## Appendices

### Appendix I. Doubtful Treatises

On Discipline and the Good of Chastity. Exhortation to Repentance. (This little book, most recently published at Bologna and discovered only after the work had appeared, had to be placed at the end of the appendices.)

### Appendix II. Spurious Treatises

Book on Gamblers. On the Singularity of Clerics. On the Twelve Abuses of the Age. On Twofold Martyrdom. Prayer of Cyprian of Antioch for the Martyrs. A prayer by the same author, delivered on the day of his passion. On the Mountains Sinai and Zion, against the Jews. Treatise against the Jews Who Persecuted Our Lord Jesus Christ, by an uncertain author. The Banquet, falsely attributed to Cyprian. Treatise on the Revelation of the Head of Blessed John the Baptist. Computation of Easter.

### Appendix III

Dissertation on Cyprian’s books *To Demetrianus* and *On the Vanity of Idols*, by Dom Nicolas Le Nourry, monk of the Order of St. Benedict. Poem to Felix, from Dom Edmond Martène’s extensive *Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments*; Martène was a monk of the same order.

### Appendix IV

Selected Notes on Cyprian from the Oxford Edition. Selected Notes of Joseph Martin Routh on Certain Books of Cyprian.

# Preface

## In Which, After an Enumeration of the Editions of Saint Cyprian’s Works, His Doctrine as a Holy Martyr Is Discussed at Greater Length

### By Dom Prudentius Maran, O.S.B.

In undertaking this preface, it seems necessary neither to pursue the praises of St. Cyprian nor to commend Baluze’s labor. The unanimous consensus of all in admiration of Cyprian has no need to court favor; and the editor is supported by his reputation for learning and by the great diligence he displayed in editing and correcting ancient writers. Many monuments of Baluze’s labors indeed survive, and he scarcely yields to anyone who has enriched the republic of letters more abundantly. Yet, apart from the fact that he came to this final work trained by long experience, at no other time does he appear to have spared himself less effort and labor in gathering ancient manuscripts from every quarter and examining them.

Ordered to leave this city in 1710, he did not abandon his plan to edit Cyprian or discontinue his labor. Nevertheless, after returning toward the end of 1713, he resumed it with renewed exertion and finally began committing it to type in 1717. The press had already completed Cyprian’s genuine works and the greater part of Baluze’s annotations when death overtook him in the midst of this useful labor, on July 28, 1718, in the eighty-eighth year of his life.

After Baluze’s death—to the regret of the whole learned world—the work of this new edition remained suspended and interrupted for a long time. But in 1724, after repeated requests from the director of the Royal Printing House, the Most Reverend Father Dom Denis de Sainte-Marthe, superior general of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, entrusted the undertaking to one of his monks. He willingly assumed the burden and, assisted by another, attempted to complete the fabric left unfinished by that most learned man: both by editing and correcting the materials that Baluze had left untouched, and, as had very advantageously been done for several other Fathers, by discussing more fully the deeds and doctrine of Cyprian.

To fulfill these promises, several teachings of the holy martyr must be examined in this preface with impartial judgment; Cyprian’s life will immediately follow it. Before that, however, it seems appropriate to review the various editions of his works.

The various editions of Cyprian’s works prepared in the very infancy of printing, and subsequently reproduced in many places, show how great was the desire to read this author. Three very early editions are recorded: the Roman edition of 1471, printed by Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz; the Venetian edition of 1471, printed by Wendelin of Speyer; and then the edition called “anonymous,” because neither the city nor the printer’s name is given.

The Oxford editor testifies that he used three editions:

> “I had at hand,” he says, “the very ancient editions: the Speyer edition of 1471; the anonymous edition, to which neither place nor date is attached; and also Rembolt’s edition of 1512.”

Yet the edition commonly called the Speyer edition was printed not at Speyer but at Venice, as several learned men have already observed. Those who attribute it to Speyer were misled by the name of Wendelin of Speyer, who completed it in 1471. For John of Speyer died at Venice in 1470, and his brother Wendelin succeeded him in his occupation and labors in the same city; this edition must therefore be credited to the latter. This is evident from the following verses, found at the end of the edition of the books of *The City of God* prepared by the same Wendelin:

> John of Speyer, who taught the Venetians that in scarcely three months  
> A hundred copies of Pliny could be printed,  
> And as many volumes of the great Cicero,  
> Had begun printing Aurelius [Augustine]; but, suddenly carried off by death,  
> He could not finish at Venice the work he had begun.  
> Wendelin, his brother, is here, no less skilled  
> In the art; and he will remain in the Adriatic city.  
> 1470.

In light of this, there appears to be the greatest doubt about the statement made, following several others, by the learned author of the *Typographical Annals*, vol. I: that Wendelin departed for Germany and published Barthold’s works there in 1471. The same writer lists books published by Wendelin at Venice in 1472 and 1477.

Another edition of Cyprian’s works appeared at Paris in 1512 from the press of Berthold Rembolt and Jean Waterloes. To this edition were added *The Cardinal Works of Christ*, an *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, and the *Passion of St. Cyprian*. The book or letter *On Gamblers*, and several other works that had been sent to Robert Fortunatus, were deferred to another time.

This Robert Fortunatus had undertaken the task of revising Cyprian’s works—or rather, as he himself testifies in the dedicatory letter to Ruricius of Blois, a man of senatorial rank, while Fortunatus was occupied either with lectures or domestic affairs, Guillaume Potet

> “reread and cleansed this distinguished work, and with great labor most handsomely furnished its margin with certain annotations not to be neglected, and with citations—or, as they say, quotations—of passages from the Bible and other authors.”

After the dedicatory letter, another letter by the same Fortunatus was appended, treating the usefulness of Cyprian’s books and his eloquence, with this inscription:

> **C. DE P. SENDS GREETINGS TO JACOPO GRASOLARI, CITIZEN OF VENICE.**

Moreover, this edition is sufficiently accurate and agrees with the manuscripts in many passages that were improperly altered in later editions.

Erasmus says that he used

> “the aid of three editions: the Roman, than which,” he says, “I have seen nothing more corrupt, though even this was useful in some places; another whose title page had been lost; and the Badius edition.”

The edition that Erasmus attributes to the celebrated Badius appears to be the same as Rembolt’s. Erasmus observes that the book *On the Cardinal Works of Christ* “is kept separate from the rest of the volume in the Badius edition”; and that can be seen in Rembolt’s edition, to which this work was added separately after the volume had already been completed. The other edition, whose title page had been lost, was perhaps the same as the anonymous edition.

As for the Roman edition, Friedrich Reinhart testifies that he used

> “both of those editions of Cyprian’s works, most kindly communicated from the library of the illustrious Republic of Nuremberg and published as early as 1471, when the art of printing was scarcely mature: the Roman edition—undoubtedly different from that which Heinrich Gravius, in the Cologne edition of 1544, writes that he used in addition to a certain Badius edition and another, though he had seen nothing more corrupt—and the Speyer edition, whose craftsman is praised as a certain Wendelin.”

Reinhart confuses Gravius with Erasmus; nor will he easily convince anyone that the Roman edition of 1471, which he says he used, differed from that mentioned by Erasmus.

Erasmus, who rendered splendid service to ecclesiastical and literary learning by his editions of so many holy Fathers, did not allow his contribution to Cyprian to be lacking. Under his supervision, Cyprian appeared at Basel in 1520, in folio, from Froben’s press, but far more complete than in the preceding editions. Erasmus was the first to publish the letters on the baptism of heretics addressed to Quintus, Jubaianus, and Pompeius; the third book of the *Testimonies*; and the opinions of the bishops at the Third Council of Carthage. To the same diligence are owed three treatises: *In Praise of Martyrdom*, *On Discipline and the Good of Chastity*, and *To Novatian the Heretic*. Although most critics deny that these are Cyprian’s, no one will deny that they are extremely ancient and worthy of Cyprian. To these were added two discourses falsely attributed to him.

Erasmus, a man of acute discernment, perceived that these works were not by Cyprian. Yet—to my considerable astonishment—he included among Cyprian’s most certain productions another work whose author mentions Diocletian and the war against the Turks: I mean the book *On Twofold Martyrdom*, addressed to Fortunatus. Upon finding it, Erasmus imagined, if we believe him, that he had discovered a great treasure:

> “We have added this,” he says, “after finding it in a very ancient library. Would that we might also be permitted to search out the rest of this man’s salutary writings!”

But Heinrich Gravius declares that Erasmus himself fabricated this book and passed off a work of his own invention under Cyprian’s name; Pamelius appears to agree with him on this point. Certainly, down to the present no one has learned which library Erasmus took this book from, nor has the manuscript he indicates that he used ever come into anyone’s hands. Both its subject matter and its language savor of Erasmus’s style; and, what increases the suspicion, several testimonies from Scripture are rendered in this book, as Pamelius observes, in precisely the same way as in Erasmus’s other compositions.

This edition was frequently reprinted in various places: at Basel by the same Froben in 1525 and 1558, in folio—Fabricius adds 1540, in folio—at Cologne in 1525 and 1544; at Lyon in 1528, 1537, 1544, and 1554; and at Paris in 1541. But those who have reviewed ecclesiastical writers or compiled catalogues of books agree so little about these matters that nothing can be established with certainty except by someone who has seen all these editions with his own eyes. I confess that this has not been my experience.

Among these editions, however, the distinguished one especially worthy of mention is that which Heinrich Gravius, the most learned Dominican, is said to have supervised at Cologne in 1544. But Baluze warns in his notes (p. 281) that this edition was not prepared by Gravius himself, but by another man who used a certain printed copy containing in its margins partly Gravius’s conjectures and partly variant readings from a manuscript.

Fabricius lists editions of Cyprian’s works published at Cologne in 1520 by Heinrich Alopecius; at Venice in 1547; and at Antwerp in 1541. He could have added the edition of 1542 by Jan Crinitus. The same Fabricius numbers Thomas James’s *Cyprian Restored to Life*, London, 1600. He may also be consulted regarding these matters, and regarding those by whom Cyprian was illustrated in vernacular languages or some of his works were published separately.

Whatever of Cyprian’s works had still lain hidden in libraries was collected so carefully by Paulus Manutius and Guillaume Morel that nothing was discovered after them that could be attributed to Cyprian. Through the labors of Paulus Manutius, the book *On Spectacles* and Letters 5, 17, 19, 23, 26, 27, 29, 30, 38, 39, 60, 78, 80, 82, and 83 in Pamelius’s order came to light. Very ancient manuscripts were used for this edition, published at Rome by Paulus Manutius in 1563.

It was dedicated to St. Charles Borromeo, who, as Manutius testifies there, had devoted himself entirely to ensuring

> “that all Cyprian’s writings, previously disfigured by errors, should be restored to their former integrity and appearance through the careful labor of learned men, after an exemplar of astonishing antiquity had also been summoned from Verona.”

Morel transferred into his own edition everything that Paulus Manutius had rescued from darkness. To these materials he added Firmilian’s letter to Cyprian; Celerinus’s letter to Lucian and Lucian’s reply; the letter of Celsus to Vigilius; the books *On Gamblers*, *Against the Jews Who Persecuted Christ*, and *On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*; the *Banquet of Cyprian*; and poems attributed to the holy martyr.

The edition appeared in 1564; but before it was completed, the most learned printer—who had rendered outstanding service to ecclesiastical and literary learning—died amid this labor. Adrianus Turnebus addressed the dedicatory letter to Charles IX. In it he begs the Most Christian King to aid by his generosity Morel’s children and wife, whom Morel had left destitute; to provide something toward paying and discharging the debt contracted through Morel’s zeal to serve the commonwealth; and graciously to order restored and paid the annual allowances granted to Morel by King Henry, which the harshness of the times and the treasury’s straits had not permitted him to enjoy.

*[Col. 0013A]*

Pamelius did not enlarge Cyprian’s corpus, but corrected it in many places with the aid of manuscripts and illustrated it with a new arrangement of the letters and other works, learned notes, a life compiled from Cyprian’s own writings, and copious indexes.

Even before the editions of Manutius and Morel appeared, Pamelius had already resolved to undertake this labor; but his theological studies and his journey into France interrupted his plan. When, however, he saw those two editions, he hoped that with their aid, that of other older editions, and that of manuscripts, he could produce something more accurate and complete in all its parts. He devoted himself to the work with such ardor that everything was ready for the press in 1566; but disturbances in the Low Countries caused delay.

The edition finally appeared at Antwerp in 1568. It was reprinted there in 1589, at Cologne in 1617, and at Paris in 1574, 1603, 1616, and 1644. The Barberini Library adds Paris editions of 1607 and 1632; Fabricius adds Paris, 1633, and Cologne, 1617 and 1632; but these details, as I have already said, are not entirely certain. An edition published at Cologne in 1575 is listed in the catalogue of the library at Leiden.

Pamelius anticipated the Englishman John Harris, formerly secretary to Thomas More, who had contemplated the same plan of editing Cyprian’s works. Harris willingly assisted Pamelius with variant readings from his own copy. John Clement, a physician and likewise an Englishman, also lent him assistance, as did Antonius and Valerius van Cauch, brothers and lawyers from Utrecht, who communicated their father’s corrections and conjectures. We learn this from Pamelius’s dedicatory letter, addressed to Viglius van Zuichem of Friesland, provost of St. Bavo at Ghent.

Simon Goulart published Cyprian’s works at Geneva in 1593, following Pamelius’s arrangement and text, but adding from his own resources lengthy observations that are laborious to read, in which he attempted to refute Pamelius and make St. Cyprian into a Calvinist.

Rigault’s edition appeared at Paris in 1648, enlarged by the book *On Rebaptism*. It was followed in the same city in 1666 by Prior’s edition, with the notes of Rigault and others. To Cyprian were appended the writings of Minucius Felix, Arnobius, and Commodian, as well as Julius Firmicus’s *On the Error of Profane Religions*.

A new edition of Cyprian’s letters, omitting the other treatises, appeared in 1681. Its title reads as follows:

> **The Eighty-Three Letters of St. Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and Finally Martyr, and of Certain Others Written to Him or on a Similar Matter; Arranged according to the Order of Pamelius; Divided into Sections from the Goulart Edition; with St. Augustine’s Replies to Cyprian’s Arguments concerning the Baptism of Heretics Appended in Their Proper Places; with Various Readings and Conjectures of Pamelius, Rigault, and Others; and with Citations from Gratian’s *Decretum*, Lombard’s Books of *Sentences*, and Thomas Aquinas’s *Summa Theologiae* Noted in the Margin; and Finally Published Separately with Several Useful Indexes. By Friedrich Reinhart, Professor of Theology at the University of Altdorf and Minister of the Church There. Altdorf, Printed and Published by Heinrich Meyer, Printer to the University.**

Next came the Oxford edition of 1682, from the Sheldonian Theatre. It was collated with manuscripts and furnished with the notes of Pamelius, Rigault, and the editor himself. It was enlarged by several treatises of Arnold of Bonneval, the *Confession* of Cyprian of Antioch, and an ancient Easter computation.

In preparing this edition, the industry of two Protestant bishops was conspicuous: John Fell, bishop of Oxford, and John Pearson, bishop of Chester. The former assumed overall responsibility for the edition; the latter composed the *Cyprianic Annals* prefixed to the holy martyr’s works, not without earning great praise for learning. This edition was reprinted at Bremen in 1690 and Amsterdam in 1699. So Fabricius states; but Casimir Oudin took a different view, recording three editions after the first Oxford edition.

Neither so many editions of Cyprian’s works nor the favorable judgments of a considerable number of men concerning the latest Oxford edition deterred Baluze from undertaking a new one. For when he saw that every edition contained its own defects—because either corrupt manuscripts were used, or earlier editions were corrected where correction was unnecessary and left uncorrected where it was necessary—he did not despair of correcting the text of the holy martyr so thoroughly that it might at last appear pure and undefiled.

Understanding that he must labor chiefly at this task, he employed as aids, in addition to the manuscripts used by Pamelius, Rigault, and the English scholars, about thirty others. I shall provide information about these below, so far as it could be gathered from Baluze’s notes. For since that learned man had inserted variant readings excerpted from manuscripts into printed copies, those copies were dispersed with the other books of Baluze’s library, and I was able to recover only a very few of them.

Baluze also added observations and notes. In these he generally explains the reason for alterations he judged necessary in the text; at times, too, rich as he was in learning, he exercised his pen in elucidating antiquarian matters. I would act most unjustly if, since his work apart from a very few pages was printed during his lifetime, I were to divert to myself any portion of the praise due to his labor. Moreover, since time did not permit me to evaluate his notes and compare them with St. Cyprian’s text itself, I shall not interpose my own judgment but assent to that of the public. Nevertheless, I cannot conceal that I have often observed Cyprian’s text to have been very advantageously corrected, as was to be expected from a most learned man enjoying such an abundance of manuscripts.

As for the works attributed to Cyprian, a substantial part had already been printed when death took Baluze from us.

*[Col. 0015]*

In addition to the three treatises *On Spectacles*, *In Praise of Martyrdom*, and *On Rebaptism*, which Baluze joined to Cyprian’s genuine works, the following had been completed: the books *On the Good of Chastity*, *On Gamblers*, *To Novatian the Heretic*, and *On the Mountains Sinai and Zion*; two discourses falsely attributed to Cyprian; the treatise of Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, *On the Lord’s Last Words on the Cross*; and, apart from two or three leaves, the same author’s book *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*. It was necessary to labor over correcting and publishing what remained.

For my own part, had I undertaken a new edition of Cyprian’s works, I confess that I would have relieved it of no small portion of so heavy a burden. But since I understood that I was contributing substitute labor toward the completion of this edition, I had to proceed more cautiously. I therefore retained everything contained in Pamelius’s edition, because that had been Baluze’s decision.

Of the works with which the English scholars burdened Cyprian, however, I considered it necessary to remove Arnold of Bonneval’s compositions *On the Works of the Six Days* and *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin*, together with his *Meditations*. I did so partly to prevent the volume from becoming excessively large—for it would have been enlarged by ten sheets—and partly because other works by the same Arnold survive in our libraries that should, by the same right as those three compositions, have been admitted into this edition. The learned men whom we consulted decided that neither group should be admitted.

Baluze had resolved to eliminate the Easter computation published by the same English scholars; and when he excerpted from the Oxford edition the works attributed to Cyprian, he deliberately omitted it. We complied with his wishes all the more readily because this little book can neither be attributed to Cyprian nor be of much benefit to anyone. Moreover, it abounds in a thicket of variant readings and in rather lengthy notes that could not be accommodated to the plan adopted for this edition.

I would certainly not number among the better monuments of antiquity the *Confession of Cyprian* published in Latin by the Oxford editor. Yet because Baluze judged that it should not be omitted, and because it was furthermore held in esteem by Gregory Nazianzen, Eudocia, and Photius, I not only refused to allow it to be absent from this edition but did not hesitate to substitute for the Latin translation—which the English scholars had given in a form defective in many places and corrupt in countless others—the Greek text itself, generously supplied from the library of the most illustrious Comte de Seignelay, together with a new translation.

Baluze had intended to publish the spurious works in the form in which they are found in the Oxford edition. This can be perceived from the materials that we have said were printed during his lifetime. But when I saw that some of these monuments were of great value and had acquired all the more blemishes the more frequently they were published with Cyprian, I summoned to my aid every old edition and ancient manuscript that could be found in this city. With their help and support, I restored to their former clarity many passages that had been very seriously disfigured, especially in the book *On the Singularity of Clerics*, the *Exposition of the Creed*, and the *Letter of Celsus to Vigilius*.

In this matter too I was unable to follow in Baluze’s footsteps: whereas he placed his notes after the text, I placed the variant readings in the margin. Neither Baluze, who sometimes allowed himself more extensive notes, nor I, who was occupied solely with correcting the text, could properly have done otherwise.

To this labor of correcting the text was added another, which, to the extent of our modest ability, we devoted to explaining St. Cyprian’s doctrine and assessing his deeds according to the standards of criticism.

# I.—Cyprian’s Teaching on the Unity and Infallibility of the Church

The statements that we undertake to draw from Cyprian’s writings in defense of the truth are the less susceptible to evasion through caviling the clearer and more accessible they are to everyone’s understanding; and the greater the admiration they received in the Church’s third century, the more suited they appear for moving those who do not dare reject the Church’s first three centuries.

Cyprian wrote alike for the learned and the unlearned. His doctrine was not confined merely to public circulation in Africa, but crossed by sea into Italy and was carried to the most distant churches of East and West. Accordingly, his testimonies concerning the Church, the sacraments—apart from the question of the baptism of heretics—the divinity of Christ, and his grace must be regarded as testimonies not merely of one bishop or one church, but of all Catholics of that age.

Just as love of unity shone especially brightly among Cyprian’s virtues, so in his writings nothing is commended more earnestly or defended more carefully than the unity of the Church. Anyone who has not cast every love of truth out of his mind will readily perceive three principal points from his statements:

1. The Church founded by Christ through the apostles is manifest and visible to all.
2. It can neither perish nor be corrupted by any error or schism.
3. It is so completely one that whatever sects have departed from it are estranged both from the true Church and from eternal salvation.

The inventions of an invisible church, devised at a far more recent date, were unknown to the holy martyr. Rather, he understands the Church in which the weeds are seen mingled with the wheat, and earthen vessels with those of gold and silver, until the day of judgment (pp. 65 and 74); the Church founded upon Peter by the Lord’s word, which

> “is one, and through the increase of its fruitfulness extends more widely into a multitude; and, flooded with the Lord’s light, stretches its rays over the whole world; in it there is one episcopate, a share of which is held wholly and jointly by each bishop” (*On the Unity of the Church*, p. 195);

and the Church in which

> “through the changes of times and successions, the ordination of bishops and the order of the Church proceed, so that the Church is established upon the bishops and every act of the Church is governed through those same presiding officers” (Letter XXVII).

In these and other similar passages there is no suggestion of an invisible church. Cyprian would not exhort the lapsed to obey the decrees of an invisible church, or confessors to return to an invisible church. Nor does an invisible church possess a succession of bishops or spread its rays throughout the whole world.

*[Col. 0017]*

But lest anyone say that the Church deserved these titles in the first centuries, whereas the condition of affairs was afterward transformed, Cyprian anticipates these slanders and maintains that this visible Church can be overthrown by no human power, overcome by no error, and divided by no schism.

What he thought about the persecutions of the emperors can be seen from the book *On the Lapsed*. There he teaches that the dreadful persecution kindled by Decius was permitted by divine counsel so that zeal for piety, chilled by a long peace, might be aroused. He similarly observes that the persecution of Gallus and Volusian broke out at Rome

> “so that, to confound the heretics and beat them back, the Lord might show which was the Church … who those were whom the enemy attacked, and whom, by contrast, the devil spared as his own” (Letter LVIII).

Since he held this view concerning the perpetuity of the Church, neither heresies nor schisms terrified him. He knew that these things had been foretold by Christ and the apostles and that no one ought to be astonished when they occurred (Letter LV).

In many places he declares that the Church can be infected by no error and corrupted by no schism, especially in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, where he speaks as follows (p. 195):

> “The bride of Christ cannot be adulterated; she is incorrupt and chaste. She knows one house; with chaste modesty she guards the sanctity of one chamber.… The Lord says: ‘I and the Father are one’; and again, concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it is written: ‘And these three are one.’ And does anyone believe that this unity, proceeding from divine steadfastness and adhering to heavenly mysteries, can be torn apart in the Church and separated by the division of conflicting wills?”

And a little later:

> “Because the people of Christ cannot be torn apart, his tunic, woven throughout and held together, was not divided by those who possessed it. Undivided, united, and interconnected, it displays the coherent concord of our people, who have put on Christ. By the mystery and sign of his garment he manifested the Church’s unity. Who, then, is so criminal and faithless, who so maddened by the frenzy of discord, as either to believe that the unity of God, the garment of the Lord, the Church of Christ, can be torn apart, or to dare to tear it apart?”

It was therefore clear to the holy martyr that although heresies attack the Church and schisms tear away some of its parts, the Church nevertheless always stands in its own strength; and neither can the truth entrusted to it by Christ be obscured by any heresy, nor its unity corrupted by schism.

Hence he establishes as great a difference between the sects that depart from the Church and the Church itself as between a work of human beings and the work of God. He charges Novatian with folly because,

> “although there is one Church from Christ, divided throughout the whole world into many members, and likewise one episcopate diffused through the harmonious multitude of many bishops, he attempts, after God’s tradition and after the interconnected and universally united unity of the Catholic Church, to make a human church” (Letter LII).

What necessarily follows from these principles—that it can never happen that there is a just cause for departing from the Church—is also frequently taught by Cyprian. For whenever he saw people departing from the Church, he said that they had been condemned by their own judgment, so that it was unnecessary to institute any further judgment concerning them.

Thus he says in Letter XLIX that Novatus,

> “who was due to be cast out and excluded from the Church, anticipated the judgment of the priests by his voluntary departure, as though anticipating the sentence meant escaping the punishment.”

And in *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 200, he says:

> “Such a person, whoever has been separated from the Church, must be shunned and avoided. A person of this kind is perverted, sins, and is condemned by himself” (see Letter XL).

From these statements it is readily perceived that the Church of Christ is altogether one and indivisible, although several sects claim that they themselves are the true Church of Christ. For there cannot be more than one Church that cannot be overthrown by error or schism, and from which no one can depart without committing a crime.

All Cyprian’s declarations wonderfully confirm this. He maintains that the Church,

> “which both lives forever and gives life to the people of God” (p. 127),

is so completely one that, if it existed with Novatian, he declares that it did not exist with Cornelius (p. 152). Hence the Church is so often called the enclosed garden and sealed fountain, as on the same page; the bride of Christ, who alone can beget children and who adheres to Christ by indivisible bonds (pp. 63, 108, 140, 147, 195).

Cyprian does not hesitate to compare

> “this unity of the Catholic Church, proceeding from the gracious favor of the divine ordering” (p. 128),

with the unity of Christ (p. 132), with the unity of God (p. 202), and with the unity of the Trinity (p. 196).

And this was the hinge upon which turned all the controversies that befell Saint Cyprian. When Felicissimus and five presbyters had drawn some of the lapsed away from communion with Cyprian, and cloaked their crime with plausible pretexts, how great was Cyprian’s grief at this destruction of the souls entrusted to him! With what charitable zeal he exhorts them to avoid the wolves who promise salvation, “lest one who has sinned should attain salvation”; who pledge the Church, while acting so that whoever believes them “may perish altogether from the Church” (*Epp.* XXXVIII and XL). Nothing, however, seemed more suitable to Cyprian for deterring those who had been deceived than to show them that they could not communicate in the Church with the bishops and the people of Christ if they followed the leaders of the schism. In fact, this doctrine—that there is absolutely one Church and that no just cause for departing from it can ever arise—had been so deeply impressed and engraved even upon the minds of the common people that the standard-bearers of schism led on and enticed those whom they had deceived with the hope of returning to the Church. But their fraud was exposed by the ordination of Fortunatus, whom they appointed as a pseudo-bishop of Carthage. “For those before whose eyes,” says Cyprian (*Ep.* LV, p. 87), “deceptive appearances were formerly displayed and to whom fallacious assurances were given that they would return to the Church together, learned, after they saw that a pseudo-bishop had been created there, that they had been frustrated and deceived; and every day they return and knock at the Church’s door.”

Just as Novatian’s faction wore a more attractive cloak of piety than Felicissimus’s, so it brought greater destruction: its counterfeit appearance dazzled even the eyes of the confessors themselves. It burdened and grieved Cyprian, to use his own words (*Ep.* XLIV), and overwhelmed him with the almost unbearable sorrow of a heart struck down and nearly prostrated, because they had separated themselves from Christ’s flock and from his peace and concord; because schismatic and heretical error had received them as they came out of prison (*Epist.* LI). Cyprian’s exhortation was of no small benefit to these confessors, urging them to repair by a happy return the injury inflicted upon unity: [Col. 0019] for “having recognized their error,” as Saint Cornelius says (*Epist.* XLVI), “they came with sincere intention to the Church from which they had departed.” They confessed their error before Cornelius and five other bishops, a Roman presbyter, and the people themselves, a great crowd of whom had assembled; and they declared that their sincere intention had always been within the Church, since they were not unaware that “there is one God, and one Christ the Lord, one Holy Spirit, and that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church.”

Yet if any sect could have escaped the stigma of schism and appeared to be a part of the true Church, Novatian’s sect above all would have claimed this for itself, since, at least in its beginnings, it violated neither the Church’s doctrines nor the outward form of religion. But Cyprian maintains that it matters little what Novatian teaches, “since he teaches outside. Whoever he may be,” he says (*Epist.* LII, p. 73), “and whatever sort of man he may be, he is not a Christian who is not in the Church of Christ.” He teaches the same in many other places, especially in the letter to Magnus, where he speaks as follows (p. 151):

> “For when our Lord Jesus Christ testified in his Gospel that those who were not with him were his adversaries, he did not designate any particular kind of heresy, but showed that absolutely all who were not with him and who, by not gathering with him, scattered his flock, were his adversaries, saying: ‘He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters.’ Likewise, the blessed Apostle John did not distinguish any particular heresy or schism or set down certain persons specifically as separated; rather, he called antichrists all who had gone out from the Church and who acted against the Church, etc.”

For this reason the holy martyr declares that not even martyrdom outside the Church delivers one from condemnation. “Though they burn in flames,” he says in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 199, “and though, delivered to the fires or thrown to wild beasts, they lay down their lives, that will not be the crown of faith but the punishment of faithlessness, nor the glorious end of religious virtue but the destruction of despair. Such a person can be killed; he cannot be crowned.” The same judgment occurs frequently elsewhere, as in the same book *On Unity*, p. 198, and in *Epist.* LII, p. 71, and LVII, p. 95.

If anyone should suspect that Cyprian, through love of unity, is carried further than is proper, he should be reminded that all the other churches agreed with Cyprian concerning these principles, although they did not draw the same conclusions as he did and did not reject the baptism of heretics. For Cyprian refuted his opponents by this argument: they admitted that the Holy Spirit can neither be possessed nor given outside the Church. “Although in other respects they are obstinate and unteachable,” he says (*Epist.* LXXVI, p. 155), “they nevertheless acknowledge at least this: that none, whether schismatics or heretics, possess the Holy Spirit; and that they can therefore indeed baptize, but cannot give the Holy Spirit. In this very point they are caught by us, so that we may show that those who do not possess the Holy Spirit cannot baptize at all.” Cyprian himself employs the same argument throughout, as does Firmilian (p. 147).

It is therefore manifest, both from Cyprian’s testimony and from the consensus of all the Christians then living, that among the various communities claiming for themselves the profession of the Christian religion, there is some one community outside which eternal salvation cannot be obtained, whether the error be slight or even if no error at all be added to schism; much less can that community itself enter with sects severed from it into the constitution of one common Church. For if sects cut off from the Church retain the marks and rights of the true Church, then in vain was the succession of bishops and the unity of the episcopate throughout the whole world raised as an objection against the ancient sects; in vain did the ancient Church maintain that she alone was the bride, that she could never err, that no legitimate cause for departing from her could ever arise, and that not even martyrdom could avail for the salvation of those who departed. An impious and cruel error must therefore be falsely ascribed to the entire ancient Church—or rather to the Apostles, from whom alone that extraordinary consensus concerning the marks of the true Church, which we see prevailing among all Christians, could have been formed.

Extraordinary are the conclusions that commended themselves to Dodwell when he examined Saint Cyprian’s position on unity. For he determines that in these arguments of the holy martyr “the subject is not the unity of that Church which we today call Catholic, which of course embraces within its compass all the particular churches throughout the world, but only the particular churches themselves” (*Dissert. Cypr.*, 7). It is indeed perfectly true, as Dodwell proves, that every bishop is the principle of unity in his own church and that all must obey him—but only if he communicates with the other bishops; not so if he departs from the universal Church. For then he would be a principle of discord and schism rather than of unity.

And, to remain with Cyprian, it can easily be demonstrated that in these discussions the unity of the Church is defended by the holy martyr in such a way that the conception of the universal Church is always before his mind. This is apparent from the very testimony Dodwell excerpted from the book *On the Unity of the Church* in defense of his case:

> “Just as there are many rays of the sun, but one light,” he says on p. 195, “and many branches of a tree, but one strength founded upon its tenacious root; and when many streams flow from one spring, although their multiplicity appears widely diffused through the abundant generosity of the overflowing supply, nevertheless unity is preserved at the source. Tear a ray of the sun away from its body: the unity of light admits no division. Break a branch from the tree: once broken, it will not be able to put forth shoots. Cut off a stream from its spring: once cut off, it dries up. So too the Lord’s Church, suffused with light, extends her rays throughout the whole world. Yet it is one light that is diffused everywhere, nor is the unity of the body divided. She extends her branches over the whole earth in the abundance of her fertility; she spreads her freely flowing streams ever more widely. Yet there is one head and one source and one mother, rich in the successive fruits of her fecundity.”

By these words—“the Lord’s Church, suffused with light, extends her rays throughout the whole world; she extends her branches over the whole earth in the abundance of her fertility”—the unity not of a particular church but of the universal, or Catholic, Church is described. The words that precede and follow confirm the same point. Before the words quoted, Cyprian spoke as follows:

> “This unity we must firmly maintain and vindicate, especially we bishops who [Col. 0021] preside in the Church, so that we may prove the episcopate itself also to be one and undivided. Let no one deceive the brotherhood with falsehood; let no one corrupt the truth of the faith by faithless betrayal. The episcopate is one, a share in which is held wholly and undividedly by each. The Church also is one, and she is extended more widely into a multitude by the increase of her fecundity.”

After the testimony adduced by Dodwell, Cyprian adds:

> “From her womb we are born; by her milk we are nourished; by her spirit we are given life. The bride of Christ cannot be adulterated; she is incorrupt and chaste. . . . Whoever, after being separated from the Church, joins himself to an adulteress is separated from the promises of the Church. He who leaves the Church of Christ will not attain the rewards of Christ. He is an alien; he is profane; he is an enemy. He can no longer have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother. If anyone who was outside Noah’s ark could escape, then one who is outside the Church also escapes.”

Dodwell is thus a charming interpreter of Cyprian, inventing for himself a particular church where the holy martyr commends the one episcopate throughout the whole world. What of the fact that in *Epist.* XL Cyprian declares to the lapsed that if anyone joins himself to Felicissimus, he “cannot afterward return to the Church and communicate with the bishops and the people of Christ”? Or that in *Epist.* XLIV he exhorts the confessors to return to the Church, and in *Epist.* LI congratulates them after their return: “because the truth of the Church and the unity of the evangelical sacrament which was maintained by us,” he says, was “also joined by their consent and bond”? Does he seem to have been speaking of particular churches without any regard for the unity established among all the churches?

Nothing is more adverse to Dodwell than Cyprian’s principle concerning the singularity of the bishop, although he believes it especially favorable to himself. For Cyprian never defended the unity of the Catholic Church more precisely than when he maintained that there ought to be one bishop in each church. When Novatian had usurped the episcopate at Rome and through his emissaries attempted the same crime in other cities, Cyprian refuted his supporters by this argument: since the only bishop is the one whose episcopate is confirmed and recognized by his other colleagues, anyone who dares to thrust himself into his place can have no communion with the bishops of the Catholic Church and consequently perishes, having been left outside.

“Cornelius was made bishop,” he says in *Epist.* LII, p. 68,

> “by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people then present, and by the college of ancient priests and good men, when no one had been made bishop before him, when the place of Fabian—that is, the place of Peter and the rank of the sacerdotal chair—was vacant. Once that place had been occupied by the will of God and confirmed by the consent of us all, whoever thereafter wishes to be made bishop must necessarily be made so outside, nor can one who does not maintain the unity of the Church possess ecclesiastical ordination.”

In the same way, Cyprian demonstrates that the bishops appointed by Novatian in other cities are not bishops of Christ’s Church but of a human church:

> “Unless perhaps you think him a bishop,” he says in the same letter, p. 73, “who strives through canvassing to be made an adulterous and alien bishop by deserters, in opposition to a bishop made in the Church by sixteen fellow bishops; and although there is from Christ one Church, divided throughout the whole world into many members, and likewise one episcopate diffused through the harmonious multitude of many bishops, he nevertheless attempts, after God’s tradition and after the interconnected and everywhere united unity of the Catholic Church, to create a human church and sends his new apostles through very many cities to establish certain novel foundations of his institution. And although bishops have long since been ordained throughout all the provinces and in each individual city—men advanced in age, sound in faith, tested under oppression, and proscribed in persecution—he dares to create other pseudo-bishops over them.”

Hence he maintains that, even if they had been legitimately ordained, they could nevertheless not be recognized as legitimate bishops, because they had departed from the Catholic Church: “He could not retain the episcopate,” he says, “even if he had first been made a bishop and then withdrew from the body of his fellow bishops and from the unity of the Church.”

## II.—THOSE WHO DENY THAT, IN CYPRIAN, BISHOPS ARE DISTINGUISHED FROM PRESBYTERS BY DIVINE RIGHT ARE REFUTED

Although the rights of the episcopate could not be defended more precisely than Cyprian defends them, there have nevertheless been those who seized upon some of his words as an opportunity for calumny. For because the holy martyr sometimes appears to divide the clergy into two orders, namely priests and ministers, and shares the titles *priest* and *prelate* with the presbyters themselves—as in *Epp.* LXV, LXVIII, LXXII, and in the book *On the Lapsed*—Salmasius and Blondel conclude from this that presbyters are not distinguished from bishops by divine right or by a different degree of priesthood. If such petty reasoning were valid, one might with equal right conclude that not even deacons and the other lower clerics are distinguished from presbyters and bishops by divine right, since the Church is often divided into clergy and people. But if deacons and lower clerics are included with presbyters and bishops under the term *clergy*, what wonder is it if presbyters, who consecrate the Eucharist and possess the power of binding and loosing, share with bishops the titles of priest and prelate?

Cyprian certainly always held presbyters in very great honor; and since it was his custom to do nothing without the counsel of the clergy, as he himself testifies in *Epist.* VI, there can be no doubt that he attributed great authority to presbyters, seeing that they sat with him. Yet he claims for himself a degree of priesthood distinct from that of the presbyters. In *Epist.* XI he complains that certain presbyters, neither mindful of the Gospel “nor reserving to the bishop the honor of his priesthood and chair,” had already begun to communicate with the lapsed. The degree of priesthood in bishops is therefore different from that in presbyters, and consequently bishops are distinguished from presbyters not only by authority and chair but also by order and character.

That this distinction within the priesthood was instituted by Christ himself is apparent from many passages in Cyprian:

> “Our Lord,” he says in *Epist.* XXVII, p. 37, “whose precepts and admonitions we must observe, when ordering the honor of the bishop and the constitution of his Church, speaks in the Gospel and says to Peter: ‘I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and [Col. 0023] the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.’ From this, through the successive changes of times and successions, the ordination of bishops and the constitution of the Church proceed, so that the Church is established upon the bishops and every act of the Church is governed through those same prelates. Since this, therefore, has been founded by divine law,” etc.

Many points must be observed here, from which the holy martyr’s position shines forth wonderfully.

First, he declares that the bishops succeeded the Apostles. Thus also in *Epist.* XLII he teaches that “the unity handed down by the Lord and through the Apostles to us, their successors,” must be maintained. See *Epist.* LXIX. Firmilian teaches the same in his letter to Cyprian, p. 148: the bishops succeeded the Apostles “by a vicarious ordination.” Likewise, at the Council of Carthage over which Cyprian presided, Clarus of Mascula says (p. 337): “We have succeeded the Apostles, governing the Lord’s Church with the same power and baptizing the faith of believers.”

Second, Cyprian pronounces that episcopal ordination was instituted by Christ and founded upon divine law. For although he had been ordained a presbyter and had ministered for some time in that degree, he nevertheless knew very well that, when called to the episcopal rank, he had need of another ordination. No one in those times remembered the practice that Salmasius and Blondel imagined to have prevailed in the first centuries: that upon the death of a bishop the senior presbyter, without a new ordination, succeeded him—or perhaps the one who appeared worthier, as Blondel holds. Not even the schismatics themselves, although ready for every crime, dared to promote presbyters to the episcopate without ordination. Novatian the presbyter knew very well that not even the semblance of the episcopate could be seized without a new ordination, since he compelled three bishops—whom he had deceitfully summoned from the most contemptible part of the Church and confined at the tenth hour, drunk and oppressed by surfeiting—to confer the episcopate upon him by force through a certain shadowy and empty imposition of hands (Eusebius, *Hist.*, bk. VI, ch. 43).

Third, from these things it is also evident that bishops received from Christ alone the power of governing the Church. Hence Cyprian so often says that “the Lord chooses and appoints priests for himself in his Church,” p. 59. On this basis Cyprian defends the episcopate of Cornelius as “received by the will of God, who makes priests” (*Epist.* LII, pp. 68–69). See *Ep.* LV, p. 82; *Ep.* LXV, p. 113; and *Ep.* LXIX, p. 121. From this conception of the episcopate arose Cyprian’s supreme constancy in governing and defending his church: because he knew himself to have been given by God as a judge over it for a time (p. 122), he guarded “with faithful courage the camp divinely entrusted” to him (p. 141).

This conviction was impressed upon the minds of the other African bishops. “If a husband setting out on a foreign journey,” says Venantius of Timisa at the Council of Carthage, p. 335, “had entrusted his wife to his friend’s custody, that friend would preserve the woman entrusted to him with all possible diligence, lest her chastity and holiness be violated by anyone. Christ our Lord and God, when departing to the Father, entrusted his bride to us.”

I do not know what sort of priesthood Rigaltius and Baluzius ascribe to deacons in their observations upon these words of Cyprian: “Likewise, the vigor of the priesthood was not lacking to the presbyters and deacons” (*Epist.* XV). In this passage Cyprian by no means attributes the vigor of the priesthood to those presbyters and deacons; rather, he shows that he himself employed that vigor in rebuking them. This is apparent both from what follows and from the sequence of the entire letter.

Nor does the opinion of Rigaltius and Baluzius receive support from the fact that Cyprian, while absent, decrees in *Epist.* XIII:

> “That those who have received certificates from the martyrs and can be assisted by their privilege before God, if they are overtaken by some infirmity and danger of illness, may—without awaiting our presence,” he says, “make the *exomologesis* [acknowledgment] of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, even before a deacon; so that, once a hand has been imposed upon them for repentance, they may come to the Lord with the peace which the martyrs desired should be granted through letters addressed to us.”

I shall not linger over explaining this difficulty, which is too closely connected with the following centuries to be examined here. But, so as not to depart from Cyprian, there is one point I should like to be observed: this duty is by no means entrusted by him to deacons so that they might receive confession of sins and impose penance. For the discipline of those times was that no one was admitted to peace, not even in the final crisis, unless before his illness he had confessed his sins and sought penance, as Cyprian testifies in *Epist.* LII. Consequently, the prescribed *exomologesis* before a deacon at the point of death was not the confession of sins, which ought previously to have been made before priests; and therefore the function of imposing penance was not shared with deacons.

Moreover, what learned men observed long ago—that there was a twofold *exomologesis*—is confirmed by Cyprian’s letters written concerning the case of the lapsed, especially *Ep.* XII, where he says that *exomologesis* is made “after the life of the person performing penance has been examined.” From this it is clear that the *exomologesis* immediately followed by absolution, after the penance of the lapsed person had already been proved and sufficiently observed, must be distinguished from the confession of sins that preceded the penance itself.

## III.—THE PRIMACY OF THE ROMAN CHURCH ALWAYS ACKNOWLEDGED BY SAINT CYPRIAN

Cyprian defended the rights of bishops in such a way as to acknowledge the legitimate primacy of the Roman See. In the disagreement he had with Stephen, he often complained that Stephen placed too much confidence in his primacy, but he did not dispute Stephen’s authority itself. Thus, without naming him, he censures Stephen in *Epist.* LXXI:

> “But neither did Peter,” he says, “whom the Lord chose first and upon whom he founded his Church, when Paul afterward disputed with him concerning circumcision, insolently claim anything for himself or arrogantly assume it, so as to say that he held the primacy and that novices and those who came later ought rather to obey him.”

Likewise, Firmilian says that he is justly indignant [Col. 0025] with Stephen (p. 148), because one who “boasts in this way of the place of his episcopate and contends that he holds the succession of Peter, upon whom the foundations of the Church were laid, introduces many other rocks and establishes new buildings of many churches, while by his own authority he defends the existence of baptism there.” And a little later: “Stephen, who proclaims that through succession he possesses the chair of Peter, is stirred by no zeal against heretics.”

Firmilian therefore acknowledges in Stephen a certain higher degree of dignity; and when he finds in him no zeal for the faith corresponding to that dignity, he admits that Peter’s primacy had passed to him by succession.

Cyprian frequently commended elsewhere the primacy of Peter and his successors. “Peter, however,” he says on p. 123, “upon whom the Church had been built by the same Lord, speaking alone for all and answering in the voice of the Church, says: ‘Lord, to whom shall we go?’” See p. 123. “One Church, founded by the Lord upon Peter as the source and principle of unity,” p. 125. “For to Peter, upon whom he built the Church and from whom he instituted and displayed the source of unity, he gave this power: that what Peter loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven. And after the resurrection he also speaks to the Apostles, saying: ‘As the Father has sent me, so I send you,’” etc. (*Epist.* LXXIII, p. 131; see pp. 148 and 250).

But an especially notable passage from the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 195, must be considered:

> “The Lord speaks to Peter: ‘I say to you,’ he says, ‘that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.’ And again, after his resurrection, he says to the same man: ‘Feed my sheep.’ Upon that one man he builds his Church, and to him he entrusts his sheep to be fed, although after his resurrection he grants equal power to the Apostles and says: ‘As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained.’ Nevertheless, to manifest unity, by his own authority he arranged that the source of that same unity should begin from one man. Certainly the other Apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership both of honor and of power; but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one.”

I have presented this testimony as it appears in this edition of Baluzius. Cyprian’s words, however, are read differently in the editions of Manutius and Pamelius. In them, after the words “to manifest unity,” there is added: “he established one chair.” Likewise, after the words “the beginning proceeds from unity,” those editions have:

> “And the primacy is given to Peter, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one and the chair one. And all are shepherds, and the flock is shown to be one, fed by all the Apostles with unanimous agreement, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. . . . Does one who deserts the chair of Peter, upon whom the Church was founded, trust that he is in the Church?”

Baluzius believed that these words had crept into the text; it will be for learned men to judge his opinion and reasons. But I should like it observed that if the words expunged by the Oxford editor and Baluzius are retained, nothing will be present that does not accord perfectly with Cyprian’s doctrine; while if they are excised, the remaining portions of this testimony will possess sufficient weight by themselves to establish the primacy of the Roman Church.

A person would indeed be a stranger and foreigner to Cyprian’s doctrine if he were surprised that Cyprian attributes the primacy to Peter and affirms one flock and one chair, since in so many places he defends the same primacy and commends one flock, one episcopate, and—specifically in *Epist.* XL—one chair. Nor is it any more surprising that he pronounces those wicked schismatics not to be in the Church, when, after trampling upon this one episcopate and deserting this one chair founded upon Peter, they were attempting to institute an entirely human church. There was therefore no reason for the Oxford editor to imagine that he had purified Cyprian’s testimony of these words as though of a certain “poison,” as he himself calls it.

Indeed, even those words in this testimony which that editor retains and which are admitted by all are by themselves sufficient to demonstrate the primacy.

First, it is evident from this passage of Cyprian and from many others that the principle of unity cannot exist without primacy. For who would deny primacy to him from whom unity begins and through whom the Church is shown to be one?

Second, just as unity did not cease after Peter, neither did the primacy and principle of unity which Christ established by his own authority, and which he instituted for the purpose of showing the Church to be one. Therefore, just as unity must persevere, so must the principle and bond of unity persevere in the Church. From this one may judge how highly Cyprian valued the Roman Church and how closely attached to the principle of unity was a man kindled with so great a love of unity. Hence his indignation (p. 86) that schismatics had dared “to sail to the chair of Peter and to the principal Church, from which sacerdotal unity arose.”

Our opponents repeatedly assert that Cyprian defended the primacy of the Roman Church not because it possessed any right over the other churches, but because it was the seat and residence of the Empire. But nothing is more absurd than this invention. No one will persuade himself that Cyprian, whose love of unity breathes throughout all his writings and deeds, either denied primacy to the Church from which he acknowledged sacerdotal unity to have arisen, or granted it because of the city’s power and greatness rather than because it was the principle of unity.

The Roman Church claimed this primacy for itself without opposition from anyone. Although the Roman clergy, while the See was vacant, did not assume all authority for themselves but preserved all the more difficult matters undecided until the election of a bishop—including the case of the lapsed—the primacy was not for that reason suspended. “The brothers who are in bonds salute you,” says that clergy (*Epist.* III among the Cyprianic letters), “as do the presbyters and the entire Church, which itself also keeps watch with the greatest solicitude over all who invoke the name of the Lord.” Hence the letters of that same clergy dealing with the lapsed were sent throughout the whole world, as Cyprian testifies in *Ep.* LII.

But in this passage of Cyprian, Fell and Simon Goulart maintain that an equal partnership of honor and power among the Apostles and their successors is wholly incompatible with primacy. Fell observes in a note on the Letter [uncertain lacuna in the source: “.....”], [Col. 0027] that “in the judgment of that blessed martyr, those must be considered desperate and lost persons who regard the authority of the bishops in Africa as less than that even of Cornelius himself, seated in Peter’s chair at Rome.”

If preconceived opinions were set aside, nothing would be easier than to grasp Cyprian’s meaning and reconcile primacy with an equal partnership of honor and power. No one is unaware that Cyprian presided over Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania. Nevertheless, the bishops of those provinces had received equal power from Christ: they certainly were what Cyprian was, endowed with an equal partnership both of honor and of power; yet the bishop of Carthage presided over them. But if Cyprian, while acknowledging an equal partnership of honor and power among bishops, did not for that reason cast aside the authority conferred upon him by ecclesiastical right, why should he be thought to have stripped Peter and his successors of the authority handed down by Christ himself?

His position is clearer than daylight. He shows that unity appeared so important to Christ that, although he granted equal power to the Apostles, he nevertheless willed that one should preside over the others. Thus the Apostles were what Peter was, but with the exception of the primacy. James and John had received power equal to Peter’s, but Christ did not will unity to begin either from James or from John; to Peter alone he granted this honor.

From these considerations another passage of Cyprian, much celebrated by the same opponents, can also be elucidated. “The episcopate is one, a share in which is held wholly and undividedly by each,” says Cyprian in the same place in the book *On the Unity of the Church*. Cyprian frequently declares elsewhere that although “a portion of the flock has been assigned to each shepherd” and although “there are many shepherds,” they nevertheless feed “one flock,” and “ought to gather and cherish all the sheep whom Christ acquired by his blood and passion”; and that for this reason there exists “a numerous body of priests joined together by the cement of mutual concord and the bond of unity, so that if anyone from their college attempts to create a heresy and to rend and ravage Christ’s flock, the others may come to its aid and, like useful and merciful shepherds, gather the Lord’s sheep into the flock” (pp. 86 and 116).

But that numerous body of priests acting in concert to feed the sheep not only detracts nothing from primacy; it necessarily requires a leader and originator. Otherwise there would be the utmost confusion in all affairs. In accordance with their zeal for unity, bishops must render mutual assistance to one another in matters of greater importance; they must unite their authority and counsels in condemning heresies. But who would deny that in matters of this kind the principal role ought to belong to him from whom Christ “by his own authority arranged that the source of unity should begin”?

## IV.—ON SAINT CYPRIAN’S DISAGREEMENT WITH SAINT STEPHEN.—STEPHEN APPROVED NO BAPTISM EXCEPT THAT WHICH WAS ADMINISTERED ACCORDING TO THE FORM PRESCRIBED BY CHRIST

Since Saint Cyprian, in the letters written concerning the baptism of heretics, says many things about his opponents or reports statements made by them, it is of no small importance for elucidating his testimony to explain what Saint Stephen and Cyprian’s other opponents believed. Many, even among Catholics, accused Stephen of error and would have it that he approved the baptism of all heretics, including those who did not preserve the form prescribed by Christ. Launoy even defends Cyprian in such a way that he considers antiquity more favorable to him than to his opponents, declaring—if I may use his own words—“that this matter concerns not faith but discipline” (vol. VIII, p. 656). I shall endeavor to demonstrate that Stephen taught nothing other than what was afterward established by universal consent, and that this teaching of his was not contrary to antiquity but flowed from the very heart of the tradition of the Apostles.

We have lost the letters written by Pope Stephen on the baptism of heretics; but what Cyprian reports from the letter written to him cuts off every opportunity for accusing the holy pontiff. For Stephen spoke as follows in his letter to Cyprian:

> “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, LET NOTHING BE INNOVATED BEYOND WHAT HAS BEEN HANDED DOWN, namely, that a hand be laid upon him for repentance; for the heretics themselves, properly speaking, do not baptize those who come to them from one another, but merely admit them to communion.”

Rigaltius most absurdly distorts the word “properly” (*proprie*) so as to refer it to those “who are properly called heretics on account of some particular cause of their own.” It is clear that this word refers to what follows, so that heretics are said, properly speaking, not to baptize—that is, not to initiate with a baptism peculiar to themselves those who come to them from one another. Compare Horace’s phrase, “it is difficult to express common things distinctively” (*difficile est proprie communia dicere*).

Only two interpretations of Stephen’s words seem possible. Either he says that each group of heretics has its own peculiar baptism, but nevertheless does not initiate with it those who come to it from another group; or he maintains that the heretics do not claim for themselves a peculiar baptism with which they baptize those coming to them, but reverence one baptism common both to their own and to other sects. The first interpretation cannot stand; the second is certain and evident.

1. Such diversity among heretics in baptizing would be entirely inconsistent with their agreement in approving and retaining the baptism of others. For why would each sect have instituted a baptism peculiar to itself and differing from those of the others, unless it considered both the Church’s baptism and those of the other sects insufficient for salvation? Accordingly, it would have been consistent for those who instituted a new baptism to reject the baptism of others.

2. In this passage Stephen proposes the heretics to Cyprian as an example for imitation. Although each man held baptism in the highest esteem, each nevertheless seemed to the other to think too little of it. Cyprian believed that the holiness and majesty of baptism were diminished if baptism given by heretics were valid; Stephen thought baptism was wronged if it were rejected even among the heretics themselves. Since, therefore, he proposes the heretics as an example for imitation, he must be praising in them something that serves to commend baptism. But if the heretics had violated the form prescribed by Christ in baptizing, and yet had not hesitated to approve the dissimilar baptism of others, this conduct would have belonged to men who treated baptism as a useless and insignificant ceremony.

3. The testimonies of Firmilian and Cyprian also help clarify Stephen’s position. “Stephen said in his letter,” says Firmilian, “that the heretics themselves also agree with one another in baptism.” After quoting Stephen’s words, Cyprian adds the following in Epistle LXXIV:

> “And although the individual heresies have their individual baptisms and their different sins, this man, by communicating with the baptism of them all, has amassed within his own bosom the accumulated offenses of them all.” [Col. 0029]

Cyprian opposes another principle to Stephen’s principle and contends that the individual heresies have their individual baptisms, because Stephen had maintained that among the heretics there was one common baptism. Yet Cyprian does not therefore count as many baptisms as there are heresies on the ground that each heresy had changed the form of baptism—for no one will suspect that—but because each is, as it were, an individual body separated from the other sects and from the Church.

Launoy, and after him the author of the *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, object that at that time very few heretics baptized in the name of the three Persons; therefore, they say, Stephen approved absolutely all heretics, including the Marcionites, as Firmilian and Cyprian reproach him for doing. But the institutions of the ancient heretics were better known to Stephen, Cyprian, and Firmilian than to modern writers. Yet Stephen and Cyprian and Firmilian agree in general, as we have just seen, that the heretics did not possess a baptism peculiar to themselves. Very few, therefore, can be excepted as having perverted the common form of baptism.

Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian may be cited as witnesses to the same opinion. The former (*Stromata* I, p. 317) observes that in Scripture the baptismal water of heretics is called “strange water”; yet he does not assign as the reason that they had corrupted the rule for administering baptism, but that they were strangers to the Church. Similarly, Tertullian (*On Baptism*, ch. 15) rejects the baptism of heretics, not on the ground that they had altered the rite for administering it prescribed by Christ, but because:

> “They have no fellowship with our discipline, since the very withdrawal of communion indeed proves them to be outsiders.”

To these is also added the testimony of Augustine, who speaks as follows in Book VI of *On Baptism*, chapter 25:

> “Who does not know that it is not Christ’s baptism if the Gospel words of which the formula consists are lacking from it? Yet heretics who do not baptize at all are more readily found than heretics who do not baptize with those words.”

Launoy vainly thinks that Augustine’s testimony must be understood of heretics contemporary with that holy Doctor, while a different judgment must be made about earlier heretics. For what Augustine observed in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Church may with even greater force be asserted of the second and third. There were indeed heresies which, after following the common rule of baptism at the beginnings of their sect, later altered it in order to obstruct with greater difficulty the return of their members to the Catholic Church. Basil expressly testifies to this concerning the Encratites in canon I. Yet not even they perverted the form prescribed by Christ, but seem merely to have added or removed certain ceremonies. Thus Basil says of them in canon 47:

> “Let them not say: ‘We were baptized into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.’”

Indeed, he does not disapprove of their baptism being held valid if some greater benefit follows from doing so. And he himself testifies in canon I that the brothers Zoïn and Saturninus, when returning from this heresy, had been received by him into the episcopal chair.

But if the Encratites had at first followed the common rites and, when they wished to introduce something new, nevertheless did not dare to violate the form prescribed by Christ, can there be any doubt that the Marcionites and others of that kind, whose relationship with the Encratites was very close, retained the baptism used in the Catholic Church?

Moreover, Cyprian is a substantial witness that Marcion baptized in the name of the three Persons, for Cyprian rejects his baptism on the ground that Marcion does not acknowledge the same Trinity as the Catholics:

> “Does Marcion hold this Trinity?” he says in the *Epistle to Jubaianus*, p. 131. “Does he affirm the same Father and Creator whom we affirm? Does he know the same Son, Christ born of the Virgin Mary?”

Cyprian therefore admitted that the three Persons were named by heretics in baptism, and he had been reduced to saying that the heretics interpreted the Trinity differently from the Catholics. By similar reasoning Firmilian rejects the baptism of the Gnostics and Montanists, because the former did not acknowledge the same Father as the Catholics, and the Montanists did not acknowledge the same Holy Spirit.

Tertullian presses Marcion with arguments drawn from baptism in such a way as to make it readily apparent that this heretic had not altered the common rite of baptism. For in Book I, chapter 28, he asks how Marcion’s god, who did not generate, regenerates; how he bestows the Spirit in baptism, when he did not first confer the soul; why he washes a human being who was never defiled in his sight, and in this entire sacrament of salvation immerses flesh that has no share in salvation.

Epiphanius relates on p. 230 that “among the Marcionites not one baptism but three are permitted after sin; others are baptized on behalf of their deceased catechumens; and women are entrusted with the power to confer baptism.” But he does not accuse Marcion of violating the baptismal form.

Stephen is also said to have held the baptism of Valentinus and Apelles valid. But this followed from his principles. For since he held it as certain, as Firmilian reproaches him, that baptism is administered “when the triad of the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is invoked,” he ought to exclude absolutely no one who was known not to depart from this rule of baptism. But if Marcion himself, who surpassed all others in impiety, baptized in the name of the three Persons, I do not see why the same should not be believed of Apelles and Valentinus.

Cyprian objects only this against heretics of that kind: that they do not confess the same Father, the same Son, the same Holy Spirit, and the same Church as the Catholics. He joins the Patripassians, Anthropians, Valentinians, Apelleians, and Ophites to the Marcionites in the *Epistle to Jubaianus*, p. 130.

Marcus, the most celebrated of Valentinus’s followers, pronounced all the words of invocation when consecrating the bread and wine, as Irenaeus testifies in Book I, chapter 12; the other heretics of the same kind celebrated the Eucharist according to the Church’s custom. Hence Irenaeus challenges them in Book IV, chapter 18, either “to change their opinion or to abstain from offering the things aforesaid.” It is unlikely that men who scrupled to depart from the customary form of celebrating the Eucharist should have failed to retain in the rites of baptism even what Christ had expressly prescribed.

Many Gnostics undoubtedly introduced much that was impious and absurd into the ceremonies of baptism. But, as Augustine observes (*On Baptism*, Book VI, no. 47):

> “Those certain Gospel words, without which baptism cannot be consecrated, possess such power [Col. 0031] that through them whatever is said amiss in a faulty prayer contrary to the rule of faith is rendered ineffective. And if an evil and perverse man introduces in some respects a perverse prayer, God is present through his own Gospel words, without which Christ’s baptism cannot be consecrated, and he himself sanctifies his sacrament.”

Stephen agrees with Augustine, for, as Firmilian reports, he said that “the presence and holiness of Christ are present to those who are baptized among heretics.”

As regards those who either did not use water or did not baptize as Christ prescribed—some such persons seem to have existed among the Gnostics, being pagans rather than heretics—there can be no doubt that Stephen would not have admitted them into the Church without baptism. Some, however, altered the words of baptism in such a way that they nevertheless wished to retain and express them; such were those who baptized:

> “Into the name of the unknown Father of all, into Truth the mother of all, into him who descended into Jesus” (Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 21, no. 3).

But there was so little controversy about heretics of this kind that Cyprian and Firmilian testify that the very interrogations customarily employed in the Church were retained by the heretics, pp. 131, 145, 154.

To these testimonies of Cyprian and Firmilian is added the authority not only of Augustine, Vincent of Lérins, and Facundus, who had no doubt whatever that Stephen had defended the Church’s common position, but also of Dionysius of Alexandria and Eusebius. The former wrote to Stephen and about Stephen in such a way as to desire in him only a more lenient position and a certain accommodation, as was fitting in a matter not yet decided by universal agreement; the latter testifies that Stephen had defended ancient tradition, *History*, Book VII, chapter 3.

## V.—ST. CYPRIAN UNDERSTOOD HIS OPPONENTS’ POSITION LESS THAN FULLY.—ON BAPTISM IN THE NAME OF CHRIST.—STEPHEN’S POSITION DERIVED FROM THE APOSTLES

But two matters remain for us to explain: whether Stephen believed that in the baptism of heretics not only was the character imprinted, but sins were also forgiven; and whether he considered it sufficient to baptize in the name of Christ, with no mention made of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Cyprian and Firmilian always refute their opponents as though the latter contended that sins were forgiven by heretics who baptized. “Does he honor God,” says Cyprian (Epistle LXXIV), “who judges that forgiveness of sins is granted among those who blaspheme God?” And Firmilian says (Epistle LXXV):

> “Stephen and those who agree with him contend that forgiveness of sins and a second birth can proceed in the baptism of heretics, among whom they themselves confess that the Holy Spirit is not present.”

And below:
