> “They say that one who is baptized outside, in whatever manner, can obtain grace by his own intention and faith.”

In the letter sent by Jubaianus to Cyprian, which Pamelius and Baronius believe to be Stephen’s, it was written “that one should not inquire who baptized, since the person baptized could have received forgiveness of sins according as he believed.”

It was not difficult for Cyprian and Firmilian to demonstrate an evident contradiction in the opinion they attribute to their opponents. For it is utterly absurd to say that someone has obtained forgiveness of sins when he has not yet received the Holy Spirit, or that someone has put on Christ in baptism when the Holy Spirit does not yet dwell in him.

But those eminent men Cyprian and Firmilian seem to interpret their opponents’ position less precisely. It is unlikely that the latter reasoned so absurdly as to believe that forgiveness of sins could be obtained without the Holy Spirit. The learned editor of the *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs* thinks that Stephen, when recognizing forgiveness of sins in baptism conferred outside heresy, is speaking either of infants, or of adults who in good faith receive baptism from a concealed heretic, or from an open heretic in extreme danger of death.

Although I greatly respect this most learned writer, I shall nevertheless take another route in explaining Stephen’s position, which seems to me capable of being clarified from these words of his cited by Firmilian:

> “Heresy, indeed,” he said, “gives birth and exposes its offspring; but the Church receives those who have been exposed.”

It is clear from these words that heresy gives birth not for itself but for the Church—or rather, that the Church gives birth through heresy as through a maidservant—so that those whom heresy bears can become children of the bride if they approach the Church, but cannot escape destruction if they are not received by the Church.

Very similar to Stephen’s doctrine is this statement of Augustine:

> “For the Church,” he says in Book I of *On Baptism*, no. 12, “gives birth to all through baptism, whether within herself, that is, from her own womb, or outside herself from the seed of her husband. Yet Esau, though born of the wife, was separated from the people of God because of fraternal discord; while Asher, born indeed under the authority of the wife but from a maidservant, received the land of promise because of fraternal concord. Hence in Ishmael’s case his mother’s status as a maidservant did not cause his separation from the people of God; rather, fraternal discord did. Nor did the wife’s authority benefit him, though he was more properly her son, because by virtue of her marital rights he was both begotten in the maidservant and received from the maidservant. Thus among these people also, whoever is born is born by the Church’s right, which is present in baptism. But if they agree with their brethren, they come through the unity of peace to the land of promise: they are not to be cast out again from the maternal womb, but acknowledged in the paternal seed. If, however, they persevere in discord, they will belong to Ishmael’s lot.”

Cyprian and Firmilian therefore wrongly thought that Stephen attributed children to heresy as though she were the bride, since he said that heresy gives birth as a maidservant, so that those whom she has borne may be received by the Church, which alone is the bride.

He seems to have recognized the forgiveness of sins in the baptism of heretics in a not dissimilar sense. For just as such baptism has the power that those whom the maidservant has borne belong to the bride when they are received by the Church, so, although it does not forgive the sins of those who remain in heresy, it nevertheless avails so that their sins are forgiven [Col. 0033] when they return to the Church. Augustine explains this excellently in Book I of *On Baptism*:

> “Let them understand,” he says (no. 18), “that in communions separated from the Church people can be baptized wherever Christ’s baptism is given and received with the same sacramental celebration; yet it benefits them for the forgiveness of sins only when, once reconciled to unity, they are stripped of the sacrilege of dissension, by which their sins were held fast and prevented from being forgiven.”

The anonymous author of the book *On Rebaptism* proves scarcely anything else than this usefulness of baptism received outside the Church for obtaining the forgiveness of sins within the Church. On p. 357 he states:

> “That prior invocation of the name of Jesus, if bare and solitary and situated in error, cannot suffice to bestow salvation, lest in this way,” he says, “we believe even pagans and heretics who misuse the name of Jesus capable of attaining salvation without the true and complete reality. Yet it is most useful to believe that this invocation of the name of Jesus, when error has been corrected, the truth of the faith acknowledged, and every stain of former conduct cut away, may, by the mystery of God duly accomplished in persons of this kind, obtain the place it otherwise would not have had; and finally that it does not hinder the true faith and the conferral of the sign in its integrity, once what was lacking has been supplied.”

Cyprian and Firmilian, therefore, since they knew their opponents’ position not from peaceful conversations and disputations but only from writings—and very obscure ones at that—seem to have understood less fully what those opponents held. They believed that their opponents admitted faith and forgiveness of sin in heretics who did not depart from heresy, although they were speaking of faith succeeding error, and said that sin was forgiven in such a way that this forgiveness took effect when one departed from heresy.

Now another error must be warded off from the holy pontiff: it is unlikely that he approved baptism in the name of Christ alone.

1. A manner of speaking supported both by the authority of Scripture and by ecclesiastical usage ought not to be censured in Stephen and his associates, as the recently praised editor of the *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs* demonstrates.

2. As regards Stephen, Cyprian does not accuse him of error in this matter, although at first sight he seems to do so. In Epistle LXXIII he says:

> “Nor is there any reason for someone, in order to circumvent Christian truth, to put forward the name of Christ and say: ‘Wherever and however they were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, they have obtained the grace of baptism.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “How, then, do some say that a pagan baptized outside the Church—indeed, both outside and against the Church—wherever and however, provided it is in the name of Jesus Christ, can obtain forgiveness of sins, when Christ himself commands the nations to be baptized in the full and united Trinity?”

To understand these words, however, it must be observed that Cyprian here does not blame his opponents for saying that one of the three Persons could be omitted in baptism, but for denying that faith in the three Persons was necessary. For since the Marcionites and other heretics of that kind poured out dreadful blasphemies against the Father, Cyprian contends that the name of Christ avails them nothing, because “the Son alone cannot benefit anyone without the Father or against the Father.”

> “How,” he says, “when God the Father is not known—indeed, is blasphemed—are those who are said to have been baptized among heretics in the name of Christ judged to have obtained forgiveness of sins?”

Cyprian therefore rejects baptism conferred by heretics in the name of Christ, not because the Father was omitted—a matter that was not in controversy—but because of their blasphemies against the Father. Hence he approves that same baptism if it is administered in Christ’s truth:

> “It is therefore apparent,” he says, “that things vaunted in the name of Christ are not immediately to be received and accepted, but those things which are done in the truth of Christ.”

Thus baptism “in the name of Christ” is the same as baptism instituted by Christ.

Firmilian, who had read this letter of Cyprian and confirms this passage now before us, as he does most others, by his own observations, considers baptism to be given in the name of Christ when it is given in the name of the three Persons. Nor does he blame his opponents for holding baptism in the name of Christ alone to be valid, but:

> “Because they do not think it necessary to ask who the person was who baptized, on the ground that the person baptized could obtain grace when the triad of the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit was invoked, as though this bare invocation of the names sufficed for the forgiveness of sins and the sanctification of baptism.”

Indeed, not only Stephen but not even the anonymous author of the book *On Rebaptism*, who poured biting vinegar upon Cyprian, seems to have approved baptism in the name of Christ alone. Tillemont nevertheless contends that he labored under this error, but entirely without justification. For that author interprets baptism in the name of Christ as baptism conferred according to the form prescribed by Christ.

The very passage that Tillemont adduces clearly demonstrates the point:

> “It makes a great difference,” says the anonymous writer on p. 358, “whether someone has not been baptized at all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, or whether he limps in some respect when he is baptized with the baptism of water, which is less, provided that afterward there is found in the baptism of the Spirit, which is undoubtedly greater, a sincere faith in the truth. And do not suppose that what the Lord said is contrary to this treatise: ‘Go, teach the nations, immerse them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit’; for although this is true and right, and is in every way to be observed in the Church, and has in fact customarily been observed, nevertheless it must be considered that the invocation of the name of Jesus ought not to seem futile to us, because of the veneration and power of that very name, in which all mighty works are customarily done, and sometimes even some by outsiders.”

From these words Tillemont concludes that this writer, although he admits that the three Persons were customarily named in the Church, nevertheless does not regard baptism as invalid if it is conferred in the name of Jesus alone. But our writer does not raise against himself from Christ’s words the phrase, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”; rather, he raises the phrase “Teach the nations.” Nor does he defend baptism that lacks the naming of the three Persons, but baptism that lacks “sincere faith”; and his words “to be observed in the Church and customarily observed” refer to [Col. 0035] the words “Go, teach the nations.”

Hence he contends that when the Apostles were baptized in the Jewish manner they believed Christ to be immortal and did not believe in his death and resurrection. He therefore concludes as follows (p. 360):

> “Thus, as regards the disciples themselves, they are found not to have possessed a whole and perfect faith, in the ways we have recounted; and, what is much more serious, as is written in the Gospel according to John, they even baptized others.”

The issue here, therefore, is not the naming of the three Persons; that is laid down as certain and entirely undisputed. Nor does “baptism in the name of Jesus” mean anything else in this writer, as is clear from the words just cited, than baptism of water, baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Now no lengthy disputation is needed to demonstrate that the practice defended by Pope Stephen flowed from the sources of apostolic tradition. This custom was certainly flourishing, apart from those churches which the decrees of councils had turned toward a different position. There is no trace in the West of repeated baptism except in Africa. In the East, Eusebius testifies (*History*, Book VII, chapter 2) that the ancient custom had prevailed of employing only the imposition of hands with prayers in receiving heretics.

We perceive the custom of Egypt from the testimonies of Dionysius of Alexandria preserved in Eusebius in the same book. Stephen had threatened not to communicate with Cappadocia, Cilicia, Galatia, and the neighboring regions; but there were no complaints whatsoever about Egypt. Indeed, Dionysius of Alexandria, to the great benefit of the Church, intervened to reconcile the dispute.

As for the fact that he thought Xystus, the Roman pontiff, ought to be consulted about a man who had long since returned to the Church but remembered that he had been initiated with an impious baptism full of blasphemy: this not only reveals Dionysius’s agreement with the Roman Church and his aversion to repeating baptism, but also proves that his predecessors Heraclas or Demetrius, who had received this man, had not customarily baptized heretics upon their return.

To this is added Basil’s testimony, who asserts in canon I that the baptism of the Montanists was approved by Dionysius of Alexandria. The objection drawn from Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* I, p. 317), that the water of heretics is “strange water,” proves that those who as adults receive baptism in heresy are not cleansed but contaminated; it does not prove that holy Clement considered their baptism invalid and nonexistent.

Jerome is more difficult to explain. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he testifies that Dionysius of Alexandria held the same view as Cyprian concerning the baptism of heretics and wrote several letters on the matter; but in this Jerome directly contradicts Basil.

Africa itself may also be cited as a witness to the tradition that it most vigorously attacked. For the Africans did not repeat baptism given by heretics before Agrippinus’s decrees. That they themselves confessed this is apparent from these words of Firmilian:

> “This, Africans, you can indeed say against Stephen: that, once you had recognized the truth, you abandoned the error of custom.”

Cyprian himself also, when he says in the *Epistle to Jubaianus* that it is not a new or sudden practice for those who come from the heretics to the Church to be baptized, but that many years had passed since the bishops under Agrippinus had established this in council, not obscurely confesses the novelty of his own opinion and recognizes Agrippinus as its source and originator.

Augustine thought that the custom introduced by Agrippinus, after drying up shortly afterward, had been revived by Cyprian. But, as Tillemont observed, this is wholly inconsistent with these words of Cyprian from the *Epistle to Jubaianus*:

> “Since from that time”—namely, from Agrippinus—“down to the present day so many thousands of heretics converted to the Church in our provinces have neither disdained nor hesitated, but indeed have reasonably and willingly embraced the opportunity to obtain the grace of the life-giving washing and saving baptism.”

But if Cyprian defended a custom already established, Agrippinus certainly introduced a new one, as Augustine observes in so many passages of his books *On Baptism*.

The agreement of the sects, which did not dare to repeat baptism received in other sects, adds very great weight to these testimonies. Who does not see that the agreement of so many churches and so many sects flowed from no other origin and source than the Apostles—especially in a matter beset by the greatest difficulties, not openly indicated in Scripture, and confirmed by no decree of the Church, yet so firmly established among both Catholics and heretics that the contrary opinion appeared a grave error?

Certainly, after the Apostles, so firm a conviction could never have been impressed upon people’s minds without a decree of the universal Church intervening. Rather, hatred of heresy and the entirely justified precaution that the Eucharist not be given to persons who had not been baptized, or that infants baptized in heresy not die without true baptism, would have led very many to regard repetition of baptism as necessary.

## VI.—THE PRINCIPAL ARGUMENTS BY WHICH ST. CYPRIAN DEFENDED HIMSELF.—HE REJECTED NEITHER SACRAMENTS ADMINISTERED BY EVIL PERSONS WITHIN THE CHURCH NOR TRADITION

Although the Church received its doctrine concerning the baptism of heretics from the very mouth of the Apostles, it must nevertheless be admitted that this tradition was not of the kind that daily preaching impressed upon everyone’s ears. No one could ever have been ignorant, without the greatest negligence, of the Church’s position concerning the divinity of Christ and the Holy Spirit, the change of the gifts into the body and blood of Christ, and other matters of that kind; nor could anyone have opposed it without the gravest crime, because these doctrines resounded in Christian ears throughout all the churches.

Whether, however, the baptism of heretics should be regarded as valid or not could become obscured and fade from use over time in many regions where there was either no occasion, or only a very rare one, for receiving heretics. We therefore need not wonder why outstanding men erred in this matter.

The truth could indeed easily have been investigated if the most ancient churches had been consulted—churches which had never lacked heretics either to oppose or to receive when they returned to [Col. 0037] the Church. Foremost among these was the Roman Church, since it is established that all the most ancient heretics made their way to that city. Yet Cyprian bears only the slightest blame for failing to take this precaution, since he did not introduce the custom of rebaptizing into his church, but found it established by the authority of his predecessors.

The arguments employed by Cyprian possess such brilliance that Augustine admits that only the Church’s authority led him to the contrary position:

> “Nor would we ourselves,” he says in Book II of *On Baptism*, no. 5, “dare to assert anything of this kind unless supported by the most harmonious authority of the universal Church. To this authority Cyprian himself would undoubtedly have yielded, if in his time the truth of this question had already been clarified and declared and then confirmed by a plenary council.”

Cyprian relied chiefly on this argument: since heresies have been cut off from the unity of the Church and consist of dead persons, they cannot sanctify, forgive sins, or give the Holy Spirit.

> “Who can give,” he says in Epistle LXX, “what he himself does not possess? Or how can one perform spiritual acts when he himself has lost the Holy Spirit?”

And in Epistle LXXI:

> “For they receive nothing there, where there is nothing.”

And shortly afterward:

> “It is evident that those who are not in the Church of Christ are counted among the dead, and that one who does not himself live cannot give life to another.”

From these and other testimonies of this kind, Cyprian by no means establishes what certain learned men thought followed from his words: that holiness is necessary in each individual minister for the valid administration of the sacraments. He speaks of the entire society, not of individuals. Just as the sacraments of the Catholic Church, when administered by evil persons, retain their force and effect through the prayers of the saints and the groans of the dove, so among heretics, where all are dead, he believed that the sacraments were deprived of their effect and were altogether nonexistent. For he could not persuade himself that the dove baptized through heretics and schismatics in heresy and schism just as she did through evil ministers in the Catholic Church.

That Cyprian’s mind must be explained in this way is evident from several passages:

> “How,” he says in Epistle LXX, “can one in whom the Holy Spirit is not present cleanse and sanctify the water? . . . Or how can one who baptizes give another forgiveness of sins, when he himself cannot lay aside his own sins outside the Church?”

And in Epistle LXXIII, p. 132:

> “Can one who is not within the Church irrigate from the Church’s fountains?”

A little afterward he admits that heretics, “if they are devoted to the Church and established within the Church, can make use both of her baptism and of her other saving goods.”

Finally, in the same epistle (p. 133), he expressly distinguishes evil persons who are within the Church from heretics:

> “Moreover,” he says, “it is one thing for those who are within the Church to speak concerning the name of Christ, and another for those who are outside and act against the Church to baptize in the name of Christ. Therefore, let those who champion heretics not put forward what Paul stated concerning brethren; rather, let them show whether he thought anything ought to be conceded to a heretic, or whether he approved their faith and baptism, or whether he established that the faithless and blasphemous could receive forgiveness of sins outside the Church.”

Firmilian has the same argument on p. 149. Hence Augustine observes (*On Baptism*, Book IV) that Cyprian distinguishes “between those who are evil outside and those who are evil within,” and demonstrates at length that it by no means follows from this distinction that the Church does not baptize outside through heretics just as she baptizes inside through evil persons.

Although Cyprian’s arguments drawn from Scripture are not destitute of every appearance of probability, the answers he gives to the tradition advanced by his opponents are wholly unworthy of the brilliance of so great a mind. He calls a human tradition what was observed with the greatest agreement in all the principal churches, established by the authority of no council, and what had not ceased to be observed even in Africa until Agrippinus.

When it was objected to him, “What, then, will become of those who in the past came from heresy to the Church and were admitted without baptism?” he answers as follows in the *Epistle to Jubaianus*:

> “The Lord is able in his mercy to grant pardon and not to exclude from the gifts of his Church those who were admitted to the Church in simplicity and fell asleep within the Church.”

In this answer one readily recognizes Cyprian’s charity and moderation of spirit. But although the objection made to him embraced both adults and infants, he extricates himself, as best he can, with regard to the adults, while regarding infants baptized in heresy and dying within the Church before the use of reason without a new baptism, he utters not even a word.

Although Cyprian answered the tradition advanced against him less than successfully, he did not on that account treat the authority of tradition as worthless. Nowhere does he express or say what Simon Goulart, in his notes on Epistle LXXIV, and many other Protestants attributed to him:

1. That every evangelical and apostolic tradition must be sought in the Gospels, Acts, or Epistles;

2. That everything which cannot be found in those books must be rejected and despised.

Heaven does not seem to be farther removed from earth than Cyprian’s position is from such fabrications. First, from his testimonies concerning the Church’s infallibility, which we cited above, one may discern whether he admitted no other rule of faith than the text of Scripture separated from tradition. Second, Cyprian and Firmilian nowhere complain that Stephen appeals to tradition as a rule of faith. They acknowledge that this tradition concerning the non-repetition of the baptism of heretics must be observed if it originated with the Apostles; but they deny that it originated with the Apostles, because the heretics who returned under the Apostles had already been baptized in the Church (Epp. LXXIV and LXXV). Firmilian adds that “those who are at Rome do not in every respect observe what has been handed down from the beginning, for example, concerning the days on which Easter is celebrated”; from this it is readily understood what Firmilian thought about unwritten traditions. Third, against the tradition adduced by his opponents Cyprian sets another about which both sides were agreed:

> “Nor let anyone say,” he writes in the Epistle to Jubaianus (p. 133), “‘We follow what we have received from the Apostles,’ since the Apostles handed down only one Church and one baptism, which is established only in that same Church; nor do we find [Col. 0039] that anyone baptized among heretics was admitted by the Apostles in that same baptism and received into communion, such that the Apostles might appear to have approved the baptism of heretics.”

And in Epistle LXXIV, p. 141:

> “This is what the priests of God, observing the divine precepts, must also do now: if in any respect the truth has faltered and wavered, we must return to the Lord’s source and to the evangelical and apostolic tradition, and the rationale of our conduct must arise from the same source from which its order and origin arose. For it has been handed down to us that there is one God and one Christ, one hope and one faith, one Church and one baptism,” etc.

Fourth, so far are Cyprian and Firmilian from severing tradition from the Scriptures, and so unlawful do they consider it to depart from the Church’s authority in interpreting the Scriptures, that they argue that the baptism of heretics is invalid also on this ground: heretics interpreted the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—and even the questions themselves, “Do you believe in the remission of sins and eternal life through the holy Church?”—differently from the Church (pp. 131, 145, 154).

## VII.—ST. CYPRIAN DOES NOT CONFUSE CONFIRMATION WITH THE IMPOSITION OF HANDS UPON RETURNING HERETICS.—HE NUMBERS CONFIRMATION AMONG THE SACRAMENTS.

A question of no slight importance must here be examined: whether Cyprian labored under the error which I see attributed to him by many, namely, that he believed the imposition of hands customarily received by returning heretics to be the sacrament of Confirmation. The learned Noël Alexandre (*Dissert. II saec.*) and the author of the new edition of the *Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs* skillfully demonstrate that the imposition of hands upon returning heretics differs greatly from the sacrament of Confirmation, and that Pope Stephen did not intend Confirmation to be repeated when he maintained that it was sufficient to lay a hand upon returning heretics so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Yet these same writers think that Cyprian did not adequately understand his opponents’ position, and therefore argued against them as though they repeated the Confirmation received in heresy. Against Cyprian the following testimonies of his own are produced:

> “But if,” he writes in the Epistle to Jubaianus, p. 131, “someone could be baptized outside according to a corrupt faith and obtain the remission of sins, then according to that same faith he could obtain the Holy Spirit; and it is unnecessary to lay a hand upon him when he comes, so that he may obtain the Holy Spirit and be sealed. For either faith outside could effect both, or one who had been outside received neither of them.”

And on p. 136:

> “Those who come from heresy to the Church must be baptized, so that those who are prepared for the kingdom of God by divine regeneration in the lawful and unique baptism of the holy Church may be born through both sacraments, because it is written: ‘Unless one has been born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.’”

And in the Epistle to Stephen, p. 128:

> “For only then can they be fully sanctified and become children of God, if they are born through both sacraments, since it is written: ‘Unless one has been born again,’ etc.”

Nemesianus of Tubunae speaks to the same effect at the Council of Carthage:

> “Some therefore misinterpret matters,” he says, “by saying that through the imposition of hands they receive the Holy Spirit and are thus received, although it is manifest that they must be born again in the Catholic Church through both sacraments.”

But these testimonies seem capable of explanation, and they do not persuade me that Cyprian, inattentive in a matter plainly before his eyes, erred and mentally confused things so distinct in their nature and in the Church’s practice. His position, moreover, may be traced by the surest indications in the Epistle to Quintus (p. 127), where he speaks as follows:

> “And they say that in this they follow ancient custom, since among the ancients heresy was still only in its earliest beginnings, so that those there were persons who were departing from the Church and had previously been baptized here; yet when they returned to the Church and did penance, it was unnecessary to baptize them. We too observe this today: when it is established that certain persons were baptized here and passed from us to the heretics, if afterward, recognizing their sin and abandoning their error, they return to the truth and to their mother, it is sufficient to lay a hand upon them unto penance; so that, because he had been a sheep, the shepherd may receive this estranged and wandering sheep back into his fold.”

The issue is not how correctly Cyprian answers his opponents, but what answer he gives. They maintained that it had been handed down by the Apostles, and always observed in the Church, that baptism received in heresy should not be repeated, but that upon heretics returning with this baptism a hand should merely be laid unto penance. Cyprian answers that in former times heretics were rightly received without baptism because they had previously been baptized in the Church; and he declares that he himself does the same, so that if he receives any heretics who had been baptized in the Church, he merely lays a hand upon them unto penance. In a word, he concedes to his opponents that this custom of receiving heretics, which they defended with such zeal, had both been practiced in former times and was practiced by himself whenever a similar case arose. But no one would say that Cyprian believed Confirmation had been repeated in the Church’s earliest days, or intended to repeat it whenever a hand unto penance was to be laid upon heretics baptized in the Church before their heresy. He is therefore unjustly accused of confusing the imposition of hands upon returning heretics with the sacrament of Confirmation. At the Council of Carthage, Crescens of Cirta confirms Cyprian’s position; he judges that all who return from heresy and schism must be baptized,

> “except, of course, those who had previously been baptized in the Catholic Church, provided nevertheless that through the imposition of hands unto penance they are reconciled to the Church.”

But why does Cyprian require that those baptized in heresy, upon returning to the Church, “be born through both sacraments”? What can those two sacraments be other than Baptism and Confirmation? This difficulty can be resolved. For there is no contradiction in supposing that Cyprian, taking the occasion furnished by his opponents, concluded that the sacrament of Confirmation must be repeated, although he did not in the least suspect that his opponents were repeating it. St. Stephen and those who sided with him, though they regarded the baptism of heretics as valid, nevertheless acknowledged that the Holy Spirit was not conferred in such [Col. 0041] baptism; consequently, another sacrament was necessary for those returning from heresy, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, whom they could not obtain in heresy. This sacrament, however, was the imposition of a hand unto penance, or the sacrament of Penance, which, according to Cyprian’s testimony, confers the Holy Spirit upon penitents. For among the other reasons that induced Cyprian to grant peace to penitents, he lists this one: that he considered it necessary to prepare penitents to endure persecution and to equip them with the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

> “But since the Lord says,” he writes, “that the Spirit of the Father speaks in those who have been handed over and placed in a state of confessing the name, how can one be found prepared or fit for confession if, having first received peace, he has not received the Spirit of the Father, who, strengthening his servants, himself speaks and confesses in us?” (Ep. LIV).

Accordingly, when Cyprian saw his opponents deny that returning heretics needed baptism, but only the imposition of a hand so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, he seized upon this as an occasion to establish that returning heretics needed two kinds of sacrament: one for the remission of sins, the other for receiving the Holy Spirit. On this general point, indeed, Cyprian and his opponents agreed that some sacrament was necessary for returning heretics so that they might receive the Holy Spirit; but it was unnecessary to identify that sacrament specifically. In a not dissimilar fashion, at the Council of Carthage Vincentius of Thibaris agrees with his opponents that the imposition of hands is necessary, but interprets it differently from them:

> “We know,” he says, “that heretics are worse than pagans.... Therefore, first through the imposition of hands in exorcism, and second through the regeneration of Baptism, can they then come to Christ’s promise.”

Vincentius agrees with his opponents concerning the imposition of hands; but they understood an imposition of hands unto penance, while he understood one in exorcism. It is therefore hardly surprising if Cyprian agrees with his opponents concerning the necessity of a sacrament for conferring the Holy Spirit, although the two sides interpret that sacrament differently.

From these things, moreover, it is evident that Confirmation was always in the Church a sacrament distinct from Baptism. Each is called a sacrament and has different effects assigned to it. For although the Holy Spirit is received in Baptism, as Cyprian observes in so many places, he is nevertheless attributed especially to Confirmation, which strengthens with new protection and the gifts of the Holy Spirit those who have already put on Christ in Baptism, so that we are said to be born again through both sacraments. And this, indeed, is wonderfully confirmed by Cyprian and the other bishops of Africa in the letter to the Numidians:

> “It is also necessary,” they say, “that one who has been baptized be anointed, so that, having received chrism—that is, anointing—he may be an anointed one of God and may have within himself the grace of Christ.”

I shall attempt briefly to explain what follows:

> “Moreover, the Eucharist,” the same bishops say, “is that from which those baptized are anointed with oil sanctified upon the altar. But one who had neither altar nor church could not sanctify the created substance of oil. Hence spiritual anointing cannot exist among heretics either, since it is established that oil cannot be sanctified and the Eucharist cannot be celebrated among them at all.”

Baluze very properly emended this passage from what was read in the old editions, “oil sanctified upon the altar”; or, in Erasmus and Pamelius by a freer conjecture, “the Eucharist, and the oil with which those baptized are anointed, is sanctified upon the altar.” Cyprian is not saying what Rigault and Fell suppose him to have said metaphorically—namely, that the Eucharist is the oil with which we are anointed—but rather that the Eucharist is that from which the oil used to anoint the baptized derives its sanctification, because, plainly, the oil was sanctified upon the altar amid the very prayers of the sacrifice.

## VIII.—THE SACRAMENT OF PENANCE IS DEFENDED FROM THE TESTIMONIES OF ST. CYPRIAN.—HOW NECESSARY HE JUDGED IT, AND HOW HOLILY HE WISHED IT TO BE ADMINISTERED, IS SHOWN.—SEVERAL OF HIS STATEMENTS ARE EXPLAINED.

From the testimonies cited it is also readily evident that Penance was numbered among the Church’s sacraments, since, as we have said, it was generally agreed between Cyprian and his opponents that Penance and Confirmation were sacraments. Hence Cyprian explicitly declares, as we have just seen, that the Spirit of the Father is bestowed in the sacrament of Penance. As he judged Baptism necessary for catechumens, so Cyprian judged absolution and peace necessary for the lapsed. For while he remained hidden in retirement, seeing that he would not return very soon and that summer had already begun—a season plagued by constant and serious illnesses—he thought provision should be made for both the hearers and the lapsed, so that neither the former should die without Baptism nor the lapsed without peace. So highly did Cyprian esteem this remission of sin effected through priests—for so he himself calls it in *On the Lapsed*, p. 191—that he regarded it as a grave sacrilege on the part of Marcianus of Arles that, through his fault and cruelty, many of the brethren had died without peace in previous years (Ep. LXVII). This same reason induced the holy Martyr, when the persecution [Col. 0043] of Gallus and Volusianus was impending, to admit to peace those who had lapsed under Decius and had not ceased doing penance from the first day of their lapse. For he did not think that one would be fit to confess Christ unless, after first receiving peace from the priests, he had received the Spirit of the Father. Moreover, he feared that if anyone, having abandoned everything and fled, and finding himself in darkness and solitude, happened to encounter robbers or died of fever and illness, it would be imputed to him that so good a soldier had died without peace and without communion (Ep. LIV). From these things it is evident how little concern for salvation moves those who make light of this sacrament and erase it from the list of the sacraments. For if any of the lapsed in former times had lacked it—not only those whose virtue was still weak, but even those whose perfect charity shone forth in their abandonment of everything for Christ—it would have been regarded as a great loss.

Cyprian defends confession of sins as a part of the sacrament that is altogether necessary and prescribed by God. He exhorts the lapsed that

> “each should confess his own offense while the offender is still in this world, while his confession can be admitted, while satisfaction and remission effected through priests is acceptable before God” (*On the Lapsed*, p. 191).

In the same book he recounts miracles of divine vengeance recently inflicted upon those who had withheld hidden sins from the priests’ knowledge; and he teaches that even if a crime was entertained in thought alone, it must be disclosed and confessed to the priests.

> “Finally, how much greater in faith,” he writes (p. 190), “and better in fear are those who, although bound by no crime of sacrifice or certificate, nevertheless, because they so much as thought of it, sorrowfully and simply confess this very thing before the priests of God, make an *exomologesis*—an acknowledgment—of conscience, disclose the burden of their soul, and seek saving medicine even for small and slight wounds, knowing that it is written: ‘God is not mocked.’”

I am astonished that the author of the Oxford edition denied that auricular confession follows from this passage. He even cites Lombert as a witness for his position:

> “The most learned Lombert,” he writes in the note on this passage, “rightly concludes from it that secret crimes must be expiated before God by confession and penance, but that auricular confession, as Pamelius wished, is not thereby established.”

Yet Pamelius and Lombert are in fact wonderfully agreed, and Lombert expressly declares that secret thoughts were confessed to priests. Nor can anything else be elicited from Cyprian’s words. For since it is established that confession of hidden crimes was not made, or at least not prescribed, publicly and in the hearing of all, it is clearer than daylight that those who confessed evil thoughts before priests, made an *exomologesis* of conscience, disclosed the burden of their soul, and sought medicine for their wounds deposited their sins in the ears of some priest. Moreover, it cannot be denied that all the circumstances in imposing penance were examined as though weighed in a goldsmith’s balance; Cyprian expressly attests this in Epistle LII. But how could priests have imposed a fitting penance upon each person for hidden sins unless the lapsed had afforded them an opportunity to inspect their consciences? Here, indeed, it should be observed that this confession of thoughts arose not from some extraordinary and unprescribed fervor of piety, but from the necessity of fulfilling a divine precept: “Knowing that it is written,” says Cyprian, “‘God is not mocked.’”

The holier Cyprian was, the more earnestly he took care that a sacrament instituted for human salvation should not be turned to human destruction. What stirred his zeal in this matter, and provided the occasion for transmitting outstanding teaching to posterity, was the wickedness of certain presbyters who, partly to cause Cyprian trouble and partly to curry favor with men by a novel device, relieved the lapsed of the burden of penance. Inflamed with zeal for the truth, the holy Martyr inveighs against such men in *On the Lapsed*:

> “They think it is peace,” he says (p. 186), “which certain men peddle with deceitful words. That is not peace but war, nor is one joined to the Church who is separated from the Gospel. Why do they call injury a benefit? Why do they designate impiety by the name of piety? Why, cutting short the lamentation of penance, do they pretend to communicate with those who ought continually to weep and beseech their Lord? Such men are to the lapsed what hail is to crops, what a stormy star is to trees, what pestilential devastation is to herds, what a savage tempest is to ships. They take away the consolation of eternal hope; they overturn the tree from its root; with diseased speech they spread a lethal contagion; they dash the ship against the rocks so that it may not reach harbor. Such easy indulgence does not grant peace but takes it away; it does not bestow communion but obstructs the way to salvation. This is another persecution and another temptation, through which the subtle enemy advances with hidden devastation to assail the still-fallen, so that lamentation may cease, grief fall silent, the memory of the offense vanish, the groaning of hearts be suppressed, the weeping of eyes be stopped, and the Lord, who has been grievously offended, not be entreated through long and full penance, although it is written: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance.’”

I shall cite no more, since anyone may see Cyprian’s position with his own eyes in those splendid letters he wrote concerning the cause of the lapsed to the clergy, the people, the confessors, and even the lapsed themselves. No less evangelical vigor shines forth in the letters of the Roman confessors, and especially in the distinguished Letter of the Roman Clergy (XXXI among Cyprian’s letters), which, as we learn from Cyprian’s Epistle LII, was sent throughout the whole world:

> “For far be it from the Roman Church,” they say, “to abandon its vigor through such profane laxity, and, with the majesty of faith overthrown, to dissolve the sinews of severity, so that, while the ruins of our overthrown brethren not only still lie prostrate but continue to fall, remedies of communion, hastily administered and certain to be of no benefit, should be supplied, and through false mercy new wounds should be impressed upon the old wounds of transgression, so that even penance is snatched away from the wretched to their greater ruin. For where can the medicine of indulgence be effective if the physician himself, cutting short penance, indulges the dangers; if he merely covers the wound and does not allow the remedies requiring time to form a scar? This is not to heal but, if we wish to speak the truth, to kill.”

So great was Cyprian’s constancy in this matter that nothing could bend him: neither the certificates of the martyrs, to which he nevertheless attached no small weight; nor the danger threatening from wicked presbyters; nor the disturbances stirred up by them, since in certain cities of the province [Col. 0045] of Carthage the multitude had attacked their rulers, and at Carthage some turbulent men, inflamed as though by torches by a letter of the confessors, had begun to blaze up more fiercely and to extort the peace granted to them. The holy Martyr persisted in what he had previously decreed: that the matter should be preserved intact for the council; and he did not hesitate to exclude from his communion anyone who dared to communicate with the lapsed before that time.

Yet Cyprian must not therefore be thought unduly severe. Nothing was gentler than he, nothing more inclined to indulgence. He took care neither to appear harsh, hard, or inhuman in cherishing the brethren, nor, conversely, to be lax and ready to loosen communion recklessly. He showed the utmost kindness to the lapsed who had written to him in supplication, saying “that they recognized their offense and were doing true penance, and were not hastening recklessly or importunately toward peace.”

> “How greatly I rejoiced for them,” he says (Ep. XXVII), “the Lord is witness, who has deigned to show what servants of such a kind and character deserve from his kindness.”

Cyprian’s gentleness shone forth especially when, as the persecution of Gallus and Volusianus approached, he gathered within the Lord’s camp absolutely all the soldiers of Christ who desired weapons and demanded battle; and with the other bishops he judged that peace should be granted to those who had not withdrawn from the Church of the Lord, but had not ceased to do penance, lament, and beseech the Lord from the first day of their lapse. He describes his gentleness as follows in Epistle LV:

> “I desire,” he says, “that all return to the Church; I desire that all our fellow soldiers be enclosed within Christ’s camp and the dwelling places of God the Father. I remit everything; I overlook much in my zeal and desire to gather the brotherhood together. Even offenses committed against God I do not examine with the full judgment of religion; by remitting offenses more than I ought, I myself almost offend. With ready and complete affection I embrace those who return with penance, confessing their sin through humble and simple satisfaction.”

Cyprian’s entire manner of acting and reasoning attests that the power of binding and loosing was committed by Christ to the bishops, and demonstrates how great the caution and foresight of mind to be employed in this judgment must be. But lest some of his statements be twisted to a worse meaning, I shall attempt briefly to explain them. The holy Martyr says in *On the Dress of Virgins* (p. 173) “that there is no pardon thereafter if you sin once you have begun to know God”; and in Book III of the *Testimonies* (c. 18, p. 314), “that one who has sinned against God cannot be forgiven in the Church.” He proves this from these words of 1 Samuel, chapter 2:

> “If in sinning a man sins against a man, they will pray to the Lord for him. But if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?”

But he himself clearly explains his position in *Exhortation to Martyrdom* (p. 264, c. 4), where he cites the same testimony. From it he proves not that sins committed against God cannot be forgiven, but only that “God does not readily pardon idolaters.” He therefore detracts nothing from the power of binding and loosing and nothing from the judgment of priests; rather, he binds judges to certain laws, so that they do not readily remit what is not readily remitted by God. Hence, when schismatics exempted the lapsed from the burden of penance, he refuted them as follows in *On the Lapsed* (p. 186):

> “Let no one mislead himself; let no one deceive himself. The Lord alone can have mercy. He alone can grant pardon for sins committed against him who bore our sins, who suffered for us, whom God handed over for our sins. Man cannot be greater than God; nor can a servant by his own indulgence remit or pardon what has been committed against the Lord by a graver offense, lest this also be added to the fallen man’s crime, if he does not know that it was foretold: ‘Cursed is the man who places his hope in man.’ The Lord must be entreated; the Lord, who said that he would deny one who denies him, who alone received all judgment from the Father, must be appeased by our satisfaction.”

Just as Cyprian in this passage does not deny that martyrs have great influence with God, but requires a certain measure and discrimination in the certificates they customarily issued, so he attacks only the power which the wicked presbyters arrogated to themselves by fair means or foul. But where the laws prescribed by Christ and the Church are observed, Cyprian teaches that the priest’s judgment is ratified before God. Hence in *On the Lapsed* (p. 191) he exhorts the lapsed to confess their sins “while satisfaction and remission effected through priests is acceptable before God.” Near the end of the same book he teaches that God can “mercifully forgive the penitent who works and prays, and accept whatever the martyrs have requested and the priests have done on behalf of such persons.” Relying on this hope, when the lapsed displayed great ardor for combat as a new persecution approached, he shortened their prescribed period of penance and judged it unlawful (Epistle LIV, p. 77)

> “that the Church should be closed to those who knock, since he who gave the law permitted that things bound on earth should also be bound in heaven, while things might be loosed there which had first been loosed here in the Church.”

In the same sense must be understood Firmilian’s statement (p. 144) that councils are held each year so that bishops may deliberate together about matters of greater importance, and

> “that a remedy may also be sought through penance for brethren who have lapsed and been wounded by the devil after the saving washing—not,” he says, “as though they obtain remission of sins from us, but so that through us they may be turned toward an understanding of their offenses and compelled to make fuller satisfaction to the Lord.”

The holy prelate does not deny the power of remitting sins, which in this very Epistle (p. 148) he claims exclusively for the Catholic Church. Rather, the words just quoted seem to contain a certain barb directed against Stephen, whom Firmilian believed to attribute more than was proper both to ministers and to the observance of the external rite, as though he held that not even heresy interrupted the effect of the sacraments. Since the matter appeared otherwise to Firmilian, he denies that it has been granted to men to remit sins at their own discretion. In a not dissimilar judgment, Origen in *On Prayer* contends that not all sins are to be remitted, or expiated by prayer and sacrifice alone, but that some must be retained—that is, subjected to penance. He refutes those who boasted that they could pardon idolatries and forgive adulteries [Col. 0047] and fornications, as though through their prayer on behalf of those who perpetrated such things, sin unto death were forgiven.

## IX.—WHETHER IN AFRICA BEFORE ST. CYPRIAN COMMUNION WAS DENIED AFTER PENANCE FOR THE GRAVEST CRIMES

But in order that Cyprian’s decrees and those of his colleagues may be judged more readily, the discipline of the African Church must be traced from somewhat farther back, and it must be briefly examined whether, before Cyprian’s age, peace after penance was or was not granted for the gravest crimes, such as idolatry and homicide.

Those who sought the penance they had scorned while in health only when they were in extreme danger were rejected, at least in Africa, during the earliest centuries, as is evident from Cyprian’s Epistle LII (p. 73):

> “And for that reason,” he says, “dearest brother, we have judged that those who do not do penance, and do not attest their sorrow for their offenses with their whole heart and by an open profession of their lamentation, must be altogether barred from the hope of communion and peace if they begin to entreat while in illness and danger, because it is not repentance for their offense but the warning of imminent death that compels them to ask; nor is one worthy to receive consolation in death who did not reflect that he was going to die.”

As regards those who sought penance in good time, no one doubts that certain bishops in Africa before Cyprian decreed that peace should be denied to adulterers. Cyprian himself expressly attests this in Epistle LII (p. 72):

> “And indeed among our predecessors,” he says, “certain bishops here in our province did not think that peace should be given to adulterers, and entirely closed the place of penance against acts of adultery.”

This decree appears to have been issued within the interval that elapsed from Tertullian to Cyprian. For in *On Modesty*, Tertullian attacks the custom of granting peace to adulterers after penance as a common practice of the Catholic Church, and admits that he himself had once thought this way while he remained within the Church:

> “This work, therefore, will also be directed against the Psychics,” he says in chapter 2, “and against my former sharing of their opinion, so that they may all the more cast this up against me as a mark of fickleness.”

The conjecture of learned men that the severe decree mentioned by Cyprian also included idolaters and murderers, whose crime is graver than adultery, does not appear very probable. For it could have happened that in certain places bishops judged that excessive license in adultery should be restrained by heavier penalties, yet did not determine the same concerning idolatry and homicide, especially since care had to be taken that Montanist institutions should not appear to be introduced into the Church. From the hatred with which everyone burned against the severity of this heresy, one might conjecture that the bishops left at least this consolation to penitent adulterers: that they should receive peace at the point of death. But these words of Cyprian, “they entirely closed the place of penance against acts of adultery,” indicate that, just as penance, so also the hope of peace was altogether barred. For why would penance not have been imposed upon those to whom peace was to be given after a year, or perhaps even sooner, if they fell into danger of death; and who, if they recovered from illness, would retain the peace they had once received and thereafter possess the same standing as the other faithful? For in those times persons who had received peace under the pressure of danger retained this benefit when restored to full health and were not compelled to complete the course of penance, as is evident from Cyprian’s Epistle LII.

But concerning adultery and the other gravest sins before the Montanist heresy, and concerning idolatry and homicide after the Montanists themselves, many great difficulties arise, which have given rise to differing opinions. Petavius held in his notes on Epiphanius (p. 231) that in the first centuries those guilty of the gravest crimes were barred from communion and were never restored to the Church, whether in health or dying; and that this most severe discipline prevailed from apostolic times almost to the age of Tertullian, but was relaxed somewhat by the pontiff Zephyrinus as far as adultery was concerned, and made greater advances toward leniency in Cyprian’s time. Morinus, Book IX of *On Penance*, chapter 20, and Noël Alexandre, Dissertation VII on the history of the third century, adopted an entirely different position. They maintain that in those first centuries peace was granted to the lapsed after they had completed penance, and was not denied to those dying during the course of penance.

What is more surprising amid this diversity of opinions is that both sides understand in the same sense a notable passage of Tertullian which is the hinge of the whole controversy. They agree that Tertullian, when he says in *On Modesty*, chapter 5, “You indeed condemn the idolater and the murderer once for all, but you except the adulterer from their midst?” and in chapter 12, “Hence it is that peace is restored by the churches neither to idolatry nor to bloodshed,” expressly teaches that among Catholics peace is denied for idolatry and homicide. But Petavius does not suspect that Tertullian was lying about a matter exposed to everyone’s eyes; Morinus and Alexandre do not hesitate to accuse him of wicked slander and a rank falsehood. I cannot wholly agree with either side: neither with Petavius, who attributes excessive severity to the first centuries, nor with Morinus and Alexandre, who brand Tertullian as a liar. I shall therefore undertake to demonstrate that those three gravest sins—idolatry, homicide, and adultery—were not excluded from penance and peace in the ancient Church, and that Tertullian did not ascribe a different doctrine to Catholics.

The first consideration, and one of no slight weight, is supplied by Tertullian himself, whose book *On Repentance*, chapter 4, contains these words: “Therefore, for all sins,” he says, “whether committed in the flesh or in the spirit, in deed or in intention, he who appointed punishment through judgment has likewise promised pardon through repentance.” He expressly declares in chapter 7 that idolaters are not excluded from this benefit: “And so,” he says, “the enemy watches, attacks, and lays siege, in the hope that he may strike the eyes with carnal desire, entangle the mind with worldly allurements, overthrow faith through fear of earthly power, or turn it from the sure path by perverse traditions: he never lacks stumbling blocks or temptations. God, therefore, foreseeing these poisons of his, although the door of forgiveness had been closed and the bar of baptism drawn across it, permitted something still to remain open. He placed a second repentance in the vestibule, to open the door to those who knock.” [Col. 0049] Thus Tertullian taught while he was still among the Catholics. After becoming a Montanist he taught otherwise, but the Catholics resisted him; he introduces them as speaking thus in *On Modesty*, chapter 2: “But God, they say, is good and supremely good, merciful and compassionate and abounding in mercy, which he prefers to every sacrifice, valuing not so much the death of the sinner as repentance, the Savior of all and especially of the faithful. Accordingly, the children of God must also be merciful, forgiving one another as Christ forgave us, and not judging, lest we be judged.”

The same Tertullian divides sins “between two outcomes” and holds that “some are remissible, others irremissible”; but he admits that the Catholics oppose him in this matter and recognize no sin whatsoever as irremissible: “But first,” he says in chapter 3, “I shall dispose of the objection raised on the other side against that kind of repentance which we have just defined as incapable of obtaining pardon. For if, they say, any repentance is without pardon, then you ought not to undertake it at all; for nothing should be done in vain. But repentance will be undertaken in vain if it is without pardon. Yet all repentance must be undertaken; therefore, let all repentance obtain pardon, lest it be undertaken in vain, since it ought not to be undertaken if it is undertaken in vain. But it will be undertaken in vain if it is without pardon.”

These testimonies of Tertullian, however, must be understood not merely of Africa but of all the churches attacked by the defender of the Montanists. For this discipline prevailed everywhere and had prevailed during the first two centuries, as may be seen from the second book of Hermas, *Mandate* 4, and especially from what Clement, in Eusebius, book III, chapter 23, relates concerning Saint John the Evangelist. Nor should we omit the letter of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, to the churches of Amastris and the other churches of Pontus, in which he instructed them to receive kindly those returning from any lapse or sin, or even from heretical depravity, as Eusebius attests in book IV, chapter 23.

2. What Petavius says is altogether improbable: that Zephyrinus relaxed something of the severity of the ancient discipline with respect to adultery, and that afterward, in Cyprian’s time, still greater advances were made toward leniency. This distribution among periods does not fit the facts. For adultery, which in Tertullian’s time, with the assent of all Catholics, obtained peace, as we have just seen, was excluded from this benefit in some churches under Cyprian’s predecessors. How, then, can the discipline be said to have been mitigated at that time, when it had acquired new increments of severity?

3. If it were permissible to draw from Tertullian’s words the conclusion Petavius drew, it would follow that in the Catholic Church peace was mercilessly denied not only to murderers and idolaters, but also to those who after receiving the faith had fallen into heresy, or who had yielded after being overcome amid tortures. For Tertullian speaks thus of heretics in chapter 13: “But if the sin of Hymenaeus and Alexander is irremissible both in this age and in the age to come—namely, blasphemy—then surely the Apostle would not, contrary to the Lord’s limit, have delivered them to Satan in the hope of pardon, since they had already plunged from faith into blasphemy; hence he also pronounced them shipwrecked with respect to faith, as not possessing the refuge of the ship that is the Church. For pardon is denied to those who, departing from faith, have denied it in blasphemy.” And in the final chapter he says of those overcome by torture: “Whatever authority,” he says, “whatever principle restores ecclesiastical peace to the adulterer and fornicator, must likewise come to the aid of the penitent murderer and idolater, and certainly of the denier—especially of one whom cruelty struck down when he had struggled against tortures in the battle of confession. Otherwise, it is unworthy of God and of his mercy, which prefers a sinner’s repentance to his death, that those who fell through copulation should return to the Church more easily than those who fell through combat. The indignity compels us to ask: will you recall bodies that have been defiled rather than bodies that have been bloodied? Which repentance is more pitiful: that which prostrates flesh that has been titillated, or flesh that has been torn?”

In these passages Tertullian appears at first sight to argue as though he agreed with the Catholics that repentance ought to be granted neither to those who had departed from the faith into heresy nor to those who had yielded after struggling against tortures. But such severity is so alien to the customs of the ancient Church that no one can ascribe it to her. In his letter to Quintus, Cyprian acknowledges that returning heretics who had been baptized in the Church ought to receive the laying on of hands for repentance, and he does not hesitate to trace the origin of this custom back to the very infancy of the Church. As for those whose body, but not their resolve, had failed under pain, and who sought pardon not with tears but with blood and wounds, the humanity customarily shown to them in the Church may be seen both from Cyprian’s book *On the Lapsed*, p. 185, and from his Letter LIII.

What, then, are we to conclude about Tertullian? He certainly goes wholly astray in Montanus’s camp and contradicts himself; nevertheless, he never raves without some glimmer of intelligence. Nor could I believe that he had become so senseless as to expose himself to everyone’s ridicule through a manifest falsehood. Therefore, the assertion, “Neither to idolatry nor to bloodshed is peace restored by the churches,” must be understood not of the Catholic churches but of those of the Montanists. Tertullian habitually claims the name “Church” for Montanus’s sect by a sort of proprietary right, as when he calls it the “Church of the Spirit,” the “Church constituted in three,” in chapter 21; or when he says in chapter 10: “I would yield to you if the writing of the *Shepherd*, which alone loves adulterers, had deserved to be included among the divine instruments; if it had not been judged apocryphal and false by every council of churches, including your own.” He seems to consider that he shows the Catholics considerable honor if he assigns second place to their churches after Montanus’s sect.

I shall offer another example from chapter 7, where he proves that the parables of the sheep and the drachma do not apply to an adulterer or fornicator, because “as soon as he has been exposed, the man is immediately expelled from the Church; he neither remains in it nor brings joy to the Church that finds him, but grief; nor does she summon neighboring women to congratulate her, but the neighboring brotherhoods to share her sorrow.” Take care not to suppose that the Church’s custom is being described, although Tertullian speaks in general terms. These things do not savor of the Church’s charity, but of the inhumanity of the Montanists, who kept the twice-married outside and “fixed the same boundary at the threshold for adulterers and fornicators also, who would shed fruitless tears for peace and receive nothing further from the Church than the public disclosure of their disgrace.” [Col. 0051] It is clear that in passages of this kind Montanus’s church, not Christ’s Church, must be understood.

Tertullian himself is witness to the great humanity with which those seeking repentance were customarily received in the Catholic Church: “And you indeed,” he says in chapter 13, “when bringing an adulterer’s repentance into the Church to entreat the brotherhood, place him in their midst, clad in haircloth and covered with ashes, fashioned into a spectacle of disgrace and horror, grasping everyone’s garments, licking everyone’s footprints, clasping everyone’s knees; and over this abasement of the man you preach, with every inducement to mercy at your command, as a good shepherd and blessed pope; and in the parable of the sheep you seek your goats, lest your sheep again leap out of the Church, as though thereafter what was not permissible even once had become permissible.” Therefore, just as Tertullian is speaking of Montanus’s church when he says that an adulterer or fornicator, as soon as he is exposed, is expelled from the Church, so his statement that peace is restored by the churches neither to idolatry nor to bloodshed must also be referred to the Montanist synagogues. The statement in chapter 13 must be interpreted in the same way: “For pardon is denied to those who, departing from faith, have denied it in blasphemy.” This severity belonged to the Montanists, not to the Catholics whom Tertullian himself attacks in chapter 19 because they granted pardon to those who had fallen into heresy “after living faith.”

But another difficulty remains to be resolved: why does Tertullian argue in this controversy as though his adversaries barred all hope of pardon to idolaters and murderers, and seize upon this as an argument for proving that adulterers and fornicators must be treated in the same way? “What,” he says in chapter 5, “does your most indulgent and humane discipline do? Either you must be this to all of them—for blessed are the peacemakers—or, if not to all, you must be ours. You condemn the idolater and murderer once and for all, but select the adulterer from their midst—the idolater’s successor, the murderer’s predecessor, and the associate of both? This is partiality: you have passed over the more pitiable forms of repentance.” And in chapter 6: “You will therefore grant pardon to idolatry also, and to every apostate . . .; you will also communicate with the murderer.” In chapter 19 he cites John’s words: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, so as to forgive them for us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness”; then adds: “Surely not from impurity? Or, if that is the meaning, then also from idolatry.” To these add what we quoted above from the final chapter: “Whatever authority, whatever principle restores ecclesiastical peace to the adulterer and fornicator must likewise come to the aid of penitent idolaters and murderers.”

For those familiar with Tertullian’s character and who have examined it closely, however, access to his meaning will be easy. He had undertaken to defend precisely what in the Montanist cause was most exposed and vulnerable to his adversaries’ weapons. Nothing brought greater odium upon that sect than its keeping adulterers, fornicators, and the twice-married outside, leaving them no hope of peace even at their last breath. What course, then, will Tertullian pursue to extricate himself from this troublesome and difficult position? He establishes two classes of sins. “Some,” he says in chapter 2, “will be remissible, others irremissible, since no one doubts that some deserve correction, others condemnation. Every offense is erased either by pardon or by punishment: pardon results from correction, punishment from condemnation.”

He then uses John’s authority, distinguishing certain sins as not unto death and others as unto death. “According to this distinction between offenses,” he says, “the condition of repentance is likewise differentiated. One kind will be capable of obtaining pardon, namely in the case of a remissible offense; another will in no way be capable of obtaining it, namely in the case of an irremissible offense.” Having laid down this principle, he declares that his purpose is “to examine specifically the status of adultery and fornication, and to which class of offenses they ought to be assigned.” But because he knew that the Catholics rejected this distinction between sins, he thinks that they must briefly be refuted before he argues that adultery is to be counted among sins that can never be forgiven: “But first,” he says, “I shall dispose of the objection raised on the other side against that kind of repentance which we have just defined as incapable of obtaining pardon. For if, they say, any repentance is without pardon, then you ought not to undertake it at all. Nothing should be done in vain. But repentance will be undertaken in vain if it is without pardon. Yet all repentance must be undertaken. Therefore, let all repentance obtain pardon, lest it be undertaken in vain, since it ought not to be undertaken if it is undertaken in vain. But it will be undertaken in vain if it is without pardon.”

Tertullian does not refute this Catholic argument very successfully. Nevertheless, after he imagines that he has overthrown it with the strongest arguments, he then concentrates solely upon proving that adultery and fornication belong to that class, as though it had now been established as a most certain principle that some sins are irremissible. Accordingly, when he says, “You condemn idolatry and murder once and for all,” he is not accusing the Catholics of actually denying peace to those sins while treating adulterers more liberally. Rather, he presses the adversary whom he imagines he has defeated and compelled to acknowledge that certain graver sins—such as idolatry, murder, and heresy after reception of the faith—ought not to be forgiven. Hence Tertullian, in conformity with his established division of sins, contends that adultery, as closely akin to murder and idolatry, must be excluded from the hope of pardon; or else, if adulterers are treated more leniently, murderers and idolaters ought to enjoy the same right. From these considerations I believe it becomes clear that the same humanity was available to penitents in Africa as in the other churches; far from its being permissible to infer from these testimonies of Tertullian, as very learned men have done, that other churches also treated the lapsed more severely.

## X.—WHETHER A NEW DISCIPLINE WAS INTRODUCED UNDER ST. CYPRIAN, WITH THE FORMER SEVERITY RETAINED ONLY AGAINST APOSTATES AND DESERTERS

[Col. 0051]

Now that we have elucidated Tertullian’s testimonies as best we could, the investigation of Cyprian’s position will be easier and less encumbered. Tertullian had misled many, causing them also to misunderstand Cyprian’s meaning. Three questions present themselves for examination: 1. whether the discipline was mitigated under Cyprian, with its former severity retained only against apostates and deserters; [Col. 0053] 2. whether peace was denied to the lapsed who were dying during the course of their repentance unless they had received certificates from the martyrs; 3. whether, at least, repentance was not imposed upon those who had sacrificed until death, and communion granted only at the point of death.

With respect to the change in discipline, Albaspinaeus, book II of the *Observations*, believes that peace began under Cyprian to be granted for idolatry and other most serious crimes, but in such a way that the ancient severity remained in force against apostates and deserters. The most learned bishop relies not only upon Tertullian’s testimonies, but also adduces as an argument the fact that neither Cyprian nor the Roman clergy dared determine anything concerning the lapsed, but waited for the authority of a council. He also appeals to Cyprian’s statement that he had “yielded to the necessity of the times” and feared suspicion of excessive leniency because “he had thought that peace should be granted to those who had stained their conscience with certificates or committed abominable sacrifices” (Letter LII, p. 67). Albaspinaeus therefore contends that there would not have been such anxious deliberation about this matter if precedents for granting peace had existed in earlier persecutions; nor would Cyprian have allowed himself to describe as a relaxation on his part something established by the authority of his predecessors. Petavius’s position, as we saw above, is not dissimilar.

But a preconceived opinion derived from Tertullian’s testimonies led that learned author into error. There is no trace of novelty in this matter in Cyprian, than whom no one was more tenacious in preserving the ancient discipline. The holy martyr observes in Letter LII (p. 62) that some of his predecessors had denied peace to adulterers and “entirely closed the place of repentance” to them; but he indicates clearly enough both that this law had been established by only a few bishops and had not existed before them, and that in his own age it had already been rescinded and abrogated. Neither he nor anyone else in Africa recalled that all hope of peace had been barred to those who fell in the earlier persecutions.

When certain presbyters gave communion to the lapsed before they had performed repentance, Cyprian abhorred their action and declared that they had acted contrary to the Gospel. Yet he reproves them only because they had granted it “before repentance had been performed,” “when it was necessary to reach these things in due order.” In all the letters he wrote concerning the lapsed, and in his book *On the Lapsed*, you will find nothing whatsoever by which the lapsed are left in doubt concerning peace, provided that they perform repentance proportionate to their sins. Rather, Cyprian lays it down as an absolutely certain principle that God “can mercifully forgive one who repents, labors, and prays, and can accept whatever the martyrs have requested and the priests have done on behalf of such persons” (p. 193). In the same book (p. 190) he urges “each individual to confess his sin while satisfaction and remission effected through the priests are acceptable.”

Similarly, the Roman clergy (in Letter XXXI among Cyprian’s correspondence), while rightly reproving “over-hasty remedies of communion, which would certainly do no good,” do not disapprove of the lapsed person’s desire for peace, provided “they do indeed knock upon the doors, but certainly do not break them down, and approach the threshold of the Church, but certainly do not leap over it.” These words also deserve notice: “A modest request, a reverent petition, necessary humility, and active patience will greatly benefit them.”

It was a very ancient custom in the Church for the recommendation of martyrs to have force in shortening the period of repentance imposed upon the lapsed. We have Tertullian as a witness to this custom in his book *To the Martyrs* and in *On Modesty*. Hence Cyprian likewise says: “In the past,” he says in Letter XI, “under our predecessors, it was always done that deacons visiting the prison guided the martyrs’ wishes by their counsels and by the precepts of Scripture.” To this may be added the agreement of all the churches, mentioned by Cyprian in Letters LII, LXVII, and LXVIII, in rejecting Novatian, whose own hand convicted him of depraved innovation. For, as Cyprian testifies in Letter LII, Novatian had written, and had read aloud in his own voice, a letter of the Roman clergy which provided “that peace should be given to the lapsed who were ill and at the point of death.” The agreement of the churches had likewise been conspicuous in rejecting the Montanists.

What led Cyprian and the Roman clergy to preserve the entire matter for decision by a council, therefore, was not the opinion attributed to them, but their distrust of their own powers in a case of this kind, which, as Cyprian says in Letter XIV, “was the concern not of a few persons, nor of one church or a single province, but of the whole world.” The circumstances and intentions of individuals had to be examined, and the various degrees of sin had each to be weighed according to its own measure. Such an examination would have been entirely useless if all who had sacrificed had, without distinction, been excluded from the hope of pardon.

Moreover, during the Decian persecution the number of the lapsed was so great, and those who, as Cyprian says in *On the Lapsed* (p. 183), betrayed their faith at the very first words of the threatening enemy, voluntarily ran to the forum, and urged one another to destruction inflicted such disgrace upon the Christian name, that it could reasonably have been debated whether something more severe than in earlier persecutions should be decreed against persons of this kind. Nevertheless, examples of leniency rather than severity appear to have been established at the Council of Carthage. For, as we shall presently see, the *libellatici*—those who had procured certificates—who had already performed repentance were admitted at the council itself; full repentance was imposed upon those who had sacrificed, yet in such a way that they would not be deprived of peace if they fell into a dangerous illness before the appointed period of repentance had elapsed. Nothing more lenient could have been enacted in those times.

It was therefore possible for Cyprian to defend the council’s leniency when Antonianus criticized it, although no new discipline had been introduced at that council. Cyprian declares that he acted in both instances only after long and carefully weighed consideration: he employed severity while the persecution was in force, and indulgence once peace had been restored. Yet he does not say that his severity consisted in decreeing that peace must be denied altogether to the lapsed, but in resisting those who sought it by every lawful and unlawful means, and in threatening excommunication if anyone communicated with them without his authorization.
