Likewise, with respect to the leniency that followed, he denies that ecclesiastical laws were violated; rather, he contends that provision was made lest the lapsed either fail through despair “or, conversely, the evangelical censure be relaxed so that they might rashly leap into communion.” In a word, he denies that either he or Cornelius did anything outside the precedents of their forebears: “For just as [Col. 0055] our predecessors often did,” he says (p. 69), “in gathering our brethren, our most beloved brother Cornelius yielded to necessity.”

Albaspinaeus, and Gotofredus after him (*Codex Theodosianus*, book XVI, p. 210), infer that Cyprian sometimes retained the former severity from these words of Letter LII: “But apostates and deserters, or adversaries and enemies and those who scatter Christ’s Church, cannot, according to the Apostle, be admitted to the peace of the Church even if they have been killed outside for the Name, since they retained neither the Spirit nor the unity of the Church.”

To explain this testimony of Cyprian, it must be observed, first, that “apostates and deserters” does not mean, as Albaspinaeus and Gotofredus think, those who, having been Christians, became pagans or Jews, but those who enrolled themselves in the schism of Felicissimus.

Second, we must recall what we said above: peace was denied at the risk of death to those who had despised repentance while healthy, because it reasonably appeared doubtful whether they were recovering their senses with a sincere disposition. What had been decreed concerning persons of that kind ought likewise to be observed in the case of several others whose wickedness appeared either incurable or dangerous to the rest of the sheep. Thus, when many, having recognized the wickedness of Felicissimus, returned and knocked at the Church, Cyprian anxiously weighed and carefully examined “who ought to be received and admitted into the Church. For some,” he says in Letter LV, p. 87, “are so obstructed either by their crimes or by the brethren’s stubborn and resolute opposition that they cannot possibly be received without scandal and danger to many.”

Cyprian’s threats in Letter XXXVIII seem to refer to these people, where he speaks as follows: “But let whoever allies himself with his conspiracy and faction know that he will not communicate with us in the Church, since he has voluntarily preferred to separate himself from the Church.” And in Letter XL: “But if anyone, refusing to repent and make satisfaction to God, should go over to the party of Felicissimus and his satellites and join himself to their heretical faction, let him know that he will afterward be unable to return to the Church and communicate with the bishops and the people of Christ.”

Cyprian did not put these threats entirely into effect. For he himself testifies in Letter LV that he received many who returned from the schism, and that the people were accustomed to rejoice and be glad when “those who could be tolerated and were less blameworthy” returned. Indeed, he sometimes persuaded, or even compelled, the people to receive some of those who were incorrigible and insolent; and one or another who was received through Cyprian’s indulgence, despite the people’s resistance and opposition, proved worse than before.

With a similar judgment, Cyprian and several other bishops decreed as follows concerning virgins who had been found with men in the same bed: “But if they obstinately persist and do not separate from one another, let them know that with this unchaste obstinacy of theirs they can never be admitted by us into the Church, lest through their sins they begin to furnish others with an example leading to ruin.” Such obstinate sinners, like pertinacious schismatics, were rightly denied not only pardon but even entry into the church. Yet if they had returned with the requisite signs of a converted heart and had knocked long and earnestly at the Church’s doors, there is no doubt that Cyprian would have received them into his paternal embrace and admitted them to repentance. Felicissimus and his principal followers, therefore, since they were men prepared for every crime, could have had every return to the Church barred to them by Cyprian without his departing from the Church’s rules. Nor should this be regarded as some vestige of a discipline observed before Cyprian against all persons guilty of graver crimes.

Third, the passage from Cyprian adduced by Albaspinaeus does not say that apostates and deserters cannot be admitted to the Church’s peace even if, after abandoning schism, they shed their blood for Christ. It says only that martyrdom outside the Church can profit them nothing toward obtaining peace, because “they retained neither the Spirit nor the unity of the Church”—a point Cyprian frequently emphasizes elsewhere. He contrasts deserters of this kind with the other lapsed who were performing repentance within the Church and whom the Lord would find inside when he appeared to judge the world.

## XI.—WHETHER ST. CYPRIAN DENIED PEACE TO THE LAPSED WHO WERE DYING DURING THE COURSE OF REPENTANCE, EXCEPTING ONLY THOSE WHO HAD RECEIVED CERTIFICATES FROM THE MARTYRS

[Col. 0055]

Having proved that Cyprian did nothing new when he granted peace to the penitent lapsed, we must next inquire whether he denied communion to those who became dangerously ill before completing their repentance, unless they had received certificates from the martyrs. Petavius contends that Cyprian granted peace only to those who had received certificates from the martyrs, and did not grant it to the rest even when they were in immediate danger of death; otherwise, there would have been no distinction between the latter and the former, who nevertheless ought to have enjoyed some better condition.

But the holy martyr’s own words must be presented: “Since, however,” he says in Letter XII, “I see that there is not yet an opportunity for me to come to you, and that summer has already begun, a season beset by frequent and serious illnesses, I think provision must be made for our brethren. Thus, those who have received certificates from the martyrs and can be helped before God by their prerogative, if they are overtaken by some ailment and danger of illness, may, without awaiting our presence, make confession (*exomologesis*) of their sin before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, even before a deacon, so that, after hands have been laid upon them for repentance, they may go to the Lord in peace—the peace which the martyrs expressed the desire should be given to them in the letters they sent to us.”

Petavius wrongly infers from this testimony that peace was denied to those who possessed no certificates.

First, who could suppose Cyprian so forgetful of equity that he would make such benevolent provision for those who evaded repentance and strove “by bold importunity and violent assault to extort peace,” “so as meanwhile to mitigate their violence by whatever means” (Letter XV), yet permit fervent penitents, who preferred to submit themselves to their bishop’s judgment rather than evade repentance, to die without peace and communion?

Second, [Col. 0057] while Cyprian was absent, the Roman clergy had advised the clergy of Carthage “that aid should be given to those who, having been overtaken by illness after their lapse, were penitent and desired communion” (Letters III and XV). Cyprian not only did not disapprove of this counsel, but in Letter XV also declares that he thought he “must abide by” their “judgment as well, lest our action,” he says, “which ought to be united and to agree in all things, should differ in any respect.” But how immeasurably Cyprian’s manner of acting would have differed from that of the Romans if, after they had advised that peace should be given to all who were truly penitent, Cyprian had employed indulgence and humanity only toward those who had added the evasion of repentance and the disturbance of the Church to their sin!

Third, Cyprian indicates with sufficient clarity in Letter XIII that those supported not by certificates but by works of repentance had a far stronger right to be given peace when dangerously ill. “Also cherish by your presence,” he says, “the remaining part of the people who have lapsed, and revive them by your consolation, so that they may not fall away from faith and from the Lord’s mercy. For those who are meek and humble and who, truly performing repentance, persevere in good works will not be abandoned by the Lord’s aid and assistance, so that provision may be made for them also by the divine remedy.”

He therefore wishes penitents of this kind to be persuaded that “provision will be made for them also by the divine remedy.” He grants them this as a consolation consistent with the Church’s laws and requiring no new decrees. For Cyprian did not deliberately write Letter XIII in order to provide for those lapsed persons for whom both the Church’s custom and the admonitions of the Roman clergy had already made sufficient provision, but to restrain the tumult of those whose complaints were setting the church of Carthage ablaze.

I believe this also to be the reason why Cyprian, in Letter XIV, while confirming what he had decreed in Letter XIII, says nothing expressly about granting peace in extreme danger to true penitents. After speaking of those who had received certificates from the martyrs, he adds: “But let the rest, who, having received no certificate from the martyrs, are arousing resentment—since this is the concern not of a few persons, nor of one church or one province, but of the whole world—await, under the Lord’s protection, the public peace of the Church herself.”

Cyprian certainly does not decree by this that peace at death should be denied to true penitents. He does not retract what he had established in the preceding letter, but rather confirms it when he says that he had “written fully on this matter in his most recent letter.” Instead, he restrains the haste of certain persons who were seeking communion before peace had been restored to the Church and before they were afflicted by grave illness. He commands these to wait until peace is restored to the Church, but he does not deny peace at death. Nor does he rebuke them because they did not wish to be barred from communion at death, but because they sought it before the exiles’ return and wished “to anticipate the confessors themselves.”

Petavius objects, however, that those who had received certificates ought to have enjoyed a better condition than those who had not; but if peace was granted to everyone, no distinction whatsoever existed between the two groups. Tillemont believes that Cyprian acted out of a certain ingenious charity, so that while he appeared to grant some special favor in honor of the martyrs, he nevertheless granted nothing special; and while promising peace only to those who possessed certificates, he excluded no one whatsoever from this indulgence, since the martyrs were so lavish with certificates that their generosity was open to all.

But if Cyprian had employed the accommodation which Tillemont supposes him to have used, and had tacitly exhorted all the lapsed to equip themselves with the protection of certificates, would he shortly afterward have burned with such indignation against Lucianus, who dared to grant to all the lapsed what Cyprian had already granted to very many? Moreover, Cyprian would most unjustly have exposed true penitents to the danger of dying deprived of peace. For it was unlikely that those who had hitherto been so timid and modest would thereafter become bolder in requesting certificates, or that the confessors themselves would not become more cautious in granting them after Cyprian had reproved their excessive facility.

Morinus interprets Cyprian as follows: Since the law was that the dying who had not done penance while in good health should not obtain peace, the learned author thinks that Cyprian decreed that, in the case of those who had received certificates from the martyrs, the severity of the law should not be observed, and that, in honor of the martyrs, peace should be granted to those who, without this support, would have sought it in vain. But this interpretation agrees neither with Cyprian’s words nor with his intention. First, Cyprian expressly requires that those who received certificates from the martyrs should be able “to be helped before the Lord in respect of their offenses by the martyrs’ privilege and assistance.” Now, in these letters and in the book *On the Lapsed*, he firmly maintains and carefully defends the position that the martyrs’ commendation does not benefit the lapsed if they refuse to do penance. Accordingly, if, after so many admonitions from Cyprian and the presbyters, the lapsed had persisted in their obstinate resolve not to do penance, would Cyprian have regarded them as fit to be helped before the Lord by the assistance of the martyrs? Furthermore, if he decreed peace for everyone who possessed certificates, whether they had done penance or not, what need was there to make a selection and to require, as a condition, that they be capable of being helped by the martyrs’ assistance? Cyprian therefore does not exempt the lapsed from the burden of penance; rather, he gently and mildly exhorts them to penance by offering peace to the dying, provided that they can be helped by the merits of the martyrs. Hence, in Epistle XIV, he praises the presbyters and deacons because they had exhorted the lapsed to penance and patience, and he declares that penance is done by the person who, meek and patient in accordance with the divine precepts and obedient to God’s priests, wins the Lord’s favor by his acts of service and righteous works. Yet he appears to concede this much to the merits of the martyrs: that, for lapsed persons who have not yet been purified by such penance as would of itself obtain peace at the point of death, the commendation of the martyrs should serve as support. Nor should this indulgence be regarded as slight, if the severity of those times is considered. For although peace was customarily given to penitents who were dangerously ill, it was nevertheless not granted without discrimination and judgment. Hence the Roman clergy, after deliberating on the matter with several bishops, judged that, “in the case of those whose imminent departure at the end of life permits no delay, once penance has been performed and abhorrence of their deeds repeatedly professed, [Col. 0059] if by tears, groans, and weeping they have manifested the signs of a sorrowful and truly penitent heart, and when, humanly speaking, no hope of life remains, only then should aid be given cautiously and carefully,” etc. (Epistle XXXI). Cyprian himself, in Epistle XIII, promises peace only to those “who, meek and humble and truly doing penance, have persevered in good works.” From this it can be seen how far Cyprian extends mildness and indulgence. Those for whom he wished provision to be made in Epistles XIII and XIV had either performed penance sluggishly or had even added to their most serious offense the further offense of avoiding penance and embroiling the Church in dissensions and complaints. By these deeds they had deserved to be denied peace when dying, even if they had begun penance shortly before their illness. Therefore the holy martyr grants to the former that whatever their penance lacked for obtaining peace should be supplied by the merits of the martyrs. He likewise makes provision for the latter and, in order to suppress the disturbance, treats them indulgently: provided that they relinquish their aversion to the remedies of penance, he commands the presbyters to ratify what, taken by itself, would appear incomplete and merely begun, once it has been made good by the merits of the martyrs.

## XII.—WHETHER THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE IMPOSED PENANCE UPON THOSE WHO HAD SACRIFICED FOR THE WHOLE PERIOD OF THEIR LIVES

Another question must now be examined: whether, at least in Cyprian’s time, penance for more serious sins was imposed for the whole period of life, with communion deferred until the very point of death. The matter can be decided from the custom then in force: those who had received peace during a grave illness, if restored to health, did not complete the remaining period of penance but possessed the same standing as the other faithful. This is evident from Cyprian’s words in Epistle LII (p. 69):

> “For if any,” he says, “are overtaken by illnesses, assistance is given to them, as was resolved. Yet after assistance has been given and peace granted to those in danger, they cannot be choked or crushed by us, or driven by our force and hand to the end of death, as though, since peace is granted to the dying, those who have received peace must necessarily die. Rather, the proof of divine goodness and paternal mildness appears chiefly in this: those who receive the pledge of life in the peace that has been granted are also preserved for life by that granted peace. And therefore, if, after peace has been received, a reprieve is granted by God, no one ought to make this a charge against the priests, since it was once resolved that assistance should be given to the brethren at the end.”

So great a degree of mildness is inconsistent with penance imposed for the whole period of life. Otherwise it would frequently have happened in practice that those who, after one or two years of penance, received communion during a grave illness would, upon recovering from the illness, have already completed their course of penance, while others in the same circumstances, and perhaps guilty of an even lighter offense, still had thirty or forty years to run. The bishops’ scrutiny in judging, and their consideration and foresight regarding every circumstance, were surely too great for them not to have avoided so serious an inequity. Nevertheless, we must consider what was decreed on this subject by the Council of Carthage, at which the case of the lapsed was adjudicated shortly after Cyprian’s return.

The holy martyr explains the decree of this council as follows in Epistle LII (p. 71):

> “And therefore,” he says, “it was resolved, after the cases of individuals had been examined, that the *Libellatici* [those who had obtained certificates] should for the present be admitted, and that assistance should be given at the end to those who had sacrificed.”

Scholars have not held a single opinion concerning this canon. The author of the *Critical Observations on the Library of Ecclesiastical Writers* denies that the *Libellatici* were immediately admitted to peace at the council itself. He sets this distinction between them and those who had sacrificed: the latter were assigned to penance for their whole lives, whereas the former were admitted “for the present,” that is, after a determinate period of penance had been completed. The author of the *Library* himself holds the same view concerning those who had sacrificed, although he thinks that peace was granted to the *Libellatici* at the council itself. Tillemont agrees with him concerning the *Libellatici* and attacks his critic; but he refutes at greater length what both had taken as certain—that those who had sacrificed had been assigned no limit to their penance other than the end of life. Tillemont’s position seems preferable on many grounds. Above all, it must be observed that these two questions, concerning the *Libellatici* and those who had sacrificed, are so closely connected that whatever is said about either must be regarded as applying to both. For if the *Libellatici* were restored to communion with great clemency immediately at the council itself, it is improbable that those who had sacrificed were relegated to the final crisis of life. Conversely, if the words “it was resolved that assistance should be given at the end to those who had sacrificed” do not prohibit peace from being given before life’s end, but instead decree that it should be granted to those who became dangerously ill within the prescribed period, it will be evident that the *Libellatici*, whose guilt was much lighter, were not assigned penance at the council but were granted communion. Otherwise it would have been decreed that assistance should likewise be given to them at the end.

As regards the *Libellatici*, it is clear that the meaning of the words “it was resolved that the *Libellatici* should for the present be admitted” is that the *Libellatici* were meanwhile admitted to peace while those who had sacrificed performed penance—that is, by the same decree peace was appointed for the *Libellatici* and penance for those who had sacrificed. Hence Cyprian says in Epistle LIV that it was decreed at this council, concerning those who had sacrificed, that they should perform full penance for a long time; but he does not include the *Libellatici* under the same decree. In the following year, when, in view of the approaching persecution, he resolved to grant communion to those who had performed penance from the first day of their lapse, this indulgence concerned only those who had sacrificed and upon whom full penance had been imposed. There is no mention of the *Libellatici*, although they above all ought to have shared in this indulgence if they had not already obtained it at the council. Indeed, it is clear from Epistle LII that Cyprian communicated with the *Libellatici* after the council. For Cyprian’s statement that he “had not previously communicated with anyone among the lapsed” while the persecution raged, “but afterward yielded to the necessity of the times,” cannot refer to those who had sacrificed—for penance had been imposed upon them—but only to the *Libellatici*. [Col. 0061] And when this communion was made a ground of odium by Novatian, Cyprian refuted him as follows in the same epistle:

> “Or if,” he says, “he has appointed himself the examiner and judge of heart and reins, let him judge equally in every case; and since he knows that it is written, ‘Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you,’ let him separate swindlers and adulterers from his side and company, since the case of the adulterer is much graver and worse than that of the *Libellaticus*, for the latter sinned under necessity, the former voluntarily.”

Novatian was therefore attacking the Catholic bishops because they communicated with the *Libellatici*. Yet peace was not granted at the council to all the *Libellatici*, but only to those who had performed penance. Consequently, the author of the *Observations on the Library* labors in vain to prove at length what no one denies: that the offense of obtaining a certificate was not forgiven without penance.

The second part of the decree is easily clarified. First, the phrase “assistance should be given at the end to those who had sacrificed” indicates not that penance was to be prolonged until the last breath, but that it was to be terminated in the event of grave illness; nor was it decreed as a penalty but as a benefit, since Cyprian, in Epistle LII, removes from this decree any suspicion of excessive leniency and explains why the bishops had descended to this degree of mildness and indulgence. Secondly, he reports the same decree in Epistle LIV, but somewhat more clearly:

> “We had resolved some time ago,” he says, “dearest brother, after sharing counsel with one another, that those who had been overthrown by the adversary and had lapsed during the assault of persecution, and had defiled themselves with unlawful sacrifices, should perform full penance for a long time; and that, if the danger of illness became urgent, they should receive peace under the stroke of death.”

The whole question therefore turns upon determining what “full penance” means: whether it embraced the whole period of life or was defined by some fixed interval. But this is readily apparent from Epistle LIX, where Cyprian complains that Therapius had granted peace to Victor, formerly a presbyter, “before he had performed full penance, before the lawful and complete period of satisfaction, without the request and knowledge of the people, and without any illness or necessity compelling it.” There was therefore some predetermined period of penance, which the bishop had power to shorten, provided that some grave cause arose. Epistle LXII supplies the same conception of full penance. In it, Cyprian and the other bishops with him decree concerning virgins who had been found with men in the same bed:

> “If they have performed penance for this unlawful cohabitation of theirs and have separated from one another, meanwhile let the virgins be carefully examined by midwives; and if they are found to be virgins, once communion has been received, let them be admitted to the Church. . . . But if any one of them is found to have been corrupted, let her perform full penance, because she who has committed this crime is an adulteress not against a husband but against Christ; and therefore, after a just period has been assessed and *exomologesis* [public confession] afterward made, let her return to the Church.”

A short penance, therefore, is imposed upon virgins found intact, but a full penance, “after a just period has been assessed,” upon those found corrupted. And just as it was decreed at the Council of Carthage that the lapsed should be admitted for the present while those who had sacrificed performed full penance, so too in this passage the bishops decree that the virgins should meanwhile be examined and that, after those found intact had been admitted into the Church, those found corrupted should perform full penance. Thirdly, if those who had sacrificed had been assigned to penance for the whole period of life, it would not have been necessary “for the circumstances, intentions, and necessities of individuals to be examined”; rather, as Tillemont observes, there would have been absolutely no distinction and no selection.

## XIII.—ON THE PRESENCE OF CHRIST IN THE EUCHARIST

The Church’s doctrine concerning the body and blood of the Lord is contained in explicit testimonies from Cyprian. Everything the holy martyr declares concerning the Eucharist tends to confirm the conception that Christ’s words convey to the mind when first heard. His position can be perceived from what he discusses concerning the sacraments of heretics. For why, in Epistle LXX, did he judge that “the Eucharist can in no way be effected among them,” unless because he thought that Christ’s words were pronounced by them in vain and that the Holy Spirit was invoked in vain to make the bread and wine the body and blood of Christ? Firmilian likewise, in order to prove that observance of the Church’s prayers and rites is insufficient to produce the effects of the sacraments, uses the example of a certain deranged woman who had frequently dared “both to pretend that, by an invocation not contemptible, she was sacrificing the bread and effecting the Eucharist, and to offer sacrifice to the Lord not without the sacrament of the customary proclamation.” Firmilian and Cyprian therefore placed this distinction between the Eucharist of Catholics and that of heretics: when heretics invoked the Holy Spirit, no change in the gifts occurred; but the prayers of Catholics never lacked this marvelous effect.

Cyprian was so fully persuaded and certain of this marvelous effect of the Church’s invocation that, concerning the lapsed who communicated before their consciences had been purified, he did not hesitate to say in the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 186):

> “Violence is done to his body and blood, and they now sin against the Lord with their hands and mouth more than when they denied the Lord.”

The body of Christ is therefore not received in the Eucharist by faith alone, but is truly received even by the unworthy themselves. Nor is the body separated from the soul and divinity; rather, the Lord himself is present, and those who communicate unworthily sin against him with their hands and mouth. Hence, in the same book, he declares that the very majesty of the Lord is present. For he speaks as follows concerning a girl who, having been carried by her nurse to an idol and afterward by her parents to church, rejected with sobbing the blood of the Lord which the deacon had poured into her resisting mouth:

> “In the defiled body and mouth,” he says, “the Eucharist could not remain. The drink sanctified in the blood of the Lord burst forth from the polluted entrails. So great is the power of the Lord, so great his majesty!” (P. 189.)

Cyprian there recounts another miracle:

> “And indeed another man,” he says, “because he too had been defiled by sacrifice, dared secretly to receive a portion with the others when the sacrifice had been celebrated by the priest; but he could not eat and handle the holy thing of the Lord, and when he opened his hands he found himself carrying ashes. By the example of one man it was shown that the Lord withdraws when he is denied.”

It was not, therefore, merely bread that had vanished from this man’s hands; rather, the Lord himself had withdrawn. [Col. 0063] Cyprian discusses these things with the intention of explaining to those who communicated too carelessly what they should think about this mystery. Consequently, it is readily apparent in what sense the bishops of the first centuries understood Christ’s words, **THIS IS MY BODY, THIS IS THE BLOOD**, etc., since from them they conclude that Christ’s body and blood are received; that those who communicate unworthily sin against the Lord himself with their mouth and hands; that the power and majesty of the Lord are present; and that the Lord himself withdrew, not without a miracle, from contaminated hands. If at that time the change of wine into the blood of Christ had not been believed, would nothing other than the blood of Christ, I ask, have been acknowledged in the chalice after those prayers in which God is asked to make the wine the blood of Christ? Indeed, Cyprian acknowledges nothing else in countless passages. Against those who offered only water in the morning sacrifices, he maintains that it is unworthy of a Christian to fear “lest by the taste of wine he should smell of the blood of Christ.”

> “Thus, therefore,” he says, “the brotherhood begins to be held back from suffering for Christ in persecutions, when in the offerings it learns to be ashamed of his blood and gore. . . . How, moreover, can we shed our blood for Christ, if we are ashamed to drink the blood of Christ?” (P. 109.)

He calls it not only blood but even gore, and does not hesitate to compare that blood with the blood flowing in our veins. He also says on p. 106:

> “Just as wine cannot be obtained for drinking unless the cluster is first trodden and pressed, so neither could we drink the blood of Christ unless Christ had first been trodden and pressed, and had first drunk the cup from which he would give believers to drink.”

Just as Cyprian condemns unworthy communions because “the holy body of the Lord” is profaned (p. 20), because “violence is done to the body and blood of the Lord” and sin is committed against the Lord “with hands and mouth” (p. 186), and just as Firmilian regarded it as a kind of sacrilege that persons who, as he thought, had not been baptized “should, by rashly usurping communion, touch the body and blood of the Lord” (p. 149), so the gifts of grace customarily received from the Eucharist are attributed to the body and blood of Christ there present. Cyprian teaches that Christ’s soldiers ought to consider that “they drink the cup of Christ’s blood daily precisely so that they themselves may be able to shed their blood for Christ.” Hence, when, with the persecution of Gallus and Volusian impending, he had resolved to grant communion to those who had lapsed under Decius, he gives this reason for the indulgence in Epistle LIV (p. 78):

> “For how,” he says, “do we teach or incite them to shed their own blood in confession of the Name, if we deny the blood of Christ to those who are about to serve as soldiers? Or how do we make them fit for the cup of martyrdom, if we do not first admit them, by right of communion, to drink the cup of the Lord in the Church?”

And in Epistle LXIII (p. 107):

> “The Lord’s cup so inebriates those who drink that it makes them sober, directs their minds toward spiritual wisdom, and brings each person back to the knowledge of God from this taste of the world. And just as by this common wine the mind is unbound and the soul relaxed, and every sorrow laid aside, so, when the blood of the Lord has been drunk from the saving cup, let the memory of the old man be laid aside, let there be forgetfulness of one’s former worldly conduct, and let the mournful and sorrowful breast, formerly weighed down by oppressive sins, be released by the joy of divine indulgence.”

Whatever, therefore, the Catholic Church teaches concerning the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, and whatever can be observed by a mind imbued with this faith, we perceive to have been impressed and engraved upon Cyprian’s mind.

The Oxford editor objects to us with this passage from Epistle LXIII:

> “Thus, in sanctifying the cup of the Lord,” Cyprian says (p. 108), “water alone cannot be offered, just as neither can wine alone. For if someone offers wine only, the blood of Christ begins to exist without us. But if there is water alone, the people begin to exist without Christ. When, however, both are mixed, then the spiritual and heavenly sacrament is completed.”

From this he concludes that the blood of Christ is in the chalice in the same manner as the people themselves are said to be contained in that chalice. But the distinction is so manifest that I am astonished that a learned man should linger over such quibbles. For who has ever said that the people are drunk in the chalice, touched by mouth and hands, that the people withdraw when the appearances have been changed, or any other such things as those we have just cited concerning the blood of Christ? Accordingly, when the people are said to be in the chalice, the figure is manifest and can neither escape anyone’s notice nor cast anyone into danger of error. But after Christ’s words, “This is the blood,” etc., had been daily commemorated and impressed upon believers, and after the daily prayers in the sacrifice that the wine should become the blood of Christ, who could have suspected a figure when hearing nothing other than that Christ’s blood is in the chalice, is offered in the chalice, and is drunk, and strengthens our souls so that we may shed our blood for Christ?

But we must briefly examine the difference between the arguments by which Cyprian maintains that water must be poured into the chalice and those by which he establishes that wine is altogether necessary. In this way the reality of the Lord’s blood will also become evident, and at the same time those will be refuted who wish to maintain that water was prescribed by Cyprian as a matter of divine, and not merely ecclesiastical, law. The holy martyr had resolved to overthrow the very bad custom that had crept in among certain persons, of offering water alone in the morning sacrifice. Consequently, he shows that water is the essential matter for the proper effect of the sacrament not in the Eucharist but only in Baptism, and that “whenever water alone is named in the Scriptures, Baptism is proclaimed, and by the designation of water Baptism is always signified.” But in the Eucharist, “the cup which the Lord offered was mixed, and that which he called his blood was wine; and by the example of his teaching he showed that the cup is to be mixed by joining wine and water.” Hence he shows that water is employed only for mystical significations:

> “For the divine Scripture declares in the Apocalypse,” he says (p. 108), “that waters signify peoples, saying: ‘The waters which you saw, upon which that harlot sits, are peoples and crowds and nations of the Gentiles and tongues.’ We perceive that this is also contained in the sacrament of the cup. For because Christ bore us all, he who also bore our sins, we see that the people are understood in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine.”

Thus far Cyprian diminishes rather than commends the necessity of water. Yet afterward he says that water [Col. 0065] alone cannot be offered, “just as neither can wine alone,” and that the union and conjunction of water and wine are so mingled in the cup of the Lord “that the mixture cannot be separated one from the other.” Cyprian’s purpose must be noted. In disputing with people who employed water alone, he uses a principle that they would readily concede: that wine alone likewise ought not to be employed. Certainly no preconceived opinion prevented them from admitting this. Therefore Cyprian declares that water alone ought not to be employed, just as neither should wine alone—not because he feared that such people would offer wine alone; not because he regarded water, equally with wine, as prescribed by Christ and pertaining to the essence of the sacrament, since he had sufficiently declared that water was employed for mystical significations; but because this comparison was suited to demonstrating the necessity of wine, and because it was evident that much graver disadvantages would result if water alone were employed than those that would follow if wine alone were employed. Hence, whenever in this epistle he declares that the cup must be mixed, he does not properly refer this to the water, but to the wine which those whom he was refuting omitted.

Cyprian defends the necessity of wine in a very different way. First, he shows from the testimony of Scripture that, just as water is designated in Baptism, so wine is designated in the Eucharist. Secondly, he shows that Christ’s most solemn command is violated if the wine is omitted:

> “Since, therefore,” he says (p. 107), “neither the Apostle himself nor an angel from heaven can proclaim or teach anything other than what Christ once taught and his Apostles proclaimed, I am sufficiently astonished at the origin of this practice whereby, contrary to evangelical and apostolic discipline, water is offered in the Lord’s cup in certain places, although water alone cannot express the blood of Christ.”

And on p. 109:

> “But if it is not lawful to relax even the least of the Lord’s commandments, how much less is it permitted to violate things so great, so momentous, and so closely pertaining to the very sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and our redemption, or by human tradition to change them into anything other than what was divinely instituted?”

Thirdly, what disadvantages does Cyprian think follow from this rash alteration of the divine institution?

> “For,” he says (p. 106), “taking the cup on the day of his Passion, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Drink from this, all of you. For this is the blood of the New Testament,’ etc. In this passage we find that the cup which the Lord offered was mixed, and that what he called his blood was wine. Hence it is apparent that Christ’s blood is not offered if wine is absent from the cup; nor is the Lord’s sacrifice celebrated with lawful consecration unless our offering and sacrifice correspond to the Passion. For,” as he says (p. 109), “the Passion of the Lord is the sacrifice which we offer.”

According to Cyprian, therefore, wine must be used in the chalice because, since Christ took wine and said, “This is the blood,” etc., if water alone is employed it will remain water, and Christ’s blood will no longer be offered; the Passion of the Lord will not be our sacrifice, nor will the same thing be offered that was offered in the Passion. Fourthly, Cyprian also recalls how many and how great are the benefits we receive “when the blood of the Lord has been drunk from the saving cup,” in order to demonstrate how harmful it is to employ water alone. He adds that it is a grave offense to be ashamed “of Christ’s blood and gore,” and that those “who are ashamed to drink Christ’s blood” can no longer “shed their blood for Christ.” It is now readily apparent in what sense Cyprian thinks the people, and in what sense he thinks Christ’s blood, to be in the chalice. He teaches that the union of the people with Christ is signified by the union of water with wine; and he acknowledges that, when the water is omitted, Christ’s blood is indeed offered and the Passion commemorated, though nevertheless it will be no slight defect if the union of the people with Christ is absent. But he declares that Christ’s blood is in the chalice because Christ said, “This is the blood,” etc.; and if the blood is absent, the sacrifice can no longer be offered and the Passion of the Lord celebrated. Indeed, we shall be utterly deprived of the gifts promised to those who drink Christ’s blood.

## XIV.—ON COMMUNION UNDER BOTH KINDS

Although Cyprian maintains that the sacrifice must be offered under both kinds, and that this was instituted and prescribed by Christ, he nevertheless did not judge communion under both kinds to be necessary, as can be seen from his principles and from the custom of that age. For he did not regard everything Christ did in instituting the sacrament as something to be observed with the force of law, but only those things that pertain to the essence of the sacrament. When it was objected to him that the Lord offered after supper, he responded as follows (Epistle LXIII, p. 109):

> “Must we therefore celebrate the Lord’s rite after supper, so that we may thus offer the mixed cup when celebrating the Lord’s rites? Christ had to offer toward the evening of the day, so that the very hour of the sacrifice might show the decline and evening of the world. . . . But we celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning.”

Why, then, does he deny that we are commanded to do in this respect the same thing Christ did, whereas in the offering of bread and wine he maintains that the priest truly acts in Christ’s stead “when he imitates what Christ did and offers according to what he sees Christ himself to have offered”? The reason lies before our eyes. It makes no difference to the nature of the sacrifice whether it is offered in the morning or after supper. But if water is offered in place of wine, the sacrifice instituted by Christ is utterly overthrown, his Passion is not celebrated, and blood will neither be offered nor drunk from the chalice, but only ordinary water. From these principles it can be perceived what Cyprian thought about communion under both kinds. He could not have believed it necessary and commanded by Christ, since it does not pertain to the essence of the sacrament. For Cyprian acknowledges the whole Christ under either kind: he reveres his majesty in the chalice and declares that he withdrew from the contaminated hands of the man in which ashes were found in place of the Eucharist.

The customs of the ancient Church agree with his faith and doctrine. We have already seen, from Cyprian, the example of the girl who communicated from the chalice alone—a custom which, as everyone knows, continued in the West until the [Col. 0067] twelfth century. It is clearer than daylight that this girl did not communicate under the species of bread. For Cyprian relates this story in order to show that the Eucharist could not remain in a defiled body and mouth; but if she had previously received the species of bread, there would have been no miracle whatever and no force in Cyprian’s reasoning. We have also cited the example of the man who found ashes in his hands in place of the Eucharist. Another very similar example occurs in the same book *On the Lapsed*, concerning a woman who, when “she attempted with unworthy hands to open her chest, in which the holy thing of the Lord had been kept, was frightened by fire rising from it and did not dare to touch it.”

## XV.—ST. CYPRIAN’S POSITION ON SACRIFICE, PURGATORY, AND THE INVOCATION OF THE SAINTS

Cyprian confirms by his testimony that the Eucharist is a true sacrifice, properly so called. In the book *On the Unity of the Church* (p. 200), he says that schismatics “profane the reality of the Lord’s victim by false sacrifices.” That true victim which Cyprian maintains is offered in the Church alone is Christ himself, immolated upon the altar in an unbloody manner.

> “Jesus Christ, our Lord and God,” he says in Epistle LXIII (p. 109), “is himself the high priest of God the Father; he first offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father, and commanded this to be done in commemoration of himself.”

Since, therefore, the same victim that was offered on the cross is offered upon the altar, Cyprian rightly says: “The Passion of the Lord is the sacrifice which we offer.” In the same epistle, he denies that “the Lord’s sacrifice is celebrated with lawful consecration unless our offering and sacrifice correspond to the Passion.” He also demonstrates the reality of the sacrifice instituted by Christ from the fact that it was prefigured by the priest Melchizedek:

> “Likewise in the priest Melchizedek,” he says (p. 105), “we see the sacrament of the Lord’s sacrifice prefigured, according to what the divine Scripture testifies and says: ‘And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine. Now he was priest of the Most High God, and he blessed Abraham.’ That Melchizedek bore the type of Christ the Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: ‘Before the morning star I begot you. You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’ This order certainly comes from that sacrifice and descends from the fact that Melchizedek was priest of the Most High God, that he offered bread and wine, and that he blessed Abraham. For who is more truly priest of the Most High God than our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered sacrifice to God the Father and offered the very same thing that Melchizedek had offered—that is, bread and wine, namely his own body and blood?”

Sacrifice is offered for the sins of the living and of the dead. Hence Cyprian complains in the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 186) that communion had been given to some of the lapsed “before their conscience had been purified by the sacrifice and the hand of the priest, and before the offense against the indignant and threatening Lord had been appeased.” In Epistle LX to the Numidian bishops, Cyprian testifies that he had appended the names of all those who had contributed readily and liberally to the redemption of captives, so that the bishops might keep them in mind in their prayers “and make a return to them for their good work in sacrifices and prayers.”

As regards the dead, we have an outstanding testimony in Epistle LXVI, addressed to the clergy and people residing at Furni. Cyprian’s predecessors had decreed that no brother, when departing this life, should appoint a cleric as guardian or administrator; and that if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him, lest the sacrifice for his falling asleep be celebrated. For the man who wished to call priests and ministers away from the altar does not deserve to be named at God’s altar in the prayer of the priests. Accordingly, when a certain Victor had dared to appoint the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian, Cyprian forbade “an offering to be made for his falling asleep, or any supplication in his name to be regularly made in the church.”

The author of the Oxford edition contends in vain that “these things were performed as a token of faith, hope, and charity, and not as assistance for souls or as relief for those burning in the fires of purgatory, because they applied principally to the martyrs.” This example of the martyrs proves nothing. Sacrifice was not offered for the sins of the martyrs, since everyone was certain that they saw God in heaven. Consequently, they were not named in the same place as others who had died in the peace of the Church; and Cyprian himself explains in Epistle XXXVII what he says in Epistle XXXIV about sacrifices customarily being offered for them, for there he says that offerings and sacrifices are celebrated “in commemoration of them.”

The case of those who died in the peace of the Church was different. Sacrifice was offered for their sins, as may be seen in the liturgy contained in Book VIII, chapter 41, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, where the following words are found:

> “Let us pray for our brethren who have rested in Christ, that God, the lover of humankind, who has received the soul of the departed, may forgive him every voluntary and involuntary sin and, becoming gracious and merciful toward him, may place him in the region of the righteous,” etc.

Nor indeed is it surprising if the ancient Christians hoped that sacrifice would benefit the faithful departed, since everyone was persuaded and fully convinced that the souls of the just who are released from the body before they have expiated all their sins are afflicted with punishments in the next life and that their beatitude is deferred. Hence the Roman clergy feared for those who died before completing their penance: “God knows,” it says in Epistle XXXI, “what he will do concerning such persons, and how he will weigh the balances of his judgment.” Cyprian thus compares such persons with those who die after shedding their lives for Christ, or at least after living holy lives:

> “It is one thing,” he says in Epistle LII (p. 72), “to stand awaiting pardon, another to attain glory; one thing, after being sent to prison, not to come out until one has paid the last farthing, another immediately to receive the reward of faith and virtue; one thing to be cleansed from sins by the torment of prolonged suffering and to be purified for a long time by fire, another to have purged away all sins through suffering; finally, one thing to remain in suspense until the day of judgment for the Lord’s sentence, another immediately to be crowned by the Lord.”

The efforts of Rigaltius [Col. 0069] and the Oxford editor to evade this testimony are entirely futile. They distort this prison, the torment of prolonged suffering, and the fire that purifies for a long time, making them refer to the penance customarily imposed by priests upon the lapsed. But:

1. They must at least acknowledge that it follows from Cyprian’s words that temporal punishments remain to be paid by those whose eternal punishments have been remitted.

2. If Cyprian is describing the sufferings of penance, this applies far more aptly to those who die before completing the course of their penance. For no one will attribute to Cyprian the opinion that such persons do not stand awaiting pardon but have attained pardon; are not sent to prison until they pay the last farthing but immediately receive the reward of faith and virtue; are not cleansed from sins by the torment of prolonged suffering and purified for a long time by fire; do not remain in suspense until the day of judgment but are immediately crowned by the Lord.

3. Cyprian compares not only martyrs with the lapsed but also virgins with adulterers. There is no doubt that he is speaking of martyrs and virgins who have died, since he declares that the crown is bestowed upon them immediately. Why, then, should we believe that he spoke of the state of penitents only in this life? A truly splendid and remarkable comparison it would be to contrast martyrs and virgins with idolaters and adulterers on the ground that the former are crowned immediately in the next life, while the latter must undergo the labor of penance in this life. But if those idolaters and adulterers die after beginning their penance, will they immediately receive the reward and crown, like martyrs and virgins, and be regarded as having purged away all their sins through penance? Who does not see that the comparison instituted by Cyprian refers principally to the future life? For in this life sacred virgins, whose manner of living was austere, equaled the labor of penitents, while martyrs far surpassed it.

4. The phrase “to remain in suspense until the day of judgment” causes the adversaries great difficulty. Nicolaus Faber and Rigaltius think that, according to Cyprian, the beatitude of the just—excepting the martyrs—is deferred until the day of judgment. But this opinion cannot be attributed to Cyprian, who in this passage, as I have already observed, speaks not only of martyrs but also of virgins. Elsewhere he frequently teaches, and especially in the book *On Mortality*, that not only martyrs but other saints as well, when they depart from this life, begin to reign with Christ; that virgins and children happily attain the reward of continence and innocence; and that the just are summoned to refreshment. The testimony now under discussion must therefore be referred to those who, having died before completing their penance, Cyprian believes are reserved until the day of the general judgment. Nor is it surprising that he defers the beatitude of such persons until that time; for since he believed the coming of the Lord to be imminent, the interval could not have seemed unduly long.

Moreover, Cyprian’s position is further clarified by his declaration that, on the day of judgment, the merits of the martyrs will benefit many who remain in suspense until that day:

> “We indeed believe,” he says in the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 187), “that the merits of the martyrs and the works of the just can avail greatly before the Judge—but when the day of judgment has come, when, after the passing away of this age and of the world, his people stand before the tribunal of Christ.”

And this concerns those who submit themselves to penance within the Church. But as for those who die outside the Church, Cyprian declares that, even if they have been killed for the Name, they will never attain the indulgence promised to others who die within the bosom of the Church:

> “And because there is no confession in the lower regions,” he says in the same Epistle LII, “nor can *exomologesis* [public confession and penance] be performed there, those who have repented and entreated with their whole heart ought to be admitted inwardly into the Church and there reserved for the Lord, who, when he comes to his Church, will assuredly judge concerning those whom he finds within it. Apostates, however, and deserters, adversaries and enemies, and those who scatter the Church of Christ—even if they have been killed for the Name—cannot, according to the Apostle, be admitted to the peace of the Church, since they have maintained neither the unity of the Spirit nor that of the Church.”

Cyprian rightly denies that the *exomologesis* prescribed in this life can be completed in the next. But it is evident that he acknowledges a certain indulgence and peace which, though closed and denied to schismatics and heretics who die outside the Church, even if they have been killed for the Name, will be granted to others who die within the Church and are reserved until the coming of the Lord.

From these facts it is clear that the communion which the Catholic Church maintains with saints and martyrs, and with the just who have died before completing their penance, is not a novel invention but a dogma known and believed in the earliest centuries. Nor is it surprising that this communion displeases those who have withdrawn from the unity of the Church. But Cyprian, among whose foremost virtues love of unity shone brightly, besides the measures enacted by him in honor of the martyrs that we have already related, testifies in two other passages to the close bond between the Church now present and the saints and martyrs.

The first occurs in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, which Cyprian concludes thus:

> “Only remember us then, when virginity begins to be honored in you.”

The other testimony is found in Epistle LVII to Cornelius, whom Cyprian addresses as follows:

> “Let us be mutually mindful of one another, harmonious and of one mind; in both places let us always pray for one another; let us relieve pressures and distresses by mutual charity; and if one of us here should, through the swiftness of divine favor, precede the other, let our affection persevere before the Lord, and let prayer for our brothers and sisters not cease before the mercy of the Father.”

The Oxford editor attempts in vain to evade these passages. He says that virginity begins to be honored when it attains the glory of confession; but Cyprian addresses all virgins generally, not martyrs alone, and therefore indicates the crown not of martyrdom but of virginity. Fell interprets the second passage as though Cyprian were making an agreement with Cornelius “that whichever of them survived, and happened to remain longer among the living, should continue to pray.” But this is manifest quibbling; for Cyprian entrusts this duty of prayer not to the one who survives, but to the one who “has gone before first.” Fell, however, denies that our interpretation entails the permissibility of praying to the saints. Yet he fails to notice how closely these words are connected with the invocation of the saints. If in the earliest centuries this had been regarded as a superstition injurious to Christ—or rather, if it had not flourished throughout the whole Church, as the most certain monuments testify that it did flourish [Col. 0071A]—it would never have occurred to Cyprian to entreat and invoke virgins and martyrs beforehand.

## XVI.—ON THE DIVINITY OF CHRIST AND HIS GRACE

I should exceed the bounds of a preface if I were to linger over a careful investigation of Cyprian’s other teachings. For, as Pamelius rightly observes, no error has been devised in these later centuries that is not refuted by testimonies from Cyprian. The holy Martyr did not expressly undertake a systematic treatment of Christ’s divinity, but his brief statements concerning God incarnate possess no less force and weight than a fuller treatment.

He customarily calls Christ our Lord and God, as when he says in Epistle VIII (p. 15):

> “We have as advocate and intercessor for our sins Jesus Christ, our Lord and God.”

In Epistle LX (p. 99), he teaches that we must labor:

> “so that through our acts of service we may merit the favor of Christ, our Judge and Lord and God.”

In Epistle LXIII (p. 104):

> “Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, the author and teacher of this sacrifice”;

and on p. 109:

> “Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, is himself the high priest of God the Father.”

In Epistle XLVII (p. 61), he gives thanks:

> “to God the almighty Father, and to his Christ, our Lord and God and Savior.”

See Epistle LVI, pp. 92 and 94; Epistle LXV, p. 113; Epistle LXXIV, pp. 139 and 140; Epistle LXXVII, p. 158.

In the book *On the Lord’s Prayer* (p. 204):

> “Let us therefore pray, most beloved brothers, as God our Teacher has taught”;

and (p. 206):

> “The God of peace and Teacher of concord, who taught unity, willed that one person should pray for all in the same manner as he himself bore all in one.”

In the book *On the Vanity of Idols* (p. 228), he similarly calls Christ our God, “God mingled with man”; in Book II of the *Testimonies*, “man and God compounded from both natures.” He proves from the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments that Christ is God and is called God, pp. 286, 287, 288, and refers to him all the most illustrious testimonies.

In the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom* (p. 267), after quoting the words of Isaiah, “I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who saves you,” he adds:

> “He also promises in the Gospel that divine aid will not fail God’s servants during persecutions, saying: ‘But when they deliver you up,’ etc.”

In the book *On the Good of Patience*, he teaches that Christ is worshiped in heaven and that the Father commanded the Son to be worshiped. To him he refers these testimonies of Scripture: “God will come manifestly”; “Our God, and he will not remain silent”; “The Lord God of hosts will come forth”; and others of this kind. He then adds:

> “But who is it that says he was formerly silent and will not be silent? Assuredly he who was led like a sheep to sacrifice.… This is our God—that is, the God not of all but of the faithful and believers—who, when he comes manifestly at his second advent, will not remain silent.”

Nor should we omit the notable passage from the Epistle to Jubaianus (p. 133), in which Cyprian explicitly teaches that the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are one God:

> “For if,” he says, “someone could be baptized among heretics, he could assuredly also obtain remission of sins. If he obtained remission of sins, he was also sanctified and made a temple of God. If he was sanctified and made a temple of God, I ask: of which God? If of the Creator, he could not have been, because he did not believe in him; if of Christ, he could not have become his temple either, since he denies that Christ is God; if of the Holy Spirit, since the three are one, how can the Holy Spirit be favorably disposed toward one who is an enemy either of the Father or of the Son?”

See the book *On the Unity of the Church*, where he cites these testimonies of Scripture: “I and the Father are one,” and “these three are one.” See also Epistle LXXVI (p. 139), where he contends that it is utterly absurd to say that those who were baptized outside the Church “had indeed put on Christ but could not receive the Holy Spirit, as though Christ could be put on without the Spirit, or the Spirit could be separated from Christ.”

That supreme devotion toward God incarnate which shines so wonderfully in Cyprian’s writings burned likewise in the hearts of the other bishops of Africa, as we can perceive from the Council of Carthage, at which eighty-seven bishops from Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania were present, together with presbyters and deacons, and also the greater part of the people.

At this council Nemesianus of Thubunae speaks thus (p. 330) concerning the Holy Spirit:

> “That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit, because the Spirit is God and was born of God.”

The Oxford editor explains the phrase “was born of God” less suitably as follows: “What is born of the Spirit is born of God.” But Nemesianus would then have had to say, “it was born of God.” Anyone who pays even moderate attention will see that the meaning of this passage is that what is born of the Spirit is spirit, because the Holy Spirit, since he is God and was born or proceeded from God—for these expressions sometimes have the same sense—by his supreme power makes those whom he regenerates spiritual.

Fortunatus of Thuccabori speaks thus at the same council (p. 332):

> “Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, the Son of God the Father and Creator, built his Church upon the rock.”

Euchratius of Thenis (p. 333):

> “God and our Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled our faith and the grace of Baptism when, teaching the Apostles with his own mouth, he said: ‘Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’”

In the same place Felix of Uthina says:

> “No one doubts, most holy fellow priests, that human presumption has far less power than the adorable and venerable majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Venantius of Timisa (p. 335):

> “Christ, our Lord and God, when departing to the Father, entrusted his bride to us.”

Just as Cyprian thought magnificently concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, so also did he think concerning the benefits received from God incarnate. Learned theologians long ago observed that the errors of the Pelagians had been refuted much earlier by the holy Martyr, and that he furnished Augustine with abundant material for the overthrow of that heresy.

Cyprian knew well [Col. 0073] that the Lord, when he came, healed “the wounds that Adam had borne” and cured “the ancient poisons of the serpent” (p. 237). Hence he believed Baptism to be absolutely necessary for everyone:

> “All those,” he says in the book *On the Dress of Virgins* (p. 180), “who through the sanctification of Baptism attain the divine washing put off the old man there by the grace of the saving bath, and, renewed by the Holy Spirit, are cleansed from the defilements of the ancient contagion through a second birth.”

Above all, however, the Catholic dogma is defended in Epistle LIX, written to Fidus not by Cyprian alone, but also by the other sixty-six colleagues who were present at the council. Through some unknown error of opinion, Fidus had imagined that infants “ought not to be baptized within the second or third day after their birth, and that the law of ancient circumcision ought to be considered, so that he did not think one who had been born should be baptized and sanctified before the eighth day.”

The judgment of everyone at the council was far otherwise, and they unanimously determined that “the mercy and grace of God must be denied to no human being who has been born.” They continue:

> “Moreover, if remission of sins is granted even to the gravest sinners and to those who have sinned greatly against God in the past, and no one is barred from Baptism and grace, how much less ought an infant to be barred—an infant who, having only recently been born, has committed no sin except that, being born according to Adam in the flesh, he contracted the contagion of ancient death in his first birth, and who approaches the reception of remission of sins all the more readily for the very reason that what is remitted to him is not his own sins but those of another.”

Against the proud inventions of the Pelagians, Cyprian teaches in many passages that we sin daily, as in the books *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 211; *On Works and Almsgiving*, pp. 238 and 243; and Book III of the *Testimonies*, p. 54.

In innumerable passages Cyprian wonderfully commends the grace of Christ. While he was still lying in darkness and blind night, he believed that what Christians taught could not happen:

> “that someone could be born anew, and that, animated into a new life by the washing of saving water, he could put off what he had previously been and, although the bodily structure remained, be changed in soul and mind” (*Epistle to Donatus*).

But he laid aside this error together with his other vices and errors, and thereafter proclaimed the grace of Christ all the more gladly in proportion to the obstinacy with which he had previously rejected it. What he discusses to this effect in the *Epistle to Donatus* may be consulted.

In the *Exhortation to Martyrdom* (p. 167), he proves from several testimonies of Scripture:

> “that the injuries and punishments of persecutions are not to be feared, because the Lord is greater in protecting than the devil in attacking.”

See pp. 262, 268, 273. In Epistle IX, he exhorts the martyrs to constancy:

> “because he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world, nor has earthly punishment greater power to cast down than divine protection has to raise up.”

See more in the same epistle and in Epistle LV (p. 88).

Many other principles of Cyprian may be referred to this subject, as when he teaches that victory is given by God (p. 79); that God makes men victorious by his favor (pp. 162, 285); that God rewards in us whatever he himself has bestowed, and honors what he himself has done (p. 169); that nothing is ours (p. 305); that no one ought to claim anything for himself (p. 212); and that everything must be attributed to God (*ibid.*).

Above all, the book *On the Lord’s Prayer* should be carefully studied. There he teaches that we must pray that God’s will may be done in us; that God’s will may be done in body and spirit; that we may be able to do what God wills; that God’s will may be done in those who do not believe, just as God’s will has been done in us through our faith—for God’s will is necessary if God’s will is to be done in us; that we who have been sanctified in Baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be; and that the sanctification and vivification received from God’s grace may be preserved by his protection [apparently correcting OCR *perfectione* to *protectione*].

[Col. 0073]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT CYPRIAN, PREPARED BY DOM PRUDENTIUS MARAN, O.S.B.

[Col. 0073] Cyprian, that great light of the Christian religion, was, for as long as he shone in the Church, a major participant in the events then taking place. His life therefore supplies the most abundant material for discussion, and an entire volume would be needed if I were to undertake to trace every kind and circumstance of the events relating to him, to set before the reader’s eyes the examples he furnished of each virtue, and to draw forth the exceptional sentiments of his soul from his epistles and other writings, in which his character is wonderfully portrayed.

But a treatment of that kind does not belong here, nor is it my purpose [Col. 0074] to discuss Cyprian’s affairs in that manner, but only to explain them in order and to assign the writings themselves to their respective dates. For since this study is published together with the writings of the holy Martyr, there is no need to append lengthy testimonies, which anyone can draw from the fountain itself; and various observations must be omitted which perhaps ought not to be omitted if the Life of St. Cyprian were published separately from his works.

## I.—ON ST. CYPRIAN BEFORE HE BECAME A CHRISTIAN.—HE MUST BE DISTINGUISHED FROM CYPRIAN OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 0075]

No one disputes that Cyprian was born in Africa. Prudentius and Suidas believed that he was a native of Carthage; but since the holy Martyr does not credit Carthage with this benefit, and says only in Epistle XXXVI, “For where could it be better or more joyful for me than there where God willed me to believe and to grow?”, some other native country appears to have brought him into the light.

He was called Thascius Cyprianus, as is clear from the proconsul’s sentence and from Epistle LXIX. Moreover, according to Jerome, he had adopted the name Caecilius, so that by this memorial he might attest his gratitude and affection toward the presbyter Caecilius, through whose agency he had been converted to Christ.

Pontius the deacon, who wrote Cyprian’s *Life*, judged the deeds he had performed before his conversion less worthy of being committed to writing. Accordingly, this part of his life lies in oblivion and darkness. We know nothing with certainty except that he taught rhetoric with the greatest distinction and was not free from those vices which are ordinarily associated with the worship of idols and ignorance of Christ.

“The fishermen were changed,” says Augustine in Sermon CCCXI (new edition), “and afterward many senators too were changed; Cyprian was changed, whose memorial we celebrate today.… He himself writes and himself testifies what kind of life he once lived—how wicked, how impious, how deserving of condemnation and detestation.”

Nevertheless, what we read in Gregory Nazianzen concerning Cyprian’s devotion to magical arts before his conversion, in Oration XVIII, by no means applies to our Cyprian. It is evident that these things concern Cyprian of Antioch, whom Gregory confuses with Cyprian of Carthage, fashioning a single person from the two. Yet because the learned Oxford editor contends that there was only one Cyprian, counts what is reported concerning the Antiochene among fables, and declares that it was composed to embellish the history of the Carthaginian, it seems useful to investigate the matter.

First, it cannot be denied that the deeds of Cyprian of Antioch were transmitted in very ancient records. According to Photius (Codex 184), the empress Eudocia celebrated him in distinguished verse. The work was divided into three books. The first contained the conversion of Justina, her virginity unconquered by demons, and the marvelous conversion of Cyprian himself after his crimes of magic, his baptism, his office of doorkeeper, his miracles, and finally his episcopate. In another book Cyprian himself set out the sequence of his experiences and recounted the magical arts by which he had transformed himself and others into various forms, his journeys, and finally his disgust with that wicked art, and how his mind was recalled by Eusebius from the despair inspired by consciousness of his crimes to hope in divine mercy. In the third, finally, the martyrdom of Justina and Cyprian was described.

It is apparent that Eudocia wrote these things not according to poetic license but with historical fidelity. This is clear both from Gregory Nazianzen, who cites the confession of crimes written by Cyprian himself and in Oration XVIII relates the same things about him as Eudocia [Col. 0076], and from the threefold record which those learned investigators of antiquity, Dom Edmond Martène and Dom Ursin Durand, published in their *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*: namely, the *Conversion of Justina and Cyprian*, the *Confession of the Same Cyprian*, and the *Passion of Both*. That tripartite work agrees so closely with Eudocia’s verses that there can be no doubt that it had been constantly in her hands.

Who, then, could persuade himself that a man never existed concerning whom records survive that are almost contemporary with the period in which he is said to have lived? Fables seek concealment in remote ages, and no one lies so foolishly as to pretend that events which no one remembers seeing or hearing occurred recently, in the clearest light and before everyone’s eyes.

Moreover, Fell himself admits—although I do not agree with him entirely on this matter—that Cyprian’s *Confession* was written before the time of Constantine, that is, around the time at which he is believed to have suffered martyrdom, namely under Diocletian and Maximian, as Eudocia testifies. Furthermore, the Acts of Justina and Cyprian had been written before this work, as we learn from the account of the passion of both.

Second, it is not credible that records of this kind were fabricated to embellish the history of Cyprian of Carthage, since there was absolutely nothing in them that could be adapted to Cyprian of Carthage: neither the time nor the place of his martyrdom and episcopate, nor his deeds and journeys.

Third, if this Cyprian of Antioch, who is said to have suffered with Justina at Nicomedia, had never existed, how could a feast day in both their names have been introduced in the fourth century into regions near Nicomedia, and how could the fame of both have been celebrated on everyone’s lips? It can be perceived quite clearly from St. Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration XVIII, delivered at Constantinople, that the Cyprian whose feast day was being observed was not the Carthaginian but the Antiochene. For Gregory proclaims his magical arts and conversion as the foremost and best-known events of his life, so much so that he doubts whether any of his hearers is ignorant of his history (p. 277). Moreover, when he says that Cyprian became a temple attendant after his conversion, he testifies that he had heard this from someone (p. 281). It is improbable that Cyprian of Carthage should have been so well known in these regions, especially from matters that did not concern him at all, that the inhabitants should instruct Gregory about him. Rather, this fame and feast day must be referred to another man.

Fell objects that St. Gregory could not have erred so carelessly as to confuse a bishop of Antioch with the bishop of Carthage. For if that Cyprian who is said to have been bishop of Antioch and to have suffered at Nicomedia had truly existed, some report of him could not have failed to reach Gregory’s ears, since Gregory ought both to have learned such marvelous events early from his father and to have discovered them for himself while traveling through Nicomedia and the surrounding regions.

But while the learned man will not permit Gregory to be censured for fashioning one Cyprian out of two, he exposes him to another reproach scarcely less serious: namely, that he referred to Cyprian of Carthage records incompatible with his age, country, and deeds.

This explanation for excusing Gregory seems more probable to me: since his acquaintance with those whom he was addressing was quite recent, and after a withdrawal of a few days he had returned just in time for the feast itself, as he testifies (p. 275), it was easy enough for him to slip and err when he had so little time to learn the facts accurately.

As for Fell’s further assertion that no Cyprian is found among the bishops of Antioch, this difficulty is easily resolved. Cyprian is not said to have been bishop of great Antioch, but of another city of that name situated in Phoenicia, as Tillemont observes, from which he was taken to Damascus to be interrogated by the judge.

Two Cyprians must therefore be distinguished, and in Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration XVIII it must be considered what applies to the Antiochene and what to the Carthaginian. Gregory’s statement that Cyprian was born of a noble and senatorial family is attributed by Tillemont to our Cyprian, as not very suitable to that other magician; but in volume V, where he discusses Cyprian of Antioch, he admits that this cannot be determined.

I shall not linger over an examination of the other conjectures customarily made concerning Cyprian, such as the opinion of Baronius and, after him, certain others that Cyprian was already an old man when he embraced the Christian religion. They rely upon a passage in the *Epistle to Donatus*, where Cyprian speaks as follows:

> “How is so great a transformation possible, I used to say, that there should suddenly and swiftly be stripped away either what, being innate, has hardened through the corruption of natural matter, or what, acquired over a long period, has become inveterate through the old age of longstanding habit?”

But Cyprian is not counting his years; he is speaking of vices, which possess antiquity even in a man who is not old, since they have, as we read in the same place, “settled with a deep root penetrating far below.”

Add to this that Cyprian is not discussing only his own circumstances, but is generally embracing every age and condition of life. Christians excluded absolutely none of these from the possibility, as they taught, of renewal and rebirth through Christ’s grace. This is clear from what follows:

> “When,” he says, “does one who has grown accustomed to sumptuous banquets and lavish feasts learn frugality? And when does one who, conspicuous in costly clothing, has glittered in gold and purple lower himself to ordinary and simple attire? A man delighted by the fasces and public honors cannot endure being a private and undistinguished person. Another, surrounded by wedges of clients and honored by the more crowded escort of an attentive retinue, thinks it a punishment to be alone. By their tenacious allurements, drunkenness must always entice him as it was accustomed to do; pride must inflate him, anger inflame him, greed disturb him, cruelty incite him, ambition delight him, lust hurl him headlong.”

I have thought it proper to relate these things so that it may be clear that those who suppose Cyprian portrayed his own character in this picture, and described the splendor and wealth of his former station, indulge their leisure without sufficient restraint. If these conjectures have any force, it will have to be said that he shone with the fasces and suffered from the vices of drunkenness and greed—something I see that no one has hitherto suspected.
