## II.—ON THE CONVERSION OF ST. CYPRIAN.—WHILE A CATECHUMEN HE DISTRIBUTED HIS PROPERTY AND BOUND HIMSELF BY A VOW OF CONTINENCE.—THE YEAR AND SEASON OF HIS BAPTISM ARE UNCERTAIN

The conversion of so great an intellect certainly brought much honor and support to the Christian religion; and truth seemed to triumph most splendidly when it captured that most celebrated teacher and defender of falsehood [Col. 0078].

Cyprian was not, however, conquered at the first assault. Rather—as is not very surprising in a man puffed up by knowledge of empty things—he long wavered between truth and error, his judgment uncertain. What the Christian religion teaches concerning a new creation in Christ he refuted as though it were a dream, using an argument drawn from his own experience: he was not yet willing to correct his vices and believed that they could not be corrected.

He himself explains in the *Epistle to Donatus* the agitation of mind that he then experienced:

> “While I was lying in darkness and blind night,” he says, “and while, wavering and uncertain, I drifted upon the sea of this tossing age with wandering footsteps, ignorant of my own life and estranged from truth and light, I considered it altogether difficult and hard, given my character at that time, to believe what divine indulgence promised me for my salvation: that someone could be born anew, and that, animated into a new life by the washing of saving water, he could put off what he had previously been and, although the bodily structure remained, be changed in soul and mind. How is so great a transformation possible, I used to say? etc.”

But at length Christ bent his mind and made him docile to the exhortations of the presbyter Caecilius, who was the agent and interpreter of so splendid a work. This was not, as some have thought, the tutor of Diadumenus, but rather the same man who in the dialogue of Minucius Felix attacks the Christian religion by fair means and foul, and afterward gladly embraces it when it has been vigorously defended by Octavius.

The friendship between Cyprian and Caecilius was bound so closely by the magnitude of this benefit that Cyprian loved him as a parent, wished to bear his name, and appears to have lived in his house:

> “He indeed shared a household,” says Pontius, “with a man of just and praiseworthy memory, Caecilius, who was at that time a presbyter both in age and in honor, and who had corrected him from the error of the world and brought him to acknowledgment of the true Divinity. Cyprian loved him with every honor and all respect, regarding him with obedient veneration, no longer as a friend equal to his soul but as the parent of his new life. Finally, Caecilius, won over by his acts of service, was deservedly moved to such immeasurable affection that, when he was departing from the world and his summons was already near, he commended his wife and children to Cyprian; and having made him a sharer in the communion of the sect, he afterward made him the heir of his filial devotion.”

This sharing of a household, which indicates that Cyprian lived in Caecilius’ house, accords poorly with the conjectures of learned men who maintain that Cyprian had a wife and perhaps even children when he embraced the Christian religion, although absolutely no trace of this is found either in his writings or in the *Life* written by Pontius.

The varying agitation of Cyprian’s mind as he vacillated delayed his conversion. But as soon as he yielded to the truth shining before his eyes, devotion poured itself wholly into him, and, cultivated by the oracles of Scripture, brought forth ripe fruits at the very beginning:

> “Among the first rudiments of his faith,” says Pontius, “he believed nothing more worthy of God than that he should preserve continence; for only then, he believed, could his heart become fit and his understanding attain the full capacity for truth, if he trampled upon the lust of the flesh with the vigorous and unimpaired strength of holiness. Who has ever remembered so great a miracle? The second birth had not yet opened the eyes of the new man with the full splendor of divine light, and already, through the mere preparation for the light, he was overcoming the former and ancient darkness.
>
> “Then—what is greater—when he had already learned certain things from the divine reading, not in proportion to the condition of his newness but in proportion to the haste of his faith, he immediately seized upon what he found would profit him in earning the Lord’s favor. Having sold his possessions and dispensed the price of whole estates for the support of the poor in their need, he united two good things at once: he both despised worldly ambition, than which nothing is more destructive, and fulfilled mercy, which God preferred even to his sacrifices and which even the man who said that he had kept all the commandments of the law did not fulfill. By the headlong speed of his devotion, he almost began to be perfect before he had learned how.”

Scholars do not agree whether Cyprian had already been initiated into the Christian sacraments when he bound himself by the law of continence and distributed his property to the poor, or whether he performed these two splendid deeds while still a catechumen. But if Pontius’ words are considered more carefully, scarcely any room for doubt will remain.

For he explicitly declares that Cyprian had not yet been regenerated by Baptism when he performed these things:

> “The second birth had not opened his eyes, but through the mere preparation for the light he was overcoming the former and ancient darkness.”

Shortly after the words quoted above, Cyprian is called “a man still untrained in the faith, and one who perhaps was not yet trusted.” The same conclusion follows from these words:

> “The threshing preceded the sowing, the vintage the vine-shoot, the fruits the root.…”

And below:

> “But what would he do as a bishop for the poor, whom he loved as a catechumen?”

Tillemont, however, a writer of the keenest judgment, believes that this testimony of Pontius—which he admittedly acknowledges ought not to be called into question—can scarcely be reconciled with the *Epistle to Donatus*. There, as we have just seen, Cyprian declares that at the beginning of his conversion he could not attain even in thought the correction of his morals and transformation of his life, much less begin with such fervent first efforts:

> “In despair of better things,” he says, “I favored my evils as though they were already my own and native to me.”

Moreover, he attributes the correction of his morals to Baptism and says that “after, with the aid of the water of generation, the stain of his former age had been washed away and light from above had poured itself into his cleansed and purified breast,” he then recognized that “what had previously seemed difficult was easy, and that what had been thought impossible could be accomplished.” How, then, could he have acquired so many ornaments of virtue before Baptism?

To resolve this difficulty, it must be observed, first, that Tillemont somewhat inaccurately refers to the beginnings of Cyprian’s Christian profession those doubtful thoughts which drew him this way and that before his conversion. For he did not yet believe in Christ when his mind was thus wavering; rather, as he himself relates, he “lay in darkness and blind night; tossed upon the sea of the restless world, he drifted uncertainly with wandering steps,” “ignorant of his own life, estranged from truth and light.” [Col. 0080] Pontius is therefore readily reconciled with Cyprian; nor is it surprising that the former testifies that Cyprian, after he had surrendered himself to the truth, soared to the summit of virtue, although Cyprian himself had despaired of reforming his conduct before receiving the gift of faith.

Second, Cyprian was not wrong to attribute the renewal of his soul and his new creation to Baptism, although he approached Baptism already furnished with many virtues. For ecclesiastical usage has always spoken in this way: although no one was admitted to Baptism except after displaying many signs of a reformed life, nevertheless renewal itself and the new creation were said to be fruits of Baptism. Hence the statement of Cyril of Jerusalem in Catechesis III (p. 45): “You descended dead in sins; you ascend made alive in righteousness.” Yet there is no doubt that among the catechumens instructed by Cyril, not a few had already made great progress in virtue; and perhaps some had even bound themselves by a vow of continence, as the most learned editor observes in his notes on Catechesis IV (p. 62). It is not the purpose of this undertaking to explain the mode of argument customarily employed by the holy Fathers and theologians; but it is certainly clear from it that Pontius and Cyprian do not conflict with one another when the former relates the illustrious deeds performed by Cyprian while preparing himself for Baptism, and the latter assigns to Baptism whatever he had attained both in the administration of Baptism itself and in the preceding meditation and discipline. I would also add whatever he attained in the sacrament of Confirmation and in communion in the body and blood of Christ, two sacraments which were customarily conferred together with Baptism.

The year in which Cyprian was converted and baptized must be estimated from the beginning of his episcopate. For, as Pontius says, “while still a neophyte and, as was thought, a novice, he was chosen for the office of the priesthood and the rank of the episcopate.” Therefore, since he was made bishop in 248 or 249, as we shall presently see, his Baptism may suitably be assigned to the year 244 or 245. Others assign it to the year 246, but nothing about these matters appears capable of being established with certainty. It is futile, moreover, to inquire at what season of the year he was baptized. Pearson and certain others think that he was initiated into this sacrament between Easter and Pentecost, “because in Africa this period was appointed for administering the baths of Baptism.” But although these days were especially consecrated to Baptism, nothing prevented Baptism from being administered at other times if reasons arose either for postponing it beyond the solemn days or even for anticipating them. In his book *On Baptism*, Tertullian proves that there is no impropriety in receiving Baptism outside the solemn days for just reasons:

> “Easter,” he says, “provides the most solemn day for Baptism. . . . Thereafter Pentecost is a very ample period for administering the baths. . . . For the rest, every day belongs to the Lord; every hour and every season is suitable for Baptism. If solemnity makes a difference, grace makes none.”

St. Gregory Nazianzen, however, sharply rebukes sluggish postponers of Baptism in Oration XL, and does not approve their customary sayings: “I am waiting for the feast of Lights; I esteem the feast of Easter more highly; I shall wait for Pentecost. It is better to be [Col. 0081] baptized with Christ, to return to life with Christ on the day of the Resurrection, and to honor the coming of the Spirit.”

Pontius says that Cyprian, while still a layman, performed many deeds after the examples of the righteous of old, and that if he saw some illustrious deed of theirs confirmed and praised by the authority of Scripture, he attempted to attain it through imitation. That Cyprian was adorned with the gift of prophecy is attested by the many things foreknown and foretold by him for the benefit of the Church. Yet there are those who infer from the *Letter to Donatus*, which he wrote soon after his Baptism, that even then he had become a participant in this gift and in several others. For he recalls those gifts and exhorts others to attain them in such a way that he does not appear to have lacked them himself:

> “Let only our breast thirst and lie open,” he says. “As much receptive faith as we bring there, so much overflowing grace do we drink in. From this there is now granted the power, with sober chastity, an uncorrupted mind, a pure voice, and sincere virtue, to extinguish the venom of poisons for the healing of the afflicted; to cleanse away, by restored health, the stains upon deranged minds; to command peace for the hostile, calm for the violent, and gentleness for the raging; and, with threatening rebukes, to compel unclean and wandering spirits which have entered into men in order to overcome them to make confession, etc.”

### III.—ON THE STUDIES AND WRITINGS OF ST. CYPRIAN FROM HIS BAPTISM UNTIL HIS ORDINATION

There is no doubt that Cyprian devoted the whole period that elapsed from his Baptism until his ordination to reading the Scriptures, studying ecclesiastical writers, and meditating upon and gathering together all those things which he later brought forth publicly and before the eyes of the whole Church. Among ecclesiastical writers, he appears to have loved Tertullian especially. Everyone knows what Jerome relates in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: that he had seen

> “a certain Paul of Concordia, a town in Italy, an old man who said that, when he himself was quite young, he had seen at Rome the secretary of the blessed Cyprian, who was then already advanced in years; and that this man used to tell him that Cyprian never allowed a single day to pass without reading Tertullian, and often said to him, ‘Give me the master,’ meaning Tertullian.”

But if Cyprian was so devoted to reading Tertullian, he exercised no less diligence in guarding against—or rather refuting—his errors. For, to say nothing of the unity of the Church, which Tertullian violated and Cyprian vigorously defended, there are as many barbs directed against Tertullian as there are statements by the holy Martyr concerning just indulgence toward the lapsed.

Not long after his Baptism, Cyprian sharpened his intellect for the defense of religion and the formation of morals. To this period belong the *Letter to Donatus* and the book *On the Vanity of Idols*. Supreme eloquence certainly shines forth in Cyprian’s other works; they possess gravity of thought and splendor of language. But the *Letter to Donatus* was composed with such artifice and adorned with so many elegant pictures that it hardly recalls those periods when Cyprian, occupied with conducting and discussing affairs of the greatest importance, no longer elaborated exquisite embellishments [Col. 0082] but poured forth the riches of his discourse without cosmetics or artificial coloring. Hence Augustine excellently says in Book IV, chapter 14, of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> “There is something of this kind,” he says, “in an epistle of the most blessed Cyprian. I think that this either happened or was done deliberately so that posterity might know what sort of language the soundness of Christian doctrine recalled from such excess and restrained within a graver and more modest eloquence—the kind securely loved, devoutly sought, and most difficult to achieve in his subsequent writings.”

Pontius lists this book first among Cyprian’s works when he says that Cyprian demonstrated “the benefit of grace advancing through faith.” Although Cyprian alone speaks, a certain dialogue form is nevertheless discernible. At Donatus’ request, Cyprian delivers the discourse he had promised during the pleasant vintage season, in a most delightful garden. He describes admirably what he had been before Baptism and what Baptism had accomplished in him; and, to commend the magnitude of the benefit received from Christ, he elegantly portrays the vices and dangers of the world. He brings his discourse to an end when the sun is already declining. Then, so that the rest of the day might be passed in gladness, he exhorts Donatus, who possessed a retentive memory and a melodious voice, to begin the Psalms according to custom at their sober banquet.

Donatus therefore appears to have been not merely Cyprian’s friend but also a member of his household. He knew what the death of crimes and the life of virtues had taken away from Cyprian and what they had conferred upon him. He had enrolled his name in the camp of the heavenly army; and since nothing was so pleasing to his ears as that which is pleasing to God, he was wonderfully captivated by Cyprian’s discourses.

Around the same period appears to have been written the book *On the Vanity of Idols*, in which many passages closely imitated, and some translated word for word, occur from Tertullian’s books against the pagans and from the dialogue of Minucius Felix. Certain statements in this book that were expressed with insufficient precision recall the beginnings of his conversion—for example, when Cyprian says that kingdoms change by lot, that Christ had to suffer, and that, after suffering, he returned again to the realms above.

### IV.—CYPRIAN IMMEDIATELY RECEIVES THE PRESBYTERATE AND PRIESTHOOD.—IN WHAT YEAR HE WAS ORDAINED BISHOP.—HIS ACTS AND WRITINGS AT THE BEGINNING OF HIS EPISCOPATE

Pontius observes that, because of Cyprian’s exceptional progress in virtue, the apostolic precept that neophytes should not be raised to the priesthood was not observed in his case: “He immediately received the presbyterate and priesthood,” he says; “for who would not believe that every degree of honor was due to one who believed with such a mind?” He adds that Cyprian performed many illustrious deeds as a presbyter, but he did not hand them down to our memory.

I readily agree with Pearson and Fell that the three books of *Testimonies* were written by Cyprian as a presbyter, or at least I would believe that they were written at the beginning of his episcopate. For in them there is no trace of those positions which Cyprian later defended with such ardor: whether when, against Felicissimus, he maintained that the lapsed were not to be received without penance, or, against Novatian, that they were not to be excluded from the hope of pardon; whether when he upheld the unity of the Church against both; [Col. 0083] or when he contended that Baptism outside the Church was null and invalid.

In the third book he produces certain testimonies of Scripture against heretics and schismatics, but he would have been much more abundant and vehement if he had written amid the very conflagration and disturbances stirred up by heretics. Furthermore, what he says in Book III, chapter 28—“That one who has sinned against God cannot be forgiven in the Church”—although I hope it was suitably explained in chapter 9 of the preface, nevertheless reveals a mind less attentive to the controversy raised by Novatian. Fell observes that the testimonies of Scripture in these books are not cited in the same manner as in Cyprian’s other works, nor are the books of Scripture designated by the same names; from this he confirms that they were written before Cyprian’s other works.

They are dedicated to Quirinus, whom Cyprian calls his son and at whose request he arranged the testimonies of Scripture under certain specified headings, adding nothing of his own except the titles and the prefaces placed before the first and third books. Those who deny that these books belong to Cyprian—or at least deny that the third, published by Erasmus, belongs to him—are refuted in Baluze’s first observation on these books, which is well worth reading.

Cyprian did not remain long in the rank of presbyter. A little later, as is clear from the testimony of Pontius, upon the death of the bishop of Carthage, he was chosen to succeed him “by the judgment of God and the favor of the people.” Yet he was not easily persuaded to undertake so great a burden. Rather,

> “when the whole people, under the Lord’s inspiration, sprang forward in love and honor toward him, he humbly withdrew, yielding to his seniors and judging himself unworthy of the title of so great an honor.”

But because the zeal of the people was necessarily kindled all the more toward him, because a numerous brotherhood besieged the doors of his house, and solicitous affection surrounded every approach, he was compelled to yield to the divine will, signified by so many manifest indications.

Although the episcopate was imposed upon him against his will and while he sought to flee it, there were some who conspired to oppose his election. Among them five presbyters in particular made their wickedness notorious. The indignation of the people blazed against Cyprian’s detractors, as is clear from Letter XL; but Cyprian omitted nothing in his effort to restore their embittered minds to health, “counting them among his closest friends and intimates, to the astonishment of many,” as Pontius says. Yet those five presbyters nourished the poison they had conceived in their very marrow, and after several years it violently erupted in an organized schism.

Augustine, in Book II, chapter 7, of *On Baptism*, calls Agrippinus Cyprian’s predecessor. But Cyprian did not succeed him immediately: first, because in Letter LXXIII he says that many years and a long period had already passed since a decree concerning the rejection of heretical baptism had been made in council under Agrippinus; and second, because in Letter LV he calls Donatus his predecessor, just as he calls Fabian the predecessor of Cornelius. It is therefore most probable that Cyprian immediately succeeded Donatus.

In Letter LV, written in the year 252, Cyprian says that he had “already proved himself to his people during four years in the episcopate.” From this those who have treated his career conclude that he was ordained in the year 248. Yet, if we calculate the matter more precisely, it is not as certain and established as those learned men [Col. 0084] suppose. It could very well have happened that, although ordained at the beginning of 249, he counted four years of his episcopate in Letter LV, which could scarcely have been written before July 252. For Cyprian customarily counts begun years as complete ones. In Letter XL he calls the period from January or February 250 until Easter 251 “two years”; similarly, in Letter LIII he interprets it as “three years.”

Therefore, if he had been ordained around Easter 249, he could have counted four years in July 252. That he was already bishop around Easter 249 is clear from Letter XXIV, written during his withdrawal, in which he says that on Easter Day he had once and again assigned the reading to Saturus. Since this Easter cannot refer to the year 250—for Cyprian was then absent—it must refer to the year 249. But perhaps, when he assigned the reading to Saturus, he was newly ordained; and nothing prevents us from saying that he was ordained at the beginning of 249. If, however, he received ordination in 248—which I do not deny could very well have happened—he certainly received it not long before July. For, according to his custom, he would have counted five years, not four, at the beginning of July 252 if he had been ordained in May 248.

Cyprian devoted the period from the beginning of his episcopate until the persecution of Decius to reforming the conduct of his people and upholding the laws of discipline. For in Letter LV he says that he had served “amid the peace of discipline.” Since he always showed the greatest concern for virgins, some appropriately assign the book *On the Dress of Virgins* to the beginning of his episcopate. Others maintain that the words, “We exhort them more by affection than by authority,” are more fitting for a presbyter than for a bishop. Pearson, however, attributes these words to Cyprian’s modesty and observes that episcopal authority is vigorous in other passages, as when Cyprian says: “Listen, therefore, virgins, as to a parent; listen, I beseech you, to one who alike teaches and admonishes you.”

Rigaltius places this book after the persecution of Decius, relying upon the argument that Pontius lists it among those works of Cyprian which the Church would have lacked if Cyprian had not escaped the violence of the pagans by a prudent withdrawal. But Rigaltius did not notice that Pontius likewise mentions the book *To Donatus* in the same manner, although no one denies that it was written at the beginning of Cyprian’s conversion. It is therefore clear that Pontius lists Cyprian’s works as occasion offers, not merely those written after his withdrawal.

Around the same period—that is, before the persecution—Letter LXVI is thought to have been written. Cyprian addressed it “to the presbyters and deacons and the people residing at Furni,” concerning a certain Geminius Victor, who in his will had appointed the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian. Cyprian orders the observance of what his predecessor bishops had long before decreed:

> “That no brother, upon departing this life, should appoint a cleric as guardian or administrator; and that if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him, nor should the sacrifice for his repose be celebrated.”

Cyprian had deliberated on the matter with the fellow bishops who were present and the fellow presbyters who sat with him. Affairs often brought African bishops [Col. 0085] to Carthage, with whom the bishop of Carthage could maintain, as it were, a continuous council. It is sufficiently clear, as Pearson and Tillemont observe, that this letter was written during a time of peace. For Geminius would not have entrusted the guardianship of his children, while persecution was raging, to a presbyter whose dignity and office would have cast him into the midst of danger. It is probable that the Geminius Faustinus whom Victor appointed guardian was afterward made bishop of the same city. For Geminius of Furni attended the Council of Carthage in the year 256.

Pearson declares that three other letters were written before the year 250: Letter LXI to Euchratius, concerning a certain actor who, although he had ceased performing in the theater, continued to teach his craft; Letter LXII to Pomponius, concerning virgins who had been discovered in the same bed with men, one of whom was a deacon; and Letter LXV to Rogatianus, concerning a certain deacon who had offered him insults and injuries, without regard for either his dignity or his age.

If these letters were written at the beginning of Cyprian’s episcopate, his reputation for wisdom must already have been supreme, since bishops everywhere sought his judgments. But it must be acknowledged that these letters contain no indication requiring them to be assigned to this period. I would rather believe that the letter to Rogatianus was written after the disturbances stirred up by Novatus and his associates; for Cyprian appears to have them in view when he says:

> “For these are the beginnings of heretics and the origins and endeavors of schismatics whose thoughts are evil: they take pleasure in themselves and in their proud swelling despise the one set over them. Thus men withdraw from the Church; thus a profane altar is established outside; thus they rebel against the peace of Christ and against the ordination and unity of God.”

Cyprian’s wisdom shines forth in these letters. In Letter LXI he declares that it accords neither with the divine majesty nor with evangelical discipline for an actor to receive communion. If poverty compels him to practice this craft, he should be supported at the Church’s expense, provided that he is content with more frugal food; or, if the Church there cannot bear these expenses, Cyprian invites him to his own church.

In Letter LXII he praises Pomponius for excluding from communion the deacon who had often remained with a virgin, as well as the others who had become accustomed to sleep with virgins. He advises that the virgins be carefully examined by midwives; and if they are found to be virgins, they should, after receiving communion, be admitted into the Church—provided, however, that they have thus far performed penance for this illicit sleeping together and have separated from one another. He threatens a graver censure if they return to the same men or live together with them in one house and beneath the same roof. He imposes full penance upon those who have been corrupted and declares that, if they obstinately persist, they can never be admitted into the Church.

In Letter LXV he praises the humility of Rogatianus because, although by the vigor of his episcopate and the authority of his chair he could have punished the deacon, he instead referred his complaints to Cyprian. He decrees that the deacon must “perform penance for his audacity, acknowledge the honor of the priest,” [Col. 0086] and make satisfaction in complete humility to the bishop set over him.

Here Cyprian’s authority is readily discerned: he is not so much offering counsel as issuing commands and orders, both because of the dignity of his see and because he gave his judgments after taking counsel with bishops and presbyters. For the letters to Pomponius and Rogatianus were written not only in Cyprian’s name but also in the names of the bishops with whom he had deliberated concerning the matters proposed. Nor is it at all surprising that he consulted bishops on weightier affairs, since from the beginning of his episcopate he had determined to do nothing according to his private judgment without the counsel of the clergy and the consent of the people.

From what we shall say hereafter, anyone will readily perceive how great Cyprian’s diligence and assiduity were in this respect, whether clerics were to be ordained or some other important matter undertaken. Pontius praises in his episcopate his devotion and vigor, his mercy and discipline, his grave yet cheerful countenance, neither gloomy severity nor excessive affability, a mind averse to secular pride yet free from affected and sordid poverty, and, finally, his supreme charity toward the poor, whom he had loved while still a catechumen.

### V.—ON THE PERSECUTION OF DECIUS AND ITS BEGINNINGS, AND ON THE GREAT NUMBER OF THE LAPSED AND THE CONFESSORS

Chosen during a time of peace, Cyprian, as he himself testifies in Letter LV, passed one year, perhaps with some additional months, in this condition of affairs. Around the beginning of the year 250, the presbyter Novatus was summoned before Cyprian for trial because he had kicked his wife in the womb and caused the child to be expelled by miscarriage, and because of other crimes. The day of the hearing had already arrived, but the persecution supervened (Letter XLIX). Pearson makes much of this example of a married presbyter. Yet Novatus did not marry his wife while he was a presbyter; nor, because he retained her as a presbyter, was the Church thereby forbidden to choose presbyters from among the continent.

The persecution of Decius opened the widest field for Cyprian’s virtues. We must say a few things about it before tracing Cyprian’s actions during these most troublesome times. After cruelly killing the two Philips and seizing the empire, Decius judged that nothing had to be done before—or rather, with greater urgency than—directing every effort of his rule against the Christian religion, which had grown wonderfully under the Philips and the preceding emperors. Accordingly, both from his hatred of the Philips and from his longing for the Roman superstitions—upon whose ruins he saw this religion being built—he began to make propitiatory offerings with the blood of Christians.

We learn that the persecution began simultaneously with the reign of Decius from an authoritative witness, Dionysius of Alexandria, who bore a very great part in defending and protecting the Church during this persecution. “But immediately,” he says in Eusebius (*History*, Book VI, chapter 41), “the change in that rule which had been most kindly disposed toward us was announced, and the gravest terror of threats was directed against us. And now the emperor’s edict was at hand, etc.” Lactantius testifies to the same in chapter 4 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, as does Orosius in Book VI, chapter 21.

Therefore, since no trace of persecution exists before January [Col. 0087] of the year 250—and it is established that Pope Fabian suffered at Rome on the twentieth day of that month—Tillemont does not agree with the learned author of the *Cyprianic Annals*, who thinks that Philip was killed in August 249 and that Decius assumed the purple at the end of July. It is indeed reasonably maintained that both Philips died before the end of 249 and did not reign seven years, as Eusebius believed. For in the *Code of Justinian* (Book IV, title 16) there survives a rescript issued in the name of Decius on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, when Aemilianus and Aquilinus were consuls. The Philips therefore appear already to have perished by then. But it is not proved that this occurred in August. Indeed, Tillemont cites from the *Code of Justinian* (Book VI, title 36) a law issued by Philip on the Ides of October, in the consulship of the same Aemilianus, to whom Peregrinus is erroneously assigned as colleague.

But whatever beginning may be assigned to the reign of Decius, it cannot be denied that the persecution was raging at the beginning of the year 250. At first it lacked the cruelty of tortures—not, indeed, everywhere, but at least at Carthage, where the confessors were initially subjected to no penalties other than imprisonment and exile. After a few months had passed, however, no kind of torment was absent. Thus Aurelius, as Cyprian says in Letter XXXIII,

> “engaged in combat before the eyes of a few when he was being driven into exile; but afterward he deserved to engage in combat in the forum with still more illustrious virtue, so that after overcoming the magistrates he also overcame the proconsul, and after exile he conquered tortures.”

Tillemont thinks that the persecution raged earlier at Rome than in Africa, and that Moses and Maximus, Roman presbyters, had already been cast into prison when the persecution began in Africa, although according to Bucherius’ *Pontifical* they were imprisoned after the martyrdom of Pope Fabian. There is certainly no inconsistency in supposing that the persecution broke out earlier at Rome than in the provinces. Yet the words of Cyprian upon which this most learned man relies do not demonstrate precisely what he thinks: namely, that the Roman confessors were imprisoned before those of Carthage. They show only that suffering and torture began at Rome before they began at Carthage. For Cyprian speaks as follows in Letter XXV, to Moses, Maximus, and the other confessors:

> “For you, made the foremost men and leaders in the battle of our time, set in motion the standards of the heavenly army. By your virtues you inaugurated the spiritual conflict which God has now willed to be waged. You were the first to break the assaults of the rising war by immovable strength and unshaken steadfastness. From you arose the happy beginnings of the struggle; from you began the auspices of victory. Here it has happened that martyrdoms were consummated through torture; but one who, by preceding others in the encounter, became an example of virtue to his brethren shares honor with the martyrs. From there you passed on to us the crowns woven by your own hands, and from the cup of salvation you gave drink to your brethren.”

Tillemont denies that it follows from these words that Moses and Maximus were the first of all to confess at Rome, since Fabian had died as a martyr before they were cast into prison. He thinks only that they gained this praise before the Carthaginians. Yet Cyprian makes no exception, and he declares that the confessors to whom he was writing, “the foremost men and leaders in the battle of our time,” had set the standards in motion. It is therefore far better to understand these words, as their entire context requires, of the martyrs’ steadfast endurance under torture.

In his book *On the Lapsed*, Cyprian traces the cause of the persecution to the sins of Christians. A long peace had so corrupted their ancient devotion that in very many persons greed for money, love of luxury, frauds and robberies, marriages with unbelievers, perjuries, hostilities, and curses were justly blamed. Corruption had infected many bishops as well. Among them Cyprian rebukes not only the administration of secular business and profitable commercial dealings conducted through foreign provinces, but also fraud, robbery, and usury.

For the correction of so many evils, God employed the persecution of Decius, which wonderfully exercised the devotion and steadfastness of the good and exposed both the cowardice and the inward stains of those who were Christians more in name than in life. This persecution possessed the distinctive characteristic of embracing absolutely all Christians—at least at Carthage—so that no one emerged from it except as either an illustrious confessor of Christ, a faithless worshiper of idols, or a *libellaticus*. For specified days were appointed to individuals for the testing of their faith, as Cyprian says in *On the Lapsed* (p. 182). Thus not only the person who boldly presented himself, but also the one who “did not make his declaration within the appointed day and withdrew after abandoning his property, confessed himself to be a Christian.”

Accordingly, there was no middle course: either life had to be poured out for Christ, or at least property had to be cast away; otherwise both could be retained only at the price of crime. That the same occurred at Alexandria is evident from Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius’ *History* (Book VI, chapter 41). The Roman confessors lament “the ruin of many throughout almost the whole world, and the great crime which spread through almost the whole world with incredible devastation” (Letter XXVI). “Look upon almost the whole world laid waste,” says the Roman clergy (Letter XXXI), “and everywhere the remnants and ruins of those who have been cast down lie prostrate.”

Cyprian likewise laments in Letter VI “the hostile tempest” which had “struck down the greater part” of his people and had also touched a portion of the clergy, although the clerics fell later. With the deepest grief he recalls in *On the Lapsed* (p. 183) that

> “at the very first words of the threatening enemy, a very great number of the brethren betrayed their faith; they were not cast down by the violence of persecution, but cast themselves down by a voluntary fall. They did not wait,” he says, “even to deny when questioned or to ascend the tribunal after being arrested. Many were defeated before the battle line and cast down without an encounter; nor did they even leave themselves the excuse that they appeared to sacrifice to idols unwillingly. Of their own accord they ran to the forum and voluntarily hastened toward death. . . . What of those who, when evening was approaching, were postponed by the magistrates, yet even begged that their destruction should not be delayed? . . . For many, their own destruction was not enough: by mutual exhortations the people were driven to their ruin, and death was offered from one to another in a deadly cup.”

Yet not all the lapsed had led blameworthy lives before the persecution. Cyprian testifies in Letter XXVII that among the lapsed there were some who were “humble and gentle, trembling and fearing God, who had always acted gloriously and nobly in the Church, and who credited their work to the Lord.”

The cowardice of so many people running from the sacred rites of Christ to the altars of demons certainly branded the Christian name with great disgrace. On the other hand, it received very great splendor not only from the courage and steadfastness of those who overcame dreadful tortures and unheard-of punishments for Christ, but also from the prudent flight of countless others who preferred to cast away their possessions rather than obey impious commands and who, in Cyprian’s judgment, are numbered among the confessors. Therefore, although at no other time had so great a multitude of the lapsed been seen, never had there been so great a number of confessors. Moreover, although the persecution raged everywhere, the demon’s arts did not everywhere succeed.

For the Roman clergy write in Letter III to the clergy of Carthage that the Roman Church stood strong in faith and that only some had fallen under the compulsion of fear. This also must be observed to the praise of religion: very few bishops fell, while countless others steadfastly guided the ship of the Church amid dreadful storms; and when peace was restored, they treated the wounds of the lapsed in such a way that those who had succumbed to the persecution of Decius, when the battle was renewed under Gallus and Volusian, proved victorious, as the author of the book *Against Novatian the Heretic* testifies.

### VI.—IN WHAT THE OFFENSE OF THOSE CALLED *LIBELLATICI* CONSISTED

While the persecution of Decius was raging, there appeared in Africa a new class of the lapsed who were called *Libellatici*, and they have provided material for the conjectures of learned men. Rigaltius, in his notes on Cyprian’s Letters XIV and XXXI, and Natalis Alexander (vol. II, p. 635) thought that those were called *Libellatici* who, after paying money to the judge, received a certificate of security and thus purchased exemption both from the imposed law requiring sacrifice and from the penalties threatened against those who resisted.

But this opinion is so entirely destitute of every supporting argument, and has been so thoroughly broken down and rejected by learned men, that it requires no new labor of refutation. For who could persuade himself that a deed was a grave sin requiring expiation through penance when it was approved by examples from Scripture and by canon 12 of Peter of Alexandria, and was never forbidden except among the Montanists, who condemned flight from persecution as equivalent to a crime?

Many other conjectures have been advanced concerning the *Libellatici*, among which judgment is not so easy. The author of the *Cyprianic Annals* (p. 17) thinks that the *Libellatici* “denied Christ in officially recorded proceedings before the magistrates.” St. Augustine interprets the *Libellatici* as those “who during the persecution had declared through written certificates that they would offer incense” (Book IV, *On Baptism*, no. 6). Baronius, under the year 253, denies that the *Libellatici* were so called because they had submitted certificates, but holds that they had received them; he nevertheless contends that they had denied Christ. Tillemont (vol. I, note 3 on the persecution of Decius) doubts whether they submitted or received certificates. He suspects that they both submitted and received them, and proves that the learned author of the book *On Frequent Communion* held the same opinion.

Many others think that the *Libellatici* were so called from the certificates they submitted, among them Bosquetus (Book III, *The Gallican Church*, p. 132); some also maintain that they signed the public records. Since this variety of opinions leaves freedom for conjecture and investigation, I shall not hesitate to explain what seems true to me. I therefore think that the *Libellatici* neither verbally nor in writing promised that they would commit any impious act, nor declared that they had committed one. Rather, they were blamed and subjected to just penance because they obtained certificates of security from the magistrates under this condition: that it should be recorded in the public acts that they had sacrificed and denied Christ, although they had done neither.

That the offense of the *Libellatici* consisted in this is clear from the fact that their fraud is compared with the proposal made to Eleazar by the king’s servants. Cyprian says in the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom* (p. 271):

> “And lest anyone embrace the evil gift of those who deceive him when an opportunity is offered by means of a certificate or anything else through which he may practice deception, Eleazar too must not be passed over, etc.”

The *Libellatici*, therefore, committed what Eleazar refused to commit: they consented to be said to have sacrificed, thus proving wholly unlike that illustrious old man. But if they had verbally pronounced or declared in writing that they had sacrificed and denied Christ, Cyprian would have warned against an act of that kind as open impiety, not as cunning simulation.

The same is clear both from those passages in which the guilt of the *Libellatici* is mitigated and in some measure excused, and from those in which it is more severely chastised. When the peace granted to the *Libellatici* at the Council of Carthage was criticized by the followers of Novatian, Cyprian defended the council’s action as follows in Epistle LII, to Antonianus:

> “Since, therefore, even among those who sacrificed,” he says (p. 70), “there is great diversity, what mercilessness and how bitter a severity it is to associate the *Libellatici* with those who sacrificed, when the person who received a certificate says: ‘I had previously read, and had learned from the bishop’s exposition, that one must not sacrifice to idols and that a servant of God ought not to worship images; and therefore, in order not to do what was unlawful, when an opportunity of obtaining a certificate was offered—though I would not have accepted even that had the opportunity not been pointed out—I either went to the magistrate or, when someone else went, gave him instructions, saying that I was a Christian, that it was not lawful for me to sacrifice, that I could not come to the altars of the devil, and that I would therefore pay a fee so that I should not do what is unlawful.’ Yet now even this man, who has been stained by a certificate, after learning through our admonitions that he ought not to have done even this—although his hand is pure and his mouth has not been polluted by any contamination from the deadly food—nevertheless has a polluted conscience; on hearing us, he weeps and laments; he is now made aware that he has sinned; and, having been deceived not so much by crime as by error, he declares that henceforth he is instructed and prepared.”

From these words it is clear:

1. That the *Libellatici* took their name not from certificates given by them, but from certificates received by them.

2. That they had secretly confessed to the magistrate that they were Christians, and that the entire matter had been handled with such careful accommodation that neither did the Christian think he was saying or doing anything impious, nor did the judge expose himself to danger.

3. That neither the hand nor the mouth of the *Libellatici* had been polluted [Col. 0091], but only their conscience, evidently because, with their knowledge, a fictitious crime had been entered in the public records. But if they had testified orally or in writing that they had sacrificed and denied Christ, would Cyprian have regarded their tongues and hands as innocent of crime and pure?

4. Finally, those who conclude from this epistle that there were two classes of *Libellatici*, one of which had sinned much more gravely than the other, are refuted by the very point they consider most favorable to themselves. For when Cyprian observes that there is great diversity “among those who sacrificed,” the only distinction he draws among the *Libellatici* is that some had gone to the magistrate while others had commissioned someone else to go. He does not doubt that both had sinned equally. Hence peace was granted to both at the same time at the Council of Carthage, which was held after Easter in the year 251. At that council, moreover, since the bishops had calculated every consideration with the utmost exactness, as Cyprian attests in this Epistle LII, they would not have dealt in the same way with all the *Libellatici* if there had been a marked diversity among them. Cyprian does not state what sin the two groups of *Libellatici* had committed—both those who had dealt with the magistrate in person and those who had acted through others—for the matter was very well known to Antonianus. Yet this much, at least, is established by his words: their sin was of such a kind that they did not even think they had sinned. But it is utterly incredible that Christians imbued with the finest moral precepts should have been so blind as to believe that they could say or write without committing a crime, “I have sacrificed to the gods; I have denied Christ,” and should have learned that they ought not to have done this only after being admonished by Cyprian. The impiety of such a deed is so manifest that it could have escaped absolutely no one except a person who had cast off every sense of religion.

The Roman clergy, in Epistle XXXI among the Cyprianic letters, chastises the guilt of the *Libellatici* with no gentle hand, yet indicates nothing other than what we have just observed:

> “That we do not say this falsely,” it states, “has been proved by our earlier letters, in which we presented our judgment to you in a lucid exposition, both against those who had betrayed themselves as unbelievers by the unlawful declaration contained in their impious certificates—as though they imagined that they would escape those ensnaring snares of the devil, although they were held no less than if they had approached the impious altars, by the very fact that they had formally attested to this—and also against those who had caused official records to be made, although they had not been present when they were drawn up, since by giving instructions that they be recorded in this manner they had, in effect, made themselves present. For the man who ordered it to be done is not innocent of the crime, nor is one free from guilt when, by his consent, a crime—although not committed by himself—is nevertheless publicly recorded. And since the entire sacrament of faith is understood to be comprised in the confession of Christ’s name, he who seeks deceptive tricks as an excuse has denied Christ; and he who wishes to appear to have complied with edicts or laws issued against the Gospel has already obeyed by the very fact that he wished to appear to have obeyed.”

This passage is plainly the twin of the other passage taken from the Epistle to Antonianus, although the one inclines toward the utmost leniency and the other toward the utmost severity. The Roman clergy attests that the *Libellatici* were so disposed in mind that they imagined they would escape the snares of the devil [Col. 0092]. This assuredly would not have occurred to Christians if they had either uttered anything impious orally or testified to it in writing.

The Roman clergy distinguishes two classes of *Libellatici*, just as in the Epistle to Antonianus: those who had been present when the record was written, and those who had not even dared or been able to be present. Both are blamed equally, because the latter, although “they had not been present when the records were made, had in effect made themselves present by giving instructions that they be recorded in this manner.” Now no one would say of those who were not present when the record was written that they had submitted a certificate or made any impious oral declaration. They are blamed only because they had ordered that the records be drawn up; because, by their “consent, a crime—although not committed by themselves—was nevertheless publicly recorded”; because they had “sought deceptive tricks as an excuse”; and because they had wished “to appear to have complied with edicts or laws issued against the Gospel.”

Those who were present, therefore, since their case is precisely the same, committed nothing more than allowing a fictitious crime to be entered in the public records before their own eyes. Consequently, when the Roman clergy says that they were held “no less than if they had approached the impious altars, by the very fact that they had formally attested to this,” this must not be understood as though they had orally declared that they had approached the altars, but as meaning that they had consented to the existence of public testimony to a crime they had not committed. In a similar sense, the same Roman clergy says that those “who had not been present when the records were made” had nevertheless caused the records to be made.

The statement concerning Martialis in Epistle LXVIII (p. 119) must be understood in the same way, as must also this passage from the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 190):

> “Nor should those who, although they did not contaminate their hands with accursed sacrifices, nevertheless polluted their conscience with certificates, flatter themselves so as to avoid doing penance. That declaration is the act of one who denies; it is the attestation of a Christian who had renounced what he was. He said that he had done whatever another actually committed by doing it.”

This passage does not differ from the judgment of the Roman clergy against those “who had betrayed themselves as unbelievers by the unlawful declaration contained in their impious certificates.” The *Libellaticus* said that he had done whatever another actually committed by doing it—not because he orally declared that he had denied Christ and sacrificed, for he told the judge that he was a Christian and that it was not lawful for him to sacrifice or to come to the altars of the devil, as we read in Epistle LII—but because that declaration in the certificate is, in a certain sense, the declaration of a person who denies.

For after examining the old editions and eight manuscript codices, I found that this passage should be read as follows:

> “And that declaration is the act of one who denies; it is the attestation of a Christian who had renounced what he was,”

evidently in the same sense in which the Roman clergy says that the man who seeks deceptive tricks as an excuse has denied Christ, and that he who wishes to appear to have complied with the edicts has already obeyed by that very fact.

As regards the certificates issued by the judges, it does not appear that the same thing was written in them as in the public records. For the sin of the *Libellatici* would have been more serious if, in addition to the testimony entered in the public records, they had preserved certificates of this kind and displayed them whenever an occasion arose. Yet neither Cyprian nor the Roman clergy charged them with this.

To the considerations of reason employed thus far I shall add one more: it was not customary [Col. 0093] for those who denied the faith to commit that denial to writing; it was merely entered in the official records. Baronius (*ad annum* 304) and Tillemont (vol. V, p. 451) think otherwise and adduce a passage from the *Acts of the Holy Martyrs Agape, Chionia, and Irene*, who are said to have been “ordered to make a written profession of their denial of Christ.” But that “written” denial—in Greek, ἔγγραφος (*engraphos*), for I believe this was the reading of the Greek text—is nothing other than a denial entered in the official records.

Thus in Eusebius (*Hist.* XI, ch. 5), certain women were compelled by the governor to λέγειν ἐγγράφως (*legein engráphōs*), “to confess by testimony spoken for the official record,” that they had been Christians and were aware of the crimes supposedly committed by Christians. The Messalians in Photius (Codex 52) are said to have been convicted ἐγγράφως (*engráphōs*), that is, “by testimony spoken for the official record,” of having returned to their errors. Hence Basil (*On Baptism*, book I, ch. 3) calls the promises by which we are bound in Baptism ὥσπερ ἔγγραφον ὁμολογίαν (*hōsper éngraphon homologían*), “as it were, a kind of formal profession before the official record.” Thus also Optatus (book II, no. 34) says: “The faith and profession of believers, which is drawn up in the records of the angels.”

Although the offense involving certificates acquired its reputation and name chiefly in Africa, it was nevertheless not unknown in other provinces. At Rome, St. Cornelius was accused of this crime by impious schismatics; in Spain, the bishops Basilides and Martialis were convicted of it. Indeed, under Peter of Alexandria in Egypt, a certain class of *Libellatici* occurs, although I do not know whether it differed from the African kind.

Peter of Alexandria (Canon 5) sentences to six months’ penance those who had engaged in pretense, as David also did: ἤτοι ὡς διελθόντες βωμοὺς, ἤτοι ὡς χειρογραφήσαντες, ἤτοι ὡς ἀνθ᾽ ἑαυτῶν βαλόντες ἐθνικούς—“either as though passing through altars, or as though giving a written undertaking, or as though putting forward pagans in their own place.” Peter admits that people of this kind had not openly displayed impiety: καὶ μὴ γυμνῶς ἀπογραψαμένοις τὰ πρὸς ἄρνησιν—“and had not openly subscribed statements tending toward denial”—where ἐπιγραψαμένοις appears to be the proper reading. Zonaras interprets that written undertaking as συνέθεντο θῦσαι (*synéthento thŷsai*), “they agreed that they would sacrifice.” But would such a promise have lacked the appearance of open impiety? I would rather believe that such people, like the *Libellatici* in Africa, accepted from the judges some condition that appeared both safe for the judge and not openly impious to the Christian.

I shall say nothing about another class of *Libellatici* which Baronius (*ad annum* 253) imagined he perceived in Pliny’s letter to Trajan, from which he quotes these words:

> “A document was posted anonymously, containing the names of many persons who denied that they were or had been Christians, etc.”

But Baronius failed to notice that this document had not been submitted by Christians, but by someone who concealed his own name and identified many people by name as Christians, although they denied that they were or had been Christians. Hence Trajan, replying to Pliny, says:

> “Anonymous accusations, however, ought to have no place in any prosecution, for this sets the worst example and does not belong to our age.”

## VII.—CYPRIAN WITHDRAWS DURING THE PERSECUTION FOR THE MOST JUST REASONS

As soon as the edict of Decius was brought to Africa, Cyprian was immediately assailed by the cries of the populace and demanded for the lion [Col. 0094]. By a prudent withdrawal he avoided the fury of the impious, preferring that his crown should be deferred to another time rather than that his presence should add fresh fuel to the fire of persecution. He was sought not once, but repeatedly; on several other occasions popular fury flared up against him in his absence. Pontius attests that he was “demanded for the lion by repeatedly renewed acclamations” and that he “attained the glory of proscription.” Cyprian himself likewise relates that he was “so often demanded and sought” (Epistle VI), “so often demanded for the lion in the circus and in the amphitheater,” and that he had even been proscribed “with the title of his episcopate appended and attached to his name” (Epistle LV):

> “When it was publicly read: ‘If anyone holds or possesses any of the property of Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of the Christians’” (Epistle LXIX).

We do not know where he withdrew. But the Roman presbyters and deacons, deceived by hostile reports, judged his withdrawal somewhat unfairly before they were more fully informed by Cyprian himself about the entire matter. There can scarcely be any doubt that certain others also criticized him; for Pontius would not have defended his action with such zeal if it had been approved by everyone and required no vindication. Perhaps this opportunity for censure was seized long ago, or may even be seized today, if someone assumes the role of censor: namely, that in his absence the greater part of the faithful disgracefully fell, whereas they might have remained more steadfast in the faith—or at least slower to commit that dreadful crime—if they had heard their bishop’s entirely fearless confession or witnessed his illustrious death for Christ.

But in order to repel every reproach from Cyprian regarding a policy that two other most eminent men, Gregory Thaumaturgus and Dionysius of Alexandria, were following at the same time, the following points must be observed.

1. He obeyed the general precept of the Gospel, which he was especially obliged to observe when the persecution was breaking out chiefly against his own name and there was danger that his presence might inflame the fury of the pagans against his congregation.

2. He was warned by God in a particular manner to depart. “For a mind dedicated to God in all things,” says Pontius, “and a faith made subject to divine admonitions believed that, unless he obeyed the Lord, who then commanded him to seek concealment, he would sin even by undergoing the Passion itself.” Cyprian defends himself by reference to the Gospel’s precept in the epistle he wrote to the Roman clergy to vindicate himself; but in another epistle, namely the tenth, he declares that the Lord had commanded him to withdraw.

3. That very great number of brethren who fell in Cyprian’s absence were not compelled by torments and tortures to deny Christ, “but at the very first words of the threatening enemy betrayed their faith,” as we read in the book *On the Lapsed*. Cyprian could not have given better counsel to people so disposed than by exhorting them through his own example to withdraw.

4. Pontius observes that Cyprian was preserved by divine counsel so that, when the Church had suffered the greatest disaster under the persecution of Decius, “he might treat the wounded—men pierced by the enemy’s varied and devastating arts—with the remedy of heavenly medicine, either cutting for a time or soothing them according to the nature of the wound.” The outcome confirmed this. For the author of the book *Against Novatian the Heretic* attests that “those who were wounded in the first battle,” that is, “in the Decian persecution, afterwards [Col. 0095] persevered so bravely in the second battle that, despising the edicts of secular rulers, they remained invincible in this: following the example of the Good Shepherd, they did not fear to surrender their lives and shed their blood, nor did they shrink from any cruelty of the raging tyrant.”

5. Finally, Cyprian was absent in body in such a way that in spirit and solicitude he remained involved in every matter and omitted none of a bishop’s duties. When departing, he had made provision for everything and had distributed money among the clergy “so that several persons might have resources from which they could minister to the needs and afflictions of individuals” (Epistle V).

During his withdrawal, he appears continually to have offered sacrifices, with Victor the deacon serving him, who had accompanied him together with several others (Epistles V, XXXVII). At times several bishops were present, and together with Cyprian they ordained Aurelius and Celerinus, as is clear from Epistles XXXIII and XXXIV. Indeed, he speaks of his sacrifices in such a way that he appears to have gathered a considerable congregation. For he says in Epistle XVI, addressed to the Roman confessors:

> “For our part, remembering you by day and night, both when we offer prayer together with many at the sacrifices and when in our withdrawal we pray in private, we ask from the Lord favor in full measure for your crowns and praises.”

Moreover, when he had entrusted the care of the Church to the presbyters and deacons and, in addition—to use his own words from Epistle XXXVIII—had sent in his place as deputies two bishops, Caldonius and Herculanus, to whom he had joined the presbyters Rogatianus and Numidicus, every matter was reported to him. Nothing was omitted by him that concerned the relief of the poor, the encouragement and at times even the chastisement of the confessors, the repair of the ruin of the lapsed, the maintenance of discipline, and the pacification of the Church. But because different scholars arrange the letters he wrote during his withdrawal in different ways, the matter must be examined by us with more than cursory attention.

## VIII.—THE LETTERS OF THE ROMAN CLERGY SENT TO CARTHAGE AFTER CYPRIAN’S WITHDRAWAL HAD BEEN REPORTED

The Roman presbyters and deacons, to whom supreme responsibility for the administration of affairs had returned after Fabian’s death, learned of Cyprian’s withdrawal from Clementius—or, as Baluzius calls him, Crementius—a subdeacon of Carthage. Since the matter had been reported “with less simplicity and less fidelity,” as Cyprian says in Epistle XV, whether by this subdeacon or by others—for Cyprian does not accuse him—they sent two letters to Carthage by the same Crementius: one to Cyprian concerning the death of Fabian, which has indeed come down to us, and another to Cyprian’s clergy, although Cyprian says that “neither the identity of the writer nor those to whom it was written were clearly stated.”

In this epistle, which occupies third place in Pamelius, although nothing is said of Cyprian by name except in honorable terms, they nevertheless speak of his withdrawal in such a way that they plainly do not approve it; they discuss the marks of good shepherds as though they found them wanting in Cyprian; and, finally, they commend the protection of the flock to the clergy of Carthage as though the church had been widowed of its bishop. It could also have troubled Cyprian that the Romans [Col. 0096] asked the clergy of Carthage to transmit a copy of this letter, or copies of their own, to as many people as possible whenever suitable opportunities arose.

Tillemont dates this letter of the Roman clergy to approximately the month of May. But it is improbable that the Romans informed Cyprian so late of the death of Fabian, who suffered martyrdom on January 20. Even if the persecution had prevented any opportunity to communicate the event, as Tillemont conjectures, there was nevertheless far too much intercourse between Rome and Carthage for “rumor to remain uncertain and opinion to waver in doubt” for four months concerning so notable an event, as Cyprian says in Epistle IV.

Furthermore, from the letter of Celerinus to Lucianus (Epistle XXI among the Cyprianic letters), we learn that sixty-five confessors came to Rome from Carthage shortly after Easter, or perhaps even before Easter, which in that year fell on April 7 according to the cycle of Victorius, or on March 31 according to the cycle of Hippolytus. Yet the Roman clergy indicates in the letter now under discussion that, apart from Clementius the subdeacon, no one had come from Carthage from whom they could learn more certainly about Cyprian’s withdrawal. It is therefore much more probable that this epistle was delivered in March.

But Tillemont objects that in Epistle XV, which is known to have been written in the summer, Cyprian speaks of this letter of the Roman clergy as though he were saying that it had been sent recently. He then asks why, although Cyprian replied to this letter immediately, the Romans wrote back so late; for they had not yet done so when Cyprian wrote Epistle XV.

The word “recently” proves nothing, since its meaning varies according to the perspective from which the matter is considered. In Epistle LXV, Cyprian says that a certain decree of his predecessors was made both long ago and recently. He could therefore say that he had recently received a letter received four months earlier, especially when no other letter had arrived during that entire period.

There is a simple and ready explanation of why the Romans had still not replied to Cyprian in July: they had not yet laid aside their suspicions, and their ears still remained open to hostile reports, as can be seen at the beginning of Epistle XV. They had therefore decided not to answer him; hence, in July, they addressed a letter not to Cyprian himself but to his clergy. Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that they had received Cyprian’s first letter, even if it had not been written before May.

## IX.—CYPRIAN’S FIRST REPLY TO THE LETTER OF THE ROMANS.—THE THIRTEEN LETTERS WRITTEN BEFORE HIS SECOND REPLY AND CONVEYED TO ROME TOGETHER WITH IT; IT IS SHOWN THAT MANY OF THEM ARE LOST

Cyprian immediately answered the first letter of the Roman clergy and congratulated them on Fabian’s glorious end, concerning which rumor had previously been uncertain. As regards the second letter, written to the clergy of Carthage, he judged that the matter must be handled prudently. Since he had noticed that in this letter “neither the identity of the writer nor those to whom it was written were clearly stated,” and since “the handwriting, the meaning, and even the paper itself in that letter disturbed him, lest something should have been either omitted from the original or altered,” he sent the same letter [Col. 0097], in its original form, back to them “so that they might verify whether it was the very letter they had given Clementius the subdeacon to deliver” (Epistle IV).

But when he had ascertained that the letter was genuine, without waiting for a reply from the Romans he wrote again in his own defense and calmly explained the reasons for his actions. He also sent them thirteen letters which he himself had written on various subjects since his withdrawal and which left no room whatever for suspicion of negligence. Cyprian enumerates these letters as follows:

> “And what I have done,” he says in Epistle XV, “is declared to you by the thirteen letters issued at their proper times which I transmitted to you. In them, so far as our humble capacity was able to exert itself according to the law of faith and the fear of God, at the Lord’s prompting, neither counsel to the clergy, nor exhortation to the confessors, nor rebuke to the exiles when it was required, nor our address and persuasion to the entire brotherhood to implore God’s mercy, was lacking. Moreover, after the tortures came, my discourse reached our brethren—whether already tortured or still confined so that they might be tortured—to strengthen and encourage them. Likewise . . . . . I composed letters in which, so far as I could, I recalled the martyrs and confessors by my counsel to the Lord’s precepts. Likewise, the vigor of the priesthood was not lacking toward the presbyters and deacons . . . . . We also composed the spirit of the people themselves, so far as we could . . . ; concerning this I also twice wrote letters to the clergy, etc.”

It is of the greatest importance to identify those thirteen letters among the Cyprianic correspondence and to investigate whether they all survive or whether some have perished. Pearson allows that none whatever is missing. In addition to Epistle V to the clergy, Epistle IX to the confessors, and five other letters concerning the lapsed—namely X, XI, XII, XIII, and XIV—which correspond exactly to the words of Cyprian just quoted, he counts Epistles LXXXI, XXXVII, XXXVI, VIII, VII, and VI among those thirteen letters sent to Rome.

Tillemont, on the contrary, maintains that four of those thirteen letters sent to Rome have perished, and thinks that Epistles VIII, VII, VI, and XXXVI were written later, namely toward the end of this year, 250. Although the loss of Cyprian’s letters is painful to learned men, I shall nevertheless be compelled to increase their sense of loss. For I agree with Tillemont concerning Epistles VIII, VII, VI, and XXXVI; but concerning Epistles LXXXI and XXXVII, I can agree neither with him nor with Pearson that they were written and sent to Rome at this time. Accordingly, of the thirteen letters sent to Rome, only seven appear to me to survive.

First, I would have it noted that in the testimony of Cyprian which we have just cited, only eleven letters are identified, although thirteen are said to have been sent. For when he expressly mentions one letter to the martyrs after the tortures and five others concerning the lapsed, seven others must necessarily be comprised in these words:

> “Neither counsel to the clergy, nor exhortation to the confessors, nor rebuke to the exiles when it was required, nor our address and persuasion to the entire brotherhood to implore God’s mercy, was lacking.”

Second, it is clear from this that those who imagine they have identified those thirteen letters among the Cyprianic correspondence are wasting both their labor and their oil. [Col. 0098] For where will they find seven epistles corresponding to these words of Cyprian? Where are those letters which he attests in Epistle XXXVII that he wrote “frequently” to the presbyters and deacons, commending to them the care of the martyrs and confessors? Only one survives before the thirty-seventh, namely the fifth. We possess no letter whatever written to rebuke the exiles, and none “to the entire brotherhood for the purpose of imploring God’s mercy.”

But these points will become more explicit and clearer from what must be said concerning Epistles VIII, VII, VI, and XXXVI. For we shall discuss the thirty-seventh in the following chapter, and the eighty-first when we come to the persecution of Gallus and Volusianus.

There can be no doubt that these four epistles were written, as Tillemont observes, when Cyprian had been encouraged by the hope of approaching peace. In the seventh, he exhorts the confessors to advance more and more in the Lord, “so that when, in accordance with his mercy, he has established the peace which he promises he will establish,” they may return to the Church as new and almost transformed persons. In the eighth, he relates that he heard in a vision divinely granted:

> “Tell him to be secure, because peace is coming; but meanwhile there is a short delay, since there are still some who must be tested.”

In the sixth and the thirty-sixth, moreover, he attests that his return is being hindered by this consideration alone: he fears that he might become the cause of breaking the peace.

But Pearson, in order to extricate himself from this difficulty, invents the following explanation:

> “At about this time the proconsul, sated with the blood of the martyrs, left Carthage, and after his departure the persecution was exercised day by day with much greater mildness by the magistrates at Carthage; for after this period no mention is made either of the proconsul or of torture or ill-treatment in prison.”

But it must be noted:

1. In the letters known to have been sent to Rome, which Pearson places after those letters, there is no trace whatever of approaching peace. “The battle line is still engaged,” Cyprian says in Epistle XIV, “and the contest is celebrated daily.” In Epistle XXV, to Moses and the other Roman confessors, which Pearson thinks was written at the beginning of August, the Oxford edition reads: “Martyrdoms are being celebrated here through tortures.” In the letter of Lucianus to Celerinus, which was written after May and when summer had already begun, one may see what the martyrs had suffered only a few days earlier, when they were tortured “with hunger and thirst, and also with the heat of fire.”

In general, in all those epistles that speak of the lapsed, there is no mention of peace—not merely of peace already granted, as Pearson supposes, but not even of peace approaching. Cyprian orders that the case of the lapsed be reserved intact until his return and decides that the Church must receive peace from the Lord before peace is granted to the lapsed. Yet nowhere does he indicate that he had learned by divine revelation that the persecution would end, although this would have been especially appropriate for calming the minds of the lapsed, who were distressed that their case was being postponed for a long time.

2. It is clear from Epistle VIII that the persecution had raged for a long time:

> “For if only two persons in harmony can accomplish so much,” he says, “what if there were harmony among all? What if, in accordance with [Col. 0099] the peace which the Lord gave us, all the brethren were in agreement? Long ago we would have obtained from divine mercy what we ask, and we would not have been tossed about for so long in this danger to our salvation and faith.”

This epistle therefore cannot have been written in April of the year 250. In the same epistle we read:

> “Finally, to his least servant—although placed among many of his chosen ones and unworthy of his gracious favor—he nevertheless deigned, in his goodness toward us, to send this command: ‘Tell him,’ he said, ‘to be secure, because peace is coming; but meanwhile there is a short delay, since there are still some who must be tested.’”

If Cyprian wrote this in April 250, why did he remain hidden in withdrawal for another year because of the persecution? Why, in Epistle XXXIII, which is known to have been written toward the end of 250, does he say that Aurelius inaugurated “peace when he dedicated his ministry as reader”?

3. Epistle VIII is addressed to the presbyters and deacons, and St. Augustine (*On Baptism*, book IV, ch. 2) attests that it was written to the clergy. Yet Pearson thinks that it corresponds to these words of Cyprian:

> “Nor was our address and persuasion to the entire brotherhood to implore God’s mercy lacking.”

Furthermore, the epistle “to the entire brotherhood” was written before the tortures, as is clear from Epistle XV; but Cyprian attests in this same Epistle VIII that tortures had already been inflicted on the confessors.

The same must be said of Epistle VII, in which Cyprian exhorts the confessors at length to preserve the glory of their confession through a praiseworthy life, and censures not a few of their faults, among them the fact that certain exiles had returned to their homeland without authorization. Pearson seizes upon this as an opportunity to prove that Cyprian is speaking about this Epistle VII when he says that rebuke to the exiles had not been lacking. But if Cyprian had mentioned this epistle in his letter to the Roman clergy, he would not have identified it from one or two words spoken, as it were, in passing, but from the purpose and design of the entire epistle.

Pearson’s opinion, moreover, has introduced the greatest disorder into the sequence of Cyprian’s letters. In Epistle VII of the Oxford edition, which is XXXVI in Pamelius, Cyprian fears that, if he returns, he may “become the cause of breaking the peace.” Yet in Epistle XI of the Oxford edition, which is VIII in Pamelius, Pearson thinks that tortures recently inflicted on the confessors are mentioned. In Epistles XIII and XIV of the Oxford edition, which are VII and VI in Pamelius, it is clear that the martyrs have already been released from prison. But in Epistle XV of the Oxford edition, which is XI in Pamelius, they are still being held confined in prison.

## X.—THE ORDER OF CYPRIAN’S LETTERS BEFORE THE FIFTEENTH LETTER WRITTEN TO THE ROMANS; FIRST, CONCERNING THE FIFTH AND THE NINTH.—THE THIRTY-SEVENTH MUST BE ASSIGNED TO ANOTHER PERIOD

With those epistles removed from a position not properly theirs, the sequence of the others will now be freer from difficulty and more intelligible: both of those which were sent to Rome and of those which Cyprian wrote later as the disturbance created by the lapsed grew more serious, and also of those which he wrote toward the end of this year, 250, when the hope of peace had been revealed by divine warning.

The first of all the letters written during his withdrawal is thought to be the one that occupies fifth place both in Pamelius and in the Oxford edition. For it corresponds to these [Col. 0100] words of Epistle XV: “Nor was counsel to the clergy lacking.” Cyprian commends care of the poor to the clergy and asks that “they should lack nothing, since the entire sum collected is there, distributed among the clergy for cases of this kind, so that several persons might have resources from which they could minister to the needs and afflictions of individuals.”
