He also urges, in order to avoid ill will, that the confessors “should not be visited in a crowd or by a multitude assembled all at once,” and that “the presbyters who offer there in the presence of the confessors should take turns, one at a time, each accompanied by a single deacon.”

I would readily grant that, among the epistles Cyprian sent to Rome in his own defense, none now survives that should be placed before this fifth epistle. But I cannot persuade myself of what Pearson and Fell maintain: that it was the very first of all and was written immediately after Cyprian withdrew. For since Cyprian, as I have already observed, does not identify each of those thirteen letters individually, and since the fall of the people of Carthage, who had renounced the faith “at the first words of the threatening enemy,” caused Cyprian the greatest grief, there can scarcely be any doubt that in such great difficulty he strengthened his clergy with his counsels and wrote them some letters before this fifth epistle; or, at the least, the letters he first wrote upon receiving news of this calamity ought to have contained some indication of so great a sorrow.

I therefore would not believe that this was the very first epistle written. But there is no doubt that it was written while “everything remained intact with regard to the safety of the clergy,” while some measure of humane treatment was still being shown to the confessors, and therefore before part of the clergy disturbed the Church by secret machinations or obeyed the edicts of Decius—indeed, before the tortures were inflicted upon the confessors in April, and before the darkness of the more intensely heated prison mentioned in Lucianus’s letter to Celerinus.

Before that same month, three other letters were also written, “in which neither exhortation to the confessors, nor rebuke to the exiles when it was required, nor address and persuasion to the entire brotherhood to implore God’s mercy, was lacking.” Cyprian indicates that they were written before the tortures, but we have shown that they have not come down to us.

Learned men observe that the tortures were inflicted on the confessors in April. Mappalicus died as a martyr under interrogation on April 17, as the martyrologies attest, after enduring extremely bitter torments on the preceding day, during which he said to the proconsul:

> “Tomorrow you will see the contest.”

Cyprian therefore wrote, probably toward the end of that month, Epistle IX to the martyrs and confessors, in which he extols their praises lavishly and exhorts them to follow:

> “that most blessed martyr and the other participants in the same conflict, companions steadfast in faith, patient in suffering, and victorious under interrogation.”

There can be no doubt that this is the very epistle which Cyprian says in Epistle XV that he wrote “after the tortures came.”

Not long afterward—that is, in the month of May—Pearson and Tillemont, following Baronius and Lombert, believe that Letter XXXVII was written. In it Cyprian commends the care of the poor to the presbyters and deacons, [Col. 0101] and repeatedly exhorts them “to devote still greater vigilance and care also to the bodies of all those who, although they have not been tortured, nevertheless die in prison by a glorious death,” and to record “the days on which they depart,” so that he might “celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs.” What follows must be carefully noted:

> Although Tertullus, our most faithful and devoted brother—in keeping with all his customary solicitude and care, which he bestows upon the brethren in every service of active charity, and who does not fail them there even in the care of their bodies—has written, continues to write, and informs me of the days on which our blessed brethren pass in prison to immortality through the glorious end of death, offerings and sacrifices are celebrated here by us in their commemoration; these, with the Lord’s protection, we shall soon celebrate together with you.

For my part, although I am greatly influenced by the authority of so many learned men, I nevertheless do not see why they would have Cyprian write these words in May—that is, at the height of the persecution’s blaze—when he himself announces that he will soon celebrate the martyrs’ commemorations with his clergy. The persecution, then, was already cooling, and was giving him hope of an early return. The same reasons that moved Tillemont to assign Letters VI, VII, VIII, and XXXI to the end of the year 250 should have moved him to render the same judgment concerning Letter XXXVII. Furthermore, in May the martyrs were being subjected to dreadful tortures; but when Letter XXXVIII was written, they were no longer obtaining the crown through the wounds of martyrdom. Rather, if any flew to heaven, they attained it by dying in prison without torture. Yet in May it would have been the days of those who poured out their lives amid tortures—not of those who died in prison without torture—that had to be recorded and reported to Cyprian. It is therefore much more probable that this Letter XXXVI was composed when the persecution was growing milder day by day, although the confessors had not yet been released from prison.

## XI.—FIVE LETTERS OF ST. CYPRIAN CONCERNING THE LAPSED.—HE DID NOT OVERLOOK THE CRIME OF THE PRESBYTERS WHO HAD GIVEN COMMUNION TO THE LAPSED.—HE THREATENS THEM NOT WITH SUSPENSION BUT WITH EXCOMMUNICATION.

Cyprian derived very great consolation from the triumphs of the martyrs; but this joy was sullied by the wicked intrigues of certain presbyters who, having always opposed him from the beginning of his episcopate, caused him the gravest troubles during his absence. The drama they enacted took as its occasion an ancient and praiseworthy custom, which they endeavored to turn to the ruin of many. It was customary in the Church for the canonical penalties of lapsed persons who had obtained certificates from the martyrs to be remitted in some measure at the judgment of the bishops. Tertullian attacks this institution near the end of his book *On Modesty*, although, while still a Catholic, he had praised it in his book *To the Martyrs*. Certificates of this kind, however, were not given by just any confessors, but by those who had been condemned to death or had at least endured some torture.

Hence Celerinus, in his letter to Lucian, asks “that whichever [Col. 0102] of the confessors is first crowned may remit the sin of Numeria and Candida.” Consequently, since the beginning of Decius’s persecution was free of torture, no certificates were being given; none of the lapsed had any opportunity to evade penance; and the presbyters who were eager for revolutionary change remained inactive. But after tortures were inflicted in April and some of the confessors were crowned with martyrdom, certificates began to appear, although due honor was still preserved both for the bishop’s dignity and for ecclesiastical laws. For the martyrs addressed a letter to Cyprian and asked “that their wishes be examined at that time, and that peace be granted when Mother Church herself has first received peace through the Lord’s mercy,” and when “divine protection” had restored Cyprian “to his Church” (Letter X).

Moreover, certificates were given to only a few, as is evident from Letter XXIII. The martyr Mappalicus, moved by familial affection, had given one only to his mother, who had lapsed; Saturninus, still confined in prison after his tortures, had given none at all. But shortly afterward moderation and discrimination ceased to be observed:

> For Lucian, himself one of the confessors, was indeed fervent in faith and strong in courage,

as Cyprian says in the same letter,

> but less well grounded in the Lord’s teaching. He attempted certain things, having long since set himself up as an authority for the ignorant populace, so that certificates written in his own hand were given indiscriminately to many in Paul’s name.

And he did this

> not only while Paul was still confined in prison, but even after his death, saying that Paul had instructed him to do so. Many certificates were likewise given in the name of Aurelius, a young man who had endured torture, written in the same Lucian’s hand because Aurelius did not know how to write.

The same Lucian appears to have been the author of certificates that Cyprian had heard were written in this form (Letter XI): “Let that person communicate with his own people.” Cyprian also censures some others “who showed partiality toward persons in dispensing” the martyrs’ favors, either granting favors from personal motives or seeking “a marketplace for illicit trafficking.”

Cyprian was not unaware that five presbyters were supplying “encouragements and incitements to certain confessors, so that they would not agree with the bishop and would not preserve ecclesiastical discipline with fidelity and tranquility in accordance with the Lord’s precepts” (Letter XL). Nevertheless, since the whole matter was being preserved intact until his return, and since in this license concerning certificates nothing was being promised to the lapsed before the peace of the Church and the bishop’s judgment, he overlooked it and maintained patience, as though a restrained silence might promote tranquility (Letter X).

But the five presbyters, mindful neither of the Gospel nor of their position, and considering neither the Lord’s future judgment nor the bishop placed over them, committed a new crime unheard of under Cyprian’s predecessors. They had given peace and the Eucharist to the lapsed “before penance had been performed, before *exomologesis*—the confession—of the most grave and extreme offense had been made, and before the hand of the bishop and clergy had been imposed in penance.” Then Cyprian understood that a matter of such importance must not be overlooked, lest excessive silence proceed to the peril alike of the people and of himself. Therefore, to suppress the progress of the evil, he wrote three letters in a single stretch of work (with the same lamp-oil and labor), [Col. 0103] full of spirit and grief: one to the martyrs and confessors, another to the presbyters and deacons, and a third to the people. In Pamelius these are Letters XI, X, and XII; in each of them the other two are mentioned.

He admonishes the martyrs “that those by whom the Lord’s faith is preserved so devoutly and courageously should likewise preserve the Lord’s law and discipline.” He shows his astonishment that, instead of being directed and instructed by the presbyters and deacons, as had formerly been customary, their pious intentions were instead being obstructed by certain presbyters who were overturning every rule. He therefore exhorts the martyrs themselves to teach the presbyters what they ought to have heard from the presbyters. He prescribes that, in granting certificates, they should follow in the footsteps of their predecessors; carefully and cautiously weigh the wishes of those making requests; examine the conduct, works, and merits of each; and consider also the kinds and qualities of their offenses. Finally, they should designate by name in a certificate those whom they themselves saw and knew, and whose repentance they perceived to be approaching satisfaction; and in this manner they should address to the bishop letters consistent with faith and discipline.

In his Letter to the Clergy, he is still more fiercely indignant against the presbyters who had dared profane the Lord’s holy body. He declares that, “if they persist any longer in the same conduct,” he will employ that admonition which the Lord commanded him to use, “so that for the time being they may be forbidden to offer.” For, in addition to nocturnal visions, “during the day as well the innocent youth of children” was being filled “with the Holy Spirit; in ecstasy they saw with their eyes, heard, and spoke those things by which” the Lord deigned “to admonish and instruct” Cyprian.

In his Letter to the People, he declares that he knows both his people’s tranquility and their fear. Nor does he doubt that the lapsed would be vigilant in making satisfaction to God and entreating him, had certain presbyters not deceived them by currying favor with them. He exhorts the people themselves to direct each person and, through their counsel and moderation, to regulate the dispositions of the lapsed in accordance with the divine precepts. He commands that the whole matter be preserved intact until his return:

> So that, when by God’s mercy we have come to you, we may summon a larger number of our fellow bishops and, in accordance with the Lord’s discipline, in the presence of the confessors and with your judgment as well, examine the letters and wishes of the blessed martyrs.

From the words in the Letter to the Clergy, “For a long time I maintained my patience,” it may be perceived that these three letters were not written before June. Tillemont, however, rather infelicitously supposes that Cyprian long endured patiently not only the license taken with certificates but also the crime of profaning the Eucharist. The following words of Cyprian in Letter LV (p. 85) misled that most learned man:

> Concerning that one matter in which the cause is not mine or that of human beings but God’s, I do not think their crime ought to be passed over in silence: from the very first day of the persecution, while the recent crimes of the offenders were still seething, and not only the devil’s altars but even the very hands and mouths of the lapsed were still smoking from their impious sacrifices, they did not cease to communicate with the lapsed and to obstruct the performance of penance.

From these words Tillemont concludes that, from the very [Col. 0104] day on which the persecution broke out, there were already persons who gave the Eucharist to the lapsed.

The most learned author interprets Cyprian far too narrowly. His words mean nothing more than that the presbyters communicated with the lapsed while their crime was still recent. In fact, if one considers the length of time customarily devoted to penance in that age, Cyprian could say without absurd exaggeration that the presbyters had communicated with the lapsed “from the very first day of the persecution.” Furthermore, since the lapsed did not all offend at the same time, but some earlier and others later, it could have happened that many received communion from the wicked presbyters only a very few days after committing their crime.

The entire sequence and connection of events makes it necessary to interpret Cyprian in this way. For the presbyters seized their opportunity to cause disorder from the martyrs’ certificates, which began to be given after the tortures; and in Letter XV Cyprian mentions, just as he does the martyrs’ certificates after the infliction of torture, so also after the certificates themselves the audacity of those “who had now begun to communicate with the lapsed.” From this it is likewise evident that the presbyters’ crime was altogether recent. He gives the same testimony in Letter XII, to the people: “Yet I hear,” he says, “that certain presbyters . . . have now begun to communicate with the lapsed.”

But most decisive for the matter and its cause is Cyprian’s declaration in his Letter to the Clergy that the presbyters’ crime is of a kind that cannot be tolerated or overlooked. He shows that he had maintained patience for a long time; but since certain persons were attempting to disturb the people’s tranquility and claim the whole matter for themselves, he ought no longer to remain silent. He had always overlooked and endured the affronts offered to his episcopate, but now there was no room for overlooking them, “when the brotherhood is being deceived by certain persons who, while seeking to become popular without regard for the restoration of salvation, are doing greater harm to the lapsed.”

Tillemont rightly refutes Lombert, who interprets the words from the same Letter to the Clergy, “so that for the time being they may be forbidden to offer,” as though Cyprian were meanwhile forbidding the presbyters to present the names of the lapsed. Tillemont contends that these presbyters were suspended, or at least threatened with suspension, but not deposed. He adds that Baronius held the same opinion, and Pamelius before him, whose observation was incorporated into the editions of Priorius and Fell.

But—with due respect to so many most learned men—by the words “so that for the time being they may be forbidden to offer,” Cyprian designates not suspension but excommunication. Nor does he impose this penalty at the present time; he only threatens it. He then adds:

> They will plead their case both before us, before the confessors themselves, and before the entire people, when, with the Lord’s permission, we have begun to be gathered again into the bosom of Mother Church.

He adds this, I say, because what was then to be deliberated was not whether these presbyters should be deposed, as Tillemont holds, but whether communion should be restored to them and, if so, on what condition and under what rule of penance. I cannot interpret Cyprian otherwise when I read Letter XXVIII, in which he congratulates his presbyters and deacons because they had refused to communicate with Gaius of Didda and his deacon, [Col. 0105] who had given communion to the lapsed. In the same letter he renews his decree that anyone who dared communicate with the lapsed should be barred from his communion.

Likewise, in Letter LII (p. 67), explaining the severity he had once employed against the lapsed, he relates that he had decreed:

> If anyone, before our deliberation and before a decision established by the counsel of all, should rashly choose to communicate with the lapsed, he himself should be excluded from communion.

Now, to be excluded from communion is not the same as to be suspended, especially in Cyprian, who uses this expression to designate excommunication—as when he says in Letter XLVIII that Felicissimus had been excluded by him; in Letter LV, that Jovinus and Maximus had been excluded in council because of their impious sacrifices; and in Letter LXVII, that Novatian had been excluded by the priests of God throughout the whole world. By the words “so that for the time being they may be forbidden to offer,” therefore, Cyprian announces that not only the priestly offering but also the offering and communion of the laity are to be taken away.

It is also evident from what we have said that Cyprian did not immediately impose this penalty, but only threatened it, in times of the greatest difficulty and requiring the highest prudence. This is further confirmed both by Cyprian’s exceptional clemency in suppressing the presbyters’ names and by the condition he appended: “if they persist any longer in the same conduct.”

The clergy did not respond to these letters. But shortly afterward Cyprian, always attentive to the guardianship of his flock, seeing that he still had no opportunity to return and that summer had already begun—a season plagued by continual and serious illnesses—thought that provision should be made both for the lapsed and for the hearers (catechumens). He therefore wrote Letter XIII to the clergy. In it he decrees that if lapsed persons possessing certificates from the martyrs should become dangerously ill, they may make *exomologesis*, or confession, of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death has begun to press upon them, even before a deacon—provided, however, that they can be assisted before God by the martyrs’ privilege. To the others, who had not received certificates but were performing penance meekly and humbly, he promises that provision would also be made for them through the divine remedy. He similarly prescribes that the Lord’s mercy must not be denied to hearers (catechumens) imploring divine grace.

By a similar decree Dionysius of Alexandria made provision for the lapsed during this persecution. For he himself testifies in his Letter to Fabius of Antioch that he had commanded “that those who were dying, if they asked—and especially if they had previously made a humble petition—should be granted pardon, so that they might depart this life filled with good hope” (Eusebius, Book VI, ch. 44). Dionysius distinguishes between those who sought penance when danger was imminent and those who had sought it before falling ill. Although in making this distinction he may not appear as precise as Cyprian, who expressly requires that those who had received certificates from the martyrs should be able to be assisted by their aid and privilege before the Lord, I nevertheless believe that both held the same opinion. Nor do I doubt that Dionysius would not have granted peace to any who had boldly [Col. 0106] rejected penance, something we see many had done in Africa.

When the clergy replied to this letter—for Cyprian had complained that they had made no reply to so many letters of his—and at the same time consulted him concerning certain immoderate persons urgently demanding to receive communion without delay, Cyprian wrote Letter XIV. In it he confirms what he had established in the preceding letter concerning dangerously ill lapsed persons, but vigorously refutes and chastises those importunate demanders of peace:

> If they are in such great haste, they have within their own power what they demand, for time itself grants them more than they demand. The battle line is still engaged, and the contest is held daily. If they truly and steadfastly repent of what they have committed and the fervor of faith prevails, one who cannot endure delay can be crowned.

In this statement Cyprian appears to permit the lapsed to present themselves to the judges. For if he had wished them to wait until a day was appointed for them, he would not have said that what they sought lay within their own power. It was indeed forbidden for anyone to offer himself voluntarily, as Cyprian declared before the proconsul Paternus; but laws of this kind sometimes yield to differing circumstances. We see many—for example, in Justin’s *Lesser Apology* and in Eusebius, Book VIII—voluntarily approaching a judge and coming forward when summoned to confess. If this liberty is not censured in them, much less must it always be censured in the lapsed, who rightly ought to repair the disgrace they had brought upon the Christian name and confess Christ where they had shamefully denied him.

In Letter LVII, Cyprian raises to heaven, with unstinting praise, the conduct of the Roman Church: when Cornelius went forward to confess, everyone who heard hurried there at once; not individual soldiers, but the whole camp together went out to battle; the entire Roman Church confessed; and very many of the lapsed were restored through a glorious confession.

## XII.—ON LETTER XV OF ST. CYPRIAN AND SEVERAL OTHERS WRITTEN SHORTLY AFTERWARD, WHEN A NEW DISTURBANCE AROSE.

After so many measures had been taken courageously and prudently to restore the Church’s peace, Cyprian wrote Letter XV to the Roman clergy in his own defense. He judged that nothing would be more suitable for repelling unjust suspicions than to send to Rome the five letters concerning the lapsed, together with eight others likewise written in his retirement. Of the latter, we have observed that only two survive: Letter V to the clergy and Letter IX to the confessors.

Cyprian’s charity and moderation of spirit shine wonderfully in Letter XV to the Romans. It contains no indication of wounded feeling and no complaints. He merely explains briefly why he withdrew and what he did during his retirement. In keeping with his supreme devotion to unity, he declares that, in what he granted to the penitent lapsed, he thought it necessary to abide by the opinion of the Roman clergy as well, lest our action, he says, “which ought to be united and to agree in all respects,” should differ in any particular.

The five letters that Cyprian had written amid the disturbances raised by the lapsed were sent not only to the Romans but also to many bishops. They had already [Col. 0107] written back to Cyprian “that they too maintained the same position in accordance with the catholic faith” when Cyprian replied to Bishop Caldonius.

Caldonius had consulted him about certain persons “who, after they had sacrificed, were arrested a second time and became exiles.” Among them was a woman named Bona, who had been dragged to the sacrifice by her husband—or rather, she herself had not sacrificed, but those who held her resisting hands had done it. She said to them, “I did not do it; you did,” and she too became an exile. Although Caldonius did not doubt that these persons, who were asking for peace, had washed away their former offense, he nevertheless wished to establish nothing unless Cyprian’s authority concurred.

Cyprian praises his prudence and replies that persons of this kind, “since they have washed away every offense and, with the Lord assisting them, have effaced the former stain by greater courage, ought no longer to lie under the devil as though prostrate.” He sends Caldonius “a book together with five letters.” Fell interprets this “book” as the collection of five letters itself; Rigaltius and Baluzius understand it to mean the book *On the Lapsed*. But that book had not yet been composed. Caldonius’s letter and Cyprian’s reply occupy the nineteenth and twentieth places in Pamelius’s arrangement.

Cyprian’s letters, in which clemency tempered just severity, ought to have healed embittered minds. But Lucian, at the instigation of the wicked presbyters, committed a new crime. In the name of all the confessors he wrote to Cyprian “that they had granted peace to everyone and wished this formula to be made known through Cyprian to the other bishops.” His addition—“concerning those for whom an account has been established of what they did after their offense”—was intended to bring odium upon Cyprian, as Cyprian himself observes in Letter XXIII. A somewhat overbold admonition likewise appears to be contained in the words: “We wish you to have peace with the holy martyrs.”

From this letter of Lucian, which is Letter XVII in Pamelius, seditions arose. In Cyprian’s province, “in several cities the multitude made attacks upon those placed over them and compelled peace to be granted to them immediately, terrifying and subduing” the weaker superiors. In the church of Carthage itself certain turbulent persons, as though set alight by this letter like so many torches, blazed still more fiercely (Letter XXIII).

Cyprian wrote Letter XVII to his clergy concerning this matter. In it he teaches that they must abide by his earlier letters; and because the confessors had said, “concerning those for whom an account has been established before you of what they did after their offense,” he concludes from this that the confessors intended the cases of the lapsed to be examined, and that those who were unwilling to await the proper time for this were acting most unjustly. In fact, although the confessors were carrying the matter beyond law and moderation, nevertheless, because Cyprian had threatened excommunication if anyone gave communion to the lapsed without consulting him, they did not dare request that peace be granted before peace had been restored to the Church and before Cyprian’s judgment. Hence Lucian, in his Letter to Celerinus, asks that several lapsed members of the Roman Church who had been commended to him should receive peace in this manner: “when the Lord has begun to grant peace to the Church itself, and after their case has been set forth [Col. 0108] before the bishop.” Cyprian also sent his clergy Caldonius’s letter and the reply he himself had written to Caldonius.

Amid these difficulties, letters from the Roman clergy and also from the confessors arrived most opportunely—not, indeed, letters to Cyprian, for they had not yet learned the details of his affairs, but the former addressed to the clergy of Carthage and the latter to the Carthaginian confessors. They were written before Cyprian’s Letter XV had been delivered at Rome. Neither has come down to us; but from Cyprian’s Letter XXIII we learn that in them there prevailed “the full vigor of the Gospel and the robust discipline of the Lord’s law,” and that they brought very great support to the struggling Cyprian as he resisted the assault of odium with all the strength of faith.

The Roman clergy mention the same letters in Letter XXXI, where they say that in their previous letters they had set forth their judgment “in a lucid exposition” against the *Libellatici*—those who had procured certificates of sacrifice—as well as demonstrated their fidelity and agreement against those who had actually sacrificed. Had Cyprian been attentive to his own rights and the honor due to him, letters of this kind, written to the clergy and confessors while bypassing him, would have offended him. But whatever benefited the Church could not fail to please him, and he immediately gave thanks to the Roman clergy and confessors as for a very great benefit.

Through Letter XXIII he informed the clergy both of Lucian’s earlier acts and of the latest disturbances he had provoked. Through Letter XXV, meanwhile, he congratulated the confessors both for the glory of their confession and for their exceptional zeal in defending discipline. Letters XXIII and XXV were carried by Saturus and Optatus, the former of whom Cyprian had made a reader and the latter a subdeacon for the purpose of carrying the letters. For since he needed to conduct his correspondence through clerics, but knew that many of his own were absent while the few who were in Carthage scarcely sufficed for the ministry of daily work, he had to appoint some new ones who could be sent.

Through the same clerics he sent six other letters to the Roman clergy: Letters XVII, XVIII, XIX, and XX, which we have already discussed, and in addition Celerinus’s letter to Lucian and Lucian’s reply, numbered XXI and XXII in Pamelius. We shall say a little about these.

## XIII.—ON CELERINUS’S LETTER TO LUCIAN AND LUCIAN’S REPLY.

While Celerinus of Carthage was staying at Rome, where he had been cast into prison for Christ and had displayed exceptional examples of constancy, he suffered very great grief over the lapse of two women, Numeria and Candida, who had sacrificed. One of them—probably Numeria—was his own sister. He says that, because of her deeds, on this day of Easter joy he had passed, and continued to pass down to the present day, his days weeping day and night in sackcloth and ashes, bathed in tears.

He also mentions another woman, named Etecusa, who had not sacrificed but had nevertheless gone up as far as the Three Fates and then come back down; for she had paid over gifts so as not to sacrifice. “Their case had now been heard, and the superiors had ordered [Col. 0109] that they remain in their present condition until a bishop should be appointed.”

Celerinus therefore asks Lucian to report the matter to the other confessors and ask them “that whichever of them is first crowned may remit such a sin for these sisters.” He makes this request not only in his own name but also in that of sixty-five confessors. When those confessors came from Carthage to Rome, these women “went down to the harbor to meet them, brought them up into the city, ministered to them, and cared for them in every respect.” Celerinus hoped that, “in view of their repentance and the works” they had performed among the confessors, “Christ would pardon them at the martyrs’ request.”

It is clear from the words “on this day of Easter joy,” which Baluzius recovered from ancient manuscripts, that this letter was written during the Easter season. Learned men believe that Celerinus wrote to other confessors as well. But it seems more probable that he wished Lucian to read this letter to the other confessors and to regard it as common to them all. Celerinus’s following words mean nothing else:

> For you must know that I have also written a letter to my lords, your brothers, and I ask that you be so kind as to read it as addressed to them.

There was no need to weary Lucian with entreaties, since he observed no moderation in matters of this kind. Accordingly, he replies to Celerinus in such a way that he does not seem to grant the lapsed women anything exceptional, but rather includes them in a benefit poured out upon all the lapsed. For he relates that all the confessors “by common agreement granted peace to everyone,” and that the martyr Paul, while he was still in the body, had said to him:

> Lucian, I tell you before Christ: if anyone asks peace of you after I have been summoned away, grant it in my name.

Hence he grants peace not only to the women whom Celerinus had commended, “but also,” he says, “to those whom you know to reach our mind”—that is, those by whose welfare we are in some way concerned. Trajan uses a similar mode of expression in Letter XXVIII to Pliny: “It matters to me,” he says, “by what route you arrive in the province.”

The persecution was now raging with exceptional severity. Lucian relates that he and the other confessors had been shut up again for eight days, and that he hoped soon to become, together with the others, a companion of the martyrs who had already been crowned. In the *Cyprianic Annals*, this letter is said to have been written “when May was already far advanced,” but this is entirely erroneous. For in it Lucian expressly declares that all the confessors had granted peace to all the lapsed; yet they did not attempt this crime until after Cyprian’s Letter XV to the Romans had been written, as Cyprian himself testifies in Letter XXIII.

In these letters of Celerinus and Lucian, a confessor named Saturninus is mentioned. Some wish him to be the same Saturninus of Carthage of whom Cyprian testifies in Letter XXIII that, while still confined in prison after torture, he had given no certificates, and to whom, together with Aurelius, the letter of the Roman confessors had been addressed. But two men named Saturninus must certainly be distinguished, one Roman and the other Carthaginian. For the Saturninus in whose name Celerinus greets Lucian had already “confessed courageously there under the punishment of the claws”; this cannot be understood of the Carthaginian [Col. 0110] Saturninus. When Celerinus wrote these words on the day of Easter joy, tortures had not yet been inflicted at Carthage—or at least news of the event had not yet arrived in Rome; still less could Saturninus himself, returned to prison after torture, have reached Rome. Hence Celerinus did not know whether any of the Carthaginian confessors had already suffered or been crowned.

Later, moreover, amid the troubles caused Cyprian by Lucian, letters from the Roman confessors addressed to Saturninus and Aurelius arrived. At the same time—that is, shortly after Cyprian’s fifteenth letter and the unrestrained grant of peace to all the lapsed—Lucian replied to Celerinus and greeted Saturninus. It is therefore necessary to distinguish two men named Saturninus.

I would indeed believe that the Carthaginian Saturninus had already been crowned when the letter of the Roman confessors addressed to him and Aurelius arrived. For Cyprian’s statement that, while still confined in prison after his tortures, he had given no certificates seems to indicate that he was released from prison only by martyrdom. Similarly, Cyprian says that “while Paul, whose death he mentions, was still confined in prison, Lucian gave certificates in Paul’s name written in his own hand.” The confessors had certainly not yet been released from prison when Cyprian wrote this Letter XXIII.

I shall attempt to emend a notably corrupt passage in Celerinus’s letter. In the printed editions it reads:

> Yet I ask of the Lord, dearest brother, that if you have first been washed in that holy blood—if you have suffered for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ before my letter reaches you in this world—or if it reaches you now, you may write back to me concerning these matters.

Editors have labored over these words without being able to explain anything. But in a manuscript formerly belonging to Baluzius and now in the Royal Library, it reads:

> Yet I ask of the Lord, dearest brother, that you may be washed in that holy blood for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ before my letter reaches you in this world; or, if it reaches you now, that you may write back to me concerning these matters.

A splendid sentiment indeed, and worthy of a martyr! The manuscript of Grenoble confirms this reading, having: “Yet I ask of the Lord, dearest brother, that by me [*a me*; uncertain reading] in that blood, etc.”

## XIV.—ST. CYPRIAN WRITES TO THE CLERGY CONCERNING THE ORDINATION OF SATURUS AND OPTATUS.—VARIOUS LETTERS FROM THE LAPSED TO ST. CYPRIAN.—THE CLERGY REMOVE GAIUS OF DIDDA FROM THEIR COMMUNION.—WHEN WERE LETTERS XXIII AND XXIX WRITTEN?—ON THE LETTERS OF THE ROMAN CLERGY AND CONFESSORS.

After Cyprian appointed Saturus and Optatus as clerics and sent them to Rome with letters, he wrote Letter XXIV to his clergy, in which he explains why he had created new clerics without consulting the clergy. Yet he shows that not even this had been done without their consultation:

> For long ago, by common counsel, we had brought them near to the clergy: both when, on Easter Day, we twice assigned Saturus the reading, and recently when, together with the presbyters who are teachers, we carefully tested the readers and appointed Optatus among the readers as a teacher of the hearers, examining whether all the qualities that ought to be present in those preparing for the clergy were in accord in them.

In subsequent centuries, those who had read once or twice were not merely close to the clergy, but also attached and formally enrolled among them. Hence Augustine, in Letter LXIII, appeals to Severus’s conscience:

> Whether a man who, in the church entrusted to my administration, had already begun to read—not once, but a second and third time—can or ought to be judged not to have been a reader.

It was decreed at the Council of Milevis in the year 402 that anyone who had read in a church even once could not be retained by another church.

Tillemont admits that he does not know which letters Cyprian means at the beginning of Letter XXIV, where he speaks as follows:

> So that nothing might escape your knowledge, dearest brothers, I have sent you copies of both letters—what was written to me and what I wrote in reply—and I believe that what I answered will not displease you.

But since Cyprian testifies in Letter XXVII, which was written shortly after Letter XXIV, that certain persons had recently written to him “from among the lapsed who were humble and meek, trembling and fearing God, and who had always labored gloriously and nobly in the Church,” and that he had congratulated them, and that the Lord had deigned “to show what servants of this kind and character merit from his kindness,” I readily believe that this letter of the lapsed and Cyprian’s reply were sent together to the clergy at Carthage with Letter XXIV.

Not all the lapsed displayed the same moderation of spirit. For some wrote to Cyprian “not asking that peace be given to them, but claiming it as though it had already been given” (Letter XXIX); and what especially provoked Cyprian’s indignation was that they wrote in such a manner as “to issue letters in the name of the Church.” Cyprian wrote Letter XXVII to them in order to restrain their rashness.

About the same time the clergy of Carthage informed him that, on the advice of the bishops who were present, they had judged that communion ought not to be maintained with Gaius of Didda and his deacon, because they had communicated with the lapsed and had presented the offerings of the lapsed, and had persisted after being admonished once and again by the bishops. Cyprian praises the steadfastness of his clergy, orders them to read to the bishops the letter he was writing to them—namely, Letter XXVIII—and directs that if any of his presbyters or deacons, or even any visiting clergy, should dare to communicate with the lapsed, he is to be barred from communion with him. The clergy had also consulted him about the subdeacons Philomenus and Fortunatus and the acolyte Favorinus, who had departed in the meantime and had recently returned. Cyprian judged that the time for deciding their case had not yet come, because many members of the clergy were still absent and the circumstances of each individual had to be thoroughly considered and carefully weighed, not only with his colleagues but also with the entire body of the people. He therefore decreed that “for the present they are merely to abstain from the monthly distribution—not in such a way that they may appear to have been deprived of ecclesiastical ministry, but so that, with every matter left intact, their cases may be deferred until our presence,” as he says. Cyprian then wrote to Rome concerning these matters in Letter XXIX, carried by the subdeacon Fortunatus; and at the same time [Col. 0112] he sent both the letter of the lapsed and his own reply, together with the letters he had subsequently written back to the clergy.

Those three letters that Cyprian sent to Rome—namely XV, XXIII, and XXIX—are so closely connected with one another that they appear to have been written almost without interruption. There is no doubt that Letter XXIII, sent by Saturus and Optatus, was dispatched before the Roman clergy had replied to Letter XV, since the Roman clergy plainly replied to it in the same response. Indeed, the last letter, sent by Fortunatus, likewise appears to have been written before Cyprian received the Romans’ letters. For in his great courtesy he would undoubtedly have thanked them for having afforded him so much consolation amid his most distressing troubles. Moreover, just as Cyprian, writing through Saturus and Optatus, said, “After the letters written to you . . . another matter arose, of which you likewise ought not to have been ignorant,” so too in the letter sent through Fortunatus he said: “After I had written to you the letters that I sent through Saturus the reader and Optatus the subdeacon, our brethren, having witnessed the rashness of certain persons who refuse to do penance and make satisfaction to God, wrote to me.” Since letters of this kind followed one another so closely, Pearson wrongly postpones the last of them until October. For they cannot be placed so late, since they were sent before the reply was received to the letter written at the beginning of July. The Roman clergy’s reply itself also appears to be placed too late when assigned to September. Many considerations prompted the Romans to respond quickly: the disturbance in the Church of Carthage demanded a swift remedy, and Cyprian had to be relieved of the distress caused him by the Romans’ silence and by unjust suspicions. It is therefore more probable that those most distinguished letters of the Roman clergy and confessors, numbered XXXI and XXIV in Pamelius, arrived during August itself. They contain an excellent reply both to Letter XV, which Cyprian had written in his own defense, and to the letter he subsequently sent through Saturus and Optatus. As is evident from Cyprian’s Letter LII (p. 67), Novatian wrote this Letter XXXI; together with it the Roman clergy sent Cyprian a letter written in the name of the Roman Church to Sicily.

Cyprian derived so much consolation from these letters of the Roman clergy and confessors, and judged that they would be so useful to everyone, that he instructed Saturus, who appears to have brought them back from Rome, to allow anyone who desired to make copies of them. He also sent them to his own clergy together with the letters he himself had written to Rome, at the same time directing in Letter XXXII that both his own writings and their replies should be made known to the brethren. Furthermore, if any visiting bishops, presbyters, or deacons were present or should arrive, they were to hear all these documents; and if they wished to transcribe copies of the letters and carry them back to their own people, they were to be given the opportunity to do so. From Cyprian’s Letter LII we learn that these letters of the Roman clergy were sent throughout the whole world and brought to the attention of all the churches and all the brethren. Hence, in Letter XL, [Col. 0113] written at the beginning of the year 251, he declares that it had once been resolved, “both by us,” he says, “and by the confessors and the clergy of the City, as well as by all the bishops established either in our province or overseas, that no innovation should be made concerning the case of the lapsed until we had all assembled together,” etc. Not long afterward the Roman clergy replied to the same effect to Cyprian’s letters. Those letters, as we have already said, had indeed been written before Saturus returned, but after he had departed from Rome they were brought to that city by the subdeacon Fortunatus and made it necessary for the Roman clergy to write again. This is Letter XXX in Pamelius. Near the end of the letter they thank Cyprian for having informed them, in his customary manner, about the matters concerning Privatus of Lambaesis. They also declare that even before his letter the deceit of this crafty man had not been able to escape their notice. “For when previously,” they say, “a certain standard-bearer from the company of his wickedness, Futurus, an adherent of Privatus, came and deceitfully attempted to extract letters from us, neither did what he was escape our notice, nor did he obtain the letters he desired.” Cyprian had therefore written some letter about this Privatus, of whom absolutely nothing appears in the three letters we have mentioned; but that letter has perished along with many others. There is no doubt that these letters from the Romans were of great use to Cyprian amid these difficult circumstances. This perhaps explains why, in the letters that we shall review as having been written during the remainder of this year, the same goads of anxiety no longer appear to torment Cyprian: the seditious and those who were silently pursuing their wicked designs had evidently been checked for a time, although at the beginning of the following year they attempted to bring those designs to completion.

## XV.—THE PERSECUTION BREAKS OUT AFRESH: THE COMING PEACE IS REVEALED TO ST. CYPRIAN.—A REVIEW OF HIS ACTS AND WRITINGS TOWARD THE END OF THE YEAR 250

I conjecture that Letter XXXVII was written about the month of October. In it Cyprian gives the presbyters and deacons the same admonition he had often given them already: that every care should be shown to the confessors held in prison and that the days on which they died in prison should be recorded. He praises the diligence of the presbyter Tertullus, both in assisting the confessors with every office of humanity and in reporting to him the days on which they passed away in prison. I have preferred to assign this letter—which Tillemont and others less suitably place at the height of the persecution—to the period when the persecution was cooling and the confessors were dying more often in prison than amid tortures, and when Cyprian hoped that, with the Lord’s protection, he would soon celebrate the sacred rites with his clergy.

Letter VIII appears to have been written not long afterward, when in a divinely granted vision Cyprian heard: “Tell him to be at ease, because peace is coming. But since there is a short delay in the meantime, there still remain some who must be tested.” The persecution was still ravaging the flock, as Cyprian immediately adds; and since it had been milder at some times and harsher at others, it appears, as Tillemont observes, to have broken out violently again near the very end. For when Cyprian says that tortures came while the confessors [Col. 0114] failed to maintain discipline, he does not appear to be recalling events that had occurred in April or May, but to be describing the present state of affairs; this is sufficiently evident from his words. “What blows,” he says, “what wounds do we not deserve, when not even the confessors, who ought to have been an example of good conduct to the rest, maintain discipline? And so, while the timid and shameless boasting of their confession insolently exalts certain persons, tortures have come. We suffer these things through our own fault and according to our deserts.” To this period should apparently be referred what Cyprian relates in Letter XL about the five leading men of Carthage, “who had recently been associated by an edict with the magistrates in order to undermine the faith of the Christians.” He is not relating a vision here, as some have thought, but an event known and attested by everyone; nor is it difficult to believe that five leading men of the city had been joined to the magistracy in either promulgating or executing some edict against the Christians. When Cyprian adds, “The same method, the same overthrow, is now once again being introduced through the five presbyters joined with Felicissimus, for the ruin of salvation,” this certainly does not indicate that the presbyters’ crime had been prefigured in some vision. It means instead that they were creating the same danger for the Church that had previously arisen from the magistrates and the five leading men of the city. Another indication that the persecution ended violently is that, although the clergy of Carthage had hitherto remained whole and pure amid so much contagion of evil, Cyprian laments the falls of certain members in letters written at the end of this year, namely VI and XXXV. That those who lapsed belonged to the presbyterate rather than to the lower ranks of the clergy may be inferred from the fact that in Letter XXXV Cyprian says that the presbyter Numidicus, whom he enrolled among the presbyters of Carthage, had been miraculously preserved so that “the Lord might attach him to the clergy of Carthage and adorn with glorious priests the ranks left depleted by the lapse of certain presbyters.” Yet he does not say the same of the glorious confessors Aurelius and Celerinus, whom he ordained readers at about the same time. At his own exhortation the presbyter Numidicus had sent before him a great number of martyrs slain by stones and flames; he had joyfully watched his wife, clinging to his side, burned together with the others. He himself, half-burned, buried beneath stones, and abandoned as dead, was found by his daughter, who searched for him anxiously; after being pulled out and revived, he had survived against his will. Cyprian had determined to promote him to the episcopate when he returned to Carthage; but meanwhile, admonished and instructed by divine favor, he enrolled him among the presbyters of Carthage and sent advance notice of this joy to the presbyters, deacons, and people in Letter XXXV.

About the same time, two distinguished confessors, Aurelius and Celerinus, were ordained readers by Cyprian and the bishops who were present—Aurelius first, and Celerinus a few days afterward. Cyprian had wished to join Celerinus to Aurelius, but Celerinus steadfastly refused the honor and was finally compelled by a vision granted during the night [Col. 0115] to yield. Cyprian informed the presbyters, deacons, and entire people of these ordinations in Letters XXXIII and XXXIV. These events occurred amid the first joys of the dawning peace, as is evident from Cyprian’s words about Aurelius in Letter XXXIII: “Meanwhile he has read for us on the Lord’s Day; that is, he has inaugurated the peace by dedicating his reading.” Aurelius was a distinguished young man, still youthful in years but advanced in the praise of virtue and faith. He had confessed twice: both before the magistrates, who sentenced him to exile, and before the proconsul, by whose order he was most cruelly tortured. Cyprian doubts whether he should praise more highly the glory of his wounds or the modesty of his conduct and his extraordinary humility. Celerinus too had endured the gravest tortures and had compelled Decius himself, before whose eyes he was being tortured, to praise and admire his courage. Examples within his own family encouraged him, for his grandmother Celerina and his paternal and maternal uncles, Laurentinus and Egnatius, had won the crown of martyrdom. Cyprian raised this illustrious pair of young men no higher than the office of reader, but even then he designated them for the honor of the presbyterate, “so that they might be honored with the same stipends as the presbyters and share in the monthly distributions in equal amounts.”

When Celerinus came from Rome to Africa and presented himself to Cyprian, he showed him how highly the Roman confessors esteemed him and how greatly they loved him. This prompted Cyprian to write Letter XVI to them. In it he describes the four seasons of the year that the confessors had passed in prison in such a manner that there can be no doubt that the letter was written after the completion, or at least near the end, of this year 250. When the short delay Cyprian had foretold came to an end, the Church of Carthage tasted a beginning of peace, and the confessors were released from prison. Most of them upheld the glory of their confession by excellent conduct; but some proved a disgrace to so great a distinction, and in Letter VII Cyprian reproaches them with drunkenness and lust, arrogance, contention, and promiscuous sleeping with women. He also touches on this in Letter VI, which he wrote at about the same time to the presbyters and deacons, while he was still involuntarily detained in retirement, in order to commend to them the care of the poor and especially of the confessors. For although the confessors had been released, a full and settled peace had not yet dawned. Therefore, although Cyprian was borne in mind and spirit toward Carthage, both to revisit his people and to put the Church’s affairs in order, he was nevertheless compelled to obey the wise advice of the presbyter Tertullus, who had counseled him not to appear so soon in the place where his presence had so often been demanded. The exiles had not yet obtained permission to return; and when a calmer condition of affairs had prompted some to return without authorization, Cyprian severely rebuked them in the same Letter VII. Indeed, even shortly before the feast of Easter he was still praying “for the fullest peace, first for the mother and then for her children” (Letter XI).

## XVI.—CYPRIAN SENDS DEPUTIES IN HIS PLACE.—THE THREATS OF FELICISSIMUS

While Cyprian remained in retirement, lest he who was obliged to consult the welfare of all should become responsible [Col. 0116] for breaking the peace, he wrote in the meantime to his presbyters and deacons in Letter XXXVI. There he says that he will come to them when they write that, “affairs having been settled, he ought to come—or if the Lord should graciously reveal it beforehand.” He then exhorts them to “exercise diligent care for the widows, the sick, and all the poor,” and also to provide expenses “for any needy strangers, from my own personal fund,” he says, “which I left with our fellow-presbyter Rogatianus. Since perhaps that entire sum has already been disbursed, I have sent him another portion through the acolyte Naricus, so that assistance may be rendered more generously and promptly to those in distress.” Tillemont observes that these words appear to show that Cyprian left a sum of money with Rogatianus when he departed from Carthage. He admits, however, that this interpretation involves him in many difficulties. First, Rogatianus made his confession before Cyprian’s retirement—or so the learned man supposes. Second, even if Cyprian had departed first, since Rogatianus lay in prison for so long, the sum of money does not appear to have been secure in his keeping. Finally, since this Letter XXXVI was written near the end of 250 or the beginning of 251, why does Cyprian wonder whether money given so long before had all been spent? Moved by these difficulties, Tillemont conjectures that instead of the words “I left with Rogatianus” (*apud Rogatianum dimisi*), the text should read “I sent to Rogatianus” (*ad Rogatianum misi*). Yet it does not appear necessary to alter the text. These words do not necessarily show that Cyprian entrusted the money to Rogatianus when departing from Carthage. They may mean that, since the holy martyr’s personal allowance was customarily sent to him while he remained hidden in retirement, he did not wish that sum of money to be brought to him in the usual manner but left it with Rogatianus. Moreover, since only a short time had passed since Rogatianus and the other confessors had left prison, Cyprian had good reason to wonder whether all this money had already been disbursed.

Besides Rogatianus, Cyprian had sent the two bishops Caldonius and Herculanus and the presbyter Numidicus as deputies in his place, so that they might meet “the needs of the brethren by providing funds; if any also wished to practice their trades, they were to assist their desires by supplying whatever additional amount was sufficient. At the same time they were to ascertain their ages, circumstances, and merits,” so that Cyprian might know everyone as well as possible and promote “all who were worthy, humble, and gentle to offices of ecclesiastical administration.” But while those bishops and presbyters were carrying out Cyprian’s instructions, Felicissimus appeared—a man of reckless temerity and extreme audacity—and intervened “to prevent anyone from having his needs discharged and to prevent the matters” Cyprian desired “from being ascertained by careful examination. With wicked exercise of power and violent intimidation he even threatened the brethren who had first come forward to have their needs discharged, saying that they would not communicate with him in death.” Afterward he rushed out “with a great many followers, rashly and furiously declaring himself the leader of a faction and the chief of sedition.” When Cyprian was informed of these events by the bishops Caldonius and Herculanus [Col. 0117] and the presbyters Rogatianus and Numidicus, he wrote Letter XXXVIII to them, in which he excommunicated Felicissimus, both for his wicked schism and because “to his frauds and robberies, which,” he says, “we have learned by clear evidence, there is also added the charge of adultery, which our brethren, men of weight, have reported that they discovered and have affirmed that they will prove.” Cyprian threatens Augendus, who had allied himself with Felicissimus, with the same penalty if he should persist any longer in association with him.

It is not easy to explain what Felicissimus meant when, “with wicked exercise of power and violent intimidation,” he threatened that those who obeyed Cyprian would not communicate with him “in death.” In place of Baluze’s reading “in death” (*in morte*), supported by the authority of ancient manuscripts, other editions have “on the mountain” (*in monte*). But whether one reads “on the mountain” or “in death,” could excommunication threatened by such a man have inspired violent terror? Would he not rather have terrified them if he had threatened to compel Catholics to communicate with him? Could deprivation of communion with a thoroughly wicked man have appeared a serious misfortune to people devoted to their bishop and detesting Felicissimus? For my part, insofar as one can conjecture in a very obscure matter, I suspect that Felicissimus threatened not merely excommunication but death itself, so that he meant that those who obeyed Cyprian would not share with him in the death he was threatening. When Cornelius appeared to have been terrified by the “murderous threats” of Felicissimus, Cyprian declared in Letter LV that it made no difference to him “either by whom or when he should be killed, since he would receive from the Lord the reward of death and blood.” If Felicissimus’ murderous threats broke out against Cornelius and Cyprian, who could wonder that ordinary people were terrified by such threats from him?

The bishops and presbyters whose deputy service Cyprian employed in his absence obeyed him diligently and excommunicated Felicissimus and his principal followers, as is evident from Letter XXXIX among the Cyprianic letters. This document, however, appears to be not so much a letter as a writ of excommunication publicly posted.

## XVII.—THE SCHISM OF FELICISSIMUS AT THE BEGINNING OF THE YEAR 251.—NOVATUS, ONE OF THE FIVE SCHISMATIC PRESBYTERS.—ON CYPRIAN’S LETTER XL

It is not worth the trouble to refute Baronius’ rather inept opinion concerning the priestly status of Felicissimus. Cyprian is an authoritative witness that Felicissimus was a layman when he created the schism, for he declares that Novatus obtained the diaconate for him by the same machinations through which he obtained the episcopate for Novatian. “It is he,” Cyprian says in Letter XLIV, “who by his factional activity and ambition made his satellite Felicissimus a deacon without either my permission or my knowledge. . . . He who made a deacon there against the Church appointed a bishop here.” Moreover, this ordination could not have occurred until after the schism had openly broken out. Pearson has no reason whatever for placing it before the schism, since, as Tillemont observes, Cyprian does not include this crime among the offenses of Felicissimus in Letter XXXVIII. Novatus himself, [Col. 0118] although the firebrand of that conflagration, nevertheless kept his wickedness almost concealed at the beginning of the schism and did not associate himself with Felicissimus publicly and openly. Had he dared to do so, he would have incurred the same excommunication as the other followers of Felicissimus.

This schism can be placed neither earlier nor later than the beginning of 251. As Tillemont demonstrates against Pearson, who assigns it to the year 258, absolutely no trace of the schism appears in the letters written in 250; nor had Cyprian received any report of it when he wrote Letter XXXVI, which gave the schismatics the opportunity to break out. Yet Felicissimus did not defect from the Church any later either, for the five presbyters who revealed themselves around Easter had already been secretly supporting his party for some time.

Cyprian had determined to celebrate Easter of this year, 251, in his own church. For he was pierced by “an exile now in its second year, a sorrowful separation from the faces and eyes” of his people, “unceasing pain and a groaning that tormented him alone with continual lamentation, and tears flowing by day and night because it had not yet fallen to the priest’s lot to cling to” his people “in embraces” (Letter XI). But to this grief, which the hope of an early return was soothing, there was added the perfidy of five presbyters. Before Easter of this year they finally broke out into open schism, which they had long been laboring to bring forth in their wicked minds. By their threats and plots they reduced Cyprian to such a position that he did not dare to return before Easter, lest upon his arrival “a still greater disturbance should arise there, and since the bishop ought in every respect to provide for peace and tranquility, he might appear to have furnished material for sedition and to have inflamed the persecution anew” (*ibid.*).

Those five presbyters had already conspired against Cyprian’s episcopate, diverted certain confessors from the reverence due to their bishop, and driven them into thoroughly dishonorable vices. They now openly “turned with their poisonous deception to the destruction of the lapsed, drew them away from the remedy for their wound,” and, “interrupting the entreaties and prayers by which the Lord had to be appeased through long and continual satisfaction, invited them into destructive rashness by the lie of a deceitful peace.” Cyprian also attributes the schism of Felicissimus to them as its secret instigators. Although so many evils had arisen from men of this kind, Cyprian nevertheless did not wish them to cast themselves out voluntarily. Yet they pronounced against themselves the sentence they had escaped through his indulgence and, “by the providence of God”—without Cyprian either willing or desiring it, indeed while he forgave and remained silent—“paid the penalties they deserved” (*ibid.*).

I am certainly surprised that the *Cyprianic Annals* excludes Novatus from the number of the five presbyters, since Cyprian speaks of him as follows in Letter XLIX: “This is the same Novatus who among us first sowed the conflagration of discord and schism, who here separated certain brethren from the bishop, who during the persecution itself became for our people another kind of persecution designed to overthrow the minds of the brethren. It is he who by his factional activity and ambition made his satellite Felicissimus a deacon without either my permission or my knowledge,” etc. Fortunatus also belonged to the same number, [Col. 0119] as Cyprian testifies in Letter LV; the schismatics subsequently made him pseudo-bishop of Carthage. Two others who may not improbably be included in the same number are Donatus and Gordius, who are discussed in Letter VI; perhaps Gaius of Didda, whom Cyprian removed from his communion in Letter XXVIII, should be placed fifth. Four presbyters—Donatus and Fortunatus, Novatus and Gordius—had written to Cyprian shortly before the schism. Cyprian does not indicate what they wrote about, but declares that he could not reply to them alone, since from the beginning of his episcopate he had resolved to conduct no business on his private judgment without the advice of the clergy and the consent of his people (Letter VI).

After Cyprian learned of the crime of the five presbyters, he wrote Letter XL to the entire people. In it he portrays the wickedness of the schismatics in its true colors, demonstrates the unity of the Church, and exhorts both those who had stood firm and those who had lapsed: the former to preserve the praise they had acquired during the persecution, and the latter “faithfully to provide for their hope and peace in this second temptation.” Finally, he declares that this is the persecution’s latest and final trial, “which itself,” he says, “will soon pass away under the Lord’s protection, so that after Easter Day I may be restored to you together with my colleagues.” Tillemont observes that Cyprian also wrote to the clergy about this matter, but that the letter has not come down to us. For in Letter XLII Cyprian mentions letters he had written to the clergy and the people concerning Felicissimus and his presbyterate, which explained both the arrangement and the grounds of what had been done.

## XVIII.—CYPRIAN RETURNS AFTER THE PERSECUTION HAS SUBSIDED AND DELIBERATES WITH HIS COLLEAGUES ON THE CASE OF THE LAPSED; BUT BEFORE THE COUNCIL HE WRITES THE BOOK *ON THE LAPSED*

When the divinely promised peace had at last dawned upon the African Church, Cyprian came out after Easter from the retirement in which he had lain hidden for about a year and four months. In Letter LII he says that the persecution had then subsided; he does not say that it had been completely brought to an end. In reality, as long as Decius lived, Christians always had reason to fear his cruelty. Hence Pope Cornelius, elected in June, sat “undaunted,” according to Cyprian’s testimony in Letter LII (p. 69), “upon the priestly chair at Rome, at a time when the tyrant, hostile to the priests of God, was uttering threats both speakable and unspeakable.” It therefore does not appear that anything else brought about this peace except the fear inspired in Decius by Lucius Priscus. While governing Macedonia, Priscus had seized imperial power in that province and joined his forces with the Goths against Decius.

Cyprian’s return presented him with a most joyful spectacle: he saw gathered in the church both the great number of confessors—among whom women, virgins, and children shone conspicuously—and the rest of the multitude of those who had stood firm, none of whom had regarded anything as so precious that it could induce them to obey the emperor’s edicts. Yet the lapsed caused him great anxiety. He was not troubled by those who had truly and sincerely embraced penance, for he had congratulated them extraordinarily and the Lord had shown him “what servants of this kind and character merit from his kindness.” Rather, he was troubled by those who had joined themselves to apostates and the faithless, or who attempted either to conceal their sin by a kind of stealth or, once it was known, to withdraw it from the laws of penance. Shortly after Cyprian’s return, God made many examples of those who had dared to approach communion without confessing their sins to the priests: “Many who daily failed to do penance or confess their guilt were filled with unclean spirits; many, losing the soundness of their minds even to the point of insanity, were shaken by the frenzy of madness.” As we learn from the book *On the Lapsed*, many other manifestations of divine wrath against people of this kind occurred both while the persecution continued and after Cyprian’s return. He relates that a certain young girl did not escape them: her nurse had taken her to the idols, and afterward her mother, unaware and ignorant of what had happened, brought her into the church while Cyprian was offering the sacrifice.

Cyprian had promised that as soon as he returned he would investigate, calculate, and judge the case of the lapsed together with his colleagues, “so that the prelates, assembling with the clergy and in the presence of the steadfast laity—to whom honor must likewise be shown on account of their faith and fear—might arrange all things with the religious scrupulousness of common deliberation” (Letter XIV). He did not fail to fulfill his promises. Yet before the council was held, he appears to have written the book *On the Lapsed*, in order to prepare the minds of the lapsed, as was proper, to receive the council’s decrees. Pearson, however, believes that this book was composed after the death of Decius, while the author of the *Observations on Dupin’s Library* places it after the Council of Carthage. Tillemont denies both claims on very weighty grounds.

Against Pearson he first employs this argument: since the Roman confessors returned to the Church in the same month in which Decius was slain, the book *On the Lapsed*, which was sent to them before their return to the Church together with the book *On the Unity of the Church*, cannot be postponed until after Decius’ death. For it is unreasonable to compress into one and the same month so many notable events: the death of Decius; the report of it throughout all the provinces; the peace of the Church; the writing and dispatch to Rome of two books by Cyprian; and the confessors’ return to the Church after reading those books.

Pearson was influenced by the words at the beginning of the book: “By divine aid and vengeance our security has been restored.” From these words he concludes that Decius had by then paid the penalty for his persecution of the Christian religion. Tillemont observes that Decius was so preoccupied by the revolt of Lucius Priscus and the advances of the Goths that even then God was manifestly avenging the blood of the Christians and establishing peace, at least in the African Church. He nevertheless regards it as unworthy of Cyprian that, although he prayed daily for the emperor, he should rejoice in the emperor’s calamity. He therefore suspects either that these words were added by Cyprian after Decius’ death or that they must be referred to the punishment of the proconsul or to some other event. But I do not see why we should hesitate to interpret Cyprian’s words as referring to Decius himself—not yet deprived of his empire and his life, but already under attack. Nothing prevented Cyprian, although he prayed daily for the emperor, from nevertheless tracing the emperor’s misfortune to [Col. 0121] divine vengeance, especially since he does not name Decius himself or say anything particularly harsh against him. After Decius’ death he was far more vehement, as may be seen in the letter to Antonianus, where he calls him a tyrant and depicts his cruelty. Thus the very fact that in the book *On the Lapsed* Cyprian contented himself with a single expression, and so mild a one, ought to serve as evidence that Decius was still reigning.

It is no more difficult to prove that the book *On the Lapsed* was written before the Council of Carthage. The council’s decrees are nowhere mentioned in this book. Peace was granted at the council to the *libellatici* (certificate-holders). Yet in this book Cyprian exhorts not only the *libellatici* but even those “who merely entertained the thought of doing this” not to cease “from doing penance and imploring the Lord’s mercy, lest what appears less serious in the nature of the offense be increased by neglect of satisfaction.”

The opening shows that the book was written amid the first joys of the restored peace:

> Behold, dearest brethren, peace has been restored to the Church; and what recently appeared difficult to unbelievers and impossible to the faithless, our security has been restored by divine aid and vengeance. . . . The day desired by the prayers of all has come. . . . With joyful eyes we behold the confessors, illustrious through the proclamation of their good name and glorious through the praises of their courage and faith; clinging to them with holy kisses, we embrace with insatiable longing those for whom we had long yearned. The radiant cohort of Christ’s soldiers is present, etc.

The book *On the Lapsed* therefore appears to have prepared the way for the Council of Carthage, which was held shortly after Cyprian’s return. Pearson places it in May of this year, 251, and this accords with Cyprian’s words: “Yet in accordance with what had previously been determined,” he says in Letter LII (p. 67), “when the persecution had subsided and the opportunity of assembling together had been granted, a great number of bishops—whom their faith and the Lord’s protection had kept whole and unharmed—assembled together.” That presbyters and deacons were present is evident from Letter LV.

When Cyprian says in the same Letter LII and in Letter LV that the bishops wrote to Cornelius and that what was decreed concerning the lapsed was established “after mutual consultation,” this appears at first sight to prove that the council was held later. For Cornelius was elected in June, and he did not immediately receive letters from the African bishops, who for some time sent their letters not to him but to his Church, until the envoys they had sent to Rome brought back a certain report concerning the dissension that had arisen there. But, as Tillemont observes, it is possible that many of the bishops who had attended the council were still at Carthage when the legitimacy of Cornelius’ election became established. Since these bishops wrote to Cornelius in their own name and in the name of the others, they were reasonably regarded as having established, in consultation with Cornelius, whatever they had decreed concerning the lapsed. Tillemont, following Pearson, interprets the words of Letter LV, “the council having been held repeatedly” (*concilio frequenter acto*), as meaning that the council was often reconvened, so that, as some bishops departed from Carthage and others succeeded them, it might be regarded as having continued in a certain fashion.

The principal deliberation of the council concerned the adjudication of the cases of the lapsed [Col. 0122]; and because there was the greatest possible variety of circumstances, every case was examined with exceptional prudence, as though in a goldsmith’s balance. Some had been defiled by impious sacrifice, others only by certificates, while still others had incurred guilt merely in intention. They were not to be treated alike, Cyprian says in Epistle LII (p. 70):

> The man who immediately rushed willingly to the impious sacrifice, and the man who resisted and struggled for a long time but was finally driven by necessity to that deadly act; the man who betrayed both himself and all his family, and the man who, personally exposing himself to danger on behalf of everyone, protected his wife, children, and entire household by undergoing the danger himself; the man who compelled his tenants or friends to commit the crime, and the man who spared his tenants and farmers, and even received under his roof and hospitality a great many brethren who were departing as exiles and fugitives, thereby presenting and offering to the Lord many souls alive and unharmed to intercede for the one that was wounded.

Finally, some had lapsed later and others sooner; some had immediately taken refuge in repentance, while others, through excessive confidence in the certificates received from the martyrs, had attempted to evade this remedy. Accordingly, at the Council of Carthage “the circumstances, intentions, and necessities of each individual were examined, and the decisions concerning each individual were recorded in a document.” (Ibid.) Baronius rightly observed that this document was not unlike penitential canons; the Oxford editor, however, has no justification whatever for understanding it, in his notes on this passage, as the book *On the Lapsed*. What we have said about the council’s decrees in the preface may be consulted.

Tillemont suspects that the same council decreed that, if a persecution were imminent, communion should be granted to the lapsed before the appointed time. He was led to this suspicion by the following words of Cyprian from Epistle LII (p. 71):

> No one can be compelled by us to repent if the fruit of repentance is taken away. If the battle comes first, he will be found strengthened by us and armed for battle. But if illness overtakes him before the battle, he departs with the consolation of peace and communion.

Yet the meaning of this passage appears to be that the hope of obtaining peace after repentance has this advantage: it raises the spirits of the lapsed and strengthens them to fight more vigorously if another opportunity should arise. For, as Cyprian had said shortly before:

> Strength for faith and courage is armed through repentance; but it cannot be armed if a man should fail through despair, if, harshly and cruelly separated from the Church, he should turn to pagan ways and worldly occupations, or, cast out by the Church, should pass over to heretics and schismatics.

Moreover, if this council had decreed that communion should be granted to the lapsed when persecution was pressing, Cyprian and the other bishops would not have omitted this in Epistle LIV.
