In that epistle they do not attempt to justify by the authority of the previous council what they had decreed concerning the reception of the lapsed into the Church because of the imminent persecution, but declare that they had so resolved “at the prompting of the Holy Spirit.” In Epistle LV Cyprian recalls another decree of the same council concerning bishops who had lapsed: men of that kind could “indeed be admitted to perform penance, but were to be barred from ordination [Col. 0123] to the clergy and from sacerdotal honor.” Felicissimus appeared before the bishops assembled in council, together with the presbyters attached to him, as is evident from Epistle XLII; but after hearing them, the bishops condemned and excluded them from communion. “Jovinus and Maximus, bishops who had been condemned by the judgment of nine bishops for impious sacrifices and crimes proved against them, were likewise excluded from communion a second time in the council,” Cyprian says in Epistle LV (p. 84).

Just as this council decreed, “not only by the bishops’ agreement, but also with a warning,” as Cyprian says in Epistle LV (p. 85), “that no one should rashly grant peace to those who were not performing penance,” so I am inclined to believe that, in accordance with the Church’s custom, some deference was shown to the just petitions of the martyrs as a mark of honor. For in the book *On the Lapsed*, which Cyprian testifies in Epistle LI that he had recently read at Carthage—from which some infer that it was read in the council itself—Cyprian, while refuting the excessive license of certain martyrs “in indiscriminately remitting and pardoning sins,” nevertheless acknowledges that something may be granted in compliance with their instructions:

> If what is to be done by God’s priest is just, if it is lawful, if it is not contrary to the Lord himself; if the consent of the person complying is ready and willing; and if there has been reverent moderation on the part of the petitioner. (p. 187)

He also acknowledges (p. 193) that God can accept whatever “the martyrs have requested and the priests have done” on behalf of those who truly repent. It is therefore likely that some concession was made to the martyr Mappalicus, who, moved by familial devotion, had commended his mother and—according to some editions—his sister; and likewise to others who had not imitated Lucianus, but who, as Cyprian directs in Epistle XI, had carefully examined “the conduct, works, and merits of each person, as well as the kinds and qualities of their offenses,” and had named individually in their certificates those whom they personally knew and “whose repentance they perceived to be approaching satisfaction.”

## XIX.—THE PRUDENCE OF SAINT CYPRIAN IN SUPPRESSING THE SCHISM OF NOVATIAN AND CONFIRMING THE EPISCOPATE OF SAINT CORNELIUS

After Cyprian had emerged from the very grave troubles caused him by the immoderate indulgence of certain martyrs and the impious recklessness of the schismatics, new difficulties arose when dissension broke out at Rome and the heresy of Novatian attempted to gain entrance into various churches. After Fabian, who died a martyr on January 20 in the year 250, the Roman Church had been without a bishop, and the cruelty of Decius had left no opportunity to choose a pastor. At last, however, while the tyrant was absent and authority in the city had been entrusted to Julius Valens, a most favorable opportunity presented itself, and Saint Cornelius was elected “upon the testimony of nearly all the clergy, by the vote of the people who were then present, and by the college of the ancient priests and good men.” He was a man endowed with every distinction; the high estimation in which Cyprian held him is evident from several of Cyprian’s epistles, especially Epistle LII. It is certain that this election took place after Easter [Col. 0124] of the year 251, since Cyprian, who returned to Carthage after the festive days had passed, was holding a council with his colleagues when news of the election arrived. Indeed, if we follow Pearson’s conjectures, which appeared probable to Tillemont, the election must be postponed as late as June 4. Of two pontifical catalogues, one published by Bucherius says that Cornelius occupied the see for two years, three months, and ten days, while the other, edited by Bollandus, assigns the holy pontiff one year, two months, and three days. Selecting from each what appeared suitable and correcting what did not agree, Pearson concludes that Cornelius occupied the see for one year, three months, and ten days. He therefore dates the election to June 4, 251, so as to reconcile it with Cornelius’s death, which, as is evident from many weighty indications, occurred on the Ides of September, September 13, in the year 252.

Novatus, who had “first sown the fire of discord and schism” in Africa, as Cyprian says in Epistle XLIX, “also sailed to Rome to overthrow the Church, and there undertook similar and equivalent enterprises.” He attached himself to Novatian and devoted to him his skills and fertile ingenuity. Relying upon this assistant, Novatian brought over to his cause five presbyters, several confessors, and part of the people, and opposed the election of Cornelius, accusing him of various crimes, including that of having defiled himself with a certificate. When both parties wrote to Africa, Cyprian and the many other bishops who had come to him understood that a matter of such importance had to be handled with every precaution. Cyprian accordingly ordered that Cornelius’s letters, “which breathed religious simplicity,” be read to the clergy and people, and “made his ordination to the episcopate known to the ears of all.” By contrast, he completely rejected in Epistle XLII the allegations that had been “heaped together with criminal acrimony” against Cornelius and his presbyters in a document sent to Carthage. Nevertheless, together with the several bishops who had assembled, he resolved that “fellow bishops Caldonius and Fortunatus should be sent as delegates to Rome, and that meanwhile everything should be held entirely in suspense until those colleagues returned, after either restoring affairs there to peace or ascertaining the truth.”

The African bishops were well aware that, according to ancient custom, it was sufficient for Cornelius to announce by letter that he had been made bishop. Yet, to deprive his adversaries of every pretext for disturbing the Church, they requested letters from the bishops by whom he had been ordained and sent delegates to bring back those letters and to report the entire affair after carefully investigating it:

> So that only then, after every scruple had been removed from each person’s heart, letters might be sent by absolutely all the bishops situated in Africa, and all his colleagues might approve and firmly maintain Cornelius and communion with him—that is, the unity and charity of the catholic Church. (Epistle XLI)

That Cyprian and his colleagues adopted these measures with the intention of confirming Cornelius’s election, not because they suspected its validity, is also evident from the fact that Cyprian “explained the matter to each person embarking on a voyage, so that they might not sail with any cause of scandal,” and exhorted them “to acknowledge and hold fast to the root and mother of the catholic Church”—that is, to remain in communion with Cornelius. Nevertheless, their letters were addressed to the presbyters and deacons, not to Cornelius. Moreover, when Cyprian and Cerealis came to Hadrumetum before the delegates returned and taught that city’s presbyters and deacons, in the absence of Bishop Polycarp, what had been decreed in the council, those clergy too began to observe what the others were observing and addressed their letters to the Roman presbyters and deacons, although letters had previously been addressed to Cornelius himself in Polycarp’s name (Ibid.).

Before the delegates returned, men sent by Novatian came to Carthage: the presbyter Maximus, the deacon Augendus, and two others named Machaeus and Longinus. When Cyprian and his colleagues learned from the letters they carried, and from their own statements and assertions, that Novatian had been made bishop, they judged that these men must immediately be barred from communion, while in the meantime refuting and blunting the claims they obstinately and persistently attempted to maintain.

After the delegates returned with letters from the bishops who had participated in Cornelius’s ordination, two other African bishops, Pompeius and Stephanus, arrived from Rome. Having seen the entire affair with their own eyes, “they too supplied manifest evidence and testimony to instruct the African bishops, in accordance with their dignity and trustworthiness” (Epistle XLI). Pearson thinks that these two bishops had been sent to Rome to participate in the election of the Roman bishop. But, as Tillemont observes, quite apart from the absence of any example of embassies of this kind, the Africans do not appear to have known anything about the forthcoming election. Certainly, if delegates had been sent to Rome for this purpose, there would have been no need subsequently to send Caldonius and Fortunatus; it would have been far more convenient to await the return of Pompeius and Stephanus, who had examined the entire affair with their own eyes. Yet Caldonius and Fortunatus returned before them. It is therefore entirely certain that they had not been sent by their colleagues but had either fled because the persecution was raging or traveled to Rome on business. Since their testimony agreed with the delegates’ report and with the letters of Cornelius’s colleagues, the legitimacy of Cornelius’s ordination became so firmly established in everyone’s mind “that it was no longer necessary even to hear the men who had been sent by Novatian.” (Ibid.)

## XX.—WHEN THE SCHISM OF NOVATIAN BROKE OUT

For determining the order of Cyprian’s actions, it is by no means unimportant to inquire when Novatian fomented his schism and when he received ordination. Valesius and Pearson believed that the schism began at the very beginning of the year 251. Tillemont denies that it occurred before Cornelius’s ordination. Of great importance to both positions is the testimony of Cornelius in his epistle to Fabius of Antioch, where the holy pontiff testifies that the holy martyr Moses, while still [Col. 0126] alive, denied communion to Novatian and five presbyters. Since both sides agree that Saint Moses dealt in this way with Novatian as an open and manifest schismatic, Valesius and Pearson conclude that the schism began with the year 251, because Saint Moses died in prison at the beginning of that year, according to Bucherius’s ancient catalogue of pontiffs. Tillemont, however, since he firmly holds that the schism did not break out before the ordination of Cornelius, places in November of the same year 251 the death of Moses, whom Cornelius says had recently suffered martyrdom. I shall therefore take a middle path between the two positions, accepting something from each while also rejecting something. For although I do not believe that the schism broke out before Cornelius’s ordination, it nevertheless appears to have been formed and prepared long beforehand through secret machinations. Thus there is no necessity to postpone Saint Moses’s martyrdom with Tillemont, nor does Saint Moses’s death compel us, with Valesius and Pearson, to date the schism to the beginning of the year 251.

Tillemont argues with compelling reasons that no schism existed at Rome before Cornelius’s ordination. First, Saint Pacianus in Epistle II (pp. 56 and 60), and the author of the book *To Novatian the Heretic*, declare that Novatian was driven into schism by envy conceived because of Cornelius’s episcopate. Second, Pearson most absurdly transfers Novatus—who was fomenting schism at Carthage in March, or at least in February—to Rome in January; Valesius transfers him there in February. Finally, it is inconceivable that the African Church should have remained unaware for so long of a schism that had arisen at Rome, and should not have sent delegates to settle the dissension until after it had been informed of Cornelius’s election. It is certainly difficult not to assent to these arguments.

Yet the testimony of Cornelius favors neither Tillemont nor his opponents; rather, it proves that Saint Moses condemned in Novatian not an open schism but secret machinations joined with many wicked deeds. The holy pontiff speaks as follows in Eusebius (book VI, chapter 43):

> Ὃν καὶ Μωσῆς ὁ μακάριος μάρτυς, παρ’ ἡμῖν ἔναγχος μαρτυρήσας καλήν τινα καὶ θαυμαστὴν μαρτυρίαν· ἔτι ὢν ἐν κόσμῳ, κατιδὼν αὐτοῦ τὴν θρασύτητα καὶ τὴν ἀπόνοιαν, ἀκοινώνητον ἐποίησε σὺν τοῖς πέντε πρεσβυτέροις τοῖς ἅμα αὐτῷ ἀποσχίσασιν ἑαυτοὺς τῆς ἐκκλησίας.
>
> Moses, the most blessed martyr, who recently among us underwent a noble and admirable martyrdom, while he was still alive perceived Novatian’s audacity and frenzy and excluded him from his communion, together with the five presbyters who likewise broke themselves away from the body of the Church with him.

The learned man vainly infers from the words “recently underwent martyrdom” that the event had occurred only one or two months earlier, since such a manner of speaking can be applied to events that occurred ten months, or even a year, before. I acknowledge that the words “together with the five presbyters who likewise broke themselves away from the body of the Church with him” appear to indicate that communion was denied to open schismatics. But the Greek words are best rendered: “together with the five presbyters [Col. 0127] who likewise broke themselves away from the Church with him.” When they are translated in this way, the schism does not appear to have preceded Moses’s denial of communion, but rather to have followed it.

Much in this same testimony confirms that interpretation. First, Cornelius relates Moses’s action and employs his testimony in such a way as both to assign Moses a distinction not shared by everyone and to brand Novatian with no slight disgrace. Yet it would have been no great distinction for the holy martyr to refuse communion to men involved in open schism and detested by so many bishops, so many presbyters, and nearly the whole people; nor would the loss of communion with a single martyr have been a great reproach to schismatics already excluded from the communion of the entire world. Furthermore, when Novatian was holding schismatic assemblies with his adherents, are we to say that he then wished to communicate with Saint Moses and was rebuffed? The time does not appear appropriate for such an event.

Second, Cornelius does not say that communion was denied to Novatian because of open schism, but because Moses perceived his audacity and frenzy. Novatian had already committed enough wicked acts for Moses to deal with him in this way, most notably when, during the persecution, he was admonished by the deacons to assist the brethren and replied that he no longer wished to be a presbyter. This was Novatian’s audacity; this was his frenzy. When the impious alliance of his plans with the five presbyters was added to it, it was not difficult for Saint Moses to foresee what they were plotting for the destruction of the Church, nor is it surprising that he refused to communicate with them.

Third, if Saint Moses had denied communion to manifest schismatics, he would have branded by the same judgment not only the five presbyters but also the confessors who had attached themselves to Novatian. For, as Cyprian says in Epistle LI, “schismatic and heretical error received” the four confessors “when they came out of prison,” and Novatian had associated them with himself from the beginning. According to the testimony of Cornelius in Eusebius (book VI, chapter 43), Moses’s judgment upon these members of Novatian’s flock should have been the same as his judgment upon the five presbyters; nevertheless, he denied communion only to the five presbyters. This is evidence that he condemned in Novatian neither open schism nor manifest war against Cornelius and all the bishops adhering to Cornelius, but impious machinations and plans undertaken with the five presbyters to disturb the Church. These, when added to Novatian’s numerous other vices, deterred Moses from communicating with him.

Fourth, Moses’s martyrdom does not appear to have occurred in November, as Tillemont thinks, but rather before the ordination of Cornelius. It is certain that the martyrs had been released from prison when Cornelius was ordained. Why, then, should Moses alone not have shared in that peace which had for so long prevented the election of a bishop? Furthermore, Moses did not die in prison, as Bucherius’s catalogue states, but shed his blood for Christ, as Tillemont demonstrates from the words of Cornelius, who declares that he underwent a splendid and admirable martyrdom. Yet from the ordination of Cornelius until the month of November, Christian blood does not appear to have been shed at Rome. Cornelius sat fearlessly “on the sacerdotal chair at Rome at a time when the tyrant, hostile to the priests of God, was threatening things speakable and unspeakable alike, when he would have heard with far greater patience and tolerance that a rival emperor had been raised up against him than that a priest of God had been established at Rome,” Cyprian says in Epistle LII (p. 69). Consequently, either Decius was unable throughout that entire period to satiate his cruelty, or he was deferring it until his return. Since Cornelius escaped, although Decius was especially hostile to him, Moses does not appear to have undergone his splendid and admirable martyrdom in November, but rather in January, as Bucherius’s ancient catalogue records, or at any rate before the end of the persecution, before the ordination of Cornelius, and before Novatian’s open schism.

## XXI.—WHEN NOVATIAN WAS ORDAINED

Critics do not agree concerning the ordination of Novatian. Pearson thinks that Novatian was ordained in the month of June itself and that his delegates came to Carthage at the beginning of July. Tillemont contends that this occurred after Cornelius’s ordination had been approved by the judgment of all Africa. Weighty reasons show that the crime was committed before Africa confirmed Cornelius’s ordination by its testimony. But before I begin to prove this, I shall observe in passing that Pearson is less than exact in arranging the events concerning Cornelius’s ordination. He says that “when June was already well advanced, Cyprian received the letters of Cornelius and his colleagues.” Yet from what we have already said and shall say below, it is evident that the African bishops, after receiving Cornelius’s letters, requested letters from his colleagues, and only then devoted themselves to confirming Cornelius’s ordination, when the delegates brought back those letters from his colleagues. Since Cornelius was ordained in June, the delegates who were sent by the Africans after news of this event had been received could not have returned with the letters during June.

As for Novatian’s ordination, it is easily proved against Tillemont that this crime was committed shortly after the ordination of Cornelius, and perhaps even at the end of June itself, as Pearson believed. For the delegates sent by Novatian to Africa arrived before Caldonius and Fortunatus returned from Rome; the African bishops had sent the latter to that city to settle the dissensions. The matter is evident from Epistle XLI, where Cyprian relates that Novatian’s delegates, immediately upon coming to Carthage and announcing that Novatian had been made bishop, were barred from communion, “while in the meantime the assertions they obstinately and persistently attempted to maintain were refuted and blunted.” He then adds:

> For I and the many colleagues who had assembled with me awaited the arrival of our colleagues Caldonius and Fortunatus, whom we had recently sent as delegates to you and to our fellow bishops who had attended your ordination, so that, when they arrived and reported the truth of what had occurred, the wickedness of the opposing party might be broken by greater authority and by the clear proof they supplied.

It is therefore evident that Novatian’s delegates, by their speed, preceded the return of the African prelates, and that they were meanwhile barred from communion as the delegates’ return was awaited. After the latter had returned, and two other bishops, Pompeius and Stephanus, who had attended Cornelius’s ordination, arrived after them, the affair was so clarified and confirmed both by the letters of the Italian bishops brought by the delegates and by the testimony of Pompeius and Stephanus “that it was no longer necessary to hear those who had been sent by Novatian.” Similarly, in Epistle XLII Cyprian relates that after the opposing party had appointed a bishop for itself, the African bishops received the letters both of Cornelius and of his colleagues, “and likewise, upon the arrival of the good men Pompeius and Stephanus, by whom all these things were firmly affirmed and proved to the common joy”; only then did they address letters to Cornelius.

Novatian’s delegates, therefore, were sent to Carthage before Caldonius and Fortunatus departed from Rome, or perhaps even before they arrived there. For if the latter had seen the events with their own eyes, why would Cyprian rely only upon the letters they brought, rather than upon their testimony as well, as he relies upon the testimony of Pompeius and Stephanus? Furthermore, Cyprian testifies in Epistle XLI that he learned “from the letters Novatian’s delegates carried with them, and from their statements and assertions, that Novatian had been made bishop.” It is therefore evident that the first news of this event was brought by Novatian’s delegates and that no one in Africa had suspected the dreadful crime before their arrival. This also confirms what we have already said: that they arrived not only before Pompeius and Stephanus, “by whom all these things were affirmed and proved”—namely, that a bishop had been appointed by seditious men “contrary to the sacrament once delivered of divine ordering and catholic unity”—but also before Caldonius and Fortunatus. For in the letters that Caldonius and Fortunatus brought from Cornelius and his colleagues, as Cornelius testifies in Epistle XLVI, many previous actions involving the confessors adhering to Novatian were described. Upon returning to the Church, the confessors acknowledged these actions with tears, including that “when they had been deceived into making themselves authors of schism and heresy, they allowed hands to be imposed upon him”—Novatian—“as though upon a bishop.” But if letters of this kind had arrived before Novatian’s delegates, Cyprian and the other bishops would not have received from those delegates the first news that Novatian had seized the episcopate.

Tillemont’s position therefore cannot be defended, and that most exact writer has no justification whatever for placing Novatian’s ordination after the return of the African delegates. Even less probable is his statement that the Church—or at least the African Church—had already agreed in approving Cornelius’s episcopate when Novatian was ordained. This agreement of the African Church became manifest only when the bishops, after being informed by Cyprian and his colleagues who were present at Carthage concerning the entire affair, wrote letters to Cornelius. But before Cyprian informed the African bishops about the affairs of the Roman Church, he sent the presbyter Primitivus to Rome with Epistle XLI, so that he might report how Novatian’s delegates had been received at Carthage. Cyprian speaks of his letters throughout Africa only in Epistle XLII, which was carried by Mettius the subdeacon and Nicephorus the acolyte, who followed Primitivus:

> But throughout our province as well, in bringing these same matters to the attention of each of our colleagues, we instructed them also to send our brethren with letters.

By the time the African bishops, having been informed by Cyprian, wrote to Cornelius, the presbyter Primitivus had already returned with Cornelius’s letters. In responding to them, Cyprian says (Epistle XLV [printed “XLX” in the source]): “It was resolved that letters should be written by absolutely everyone situated here, as in fact they have been,” etc. Thus many events intervened between Novatian’s ordination and Africa’s agreement in approving Cornelius’s episcopate: the arrival of Novatian’s delegates, the return of the African delegates, and the outward and return journeys of the presbyter Primitivus.

First, Tillemont relies upon these words of Cyprian from Epistle LII:

> Once that place of Peter has been occupied by the will of God and confirmed by the agreement of us all, whoever thereafter wishes to be made a bishop must necessarily be made one outside.

From this he concludes that Cornelius’s rights had already been confirmed by all the bishops, or at least by the African bishops, when Novatian was ordained. But the most learned critic pays insufficient attention to the fact that Cyprian is speaking about the state of affairs that existed at the time he wrote. For since the consensus of the whole world united in defense of Cornelius, while Novatian nevertheless did not desist from his endeavors, Cyprian rightly opposes this consensus to him and by this argument attacks not so much his ordination as his obstinate determination to retain it. Here in the same Epistle LII, when speaking of Novatian’s ordination, Cyprian objects only that, “after a bishop had been appointed in the Church by sixteen bishops, he attempted through canvassing to be made by deserters an adulterous and alien bishop.” Similarly, Cyprian did not confront Novatian’s delegates with the consensus of the whole world, but with the testimony of the colleagues by whom Cornelius had been ordained, recorded in the letters brought by Caldonius and Fortunatus, as is evident from Epistle XLI.

Second, Tillemont asks why Novatian’s ordination was immediately rejected by the Africans “as unlawful and performed contrary to the Church,” and why his delegates were barred from communion, if the African bishops had not yet approved Cornelius’s ordination. But the answer is ready and straightforward. For Cyprian, as we have just seen, never doubted that Cornelius’s ordination was legitimate. Nevertheless, after letters had been received from both parties, he wished everything to remain undisturbed until the delegates returned, so as to leave no occasion for discord. It is therefore hardly surprising that he was moved by the greatest indignation as soon as he learned of Novatian’s impious ordination.

Third, Tillemont thinks that it can be inferred from Epistle LXVII that Novatian, when he sent delegates to Africa, had already been judged an enemy of the Church, or at least that Cornelius was already regarded throughout Africa as the legitimate bishop of Rome. But nothing of the kind can be read in Epistle LXVII. Cyprian does indeed say [Col. 0131] that Novatian had formerly been judged an enemy of the Church and that, when he sent delegates to Africa, he had there received the judgment of a council of very many priests. He adds that Novatian had recently been blunted and refuted, and excluded from communion by God’s priests throughout the entire world. Yet he does not reproach him for having been ordained when Cornelius’s episcopate had already been confirmed by the authority of the entire world. Instead, he reproaches him because, “after Cornelius had been ordained in the catholic Church by the judgment of God and the vote of the clergy and people, he attempted to erect a profane altar, establish an adulterous chair, and offer sacrilegious sacrifices in opposition to the true priest.”

Fourth and finally, Tillemont observes that Antonianus, to whom Cyprian wrote Epistle LII, had already, on Cyprian’s advice, embraced communion with Cornelius before he was moved by Novatian’s letters to entertain unjust suspicions concerning Cornelius and Cyprian. Yet the example of Antonianus completely overthrows Tillemont’s position. For Antonianus had written to Cyprian not only that he “maintained one and the same agreement with Cornelius,” but also that he “did not communicate with Novatian.” Thus he simultaneously approved Cornelius’s ordination and rejected his rival Novatian. The fact that he appears to have read Novatian’s letters later—namely, after at Cyprian’s exhortation he had already declared his communion with Cornelius—is easily reconciled with this. For after Novatian’s delegates were rejected at Carthage, they began to travel from town to town through the cities; consequently, they may have reached Antonianus later. Moreover, Novatian subsequently sent another delegation and other letters, and nothing prevents us from understanding Cyprian to be referring to these.

## XXII.—THE ORDER OF SAINT CYPRIAN’S ACTIONS IN THE CAUSE OF CORNELIUS

We can therefore construct the entire sequence of events as follows. As soon as the delegates’ return had surrounded the truth with such light that there was no need to hear Novatian’s delegates again, Cyprian wrote to Rome by the presbyter Primitivus, whom he had instructed to relate to Cornelius matters that would have taken too long to include in a letter. This is the forty-first epistle in Pamelius’s edition. The bishops who were present at Carthage then wrote to the other bishops throughout Africa, informing them about the affairs of Cornelius and the schism of Novatian, and instructing them to send brethren with letters to Rome. What they urged the others to do, they themselves were the first to perform, and they wrote jointly to Cornelius.

There can scarcely be any doubt that these are the letters of Cyprian and his colleagues in which, Eusebius testifies (book VI, chapter 43), it was decreed that assistance should be given to the lapsed and that the author of the impious heresy should be expelled from the Church. The same letters contained much concerning Felicissimus and his associates: the bishops informed Cornelius what judgment they had formed after hearing those men and what sentence they had pronounced. Both of these conciliar letters—the one to the African bishops and the one to Cornelius—are mentioned by Cyprian in Epistle LXII [apparently XLII], which was sent by Mettius the subdeacon and Nicephorus the acolyte [the titles are restored from the uncorrupted wording above]. By the same clerics Cyprian sent copies of the letters he had written concerning Felicissimus and his presbyterate to the clergy and people of Carthage, which he had previously sent to Cornelius by Caldonius and Fortunatus. He exhorts Cornelius to order that they be read to the brethren.

This Epistle XLII was sent before the presbyter Primitivus returned; for Cyprian had not yet learned from the letters Primitivus brought that Cornelius was displeased because Cyprian had advised the people of Hadrumetum to write not to Cornelius by name, but to the Roman Church. Nevertheless, suspecting something and fearing that some offense might have entered Cornelius’s mind, Cyprian demonstrates in the same Epistle XLII that he had been moved by zeal for peace and unity to preserve everything intact while letters from the bishops of Italy were awaited.

Besides Epistle XLII, another, shorter letter was entrusted to Mettius for Cornelius; this is Epistle XLIII. In it Cyprian informs him that he had written to the schismatic confessors, but had instructed Mettius to read these letters to Cornelius and not deliver them unless Cornelius judged that they should be delivered. It is unlikely that Mettius was sent by Cyprian to Rome twice—once with Nicephorus to carry Epistle XLII, and again to carry the forty-third epistle concerning the schismatic confessors. This, I say, is not probable, for Nicephorus, who probably returned with Mettius, brought Cyprian the most welcome news of the confessors’ return. Why, then, did Cyprian give him two letters for Cornelius at the same time? Tillemont resolves the matter. Since Cyprian knew very well that his letters were customarily read publicly at Rome, he prudently entrusted to the shorter epistle the matters he did not wish to be made public. Besides Epistle XLIV to the confessors, Cyprian sent them his books *On the Lapsed* and *On the Unity of the Church*. From this it is easy to conjecture that the book *On the Unity of the Church* was written around this time; this is confirmed by the testimony of Pontius, who lists it immediately after the book *On the Lapsed*.

Before Cornelius received these letters, he wrote to Cyprian by the presbyter Primitivus and indicated that he disapproved of the advice Cyprian had given to the people of Hadrumetum. Cyprian answered him in Epistle XLV, which was written at the time when African bishops from every region were writing to Rome to testify that they adhered to Cornelius. In matters of such importance, it is unlikely that either Cyprian or the clerics he sent to Rome remained inactive; nor does much time appear to have elapsed between Epistles XLI, XLII, and XLV. For the forty-first was sent through the presbyter Primitivus shortly after the delegates’ return; the forty-second, shortly after the council’s letter to Cornelius, before Primitivus returned and before letters were being written to Cornelius from the various provinces of Africa; and this latter action was taking place when, after Primitivus brought the letters, Cyprian replied in Epistle XLV.

## XXIII.—NEW ATTEMPTS BY NOVATIAN.—RETURN OF THE ROMAN CONFESSORS TO THE CHURCH AT CYPRIAN’S EXHORTATION: IT IS SHOWN THAT THIS OCCURRED BEFORE THE ROMAN COUNCIL OF THE YEAR 251

[Col. 0133]

When Maximus, Longinus, and Machaeus, Novatian’s legates, had been expelled by Cyprian and his colleagues, Novatian sent others into Africa, namely Nicostratus, Novatus, Evaristus, Primus, and Dionysius. Cornelius warned Cyprian of this in a letter sent by Augendus the confessor, which is no longer extant. Not long afterward, when another opportunity arose, he again wrote to Cyprian through Nicephorus the acolyte—the letter numbered XLVIII among the Cyprianic letters—in which he asks that, through Cyprian’s efforts, all his fellow bishops and brethren should be informed that Nicostratus was guilty of many crimes: he had not only defrauded and robbed his secular patroness, whose accounts he administered, but had also carried off substantial deposits entrusted to the Church. Evaristus, moreover, had been an instigator of the schism, and Zetus had been appointed bishop in his place as successor over the people whom Evaristus had formerly governed. On the day after Novatian’s legates arrived, Nicephorus the acolyte came with Cornelius’ letters, from which Cyprian learned—and informed the other bishops—of the matters concerning Nicostratus and Evaristus. He afterward thanked Cornelius in Letter XLIX.

But the same Nicephorus brought other and far more joyful letters, in which Cornelius informed Cyprian of the return of the four confessors Maximus, Urbanus, Sidonius, and Macharius. When certain brethren had reported that the confessors were returning to their right minds, and Urbanus and Sidonius had afterward come to the presbyters, affirming that Maximus, a presbyter and confessor, likewise wished to return with them into the Church, Cornelius decided that what they had communicated through the delegation should be heard from their own mouths and confession. When they came and were questioned by the presbyters about what they had done, they declared that they had been deceived and that they had not known what was contained in the letters sent throughout all the churches in their name; they begged that their preceding actions be annulled and erased from memory. When the whole proceeding had been reported to Cornelius, he ordered the presbyteral council to assemble. Five bishops were present, and after the matter had been submitted for deliberation, each gave his opinion; Cornelius appended these opinions to his letter to Cyprian. Once this had been done, the four confessors and very many brethren who had joined them came before the presbyteral council, earnestly entreating that their former actions should be consigned to oblivion. When a great gathering of the brotherhood had assembled, there was, Cornelius says, one voice among them all as they gave thanks to God, expressed the joy of their hearts in tears, and embraced the confessors as though they had been released that very day from the punishment of imprisonment. The confessors declared that they acknowledged Cornelius as bishop of the most holy catholic Church. They confessed that they had suffered deception and been circumvented, but that their sincere intention had nevertheless always remained within the Church, since they were not unaware that there is one God, one Christ [Col. 0134] the Lord, and one Holy Spirit, and that there ought to be one bishop in the catholic Church. Moved by these events, Cornelius ordered Maximus the presbyter to resume his own position, received the others with the overwhelming approval of the people, and committed everything else to Almighty God. At that very hour and moment he transmitted this news in writing to Cyprian—namely, in the letter numbered XLVI among the Cyprianic letters—and immediately sent on Nicephorus the acolyte, who was preparing to go down to embark. Cornelius’ letters filled the Church of Carthage with joy; nor can there be any doubt that Cyprian sent them to the other churches of Africa, as Cornelius had requested. Cyprian replied to him in Letter XLVII. The confessors also wrote to Cyprian; their letter is numbered L among the Cyprianic letters. Cyprian replied to them in Letter LII.

What we have related from Cornelius’ letters proves that the confessors were not the only persons to return. There came with them before the presbyteral council “very many brethren who had joined them”; this can hardly be understood as referring to catholic laypeople interceding for the confessors. Cornelius afterward relates the gathering of the brotherhood, which he indicates took place only when he judged that this whole proceeding should be made known to the people. It is certainly difficult to suppose that confessors who had drawn many away by their authority had no companions or imitators when they returned. Cyprian understood Cornelius’ words in precisely this way:

> “How much greater,” he says (Ep. XLVII), “is the joy both on earth and equally in heaven over confessors returning to the Church of God with their glory and praise, and by the faithfulness and proof afforded by their example making a path of return for the others! For here error had misled some of our brethren, because they thought that they were following the communion of the confessors. Once that error was removed, light was poured into every heart, and it was shown that the catholic Church can neither be split nor divided.”

It therefore seems remarkable that Tillemont should think Cyprian was speaking only of the confessors. The entire affair is related by that same learned author as though it had been completed in one and the same day. Yet Cornelius’ words, “There were also present five bishops, who were present again today,” make it clear that two days were occupied: the first was devoted to deliberation about receiving the confessors, while on the following day, amid a great gathering of the brotherhood, the decisions made on the preceding day were completed and put into effect.

Tillemont and Pearson assign this notable event to November of the present year, 251, after the Roman council which Cornelius held in that year with sixty bishops—in October, according to Pearson, or much earlier, according to Tillemont, and before Novatian’s ordination. But those four confessors seem to have returned to the Church at a considerably earlier date, or at least before the Roman council.

The confessors’ return followed Novatian’s new delegation by only a few days. “For when Novatus departed from you there,” says Cyprian (Ep. XLIX), “that is, when the storm and whirlwind withdrew, some measure of calm arose there.” Furthermore, not much time elapsed between the first delegation and this new one; for Novatian, “struck down by the mighty works of God,” as Cornelius says (Ep. XLVIII), “rose up again when Maximus, Longinus, and Machaeus had been expelled by Cyprian and his colleagues.” These words make it clear that Novatian did not remain inactive from July until November, but wished to repair his losses immediately by sending more experienced and energetic legates. Therefore, the return of the confessors, which occurred very close to the departure of the new delegation, cannot be postponed until November.

Moreover, Nicephorus, the acolyte who brought both letters—one concerning the new delegation and the other concerning the confessors’ return—does not appear to have been a Roman cleric, but rather that same Nicephorus the acolyte whom Cyprian had sent to Rome with Mettius the subdeacon at the end of July or the beginning of August. For Cornelius speaks of him as follows in Epistle XLVI:

> “These things, therefore, dearest brother, we have transmitted to you in writing at this very hour and moment; and I have immediately sent Nicephorus the acolyte on to you, as he was preparing to go down to embark.”

These words make it clear that this cleric had not been expressly sent by Cornelius. Rather, as he was returning after completing the business for which he had come, the holy pontiff took advantage of the opportunity. Cornelius had already given him the letter to carry concerning Novatian’s new attempts; yet that letter was by no means so necessary, nor of such a kind as to require a cleric to be sent, since Augendus the confessor had already been dispatched concerning the matter and there was no need to send another afterward to report the same thing. Furthermore, if this is the Nicephorus the acolyte who carried Cyprian’s Letter XLII with Mettius, his return is postponed to November without reason. It matters little that Cornelius’ letter makes no mention of Mettius the subdeacon, with whom Nicephorus the acolyte had set out from Carthage; for similarly, as we saw above in Epistle XLIII, Mettius alone is named, although Nicephorus had been assigned as his companion.

As for the Roman council, it appears to have taken place altogether after the return of the confessors. There is absolutely no trace of this council in the letters sent to Rome or Carthage during the interval between Cornelius’ ordination and the confessors’ return. The legates Caldonius and Fortunatus, who returned to Carthage after Novatian’s ordination, brought letters from no more than sixteen bishops. Who, then, could believe that Cornelius’ ordination had already been confirmed in a council of sixty bishops, as Tillemont conjectures?

Moreover, according to Eusebius (book VI, chapter 43), this council decreed that “Novatus and those who had insolently exalted themselves together with him, and all who had presumed to assent to his utterly inhuman opinion, so alien to brotherly charity, were to be regarded as strangers to the Church.” Yet the confessors conducted themselves before their return, and were received upon returning, in such a way that they do not appear to have been excommunicated by a council of sixty bishops. For if they had been summoned to judgment by this synod, excommunicated, and then hardened themselves in schism, could they have said that they had been deceived, had suffered imposture, and that their intention had always remained within the Church? Who could believe that Cornelius would then have received them in such a manner as to commit everything else to Almighty God? That is not the customary manner of dealing with persons who have already been judged and excommunicated. The council, therefore, was later than the confessors’ return, though not much later; for there were most serious reasons why it should be held quickly: both to break Novatian’s party completely and to adjudicate the case of the lapsed, which had been referred to a council.

## XXIV.—THE ACTS AND WRITINGS OF ST. CYPRIAN IN THE YEAR 252, BEFORE THE PERSECUTION

Though condemned throughout the whole world, Novatian did not lose heart, but sent his new apostles through a great many cities, so that he might lay foundations for his newly established sect and set up other pseudo-bishops over the lawful bishops. Cyprian bears witness to this in his Letter to Antonianus, written at the end of 251 or the beginning of 252. Cyprian had long before received a letter from this Numidian bishop, in which Antonianus declared that he was not in communion with Novatian but remained attached to Cornelius, and requested that a copy of the same letter be sent to Cornelius. Later, however, another letter arrived in which he appeared to waver, having been influenced by Novatian’s letters. He asked what heresy Novatian had introduced, and on what grounds Cornelius communicated with Trophimus and with those who had offered incense; nor did he calmly accept even Cyprian’s humane treatment of the lapsed. Cyprian replies to him in this Letter LII in such a way as both admirably to defend himself and Cornelius and to demonstrate that no one could communicate with Novatian unless he rejected the communion of the whole Church.

It is clear that the letter was written after the return of the confessors, whom he says were united with Cornelius in the Church, and after the death of Decius, whom he calls a tyrant, but nevertheless before the indulgence granted to the lapsed in the present year, 252. For Cyprian’s defense concerns only what had been granted in the preceding year to the *libellatici*—those who had obtained certificates—and to the others who were in danger of death. It is not unreasonable to think that this Antonianus is the same person listed among the Numidian bishops in the heading of Epistle LXX; this is also evidence that he did not resist Cyprian’s admonitions.

At about this time, Novatian’s emissaries made Maximus pseudo-bishop of Carthage. But this crime was so contemptible and obscure that Cyprian did not even consider it worth writing to Rome about. For shortly before, on the advice of his colleagues, he had sent Cornelius the names of the sound and catholic bishops in Africa, so that Cornelius and his colleagues might know to whom they ought to write and from whom they ought in turn to receive letters. If anyone apart from those whom Cyprian had included in his letter dared to write, they were to know that he was either stained by sacrifice or by a certificate, or was one of the heretics—that is, a perverse and profane man.

[Col. 0137] Cyprian’s most excellent work *On the Lord’s Prayer* is thought to have been written in this year. Pontius lists it after the book *On the Unity of the Church*; and since much is said in that same book, forcefully and abundantly, against schismatics, it is reasonably concluded that the schisms of Felicissimus and Novatian had already appeared when Cyprian wrote it.

Around the first solemnities of Easter, Cyprian wrote Letter LIII to the bishops Fortunatus, Ahymnus, Optatus, Donatianus, Fortunatus, and Felix. While they were in the city of Capsa for the ordination of a bishop—probably Donatulus, bishop of Capsa, who delivered the sixty-ninth opinion at the Council of Carthage in 257—they had been consulted by Superius as to whether Ninus, Clementianus, and Florus should now be admitted to communion. These men had confessed Christ before the magistrate and the people, but had subsequently been overcome under torture before the proconsul; they had not ceased to do penance throughout these three years, not indeed three completed years, but a third year already begun. Not daring to decide the matter, the bishops referred it to Cyprian and wrote “that he should deliberate most fully upon this very matter with a larger number of colleagues.” Cyprian replies that communion should be restored to men of this kind, and promises that he will deliberate on the matter with the bishops “when they have fulfilled their obligation to celebrate the solemnity among their own people” and “have come” to Carthage.

There can scarcely be any doubt that he fulfilled this promise in the council held at Carthage on the Ides of May of this year, as he himself testifies in Epistle LV (p. 84). In that letter he writes that “Privatus, an old heretic, condemned in the colony of Lambaesis almost many years before for many serious offenses by the judgment of ninety bishops, and most severely censured in letters from Pope Fabian and Donatus,” bishop of Carthage, was not admitted when “he declared that he wished to plead his case before this council.”

Sixty-six bishops attended this council, if it was there—as is most probable—that a reply was given to the questions proposed by Bishop Fidus. Fidus had complained by letter that Therapius, bishop of Bulla and a confessor—as Pamelius conjectures from the Council of Carthage of 256—had granted peace prematurely to Victor, formerly a presbyter, before Victor had performed full penance. Fidus also proposed a certain novel opinion concerning infants: he thought that the custom of ancient circumcision ought to be observed in their case, so that they should not be baptized before the eighth day. Among other arguments, he offered this one:

> “The foot of an infant in the first days after its birth is not clean, and everyone shrinks from kissing it.”

The sixty-six bishops replied in Epistle LIX that Therapius had been rebuked, but that communion had nevertheless not been taken away from Victor. As for Fidus’ opinion concerning infants, they unanimously rejected it and defended the baptism of infants “immediately from the very beginning of their birth” with most distinguished and weighty arguments. It is evident that this council of sixty-six bishops is precisely the same as the one held on the Ides of May in the present year, 252. For the fact that granting lay communion to Victor, formerly a presbyter, did not escape censure is evidence that nothing had yet been subtracted or softened from the preceding year’s decree, and that peace had not yet been restored to penitents. Yet that indulgence was granted to them very few months after the council held on the Ides of May.

[Col. 0138] Pearson rightly censures Lombert for placing this council of sixty-six bishops not long after the council of the preceding year. It is not probable that, after a council which had been occupied for so long in adjudicating the cases of the lapsed, another council attended by so many should have been convened in the same year, especially since no trace of such an event exists in the letters written during that preceding year.

Yet Pearson himself postpones this council, in which sixty-six bishops replied to Fidus, until September 253, when, as he supposes, the bishops were deliberating on ecclesiastical affairs after peace had been restored. That opinion does not agree with these words of the bishops:

> “This matter,” they say, “moved us sufficiently, namely, that there had been a departure from the authority of our decree, so that before the lawful time and the completion of satisfaction, and without the petition or knowledge of the people, with no illness pressing and no necessity compelling, peace was granted to him.”

These words agree perfectly with the Ides of May 252. Victor had already completed a considerable part of his penance; the sole ground for censure was that he had not completed the full period. Indeed, there would have been no censure at all if peace had been granted at the people’s request. But the bishops could certainly never have acted so leniently in 253, at the very beginning of the peace. For those who, once Decius’ persecution had subsided, had displayed such severity that they threatened excommunication if anyone admitted the lapsed to communion—could they, when the persecution of Gallus and Volusian had ended and the hands of the lapsed were still smoking from impious sacrifices, have been so indulgent as to say that they would not have censured the granting of peace if only it had not been granted “without the petition or knowledge of the people”?

Moreover, councils do not appear to have been necessary after the persecution of Gallus and Volusian, because the entire matter could easily be decided from what had been decreed concerning the lapsed in the earlier council; or rather, because either no one, or at least very few, appear to have fallen in this persecution. Cyprian testifies in Epistle LVII that those who had fallen at Rome under Decius obtained the praise of confession in this second battle. The author of the book *To Novatian* (p. 11) gives the same testimony, at least concerning Africa. Hence, in Epistle LXXXI to the Martyrs, Cyprian does not lament the disasters and deaths of his people as he had done under Decius in Epistle IX. Nor is it surprising that those whom Epistle LIV shows to have been prepared for battle with such ardor of spirit proved victorious in this struggle.

About the same time, as Tillemont observes, Epistle LXIV was written to Epictetus and the people of Assuras against Fortunatianus, formerly bishop of that city. Having been deposed from the priesthood because of the worship of idols, he “wished to behave as though he were unimpaired” and had begun to claim the episcopate for himself. Epictetus, whom Cyprian calls his brother, appears to have been appointed in Fortunatianus’ place.

Fortunatianus was not the only one among the lapsed bishops to attempt a crime of this kind. Cyprian observes that several others had undertaken the same thing because [Col. 0139] “they long for the contributions, offerings, and profits upon which they formerly fastened with insatiable greed, and even now crave the dinners and banquets whose drunken excess they lately belched forth day after day with unabated indigestion.” Since, moreover, he exhorts all the lapsed that, “acknowledging the magnitude of their offense, they should not cease entreating the Lord, but should persevere in acts of satisfaction and knock at the Church’s door,” this letter is reasonably thought to have been written before indulgence was generally granted to the lapsed.

Privatus, rejected by the Council of Carthage as we have just said, established Fortunatus as a pseudo-bishop at Carthage. Fortunatus was “one of the five presbyters who had long since fled from the Church and had been condemned by the judgment of our fellow bishops,” Cyprian says in Epistle LV (p. 83), “many men of the greatest authority who in the preceding year had written to Cornelius concerning this matter.”

According to the holy martyr in the same passage, assistance in this crime was given by a certain Felix who had come with Privatus and whom Privatus himself had formerly appointed as a pseudo-bishop outside the Church, in heresy; by Jovinus and Maximus, who had been condemned by the judgment of nine bishops for impious sacrifices and crimes proved against them, and had again been excluded by many others at the council of the preceding year; and by Repostus of Saturnica, who had not merely fallen personally during the persecution but had also cast down the greater part of his people by sacrilegious persuasion. These five, together with a few men who had either sacrificed or had guilty consciences, chose Fortunatus as their pseudo-bishop.

But the crime did not succeed as they had intended. Although they repeatedly claimed that twenty-five bishops would come to Carthage, only five were found there, not without bringing upon themselves the disgrace of falsehood. Furthermore, when those whom they had formerly deceived and sustained with the false hope of returning to the Church saw the pseudo-bishop, they discovered the fraud and returned to the Church. Consequently, if the presbyters and deacons are counted, more persons had passed judgment upon those impious men than then appeared to be united with them.

Nevertheless, Cyprian investigated and carefully examined which persons ought to be admitted and received into the Church. Some could not be received “without scandal and danger to very many.” For the people seethed and resisted “whenever the incorrigible and insolent, those polluted either by adulteries or sacrifices, and thereafter additionally by schism, returned to the Church.” Cyprian could scarcely persuade the people—indeed, he had to compel them—to consent to the reception of such men; and the brotherhood’s indignation had become more justified because one or another person whom Cyprian had received through his leniency, despite the resistance and contradiction of the people, had proved worse than before (*ibid.*).

Cyprian was so little disturbed by Fortunatus’ ordination that he did not judge it necessary to write to Cornelius about it immediately. Nevertheless, when the opportunity arose through a very close friend and cleric—Felicianus the acolyte, whom Cornelius had sent to Africa with Bishop Perseus—Cyprian also wrote to Cornelius about this Fortunatus. But while Felicianus was delayed at Carthage, either by the wind or while waiting to receive other letters, Felicissimus forestalled him by hurrying to Rome. Felicissimus was being sent to Rome with letters from Fortunatus to Cornelius, because that impious faction, excluded on every side and everywhere notorious in [Col. 0140] Africa for the infamy of its crimes, had decided to sail to Rome.

Felicissimus therefore came to Rome accompanied by a throng and faction of desperate men, but was rejected by Cornelius and, “with the full vigor with which bishops ought to act,” driven from the Church. Yet the impious men repeatedly claimed that Fortunatus had been ordained by twenty-five bishops, and they “assailed Cornelius with threats that, if he did not receive the letters they had brought, they would read them publicly and utter many shameful and disgraceful things worthy of their own mouths.” Cornelius, who was troubled by Cyprian’s silence and “somewhat disturbed by their threats and terrors,” wrote two letters at the same time to Cyprian through Saturus the acolyte. The first indicated that Felicissimus had been resolutely expelled; the second revealed that Cornelius’ own mind had been disturbed and alarmed.

Cyprian was deeply distressed that, although he had displayed the greatest courage in defending Cornelius’ episcopate, Cornelius did not render the same support to him in a very similar affair. He therefore wrote Letter LV to Cornelius, making no attempt to conceal his distress that Cornelius had granted a hearing to schismatics stained with every mark of crime and condemned in council, against a bishop chosen in peace by the suffrage of all the people, protected by God’s help during persecution, faithfully united with all his colleagues, proved to his people over the course of four years, serving discipline in times of calm, proscribed in time of storm with the title of his episcopate attached to his name, so often demanded for the lion, honored in the circus and amphitheater by the testimony of the Lord’s favor, and recently demanded once again for the lion by the shouting of the populace.

He demonstrates that it was an impious act for schismatics to carry letters “to the chair of Peter and to the principal Church, from which priestly unity took its rise,” since, he says:

> “It has been established among us all, and is equally fair and just, that each person’s case should be heard in the place where the offense was committed . . . unless, perhaps, a few desperate and ruined men think that the authority of the bishops established in Africa is inferior,” etc.

Cyprian so defends the rights of his own episcopate as to acknowledge the origin of unity in the Roman Church as the principal church. Just as elsewhere, while admitting an equal power among the Apostles, he acknowledges that the origin of unity was established in Peter, so too in this passage, although he denies that the authority of the African bishops is inferior, the Oxford editor wrongly pronounces that Cyprian denies the primacy. But we have already discussed these matters in the preface.

Although this letter might appear capable of detracting somewhat from Cornelius’ reputation for prudence and constancy, Cyprian nevertheless does not hesitate to admonish and ask him, in accordance with his custom, to read the letter to the clergy who presided with him and to the most holy and numerous people—so well known and fully tested was Cornelius’ virtue in Cyprian’s eyes.

It is certain that this letter was written in the present year, 252; for Cyprian mentions the council of the preceding year and also another held on the most recent Ides of May. Thus he says that he had now been proved to his people for four years. The letter, however, does not seem to have been written before the end of June or the beginning of July.

## XXV.—THE PERSECUTION IS REVEALED TO CYPRIAN.—HE EXHORTS THE PEOPLE OF THIBARIS TO THE CONTEST.—IN A COUNCIL, WHICH MUST BE DISTINGUISHED FROM THE OTHER COUNCIL HELD ON THE IDES OF MAY, HE RESTORES PEACE TO THE PENITENT LAPSED

[Col. 0141]

Since a considerable interval elapsed between the Council of Carthage, which we have said was held on the Ides of May, and the persecution, it is evident that the emperors Gallus and Volusian, who had obtained the imperial power at the end of 251, did nothing hostile against the Christians throughout that whole interval, and did not unleash their fury against them before the middle of the present summer. But the persecution was violent and did not end until the lives of the emperors themselves ended.

Some sparks had already appeared when Cyprian wrote Letter LV to Cornelius. For he says that “in these very days” in which he was writing, “because of the sacrifices which the people were ordered by a published edict to celebrate,” he had “again been demanded for the lion by the cries of the populace” “in the circus.” The occasion for ordering these sacrifices appears to have been the plague which raged with dreadful violence under Gallus and Volusian and the subsequent rulers.

Not long afterward came the edicts of the emperors Gallus and Volusian against the Christians. When Cyprian received foreknowledge of them through many visions divinely presented to him, he wrote Letter LVI to the people of Thibaris. He had previously intended to visit them, but was then unable to carry out his plan, and therefore sent letters in his place. In it he warns them that, “by the favor of the Lord who instructs us,” he had learned—and that they must know, believe with certainty, and hold fast—that a struggle more severe and savage than the former one was now imminent. He then draws from the Holy Scriptures and from the principles of the Christian religion everything capable of encouraging them steadfastly to endure the persecution.

Cyprian appears to have been prevented from satisfying the wishes of the people of Thibaris by the necessity laid upon him to make provision for the affairs of his own church as persecution approached. He judged that nothing should take precedence, at this most difficult time, over gathering within the Lord’s camp absolutely all the soldiers of Christ who desired weapons and demanded battle. He therefore decreed in council with forty-one bishops that, after the individual cases had been examined, peace should be granted to those lapsed persons who had not ceased to perform penance from the first day of their fall.

The bishops informed Cornelius of this in Letter LIV, saying that they had so determined “at the prompting of the Holy Spirit.” They demonstrate that the blood of Christ should not be denied to those who promised that they would shed their own blood for Christ and fight valiantly. They add that they hoped the decision would be pleasing to Cornelius “in consideration of paternal mercy.”

I am surprised that Pearson confuses this council with the one held on the Ides of May.

1. No letters were written to Cornelius in the name of the synod concerning the matters deliberated upon on the Ides of May. Indeed, even concerning Privatus, whom the synod had refused to admit, Cyprian wrote to Cornelius in his own name only when an opportunity was offered through Felicianus the acolyte.

2. In Epistle LV, from which we say that a council was held on the Ides of May, there is no trace of indulgence having been granted to the lapsed; only the necessity of penance is defended against Felicissimus and his satellites. From this it is clear that, in the Oxford edition, this letter is wrongly placed before Letter LIV, through which Cornelius was informed of the communion granted to the lapsed.

3. The council of forty-one bishops in which communion was granted to the lapsed was held when persecution was imminent and the enemy had announced the battle. The lapsed “desired and demanded weapons,” as Epistle LIV says, and professed that they “were prepared for battle and would stand courageously and fight for the name of their Lord and for their own salvation.” For this reason, the decision must immediately have preceded the confession of Cornelius, who was the first to confess at Rome. But many events intervened between the council held on the Ides of May and the persecution and confession of Cornelius: Fortunatus’ ordination, the delegation sent by him to Rome, Cornelius’ letters to Cyprian, and Cyprian’s reply.

## XXVI.—ST. CYPRIAN CONGRATULATES ST. CORNELIUS UPON THE GLORY OF HIS CONFESSION.—HE EXHORTS THE CARTHAGINIAN CONFESSORS IN EPISTLE LXXXI, WHICH IS SHOWN TO HAVE BEEN WRITTEN DURING THIS PERSECUTION IN THE YEAR 252

Cyprian’s prediction of the coming persecution was not empty, nor did the precautions he took to strengthen the Christians fail to produce the desired result. At Rome the adversary sprang forth to disturb Christ’s camp with violent terror. But there the courage of the bishop who led them was publicly proved, and in a certain sense the entire Roman church confessed. It was not individual soldiers who went out to battle, but the whole camp; everyone who heard hurried forward and came. Very many of those who had fallen under Decius were restored through glorious confession, having been made stronger for battle by the very grief of their penance, so that it became apparent that in the first persecution they had trembled because of fear at something new and unfamiliar.

We learn this from Cyprian’s Epistle LVII, in which he congratulates Cornelius, then an exile at Centumcellae, upon the glory of his confession and shares with him what he had learned when instructed by the providence of the Lord who warns us:

> “The day of our contest and struggle,” he says, “is now drawing near.”

Finally, he asks that whichever of them should first depart to the Lord should pray to God for the other and for the brothers and sisters. Not long afterward this prediction was fulfilled in Cornelius, who died as a martyr at Centumcellae on September 14 of the present year, 252, as is agreed among the most learned authorities.

Meanwhile Novatian, as Cyprian observes, remained inactive and was touched by no persecution at all, just as he had no share either in the unity of the Church or in its triumphs. Lucius, who succeeded Cornelius, obtained the glory of the priesthood and of exile at almost the same time. But he was recalled shortly afterward and died as a martyr on the fourth or fifth of March in 253, after having presided for five months and a few days.

Cyprian had congratulated Lucius upon his priesthood and confession in letters that have not come down to us; he also congratulated him upon his return in Epistle LVIII, in his own name and that of his colleagues. Beyond this service of correspondence, by which he testifies that his own joy was added to the common joy of the Roman Church, he says that he did not [Col. 0143] cease “in the sacrifices and prayers to give thanks to God the Father and to Christ his Son our Lord, and equally to pray and petition that he who is perfect and makes perfect might preserve and bring to perfection”—in Lucius—“the glorious crown of confession,” etc. As though foreseeing what subsequently occurred, he suspects that Lucius had been recalled from exile so that he might shed his life for Christ before the eyes of his own church.

From Cyprian we learn that Lucius confirmed Cornelius’ decrees concerning the lapsed. Cyprian calls Lucius and Cornelius blessed martyrs and says that he honors their memory. He testifies that, filled with the Spirit of God and established in glorious martyrdom, they judged that peace should be granted to the lapsed and recorded in their letters that, once penance had been performed, the fruit of communion and peace ought not to be denied (Epistle LXVII).

Although Cyprian was demanded for the lion when the sparks of persecution broke forth, he did not withdraw as he had during the persecution under Decius, nor was he driven out or proscribed. The first at Carthage to endure the attack of the raging populace, as may be seen from Epistle LXXXI, was the glorious old man Rogatianus, a presbyter who had confessed during Decius’ persecution and who, after being released from prison, had been assigned by Cyprian to govern the Church of Carthage together with two bishops and the presbyter Numidicus.

When Rogatianus was the first to be cast into prison during this persecution of Gallus and Volusian, together with Felicissimus—whom Cyprian calls an ever-peaceful and sober brother—he was crowned with him. Cyprian exhorts the other confessors confined in prison (in Epistle LXXXI) to imitate Rogatianus, and says that he continually prays to the Lord that they may obtain the same crown as he did.

Among these confessors boys and women were conspicuous, something that we also see to have occurred during Decius’ persecution from the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 181), and during Valerian’s persecution from Epistle LXXVII. Those who had fallen under Decius likewise obtained the glory of confession, as we observed in chapter 24. This must indeed be understood of very many, though not of all; for the author of the book *To Novatian* mentions others from among their number who were still devoted to penance.

But because some assign Epistle LXXXI to Valerian’s persecution and others to that of Decius, we must explain why it appears preferable to refer it to this persecution under Gallus and Volusian.

Pamelius and Baronius number this epistle among Cyprian’s last and believe that it was written during the persecution of Valerian. They are led chiefly by this consideration: in this Epistle LXXXI, the presbyter and confessor Rogatianus—who is known to have survived the persecution of Decius—is said to have shed his life for Christ together with Felicissimus. This indeed accords with the ecclesiastical calendars, in which, Baronius says, the solemn commemoration of the martyrdom of Rogatianus and Felicissimus, “who suffered on the same day, is recorded for the seventh day before the Kalends of November” [October 26]. Pearson, on the contrary, contends that this epistle was written under Decius, while Cyprian was in hiding, and proves this from the epistle’s opening words: “I greet you, dearest brothers, myself also longing to enjoy the sight of you, if the circumstances of my position permitted me to reach you.” Cyprian, however, is accustomed to speak in this way from his place of retreat, as in [Col. 0144] Epistle V: “And since the circumstances of my position do not now permit me to be present”; and in Epistle XXXVII, to the same clergy: “Would that the circumstances of my position and rank permitted me to be present in person now!” Pearson therefore concludes that these words signify, not Cyprian’s exile under Valerian, but his retreat under Decius. He believes, moreover, that the passage from which Rogatianus is judged to have died must be understood in an entirely different sense, and that an error crept into the ecclesiastical calendars when Usuard, Ado, and others uncritically followed Bede, who cites this letter of Cyprian and teaches from it that Rogatianus and Felicissimus were crowned with martyrdom.

Pearson’s opinion appeals to Tillemont; yet many considerations make it clear that this epistle was written not in retreat but at Carthage, when Rogatianus had already died—not, however, under Valerian, but under Gallus and Volusianus. Cyprian’s context is far too explicit for us to deny that Rogatianus and Felicissimus had been crowned with martyrdom before Cyprian wrote this epistle. Let us examine the passage:

> “Maintaining this faith yourselves,” he says, “and meditating upon it day and night, ready for God with your whole heart and, in contempt of present things, thinking only of those to come, you seek to attain the fruit of the eternal kingdom, the embrace and kiss of the Lord, and the sight of him, so that in all things you may follow Rogatianus the presbyter, that glorious old man, who by religious courage and divine favor is making for you a path to the glory of our time. Together with our brother Felicissimus, always quiet and sober, he met the assault of the raging populace, first prepared lodging for you in prison, and, as it were, your quartermaster, now also goes before you. That this may be brought to completion in you, we beseech the Lord in continual prayers, so that, as your beginnings proceed toward the highest consummation, he who makes you confessors may also make you crowned.”

There is scarcely a word in this passage that does not indicate that Rogatianus suffered for Christ. Cyprian calls him “a glorious old man,” which is evidence that he had attained glory. He praises the confessors because they think only of things to come, so that they may reach the Lord’s embrace and follow Rogatianus in all things, whom they had already imitated in many. Rogatianus, therefore, had already come into the Lord’s presence, since attaining the Lord’s presence is identified with following Rogatianus in all things. Rogatianus had prepared their first lodging in prison. Where was he preparing the second, unless in heaven, going before them like a kind of quartermaster? Finally, Cyprian prays to God that the thing in which Rogatianus had preceded them might be brought to completion in them also, and that they might attain the crown. Rogatianus, therefore, had already attained this crown. Since he did not obtain it in the persecution of Decius, but left prison before Cyprian emerged from his retreat, this epistle must necessarily be assigned to another time. Tillemont relies on the words “making the path” and “goes before you” to prove that Rogatianus had not died when this epistle was written. But who does not know that the poverty of the Latin language often compels the use of words of this kind? In Epistle LXXVIII, the martyrs praise Cyprian [Col. 0145] because, when he was the first to raise the standard of confession, his soul “not only began to share the company of the martyrs already departing from the world, but also united itself in heavenly friendship with those yet to come.” In precisely the same manner, in Epistle IX Cyprian exhorts the confessors to follow the martyr Mappalicus:

> “It is both my wish and my exhortation,” he says, “that the rest of you also follow this now most blessed martyr and the others who shared in the same contest and were his companions—steadfast in faith, patient in suffering, victorious under examination—so that those whom the bond of confession and the lodging of prison joined together may also be joined by the consummation of courage and the heavenly crown.”

Pearson has not understood well the words, “if the circumstances of my position permitted me to reach you.” For he says that by these words Cyprian signifies “the place where he especially longed to be present and to enjoy the sight of the confessors, but the condition of the place—that is, of Carthage, where the persecution was already raging—did not permit it.” Yet numerous testimonies from Cyprian make it clear that this word designates not Carthage but episcopal authority. Thus in Epistle XI: “The responsibility of our position and the fear of the Lord compel us”; “Since they”—the martyrs—“mindful of our position, have directed letters to me” (Epistle X); “It befits the position itself and the office of our priesthood” (Epistle LXIII). See Epistle LXV.

Consequently, when Cyprian says in this Epistle LXXXI:

> “I greet you, dearest brothers, myself also longing to enjoy the sight of you, if the circumstances of my position permitted me to reach you. For what could happen to me more desirable or joyful than to cling to you now, so that you might embrace me with those hands which, pure and innocent and preserving the Lord’s faith, rejected sacrilegious acts of homage? What could be more delightful and sublime than now to kiss your faces and to be seen by your eyes while present among you?”

when Cyprian says this, I repeat, he indicates that one thing alone keeps him from visiting the martyrs: his fear that, conspicuous because of his rank, he might be unable to escape the eyes of the pagans. Nor is it necessary that he was absent from Carthage in order to write in this way. His rank could have restrained him from visiting the holy martyrs even if he had been present in Carthage. For one who took care that the martyrs “should not be visited in a crowd or by an assembled multitude, but that even the presbyters who offered sacrifice there among the confessors should take turns, each accompanied by a single deacon” (Epistle V), would still less have allowed himself to catch the pagans’ eyes and thereby kindle new conflagrations.

Indeed, this custom prevailed in Africa even before Cyprian: the bishop did not visit the confessors. For Cyprian testifies in Epistles X and XXI that under his predecessors it had always been done in the past in such a way that the presbyters and deacons instructed the martyrs and confessors most fully concerning the law of the Gospel, while the deacons who went to the prison guided the martyrs’ desires by their counsel and the precepts of Scripture. Nothing, therefore, prevents us from thinking that Cyprian wrote these things while in the city itself, though necessary considerations and the example of his predecessors kept him from the sight of the confessors. I would even venture to say that he would not have spoken in this way [Col. 0146] if he had been absent from Carthage. For how could his rank alone have kept a man who was absent and concealed in a hidden place from embracing the martyrs, when, had he been in the city itself, necessary precautions and the examples of his predecessors would have excluded him from that joy? Hence, in Epistle IX, which is known to have been written to the martyrs and confessors during his retreat, he does not say that his retreat was burdensome to him because he could not visit them. In Epistle XXXVII he expresses his longing for the city, but by no means so that he might remain in the martyrs’ embraces; rather, it was “so that, ready and willing, I might fulfill, in solemn ministry, all the duties of affection toward my most courageous brothers.”

This epistle, therefore, does not fit the time of Decius, nor does it fit the persecution of Valerian, whose first assault Cyprian himself withstood.
