Rogatianus and Felicissimus did not then carry the torch before all others in confessing Christ’s name; Cyprian himself did, as we shall see below. Epistle LXXXI is assigned far more appropriately to the persecution of Gallus and Volusianus, during which Cyprian was neither expelled from Carthage nor withdrew voluntarily. Yet there is no doubt that he sent his letters to serve in his place before the ears and eyes of the confessors, since his rank, exposed to everyone’s notice, did not permit him to visit them. In October of the year 252, when Rogatianus and Felicissimus are said in the ecclesiastical calendars to have suffered, the persecution was raging. Cornelius bears witness to this fact, since he died a martyr in September of that year. From the assault of the raging populace which Rogatianus is said to have met, Pearson concludes that Epistle LXXXI pertains to the persecution of Decius, because popular violence often broke out against Cyprian during that persecution. But Cyprian experienced the same violence of the populace during the persecution of Gallus, as he himself relates in Epistle LV. Moreover, the dreadful plague that accompanied Gallus’s persecution seems far more suited to stirring popular disturbances, since the Christians were blamed as the cause of the calamity.

## XXVII.—THE WONDERFUL CHARITY OF ST. CYPRIAN DURING THE CALAMITY OF THE PLAGUE.—HE DEFENDS RELIGION AGAINST DEMETRIANUS.—THE ABUNDANT GENEROSITY OF THE WHOLE CHURCH OF CARTHAGE IN RANSOMING CAPTIVES

To the persecution was added a dreadful plague which, having probably begun under the Decii themselves, raged with far greater force under Gallus and Volusianus. Here Cyprian’s charity shone forth before the very eyes of the pagans and redounded to the highest benefit of the commonwealth. For while all the pagans recoiled from and fled contagion and impiously abandoned their own people, and while corpses lay throughout the whole city and no one regarded anything except cruel profit, then indeed the bishop of Christ and God gathered the people in one place and by vigorous exhortation induced them to perform the duties of compassion not only toward the household of faith but even toward the pagans themselves. Inflamed with charity, he said things which, Pontius declares, “if the Gentiles could have heard, they might perhaps have believed immediately.”

Duties were accordingly distributed at once according to the condition and rank of each person. Many who, because of the constraints of poverty, could not practice beneficence through expenditure offered more [Col. 0147] than expenditures could provide, compensating by their own labor and gaining a reward dearer than all riches. Thus, through the abundance of overflowing works, good was done to everyone, not only to the household of faith.

Amid these calamities of persecution and plague, Cyprian wrote his book *Against Demetrianus*, which Pontius designates in these words: “Through which the Gentiles were defeated, when the charges they hurl against us were turned back upon themselves.” Demetrianus used repeatedly to come to Cyprian; but Cyprian judged him, “barking against God and making a clamor with impious words,” wholly unfit for debate, “since he seemed able neither to teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious by religion, nor curb the raging by gentleness.” But when Demetrianus continually asserted that “wars arise more frequently, that plague and famine rage, and that long periods of clear weather withhold rains and showers,” and that this was imputed to the Christians, Cyprian was unwilling to remain silent any longer. Lest his silence be attributed to lack of confidence rather than to modesty, he resolved that this man must be answered, “together with the others whom he himself had perhaps incited and, by sowing hatred against Christians with slanderous words, had made his companions through the proliferation of his own root and stock.”

He therefore demonstrates that the calamities do not arise because the Christians worship God, but because the Gentiles do not worship him and torment his worshipers with every kind of torture. Although these calamities touch the Christians themselves as well, they nevertheless harm only the Gentiles, not the Christians, whom they conduct to eternal joys. Lactantius (book V, chap. 4) thought Cyprian had acted somewhat inappropriately by citing the testimony of Scripture rather than of poets and philosophers in order to break and refute Demetrianus. But, besides the fact that the Scriptures had to be employed so that what Christians believed and hoped might be readily apparent, there is assuredly such power and such majesty in the testimonies of the Holy Spirit that they can move even those who are most hardened. (See Baluze’s note.)

That this book was written during the persecution of Gallus and Volusianus is clear from the testimony of Pontius, who lists it among the books *On the Lapsed* and *On the Unity of the Church*, written after the persecution of Decius, and the book *On Patience*, which preceded the persecution of Valerian. The same conclusion may also be drawn from these words of Cyprian (p. 221):

> “To say nothing of ancient records, and without rehearsing, with any proclamation of the voice, the acts of vengeance repeatedly exacted on behalf of God’s worshipers, the evidence of a recent event is sufficient: the defense that recently followed so swiftly—and, in such swiftness, so mightily—in the collapse of affairs, the loss of wealth, the loss of soldiers, and the diminution of armies.”

Earlier editions read “in the collapse of kings,” by which words learned men believed that the Decii were designated. But although Baluze, on the authority of ancient manuscripts, printed “in the collapse of affairs,” the passage is no less clearly a description of what befell the Decii because of their persecution of the Christians, and cannot be referred to the Gordians or the Philips, who did not persecute the Christians.

[Col. 0148] Some have believed that the Demetrianus whom Cyprian refutes was the proconsul of Africa; others, that he was one of the judges. I would be more inclined to believe that he was one of the sophists. This is sufficiently suggested by his frequent disputes with Cyprian, the calumnies against the Christians, and the accusations for which Cyprian reproaches him, without in any way indicating that power was joined to this malicious disposition. Learned men seem to have been misled by these words (p. 219): “You who judge others, be at last your own judge as well.” But these words do not pertain to a forensic judgment, nor does Cyprian direct them specifically at Demetrianus. He speaks generally to the Gentiles, who, as he says in the same place, had leisure “to be wicked amid the very adversities and, amid such great dangers, to pass judgment not primarily upon themselves but upon another.” Nor do these words (p. 220) properly apply to Demetrianus: “You deprive the innocent, the just, and those dear to God of their homes; you despoil them of their property, weigh them down with chains, shut them in prison, and punish them by the sword, wild beasts, and fire, etc.” Rather, they apply generally to all pagans, whom—as is customary in speeches of this kind—he addresses sometimes in the singular and sometimes in the plural. Shortly before he had said: “Furthermore, you harass the servants of God and those dedicated to his majesty and name with unjust persecutions. It is not enough that you yourself do not worship God; in addition, you persecute with sacrilegious hostility those who do worship him.”

Inflamed by Cyprian’s exhortations, the people of Carthage gladly seized any opportunity that presented itself for the exercise of charity. They showed this most clearly when eight bishops of Numidia, gravely afflicted because the barbarians had carried off many Christians from Numidia—including virgins consecrated to Christ—implored Cyprian’s aid. Then indeed the common “grief and anguish over the peril of the virgins” came upon the Church of Carthage, for whom they believed they must mourn “not only the loss of freedom but also that of chastity.” Accordingly, “everyone promptly, willingly, and generously contributed monetary assistance for the brothers. They were always inclined toward God’s work in accordance with the steadfastness of their faith, but now,” says Cyprian, “they were still more inflamed toward works of salvation by contemplation of so great a sorrow.”

Cyprian therefore wrote Epistle LX to the bishops of Numidia and sent “one hundred thousand sesterces, collected by the contributions of the clergy and people.” The holy martyr asks them that, if anything of this sort should happen again, they should report it without delay by letter, “holding it certain that the Church” of Carthage “and the entire brotherhood pray that these things may not happen again; but, if they should happen, will willingly and generously provide assistance.” Cyprian also appended the names of each of those who had promptly and willingly taken part in this most necessary work, so that in their sacrifices and prayers the bishops might make a return to them for their good work. He also added the names of his colleagues and fellow priests, who themselves, when present, had contributed certain sums according to their ability, both in their own name and that of their people; and he recorded and sent the amounts of their contributions.

Pearson believes that these events occurred at the beginning of the year 253, when Gallus’s negligence left the Roman frontiers [Col. 0149] open to barbarian nations. At least this much seems capable of being established: this epistle was written after the persecution of Decius. For if anyone compares the book *On the Lapsed* with this epistle, he will readily understand that the Carthaginians had been so purified by persecution and so transformed by Cyprian’s cares and labors that one could scarcely recognize them as the same people. Previously, a long period of peace had corrupted very many in this Church, and love of property had driven them to sacrifice to idols. But now, when they receive news of what had happened in Numidia, all account the captivity of their brothers as their own; all grieve and suffer anguish at the peril of the virgins; all vie with one another in pouring out their wealth to ransom the temples of God; all pray that these things may not happen again; yet if they should happen, all promise willing and generous assistance.

## XXVIII.—ON THE BOOKS AND EPISTLES WRITTEN AFTER THE PERSECUTION, UNDER VALERIAN AND AT THE BEGINNING OF THE PONTIFICATE OF POPE STEPHEN, IN THE YEARS 253 AND 254

Not long after the martyrdom of Lucius, which occurred on the fifth day of March in this year 253, Stephen was elected, perhaps because the disturbances arising in the empire were already allowing the Christians to breathe freely. For in May, as the most learned critics believe, vengeance for the blood of the Christians was manifested in Gallus. When his own soldiers saw that he was unequal to the task of repelling Aemilianus, who had already occupied Italy, they deprived him of both empire and life. Then, when Aemilianus himself was killed around the month of August by the soldiers who had conferred the imperial power upon him, Valerian obtained the empire without opposition. Through his justice and exceptional favor, the Church enjoyed the brightest peace.

But once the storm of persecution had been calmed, the plague grew worse. Cyprian therefore observed that “among the people some, whether through weakness of spirit, slightness of faith, attachment to worldly life, softness of sex, or—what is more serious—error concerning the truth, stood with less courage and did not display the divine and unconquered strength of their breast.” He did not neglect the opportunity to teach the truth, but wrote the outstanding book *On Mortality*, in which he demonstrates that death is feared by one who is unwilling to go to Christ, whereas those who truly believe in Christ ought to rejoice when they are called to Christ.

He relates that a certain bishop who asked to escape his illness was rebuked in a vision:

> “To us also,” he says (p. 234), “the least and the last, how often has it been revealed, how frequently and clearly has it been commanded by God’s favor, that I should testify continually and preach publicly that our brothers, freed from the world by the Lord’s summons, are not to be mourned!”

Pontius thus describes this book, after the work *Against the Gentiles* and before the books *On Works and Almsgiving* and *On Patience*: “By which Christians of a more tender disposition at the loss of their own—or, what is more serious, of weaker faith—might be consoled by the hope of things to come.” It seems to have been written during the peace under Valerian, for it contains no indication of a persecution joined to the plague. Indeed, Cyprian declares that through this calamity Christians were being armed and prepared to conduct themselves courageously when persecution should come:

> “[Col. 0150] See,” he says, “virgins depart in peace, safe with their glory. . . . The lukewarm are set aflame, the lax are braced, the sluggish are roused, deserters are compelled to return, Gentiles are constrained to believe, the old population of believers is called to rest, and a fresh and numerous army is mustered with greater strength for the battle line. When the battle comes, those who enlist for service in the time of mortality will fight without fear of death.”

Hence some also concealed their fear under the pretext that the plague might snatch away from them the opportunity for martyrdom—an excuse they could not have used if a persecution had then opened an entrance to martyrdom.

Pearson nevertheless believes that this book was written under Gallus, in the year 252, “because Cyprian extensively pursues an argument drawn from the imminent persecution and the coming Antichrist.” But since the holy martyr had long believed that the end of the world and the advent of Antichrist were imminent, he must have retained this opinion even during the peace, especially since the plague then raging appeared to be one of the events that would precede the end of the world. Hence the same suspicions concerning the perishing world and the approaching Antichrist occur in books and epistles written after the persecution, as in the book *On the Unity of the Church* (pp. 199 and 200), and in Epistle LXVIII, concerning Basilides and Martialis (p. 120). It is therefore more probable that the book *On Mortality* was written under Valerian, in the year 253 or 254.

The book *On Works and Almsgiving* is listed by Pontius immediately after the book *On Mortality* and was consequently written under Valerian. The conclusion of the book indicates a time of peace:

> “If the day either of our recompense or of persecution finds us unencumbered, swift, and running in this contest of works,” says Cyprian, “the Lord will nowhere fail to reward our merits. In peace he will give to those who conquer the white crown for their works; in persecution he will double it with the purple crown for suffering.”

Epistle LXIX, which Cyprian wrote to Florentius Pupianus when he had already governed the Church of Carthage for six years, is assigned to the beginning of the year 254. This Pupianus had been in the Church before the persecution and had been in communion with Cyprian; but afterward, joining himself to the schismatics, he had rashly believed things about Cyprian that were “unspeakable, shameful, and execrable even to the Gentiles.” Indeed, he even dared to write letters to him in which, constituting himself judge of his own bishop, he said that priests ought to be humble; that a scruple into which he had fallen must be removed from his mind; that because of Cyprian the Church had a portion of itself scattered abroad; that all who communicated with him were polluted by his polluted mouth; and that they had lost the hope of eternal life through the contagion of communion with him.

Cyprian defended his innocence with the gravity and steadfastness becoming a bishop, and offered forgiveness to his shameless detractor if, even belatedly, he should begin to repent of his rashness, pride, and insolence:

> “Yet,” he says, “the regard and fear of the divine judgment remain with us, so that I must first consult my Lord as to whether, by his manifestation and admonition, he permits peace [Col. 0151] to be given to you and you to be admitted to the communion of his Church.”

It is clear from these words that this man was not a bishop, as some have imagined, but a layman subject to Cyprian’s jurisdiction, from which he had nevertheless withdrawn himself through wicked schism. Nor is the opinion of those who contend that Pupianus suffered something during the persecution any more probable, merely because Cyprian says to him (p. 121): “Lest perhaps the dignity of your splendor and martyrdom be stained by communion with us.” And on p. 122: “For when persecution came, it advanced you to the highest sublimity of martyrdom, but weighed me down with the burden of proscription when it was publicly proclaimed: ‘If anyone holds or possesses anything from the property of Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of the Christians.’” But there is manifest irony in these words. Dionysius of Alexandria refutes the calumnies of Germanus in a manner not dissimilar: “But perhaps Germanus,” he says in Eusebius (book VII, chap. 11), “boasts of many confessions of faith and can proclaim many things done against himself.” Indeed, Cyprian indicates that material for reproach would not be lacking if inquiry were made into Pupianus’s conduct both during the persecution and in peace. “But concerning the things you have done,” he says (p. 124), “whether in persecution or in peace, it is foolish for me to wish to judge you, since you have all the more appointed yourself our judge.”

There is no doubt that Cyprian wrote Epistles LXVII and LXVIII at the beginning of Pope Stephen’s pontificate, while peace prevailed under Valerian. The occasion of the sixty-seventh was as follows. Marcianus, bishop of Arles, had joined himself to Novatian and departed from the unity of the Catholic Church. He closed the aid of divine mercy to the servants of God who were penitent and sorrowing and who knocked upon the Church with tears, groaning, and grief. Since he did not appear to have been excluded from communion by the bishops, he boasted and proclaimed that, by supporting Novatian and following his obstinacy, he had separated himself from the communion of the bishops.

Faustinus of Lyons wrote to Cyprian about this matter once and again. After receiving his letters, Cyprian writes to Pope Stephen and repeatedly urges him to send the fullest possible letters to the province and to the people established at Arles, so that Marcianus may be excluded from communion and another substituted in his place. Since many of the brothers had died without peace in previous years, he asks that aid at least be given to the others who remain and who groan day and night. He also asks Stephen to inform him who had been substituted for Marcianus at Arles, so that he might know to whom he should direct the brothers and to whom he ought to write. Launoy denied this epistle to Cyprian, but his opinion has been so thoroughly rejected among the learned that anyone wishing to refute it would merely be doing what has already been done.

At about the same time, another affair in Spain moved Cyprian’s charity—which was not confined within the boundaries of Africa—to aid foreign churches. Two bishops, Basilides and Martialis, who had been deposed for most serious offenses, dared to claim for themselves the priesthood that had rightly been taken away from them. Each had been stained by an impious certificate of idolatrous compliance. Basilides, furthermore, in addition to the stain of the certificate, had blasphemed against God [Col. 0152] while lying ill, had confessed that he had blasphemed, and had voluntarily laid aside the episcopate because of the wound to his conscience. He had turned to doing penance and beseeching God, quite thankful if it should fall to his lot to communicate even as a layman. Martialis likewise, besides having long frequented the shameful and filthy banquets of the Gentiles in an association, had placed his sons in the same association at profane tombs according to the custom of foreign nations and buried them with aliens. He had also declared in publicly recorded proceedings before a *procurator ducenarius* [a procurator receiving 200,000 sesterces] that he had complied with idolatry and denied Christ.

When each had been deposed for these and many other offenses, Basilides—Sabinus having been substituted in his place by the vote of the entire brotherhood and the judgment of the bishops—went to Rome and deceived Stephen, who was far away and ignorant of both the events and the truth, so as to procure his unjust restoration to the episcopate from which he had rightly been deposed. Cyprian does not expressly say that Martialis also went to Rome, but sufficiently indicates it when he says: “Nor could deceit have profited Martialis, so as to enable him, himself also entangled in serious offenses, to retain the episcopate.”

Some bishops in Spain appear to have favored those deposed bishops. But the Churches of León, Astorga, and Mérida wrote about the matter to the African bishops and sent as delegates Sabinus and Felix, who were probably substituted in place of Basilides and Martialis. Another Felix, of Zaragoza, whom Cyprian calls a cultivator of the faith and defender of the truth, confirmed by his own letter everything those Churches had written and entrusted to their delegates. The letters were read and the delegates heard in a council of thirty-seven bishops. Cyprian, who presided, and the other bishops replied through Epistle LXVIII that the offenses of Basilides had not so much been erased as increased; that an ordination rightly performed could not be rescinded; and that deceit could not benefit Martialis either. Such men attempted in vain to usurp the episcopate for themselves, since it was manifest that men of this kind could neither preside over the Church of Christ nor offer sacrifices to God.

They express their indignation against the bishops who favored their deposed colleagues and warn the people themselves that they must not communicate with such men, and that those who mingle with them in unlawful communion are polluted by contact with them. This judgment, indeed, not only does not loosen the reins of popular license, but even restrains it, lest the people pass judgment upon their own bishop at their own discretion, either by rejecting one lawfully ordained by other bishops or by retaining one lawfully deposed.

## XXIX.—THE DISSENSIONS CONCERNING BAPTISM THAT AROSE AT THE END OF THE YEAR 253; AND ST. STEPHEN CONTENDED WITH THE EASTERNERS BEFORE HE CONTENDED WITH THE AFRICANS

At last, in the course of our discussion, we have reached that most celebrated controversy concerning the baptism of heretics. In this controversy, it was not some small band of heretics or schismatics that declared war upon the universal Church; rather, distinguished churches—Africa, Cappadocia, Cilicia, and the neighboring provinces—contended with other churches [Col. 0153] over a matter of the greatest gravity. Although, amid the very conflagration of dissension, the state of affairs presented a sorrowful appearance, nevertheless, from the benefits that flowed into the Church from this controversy, it may readily be seen that it arose under Christ’s providence and ordering. This was not only so that a matter of such importance might eventually be confirmed by the united and harmonious consent of all, but also so that posterity might have something to imitate in dissensions of this kind.

For the defenders of the baptism of heretics did not break the covenant of fraternal charity with those whom they regarded as inflicting the greatest injury upon the sacraments. The latter, for their part, did not hesitate to communicate both with those whom they believed had not even been initiated by Baptism and with those who appeared to deny Baptism to dying infants and to offer the Eucharist to the unbaptized.

Tillemont assigns the beginning of the dissension to the year 256, although he does not reject Pearson’s view that the first Council of Carthage was held in the autumn of 255. Both believe that the conflict began in Africa before it did in the East. Those who maintain that Stephen died in the year 255 contend that the dissension broke out earlier. But although Tillemont and Pearson believe, for weighty reasons, that Stephen died in 257, they nevertheless seem to place the beginnings of the dissension far too late. I shall undertake to prove that the controversy began to be agitated at the end of the year 253, and that Stephen contended with the Easterners before he did with the Africans.

1. My authority for believing that debate concerning baptism began in the year 253 is Eusebius, who expressly declares (book VII, chap. 4) that Dionysius, in a letter to Stephen concerning Baptism, indicated that “all the churches everywhere, once the fury of the persecution had abated, detesting the turbulent novelty of Novatus, had made peace with one another.” The persecution had therefore scarcely ended when Dionysius attempted to settle the controversy that had arisen concerning Baptism. Moreover, since the persecution was brought to an end in May of 253, Dionysius does not appear to have written to Stephen about Baptism later than the end of that year.

Pearson, with Tillemont not dissenting, judges that Eusebius erred by believing that what Dionysius had said about the peace established after the dissensions stirred up by the Novatians was said about the peace that followed the persecutions of the pagans. But before we say that Eusebius blundered so carelessly, there must be some weighty reason for doing so. He accurately distinguishes the fury of persecution from the turbulent novelty, and the peace established among the churches from the abatement of the fury of persecution. Who, therefore, could believe that nothing at all was said in Dionysius’s letter about the persecution having been brought to an end, although Eusebius testifies that he read precisely this?

2. In the same letter concerning Baptism, Dionysius reported to Stephen, as an entirely recent event, that the disturbances which the Novatian heresy had stirred up in the East had been calmed. But if the beginnings of the controversy concerning Baptism were connected with the end of this dissension, they ought not to be placed later than the year 253. For Dionysius speaks of the dissension having been settled in such a way that this seems to have occurred not long after the persecution. His statement that “all the bishops everywhere were of one and the same mind and rejoiced beyond belief at the peace unexpectedly [Col. 0154] made” sufficiently indicates that the evil had been suppressed before it took root, and that peace was ratified when there was fear that the dissension might grow worse. But if conflict over the opinion of the Novatians had continued in the East until the year 256, it does not seem that a conflagration strengthened over so many days could have been extinguished so completely that not even any smoke at all remained.

To this is added the authority of Cyprian, who, in a letter to Stephen written around the year 254, testifies that Novatian had “always been repulsed and refuted and excluded from communion by the priests of God throughout the whole world.” If, therefore, the whole world had already agreed at that time in condemning Novatian, the letter of Dionysius that reported this agreement among bishops who had previously dissented cannot be assigned to the year 256. Another argument for the same position is supplied by what we undertook to prove in the second place: the controversy began in the East before it did in Africa. For if the dissension arose in the East before Africa, it cannot be placed later than the year 254 or the end of 253.

That dispute, however, had flared up in Cappadocia, Cilicia, and the neighboring provinces before it did in Africa, as is clear from these words of Firmilian against Stephen: “What could be more humble or gentle than to have disagreed with so many bishops throughout the whole world, breaking peace with individuals through various kinds of discord—now with the Easterners, as we trust is not unknown even to you, and now with you who are in the South?” (p. 150). Tillemont excellently observes that Stephen’s dispute with the Easterners, which Firmilian mentions, arose not from the Novatian schism, as Lombert thought, but from Baptism. For that schism was suppressed in the East at the beginning of Stephen’s pontificate; nor did the Easterners, Firmilian among them, show any less zeal than Stephen himself in extinguishing that schism, much less did peace between them and Stephen thereby come to be broken. Very few favored this schism, and they were at Antioch, as is clear from Dionysius’s Letter to Cornelius in Eusebius (book VI, chapter 46). Firmilian is therefore speaking about Baptism. From his words, moreover, it may be gathered that Stephen did not contend with the Easterners and the Africans at the same time, but at different times and in different ways; and that affairs in the East had become calmer at the time when they were being disturbed far more seriously in Africa. Hence Dionysius himself, in the letter which, after Stephen’s death, he wrote to Philemon, a Roman presbyter, interposes himself as an advocate for the Africans alone; and, in order to mollify the Romans, he demonstrates (in Eusebius, *History*, book VII, chapter 5) “that this custom had not then been introduced for the first time by the Africans alone,” but that the same practice had previously been established by the Easterners in councils. This argument would indeed appear utterly absurd if Rome had not been more conciliatory toward the latter than toward the Africans.

In his Letter to Xystus, however, when discussing Stephen and his conflict with the Africans, Dionysius said that “Stephen had previously written to him concerning Helenus and Firmilian, and finally concerning all the priests established throughout Cilicia, Cappadocia, and all the neighboring provinces; and that for the same reason he intended to withdraw from communion with them, because, he said, they rebaptized heretics” [Col. 0155]. The word “previously” proves that Stephen had fought over this same baptism of heretics with Cilicia and the neighboring provinces before he did with Africa; and when he complained bitterly to Dionysius about Helenus and Firmilian, Cyprian and the African bishops had not yet given him offense. Dionysius further added: “Concerning all these matters I wrote to him, praying and entreating him.” Who would not gather from these words that the letter which, according to Eusebius, he wrote—the sole letter he wrote—to Stephen was composed not on behalf of the Africans, as Tillemont and Pearson supposed, but on behalf of those about whom Stephen had written, namely Helenus and Firmilian? They therefore benefited from Dionysius’s assistance and commendation before the Africans did.

The opinion we are refuting also involves this difficulty: Tillemont and Pearson compress far too many events within a single year—three councils of Carthage, so many letters of Cyprian, Stephen’s letters to Dionysius and Cyprian, and his disputes first with the Easterners and then with the Africans. It is far preferable to distinguish this diversity of events by assigning them to different times.

But perhaps an objection will be raised from what Eusebius says in book VII, chapter 3: πρῶτος τῶν τότε Κυπριανός, etc.: “Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was the first of those then living to hold that heretics should be admitted only after first being cleansed from error through baptism.” Gerardus, Johannes Vossius, and Valesius accuse Eusebius of error. Pearson, however, although he rightly observes against Valesius that Eusebius’s words πρῶτος τῶν τότε should be rendered “the first of those then living,” and not, as Valesius rendered them, “the first of all,” nevertheless made little progress in exonerating Eusebius. For Firmilian, a contemporary of Cyprian, had rejected the baptism of heretics long before Cyprian did, at the Council of Iconium, which he testifies in his Letter to Cyprian that he attended. Eusebius will therefore equally be convicted of error whether he said that Cyprian was the first of all or merely the first of his contemporaries to establish this position. It is thus far more probable that primacy is assigned to Cyprian because he added very great weight to this position, and because his controversy with Stephen became much more celebrated than that of the Easterners.

## XXX.—THE ORDER AND SEQUENCE OF EVENTS IN AFRICA IN THE YEARS 255 AND 256, DOWN TO THE THIRD COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE

There is no need to labor greatly over the beginnings of this dispute in Africa, for the entire matter rests upon conjecture. Pearson assigns the first Council of Carthage to the autumn of the year 255. Tillemont, who compresses everything within the span of the year 256, does not reject Pearson’s view; nor perhaps would one be wrong to trace the controversy back to the very beginning of 255. This much alone we can establish: the Africans first contended among themselves before they contended with Stephen. In the Letter to the Numidians, “those who defend heretics” are refuted. Cyprian touches upon the same men in his Letter to Quintus: “For I do not know,” he says, “by what presumption certain of our colleagues are led to think that those who have been baptized among the heretics [Col. 0156] ought not to be baptized when they come to us.” Yet peace and favor were not broken apart by this diversity of practices, as is evident from the Letter to Stephen. “Moreover, we know,” says Cyprian, “that some are unwilling to relinquish what they have once imbibed,” or readily to change “their own purpose, but, while preserving among colleagues the bond of peace and concord, retain certain practices of their own which have once been adopted among them.”

These words of Cyprian in the Letter to Jubaianus appear to refer to some bishops from Africa: “And now among some of our own the baptism of heretics is asserted as valid.” Through this same Jubaianus a letter written against those who rebaptized came into Cyprian’s hands. But it seems to have been composed neither by Pope Stephen nor by any bishop from across the sea—for in that case it would have reached Cyprian at Carthage by a direct route—but by some African. Jubaianus himself did not altogether agree with Cyprian, but indicated that his mind was averse to rebaptism, because the Novatianists, if they enticed any Catholics over to their party, rebaptized them in a dreadful act of sacrilege.

Eighteen Numidian bishops first gave Cyprian an occasion to proclaim his position publicly and openly. For although they were accustomed to reject baptism administered by heretics, nevertheless, when a synod was held at Carthage, they thought it should be consulted “concerning those who appear to have been baptized among heretics and schismatics: whether, when they come to the Catholic Church, which is one, they ought to be baptized.” Cyprian and the other bishops, thirty-one in number, as is clear from the title of Letter LXX, praise the Numidians because “they too hold to the truth and firmness of the Catholic rule,” and profess their agreement with them that no one can be baptized outside the Church. Not long afterward, when Cyprian was consulted on the same matter by Quintus, a bishop in Mauretania, through the presbyter Lucianus, he wrote Letter LXXI to him; and so that Quintus might know “what his fellow bishops, together with the fellow presbyters who were present, had decided in council,” he sent him a copy of the earlier letter to the Numidians.

Nor did much time elapse between this letter and the second Council of Carthage, “in which many matters indeed were brought forward and transacted,” but above all this: Cyprian wrote to Pope Stephen, in the name of the seventy bishops who had sat with him, that those baptized among heretics or schismatics ought to be baptized when they returned to the Church. Cyprian testifies that this had “recently been carefully set forth,” both in the Letter to Quintus and in the letter to the Numidian bishops. He sent Stephen a copy of each letter along with Letter LXXII. He adds that at the same council it was established by common consent and authority:

> That even if certain presbyters or deacons had first been ordained in the Catholic Church and afterward had stood as faithless rebels against the Church, or had been advanced among the heretics by pseudo-bishops and antichrists through a profane ordination contrary to Christ’s appointment, and had attempted outside the Church to offer false and sacrilegious sacrifices against the one altar and divine sacrifice, they too [Col. 0157] should be received on this condition when they return: that they communicate as laymen and be content that they are admitted to peace, though they had proved themselves enemies of peace; and that, upon returning, they ought not to retain among us those weapons of ordination and honor with which they had fought against us.

I am compelled to assign to this time the embassy of the bishops whom the African council sent to Stephen. Firmilian says that Stephen received these episcopal envoys in such a way “that he would not admit them even to the conversation of a common conference, and furthermore . . . commanded the whole brotherhood that no one should receive them into his house, so that, when they arrived, they would be denied not only peace and communion, but also shelter and hospitality” (p. 150). Firmilian also complains that Stephen called Cyprian “a false Christ, a false apostle, and a deceitful worker” (p. 151). These things would indeed be incredible if they were not supported by the testimony of two men whose credibility cannot be impugned—I mean Firmilian and Cyprian, who translated Firmilian’s letter into Latin, or at least published it under his own authority. But we must examine Firmilian’s individual words, both to avoid adding anything to his complaints, which are sufficiently grave in themselves, and to determine at what time and in what manner these events occurred.

First, I think I can discern that these envoys did not arrive with the greatest speed, but that a report of their coming preceded them. For Stephen forbade anyone to receive them into his house, “so that, when they arrived, they would be denied not only peace and communion, but also shelter and hospitality.” They had therefore not yet arrived when Stephen issued this decree, and their delay gave him time to learn both of their coming and of the proceedings of the council. From this I gather that the embassy cannot be assigned to the third Council of Carthage, although Tillemont thinks otherwise. For it is agreed that Rogatianus was not sent by Cyprian into Cappadocia until after the episcopal envoys had returned from Rome. But since the third Council of Carthage was celebrated on the Kalends of September, and since Rogatianus, according to Firmilian, hastened to return because winter was pressing on, how could it have happened that after the council the episcopal envoys went to Rome and returned, and that after their return Rogatianus was sent into Cappadocia and still had time to return before winter? Tillemont admits that these things could not easily have happened; he nevertheless maintains that they are not impossible, provided, of course, that both embassies hastened their outward and return journeys. Yet we see that the arrival of the bishops sent to Rome was not very swift but rather delayed. Had Tillemont noticed this, I believe he would have judged otherwise.

Furthermore, since Stephen, in his Letter to Cyprian, which was sent before the third council, held that those who rebaptized should be excluded from communion, I very much doubt whether this council would have exposed episcopal envoys to such a danger that communion would be denied them at Rome. It is therefore more probable that the embassy was sent after the second council.

From Firmilian’s words it may also be inferred that Stephen’s edict [Col. 0158] was not fully put into effect.

1. It is incredible that in so holy a Church the episcopal envoys, denied hospitality by the brethren, were compelled to seek it among unbelievers.

2. Firmilian distinguishes shelter and hospitality from peace, communion, and the conversation of a common conference. He declares in express words that the bishops “were not admitted even to the conversation of a common conference.” As regards shelter and hospitality, however, he reproaches Stephen only for threats and commands, not for their actual execution; yet he would not seem likely to have omitted that fact if they had also been deprived of this duty of humanity.

3. It is probable that in the Roman Church, which abounded in holy presbyters, there were some at that time who interposed themselves as mediators between Stephen and Cyprian. Even if they did not prevail upon Stephen to admit the envoys to communion and conversation, they may at least have deterred him from forbidding others to receive them as guests.

For we cannot assign to a more appropriate time what Dionysius says (in Eusebius, *History*, book VII, chapter 5) in his Letter to Xystus:

> καὶ τοῖς ἀγαπητοῖς δὲ ἡμῶν καὶ συμπρεσβυτέροις Διονυσίῳ καὶ Φιλήμονι, συμψήφοις πρότερον Στεφάνῳ γενομένοις, καὶ περὶ τῶν αὐτῶν μοι γράφουσι· πρότερον μὲν ὀλίγα, καὶ νῦν δὲ διὰ πλειόνων ἐπέστειλα.
>
> “I also wrote to our beloved brothers and fellow presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, who had formerly agreed with Stephen and had written to me about the same matters—briefly before, but now at greater length.”

It is clear from these words that Dionysius and Philemon, although they had previously agreed with Stephen in everything, afterward disagreed with him on some point. Launoy (vol. VIII, p. 603), however, most absurdly concludes from these words that these two presbyters, who had previously not rejected baptism conferred by heretics, afterward went over to Cyprian’s position. I think very few will fail to reject Launoy’s conjecture. For the issue here is not so much doctrine as the manner of defending doctrine. Dionysius does not disapprove of Stephen’s teaching, since he himself followed it, but requires gentleness and moderation of spirit from him.

Accordingly, when Dionysius says that Dionysius and Philemon had previously agreed with Stephen and had written to him concerning the same matters, this must be understood of Stephen’s position that communion should not be maintained with Helenus, Firmilian, and the other rebaptizers. This position was both the principal origin of the dissensions and the subject of Dionysius’s cares and anxieties. But if Dionysius and Philemon at some point ceased to approve Stephen’s manner of proceeding, they seem especially to have done so when they saw him carried away into those extreme demonstrations of discord. Not without reason, therefore, do we suppose that their wisdom mitigated Stephen’s edict, which not even Firmilian says was carried into effect so as to deny the episcopal envoys shelter and hospitality.

It is now not difficult to answer Tillemont’s arguments. He does not think it probable that Stephen became so violently inflamed at the first report of the African decree. But this difficulty, which appeared great to Tillemont because he thought the dispute had begun in Africa, vanishes in light of what we have said about the East. Nor is it now surprising if the African decrees added fresh fuel to Stephen’s indignation, already kindled by what had occurred between him [Col. 0159] and the Asians.

Tillemont also asks why Stephen wrote to Cyprian if he had admitted the envoys neither to communion nor to conversation. Yet there is no inconsistency in supposing that the two presbyters whom we have mentioned prevailed upon the holy Pontiff at least to write to Cyprian. Although, since Stephen in this letter held that those who rebaptized should be excluded from communion, he does not appear to have departed very far from his manner of treating the envoys.

Tillemont also employs as an argument the fact that Cyprian said nothing in the third Council of Carthage about these injuries inflicted upon the envoys. From this the most learned writer concludes that the embassy must be placed after the third council. But this silence must be attributed to the gentleness that was supreme in Cyprian. In the letter to Pompeius, however, in which Stephen’s letter is refuted, certain statements escaped the holy martyr that were somewhat harsh toward Stephen; amid such great moderation of spirit, they reveal the pain produced by the gravest insults. The same is proved by these words from the Letter to Jubaianus, written before the third council and not long after the second: “Why,” he asks (p. 133), “are we regarded as transgressors of the truth and betrayers of unity?”

The embassy was immediately followed by the letter to Bishop Jubaianus. He had consulted Cyprian concerning baptism conferred by heretics, and at the same time had sent him a letter written not by himself but by another against Cyprian’s position. Cyprian refutes this letter and gathers with the greatest diligence everything that he thought capable of supporting his cause, while always preserving moderation of spirit and charity, which he held dearer than anything else. He also sends Jubaianus a copy of his letters to the Numidians and to Quintus, and perhaps also the decrees of the recent synod, of which he speaks as follows: “And now also, when seventy-one bishops from both the province of Africa and Numidia had assembled together, we again confirmed this same position by our judgment” (p. 120). From these words it is clear that this letter was written not long after the council, yet after letters had arrived from Stephen. For in the Letter to Stephen Cyprian testifies that some disagreed with him, “but with the bond of peace and concord among colleagues preserved.” By contrast, in the Letter to Jubaianus he says (pp. 129, 132): “Why are we regarded as transgressors of the truth and betrayers of unity?” By then, therefore, he was missing in his opponents the zeal for peace and concord which he had praised when writing to Stephen.

He sent Jubaianus another gift as well, the treatise *On the Good of Patience*, of which he speaks as follows (p. 137): “We patiently and gently preserve charity of spirit, the honor of the episcopal college, the bond of faith, and the concord of the priesthood. For this reason, as far as our modest ability could accomplish, with the Lord permitting and inspiring, we have also written a treatise *On the Good of Patience*, which we have sent to you in mutual affection.” Learned men have excellently observed that this book was written with such restraint that Cyprian no more touched upon the controversy then raging [Col. 0160] than if it had never existed at all. Not long afterward he wrote another book, *On Jealousy and Envy*, with the same purpose. Pontius lists both after the book *On Works and Almsgiving*.

When Stephen’s letter had been brought to Africa, Pompeius, bishop of Sabrata—the same man, it seems probable, who had taken part in the ordination of St. Cornelius—informed Cyprian that he wished to see Stephen’s letter. Cyprian complied with his request and refuted the letter with somewhat greater agitation, because Stephen held that “the priests of God who maintained the truth of Christ and the unity of the Church should be excluded from communion” (Letter LXXIV). At the same time, he sent Pompeius copies of other letters in which he had discussed the baptism of heretics.

The book *On the Baptism of Heretics*, whose author was a bishop, as we shall prove elsewhere, assails Cyprian with such unworthy abuse that I do not doubt it was written after the time when Cyprian, writing to Stephen, testified that charity and concord had been preserved by those from whom he disagreed.

Letter LXXV to Magnus was also written after the heat of the dispute had swept some of Cyprian’s opponents into abuse and malediction. For his calling them “obstinate and unteachable,” and his statement that “transgressors of the faith and betrayers of the Church stand against the Church within the very enclosures of the Church,” show his grief that he did not find in all his opponents the moderation of spirit and zeal for unity which he especially wished to preserve. Nevertheless, Baronius and Pearson maintain that this was the first of all his letters written on Baptism, because Cyprian does not mention his earlier letters in it. But neither is this letter mentioned in his letters to Quintus, Jubaianus, and others. Moreover, Magnus seems, as Tillemont observes, to have known and thoroughly understood Cyprian’s earlier letters. For he agreed with him in everything, and only one scruple remained in his mind: whether, among the other heretics, those who came from Novatian ought to be baptized.

Magnus had also asked Cyprian what he thought about those “who receive the grace of God in weakness and sickness: whether they should be regarded as legitimate Christians,” because they had not been washed with saving water but merely had water poured or sprinkled upon them. Cyprian replies that such persons are legitimate Christians and that it matters little whether water was poured or sprinkled upon them. Yet he censures those who approve the baptism of heretics and diminish the majesty and sanctity of ecclesiastical Baptism in such a way as to indicate, by no obscure implication, the Roman Church, in which it is known that *clinici*—those baptized on a sickbed—were excluded from the clergy.

## XXXI.—ON THE THIRD COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE—CYPRIAN SENDS THE DEACON ROGATIANUS TO FIRMILIAN—ON FIRMILIAN’S LETTER TO CYPRIAN

The immoderate zeal of his opponents had given Cyprian the most just cause to fear that some wound might be branded upon the unity of the Church. Therefore, to forestall so great an evil, [Col. 0161] he convened a more fully attended council than before and joined counsels for fostering peace and unity with certain bishops of foreign peoples.

It is worth investigating in what year this synod was held. The whole matter depends upon the death of Pope Stephen. For since no one doubts that he died on the second day of August, it is necessary to say that the third Council of Carthage, held on the Kalends of September while he was still alive, took place in the year preceding his death. It is generally agreed that Stephen was ordained in 253. Some, however, think that he occupied his see for only two years and died in 255; others assign him four years of pontificate and place his death in 257. The latter opinion, which Tillemont and Pearson followed, seems less constrained and more intelligible. For if Stephen’s death is assigned to 255, the third Council of Carthage must be assigned to the Kalends of September 254, and Stephen’s conflicts with the Africans and the Easterners would then have occurred simultaneously, although we have proved that they were separated in time.

To this may be added the weight of the arguments upon which Tillemont and Pearson rely. First and foremost, Firmilian testifies in his Letter to Cyprian that “nearly twenty-two years earlier, in the period after the emperor Alexander, many calamities befell Cappadocia and Pontus, with the result that a severe persecution was also raised against us who bear the Christian name.” Since Alexander died in 235, the twenty-second year after his death is precisely 256; consequently, the dispute concerning Baptism was especially intense in that year, and Stephen had not yet died.

2. If Stephen had died in 255, how could Cyprian, who poured out his life for Christ on the Ides of September 258, have remained silent for so long in a matter of such importance? For nothing could be assigned to that whole interval which he might be said to have done either in defense of his cause or for the pacification of affairs. But if the controversy over Baptism is assigned to the year 256, it will not appear very surprising that Cyprian remained silent after the third Council of Carthage and after writing to Firmilian, because the persecution that began in 257 left no opportunity for the discussion of these matters.

3. Tillemont proves by several arguments that St. Stephen died as a martyr. Since persecution did not break out until 257, he concludes that the holy pope’s death must be assigned to August of that same year, and consequently that the third Council of Carthage, celebrated while he was still alive, and Cyprian’s letter to Firmilian, likewise written under this Pontiff, belong to 256.

The principal difficulties obstructing this opinion of Tillemont and Pearson seem capable of being resolved by what we have just observed: that the dispute arose later in Africa than in the East. Once this distinction is noted, the authority of Eusebius no longer presents an obstacle, nor is it necessary to attribute an absurd blemish to so careful a writer. Tillemont admits that it cannot easily be explained [Col. 0162] why Dionysius of Alexandria, if Xystus presided for not even a full year, nevertheless sent him three letters—and did so while burdened by the hardships of persecution and exile—whereas he wrote only once to Xystus’s predecessor Stephen, under whom the disputes were more bitter. This difficulty, which at first sight suggests that some years should be subtracted from Stephen and added to Xystus, is substantially diminished if Dionysius is said to have written to Stephen about Eastern affairs and afterward to Xystus about African affairs. For although Stephen’s dispute with the Easterners had not been settled, it had nevertheless been mitigated; and while they peacefully retained their custom, the war, so to speak, was afterward transferred to Africa. It is therefore not at all surprising if Dionysius wrote no further to Stephen and did not renew his efforts toward pacification until he had definite knowledge of the affairs of the Africans, who perhaps appealed for his assistance only later.

The acts of this third Council of Carthage survive. It was attended by eighty-five bishops from the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania—or even eighty-seven, if the two absentees are counted: Pompeius of Sabrata and Dioga of Leptis Magna, who entrusted their proxies to Natalis of Oea. When, therefore, they assembled on the Kalends of September together with presbyters and deacons, and with a very large part of the people also present, Jubaianus’s letter to Cyprian was read, as was Cyprian’s to Jubaianus, together with the reply that Jubaianus subsequently wrote to Cyprian. Cyprian then exhorted them to state their judgment freely and peacefully:

> “Judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should hold a different opinion. For none of us,” he said, “sets himself up as a bishop of bishops or drives his colleagues by tyrannical terror to the necessity of obedience.”

Baronius observes that Stephen is censured in these words. All pronounced the same judgment with one voice, and Cyprian, speaking last of all, declared that his position had been most fully expressed in the Letter to Jubaianus.

Cyprian resolved to fortify with new safeguards the unity established among the Africans by this deliberation. He sent the deacon Rogatianus with letters to Firmilian, informing him of the dispute with Stephen. He also appears to have sent the letters he had written to others concerning the baptism of heretics, for Firmilian praises Cyprian’s replies against Stephen and cites several statements found in the Letter to Jubaianus. Cyprian’s writings were most welcome to Firmilian, who testifies that he received them as though they were his own. He did not read them merely in passing, but committed them to memory by frequent repetition. His reply to Cyprian reviews what Cyprian had said in order to confirm the truth and adds certain points to augment the proof. But because he wrote hastily, many excessively angry statements against Stephen escaped him. Firmilian, given his exceptional moderation of spirit, might perhaps have corrected them had Rogatianus, impatient of delay, not deprived him of the time needed to reread the letter properly. This letter of Firmilian, preserved in Latin as Letter LXXV among the Cyprianic corpus, so strongly recalls Cyprian’s [Col. 0163] style that it seems to have had no other translator.

The faithful translator retained the idiom of the Greek language in several places. Shortly after the beginning (p. 143):

> “The angels are saddened when they see the divergent minds and divided wills of certain people, as if they do not merely invoke one and the same God together, but, being separated and divided from one another, could no longer have either conversation or common discourse.”

That is, “as if they do not together invoke one and the same God”; the final negation is sometimes omitted among Latin writers, but more frequently among Greek writers.

At p. 145: “Unless Paul was inferior to these bishops who are now.” Pamelius thought it should read, “of whom now”; but this is an evident Hellenism: τούτοις ἐπισκόποις τοῖς νῦν, “to these bishops now existing.”

The Hellenism is more easily detected in these words (p. 147): “It is the same error; it is the deceit of demons itself”—that is, “the same deceit.”

Firmilian relates (p. 146) the story of a woman inspired by a demon, who:

> “Frequently even dared to do this: to pretend both that she sanctified bread by an invocation not to be despised and that she performed the Eucharist, and she was accustomed to offer sacrifice to the Lord, not without the sacramental formula of the customary proclamation,” etc.

Rigaltius, whose note is appended in the Oxford edition, reads “customary prayer.” But absolutely nothing should be changed, for these words have been accurately rendered from the Greek. The prayers customarily made in the sacrifice are called by Basil (*Letter* CCXLI) ἐκκλησιαστικὰ κηρύγματα, “ecclesiastical proclamations.”

Since Firmilian thought that his opponents acknowledged Christ’s grace in baptism received by adults outside the Church, he refutes them as follows (p. 147):

> “For if the Apostle does not lie when he says, ‘As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ,’ then certainly the man who has been baptized into Christ there has put on Christ. But if he has put on Christ, he was also able to receive the Holy Spirit, who was sent by Christ; and the hand is imposed upon him in vain when he comes to receive the Spirit—unless after Christ he puts on the Spirit, so that Christ indeed is present among the heretics but the Holy Spirit is not present there.”

The words “unless after Christ he puts on the Spirit” have the same meaning as “after putting on Christ”; the conjecture of Cauchius and Pamelius, who think it should read, “unless he does not put on the Spirit from Christ,” is not probable.

I shall attempt to emend another, far more difficult passage. Concerning those who were baptized outside the Church and died within the Church without a new baptism, Firmilian states as follows (p. 149):

> “If they have departed from this world, they are reckoned among the number of those who were indeed catechized among us but died before they were baptized. They do not merely say the benefit of the truth and faith which they had attained after abandoning error, although, being overtaken by death, they did not obtain the consummation of grace.”

Rigaltius thinks that the verb “they have” should be inserted after “they are reckoned,” and emends it thus: “They have; they do not merely learn the benefit of truth and faith.” But it could far more suitably be read: “They have no small benefit,” in place of “they say not merely” or “they learn not merely.”

## XXXII.—SOME OBSERVATIONS ARE ADDED ON THIS CONTROVERSY CONCERNING BAPTISM

[Col. 0164]

There is absolutely no surviving record of what Stephen and Cyprian did thereafter in this cause. Perhaps the persecution that arose a few months later diverted their minds from domestic disputes to the defense of religion. Yet nothing else averted the danger of schism from the Church except the love of unity impressed and engraved upon the minds of both parties.

Each party believed itself to be defending a position of the greatest importance. Cyprian’s opponents were well aware of the grave injury done by those who rebaptized—to the sacraments of Christ, to apostolic tradition, and to so many churches which, if Cyprian’s opinion had been true, had granted communion to unbaptized persons and had often even caused infants to die deprived of baptism. That these objections were made to Cyprian is clear both from his own letters and from the book *On Rebaptism*.

On the other side, Firmilian and Cyprian, since this question had not yet been placed in the clearest light or decided by the settled judgment of the Church, thought that a most corrupt custom had crept in and that their opponents were gravely at fault. “What is this obstinacy,” Cyprian asks in the Letter to Pompeius (p. 139), “or what presumption is it to prefer human tradition to divine ordinance and not to perceive that God is indignant and angry whenever human tradition dissolves and disregards divine commands?” In the same letter he complains that authority is attributed to heretics and that faith and truth are betrayed (p. 141). He believed that, by a singular benefit of God, the truth had been disclosed to himself and to others who held the same opinion, so that he might present it to the other churches.

“Therefore it is in vain,” he says in the Letter to Jubaianus (p. 133),

> “that certain people, when defeated by reason, oppose custom to us, as if custom were greater than truth, or as if, in spiritual matters, we ought not to follow whatever has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit. A person who errs in simplicity can indeed be forgiven, as the Apostle Paul says of himself: ‘I who formerly,’ he says, ‘was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an injurious man; but I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance.’ But after inspiration and revelation have been given, whoever knowingly and consciously persists in the error in which he had been involved sins without the pardon due to ignorance. For he relies upon a certain presumption and obstinacy when he is overcome by reason.”

Firmilian likewise says: “What an offense it is,” he asks (p. 149), “whether on the part of those who are admitted or of those who admit them, that without the stains having been washed away through the laver of the Church and without their sins having been laid aside, they rashly usurp communion and touch the body and blood of the Lord?”

But the greater the importance each side attached to its own position, the more clearly the love of unity shines forth in both. In the East there does not appear to have been any great contention of minds, although several provinces differed from the ancient and common position. When Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to Stephen, seeking to induce him to come to terms with the Asians who rebaptized, he praised the complete concord of the bishops in the East. From [Col. 0165] this it is evident that the Eastern bishops dealt more generously with the Asians than Stephen did. Indeed, Helenus and Firmilian were always held in high esteem by their colleagues. In the West, too, hatred and avoidance of schism were conspicuous. Although the author of the book *On Rebaptism* assails Cyprian with unworthy reproaches and abuse, he nevertheless acknowledges that this entire question was debated among brethren. “I observe,” he says at the beginning of the book, “that it has been asked among the brethren what ought preferably to be observed in the case of those who, though in heresy, have nevertheless been baptized in the name of our God Jesus Christ, etc.” Stephen was more vehement than was proper; yet Africa did not on that account cease to remain in communion with the other churches, including the Roman Church. Certainly no document survives showing that other bishops refused communion with the Africans and thought that those who rebaptized ought to be excluded, as Stephen had thought. Indeed, since in the Roman Church itself two most eminent presbyters, Philemon and Dionysius, as we have just seen, promptly perceived wherein Stephen’s excessive severity was at fault, I believe I am justified in thinking that, even under this pontiff, that whole disagreement did not produce the consequences that might have followed from the first heat of tempers. Under St. Xystus, Stephen’s successor, although persecution ought to have suppressed domestic quarrels, or at least imposed a truce, the controversy over Baptism nevertheless does not appear to have cooled immediately, since Dionysius of Alexandria, amid the hardships of exile and in the very blaze of persecution, wrote three letters to Xystus in order to summon him to moderation and concord. The most holy martyr followed Dionysius’s counsels; and for this reason he is believed to have been called “a good and peaceable priest” by Pontius, and to have been entered among the martyrs in the diptychs of the African Church, because he settled the controversy that had arisen under Stephen. That communion between him and Cyprian was not interrupted is clear from Epistle LXXXII, in which Cyprian relates that he had sent men to Rome to bring back reliable information about the affairs of the Church. As for Dionysius, there can be no doubt that he dealt generously with the Africans, since, while still a presbyter, he had ceased to approve Stephen’s excessive severity. The same humanity was maintained by the other pontiffs, “until,” as Augustine says (*On Baptism*, book I), “what was most salutarily held should be confirmed, with all doubts removed, by a plenary council of the whole world.”

But the love of unity was especially displayed by Cyprian, to whom the Lord “undoubtedly did not reveal the truth for this reason,” Augustine says (*On Baptism*, I.18), “that his piety, humility, and charity in preserving the Church’s peace in a salutary manner might be made manifest, and might be recorded, not only for the Christians of that time but also for posterity, as medicinal knowledge, so to speak.” Although he seemed to himself to perceive a grave error in his opponents, nevertheless, “in those questions which,” as Augustine says (*On Baptism*, III.3), “have not yet been examined with the clearest insight,” he had no doubt that “every bishop possesses, by virtue of the liberty and power granted him, his own freedom of judgment, and can no more be judged by another than he himself can judge another.” Thus he addresses his colleagues at the Council of Carthage [Col. 0166]: “It remains for each of us to set forth what he thinks concerning this very matter, judging no one and removing no one from the right of communion if he should think differently.” The Donatists formerly used to say of St. Cyprian, “as though to his praise,” that he had lied “and had planned to catch his more simple-minded colleagues in their words, so that, once they had disclosed that they thought differently, he might then, contrary to his promise, resolve that they ought to be excommunicated.” But Augustine refutes this calumny in *On Baptism*, III.3. Firmilian was certainly hot-tempered and more vehement than was proper; yet a love of unity breathes throughout his whole letter, and nothing more significant concerning the unity of the Church could be said. Hence, although he seemed to himself to be defending a truth of the greatest importance, because the judgment of the Church had not yet intervened, he thought that the matter ought to be handled in the same way as the various institutions pertaining to discipline. “Accordingly,” he says (p. 144), “in very many other provinces too, many things vary according to differences of place and name; and yet there has never on that account been any departure from the peace and unity of the Church.”

### XXXIII.—ON CYPRIAN’S EPISTLE LXIII AGAINST THOSE WHO USED WATER ALONE IN THE MORNING SACRIFICE

Besides the letters that Cyprian wrote in defense of his cause, I conjecture that another letter, written not on the same subject but at about the same time, was the sixty-third, addressed to Bishop Caecilius, who was most probably from Bilta and was the first to give his opinion at the Council of Carthage. The occasion for this letter was a corrupt custom introduced among certain persons, namely, that they used water alone in the morning sacrifice. They did not, however, commit this offense, as the Encratites did, out of hatred for wine created by God, for in the evening they offered a cup mixed with wine. Cyprian demonstrates that by this corrupt custom both Christ’s command is violated and the sacrament utterly overthrown, since the blood of Christ cannot be in the cup unless wine is used. Moreover, from these words, “And let him see to it, dearest brother, if any of our predecessors, whether through ignorance or simplicity, did not observe this,” it is readily perceived that this fault had not then appeared for the first time, but had become entrenched over many years, and consequently had been introduced not into any prominent church but rather into certain rural districts. For if anything of this kind had occurred in the larger cities, the matter would quickly have become known to the other churches and aroused the indignation of all. Pearson therefore thinks without justification that it originated with one of the bishops of Carthage. For the phrase “if any of our predecessors” refers no more to Cyprian’s predecessors than to Caecilius’s; rather, since the episcopate is one, Cyprian calls those who had long ago presided over the Church both his own and Caecilius’s predecessors.

Why, however, I think that this letter was written after the controversy over Baptism arose, I conjecture from these words: “And because his second coming is now drawing near to us, his benign and abundant condescension illuminates our hearts more and more with the light of truth.” [Col. 0167] These words indicate something greater than that they should be understood solely of the matters treated in this letter. For it was well established among all Christians that the blood of Christ could not be in the cup unless wine was offered; and very few erred in this respect, doing so more from fear and a perverse sense of shame than from obstinate error. But in the controversy over Baptism that Cyprian had with so many churches, he maintained that the truth had been revealed by a singular favor to himself and to the colleagues who shared his view, as we observed in the preceding chapter. He appears incidentally to touch upon this fuller illumination, this benign and abundant condescension of Christ, in Epistle LXIII. To this may be added the fact that in the letters written about Baptism he refutes the authority attributed to custom in the same way as in the sixty-third.

Pearson, however, places this letter in the year 253, during the persecution of Gallus and Volusianus. He infers a time of persecution both from the expectation of Christ’s coming and from these words (p. 109): “Unless perhaps someone fears this in the morning sacrifices, lest through the taste of wine he should smell of the blood of Christ. Thus, therefore, the brotherhood begins to be held back from Christ’s passion in times of persecution, when in the offerings it learns to be ashamed of his blood and gore.”

As regards Christ’s coming, expectation of it is no less explicit, as we said above in chapter 28, in certain works of Cyprian that are known to have been written in a time of peace. In the passage cited, moreover, Cyprian does not reproach those whom he is refuting with the fear that someone might infer from the smell of wine that they were Christians. For how could the pagans have suspected this, when what took place in the mysteries of the Christians was entirely hidden from them? Rather, they feared that the smell of wine in the morning might present an appearance insufficiently respectable and unworthy of a sober person. Hence Cyprian indicates a time of peace rather than of persecution when he says that those who dread so slight an inconvenience from communion in Christ’s blood are thereby made more reluctant to shed their own blood in persecutions—although he reproves that empty fear not by asserting it as fact, but rather by conjecturing it.

### XXXIV.—CYPRIAN’S CONFESSION AND MARTYRDOM

It seemed that nothing could be added to Cyprian’s many outstanding services to the Church and his many illustrious achievements except the glory of confession and martyrdom. By Christ’s gift he attained both during the persecution of Valerian, who, after treating the Christians for some time with every kindness both privately and publicly, was afterward induced by Macrianus’s intrigues to hope that he would become a certain great and fortunate emperor if he attacked the Christian religion. When persecution was impending in Africa, Bishop Fortunatus—perhaps the same person who at the Council of Carthage is described as bishop from Tuccabori—asked Cyprian to compose exhortations from the divine Scriptures to prepare and strengthen the minds of the brethren. Cyprian gladly complied, judging it insufficient that he should rouse the people of God with the trumpet-call of his own voice unless he also strengthened the faith of believers and their virtue, dedicated and devoted to God, by the [Col. 0168] reading of Scripture. He therefore wrote the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, composed almost entirely of testimonies from Scripture. Baronius and Fell place this work under Gallus, but in vain; for Pontius the deacon lists it after the books *On Patience* and *On Jealousy and Envy*, as Tillemont observes. Since, moreover, Cyprian’s confession and martyrdom are recorded in his Acts, which we shall append below, I shall not consume time by recounting the same events, but it will be sufficient briefly to review the letters written during this persecution.

When Valerian had decreed that Christians were not to hold assemblies or enter cemeteries, and that anyone who did not obey this command was to be put to death, Cyprian appears to have been the first of all in Africa to receive the onset of the persecution. Learned men have indeed observed this from the words of Epistle LXXVIII, where the martyrs address Cyprian as follows: “Like a good and true teacher, you were the first to declare before the proconsul’s official record what we disciples, following you, ought to say before the governor; and, sounding God’s trumpet, you roused the soldiers equipped with heavenly arms to the battle of conflict, and, fighting in the front line, slew the devil with the spiritual sword; you also arrayed the companies of the brethren on this side and that with your words,” etc.

Having confessed Christ with the greatest firmness of spirit before the proconsul Paternus on the third day before the Kalends of September in the year 257, he was deported into exile to a remote and secluded place called Curubis. Pontius the deacon, who wrote his life, accompanied him in exile. On the day when they first stayed at the place of exile, Cyprian was warned in a nocturnal vision of his future martyrdom; but he obtained a postponement until the morrow, so that on that day, which had been granted him, he might put his affairs in order. Yet “this one day signified a year,” says Pontius; “for he was crowned on that same day after the completion of a year on which this had been shown to him a year before.” He was all the more readily able to provide for the affairs of his church, and especially to devote his care to relieving the poor, because under Xystus, “a good and peaceable priest,” as Pontius says, the settling of the disagreements had freed him from great troubles. While Cyprian remained in exile, many bishops imitated his constancy; following their example, a numerous portion of the people likewise confessed together with them and was crowned together with them, not separated from its leaders either in prison or in the mines. Nor were virgins and children absent from this number. Some of the blessed martyrs were crowned, while others remained in prison; still others were condemned to the mines, where the many hardships they endured may be seen from Epistle LXXVII, which Cyprian wrote to them more to congratulate than to console them. Their feet were bound with transverse bars and fetters; they lay on the ground without beds; scant bread was provided; those who were freezing lacked clothing; and the hair bristled on their half-shaven heads. The letter is addressed to fellow bishops, presbyters and deacons, and to the other brethren. At the same time, in his own name and that of Quirinus, he sent a sum of money through Herennianus the subdeacon and Lucanus, Maximus, and Amantius, acolytes. The confessors gave thanks in three separate letters, because they were suffering in various places. These letters survive [Col. 0169] and are numbered LXXVIII, LXXIX, and LXXX among the Cyprianic letters.

Cyprian’s charity was not confined within the boundaries of Africa; rather, if the most ancient manuscript is to be trusted, he exhorted by letter two other martyrs, Augustine and Felicitas, who are said to have suffered at Capua in Campania during the same Valerianic persecution. The names of both are found in the ancient martyrologies attributed to Jerome. Tillemont thinks that, besides the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom* and the letters to the confessors, Cyprian wrote another work to the same effect. For after mentioning the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, Pontius adds: “Who, finally, would animate with the clarion-call of the heavenly trumpet so many confessors, marked on their foreheads with a second inscription and preserved alive as an example of martyrdom?” Now, since Pontius is reviewing in this passage the books written by Cyprian and says nothing about his letters, the learned man thinks that these words indicate some book.

After Cyprian had remained for a long time at Curubis, the proconsul Paternus was succeeded by Galerius Maximus, who recalled Cyprian from exile and ordered him to remain in his gardens until he passed sentence upon him. Cyprian had sold these gardens at the beginning of his conversion and distributed its price to the poor; but we learn from Pontius the deacon that by God’s indulgence it had been restored to him. While he was looking after his church and waiting from day to day to be crowned with the martyrdom promised in the vision, various and uncertain reports spread among the populace induced him to send men to Rome who could bring back sure and verified information about the affairs of the Church.
