Upon their return, they reported that Valerian had written back to the senate that bishops, presbyters, and deacons were to be punished immediately; that senators, men of distinguished rank, and Roman knights, after losing their rank, were also to be stripped of their possessions, and, if they persisted in being Christians after their property had been taken away, were also to be put to death; that matrons, after the confiscation of their property, were to be sent into exile; and that any members of the imperial household who had either confessed before or should confess now were to have their property confiscated, be put in chains, registered, and sent to imperial estates. They added that Xystus had been put to death in the cemetery on the eighth day before the Ides of August, and four deacons with him; and further, that the prefects were pressing the persecution daily, so that any persons brought before them should be put to death and their goods claimed for the treasury. Cyprian would gladly have informed his colleagues more fully about these matters, but he had no clergy available to send, for all of them, standing under the stroke of the contest, were utterly unable to leave Carthage, all prepared, according to the devotion of their hearts, for divine and heavenly glory. At last, when an opportunity presented itself, he wrote to Bishop Successus—Epistle LXXXII—about the reports brought from Rome, asking him to make them known through himself to their colleagues, so that the brotherhood everywhere might be strengthened by their exhortation. Where Valerian is said to have written back that members of the imperial household, “any who had either confessed before or should confess now, were to have their property confiscated and be put in chains, registered, and sent to imperial estates,” it would be far more appropriate to read “and enrolled,” as in the Verona manuscript, or “and inscribed,” [Col. 0170] as in Colbert. 2442. Among the punishments was that disgrace of an inscribed forehead, as is clear from these words of Pontius: “Who, finally, would animate with the clarion-call of the heavenly trumpet so many confessors, marked on their foreheads with a second inscription and preserved alive as an example of martyrdom?”

After Cyprian received word that the *frumentarii* had been sent to conduct him to Utica, he agreed, on the advice of his dearest friends, to withdraw from his gardens to some secluded place. From there he wrote his final letter to his church, Epistle LXXXIII, and relates that his reason for withdrawing was that he had been unwilling to allow sentence to be passed upon his confession in a foreign city and then to depart thence as a martyr to the Lord: “since,” he says, “both for myself and for you, I beseech with continual prayers, desire with every longing, and ought to desire, that I may confess among you, suffer there, and depart thence to the Lord.” He exhorts them to preserve quiet and tranquility, and that no one should cause a disturbance or voluntarily offer himself to the pagans.

When the proconsul had returned to Carthage, Cyprian returned to his gardens, awaiting the executioner. “Meanwhile,” says Pontius, “many men of distinguished and illustrious rank and birth, noble also by worldly status, gathered together and, because of their long-standing friendship with him, repeatedly advised withdrawal; and lest bare persuasion should be insufficient, they even offered him places to which he might withdraw.” Not a few of the faithful advised the same. Cyprian would not have hesitated to depart if God had commanded it, as Pontius likewise observes. But at that time he by no means assented to their persuasion; instead, eager to die for Christ, he did not cease exhorting others also to constancy. At last the chief officer came to the gardens at the proconsul’s command with his soldiers, and Cyprian, having been arrested, confessed Christ on the following day—that is, 14 September 258—and shed his blood for him, as may be seen from his life written by Pontius and from the Proconsular Acts, where the various circumstances of his confession and martyrdom, to which we refer the reader, are carefully described. We have excerpted the text of both documents from the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs*, since it is more accurately corrected there than in the editions of Cyprian, together with some notes by the most learned editor. I shall add only one thing in praise of St. Cyprian: that his sacred relics have been preserved with the greatest veneration in the monastery of Compiègne since the time of Charles the Bald. For that emperor magnificently constructed this basilica within his palace and endowed it with most splendid privileges; and he wished the body of the holy martyr—which Aaron, king of the Persians, had granted to Charlemagne’s envoys and which had been deposited at Arles and afterward at Lyons—to be placed there as an exceptional safeguard and ornament, as Ado of Vienne and the most trustworthy charters of that monastery attest.

### XXXV.—ON THE BOOKS ATTRIBUTED TO CYPRIAN, AND FIRST ON THE THREE LETTERS PUBLISHED BY BALUZE.—A REVIEW OF THE BOOKS *ON THE SPECTACLES*, *ON THE PRAISE OF MARTYRDOM*, *ON REBAPTISM*, *ON CHASTITY*, *TO NOVATIAN*, ETC.

[Col. 0171]

To what we have discussed concerning Cyprian’s deeds and writings, it seems that some remarks should be appended concerning the works attributed to his name, especially those commended by their antiquity. Baluze extracted three letters from ancient manuscripts, but that learned critic does not pronounce them genuine. The first, purportedly from Pope Cornelius to Cyprian against the corrupt novelty of rebaptism, bears a manifest mark of fraud and falsehood, since it is established that this controversy did not arise under Cornelius and that complete agreement always prevailed between Cornelius and Cyprian. The second is issued under Cyprian’s name to the people of Carthage; but it does not reflect Cyprian’s age, for it speaks of nothing except those who surrendered the Scriptures, and is even further removed from his style. The third is said to have been written by Cyprian to his blessed and most beloved father Turasius, to console his spirit, distressed by grief over the falling asleep of his daughter. It contains some passages very similar to those read in Cyprian’s book *On Mortality*, but the style is altogether different. Moreover, I shall note that this letter, long since published among Jerome’s works, is found in both old and more recent editions under Jerome’s name, addressed to Tyrasius.

The book *On the Spectacles* is not unworthy of Cyprian, whether one considers its eloquence or its evangelical vigor; many plausible considerations converge in favor of attributing it to him. A bishop writes to his church, from which he was absent against his will; he writes at a time when the custom of carrying the Eucharist home was prevalent and when Christians especially needed to beware of pagan customs. Many passages are shaped in imitation of Tertullian, who had long before discussed the same matters at Carthage. Nor is it surprising if, in that great city, which lacked no kind of spectacle, the contagion of evil tempted Christians themselves. Nevertheless, the grounds do not appear sufficiently weighty for assigning the book *On the Spectacles* to Cyprian. Pontius makes no mention of it; and although, among the works published as Cyprian’s, none approaches the holy martyr’s style more closely, there is nevertheless a certain dissimilarity that ears accustomed and well trained by reading Cyprian may readily perceive.

The book *On the Praise of Martyrdom* has been attributed to Cyprian; Erasmus, Dupin, and Fell thought it the product of an idle declaimer. Yet a more equitable judgment surely ought to have been made of this excellent work, composed to exhort confessors with a certain vivid ardor of piety that a cold artificer of words could not easily imitate. The antiquity of this work is also commended by the fact that in several places its author laments the dreadful plague that raged under Gallus and Volusianus. But since the little book is addressed to Moses and Maximus, who are known to have been crowned with martyrdom in the year 251, and the plague did not break out before the reign of Gallus and Volusianus, Fell infers from this that the book’s author ineptly invented events remote from his own time. But Baluze cuts the knot by testifying that this title, *To Moses and Maximus*, is absent from the ancient manuscripts. Add to this Tillemont’s observation: from a certain testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius (VII.11), concerning deacons consumed by the plague—a testimony that appears necessarily to refer to the time of Decius—he concludes that this plague began under that emperor, although it raged most fiercely under Gallus and Volusianus. Moreover, although I maintain that this work is ancient, I would not on that account assign it to Cyprian; so great is the stylistic discrepancy between this little book and Cyprian’s writings.

Next in Baluze’s edition comes the book *On Rebaptism*, or *Against Those Who Rebaptize*, concerning which Baluze’s notes may be consulted. The work is attributed by some to Ursinus the monk, whom Gennadius attests to have written in the fourth century against those who rebaptized. What Gennadius says was contained in Ursinus the monk’s book may readily be observed in this treatment of rebaptism, for the author, whoever he may ultimately have been, does nothing other than prove that those baptized in heresy are not to be rebaptized, but that hands are to be imposed upon them once they have been converted to a sounder faith. But Ursinus the monk cannot appear to be the author of this little book unless he is said to have been a bishop in the third century. Our writer explicitly declares himself to be a bishop: “For Baptism,” he says (p. 360), “will either be administered by us, completely, solemnly, and in accordance with everything written, and will be administered without the omission of anything whatsoever; or, if it has been administered by the lower clergy under necessity, we shall await the outcome, so that it may either be completed by us or left to be completed by the Lord.” Clear indications of the third century occur in the same writer. For he speaks of that whole controversy in such a way as to indicate that it had recently arisen and was still active. He says (p. 354) that “it is like a monstrosity for bishops to devise such scandals”; that the aim of turbulent men is “to persuade others that they should begin even now to pursue their own enterprise.” In the very passage that Baluze adduces against this, he holds it useful (p. 357) “to acquiesce with good reason in the authority of so many years and so many churches, and likewise of the Apostles and bishops, since it is the greatest injury and loss to the most holy mother Church to rise up against ancient decisions, after so long a succession of so many ages, now for the first time, suddenly and without reason.” It should not be inferred from these words that the author lived in the fourth century, but only that he was not very restrained in his exaggeration. For, apart from the fact that not even in the fourth century could he have alleged “so long a succession of so many ages” without absurd exaggeration, he certainly declares in express words that the controversy over the baptism of heretics had then broken out for the first time; this properly agrees with the third century. Indeed, without naming him, he attacks Cyprian himself as still living and supporting one side with his authority. For he asserts (p. 353) that the only fruit of such a controversy is that one man, whoever he may be, should be proclaimed among certain frivolous men, with empty boasting, as possessing great prudence and constancy; and that, endowed with the folly of heretics, whose only consolation is not to appear to sin alone, he should be celebrated among those most like and equal to himself as having corrected the errors and faults of all the churches. Who would have reviled Cyprian in such unworthy terms after he had washed away by martyrdom the stain of the error that he had defended with the greatest moderation of spirit in a matter not yet decided, and after his name, once the heat of contention had cooled, had attained the highest renown in all the churches?

Pamelius thought that the book *On Chastity* was written by Cyprian in his retirement; and indeed it does not appear unworthy of the holy martyr, so distinguished is it by marks of piety. It is also certain that it was written by a bishop absent from his church. But to its dissimilarity of style must be added the silence of Pontius, who ought especially to have mentioned the works written during the retirement. The author, whoever he may ultimately have been, is very ancient and wrote while the persecutions had not yet ceased. “Virginity,” he says (p. 4), “cannot fear persecution, since from its state of security it can challenge it.” Tillemont nevertheless conjectures that this may be understood of the persecutions of the Vandals; and from its splendid testimonies concerning the grace of Christ, he suspects that this writer was later than Augustine. But this conjecture is less probable, since in Cyprian himself there occur many more testimonies of this kind, and perhaps even more explicit ones.

It is certain that the author of the book *To Novatian* was a contemporary of Cyprian, and there can be no doubt that he wrote during the peaceful beginnings of Valerian’s reign, when the Church enjoyed imperial favor. For after the persecution that raged under Decius, he counts only one persecution, and says that those who fell in the first were victorious in the second (p. 11). He also appears to have been an African, both because he makes this play upon the name of Felicissimus, who was scarcely known outside Africa—“What can those most perverse Novatians answer to this, or rather those few who are now most *un-fortunate* [*infelicissimi*]?” (p. 9)—and because, in declaring that the Church alone baptizes by a heavenly principle, he rejects the baptism of heretics in no obscure terms (p. 10). Dissimilarity of style alone deterred Tillemont from attributing this work to Cyprian. Yet, besides this reason, another can apparently be advanced. At the very beginning, the author of this book declares that, while he “was considering [to himself and] suffering intolerable anguish in his mind over what he [ought] to do concerning the pitiable brethren who, wounded not by their own will but by the assault of the raging devil, were still enduring punishment—that is, throughout a long succession of time—there arose against him” another enemy, the heretic Novatian, an adversary of his own paternal compassion. By these words he indicates that he was a bishop and that, while compassionately taking thought for the lapsed who had long been doing penance, he was distressed to have the heretic Novatian opposing his leniency. Hence also, further on, after speaking of those who “were wounded in the first battle line, that is, in the Decian persecution, and afterward were victorious, that is, in the second battle,” he adds that their “equals—that is, those still remaining in the same guilt of their lapse—were judged by the Novatians not to be admitted to penance.” [Col. 0174] Therefore, the author of this work had not yet granted peace to those who had lapsed under Decius. For he speaks of no others: he calls them the equals of those who were defeated in the first battle but victorious in the second; he says that after a long succession of time they were enduring punishment and were still remaining in the same guilt of the lapse that others had expiated by martyrdom. But when the persecution of Gallus and Volusianus was imminent, Cyprian had gathered into the Lord’s flock the lapsed who had done penance from the first day of their lapse, and had given them Christ’s blood to arm them for shedding their own blood for Christ.

In this book (p. 14), Novatian is said, while he was in the Church, to have mourned the offenses of others as his own. But it is remarkable how he acquired this reputation for humanity and diligence in caring for the lapsed. The testimony of Cornelius appears contradictory, for in Eusebius (VI.43) he attests that during the persecution of Decius Novatian refused to assist the brethren who needed help. But perhaps this reputation for humanity came to Novatian from the most distinguished letter of the Roman clergy, numbered XXXI among the Cyprianic letters, which was written by Novatian and sent throughout the whole world, as Cyprian attests in Epistle LII.

All agree that the book *On Gamblers* is not Cyprian’s. It is evident from its beginning that it is the product of some bishop, or even, as Bellarmine thought, of a Roman pontiff. Its manner of citing Scripture demonstrates that it is an ancient work. Yet it would not unjustly be thought to have been written later if, as some have supposed, it censured the corrupt habit of gambling among presbyters themselves. But nothing prevents these words from being understood of laymen: “The hand that has been admitted to the Lord’s sacrifice, and receives by condescension what pertains to the salvation of the whole person, the hand that completes the divine sacraments.” Nor can the book *On Mounts Sinai and Zion*, the two prayers falsely attributed to Cyprian, and the book *On the Twelve Cardinal Works of Christ* give rise to any controversy. This last work is very famous, and Pamelius contends that it was written either by Cyprian or by a contemporary author. But it has long since, on the evidence of manuscript codices, been assigned to Arnold, abbot of Bonneval in the diocese of Chartres. Certain poems follow; attributed in ancient manuscripts sometimes to Cyprian and sometimes to Tertullian, they are denied to both by all critics.

### XXXVI.—ON *THE SINGULARITY OF CLERICS*, THE EPISTLE OF CELSUS TO VIGILIUS, AND CERTAIN OTHER WORKS

Those who attributed the book *On the Singularity of Clerics* to Cyprian, Origen, or Augustine erred considerably. Dissimilarity of style wholly excludes Cyprian and Augustine, while the episcopal dignity with which the author of this work appears to have been invested excludes Origen. Some thought there was a plausible reason for assigning this book to Origen, because they believed that it praises those who emasculated themselves out of zeal for chastity. But such men are by no means praised; rather, the author takes care not to appear to praise them. For he says: “Concerning them I suspend judgment for the present by way of examination, leaving the opinion to be set forth in another discussion.” And even if an act of this kind [Col. 0175] were approved in this book, would it therefore have to be attributed to Origen, who at a more mature age disapproved what he had done as a youth?

But no one has strayed further from the truth than the Oxford editor, who thinks this book was written around the time of Bede. It is clear that this writer lived when persecutions had not yet ceased: “I am lying,” he says, “if we do not see that the destruction of many has resulted from this. How many bishops and clerics, and laymen as well, and of what quality, are known to have suffered shipwreck with all these things after passing through the contests of confessions and victories, and after mighty deeds, signs, and wonders had been displayed everywhere, because they wished to sail in a fragile vessel!” The clerics whom he refutes objected that some men “who kept women in their houses had attained martyrdom, so that their innocent conscience was thereby proved. In martyrdom,” they said, “we are pardoned, just as our forebears were granted indulgence.” The writer’s antiquity is also evident from his opinion concerning the Angels, whom he thinks “fell with women.” Moreover, when he says that Christ did not dare to compare himself with God, this certainly smacks of an age before Arius, which was sometimes more attentive to distinguishing the Persons than to defending their equality.

The Oxford editor relies on these arguments (note 1): that around Bede’s time the controversy over clerical celibacy was at its fiercest, especially in the West; that at that time the marriage of priests was said to have been prohibited by revelations, as it is in this very book; and that it is certain that this book was written after the Vulgate version had come into use. But the argument drawn from revelations accomplishes absolutely nothing, for revelations were far more frequent in the third and fourth centuries than around Bede’s time. Already in the third century, clerics had been forbidden to keep “subintroduced women” in their houses. For among the many other charges that the Fathers of Antioch brought against Paul of Samosata, they also counted this against him: that both he himself kept women of this kind and, with his connivance, presbyters and deacons did likewise. Cyprian’s Epistle LXII may also be read. As regards the Vulgate version, does this writer, I ask, follow it when he cites the Apostle thus: “Forgetting indeed what lies behind, reaching toward what lies before, I pursue according to the rule, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of our Lord Jesus Christ”? Copyists did indeed do this in the present book and in many others: they conformed scriptural testimonies to the Vulgate; but the true reading can often be discerned from ancient manuscripts.

It may therefore be concluded that this writer lived in the third century or at the beginning of the fourth. That he was a bishop is shown by his concern for governing the Church and admonishing the clergy. To them he testifies that his letters had never failed them—letters which, he says, “during our absence compensated everyone for our personal attendance.” Before this book he had written them a letter “which, commending from the law the principles governing every form of conduct, contained in summary everything generally pertinent to all clerics for directing the rule of discipline.”

I shall say nothing of the *Exposition of the Creed*, that outstanding work, also attributed to Jerome, which by the judgment of all [Col. 0176] is now restored to its legitimate author, Rufinus. The *Letter of Celsus to Vigilius* must be examined somewhat more carefully. This little work is nothing other than the preface or dedicatory letter of a certain Celsus, an elderly Christian, to the *Disputation of Jason and Papiscus*. He had translated that work from Greek into Latin and dedicated it to Bishop Vigilius. We have suffered the loss both of that very ancient book and of its Latin translation; only the preface, or dedicatory letter, survives. After Jason, a Hebrew Christian, had debated with Papiscus, an Alexandrian Jew, about the truth of the Christian religion, and the Jew, after many displays of obstinacy, had at last yielded to the truth he had opposed, the arguments debated so earnestly between them were committed to writing in Greek. It is not established that Jason himself wrote the dialogue, although no one appears to have been better able to do so. Clement of Alexandria attributed the work to St. Luke in the sixth book of his *Hypotyposes*, as Maximus testifies in his scholia on chapter 1 of Dionysius’ *Mystical Theology*; but this is wholly improbable. Maximus himself there assigns it to Aristo of Pella.

When Celsus the Epicurean contended that the histories of the Jews and Christians were fables, and disparaged the labor expended by both groups in interpreting certain things allegorically, he cited as an example the ἀντιλογία (*disputation*) of a certain Papiscus and Jason, which he judged to deserve pity and hatred rather than laughter, and therefore not even to merit refutation. Origen observes (*Against Celsus* IV, p. 199) that, from all the Christian books containing allegories and expositions in a style not to be despised, Celsus selected the one that was of less value and better suited to instructing the multitude and simpler people in the faith than to moving the more intelligent. Origen nevertheless maintains that nothing occurs in it deserving hatred, and asks nothing more for the condemnation of Celsus than that the book be read, “in which a Christian is represented debating with a Jew from the Jewish Scriptures and demonstrating that the prophecies concerning Christ apply to Jesus, while the other vigorously resists this argument in a manner appropriate to the character of a Jew.” From these remarks one may perceive what subjects were treated in this book. Tillemont gathers from Origen that the author of the book diligently inculcates this proposition: “that the source and beginning of all wisdom is to believe in the God of all things, and to direct all one’s actions to the end of pleasing him in every matter, and not even to think anything displeasing to him, since not only words and deeds but even thoughts must be judged.” But Origen does not make this proposition peculiar to Jason; he mentions it as a principle common to all Christian books. Jerome, in his *Questions on Genesis*, testifies that the opening of Genesis is explained thus in the *Disputation of Jason and Papiscus*: “In the Son God made heaven and earth.” He also cites from the same book λοιδορία Θεοῦ ὁ κρεμάμενος, “The one who is hanged is God’s curse,” in book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*. Add to these Maximus, who says in the passage cited above that he had read of seven heavens in the dialogue of Jason and Papiscus. That this treatment was brief is indicated by the Latin translator, who says that “the obstinate hardness of the Jewish [Col. 0177] heart was softened by a brief admonition and gentle rebuke.” For so we have emended what was previously read as “by a Hebrew admonition.”

Pamelius supposed that Jason, the Hebrew Christian who brought Papiscus, the Alexandrian Jew, to the Christian religion, was the same man mentioned in Acts 17 and Romans 16; but this conjecture rests on no evidence whatever. There is no doubt that he lived in the second century, since his disputation was known to Celsus. I would believe that he was a bishop, or at least a presbyter, since Papiscus, struck by the light of truth, entreated Jason and asked to receive the seal.

As for the Latin translator, he says that he is an old man and is named Celsus. He undertook to set forth in Latin the disputation of Jason, the Hebrew Christian, and Papiscus, the Alexandrian Jew, “with the aid of God giving life to the undertaking and with the proper force of the words preserved,” so that he might convey to those ignorant of Greek knowledge of the most glorious victory that truth had won from the heart of Papiscus. He dedicates his translation to Bishop Vigilius: first, so that Vigilius, as a priest skilled in both languages and reverently submissive to the Holy Spirit, might by the authority of the Holy Spirit approve and correct the work; and second, so that by this first request of affection Celsus might be received by him into the number of his disciples. From this it is clear that Celsus had arrived in the city over which Vigilius presided not long before offering him this gift. The fame of Vigilius had drawn him to that city from another part of the province; neither old age, nor the length of the journey, nor the distress of poverty and want had deterred him. Pamelius conjectures that this Vigilius was bishop of Trent. But Celsus congratulates his Vigilius on his future martyrdom and says that, when in a marvelous manner he was appointed bishop, he had been destined by God’s judgment to become a martyr. This cannot be applied to Vigilius of Trent, whom no one, while he lived at the end of the fourth century in the profound peace of the Church, could have called a martyr in hope and expectation.

There follows another treatise against the Jews, which must be entirely denied to Cyprian. Still more absurdly acted those who published among Cyprian’s works the book *On the Revelation of the Head of Blessed John the Baptist*. This fabulous work is found in the very ancient Speyer edition printed by Vindelinus. H. Gravius and Pamelius branded the name of Erasmus with no slight disgrace when they judged that the book *On the Twofold Martyrdom* had been composed by him and falsely ascribed to Cyprian. We have discussed this little book in the preface. Various conjectures have been offered concerning *The Twelve Abuses of the Age*, some assigning it to a certain layman named Erard, others to St. Patrick, apostle of the Irish. In many ancient manuscripts the work is attributed to Augustine, and it has been published with his works. Fell testifies that it was once translated into the language of the English and is found in a manuscript volume of Saxon homilies under this title: *On the Twelve Abuses, According to the Disputation of St. Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr*. Yet no monument whatever stands farther from Cyprian’s piety than the *Supper [Col. 0178] of Cyprian*. It contains nothing but the most foolish jokes, drawn not from profane subjects but—something Tillemont considers more worthy of a Turk than a Christian—from the Holy Scriptures by fair means and foul. Salmasius testifies in his notes on Flavius Vopiscus (p. 396) that, through the kindness of the very learned jurist Juret, he possessed this little work in manuscript, rendered into verse by Azelin, a monk of Rheims, with this title: “The *Supper* of Azelin, monk of Rheims, which he composed for Emperor Henry in imitation of Cyprian of Carthage.” On the same book, see Casimir Oudin.

Several other works bear Cyprian’s name, such as the *Notae* of Tiro and Seneca. Following Trithemius, Gruter—by whom these *Notae* were published—believes that Cyprian enlarged them with terms suited to Christian usage. The English published under Cyprian’s name an Easter computation, which they think was the work referred to by Paul the Deacon when he says that Cyprian composed a very useful chronicle. The computation indicates the writer’s date, for it extends to the fifth year of Gordian and the consulship of Arrianus and Papus. It is not wholly inconsistent to suppose that Cyprian had already been converted at that time, although Pontius the deacon suggests that this happened later. But the barbarity of this writer’s style does not accord with the elegance of language which Cyprian clearly cultivated at the beginning of his conversion, as appears from the *Letter to Donatus*. The Oxford editor found two little books under Cyprian’s name, one written in Latin and the other in Greek. The title of the first is *The Secrets of Cyprian*; that of the other, Εὐαὶ Κυπριάνου, “Woes of Cyprian.” He judged both utterly unworthy of the light of publication, since they are filled with the foulest superstition. These works, however, appear to have been falsely attributed to Cyprian of Antioch, whom we must now discuss.

### XXXVII.—ON THE PENITENCE OF ST. CYPRIAN OF ANTIOCH AND TWO OTHER LITTLE WORKS RELATING TO HIM

Above we attempted to prove that Cyprian of Antioch was not a fictitious person, as the Oxford editor supposed. We must now consider his *Penitence*, or *Confession*, a work published in Latin by the English and which we have thought fit to publish in Greek and Latin. We shall also discuss two other little works, namely the *Conversion of Justina and Cyprian* and the *Passion of Both*. These, together with the *Confession*, were recovered from an ancient manuscript of St. Ouen at Rouen and published in Latin not long ago by two learned men, Dom Edmond Martène and Dom Ursin Durand, in volume III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*.

St. Gregory Nazianzen believed that the *Confession* was written by the martyr himself. For in Oration XVIII (p. 278) he says that Cyprian “assailed the baseness of his own life in a lengthy discourse, so that he might offer even the confession of his crimes to God as a gift, and might provide a way toward better hope for the many who turn their minds away from a wicked and shameful manner of life.” Tillemont and the editors who published those three monuments believe the same. But I am prevented from agreeing with them not only by certain effects of magical art that savor of fable, but also by the lengthy description of magical operations and [Col. 0179] the elaborate circumlocutions concerning every particular form of vice. These seem entirely frigid and to arise more from curious reflection than from sorrow piercing the innermost feelings. Moreover, the author who introduces Cyprian as speaking in this book indicates with sufficient clarity that in recounting his crimes he does not always follow information that is certain and verified, but conjectures what Cyprian had done from the things magicians are accustomed to do. For Eusebius says to Cyprian: “I approve your confession, in which you have recounted to me both the impieties you committed and those you did not commit.” Cyprian himself would never have written this. Rather, by these words another author warns us that he attributed so many crimes to Cyprian not because he knew with certainty that Cyprian had committed them all, but because it did not seem that so famous a magician would have avoided most acts customarily perpetrated by magicians. In this he performed the office of a candid writer, unwilling to deceive his readers if he took some license in writing. Therefore, although this work was not written by Cyprian himself, his conversion must not on that account be assigned to the realm of fable. Nor, if someone chose this event as a subject to adorn and amplify, must the substance of the history therefore be called into question—especially since that writer may have used earlier monuments containing the acts of the martyrdom of Cyprian and Justina “written from beginning to end,” as we read near the end of the little book on the passion of both.

As for the time when the *Confession* was written, although the Oxford editor places no faith whatever in this work, he nevertheless considers it earlier than the reign of Constantine. Yet in the *Conversion*, which appears to be the product of the same writer as the *Confession*, Christians are called “Galileans.” This has a strong connection with the age of Emperor Julian, whom everyone knows to have customarily addressed Christians by that name. What is read in both little works concerning the futile efforts of magical art against Christians appears quite appropriate to that period.

The administration of a monastery of virgins entrusted to Justina, as we read near the end of the *Conversion*, does not conflict with the institutions of the third century. For it appears from the *Life of St. Antony* that communities of such virgins already existed at that time: according to Athanasius (§3), Antony took his sister to be raised in a παρθενών (*house of virgins*) about the year 271. But the statement near the end of the *Confession* that Justina cut her hair for God agrees more closely with the fourth century than the third. Jerome testifies in his *Letter to Sabinianus* that it was customary in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria for both virgins and widows who had vowed themselves to God to offer their hair to the mothers of the monasteries to be cut. He adds that this was done for cleanliness, because women of this kind used neither baths nor oil. Here, however, I shall observe that virgins of this kind differed greatly from those whom the Synod of Gangra condemned with an anathema and concerning whom Theodosius also decreed in the year 390: “Women who, contrary to divine and human laws, have cut off their hair under the impulse of a professed calling shall be kept away from the doors of the church . . . to such a degree that if a bishop permits a woman with a shorn head to enter, he too shall be excluded together with [Col. 0180] communities of this kind,” etc. (*Theodosian Code*, vol. VI, p. 61). Gothofredus believes that absolutely every custom of shaving the head in women was condemned by the Synod of Gangra and by Theodosius. Hence that very learned man inveighs against the custom adopted by the monasteries of Syria and Egypt, and afterward by others, as though against a great crime; and not without profound sorrow he complains “that custom finally brought human and divine laws under its own power.” But it is clearer than daylight that neither the Synod of Gangra nor Theodosius had in view those virgins who, Jerome testifies, wore their heads veiled and bound even though they cut their hair, but other and very different women who, as the Synod of Gangra says, were “dissolving the command of subjection,” ἀναλύουσα τὸ πρόσταγμα τῆς ὑποταγῆς, because they went about with uncovered heads. Hence Theodosius, since women of this kind could be seen by everyone, orders bishops to be deposed if they grant them entrance into the church.

Since, therefore, those three monuments bear several marks of the fourth century and are thus separated by some interval from Cyprian of Antioch, it could have happened that certain things were added to the substance of the history for the sake of adornment or amplification. For I am displeased by the picture of Justina sitting at a window while listening to the deacon Praelius discoursing on the Gospel, and by the claim that she was accustomed to be instructed each day through the window by the same deacon. The same thing is said in the *Life* of the virgin Thecla when she listens to Paul. Moreover, those works that survive only in Latin must not be assigned as much weight as the Greek text itself would possess. For, when comparing the Latin translation of the *Confession* with the Greek text, I discovered that the translator had omitted much, added much, and in very many places departed from the true sense; I fear that the same may have happened in the other two parts. Hence in the *Conversion* you will find nothing about the celebrated prayer in which Justina, according to Gregory Nazianzen, prayed to the Mother of God in the very crisis of temptation that a virgin might come to the aid of a virgin; nothing about Cyprian’s burning his magical books before baptism; and nothing about the office of doorkeeper entrusted to him after baptism. Perhaps for the same reason, in the *Passion of Cyprian and Justina* the judge who condemned them is called Count of the East and writes thus to Diocletian: “To Claudius [Diocletian in the Colbert manuscript], great Caesar, lord of land and sea, greetings.” Thus also Cyprian and Justina are summoned to Damascus, although according to Photius Justina had already moved to that city, while Cyprian alone was then conducted there.

That Cyprian suffered with Justina at Nicomedia under Diocletian and Maximian, while Diocletian was residing at Nicomedia, is clear both from Eudocia’s testimony preserved by Photius and from the *Passion* itself. But if they suffered on September 26, the day on which the Latins celebrate their feast, or, according to the Greeks, on October 2, it must have occurred in the year 304, as Tillemont observes. For it could not have occurred in 303, because about November of that year Diocletian was at Rome, and the persecution did not rage against the laity before 304; nor [Col. 0181] could it have occurred in 305, because by May of that year Diocletian had already abdicated the imperial power.

Cyprian appears to have been advanced in years when he gave his life for Christ. At the age of thirty he went from Egypt to Chaldaea; after remaining there, he returned to his native country, where he acquired fame and reputation through many crimes. [Col. 0181] At length, when he perceived that the efforts of his impious art against Justina were futile, he enrolled himself in the Christian religion. After a year he was made a presbyter; and after spending sixteen years in that rank [Col. 0182] he succeeded Bishop Anthimus. He must have passed several years in the episcopate, “since he illuminated the hearts of many through the word of God, converted them from every heresy, and increased Christ’s flock.” Anthimus, Cyprian’s predecessor, had succeeded Optatus, by whom Aedesius and Cledonia were baptized together with their daughter Justina. Aedesius was also made a presbyter and discharged that ministry for one year and six months.

[Col. 0181]

## ACCOUNT OF THE MANUSCRIPTS USED IN PREPARING THIS EDITION

[Col. 0181] Baluze had collated with manuscripts many printed copies of Cyprian’s works which we were not permitted to inspect. From his notes, however, one may judge how much industry and labor he expended on this work. For in addition to the manuscripts used by Manutius, Pamelius, Rigaltius, and the English editors, Baluze possessed and diligently collated with the printed texts several manuscripts from the Royal Library, among them an ancient manuscript formerly belonging to St. Martin’s at Tournai; from the Colbert Library, manuscripts 137, 782, 801, 2442, and the extremely ancient no. 1305, formerly belonging to the library of de Thou, as well as another formerly belonging to the College of Foix; from the library of St. Remigius, one extremely ancient manuscript and another more recent one; one from the monastery of St. Denis in the same city; and several both from St. Victor’s in Paris and from Baluze’s own library. Add to these the Séguier manuscript, written a thousand years ago; the manuscripts of Bec, Dijon, Corbie, Grenoble—this last belonging to the distinguished Gaspard Bon—the Burgundian, Fossés, Chartres, Lamoignon, Compiègne, Pithou, Sorbonne, and Münster manuscripts, the last now preserved in Paris in the library of the Augustinians [Col. 0182] of the suburb of Saint-Germain; the Fleury and Moissac manuscripts; an ancient book that belonged to Raymond, bishop of Acre; and finally others from the monasteries of St. Arnulf at Metz, Mont-Saint-Michel, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, St. Gall, and Mont-Saint-Éloi. Moreover, variant readings excerpted from Vatican manuscripts were sent to Baluze, as is evident from his notes on Cyprian’s Letter XLVIII. Some of the manuscripts we have enumerated are regularly cited by the English editors; but Baluze nevertheless employs them in such a way as to suggest that he collated them with the printed texts or at least consulted them.

For the works attributed to Cyprian, we also used ancient books from the Royal, Colbert, Sorbonne, St. Victor, and Saint-Germain libraries. But for the accurate correction and emendation of the more valuable works, three extremely ancient manuscripts were especially useful: one from St. Remigius for the *Letter of Celsus to Vigilius*, and two from Saint-Germain for the book *On the Singularity of Clerics* and the *Exposition of the Creed*.

## ORDER OF THE LETTERS AND TREATISES OF ST. CYPRIAN, ADAPTED TO WHAT WE HAVE DISCUSSED IN THE LIFE OF THE HOLY MARTYR

Not long after his baptism: the *Letter to Donatus* and the book *On the Vanity of Idols*.

Cyprian wrote the three books of *Testimonies* and the book *On the Dress of Virgins* either as a presbyter or at the beginning of his episcopate.

Letter LXVI was written at the beginning of his episcopate, before the persecution of Decius. In the *Cyprianic Annals*, Letters LXI, LXII, and LXV are thought to have been written about the same time; but the last appears rather to have been written after the Novatianist heresy. The first two bear no indication of date.

In the year 250, during St. Cyprian’s withdrawal: Letter III, which is from the Roman clergy, and IV, which is Cyprian’s reply. Thirteen letters are mentioned in Letter XV, of which we possess only seven, namely V, IX, XI, X, XII, XIII, and XIV. These were sent to Rome with Letter XV, when summer was already under way. Shortly afterward came XIX, which is Caldonius’ letter to Cyprian; XX, Cyprian’s reply; XVII, from Lucianus and the confessors; XVIII, to the presbyters and deacons; and XXII, Lucianus’ reply to Celerinus. The letter of Celerinus, which is XXI, had been written during the days of Easter. Those six letters were sent to Rome with Letters XXIII and XXV, written shortly afterward. Letter XXIV was written at the same time, and not long afterward XXVII, XXVIII, and XXIX. After Cyprian’s twenty-ninth letter, Letters XXXI and XXVI arrived from Rome. Cyprian then writes Letter XXXII and shortly afterward receives Letter XXX from Rome. About October: Letter XXXVII. Not long afterward: Letter VIII. In the same year 250, at its close—or, if anyone prefers, at the beginning of 251—Letters XVI, XXXV, XXXIII, XXXIV, VII, VI, XXXVI, XXXVIII, and XXXIX were written. Letters XVI and XXXV make no mention of peace; indeed, in Letter XVI Cyprian praises and exhorts the confessors as though in the midst of persecution.

In the year 251, shortly before Easter: Letter XI, while Cyprian was still in retirement. Not long after Easter and Cyprian’s return: the book *On the Lapsed*. Shortly after the envoys’ return: Letter LXI, carried by the presbyter Primitivus; and before his return, Letter XLII, together with XLIII and XLIV and the book *On the Unity of the Church*. Then Letter XLV, shortly after Primitivus’ return. Letters LXVIII and XLVI, which are from Cornelius, and L, which is from the confessors, were brought by Nicephorus, who probably had carried Letters XLII, XLIII, and XLIV together with Mettius. Cyprian replies to these matters by Letters XLIX, XLVII, and LI.

At the beginning of the year 252: Letter LII. In the same year: the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*. About Easter: Letter LIII. After May 15: Letters LIX and LXIV, then LV, LVI, LIV, and LVII.

At the end of the year 252: Letters LVIII and LXXXI.

In 252 or 253: the book *Against Demetrianus* and Letter LX.

In 253 or 254: the book *On Mortality*; and not long afterward the other work, *On Works and Almsgiving*.

In 254: Letter LXIX. Perhaps in the same year, or at least before the disagreement of the Africans with Stephen: Letters LXVII and LXVIII.

In 255, about autumn: Letter LXX, then LXXI.

In 256, shortly after Easter: Letters LXXII, then LXXIII, LXXIV, and LXXVI. About the same time the books *On Patience* and *On Jealousy and Envy* were written. In the same year, on September 1: the Third Council of Carthage; then, as winter approached, Letter LXXV, from Firmilian to Cyprian. Letter LXIII was written after the controversy concerning baptism arose, perhaps in 257.

In 257: the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*. In the same year or in 258: Letters LXXVII, LXXVIII, LXXIX, and LXXX.

In August 258: Letter LXXXII; and shortly before the martyrdom: Letter LXXXIII.

# FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF THE DIVINE THASCIUS CAECILIUS CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE AND MARTYR.—LETTERS

[Col. 0191]

## [LETTERS (C, S)]

[Note: [Col. 0191A]

369. LETTER I.—All editions and most ancient books contain this letter. It is not found, however, in one manuscript of the Royal Library, in one from the monastery of St. Remigius at Rheims, in two from the monastery of Compiègne, in the one I obtained from the monastery of Mont-Saint-Michel, nor, finally, in the Corbie manuscript. I have thought this worth [Col. 0191B] noting because the very learned Nicolas Rigault, doubtless through a lapse of memory or inadvertence, records in his observations on the works of St. Cyprian several variant readings of this letter from the Corbie manuscript, in which it is not contained.

It occupies first place in many ancient manuscripts: namely, in the Verona manuscript, the oldest of all; in the likewise very ancient Séguier manuscript; in two Vatican manuscripts; in all those used by Guillaume Morel; in the manuscript that belonged to Raymond, bishop of Acre, as I found noted in the hand of Simon Goulart, who used it; and in twenty-one of those with which I collated the works of the blessed Martyr. Indeed, in the manuscript of St. Eligius at Arras I saw the following written at the end of this letter: “Here ends the first letter.”

Augustine cites this letter and quotes passages from it in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 14, and [Col. 0191C] in Sermon 312, p. 1256 of the new edition. He severely censures Cyprian for adorning it with a frothy circumlocution of words, because, I suppose—to use the words of Sulpicius Severus in the prologue to his *Life of Saint Martin*—he believed that the kingdom of God consists not in eloquence but in faith. For my part, I have very often wondered at Augustine’s judgment on this letter, which is wholly concerned with God and with censuring the corrupt morals of a depraved age: he censures the dignity and eloquence of its language, as though it were not permissible to adorn the things of God rhetorically with the choicest words and weightiest sentiments. On the contrary, if eloquence is needed anywhere, then in my opinion it plainly ought above all to have a place [Col. 0192A] in compositions concerning the majesty and glory of the supreme God, although, as Saint Hilary says in Book II of *On the Trinity*, all language is inadequate for expounding the things of God. Macarius Mucius likewise says in the preface to his poem *On the Triumph of the Cross*: “I would not dare deny that divine subjects possess such power and dignity that we cannot attain to them by any style; yet I do not consider them so remote that I should deem them inaccessible to the Muses.” [Col. 0192B] For, as Novatian says in his book *On the Trinity*, “When it comes to conceiving and expressing the majesty of God, all eloquence is deservedly mute, and the mind is too slight.” All literature is full of examples of this kind. Who has ever censured eloquence in Saint John Chrysostom? What is more learned or more acute than Tertullian’s *Apology*, which, as Saint Jerome says in his letter to Magnus against Jovinian, contains the whole learning of the secular world? What is more elegant than the *Octavius* of Minucius Felix? Nor was Arnobius without eloquence of his own. Everyone agrees that Lactantius’s books of the *Divine Institutes* breathe Ciceronian eloquence. Even the works of Saint Jerome—although in his letter to Pammachius he writes that elegance of expression must be concealed and avoided in ecclesiastical interpretation, as he himself avoided it in translating the books of sacred Scripture—nevertheless abound everywhere in rhetorical flourishes [Col. 0192C] and elaborate eloquence; and in the same letter to Magnus he undertook the defense of those who employ this manner of writing. From this it necessarily follows that the ecclesiastical authors of higher distinction are liable to censure if Saint Augustine’s judgment against this letter of Cyprian is just and legitimate. I therefore believe that Lactantius’s view should be embraced without reservation. He says (*Book V*, chapter 1) that literary learning not only does no harm to religion and justice, but is also of the greatest benefit, provided that the person who has acquired it is better furnished with virtues and wiser in the truth. The man who supervised the 1483 Venetian edition of Saint Cyprian’s works [Col. 0193A] likewise speaks as follows in his preface: “For I can by no means patiently endure the novel heresy of certain modern writers, who pursue no flower of speech and suppose that whatever is treated in polished and refined language does great harm to sacred subject matter.” And shortly afterward: [Col. 0193B] “For if they acknowledge that eloquence is a morally neutral thing, which we can use either rightly or wrongly, what sane person dares to say that those who profess Christian doctrine ought not to use in defending truth that which all the pagans abused in exalting falsehood?” John Maldonatus expressed the same view when writing to Peter Madurus: “For why,” he asks, “should Christ not have better orators than the devil?” John Sichardus’s preface to the books of Saint Clement’s *Recognitions* makes clear that he too held the same opinion. Among the collected *Orations* of Marcus Antonius Majoragius there is a speech against those who censure the cultivation of ornamented discourse and elegance in speaking; he calls their opinion a heresy. Paul Cortesius also, in the proem to his book of *Sentences*, condemns those theologians who separate elegance in disputation from theology. Nevertheless, what Saint Jerome says in his letter *On the Prodigal Son* to Pope Damasus is true: in ecclesiastical matters it is not words but meanings that are sought. Faustinus the bishop expressed the same view in the preface to his book *On Faith against the Arians*: [Col. 0193C] “In a matter of faith,” he says, “loftiness of language is not to be sought, since the testimonies alone suffice.”]

# FIRST LETTER: TO DONATUS

[Note: [Col. 0191A] *To Donatus, on the errors of the world and contempt for it*: Camb., Dun., Vict. *On Discipline, to Donatus*: Voss. 4. *On* [Col. 0192A] *the Grace of God*: Oxon., Gold.]

(Erasm., Pamel., Letter II; Rigal., Letter I; Oxon., Lips., *Book on the Grace of God*.)

[Col. 0191A]

## SUMMARY

Cyprian had promised Donatus that he would converse with him about divine matters. Now, reminded of his promise, [Col. 0192A] he fulfills it. While commending at length the grace of God conferred through Baptism, he explains how greatly he has been changed by it; and, after vividly demonstrating the errors of the world, he exhorts Donatus to despise it and, finally, to continual reading and prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0193C]

### I.—“You remind me well”

In the manuscript of Foix it is written, “You truly remind me,” and in the margin: “Others say: ‘You remind me well.’” Besides the authority of the ancient copies, that this latter reading is better is also proved by the authority of Rufinus in the prologue to Origen’s *Homilies on Numbers*, as printed by Henri de Valois in his annotations on Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* (p. 129), where the passage reads as follows: “I use for you, brother, the words of the blessed martyr: ‘You remind me well, dearest Donatus. For I also remember that I made a promise.’” And shortly afterward: “But for discharging the promise, the time was not timely, as he says, but stormy and troubled for us.” From these words of blessed Cyprian it may provisionally be inferred that in this letter he is answering one in which Donatus had reminded him to fulfill his promises and his obligation. Nevertheless, it must not be inferred from this that the short letter Pamelius found in the manuscript of Cambron—and which we also found [Col. 0193D] in the old book formerly belonging to François Pithou—was the reminder that moved Cyprian to send this letter to him, merely because its heading gives the name of Donatus as writing to Cyprian. Pamelius did not doubt that it was a genuine production of Donatus, and the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius readily embraced that judgment in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*. Others rejected it as spurious, and I willingly concur with their opinion. Yet I think that it ought to be placed here, as Rigaltius and the Bishop of Oxford have done, lest an inquisitive reader charge me with any negligence. It reads as follows:

**Donatus to Cyprian.** I believe you remember, most holy Cyprian, the talkativeness we shared among the orators: one perception, one thought, an undivided affection. Why, then, are our minds not strengthened in the same way by divine reading? Or was this not always our thought, as we used to promise, that we should believe together?

[Col. 0194A] **Donatus.** The name Donatus was very common in Africa, as is also written in chapter 3 of Saint Augustine’s second letter to Eleusius, Glorius, and Felix. In the following century Lactantius wrote his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* to Donatus the confessor, [Col. 0194B] the very same man, as we may suppose, to whom he also dedicated his book *On the Anger of God*. For I persist in the opinion I expressed when I edited the *Deaths of the Persecutors*. I know that the excellent and venerable Nicolas Le Nourry thought otherwise, and believed that the Donatus to whom the *Anger of God* is dedicated was different from the man whose name appears at the beginning of the book I edited. The excellent scholar believed that he had proved they were different on the ground that the *Anger of God* makes it clear that the Donatus to whom it was dedicated had recently been converted to the religion of Christ, which, he says, cannot be said of the other. The most distinguished man was mistaken about the name. He transferred to Donatus what pertained to Demetrianus, to whom the book *On the Workmanship of God* was dedicated; from that book it is clear that Demetrianus was still uninitiated in our mysteries.—371 **Donatus.** In the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul of Metz it is written: “You remind me well, dearest brother Donatus.”

**The vintage granting respite.** Ennodius, Book IX, Letter 2: “Let conversation between us take the place of prosperous vintages.”

[Col. 0194C] **Customary and fixed.** The old manuscripts vary greatly at this point. Some have “appointed” instead of “fixed”; others “fixed and secure,” or merely “fixed.” One, however, has “customary and fixed,” with “or appointed” written above the line. I prefer the commonly printed reading, which seems to me the best and most certain. For Cicero somewhere speaks of “a customary and fixed sacrifice.” In Law III of the *Code*, *On Delays*, we read: “Holidays are either extraordinary or customary.” Jurists say that customary holidays are those that are annual and legally established. Cyprian was therefore right to speak of customary and fixed truces or holidays; Festus says that they are called “fixed” because they are observed on a definite, appointed day. See Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 16, and Juretus on Symmachus, Book III, Letter 21, at that passage, and “remnants of holidays.”

**The place also.** Cicero in his book *On Famous Orators*: “But, so that our conversation may unfold more easily, let us conduct it seated, if you agree.” When this also pleased them, “we then sat down in the open space beside the statue of Plato.” Jerome, Book II [Col. 0194D] *Against Jovinian*: “The Platonists too and the Stoics used to spend their time in the precincts and porticoes of temples.” Rusticus the deacon, in the preface to his dialogue *Against the Acephali*: “The silence of the place, the convenience of the time, our common agreement, and our temporary freedom from other affairs all concur together for us.”

**Fading.** That is, weary and failing, as in Virgil and Ovid. I found this reading, which is the best and truest, only in one excellent old manuscript of mine. All the others and all editions have “wearisome.” Lucretius, in Book III, speaking of the soul, after saying that it dissolves like smoke into the lofty breezes of the air, adds:

> At the same time, exhausted by age, it fades away.

And in Book V he says that all things are conquered by time, even rocks and lofty towers:

> And the temples and images of the gods, exhausted, fade away.

Lucas Holstenius noted a similar error in the *Acts of the Holy Martyrs Perpetua* [Col. 0195B] *and Felicity*, where, instead of the reading *defatigationibus* (“exhaustions”), he thinks *de factionibus* (“concerning factions”) should be read. (Baluzius wrongly replaced the reading *fatigantis*, supported by nearly all the manuscripts and editions, with *fatiscentis* from a single manuscript. For *fatigantis* means the same as “jesting” or “playing.” Compare Chr. Gfr. Müller, *Observations on Five Passages in Cyprian’s Letters*, Gera, 1776, pp. 2 ff. **GOLDHORN.**)

**With studied tales.** I have always thought this passage corrupt and that the most learned scholars have thus far labored in vain to emend or explain it. While seeking a remedy for it, it occurred to me that perhaps the word *studentibus* (“studied”) should be exchanged for *ludentibus* (“playful”), so that the passage would read “with playful tales,” just as Minucius has “with deceptive tales.” For Ausonius used the expression “to play with tales” in the third letter addressed to his book, bidding it go to Probus: “Let it grow accustomed to jest and play at the same time with skillful tales.” Cyprian and Donatus were therefore conducting their conversation with playful, yet skillful and serious, tales. For we must not suppose that their discussions were frivolous or their conversations concerned trivial matters, since topics of the greatest importance, pertaining to the glory [Col. 0195C] and worship of the supreme God, were being treated between serious men—unless Cyprian, following the convention of dialogues, represented Donatus and himself as saying things they had never said, as Cicero remarks about himself and Varro at the beginning of the *Academic Questions*. Julius Firmicus, in the preface to his books *On Instruction in Astrology*: “We were weaving honorable and varied conversational tales.”

**To instruct.** Something is missing here, for the sense is incomplete. But there are many such passages in Cyprian. Lombert, seeing that the sense was incomplete, translated this passage as though Cyprian had written, “It is pleasing to instruct the conscience of the heart.”

**Of the noisy household.** Saint Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias *On Preserving Virginity*, praises her because, “amid jewels and silk, amid troops of eunuchs and girls, amid the flattery and service of a noisy household, and amid the exquisite feasts supplied by the abundance of a great house,” she had sought the labor of fasting, rough clothing, and restraint in food. Likewise, in his letter to Laeta *On the Education of Her Daughter*, he warns that she should not take part in the servants’ gossip or mingle in the games of the noisy household. And at the end of his book *Against Helvidius*, among the disadvantages of marriage he again includes a noisy household.

**Let us seek this seat.** Abelard cites this passage at the end of Book II of *Christian Theology*.

**The wandering interlacings of the vine shoots.** Cicero in his book *On Old Age*: “The vine, indeed, which by nature falls down and, unless supported, is borne to the ground, nevertheless, in order to raise itself, embraces with its tendrils, as though with hands, whatever it has found; and while it creeps with a manifold and wandering course, the pruning-hook restrains it by cutting it back, lest it grow wild with shoots and spread in every direction.” 372 Sidonius, Book V, Letter 17: “Here one part lay beneath the shade of a mature vine, which had formed a covering by means of foliage drawn over raised supports and hanging in a latticework.” See below, in the notes on Book I of the *Testimonies against the Jews*, chapter 21, under the word “haircloth.”

[Col. 0196B] **A vine portico.** Virgil, *Georgics*, Book III:

> Here they pass the night in play and merrily imitate cups  
> Of wine with fermented and sour rowanberries.

Prudentius in the *Hamartigenia*:

> And vineyards are enclosed with dense hedges.

And in the *Hymn before Food*:

> Here, where the vine’s arms luxuriate  
> With a branch of leafy shoots.

**Leafy roofs.** From Virgil, *Georgics*, Book IV:

> And always seek  
> Leafy roofs.

Ovid, *Fasti*, Book III:

> A hut was made of foliage.

Arator, Book II of the *Acts of the Apostles*, spoke of “the leafy tresses of spring.” Similarly, when Cicero was about to relate the discussions concerning laws held between himself, his brother Quintus, and Titus Pomponius Atticus, he first said that Plato, with Clinias and Mogillus the Lacedaemonian, had debated the institutions of commonwealths and the best laws on a summer day amid the cypress groves and woodland paths of Cnidus. He then says that he, Quintus, and Atticus, while walking [Col. 0196C] among very tall poplars on a green and shady bank and afterward sitting down, investigated the same matters somewhat more fully than forensic practice requires. Likewise Lucian, in *The Hall*, says that Socrates sat with Phaedrus of Myrrhinus beneath a leafy plane tree, amid green grass and beside a clear spring. See Sirmond’s notes on Sidonius, Book II, Letter 1, under the word *hippodrome*.

**Into the ears.** The manuscript of Bec has “into the breezes,” which accords well enough with what follows.

**The mind at the same time.** The same manuscript has: “At the same time both the hearing of the soul is instructed and the gaze is nourished.”

**Your eye.** This is the reading of the old editions and of most of the ancient manuscripts of the best quality. Rigaltius was the first to change it and print: “you are fixed, your eyes.” The English edition afterward followed Rigaltius, although it notes that the reading which we have restored is found in several ancient manuscripts. I am astonished that a reading which is not Latin could have pleased learned men. It plainly arose from the interchange of the letters *o* and *u*, which Quintilian, Book I, chapter 4, notes were very often interchanged in ancient writing; I also found this noted in Book I of Priscian. Thus, in the very ancient manuscript of Saint Cyprian’s letters, no. 1305 of the Colbertine Library, formerly belonging to De Thou, “you are fixed, your eyes” is clearly written; but the letter *u* is joined above the line to those two words, so that the reader might know that this was a correction and that the true reading was the one written above them. For I have often seen the same method of correction used in ancient manuscripts of other writers: namely, where *o* had been written by mistake, *u* was placed above it, and vice versa. The reading of the Colbertine manuscript is also confirmed by the one formerly belonging [Col. 0197B] to Raymond, Bishop of Acre, in which was written, “your eye is fixed.” In my opinion, therefore, Lucas Fredericus Reinhartus acted rightly when, in his edition of the holy martyr’s letters, he restored the ancient reading and relegated to the margin the one Rigaltius had substituted. Pliny, Book XI, chapter 37: “It is with the mind that we see, with the mind that we discern. The eyes, like certain vessels, receive and transmit its visible part.”

**As much with the ear.** Previously it read, “as much with the mouth as with the mind,” which gives a very bad sense. For we do not hear with the mouth but with the ear. Psalm 48: “Receive with your ears the words of my mouth,” and often elsewhere. I had emended this passage of Cyprian by a most certain conjecture. I believed that I had been the first to emend it, but later discovered [Col. 0197C] that Rigaltius had made the correction before me in his observations. Nor do I approve Gronovius’s judgment that this emendation by Rigaltius is illegitimate. For the words of Pliny, “attentive and hanging upon,” which Gronovius cites in Book III of his *Observations*, chapter 12, to show that “mouth” ought not to be changed to “ear,” have no bearing on this passage.

**Entirely a hearer.** Pliny, Book I, chapter 7, speaking of God: “He is wholly sight, wholly hearing.” Likewise Novatian in his book *On the Trinity*: “But he himself is wholly eye, because he sees wholly; wholly ear, because he hears wholly.” Hence Saint Leo the pope in his sermon on the Nativity of the Lord: “Your Lord is present everywhere.” And Cyprian himself, at the beginning of his book *On the Lord’s Prayer* (p. 204), says: “God is present everywhere, hears all, and sees all.”]

## I

Caecilius Cyprianus sends greetings to Donatus.

You remind me well, [Col. 0193A] dearest Donatus. For I both remember that I made a promise and recognize that this is altogether the timely moment to discharge it: now that [Note: [Col. 0193A] *Quod*: Ar., Ben., Bod. 3. *Quo*: Lamb., Eb., Lin., NC. 1, Spir., Thu., Voss., Vict. “Released into leisure when the vintage has granted respite”: Voss. 4.] the vintage grants respite, the mind, released [Col. 0194A] into leisure, obtains the customary and fixed truce of the fading year [Note: [Col. 0193A] “Appointed”: Lam., Ben., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, Reg., Voss. 4. [Col. 0194A] But wrongly. “Fixed”: Foss., Vict.] [Note: [Col. 0194A] “May obtain”: Lam., Bod. 3, Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, Ben., Foss., Vict., Voss. 4. “May keep holiday”: Thu.]. The place also accords with the day, and the pleasant appearance of the gardens, soothing and cherishing the senses beneath the gentle breezes of caressing [Col. 0195A] autumn, is in harmony with it. Here it is delightful to pass the day in conversation and, through discussions directed toward divine precepts, to instruct the conscience of the heart [Note: [Col. 0195A] “Astonished”: Vict.]. And lest a profane observer interrupt our conversation [Note: [Col. 0195A] “Discourse”: Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1, Ben.], or the unrestrained din of a noisy household deafen us, let us seek this seat. The neighboring seclusion affords retirement: here, while the wandering courses of the vine shoots creep over supporting reeds in hanging interlacings, [Col. 0196A] they have made a vine portico with a leafy roof. It is good here to devote our studies to our ears; and while we delight our eyes by the pleasing prospect of the trees and vines [Note: [Col. 0195A] “The vines we see”: Eb., Ar., Pem., Lam., Reg. “The vines which we see”: Bod. 3, NC. 1, Spir., Pem., Et., Man., Fossat. “We see [Col. 0196A] the delightful prospect”: Thu. “And vines”: Oxon.], hearing at the same time instructs the mind and the gaze nourishes it [Note: [Col. 0196A] “As the gaze nourishes”: Salis.]. Yet now your sole delight, your sole concern [Note: [Col. 0196A] “Concern now”: Mich., Vict.], is our conversation. Disregarding the enticements of the pleasurable view, your eye is fixed [Note: [Col. 0196A] “You are fixed, your eyes”: Oxon.] upon me. [Col. 0197A] As much with your ear as with your mind [Note: [Col. 0197A] “By what mouth, by what mind”: Lam., Lin., NC. 1, Ebor., Voss. 2. “As much with the mouth as with the mind”: Bod. 3, Fossat., Spir., Rem., Erasm., Moen., Morell. “By what manner, by what mind”: Thu., Vict. “O, with how upright a mind”: [Col. 0197B] Voss. 4. “As much with the mouth, as much with the mind”: Oxon.], you are entirely a hearer—and this because of the love with which you cherish me.

[Note: [Col. 0197C]

### II.—“Of a slight talent”

Jerome in the preface to Book III of his commentary *On the Epistle to the Galatians*: 373 “Perceiving a rivulet of slight talent, scarcely murmuring with a faint sound.” Ruricius, Bishop of Limoges, Book I, Letter 10: “You should know that I labor under the poverty and barrenness of a slight talent.” Symmachus, [Col. 0197D] Book IX, Letter 10: “The slightness of my talent inspires little admiration.” Lactantius expressed the same thing in different words in the first chapter of *On the Workmanship of God*: “So far as the capacity of my understanding perceives.” Cassian in the preface to the *Conferences*: “So far as the feebleness of our talent sufficed.” Julius Firmicus in the preface to *Instruction in Astrology*: “Our talent is slight.” Instead of this, Martial, Book IX, epigram 51, said “a very small talent.” Jerome in his epitaph for Nepotian: “Small talents cannot sustain great subjects.” Arnold of Bonneval in the English edition: “Lofty subjects require expositors of lofty talent.” Correctly so. For great talents, as Velleius Paterculus says, need great assistance. Quintilian speaks admirably in the preface to his *Institutes of Oratory*: “Nevertheless, it must first of all be affirmed that precepts and arts have no efficacy unless nature assists them. Therefore, these writings are no more intended for someone who lacks talent than writings about agriculture are intended for barren lands.” The same author, Book VIII, chapter 4, says that just as land is made richer by cultivation, so the soul is enriched by instruction. Ammianus Marcellinus, at the beginning of Book XVI: “If they suffice, I shall set in motion all the resources of a moderate talent.”

[Col. 0198B] **Summits.** Thus all editions before that of Pamelius. The ancient copies also agree. Although the word *culmis* (“stalks”), which Pamelius substituted for the other, is good and yields a good sense, I thought the ancient reading should be restored, since it too is excellent: for *culmen* means the highest point of something. In the Tours manuscript “summits” is written, and above the line, “or stalks.”

**Not upon the powers of eloquence.** Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius in defense of his books *Against Jovinian*: “Furthermore, do not demand in humble works the eloquence that you despise in Cicero for Christ’s sake. Ecclesiastical interpretation, even if it possesses elegance of expression, ought to conceal and avoid it.”

**Not eloquent.** Jerome, in his letter to Nepotian *On the Life of Clerics*: “Hear, then, as blessed Cyprian says, words not eloquent but powerful.” Ruricius, Book I, Letter 17: “We are certain that you desire to hear words not so much eloquent as powerful.” Julianus Pomerius, Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 34: “Sensible men are pleased not by ornamented words but by powerful ones.”

**Nor for the audience’s.** The manuscript of the Bishop of Acre: “Nor painted over with polished language for the enticement of a popular audience.”]

## II

But what, or how much, can come from me and enter your heart? The narrow mediocrity of a slight talent produces very meager fruits and bears no heavy crowns [Note: [Col. 0197B] “Stalks”: Oxon.] such as spring from an abundance of fertile soil. Nevertheless, I shall undertake it with such ability [Note: [Col. 0197B] “Ability” in the accusative: Ben.] as I possess; for the subject of the discourse is also on my side [Note: [Col. 0197B] “Fear”: Goul.]. In trials, in an address [Note: [Col. 0197B] “In the contention of a trial”: Vict., Lin., Goul. “In the address of a trial”: [Col. 0198A] Thu., Foss.] before the rostra, let opulent eloquence parade itself with fluent ostentation [Note: [Col. 0198A] “Noble”: Fab.]. But when the voice speaks of the Lord [Col. 0198A] God [Note: [Col. 0198A] “Of the Lord and of God”: Foss. “And of the Lord and of God”: Thu.], the voice’s pure [Note: [Col. 0198B] “Of a pure voice”: Voss. 4.] sincerity relies, in presenting the proofs of faith, not upon the powers of eloquence,^2 but upon the subject matter itself. Accordingly, accept words not eloquent but powerful, not painted over with polished language [Note: [Col. 0198B] “Enticements”: Ar., Lam.] for the enticement of a popular audience [Note: [Col. 0198B] *Fucatam*: Thu.], but simple in their unadorned truth, for proclaiming divine generosity. Accept what is experienced before it is learned, what is not gathered through delays of time by a prolonged acquisition of knowledge, but is imbibed by the shortcut of grace as it brings us to maturity.

[Note: [Col. 0198C]

### III.—“When I lay in darkness”

Saint Augustine cites this passage in Sermon 312 of the new edition. Sedulius, moreover, appears to have borrowed from this passage what he writes about his own conversion to God in his letter to Macedonius:

“While I was therefore occupied with secular studies, I expended the force of an impatient talent, which the providence of the Divinity had engendered in me, not for the benefit of my soul but upon an empty life; and I devoted the consolations of literary training, through the diversions of fruitless labor, not to their Author. At last, God, the merciful Creator of all things, looked with greater compassion upon the structure that was rightfully his own; he grieved that the perceptions of worldly wisdom had been entertained in me for too long, and seasoned the foolish talent of mortal prudence with heavenly salt. As soon as the inner darkness abandoned the eyes of my flesh, I redirected my footsteps, which had been wandering through the thorns of scrubby ground, onto the grass of a flowered turf; and with the secure endeavor of a better judgment, I dedicated the cultivation of an enlightened heart to God.”

Minucius Felix, speaking of himself: “When, the darkness having been dispelled, I emerged from the depths of shadow into the light of wisdom and virtue.” Lucian, the presbyter of Antioch, in Rufinus, Book IX, chapter 6, asserting our faith against the pagans: “We too once wandered in error, and believed that the images we ourselves had fashioned were the gods who created heaven and earth.” Commodianus, *Instruction* 26: “I too was a pagan; I persisted with a perverted mind and believed that the life of this age was the true life.” See also *Instructions* 1 and 33.

[Col. 0199C] **In blind night.** That is, in idolatry. Jerome on the third chapter of Jonah: “Let us set before us blessed Cyprian, who was previously a defender of idolatry and rose to such renown in eloquence that he even taught oratory at Carthage; yet at last he heard Jonah’s discourse, was converted to repentance, and attained such virtue that he publicly proclaimed Christ and bent his neck to the sword for him.”

**To be reborn.** For we are not born Christians but reborn as Christians. Tertullian in the *Apology*: “Christians are made, not born.” Likewise Jerome in his book *Against Vigilantius* and in his letter to Laeta *On the Education of Her Daughter*. In Primasius’s prologue to his commentary on the *Epistles of Paul*, Christians say to the Jews: “Birth does not make sons of Abraham; faith does.” See what Munnulus of Girba says about the birth of Christians at the Council of Carthage, and what Pontius the deacon says about heavenly birth in his *Life of Cyprian*.

**In gold . . . purple.** Jerome in his letter to [Col. 0199D] Heliodorus *In Praise of the Solitary Life*, and in his letter to Laeta *On the Education of Her Daughter*: “To play amid gold and purple.” Marcus Cato in Aulus Gellius, Book II, chapter 18: “Thieves guilty of private crimes spend their lives in stocks and shackles; public thieves live amid gold and purple.” Saint Ambrose, or whoever else wrote Book III of *On Duties*, chapter 3, says: “The thefts of slaves, however, are concealed; the plunder of the rich is public.” Seneca, Letter 76: “None of those whom you see clad in purple is happy, any more than those to whom a theatrical play assigns a scepter and a military cloak.”

**That man with the fasces.** William Cave thought Cyprian had written these words about himself, because he believed that Cyprian had held public honors before becoming a Christian. But since we find nowhere that he held honors, magistracies, or commands, no reason can move us to think that those words refer to Cyprian. We know that he was a rhetorician, but not a proconsul, praetor, or governor, nor did he hold any other magistracy. This error arose because our Cyprian [Col. 0200C] was confused with Cyprian of Antioch. Columella, moreover, spoke of “the dignity and authority of the fasces” in the preface to his books *On Agriculture*.

**Of the attentive throng.** One of my old manuscripts reads “of the more honorable throng.” The manuscript of the Bishop of Acre had the same reading.

**He considers it a punishment.** See what Casaubon notes on Book III of Suetonius under the words: “If you do not rule.”

**Enticements.** The word “accustomed” is added in the editions of Pamelius and Rigaltius. The English editors note that Pamelius added that word against the evidence of all the ancient copies. This is true, for I found it only in a single royal manuscript formerly belonging to Saint Martin of Tournai. In the Dijon manuscript, in the more recent manuscript of Saint-Remi, and in one of my own, “devoted” is written.
