This suggests that the word was added by someone who thought something was missing here. I therefore concluded that the English editors were right [Col. 0200D] to judge that it should be removed.

**Lust hurls him headlong.** Seneca, Letter 10: “Then it sharpens audacity, excites lust, and provokes anger.” Commodianus, *Instruction* 63: “Lust hurls headlong.” Here it should be noted in passing, although the matter is of slight importance, that an old manuscript of Commodianus has “You desire to wage war” where Rigaltius printed “You seek to wage war.”]

## III

When I [Note: [Col. 0198B] “Therefore I”: Pamei.; he supplied “without any defenses.”] lay in darkness and blind [Col. 0199A] night, when I drifted upon the sea of this [Note: [Col. 0199C] “Of this”: Voss. 4.] tossing world, wavering and uncertain, with wandering steps, ignorant of my life’s course [Note: [Col. 0199C] Perhaps “way”: Oxon.], estranged from truth and light, I considered it altogether difficult and hard, given my character at that time, to believe what divine generosity promised me for my salvation: that a person could be born anew, [Col. 0199B] and, animated into new life by the bath of saving water [Note: [Col. 0199C] “Armed”: Ar., Lam., Eb.], could put off what he had formerly been and, although the structure of the body [Note: [Col. 0199C] Nearly all printed editions and manuscripts wrongly punctuate: “could put it off: although the body.” “Corporeal”: Rigalt.] remained [Note: [Col. 0199C] “The material remaining”: Thu.], could change the person in soul and mind [Note: [Col. 0199C] “The person and the mind”: Vict.].

“How,” I said, “is so great a transformation possible [Note: [Col. 0199C] ‘What is more impossible, I said, than that’: Pem., Lam., Eb., Reg. ‘Indeed’: Pem., Foss., Spir., Rem., Manu. ‘For whom’: Goul., Lam. ‘In what way’: Voss. 4.], that suddenly and swiftly there should be stripped away what, either innate, has hardened through the decay of its natural substance [Note: [Col. 0199C] “Begotten in the bosom,” marginal note in an old manuscript. “In a double [Col. 0200C] condition”: Voss. 4, Spir. “Begotten in the bosom”: Bod. 3.], or, acquired over a long period, has become ingrained through age and long standing? These things have settled deep and far down, with profound roots. When does a man accustomed to sumptuous dinners and lavish banquets learn frugality? And when does one who, conspicuous in costly clothing, has glittered in gold and purple, lower himself to the plain and ordinary dress of the common people? The man delighted by the fasces and public honors cannot bear to be a private person without distinction. The man surrounded by wedges of clients, [Col. 0200A] honored by the more numerous company of an attentive throng, considers it a punishment whenever he is alone. Held by tenacious enticements, he must inevitably be invited, as he was accustomed, by drunkenness, puffed up by pride, inflamed by anger, disturbed by greed, incited by cruelty, delighted by ambition, [Col. 0200B] and hurled headlong by lust [Note: [Col. 0200C] “And hurled headlong by lust”: Thu.].”

[Note: [Col. 0200D]

### IV.—“Errors”

Most of the old manuscripts and all editions before the Manutian edition present “horrors.” Yet many manuscripts have “errors,” which I think is better here. By contrast, a little below in this same letter I have retained “horrors,” as will be explained in its proper place.

**I resisted.** I have seen *offavebam* written in several old manuscripts; the older editions before that of Rigaltius have *adfavebam*. Below, in Letter 52, we find *offocari* for *suffocari* (“to be suffocated”) and *offectura* for *effectura* (“going to bring about”) in the opinion pronounced by Munnulus of Girba at the Council of Carthage in the controversy over the baptism of heretics.]

[Col. 0201B] **In one’s own praises.** Ruricius, book II, Letter I: “In one’s own praises, as the saying goes, boasting is odious.” Thus the old manuscript of St. Gall; in its place Canisius printed *jactantia* (“ostentation”). It is sufficiently established that Cyprian used this word. That maxim of Cyprian is indeed true. Hence the familiar saying: “Praise grows sordid in one’s own mouth.” Proverbs 21: “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth.” Augustine, in his Letter to Count Valerius: “And therefore the account concerning you was sweeter to us because he related things which you yourself could not have written back—not even in response to my inquiry—lest you become the herald of your own praises, which Holy Scripture forbids.” In Eusebius, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 30, [Col. 0201C] Paul of Samosata is sharply reproached because he spoke grandly of himself, not as a bishop but as a kind of sophist and impostor. Pliny, book I, Letter VIII: “For if even the praises of others are commonly received with somewhat unfavorable ears, how difficult it is to ensure that a discourse in which someone discusses himself or his own people does not appear tiresome.” Dionysius of Halicarnassus says at the beginning of his *Histories* that he will not dwell at length upon his own praises, since he knew that they were burdensome and tiresome to listeners. Symmachus, book I, Letter I: “No doubt you ridicule me because I proclaimed certain things about myself more indulgently than was proper. And this is a true and deserved reproach. For all ostentation is attended by suspicion of falsehood, because whatever is arrogated is not regarded as one’s own. Moreover, boastfulness, greedy for praise, greatly diminishes modesty.” From this perhaps comes that saying of Symmachus praised by Sidonius: “As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.” Pope Anastasius accords with this maxim in his letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem: “For a twofold reason constrains me to ask this: lest false praise bring pain to the mind of your fellow priest, or true praise kindle his embarrassment.” [Col. 0201D] Quintilian, book IV, chapter 1: “Sometimes it becomes necessary to recount merits, concerning which a man praising his own deeds will have to speak more modestly than one praising another’s.” And book XI, chapter 1: “All boasting about oneself is objectionable, and brings listeners not merely disgust but very often hatred as well.” Before him Cicero had said in book I of *On Duties*: “It is also unseemly to proclaim one’s own merits.” For he knew the truth of what Julius Caesar says in book II of the *Commentaries on the Civil War*: that men gladly proclaim their own praises—something Dio Cassius, book XXXVII, reports that Caesar himself did not habitually do. Yet Cicero himself thought that it was sometimes permissible to speak grandly of oneself. For he says in *On Duties*: “I may indeed boast before you, my son Marcus, to whom both the inheritance of this glory and the imitation of these deeds belong.” The same author, in the speech *On the Responses of the Haruspices*: “Can anyone who has conducted great affairs amid hostility respond with sufficient force to an enemy’s abuse without praising himself?” Plautus, in the *Amphitryon*: “It is fitting for one who has done no wrong to be bold, [Col. 0202B] and to speak confidently and defiantly in his own defense.” For it is sometimes permissible to launch into one’s own praises, after the example of the holy apostle Paul in the Second Letter to the Corinthians (11:22): “In whatever anyone dares—I speak as a fool—I too dare. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one less wise: I am more—through very many labors, through imprisonments more abundantly, through blows beyond measure, through frequent dangers of death,” etc. Saint Augustine explains, in his commentary on Psalm 144, how someone may sometimes praise himself. There is extant among Plutarch’s works a little book on how one may praise oneself without incurring envy. Aristotle, speaking about himself, [Col. 0202C] used to declare that one ought to speak neither favorably nor unfavorably, as Valerius Maximus reports in book VII, chapter 3, since self-praise belongs to the vain and self-reproach to the foolish. For speaking against oneself is generally characteristic only of buffoons, as Quintilian says in book VI, chapter 3. See Demosthenes’ speech *On the Crown*.

**Fear is the guardian of innocence.** Columella, in the preface to book XII: “Fear contributes greatly to diligence in guarding.” Livy, book XXXIV: “Discipline is the guardian of weakness, which among the stronger is best restrained by fear.” Vegetius, book IV, chapter 12: “Fear breaks the inexperienced more readily.” Tertullian, book II of *The Apparel of Women*: “Fear is the foundation of salvation.” In Psalm 118: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” And elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” Lactantius, in *On the Anger of God*, chapter 11, says that religion cannot exist where there is no fear. Likewise that saying in book III of the *Thebaid* and in Petronius:

> Fear first made gods in the world.

The report of Pope Leo II to the emperor Constantine, inserted into the acts of the Sixth Synod: “For your piety [Col. 0202D] is the fruit of mercy, while authority is the guardian of discipline.” Ennodius, in the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*, says that modesty is the mother of good works.

**Lest security.** Cyprian, in *On the Lapsed*, p. 132: “A long peace had corrupted the discipline handed down to us.” For favorable circumstances, as Livy says in book VI, create negligence; and therefore, as he also says in book XLII, they should not be trusted too greatly. See our notes on book VI of Salvian.]

### IV

I myself often reflected upon these things. [Note: [Col. 0200C] “I remember,” Ebor., Ben.] For just as I myself [Note: [Col. 0200C] “For I myself also,” Lam., Ebor., Voss. 2, Vict.] was held entangled in very many errors of my former life [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Ensnared,” Thu., Foss.], from which I did not believe that I could free myself, so I was compliant toward the vices that clung to me [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Sluggish in vices,” Thu.], and, despairing of better things, [Note: [Col. 0200C] “I was, in despair,” Thu., Voss., Fict.] I favored my evils as though they were already my own and native to me. But afterward, when, by the aid of the life-giving water, the stain of my former age had been washed away, a serene and pure light from above poured itself into my cleansed heart [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Light from above poured itself” is absent from Pam., Rig.]; when, after I had drawn in the Spirit from heaven, a second birth restored me as a new man, then, wondrously and at once, doubtful things began to become certain, closed things to open, dark things to shine [Note: [Col. 0200C] Voss. 4 adds “began”]; what had previously seemed difficult became possible, and what had been thought impossible could be accomplished [Note: [Col. 0200C] “Was thought to be, to recognize that what formerly, as though it truly belonged to God . . . . . had been earthly,” Lam., Et., Goul., Vict.]. Thus it became possible to recognize [Col. 0201A] that what, having previously been born according to the flesh, lived subject to sins had been earthly, and that what the Holy Spirit now animated had begun to belong to God.

You yourself certainly know and acknowledge together with me what this death of crimes and life of virtues has taken from us and what it has bestowed upon us. You yourself know; I do not proclaim it. Boasting in one’s own praises [Note: [Col. 0201B] “To write in one’s own praises,” Ben., Ebor., Lam.; “in one’s own praises,” Pem.] is odious [Note: [Col. 0201B] “Idle,” Spir., Rem., Eras., Foss., Vict.]; although whatever is attributed not to human virtue but proclaimed as deriving from God’s gift may be not boasting but gratitude. Thus, no longer to sin has begun to belong to faith, whereas having sinned before belonged [Note: [Col. 0201B] “Had been sin,” Lam., Ar., Eb.; “of the race,” NC. 1.] to human error. It is God’s, I say; it is God’s [Col. 0202A]—everything [Note: [Col. 0201B] “Everything is God’s,” Oxon.] that we can do. From him we live; from him we have strength; from him, having received and conceived our vigor [Note: [Col. 0201B] “Having received vigor,” Voss. 4.], we foreknow, while still placed here, the signs of things to come.

Only let fear be the guardian of innocence, so that the Lord, who mercifully flowed into our minds with the descent of heavenly indulgence [Note: [Col. 0201B] “What the Lord mercifully poured into our minds,” Ar., Ebor.; *inflixit*, Ben., Lam., Bod. 3, Voss. 4, Spir., NC. [Col. 0202B] 1, Pem., Eras., Manut.; *inluxit*, Morell., Vict.], may be retained within the lodging of the delighted soul through due obedience [Note: [Col. 0202B] “Through righteous prayer,” Ben., Ar.], lest the security we have received [Note: [Col. 0202B] “Lest, when it has been received …,” old Pem., Lam., Eb., Ben., Voss. 2; “nor the security received,” Foss.] give birth to negligence and the old enemy steal upon us again.

[Note: [Col. 0202D]

### V.—Keep to the path

Certain old manuscripts give “track.” Pamelius, from whom the others received it, printed: “If you keep to justice, if you walk with the unslipping firmness of your step, if you depend upon God with all your strength,” etc.

**Unslipping.** That is: if you keep to the path of justice with so firm a foot that you do not turn aside from it or slip: *illapsa*, that is, “not slipped.” The *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus: “With the unslipping firmness of one’s step.” These are Cyprian’s words.

**With sincere virtue.** These words dropped out of the editions of Pamelius [Col. 0203B] and Rigaltius. They are, however, extant in the others and in many ancient manuscripts. The English edition restored them.

**For the healing of the suffering.** Thus the manuscript of the monastery of Bec and the manuscript of the bishop of Acco. The Verona manuscript and one Vatican manuscript have *medellam dolentium*. The old editions [Col. 0203C] had “in the marrow of young men.” Morellius printed “in the marrow of those growing up.” In the manuscript of St. Arnulf of Metz it is written “in the healing of those growing up.” In one royal manuscript and in one of mine: “then the healing of the languishing.” Rigaltius seems to have considered this last reading better, and he judges that the word “suffering,” which is now found in the commonly used editions, comes from an interpreter rather than from the author. And because he saw that “in the marrow of young men” was written in the old editions—a reading confirmed by certain old copies—he concluded from this that the passage would be most correctly emended if one wrote “for the healing of those in pain” (*in medelam dolescentium*). I, however, have found this word nowhere. I therefore think that the reading of the old manuscripts, which I have retained, is to be preferred to a new word whose sole origin is Rigaltius’ conjecture. In Letter LIV, p. 77, it is written: “Deservedly was the repentance of the suffering prolonged.” Furthermore, the reader will be able to see, in the volume [Col. 0203D] of the *Capitularies*, p. 1011, that *medulla* (“marrow”) was sometimes mistakenly written by scribes for *medela* (“healing”).

**Of poisons.** Two old manuscripts have “of lethargies.”

**Wandering spirits.** Below, in *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 226: “Impure and wandering spirits.” See the notes there.

**Wailing.** Tertullian, in the *Apology*: “Fearing Christ in God and God in Christ, they are subjected to the servants of God and Christ. Thus, when seized through our touch and breath, through the contemplation and representation of that fire, they depart from bodies at our command, even unwillingly and in pain, and blush in your presence.” The same author, *Against Scapula*: “We not only reject demons, but also refute and expose them daily and drive them out of human beings, as is known to very many.” Minucius Felix: “Most of you know all these things: the demons themselves confess them about themselves whenever they are driven from bodies by us, through the torments of words and the fires of prayer.” Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “Thus, when lodged in human bodies, [Col. 0204B] your gods are tormented by the word of God in the fire of spiritual flames; and those who are worshiped among you as gods are, among us, through the healing of religious faith and the grace of Christ, subjected to human authority; though resisting, they endure torments, and, defeated, are subdued by avenging punishments.” Lactantius, book IV, chapter 27: [Col. 0204C] “Anyone who has seen how demons, adjured through Christ, flee from the bodies they have possessed will know how great a terror this sign is to them.” Even the relics of martyrs put demons to flight. For in the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus it is written concerning the power of the relics of the martyr Rufinianus: “The people of Naples in Campania know this, where the relics of his blood afflict demons in possessed bodies.” See Jerome in the book *Against Vigilantius*, where he testifies to the same thing concerning the relics of the martyrs.]

### V

But if you keep to innocence, if you keep to the path [Note: [Col. 0202B] “The track of justice,” Lin.] of justice, if you walk with the unslipping [Note: [Col. 0202B] “Keep to it with the unslipping firmness of your step,” Lam., NC. 1, Ebor., Thu., Foss.] firmness of your step [Note: [Col. 0202B] “With your steps,” Voss. 4, Morel.], if, depending upon God with all your strength and all your heart, you are only [Col. 0203A] what you have begun to be, then as much freedom is granted to you as spiritual grace is increased. For the heavenly gift is not received after the manner of earthly benefits³ [Note: [Col. 0203B] “The divine gift,” Vict.], with any measure [Note: [Col. 0203B] “Judgment,” Lam., Eb., Lin.] or limit. The Spirit, flowing forth abundantly, is confined by no boundaries, nor is it restrained [Note: [Col. 0203B] “Reined back,” Lam., Ben., Ebor., Thu., Vict.] within fixed limits by enclosing barriers: it flows continually and overflows copiously. Let only our breast thirst and lie open: as much receptive faith as we bring there [Note: [Col. 0203B] “Faith there,” Viet.], so much of the inundating grace do we drink.

From this comes the power, with sober chastity, an uncorrupted mind, a pure voice, and sincere virtue [Note: [Col. 0203B] “Holy,” Ben.], to extinguish the venom of poisons for the healing of the suffering [Note: [Col. 0204B] “For it to be extinguished,” Thu.]; to cleanse the stains of deranged minds by restoring health; to command peace for the hostile, calm for the violent, and gentleness for the raging; to compel the unclean and wandering [Col. 0203B] spirits that have plunged themselves into human beings in order to conquer them [Note: [Col. 0204B] “To conquer human beings,” Vict.] [Note: [Col. 0204B] “Had plunged themselves,” Thu.] to confess and depart by rebuking them with threats, and to press them with harsh blows; [Col. 0204A] to stretch them out as they struggle, wail, and groan under the mounting, spreading punishment; to scourge them with lashes and scorch them with fire. The deed is done there, though it is not seen: the wound is hidden, but the punishment [Note: [Col. 0204B] “But the punishment,” Thu.] manifest.

Thus, insofar as concerns what we have now begun to be, the Spirit we have received exercises his own freedom; insofar as we have not yet changed our body and limbs, our fleshly sight is still blinded by the cloud of this world. How great is this dominion of the soul, how great its power: not only itself to be withdrawn from the world’s destructive contacts, so that, purified and clean, it is seized by no defilement of the assailing enemy, but to become still greater and stronger in power, so that it rules by sovereign right over the whole army of the attacking adversary!

[Note: [Col. 0204C]

### VI.—Of evils

Erasmus added “flattering.” But this word is found neither in the old manuscripts nor in the ancient editions. Below, however, one reads “the poison of flattering evils.” Erasmus therefore seems to have taken it from there.

**Covered.** I do not know upon what authority Rigaltius preferred to print the feminine *opertas*, contrary to the testimony of all the old manuscripts and editions. For that epithet is in no way appropriate to darkness, which is always covered. Unless perhaps he saw the manuscript of St. Arnulf of Metz, in which alone I found *opertas* written. I know that Apuleius [Col. 0204D] wrote: “and spontaneously longs for night and covered darkness.” But his authority is not so great that Cyprian’s wording should be changed on that account. For Cyprian himself, in *On Works and Alms*, p. 242, said: “Eyes overspread with the darkness of blackness and covered by night.” And Virgil:

> Night covers the lands.

In Ovid: “Mount Haemus covered with clouds”;

> . . . And the ether covered with flowing clouds.

Palladius, book I of *Agriculture*, title 3: “Places freed from mist at night.” Nevertheless, the English retained Rigaltius’ edition. I am surprised, however, that he noted that *operti* was written in the Corbie manuscript, in which it is certain that the Letter to Donatus is not contained.

**On the lofty mountain.** Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Nepotianus*: “O, if only we could ascend to such a watchtower, from which we might behold the entire earth beneath our feet! I would now show you the ruins of the whole world, nations dashed against nations [Col. 0205B] and kingdoms against kingdoms.” Matteo Bosso, book I, Letter I to Filippo of Parma, in which he discusses flight from and contempt for the world: “So that you too may perceive this fully, I ask you to turn your mind away from other things for a little while and to place and station it as though upon a lofty watchtower, from which you may see and behold at a single glance the pitiable and dreadful things being done down here among human beings.” Thus Mercury, in Lucian’s *The Observers*, wishing to show Charon what was being done throughout the world, leads him onto a lofty mountain thick with trees so that he may see everything from there.

**When they commit homicide.** Seneca: “Cruel deeds are performed by decrees of the senate and resolutions of the plebs, and things forbidden in private are commanded publicly.” In the comedy *Querolus*, it is written that no one speaks the truth, and that speaking falsely is not a crime because it is common—that is, because it is generally done and is therefore lawful. The ancient author of the *Debate of the Synagogue and the Church*, fol. 41: “But because it was customary, it was not a crime.”

**It is called virtue.** Lactantius, book I, chapter 18: “The more human beings they have afflicted, despoiled, and killed, the more noble and illustrious they consider themselves; captivated by the semblance of empty glory, they impose the name of virtue upon their crimes.” Seneca, *Hercules Furens*: “Successful and fortunate crime is called virtue.” The same author, *Hercules Oetaeus*: “Unrestrained vice is called virtue.” Lucan, book I: “And an unspeakable crime will bear the name of virtue.” The author of the *Second Letter to a Sick Friend*, among Jerome’s works: “To have inflicted injury is virtue.”]

### VI

And so, that the signs of the divine gift may shine more brightly when the truth has been disclosed, I shall give you light for understanding; [Col. 0204B] once the gloom of evils has been wiped away [Note: [Col. 0204B] “Washed away,” Lam.], I shall reveal the darkness of the covered world. Imagine yourself withdrawn for a little while to the loftier summit of a lofty mountain; from there survey [Col. 0205A] the aspects of the things lying below you, and, with your eyes extended in every direction, yourself free from earthly contacts, contemplate the whirlwinds of the tossing world. You will soon pity the world yourself, and, reminded of your own condition and made more grateful to God, you will rejoice with greater joy that you have escaped.

Look: [Note: [Col. 0205B] “You will look,” Ar., Pem.] the roads are closed by robbers, the seas beset by pirates, and wars spread everywhere amid the bloody horror of military camps [Note: [Col. 0205B] “Diffused,” Ar., Lam., Ebor., Ben.]. The world is drenched in mutual bloodshed; and homicide, when individuals commit it, is a crime, but when it is conducted publicly it is called virtue. It is not the consideration of innocence but the magnitude of cruelty [Note: [Col. 0205B] “Of vice,” Lin.] that secures impunity for crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0205C]

### VII.—A crowd

By contrast, in the Letter of Pope Zosimus to Hesychius: “The solitude of monks is greater than any crowd.” For, as Jerome says in the *Epitaph of Marcella*, there was an excessive multitude of monks. Indeed, monks, to whom cities had been forbidden, [Col. 0205D] are commanded to seek out and inhabit deserted places and vast solitudes, as stated in the Theodosian Code. Jerome wrote in his Letter to the monk Rusticus: “Why do we desire the crowds of cities, we who are judged by our solitude?” But, as commonly happens, this discipline was changed into its opposite in subsequent times, and monks gradually abandoned their dwellings and made their way into cities. I do not condemn this later institution, since I know that, while the one and only irreformable rule of faith remains, as Tertullian says, other aspects of conduct and discipline admit the novelty of correction. Moreover, I know—and the whole world knows with me—that enormous advantages have come to the Christian commonwealth from the conduct of monks dwelling among us and from their studies directed toward the common and indeed great benefit of the Church.

But I cannot prevail upon myself not to condemn certain Sarabaites and Gyrovagues who claim to be hermits and are nothing of the kind, since they very frequently abandon their solitudes and visit cities, openly contrary to the form of life which they prescribed for themselves. [Col. 0206B] Above all I have often marveled that, a little less than three hundred years ago, there was a bishop—namely John, bishop of Jaén—who, after resigning his episcopate, openly and publicly professed that he wished to lead the eremitical life, and yet always resided at the Roman Curia. Though by the terms of his chosen institution he ought to have remained far removed from the conduct of public affairs, he devoted himself wholly to embroiling matters at the beginning of that unspeakable schism which arose in the Roman Church after the death of Pope Gregory XI.

[Col. 0206C] **A human being is killed.** Seneca, Letter VII: “Now, all trifling aside, they are sheer murders.” The same author, book I of *On the Happy Life*, chapter 2: “Why does the populace become angry with gladiators, and so unfairly that it regards as an injury the fact that they do not perish willingly? It judges itself despised, and in expression, gesture, and passion it is transformed from spectator into adversary.” Tertullian, in *On the Spectacles*: “Gladiators who are innocent certainly come into the games to become victims of public pleasure. Even those condemned to the games—what sort of reformation is it that they advance from a lesser offense into becoming murderers?” And a little later: “Indeed, the very man who comes to the spectacle to approve the punishment of a murderer drives an unwilling gladiator to homicide with lashes and rods.” The *Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*: “When the people demanded that they be brought into the center, so that, as the penetrating sword entered their bodies, they might join their eyes as accomplices in the homicide,” etc. Prudentius, in the *Hamartigenia*:

> A public assembly presents spectacles  
> Of human blood.

“They watch a populace made cheerful by death.” [Col. 0206D] The same author, book I *Against Symmachus*:

> Human blood is shed at a Latian funeral,  
> And there the assembly, looking on at the altar, fulfills  
> The savage vows of its own Plato.

See Lactantius, book V, chapter 20; Cassiodorus, book V, Letter 42; and Muretus on Seneca’s Letter VII.

**Whom no one condemned.** Morellius’ edition reads: “whom no one condemned to the beasts.” But this is a pure gloss.

**In the prime of life.** Pacuvius, in Aulus Gellius, book XIII, chapter 28: “A man in the prime of life, of fierce disposition, and tall in appearance.”

**Of comely appearance.** The Grenoble manuscript has “graceful.”

**In costly clothing.** Below, in *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 175: “Or in costly clothing,” from Paul.

**Living.** Pamelius added “young men” from the Cambron manuscript. But since that authority stands alone, and it is not established that the subject here is young men rather than strong men, this word was removed in subsequent editions. [Col. 0207B] Nevertheless, the reading that contains “young men” can be confirmed from the passages of ancient authors cited by Bulenger in *On the Hunts of the Circus*, chapter 3.

**(i) For a self-chosen death.** That is, they willingly and spontaneously consign themselves to death. Here *funus* signifies death or a corpse, not the solemn rites of burial, as we shall demonstrate more fully in our note on Cyprian’s Letter XXXI. Lombert therefore failed to grasp the meaning of this passage. For he translated it thus: “People in the flower of their age, well formed and well dressed, coolly prepare to conduct their own funerals.”

**They fight against beasts.** Rigaltius wrote: “Beasts fight against beasts.” He seems to me to have taken this from Nicolas Le Fèvre’s marginal annotation on the Pamelian edition, where that most learned man wrote: “Beasts fight against beasts—not by designation, but by fury.” Yet he did not indicate [Col. 0207C] the source from which he obtained this reading. I, however, found it written thus in the Verona manuscript. But the word “beasts,” which is certainly useless in this passage, I found neither in the other ancient manuscripts nor in the ancient editions. Lombert also translated this passage unsuccessfully—not through his own fault, but because he wished to express what he read in Rigaltius’ edition. He therefore translated it thus: “Beasts fight in this way against beasts, not to expiate their crimes but to satisfy their fury.”

The true meaning is this: “Gladiators fight against beasts,” that is, with beasts; “not by reason of crime,” that is, not because they have been condemned to the beasts for their crimes, “but from fury”—namely, to show themselves brave and skilled in gladiatorial art. The English therefore rightly removed the word “beasts” from this passage, since, as they themselves say, when the author is speaking about human beings, he can hardly be thought to have called them beasts by means of a vulgar and hackneyed insult. Seneca spoke of “the beast-show” and “beast-fighters” in Letters LXVI and LXX. See the same author, book II of *On the Anger of God*, chapter 8, and Symmachus, book II, Letter XLVI, with Juret’s notes. Furthermore, I note [Col. 0207D] that Rigaltius, in the additions to his observations, says that “error” was written for “fury” in Nicolas Le Fèvre’s book. This is not true.

**Not by reason of crime.** Arnobius, book II: “Others kill themselves for no cause deserving it, but for the welcome pleasure of the spectators.” Rufinus, book XI, chapter 18: “Vengeance is granted not to crime but to fury.”]

### VII

Now, if you turn your eyes [Note: [Col. 0205B] “Your eyes toward the cities,” Bod. 1.] and face toward the cities themselves, [Col. 0206A] you will encounter a crowd more dismal than any solitude. A gladiatorial show is prepared so that blood may delight the lust of cruel eyes. The body is filled out into bulk [Note: [Col. 0205B] “Dry,” Spir., Bem.] with stronger foods, and the robust mass of the limbs grows fat upon layers of grease [Note: [Col. 0206B] “For the ruin of the body’s limbs,” Ben., Lam., Ebor., NC. 1; “and from the dew of fat,” Spir., Rem.; “from the continual smell of cooking fat,” Eras.], so that, fattened for punishment, it may perish at a higher price.

A human being is killed for another human being’s pleasure; and the ability to kill is expertise, practice, and art. Crime is not merely committed but also taught. What more inhuman, what more bitter can be said? It is a discipline that enables someone to kill, and it is a glory that he kills [Note: [Col. 0206B] “Has killed,” Foss.].

What, I ask you, is that practice by which men whom no one has condemned expose themselves to wild beasts—men in the prime of life, of sufficiently comely [Col. 0207A] appearance, and in costly clothing? While still alive, they are adorned for a self-chosen death; in their own misfortunes the wretched men glory. They fight against beasts, not because of crime but from fury. Fathers watch their sons; a brother is in the arena and his sister stands nearby. And although the more lavish preparation of the exhibition increases the price of the spectacle, so that a mother may be present at her own sorrows, the mother—alas, what grief! [Note: [Col. 0207B] “Alas for the grief!” Vict.]—even purchases this; and amid spectacles so impious, so dreadful and deadly [Note: [Col. 0207B] “Amid harsh crimes,” Pem., Voss. 2, Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.], they do not consider themselves parricides through their own eyes [Note: [Col. 0207B] “The eyes,” most manuscripts and printed editions.].

[Note: [Col. 0207D]

### VIII.—Of a different spectacle

Thus almost all the old manuscripts and the old editions. In its place Pamelius, and others after him, printed “different spectacles.” To conceal nothing, I found that reading in two ancient manuscripts.

**Contagions.** I gladly seize the opportunities that arise to emend passages of ancient writers which seem to me to have been corrupted. In the fifth Letter of Pope Hormisdas to the bishops established throughout Spain, the commonly printed text reads: “Separate yourselves from every communion of those who err,” with “contagion” in the margin. But in the very old and excellent manuscript of the Colbertine Library the reading is *cognatione* (“kinship”), and in another likewise very old manuscript belonging to the monastery [Col. 0208B] of Saint-Remi at Reims it is *cognitione* (“knowledge”). Although both readings are false, they show that *contagione* (“contagion”) must be read. The preceding words confirm this reading.

**Acts of parricide.** I have seen this written in the Morellian edition and in thirteen ancient manuscripts. Gronovius also testifies that he read it thus in his own manuscript, in chapter 3 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*. Other editions and ten old manuscripts have “parricides” in the dative or ablative. I shall also add the following, although it may perhaps be beside the point: in the *Dialogue Against the Pelagians*, Jerome calls a man who is able to free someone from death but does not do so a parricide; and in book II *Against Jovinian*, following the opinion of the Pythagoreans, he calls anyone who cuts down a fir tree a parricide. Optatus, however, in book VII *Against the Donatists*, says that a man is a murderer if, compelled by no necessity, command, or authority, but driven by fury, he has done of his own volition what the laws prohibit. The monk Widus, in his Letter to Archbishop Heribert in book I of our *Miscellanies*, p. 412: “Whoever can defend his brother from death but fails to do so incurs the guilt of his brother’s death.” Apuleius, book VII of the *Metamorphoses*: “Do you not know that even those who deny saving assistance to persons about to die are commonly punished, because in doing this they have acted against good morals?” [Col. 0208C]

**Horror.** I have retained this word, although the English, relying upon the authority of Gronovius’ manuscript, removed it and wrote “error” in its place—a reading that I also found in the Foix manuscript. But “horror” is written in all the other ancient manuscripts, twenty-two in number, and in the ancient editions. I therefore do not dare to make a change contrary to so many authorities, particularly since it is certain that this reading produces good sense. Thus Dionysius Lambinus observes that in Cicero’s speech *For Milo* one ought to read, “Yet they bring something of horror to the orator,” not “of terror.” In Avitus of Vienne, Letter VI, one reads: “Who, then, would attempt to persuade me that a tomb can be cleansed after the errors of funerals?” In the Marnaesius manuscript, “horrors” is written in place of “errors.” Conversely, in the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus, where the common edition reads “which may move one to horror,” certain very old manuscripts have “which may move one away from error.” Meanwhile, this passage may prove useful for emending similar errors where the authority of old copies is lacking. [Col. 0208D]

**By the instruction.** At first sight it seemed to me that there was a corruption in this passage and that it ought to be emended to read “the instruction” in the nominative or accusative. For I saw it written thus in two ancient manuscripts. But all the others oppose this, as do all the editions. Finally, upon examining more deeply what Cyprian meant to say, I became convinced that he wrote “by the instruction,” intending to say that the multitude takes pleasure in seeing mimes act out obscenities and actors represent shameful deeds. He says that this is done “by the instruction of obscenities,” that is, by the instruction [Col. 0209A] of an immodest art—or, as in Letter LXI to Euchratius, by “the art which is the mistress of teaching obscenities”—because mimes are teachers who exhibit indecencies.

For a wanton age derived great pleasure from that license of the theaters. Hence, since games ought to be more chaste when a censor is watching, as Flavius Vopiscus says in his *Carinus*, when Marcus Porcius Cato was watching the Floralian Games, as Valerius Maximus testifies in book II, chapter 10, the people were ashamed to demand that the mime actresses strip naked; and when he departed, public rejoicing immediately followed. For in the celebration of the Floralian Games, as Lactantius reports, women stripped naked to satisfy the lust of young men’s eyes. Seneca also testifies to this in Letter LXXIX. This therefore illuminates Cyprian’s somewhat obscure passage [Col. 0209B].]

**Adultery is learned.** Seneca, *Epistle* VII: “When people teach, they learn.” It is certain that the Floralia were games of shamelessness, and that among the Romans theatrical license was unrestrained and boundless; many criminal obscenities and, to use Salvian’s words, many impurities in the spectacles were customarily committed there. Tertullian inveighs against the shamelessness of the theaters as follows in *On the Spectacles*, ch. 17:

> “Similarly,” he says, “we are commanded to put away all shamelessness. In this way, therefore, we are also separated from the theater, which is the private council chamber of shamelessness, where nothing is approved except what is disapproved elsewhere. Thus its highest appeal is largely contrived from filthiness: the Atellan actor represents it by gesture, and the mime represents it even through women, banishing modesty from the sex, so that they blush more readily at home than on the stage; and finally the pantomime suffers it in his body from boyhood so that he may become an artist. Even prostitutes themselves, victims of public lust, are brought forward on the stage—more wretched in the presence of women, [Col. 0209C] to whom alone they had remained unknown—and are paraded before the faces of every age and every rank; their place, price, and advertisement are proclaimed even to those who have no need of them. I say nothing of the rest, things which ought to have lain hidden in their own darkness and dens, lest they pollute the daylight. Let the senate blush; let every order blush. Those very destroyers of their own modesty, terrified to bring their gestures into the light and before the people, blush once a year. But if all shamelessness must be abominable to us, why should it be permissible to hear what it is not permissible to say? Since we also know that buffoonery and every idle word are judged by God, why should it likewise be permissible to see what it is a disgrace to do?”

So great a love of the theaters was implanted in pagan minds that, according to Tertullian, the peril of pleasure drew more people away from the Christian sect than did the peril of life. Nor were there lacking those who thought that Christians—a kind of people ready for death—were trained for this obstinacy by the renunciation of pleasures, so that they might despise life more readily once, as it were, its restraints had been severed (*ibid.*, chs. 1 and 2).

Although spectacles were forbidden to Christians, and although the pagans themselves were not unaware of this strictness of the Religion [Col. 0209D], there nevertheless sometimes remained in certain Christians, as it were, some fibers of this vice—that is, of the love of spectacles—which the holy Fathers labored vigorously to tear out. Among the weighty arguments they customarily employed, a memorable one appears to have been drawn from the promises of Baptism, as may be seen from two authoritative witnesses, Tertullian and Cyril of Jerusalem. The former speaks as follows in *On Baptism*, ch. 24:

> “In how many more ways,” he says, “shall we argue that nothing assigned to the spectacles is pleasing to God or fitting for God’s servants, since we have shown that it is not pleasing to the Lord, because all such things were instituted for the devil and furnished from the devil’s possessions? For whatever is not God’s, or displeases God, is necessarily the devil’s. This will be the devil’s pomp, against which we swear in the seal of faith. But that which we swear against we ought not to share in by deed, word, sight, or observation. Otherwise, do we not swear against and break the seal [Col. 0210A] by breaking its attestation? Does it therefore remain for us to demand an answer from the pagans themselves? Let them now tell us whether Christians may attend a spectacle. Yet it is especially from this that they understand a man to have become a Christian: from his repudiation of spectacles. Thus whoever removes that by which he is recognized plainly denies his faith. What hope, moreover, remains for such a man? No one passes into the enemy’s camp unless he has cast away his own arms, deserted the standards and military oaths of his prince, and at the same time covenanted to perish. Did that man think again about God at the time when he was stationed where there is nothing of God? He will, I suppose, have peace in his mind while contending for a charioteer; he will learn chastity while gaping at mimes. Indeed, in every spectacle no greater stumbling block will confront him than the very elaborate adornment of women and men: their very agreement, [Col. 0210B] or their conspiracy or disagreement in their partisan enthusiasms, fans the sparks of lust among them through their intercourse. Finally, no one entering a spectacle thinks first of anything except seeing and being seen. But while the tragic actor is shouting, he will ponder the exclamations of some Prophet. Amid the rhythms of effeminacy he will call a Psalm to mind; and when the athletes perform, he will be ready to say that one must not strike back. He will even be capable of being moved to mercy while intent upon the bites of bears and the sponges of the net-fighters (*spongiae retiariorum*). May God avert from his own people so great a craving for deadly pleasure. For what is it like to go from the Church of God to the church of the devil? From heaven, as they say, into filth? To weary by applauding an actor those hands which you have raised to the Lord? With the mouth by which you pronounced Amen over the holy thing, to bear witness for a gladiator? To say *Εἰς αἰῶνας* (“For ever”) to anyone at all except Christ God?”

So too Cyril of Jerusalem, in *Mystagogical Catechesis* I, teaches that Christians renounced spectacles when in Baptism they renounced the devil’s pomp:

> “Afterward,” he says, “you say, **AND ALL HIS POMP**. The devil’s pomp [Col. 0210C], however, is the madness of the theaters, horse races in the hippodromes, hunts in the circus, and the rest of this kind of vanity, from which the holy man, asking to be delivered, says to God: ‘Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity’ (Ps. 118:37). Do not make the madness of the theater your eager concern and delight, where you may see the insolences of mimes, overflowing with every insult and dishonor, and the dances of effeminate men, full of frenzy and madness. Nor make those men your concern who expose themselves to wild beasts in the circus hunts in order to soothe their unhappy belly; who, in order to pamper their stomach with food, themselves truly become food for the bellies of savage beasts; and, to speak more accurately, for the sake of the belly, which they have known as their one god, cast their own life headlong into danger in single combats. Flee also horse races, an utterly mad spectacle that casts souls downward. For all these things constitute the devil’s pomp.”

Nor should what is read in the book *On the Spectacles*, attributed to St. Cyprian, be omitted. The author says on p. 341:

> “But to pass from this shameless pollution of the stage: I am ashamed to report what [Col. 0210D] is said; I am ashamed even to accuse what is done—the twists of plots, the deceptions of adulterers, the shamelessness of women, scurrilous jokes, sordid parasites, and even the toga-clad heads of households themselves, now stupefied, now obscene, foolish in everything, shameless in everything. And although no class or profession of humanity is spared by the speech of these wicked men, all nevertheless assemble for the spectacle. The common disgrace gives pleasure: people come to see, recognize, or learn vices. They flock there to the public shame of the brothel, to the school of obscenity, lest anything less be done in secret than is learned in public; and amid the very laws everything forbidden by the laws is taught. What is a faithful Christian doing among these things, when he is not permitted even to think about vices? Why does he delight in representations of lust, so that, once modesty has been cast aside in their very presence, he may become bolder for crimes? He also learns to do them while becoming accustomed to see them.”

**Matron.** A woman who enters into marriage with a man, as Aulus Gellius says, but especially a noblewoman of the first rank, not one of the common people. Hence in Tertullian’s book [Col. 0211C] *On the Pallium* we read of matrons rebuked for being without the *stola*, because the *stola* was the distinctive garment of matrons, which husbands gave to newly married women, as Cicero also teaches in the Second *Philippic*. And in Book II of the same Tertullian’s *To His Wife*, a rich woman is described as “puffed up with the title of matron.” And in Rufinus, Book I *On Hosea*: “A woman distinguished by the insignia of a matron.” In the *Acts of the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity* it is written as follows: “Vibia Perpetua, honorably and liberally educated, a matron though married, having a father and mother.” Lucas Holstenius labored to understand this passage, doubtless because of faulty punctuation, since it should be read: “a matron, though married, having a father and mother.” Hence “matronly diligence” in Columella, in the Preface to Book XII; “matronly dignity” in Pliny, Book V, *Epistle* 16; “matronly ornaments” in Book II of Tertullian’s *On the Apparel of Women*; and the “Matronalia festival” in *On Idolatry*. Lampridius, in *Heliogabalus*: “Ridiculous decrees of the Senate were enacted concerning the laws of matrons.” An elegant passage of Columella concerning husbands wishing to depart for their country estates is also worthy of being quoted. Thus he says in Book I, ch. 4:

> “It will therefore be more pleasant for the husband if a matron also accompanies him; as her sex is more delicate, so too is her disposition. She will accordingly have to be won over by some amenity, so that she may remain with her husband more patiently.”

In the little book of the *Petition* of Marcellinus and Faustinus, it is written that Pope Damasus was loved by matrons to such an extent that he was called their “ear-scratcher.” But these things were written by his adversaries. In Ovid, Book II of the *Metamorphoses* and Book VI [not XVI] of the *Fasti*, and also in Silius Italicus, Juno is called “the matron of the Thunderer.” See Lambinus on Horace, Book III, Ode 2.

**She returns shameless.** Below, in *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 179: “How far a virgin falls from her purpose when she who had come chaste departs shameless!” Salvian, Book VI, ch. 3: “And so, in those representations of fornications, the whole populace fornicates in mind; and those who perhaps came pure to the spectacle return from the theater adulterers.”

**The males are emasculated.** The Laetian codex reads: “The honor and vigor of the male is blunted in human beings,” etc.

[Col. 0212C] **Has broken the man into a woman.** Below, *Epistle* LXI: “Teaching how the male is broken into a woman.” Salvian, Book VII, ch. 19: “For men assumed women’s dress and minced their steps more than women.” Arnobius, Book II: “To expose the vigor of manhood and soften it into the dress and delicacies of women.” Jerome, in the *Epistle to Heliodorus*: “An actor broken into a woman.” Tertullian, in *On the Spectacles*: “Those things that are private and peculiar to the stage, in the gesture and bending of the body, sacrifice their softness to Venus and Liber.” Lactantius, Book VI, ch. 20:

> “What else do the shameless movements of actors teach and incite but lusts? Their enervated bodies, softened into a woman’s gait and dress, imitate shameless women with dishonorable gestures.”

St. Ambrose, in the *Epistle to Bishop Sabinus*: “What, indeed, is so shameful to behold as to writhe in theatrical gestures and soften the limbs according to womanly practice?” Prudentius, in the *Hamartigenia*: “One watches the shameful limbs of half-men being whirled in a theatrical gyration.” And below: “You may see aged heroes growing soft through their adornment.” Columella, in the Preface [Col. 0212D] to the *Books on Agriculture*, says that his age admired the gestures of effeminate men, because they feigned through feminine movement the sex denied to men by nature and deceived the eyes of the spectators. See Quintilian, Book II, ch. 1.

**The more skilled, the more shameful.** Phaedra to Hippolytus in Ovid:

> A shameful adulterer does more harm than adultery.

**Religious crimes.** Lactantius, Book I, ch. 20: “What wonder if every crime has flowed from this nation, among whom the vices themselves are religious?”

## VIII

Turn your face from here toward the no less regrettable corruptions of a different [Note: [Col. 0207B] “Different things,” Oxon.] spectacle. [Col. 0207B] In the theaters [Col. 0208A] too you will see what must cause you both pain and shame. The tragic buskin recounts ancient crimes in verse [Note: [Col. 0208B] “In ancient verse,” Bod. 3. “The crimes of poems,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. Ben. Thu. Vict. “Ancient crimes of poems,” Oxon.]. The ancient horror of parricides and incest is reenacted, in a performance expressed after the likeness of reality, lest, as the ages pass, what was once committed should fade from memory. Every age is warned by hearing that what has been done can be done. Crimes never die from the old age of time; wrongdoing is never buried by the passing years; wickedness is never entombed in oblivion. Things that have now ceased to be crimes become examples.

[Col. 0208B] Then in the mimes it gives pleasure, under the instruction of obscenities [Col. 0209A], either to recognize what one has done at home or to hear what one might do. Adultery is learned while it is seen; [Col. 0210A] and, with the evil of public authority acting as a pimp for the vices, the matron who had perhaps gone to the spectacle chaste [Col. 0211A] returns from the spectacle shameless.

Then again, what great decay of morals, what kindling of disgraces, what nourishment [Note: [Col. 0211B] “Incitements,” Vict.] of vices there is in being polluted by theatrical gestures; in seeing, contrary to the compact and law of birth [Note: [Col. 0211B] “And the law of birth,” Voss. 4.], the carefully practiced passivity of unnatural obscenity! Males are emasculated; all the honor and vigor of their sex is softened by the disgrace of an enervated body, and whoever has more thoroughly broken the man into a woman gives greater pleasure there. His praise grows out of his crime [Note: [Col. 0211B] “And he attains praise,” Vict.], and he is judged the more skilled [Note: [Col. 0211B] “The more skilled,” Bod. 3.] the more shameful he is. Such a man is watched—oh, the wickedness!—and watched gladly [Note: [Col. 0211B] “Is gladly admitted,” Voss. 4.]. What might a man of that kind not persuade others to do? He stirs the senses, soothes the affections, and storms the stronger conscience of a good heart. Nor does seductive disgrace lack authority, so that ruin may creep into human beings through the more soothing experience of hearing.

They portray a shameless Venus, an adulterous Mars, and that Jupiter [Col. 0211B] of theirs, chief no more in sovereignty than in vices, burning for earthly loves together with his very thunderbolts—now growing white in the feathers of a swan [Note: [Col. 0211B] “Bursting into flower,” Spir. Rem.], now flowing down in a golden shower, now leaping forth to abduct adolescent boys with birds as his servants. Ask now whether one who watches can remain uncorrupted or chaste. They imitate the gods [Col. 0212A] whom they worship [Note: [Col. 0211B] “When they imitate their gods,” Voss. 4.]; and for the wretched even their crimes become religious [Note: [Col. 0212B] “For the wretched, religious,” Bod. 3.].

[Note: [Col. 0212D]

## IX.—As though his conscience

Three old books give: “as though it were not enough that he cannot escape his own conscience.”

**People of this kind. With that mouth.** It was formerly read as “with that mouth of this kind.” Certain old copies have taught me that this passage should be established and punctuated in this way. Gronovius had already made the same observation before me in Book III of the *Dissertations*, [Col. 0213B] ch. 12. Moreover, these final two words are wrongly joined to what precedes them in the commonly received editions, since what is said above has no connection with these words. For nothing is written there about a mouth. Erasmus, Manutius, and Pamelius printed “with that polluted mouth.” But neither the old books, with one exception, [Col. 0213C] nor the old editions recognize this last word.]

## IX

O, if only, stationed upon that lofty watchtower, you could direct your eyes into hidden places, open the closed doors of bedrooms, and, for the consciousness of your eyes, disclose their concealed inner chambers! You would behold the shameless doing what a modest countenance cannot even behold [Note: [Col. 0212B] “Mind,” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor.]; you would see what it is a crime even to see; you would see those driven mad by the frenzy of vice [Note: [Col. 0212B] “Groaning,” Spir. Rem.; Eras.] denying that they have done what they hasten to do. Men rush upon men in insane lusts; things are done which cannot please even [Note: [Col. 0212B] “Even those very men,” Pam.] those who do them.

I am lying if a man of this kind does not reproach others. A shameful man defames the shameful and believes that, though conscious of his guilt, he has escaped, as though his conscience alone were not enough. The same men are accusers in public and defendants in secret, at once censors [Col. 0212B] and guilty men against themselves. Outside they condemn what they practice within; they gladly commit what, once they have committed it [Note: [Col. 0212B] “And others, when they have committed it,” Mor.], they denounce as criminal: boldness acting entirely in concert with the vices [Note: [Col. 0212B] “Acting in place of invectives,” Eras.; “favoring,” Lam. Ben. Ebor.; “acting with invectives,” Spir. Rem.], and impudence agreeing with the impudent. I do not want you to marvel at what people of this kind say: with that mouth, whatever offense is now committed by the voice is the lesser thing.

[Col. 0213A] [Note: [Col. 0213C]

## X.—Amid the laws themselves

Jerome, Book I, p. 4, *Against Jovinian*: “Every day the blood of adulterers is shed, adulteries are condemned, and amid the very laws, axes, and tribunals, blazing lust holds dominion.” Symmachus, Book II, *Epistle* 52: “We invoke the empty name of laws.” Valerius Maximus, Book IX, ch. 1: “Audacity, the conqueror of laws.” Seneca, in *Hercules Furens*, says that arms conquer laws. And in Cicero’s speech *For Milo*: “The laws fall silent amid arms.” Ovid, Book V of the *Tristia*:

> They do not fear the laws, but justice yields to force,  
> And conquered rights lie beneath the warrior’s sword.

In Livy, however, Book X: “The laws are now ruled, and do not rule.” Seneca, Book IX [read: VII] of *On Benefits*, ch. 28: “Those who have most offended against the laws are protected by the shelter of the laws.” Tacitus, Book I of the *Annals*: “The protection of the laws being ineffective”; and below: “The law has without doubt been defeated.” Agobard also cites this passage of Cyprian, but greatly abbreviated, as is his custom.

[Col. 0213D] **Amid the togas.** Below, in the book *Against Demetrianus*, p. 219: “You complain that an enemy is rising up, as though, even if an enemy were absent, peace could exist amid the very togas.” Seneca, Book II of *On Anger*, ch. 7: “Among those whom you see wearing togas there is no peace.” Tertullian, in *On the Pallium*: “Togas have done more harm to the commonwealth than breastplates.” Florus, Book IV, ch. 12: “They saw togas and laws more savage than arms.” It is also not inappropriate to note that the Tournai codex of the royal library reads: “Amid kings, with peace broken,” and above the line, “or togas.” But it is agreed that this reading also is utterly false, as is the one found in the Fuxensian book, “amid truces, with peace broken,” since the word *treugae* (“truces”) had not yet been invented.

**Than limbs.** Other editions have “than there are limbs.” So too it is read in five old books. But since that final word does not occur in the other ancient copies I used, nor in several English ones, and since the expression is more elegant without that word, which I believe came from a gloss, I removed it. Below, [Col. 0214B] *Epistle* VIII, p. 16: “Although in the servants of God it was no longer limbs but wounds that were being tortured.”

**He substitutes a will.** Some codices have *subducit* (“withdraws”), others *substituit* (“substitutes”), that is, “supposes” or “puts falsely in place.” Valerius Maximus, Book IX, ch. 4: “When certain men in Greece had substituted a false will.” Aulus Gellius, Book V, ch. 9: “To substitute a false lot bearing a name.” Julius Paulus, Book IV of the *Sentences*, title 7: “Not only he who substituted a will.” Cicero, in the *Paradoxes*: “Substituted wills.” Arnobius, Book II: “Did he therefore send souls so that some might infest the passages of the roads, others entrap the ignorant and substitute false wills?” Lactantius, Book V, ch. 9: “For those who hunt after inheritances and substitute wills always arise not from our number but from theirs.” Pliny, Book XXIX, ch. 1, speaks of “snares involving wills.”

**No fear of the laws.** Cassiodorus, in the Preface to the *Variae*: “Then by the ruler’s authority you correct depraved morals, break audacity, and restore fear of the laws.” Livy, Book II, said: “Law overwhelmed by force.” Horace, Book I, Satire 3:

> You must admit that laws were devised through fear of injustice.

**Of the examiner.** The one who conducts judicial examinations, who presides over capital trials, as Pomponius says in Book II of the *Digest*, *On the Origin of Law*. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXIX, says that the injustice of the examiner is more grievous than every crime. Prudentius, in the poem on St. [Col. 0214D] Hippolytus:

> Then the raging examiner says: “Now, torturer, cease  
> With one alone. If the examination is fruitless, the matter is pursued to death.”

The office of the *quaesitor* is something different in Julian the law professor.

**What can be redeemed.** In the Salic Law, title LV, a hand that ought to have been cut off according to the law is redeemed for a price. And in Book III of the *Capitularies*, ch. 10, the penalty established against a perjurer is that he lose his hand or redeem it. See the *Notes on Regino*, p. 593. And yet there were certain offenses that could not be redeemed: for example, if someone had committed perjury, Book V of the *Capitularies*, ch. 196; or if someone killed his enemy after peace had been made with him, Book VI, ch. 272. For such persons must lose a hand, and they are not permitted to redeem it.

**Whoever does not imitate the wicked.** Tacitus, Book IV of the *Annals*: “Even glory and virtue have enemies, since by too close a contrast they reproach what differs from themselves.” For, as Lactantius, Book V, ch. 9, and Jerome, in the *Epistle to an Exiled Virgin*, say, whoever dissents from another’s way of life seems to rebuke it. Sulpicius Severus, Book II of the *Sacred History*: “Indeed, vices are always hostile to virtues, and all the best men are regarded by the wicked as though they were reproaching them.” For there is, as Quintilian says in Book II, ch. 12, and Book III, ch. 7, [Col. 0215C] a certain proximity between virtues and vices. And Seneca, *Epistle* XLV, says that vices creep in under the name of virtues and, mingled with them, drag them along with themselves. Livy truly said that evils cling to good things and are more powerful in human minds. See Aulus Gellius, Book VI, ch. 1.

**It began to be lawful.** Tertullian, in *On the Crown*: “But what is not prohibited is voluntarily permitted. Rather, what is not voluntarily permitted is prohibited.” St. Ambrose, in the *Epistle to Paternus*:

> “For in your letter you allege that a marriage of this kind between such relatives is considered permitted by divine law because it is not prohibited. But I maintain that it is prohibited.”

And a little later:

> “But if you think it permitted for the reason that it is not specifically prohibited, you will not find it prohibited by the wording of the law that a father should take his own daughter as wife. . . . Is it therefore lawful because it is not prohibited?”

For whatever is permitted is so by indulgence, as Tertullian says in *Exhortation to Chastity*. In the comedy *Querolus* it is written that speaking falsely is not a crime because it is common; that adultery too is not a crime, and is therefore lawful, because it can neither be permitted nor prohibited. The ancient author of the *Altercation of the Synagogue and the Church*: “Jacob’s four wives are charged against him as a great crime. But because it was the custom, it was not a crime. Now, however, it is a crime because it is not the custom.”]

## X

But perhaps, after treacherous roads, after the manifold conflicts of every kind throughout the whole world, after spectacles either bloody or shameful, after the disgraces of lust either prostituted in brothels or enclosed within domestic walls—whose guilt is the bolder, the more secret it is—the forum may seem to you immune, as though it were free from assailing wrongs and polluted by no contact with evils.

Turn your gaze in that direction. You will find more things there to detest; you will turn your eyes away from it all the more. Although the laws have been engraved upon the Twelve Tables, and legal rules have been publicly prescribed upon bronze set up for all to see [Note: [Col. 0213B] “Upon public bronze set up,” Pem. Lam. Eb. NC. 1. Voss. 2. “Public,” Voss. 4. “Set up,” Spir. Rem.], offenses are committed amid the very laws, and sins amid the legal rules. Innocence is not preserved even where it is defended.

The frenzy of men in mutual conflict rages, and amid the togas, when peace has been broken, the forum bellows, mad with lawsuits. The spear, sword, and executioner stand ready there; the claw gouges, [Col. 0213B] the rack stretches, and fire burns: for the one body [Col. 0214A] of a human being there are more punishments than limbs. Who will bring help amid these things? The advocate [Note: [Col. 0213B] “The advocate, of course,” Voss. 4.]? He betrays his client and deceives him. The judge? But he sells his sentence [Note: [Col. 0213B] “The judge sells his sentence,” Voss. 4.]. The man who sits to punish crimes commits them; and so that an innocent defendant may perish, the judge becomes guilty.

Crimes blaze everywhere, and throughout society the guilty poison of wrongdoing operates through wicked minds in its manifold forms. This man substitutes a will; that man writes a false one in a capital fraud. Here children are barred from inheritances; there strangers are endowed with property. An enemy makes an accusation; a slanderer attacks; a witness defames. On both sides [Note: [Col. 0213B] “An enemy makes an accusation, slanders and attacks; witnesses defame the truth; everywhere,” Vict.] the venal audacity of a voice prostituted to falsehood runs riot with accusations [Note: [Col. 0214B] “Of an accusation,” Rig. Pem. Bod. 3. Voss. 2. Lin. Spir. Rem. Man. Mor.], while meanwhile the guilty do not perish even with the innocent [Note: [Col. 0214B] “The innocent perish with the guilty,” Lam. Ben. Ar. NC. 1.].

There is no fear of the laws; no dread of the examiner or the judge. What can be redeemed is not feared. Among the guilty, it is now a crime [Col. 0214B] to be guiltless [Note: [Col. 0214B] “It belongs to crime,” Oxon.]. Whoever does not imitate the wicked gives offense [Note: [Col. 0214B] “Whoever is wicked while he does not imitate,” Ebor. Lam.]. [Col. 0215A] The laws have come to an agreement with sins, and what is public has begun to be lawful. What sense of shame can there be in such affairs, what integrity can possibly exist, where there are none to condemn the wicked, and only those [Note: [Col. 0215B] “Only where,” Lam. Ebor. An. Thu. Eras. Morel. Voss. 4.] who ought to be condemned are encountered?

[Note: [Col. 0215D]

## XI.—Once the thing has been drunk

The old books and old editions vary greatly in this passage. Some read “it has been drunk”; others *epotata*, *epotaris*, “it has been drunk up,” and even “it must be drunk.” But since the reading we prefer is found in many more ancient codices than the others, and since it is also confirmed by the Séguier codex and the editions preceding that of Pamelius, we judged that it should be restored.

Moreover, because Pamelius, in order to add the authority of some earlier scholar to his edition, noted that Gravius had restored this passage in that way, the reader must be warned that this is not true. For in the edition called that of Gravius it is plainly written, “once the thing has been drunk,” and in the margin, “we have drunk it.” Gronovius, Book III of the *Observations*, ch. 24, notes that he saw “once the thing has been drunk” written in the [Col. 0216B] Fuxensian codex. This is true.

**Morning caller.** Virgil, Book II, p. 5, of the *Georgics*:

> Unless, at dawn, the lofty house pours from all its chambers  
> A mighty wave of callers through its proud doors.

[Col. 0216C] Martial, Book X, Epigram 10:

> As a morning caller, may you wear away a thousand thresholds.

For this reason Horace wrote in *Epode* XI of “the proud thresholds of powerful citizens.” Claudian, Book I, *Against Rufinus*: “There the crowd of callers fills the spacious house with its din.” The ambition surrounding morning salutations had reached such a point that those who wished to be the first callers spent the night awake before the doors of eminent officials, as Symmachus teaches in Book IV, *Epistle* XLI.

Suetonius notes that Caligula, being timid and distrustful by nature, always stationed extremely harsh searchers against those who came to salute him, but that this custom was abandoned by Vespasian. Aelius Lampridius, in the *Life of Alexander Severus*, writes that Alexander admitted callers as though he were merely one of the senators, with the curtain open and the admission officers removed, whereas previously it had not been possible to salute the emperor because he could not see them. Once he had been saluted, says the same author, he offered seats to all the senators. For that reason he admitted to the salutation none but honorable men of good reputation, and ordered that no one should enter unless he knew himself to be innocent. [Col. 0216D] He proclaimed through a herald that no one who knew himself to be a thief should salute the emperor.

By contrast, Maximinus the Younger, as Julius Capitolinus relates, was exceedingly arrogant at salutations: he held out his hand and allowed his knees to be kissed, and sometimes even his feet. Something similar occurs in Lucian’s *Necromancy*, where he mocks those who, when established in power, thought that they would make the people saluting them happy and blessed if they offered their breast or right hand to be kissed. Many constitutions concerning the honor and right of salutations survive in the Theodosian Code. More could be said on this subject, but these observations are sufficient. See nevertheless Seneca, *Epistle* XCI; Aulus Gellius, Books IV and XX, ch. 1; and St. Augustine, *Confessions* VI.1.

**A hunter of opportunities.** One who hunts for the opportune moment, as Cicero says in the speech *For Roscius of Ameria*. It is agreed that fawners—that is, flatterers—do this. Some ancient codices and editions read *anceps* (“wavering” or “doubtful”).

**The attendant has disgraced it.** That is, has left the side exposed, as is correctly explained in the English edition. Tacitus notes in Book XIII of the *Annals* that this happened to Agrippina, Nero’s mother, where he says that she was deserted by the crowd of callers after Nero removed both her military watch and her German guards. Jerome, in the *Epistle to Furia on Preserving Widowhood*: “Let neither a curled steward, nor a handsome foster-brother, nor a fair and ruddy attendant cling to your side.” Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, in the constitution issued against the eunuch Eutropius, law XVII of the Theodosian Code, *On Punishments*: “The filthy prodigy disgraced by his contamination the divine reward of the consulship.” Hence the familiar saying: “All portents yielded to the eunuch as consul.”]

## XI

But lest we perhaps appear to select the worse things, and, from an eagerness to demolish them, to lead your eyes over sights whose grim and abhorrent appearance offends the expression and countenance of a better conscience, I shall now show you those things which secular ignorance regards as good. There too you will see things that must be fled.

What you suppose to be honors and fasces, abundance in riches and power in military commands [Note: [Col. 0215B] Rigalt. removed all the repeated interrogative expressions.], the splendor of purple in magistracies and the power of license in sovereignty [Note: [Col. 0215B] “In magistracies—in sovereignties,” NC. 1. Eb. Lam.], is the hidden poison of flattering evils [Note: [Col. 0215B] “And” omitted, Oxon.] and the countenance of smiling wickedness, cheerful indeed, yet an alluring deception concealing disaster [Col. 0215B] [Note: [Col. 0215B] “Of concealed disaster,” Pem. Voss. 2, but omitted]: a kind [Col. 0216A] [Note: [Col. 0216B] “A certain kind,” Voss. 2.] of poison in which sweetness is sprinkled upon deadly juices and, by the cunning of deception, the flavor is medicated, so that what is taken seems to be a drink; but once the thing has been drunk, the destruction swallowed down runs riot.

Indeed, you see that man who, conspicuous in more splendid clothing, imagines that he shines in purple. With what filth did he purchase this brilliance? What disdain from arrogant men did he first [Note: [Col. 0216B] “First” omitted, Voss.] endure? What proud doors did he besiege as a morning caller? How many insulting footprints of swollen men [Note: [Col. 0216B] “What swollen . . . ,” Bod. Spir. Ren. Foss.; “with insulting footsteps,” Ar. Ben. Lam. Ebor.] did he precede, hemmed into the massed ranks of clients [Note: [Col. 0216B] “Hemmed in by clients,” Spir. Eras.; “in ranks,” Oxon.], so that afterward, once he himself had been saluted [Note: [Col. 0216B] “Of those saluting,” Lamb. Eras.], a procession might likewise precede him as his escort—a procession subservient not to the man but to his power! For he did not deserve to be honored for his character, but for his fasces.

Finally, you may see the shameful ends of such men, when the flattering hunter of opportunities has withdrawn and when the deserting attendant has disgraced the private citizen by leaving his side exposed. [Col. 0216B] Then the wounds of the mutilated household [Col. 0217A] strike the conscience; then the losses of an exhausted estate [Note: [Col. 0217A] “Exhausted,” Spir. Rem. Eras.] are recognized—the losses by which the favor of the crowd was purchased and popular acclaim was sought through transient and empty aspirations. It was an altogether foolish and empty waste [Note: [Col. 0217A] “Boasting,” Pem. Voss. 2.] to have wished, for the pleasure of a disappointing spectacle, to acquire something which the people did not receive and the magistrate would lose!

[Note: [Col. 0217B]

## XII.—Let the jewel drink

Virgil, Book II of the *Georgics*: “So that the jewel may drink”; and Book I of the *Aeneid*:

> [Col. 0217C] Here the queen called for a heavy bowl,  
> Laden with jewels and gold, to be filled with wine.

Seneca, ch. 3 of *On Providence*: “How much more should this man be envied than those who are served with a jewel.” Julius Capitolinus, in *Aelius Verus*: “Golden and silver cups, including jeweled ones, were also given.” Likewise, in *Gallienus*: “He made jeweled vessels.” Martial, Book XII, Epigram 12: “It is fitting for you to drink from a jewel,” that is, from a jeweled vessel, a vessel adorned with jewels. Juvenal, Satire X: “When you take up jeweled cups.” The same author says in Satire V that if a golden vessel is offered to a parasite at a banquet, a guard is assigned to him to count the jewels. Propertius, Book III, Elegy 3: “Nor does my thirst drink from a costly jewel.” Silius Italicus, Book XIII: “And cups that stimulate luxury with eastern gems.” Statius, Book I of the *Thebaid*: “Nor is there any concern about entrusting jewels to wine.” Aelius Spartianus writes that Zenobia used jeweled golden vessels at banquets. Latinus Pacatus Drepanius, in the *Panegyric of Theodosius*: “Unless the flame had broken the summer ice in capacious jeweled vessels.” [Col. 0217D] Sidonius, Book II, *Epistle* 13: “Capacious jeweled cups would steam with Falernian wine.” The same author, in Poem 2: “The king himself retaining the jeweled bowl.” Lucian, in the *Downward Journey*, mentions cups set with jewels; and Apuleius, Book II of the *Metamorphoses*, mentions jewels fashioned into wine cups.

Jerome, in the *Life of Paul the Hermit*: “You drink from jewels; he satisfied his need with the hollow hands nature gave him.” The same author, in the *Epistle to Paul on the Hebrew Alphabet*: “Let others, if they wish, keep their riches for themselves; let them drink from jewels.” Seneca, *Epistle* CXIX: “Whether the cup is golden, crystalline, murrhine, a Tiburtine goblet, or a hollow hand makes no difference.”

Moreover, it should be noted here that Rigaltius printed “let him drink jewels,” and that Lombert, who used his edition, therefore translated it badly as *ils boivent des perles et de l’ambre gris* (“they drink pearls and ambergris”). Lombert nevertheless added the latter word, although nothing similar occurs in Cyprian. Some think that this kind of liquid was unknown to the ancients. Others, however, say that it is amber, concerning which see Diodorus Siculus, Book V.

[Col. 0218B] **He lies awake upon down.** Seneca, *On Providence*, ch. 3: “He will lie as wakeful upon down as that man upon the cross.” Martial, Book IX, Epigram 94: “See, Gaius lies sleepless upon down.” Jerome, in the letter to Marcella concerning Blesilla’s illness: “At that time even the soft yieldingness of down seemed hard, and she could scarcely lie upon the piled-up couches.” Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*: “Golden-roofed halls never bring repose, and purple draws out sleepless nights.” Prudentius, in the *Hamartigenia*: “But we spread out the luxury of down and woven linen.” Rigaltius wrote, “yet he lies awake upon down,” contrary to the authority of all the ancient manuscripts and editions. I think, however, that he added the word “yet” from a copy of the Pamelian edition used by Nicolas Le Fèvre, in whose margin that most learned man had written it in his own hand, without mentioning the place where he had found it. [Col. 0218C] It certainly does not occur in the ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, with which he collated many passages of Saint Cyprian. The English edition nevertheless retained the word. Reinhart rejected it. It is certainly unnecessary.

**Is possessed rather.** Below, in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 185: “They believe that they possess, when they themselves are possessed instead.” Jerome, in the letter to Paulinus concerning the training of a monk: “Crates of Thebes, once an exceedingly wealthy man, when setting out for Athens to pursue philosophy, cast away a great weight of gold: he did not think that he could possess both virtues and riches at the same time.” Likewise, in Book II *Against Jovinian* and in the consolatory letter to Julian: “Crates of Thebes, after casting into the sea no small weight of gold, said: ‘Away to the depths, evil desires! I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’” In casting his wealth into the sea, however, as Gregory Nazianzen teaches in his oration *In Praise of Basil*, he said: “Crates sets Crates the Theban free.” Philostratus reports [Col. 0218D] in his *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book II, ch. 10, that Apollonius of Tyana blamed him for this. Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, ch. 22: “My riches belong to me; you belong to your riches.” Likewise, Letter 115: “Money is possessed with greater torment than it is acquired.” Likewise, Letter 119: “As for those whom the name of riches has falsely seized—poverty under occupation—they possess riches in the same way that we are said to ‘have a fever,’ although it is the fever that has us. Conversely, we ought to say, ‘A fever holds him.’ In the same way one should say, ‘Riches hold him.’” Valerius Maximus, Book IX, ch. 4: “Beyond doubt, that man does not possess riches, but is possessed by riches.” Something similar appears in Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book V, ch. 8.

**And resources.** These two words, which I did not find in the old editions or in any of the ancient copies that I use, were added by Pamelius; and Gronovius, *Observations*, Book III, ch. 12, advised that they should be deleted. I too had thought that they ought to be omitted, especially since I saw that Cicero, in his book *On Friendship*, distinguishes between *divitiae* (“riches”) and *opes* (“resources”).
