For he says: “Riches, so that you may use them; resources, so that you may be honored.” But [Col. 0219B] I did not wish to change anything, because I see that this reading has been accepted. It can indeed be supported by the distinction Cicero draws between riches and resources. Lombert translated this passage as though those words were not Cyprian’s, because among the French *divitiae* and *opes* are expressed by the same word.]

XII. But even those whom [Note: [Col. 0217A] *Quod* Pem. Mor.] you suppose to be rich—joining estate to estate and, after excluding the poor from the neighboring lands, extending boundless and limitless tracts ever farther; those who possess a very great weight of silver and gold, and either raised heaps or buried stores of immense sums of money—[Col. 0218A] even amid their riches are tormented by the anxious fear of uncertain thought: lest a robber lay waste to them, lest an assassin attack them, lest the hostile envy of some wealthier man harass them with malicious lawsuits. Neither food nor sleep comes to such a man in security. [Note: [Col. 0217A] *Securus* Lam. York. Spir. Rem. Eras. *Securos* Voss. [Col. 0217B] 2. Mor. *Securum* Voss. 4.] He sighs at the banquet, though he drink from a jeweled cup; and when a softer couch has received his body, enervated by feasting, within its deep embrace [Note: [Col. 0218A] *Condat* Lam. York. Lin. Ben. *Condidit*.], he lies awake upon down. In his wretchedness he does not understand that these splendid things are instruments of punishment for him, that he is held bound by gold, and that he is possessed by riches and resources rather than possessing them. And—oh, the detestable [Note: [Col. 0218A] “Riches. O detestable” York. Lin. “And indeed detestable” Lam. *Instabilis* Mor. NC. 1. York, with the sense continuing. “Resources. O detestable” Oxon. “Riches and, O detestable” Gold.] blindness of minds and [Col. 0219A] deep darkness of insane greed! Though he could unburden himself⁶ and gain relief from those weights, he instead continues to brood over the fortunes that torment him and continues stubbornly to cling to his punitive hoards. From them comes no generosity toward dependants, no distribution to the needy [Note: [Col. 0219B] *Participatio*, *portio* Lam. York. Ben. M. A.]; and they call “their own money” that which, as though it belonged to another, they keep locked up at home with anxious effort, from which they grant nothing to friends, nothing to their children, and finally nothing even to themselves. They possess it solely so that another may not be permitted to possess it. And, oh, how great the discrepancy in names! They call “goods” those things of which they make no use except for evil purposes.

[Note: [Col. 0219B]

**XIII.—He is compelled to fear just as much.** Cicero, in Book I of *On Duties*: [Col. 0219C] “For those who wish to be feared must themselves fear the very people by whom they are feared.” The same author, in *On Friendship*: “For who loves either the man whom he fears, or the man by whom he believes himself to be feared?” Seneca, *On Clemency*, Book I, ch. 9: “For he must necessarily fear as much as he has wished to be feared.” The same author, Letter 105: “Add now that he who is feared is himself afraid.” The same author, *On Benefits*, Book IV, ch. 19: “Nor does anyone love those whom he fears.” For, as the same author says in Letter 47, “love cannot be mingled with fear.” Seneca, *Oedipus*: “The savage man who rules two scepters with imperious power fears those who fear him.” The same author, *Agamemnon*: “They desire to be feared, and fear being feared.” There is an elegant dialogue between Nero and Seneca in the same author’s *Octavia*. Nero says: “The sword protects the prince.” Seneca replies: “Loyalty does so better.” Nero retorts: “Caesar ought to be feared.” Seneca answers: “But he ought still more to be loved.” Quite rightly. For Velleius Paterculus records that Caesar—whom Dio Cassius, Books XXXVIII and XLII, writes was mild by nature, exceptionally gentle, and by no means prone to anger—as well as Augustus, who, as the same Dio testifies in Book XLVII, had been so instructed by his father—[Col. 0219D] Velleius records, I say, that when Pansa and Hirtius advised Caesar to retain by arms the supremacy he had acquired by arms, he replied that he preferred to be loved rather than feared. In this he was plainly unlike Maximinus, who, according to Julius Capitolinus, was persuaded that imperial power could not be retained without cruelty. For Symmachus, Book X, Letter 54, or in the *Report to the Emperors*, wrote that to be loved, honored, and cherished is greater than imperial power. Sidonius, Book II, Letter 3, praises Theodoric, king of the Goths, and places among his chief commendations: “I shall say what I think: he fears being feared.” Yet sometimes fear is a sign of love, and Martial says in Book X, Epigram 59: “Fear is an imperious thing.” Vulcacius Gallicanus says of Avidius Cassius: “He deserved to be feared because he did not fear.” Lucan had said this very thing in Book V: “Not fearing, he deserved to be feared.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XV, notes that the emperor Julian was loved most ardently while he was feared; and in Book XXVII, that Praetextatus, prefect of the city, did not lose the citizens’ love even while he was feared, because, as Mamertinus says, [Col. 0220B] “the greatest fear was joined to the greatest love.” By contrast, Flavius Vopiscus laments the unhappy condition of the emperor Aurelian, who, although an excellent man, was indeed feared but was not loved. Subjects are sometimes insolent and defiant, for, as Xenophon says in Book V of the *Education of Cyrus*, fear and law are sufficient to restrain affection. Sometimes princes [Col. 0220C] have so little love for their subjects that they do not care to be loved by them, as Seneca testifies concerning Alexander the Great in *On Benefits*, Book I, ch. 15, saying that he regarded it as the highest good to be an object of terror to all mortals. Certainly it is just for peoples to obey their princes and fear them. Otherwise the state collapses. Yet princes ought to strive with every effort to desire to be loved more than feared, as the emperor Titus did, for which reason he was called “the Delight of the Human Race.” In this way they will render themselves safe from plots and conspiracies, and free themselves from fear. For what many have handed down is true: the man whom many fear must necessarily fear many. As Seneca says in Letter 105, no one can be both terrifying and secure.

**His flank guarded.** From this arose, during the decline of the Roman Empire, the rank of the Protectors, who were so called because they protected the emperor’s flank. The emperors Honorius and Theodosius, law 9 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Domestics and Protectors*: “We do not permit the most devoted Protectors—who, on entering armed military service, undertake responsibility not only for the defense of their own persons but also for the protection of our flank, [Col. 0220D] whence they have also received the name ‘Protectors’—to remain without distinction.”

**He smiles in order to rage.** Below, in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 130: “Here the devil flatters in order to deceive, smiles in order to harm, entices in order to kill.” Ruricius, Book II, Letter XII: “He flatters in order to capture, serves in order to hold, entices in order to kill.”

**Honors.** I am surprised that the author of the edition called Graevius’s, Pamelius, Rigaltius, and the English editors preferred to write “goods.” For all the old editions and all the ancient copies I have used have “honors” or “honor.” In one Royal manuscript, however, which once belonged to the monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai, “goods” has been written erroneously.]

XIII. Or do you perhaps suppose that those men are safe—at least those who, amid the insignia of honors and abundant resources, shine with the splendor of a royal court and are surrounded by the protection of armed guards keeping watch? Their fear is greater than that of others. [Col. 0219B] A man is compelled to fear just as much as he is feared. Lofty rank exacts punishment from the more powerful man as well, although he may be enclosed by a band of attendants [Note: [Col. 0219B] *Septum* Bod. 3.] and may protect his enclosed [Col. 0220A] and guarded flank with a numerous escort. To the same degree that his power does not permit his subjects to be secure, he too must necessarily be insecure. His power terrifies, before anyone else, the very men whom it makes [Note: [Col. 0219B] “Which it makes” Aod. 3.] terrifying. It smiles in order to rage, flatters in order to deceive, entices in order to kill, exalts [Note: [Col. 0220B] “Deceive, exalts” Pem. Voss. 2.] in order to cast down. By a kind of interest charged upon wrongdoing, the larger the principal sum of rank and honors has been, the greater is the interest exacted in punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0220D]

**XIV.—And perpetual.** These words are absent from twelve of the best and most ancient copies. They do, however, occur in seven. If the respective numbers had to be considered, they should be deleted. They appear, however, to have originated in a gloss.

**Established.** We have restored this reading, following the authority of the best manuscripts and the old editions, in place of *fundetur* (“may be established”), which [Col. 0221C] Rigaltius printed. Yet that reading too is found in certain ancient manuscripts.

**A gratuitous gift from God.** Morel says that because some did not understand this sentence, they inserted other words, and so arranged for it to be printed: “A gratuitous gift from God is received with a religious mind and is easy.” He is referring to Erasmus’s edition.

**Reality.** So reads the Séguier manuscript and other ancient copies, [Col. 0221D] including the one used by Florus. In its place Rigaltius was the first of all to put “firmness,” from, I think, the manuscript of Nicolas Le Fèvre that I mentioned above. I am surprised, however, that this reading, which Rigaltius himself says he considers utterly false, was nevertheless placed by him in Cyprian’s text. The English editors and Reinhart followed Rigaltius’s edition.

**Day gives light.** These words occur in all editions before that of Rigaltius and in most manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript and the one used by Florus, as well as those seen by the English editors. Yet they too omitted the words from their edition. Lombert also omitted them from his translation for no reason other than that they did not occur in Rigaltius’s edition. Reinhart printed, “day illuminates.”]

XIV. There is, then, one serene and faithful tranquility, one solid, firm, and perpetual security: if a person, withdrawn from the storms of this restless world and established in the anchorage of the harbor of salvation, should raise his eyes from earth to heaven [Note: [Col. 0220B] “Raises his eyes” Voss. 2.], and, admitted to the gift of the Lord and already close to his God in mind, should glory that whatever among others appears lofty and great in human affairs lies beneath his own conscience. One who is greater than the world can no longer crave or desire anything from the world. How stable, how unshaken a protection [Col. 0221A] it is; what a heavenly defense, rich in everlasting blessings [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Rich in blessings” Goul. Morel.], to be released from the snares of the entangling world and, cleansed from earthly dross, to enter the light of eternal immortality! Let him see [Note: [Col. 0221C] *Videre* Mor. *Videri* Lam.] what insidious destruction wrought by the enemy who formerly assailed us raged against us. We are compelled to love all the more what we shall become, since we are permitted both to know and to condemn what we once were. Nor is there need for money, canvassing, or force to attain this, so that the highest dignity or power of man may be acquired through laborious exertion [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Force” Lin.]; rather, it is a gratuitous [Note: [Col. 0221C] “And gratuitous” Voss. 2. “The gift is received with a religious mind” Voss.] and readily obtained gift from God [Note: [Col. 0221C] “It is easy. Spontaneously” Lam. York.]. As the sun radiates of its own accord, day gives light, the spring supplies water, and the rain moistens, so the heavenly Spirit pours himself into us. After the soul, gazing toward heaven, has recognized its author, it rises higher than the sun [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Higher than the ground” Oxon.] and more exalted than all this earthly power, and begins to be what it believes itself to be.

[Col. 0221B] XV. You only—whom the heavenly army has now marked out for the spiritual camp—maintain discipline incorrupt and sober through religious virtues. Let either prayer or reading be continual for you: now speak with God, now let God speak with you; let him instruct you by his precepts, let him direct you. No one will make poor the man whom he has made rich [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Whom he has made rich in his commandments” Pem. Voss. 2. Fab.]; there can now be no want for one whose breast the nourishment of heaven has once satisfied [Note: [Col. 0221C] “When once his breast” Ar. Pem.]. Coffered ceilings adorned with gold and homes clad with veneers [Col. 0222A] of precious marble will now seem sordid to you, once you know that you yourself must be cultivated more, that you yourself must rather be adorned, and that this is the more precious house for you—the house in which the Lord has taken his seat as in a temple, and in which the Holy Spirit has begun to dwell. Let us paint this house with the colors of innocence; let us illuminate it [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Let us illuminate” Pam. Rig.] with the light of righteousness. This house will never collapse into ruin through the aging of antiquity, nor will it be disfigured when the pigment of its wall or its gold [Note: [Col. 0222C] “The pigment of the wall with gold” Lam. York. Lin. NC. 1.] grows old and fades. Whatever is artificially embellished is perishable, and things that lack the reality [Note: [Col. 0222C] “For their possessors” Pem. Lam. Bod. 3.] of permanent possession provide their owners with no stable confidence. This house remains [Note: [Col. 0222C] “Firmness. It remains” Voss. 3.] with its adornment perpetually fresh, its honor unimpaired, and its splendor enduring. It cannot be effaced or extinguished; when the body returns,⁷ it can only be fashioned into something better.

[Note: [Col. 0221D]

**XVI.—Now there is leisure from business and repose.** I think those people are mistaken who have inferred from these words and from those immediately following that Cyprian was still attending the forum at the time when he wrote this letter. For since it is established that the letter was written after Cyprian embraced the faith of Christ, it is not probable that, when he wrote it, he was attending the forum against which he declaims so forcefully. Add [Col. 0222C] that Pontius says in his *Life* that Cyprian immediately received the presbyterate and the episcopate. Finally, it is nowhere found that he was a senator and attended the forum.

**The hour of the banquet.** Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*: “If the purpose of the banquet is honorable, judge the remainder of its order by its conformity to the service of religion. It admits nothing base, nothing immodest. One does not recline at table before first tasting prayer to God. Prayer likewise concludes the banquet.” Optatus, Book VII: “Let every discourse in the Church begin with the name [Col. 0222D] of God and end with the name of that same God.” Jerome, in the letter *On Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*: “Meanwhile, let some reader’s voice resound at the table and, amid the Psalms, with sweet modulation in your ear, etc.” The same author, in the letter to Marcella inviting her to move to Bethlehem: “Our Ambrose relates that in Origen’s presence he never took food without a reading, and never went to sleep unless one of the brothers’ voice was sounding forth the sacred writings. He did this by day and night, so that reading followed prayer and prayer followed reading.” This Ambrose, who was Origen’s friend, is splendidly mentioned, as I may also note in passing, by Eusebius, Book IV, ch. 18. Again Jerome, in the letter to Eustochium concerning the little gifts received from her, says: “You must always eat in such a way that both prayer and reading follow the meal.” Likewise, in the book *Against Vigilantius*: “He philosophizes among the drinking bowls, and while licking his lips over pastries is soothed by the chanting of Psalms.” See what our most learned and excellent friend Dom Bernard de Montfaucon has noted on this subject from Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius of Caesarea in his notes on Philo’s book *On the Contemplative Life*, p. 129.

[Col. 0223B] **Sweetness.** Aulus Gellius, Book XIX, ch. 9: “And he taught exercises in that language which possessed many pleasures but none of the sweetness of Venus and the Muse.” Saint Jerome—or some other author—in the letter to a sick friend: “For the benefit of brotherly consolation is undoubtedly a part of the greatest remedies, and the sustaining sweetness of consoling words has introduced relief to weary minds.” Boethius, Book II of *The Consolation of Philosophy*: “She had now finished her song, while the sweetness of the music held me fixed in astonishment, eager to hear, with my ears still straining.” Sidonius, Book V, Letter XVII: “When the observance of the vigils was completed—which monks and clerics singing psalms had celebrated together with alternating sweetness—we withdrew, each in a different direction.” Two hundred years ago a certain Brother Berthold of the Order of Preachers used the word *mulcebritas* (“soothing sweetness”) in a little work entitled *The Clock of Devotion*. Among the witticisms of André Arnaud [Col. 0223C] appears the following couplet by an unknown author:

> Those whom the dreadful serpent fed with sorrowful sweetness,  
> The wondrous blood of Christ washed with sweetness.

]

XVI. So much for now, in brief, my dearest Donatus. [Col. 0222B] For although saving instruction delights your ready patience born of goodness [Note: [Col. 0222C] “If receptive—the patience of goodness” Voss. 2.], your steadfast mind [Note: [Col. 0222C] “A mind steadfast in God” Ar. Pem. Lin.], and your secure faith, and nothing is so pleasing to your ears as that which is pleasing in God [Note: [Col. 0222C] “In the Lord” Lin. “In God” Oxon.], nevertheless, since we are together and shall converse more often, we must set limits upon what is to be said [Note: [Col. 0222C] “In speaking” Fab. “In God” Spir. Rem. Man. Morel. Absent from Rig. and Pamel.] [Note: [Col. 0222C] “Shall speak” Lin. Voss. 2. York. Nearly all the printed editions.]. And since there is now leisure from business and a time of repose, let us happily spend whatever remains of this day as the sun now sinks toward evening [Note: [Col. 0222C] “As the sun is sinking” Voss.], and let not even the hour of the banquet be without heavenly grace. Let the sober banquet resound with psalms [Note: [Col. 0222C] “A psalm” Voss.] [Col. 0223A]; and since your memory is retentive and your voice melodious, undertake this office as usual [Note: [Col. 0223A] “Rather, from your mouth” Morel. “Rather, for” Fab.]. You will nourish those dearest to you all the more if we have a spiritual hearing [Note: [Col. 0223A] “You will nourish them: let there be” Lam. York. Bod. Lin. NC. 1.] and religious sweetness entice our ears.

[Note: [Col. 0223C]

**LETTER II.—** We had two ancient copies of this letter, one from our own library and the other from the city of Grenoble. The English editors had one from the Bodleian Library. Guillaume Morel, who first published the letter, noted that its title stated that it was written by Celerinus to Lucian—doubtless because, in the ancient manuscript from which he transcribed it, it followed, as it does in one of my own ancient Grenoble manuscripts and in Vatican manuscript 199, after Lucian’s letter to Celerinus. Pamelius, however, who saw that it had not been written by a single individual but by several, and that it was addressed not to Lucian alone—who was not a presbyter—but composed for several presbyters, did not hesitate to alter this title, particularly since the similarity of the letters could have caused someone mistakenly to substitute “of Celerinus” for what had been “of the Roman clergy.” And because this emendation of Pamelius [Col. 0223D] is sound, the later editions followed it. Thus, in my ancient manuscript one reads: “Here begins the letter written in reply to Cyprian by the Roman clergy.” That is somewhat better than the reading in Morel’s edition. In the Grenoble manuscript, however, it is written: “The reply of Celerinus to Lucian concerning a pastor’s care and resistance to idolatry.” I do not know why the English editors relegated the heading of this letter to the margin. For the reader should have been informed at first glance by whom and to whom the letter was written. The same editors refute Rigaltius, who had written that the word *clerus* (“clergy”) was wrongly extended to designate ecclesiastical persons and men admitted to sacred orders. Rigaltius’s extremely lengthy observation is certainly a genuine paralogism, in which nothing sound and nothing true has been written. Tertullian, in the book *Exhortation to Chastity*: “The authority of the Church established the distinction between the order and the laity.” See the *Minor Works* of Pierre de Marca, p. 72, [Col. 0224B] where he discusses the distinction between clerics and laity according to divine law.]

## LETTER II

*(Pamelius, III; Rigaltius, Baluze, Paris, II; Oxford, Leipzig, VIII.)*

### THE ROMAN CLERGY TO THE CARTHAGINIAN CLERGY, CONCERNING THE WITHDRAWAL OF SAINT CYPRIAN

**ARGUMENT.—** The Roman clergy had learned from Crementius the subdeacon that Cyprian had withdrawn during the persecution. Therefore, in accordance with their zeal for the faith, they admonish the Carthaginian clergy concerning their duty [Col. 0224A] and instruct them what should be done about the lapsed while their bishop is absent.

[Note: [Col. 0224B]

**I.—Blessed.** In this passage “Blessed” is not a proper name, as Sirmond observed in his notes on Sidonius, but an epithet with which many writers adorned Christian men. To the examples supplied by that most learned man I add that Tertullian, in the book *On Modesty*, calls Zephyrinus “the blessed pope.”

**Pope.** My ancient manuscript has *Papatem*. So too in the manuscripts cited in the English edition and in Morel’s annotations. Latinus Latinius likewise read it so in his ancient manuscripts. See Letters XVI and XL.

**Crementius.** So reads my manuscript and Morel’s edition. I also find him named in this way in most ancient manuscripts. I think this is the true reading. For the martyr Crementius is also mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0224C] **Because.** These two words, which were absent from Rigaltius’s edition, we have restored because they occur in the editions of Morel and Pamelius and in one excellent manuscript of mine. Rigaltius had no ancient copy of this letter whose authority he could use to alter this reading. Latinius thought that the word “that” should be deleted.

**A person of distinction.** That is, someone to whom reverence is owed, as Quintilian says in Book VI, ch. 1; for this reason King Childebert calls such a person “a person of greater honor” in a constitution published by Sirmond. In ch. 2 of King Pepin’s Capitulary of Metz: “But concerning ecclesiastics who have committed the aforesaid crimes, if he should be a person of good standing”—that is, distinguished, as is clear from what follows. Philip, bishop of Fermo and legate of the Apostolic See, used “an AUTHENTIC person” to mean “a DISTINGUISHED person” in ch. 26 of the council that he celebrated at Buda in the year 1279. See vol. IV of the *Capitularies*, p. 1030, at the end.

**We who appear to have been placed in authority.** This is plainly because, after the death of the Roman bishop, responsibility for that church rested upon the clergy [Col. 0224D] of the city. No one should, with Baronius, Binius, or Papebroch, apply these words to the prerogative of that Church, to which, when the see is vacant, the care of all the churches allegedly belongs, so that the Roman clerics, as ministers of Peter’s Church, had been entrusted with the care of the universal flock. For even in our own times, although it is established that the authority and power of the Apostolic See have been greatly developed and enlarged, the cardinals—who succeeded the city’s clerics and in whose hands rests the government of the Roman Church while the see is vacant—nevertheless extend their care and concern in no way to other churches. Guillaume de Montlauzun also testifies to this in the chapter *Ubi majus*, *On Election*, in the *Sext*. Likewise Álvaro Pelayo, Book I of *The Lament of the Church*, ch. 20, where he expressly writes that while the papacy is vacant no one succeeds to the pope’s jurisdiction—not even the college of cardinals—except in matters of the least importance. See also Jacobazzi, Book IV, art. 3, and Augustine of Ancona, *On Ecclesiastical Power*, question III, art. 8. [Col. 0225B] It is certainly evident from the context of the letter that the Roman clergy were then concerned with governing no church other than their own, in accordance with the practice accepted everywhere that a church deprived of its bishop should be governed by the clergy of the vacant church. This is also acknowledged by Naclantus, bishop of Clugium, in his treatise *On the Power of the Pope and the Council*. It is also clear from the fact that, after the death of Pope Martin [Col. 0225C] I, because the episcopate was vacant for thirty-five days, the presbyters presided over the Roman Church, as is read in the pontifical records—that is, those members of the Roman presbyterate who held precedence over the others: the archdeacon, archpriest, and primicerius, as a letter of that same Martin to Eliterus teaches. For these men represented the pontiff’s office. Here I shall note in passing that it appears to have been due to a copyist’s error that the archdeacon is there named before the archpriest—unless the discipline of the Roman Church had already declined so far at that time that the archdeacon was preferred to the archpriest. For it is established from the *Book of the Daily Office of the Pontiffs* that the archpriest was named first, before the archdeacon, in a letter written by the Roman clergy to the exarch concerning the pontiff’s death.

**In the pastor’s stead.** The ancient manuscripts have “of the pastors.” We nevertheless wished to change nothing, because it is established that this letter was written by the Roman clergy to Cyprian at a time when the Roman Church had no pastor. David Blondel, in order to show that presbyters are [Col. 0225D] equal to bishops and are likewise vicars of Christ, added at this point, after the word “pastor,” the words “namely, of Christ.” But he was certainly gravely mistaken. For here the word “pastor” plainly means the Roman bishop. At that time, after Fabian’s death, the Roman clergy governed the Church in the pastor’s stead until another bishop should be appointed in Fabian’s place.

**Our predecessors.** These words, which possess a certain obscurity, were applied by the English editors to the priests of the Jews, because it is certain that they were written against them by Ezekiel.

**Because we did not seek what was lost.** This passage of Ezekiel, which is severely mutilated here, occurs in much more complete form in Letter LIV. Saint Jerome, in explaining these words and those that follow, applied them to the pride of bishops, whom he sharply censures. These are his words: “This pertains particularly,” he says, “to the arrogance of bishops—namely, those who dishonor the dignity of their title by their deeds and assume pride in place of humility, so that they think they have received an honor, not a burden; and whenever they see men in the Church who are exceedingly powerful and possess [Col. 0226B] the word of God, they appear to oppress them.” Far removed from these men was the humble manner of conduct shared by Valerius and Augustine, which was free from the love of personal praise.

**Their milk.** In one ancient manuscript one reads *lactem*. The Glosses of Philoxenus: “*Lactem*, γάλα (*gala*, ‘milk’).” Plautus, *The Two Bacchises*: “Which have neither milk nor any wool.” Similarly, in Apuleius, Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, Nonius Marcellus [Col. 0226C] notes that the ancients used *lacte* in the nominative.

**The wolf coming.** Jerome, in the same place: “Hirelings consider only the profit from the flocks, and flee when they see the wolf coming; through their negligence the Lord’s flock is devoured by the beasts of the field.”

**By the course he took.** An obscure passage. Latinius noted that one ancient manuscript reads *gessit* (“he did”), and another *gestum* (“the deed”). But my manuscript and Morel’s edition read *cessit*. Rigaltius refers these words to the time when, after Christ had been seized by the Jews, Peter did not strictly flee but withdrew—that is, departed or went away. For, as the Gospel says, he did follow Christ, but at a great distance, which gave the appearance of flight; and thus the Gospel says that all the disciples abandoned Christ and fled. But, with the pardon of Rigaltius and of the English editors who adopted his observation, the meaning of this passage is: we know that Christ’s command, “Feed my sheep,” was fulfilled in the deed itself by the course Peter took—that is, by the outcome he met. For the Roman clergy contrast Christ and the apostles with the pastors of the Jews; they do not reproach Peter [Col. 0226D] for fleeing during Christ’s Passion, but praise his diligence in feeding the sheep, just as Christ had commanded him after the Resurrection.

**And the other disciples.** Rigaltius adds that this letter of the Roman clergy places a still heavier burden upon Peter because it says, “and the other disciples acted similarly,” as though they had followed Peter’s example. But this observation is false, as I have already said. Nor do the Roman clergy, by the words “and the other disciples acted similarly,” indicate that the apostles followed Peter as he fled, but rather that, after his example, they applied the greatest diligence in feeding the sheep. Nothing could be more foreign to the purpose of the Roman clergy than to derive from Peter and the other disciples an example of cowardice in feeding the sheep. Moreover, Rigaltius’s reasoning limps: Peter fled; the other disciples also fled; therefore they fled after Peter’s example, since he gave them an example of flight. For Matthew and Mark say that all the disciples abandoned Christ and fled, without any mention of Peter.]

I. We learned from Crementius the subdeacon, who came to us from you, that the blessed Pope Cyprian has withdrawn for a definite reason. He certainly acted rightly, because he is a person of distinction. And with a contest impending—which God has permitted in the world for the purpose of struggling with the adversary together with his servants [Note: [Col. 0224A] “For the purpose of struggling, together with” Vat. 1.]—God also wills to make this contest manifest to angels and human beings, so that the victor may be crowned, while the defeated man will have brought upon himself [Note: [Col. 0224A] “Will have borne” Oxon.] the sentence that has been revealed to us.

And since it falls upon us, who appear [Col. 0225A] to have been placed in authority and to guard the flock in the pastor’s stead, if we are found negligent, we shall be told what was also said to our predecessors, who were such negligent rulers: that we did not seek what was lost, did not correct the wandering, did not bind up the lame [Note: [Col. 0225B] “We gathered” Vat. 1.], and were consuming their milk and clothing ourselves in their wool (Ezek. 34:3–4). Finally, the Lord himself, fulfilling what had been written in the Law and the Prophets, teaches when he says [Note: [Col. 0225B] “Said in the Prophets” Vat. 1.]: “I am the good shepherd, who lays down my life for my sheep. But the hireling, to whom the sheep do not belong, when he sees the wolf coming, abandons them and flees [Note: [Col. 0225B] “Abandoning them, he flees” Vat. 2.], and the wolf scatters them” (John 10:11–12). And he also says to Simon [Note: [Col. 0225B] “He says to Simon” Vat. 1.]: “Do you love me?” He answered, “I love you.” He said to him: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). We know that this command [Col. 0225B] was fulfilled in the deed itself by the course he took, and the other disciples acted similarly.

[Col. 0226A] [Note: [Col. 0226D]

**II.—Going up:** namely, to the Capitol, there to sacrifice to the gods of the gentiles. But we shall discuss this matter at greater length in connection with Letter LV.

[Col. 0227C] **The Church:** the Roman Church, which it calls strong because it remained firm and immovable amid the harshest persecutions. Yet even in this Church there was no lack of lapsed persons, since the clergy preserved their case undecided until the election of a bishop. But these were fewer in number than at Carthage.]

## II

We therefore do not wish you, most beloved brothers, to be found as hirelings [Note: [Col. 0225B] “to find,” *Imp.*], but as good shepherds, since you know that no slight danger then threatens if you have not exhorted our brothers to stand [Note: [Col. 0225B] “your brothers to stand,” *Vat. 1, Oxon.*] immovable in the faith, lest the brotherhood be utterly uprooted by those rushing headlong [Note: [Col. 0226B] “lest one going headlong,” *Oxon.*] into idolatry. Nor do we exhort you to this by words alone; rather, you will be able to learn from many who come from us to you that, with God’s help, we have done and continue to do all these things with every solicitude and at secular peril, keeping before our eyes the fear of God and everlasting punishments more than [Note: [Col. 0226B] “keeping before our eyes—more than,” *Vat. 2.*] the fear of men and a brief injury. We do not abandon the brotherhood, but exhort them to stand in the faith and to be ready to go [Note: [Col. 0226B] “that they ought to be ready to go,” *Oxon.*] with the Lord. Indeed, we have also called back those who were going up [Col. 0226B] to that [Note: [Col. 0226B] “attending to that,” *printed editions*] which they were being compelled to do.

The Church [Col. 0227A] stands [Note: [Col. 0227B] “That Church is strong in faith,” *printed editions*] in the faith, although some, compelled by the terror itself—whether because they were distinguished persons or because, having been arrested, they were afraid through fear of men [Note: [Col. 0227B] “they return,” *Imp.*; “they fell,” *Oxon.*]. Though separated from us, we have not abandoned them, but have exhorted them and continue to exhort them to do penance, so that they may perhaps be able to receive pardon from him who is able to grant it, lest, if they are abandoned [8] by us, they become worse.

> **[Note: [Col. 0227C]**
>
> **III.—*Clinomeni*.** My manuscript has *domeni*; the Grenoble manuscript, *chlidomeni*; Morel printed *clydomeni*; Latinius and Rigaltius, *clinomeni*. The English edition later followed; rejecting the other readings without any authority from the ancient manuscripts, and proceeding solely from a conjecture drawn from Pope Cornelius’s letter to Fabius, bishop of Antioch—which survives in Greek in Eusebius—it printed *thlibomeni*. Although that emendation may appear sound, it ought not to have been transferred into the text without greater authority, for the other readings may also be sound.
>
> Moreover, [Col. 0227D] the emendation which the English appear to have taken from the annotations of Henri de Valois on Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* belongs neither to Valois nor to the English, but to the most illustrious François Bosquet, who first proposed it in 1633, in the first book of his *Histories of the Gallican Church*. Those whom the Greeks call *thlibomenoi* (θλιβόμενοι, “the afflicted”), Rufinus translates as “the needy,” and Baronius as “the wavering,” with a very different meaning. See the first *Cyprianic Dissertation* of the most distinguished Henry Dodwell. (The Leipzig edition follows Dodwell’s conjecture in *Cyprianic Dissertation* I.7, reading *Clydonizomeni*.)
>
> **Catecumini.** We have chosen to write it thus, not only because we found it so written in all the ancient manuscripts, but especially on the authority of Commodian, who leaves us no room to doubt that in ancient times this word was spelled in this way. Indeed, in an old glossary of the royal library I read: “CATECUMNUS: one instructed, a hearer.” Likewise, in an old glossary of my own: “CATECUMENUS: one instructed or a hearer, because he is still hearing the doctrine of the faith but has not yet received Baptism.” [Col. 0228C] In the Corbie and Fux manuscripts, moreover, where this class of persons is discussed, the reading is *Caticuminos*, which is the same thing. It is well known that the letters *i* and *e* were often interchanged by the ancients.
>
> Holstenius notes, in his annotations on the *Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, that *cathecumini* is written in the ancient Cassinese manuscripts and in Mombritius; he believes that words of this kind were pronounced in this manner in that age. Jerome, in the *Letter to Oceanus* concerning the marriage case: “Let the *cathecumini*, who are candidates for the faith, hear.” Thus, in our edition of Marius Mercator, p. 347, *catecismi* is read for *catechismi*. See Caelius Calcagninus, Book I, Letter IX, and the notes on the *Capitularies*, p. 1250.
>
> **Bodies of the martyrs.** Just as human dispositions differ, so do opinions. Rigaltius interpreted this passage as concerning only the duty of burying the martyrs. I, however, used it to demonstrate [Col. 0228D] that those who contend that the ancient Christians took no care for the relics of holy persons are gravely mistaken. I demonstrated this in the address which I delivered publicly at Paris when, in the Royal College, I was expounding the title of the *Decretals* concerning Relics and the Veneration of Saints. For so great at that time was the care taken in burying holy persons that they omitted nothing capable of demonstrating their remembrance of and veneration for them. Thus Tertullian testifies in the *Apologeticum* that the Christians expended more costly and precious merchandise in burying Christians than the pagans did in burning incense to their gods. From this it may seemingly be inferred that they also embalmed their bodies with Arabian spices, which are known to have been employed in the burial of bodies.
>
> Indeed, Pliny, Book XII, chapter 18, writes that Nero burned more cinnamon at Poppaea’s funeral than Arabia produces in one year. See Baronius in the *Annotations on the Roman Martyrology*, under August 4.
>
> **Bassianus.** I agree with Pamelius, who thinks that he belonged to the Roman clergy. He is also mentioned [Col. 0229B] in Letter XXII, which is Lucian’s letter to Celerinus, then residing at Rome.]  

## III

You see, therefore, brothers, that you too ought to do this: so that even those who have fallen, correcting their dispositions through your exhortation, may confess if they are arrested a second time and thus be able to correct their former error. There are also other duties incumbent upon you, which we too have added below: if any who have fallen into this trial begin to be overtaken by illness, repent of what they have done, and desire communion, help must certainly [Col. 0227B] be given to them. Whether they are widows, or *clinomeni* who cannot present themselves, or those who are in prison, or those driven from their homes [Note: [Col. 0228B] “expelled from their homes,” *Vat. 1*], they certainly ought to have persons who minister to them. Catechumens overtaken by illness must not be denied assistance either.

And, what is most important, if the bodies of martyrs or of others are not buried, great danger threatens those upon whom this work is incumbent. Therefore, whichever of you has, on any occasion, accomplished this work, we are certain that he will be reckoned a good [Col. 0228A] servant, so that he who was faithful in the least may be placed over ten cities. May God, who grants all things to those who hope in him, bring it about that all of us may be found engaged in these works.

The brothers who are in chains greet you, as do the presbyters and the whole Church, which itself keeps watch with the greatest solicitude over all who invoke the name of the Lord. We also [Note: [Col. 0228B] “But we too,” *Imo.*] ask that you, in turn, remember us.

Know that Bassianus has reached us. We ask you who possess zeal for God to transmit a copy of this letter to as many as you can when suitable opportunities arise, or to make copies of your own, or send a messenger, so that they may stand strong and immovable in the faith. We wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well.

> **[Note: [Col. 0229B]**
>
> **LETTER III—I. “Good man.”** Fabian, bishop of Rome. Cyprian customarily bestows this epithet upon deceased bishops, as in Letter LXXII upon Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage. Jerome, in his *Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus*, mentions letters written by Origen to Fabian, bishop of the city of Rome; so too does Rufinus in the first book of his *Apologies against Jerome*.
>
> **“Superior.”** Baronius, speaking of Pope Fabian’s death, notes that Cyprian calls him sometimes [Col. 0229D] “colleague” and sometimes “superior,” because, although he was a fellow bishop, in power and in the hierarchical order of the Church he was nevertheless set above the other bishops. Baronius could have confirmed that opinion of his by the authority of the letter of Pope Boniface II to Eulalius, in which the Roman bishop is called “the one superior to whom recourse may be had.” But Baronius knew that this letter was spurious.
>
> It is my duty to note errors committed in interpreting what is found written by Cyprian. Baronius’s observation might have an appearance of truth if Cyprian called only the pope a “superior.” But since it is certain that he commonly calls all bishops “superiors,” Baronius’s position collapses altogether. Thus Cyprian here calls Pope Fabian a superior because he was a bishop and a colleague of Cyprian the bishop. Historical matters must be treated candidly, far removed from every partisan inclination; otherwise confidence in the facts is lost.]  

# LETTER III

*(Erasm., III.21; Pamel., IV; Rig., Baluz., Paris., III; Oxon., Lips., IX.)*

## TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS RESIDING AT ROME

[Col. 0228B]

**SUMMARY.—**This is a personal letter and therefore requires no summary, especially since its contents may be sufficiently inferred from the title itself. The letter of the Roman clergy to which Cyprian replies, however, is missing.

## I

Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome, his brothers: greetings.

When the report of the death [Col. 0229A] of that good man, my colleague, was still uncertain among us, dearest brothers, and doubtful opinion remained wavering, I received the letter you sent me through Crementius [Note: [Col. 0229B] “Clementius,” *Oxon.*], the subdeacon, by which I was most fully informed of his glorious departure. I rejoiced greatly that, in keeping with the integrity of his administration, his end too proved honorable.

In this matter I also congratulate you most warmly because you honor his memory with so renowned and illustrious a testimony. Through you we have learned what was glorious for you also in your remembrance of your superior, and what furnished us as well with an example of faith and courage. For just as [Note: [Col. 0229B] “In proportion as,” *Lam., Ebor., NC. 1*] the fall of a superior is a ruinous thing, leading those who follow him into a fall, so, conversely, it is useful and salutary when a bishop, through steadfastness of faith, offers himself to the brothers as one to be imitated.

> **[Col. 0229B] [Note: [Col. 0229D]**
>
> **II.—“Nor who wrote it.”** We have retained the reading favored by the old editions and confirmed by all the ancient manuscripts. [Col. 0230B] Manutius was the first to print “nor those who wrote it.” That reading is unsound, for a letter written in the name of all was written by one person, as at the end of Letter XVI: “Lucian wrote this”; this is also shown by Letter XXII, Cyprian’s letter to the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome. Thus in councils one person spoke for all, as we observed in the dissertation on the Council of Telepte.
>
> **“I have sent the letter back.”** See what is said about this matter below, in connection with Letter XX.
>
> **“Handwriting and signature.”** Thus the old manuscripts and editions. Manutius’s edition reads, “the handwriting and signature” in the nominative. [Col. 0230D] The later editions followed that authority, and Gronovius, chapter 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, says that the reading was improperly changed.
>
> **“Whether it is yours.”** In the Fux manuscript it is written, “whether it is from your hand.” I think this arose from a gloss, since it is certain, as I said just now, that letters were customarily written by one person. In the Council of Chalcedon, p. 1091 of our recension, we read, “whose hand it is.” See Rusticus’s annotation there.]  

## II

I have also read another letter [Note: [Col. 0230B] “I have also read a letter,” *Oxon.*] in which neither who wrote it nor to whom it was written is expressly stated. And because in that letter its handwriting, its meaning, and even the sheets themselves led me to suspect that something might have been either removed from or altered in the truth, I have sent the same original letter back to you, so that you may ascertain whether it is the one you gave to Crementius the subdeacon to deliver.

For it is an exceedingly serious matter if the truth of a clerical letter has been corrupted by some falsehood and fraud. Therefore, so that we may know [9] this, ascertain whether the handwriting and signature are yours, and write back to us what the truth is. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well.

> **[Note: [Col. 0230D]**
>
> **LETTER IV.—**The first edition of this letter came from the press of Manutius. Ancient copies of it are exceedingly rare. I possessed five: one from my own library; another formerly belonging to the Collège de Foix; a third from the monastery of Saint-Denis at Reims; a fourth from the monastery of Mont-Saint-Éloi; and a fifth from the city of Grenoble.]  

# LETTER IV

*(Pamel., V; Rig., Baluz., Paris., IV; Oxon., Lips., V.)*

## TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS

[Col. 0230A]

**SUMMARY.—**Saint Cyprian, now in retirement, exhorts his clergy to discharge his duties in his place and to ensure that neither those confined in prison nor the other poor lack anything. He then urges them to keep the people calm, lest, if they crowd together to visit the martyrs in prison, this should ultimately be forbidden them.

> **[Note: [Col. 0230D]**
>
> **I.—“Small sum.”** Previously the reading was “sum.” We have chosen to follow the authority of the old manuscripts. The Saint-Denis manuscript nevertheless has “sum.”
>
> **[Col. 0231C] “Not in crowds.”** Holstenius used this passage in his *Notes on the Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity* to prove that Christian believers generally approached the prisons cautiously and timidly, and almost one at a time, lest they destroy themselves or arouse hostility among the persecutors by streaming there in bands. In Book I of Angelo Poliziano’s *Letters* there survives a letter of Pomponius Laetus to Poliziano which reads: “When I consider the loftiness of your genius, I cannot but wonder why our people do not fly to you in chattering flocks and troops.”
>
> **[Col. 0231D] “Lose everything.”** Guillaume Durand, bishop of Mende, in Book II, chapter 7, of *The Manner of Celebrating a General Council*: “There is a common proverb: ‘He who wants everything loses everything.’ The Roman Church claims everything for itself. Hence there is reason to fear that it may lose everything.” See our addition to chapter 1 of Book I of *The Concord of Priesthood and Empire*.
>
> **“They greet you.”** In the Saint-Éloi manuscript the reading is: “Victor the deacon and the brothers who are with him greet you.” In the Grenoble manuscript: “Victor greets you, and those who are with me send greetings.”]  

## I

Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons, his dearest brothers: greetings.

By God’s grace I greet you in good health, dearest brothers, rejoicing that I have learned that everything also remains unimpaired with respect to your welfare. [Col. 0230B] And since the circumstances of my location do not now permit me to be present, I ask you, in accordance with your faith and religious devotion, to perform there both your own duties and mine, so that nothing may be lacking either in discipline or in diligence.

As for supplying expenses, whether to those who have confessed the Lord with a glorious voice and are confined in prison, or to those poor and needy persons who suffer hardship yet persevere in the Lord, I ask that nothing be lacking. The entire small sum collected there has been distributed among the clergy for cases of this kind, so that a greater number might possess the means to attend to the needs and afflictions of individuals.

## II

I also ask that your resourcefulness and solicitude not fail [Note: [Col. 0230B] “not cease,” although *Morel., Pem., Rig.*] in preserving quiet. For although, in their love, the brothers are eager [Col. 0231A] to assemble and visit the good confessors whom divine favor has already distinguished by glorious beginnings, I nevertheless think that this should be done cautiously, not in crowds or by a multitude assembled together. Otherwise hostility may be aroused by this very conduct, access may be denied, and, while in our insatiability we want everything, we may lose everything.

Consult together, therefore, and take care that this may be done more safely and with moderation [Note: [Col. 0231C] “that this may be fulfilled more safely,” *Vat. 1*]. The presbyters who make the offering there among the confessors should also take turns, each accompanied by one deacon, because both the changing of persons and the rotation of those assembling diminishes hostility.

In all matters we ought to be gentle and humble, as befits servants of God: accommodating ourselves to the times, looking to peace, and caring for the people. I wish you, my dearest and most longed-for brothers [Col. 0231B] [Note: [Col. 0231C] “most longed-for,” *Oxon.*], always to fare well and to remember us. Greet the whole brotherhood. Victor the deacon and those who are with me greet you. Farewell.

> **[Note: [Col. 0231D]**
>
> **LETTER V.—**The English edition notes that few copies of this letter are found. I possessed nine.]  

# LETTER V

*(Erasm., III.20; Pamel., IV; Rig., Baluz., Paris., V; Oxon., Lips., XIV.)*

## TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS

**SUMMARY.—**Its subject is almost the same as that of the preceding letter, except that he also wishes the confessors to be admonished by the clergy concerning their duty: they are to devote themselves to humility and obey the presbyters and deacons. In passing, he also explains the reason for his retirement. This too is among the thirteen letters mentioned below in Letter XV.

> **[Col. 0231C] [Note: [Col. 0231D]**
>
> **I.—“Whom both in faith.”** The Fossés and Chartres manuscripts and the old editions read, “whom in constancy and in the strength of faith.” Manutius changed this and introduced another reading. The reader [Col. 0232C] will judge which is better, for both are sound.
>
> **“Determine.”** Thus the old manuscripts and editions, including Erasmus’s. Manutius’s and Morel’s editions and the Grenoble manuscript have “polish.” Nonius Marcellus: “to polish, to determine.” Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 11: “Others sprinkle filed bronze dust with vinegar.” In the bull of Pope Hadrian I for the monastery of Saint-Martin of Tours: “But if the abbot of that monastery is [Col. 0232D] in no way willing for the matter to be determined between them,” etc. In a similar privilege for the monastery of Saint-Denis in Francia it is written: “But if the abbot of that monastery is in any way willing for it to be declaimed between them.” For this I think “determined” should be written, as in the bull for Saint-Martin. The bull of Pope Gregory V for the same monastery of Saint-Martin reads: “But if the abbot of that monastery is in no way willing to determine a judgment between them.”
>
> **391 “Demanded.”** Namely, demanded for the lion, as below in Letters XIV and XV.]  

## I

Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons, his brothers: greetings.

I had indeed wished, dearest brothers, to greet our entire [Col. 0232A] clergy as safe and unharmed in my letter. But because the hostile tempest which has struck down the greater part of our people has added this further culmination to our sorrows, so that it has also grazed a portion of the clergy with its devastation [Note: [Col. 0231C] “hence also,” *Foss., Vict., Bod. 1*], we pray the Lord that at least you, whom we have learned to stand firm both in faith and courage, may also be greeted as safe hereafter through divine mercy.

Although the circumstances compelled me to hasten and come to you myself—first, because of my eagerness and longing for you, which is the highest of my desires, and then so that we might together discuss what the common good requires concerning the governance [Note: [Col. 0231C] “helm,” *Oxon.*] of the Church, and, after examining it by the counsel of many [10], determine it—nevertheless, it seemed better for the present still to remain in concealment and quiet, out of consideration [Col. 0232B] for other interests pertaining to the peace and salvation of us all. An account of these will be given to you by our dearest brother Tertullus. In keeping with the rest of his care [Note: [Col. 0232C] “sincere care,” *Vat. 2*], which he earnestly [Note: [Col. 0232C] “devoting,” *Oxon.*] bestows upon divine works, he also advised this course: that I should conduct myself cautiously and with restraint, and not rashly expose myself to public view, especially in that place where I had so often [Note: [Col. 0232C] “nor in those places in which so often,” *Foss.*] been demanded and sought.

> **[Note: [Col. 0232D]**
>
> **II.—“In regard to the steadfast.”** That is, those strong in faith, as the Apostle speaks. It is certain that several ancient copies and all editions before Manutius’s, including the Speyer edition, favor this reading. The alternative, “in regard to faith,” also survives in several ancient manuscripts and later editions. I think the first is better. The comparison is between the *fidentes*, that is, the strong, and the *laborantes*, that is, the poor and needy—as Cyprian speaks in Letter IV—those suffering want of sustenance. Cyprian therefore says that it must be feared that those who stood firm in unshaken faith, or were strong, may be brought down by necessity [Col. 0233C] if relief is not given to their poverty.
>
> Cicero, Book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “He who is brave is likewise confident.” Seneca, Letter LXXXV: “He who is brave is without fear.” Cicero, Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Let him advance toward death with a confident spirit.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI: “These were of a quiet and cautious spirit; those were confident, relying on their immense bodies”; and a little later: “whom the Roman now laid low with confidence.” Horace, Book III, Ode 3:
>
> > Youth confident, fearsome in its strength of arm.
>
> [Col. 0233D] Seneca the tragedian, *Hercules Furens*: “Whomever you see to be brave, deny that he is wretched.” Cyprian himself in Letter LII to Antonianus, p. 72: “But the strength of the confident remains immovable, and among those who fear and love the Lord with their whole heart, integrity perseveres steadfast and strong.” The same author, in *On Mortality*, p. 232: “Protection is granted more swiftly to the confident, punishment to the faithless.” In *Against Demetrianus*, p. 221, “certain and confident” occurs in another sense. There the word *fidentes* signifies those who trust in Christ’s promises.
>
> Josephus, in *On the Rule of Reason*, in Erasmus’s translation: “He, therefore, who is wise and brave is master of every passion, since he considers beforehand what has been well considered, and nowhere rejects what has been accepted.” In this same latter sense in which Cyprian employs *fidentes*, Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII, said: “Intending humbly to request peace, they came confidently into the emperor’s presence.”
>
> **“Of the disciples.”** Previously the reading was “of the Apostles.” But because the manuscripts and old editions [Col. 0234C] have “of the disciples,” which is also how it is written in the Gospel according to John, we have restored that reading.]  

## II

Relying, therefore, upon your love and religious devotion, which I know well, by this letter I both exhort and instruct you—whose presence there arouses the least hostility and is not so dangerous—to act in my place in conducting what religious administration requires.

Meanwhile, as far and in whatever way possible, care should be taken for the poor—those, however, who, standing firm in unshaken faith, have not abandoned Christ’s flock. Through your diligence, expenses should be supplied to help them endure deprivation, [Col. 0232C] lest necessity accomplish among those who suffer what the tempest did not accomplish among the steadfast. [Col. 0233A]

More generous care should also be bestowed upon the glorious confessors. Although I know that many of them have been taken in by the goodwill and love of the brothers, nevertheless, if any lack either clothing or funds, they should be supplied with everything necessary, just as I wrote to you some time ago while they were still confined in prison. They must, however, be told by you, instructed, and taught what ecclesiastical discipline requires according to the teaching of the Scriptures: that they ought to be humble, modest, and quiet, so that they may preserve the honor of their name; and that those who were glorious in their confession [Note: [Col. 0233C] “so that those who … were,” *Man., Oxon.*] may also be glorious in conduct. Let them make themselves worthy, so that, pleasing the Lord in all things, they may reach the heavenly crown through the consummation of their praise.

For more remains than appears to have been completed, since [Col. 0233B] it is written: “Praise no man before his death” (Ecclus. XI.30). And again: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Apoc. II.10). The Lord also says: “He who endures unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X.22).

Let them imitate the Lord, who at the very time of his Passion became not prouder but humbler. For it was then that he washed his disciples’ feet, saying: “If I, your teacher and Lord, have washed your feet, you too ought to wash the feet of others. For I have given you an example, so that as I have done, you too may do” [Note: [Col. 0233C] “may do to others,” *Foss., Vict., Man.*] (John XIII.14–15).

Let them likewise follow the instruction of the apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0233C] “Let us follow,” *Man.*], who, after repeated imprisonment, after scourging, after the beasts, persevered in all things gentle and humble; nor, even after the third heaven and paradise, did he arrogantly claim anything for himself, saying: [Col. 0234A] “Nor did we eat bread from any of you without payment, but [Note: [Col. 0233C] “from anyone, but,” *Man.*] worked night and day in labor and weariness, lest we burden any of you” (II Thess. III.8 [printed here as II.8]).

> **[Note: [Col. 0234C]**
>
> **III.—“Illicit unions.”** Below, Letter IV, p. 12: “in a shameful and infamous union.” Likewise Letter LXII, p. 103: “How much wickedness and crime does the shameful and foul sleeping together of two persons confess?” Jerome, in the letter *On Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*: “Finally, I say this: even if such conduct bears no wound of guilt upon the conscience, it nevertheless bears the disgrace of ill repute.” Cassian, *Conference* XXI, chapter 33: “The very desire is culpable, and the habit of sleeping together is swept toward the swiftest [Col. 0234D] excesses of adultery.”
>
> Concerning the women who cohabited with clerics, see Fronton du Duc’s notes on Saint John Chrysostom’s book *Against Those Who Keep Subintroduced Women*; Petavius’s observations on Epiphanius’s treatment of the heresy of the Antidicomarianites; and Henri de Valois’s *Annotations* on Book VII, chapter 30, of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*.]  

## III

I beg you, impress each of these things upon our brothers. And because “he who humbles himself shall be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0234C] “those who humble themselves shall be exalted,” *Bod. 1*] (Luke XIV.11), now is the time for them to fear all the more the adversary who lies in wait. He attacks each of the stronger more fiercely, and, made more savage by the very fact that he has been defeated, endeavors to defeat the victor.

May the Lord grant that I too may soon [Note: [Col. 0234C] “sooner,” *Ver.*] see them again and, by salutary exhortation [Note: [Col. 0234C] “to greet and by exhortation,” *Man.*], compose their minds for the preservation of their glory. For I grieve when I hear that some are running about shamelessly and insolently and giving themselves over to follies or quarrels; that members of Christ, who have already confessed Christ, are being defiled through illicit unions; and that they cannot be governed by [Col. 0234B] deacons or presbyters, but so conduct themselves that the honorable glory of the many good confessors is stained by the corrupt and evil conduct of a few. They ought to fear lest, condemned by the testimony and judgment of the good confessors themselves, they be deprived of their fellowship. For only that confessor [11] is ultimately illustrious and true of whom the Church is not afterward ashamed, but in whom she glories.

> **[Note: [Col. 0234D]**
>
> **IV.—Fortunatus.** This man’s name is absent from the old editions and from most ancient manuscripts. It nevertheless survives in one of my best manuscripts and in the Grenoble manuscript. Manutius’s edition introduced it; Pamelius noted that it was missing from the Affligem manuscript.
>
> **Novatus.** This name too is missing from the Fux manuscript, although this letter was copied there twice.
>
> **“I wish you.”** All these words are absent from the ancient manuscripts and editions and were first published by Manutius. They nevertheless survive in my manuscript and in the Grenoble manuscript.]  

## IV

As for what our fellow presbyters Donatus and Fortunatus, Novatus and Gordius, wrote to me, I could make no reply by myself, since from the beginning of my episcopate I determined to do nothing on my private judgment without your counsel and without the consent of the people. But when, by God’s grace, I come to you, we shall then discuss together what has either been done or must be done, as our mutual honor requires.

I wish you, [Col. 0235A] my dearest and most longed-for brothers, always to fare well and to remember me. Give many greetings from me to the brotherhood that is with you, and admonish them to remember us. Farewell.

# LETTER VI

*(Erasm., I.5; Pamel., VII; Rig., Baluz., Paris., VI; Oxon., Lips., XIII.)*

## TO ROGATIANUS THE PRESBYTER AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS

**SUMMARY.—**He exhorts Rogatianus and the other confessors to observe discipline, lest those who had confessed Christ by their voice should appear to deny him by their deeds. In passing, he also rebukes certain of them who, though made exiles [Col. 0235B] because of the faith, nevertheless did not fear to return to their homeland without authorization. This is what Cyprian says below in Letter XV: that, when necessary, rebuke had not been withheld from the exiles. It is consequently evident that this letter was written during his retirement.

> **[Note: [Col. 0235C]**
>
> **LETTER VI—I.—“To Rogatianus.”** Pamelius judged this Rogatianus to be different from the man to whom Letter LXXXI is addressed, whom certain editions and some old manuscripts call a young man. From that letter he inferred that the Rogatianus to whom the present letter was sent had been perfected by martyrdom by the time the other was written, because Saint Cyprian says that he had prepared lodging in prison for the other confessors, into which he had been cast with Felicissimus, and that he now precedes them. These points do indeed appear to show that Rogatianus was a candidate for martyrdom, but they do not prove that he underwent martyrdom.
>
> [Col. 0235D] **“The glory of the superior.”** Some old manuscripts have “honor.”]  

## I

Cyprian to Rogatianus the presbyter and the other confessors, his brothers: greetings.

I had already sent you a letter some time ago, my dearest and bravest brothers, in which I congratulated your faith and courage with exultant words; and now, first and foremost, my speech embraces nothing other than the frequent and continual proclamation, with joyful spirit, of the glory of your name. For what greater or better object could there be among my prayers than to see Christ’s flock illuminated [Col. 0235C] by the honor of your confession?

Although all the brothers ought to rejoice in this, the bishop has the greater share [Col. 0236A] in the common joy, for the glory of the Church is the glory of its superior. As much as we grieve over those whom the hostile tempest has struck down, so much do we rejoice over you, whom the devil was unable to overcome.

> **[Note: [Col. 0235D]**
>
> **II.—392 “Concerning our life.”** That is, every day we are in danger of losing our life. This is the true and genuine meaning of these words. I therefore cannot agree with Rigaltius, who writes that eternal life is being discussed here. Nor is it any more true that the words from Letter XIII, p. 23, “it concerns the very life of us all,” have that meaning.
>
> In Letter XXVI, p. 36, it is written: “For your sake we are killed all day long,” corresponding to what is read in chapter 8 of the Letter to the Romans: “For your sake we are put to death all day long.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Rusticus*: “Nothing is more laborious than the Christian’s condition, for he risks his life every day.” The same author, in the *Letter to Sunnias and Fretela*, discussing the passage of Psalm CXVIII, “My soul is always in my hands,” says that the meaning is: “Every day I am in danger, [Col. 0236C] and I carry my blood, as it were, in my hands.” Gaius Caesar in Sallust’s *Catiline*: “Our liberty and life are in jeopardy.”
>
> **“To be able to preserve.”** Ovid, Book II of *The Art of Love*:
>
> > It is no less a virtue to guard what has been gained than to seek it.
>
> Julius Caesar, in his address to his legates and centurions [Col. 0236D] in Cassius Dio, Book XXXVIII, says that good things are both acquired and retained by the same arts. Marcus Antonius, in the funeral oration for Caesar in the same Dio, Book XLIV, states that it is more difficult to preserve things than to procure them. That Maecenas also thought this is evident from his address to Augustus in Book LII of the same Dio. In Livy: “You know how to win, Hannibal; you do not know how to use victory.”
>
> **“Suppose that he says this.”** This clause was absent from the old editions. Erasmus restored it, and it survives in many ancient manuscripts. It is absent from the Saint-Arnoul manuscript.]  

## II

Yet we exhort you by our common faith and by the true and sincere love of our heart toward you: since you have overcome the adversary in this first encounter, retain your glory with brave and persevering [Note: [Col. 0235C] “bravely,” *NC. 2*] courage.

We are still in the world; we are still stationed in the battle line; every day we contend for our life. Care must be taken that after these beginnings there may also be growth, and that what you have already begun to be through these fortunate first lessons may be brought to completion in you. It is a small thing to have been able to attain something; the greater thing is to be able to preserve what you have attained. Faith itself and saving birth [Col. 0236B] give life not by being received, but by being preserved. It is not immediate attainment, but consummation, that preserves a person for God.

The Lord taught this in his instruction, saying: “Behold, you have been made well; now sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” [Note: [Col. 0235C] “lest something worse befall you,” *Bod. 1*] (John V.14). Suppose that he says this also to his confessor: “Behold, you have become a confessor; now sin no more, lest something worse happen to you.”

Thus Solomon and Saul and many others were able to retain the grace given to them as long as they walked in the ways of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0235C–0236C] “They did not walk … they were unable to retain,” *Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1, 3*]. When the Lord’s discipline withdrew from them, grace also withdrew.

> **[Note: [Col. 0236D]**
>
> **III.—“The confessors ought to fulfill this.”** Rigaltius wrote, “you confessors ought to fulfill this.” I removed the word “you,” which is found neither in the old editions nor in the ancient manuscripts. I know that it does no harm to Cyprian’s meaning. But because I found it nowhere except in Rigaltius’s edition, I judged that it should be removed. I mention this lest anyone charge me with rashness.
>
> **[Col. 0237C] “Shine like.”** See Erasmus’s annotations on chapter 2 of Paul’s Letter to the Philippians.]

*Detrectant* (“disparage”). We have restored this reading, following the better manuscripts and the old editions. The Fuxensis manuscript and Rigault’s edition have *retractant*. But in Latin *retractare* is one thing, *detrectare* another. Livy, book XXXVIII: “Envy is blind and knows nothing but how to disparage virtues.” In the same sense Apuleius, in the first book of the *Florida*: “In a great city this sort of person is also found: those who would rather disparage their betters than imitate them.”]

III. We must persevere on the confined and narrow path of praise and glory. And although repose, humility, and the tranquility of good conduct befit all Christians, according to the word of the Lord, who regards [Note: [Col. 0236C] *Looks after*, Ebor. NC. 1. *Receives*, Lin.] none but the humble and quiet person who trembles at his words [Col. 0236C] (Isa. 66:2), nevertheless confessors especially ought to observe and fulfill this, [Note: [Col. 0236C] *Confessors on earth*, Lam. NC. 1.] since you have become an example [Col. 0237A] to the other brothers, by whose conduct the life and actions of everyone ought to be inspired. For just as the Jews were estranged from God because through them God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles, so, conversely, those through whose discipline the Lord’s name is proclaimed by praiseworthy testimony are dear to God, 12 as it is written, with the Lord warning beforehand and saying: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). And the apostle Paul says: “Shine like lights in the world” (Phil. 2:15). Peter likewise exhorts us: “As guests,” he says, “and strangers, abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul, maintaining good conduct [Note: [Col. 0237B] *Your conduct*, Pem.] among the Gentiles, [Note: [Col. 0237B] *Among the nations*, Ebor. NC. 1. Lam.] so that, when they disparage you as evildoers, they may behold your good works and magnify [Col. 0237B] the Lord” (1 Pet. 2:11–12). The greater part of you, to my joy, does indeed take care to do this and, having been made better by the honor of the confession itself, [Note: [Col. 0237B] *From the honor of the confession itself*, Bod. 3. Lin.] guards and preserves its glory through tranquil and good conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0237C]

IV.—*Some drunken man.* Previously the reading was *alius ab aquis tumulentus* (“another swollen up from the waters”), that is, from Baptism, as Rigault interprets it. Other editions, as he likewise notes, have *quando alius aliquis* (“when some other person”) or *quando unus aliquis* (“when some one person”). This last [Col. 0237D] reading occurs in the Thuanus manuscript. The old manuscript of Saint Remigius at Reims has *apud aquas* (“at the waters”); the Corbeiensis, *apud aquas temulentus* (“drunken at the waters”); the Turonensis, *quando unus apud aquas* (“when one person at the waters”). The English editors retained the old edition, offering no authority for the reading conjectured by Rigault other than Rigault himself, whose reading they nevertheless refute. Reinhart likewise restored the old reading. I have followed the authority of the Seguierianus, Metensis, Beccensis, Gratianopolitanus, and Lamonianus manuscripts.

*Demoratur.* This reading is constant both in the old and in the modern editions, and in the ancient manuscript copies. Yet Goulart notes that some write *denotatur*, and in the margin of his printed book he wrote that Beza read it so. Reinhart likewise recorded this variant reading in the margin of his edition, evidently from Rigault, who says in his observations that certain copies of Cyprian have *denotatur*. But I found that reading only in a single Vatican manuscript cited in the margin of my copy of the Manutius edition, and in a copy of Pamelius’s edition that belonged to Nicolas Le Fèvre. I also found it written by some scholar in the margin of the [Col. 0238C] Lyon edition of 1550. Goulart, however, thinks that the reading *demoratur*, if retained, may signify the same as *moratur*, with the first syllable long—that is, “he is mad” or “plays the fool”—which, he says, was taken from the Greeks and used by Suetonius in his *Nero*.

*Apprehended.* I restored the word that seemed to accord better with Cyprian’s style. For some old manuscripts and certain editions have *ut deprehensus* (“as one caught”); others, indeed the best ones, have *unde apprehensus* (“so that, once apprehended”). See what I noted on the book *On the Lapsed*.

*As a Christian.* In Rufinus, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 8, it is reported from Apollonius that Alexander, an associate of the prophetess Prisca who called himself a martyr, was tried before Aemilius Frontinus, proconsul at Ephesus, not for the name of Christ but for certain robberies. Before Cyprian, Saint Peter had said in the fourth chapter of his First Epistle: “Let none of you suffer as a thief or murderer, or as an evildoer, or as one who meddles in others’ affairs, but as a Christian.”]

IV. But I hear that certain men are tainting your number and destroying the honor of your distinguished name by their depraved conduct. You yourselves, as lovers and guardians of your own honor, [Note: [Col. 0237C] *Of conduct and honor*, Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. [Col. 0238B] 1, 2.] ought to rebuke, restrain, and correct them. For with what great shame to your name is an offense committed when one man, drunk and wanton, behaves like a madman, while another returns to the country [Col. 0238A] from which he was banished, only to be apprehended and perish no longer as a Christian but as a criminal? I hear that some are becoming puffed up and swollen with pride, although it is written: “Do not be haughty, but fear. For if the Lord did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either” (Rom. 11:20–21). Our Lord was led like a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7). “I am not rebellious,” he says, “nor do I contradict. [Note: [Col. 0238B] *Contradicting*, Lin. NC. 1, 2.] I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to blows. Nor did I turn my face away from the foulness of spittle” (Isa. 50:5–6). And does anyone who now lives through him and in him dare to exalt himself and behave proudly, forgetful both of the deeds he performed [Note: [Col. 0238C] *He performed in the law*, Voss. 2.] and of the commandments he handed down to us, whether by himself or through his apostles? [Col. 0238B] But if “the servant is not greater than his lord” (John 13:15–16), let those who follow the Lord imitate his footsteps in humility, quietness, and silence, since the more lowly a person has been, the more exalted he shall become, as the Lord says: “Whoever is least among you, he shall be great” (Luke 9:48).

[Note: [Col. 0238D]

V.—*Temples of God.* Jerome, in the *Letter to Paulinus on the Formation of a Monk*: “The true temple of Christ is the soul of the believer.”

*Beds with women.* He treats a very dangerous matter, as Marbod, bishop of Rennes, also notes in his *Letter to Robert of Arbrissel*. For Robert was said, out of excessive zeal for continence, to sleep at night between two girls and in this way to attempt to extinguish the kindled heat of the flesh—by a new and unheard-of, as Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writes to him, but fruitless kind of martyrdom. Geoffrey adds that something known to have been undertaken contrary to reason can in no way be useful or fruitful. Geoffrey, however, appears to have borrowed what he said about a new kind of martyrdom [Col. 0239C] from the first book of Saint Ambrose’s *On Virgins*, chapter 2, where, speaking of Saint Agnes, he says: “A new kind of martyrdom. Not yet fit for punishment, yet already mature for victory; unequal to the contest, yet readily crowned,” and so forth. Jerome writes elegantly, as usual, and prudently in his *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “Some think it a sign of greater virtue to despise a pleasure that is present. Yet I think it belongs to a safer continence not to know what it would desire.”

*Promiscuous.* This reading, which all editions have and the old books confirm, is excellent. Yet Rigault preferred to this sound reading an erroneous one found in the Thuanus manuscript, in which, through the omission of a single letter by the copyist, *promisca* was written. There is therefore an error in the English edition, where it is noted that *promiscua* is written in the Thuanus manuscript, whereas Rigault, on the contrary, explained in his observations why he rejected this reading. In Aulus Gellius, *promisca*, *impromisca*, and *impromisce* are read in Henri Estienne’s edition. Niccolò Perotti, pp. 752, 1185, notes that the ancients wrote *promiscam* for *promiscue*. In Henri Estienne’s edition I read *promisce* in Macrobius for *promiscue*.

*The tongue that confessed Christ.* Cyprian likewise says in the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 11: “First the tongue that had confessed God was drawn out and cut off.” Pliny, book VII, chapter 23: “When Anaxarchus was being tortured, he bit off his tongue—the one means of extracting information—and spat it into the tyrant’s face.” Valerius Maximus recounts the same story more fully in book III, chapter 3. See Cujas, book XIX of the *Observations*, chapter 6.]

V.
