What, then, of that other thing which ought to seem accursed to you, and which we learned, with the greatest groaning and grief of our soul: that there are some who further defile the temples of God and the members sanctified and made illustrious after their confession by their shameful intercourse, joining their beds [Col. 0239A] promiscuously with women? [Note: [Col. 0239B] *Mingle them with women*, Lin. NC. 1.] Even if their consciences are free from fornication, this very fact is a grave crime: through the scandal they cause, examples arise that lead others to ruin. [Note: [Col. 0239B] *Examples are displayed*, Lam.; *may arise*, Bod. 1. Ebor. Lin.] Nor ought there to be any quarrels or rivalries among you, since the Lord left us his peace and it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. But if you bite and accuse one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5:14–15). I also beg you to abstain from insults and curses, [Note: [Col. 0239C] *From insulting abuse*, NC. 2. Lam.] since revilers do not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6:10), and the tongue that confessed Christ must be preserved sound and pure together with its honor. For whoever speaks peaceful, good, and just things according to Christ’s command confesses Christ every day. We had renounced the world [Note: [Col. 0240B] *We renounce the world*, Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. NC. 1, 2.] when we were baptized. [Col. 0239B] But now we have truly renounced the world, when, having been tried and proved by God, we left everything we possessed, followed the Lord, and stand and live by faith in him and fear of him.

[Note: [Col. 0239D]

VI.—*And although to the clergy.* Although Rigault, who first discovered this passage in the manuscript of Saint Remigius, did not publish it with the letter itself but included it among his observations, and although the English followed Rigault’s example, I have nevertheless attached it to the letter. I do not doubt that it is Cyprian’s, even though it was found in only one [Col. 0240C] old book. Reinhart did not attach it to the letter but added it at the end, noting that Rigault had published it from the Reims manuscript.

*From my own modest funds.* Or “from my own resources,” as Cyprian himself speaks in Letter XXXVI, p. 49—that is, from the property belonging to Caecilius Cyprian, which is mentioned in Letter LXIX to Florentius. For I do not think this should be understood as referring to that portion of the Church’s revenues that belonged to the bishop, since the division of property had not yet been devised, because the Church did not yet possess riches and wealth. At that time it was supported by the offerings of the faithful, which were free and voluntary, not compulsory. Tertullian in the *Apologeticum*: “Each person contributes a modest offering on the monthly day, or whenever he wishes and only if he can. For no one is compelled, but contributes voluntarily. These are, as it were, deposits of piety. For they are not spent on banquets, drinking parties, or thankless eating-houses, but on feeding and burying the needy.” [Col. 0240D] It is certain that Cyprian possessed property: Cyprian himself, in Letter LXIII, and Pontius the deacon, in his *Life* of Cyprian, testify concerning the gardens that he sold at the beginning of his faith and that were restored to him by God’s favor.

*I wish you well.* I have retained the common edition, which is sound. I note, however, that the Speyer edition, the old Venetian edition, Rembolt’s, Erasmus’s, and Morel’s prefer, “I wish you well, brother,” and that it is also written so in sixteen ancient manuscripts. This too is an excellent reading. For although the letter was written to several people, it was nevertheless written especially and by name to Rogatianus, a distinguished person. Therefore, when Cyprian brought it to an end, he could, as was his custom, have directed the valedictory closing to him.]

VI. Let us strengthen one another with mutual exhortations, [Note: [Col. 0240B] *With exhortations and prayers*, Lin. NC. 2.] and let us advance more and more in the Lord, so that when, in accordance with his mercy, he has established the peace that he promises he will establish, we may return to the Church renewed and almost transformed; and so that both our brothers and the Gentiles may receive us as persons corrected [Note: [Col. 0240B] *Uncorrupted*, Bod.] in every respect and reformed for the better, and those who formerly marveled at the glory displayed in our acts of courage may now 13 [Col. 0240A] marvel at the discipline displayed in our conduct. And although I have written very fully to our clergy, both recently, while you were still confined in prison, and now once more, directing that whatever may be necessary for your clothing or food be supplied, I myself have also sent you 250 from the modest personal funds I was carrying with me; and shortly before this I had sent another 250. Victor, formerly a reader and now a deacon, who is with me, has also sent you 175. I rejoice whenever I learn that very many of our brothers, moved by their love, are eagerly coming forward in rivalry with one another and assisting your needs through their contributions. I wish you, dearly beloved brothers, always to fare well and to remember me.

[Note: [Col. 0240D]

394 LETTER VII.—*On praying to God.* I am astonished that Rigault—who knew that Saint Augustine, in book IV of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, chapter 2, cited these words as Cyprian’s, and knew besides that they occurred in certain old editions—omitted them from his own edition. [Col. 0241D] The English also omitted them. We have restored them on the authority of Augustine and a great many old books.]

## LETTER VII

(Erasmus, IV, 4; Pamelius, VIII; Oxford, Leipzig, XI; Rigault, Baluze, Paris, VII.)

### TO THE CLERGY, ON PRAYING TO GOD

[Col. 0240B]

**ARGUMENT.—**Its subject is almost the same as that of the two preceding letters, except that here he exhorts them to unremitting prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0241D]

I.—*Religious solicitude.* This is the reading of all the old books and editions. Rigault’s edition, however, has *your religion*. The English restored the old reading.

*We do not keep to the way of the Lord.* Saint Augustine also cites this [Col. 0242D] passage in the work praised just above, chapter 3.]

I. Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons, his brothers: greetings. Although I know, dearly beloved brothers, that because of the fear each of us owes to God you too are there applying yourselves urgently [Col. 0241A] to constant prayer and earnest entreaties, I myself nevertheless admonish your religious solicitude that, in order to appease and entreat the Lord, we should groan not with the voice alone but also with fasting, tears, and every kind of supplication. For we must understand and confess that the turbulent devastation of this tribulation, which has laid waste to the greater part of our flock and continues to lay it waste even now, has come upon us in accordance with our sins, because we do not keep to the Lord’s way or observe the heavenly commandments given to us for salvation. Our Lord did the will of the Father, but we do not do the Lord’s will: we devote ourselves to property and profit, pursue pride, occupy ourselves with rivalry and dissension, neglect sincerity and faith, renounce the world in words alone and not in deeds, [Col. 0241B] each pleasing himself and displeasing everyone else. We are therefore beaten as we deserve, since it is written: “But that servant who knows his lord’s will and has not obeyed [Note: [Col. 0241D] *Has done*, M. R.] his will shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47). But what wounds, what blows, do we not deserve, when not even the confessors, who ought to have been an example of good conduct to others, maintain discipline? Thus, while the swollen [Note: [Col. 0241D] *Swelling*, Corb.] and shameless boasting of their confession insolently exalts certain men, tortures have come—tortures [Note: [Col. 0241D] *They have come into tortures, tortures*, Corb.] without any end imposed by the torturer, without release through condemnation, without the comfort of death; tortures that do not readily discharge them toward the crown but torment them until they cast them down—unless someone, removed by divine favor, should advance [Note: [Col. 0241D] *Should fail*, Oxford.] amid the very torments and attain glory, not through the termination of his punishment but [Col. 0241C] through the swiftness of his death.

II. We suffer these things through our own offense and desert, just as divine judgment warned beforehand when it said: “If they forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, [Note: [Col. 0241D] *In my ways*, Voss. 1. Pem.] if they profane my ordinances and do not observe my commandments, I shall visit their crimes with a rod and their offenses with scourges” (Ps. 88:31–33). We therefore feel rods and scourges, because we neither please God by good deeds nor make satisfaction for our sins. Let us entreat God’s mercy from the depths of our heart and with our whole mind, for he himself added: “But I shall not take my mercy away from them” (ibid.). Let us ask and we shall receive; and if there is delay and tardiness in our receiving because we have offended gravely, let us knock, because the door will be opened to the one who knocks (Matt. 7:7–8; 18:19; Luke 11:9–10), [Col. 0242A] provided that our prayers, groans, and tears knock at the door. We must persist and remain in these, and the prayer must be unanimous. 14

III. You should know that what especially persuaded and compelled me to write this letter to you was what the Lord deigned [Note: [Col. 0242D] *Deigns*, Oxford.] to show and reveal. It was said in a vision: “Ask, and you obtain”; [Note: [Col. 0242D] *You will obtain*, Bod. 3. Old anonymous edition.] then the people standing by were instructed to pray for certain persons designated to them. In their praying, however, their voices were discordant and their wills divergent, [Note: [Col. 0242D] *Discordant voices and scattered wills*, Lin.] and this greatly displeased him who had said, “Ask, and you obtain,” because the disharmony of the people was at variance, and there was no single, sincere, and united concord among the brothers, although it is written, “God, who causes those of one mind to dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7); and in the Acts of the Apostles we read: [Col. 0242B] “The multitude of those who had believed acted with one soul and one mind” (Acts 4:32); and the Lord commanded in his own voice, saying: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John 15:17). And again: “But I say to you that, if two of you agree [Note: [Col. 0242D] *If two of you agree*, Bod. 1, 3. Voss. 1, 2; *if you agree*, Rig.] on earth, whatever matter you ask for shall be granted to you by my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18:19). If two persons of one mind can accomplish so much, what if unanimity existed among everyone? What if all the brothers agreed in accordance with the peace the Lord gave us? We would long ago have obtained from divine mercy what we ask and would not have been tossed about for so long in this peril to our salvation and faith. Indeed, these evils would not have come upon the brothers if the brotherhood had been animated as one.

[Col. 0242C] [Note: [Col. 0242D]

IV.—*Should arise.* In one royal manuscript the reading is: “The force of this devastation should advance, and the assault of our wickedness should rush upon us.” But the other manuscripts and all the editions oppose it. In the very old Remigianus manuscript it is written: “The tempest of this devastation should arise.” In the Lamonianus: “The tempest of this wasteland should operate.”

]

IV. This too was shown: the head of a household was sitting, with a young man seated at his right hand. The young man, troubled and somewhat indignantly sorrowful, sat holding his cheek in his hand, his expression mournful. Another person, however, standing on the left, was carrying a net that he threatened to cast in order to catch the people standing around. When the person who saw this wondered what it meant, he was told that the young man sitting in this manner on the right was grieved and sorrowful because his commands were not being observed, while the person on the left was exulting because an opportunity was being given him to obtain from the head of the household the power to act savagely. This was shown long before the tempest of this devastation arose. [Note: [Col. 0242D] *Operated*, Lin. *And we see*, old anonymous edition.] And we have seen the fulfillment of what was shown: while we despise the Lord’s commands and fail to observe the saving precepts of the law given to us, [Col. 0243A] the enemy received the power to do harm and, by casting his net, enveloped those who were less well armed and less cautious in resisting.

[Note: [Col. 0243D]

V.—*Of our heart.* There are two readings of this passage in the ancient manuscripts. We found the one we retain in eight manuscripts. The other, which has *of our sin*, is offered by all editions preceding that of Pamelius and is also preferred by eleven old books. It can be supported by what occurs at the beginning of the book of Job: “That you might seek my iniquity and examine my sin.” Our reading, however, is confirmed by numerous passages of sacred Scripture in which God is called the searcher of heart and reins, as is also noted at the end of Letter VIII. In Flori’s manuscript, *of our sin* was written.

]

V. Let us pray urgently and groan in constant entreaty. For you should know, dearly beloved brothers, that not long ago [Note: [Col. 0243C] *Long ago already*, Erasmus.] this too was reproached to us through a vision: that we sleep during our prayers and do not pray watchfully. And surely God, who loves the person he corrects (Prov. 3:12), corrects in order to amend, and amends in order to preserve. Let us therefore shake off and break the bonds of sleep, and let us pray urgently and watchfully, as the apostle Paul commands when he says: “Persist in prayer, keeping watch in it” (Col. 4:2). For the apostles did not cease to pray by day and night, and the Lord himself—the master of discipline and the way of our example—prayed frequently and watchfully, [Col. 0243B] as we read in the Gospel: “He went out onto the mountain to pray and spent the night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). Surely, when he prayed, he prayed for us, since he was not himself a sinner but bore the sins of others. [Note: [Col. 0243C] *Our sins*, Lin. Voss. 1, 2. Bod. 1. Pem.] So greatly did he intercede for us that we read elsewhere: “The Lord said to Peter: ‘Behold, Satan has asked to buffet you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail’” (Luke 22:31). If he labored, kept vigil, and prayed for us and for our offenses, how much more ought we to persist in entreaty and prayer, first beseeching the Lord himself and then, through him, making satisfaction to God the Father? 15 We have Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, as advocate and intercessor for our sins, provided that we repent of having sinned in the past, [Col. 0243C] and, confessing and understanding the offenses by which we now displease the Lord, promise that at least henceforth we shall walk in his ways and fear his commandments. The Father corrects and protects us, provided that we stand in faith and amid tribulations and distresses—that is, firmly adhering to his Christ—as it is written: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8:35). None of these things can separate believers; nothing can tear away those who adhere to his body and blood. This persecution is the testing and examination [Col. 0244A] of our heart. God willed us to be shaken and tested, just as he has always tested his own; yet in his trials his help has never failed believers.

VI. Finally, to his least servant—although burdened with very many offenses and unworthy of his favor—he nevertheless deigned, in accordance with his goodness toward us, to give this message: “Tell him,” he said, “to be secure, because peace is coming; but since there is a slight delay in the meantime, there still remain some who are to be tested.” By divine favors we are also admonished concerning frugal food and sober drink, evidently lest worldly enticement enervate a heart already raised on high by heavenly strength, or lest a mind weighed down by richer meals be less wakeful for the entreaties of prayer.

[Col. 0244B] [Note: [Col. 0243D]

VII.—*Nor, finally, should you yourselves.* Although the former reading, which has *certainly*, is sound, I have preferred the one supported by the authority of almost all the old copies.

*To suppress*—that is, to withhold, in a manner of speaking very remote from the proper signification of this word. Yet [Col. 0244D] Tacitus, in the *Life of Agricola*, appears to have used the word in the same sense as Cyprian. For he says: “Nor did Agricola, greedy for credit, ever appropriate deeds performed by others; instead, centurion and prefect alike had in him an incorruptible witness to the deed.” Likewise Seneca, in *On Benefits*, p. 17: “The consciousness of an appropriated benefit burns and torments him.” Quintus Curtius, book XV: “To appropriate glory obtained by another’s blood.” Arnobius, book III: “For to suppress writings and wish to submerge a published text is not to defend the gods but to fear the testimony of truth.” Cassian, book IX, chapter 11: “Interrupting the efficacy of prayers”; and *Conferences*, book I, chapter 11: “That charity may at no time be interrupted.”

*Lost.* Thus the old editions and almost all the old books. In one of my manuscripts, however, *imposes* is written, which appears better. In the very old Remigianus, *cut down* is written.]

VII. I ought not to have passed over these individual matters or concealed them alone within my own conscience, since through them each of us can be instructed and governed. Nor, finally, [Note: [Col. 0244C] *Certainly you yourselves*, Oxford.] should you keep this letter hidden among yourselves, but should arrange for it to be read to the brothers. For to suppress the things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us is the act of one who does not wish his brother to be admonished and instructed. Let them know that we are being tested by our Lord, and let them never fail in the faith by which we once believed in him because of the struggle of the present tribulation. Let each person acknowledge his own offenses and, at least now, put off the conduct of the old man. For no one who looks backward after putting his hand to the plow is fit for the kingdom of God. Finally, Lot’s wife, though she had been delivered, looked back contrary to the command and lost what she had escaped. [Col. 0244C] Let us direct our attention not to what lies behind, whither the devil calls us back, but to what lies ahead, whither Christ calls us. Let us raise our eyes to heaven, lest the earth deceive us with its delights and enticements. Let each person pray to God not only for himself but for all the brothers, just as the Lord taught us to pray. There he does not command individuals to offer a private prayer, but instructed those praying to pray for everyone in a common supplication and harmonious prayer. If the Lord sees us humble and quiet, united with one another, fearful of his wrath, corrected and amended by the present tribulation, he will keep us safe from the enemy’s attacks. [Col. 0245A] Discipline has gone before; pardon will follow.

VIII. Let us only beseech the Lord without ceasing to ask and with faith that we shall receive, sincere and of one mind, imploring him with groaning and weeping alike, as it is fitting for those who are placed among the ruins of those who mourn and the remnants of those who fear, amid the vast slaughter of the infirm [Note: [Col. 0245C] *Of those lying down*, Bod. 1. *The small number of those standing*, Lin. Pem. Bod. 1, 3. Voss. 2. Thu. Foss.] and the slight steadfastness of those who stand. Let us ask that peace [Note: [Col. 0245C] *Peace for his Church*, Voss. 1. Bod. 3.] be restored more quickly; that aid come swiftly to us in our hiding places and dangers; that the things the Lord deigns to reveal to his servants be fulfilled; [Note: [Col. 0245C] *In most*, Foss. Corb.] that the Church be restored and our salvation secured; that after rains come clear skies, after darkness light, after storms and whirlwinds tranquil calm; and that there come the loving assistance of paternal affection and the customary wonders of divine majesty, [Col. 0245B] by which the blasphemy of the persecutors 16 may be beaten back, the repentance of the lapsed restored, and the courageous and steadfast confidence of those who persevere glorified. I wish you, dearly beloved brothers, always to fare well and to remember me. Greet the brotherhood in my name, and admonish them to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0245D]

LETTER VIII.—*The Church glories.* In the manuscript of Saint Arnulf at Metz the reading is *The Church rejoices. And recently indeed*. In the Chartres manuscript: *rejoices* or *glories. And recently*.

*You returned with devotion.* The same manuscripts have *you came forth*.

*Interrogation under torture.* I have restored this reading, which both the old books and the ancient editions prefer. In the Manutius edition, *butchery* is written. Pamelius printed it thus as well. But our reading, which rests on authority, accords properly with what was said shortly before: “You endured the harshest interrogation under torture,” and below, “victors under interrogation.” The English editors produced certain variant readings that can demonstrate that the other reading may also be sound.

*Believing.* The old [Col. 0246D] books and editions prefer this reading, except that I have sometimes seen *of one believing* written. In the Dijon manuscript, however, and in the more recent Remigianus, the consistent reading is *steadfastly*. This seems better to me, but I have not dared to change the text because the other copies oppose it.

395 *Tortured … stronger.* Sulpicius Severus, in the *Letter to Eusebius*: “But the special courage of the righteous has always lain in enduring and overcoming these things: patient throughout every trial and always unconquered, they triumphed the more courageously the more grievously they suffered.” In Rufinus, book V, chapter 1, in the history of the martyrs of Lyon: “Indeed, from the very endurance of the saints an even fiercer rage for the contest was kindled against them, and they were wearied by a kind of shame, because greater courage resided in those being tortured than in those torturing them.”

[Col. 0247C] *No longer limbs.* Thus above, in the letter to Donatus, p. 5: “No longer limbs, but wounds.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIX, in recounting the butchery inflicted upon a certain Diogenes to make him speak words pleasing to the emperor, says that, when his limbs no longer sufficed for the punishments, he was burned alive. The same author, in book XIV, speaking of a certain Eusebius who was wretchedly tortured, says he was so disemboweled that his limbs failed before the torments did. Saint Ambrose, in book I of *On Virgins*, speaking of the martyrdom of Saint Agnes: “Was there any place on that little body for a wound?” Livy, book IV: “What place was now left intact upon the body to receive new wounds?” Justin, book II: “As though punishments were being exacted from each individual limb.” Those varied kinds of torments and tortures [Col. 0247D] are elegantly described in book I of Silius Italicus:

> Neither fires nor glowing steel, nor scourges everywhere  
> Tearing the lacerated body with countless blows,  
> Nor executioners’ hands, nor corruption poured deep into the marrow,  
> Nor flames gleaming within the open wound  
> Ever ceased.

*A spectacle for the Lord.* The manuscripts of Saint Arnulf and Chartres have *of the Lord*.

*How joyful there.* The same manuscripts prefer *among them*.

*Mappalicus.* The Carthaginian Calendar published by Mabillon has: “On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, the martyr Mappalicus.” But in the martyrology of the monastery of Einsiedeln, also published by Mabillon, it is the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, as it is also in the ancient writers of martyrologies. Victor of Vita, book I, chapter 5, writes that Saint Cyprian was buried in a place called Mappalia.

[Col. 0248C] *Foretold.* The old editions earlier than the Manutius edition and certain old copies prefer *promised*.

*Will receive.* In certain ancient manuscripts, *will conceive* is written. So too in the editions preceding that of Erasmus.

*The crown of glory.* From the First Epistle of blessed Peter: “You shall receive the unfading crown of glory.” This passage of Cyprian is read variously in the old manuscripts. Some have *the crown of glory*, others *the glory of the crown*. The copyists’ audacity introduced this discrepancy. Flori’s manuscript also had the sound reading. In Cassian, book VI, chapter 3, I read *the glory of the crown*, [Col. 0248D] for which perhaps *the crown of glory* should be restored.

*That you may obtain it.* In certain very old manuscripts and editions the following then appeared: “But everyone who contends in the arena exercises self-control in all things.” But since that passage is not found in many manuscripts and is absent from the editions of Manutius and Morel; since I see this same passage of Paul copied in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 26, without that section; and since, again, it does not occur in the *Letter to Fortunatus on Exhortation to Martyrdom* in the best and oldest copies, I have struck it out everywhere, because I think it was added by some scholar from Paul’s Epistle, where it does occur. Thus, in several passages of Cyprian, sections were added from the books of sacred Scripture by those who believed they had been omitted. See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of Paul.

*Of the same contest.* The manuscript of Saint Arnulf has *agreement*; the Chartres manuscript, *agreement* or *contest*.

[Col. 0249C] *The will unimpaired.* Jerome, book II *Against Jovinian*: “For in the martyr it is the will, from which death itself arises, that is crowned.” See the notes on Letter LII at the words *he suffered*.

*To the crown concerning him.* The same manuscripts have *to the crown of God*. So too certain editions.

*Dearly beloved brothers.* The manuscript of Saint Arnulf has *most beloved brothers*. [Col. 0249D]

*Having received a reprieve.* That is, permission to remain in this life, as Rigault correctly explains in his notes on Tertullian’s book *On Flight in Persecution*.

Peace and battle line. In the book *On Jealousy and Envy*, p. 260: “Peace too has its crowns.” 396 And in the book *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 246: “To those who conquer in peace he will give a white crown for their works; in persecution he will double it with a purple crown for suffering.” In the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom, Addressed to Fortunatus*, p. 274: “In persecution military service will be crowned; in peace, conscience.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Furia on the Preservation of Widowhood* and in the *Letter to Heliodorus in Praise of the Solitary Life*: “The lilies of virgins and the roses of martyrs.” The same author, in the *Life of Malchus the Monk*: “Chastity preserved also has its own martyrdom.” Saint Ambrose, in the *Letter to Simplicianus*: “For us there are battles even in peace, and peace in war.”

I wish you well. These words are absent from the Chartres manuscript.]

## LETTER VIII

*(Eras., II, 6; Pamel., IX; Rig., Baluz., Paris., VIII; Oxford, Leipzig, X.)*

### TO THE MARTYRS AND CONFESSORS

[Note: [Col. 0248B] This note appears at the foot of column 248, but its callout letter, (f), is not printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0248B] *I am already being sacrificed*, Bod. 3. *I am being poured out*, Foss., Corb.]

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian, commending the martyrs of Africa in extraordinary terms for their steadfastness, invites them to persevere, following the example of their colleague Mappalicus.

[Col. 0245C] Cyprian to the martyrs and confessors in Christ our Lord and in God the Father: everlasting salvation.

I rejoice with gladness and congratulate you, most valiant and blessed brothers, now that I have learned of your faith and courage, in which Mother Church glories. Indeed, she gloried recently as well, when, your confession remaining steadfast, you endured the punishment that made Christ’s confessors [Col. 0246A] exiles. Yet the present confession, the stronger it is in suffering, is so much the more illustrious and greater in honor. The struggle has grown, and the glory of those who struggle has grown with it. You were not held back from the battle line by fear of tortures; rather, by the tortures themselves you were provoked more and more to battle, and, strong and steadfast, you returned with ready devotion to the combat [Note: [Col. 0245C] *Prize of the contest*, Pem.; *price*, Corb.] of the greatest contest.

Of your number I have learned that some have already been crowned, while others are now on the very threshold of the crown of victory [Note: [Col. 0245C] *Nearest to victory*, Oxford]; and all whom the prison has enclosed within its glorious company are animated by an equal and like ardor of courage for waging the contest. This is how Christ’s soldiers ought to be in the divine camp: neither blandishments should beguile the incorruptible steadfastness of their faith, nor threats terrify it, nor torments and tortures overcome it, because “greater is he who is in us than he who is in this world” (1 John 4:4); nor [Col. 0246B] has earthly punishment more power to cast us down than divine protection has to raise us up.

The truth of this has been proved by the glorious contest of our brothers, who, becoming leaders for the rest in overcoming tortures, furnished an example of courage and faith, engaging in battle until the battle line itself succumbed in defeat. With what praises shall I proclaim you, most valiant brothers? With what trumpet-call of speech shall I adorn the strength of your hearts and the perseverance of your faith? You endured [Note: [Col. 0245D] *Enduring*, Pem.; *certainly*, Bod. 1] the harshest interrogation under torture until the consummation of glory; you did not yield to the torments, but rather the torments yielded to you. The crowns put an end to the pains [Note: [Col. 0246C] *An end to the sorrows*, Oxford] to which the instruments of torture gave no end. The still more grievous interrogation [Note: [Col. 0246C] *Butchery*, Oxford; *mangling*, Pem.; *the delay of mangling*, Bod.; *a more grievous butcher*, Ben.; *interrogation*, Thu.] continued so long for this purpose: not to cast down a faith that stood firm, but to send God’s people more quickly to the Lord.

The assembled multitude looked on in wonder at the heavenly contest, [Col. 0246C] the contest of God, the spiritual contest, the battle of Christ [Note: [Col. 0246C] *A spiritual contest, a battle*, Oxford; *the spiritual battle of Christ*, Voss. 2, Bod. 1, 3, Pem.]: his servants stood with unfettered voice, uncorrupted mind, and divine courage, naked indeed of worldly weapons, but armed, as believers, with the weapons of faith [Note: [Col. 0246C] *Armed with burning faith*, Pem.]. Those being tortured stood stronger than their torturers, and their struck and mangled limbs defeated the claws that struck and mangled them. The long-raging, repeatedly inflicted scourge could not overcome their unconquerable faith, although, once the structure of their entrails had been torn apart, [Col. 0247A] it was no longer limbs but wounds that were being tortured in God’s servants.

Blood flowed that would extinguish the conflagration of persecution and quench the flames and fires of Gehenna with glorious gore. Oh, what a spectacle that was for the Lord—how sublime, how great, how acceptable in God’s eyes through the oath of allegiance and devotion of his soldier! As it is written in the Psalms, the Holy Spirit speaking to us and likewise admonishing us: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his righteous ones” (Ps. 115:15). Precious is this death, which purchases immortality 17 at the price of its own blood [Note: [Col. 0247B] *Precious power of the blood*, Corb.], which has received the crown from [Note: [Col. 0247B] *the crown of God*, Bod. 3, Pem.] the consummation of courage.

How joyful Christ was there! How gladly, in such servants of his, did he both fight and conquer—the protector of faith, giving to believers as much as the recipient believes himself capable of receiving! He was present at his own contest; he raised up, strengthened, and animated the champions [Col. 0247B] and defenders of his name. And he who once conquered death for us always conquers in us.

“When they hand you over,” he says, “do not consider what you are to say, for in that hour it will be given to you what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20). The present combat furnished proof of this fact. A voice full of the Holy Spirit burst forth from the martyr’s mouth when the most blessed Mappalicus said to the proconsul amid his tortures: “Tomorrow you will see a contest.” And what he said with a testimony of courage and faith, the Lord fulfilled. A heavenly contest was displayed [Note: [Col. 0247B] *In the contest of the heavenly exhibition*, Voss. 2; *was displayed*, [Col. 0247C] Bod. 1], and God’s servant was crowned [Col. 0248A] in the combat of the promised contest.

This is the contest that the prophet Isaiah foretold, saying: “Is it a small contest for you to contend with men, since God provides the contest?” (Isa. 7:13). And, to show what this contest would be, he added: “Behold, a virgin shall receive in her womb [Note: [Col. 0248B] *In the womb*, Thu., Foss., Bod. 1, 2, and *Against the Jews*] and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (ibid. 14).

This is the contest of our faith, by which we engage, by which we conquer, by which we are crowned. This is the contest that the blessed apostle Paul set before us, in which we must run and reach the crown of glory: “Do you not know,” he says, “that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but only one receives the palm? Run in such a way that you may secure it. They do so to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible one” [Note: [Col. 0248B] *Incorruptible*, Voss. 2, Bod. 1] (1 Cor. 9:24–25).

Likewise, displaying his own contest and promising that he would soon become the Lord’s sacrificial offering, [Col. 0248B] he says: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my taking up is at hand. I have fought the good contest, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith. There now remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, that righteous judge, will give me on that day—and not only to me, but also to all who love his coming” (2 Tim. 4:6–8).

This contest, therefore—foretold beforehand through the Prophets, instituted by the Lord, and waged by the Apostles—Mappalicus solemnly promised to the proconsul in his own name and that of his colleagues. Nor did his faithful voice prove false in its promise: he displayed the fight he had pledged, and received the palm he had earned.

I both wish and exhort you likewise to follow this most blessed martyr, and the other participants in the same contest—soldiers and comrades steadfast in faith, patient in pain, [Col. 0249A] victorious under torture—so that the consummation of courage and the heavenly crown may also unite those whom the bond of confession and the lodging of prison joined together; so that by your joy you may wipe away the tears of Mother Church, who mourns the falls and deaths of so many; and so that by the incitement of your example you may strengthen the steadfastness of the others who still stand.

If the battle line summons you [Note: [Col. 0249C] *Challenges you*, Oxford], if the day of your contest comes, serve as soldiers bravely and fight steadfastly, knowing that you fight beneath the eyes of the Lord who is present, and that through confession of his name you attain his own glory. For he is not one who merely watches his servants: he himself wrestles in us, he himself engages in combat, and in the contest of our struggle he both crowns and is crowned.

But if, before the day of your contest, [Col. 0249B] peace should arrive through the Lord’s indulgence, nevertheless may your resolve remain unimpaired and your conscience glorious. Let none of you be saddened as though he were inferior to those who endured tortures before you and, having conquered and trampled upon the world, came to the Lord by a glorious journey. The Lord searches the kidneys and the heart; he sees through secrets and beholds hidden things. To earn a crown from him [Note: [Col. 0250C] *of God*, Oxford], the testimony alone 18 of him who will judge is sufficient.

Thus both conditions, dearly beloved brothers, are equally sublime and illustrious: the former is more secure—to hasten to the Lord through the consummation of victory; the latter more joyful—to receive, after glory, leave to remain, and flourish in the praise of the Church.

O blessed Church of ours, which the honor of divine favor thus illumines, which in our times the glorious blood of the martyrs [Col. 0249C] makes illustrious! Before, she was white in the works of the brothers; now she has been made purple in the martyrs’ blood. Neither lilies nor roses are lacking among her flowers. Let each person now contend for the fullest dignity of both honors. Let them receive either white crowns from works or purple crowns from suffering. [Col. 0250A] In the heavenly camp both peace and the battle line have their own flowers, with which Christ’s soldier may be crowned for glory.

I wish you, most valiant and blessed brothers, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0249D]

**LETTER IX.—**The title of this letter, in the form in which it is given [Col. 0250C] here, was copied from our Fossatensis manuscript, the old Victorinus manuscript, the Michaelinus manuscript, and the Speyer edition, as well as from the old Venetian edition. The English editors placed its summary—an extremely poor one—in the margin.]

## LETTER IX

*(Erasm., III, 14; Pamel., X; Rig., Baluz., Paris., IX; Oxford, Leipzig, XXI.)*

### TO THE CLERGY, CONCERNING CERTAIN PRESBYTERS WHO RASHLY GRANTED PEACE TO THE LAPSED WHILE THE PERSECUTION HAD NOT YET SUBSIDED AND WITHOUT THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE BISHOPS

**SUMMARY.—**You have the summary of this letter below in the following words, Letter XIV: “The presbyters and deacons,” he says, “did not lack priestly vigor to restrain certain men who, less mindful of discipline and driven headlong by rash haste, [Col. 0250B] had already begun to communicate with the lapsed.”

[Note: [Col. 0250C]

**I.—I maintained patience.** The emperors Arcadius and Honorius, book XIV of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Deserters*: “As we maintain patience in these matters.”

**Some of the presbyters.** The English editors think that this concerns the five seditious [Col. 0250D] presbyters; on them, see our notes to Letter XXXVIII.

**Our predecessors.** Below, Letter LXX, to the Numidian bishops: “We put forward no new judgment of our own, but one established long ago by our predecessors.” The subject here is not Cyprian’s predecessors as bishops of Carthage, but the bishops generally who governed the African Church before Cyprian—namely, the seventy bishops whom Saint Augustine teaches to have attended the council held under Agrippinus, in the book *On the One Baptism, Against Petilianus*, and book III of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 12.]

### I

Cyprian to his brothers the presbyters and deacons: greetings.

For a long time I maintained my patience, dearly beloved brothers, as though our restrained silence might contribute to peace. But since the unbridled and headlong presumption of certain men attempts by its rashness to disturb both the honor of the martyrs, the modesty of the confessors, and the tranquility of the whole people, one ought no longer to remain silent, lest excessive silence advance to the peril alike of the people and of ourselves. For what danger from offending the Lord ought we not to fear, when some of the presbyters, mindful neither of the Gospel nor of their own position, considering neither the Lord’s future judgment nor the bishop now set over them [Col. 0250C], claim everything for themselves with insult and contempt for their superior—a thing that was never done at all under our predecessors?

[Note: [Col. 0250D]

**II.—With the salvation of our brothers laid low.** So read almost all the old copies and all editions before the Aldine, which reads *against the salvation of our brothers*. But I found this reading in only two ancient manuscripts. Reinhart preferred the old reading. It is moreover supported by these words in Letter XI, p. 21: [Col. 0251C] “laid low by the assault of persecution”;  and Letter XXXVII, p. 50: “laid low by the tempest of persecution.” Optatus of Milevis, book I: “Persecution laid some low in a deadly death.” Lambinus thinks that in Cicero’s *Second Oration Against Catiline* one ought to read: “He now lies there, and has been laid low.” And shortly afterward he says: “For it is more to have been laid low than to lie.” This judgment of Lambinus agrees with these words of Cyprian from Letter XL, p. 54: “Let no one lay low and press down those who lie fallen.”

**But is guilty.** In place of these words, the older Remigianus manuscript reads, “neither in this age nor in the age to come,” which is taken from chapter 12 of the Gospel according to Matthew. Jerome, in the *Letter to Marcella on Blasphemy Against the Holy Spirit*: “Let Novatian, therefore, prove that any of those who were compelled to sacrifice answered before [Col. 0251D] the judge’s tribunal that everything written in the Gospel proceeded not from the Son of God but from Beelzebub, prince of demons; then he will be able to establish that this blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable.”

**Wretched people.** The Fuxensis manuscript reads *innocent people*. What I am about to say does not concern the explanation of this passage of Cyprian; nevertheless, I shall say it because of this word, by which even the wretched are denoted in Ammianus Marcellinus. He writes in book XXVIII that Valentinian, an openly ferocious man, at the beginning of his reign ordered two men by no means wicked to be killed: Diocles, formerly Count of the Largesses of Illyricum, and Diodorus, formerly an *agens in rebus*. “Honoring their memory at Milan,” says Marcellinus, “Christians even now call the place where they were buried *at the Innocents*.” And shortly afterward he says that Christians honored them as martyrs.

**Doing penance.** The old copies vary greatly in this passage. I have adopted the reading that seemed better to me. Meanwhile I note [Col. 0252C] that, in place of *merciful* as written here, the old editions before the Aldine offer *unto mercy*. I also found this reading in the Fossatensis manuscript, the old Compendiensis manuscript, and the more recent Remigianus manuscript. The old Victorinus has both readings. For although *merciful* had first been written in it, *or unto mercy* was added above the line.

397 **Their name is offered.** Five old books have this reading, which is the common one. In two others one reads, *their names are offered*; in the Fuxensis, *for their name*. Four others and the Aldine edition read, *it is offered in their name*. There is a notable passage in Tertullian’s book *On Monogamy*, where, discussing a woman joined to a husband whom she cannot divorce, he says: “Indeed, she prays for [Col. 0252D] his soul, meanwhile asks refreshment for him and fellowship in the first resurrection, and makes an offering on the annual days of his falling asleep.” See the scholia of Jacques de Billy on Gregory Nazianzen’s *Oration in Praise of His Brother Caesarius* and Henry Dodwell’s fifth *Cyprianic Dissertation*. See also volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1129.]

### II

And would that they did not claim everything for themselves while the salvation of our brothers lies prostrate! I could overlook and endure [Note: [Col. 0251B] *I can overlook the insult …*, Oxford] the insult to our episcopate, [Col. 0251A] as I have always overlooked and endured it. But now there is no room for overlooking it, when our brotherhood is being deceived by certain men among you who, while wishing to win favor without regard for the restoration of salvation, do the lapsed greater harm.

Even those who committed it know that what the persecution compelled them to commit is the gravest offense, since our Lord and judge said: “Whoever confesses me before men, him will I also confess before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me, him will I also deny” (Matt. 10:32–33); and again: “All sins and blasphemies [Note: [Col. 0251B] *of men. But whoever*, Bod. 2] will be forgiven the sons of men. But whoever blasphemes against the Holy [Note: [Col. 0251B] *blasphemes the Spirit*, Oxford] Spirit will not have [Note: [Col. 0251C] *does not have*, Ar., Ebor., Lam., NC. 1] forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin” (Mark 3:28–29). Likewise, the blessed Apostle said: [Col. 0251B] “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20–21).

Whoever withholds these things from our brothers deceives the wretched, so that those who could do true penance and make satisfaction to God, the merciful Father, [Note: [Col. 0251C] *who can do penance and make satisfaction to God the Father*, Ar., Lam., [Col. 0252B] Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1] by their prayers and works are led astray so as to perish all the more, and those who could raise themselves up fall still farther. For when sinners guilty of lesser sins do penance for the proper period and, according to the order 19 of discipline, come to *exomologesis*—public confession—and receive through the imposition of the bishop’s and clergy’s hands [Col. 0252A] the right of communion, now, at this raw moment, while the persecution still continues and peace has not yet been restored to the Church herself, they are admitted to communion; their name is offered, and, though penance has not yet been done, *exomologesis* has not yet been made, and the bishop and clergy have not yet laid a hand upon them, the Eucharist is given to them, although it is written: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

[Note: [Col. 0252D]

**III.—Mindful of their position.** So the Fuxensis manuscript and the Aldine edition. The earlier editions and several old books cited in the English edition have *of our law*. Gronovius especially approves this reading in chapter 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*. He says that Cyprian here means the evangelical law, from which he derives ecclesiastical discipline; and to show that his opinion is sound, he cites this passage from the next letter, which reads: “They, contrary to the evangelical law,” and then several similar passages from certain other letters.

**The Lord’s law.** In the Beccensis manuscript it is written, “the observance of the Lord’s law being despised.”]

### III

But now those who have a less complete grasp of the law of Scripture are not guilty. Those who preside will, however, be guilty [Note: [Col. 0252B] *Those who did not keep the law, however, are guilty—those who preside*, Ar., Bod. 2, Lam., NC. 1] and do not set these things before the brothers, so that, instructed by their superiors, they may do everything with fear of God and with the observance given and prescribed by him.

They then expose the blessed martyrs to ill will [Note: [Col. 0252B] *They expose through ill will*, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1] and bring the glorious servants of God into conflict with God’s priest [Col. 0252B]. For, although they, mindful of our position [Note: [Col. 0252C] *mindful of our law*, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2], sent letters to me and asked that their wishes be examined then, and peace granted when our Mother Church herself has first received peace through the Lord’s mercy and divine protection has restored us to his Church, these men—setting aside the honor that the blessed martyrs together with the confessors preserve for us, and despising the Lord’s law and the observance that those same martyrs and confessors command to be maintained—communicate with the lapsed, make offerings, and deliver the Eucharist before the fear of persecution has been extinguished, before our return, almost before the martyrs’ own departure [Col. 0253A]. Even if the martyrs, in the heat of glory and giving less consideration to Scripture [Note: [Col. 0253D] *considering contrary to God’s law*, Oxford; *the law of the Lord*, Leipzig], desired something more, they ought to be admonished by the counsel of the presbyters and deacons, as was always done in the past.

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

**IV.—Admonition.** That is, the censure of suspension, as Baronius interprets this passage of Cyprian when citing it.]

### IV

Thus divine censure does not cease to chastise us by night or by day. For besides the visions of the night, by day as well the innocent youth of children among us is filled with the Holy Spirit; in ecstasy it sees with its eyes, hears, and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us. And you will hear everything when the Lord, who ordered me to withdraw, has restored me to you.

Meanwhile, let certain rash [Note: [Col. 0253D] *Meanwhile, to delay*, Foss., Vict., Mich.], incautious, and arrogant men among you, who give no thought to man, at least fear God, knowing that if they continue any longer in the same conduct, [Col. 0253B] I shall employ that admonition [Note: [Col. 0253D] *if they have continued to avoid admonition*, manuscripts of R.] which the Lord commands me to employ: namely, that for the present they be forbidden to make offerings and that they plead their case both before us, before the confessors themselves, and before the whole people, when, by the Lord’s permission, we begin to be gathered again into the bosom of Mother Church.

Concerning this I wrote letters to the martyrs and confessors and to the people, both of which I directed to be read to you. I wish you, dearly beloved and deeply longed-for brothers, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

**LETTER X.—**We have given this letter the title that we found in very many ancient copies and in the older editions.]

## LETTER X

*(Erasm., III, 15; Pamel., XI; Rig., Baluz., Paris., X; Oxford, Leipzig, XV.)*

### TO THE MARTYRS AND CONFESSORS WHO ASKED THAT PEACE BE GIVEN TO THE LAPSED

[Col. 0253C] **SUMMARY.—**You have the summary of this letter below in the following words, Letter XVI: “When I had discovered that those who had stained their hands and mouths by sacrilegious contact, or had likewise polluted their conscience by impious certificates, were everywhere canvassing the martyrs and corrupting the confessors as well by importunate and ingratiating entreaty, so that thousands of certificates might be granted without discrimination or examination of individuals, contrary to the law of the Gospel, I wrote letters in which, as far as I could by my counsel, I called the martyrs and confessors back to the Lord’s precepts.”

[Note: [Col. 0253D]

**I.—Brothers.** Previously *martyrs* was read, a usage not customary for Cyprian. I corrected it from the old manuscript of Saint-Michel-en-l’Herm. For even in this very letter, writing to them, Cyprian says, “most valiant and dearly beloved brothers.”

**By the bishop and clergy.** So also in the following letter. Therefore, the bishop did not alone lay his hand upon the lapsed returning to the Church. See Petavius’s observation [Col. 0254D] on Epiphanius, heresy LIX, which is that of the Novatians.

**Make offerings for them.** So the old books and old editions. It is also written in this manner in the following letter. Aldus printed *offer peace to the lapsed*. Morel, disregarding that alteration, retained the old reading. Rigault preferred to follow the Aldine edition. The English editors restored the old reading. Reinhart followed the editions of Aldus and Rigault. Such are the dispositions of men.]

### I

Cyprian to the martyrs and confessors, his dearly beloved brothers: greetings.

Concern for our office and fear of the Lord [Col. 0254A] compel me, most valiant and blessed brothers, to admonish you by this letter, so that those by whom the faith of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0253D] *in the Lord*, Oxford] is so devoutly and courageously preserved may also preserve the Lord’s law and discipline. For although all the soldiers [Note: [Col. 0254D] *honorable soldiers*, Verona] of Christ ought to keep the commandments of their 20 commander, it is more fitting that you above all obey his commandments, since you have become to the rest an example both of courage and of the fear of God.

I had indeed believed that the presbyters and deacons present there were admonishing and very fully instructing you concerning the law of the Gospel, as was always done in the past under our predecessors: the deacons, visiting the prison, would guide the martyrs’ [Note: [Col. 0254D] *meeting the martyrs*, Verona] wishes by their counsel and the precepts of the Scriptures. But now, to my soul’s profound grief, I learn not only that the divine precepts are not being set before you there, [Col. 0254B] but rather that you yourselves are being hindered [Note: [Col. 0254D] *found*, Corb., printed edition], so that what you do cautiously toward God and honorably toward God’s priest is undone by certain presbyters who consider neither the fear of God nor the honor of the bishop.

For although you sent letters to me in which you asked that your wishes be examined and peace be given to certain of the lapsed when, after the persecution had ended, we had begun to assemble together with the clergy and to be gathered again, they, contrary to the law of the Gospel and also contrary to your honorable petition, dare—before penance has been done, before *exomologesis* has been made for the most grievous and extreme offense, and before the bishop and clergy have laid a hand upon them for penance—to make offerings for them and give them the Eucharist; that is, to profane the Lord’s holy body, although it is written: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body [Col. 0254C] and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

[Note: [Col. 0254D]

**II.—Hastening.** So in the following letter: “Nevertheless, I do not think we should hasten, nor that anything should be done incautiously and hurriedly.” Letter XII: “Rash haste being laid aside.”

[Col. 0255C] **First it is necessary.** So the old editions before the Aldine. The English editors introduced a new reading that I have found nowhere else. For they printed, “that Mother Church receive peace from the Lord,” omitting the word *first*.

**Your wishes.** The Fuxensis manuscript reads *your petition*.]

### II

The lapsed can indeed be granted pardon for this. For who that is dead would not hasten [Note: [Col. 0254D] *wish*, Corb.] to be brought to life? Who would not hurry to attain his salvation? But it belongs to those set over them to uphold the commandment and instruct those who are either hasty or ignorant, lest those who ought to be shepherds of the sheep become butchers. For to grant things that turn to destruction is to deceive; the lapsed person is not raised up in this way, but is driven all the more toward ruin by offending God.

Let them therefore learn from you what they themselves ought to have taught. Let them reserve your petitions and wishes for the bishop, and await a mature and peaceful time for granting the peace you request [Col. 0255A] [Note: [Col. 0255C] *Let them reserve them, awaiting peace …*, Ar., Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2]. First it is necessary that Mother Church receive peace from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0255C] *Peace from the Lord*, Oxford, from the manuscripts Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, R., Bod. 1, Foss., Corb.; *before the Lord’s peace*, printed edition]; then, in accordance with your wishes, the peace of her children may be considered [Note: [Col. 0255C] *will be considered*, Verona].

[Note: [Col. 0255D]

**III.—Shamelessness.** The same manuscript and the Verona manuscript read, *by certain shameless men*. I also saw it written thus in the manuscript of Saint-Denis of Reims.

**Unviolated.** The same Fuxensis manuscript reads *unstained*.]

### III

And since I hear, most valiant and dearly beloved brothers, that you are being hard-pressed by the shamelessness of certain men and that force is being inflicted upon your modesty, I entreat you with all the prayers I can: mindful of the Gospel, and considering what concessions, and of what kind, your predecessors the martyrs made in the past [Note: [Col. 0256C] *agreed to*, Ar., Lam., Bod. 2], and how careful they were in all things, you too should carefully and cautiously weigh the wishes of those who petition you [Note: [Col. 0256C] *carefully [weigh] the wishes of those who petition*].

As friends of the Lord who will afterward judge with him, inspect the conduct, works, and merits of each person; consider also the kinds and qualities of their offenses, lest, if anything should be either promised by us or done by us precipitately and unworthily, our Church begin to blush even before the pagans [Col. 0255B] themselves. For we are frequently visited and chastised, and admonished that the Lord’s commandments remain uncorrupted and inviolate. I know that this does not cease among you there either: through divine censure it instructs many of you as well in the discipline of the Church.

All this can be done if you regulate what is asked of you with religious consideration, recognizing and restraining those who, showing partiality, either curry favor [Note: [Col. 0256C] *so that they may either curry favor*, Ar., Ebor., Lam., NC. 1] through your benefactions or seek the marketplace of unlawful trafficking.

[Note: [Col. 0255D]

**IV.—Let So-and-so communicate.** The person’s name was placed here. Formerly, as is evident from the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, Jerome, Cassiodorus, and other passages, this was how names that were to be inserted were indicated. A later age substituted the letter N, omitting the old formula.

**Indefinite and blind.** This reading is certain. Nevertheless, five old books and the older editions have *indefinite and definite*. Thus the audacity of copyists introduced many errors into the nocturnal labors of the better writers.

**Whose repentance you see to be close to satisfaction.** So the old books and old editions. Rigault wrote, “whose repentance you know.” I think he took this from the Verona manuscript, in which, undoubtedly through the copyist’s carelessness, these two words, [Col. 0256C] *close to 398 satisfaction*, had been omitted; they are also omitted in the Fuxensis manuscript. That they were absent from the Verona manuscript was noted in the margin of my copy of the Aldine edition. From this it may be gathered that Rigault, who used a copy of that same edition containing the same variant readings as my own, deleted these words from his edition on the authority of that copy. The English editors restored them.]

### IV

Concerning this I wrote letters both to the clergy and to the people, and directed that both be read to you. But you must also bring the following matter under your careful attention and correct it: you should designate by name those to whom you desire peace to be granted. [Col. 0255C] For I hear that certificates are being drawn up for certain persons in such a way that they 21 say: “Let So-and-so . . . communicate with his people,” something the martyrs have never done at all; otherwise an indefinite and blind [Col. 0256A] petition may afterward heap ill will upon us.

For the phrase “So-and-so with his people” extends widely, and twenty, thirty, or more persons may be presented to us who assert that they are relatives, connections by marriage, freedmen, or members of the household of the person who receives [Note: [Col. 0256C] *received*, Lam., Ebor., NC. 1] the certificate. I therefore ask that you designate by name in the certificate those whom you yourselves see and know, and whose repentance you perceive to be close to satisfaction, and thus direct to us letters consistent with faith and discipline.

I wish you, most valiant and dearly beloved [Note: [Col. 0256C] *most faithful*, Verona] brothers, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0256D]

**LETTER XI.—**From this letter Rigault inferred that not only clerics but also laypeople then judged together with the bishop and clergy concerning matters of the greatest importance: namely, the penance of the lapsed, the reception of the lapsed into the Church, the certificates they themselves had obtained from the martyrs, and the peace granted to the lapsed by the martyrs. Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 23: “That a bishop hear no one’s case without the presence of the clergy and the people.” For so it reads in the very ancient manuscript of the Church of Urgell. See Letters XIII, XXVI, XXVIII, and XXXI.]

## LETTER XI

*(Erasm., III, 16; Pamel., XII; Rigault, Baluz., Paris., XI; Oxford, Leipzig, XVII.)*

### TO THE PEOPLE

[Col. 0256B] **SUMMARY.—**The often-cited Letter XIV also gives the summary of this letter: “As far as we could,” he says, “we composed the spirit of the people themselves also and instructed them that they should be preserved within ecclesiastical discipline.”

[Note: [Col. 0256D]

**I.—Falls.** Rigault and the English edition have the singular *fall*. But all the old copies and all the editions contradict this reading. Cyprian also commonly writes in this way.

**I myself also . . . groan.** These words are absent from six ancient manuscripts and from the editions preceding [Col. 0257C] the Aldine. They are nevertheless extant in many old books.]

### I

Cyprian to the brothers who stand among the people: greetings.

I know from myself, dearly beloved brothers, that you groan and grieve over the falls of our brothers, since I myself also groan and grieve together with you for each one, and suffer and feel what the blessed Apostle said: “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29). And again he wrote in his letter: “If one member suffers, the other members suffer with it; and if one member rejoices, the other members rejoice with it” (1 Cor. 12:26).

[Col. 0256C] I therefore sympathize and grieve for our brothers who, having lapsed and been laid low by the assault of persecution, have dragged away with themselves a part of our own entrails and, by their wounds, inflicted an equal pain [Col. 0257A] upon us. Divine mercy has power to give them healing. Nevertheless, I do not think we should hasten [Note: [Col. 0257C] *We hasten, provided, however, that I do not think*, Lam., Ebor., NC. 2], nor that anything should be done incautiously and hurriedly, lest, while peace is rashly claimed [Note: [Col. 0257C] *lest, if peace is rashly claimed*, Ar., Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1], an offense more gravely provoke divine indignation.

The blessed martyrs have sent us letters concerning certain persons, asking that their wishes be examined. When peace has first been given to us all by the Lord and we have begun to return to the Church, then [Note: [Col. 0257C] *Then* omitted by Oxford from manuscript R. 2] the individual cases will be examined in your presence and with you participating in the judgment.

## II

I hear, however, that some of the presbyters, neither mindful of the Gospel, nor considering what the martyrs have written to us, nor reserving for the bishop the honor due to his priesthood and chair, have already begun to communicate with the lapsed, to offer sacrifice for them, and to give them the Eucharist, [Col. 0257B] although these things ought to be approached in due order. For when, even in lesser offenses not committed against God, penance is performed for the proper period, and public confession (*exomologesis*) is made after the life of the person doing penance has been examined, and no one can come to communion unless the bishop and clergy have first laid a hand upon him, how much more carefully and moderately, according to the discipline of the Lord, must everything be observed in these [Note: [Col. 0257C] “How much greater in these,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2.] most grave and extreme offenses? Our [Note: [Col. 0258C] “Our people,” Ar. Lam. Bod. NC. 1. Ebor.] presbyters and deacons certainly ought to have admonished them, so that they might cherish the sheep entrusted to them and instruct them by divine teaching in the path of entreating for salvation. I know equally well both the peaceable disposition and the fear of our people; they would have kept watch in making satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0258C] “Fear in making satisfaction,” Ar. Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. NC. 1.] to God and in supplication, had not certain presbyters deceived them by currying favor with them.

[Col. 0257C] [Note: [Col. 0257D]

### III.—“Let him hasten”

So Manutius and others after him. The earlier editions have “he is able.”

“And your judgment also.” We have decided to retain this passage, which appears in the editions of Manutius and Morel and which we ourselves also found in four ancient books. Pamelius expunged it, declaring that he did so because nowhere in Cyprian had he found so much authority granted to the laity that they were permitted to express their judgment. But that Pamelius is wrong in this is clear from what was said shortly before and from several other passages of the holy martyr. I am surprised, moreover, that Rigaltius omitted this passage from his edition. I am also surprised that the English editors, who had found it in their manuscripts, nevertheless omitted it. I think, however, that they omitted it because it was inconvenient for the criticism they themselves advanced against Rigaltius’s observation concerning the vote of the laity in ecclesiastical judgments. It is also omitted from Reinhart’s edition.]

## III

You, therefore, must guide each one, and by your counsel and moderation temper the spirits of the lapsed in accordance with the divine precepts. Let no one pluck unripe fruit before its time. Let no one commit his ship, battered and pierced by the waves, once more to [p. 22] the deep before he has carefully [Col. 0258A] repaired it. Let no one hasten to take up and put on a torn tunic unless he has seen it mended by a skilled craftsman and has received it back after treatment by a fuller. Let them, I ask, patiently hear our counsel [Note: [Col. 0258C] “My counsel,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 2.]; let them await our return, so that, when by God’s mercy we have come to you, we may, with a greater number of fellow bishops assembled, examine the letters and wishes of the blessed martyrs according to the discipline of the Lord, in the presence of the confessors and with your judgment also [Note: [Col. 0258C] Thus Bod. 2.]. On this matter I have written letters both to the clergy and to the martyrs and confessors, and I directed that both be read to you. I wish you, dearest and most longed-for brothers, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0257D]

### Letter XII

In an old manuscript of the monastery of Saint Eligius at Arras, this letter is said [Col. 0258C] to have been written to the clergy of Capua. This reading might perhaps provide grounds for supposing that canon 48 of the collection of canons of the African Church, which treats of a plenary [Col. 0258D] synod at Capua, ought not to be understood of the council held at Capua in Campania concerning the affairs of the Church of Antioch and of Bonosus, the Macedonian bishop who denied the virginity of the Mother of the Lord, but rather of some plenary African synod held at Capua. This conjecture may be supported by a fragment of an old manuscript in the Bodleian Library, in which it is written that Saint Cyprian, by letters, exhorted Augustine and Felicitas, who suffered in the city of Capua, the metropolis of Campania. At this point the most illustrious Bishop of Oxford, who published that fragment with the works of Saint Cyprian, suspects that the words “the metropolis of Campania” are an addition by a copyist, to whom Italy was better known than Africa. The most learned bishop therefore believed that there had been a city called Capua in Africa. Correctly so. For it is scarcely permissible to suppose that the plenary synod mentioned by the African canon was held anywhere but in Africa. Yet where this African Capua was situated, if indeed there was any such place, is difficult [Col. 0259C] to determine. Capsa, however, was in the province of Byzacena. See Jean Tristan de Saint-Amant, volume II of his *Commentaries*, p. LX.]

# LETTER XII

*(Erasm., III, 17; Pamel., XIII; Rigalt., Baluz., Paris., XII; Oxon., Lips., XXIII.)*

## TO THE CLERGY, CONCERNING THE LAPSED AND THE CATECHUMENS, THAT THEY MAY NOT DEPART EMPTY-HANDED

[Col. 0258B]

### SUMMARY

The subject of this and the following letter is also given below, Letter XIV: “Afterward, however,” he says, “when certain of the lapsed, whether of their own accord or at someone else’s instigation, broke forth with audacious demands and endeavored violently to extort the peace promised to them by the martyrs and confessors, I also wrote twice to the clergy on this matter and directed that the letters be read to them, so that, meanwhile, to mitigate their violence by whatever means possible, if any who had received a certificate from the martyrs were departing from this world, they might, after making public confession and having a hand laid upon them in penance, be sent to the Lord [Col. 0258C] with the peace promised to them by the martyrs,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0259C]

### I.—“Nothing to me”

This is the reading of the old books and old editions. The Verona and Fuxensis manuscripts, however, have “never to have written back to me.” From this, therefore, arose the reading preferred by the editions of Rigaltius and the English editors.

“Nevertheless, since.” See Fernando de Mendoza [Col. 0259D] on canon 32 of Elvira.

399 “Because this season is beset by constant illnesses.” Thus Ruricius, Book II, Letter 32, excusing himself to Caesarius of Arles for not having attended the Synod of Agde, says that he could not be present because of the heat of that region—namely, First Narbonensis, in which Agde is situated: “Because even in summer,” he says, “I am unable to endure that habitual infirmity either in my own residence or in cool places.”

“And their prerogative . . . can.” These words, which are certainly not necessary, are absent from six ancient books. Pamelius nevertheless thinks them Cyprian’s, just as I do not deny that they may be Cyprian’s. Manutius added them, from the Verona manuscript, as I suppose. They appear in the Fuxensis manuscript, which I think was copied from the Verona manuscript or from another similar one, and in the Bec manuscript. They also appear in Morel’s edition.

“Before a deacon.” See Petavius’s treatise on Penance and Reconciliation as received in the customs of the ancient Church, chapters 2 and 4.

“Public confession.” See the same treatise, chapters 1 and 2, and the observations of the same Petavius on Epiphanius, pp. 71, 233, and 230 of the Paris edition.]

## I

Cyprian to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons: greetings.

I am surprised, dearest brothers, that you have written no reply to the many letters [Col. 0259A] that I have frequently sent you, since the welfare or necessity of our brotherhood can surely be properly governed only if, once informed by you, we are able to refine our plan for what must be done. Nevertheless, since I see that there is not yet an opportunity for me to come to you, and summer has already begun—a season beset by constant and serious illnesses [Note: [Col. 0259C] “Besets,” Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. NC.]—I think provision must be made for our brothers. Thus, those who have received certificates from the martyrs and can be aided before God by their prerogative, if they are overtaken by some ailment and danger of illness, may, without awaiting our presence, make public confession of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, even before a deacon, so that, with a hand laid upon them [Col. 0259B] in penance, they may come to the Lord with the peace which the martyrs, in letters written to us, desired to be given them.

## II

Cherish by your presence also the remaining part [Note: [Col. 0259C] “They desired. The part,” Rig.] of the people who have lapsed, and sustain them by your consolation, so that they do not fail in faith in the Lord and in his mercy. For those who are meek and humble, who truly perform penance and persevere in good works [Note: [Col. 0259C] “Had persevered in deeds,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1; “in opinions,” Neap.], will not be abandoned by the Lord’s assistance and aid, so as to prevent provision from being made for them also by the divine remedy. Let your vigilance not fail the hearers (*audientes*, catechumens) either, if any are overtaken by danger and placed at the point of death; nor let the Lord’s mercy be denied to those imploring divine grace. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well and to remember me. Greet the entire brotherhood in my name, and [Col. 0259C] admonish [Note: [Col. 0260C] “Remember to entreat,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] and ask them to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0260C]

### Letter XIII

I have given this letter the following title; I found a double form in all the ancient copies except two, in which one reads “the Eucharist for peace.” It is also read in this way in the old Venetian edition, in the edition issued by Rembolt, and in the [Col. 0260D] editions of Erasmus and Morel. But the Speyer edition, the Manutian edition, and the others have “peace.” The English editors gave a different title according to their own understanding.]

# LETTER XIII

*(Erasm., III, 18; Pamel., XIV; Rigalt., Baluz., Paris., XIII; Oxon., Lips., XIX.)*

## TO THE CLERGY, CONCERNING THOSE WHO HASTEN TO PEACE

[Col. 0260A]

### SUMMARY

Peace must be reached through penance, and penance is performed by keeping the commandments. Those oppressed by illness may, if supported by the intercessions of the martyrs, be admitted to peace; the others must be held back until peace has been granted to the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0260D]

### I.—“Mindful of the divine precept”

We supplied this passage on the authority of the ancient Regius manuscript. Cyprian is referring to the following passage from the Gospel according to Matthew: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.”

“Works.” Thus the manuscript of Saint-Denis at Reims and the Grenoble manuscript, as well as the old Venetian edition and Morel’s. The other old editions and nine old books have “opinions.” I prefer “works,” a word customary for the holy Martyr.]

## I

Cyprian to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons: greetings.

I have read your letter, dearest brothers, in which you wrote that your salutary counsel has not been withheld from our brothers: that, laying aside reckless haste, they should show reverent [Col. 0260B] patience toward God, so that, when through his mercy we have come together, we may [p. 23] deliberate upon every class of case according to ecclesiastical discipline—especially since it is written: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance” (Rev. 2:5). But the person who performs penance is the one who, mindful of the divine precept, meek [Note: [Col. 0260C] “Meek according to the divine precepts,” Oxon.; “divine, meek,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and patient and obedient to the priests of God, wins the Lord’s favor by his acts of service and righteous works.

[Note: [Col. 0260D]

### II.—“By me to you”

In the Bec manuscript one reads: “You should know that I have written fully that letters should be given to you by me.”

“Those who have received a certificate.” See Petavius’s observations on Epiphanius, pp. 233 and 250 of the Paris edition, and Dallaeus, Book VII, *On Human Penalties and Satisfactions*, chapter 16, p. 709.

“Have received.” The Grenoble manuscript has: [.....] [Col. 0261C] “If they have received one and can, through their assistance, be aided before the Lord in their offenses, should they begin to be oppressed by some illness and danger, then, after public confession has been made and a hand laid upon them by you in penance, let them be sent to the Lord with the peace promised by the martyrs. But the others, who have no certificate,” etc.

“Public confession.” That is, satisfaction, if Dallaeus’s interpretation is correct. But Tertullian, in his book *On Monogamy*, says that *exomologesis* is a petition for pardon, because one who asks pardon confesses his offense. See the same author in his book *On Repentance*.

“With peace.” That is, with the viaticum. See Beveridge on canon 13 of Nicaea.

“Of the Church itself.” The old Reims manuscript reads, “first await the public peace of the Church.” Above, Letter X: “The first thing is that the Mother herself should first receive peace from the Lord.”

“The superiors together with the clergy.” Two old books prefer: “That several bishops, assembling together.” Correctly. For Cyprian commonly means bishops by “superiors.”

“With the laity who have stood firm.” Jerome, in his letter to Salvina *On Preserving Widowhood*: “From this we understand that he offers a crown not to those who stand, but a hand to those who lie fallen.”

“But if they are in excessive haste.” This passage is quoted below in Letter LII to Antonianus, p. 67.

“Granting.” I found this word nowhere except in the Grenoble manuscript. In the others one finds either “generously” or “abundantly,” and one or the other of these words there forms the beginning of the next sentence: “Abundantly—the battle line is still engaged.”]

## II

Nevertheless, since you indicate that some are immoderate and urgently press to receive communion at once, and since you wished a rule to be given you by me in this matter, I believe that I wrote sufficiently fully on this subject in my most recent letter to you: namely, that those who have received a certificate from the martyrs and can be aided [Col. 0260C] before the Lord in their offenses by the martyrs’ assistance, should they begin to be oppressed by some illness and danger, may, after making public confession [Col. 0261A] and having a hand laid upon them by you in penance, be sent to the Lord with the peace promised to them by the martyrs. But the others, who provoke ill will although they have received no certificate from the martyrs, must await, under the Lord’s protection, the public peace of the Church itself, since this is the cause not of a few persons, nor of one church or one province, but of the whole world.
