For it accords with modesty, discipline, and the very life of us all that the superiors, assembling with the clergy and also in the presence of the laity who have stood firm [Note: [Col. 0261C] “And the laity who have stood firm,” Oxon.; “with the laity standing by,” Benev.]—to whom honor must also be shown for their faith and fear—should be able to arrange everything with the reverence proper to common deliberation. Moreover, how irreverent, and how destructive even to those who are in haste, it is that, while the confessors themselves, exiled and driven from their homeland and stripped of all their possessions, have not yet returned to the Church, [Col. 0261B] some of the lapsed should hasten to precede the confessors themselves and enter the Church before them! [Note: [Col. 0261C] “And enter the Church before them,” Oxon.] But if they are in excessive haste, what they seek lies within their own power, since the present time grants them more than they ask. The battle line is still engaged, and the contest is held daily. If someone truly and steadfastly repents of what he has done, and the ardor of faith prevails [Note: [Col. 0261C] “The ardor remains,” Ar. NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.], the one who cannot bear delay can be crowned. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well and to remember me. Greet the entire brotherhood in my name, and admonish them to remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0262C]

400 ### Letter XIV

The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius says that this letter was written by Cyprian to the Roman clergy, to whom Cyprian, as was proper, gave an account of his conduct. But that most learned man was mistaken. It was written to those members of the Carthaginian clergy who were then at Rome, as is manifestly evident from the final words of the letter, in which Cyprian writes that he is awaiting them so that, with their counsel, he may arrange and reform the individual matters. Consequently, one cannot infer from this that Cyprian, as a matter of obligation, wrote to the Roman clergy, who, as I said before, demonstrably [Col. 0262D] did not have charge of the universal Church while the see was vacant. The English editors nevertheless believed that the letter was written to the Roman clergy, as did Reinhart, who supplied a new title.]

# LETTER XIV

*(Erasm., III, 5; Pamel., XV; Rigalt., Baluz., Paris., XIV; Oxon., Lips., XX.)*

## TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS RESIDING AT ROME

[Col. 0261C]

[Col. 0262A]

### SUMMARY

He gives an account of his withdrawal and of what he did during it, sending to Rome, in his own defense, copies of the letters he had written to his people—indeed, using the very same words employed there. Compare Letter XXII, to the Roman Clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

### I.—“As the Lord’s commands”

Two old books have: “As we are instructed by the Lord’s commands.”

“Having arisen.” It is surprising that this word—without which the sense can stand, but which nevertheless makes it clearer—is absent from ten of the best ancient copies and from the ancient editions. Manutius was the first to add it; Morel rejected it. It nevertheless appears in six ancient manuscripts.]

## I

Cyprian to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome: greetings.

Since I have learned, dearest brothers, that the things which have been and are being done here by us are being reported to you with insufficient candor and fidelity, I thought it necessary to write this letter to you, so that an account might be rendered to you of our conduct, discipline, and diligence. For, as the Lord’s commands instruct us, immediately after the first outbreak of turmoil had arisen, when the populace had repeatedly demanded me with violent clamor, I withdrew for the time being, thinking not so much of my own safety as of the public peace of the brothers, [Col. 0262B] lest through my obtrusive [Note: [Col. 0262C] “Modest,” Lin.] presence the disturbance that had begun should be provoked still further. Yet although absent in body, I failed neither in spirit [Note: [Col. 0262C] “Nor in writings,” Bod. 1.] nor in action nor in my admonitions to provide, in my humble capacity [Note: [Col. 0262C] “My humble capacity might be able,” Lin.], for our brothers wherever I could, according to the Lord’s precepts.

[Note: [Col. 0262D]

### II.—“To the exiles”

That is, to those who had gone into exile, voluntarily or under compulsion, for the cause of the faith. In certain ancient manuscripts one reads “to those driving into exile.” See Letter XXXIX and the Cyprianic annals for the year 250. See also Charles Guyet, Book II of the *Heortology*, p. 173.

“Fear of God.” The Fuxensis manuscript reads: “and according to the fear of the Lord our humble capacity was able to suggest. But afterward,” etc.

“To strengthen.” Rigaltius printed “to confirm,” contrary to the authority of all the ancient manuscripts and editions. I am surprised that the English editors, who found the reading which we restore even in their oldest copies, retained what was written in Rigaltius’s edition. Reinhart restored “to strengthen.”

“Was not lacking to the deacons.” They occupied the third order of ministry, as Optatus says in Book I, and could do many things in the absence of bishops and presbyters. Cyprian therefore rightly says that priestly vigor was not lacking to them. See the letter of Augustine the presbyter to Valerius.

“Spirit.” The Manutian edition added this word, which was absent from the other editions and is absent from many ancient manuscripts. I found it, however, in eight manuscript codices. Rigaltius printed the plural, “spirits.”]

## II

And what I have done is declared to you by the thirteen letters issued as circumstances required, [p. 24] which I have transmitted to you; in them, to the extent that, according to the law of faith and the fear of God and by the Lord’s prompting, my humble capacity was able to exert itself, neither counsel to the clergy, nor exhortation to the confessors, nor rebuke to the exiles when necessary, nor my address and persuasion to the entire brotherhood to entreat God’s mercy was lacking. [Col. 0262C] But afterward, when the tortures came, my discourse reached our brothers—whether those already tortured [Col. 0263A] or those still imprisoned to be tortured—in order to reinforce and strengthen [Note: [Col. 0263C] Thus Lam. Lin. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1. Ebor.] them. Likewise, when I had learned that those who had stained their hands and mouths by sacrilegious contacts, or had equally polluted their consciences by impious certificates, were everywhere canvassing the martyrs and corrupting the confessors also by importunate, favor-seeking entreaty, so that thousands of certificates were being given out daily, without any distinction or examination of individuals, contrary to the law of the Gospel, I wrote letters in which, by my counsel and so far as I could, I recalled the martyrs and confessors to the Lord’s precepts. Likewise, the vigor of the priestly office was not lacking to the presbyters and deacons, so that certain men, insufficiently mindful of discipline and rushing headlong with reckless haste, who had already begun to communicate with the lapsed, might be restrained [Col. 0263B] through our intervention. We also settled the spirit of the people themselves as far as we could, and instructed them to preserve ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. 0263C] “That they should preserve ecclesiastical discipline,” Bod. 1, 2.].

[Note: [Col. 0263D]

### III.—“Or at someone’s instigation”

In the Fuxensis manuscript one reads: “without some disputant.” In the Dijon manuscript and in one Reims manuscript: “with some disputant or other inciting them.”

“Broke forth.” Thus all the old books and editions, including Reinhart’s. The Verona manuscript has “burst forth.” From this, therefore, arose the alteration which Rigaltius introduced into this passage.]

## III

Afterward, however, when certain of the lapsed, whether of their own accord or at someone’s instigation, broke forth [Note: [Col. 0263C] “Had broken forth,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2.] with audacious demands and endeavored violently to extort the peace promised to them by the martyrs and confessors, I also wrote twice to the clergy on this matter and directed that the letters be read to them. This was so that, meanwhile, to mitigate their violence by whatever means possible, if any who had received a certificate from the martyrs were departing from this world, they might, after making public confession and having a hand laid upon them in penance, be sent to the Lord with the peace promised to them by the martyrs. Nor did I lay down a law in this matter or rashly set myself up as its author. But since it seemed both that honor must be shown to the martyrs [Col. 0263C] and that the violence of those who wished to throw everything into confusion must be restrained, and since, moreover, I had read the letter you had recently sent here to our clergy through Crementius [Note: [Col. 0264C] “Clementius,” Oxon.] the subdeacon, stating that assistance should be given to those who, after lapsing, had been overtaken by illness and, being penitent, desired communion, I thought that I should stand [Col. 0264A] in agreement with your judgment, lest our conduct, which ought to be united and to agree in all matters, should differ in any respect. I expressly directed that the cases of all the others, even though they had received a certificate from the martyrs, should be deferred and reserved until my presence, so that, when peace has been given to us by the Lord and several superiors have begun to assemble together, we may, after sharing counsel with you also, arrange and reform each matter. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well.

# LETTER XV

*(Erasm., II, 4; Pamel., XVI; Rig., Baluz., Paris., XV; Oxon., Lips., XXXVII.)*

## TO MOYSES, MAXIMUS, AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS

[Col. 0264B]

### SUMMARY

The subject of this letter is given below in Letter XXXI, where the Roman clergy say:

“At this point we owe you, and render you, the greatest and most abundant thanks: because you illuminated the darkness of their prison with your letters; because you came to them in the only way you could enter; because by your addresses and letters you refreshed their spirits, already strong through their faith and confession; because, having celebrated their blessed condition with fitting praises, you kindled them to a far more ardent desire for heavenly glory; because you urged forward those already inclined; because, as we believe and hope, you animated by the power of your discourse those who were to become victors—so that, although all this appears to arise from the faith of the confessors and from divine indulgence, they nevertheless seem, in some measure, to have become indebted to you in their martyrdom.”

[Col. 0264C] [Note: [Col. 0264C]

### Letter XV—I.—Celerinus

Saint Cyprian recalls his distinguished merits [Col. 0264D] in Letter 34, to the clergy and people (p. 47), and he is mentioned in highly honorable terms in Pope Cornelius’s letter to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 43, written, as I suppose, at the time when Celerinus was with Cornelius. For I agree entirely with the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius that the Celerinus praised in this letter of Cornelius is the man who was lector of the Church of Carthage. I would observe in passing, however, that Mariano Vittori, in his annotations on the works of Saint Jerome, confused this Fabius, bishop of Antioch, with Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, who is frequently mentioned at the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon. That most learned man was led [p. 401] into this error by a false reading that long ago crept into Saint Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men*, where it is written that Pope Cornelius wrote four letters to Flavian, bishop of Antioch; in place of this, the old copies of that book and the latest edition of Jerome’s works correctly give [Col. 0265C] the name Fabius. This Celerinus’s letter to Lucianus, moreover, appears below among the letters of Saint Cyprian. See the notes on Letter XXXIV.

Saint Jerome, in his letter to Ageruchia, mentions another Celerinus, who was Ageruchia’s father; there is also an old inscription concerning another, published by Reinesius, p. 161. The name of Celerinus the praetor appears in the history of the passion of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria in Surius, vol. V.

“You in him.” Ruricius, Book II, Letter 32: “Our brother and fellow presbyter Capillutus has on this occasion proved doubly welcome to us, since he himself, long desired by us, has come to us, and through your letters he makes a kind of presence of you manifest.”

“Ornaments.” Thus Rigaltius, who was criticized for it [Col. 0265D] in the English edition. Yet he had the Manutian edition as authority for this reading, for it is written in this way there, and nine old copies agree with that text. Certainly the word “encouragement,” preferred by the old editions and likewise by ten old copies, can be a good reading. Reinhart therefore preferred it. It can also be supported by this passage from the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 183): “Very many bishops, who ought to be both an encouragement and an example to the others.”

“In withdrawal.” Two old books have “in private,” which seems better. We nevertheless did not wish to alter it, because nearly all the old books and all the editions have “in withdrawal.”

“Favor from the Lord.” The Chartres and Bec manuscripts have “the Lord’s favor.” Festus says: “*Faventia* signifies a favorable utterance.” Accius, *Oenomaus*, in Nonius Marcellus: “May they accept with every auspicious sign a favorable utterance.” Hadrianus Junius correctly emended this passage in this way.

“Breathing.” The Chartres manuscript has “hoping”; the manuscript of Saint-Arnulf at Metz, “breathing or hoping.”

[Col. 0266C] “The very delay of suffering.” The Fuxensis and Saint-Eligius manuscripts have “the very hour.” The Corbie manuscript has “until the very hour.”

“You do not draw out.” The Chartres manuscript has “you do not diminish.”]

## I

Cyprian to Moyses and Maximus, presbyters, and to the other confessors, his brothers: greetings.

When Celerinus arrived—your companion in faith and virtue and a soldier of God in glorious encounters [Note: [Col. 0264C] “Conflicts,” Oxon.]—he made all of you together and each one individually present to my affections, dearest brothers. [Col. 0265A] When he came, [p. 25] we saw you all in him; and when he spoke sweetly and often of your love [Note: [Col. 0265B] “Concerning love,” Corb.] toward me, we heard you in his words. I rejoice exceedingly whenever such reports are brought from you by such men. In a certain manner, we too are there with you in prison; we believe that we experience with you the ornaments bestowed by divine favor, since we cling so closely to your hearts [Note: [Col. 0265B] “Adhere,” Oxon.]. Your inseparable love [Note: [Col. 0265B] “Our,” Ebor.] joins us to your honor; the love of the spirit does not permit separation [Note: [Col. 0265B] “For separation,” Lam.]. Confession confines you there; affection [Note: [Col. 0265C] “Me here,” NC. Fab.] confines me.

For our part, remembering you by day and night—both when we pray with the congregation at the sacrifices and when, in withdrawal, we pray with private prayers—we ask from the Lord complete favor for your crowns and praises [Note: [Col. 0265C] “The Lord’s favor,” Lam. Bod. 3. NC. 1, 2. Lin.]. But our humble capacity is too small to repay you in kind. You give more when you remember me in prayer, for, already breathing [Note: [Col. 0266B] “Hoping,” Bod. 1. Vat. Thu. Corb.] only heavenly things and meditating solely upon divine things, you ascend to higher summits through the very delay of your suffering, and through the long passage of time you do not draw out [Note: [Col. 0266B] “Diminish,” Bod. 1. Thu. Foss. Corb.] your glories, but increase them. A first and single confession makes a person blessed. You confess as many times as, when asked to leave prison, you choose prison instead through faith and courage. Your praises are as numerous as your days; as many courses of months as there are, so many increases of merit. He conquers once who suffers at once; but the one who remains [Note: [Col. 0266B] “Remains in the battles,” Lam.] and continually engages with pain amid torments without being conquered is crowned every day.

[Note: [Col. 0266C]

### II.—“Annual honor”

The old Reims manuscript has “with the annual honor of glory.”

“Has been marked.” The manuscript of Saint-Arnulf has “is marked.”

“Terrible to the others.” The Chartres manuscript has “of the prison, or to the others.”

“Months.” The old books have *mensuum*. I have also often seen it written in this way in ancient manuscript copies of other early authors. *Mensum* in place of *mensuum* is frequently written in the Theodosian Code. *Mensum* is also read in Aulus Gellius, Book I, chapter 25. See Denis Lambin’s annotations on Cicero’s second speech against Verres.

[Col. 0266D] “Winter.” The text formerly printed was “the winter season.” I removed the word “season,” because most manuscripts do not have it, and it therefore seems to derive from a gloss; and because the ancients used “winter” by itself. Seneca, Letter XV: “One winter undid Hannibal.” Tertullian, Book I *Against Marcion*: “The whole year is winter.” There are other examples as well, but these suffice. See the notes on the *Capitularies*, p. 1185.

“You counterbalanced.” The manuscript of Saint-Arnulf has “you counterbalance,” which seems better.

“Were present.” Thus most of the old books. In five, however, and in the old editions, “clung to” is written. Morel printed “cling to.”

“You harvested.” The Chartres and Saint-Arnulf manuscripts have “you harvest.”

“Purified.” The old editions, including those of Erasmus and Manutius, prefer “tested.” So too do many old books. Pamelius preferred “purified,” though he cited no old book. We followed his emendation because we believed it to be good and saw it confirmed by the authority of some [Col. 0267C] old books.

“Your winepress.” Thus I read in eight ancient manuscripts. But the old editions before that of Pamelius and nine old copies have “our.” Our edition is better.

“You experience your winepress as the prison tortures you.” I found this reading in all the old books and all the editions, except that the Tours manuscript has “you have poured out” in place of “you experience.” I do not know where Rigaltius obtained the text in his edition, where only “torturing” is read. 402 I think, however, that he was led into this error by the Corbie manuscript, in which the word “you experience” was omitted through a copyist’s carelessness. For all else is the same. I am surprised [Col. 0267D] that the English editors preferred Rigaltius’s edition, which introduces obscurity into this passage. The old reading, which is ours, is plain and not at all difficult to understand.]

## II

Let magistrates and consuls or proconsuls now proceed on their way and boast in the emblems of their annual dignity and in their twelve fasces. Behold, heavenly dignity has been marked in you by the splendor of an annual honor and, through the duration of victorious glory, has already passed beyond the revolving circle of a returning year. The rising sun and the moon traversing its course illuminated the world; but for you the one who made the sun and moon was a greater light in prison, and the brilliance of Christ, shining in your hearts and minds, irradiated with that eternal and radiant light the darkness of the place of punishment, terrible and deadly to others.

Winter passed through the successive changes of the months; but while enclosed [Col. 0266B] you counterbalanced the seasons of winter with the winter of persecution [Note: [Col. 0266B] “You counterbalance,” Bod. 1. Thu.]. The mildness of spring followed winter, rich with roses and crowned with flowers; but for you roses and flowers from the delights of paradise were present, and heavenly garlands crowned your heads. Behold, summer is fruitful with the abundance of harvests, and the threshing floor is filled with grain; but you, who sowed glory, harvested the fruit of glory and, standing upon the Lord’s threshing floor, you behold [Note: [Col. 0266C] “Perceive,” Bod. 1. Corb.] the chaff being burned in unquenchable fire, while you yourselves, like purified grains of wheat and precious grain, already purified and stored away, regard the lodging [Col. 0267A] of the prison as a granary.

Nor does autumn lack the season’s spiritual grace for discharging its functions [Note: [Col. 0267C] “Of the season for fleeing,” Lam.]. Outside, the vintage is being pressed, and grapes destined to fill cups are trodden in winepresses. You are rich clusters from the Lord’s vineyard and bunches already heavy with ripe fruit; trodden by the assault of worldly oppression, you experience your winepress as the prison tortures you, and instead of wine you pour out blood. Strong in enduring suffering, you willingly drain the cup of martyrdom. Thus the year unfolds among God’s servants; thus the succession of the seasons is celebrated with spiritual merits and heavenly rewards.

[Note: [Col. 0267D]

### III.—“Companions”

In certain ancient manuscripts “soldiers” is written, a reading I do not approve. I cite it only so that I may occasionally present examples of the liberties taken by ancient copyists.

“Your struggle.” This is, in my opinion, the true reading of this passage, confirmed both by the old editions and by several of the best books. The other reading which follows seems to derive from a gloss. Accordingly, in certain manuscripts one reads “your confession or struggle.” Morel’s edition has only “your confession.” That reading is supported by the words shortly above: “A first and single confession makes a person blessed.”

“Is subdued.” The Chartres and Saint-Arnulf manuscripts have “is subjected.”]

Nor is death feared. Tertullian, in his book *On the Spectacles*, says that Christians are “a people ready for death.” Antoninus Pius, in his rescript to the Asians, as preserved by Rufinus, [Col. 0268C] book IV, chapter 13, says that Christians lay down their lives for their God and willingly embrace death. See Lucifer of Cagliari in his book addressed to Constantius, *On Dying for the Son of God*.]

### III

Blessed indeed are those among you who, journeying along these paths of glory, have already departed from the world and, having completed the course of courage and faith, have come to the Lord’s embrace and kiss, while the Lord himself rejoices. [Col. 0267B] Yet your glory too is no less: still engaged in the contest and destined to follow the glories of your companions [Note: [Col. 0267C] “the glory of your companions” Pem. Lin. Ebor. NC. 1, 2.], you wage the struggle for a long time, and, steadfast with an unmoved and unshaken faith, you daily present to God a spectacle of your virtues. The longer your struggle [Note: [Col. 0267C] “confession” Thu. Bod. 1.], the more exalted is your crown. The contest is one, but composed of a manifold multitude of battles. You conquer hunger and scorn thirst, and by the vigor of your strength you trample upon the filth of the prison and the horror of the penal enclosure. There punishment is subdued, torture is crushed, and death is not feared but desired; for death itself is conquered by the reward of immortality, so that whoever has conquered may be crowned with eternal life [Note: [Col. 0268C] “may be honored” Man. Voss. 1. 3. M. R. Thu. Foss. Corb. “those who have conquered may be honored” Bod. 1. 3.]. What spirit is now in you, how exalted and capacious a heart, in which things so great and of such a kind are pondered, where nothing but God’s [Col. 0268A] commandments and Christ’s rewards are contemplated! There is present only the will of God; and although you are still placed in the flesh, the life already being lived is not that of the present age but of the age to come.

[Note: [Col. 0268C]

**IV.—“From the goodness of the Lord.”** This is the reading of all the editions published before Rigault’s, who printed *voluntate* (“will”) here. He took this reading from an ancient manuscript belonging to the monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims, from the Corbie manuscript, and from the Foix manuscript; for he used these three copies. The same reading occurs in the Tours manuscript. Nearly all the other ancient books, including those mentioned by the English edition, present the good reading, which is ours. Nevertheless, the English editors retained in [Col. 0268D] the text a reading that even the words that follow show to be unsound. Two ancient books give preference to *pietate* (“mercy”).

**“From the indulgence of the Lord.”** In the Tours and Corbie manuscripts the reading is: “from the indulgence and will of the Lord, what you cannot obtain.” See our notes on chapter 36 of Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

**“The discipline of the Gospel.”** Before the Aldine edition, the reading was “the way of the Gospel.” But I found this reading in none of the ancient manuscripts I used. It nevertheless pleased Morel.]

### IV

Now, dearly beloved brothers, remember me; amid your great and divine reflections, turn us too over in your hearts and minds. Let me be present in your prayers and supplications when that voice—made illustrious by the purity of its confession and praiseworthy for the constancy of its enduring honor—penetrates to the ears of God and, with heaven opened to it, is transmitted from these regions of the conquered world to the heights above, obtaining from the Lord’s goodness what it asks. For what do you ask from the Lord’s indulgence that you should not deserve to obtain—you who have thus kept the Lord’s commands, who have maintained the discipline of the Gospel with the sincere vigor of faith, and who, standing courageously with the Lord’s precepts [Col. 0268B] and with his apostles in the incorruptible honor of courage, have strengthened the wavering faith of many by the truth of your martyrdom? Truly witnesses of the Gospel and truly martyrs of Christ, supported by his roots and founded in a mighty mass [Note: [Col. 0268C] “upon the mighty mass of the rock” Bod. 3.] upon the rock, you have joined discipline to courage; you have stirred others to fear God; you have made your martyrdoms into examples. I wish you, most courageous and most blessed brothers, always good health and remembrance of us.

[Note: [Col. 0268D]

**LETTER XVI.—**Of this letter, which first appeared in the Aldine edition, I had two ancient copies, one from my own library and the other from Grenoble. The English editors cite none except the Verona text—that is, as I think, the Aldine edition—just as Rigault sometimes cites the Verona manuscript in place of the Aldine edition. Correctly, in my opinion; for I am convinced that those who prepared that edition used the Verona manuscript.

**“To Bishop Cyprian.”** My manuscript and the Aldine edition have *Papati*. Latinus Latinius likewise read it so in his ancient books. See volume IV of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, page 104. Thus also *Thomati* for *Thomae* in the collation [Col. 0269C] with the Severian texts, and *Menati* for *Menae* in ancient manuscripts of Liberatus. The title *papa* was formerly common to all bishops. Later this displeased the Romans. On this matter see what we once said on Letter 81 of Lupus of Ferrières, and Ludovico Celio Ricchieri, book VI, chapter 43.

**“Granted peace.”** This passage too demonstrates the error of Goulart, who writes that neither in Tertullian nor in Cyprian is it found anywhere that the martyrs granted peace to the lapsed. Furthermore, from Lucian’s letter to Celerinus and the latter’s letter to Lucian, it is evident that Paul and the others held in prison granted peace to the lapsed. And the storm that arose in the African Church because Cyprian refused to grant peace to those to whom it had been conceded by the martyrs is well known. Tertullian says in his book *On Modesty*: “Some who did not possess peace in the Church were accustomed to entreat it from the martyrs in prison.” See Henri Valois’ notes on book VI, chapter 42, of Eusebius’ *Ecclesiastical History*.

**“We wish you.”** The English editors thought that these words contained a threat, namely that if Cyprian did not adequately perform these things, the martyrs would not remain in communion with him. 403 They repeat this observation as certain and entirely unambiguous in their observations on Letter XXII, which was addressed to the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome. But I do not see how excommunication can be understood from these words. Lucian and the other confessors who were with him saw that Cyprian showed himself very reluctant to receive the lapsed to whom the martyrs and confessors—whom they believed to possess great authority in this matter—had granted peace, and to whom Lucian and the others had granted peace in the name of the martyrs and confessors. They took that strict discipline of their bishop badly, considering it contrary to fairness and justice. Because sedition had consequently been stirred up in certain towns of the province, they write that they wish him to have peace with the martyrs and to temper severity with mercy, so that harmony and peace might thus be restored [Col. 0270B] between him, the martyrs, and the agitated people. Are they therefore threatening him with excommunication if he does not acquiesce in their desires? Certainly not. [Col. 0270C] These are prayers, not commands or threats. To wish is one thing, to command another, and to threaten punishment yet another. “No one makes a request in such a way as to threaten,” says Jerome in the *Life of Paul, the First Hermit*. Likewise Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, book I, letter 8: “What is requested is customarily obtained by prayers, not threats; by acts of deference, not insults.” Cyprian indeed complains very vehemently about Lucian’s audacity, yet not because of threats of excommunication, which he does not mention even in a single word, but because Lucian—something neither fitting nor permissible for him—had granted peace to the lapsed in the name of the martyrs and confessors without any intervention by episcopal authority, and because he had set himself up as the leader of the ignorant populace, when it was known that many seditions had been made and fomented at his instigation. This is Cyprian’s complaint against Lucian. Although it was serious and just, Cyprian nevertheless did not threaten him with excommunication. See our annotations on Letter XXX.

**“In the presence.”** This word is absent from my ancient book, where a blank space has been left. In the Grenoble manuscript *Praeterea* (“Furthermore”) is written. The Aldine edition has *presbyter* (“presbyter”). I think the text should read “in the presence of a member of the clergy, an exorcist, and a reader,” to signify that the confessors intended to say that the letter was written in the presence of an exorcist and a reader, using singular *praesente* for plural *praesentibus*, just as I remember reading *praesente nobis* in Plautus. According to Nonius Marcellus, they used to say *absente nobis* and *praesente nobis* for *absentibus nobis* and *praesentibus nobis*, “in our absence” and “in our presence.” He immediately afterward cites a passage from Plautus’ *Amphitryon*. See also under the word *Praesente*, and Salmasius on the writers of the *Augustan History*, page 91.

**“Lucian.”** Cyprian teaches in Letter XXII that this letter was written by him.]

## LETTER XVI

*(Pamelius, XVII; Rigault, Baluze, Paris, XVI; Oxford, Leipzig, XXIII.)*

### THE CONFESSORS TO CYPRIAN

**SUMMARY.—A certificate written by Lucian in the name of the martyrs.**

All the confessors send greetings to Bishop Cyprian. [Col. 0269A] Know that we have granted peace to all concerning whom an account has been established before you [Note: [Col. 0269B] “before you” Verona.] of what they have done after their transgression, and we wished this rule to be made known through you to the other bishops as well. We wish you to be at peace with the holy martyrs. In the presence of a member of the clergy, an exorcist, and a reader, Lucian wrote this.

[Note: [Col. 0270D]

**LETTER XVII.—**Pamelius, in his annotations on Letter XXI, remarks that this letter is spurious. I cannot, however, divine what reasons moved him to think so.

**“Awaits the judgment.”** Better in the Chartres manuscript: “has regard to the judgment.” And I would have printed it so if I had possessed that manuscript—which came late into my hands—at the time this letter was being printed.

**“Patience.”** I found this reading in only two ancient books. The others and the early editions give preference to “penitence.” Either reading may be sound. I therefore wished to change nothing, for I have very often seen *patientia* (“patience”) placed for *poenitentia* (“penitence”) in ancient manuscripts, and conversely. Pamelius preferred the latter reading. Reinhart also approved it.

**“To their own transgression.”** The Chartres manuscript has “to their former transgression.” Correctly; it should be restored accordingly.

**“While they are willing to obey neither us.”** Gronovius rejects this reading [Col. 0271C] in chapter 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, saying that the most blessed Cyprian never possessed such arrogance as to complain that anyone—not merely those people—was unwilling to serve him. I think this observation false and Pamelius undeservedly abused by Gronovius in his edition of this passage. Pamelius was not the first to write it so, since he declares that he reproduced the editions of Aldus and Morel. Cyprian himself says in Letter XXXVIII, “nor moved by the honor of my office.” There are also other passages in which he mentions his dignity and authority as bishop.]

## LETTER XVII

*(Erasmus, III, 19; Pamelius, XXIII; Rigault, Baluze, Paris, XVII; Oxford, Leipzig, XXVI.)*

### TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS, CONCERNING THE PRECEDING AND THE TWO FOLLOWING LETTERS

**SUMMARY.—No account is to be taken of the martyrs’ certificates before peace has been restored to the Church.**

[Col. 0269B] Cyprian sends greetings to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons. The Lord speaks and says: “Upon whom shall I look, if not upon the humble and quiet man who trembles at [Col. 0270A] my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Although we should all be such persons [Note: [Col. 0269B] “be such persons” Lam. Ebor. NC. 2.], at the present time [Note: [Col. 0269B] “all the more” Bod. 1. Aldine; “especially now” Neap.] those in particular ought to be so who must labor, after a grave fall, to become worthy of the Lord through true penitence and complete humility. I have also read the letter of all the confessors, which they wished to be made known through me to all our colleagues, and the peace granted by them to reach those concerning whom an account has been established before us of what they have done after their transgression. Since this matter awaits [Note: [Col. 0270B] “has regard to” M. R. Aldine; “awaits” Oxford, Baluze, Leipzig.] the counsel and judgment of us all, I do not dare to prejudge it or claim for myself alone a matter common to all. Therefore, meanwhile, insist upon the letters that I recently wrote to you, copies of which I have already sent to many colleagues. They have replied [Note: [Col. 0270B] “have written fully” Aldine.] that they approve what we decided and that we must not depart from it until, once peace has been restored to us by the Lord, we can assemble together and examine the cases of individuals. But so that you might also know what my colleague Caldonius wrote to me and what I wrote back to him, I enclosed copies of both letters with [Col. 0271A] my own. I ask that all of this be read to our brothers, so that they may be disposed more and more toward patience, and may not add yet another transgression to their own, by being willing to obey neither us nor the Gospel and by refusing to allow their cases to be examined in accordance with the letter of all the confessors. I wish you, dearly beloved brothers, always good health and remembrance of us. Greet the whole brotherhood. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0271C]

404 **LETTER XVIII.—**The first edition of this letter came from the press of Aldus. I found it in none of the ancient copies I use except one of my own, the Grenoble manuscript, and the one I obtained from the monastery of Saint-Denis at Reims. The English editors possessed one from the Bodleian Library. Pamelius appears to have possessed none, nor did Rigault.

**“Caldonius to Cyprian.”** I added this heading, which is certain, from my own book.

**“The times.”** Thus the Reims and Bodleian manuscripts, with which the editions of Aldus and Rigault agree. But Morel’s and the English edition prefer “the time.” That reading is also found in my manuscript and in the Grenoble manuscript.

**“Arrested a second time.”** We have emended the text thus, although the ancient manuscripts and editions oppose it. The emendation is certain. For Celerinus too will say on page 28, “you, arrested for the name of our Lord,” and Lucian on page 30, “we were imprisoned a second time.” There are also other similar passages in Cyprian’s works. Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* I, chapter 14: “arrested and put in chains.” Rufinus, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16: “Which of them was not arrested for the name of the Lord?” The pontifical acts edited by Emmanuel Schelstrate, page 431: “arrested by Maximian.” Jerome, in his letter to Lucinianus of Baetica: “That young man who followed Jesus covered with a linen cloth escaped naked, casting away his earthly covering, because he had been arrested by the attendants.” Rabanus, in his book *On Computation*, chapter 64: “the Lord, arrested by the Jews that same evening.” Correctly; for in Matthew’s Gospel it is written that the Jews laid hands on Jesus and seized him. Hence, in the acts of Saint Sabinus, bishop and martyr, in book II of our *Miscellanies*, page 47, the emperor Maximian says: “Nevertheless, Conscript Fathers, I shall grant permission that Christians, wherever they are found, be detained by the prefect.” In Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVI: “but the barbarian arrogance laughed, while the envoys were detained until the work on the camp had been completed.” Antoninus of Constantine, in his consolatory letter to Arcadius: “Behold, you have been arrested for a man.” See the acts of the passion of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr.

[Col. 0272C] **“Was supplying the presbyterate.”** Although others think differently, I consider Pamelius’ opinion preferable: that Felix is here understood to have discharged Decimus’ duties in the church entrusted to Decimus’ care, since Decimus, being either an exile or imprisoned after arrest, could not perform his ministry.

**“Nearest to me in chains.”** It seemed right to restore this reading, which is preferred by Morel’s edition and also by the ancient manuscripts. For it is the best. The other reading, which has *vicinus* (“neighboring”) instead of *vinculis* (“in chains”), cannot be sound.

**“Felix and Victoria.”** An ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage published by Mabillon reads: “On the fifth day before the Ides of February, the saints Felix, Victor, and Januarius.”

**“Exiles.”** The Saint-Denis manuscript and my own have *extorrentes*. In the same manuscript of mine *extorrentes* is written in Letter 20, page 29, and *de extorrentibus* in Letter 39, page 52. It is also printed in this form in [Col. 0272D] the Aldine edition. I therefore infer that the Verona manuscript likewise had it, since in the variant readings copied from that manuscript into the margin of my copy of the Aldine edition, no variant is appended at this letter. An *extorris*, moreover, is one who has been cast outside his native soil and native land. Cyprian, in his book *On the Lapsed*, page 184: “One had to abandon one’s country and suffer the loss of one’s patrimony.” See Baronius under the year 25 and in the annotations on the *Roman Martyrology* for January 2. See also Du Cange’s *Latin Glossary*.

**“But also a woman.”** Morel’s edition reads: “but also, whether through herself or through those same persons, a woman named Bona.” The Reims manuscript: “but also over herself by the same deed a woman named Ibono.” The Bodleian: “but also over herself and for the same.” The Grenoble manuscript: “but there also remains, or by the same.” Mine: “but also over herself by the same deed a woman named Bono.” Another Bona is mentioned in the *Roman Martyrology* on April 24, but she was from Reims. Another Bona mentioned by Peter de Natalibus, book VIII, chapter 71, was Egyptian [Col. 0273C] and was called Cordimunda by another name among her fellow Egyptians.

**“Who, in her conscience.”** The Aldine edition and the Reims manuscript read: “who did not commit it in her conscience.” Morel: “who also, in the conscience of what I did not commit.” The same is found in my ancient manuscript. Rigault: “who, in the conscience of what I did not commit.” The Grenoble manuscript: “who did not commit it in her conscience.”

**“They sacrificed.”** Thus Morel’s edition and the Reims manuscript. [Col. 0273D] It is likewise read in my manuscript and the Grenoble manuscript. The other editions have “were sacrificing.” Afterward the same manuscripts and Morel’s edition add, “thus she herself began to say.”

**“Counsel.”** Previously the text read *consultum*. But that word has another meaning, namely something decided after deliberation. It has been emended from the manuscripts.

**“Appear to be obliged.”** The Reims, Grenoble, and my manuscripts read: “appear and ought to receive.” So too Morel’s edition.

**“Greet our people.”** The English editors remark that “your people” should be read. The conjecture appears sound, but the editions and written books oppose it.

**“I wish you.”** We have restored this from the same Reims manuscript, where previously the reading was: “I wish you most fortunate men good health.”]

## LETTER XVIII

*(Pamelius, XIX; Rigault, Baluze, Paris, XVIII; Oxford, Leipzig, XXIV.)*

### CALDONIUS TO CYPRIAN

**SUMMARY.—When some of the lapsed, under the pressure of a new [Col. 0271B] persecution, had confessed Christ and, before departing into exile, were therefore requesting peace, Caldonius consults Cyprian as to whether peace ought to be granted to them.**

Caldonius sends greetings to Cyprian and the fellow presbyters residing at Carthage. The necessity of the times makes it imperative that we not grant peace rashly. But I had to write to you, because those who, after sacrificing, were arrested a second time and became exiles. They therefore seem to me to have washed away their earlier transgression by abandoning their possessions and homes and, doing penance, following Christ. Thus Felix, who was supplying the presbyterate under Decimus and who was nearest to me in chains—I came to know this same Felix more fully—his wife Victoria [Note: [Col. 0271B] “nearest to me in fetters” Bod. 1.] [Note: [Col. 0272B] “his spouse” Oxford, Leipzig.], and Lucius, all faithful believers, became exiles and left behind possessions that the treasury now holds. But [Col. 0272B] there is also a woman named Bona, who was dragged by her husband [Col. 0273A] to sacrifice. Conscious that she had not committed the act herself, because they took hold [Note: [Col. 0273C] “but taking hold” Bod. 1.] of her hands and themselves performed the sacrifice, she began [Note: [Col. 0273C] “thus she herself began” Bod. 1.] to cry out against them, “I did not do it; you did it!” Thus she too became an exile.

Since, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0274C] “Since to me, therefore” Bod. 1.] they were all requesting peace, saying, “By doing penance we have recovered the faith that we had lost, and we have publicly confessed Christ,” although they seem to me to be entitled to receive peace, I nevertheless referred them to your counsel, lest I appear to have presumed anything rashly. If, therefore, any decision is approved by common counsel, write to me. Greet our people. Our people greet you. I wish you, dearly beloved brothers, always good health.

[Note: [Col. 0273D]

**LETTER XIX.—“To be granted.”** I found this reading in fourteen ancient copies. The Speyer edition and the old Venetian edition, although corrupt in this passage, nevertheless show that this reading is sound, for they have *impertinentiam*. Rembolt has *impertitam*.

**“The former stain.”** Most ancient books and editions have “the first stain.”

**“By a stronger courage.”** Some ancient manuscripts prefer “by a later courage.”

**“A book.”** *On the Lapsed*, as Rigault interprets it. [Col. 0274D] The English editors, by contrast, reject Rigault’s opinion and interpret this as a bundle of letters. But they have clearly erred, since Cyprian most plainly distinguishes the book from the letters: “I sent the book together with five letters.”]

## LETTER XIX

*(Erasmus, III, 20; Pamelius, XX; Rigault, Baluze, Paris, XIX; Oxford, Leipzig, XXV.)*

### HE REPLIES TO CALDONIUS

[Col. 0273B]

**SUMMARY.—Cyprian deals with nothing distinctive in this letter except that he agrees with Caldonius’ judgment: namely, that peace should not be denied to those among the lapsed who have merited it through true penitence and confession of Christ’s name and have thereby restored it to themselves.**

Cyprian sends greetings to his brother Caldonius. We have received your letter, dearly beloved brother, a thoroughly sober letter, full of integrity and faith. Nor are we surprised that, being trained and experienced in the Lord’s Scriptures, you conduct everything cautiously and deliberately. You judged correctly concerning the granting of peace to our brothers, who restored it to themselves by true penitence and the glory of confessing the Lord, [Col. 0273C] being justified by the words through which they had previously condemned themselves. Since, therefore, they have washed away every transgression and, with the Lord standing by them, have effaced their former stain through a stronger [Col. 0274A] courage, those who became exiles, were stripped of all their goods, raised themselves up, and began to stand with Christ ought no longer to lie beneath the devil as though prostrate.

And would that the others too, repenting after their fall, might thus be restored to their former condition! So that you might know how we have ordered matters concerning those who now press us and rashly and importunately extort peace, I sent you the book together with five letters, which I wrote to the clergy, to the people, and also to the martyrs and confessors. These letters, already sent to very many of our colleagues, have met with their approval, and they have written back that they too stand with us in the same counsel, in accordance with the catholic faith. Transmit [Note: [Col. 0274C] “to transmit” Ar. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1.] this same material to as many of our colleagues as you can, so that one course of action and one agreement, in accordance with the Lord’s commands, [Col. 0274B] may be maintained among all. I wish you, dearly beloved brother, always good health.

[Note: [Col. 0274D]

**LETTER XX.—**Morel was the first of all to publish this letter. Pamelius afterward reprinted it, admitting that he had possessed no ancient copy of it, and sometimes emending it by conjecture. Latinius possessed two ancient copies, and in his annotations on Cyprian, page 195, it is stated that he successfully emended this letter. That is not true, since it is extremely difficult to emend it well because of the errors that crept into the ancient copies. I possessed two: one from Grenoble and the other from my own library. The English editors cite one Vatican and one Bodleian manuscript. It certainly survives even today in Vatican 199, one of those, as I suppose, that Latinius had examined.]

## LETTER XX

*(Pamelius, XXI; Rigault, Baluze, Paris, XX; Oxford, Leipzig, XXI.)*

### CELERINUS TO LUCIAN

**SUMMARY.—Celerinus requests from the confessors at Carthage peace for his sisters at Rome who had lapsed.**

[Note: [Col. 0274D]

**I.—“Of this world.”** The previous reading was *hujusmodi* (“of this kind”), which makes no sense. The English editors produced the true reading. [Col. 0275B] Latinius remarks that it occurs in his copies. It is likewise read in my manuscript and the Grenoble manuscript.

[Col. 0275C] **“You knew.”** Although this reading occurs in the editions of Morel, Pamelius, and Rigault, as well as in the Vatican manuscript, and although it is confirmed by the two ancient copies I use—even though my manuscript mistakenly has “I knew”—the English editors nevertheless preferred “you may write.” But if they had noticed that Celerinus is complaining that Lucian had not written to him by Montanus, whom Lucian knew would be coming to him, they would have thought differently. It is therefore certain that the reading we have retained is sound.

**“For, so that to you.”** Here we have reproduced the reading of the ancient books and editions. The English editors, by conjecture—for they cite no ancient copy—wrote: “For, so that I too may then be called your most humble servant or brother, if I am worthy; Celerinus would be heard.” Certainly Latinius, when he saw in the Vatican manuscript what is found in my manuscript and the commonly printed editions, thought it should be read approximately as the English editors printed it. The Grenoble manuscript reads: “that you had forgotten to write to me, so that I too may speak of your most humble servant or brother,” etc.

[Col. 0275D] 406 **“When I was … in so.”** That is, when I was confined in prison on account of the Lord’s name.

**“That if before.”** This is the reading of Morel’s edition. The same occurs in my ancient book and in the Bodleian. The Grenoble manuscript wrongly reads, “that by me with that blood.” Pamelius, supposing that Lucian would have been unable to write back after shedding his blood for Christ, believed that a negation was missing from this passage and did not hesitate to insert it. Latinius disapproved of this boldness, judging that the sentence needed no negation. The English editors held the same view regarding the negation, but transferred the argument to something else. For they interpret this otherwise sufficiently obscure and involved passage as though Celerinus, fearing that Lucian might depart before granting peace and pardon to his sisters who had lapsed, had asked the Lord to take pity on them and, after Lucian’s departure, to grant them the pardon that Lucian, forestalled by death, had not granted. But this interpretation cannot be accepted, since Celerinus’ sisters [Col. 0276B] had not previously been mentioned. The true and genuine meaning of this passage, therefore, in my judgment, [Col. 0276C] is as follows. Celerinus had complained about Lucian’s negligence in writing: although Lucian knew that Montanus would be coming to Celerinus, he had written nothing through him about his health or about what was happening where he was. Celerinus now asks that if Lucian has breathed out his spirit before these letters reach the place where he is staying, he should write nothing back, but that he should write back if he is still alive when they reach him.]

### I

Celerinus sends greetings to Lucian. When I wrote these things to you, my lord and brother, I was both joyful and sad: joyful because I heard that you had been arrested for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, and had confessed his name before the magistrates of this world; but sad because, since the time I escorted you away, I have never [Col. 0274C] been able to receive a letter from you. And just now a twofold sadness has fallen upon me, because, although you knew that Montanus, our common brother, would be coming from you in prison to me, [Col. 0275A] you gave me no information about your health or about what is happening where you are. But this is customary [Note: [Col. 0275B] “And this is customary” Oxford.] among God’s servants, especially those who are engaged in confessing Christ. For I know that each now pays no attention to the things of this age, because he hopes for the heavenly crown.

I therefore said that perhaps you had forgotten to write to me. For, so that I too may be called your most humble servant or brother, if I shall have been [Note: [Col. 0275B] “may be called, if I shall have been” early editions; “that you might hear” P. Salv.] worthy to hear the name Celerinus, nevertheless, when I too was in so flourishing a confession, I remembered my brothers of longest standing, and in my letters reminded them that their former affection remains with me and mine even now. Yet I ask, dearest brother, of the Lord that, if you wash yourself first in that holy blood—if you suffer for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ before my letter reaches you in [Col. 0275B] this world—or if they have reached you now, you should write back to me concerning these matters. May he whose name you have confessed thus crown you [Note: [Col. 0275B] “If he crown you” Vat.]. For I believe that even if we do not see one another in this world, in the future we shall nevertheless embrace one another before Christ [Note: [Col. 0275B] “before or with Christ” Bod. Vat.]. Ask that I too may be worthy [Note: [Col. 0275B] “through you may I be worthy” early editions.] to be crowned among your company.

[Col. 0276A]

[Note: [Col. 0276C]

**II.—“In the joy of Easter.”** The Grenoble manuscript has “on this day of joy.” Cassiodorus, book IV, Letter 42: “The complaint of Marcianus and Maximus has assailed us, since during the paschal days they were wounded by the blow of a father’s mourning and at the very time of joy,” etc.

**“Easter.”** The ancients wrote it thus, *Paschae*. Tertullian, in his book *On the Crown*: “We enjoy the same immunity from Easter Day until Pentecost.” The same author, book II *To His Wife*: “Who, finally, will without anxiety tolerate her spending the entire night at the solemn observances of Easter?” Likewise book IV *Against Marcion*: “For from all the festivals of the Jews he chose Easter Day.” The Council of Cabarsussi: “before the day of the coming Easter.” [Col. 0276D] The appendix to the memorandum of the emperor Honorius in the case of Eulalius and Boniface, who were contending over the Roman episcopate, as given by Baronius: “the approaching days of holy Easter.” Arator, book II of the *Acts of the Apostles*: “You celebrate the joys of Easter with the chosen thief.” Rufinus likewise uses it in the books of the *Ecclesiastical History* and in the books of the *Recognitions of Saint Clement*. See Sirmond’s notes on the First Council of Arles.

**“May come to the aid.”** I added this word by conjecture merely to establish the sense in this way. If anyone prefers to substitute another word, I do not object.

**“You will ask.”** The Grenoble manuscript reads: “it must be requested that he come to the aid of so dreadful a shipwreck.”

**“For our sisters.”** Thus the English edition, confirmed by the Grenoble manuscript. Latinius likewise testifies that he saw it written so in two ancient manuscripts. Mine reads “through our sisters.”]

### II

Know, however, that I have been placed in great tribulation [Note: [Col. 0276B] “know that I have been greatly afflicted” early editions.], and, as though you were present with me, I remember our former affection day and night. God alone knows. Therefore I ask you to assent to my desire and grieve with me over the death of my sister, who fell away from Christ in this devastation. For she sacrificed and provoked our Lord to anger. This seems manifest to us. On account of what she did, I have spent—and continue to spend down to the present day—tearful days, weeping day and night in sackcloth and ashes on this day of Easter joy [Note: [Col. 0276B] “tearful days” Vat.], until the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ [comes to aid] and compassion comes through you or through those lords of mine who shall have been crowned, whom you are to ask that those dreadful shipwrecks may receive pardon [Note: [Col. 0276B] “from whom it must be requested, if he should come to the aid of so dreadful a shipwreck” Vat.; “may he come to the aid of so dreadful a shipwreck” Leipzig.].

For I have remembered [Note: [Col. 0276B] “For I am mindful” Vatican.] your former affection, because you grieve with everyone [Col. 0276B] for our sisters, whom you too know well—that is, Numeria and Candida. Because they have us as brothers, we ought to keep vigil on account of their sin. For I believe that, in accordance with their penitence and the works they performed among our colleagues—exiles who came from you, from whom you will hear directly about their works [Col. 0277A]—Christ will now grant them pardon at the petition of you, his martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0277B]

**III.—“And now above them.”** My manuscript reads: “and now, having been made above them, he recognized the priests of God, that is, a minister.” The Grenoble manuscript has the same, except that *antistes* (“priest”) is singular there. Sidonius, book VII, Letter 17: “I ask that our brother Auxanius be abbot, but that you be even above the abbot.”

**“To your brothers.”** Thus the ancient books and editions. The English edition wrongly has: “to your brothers and mine, my lords.”

**“Etecusa.”** Gisbert Cuper, in a letter to Paulus Voetius, remarks that the bishop of Chester wrote back *Aecusa*. Julius Firmicus used *Aecusa* in certain editions, but *Aethusa* in others. Yet that Aecusa differs greatly from Etecusa. (Dodwell’s conjecture in his *Cyprianic Dissertation* on Letter 22 (?) that *aecusam* should be read would certainly not be negligible; for they were called ἀεκοῦσαι (*aekousai*, “unwilling women”) when, overcome by force and insults against their will, they yielded—if only the manuscripts supported it. GOLDAST.)]

**The Three Fates.** Thus the Vatican manuscript cited in the English edition, two old copies belonging to Latinius, and one from my own library. Nor is there any doubt that this is the true reading. Yet this passage, which, in my judgment at least, presents no difficulty, has been greatly vexed by interpreters who thought that reading unsatisfactory. And yet I am convinced [Col. 0277D] that no reading other than this can be correct. Moreover, passages drawn by the most learned men from the pontifical records to explain this passage confirm it. For it cannot be denied that at Rome, from which this letter was written, there was a place called the Three Fates (*Tria Fata*). Procopius is an ample witness to this fact in book I, chapter 25, of *The Gothic War*, where he writes that Janus had a shrine in the Forum, opposite the Curia, above the Three Fates. It is clear, moreover, that the woman discussed in this letter of Celerinus had gone up—namely, to the Capitol—to sacrifice, 407 but had stopped at the Three Fates and had come back down from there, evidently moved by repentance.

Now since Procopius writes that the Three Fates were near the shrine of Janus, opposite the Curia; since P. Victor places the temple of Janus near the Forum; since Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II, teaches that the Forum lay in the space midway between the Capitol and the Palatine, on the plain beneath the Capitol; since Onofrio Panvinio, in his description of the city of Rome, observed that the Palatine Hill had the Roman Forum and Capitol to the west, and the Sacred Way to the north; since the author of the *Pontifical Records* relates [Col. 0278B] that the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which stood at the Three Fates, was situated on the Sacred Way—which Ovid, in book III of the *Tristia*, places near the Forum and the Palatine, where Cicero, in his speech *For Gnaeus Plancius*, teaches that the Arch of Fabius stood; since Seneca, in chapter II of the book *That the Wise Man Cannot Suffer Injury*, teaches that this arch was near the Rostra; since Asconius Pedianus, in his commentary on the first pleading against Verres, wrote that the arch was situated on the Capitoline slope and that from there a direct road ran to the Forum, through the Forum and through the Three Fates; and since Dio Cassius, book LIV, and Herodian, book IV, say that the approach to the Forum was by way of the Sacred Way—it is manifest that the reading we have retained is true.

I therefore wish that the most learned men had not been so ready to accept Gronovius’ conjecture, who writes in chapter 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers* that *dryfacta* should be restored in this letter of Celerinus in place of *Tria Fata*, since it is certain that this emendation was attempted against the authority of all the ancient books and editions, and without any necessity. It was therefore rightly and deservedly rejected in the English edition.

Furthermore, that Celerinus was then at Rome—which we must now establish—has already been noted by others and is clear from a passage in the letter itself, page 29, where Celerinus says that the case of certain women had been deferred until a bishop should be appointed; that is, [Col. 0278D] until the see of Peter, which had been vacant after Fabian’s death, should receive a bishop. It is especially clear from Letter 22, page 32, in which Cyprian writes that he is sending to the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome Celerinus’ letter to Lucianus, so that they may ascertain whether it is genuine. That it was sent through Crementius the subdeacon may readily be inferred from Letters IV and XIV.

**Those in authority.** That is, those members of the clergy who governed the Roman Church after Fabian’s death.]

### III

For I have heard that you received the ministry of the more illustrious confessors.

[Note: [Col. 0277B] *Splendidly, the ministry of all of them*, Vat.]

O happy man, to receive, even while sleeping on earth, the fulfillment of the prayers you always desired!

[Note: [Col. 0277B] *Receive*, printed editions.]

You wished to be sent to prison for his name; this has now befallen you, as it is written: “May the Lord grant you according to your heart” (Ps. XIX, 5). And now, having been made God’s overseer over them, the same minister has acknowledged it.

[Note: [Col. 0277B] *For the minister*, Bod. 1.]

I therefore ask and entreat you, lord, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to report the matter to your other colleagues—your brothers and my lords—and to ask them that whichever of you is first crowned should remit such a sin to these sisters of ours, Numeria and Candida. For I have always called this very woman Etecusa; God is our witness [Col. 0277B] that she paid gifts on her own behalf so that she would not [Col. 0278A] sacrifice. But she appears only to have gone up as far as the Three Fates,

[Note: [Col. 0277B] *Three deeds*, printed editions.]

and to have come back down from there. I therefore know that this woman did not sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 0278B] *These women*, Vat.]

Their case has now been heard, and those in authority ordered that they should remain in their present condition until a bishop is appointed. But I ask that, through your holy prayers

[Note: [Col. 0278B] *Works*, Vat.]

and petitions, in which we

[Note: [Col. 0278B] *for us*, Vat.]

place our trust, since you are both the friends and witnesses of Christ, you

[Note: [Col. 0278B] *who*, Vat.]

grant pardon in all things.

[Note: [Col. 0278D]

### IV.—*Sanctimonio*

Thus the old books read both here and elsewhere. I could produce many examples to show that the ancients commonly wrote it this way. But I refrain, because I think readers will readily give me credence. In the same way they said *blasphemium* in place of *blasphemia*, as we noted on Marius Mercator, page 451. I add, however, that the most learned monks to whom we owe the new edition of Saint Augustine’s works printed *sanctimonii et continentiae* in Letter LXI. Likewise in the rescript of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Aurelian against the Pelagians.

[Col. 0279C] **But also Statius.** Thus my manuscript and the Grenoble manuscript. It is also clear that the old copies belonging to Latinius had this reading. Pamelius had likewise judged that this was how it should be read, where previously *statim* (“immediately”) had been written. See the notes on Letter LIV.

**Macharius.** I know perfectly well that *Macarius* ought to have been written if it were established that the Africans wrote as the Greeks did. But since I found this word written with an aspirate in ancient copies of Cyprian, and knew, moreover, that the Africans and most Latin writers spelled certain words differently—as is evident in *catecuminus*, *acolytus*, and also *Arrius*—I judged [Col. 0279D] that in this passage I ought to follow the spelling of the ancient copies of Saint Cyprian. Francis Maria Florentinius also writes in his edition of the very ancient martyrology, on the sixth day before the Ides of December: “In Africa, the saints Primus, Macharius, and Justus.” And in Saint Augustine’s Letter XXIX, in the new edition, *Machario* is written in accordance with the authority of the Cistercian manuscript from which it was edited.]

### IV

I therefore ask, dearest lord Lucianus, that you remember me and grant my petition. By that holy crown which Christ has bestowed upon you not only in confession but also in the holy life in which you have always run your course—always being an example of the saints and a witness—I ask that you report this deed to all my lords, your brothers the confessors, so that these women may receive assistance [Col. 0278B] from you.

For you ought to know this, lord brother: not only am I asking this on their behalf, but Statius and Severianus and all the confessors who came here from you also ask it. The women went down to meet them at the harbor, took them up into the city, ministered to sixty-five of them, and have supported them in everything to this very day. For they are all staying with those women. Yet I ought not to burden that holy heart of yours any further, since I know that you act with a ready will.

Macharius greets you, together with his sisters Cornelia and Emerita, who rejoice in your glorious confession, and in that of all the brothers. Saturninus also greets you: he too has wrestled with the devil; he too has courageously confessed the name of Christ;

[Note: [Col. 0279C] *has confessed*, Oxford.]

he too, there under torture by the claws, [p. 30] courageously confessed; and he too most earnestly asks and petitions for this. Your brothers Calphurnius and Maria and all the holy brothers greet you. You must also know [Col. 0279B] that I have written [letters] to my lords, your brothers; I ask that you be so good as to read them to them.

[Note: [Col. 0279D]

**LETTER XXI.**—I had only two old copies of this letter, one from the city of Grenoble and another from my own library. The English editors cite one from the Vatican, doubtless, as I think, the one marked number 199 in the Vatican Library. Latinius testifies that he had it in his manuscripts, [p. 408] but in so corrupt a state that its meaning could scarcely be understood. Pamelius and Rigaltius acknowledge that they had no old copy of it.]

## LETTER XXI

*(Pamel., XXII. Rig., Baluz., Paris., XXI. Oxford, Leipzig, XXII.)*

### LUCIANUS REPLIES TO CELERINUS

**SUMMARY.—Lucianus grants Celerinus’ petition.**

[Note: [Col. 0279D]

### I.—*The greater serpent*

That is, the emperor Decius, whom Lactantius calls an accursed beast in his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. Thus Prudentius, in his poem on Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Tarragona, calls [Col. 0280C] the governor Aemilianus a bloodstained serpent. Thus Huneric, king of the Vandals, is called a torpid old serpent in the account of the passion of the martyrs who suffered at Carthage under his reign on the sixth day before the Nones of July. And the author of the *Life of Pope Gregory IX*, in Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1238, § 72, calls Emperor Frederick II a twisting serpent. Nebuchadnezzar is called a great eagle by Jerome and Theodoret, as Fronto Ducaeus notes in his annotations on the first volume of Saint John Chrysostom’s works. These words of Cyprian about Celerinus in Letter XXXIV, page 47, refer to Decius: “At the beginning of the persecution, he engaged in combat with the very prince and author of the assault”; [Col. 0280D] and perhaps also the things he says in Letter XLVI, page 60, about the poisonous cunning of an evil man, like that of a serpent.

**Quartermaster of Antichrist.** Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, calls Constantius, the Arian emperor, the forerunner of Antichrist, which amounts to the same thing. Lactantius, by contrast, in book IV, chapter 11, calls Christ the quartermaster of God’s temple, that is, of the Church. On quartermasters, see what is said below on Letter LXXXI.

**I know you.** Although Morel’s edition, from which the others derive, has *tenoris*, the old books—including one cited by Latinius—have *te novi* (“I know you”). I therefore judged that this reading should be retained, both because it rests upon the authority of the old books and because it appears better.]

### I

Lucianus to his lord Celerinus—if I should be worthy to be called his colleague in Christ—greetings.

I received your letter, dearest lord and brother, in which you placed so great a burden upon me that, because of the weight of it,

[Note: [Col. 0279C] *under a perpetual burden*, printed editions.]

I almost fell away from the great joy with which I exulted at reading, after so long a time, the letter that I myself had desired to read, in which, through the favor of your great humility, you deigned to make mention of me;

[Note: [Col. 0279C] *to be mentioned*, Oxford, from Vat.]

for in writing to me you said:

[Note: [Col. 0279C] *you say*, printed editions.]

“If I should be worthy to be called your brother”—I, a man who, in the presence of lesser men, confessed the name of God with fear. But you, by God’s will, confronted the greater serpent, the quartermaster of Antichrist,

[Note: [Col. 0280C] *the greater and more savage*, Vat.]

and not only confessed Christ but terrified and conquered that serpent with those declarations and divine words. From these I know you to be, as it were, a lover of the faith and jealous guardian of the discipline of Christ, and I rejoice that you live with vitality in that discipline.

Now, dearest brother, already to be numbered among the martyrs,

[Note: [Col. 0280C] *those to be numbered*, Vat.]

you chose to burden us with your letter, in which you informed us about our sisters. On their behalf, would that it were possible for us to make mention of them without so great a crime having been committed! We would certainly not be bowed down [Col. 0280B] with such tears as we are now.

[Note: [Col. 0280D]

### II.—*Since in part*

I restored this reading, following the authority of my old book and the Grenoble manuscript. The Vatican manuscript cited in the English edition has *quoniam partem*. The editions read *quod tam placuit*.

[Col. 0281C] **They would afflict.** Thus Morel’s edition and the rest. The manuscript of Latinius and my own read, “so that it did not afflict.” The Grenoble manuscript reads, “so that it was not being effected.”

**Bassus in the *pejerarium*.** Thus Morel. Rigaltius conjectured that it should read *in petrario*, that is, “in the quarry.” The Vatican manuscript and that of Latinius have *in perario* or *imperario*, which may support Rigaltius’ conjecture. One Bodleian manuscript has *pegrario*; mine, *pignerario*; the Grenoble manuscript, *imperario*, as in Latinius’ manuscript. The English editors placed Rigaltius’ conjecture in the text. Maximus, bishop of Turin, says in his homily *On Not Fearing Carnal Enemies*: “*Piraterium* in Latin can be called a trial.” This homily formerly appeared in editions of Saint Ambrose’s works. But the Benedictine monks correctly observed that it is by Maximus.

**Under examination.** Below, Letter LXIX, page 123: “so many confessors interrogated and brave—not that the truth might be sought, but that through the torments of examination they might be compelled to abandon the truth.” Hence, in the acts of Saints Lucianus and Marcianus, those whose duty it was to put defendants to the question and harry them with tortures were called *quaestionarii*, “torture-officers.” They were also called executioners, as our former and most learned friend Charles du Fresne du Cange shows in his Latin glossary. The torments of examination sometimes compelled innocent people to confess crimes of which they were accused, as we noted in the notes on the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*, page 599.

**Mind.** The Vatican manuscript and mine, as well as the one that belonged to Latinius, have “soul.”]

### II

You ought to have known what has taken place among us. While the blessed martyr Paul was still in the body, he called me and said to me: “Lucianus, I tell you before Christ that if anyone, after I have been summoned away, asks you for peace, grant it

[Note: [Col. 0280C] *may you grant*, Oxford.]

in my name.” Moreover, all of us whom the Lord deigned to summon amid so great a tribulation jointly sent letters granting peace to everyone.

You see, therefore, brother, that we acted partly because of what Paul commanded me and partly because of what all of us who were in this tribulation decided, when we were ordered

[Note: [Col. 0280C] *when we ordered*, printed editions.]

to be killed by hunger and thirst in accordance with the emperor’s decree and were shut up in two cells, [Col. 0281A] so that they might afflict us with hunger and thirst. Moreover, the fiery heat produced by the instrument of our confinement was so intolerable

[Note: [Col. 0281C] “The fiery heat; and our confinement was intolerable,” Oxford.]

that no one could bear it. But now we have attained that very glory.

And therefore, dearest brother, greet Numeria and Candida. In accordance with the command of Paul and of the other martyrs, whose names I give below—Bassus in the *pejerarium*, Mappalicus under examination, Fortunio in prison, Paul after examination, Fortunata, Victorinus, Victor, Herennius, Credula, Herena, Donatus, Firmus, Venustus, Fructus, Julia, Martialis, and Aristo—who, by God’s will, were killed by hunger in prison, they are to have peace. Within a few days you will hear that we too are to become their companions. For on the day on which I wrote this letter to you, it had already been eight days since

[Note: [Col. 0281C] *For as*, Oxford.]

we were shut up again. Moreover, during the preceding eight days, for five intervening days we received a little bread [Col. 0281B] and a measured ration of water.

I therefore ask, brother, that when the Lord begins to give peace to the Church here, in accordance with Paul’s command and our deliberation, they should have peace after their case has been presented before the bishop and an *exomologesis*—a public confession—has been made: not only these women, but also those whom you know to be dear to our hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0281D]

### III.—*Companions*

Thus Morel’s edition. The English editors preferred *omnibus* (“all”), attesting that they had seen it written thus in the Vatican manuscript. So too the manuscript of Latinius. But the Grenoble manuscript [Col. 0282C] has *comitibus* (“companions”). Mine has *motibus*, which is closer to *comitibus*.

**Maris, Collecta.** This reading is found in Morel’s edition, in my old book, and in the Grenoble manuscript. Pamelius altered it according to his own judgment, without the authority of any old copy, and printed “Macarius, Cornelia,” because he saw that the feast of Macarius and ten other martyrs was celebrated on the sixth day before the Ides of April. Yet the name Maris is by no means unknown in ecclesiastical history. Maris, bishop of Chalcedon, was distinguished in the time of Emperor Julian. Another Maris, likewise bishop of Chalcedon, attended the Council of Chalcedon; Maris of Doliche attended the First Council of Constantinople. Well known is the controversy at the Fifth Council concerning the letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, [Col. 0282D] to Maris the Persian, which was also mentioned at Ephesus. Theodoret mentions the monk Maris in chapter 20 of his *Religious History*.]

### III

All my colleagues greet you. 31 Greet the Lord’s confessors who are there with you and whose names you communicated, among whom are Saturninus with his companions, and also my colleague, and Maris, Collecta and Emerita, Calphurnius and Maria, Sabina, Spesina, and the sisters Januaria, Dativa, and Donata. We greet Saturus with his companions, Bassianus, and the entire [Col. 0282A] clergy; Uranius, Alexius, Quintianus, Colonica, and all whose names I have not written because I was already weary. They therefore ought to forgive me.

I wish you good health—Alexius and Getulicus, the silversmiths, and the sisters. My sisters Januaria and Sophia, whom I commend to you, greet you.

[Note: [Col. 0282D]

409 **LETTER XXII.**—Of the old copies that I use, I found this letter, first printed in the Manutius edition, only in the Foix manuscript, the Grenoble manuscript, one of my own, and the one preserved in the monastery of Saint Denis at Reims. The English editors had a single copy from the Bodleian Library. Pamelius had found it in an English manuscript belonging to John Harris.]

## LETTER XXII

*(Pamel., XXIII. Rigalt., Baluz., Paris., XXII. Oxford, Leipzig, XXVII.)*

### TO THE CLERGY RESIDING AT ROME, CONCERNING THE MANY CONFESSORS, THE SHAMELESSNESS OF LUCIANUS, AND THE MODESTY OF THE CONFESSOR CELERINUS

**SUMMARY.—In this letter Cyprian informs the Roman clergy of the seditious demand of the lapsed that they be restored to peace, and of the shamelessness [Col. 0282B] of Lucianus. To make these matters better understood, Cyprian arranges for both his own letters and those of Celerinus and Lucianus to be transmitted.**

[Note: [Col. 0282D]

### I.—*After letters had been written*

Morel’s edition, my manuscript, the Grenoble manuscript, and one Bodleian manuscript have: “After letters had been written to you.”

**Long since through his lack of skill.** The word *jampridem* (“long since”) is absent from the Reims manuscript. The Foix manuscript reads *imperitia sua pridem se* (“long since through his own lack of skill”). This reading appears to agree with what Cyprian said shortly before about Lucianus: that he was less firmly grounded in the reading of the Lord’s teaching. He is again called [Col. 0283B] unskilled in this very letter. Saint Jerome says in his letter to Nepotianus on the life of clerics: “To excite the admiration of an ignorant crowd by rapidity of speech is the mark of unlearned men.” And below: “Nothing is as easy as deceiving a cheap rabble and an unlearned assembly by fluency of tongue, for it admires all the more whatever it does not understand.” Arnulf of Lisieux, Letter XXXII: “There are some who esteem difficult things more highly because they understand them less, and who regard as childish whatever the pleasing clarity of lucid discourse illuminates.” Quintilian’s report, book VIII, chapter 2, about a certain teacher who ordered his pupils to make obscure whatever they said, is well known.

**A written certificate.** The Foix manuscript, in which this letter is copied twice, has in one place: “a written certificate was to be given collectively to many in Paul’s name.”

**Many.** The Saint-Denis manuscript of Reims reads *ructis*; the Foix manuscript, *rustis*.
