In the *Life of Saint Tygris*, a virgin of Maurienne in Savoy, published in the fifth volume for June of the Bollandists, page 75, one reads: “He also granted the Cottian valley, built around Maurienne, and the *rustes* and *fivum*, which would minister to the walls and roofs of the church.” There Daniel Papebroch conjectures that *rustes* should be understood to mean countrymen, whom we otherwise call serfs bound to the soil. From this it might perhaps be inferred that *rusticis* (“to the country people”) ought to be restored here, as though Cyprian were persisting in what he had said shortly before, that Lucianus had made himself the leader of the ignorant common people. Anyone who approves this conjecture may use it.

**His mother.** This much is found only in Manutius’ edition. Morel and Pamelius added “and sister.” There is no mention of a sister in the Reims or Foix manuscript, which read “who had lapsed.” Nor is there any mention of a sister in the variant readings I possess from the Verona manuscript. It is found, however, in my manuscript and the Grenoble manuscript.

**Under his name.** The Reims manuscript reads: “he persisted under an occasion of this kind.”

**He did not know letters.** From this it may be inferred that this Aurelius is different from Aurelius, the reader of the Church of Carthage, whose ordination is discussed in Letter XXXII. Thus, in the first conference at Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists, chapter 133, Trifolius, bishop of Abora, signs on behalf of Paulinus of Zuma, who was present but did not know letters. And in the profession of Zeno, a chorepiscopus of the Quartodeciman sect, recorded in the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, Flavius Palladius signs for him because Zeno, though present, said that he was ignorant of letters. Indeed, at the Council of Chalcedon, after certain acts of the First Synod of Ephesus had been reread, Elias, bishop of Hadrianopolis, signs through Romanus, bishop of Myra, “because I did not know letters”; and Cajumas, bishop of Phoenice or Phauna, as it appears in the old books, signs through his fellow bishop Dionysius, [Col. 0284B] “because I am ignorant of letters.”

A later age therefore made provision against this disadvantage and decreed that the illiterate should not be admitted to ecclesiastical service, because one who lacks letters cannot be suited to sacred offices, as is read in the letter of Pope Gelasius to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, writing to Robert, king of the Franks, in Letter 88 concerning the election of Franco, bishop of Paris, says that he approves the election if Franco is excellently learned. In the year 1097, when the church of Prague was vacant, Normannus the deacon was elected bishop there, “a man,” says Cosmas, dean of Prague, “exceedingly learned—which is the first virtue in a cleric.” At the Council of Reims in the year 991, Arnulf, bishop of Orléans, says in chapter [Col. 0284C] 28 that there was [p. 410] scarcely anyone at Rome at that time who had learned letters.

In this letter, however, and in several others written to the same effect, Cyprian speaks of the martyrs’ certificates in such a way that he by no means denies that the lapsed can be aided by the martyrs’ merits. For in Letter XIII he declares that those who have received certificates from the martyrs and can be aided before God by their prerogative may, if they are overtaken by some affliction and danger of sickness, without awaiting Cyprian’s own presence, make an *exomologesis* of their offense before any presbyter who is present—or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press, even before a deacon—and so forth. Cyprian therefore believed that they could be aided before the Lord in their offenses by the martyrs’ prerogative, or, as he says in Letter XIV, by their assistance.

Likewise, in the book *On the Lapsed*, page 187, he acknowledges that something can be granted at the martyrs’ command, provided that it is just and lawful; that it is not contrary to the Lord himself for God’s priest to do it; that the consent of the person complying is easy and ready; and that the petitioner’s moderation is religious. Thus [Col. 0284D] he condemns not the custom itself, which had long prevailed in the Church, but its abuse and the excessive license of certain confessors—especially Lucianus—who issued certificates written in this form: “Let so-and-so receive communion with his household.” Nor did they observe what Cyprian had commanded in Letter XI: that they should carefully examine the conduct, works, and merits of each person, as well as the kinds and qualities of the offenses themselves, and should designate by name in the certificates those whom they personally knew and whose repentance they perceived to be approaching satisfaction.

Two further points must be observed: first, that the confessors did not grant peace, but asked that it be granted; second, that they did not even venture to demand that peace be granted to the lapsed before Cyprian’s return, but in this matter deferred to their bishop. Accordingly, the five presbyters were induced to admit the lapsed to communion before the bishop’s return, entirely without consulting him, not by the confessors’ authority but by their own wickedness.]

### I

Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome, his brothers, greetings.

After letters had been written to you, dearest brothers, in which our conduct was explained and some account, however slight, of our discipline and diligence was given, another matter arose of which you likewise ought not to remain unaware. For our brother Lucianus, himself one of the confessors—ardent indeed in faith and steadfast in courage, but less firmly

[Note: [Col. 0282C] *steadfast, but less*, printed editions.]

grounded in the reading of the Lord’s teaching—has attempted certain things. Long since making himself the leader of an ignorant populace,

[Note: [Col. 0282C] *unskillfully now making himself the patron*, Verona.]

[Col. 0283A] he arranged for certificates written in his own hand to be issued collectively to many people in Paul’s name. Yet the martyr Mappalicus, prudent and modest, mindful of the law and discipline, wrote no letters contrary to the Gospel. Moved only by family devotion, he directed that peace be given to his mother, who had lapsed.

[Note: [Col. 0283B] *And to his sister, both of whom had lapsed*, Oxford.]

Saturninus also, after his tortures and while still confined in prison, issued no letters of that kind.

Lucianus, however, not only distributed certificates everywhere in Paul’s name, written in his own hand while Paul was still in prison, but even after Paul’s death he persisted in doing the same under his name, saying that Paul had commanded him to do so,

[Note: [Col. 0283B] *that this had been commanded him by Paul*, Bod. 1.]

without knowing that one must obey the Lord rather than a fellow servant. [Col. 0284A] Many certificates were also issued in the name of the young man Aurelius, who had suffered torture, written in the hand of the same Lucianus, because Aurelius himself did not know letters.

[Note: [Col. 0284D]

### II.—*The rule of the Gospel*

The Foix manuscript reads: “the discipline of the evangelical tradition.”

**Lucianus wrote a letter.** That is, Letter XVI.]

### II

So that some resistance might be offered to this practice, I wrote them the letter that I transmitted to you under cover of my previous letter. In it I did not cease to ask and advise that the rule of the Lord’s law and of the Gospel should be maintained.

But after I had sent them the letter, so that something apparently more moderate and restrained might be done, the same Lucianus wrote a letter in the name

[Note: [Col. 0284B] *this in the name*, Vat.]

of all the confessors, by which almost every bond of faith, the fear of God, the Lord’s commandment, and the sanctity and stability of the Gospel were dissolved. For he wrote in the name of them all that they had granted peace to everyone, and that they wished this formula [Col. 0285A] to be made known through me to the other bishops. I transmitted a copy of his letter to you.

To be sure, this qualification was added: “concerning those for whom an account has been established of what they did after their offense.” This matter creates greater hostility against us, so that when we begin to hear and examine the individual cases, we shall appear to be denying to many what all now boast that they have received from the martyrs and confessors.

[Note: [Col. 0285D]

### III.—*The peace which once*

Tertullian, in his book *To the Martyrs*: “Certain people who did not possess peace in the Church were accustomed to beg it from the martyrs in prison.” See Dallaeus, book VII of *Human Penalties and Satisfactions*, chapter 16.

**Caldonius.** His letter to Cyprian is Letter XVIII among Cyprian’s letters. Cyprian replies to him in Letter XIX.

**Lucianus.** Doubtless the same person who is mentioned in Letter LXXVIII, page 161, where he is called Lucanus in certain ancient manuscripts and editions.

**Our sect.** This is how the Catholic Church was formerly described. Today that word is invidious, as Erasmus long ago observed on chapter XXIV of Acts. See Pamelius’ notes on this letter and Xystus Betuleius’ notes on Lactantius, page 482.

(The word *secta* is frequently used in a favorable sense by Tertullian for the Christian confession, as may be seen in his books *On Flight in Persecution*, *On the Pallium*, and the *Apology Against the Gentiles*. Cyprian imitates him in his customary manner, both here and in Letter XXXIV, concerning Celerinus, and in the preface to book I of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*. Likewise, Bede, in his *Retraction on Acts*, bears witness that in Acts XXVI the apostle used αἵρεσιν (*hairesin*, “sect”) in a favorable sense; our translator therefore did not badly render it there as *sectam*. PAMEL.)

**Less skilled.** The Reims and Foix manuscripts read “unskilled.”

**Troublesome.** The Reims and Grenoble manuscripts and Manutius’ edition have “modest.” The same is written in my old book. One copy in the Foix manuscript has “troublesome,” the other “immodest.”]

### III

Finally, the beginning of this sedition has already appeared. For in several cities of our province an assault has been made upon those in authority by the multitude,

[Note: [Col. 0285C] *of multitudes*, printed editions.]

32 and they compelled their terrified and subdued superiors—who were less able to resist through strength of spirit and firmness of faith—to furnish them immediately with the peace which all loudly proclaimed had once

[Note: [Col. 0285C] *although once*, Verona; *which of the way*, Lat.]

been granted by the martyrs and confessors.

Among us also, certain turbulent persons, who in the past could scarcely be governed by us and whose cases were being deferred until we should be present,

[Note: [Col. 0285C] *until our judgment*, Bod. 1.]

were set ablaze by this letter as though by torches and began to burn still more fiercely and to extort the peace they claimed had been given them. I have sent you a copy of the letter I wrote about them to our clergy. I have also transmitted both the letter which my colleague Caldonius wrote to me out of his integrity and faith, and my reply to him, for you to read.

I have likewise sent you copies of the letter which the good and steadfast confessor Celerinus wrote to the same confessor Lucianus, and of Lucianus’ reply to him, so that you might know both our labor

[Note: [Col. 0285C] *that we labor*, Bod. 1.]

and diligence in all things, and might learn the truth itself:

[Note: [Col. 0285D] *from the truth itself*, Bod. 1.]

how moderate and prudent the confessor Celerinus is, modest in humility and reverent fear toward our sect; and how Lucianus, as I have said, is less skilled

[Note: [Col. 0286C] *as we have said, unskilled*, Bod. 1.]

in understanding the reading of the Lord’s teaching, and, through his readiness to expose us to odium, troublesome to our modesty.

For although the Lord said that the nations are to be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII, 19), and that past sins are forgiven in Baptism (John III, 5), this man, ignorant of the commandment and the law, directs that peace be granted and [Col. 0286A] sins forgiven in Paul’s name. He says that Paul commanded him to do this, as you will observe in the letter written by the same Lucianus to Celerinus. In this he gave no consideration

[Note: [Col. 0286C] *gave less consideration*, Bod. 1.]

to the fact that martyrs do not make the Gospel, but are themselves made martyrs through the Gospel. For the apostle Paul also, whom the Lord called his chosen vessel (Acts IX, 15), wrote in his epistle:

“I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you into grace, to another gospel—which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim something different from what

[Note: [Col. 0286C] *beyond what*, Bod. 1; *beyond what we proclaimed*, Oxford.]

we proclaimed to you, let him be anathema. As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone proclaims to you anything beyond what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. I, 6, 8).

[Col. 0286B]

[Note: [Col. 0286D]

### IV.—*According to the law of the Gospel*

In the Reims manuscript and in one copy of the Foix manuscript it reads: “I sent the law, and may your judgment also concur with us courageously and unanimously.”]

### IV

Your letters arrived at an opportune time. I received the letter addressed to the clergy, and likewise the letter which the blessed confessors Moses and Maximus, Nicostratus and the others, sent to Saturninus, Aurelius, and the rest. These contain the full vigor of the Gospel and the robust discipline of the Lord’s law.

As we labored here and resisted the assault of hostility with all the strength of faith, your discourse greatly assisted us, so that relief was granted by God: even before the letters that I recently sent you arrived, you made clear to us that your judgment too concurred with us courageously and unanimously according to the law of the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0286C] *presence*, Bod. 1.]

I wish you, dearest and most longed-for brothers,

[Note: [Col. 0286D] *most beloved*, Oxford, Leipzig.]

ever good health.

## [NOTE]

Since the works of Saint Cyprian are commonly cited [Col. 0286C] according to the order they occupy in the editions of Pamelius and Rigaltius, and since we have resolved to follow this order, although the printer from whose workshop the Rigaltius edition emerged skipped the number XXIII in publishing the Letters, it seemed proper to warn readers that we too have retained the same error, for the reason given at the beginning of this notice.

**D. PR. MARAN.**

[Note: [Col. 0287D]

**LETTER XXIV.—And what I wrote in reply.** These words are absent from the editions preceding that of Manutius. They are also absent from eight ancient manuscripts that I have seen and from certain English manuscripts.

**To the clergy.** That is, to those members of the Carthaginian clergy who were then at Rome, to whom Letter XXII was written.

**The ministry of daily work.** My old book reads, “the work of daily ministry.” The Foix manuscript reads, “the daily ministry is insufficient.” The manuscripts of Bec and Chartres read, “the ministry of daily work is sufficient.”

**Together with the presbyters.** This passage is greatly disordered in the ancient copies. Pamelius says that he pieced together the reading we have retained.]

Everything. Thus all the old manuscripts and editions. But because in Rigault’s edition *monia* was misprinted [page 411] instead of *omnia* (“everything”), the English editors, without the authority of any ancient manuscript and doubtless supposing that the syllables *testi-* had dropped out through the fault of Rigault’s printers, substituted *testimonia* (“testimonies”). And yet [Col. 0288D] Rigault had warned in the errata that *omnia* was to be read.]

## 33 LETTER XXIV

(Erasm., IV, 22. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXIV. Paris., XXIII. Oxon., Lips., XXVIII.)

### TO THE CLERGY, CONCERNING THE LETTERS SENT TO ROME AND THE APPOINTMENT OF SATURUS AS READER AND OPTATUS AS SUBDEACON

[Col. 0287A]

**Summary.—**By this letter the clergy are informed of the ordination of Saturus and Optatus, and of what Cyprian wrote to Rome.

Cyprian to his brothers the presbyters and deacons, greetings.

So that nothing might escape your knowledge, dearly beloved brothers, I have sent you copies of both letters—what was written to me and what I wrote in reply; [Col. 0287B] and I believe that what I answered will not displease you. But I was also obliged to inform you by my letter that, because the matter was urgent, I sent a letter to the clergy residing in the City. And since it was proper for me to write through clerics, while I know [Note: [Col. 0287C] “For I know,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. M A.] that very many of our own clergy are absent, whereas the few who are there are scarcely sufficient for the ministry of the daily work, it became necessary to appoint some new men to be sent: [Note: [Col. 0287C] “To minister,” Ar. Ebor. Lam. NC. 1. MR.].

You should therefore know that I have made Saturus a reader and Optatus the confessor a subdeacon. Long ago, by common deliberation, we had placed them next in rank to the clergy: in Saturus’s case, when on Easter Day we assigned him the reading once and again; and in Optatus’s case, when, together with the presbyters who serve as teachers, we carefully examined the readers and appointed Optatus among them as an instructor of the hearers, testing whether all the qualities [Col. 0287C] that ought to be present in those being prepared for the clergy were fittingly present in them. Therefore, nothing new has been done by me in your absence; rather, what had long ago been begun by the common deliberation of us all has, under the pressure of necessity, been carried forward.

I wish you, dearly beloved brothers, always to fare well and to remember us. Greet the brotherhood. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0288D]

**LETTER XXV.—**In the ancient manuscript of Saint-Remi, this letter is said to have been written to Moses, Maximus, Nicostratus, and the others. In the ancient catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Rome, which Rigault cites from the manuscript of Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, it reads: “After the suffering of Fabius, the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus were arrested and sent to prison.” So too in another catalogue that Aegidius Bucherius published from Cuspinian; from this it is inferred that *Fabianus* should be restored in place of *Fabius*, which stands in Peiresc’s manuscript. Pope Cornelius, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 3, attests that Maximus was a presbyter of the Church of Rome. See Baronius’s annotations on the *Roman Martyrology* for November 19.]

## LETTER XXV

(Erasm., IV, 3. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXV. Paris., XXIV. Oxon., Lips., XXVIII.)

### TO MOSES AND MAXIMUS AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS

[Col. 0288A]

**Summary.—**This is a letter of congratulation to the Roman confessors.

### I

Cyprian to the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the other confessors, his dearly beloved brothers, greetings.

I had long since learned by report of the glory of your faith and courage, most valiant [Note: [Col. 0287C] “Dearest,” Lam. Ebor.] and most blessed brothers, and I rejoiced exceedingly and offered abundant congratulations because, through the confession of his name, a singular act of favor has prepared you [Note: [Col. 0287C] “Has distinguished you,” Ver.] for the crown of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, having become the foremost men and leaders in the battle of our time, you set the standards of the heavenly army in motion. You imbued with your virtues the spiritual contest [Col. 0288B] that God has now willed to be fought. With immovable strength and unshaken steadfastness [Note: [Col. 0287C] “With the unshaken steadfastness of faith,” Lam.] you were the first to break the assault of the rising war. From you arose the auspicious beginnings of the fight; from you commenced the favorable omens of victory.

It has happened [Note: [Col. 0287C] “It happens,” Oxon.] here that martyrdoms are brought to completion [Note: [Col. 0287D] “To complete,” Ver.] through torture. But he who, taking the lead in the encounter, [Note: [Col. 0288C] “In the confession,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] became an example of courage to the brothers shares equally in honor with the martyrs. You have passed from there to us the crowns woven by your hand [Note: [Col. 0288C] “Your crowns,” MR.], and have offered your brothers drink from the cup of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0288D]

**II.—“United to the Lord.”** In the Bec manuscript it is written “of the Lord.”

[Col. 0289D] **“Apart from the Lord.”** In most ancient manuscripts it is written “through the Lord.” In one of my own: “For, apart from the Lord, to become a martyr” [the reading is fragmentary]. In the Bec manuscript: “Nor, on account of the Lord, for martyrdoms to occur” [fragmentary]. The Chartres manuscript is almost the same.

**“Honored.”** The Grenoble manuscript has *honeratis*. Certain ancient manuscripts and certain editions have “crowned.”

**“Our age.”** We have restored this reading, following the authority of the early editions and eight ancient copies. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that the reading “in our age” also survives in eight ancient manuscripts.

At the end of this Letter and at the end of Letter XXXIV, the following was written in ancient times in Pithou’s manuscript: “Justinus corrected this at Rome.”]

### II

To the glorious beginnings of your confession and the auspicious commencement of your victorious service [Note: [Col. 0288C] “To the beginnings of glorious service,” Pem. Voss.] there has been added that constancy of discipline which we perceived in the forcefulness of your letter, which you recently sent [Note: [Col. 0288C] “Did,” Ver.] with an earnest admonition to your colleagues in confession, joined with you to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0288C] “Of the Lord,” Bod. 1.] [page 34], so that the holy precepts of the Gospel and the life-giving commandments delivered to us once for all should be maintained with courageous and steadfast observance. [Col. 0288C]

Behold another lofty degree of your glory; behold a second title to merit before God, now doubled together with your confession: to stand with firm [Note: [Col. 0288C] “Steadfast,” Bod. 1.] footing and, by the strength of faith, to drive from this battle line those who attempt to break into the Gospel and stretch out impious hands [Col. 0289A] to overthrow the Lord’s precepts; [Note: [Col. 0289C] “And to bring impious hands against this battle line, which is the Gospel—,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. “Which is crowned in the Gospel,” Ver. Vat. anonymous. Spir. Remb.] to have offered examples of courage at the beginning, and now also to offer instruction in conduct.

After his resurrection, the Lord sends the apostles and commands them, saying: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go, therefore, and teach all nations, immersing [*tingentes*] [Note: [Col. 0289C] “Baptizing,” Ebor. NC. 1.] them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19). And the apostle John, mindful of the commandment, later sets it down [Note: [Col. 0289C] “Sets it down and says,” Pem. Lin. Voss. 2.] in his Epistle: “By this,” he says, “we understand that we have known him: if we keep his commandments. He who says that he has known him and does not observe his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him” (1 John 2:3–4).

You urge that these precepts be kept; you observe the divine and heavenly commandments. This is to be a confessor of the Lord; this is to be a martyr of Christ: to preserve in every respect the inviolable and solid constancy of his utterance. [Col. 0289B] For to wish to become a martyr apart from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0289C] “For the Lord,” NC. 2.] while attempting to destroy the Lord’s precepts, to use against him the favor that he has granted you, and in some fashion to become a rebel with weapons received from him—this is to wish [Note: [Col. 0289C] “Not to wish,” Pem.] to confess Christ while denying the Gospel of Christ.

I therefore rejoice on your account, most valiant [Note: [Col. 0289C] “Most beloved brothers,” Lam. Lin. Ebor. NC. 1.] and most faithful brothers. As greatly as I congratulate the martyrs honored there [Note: [Col. 0289D] “Those martyrs,” Pem.] for the glory of their strength, so equally do I congratulate you for the crown of the Lord’s discipline as well. The Lord has poured forth his favor in manifold forms of generosity; in abundant variety he has distributed the praises of good soldiers and their spiritual glories. We too share in your honor and reckon your glory as our own, for so great a felicity has illumined our times [Col. 0289C] that it has fallen to our age to behold God’s proven servants and Christ’s soldiers crowned.

I wish you [Note: [Col. 0290C] The remainder is absent from Corb.], most valiant and most blessed brothers, always to fare well and to remember us.

[Note: [Col. 0289D]

**LETTER XXVI.—**In the very ancient manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims, the title of this Letter was written in ancient times as follows: “Here begins the reply of Myseus and Maximus to Cyprian, which Novatian dictated.” In the Grenoble manuscript [Col. 0290D] the man whom we commonly call Moses is frequently called Myseus. In the martyrology published by Florentinius, under February 15, it reads: “In the city of Asta, of Moyses.” In the fragments of Pacian, in Florus’s manuscript, the following is read in the *Exhortation to Repentance*: “among Moseus and the ancients”; and a little later, “Moyseus as a blasphemer.” At the beginning of Arnobius’s disputation with Serapion, *Moseus* is read. See the preface of the most illustrious Dom Bernard de Montfaucon to Athanasius, p. 34. On the eloquence of Novatian, by whom this letter is said to have been dictated, see the observations below on Letter XXX.]

## LETTER XXVI

(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXVI. Paris., XXV. Oxon., Lips., XXXI.)

### MOSES, MAXIMUS, NICOSTRATUS, AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS REPLY TO THE PRECEDING LETTER (C, G)\*

[Col. 0290A]

**Summary.—**The Roman confessors gratefully acknowledge the consolations that they received from Cyprian’s letter.—Martyrdom is not a punishment but a felicity.—The words of the Gospel are torches for kindling faith.—Agreement with Cyprian’s judgment in the case of the lapsed.

[Note: [Col. 0290D]

**I.—“To Caecilius Cyprian.”** We have taken this address from the same manuscript of Saint-Remi. We have included it chiefly for this reason: that from it we may learn the epistolary form of those times. For the letter was doubtless addressed in precisely the form in which it is read in that ancient book.

**“Fed and fattened.”** Above, in the Letter to Donatus, p. 3 (col. 192): “The body is filled out into flesh by richer foods, so that, once fattened, it may perish at greater cost under punishment.” It was formerly customary, as Holstenius observes on the *Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, for those who had either been condemned as punishment to the gladiatorial or beast-fighting spectacle, or had voluntarily bound themselves to those same contests, first to be fattened by the masters of the training school, so that they might be brought forward fitter and stronger. In Livy, book V, it is written that the popular leaders “fattened the plebs so that they might be slaughtered.” Tacitus, in book II of the *Histories*: “There Vitellius distributed prepared food and gladiators’ fattening rations to the soldiers.” Jerome, in book II *Against Jovinian*: “Athletes, whose life and craft consist in fattening.” Quintus Curtius, book IX: “Dionysius of Athens, a celebrated boxer, attended the banquets and, because of the exceptional power of his strength, had been advanced and favored by the king. The envious and malicious reproached him, amid serious business and jesting alike, saying that he went about as a useless beast with a fattened body.” [Col. 0291D] See Cassian, book VI, chapter 7, *On the Institutes of Those Who Renounce the World.*]

### I

To Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of the Church of the Carthaginians: Moses and Maximus, presbyters; Nicostratus and Rufinus, deacons; and the other confessors persevering in the faith of truth in God the Father, in his Son [Col. 0290B] Jesus Christ our Lord, and in the Holy Spirit: greetings.

Although placed amid various and manifold sorrows, brother, because of the present falls of many brothers [Note: [Col. 0290C] “Of the brothers” omitted by Oxon.] throughout almost the whole world, this singular consolation came upon us: upon receiving your letter we were raised up [Note: [Col. 0290C] “And most upright,” Bod. 2. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. “And refreshed,” Ben.] and received soothing remedies for the griefs of our sorrowing mind. [Note: [Col. 0290C] “A strengthening remedy for the sorrowing soul,” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] From this we can now understand that perhaps divine providence wished to keep us confined for so long in the chains of prison for no other reason than that, instructed [Note: [Col. 0290C] “More fully instructed,” Manut.] and more resolutely encouraged by your letter, we might be able to reach the appointed crown with a readier desire.

For your letter shone upon us like clear weather amid a storm [page 35], like longed-for [Note: [Col. 0290C] “Arisen,” Bod. 2. Ben. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] calm upon a troubled sea, like rest amid labors, like health amid dangers and sufferings, and like bright and radiant light amid the thickest [Col. 0290C] darkness. [Note: [Col. 0290C] “Radiant light,” Ben. Bod. 2.] We drank it in so deeply with a thirsty spirit and received it with a hungry desire that we rejoice to have been sufficiently fed and fattened by it for the contest with the enemy. [Note: [Col. 0290D] “The contest of the mind,” Lam. Bod. 2. Ebor.]

The Lord will repay you for this love of yours [Col. 0291A] and will render the fruit owed for so good a work. For the man who has exhorted is no less worthy of the reward of the crown than the man who has suffered; the man who taught is no less worthy of praise than the man who acted; and the man who admonished is no less deserving of honor than the man who fought—except that sometimes a greater accumulation of glory overflows upon the instructor than upon the one who offered himself as a teachable disciple. For the latter would perhaps not have possessed what he put into practice unless the former had taught him.

[Note: [Col. 0291D]

**II.—“Celebrated.”** [page 412] We have restored *prosequendi* (“to be celebrated”), following the authority of the ancient Saint-Remi manuscript, whereas *personandi* (“to be sounded forth”) was previously read. And certainly our reading will always appear superior.

**“Bearing witness.”** The Foix manuscript has “bearing witness and rendering.”]

### II

We have therefore received—we say it again, brother Cyprian—great joys, great consolations, great soothing remedies, especially because you celebrated the glorious—what shall I call them? not deaths, but immortalities—of the martyrs with glorious and fitting praises. For such departures had to be celebrated in such words, so that the events recounted might be expressed as they occurred. [Col. 0291B]

From your letter, therefore, we beheld those glorious triumphs of the martyrs; with our own eyes, as it were, we followed them as they sought heaven, and we contemplated [Note: [Col. 0291C] “As though we contemplated,” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor. Ben. Bod. 1, 2. Vat. ancient anonymous manuscript.] them stationed among the angels, powers, and heavenly dominions. But with our own ears, as it were, we also perceived [Note: [Col. 0291C] “Similarly perceived,” Bod. 2. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.] the Lord bearing witness [Note: [Col. 0291C] “Rendering,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.] before the Father on their behalf, as he had promised. This, then, is what raises our spirit day by day and kindles [Note: [Col. 0291C] “Sets alight,” Ben.; “stretches,” printed editions.] us to attain the successive degrees of so great a favor.

[Note: [Col. 0291D]

**III.—“In the very act of destruction.”** In the edition of Manutius, to whom the first edition of this letter is owed, and in the editions that subsequently followed it, *interritum* (“undaunted”) is read. Since the most learned Denis Pétau considered this corrupt, he judged in his notes on Themistius that *inter ictus* (“amid the blows”) ought to be restored. This conjecture seemed to him very suitable to the passage; and I strongly approved it, especially since it appeared capable of confirmation [Col. 0292C] even from Cyprian’s authority, for in Letter LIV, p. 71, he writes “under the blow of death”; in Letter LXV, p. 113, “under the blow of suffering”; likewise in the deacon Pontius’s *Life* of him; in Letter LXXXI, p. 165, “under the blow of the contest”; and at the end of the book *Against Demetrianus*, p. 224, “at the very departure of life.” But once the true reading has been found, there is no need to employ conjectures. I found the reading restored by me in the same Saint-Remi manuscript. It is sufficiently evident that the English editors had this same reading in their manuscripts.

**“Than, by divine favor, to have been made judge of his own judge.”** This passage is absent from three ancient manuscripts, namely the Saint-Remi, Dijon, and Sorbonne manuscripts. [Col. 0292D]

**“Not to have departed.”** That is, not to have departed from life. Cyprian himself, in the book *On Mortality*, p. 234: “You fear suffering; you do not wish to depart.” Hence *departure* frequently means death in the same Cyprian.]

### III

For what more glorious or happier could befall any human being by divine favor than to confess the Lord [Col. 0292A] God amid the very executioners, in the very act of destruction; than, amid the varied and ingenious torments of raging [Note: [Col. 0292C] “Raging men,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] secular power, to confess Christ, the Son of God, even when the body has been racked, tortured, [Note: [Col. 0292C] “The body tortured,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2.] and butchered, with a spirit departing indeed, yet free; than to have left the world and sought heaven; than, abandoning human beings, to stand among angels; than, having broken every secular impediment, to present oneself already free in the sight of God; than to possess the heavenly kingdom without any delay; than to have become, in Christ’s name, Christ’s companion in suffering; than, by divine favor, to have been made judge of one’s own judge; than to have brought back an unstained conscience from the confession of the Name; than not to have obeyed human and sacrilegious laws opposed to the faith; than to have borne witness publicly to the truth; than, by dying, to have subdued death itself, which all fear; than through death itself [Col. 0292B] to have attained immortality; than, butchered and racked [Note: [Col. 0292C] “Flayed,” Lam. Bod. 2. Ebor.] by every instrument of cruelty, to have overcome the torments by the torments themselves; than to have struggled by strength of spirit against every pain of a mangled body; than not to have recoiled from one’s flowing blood; than, after embracing the faith, to have begun to love one’s punishments; than to regard not having departed [Note: [Col. 0292C] “Having lived,” Vat. Bod. 2. “Having conquered,” Ver. Ben.] as the loss of one’s life?

[Note: [Col. 0292D]

**IV.—“And he who loves his life more.”** These words, which appear in Manutius’s edition and are absent from Morel’s, were omitted by Pamelius on the basis of judgment rather than authority, because, as he says, they are found neither in Greek nor Latin manuscripts. But in emending Cyprian’s works I do not ask what is found in Greek and Latin copies of the Holy Scriptures, but what Cyprian wrote. This sentence appears in two ancient manuscripts of Saint-Remi of Reims, in the Sorbonne manuscript, and in the Foix manuscript—that is, in nearly all the ancient manuscripts. For I had only six ancient copies of this letter. It also appears in four ancient manuscripts cited in the English edition.

**“Hated.”** Thus the ancient Saint-Remi, Sorbonne, Dijon, Grenoble, and Foix manuscripts. So too the Manutius edition.

**“Their fathers.”** These words are absent from the Saint-Remi and Foix manuscripts.

**“Authorities.”** The same ancient manuscripts have “governors.”

**“Victims.”** So too in the Letter to Fortunatus, *An Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 6, and book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 18. But three of our manuscripts and five cited in the English edition prefer “for slaughter,” while the Foix manuscript has “for butchering.” The Vulgate edition of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans has “for slaughter.” Saint Augustine also cites it thus in *Retractations*, book I, chapter 7, and *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 20. So too Primasius. See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of Paul.

[Col. 0293D] **“We more than conquer” (*supervincimus*).** When I saw that in place of this word, which is not Latin, *speramus* (“we hope”) was written in the ancient Saint-Remi, Grenoble, and Dijon manuscripts, and also in five manuscripts whose variant readings appear in the English edition, my inclination was strongly to expunge the non-Latin word and substitute the Latin one, especially since the latter appears in the Vulgate edition of Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, and the holy martyr likewise uses it in the book *An Exhortation to Martyrdom*, addressed to Fortunatus. But when I saw that he had written *supervincimus* in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 18, and that this word was retained by Tertullian in the *Scorpiace* and by Saint Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 20, and *The City of God*, book II, chapter 23, as well as in Evodius’s letter to Augustine, I judged that nothing should be changed. Thus *supersperavi* (“I hoped beyond”) is often read in the Psalms; in Tertullian’s book *On Repentance*, *superscenditur* (“it is climbed above”); in Symmachus, book I, Letter 56, *superpingo* (“I paint over”); and in Sidonius, book IX, Letter 3, *superinspicis* (“you inspect from above”). Meanwhile it should be noted here that the Verona manuscript [Col. 0294C] has *supervincimus*, not *speramus*, in the book addressed to Fortunatus.]

### IV

For the Lord rouses us to this battle, as though by a trumpet-call of his Gospel, saying: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves his life [Note: [Col. 0292C] Thus Ben.; omitted by Oxon.] more than me is not worthy of me; he who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” [Col. 0293A] (Matt. 10:37).

And again: “Blessed are those who have suffered [Note: [Col. 0293B] “Suffer,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed will you be [Note: [Col. 0293B] “Blessed are you,” Bod. 1.] when they persecute you and hate you. [Note: [Col. 0293B] Thus Lam. Ebor. NC. 1; “hate,” Oxon.] Rejoice and exult. For thus did their fathers persecute the prophets who were before you” (Matt. 5:10, 12).

And again: “For you will stand [page 36] before kings and authorities, [Note: [Col. 0293B] “Governors,” Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and brother will hand brother over to death, and a father his son; and he who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:18, 21–22).

And: “To him who conquers I shall grant to sit upon my throne, just as I too conquered and sat upon my Father’s throne” (Rev. 3:21).

And the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0293B] “Paul,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.] also says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been reckoned as sheep [Col. 0293B] for sacrifice.’ But in all these things we more than conquer because of him who loved us” (Rom. 8:35–37).

[Note: [Col. 0294C]

**V.—“We challenge.”** That is, we voluntarily offer ourselves to the persecutors, desiring to die, as the martyrs of Lyons and Vienne had once done, according to Eusebius. Tertullian, in the book *To Scapula*: “In short, we vie with all your cruelty, even bursting forth voluntarily.” See the *Acts of the Passion of Saint Stephen, Pope and Martyr*, at its very beginning. And yet the public discipline of that time prohibited anyone from offering himself voluntarily, since divine Scripture forbids this, as we read in the proconsular Acts concerning Cyprian’s martyrdom; for it is not rashness but faith and modesty that is crowned, [page 413] as we read in the letter of the Church of Smyrna according to Rufinus’s translation in Eusebius. Furthermore, Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, prohibited this so severely that he even forbade honor to be given to Christians who, without having been arrested, offered themselves to persecution, as we have discussed at greater length in our comments on chapter 11 of Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. See also Saint Ambrose—or whoever else is the author—*On Duties*, chapter 37; the Council of Elvira, canon 60; and Rigault on Cyprian’s Letter IV. [Col. 0294D]

**“To pour out.”** This is the reading of the ancient Saint-Remi manuscript and certainly the best. Three ancient manuscripts cited in the English edition also have it.

**“Let no one judge this.”** The same Saint-Remi manuscript reads: “Let no one judge this love of ours to be a form of madness.”

**“Which impedes glory.”** This is absent from the same Saint-Remi manuscript.

**“Has trained and tested.”** The Dijon and more recent Saint-Remi manuscripts have “has both tested and tests.” In them, however, the word “trained” is omitted.

**“The helmet of salvation.”** We added this from the ancient Saint-Remi manuscript, also following the authority of five ancient English copies.]

### V

When we read these and similar passages brought together in the Gospel, [Note: [Col. 0293B] “We have read,” Oxon.] and feel that the Lord’s words have been set beneath us like torches to kindle faith, we not only no longer dread the enemies of truth, but even challenge them. By the very fact that we have not yielded, we have already conquered [Note: [Col. 0293B] “We conquer,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] God’s enemies and subdued the sacrilegious laws [Col. 0294A] opposed to truth. [Note: [Col. 0293B] “The laws of the city,” Ver.]

And if we have not yet poured out our blood, but are prepared to pour it out, [Note: [Col. 0293C] “Have poured it out,” Oxon.] let no one judge this delay imposed upon us to be clemency. It harms us, impedes our glory, defers heaven, and withholds the glorious sight of God. For in such a contest and in such a battle, where faith contends, [Note: [Col. 0294B] “In a contest where faith contends,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.] true clemency would have been not to delay the martyrs with postponement. [Note: [Col. 0294B] “Not martyrs in battle,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.]

Therefore pray, dearest Cyprian, that through his grace the Lord may day by day arm and illuminate each and every one of us more abundantly [Note: [Col. 0294B] “More freely,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and readily, and may strengthen and fortify [Note: [Col. 0294B] “Test and form,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.] us with the powers of his might; and that, like the finest [Note: [Col. 0294B] “Whereby the best,” Ver.; “because,” Vat.] commander, he may now lead forth into the field of the appointed contest his soldiers, whom until now he has trained and tested in the camp of the prison. May he extend to us [Col. 0294B] the divine arms, those weapons that know no defeat: the breastplate of righteousness, which is never broken; the shield of faith, which cannot be pierced; the helmet of salvation, which cannot be shattered; [Note: [Col. 0294B] “The helmet—to be shattered” omitted by Oxon.] and the sword of the Spirit, which cannot be wounded. For whom should we charge to pray for these things on our behalf more properly than so glorious a bishop, so that victims destined for sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0294B] Feminine form, “destined,” Ver. Ben.] may seek aid from a priest?

[Note: [Col. 0295C]

**VI.—“Although meanwhile.”** In the same ancient Saint-Remi manuscript it reads: “although meanwhile, at the outset, the brothers were, in view of the conditions of the time, *destricti*”—doubtless in error for *distracti* (“scattered”). Five English manuscripts also have this.

**“With fitting severity.”** The same Saint-Remi manuscript reads: “with your fitting severity, worthily rebuked them.” So too the more recent Saint-Remi and Compiègne manuscripts.

**“Rebuked them.”** This passage refers to Letter XXII, which concerns the peace that certain troublemakers claimed had been granted to them by the confessors and martyrs. This affair had aroused great hostility against Cyprian, because he said that it had been done contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. See also Letter XIV.

**“Through your absence.”** The Manutius edition and four ancient manuscripts have “through impatience.” Either reading may be sound. [Col. 0295D]

**“To dogs.”** This word, as well as the word “to swine,” is absent from all the ancient manuscripts.

**“The laity who stood firm.”** That is, laypeople who had remained steadfast in confessing the Name, who had not yielded to tortures and had not sacrificed to idols. Hence in the following Letter it is written that the Church is constituted also in those who stand firm. See also Letter XXX.

**“For when.”** The ancient Saint-Remi manuscript reads: “For there the fear of God is abandoned when pardon is so readily granted to sinners.” Several other ancient manuscripts also have the word “fear.”

**“And instructed from the Scriptures.”** These words are absent from three ancient manuscripts.

**“Because they are many.”** Tertullian, at the beginning of the book *On Modesty*: “As though it were not easier to err with the many, since truth is loved among the few.” Jerome, in the dialogue *Against the Pelagians*: “The multitude of your companions will never prove you a catholic, but a heretic.” For, as he says elsewhere, the multitude of sinners does not seek a defense for error. Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, chapter 2: “Human affairs are not so well conducted that better things please the majority. A crowd is proof of what is worst.” The same author, *On Clemency*, book I, chapter 21: “For the multitude of sinners has established the habit of sinning.” Quintilian, book I, chapter 6: “For whence could such goodness come, that true things should please the majority?” Ovid, *The Art of Love*, book I:

> Most things are always worse than the good.

Matteo Bosso, in the disputation *On Joy*: [Col. 0296D] “A crowd is always the author of fickleness and the worst error.” And Cicero, at the beginning of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “The multitude consenting to vices.” Nonius Marcellus observes that the ancients used the number of the few to signify the good, just as they used that of the many to signify the bad. Livy, book XXI: “A few, and all the best men, agreed with Hanno.”

**“To avail.”** This word does not appear in Morel’s edition and is also absent from five ancient manuscripts. In its place, however, the ancient Saint-Remi manuscript offers “to make progress.”

**“Patience.”** Certain manuscripts have “repentance,” through an easy and very common error, as we noted on Letter XVII, p. 403. The Grenoble manuscript and Morel’s edition have “wisdom.”

**“The ruins of the downcast mind.”** The ancient Saint-Remi manuscript reads: “raises and lifts up the declining and trembling ruins.”

**“Quenches the heat.”** Three ancient manuscripts have “extinguishes”: “The physician gives suitable foods to the sick. For he does not,” etc. [Col. 0297C] The ancient Saint-Remi manuscript reads: “quenches and ends the disease.” So too the Grenoble manuscript.]

### VI

Behold another source of our joy: although in the discharge [Col. 0295A] of your episcopal office you are meanwhile separated from the brothers by the conditions of the time, you have nevertheless not failed them. You have repeatedly strengthened the confessors by your letters; you have also supplied the necessary expenses from your rightful earnings; in every matter you have always made yourself in some sense present; and in no part of your duty have you faltered like a deserter.

But we cannot keep silent about what has roused [Note: [Col. 0295B] “You have roused,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.] us still more powerfully to greater joy; rather, we must celebrate it with the full testimony of our voice. For we have observed that with fitting severity you worthily rebuked both those who, forgetful of their own offenses, through your absence extorted peace from the presbyters with hasty and precipitous eagerness, [Note: [Col. 0295B] “Are said to have extorted,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1.] and those who, without regard for the Gospel, with profane [Col. 0295B] [Note: [Col. 0295B] “Ready,” Ver.] facility gave the Lord’s holy thing to dogs and pearls to swine.

For a grave offense, which has raged with incredible devastation throughout almost the whole world, ought to be treated only, as you yourself write, cautiously and moderately, after consultation with all the bishops, presbyters, deacons, confessors, and the laypeople themselves who stood firm, as you too attest in your letters. Otherwise, while wishing to aid the fallen at an improper time, we may appear to be preparing other and greater falls. For how is the divine [Note: [Col. 0295B] “Fear of God,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1. NC. 1.] word not abandoned if pardon is granted so readily to sinners?

Their spirits [Note: [Col. 0295B] “The spirits of the lapsed,” Vat.] must indeed be cherished and nourished [Col. 0296A] until their proper time of maturity, and they must be instructed from the Holy Scriptures concerning how enormous and surpassingly grave an offense they have committed. Nor should they be encouraged because they are many; rather, they should be restrained all the more precisely because they are not few. A shameless multitude has never been able [Note: [Col. 0295C] “A shameless one has contributed,” Vat.] to diminish an offense. Rather, shame, modesty, patience, [page 37] discipline, humility and submission, [Note: [Col. 0295C] “Submission: this is,” Lam. Ebor.] awaiting another’s judgment upon oneself, and enduring another’s sentence concerning one’s own action [Note: [Col. 0295C] “Concerning one’s own action,” Bod. 1.]—these are what prove repentance. These are what draw a scar over the wound that has been inflicted; these are what raise and lift up the ruins of the downcast mind; these are what quench and end the burning heat of seething offenses.

For a physician will not give sick people what belongs to healthy bodies, [Note: [Col. 0295C] “For healthy bodies; but a physician will be given to the sick,” Lam. [Col. 0296B] Ebor. 2. NC. 1.] lest food administered at the wrong time should not suppress but inflame the violence [Col. 0296B] of a raging illness; [Note: [Col. 0296B] “Raging” omitted by Lam. NC. 1. Ebor.] that is, lest what could have been reduced more quickly by fasting [Note: [Col. 0296B] “Cured by attenuation,” Lam. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1. “Attenuated,” Ver.] should, through impatience, be prolonged further by feeding the undigested condition. [Note: [Col. 0296B] “Should appear to be prolonged,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. Ben. Manut.]

[Note: [Col. 0297C]

**VII.—**[page 414] **“Nothing but patience.”** The same Saint-Remi manuscript reads: “There is no impatience.” So too the Sorbonne, Foix, and Grenoble manuscripts. The more recent Saint-Remi and Dijon manuscripts read: “In illnesses there is nothing but patience.” Lucan, IX:

[Col. 0297D]

> Patience rejoices in hardships.

**“With intolerable haste.”** The ancient copies have “the intolerable haste of communion.” But Pamelius says that this reading is exceedingly bad.

**“Complaining.”** Certain ancient manuscripts have “querulous.”

**“We wish you.”** We have restored this concluding clause from the early editions and also found it in four ancient manuscripts. I do not know on what authority Rigault introduced a different clause, which I have found nowhere. The English editors nevertheless retained it.]

VII. Therefore hands stained by impious sacrifice must be cleansed by good works [Note: [Col. 0296B] “Evil works,” Ben. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.], and wretched mouths [Note: [Col. 0296C] Lam. NC. 2. Ben. omit “wretched.”] polluted by sacrilegious food must be purified by the words of true repentance [Note: [Col. 0296C] NC. 1 adds “patiently.” “By true words,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.]; and in the secret places of the heart the faithful spirit must be renewed and consecrated [Note: [Col. 0296C] “The spirit must be renewed,” Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.]. Let the frequent groans of penitents be heard; not merely once, but [Col. 0297A] again and again let faithful tears pour from their eyes, so that those very eyes which wickedly gazed upon idols may, by tears making satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0297C] “Making satisfaction,” Lam. Ebor. 1. NC. 1. Ben.] to God, wash away the unlawful deeds they committed.

Nothing but patience is necessary for illnesses. Those who are sick struggle with their pain, and only then do they hope for health, if by endurance they overcome the pain. For a scar which a hurried physician has closed too quickly is unreliable, and at any mishap the remedy is torn open again [Note: [Col. 0297C] “Is extinguished,” Vat.], unless remedies are faithfully furnished through the very slowness of the treatment [Note: [Col. 0297C] “For which remedies are not,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ben.]. The flame is quickly rekindled into a conflagration [Note: [Col. 0297C] “Are furnished. The conflagration of the flame,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. “The plate is recalled,” Ver.], unless the fuel of the entire fire, even to the final spark, is extinguished; so that people of this kind may rightly understand that even the delay itself is more to their advantage and that more trustworthy remedies are being furnished through necessary postponements.

Besides, what meaning will there be in the fact that those who confess Christ are confined in the custody of a filthy prison [Col. 0297B] [Note: [Col. 0297C] “Besides, what meaning will there be in the fact that they undergo trials and are confined in prison?” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Ben.], if those who denied him are in no danger to their faith? What meaning will there be in the fact that they are bound within encircling chains in the name of God, if those who did not maintain their confession of God [Note: [Col. 0297C] “Who rejected God,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Manut.] are not excluded from communion? What meaning will there be in the fact that imprisoned martyrs lay down their glorious [Note: [Col. 0298C] “What meaning will there be if those who are imprisoned lay down their glorious…,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Manut.] lives, if those who abandoned the faith do not feel the magnitude of their dangers and offenses?

But if they display excessive impatience [Note: [Col. 0298C] “Display the least patience,” Ben. Vat. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2. NC. 2. “Display their impatience,” Oxon.] and demand communion with intolerable haste, they hurl in vain those querulous, odious insults—which have no force against the truth—from insolent and unbridled mouths, since it had been within their power to retain by their own right what they are now compelled [Col. 0297C] to request because of a necessity they voluntarily sought [Note: [Col. 0298C] “Now by necessity,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]. For the faith which was able to confess Christ [Col. 0298A] was also able to be retained by Christ in communion. We wish you, most blessed and most glorious pope [Note: [Col. 0298C] “We wish you, brother,” Rigalt. Oxon.], always to enjoy good health in the Lord and to remember us.

[Note: [Col. 0297D]

EPISTLE XXVII.—In the old manuscript of Saint-Denis of Reims and in one of my own, this epistle has no title. In the Morel edition it is said to be from Celerinus to the lapsed. In the Manutius edition, which is the earliest of all, and in the Foix manuscript, it is “Cyprian to the Lapsed.” This is the correct reading.]

## EPISTLE XXVII

(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXVII; Paris., XXVI; Oxon., Lips., XXXIII.)  
**CYPRIAN TO THE LAPSED**

**ARGUMENT.—**You have the subject of this epistle below, in Epistle XXIX. “They wrote letters to me,” he says, “demanding not that peace be granted to them, but claiming it as though it had already been granted to them, because they say that Paul granted peace to everyone, as you will read in their letter, a copy of which I sent to you, together with the brief reply which I made to them.” The letter of the lapsed to whom he replies is, however, missing.

[Col. 0297D] [Note: [Col. 0297D]

I.—*Whose precepts.* At this point I have chosen to follow the text of the Foix manuscript, which I believe to be better than that preferred by the editions of Manutius and Morel and by my old manuscript, where it is written: “whose precepts we ought to fear and observe.” The manuscript of Saint-Denis of Reims reads: “to serve and observe the precepts.”

*They will not overcome it.* So also in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, [Col. 0298D] p. 194. The Foix manuscript reads: “they will not prevail against it.” In Pacian’s letter to Sympronianus against the treatises of the Novatianists: “they will not gain strength against it.”

*I will give you the keys.* Although here the keys are not given to Peter but promised, the ancients nevertheless believed—and rightly—that they were given; and Optatus says that Peter alone received them, though they were to be shared with the others. For, as Saint Augustine says, he bore in his person, by a figurative universality, the representation of the whole Church; and the other apostles were assuredly what Peter was, endowed with an equal fellowship both of honor and of authority, as Cyprian says in the book *On the Unity of the Church*. See the letter of Stephen, bishop of Larissa, to Pope Boniface II, published in Holstenius’s Roman collection; the letter of Mapinius, bishop of Reims, in Freher and Duchesne; and Francis Mason, *On the English Ministry*, book IV, chapters 3 and 4.

[Col. 0299D] *So that the Church … should conduct.* These words were added from my old manuscript and from Morel’s edition. I am surprised that Pamelius and Rigaltius omitted them, since without them the sense is incomplete. The English editors therefore did right to restore them. Reinhart omitted them because he did not find them in Rigaltius’s edition.

*Since the Church.* These are the words of the lapsed to Cyprian.

*Unconquered.* I would not call attention to the fact that I have placed this word here—the reading preferred by the editions of Manutius, Morel, and Pamelius, and also found in my old manuscript and in the Grenoble manuscript—were it not that Rigaltius and the English edition have “ill-will” (*invidiam*) in its place, which yields no sense, or at least a very bad one. I think that Rigaltius obtained this corrupt reading from the Foix manuscript, which it is established that he used.]

### I

Our Lord, whose precepts and admonitions we ought to observe, when establishing the honor of the bishop and the ordering of his Church, speaks [Note: [Col. 0298C] “Speaks to the Church,” Bod. 1.] in the Gospel and says to Peter:

> I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not overcome it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind upon earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth will be loosed also in heaven.  
> (Matt. 16:18–19)

From this, through the successive changes of times and successions, the ordination of bishops and the ordering of the Church have come down to us, so that the Church is established upon the bishops, and every act of the Church is governed by these same presiding officers. Since this, therefore, has been founded by divine law [Note: [Col. 0298C] “Since this has thus been founded by divine law,” Bod. 1.], I am astonished that some have wished, with such audacious rashness, [Col. 0299A] to write to me in such a way as to issue letters in the name of the Church: “since [Note: [Col. 0299C] “Wished, since,” printed editions] the Church is constituted in the bishop and clergy and in all who stand firm.”

Far be it from us—and may neither the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 0299C] “May the Lord’s,” Oxon.] mercy nor his unconquered power permit—that the number of the lapsed should be called the Church, since it is written: “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32). We do indeed desire that all should be restored to life, and we pray with our petitions and groans that they may be restored to their former condition. But if certain of the lapsed wish themselves to be the Church, and if the Church is among them and in them, what remains but that we should ask them to deign to admit us into the Church?

Those who, mindful of their offense, owe satisfaction to God must therefore be submissive, quiet, and modest; nor should they issue letters in the name of the Church, since they know that it is rather to the Church [Col. 0299B] that they are writing.

[Note: [Col. 0300D]

II.—*Kindness.* My manuscript and the Morel edition read “goodness.”]

### II

Recently, however, some of the lapsed wrote to me who were humble, meek, trembling, and God-fearing, and who had always acted gloriously and nobly in the Church, yet had never credited their work to the Lord as a claim upon him, knowing that he said: “And when you have done all these things, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17:10).

Reflecting on these things, although they had received certificates from the martyrs, they nevertheless wrote to me in supplication, so that their satisfaction might be accepted by the Lord. They acknowledged their offense and declared that they were practicing true repentance; that they were not rushing rashly or importunately toward peace, but were awaiting our presence, saying that peace itself would also be sweeter to them if they received it while we were present. How greatly [Col. 0299C] I rejoiced over them, the Lord is witness—the Lord who has deigned to show what servants of this kind and character deserve from his kindness.

Since I recently received that letter and have now read that you have written something different, I ask you to distinguish your wishes, and that all of you who have now sent this letter append your names to the petition and transmit the petition to me with each person’s name. For I must first know to whom I am to reply. Then, in accordance with the limited capacity of my position and activity, I shall reply to each of the points you have written. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to enjoy good health and to act peacefully and quietly in accordance with [Col. 0300A] the Lord’s discipline. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0300D]

EPISTLE XXVIII.—This epistle was first published by Manutius. Pamelius possessed no old copy of it. The English editors had one from the Bodleian Library. I possessed one from the Colbert Library, which formerly belonged to the College of Foix; I also had one from my own library and another from the city of Grenoble. Moreover, this epistle is copied twice in the Foix manuscript.]

## EPISTLE XXVIII

(Pamel., Rig., Baluz., XXVIII; Paris., XXVI; Oxon., Lips., XXXIV.)  
**TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS**

**ARGUMENT.—**The subject of this epistle agrees sufficiently with that of the preceding one, and I believe this is the epistle of which he speaks in the following letter. For he praises his clergy because they had excluded from communion Gaius, presbyter of Didda, and his deacon, who were rashly admitting the lapsed to communion; and he urges them to do the same in the case of certain others.

[Note: [Col. 0300D]

I.—*Contrived.* Thus the Foix manuscript and the editions of Manutius and Morel. But my manuscript and the Grenoble manuscript prefer “corrupt.” The English editors report that they also read it thus in one Bodleian manuscript.]

### I

Cyprian to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons: greetings.

You acted with integrity and discipline, dearest brothers, when, with the counsel of my fellow bishops who were present, you determined that communion should not be granted to Gaius, presbyter of Didda, and his deacon. They had repeatedly been caught in their perverse errors—communicating with the lapsed and offering the lapsed persons’ oblations—and, although they had been warned once and again by my colleagues, as you wrote to me, not to do this, they stubbornly persisted in their presumption and audacity, deceiving certain brothers from among our people.

We desire to care for these people with all humility [Note: [Col. 0299D] “Advantage,” Bod. 1.], and we look after their salvation not with contrived flattery but with sincere faith, so that through true repentance, groaning, and fullness of sorrow they may entreat the Lord [Note: [Col. 0300C] “Of the Lord,” Bod. 1.], because it is written: “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent” (Rev. 2:5). And again divine Scripture says: [Col. 0300C] “Thus says the Lord: When you turn and groan, then you will be saved, and you will know where you were” (Isa. 30:15).

[Note: [Col. 0300D]

II.—*Flatteries.* Tacitus, *Histories*, book I: “Flattery is the worst poison of genuine affection.” And in the *Life of Agricola*: “Those who praise are the worst kind of enemies.” Cicero, in the book *On Friendship*, says that there is no plague greater than adulation, flattery, and sycophancy. Dio Chrysostom, Oration III, writes that flattery is the basest of all vices. Jerome, in the letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “Everyone who flatters is a coaxing enemy.” The same author, in the *Dialogue Against the Pelagians*: “Flattery is always treacherous, crafty, and coaxing.” Saint Ambrose—or whoever the author may be—in *On Duties*, book III, chapter 16: “For there is no true friendship where there is deceitful flattery.” Seneca said in Epistle XLV that flattery resembles greed. In Plutarch there is a book on how a flatterer may be distinguished from a friend. Symmachus, book I, Epistle 31: “Those who continually flatter are of shattered fidelity.” Ovid, *Amores*, book III, elegy 8:

> Impious poisons lurk beneath sweet honey.

[Col. 0301D] An old author of a gloss on Charlemagne’s capitulary concerning Italian cases calls flatterers *Placentini*, as we noted in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1043.

*Disobedience.* The Foix manuscript reads *inobedientiam* (“disobedience”). Yet the same manuscript, in Epistle XLII, p. 56, has: “which causes scandal to the contentious and disobedient.” Tertullian, in the book *Exhortation to Chastity*, used *obaudientiam* (“obedience”).]

### II

But how can those people groan and repent when some of the presbyters intervene against their groans and tears, rashly supposing that they ought to communicate with them? They do not know that it is written: “Those who call you happy [Note: [Col. 0300C] “Not knowing that it is written: Those who call you happy and blessed,” Bod.] lead you into error and disturb the path of your feet” (Isa. 3:12).

Our wholesome and truthful counsels therefore rightly accomplish nothing, while saving [Col. 0301A] truth is obstructed by pernicious flatteries [Note: [Col. 0300D] “By one who flatters,” Rigaltius conjectures.] and caresses. The wounded and sick mind of the lapsed suffers what the physically sick and infirm also often suffer: while rejecting wholesome foods and beneficial drinks as though they were bitter and repulsive, and desiring things which delight them and seem sweet for the present, through disobedience and lack of restraint they bring destruction and death upon themselves. The practitioner’s true remedy makes no progress toward their salvation while sweet enticement deceives them with its blandishments.

[Note: [Col. 0301D]

III.—*I could not give myself alone.* Thus Manutius and Rigaltius. But my old manuscript, the Grenoble manuscript, and one Bodleian manuscript read: “I do not think that I alone ought to give judgment.” So also in Morel’s edition, except that he placed “could” in place of “think.”

*Their place.* Thus Pamelius and the others. Manutius published “this alone,” which is also how it reads in the Foix manuscript. I also found that it had been written thus in one Vatican manuscript.

[Col. 0302C] *Late.* This is the reading of the Manutius edition and of the Grenoble manuscript. Morel’s edition and one Bodleian manuscript read *sorte* (“by chance”). Mine has *sorore* (“sister”), in place of *sorte*, as I believe.

*Ministers.* Although I do not doubt that this reading is sound, I must nevertheless note that in the Foix manuscript—in which, as I said above, this epistle is copied twice—it is consistently written “all the men.” I know that it was also written this way in the Verona manuscript. But the other old manuscripts and editions prefer “ministers.”

*From the monthly distribution.* Morel thus published it in place of *dictione* in Manutius’s edition. But in Latinius’s manuscript and in the Verona manuscript, and also in the Foix manuscript, it is written *a dictione*. My manuscript confirms Morel’s edition.

*Monthly.* Below, Epistle XXXIV, p. 28: “Let the monthly distributions be divided in equal quantities.” Rufinus, book IV, chapter 28: “one hundred and fifty denarii of monthly [Col. 0302D] allowance.” The Foix and Grenoble manuscripts and Morel’s edition read “of those measuring”; mine reads “of those repeatedly measuring.”]

### III

Accordingly, as you faithfully and beneficially take counsel in accordance with my letters, do not retreat from your better counsels. Read these same letters also to my fellow bishops, if any are present or should arrive, so that, with one mind and in concord, we may maintain a beneficial policy for tending and healing the wounds of the lapsed. We shall discuss [Col. 0301B] everything most fully when, through the Lord’s mercy, we have begun to assemble together.

Meanwhile, if anyone immoderate and headstrong—whether one of our own presbyters or deacons or one from abroad—should dare to communicate with the lapsed before our judgment, let him be excluded from our communion. He will have to state before us all the case for his rashness when, with the Lord’s permission, we have assembled together.

You also wished me to reply with my opinion concerning the subdeacons Philumenus and Fortunatus, and the acolyte Favorinus, who departed in the intervening period and have now returned. In this matter I could not appoint myself sole judge, since many of the clergy are still absent and have not thought that they should reclaim their place, even [Col. 0302A] belatedly. The case of each person must be considered and examined more fully, not only with my fellow bishops but also with the entire people itself. For the matter must be weighed with balanced moderation and then decided, since it is to establish a precedent concerning the ministers of the Church for the future.

Meanwhile, let them merely abstain from the monthly distribution, not as though they were deprived of ecclesiastical ministry, but so that, with everything left intact, their cases may be deferred until our presence [Note: [Col. 0301C] “Let this inquiry be deferred,” Bod. 1.]. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to enjoy good health. Greet the whole brotherhood, and farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0302D]

EPISTLE XXIX.—I possessed three copies of this epistle, which we owe to the Manutius edition: one from the Colbert Library, which formerly belonged to the College of Foix; another from my own library; and a third from the city of Grenoble. The English editors had one from the Bodleian Library.

*Subdeacon.* In all editions published after the Manutius edition, the words “our brothers” are added after this. We removed these words, plainly added by Morel, as superfluous, because they are not found in our old manuscripts. Nevertheless, in the Grenoble manuscript “our brother” is added after “subdeacon.”

*The concerted rashness of certain men.* I do not know on what authority Morel added “the observed rashness of certain men.” For apart from the fact that the word “observed” is unnecessary there, it is not found in the Manutius edition, in our old [Col. 0303C] manuscripts, or in the English manuscripts. It is therefore surprising that it was retained in the English edition.

*Wholesome.* At this point we have followed the authority of the old copies and Morel’s edition. Rigaltius and the English editors preferred the reading “saving.”]

## EPISTLE XXIX

(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXIX; Paris., XXXIII; Oxon., Lips., XXXV.)  
**TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS RESIDING AT ROME**

[Col. 0302B]

**ARGUMENT.—**The Roman clergy are informed of the rashness of the lapsed who were demanding peace.

Cyprian to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome: greetings.

Both our common affection and reason itself require, dearest brothers, that I withhold from your awareness nothing concerning the matters being conducted among us, so that we may share a common counsel regarding the benefit of ecclesiastical administration.

For after I wrote to you the letter which I sent through Saturus the reader and Optatus the subdeacon, the concerted rashness of certain lapsed persons [Note: [Col. 0301C] “The observed rashness of certain men,” Oxon. “Concerning the rashness of certain men,” [Col. 0302C] Manut.]—who refuse to repent and make satisfaction to God—caused them to write to me, demanding not that peace be granted to them, but claiming it as though it had already been granted to them, because they say that Paul granted peace to everyone. You will read this in their letter, a copy of which I sent to you, together with what I briefly replied to them in the meantime. I also sent you a copy of the letter which I subsequently wrote to the clergy, so that you might know its character.

But if their rashness is not restrained by either my letters or yours, and if it does not obey wholesome counsels, we shall do what the Lord commanded to be done in accordance with the Gospel. I wish you, dearest brothers, always to enjoy good health. Farewell.

## EPISTLE XXX

(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXX; Paris., XXIX; Oxon., Lips., XXXVI; *Works of Novatian*, ed. Jackson, p. 309.)  
**THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS RESIDING AT ROME TO CYPRIAN** (C, G)\*

[Col. 0303B]

**ARGUMENT.—**The Roman Church sets forth its judgment concerning the lapsed, a judgment agreeing with the decrees of the Church of Carthage.—The indulgence to be applied to the lapsed is to be measured according to the standard of the Gospel.—That the peace granted by the confessors rests only upon grace and favor is evident from the fact that the lapsed are referred to the bishops.—The seditious demand for peace is imputed to the faction of Felicissimus.

[Note: [Col. 0303C]

416 EPISTLE XXX.—I. Manutius was the first to publish this epistle. Old copies of it are exceedingly rare. [Col. 0303D] I possessed two: one from my own library, the other from the city of Grenoble. In correcting it, the English editors used one Bodleian manuscript.

Lombert and William Cave say that it was written by Novatian in the name of the Roman clergy before he created the schism, but they offer no proof. Perhaps they inferred this from these words of Epistle LII, p. 67: “Novatian then serving as writer.” In an old Reims manuscript it is noted that Epistle XXVI was dictated by Novatian, as we observed there. Jerome, in the letter *On Five Questions* to Pope Damasus, calls Novatian a most eloquent man; and in the letter to Paul of Concordia he mentions Novatian’s letters. Cyprian himself, in Epistle LII, p. 73, speaking to Antonianus about Novatian, says: “Let him boast as he pleases, and proclaim his philosophy or his eloquence in proud tones.” [Col. 0304C] We possess his treatise *On the Trinity*, published with the works of Tertullian.

*Pope.* In my old manuscript, in manuscript 199 of the Vatican Library, and in the Grenoble manuscript, it is written *papati*. Similarly, in Liberatus, chapter 23, four ancient manuscripts have *Menate* in place of what the editions read as *Menna*, as we noted at Epistle XVI. See also the notes on the second epistle, p. 387.

*The rashness of the words.* This passage may support the opinion of the most illustrious Bishop of Oxford, who believes that certain less well-considered words found in Epistle XVIII of the confessors to Cyprian contain threats of excommunication. Yet since the holy martyr makes no mention of threats of this kind in Epistle XXII, where he complains of Lucian’s rashness, it seems evident that “the rashness of the words” censured here refers only to the rashness noted in the preceding epistle.

*Because it differs from him.* Previously the text read “from God.” We corrected it on the authority of the Vatican manuscripts cited in the margin of the Manutius edition, in the printed copy which I possess, as well as on that of the Grenoble manuscript and one excellent manuscript of my own. The sense also requires that it be written in this way.]

### I

The presbyters and deacons residing at Rome to Pope Cyprian: greetings.

When we had read through your letter, dearest brother, which you sent through the subdeacon Fortunatus, we were struck by a twofold pain and overwhelmed by a double grief: first, because no repose [Col. 0303C] was being granted to you amid such great necessities of persecution; and second, because the unrestrained insolence of our lapsed brothers was shown to have proceeded as far as a dangerous rashness of speech.

But although these things of which we have spoken grievously afflicted us and our spirits, [Col. 0304A] your vigor and the severity you applied in accordance with evangelical discipline moderated [Note: [Col. 0303C] “Was moderated,” Bod. 1.] the exceedingly heavy burden of our grief. For you both justly restrain the wickedness of certain people and, by exhorting them [Note: [Col. 0303C] “Justly restrains and, by exhorting,” Oxon.] to repentance, show [Note: [Col. 0304C] “Shows,” Oxon.] them the lawful way of salvation.

We were indeed greatly astonished that they wished to leap so far as to demand peace for themselves so urgently, at so untimely and bitter a moment, and in the face of so great and immeasurable a crime and offense—not so much requesting peace as claiming it, and even saying that they already possessed it in heaven. If they possess it, why do they request what they hold? But if the very fact that they request it proves that they do not possess it, why do they not await the judgment of those from whom they thought they should request the peace which they certainly do not possess?

But if they believe that they possess the prerogative of communion from some other source, [Col. 0304B] let them attempt to compare it with the Gospel, so that only then may it be firmly valid, if it does not disagree with evangelical law.
