Otherwise, how will something decreed contrary to evangelical truth be able to furnish evangelical communion? For every prerogative pertains to the privilege of indulgence only if it does not differ from the one with whom it seeks to be united. Because it differs from the one with whom it seeks to be united, it must lose the indulgence and privilege of fellowship.

[Note: [Col. 0304D]

II.—*From which they become martyrs.* Above, Epistle XXII, [Col. 0305C] p. 32: “He gave no consideration to the fact that martyrs do not make the Gospel, but that martyrs are made through the Gospel.” Below, Epistle XXXIII, p. 46: “To read the Gospel of Christ, from which martyrs are made.” And in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 188: “Those who become martyrs through the Gospel.”

*So insolently*; that is, by stirring up sedition against their presiding officers so that they might extort peace from them, as may be seen in Epistle XXII, p. 32.]

### II

Let them therefore consider what they are attempting to do [Note: [Col. 0304C] “What they will be compelled to do,” Bod. 1.] in this matter. For if the Gospel says one thing while the martyrs are said to have established a different decree, the martyrs, by coming into conflict with the Gospel, will be endangered on both sides. The majesty of the Gospel will appear already broken and prostrate [Col. 0304C] if it could be overcome by the novelty of a different decree; and the glorious crown of confession will be removed from the martyrs’ heads if they are not found to have obtained it by preserving the Gospel, from which they become martyrs. Thus it is rightly fitting for no one more than for the person who struggles [Note: [Col. 0305C] “Struggled,” Oxon.] to receive the name of martyr from the Gospel to decree nothing contrary to the Gospel.

We would, moreover, wish to learn this: if martyrs become martyrs for no other reason than that, by refusing to sacrifice, they may preserve the Church’s peace even to the shedding of their blood—lest, overcome by the pain of their tortures and losing peace, they should lose salvation—how can they think that the salvation which they believed they would not possess if they had sacrificed should be granted to those who are said to have sacrificed? For they ought to maintain in the case of others the law which they themselves appeared previously to have laid down for themselves.

In this matter, we observe that the very thing which they thought they were doing for their own benefit has been brought forward against themselves. For if the martyrs thought that peace should be granted to them, why did they not grant it themselves? Why did they decide, as they themselves say, that those people should be referred to the bishop? [Col. 0305B] For the person who orders something to be done is surely capable of doing what he orders to be done.

But, as we understand—or rather, as the matter itself speaks and cries aloud—the most holy martyrs thought that a due balance of both modesty and truth should be applied on both sides. For since they were being pressed by many people, by referring them to the bishop [Note: [Col. 0305C] “Who refer them to the bishop,” Bod. 1.] they thought they should protect their own modesty, lest they be disturbed any further; and by not themselves admitting those people to communion, they judged that the unblemished integrity of evangelical law must be preserved.

[Note: [Col. 0305C]

III.—*We know its foundation.* I believe that the Romans are speaking here of the foundation or beginnings of the Church of Carthage. In the book *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 15, Saint Augustine concluded that it had received the faith of Christ in the early days of the Church’s foundation, because it is established by the clearest testimony that the Church was then spread throughout the whole world. It is evident that Tertullian held this view as well, from his book [Col. 0305D] *Against the Jews* and from the book *On Prescriptions*; from the latter one may infer that he believed the African Church owed the beginnings of its faith to the Roman bishops. For he says: “But if you are near Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is also available to us.” Augustine, too, in his letter to Severinus, says that the authority of the Christian faith flowed into Africa from the Church across the sea, that is, the Roman Church.

This opinion may be confirmed by the authority of the letter which Pope Innocent wrote to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio. In it he says that it is evident that no one founded churches in Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily except those whom the venerable Peter or his successors appointed as priests. From this he concludes that those churches ought to follow what the Roman Church observes—the Church from which they undoubtedly received their beginning—lest, while pursuing foreign [Col. 0306C] assertions, they appear to neglect the source of their institutions.

Saint Gregory likewise, book VII, indiction I, Epistle 32, writing to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, says: “Knowing, moreover, whence the priestly order in the regions of Africa took its beginning, you act commendably when, by loving the Apostolic See, you return with prudent recollection to the origin of your office.” In the same spirit Pope Saint Leo wrote thus to the bishops appointed throughout Sicily: “You could in no way have fallen into this fault if you had taken the law governing your entire observance from the same source from which you received the consecration of your honor, and if the see of the blessed apostle Peter, which is the mother of your priestly dignity, had been the teacher of your ecclesiastical order.”

Salvian, almost a contemporary of Innocent and Leo, did not doubt that the Church of Carthage had been founded [Col. 0306D] by the apostles. In the age of Gregory the Great, the Numidians also believed that the African Church had been founded by the apostles. Moreover, the most illustrious Bishop of Oxford, in his notes on the book of Pontius the deacon *On the Life of Saint Cyprian*, believed that Simon the Zealot had been the apostle of the Africans, while Eysingrenius believed it was Saint Crescens.

*That certain things.* It is difficult to establish the reading of this passage with certainty. But so that the reader may know wherein the difficulty consists, I shall give the readings of the old manuscripts. In my excellent old manuscript it is written thus: “that certain things interpret a letter thrust in more harshly” [*quod quaedam interpretare Epistolam injecta durius*]. In the Grenoble manuscript it reads: “that certain things were thrust more harshly against you by an interpreter through a letter” [*quod quaedam interprete per epistolam injectam durius*].]

### III

Nevertheless, brother, in accordance with your charity, never cease to moderate the spirits of the lapsed and to furnish the medicine of truth to those who err, even though the disposition of the sick [Note: [Col. 0305C] “The ailing disposition,” Bod. 1.] is accustomed to reject the care of those who treat them.

This wound of the lapsed is recent; the injury is still swelling into a tumor. [Col. 0306A] We are therefore certain that, once this violent impulse has grown old over a more extended period, they will appreciate the very fact that they were held back for faithful treatment—provided, however, that there cease to be people who arm them to their own peril and, by instructing them perversely, demand for them the deadly poisons of hasty communion in place of the saving remedies of postponement [Note: [Col. 0306C] “Of postponement,” singular, Bod. 1.].

For we do not believe that they would all have dared, without the instigation of certain people, to claim peace for themselves so insolently. We know the faith of the Church of Carthage; we know its foundation; we know its humility. Hence we were also astonished when we observed that certain things had been thrust against you rather harshly through a letter, since we had often ascertained your mutual love and charity through many examples of reciprocal [Col. 0306B] affection toward one another.

It is therefore time for them to repent of their offense, to demonstrate grief over their fall, to show modesty, to display humility, to exhibit self-restraint, to call forth God’s clemency toward themselves by their submission, and, by rendering the honor due to God’s priest [Note: [Col. 0306C] “In God’s priest,” Oxon.], to elicit divine mercy toward themselves. How much better their own letter would have been if the prayers of those who stand firm on their behalf had been assisted by their own humility! For what is requested is obtained more readily when the person for whom it is requested is worthy that the request should be granted.

[Note: [Col. 0306D]

IV.—*Privatus of Lambaesis.* See the *Cyprianic Annals*, under the year 252, § 8, and Pamelius on Cyprian’s Epistle LV.

[Col. 0307C] *Standard-bearer*, that is, the standard-bearer of sedition, as he is called in Epistle LV, p. 83, to Cornelius; in the same way that Paschasius is called the standard-bearer of fury in the letter of the Council of Aquileia to Emperor Gratian; and likewise in the same way that Latinus Pacatus Drepanius called the commander of the forces of the usurper Maximus the standard-bearer of a sacrilegious faction, in the panegyric which he delivered to the emperor Theodosius, while the author of the panegyric addressed to the emperor Maximian calls Maximian’s adversary the standard-bearer of a wicked faction. Thus Robert, son of Gervase and bishop of Senez, in his treatise *On Schism*, calls Bartholomew, archbishop of Bari, the standard-bearer of schismatic depravity; see the notes on the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*, p. 1270.

*Futurus.* Thus the Verona manuscript. I am surprised that the English editors, who customarily follow Rigaltius’s edition, printed *Futurus*. Reinhart did very badly when, rejecting Rigaltius’s edition—which is sound—he restored the old reading and wrote: “of Privatus, and stealthily and fraudulently.” My old manuscript reads: “to be, and fraudulently” [*futuros ac fraudolenter*]. Pamelius believed [Col. 0307D] that Futurus and Felicissimus were the same man.]

### IV

As for Privatus of Lambaesis, you acted in your customary manner when you wished to report the matter to us as one requiring concern [Note: [Col. 0306C] Oxon. deletes “as.”]. For it is fitting that all [Col. 0307A] of us should keep watch [Note: [Col. 0307B] “Teaches us,” Bod. 1.] over the body of the whole Church, whose members are distributed throughout the various provinces.

Yet even before your letter, the deceit of that crafty man could not escape our notice. For when a certain standard-bearer from the cohort of his wickedness, Futurus, an adherent of Privatus, had previously come and sought fraudulently to elicit letters from us, neither did his identity remain hidden nor did he receive the letters he wanted. We wish you good health in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0307D]

[The supplied source breaks off here.]

**EPISTLE XXXI.**—This Epistle is badly mutilated and nevertheless interpolated in the manuscript of Saint-Arnulf of Metz. Shortly after its beginning, a lengthy fragment from the book *On the Praise of Martyrdom* has been inserted, namely from the words on p. 343, “so that, as much as in expressing,” as far as “turning it over within himself.” After that, however, the Epistle resumes at the words on p. 44, “not having a wedding garment,” and continues to the end. Furthermore, a large part of this Epistle appears above, detached from it, in that manuscript after Epistle XVII, which is addressed to Cornelius and begins: “And that we have acted.”]

42 **EPISTLE XXXI**

(Erasm., II, 7. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXI. Paris., XXX; Oxon., Lips., XXX; *Works of Novatian*, ed. Jackson, p. 277. Galland., *Biblioth. Vett. PP.* III, p. 291.)

**THE ROMAN CLERGY TO CYPRIAN**  
(C, G)\*

**SUMMARY.**—What the Roman Clergy treated briefly in the preceding Epistle they now discuss more fully and solidly, also replying to another letter of Cyprian, from which they quote several words, though that letter is not thought to survive. In passing, they also thank Cyprian for the letters sent to the Roman martyrs and confessors. It was written, like the preceding letters of the Roman Clergy, while the See was vacant after Fabian’s death.

[Note: [Col. 0307D]

**I.—Although … within himself.** In various excerpts found at the end of the works of Saint Cyprian in an ancient manuscript that formerly belonged to the monastery of Fossés and is now mine, the beginning of this Epistle is transcribed, and its title [Col. 0308C] reads as follows: “Here begins the letter to the Romans. Although well conscious within himself.” At the end this has been added: “Here ends the letter to the Romans.” But the tenor of the Epistle itself establishes that this is false, since it was certainly written by the Roman Clergy to Cyprian, as is also noted at the head of the Epistle in the Grenoble manuscript: “The Roman Clergy to Cyprian.” Nevertheless, Hincmar, in his book *On Predestination against Gottschalk*, p. 73, cites it as from the “Epistle to the Romans.” From this it is clear that the error is ancient.

**By the heavenly decrees.** I found this reading in eight ancient manuscripts. The English editors note that the Vatican manuscript reads “by the heavenly camps.” Rigault rightly says that this reading does not please him. On “the heavenly camps,” see the notes on Epistle XLIV.

**While we approve them.** Below, Epistle LXXI, p. 127: “What is beneficially suggested, if true and legitimate, let us regard rather as our own. For what we approve we make our own,” as Emperor Justinian says in the [Col. 0308D] constitution *On the Composition of the Digest*. Likewise Pope Celestine—or whoever may be the author of a certain collection circulated among his decrees—speaking of Saint Augustine’s opinions on the grace of Christ, says that the apostolic bishops made them their own when they approved them. Cassian, Book VI of *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 9: “Let us repeat both the creed’s confession and yours. For what belongs to it is yours, because by confessing its confession you have made it your own.” John of Salisbury, in the prologue to the *Policraticus*: “Whatever has been well said anywhere, 418 I make my own.” The same author, Epistle CCXXX: “Do we not also make our own all things upon which we bestow our authority?”]

### I

The presbyters and deacons residing at Rome send greetings to Pope Cyprian.

Although a mind that is well conscious within itself, supported by the strength [Note: [Col. 0307B] “Rigor,” Bod. 1.] of evangelical discipline, [Col. 0308A] and made a true witness to itself in the heavenly decrees [Note: [Col. 0307B] “Camps,” Vat.], is ordinarily content with God alone as judge and neither seeks another’s praise nor fears accusations, nevertheless those are worthy of double praise who, although they know that they owe an account of their conscience to God alone as judge, still desire their actions to be approved even by their own brothers.

It is not surprising, brother Cyprian, that you should do this, since, in accordance with your modesty and the native [Note: [Col. 0307B] “And native” omitted by Lin.] diligence of your deliberations, you wished to find us not so much judges as participants in your counsels, so that, while we approve your actions, we might share their praise with you and, because we also affirm them, might become coheirs [Note: [Col. 0308B] “Heirs of your counsels,” Snir., Lin.] of your good counsels. We are all believed to have performed [Note: [Col. 0308B] “To perform,” Lin.] the same act when we are found to be united by the same agreement in judgment and discipline.

[Col. 0308B] [Note: [Col. 0308D]

**II.—The ship.** The manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims reads: “dash the ship of ecclesiastical discipline.” The Dijon manuscript and the more recent manuscript of Saint-Victor read: “dash the ship of the Church upon false reefs.”

[Col. 0309C] **Ancient … severity.** These words, which were added in the Aldine edition, are absent from the old editions and from two ancient manuscripts. They are, however, present in the others.

**The letters have proved.** In the Saint-Arnulf manuscript a fragment from the book *On the Praise of Martyrdom* follows at this point.]

### II

For what is more appropriate in peace, or more necessary in the warfare of persecution, than to maintain the due [Note: [Col. 0308B] “Than that it ought to,” Lin.] severity of divine strength? Whoever relaxes it must always go astray [Note: [Col. 0308B] “Fall,” Lin.] amid the unstable course of events, be scattered this way and that by the varied and uncertain storms of circumstances, and—as though the helm of deliberation had been torn from his hands—dash the ship of ecclesiastical salvation upon the reefs. Thus it becomes evident that [Col. 0309A] provision can be made for the Church’s salvation in no other way than by repelling those who act against it like hostile waves, and by always preserving the rule of its discipline like a saving helm amid the storm.

Nor is this a counsel only recently devised by us, nor have these defenses against the wicked suddenly occurred among us only now. Rather, this severity among us is ancient, our faith is ancient, and our discipline is shown to be ancient. For the Apostle would not have uttered such great praise of us when he said, “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Rom. 1:8), unless that strength had already drawn the roots of faith from those times; and it is a very great offense to have proved unworthy [Note: [Col. 0309B] “Unworthy” in the plural, Lin.] of that praise and glory. For it is less disgraceful never to have attained the proclamation of praise [Col. 0309B] than to have fallen from the summit of praise. It is a lesser [Note: [Col. 0309B] “Of less,” Bod. 1.] offense never to have been honored by favorable testimony than to have lost the honor of favorable testimonies. It is less disgraceful to have lain obscure and unpraised, without any proclamation of one’s virtues [Note: [Col. 0309C] “To have remained silent,” Lin.], than to have been disinherited from the faith and lost one’s own praises. For unless what is proclaimed to someone’s glory is preserved by anxious and watchful labor, it swells into an indictment of the gravest offense.

[Note: [Col. 0309C]

**III.—Entangling.** One of my ancient books reads “retaining”; the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis reads: “in retaining those snares of the devil.”

**By commissioning.** Thus, in the acts of the Conference of Carthage between the Catholics and the Donatists, we see that several bishops commissioned their colleagues to represent their presence by signing on their behalf. Likewise, not to seek examples only from remote times, Natalis of Oea delivered an opinion at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian on his own behalf and on behalf of Pompeius of Sabrata and Dioga of Leptis Magna, “who commissioned me.”

[Col. 0309D] **Is not innocent.** Cicero, as quoted by Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII: “For what difference is there between one who advises an act and one who approves it?” This is taken from the Second *Philippic*. Seneca, *Troades*: “He who did not prevent wrongdoing when he could have done so commands it.” And below: “The guilt of a coerced crime returns to its instigator.” The author of the *Epistle to Celantia*, among the works of Jerome: “For as far as the reckoning of sin is concerned, one who resolved to harm has already harmed.” Valerius Maximus, Book IX, chapter 2: “To look upon a crime with an approving mind was to commit the crime.” Arator, Book II of *The Acts of the Apostles*: “Punishment does not separate those whom equal guilt binds.”

**Commanded.** This reading seems the best. Nevertheless, I found it in only one ancient book. The others and the older Pamelian editions have “procured.” Pamelius changed it, following Coster’s conjecture, although he admits that he had read “procured” everywhere. Thus, in Epistle XLIV of the *Encyclical Codex*, the [Col. 0310C] Beauvais manuscript writes “whom to procure by divine judgment” instead of “whom to command.” It is an easy error, and it was also admitted into another ancient manuscript of the same church, namely into chapter 18 of Liberatus’s *Breviary*, where, instead of “he dismissed them, having procured nothing,” as the editions and three ancient books read, the manuscript of the Church of Beauvais has “commanding.” Likewise, in Fulgentius Placiades, Book II of the *Mythologies*, where he treats of Vulcan and Minerva, one should read “Jupiter commanded,” instead of the “procured” that is read there.

Lactantius confirms the reading I have retained in this passage of Cyprian, in chapter 64 of the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*: “The ancient precept is not to kill. This must be understood in such a way that we are commanded not merely to keep our hands from homicide—which was long ago forbidden by public laws—but that it is unlawful to bring danger upon anyone either by issuing a command or by a word.” Emperor Constantine, under the title of the Theodosian Code concerning the Julian Law of Treason, declared that the man by whose advice and instigation another proceeded [Col. 0310D] to make an accusation ought to be subjected to torture. And in Julius Paulus, Book V, title 23: “Those who commission a killing are to be punished in the same way as murderers.” Salvian, Book VII, chapter 19: “For great and most powerful authority, which can prevent a very great crime, seems to approve that it ought to be done if it knowingly allows it to be committed. For one who has it in his power to prohibit an act commands it to be done if he does not prohibit its commission.” Ennodius, Book I, Epistle V: “He who is said to have been able to commit a crime is believed to have committed it.” Pacian, in the *Exhortation to Repentance*: “I add that it is not hands alone that are punished in a case of murder, but also every counsel that has driven another’s life into death.” The Epistle of the Bishops of Egypt to Emperor Leo, in chapter VII of the *Encyclical Codex*: “Afterward, too, he who brings this crime about is virtually a murderer with his own hands and therefore deserves condemnation, since in punishment the person who orders evil to be done stands next to the person who does it.”

[Col. 0311C] **Be effective.** I judged that this should be corrected thus, following the authority of the ancient copies and editions, instead of “proceed,” which the later editions prefer. Yet I admit that I found this last reading in two of my ancient books, the Grenoble manuscript and one manuscript of Saint-Victor, as well as in the Aldine edition. The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis and the Lamonian manuscript have [Col. 0311D] “be beneficial,” with the same sense.]

### III

Our previous letters proved that we do not say this falsely. In them we set forth our judgment to you in a clear exposition, both against [Col. 0310A] those who had betrayed themselves as unbelievers by an unlawful declaration in impious certificates and who appeared likely to escape those entangling snares of the devil [Note: [Col. 0310B] “That they would escape in retaining those snares of the devil, which,” Lin.], although they were bound by the very fact that they had attested to it no less than if they had approached the impious altars; and also against those who had caused official records [Note: [Col. 0310B] “Received,” Lin., Bod. 1, Benev., Manut., Oxon., Lips.] to be made, even though they had not been present when they were made, since by commissioning it they had caused their presence to be entered in the record.

For one who commanded that a crime be committed is not innocent of it, nor is one free from an offense 43 when an offense, though not committed by him personally, is nevertheless publicly recorded with his consent. And since the entire sacrament of faith is understood to be comprised in the confession of Christ’s name, the man who seeks deceptive tricks as an excuse has denied him; and the man who wishes to appear to have complied with edicts or laws enacted [Col. 0310B] against the Gospel has already obeyed by the very fact that he wished to appear to have obeyed.

We have also shown our faith and agreement against those who had polluted their hands and mouths with unlawful sacrifices after first polluting their own minds, from which their hands and mouths themselves were also polluted. Far be it from the Roman Church to surrender its strength through such profane leniency and to relax the sinews of severity after the majesty of faith has been overthrown; so that, while the wreckage of our fallen brothers is still not merely lying there but continues to fall, remedies administered with excessive haste should confer a communion that will certainly be of no benefit, [Col. 0311A] and through false mercy new wounds [Note: [Col. 0311C] “Wounds made,” Lin.] should be impressed upon the old wounds of transgression, with the result that repentance too is taken from the wretched for their greater ruin. For where will the medicine of indulgence be able to take effect if the physician himself, by cutting short repentance, is indulgent toward the sources of danger—if he merely covers the wound and does not permit the necessary remedies of time to draw a scar over it? This is not to heal but, if we wish to speak the truth, to kill.

[Note: [Col. 0311D]

**IV.—The honor of martyrdom.** This fragment of the Epistle appears, as we have said, in the wrong place in the Saint-Arnulf manuscript.]

### IV

Although you also have a letter in agreement with ours from the confessors whom the dignity of their confession still keeps enclosed here in prison, and whom their faith, already glorious in confession, has once crowned for the evangelical contest, a letter in which they set forth the severity of evangelical discipline and turned unlawful petitions away [Col. 0311B] from the Church’s sense of shame. Had they not done this, the ruins of evangelical discipline would not easily be repaired [Note: [Col. 0311C] “Would repair,” Bod. 1.], especially since it was more fitting for no one than for those who had surrendered themselves to raging men to be tortured and mangled for the Gospel to preserve inviolate the rule of evangelical strength and its dignity [Note: [Col. 0311C] “To preserve with inviolate dignity,” Vat.], lest they deservedly lose the honor of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0311C] “Had surrendered themselves—the martyr,” Bod. 1.] if, on the occasion [Note: [Col. 0311C] “At the killing,” Lin.] of martyrdom, they had wished to become transgressors of the Gospel. For whoever does not preserve what he has in the very basis from which he possesses it loses what he possessed when he violates the basis from which he possesses it. [Note: [Col. 0311C] “Violates, violates what,” Oxon.]

[Note: [Col. 0311D]

**V.—And ruins.** The Speyer edition and three ancient books do not have these two words. The old Venetian edition has them. Two other ancient books prefer “snares” to “ruins.”

**Corpses.** The Saint-Arnulf manuscript has “wounds.” This reading seems better to me, 419 and I would have placed it in the text if I had possessed that manuscript when this passage was being printed. But if anyone thinks that the word “corpses” (*funera*) should be retained, it must be understood as “deaths,” or rather “the bodies of the dead.” Above, in the Epistle to Donatus, p. 3: “Though living, they are adorned for a voluntary funeral.” For *funus* is frequently used for a dead body or corpse. In Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, “a mangled corpse,” that is, a torn body, as Servius interprets it. Juvenal in the First Satire:

> A corpse is borne along, to be mourned by angry friends.

[Col. 0312C] Statius at the beginning of the *Thebaid*: “and the corpses of kings lacking tombs.” Silius Italicus, Book VIII:

> And amid the strewn corpses  
> he sought the prostrate body  
> of his brother Mancinus.

Tacitus, *Annals* I: “that the corpse should be borne through the triumphal gate.” See Freinsheim’s notes there. The *Epitome of Aurelius Victor*, under Diocletian: “His corpse is placed in Gallienus’s tomb.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII: “The corpse [Col. 0312D] is carried to burial, while the whole people accompanies the funeral procession.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVI: “King Chnodomarius, having fallen over heaps of corpses.” The same, Book XXIX: “His corpse was carried in by the undertakers, while a great many dignitaries, dressed in mourning, preceded it.” Likewise Book XXXI: “The emperor, surrounded by dreadful terrors and gradually climbing upon a pile of corpses, fled to the lancers.” Julius Capitolinus, in *Antoninus the Philosopher*: “Finally, before the corpse was buried.” Optatus of Milevis, Book II: “One corpse is enough for each tomb, and then it is closed.” Jerome, in the *Epistle to Paulinus on the Education of a Monk*: “How many today, by living in this manner, carry their own corpses and, like whitewashed tombs, are full of dead men’s bones.” The same, in the *Epitaph of Nepotian*: “We hold as a corpse the man whom we thought our heir.” The same, in the *Life of the Monk Malchus*: “He therefore escorted me out of the monastery as though he were carrying out a corpse.” Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History* I, chapter 8: “The corpses of their children.”

A petition submitted to the Augusti Valentinian and Marcian [Col. 0313C] by Bassus, bishop of Ephesus, at the Council of Chalcedon: “Moreover, they delivered many of my people to death by various blows, so that certain men exposed their corpses before the doors of the Holy Church of God.” Here the editors of the Roman edition placed “cadavers” in the margin in the manner of an interpretation for “corpses.” Sulpicius Severus, Book II of the *Sacred History*, speaking of the discovery of the Holy Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ: “They then formed the plan of bringing someone recently dead into contact with the crosses. Without delay, as though by God’s providence, the corpse [Col. 0313D] of a dead man was being carried in a solemn funeral procession, and amid the crowding of all the people the body was snatched from the bier.—The corpse sprang up and stood among its own spectators.” The comedy *Querolus*: “And we ourselves were carrying that corpse—I do not know where.” Sidonius, Book VII, Epistle 17: “Maximus himself claims for himself the role of honoring the corpse.” The same, at the end of Poem XVI: “Or rather, his mind distracted by corpses needing burial.” Cassiodorus, Book III, Epistle 19: “Plots for burying corpses.” The Acts of the Council of Bagai: “The shores are full of the corpses of those who perish.” Liberatus, chapter 11, speaking of the death of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria: “He is killed, mangled, cast out, and his corpse is burned; even his ashes are scattered to the winds.” I agree with Livineius and Acidalius, who think that where Drepanius’s panegyric for the Emperor Theodosius reads “they had handled the reins of the condemned,” “the corpses of the condemned” should be restored.]

### V

At this point we owe you and do give you the greatest and most abundant thanks: because you illuminated [Note: [Col. 0312C] “Animated,” Fab.] the darkness of their prison with your letters; because you came to them in whatever way you could gain entrance; because you refreshed through your exhortations and letters their spirits, already strengthened [Col. 0311C] by their faith and confession; because, having celebrated [Note: [Col. 0312C] “Persecuted,” Oxon.] their blessed condition [Col. 0312A] with fitting praises, you kindled them to a far more ardent desire for heavenly glory; because you urged forward those already inclined; and because, as we believe and hope, you animated [Note: [Col. 0312C] “Armed,” Bod. 1.] by the strength of your discourse those who will be victors. Thus, although all this appears to proceed from the faith of those who confess [Note: [Col. 0312C] “This entire confidence,” Bod. 1.] and from divine indulgence, they may nevertheless appear to have become indebted to you in some degree in their martyrdom.

But, to return once more to the point from which our discourse appeared to digress, you will find appended the kind of letter that we also sent to Sicily. Yet a greater necessity of postponing this matter rests upon us, since, after the death of Fabian, a man of most noble memory, no bishop has yet been appointed among us because of the difficulties of affairs and the times—one who might govern [Note: [Col. 0312C] “Remedy,” Lin.] all these matters and, with authority [Col. 0312B] and deliberation, take account of those who have fallen.

Nevertheless, in so momentous a matter we approve what you yourself have considered: first, that the peace of the Church must be awaited [Note: [Col. 0312C] Oxon. punctuates: “first; the Church’s peace”]; and then that the case of the fallen should be treated through a joint conference of counsels with bishops, presbyters, deacons, confessors, and the laypeople who have remained standing. For it seems to us both exceedingly 44 invidious and burdensome that what appears to have been committed by many should not be examined by many, and that one person should pronounce judgment when so great an offense is shown to have spread through many. For no decree can be secure that does not appear to have gained the agreement of a very great number.

Look upon almost the whole world laid waste, with the remnants and ruins of the fallen lying everywhere, and understand that counsel as great as the offense appears to have spread widely is therefore required. [Col. 0312C] Let the medicine not be smaller than the wound, nor the remedies smaller than the corpses; so that, just as [Col. 0313A] those who fell did so because in blind rashness they were excessively incautious, those who strive to settle this matter may employ every measure of deliberation, lest anything improperly done be judged invalid by all.

[Note: [Col. 0313D]

**VI.—For the ecclesiastical name.** We restored this reading [Col. 0314C] by following the English edition and the authority of certain ancient books. If anyone should nevertheless prefer to read “in the name,” I do not object.

**Not instantaneous.** For some circumstances require neither slow remedies nor sluggish physicians, as Alexander the Great said of himself in Quintus Curtius, Book III. Thus the Epistle of the Council of Chalcedon to the Emperors reads in the edition of Rusticus the deacon: “Great sufferings require powerful medicines and wise physicians.”

**Require.** Two ancient books have: “ought to require medicine.”

[Col. 0314D] **Repentance.** Previously “repentance” was read in the accusative, and that reading is confirmed by the old editions and seven ancient copies. Our reading, which seems better, is confirmed by three ancient manuscripts.

**Let them send ambassadors.** Tertullian, in the book *On Repentance*: “To prostrate oneself before the presbyters, to kneel before those dear to God, and to charge the brothers with embassies of one’s supplication.”]

### VI

Therefore, with one and the same purpose, prayers, and tears, let both we, who until now appear to have escaped the ruins of this time, and those who appear to have fallen into these calamities of the time, beseech the divine majesty and ask for peace for the ecclesiastical name. Let us cherish, guard, and arm one another with mutual prayers. Let us pray for the fallen, that they may be raised up; let us pray for those who stand, that they may not be tested to the point of ruin; let us pray that those who are reported to have fallen may recognize the magnitude of their offense and understand [Col. 0313B] that it requires neither instantaneous nor overhasty medicine.

Let us pray that both the effect of indulgence and the repentance of the fallen may follow, so that, having understood their own offense, they may be willing meanwhile to show patience toward us and may not disturb the Church’s still-unsettled condition, lest they appear to have kindled an internal persecution against us themselves and thus add to the sum of their offenses the fact that they were also disruptive. For modesty is especially fitting for those whose immodest mind is condemned in their offenses.

Certainly let them knock at the doors, but by no means break them down. Let them approach the threshold of the Church, but by no means leap over it [Note: [Col. 0313C] “So that they may leap over it,” old unnamed manuscript, Spir.]. Let them keep watch at the gates of the heavenly camp, but armed with the modesty by which they understand that they have been deserters. Let them take up again the trumpet of their prayers, but not so as to sound a call to war. Let them indeed arm themselves [Col. 0313C] with the weapons of modesty and take up again the shield of faith that, from fear of death, they had abandoned by their denial; but let them consider themselves armed now against the enemy, the devil, not against the Church, which grieves over their fall.

[Col. 0314A] A modest petition, a respectful request, necessary humility, and patience that is not idle will benefit them greatly. Let them send tears as ambassadors for their grief; let groans drawn from their innermost breast perform the work of advocates, proving their sorrow and shame over the offense they committed.

[Note: [Col. 0314D]

**VII.—Banquet.** So it is written in the Morel edition and in three ancient manuscripts. The old editions and five ancient books prefer “at the banquet.”]

### VII

Indeed, if they shudder at the magnitude of the disgrace they have incurred; if with a truly healing hand they treat the mortal wound of their breast and conscience and the deep recesses of the winding wound, let them even be ashamed to ask—except that it would once more entail greater danger and shame not to have asked for the assistance of peace.

But let all this be done within the sacrament, under the law governing the petition itself, with moderation afforded by time, with a submissive request and a subject prayer. For the one who is petitioned must be moved, not provoked [Note: [Col. 0313C] “Summoned,” Lin.]. And just as divine clemency must be regarded, so [Col. 0314B] must divine judgment also be regarded. Just as it is written, “I forgave you the whole debt because you asked me” (Matt. 18:32), so it is written: “Whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him before my Father and before his angels” (Matt. 10:33).

For just as God is indulgent, so he is an exactor—and indeed a diligent exactor—of his commandments. Just as he calls people to the banquet, so he binds hand and foot the man who does not have a wedding garment [Note: [Col. 0314C] “The hand of those not having,” Bod. 1.] and casts him outside, away from the assembly of the saints. He has prepared heaven, but he has also prepared Tartarus. He has prepared places of refreshment, but he has also prepared eternal punishments. 45 He has prepared inaccessible light, but he has also prepared the vast and eternal darkness of perpetual night [Note: [Col. 0314C] “And gloomy,” Vat.].

[Note: [Col. 0314D]

**VIII.—Neighboring bishops.** When these bishops saw that opinions in the Church of Christ differed concerning the fallen, and judged that the evil arising must be met, they traveled to Rome to deliberate about their case. It was a common cause that stirred the universal Church. They knew, moreover, that it was incumbent upon individual bishops [Col. 0315C] to take care that the Church suffered no harm. Accordingly, having gone to Rome by mutual agreement—and not having been summoned by the Roman Clergy, as Baronius thought—they held a synod with the presbyters and deacons of the city so that, after their counsel had been established, they might determine by everyone’s agreement what ought to be observed concerning those persons, as Cyprian writes in Epistle XL.

From this Baronius concluded that a Council was held at that time by the Roman Clergy. I do not deny that a Council was held at Rome at that time. For it is certain that there is a Council when bishops assembled in a matter of religion deliberate in common. Nevertheless, the Reverend Father Hardouin thought otherwise. For he makes no mention of this Council in his edition of the Councils, although Binius and Labbe had included it in theirs. But Simon Starowolski’s claim that this Council was convened by the Roman Clergy at Saint Cyprian’s request is pure invention.

**In suspense.** Morel corrected it thus from what had previously been read, “in suspension.” One of my books has [Col. 0315D] “with the intention suspended.”

**Can endure delays.** The Grenoble manuscript reads: “who can endure affection outside.” The older editions read: “who can be sustained outside by delay.”

**We, nevertheless.** The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis reads: “We, however, have taken anxious care.”

**We wish.** One of my ancient manuscripts reads: “I wish you, dearest and holiest brother, always to fare well and to remember us.” The Grenoble manuscript reads: “I wish you, most glorious and blessed Pope, always to fare well in the Lord.”]

### VIII

Seeking here to maintain the governance of this moderation for a long time, we—many of us indeed, and together with certain bishops who are our neighbors and live nearby, as well as bishops whom the heat of this persecution had driven from other, far-distant provinces—judged that nothing should be changed before the appointment [Col. 0315A] of a bishop. Rather, we believe that care for the fallen must be governed with measured moderation.

Thus, while we await a bishop being given to us by God, the case of those who can endure the delays of postponement should meanwhile be held in suspense. But for those whose approaching departure at the end of life cannot bear delay, after they have performed repentance and repeatedly professed their abhorrence of their own deeds—if through tears, groans, and weeping they have revealed signs of a sorrowing and truly repentant mind, and when no hope of survival according to human judgment remains—only then should assistance be rendered cautiously and carefully. God himself knows what he will do with such persons and how he will weigh the balances of his judgment; we, nevertheless, take anxious care that neither [Note: [Col. 0315B] “That in this,” Bod. 1.] may wicked people praise our ready leniency nor the truly repentant condemn [Col. 0315B] what they regard as our harsh cruelty.

We wish you, most blessed and glorious Pope, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember us.

[Note: [Col. 0315D]

**EPISTLE XXXII.**—In the Speyer edition, the Fossés manuscript, the ancient Compiègne manuscript, the Pithou manuscript, the Bec manuscript, one manuscript of Saint-Victor, and the Michel manuscript, this Epistle is entitled “First Epistle to the Romans.” In the ancient manuscript of Saint-Victor, the Liessies manuscript, the Saint-Arnulf manuscript of Metz, and the Bigot fragments it is entitled “Epistle of Cyprian to the Romans.” Better in the more recent Saint-Remi and Dijon manuscripts: “Epistle of the Blessed Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons [Col. 0316C] of Carthage.” One of my ancient manuscripts reads: “To the clergy of Carthage concerning what he had written to the confessors and Roman Clergy and concerning their replies.” But in another of my ancient manuscripts it is written thus: “To the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome.” In the old Venetian edition: “To the presbyters residing at Rome.” The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis reads: “To the brothers, the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome.” From some similar manuscript, therefore, arose the reading of Rembolt, Erasmus, and Morel, which has: “To the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome.” Pamelius deleted the words “residing at Rome,” because the text itself established for him that this letter was addressed not to the Roman but to the Carthaginian clergy.

**Become known.** This is the best reading, and several ancient books and editions prefer it. But several ancient books, the Speyer edition, and the old Venetian edition have the alternative reading “make known.” That reading, too, is excellent. See the notes on Agobard’s book *On the Insolence of the Jews*.

**Of foreign bishops.** The Saint-Arnulf manuscript reads: “But also if [Col. 0316D] any visiting bishops.”

**And to their own people.** The remainder of this Epistle is absent from the same Saint-Arnulf manuscript, and in its place appears a lengthy fragment of Epistle XXXI, p. 42, from the words “our judgment to you in a clear,” as far as “the honor of martyrdom.”

**To Saturus the reader.** The Aldine edition reads “always to Saturus the reader”; the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis and the Lamonian manuscript read “to Satyrus, a fellow reader.” These readings, however, are not sound.

**One and faithful.** Thus, more or less, the ancient copies read. Some, however, have “one faith.” From this one might perhaps infer that Rembolt’s reading is correct; he printed “one agreement of faith.” Erasmus, Morel, and Pamelius retained this reading. Rigault changed it. The English edition approved Rigault’s alteration. I readily agree with their opinion. For the issue here is not [Col. 0317B] the doctrine of faith but the good of discipline. Reinhart, however, preferred Rembolt’s edition. The Chartres and Saint-Arnulf manuscripts confirm it.

**When we begin to assemble.** The Foix manuscript reads: “when, with the Lord’s permission, we have assembled as one.”]

## EPISTLE XXXII

(Erasm., III, 4. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Oxon., Lips., XXXII.)

**TO THE CLERGY OF CARTHAGE, CONCERNING THE LETTERS SENT TO ROME AND RECEIVED FROM THERE**

**SUMMARY.**—The clergy of Carthage are instructed [Col. 0316A] to ensure that the letters of the Roman Clergy and Cyprian’s replies are circulated.

Cyprian sends greetings to his brothers, the presbyters and deacons.

Dearest brothers, so that you might know what kind of letter I wrote to the Clergy serving at Rome, what they wrote back to me, and what Moses and Maximus the presbyters, Nicostratus and Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0315B] “Rufus,” Lam.] the deacons, and the other confessors held in custody with them likewise wrote in reply to my letter, I have sent you copies to read.

Take care, so far as you can and in keeping with your diligence, that our writings and their replies become known to our brothers. Moreover, if any of my fellow bishops from abroad [Note: [Col. 0315B] “Bishops,” Bod. 1.], or any presbyters or deacons [Note: [Col. 0315B] “Deacons,” Ar., Lam., Ebor., NC. 2.], are present or should arrive, [Col. 0316B] let them hear all these things from you. If they wish to transcribe copies of the letters [Note: [Col. 0316B] “Transfer,” Neap.] and carry them to their own people, let them be given the opportunity to make transcripts.

I have also instructed our brother Saturus the reader [Note: [Col. 0316B] “Our reader,” Lam., Bod. 2.] to grant each person who desires it the opportunity to make a copy, so that, while the condition of the churches is meanwhile being set in order in whatever way possible, one faithful agreement [Note: [Col. 0316B] “One faith,” Lin., Bod. 1. “Faithful,” NC. 1. “One faithful.”] may be preserved by all.

As for the other matters that will have to be addressed, as I have also written to very many of my colleagues, [Col. 0317A] we shall treat them more fully by common counsel when, with the Lord’s permission, we begin to assemble.

I hope that you, dearest and most longed-for brothers, always fare well. Greet the brotherhood. Farewell.

46 **EPISTLE XXXIII**

(Erasm., II, 51. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXIII. Paris., XXXII. Oxon., Lips., XXXVIII.)

**TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE, CONCERNING AURELIUS’S ORDINATION AS READER**

**SUMMARY.**—Cyprian informs the clergy and people that he has ordained Aurelius the confessor as a reader, incidentally commending his virtue and constancy of spirit, qualities by which he deserved an even higher rank in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0317B]

**EPISTLE XXXIII.—I. To the presbyters … entire.** The same also occurs in the following Epistle. In the margin of Nicolas Le Fèvre’s printed book it is written thus: “To the presbyters and deacons and the entire people of Hippo.” From this it might be inferred that this Epistle was encyclical and was sent to all the African churches, or at least to those situated in the proconsular province.

**In clerical ordinations.** This is the true reading. Certain [Col. 0317C] ancient manuscripts, however, have “of clerics,” but by way of correction. For “to clerics” was first written in them, and the correction was placed above the line. The Grenoble manuscript and the old Venetian edition read: “In ordaining clerics.” The Saint-Arnulf manuscript reads: “On ordaining clerics.”]

We are accustomed to consult you beforehand. That discipline was then received everywhere: bishops admitted no one into the clergy except with the consent of clergy and people; and this was always observed unless some weighty reason required haste. It is therefore no wonder that the Roman bishop who ordained Novatian a presbyter—although the entire clergy and many of the people opposed its being done, and for good reason—asked everyone, as Rufinus writes in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 31, for a special concession allowing him this one case. A special concession, therefore, was granted to the bishop by clergy and people so that he might ordain Novatian a presbyter. Yet Baronius, strangely enough, here praises the admirable modesty [Col. 0317D] of the Supreme Pontiff: although his authority in the Church was supreme, he was nevertheless accustomed to do everything not according to his own judgment but with the consent of his brethren; when he saw them resisting him, he did not compel them by any force or authority but entreated them humbly. Baronius is indulging in rhetoric here and, as is his custom, accommodating the practices of those times to our own: he attributes to the obliging character of that good pope the special concession made to him by clergy and people, as is manifestly clear from that history. In historical matters we seek not the semblance of exposition but fidelity, to use Quintilian’s words.

**Aurelius . . . a young man.** From this it is clear that this Aurelius is different from the one mentioned in Letter XXII, p. 31.

**Dear to God.** So nearly all the old copies. Two, however, read “dear to his God,” which pleased Rigaltius better. I think the other reading is better.

**Still very young in years.** It is no wonder that Aurelius, who here [Col. 0318B] is called “still very young in years” and “a young man,” was made a reader in the church of Carthage, since in Victor of Vita, book V, chapter 9, we see that very many readers in that church were little children under Bishop Eugenius.

**In the course.** So the editions of Morel and Rigaltius. The English editors printed *incursu*, as one word, as it is written in the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul and in the Chartres manuscript. An old manuscript of the church of Saint-Martin of Tours has *excursu*; the Corbie manuscript, *ex cursu*. Rigaltius retained the reading that makes two words. Yet in his observations he preferred the other, saying that *excursus* means a preliminary exercise for a more strenuous contest, which he proves from the authority [Col. 0318C] of Vegetius. In *On the Lapsed*, p. 182, Cyprian says “in the onset (*incursu*) of perfection”; for this the Foix manuscript has “impetus.” Elsewhere *incursus* means something altogether different, if the reading of the old manuscripts and old editions of Victor’s *Epitome of the Caesars* is correct. In these it is said that Augustus, moved by grief at the loss of an army beyond the Rhine, struck the wall “in a fitful assault of the brain” (*cerebri vario incursu*). But this reading did not please Andreas Schott, who, disregarding that authority, restored *incussu*, “by a blow.” It is certain, however, that Augustus was so dismayed by that disaster that for successive months he let his beard and hair grow and sometimes struck his head against the doors.

**Of suffering.** So all the old books and every edition before that of Rigaltius. I do not know, however, whence he obtained the word “confession,” which he placed here.

**As often as.** In old books we very frequently find *quotiens* and *totiens* written, including those containing the works of Saint Cyprian. When I saw such agreement among the ancients in retaining that spelling, I was readily induced to write it so myself. I nevertheless refrained, considering correct the observation of Dionysius Lambinus, a most learned man, who in his annotations on Cicero’s speech *For Publius Quinctius* advised that *quoties* and *toties* must always be written. He said that the error of those who wrote *quotiens* and *totiens* arose from a custom employed by the earliest Romans: they sometimes marked the vowel *e*, if long, with a thin and not very long line, thus: *quotiês, totiês*. Hence it came about that unlearned copyists, supposing that little stroke to stand for the letter *n*, wrote *quotiens* and *totiens*. Lambinus adds that this spelling had long since been rejected and discarded by everyone’s tacit consent. See also what Antonio Agustín wrote on this subject in book II, chapter 6, of his *Emendations*.

**Most ready and most courageous.** I found this reading in eleven ancient manuscripts. Another has “most courageous and most ready.”

## I

Cyprian to the presbyters, deacons, and all the people: greetings.

In clerical ordinations [Note: [Col. 0317B] “Concerning ordinations,” Bod. 1; “in ordaining,” Pem., Corb.; “in ordinations of clerics,” Bod. 3, N C. 2, Lin.], dearest brethren, we are accustomed to consult you beforehand and to weigh the character and merits of each person by common deliberation. But human testimonies must not be awaited when divine approval has preceded them. Our brother Aurelius, an illustrious young man, already proved by the Lord and dear to God [Note: [Col. 0317B] “Has been proved,” Voss. 2; “and in God,” Oxon.], is still very young in years but advanced in the praise of virtue [Note: [Col. 0318B] “In virtue,” Lem., Ebor., Lin., Bod. 1.] and faith; younger by reason of his age, but greater in honor. Here he has contended in a twofold struggle: twice a confessor and twice glorious in the victory of his confession—both when, victorious in the course [Note: [Col. 0318B] “Victorious in the preliminary contest,” Corb.], he was made an exile, and when he fought again in a more strenuous contest [Note: [Col. 0318B] “Fought back,” Lam., Lin.], triumphant and victorious in the battle of suffering.

As often as the adversary wished to challenge the servants of God, so often this most ready and most courageous soldier both fought and conquered. It had been too little for him to have engaged in combat before the eyes of only a few when he was being made an exile; he deserved also to engage in a more public forum with more illustrious courage, so that after defeating the magistrates he might defeat the proconsul as well, and after exile might overcome tortures. Nor can I decide what in him I ought more to proclaim: the glory of his wounds or the modesty of his character; whether the fact that he is distinguished by the honor of courage or that he is praiseworthy for his admirable reserve. He is at once so exalted in dignity and so unassuming in humility that it is apparent that he was preserved by divine providence to serve as an example to others in ecclesiastical discipline: how the servants of God should conquer through their virtues in confession and, after confession, excel in their conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0319C]

**II.—Not according to his years.** Virgil, *Aeneid*, book IX:

> Bearing before his years the spirit and concern of a man.

Nazarius says in his panegyric to Constantine: “You have shown that the course of age need not be awaited when virtue hastens.” And shortly afterward, concerning Crispus: “In him swift virtue, not delayed by the tardiness of age, anticipated his boyish years with triumphal swords.” In Victor of Vita, book V, chapter 10, mention is made of twelve child clerics of the church of Carthage whom the Arians could not entice by their blandishments away from the profession of the right faith; they were found superior to their years. For they were afflicted with the gravest tortures, and yet their tender age did not fail amid suffering. Pierre Corneille, a man worthy of comparison with the ancients, expressed this very thought in most elegant verses in the tragedy *Le Cid*. His words deserve to be copied here:

> I am young, it is true; but in souls nobly born,  
> Valor does not await the tally of the years.

**To the pulpit**, that is, the tribunal of the church, as Cyprian will say below in Letter XXXIV, p. 48. A later age called it the *ambo*. The Council of Laodicea, canon 15, according to the translation of Dionysius Exiguus: “Concerning those who ought to sing psalms in the ambo, that is, in the pulpit.” See Ciampini, *Sacred Buildings*, pp. 15, 52, and *Collection of Ancient Monuments*, p. 18. See also our notes on the *Capitularies*, p. 1147.

**The scaffold.** See Victor Giselinus in his notes on Prudentius’s hymn concerning the martyrs of Calahorra.

**Joy hastens.** Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias on the preservation of virginity, says that throughout Italy and Africa, and in the islands, when the resolve of the holy virgin was heard, everyone was filled with this report, and that joys ran farther with unimpeded foot. Symmachus, book I, Letter 32, writes that patience in joy is difficult. Martial, book VIII, epigram 21: “Morning Star, restore the day: why do you delay our joys?” Saint Leo the pope, Letter 52, to the bishops of Gaul: “For we do not wish our brother Ingenuus to be delayed by this expectation, since for this very reason he ought to have returned more quickly, lest the source of everyone’s joy remain unknown to you any longer.” Cassiodorus, book IV, Letter 4: “Joys always make the spirits restless. For a limit is rarely imposed on happy circumstances, though it is more often found in sorrowful ones.” For, as [Col. 0320C] Tertullian says in *On Modesty*, sad things linger more than joyful ones. Symmachus, book VII, Letter 1: “Things that are deferred become longer.” Petronius, concerning Ascyltos: “It is tardy to defer what pleases.” Cicero, in book IV of the *Tusculan Disputations*, distinguishes between joy and gladness. Lactantius, book VI, chapter 11: “Gladness is nothing but unrestrained joy.” Jerome, on chapter 4 of the *Epistle to the Galatians*: “For they say that joy is the exaltation of a spirit exulting over things worthy of it, whereas gladness is the exaltation of an unbridled spirit that knows no mean and rejoices even in things mingled with vice.” See Ludovico Celio Ricchieri, book V, chapter 33.

**Nor delays.** “For every excessively long delay is a delay to one who hastens,” as Seneca says in *Agamemnon*. Hero’s letter to Leander in Ovid: “Long to us is every delay that postpones joys.” Seneca, *Hercules Furens*: “True love hates and does not endure delays.” The same author, *Thebaid*: “I pass over the sluggish punishments of long delay.” Apuleius, book IV of the *Metamorphoses*, used the phrase “the impatience of the soul.” Juvenal, [Col. 0320D] Satire 6: “Impatient of delay, she falls silent.” Lucan, book VII: “For he is sick with delay and burning with desire for the throne.”

**The Lord’s Day.** In *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 242: “Do you think that you are celebrating the Lord’s rite?” Letter LXIII, p. 109: “Must we therefore celebrate the Lord’s rite after supper?” See the *Acts of the Donatist Martyrs* in book II of our *Miscellanies*, pp. 61, 63, 64, 66.

**That is.** So eight old books. Some others have “the same,” others “for this”—undoubtedly through copyists’ error. The Chartres manuscript has “on this day.” In the more recent Reims manuscript it is written: “On the Lord’s Day, meanwhile, he reads for us. Meanwhile, on this day, he has inaugurated peace for us.”

**He inaugurates.** That is, “begins” or “commences,” as is plain. Whether it may truly be inferred from this that Aurelius, when authority to read the Gospel had been granted to him, addressed and greeted the people and bestowed the peace and blessing of Christ the Lord upon the faithful, I leave for others to examine. See Albaspinaeus’s notes on the Third Council of Carthage.]

## II

Such a man deserved further ranks of clerical ordination and greater advancement, since he was to be judged not according to his years but according to his merits. For the present, however, it has pleased us that he should begin with the office of reader, since nothing is more fitting for the voice that confessed the Lord in glorious proclamation than to resound in the celebration of the divine readings [Note: [Col. 0319B] “Than for those celebrating,” Lam., N C. 1, 2, Lin.]; after the sublime words that declared Christ’s martyrdom, to read Christ’s Gospel, from which martyrs are made; to come to the pulpit after the scaffold; there to have been conspicuous to the multitude of pagans, here to be seen by his brethren; there to have been heard with amazement by the surrounding people, here to be heard with the joy of the brotherhood.

Know, therefore, dearly beloved brethren, that he has been ordained by me and by the colleagues who were present. I know that you both gladly embrace this and desire that very many such men be ordained in our church. And because joy always hastens and gladness cannot endure delays, on the Lord’s Day he has meanwhile read for us—that is [Note: [Col. 0319B] “Today,” Ebor.], he inaugurated peace when [Note: [Col. 0319B] “He inaugurated it, when,” Ebor.] he opened his ministry of reading. Persist frequently in prayer, and support our petitions with your petitions, so that the Lord’s mercy, favoring us, may soon restore to his people both their priest unharmed and, together with the priest, the martyr as their reader. I wish you, dearest brethren [Note: [Col. 0320B] “Always” added by Pem., Voss. 2, Lam., Lin., N C. 1, 2; “and to remember us,” Lam., N C. 1.], always to fare well in God the Father and Christ Jesus.

[Note: [Col. 0320D]

**LETTER XXXIV.—**In manuscript 137 of the Colbert Library [Col. 0321C], the title of this letter is written as follows: “Here begins the letter of Saint Cyprian the bishop, concerning Celerinus the reader, to the people; his feast is celebrated on the third day before the Nones of February.” Correctly so, for he is mentioned on this day in the martyrologies. But in the church dedicated to his name, which I shall discuss shortly, his feast is celebrated on the seventh of May. In the very ancient martyrology of the monastery of Gellone, with which an old manuscript of the monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland agrees, Celerinus is named on that day, though without a title; in the additions to the new edition of Usuard, however, he is called a bishop and confessor.

In the diocese of Le Mans there is a parish church under the name of Saint Celerinus, on the river Sarthe, halfway, as they say, between Beaumont and Alençon. There is a priory of the Order of Saint Benedict there. In the Le Mans cartulary of the Great Monastery of Tours, upon which this priory depends, there are several old charters mentioning this parish of Saint Celerinus; in one of them he is called Serenicus, by error, as I think. For it is established that [Col. 0321D] that church and the fortress situated in the same place have always borne from antiquity, and still bear, the name of Saint Celerinus. From this it may readily be inferred that the fortress of Saint-Céneri mentioned in the *Ecclesiastical History* of Orderic Vitalis is different from this one. Consequently, those are mistaken who, appealing to Orderic’s authority, charge with error the historians who mention the war fought in 1432 between the French and the English over the fortress of Saint-Célerin.

To return to the point from which I digressed: in the cartulary named above, I find a gift made in the time of Abbot Bartholomew by Hugh, lord of Brajetellum. With the approval of his wife and the consent also of Geoffrey, his son-in-law, and of his daughter Hervisa, he gave a certain church that he had begun to build in honor of the Holy Trinity in the parish of Saint Celerinus, together with the church of Saint Celerinus itself and all revenues belonging to it.]

# 47. LETTER XXXIV

*(Erasm., IV, 5. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXIV. Paris., XXXIII. Oxon., Lips., XXXIX.)*

## To the Clergy and People, Concerning the Ordination of Celerinus as Reader

[Col. 0320B]

**Argument.—**Its argument is almost the same as that of the preceding letter, except that it commends at length Celerinus’s steadfastness in the confession of the faith. The circumstances of the text itself sufficiently indicate that both letters were written in retirement.

[Note: [Col. 0322C]

**I.—A respite.** That is, permission to remain somewhat longer in this world, as Rigaltius explains—and rightly. Jerome, in his letter to Paula on the death of her daughter Blaesilla: “And so, while the spirit governs these limbs, while we enjoy the respite of this life.”

**He who had greater authority.** The punctuation must be placed thus. The sense itself advised me to do so, and for this punctuation I had as authorities manuscript 801 of the Colbert Library and Nicolas Le Fèvre, who corrected it thus in his own hand in his printed book. See Latino Latini’s observations on this passage.]

## I

Cyprian to the presbyters, deacons, and all the people, brethren in the Lord: greetings.

The divine benefits must be acknowledged and embraced, dearly beloved brethren, by which the Lord has deigned in our times to illuminate and honor his Church, granting a respite to his good confessors and glorious martyrs so that those who had sublimely confessed Christ might afterward adorn Christ’s clergy in ecclesiastical ministries.

Exult, therefore, and rejoice with us at our letter [Note: [Col. 0321B] “When this letter had been read,” Oxon., from many editions and manuscripts.], in which I and my colleagues who were present report to you that our brother Celerinus, glorious alike in virtues and conduct, has been joined to our clergy not by human approval but by divine favor. When he hesitated to consent to the Church’s request, he was compelled by the Lord’s own admonition and exhortation in a vision by night not to refuse [Note: [Col. 0321B] “Was to refuse,” Rigalt.] us when we urged him. He who had greater authority also compelled him, because it would have been neither right nor fitting for one whom the Lord had so honored with the dignity of heavenly glory to remain without ecclesiastical honor.

[Note: [Col. 0322C]

**II.—Though imprisoned, greater than his imprisoners.** Thus Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus concerning the books of sacred history, speaking of Plato when he was sold, says: “He was greater than the man who bought him.” Reader, see Erasmus’s scholion on this passage of Jerome: you will laugh.

**Trampled.** This reading is certain. Nevertheless, some old books have “helmeted.”

**Nor is the evidence of the eyes lacking.** Plautus:

> One eyewitness is worth more than ten who merely heard:
>
> Those who hear know what they have heard; those who see know plainly.

Moses the hermit, in Rufinus, book XI, chapter 6: “Can faith received through the ears possibly be truer than that which is clearly perceived by the eyes?” Apuleius, by contrast, at the beginning of book I of the *Florida*, reports that Socrates did not agree with Plautus in this matter and reversed the sense of this verse. But he referred these things to the eyes of the mind and the judgments of the soul. See Lambinus on the passage of Horace’s *Art of Poetry*:

> What enters through the ear stirs minds more slowly  
> Than what is set before the faithful eyes.

]

## II

He was the first to enter the battle of our time [Note: [Col. 0321B] “The first to enter,” Lam., Ebor., Ben., N C. 1.]; he was the standard-bearer among Christ’s soldiers; amid the blazing beginnings of the persecution he engaged the very prince and author of the assault. By defeating the adversary through the unconquerable firmness of his struggle, he opened for others the path to victory. He was not a victor by the brief expedient of wounds, but a triumphant victor by the marvel of a long struggle, with punishments clinging to him and continuing for a long time.

For nineteen days he was confined under prison guard, in the stocks and in chains; but although his body was placed in bonds, his spirit remained unfettered and free. His flesh wasted away through prolonged hunger and thirst, but God fed his soul, alive through faith and courage, with spiritual nourishment. Amid punishments he lay stronger than his punishments; though imprisoned, greater than his imprisoners; lying down, loftier than those standing; bound, firmer than those binding him [Note: [Col. 0322B] “Defeated . . . although defeated,” Ebor., N C. 4.]; condemned, more exalted than his judges. And although his feet were bound in the stocks, the serpent was trampled, crushed, and conquered.

Bright marks of wounds shine upon his glorious body; traces impressed by prolonged wasting stand out and appear [Note: [Col. 0322B] “Stand out visibly,” Lam., Bod. 1, 3.] in the sinews and limbs of the man. Great and marvelous are the things that the brotherhood may hear concerning his courage and praises. And if there should be anyone like Thomas who puts less trust in his ears, neither is the evidence of the eyes lacking, so that one may also see what one hears. In the servant of God the glory of his wounds effected the victory; the memory of his scars preserves the glory [Note: [Col. 0322B] “The glory of his scars preserves the memory,” Lam., Ebor., N C. 1.].

[Note: [Col. 0322D]

**III.—He walks in the footsteps of his kindred.** Something similar occurs in Cassiodorus, book III, Letter 6.

**Celerina.** This Celerina is mentioned, as I think, in book I of Victor of Vita’s account of the African persecution. Another of that name is likewise mentioned in the *Book of Inscriptions of Saint Paul in the City*, p. 26. In the new edition of Saint Augustine, Sermons 48 and 174 are noted as having been delivered in the Basilica of Celerina.

[Col. 0323D] **Palms from the Lord.** So the old editions and certain old books. I think this reading better than the one that offers “the Lord’s palms,” although the latter rests upon the authority of a greater number of old manuscripts. The Tours manuscript has “palms from God.”

**Egnatius.** So the de Thou manuscript and several others. In others, however, he is called Ignatius. Either reading is sound. Pamelius preferred to write Ignatius. But Latini thought differently; he says that those who followed the testimony of the better manuscripts and printed Egnatius acted correctly. See Cotelier on the martyr Ignatius’s *Letter to the Ephesians*.

**And days.** These words are absent from manuscript 801 of the Colbert Library. I think they can be omitted without any difficulty.

**Nobly born.** I have no doubt that this reading is the best. I nevertheless note that “glorious” is read in four ancient manuscripts.

**Height.** The same Colbert manuscript has “loftiness.”]

## III

Nor is this title to glory in our dearest Celerinus untried or new. He walks in the footsteps of his kindred and is made equal to his parents and relatives in the like honor of divine favor. His grandmother Celerina was crowned with martyrdom long ago. Likewise his paternal and maternal uncles, Laurentius [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Laurentinus, Egnatius,” Oxon.] and Egnatius, had once served in worldly camps themselves; but as true and spiritual soldiers of God, by overthrowing the devil through the confession [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Encounter,” Oxon.] of Christ they merited palms from the Lord [Note: [Col. 0323C] “The Lord’s palms,” Oxon.] and crowns through an illustrious suffering.

As you remember, we always offer sacrifices for them whenever we celebrate the sufferings and anniversary days [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Anniversaries,” Pem.] of the martyrs with annual commemoration. He could not, therefore, be degenerate or inferior when the dignity of his family and his noble lineage, 48 through its domestic examples of courage and faith, summoned him on. But if in a worldly family it is a matter of renown [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Of greater praise,” Lam.] and praise to be a patrician, how much more praiseworthy and honorable it is to become noble in heavenly renown!

I cannot decide whom I should call more blessed: those who have so illustrious a descendant, or this man who has so glorious an ancestry. [Col. 0323B] Divine favor thus returns and passes equally between them, so that the dignity of their offspring illuminates their crown [Note: [Col. 0323C] “The offspring of dignity,” Lam., Ebor., N C. 1.], while the loftiness of his lineage sheds light upon his glory.

[Note: [Col. 0324D]

**IV.—To advance.** I have retained this reading, although the earlier editions and six ancient copies offer *proficisci*, “to proceed,” because the present reading rests upon the authority of a greater number of old books and editions. For I found it in seven ancient manuscripts. Neither, however, is good. One might conjecture that *praefici*, “to be appointed,” should be read. But that construction would not be Latin. *Promoveri*, “to be promoted,” would be better. Yet all the old books and all the editions oppose it.

**With Aurelius.** His ordination was treated in the preceding letter.]

## IV

When this man came to us with so great a mark of the Lord’s favor, dearly beloved brethren—rendered illustrious by the testimony and astonishment of the very man who had persecuted him—where else should he have been placed but upon the pulpit, that is, upon the tribunal of the church? Thus, supported by the height [Note: [Col. 0323C] “Celebrity,” Pem.] of a loftier position and visible to the whole people in keeping with the distinction of his honor, he may read the precepts and Gospel of the Lord, which he follows courageously and faithfully. Let the voice that confessed the Lord be heard daily in the words spoken by the Lord.

Whether there is a further rank in the Church to which he may advance [Note: [Col. 0324C] “Proceed,” Bod. 3.] will be seen hereafter. There is nothing in which a confessor may benefit [Note: [Col. 0324C] “May be able,” Pem., Voss. 2.] his brethren more than this: when the Gospel reading is heard from his mouth, everyone who hears may imitate the reader’s faith.

He had to be joined with Aurelius in reading, since he has also been joined with him in participation in divine honor and united with him in every distinction of courage and praise [Note: [Col. 0324C] “And faith,” Lam., N C. 1, Ebor.]. The two are equals and each resembles the other: as exalted in glory as they are humble in modesty; as elevated by divine favor as they are unassuming in their own quietness and tranquillity. They provide every person with examples alike of virtues and character and are fitted both for conflict and for peace, praiseworthy there for strength, here for modesty.

[Note: [Col. 0324D]

**V.—Let the brotherhood’s course of life follow them.** So the Pithou manuscript. The common editions, with which other old books agree, have “the brotherhood having followed them.” It is sufficiently clear, however, that our reading is better, especially since it was taken from an old manuscript corrected in ancient times at Rome by a certain Justinus, as is noted at the end of the letter in the Pithou manuscript.

**Monthly distributions.** The old books vary greatly at this place. Some offer “monthly distributions” (*divisiones mensurnas*); others *divisiones menstruas*, *divisiones mensuras*, *divisiones mensuriae*, or *divisiones mensurae*. Hadrianus Saravia preferred *menstruas*, “monthly.”]

## V

In such servants the Lord rejoices; in confessors of this kind he glories. Their course of life and conduct so advance the proclamation of glory that they furnish others with instruction in discipline. For this reason Christ willed them to remain here in the Church for a long time; for this reason he snatched them from the midst of death and preserved them unharmed by effecting, so to speak, a kind of resurrection in their case: so that, when the brethren behold nothing more exalted in honor and nothing more unassuming in humility, the brotherhood’s course of life may follow these same men [Note: [Col. 0324C] “Having followed,” Oxon.; “allotted,” Bod. 3.].

Know, nevertheless, that they have meanwhile been appointed readers, because the lamp had to be placed upon the lampstand so that it might shine for everyone, and their glorious faces had to be set in a higher place, where, seen by the entire surrounding brotherhood, they might offer those who behold them an incentive to glory. Know, moreover, that we have already designated the honor of the presbyterate for them, so that they may be honored with the same allowances as the presbyters and share monthly distributions [Note: [Col. 0324C] “Monthly,” Pem., Lam.] in equal amounts [Note: [Col. 0324C] “Equal,” Bod. 1, Ebor., N C. 1.]; they will sit with us when their years have advanced and matured. Yet one who has attained full age in the dignity of glory can in no respect appear inferior by reason of his age.

I wish you, dearest and most greatly longed-for brethren, always to fare well.

[Note: [Col. 0325C]

**LETTER XXXV.—Numidicus the presbyter.** I have retained the common reading. The word “presbyter” is absent from two ancient manuscripts. Cyprian enrolls him in the number of the presbyters of Carthage. It seems that no one except a bishop could accomplish this. It may therefore appear strange that Cassian says in *Conference* IV, chapter 1, that Daniel, the deacon of the presbyter Paphnutius, was promoted by him to the honor of the presbyterate, without any mention of a bishop. Alardus Gazaeus, however, offers a sufficiently convenient interpretation of this passage: Daniel was not promoted by Paphnutius but sent to a bishop so that he might be promoted by him. The examples from later times were adduced by Gazaeus.

**Of the presbyters.** Other editions and three old copies have “of the Carthaginian presbyterate.” That reading is also good. But the one I printed, which I found in more ancient manuscripts, seems better to me.

**A number of martyrs.** In the de Thou and Foix manuscripts it is written, “a true martyr.” But this reading is not good. The Grenoble manuscript has: “He sent good and true martyrs, killed by stones and flames, before him.”

**Burned.** Lamonius’s manuscript has “entirely burned.”

**From his companions.** Three old copies offer “out of his companions,” which means the same thing. For Cyprian says that Numidicus remained behind, or survived, his companions or associates in martyrdom, in the same way that Bishop Domnus of Antioch remained after the deposition of the orthodox, as we said in chapter 37 of our preface to the Council of Chalcedon. See again our notes [Col. 0326C] on the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*.

**Of our presbyters.** I found this reading in eight ancient manuscripts and in the editions preceding that of Pamelius. Pamelius preferred “of our presbyterate.” The presbyterate did not lapse, but certain presbyters did. Our reading is therefore better.
