**When God permits.** Certain very old copies and editions read, “when time permits.”

**Of his district.** Previously “of his religion” was read. I found this correction, which is excellent, in two old books. It is well known that cities were divided into districts. A more extensive position within a district is correctly spoken of, but not within a religion. In Lactantius, book II, chapter 18: “It must be sought not in one religion but in the highest religion.” For this certain old books have “district.” Likewise, in book IV, chapter 27, “through the various regions”; for this the Bologna manuscript cited by Thomasius offers “religions.” The reading “of his religion,” however, can have a good sense.]

# LETTER XXXV

*(Erasm., IX, 10. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXV. Paris., XXXIV. Oxon., Lips., XL.)*

## To the Same, Concerning the Ordination of Numidicus as Presbyter

[Col. 0324C]

**Argument.—**He announces to the clergy and people that Numidicus has been ordained a presbyter by him, and briefly commends his distinction.

Cyprian to the presbyters, deacons, and all the people, his dearest and most greatly longed-for brethren: greetings.

I had to announce to you, dearest brethren, something that concerns both our common joy and the greatest glory of our church. For know that we have been admonished and instructed by divine favor 49 that Numidicus the presbyter should be enrolled among the presbyters of Carthage and sit with us among the clergy: illustrious with the brightest light of confession [Note: [Col. 0325B] “For the office of confession,” N C. 2; “with the honor of confession, courage, and faith,” Ebor., Lin.] and exalted by the honor of courage and faith.

Through his exhortation he sent before himself a great number of martyrs [Note: [Col. 0325B] “A glorious, true martyr,” Ben., Ver., Lam., Ebor., Lin., Bod. 1, 2.], killed by stones and flames [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Sent before him beforehand,” Ben.]. His wife, clinging to his side and burned [Note: [Col. 0325C] “Burned by fire,” N C. 2.] together with the others—preserved, I should rather say—he joyfully beheld. He himself was half-burned, buried beneath stones, and abandoned as dead. Afterward, when [Note: [Col. 0326B] “Left almost entirely. Finally, when,” Ben.] his daughter, with the anxious devotion of filial duty, searched for her father’s body, he was found half-alive, drawn out, and [Note: [Col. 0326B] “Drawn back and scarcely,” Ver., Manut.] revived. Unconquered, he remained behind his companions whom he himself had sent ahead [Note: [Col. 0326B] “Having been revived, he remained unwillingly,” Bod. 1.].

But the reason for his remaining, as we see, was that the Lord might join him to our clergy and adorn with glorious priests the number left desolate by the lapse of some of our presbyters [Note: [Col. 0326B] “The number of our presbyterate,” Oxon.; “our number of presbyters,” Lam., Ebor., Lin., Bod. 1.]. He will indeed be promoted, when God permits, to a more extensive position in his own district, when, under the Lord’s protection, we have come into your presence.

Meanwhile, let what has been indicated be done, so that we may receive this gift of God with thanksgiving, hoping from the Lord’s mercy for many ornaments of this kind, so that, when the strength of his Church has been restored, he may cause men so gentle and humble to flourish in the honor of our assembly.

I wish you, dearest and most greatly longed-for brethren, always to fare well.

[Note: [Col. 0326D]

**LETTER XXXVI.—**This letter has the same argument as the fifth; consult it.

**Show.** Through a vision, in sleep. A manner of speaking frequently employed by Cyprian.

**Or happier . . . grow.** These words are absent from the old editions. The Manutius edition therefore filled the gap thus: “or happier than there where the Lord decreed that I should be.” Morel, however, has: “Where God willed me both to believe and to grow.” Pamelius thought that they had supplied these words by conjecture. In vain: for Morel’s words occur in one Vatican manuscript and in three other ancient manuscripts seen by me, except that in one of them—the Foix manuscript—*secedere*, “to withdraw,” is written in place of *credere*, “to believe.”

**To grow.** [Col. 0327C] Pope Celestine, to the bishops appointed throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne: “It is no wonder if those who did not grow up in the Church act contrary to ecclesiastical custom.” I agree with the most illustrious Bishop of Oxford, who thinks that Carthage is meant in this passage: there Cyprian first believed in Christ, there he was baptized, and there he grew, having been made bishop in that place.

**From my own funds.** See the notes on the final part of the sixth letter, p. 393.

**Those in distress.** The poor and needy, whom Emperor Constantine, in laws III and VI of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*, says must be supported from the riches of the churches. In his tenth *Sermon on the Words of the Lord*, Augustine used “those in distress” to mean the needy, as did the Greek bishop of Marseille when writing to Ruricius of Limoges. Symmachus, book IV, Letter 18: “Meanwhile there is murmuring among those in distress.” See above, p. 391.]

# LETTER XXXVI

*(Erasm., III, 24. Pamel., Rig., Baluz., XXXVI. Paris, XXXV. Oxon., Lips., VII.)*

## To the Clergy, Concerning the Care of the Poor and Strangers

**Argument.—**He warns them not to visit the martyrs in crowds, and not to neglect widows, the sick, the poor, or strangers.

Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons, his most beloved brothers: greetings.

I greet you, most beloved brothers, safe by God’s grace, hoping to come to you soon, [Col. 0326B] so that both my longing and yours, and that of all the brothers, may be satisfied [Note: [Col. 0326C] “May be satisfied concerning the brothers,” S. Mich.]. Nevertheless, we must take thought for the peace of all and must sometimes, though to the distress of our own spirit, remain absent from you, lest our presence provoke the hostility and violence of the Gentiles and we become responsible for breaking the peace, when we ought rather to provide for the tranquility of all. Therefore, when you write that affairs have been settled and that I ought to come—or if the Lord should deign to indicate this beforehand—then I shall come to you. For where could it be better or more joyful for me than there, where God willed me both to believe and to grow?

I ask that you diligently care for the widows, the sick, [Col. 0327A] and all the poor. And if any strangers are in need, provide them with funds from my own personal allowance, which I left with Rogatianus, our fellow presbyter. Lest that allowance perhaps has already been entirely distributed, I have sent him another portion through Naricus the acolyte, so that charitable assistance may be given more generously and promptly to those in distress. I hope that you, most beloved brothers, will always fare well and remember me. Greet the brotherhood in my name, and admonish them to remember me.

[Note: [Col. 0327D]

**LETTER XXXVII.**—In an old codex of Saint Lambert at Liège, the title of this letter is written as follows: “Cyprian to the clergy, explaining that he could not rashly come to Carthage, and directing that every humane service be rendered to those confessors who are confined in prison.” In the Compiègne codex, however: “Here begins the letter to the clergy, explaining that he could not rashly come to Carthage because of the bodies which they delivered up in Carthage.” Such titles were supplied according to the understanding and ability of the ancient copyists.]

## 50 LETTER XXXVII

*(Erasm., III, 6. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXVII. Paris., XXXVI. Oxon., Lips., XII.)*

### TO THE CLERGY, THAT EVERY HUMANE SERVICE BE RENDERED TO THE CONFESSORS CONFINED IN PRISON

[Col. 0327B]

**SUMMARY.**—He exhorts his clergy to employ every humane service and care toward the confessors, both those living and those who died in prison; to record carefully the days of their deaths, so that their memory might be celebrated annually; and finally, not to forget the poor either.

[Note: [Col. 0327D]

**I.—Persevered.** Certain old books—and indeed the best of them—have *arrived*.

]

### I

Cyprian to the presbyters and deacons, his brothers: greetings.

Although I know, most beloved brothers, that you have frequently been admonished by my letters to show every diligence toward those who have confessed the Lord with a glorious voice and are confined in prison, nevertheless I urge you repeatedly, lest anything be lacking in the care of those who lack nothing for glory. And would that the condition of my position and rank [Col. 0327C] permitted me to be present there myself now! Ready and willing, I would fulfill with solemn ministry every duty of love toward our most courageous brothers. But let your diligence, I beg you, represent my service and do everything that ought to be done for those whom divine favor has distinguished by such merits of their faith and courage [Note: [Col. 0327C] “Their” is absent from the Oxford edition.].

Let still greater vigilance and care also be devoted to the bodies of all those who, although they were not tortured in prison, nevertheless depart this life by a glorious death. For neither their courage nor their honor is any less, so as to prevent them too from being numbered among the blessed martyrs. So far as it lay with them, they endured whatever they were ready and willing to endure. The man who offered himself to torture and death before the eyes of God suffered whatever he wished to suffer [Note: [Col. 0327C] “Was able to suffer,” Bod.]; for it was not he who failed the tortures, but the tortures that failed him [Col. 0328B] [Note: [Col. 0327C] The Oxford edition adds, from Bod. 1: “As it is written.”].

“Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10:32), says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0327C] “Says the Lord” is absent from the Oxford edition.]. They confessed him. “He who endures to the end, this man will be saved” [Note: [Col. 0328C] “Will be saved,” Bod. 1.] (ibid., 22), says the Lord. They endured, and to the very end they maintained the merits of their virtues uncorrupted and unstained. And again it is written: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2:10). Unto death they remained faithful, steadfast, and unconquered. When the end imposed by death is added to the will and to the confession of the Name in prison and in chains, the martyr’s glory is complete.

[Note: [Col. 0328C]

**II.—Their days.** Tertullian, in the book *On the Crown*: “We make offerings for the dead and for their anniversaries on the annual day.” Likewise, in the book *Exhortation to Chastity*, he mentions the offerings made for the dead and for their spirit. See the scholia of the most learned Jacques de Billy on Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration in Praise of His Brother Caesarius, and Goar’s *Euchologion*, p. 143.

**Tertullus.** Because Saint Cyprian says here that Tertullus had informed him of the days on which the martyrs passed to immortality by the departure of a glorious death, the English editors supposed that Tertullus had learned shorthand under Cyprian the rhetorician, whom they consider sufficiently certain to have known that art and to have used shorthand signs to record the acts of the martyrs. But this passage does not concern the recording of the acts of the martyrs, where shorthand signs might have been necessary, but only the notification of the days on which the martyrs had died. That certainly could easily be done without the use of shorthand. The English therefore did not rightly infer from this passage that the duty of transcribing the acts of the martyrs had been entrusted to Tertullus during the Decian persecution. Whether Cyprian knew the art of shorthand, however, I leave to others to investigate. Another mention of a Tertullus, a deacon of the Roman Church, survives in our new collection of Councils, p. 1464, in the time of Pope Symmachus. In that same period there lived another Tertullus, a Roman citizen, who entrusted his son Placidus to Saint Benedict for instruction.

[Col. 0329C] **Immortality.** The Fuxensis codex has: “They pass, by the departure of death, to the palm of glorious immortality.” Sallust in the *Jugurtha*: “For no one has been made immortal by cowardice.”

**Driven.** Thus most old books and editions. Morel printed *added*, a reading that I found in the Grenoble manuscript. The English wrote *overcome*, on the authority of the Bodleian codex. I found that same reading in seven ancient codices. Nevertheless, I prefer the old one.

**The poor.** The old Reims codex has *the brothers*.]

### II

Finally, record also the days on which they depart, so that we may celebrate their commemorations among the memorials [Col. 0328C] of the martyrs. Yet Tertullus, [Col. 0329A] our most faithful and devoted brother—in keeping with his customary solicitude [Note: [Col. 0329C] “With sure solicitude,” Ver.] and the care that he devotes to the brothers in every service of charitable activity, and who does not fail there either in caring for their bodies—has written, continues to write, and informs me of the days on which our blessed brothers in prison pass to immortality by the departure of a glorious death. Here we celebrate offerings and sacrifices in their commemoration, and these, with the Lord’s protection, we shall soon celebrate together with you.

Nor, as I have often written already, should your care and diligence fail the poor—yet especially those who, standing firm in the faith and fighting courageously at our side, have not deserted the camp of Christ. Indeed, greater love and care must now be shown them by us because, neither driven by poverty nor struck down by the storm of persecution, they serve the Lord faithfully [Col. 0329B] and have also furnished the other poor with an example of faith.

I hope that you, most beloved and deeply longed-for brothers, will always fare well and remember me. Greet the brotherhood in my name. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0329D]

**LETTER XXXVIII.**—This letter was first published in the Manutian edition. The English had two old copies of it, one from the Vatican Library and another from the Bodleian. I collated it with four ancient manuscripts: one survives in the library of Saint-Remi at Reims; another, formerly belonging to the Collège de Foix, now survives in the Colbert Library; a third is in my own library; and the fourth I obtained from Grenoble.]

## 51 LETTER XXXVIII

*(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXVIII. Paris., XXXVIII. Oxon., Lips., XLI.)*

### TO CALDONIUS, HERCULANUS, AND THE OTHERS, ON EXCLUDING FELICISSIMUS

**SUMMARY.**—Felicissimus, together with the associates of his sedition, must be barred from everyone’s communion.

[Note: [Col. 0329D]

**I.—Strike off.** The register of needs contained the names of persons in want. Therefore, when someone’s need was relieved by the generosity of the brothers, his name also was struck off. Thus generosity struck off both the need and, together with the need, the name of the needy person. RIGALT.

**By an addition.** The Fuxensis codex has: “He added, however, that they should practice their trades, as though their wishes were sufficient.” Mine has: “They should practice; I added, however, as though their wishes were sufficient.”

**Had approached.** The codex of Saint-Denis has *were being summoned*.

**In death.** Thus the old books. Manutius, Morel, and Pamelius preferred *on the hill*. So too the English, although they note that the Vatican codex reads *in death*. I do not know what hill near Carthage Pamelius imagines here. Rigaltius nevertheless strongly approved his opinion. See what the same Rigaltius writes about the hill of Bellona in the additions to his observations on Tertullian, p. 127. Baronius, under the year 254, reads *on the hill*, and from this derives the origin of the Montenses, or Donatists. See our notes on chapter 11 of Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* and on the acts concerning the vindication of Caecilianus.]

### I

Cyprian to his colleagues Caldonius and Herculanus, and likewise to his fellow presbyters Rogatianus and Numidicus: greetings.

I was profoundly saddened, most beloved brothers, on receiving [Col. 0329C] your letter. For although it has always been my purpose and prayer to preserve our entire brotherhood unharmed and, as love requires, to keep the flock inviolate, you now report that Felicissimus has wickedly and treacherously undertaken many things. In addition to his old frauds [Note: [Col. 0329C] “His frauds,” Bod. 1.] and robberies, about which I learned much long ago, he has now also attempted to divide a portion [Col. 0330A] of the people from its bishop—that is, to separate the sheep from their shepherd and the children from their parent [Note: [Col. 0329C] “To separate the sheep from the shepherd and divide the children from the parent,” Bod. 1.]—and to scatter Christ’s members.

I sent you as my representatives to strike the needs of our brothers from the register by providing funds; and, if any also wished to practice their trades, to assist their desires by an additional grant sufficient for the purpose. At the same time you were to learn their ages, circumstances, and merits, so that even now I—upon whom rests the duty of knowing everyone thoroughly—might promote all who are worthy, humble, and gentle to the offices of ecclesiastical administration. Yet he [Note: [Col. 0330C] “They,” Rig.] intervened so that no one could be struck off the register and so that the matters I had requested could not be distinguished by careful [Note: [Col. 0330C] “By your careful examination,” Bod. 1.] examination. He even threatened those of our brothers who first came forward to be struck off the register, with insolent domination and violent intimidation, that those who wished to obey us would not communicate with him [Col. 0330B] in death [Note: [Col. 0330C] Thus the editions and Vat. “On the hill,” Manut., Morel., Pamel., Oxon., Lips.].

[Note: [Col. 0331B]

**II.—Augendus.** This man must not be confused with the confessor Augendus mentioned in Letter XLVIII, p. 62.

**Carthage.** There was recently a certain learned and erudite man who, judging this passage to be corrupt, thought that this word should be removed from here and that *Rome* should be written instead. Indeed, his arguments are so strong and cogent that this correction appears necessary, although all editions and all old copies—as he himself notes, and truly—have *Carthage*. This opinion also seems capable of confirmation from the fact that this letter was written at the beginning of Felicissimus’ schism; Felicissimus was contemplating a journey to Rome, as Cyprian teaches in Letter LV, p. 85. It therefore seemed worthwhile to forestall him and warn the Roman clergy not to allow themselves to be deceived and misled by the fraud and perfidy of a criminal man.]

### II

After all this, neither moved by the honor of my office nor restrained by your authority and presence, but disturbing the peace of the brothers on his own impulse, he rushed forward with very many followers, rashly and furiously declaring himself leader of a faction and chief of a sedition. In this matter, indeed, I rejoice that very many brothers have withdrawn from this audacity and preferred to submit to you, so that they might remain with Mother Church and receive her allowances as distributed by her bishop. I know for certain that the others too will do this peaceably and soon withdraw from their rash error.

Meanwhile, since Felicissimus has threatened that those who obeyed us—that is, those who communicated with us—would not communicate with him in death, let him receive the sentence that he first pronounced: let him know that he is excluded from us. For to his frauds and robberies, which we have learned with manifest certainty, is added the charge of adultery, which our brothers, men of weight, have reported that they detected and have solemnly declared they will prove. We shall investigate all these matters when, by the Lord’s permission, we have assembled together with a larger number of colleagues.

Augendus also, who, taking thought neither for the bishop nor for the Church, has likewise allied himself with Felicissimus in conspiracy and faction, must bear the sentence that this factious and reckless man has called down upon himself, if he persists any longer with him. And whoever joins his conspiracy and faction should know that he will not communicate with us in the Church, since he has voluntarily preferred to be separated from the Church.

Read this letter of mine to our brothers, and also transmit it to the clergy at Carthage, adding the names of those who have joined Felicissimus. I hope that you, most beloved brothers, will always fare well and remember me. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0331C]

**LETTER XXXIX.**—This letter, of which I had only two old copies, one from my own library and the other from Grenoble, was first published by the press of Manutius. Opinions differ concerning the person or persons to whom it was written. I do not doubt that it is Caldonius’ account to Cyprian of what had been done by him and the other colleagues serving with him as representatives [Col. 0331D] against Felicissimus and his associates. Therefore, the reading of the books that have *you ought* in the singular is the best. For Caldonius alone writes in his own name and in that of his colleagues. I believe, however, that the letter written to the Roman clergy had another form and explained Felicissimus’ case more fully, as was fitting, and that the names of those who had joined Felicissimus were moreover appended, as Cyprian had prescribed. This opinion of mine is confirmed by the Bodleian codex cited by the most illustrious Bishop of Oxford, in which this letter is said to have been written to Cyprian. But I cannot agree with those who think it was a public notice affixed and posted in the church at Carthage. It is certainly a letter of Caldonius. This does not, however, prevent something similar from having been published in the church.

**Exiles.** The old books and Manutius’ edition have *those causing exile* both here and a little below. That reading can be confirmed from the observations made above on Letters XIV and XVIII.

[Col. 0332B] **Seamstress.** Salmasius, in his notes on the writers of the *Augustan History*, p. 408, wrote *farcinatricem*, perhaps through a printer’s error. Nonius Marcellus: “*Sarcinatricis*, not, as some maintain, *sarsitricis*, as though from sewing, but rather from bundles, because they handle many garments.” Varro, *Onos Lyras*: “Country people singing an unpolished song during the grape harvest, like seamstresses at their machines.”

**Subscription.** That is, a signature. See our new collection of Councils, pp. 1011, 1090.

**You ought.** Thus Manutius’ edition and the old books. Morel and Pamelius printed the plural *you ought*, as did the English edition. But that reading is not good. For, as I have said, the letter is from Caldonius, writing in his own name and that of his colleagues to Cyprian. Rigaltius, although he printed the plural *you ought* in the text, judges in his observations that the singular *you ought* should be read.

**Budinarius.** My old book has *budianarius*. But Salmasius, in the passage cited just above, judges that *butinarius* should be restored, from the Greek word βουτίνῳ in Hesychius, and that *butinum*, meaning a small cup, was derived from it. If that conjecture were certain, I would readily embrace Salmasius’ opinion, since Quintilian, book I, chapter 4, writes that there is a certain kinship between the letters *t* and *d*. I would therefore readily suppose that Cyprian [Col. 0332D] is speaking here of a craftsman who made small cups or flasks, as Du Cange interprets it—that is, small vessels in which oils, wines, and other liquids are stored—especially since John Damascene, cited by Du Cange, uses the word *butina*. Pliny, book XXI, chapter 34, writes that when the measure of an *acetabulum* is mentioned, a quarter of a hemina is meant, that is, fifteen drachmas. The most illustrious Bishop of Oxford contends that *burdonarius* should be read here in Cyprian, a word which he says means a muleteer. But this conjecture does not commend itself to me, since there is nothing in the word *budinarius* from which it could be derived, especially since *burdonarii* are nowhere found among authors writing in Latin. If the kind of sausage that we call *bodins* had once existed in Africa, and a word approaching our vernacular term could be discovered in some ancient writer, the matter would be settled. But I find nothing of the kind.]

## 52 LETTER XXXIX

*(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XXXIX. Paris., XXXVIII. Oxon., Lips., XLII.)*

### LETTER OF CALDONIUS, HERCULANUS, AND THE OTHERS TO CYPRIAN, CONCERNING FELICISSIMUS AND HIS FOLLOWERS BEING EXCLUDED

[Col. 0331B]

**SUMMARY.**—Caldonius, Herculanus, and the others carry out what he had ordered them in the preceding letter.

Caldonius, together with his colleagues Herculanus and Victor, and likewise with the presbyters Rogatianus and Numidicus:

We have excluded from communion Felicissimus and Augendus, as well as Repostus of the exiles, Irene of the Rutili, and Paula the seamstress; you ought to have learned this from my written notice. We have likewise excluded Sophronius, himself also of the exiles, and Soliassus the *budinarius* [possibly a maker of small vessels; uncertain].

## LETTER XL

*(Erasm., I, 8. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XL. Paris., XXXIX. Oxon., Lips., XLIII.)*

### TO THE PEOPLE, CONCERNING THE FIVE SCHISMATIC PRESBYTERS OF FELICISSIMUS’ FACTION

**SUMMARY.**—Just as Cyprian, in the second letter before this one, informed the clergy, so now he informs the people that Felicissimus must be avoided together with the five presbyters of his faction, who both granted peace indiscriminately to the lapsed and stirred up sedition and schism against him.

[Note: [Col. 0332D]

**LETTER XL.—I. Virtius.** I have written it thus, following Manutius’ edition and because I saw it so written in many ancient codices. Certain editions and some old books have *Briccius*. These matters are of little importance. Nevertheless, they had to be noted.

**Ecclesiastical administration.** Certain old books have *the administration of ecclesiastical discipline*.

**Render.** The Fuxensis codex has *furnish*.

**Certain presbyters.** They are named in Letter LV, p. 84; consult it.

**Conspiracy.** The case of Felicissimus is being discussed here, as is also clear from what follows and from Letter XLII, p. 57: “But as far as the case of certain presbyters and of Felicissimus here is concerned,” etc.

**Their old attack against us.** Since the testimony of Pontius the deacon establishes that certain persons opposed Cyprian’s election, it seems possible to infer from this that Felicissimus was among their number, and perhaps the leader of that faction.

**Renew.** We have restored the ancient reading, which rests on the authority of several old books. Rigaltius printed *recall*, because he found it so written in the Fuxensis. That reading also survives in the Michaelinus and Lamonius codices. The others and the editions earlier than Rigaltius have the reading we have restored. Nevertheless, the English preferred to follow Rigaltius’ edition, while citing no evidence for their opinion from the old books and indeed adducing several witnesses in favor of the older editions. Reinhart likewise retained Rigaltius’ text.

**Showing indulgence.** In one English codex it is written *being ignorant*. Nicolas Le Fèvre also wrote it thus in the margin of his printed book.

**Paid.** I would not point out that all the old editions [Col. 0334C] and almost all the old copies prefer this reading, had Rigaltius not published *repaid*. That reading indeed rests on the authority of the Verona codex and of the one I obtained from the monastery of Saint-Eloi at Arras.

**Of their own accord.** The codex of Saint-Arnoul has *themselves*.]

### I

Cyprian to the whole people: greetings.

Although, most beloved brothers, Virtius [Note: [Col. 0331B] *Viritus*, MR. Thu.], a most faithful and upright presbyter, as well as Rogatianus and Numidicus, [Col. 0333A] presbyter-confessors distinguished by the glory of divine favor, and also the deacons—good men devoted through every service to ecclesiastical administration—together with the other ministers [Note: [Col. 0333C] “Ministries,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Thu., Mich.], offer you the full diligence of their presence and do not cease to strengthen each one by constant exhortations, and also to guide and reform the minds of the lapsed by salutary counsels, nevertheless, so far as I can, I admonish you, and in the way I can, I visit you through my letters.

Through letters, I say, most beloved brothers; for the malice and perfidy of certain presbyters have brought it about [Note: [Col. 0333C] “Bring it about,” Rigalt., Vict.; “endures it,” Bod. 3.] that I was not permitted to come to you before Easter Day. Mindful of their conspiracy and retaining that old venom directed against my episcopate—or rather, against your vote and God’s judgment—they revive their old attack [Col. 0333B] upon us and once again renew their sacrilegious schemes by their customary intrigues. Yet by God’s providence, although we neither willed nor desired this but rather showed indulgence and remained silent, they paid the penalties they deserved: they were not cast out by us, but cast themselves out of their own accord; by their own conscience they pronounced sentence upon themselves; and, in accordance with your votes and God’s, these conspirators and criminals voluntarily expelled themselves from the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0334C]

**II.—Against the priesthood.** One Vatican codex and the Lamonius read: “Against the Lord’s ordinance and against God’s priesthood.” Here it is appropriate to note that this reading is not found in the Thou or Saint-Maur-des-Fossés codices, in which the English said that it occurred.

]

### II

It has now become apparent [Note: [Col. 0333C] “It will now become apparent,” Lin.] where Felicissimus’ faction [Note: [Col. 0334C] “Advanced,” Vic., Fat.; “advance,” Thu.] came from, and upon what roots and forces it rested. These men had long been furnishing certain confessors with incentives and encouragement not to agree with their bishop, not to maintain ecclesiastical discipline with faith and tranquility in accordance with the Lord’s precepts, and not to preserve the glory of their confession through conduct uncorrupted and unstained. And as though it had been too little to corrupt the minds of certain confessors and to attempt to arm against God’s priesthood a portion of the severed brotherhood, they have now turned their poisonous deception toward the destruction of the lapsed. The lapsed are sick and wounded and, because of the calamity of their fall, less fit and less steadfast in adopting stronger counsels; yet these men call them away from the healing of their wound and, abandoning the entreaties and prayers by which the Lord must be appeased through long and continuous satisfaction, invite them [Col. 0334A] to destructive recklessness by the lie of a deceitful peace.

[Note: [Col. 0334C]

**III.—Undermine.** Thus all the old books and the editions earlier than Rigaltius, except the first three, which read *overwhelm*. Of the codices I have seen, only the Fuxensis has *overturn*. I know, however, that it was also written thus in the Verona codex. But the other reading pleases me more, and it is clear that it is supported by the reading of the old editions.

**Slender.** In the Verona codex and in one English codex, *frail* is written. Nicolas Le Fèvre likewise wrote this in the margin of his printed book. In Lamonius’ codex *of the slender* is read, as though it referred to the brothers.

**The clergy of the City.** That is, the Roman clergy, because in antiquity the word *City* meant Rome, mistress of the nations, as Quintilian says, book VI, chapter 3, and book VIII, chapter 12. Optatus, book I: “to Zephyrinus of the City,” and book II, “residence in the City”; and in Victor of Vita, book I, chapter 8, “captives of the City” . . . See Heribert Rosweyde’s notes on Saint Paulinus, p. 745. In the preface to the creed published at the First Council of Toledo, it reads: “by command [Col. 0335C] of Leo, pope of the city of Rome.” But in three very ancient and excellent manuscript codices—one belonging to the most illustrious Church of Lyon; another formerly belonging to Leidrad, Archbishop of Lyon, and now thought to be in the Séguier Library; the third belonging to the Colbert Library—which contain an old collection of canons made, as I think, shortly after the Twelfth Council of Toledo, in those three codices, I say, the word *Rome* is absent, and it reads simply: “by command of Leo, pope of the City.” There survives a letter of Jerome to Paul of the City, beginning “The day before yesterday,” and in Augustine’s letter to Casulanus one reads “the discourse of a certain man of the City.” In Burchard, book III, chapter 226; Ivo, [Col. 0335D] part III, chapter 270; and Gratian, distinction 2, *On Consecration*, there is found a certain decree from a Council of the City, which runs as follows: “At the altar at which a bishop has celebrated Mass, a presbyter shall not presume to celebrate another on the same day.” This is also found in canon ten of the Synod of Auxerre under Aunacharius. Yet it is not always true that the word *urbicus* signifies a Roman citizen. For in Evodius’ letter to Augustine, a certain female citizen of an African town is called *urbica*, that is, a citizen of that place: “But behold, after two years, a certain respectable widow, a citizen among the Frigentes.”

**Across the sea.** That is, Rome. Hence overseas appeals were later prohibited in the code of canons of the African Church, as was the departure of African bishops across the sea unless they had consulted the bishop of the first see; this too was confirmed by Pope Innocent. Overseas judicial proceedings were also prohibited. See the code of canons of the African Church, chapters 23, 25, 56, and 94.]

### III

But I beg you, brothers: keep watch against the snares of the devil and, solicitous for your salvation, maintain still greater vigilance against his death-dealing deceit. This is another persecution and another temptation. Those five presbyters are nothing other [Col. 0334B] than those five chief men who had recently been joined to the magistrates by the edict in order to undermine our faith and, by betraying the truth, to turn the slender hearts of the brothers aside toward deadly [Note: [Col. 0334C] “Entice toward,” Bod. 1, Thu.] snares.

The same design, the same overthrow, is now being introduced anew through the five presbyters allied with Felicissimus, to the ruin of salvation: that God should not be entreated, nor the one who denied Christ implore that same Christ whom he denied; that after the guilt of the crime, repentance too should be removed; that satisfaction should not be made to the Lord through bishops and priests; but that, with the Lord’s priests abandoned, a new tradition of sacrilegious institution should arise contrary to the discipline of the Gospel.

Although it was once agreed by us, by the confessors and clergy of the City, and likewise by all the bishops appointed either in our province or across the sea [Col. 0335A], that nothing should be changed concerning the case of the lapsed until we had all assembled together and, after comparing our counsels, had established a judgment tempered equally by discipline and mercy, our counsel is now being rebelled against, and all priestly authority and power is being destroyed by factious conspiracies.

[Note: [Col. 0336C]

**IV.—Whom with such love.** The codex of Saint-Eloi at Arras has: “whom you appointed with such honor and love.” The Fuxensis: “with such ardor, with equal grief.” Here it appears that *with equal honor* should be read. See Pontius the deacon where he discusses Cyprian’s election.

**Peace and tranquility.** Almost all the old books have the accusative, *peace and tranquility*.

**Might appear.** Lamonius’ codex has *that we might appear*.]

### IV

What sufferings I now endure, most beloved brothers, because I cannot come to you personally at present, approach each one personally, and exhort you personally according to the teaching [Note: [Col. 0335C] “Ministry,” Nic. Fab.] of the Lord and his Gospel! My exile, now two years long, my mournful separation from your faces and your eyes, the unceasing pain and groaning that torments me alone without you through continual lamentation, and the tears flowing day and night were not enough [Note: [Col. 0335C] “It afflicts us,” Lam.; “had afflicted,” Ebor., NC. 1.]: it has still not fallen to the priest whom you appointed with such love and ardor to greet you or cling to your embraces.

To this wasting of our spirit has been added a greater sorrow: that amid such anxiety and need I cannot hasten to you myself. Because of the threats and intrigues of the perfidious, we take care lest a greater disturbance arise there upon our arrival and lest the bishop, who ought in every respect to provide for peace and tranquility, should himself appear to have supplied material [Note: [Col. 0335C] “Teaching,” Thu.] for sedition and to have inflamed the persecution anew.

From here, nevertheless, most beloved brothers, from here I alike admonish and counsel you: do not rashly believe destructive voices; do not readily grant assent to deceitful words; do not take darkness for light, night for day, hunger for food, [Col. 0336A] thirst for drink, poison for medicine, or death for salvation. Do not [Note: [Col. 0335C] “Nor,” Pem., Bod. 3, Voss. 2, Lam., Thu., Foss., Vict.] be deceived by their age or authority. They correspond to the ancient wickedness of the two elders in Daniel 13: just as those men attempted to corrupt and violate the chaste Susanna, so these men too attempt to corrupt the chastity of the Church with adulterous doctrines and to violate the truth of the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0336C]

**V.—Cancer.** Two old books prefer *cancerem*; four others, *canorum*; the Michaelinus, *cancerum* or *canerum*. I have retained the commonly received reading, which most codices present, because this passage is generally cited in this form.

**Upon the rock.** The old editions and seventeen old books write it thus [Col. 0336D]. Manutius printed *Peter*. Pamelius retained that reading, though he testified that the other was found in ancient codices. From there it was propagated into later editions, including the English edition. It is certainly true, as Pamelius notes, that elsewhere Cyprian very frequently says that the Church was founded upon Peter, and therefore it would not be surprising if he spoke in that way here as well. I am not disputing whether the Church was founded upon Peter. For I know that Cyprian held this view. But I say that in this passage the reading preferred by the greater number of old books and by the old editions must be retained. No one doubts that Christ was the rock and that the Church was founded upon this rock. On this matter see what we note below on the book *On the Unity of the Church*. Moreover, from the corrupt reading that crept into this passage, the author of Pelagius II’s Letter II to the bishops of Istria may have derived what he wrote: “He who abandons the Chair of Peter, upon whom the Church was founded.”

[Col. 0337C] **Will be put to death.** This word is absent from the old editions and from all the ancient codices I used. I know, however, that it occurred in the Verona codex and in one Neapolitan codex. In Lamonius’ codex *will die* is written, with the same meaning. In one old codex of mine it reads, “to cause you to stray [Col. 0337D] from the Lord your God,” and so forth. From this it is easy to infer that some material had to be added in this passage. Accordingly, since several words had to be added, it was not sufficient to add the word *will be put to death* or *will die*. Erasmus was the first to write *will be put to death*. The whole passage from chapter 13 of Deuteronomy should instead have been added, or it should be edited as it survives in the old books, with that word omitted.

**From the Lord’s ways.** This is the reading of many old copies and of the Manutian edition.

**Let them perish by themselves alone.** I do not know whether the reading of one of the ancient codices of the Royal Library should be preferred; there it reads: “Let those men alone perish.”

**Now according to.** Thus Manutius’ edition and seven old books. The more recent Reims codex has *and according to*; the Sorbonne codex incorrectly has *nor*, and the Saint-Eloi codex *not*. In the old editions and in six ancient codices it is written: “formerly according to God’s judgments.”]

V. The Lord cries out and says: “Do not listen to the words of the false prophets, because the visions of their own hearts deceive them. They speak, but not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who reject the word of the Lord: ‘Peace shall be yours’” (Jer. 23:16–17). Those who themselves do not possess peace now offer peace. Those who have withdrawn from the Church promise to bring back and recall into the Church [Note: [Col. 0336C] “the fallen in the Church” (*in Ecclesia lapsos*) Vict.] those who have fallen. There is one God and one Christ (Eph. 4:5), [Col. 0336B] and one Church, and one Chair founded upon the rock by the Lord’s word. No other altar can be established, nor can a new priesthood be created, apart from the one altar and the one priesthood. Whoever gathers elsewhere scatters. Whatever is established by human frenzy in order to violate the divine ordering is adulterous, impious, 54 and sacrilegious. Withdraw far from contact with people of this kind, and flee and avoid their words as though they were a cancer and a plague, as the Lord forewarns and says: “They are blind leaders of the blind. But when the blind leads the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. 15:14). They obstruct your prayers, which [Note: [Col. 0336C] “the prayers which” Ver.; “our prayers” Rig.] you pour out to God with us by day and night so that you may appease him through due satisfaction. They obstruct your tears, with which you wash away [Col. 0337A] the guilt of the offense you committed. They obstruct the peace which you truly and faithfully seek from the Lord’s mercy; nor do they know that it is written: “And that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams, who spoke in order to make you stray from the Lord your God, shall be put to death” (Deut. 13:6). Let no one, dearest brothers, make you stray from the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 0337C] “the Lord’s” (Dominicis) Pem. Bod. 1.] ways; let no one tear you, Christians, away from the Gospel of Christ; let no one remove the children of the Church from the Church. Let those who have chosen to perish perish by themselves alone; let those who have withdrawn from the Church remain alone outside the Church. Let those who rebelled against the bishops alone be without the bishops. Let those alone undergo the penalties of their conspiracy who formerly, in accordance with your [Note: [Col. 0337C] “our” Nic. Fab.] votes, and now in accordance with the judgments of God, have deserved to undergo sentence for their conspiracy and malice.

[Note: [Col. 0337D]

VI.—“A single fall.” So sixteen old books and the Manutius edition. [Col. 0338C] The old editions and three old manuscripts have “their own fall.”

“Does not assent to sound words.” Six old books have “does not assent to sound discourses.” So too in the commonly received edition of Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians.

[Col. 0338D] “Withdraw from such a person.” I have seen it written thus in fourteen ancient manuscripts. The rest vary greatly.

“Disobedience.” So too in Epistle LXIV, p. 112, and in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 202. See Erasmus’s *Annotations* on this passage of Paul.]

VI. The Lord admonishes us in his Gospel, saying: [Col. 0337B] “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition” (Mark 7:9). Those who reject God’s commandment and attempt to establish their own tradition should be vigorously and firmly rejected by you. Let one fall suffice for the fallen. Let no one, through his deception, cast down those who wish to rise; let no one more grievously overthrow and crush those who lie fallen, for whom we pray that they may be raised up by God’s hand and arm; let no one turn away from every hope of salvation those who are half-dead and implore that they may recover their former salvation; let no one extinguish every light upon the saving path for those who stagger in the darkness of their fall [Note: [Col. 0337C] “gift” Lin.]. The Apostle instructs us, saying: “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to his doctrine, being puffed up with stupidity [Note: [Col. 0337C] “pride” Erasm.], withdraw from such a person” (1 Tim. 6:3–5). And he himself says again: “Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things [Col. 0337C] the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Therefore do not become their partners” (Eph. 5:6–7). There is no reason for you, deceived by empty words, to begin sharing in their depravity [Note: [Col. 0338C] “Let there be no reason for you, deceived by empty words, not to begin sharing in their depravity” Nic. Fab.]. Withdraw from such people, I beg you, and assent to our counsels—we who [Col. 0338A] daily pour out unceasing prayers to the Lord on your behalf, who desire that through the Lord’s mercy you be recalled [Note: [Col. 0338C] “to recall” Vict. Foss.] to the Church, and who ask God for the fullest peace, first for the mother and then for her children. Join your own prayers and petitions to our prayers and petitions; unite your tears with our weeping. Avoid the wolves who separate the sheep from the shepherd. Avoid the poisoned tongue of the devil, who, ever deceitful and mendacious from the beginning of the world, lies in order to deceive, flatters in order to harm, promises good in order to confer evil, and pledges life in order to kill. Even now his words shine brightly, and his poisons are manifest: he promises peace so that peace cannot be attained; he promises salvation so that one who has sinned may not come to salvation; he guarantees the Church, while acting so that whoever believes him may perish utterly outside the Church. [Col. 0338B]

[Note: [Col. 0338D]

VII.—“Now it is, brothers.” The old editions have: “Now care must be taken, brothers.” The Manutius edition deleted the word “care must be taken.” It is absent from five ancient manuscripts and appears to derive from a gloss.

“I may be restored to you.” Four old books have “I may restore myself to you.”

“Of us all.” In most very old manuscripts it is written “of our mind.”

“To the party of Felicissimus.” The old editions before the Manutius edition and seven old manuscripts prefer “to the party of the most unfortunate man” (*ad infelicissimi*). Manutius, Morel, and likewise eight old manuscripts have “among those of Felicissimus” (*in felicissimi*). Two other old manuscripts have “to that of Felicissimus.”

“Has gone over.” The Fuxensis codex has “has consented.”

[Col. 0339C] “Mercy.” The Laetiensis codex has “clemency.” But [Col. 0339D] this final portion is absent from the codex of Saint Arnulf.]

VII. Now, dearest brothers, those of you who stand must persevere bravely and preserve with perpetual steadfastness the glorious constancy which you maintained during the persecution; and if [Note: [Col. 0338C] “and those who” Pem. Voss. 2. Bod. 1, 2. Lam.] any of you have fallen through the adversary’s deception, you must in this second temptation faithfully take thought for your hope and peace. And so that the Lord may forgive you, do not withdraw from the Lord’s priests, since it is written: “And any man who acts arrogantly, so as not to obey the priest or whatever judge shall be in those days, that 55 man shall die” (Deut. 17:12). This is the latest and final trial of this persecution, and it too, under the Lord’s protection, will soon pass, so that after Easter Day I may be restored to you together with my colleagues. In their presence, in accordance also with your judgment and [Col. 0338C] the common counsel of us all, we shall be able jointly to arrange and refine what must be done, as was once resolved. But if anyone refuses to do penance and make satisfaction to God, goes over to the party of Felicissimus and his satellites, and joins himself to a heretical faction, [Col. 0339A] let him know that afterward he cannot return to the Church or communicate with the bishops and Christ’s people. I wish you, dearest brothers, always good health, and that you persevere with us in continual prayers to implore the Lord’s mercy.

## EPISTLE XLI

(Erasm., II, 11. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XLI. Paris., XL. Oxford, Leipzig, XLIV.)

### TO CORNELIUS: THAT HE DID NOT ACCEPT THE ORDINATION OF NOVATIAN

**SUMMARY.—**The messengers sent by Novatian, who had announced his ordination to the Church of Carthage, are rejected by Cyprian.

(We have deferred this epistle to volume III of this collection, where it is to be joined with the epistles of Saint Cornelius the pope.)

## 56 EPISTLE XLII

(Erasm., II, 10. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XLII. Paris., XLI. Oxford, Leipzig, XLV. Coustant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, I, p. 127. Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, III, p. 334.)

### TO CORNELIUS, CONCERNING HIS ORDINATION AS APPROVED BY CYPRIAN AND CONCERNING FELICISSIMUS

[Col. 0339B]

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian excuses himself for not having placed unquestioning confidence in the ordination of Cornelius before the letters of his colleagues Caldonius and Fortunatus reached him, through which it was confirmed to have been legitimate. Because of the rival faction of Novatian’s party, he incidentally reiterates that he did not adhere to it at once, at its very beginnings, but instead adhered to Cornelius—to such an extent that he refused to entertain accusations against that ordination.

(Like the preceding and following epistles, we have thought that this epistle should be transferred [Col. 0339C] to volume III, where the epistles of Saint Cornelius the pope are treated.)

## 58 EPISTLE XLIII

(Erasm., II, 9. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XLIII. Paris., XLII. Oxford, Leipzig, XLVII. Coustant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, I, p. 130. Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, p. 335.)

### TO THE SAME: THAT HE HAD WRITTEN TO THE CONFESSORS SEDUCED BY NOVATIAN

**SUMMARY.**—The title of the epistle sufficiently indicates its subject; it is clear, however, from the message that this epistle and the following one were sent together with the present one.

(See the note appended to the two preceding epistles.)

[Note: [Col. 0339D]

EPISTLE XLIV.—“Nicostratus.” A deacon of the Roman Church, as Pamelius notes. He was an associate of Maximus, whom we said above, at Epistle XLI, had returned to the Church. Nicostratus, however, did not return, but was made a bishop in Africa by the faction of the Novatianists.

“Against the ecclesiastical ordering.” Two old books have “divine.” Certain others have neither “ecclesiastical” nor “divine.” Gronovius, chapter 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, says that he prefers what appeared in the manuscripts: “against the ordering of God.”

“Another bishop.” Novatian, who seized the Apostolic See after the election of Cornelius. See Epistle II of Pacian to Sympronian and Henri Valois’s annotations on book VI, chapter 43, of Eusebius.

“Consented.” In the old editions and in the old book of Saint Eligius at Arras, it reads “judged.” It is clear, however, that the people in question here are those whom Pacian censures in the same Epistle II to Sympronian.

[Col. 0340C] “Another Church.” Certain old books have “a second,” [Col. 0340D] in the same sense.

“One body.” The word “one,” which is certainly unnecessary and can be omitted without any harm, is absent from the Grenoble codex.

“Return to your mother.” As we said at Epistle XLI that they did.

“Nor should you think.” Twelve of our ancient codices and six English codices have “Nor can you.”

“Domestic camp.” Although I know that Juvenal used the phrase “domestic camp” in Satire 10, I would prefer “the Lord’s camp” (*castra dominica*) here, as Cyprian himself says in Epistle LIV, p. 77. Prosper, book II of *The Promises and Predictions of God*, chapter 6: “Thus, corrupted throughout by the stain of leprosy, they too were driven from the Lord’s camp.” The *Acts of the Donatist Martyrs*, in book II of our *Miscellanies*, p. 57: “Wherever each person encountered the enemy, there he established the Lord’s camp.” Pope Nicholas I, Epistle VII: “To burst suddenly out of the laity and force one’s way into the Lord’s camp.” Cyprian said “spiritual camp” in the Epistle to Donatus, p. 6; elsewhere he often says “Christ’s camp” and “the heavenly camp.” [Col. 0341D] Lucifer of Cagliari, in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*: “Unless you make the passage from the devil’s camp to the army established in the heavenly camp.”

434 “Our brotherhood.” So the old Speyer edition and others. Rembolt printed “your,” and that reading has the agreement of eighteen of our old books and seven English ones. Either reading is good.]

## EPISTLE XLIV

(Erasm., III, 2. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XLIV. Paris., XLIII. Oxford, Leipzig, XLVI.)

### TO THE ROMAN CONFESSORS, THAT THEY SHOULD RETURN TO UNITY

**SUMMARY.—**He exhorts the Roman confessors who had been seduced by the faction of Novatian and Novatus to return to unity.

Cyprian to Maximus, Nicostratus, and the other confessors: greetings.

Since you have frequently learned from my letters, dearest brothers, what honor for your confession [Col. 0340B] and what love for our united brotherhood I have maintained in my discourse, please believe and assent to this letter of mine, in which I both write to you concerning your conduct and praises and offer you simple and faithful counsel. For it weighs upon and saddens me, and an intolerable grief constricts my heart, which has been struck and almost laid prostrate, since I learned that there you had consented, contrary to ecclesiastical ordering, contrary to the law of the Gospel, and contrary to the unity of the catholic institution [Note: [Col. 0339C] “catholic truth” Lam. Bod. 2.], to the creation of another bishop—that is, to what it is neither right nor lawful to do: that another church should be established, Christ’s members torn apart, and the one soul and body of the Lord’s flock mangled by divisive rivalry.

I beg that at least among you this unlawful division of our brotherhood may not persist, but that, mindful both of your confession and of the divine tradition, [Col. 0340C] you return to the mother from whom you came forth, from whom you came to the glory of confession amid that same mother’s rejoicing. Nor should you think [Note: [Col. 0340C] “Nor can you” Lam. York, Lin., NC. 1, 2.] that you are defending Christ’s Gospel in this way, while separating yourselves from Christ’s flock and from his peace and concord, since it is more fitting for glorious and good soldiers to remain within their domestic camp and, stationed inside it, to manage and provide for the matters that must be considered in common. For [Col. 0341A] since our unanimity and concord must by no means be divided, and since we cannot abandon the Church, go outside, and come to you, we petition and entreat you with every exhortation available to us that you instead return to Mother Church and to our [Note: [Col. 0341D] “your” Ben. Neap. Lam. York, NC. 1, 2.] brotherhood. I wish you, dearest brothers, always good health.

(Erasm., II, 8. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., XLIX. Paris., XLVIII. Coustant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, I, p. 139. Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, III, p. 338.)

### CYPRIAN’S REPLY TO CORNELIUS, CONCERNING THE CRIMES OF NOVATUS

**SUMMARY.—**He praises Cornelius for having warned him at the opportune moment, since he received Cornelius’s letter on the day after the guilty faction came to him. He then describes at length the crimes of Novatus and the schism that Novatus had previously stirred up in Africa.

[Col. 0342B] (See volume III.)

[Note: [Col. 0341D]

439 EPISTLE L.—“That we, after taking counsel.” It is certain that the construction of this sentence is not coherent. Nevertheless, all the old books and all editions before Pamelius present it in this form. Pamelius deleted the word “that” without manuscript authority, I suppose because the construction offended against the rules of grammar. But that reason does not suffice. Similar errors are sometimes found in the best authors, even in Cicero. [Col. 0342D] Saint Augustine supplies a notable example in book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 13, where the following is read: “Even the expression that I now cannot remove from the mouths of the singing peoples, ‘But upon him my sanctification shall bloom,’ certainly detracts nothing from the meaning. A more learned hearer, however, would prefer this to be corrected, so that ‘shall bloom’ be expressed not as *floriet* but as *florebit*. Nothing prevents the correction except the singers’ custom.” Indeed, Jerome, in a certain epistle to Augustine, testifies of himself that he incurred severe reproach because in the fourth chapter of Jonah he had corrected a passage that seemed faulty to him 440 and substituted the reading he thought better. Yet in this epistle of Cyprian, “we made” could be restored in place of “to have made,” since most English codices prefer that reading.]

## 64 EPISTLE L

(Erasm., III, 3. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., L. Paris., XLIX. Oxford, Leipzig, LIII.)

### MAXIMUS AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS TO CYPRIAN, CONCERNING THEIR RETURN FROM SCHISM

**SUMMARY.—**They inform Cyprian that they have returned to the Church.

Maximus, Urbanus, Sidonius, and Macharius to their brother Cyprian: greetings.

We are certain, dearest brother, that you too rejoice with us with an equal desire that we [Note: [Col. 0341D] “that we” Lam. Ar. York, Bod. 1, 2. NC. 1.], after taking counsel and taking greater thought for the interests and peace of the Church, leaving all other matters aside and reserving them for God’s judgment, have made peace equally with Cornelius our bishop and with the entire clergy [Note: [Col. 0342D] “we made” Lam. Ar.]. Amid the joy of the whole Church and the ready love of everyone, [Col. 0342C] you certainly ought to have learned from this letter of ours that this has taken place. We pray, dearest brother, that you may enjoy good health for many years.

## 65 EPISTLE LI

(Erasm., III. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LI. Paris., L. Oxford, Leipzig, LIV.)

### CYPRIAN TO THE CONFESSORS: CONGRATULATIONS ON THEIR RETURN FROM SCHISM

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian congratulates the Roman confessors on their return to the Church and replies to their letter.

[Note: [Col. 0343C]

440 EPISTLE LI.—I. “Christ had prepared.” So most of our best books. Certain others and the old editions earlier than Pamelius have “Christ’s Church had prepared.”

]

I. Cyprian to Maximus the presbyter, and likewise to Urbanus, Sidonius, and Macharius, his brothers: greetings.

Having read your letter, dearest brothers, which you sent to me concerning your return, ecclesiastical peace, and fraternal restoration, [Col. 0343A] I confess that I rejoiced as greatly as I had rejoiced before, when I learned of the glory of your confession and received with congratulations the heavenly and spiritual praise [Note: [Col. 0343C] “heavenly and spiritual joy” Lin.] of your service. For this too is another confession of your faith [Note: [Col. 0343C] “of this faith” Ar. Lam. NC. 1. York.] and praise: to confess that there is one Church, not to become a participant in an alien error—or rather depravity—and to return to the same camp from which you came forth and from which you sprang forward with the most valiant strength to wage battle and subdue the adversary. For the trophies had to be carried back from the battle line to the place from which the weapons had been taken up for battle, lest Christ’s Church fail to possess as glorious those whom Christ had prepared for glory. But now you have both maintained, through the Lord’s peace [Note: [Col. 0343C] “the Lord’s peace” in the accusative, Lam. Bod. 2. MR. Ar. NC. 2. York, Mich.], the tenor appropriate to your faith and the law of indivisible love and concord, and by your journey you have furnished others an example of love and peace, so that the Church’s truth and the unity of the evangelical sacrament [Note: [Col. 0343C] “of the Gospel and” Ben. Bod. 1. Ver.; “evangelical” Ar. Lam. York, NC. 1. Bod. 2.], which we maintained, might also be joined by your consent and bond, and so that the confessors of Christ should not become leaders of error after having proved praiseworthy authors of courage and honor.

II. Let others see how greatly they congratulate you, or how greatly each person glories within himself. I confess that I congratulate you more and glory more than others in this peaceful return [Note: [Col. 0343C] “entry” Ar.] and love of yours. For you ought to hear plainly what was in my heart. I grieved vehemently and was sorely distressed because I could not communicate with those whom I had once begun to love. [Col. 0344A] After you [Note: [Col. 0343C] “For after you” Ver.] came out of prison and schismatic and heretical error received you, it was as though your glory had remained in prison. For the dignity of your name seemed to have remained [Note: [Col. 0344C] “withdrawn” Ar. Lam. York, NC. 1.] there when Christ’s soldiers did not return from prison to the Church, although they had previously entered that prison amid the praise and rejoicing of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0343C]

III. “Weeds.” Certain codices here and a little later have the singular, “weed.” The Grenoble codex: “For although there seems to be weeds in the Church.” Tertullian and Symmachus used “wild oats” for “weeds.” Jerome also seems to have thought so in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*: “Not only birds,” he says, “remain in the Church, nor do only [Col. 0343D] clean birds fly there; rather, wheat is sown in the field, and among the shining crop burs and thistles and barren wild oats hold sway.”

III.—“That we may be able to be wheat.” Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 5: “Hear Cyprian; tolerate the weeds; be wheat.” See also the Epistle to Macrobius, where Cyprian’s words are quoted. Tertullian, in the book *On Flight in Persecution*: “This is that winnowing shovel which even now cleanses the Lord’s threshing floor—that is, the Church—winnowing the mingled heap of the faithful and separating the martyrs’ wheat from the chaff of the deniers.” Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, in Eusebius, book III, chapter 36: “I am Christ’s wheat; may I be ground by the teeth of beasts.” See Samuel Petit in his commentary on the Attic laws, p. 136.

“Golden vessels.” We have printed this following the authority of the old manuscripts. It is also written thus in Epistle [Col. 0344C] LII, to Antonianus, p. 78. So too Saint Leo in the Epistle to the Bishops of Caesarian Mauretania.

“So that he thinks himself.” One old codex of mine has: “he thinks that he already bears the winnowing fan for winnowing and cleansing the threshing floor.” This reading of my book also appears in Saint Augustine’s Epistle to Macrobius. Goulart likewise writes that he found it in the book of the bishop of Accon. In the book of Saint Arnulf it is written [Col. 0344D] “thinks himself entitled to claim.” The old translator of Matthew also used “winnowing fan” in place of “shovel.” Yet the winnowing fan is a farmer’s implement distinct from a shovel. Columella, book II, chapter 10: “For when the heap, mixed with chaff and grain, has been gathered into one place, it is gradually tossed from it across a considerable space with winnowing fans.” Plautus in the *Poenulus*: “He says that he was given shovels to sell and mattocks with which to dig the garden and harvest the grain.” Grammarians say that a *marga* is a fork with which heaps of produce are made. See the notes of the most learned Fronton du Duc on Saint Basil’s *Homilies on the Hexaemeron*, p. 4.

“To separate by human judgment.” I found this reading, which I think better, in the codex of Florus and in several others. Below, in Epistle LII, p. 74: “attempts to separate the chaff from the wheat.”

“Frenzy assumes.” The Verona and Fuxensis codices read: “a depraved man foolishly assumes.”]

III. For although there appear to be weeds in the Church, neither our faith nor our love ought therefore to be hindered, so that, because we perceive that there are weeds in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church. Our only task [Note: [Col. 0344C] “Dearest brothers, our task” Ver.] is to labor so that we may be able to be wheat, so that when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord’s barns, we may receive fruit for our work and labor. The Apostle says in his epistle: “But in a great house there are not only [Col. 0344B] vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some indeed are honored, but others dishonored” (2 Tim. 2:20). Let us apply ourselves, dearest brothers, and labor as much as we can so that we may be vessels of gold or silver [Note: [Col. 0344C] “may be able to be of gold or silver” Ver.; “may be a vessel of gold or silver”]. But permission to shatter the earthenware vessels has been granted to the Lord alone, to whom the iron rod has also been given. A servant cannot be greater than his master; nor can anyone claim for himself what the Father has granted to the Son alone, so that he thinks he can bear the shovel for winnowing and cleansing the threshing floor [Note: [Col. 0344C] “bear the winnowing fan” Cod. Goulart.], or separate all the weeds from the wheat by human judgment [Note: [Col. 0344C] “segregate” Oxford, Leipzig.]. That is arrogant obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption, which depraved 66 frenzy assumes for itself; and while certain people, always claiming for themselves a degree of authority beyond what gentle justice demands [Note: [Col. 0344C] “And while they claim for themselves something further” Lin. NC. 2.; “always something” Ver. Ben. Aug.], perish from the Church, [Col. 0345A] and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling pride, they lose the light of truth. Therefore we too, maintaining due balance, contemplating the Lord’s book, and considering the loving-kindness and mercy of God the Father, after long and extensive deliberation among ourselves, have weighed with just moderation what must be done.

[Note: [Col. 0345C]

IV.—“The unity of the catholic Church.” Cyprian refers to his book *On the Unity of the Church*, which this passage shows to have been written at the time when Novatian created the schism.

“You now read it in such a manner.” Imitated from the poem on the works of Virgil attributed to Augustus:

> Let it be praised, flourish, please, be read again, and be loved.

Likewise, in the poem accompanying the sacred books presented to King Charles the Bald by Vivian, abbot of Saint Martin of Tours, published in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1572:

> In whose honor they pray that it may please, be praised, and be loved.

]

IV. You can examine all these matters thoroughly by reading the treatises which I had recently read here and had also sent to you to read because of our shared love. In them the fallen lack neither censure to rebuke nor medicine to heal. Moreover, our modest ability expressed as fully as it could the unity of the catholic [Note: [Col. 0345C] “the unity of the Church’s love and peace” Ar. York.] Church. I trust that this treatise pleases you more and more now, since you already read it in such a manner that you both approve and love it; [Col. 0345B] for you fulfill in deeds what we composed in words when you return to the Church in the unity of love and peace. I wish you, dearest and most deeply longed-for brothers, always good health.

## EPISTLE LII

(Erasm., IV, 2. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LII. Paris., LI. Coustant, *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, I, p. 159. Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, III, p. 347.)

### TO ANTONIANUS, CONCERNING CORNELIUS AND NOVATIAN

**SUMMARY.—**When Antonianus, after receiving a letter from Novatian, had begun to incline in spirit toward his party, Cyprian confirms him in his former position—namely, that he should continue to communicate with Cornelius, that is, with the catholic Church. To persuade him, he weaves together the history of the whole tragedy [Col. 0345C] between Cornelius and Novatian, [Col. 0346A] and shows that Cornelius was an excellent man and lawfully elected, whereas Novatian, guilty of many crimes, had usurped an unlawful election. At the beginning of the epistle he incidentally excuses himself for changing his position regarding the treatment of the fallen, and at the end explains in what the Novatianist heresy consists.

(It has seemed best to assign this epistle a more appropriate place in volume III, where the whole history of Novatian’s schism is described together with all the documentary evidence.)

[Note: [Col. 0345D]

450 EPISTLE LIII.—I. “Superius.” I know that this was written in the extremely old Verona codex, and Rigaltius also notes it. Manutius likewise printed it. Pamelius testifies that the English codex he used has the same reading as Manutius. Nevertheless, the recent English edition cites no old witness for that reading except the Verona codex. It is nonetheless supported by the codices of Saint Eligius and Bec, in which *superus* is written, and by ten other old codices, which have *super*. The old editions, including the Morel edition, and three old manuscripts prefer “recently” (*nuper*). Another presbyter named Superius appears in book II of our *Miscellanies*, p. 101, and Superius the *stationarius* (an official assigned to a post) appears in Optatus of Milevis at the end of book I. In the copy of the Basel edition of 1540 that belonged to Jacques Cujas and is now in my possession, that most learned man wrote in the margin, from a certain 451 old book, *superus*, as in the codices of Saint Eligius and Bec.

[Col. 0346C] “Ninus.” In two ancient codices it is written “Saturninus.” Saturninus is mentioned in various epistles of Cyprian. Ninus, so far as I know, is mentioned nowhere else, and this might perhaps support the reading of those two old books. Yet there is no record anywhere of Saturninus’s fall. Therefore, if the reading is correct, either this was another Saturninus, or else the name Ninus must certainly be retained here. It might be inferred from this passage that he was a bishop, because Cyprian calls him “brother,” were it not clear that Cyprian also called presbyters [Col. 0346D] brothers. Cyprian bears ample witness that Ninus repented after breaking faith, and I therefore think that he subsequently restored his glory. For in the extremely old martyrology, at the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, it is noted: “In Mauretania, Ninus”; and at the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January: “In Africa, Ninus.” He is not said to have been a martyr. It might therefore be thought that he is not distinct from Ninus the confessor, who is mentioned in the account of a certain man who saw the Son of God. That account survives in the Fossatensis codex. It begins as follows: “There was a certain very devout presbyter named Airgils, who frequently celebrated the solemn rites of Mass at the body of Saint Ninus, bishop and confessor.”

“The proconsul”—of Africa, of course. The testimony of Salvian makes clear that he possessed great dignity and authority; in book VII, chapter 16, Salvian says that in title he was indeed a proconsul, but in power a consul. The proconsuls of Africa are frequently mentioned by the ancient historians. [Col. 0347D] Moreover, the Theodosian Code contains many constitutions of the emperors addressed to the proconsuls of Africa.]

## 76 EPISTLE LIII

(Erasm., III, 23. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LIII. Paris., LII. Oxford, Leipzig, LVI.)

### TO FORTUNATUS AND OTHER COLLEAGUES, CONCERNING THOSE OVERCOME BY TORTURE

**SUMMARY.—**When Cyprian was consulted by his colleagues as to whether certain fallen persons who had been overcome by torture [Col. 0346B] should be admitted to communion, he replies that, since they had already done penance for three years, it did indeed seem to him that they should be admitted; but because a council of bishops was to be held at his residence after the Easter solemnities, he would discuss the matter with them.

I. Cyprian to his brothers Fortunatus, Ahymmus, Optatus, Privatianus, Donatulus, and Felix: greetings.

You wrote to me, dearest brothers, that when you were in the city of Capsa for the ordination of a bishop, our brother and colleague Superius reported to you that our brothers Ninus, Clementianus, and Florus—who had earlier been arrested during the persecution, confessed the name of the Lord, and overcome the violence of the magistrate and the attack of the raging populace [Note: [Col. 0346C] “crowded populace” Bod. 1.]—were afterward, when they were being tortured with severe punishments before [Col. 0346C] the proconsul, overcome by the violence of the tortures [Col. 0347A] and fell away under prolonged torments from the degree of glory toward which they had been striving with the full strength of faith [Note: [Col. 0347C] “which they had attained” Ver.]. Nevertheless, after this grievous fall, incurred not voluntarily but under compulsion, they had not ceased to perform penance throughout these three years [Note: [Col. 0347C] “had been received for the performance of penance” Thu. Mich.]. Concerning them, you thought that counsel should be taken as to whether it was now lawful to admit them to communion.

[Note: [Col. 0347D]

II.—“The name of the Lord.” I added the word “Lord,” although I know that it is not necessary in this passage, because I found it written thus in almost all the very old manuscripts I used and in the old editions. Pamelius deleted it.

“At the last.” That is, afterward. I judged that this should be restored in place of “most recently,” which Rigaltius and the English editors printed. For all the old books and editions before Rigaltius have the reading I restored. I therefore wonder that the English editors, who knew that it appeared in our old books, preferred a reading found nowhere except in Rigaltius’s edition. What if we attribute the error in that edition to the printer?

“Clemency.” The Fuxensis codex has “mercy.”

“They were not permitted.” Jerome quotes this passage in the *Life of Paul the Monk*: “But the cunning enemy, devising punishments that delayed death, desired to slaughter souls; and, as Cyprian, who himself suffered from him, says, those who wished to die were not permitted to be killed.” The Fuxensis codex here in Cyprian has “they were not allowed to suffer.” But Jerome had “they were not permitted” in his copy. Lucan, book VI:

> Ah, wretched is he from whom the final gift of an unjust death  
> Is snatched away—the power to die.

Seneca, *Thebaid*: “To forbid someone who longs to die from dying is to kill him.”

“Begin to come.” From this it may seem possible to infer that it was customary at that time for the African bishops to convene at Carthage with the bishop of that great church, just as the bishops of Italy and Sicily convened with the Roman bishop, but that they nevertheless had to be in their own cities on the principal feast days. The English edition wrongly interpreted this passage as referring to synods held twice a year. That rule had not yet been devised.]

## II

And indeed, so far as my own judgment is concerned, I think that the Lord’s indulgence will not fail those who are known to have stood in the battle line, to have confessed the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0347C] “of the Lord” is absent from the Oxford manuscript], and to have overcome the violence of the magistrates and the assault of the raging populace by the steadfast resolve of an immovable faith; who endured imprisonment and, for a long time, amid the proconsul’s threats and the roar of the surrounding populace, resisted torments that mangled them and tortured them through prolonged repetition [Note: [Col. 0347C] “tortures,” Mich.]. [Col. 0347B] Thus, what appears at the very end [Note: [Col. 0347C] “at the very last,” Oxford, Rigaltius] to have been overcome through the weakness of the flesh may be relieved by the defense of their preceding merits; and for such persons it should be enough to have lost their glory. We ought not, however, also to close to them the opportunity for pardon and deprive them of paternal compassion and of communion with us. For them, we think, it may suffice in imploring the Lord’s mercy that for three years continuously and sorrowfully, as you write, they have mourned with the utmost lamentation of repentance.

Certainly, I do not think that peace is being entrusted incautiously and rashly to those whom we see, through the courage of their military service, not to have failed in the earlier battle [Col. 0347C] and to be capable of recovering their glory if the battle line should form again. For since it was resolved in council that those doing penance should be assisted when in danger from illness and should be granted peace, those whom we see to have fallen not from weakness of spirit, but to have entered battle and been wounded, and through the frailty of the flesh to have been unable to bear the crown of their confession, ought surely to take precedence in receiving peace—especially since, although they desired to die, they were not permitted to be killed; rather, the tortures continued to mangle them in their exhaustion until they wore down, not the faith, which is unconquered, but the flesh, which is weak [Note: [Col. 0348C] “which was conquered,” Lam., York, NC. 1].

## III

Nevertheless, since you have written asking me to discuss this very matter as fully as possible with a greater number of colleagues [Note: [Col. 0348C] “when very many colleagues,” Ver.; “once it had been held,” Lam., York, Bod. 2; “I should discuss it more fully,” York, Lincoln, NC. 1], and since so [Col. 0348A] important a matter requires a greater and more earnest consultation based upon the deliberation of many, while at present almost all remain among their own people with the brethren during the first solemnities of Easter, I shall discuss it more fully with each of them when they have discharged their duty of celebrating the solemnity [77] among their own people and have begun to come to me. Thus, concerning the matter on which you have consulted us, a settled judgment, weighed by the counsel of many bishops, may be established among us and reported back to you. I wish you, dearest brethren, always good health.

# Letter LIV

*(Erasmus, I, 2; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, LIV; Paris, LIII; Oxford, Leipzig, LVII; Coustant, Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, I, p. 167; Galland, Library of the Ancient Fathers, III, p. 350; Routh, Sacred Remains, III, p. 69.)*

## To Cornelius, on Granting Peace to the Lapsed

[Col. 0348B]

### Argument
