The African bishops had previously determined in a certain council that the lapsed should not be admitted to peace unless they had performed penance for a long time, except perhaps when danger from illness pressed upon them. Now, with a new persecution imminent, they determined that peace should be granted to all who had done penance, so that they might be stronger for the battle of suffering. Cyprian announces this decree of the bishops to Pope Cornelius in the name of the whole synod; accordingly, this letter belongs not so much to Cyprian himself as to the African synod.

*(You will find this letter, as also the other omitted letters, in their proper place among the pontifical letters in the preceding volume.)*

[79]

# Letter LV

*(Erasmus, I, 3; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, LV; Paris, LIV; Oxford, Leipzig, LIX; Coustant, Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, I, p. 172; Galland, Library of the Ancient Fathers, III, p. 352.)*

## To Cornelius, on Fortunatus and Felicissimus, or Against the Heretics

[Col. 0348C]

### Argument

In this letter Cyprian first admonishes Cornelius not to listen to the slanders of Felicissimus and Fortunatus against him, nor to be frightened by their threats, but to be strong in spirit, as befits a priest of God confronting heretics. For, according to the custom commonly practiced by heretics, they began their heresy and schisms out of contempt [Col. 0349A] for the one bishop in the Church. In passing, he also indicates the usual source from which heresies and schisms arise; hence Morel rightly gave it the title **Against the Heretics**.

*(See the note on the preceding letter.)*

[90]

# Letter LVI

*(Erasmus, IV, 6; Pamelius, Rigaltius, Baluze, LVI; Paris, LV; Oxford, Leipzig, LVIII.)*

## To the People of Thibaris, an Exhortation to Martyrdom

### Argument

Cyprian first excuses himself to the people of Thibaris for not having visited them, and warns them of the impending persecution; he then adds incentives for undertaking martyrdom eagerly.—Next are presented examples of the devout from the beginning of the world who suffered martyrdom. Foremost among them is the Passion of our Lord, which surpasses all examples.—Moreover, are not the contests of the stadium and theater, when endured bravely [Col. 0349B] and eagerly, an incentive to the sufferings of martyrdom?—Finally, let the future reward be considered, which even now more than sufficiently encourages and inflames us to endure all things.

> [Note: [Col. 0349C]
>
> **462 LETTER LVI.—I. “To the people residing at Thibaris.”** Vincentius of Thibaris was present at the Council of Carthage held under Saint Cyprian; and at the Conference of Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists there were Victor, the Catholic bishop of Thibaris, and Victorinus, the Donatist bishop of Thibaris, who are named among the bishops of the province of Byzacena. It may therefore be supposed that Thibaris was in that province, especially since it is clear from this letter that the city was not far removed from Carthage. Otherwise, that congregation would not have asked Cyprian to come to them.
>
> **“The brotherhood.”** I deleted the word “your,” which followed in the editions, not only because it seemed superfluous to me [Col. 0349D], but especially because it is found neither in the ancient manuscripts nor in the early editions. Pamelius added it from the Cambron and Affligem manuscripts, as he himself says.
>
> **“More frequently.”** In the editions this was followed by the word “further,” which I removed because it exists neither in the old books nor in the early editions. Pamelius added it from the same two old books.
>
> **“For this is what it means to desire.”** The passage from here through “We are children” is absent from the Bec manuscript. In its place, however, the following has been substituted: “the sacred blood of Christ, prefigured as a certain testimony of Christ. John the Baptist also, the forerunner of the Lord, who immersed Christ in water; and by him the very Spirit who came upon John was made a figure of what is in us today [the syntax of the manuscript’s substituted text is uncertain], as the Apostle exhorts us, saying: ‘The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit 463 that we are children of God.’” Immediately thereafter follows: “We are [Col. 0350C] children,” etc. But I have found this material nowhere except in the Bec manuscript.
>
> **“That which Christ.”** Certain old books read, “if we imitate that which Christ wished to be done.” Even some which have “if that which Christ” do not have “imitate.”]

## I

Cyprian to the people residing at Thibaris: greetings.

I had indeed intended, dearly beloved brethren, and had it among my prayers, if the course of events and the circumstances of the time permitted, to come to you myself, as you have frequently desired, and by my personal presence there to strengthen the brotherhood with such modest power of exhortation as I possess [Note: [Col. 0349C] “the brotherhood present,” York, Bod. 2, NC. 1; “your brotherhood,” Oxford]. But because the pressure of events so detains us that we are not given the opportunity to travel far from here and be absent for long from the people over whom, by divine indulgence, we preside, I have meanwhile sent you this letter to serve in my place. For since, by the favor of the Lord who instructs us, we are more frequently [Col. 0349C] impelled and admonished, we ought also to bring the solicitous care of our admonition to your conscience.

[Col. 0350A] You should know, and believe and hold as certain, that the day of affliction has begun to hang over our heads and that the end of the age and the time of Antichrist have drawn near, so that we may all stand ready for battle and think of nothing but the glory of eternal life and the crown of confessing the Lord. Nor should we suppose that the things which are coming will be such as those which have passed. A more grievous and more savage battle now impends, for which Christ’s soldiers must prepare themselves with uncorrupted faith and robust courage, considering that they drink the cup of Christ’s blood daily precisely so that they themselves may be able to shed their blood for Christ. For this is what it means to desire to be found with Christ: to imitate what Christ both taught and did [Note: [Col. 0350C] “let us imitate what Christ wished to be done,” Lam., York], in accordance with the words of the apostle John: “He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk as Christ walked” [Col. 0350B] (1 John 2:6). Likewise, the blessed apostle Paul exhorts and teaches us, saying: “We are children. But if children of God, then heirs of God and coheirs with Christ, provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him” (Rom. 8:16–17).

> [Note: [Col. 0350C]
>
> **II.—“Service.”** Thus read all our books and the English books, and also the early editions. Pamelius, who printed “worship,” writes that he substituted this word, from the two manuscripts praised a little above, for what had been “service.” To be sure, the Vulgate edition of the New Testament reads “worship.” But that authority is of no weight against the fidelity of so many ancient copies and editions. [Col. 0350D] Moreover, the fact that Cyprian is known to have used a translation other than the one we call the Vulgate proves that the word “worship” should not be retained here; and “service” is also read in chapter 11 of the Letter to Fortunatus, *An Exhortation to Martyrdom*, and in Augustine’s Letter to Count Boniface. Nevertheless, against what we have argued it may be objected that the passage is quoted in Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 16, and that “worship” is read there. To this I reply that the word certainly occurs in some ancient manuscripts and is absent from others, doubtless according to the differing preferences of ancient copyists. See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage in John, on chapter 9 of Paul’s Letter to the Romans, and on chapter 2 of the Letter to the Philippians.
>
> **“We are children.”** Read: “We are children of God.” A typographical error.
>
> **“You may remember.”** Four old books have “remember.” [Col. 0351C] So also in the Vulgate edition of the New Testament. But the reading asserted by the editions and the greater part of the old books should be retained here.
>
> **“We may be joined.”** The remainder of this letter is absent from the manuscript of Bec Abbey.
>
> **“Do not be surprised.”** So also in the Letter to Fortunatus, *An Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 9. This was taken from the First Letter of Saint Peter, chapter 4, where it reads, “Do not regard the fiery trial as foreign.” The more recent translators differ greatly both from it and from Cyprian’s [Col. 0351D] version. See Erasmus’s commentary there.
>
> **“Anything new.”** I added the word “anything,” following the authority of two old books. It is also present in Peter’s Letter.
>
> **“Or sisters.”** These words are absent from all the manuscripts of Cyprian. They occur, however, in chapter 10 of the Gospel according to Mark, though not in chapter 18 of Luke, where this passage is related.
>
> **“Sevenfold.”** I read “a hundredfold” in three old books, as it is also read in the Gospel of Saint Mark. In other ancient books and in the editions “sevenfold” is written, as also in the book *On the Lapsed* and Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 16. It is clear from the letter of Pope Gregory IX to Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, in Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1232, §51, that he too read it thus.]

## II

All these things must now be considered by us, so that no one may desire anything from an age already dying, but may follow Christ, who both lives forever and gives life to his servants established in faith in his name. For the time is coming, dearly beloved brethren, which our Lord long ago foretold and taught would come, saying: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God. But they will do these things because they have known neither the Father nor me. I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that [Col. 0350C] I told you” (John 16:2–4).

Nor should anyone be surprised that we are wearied by continual persecutions and frequently pressed by constricting afflictions [Col. 0351A], since the Lord foretold that these things would happen in the last times and prepared us for our military service by the instruction and encouragement of his word. His apostle Peter also taught that persecutions occur so that we may be tested and, following the example of the righteous who went before us, may ourselves be joined to the love of God through death and sufferings. For he wrote in his Letter, saying:

> “Dearest friends, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that comes upon you and takes place for your testing, nor fall away as though anything new were happening to you. Instead, whenever you share in Christ’s sufferings, rejoice in every way, so that when his glory is revealed you may rejoice and exult. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the name of the Lord’s majesty and power rests upon you; according to them it is [Col. 0351B] [91] blasphemed, but according to us it is honored” (1 Pet. 4:12–14).

The Apostles taught us those things which they themselves had learned from the Lord’s precepts and heavenly commandments, the Lord himself, of course, strengthening us and saying:

> “There is no one who leaves house, or field, or parents, or brothers, or sisters, or wife, or children for the kingdom of God and does not receive seven times as much in this present time, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10:29; Luke 18:29–30).

And again:

> “Blessed,” he says, “will you be when people hate you, separate you from themselves, drive you out, and revile your name as evil because of the Son of Man. Rejoice on that day and exult; for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke 6:22–23).

> [Note: [Col. 0351D]
>
> **III.—“Soldiers of God.”** Four old books have “soldiers of Christ,” as Cyprian is fond of saying. Lactantius [Col. 0352C], chapter 16 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “This is to be a disciple of God; this is to be a soldier of Christ.”
>
> **“To die.”** We have restored this reading, which all the old books and all the early editions prefer. Pamelius printed “death” on the authority of a single manuscript and claims glory for himself from that emendation. Yet below, Letter LVII, p. 95, Cyprian says that Christians are unconquered precisely because they do not fear to die.]

## III

The Lord wished us to rejoice and exult in persecutions [Col. 0351C], because when persecutions occur, then the crowns of faith are bestowed [Note: [Col. 0351C] “the crown is bestowed,” Lam., Bod. 3], then the soldiers of God are tested [Col. 0352A], then heaven lies open to the martyrs. For we did not enlist in military service on the condition that we should think only of peace and ought to evade and refuse military duty, since in that very service the Lord—the teacher of humility, endurance, and suffering—marched first, so that he might first do what he taught must be done, and might himself first suffer for us what he exhorts us to suffer [Note: [Col. 0351C] “who first exhorts,” Bod. 1, 4].

Let it stand [Note: [Col. 0351C] “If before your eyes,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Rigaltius] before your eyes, dearly beloved brethren, that he who alone received all judgment from the Father and who is to come as judge has already pronounced the sentence of his judgment and of the future examination [Note: [Col. 0352C] “the future sentence,” Lam.], foretelling and solemnly declaring that before his Father he will confess those who confess him and deny those who deny him.

If we could escape death, we would rightly fear to die. But since one who is mortal must die, let us embrace the opportunity that comes from the divine promise and favor [Col. 0352B] [Note: [Col. 0352C] “divine favor,” Lam., York, Bod. 2, NC. 1], and let us undergo the departure of death with the reward of immortality. Let us not fear to be killed, since it is established that when we are killed we are crowned.

> [Note: [Col. 0352C]
>
> **IV.—“It is not permitted to kill.”** Tertullian in the *Apologeticum*: “If under this discipline it were not more permissible to be killed than to kill.” Lucifer of Cagliari, in the book addressed to Constantius, *On Dying for the Son of God*: “For he is the enemy of the religion of God, in which piety, humanity, and all justice are practiced; in which we are taught not to repay evil for evil; in which we are taught not to kill, but to be killed for the Son of God.…” Gerhoh of Reichersberg, in the book *On the Corrupt State of the Church*, p. 215: “With every intention of killing anyone entirely set aside—something men committed to a spiritual purpose are not permitted to do, since they ought to prefer being killed to killing.” See above, pp. 402, 461.
>
> **“He is not alone.”** Saint Fulgentius quotes this passage in chapter 17 of Book II *To Thrasamund*.
>
> **“In the wilderness and mountains.”** Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 31: “Why indeed should I recall how great were the multitudes who, wandering in deserts and mountains, were consumed by hunger, thirst, cold, disease, robbers, and wild beasts?”
>
> [Col. 0353D] **“Resurrection.”** The old editions and the Tours manuscript have “rising.” So also Arator, Book I of *The Acts of the Apostles*. But all the other old books prefer 464 “resurrection,” and the English editors placed that reading in their edition. Other editions, including Rigaltius’s, have “persecution.” Yet in his *Observations* he says that he does not see why the text which has “resurrection” ought to have been deleted.
>
> **“Because of Christ.”** One manuscript from Reims has “for Christ,” with the same meaning.]

## IV

Nor should anyone, dearly beloved brethren, be disturbed when he sees our people put to flight and scattered by fear of persecution, because he does not see the brotherhood assembled or hear the bishops discoursing. At such a time, all those for whom it is not permitted to kill, but who must be killed, cannot be together.

Wherever each of the brethren may be in those days, separated for the time from the flock by the necessity of the circumstances in body but not in spirit [Note: [Col. 0352C] “separated in spirit,” Lincoln], let him not be shaken by the horror of that flight, nor, when withdrawing and hiding, be terrified by the solitude of a deserted place. He is not alone whose companion in flight is Christ; he is not alone who, preserving the temple of God, is nowhere without God, wherever he may be [Col. 0352C].

And if, as he flees through solitude and mountains, a robber overpowers him, a wild beast attacks him, hunger or [Col. 0353A] thirst or cold afflicts him, or a storm and tempest submerge him as he hastens over the seas on a perilous voyage, Christ watches his soldier fighting wherever he may be; and to one who dies because of persecution for the honor of his name, he grants the reward which he promised that he would give at the resurrection. Nor is the glory of martyrdom any less when a person perishes not publicly and among many, provided that the cause of his perishing is to perish because of Christ. For testimony to his martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0353C] “the testimony of his martyr,” York, Bod. 1, 2, NC. 1, 2], that Witness who tests and crowns martyrs is sufficient.

> [Note: [Col. 0353D]
>
> **V.—“Abel inaugurated.”** So also in the book *On the Benefit of Patience*, p. 250. Prosper, Book I of *The Promises and Predictions of God*, chapter 6, speaking of Abel’s murder [Col. 0354D]: “From this point illustrious martyrdoms shone forth, as the righteous were killed by the impious.” See the eighth homily of Saint John Chrysostom *Against the Jews* in the new edition, p. 686.
>
> **“With faith and freedom.”** We have restored the reading of the early editions, which almost all the old books also present. For I have found Erasmus’s emendation, which printed “with freedom of faith,” in no other book than the Tours manuscript. Reinhart nevertheless retained it and rejected the other reading.]

## V

Let us imitate, dearly beloved brethren, righteous Abel, who inaugurated martyrdoms when he was the first to be killed for righteousness. Let us imitate Abraham, the friend of God, who did not hesitate to offer his son as a sacrificial victim with his own hands when he obeyed God with the faith of devotion [Note: [Col. 0353C] “with faith and devotion,” NC. 2].

Let us imitate [Col. 0353B] the three young men—Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael—who, neither terrified by their youth nor broken by captivity, after Judea had been conquered and Jerusalem captured, overcame the king in his own kingdom through the courage of faith. When ordered to worship the statue which King Nebuchadnezzar had made, they proved stronger than both the king’s threats and the flames, proclaiming and [92] testifying to their faith in these words:

> “King Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you concerning this matter. For the God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of burning fire, and he will free us from your hands, O king [Note: [Col. 0353C] “he will free us from your hands,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2]. But if not, let it be known to you that we do not serve your gods, nor do we worship the golden image which you have set up” (Dan. 3:16–18).

They believed that, according to their faith [Note: [Col. 0353C] “their faith,” York, NC. 2, Lam., Bod. 2], they could escape; but they added “but if not,” so that the king might know that for the sake of the God whom they worshiped they were also able to die [Col. 0353C]. For this is the strength of courage and faith: to believe and know that God can deliver one from present death, yet not to fear death or yield, so that faith may be tested all the more strongly.

The uncorrupted and unconquered vigor of the Holy Spirit burst forth through their mouths, so that the truth of what the Lord said in his Gospel might become manifest [Note: [Col. 0353C] “declared,” Bod. 1, 2; “said, saying,” Lam., Bod. 3, 4]:

> “But when they arrest you [Note: [Col. 0353D] ‘hand you over,’ Lam., Bod. 2], do not consider what you are to say, for in that hour what you are to say will be given to you. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20).

[Col. 0354A] He said that what we can say and answer is divinely given and supplied to us in that hour [Note: [Col. 0353D] “is supplied to us divinely in that hour,” Bod. 3], and that it is not we who then speak, but the Spirit of God the Father, who, since he neither withdraws nor is separated from those who confess, himself both speaks and is crowned in us.

So too Daniel, when he was compelled to worship the idol Bel, whom the people and king were then worshiping, burst forth with complete faith and freedom [Note: [Col. 0354C] “in asserting … honor,” Bod. 3] to vindicate his God’s honor, saying: “I worship nothing except [Note: [Col. 0354C] “except the one God,” Bod. 2] the Lord my God, who created heaven and earth” (Dan. 14:4).

> [Note: [Col. 0354D]
>
> **VI.—“An age not yet fit.”** See what was related above, p. 393, concerning Saint Agnes from Ambrose.
>
> **“Me before you.”** Two old books have “me first.”]

## VI

What of the Maccabees—the grievous torments of the blessed martyrs, the manifold punishments of the seven brothers, and their mother encouraging her children amid their punishments and herself dying with her children? Do they not testify to examples of great [Note: [Col. 0354C] “great,” singular, Lam., Bod. 2] courage and faith, and by their sufferings exhort us to the triumph of martyrdom [Col. 0354B]?

What of the prophets, whom the Holy Spirit inspired with foreknowledge of future things? What of the Apostles, whom the Lord chose? When the righteous [Note: [Col. 0354C] “who, being righteous,” Oxford] were killed for righteousness, did they not teach us also to die?

Christ’s nativity began immediately with the martyrdoms of infants, when those two years old and younger were killed because of his name. An age not yet fit for battle proved fit for the crown. To show that those who are killed for Christ are innocent, innocent infancy was slain because of his name. It was shown that no one is immune from the danger of persecution, since even such as these accomplished martyrdoms.

How grave a thing it is [Note: [Col. 0354D] “therefore,” Oxford] for a Christian man to be unwilling to suffer when the Lord suffered first, and for us to be unwilling to suffer for our sins when he, having no sin of his own [Col. 0354C], suffered for us! The Son of God suffered to make us sons of God, and the son of man is unwilling to suffer so that he may continue to be a son of God!

If we labor under the hatred of the world, Christ first endured the world’s hatred. If we endure insults in this world, if exile, if torments, the Maker and Lord of the world experienced things more grievous, and he also admonishes us, saying:

> “If the world hates you,” he says, “remember that it hated me before you. If you belonged to the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you do not belong to the world and I chose you out of the world, [Col. 0355A] therefore the world hates you [Note: [Col. 0355C] ‘the world … the world,’ Bod. 3]. Remember the word which I spoke to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:18–20).

Whatever our Lord and God taught, he also did, so that a disciple who learns but does not act may have no excuse.

> [Note: [Col. 0355C]
>
> **VII.—“By fear of the coming persecution.”** One royal manuscript has “fear the coming persecution.”
>
> **“Kill in Gehenna.”** The same two books have “destroy.”
>
> **“His image.”** In the Grenoble manuscript the following comes next: “We ought to persist more earnestly in prayers and to pray, first entreating him himself, and then making satisfaction to God the Father. For we have as advocate and intercessor for our sins Jesus Christ our Lord and God, provided only that we repent of having sinned in the past and, confessing and understanding the debts by which we now offend the Lord, promise that henceforth we shall walk in his ways and fear his commandments.” I have not dared to place this in the text, because it does not seem to me to cohere with the subject being treated here.]

## VII

Nor should any one of you, dearly beloved brethren, be so terrified by fear of the coming persecution or by the imminent advent of Antichrist that he is not found armed for all things by the exhortations and precepts of the Gospel and by heavenly admonitions.

Antichrist is coming, but Christ too is coming immediately afterward. The enemy runs rampant and rages, but the Lord also follows at once [93] to avenge our sufferings and wounds. The adversary is angry and threatens, but there is one who can deliver us from his hands. He is to be feared whose wrath no one will be able to escape, as he himself forewarns and says:

> “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can kill both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

And again:

> “He who loves his soul will lose it, and he who hates his soul in this age will preserve it for eternal life” (John 12:25).

And in the Apocalypse he instructs and forewarns us, saying:

> “If anyone worships the beast and his image, and receives the mark on his forehead and on his hand, he too will drink from the wine of God’s wrath, mixed in the cup of his wrath, and will be punished with fire and sulfur before the eyes of the holy angels and before the eyes of the Lamb. The smoke of their torments will ascend for ages of ages, and they will have no rest by day or night, whoever worships the beast and his image” (Rev. 14:9–11).

[Col. 0355C]

> [Note: [Col. 0355D]
>
> **VIII.—“Opening.”** The Pithou manuscript has *spandens*. Perhaps *expandens* (“spreading open”) should be restored, just as I have often seen *spectans* written in many books for *expectans*, and conversely. See Du Cange’s Latin glossary under the word *spando*. Thus *splendor* occurs for *explendor* in Tertullian’s book *On the Soul*, as Rigaltius notes. Likewise, in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 984, *straneis* occurs for *extraneis*. Thus also I have often read *strumenta* [Col. 0356C] for *instrumenta* elsewhere in ancient manuscripts and public documents. See Obsopoeus on Seneca’s Letter LX.
>
> **“Let us be armed and prepared.”** Thus the early editions, eleven of our old books, six English books, and Florus’s manuscript. So also the editions of Manutius and Morel. The other reading, “The blessed Apostle arms and prepares us, saying” [Col. 0356D], pleased Pamelius, Rigaltius, and the English editors.
>
> **“The whole armor.”** In Erasmus’s edition, which Pamelius, Rigaltius, and the English editors followed, the word “of God” is added. But I found this addition nowhere in the ancient copies. The Sorbonne manuscript reads, “Put on the armor of light.” The Pithou manuscript has, “Put on the whole armor.”
>
> **“Which is the word of God.”** Three ancient manuscripts read, “which is the word of God,” using *verbum* rather than *sermo*, with the same meaning. Nevertheless, it seemed necessary to draw attention to this because of the difference between the versions.]

## VIII

People are trained and prepared for a worldly contest, and they reckon it a great glory to their honor if they should have the good fortune to be crowned while the people watch and the emperor is present. Behold the lofty and mighty contest, glorious with the prize of a heavenly crown: that God should watch us contend and, opening his eyes over those whom he has deigned to make his sons [Col. 0356A], should take pleasure in the spectacle of our struggle.

God watches us as we do battle and fight in the conflict of faith; his angels watch; Christ also watches [Note: [Col. 0355C] “his Christ,” Lam., York, Bod. 2, NC. 1]. How great is the dignity of glory and how great the happiness of entering the contest in God’s presence [Note: [Col. 0356C] “with God presiding,” Bod. 1, 2, Lincoln, NC. 1, 2, York] and being crowned with Christ as judge!

Let us be armed, dearly beloved brethren, with all our strength and be prepared for the contest with uncorrupted minds, complete faith, and devoted courage. Let the camp of God advance to the battle line appointed for us. Let those who have remained intact be armed, lest one who is intact lose that for which he recently stood firm. Let the lapsed also be armed, so that even one who has fallen may regain what he lost. Let honor summon the intact to battle, and sorrow the lapsed.

The blessed apostle Paul teaches us to be armed and prepared, saying:

> “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers and rulers of this world and of this darkness, against the spirits of wickedness [Note: [Col. 0356C] ‘wicked spirits,’ York, NC. 1] in the heavenly places. Therefore put on the whole armor, so that you may be able to resist on the most evil day; so that, when you have accomplished all things, you may stand with your loins girded in truth, wearing the breastplate of righteousness and your feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6:12–17).

> [Note: [Col. 0356D]
>
> **IX.—“The saving helmet.”** Erasmus introduced this reading, and Manutius and Morel retained it. Three old books have it. But five others and the earlier editions prefer “the spiritual helmet.” So also in the excerpts of Florus. Above, in Letter XXVI, p. 36, “the helmet of salvation” is read. See Erasmus’s annotations on chapter 6 of the Letter to the Ephesians.
>
> [Col. 0357C] **“The sign of God.”** Placed upon the forehead. Lactantius, chapter 10 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “They placed the immortal sign upon their foreheads.” The same author, Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 27: “When the sign has been placed upon their foreheads,” and “those whom the immortal sign has fortified.” Likewise Cyprian, in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 200: “He was stained upon the forehead by the mottling of leprosy, marked, because the Lord had been offended, upon that part of the body where those who win the Lord’s favor are signed.” Victor of Vita, Book I, chapter 14: “The forehead upon which Christ had fixed the standard of his cross.” See Savaron on Sidonius, Book III, Letter 12.
>
> **“Let us also arm the right hand.”** The Most Eminent Cardinal Giovanni Bona quotes and admirably elucidates this passage [Col. 0357D] in Book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 17; consult him.
>
> **“Received the Lord’s body.”** In the right hand, that is. See what the same Most Eminent Cardinal said on this matter in the passage just cited. For I gladly employ the authority of this excellent and most learned man, whose friendship I used to boast of and to whom, in my preface to the *Capitularies*, I professed myself greatly indebted.
>
> **“Let it embrace him.”** A more recent Victorine manuscript reads, “let it embrace its Lord in him, since it will afterward receive the Lord.” So also in Morel’s edition, except that at the end it has “from the Lord.”]

## IX

Let us take up these weapons and fortify ourselves with these spiritual and heavenly defenses, so that on the most evil day we may be able to resist and repel the devil’s threats. Let us put on the breastplate of righteousness, so that the breast may be fortified and protected against the enemy’s darts. Let our feet be shod and armed with the teaching of the Gospel, so that when the serpent begins to be trampled [Col. 0356C] and crushed by us, it may not be able to bite or trip us.

Let us bravely carry the shield of faith, under whose protection whatever the enemy hurls may be extinguished. Let us also receive the saving helmet as a covering for the head: let the ears be fortified, so that they do not hear the deadly edicts; let the eyes be fortified, so that they do not see the detestable images; [Col. 0357A] let the forehead be fortified, so that the sign of God may be preserved unharmed; let the mouth be fortified, so that the victorious tongue may confess Christ its Lord.

Let us also arm the right hand with the spiritual sword, so that it may resolutely reject the deadly sacrifices; so that, mindful of the Eucharist, the hand which received the Lord’s body may embrace him, being destined afterward to receive from the Lord the reward of heavenly crowns.

> [Note: [Col. 0357D]
>
> **X.—“Set ablaze with burning.”** This is exactly what is written in one old book of the royal library. I readily prefer this reading, both because the expression is Latin and because I think that the word *damnare* (“condemn”), which is placed here instead of *flammare* (“set ablaze”) in other ancient copies and editions, was substituted by some unskilled copyist to whom the other reading was not sufficiently familiar. For through ignorance of ancient Latinity, unskilled copyists have spattered these most elegant writings with no small number of blemishes, as Joseph Scaliger complains at the beginning of his notes on Varro’s books *On Agriculture*. This passage from the book *Against Demetrianus*, p. 224, also seems to confirm the emendation: “Gehenna, burning forever, will consume those sentenced to it.”
>
> **“What glory there will be.”** The Fux manuscript has, “What dignity of glory there will be.” Another passage from the book *Against Demetrianus*, p. 224, can support this reading: “What glory faith will then have, what punishment faithlessness will have, when the day of judgment comes.”
>
> **“With the righteous.”** Two old books have, “with all the righteous [Col. 0358D] and the friends of God.”
>
> **“Brightness.”** The same two old books have “glory.” Copyists have often changed words in this way in Cyprian and other ancient writers. But Cyprian himself teaches that “brightness” must be read: when reproducing this passage of Paul in Letter LXXII, to Nemesianus and the others, in the Letter *An Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 12, and in Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 17, he always uses “brightness.”]

Deserters of God . . . rebels. Below, Epistle LXXIII, p. 131: “It is the duty of a good soldier to defend the camp of his commander against rebels and enemies.” Accordingly, those who deserted their commander’s camp were so hated and detested that, if they were caught deserting, they were exposed to the utmost danger, as Saint John Chrysostom says at the beginning of his *Second Exhortation to Theodore after His Fall*; and if a slave betrayed a deserter, he was rewarded with freedom. On this subject, one should consult what Godescalcus Stewechius learnedly wrote concerning deserters in his notes on Vegetius.]

### X

O what a day that will be, and how great, when it comes, dearly beloved brethren—when the Lord begins to review His people and, by the examination of divine knowledge, to assess the merits of each person; to send the guilty into hell, and to set our persecutors aflame with the perpetual burning of the penal fire, but to pay us the reward of faith and devotion! What glory and how great a joy it will be to be admitted to the sight of God; to be honored by receiving, with Christ [Col. 0357B] your Lord and God, the joy of salvation and eternal light; to greet Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, and all the patriarchs and prophets and apostles and martyrs; to rejoice with the righteous and the friends of God in the kingdom of heaven, in the delight of the immortality bestowed upon us; there to receive what neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2:9)! For the Apostle proclaims that we shall receive greater things than what we either accomplish or suffer here, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come, which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). When that revelation comes, when God’s glory shines upon us, we shall be as blessed and joyful, honored by the Lord’s gracious favor, as those who, being deserters of God or rebels against God, have done the devil’s will shall remain guilty and wretched, so that they must be tormented together with him in unquenchable fire.

[Col. 0358A]

### XI

Let these things, dearly beloved brethren, cling to our hearts [Note: [Col. 0357C] “To your hearts.” Rigault: “Let these things be our meditation by day.”]. Let this be the preparation of our arms, let this be our meditation by day and night: always to keep before our eyes, and to revolve in thought [Note: [Col. 0358C] “To keep before our eyes and to consider”: Lambeth, Bodleian 2, 3.] and in our senses, the punishments of the wicked and the rewards and merits of the righteous—what punishment the Lord threatens against those who deny Him, and, conversely, what glory He promises to those who confess Him. If the day of persecution overtakes us while we are thinking and meditating upon these things, the soldier of Christ, instructed by His precepts and admonitions, does not tremble at the battle, but is ready for the crown. I wish you, dearest brethren, always to fare well.

## EPISTLE LVII

*(Erasmus, I, 1; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LVII; Paris, LVI; Oxford, Leipzig, LV.)*

### TO CORNELIUS IN EXILE, CONCERNING HIS CONFESSION

[Col. 0358B]

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian praises in Cornelius and his people their confession of the name of Christ even to the point of exile, and exhorts them to steadfastness and to mutual prayers for one another, both because the day of conflict in this life is imminent and for the time after death. Damasus, moreover, mentions this letter in his *Life of Cornelius*, since, because of the slander occasioned by it, the tyrant found a pretext for killing him.

*(This letter of Cyprian is rightly appended to volume III of the Pontifical Epistles.)*

## 96 EPISTLE LVIII

*(Erasmus, III, 1; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LVIII; Paris, LVI; Coustant, Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs, I, p. 207.)*

### TO LUCIUS, BISHOP OF ROME, UPON HIS RETURN FROM EXILE

[Col. 0358C]

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian, together with his colleagues, congratulates Lucius [Col. 0359A] upon his return from exile, teaching that a martyrdom deferred does not diminish its glory. Then, indicating that the martyrdom of Cornelius and the exile of Lucius had occurred by divine providence in order to confound the Novatianists, he foretells Lucius’s imminent martyrdom; God so ordaining it that his martyrdom should be consummated not abroad, but among his own people.

*(See the note on the preceding Epistle.)*

## 97 EPISTLE LIX

*(Erasmus, III, 8; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LIX; Paris, LVIII; Oxford, Leipzig, LXIV; Routh, Remains of Sacred Writers, III, pp. 74 and 116.)*

### TO FIDUS, CONCERNING THE BAPTISM OF INFANTS

**SUMMARY.—**Saint Augustine briefly states the principal subject of this letter in Epistle XXVIII to Jerome: “The blessed Cyprian,” he says, “was not establishing some new [Col. 0359B] decree, but preserving the Church’s most firmly settled faith, when, together with certain of his fellow bishops, he decided, in correction of those who thought that an infant ought not to be baptized before the eighth day from birth, that a child could properly be baptized immediately after being born.” Incidentally, however, near the beginning of the letter, he does not revoke the peace granted to a certain Victor, even though it had been granted contrary to the decrees of the synods concerning the lapsed; rather, he forbids Bishop Therapius to act in that way thereafter. From this passage it is sufficiently clear that this letter was written after both synods concerning the lapsed, mentioned above at Epistle LIV. Whether it was written a little or a long time afterward, however, is uncertain; its context nevertheless indicates that it was written in time of peace.

*(This letter is listed above among the acts of the Councils of Carthage held under Saint Cyprian.)*

[Note: [Col. 0359D]

**470 EPISTLE LX.—**The English editors say that this letter occurs very rarely in ancient copies and that they had seen none in which it was found. I possessed one from the monastery of Saint Denis at Reims. Furthermore, although this letter contains no mention either of the bishops of Numidia or of Numidian affairs, it is nevertheless sufficiently clear that it was written to the Numidian bishops, as the author of the *Cyprianic Annals* rightly judged. This is established by the inscription found in the Manutius edition, where the letter was first published, and in the Reims manuscript; and also because it seems to be mentioned in Epistle LXXII, p. 128, [Col. 0360D] in these words: “Likewise in the letters which our colleagues previously sent to the bishops presiding in Numidia.” Epistle LXXII is also addressed to the same men. Hadrianus Saravia nevertheless thought that it had been written to the bishops of Mauretania, in chapter 11 of his treatise *On the Honor Due to Prelates and Presbyters*.]

## 99 EPISTLE LX

*(Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LX; Paris, LIX; Oxford, Leipzig, LXII.)*

### TO THE NUMIDIAN BISHOPS, CONCERNING THE RANSOM OF THE BRETHREN FROM CAPTIVITY AMONG THE BARBARIANS

[Col. 0359C]

**SUMMARY.—**After first lamenting the captivity of the brethren, of which Cyprian had been informed by the Numidian bishops, he says that he is sending one hundred thousand sesterces, and appends the names both of the individual brothers and sisters and of the colleagues who had contributed something. It is probable that this captivity was inflicted by those barbarians against whom Decius set out to war and was killed. Manutius and Morel were the first to publish this letter in recent times.

[Col. 0359D]

[Note: [Col. 0360D]

**Captivity. I.—**See the *Cyprianic Annals* for the year 253.]

### I

Cyprian to his brothers Januarius, Maximus, Proculus, Victor, Modianus, Nemesianus, Nampulus, and Honoratus, greetings. With the deepest anguish of our soul and not without tears, we read your letter, dearest brethren, which in the solicitude of your love you sent us concerning the captivity of our brothers and sisters. For who would not grieve at such misfortunes? Or who would not reckon his brother’s grief as his own, when the Apostle Paul speaks and says: “If one member suffers, the other members suffer with it; if one member rejoices, the other members rejoice with it” (1 Cor. 12:26)? And elsewhere he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Accordingly, the captivity of our brethren must now be accounted our own captivity, and the suffering of those in danger must be reckoned as our own suffering, since the body of our unity is one; and not only love, but also religion ought to urge [Col. 0360B] and strengthen us to ransom the members of our brethren.

[Note: [Col. 0360D]

**II.—With shame.** The Reims manuscript reads: “and with the love of the marital bond.”]

### II

For since the Apostle Paul says again, “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16), even if charity compelled us less urgently to bring aid to the brethren, we should nevertheless have considered here that it is the temples of God that have been taken captive. We ought not, through prolonged inaction and indifference to their suffering, to allow the temples of God to remain captive for a long time, but should strive with all the strength we possess, and act swiftly, so that by our acts of service we may merit the favor of Christ, our Judge and Lord and God. For since the Apostle Paul says, “As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27), Christ must be contemplated in our captive brethren, and He who redeemed us from the danger of death must be redeemed from the danger of captivity, [Col. 0360C] so that He who snatched us from the jaws of the devil—He who now remains and dwells in us—may Himself be snatched from the hands of the barbarians; and so that He who redeemed us by the cross and by His blood may be redeemed by a sum of money. He therefore allows these things to happen for a time so that our faith may be tested: whether each person will do for another what he would wish to be done for himself, if he himself were held captive among the barbarians.

For who, if he is mindful of humanity and reminded of mutual love, would not, if he is a father, reckon that his own children are now there; or, if he is a husband, think with equal grief and shame for the marital bond that his own wife is held captive there? And how great is the grief and anguish common to us all over the danger of the virgins held there! In their case we must lament not only the loss of freedom, but also of chastity, [Col. 0360D] and must deplore not so much the chains of the barbarians as the violations inflicted by pimps and brothels, lest members dedicated to Christ and devoted forever in chaste virtue to the honor of continence [Col. 0361A] be defiled by the lust and contamination of those who assault them.

[Note: [Col. 0361C]

**III.—Sesterces.** Here we have followed the editions of Manutius, Pamelius, and Rigault. The English editors printed *sestertium*, but without mentioning any ancient manuscript, merely because Rigault had advised that it should be written thus, and because of linguistic analogy, since they knew that ancient authors of the Latin language wrote *sestertium* in the plural. That this was not always so, however, is proved by these words of Sosipater Charisius: “We cannot simply say *centies nummum*, but *centies sestertium*; yet we do not say *quinquaginta sestertium*, but *quinquaginta sestertia*.” Juvenal, Satire I:

> Is it mere madness to squander  
> A hundred thousand sesterces?

And Satire IV:

> He bought a mullet for six thousand,  
> A fish whose weight indeed matched its cost in sesterces, pound for pound.

471 See Lambinus’s *Annotations on Cicero’s Speech for Sextus Roscius of Ameria*, and Jean Tristan de Saint-Amant, volume II of his *Commentaries*, p. 576. See also Baronius, under the year 254, near the end.]

### III

Our brotherhood here, reflecting upon and sorrowfully considering all these matters in accordance with your letter, has promptly, willingly, and generously contributed financial aid for the brethren. They have indeed always, in accordance with the firmness of their faith, been disposed toward the work of God, but now they have been kindled still more strongly toward saving works by the contemplation of so great a suffering. For since the Lord says in His Gospel, “I was sick, and you visited Me,” with how much greater a reward for our work will He now also say: “I was captive, and you redeemed Me” (Matt. 25:36)! And since He says again, “I was in prison, and you came to Me,” how much greater will it be when He begins to say: “I was in the prison of captivity, and I lay confined and bound among the barbarians, [Col. 0361B] and you freed Me from that prison of slavery,” when, at the coming of the day of judgment, you are to receive a reward from the Lord?

Finally, we give you the greatest thanks because you wished us to share in your solicitude and in so good and necessary a work, thereby offering us fertile fields in which we might sow the seeds of our hope, while awaiting a harvest from the most abundant fruits that arise from this heavenly and saving work. We have sent one hundred thousand sesterces in coin, which were collected here, in the church over which by the Lord’s gracious favor we preside, through the contributions of the clergy and the people established among us. You will distribute them there with your customary diligence.

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

**IV.—Holding it as certain.** The Reims manuscript adds: “and knowing.”]

### IV

We indeed wish that nothing of this kind may happen in the future and that our brethren, protected by the Lord’s majesty, may be preserved unharmed from dangers of this sort. If, however, something of this kind should occur in order to test the charity of our mind and examine the faith of our heart, do not hesitate to inform us of it by your letters. You may hold it as certain that our church and the entire brotherhood here pray that these things may not happen again; but if they do happen, they will willingly and generously furnish assistance.

So that you may remember in your prayers our brothers and sisters who have contributed promptly and willingly to this most necessary work, and so that you may make a return to them for their good work in your sacrifices and prayers, I have appended the names of each of them. I have also added the names of our colleagues and fellow priests who, being present themselves, contributed certain amounts according to their means both in their own name and in the name of their people. In addition to our own personal amount, I have also specified and sent the small sums contributed by them all. You ought, as faith and charity require, to remember every one of them in your prayers and supplications. We wish you, dearest brethren, always to fare well and to remember us.

[Note: [Col. 0361D]

**EPISTLE LXI.—**I found this letter in twenty-three ancient copies. Some of them give the name of Euchratius in different forms, but almost all have it as we have printed it. Euchratius, bishop of Thenis, attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. [Col. 0362C] Thenis, or the colony of Thenae, was in the province of Byzacena, not far from Usula, as we have said elsewhere.]

## EPISTLE LXI

*(Erasmus, I, 10; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LXI; Paris, LX; Oxford, Leipzig, II.)*

### TO EUCHRATIUS, CONCERNING AN ACTOR

[Col. 0362B]

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian forbids an actor, if he persists in his shameful craft, to receive communion in the Church. Nor, indeed, ought he to be excused on the ground that he does not himself practice acting, so long as he teaches it to others; nor because of poverty in his personal affairs, since he can be supplied with food at the Church’s expense. Indeed, if the resources of Euchratius’s church are insufficient, Cyprian advises that the man come to Carthage.

[Note: [Col. 0362C]

**I.—Because of your affection.** The Chartres and Bec manuscripts, as well as Morel’s edition, prefer: “Because of your affection and our mutual respect.”

**Actor.** Plutarch asks in his *Roman Questions* why performers of the stage, who are consecrated to Bacchus, are called *histriones*.

[Col. 0362D]

**Master and teacher:** that is, a teacher of theatrical arts, as Ammianus Marcellinus puts it in Book XIV. Lactantius, in the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*, ch. LXIII: “There are also the shameless gestures of actors, by which they imitate infamous women; they teach the lusts which they represent in dance.” See also Book VI, ch. 20. Tacitus, in Book I of the *Annals*: “There was in the camp a certain Percennius, formerly a leader of theatrical companies and afterward a common soldier, insolent in speech and skilled through his theatrical profession in stirring up assemblies.” The same author writes in Book II of the *Histories* that Vitellius kept around him buffoons, actors, and charioteers, in whose degrading friendships he took extraordinary pleasure.

**Shameful gestures.** See Theodoret, Book IV, ch. 22 of the *Religious History*.

**Through the teaching of a shameless art.** Apuleius, in his *Apology*: “For it is denied that he possessed anything of the actor except shamelessness.”

**Which I think.** I do not know what induced Pamelius [Col. 0363C] to alter, on the authority of Cauch’s single manuscript, the reading of the earlier editions, which is the reading we give here. All the ancient copies present this reading. It is probable that the reading in Cauch’s manuscript arose from a copyist’s error, as frequently happens in manuscripts of the ancients, but especially in the works of Saint Cyprian, of which no ancient copies are found that do not contain errors of this kind.]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Euchratius, greetings. Because of our mutual affection and your respectful regard, you thought it proper to consult me, dearest brother, as to what I think concerning a certain actor who is living among you, yet continues in the disgrace of his same craft, and, as a master and teacher not of boys who are to be educated but of boys who are to be ruined, instills into others as well what he himself learned wickedly: whether such a man ought to receive communion with us. I think it accords neither with the divine majesty nor with the discipline of the Gospel that the modesty and honor of the Church should be defiled by so shameful and [Col. 0363A] infamous a contamination. For since men are forbidden in the Law [Note: [Col. 0363C] “In the Law of God”: Lambeth, York, Bodleian 2.] to put on women’s clothing [Note: [Col. 0363C] “A man is forbidden”: Lambeth, Bodleian 2.], and persons of that sort are judged accursed, how much greater is the crime not only of taking up women’s garments, but also of portraying shameful, effeminate, and womanly gestures through the teaching of a shameless art?

[Note: [Col. 0363C]

**II.—Substitutes.** Thus the ancient editions and eleven ancient manuscripts. This word, moreover, occurs in Plautus, in whose works, according to the variations sometimes found in the ancient manuscripts, it is occasionally written *succidaneos*. That is the reading of nine ancient copies of Saint Cyprian. [Col. 0363D] See Aulus Gellius, Book IV, ch. 6.

**The sex is altered by art.** The constitution of Constantius and Constans in the title of the Theodosian Code *Concerning Adulterers* says: “where sex has lost its place.” Seneca, Epistle CXXII: “Does a man who has exchanged clothing with women not seem to you to live contrary to nature?” Quintilian, Book V, ch. 9, says that if a man assumes women’s clothing, it is a sign that he is effeminate and scarcely a man. Dio Chrysostom tells a monstrous story concerning Nero’s male prostitute in Oration XX. See William Beveridge’s annotations on canon XIII of the Synod of Gangra.

**Let him gain.** Four ancient manuscripts have “let him acquire.” Nearly all the ancient manuscripts, however, separate the following words from this verb and begin another sentence. We judged that this should be followed.

**Eternal life.** We corrected this from the Fuxensis and Grenoble manuscripts, whereas it was formerly misread as “his own life.” Below, Epistle LXXI, p. 127: “Since the Church is one, which has obtained the grace of eternal life.” Some ancient manuscripts nevertheless have “his own life.”

**Dearest brother.** This is the true reading, presented by many ancient manuscripts and the early editions, including Morel’s and also the one which Simon Goulart issued after that of Pamelius. Pamelius, however, who saw “son” written in the Manutius edition, printed it thus in his own. From there this corrupt reading passed into Rigault’s edition and the English edition. It seemed proper to issue this warning so that no one might hereafter be misled by it. For the man who recently composed a life of Saint Cyprian, deceived by that false reading, thought that from it an argument could be derived [Col. 0364D] for asserting episcopal rank for Magnus, to whom Epistle LXXVI was written, even though Cyprian there calls him “son,” not “brother,” as is his custom when writing to bishops. For he knew that Euchratius was a bishop, and nevertheless saw him called “son” at the end of this Epistle.]

### II

Nor should anyone excuse himself on the ground that he has personally withdrawn from the theater, while nevertheless teaching it to others. For he cannot be regarded as having withdrawn when he appoints representatives and provides many substitutes for himself alone, contrary to God’s ordinance, instructing and teaching how a male may be broken down [Note: [Col. 0363C] “fashioned”: MR.] into a female and the sex be altered by art, and how the devil may be gratified, as he stains God’s handiwork through the sins of a corrupted and enervated body.

But if such a man pleads his destitution and the necessity of poverty, [Col. 0363B] his need can be relieved among the others who are supported by the Church’s provisions, provided that he is content with food that is more frugal but innocent [Note: [Col. 0363C] “more frugal and innocent food”: NC 1, 2; Lambeth; [Col. 0364C] York; Lincoln.]. Nor should he think that he must be bought off with a salary in order to cease from sin, since he renders this service not to us but to himself. Besides, however much he wishes [Note: [Col. 0364C] “however much he wants”: Lambeth, York, NC 1, Bodleian 2.] to gain from it, what sort of gain is it that snatches men away from the banquet of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and, after they have been wickedly and ruinously fattened in this world, leads them to the punishments of eternal hunger and thirst?

Therefore, so far as you are able, recall him from this depravity and disgrace to the path of innocence and the hope of eternal life, so that he may be content with the Church’s provisions, more sparing indeed, but conducive to salvation. But if the church there does not have sufficient means to furnish food to those in distress, he may transfer himself to us and here receive whatever [Note: [Col. 0364C] “and that which”: Lambeth, York, Bodleian 2.] is necessary for his food [Col. 0364A] and clothing, so that he may no longer teach others outside the Church things that bring death, but may himself learn within the Church things that bring salvation. I wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

## 102 EPISTLE LXII

*(Erasmus, I, 11; Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LXII; Paris, LXII; Oxford, Leipzig, IV.)*

### TO POMPONIUS, CONCERNING VIRGINS

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian, together with several colleagues, replies to his colleague Pomponius that virgins who had resolved to maintain their state continently and steadfastly, but were afterward found in the same bed with males, are to be received into communion and admitted to the Church if they are still found to be virgins; but if not, since they are adulteresses not against a husband but against [Col. 0364B] Christ, they must be compelled to undergo full penance; and those who stubbornly persist are to be cast out of the Church. Incidentally, he sets forth a form of discipline by which virgins may be kept to their duty, as well as certain points concerning the power of excommunication in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0364D]

**EPISTLE LXII.—I. To Pomponius,** bishop of Dionysiana in the province of Byzacena. He attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Fortunatus, bishop of Dionysiana, subscribed to the Council of Cabarsussi. At the Conference of Carthage between Catholics and Donatists, Victor, the Donatist bishop of Dionysiana, was present and declared that he had no opponent. This was immediately denied, however, by Aurelius, the Catholic bishop of Macomades.

**With the presbyters.** In one of my ancient manuscripts the reading is “with the Roman presbyters.”

**Since they had once resolved to maintain their state.** We have restored the reading of the ancient [Col. 0365B] manuscripts which we used. The English edition attests that it is also read thus in one Bodleian manuscript. Rigault had printed: “since they had resolved to remain in their own state and steadfastly to maintain continence.” I saw this reading written in the margin of my copy [Col. 0365C] of the Manutius edition, where it was noted as coming from the Verona manuscript. The Fuxensis manuscript also appears to agree with it, reading thus: “since, once they were in that state, they had resolved steadfastly to maintain continence.”]

### I

Cyprian, Caecilius, Victor, Sedatus, and Tertullus, together with the presbyters who were present, to their brother Pomponius, greetings. We have read your letter, dearest brother, which you sent through our brother Paconius, asking and desiring us to write back to you what we think concerning those virgins who, after once resolving to maintain their state continently and steadfastly, were afterward discovered to have remained together in the same bed with males, one of whom you say is a deacon; and specifically concerning those same women who, although they have confessed that they slept with men, [Col. 0365A] assert that they remain intact.

Since you desired our counsel on this matter, you should know that we do not depart from the traditions of the Gospel and the Apostles, so that our brothers and sisters may be advised with constancy and resolution [Note: [Col. 0365B] “that we might advise with resolution”: Lincoln.], and so that ecclesiastical discipline may be preserved along every path of benefit and salvation [Note: [Col. 0365B] “along every path of ecclesiastical discipline”: Bodleian 1, 2. “All the benefits and means of salvation belonging to ecclesiastical discipline”: York, Lambeth, NC 1.]. For the Lord speaks and says: “And I will give you shepherds according to My heart, and they shall feed you, feeding you with discipline” (Jer. 3:15); and again it is written: “He who rejects discipline is unhappy” (Wis. 3:11); and in the Psalms also the Holy Spirit admonishes and instructs us, saying: “Hold fast to discipline, lest the Lord perhaps become angry, and you perish from the right way, when His wrath is quickly kindled against you” (Ps. 2:12).

[Note: [Col. 0365C]

**II.—Belching.** Previously the reading was “fruit,” not only in the editions but also in the ancient manuscripts. Rigault observed that “belching” was written in the Verona manuscript and pronounced that reading entirely correct. I, on the contrary, thought it entirely incorrect. “For what,” I said, “does personal choice have in common with belching, which signifies an indecent act that the Stoics, as Cicero attests, wished to place on the same footing as breaking wind; Columella, Book VI, ch. 6, with a sound of the belly; and Jerome, in the *Epistle to the Virgin Principia* and Book II *Against Jovinian*, with the breaking of wind that arises from a full and overheated belly?” I therefore conjectured that perhaps the reading should be “according to their own choice and custom,” as in Jerome’s Book II *Against Jovinian*, or “nod,” as in Livy, [Col. 0365D] Book IV: “under the nod and choice”; and in Cyprian, Epistle LXIX, where Christ is said to govern the Church by His own choice and nod. But when I noticed that the word “belch” was used in the same sense by Pontius the deacon in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, I embraced the reading that Rigault says is entirely correct. These are the words of Pontius: “Far be it from me to admit this evil into the conscience of a religious mind, so that a man’s belch should pass judgment on so blessed a Martyr.”

**Virgins with males.** Jerome, in the *Epistle to Paul of Concordia*: “The wretched man said only that virgins ought more often to be with women than with males, and I offended the eyes of the whole city and was pointed at by everyone’s fingers.” See Saint John Chrysostom’s Homily *Against Those Who Keep ‘Subintroduced’ Virgins in Their Homes*, and likewise his Homily *That Women under a Rule Ought Not to Live with Men*.

[Col. 0366B]

**Must be stripped away.** Coster, as Pamelius attests, thought that the reading should be “must be rescued,” as I found in two excellent ancient manuscripts. Gronovius, however, refutes this conjecture with several arguments in chapter XIV of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*.

**Near danger.** Jerome, in the *Epistle to Paula on the Interpretation of the Hebrew Alphabet*: “No one, as the blessed Cyprian says, is sufficiently safe when near danger.” The same author, in the *Epistle on Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*: “It is safer to have been able to perish than not to have perished beside danger.”

**So that they may be separated.** I do not know how it happened that these words, and those that follow—“afterward, when they have adhered through a most grievous bond of conscience”—were omitted in Rigault’s edition, although they appear in all the earlier editions and in all our ancient manuscripts, as well as in six English manuscripts. It is all the more remarkable that the English editors also omitted that part in their edition. The ancient manuscripts of Saint-Remi and Fux have: “They have adhered through the glue of conscience.” Jerome, in the *Epistle on Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*: “If I thought that you had adhered through the glue of sins.”

**Without any public tale.** That is, without the matter being widely circulated, as Varro says in Book V of *The Latin Language*. Horace, Satire I:

> Change the name, and the tale  
> Is told of you.

[Col. 0366D]

Petronius, in the *Story of the Matron of Ephesus*: “Thus there was but one tale throughout the whole city.” Apuleius, *Apology*: “A woman of sacred chastity, after so many years of widowhood, without blame, without scandalous report.” Ovid, Book II of the *Tristia*:

> So that no tale may ever tarnish your name.

Book IV, Elegy 10:

> No tale was ever attached to my name.

Book III of the *Amores*, Elegy 1:

> You are a tale spread throughout the whole city, yet do not perceive it.

Book II of *The Art of Love*:

> Whichever woman you touch will become the subject of a shameful tale.

I could produce many similar examples, but these will suffice.

**It is better that they marry.** Protestants seize from this an opportunity to declaim against vows. But if it follows from Cyprian’s words that marriages of virgins were once tolerated in certain churches, it by no means follows that they were approved. For Saint Augustine, who says of certain virgins, “It would be better for them to marry than to burn,” in *On Virginity*, ch. 34, proves from the Scriptures that for virgins not only to enter into marriage, but even to wish to marry although they do not do so, is condemnable, in *On the Good of Widowhood*, ch. 9. But the words of the holy Doctor should be quoted:

“Many of them,” he says in *On Virginity*, ch. 34, “are restrained from marrying not by love of their noble resolve, but by fear of manifest disgrace—a fear itself arising from pride, by which they dread displeasing human beings more than displeasing God. Therefore, those who wish to marry, and do not marry for the reason that they cannot do so with impunity—those for whom it would be better to marry than to burn, that is, than to be ravaged in their very conscience by the hidden flame of concupiscence; those who regret their profession and are ashamed of their confession—unless they direct their corrected heart aright and once more conquer lust through fear of God, must be counted among the dead.”

And in *On the Good of Widowhood*, ch. IX:

“For if chastity is preserved within the marital bond, damnation is not feared; but in the continence of widowhood and virginity, the excellence of a greater gift is sought. Once that excellence has been sought and chosen and offered under the obligation of a vow, it is now condemnable not only to enter into marriage, but even to wish to marry although one does not do so. For to demonstrate this, the Apostle did not say, ‘After living in indulgence against Christ, they marry,’ but ‘they wish to marry,’ saying that they ‘have condemnation because they have made void their first faith’—even if they do not marry but only wish to do so. It is not that marriage itself, even for such women, is judged condemnable; rather, the deceit against their resolve is condemned, the broken faith of their vow is condemned, not their undertaking of a lesser good, but their fall from a higher good. In short, such women are condemned not because they later entered into the marriage covenant, but because they made void their first pledge of continence” (1 Tim. 5:11–12).

How inviolable Cyprian believed vows to be can be perceived from this very letter, from Epistle LX, and from the book *On the Dress of Virgins*. He declares that corrupted virgins are adulteresses not against a husband but against Christ, pp. 103 and 172. Hence he judged that so severe a penance should be imposed upon them. He teaches that they have dedicated themselves to Christ and vowed themselves to God in both flesh and mind, p. 174, and that their members have been dedicated to Christ and devoted forever in chaste virtue to the honor of continence, p. 100.]

### II

Therefore, in the first place, dearest brother, both the presiding clergy [Col. 0365B] and the people must labor for nothing else than this: that we who fear God should keep His divine precepts with complete observance of discipline. We must not permit our brethren to go astray and live according to their own choice and belching, but must faithfully provide for the life of each individual. Nor must we permit virgins to live with males—I do not say to sleep together, but not even to live together—since both the weaker sex [Col. 0366A] and an age still prone to slipping must be restrained and governed by us in every respect, lest an opportunity to inflict harm be given to the devil who lies in wait and desires to rage, since the Apostle also says: “Give no place to the devil” (Eph. 4:27).

A ship must be vigilantly freed from dangerous places lest it be shattered among reefs and rocks. A burden must quickly be removed from the fire before the advancing flames consume it. No one is safe for long [Note: [Col. 0366B] “long-lasting”: Bodleian 1.] when near danger; nor will a servant of God who has entangled himself in the devil’s snares be able to escape the devil [Note: [Col. 0366B] “the hands of the devil”: Lincoln, NC 2.]. We must quickly intervene with such persons so that they may be separated while they can still be separated in innocence, because afterward our intervention will not be able to divide them once they have become joined in most grievous guilt. In short, we see what grievous falls of many people arise from this, and with the deepest sorrow of our soul we behold very many virgins being corrupted through such [Col. 0366B] illicit and dangerous unions.

But if they have in faith dedicated themselves to Christ, let them persevere chastely [Note: [Col. 0366B] “If chastely”: Bodleian 2.] and purely, without any public scandal, and thus, being strong and steadfast, await the reward of virginity. If, however, they are unwilling or unable to persevere, it is better that they marry than that through their sins [Col. 0367A] [Note: [Col. 0367A] “as punishment for their sins”: Lambeth, York, NC 1.] they fall into the fire. Certainly, they must cause no stumbling block to their brothers or sisters, since it is written: “If food causes my brother to stumble, I will not eat flesh forever [Note: [Col. 0367A] “for eternity”: Lambeth, York, Bodleian 2, Lincoln.], lest I cause my brother to stumble” (1 Cor. 8:13).

[Note: [Col. 0367D]

**III.—The eyes are often deceived.** Thus the early editions, seven of our ancient copies, and two English copies. Two other copies of ours and likewise two English copies have: “it often deceives the eyes.” Six other copies of ours and the Manutius edition have: “the eye is often deceived.” The familiar saying is: “Forehead, eyes, and expression very often lie.”

**She may be a woman.** The designation *mulier* (“woman”) is general and signifies females universally, whether they have or have not experienced sexual intercourse—that is, virgins as well. Hence Jerome’s remark in the *Epistle on Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*: “Women quickly grow old, especially those who are near men.” Ovid pertinently says on this subject in Book III of *The Art of Love*:

> Add that childbirth also makes the years of youth shorter—
Times. Nevertheless, the word *mulier* (“woman”) is often used only of those who have had experience of men, as here and in Tertullian, [Col. 0368A] in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. Quintilian, Book VI, chapter 1, reports that Cicero, when certain persons reproached him because at the age of sixty he had married the virgin Popilia, replied: “Tomorrow she will be a woman.” Ulpian, in the book *Alioquin*, *Digest*, *On Contracting a Sale*, says: “What if I [Col. 0368B] thought I was buying a virgin, when she was a woman? The sale will be valid, for no mistake was made concerning her sex.” Lactantius, Book I, chapter 17: “If she was a virgin at first, she was afterward a woman.” Jerome, in his book *Against Helvidius*, in the first book *Against Jovinian*, and in the Letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*, cites the passage of the Apostle Paul from the seventh chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, where, instead of what is written in the Vulgate edition, “the unmarried woman and the virgin,” the old translator rendered it: “The virgin and the woman are divided.” Tertullian likewise cites this passage from that old version in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*. From this it is evident that this old translator called one who is not a virgin a *mulier*. Saint Ambrose—or whoever else was the author—in Book III of *On Duties*, chapter 8, understood the term in the same way when he wrote that their women and children would be exposed to plunder. Optatus of Milevis, Book II: “Returning from there, Urbanus of Forma and Felix 474 of Idicra found the mothers whom they had made women from among the consecrated virgins.” Hence Catullus’s “new woman” in his poem on Attis. M. [Col. 0368C] Cato, in Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 6, used these words when advocating the Lex Voconia: “To begin with, a woman has brought you a large dowry.” Jeremiah, chapter XV: “They humbled women in Zion and virgins in the cities of Judah.” Even now, we Limousins call a female who is married *Moulier*, the word plainly being derived from the Latin term *mollier*, which Varro, as quoted by Lactantius in chapter 12 of *On the Workmanship of God*, says was so called from softness (*mollities*). The Italians say *moglie*. See vol. II of the *Capitularies*, p. 796.

**Could be corrupted.** Thus read all the editions and almost all our old manuscripts, as well as three English ones. Three, however, have “could be violated.” Rigaltius was the first to introduce that expression into Cyprian’s text. That our emendation is sound can also be gathered from the fact that a little earlier in this letter it is written that “very many virgins are corrupted.”

**Kissing together (*inosculatio*).** This is the reading of the old editions and of seven manuscripts, and I believe it to be sound, although, [Col. 0368D] so far as I know, the ancient Latin writers do not recognize it. For *inosculatio* can be formed in the same way as we see that the ancients called *inoculatio* a kind of grafting performed by budding, when the eye of one tree is applied to another, or an eye is opened in a tree, as may be seen in Pliny and Columella. Thus *inosculatio* is the application of kiss to kiss. Manutius and those who followed him afterward printed *osculatio* (“kissing”). I found that reading in seven old books. Jerome, Book I *Against Rufinus*: “In accordance with the idiom of their language, the Hebrews use *deosculatio* for veneration.” Here, then, in Jerome is a word as rare in Latin as *inosculatio*.

**If a husband should come upon them.** In Xenophon, Book V of the *Education of Cyrus*: “If anyone were to indulge your wife in such a way as to make her more friendly to him than to you, would that service make you glad?” See what Venantius of Timisa said on a similar subject in Saint Cyprian’s Council of Carthage, p. 335.

[Col. 0369B] **The anguish of jealousy.** Thus read all the old books and all the editions. Rigaltius printed “the lividity of jealousy,” and the English editors retained that reading, although they acknowledge that “anguish” is read in eight ancient manuscripts. I nevertheless note that the Verona and Foix manuscripts have “lividity.” Rigaltius therefore took it from there.

**The superiors and deacons.** Cyprian commonly applies the term “superiors” to bishops. Here, however, he seems to be speaking of presbyters, joining them with deacons. This is clearer below, Letter LXV, p. 113: [Col. 0369C] “Deacons ought, moreover, to remember that the Lord chose the Apostles—that is, bishops and superiors.” Certainly the presbyters governed the Church together with the bishop. Cyprian is a witness to this, for he did nothing of any importance unless the presbyterate had been convened. The Roman clergy speak of themselves in this way, p. 7: “And since it falls to us, who appear to be the superiors and to guard the flock in the shepherd’s stead.” Celerinus likewise speaks in this way concerning the Roman clergy: “When their case had now been heard, the superiors ordered that they remain thus for the time being, until a bishop should be appointed.” Cyprian, in Letter XI, which is addressed to the Martyrs and Confessors, designates his own clergy by the same word. “But it is the duty of the superiors,” he says, “to uphold the commandment and to instruct those who are either too hasty or ignorant, lest those who ought to be shepherds of the sheep become butchers.” Presbyters are also called priests by Cyprian, as when he says in Letter XXXV, p. 49, that Numidicus remained alive so that the Lord might add him to the clergy of Carthage and adorn the company left desolate by the lapse of certain presbyters with glorious priests. See Letter XL, [Col. 0369D] p. 53.]

### III

Nor should any woman suppose that she can be defended by the excuse [Note: [Col. 0368A] “Can” is absent from the Oxford manuscript.] that she can be examined and tested to determine whether she is a virgin, since both the hands of midwives and their eyes are often deceived; [Col. 0368A] and even if the virgin is found intact in that part of herself by which she can become a woman, 103 she may nevertheless have sinned with another part of the body that can be corrupted and yet cannot be inspected. Certainly the very lying together, the very embrace, the very conversation and mutual kissing, and the shameful and foul sleeping of two persons lying together—how much disgrace and guilt this attests to! If a husband, arriving unexpectedly, should see his betrothed [Col. 0369A] lying with another man, does he not become indignant and rage, and perhaps, through the anguish of jealousy, even take a sword in his hand? How indignant and angry, then, is Christ, our Lord and Judge, when he sees his virgin, dedicated to him and destined for his holiness, lying with another man; and what punishments does he threaten against such incestuous unions! In order that each of the brethren may escape his spiritual sword and the coming day of judgment, we must take every precaution and labor with every counsel. And although it is altogether necessary for everyone to maintain discipline, it is much more right that the superiors and deacons should attend to this, since they must furnish the rest with an example and lesson through their conduct and morals. For how can they preside over integrity and continence if corruptions and [Col. 0369B] instruction in vice begin to proceed from themselves?

[Note: [Col. 0369D]

### IV.—The deacon who was with a virgin

See Jerome’s letter to Sabinianus the deacon.

**Let them meanwhile be examined.** This is also the reading in Ivo, part VII, chapter 128. But in Gratian, XXVII, question 1, chapter *What if Penance*, “again” is read. The gloss, however, notes that elsewhere “meanwhile” is read, which is the true reading.
