**Let the virgins be examined.** Since everything pertaining to virgins ought to be chaste and modest, I am astonished that the ancients sometimes adopted the view that they should order them to be examined by midwives, so that it could be learned whether they were virgins, as Saint Cyprian did. Indeed, boldness formerly went so far that, according to Clement of Alexandria in the seventh book of the *Stromata*, certain persons said that after the Virgin Mary had given birth she was examined by midwives and found to be a virgin. Matthaeus [Col. 0370B] Bossus vehemently flares up against this tale in Book I, Letter LXXVII, to Polycletus. Nevertheless, it can easily be proved that this custom was retained for a long time in the Church of God. Saint Ambrose, in his Letter to Bishop Syagrius, relates the story of Indicia, a virgin of Verona. When she had been accused of immodesty, 475 and Syagrius wished her to be examined and inspected by midwives, his demand was rejected, since it had been proved by reliable testimony that she was a virgin of unimpaired profession. Saint Augustine, Book III of *The City of God*, chapter 18: “A midwife, while examining, as it were, the integrity of a certain virgin [Col. 0370C] with her hand, whether through malice, ignorance, or accident, destroyed it in the course of the examination.” For the examination itself also often produces a false finding, as Quintilian says, Book V, chapter 6. Rigaltius was therefore right to say, on this passage of Saint Cyprian, that the examination of virgins is a disgraceful business and that virginity is slain between the hands of midwives. For the midwife’s art is very obscure and uncertain in these matters; and Laurentius Joubertus, Book V of *Popular Errors*, chapter 4, contends that nothing certain can be established by inspecting that part by which a virgin can become a woman. Victor of Vita, Book II, chapter 7, speaking of the persecution under Huneric, king of the Vandals: “He then ordered the consecrated virgins to be assembled, sending Vandals with midwives of their own nation to inspect and handle, contrary to the laws of modesty, the modest organs of chastity.” See Matthaeus Bossus in the Letter to Polycletus cited shortly above. See also the chapter *You Have Proposed*, under the title *On Proofs* in the *Decretals*.

**Under the same roof.** Jerome, in his Letter *On Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*: “Let your houses be separate [Col. 0370D] and your meals divided, lest malicious people, seeing you remain under one roof, accuse you of also sharing a bed.”

**Have lived.** The Foix manuscript reads: “have wished to live.”

**Such women should afterward readily.** Thus read eight of our old books, five English manuscripts, and the old editions. The word “such” is absent from six other ancient manuscripts. The greater part of the old manuscripts and editions persuaded us to restore it.

**Any one of them is found corrupted.** The old editions and six old manuscripts have: “any of them are found corrupted.” The old Reims and Foix manuscripts have: “any of them are found contumacious.” The Pithou manuscript likewise reads so. But in that manuscript the word “corrupted” is written above “contumacious” by way of emendation. The reading that has “contumacious” can be supported by what follows a little later: “the proud and contumacious are slain.”

[Col. 0371C] **Wholesome precepts.** The old editions and two old books prefer “saving counsels.” But all the other books have “precepts.” After the word “wholesome,” nothing further from this letter appears in the manuscript of Saint Arnulf; and in place of what is missing there are appended consecutively two fragments of other letters, namely one from Letter LXIV, to Epictetus, and another from Letter LXXI, to Stephen, extending to the end.]

### IV

And therefore you acted prudently and vigorously, dearest brother, by excluding the deacon who frequently remained with a virgin, as well as the others who had been accustomed to sleep with virgins. But if they have done penance for this unlawful lying together [Col. 0370A] and have withdrawn from one another, let the virgins meanwhile be carefully examined by midwives; and if they are found to be virgins, let them receive communion and be admitted to the Church, yet with this warning: if they afterward return to those same men, or if they live together with them in one house and under the same roof, they are to be expelled under a more severe sentence, nor afterward are such women readily to be received into the Church. But if any one of them is found corrupted, let her perform full penance, because a woman who has committed this crime is an adulteress not against a husband but against Christ; and therefore, after a just period has been assessed, let her make public confession (*exomologesis*) and return to the Church. But if they obstinately persist and do not separate from one another, let them know that with this immodest obstinacy of theirs they can never [Col. 0370B] be admitted by us into the Church, lest through their sins they begin to provide the rest with an example leading to ruin. Nor should they suppose that any reckoning of life or salvation remains secure for them if they refuse to obey the bishops and priests, since in Deuteronomy the Lord God says: [Col. 0371A] “And whatever man acts presumptuously, so as not to heed the priest or whatever judge shall be in those days, that man shall die; and all the people, when they hear of it, shall be afraid and shall not act impiously any longer” (Deut. XVII, 12–13). God ordered those who did not obey his priests and who refused obedience to judges appointed by him for the time to be killed [Note: [Col. 0371C] Bod. 1: “Thus he appointed the time of his judgment for the disobedient, and …” [reading corrupt].]. And at that time they were indeed slain with the sword, when circumcision of the flesh still remained. But now, because spiritual circumcision has begun to exist among God’s faithful servants, the proud and contumacious are slain with the spiritual sword when they are cast out of the Church. For they cannot live outside it, since the house of God is one and salvation can belong to no one except in the Church. That the undisciplined perish when they neither listen to nor obey wholesome precepts is attested by divine Scripture [Col. 0371B], which says: “The undisciplined man does not love the one who corrects him. But those who hate reproofs shall be shamefully consumed” (Prov. XV, 12, 10).

[Note: [Col. 0371C]

### V.—We enter

Rigaltius printed “we walk,” evidently from the Verona manuscript, with which the Foix manuscript also agrees. The old Reims manuscript has “he walks.” The true reading, which we have restored, is presented by all [Col. 0371D] the other old manuscripts, seven English manuscripts, and all editions earlier than that of Rigaltius. Reinhartus therefore did rightly in retaining the reading of the old editions. The English editors preferred “we walk.”

**We have gained the brethren.** I found these words in only three ancient manuscripts. The others—that is, fourteen of ours and seven English manuscripts—have approximately the following: “It is most welcome to us. We have likewise instructed them by our discourse to stand firm unto salvation.” It is difficult to determine among these readings what Cyprian wrote. If conjecture is permissible, I would suppose that the text should be read as in the old books and editions: “But if they obey, it is most welcome to us. We have formed them, standing firm, for salvation likewise by the condescension of our discourse.”

**Christ the Lord.** Seven old manuscripts prefer this reading. Eight others and four English manuscripts have: “Let us please Christ the Lord and our God by keeping his precepts.”]

### V

Therefore, lest the undisciplined be consumed and perish, take pains, dearest brother, insofar as you can, to govern the brotherhood with saving counsels [Note: [Col. 0371C] “Wholesome” in Lam., Ebor.] and to counsel each individual for his salvation. Narrow and constricted is the way by which we enter into life, but supreme and great is the fruit when 104 we arrive at glory [Note: [Col. 0372C] “The fruit of one arriving at glory,” Bod. 1.]. Those who have once made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven should please God in all things, and should not offend the priests of God or the Church of the Lord by the scandal of their depravity [Note: [Col. 0372C] “Should not offer themselves as a scandal to the brethren,” Lam., Bod. 2, NC. 1.]. [Col. 0372A] And although at present some of our brethren appear to be saddened by us, let us nevertheless remain steadfast in wholesome persuasion, knowing that the Apostle too said: “Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (Gal. IV, 16). But if they obey us, we have gained the brethren, and by our discourse have formed them alike for salvation and dignity. If, however, some of the perverse refuse to obey, let us follow the same Apostle when he says: “If I pleased men, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. I, 10). If we cannot persuade some so as to cause them to please Christ, let us at least, for our part, please Christ the Lord and our God by keeping his precepts. I wish you, dearest and most greatly longed-for brother, good health in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0371D]

**LETTER LXIII.**—Saint Augustine cites this letter and quotes a large fragment from it in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21. And just as he had said that Cyprian’s Letter to Donatus was adorned with a florid circumlocution of words, so he says that this one was written [Col. 0372C] in a subdued style. Goulartius, on the contrary, thinks that Cyprian was vehement here.]

# LETTER LXIII

*(Erasm., II, 3; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXIII; Paris., LXII; Oxon., Lips., LXIII.)*

## TO CAECILIUS, ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE LORD’S CUP

[Col. 0372B]

**SUMMARY.—**Against the Aquarians, Cyprian teaches that not water alone, but wine mixed with water, must be offered in the Lord’s cup; that in the Scriptures water signifies Baptism, but by no means the Eucharist. By types drawn from the Old Testament, the use of wine in the sacrament of the Lord’s body is illustrated, and it is declared that the Christian people are signified by the symbol of water.

[Note: [Col. 0372C]

### I.—To Caecilius

Although what I am about to say may appear to some to be of little importance, I shall nevertheless say it. After Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was published, there were those who debated 476 whether the name Caecilius should be written with or without a diphthong. I, however, say that very many old manuscripts of Saint Cyprian’s works—including the Séguier manuscript, the oldest of all ours—many ancient inscriptions, and old coins have the diphthong. Nevertheless, relying upon the support of this recent controversy, the most illustrious man [Col. 0372D] who lately furnished a new edition of this book of Lactantius wrote that author’s name without the diphthong, because he saw it written thus in the old manuscript from which that book was brought before the public. He failed to observe that old scribes frequently committed many orthographic errors, and that such errors also occur in ancient inscriptions and coins. That excellent man also contends—to mention this as well—that the book is not Lactantius’s, because Lactantius’s name does not appear in the old manuscript. It was evidently omitted by a hurried scribe who, as Sirmond, a man highly expert in such matters, said in a similar case, did not wish, for brevity’s sake, to copy all the author’s names and therefore ignorantly selected, in place of the last name, which was the proper one, the name that occurred first. When that new editor did not find in Sirmond’s edition of Sidonius this observation of that celebrated scholar, which I had employed, he wished to cast suspicion upon my good faith, as if I had falsely invoked Sirmond’s authority to prove what I had undertaken to prove. He undoubtedly would not have done so had he read Sirmond’s brief preface concerning the proper names of the Middle Ages, published at the beginning of his notes on Sidonius. I wish, moreover, that the most learned [Col. 0373B] and excellent Christoph Matthäus Pfaff had not written in the preface to his edition of Lactantius’s *Epitome* that no ancient manuscript of Lactantius’s works has the name Lucius Caecilius. For long before that edition of the *Epitome* appeared, I had noted that two very ancient manuscripts existed here in Paris in the royal library, in one of which he is called Lucius Caecilius, and in the other Lucius Caelius—which comes to the same thing.

**To the brother Caecilius.** A bishop, as I believe, of Bilta in the Proconsular province. For a Caecilius of Bilta is found to have attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Another Caecilius was the presbyter who corrected Cyprian’s secular error and brought him [Col. 0373C] to acknowledgment of the true divinity. For it is clear from the book that Pontius the deacon wrote *On the Life of Cyprian* that this man departed from life before Cyprian, commending his wife and children to Cyprian as he left this world. Baronius reverses this story, saying, through a misuse of Pontius’s testimony, that Cyprian, when he embraced the religion of Christ, commended his dearest wife and most beloved children to the presbyter Caecilius. The same Baronius believed that this presbyter had at one time been the teacher of the emperor Diadumenian. But the most learned Pearson showed in his *Cyprianic Annals* that this opinion could not be true.

**These letters to you.** Better, in my opinion, is the reading in the Bec manuscript: “about this to you.” I had not yet seen this book when this letter was printed.

**Our own and human.** The Séguier manuscript prefers this reading. The Chartres manuscript and Morellius’s edition read: “our own and human mind.” The Foix manuscript [Col. 0373D] reads: “with this human mind,” omitting “our own and,” which are also absent from the Corbie and Tours manuscripts. The Bec manuscript reads: “our own and human conscience.” The two Bodleian manuscripts read: “human and novel institution.” See Rigaltius’s observations.

**Is held.** I would not have recorded the variant readings of this passage found in ancient manuscripts had Rigaltius not noted that in certain old books he had read “is darkened,” which he preferred to the commonly received reading. He found it in the margin of the Manutius edition, where a certain scholar recorded variant readings from Italian manuscripts and noted that “is darkened” was written in two Vatican manuscripts. But although I have collated so many old manuscripts with Cyprian’s works, I found “is darkened” in only two. All the others have “is held,” “was held,” “was being held,” or “are held.” For the rest, I think Rigaltius’s view can please no one. Cicero said in his *Speech on His Consulship*: “I know not what error holds me.” And in the *Speech for Marcellus*: [Col. 0374B] “Even if I am held by some fault of human error.” Ovid, Book III of the *Metamorphoses*:

> So great an error holds the lover.

Virgil, Book X of the *Aeneid*, said “to be held by a grievous error.”

**When anything.** This fragment is quoted by Pope Paschal II in his Letter to Pontius, Abbot of Cluny, which is published in the volumes of the *Councils*.

**Inspiring.** Thus read the old editions. I have found nowhere else the word “breathing upon,” which Rigaltius substituted. Although the English editors saw “inspiring” written in their ancient manuscripts, they retained Rigaltius’s text. Reinhartus rejected it. It appears in the letter of Pope Paschal.]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Caecilius, greetings. Although I know, dearest brother, that very many bishops, set by divine favor over the Lord’s churches throughout the whole world, maintain the rule of evangelical truth and the Lord’s tradition and do not depart, through a human and novel institution [Note: [Col. 0373B] “A human and novel institution,” Bod. 3, 4.], from what Christ the Master both commanded and performed; nevertheless, because certain persons, whether through ignorance or simplicity, in consecrating the Lord’s cup and ministering it to the people do not do what Jesus Christ our Lord and God, the author and teacher of this sacrifice, did and taught, I have considered it both a religious duty and a necessity to address these [Note: [Col. 0373B] “I have considered it necessary to address you concerning this,” Lam., NC. 1, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] letters to you, so that if anyone is still held [Note: [Col. 0374B] “Is darkened,” NC. 2, Vat.] in this error, then, once he has beheld the light of truth, [Col. 0374A] he may return to the root and origin of the Lord’s tradition. Nor should you suppose, dearest brother, that we are writing things of our own and human devising, or that we are boldly assuming this responsibility by our spontaneous will, since we always preserve our modest station with humble and restrained moderation. But when anything is commanded by God’s inspiration and ordinance, the faithful servant must obey the Lord; he is excused before everyone from the charge of arrogantly assuming anything for himself, because he is compelled to fear offending the Lord if he does not do what he is commanded.

[Note: [Col. 0374C]

477 ### II.—Commemoration

Thus read the old editions earlier than the Manutius edition, six of our old books, five English manuscripts, and also Rabanus, Book I of *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, chapter 31, where he quotes this passage of Cyprian. Rightly so, in my opinion. For in chapter XXII of the Gospel according to Matthew and in chapter XI of the First Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians, Christ, when instituting the sacrament of the Eucharist, is reported to have said to his disciples: “Do this in commemoration of me.” It must not, however, be concealed that Manutius’s reading, namely “in commemoration,” is found in eight old books. Pamelius and Reinhartus printed the accusative *commemorationem*; Rigaltius, the ablative *commemoratione*. Yet the same Rigaltius, at the end of this letter where these words are repeated, twice wrote the accusative *commemorationem*. The English editors retained Rigaltius’s reading.

**Should be offered mixed with wine.** The Third Council of Carthage, canon 24: “In the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, let nothing more be offered than the Lord handed down, [Col. 0374D] namely bread and wine mixed with water.” The wine, however, ought to be present in a greater quantity than the water, as Richard, Archbishop of Armagh, also writes in Book IX, chapter 9, of *Questions Concerning the Armenians*. Consequently, since the contrary practice once prevailed in the Kingdom of Sweden, Pope Honorius III, writing to the Archbishop of Uppsala, prohibited its being done thereafter, saying that it was very pernicious. His constitution on this matter appears in the books of the *Decretals* and in the fifth compilation. See Emmanuel Gonzalez’s commentary on the title *On the Celebration of Masses* in the *Decretals*. A remarkable synodal constitution of Diego Escolano, Bishop of Majorca, published in 1659, reads as follows: “Since the most sacred sacrifice of the altar, in which the source of all sanctity and purity is contained, is performed with less propriety when red wine is consecrated, because the cleanliness of the altar can scarcely be preserved in this way, we therefore exhort all the presbyters of this diocese to use white wine hereafter in the celebration of Masses.”

[Col. 0375B] **Christ’s blood is not water.** Pope Innocent VIII had doubtless not read this passage of Cyprian when he permitted the Norwegians to celebrate the sacrifice of the Mass without wine. Raphael of Volterra, Book VII, p. 159, testifies that he granted this to them: “By a concession of Pope Innocent VIII, Norway was permitted to offer the sacrifice of the cup [Col. 0375C] without wine, because, on account of the immense cold, wine imported into that region turns sour. An embassy was sent for the sake of this matter.” In an old manuscript missal of the Church of Saint Martin of Tours, I read the following: “If through negligence it should happen that, after the canon has been read and the consecration performed, neither wine nor water is found in the cup, both must immediately be poured in, and the priest shall repeat the consecration from that place in the canon, namely, ‘In like manner, after he had supped,’ to the end, yet in such a way that he omits those two crosses that he made separately over the bread. But if the consecration is performed with wine alone, or with water without wine, the wine is reckoned as the sacrament, but the water is not so reckoned. And therefore this negligence concerning water is greater and must be corrected by a greater penance.” The Armenians, as Guido of Perpignan reports, said that water was not to be mixed with wine in the sacrament of the altar, and that if water was added, there was no sacrament. Pope Eugenius IV refuted this error of theirs, as reported by Odoricus Raynaldus under the year 1439, § 15. Giovanni Battista Casali also shows that in antiquity certain persons used milk instead of wine in the sacrifice of the Mass, [Col. 0375D] in his work *On the Ancient Sacred Rites of Christians*, chapter 11, where he treats the use of the cup. See also the Letter of John, Deacon of the Holy Roman Church, to Senarius, chapter 12, in volume I of Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum*, p. 75, and Cotelerius’s notes on Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 8.

**Made alive.** One royal manuscript and the editions of Rabanus have “justified.” But two manuscripts in the royal and Colbert libraries containing Rabanus’s books *On the Instruction of the Clergy* prefer “made alive.” And this is the true reading.]

### II

Know, moreover, that we have been admonished [Note: [Col. 0374B] “You should know,” Augustine.] that in offering the cup the Lord’s tradition is to be observed, and that nothing else is to be done by us than what the Lord first did for us: namely, that the cup offered in commemoration of him should be offered mixed with wine. For since Christ says, “I [Col. 0375A] am the true vine” (John XV, 1), Christ’s blood is certainly not water, but wine. Nor can his blood, by which we have been redeemed and made alive, appear to be in the cup when the cup lacks wine, by which Christ’s blood is manifested—the blood proclaimed by the sacramental meaning and testimony of all the Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0375B] “Which is proclaimed as poured out by the testimony of all the Scriptures,” Oxford.].

[Note: [Col. 0375D]

### III.—Reclining

Thus read the old editions, most of the old books, and Reinhartus’s edition. Pamelius wrote “reclining at table,” drawing his authority, as I believe, from Rabanus. For he cites no old book from which he took this reading. Rigaltius found it in the Corbie manuscript. Certainly the reading of Pamelius, taken, as I have said, from Rabanus, appears in manuscript 4064 of the [Col. 0376B] royal library and manuscript 584 of the Colbert library, in which this book of Rabanus is found. But manuscript 4063 of the same royal library, and two very ancient and excellent Colbert manuscripts in which the same book appears, prefer “reclining.”

**Exposed.** Thus read the old editions and most of the old books. [Col. 0376C] One royal manuscript, one English manuscript, the Grenoble manuscript, the Foix manuscript, two cited by Pamelius, and Saint Augustine read “uncovered”; in the ninth chapter of Genesis and in Rabanus, “made naked”—that is, disclosed or revealed. In the old manuscripts of Rabanus, however, “marked” is written. Jerome, in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*: “The elder son mocked his naked father, and the younger covered him.” Tertullian, in his book *On the Dress of Women*: “Goodness does not love darkness; it rejoices to be seen and exults even in its own exposures”—that is, manifestations, as Pamelius rightly interprets it. Cassian, *Conference* 12, chapter 9: “If any parts should perhaps have been uncovered somewhat immodestly,” 478 that is, exposed. Thus here the words “exposed” and “uncovered” have the same meaning. Tertullian uses the term in another sense in Book I *To the Nations*, chapter 10; see Gothofredus’s notes there.]

### III

For we find that in Genesis this same thing occurred beforehand in connection with the sacramental mystery in Noah, and that a figure of the Lord’s passion existed there: he drank wine; he became drunk (Gen. IX, 21); he was uncovered in his house; he lay reclining with his thighs naked and exposed; the nakedness of the father was exposed by the middle son and reported outside, but covered by the other two, the elder and the younger; and the other details, which there is no need to pursue. It is enough to embrace this one point: 105 Noah, exhibiting a type of the truth to come, [Col. 0375B] drank not water but wine, and thus expressed an image of the Lord’s passion.

[Note: [Col. 0376C]

### IV.—I have begotten you

In the old editions and in five ancient manuscripts, there follows: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent.” But these words are absent from [Col. 0376D] the other ancient manuscripts, including the Verona and Séguier manuscripts, and from Rabanus. They are nevertheless present in Psalm CIX, from which this passage was taken, and in Book I of the *Testimonies*, chapter 17. Manutius deleted them, Morellius restored them, and Pamelius rejected them. The later editions followed that of Pamelius. Certainly, without that addition, which appears superfluous, the meaning is properly coherent. The Letter to Demetrias published among Jerome’s works, which certain learned men believe to be by Pelagius, says: “Melchizedek is described as a priest of God. His merit can readily be understood from the fact that he prefigured the Lord’s sacrament, which was to come much later, and by the sacrifice of bread and wine expressed the mystery of the body and blood and, by the type of his priesthood, represented the sacrament of Christ.” Alcuin cites this passage of Cyprian in his Letter to Charlemagne, published in the first book of our *Miscellanies*. On the temporal priesthood of Christ, moreover, see Matthaeus Bossus, Book I, Letter 77, to Polycletus.

[Col. 0377C] **Foreseeing, moreover.** The old editions and five old books have “foreseeing beforehand.” Either reading is good.

**Have been blessed.** The old editions and certain old books prefer “will be blessed.” But the commonly received reading, which is also ours, is confirmed by the editions of Manutius, Morellius, and Pamelius, and also by thirteen old manuscripts.

**The fullness of truth.** Thus we have restored the text on the authority of three old manuscripts, in which it is written as follows: “The fullness of truth fulfilled the truth of the prefigured image.” Cyprian, Letter 74, p. 171: “Custom without truth is the antiquity of error. Therefore, having abandoned error, let us follow truth”; and a little later: “Christ, showing us this truth, said in his Gospel: [Col. 0377D] ‘I am the truth.’” This passage is cited in Gratian, distinction 8, from Gregory’s Letter to Wimund, Bishop of Aversa, as is another from the Letter to Pompeius. See our notes on Gratian, p. 443. I now return to the path. Tertullian, in his book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “Our Lord Christ called himself truth, not custom.” The Foix manuscript confirms this emendation of ours, for it reads: “He who is the fullness of truth fulfilled the prefigured image.” There the word “truth,” which the other manuscripts have, has fallen out. That this error is ancient can be gathered from the fact that when certain scribes copying the works of Saint Cyprian read “of the prefigured image” and saw that the sentence was not complete, they added the word “reality,” thus writing: “the fullness of truth fulfilled the reality of the prefigured image.” For so it is written in three ancient manuscripts. They appear to have been moved to add this word because a little earlier one reads: “which reality the Lord perfected and fulfilled.”]

IV. Likewise, in the priest Melchizedek we see prefigured the sacrament of the Lord’s sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0375B] Augustine: “The mystery of the Lord’s sacrament was prefigured.” [Col. 0376B]], in accordance with the testimony and declaration of divine Scripture: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine” (Gen. 14:18). He was, moreover, a priest of the Most High God, and he blessed Abraham. That Melchizedek bore the type of Christ is declared in the Psalms by the Holy Spirit, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son: “Before the morning star I begot you. You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4–5). This order, of course, is the one deriving from that sacrifice and descending from it: that Melchizedek was a priest of the Most High God, that he offered bread and wine, and that he blessed Abraham. For who is more truly a priest of the Most High God than our Lord Jesus Christ, who offered a sacrifice to God the Father and offered precisely what Melchizedek had offered—that is, bread and wine, namely his own body and blood?

And that earlier blessing concerning Abraham [Col. 0376B] pertained to our people. For if Abraham believed God and it was reckoned [Note: [Col. 0376B] “Accounted,” NC. 1, 2; Ebor.] to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:6), then surely whoever believes God and lives by faith is found righteous, and is shown already long ago to have been blessed and justified in faithful Abraham, [Col. 0377A] just as the blessed apostle Paul proves when he says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned [Note: [Col. 0377C] “Accounted,” NC. 1, 2; Ebor.] to him as righteousness” (Gal. 3:6–7). “You know, therefore, that those who are of faith are the children of Abraham. And Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham that all nations would be blessed in him” (Gen. 12:3). Therefore, those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham. Hence in the Gospel we find that children of Abraham are raised up from stones—that is, gathered from the nations (Matt. 3:9). And when the Lord commended Zacchaeus, he answered and said: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:9).

Therefore, so that in Genesis the blessing concerning Abraham might duly be celebrated through the priest Melchizedek, the image of Christ’s sacrifice, [Col. 0377B] consisting namely in bread and wine, came first [Note: [Col. 0377C] “Of the sacrifice in bread,” Bod. 1, 2, 3; NC. 1, 2; Lin.; Ebor.]. Bringing this reality to completion and fulfillment, the Lord offered bread and a cup mixed with wine; and he who is the fullness of truth fulfilled the truth of the prefiguring image.

[Note: [Col. 0378C]

V.—“Showing beforehand the sacrificed.” The old manuscript of Saint-Remi reads: “Christ announcing beforehand that he would sacrifice.”

“Set beneath.” To conceal nothing, I would readily have changed this reading and preferred the one I found in the manuscript of Saint Eligius at Arras, where “he hewed out” is read. This is also how it is written in the ninth chapter of Proverbs. For the word “set beneath” does not signify what Solomon intended to say. Yet I did not dare alter it against the authority of so many old books and editions, especially since I see “set beneath” written in Book III of the *Testimonies*, and because Prosper—or whoever else wrote Book II of *The Promises and Predictions of God*, chapter 2—also reads it in this way. Saint Augustine, in Book VII of *The City of God*, chapter 20, reads “supported,” and in chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Galatians, “set in place.” What if *subscidit* (“he cut beneath”) were placed here in Cyprian instead of *subdidit* (“he set beneath”)? See Flaminius Nobilius’s notes on Proverbs 9.

“Slaughtered.” Four old books have “killed”; the Vulgate edition of sacred Scripture has “sacrificed.” See Nobilius again.

“His servants.” So also in Book II of the *Testimonies*, chapter 2. In the book of Proverbs the Vulgate edition has “his maidservants.” But the Greek Septuagint reads δούλοις, “servants.”

479 “Lofty.” One royal manuscript has “great”; the old Saint-Remi manuscript, “sublime.” From this alone it is evident how much license and authority the ancient scribes arrogated to themselves.]

V. Moreover, through Solomon the Holy Spirit, showing beforehand the type of the Lord’s sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0377C] “Sacrament,” Lam.; Bod. 2; Ebor.; NC. 1.] and making mention in advance [Note: [Col. 0377C] “Shows beforehand,” Oxon.] of the sacrificed victim, the bread and wine, the altar, and the Apostles, says: “Wisdom built herself a house and set beneath it seven columns. She slaughtered her victims, mixed her wine in a bowl, and prepared her table. And she sent her servants, summoning them to the mixing bowl with a lofty proclamation and saying: [Col. 0378A] ‘Whoever is foolish, let him turn aside to me.’ And to those lacking understanding she said: ‘Come, eat of my breads, and drink the wine that I have mixed for you’” (Prov. 9:1–5). She declares the wine to be mixed—that is, by a prophetic voice she announces beforehand the Lord’s cup mixed with water and wine—so that it may be apparent that in the Lord’s Passion there occurred what had previously been foretold.

[Note: [Col. 0378D]

VI.—“Reclines.” I am accustomed, as you see, reader, frequently to note the audacity of the ancient scribes, which was considerable even in this passage. For some old books have “reclines sleeping,” others “lies sleeping,” others “reclines,” “reclined,” “let him recline and sleep,” “reclining and sleeping,” and “reclined.”]

VI. The same thing is also signified in Judah’s blessing, where here too the figure of Christ is expressed: that he would be praised and adored by his brothers; that with his hands—by which he endured the cross and conquered death—he would press down the backs of his enemies as they yielded and fled; that he himself is the lion of the tribe of Judah; that he reclines sleeping [Note: [Col. 0378C] “Reclining and sleeping in the Passion and rising,” Lin.] in the Passion and rises; and that he himself is the hope of the nations. To these things divine Scripture adds and says: “He will wash his robe in wine [Col. 0378B] and his garment in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49:11). Now when “the blood of the grape” is spoken of, what else is shown but the wine of the cup of the Lord’s blood?

VII. Likewise, in Isaiah the Holy Spirit testifies to this same thing concerning the Lord’s Passion, saying: “Why are your garments red, 106 and your clothes like those from the treading of a full and thoroughly trodden winepress?” (Isa. 63:2). Can water make garments red? Or is it water in a winepress that is trodden by feet or squeezed out by a press? Wine is assuredly mentioned [Note: [Col. 0378C] “Thus mixed wine,” Ebor.; NC. 2.] so that the Lord’s blood may be understood [Note: [Col. 0378C] “May be understood through wine,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Ebor.; NC. 1.], and so that what was afterward manifested in the Lord’s cup [Col. 0379A] might be foretold through the proclamation of the Prophets [Note: [Col. 0379C] “Is proclaimed,” Lin.; Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; NC. 1. “May be proclaimed,” NC. 2.]. The treading and pressure of the winepress are also specified, because just as wine cannot be made available for drinking unless the cluster is first trodden and pressed, so neither could we drink Christ’s blood [Note: [Col. 0379C] “Can we,” Bod. 1. “Drink down,” Lin.; NC. 1.] unless Christ had first been trodden and pressed, and had first [Note: [Col. 0379C] “Previously,” NC. 2.] drunk the cup from which [Note: [Col. 0379C] “Into which,” Bod. 2.] believers would be given drink.

[Note: [Col. 0379C]

VIII.—“Is foretold.” The reading of those editions that have “is sung beforehand” is undoubtedly good. Nevertheless, I thought the reading of the old editions [Col. 0379D] and thirteen old copies should be restored. The manuscript of Saint-Albin does indeed have “is foretold”; but it was corrected in antiquity, and “is sung beforehand” was entered. In one of my old manuscripts “is sung beforehand” is written.

“Is predicted beforehand.” Here too I decided to follow the text of the old editions and our old books, with which several English manuscripts also agree. In the Verona manuscript “is proclaimed” was written.

“Will be split.” Although I know that all editions and nearly all the old books have “will be split,” I would readily have preferred the reading of the Fuxensis manuscript, in which “will be cleft” is written, because Isaiah 48, to which this passage refers, reads: “He brought water out of the rock for them, and cleft the rock, and the waters flowed.” But since I saw that “will be split” was also written in Book I of the *Testimonies*, chapter 12, I did not dare alter it.

“Blessed are those who hunger.” So all the editions and six old books, among which I name the Séguier manuscript. Quite rightly indeed. For in Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 1, [Col. 0380C] it reads: “Blessed are those who hunger for righteousness”; there the English edition notes that eight ancient manuscripts read: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst.” I nevertheless thought it necessary to point out [Col. 0380D] that ten ancient copies here prefer: “Blessed are those who thirst and hunger.”]

VIII. Whenever water alone is mentioned in the holy Scriptures, Baptism is proclaimed, as we see signified in Isaiah: “Do not,” he says, “remember the former things, and do not consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing new things, which will now arise, and you will know them [Note: [Col. 0379C] “You will know the truth,” Lam.; Bod.; Ebor.; NC. 1.]; and I will make a road in the desert, and rivers in a waterless place [Note: [Col. 0379C] “Waterless places,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.] to water my chosen race, my people whom I acquired, that they might declare my mighty works” (Isa. 43:18–21). [Col. 0379B] There God foretold through the prophet that among the nations, in places that had formerly been without water, rivers would afterward overflow and water God’s chosen race—that is, those made children of God through the generation of Baptism.

Likewise, it is again foretold and predicted beforehand that if the Jews thirst and seek Christ, they will drink among us—that is, they will obtain the grace of Baptism: “If they thirst,” he says, “he will lead them through deserts; he will bring forth water for them [Note: [Col. 0380C] “Water for them,” Bod. 1, 2; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1.] from the rock; the rock will be split, and water will flow, and my people will drink” [Note: [Col. 0380C] “And you will drink, O people,” Bod. 1.] (Isa. 48:21). This is fulfilled in the Gospel, when Christ, who is the rock, is split by the thrust of the lance in the Passion. And, calling attention to what had previously been foretold through the prophet, he cries out and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says [Note: [Col. 0380C] “As it is written,” Lam.], rivers of living water will flow from his [Col. 0379C] belly” (John 7:37–39).

And so that it might be still more evident that the Lord is speaking there not of the cup but of Baptism, Scripture added, saying: [Col. 0380A] “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive.” For through Baptism the Holy Spirit is received, and thus those who have been baptized and have obtained the Holy Spirit come to drink the Lord’s cup. Nor should anyone be troubled because, when divine Scripture speaks of Baptism, it says that we thirst and drink, since the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6); for that which is received with eager and thirsty desire is imbibed more fully and abundantly. Likewise, in another place the Lord speaks to the Samaritan woman, saying [Note: [Col. 0380C] “Speaks and says,” Lam.]: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give will never thirst forever” (John 4:13–14). By this too the Baptism of saving water is signified [Note: [Col. 0380C] “Was signified,” Bod. 3.], which is of course received once [Col. 0380B] and is not repeated. The Lord’s cup, however, is always both thirsted for and drunk in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0380D]

IX.—“For this is.” This is the reading of nearly all the old copies. Three old copies and the early editions, however, prefer “For this thing is.” Nicholas Le Fèvre likewise noted in the margin of his copy of Pamelius’s edition that he had read it this way in the oldest edition he possessed.

“Of the new covenant.” The word “new” is absent from thirteen ancient manuscripts.

“New wine.” The word “wine” is absent from Matthew’s Gospel, from Jerome in the title of the second question to Hedibia, from eleven ancient manuscripts, and from the editions of Manutius and Morel. It is also known to be absent from nine English manuscripts. The Vulgate reading, which has “When I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father,” pleased Pamelius more; he testified that he had found it in the Affligem manuscript. In Varro, Book V of *On the Latin Language*: “I drink new old wine.”

[Col. 0381C] “To be offered.” The Münster manuscript adds “or to be celebrated.”

“If wine is absent.” The Fuxensis manuscript reads: “unless wine is mixed into the cup.”]

IX. Nor are many arguments needed, dearest brother, to prove that Baptism has always been signified by the designation “water,” and that we must understand it so [Note: [Col. 0380C] “We ought,” NC. 2.], since the Lord, when he came, revealed the truth of Baptism and of the Cup: he commanded that faithful water, the water of eternal life, be given to believers in Baptism, while by the example of his teaching he taught that the cup should be mixed by joining wine and water. For on the day of his Passion, taking the cup, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Drink from this, all of you. For this is the blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins. I tell you, from now on I shall not drink from this product of the vine until that day [Col. 0380C] when I shall drink new wine with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26:28–29). In this passage we find that the cup the Lord offered [Col. 0381A] 107 was mixed, and that what he called his blood was wine. Hence it is apparent that Christ’s blood is not offered if wine is absent from the cup, nor is the Lord’s sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0381C] “The Lord,” Bod. 3, 4; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2; Lin.] celebrated with legitimate consecration unless our offering and sacrifice correspond to the Passion. How, moreover, shall we drink new wine from the product of the vine with Christ in the kingdom of the Father if we do not offer wine in the sacrifice of God the Father and of Christ, nor mix the Lord’s cup according to the Lord’s tradition?

[Note: [Col. 0381C]

X.—“Gave thanks.” This is the reading of all editions preceding Pamelius’s. Pamelius, however, changed it on the authority of the single Cambron manuscript and printed “giving thanks, broke it.” We have likewise seen it written this way [Col. 0381D] in the Saint-Éloi and Reims Saint-Denis manuscripts. But since nearly all our old books, as well as the English manuscripts, prefer the reading Pamelius rejected, we judged that it should be restored. Yet whether one reads it this way or the other, the sense is the same; and therefore the old reading ought to have been retained.

“Should proclaim otherwise.” In the Séguier manuscript “has evangelized” is written.]

X. The blessed apostle Paul also, chosen and sent by the Lord and appointed a preacher of the truth of the Gospel, sets forth these same things in his Epistle, saying [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Sets forth and says,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2.]: “The Lord Jesus, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and gave thanks [Note: [Col. 0381C] “And gave thanks,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2. “Giving thanks, broke it, and,” Oxon.] and broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which will be handed over for you. Do this in [Col. 0381B] remembrance of me.’ In the same way [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Likewise,” Lam.] he also took the cup after supper, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant [Note: [Col. 0381C] “This is the cup of the new covenant,” Lam.; Lin.; Ebor.] in my blood. Do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me. For whenever you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes’” (1 Cor. 11:23–26).

If this is both commanded by the Lord [Note: [Col. 0381C] “Should be commanded,” Bod. 3.] and confirmed and handed down by his Apostle, so that whenever we drink, we do in remembrance of the Lord what the Lord himself did, we find [Note: [Col. 0382C] “We shall find,” Bod. 1.] that what was commanded is not observed by us unless we too do the same things the Lord did and, mixing the Lord’s cup in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Mixing the cup in the same manner,” Bod. 1, 2, 3; Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2; Lin.], do not depart from divine instruction. That one must not depart at all from the Gospel’s precepts [Note: [Col. 0382C] “One does not,” Lam.], and that the disciples too must observe [Col. 0381C] and do the same things the teacher taught and did, [Col. 0382A] the blessed Apostle teaches still more resolutely and forcefully in another passage [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Blessed Paul teaches,” Lin.], saying: “I marvel that you are so quickly changing [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Being transferred,” NC. 2.] from him who called you to grace, to another gospel—which is not another—except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should proclaim otherwise than what we proclaimed to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone proclaims to you anything other than what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:6–9).

[Note: [Col. 0381D]

XI.—“Exceedingly.” It is written so here and a little later in eighteen of our copies and in six English manuscripts. That Joachim Vadian read it this way can also be seen in Book II of his *Aphorisms on the Eucharist*. The editions earlier than Pamelius’s likewise have it. Pamelius, therefore, was the first of all to print “how supremely excellent,” saying that this was probably Cyprian’s genuine reading. But I think he erred in this. For *perquam* (“exceedingly”) is an adverb customarily placed before a word for emphasis, and Cyprian used it [Col. 0382C] in Epistle III, page 8: “For it is exceedingly serious”; and in Epistle XXXI, page 43: “For it seems exceedingly odious and burdensome to us,” even in Pamelius’s edition. And to take examples from secular literature: Cicero said in Book II of *On the Orator*: “The variety greatly to be desired by us, and that incredible power of speech possessed by Carneades.” Valerius Maximus, Book VII, chapter 4: “By an exceedingly excellent kind of counsel.” [Col. 0382D] Aulus Gellius, Book I, chapter 4: “The rhetorician Antonius Julianus was of an exceedingly honorable and agreeable disposition.” See also Quintilian, Book VIII, in the Preface and chapter 3, and Book IX, chapter 1. Meanwhile, it must not be concealed that I used four ancient copies in which 480 “how supremely excellent” was written. Moreover, Pamelius’s claim that Rembolt was the first to write “exceedingly excellent” is certainly untrue. For that reading occurs in the Speyer edition and in the old Venetian edition, which are much older than the one Rembolt published.

“Restore.” The Fuxensis and one Bodleian manuscript read “bring back.” One of my manuscripts and the Münster manuscript read “restore to spiritual love.”

“Taste.” This passage is variously written. In the editions earlier than Pamelius’s, in nine of our old books, in three English manuscripts, and also in the Cambron manuscript praised by Pamelius, “slumber” is read. But “taste” is preferred by nine other old copies of ours and [Col. 0383C] two praised by Pamelius. That there was doubt in antiquity about how it should be written appears inferable from one of my old books, in which “slumber” is written, and above the line “or taste.” Pamelius preferred “taste” on the basis of his own earlier conjecture, which he was glad to find confirmed by the authority of the Affligem and Cologne manuscripts.

“May hold to the Lord’s truth.” The Fuxensis manuscript reads: “May hold to the truth with the Lord’s mind.”]

XI. Since, therefore, neither the Apostle himself nor an angel from heaven can proclaim or teach anything other than what Christ once taught and his Apostles proclaimed, I marvel greatly at where the practice arose that, contrary to the discipline of the Gospel and the Apostles, water should be offered by itself in the Lord’s cup in certain [Col. 0382B] places, although water alone cannot represent Christ’s blood. The Holy Spirit does not remain silent about the mystery of this matter even in the Psalms, but mentions the Lord’s cup and says: “Your intoxicating cup is exceedingly excellent” [Note: [Col. 0382C] “How supremely excellent,” Oxon.] (Ps. 22:5). But a cup that intoxicates is surely mixed with wine [Note: [Col. 0382C] “Must be mixed. For water alone,” Lin.], for water cannot intoxicate anyone. The Lord’s cup intoxicates in the same way that Noah, drinking wine in Genesis, became intoxicated. But because the intoxication of the Lord’s cup and blood is not of the same kind as the intoxication of ordinary wine, when the Holy Spirit said in the Psalm, “Your intoxicating cup,” he added “exceedingly excellent,” because the Lord’s cup so intoxicates those who drink that it makes them sober, restores their minds to spiritual wisdom, and causes each person to recover his senses, turning from this worldly taste to the understanding of God. [Col. 0382C]

And just as with this common wine the mind is loosened, the soul relaxed, and every sorrow laid aside, so, when the Lord’s blood and the cup of salvation have been drunk [Note: [Col. 0383C] “And having been drunk,” Lam.; Ebor. “And having drunk,” Ver.; Bened. “Drinking,” Lin. “Having drunk the blood,” NC. 2. “When drunk,” Oxon.], let the memory of the old man be laid aside, let there be forgetfulness of one’s former worldly manner of life, and let the mournful and sorrowful breast, formerly oppressed by distressing sins, be released by the joy of divine forgiveness. Yet what is drunk can gladden the drinker in the Lord’s Church only if it 108 holds to the Lord’s truth.

[Note: [Col. 0383C]

XII.—“Among the Jews.” The words immediately following, down to “wine from water,” are absent from the Bec manuscript, and in their place the following words have been inserted: “For the things offered among the Jews signified a spiritual understanding. Everything the Jews offered under the old covenant has now been fulfilled, because the old law was a shadow. Afterward, in the New Covenant, in Cana of Galilee and before the Jews, the Lord made from water,” etc. [Col. 0383D]

“And multitudes.” These words are not found in Revelation 17. Moreover, instead of “and multitudes,” the Reims Saint-Denis manuscript has “and tribes.”]

XII. How perverse and contrary it is that, although the Lord made wine from water at the wedding (John 2:7), we should make water from wine, when the mystery of that event too ought to admonish and instruct us to offer wine, rather, in the Lord’s sacrifices. For because spiritual grace had failed among the Jews, the wine also failed: for “the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth [Col. 0383B] was the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7). But Christ, teaching and showing that the people of the nations would succeed them, and that through the merit of faith we would afterward attain the place the Jews had lost, made wine from water—that is, he showed that, when the Jews had ceased, the people of the nations would instead flow and gather together for the wedding of Christ and the Church. For divine Scripture declares in Revelation that waters signify peoples [Note: [Col. 0383C] “By waters … peoples are signified,” NC. 2.], saying: “The waters that you saw, upon which that harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations of the Gentiles and languages” (Rev. 17:15). We plainly see that this is also contained in the sacrament of the cup.

[Note: [Col. 0383D]

XIII.—“We see in the water.” These words, which are certainly not those of Pope Julius, are nevertheless quoted from Julius by Eugenius IV in the *Confession Sent to the Armenians*, in Odoricus Raynaldus, under the year 1439, §15. Regino, however, in Book I, chapter 66, cites them from the Council of Worms, chapter 29, where they appear as canon four in editions of the councils. See the notes on Regino, page 550.

“The people of believers.” The Verona manuscript reads: “The people of believers is coupled and joined to his blood, in which it has believed.”

“So that the mingling.” In the Bec manuscript it is written: “So that that mingling may not be separated within itself, and the unity of the Church—that is, of the people established in the Church—may be understood, if it has faithfully and steadfastly persevered in what it believed; nothing will be able to separate it, so that it may always remain in undivided love—[the final words are textually uncertain]—not even from that which was less.”

“Undivided love.” I found this reading, which is excellent, in fourteen old books and in Pamelius’s edition, which first brought it forward. But the editions of Manutius and Morel and the Bec manuscript have “with undivided love.” The old editions and four old books have “in divine love.” That reading is better than the one I retained. For Epistle LVII, page 96, also has: “May our love persevere with the Lord.”

“For if wine.” I think Paschasius Radbertus, when using this passage, altered Cyprian’s words so as to make them his own. For in chapter 11 of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* he wrote as follows: “For if wine is offered without water, Christ’s blood begins to be without us. But if there is water alone, the people now appears to be without Christ. When, however, both are mixed and joined, then the mystery of the Church is rightly accomplished spiritually.”

“The heavenly is accomplished.” The remainder of this epistle was not copied in the Bec manuscript.

“In consecrating.” Two of our old books and two English manuscripts prefer “in sacrificing.”

“Many grains.” Below, Epistle LXXVI, page 153: “For when the Lord calls his body bread, compacted from the uniting of many grains.”

“And ground together.” These words are absent from Florus’s excerpts, but are present in the Séguier manuscript.]

XIII. For since Christ bore us all, as he also bore our sins, we see that the people is understood in the water, while Christ’s blood is shown [Note: [Col. 0384C] “He shows,” Rigalt.] in the wine. [Col. 0384A] When water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people is united to Christ, and the congregation of believers is coupled and joined to him in whom it has believed. This coupling and joining of water and wine is so effected in the Lord’s cup that the two cannot be separated from one another. Hence nothing will be able to separate from Christ the Church—that is, the people established in the Church, faithfully and steadfastly persevering in what it has believed—so as to keep it from always clinging to him and its love from remaining undivided.

Thus, in consecrating the Lord’s cup [Note: [Col. 0384C] “Cup,” Lin.; NC. 1, 2.], water cannot be offered alone, just as wine cannot be offered alone. For if someone offers wine only, Christ’s blood begins to be without us; but if there is water alone, the people begins to be without Christ. When, however, both are mixed and are coupled to one another in a blended union, then the spiritual and heavenly sacrament is accomplished. Thus the Lord’s cup [Col. 0384B] is not water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed together, just as the Lord’s body cannot be flour alone or water alone unless both have been united and joined and consolidated into the structure of a single loaf. By this very sacrament our people too is shown to be united, so that, just as many grains, gathered into one and ground and mixed together, make one loaf, so we may know that in Christ, who is the heavenly bread, there is one body, to which our whole number is joined and united.

[Note: [Col. 0385C]

XIV.—“If Christ alone.” Gratian cites this passage in distinction 8, chapter *Si solus*, chapter *Si consuetudinem*, and chapter *Consuetudo*. On this passage of Cyprian, where he says that Christ alone must be heard, John, Cardinal of Torquemada, says that the word “alone” does not exclude the pope, prelates, other teachers, or good preachers, but only antichrists—that is, those opposed to Christ who preach contrary things.

“Someone else before us.” We found it written this way in seven ancient manuscripts. The old editions, including those of Manutius and Morel, have “what someone before us.” The Thou and Chartres manuscripts likewise read so, as do two old books praised in Pamelius’s edition. 481 [Col. 0385D] In the Fuxensis manuscript it is written “another something before”; in the Tours manuscript, “something else someone”; in the Corbie manuscript, “another someone.”

“For neither.” The Münster manuscript reads: “Nor ought anyone to follow another person’s custom.”

“Alter by tradition.” One royal manuscript has “cast headlong by reasoning.”]

XIV. There is therefore no reason, dearest brother, for anyone to think that the custom of certain people should be followed, if any in the past thought that water alone ought to be offered in the Lord’s cup. For one must ask whom [Col. 0385A] they themselves followed. For if, in the sacrifice Christ offered, none but Christ is to be followed, surely we ought to obey and do what Christ did and commanded to be done, since he himself says in the Gospel: “If you do what I command you, I no longer call [Note: [Col. 0385C] “I shall not call,” Lam.; Bod. 1, 2; NC. 2; Ebor.] you servants, but friends” (John 15:14–15). And that Christ alone must be heard is also attested by the Father from heaven, saying: “This is my most beloved [Note: [Col. 0385C] “Beloved,” Bod. 2; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2.] Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 17:5).

Therefore, if Christ alone must be heard, we ought not to attend to what someone else before us thought should be done, but to what Christ, who is before all, did first. For one ought not to follow human custom but God’s truth, since God speaks through Isaiah the prophet and says: “In vain they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men” (Isa. 29:13). And again the Lord [Col. 0385B] repeats this same thing in the Gospel, saying: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition” (Mark 7:13). And in another place he states and says: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and so teaches people will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

But if it is not permissible to break even the least of the Lord’s commandments, how much more is it unlawful to violate such great and weighty things, pertaining as they do to the very sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and our redemption, or to alter by human tradition what has been divinely instituted into something else? For if Jesus [Note: [Col. 0385C] “For Jesus,” Bod. 1.] Christ our Lord and God is himself the high priest of God [Note: [Col. 0385C] “Himself the high priest,” Bod. 1.] [Col. 0385C] the Father, and first offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father [Note: [Col. 0385C] “Offered himself to God the Father,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.], [Col. 0386A] and commanded that this be done in remembrance of him [Note: [Col. 0386C] “In remembrance,” Bod. 1, 2; Lin.; Ebor.; NC. 1, 2.], then surely that priest truly performs the office of Christ who imitates what Christ did; and he then offers a true and full sacrifice in the Church to God the Father if he begins to offer in accordance with how he sees that Christ himself offered.

[Note: [Col. 0385D]

XV.—“Smell of blood.” The Corbie manuscript afterward adds: “[The text is materially uncertain:] a scent, fragrant from an unbelieving conscience, may have been recognized in the morning shadows, and he is known to be a Christian while we are ashamed of the blood of Christ.” I marvel that Rigault did not notice this. I also found this addition in the Tours and Fuxensis manuscripts. But it is not present in the Séguier manuscript, the oldest of all. Jerome, in the *Epistle to Nepotianus on the Life of Clerics*: “Never smell of wine, lest you hear the philosopher’s saying: ‘This is not offering a kiss but offering wine to drink.’” Tertullian in the *Apology*: “For this reason it was even necessary to offer kisses to their relatives, so that they might be judged by their breath. But now among women, because of wine, no kiss is free.” He is referring to the customs of Roman women, who were not permitted to drink wine, as Pliny, Book XIV, chapter 13, and Aulus Gellius, Book X, chapter 23, teach. On the customs of Christians, however, with which this passage of Cyprian is concerned, see Petavius’s observations on Epiphanius, page 265, and Josephus Vicecomes, Book III of *The Rites of the Mass*, page 236.

“Who is ashamed.” So most of the old books. But in one Saint-Remi manuscript, in the Dijon manuscript, and in the Grenoble manuscript [Col. 0386D] it reads: “Whoever confesses me before men, the Son of Man will confess him.” So also in the Pithou manuscript, except that it reads “will confound” instead of “will confess.” But in *On the Lapsed*, page 190, he writes: “Who is ashamed of me,” etc. See Pamelius’s notes on this passage.]

XV. Furthermore, the whole discipline of religion and truth is overturned unless what is spiritually commanded is faithfully preserved [Note: [Col. 0386C] “Is received in a special manner and faithfully observed,” Vat.]—unless, indeed, someone at the morning sacrifices fears that through the taste of wine he may smell of Christ’s blood. Thus, then, the brotherhood begins to be held back from Christ’s Passion in persecutions, when in the offerings it learns to be ashamed of his blood and gore. Yet the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is ashamed of me, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him” [Note: [Col. 0386C] “Whoever is ashamed of me before men, he will put him to shame,” Bod. 2; NC. 1; Ebor.] [Col. 0386B] (Mark 8:38). And the Apostle also speaks, saying: “If I were pleasing men, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). How, then, can we shed our blood for Christ when we blush to drink Christ’s blood?

[Note: [Col. 0386D]

XVI.—“Celebrate the Lord’s rite,” that is, offer divine sacrifices, sacrifice, as Pamelius correctly explains. Elsewhere *Dominicum* signifies the church in which Christians gathered to celebrate the mysteries. See Baronius under December 25; Cardinal Bona, Book I, chapters 3 and 19 of *Liturgical Matters*; and Du Cange’s Latin glossary. The *Acts of the Donatist Martyrs* in Book II of our *Miscellanies*, page 66: “Do you not know, Satan, that the Christian is constituted in the Lord’s house and the Lord’s house in the Christian?” *Dominicum* seems to mean something else in the spurious Epistle of the Council of Nicaea to Pope Sylvester published in Merlin’s collection.

“After supper.” See Durandus, Book II, chapter 51 of *The Rites of the Catholic Church*.]

XVI. Does anyone flatter himself with the consideration that, although water alone seems to be offered in the morning, nevertheless, when we come to supper, we offer a mixed cup? But when we sup, we cannot summon the people to our banquet so as to celebrate the truth of the sacrament with the whole brotherhood present. Yet the Lord offered the mixed cup not in the morning but after supper. Must we therefore celebrate the Lord’s rite after supper [Col. 0386C], so that we may thus offer the mixed cup when celebrating the Lord’s rites [Col. 0387A]? It was fitting for Christ to make his offering toward the evening of the day, so that the very hour of the sacrifice might show the decline and evening of the world, as it is written in Exodus: “And the whole multitude of the congregation of the children of Israel shall kill it toward evening” (Exod. 12:6). And again in the Psalms: “The lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2). We, however, celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning.

[Note: [Col. 0387C]

**XVII.—For Scripture.** Eleven old manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, omit mention of the bread and give this passage as follows: “For Scripture says that whenever we offer the cup in commemoration of the Lord and of his passion,” etc.

**And let him see.** Here again this passage reveals the audacity, negligence, and carelessness of the ancient copyists. [Col. 0387D] For some old manuscripts have *et viderit* (“and let him see”), others *et videris* (“and you will see”), *sed vide* (“but see”), *sed videris* (“but you will see”), or *sed videamus* (“but let us see”). Some of these readings must necessarily be false.]

### XVII

And because in all sacrifices we make mention of his passion—for the sacrifice we offer is the Lord’s passion—we ought to do nothing other than what he did. For Scripture says: “For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. XI, 26). Therefore, whenever we offer the cup in commemoration [Col. 0387B] of the Lord and of his passion, let us do what it is established that the Lord did.

And let him see to it, dearest brother: if any of our predecessors, whether through ignorance or in simplicity, did not observe and maintain what the Lord taught us to do by his example and instruction, pardon can be granted to his simplicity through the Lord’s indulgence. But we will not be able to be forgiven, since we have now been admonished and instructed by the Lord to offer the Lord’s cup mixed with wine, in accordance with what the Lord offered. We must also send letters concerning this matter to our colleagues, so that the law of the Gospel and the Lord’s tradition may everywhere be observed, and so that there may be no departure from what Christ both taught and did.

[Note: [Col. 0387D]

**XVIII.—Rebuking.** Four ancient manuscripts punctuate it thus: “the Lord’s reproach.” The word *increpantis* (“rebuking”) occurs in the Psalm.

**You ran with him.** So too in Epistle LXIII, p. 120, where this passage is quoted, Tertullian in his book *On the Spectacles*, and certain old manuscripts have: “you ran with him” (*concurrebas cum eo*). It is also read in this form in Pope Siricius’s Epistle to Himerius. Certain others have: “you ran together with him” (*simul currebas cum eo*). Pamelius says that he found this reading in the Affligem and Cologne manuscripts.

**A share.** In certain ancient copies the reading is “a portion.” It is written in this form also in Epistle LXVIII and in the Epistle of Siricius.

**To the prophets.** In two old manuscripts [Col. 0388C] it is written “false prophets.” This is perhaps better, for Cyprian, in his book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 197, when quoting another passage from the same chapter of Jeremiah, is read as having said: “Do not listen to the words of the false prophets.”

**The light of the age.** I have retained this reading because I found it in sixteen ancient manuscripts. Otherwise I would have preferred [Col. 0388D] the reading “the light of the world,” which is presented both by the old editions and by five old manuscripts, except that in the Chartres manuscript it is written “of the world or of the age.” For the Greek *κόσμον* (*kosmon*), which occurs in the Greek text, properly signifies “world.” Hence, as Tertullian says in the *Apologeticum*, the Greeks gave the world the name *κόσμον* (“order, ornament”). So too Saint Hilary in Book I of *On the Trinity*. Pliny, Book II, chapter 4: “For that which the Greeks called *κόσμον*, from the word for ornament, we too called *mundum* from its perfect and complete elegance.” See Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, Book I, chapter 5, p. 482. It is nevertheless true that ecclesiastical writers frequently use *saeculum* (“age”) for *mundus* (“world”).

**Immersing.** Five old manuscripts and the Affligem manuscript praised by Pamelius have “baptizing,” with the same meaning. Thus copyists saw fit to alter Saint Cyprian’s expressions at their own discretion.]

### XVIII

To despise these things any longer and persevere in the former error—what else is this but to incur [Col. 0387C] the reproach of the Lord, who rebukes in the Psalm and says:

> “Why do you expound my statutes and take up my covenant upon your lips? Yet you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and among adulterers you placed your share” (Ps. XLIX, 16–18).

For to expound [110] the Lord’s statutes [Col. 0388A] and covenant, and yet not do what the Lord himself did—what else is this but to cast away his words and despise the Lord’s discipline, and to commit not earthly but spiritual thefts and adulteries, when someone steals our Lord’s words and deeds from the truth of the Gospel and corrupts and adulterates the divine commandments? As it is written in Jeremiah:

> “What,” he says, “has chaff to do with wheat? Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who steal my words, each from his neighbor, and who lead my people astray by their lies and their errors” (Jer. XXIII, 28, 30, 32).

Likewise, in another passage of the same prophet:

> “And she committed adultery,” he says, “with wood and stone, [Note: [Col. 0387C] ‘from wood and stone,’ NC. 2.] and in all these things she did not return to me” (Jer. IX, 10).

We must take care, diligently, fearfully, and religiously, that this theft and adultery do not fall upon us as well. [Col. 0388B] For if we are priests of God and Christ, I find no one whom we ought to follow more than God and Christ, since he himself expressly says in the Gospel:

> “I am the light of the age. Whoever follows me will not walk [Note: [Col. 0387C] ‘does not walk,’ York.] in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII, 12).

Therefore, lest we walk in darkness, we ought to follow Christ and observe his commandments, because in another place, when sending the Apostles, he also said:

> “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, therefore, and teach all nations, immersing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded [Note: [Col. 0388C] ‘enjoined,’ NC. 2.] you” (Matt. XXVIII, 18–20).

Therefore, if we wish to walk in the light of Christ, let us not depart from his commandments and admonitions, giving thanks that, while he instructs us for the future as to what we ought to do, [Col. 0388C] he forgives what in the past we erred in through simplicity. And because his second coming is now drawing near to us, his gracious and abundant favor increasingly illuminates our hearts with the light of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0389C]

**XIX.—I wish you.** The old Reims manuscript reads: “Always fare well in God the Lord, dearest brother.”]

### XIX

It therefore accords with our religion and fear, [Col. 0389A] and with the very position and office of our priesthood, dearest brother, that in mixing and offering the Lord’s cup we preserve the truth of the Lord’s tradition, and that, at the Lord’s admonition, we correct what appears previously to have been done erroneously among certain persons. Thus, when he begins to come in his glory and heavenly majesty, he may find us maintaining what he admonished, observing what he taught, and doing what he did.

I wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

## EPISTLE LXIV

*(Erasm., I, 7; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXIV; Paris., LXIII; Oxford, Leipzig, LXV.)*

### TO EPICTETUS AND THE PEOPLE OF ASSURAS, CONCERNING FORTUNATIANUS, FORMERLY THEIR BISHOP

**SUMMARY.—**He admonishes Epictetus and the people of Assuras not to permit Fortunatianus—formerly their bishop, but subsequently fallen—to return to the episcopate, both for other reasons and because it had been decreed that fallen bishops should not be admitted to their former rank.

[Note: [Col. 0389C]

**EPISTLE LXIV—I. To Epictetus, bishop of Assuras in the Proconsular province.** It is clear from Saint Cyprian’s Council of Carthage that Victor succeeded him in that see. At the Council of Bagai, Praetextatus, bishop of Assuras, was condemned, and in his place the Donatists installed [Col. 0389D] Rogatus. At the Conference of Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists, Evangelus, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Assuras, was present.

**Dearest brothers.** Three old manuscripts give preference to “dearest brother.” That reading may well be correct. For the epistle was written to the bishop and the people, and Cyprian could have written in the manner in which he is found to have written Epistle LVII to Cornelius. Although that epistle was written equally to Cornelius and to the entire Roman Church, he nevertheless says: “We have learned, dearest brother,” and Cyprian immediately turns his style toward them all, who are accordingly called “dearest brothers” a little later. This discrepancy among the readings in Cyprian seems to have arisen from abbreviations. For I have observed that *frater charissime* and *fratres charissimi* are sometimes written in ancient manuscripts as *F. K.* and *FF. CC.*, just as I have often seen *dilectissimi* written as *DD.*

**Fortunatianus**, whom apostasy had cast down from the episcopate when he sacrificed to idols. Hence, in the Saint-Arnoul manuscript, [Col. 0390C] when *apepiscopum* had been written, *apostatam* was written above the line, apparently by the same hand. Cyprian therefore says that he was formerly a bishop but is one no longer. We have noted a similar manner of speaking in Epistle LIX, p. 97, concerning Victor, formerly a presbyter.

**Which he betrayed.** The Saint-Arnoul manuscript has “which he lost.”

**Of faith and courage.** Although this reading, which both the old editions [Col. 0390D] and twelve old manuscripts prefer, is excellent, I ought nevertheless not to pass over in silence the fact that the Morel edition and five old manuscripts have “of courage and faith.”]

[Note: [Col. 0392C] This note appears at the foot of column 392, but its callout letter, (f), has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0392C] “Consecrated,” Verona.]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Epictetus and to the people dwelling at Assuras [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Asturas,” Lin., Thu., Foss., Corb.], greetings.

I have been deeply and painfully distressed, dearest brothers, because I have learned that Fortunatianus, formerly bishop among you, after his grievous fall, now wishes to conduct himself as though he were still unimpaired and has begun to claim the episcopate for himself.

This matter has saddened me, first on his own account. The wretched man, either wholly blinded by the darkness of the devil or deceived by the sacrilegious persuasion of certain persons, ought to be making satisfaction and devoting himself day and night, with tears, [111] prayers, and entreaties, to entreating the Lord. Yet he still dares to claim for himself the priesthood which he betrayed, as though, after serving at [Col. 0389C] the altars of the devil, it were permissible to approach the altar of God; or as though he would not provoke against himself still greater wrath and indignation from the Lord on the day of judgment. Although he was unable to be a leader of faith and courage to the brothers, he sets himself up as a teacher of faithlessness, audacity, and rashness; and though he did not teach the brothers to stand bravely in battle, he would teach those who have been defeated and cast down not even to entreat, although the Lord says:

> “To them you poured out drink offerings, and upon them you placed sacrifices; therefore, after all these things, [Note: [Col. 0389C] “Asturas,” Lin., Thu., Foss., Corb.] shall I not be indignant? says the Lord” (Isa. LVII, 6).

And in another place:

> “He who sacrifices to gods shall be utterly destroyed, unless it is to the Lord alone” (Exod. XXII, 19).

Likewise, the Lord speaks again and says:

> “They worshiped those things which their fingers had made, and man bowed down and the man was humbled; and I will not forgive them” (Isa. II, 8–9).

In the Apocalypse also we read the Lord’s wrath as he threatens and says:

> “If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives a mark on his forehead and on his hand, he too will drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed in the cup of his anger, and he will be punished with fire and sulfur before the eyes of the holy angels and before the eyes of the Lamb. And the smoke of [Col. 0390B] their torments will ascend for ages of ages, and those who worship the beast and its image will have no rest by day or night” (Rev. XIV, 9–11).

[Note: [Col. 0390D]

**The devil’s priests.** The Foix manuscript reads: “the devil or his priests.”

**By sacrilege and crime.** The Grenoble manuscript reads: “which had been taken captive by sacrilege and crime.” The Corbie manuscript has “of sacrileges and crimes.” This reading appears better if the word “captive” is retained. Jeremiah chapter XLIX has “the captives of the children of Ammon.” For one does not say “a servant to a master,” but “a servant of a master.” Hence Cicero has “slaves of laws, seditions, and desires.” The same must be said of captives, who are not under their own authority.

**To the altar of the holy place.** So read nearly all the old manuscripts, including the English manuscripts, and all editions before the Erasmian edition. The Erasmian edition reads “to the holy altar,” a reading that two old manuscripts also prefer. Rigault, omitting the word “altar,” printed “to the holy place,” on the authority, as he himself says, of the Verona manuscript. I did not, however, find this [Col. 0391C] in the margin of my copy of the Aldine edition. He declares that reading to be entirely correct, failing to notice that this same passage was printed below by himself in Epistle LXVIII, p. 117, and Epistle LXII, p. 129, in precisely the same form in which I have restored it here. The copyist of the Foix manuscript wrote “to the altar of the Lord,” which confirms our emendation.

Pamelius, however, says that he was unable to discover which passage of Scripture Cyprian is citing. Goulart, on the other hand, says that he is alluding to various statements by Moses in Exodus, especially concerning the office of the priests who served at the altar of Jehovah. This is certainly correct, for this passage was taken from chapter XXVIII of Exodus according to the Septuagint translation. In our edition of the Vulgate Sacred Scripture the reading is: “Or when they approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest they die guilty of iniquity.” The version [Col. 0391D] used by the holy Martyr is clearer and makes the sense of this passage easier to understand. In his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, Jerome read: “when they approach to minister in holy things.” That reading comes very close to the one cited from the Verona manuscript.

**The hearts of certain persons.** The Grenoble manuscript reads: “certain sinners.”]

### II
