Since, therefore, the Lord threatens these torments and these punishments on the day of judgment against those who obey the devil and sacrifice to idols, how does he think that he can act as a priest of God when he obeyed and served the devil’s priests? Or how does he think that his hand, which was taken captive by sacrilege and crime, can be transferred to the sacrifice of God [Note: [Col. 0389C] “of God” is absent from Corb.] and to prayer to the Lord, when in the divine Scriptures God forbids even priests involved in a lesser offense to approach the sacrifice, and says in Leviticus:

> “A man in whom there is a defect or blemish shall not approach to offer gifts to God” (Lev. XXI, 17).

Likewise in Exodus:

> “And let the priests [Col. 0390C] who approach the Lord God be sanctified, lest perhaps the Lord abandon them” (Exod. XIX, 22).

And again:

> “And when they [Note: [Col. 0390C] “Those who approach,” Bod. 1, 2; Lam.; York; NC. 1, 2; Lin.] approach to minister at the altar of the holy place, they shall not bring guilt upon themselves, lest they die” (Exod. XXIX, 43).

Those, therefore, who have brought grievous offenses upon themselves—that is, those who by sacrificing to idols have performed sacrilegious sacrifices—cannot claim God’s priesthood for themselves, nor can they offer any prayer before him on behalf of the brothers, since it is written in the Gospel:

> “God does not hear a sinner; but if anyone [Note: [Col. 0391B] “if any person,” Oxford.] worships God and does his will, him he hears” (John IX, 31).

Nevertheless, the profound darkness of the shadows descending [Note: [Col. 0391B] “rushing upon them,” Lin., NC. 1.] has so blinded the hearts of certain persons that they admit no light from the saving commandments. Having once turned aside from the straight boundary of the true path, they are swept headlong over the precipice and through the abyss [Note: [Col. 0391C] “through the abysses,” Bod. 1.] by the night and error of their crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0391D]

**III.—[p. 483] Gluttonous indigestion.** Jerome, in his Epistle to the monk Rusticus, speaks of “belching forth gluttonous indigestion, which is the parent of lusts.” Salvian, Book IV, chapter 3, has “you are distended with gluttonous indigestion,” where the Corbie manuscript has “cruelty”; and Book VII, chapter 16, “others distended with gluttonous indigestion,” where the Colbert manuscript has “cruelty.” Likewise, in Avitus of Vienne, Epistle LXXXV, the reading is “the separation of the nations [produces] gluttonous indigestion.” In place of this, the Vienne manuscript of Marnaesius has “cruelty.” Ancient copyists therefore sometimes interchanged *crudelitas* (“cruelty”) and *cruditas* (“indigestion”).

**To the defilements of the altar.** This passage above all reveals the audacity and ignorance of the ancient copyists. For the Foix, Metz, Saint-Arnoul, and Grenoble manuscripts [Col. 0392C] have *impia mente* (“with an impious mind”); the Münster manuscript has *amplas mentes* (“ample minds”); the Dijon manuscript and one Reims manuscript have *per simplas mentes* (“through simple minds”); and one old manuscript of mine has *per simplicia merita* (“through simple merits”). None of these readings is sound. Six English manuscripts have: “with an impious mind they approach the sanctification of the altar,” where the word “sanctification” appears to have been added by a copyist who did not understand what he was writing.

**Defilements.** Festus Pompeius: *impiatus*, “made wicked.” The word is derived from the verb *impio*, which means to commit a crime against piety. Hence in Plautus’s *The Rope* one reads: “If I have acted impiously toward a parent or the gods,” which commentators explain as though Plautus had said: “If I have been impious toward my parents.” Apuleius, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*: “So that I still believe myself to be spattered and polluted with human blood”; and Book II: “You therefore have the accused, polluted by so many murders.” Conversely they also used the word *piamentum* (“expiation”). Pliny, Book XXV, chapter 4: “After it has been pulled up, religious custom requires that the trench be filled with various kinds of produce as an expiation for the earth”; and chapter 9: “After honeycombs and honey have first been given as an expiation for the earth”; Book XXXVII, chapter 1: “There would appear to have been sufficient expiation in the voluntary loss of a single gem.” *Piare* is an ancient verb found in Plautus, Horace, Seneca, and others. It means to cleanse or expiate.

**And we must strive with all our strength.** Since these words occur in all the ancient editions, in all our manuscripts, and in the English manuscripts, it is remarkable that they disappeared from Rigault’s edition. Reinhart and the English editors restored them.]

### III

Nor is it surprising if those who denied the Lord now reject our counsels or the Lord’s commandments. They desire contributions, offerings, and profits, upon which they formerly preyed insatiably; and even now they gape after dinners and feasts, the surfeit of which they daily belched forth until recently while their indigestion persisted. They now demonstrate with complete clarity that even before this they had served not religion but rather their bellies and their profits, with profane greed.

Hence we perceive and believe that this judgment itself came from God’s testing, so that the unchaste, the faithless, the profane, the earthly, and the sacrilegious might no longer persist in standing at the altar and handling, respectively, modesty, faith, religion, divine things, and holy things. Lest such persons return once more to the defilement of the altar and the contamination of the brothers, we must keep watch [Col. 0392A] with all our powers and strive with all our strength to repel them, so far as we can, from this audacity born of their own crime. They must not still attempt to act as priests [Note: [Col. 0392B] “to act the priest,” Lin.], when, cast down to the final extremity of death, they have fallen under the weight of a greater ruin, beyond even the fallen laity. [Note: [Col. 0392B] “a fallen layman,” Oxford.]

[Note: [Col. 0392D]

**IV.—But let them preserve.** In one royal manuscript the reading is: “But let them, being unimpaired, preserve the continuity of their salvation and the perpetual strength of integrity, and guard it.” Better is the reading in the Saint-Arnoul manuscript: “the continuity of their salvation and the perpetual strength of the integrity preserved and guarded by them.” I think that it ought to be restored in that form. In the Grenoble manuscript the words “being unimpaired, the continuity of their salvation” are absent.]

### IV

But if an incurable frenzy [112] persists among the mad, and if, after the withdrawal of the Holy Spirit, the blindness which has begun remains in its own night, our counsel will be to separate each of the brothers from their deceit and to remove them from their contagion, lest anyone fall into the snares of error. For an offering cannot be sanctified where the Holy Spirit is not, nor can the Lord benefit anyone through the prayers and entreaties of a man who has himself violated the Lord.

But if Fortunatianus—either forgetful of his own crime through the blindness of the devil, or having become the devil’s [Col. 0392B] minister and servant in order to deceive the brotherhood—persists in this frenzy of his, labor as much as you can. Amid this darkness of the raging devil, call the minds of the brothers back from error, lest they readily consent to another’s madness or make themselves participants in the offenses of the desperate. Instead, let them, being unimpaired, preserve the perpetual continuity of their salvation and of the integrity which they themselves have preserved and guarded.

[Note: [Col. 0393C]

**V.—Deceptive and deadly.** So Erasmus and four old manuscripts. But the older editions and likewise four old manuscripts have: “by false and deadly deception.”

**Deception.** I was moved to restore this reading by the authority of the old editions and of nearly all the old manuscripts. For I found the word “circumvention,” which Erasmus introduced, in only three ancient manuscripts. The English editors testify that it was not present in theirs.

**Most greatly missed.** I have restored these words, which occur in eleven ancient manuscripts and in the old editions, but which Erasmus expunged and others afterward omitted. I did so also because I know that Cyprian frequently used this formula in writing. Besides the authority of the old copies of Saint Cyprian, in which I have always seen *desiderantissimi* written, an ancient inscription given by Spon, p. 208, likewise contains this form. Similarly Julius Capitolinus, in his *Albinus*, has: “to his most loving and most greatly missed brother.” In editions of the Epistles of Saint Leo the Pope, the address to Eutyches reads: “To the most beloved son Eutyches.” But in the manuscripts of the deacon Rusticus the reading is: “To the most greatly missed son Eutyches”; and at the end, instead of “most beloved son,” the reading is “most greatly missed son,” as I noted in my edition of the Councils, p. 1011. On p. 1514 of that same work, in Cyril’s Epistle to the Monks published in the acts of the Fifth Council, I read *desiderantissimis*, where the common text likewise reads *desiderantissimis*. And indeed, since this word descends from the participle *desiderans*, it is necessary that we write *desiderantissimus*. Our Benedictines have sometimes written it in this form in their edition of the Works of Saint Augustine.]

### V

But let the fallen, recognizing the magnitude of their offense, not cease to entreat the Lord, nor abandon the Catholic Church, which was established by the Lord as one and alone. Instead, let them persist in acts of satisfaction [Col. 0393A] and implore the Lord’s mercy; let them knock at the Church, so that they may be received there where they formerly were, and let them return to Christ, from whom they departed.

Nor should they listen to those who deceive them by deceptive [Note: [Col. 0393B] “who deceive them by false,” Bod. 1, NC. 2.] and deadly seduction, since it is written:

> “Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Therefore, do not become their participants” (Eph. V, 6–7).

Therefore, let no one accompany the disobedient, those who do not fear God and who withdraw entirely from the Church. But if anyone is too impatient to entreat the Lord who has been offended, and refuses to obey us, but follows the desperate and the lost, he will have himself to blame [Note: [Col. 0393B] “it will be imputed to him,” Lam., NC. 1, Bod. 2, York.] when the day of judgment comes. For how will he be able to entreat the Lord on that day, when he has previously denied Christ and now also denies the Church of Christ and, refusing to obey bishops who are sound, unimpaired, and living, has made himself a companion and participant of those who are dying? [Col. 0393B]

I wish you, dearest and most greatly missed brothers, always to fare well.

[Note: [Col. 0393D]

**EPISTLE LXV.—**Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, copied almost this entire Epistle and made it his own in Book IV, Epistle XXII, when writing to Amblard, abbot of Saint-Martial at Limoges, with the necessary alterations. For what is said here about a proud deacon, Geoffrey [p. 484] applied to a monk who was disobedient and insulting [Col. 0394C] toward his abbot. Another proud deacon, named Maximianus, is mentioned by Augustine in his book *On the Correction of the Donatists*, chapter 4, and in his Epistle to Count Boniface.

**Concerning the deacon.** We have retained this title, which is preferred both by the old editions and by nearly all the old manuscripts. Some have only “Concerning the deacon”; others “Concerning his deacon”; and still others “Concerning the disobedient deacon.”]

## EPISTLE LXV

*(Erasm., III, 9; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXV; Paris., LXIV; Oxford, Leipzig, III.)*

### TO ROGATIANUS, CONCERNING A DEACON WHO CONTENDED AGAINST HIS BISHOP

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian admonishes Bishop Rogatianus to restrain the pride of the deacon who had provoked him with insults and to compel him to repent of his audacity. On this occasion he repeats once more all that was said above in Epistle LV concerning priestly or episcopal authority. It is not sufficiently clear at what time it was written, except that the similar opening of both epistles suggests that it was written at the same synod as the following epistle.

[Note: [Col. 0394C]

**I.—To Rogatianus.** Bishop of Nova in Mauretania. He attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. At the Conference of Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists, Felix, the Catholic bishop of Nova, was present. There was another Nova in Moesia Secunda, whose bishop Peter is named in chapter 19 of the Encyclical Codex in our edition, and chapter 12 in Hardouin’s edition. Hardouin refused to follow our edition, but disturbed the order established by the man who first collected the Epistles contained in the Encyclical Codex. Yet he knew that I had complained about those who supervised the Roman edition of the Councils, because they had changed the ancient order contrary to the intention of the man who collected [Col. 0394D] the Encyclical Epistles.

**My colleagues.** The English editors, who read the word “my” in their manuscripts, nevertheless omitted it from their edition. I have been unable to divine why they did so, unless I suppose that, as often elsewhere, they wished to retain the readings of Rigault’s edition. Yet they could easily have recognized that there was an error in that edition, an error also indicated by the following Epistle, at the beginning of which it is written: “I and my colleagues who were present were deeply distressed.” Moreover, the word omitted by Rigault and the English editors is preferred by all the old editions, eighteen of our old manuscripts, and even certain English manuscripts. Therefore, if it is absent from certain copies—and these are certainly few—it must be supposed that this resulted from the copyists’ negligence and carelessness.

**Concerning your deacon.** If the reading of the Lamonian manuscript and of another old manuscript cited in the English edition [Col. 0395C] is reliable, that deacon was named Cassius. Cassius, bishop of Macomades, attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian.

**To have acted proudly.** I found this reading in only three old manuscripts. It does, however, occur in the old editions. Aldus Manutius printed *superbi esse* (“to be proud”). So too seven [Col. 0395D] of our old manuscripts and seven English manuscripts. Morel wrote *superbire* (“to act proudly”).

**Might be demonstrated.** So twelve of our old manuscripts and seven English manuscripts. The old editions before Pamelius have “might be demonstrated” in the plural. Pamelius himself emended the reading from four manuscripts and an old printed edition, in place of the plural form which Rembolt had printed. In this Pamelius is mistaken, for the Speyer edition and the old Venetian edition also have the same plural reading; and we have likewise found it in eight manuscript copies.]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Rogatianus, greetings.

I and my colleagues who were present were deeply and painfully distressed, dearest brother, when we read your letter in which you complained that your deacon, forgetful of your priestly position and office and oblivious of his own ministry, had provoked you with his insults and injuries.

You, indeed, acted honorably toward us and in accordance with your customary humility [Col. 0394B] by preferring to complain to us about him, although, by virtue of the strength of the episcopate and the authority of your chair, you possessed the power by which you could immediately have punished him. You could be certain that all your colleagues would approve [Note: [Col. 0394B] “regard as valid,” Erasmus.] whatever you had done to your insulting deacon by priestly authority, since you have divine commandments concerning such persons. For the Lord God says in Deuteronomy:

> “And any man who acts proudly by refusing to listen to the priest or the judge, whoever shall be serving in those days—that man shall die; and all the people [Col. 0395A] will hear and be afraid, and they will not act impiously any longer” (Deut. XVII, 12).

And so that we may know that this declaration of God [113] proceeded from his true and supreme majesty [Note: [Col. 0395C] “his” omitted by Oxford.] for the honoring and vindication of his priests: when three of the ministers—Korah, Dathan, and Abiram—dared to act proudly against Aaron the priest, to raise their necks, and to make themselves equal to the priest set over them, they were swallowed up and devoured by the gaping earth and immediately paid the penalty for their sacrilegious audacity. Nor were they alone punished. The other two hundred and fifty who had accompanied them in their audacity were consumed by fire bursting forth from the Lord, so that it might be demonstrated that God’s priests are vindicated by him who makes them priests.

In the Book of Kingdoms also, when Samuel the priest was despised by the Jewish people on account of his old age, just as you now are, the Lord cried out in anger and said:

> “They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me” (1 Sam. VIII, 7).

And to avenge this, he raised up Saul as king over them, who afflicted them with grievous injuries and trampled and oppressed the proud people through every kind of insult and punishment, so that the despised priest might be vindicated against the proud people by divine vengeance.

[Note: [Col. 0395D]

**II.—Your people.** Seven old manuscripts have “your congregation.” But in Epistle LV, p. 80, Epistle LXIX, p. 122, and Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 12, it is written “your people.” So too in the commonly received edition of the New Testament, Acts chapter XXIII. See above, p. 454.

**The Lord also.** Ivo quotes this passage in a greatly abbreviated and mutilated form in Part V, chapter 355, as does Gratian [Col. 0396C] in distinction 93. The Roman Correctors supplied the omissions from Cyprian’s Epistle.

**Under the blow of the passion.** In his book *On Prayer*, Tertullian said “under the imminence of the passion,” as Rigault correctly noted; he also quotes a similar passage from Saint Leo’s eighth sermon *On the Passion of the Lord*. Pamelius, however, printed “the substance of the passion.” This is also the reading [Col. 0396D] in Agobard’s book in the Royal Library.

**Prove.** So too in Epistle LXIX to Florentius, p. 122. In Jerome, Book II *Against the Pelagians*, the reading is: “rebuke concerning jealousy,” or “concerning sin.”

**All these things.** See our notes on Agobard, p. 107.]

### II

But Solomon also, established in the Holy Spirit, testifies and teaches what priestly authority and power are, saying:

> “Fear God with all your soul, and sanctify his priests.”

And again [Note: [Col. 0395C] “he says” added by Lam., Bod. 1, 2.]:

> “Honor God with all your soul, and honor [Note: [Col. 0395C] “and honor,” Bod. 1.] his priests” (Sir. VII, 29, 31).

Mindful of these commandments, the blessed apostle Paul, according to what we read in the Acts of the Apostles, when it was said to him, “Do you thus assail God’s priest with curses?” answered and said [Note: [Col. 0395C] “answered, saying,” Bod. 2, Lam.]:

> “I did not know, [Col. 0395C] brothers, that he is the high priest. For it is written: ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people’” (Acts XXIII, 4).

Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, our king, judge, and God, [Col. 0396A] preserved honor toward high priests and priests until the day of his passion, although they had preserved neither the fear of God nor the recognition [Note: [Col. 0396C] “esteem,” Bod. 1.] of Christ. For when he had cleansed the leper, he said to him:

> “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift” (Matt. VIII, 4).

With the humility by which he taught us also to be humble, he still called “priest” one whom he knew to be sacrilegious.

Likewise, under the blow [Note: [Col. 0396C] “subjected to,” Lin.] of his passion, when he had received a blow to the face and was asked, “Is this how you answer the high priest?” he said nothing insulting against the person of the high priest, but rather defended his own innocence, saying:

> “If I have spoken wrongly, prove [Note: [Col. 0396C] “disprove the testimony,” Lam., York, Bod. 2, NC. 1, 2.] the wrong. But if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John XVIII, 23).

All these things were done by him humbly and patiently so that we might have an example of humility and patience. For by conducting himself in this way even toward false priests, he taught that true priests [Col. 0396B] are lawfully and fully to be honored.

[Note: [Col. 0396D]

**III.—The deacons … the Apostles appointed.** See Tertullian in his book *An Exhortation to Chastity*.

**Ascension.** So sixteen old manuscripts. The old editions, including Morel’s, have *ascensam*, in the manner in which Tertullian and Cyprian customarily write *defensam* for *defensionem* (“defense”) and *remissam* for *remissionem* (“remission”). Yet I found the word *ascensam* here in only four ancient manuscripts. One has *ascensionem* (“ascension”).

**And the honor of the priest.** The Bec manuscript reads: “and that he acknowledge the honor of the priest.” The Chartres manuscript: “that he acknowledge the honor of the priest.” The Metz Saint-Arnoul manuscript: “and that he acknowledge the honor of the priest.”

[Col. 0397C] [p. 485] **Toward him.** Although this reading can be accepted, I would nevertheless prefer the reading given by five old copies, in which it is written “against him.” For I have often seen *circa* (“toward”) written for *contra* (“against”) in ancient manuscripts, and conversely. Nevertheless, I have been unwilling to alter anything.]

### III

Deacons, moreover, ought to remember that the Lord chose the Apostles—that is, the bishops and superiors—whereas, after the Lord’s ascent into heaven, the Apostles appointed deacons for themselves as ministers of their episcopate and of the Church. If we are able to presume to do anything against God, who makes bishops, then deacons too, who are made by us, may presume to act against us. And therefore the deacon [Note: [Col. 0396C] “The deacon Cassius ought,” Lin.] about whom you write ought to repent of his presumption, acknowledge the honor due to the priest, and make full satisfaction to the bishop who is his superior, in complete humility. For these are the beginnings of heretics and the origins and endeavors of schismatics whose thoughts are evil: they become self-satisfied and, swollen with pride, despise their superior. Thus men withdraw from [Col. 0396C] the Church; thus a profane altar is set up outside it; thus they rebel against the peace of Christ and against the ordinance and unity of God.

But if he should further exasperate and provoke you by his insults [Col. 0397A], exercise against him the authority belonging to your office, either by deposing him or by excluding him from communion. For if the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, said, “Let no one despise your youth” [Note: [Col. 0397C] “Contemn,” Lam. NC. 1, Ebor.] (1 Tim. 4:12), how much more should your colleagues say to you, “Let no one despise your old age.” And since 114 you have written that a certain person has associated himself with this deacon of yours and shares in his pride and presumption, you will also be able to restrain or exclude him—and any others who prove to be of the same kind and act against the priest of God—except that we exhort and admonish them rather to recognize that they have sinned and to make satisfaction, and to allow us to maintain our settled purpose. For we would rather overcome the insults and injuries of individuals by merciful patience than [Col. 0397B] avenge them by priestly authority. I wish you, dearest brother, always to fare well.

[Note: [Col. 0397C]

**LETTER LXVI.—I. Furni.** At the Conference of Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists there was present Florentius, the Donatist bishop of Furni; at the Council of Carthage under Bishop Boniface, however, Simon was bishop of the people of Furni. But at the time when Cyprian was writing this, the bishop of the people of Furni was Geminius, as the acts of the Council of Carthage held under Cyprian show—perhaps the same man who is named Geminius Victor here, as Pamelius conjectured. Pearson refutes him in the *Cyprianic Annals* under the year 249.

**In the council.** So far as I know, this council is mentioned nowhere except in this Letter. Rigaltius thought that these words of Cyprian had been transcribed by him from a decree of the council. I do not know, however, whether that opinion can be correct. See Julius Nigronius, *Ascetical Treatise* XIV, ch. 2.

**In clerical ministry.** I prefer this reading, which eleven old books exhibit, because I think it accords better with Cyprian’s style. Nevertheless, it is difficult to establish the true reading of this passage. The old editions and four old books have [Col. 0398C] *clericali ministerio* (“in clerical ministry”); the Manutian edition and eleven old books have *clerico ministerio* (“in clerical ministry”), with which an old manuscript of Reims agrees, although through error it has *cleri comministerio* (“in the clergy’s fellow-ministry”). The manuscripts of Foix and Bec have *cleri ministerio* (“in the ministry of the clergy”); the Pithou manuscript, *clericorum ministerio* (“in the ministry of clerics”).

**How much more by worldly burdens.** Rigaltius printed *quanto magis clerici molestiis* (“how much more ought clerics by burdens…”). But the word *clerici* (“clerics”) is not recognized [Col. 0398D] by the other editions, except the English edition, which follows that of Rigaltius, nor by the old copies. It is certainly superfluous and useless. Reinhart therefore rightly expunged it. We have followed the old copies and old editions.

**By clerical ordination.** I also prefer this reading because of its agreement with the style of Saint Cyprian, although I have found it only in five old books and in the Manutian edition. The Morellian edition and one old royal codex have *ordinatione clericali* (“by clerical ordination”); the Verona manuscript and eight others, *ad ordinationem clericam* (“to clerical ordination”); the old editions and eight old copies, *ad ordinationem clericalem*. My reading is also confirmed by the authority of Cyprian, who said in Letter XXXIII, p. 46: “Such a man deserved the further grades of clerical ordination.” Likewise, in his translation of Firmilian’s Letter, p. 149: “Assuming for themselves the power of clerical ordination.”]

# LETTER LXVI

*(Erasm., I, 9. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXVI. Paris., LXV. Oxon., Lips., I.)*

## TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE RESIDING AT FURNI, CONCERNING VICTOR, WHO NAMED THE PRESBYTER FAUSTINUS AS GUARDIAN

**SUMMARY.—** Since Geminius Victor, contrary to the decree of a council of bishops, had named the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as his guardian or curator in his will, Cyprian forbids an offering to be made for Victor or a sacrifice to be celebrated for his repose. In passing, drawing a conclusion from the example of the Levitical tribe, he explains that clerics ought not to involve themselves in worldly burdens.

[Col. 0397C] **I.** Cyprian sends greetings to the presbyters and deacons and to the people residing at Furni.

We were deeply disturbed [Col. 0398A]—both I and my colleagues who were present, and our fellow-presbyters who were seated beside us [Note: [Col. 0397C] “Were standing beside us,” Foss. Spir. Remb.; “with us,” Thu. Corb.]—dearest brothers, when we learned that our brother Geminius Victor, on departing from this world, had named the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian in his will. For it was decreed long ago in a council of bishops that no one should appoint any member of the clergy or minister of God as guardian or curator [Note: [Col. 0397C] “Custodian,” Lam. Ebor. Ben.] in his will, since those individually honored with the divine priesthood and appointed to clerical ministry ought to serve only the altar and the sacrifices, and to devote themselves to prayers and supplications. For it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles [Note: [Col. 0397C] “Involves,” Foss.] himself in worldly burdens [Note: [Col. 0397C] “Affairs,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.], so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2:4).

Although this was said of everyone, how much more ought those occupied with divine and spiritual [Note: [Col. 0398C] “Good things,” Bod. 2, Ebor. NC. 2, Lam.; “those who are occupied with spiritual things,” printed text.] matters not to be bound [Col. 0398B] by worldly burdens and snares, since they cannot withdraw from the Church and devote themselves to earthly and secular affairs? The Levites formerly observed in the Law the pattern of this ordinance and religious practice. When the eleven tribes divided the land and apportioned their possessions, the tribe of Levi, which devoted itself to the temple, the altar, and the divine ministries, received nothing from that apportioned share. Instead, while the others cultivated the land, that tribe worshiped God alone and received from the eleven tribes, for its livelihood and sustenance, tithes from the produce that grew [Note: [Col. 0398C] “Received,” Oxon.]. All this was done by divine authority and arrangement, so that those who devoted themselves to divine works might not be called away to any other matter or compelled to think about or conduct secular affairs.

This same principle and pattern is now maintained among the clergy: those who are advanced in the Lord’s Church [Col. 0398C] by clerical ordination are not to be called away in any respect from divine service or bound to worldly burdens and affairs [Col. 0399A]. Instead, supported by the contributions of their brothers and receiving them as though they were tithes from the produce, they are not to withdraw from the altar and the sacrifices, but to serve heavenly and spiritual things by day and by night.

[Note: [Col. 0399D]

**II.—For his repose.** Here once again the ignorance and carelessness of the old copyists must be observed. Two old books have *ordinatione* (“ordination”) instead of *pro dormitione* (“for his repose”), producing a false and inept sense. The same must be said of the word *deprecatio* (“supplication”), which follows shortly afterward and for which the Corbie and Foix manuscripts read *delegatio* (“delegation”). The English editors note that the Thuanus manuscript is also so written. This is not true, since both words—or rather, *deprecatio*—are absent from it, and nothing is placed in their stead.

**Repose.** As Rigaltius observes on the third Letter, Christians avoided the word “death” as much as they could because of their hope in the resurrection and eternal life. Thus, instead of “dead,” they said “sent on ahead”; and instead of “death,” they used “departure,” “passing,” “repose,” and “assumption,” as could readily be demonstrated from the testimony of Tertullian, Cyprian, Jerome, and others. See Erasmus’s annotations on Luke 9. I have frequently found “the Assumption of Peter,” “the Assumption of Paul,” and that of others in ancient [Col. 0400D] codices containing lives of the saints. The controversy that arose in our own age in the Church of Paris concerning the Assumption of the most blessed Virgin Mary is well known. This is not the place to reopen it. I shall say only this: Pope John XXII thought that she had not yet gone into heaven and would not enter into the joy of her Lord before the day of judgment. See our notes on the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*, p. 789.

**Priests and ministers.** The Foix codex reads: “They draw away the priests and ministers of God from his altar and Church and summon them to worldly burdens.”

**Ministers.** The editions of Erasmus and Morel add “his Levites.” I found this Letter in nineteen ancient copies, and I did not find this addition in any of them. Manutius and the others therefore did well to reject it.]

**II.** Our predecessor bishops, considering this religiously and making salutary provision, decreed that no brother, when departing this life, should name a cleric to a guardianship or curatorship, and that, if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him [Note: [Col. 0399C] “No sacrifice for him, nor for his repose,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1, 2.], nor should a sacrifice be celebrated for his repose. For a man who wished to call priests and ministers away from the altar does not deserve to be named at God’s altar in the prayer of the priests.

Therefore, since Victor dared, contrary to the rule recently laid down by the priests in council, to appoint the presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian, 115 no offering for his repose is to be made among you [Col. 0399B], nor is any supplication in his name to be regularly offered in the Church. Thus the decree of the priests, made religiously and necessarily, may be observed by us; and at the same time an example may be given to the other brothers, so that no one may summon the priests and ministers of God, who devote themselves to his altar and Church, to worldly burdens. For it will be possible to ensure that such a thing is not hereafter done again with respect to members of the clergy, if what has now been done is punished. [Note: [Col. 0400C] The following words are absent from Lam. Ebor. NC. 1; indeed, this valedictory formula is regularly absent from most manuscripts.] I wish you, dearest brothers, always to fare well.

# LETTER LXVII

*(Erasm., III, 13. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXVII. Paris., LXVI. Lips., Oxon., LXVIII. Coustant, Epist. Rom. Pont. 4, p. 211.)*

## TO STEPHEN, CONCERNING MARCIAN OF ARLES, WHO SIDED WITH NOVATIAN

[Col. 0399C] **SUMMARY.—** Since Marcian, bishop of Arles, had followed the sect of Novatian, led many astray, and separated himself by schism from communion with the other bishops, Cyprian admonishes Stephen, the supreme pontiff, to use his authority, in Marcian’s absence, to substitute another in his place; and, after penance has been performed, to grant peace and permit a return to the Church both to the lapsed and to those whom Marcian had led astray.

# 117 LETTER LXVIII

*(Erasm., I, 4. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXVIII. Paris., LXVII. Oxon., Lips., LXVII. Routh, Rell. Scr., III, pp. 77 and 122.)*

## TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE RESIDING IN SPAIN, CONCERNING BASILIDES AND MARTIALIS

[Col. 0400A]

**SUMMARY.—** Since the bishops Basilides and Martialis had lapsed and had been defiled by certificates of idolatry, Cyprian and his fellow-bishops commend the clergy and people of the Spains for having substituted Sabinus and Felix in their place by a lawful election—especially since, according to the decree of Cornelius, lapsed bishops could indeed be admitted to perform penance, but were barred from priestly office. In passing, he also touches upon certain matters concerning the ancient rite for the election of bishops. The context indicates that it was written during the pontificate of [Col. 0400B] Stephen.

# 121 LETTER LXIX

*(Erasm., IV, 9. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXIX. Paris., LVIII. Oxon., Lips., LXVI.)*

## TO FLORENTIUS PUPIANUS, CONCERNING DETRACTORS

**SUMMARY.—** Cyprian clears himself before Florentius Pupianus of various crimes alleged by him and reproves his fickleness of mind because he so rashly believed detractors. Moreover, because he says that he had then already held the episcopate for six years, it is sufficiently clear that the Letter was written under Stephen.

[Note: [Col. 0400D]

**493 LETTER LXIX.—I. Pupianus.** John Tristan of Saint-Amant, in the second volume of his *Commentaries*, [Col. 0401D] p. 493, suspects that *Pupienus* could be read here, because in the *Historia Augusta* he found several people bearing that name. (I would believe that Pupianus grudged Cyprian the name Caecilius and, out of contempt, greeted him by the title Thascius, by which he was known among the pagans. OXON.)

**Smaller things.** The Chartres codex reads “the smallest things.”]

**I.** Cyprian, also called Thascius, sends greetings to Florentius, also called Pupianus, his brother.

I had believed, brother, that you had at last now turned to repentance for having in the past so rashly either heard or believed such unspeakable, such shameful things about us—things execrable even to pagans. But now I observe in your letter that you are still the same man you were before: that you believe the same things about us and persist in what you have believed; and that, lest perhaps the dignity of your glory and martyrdom be stained by communion with us, you are diligently investigating our conduct and, after God the Judge, [Col. 0401A] who makes priests, you desire to judge—not merely me (for how important am I [Note: [Col. 0401C] “Am” is absent from Spir. Innom. Erasm.]?)—but the judgment of God and Christ.

This is not to believe in God; this is to stand as a rebel against Christ and his Gospel. For he says, “Are not two sparrows sold for an as? And neither of them falls to the ground without the will of the Father” (Matt. 10:29), and his majesty and truth thereby prove that even smaller things do not happen without God’s knowledge and permission; yet you suppose that priests of God are ordained in the Church without his knowledge. For to believe that those who are ordained are unworthy and unchaste—what else is this than to believe [Note: [Col. 0401C] “To contend,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1, 2. Ben. Neap.; “to concede,” Ver.] that his priests are appointed in the Church neither by God nor through God?

[Note: [Col. 0401D]

**II.—But the assurance of truth is genuine.** The codex of Saint-Arnoul reads: “But the assurance of truth would be uncertain unless another were the proclaimer and witness.”

**He is a witness concerning me.** The Foix codex reads: “He bears witness concerning me.”

**By the strength of its faith.** Thus I have read in eleven ancient copies and in the editions of Manutius and Morel. The Speyer manuscript, the old Venetian edition, the Erasmian edition, and five other old copies have “by God’s rights,” undoubtedly through an error of the copyists. For in ancient manuscripts I have often seen *juribus* (“rights”) written for *viribus* (“strength”) and conversely.]

**II.** Do you think that my own testimony concerning myself is greater than God’s testimony, when the Lord himself teaches and says that testimony is not true if someone appears as a witness concerning himself? For everyone naturally favors [Note: [Col. 0401C] “Pleases,” Ver.] himself, and no one produces accusations hostile and adverse to himself. But the assurance of truth is genuine [Note: [Col. 0401C] “It is genuine if truth,” Lin.] if in our proclamations another is the proclaimer and witness: “If I bear witness concerning myself,” he says, “my testimony is not true. For there is another who bears witness concerning me” (John 5:31–32).

If the Lord himself, who is afterward to judge all things [Note: [Col. 0401C] “Since all things,” Lam. NC. 1; “who all things,” Pem. Bod. 1. [Col. 0402C] “Is to judge,” Lam. Lin. Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. NC. 1, 2.], did not wish his own testimony to be believed on its own, but preferred to be vindicated by the judgment and testimony of God the Father, how much more ought his servants to observe this principle? They are not only vindicated by God’s judgment and testimony, but even glory in it.

Yet with you, against the divine verdict and against our conscience, which rests upon the strength of its faith, the fabrication of enemies and malicious men has prevailed—as though among the lapsed and profane, those placed outside the Church, from whose breasts the Holy Spirit has departed, there could be anything except a depraved mind, a deceitful tongue, poisonous hatreds, and sacrilegious lies. Anyone who believes them must necessarily be found among them when the day of judgment comes.

[Note: [Col. 0401D]

**III.—Because both the Lord.** The codex of Saint-Arnoul reads: “Because [Col. 0402D] the Apostles too were humble.”

**To exert himself.** The same codex reads “to put himself to the test.”

**People.** I have retained this reading because it agrees with several ancient codices and because it is so read in Letter LV, p. 81, and Letter LXV, p. 113. Nevertheless, “your people” is written in twelve of our very old copies, in seven English manuscripts, in the old editions, and also in the Manutian and Morellian editions.

**For the persecution.** The codex of Saint-Arnoul reads: “For the persecution, coming upon you, to the highest…”]

**III.** As for your assertion that priests ought to be humble [Col. 0402A], because both the Lord and his Apostles were humble: all the brothers, and even the pagans, know and esteem my humility exceedingly well. You too knew and esteemed it, 122 when you were still in the Church and in communion with me. Which of us, then, is far removed from humility? Is it I, who daily serve the brothers and receive each person who comes to the Church kindly, eagerly, and joyfully? Or is it you, who appoint yourself the bishop of a bishop and the judge of a judge appointed for a time by God [Note: [Col. 0402C] “Bishop over a bishop, and judge over a judge,” Bod. 2. Lam. Ebor.]?

The Lord God says in Deuteronomy: “And whatever man acts proudly, so as not to obey the priest or judge, whoever shall be in those days, that man shall die; and all the people, when they hear, shall fear, and they shall no longer act impiously” (Deut. 17:12–13). Again, he speaks to Samuel and says: [Col. 0402B] “They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me” (1 Kings [1 Sam.] 8:7). And furthermore, when it was said to the Lord in the Gospel, “Is this how you answer the high priest?” he observed and taught that priestly honor ought to be maintained. He said nothing against the high priest, but merely vindicated his own innocence, answering: “If I have spoken evil, give evidence of the evil. But if well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23).

Likewise, when it was said to the blessed Apostle, “Is this how you leap upon the priest of God with curses?” (Acts 23:4–5), he said nothing insulting against the priest, although he could steadfastly have asserted himself against those who had crucified the Lord and who had already lost [Note: [Col. 0402C] “Had forfeited,” Lin. NC. 2.] God and Christ and the temple and priesthood. Rather, although the priests were false and despoiled, he nevertheless considered even the empty shadow of the priestly [Col. 0402C] name and said: “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest. For it is written: ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people [Note: [Col. 0402C] “Congregation,” Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.]’” (Exod. 22:28).

[Note: [Col. 0402D]

**IV.—But me.** The old books vary greatly in this passage. In the Dijon manuscript, the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul at Metz, and the Lamonian manuscript it is written: “But me he cast down by the honor of proscription, when it was rather publicly read: ‘If anyone possesses any of the property of Caecilius Cyprian the bishop.’” One old manuscript of mine has almost the same reading. One Reims manuscript reads: “But when the proscription of Caecilius Cyprian was read concerning me, ‘If anyone holds or possesses,’ it cast me down by honor, when it was rather publicly read: ‘If anyone holds [Col. 0403C] any of the property of Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of the Christians, let him be proscribed,’ so that even…” etc.

**Burden.** Six of our old books, two Angelican manuscripts, and the Verona manuscript have “honor”; similarly, in the passages cited shortly before, three have “terror.” See the observations of Rigaltius.

**Bishop of the Christians.** Erasmus’s edition adds “let him be proscribed.” I have found this nowhere except in the Reims manuscript cited shortly before. But there everything is extremely confused and intermingled.

**By a vicarious ordination.** See our notes on Lupus of Ferrières, pp. 422, 425, 427.]

**IV.** Unless perhaps I was a priest for you before the persecution, when you were in communion with me, but ceased to be a priest after the persecution. For the persecution came and raised you to the highest sublimity of martyrdom, but cast me down [Col. 0403A] beneath the burden of proscription, when it was publicly read: “If anyone holds or possesses any of the property of Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of the Christians”—so that even those who did not believe God when he appointed me bishop might at least believe the devil [Note: [Col. 0403B] “He believed … he might believe,” Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.] when he proscribed me as bishop.

I do not set these things forth boastfully, but in grief, since you appoint yourself judge of God and Christ. Christ says to the Apostles, and through them to all superiors who succeed the Apostles by a vicarious ordination: “He who hears you hears me, and he who hears me hears him who sent me. And he who rejects you rejects me and him who sent me” (Luke 10:16).

[Note: [Col. 0403C]

**V.—For from this.** The old editions, the Morellian edition, and eight old copies have: “For whence have schisms and heresies arisen, and whence do they arise, except when the bishop…” [Col. 0403D] We have followed the authority of the greater number of old copies.

**Unworthy in the judgment of men.** This reading is confirmed by eleven old books and the editions of Manutius and Morel. But the early editions and two manuscript books prefer “by unworthy men.” Thus Paulinus, bishop of Trier, was judged unworthy of the Church by the Arian bishops, as we noted on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 486.

**Nor the brotherhood.** The Foix codex reads: “Nor has the clergy had a bishop.” I would gladly prefer this reading if it rested on the authority of more old books.

**And communion.** Four old books read: “and the law of communion handed down.”

**By the authority of your judicial examination.** Three old books read: “to restore by the judgment of your examination.” Two others: “to restore by the vigor of your examination.” So too the Sorbonne manuscript, except that the word “vigor” has dropped out through a copyist’s error. In the Thuanus manuscript it is written, “to form by the victor of your examination”; in the Lamenian manuscript, “the victor of your examination.” All these readings would seem perhaps to suggest that *cognitionis tuae vigore* (“by the vigor of your examination”) ought to be read.]

**V.** For from this have schisms and heresies arisen, and from this they continue to arise: the bishop, who is one and presides over the Church, is despised through the proud presumption of certain people, and a man honored by God’s gracious favor is judged unworthy by men [Col. 0403B].

What swelling of pride is this? What arrogance of spirit, what inflation of mind—to summon superiors and priests before your own tribunal, so that, unless we have been cleared before you and acquitted by your sentence, behold: for six years now the brotherhood has had no bishop, the people no superior, the flock no shepherd, the Church no governor, Christ no high priest [Note: [Col. 0403C] “The Holy Spirit no high priest,” Lin.], and God no priest. Let Pupianus come to the rescue; let him pronounce sentence and enter the judgment of God and Christ as received and approved, lest so great a number of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0403C] “A new body of believers,” Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. [Col. 0404C] 1, 2.]—who have been summoned under our ministry—should appear to have departed without hope of salvation and peace; lest the new body of believers be judged to have obtained through us no grace of Baptism and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0404A]; and lest the peace granted to so many lapsed penitents, and the communion conceded after our examination, be annulled by the authority of your judgment.

Consent at last, and deign to make a pronouncement concerning us and to confirm our episcopate by the authority of your judicial examination, so that God and his Christ may be able to thank you because through you a high priest and ruler has been restored both to their altar and to their people.

[Note: [Col. 0404C]

**VI.—And livestock a leader.** Some old books omit the word “livestock” here and have “judge” written instead of “leader.”

**Robbers obey their chief.** That is, their prince, their leader, or their superior, as Cyprian will say shortly afterward. Lucifer of Cagliari, in his *Second Apology for Saint Athanasius*, says: “By your fruits, Emperor Constantius, you are recognized as being not a Christian but plainly a servant of robbers.” Suetonius, in his *Vespasian*, called a man who used to travel every year from Umbria into the Sabine country to cultivate fields a *manceps operarum* (“contractor of labor”). Prudentius [Col. 0404D], in his poem on Saint Vincent the martyr, calls the prison guard a *manceps*: “Then the keeper of the prison himself and the doorkeeper of the chains.” Cicero, *On Duties* I: “Even robbers are said to have laws which they obey and observe.” Likewise, in the speech *For His House*: “Finally, he cannot discover that I had become even a contractor or robber in a partnership of plunder.” Caelius Calcagninus, book I, Letter 21, interprets *mancipes* as lessees and tax-farmers. See the notes of Jacques Godefroy on Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 9.

**How much more straightforward.** Five old books have: “How much more straightforward and better than you are the brute, savage, and raging…” In one manuscript in which the same reading is found, “mute” is written instead of “brute.” The Foix manuscript reads: “How much more straightforward and better are the brute animals.”]

**VI.** Bees have a king, and livestock has a leader, and they remain faithful to him; robbers obey their chief [*manceps*] with submission full of 123 humility [Note: [Col. 0404B] “And they remain faithful; robbers obey their chief,” Oxon.; “slaves,” [Col. 0404C] Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Ebor. NC. 1.]. How much more straightforward and better than you are brute livestock and mute animals—and even plunderers, though bloodthirsty and raging amid swords and weapons! Among them a superior is acknowledged and feared, though no divine sentence appointed him; instead, a ruined faction and a criminal band agreed upon him [Col. 0404B].

[Note: [Col. 0405C]

**VII.—So many bishops.** I have restored the reading of the old editions, which is confirmed by the authority of the old copies. Manutius and Morel printed “fellow-bishops.” That reading is found in seven ancient codices.

**Put to the question.** That is, subjected to judicial examination under torture. Executioners are called *quaestionarii* (“torturers”) in the old translation of the Council of Ephesus and in Marius Mercator. See above, p. 408.

**Alone unimpaired.** Thus Jerome, in his Letter to Pammachius, addressing John of Jerusalem, says: “You, most blessed Pope and disdainful high priest, alone rich, alone wise, alone noble and eloquent, look down with wrinkled brow and sidelong eyes upon your fellow-servants, who were redeemed by your Lord’s blood.” In the opposite sense, in Apuleius’s first book of the *Metamorphoses*, Socrates is called *integer*: sound and unharmed.]

**VII.** You said, certainly, that a scruple into which you had fallen had to be removed from your mind. You did fall into it—but through your irreligious credulity. You did fall into it—but through your sacrilegious mind and will, since you readily listen to unchaste, impious, and unspeakable accusations against a brother, against a priest; gladly believe them; and defend another’s lies as though they were your own private lies. You do not remember that it is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and refuse to hear a wicked tongue” (Sir. 28:28). And again: “An evil man listens to the tongue of the wicked, but a righteous man pays no heed to lying lips” (Prov. 17:4).

Why did the martyrs, filled with the Holy Spirit and already drawn near through suffering to the sight [Col. 0405A] of God and his Christ, not fall into this scruple? From prison they sent letters to Cyprian the bishop, acknowledging him as a priest of God and bearing witness to him. Why did so many bishops, my colleagues, not fall into this scruple—those who, when they departed from our midst [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Departed,” Bod. 1.], were proscribed; or were arrested, thrown into prison, and held in chains; or, banished into exile, journeyed to the Lord by a glorious path; or, executed in certain places, received heavenly crowns through the Lord’s glorification?

Why did so many from this people of ours, who are with us and have been entrusted to us by God’s gracious favor, not fall into this scruple: so many confessors put to the question and tortured, glorious in the remembrance of their distinguished wounds and scars; so many undefiled virgins; so many praiseworthy widows; and, finally, whole churches throughout the entire [Col. 0405B] world joined with us by the bond of unity? Unless perhaps all these people [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Unless all this,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 2. NC. 1.] who are in communion with me have, as you wrote, been polluted by our polluted mouth and have lost the hope of eternal life through contamination by our communion. Pupianus alone is unimpaired, inviolate, holy, and chaste; he, who refused to associate with us, will alone dwell in paradise and in the kingdom of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0405D]

**VIII.—Would have had to be cast out.** Rufinus, speaking of people of this kind in his treatment of Psalm 24, says: “For enemies are not lacking only outside, but even within the communion of the Church itself.”

**To be built.** This is unquestionably how it must be written. For when these words were spoken by Peter, Christ had not yet made him the promise concerning the Church that was to be built upon him. Most ancient codices and the old editions prefer this reading. See Erasmus’s annotations on Matthew 16.

**495 In the name of the Church.** Because Peter, in a figurative universality, represented the person of the whole Church, as Augustine says. Those who attempt to transfer this argument elsewhere torment themselves to no purpose.

[Col. 0406C] **Of those unwilling to obey.** Thus the old editions and four old books. So too in Nicholas of Cusa, *On the Concordance of the Catholic Church*, book XI, ch. 14. Manutius printed “of those willing.” This also pleased Morel, Pamelius, and Rigaltius, although Rigaltius noted in his Errata that “unwilling” should be read. The English editors did not notice this; although they otherwise almost always follow Rigaltius’s edition, they printed “willing” in their own. Reinhart accepted Rigaltius’s correction. This is the true reading. The other cannot be sustained.

**You ought to know.** In Ivo, part V, ch. 360, and in Gratian, VII, q. 1, this is cited from Cyprian’s Letter to Papaianus—or Papinianus, as others wrote. The Roman Correctors amended this and noted that it survives in the Letter to Florentius Pupianus. From this passage Juan de Torquemada drew an argument for inveighing against titular bishops, who have neither a church nor a people. We recently said some rather curious things about them in book III, ch. 19 of the *History of Tudela*. Their abolition was discussed on Saturday, 5 February 1547, at the Council of Trent, because the Church sustains many losses and disadvantages from them and receives no or very little benefit, as Odorico Raynaldi demonstrated from a manuscript codex of the Vatican archive under the year 1547, § 76. Their abolition was most recently discussed again following the report of the most illustrious François Bosquet, bishop of Lodève, in 1656, at the Assembly of the Gallican Church. See the *Acts*, pp. 300, 344.

**The bishop is in the Church.** It is absolutely certain that the bishop is in the Church [Col. 0407C] and the Church in the bishop. For the Church is the people adhering to the priest. There was a certain not undistinguished writer who, at the close of the sixteenth Christian century, explained this passage of Cyprian as though Cyprian had held that the supreme pontiff was above a council, although no mention is made here either of the Roman bishop or of a council. Thus it often happens that zeal sweeps people away into distorted opinions.]

**VIII.** You also wrote that the Church now, because of me, has a portion of itself dispersed, when the entire people of the Church is gathered and united and joined to itself in undivided concord. Only those have remained outside who, even if they had been inside, would have had to be cast out. Nor does the Lord, the protector and guardian of his people, allow the wheat to be snatched away from his threshing floor; only the chaff can be separated from the Church. For the Apostle says: [Col. 0405C] “For what if some of them have fallen away from the faith? [Col. 0406A] Has their unbelief made the faithfulness of God void? By no means. For God is true, but every man a liar” (Rom. 3:3–4).

And in the Gospel too, when his disciples abandoned him as he spoke, the Lord turned to the Twelve and said, “Do you also wish to go away?” Peter answered him, saying: “Lord, to whom shall we go [Note: [Col. 0405C] “Are we going,” Rigalt., against the manuscripts and editions.]? You have the word [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Words,” Oxon.] of eternal life, and we believe and have come to know that you are the Son of the living God” (John 6:67–69).

Peter speaks there—the one upon whom the Church was to be built—teaching and showing in the name of the Church that, even if a defiant and proud multitude of those unwilling to obey should depart, the Church nevertheless does not depart from Christ. And the Church consists of the people united to the priest and the flock adhering to its shepherd. Hence you ought to know that the bishop is in the Church and the Church in the bishop [Col. 0406B]; and that if anyone is not with the bishop, he is not in the Church. Those who do not have peace with the priests of God, but insinuate themselves among certain persons and secretly believe that they are in communion, flatter themselves in vain. For the Church, which is catholic and one, is neither torn nor divided, but is assuredly joined and held together by the cement of priests who adhere 124 to one another.

IX. Therefore, brother, if you will reflect upon the majesty of God, who appoints priests; if you will at some point look to Christ [Note: [Col. 0406C] “Christ appoints” Lam., Lin., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1, Spir., Innom.], who by his judgment, command, and presence governs both the rulers themselves and the Church together with its rulers; if, concerning the innocence of the priests, you will trust not human hatred but divine judgment; if you will begin, even belatedly, to repent of your recklessness, pride, and insolence; if you make the fullest satisfaction to God and his Christ, whom I serve [Col. 0406C] and to whom, with a pure and unstained mouth, I unceasingly offer sacrifices [Col. 0407A] alike in persecution and in peace—we shall be able to take your communion into consideration. Nevertheless, regard and fear for the divine judgment will remain with us, so that I may first consult my Lord as to whether, by his revelation and admonition, he permits peace to be granted to you and you to be admitted to the communion of his Church.

[Note: [Col. 0407C]

**X.—What has been shown to me.** In those ancient times revelations were received in sleep, as is evident from Tertullian, Cyprian, Rufinus, and others. Later, when the Christian religion enjoyed complete freedom, Christ, the blessed Virgin Mary, the apostle Peter, and the other [Col. 0407D] saints made themselves visible to pious and credulous people and spoke with them face to face, as a friend is accustomed to speak with his friend. Countless examples of these visions survive in ecclesiastical history. Saint Vincent Ferrer, in his *Sermon on the Octave of the Holy Innocents*: “There are many dreams that are believed to be divine revelations but are illusions.” See above, p. 452.

**Dreams.** Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV, relates that certain learned men regretted that they had not been born among the Atlanteans, among whom it is recorded that dreams are not seen. Martianus Capella likewise attests this in book VI, in his *Description of Inner Africa*.

**Foolish visions.** Aelius Spartianus, in his *Hadrian*, after recounting the story of a certain woman who said that she had been warned in a dream to inform Hadrian that he should not kill himself, adds that Marius Maximus records that these things were done as a pretense. For the pagans attributed great importance [Col. 0408C] to such nocturnal visions, as is evident from the final part of Apuleius’ *Metamorphoses*, from book II of Livy, Valerius Maximus, and others. Quintilian, book IV, chapter 2: “The embellishments drawn from dreams and superstitions have by now lost their authority through their very facility.” See also Lactantius, book II, chapter 8, and Nicolaus Gerbelius’ preface to the book of the *Shepherd*.

**Both will be read aloud.** Thus the old editions, twelve of our old manuscripts, and one Bodleian manuscript. Manutius printed: “Both letters will be read aloud.” Although I know that this latter reading exists in three ancient copies and can be sound, I do not doubt that the reading I have retained is to be preferred.]

X. For I remember what has already been shown to me—or rather, what has been commanded to an obedient and God-fearing servant [Note: [Col. 0407C] “what to a servant” Oxon.] by the authority of the Lord and of God. Among the other things that he deigned to show and reveal, he also added this: “Thus, he who does not believe Christ when he makes a priest [Note: [Col. 0407C] “would believe” Impr.] will afterward begin to believe Christ [Note: [Col. 0408C] “begins” Rigalt.] when he vindicates the priest.”

Although I know that dreams seem ridiculous and visions foolish to some, they certainly seem so to those [Col. 0407B] who prefer to believe against priests rather than to believe a priest. Yet this is no wonder, since Joseph’s brothers said of him: “Behold, that dreamer is coming. Come now, therefore; let us kill him” (Gen. XXXVII, 19–20). And afterward the dreamer obtained what he had dreamed, while his murderers and sellers were put to confusion, so that those who had not believed words beforehand might subsequently believe deeds.

As for the things that you have done, whether during persecution or during peace, it would be foolish for me to wish to judge you, since you have instead appointed yourself as our judge. I have written this reply from the pure conscience of my mind and from confidence in my Lord and God. You have my letter, and I have yours. On the day of judgment, before the tribunal of Christ, both will be read aloud [Note: [Col. 0408C] “Both letters will be read aloud” Oxon.].

## LETTER LXX

*(Erasm., I, 2. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Oxon., Lips., LXX. Paris., LXIX. Routh, Rell. scr. III, pp. 84 and 135.)*

### TO JANUARIUS AND THE OTHER NUMIDIAN BISHOPS, ON BAPTIZING HERETICS

[Col. 0408A]

**SUMMARY.—**You have the subject of this and the following letter in the third letter after this one, addressed to Stephen, in these words:

> “That the baptism used by heretics is no baptism, and that no one among those who oppose Christ can profit through the grace of Christ, was carefully set forth recently in the letter written in reply to Quintus, our colleague stationed in Mauretania, concerning this matter; likewise in the letter that our colleagues previously sent to the bishops presiding in Numidia. I have appended copies of both letters.”

[Col. 0408B] Both are also mentioned in the letter to Jubaianus, and this letter is mentioned in the following one.

## 126 LETTER LXXI

*(Erasm., to Quintinus, p. 337. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Oxon., Lips., LXXI. Paris., LXX.)*

### TO QUINTUS, ON BAPTIZING HERETICS

**SUMMARY.—**A reply is made to Quintus, a bishop in Mauretania, who had consulted Cyprian about baptizing heretics.

[Note: [Col. 0408D]

**497 LETTER LXXI.—I.** The first edition of this letter is owed to Erasmus, who published it in 1519. But because it stands outside the sequence of the letters and was placed after the books of the *Testimonies*, following the letters to Jubaianus and Pompeius, Eck, failing to notice that it lay outside the numbering of the letters, although he possessed a copy of it, cited a passage from it as though it were unpublished in book II, chapter 1, of *The Primacy of the Pope*. He also transcribes some of its words from book II, chapter 1, of Augustine’s work against the Donatists. I emended it by collating it with sixteen ancient manuscripts.

**To the brother Quintus.** The following letter will show that he was a bishop in Mauretania.

**Lucianus.** I think that he is the man who wrote Letters XVI and XXI, and who is also mentioned in Letter XXII.

**At the council.** See Letter LXX to the Numidians.

[Col. 0409C] **Some of our colleagues**, such as Florentius, surnamed Pupianus, as is evident from Letter LXIX written to him.

**Namely, it is one.** I have retained the reading of five old [Col. 0409D] manuscripts, which seems to me the best. Erasmus and others after him printed: “Namely, it is one in the Catholic Church. If that Church is one, baptism cannot exist outside the Church.” Some old manuscripts have “apart from the Church.”

**Two baptisms.** The editions of Erasmus and Morellius add “or many.” But these words are absent from fourteen old manuscripts. They are present, however, in the Corbie manuscript. Arator, book II of the *Acts of the Apostles*: “Why do you profanely desire to counterfeit a twofold baptism?” Optatus, book I: “You see, therefore, brother Parmenianus, that the heretics, exiles from the house of truth, alone possess various and false baptisms, by which one who is defiled cannot wash clean, one who is unclean cannot cleanse, and a supplanter cannot set upright.” Here everyone sees that “one who has been supplanted” must be read.

**Enemy and adversary.** We have restored this passage in this form in place of what the other editions have, “enemies and adversaries,” because we saw it written thus in all the ancient manuscripts.

[Col. 0410C] **498 He who is baptized.** Saint John Chrysostom explains this custom at the beginning of Homily XL on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians. See Rigaltius’ observations on Tertullian’s book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*; Christoph Justellus’ notes on Canon XII of the Synod of Antioch; and the dissertations published by Friedrich Spanheim and Jean Hardouin on baptism for the dead. See also Amboise’s preface to Abelard, p. 24.]

I. Cyprian to his brother Quintus, greetings.

Our fellow presbyter Lucianus has reported to me, dearest brother, that you desired us to tell you what we think about those who appear to have been baptized among heretics and schismatics. So that you might know what many of our fellow bishops, together with the fellow presbyters who were present, recently decided about this matter in council, [Col. 0409A] I have sent you a copy of that same letter.

For I do not know by what presumption some of our colleagues are led to think that those who have been dipped among heretics [Note: [Col. 0409C] “and schismatics” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2.], when they come to us, ought not to be baptized, on the ground that they say there is one baptism. It is one, of course, precisely because the Church is one, and baptism cannot exist outside the Church. For since there cannot be two baptisms, if heretics truly baptize, then they themselves possess baptism. And whoever, on his own authority, grants them this protection yields to them and agrees that an enemy and adversary of Christ should appear to possess the power to wash, purify, and sanctify a human being.

We, however, say that those who come from there are not rebaptized among us, but baptized. For they receive nothing there, [Col. 0409B] where there is nothing; rather, they come to us so that they may receive here, where all grace and truth are, because grace and truth are one.

Moreover, some of our colleagues prefer to give honor to heretics rather than agree with us. While, because of their affirmation that there is one baptism, they refuse to baptize those who come to us, they either create two baptisms themselves, since they say that baptism also exists among heretics, or else—which is more serious—they strive to set the filthy and profane dipping of heretics before and above the true, unique, and legitimate baptism of the Catholic Church. They fail to consider that it is written: “He who is baptized by a dead man—what profit does he gain from his washing?” [Note: [Col. 0409C] “from the washing” Bod. 1, Lin.] (Ecclus. XXXIV, 30).

It is evident that those who are not in the Church of Christ are counted among the dead, and that one who does not himself live cannot give life to another, 127 [Col. 0409C] since there is one Church, which has obtained the grace of eternal life, lives forever, and gives life to the people of God.

[Note: [Col. 0410D]

**II.—Estranged.** Three old manuscripts have *abigeatam* (“driven away”), eight others *abjectam* (“cast away”), another *abactam* (“driven off”), and one royal manuscript “cast away and trembling into the fold.” Rigaltius prefers *abigeatam*.

]

II. They say that in this matter they follow the ancient custom, when among the ancients heresy and schisms were still only in their beginnings, so that those found there were people who had withdrawn from the Church and had previously been baptized here. [Col. 0410A] When they returned to the Church and did penance, it was therefore unnecessary to baptize them.

We too observe this today: if persons who are known to have been baptized here and to have passed from us to the heretics should afterward recognize their sin, cast off their error, and return to the truth and to their mother, it is sufficient to lay a hand upon them for penance. Thus, because such a person had already been a sheep [Note: [Col. 0410C] “had been a sheep” Oxon.], the shepherd receives this estranged and wandering sheep back into his own fold.

But if one who comes from the heretics was not previously baptized in the Church, but comes as someone altogether alien and profane, he must be baptized so that he may become a sheep, because there is one water in the holy Church that makes sheep. And therefore, since nothing can be common to falsehood and truth, darkness and light, death and immortality, antichrist and Christ, [Col. 0410B] we must maintain the unity of the Catholic Church in all respects and yield in nothing to the enemies of faith and truth.

[Note: [Col. 0410D]

**III.—For neither did Peter.** Saint Augustine quotes this passage at the beginning of the second book of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*.

**That he held the primacy.** In the gloss inserted into the book *On the Unity of the Church*: “The primacy is given to Peter so that it may be shown that there is one Church of Christ and one Chair.” See Rigaltius’ observations there.]

III. Custom must not be pleaded as a bar; rather, one must prevail by reason. For neither did Peter, whom the Lord chose first and upon whom he built his Church, when Paul later disputed with him about circumcision, insolently claim anything for himself or arrogantly assume the right to say that he held the primacy and that newcomers and later arrivals ought rather to obey him. Nor did he despise Paul because Paul had previously been a persecutor of the Church. Instead, he accepted the counsel of truth and readily agreed with the legitimate reasoning that Paul maintained (Gal. II, 14), thereby furnishing us with a lesson in harmony and patience: we are not stubbornly to cherish what is our own, but, if the things sometimes suggested beneficially and wholesomely by our brothers and colleagues are true and legitimate, we should instead regard those very things as our own [Note: [Col. 0410C] “we should rather embrace those very things” Thu.; “those things” Foss.].

Paul too, looking to this matter and faithfully providing for harmony and peace, wrote in his epistle: “Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others examine what is said. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent” (I Cor. XIV, 29–30). [Col. 0411A] In this passage he taught and showed that many things are revealed to individuals for the better, and that no one should contend stubbornly merely for what he had once imbibed and held; rather, if something better and more beneficial emerges, he should embrace it willingly.

For we are not defeated when better things are offered to us, but instructed—especially in matters pertaining to the unity of the Church and to the truth of our hope and faith. Thus we, as priests of God and rulers of his Church by his gracious appointment, should know that the remission of sins can be given only in the Church, and that the adversaries of Christ cannot claim for themselves anything concerning his grace.

[Note: [Col. 0411C]

**IV.—Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in book II, chapter 9, of *On Baptism, against the Donatists*. But in this passage of Cyprian I do not find what Augustine says a little earlier that Cyprian had said: namely, that the custom of receiving heretics without a new baptism had, as it were, begun to be corrected through Agrippinus. Augustine immediately afterward says on his own account that through Agrippinus it began to be corrupted, not corrected. These matters must be explained.

Augustine says that in Cyprian’s time the question of repeating baptism had not yet been carefully examined, [Col. 0411D] but that the Church—clearly meaning the Roman Church, as is evident from Firmilian’s letter—nevertheless maintained the most salutary custom of correcting, even in schismatics and heretics, what was perverse, but not repeating what had been given. The custom of the African Church was different.

And because Pope Stephen offered nothing but custom in support of his opinion, Cyprian censures this method of disputation and says in Letter LXXI, p. 127, and Letter LXXIV, p. 141, that the matter must be handled by reason, not by custom, which he calls “the antiquity of error.” For although custom imitates law and is observed no less than what has been written, nevertheless long custom must not be pleaded as a bar unless it is reasonable and has endured for so long that its beginning is not retained in human memory. Jurisconsults say that custom is a reasonable practice confirmed by a suitable period of time [Col. 0412C] and interrupted by no contrary act.

Against the custom of the Romans—which, as even Baronius acknowledged, Cyprian said did not flow from the apostolic source—Cyprian opposed the custom of truth, which he believed to exist in the African Church. Augustine indeed says that custom must yield to truth once revealed. And because that truth had not been revealed in Cyprian’s age, since the question had not yet been carefully examined, Augustine therefore excuses him and thinks that he would have accepted the truth if it had then been revealed, as it afterward was [Col. 0412D] at a plenary council.

It must, however, be noted here that the discipline of baptizing heretics who came to the Church had been accepted long before Cyprian, as we shall say in the notes on the Council of Carthage; and therefore Nicephorus Callistus was wrong when he wrote that Cyprian was the first to judge that heretics must be baptized.

I shall add here that Pope Gregory VII used Cyprian’s authority against a custom whose practice is contrary to truth, because every custom, however ancient and however widespread, must be subordinated to truth. This letter of Gregory appears in Gratian, distinction VIII, chapter *Si consuetudinem*.

**Having weighed.** Three old manuscripts have: “having weighed it in common counsel.” Seven others and Erasmus’ edition have: “having weighed it by the examination of common counsel.” This manner of expression also occurs at the beginning of the following letter.]

IV. This is indeed what Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, together with his fellow bishops who at that time governed the Lord’s Church in the provinces of Africa and Numidia, decreed and confirmed after weighing the matter through the examination of their common counsel. [Col. 0411B] We too have followed their judgment, which was devout, legitimate, salutary, and consonant with the faith and the Catholic Church.

So that you might know what kind of letter we composed on this matter, out of our common affection we have sent a copy of it for the information both of you and [Note: [Col. 0411C] “of you as” Bod. 2.] of our fellow bishops who are there. I wish you, dearest brother, always good health.

## 128 LETTER LXXII

*(Erasm., II, 1. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Oxon., Lips., LXXII. Paris., LXXI. Coustant, Epist. Rom. Pont., I, p. 216. Routh, Rell. scr. III, pp. 88 and 144.)*

### TO POPE STEPHEN, CONCERNING THE COUNCIL

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian, together with his colleagues at a certain council, [Col. 0411C] informs Stephen, the Roman Pontiff, that they had decreed both that those returning to the Church from the heretics should be baptized and that bishops or presbyters coming from those same groups should not [Col. 0412A] be received on any condition other than that they communicate as laymen.

## 129 LETTER LXXIII

*(Erasm., to Jubaianus on the Baptism of Heretics, p. 322. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Oxon., Lips., LXXIII. Paris., LXXII.)*

### TO JUBAIANUS, ON BAPTIZING HERETICS

**SUMMARY.—**You have the subject of this letter at the beginning of the Synod of Carthage, above, vol. III, in these words:

> Cyprian said: “You have heard, dearly beloved colleagues, what Jubaianus, our fellow bishop, wrote to me, consulting our humble person about the unlawful and profane baptism of heretics; and what I wrote back to him, namely, giving the judgment that we have given once, twice, and often: that heretics who come to the Church ought to be sanctified and baptized with the Church’s baptism.”

[Col. 0412B] This letter therefore also pertains to the error of Cyprian and his fellow bishops.

*(This letter, moreover, like the preceding one, we have included among the records of the great controversy over rebaptism. See vol. III.)*

## 138 LETTER LXXIV

*(Erasm., to Pompeius against Stephen’s Letter, p. 332. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXIV. Paris., LXXIII. Oxon., Lips., LX.)*

### TO POMPEIUS, AGAINST STEPHEN’S LETTER ON BAPTIZING HERETICS

**SUMMARY.—**The summary of this letter is given by St. Augustine in book V, chapter 23, *Against the Donatists*:

> “Cyprian,” he says, “also writes to Pompeius about this same [Col. 0412C] matter, where he plainly indicates that Stephen, whom we have learned to have been bishop of the Roman Church at that time, not only did not agree with him on these points, but even wrote and issued commands to the contrary.”

Again, concerning this, in chapter 25:

> “I do not wish to reconsider the things he poured out against Stephen in anger, because there is no need. The very same things are said there that have already been sufficiently discussed; and it is better to pass over matters that carried the danger of pernicious dissension.
