Stephen, however, had thought that those who attempted to overturn the ancient custom concerning the reception of heretics should be excluded from communion. But Cyprian, moved by the difficulty of the question itself and most abundantly endowed with the holy affections of charity, held that those who thought differently should remain in unity. Thus, although he expressed his indignation with some vehemence, yet did so fraternally; and the peace of Christ prevailed in their hearts, so that amid such disagreement no evil of schism arose between them.”

Thus far Augustine. We have quoted these words [Col. 0413B] at greater length because they serve as an antidote against those who strive to use this episode to confirm their schism from the Roman Pontiff.—You will find this letter, like the preceding one, among the documents of the same dispute of the rebaptizers, in the same volume III. **EDS.**

## 142 LETTER LXXV

*(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., Oxon., Lips., LXXV. Paris., LXXIV. Routh, Script. Ecclesiasticor. Opusc. praecip., I, p. 221.)*

### FROM FIRMILIAN, BISHOP OF CAESAREA IN CAPPADOCIA, TO CYPRIAN, AGAINST STEPHEN’S LETTER

**SUMMARY.—**Its subject is entirely the same as that of the preceding letter, but it was written somewhat more vehemently and bitterly than befits a bishop. This was chiefly, as I suspect, because Stephen had also written another [Col. 0413C] letter to Firmilian, Helenus, and the other bishops of those regions, saying that he would not communicate with them as long as they persisted in that opinion concerning the baptism of heretics. Eusebius teaches this from the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Xystus, Stephen’s successor, in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 4.

Perhaps, therefore, it would have been more prudent if this letter had never been published, so that I think Manutius omitted it deliberately. But since Morellius published it, I was unwilling to pass it over: both because it contains certain memorable matters and because the words of the aforementioned Dionysius’ letter to Stephen may serve as an antidote. Eusebius gives this letter in the aforementioned book, chapter 3, and Nicephorus repeats it more fully in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 7. From these words it is evident that Firmilian sang a palinode, as they say—that is, recanted:

> “Know, brother,” he says, “that the Eastern churches, as well as those farther away, which [Col. 0413D] were previously divided, have been restored to unity, and that all their prelates, being of one mind and in agreement, rejoice beyond measure over the peace and harmony that have arisen contrary to expectation: first and foremost Demetrianus of Antioch; Theoctistus of Caesarea; Mazabenes of Aelia, the successor of the deceased Alexander; Marinus of Tyre; Heliodorus of Laodicea, who was appointed in place of Thelymedres; Helenus of Tarsus; and all the churches of Cilicia; [Col. 0414A] Firmilian and all Cappadocia. For I have named only the principal bishops, lest the letter become too long and I grow wearisome through many words. But all Syria and Arabia as well, Mesopotamia itself, Pontus, and Bithynia—and, to say it once for all, everyone everywhere—exult, glorifying God in harmony and brotherly charity.”

Thus far Dionysius. Similar things may be seen in St. Jerome’s work *Against the Luciferians* and in St. Augustine, book III, chapters 1, 2, and 3, *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*. There, from the confession of the Donatists themselves, Augustine relates that the Eastern bishops rescinded—or rather corrected—their judgment that they ought to agree with Cyprian and the African Council on this question of baptism.—Concerning the character, authenticity, [Col. 0414B] authority, and tenor of this and the other letters pertaining to the rebaptizers’ controversy, please see the discussion in the preceding volume. **EDS.**

## 151 LETTER LXXVI

*(Erasm., I, 6 [I–XI], and IV, 7 [XII–XVI]. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXVI. Paris., LXXV. Oxon., Lips., LXIX.)*

### TO MAGNUS, ON BAPTIZING NOVATIANS AND ON THOSE WHO RECEIVE GRACE IN BED

**SUMMARY.—**The first part of the letter has the same subject as the preceding letters, except that here Cyprian emphasizes concerning the Novatians what he had previously said generally about all heretics. He also incidentally indicates that legitimate succession in the Chair of Peter is a mark by which the Church may be recognized.

In the second part—which, as its title sufficiently indicates, has until now wrongly been published as a separate letter—he teaches that the baptism performed by sprinkling upon a bed is just as true a baptism as that performed by immersion in the Church. See vol. III, col.

## 158 LETTER LXXVII

*(Erasm., III, 25. Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXVII. Paris., Oxon., Lips., LXXVI.)*

### TO NEMESIANUS AND THE OTHER MARTYRS STATIONED IN THE MINES

**SUMMARY.—**He extols with extraordinary praises the martyrs condemned to the mines, setting a corresponding consolation against each torment in a beautiful antithesis. It can be gathered from the following words that the letter was written in exile: “Had the boundaries of my assigned place not kept me away because I was banished for confessing the Name.”

[Note: [Col. 0413D]

**517 LETTER LXXVII.—I. In the mine.** At Sigus, in Letter XXX. On Christians condemned to the mines, see Baronius’ notes on February 16.

**Confession of the Name.** The old editions and three [Col. 0415C] old manuscripts add “the name of Christ.” Manutius deleted the words, quite rightly. For they do not occur in nineteen ancient manuscripts. That they are unnecessary is evident from many similar passages in Cyprian. See Pamelius.

**In body and step.** The Fuxensis manuscript and one English manuscript have “with bodily step.”

[Col. 0415D] **Destined to possess as many rewards.** Sulpicius Severus, in his *Letter to His Sister Claudia*: “How great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heaven is taught to us, apart from the testimonies of Scripture, also by the custom of the Church, by which we say that a distinctive merit belongs to that which has a special consecration.” This letter had previously been published among the works of Jerome. Indeed, in manuscript 1128 of the Colbertine Library it is inserted into the *Letter to Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*. But at the Council of Aachen of 816, book II, chapter 6, it is said to be by St. Athanasius; likewise in the appendix to the *Code of Rules* published by Holstenius.

**Counts.** I prefer this reading to what was formerly read, “are counted.” This restoration is supported by fifteen old manuscripts; and I think it can also be supported by the authority of two English manuscripts, in which “they count” is written. I have also read it in that form in some of our manuscripts.

[Col. 0416C] **Having preserved the tenor of the faith.** Thus six old manuscripts. Four others have: “you flourished by the tenor of the faith preserved.” So too seven English manuscripts. Three others have: “you maintained the vigor of the faith preserved.” See Pamelius.

**The Lord’s commands.** Two old manuscripts have “the divine commands,” with the same meaning.

[Col. 0416D] **By presenting yourselves as leaders of courage.** The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul has “by displaying virtues.”]

I. Cyprian to his fellow bishops Nemesianus, Felix, Lucius, the other Felix, [Col. 0414D] Litteus, Polianus, Victor, Juder, and Dativus; likewise to his fellow presbyters and deacons, and to the other brothers stationed in the mines, martyrs of God the almighty Father and of Jesus Christ, our Lord, God, and Savior: eternal salvation.

Your glory indeed required, most blessed and beloved brothers, that I should come in person to see and embrace you, had not the boundaries of my assigned place kept me away as well, because I was banished for confessing the Name. Yet [Col. 0415A] I make myself present to you as I am able. Even though I am not permitted to come to you in body and step, I nevertheless come in affection and spirit, expressing my mind in this letter: I joyfully exult in these courageous deeds and praises of yours and count myself a participant with you, if not through the suffering of the body, then through the fellowship of charity.

Could I remain silent and suppress my voice when I learn of so many glorious things among my dearest friends, with which divine favor has honored you? Some of you have already gone ahead by completing their martyrdom and are to receive from the Lord the crown of their merits. Others still remain within the confines of prisons or in the mines and chains [Note: [Col. 0415C] “remain in the mines” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1.]. Through the very prolongation of their punishments, they furnish still greater lessons for strengthening and arming the brothers, advancing toward more ample titles of merit [Note: [Col. 0415C] “titles of martyrdom” Pem., Voss. 2.] [Col. 0415B] through the delay of their torments, destined to possess as many rewards among the prizes of heaven as the days they now count under punishment.

That these things have happened to you, most courageous and blessed brothers, in accordance with the merit of your religion and faith, does not surprise me. The Lord has thus advanced you to the lofty summit of glories through the honor of his glorification because you have always flourished in his Church while preserving the tenor of the faith. You have firmly kept the Lord’s commands: innocence in simplicity, harmony in charity, modesty in humility, diligence in administration, vigilance in assisting those who labor, mercy in sustaining the poor, constancy in defending the truth, and corrective judgment in the strictness of discipline.

And lest anything be lacking in you as an example of good works, now also, through the confession of your voice [Col. 0415C] 159 and the suffering of your body, you summon the minds of the brothers to divine martyrdoms, presenting yourselves as leaders of courage. Thus, while the flock follows its shepherds and imitates what it sees its rulers doing, it too may be crowned by the Lord for equal merits of obedience.

[Col. 0416A]

[Note: [Col. 0416D]

**II.—Glorious beginnings.** Formerly “religious beginnings” was read. The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul also has this. The reading I have maintained seems to me more consistent with the style and thought of the holy Martyr. I found it in five ancient copies.

**The nature of the mines transformed.** Rufinus, book II, chapter 6: “At the same time, the Church, as though refined in the fire of persecution, shone more purely with the metal of gold.”

**Persons dedicated to God.** The observations Cotelerius made on a similar subject in St. Ignatius’ *Letter to the Ephesians* illuminate this passage.

**They bind the feet together.** Seneca, chapter 11 of *On Tranquility of Mind*: “He cuts apart hands bound and joined in fellowship.”

**Crossbars.** Thus Morellius’ edition and twelve old manuscripts. Five others and Manutius’ edition have the alternative spelling *transversariis*. See Du Cange’s Latin glossary.

[Col. 0417D] Below, Letter LXXVIII, p. 161: “You matched the hair-covering of a half-shorn head.” The most learned Jean Morin observes in Exercise XV, chapter 1, §9, *On Clerical Tonsure*, that being clipped and shaved was disgraceful and a mark of slavery, which he proves with numerous examples. Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, in book IV of the Theodosian Code, *On the Clothing to Be Worn within the City*, say: “We command that long hair and garments made of skins be forbidden within the most sacred city, even among slaves.” See the Council of Epaon, canon 39. For Romans were accustomed to go about with beard and head shorn, as Baronius observed in the first volume of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*.]

II. As for the fact that, after first being severely beaten and afflicted with clubs, you inaugurated the glorious beginnings of your confession through punishments of this kind, this is not something execrable to us. For the Christian body did not shrink from clubs, since all its hope is in the wood. The servant of Christ recognized the sacrament of his salvation: redeemed by wood for eternal life, by wood he was advanced to the crown.

What wonder is it, moreover, if you, vessels of gold and silver, have been sent into the mine—that is, the dwelling place of gold and silver—except that the nature of the mines has now been transformed, and the places that were previously accustomed to yield gold and silver have begun to receive them?

They also placed fetters upon your feet and bound your blessed limbs, the temples of God, with infamous chains, as though the spirit too were bound together with the body [Note: [Col. 0416C] “as though Christ too were bound” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2, NC. 1.], or as though your gold could be stained [Col. 0416B] by contact with iron. For persons dedicated to God and testifying to their faith with devout courage, these are ornaments, not chains. They do not bind Christian feet together for disgrace, but glorify them for the crown.

O feet blessedly bound, which are released not by a smith but by the Lord! O feet blessedly bound, which are directed along the path of salvation toward paradise! O feet chained for the present in this world, so that they may be forever free with the Lord! O feet lingering for a time in fetters and crossbars, but soon to run to Christ upon a glorious path [Note: [Col. 0416C] “to run back here” Bod., NC. 1, Ebor.; “it is run” Pem.]!

Let envious or malicious cruelty detain you here in its bonds and chains as long as it wishes: you will soon come from the earth and these punishments to the kingdoms of heaven. In the mines the body is not comforted with a bed and cushions, but it is comforted by the refreshment and consolation of Christ. Limbs weary from labor lie upon the ground; but it is no punishment to lie with Christ. The limbs grow squalid without baths, disfigured by neglect and dirt; but what is carnally soiled outside is spiritually washed within.

Bread is scarce there; yet “man does not live by bread alone, but by the word of God” [Col. 0417A] (Deut. VIII, 3). Clothing is lacking to those who suffer from the cold; but whoever has put on Christ is both abundantly clothed and adorned. The hair of the half-shorn head bristles; but since Christ is the head of man, whatever condition that head bears must be fitting when it is distinguished for the Lord’s name.

With what splendor will all this deformity, detestable and dreadful to the Gentiles, be repaid? For the reward of what bright and eternal honor will this worldly and brief punishment be exchanged, when, according to the words of the blessed Apostle, the Lord “transforms the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory” (Phil. III, 21)?

[Note: [Col. 0417D]

**III.—**In Florus’ manuscript: “sacrifices. You celebrate divine rites.” In Lamonius’ manuscript: “the divine duties of sacrificing.”

**Pleasing to God.** The Verona manuscript adds: “your reasonable service.”]

III. Nor, beloved brothers, can any loss of religion or faith be felt in the fact that the priests of God are not now given the ability there to offer and celebrate the divine sacrifices. You do celebrate—indeed, you offer—a sacrifice [Col. 0417B] to God that is at once precious and glorious and will profit you greatly toward the recompense of heavenly rewards, since divine Scripture speaks and says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L, 18).

This sacrifice you offer to God; this sacrifice you celebrate without interruption by day and night, having yourselves become offerings to God and presenting yourselves as holy and unstained victims, just as the Apostle exhorts and says:

> “I beseech you, therefore, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; and do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your understanding, so that you may discern what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Rom. XII, 1; Phil. III, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0417D]

IV.—**Gaudebundus** (“rejoicing”). Thus the old manuscripts and editions. Others have *gaudibundus*, which means the same thing. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VIII: “rejoicing in the offspring of the newly married couple” [Col. 0418D]. In the book *On the Passion of Maximian and Isaac, Donatist Martyrs*, published by the most learned Louis Ellies du Pin, we read: “Rejoicing, he showed this miracle to everyone present.” From the same source arose many similar words, such as *nudabundus* (“naked”) in Cyprian’s *Letter to Donatus*; *cruciabundus* (“being tortured”) in Letter XV, *To Cornelius*; *turchinabundus* and *lurchabundus* in Quintilian; in Suetonius, *ludibundus* (“sporting”), *gratulabundus* (“congratulating”), and *osculabundus* (“kissing”); in Seneca, *reptabundus* (“crawling”); in Aulus Gellius, *amorabundus* (“loving”), *stomachabundus* (“indignant”), and *errabundus* (“wandering”); in Apuleius, *bacchabundus* (“reveling”), *murmurabundus* (“murmuring”), *imaginabundus* (“imagining”), and *munerabundus* (“bestowing gifts”). This author, moreover, abounds in similar words, which need not be enumerated. In Quintus Curtius, *bacchabundus*. In Nonius Marcellus, *vitabundus* (“avoiding”).

**Constitutos** (“placed”). Three old manuscripts required us to add this word. Nevertheless, I do not think it necessary.]

IV. For this is what especially pleases God; this [Col. 0417C] is that in which our works advance through greater [p. 160] merits toward deserving God’s favor; this alone is what repays the Lord [Note: [Col. 0417C] “the Lord for all things”: *Vos.* 2, *Lam.*, *Ebor.*] with the service of our faith and devotion for his great and saving benefits, as the Holy Spirit proclaims and solemnly declares in the Psalms: “What,” he says, “shall I repay the Lord for all that he has bestowed upon me? I shall take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in the sight of the Lord [Col. 0418A] is the death of his righteous ones” [Note: [Col. 0417C] “his holy ones”: *Lam.*, *Ebor.*, *Bod.* 1.] (Ps. 115:12, 13, 15). Who would not willingly and readily [Note: [Col. 0417C] “willingly and prosperously”: *NC.* 2.] take the cup of salvation? Who would not joyfully and gladly desire that by which he himself might repay something to his Lord? Who would not courageously and steadfastly accept a death precious in the sight of the Lord, thereby pleasing the eyes of him who looks down from above upon us, stationed in the contest for his name, approves those who are willing, assists those who fight, and crowns those who conquer—rewarding in us, by the recompense of his fatherly goodness and loving-kindness [Note: [Col. 0418C] “of fatherly goodness”: *Lam.*, *Bod.* 2, *Ebor.*, *NC.* 1.], whatever he himself has granted [Note: [Col. 0418C] “among the good things”: *Lam.*, *Bod.* 2, *NC.* 1, *Ebor.*], and honoring what he himself has accomplished?

V. That our victory, and our attainment of the palm of the greatest contest after the adversary has been subdued, belong to him is declared and taught by the Lord in his Gospel, when he says: “But when they hand you over, do not consider [Col. 0418B] how or what you are to say; for in that hour it will be given to you what you are to say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20). And again: “Settle it in your hearts not to prepare your defense beforehand. For I shall give you a mouth and wisdom that your adversaries will be unable to resist” (Luke 21:14–15). In this there is indeed both great confidence for believers and a most grievous guilt on the part of the faithless: not to believe him who promises that he will give his aid to those who confess him, and, conversely, not to fear the same one who threatens eternal punishment to those who deny him.

[Note: [Col. 0419C]

VI.—**Gemina** (“twofold”). Thus the old editions, fourteen of our manuscripts, and seven English manuscripts. The other reading, *geminata* (“doubled”), which Erasmus introduced and Manutius and Morel retained, occurs in five ancient manuscripts.

**In pueris quoque** (“among the children also”). Below, Letter LXXXI, p. 164: “Divine favor also joined children to you in glorious confession.” Antiquity supplies us with many examples of children’s courage and faith. From the many that could be produced, I shall offer only a few of the more illustrious. In Eusebius [Col. 0419D] we see Pontius, a boy of fifteen, subjected to martyrdom together with Blandina, the martyr of Lyons, and Dioscorus, likewise a boy of fifteen, who under Decius suffered many things at Alexandria for the name of Christ. Prudentius, in his poem on Saint Romanus, the martyr of Antioch, celebrates the almost incredible steadfastness of a child who was still nursing. In the *Acts of the Donatist Martyrs*, published in the second book of our *Miscellanies*, p. 70, chap. 15, mention is made of the little Hilarianus, who suffered courageously for the name of Christ. Victor of Vita commemorates the approximately seven-year-old son of a certain Carthaginian nobleman, who after many tortures was drowned in a whirlpool. In the *Passion of the Most Blessed Martyrs* who suffered at Carthage on the sixth day before the Nones of July under Huneric, king of the Vandals [p. 519], a very young child named Maximus is named as having been tortured and put to death with them. These examples suffice.

[Col. 0420C] **Exultantia** (“exultation”). Five old manuscripts prefer *exultatio*.

**De judicio Dei** (“secure concerning God’s judgment”). Although I found this reading in only three old manuscripts, I nevertheless do not doubt that it is better than the one that has *de judicii die* (“concerning the day of judgment”). Yet that reading occurs in more ancient manuscripts. I therefore note this so that anyone who prefers it may know that he can do so with manuscript authority.

**In metallis** (“in the mines”). Thus the old editions and twenty-seven old manuscripts. Rufinus, book VII, chap. 7: “those condemned to the mines”; and book IV, chap. 23: “the brothers banished to the mines.” Manutius [Col. 0420D] printed *in metallo* (“in the mine”).]

VI. All these things you, most courageous and faithful soldiers of Christ, have made known to our brothers, fulfilling [Note: [Col. 0418C] “completing”: *Bod.* 1, 2, *Lam.*, *Ebor.*, *NC.* 1, 2.] in deeds what you previously taught in words, destined to be greatest in the kingdom of heaven, as the Lord promises and says: “Whoever [Col. 0418C] does and so teaches shall be called greatest in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). Indeed, following your example, a great portion of the people confessed with you and was crowned together with you, bound to you by the bond of most steadfast love and separated from its leaders neither by prison nor by the mines. Nor are virgins absent from their number: for them the hundredfold fruit has been added to the sixtyfold (Matt. 13:8), and a twofold glory has advanced them toward the heavenly crown [Col. 0419A]. Among the children also, courage greater than their age surpassed their years through the glory of confession, so that every sex and every age might adorn the blessed flock of your martyrdom.

VII. What vigor of a victorious conscience is now yours, dearly beloved brothers; what elevation of spirit; what exultation within the mind; what triumph in the heart—to know that each of you stands ready for God’s promised reward, is secure concerning God’s judgment, and walks in the mines with his body indeed captive but his heart reigning [Note: [Col. 0419C] “to know that he walks in the mines, captive indeed in body but reigning in heart”: *Lam.*, *Bod.* 2, *Ebor.*]; to know that Christ is present with him, rejoicing in the endurance of his servants as they proceed along his footsteps and ways toward the eternal kingdoms? Each day you joyfully await the saving day of your departure, and, being now on the very point [Note: [Col. 0419C] “and even”: *Voss.* 2.] of withdrawing from the world, you hasten toward the rewards of the martyrs [Col. 0419B] and the divine dwellings. After this world’s darkness you will see the brightest light, and you will receive a splendor greater than all your sufferings and conflicts, as the Apostle solemnly declares and says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming splendor that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

Assuredly, because your speech is now more efficacious in prayer, and your petition more readily obtains what is sought amid afflictions, petition more earnestly and pray that divine favor may bring the confession of us all to completion; that God may deliver us also, together with you, whole and glorious from this world’s darkness and snares; and that we who, joined by the bond of love [p. 161] and peace, have stood together against the outrages of heretics and the afflictions inflicted by the gentiles may rejoice together in the heavenly kingdoms. I wish you, most blessed and dearly beloved brothers, always to fare well in the Lord and to remember us always and everywhere.

## LETTER LXXVIII

*(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXVIII; Paris., Oxon., Lips., LXXXII.)*

### THE REPLY OF NEMESIANUS, DATIVUS, FELIX, AND VICTOR TO CYPRIAN

[Col. 0420A]

**SUMMARY.—**This letter and the two that follow contain nothing other than replies to the preceding letter, since they offer thanks both for consolation by letter and for the assistance sent with it. From the fact that three different letters were written in reply to Cyprian’s single letter, it may be inferred that the bishops who wrote them were stationed in different mines. This is confirmed by Letter LXXX, where a particular mine is mentioned.

[Col. 0420B] [Note: [Col. 0420D]

**LETTER LXXVIII—I. Et amatorem** (“and our devoted friend”). These two words are not found in the edition of Manutius, who first published this letter. They are also absent from the Moissac, Foix, and Lamonian manuscripts. They do, however, occur in several other ancient manuscripts, including the Verona manuscript, and in Morel’s edition.

Taking this opportunity, I shall also correct a very corrupt passage in Letter XXXV of Avitus, bishop of Vienne, which reads as follows: “For through the elder of the house of Tullius, who your affection, my lord Sigismund, from your father,” etc. This passage greatly tormented that most distinguished man Jacques Sirmond—and certainly not without reason. But if Sirmond had seen the old manuscript belonging to Pierre de Marca, senator of Grenoble, he would have had no difficulty explaining this passage. For in that old manuscript it is written thus: “For through the elder of your house, who the condemner, my lord [Col. 0421C] Sigismund, from your father,” etc. There, however, *amatorem* (“devoted friend”) must be restored in place of *damnatorem* (“condemner”). A similar correction should perhaps be applied to Letter XI of Pope Nicholas I, in which we read: “It is apparent that you devote less attention to the common welfare than to your private lot.” For in an old manuscript from the monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims, it is written: “than to private affection.”

]

I. Nemesianus, Dativus, Felix, and Victor to their brother Cyprian: eternal salvation in the Lord. You have always spoken in your letters with lofty understanding suited to the circumstances, dearly beloved Cyprian. By their continual reading, both the corrupt are corrected and people of sound faith are strengthened. For since you never cease to disclose the mysteries in your treatises, you make us grow in faith [Note: [Col. 0420C] “the faith”: *Voss.* 2.] and cause people from the world to approach belief. Indeed, in setting forth all the good things contained in your many books, you unknowingly described yourself to us; for among all people [Note: [Col. 0420C] “for indeed, among all”: *NC.* 2.] you are loftier in exposition, more eloquent in speech, wiser in counsel, more guileless in patience, more generous in deeds, holier in abstinence, humbler in service, and more innocent in good conduct. You yourself know, dearest brother, that it is our cherished desire to see you [Col. 0420C], our teacher and devoted friend, attain the crown of a great confession.

[Col. 0421A] [Note: [Col. 0421D]

II.—**Cadaveris** (“of the corpse”). Two old manuscripts have: “that the corpses of the public enemy himself and his severed sinews might be trampled.” Three English manuscripts likewise read thus. I have also ascertained that the Verona manuscript, the oldest of all, had this reading. Supported by these authorities, I established the true reading. For besides this, it is certain that a single enemy does not have several corpses.

]

II. For like a good and true teacher, you first declared in the proconsul’s official proceedings what we, as disciples following you, ought to say before the governor. Sounding the trumpet, you aroused God’s soldiers, equipped with heavenly weapons, to the battle of encounter; fighting in the foremost line, you slew the devil with the spiritual sword; and by your words you arrayed the ranks of the brothers on this side and that, so that snares might be laid everywhere for the enemy and the severed sinews of that public enemy’s corpse might be trampled underfoot.

Believe us, dearest brother: your innocent soul is not excluded from the hundredfold reward. It neither feared the world’s first assaults, nor refused to go into exile, nor hesitated to leave the city, nor shuddered at dwelling [Note: [Col. 0421C] “remaining”: *Lin.*, *NC.* 2.] in a desert place. Because it gave many people a model of confession, it itself led the way before the martyrs. [Col. 0421B] For by its example it summoned others to undergo martyrdom; and it not only began to be the companion of martyrs already departing from the world, but also joined itself in heavenly friendship with those yet to come.

[Note: [Col. 0421D]

III.—**Per Herennianum** (“through Herennianus”). The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis reads: “to be distributed through Felix, Herennianus the subdeacon, Lucianus, Maximus, Augustus, and Amandus the presbyter,” etc. Almost the same reading occurs in two English manuscripts. Baronius thinks that this Herennianus is the man through whom Cyprian, while in exile, sent financial assistance [Col. 0422C] to the confessors condemned to the mines.

]

III. Those condemned together with us therefore give the greatest thanks to God for you, dearly beloved Cyprian, because by your letters you refreshed their weary hearts, healed their limbs wounded by clubs, released their feet bound in fetters, evened out the hair on their half-shorn heads [Note: [Col. 0421C] “heads”: *Lin.*], illuminated the darkness of the prison, leveled the mountains of the mine into a plain, placed fragrant [Note: [Col. 0421C] “burning”: *Voss.* 2.] flowers before their nostrils, and expelled the foul smell of smoke [Note: [Col. 0421C] “dispersed”: *Pem.*, *NC.* 2, *Voss.* 2.].

Your ministry and that of our dearly beloved Quirinus also brought it about that, through what you sent by Herennianus the subdeacon and Lucianus, Maximus, and Amantius the acolytes [Col. 0421C] for distribution [Note: [Col. 0421C] “ordered”: *Pem.*], whatever was lacking for our bodily necessities was supplied. Let us therefore assist one another by our prayers, and let us pray, as you instructed, that we may have God and Christ and the angels as helpers in all our actions. We wish [Col. 0422A] you, lord and brother, [p. 162] always to fare well and to remember us. Greet everyone who is with you. All our companions who are with us love and greet you, and desire to see you.

[Note: [Col. 0422D]

**LETTER LXXIX.—**It is difficult to determine with certainty whether this letter is Cyprian’s or Lucius’s, although it appears to be Cyprian’s rather than Lucius’s. For in three ancient manuscripts it is said to have been written by Cyprian to Lucius and those who were with him, but in others by Lucius to Cyprian. Two, moreover, attribute it to Lucius, bishop of Rome. Pamelius nevertheless thinks that this Lucius was different from the one who was bishop of Rome. This opinion of Pamelius seems capable of confirmation from the fact that, if this letter is Cyprian’s, then, since it was sent through the same people who had brought the one written to Nemesianus, it appears to have been sent into Africa to a certain Lucius. Certainly, in Cyprian’s Letter LXXVII, *To the Martyrs Stationed in the Mines*, p. 158, Lucius is named among the African bishops to whom it was written.]

## LETTER LXXIX

*(Erasm., IV, 7; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXIX; Paris., Oxon., Lips., LXXVIII.)*

### THE REPLY OF LUCIUS AND THE OTHER MARTYRS TO THE SAME CYPRIAN

**SUMMARY.—**The very words of the letter show that its subject is the same as that of the preceding letter. It is therefore a letter not of Lucius, the Roman pontiff, but of Lucius, an African martyr and bishop; still less is it a letter from Cyprian to Pope Lucius.

[Col. 0422B] [Note: [Col. 0422D]

I.—**Parem gratiam** (“the same grace”). Two old manuscripts have *parem gloriam* (“the same glory”).

]

I. To Cyprian, brother and colleague, from Lucius and all the brothers who are with me: greetings in the Lord. While we were exulting and rejoicing in God because he had armed us for the encounter [Note: [Col. 0421C] “in the encounter”: *Ar.*; “and for the encounter”: *Lam.*, *Bod.* 2.] and by his favor had made us victors in the battle, your letters arrived, dearest brother, which you sent to us through Herennianus the subdeacon and Lucianus, Maximus, and Amantius the acolytes. When they had been read, we received [Note: [Col. 0422C] “we have received”: *Oxon.*] relief in our bonds, consolation in affliction, and protection in need; and we were roused [Note: [Col. 0422C] “trained”: *Ar.*, *NC.* 1.] and more strongly encouraged to endure whatever further punishments there might be.

For before our suffering you summoned us to glory, since you first provided us leadership toward confession of Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 0422C] “bestowed”: *Bod.* 2, *NC.* 1, *Ebor.*]. We, following the footsteps of your confession, hope to share the same grace [Col. 0422C] with you. For whoever is first in the race is also first to the prize; and because you were first to take possession of that which you began, you thereby shared it with us, clearly demonstrating indivisible love [Note: [Col. 0422C] “You thereby shared the same thing with us, namely the demonstration of indivisible love”: *NC.*, *Ar.*, *Voss.* 2, *Lin.*, *Bod.*; “You clearly demonstrated indivisible love”: *Pem.*], because you have always loved us—so that those who possessed one spirit in the bond [Col. 0423A] of peace might possess the grace of your prayers [Note: [Col. 0423C] “of united prayers”: *Oxon.*] and one crown of confession.

[Note: [Col. 0423C]

II.—**Quas patimur** (“which we suffer”). The Verona manuscript, eight of our manuscripts [Col. 0423D], and two English manuscripts prefer the form we have printed. It was formerly read *quas patienter ferimus* (“which we patiently endure”). But I think that reading arose from an itch to make corrections.

]

II. To the crown of confession there has also been added for you, dearest brother, an abundant measure of recompense for your works, which you will receive from the Lord on the day of reward. Through your letters you made yourself present to us, so that you might reveal that pure and blessed heart of yours, which we have always known, and, in accordance with its breadth, utter praises to God together with us—not as much as we deserve to hear, but as much as you are capable of saying. For by your words you both adorned whatever in us had been less fully equipped and strengthened it to sustain the same sufferings that we endure, making us secure concerning the heavenly reward, the crown of martyrdom, and the kingdom of God through the prophecy that, filled with the Holy Spirit, you promised in your letter. All this [Note: [Col. 0423C] “this, however”: *Ar.*; “only”: *Bod.* 2.] will come to pass, dearly beloved brother, if you keep us in mind in your prayers [Col. 0423B], which I trust you do, just as we assuredly do.

III. We have therefore received, most longed-for brother, what you sent from Quirinus and from yourself: a sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0423C] *Lin.*, *NC.* 2 add “your.”] consisting entirely of a pure work. Just as Noah offered to God, and God delighted in the sweet fragrance and looked favorably upon his sacrifice, so may he also look favorably upon yours and delight [Note: [Col. 0423C] “he will look favorably and delight”: *Ver.*; “rendering”: *Lin.*, *NC.* 2.] in repaying you the reward for so good a work. I ask, moreover, that you order the letter we wrote to Quirinus [Note: [Col. 0424C] “Cyrinus”: *Ver.*] to be forwarded. I wish you, dearest and most longed-for brother, always to fare well and to remember us. Greet everyone who is with you. Farewell [Note: [Col. 0424C] “order it to be forwarded. Farewell”: *Sem.*, *Voss.* 2, *Bod.* 1.].

[Note: [Col. 0423D]

[p. 520] **LETTER LXXX.—**The first edition of this letter was produced in the printing house of Manutius. That edition places Victorius before Herennianus. But the name Victorius appears in none of the old manuscripts against which I collated the works of Saint Cyprian, nor in the editions that followed, with the sole exceptions of Rigault’s edition and that prepared by Reinhart.

**Siguense.** Thus two old manuscripts. Six others have *Singuense*; Manutius, *Sibuense*. The most illustrious Dom Bernard de Montfaucon, in volume II of his new collection of the Greek Fathers, published Cosmas Indicopleustes’ book *On the Christian View of the World*. There, book II, p. 142, Cosmas, speaking of an ancient inscription of Ptolemy Euergetes, relates that when Ptolemy went into Egypt he subdued Agame and Siguen. From this it might perhaps be inferred that the confessors had been cast into the deserts [Col. 0424C] of Egypt. But Baronius, under the year 260, thinks that this refers to the mine of Siga in Mauretania [Col. 0424D] Tingitana. This is perhaps the better view.

**Quas scripsisti** (“which you wrote”). Five old manuscripts, likewise five English manuscripts, and the editions of Manutius and Morel have *quas misisti* (“which you sent”), with the same meaning.

**Tamquam filios** (“as sons”). Three old manuscripts add *tuos* (“your”).

**Felix scripsi** (“I, Felix, wrote this”). This was added from the English edition. For I did not find it in the other editions or in our manuscripts. Accordingly, if this is the true reading—as I think it is—this letter was written by Felix, who is named first among the bishops from whom the letter came. Jader, who is named second, signed it; Polianus, who is named third, read it.]

## [p. 163] LETTER LXXX

*(Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXX; Paris., Oxon., Lips., LXXIX.)*

### THE REPLY OF FELIX, JADER, POLIANUS, AND THE OTHER MARTYRS TO CYPRIAN

[Col. 0423C]

**SUMMARY.—**The aforementioned martyrs gratefully acknowledge the assistance sent by Cyprian.

To their dearest and most beloved Cyprian, from Felix, Jader [Col. 0424A], Polianus, together with the presbyters and all who are staying with us at the Siguense mine: eternal salvation in the Lord. We return your greeting, dearest brother, through Herennianus [Note: [Col. 0424C] “Victorius, Herennianus”: *Imp.*] the subdeacon, and Lucianus and Maximus, our brothers, who are courageous and unharmed through the assistance of your prayers. From them we received, under the name of an offering, no small amount, together with the letters you wrote, in which you graciously strengthened us as sons with heavenly words.

We have given and continue to give thanks to God the almighty Father through his Christ, because we have thus been comforted and strengthened through your address. Appealing to the purity of your heart, we ask that you graciously keep us in mind in your continual prayers, so that he may bring to completion your confession and ours, which the Lord has graciously conferred upon us. Greet all who are staying with you. We wish [Col. 0424B] you, dearest brother, always to fare well in God. I, Felix, wrote this. I, Jader, signed it. I, Polianus, read it. I greet my lord Eutychianus [Note: [Col. 0424C] “Eutychianus” is absent from the manuscripts *Lam.*, *Ebor.*, *NC.* 2.].

## LETTER LXXXI

*(Erasm., IV, 1; Pamel., Rigalt., Baluz., LXXXI; Paris., LXXX; Oxon., Lips., VI.)*

### CYPRIAN TO SERGIUS, ROGATIANUS, AND THE OTHER CONFESSORS STATIONED IN PRISON

**SUMMARY.—**He consoles Rogatianus and his fellow confessors, who are stationed in prison, and strengthens their spirits by the example of the martyrs Rogatianus the elder and Felicissimus. [Col. 0424C] The letter itself indicates that it was written in exile.

[Note: [Col. 0424D]

**LETTER LXXXI—I. Sergio** (“to Sergius”). Thus Pamelius and others after him printed it, and this reading is presented by three old copies. Others have *Seagrio* or *Seugeio*. In the old Reims manuscript: “Cyprian to Sergius, Rogatianus, Victor, Felicissimus, and the other confessors.” The English editors rightly judged that the reading found in some old manuscripts and editions, “to Rogatianus the younger,” had been incorrectly inserted [Col. 0425C], and demonstrated the truth of their judgment with many arguments.

Furthermore, the name Sergius is not found in Vatican manuscript 195, the Grenoble manuscript, or, finally, the Lamonian manuscript. It is also clear from a note by Nicolas Le Fèvre in a copy of Pamelius’s edition that it did not occur in an excellent old manuscript; for that most learned man observed that this manuscript read simply “to Rogatianus and the other confessors,” as is also found in the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul.

**Complecteremini me** (“that you might embrace me”). This is the true reading, confirmed by almost all the old manuscripts and every early edition. Nevertheless, Pamelius disregarded this authority and altered the text, printing *ut complecterer manus illas* (“that I might embrace those hands”), merely because he had found that reading added in the margin of the Affligem manuscript. The reading we restore is preferred by eighteen of our manuscripts and ten English manuscripts. Only two support Pamelius.

**Dominum confessa** (“which confessed the Lord”). The Burgundian manuscript has “which confessed the name of the Lord.”

**O beatum carcerem** (“O blessed prison”). Tertullian, in the book *To the Martyrs*, says while speaking of their prison: “For if we reflect that the world itself is much more truly a prison, we shall understand that you have gone out of prison rather than entered into prison.” And shortly afterward he adds concerning the prison: “It has darkness, but you yourselves are light. [Col. 0426C] It has chains, but you have been set free for God.” Arator, book II of *The Acts of the Apostles*:

> O place made blessed by disaster, for which radiant lights  
> Shine brilliantly in place of darkness.

**Dei mittit** (“sends God’s people”). Two old manuscripts have: “sends people to heaven.” The old Reims manuscript: “sends God’s people to heaven.”]

I. Cyprian to Sergius, Rogatianus, and the other confessors: perpetual salvation in the Lord. I greet you, dearest and most blessed brothers, desiring that I too might enjoy the sight of you, if the condition of the place permitted me to reach you. For what more desirable or joyful thing could happen to me than to cling to you now, so that [Col. 0425A] you might embrace me with those hands that, remaining pure and innocent and preserving the Lord’s faith, rejected sacrilegious acts of worship? What could be more delightful and sublime than now to kiss your mouths, which confessed the Lord with a glorious voice, and to be seen in person by your eyes, which, after despising the world, have proved worthy to behold God?

But because I am not given the opportunity to share in this joy [Note: [Col. 0425C] “it is not granted to share”: *Lam.*], I send these letters in my place to your ears and eyes. Through them I both congratulate and exhort you to persevere courageously and steadfastly in the confession of heavenly glory, and, having entered the way of the Lord’s favor, to proceed with spiritual courage toward receiving the crown [Note: [Col. 0425C] “the crown of life with spiritual courage”: *Ebor.*, *Pem.*, *Lam.*, *Bod.* 1, 2, 3.], having the Lord as protector and guide, who said: “Behold, I am with you every day, even to the consummation of the world” [Note: [Col. 0425C] “of the age”: *Lam.*, *Ebor.*, *Bod.* 2.] (Matt. [Col. 0425B] 28:20).

O blessed prison, which your presence has illuminated! O blessed prison, which sends people to heaven! O darkness brighter than the sun itself and more radiant than this world’s light, where God’s temples have now been established, and your limbs are being sanctified by divine confessions!

[Note: [Col. 0426D]

II.—**Tolerantiam** (“endurance”). Holstenius illustrates this passage in his notes on the *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas*, where the author uses *sufferentia* for what Cyprian called [p. 521] *tolerantia*. It is an African word, also found in the *Acts of the Donatist Martyrs* in book II of our *Miscellanies*, p. 60 and the following pages. See Du Cange’s *Latin Glossary*.

**Fulgebunt . . . discurrent** (“They will shine . . . they will run about”). These words are absent from eleven manuscripts and from the edition of Manutius. They were also absent from chapter 12 of the letter to Fortunatus, *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*. We have restored them.

**In gehennam** (“into Gehenna”). The remainder of this letter is absent from the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul. In place of what is missing there, a large portion of the letter *To Antonianus* was subsequently inserted, beginning with these words on p. 71: “There is no confession in the lower world,” etc., and continuing to the end [Col. 0427C] of the letter *To Antonianus*. At the end it is written: “To Antonianus, concerning Cornelius and Novatian, ends.” The same occurs in the De Thou manuscript. Furthermore, the first part of the letter *To Antonianus* is missing in both manuscripts, and each begins with the words, “There is no confession in the lower world,” etc.

**Claritatem** (“splendor”). The Foix manuscript has “the crown of glory.”]

II. Let nothing occupy your hearts and minds [p. 164] except the divine precepts and heavenly commandments by which the Holy Spirit has always encouraged you to endure suffering. Let no one think of death, but of immortality; not of temporary punishment, but of everlasting glory, since it is written: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his righteous ones” [Note: [Col. 0425C] “his holy ones”: *Lam.*, *Bod.* 2, *Ebor.*, *NC.*] (Ps. 115:15). And again: “A sacrifice to God [Note: [Col. 0426C] “a sacrifice of God”: *Bod.* 1.] is a troubled spirit; a contrite [Col. 0425C] and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

And again, where divine Scripture speaks of the torments that consecrate God’s martyrs and sanctify them in the very trial [Col. 0426A] of suffering: “Even if they have suffered torments before human beings, their hope is full of immortality. Though chastened in a few things, they will be well rewarded in many, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself. Like gold in a furnace he tested them, and like the victim of a whole burnt offering he accepted them; and in due time their visitation will come. The righteous will shine, and like sparks among reeds they will run about. They will judge nations and rule over peoples, and their Lord will reign forever” (Wis. 3:4–8).

Therefore, when you consider that you are to judge and reign with Christ the Lord, you must exult and trample present torments underfoot in the joy of things to come, knowing that from the beginning of the world it was so ordained that righteousness should suffer here in the conflict of this age. Thus, at the very beginning [Note: [Col. 0426C] “at the beginning of the world”: *Bod.* 3.], righteous Abel was immediately the first to be killed; and thereafter all the righteous, the Prophets, and the Apostles were sent forth [Col. 0426B]. The Lord himself also established in his own person an example for all of them, teaching that none reach his kingdom except those who have followed him along [Note: [Col. 0426C] “those who always”: *Bod.*, *Lam.*, *Ebor.*, *NC.* 1.] his way. He says: “Whoever loves his life in this world will lose it. And whoever hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life” (John 12:25). And again: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

Paul also exhorts us that, if we desire to attain the Lord’s promises, we must imitate the Lord in all things: “We are,” he says, “children of God. But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God and coheirs with Christ—provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified together” [Note: [Col. 0426C] “so that we may thus be glorified”: *Veron.*; “so that we may also be glorified together”: *Bod.* 1, 2, *Lam.*, *Lin.*, *Ebor.*]. [Col. 0426C] (Rom. 8:16). He also added a comparison between the present time and future splendor, saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming [Col. 0427A] splendor that will be revealed in us” (*ibid.*, 18). Considering the glory of that splendor, we ought to endure every affliction and persecution, because although the afflictions of the righteous are many, those who trust in God are nevertheless delivered from them all.

[Note: [Col. 0427C]

III.—**Sexu suo fortiores** (“stronger than their sex”). Below, in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 175: “A woman is found stronger than the men who torture her.” Lactantius, book V, chap. 13: “Behold, the weak sex and fragile age endures being torn apart and burned throughout the whole body.” Jerome, in the letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “The blessed martyr Agnes conquered both her age and the tyrant, and consecrated the title of chastity by martyrdom.” The same author, in the letter *On the Woman Struck Seven Times*: “A woman, weaker in sex, stronger in courage.” Eusebius, book VI, chap. 41, relates the history of Saint Apollonia. Rufinus likewise relates it, book VI, chap. 31; after saying that she voluntarily leapt into the fire with which the persecutors were threatening her, he adds: “So that even the very authors of the cruelty were terrified, because the woman was found more ready for death [Col. 0427D] than the persecutor was to inflict punishment.” See also the history of the martyr Blandina in the same Eusebius.

Florus, book II, chap. 15, recalls a certain Carthaginian woman who, during the destruction of the city of Carthage, cast herself from the roof of her house into the midst of the fire, at the very time when forty thousand men surrendered under the leadership of Hasdrubal. Florus therefore says: “How much more courageously the woman acted!” Aelius Spartianus says of Zenobia, the wife of Odaenathus: “In the judgment of many, she is said to have been more courageous than her husband.” Statius, book IX of the *Thebaid*:

> She herself, fearing nothing and forgetting her weaker sex.

**Refrigerium** (“refreshment”). Thus the old editions and four old manuscripts. Manutius printed *refrigerii locum* (“a place of refreshment”). This is also how it is read in eleven manuscripts and in Morel’s edition.

[Col. 0428C] **De hoc verbo** (“concerning this statement”). The Pithou manuscript has *de hoc sermone* (“concerning this discourse”). Yet Cyprian, in Letter LV *To the Thibaritans*, in chapter XI of the letter to Fortunatus *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, and in book III of the *Testimonies*, chap. 10, always uses *de hoc verbo*. It therefore should not have been altered here. See Erasmus’s notes on the first chapter of the Gospel according to John.]

III. Blessed also are the women who are with you and have been placed in the same glory of confession. Holding fast to the Lord’s faith and proving stronger than their sex, they are not only themselves very near the crown of glory but have also offered the other women an example of their steadfastness. And lest anything should be lacking from the glory of your company [Note: [Col. 0427B] “from your number”: *Neap.*; “from your service”: *Ver.*], so that every sex and every age might be honored together with you, divine favor has also joined children to you in glorious confession. It thereby presents to us something like what the illustrious children Ananias, Azarias, and Misael once did [Col. 0427B]. When they were shut in the furnace [Note: [Col. 0427B] “in the furnace”: *Lam.*], the fires yielded to them and the flames gave them refreshment, because the Lord was present with them and proved that the heat of Gehenna could have no effect upon his confessors and martyrs, but that those who believed in God [Note: [Col. 0427B] “entrusted themselves to God”: *Bod.* 1, 2, *Lam.*, *NC.* 1, 2, [Col. 0428B] *Ebor.*, *Lin.*] would always persevere unharmed and secure in all things.

I ask that, in accordance with your religious devotion, you consider more carefully what kind of faith there was in those children—a faith that was more fully able to merit the Lord’s favor. For, prepared for everything, as we all ought to be, they say to the king: “King Nebuchadnezzar, there is no need [Col. 0428A] for us to answer you concerning this matter. For the God whom we serve is able to rescue us from the furnace of burning fire, [p. 165] and he will deliver us from your hands, O king. But if not, let it be known to you that we do not serve your gods and will not worship the golden image that you have erected” (Dan. 3:16–18).

Although they believed, and knew that because of their faith they could even be delivered from the present punishment, they nevertheless refused to boast of this or claim it for themselves, saying, “But if not,” lest the courage of their confession should be diminished through the absence of the testimony of suffering. They added that God was able to do all things, yet they did not place their confidence in desiring to be delivered for the present; instead, they looked toward that glory of eternal freedom and security.

[Note: [Col. 0428C]

**IV.—You ponder.** We have emended this passage on the authority of two ancient manuscripts.

**Your quartermaster.** This word, which has several meanings, originated in the art of agriculture. For those who arrange trees in a nursery or plantation and set them out in a certain order are so called, the term being derived from *meta*, that is, the boundary or line of fields from which measurement begins for arranging the trees. Here it refers to one who goes ahead of the soldiers, lays out the camp, and prepares quarters. Vegetius, Book II, chapter 7: “*Metatores* are those who go ahead and choose a site for the camp.” Nonius Marcellus: “*Metari*: to prepare. Hence also *metatores*.” Celsus’s preface to the *Debate between Jason and Papiscus*: “Everywhere there recurs [Col. 0428D] or is made manifest the prophecy of all those who, forewarned by the Holy Spirit, were accustomed to be the forerunners (*metatores*) of the Lord’s advent.” Victor of Vita, Book V, chapter 12: “Or could deceitful water overcome the resolve of so great a will, which the man of God had already sent as a legacy to heaven, his tears marking out the way?” The same officials are called *mensores* (“surveyors”) in the title of the Theodosian Code *On Billeting*. Lucian, in his *Letter to Celerinus*, p. 50, calls Decius the forerunner (*metator*) of Antichrist. Rigault wrongly referred that passage to agriculture, as though Lucian, in writing thus, had in mind the line or cord of a surveyor arranging his trees. (Vegetius, *Military Institutions*, II, 7: “Those who go ahead and choose a suitable site for the camp are called *metatores*.” GOLDAST.)

**Goes before.** It is certain that the *metatores* were called *antecessores* (“forerunners”), because they go ahead of the soldiers to prepare quarters for them. Saint Cyprian therefore employed a military term. See Vegetius.

**Victor the deacon.** These words were added from an ancient manuscript of Reims.]

### IV

Holding fast to this faith yourselves and meditating upon it day and night, ready for God with your whole heart and despising present things, [Col. 0428B] you ponder only those to come, so that you may attain the fruit of the eternal kingdom, the embrace and kiss of the Lord, and the sight of him; and so that in everything you may follow Rogatianus the presbyter, that glorious old man, who by religious courage and divine favor is making for you [Note: [Col. 0428B] “For us,” Oxford.] a path to the glory of our time. Together with our brother Felicissimus, always calm and sober, he withstood the onslaught of the raging populace, prepared your first lodging in prison, and, as it were, your quartermaster; and now too he goes before you. [Col. 0429A] That this may be brought to completion in you, we beseech the Lord in continual prayers: as your beginnings advance toward the highest consummation, may he who caused you to confess also cause you to be crowned.

I wish you, most beloved and most blessed brothers, always to fare well in the Lord and to attain the crown of heavenly glory. Victor the deacon and those who are with me greet you.

[Note: [Col. 0429C]

**522 LETTER LXXXII.—**For this letter, whose first edition we owe to Manutius, I had ten ancient manuscripts. Pamelius had two. The English editors had none.]

# LETTER LXXXII

*(Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LXXXII; Paris, LXXXI; Oxford, Leipzig, LXXX.)*

## TO SUCCESSUS, CONCERNING THE MESSENGERS RETURNED FROM ROME WHO ANNOUNCED THE PERSECUTION

**SUMMARY.—**Cyprian reports to Bishop Successus that, after a more severe persecution had now been decreed by the emperor Valerian—undoubtedly together with Gallienus—Pope Xystus suffered at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of August; and he asks Successus to notify his other colleagues, so that each may encourage his own flock toward martyrdom. Since Cyprian himself suffered shortly afterward, in the month of September, there can be no doubt that this letter was written near the end of his life.

[Note: [Col. 0429C]

**I.—Successus.** Bishop of Abbir Germaniciana, who attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. That he ended his life in martyrdom is taught by the *Acts of the Passion of Saints Montanus, Lucius, and Others*, published by the Bollandist associates and by Thierry Ruinart.

**That circumstance caused.** Thus the text should be read in Ruricius, Book II, Letter 14. In Caesarius of Arles’s *Exhortation to Charity*: “That circumstance especially causes.”

**Under the stroke of the contest.** The *Acts of the Holy Martyrs* that [Col. 0429D] we cited just above: “He denied that there was pain under the stroke of suffering.” See what was said above on Letter XXVI, at “in the very moment of death,” p. 412.

**Clergy.** Ecclesiastical letters were customarily sent through them, as others have observed and as is sufficiently clear even from Cyprian alone. Jerome, in his *Epitaph of Paula*: “He sent you a letter through his cleric.”

**All prepared.** The Morel edition and five ancient manuscripts read: “all prepared, through the resolve of their souls, for divine and heavenly glory.”

**Valerian.** See our notes on chapter V of Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

**Xystus.** Pontius the deacon, in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “News had already come from the City concerning Xystus, that good and peaceable priest and therefore most blessed martyr.” See the *Cyprianic Annals* and Dodwell’s eleventh *Cyprianic Dissertation*. Jerome, in his *Letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians*: Evagrius Ponticus confused Xystus the Pythagorean with Sixtus, martyr and bishop of the Roman Church.

**Be punished with death.** Three ancient manuscripts have “be punished”; two, “suffer punishment.”

**On the eighth day before the Ides.** Five ancient manuscripts prefer “the fifth day before.” But the martyrologies have “the eighth day before,” and the *Pontifical Acts*, “the sixth day before.”

**Four deacons.** I know that some ancient manuscripts and later editions read here “and Quartus with him.” But I prefer the reading of Manutius and Morel, and I think the reading “Quartus” in the ancient manuscripts arose from a corrupt reading of this passage in Cyprian. The error arose, in my opinion, because in one ancient manuscript the words were written in abbreviation as *et cum eo d. IV* (“and with him four d[eacons]”), just as I too have seen “IV” written in one ancient manuscript. From this subsequent copyists made “and Quartus with him.” For there are some ancient manuscripts that have only “and with him four,” omitting the word “deacons.” Moreover, it is certain that no mention of Quartus is found elsewhere except among martyrologists who cite Cyprian’s letter. It is also certain that the deacons Felicissimus and Agapitus were beheaded with Xystus. I therefore think Pamelius’s observation—that the reading of Manutius and Morel can in no way be defended—is false. Certainly four deacons who suffered with Xystus are commemorated here. Yet in his *Acts* only two are said to have been beheaded with him. In the *Pontifical Acts*, however, which are also cited in the ancient martyrologies, it is written that six suffered with him. But this discrepancy is of no importance. Felicissimus and Agapitus died with Xystus; the others on one of the following days.]

### I

Cyprian to his brother Successus, greetings.

Most beloved brother, the circumstance that caused me not to write to you immediately was that all the clergy, being placed under the stroke of the contest, were wholly unable to depart from here, all prepared, through the resolve of their souls, for divine and heavenly glory. You should know, however, that those whom I had sent to the City for this purpose have returned, so that, whatever rescript had been issued concerning us, they might ascertain the truth for themselves and bring it back to us. [Col. 0430A] For many varied and uncertain reports are being bandied about in public opinion.

The truth of the matter is as follows. Valerian has sent a rescript to the senate ordering that bishops, presbyters, and deacons be punished immediately; that senators, men of distinguished rank, and Roman knights [Note: [Col. 0429C] The Leipzig editor deleted “and,” at the suggestion of Neander, *Kg.* I, p. 141, n. 3, with whom Münter agreed, *Primordia Ecclesiae Africanae*, p. 171, n. 1.], after losing their rank, also be stripped of their property; and that, if they persist in being Christians after their resources have been taken away, they also be punished with death. Matrons, after their property has been taken away, are to be sent into exile. Any members of the imperial household who either had confessed previously or now confess are to have their property confiscated and, after being put in chains and registered for labor on the imperial estates [Note: [Col. 0430C] “And enrolled,” Verona.], are to be sent there.

The emperor Valerian also appended to his address a copy of the letters he had written concerning us to the provincial governors. We expect those letters to arrive daily, standing firm, in accordance with the steadfastness of our faith, to endure suffering, and awaiting from the Lord’s help and mercy the crown of eternal life.

You should also know that Xystus was executed in the cemetery on the eighth day before the Ides of August, and four deacons with him [Note: [Col. 0430C] “Quartus,” Verona; “and Quartus with him,” Oxford.]. The prefects in the City are also pressing this persecution daily, so that any who are brought before them may be executed and their property claimed for the treasury. 166

### II

I ask that through you these facts be made known to the rest of our colleagues, so that everywhere the brotherhood may be strengthened by their exhortation and prepared for the spiritual contest; so that each of our people may think not so much of death as of immortality and, dedicated to the Lord with complete faith and total courage, may rejoice rather than fear in this confession, [Col. 0431A] in which they know that the soldiers of God and Christ are not destroyed but crowned.

I wish you, most beloved brother, always to fare well in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0431C]

**LETTER LXXXIII.—I. Prison officials.** Manutius, to whom we owe the first edition of this letter, and Morel printed “military intelligence agents” (*frumentarios*); this reading is also preferred by the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis. All the others, including the two cited by Pamelius, have *commentarios*. Pamelius said that he approved this reading more highly, yet printed *frumentarios*. The *commentarii* or *commentarienses*, who are mentioned many times in the Theodosian Code, where they are called “most wicked,” were, as Julius Firmicus says in his book *On the Instruction of Astrology*, those entrusted with the care of the condemned, or prison guards, whom we call jailers, *geôliers*. Thus [Col. 0431D] they are correctly explained in the *Acts of the First Entry of Jean d’Orléans, Bishop of Orléans, into His City in 1552*: “the *commentarienses*, or jailers, of the prisons of the bishopric of Orléans.” According to Firmicus, they were likewise entrusted with the care of public chains. On them see also Lodovico Celio Rhodigino, Book IX, chapter 34. Cyprian is therefore right to say that prison officials were sent to conduct him to Utica. The same men are called lictors in Jerome’s *Letter concerning the Woman Struck Seven Times*: “The neighboring city is disturbed by such news, and the entire troop of lictors gathers; from their midst the one responsible for the condemned bursts forth,” etc. On the *frumentarii*, see André Schott’s notes on Aurelius Victor; Henri Valois on Book VI, chapter 30, of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*; and Du Cange’s Latin glossary. In another sense, Jacques de Billy, in his scholia on Gregory Nazianzen’s *Oration on the Plague of Hail*, calls those who buy grain in order to oppress their brothers *frumentarii*.]

# LETTER LXXXIII

*(Pamelius, Rigault, Baluze, LXXXIII; Paris, LXXXI; Oxford, Leipzig, LXXXI.)*

## TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE, CONCERNING HIS RETIREMENT SHORTLY BEFORE HIS MARTYRDOM

**SUMMARY.—**Near the end of Cyprian’s life, when, after his return to his gardens, he was informed that men had been sent to drag him to Utica for execution, he withdrew. But lest it be believed that he had done this from fear of death, in this letter he explains his reason: namely, that he might undergo martyrdom nowhere but at Carthage, in the sight of his own people.

[Note: [Col. 0432C]

**From our gardens.** See what was said concerning these gardens in the notes on Letter VI, p. 393.]

### I

Cyprian to the presbyters, deacons, and [Col. 0431B] all the people, greetings.

When word had been brought to us, most beloved brothers, that prison officials had been sent to conduct me to Utica, and when, on the advice of those dearest to me, I had been persuaded to withdraw for a time from our gardens, I consented, since a just cause intervened. For it is fitting that a bishop should confess the Lord in the very city in which he presides over the Lord’s Church, and that the whole people should be glorified by the confession of their present leader. For whatever a bishop-confessor says at the moment of his confession, he says, by God’s inspiration, with the mouth of all.

Otherwise, the honor of our so glorious church would be impaired if I, the bishop set over another church, were to receive sentence at Utica for my confession and depart from there as a martyr to the Lord; since both for myself and for you I pray in continual supplications, long with every desire, and am bound, [Col. 0431C] to confess among you, to suffer there, and to depart from there to the Lord. [Col. 0432A]

We therefore wait here, established in a hidden place of retirement, for the arrival of the proconsul returning to Carthage, so that we may hear from him what the emperors have commanded concerning Christian laypeople and bishops, and may say what the Lord wishes to be said at that hour.

[Note: [Col. 0432C]

**II.—The proconsul pronounces sentence.** Five ancient manuscripts read: “the proconsul’s sentence strikes.”

**In common.** Although this reading is excellent, the one presented by manuscript 2442 of the Colbert Library and by the Foix manuscript does not displease me. They read *in comminus*, that is, “when we shall be together, when we shall have assembled in one place.” Since I have often observed that the Verona and Foix manuscripts prefer the same [Col. 0432D] readings, this observation of mine is also supported by the testimony of this passage. For the Verona manuscript had *comminus*. I have also seen the word written in this fashion in Suetonius’s *Life of Caesar*. Apollonius in Rufinus, Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18: “Or, if they are confident, let them come into close quarters.”

**So may it be.** We added this from the Foix manuscript.]

### II

But you, most beloved brothers, in accordance with the discipline you have always received from me out of the Lord’s commandments, and according to what you have very often learned from my exposition, maintain quiet and tranquility. Let none of you cause any disturbance among the brothers or voluntarily offer himself to the gentiles. For one who has been arrested and handed over ought to speak, since the Lord placed within us speaks at that hour—the Lord who wished us to confess when questioned rather than profess unbidden [Note: [Col. 0431C] “Recklessly profess,” Vatican 1.].

As to what else it is fitting for us to observe [Col. 0432B] before the proconsul pronounces sentence upon me concerning the confession of God’s name, we shall arrange it together, under the Lord’s instruction. May our Lord cause you, most beloved brothers, to remain unharmed in his Church, and may he deign to preserve you. So may it be through his mercy. [Note: [Col. 0432C] Oxford and Leipzig reject these final words.]

167 The three letters that follow are found among Cyprian’s letters in certain ancient manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0432D] Although I do not wish to guarantee that these three letters are Cyprian’s, I nevertheless thought I ought to publish them here because they are included in certain ancient manuscripts of Saint Cyprian’s letters. Learned men will examine them. The first, which purports to be from Pope Cornelius, was found, as stated at Letter LXX, in two ancient manuscripts; the second in the Foix manuscript of the Colbert Library; the third in that same Foix manuscript and in the one preserved at Reims in the Abbey of Saint-Denis.]

# LETTER OF POPE CORNELIUS TO CYPRIAN  
*(C, S)\**

I have received writings from your Charity that are neither pleasing nor in accordance with the rule of faith. In them I recognized nauseating things, and I did not approve the poison of your words against the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, over which you sowed dreadful tares. I ask that you quickly remove and condemn them beforehand. You should indeed have done this before [Col. 0432C] the deadly poison scattered throughout the world killed the minds of the simple and innocent.

[Col. 0433A] It is therefore not proper to rebaptize. Therefore uproot and disentangle, as we have said, by eloquent and worthy words in a subsequent letter, those earlier writings which the offspring of vipers have judged should be maintained against the Catholic faith. For it does not befit the bishop of so great a city and so excellent a teacher, while thinking that the baptism of heresy must be condemned, to be heard staining true Baptism with words which, to your grief, clearly conflict with the Apostle’s statement: “One God, one faith, one Baptism.”

# TO THE PEOPLE OF CARTHAGE  
*(C, G, S)*

Cyprian to the people residing at Carthage, eternal salvation in the Lord.

We indeed give thanks to God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who has united you and restored you to your assemblies. For this reason we have called the matter to mind [Col. 0433B] and have wished to reserve the written judgment of the most blessed martyrs and confessors for our council. Majesty from above and the Holy Spirit command it; his saving grace is a witness within us. For when Scripture treats of the betrayers, it commands both in the Gospel and in the Apostle, both in the Psalms and in the Prophets and the other Scriptures: “Search the Scriptures” (John 5:39).

When this had been investigated by us, it was found [Note: [Col. 0433D] Baluze conjectures, “It was found.”] that those who surrendered the Holy Scriptures do not deserve to join our council—that is, to abide in its counsel. For there is no one who enters this council [Note: [Col. 0433D] Perhaps “joins.” Editors.] who does not look toward heaven.

For that reason we have recalled that those who treated the Scriptures in such a manner should be brought before the standing assembly of the people and the judgment delivered by them; that no action should be initiated by them, nor should they stand near either the sacrifice or the people [Col. 0433C]—for they had, to be sure, long since abandoned the people, stripped the altars, and made the sacrifices ready [Note: [Col. 0433D] Perhaps “they abandoned.” Editors.].

Rightly recalling these matters with sorrow and anguish of spirit, with the Lord as witness, we have advanced and established what we were bound to establish, since all disputes, dissensions, heresies, and scandals had consumed them, so that people of little faith or people careless in the Scriptures might provoke themselves no further. This we have decided and do decide [Note: [Col. 0434D] “And we decide.” These words are redundant and betray the copyist’s manner. Editors.], and we are unwilling to depart from our decree: if any prelate assigned to this people committed betrayal, they should deserve a bishop administering at the altar with his body intact. But those to whom we have given commands, and by whom we also order the sacrifice to be offered, ought rightly to obey these commands. 168 Nothing else will occur than what the sincere evangelical voice according to John immediately says: “I do not desire sacrifices from your hands, because you have not come to me with a clean offering.” [Col. 0433D] Whoever does not offer a clean sacrifice—no offering from his hands ascends.

For again we read: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Those who, through the Word, have fashioned a fabrication so as to deliver things uninhabitable among them—whether genuine Holy Scriptures or fabricated ones—he who gives voice and gives the desires nearest at hand, whoever indeed devises surrender, will complete the act of betrayal. [The text is materially corrupt here.]

Rightly, we wish those fathers who denied to have pardon for the time being if they confess. For one who says that he does not possess the Scriptures was surely prepared even [Col. 0434A] to be tortured; of such men we have examples. They denied a third time, and did not surrender the sacred object. But those who offered it without even being questioned shall communicate as laypeople until the council is constituted.

Nevertheless, when the council is constituted, we wish whatever Holy Scripture has brought forward to be completed in accordance with the settled judgment of the saints and friends of God, since witnesses and those nearest to the matter—our predecessors—had already established something long ago. For this reason it is necessary that we consent to, embrace, and complete the testimony.

I wish you always to fare well in the Lord. Amen. Thanks be to God.

# TO THE PRESBYTER TURASIUS  
*(C, G, S)*

Cyprian to his blessed and most beloved kinsman Turasius, eternal salvation in the Lord.

I received the letter of your Charity [Col. 0434B], from which I learned that your spirit had been shaken by grief at your daughter’s falling asleep. Nothing primarily astonished me more than that the courage of a Christian heart had been cast down in you, so that you inclined your spirit toward grief. I am amazed that the wall of faith was pierced by the wounds of bereavement when hope in the resurrection and the heavenly kingdom ought to have fortified it. Hope never agrees with grief, nor does faith ever experience any loss.

We believe that the dead will rise, and yet we mourn them. What would we do if God commanded that they merely die, without resurrection? His will alone should surely suffice for consolation, since we know that no affection should be placed before it. He who had given her and created her has taken her away. Why do you strive to mourn what you had received only for a time? He had lent her to you so that you might have her for however long he willed, and so that he might take her back again [Col. 0434C] whenever he willed. He who deigned to take back what was his own took away nothing of yours. It was fitting that the creditor should recover what he had entrusted, and nothing better befits the borrower than to give thanks to his creditor.

Thus we read the most devout words of Job, which we should follow: “The Lord gave,” he says, “the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). It was no small consolation against mourning that no one ought to grieve when he has returned something belonging to another, since it was not right for what its owner needed to be detained in another’s possession.

Another providential consolation is added, one that may meet the darts of bereavement. We ought to rejoice over those who depart from the world, if we ourselves perceive the world’s hostilities against us; yet we mourn the Lord’s beneficence, although whatever he grants us, he grants for our weakness. [Col. 0434D] The person who grieves over one who has fallen asleep wished that person still to be exposed to danger and longed to see the wretch laboring amid the waves of the present life. Why do you think that a Christian and faithful soul should have remained within the prison of the world, when the whole world is shipwreck to it? It has escaped so many and such storms of life, so many assaults of the devil, so many wars of the body, so many disasters of the age, and so many calamities. Yet you shed tears as though unaware of what you yourself suffer every day.

For this reason the Lord admonishes his apostles thus: [Col. 0435A] “If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father” (John 14:28).

He certainly wept for the dead Lazarus, but not with tears like yours. The one who promised resurrection could not grieve in such a way as to make the faith he taught into faithlessness. He grieved not for Lazarus asleep, but rather for Lazarus about to rise; and he wept for the man whom, in order to save others and confound unbelievers, he was compelled to summon back into the world. The Lord groaned as he gave that life whose removal you grieve. Your tears oppose his tears, and your love does not accord with his love. His weeping has no equal.
