He did not wish to restore to toil the man he had loved; and do you believe that you love someone for whom you wished the torments of toil still to remain?

Besides, if you think that he grieved for Lazarus because he was dead, he would not earlier have allowed to depart one whose death he could prevent; or at least he who possessed the power later to raise the dead man would not have wept. [Col. 0435B] Hence it is evident that he was moved for this reason alone: that, for the sake of some who were to believe or for the confounding of unbelievers, he was compelled to summon his dearest friend back once more to a hostile life. Finally, the Lord continued as follows: “Therefore, Father, that they may believe that you sent me,” and he said in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11:43). And it was done.

You therefore ought to rejoice over what compelled him to weep, lest you appear to envy the happiness of one who sleeps. She has passed from an alien world to her own; she has passed to the Lord and migrated from a hostile country to her fatherland, to heaven, as the Apostle says: “We know that, if our earthly house of this body is dissolved, we have an eternal dwelling in heaven, not made by hand” [Col. 0435C] (2 Corinthians 5:1).

She has therefore escaped a house that she ought never even to have known; she has escaped evil fellow citizens whose hatred she endured, so that she should no longer be a pilgrim in an alien land, as the Apostle recalls when he says: “As long as we are in this age, we are absent from the Lord” (ibid., 6).

Grief therefore ought not to overwhelm us whenever anyone has been deemed worthy to return from exile to his own country, especially since it is known that one who has acquired the profit of Christianity—the reason he came to the world’s marketplace—does not return empty and destitute. He completed his business, returned, and paid his debt to God. He acquired the purchase for which he had descended and hastened to return to the Lord, to whom he might present his merchandise and receive both security and honor for the goods he had acquired.

“But I,” you will say, “am disturbed by no doubt concerning the heavenly promises [Col. 0435D]; I am merely inflamed by separation from the one who died, and, deprived of the comfort of my beloved child, I am tossed about.” This is undoubtedly an excuse arising from human frailty, but it cannot defend lack of faith. For if people were unable to bear desolation, they would never allow their dear ones to leave them at all. They complain that the dying have left them bereft, yet they entrust living children to foreign lands for the sake of education, honors, or business. They are happy to remain their whole lives without those they love, provided that they may obtain what they desire their dear ones to attain. They send them abroad so that they may proceed to palaces. They compel them to sail away to pursue the acquisition of rank, or to depart through toil and danger to settle questions of inheritance, [Col. 0436A] and do not permit those whom they love to remain at leisure with them.

Yet when their children may safely attain the palace of heaven, the school of Christ, the honor of perpetual life, and the inheritance of eternal possession, 170 no one gladly congratulates them on departing from him. For uncertain ends, each person compels a son, brother, or parent to journey through uncertainties; for certain ends, no one permits any of his own to depart by a certain way. At the devil’s prompting, parents rejoice to be separated from their children, and children from their parents, for the sake of acquiring sins; but when God calls, they are unwilling to be separated from one another in order to receive forgiveness.

Thus it becomes apparent that we do not grieve, as our reason claims, for whomever we seem to lose; rather, we reveal a sign of distrust, since we cannot endure the departure to the Lord of those whose travels in the world [Col. 0436B] we celebrate. Because we believe in worldly profits, we tolerate the severing of the members of our own body. If we believed God’s promises, after the departure of our dear ones the joy of our hearts ought to resound with nothing but thanksgiving.

Believe me: unbelief always grieves in everything; and just as faith can know nothing at which to grieve, so distrust alone is held as grief’s slave. For if we call them sleepers, we surely ought to believe that they are sleeping—not dead, but resting for a time—according to the trustworthy words of the Lord: “Everyone who believes in me, though he die, shall live” (John 11:25).

If a human physician promised someone something, his promise undoubtedly could not wholly be denied the response of joy. Now, because the Lord Christ, the Maker and Raiser of the dead, makes the promise, [Col. 0436C] you are not afraid to mourn, so as seemingly to judge a physician both more trustworthy than Christ and more powerful in keeping promises.

“But,” you say, “I grieve over my forsaken old age, because I ought rather to have gone before my children, lest I remain amid hardships.” Whenever anything concerning spiritual goods is considered, nothing carnal should be set before one’s eyes at all. I declare that events have turned out better for you [Col. 0436D], because I consider not carnal but spiritual faithfulness in your regard. You say that the death of a dear one has broken you in old age. I, on the contrary, affirm that your old age has been relieved. The Lord has cut away the anxiety that tormented you about your living daughter, lest she perish. Surely it is better that, dead to the world, she has now returned alive to the Lord than that you should perhaps grieve over her being alive to the world but dead before the Lord.

Rejoice that you will be deemed worthy to follow a Christian woman whom, after following her, you may joyfully embrace again in heaven. She has not deserted you but gone before you; and, lest she grieve at the departure of her father, she hastened to receive him. You have not lost the one you nurtured. If you recoil from mourning and, though old, can reckon that you have offered your dear one to the Lord, then, even if you cannot hold first place, you can, as you desire, hold second place after Abraham: what he did not tremble to offer, you may at least be seen to rejoice over when it has been taken away. From him the Lord asked; from you he took. He obeyed the command; you consented to the will. Through an act forbidden by the law of nature the Lord proved him devoted to himself; through the lawful condition of religion may he at least enroll you as devout and summon you as devout. For whether by will or under the compulsion of necessity you present something of devotion to the Lord, [Col. 0437A] in what respect will you be able to prove yourself a Christian? [The syntax of this sentence is uncertain.]

Let our unbelief be ashamed before the gentiles, if it wishes to be subject to the Lord. The outcome of death is common to us and them, yet we surpass their griefs with griefs of our own. What would we do if something were required specifically of us that would redound to our disgrace? Gentiles often despise grief, though they are carried not toward heavenly promises but toward the punishments of Tartarus. Yet we 171 mourn those who go to heaven.

Let such a Christian consider what he will deserve hereafter, when he neither strives to imitate the examples of the saints nor shows the contempt exhibited by gentiles. In despair they disdain mourning, while we, in hope, merely attempt to disdain it. Indeed, they often do not hesitate to sell their children, so that, worse still, they may despise them while they are alive. [Col. 0437B] Yet not even the deaths of our deceased relieve us. We wish those removed from captivity and given freedom still to serve. They fearlessly entrust their children to mortal human beings; yet with sacrilegious minds we hesitate to release both our own selves and our children so that they may be delivered, as though we judged it safer for one of our children to be entrusted to human beings than to the Lord.

A Christian among the gentiles is something shameful—I know not what reproach. Such Christians are undoubtedly judged worse than the gentiles, whom it would have been culpable, I do not say to regard as better, but even to regard as their equals. Christians are unwilling even to accompany their dear ones with congratulations toward good things; gentiles do not hesitate to hand theirs over to evils.

Finally, let us be compelled to incline our minds at least by the very happiness of our dying loved ones, and let our desires cease to oppose theirs. Those who depart rejoice as they come to rest. [Col. 0437C] Let us too rejoice with them, at least by considering the blessedness of our loved ones as they depart. If the one who has escaped is religious or a novice, if you cannot rejoice for any other reason, at least exult because you know that a sharer in your blood has pleased Christ—especially because, even from the circumstances, [Col. 0438A] you ought to endure the Lord’s will, which you cannot oppose. [The wording of this sentence is uncertain.]

And since this event is common to everyone, grief is vain when its sufferer is seen to be neither the first nor the only one. But you say: “No anguish of my own desolation lacerates me; rather, human affection drives me on account of the sins of the little one who died.” Not even this may disturb a Christian spirit, lest it struggle against Christ’s commands.

What does it matter that we have left behind children of whatever number or kind, whom the Lord commands us to hate for devotion’s sake? The one who dies now saves his soul better. He departs in peace, lest he should have been unable to escape persecution without his own destruction. He himself assists in the world those whose mother dwells in heaven; and he who comes to the mother’s aid certainly brings help to the children as well. [This passage is textually corrupt; pronoun references are uncertain.]

Finally, consider whether anyone has reason [Col. 0438B] to be shattered by grief where someone may be wearied without any remedy. One who grieves ought to grieve wisely, lest he lose without cause the very thing for which he grieves. But now weapons must be taken up against mourning, so that our hope may gain the victory.

First, let us rejoice that the Lord willed to receive her. Then, because this is common to everyone in the world, there is added what is privately and particularly ours: that we are called back to rest. There follows the consummation of every joy, when the Lord restores us and we are returned to one another in the resurrection, as the Apostle promises: “We do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also will he bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 4:12).

These things [Col. 0438C], blessed one, I have sent you out of our mutual charity. Yet I know that you are well and that you console others. Bereavement will then find you impenetrable if you do not cease to arm others against it.

I wish you, most beloved brother, always to fare well and to remember us.

# PART II OF THE WORKS OF THASCIUS CAECILIUS CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE AND MARTYR

## TREATISES

*BOOK ON THE DRESS OF VIRGINS. BOOK ON THE LAPSED. BOOK ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH. BOOK ON THE LORD’S PRAYER. TO DEMETRIANUS. ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS. ON MORTALITY. ON WORK AND ALMSGIVING. ON THE GOOD OF PATIENCE. ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY. TO FORTUNATUS, AN EXHORTATION TO MARTYRDOM. TO QUIRINUS, TESTIMONIES AGAINST THE JEWS, THREE BOOKS.*

[Col. 0439]

173 [Note: [Col. 0439B] The title was formerly read *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*. I was compelled to change it on the authority of the ancient manuscripts, especially that of Seguier, the oldest of all, and because Saint Augustine cites this book under that title in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21. Jerome writes of it as follows in his *Letter to Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*: “Read Tertullian’s work addressed to his philosopher friend, other little books on virginity, and the excellent volume of the blessed Cyprian.” Likewise in his *Letter to Demetrias on the Preservation of Virginity*: “Certainly the blessed Cyprian too published an excellent volume on virginity.” These words are also found in Letter 79 of Hildebert. I think that this alteration of ours in the title of this book can also be confirmed by the authority of Cassian, who called the books he published *On the Institutions of Monks* by the title *On the Dress of Monks*. [Col. 0440B] For thus it reads in the Corbie manuscript: “Here begins the first book *On the Dress of Monks*.” And at the end: “Here ends the first book *On the Dress of Monks*.” So too in manuscript 782 of the Colbert Library. Indeed, in Christopher Plantin’s Antwerp edition the opening reads: “First Book *On the Dress of the Monk*.” There survives a distinguished book by Saint John Chrysostom *On Virginity*.]

# BOOK ON THE DRESS OF VIRGINS  
*(C)*

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0439A]

Pontius, in his *Life of the Blessed Cyprian*, summarizes the subject of this book in a few words: “Who,” he says, “would restrain virgins, as though with certain reins supplied by the Lord’s teaching, within a discipline befitting chastity and a manner of life worthy of holiness?” First—to explain the subject somewhat more fully—Cyprian celebrates a panegyric on discipline and establishes its usefulness from the Scriptures. Then, after treating the glory, distinction, and merits of virginity and of those women who had vowed and dedicated their virginity to Christ, he teaches that continence consists not merely in bodily integrity but also in the dignity and modesty of dress and adornment. Nor, indeed, can riches excuse excessive concern for adornment in women who have already renounced the world. Rather, since the Apostle prescribes that even married women’s adornment be restrained within proper limits, a virgin [Col. 0439B] ought much more to observe this; and therefore, although they may be wealthy, they must consider that riches are indeed to be used, but for good works—that is, spent upon the poor, as God has commanded.

After this, he teaches from the Apocalypse that conspicuous ornaments and clothing [Col. 0440A] are more suitable for prostitutes than for virgins; and from Isaiah chapter 3 he likewise shows how greatly such varied and costly feminine ornaments offend God. Then, passing from excessive ornament to the various kinds of cosmetics, he absolutely forbids these not only to virgins but also to married women, since they will not escape punishment for attempting to remake, transform, and adulterate God’s handiwork. Moreover, he also forbids virgins practices that had come into use through negligence: both attending weddings and frequenting mixed baths. Finally, in a brief epilogue, having explained in what one might call three words what good the virtue of continence contains and from what evil it is free, he concludes the book with this exclamation: “Persevere bravely, advance spiritually, arrive happily; [Col. 0440B] only remember us then, when virginity begins to be honored in you.” PAMELIUS.

[Note: [Col. 0440B]

I.—*Discipline is the guardian of hope.* Livy, book XXXIV: “Discipline is the guardian of weakness.” Cyprian, in the *Letter to Donatus*, p. 2: “Fear is the guardian of innocence.” Cicero, in the *Speech against Lucius Calpurnius Piso*: “That ancient censorial severity, the mistress of decency and modesty.” Apuleius, book IX of the *Metamorphoses*: “The enemy of fidelity, the foe of chastity.” A fine commendation of chastity is found in Ludovicus Caelius Rhodiginus, book VII, chapter 27.

[Col. 0441C] 524 *Turn away from.* The manuscripts of Saint-Arnoul and Bec, as well as Morel’s edition, have *oppose*. So also the Thou and Fossé manuscripts, as is correctly noted in the English edition.

*From the straight way.* In the Saint-Arnoul manuscript, *just* is written, with *or straight* above the line.

*Why do you set forth?* The same manuscript and the Bec manuscript have, “For what purpose?” So also Morel’s edition.]

## I

Discipline, the guardian of hope, the support of faith, the guide upon the way of salvation, the kindling and nourishment of a good disposition, and the mistress of virtue, causes us always to abide in Christ, continually to live for God, and to attain the heavenly promises and divine rewards. To pursue it is salutary, but to turn away from it and neglect it is deadly.

In the Psalms the Holy Spirit speaks [Note: [Col. 0441B] *The Holy Spirit, saying*, Ver.]: “Hold fast to discipline, lest perhaps the Lord become angry, and you perish from [Note: [Col. 0441B] *from the way*, Bod. 1.] the straight way, [Note: [Col. 0441C] *the right way*, Lam. Ebor. NC. 2. Corb. Thu.] when his anger quickly [Note: [Col. 0441C] *in a short time*, Vat. 2.] blazes out against you” (Ps. 2:12). And again: “But to the sinner God said: Why [Note: [Col. 0441C] *For what purpose?* Vel. Innom. Voss. 1. Bod. 1. Thu. Foss.] do you set forth my ordinances and take up my covenant in your mouth? Yet you have hated discipline and cast my words behind you [Note: [Col. 0441C] *backward*, Pem. Bod. 4; *behind himself*, NC. 2.]” (Ps. 49:16–17). And once more we read: “He who casts away discipline is unhappy” (Wis. 3:11). And from Solomon we have received the commandments of Wisdom admonishing us: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor lose heart when corrected by him; for the one whom God loves he corrects [Note: [Col. 0442B] *thus he corrects*, Foss.]” (Prov. 3:11–12).

But if God corrects the one whom he loves, and corrects him for the purpose of amendment, then brethren also—and especially priests—do not hate but love those whom they correct so that they may amend, since God also foretold through Jeremiah and signified our own times when he said: “And I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed you, feeding you with discipline” (Jer. 3:15).

[Note: [Col. 0441C]

II.—*In the Holy Scriptures.* In Erasmus’s edition and those that followed it, the words *consistently, in both the Old and the New* are added; Rigault says that this addition is superfluous. It is certainly absent from the early editions. Pamelius notes that this is true, but nevertheless states that the manuscripts contain it. I, however, can testify that among the very large number of ancient copies against which I collated Saint Cyprian’s works, I found it only in one comparatively recent manuscript belonging to Saint-Victor in Paris. It is certainly absent both from the Séguier manuscript and from the letter of Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria, where this passage is quoted. The edition commonly called Gravius’s does indeed contain it, but in smaller type, and a marginal note states that these words are not found elsewhere—that is, anywhere other than Erasmus’s edition, which appeared before the one called Gravius’s. Lombert, who translated the holy Martyr’s works into French, omitted it from his translation. The English editors also deleted it.

*God’s gifts.* Previously the text read *Christ’s gifts*. That is certainly a good reading. Nevertheless, because Morel’s edition and all the ancient books I have seen, with only two exceptions, read *God’s gifts*, I judged that I should yield to the authority of so many ancient copies, [Col. 0442C] especially since the same wording occurs below in the book *Against Demetrianus*, p. 223. And although *Christ’s rewards* is read in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 195, it cannot be inferred from that that the word *Christ* must be retained here, although that reading too is good.

*By which he has formed us.* Three ancient manuscripts read, “in which we have succeeded.” But the verb “have succeeded,” which certainly has no place here, is absent from all the others.

*Glorify.* So seventeen ancient books read, followed shortly afterward by *let us glorify*. I would not have mentioned that I printed the text in this form had the alternative reading—*give glory* and *let us give glory*—not prevailed in every edition except Morel’s. I preferred the former because of the authority of the ancient copies and because Saint Cyprian is fond of speaking in this way.

*With a clean body.* Florus’s manuscript read *with a clean heart*.

*And let us take care.* These words are absent from the Saint-Arnoul manuscript.

*Rule.* We have corrected the text to this from the Burgundian manuscript, in place of *custom*, which the old editions have, and *fear*, which our thirteen manuscripts and five English manuscripts have. Relying upon that weight of evidence, the English editors printed *fear*. But I consider that reading utterly false, and the one preferred by the Burgundian manuscript entirely correct. Pliny appears to confirm it in the *Panegyric*, where, speaking of Trajan’s wife and sister, he says: “Both have the same purpose, the same rule of life.” Cyprian himself says in Letter LXIV: “Let those who remain unimpaired maintain the perpetual rule of their salvation,” as we corrected the text with the aid of the Foix manuscript. Statius, in the *Lament for Etruscus*: “and the course of a life without blemish.” Tacitus, in the *Life of Agricola*: “The same course of his praetorship.” Likewise Cyprian, Letter XXV, p. 33, wrote “the rule of discipline”; Letter LII, p. 72, “the rule of glory”; Letters LI, p. 65, and LXXVII, p. 158, “with the rule of faith preserved.” Arnobius, book II: “We preserve and maintain unimpaired the rule of all the virtues.” Lactantius, book V, chapter 9: “Piety, holding the rule at the highest point, preserves its own course.” Dido, in the *Letter to Aeneas* in Ovid:

> The course of our fate that existed before endures to the end  
> And accompanies the final moments of life.

There are many other examples of this kind in the same Ovid, Suetonius, Valerius Flaccus, Lucretius, Virgil, and others, which I refrain from citing. I shall nevertheless add a passage from Pontius the deacon’s *Life of Cyprian*, as it reads in the Bodleian manuscript: “he trampled down concupiscence by the rule of holiness,” in place of *by the vigor of holiness*, which the editions have.

*With less attentive.* The Tours manuscript reads, “with less cautious and attentive fear.”

*Be maintained.* After these words Pamelius added from the Cambrai manuscript, where it is written: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved.” But I deleted that addition because I found it nowhere in the ancient manuscripts against which I collated the holy Martyr’s works, and it is also absent from nine English manuscripts.]

## II

But if discipline is frequently and everywhere commanded in the Holy Scriptures, and the entire foundation of religion and faith proceeds from observance and fear, [Col. 0442A] what ought we to desire more eagerly, what ought we more earnestly to wish for and hold fast, than that, with our roots more firmly fixed and our dwellings established in a solid structure upon the rock, we may stand unshaken against the storms and whirlwinds of the world, so that through the divine commandments we may attain God’s gifts? We must at the same time consider and know that our members are temples of God, cleansed from every dreg of the old contagion by the sanctification of the life-giving bath [Note: [Col. 0442B] *saving*, Ar. NC. 1. Ebor. Lam. MR.; so in *To Donatus*.], and that it is unlawful for them to be violated or polluted, since anyone who violates them is himself violated.

We are the worshipers and guardians of those temples. Let us serve him whose possession we have now begun to be. Paul says in his letters [Note: [Col. 0442B] *sets down and says*, Foss.; *by which successes*, Voss. 3.]—through which he formed us for the courses of life by divine instruction—“You are not your own. For you were bought at a great price [Note: [Col. 0442B] *You were bought at a great price*, Bod. 2, 4. NC. 1. Voss. 1, 2. Pem. [Col. 0442C] Lam. Ebor. Ver. MR.]. Glorify [Note: [Col. 0442C] *Give glory to*, Oxon.] and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20).

Let us glorify [Col. 0442B] and bear God with a pure and clean body and with a more excellent observance; and since we have been redeemed through the blood of Christ [Note: [Col. 0442C] *redeemed through the blood of Christ our Lord*, Thu. Foss.], let us obey our Redeemer’s command in every act of dutiful service. Let us take care that nothing unclean or profane is brought into God’s temple, lest, once offended, he abandon the dwelling he inhabits.

These are the words of the Lord who saves [Note: [Col. 0442C] *who dwells as a guest*, Bod. 4; *who raises up*, Voss. 3.], teaches, heals, and at the same time admonishes: “Behold,” he says, “you have been made well; now sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). After granting health, he gives a rule of life and a law of innocence. He does not afterward permit the man to wander with loose and unrestrained reins; rather, he threatens more severely the man now bound to the very restraints by which he had been healed. For there was, of course, less guilt in sinning before, when you did not yet know God’s discipline; but there is no further pardon [Note: [Col. 0443C] *you do not obtain pardon*, Voss. 3.] for sinning after you have begun to know God.

And indeed this must be observed and attended to by men and women alike, by boys as well as 174 girls, by every sex and every age, in accordance with the religion and faith that each owes to God, lest what is received as holy and pure through the Lord’s favor be maintained with insufficiently attentive fear.

[Note: [Col. 0444C]

III.—525 *Our discourse now concerns virgins.* Saint Augustine quotes this passage in book VI of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21.

*Holiness.* The Saint-Arnoul manuscript has *a holy object*. See above, p. 407.

*Abundant.* Augustine has *glorious*; the Fleury manuscript cited there has *noble*. So also Morel in an ancient manuscript.]

## III

Our discourse now concerns virgins; the more exalted their glory, the greater also is the care they require. They are the flower [Note: [Col. 0443C] *These are the flowers of the Church’s offspring*, NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. Oxon.] of the Church’s offspring, the beauty and ornament of spiritual grace, joyful offspring, a work of praise and honor whole and uncorrupted, the image of God corresponding [Col. 0443B] to the Lord’s holiness, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock. Through them and in them the glorious fecundity of Mother Church rejoices [Note: [Col. 0443C] *and through them*, Pem.] and richly flourishes; and the more abundant virginity adds to its number, the more the mother’s joy [Note: [Col. 0443C] *adds to the mother’s joy*, Thu. Corb. Foss.] increases.

We speak to these women and exhort them from affection rather than authority. This is not because we—the least and lowest [Note: [Col. 0443C] *authorities, the least and lowest*, Ar.], and thoroughly conscious of our own humility—claim for ourselves any license [Note: [Col. 0443C] *conscious of any such thing*, Bod. 2. Lam. Ebor. Ben. NC. 1.] to pass judgment, but because [Note: [Col. 0443C] *nor because*, Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Thu. Corb.; *nor whereby*, [Col. 0444C] MR.; *because*, Foss.], being more cautious out of concern [Note: [Col. 0444C] *belongs to concern*, Ver.], we fear the devil’s assault all the more.

[Note: [Col. 0444D]

IV.—*Eunuchs.* See Erasmus’s annotations on Matthew chapter 19.

*The angel’s voice.* Two ancient manuscripts have *the archangel’s*; nine have *the Gospel’s*. Morel likewise found this in an ancient manuscript.]

## IV

For this caution is not empty, nor is this fear vain, since it takes counsel for the way of salvation and guards the Lord’s life-giving commandments. Its purpose is that women who have dedicated themselves to Christ and, withdrawing from carnal desire, have vowed themselves to God in both body and mind, may complete their work [Col. 0443C] destined for a great reward; and that they may no longer endeavor to adorn themselves or to please anyone except their Lord, from whom they also await the reward of virginity. He himself says:

> Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it has been given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb; there are eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

(Matt. 19:11–12)

Again, through this angel’s voice the gift of continence is revealed and virginity proclaimed:

> These are they who have not defiled themselves with women, for they have remained virgins. These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

(Rev. 14:4)

For the Lord does not promise the grace of continence [Note: [Col. 0444C] *the Lord promises continence*, MR.] only to males while passing women over. Rather, because woman is a portion of man, taken and formed from him, God [Col. 0444B] speaks in almost all the Scriptures to the first-created man, since the two are one flesh and woman is signified together with man in the male.

[Note: [Col. 0444D]

V.—*But continence.* See what we said concerning continence above, in connection with Letter LII, p. 442.

*The unmarried man thinks.* So also book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 32. Jerome, however, in his *Letter to Eustochium on Preserving Virginity*, quotes this passage differently from a certain ancient version:

> He who is without a wife is concerned about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But he who has a wife is concerned about the things of this world, how he may please his wife. The woman and the virgin are divided. She who is unmarried thinks about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit.

Yet the same Jerome, in book I *Against Jovinian*, rejects [Col. 0445C] this version and says that it does not represent the apostolic truth. Nevertheless, in the book *Against Helvidius*, when quoting the same passage, he says: “Why do you bark? Why do you resist? The vessel of election speaks, saying, ‘The woman and the virgin are divided.’” It is clear from his book *On the Veiling of Virgins* that Tertullian used the same version.

*So too the virgin.* The Saint-Arnoul and Bec manuscripts and Morel’s edition read: “So too the woman and the unmarried virgin.”

*Doubt whether she is a virgin.* The Grenoble manuscript reads, “doubt whether she is married or a virgin.” Tertullian [Col. 0445D] in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “It is difficult for a woman to become one only once if she does not fear becoming one; and once she has become one, she can falsely claim before God to be a virgin.” In Cassius Dio, book XXXVII, we read that Caesar repudiated his wife when she was suspected of adultery—not because he believed the reports circulated about her, but because he said that he could not have as his wife a woman who had once fallen under suspicion of having committed adultery. For a chaste woman must not merely refrain from wrongdoing; she must not give rise to even the slightest base suspicion concerning herself.

*Equal.* The Séguier manuscript reads: “May your integrity show you to be such.”

*Not only in body.* I must not conceal that nineteen ancient copies, including the Séguier manuscript, have “not only bodily but spiritually.” I found the commonly printed reading only in the old editions and two ancient books. I have nevertheless retained it because it is more elegant, although I know that in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 204, some ancient books have *more spiritual* where the text printed there has *spiritual to a greater degree*.

*To be adorned (comi).* So most ancient books. The same is also found in Aldhelm’s book *On the Praise of Virginity*. Yet I do not dislike the alternative reading, *grow her hair*. Below, in this same book, p. 178: “What you think is adorning yourself, what you think is being adorned (comi), is an assault upon God’s handiwork.”]

## V

But if continence follows Christ and virginity is destined for God’s kingdom, what have virgins to do with worldly adornment and ornaments? While striving to please men through these things, they offend God, failing to consider that it was foretold: “Those who please men have been put to confusion, because God has reduced them to nothing” (Ps. 52:6); and that Paul also proclaimed gloriously and sublimely [Note: [Col. 0444C] *Paul proclaiming*, Bod. 4. Ver.; *Paul also proclaims*, Voss. 3.]: “If I wished to please men [Note: [Col. 0444C] *If I pleased men*, Lam. NC. 1. Voss. 1. Corb.], I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10).

But continence and chastity consist not merely in bodily integrity, but equally in dignity and modesty of dress and ornament, so that, according to the Apostle, an unmarried woman may be holy both in body and in spirit. Paul instructs and teaches us, saying [Note: [Col. 0444C] *Paul also says*, Oxon.]:

> The unmarried man thinks [Col. 0444C] about the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but [Col. 0445A] he who has contracted marriage thinks about the things of this world, how he may please his wife. So too the virgin and the unmarried woman think about the things of the Lord, that they may be holy both in body and in spirit.

(1 Cor. 7:32–34)

A virgin must not merely be a virgin; she must also be understood and believed to be one. When anyone sees a virgin [Note: [Col. 0445C] *sees a virgin*, Oxon.; *were to see*, Lin. Voss. 1. Lam. Ebor.], let him not doubt whether she is a virgin. Let your integrity show itself equal in all respects, and let the adornment of the body not bring the goodness of the mind into disrepute. Why does she go out adorned, why with her hair arranged, as though she either had a husband or were seeking one? If she is a virgin, she should rather fear to please; nor should one who preserves herself for better and divine things seek out danger to herself.

Women who have no husband whom they might pretend to please should persevere whole and pure, not only in body but also in spirit. For it is not lawful for a virgin to adorn herself for the display of her own beauty or to glory in her flesh and its 175 beauty, [Col. 0445B] since she has no greater struggle than the struggle against the flesh, no more resolute contest than that of conquering and subduing the body.

[Note: [Col. 0446C]

VI.—*Since you are a candidate for integrity.* Two ancient books have, “with an affection for integrity.” Three others: “since you are radiant with integrity and modesty.”

*Candidate.* So Erasmus’s edition, whereas the previous reading had been *radiant*. I found that reading in eleven ancient books. I found the other in Manutius’s and Morel’s editions and in eight other manuscripts. Tertullian said in book II *To His Wife*: “He is himself God’s candidate through fear.” And in the book *On Baptism*: “Thus a baptism of repentance was being administered as, so to speak, a candidate for the forgiveness and sanctification that were to follow in Christ.”

*Word.* Most ancient books, as frequently elsewhere, have *utterance*. See above, p. 465, and the notes on Letter LXXXI, p. 521.]

## VI

Paul proclaims in a strong and exalted voice: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14)—and does a virgin in the Church glory in the beauty of her flesh and the attractiveness of her body?

Paul adds and says: “For those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24)—and is she who professes to have renounced the desires and vices of the flesh found among the very things she had renounced?

You are caught, virgin; you are exposed. You boast that you are one thing, yet pursue another. You sprinkle yourself with the stains of carnal desire [Note: [Col. 0445C] *of the flesh*, Bod. 4.], although you are a candidate for integrity and modesty.

“Cry out,” says God through Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides forever” (Isa. 40:6–8). No Christian ought—and above all no virgin ought—to reckon [Note: [Col. 0445C] *put forward*, Ar. Lam. NC. 1. Ebor. Bod. 2. Ben.] any glory or distinction of the flesh as valuable, but only to desire the word [Note: [Col. 0445C] *utterance*, Bod. 4. Foss.] of God and embrace the good things that will abide forever.

Or, if one is to glory in the flesh, then it is certainly when the flesh is tortured for confessing the Name [Note: [Col. 0446C] *the name of Christ*, NC. 1. Lam. Bod. 2. Ben.], when a woman is found stronger than the men who torture her, when she endures fires, crosses, the sword, or wild beasts in order to be crowned. Those are the flesh’s precious necklaces; those are the body’s better ornaments.

[Note: [Col. 0446D]

VII.—*Possession.* The old editions and ten ancient books have *dwelling*.

*Earnestly declaring.* I have seen this written in most manuscripts. Some manuscripts, however, as well as the old editions, prefer *strengthening*. Below, in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 183: “strengthening God’s servants with a heavenly voice.”

[Col. 0447C] *Christ said.* So all the ancient books except the Thou manuscript, which reads *did*. So also Erasmus. The reading of the ancient books is better, for Cyprian is here referring back to the words of Christ quoted shortly before.]

## VII

But there are some women who are rich and wealthy with an abundance of resources, who parade their riches and maintain that they ought to use their goods. Let them know first that the rich woman is she who is rich in God, that the wealthy woman is she who is wealthy in Christ, and that the true goods are those that are spiritual, divine, and heavenly—those that lead us to God and remain with us before God as a perpetual possession.

All earthly things, however, which have been received in the world and will remain here with the world [Note: [Col. 0446C] *in the world and will remain with the world*, Bod. 1; *received*, Lam. Ebor.], ought to be despised just as the world itself is despised. We renounced its displays and pleasures at the very time when, by a transition to better things, we came to God.

John arouses and exhorts us, earnestly declaring in a spiritual and heavenly voice:

> Do not love the world or the things that are in the world [Note: [Col. 0446C] *or the things that are in the world*, Pem. Voss. 2.]. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, [Col. 0447A] and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the desire of the age. And the world will pass away, together with its desire. But he who does God’s will abides [Note: [Col. 0447C] *will abide*, Thu.] forever, just as God abides forever.

(1 John 2:15–17)

Therefore, eternal and divine things must be pursued, and everything must be done according to God’s will, so that we may follow the footsteps of our Lord and his divine teachings [Note: [Col. 0447C] *divine* omitted by Oxon. and Man. from the manuscripts Ver. Lam. Ebor. Lin. Voss. 2.; *we follow*, Ar. Lam. Lin. Bod. 1, 2.]. He admonished us and said: “I did not descend from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

But if the servant is not greater than his master, and the one who has been liberated owes obedience [Note: [Col. 0447C] *service*, Bod. 1, 3, 4.] to his liberator, then we who desire to be Christians ought to imitate what Christ said and did. It is written, read, heard, and proclaimed by the Church’s voice as an example for us: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk just as Christ walked” [Col. 0447B] (1 John 2:6).

We must therefore walk with matching steps; we must strive to follow with emulous progress. Then the pursuit of truth corresponds [Note: [Col. 0447C] *will correspond*, Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4. MR.] to faith in the Name, and the believer is given [Note: [Col. 0448C] *will be given*, Ben. MR.] his reward if what is believed is also practiced.

[Note: [Col. 0447C]

VIII.—*Within proper limits.* The Thurn manuscript has *by justification*. So also the Saint-Arnoul manuscript.]

## VIII

You say that you are wealthy and rich. But Paul confronts your riches, and by his own voice prescribes that your dress and adornment be restrained within proper limits:

> Let women array themselves with reserve and chastity, not with braided hair, nor with gold, nor pearls, nor costly clothing, but—as befits women who profess chastity—through good conduct.

(1 Tim. 2:9)

Peter likewise agrees with these same commandments and says: “Let a woman’s adornment be not the outward adornment of ornaments, gold, or clothing, but the adornment of the heart” (1 Pet. 3:3–4).

[Col. 0448A] But if they also admonish that even those women who are accustomed to excuse their adornment on account of a husband [Note: [Col. 0448C] *husbands*, Voss. 1.] must be restrained and regulated by religious observance in accordance with the Church’s discipline, how much more proper is it for a virgin to observe this? She can have no excuse for her adornment, nor can the false pretext for her fault [Note: [Col. 0448C] *the fault of the falsehood*, Bod. 1.] be shifted to another; she alone remains responsible for the offense.

[Note: [Col. 0447C]

IX.—*If you adorn yourself more expensively.* Jerome, in the *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “Take care not to pierce her ears, nor paint with white lead and rouge the face consecrated to Christ,” etc. The same author, in the *Letter to Furia on Preserving Widowhood*: “What are rouge and white lead doing on a Christian woman’s face?” See in book IV of Livy the story of the Vestal virgin accused because of her more attractive dress. In Matteo Bosso’s *Nights of Fiesole* there is an exhortation to Bessarion that feminine ornaments should not be restored to the women of Bologna. See also Letter VI of the same Matteo.

*Eyes toward yourself.* Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “To see and to be seen belong to the same lust.” Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 2, chapter 12: “A woman’s first virtue is not to be seen.” Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 5, records that Spurinna, a young man of exceptional beauty, when his remarkable appearance was attracting the eyes of many distinguished women, disfigured the beauty of his face with wounds because he did not wish his appearance to become an incitement to another’s lust. The same author, book VI, chapter 3, says that Gaius Sulpicius Gallus dismissed his wife because he had learned that she had been outside with her head uncovered. “For the law,” he says, “appoints only my [Col. 0448C] eyes as those before which you may display your beauty. Any further sight of you, sought through needless provocation, must necessarily remain subject to suspicion and accusation.”

*Fuel for sighing.* It is remarkable how great the disagreement among the manuscripts is in this passage. Two have *for sighing*; eight and Manutius’s edition, *for hoping*; one, *for perishing*; another, *for crowding*; another, *for debauching*; and yet another, *for sinning*. In Aldhelm’s book *On the Praise of Virginity* there is *for breathing*, perhaps in place of *for sighing*. Tertullian, in *On the Dress of Women*: “She draws the sighs of young men after her.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Eustochium on Preserving Virginity*: “These are the women who walk conspicuously in public and draw troops of young men after them by secret signals of the eyes.” The same author, in the *Letter to Geruntia on Monogamy*: “Let not overly elaborate dress bring the resolve of a widow into disrepute. Let her not draw troops of young men after her with signals of the eyes and a cheerful expression.”

*Like a sword.* Tertullian, book II *On the Dress of Women*: “For the moment he desires your beauty, he perishes, and you have become a sword to him.” See Saint John Chrysostom’s homily *That Women Subject to a Rule Ought Not to Live with Men*.]

## IX

You say that you are wealthy and rich. But not everything that can be done ought to be done, nor should far-reaching desires born of worldly ambition be extended beyond the dignity and modesty of virginity, since it is written: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient; all things are lawful, but not all things build up” (1 Cor. 10:23).

But if you adorn yourself more expensively, walk conspicuously in public, entice the eyes of the young toward yourself, draw the sighs of young men [Col. 0448B] after you, nourish the lust of desire, and kindle fuel for sighing, so that—even if you do not yourself perish—you nevertheless cause others to perish, offering yourself to those who see you like a sword and poison, you cannot be excused on the ground that you are chaste and modest in mind. Your improper dress and shameless adornment convict you. You can no longer be counted among Christ’s maidens and virgins, since you live in such a way that you can be loved with passion.

[Note: [Col. 0448D]

X.—*Those who buy as though they were not buying.* Although I know that this clause is not present in Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, from which this passage is taken, and although I know that it is rarely found in ancient manuscripts of Saint Cyprian’s works, I have nevertheless added it, because I found it in the Pithou manuscript, with which the Cambrai manuscript cited by Pamelius agrees, and because [Col. 0449C] Cyprian, in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 11, also includes this clause when quoting the same passage. For, as I said before, in correcting the holy Martyr’s works I do not ask what is found in manuscripts of the Holy Bible, but what Cyprian wrote. It appears that he wished to make the sense complete when he added these words.]

## X

You say that you are wealthy and rich. But it is not fitting for a virgin to parade her riches, since divine Scripture says: “What profit did pride bring us, or what did the ostentatious display [Note: [Col. 0448C] *ostentation*, Thu.] of riches confer upon us? All those things have passed away like a shadow” (Wis. 5:8).

And again the Apostle admonishes and says:

> Let those who buy be as though they were not buying, those who possess as though they did not possess, and those who use this [Col. 0449A] world as though they did not use it [Note: [Col. 0449C] *use it*, Ar. Lam. NC. 1. Ebor.]. For the form of this world is passing away.

(1 Cor. 7:30–31)

Peter also—to whom the Lord entrusted his sheep to be fed and protected, and upon whom he placed and founded the Church [Note: [Col. 0449C] *his Church*, Bod. 4.]—denies that he possesses gold or silver (Acts 3:6), but says that he is rich in Christ’s grace and wealthy in his faith and power. Through these he performed many mighty works with miracles; through these spiritual goods [Note: [Col. 0449C] *gifts*, Bod. 4.] he abounded unto the grace of glory. A woman who prefers to be rich in the world rather than in Christ cannot possess these resources, these riches.

[Note: [Col. 0449C]

XI.—*With your patrimony.* Pamelius, and Rigault after him, printed: “Lend your patrimony to God.” I found that reading in four ancient copies. The old editions and eleven ancient copies have: “Lend your patrimonies to God.” The reading I have retained, however, is preferred by twelve ancient books and by both the Manutius and English editions.

*Love songs must be sung.* Seneca the rhetorician, in the preface to the *Controversies*: “Nowadays obscene pursuits of singing and dancing occupy the effeminate.” Quintilian, book I, chapter 2: “Every banquet resounds with obscene songs; things shameful even to mention are displayed.” The Council of Vannes, canon 11: “Priests, deacons, and subdeacons must avoid wedding banquets and must not mingle in gatherings where love songs and obscene songs are sung.” So also canon 37 of the Council of Agde. Burchard, book II, chapter 134, quotes this decree of the Synod of Agde from the sayings of Augustine. So also Ivo of Chartres, part 6, chapter 209; but Gratian correctly attributes it to the Council of Agde. Obscene songs are forbidden in chapter 11 of the Council of Trosly. Jerome, in the *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “Let her not understand obscene words; let her be ignorant of worldly songs.” Aelius Spartianus records that the emperor Hadrian wrote love songs.

*Iron for cultivation.* Ovid, book II of the *Tristia*:

> Both the robber and the cautious traveler gird themselves with a sword;  
> The one carries it for ambush, the other as protection for himself.

Quintilian, book II, chapter 16: “Let no sword be forged for the soldier; a robber can use the same iron.” Tertullian, 627 in the book *On the Shows*: “Iron is a thing of God. Yet did its Creator provide it for killing a human being?”]]

XI. You say that you are wealthy and rich, and you think that you should make use of the things which God has willed you to possess. Use them—but for salutary purposes; use them—but for good works [Note: [Col. 0449C] “For salutary purposes and for good works,” Lam. Lin. Foss.]; use them—but for those things which God commands, which the Lord reveals. [Col. 0449B] Let the poor perceive that you are rich; let the needy perceive that you are wealthy. Lend your patrimony to God; feed Christ. By the prayers of many obtain the privilege of preserving the glory of virginity and the good fortune of attaining the Lord’s rewards. Entrust your treasures there where no thief may dig them up, where no predatory assailant lying in wait may break in. Acquire for yourself possessions that are heavenly above all, where your fruits are unfailing and everlasting and immune from every touch of worldly injury [Note: [Col. 0449C] “Immune, where neither judge may intrigue nor investigator inquire,” Vat. 1.], where neither rust wears them away, nor hail strikes them, nor sun scorches them, nor rain spoils them. For in this very matter you sin against God if you believe that riches were given to you by him so that you might not enjoy them to wholesome purpose. God also gave the human being a voice [Note: [Col. 0449C] “Gave human beings,” Lin.], yet amorous or shameful songs are not therefore to be sung [Note: [Col. 0450C] “Therefore” omitted by Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2.]; and [Col. 0450A] God willed iron to exist for cultivating the earth, yet murders are not therefore to be committed; nor, because God established incense, wine, and fire, must sacrifice therefore be offered with them to idols; nor, because flocks of livestock abound in your fields, must you sacrifice victims and offerings to the gods. Otherwise, a great patrimony is a temptation unless wealth is employed for good purposes, so that through his patrimony [Note: [Col. 0450C] “And through his patrimony,” Thu.] each person ought rather to redeem than to increase his sins.

[Note: [Col. 0450D]

**XII.—The Harlot City.** I do not know what the word *city* is doing here. For the Apocalypse is not dealing with any city, but with the great harlot. Cyprian therefore appears to have taken it from Book II of Tertullian’s *On the Dress of Women*, where one reads: “That mighty city which presides over seven mountains and very many waters.” He likewise calls it a prostituted city in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. In the first chapter of Isaiah one reads: “How has the faithful city become a harlot?” Jerome, in the *Letter to Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*: “I beseech you, let not faithful Zion become a harlot city.” See Estius on that chapter of the Apocalypse.

**The ornaments of harlots.** See Nicolaus Abram’s notes on Cicero’s *Speech for Marcus Caelius*, p. 491, and Jean Bourdelot’s commentary on Petronius, p. 277.]

XII. The marks of ornament and clothing, and the enticements of beauty, 177 are appropriate only to prostituted and shameless women; and scarcely any women’s adornment is more costly than that of those whose modesty is cheap. Thus in the Holy Scriptures, by which the Lord willed us to be instructed and admonished, the harlot city is described as more beautifully arrayed and [Col. 0450B] adorned, and as destined to perish together with her ornaments—and indeed chiefly because of those very ornaments:

> “And there came,” he says, “one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls, and he approached me, saying: ‘Come, I shall show you the condemnation of the great harlot who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication.’ And he carried me away in the spirit. And I saw a woman sitting upon a beast; and that woman was clothed in a purple [Note: [Col. 0450C] “A purple cloak,” Lin. NC. 1. Pem. Ver. Neap. Thu. Corb.] and scarlet cloak, and she was adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, holding in her hand a cup full of abominations and of the impurity [Note: [Col. 0450C] “All the impurity,” Ver.] and fornication of the whole earth” (Rev. 17:1–4).

Let chaste virgins and modest women flee the adornment of the unchaste, the attire of the shameless, the insignia of brothels, the ornaments of harlots.

[Col. 0451A] [Note: [Col. 0451B]

**XIII.—Corrupted by clothing.** So all the old books and editions read. Erasmus nevertheless thought that the word *corruptas* (“corrupted”) had been wrongly placed and conjectured that *comptas* (“adorned”) should be read. A little later Cyprian will say that “from this virgins have been corrupted,” and soon afterward that “once corrupted, they have earned ugliness and foulness.”

**The pleasures of the world.** Four of our books and one English manuscript have “riches.”

[Col. 0451C] **Crescents.** Men too used to wear little crescents, though certainly not upon the head but on their shoes, as Plutarch teaches in his *Roman Questions*. We too wore crescents on our shoes in our youth. See Lodovico Celio Ricchieri, Book XI, chap. 28.

**Hair-parting pins.** Jerome, in the *Apology Against Rufinus*: “He used to pierce the truth-telling tongue with a hair-parting pin.” In the *Apology* of Apuleius, there is mention of arranging the hair. Ovid, Book III of *The Art of Love*:

> A long face approves a parting on an unadorned head.

Plutarch asks in his book of *Roman Questions* why the Romans part the hair of brides with the point of a spear. See Martini’s lexicon and Du Cange’s Latin glossary.

**Bracelets.** Jerome, in his *Letter to Eustochium on the Little Gifts Received from Her*: “Bracelets belong to the arms.” So too Diodorus Siculus, Book V, when discussing the Gauls. Tertullian, Book I of *On the Dress of Women*: “Rings of gold with which the arms are bound.” The same Jerome, [Col. 0451D] in his *Letter to Demetrias on the Preservation of Virginity*: “They have tight-fitting sleeves.” See Cotelier’s notes on Book I of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chap. 3.

**Botronatum.** If Cyprian had rendered Isaiah’s words in the order they occupy in the book of Isaiah, it would readily be possible to understand from this what the word means. But he evidently used another version, or else disturbed the order of the words. See Salmasius in his *Plinian Exercises*, p. 763, and in his notes on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, p. 339, as well as Martini’s lexicon. See also Vossius’ *Etymologicum* under the word *botrus* (“cluster”).

**Right-arm ornaments.** Numbers, chap. 31: “rings, right-arm ornaments, and necklaces.” Lucifer of Cagliari, in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin Against God*: “We ought to revere the diadem of your kingdom, as well as the earring and the *dextrocherium*.” Here Jean du Tillet, bishop of Meaux, to whom we owe the first edition of Lucifer’s works, said that *dextrocherium* seemed to him to be a word compounded from Latin and Greek, denoting some ornament on the right hand. See Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, [Col. 0452B] p. 251, Martini’s lexicon, and Du Cange’s Latin glossary. See also Lodovico Celio Ricchieri, Book V, chap. 13.

**Earrings.** Below, in this very book, p. 177: “Did God will wounds to be inflicted on the ears?” And again below, p. 179: “Let no wounds be inflicted on the ears.” Tertullian, [Col. 0452C] Book II of *On the Dress of Women*: “God inflicted troublesome wounds upon the ears, and valued so highly the maltreatment of his handiwork and the tortures of innocent infancy, then feeling pain for the first time, that from those scars in a body born for iron should hang certain beads or other.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “Take care not to pierce her ears.” The same author in the *Epitaph of Marcella*: “To hang the most precious beads of the Red Sea from pierced ears.” Pliny, Book XII, chap. 1: “For this purpose wounds to the ears were devised—evidently because it is not enough for them to be worn upon the neck and hair unless they are also driven into the body.” Gregory of Nazianzus, in his *Poem to Olympias*, warns her not to place the adornment of her ears in pearls. See Diodorus Siculus, Book V, where he treats of Panchalia.]

XIII. Isaiah too, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries aloud and rebukes and reproves the daughters of Zion, corrupted by gold and silver and clothing, overflowing with destructive wealth and departing from God [Note: [Col. 0451B] “From the Lord,” Voss. 3.] through the pleasures of the world:

> “The daughters of Zion have been exalted,” he says, “and have walked with neck held high [Note: [Col. 0451B] ‘Advanced with lofty neck,’ Neap. Foss.; ‘Walked with lofty neck,’ Ben.], signaling with their eyes, trailing their tunics with the movement of their feet, and playing with their feet together. And God will humble the foremost daughters of Zion, and the Lord will expose their attire; and the Lord will remove the glory of their clothing, and their ornaments, and their hair, and curls, and crescents, and hair-parting pins, and bracelets, and *botronatum*, and right-arm ornaments, and rings, and earrings, and silken fabrics woven together with gold and hyacinth-blue. And instead of a sweet fragrance there will be dust; and instead of a girdle you will be girded with rope; and instead of a golden ornament for the head you will have baldness [Note: [Col. 0451B] ‘They will have baldness,’ Pem. Voss. 1]” (Isa. 3:16–24).

God condemns this; this he censures. [Col. 0451B] From this, he declares, virgins have been corrupted; from this they have departed from true and divine worship. Exalted, they fell [Note: [Col. 0452B] “Exalted, he says, they fell,” Veron.]; adorned, they earned ugliness and foulness. Those clothed in silk [Col. 0452A] and purple [Note: [Col. 0452B] “In silk and purple,” Vat. 3. Foss.] cannot put on Christ. Adorned with gold and pearls and necklaces, they have lost the ornaments of heart and breast. Who would not abhor and flee that which has brought destruction upon another [Note: [Col. 0452B] “Others,” Foss.; “Destruction,” Voss. 1.]? Who would seek and assume that which has served as sword and weapon for the death of another? If a person died after drinking from a cup, you would know that what he drank was poison. If someone died after taking food, you would know that what was taken was deadly, since it could kill the recipient; nor would you eat or drink from that which you had seen others perish before you. How great, then, is this ignorance of the truth [Note: [Col. 0452B] “Of yourself,” Foss.], how great this madness of mind: to desire that which both has always harmed and still harms, and to suppose that you yourself will not perish from that by which you know others have perished!

[Note: [Col. 0452C]

**XIV.—To dye wool.** Tertullian, in Book I of *On the Dress of Women*: “Preparations made from dye, with which wool is colored.” Virgil, *Eclogue* IV:

> Nor shall wool learn to counterfeit various colors.

Horace, Book III, Ode 3:

[Col. 0452D]

> Nor does wool treated with dye  
> Recover its lost colors.

Jerome, in the *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “Who can restore shellfish-dyed wool to its original whiteness?”

**528. With little stones.** Although the ancient manuscripts and editions read thus, I think *capillis* (“hair”) should be written instead of *lapillis* (“little stones”). The ancients used to mix filings of gold with their hair so that it would appear more golden. Indeed, a golden color—as is clear also from Virgil’s testimony in Book IV of the *Aeneid*—was esteemed in the beauty of the face and head. Julius Capitolinus teaches this in his *Verus*: “He is said, indeed, to have taken such care over his golden hair that he sprinkled filings of gold upon his head, so that his illuminated locks might shine more golden.” The same author in his *Commodus*: “His bodily form was indeed well proportioned, his head always dyed and made radiant with filings of gold.” Trebellius Pollio in his *Gallienus*: “He sprinkled gold dust upon his locks.” The author of the *Letter to Demetrias* published among Jerome’s works: “This is their chief daily concern: to entwine the hair with gold and to make the glowing stones of shellfish the glory of the head.” Martianus Capella, [Col. 0453B] Book I: “Juno too had added to her hair, as a companionable bond, a shining vein of more refined gold.” Shortly afterward the same author says that Phoebus is called “golden-haired”: “For the sun’s majestic head,” he says, “bathed in rays and encircled by blazing light, resembles the gilded hair of a radiant crown.” Hence in Tacitus, *Histories*, Book IV: “reddened hair.” Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book XI, uses “hair-gold.” Ovid, *Amores*, Book III, Elegy 12:

> A maiden’s hair is weighed down with gold and gems.

In the same book, Elegy 14:

> Yet it was not black, nor was its color golden;  
> Though neither one, its color blended both.

Likewise, in the *Letter of Cydippe to Acontius*: “He himself gave gems for your fingers and gold for your hair.” Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book IV:

> She presses a leaf upon her hair, arranging it, and entwines it with gold.

Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 10: “Do not defile beauty with gold.” Pliny, Book III, chap. 1: “Gold entwined in men’s hair.” [Col. 0453C] Seneca, *Medea*: “The gleam of jewels adorns the gold with which hair is customarily bound.” The same author in *Hercules on Oeta*: “Why does the hair lie bare of gold and gems?” Prudentius in the *Hamartigenia*: “And her plaited hair stands stiff with little golden chains.” In Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book V, Venus, enraged with her son, says: “I shall believe that satisfaction has been made for the wrong done me when I have shaved off her hair, which with these very hands of mine I have often stroked to a golden sheen.” And in Book X: “There appeared a splendid naked boy, conspicuous everywhere for his golden hair, and amid his locks little golden wings projected, joined to them by a similar kinship.” See Bourdelot’s notes on Petronius, p. 241.

After our edition of Cyprian’s works had been published, and after I had attempted to emend this passage, I at last found the true reading in an old and excellent manuscript from the monastery of Bec, in which *capillis* (“hair”) is written explicitly. The emendation is therefore certain. I would moreover have placed it in the text of this work of Cyprian if I had possessed the Bec manuscript, [Col. 0453D] which came into my hands late, at the time when this passage was being printed by the typographer.

Roman women used another device, as Valerius Maximus says in the first chapter of his second book: to make their appearance more elegant, they reddened their hair with ashes with the greatest care. Sosipater Charisius, Book I: “A woman’s attendant is called a *cinerarius* (‘ash-man’).” For Cato says in his *Origins*: “Our women used to anoint their hair with ash so that their locks would be red-gold.” The Council of Elvira, canon 67: “It must be forbidden for any female believer or catechumen to keep either long-haired men or male ash-dressers.” I reproduce these words of the synod as they are written in three very ancient and excellent manuscripts and in García de Loaysa’s edition. I note this because Fernando de Mendoza says that he does not approve this reading, since reason and the other manuscripts agree with the common edition, in which “actors or theatrical men” is written. See what [Col. 0454B] Juan Luis de la Cerda noted on Book II of Tertullian’s *To His Wife*, p. 642. By contrast, in chapter 2 of Jeremiah’s *Lamentations*, we read that the squalid and desolate daughters of Zion sprinkled their heads with ashes—evidently to disfigure their appearance and thus display their wretched condition.

From what I have noted about hair mixed with gold, I think a conjecture may be drawn for emending a passage of Juvenal from the Satire in which he depicts the depraved conduct of Messalina, whom he says stood naked in a brothel “with gilded nipples.” In place of *papillis* (“nipples”), I could readily believe that *capillis* (“hair”) should be read. For I do not see what Juvenal could have meant if he had written that her nipples were gilded. What contribution does gold on the nipples make to lust? I further think that this conjecture can be supported by Juvenal’s statement shortly before that she concealed her black hair beneath a golden wig. For the golden color rightly corresponds with gold, as the passages of the ancients cited above demonstrate. And Ovid, in Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, spoke of hair resembling gold, [Col. 0454C] that is, golden hair. (Baluze emended it to *capillis*, with insufficient caution and in utter defiance of the sense. **GOLDHORN.**)

**You should conceal.** Three old books have “she should conceal.” So too Morellius.

**With blackness drawn around them.** The manuscript of Saint-Aubin reads: “with the blackness of powder drawn around them.” Tertullian, in Book I of *On the Dress of Women*: “That very black powder with which the outlines of the eyes 529 are extended.” In Commodianus, *Instruction* 60, one reads: “Your eyes smeared with soot.”

**The cheeks with a falsehood.** Origen, Homily I on the *Song of Songs*: “For women’s beauty is said to reside especially in the cheeks.” Pliny, Book XI, chap. 37, speaking of the cheeks: “This is the seat of modesty. There the blush is displayed most of all.” Ovid, in the book *On Cosmetics for the Female Face*:

> Let neither white lead nor the foam of reddening soda  
> Be lacking to you . . .

Seneca, Book V, *Controversy* 6: “He put on a woman’s garment, arranged his hair in a woman’s fashion, encircled his eyes with a girl’s cosmetic allure, and colored his cheeks.” [Col. 0454D] Apuleius, in his *Apology*, spoke of “purple-painted cheeks.” Commodianus, *Instruction* 59: “And you also apply false preparations to your cheeks”; and *Instruction* 60: “You treat your cheeks with a certain layer of rouge.” Today nothing is more common. It is noted in the *Thesaurus of the Latin Language* that this custom came to us from the Italians; there one reads that women formerly used *purpurissum* to color their lips and cheeks, just as we generally see done among the Italians today.

**By the assault of corruption.** Erasmus would prefer *impigmatione* (“by pigmentation”), from which, as he says, the word *pigmenta* appears to be derived. But I have not read *impigmationem* elsewhere.]

XIV. For God did not make scarlet or purple [Col. 0452B] sheep, nor did he teach anyone to dye and color wool with the juices of plants and shellfish. Nor did he institute necklaces made with little stones and pearls set apart with gold, arranged in a woven series and elaborate structure, [Col. 0453A] so that you should conceal the neck which he made, and what God formed in a human being should be covered while what the devil devised is displayed above it. Did God will wounds to be inflicted upon the ears, so that infancy, still innocent and ignorant of worldly evil, might be tortured, and afterward costly beads might hang from the scars and cavities of the ears—heavy, if not by their own weight, then at least by the value [Note: [Col. 0453A] “By their weight, nevertheless,” Neap. Bod. 2.] of the merchandise? All these things sinful [Note: [Col. 0453A] “Transgressing,” NC. 2.] and apostate angels disclosed through their arts when, having sunk down to earthly contagions, they withdrew from heavenly vigor. They taught women to paint their eyes with blackness drawn around them, [Col. 0454A] to stain their cheeks with the falsehood of a blush, to alter their hair with counterfeit [Note: [Col. 0453A] “Adulterous,” Ver. Corb.] colors, and to assail all the truth of face and head with the assault of their own corruption.

[Note: [Col. 0454D]

**XV.—To adulterate God’s modeling.** Tertullian, Book II of *On the Dress of Women*: “God’s modeling plainly displeases them.” And a little earlier he had said: “For beauty is not to be accused, since it is a bodily good fortune, an addition to the divine modeling.” And in the book *On the Shows*: “Having overstepped God’s modeling.”

**With a golden color.** Juvenal, Satire 6: [Col. 0455C] “concealing her hair beneath a golden wig.” Dio Chrysostom, Oration 21, says that Achilles’ hair was golden. Apuleius, Book II of *The Golden Ass*: “A tempered blush, golden and unaffected hair.” The same author, Book V: “By those cinnamon-colored locks of yours, hanging down on every side.” Ovid, Book III of *The Art of Love*:

> A woman dyes her gray hair with genuine herbs,  
> And art seeks a color better than the true.

**It is God’s work.** Cyprian imitated his master. For Tertullian says in Book II of *On the Dress of Women*: “What is born is God’s work. Therefore, what is fabricated is the devil’s business.”

**They lay hands upon God.** Tertullian in the same place: “He unquestionably devised contrivances of this kind, so that it may be evident in you that you are, in a certain fashion, laying hands upon God.”

**If any painter.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chap. 21.]

XV. And indeed, at this point, in view of the fear which faith inspires in us and the love which fellowship requires, I think that not only virgins or widows, but married women as well—and indeed all women without exception—must be admonished that God’s work and creation and modeling ought in no way to be adulterated by the application of golden dye [Note: [Col. 0454A] “That they ought in no way to adulterate his creation and model,” Ar. Lam. NC. 1. Voss. 1.], black powder, rouge [Note: [Col. 0454A] “Or rouge” absent from MR.], or, in short, any preparation that corrupts the natural features. [Col. 0455A] God says [Note: [Col. 0455C] “Since God says,” Lin.]: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). And does anyone dare to alter and transform what God made? They lay hands upon God when they strive to remodel and transfigure what he formed, not knowing that everything born is God’s work, while whatever is altered [Note: [Col. 0455C] “Whatever is added and altered,” Ar. Neap. Bod. 4.] belongs to the devil. If some painter had portrayed a person’s face and appearance and bodily character in a faithfully matching color, and, once the likeness had already been portrayed and completed, another laid hands upon it in order to remake, as though more skillful, what had already been formed and painted, it would be regarded as a grave injury to the first artist and a just cause for indignation. Do you imagine that you will bear with impunity the audacity of such wicked temerity—an offense against God the artist? For although you may not be immodest or unchaste toward men through alluring cosmetics, [Col. 0455B] by corrupting and violating the things that belong to God you are convicted as a worse adulteress. What you suppose is adorning yourself, what you suppose is beautifying yourself, is an assault upon the divine work, a transgression against the truth [Note: [Col. 0455C] “An assault upon the truth,” NC. 1. Pem.].

[Note: [Col. 0455D]

**XVI.—Flame-colored hair.** Tertullian in the same place: “With a flame-colored head, they make an ill—indeed, the worst—omen for themselves.” See Book III of Cuper’s *Observations*, chap. 14.

**His hair was white.** The *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*: “And in that same place we saw sitting one who resembled a gray-haired man and had snow-white hair.”]

XVI. It is the voice of the Apostle admonishing us:

> “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, just as you are unleavened [Note: [Col. 0455C] ‘Unleavened bread,’ Ver.]. For Christ our Passover has also been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast [Note: [Col. 0455C] ‘Therefore let us feast,’ Voss. 3.], not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:7).

Do sincerity and truth remain when sincere things are polluted by adulterations of color [Note: [Col. 0456C] “By adulterous colors,” Bod. 2.], and true things are changed into falsehood by the counterfeit cosmetics of preparations [Note: [Col. 0456C] “By the juices of preparations,” Lam. Bod. 1; “counterfeit” deleted by Oxon.]? Your Lord says: “You cannot make one hair white or black” (Matt. 5:[Col. 0455C]36); and do you wish to be [Col. 0456A] more powerful than your Lord, so as to overcome his declaration? With an audacious endeavor and sacrilegious contempt, you dye your hair; with an evil omen of the things to come, you already make your hair flame-colored, and—horrible to say!—you sin with your head [Note: [Col. 0456C] “Horrible to say! against the head,” Bod. 1.], that is, with the superior part of the body. And although it is written of the Lord, “His head and his hair were white as wool or snow” (Rev. 1:14), you curse gray hair and abhor the whiteness that resembles the Lord’s head.

[Note: [Col. 0455D]

**XVII.—Lest he recognize you.** Julius Firmicus, in the book *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “When your company approaches the tribunal of God the judge, you will bring with you nothing that God, who made you, may recognize.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Furia on the Preservation of Widowhood*: “With what confidence does she raise toward heaven faces which the Creator does not recognize?” In Victor of Vita, Book V, chap. 9, there survives a rebuke delivered by Muritta, a deacon of Carthage, to Elpidophorus, formerly a Christian, who had been assigned the task of savagely mutilating the limbs of Christ’s confessors with tortures. Among other things, Muritta therefore tells him that God will not recognize him when the last day comes and will say: “I do not perceive the countenance bearing my seal; [Col. 0456D] I do not see the mark of the Trinity.” Emperor Constantine, in the title *On Punishments* of the Theodosian Code: “If anyone has been condemned to the gladiatorial school or the mines in proportion to the nature of the crimes discovered, no mark shall be inscribed upon his face, since the writing that records the sentence can be placed on his hands and calves, so that the face, which is fashioned in the likeness of heavenly beauty, may in no way be defiled.”

**Painted eyes.** Pliny, Book XI, chap. 37: “Human beings have eyelids on both sides, upon the cheeks. In women they are even stained in a certain fashion. So great is the pursuit of disfigurement that even the eyes are dyed.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Furia on the Preservation of Widowhood*, says: “Nor the orbs—that is, the eyes—blackened with antimony.”

**To be feared.** Erasmus noted that *meditanda* (“to be considered”) is read elsewhere, and I found that reading in the Fuxensis manuscript.]

XVII. I ask you, woman of such a kind: do you not fear that when the day of resurrection comes, your Maker may fail to recognize you, remove and exclude you when you come to receive his rewards and promises, and, rebuking you with the severity of censor and judge, say: “This is not my work, nor is this our image. You have polluted your skin with false cosmetics; you have altered your hair with counterfeit color; your face has been conquered by falsehood; [Col. 0456B] your form has been corrupted; your countenance is alien. You will not be able to see God, since your eyes are not those which God made but those which the devil has stained. You have followed him; you have imitated the glowing and painted eyes of the serpent; adorned by your enemy, you are destined to burn together with him.”

Should not these things, I ask, be considered by God’s servants? Should they not always be feared, by day and by night? Let married women see what comfort they may flatter themselves that they derive from their husbands through their eagerness to please; for while they put them forward as their excuse, they enlist them into complicity in their criminal consent. As for virgins, certainly, whom this discourse now counsels: those who have adorned themselves with arts of this kind should not, in my judgment, be numbered among virgins, but should be kept away from the holy and pure flock of virginity [Col. 0456C] like infected sheep and diseased livestock [Note: [Col. 0456C] “Livestock” absent from NC. 2.], lest by their contagion they pollute the others while they dwell [Col. 0457A] together, and lest those who have perished destroy others.

[Note: [Col. 0457B]

**XVIII.—To attend weddings.** He condemns Christian virgins who attended weddings, where, certainly, even in more respectable gatherings many things take place which do not appear appropriate for those who profess virginity. For the Fescennine songs sung at weddings gave expression to the greatest license and wantonness. The holy Martyr vigorously pursues this subject in the present passage. Jerome, in the *Letter to Demetrias on the Preservation of Virginity*: “The shrill sound of the Punic tongue will sing wanton Fescennine verses to you.” [Col. 0457C] But on the Fescennine verses, see Muretus on Catullus. Indeed, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus urges Olympias, who was married, not to attend a wedding feast where people drink deeply and, in short, indulge in tasteless jests. For “every banquet,” as Quintilian says in Book I, chap. 2, “resounds with obscene songs, and things shameful to utter are watched.” And Prudentius said in the *Hamartigenia*: “The flesh of heated convivial wickedness.”

**Amid that freedom of the wanton.** Eleven old books and Manutius’ edition read thus. Nevertheless, I do not dislike the reading of the old editions, in which it is written, “amid that wanton freedom.” That reading is also found in five old books. The Bec manuscript has, “amid that freedom of the banqueters.” Horace spoke of “wanton license” in Book I, Ode 19.

**The bridegroom to boldness.** Hildebert, Letter 36: “Virgins do not know what a woman’s weakness endures under marital license.” A description of marital license survives in an old epigram included among Salmasius’ notes on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, p. 285.

[Col. 0457D] **When modest.** This passage is read in different ways in the manuscripts and common editions.
