Some of them have: “how she who had come modest departs immodest.” Others, with the opposite sense: “when she who had come immodest departs even more immodest.” I prefer the former reading, also because Cyprian, in a similar argument, writes in *To Donatus*, p. 4: “The matron who had perhaps gone to the show modest returns from the show immodest.” Thus Martial, Book I, Epigram 30, speaking of the chaste Levina who became an adulteress at the baths, says: “She came as Penelope; she leaves as Helen.” Rigaltius thought otherwise. For although he placed in the text the reading I prefer, in his observations he approves more strongly the one which has: “she who had come more immodest departs modest.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Salvina on the Preservation of Widowhood*: “A reputation for chastity [Col. 0458B] is a fragile thing in women.” In Ovid’s *Letter of Oenone to Paris*:

> Chastity, once harmed, can be restored  
> By no art. Once lost, it is gone.

“For what,” Lucretia asks in Livy, “remains safe for a woman when chastity has been lost?” Seneca, *Hippolytus*: “It is the mind, not circumstance, that ordinarily makes a woman unchaste.”]

XVIII. And since we seek the good [Note: [Col. 0457B] “Gift,” Voss. 1.] of continence, let us avoid everything destructive and hostile [Note: [Col. 0457B] “We avoid,” Oxon., from four manuscripts; “unchaste,” Lam.]. Nor do I pass over those practices which, while becoming customary through negligence, have claimed license for themselves by habitual use against modest and sober conduct. Some women are not ashamed to attend weddings and, amid that freedom of wanton people, to mingle unchaste conversation with their speech, to hear what is improper, to say what is unlawful [Note: [Col. 0457B] “What is unlawful . . . what is improper,” Voss. 1. Bod. 2.], to be watched and to be present amid shameful words and drunken banquets, by which the fuel of lust is kindled, the bride is encouraged to endure sexual violation, and the bridegroom to boldness. What place does she have at a wedding whose mind is not set upon marriage [Note: [Col. 0457B] “What place do they have . . . whose,” Lin. Bod. 4.]? Or what pleasure [Note: [Col. 0458B] “Voluntary things,” Thu.] and joy can be there where both pursuits and desires are different? What is learned there; what [Col. 0457B] is seen? How far does a virgin fall away from her purpose when she who came modest departs immodest? Although she may remain a virgin in body and mind, she diminishes through her eyes, [Col. 0458A] ears, and tongue what she possessed.

[Note: [Col. 0458B]

**XIX.—Mixed baths.** Women bathing [Col. 0458C] with men was once considered a sign of adultery, as may be seen in Quintilian, Book V, chap. 9. Jerome, in the *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “In a grown virgin I wholly disapprove of baths; she ought to blush at herself and be incapable of allowing herself to be seen naked.” A little afterward he says, on the contrary, that she arouses dormant fires with the warm fomentations of baths. For the heat of baths, as he likewise writes in the *Letter to Furia on the Preservation of Widowhood*, inflames the fresh blood of a young woman. The same author, in the *Letter to Rusticus the Monk*: “Let him who desires to extinguish the heat of the blood with the chill of fasting not seek the warm fomentations of baths.” Aelius Spartianus reports that Emperor Hadrian separated the baths according to sex. Julius Capitolinus writes that Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher abolished mixed baths. Aelius Lampridius teaches that Alexander Severus prohibited mixed baths from being provided at Rome and willed eunuchs to supervise nothing in the palace except the women’s baths. The Council of Laodicea, canon 30: “Those dedicated to sacred offices, clerics, ascetics, or any Christian layman ought not to bathe with women, because this is the foremost reproach among the gentiles.” [Col. 0458D] Quite rightly. For, as Ovid says in Book III of *The Art of Love*: “The baths conceal many secret games”; here I think *mista* (“mixed”) should be read. See Petau’s observations on Epiphanius, in Heresy 30, that of the Ebionites; Cotelier’s notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, p. 131 of the Paris edition; and Beveridge’s annotations on Trullan canon 77.

**Modesty is stripped off.** Herodotus, Book I: “When a woman removes her tunic, she removes her modesty.” Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinian*?: “Herodotus writes that when a woman puts off her garment she also puts off her modesty.” Rufinus, Book I on Hosea: “She had driven from her face the modesty which customarily impedes obscenity.” Pliny, Book XXXV, chap. 10, mentions the noteworthy modesty of a new bride. Justin, Book XIV, reports that Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great, as she was dying, covered her legs with her hair and clothing so that nothing indecorous might be seen on her body. Quintus Curtius, Book V, says that the attire of Babylonian women entering banquets was modest at first; then they removed each upper covering and gradually profaned their modesty, finally exposing the lowest parts of their bodies. [Col. 0459B–C] On this subject, see Lodovico Celio Ricchieri, Book V, chap. 11. Aulus Gellius, Book XV, chap. 10, writes from Plutarch that, when the Milesian maidens were taking their own lives by hanging without any evident cause, the Milesians decreed that all who died with their bodies suspended should be carried out naked with the same noose with which they had girded themselves; and after this decree the maidens no longer sought voluntary death, deterred solely by shame at so dishonorable a funeral. I shall close these notes with a distinguished passage of Valerius Maximus, who says in Book IV, chap. 5, that modesty is the parent of every honorable resolution, the guardian of solemn duties, and the mistress of innocence, and that at all times it presents an agreeable countenance. The same author, Book VI, chap. 1, says that chastity is the chief support of men and women alike. But nakedness was censured not only in women but also in men. For Masurius Sabinus, as reported by Aulus Gellius, Book X, chap. 15, relates that the Flamen Dialis could not remove his under-tunic [Col. 0459D] except in a covered place, lest he be naked beneath the sky, as though before the eyes of Jupiter.

**Modesty is laid aside.** Although it is written thus in nearly all the manuscripts and editions, I would nevertheless prefer *caeditur* (“is struck down”), as is read in one manuscript from Saint-Remi and in the Bec manuscript, and as Morellius and Pamelius testify that they read in several old books. For a little afterward I see written there: “the honor of continence and modesty is struck down.” This reading also seems to be confirmed by the Cambron manuscript cited by Pamelius, and likewise by another Neapolitan manuscript noted in the margin of my copy of the Manutian edition, in which *laeditur* (“is injured”) was written. Yet although these things are true, I did not dare to alter the text against the authority of 531 so many old manuscripts and editions. Gregory of Nazianzus, in the *Poem to Olympias*, says that the loss of modesty is the surest parent of every disgraceful act.

[Col. 0460B] **To be exposed.** That is, to be stripped naked. See the notes on Letter 63, p. 477.

**To be handled.** It must not be concealed that *conspectanda* (“to be gazed upon”) is written in one old book cited in the margin of the Lyon edition of 1544, in which variant readings from several ancient manuscripts are recorded.

[Col. 0460C] **Be modest.** The Burgundian manuscript reads: “Let virginity be modest among men.”]

### XIX

But what of those who frequent mixed baths, who prostitute bodies dedicated to modesty and chastity before eyes made inquisitive by lust? When they shamefully see men naked and are themselves seen naked by men, do they not themselves furnish an enticement to vice? Do they not arouse and invite the desires of those present to their own corruption and dishonor? “Let each person,” you say, “see with what intention he comes there; my concern is merely to refresh and wash my poor little body.” That defense does not cleanse you [Note: [Col. 0458B] “That filthy defense,” Pem. Voss. 2.], nor does it excuse the charge of wantonness and insolence. Such bathing soils; it does not wash. It does not cleanse the limbs but stains them. You look upon no one immodestly, but you yourself are looked upon immodestly. You do not pollute your own eyes with shameful pleasure; but [Col. 0458B] while you give pleasure to others, you yourself are polluted. You turn the bath into a spectacle. The places where you assemble are fouler than the theater [Note: [Col. 0458B] “Theaters,” Voss. 1. Old anonymous edition.]. There all modesty is stripped away; together with the covering [Col. 0459A] of clothing, the body’s honor and sense of shame are laid aside; virginity is exposed to be marked out and handled. Consider now whether, when you are clothed, you are modest among men, when the audacity of nakedness advances you toward shamelessness.

[Note: [Col. 0460C]

### XX.—The besieging enemy

The old editions and five old manuscripts have *expugnatus* (“the conquered enemy”). That reading may be sound. I nevertheless prefer the other, both because it appears in the editions of Manutius and Morellius and in twelve ancient manuscripts, and because below, in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 184, we read: “They would not now have the enemy and besieger within their own household.”

**Widows before they were brides.** Jerome, in the *Letter to Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*: “You may see very many women who are widows before they have been brides, covering an unhappy conscience merely with a deceptive garment.” In Apuleius’s *Apology*: “Perhaps she would still have remained at home, a widow before she was a bride.” Ovid, *Fasti*, Book II: “Refrain, widowed maidens.”]

### XX

Thus, then, the Church frequently mourns her virgins; thus she groans over their infamous and detestable stories; thus the flower of virgins is extinguished, the honor of continence and modesty is cut down [Note: [Col. 0459B] “Is cut down,” Neap.; “is laid aside,” Vat. 1, 2, 3.], and all their glory and dignity are profaned! Thus the besieging enemy insinuates himself through his devices; thus the devil creeps in by snares that deceive in secret. Thus, while virgins wish to adorn themselves more elaborately and to wander about more freely, they cease to be virgins: corrupted by hidden disgrace, widows before they are brides, adulteresses not of a husband but of Christ. Just as, while virgins, they had been destined for immense rewards, so they will experience immense punishments [Col. 0459B] for the virginity they have lost.

[Note: [Col. 0460C]

### XXI.—Fearing

Nearly all the old manuscripts and editions prefer this reading. Pamelius printed *docentem* (“teaching”); I found that reading in six ancient manuscripts, in one of which *timentem* (“fearing”) had first been written but was later erased so that *docentem* might be written. Twenty others have *timentem*. Cyprian therefore says that he fears for the virgins dedicated to God if they do not maintain a life consistent with their profession, and so he admonishes them to persevere in what they have begun.

**You who are a virgin.** In Erasmus’s edition, from which others adopted it, the words “you who serve God” follow. But because I did not find this in more than one old manuscript, whereas it is absent from all the others—that is, twenty, and especially from the Séguier manuscript—I judged that it was not Cyprian’s and had been added by some scholar, perhaps in the margin, in the guise of an interpretation. I therefore deleted it.

**With the hundredfold.** I retained this reading because it occurs in all the ancient manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, and [Col. 0461B] in the editions preceding that of Manutius. Prudentius, in his *Poem on Saint Agnes*, says:

> Meanwhile God encircles  
> The brow of the unwedded martyr with two crowns.  
> A reward yielded seven times tenfold  
> Completes the one with everlasting light.  
> In the other stands the hundredfold fruit.

[Col. 0461C] In the Pithou and Verona manuscripts the reading here is: “The first with the hundredfold.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*: “The hundredfold and sixtyfold fruit come from the one seed of chastity.” John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book VIII, chapter 11: “Yet I do not say this to detract from marital chastity; but although the hundredfold or sixtyfold fruit springs from the root of the thirtyfold, I by no means consider it comparable to the thirtyfold.”

**Sixtyfold.** Prudentius, Book II *Against Symmachus*:

> Our virgins too have most beautiful rewards.

And shortly afterward:

> Here fruits six times ten are gathered into the barns.

**Thought.** So nearly all the old manuscripts. Two, however, have “struggle.” In the Verona manuscript “struggle” was written first, but “thought” was written above the line.]

### XXI

Hear me, therefore [Note: [Col. 0459B] “Me” is absent from Oxon.], virgins, as a parent; hear, I beg you, one who fears for you even as he admonishes you; hear one who faithfully counsels you for your own advantage and benefit. Be such as God the Craftsman made you; [Col. 0460A] be such as the Father’s hand fashioned you. Let your face remain uncorrupted, your neck pure, your appearance unfeigned. Let no wounds be inflicted upon your ears, nor let a costly chain of bracelets and necklaces enclose your arms or necks. Let your feet be free from golden fetters, your hair unpainted by any dye, your eyes worthy of looking upon God. Let your bathing be conducted with women, among whom your washing is chaste [Note: [Col. 0459B] “Chaste toward you,” nearly all printed editions; “it ought to be toward you,” Oxon.]. Let shameless wedding celebrations and wanton banquets [Note: [Col. 0459B] “Drunken,” Ver.] be avoided, for their contagion is dangerous. You who are a virgin, overcome clothing; you who overcome the flesh and the world, overcome gold. It is not characteristic of the same [Note: [Col. 0460B] “Of the same virtue and spirit,” Voss. 2.] person to be incapable of being overcome by greater things and yet to be found unequal to lesser ones. Narrow [Note: [Col. 0460B] Lin. adds: “Integrity proves itself equal in all things; nor should adornment bring the good of virginity into disrepute.”] and confined is the way that leads to life (Matt. 7:14); hard and steep [Note: [Col. 0460B] “Confined,” Bod. 2.] is the boundary-path that tends toward glory (ibid., 13). Along this boundary of the way the martyrs advance, the [Col. 0460B] virgins go, and all the righteous proceed. Avoid the broad and spacious roads. There are deadly enticements and death-dealing pleasures there. 180 There the devil flatters in order to deceive, smiles in order to harm, entices in order to kill. The first fruit, with the hundredfold, belongs to the martyrs; the second, the sixtyfold, belongs to you. [Col. 0461A] Just as among the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0461B] “The martyr,” Oxon.; *martyras* [uncertain form], Thu. Corb.] there is no thought of the flesh and the world, nor is the encounter slight, easy, and delicate, so also among you, for whom the second reward in grace is appointed [Note: [Col. 0461B] “In relation to grace,” Bod. 1, 2. Thu. Foss. Corb. MR.], let your courage in endurance be correspondingly close to theirs. There is no easy ascent to great things. What sweat, what labor do we endure when we try to climb hills and mountain peaks? What, then, when we are to ascend to heaven? If you look to the promised reward, the labor you undergo is less. Immortality is given to the one who perseveres [Note: [Col. 0461B] “To those who persevere,” Bod. 1.]; everlasting life is promised; the Lord promises a kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0461C]

### XXII.—They do not marry

The Foix manuscript has, “They will neither marry nor be given in marriage.” The Séguier manuscript and one other old manuscript have only, “They are not given in marriage.” The word *nubere* (“to marry”) is often found in an obscene sense, as the most learned [Col. 0461D] John Selden noted after Lipsius in Book V, chapter 4 of *The Law of Nature and Nations*, and as we too have observed elsewhere. Servius the grammarian likewise seems to have understood it so in his commentary on Book II of the *Aeneid*: “Unmarried: she who has never *nubit*. For a virgin too can *nubere*.” Tertullian, Book IV *Against Marcion*: “While a marriage remains in force, *nubere* is adultery.” The same Tertullian, speaking of Christ’s incarnation in the *Apology*, says that the Son of God had no mother arising from unchastity; even she whom he seemed to have as mother had not *nupserat*. Here it is evident that *nupserat* is used for a woman’s intercourse with a man. Otherwise what Tertullian says would be false, since it is certain that Mary, the mother of Christ, had been taken in marriage by Joseph, had been married to Joseph, and had been his wife; and that Christ was therefore thought to be the carpenter’s son, because he was the son of the woman who was the carpenter’s wife—for the son is he whom marriage identifies. Hence, in Saint Cyril’s scholia *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 25, we read: “For he was born of a virgin and alone has an [Col. 0462B] unmarried mother,” that is, a virgin who had not had intercourse with a husband. Rufinus too, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 6, used “unmarried” for “virgin.” In place of this, Jerome, at the beginning of his book *Against Helvidius*, said that Mary was a mother before she was married, because, of course, she had conceived by the Holy Spirit before she became Joseph’s wife instead of merely his betrothed. And Saint Ambrose, in his letter concerning [Col. 0462C] Bishop Bonosus, who was accused at the Synod of Capua of saying that the Virgin Mary had several children, wrote: “For the Lord Jesus would not have chosen to be born through a virgin if he had judged that she would be so incontinent as to defile by the seed of human intercourse that generative sanctuary of the Lord’s body, that court of the eternal King.” Moreover, to mention this too in passing, Rigault thought that this passage from Tertullian’s *Apology* should be written so as to say that Christ had no mother “arising from chastity,” because he saw that Latino Latini and Pamelius had read it so in certain very old copies. I, by contrast, think the commonly received reading should be retained, since it rests upon the authority of the oldest and best manuscripts. The sense is that Christ’s mother suffered no stain of unchastity—not even, to use Rufinus’s words, the outrage of an obscene handling—since she never engaged in marital intercourse with a husband or, to speak with Lactantius, was never joined to a husband through the enticements of pleasure. See Erasmus’s annotations [Col. 0462D] on this passage of Matthew.

**You have already begun to be.** Jerome, in his exposition of Psalm 44 addressed to Principia: “Sex is swallowed up by the virgin. She bears Christ in her breast. She already possesses what she is to become.” The same author, in his *Letter to Eustochium on the Guarding of Virginity*: “Rejoice, sister; rejoice, daughter; rejoice, my virgin, because you have truly begun to be what other women merely pretend to be.”

**Grace.** Nearly all the old manuscripts and old editions prefer this reading. Manutius preferred “glory,” and the later editions adopted it from him. I do not dare to disregard the authority of so many old copies and editions that read otherwise. If anyone nevertheless prefers “glory,” let him enjoy his own judgment.

**You persevere chaste and virgins.** Jerome, in his *Letter to Eustochium on the Guarding of Virginity*: “And because they have experienced the dominion of husbands, they are called chaste women and *nonnae*.” For what *nonnae* are, consult Du Cange’s Latin glossary.]

### XXII

Preserve [Note: [Col. 0461B] “Preserve what you owe,” Foss.], virgins, preserve what you have begun to be; preserve what you will be. A great recompense awaits you: a great reward of virtue, the greatest gift of chastity. Do you wish to know what evil the virtue of continence lacks and what good it possesses? “I will multiply,” God says to the woman [Col. 0461B], “your sorrows and your groanings, and in sorrow [Note: [Col. 0462B] “With sorrow,” Ver.] you will bear children; and your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you” (Gen. 3:16). You are free from this sentence; you do not [Col. 0462A] fear women’s sorrows and groanings. You have no fear concerning the bearing of children, nor is a husband your lord; instead, your Lord [Note: [Col. 0462B] “The Lord, the Lord your God,” Bod. 1, 2, 4.] and head is Christ, in the image and place of the male. Your lot and condition are shared with men. It is the Lord’s voice that says in that passage: “The children of this age beget and are begotten. But those who shall have been deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor contract marriage. For they will no longer begin to die; for they are equal to the angels of God, since they are children of the resurrection” (Luke 20:31–36). What we are to become, you have already begun to be. You already possess the glory of the resurrection in this age; you pass through the age without the age’s contagion, provided that you persevere chaste and virgins. You are equal to the angels of God. Only let virginity remain and endure sound and unharmed, and as it began courageously, let it persevere continually. [Col. 0462B] Let it seek the adornments not of necklaces or garments, but of conduct. Let it look upon God and heaven, and not lower eyes raised on high toward the desire of flesh and the world, nor cast them down [Note: [Col. 0462B] “Nor toward earthly things,” Bod. 2.] toward earthly things.

[Col. 0463A] [Note: [Col. 0463B]

### XXIII.—Dwelling places

The Foix manuscript has “mansions,” which is perhaps better. For in chapter 14 of the Gospel [Col. 0463C] according to John, to which Cyprian refers here, the Vulgate edition reads: “In my Father’s house are many mansions.” But here it must be remembered that Cyprian used a version different from the one we use.

**To the divine bath.** I printed this, following the testimony of one of my old manuscripts. This reading seems best to me. For the other is exceedingly convoluted and reads as follows: “All, indeed, who attain to the divine and paternal gift through the sanctification of Baptism.” For 533 what is the word “paternal” doing here? And yet that reading occurs in the Séguier manuscript and six others. Seven others and the old editions prefer “patrimony”; the Bec manuscript has “fatherland.” But, in my judgment, none of these words suits this passage. If anyone nevertheless wishes to retain one of them, I do not object.

**As we have borne.** Saint Augustine reproduces this final portion of the book in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book IV, chapter 21.]

### XXXIII

The first pronouncement commanded growth and procreation; the second commended continence. While the world was still new and empty [Note: [Col. 0463B] “Was,” Oxon., from all the manuscripts; “is,” printed editions.], we were propagated through procreation in abundance [Note: [Col. 0463B] “Abundant,” Ar.; “an abundance of fecundity,” Bod. 1, 2. Ver. Voss. 1.], and we increased for the multiplication of the human race. Now that the earth is filled and the world is full, those who can receive continence, living in the manner of eunuchs, make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom. The Lord does not command this but exhorts to it; nor does he impose a yoke of necessity, since freedom of choice remains. But when he says that there are many dwelling places with his Father (John 14:2), he indicates lodgings in a better habitation. You seek these better dwellings; by making eunuchs of the flesh’s desires, you obtain in heaven the reward of greater grace. All, indeed, who attain to the divine bath through the sanctification of Baptism put off the old person there [Col. 0463B] through the grace of the saving bath; and, renewed by the Holy Spirit, they are cleansed from the filth of their ancient contagion through a repeated birth. But the greater holiness and reality of that repeated birth belong to you, in whom there are now no desires of flesh and body. In you only those things that belong to virtue and spirit have remained for glory [Note: [Col. 0464B] “For glory” is absent from Ar. MR.]. It is the voice of the Apostle whom the Lord called his chosen vessel and whom God [Col. 0464A] sent to declare [Note: [Col. 0464B] “To earn,” MR.] the heavenly commandments: “The first man,” he says, “was from the clay of the earth, the second man from heaven [Note: [Col. 0464B] ‘The second from heaven,’ Thu. Foss. Corb.]. As the man of clay was, so also are those who are of clay; and as the heavenly man is, so also are the heavenly. As we have borne the image of him who is of clay, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47–49). Virginity bears this image; integrity bears it; 181 holiness and truth bear it. Those mindful of God’s discipline bear it: those who retain righteousness together with religion, steadfast in faith, humble in fear, courageous in every endurance, gentle in bearing injury, ready to practice mercy, of one mind and harmonious in fraternal peace.

[Note: [Col. 0463D]

### XXIV.—You who are younger, furnish an example

After these words Pamelius, preceded by the edition called that of Gravius, added from the Afflighem and Cologne manuscripts, “service to those who are older,” and says that this fits perfectly. I do not dispute whether it fits perfectly. I say only that I deleted these two words because I did not find them in the old editions [Col. 0464B] or in any of the old copies I used—that is, twenty-seven.

[Col. 0464C] **Virginity begins to be honored.** That is, when the Lord begins to honor martyrdom in you, as it is written in the book *In Praise of Martyrdom*, p. 352: when, as the holy Martyr says in this very book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 175, you endure fires or crosses, the sword, or wild beasts, so that you may receive the crown of martyrdom. Prudentius, in his *Poem on Saint Fructuosus, Bishop of Tarragona*: “For worshipers of Christ, prison is a step toward the crown.” Jerome, in Question XI addressed to Hedibia: “The triumph of God is the suffering of the martyrs, the shedding of blood for Christ’s name, and joy amid torments.” Virginity therefore begins to be honored when a Christian virgin begins to suffer for Christ’s name. Cyprian, in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 201: “Confession is the beginning of glory, not yet the merit of the crown; it does not complete praise but inaugurates dignity”; and Letter 77, *To the Martyrs*, p. 159: “First severely beaten and afflicted with clubs, through punishments of that kind you inaugurated the glorious beginnings of your confession.” Hence the complaint of Secunda, virgin and martyr, who, when she saw [Col. 0464D] her sister Rufina being scourged, cried out to the judge: “Why do you bestow glory upon my sister, yet do not permit me to share in that glory?” Celerinus, in his *Letter to Lucianus*, p. 29: “May he whose name you have confessed crown you thus.”]

### XXIV

Each of these things, good virgins, you must observe, cherish, and fulfill—you who, free for God and Christ, advance toward the Lord to whom you have dedicated yourselves, with a greater [Col. 0464B] and better portion. You who are advanced in years, provide instruction for the younger; you who are younger, furnish an incentive to your contemporaries. Spur one another on by mutual exhortations; challenge one another toward glory by mutually emulating examples of virtue. Endure courageously; advance spiritually; arrive successfully. Only remember us then, when virginity begins to be honored in you.

[Col. 0463]

# BOOK ON THE LAPSED

[Note: [Col. 0463D]

## ON THE LAPSED

As others have already observed, Cyprian himself mentions this book in Letter 51, p. 66, as does Pontius the deacon in his *Life* of Cyprian; so too do [Col. 0464D] Saint Augustine and Saint Fulgentius in the passages noted below. Some add Eusebius of Caesarea, but incorrectly. Carelessness deceived them. For since Rufinus [Col. 0465C] translated Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* into Latin, they believed that he had translated it straightforwardly and added nothing of his own; they therefore persuaded themselves that what is read in the translator concerning this book of Cyprian is also found in Eusebius. That is not true. These are Rufinus’s words: “Cyprian published a magnificently [Col. 0465D] written book about them—that is, about the Lapsed—in which he determined both that the Lapsed should be exhorted to repentance and that those who opposed this were alien to the heart of Christ.” Moreover, Venericus, bishop of Vercelli, frequently cites this book and the book *On the Unity of the Church*.]

(C)

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0463D]

Cyprian had frequently promised that, as soon as peace was restored to the Church, he would [Col. 0464D] write something more definite about the proper treatment of the lapsed; in this book, therefore, he fulfills his promises. First, he sets [Col. 0465A] before the reader with joy the Church’s wholly unexpected peace and the steadfastness of the confessors and of the others who stood firm in the faith; then, with the greatest sorrow, the ruin of the lapsed. After explaining the causes of the preceding persecution—namely, the neglect of discipline and the sins of the faithful—he sternly rebukes the lapsed because, at the very first words of the threatening enemy, they sacrificed to idols instead of withdrawing in accordance with Christ’s counsel. He likewise rebukes them because, already stained by sacrifices and contrary to the law of the Gospel, before their offenses had been expiated and before an *exomologesis*—a public confession—of their crime had been made, they violated the body and blood of the Lord and extorted communion and peace from certain presbyters without the bishop’s judgment.

He therefore urges many toward confession of their offense, public repentance, and full satisfaction: first frightening them by the divine punishment of some of the lapsed who had communicated unworthily—while incidentally mentioning the *libellatici*, those who had obtained certificates, and explaining that they were not thereby excused from guilt—and [Col. 0465B] then encouraging them by the example of those who, although implicated in no crime of sacrifice or certificate, nevertheless painfully and simply confessed before God’s priests that they had even thought of doing this, and so performed *exomologesis*. Finally, he warns that the Novatians must be avoided, refuting their heresy by several passages of Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0465D]

### I.—Peace restored to the Church

After the death of Decius, as Pearson demonstrates in his *Cyprianic Annals*.

**Cloud.** Rigault added “and darkness.” But this addition, which is doubtless derived from a gloss, is unknown to the other editions and the old manuscripts. It was found in only two: one royal manuscript, from which I think Rigault took it, and the Moissac manuscript.

**By the prayers of all.** The Foix manuscript has, “by all voices and prayers.”]

### I

BEHOLD, dearly beloved brothers, peace has been restored to the Church; and our security, which recently seemed difficult to the unbelieving and impossible to the faithless, has been restored by divine aid and vengeance. Our minds return to joy, and, the storm of oppression and the cloud [Note: [Col. 0465C] “The cloud having been scattered and the darkness dispersed,” Ar. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Lam. Ebor.; “pressed by the storm,” Voss. 3; “cloud and darkness,” Oxon. Rigault.] having been dispersed, tranquility and serenity shine forth. Praise must be given to God, and his benefits and gifts must be celebrated with thanksgiving, [Col. 0465C] although our voice [Note: [Col. 0465C] “Our voice is fitting,” Bod. 4.] did not cease to give thanks even during the persecution. For [Col. 0466A] the enemy cannot be permitted so much that we, who love the Lord with our whole heart and soul and strength [Note: [Col. 0465C] “We who love God with our whole heart and soul do not,” Voss. 3.], should fail always and everywhere to proclaim his blessings and praises with glory. The day desired by the prayers of all has come, and after the dreadful and hideous darkness of a long night, the world, illumined by the Lord’s light, has shone forth [Note: [Col. 0465C] “Has shone forth, and the confessors,” Bod. 4.].

[Note: [Col. 0465D]

### II.—A white-robed cohort

Tertullian, in Book I *To His Wife*: “That entire Church is enrolled in white by holiness.” See Rigault there. The same Tertullian, in the book [Col. 0466C] *On the Crown*: “And all the better to be crowned with the laurel crown of martyrdom.” See the notes of Juan Luis de la Cerda, p. 649. On the “white-robed host,” see Baronius under the years 261 and 303.

**Sacrilegious sacrifices.** Seven old manuscripts have, “sacrifices and sacrileges.”

[Col. 0466D] **Reserved.** Two old manuscripts have, “bound over.”

**They overcame their sex.** Above, Letter 31, p. 164: “stronger than their sex.” See the notes there.

**Passing beyond their years in virtues.** So the old editions, twenty-three of our manuscripts, and four English manuscripts. One royal manuscript and the Moissac manuscript read, “passing beyond their years in the virtues of continence.” But since the word “continence” is absent from so many ancient manuscripts and does not suit 534 this passage, as Latini says, we judged that it should be deleted. Pamelius, to be sure, added it from the edition called that of Gravius and from a certain old manuscript. But Latini himself long ago declared that this authority was not of sufficient weight to persuade us that the word should be retained.

[Col. 0467C] **Of those standing firm.** The old editions, the Séguier manuscript, the Grenoble manuscript, the more recent Victor manuscript, and one Vatican manuscript have, “of those standing around.” But this reading is not sound. The Lamonian manuscript has, “of those standing by.”

**Losses.** This word is absent from the ancient editions and from thirteen old manuscripts. Erasmus added it. I found it in only five manuscripts. I nevertheless retained it because it seems necessary.

**For the testing.** Sixteen [Col. 0467D] old copies present this reading. The Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis has: “Days were being appointed for the assault upon their faith.” The Burgundian manuscript has, “were being announced beforehand.” The old editions have, “were feared in advance.”]

### II

We behold the confessors, illustrious through the renown of a good name [Note: [Col. 0465C] “Of the divinity,” Ben.; “of light,” Ar. Voss. 1. Lam. Bon. 3.] and glorious through the praises of courage and faith, with joyful faces; we cling to them with holy kisses and embrace with insatiable longing those for whom we had long yearned. Present is the white-robed cohort of Christ’s soldiers, who broke the raging turbulence of the persecution’s violence by an unshaken encounter, prepared to endure prison and armed to bear death. You resisted [Note: [Col. 0466C] “Resisting,” Bod. 1, 3.] the world courageously; you presented a glorious spectacle to God [Note: [Col. 0466C] “To those who would follow God,” Voss. 1.] and became an example to the brothers who would follow. [Col. 0466B] A devout voice spoke Christ’s name [Note: [Col. 0466C] “Christ’s,” Bod. 1, 4.], confessing him in whom it had once placed its faith. Illustrious hands, accustomed only to divine works, resisted sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly food, after receiving the Lord’s body and blood, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your head remained free from the impious and accursed veil with which the captive heads of those sacrificing were covered there. Your brow, pure with God’s sign, could not bear the devil’s crown; it reserved itself for the Lord’s crown. How joyfully Mother Church receives you into her bosom [Note: [Col. 0466C] “You joyful ones into her bosom,” Voss. 1, 2, 3; “with joyful bosom,” Oxon. printed editions.] as you return from battle! How blessedly and gladly she opens her gates, so that you may enter in united ranks, bearing trophies from the defeated enemy! With the triumphant men come women also, who, in battling with the world [Note: [Col. 0466C] “With the world and also their sex,” Bod. 1, 3, 4. Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1, 3. Thu. Corb. Vat. 2. MR.], [Col. 0466C] overcame their sex as well. Virgins also come, with the glory of their service doubled, and children passing beyond their years in virtues. Moreover, the rest of the multitude who stood firm [Col. 0467A] follows your glory and accompanies your footsteps with badges of praise very near and almost equal to your own. In them is the same sincerity of heart, the same integrity of tenacious faith. 182 Rooted immovably in the heavenly commandments and strengthened by the traditions of the Gospel, they were not terrified by the exile prescribed for them, the torments appointed for them, the loss of their property, or bodily punishments. Days were being fixed for the testing of their faith. But one who remembers that he has renounced the world recognizes no day belonging to the world; nor does one who hopes for eternity from God any longer reckon earthly times.

[Note: [Col. 0467D]

### III.—Through prudent withdrawal

Concerning this withdrawal of the holy Martyr, Pontius the deacon writes, among other things, as follows: “It remains for us to prove that this withdrawal was not conceived from human faintheartedness but, as was truly the case, was divine.” Jerome likewise says of Paul the Hermit: “When the storm of persecution was threatening, he withdrew to a more remote and secluded country estate.” See Tertullian’s book *On Flight in Persecution*.]

### III

No one [Note: [Col. 0467C] “No one, brothers, no one,” Voss. 1. Lam. MR.], dearly beloved brothers, must mutilate this glory; no one must weaken by malicious disparagement the uncorrupted steadfastness of those who stood firm. When the day appointed for denying the faith [Note: [Col. 0467C] “Of those denying,” Voss. 1, 3.] had passed, whoever had not made a declaration within that day [Col. 0467B] thereby confessed that he was a Christian [Note: [Col. 0467C] “Did not confess himself?” Lam.]. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord when seized by the hands of the pagans; the second step toward glory [Note: [Col. 0467C] “The step is, when someone,” Voss. 1.] is to be withdrawn through prudent seclusion and reserved for the Lord [Note: [Col. 0467C] “Reserved,” Voss. 1.]. The former is a public confession; the latter, a private one. The former overcomes the judge of the world; the latter, content with God as his judge, preserves a pure conscience through integrity of heart. There courage is more ready; here circumspection is more secure. The former, when his hour approached, was already found mature; the latter has perhaps been deferred: one who abandoned his patrimony withdrew precisely because he would not deny the faith; certainly he too would have confessed if he had been arrested.

[Note: [Col. 0467D]

### IV.—Hard or iron-hearted

Cicero, Second Action *Against Verres*: “Who at that time was so hard and iron-hearted, who so inhuman?” Juvenal, Satire I:

> For who can be so patient  
> With this unjust city, so iron-hearted, as to restrain himself?

**Assault.** The Foix manuscript has, “attack.” A little later in this same book: “nor was he cast down by the attack of persecution.” [Col. 0468C] See what we noted concerning “assault” at Letter 23, p. 421.

**Among the fallen.** Optatus, Book I: “It cast some down into deadly death.”]

### IV

One sorrow casts a shadow over these heavenly crowns of the martyrs, these spiritual glories of the confessors, and these greatest and most extraordinary virtues of the brothers who stood firm: [Col. 0467C] namely, that the violent [Col. 0468A] enemy, through the devastation wrought by his ravaging, tore away and struck down a part of our own inward being. What am I to do here, dearly beloved brothers? Tossed by the mind’s conflicting surges, what am I to say, and how am I to say it? Tears rather than words are needed to express [Note: [Col. 0468C] “To extend,” Ar. Lam. Ben. Ebor. NC. 2. Bod. 2.] the grief with which the wound of our body must be lamented and the manifold loss of a people once numerous must be mourned. For who is so hard or iron-hearted, who so forgetful of brotherly love [Note: [Col. 0468C] “So forgetful of the calamity,” Lam.], that, standing amid the various ruins of his own people and their mournful remnants, disfigured by great squalor, he can keep his eyes dry and does not, when weeping immediately bursts forth, express his groans in tears before giving them voice? I grieve, brothers; I grieve with you. My own integrity and private well-being do not beguile me into soothing my sorrows, since a shepherd is wounded more deeply by the wound of his flock. I join my heart to each one [Col. 0468B] and share the mournful burdens of grief and death. I lament with those who lament; I weep with those who weep; with those who lie fallen, I believe myself to lie fallen. Those missiles of the raging [Note: [Col. 0468C] “Raging,” Lin. NC. 2.] enemy struck my own limbs as well; the raging swords passed through my inward parts. My spirit could not remain exempt and free from the persecution’s assault. In my fallen brothers, my affection cast me down as well.

[Note: [Col. 0468C]

### V.—A long peace had corrupted us

Saint Augustine, in his *Letter to Count Boniface*: “For anxiety fittingly disciplined those whom security had rendered negligent.” Sulpicius [Col. 0468D] Severus, Book II of the *Sacred History*: “Most of them, corrupted once again by a long peace.” And below: “Again corrupted by the evil of a long peace, they poured libations to idols.” Velleius Paterculus, Book II: “Pannonia, made insolent by the blessings of a long peace.” Tacitus, in Book IV of the *Annals*, relates that Piso was rendered careless by peace. Juvenal, Satire VI: “Now we suffer the evils of a long peace.” Lucan, Book V: “The first frenzy of war scattered those who had rested throughout a long peace.” Modestus, in the book *On the Vocabulary of Military Affairs*: “The prolonged security of peace diverted men partly toward the enjoyment of leisure, partly toward civil duties.” Caesar, Book II *On the Civil War*: “The multitude, made insolent by the long duration of leisure.” Cassian, Book V, chapter 19: “This is so that the soldier of Christ, growing sluggish in the leisure of peace, may not begin to forget the glorious contests of his profession and, dissolved by the inertia of security, be deprived of the rewards of service and the merits of triumphs.” Saint Leo the Pope, Sermon II for the Solemnity of Epiphany: “We must vigilantly guard against those dangers that arise from the very leisure of peace.” See our notes on Book VI of Salvian.

[Col. 0469B] **We deserved still more.** So the ancient editions. Erasmus wrote, “we deserved to suffer still more”; I found this in four ancient copies. The edition called that of Gravius also had it, but printed in smaller type to indicate that it appeared doubtful whether it belonged to Cyprian. The word “suffer,” however, is not found in eighteen of our copies, in the five English manuscripts, or in the editions of Manutius and Morellius. I judge that it was inserted by some petty scholar who thought the sense incomplete without that word, just as Freinsheim, on Book II of Tacitus’s *Histories*, where the text reads, “thinking victory had begun,” believes that the word “thinking” was added by an outsider who supposed something to be missing there. Erasmus’s edition could nevertheless be supported by what follows a little later: “What would such people not deserve to suffer for sins of this kind?”]

### V

Nevertheless, dearly beloved brothers, account must be taken of the truth. The dark [Note: [Col. 0468C] “Enticing,” Voss. 1, 3.] gloom of the hostile persecution ought not so to have blinded mind and understanding that no light or illumination remained by which the divine commandments could be discerned. If the cause of the calamity is recognized, a remedy for the wound is also found. The Lord wished his household to be tested; and because the long peace had corrupted the discipline divinely delivered to us [Col. 0468C], heavenly correction raised up our prostrate and almost [Note: [Col. 0468C] “And so that almost,” Lam. Bod. 2.], [Col. 0469A] so to speak, sleeping faith. And although by our sins we deserved still more, the most merciful Lord so moderated all things that everything which occurred seemed a testing rather than a persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0469C]

### VI.—Among the ministers

Two old manuscripts have “in the ministries.”

Hair dyed with false color. Below in this book, p. 191: “and you who dye your hair.” Ovid, *The Art of Love*, book III: “A woman dyes her gray hair with genuine herbs.” Martial, book VI, Epigram 57: “Phoebus, you falsely claim as yours hair manufactured with ointment.” Columella, in the preface to his books *On Agriculture*: “I have not only heard hairdressers who arrange heads and hair, but have myself seen them.” See the notes on the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, at the word “precious stones,” p. 528.

To join with unbelievers. Saint Augustine cites this passage in *On Adulterous Marriages*, book I, [p. 535] ch. 21: “Although the most blessed Cyprian has no doubt about the matter, nor counts among slight sins the forming of the marriage bond with unbelievers, and says that this is to prostitute the members of Christ to pagans.” Likewise in *On Faith and Works*, ch. 19, where he concludes from this that certain things tolerated in one age were not permitted in another. Tertullian, to be sure, teaches that the rule of faith alone is immutable, [Col. 0469D] while other matters of correction and discipline admit innovation in correction. See again Saint Augustine in his Letter to Boniface concerning the different customs of churches and provinces. Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I: “They are joined to pagans and prostitute the temples of Christ to idols.” The same author, in his Letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “But if even those who are virgins are nevertheless not saved by bodily virginity because of other faults, what will happen to those who have prostituted the members of Christ?” The First Council of Arles, canon 11: “Concerning faithful girls who are joined to pagans, it was resolved that they should be excluded from communion for a period of time.” See Rigault’s observations on book II of Tertullian’s *To His Wife*. In the title of the Theodosian Code *On Marriages with Gentiles*, it is prescribed that no provincial, of whatever rank or station he may be, is to enter into marriage with a barbarian woman, nor is any provincial woman to be joined to a gentile; and if this is done contrary to the law, it is to be atoned for by capital punishment. [Col. 0470B] As Jacques Godefroy correctly observes, “gentiles” there does not mean people defined in relation to faith or religion, but barbarians defined in relation to the Romans—specifically, those who had come from various nations and placed themselves under the empire in pursuit of Roman prosperity. They are therefore contrasted with provincials, that is, Romans, not with Christians.

An exhortation. This is the reading of Manutius’s edition, whereas the earlier editions had “an ornament.” I found the Manutian reading in twelve ancient manuscripts. The other occurs in seven others, in Morel’s edition, and in Saint Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book III, ch. 36. See what I noted in a similar case on Letter XV, p. 401. In the Third Council of Toledo, canon 10, one reads “by the exhortation of the council,” but elsewhere “by the ornament of the council.”

Agents. This was always forbidden in the Church [Col. 0470C] of God. There is a notable passage on this matter in canon 16 of the Council of Carthage held after the consulships of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII; it is also found in Gratian, cause 21, question 2: “It was resolved that bishops.” See Antonio Agustín’s *Epitome of Pontifical Law*, book IV, title 73, and our notes on Agobard’s book *On the Manner of Ecclesiastical Government*. See also the invective of James, Cardinal of Pavia, against John, Cardinal of Arras. Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book I, after saying that the Levites were given no authority, so that they might serve God with greater freedom, adds: “I, for my part, would not pass over this example in silence and would gladly press it upon the ministers of the churches as something to be read. For they seem to me not merely forgetful of this command but even ignorant of it. So great a desire for acquisition has in our time invaded their minds like a wasting disease. They gape after estates, cultivate landed properties, brood over gold, buy and sell, and pursue profit in everything.” See Saint Gregory, book VIII, Letter XI, against Basil, bishop of Capua. Jerome, in his Letter to Nepotian *On the Life of Clerics*: “How can clerics be agents [Col. 0470D] and stewards of other people’s households when they are commanded to despise their own possessions?” To this may also be referred what we said in the notes on the *Capitularies*, p. 1169.

His episcopal chair abandoned. Contrary to the rules of ecclesiastical discipline. See the African councils.

Their brothers in the Church. In Pamelius’s edition the words “to give them no assistance” were added. But I have not found that addition in the ancient books I have examined, nor in the English manuscripts. The Pithou manuscript, however, has “to give them nothing.” Pamelius attests that it was also written in this form in the Cambrai manuscript. Yet this addition appears to me entirely unnecessary. Cyprian censures bishops who, while seeing their brothers starving in the Church, thirsted for gold and silver. I have said “gold and silver” because one of my ancient manuscripts reads: “to wish to possess gold in abundance while their brothers in the Church were starving,” and another has “silver” in place of [Col. 0471C] “gold.” But—and this strikes at the throat of the argument—Saint Augustine, when quoting this same passage in his Letter to Macrobius, *Against Cresconius*, book III, ch. 36, and in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book IV, ch. 9, does not have this addition. It is also absent from Venericus, bishop of Vercelli, in his book *On the Unity of the Church*, and from Thomas Waldensis in Doctrine X *On the Sacramentals*. Jerome, in his Letter to Nepotian *On the Life of Clerics*: “It is a bishop’s glory to provide for the poverty of the poor. It is the disgrace of every priest to pursue wealth of his own.” See Prosper—or Julianus [Col. 0471D] Pomerius—*On the Contemplative Life*, book III, p. 536, ch. 24.

To seize estates. Saint Augustine cites this passage in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book IV, ch. 10, and in his Letter to Macrobius. Julianus Pomerius, speaking of bishops in *On the Contemplative Life*, book I, ch. 13: “They extend the boundaries of estates without any limit to their greed, and everywhere surrender themselves to elaborate luxuries that weaken both mind and body.” Concerning Potamius, bishop of Lisbon, the following is written in Marcellinus and Faustinus’s *Book of Petitions*: “Nor did Potamius’s betrayal of the sacred faith go unpunished. For while he was hurrying toward the estate that he had earned the right to obtain from the emperor in return for his impious subscription concerning the faith, he paid a new penalty with the tongue by which he had blasphemed: he died on the road, without deriving any benefit from the estate even by seeing it.” Jerome, in his Letter to Nepotian *On the Life of Clerics*: “It is shameful for the lictors of consuls and soldiers to stand guard before the doors of a priest of Christ, who was crucified and poor and even ate food belonging to others, and for the governor of the province to dine better at your house than in the palace.” To this passage may rightly be added what Ammianus Marcellinus says in book XXVII about the banquets of the Roman bishops of his own time: he says that they provided lavish feasts, so much so that their banquets surpassed royal tables. See above, p. 444.

Statutes. Nine of our manuscripts, six English manuscripts, and Morel’s edition prefer “acts of righteousness.”]

## VI

Individuals devoted themselves to increasing their estates and, forgetting what believers had either done previously under the Apostles or ought always to do, applied themselves to enlarging their resources with the insatiable ardor of greed. Among the priests there was no devout religious commitment; [Note: [Col. 0469B] “Among the priesthoods,” Bod. 1, 4.] among the ministers [Note: [Col. 0469B] “Among the ministries,” Bod. 2, 4; Thu.; Foss.; Lam.; Manut.; Gronov.; Lips.] no uncorrupted faith; in their works no mercy; in their conduct no discipline. Men’s beards were disfigured; women’s appearance was painted; eyes were falsified after the hands of God had made them; [p. 183] hair was dyed with false color. There were cunning deceptions to mislead the hearts of the simple and treacherous intentions to entrap their brothers. They joined in the bond of marriage with unbelievers and prostituted the members of Christ to pagans. [Note: [Col. 0470B] “To prostitute the members of Christ among the nations,” NC 1; Pem.] They not only swore rashly but even committed perjury; they despised their superiors with arrogant pride, cursed one another with venomous mouths, and were divided from one another by persistent hatreds.

Very many bishops, who ought to serve as both an exhortation and an example to others, despised their divine charge and became agents of secular affairs. Abandoning their episcopal chair and deserting their people, they wandered through foreign provinces, hunting after the markets of profitable trade; [Note: [Col. 0470B] “profitable markets,” Bod. 4.] while their brothers in the Church were starving, they wished to possess silver in abundance; [Col. 0471A] they seized estates by insidious frauds and increased their profits by multiplying interest charges. What would we, being such people, not have deserved to suffer for sins of this kind, when the divine censure [Note: [Col. 0471C] “Scripture,” Voss. 1, 2.] had long before warned and said:

> If they forsake [Note: [Col. 0471C] “My sons,” added by Voss. 1.] my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my statutes and do not observe my commandments, I shall visit their crimes with the rod and their offenses with scourges. [Note: [Col. 0471C] “Their iniquities and their offenses with scourges; but I shall not withdraw my mercy from him—from them,” Voss. 3.]  
> (Ps. 88:31–33)

## VII

These things were announced to us beforehand and foretold in advance. But we, forgetful of the law given to us and of its observance, brought it about through our sins that, because we despised the Lord’s commandments, we had to come under harsher remedies for the correction [Note: [Col. 0471C] “reproof,” Ar.; Lam.; Voss. 1.] of our offense and the testing of our faith. Not even belatedly did we turn to the fear of the Lord, so that we might patiently [Col. 0471B] and courageously endure this reproof of ours and divine testing. [Note: [Col. 0471C] “patiently endure,” Voss. 3; Lin.] At the very first words of the threatening enemy, a very great number of the brothers betrayed their faith. They were not cast down by the force of persecution, but cast themselves down by a voluntary fall.

What unprecedented thing, I ask, what novelty had occurred, that, as though unfamiliar [Note: [Col. 0471C] “unknown,” Voss. 1.] and unexpected events had arisen, the sacramental pledge to Christ should be broken with headlong rashness? Had not both the Prophets beforehand and the Apostles afterward announced these things? Filled with the Holy Spirit, had they not always foretold the afflictions of the righteous and the injuries inflicted by the pagans? Does not divine Scripture, always arming our faith and strengthening God’s servants with a heavenly voice, say:

> You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.  
> (Deut. 6:13; Matt. [Col. 0472A] 4:10)

And does it not, displaying the wrath of divine indignation and warning beforehand of the fear of punishment, say again:

> They worshiped those [Note: [Col. 0472C] “They worship gods,” Voss. 3, p.] which their fingers had made; and man bowed down and the man was humbled, and I shall not forgive them.  
> (Isa. 2:8)

And again God speaks, saying:

> Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be uprooted, unless it is to the Lord alone.  
> (Exod. 22:19)

Later, too, in the Gospel, the Lord—the teacher in words and the fulfiller [Note: [Col. 0472C] “the teacher; he is fulfilled in deeds,” Thu.; Foss.] in deeds—both teaching what was to be done and doing everything that he had taught: did he not warn beforehand of everything now taking place and yet to take place? Did he not establish beforehand both eternal punishments for those who deny him [Note: [Col. 0472C] “his own future things,” Bod. 4.] and saving rewards for those who confess him?

[Note: [Col. 0472D]

### VIII—Were Taken Up Under Arrest

This is the reading of the English edition, confirmed by the ancient copies and pronounced absolutely correct by Rigault in his observations. Manutius and Morel, however, were not the first to introduce it, as Rigault seems to have thought, for it is found in the early editions. See what we note on Letter VI, p. 392.

### To the Forum

And from there to the Capitol. For above, p. 407, it was noted that the Forum was beside the Capitol.

### Deny Him

After these words Manutius and Pamelius add “so that they might burn incense.” Rigault rightly rejects this reading, although he retained it. Indeed, it is nowhere found in the ancient copies, except that the English editors cite one manuscript from the Vatican Library.

### Which They Had Always

Sixteen ancient manuscripts and Morel’s edition have “gladly.”

### How Many of Them

The Séguier manuscript reads: “that, when questioned, they should deny him, lest their destruction be postponed; and they begged.”

### Their Arms Collapsed

The Séguier manuscript reads: “their limbs collapsed.”

### Intending to Sacrifice

Some ancient manuscripts and early editions have “intending to sacrifice, or to supplicate.” Thus one ancient copyist wrote “intending to sacrifice.” Another wrote above the line, as was then customary, “or to supplicate.” From these two readings, those who followed later chose whichever pleased them more. I prefer the reading “intending to sacrifice,” which I do not doubt was the original. For immediately afterward there also follows: “Here you sacrificed your salvation.” The other reading may be supported by these words of Tertullian from his book *On Fasting*: “Wrapped in sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes, they present their suppliant ill-will to their idols.”]

## VIII

For some, all these things—what an outrage!—had slipped away and receded from memory. They did not wait even to be taken up under arrest and to deny him when questioned. [Note: [Col. 0472C] “They waited at least to be questioned and begged to burn incense,” Voss. 3; printed edition.] [Col. 0472B] Many were defeated before the line of battle and cast down without an encounter. They did not even leave themselves the plea that they appeared to sacrifice to the idols unwillingly. Of their own accord they ran to the Forum and voluntarily hastened toward death, as though they had long desired it, as though they were embracing an opportunity offered to them which they had always wished for.

How many there [Note: [Col. 0472C] “What there,” Voss. 4; “what did they,” Oxford.] were postponed by the magistrates because evening was approaching? How many even begged that their destruction not be delayed? What violence can such a person allege in order to excuse his crime, when he himself exerted even greater violence to bring about his own destruction? When he came voluntarily to the Capitol and approached of his own accord to comply with the dreadful crime, did his step not falter, [Note: [Col. 0472C] “Did he not fall,” Boss. 1.] his sight grow dim, his entrails tremble, and his arms collapse? Did his senses not become numb, [Col. 0473A] [p. 184] his tongue stick fast, and his speech fail? Could a servant of God stand there and speak and renounce Christ, when he had already renounced the devil and the world? Was not that altar, which he approached to die, a funeral pyre for him? When he saw the devil’s altar smoking and reeking with its foul stench, ought he not to have recoiled from it and fled it as the funeral and tomb of his own life? [Note: [Col. 0473C] “ought he not to have,” Voss. 1.]

Why, wretched man, do you bring an offering with you; why do you place a victim upon it, intending to sacrifice? You yourself came to the altar as an offering; you yourself came as the victim. There you sacrificed your salvation; you burned up your hope and your faith in those deadly flames.

[Note: [Col. 0473D]

### IX—Even Infants

Saint Augustine cites this passage in his Letter to Bishop Boniface. Optatus, book III: “In every place there was a temple or a crime. Old men near death were defiled; [Col. 0474D] unknowing infancy was polluted; little children were carried by hand to the abomination; parents were compelled to commit bloodless parricides.”

### The Little Ones Lost

Saint Augustine also quotes this passage in his Letter to Bishop Boniface, in order to prove from Cyprian’s testimony that the faithlessness of their parents does not harm little children before God.

### We Were Ensnared by Another’s Deceit

Thus six ancient manuscripts and Saint Augustine. Most manuscripts, however, have “they would die”; five have “they would die through another’s death.”]

## IX

For many, their own destruction was not enough. Through mutual exhortations the people were driven toward ruin; [Note: [Col. 0473C] “their own departure,” Oxford.] death was served to one another in a lethal cup. And so that nothing might be lacking to the accumulation of crime, even infants, either set down or dragged by their parents’ hands, lost as little children what they had obtained at the very beginning of birth. [Col. 0473B]

When the day of judgment comes, will they not say:

> We did nothing evil. [Note: [Col. 0473C] I do not know why Baluze inserts “evil” here; Goldh.] We did not voluntarily forsake the Lord’s food and cup and hasten toward profane defilements. Another’s faithlessness destroyed us; we found our parents to be parricides. They denied us the Church as mother and God as Father, so that, while we were little, without foresight, and ignorant of so great a crime, we were joined through others to fellowship in their crimes and ensnared by another’s deceit.

## X

Nor, alas, is there any just and weighty cause that might excuse so great a crime. One would have had to leave one’s homeland and suffer the loss of one’s property. For what person, being born and dying, does not at some point have to leave his homeland and suffer the loss of his property? [Note: [Col. 0473C] “suffer loss? So that Christ,” Oxford.] Christ must not be abandoned; the loss of salvation and of an eternal dwelling must be feared. [Col. 0473C]

Behold, the Holy Spirit cries through the prophet:

> Depart, depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean. Go out from its midst; separate yourselves, [Note: [Col. 0473C] “Sell yourselves,” Man.; “You who carry,” Lin.; Bod.] you who carry the vessels of the Lord.  
> (Isa. 52:11)

Yet those who are the Lord’s vessels and God’s temple do not go out from its midst or withdraw, lest they should be compelled to touch what is unclean and be polluted and violated by death-bearing food! Elsewhere, too, a voice is heard from heaven, warning beforehand what it is fitting for God’s servants to do and saying:

> Come out from her, my people, lest you share in her offenses and lest you be struck by her plagues.  
> (Rev. 18:4)

Whoever goes out and withdraws [Note: [Col. 0473C] “and separates himself,” Pem.; Lin.; Voss. 3.] does not become a participant in the offense; but whoever is found to be an accomplice in the crime is himself struck by the plagues. For this reason the Lord commanded people to withdraw and flee during persecution; and, so that this might be done, he both taught it and did it. For since the crown descends through God’s gracious favor and cannot be received unless the hour for receiving it has arrived, whoever meanwhile withdraws while remaining in Christ does not deny the faith but awaits the proper time. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “the hour,” Voss. 3.] But whoever fell because he did not withdraw remained only in order to deny him.

[Note: [Col. 0474D]

### XI—Those Chains

Saint Augustine, Tractate X on the Gospel of John: “Greed will be a chain upon your feet.”

### Those Who Cling to Earthly Things

Pamelius added “desires,” on rather weak manuscript evidence. Shortly afterward, on similar authority, he likewise added “and advising” after the word “warning beforehand.” But these words do not occur in the ancient manuscripts or early editions. The English editors nevertheless retained them, although their own manuscripts lacked them. The word “desire” was undoubtedly added by some learned reader who read below, “who are weighed down by earthly desires.”]

## XI

The truth, dearly beloved brothers, must not be concealed, nor must the source and cause of our wound be left unspoken. A blind love of their property deceived many, and those whose wealth bound them like fetters could not be prepared or unencumbered enough to withdraw. Those possessions were fetters for the people who remained; those were the chains by which their courage was hindered, their faith crushed, their mind bound, [Note: [Col. 0474C] “their faith betrayed and their mind defeated,” Voss. 1.] and their soul obstructed. Thus those who clung to earthly things became prey and food for the serpent who, according to God’s sentence, devours the earth.

And therefore the Lord, the teacher of good things and one who warns us concerning the future, [Note: [Col. 0474C] Thus eleven MSS. “both warning and advising,” Oxford.] says:

> If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.  
> (Matt. 19:21)

If the rich did this, they would not perish through their riches. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “not their own,” Lam.; Thu.; Foss.; Voss.] By storing up treasure in heaven, they would not now have an enemy and assailant within their own household. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “an enemy now, an assailant,” Oxford.] Their heart, mind, and understanding would be in heaven [Col. 0474C] if their treasure were in heaven. Nor could someone be defeated by the world if he had nothing in the world by which he might be defeated. [Note: [Col. 0474C] “bound,” Gronovius proposes in *Obs. mon.*, p. 40.] Unburdened and free, [Note: [Col. 0474C] “secure and free,” Bod. 4.] he would follow the Lord, as the Apostles and many under the Apostles, and certain people often afterward, have done: abandoning both their possessions and their parents, [p. 185] they adhered to Christ with inseparable bonds. [Col. 0475A]

[Note: [Col. 0475C]

### XII—They Believe That They Possess

See above, p. 384.

### Nor Masters of Their Money

Five ancient manuscripts have “nor of their money.” Two others have “nor masters of the money, but rather they themselves belong to the money.” [p. 537]

### Wandered Away

We have necessarily restored this reading, which Manutius had removed and replaced with “made shipwreck.” Manutius was not, however, the first author of that alteration, since this reading already occurred in the margin of the edition said to be that of Gravil. The reading we have restored occurs in the early editions and in nineteen ancient copies. I found the Manutian reading in only five. Although Pamelius retained it in the text, in his observations he approves the other reading more highly. In one manuscript, however, following the custom of ancient copyists, both “made shipwreck” and “wandered away” are written. [Col. 0475D] Nevertheless, Cyprian has “made shipwreck of the faith” in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 210; in *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 240; and in *Testimonies*, book III, ch. 61.

### Sevenfold

Four ancient manuscripts and the Manutian edition have “a hundredfold.”]

## XII

But how can those who are held by the bond of their property follow Christ? Or how do those who are weighed down by earthly desires seek heaven and ascend to the sublime heights? They believe that they possess, though they themselves are possessed: slaves of their property, not masters of their money, but rather enslaved to money.

The Apostle identifies this time and these people when he says:

> But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare [Note: [Col. 0475C] “a snare of the devil,” Voss. 3.] and many useless and harmful desires, [Note: [Col. 0475C] “many harmful desires,” Oxford, from MSS.] which plunge a person into destruction and ruin. For greed is the root of every evil; by seeking it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.  
> (1 Tim. 6:9)

With what rewards does the Lord invite us to contempt for our property? With what recompense does he balance these small and slight losses of the present time?

> There is no one, he says, who leaves house or field, or parents or brothers, or wife or children, for the sake of God’s kingdom, and does not receive seven times as much in this present time, and eternal life in the age to come.  
> (Mark 10:29)

Once these things are known and the truthfulness of the Lord’s promise is established, a loss of this kind is not merely not to be feared but even to be desired, as the Lord himself again proclaims [Note: [Col. 0475C] “and God,” Voss. 1, 3.] and admonishes:

> Blessed will you be when they persecute you, [Note: [Col. 0475C] “when men persecute you,” Ar.; Bod. 2, 3.] and separate you, and cast you out, and curse your name as evil because of the Son of Man. Rejoice on that day and exult; for behold, your reward is great in heaven.  
> (Luke 6:22)

[Col. 0476A]

[Note: [Col. 0475D]

### XIII—Had Come

Thus the early editions and twenty-seven ancient manuscripts, among which I include the Verona and Séguier manuscripts, except that three of them have “came.” Erasmus wrote “were going to come.”

### In Pain

Lamon’s manuscript has “through pain,” which is perhaps better. See Basil’s Letter III to Amphilochius, where he discusses those who, unable to endure pain, were driven to deny Christ.

### While Resisting

Four ancient manuscripts prefer “in their struggles”; another has “in their contests.”

### In the Encounter

The Fuxensis manuscript has “in the struggle.”

### Wearied

Morel and Pamelius add “the body, now exhausted.” I deleted these words because I did not find them in any [Col. 0476C] ancient manuscript except the Bec manuscript. Nevertheless, among variant readings entered by a learned man in the margins of the Lyon edition of 1544, I saw “now exhausted” noted beside this passage. Caesar, *The Gallic War*, book I, said “a body exhausted by blows.”

### Failed in Pain

Jerome, on chapter 1 of Paul the Apostle’s Letter to the Galatians: “In martyrdom, the person who immediately rushed to denial without struggle or torture is not punished with the same penalty as one who, twisted upon racks, cords, and fires, was compelled to deny what he believed.” And on chapter 6: “If anyone, after being tortured for confessing Christ’s name, sees another deny him under torture, let him sympathize with the denier’s wounds and wonder not so much that the other was defeated as that he himself was victorious.”

### Castus and Aemilius

The ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage published by Mabillon reads: “On the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, the saints Castus and Aemilius.” In the martyrologies of Bede and others, the following is read on the same day: “In Africa, Castus and Aemilius, who completed their martyrdom through the suffering of fire. Cyprian writes of them in his book *On the Lapsed*.” Among the sermons of Saint Augustine there survives a sermon for the feast day of several martyrs beginning, “Of the holy martyrs”; recent editors of Saint Augustine’s works concluded from Possidius’s index that it was delivered on the feast day of Saints Castus and Aemilius.

### Victors in the Second Battle

Similarly Saint John Chrysostom, at the beginning of his second *Exhortation to the Fallen Theodore*, says that many who had been broken by the force of torture and denied Christ, after renewing the contest, carried off the crown of martyrdom.

### Half-Burned

Lamon’s manuscript has “from a half-burned side.”]

## XIII

But the torments came afterward, and severe tortures threatened those who resisted. The person who has been overcome by torments can complain of torments. The person who was defeated in pain can allege pain as an excuse. Such a person can plead and say:

> I did indeed wish to contend courageously and, mindful of my sacramental pledge, took up the weapons of devotion and faith. But while I was fighting in the encounter, various tortures and prolonged punishments defeated me. My mind remained steadfast and my faith strong, and for a long time my soul struggled unshaken against the torments inflicted upon it. But when the savagery of the most cruel judge flared up again, now the whips tore my already wearied body, [Note: [Col. 0476C] “the whips still,” Bod. 1, 3, 4.] now clubs battered it, now the rack stretched it, now the claw gouged it, now flame scorched it. My flesh abandoned me in the struggle; the weakness of my entrails yielded, and it was not my spirit but my body [Col. 0476B] that failed in pain.

Such a cause may quickly advance toward pardon. An excuse of this kind may be worthy of compassion. Thus the Lord once forgave Castus and Aemilius; [Note: [Col. 0476C] “Thus, thus,” Lam.; Voss. 1; Foss.; Spir.; recent printed edition.] thus he made those defeated in the first encounter victors in the second battle, so that those who had previously yielded to the flames might be made stronger by the flames, and that they might prevail by the very means through which they had been overcome. They pleaded not by the appeal of tears but by that of their wounds, not by a lamentable voice alone but by the rending and pain of their bodies. Blood flowed in place of weeping, and gore streamed from their half-burned entrails in place of tears.

[Note: [Col. 0476D]

### XIV—What Wounds

The Séguier manuscript reads: “what violence, what wounds.”

### The Physician Is Unskilled

Tertullian, in his book *On Repentance*: “It is wretched to be cut, burned with a cautery, and tortured by the biting force of some powder. Yet treatments that heal through their unpleasantness excuse their offensiveness by the benefit of the cure and commend the present injury for the sake of the advantage that will follow.” The same author in *Scorpiace*: “And medicine certainly has what might be called a cruelty of the knife and the cautery and the burning of mustard. Yet being cut, burned, and eaten away is not for that reason an evil, because it brings useful pains.” And below: “Finally, the man howling, groaning, and bellowing under the physician’s hands will afterward heap the same man with reward, proclaim him the finest practitioner, and no longer call him cruel.”

Lucifer of Cagliari, in his book *On Dying for the Son of God*: “For although the physician cuts with the knife, burns with the cautery, and brings the patient to every kind of pain through the burning of mustard, nevertheless being cut, burned, eaten away, and bitten would not be harmful, precisely because it is good insofar as it removes useless pains by means of pains applied for the sake of health.” Cassian, *Conference* VI, ch. 6: “For the saving incision or burning that a physician mercifully inflicts upon those who have rotted through the infection of ulcers is regarded as an evil by those who endure it.”

Pacian, in his *Exhortation to Repentance*: “Sensible patients do not fear physicians, even when the latter intend to cut and burn the hidden parts of their bodies. We remember some who, without shame, endured the knife, [Col. 0477D] the cautery, and that most severe [p. 538] biting powder even upon remote and private members.” Fulgentius Placiades, *Mythologies*, book I, calls this “the butchery of surgery.”

Jerome, in his Letter to Marcella *On Onasus*: “The physicians called surgeons are regarded as cruel, and they are wretched. Is it not wretchedness not to feel pain at another’s wounds and to cut away dead flesh with an unsparing knife?” The same author, in his Letter to the Presbyter Amandus: “Rotten flesh requires the knife and the cautery. The fault lies not with the treatment but with the wound, when the physician, with compassionate cruelty, does not spare in order that he may spare, and rages in order that he may show mercy.” The same author, in his Letter to a Mother and Daughter: “Rotten flesh is treated with the knife and the cautery.”

Pope Siricius, in his Letter to Himerius: “Wounds that have felt no healing from soothing applications must necessarily be cut away with the knife.” Ennodius, in his *Life of Epiphanius*: “No patient was ever brought to the fullest cure by a physician who did not first cut away rotten limbs with the knife and draw out the corruption hidden deep within the cavity of the entrails.” Xenophon, in book V of the *Education of Cyrus*, says that physicians burn and cut those who are more gravely ill in order to cure them. [Col. 0478B]

Prudentius, in his poem on the martyr Romanus:

> Suppose that surgeons are applying their grim knife  
> To my ribs, cutting them for my health.  
> That by which health is restored is not bitter.

[Col. 0478C] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book I:

> Everything must first be attempted; but an incurable wound  
> Must be cut away with the sword, lest the healthy part be infected.

The same author, *Remedies for Love*, book I:

> To redeem the body, you must endure the knife and fire.

### Let Him Cry Out

Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II: “For what if you say that he ought to be a physician, yet accuse his instruments because they cut, burn, amputate, and constrict, when a physician cannot practice without the instruments of his art?” A letter written under Jerome’s name *To a Sick Friend*: “A physician’s hands bestow health by making many cuts, though not without the patient’s murmuring.”

### The Impatient Patient

Above, Letter XXVI, p. 37: “Nothing but patience is necessary in illness.”

### When He Has Experienced Health

Julius Firmicus, in his book *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “Thus, when a person has recovered health and been restored to well-being, he acknowledges by the judgment of a sound mind that everything he unwillingly endured because of his diseased body was done entirely for his benefit.”
