Pope Innocent III, book XI, Letter 211: “Accordingly, if we find your disease—which God forbid—to have become hardened, you will compel us to employ a more violent treatment, as the necessary cure demands. Although you may perhaps shrink from its harshness at present, once health has been restored you will praise its effect and bless the skillful physician as well.” Seneca, *On Benefits*, book V, ch. 20: “We must consider not whether someone feels pain upon receiving a benefit, but whether he ought to feel pain.”]

## XIV

But now what wounds can the defeated display, [Col. 0477A] what gashes in their gaping entrails, what tortures of their limbs, when it was not faith that entered the encounter and fell, but faithlessness that anticipated the encounter? Necessity does not excuse the person overwhelmed when the crime was voluntary. I do not say this in order to burden the cases of the brothers, but rather to urge the brothers toward the prayer of satisfaction. For since it is written:

> Those who call you happy lead you into error and disturb the paths of your feet,  
> (Isa. 3:12)

the person who caresses the sinner with flattering blandishments [Note: [Col. 0477B] “words,” Voss. 3.] supplies fuel for further sinning. He does not suppress offenses but nourishes them. But the person who rebukes and at the same time instructs his brother with stronger counsels advances him toward salvation.

> Those whom I love, says the Lord, I rebuke and discipline.  
> (Rev. 3:19)

Thus God’s priest must not deceive through misleading indulgence, but provide saving remedies. [Col. 0477B] A physician is unskilled if he handles the swollen hollows of wounds with a sparing hand and, by preserving the poison enclosed in the deep recesses of the entrails, makes it worse. The wound must be opened and cut; the putrid matter must be removed, and the wound treated with a stronger remedy. Although the impatient patient may cry out, shout, and complain [Col. 0478A] because of the pain, he will afterward give thanks when he has experienced health.

[Note: [Col. 0478D]

### XV—A Null and False Peace

Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book X, Letter 1: “Concerning peace, I think as you do: that it is an open pretense and that a most bitter war is being prepared.” See above, p. 457.

### Patient Endurance for Healing

Florus’s manuscript has “repentance.” Shortly afterward, in place of “medicine,” the Lamon manuscript has “repentance.”

### Driven Out

Thus twelve ancient manuscripts. Eleven others and the early editions have “excluded.” Both readings are sound. The Fossatensis manuscript reads: “Repentance has been driven out of sinners—or excluded.” [Col. 0479C] The copyist supplied both readings so that the reader would understand that he was free to prefer whichever pleased him more, as often happens in ancient manuscripts.

### His Uncleanness

The same reading also occurs in *Testimonies*, book III, ch. 94. But Cassian, book VI, ch. 8; *Conference* XII, ch. 2; and *Conference* XXII, ch. 5, reads: “in whom there is uncleanness shall perish before the Lord.”]

XV. For there has arisen, most beloved brothers, a new [Note: [Col. 0477B] “Against us, a new,” Voss. 3.] kind of calamity; and, as though the storm of persecution had not raged enough, there has been added to the sum of our woes, under the name of mercy, a deceptive evil and seductive destruction. Contrary to the vigor of the Gospel, contrary to the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0478B] “Contrary to God and God’s law,” Voss. 3.] and of God, through the rashness of certain persons communion is relaxed for the unwary: a futile and false peace, dangerous [Note: [Col. 0478B] “Destructive,” Ebor.] to those who grant it and of no benefit to those who receive it. They do not seek the patient endurance required for healing, nor the true remedy that comes from satisfaction. Repentance has been cast out of their hearts, and the memory of their most grievous and final sin has been removed. The wounds of the dying are covered over, and the lethal injury lodged deep in their innermost organs is concealed while its pain is ignored. Returning from the altars of the devil, [Col. 0478B] they approach the holy thing of the Lord with hands filthy and infected by the stench. Still almost belching the death-bearing food of idols, with throats even now exhaling their crime and reeking of deadly contagion, they seize upon the body of the Lord, although divine Scripture confronts them and cries aloud, saying: “Every clean person shall eat the flesh, [Col. 0479A] and any soul who eats of the flesh of the saving sacrifice that belongs to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him, that soul shall perish from among his people” (Lev. 7:20). The Apostle likewise bears witness and says [Note: [Col. 0479C] “Threatens and declares,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.]: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10:21). He likewise threatens and solemnly warns the obstinate and stubborn, saying: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

[Note: [Col. 0479D]

XVI.—Having Spurned All These Things. We have restored this passage as it is found in the ancient copies, in the Morel edition, and in the edition known as Gravius’s. In doing so we followed Rigault’s judgment; for although he retained the old reading in the text, he declares in his observations that the reading we have restored is the most authentic.

Before exomologesis had been made. That is, before the priests of God, as Cyprian says below in this book, p. 190. Rufinus on Psalm 31: “Although God forgives sins from the moment a person repents in his will, they must nevertheless be confessed to the ministers of the Church.” See Socrates, book V, chapter 19, with the annotations of Henri Valois. See also below, in the notes to page 209, “to sin and not make satisfaction.” 539.

With deceptive words. The Séguier manuscript reads “with words that deceive.”

Tree. This word is absent from sixteen ancient manuscripts and from the older editions. It was also absent from another old manuscript, but was later added above the line. The letter written in Jerome’s name *To a Sick Friend*: “For no tree is sound or robust unless, when its trunk has been shaken by the continual assault of a whirlwind, it is tested by being bent this way and that, and unless the blast of stormy winds repeatedly strikes it. For by these very afflictions it is tightened, compressed, and more quickly strengthened as its roots become firmly fixed.”]

XVI. All these things being spurned and treated with contempt—before the sins have been expiated, before exomologesis of the crime has been made, before the conscience has been cleansed by the sacrifice and hand of the priest, before the offense of the indignant and threatening Lord has been appeased—violence is done to his body and blood; and now they sin against the Lord with their hands and mouth more [Col. 0479B] than when they denied the Lord [Note: [Col. 0479C] The words “before the offense … denied” are inserted by the Ver. Impr. editions, except Baluze’s, between “treated with contempt” and “before the sins have been expiated.” The Oxford edition reports no variant reading here.]. They think that what certain persons hawk with deceptive words is peace. That is not peace, but war; nor is one joined to the Church who is separated from the Gospel. Why do they call injury a benefit? Why do they give impiety the name of piety? Why, after cutting short the lamentation of repentance for those who ought continually to weep and entreat their Lord, do they pretend to admit them to communion? Such people are to the lapsed what hail is to crops, what a stormy constellation is to trees, what a pestilential devastation is to herds, what a savage tempest is to ships. They take away the consolation of eternal hope [Note: [Col. 0479C] “The consolation of hope,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Voss. 1. “They take away … from the root,” [Col. 0480C] Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.]; they overturn the tree by its roots; with diseased speech they creep onward into lethal contagion; they dash the ship upon the rocks so that it cannot reach the harbor. This easy indulgence does not grant peace but takes it away; it does not bestow communion [Col. 0479C] but impedes the way to salvation. This is another persecution and another temptation, through which the subtle enemy proceeds with hidden devastation to attack [Col. 0480A] those who are still lapsed [Note: [Col. 0480C] “To attack people,” Voss. 2, 4; Pem.], so that lamentation may cease, pain fall silent, the memory of the sin vanish, the groaning of their breasts [Note: [Col. 0480C] “Of sinners,” Lin.; Voss. 1.] be suppressed, the weeping of their eyes be stopped, and the Lord, grievously offended, not be entreated through long and complete repentance, although it is written: “Remember whence you have fallen, and repent” (Rev. 2:5).

[Note: [Col. 0480D]

XVII.—The Lord Alone Can Show Mercy. Tertullian in the book *On Baptism*: “But neither does anyone forgive sin nor grant the Spirit except God alone.” Likewise in the book *On Modesty*: “For who forgives sins except God alone?” Saint John Chrysostom, Homily IV on chapter 1 of Matthew, says that no one can forgive sins except the Divine Nature alone. Guido of Perpignan, writing *Against the Errors of the Armenians*, says: “They also say that no one except God alone can remit sins.” Ruricius, book II, Letter 41: “His mercy, as we believe, will grant that he who deigned to inspire in you the disposition to repent—who alone can both heal what has been corrupted, restore what has collapsed, and erase what has been committed—will do so.” See Maldonado’s *Treatise on the Sacraments*, p. 255 of the second edition.

The very great merits of the martyrs. The old editions and eight ancient manuscripts read “that the merits of the martyrs are very powerful.” But the word “are powerful” does not occur in the other ancient copies.]

XVII. Let no one mislead himself; let no one deceive himself. The Lord alone can show mercy. 187 He alone can grant pardon for sins committed against himself—the one who bore our sins, who suffered for us, whom God delivered up for our sins. A human being cannot be greater than God; nor can a servant by his own indulgence remit or pardon what has been committed against the Lord as a graver offense, lest this too be added to the crime of one still fallen, [Col. 0480B] if he fails to recognize what was foretold: “Cursed is the man who places his hope [Note: [Col. 0480C] “Trusts,” Ar.; Bod. 2; Ben.] in man” (Jer. 17:5). The Lord must be entreated; the Lord must be appeased by our satisfaction—the one who said that he would deny whoever denied him, who alone received all judgment from the Father. We do indeed believe that the merits of the martyrs and the works of the righteous can have very great weight before the Judge, but only when the day of judgment has come, when, after the passing away of this age and world, his people stand before Christ’s tribunal.

[Note: [Col. 0480D]

XVIII.—Capacity. The old editions and nine ancient manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, prefer “facility.” Four others have “felicity,” evidently, in my opinion, in place of “facility.”

Good. Pamelius printed “worthy,” on what authority I do not know. I, for my part, have seen “good” written in all the ancient editions and all the old manuscripts.

Avenged. Those who think that this word should be understood here in the sense in which it is used by Optatus when he speaks of the bones of a certain martyr not yet vindicated are certainly mistaken. For here that word must, as a necessary consequence, be referred to what precedes, from which it is clear that Cyprian believed the merits of the martyrs and the works of the righteous could have very great weight before the Judge, but only when the day of judgment had come, when, after the passing away of this age and world, his people stood before Christ’s tribunal. Cyprian then immediately adduces the passage from Revelation in which the souls of the slain martyrs, placed beneath God’s altar, ask God to avenge them upon their persecutors. The case was different with martyrs who had not yet been slain: Cyprian says that they cannot remit or pardon sins, nor can they defend others before they themselves have been avenged, as the souls of the slain martyrs were requesting. In the same sense he says in Letter LVI, p. 93, that the Lord will avenge our sufferings and wounds. See also the final part of the book *On the Good of Patience*, p. 255. Tertullian in the book *On Flight in Persecution*: “You can therefore claim vindication for yourself as a martyr, knowing that it is a great thing to be avenged [Col. 0482C] by him.” Lucifer of Cagliari in the First *Apology for Saint Athanasius*: “Such is the custom of God’s worshipers that they reserve everything to God, knowing that it is a great thing to be avenged by him.” See Rigault’s observations on Tertullian’s book *On Prayer*. Julius Capitolinus said in his *Pertinax*: “He even avenged some who were dead.” This, however, cannot be referred to dead persons vindicated in Optatus’s sense.

If not contrary. Rigault says here that these words should be carried forward in a single continuous construction: “if what is to be done by God’s priest is not contrary to the Lord himself, let there be the ready and willing consent of the one complying”; and he considers this reading the most authentic. He commends the Verona manuscript, in which “let there be” was written in place of “if there are.” So too in the Morel edition. But the Séguier manuscript reads: “The martyrs command something to be done: if it is just, if lawful, if not contrary to the Lord himself, it is to be done by God’s priest. Let there be the ready and willing consent of the one complying, if there has been religious moderation on the part of the petitioner.” The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul reads almost the same way.]

XVIII. But if anyone rashly thinks that, by premature haste, he can grant remission of sins to everyone [Note: [Col. 0480C] “Grant to everyone,” Impr.; “grant, that he can,” Bod. 2.], or dares to annul the Lord’s precepts, he not only gives no help but actually harms the lapsed. This is to provoke wrath, not to observe the sentence; it is not to think that God’s mercy must first be implored, but, with the Lord treated with contempt, to presume upon one’s own capacity. Beneath God’s altar the souls of the slain martyrs cry out with a loud voice, [Col. 0481A] saying: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Rev. 6:10). And they are commanded still to rest and remain patient. Yet does anyone imagine that a person can choose to act as a benefactor against the Judge by remitting and indiscriminately pardoning sins, or that he can defend others before he himself has been avenged? The martyrs command something to be done—but only if it is just, if lawful, if what is to be done by God’s priest [Note: [Col. 0481C] “To God’s priest.”] is not contrary to the Lord himself, if the consent of the one complying is ready and willing, if the petitioner has shown religious moderation. The martyrs command something to be done [Note: [Col. 0481C] “To be done? If,” Oxford.]; but if what they command has not been written in the Lord’s law, we must first know that they have obtained from God what they request, and only then do what they command. For what has been promised by human assurance cannot immediately be regarded as granted by the divine Majesty. [Col. 0481B]

[Note: [Col. 0482D]

XIX.—They Made Golden Gods for Themselves. These words are absent from the ancient editions and from fourteen manuscripts. They do, however, occur in seven others, and in some “and silver gods” is added; this is absent from the Fuxensis manuscript and the Morel edition. In chapter IV of the letter to Fortunatus *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, one reads: “They made golden gods for themselves.” But in book I of the *Testimonies*, chapter 1: “They made golden and silver gods for themselves.” In chapter 32 of Exodus: “And they made golden gods for themselves.”

]

XIX. For Moses too petitioned on behalf of the people’s sins, yet when he petitioned he did not obtain pardon for the sinners: “I beseech you, Lord,” he said, “this people has committed a great sin and made golden gods for themselves; and now, if you forgive them, forgive their sin; but if not, erase me from the book that you have written” [Note: [Col. 0481C] “From your book,” Lam.; “which I have written,” Voss. 1.]. And the Lord said to Moses: “If anyone sins [Note: [Col. 0481C] “Has sinned,” Voss. 1; Pem.] before me, I shall erase him from my book” (Exod. 32:31). That friend of God, who often spoke face to face with the Lord, could not obtain what he requested, nor did he appease by his entreaty the offense of the indignant God. God praises and proclaims Jeremiah, saying: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the vulva I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1:5). And to that same man, as he repeatedly entreated and prayed on behalf [Col. 0481C] of the people’s sins, [Col. 0482A] God said: “Do not pray for this people, and do not petition for them in supplication and prayer, because I shall not hear them when they call upon me, in the time of their affliction” [Note: [Col. 0481C] “The Lord said,” Oxford.] (Jer. 11:14). Who indeed was more righteous than Noah, who, when the earth was filled with sins, alone was found righteous upon the earth? Who was more glorious than Daniel? Who was more robust than he in firmness of faith for undergoing martyrdoms, more blessed [Note: [Col. 0482C] “More readily disposed,” Voss. 2.] in God’s favor—he who so often conquered when he fought and survived when he had conquered? Who was more prompt than Job in works, stronger in temptations, more patient in pain, humbler in fear, truer in faith? Yet God said that even to these men, if they were to petition him, he would not grant it. When the prophet Ezekiel entreated on account of the people’s sin, he said: “Any land whatsoever that sins against me by committing an offense—I shall stretch out my hand [Col. 0482B] over it, crush the support 188 of bread, send famine into it, and remove man and beast from it. And even if these three men were in its midst—Noah, Daniel, and Job—they would deliver neither sons nor daughters; they alone would be saved” (Ezek. 14:13). Thus [Note: [Col. 0482C] “From God,” Voss. 2.] not everything that is requested lies in a prejudgment made by the petitioner [Note: [Col. 0482C] “In the judgment of the powerful one’s prayers,” Voss. 1.], but in the discretion of the giver; nor does a human judgment usurp and claim anything for itself unless the divine decree gives its assent.

[Note: [Col. 0483D]

XX.—Most Beloved. Three ancient manuscripts read: “No one, most beloved brothers, let no one mutilate or dishonor this glory.”

]

XX. In the Gospel the Lord speaks, saying: “Whoever confesses me before men [Note: [Col. 0482C] “Before men,” Bod. 4.], I too shall confess him before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me, I too shall deny him” (Luke 12:8). If he does not deny the one who denies him, neither does he confess the one who confesses him. The Gospel cannot stand firm in one part and waver in another: either both must possess force, [Col. 0482C] or both must lose the force of truth. [Col. 0483A] If those who deny him are not guilty of the crime, neither shall those who confess him receive the reward of virtue. Moreover, if the faith that conquers is crowned, it is necessary that the faithlessness that is conquered be punished. Thus the martyrs either have no power at all, if the Gospel can be annulled; or, if the Gospel cannot be annulled [Note: [Col. 0483C] “If the Gospel can be annulled, or if it cannot be annulled, contrary to …,” Lin.; Lam.; NC. 1, 2; Pem.; Ebor.; Voss. 1; Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], those who become martyrs by the Gospel cannot act contrary to the Gospel. No one, most beloved brothers, let no one dishonor the dignity of the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0483C] “Let no one mutilate this glory,” Bod. 3.]; let no one destroy their glories and crowns. The strength of an incorrupt faith remains unimpaired; nor can one whose hope, faith, virtue, and all glory are in Christ say or do anything contrary to Christ. Those who themselves fulfilled God’s commands cannot authorize bishops to act contrary to God’s command. Or is anyone greater than God, or more merciful than the divine goodness—someone who either wishes what God has permitted to happen to be undone, or thinks that we can be saved by his help, as though God had lacked sufficient power to protect his Church? [Col. 0483B]

XXI. Unless perhaps these things were done without God’s knowledge, or all these events occurred without his permission [Note: [Col. 0483C] “Or with his permission,” Lin.], although divine Scripture teaches the unteachable and admonishes the forgetful when it speaks, saying: “Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to those who despoiled him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned? And they refused to walk in his ways or to hear his law; and he brought upon them the wrath of his indignation” (Isa. 42:24). And elsewhere it bears witness and says: “Surely God’s hand is not powerless to save, nor has he made his ear heavy so that he cannot hear. But your sins separate you from God, and because of your offenses he has turned his face away from you, so as not to show mercy” [Col. 0483C] (Isa. 59:1). Let us instead take account of our sins; reviewing our deeds and the secrets of our minds [Note: [Col. 0483D] “Our deeds,” Bod. 1, 2, 4.], let us weigh the deserts of our conscience. Let it return to our hearts that we have not walked in the Lord’s ways, that we have cast aside God’s law, and that we have never been willing to observe his commands and saving admonitions.

XXII. What good can you think of such a man? What fear do you suppose was in him, what faith do you believe him to have had, when neither dread could correct him nor persecution itself reform him? His high and stiff neck was not bent even by his fall. His swollen and proud spirit was not broken [Col. 0484A] even by defeat. Lying wounded while others stand firm and whole, he expresses indignation; and because he does not immediately receive the Lord’s body with defiled hands or drink the Lord’s blood with a polluted mouth, he sacrilegiously grows angry with the priests. And—O your excessive madness, you madman! You are angry with the one who strives to turn God’s anger away from you; you threaten the one [Note: [Col. 0484C] “Strives, and,” Bod. 1, 2, 3.] who implores the Lord’s mercy on your behalf, who feels your wound when you yourself do not feel it, who sheds tears for you which perhaps you yourself do not shed. You further burden and heap up your crime; and although you yourself are implacable [Note: [Col. 0484C] “Being implacable, you are angry,” Oxford; “You are angry with God’s bishops and priests, and,” Lin.; Voss.] toward the bishops and priests of God, you think that the Lord can be placated toward you?

[Note: [Col. 0483D]

XXIII.—We Weep. The Burgundian manuscript adds “and grieve.” I found it noted in the English edition that this was also written in the Vatican manuscript. 540.

The day of punishment has come. The Séguier manuscript reads: “The day of judgment has come.”

May be corrected. Thus Erasmus and others after him. This is certainly a good reading. Nevertheless, the ancient editions and thirteen of our manuscripts, together with three English ones, prefer “may be directed.”]

XXIII. Instead, receive and admit what we say. Why do deaf ears not hear the saving precepts that we admonish them to obey? Why do blind eyes not see the path of repentance [Col. 0484B] that we show them? Why does a stricken [Note: [Col. 0484C] “Closed,” Pem.; Voss. 1, 2; NC. 2; Bod. 2.] and alienated mind not perceive the life-giving remedies that we both learn and teach from the heavenly Scriptures? Or, if certain unbelievers have too little faith in future things, let them at least be terrified by present ones. Behold the punishments we witness among those who denied him, whose sorrowful ends we lament! Even here they cannot be without punishment, although the day of punishment has not yet come. Meanwhile some are chastised [Note: [Col. 0484C] “On earth,” NC. 2.] so that the others may be corrected. The torments of a few are examples for all.

[Note: [Col. 0483D]

XXIV.—Of prayers. This too had to be altered [Col. 0484D] because of the authority of the ancient copies and the Speyer edition. Erasmus was the first to print “of praying.” But I found that reading only in the Tours manuscript. The Fuxensis manuscript, moreover, has “remedy” in place of “mercy.”

Seized, she mangled. Erasmus wrote: “Seized, she fell and mangled.” But the word “fell” is recognized by none of our ancient manuscripts, except that two of them have “collapsed.” I have also ascertained that it does not occur in the Verona or Benevento manuscripts, nor in the Séguier manuscript.]

XXIV. One of those who voluntarily ascended the Capitol intending to make his denial became mute after he denied Christ. His punishment began from the very point at which his crime began, so that he could no longer make supplication, since he had no words with which to implore mercy. Another woman, while at the baths—for this alone had been lacking to complete her crime [Col. 0484C] and misfortunes [Note: [Col. 0484D] “Had not been lacking,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.]: that she should proceed immediately to the baths after losing the grace of the life-giving washing—was there, unclean herself, seized by an unclean spirit, and with her teeth mangled the tongue by which she had either been impiously fed or had spoken. After the criminal food had been consumed, the frenzy of her mouth was armed for her destruction. She became her own executioner and afterward could not survive long: tormented by pains of the belly and entrails, she expired.

[Note: [Col. 0484D]

XXV.—Less. Pamelius later inserted the word “for themselves” on Cauchy’s conjecture, admitting that it was not found in the other copies. I, for my part, found it nowhere in those I used.

Bread with wine. Thus all the ancient manuscripts and editions. The Pithou manuscript, however, has: “she bit bread mixed with wine.”

Prevent. Four ancient manuscripts prefer “guard against.” In one, however, “prevent” is written, with “or guard against” above the line.

An inexperienced soul. Below, in the book *On the Good of Patience*, p. 251: “An inexperienced soul bears witness by weeping and groaning.” Tertullian in the *Apologeticum*: “Wait for the fleeing soul while it is new; catch the fresh blood.” Jerome in the letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians: “You assert that a human being can be without sin if he wills, and after a most profound sleep you vainly try to add, for the deception of inexperienced souls, ‘not without God’s grace.’”

Confessed. Two ancient manuscripts read “testified.”

The deacon [offered] the cup. See Beveridge on canon II of the Synod of Ancyra. Prosper tells an almost similar story about a certain young woman of Arab nationality in the book entitled *Half the Time*, chapter 6.

Closing tightly. Thus fifteen ancient manuscripts and the Manutius and Morel editions. The old editions and eight ancient copies read “hardening.” This discrepancy arose from an interchange of letters.]

XXV. Hear what happened, with me myself present as a witness. Her parents happened to flee and, taking too little thought in their terror, left their little daughter under the care of a nurse. The nurse brought the abandoned child to the magistrates. Because she was not yet able to eat meat on account of her age, they gave her, at the idol where the people were gathering, bread mixed with wine, which itself had nevertheless been left over from the sacrifice of those who were perishing. Her mother subsequently received her daughter back. But the girl was no more able to speak of and disclose the outrage committed against her than she had previously been able to understand or prevent it. Through ignorance, therefore, it came about that while we were celebrating the sacrifice, her mother brought the girl in with her. But the girl, when mingled with the holy people, could not endure our prayer and supplication: now she began to be shaken by weeping, now to be tossed restlessly about by an agitation of mind; and, as though compelled by a torturer, the inexperienced soul, still in her innocent years, confessed its consciousness of the deed by such signs as it could. But when the solemn rites had been completed and the deacon began to offer the cup to those present, and, after the others had received it, her turn [Col. 0485B] arrived, the little girl, under the impulse of the divine Majesty, turned away her face, pressed her mouth shut by tightly closing her lips, and refused the cup. The deacon nevertheless persisted and, though she resisted, poured some of the sacrament of the cup into her mouth. Then followed sobbing and vomiting. The Eucharist could not remain in a body and mouth that had been violated. The drink sanctified in [Col. 0486A] the Lord’s blood burst forth from her polluted entrails. So great is the Lord’s power, so great his majesty! The secrets of darkness were exposed beneath his light; even hidden crimes did not deceive God’s priest.

[Note: [Col. 0485D]

XXVI.—While We Were Celebrating the Sacrifice. Eight ancient manuscripts and the Morel edition present this reading. But the old editions, including the Manutius edition, and thirteen ancient manuscripts do not have the word “we,” which I therefore consider unnecessary. I have nevertheless not dared to delete it, because it does no harm to the holy martyr’s meaning. Something similar occurs in Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 10, where certain ministers who knew the Lord, while standing beside one offering sacrifice, placed the immortal sign upon their foreheads. That passage presents no difficulty. For the ministers who knew the Lord can be none other than Christians, especially since Lactantius immediately says that they placed the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. Yet recently there was someone who considered this manner of speaking ambiguous, since it was doubtful, he thought, whether those ministers were ministers of Diocletian or Christians. That they were Christians is also shown [Col. 0486B] by what follows in this passage of Lactantius, and also by another passage of his from book IV of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 27, where, in treating this very matter, he writes that “certain of our ministers stood beside their masters while they were sacrificing.”

[Col. 0486C] Within. I would not mention that I changed the “among” printed by Pamelius if the authority of the ancient copies had not compelled me to do so. For all of them, with only two exceptions, have “within.” So too does the Morel edition.

Admitting into her breast. Following the authority of the Cambron manuscript, Pamelius printed “admitting blood into her breast.” Rigault retained that reading; the English editors deleted it. Correctly, for it does not occur in our manuscripts or in the two Petau manuscripts cited by Albertinus.

Her box. Hospinianus, book II, chapter 5, *On Temples*, adduces this passage of Saint Cyprian and argues at length against us, because we enclose the Eucharist in a chest—that is, in a case or cupboard—and says that no command to enclose the Eucharist exists from either Christ or the Apostles. Hospinianus certainly wrote all this to no purpose, for we readily concede it. In the infancy of the Church, when it lived among its persecutors and Christians celebrated the divine mysteries in secret, there was no safe and fixed [Col. 0486D] place in which the Eucharist could be enclosed. It was therefore distributed to the faithful by the ministers, and each person carried his portion home in order to receive communion. But afterward, when the whole world had become Christian, it seemed fitting and appropriate to place it in a fixed and safe place, 541 so that it could immediately be distributed to those wishing to receive it—not secretly, as in the first centuries of the Church, but openly and publicly, whenever anyone desired.

The holy thing of the Lord. That is, the Eucharist, which in the beginnings of the Christian religion each person carried home so that he might freely administer to himself the communion of Christ’s body. Tertullian in book II *To His Wife*: “Will your husband not know what you taste in secret before any other food?” See our notes on the book *On the Good of Patience*.

With unworthy hands. The Verona manuscript, one of mine, and two English manuscripts have “with defiled hands.”

[Col. 0487C] Holiness fleeing. The Séguier manuscript reads: “the holy thing fleeing from there.” Shortly before, he said: “in which the holy thing of the Lord had been.” Thus that reading appears better. But I have not dared to alter it, because the remaining manuscripts prefer “holiness.” That reading too, after all, yields good sense. I shall, however, take this opportunity to correct the final part of Pelagius II’s third letter to the bishops of Istria, where one reads “with holiness preserving.” That one should write “preserved” instead is shown by the ancient manuscript from which it was edited. In the same place, a little earlier, three words that dropped out through an ancient copyist’s error must be added. It should therefore read: “He reported that the man who had written on the repetition of baptism died in Catholic unity.” Thus Augustine in the book *On the One Baptism*, chapter 12.

Not repenting … confessing. These words first emerged from the Manutius press. I found them in three ancient manuscripts. They are absent, however, from sixteen and from the Morel edition.

Which for himself. Previously, “whom” was read in all the editions and almost all the manuscripts. It was easy to suppose that “which” should be restored. Yet I found that reading, which I consider the most authentic, nowhere except in the Reims manuscript of Saint-Denis. One English manuscript prefers “which things.”

Wrath. This is the reading of twenty of our ancient copies and eight English ones. Their authority persuaded me to print it instead of the “censure” found in the editions, although this latter reading is also good and occurs in some ancient manuscripts.]

XXVI. This happened in the case of an infant who did not yet possess the age to express the crime committed against her by another. But the woman who, being advanced in age and now in mature years, secretly slipped in while we were celebrating the sacrifice—taking for herself not food but a sword, and admitting, as it were, deadly poisons within her throat and breast—subsequently began to be strangled and suffocated as her soul seethed within her. And suffering now not the oppression of persecution but of her own sin, she collapsed, palpitating and trembling. The crime of her dissembled conscience did not long remain unpunished or concealed. She who had deceived a human being felt God as her avenger. And [Col. 0486B] when a certain woman attempted to open with unworthy hands [Note: [Col. 0485B] “Defiled,” Pem.; Voss. 2.] her box, in which the holy thing of the Lord had been, she was frightened by fire rising from it and did not dare touch it. And indeed another man [Note: [Col. 0485B] “And when another man,” Bod. 1.], because he too had been stained by sacrifice, dared secretly to receive a portion with the others [Note: [Col. 0486B] “With the others who were receiving,” Pem.; Voss. 2.] from the sacrifice celebrated by the priest; but he could not eat or handle the holy thing of the Lord, and on opening his hands discovered that he was carrying ashes. 190 [Col. 0487A] By this one example it was shown that the Lord withdraws when he is denied, and that what is received does not benefit the undeserving unto salvation, since the saving grace is changed into ashes when holiness flees. How many each day [Note: [Col. 0487C] “How many unclean persons each day,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Spir.], failing to repent or confess the consciousness of their sin, are filled with unclean spirits! How many, bereft of reason even to the point of insanity, are shaken by the fury of madness! There is no need to pass through the ends of individuals, since amid the manifold ruins of the world the punishment of sins is as varied as the multitude of sinners is numerous. Let each person consider not what another has suffered, but what he himself deserves to suffer. Nor should he believe that he has escaped if punishment has spared him for the moment, since he ought all the more to fear what the wrath of God the Judge has reserved for him [Note: [Col. 0487C] “The wrath of God has reserved,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1. “Censure,” Oxford.].

[Col. 0487B] [Note: [Col. 0488C]

XXVII.—Escape. Previously “evade” was read, a reading that I consider the best; but the authority of the ancient manuscripts required me to alter it. Sixteen in number support this alteration.

In hidden places. There are two readings of this passage in the manuscripts. Some have “in hidden places,” others “in secret places.” Both readings are good.

Do I not fill heaven? These words are absent from the ancient editions and fifteen ancient manuscripts.

Formed. The Fuxensis manuscript reads “contemplating,” which is not a bad reading.]

XXVII. Nor should those who, although they did not contaminate their hands with abominable sacrifices, nevertheless polluted their conscience with certificates, flatter themselves so as to avoid repentance. That declaration of one who denies is the sworn attestation of a Christian who renounces what he had been [Note: [Col. 0487C] “What he had been,” Lam.]. He said that he had done whatever another committed by actually doing it. And since it is written, “You cannot serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24), the man who obeyed the secular lord’s edict served a secular lord; he heeded human authority more than God. Let him see whether he publicly declared before men what he had committed with less disgrace or less guilt. Yet he will not be able to flee and evade God the Judge, since the Holy Spirit says in the Psalms: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 138:16). And again: “Man sees the face, [Col. 0488A] but God the heart” [Note: [Col. 0488C] “Into the heart,” Ver.; Ben.] (1 Sam. 16:7). The Lord himself likewise forewarns and prepares us, saying: “And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of kidney and heart” (Rev. 2:23). He perceives hidden things and examines secret and concealed things. Nor can anyone escape the eyes of God, who says: “I am a God who draws near, and not a God from afar. If a man should hide in hidden places, shall I therefore not see him [Note: [Col. 0488C] “Shall I not see him? He sees,” Ben.; Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1.]? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. 23:23). He sees the hearts and breasts of individuals and will judge not only our deeds but also our words and thoughts; he beholds the thoughts and intentions of all, conceived while still within the secret recesses of the closed breast.

[Note: [Col. 0488D]

XXVIII.—Greater in Faith. The ancient editions, ten of our manuscripts, and six English ones prefer “with greater faith and better fear.” Sixteen others also read this way, except that in them “better” is written in the plural. Four have “greater men.” The *Epitome* of Lactantius, chapter 43: “When the ungrateful people had been removed from the inheritance, he might gather for himself another, more faithful people from foreign nations.”

Whoever is ashamed. Thus the ancient editions and thirteen ancient manuscripts. Three others have: “Whoever is ashamed of me, I too shall put him to shame before my Father who is in heaven.” The Bec manuscript reads: “Whoever is ashamed of me before men, he shall put him to shame.” By contrast, in two others it is written: “Whoever confesses me, the Son of Man shall confess him.” So too above, Letter IX, p. 18. But the reading containing “Whoever is ashamed” also occurs above, Letter LXIII, p. 109. I think that this discrepancy must be attributed to the rashness of copyists.]

XXVIII. Finally, how much greater in faith and better in fear are those who, although bound by no crime of sacrifice or certificate [Col. 0488B], nevertheless, because they merely thought of doing so, confess this very thing sorrowfully and candidly before God’s priests, make an *exomologesis*—a confession—of conscience, disclose the burden of their soul, and seek a saving remedy even for slight and minor wounds, knowing that it is written: “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6:7). God cannot be mocked or circumvented, nor can he be deceived by any fraudulent cunning. Indeed, the person who thinks of God in human terms and believes that he escapes punishment for his crime if he did not commit it openly sins all the more. Christ says in his commandments: “Whoever is ashamed of me, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him” (Mark 8:38). And does one who is ashamed [Note: [Col. 0488C] “Or” is absent from Oxford.] or afraid to be a Christian think himself a Christian? How can one be with Christ when he is either ashamed or afraid to belong to Christ? [Col. 0489A] Certainly, he will have sinned less by not seeing the idols, by not profaning the sanctity of the faith before the eyes of a surrounding and jeering crowd, by not polluting his hands with deadly sacrifices, or staining his mouth with criminal foods. This makes his guilt less; it does not make his conscience innocent. He can more readily attain forgiveness for his crime; yet he is not free from crime. Let him therefore not cease to do penance and to implore the Lord’s mercy, lest what appears to be less in the character of the offense [Note: [Col. 0489C] “Less of an offense,” Lam. York NC. 1. Bod. 2. Len.] be increased by neglecting satisfaction.

> **Note: [Col. 0489C]**
>
> **XXIX.—I beseech you, brothers.** After these words the Verona manuscript continued: “Let each person confess his offense.”
>
> **While his confession can be admitted.** For after death it is not admitted. There is no *exomologesis* in the lower world, as Cyprian says. See Pamelius.
>
> **With your heart.** The Pithou manuscript adds: “and with your whole soul.”

XXIX. I beseech you, dearly beloved brothers, [191] let each one confess his own offense, while the offender is still in this world, while his confession can be admitted, while the satisfaction and remission effected through the priests are acceptable before the Lord. Let us turn to the Lord with our whole mind [Col. 0489B] and, expressing repentance for our crime with genuine sorrows, implore God’s mercy. Before him let the soul prostrate itself [Note: [Col. 0489C] “Let it prostrate itself before him,” Ben.]; to him let its grief make satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0489C] “Let it make satisfaction to his majesty,” Voss. 1.]; upon him let all its hope rest. He himself tells us how we ought to pray: “Return to me,” he says, “with your whole heart, together with fasting, weeping, and mourning; and rend your hearts, and not your garments” (Joel 2:12). Let us return to the Lord with our whole heart. As he himself admonishes, let us appease his wrath and displeasure with fasting, weeping, and mourning.

> **Note: [Col. 0489D]**
>
> **XXX.—With women.** So all editions before that of Pamelius. Pamelius therefore expunged these words, both because he did not find them in his manuscripts and because he believed them unnecessary. They are indeed absent from thirteen of ours. But they occur in fifteen others and in one English manuscript. I do not see why they should be expunged, since above, in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 179, virgins are forbidden mixed bathing with men and women. From this it is inferred that women were accustomed to bathe with men. See the notes on the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 530.
>
> **542 Plucks his beard.** See book III of the *Testimonies*, ch. 84; Savaron and Sirmond on Sidonius, book IV, Epistle 24. See also Francesco Giorgio Veneto [Col. 0490C] in *On the Harmony of the World*, canticle II, ch. 6, and our notes on Gratian, distinction 22, chapter *Prohibete*, p. 453.
>
> **Wounds of sinning.** Lamon’s manuscript reads “kinds.”
>
> [Col. 0490D] **To have sinned and not made satisfaction.** Quintilian, book XI, ch. 1: “Therefore, the most useful thing in repentance is confession and satisfaction for guilt.” Tertullian in the book *On Repentance*: “For confession is the counsel of satisfaction.” See above, p. 538, before the *exomologesis* was made.

XXX. Do we think that a person laments with his whole heart and implores the Lord with fasting, weeping, and mourning if, from the very first day of his crime, he frequents the baths daily with women, feeds at lavish banquets and swells himself with richer fattening fare, belches up his indigestion the next day, and does not share his food and drink with the needy poor? [Col. 0489C] How does one who walks about cheerful and joyful mourn his own death? And although it is written, “You shall not disfigure the form of your beard” (Lev. 19:27), he plucks his beard and adorns his face! Does one who displeases God now strive to please anyone else? Or does that woman groan and mourn who has leisure to put on the finery of costly clothing but not to reflect upon the garment [Col. 0490A] of Christ that she has lost, to acquire costly ornaments and elaborate necklaces [Note: [Col. 0489C] “wrought,” Lips. Gronov., from the manuscripts.], but not to mourn the loss of divine and heavenly adornment? Although you put on foreign garments and silken robes, you are naked. Although you adorn yourself with gold, pearls, and gems, without Christ’s adornment you are disfigured. You who dye your hair, at least cease now amid your sorrows; and you who paint the outlines of your eyes with a stroke of black powder [Note: [Col. 0490C] “with a black stroke of powder,” Ver.; “with an application,” Pem.], at least now wash your eyes with tears. If you had lost one of your dear ones [Note: [Col. 0490C] Thus nine manuscripts. “Dear ones,” Oxford.] through the departure of death, you would groan sorrowfully and weep; with face unadorned, clothing changed, hair neglected, countenance clouded, and expression downcast, you would display the signs of grief. Wretched woman, you have lost your soul [Note: [Col. 0490C] “your wretched soul,” Voss. 1, 2; Pem.; Lin.]; spiritually dead, you have begun to survive yourself here and, walking about, to carry your own corpse—and you do not mourn bitterly, do not groan continually [Col. 0490B], and do not hide yourself either from shame at your crime or through unremitting lamentation! See, here are still worse wounds of sinning; see, here are greater offenses: to have sinned and not made satisfaction, to have transgressed and not mourned one’s offenses.

> **Note: [Col. 0490D]**
>
> **XXXI.—In sackcloth.** Five ancient manuscripts read “in haircloth and sackcloth”; the Séguier manuscript, “in ashes, in haircloth.” Below, at the end of this book, p. 192: “to cling to spread sackcloth amid ashes, haircloth, and filth.” Tertullian said in the book *On Repentance*: “to lie upon sackcloth and ashes, to darken the body with filth,” and “amid the harshness of sackcloth and the horror of ashes.” Sackcloth, as Jerome says in his *Letter to Marcella on Gifts Received*, is a sign of prayer and fasting.
>
> **Who keep.** The old editions and four ancient manuscripts add “and order.” Three others have “order,” but do not have “keep.”
>
> [Col. 0491D] **To you, Lord, righteousness.** Erasmus printed: “To you, Lord, glory; to you, righteousness.” But I have nowhere found the word “glory” in the manuscripts. Nor does it occur in chapter 3 of Daniel’s prophecy, from which these words were taken.

XXXI. Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, illustrious and noble young men, did not cease making *exomologesis* to God even amid the flames and fires of the blazing furnace. Although conscious of having acted rightly and having often won the Lord’s favor by the obedience of their faith and fear, they nevertheless did not cease to maintain humility and make satisfaction to the Lord even amid the glorious martyrdoms of their virtues. Divine Scripture says: “Azarias stood and prayed, and opened his mouth, and made *exomologesis* to God together with his companions in the midst of the fire” (Dan. 3:25). Daniel likewise, after the manifold favor granted to his faith and innocence [Col. 0490C], after the Lord’s approval of his virtues and praises had often been repeated, still strives to win God’s favor by fasting, rolls in sackcloth and ashes, and makes sorrowful *exomologesis*, saying: “Lord God, great and mighty and to be feared, who keep your covenant and mercies toward those who love you and observe [Col. 0491A] your commandments: we have sinned, committed wickedness, acted impiously, transgressed, and forsaken your commandments and judgments; we have not listened to the words of your servants the prophets, who spoke in your name concerning our kings and all nations and the whole earth. To you, Lord, belongs righteousness [Note: [Col. 0491C] Editions from Erasmus through Oxford add “glory.”], but to us confusion” (Dan. 9:4–7).

XXXII. These are the things the gentle, the candid, and the innocent [192] did in order to win the favor of God’s majesty; and now those who have denied the Lord refuse to make satisfaction and beseech him! I beg you, brothers, consent to these health-giving remedies; obey the better counsels. Join your tears to ours, unite your groans with our groaning. We beg you so that we may be able to beg God for you. We first direct toward you [Col. 0491B] the very prayers with which we ask God to have mercy upon you. Perform full penance; demonstrate the grief of a sorrowing and lamenting soul.

> **Note: [Col. 0491D]**
>
> **XXXIII.—So grave a crime.** Fourteen of our manuscripts and eight English manuscripts prefer this reading to the “so great” written elsewhere.

XXXIII. And do not be disturbed by the improvident error or empty stupefaction of certain people who, although held in so grave a crime, have been struck with blindness of mind, so that they neither understand nor mourn their offenses. This is a greater scourge from an indignant God, as it is written: “And God gave them a spirit of insensibility” (Isa. 29:10). And again: “They did not receive a love of the truth that they might be saved; and for this reason God will send them an operation of error, that they may believe a lie, so that all who did not believe the truth but take pleasure in unrighteousness may be judged” (2 Thess. 2:10). Unrighteously pleased with themselves and driven mad by the alienation of a stupefied mind, they despise the Lord’s commandments [Col. 0491C], neglect the remedy for their wound [Note: [Col. 0491C] “being negligent,” Lam. York Bod. 2.], and refuse to do penance. Improvident before committing the crime, obstinate after it—neither steadfast beforehand nor suppliant afterward. When they ought to have stood, they fell; when they ought to fall down and prostrate themselves before God, they think that they stand. They have taken peace for themselves unbidden, though no one granted it. Seduced by a false promise and joined to apostates and faithless persons, they accept error for truth. They regard the communion [Col. 0492A] of those not in communion as valid; they believe human beings against God, though against human beings they did not believe God.

> **Note: [Col. 0491D]**
>
> **XXXIV.—Passes across.** Thus commonly the ancient manuscripts and editions. Some, however, read differently: two have “pierces through,” and another “girds across.”
>
> **There remains.** Pamelius printed “there alone remains,” from manuscripts and an old printed copy. But the word “alone,” which is superfluous, is absent from all our manuscripts except one from Grenoble and from seven English manuscripts.

XXXIV. Flee people of this kind as far as you can [Note: [Col. 0491C] “Flee,” Oxford manuscripts, Pem. NC. 2.]; avoid with salutary caution those who cling to destructive associations. Their speech creeps like a cancer; their conversation passes across like a contagion; their harmful and poisonous persuasion kills more grievously than persecution itself. There remains the penance that makes satisfaction; but those who take away repentance for the crime close the path of satisfaction. Thus it happens that, while a false salvation is either promised or believed through the recklessness of certain people, the hope of true salvation is taken away.

> **Note: [Col. 0491D]**
>
> **XXXV.—One ought to pray.** Beatus Rhenanus, after discussing repentance and confession at length in the argument to Tertullian’s book *On Repentance*, finally transcribes this passage of Cyprian as the completion, as it were, of his observations. Meanwhile, I note that this argument by Beatus Rhenanus is absent from later editions of Tertullian’s works.
>
> **What the adversary was taking away.** Below, in the book *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 243: “An estate entrusted to God is neither seized by the state nor invaded by the treasury.” Saint Augustine, in the book *Fifty Homilies*, Homily 48: “The treasury takes what Christ does not receive.” See the same author, *Exposition of Psalm 146*. Lactantius, ch. 8 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*: “The most bloodthirsty treasury overflowed with ill-gotten wealth.” Pliny in the *Panegyric to Trajan*: “The treasury is defeated rather frequently, though its case is never bad except under a good emperor.” In Victor’s *Epitome*, Trajan is said to have called the treasury a spleen, because as it grows, the other limbs waste away. Symmachus, in his report concerning the altar of Victory: “The treasury of good emperors is increased not by losses imposed upon priests, but by spoils taken from enemies.” [Col. 0493B] The Novel of the Emperor Anthemius *On Ownerless Property*: “For nothing else seems fitting to imperial majesty [Col. 0493C] than to preserve common justice for all its subjects and to permit good emperors nothing more than is permitted to private persons.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII, treating the prefecture of Olybrius, says: “A most vigorous persecutor of malicious accusations, cutting off the treasury’s profits wherever he could.”
>
> **Poison.** Some editions have “things to be sold,” and Pamelius prefers that reading. Ours is supported by sixteen of our manuscripts and eleven English manuscripts. Nor can there be any doubt that it is the truest reading. All the ancient editions, including those of Manutius and Morel, also prefer it.
>
> [Col. 0494B] **Let it be lent to the Lord.** I have chosen to write it so because Cyprian speaks thus in the book *On the Dress of Virgins* [Col. 0494C], p. 167. Some ancient manuscripts and the Speyer edition, as well as the old Venetian edition, also read thus. Jerome in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*: “He lends to God.” Martial, book I, Epigram 44: “She alone lends all these things to the gods.”

XXXV. But you, dearly beloved brothers, whose fear of God is readily disposed and whose mind, though brought to ruin [Col. 0492B], remains mindful of its evil: as penitents who grieve over your sins, examine them; acknowledge the most grievous crime upon your conscience; open the eyes of your heart to understand your offense, neither despairing of the Lord’s mercy nor yet claiming pardon as your right. As God, in the affection of a father, is always indulgent [Note: [Col. 0491C] “merciful,” Pem. Voss. 2.] [Note: [Col. 0491C] “always, always and good,” Pem.] and good, so, in the majesty of a judge, he is to be feared. As greatly as we have sinned, so greatly let us mourn. Let a deep wound not lack diligent and prolonged treatment. Let the penance not be less than the crime. Do you think that the Lord can quickly [Note: [Col. 0492C] Thus eight English manuscripts. “Quickly” is absent from the old printed editions.] be appeased—the Lord whom you denied with faithless words, to whom you preferred your estate, whose temple you violated by sacrilegious contamination? Do you think that he easily has mercy [Note: [Col. 0492C] “can have mercy upon you,” Pem.] upon you, when you said that he was not yours? One ought to pray and beseech more earnestly, to spend the day in mourning [Col. 0492C], to pass the nights in vigils and weeping, to occupy all one’s time with tearful lamentations, to cling prostrate [Note: [Col. 0492C] “Let him abound upon the spread ground” [reading uncertain], Thu. Foss.; “to cling prostrate to the ground and ashes,” Oxford Lips.] to the ground, to roll in ashes, haircloth, and filth; after losing the garment of Christ, to desire no clothing now; after the devil’s food, to prefer fasting; to apply oneself to righteous works, by which sins are purged; to devote oneself frequently to almsgiving, by which souls are delivered from death. Let Christ receive what the adversary was taking away. [Col. 0493A] An estate by which a person has been deceived and defeated ought no longer to be retained or loved. Property must be avoided as an enemy, fled as a robber, and feared by those who possess it [193] as a sword and poison. Let what remains be useful only for this: that the crime and guilt may thereby be redeemed. Let the work be performed without delay and generously; let the entire estate be expended upon treating the wound; let our wealth [Note: [Col. 0493B] “works,” Lin. Pem. NC. 2. Bod. 3.] and possessions be lent to the Lord who is to judge concerning us [Note: [Col. 0493B] “who from our goods,” Thu. Voss.]. Thus faith flourished under the apostles; thus the first community of believers kept Christ’s commandments. They were ready and generous [Note: [Col. 0493B] “They were generous in making distributions,” Pem.]; they gave everything to be distributed through the apostles—and they were not redeeming offenses such as these.

> **Note: [Col. 0494C]**
>
> **XXXVI.—Turn aside.** The Moissac manuscript adds “to remit offenses.”
>
> **He gives weapons.** Lamon’s manuscript: “He gives the weapons of righteousness with which the righteous person may be armed.”
>
> **Will merit God’s pardon.** That is, “will obtain it,” as Lactantius says, book IV, ch. 17.

XXXVI. If someone prays with his whole heart, if he groans with the genuine lamentations [Note: [Col. 0493B] “laments,” Lam. York.] and tears of repentance, if by righteous and continual [Col. 0493B] works he moves the Lord to forgive his offense, he who has declared his mercy can have mercy upon such people, saying: “When you turn and groan, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been” (Isa. 30:15). And again: “‘I do not desire the death of the dying person [Note: [Col. 0493B] “sinner,” Lin.],’ says the Lord, ‘so much as that he should return and live’” (Ezek. 33:11). And the prophet Joel, with the Lord himself admonishing, declares [Col. 0494A] the Lord’s loving-kindness [Note: [Col. 0494B] “declares, saying,” Bod. 2. Lam. York.]: “Return,” he says, “to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious, patient and abundant in compassion, and one who turns aside his sentence against the evils inflicted” (Joel 2:13). He can grant pardon; he can turn aside his sentence. He can mercifully forgive one who repents, works, and prays; he can reckon as acceptable whatever the martyrs have both requested and the priests have done for such people. Or if someone moves him still more by his acts of satisfaction, if by a righteous entreaty he appeases his wrath and the displeasure of his indignation, he once again gives weapons with which the defeated person [Note: [Col. 0494B] “virtue may be armed,” Bod. 1.] may be armed; he repairs and strengthens the powers by which restored faith may be invigorated. The soldier will resume his contest, repeat the battle, and challenge the enemy—and indeed he will have been made stronger for battle through his sorrow. One who has thus made satisfaction to God [Col. 0494B], who through repentance for his deed and shame at his offense [Note: [Col. 0494B] “repentance for his deed, who shame at his offense,” Bod. 1, 3, 4. Thu.] has gained greater courage and faith from the very sorrow of his fall, will be heard and aided by the Lord and will make glad the Church that he had lately saddened; and he will merit not merely God’s pardon, but also the crown.

[Col. 0493]

# BOOK ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH

> **Note: [Col. 0493D]**
>
> **543** Since the English edition has splendidly demonstrated and proved that the true title of this book is *ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH*, as it is cited by ancient authors and as nearly all the ancient manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, entitle it, I have chosen to follow that opinion, which seems to me the best [Col. 0494D]. I will add only this: François Baudouin, in the *Letter to Lucanius, or Calvin* prefixed to his *Annotations on Optatus*, testifies that while he was at Trent he read this very title in Antonio Agustín’s Apulian manuscript.

(C, S)\*

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0493D]

Cyprian wrote this book on the occasion of Novatian’s schism in order to deter his Carthaginians, who otherwise were not very averse to it because of Novatus and certain other presbyters of his own Church, the authors of the whole tragedy. First, after exhorting them to steadfastness once he had fortified them against those men’s snares, he teaches that the cause of heresies is that the head of the Church is not sought, Peter’s primacy is despised, and the one chair, the one Church, and the one episcopate are abandoned. He then establishes the unity of the Church from both the Scriptures and the figures of the Old and New Testaments. Furthermore, after briefly discussing, as if incidentally, the Novatians’ ambition in usurping the Roman episcopate, he demonstrates at length [Col. 0495A] that Matthew 18—“Wherever two or three have gathered in my name,” etc.—does not accomplish anything for them against the Church on account of their small number, and that martyrdom outside the Church cannot benefit them. After this, he teaches that they ought not to be surprised that heresies flourished, since they had long ago been foretold by Christ—incidental mention being made of the punishments of schismatics—nor that certain Roman confessors assented to the schism, since no one is blessed before his death, and Judas the traitor existed within the very company of the apostles. He likewise teaches that association with schismatics and heretics must be avoided. Finally, through the Scriptures he exhorts his readers to peace and unanimity.

> **Note: [Col. 0495C]**
>
> **I. We have put on.** Thus twelve of our manuscripts and one Voss manuscript. This is certainly a better reading than the other, “we are clothed.” Below, in this same book, p. 196: “The closely woven tunic displays the coherent concord of our people, who have put on Christ.” Similarly, where the old translation of Irenaeus in the preface to the first book read “and we are for the most part occupied with a barbarous language,” a reading that is certainly false, as the most learned Dom René Massuet demonstrated, he restored “we devote ourselves for the most part to a barbarous language,” noting that this error was easy because of the resemblance between the letters *s* and *r*, and that hurried copyists could consequently readily write the latter in place of the former.
>
> **Precaution is easier.** Demosthenes writes in the *First Philippic* that nothing is terrifying to those who take precautions; Cicero, book I of *On Duties*, says that things which happen in some sudden manner are less serious than those inflicted after forethought and preparation. And in book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “It is therefore certainly beyond doubt that all things regarded as evils are more serious when unforeseen.” Rufinus, on Psalm 45: “Weapons that are not foreseen strike more grievously.” See the book *On Jealousy and Envy*, p. 255. See also above, p. 466.
>
> **Manifest.** Manutius printed “more manifest,” on what authority I do not know. For both the ancient editions and twenty-one of our manuscripts, among which I name the Séguier manuscript, as well as eight English manuscripts, prefer “manifest.” I judge that reading better. A little later, on p. 194, we read: “But we must guard not only against things that are openly manifest.”
>
> [Col. 0496C] **Confesses.** Thus all editions earlier than Pamelius, twenty-six of our copies, and five English manuscripts. On the authority of the Cambron manuscript, Pamelius wrote “professes.” I cannot agree with him. The well-known expression in Petronius is: “You have the accused confessing”; and Cicero’s in a certain *Letter to Atticus*: “When wicked men confessed to the murder of their father.”
>
> **Of circumventing a person.** One ancient Colbert manuscript reads “of circumventing people.” So also two English manuscripts.
>
> [Col. 0496D] **Hidden.** One royal manuscript and one English manuscript have “dark.”

I. SINCE the Lord admonishes and says, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13), and since he commands us to be guileless in innocence [Col. 0495B], yet prudent together with our guilelessness (ibid. 10:16), what else is fitting for us, dearly beloved brothers, but to exercise foresight and, keeping watch with an anxious heart, both to understand and to guard against the snares of the deceitful enemy, lest we who have put on Christ, the Wisdom of God the Father, should seem insufficiently wise in preserving our salvation? For it is not persecution alone, nor only those things that advance in open assault [Note: [Col. 0495C] “That is to be feared which . . . attacks,” Voss. 1, printed editions.] [Note: [Col. 0495C] “That which . . . attacks,” Oxford from ten editions; Lipsius considers it less satisfactory.] to undermine and cast down God’s servants, that must be feared. Precaution is easier where the danger is manifest, and the mind is equipped beforehand for the contest when the adversary confesses himself. The enemy is more to be feared [Note: [Col. 0495C] “feared,” Salisbury, Bod. 1, 2, 3. Cambron.] and guarded against when he creeps up secretly, when, deceiving through an appearance of peace, he crawls forward by hidden approaches; hence he also received the name “serpent.” Such is always his cunning [Col. 0496A], such his blind and hidden deceit in circumventing a person. Thus, immediately from the beginning of the world, he deceived; flattering with [194] lying words, he misled inexperienced souls through incautious credulity. When he attempted to tempt the Lord himself, he approached secretly, as though he might once more creep upon him and deceive him. Yet he was understood and beaten back [Note: [Col. 0495C] “thrust back,” Lam. NC. 1, 2. York Vat. 4.]; and he was therefore laid low because he was recognized and exposed.

> **Note: [Col. 0496D]**
>
> **II.—I say.** Pamelius wrote “I shall say,” and says this reading is better. Yet above, p. 108, in Epistle LXIII to Caecilius, where the same passage is transcribed, he printed “I say.” It is likewise written in this way in nearly all the ancient manuscripts and in the editions preceding that of Pamelius. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that five ancient manuscripts have “I shall say.”
>
> **Upon the rock.** That is, upon Christ and the faith that is in him. Jerome, in the *Explanation of Psalm 44 to Principia*: “The Church has been founded by steadfast reason upon the rock, Christ.” See Saint Augustine, Sermon LXXVI *On the Words of the Gospel According to Matthew*, Sermon CCXCV *On the Birthday of the Apostles Peter and Paul*, and book I of the *Retractations*, ch. 1; also Hincmar of Rheims, in the *Letter to the Bishop of Laon*, ch. V, p. 402.

II. From this an example has been given us: to flee the path of the old man and follow in the footsteps of the living Christ [Note: [Col. 0495C] Some read “conquering.” Baluze—I do not know why.], lest we again, through lack of caution, roll back into the snare of death, but, being provident [Note: [Col. 0495C] “provident and cautious,” York NC. 1. Bod. 2. Ben.] against danger, attain the immortality we have received. But how can we attain immortality unless we keep those commandments of Christ by which death is attacked and conquered, since he himself admonishes and says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17)? And [Col. 0496B] again: “If you do the things [Note: [Col. 0495C] “If you do what,” York Voss. 1. Pem. Lam. NC. 1. [Col. 0496C] Ver. Naples Thu. Foss.] that I command you, I no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:14–15). These, finally, he calls strong and steadfast; these he describes as founded upon a rock in a solid mass [Note: [Col. 0496C] “solid and firm,” Voss. 1, 3.]; these he presents as established with immovable and unshaken firmness against every storm [Note: [Col. 0496C] “all troubles,” Speyer.] and whirlwind of the age. “Whoever hears my words,” he says, “and does them, I shall liken him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. The rain descended, the rivers came [Note: [Col. 0496C] “arrived,” Lam. York Pem. Ar. Ver. MR. Voss. 3; “and came,” Thu. Foss.], the winds blew and beat upon that house, and it did not fall; for it had been founded [Note: [Col. 0496C] “was,” Lam. Pem. York NC. 1.] upon a rock” (Matt. 7:24–25). We must therefore stand upon his words and learn and do everything that he both taught and did. Besides, how does a person say that he believes in Christ [Note: [Col. 0496C] “believes Christ,” Thu. Voss. 3.] when he does not do what Christ commanded to be done? Or how will one attain [Col. 0497A] the reward of faith if he refuses to keep faith with the commandment? He must necessarily waver and wander and, carried off by a spirit of error, be blown about like dust shaken by the wind. Nor will one advance toward salvation by walking if he does not hold to the truth of the saving way.

> **Note: [Col. 0497B]**
>
> **III.—To the origin of truth.** Although this reading is good, I would nevertheless prefer “unity,” as is written a little later, “the origin of that same unity,” since the holy martyr immediately presses unity with the utmost vigor. Tertullian in the book *On the Prescriptions Against Heretics*: “Every kind must necessarily be assessed according to its origin.” Likewise, in place of what is commonly read at the beginning of Epistle XLII, p. 56, “Holiness and truth equally required,” the Rheims manuscript of Saint-Denis has “unity.” And we read “by the bond of unity” in Firmilian’s letter, p. 143. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, said at the Council of Tours: “Unless the Church possesses unity, it will not be one. If it is not one, it will not exist.” But Juan de Torquemada interprets this unity in the *Summary on the Church*, book III, ch. 30, as referring to the one supreme governing power of the whole Church, which resides in the pope. I prefer to speak with Saint Cyprian [545] rather than follow those empty and distorted interpretations of the scholastic theologians, which were unknown to antiquity.

III. But, dearly beloved brothers [Note: [Col. 0497B] These two words are absent from thirteen English manuscripts.], we must guard not only against things that are open and manifest [Note: [Col. 0497B] “openly manifest,” Voss. 3. Speyer.], but also against those that deceive through the subtlety of cunning fraud. Yet what could be more cunning or subtle than this: that the enemy, exposed and laid low by Christ’s advent, after light came to the Gentiles and the saving radiance shone forth for the salvation of humanity—so that the deaf might receive the hearing of spiritual grace, the blind might open their eyes to God, the infirm might recover through eternal health [Note: [Col. 0497B] “salvation,” Lam. York NC. 1.], the lame might run to the Church, and the mute might pray with clear voices and petitions—seeing the idols abandoned and his own seats and temples deserted because of the vast multitude of believers [Col. 0497B], should devise a new fraud by which to deceive the incautious under the very title of the Christian name? He invented heresies and schisms by which he might overthrow faith, corrupt truth, and rend unity. Those whom he cannot hold in the blindness of the old way [Col. 0498A], he encloses and deceives through the error of a new path. He snatches people from the Church itself; and while they seem to themselves already to have drawn near the light and escaped the night of the world, he again pours other darknesses upon them without their knowledge. Thus, although they do not stand by Christ’s Gospel, observance, and law, they call themselves Christians; and although walking in darkness, they suppose that they possess the light, while the adversary flatters and deceives them. In the Apostle’s words, he transforms himself as though he were an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14) and equips his ministers as though they were ministers of righteousness, who assert night in place of day, destruction in place of salvation, despair under the guise of hope, faithlessness under the pretext of faith, and Antichrist under the name of Christ, so that, while telling plausible lies, they may by their subtlety frustrate the truth. This happens, dearly beloved brothers, because there is no return to the origin of truth [Col. 0498B], the head is not sought, and the teaching of the heavenly Master [Note: [Col. 0498B] “of the heavenly teaching,” Lam. York NC. 1. Bod. 2. Ver.] is not preserved.

> **Note: [Col. 0497C]**
### IV.—The Lord Speaks

Since this passage, as interpolated, is the foundation of the greatest controversy between us and our adversaries, it seems necessary to me—although I have not placed it in its context in this interpolated form, where it does not belong—to reproduce it as it stands in the Manutian and Rigaltian editions. It therefore reads as follows:

> “The Lord speaks to Peter. ‘I say to you,’ he says, [Col. 0497D] ‘that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.’ And to the same man, after his resurrection, he says: ‘Feed my sheep.’ And although after his resurrection he bestows equal power upon all the Apostles and says, ‘As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit: if you forgive anyone’s sins, they shall be forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained,’ nevertheless, in order to make Unity manifest, he established one Chair, and by his own authority arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one man. Certainly the other Apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal fellowship both of honor and of power. But the beginning proceeds from Unity, and [Col. 0498B] the Primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ and the one Chair may be shown. And all are shepherds, and one flock is shown, which is fed by all the Apostles in unanimous agreement, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one, etc.”

And a little later:

> “Does one who does not hold this Unity of the Church believe that he holds the faith? Does one who opposes [Col. 0498C] and resists the Church, who abandons the chair of Peter, upon whom the Church was founded, trust that he is in the Church?”

It must be admitted that this passage exists in this form not only in the ancient codex of Marcellus II, which Onofrio Panvinio used, but also—and this carries greater authority and weight—in the second letter of Pope Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria. It might therefore reasonably seem that the following conclusion should be drawn: these words, which in my judgment are not Cyprian’s, are nevertheless ancient, and in the age of Pelagius—that is, a thousand years ago—they were believed genuinely to be Cyprian’s.

Nevertheless, the text that we follow in the main context is supported not only by editions earlier than the Manutian, but also by the authority of manuscript codices. Two are especially noteworthy: the Veronese and the Séguier codices. Latini and Aldus Manutius, son of Paulus, long ago testified that the Veronese codex had been written a thousand years before their time. Likewise, the Séguier codex, which I use, is acknowledged by the judgment and agreement of all who have seen it to have been written a thousand years ago. Latini says that this addition, [Col. 0498D] which we have removed from the text, is not found in seven Vatican codices. I myself have seen twenty-seven in which it is likewise absent.

Cyprian’s words without the addition were reproduced and cited by Callixtus II in writing to Humbald, archbishop of Lyons; by the cardinals assembled in the town of Livorno in 1408; and by the Roman correctors, who in their edition printed this passage in the form in which Gratian had transmitted it, although they knew that it appeared differently in the Manutian edition.

To these considerations, I think it should be added that the codex of Pelagius’s Letters to the bishops of Istria—the only one—is not contemporary with Pelagius, but was written at least five hundred years after his death. It follows that the codices of the works of Saint Cyprian which do not contain that clause possess at least the same authority as the codex of Pelagius’s Letters. I add that it seems probable that the German codices did not contain it in the age of Venericus, bishop of Vercelli.

[Col. 0499C]—These evidentiary considerations, on which the critics will pass judgment, had led Baluze to expunge certain words from this testimony. They were restored to the text, however, because they had been preserved in all the editions published in France during the preceding hundred and fifty years, including Rigault’s. Indeed, it was necessary to alter quite a few things in Baluze’s Notes, and more would have been altered if this could conveniently have been done. **MARAN.**

Certainly the many passages missing from these pages testify that quite a few things were altered, and indeed omitted, in Baluze’s notes. Yet anyone who weighs the surviving notes in a Catholic balance will surely have no doubt that the distinguished editor of Baluze was seized by justified anxiety. Perhaps there will even be someone who wishes that more had been omitted, especially if he thoroughly examines the note “On the Bridegroom of the Church,” which is to be appended shortly. Yet we judged that these and other similar contributions, whose learning is not entirely sound, although their considerable abundance is not to be despised, should be preserved, lest this complete body of Baluze’s edition, known to everyone and commended by its widespread reputation, be impaired. But [Col. 0499D] if you wish to correct what requires amendment here and there, see the dissertations and notes on Pontifical Authority among the Africans in the preceding volume. **EDS.**

#### The Primacy Is Given to Peter

Latini says that everything added here consists of marginal summaries that were eventually transferred into the text, not on one occasion but at different times.
