He says that the variation is apparent from the fact that the oldest surviving copies contain very few or none of these inserted summaries. This can readily be seen from the Veronese codex, which Latini maintained had been written a thousand years before his own day, since nothing of this sort appears in it, while all such words are absent from seven other Vatican codices.

He adds that these summaries were marginal and were gathered from Cyprian’s words, [Col. 0500C] something anyone can readily understand even from that summary alone which Pamelius teaches was present in Cardinal Hosius’s manuscript codex. There the following was written continuously in the text: “Here the primacy is given to Peter.” 547 For, Latini continues, what a diligent and studious reader had inferred from Cyprian in order to find the passage immediately and more easily, he had noted in the margin in a few words, perhaps also so as to construct an index from them as though they were headings and commonplaces.

From these facts that same most learned man and keen-scented critic concluded that the reading of the older and more numerous codices ought to have been retained in the text, while the words found in more recent codices should nevertheless have been indicated, but not immediately incorporated into Cyprian’s text. I found a similar observation in Denis Lambin’s annotations on Cicero’s *Pro Cluentio* and *Second Oration against Catiline*.

#### All Are Shepherds

That is, all bishops are shepherds of Christ’s flock. Hence we see that in Cyprian and elsewhere they call one another brothers and colleagues. [Col. 0500D] Later, humility—which ought to be the foremost virtue in a bishop, as is clear from Cyprian’s Letter LXIX—caused bishops to call themselves “servants of the servants of God.” Saint Pope Gregory did so, as did several other Roman bishops after him, though not all until the most recent times. See John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, book VIII, chapter 23.

#### This Unity of the Church

Ivo, part V, chapter 361, printed: “Does one who does not hold Peter’s Unity.…” This was copied from a gloss.

#### Resists

Pamelius added: “who abandons the chair of Peter, upon whom the Church was founded.” These words also exist in the second Letter of Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria and in the Acts of Alexander III, in Baronius; likewise [Col. 0501B] in Ivo at the place cited shortly before and in Gratian, distinction 93. There the Roman correctors note that these words, which Gratian and Ivo reproduce, exist in one Vatican codex of the works of Saint Cyprian and likewise in another belonging to the monastery of San Salvatore at Bologna.

They are not, however, found in the ancient editions or in our ancient books. The English edition does indeed note that they exist in four ancient English codices. Pamelius testifies that he found them in the Cambrai codex. Cyprian, Letter XL, p. 53: “The one Chair, founded upon the rock by the Lord’s voice.”

[Col. 0501C]

#### One Body

Pope Paul II copied this passage, citing Cyprian, in a letter written to the archbishop of Colossae in 1460, on 19 July:

> “Because all of us who proclaim and worship one Lord, one God, and one faith are one body and one spirit. Therefore all bishops ought firmly to hold and defend Unity, so that we may also prove the episcopate, as the blessed Cyprian says, to be one and indivisible.”

Meanwhile, I note here that “we may prove it indivisible” is also written in the Burgundian codex. From this it appears that Pope Paul used a similar copy.]

### IV

If anyone considers and examines these things, there is no need of a lengthy treatise or arguments. The proof of faith is easy in a concise statement of the truth.

The Lord speaks to Peter:

> “I say to you,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0498B] “He says, Peter,” Voss. 2.] “that you are Peter, and [Col. 0499A] upon this [Note: [Col. 0499B] Thus Ar. Bod. 4. Impr.; “that,” Oxon.] rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I [Note: [Col. 0499B] “It; I will give you,” Thu. Voss.] will give you the keys 195 of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever [Note: [Col. 0499B] “Whatever things,” Pem.] you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:18–19).

And again, after his resurrection, he says to the same man:

> “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15).

Upon that one man [Note: [Col. 0499B] Thus Pem. Voss. 2, 3. Impr. vett. and more recent editions. “Upon one man,” Oxon., with Spir. Vet. innom. Rem. Erasm. Grav. Morel. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1. NC. 1. Lin. Paris. Ben. Lips. ed. enclosed these words in brackets: “Upon that one man … his sheep.”] he builds his Church, and commands that his sheep be fed by him [Note: [Col. 0499B] “And commands that his sheep be fed by him.” The Oxford edition omitted these words.].

And although after his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0499B] “After his resurrection” is absent from Oxon. and four codices: Pem. Paris. Voss. 2. Bod. 4.] he bestows equal power upon all the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0499B] “Bestows, and says,” Spir. and innom. Pem. Erasm. Grov. Morel. Pamel. Rig. “Bestows power; nevertheless, he established one chair and by his own authority arranged the origin and principle of unity. Certainly the others were what Peter also was, but the primacy …,” Bod. 4.] and says:

> “As the Father has sent me, so I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit: if you forgive anyone’s [Note: [Col. 0499B] Thus five English codices. “If to anyone,” Oxon. and the other old editions.] sins, they shall be forgiven him; if you retain anyone’s sins, they shall be retained” [Note: [Col. 0499B] “They shall remain retained,” Lam.] (John 20:21–23),

nevertheless, in order to make unity manifest [Note: [Col. 0499B] “In order to make unity—the origin of that same unity beginning from one man—manifest,” MR.], he established one chair [Note: [Col. 0499B] “He established one chair.” Thus Manut. Pamel. and Bod. Rigalt. 1. Impr. cod. Pem. Voss. 2. Vatic. 1. Camberon. [Col. 0500B] Baluze had omitted these words, and D. Maran did not restore them when restoring the others; the Leipzig editor brackets them as spurious.], and by his own authority [Note: [Col. 0500B] “Its same origin of unity,” Paris.] arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one man [Col. 0500A] [Note: [Col. 0500B] “With one man beginning it,” Bod. 1, 4. Note: [Col. 0500B] “Its origin by his own authority,” Pem. Voss. 2.].

Certainly the other Apostles were what Peter was [Note: [Col. 0500B] “What Peter also was, but the primacy …,” Bod. 4.], endowed with an equal fellowship both of honor and of power; but the beginning proceeds from unity [Note: [Col. 0500B] Ar. Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Ben. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2 read: “proceeds, so that there may be one Church.” Hence Oxon. and Lips.], and the primacy is given to Peter [Note: [Col. 0500B] “The primacy is given to Peter,” codd. Pem. Voss. 2. Vat. 1. Bod. 3. and almost all printed editions. The Leipzig editors bracket the words “And the primacy … may be fed” and call them spurious in their notes.], so that the one Church of Christ and the one Chair may be shown [Note: [Col. 0500B] “So that the one Church of Christ … which one,” Pamel. Rigalt. and numerous printed editions. English codd. Pem. Voss. 2. Vatic. 1: “may be fed, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. Which,” Manut. “Proceeds, so that the Church may be shown to be one,” Oxon.].

And all are shepherds, and one flock is shown, which is fed by all the Apostles in unanimous agreement, so that the Church of Christ may be shown to be one. This one Church the Holy Spirit also designates in the *Song of Songs*, speaking in the person of the Lord:

> “One is my dove, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” (Song 6:9).

Does one who does not hold this unity of the Church [Note: [Col. 0500B] Thus Pamel. Rigalt. Oxon. “This unity of Peter,” Pem. Voss. 2. “The unity of Paul,” Bod. 4.] believe that he holds the faith? Does one who opposes and resists the Church, who abandons the chair of Peter, upon whom the Church was founded [Note: [Col. 0500B] Thus Pem. Voss. 1. Vat. 1. Bod. 3 and several editions. “Resists, [does he trust that] he is in the Church?” Oxon.], trust that he is [Col. 0501A] in the Church, when even the blessed Apostle Paul teaches this same thing and reveals the mystery of unity, saying:

> “One body and one spirit, one hope of your calling, one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, one God” (Eph. 4:4–6).

[Note: [Col. 0501C]

### V.—Let No One Deceive the Brotherhood

Pope Pius II used these words, though slightly altered and mutilated, as his own at the assembly of Mantua, as may be seen in volume IX of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 312.

#### The Episcopate Is One

Pius II omitted this paragraph at the assembly of Mantua. Yet he might usefully have employed it according to the opinion of those who interpret “one bishop” as referring to the Roman bishop, who in their opinion is the bridegroom of the Catholic—that is, universal—Church, as we noted above, p. 436. See Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book II, chapter 16, and Letter LXXIII of Cardinal Stanislaus Hosius, who interprets the one priest as the one whom we customarily call the vicar of Christ.

#### Just as the Sun’s

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, inserted this and several other passages from this work of Cyprian as his own, without any mention of Cyprian, in the *Sermon on Peace* in the new edition, p. 709.

#### Break a Branch from the Tree

Saint Augustine cites this passage in Sermon CCLXXXI, chapter 20, and in book III, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 33.

#### Once Cut Off, It Withers

In volume IX of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium* the reading is “diminishes.” But in the ancient papers from which this oration of Pius was published, “withers” is expressly written. So also in the new edition of Hildebert, p. 710.]

### V

We ought firmly to hold and defend this unity, especially those of us who preside as bishops in the Church, so that we may also prove the episcopate itself to be one and undivided.

Let no one deceive the brotherhood with a lie; let no one corrupt the truth of the faith by faithless treachery. The episcopate is one, a share of which is held wholly and jointly by each bishop. The Church likewise is one, though through the increase of her fruitfulness she extends more widely into a multitude.

Just as the sun has many rays but one light; and a tree many branches but one strength, founded upon its tenacious [Col. 0501B] root [Note: [Col. 0501B] “But the tree is one, founded upon its tenacious root,” Pem. Voss. 2. Ver. Man.]; and just as, when many streams flow [Col. 0502A] from a single spring, although their multiplicity appears widely dispersed through the abundance of the overflowing supply, unity is nevertheless preserved in their source.

Tear a ray away from the body of the sun: the unity of light [Note: [Col. 0501B] “Of the body of light,” Ben. NC. 1. Lam. Pem. Bod. 2. “Does not [Col. 0502B] admit,” Voss. 3.] does not admit division. Break a branch from the tree: once broken, it will not be able to bud. Cut a stream off from its source: once cut off, it withers.

So too the Lord’s Church, flooded with light, extends her rays throughout the whole world; yet it is one light that is diffused everywhere, nor is the unity of the body divided. In the abundance of her fertility she extends her branches over the whole earth and spreads her copiously flowing streams ever farther [Note: [Col. 0502B] “Flowing streams,” Lam. Ebor.; “spreads farther,” Thu.]; yet there is one head and one source, and one mother rich in the successive fruits of her fertility. From her womb we are born, by her milk we are nourished, by her spirit we are given life.

[Note: [Col. 0502B]

### VI.—Cannot Be Defiled by Adultery

Saint Fulgentius reproduces this passage in book I, chapter 1, *On the Remission of Sins*.

When I saw that in this passage of Cyprian and in the works of other ancient writers the Church was called the bride of Christ, while Christ was called her Bridegroom, and indeed her only Bridegroom; and when I read in the same passage of Cyprian that the bride of Christ cannot be defiled by adultery—the bride whom he has not abandoned, does not abandon, and will not abandon, nor cast away or alienate from himself; whom the Father betrothed to him, as Peter, abbot of Celle, says in book IX, Letter II; whom Pope Innocent III, in book I, Letter IV, [Col. 0502C] says was betrothed to Christ; when, [p. 549] I say, I read in this passage of Cyprian that the bride of Christ cannot be defiled by adultery, and that even the Roman pontiffs—Boniface I; Leo I in his Letter to Anatolius; Leo IX in his Letter to Robert, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu in Auvergne; Alexander III in his Letter to the people of Bologna; Alexander’s rival Octavian in his encyclical letter concerning his own election; Innocent III in numerous letters; Honorius III in his Letter to the king of Portugal; Clement V at the Council of Vienne; the cardinals writing to Emperor Frederick, in Baronius, year 1159, § LXIII; and others—call the Church the bride of one husband, Christ, and Christ the true and sole Bridegroom of the holy Church, I thought it could not unreasonably be inferred from this that the Church has but one husband (*univira*), as I once said in my Notes on Agobard.

I saw, moreover, that she whom Tertullian, at the very beginning of his book *To the Martyrs*, calls “Lady Mother Church” had been called the mother and mistress [Col. 0502D] of the Roman pontiff by Paschal II at the Lateran Council and by Clement V at the Council of Vienne. From this, as it seemed to me, I rightly concluded that she could not be the bride of one whose mother and mistress she was.

Nevertheless, people were later found who said that the pope too is the bridegroom of the Church—not only of the Roman Church, which is beyond dispute, but also of the whole or universal Church. That Pope Gregory X held this view is clear from his decrees published at the Council of Lyons. Later John Monachus, cardinal, after saying in the chapter *Felicis*, *On Penalties*, in the *Sext*, that there is one Church outside which no one is saved, immediately adds: “And the Pope is the bridegroom of this Church.” Then Giovanni d’Andrea, in the chapter *Pia consideratione*, *On Excesses*, in the *Sext*, says that the pope is the general bridegroom of the Church.

Pope Eugenius IV, writing to Charles VII, king of France, in Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1437, § XXIV, says that he is the true Vicar of Jesus Christ and [Col. 0503B] the sole bridegroom of his Church. Cardinal Giles of Viterbo, in an address delivered to Pope Julius II at the Lateran Council in 1511, on 3 May:

> “I therefore appeal to you, Julius, supreme pontiff. That most high God appeals to you, who willed you to represent him on earth, who long ago chose you alone from so great a senate, who has preserved you as the bridegroom of his Church even into the ninth year.”

Similarly Odoricus Raynaldus, in the dedicatory letter of volume XIII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* to Innocent X, says that the Church spread throughout the entire world is his bride.

Alexander of the Tower saw that this matter involved a great difficulty and a great danger, whether it were said that the Church does not have only one husband, or whether it were denied [Col. 0503C] that the pope is the bridegroom of the universal Church. Accordingly, although in book IV, chapter 14, *On the Resplendent Ray of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, he had said that Christ is the sole and singular Bridegroom of the Church—which appears to be most true—he nevertheless also wished the pope, whom he calls the ecumenical bishop of the Church, to be the bridegroom of the universal Church. He therefore resorted to the quibbles and subtleties of sophists and, following their understanding, said that the Church has two bridegrooms: one invisible, namely Christ, and the other visible, namely the pope.

Nothing more absurd could be devised. For what could be more absurd than to say that a woman is joined in marriage to two husbands, one real and the other imaginary? Yet Bellarmine, in book II, chapter 31, *On the Roman Pontiff*, ventured to hold the same opinion, saying that the pope is called the bridegroom of the Church in Christ’s place, as Christ’s vicar and minister.

Those who devise such empty and futile opinions certainly render no good service to the Roman pontiff. He is content with his own supreme dignity, than which none is higher, more excellent, more eminent, or [Col. 0503D] more exalted upon earth, and with which no power can be equated, as Pope Pius II says in writing to Charles VII, king of France, in Bzovius, year 1461, § IX.

Christ is the Bridegroom, the Church the bride, and the Roman pontiff the Bridegroom’s friend. When Christ was about to ascend into heaven, as Saint Augustine says, he entrusted her to his disciples, not so that she should love any of them, but that she should love him as her Bridegroom and them as the Bridegroom’s friends.

Saint Bernard therefore wrote splendidly in Letter CXCI of Mabillon’s edition, speaking in the name of the bishops to Pope Innocent:

> “The bride of Christ has been entrusted to you, friend of the Bridegroom. It is your duty to present her to Christ as a chaste virgin pledged to one husband.”

Bernard likewise warned Pope Eugenius III that, if he were the Bridegroom’s friend, he ought not to call the Church his princess, but rather his Bridegroom’s princess, just as Jerome says that he called Eustochium—who had dedicated her virginity to Christ—his lady, since she was the bride of his Lord.

For the virgins [Col. 0504B] who have consecrated themselves to Christ the Church customarily calls the brides of Christ, as Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, also once wrote to Proba *On Virginity*: “There is one Bridegroom of all sacred virgins.”

Pope Innocent III was therefore entirely correct when, in Sermon III *On the Consecration of a Pontiff*, after discussing the sacramental union of Christ and the Church and, [p. 551] calling Christ the Bridegroom and himself the Bridegroom’s friend, he added that he was the bridegroom of the Roman Church. I add that Alypius and Augustine, writing to Juliana, expressly call Christ the sole Bridegroom of the universal Church.

#### If He Was Able to Escape

Alexander III used this passage [Col. 0504C] against Emperor Frederick, as is clear from his Acts in Baronius, year 1164, § XLI.

#### And These Three Are One

See Erasmus on chapter 5 of the First Letter of John, the Notes of the English editors on this passage, and Richard Simon, *Critical History of the New Testament*, vol. I, chapter 18, p. 212. See also the *Itinerary* of the Reverend Father Edmond Martène, part II, p. 79.]

### VI

The bride of Christ cannot be defiled by adultery; she is incorrupt [Col. 0502B] and chaste. She knows one home; with chaste modesty she guards the sanctity of one bridal chamber. She preserves us for God; she assigns to the kingdom the children whom she has borne.

Whoever is separated from the Church and is joined to an adulteress is separated from the promises of the Church. One who abandons the Church of Christ will not attain Christ’s rewards. He is an alien, he is profane, he is an enemy. One can no longer have God as Father if he does not have the Church as mother.

If anyone who was outside Noah’s ark was able to escape, then one who is outside the Church [Note: [Col. 0503B] “Outside the Church’s doors,” Thu.] will escape.

The Lord warns us and says:

> “He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30).

One who breaks Christ’s peace and concord acts against Christ. One who gathers anywhere apart from the Church scatters Christ’s Church.

The Lord says:

> “I and [Col. 0504A] the Father are one” (John 10:30).

And again it is written of the Father, the Son, and the Holy 196 Spirit:

> “And these three are one” (1 John 5:7).

And does anyone believe that this unity, which comes from the divine steadfastness and coheres with the heavenly mysteries, can be torn apart in the Church and separated by the division of conflicting wills? One who does not hold this unity does not hold God’s law, does not hold the faith of the Father and the Son, and does not hold life and salvation [Note: [Col. 0503B] “Does not hold the truth unto salvation,” Oxon. Pem. Ar. Bod. 2. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. “Nor salvation,” Voss. 3.].

[Note: [Col. 0504C]

### VII.—Who Should Put On Christ

I know that Manutius and others after him, with the sole exception of Morel, printed “it itself” in place of “Christ,” just as I too saw “it itself” written in one old book, and “it” in two other old books. But since I see that our twenty-five old books, the four English books, and all the old editions have “Christ,” I judged that this reading, which can yield a sound meaning, should be retained. The sense would be that Cyprian meant to say that the soldiers cast lots to determine who should put on Christ—that is, the garment with which Christ had been clothed. This is certainly an unusual usage, but nevertheless a genuine one.

[Col. 0504D] In almost the same manner the Apostle Paul writes that those who were baptized into Christ “put on Christ”—that is, possessed Christ’s garment, as Jerome interprets it. Cyprian also uses this manner of speaking in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 192.

This error in Cyprian undoubtedly arose because in an ancient copy—similar to one that I have seen—“XPM” was written; and the man who copied the holy Martyr’s works from that codex, being unable to read these characters, ignorantly wrote “it itself,” with reference to the tunic. Others afterward wrote “it,” doubtless thinking that this word fitted the passage better than “it itself.” For it is certain that the ancient scribes who copied the holy Martyr’s works frequently took the liberty of changing Cyprian’s words and substituting other, similar words, as we have shown by numerous examples in these notes. This is the source of the many synonyms that occur in the old books of Cyprian.

#### Undivided

So read eleven of our books and seven English books, [Col. 0505D] certainly better than the others, in which “indivisible” is written. An indivisible thing is one that cannot be divided; an undivided thing is one that has not been divided. It is certain that Christ’s garment could have been divided but was not divided.

Nevertheless, Cyprian later calls the same tunic indivisible, doubtless because of the argument he was treating, in order to show that the concord of the Christian people ought to be indivisible and perpetual. Rufinus on Psalm 21:

> “But in that they did not divide the seamless and better garment, they prefigured the concord of the Church.”

Tertullian at the end of the book *On Patience*:

> “When, therefore, the Spirit of God descends, indivisible patience accompanies him.”

It may, however, be doubted whether the account given by Rupert, Saint Antoninus, and certain others, who write that the seamless tunic was made by the Blessed Virgin Mary, is true. (This tradition is nevertheless supported by a by no means undistinguished little work of Dom Gerberon on the subject, entitled *History of the Seamless Robe of Our Lord Jesus Christ, Which Is Venerated in the Church of the Benedictine Monastery of Argenteuil*, 1676, duodecimo. **EDS.**)]

### VII

This mystery of unity, this bond of inseparably coherent concord, is shown when in the Gospel the tunic of the Lord Jesus Christ is neither divided at all nor torn. Instead, as they cast lots concerning Christ’s garment to determine who should put on Christ [Note: [Col. 0503B] “Who should rather put it on.” Thus the old editions and many codices. Baluze [Col. 0504B] omitted “rather.” The Leipzig editor says that it should indeed be retained, since it most clearly expresses the point upon which the whole force of this argument rests.], the garment is received intact, and the tunic is possessed uncorrupted and undivided.

Divine Scripture speaks and says:

> “But concerning the tunic, since it was not sewn together from the upper part but had been woven throughout, they said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, to determine whose it shall be’” (John 19:23–24).

That tunic [Note: [Col. 0505C] “That man,” Lam. Ebor. NC. Pem. Bod. 1, 2, 3. Paris. Voss. 3. Thu. Foss. Spir.] bore a unity coming from above—that is, coming from heaven and from the Father—which could not be torn at all by the person receiving and possessing it, but inseparably retained its entire and solid [Note: [Col. 0505C] “Its solidity once and for all,” Paris. “Once and solid,” Oxon.] strength.

One who tears and divides the Church of Christ cannot possess Christ’s garment.

By contrast, when Solomon died and his kingdom and people were divided, the prophet Ahijah met King Jeroboam in the open country, tore his garment into twelve pieces, and said:

> “Take ten pieces for yourself, because the Lord says this: ‘Behold, I tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand, and [Col. 0505B] I will give you ten scepters; and two scepters shall remain to him because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen, that I might place my name there’” (3 Kings 11:31–32, 36).

When the twelve tribes of Israel were divided, the prophet Ahijah tore his garment. But because Christ’s people cannot be divided, his tunic, woven throughout and coherent, was not divided by those who possessed it. Indivisible, joined, and connected [Note: [Col. 0505C] “An indivisible bond, connected,” Voss. 3. Innom.], it shows the coherent concord of our people, we who have put on Christ. By the mystery and sign of his garment [Note: [Col. 0505C] “Declared by your garments,” Foss. Spir.], he manifested the unity of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0506D]

### VIII.—And There Shall Be One

Almost all the old books have “and they shall be.”

#### Schisms

Three old books have “dissensions.” Morel likewise notes that he read it thus in an old book.

#### Your Father’s Whole Household

The Bec codex reads: “You shall gather your whole family.”

#### The Holy Thing of the Lord

That is, the Eucharist, as we said above, p. 541.]

### VIII

Who, then, is so criminal and faithless, who is so deranged by the frenzy of discord, as either to believe that God’s unity—the Lord’s garment, the Church of Christ—can be torn apart, or to dare to tear it apart?

He himself warns and teaches in his Gospel, [Col. 0505C] saying:

> “And there shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

And does anyone think that in one place there can be either many shepherds or several flocks?

The Apostle Paul likewise, impressing this same unity upon us, begs and exhorts us, saying:

> “I beg you, brothers,” he says, “by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you. [Col. 0506A] But be united in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Cor. 1:10).

And again he says:

> “Bearing with one another in love, earnestly striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the joining of peace” [Note: [Col. 0506C] “In the bond of peace,” Voss. 3.] (Eph. 4:2–3).

Do you think that someone who withdraws from the Church and constructs other seats and separate dwellings for himself can stand and live, when Rahab—in whom the Church was prefigured—was told:

> “You shall gather your father and your mother and your brothers and your father’s whole household to yourself in your house; and everyone who goes outside the door of your house shall himself bear the guilt” (Josh. 2:18–19)?

Likewise, the mystery of the Passover in the law of Exodus contains [Note: [Col. 0506C] “Contains,” Pem. Voss. 2. “Is contained,” Voss. 3.] nothing other than this: that the lamb which is slain as a figure of Christ is to be eaten in one house. God speaks, saying:

> “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not carry any of its flesh outside the house” (Exod. 12:46).

The flesh [Col. 0506B] of Christ and the holy thing of the Lord cannot be cast outside, nor is there any other [Note: [Col. 0506C] “Nor any one other,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] home for believers apart from the one Church.

The Holy Spirit designates and proclaims this house, this dwelling place of unanimity [Note: [Col. 0506C] “Of unity,” Voss. 1.], when he says in the Psalms:

> “God, who causes those of one mind to dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7).

In the house of God, in the Church of Christ, those of one mind dwell; they persevere in concord and simplicity.

[Note: [Col. 0506D]

### IX.—A Simple Creature

Tertullian in the book *On the Soul*:

> “The Spirit in the form of a dove descended upon the man, so that the nature of the Holy Spirit might be manifested through a creature of simplicity and innocence, since the dove even physically lacks gall.”

Rufinus on Psalm 67:

> “The holy Church is rightly called a dove, because she has no gall of bitterness and because she is strong in the virtue of simplicity.”

#### Neither the Doves nor the Sheep

Above, in Letter LVII, p. 95, he said of the devil:

> “By first attacking one person, he had attempted, like a wolf, to separate a sheep from the flock, and, like a hawk, to separate a dove from the company of those in flight.”

John Ruusbroec seems to have been a severe enemy of the bishops of his own time [Col. 0507C] in chapter 135 of his *Commentary on the Tabernacle of the Covenant*, comparing them to a hawk and saying that they rule and govern [Col. 0507D] the Lord’s people not as shepherds, but in the manner of secular men. He adds:

> “And just as the hawk, once its young are strong, compels them to fly out and seize prey, and is fierce and cruel, so perverse prelates compel their young—that is, those who discharge their office—to take spoil wherever they can. For whenever they hope for gains in temporal possessions, they are cunning, harsh, and cruel, although almighty God has forbidden every form of harshness and cruelty to the prelates of the Church no less than he forbade every kind of hawk to the Jews.”

See also Nicholas of Cusa, *On Catholic Concordance*, book III, chapter 29.

#### Bitterness with Sweetness

[p. 552] Cornelius Celsus, book IV, chapter 9:

> “All sweet things are harmful.”

Arnobius, book VII:

> “For bitterness cannot transform itself into sweetness.”

Jerome, in the preface to the Letter to Algasia:

> “Some prefer sweet things; others delight in things somewhat bitter. Sour things revive the stomachs of the latter; insipid things sustain those of the former.”

[Col. 0508C] See our notes on the fifth book of Salvian.]

### IX

For this reason the Holy Spirit also came in the form of a dove: a simple and joyful creature, not bitter with gall, not savage with bites, not violent in tearing with its claws [Note: [Col. 0506C] “not joyful with bites, not hoofed,” Thu. Foss. Spir.], [p. 197] loving human dwellings [Note: [Col. 0506C] “is accustomed to human dwellings,” Lam. Ebor. Ben. NC. 1.], knowing the fellowship of a single home; when they breed, rearing their young together; when they travel, clinging to one another in flight; passing their lives in common companionship; acknowledging the concord of peace with the kiss of the beak; and [Col. 0506C] fulfilling in all things the law of unanimity. This is the simplicity that must be recognized in the Church; this is the charity that must be maintained: brotherly love should imitate the doves, and gentleness and mildness should equal that of lambs and sheep. What place have the ferocity of wolves, the madness of dogs, the deadly venom of serpents, and the bloody savagery of beasts in a Christian breast? We should rejoice when such persons are separated from the Church, lest the doves and [Col. 0507A] the sheep of Christ be preyed upon by their savage and poisonous contagion.

Bitterness cannot adhere to and be joined with sweetness, darkness with light, rain with fair weather, conflict with peace, sterility with fruitfulness, drought with springs, or storm with tranquillity. Let no one suppose that the good can depart from the Church. The wind does not carry off the wheat, nor does a storm overturn a tree founded upon a solid root. Empty chaff is tossed about by the tempest; weak trees are overthrown by the onset of the whirlwind. The apostle John execrates and strikes at such persons when he says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us” [Note: [Col. 0507C] “They would have remained with us,” Thu. Foss.] (1 John 2:19).

> **Note [Col. 0508D]**
>
> **X—Without divine authorization.** As Novatian did at Rome against Cornelius. See what we note concerning Lucian at Epistle XVI, p. 403.
>
> **Discourse (*tractatus*).** The earlier editions read *tractus*. Rembolt published *tactus*. This reading appealed more to Erasmus, Manutius, Pamelius, and Rigaltius, but not to Morellius, who printed *tractatus*. That is the true reading, confirmed by twenty-six of our manuscripts and ten English manuscripts, as well as by the Venetian edition of 1547. Although Rigaltius did not place this reading in the text, he nevertheless says in his observations that it unquestionably ought to be written so. The English edition followed this judgment.

### X

From this source heresies have frequently arisen and continue to arise: a perverse mind does not possess peace, and discordant faithlessness does not preserve unity [Note: [Col. 0507C] “a perverse mind does not preserve unity,” Ar.]. The Lord, however, [Col. 0507B] permits and allows these things to happen, while the free choice of each remains intact, so that, while the test of truth examines our hearts and minds, the unimpaired faith of those who have been approved may shine forth in manifest light. Through the Apostle the Holy Spirit warns us beforehand and says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19). Thus the faithful are tested; thus the faithless are exposed. Thus, even here before the day of judgment, the souls of the righteous and the unrighteous are already divided, and the chaff is separated from the grain [Note: [Col. 0507C] “from the wheat,” Voss. 3.].

These are the persons who, on their own initiative and among reckless bands of newcomers [Note: [Col. 0507C] “assemblies,” Voss. 3.], set themselves up as leaders without divine authorization; who appoint themselves as prelates without any law of ordination; who assume the name of bishop for themselves although no one has granted them the episcopate. The Holy Spirit identifies them in the Psalms as those who sit in the seat of pestilence (Ps. 1:1): pests and plagues of the faith, deceiving with a serpent’s [Col. 0507C] mouth, craftsmen in the corruption of truth, vomiting deadly poisons from pestilential tongues. Their speech spreads like a cancer (2 Tim. 2:17), and their discourse pours mortal venom into the breasts and hearts of individuals.

### XI

The Lord cries out against persons of this kind; from them he restrains and recalls his wandering people, saying:

> “Do not [Col. 0508A] listen to the words of the false prophets, because the visions of their own hearts deceive them. They speak, but not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who reject the word of God, ‘Peace shall be yours’; and to all who walk according to their own wills, ‘No evils shall come upon anyone who walks in the error of his own heart.’ I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. If they had stood in my counsel and had heard my words, and if they had taught my people, I would have turned them from their evil thoughts” (Jer. 23:16–17, 21–22).

The Lord again identifies and marks out these same persons when he says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (ibid. 2:13). Although there cannot be any baptism besides the one, they suppose that they themselves are able to baptize. Having abandoned the fountain of life, they promise the grace of life-giving and saving water. People are not washed there [Note: [Col. 0508C] “by them,” Oxon.], [Col. 0508B] but are instead defiled; sins are not cleansed but rather accumulated. That birth generates children not for God but for the devil. Born through falsehood, they do not obtain the promises of Truth; begotten from faithlessness, they lose the grace of faith. Those who have shattered the Lord’s peace through the fury of discord cannot attain the reward of peace. [p. 198]

> **Note [Col. 0508D]**
>
> **XII—Corruptors of the Gospel.** Rufinus, explaining against the heretics the words in Psalm 110, “because behold, sinners have burned the ark,” says: that is, they have adapted Holy Scripture to their own errors and opinions. The same author, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 28: “They corrupted the divine Scriptures without any reverence arising from the fear of God.”

### XII

Nor should certain persons deceive themselves through a futile interpretation of the Lord’s words: “Wherever two or three have been gathered in my name, I am with them” (Matt. 18:19–20). Corruptors of the Gospel and false interpreters cite the final words and pass over what precedes them, remembering one portion while craftily suppressing another [Note: [Col. 0508C] “partly remembering and partly,” Bod. 1; Voss. 1; Paris.; Thu.]. Just as they themselves have been torn away from the Church, so they tear apart the sense of a single passage. For when the Lord was urging unanimity and peace upon his disciples, he said:

> “I tell you [Col. 0508C] that if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatsoever that you ask, it shall be granted to you by my Father who is in heaven. For wherever two or three have been gathered in my name, I am with them” (ibid.).

He thereby showed that the greatest efficacy is granted not to the multitude but to the unanimity of those who pray. “If two of you,” he says, “agree on earth.” He placed unanimity first; he set the concord of peace before all else; he taught that we must agree faithfully and steadfastly. But how can someone agree with another when he does not agree with the body of the Church itself and with the universal brotherhood? How can two or three be gathered in Christ’s name when it is evident that they are separated from Christ and from his Gospel? For we did not withdraw from them; they withdrew from us. And since heresies and schisms arose afterward, when they established separate conventicles for themselves, they abandoned the head and origin of truth.

The Lord, however, [Col. 0509A] is speaking about his Church, and he is speaking to those who are within the Church: if they are in concord; if, in accordance with his command and admonition, even only two or three pray together with one mind, then, though they are only two or three, they can obtain from God’s majesty what they ask. “Wherever [Col. 0509B] two or three have been gathered in my name, I,” he says, “am with them”—that is, with the simple and peaceable [Note: [Col. 0509C] “peace-making,” Ver.; “appeased,” Voss. 3.], with those who fear God and keep God’s commandments.

He said that he would be with even two or three, just as he was with the three young men in the fiery furnace (Dan. 3); because they remained simple toward God and unanimous among themselves, he revived them with a dew-laden spirit while the flames surrounded them. Likewise, when the two Apostles were confined in prison (Acts 5), because they were simple and unanimous, he himself came to them; he himself broke open the barriers of the prison and again brought them into the public square, so that they might deliver to the multitude the word they faithfully preached.

Therefore, when he lays it down among his commandments and says, “Where two or three have been gathered in my name, I [Note: [Col. 0509C] “I,” he says, “am with them,” Ar. Paris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lam. Lin.] am with them,” he who instituted and made the Church is not separating people from the Church. Rather, rebuking the faithless for their discord and commending peace to the faithful by his own voice, [Col. 0509C] he shows that he is more truly with two or three praying unanimously than with a great many who are divided, and that more can be obtained by the harmonious prayer of a few than by the discordant prayer of many [Note: [Col. 0509C] “the peace of those in concord than the prayer of the many in discord,” Voss. 3.].

> **Note [Col. 0509D]**
>
> **XIII—At peace (*pacatum*).** Three old manuscripts have *placatum* (“appeased”). Three others and the oldest editions add “or peace with God.” But these words are absent from the other editions and from fifteen ancient copies. Pamelius rightly judges that they crept into the text from the margin. I would more readily believe that they were added above the line in ancient manuscripts, as we have often noted above had occurred. The Tours manuscript has: “For he could not have peace with God.” The Foix manuscript: “For he could not have the Lord’s peace.” In the second letter of Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria, one reads: “For he could not have the Lord at peace with him.” Ludovicus Romanus expressed this passage of Cyprian differently in the address he delivered at the Council of Basel. He wrote: “For he who does not have peace with his brother, but rather the discord of jealousy, cannot have God at peace with him.”

### XIII

Therefore, when he gave the rule of prayer, he also added: “And when you stand in prayer, forgive whatever [Col. 0510A] you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25). He calls back from the altar the person who approaches the sacrifice while in dissension, and commands him first to be reconciled with his brother and then, returning in peace, to offer his gift to God (Matt. 5:24). For God did not look with favor upon Cain’s offerings either (Gen. 4:5): one who did not have peace with his brother because of jealous discord could not have God at peace with him. What peace, then, do enemies of their brothers promise themselves? What sacrifices do rivals of the priests believe themselves to celebrate? Or do those who gather outside Christ’s Church suppose that Christ is with them when they have gathered?

> **Note [Col. 0509D]**
>
> **XIV—Such persons, even if.** The most learned John Pearson, bishop of Chester, in chapter 9 of his *Vindication of the Letters of Saint Ignatius*, judges that [Col. 0510D] Saint John Chrysostom had this passage in view when, in his eleventh homily on the Epistle to the Ephesians, he says that a certain holy man had declared that not even the blood of martyrdom could wash away the sin of schism.
>
> **That I may be burned.** So also in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 3. But Jerome, on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Galatians, reports that in the old version *that I may glory* was read instead of *that I may be burned*. Jerome appears to prefer that reading, since shortly afterward he says that the text containing *that I may be burned* is an error that has become established among our people.
>
> **Charity is magnanimous.** So also in the book *On Jealousy and Envy*, p. 259; in the book *On the Benefit of Patience*, p. 252; and in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 3. See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians.
>
> **Will not be able to belong.** Most old manuscripts prefer: “He who violates love will not be able to belong to Christ.” We have retained the reading of the manuscripts that are more numerous.

### XIV

Such persons, even if they are killed while confessing the Name, are not washed clean of this stain even by blood: the inexpiable and grave guilt of discord is not purified even by suffering. [Col. 0510B] One who is not in the Church [p. 199] cannot be a martyr; one who abandons her who is destined to reign will not be able to attain the kingdom. Christ gave us peace; he commanded us to be harmonious and unanimous; he ordered the bonds of love and charity to be preserved uncorrupted and inviolate. One who has not maintained brotherly charity cannot present himself as a martyr.

The apostle Paul also teaches and affirms this, saying:

> “Even if I possess faith so that I can move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And even if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and even if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, I gain nothing. Charity is magnanimous; charity is kind; charity does not envy, does not behave perversely, is not puffed up, is not provoked, does not think evil [Note: [Col. 0510C] “does not behave perversely, is not inflamed, does not rejoice over injustice,” Lam. Lin.]; it loves all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. [Col. 0510C] Charity never fails” [Note: [Col. 0510C] Nine English manuscripts have “will fail.”] (1 Cor. 13:2, 5, 7, 11).

“Charity,” he says, “never fails.” For it will always exist in the kingdom; it will endure forever in the unity of a brotherhood that clings together. Discord cannot attain the kingdom of heaven. One who through faithless dissension has violated Christ’s love cannot belong [Col. 0511A] to the rewards of Christ [Note: [Col. 0510C] “Nor the reward of Christ,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1, 2, 3. NC. 1. Paris. Thu.], who said: “This is my commandment, that you love one another just as I have loved you” (John 15:12).

One who does not have charity does not have God. This is the declaration of the blessed apostle John: “God,” he says, “is love; and one who remains in love remains in God [Note: [Col. 0511C] “remains in God. With God,” Pem. Lin. Voss. 1. NC. 2.], and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16). Those who refused to be unanimous in the Church of God cannot remain with God. Though they burn after being handed over to the flames and fires, or lay down their lives after being thrown to the beasts, that will not be a crown of faith but a punishment for faithlessness; not the glorious end of religious virtue but destruction born of despair. Such a person can be killed, but cannot be crowned.

He professes himself a Christian in the same manner as the devil often falsely claims to be Christ, as the Lord himself forewarned when he said: “Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am Christ,’ and they will deceive many” (Mark 13:6). Just as the devil is not Christ, although [Col. 0511B] he deceives in the Name, so neither can one be regarded as a Christian who does not remain in the truth of Christ’s Gospel and faith.

> **Note [Col. 0511D]**
>
> **To perform great works of power.** See our notes on Agobard’s book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*.

### XV

To prophesy, cast out demons [Note: [Col. 0511C] “expel,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 2.], and perform great works of power on earth is certainly a sublime and admirable thing. Yet no one found to possess all these things attains the heavenly kingdom unless he proceeds in observance of the upright and righteous path. The Lord declares and says:

> “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons in your name, and perform great works of power in your name?’ And then I shall say to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you who practice [Note: [Col. 0511C] “practiced,” NC. 1, 2. Pem. Voss. 2. Thu.] lawlessness’” (Matt. 7:22–23).

Righteousness is necessary if anyone is to be able to merit the favor of God as judge. His commandments and admonitions must be obeyed, so that our merits may receive their reward. [Col. 0511C] When the Lord in his Gospel was directing the path of our hope and faith in a concise summary, he said:

> “The Lord your God is one God”; and: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. This is the first commandment; and the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself [Note: [Col. 0511C] “as your own self,” Pem. Lin. Voss. 3.]. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Mark 12:29–31).

[Col. 0512A] Through his teaching he taught unity and love together; he enclosed all the Prophets and the Law within two commandments. But what unity does one preserve, what love does one maintain or contemplate, if, maddened by the fury of discord, he divides the Church, destroys the faith, disturbs peace, scatters charity, and profanes the sacrament?

> **Note [Col. 0511D]**
>
> **XVI—Most faithful.** So all the old editions, twenty of our manuscripts, and seven English manuscripts. Morellius printed “most beloved.” But I have found that reading in only three ancient manuscripts. Pamelius nevertheless retained it, both because he found it in the margin of the edition called that of Gravius and in the Cambrai manuscript, and also because he says that the word “most faithful” is unknown to Cyprian. This is not true. Indeed, I have observed that in several ancient copies “most faithful” is written in several places where other copies read “most beloved.”
>
> **Disobedient to parents.** The Thuanus manuscript has: “disobedient to parents in what is spoken.” So also the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul and the Chartres manuscript. But the Bec manuscript has: “not listening to parents in what is spoken.” Six of our manuscripts and two English manuscripts prefer *inaudientes* (“not listening”), and some have *obaudientes* (“obedient”). [Col. 0512D] In Tertullian’s book *Exhortation to Chastity*, I read *obaudientia* (“obedience”). See Gronovius, chapter XIV of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*.
>
> **Resist the truth.** The addition called that of Gravius afterward adds: “[p. 553] men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith.” But I have not found those words in any of the old copies I use. They are also absent from some English manuscripts and from the old editions. Pamelius testifies that they are lacking in the manuscripts, with the exception of the Cologne manuscript, and in all the printed editions; he adds that Cyprian could have omitted them. I certainly know that they occur in Paul’s Second Epistle to Timothy. But it is not therefore necessary to place them in Cyprian’s text, since they do not occur in ancient copies of his works. For he does not always transcribe in full the passages that he takes from Paul’s Epistles, and he sometimes adds things that do not occur in them, as was observed above, p. 526.

### XVI

This evil, most faithful brothers, began long ago; but now the destructive calamity of that same evil has increased, and the poisonous ruin arising from heretical perversity and schisms has begun to rise and sprout more abundantly. For so it was fitting that it should happen at the decline of the world, as the Holy Spirit announced and warned us beforehand through the Apostle:

> “In the last days,” he says, “distressing times will be at hand, and people will be self-satisfied, proud, swollen with conceit, greedy, blasphemous, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, impious, without [Col. 0512B] affection, without fidelity [Note: [Col. 0511C] “without mercy,” Voss. 3.], slanderers, incontinent, savage, not loving what is good, traitors, insolent, puffed up with folly [Note: [Col. 0511C] “inflated, proud,” Ar.; “ambitious,” Voss. 1, 3.], loving pleasures more than God, possessing the outward form of religion but denying its power. From among these are those who creep into houses and prey upon weak women burdened with sins, who are led by various desires, always learning and never attaining knowledge of the truth. And just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so too these resist the Truth; but they will not advance [Note: [Col. 0512C] “the Truth; but they will not advance,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. Lin. Thu. Foss. Ben. NC. 1. Voss. 1. Thu.] very far. For their ignorance will be manifest to everyone, just as theirs was” (2 Tim. 3:1–9).

Everything that was foretold is being fulfilled and, as the end of the age now approaches, has come to pass through the testing [Note: [Col. 0512C] “the tests,” Ver. Voss. 3.] alike of people and of times. As the adversary rages more and more, error deceives, folly exalts, envy inflames, [Col. 0512C] greed blinds, impiety corrupts, pride puffs up, discord embitters, and anger hurls headlong. [p. 200]

> **Note [Col. 0513C]**
>
> **XVII—Condemned by himself.** In the Burgundian manuscript the following is added immediately afterward: “Those who separate themselves from the Church of Christ have been condemned by themselves.” And shortly after the words “against the priests of Christ,” the same old manuscript adds: “He who acts against a priest of Christ will not be regarded as being with Christ.” But everyone can see that these are mere glosses that crept into the text from the margin of the book. Moreover, they are found in no manuscript other than the Burgundian, and no edition contains them. From this [Col. 0513D] it may meanwhile be inferred that material found inserted among the works of ancient authors in old manuscripts should not immediately be transferred into the text, and that mature judgment must be employed in dealing with it. See Erasmus’s annotations on chapter 3 of Paul’s Epistle to Titus.
>
> **From his clergy.** The Verona manuscript has: “from his Church and people.” The Lamonianus manuscript: “who separates himself from his clergy and people.”
>
> **And does not know.** This wording is found in all the ancient manuscripts and editions, except that the Burgundian manuscript reads, “He does not know that.” Some, though few, read “not to know.” Manutius published, “and does not deign to know.” Pamelius says that he did so correctly in order to avoid a hyperbaton, while noting that the word “deigns” does not occur in the manuscripts. I certainly have not found it in any of the old copies I use. It is also absent from seven English manuscripts, so there can be no doubt that it ought to be deleted.

### XVII

Nevertheless, let not the excessive and headlong faithlessness [Note: [Col. 0512C] “terrify,” Voss. 1, 3; “the ruin and headlong collapse,” NC. 1, 3.] of many move or disturb us; rather, since the truth of the matter was announced beforehand, let it strengthen [Note: [Col. 0512C] “let the novelty foreknown strengthen our faith,” Ben.; “of the matter foretold,” Paris.; “by the truth of the matter—the event itself,” Vat. 3.] our faith. Just as certain persons began to become such because these things had been foretold, so let the other brothers beware of persons of this kind, because these things too were foretold, as the Lord instructs and says: “But [Col. 0513A] you, beware; behold, I have foretold everything to you” (Mark 13:23).

Avoid such people, I beg you, brothers, and ward off their destructive conversations from your sides and ears as though they were the contagion of death, as it is written: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue” (Sir. 28:28). And again: “The worst conversations corrupt good characters” (1 Cor. 15:33). The Lord teaches and warns that one must withdraw from such persons. “They are blind guides of the blind,” he says. “But when a blind man leads a blind man, they fall together into the pit” (Matt. 15:14).

Anyone who has been separated from the Church must be rejected and avoided. Such a person is perverse and sins, and is condemned by himself (Titus 3:11). Does one who acts against the priests of Christ, who separates himself from the fellowship of Christ’s clergy and people, [Col. 0513B] suppose that he is with Christ? He bears arms against the Church and fights against God’s ordinance. An enemy of the altar, a rebel against Christ’s sacrifice, faithless in place of faithful, sacrilegious in place of religious, a disobedient servant, an impious son, a hostile brother—after despising the bishops and abandoning the priests of God, he dares to establish another altar, to offer another prayer in unlawful words, and to profane the reality of the Lord’s sacrifice by false sacrifices. Nor does he know that anyone who strives against God’s ordinance is punished by divine judgment for his reckless audacity.

> **Note [Col. 0513D]**
>
> **XVIII—Yield.** The Manutian edition has “believe.” [Col. 0514C] That reading could be good. But since it is found in only five ancient manuscripts, while the other reading occurs in the old editions and in twenty-one old manuscripts, we have chosen to follow the English edition, in which “yield” is written.
>
> **Where those are marked.** That is, on the forehead, as was stated a little earlier. Jerome, in the preface to the Book of Job: “I am a Christian, born of Christian parents, and I bear the banner of the Cross on my forehead.” See Hospinianus, [Col. 0514D] *On Churches*, book II, chapter 10, p. 164, and our notes on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*.

### XVIII

Thus Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who attempted to claim for themselves the right to sacrifice in opposition to Moses and the priest Aaron, immediately paid the penalty for their undertakings (Num. 16:27). The earth, its joints torn apart, opened into a deep gulf, and the chasm of the receding ground swallowed them while they stood [Col. 0513C] alive. Nor did the wrath of an indignant God strike only those who had been the instigators. Fire went out from the Lord and, in swift vengeance, consumed the other two hundred and fifty participants and companions in the same madness, who had joined together with them [Col. 0514A] in this act of audacity. This plainly warned and demonstrated that whatever the wicked attempt by human will in order to destroy God’s ordinance is done against God.

Thus also King Uzziah, when he carried the censer (2 Chron. 26:19) and violently claimed for himself the sacrifice contrary to God’s law, refused to obey and yield when the priest Azariah resisted him. He was confounded by divine indignation and stained on the forehead with the variegation of leprosy (2 Kings 5), being marked, because the Lord had been offended, on that part [p. 201] of the body where those who merit the Lord’s favor are marked. And the sons of Aaron, who placed upon the altar strange fire that the Lord had not commanded, were at once extinguished in the Lord’s presence by an avenging punishment.

> **Note [Col. 0514D]**
>
> **XIX—This crime is worse.** The Grenoble manuscript has: “This crime is worse than that which those who sacrificed are seen to have committed after lapsing.” But this is a gloss that crept into the text from the margin of the book. The author of the second letter of Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria, in order to adapt these words to his purpose, wrote: “The crime of schism is worse.”
>
> **In his sin.** The manuscript of Flori has “in his breast.” Here *peccatore* (“sinner”) has been printed through a printer’s error. It must be emended.
>
> **Afterward.** So all the old manuscripts. The old editions, including Erasmus’s, have *primitionem*. I note this because it is exceedingly surprising that this man—obviously most expert in the Latin language, who could not have been ignorant that this word is not Latin and means nothing, and who knew, moreover, that *postmodum* was read elsewhere—should, I say, have retained the corrupt reading in the text and placed the good reading in the margin. [Col. 0515D] The edition called that of Gravius prefers the correct reading. The other editions took it from there.

### XIX

They plainly imitate and follow these persons who, [Col. 0514B] after despising God’s tradition, seek foreign doctrines and introduce teachings of human invention. The Lord rebukes and reproves them in his Gospel, saying: “You reject God’s commandment in order to establish your own tradition” (Mark 7:9).

This crime is worse than that which the lapsed are seen to have committed [Note: [Col. 0513C] “those who sacrificed,” Pem. Voss. 2.]; yet, established in repentance for their crime, they beseech God with full acts of satisfaction. Here the Church is sought and entreated; there the Church is opposed. Here necessity may have existed; there the will is held fast in wickedness. Here the person who lapsed harmed only himself; there one who attempted to create a heresy or schism deceived many by drawing them with him. Here there is the loss of a single soul; there the danger of many. Certainly the former both understands that he has sinned and laments and mourns; the latter, swollen in his own breast and [Col. 0514C] taking pleasure in his very offenses, separates children from their mother, entices sheep away from their shepherd, and disturbs God’s sacraments. And while the lapsed person sinned once, the other sins every day.

Finally, the lapsed person, if he afterward attains martyrdom, can receive [Col. 0515A] the promises of the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0515C] “the kingdom of heaven,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. Ben.]; the other, if he is killed outside the Church, cannot attain the Church’s rewards.

> **Note [Col. 0515D]**
>
> **XX—The Lord’s grace.** After these words Manutius added: “As it is written: ‘And the Lord raised up Satan against Solomon himself’; and therefore in the Apocalypse the Lord gravely threatens John.” Rigaltius says that these words occur in the old Verona manuscript. Pamelius did not approve of Manutius’s addition, evidently because, as he says, the Lord in that passage speaks not to John but to the angel of Philadelphia. Pamelius therefore retained the addition but deleted what is quoted from the Apocalypse. Rigaltius did likewise. I, however, suppress everything, because I have not found these words in any of our old copies, because they are absent from eleven English manuscripts, and because they are absent from the editions earlier than the Manutian edition.

### XX

Nor should anyone be surprised, most beloved brothers, that even some of the confessors advance to such things [Note: [Col. 0515C] “advance to this dissension,” Bod. 3; “leap forward,” Ver.], and that among them too certain persons commit sins so unspeakable and grave. For confession does not make a person immune from the snares of the devil, nor does it defend one who is still situated in the world with perpetual security against secular temptations, dangers, assaults, and attacks. Otherwise, we would never subsequently see frauds, fornications, and adulteries among confessors—things that we now groan and grieve to see in some of them.

Whoever that confessor may be, he is not greater or better than Solomon, nor dearer to God. Yet for as long as Solomon walked in the Lord’s ways, [Col. 0515B] he retained the grace he had received from the Lord; after he abandoned the Lord’s way, he also lost the Lord’s grace. And therefore it is written [Note: [Col. 0515C] “And therefore,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Paris. [Col. 0516C] Voss. 1, 2; “And therefore in the Apocalypse the Lord gravely threatened John,” Ver. Manut.]: “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Rev. 3:11). The Lord would certainly not threaten that the crown of righteousness could be taken away unless, when righteousness departs, the crown must necessarily depart as well.

> **Note [Col. 0515D]**
>
> **XXI—One ascends.** The manuscript of Saint-Denis of Reims has *extenditur* (“is extended”). [Col. 0516D] Perhaps *escenditur* (“one ascends”) should be read instead, as in Tacitus, *Annals*, book XIII, “to ascend the emperor’s platform,” and afterward in book XV, “to ascend.”
>
> [p. 554]
>
> **A confessor through the Gospel.** Above, Epistle XXX, p. 40: “If they are not found to have attained through preservation of the Gospel that by which martyrs are made.” See our notes there, p. 416.
>
> **Squandered.** The Verona manuscript and sixteen of our manuscripts have this reading. Pamelius first introduced it, following, as he himself says, the edition of Gravius. In that edition, however, I have read *prodiderit* (“betrayed”). This latter reading is found in all editions preceding Pamelius’s and in ten ancient manuscripts. I think it is the better reading. Above, Epistle LXXIV, p. 61: “betrayers of the faith and assailants of the Catholic Church.” I have therefore retained the reading supported by the authority of the greater number of old manuscripts. For the other reading is also good.

### XXI

Confession is the beginning of glory, not yet the merit of the crown; it does not complete one’s praise but inaugurates one’s dignity. And since it is written, “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22), whatever occurs before the end is a step by which one ascends to the summit of salvation, not the terminus at which the highest point has already been attained.

He is a confessor; but after confession the danger is greater, because the adversary has been provoked all the more. [Col. 0515C] He is a confessor; for this very reason he must stand all the more firmly with the Lord’s Gospel, since through the Gospel he has attained glory from the Lord. For the Lord says: “From one to whom much is given, much is required; and from one to whom greater dignity is assigned, greater service is demanded” [Note: [Col. 0516C] “the duty of service,” Bod. 3.] (Luke 12:48).

Let no one perish through a confessor’s example; let no one learn injustice, insolence, or faithlessness from a confessor’s conduct. He is a confessor: let him be humble and quiet; let him be modest and disciplined [Col. 0516A] in his conduct, so that one who is called a confessor of Christ may imitate the Christ whom he confesses. For since Christ says, “He who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 18:14), and since he himself was exalted by the Father because he—the Word and Power and Wisdom of God the Father—humbled himself on earth, how can one love self-exaltation when Christ both commanded us humility by his law and himself received from the Father the most exalted name as the reward of humility?

He is a confessor of Christ—but only if the majesty and dignity of Christ are not afterward blasphemed through him. Let the tongue that has confessed Christ not speak curses; let it not be turbulent; let it not be heard clamoring with insults and quarrels; after words of praise [Note: [Col. 0516C] “words of praise and confession,” Ver.], let it not hurl serpent’s venom against the brothers and the priests of God.

But if he afterward becomes blameworthy and detestable; if he squanders his confession through evil conduct; if he stains his life with shameful foulness; if, finally, by abandoning the Church in which he became a confessor and tearing apart the concord of unity, he exchanges his first faith for subsequent faithlessness, he cannot flatter himself on account of his confession as though he had been chosen for the reward of glory, since for this very reason his deserts of punishment have increased all the more. [p. 202]

## XXII

For the Lord chose Judas also among the Apostles, and yet Judas afterward betrayed the Lord. Nevertheless, the faith and steadfastness of the Apostles did not therefore fall because Judas the traitor defected from their fellowship. So too in this case, the holiness and dignity of the confessors was not immediately diminished because the faith of certain among them was broken. The blessed Apostle Paul says in his Epistle: [Col. 0516C] “For what if some of them fell away from the faith? Did their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means. For God is true, but every man a liar” (Rom. III, 3–4).

The greater and better part of the confessors stands firm in the strength of its faith and in the truth of the Lord’s law and discipline. Those who remember that, by God’s gracious favor, they obtained grace within the Church do not withdraw from the peace of the Church; and by this very fact they obtain still greater praise for their faith: separated from the faithlessness of those with whom they had been joined in the fellowship of confession, [Col. 0517A] they have withdrawn from the contagion of their crime. Illuminated by the true light of the Gospel, radiant with the pure and shining light of the Lord, they are as praiseworthy for preserving the peace of Christ as they were victorious in their conflict with the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0517C] “And by this very fact they obtain greater praise for their faith—indeed, still greater praise—because . . . separated from those with whom they had been joined in the fellowship of confession”: Ver., Paris. “Who were joined in confessions”: Paris.]

[Note: [Col. 0517C] “But they stood firm”: Bod. 3. “But indeed”: Bod. 1, 2.]

## XXIII

I earnestly desire, dearly beloved brothers, and alike advise and urge, that, if it is possible, none of the brothers should perish, and that the mother may joyfully enclose within her bosom the one body of a people living in concord. [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Mother Church”: Voss. 3.] Yet if sound counsel cannot recall to the way of salvation certain leaders of schisms and authors of dissension who persist in blind and obstinate madness, then you others—whether ensnared through simplicity, led astray by error, or deceived by some cunning subtlety of beguiling craft—free yourselves from the snares of deception; [Col. 0517B] release your wandering steps from error; recognize the straight course of the heavenly way.

The voice of the Apostle solemnly warns: “We command you,” he says, “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw from all brothers who walk in a disorderly manner and not according to the tradition they received from us” (II Thess. III, 6). And again he says: “Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Therefore do not become their partners” (Eph. V, 6–7).

[Note: [Col. 0517D] “Distrust”: Ar., Lam.]

One must withdraw from those who do wrong—or rather, flee from them—lest anyone, by joining those who walk wickedly and proceeding along the paths of error and crime, stray from the course of the true journey and himself be held guilty of an equal crime.

There is one God, and one Christ, and one Church of his, and one faith, and one people, joined into the solid unity of one body [Col. 0517C] by the cement of concord.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] “In unity”: Bod. 1, 4.]

Unity cannot be divided, nor can the one body be separated by sundering its structure or be torn into pieces when its inward parts are wrenched apart by laceration. Whatever has departed from its mother cannot live and breathe separately; it loses the substance of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0517D]

### XXIV—“Deceitfully”

The Compiègne codex has “fraudulently,” four others “deceit,” the Burgundian codex “iniquity,” and the Saint-Éloi codex “falsehood.”

### “He gave as an inheritance”

Manutius has, “Christ gave as an inheritance.” But the word “Christ,” which is certainly unnecessary, is not recognized by the old manuscripts or by the old editions.

### “Coheirs”

It must be acknowledged that the greater part of the old manuscripts has simply “heirs,” and that the reading I retain is found in only seven manuscripts and in the oldest editions, among which I include Morel’s. Although the greater part of the old manuscripts has “heirs,” I prefer the other reading, because in chapter [Col. 0518D] VIII of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, from which this passage is taken, it reads: “But if children, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, but coheirs with Christ.” This passage is likewise cited in Epistle LVI, p. 90; Epistle LXXXI, p. 164; the *Epistle to Fortunatus on Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter II; and book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 16.]

## XXIV

The Holy Spirit admonishes us and says: “Who is the man who desires life and loves to see the best of days? Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceitfully. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. XXXIII, 13–15).

A son of peace ought to seek and pursue peace; one who knows and loves the bond of charity ought to restrain his tongue [Col. 0518A] from the evil of dissension. Among his divine commandments [Note: [Col. 0517D] “Finally, among his commandments”: Ver.] and saving teachings, the Lord, when already near his Passion, added these words: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John XIV, 27). This he gave us as an inheritance; he promised all the gifts and rewards of his pledge on the condition that peace be preserved. If we are coheirs with Christ, let us remain in the peace of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0518C] “Let us enter into the peace of Christ”: Cor. “Let us remain”: Ar.]

If we are children of God, we ought to be peacemakers. “Blessed,” he says, “are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V, 9). The children of God ought to be peaceable: gentle in heart, straightforward in speech, harmonious in affection, faithfully bound to one another by the bonds of unanimity.

[Note: [Col. 0518D]

### XXV—“Who had been”

I have restored this reading, which is also found in almost all the old manuscripts and in the editions earlier than that of Pamelius. Pamelius printed “who was,” following a manuscript codex and because he read it that way in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*. But I found that reading only in the Reims codex of Saint-Denis. We shall later see, on p. 556, that Pamelius printed “was” in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*.]

## XXV

This unanimity once existed under the Apostles. In this way the Lord’s new people of believers, keeping his commandments, preserved their charity. Divine Scripture confirms this when it says: “Now the multitude of those who had believed acted with one soul and one mind” (Acts IV, 32).

[Note: [Col. 0518C] “Had one soul and one mind”: Bod. 3.]

And again: “And they were all continuing unanimously [Col. 0518B] in prayer with the women, and with Mary who had been the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers” (Acts I, 14).

[Note: [Col. 0518C] “Continuing unanimously”: Lam., Ebor., Lin.]

And therefore, because they prayed with effectual prayers, they were able confidently to obtain whatever they asked of the Lord’s mercy.

[Note: [Col. 0519B]

### XXVI—“Encumbered and entangled”

Pamelius wrote “us encumbered and entangled.” I did indeed find that reading in three ancient copies. But the remaining manuscripts and the old editions do not recognize the word “us.” [Col. 0520B] Moreover, the sense is complete without that word. I have therefore deleted it.]

## XXVI

Among us, however, unanimity has been so diminished that generosity in works has also been broken.

[Note: [Col. 0518C] “That the generosity of active charity has been broken. Houses”: Ver. “Has been broken”: Voss. 3.]

At that time they sold houses and estates, and, laying up treasures for themselves in heaven, offered the proceeds to the Apostles to be distributed for the needs of the poor. But now we do not give even tithes from our patrimony; and although the Lord commands us to sell, we instead buy and increase our possessions. Thus the vigor [Col. 0518C] of faith has withered among us; thus the strength of believers has grown feeble.

And therefore the Lord, looking ahead to our times, says in his Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth?” (Luke XVIII). We see happening what he foretold. There is no faith in the fear of God, in the law of righteousness, in love, or in works. No one thinks about fear of things to come; [Note: [Col. 0518D] “Thinks about fear—the day”: Bod. 1, 4, printed edition.] no one considers the day of the Lord, the wrath of God, the punishments that will come upon unbelievers, or the eternal torments decreed for the faithless. Our conscience would fear these things if it believed; because it does not believe at all, it does not fear. But if [Col. 0519A] it believed, it would also take heed; if it took heed, it would escape.

Let us rouse ourselves as much as we can, dearly beloved brothers, and, shaking off the sleep of our former inertia, let us keep watch to observe and carry out the Lord’s precepts. Let us be such as he himself commanded us to be when he said: “Let your loins be girded and lamps be burning in your hands; and you yourselves be like men awaiting their master when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks they may open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke XII, 35–37).

We ought to be girded, lest, when the day of departure comes, it find us encumbered and [Col. 0520A] entangled.

[Note: [Col. 0519A] “The day of betrayal”: Pem., printed edition.]

Let our light shine and gleam in good works, so that it may lead us from this night of the world to the light of eternal splendor. Let us always await the Lord’s sudden advent with attentiveness and caution, so that, when he knocks, our faith may be awake to receive from the Lord the reward of vigilance. If these commandments are observed, if these admonitions and precepts are maintained, we cannot be overwhelmed in sleep through the devil’s deception; as watchful servants, we shall reign under Christ’s dominion.

[Note: [Col. 0520A] “We shall reign. Amen”: Voss. 3.]

[Col. 0519]

204

# BOOK ON THE LORD’S PRAYER

[Note: [Col. 0519D]

## 555. ON THE LORD’S PRAYER

Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, speaks thus of this book in chapter 5 of his *Commentary on Matthew*: “As for the mystery of prayer, Cyprian of holy memory will relieve us of the necessity of commenting upon it.”

Saint Augustine, in his *Epistle to Valerianus*: “We also read to them the book of the most blessed martyr Cyprian *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and showed how he taught that everything pertaining to our conduct, by which we live rightly, must be sought from our Father who is in heaven, lest, presuming upon free will, [Col. 0520D] we fall away from divine grace.”

We have a book on the same subject by Tertullian. At the Council of Girona it was decreed that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited every day after matins and vespers. Yet afterward some priests were found—as is stated in canon ten of the Fourth Council of Toledo—who recited the Lord’s Prayer not daily, but only on Sunday. See the *Treatise on Prayer* by Wessel Gansfort of Groningen.]

(C, S)

## SUMMARY

Saint Cyprian’s treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, in which he follows Tertullian’s book *On Prayer*, comprises three parts. In the first, he shows [Col. 0519C] that the Lord’s Prayer is the most excellent of all prayers, supremely spiritual, and supremely efficacious for obtaining what is sought. In the second part, he provides an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer and, following in Tertullian’s footsteps, proceeds through its seven principal divisions. Finally, in the third part he examines the conditions of prayer and teaches that prayer ought to be:

1. persevering and constant, after the example of Christ the Lord;

2. vigilant and poured forth from the whole heart, after the example of the priest who “before the prayer prepares the minds of the brothers by first reciting the preface, saying: ‘Lift up your hearts,’ and the people respond: ‘We have them lifted up to the Lord’”;

3. joined with good works and almsgiving, like the prayers of Tobias and Cornelius;

4. offered at all hours of the day, but especially at the three hours appointed by the Church for prayer—namely the third, sixth, and ninth—and likewise in the morning [Col. 0519D] and evening.

**EDD.**

## I
