The precepts of the Gospel, dearly beloved brothers, are nothing other than divine teachings: foundations for building up hope, [Col. 0520B] supports for strengthening faith, nourishment for sustaining the heart, rudders for directing our journey, and protections for obtaining salvation. While they instruct on earth the teachable minds of believers, they lead them to heavenly kingdoms.

[Note: [Col. 0519D] “Foundations for strengthening faith, nourishment for building up hope, a support for sustaining the heart”: Voss. 3.]

God willed many things to be spoken and heard through the Prophets, his servants; but how much greater are the things the Son speaks—the things that the Word of God, who was present in the Prophets, declares in his own voice! He no longer commands that the way be prepared for one who is coming, but comes himself and opens and reveals the way to us, so that we who formerly wandered in the darkness of death, improvident and blind, might, when enlightened by the light of grace, hold to the way of life with the Lord as our guide and director. [Col. 0520C]

[Note: [Col. 0519D] “Better”: Voss. 2, Pem.]

[Note: [Col. 0520D] “The course of the way, with the Lord as guide”: Lin., NC. 2, Bod. 1, 2, 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0521C]

### II—“More spiritual”

Pamelius noted that “more spiritual” was written in four ancient codices. I likewise [Col. 0521D] found it thus in six. See the notes on the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 525.

### “Which was given by Christ”

Manutius printed “which was truly given by Christ.” But I rejected the word “truly,” which is found neither in the old editions nor in our ancient manuscripts and is useless. For no one can doubt that the Lord’s Prayer was composed by Christ. The English edition also rejected that word.]

## II

Among his other saving admonitions and divine precepts, by which he provides for the salvation of his people, he also personally gave the form of prayer and personally admonished and instructed us what to pray for. He who gave us life also taught us to pray, with that same kindness, of course, by which he deigned to give and bestow all other things. Thus, when we speak before the Father in the petition and prayer [Col. 0520D] taught by the Son, we may be heard more readily.

[Note: [Col. 0520D] “Prayer”: Voss. 3.]

He had already foretold that the hour was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and in truth (John IV, 23), and he fulfilled what he had previously promised: so that we who received the Spirit and truth through his sanctification might also, through the tradition handed down by him, worship truly and spiritually. [Col. 0521A]

[Note: [Col. 0521C] “Satisfaction” in place of “sanctification”: Oxon.]

For what prayer can be more spiritual than the one given to us by Christ, by whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? What petition before the Father can be truer than the one uttered from the mouth of the Son, who is the Truth? Thus, to pray otherwise than he taught is not merely ignorance but also an offense, since he himself declared: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your own tradition” (Mark VII, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0521D]

### III—“To ask God with what belongs to him”

Seneca, *Epistle* 10: “Ask God boldly, since you will ask for nothing belonging to another.”

### “Through the prayer of Christ”

In this passage we have followed the edition of Rigault, which he himself proves to be the true reading by reason and example. It is supported by the authority of several old manuscripts.]

## III

Let us therefore pray, dearly beloved brothers, as God the Teacher taught us.

[Note: [Col. 0521C] “The Lord as Teacher”: Ar. “The Teacher taught”: Bod. 2, 3.]

It is a friendly and intimate prayer to ask God with what belongs to him, and to ascend to his ears through the prayer of Christ. Let the Father recognize the words of his Son when we offer our prayer. Let the one who dwells inwardly in the breast also be present in the voice. And since we have him before the Father as advocate for our sins (I John II, 1), when we sinners petition concerning our offenses, let us utter the words of our Advocate. For since he says that whatever we ask from the Father in his name he will give us (John XVI, 23), how much more effectually shall we obtain what we ask in Christ’s name if we ask it in Christ’s own prayer?

[Note: [Col. 0521D]

### IV—“Finally, by his teaching”

Saint Fulgentius cites this passage in book II *To Thrasamund*, chapter 16.

### “In hidden and secluded places”

The old editions and three old manuscripts present “in hidden and secret or secluded places,” so that the reader might adopt whichever reading he preferred. Accordingly, some had “in hidden and secret places,” while others had “in hidden or secluded places.” [Col. 0522C–D]

### “The thoughts of men”

The word “men” is absent from the oldest edition of this book that I possess, from certain other editions, and from certain ancient codices. It is certainly unnecessary.]

## IV

The speech and petition of those who pray should be disciplined, preserving quietness and modesty. Let us remember that we stand in the sight of God. Both the posture of the body and the manner of the voice must be pleasing to the divine eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0521C] “The measured tone of the voice”: Victor, Voss. 2.]

For just as it is characteristic of the shameless to make a din with shouting, so, conversely, it befits the modest to pray with restrained petitions. Finally, in his teaching the Lord commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and secluded places, in our very chambers. This is more fitting to faith, so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears and sees everyone, and by the fullness of his majesty penetrates even hidden and secret places, as it is written: “I am a God who is near, [Col. 0522A] and not a God far away. If a man should be hidden in secret places, shall I then not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jer. XXIII, 23–24).

[Note: [Col. 0521C] “I fill, says the Lord”: Victor.]

And again: “In every place the eyes of God observe the good and the evil” (Prov. XV, 3).

And when we assemble as one with the brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest, we ought to be mindful of modesty and discipline: we should not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in ill-formed outcries, nor cast toward God with tumultuous loquacity a petition that should be commended to him with restraint, because God hears not the voice but the heart. Nor does he who sees the thoughts of men need to be admonished by shouting, as the Lord confirms when he says: “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?” (Luke V, 22). And elsewhere: “And all the churches shall know that I am the one who searches the kidneys [Col. 0522B] and the heart” (Rev. II, 23).

[Note: [Col. 0522D]

### V—“Her lips were moving”

Horace, *Epistles*, book I, 16: “You move your lips, fearing to be heard.” Persius, *Satire* 5: “You move your lips in silence”; that is, praying well in secret, as Volscus says in interpreting this passage. Judith is likewise commended because she prayed with tears and with the movement of her lips in silence. Augustine, in the book *Fifty Homilies*, Homily XXIII: “She spoke silently; she did not petition with speech, but displayed her devotion.” In another sense, in Petronius, Quartilla “moved her lips obscenely.”

### “Speak in your hearts”

Four old manuscripts, among them the Séguier codex, have: “Speak in your hearts and be pierced with compunction upon your beds.” This agrees with the Vulgate version of Psalm IV.]

## V

Hannah, in the First Book of Kingdoms, bearing a type of the Church, observed and preserved this practice. She prayed to the Lord not with a clamorous petition but silently and modestly, within the very recesses of her breast.

[Note: [Col. 0522C] “With a clamorous voice, nor with a petition”: Ebor.]

She spoke with a hidden prayer but manifest faith. She spoke not with her voice but with her heart, because she knew that God hears in this way; and she effectually obtained what she sought because she asked faithfully. Divine Scripture declares this when it says: “She spoke in her heart, and her lips moved, but her voice was not heard; and God heard her” (I Kings I, 13).

Likewise, we read in the Psalms: “Speak in your hearts and upon your beds, and be pierced through” (Ps. IV, 5). Through Jeremiah also the Holy Spirit suggests and teaches these same things, saying: “But in your understanding God ought to be worshiped by you” (Baruch [Col. 0522C] VI, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0522C] “We ought to worship you”: Paris. “But worship of the Lord ought to be present to you in your understanding”: Ver. “But in the heart”: Vict.]

[Note: [Col. 0523C]

### VI—“He more deserved to be sanctified”

On the authority of the Cambrai codex, Pamelius printed “this publican more deserved to be sanctified.” But the word “publican,” which is exceedingly superfluous and useless in this passage, is found neither in our ancient copies, nor in the English manuscripts, nor, finally, in the old editions. The English editors therefore acted correctly in deleting it. Gronovius, chapter 14 of his *Observations [Col. 0523D] on Ecclesiastical Writers*, had already said that it was an addition arising from interpretation.

### “Who forgives the humble”

Following the same Cambrai codex, Pamelius wrote, “who always forgives the humble.” The old editions and manuscripts do not have the word “always.” Yet the English editors retained it, although eight of their manuscripts do not have it.

### “Was unwilling to raise his eyes to heaven”

The Séguier codex has, “raised his eyes to heaven.” The same reading occurs in another old manuscript. In the Gospel according to Luke: “He was unwilling even to raise his eyes to heaven.” See Erasmus’s annotations there.]

## VI

But one who worships, dearly beloved brothers, should not be ignorant of how the publican prayed in the temple together with the Pharisee. He did not shamelessly raise his eyes to heaven, nor insolently lift up his hands; instead, beating his breast and bearing witness to the sins enclosed within, he implored the aid of divine mercy.

And while the Pharisee was pleased with himself, the publican who prayed in this way more deserved to be sanctified, because he placed his hope of salvation not in confidence [Col. 0523A] in his own innocence—since no one is innocent—but confessed his sins and prayed humbly; and he who forgives the humble heard him as he prayed.

[Note: [Col. 0523C] “Not confidence”: Gronovius, *Monob.* p. 151, notes that this is the genuine reading, which nevertheless no one has adopted.]

The Lord sets this forth in his Gospel and says: “Two men went up into the temple to pray: [Note: [Col. 0523C] “To worship”: all editions before the Oxford edition.] one a Pharisee and one [Note: [Col. 0523C] “And the other”: Ebor., Voss. 3. “And another”: Ver., Lan., NC. 1, MR.] a publican. The Pharisee, [Note: [Col. 0523C] “But the Pharisee”: Lam., Ebor.] when he had taken his stand, prayed thus within himself: [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Prayed, saying”: NC. 1, Lam.] ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men—unjust, extortioners, adulterers—or like this publican. I fast twice on the Sabbath; I give tithes of everything I possess.’

“But the publican stood at a distance and was unwilling even to raise his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’ I tell [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Amen, amen, I tell”: Bod. 1.] you, this man went down to his house justified rather than [Col. 0523B] that Pharisee. For everyone who exalts [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Raises up”: Ar., Lam., Paris, Bod. 2.] himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XVIII, 10–14).

## VII

Learning these things from the divine reading, dearly beloved brothers, and having come to know how we ought to approach prayer, let us also learn, through the Lord’s teaching, what we ought to pray. “Pray thus,” he says:

> **OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN, HALLOWED BE THY NAME; THY KINGDOM COME; THY WILL BE DONE [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Thy will in heaven and”: Bod. 1, 4.] ON EARTH AS IT IS IN HEAVEN. GIVE US THIS DAY OUR DAILY BREAD, AND FORGIVE [Note: [Col. 0523C] “Remit”: Pem., Ebor., Paris, Lam., Ver.] US OUR DEBTS, AS WE ALSO FORGIVE OUR DEBTORS; AND SUFFER US NOT [Note: [Col. 0524C] “And lead us not”: Ar., Ebor., Pem., Lin., Voss. 2, Bod. 3, 4. “And do not suffer us to be led”: Ver.] TO BE LED INTO TEMPTATION, BUT DELIVER US FROM EVIL. AMEN.**  
> (Matt. VI, 9–13)

[Note: [Col. 0523D]

### VIII—“Teacher of unity”

The Foix codex has, “lover and teacher of unity.”

### “Individually” (*singillatim*)

Thus seventeen old manuscripts. But the ancient editions, including those of Manutius and Morel, and eleven old copies present *singulatim*. Likewise, in our new edition of the Councils, p. 1097, [Col. 0524C] we noted that the old codices of the Council of Chalcedon have *singillatim* where the editions have *singulatim*.

### “For himself alone”

The Tours codex has, “not for himself alone.” This reading seems to be confirmed by one of my old manuscripts, in which it is written: “Lest anyone, when he prays, pray only for himself.”

### “Christ had taught”

Following the Cambrai codex, Pamelius printed, “Christ, who was seen in the flesh, had taught.” Rigault and the English editors followed the edition of Pamelius. But because neither the old manuscripts nor the old editions contain this exceedingly superfluous addition, I have deleted it. [Col. 0524D]

### “Ascent” (*ascensum*)

Two old editions and three manuscript books have *ascensam*, and two have *ascensionem*. I would prefer *ascensam* if almost all the old manuscripts did not oppose it. For Tertullian and Cyprian customarily write *remissam* for *remissionem*. See Du Cange’s Latin Glossary.

### “Who had been”

Thus all the old editions and all the ancient copies. Pamelius, following the single Cambrai codex, printed “who was.” See the notes on the final part of the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 554. I do not see why this needed to be changed, since both readings have the same meaning.]

## VIII

Before all else, the teacher of peace and master of unity did not wish prayer to be offered individually and privately, so that one who prays should pray only for himself. For we do not say, “My Father, who art in heaven,” or “Give me my bread today”; nor does each person ask that his own debt alone be forgiven, or petition solely for himself that he not be led into temptation and that he be delivered from evil. [Col. 0524A]

Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we pray not for one person but for the whole people, because the whole people are one. The God of peace and teacher of concord, who taught unity, wished one person to pray for all just as he himself bore all in one.

The three young men enclosed in the fiery furnace observed this law of prayer: they were harmonious in their petition and concordant in the agreement of their spirits. The reliability of divine Scripture declares this; and by teaching us how such men prayed, it gives an example we ought to imitate in our prayers, so that [Col. 0524B] we may be such as they were:

[Note: [Col. 0524C] “It gives such an example”: Voss. 3.]

“Then those three,” it says, “as though from one mouth, sang a hymn and blessed the Lord” (Dan. III, 51). They spoke as though from one mouth, even though Christ had not yet taught them to pray. And therefore their words in prayer were effectual and efficacious, because a peaceful, straightforward, and spiritual prayer won the Lord’s favor.

We find that the Apostles with the disciples prayed in this way after the Lord’s ascension: “They were,” it says, “all continuing unanimously in prayer with the women, and with Mary who had been the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers” (Acts I, 14). They continued unanimously in prayer, displaying at once both the persistence and the concord of their prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0524C] “By the persistence and concord of their prayer displaying at once that . . .”: Lipsius’s edition, which notes that its reading seems more probable, since it is attested in three editions; cited by J. Walker in Dorville and Burman, *Miscellaneous Observations*, vol. III, tome I, p. 13.]

For God, “who causes those who are unanimous to dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII, 7), admits into the divine and eternal house only those among whom prayer is unanimous.

[Note: [Col. 0524C] “In one house”: Pem., Voss., Bod. 4.]

## IX

What and how great are the mysteries of the Lord’s Prayer, dearly beloved brothers! How many they are and how great, [Col. 0525A] gathered briefly in its words, yet spiritually abundant in power, so that absolutely nothing is omitted that is not embraced in this concise compendium of heavenly teaching within our petitions and prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0525C] “How great, how grand”: Ar., Bod. 2, MR.]

“Pray thus,” he says: **OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN.**

The new man, reborn and restored to his God by his grace, first says “Father,” because he has already begun to be a son. “He came,” it says, “to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave the power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name” (John I, 11–12).

Therefore, one who has believed in his name and become a child of God ought to begin from this point: he should both give thanks and profess that he is a child of God when he names God in heaven as his Father. He should also testify, among the very first words of his new birth, that he has renounced an earthly and carnal father, and has begun to know and possess as Father only the one who is in heaven, as it is written: “Those who say to father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and who did not acknowledge their own children—these have kept your commandments and preserved your covenant” (Deut. XXXIII, 9). [Col. 0525B]

Likewise, the Lord commanded in his Gospel that we should call no one on earth our father, because, namely, we have one Father, who is in heaven (Matt. XXIII, 9). And to the disciple who had mentioned his deceased father, he replied: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII, 22). For the disciple had said that his father was dead, although the Father of believers is living.

[Note: [Col. 0525D]

### X—“I have begotten children”

I found this reading in ten old manuscripts and in the Manutius edition. But in the other editions and in seventeen ancient copies it reads, “I have begotten.”

### “Woe, sinful nation”

I have followed the English edition because I saw that it was confirmed by the authority of the old editions and fourteen old manuscripts. For Tertullian also cites this passage in precisely this manner in his book *Against the Jews*, as Pamelius too noted. I found the other reading—“Woe to the sinful nation, a people full of sins”—in thirteen ancient copies. One of my manuscripts has, “a people heavy with iniquity.” It is also written in this way in chapter I of Isaiah in the Vulgate edition. Arnobius, book I, observes that the pagans reproached us because our writings were filled with barbarisms and solecisms and defiled by the deformity of errors. See book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 3, p. 276.

### “Wicked seed”

The Septuagint, as Jerome says, translated this “most wicked seed.” Three of our old manuscripts also have it in this form. [Col. 0526D]]

## X

Nor is this alone what we must observe and understand, dearly beloved brothers—that we call him “Father” who is in heaven—but we also join the word “our” and say, **OUR FATHER**: that is, the Father of those who believe, of those who, sanctified through him and restored by birth from spiritual grace, have begun to be children of God. [Col. 0525C]

This expression also censures and strikes the Jews, who not only faithlessly rejected Christ—announced to them through the Prophets and sent first to them—but also cruelly killed him. They can no longer call God their Father, since the Lord confounds and rebukes them, saying: “You were born of the devil as your father, and you wish to fulfill [Col. 0526A] the desires of your father. For he was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him” (John VIII, 44).

And through Isaiah the prophet God cries out indignantly: “I begot children and exalted them, but they despised me. The ox recognized its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me. Woe! Sinful nation, a people full of sins, wicked seed, criminal children! You have abandoned the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to indignation” (Isa. I, 2–4).

To their reproach, when Christians pray we say **OUR FATHER**, because he has begun to be ours and has ceased to be the Father of the Jews, who abandoned him. Nor can a sinful people be his child; rather, the name of children is assigned to those to whom forgiveness of sins is given, and eternity is promised to them, as the Lord himself says: [Col. 0526B] “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. But a slave does not remain in the house forever; a son, however, remains forever” (John VIII, 34–35).

[Note: [Col. 0525C] “Forgivenesses of sins are given”: Bod. 1, 4. “Forgiveness”: Vict.]

[Note: [Col. 0526D]

### XI—“Glorify”

The Münster codex has “glorify or magnify.” This accounts for the fact that some old manuscripts have “glorify,” and others “magnify.” See the notes on the book *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 524.]

## XI

How great is the Lord’s indulgence, how abundant his gracious favor and goodness toward us, that he has willed us to celebrate prayer in God’s sight in such a way that we call God our Father, and that, just as Christ is the Son of God, so we too call ourselves children of God!

[Note: [Col. 0526C] “Call ourselves children”: printed editions before the Oxford edition.]

None of us would dare to approach this name in prayer unless he himself had permitted us to pray in this way. Therefore we ought to remember and know, dearly beloved brothers, that when we call God our Father, we must act as children of God, so that, just as we are pleased to have God as Father, he too may be pleased with us.

Let us conduct ourselves as temples of God, so that it may be evident that God dwells within us. Let our conduct not be unworthy of the Spirit; rather, since we have begun to be heavenly and spiritual, let us think and perform nothing except what is spiritual and heavenly. For the Lord God himself also said: “Those who magnify me I shall magnify, and he who despises me shall be despised” (I Kings II, 30). [Col. 0526C]

The blessed Apostle likewise wrote in his Epistle: “You are not your own. For you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 19–20).

[Note: [Col. 0526C] “You were bought at a great price”: NC. 1, 4, Lam., Bod. 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0526D]

### XII—“Hallowed be thy name”

Saint Augustine cites this passage in book IV *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 9.

Jerome, in his *Epistle to Sunnia and Fretela*: “‘Hallowed be thy name’: not that what is holy in itself may be sanctified through our prayer, but so that we may ask that what is holy by its own nature may be sanctified in us.”

Rufinus, on Psalm LXXV: “‘Hallowed be thy name.’ This is not requested as though God’s name were not holy, but so that it may be regarded as holy by men—that is, that God may become so known to them that they consider nothing holier which they would more greatly fear to offend.”

See Tertullian in the book *On Prayer*.

### “Those who seek males”

Five old manuscripts have “those who lie with males.” [Col. 0527D] Morel likewise testifies that he read it this way in a very ancient codex, and the English edition reports it in one Bodleian codex. The Vulgate edition of Saint Paul’s Epistles also has it thus.

### “Fraudulent”

The Foix codex has “defrauders or fraudulent,” leaving the reader wholly free to retain whichever reading pleased him more. I prefer the latter because I found it in twenty-five old manuscripts. I rarely found the other.

### “Given life”

Thus all the old manuscripts and all the ancient editions. The Manutius edition has “justified.” Morel retained the old reading. Pamelius and Rigault preferred “justified.” So too did the English editors, although they had the authority of several ancient copies holding the contrary reading. See the Council of Carthage, in Cyprian, p. 332, in the address of Felix of Bagai.]

Source/review notes: The source ends with an empty, unclosed note marker (“[Note: [Col. 0537D]”); the draft faithfully preserves this inherited incompleteness.

XII. After this we say: **HALLOWED BE YOUR NAME.** Not because we desire for God to be sanctified by our prayers [Col. 0527A], but because we ask him that his name may be sanctified in us. For by whom could God be sanctified, since he himself sanctifies? But because he himself said, “Be holy, for I too am holy” (Lev. 11:44 [printed: II, 44]), we ask and pray that we who have been sanctified in Baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be. And for this we entreat daily. For we need daily sanctification, so that we who sin daily may cleanse our offenses away through continual sanctification [Note: [Col. 0527C] “Satisfaction,” Ar.]. The Apostle proclaims what this sanctification is that is bestowed upon us by God’s gracious favor, saying: “Neither fornicators, nor servants of idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who seek intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the fraudulent, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will obtain [Note: [Col. 0527C] “Possess,” Pem. Bod. 4. Voss. 1.] the kingdom of God. And such [Col. 0527B] indeed were you; but you have been washed, but you have been justified, but you have been sanctified” [Note: [Col. 0527C] “He says that we have been sanctified,” Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:9–11). He says that we have been sanctified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. We pray that this sanctification may remain in us. And because our Lord and judge, after healing and giving life to a man, threatens him that he must sin no more, lest something worse befall him, we offer this prayer continually; day and night we ask that the sanctification and life-giving received from God’s grace may be preserved by his protection.

[Note: [Col. 0528D]

557 XIII.—**He himself is the resurrection.** All editions except Morel’s have “he himself is our resurrection.” But the word *our* is absent from all our manuscripts and from eight English ones. It certainly does not appear necessary. Moreover, Ciceronians, and those who wish to write nothing that is not pure Latinity, will refuse to use the word *resurrection*. Christians, however, simple people more concerned with things than words, believed themselves permitted to use the single term that would signify Christ’s return to life. Accordingly, they said *resurrection*. Nothing is more common in the books of the ancient ecclesiastical writers.

**Will be cast out.** The Grenoble manuscript reads “will be thrown out”; the Lamonian manuscript, “will be sent.”]

XIII. Next in the prayer comes: **YOUR KINGDOM COME.** We also ask that God’s kingdom be made present to us, just as we ask that his name be sanctified in us. For when does God not reign? Or when does something begin with him that always existed and never ceases to exist? We ask that our kingdom may come—the kingdom promised to us by God and acquired by Christ’s blood and Passion—so that we who formerly served in this world may afterward reign when Christ holds dominion, just as he himself promises and says: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the 208 foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34). Indeed, dearly beloved brothers [Col. 0528A], Christ himself can also be the kingdom of God: we desire his coming daily and wish that his advent may swiftly be made present to us. For since he himself is our resurrection [Note: [Col. 0527C] “Our” is absent from eight English manuscripts and many printed editions, including the most recent Leipzig edition.], because in him we rise again, so too he himself can be understood as the kingdom of God, because in him we are to reign. We rightly ask for God’s kingdom—that is, the heavenly kingdom—because there is also an earthly kingdom. But one who has already renounced the world is greater than both its honors and its kingdom. Therefore one who dedicates [Note: [Col. 0528C] “Has dedicated,” Lam. Ben. Bod. 2, 3; “may dedicate,” Bod. 1, 4. Paris.] himself to God and Christ desires not earthly but heavenly kingdoms. Yet continual prayer and supplication are needed lest we fall away from the heavenly kingdom, just as the Jews, to whom it had first been promised, fell away, as the Lord reveals and affirms: “Many,” he says, “will come from East and West and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom [Col. 0528B] of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness. There will be weeping [Note: [Col. 0528C] “There will be lamentation,” Bod. 1, 2.] and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:11–12). He shows that the Jews were formerly children of the kingdom, while they also persevered in being children of God. After the paternal name ceased to apply to them, the kingdom ceased as well. Therefore we Christians, who have begun in prayer to call God Father, also pray that God’s kingdom may come to us [Note: [Col. 0528C] “Have begun to know ourselves,” Lem. Pem. Voss. 2, 3. Ben. Bod. 2; “desire,” Ar.].

[Note: [Col. 0528D]

XIV.—**We also add.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in book IV of *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 9.]

XIV. We also add and say: **YOUR WILL BE DONE, AS IN HEAVEN, SO ALSO ON EARTH** [Note: [Col. 0528C] “Your will in heaven,” Paris. Augustine.]; not so that God may do what he wills, but so that we may be able to do what God wills. For who can hinder God from doing what he wills? But because the devil hinders us from having our mind and actions obey God in every respect, we pray and ask that God’s will be done in us. For this to be done in us, we need God’s will—that is, his aid and protection—because no one is strong through his own powers, but is kept safe by God’s indulgence and mercy. Finally, the Lord himself, showing the weakness of the human nature he bore, said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39). And, giving his disciples an example that they should do not their own will but God’s, he added: “Nevertheless, not what I will [Col. 0529A], but what you will” [Note: [Col. 0529C] “What you will,” Voss. 3.] (Matt. 26:39). Elsewhere he says: “I did not descend from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38 [printed: VI, 32]). But if the Son obeyed so as to do his Father’s will, how much more ought a servant to obey so as to do his lord’s will? Thus John too, in his Epistle, exhorts and instructs us to do God’s will, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love [Note: [Col. 0529C] “Affection,” Ebor. Thu. Foss. Lin.] of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the desire of the world [Note: [Col. 0529C] “The desire of the age, and the world,” Thu. Foss.; “passes away,” Paris.]; and the world will pass away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God too remains forever” (1 John 2:15–17). [Col. 0529B] We who wish to remain forever must do the will of God, who is eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

XV.—**Under interrogation.** See the notes on Epistle XXI, p. 408.]

XV. Now the will of God is what Christ both did and taught: humility in conduct, steadfastness in faith, modesty in words, justice in deeds, mercy in works, discipline in morals; not knowing how to inflict injury and being able to endure one inflicted; maintaining peace with the brothers; loving God with one’s whole heart; loving in him the fact that he is Father and fearing the fact that he is God; preferring absolutely nothing to Christ, because he preferred nothing to us; cleaving inseparably to his love; standing bravely and confidently by his cross [Note: [Col. 0529C] “Bravely and faithfully,” Bod. 3, 4; “to stand by it bravely and willingly,” Ver.]; when the contest concerns his name and honor, displaying in speech the constancy by which we confess, under interrogation the confidence by which we enter the contest, and in death the patience [Col. 0529C] by which we are crowned. This is to will to be Christ’s coheir; this is to carry out God’s command; this is to fulfill the will of the 209 Father.

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

XVI.—**Now we ask that it be done.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in the book just praised and in book II of *Against Julian the Pelagian*, chapter 3.

**Earnestly.** This adverb is absent from twenty-one ancient manuscripts and from Florus’s excerpts. In the edition called Gravius’s it is printed in smaller type, to indicate that it was doubtful whether it ought to be retained. I have retained it because it occurs in the Séguier manuscript.]

XVI. Now we ask that God’s will be done in heaven and on earth; both pertain to the consummation of our well-being [Note: [Col. 0529C] “Will,” Pem. Man.] and salvation. For since we possess a body from the earth and a spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven; and in both—that is, both body and spirit—we pray that God’s will may be done. There is a struggle between flesh and spirit, and, as they disagree with one another, a daily conflict, so that we do not do the very things [Col. 0530A] we wish to do, while the spirit seeks heavenly and divine things and the flesh desires earthly and worldly things. And therefore we earnestly ask [Note: [Col. 0529D] Lipsius rejects “earnestly.”] that harmony be established between these two by God’s aid and assistance, so that, while God’s will is carried out both in spirit and in flesh, the soul reborn through him may be preserved. The apostle Paul declares this openly and plainly [Note: [Col. 0530C] “Paul openly,” Paris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Manut.] in his own words: “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these oppose one another, so that you do not do the very things you wish. Now the works [Note: [Col. 0530C] “Deeds,” Lin. NC. 2. Paris. Bod. 1, 3, 4. Manut.] of the flesh are manifest: adulteries, fornications, impurities, obscenities, idolatry, sorcery, murders, enmities, contentions, jealousies, fits of anger, provocations, feuds, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these; I warn you, as I warned you before, that [Col. 0530B] those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the spirit is love [Note: [Col. 0530C] “*Agapē* [ἀγάπη, love] … gentleness, kindness,” Ver. Man.], joy, peace, patience, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5:17–22). And therefore in daily—indeed, continual—prayers we entreat that God’s will concerning us be done both in heaven and on earth, because this is God’s will: that earthly things yield to heavenly things, and spiritual and divine things prevail.

[Note: [Col. 0529D]

XVII.—**It can also be understood in this way.** Saint Augustine likewise cites this passage in his *Letter to Valentinus*.

[Col. 0530D] **For those who persecute us.** That is, for our enemies who have not yet believed in Christ, as Augustine explains in the same book IV of *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 10.

**In those who do not believe.** The negation is absent from almost all our manuscripts, the English manuscripts, and also the ancient editions. It does occur, however, in the edition called Gravius’s and in Morel’s. That the manuscript used by Saint Augustine contained it appears clearly inferable from his *Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 8. (Commonly, “in those who do not believe”; but almost all editions and ancient manuscripts oppose this reading. Nor need Augustine have read it [Col. 0531B] in *Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 84. The meaning of our reading is straightforward: for those who are earthly, wherever God’s will is done in them, become heavenly—that is, believers.—GOLDHORN.)]

XVII. It can also be understood in this way, dearly beloved brothers: since the Lord commands and admonishes us even to love our enemies and to pray also for those who persecute us, we should ask also for those who are still earth [Note: [Col. 0530C] “Are earthly,” Ar. cod. 1, 2. Thu. Foss.; “mind earthly things,” Vict.] and have not yet begun to be heavenly, that God’s will may be done concerning them also—the will that Christ accomplished by preserving and restoring humanity. For since the disciples are no longer called earth by him [Col. 0530C], but “the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13), and the Apostle calls the first man from the clay of the earth but the second from heaven, fittingly we too, who ought to be like God the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), pray and ask, as Christ admonishes, that we offer prayer for the salvation of all: so that, just as in heaven—that is, in us—God’s will has been done through our faith, making us heavenly, so also on earth—that is, in those who do not believe [Note: [Col. 0530D] “In those who believe,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Foss. Vict. [Col. 0530D] Man.]—God’s will may be done, so that those who are still earthly by their first birth [Col. 0531A] may begin to be heavenly, born of water and spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0531B]

XVIII.—**Our daily bread.** See Jerome on chapter II of the *Epistle to Titus*, and Maldonado’s commentary on chapter V of Matthew in its first edition, for the later editions do not agree with it. A remedy for this defect was provided by the man who in 1677 issued a new edition of Maldonado’s treatise *On the Sacraments*. In his preface he printed Maldonado’s words as they occur in the first edition of the *Commentaries on the Gospels*.

**Their Christ.** We have emended this passage on the authority of eighteen of our manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, and ten English manuscripts, in which “touch” is also read. This emendation is confirmed by the words that follow shortly afterward: “It is manifest that those who touch his body live.” (I could not but follow Baluze here. All the others without exception read: “because our Christ, we who touch his body.” Walker, *Miscellaneous Observations*, p. 53, advises restoring this passage from the manuscripts as follows: “just as we say ‘our Father,’ because—call Christ, because he belongs to those of us who touch his body.” I would have preferred the reading commonly received before Baluze, changing only “Christ our,” had not the address “Our Father” been a solemn form among the ancients.—GOLDHORN.)

**Now this bread.** This passage is cited by Saint Augustine [Col. 0531D] in book IV of *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 9; in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 10; and by Adrevaldus in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, in volume XII of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 36. (It is sufficiently clear from this that in Cyprian’s time the faithful still received communion daily; that this practice had been customary from the time of the Apostles is clear from more than one passage in the Acts of the Apostles. That custom persisted at Rome until the age of Saint Jerome, as he himself testifies in the *Letter to Lucinius of Baetica* and the *Apology to Pammachius for the Books Against Jovinian*; at Milan until Saint Ambrose, as may be gathered from the last chapter of books IV and V *On the Sacraments*; and in Africa until Saint Augustine’s age, as is clear from Letter 118. But in the East that custom had long since ceased, as is clear both from the said book V of Ambrose’s *On the Sacraments* and book II of Saint Augustine’s *Sermon on the Mount*, and from Saint Chrysostom’s Homily LXI *To the People of Antioch*, Homily III *On the Epistle to the* [Col. 0532B] *Ephesians*, and Homily XXII *On Hebrews*. There he offers various observations concerning those who communicated at the solemn seasons of Advent and Lent; those who did so only at Easter, or twice or three times a year; and hermits who, from a certain humility, did so once every year or every two years. Therefore Saints Chrysostom and Jerome do not urge daily communion so much as a worthy reception of the Eucharist.—PAMELIUS.)

[Col. 0532C] **Excluded from communion.** The Grenoble manuscript has “abstaining”; the Lamonian, “absent.” And shortly afterward the Grenoble manuscript reads, “he who abstains is separated.” From this it might perhaps be inferred that “those abstaining” ought to be read in Augustine, in the passage just cited and in book II of *The Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 4, instead of “those absent,” as the old editions had. Yet in the new edition of Saint Augustine’s works it is noted that “excluded from communion” is invariably written in the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.

**But the bread which.** See Gronovius, chapter 14 of the *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*.

**And one must pray.** These words are absent from two ancient copies. Although they occur in many others and in the editions, I think them superfluous. Nevertheless, I have not ventured to delete them against the text of so many ancient manuscripts.

**Remain far removed.** Since I found the word “far” in none of our ancient manuscripts except the de Thou manuscript, I was strongly inclined to delete it. The sense is complete without that word. For “far,” the Séguier manuscript has “alien”; one of mine and another ancient manuscript have “remain separated”; eight of our manuscripts and four English ones have “alien.” These variants appear to have been introduced by those who did not know that “remain” alone yields an excellent sense, as I once said on a similar matter in chapter 37 of my preface to the Council of Chalcedon. Rufinus, book VIII, chapter 9: “But each feared this one thing alone: that perhaps, while they hurried and the pressing sun brought the day to its close, he might remain separated from the fellowship of the martyrs.” Saint 558 Ambrose, book I of *Duties*, chapter 41, speaking of Saint Lawrence: “When he saw his bishop Xystus being led to martyrdom, he began to weep—not over the other man’s suffering, but over his own being left behind.” Likewise Pontius the deacon says in the book he wrote on the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “What shall I do here, between joy at his Passion and grief at being left behind?”

**Our bread, that is, Christ.** This passage is cited in canon 10 of the Fourth Council of Toledo.]

XVIII. As the prayer proceeds, we ask and say: **GIVE US TODAY OUR DAILY BREAD.** This can be understood both spiritually and literally, because either understanding, through divine usefulness, advances salvation. For Christ is the bread of life, and this bread does not belong to everyone, but is ours. And just as we say “Our Father,” because he is the Father of those who understand and believe, so too we call it “our bread,” because Christ is the bread of those who touch his body [Note: [Col. 0531B] “Ours (we who touch his body),” Oxford.]. We ask that this bread be given to us daily, lest we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily as the food of salvation, when some more serious offense intervenes and we, being excluded from communion and not communicating, are forbidden the heavenly bread, should be separated from Christ’s body—as he himself [Col. 0531B] proclaims and admonishes [Note: [Col. 0531B] “Says,” Bod. 1, 4. Paris. Vict. Augustine, frequently.]: “I am the bread of life who descended from heaven. If anyone eats of my bread, he will live forever. And the bread [Note: [Col. 0531B] “But the bread,” Lipsius, who adds: “Thus the old editions, with Gronovius approving [Col. 0532B] in *Observations*, p. 151.”] that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the age” [Note: [Col. 0532B] “World,” Voss. 3.] (John 6:51). Therefore, when he says that anyone who eats of his bread lives [Col. 0532A] forever, just as it is manifest that those who touch his body and receive the Eucharist by the right of communion live, so conversely we must fear and pray that, when anyone excluded from communion is separated from Christ’s body, he may not remain far removed from salvation, since Christ himself threatens and says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you” (John 6:53). Therefore we ask that our bread—that is, Christ—be given to us daily, so that we who remain and live in Christ may not withdraw from his sanctification and body.

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

XIX.—**Take thought.** After this, two of our manuscripts and three English ones continued, “what you eat or what you drink.” This reading may appear capable of confirmation from these words of Matthew 6:31: “Do not take thought, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’” These words are quoted on the following page. Seneca, Letter XII: “He is happiest and most secure who awaits tomorrow without anxiety.”

**Sustenance.** The same term occurs below in the book *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 240. The ancient manuscripts and some old editions prefer “livelihood.” Tertullian, in *On Idolatry*: “If the necessity of sustenance is alleged in this way.” And below: “We wrongly reassure ourselves about the necessities of human sustenance.” The same author, in *On Monogamy*: “What if someone pleads poverty, thereby openly professing that his flesh has been put up for sale, marrying for the sake of sustenance, forgetful that one must not take thought for food and clothing?” Cassian, book I, chapter 3, wrote “food and coverings,” condemning translators who rendered “coverings” as “garments.”]

XIX. It can also be understood in this way: we who have renounced the world and cast aside its riches and displays through faith in spiritual grace should ask only for our food and livelihood, since the Lord instructs and says: “Whoever does not [Col. 0532B] renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). But one who has begun to be Christ’s disciple, renouncing everything according to his Master’s word, ought to ask for food for the day and not extend the desires of his petition far [Col. 0533A] into the future, since the Lord himself again prescribes and says: “Do not take thought for tomorrow; for tomorrow itself will take thought for itself. Sufficient [Note: [Col. 0533C] “For sufficient,” Ar. Bod. 2.] for the day is its own trouble” (Matt. 6:34 [printed: VI, 54]). Rightly, therefore, Christ’s disciple asks for his livelihood one day at a time, since he is forbidden to take thought for tomorrow; for it becomes self-contradictory and inconsistent for us to seek to live long in this world when we ask that God’s kingdom come swiftly. Thus also the blessed Apostle admonishes us, forming and strengthening the firmness of our hope and faith: “We brought nothing,” he says, “into this world, and indeed we can take nothing away. Therefore, having sustenance and covering, let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many harmful desires, which plunge a person into perdition and destruction. For greed is the root of all evils; some, in pursuing it, have made shipwreck of the faith and impaled themselves upon many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:7–10).

XX. He teaches that riches are not only to be despised but are also dangerous, and that there lies the root of seductive evils [Note: [Col. 0533C] “The root of all evils,” Pem. Voss. 2. Bod. 4.], which deceive the blindness of the human mind by hidden guile. Therefore God also rebuked the foolish rich man who was thinking about his worldly stores and boasting in the abundance of his overflowing crops, saying: “Fool, this very night your soul is demanded of you. Then whose will the things you have prepared be?” (Luke 12:20). The fool rejoiced in the crops though he was to die that very night; and when life itself was already failing him, he was thinking about an abundance of provisions. By contrast, the Lord teaches that one becomes perfect and complete who, after selling all his possessions and distributing them for the use of the poor [Col. 0533C], lays up treasure for himself in heaven. He says that the one capable of following him and imitating the glory of the Lord’s Passion is the one who, unencumbered and girded for action, is entangled in no snares of property, but, released and free, himself follows his resources, which he has sent on ahead to God (Matt. 19:21). So that each of us may be able to prepare himself for this, let him thus learn to pray and learn from the law of prayer what sort of person he ought to be.

[Note: [Col. 0533D]

XXI.—**To those seeking the kingdom.** In the Grenoble manuscript [Col. 0534D] it reads as follows: “What things? The kingdom of God and his righteousness.”]

XXI. For daily food cannot be lacking [Col. 0534A] to a righteous person, since it is written: “The Lord will not kill the righteous soul by hunger” (Prov. 10:3 [printed: X, 93]). And again: “I was young [Note: [Col. 0533C] “Younger,” Paris. Bod. 1, 2, 3. Thu. Foss.], and I grew old; and I did not see the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread” (Ps. 36:25). Likewise, the Lord promises and says: “Do not take thought, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the nations seek these things. But your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:31–33). He promises that all things will be added to those seeking God’s kingdom and righteousness. For since all things belong to God, nothing will be lacking to one who has God, provided he himself does not fail God. Thus a meal is divinely procured for Daniel when, by the king’s command, he is confined in the lions’ den; and among beasts that hunger yet spare him [Note: [Col. 0534C] “Hunger and roar,” Pem. Voss. 2. Bod. 1, 4.], the man of God is fed (Dan. 14:30). Thus Elijah [Col. 0534B] is nourished in flight; and in the wilderness, with ravens serving him and birds bringing him food, he is sustained amid persecution (3 Kings 17:6). O detestable cruelty of human wickedness! Beasts spare him, birds feed him, and human beings plot against him and rage.

[Note: [Col. 0534D]

XXII.—**How necessarily.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in book IV of *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 9.

**And forgiving.** See Erasmus on this passage of Matthew and on chapter XI of Luke.

**Debts.** These he later calls sins. Yet there are some who think there is a distinction between debts and sins, and between offenses and sins. See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of Luke. See shortly below concerning “debtors.”

**Be pleased with himself as innocent.** After this Pamelius added from the Cambrai manuscript, “since no one is innocent.” But this addition is found neither in the old editions nor in our ancient manuscripts—with the sole exception of the Pithou manuscript—nor in ten English manuscripts. And yet the English retained it in their edition. It is a learned reader’s repetition from the beginning of this book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 205.

**We deceive ourselves.** The Grenoble manuscript reads “we lead ourselves astray.”]

XXII. After this we also entreat for our sins, saying: **AND FORGIVE** [Note: [Col. 0534C] “Remit,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Augustine. Ver.] **US OUR DEBTS, AS WE ALSO FORGIVE OUR DEBTORS.** After the support of food, pardon for wrongdoing is sought, so that one who is fed by God may live in God, and provision may be made not only for the present and temporal life but also for eternal life. That life can be reached if sins are forgiven—sins that the Lord calls debts, as he says in his Gospel: “I forgave you the entire debt because you asked me” (Matt. 18:32). How necessarily, providently, and beneficially we are admonished [Col. 0534C] that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for forgiveness of our sins! Thus, while pardon is sought from God, the mind is reminded of its own conscience. Lest anyone be pleased with himself as if innocent and perish all the more by exalting himself, he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is commanded daily to pray for forgiveness of sins. Thus John too admonishes us in his Epistle, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves [Note: [Col. 0534C] “Lead ourselves astray,” Voss. 1.], and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins [Col. 0535A], the Lord is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:8–9 [printed: I, 8]). In his Epistle he embraced both points: that we ought to pray for forgiveness of sins, and that we obtain pardon when we pray. Therefore he also called the Lord faithful in forgiving sins, because he keeps faith with his promise; for he who taught us to pray for debts and sins promised paternal mercy and the pardon that would follow.

[Note: [Col. 0535C]

XXIII.—**Toward our debtors.** Three ancient manuscripts have “sinners.”

**Is confined.** So read almost all the ancient manuscripts. For what is written in the Moissac and Grenoble manuscripts, “is banished,” certainly arose from a transposition of letters. Those who afterward retained this reading—that is, Manutius and others—thought that the word “is banished” combined better with the accusative than “is confined,” failing to notice that Tertullian and Cyprian frequently [Col. 0535D] wrote “into prison” where we would use “in prison,” as is read in the ancient manuscripts.]

XXIII. He plainly joined and added a law, binding us by a definite condition and pledge: that we should ask for our debts to be forgiven in accordance with our own forgiveness of our debtors, knowing that what we seek for our sins cannot be obtained unless we ourselves have acted in like manner toward our debtors. Therefore he also says elsewhere: “With the measure by which you measure, it will be measured back [Col. 0535B] to you” (Matt. 7:2). And the servant who, after his lord had forgiven him his entire debt, refused himself to forgive his fellow servant (Matt. 18:34), is confined in prison: because he refused to pardon his fellow servant, he lost what had been granted to him by the Lord. Christ presents this even more forcefully in his commands, with the greater severity of his judgment: “When you stand for prayer,” he says, “forgive if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins” (Mark 11:25–26). No excuse remains for you on the day of judgment, since you will be judged according to your own sentence, and you yourself will suffer what you have done. For God commands that those in his house be peaceable, harmonious, and of one mind, and [Col. 0535C] he wills that we who have been reborn should persevere as he made us through the second birth: so that we who have begun to be children of God may remain in God’s peace, and those who have one Spirit may also have one mind and one disposition. Thus God does not receive the sacrifice of one who is at variance, but commands him to turn back from the altar and first be reconciled to his brother [Col. 0536A] (Matt. 5:24), so that God too may be appeased by peaceable prayers. A greater sacrifice to God is our peace and fraternal harmony: a people united from the unity of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0535D]

XXIV.—**Innocently.** For this word the Fuxensis manuscript has *mutones*, that is, wethers. This appears to accord better with the narrative.

**Will judge.** Although I know that all editions except Morel’s, and fourteen ancient copies, have “will be vindicated,” I prefer the reading of Morel’s edition, which is supported by seven ancient copies, because in the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter XIX, and according to Luke, chapter XXII, Christ says that in the regeneration, when the Son of Man comes upon the throne of his majesty, his disciples will judge the twelve tribes of Israel with him. Saint Augustine says in Sermon 351, *On Penitence*, that within this number of judges “are understood all who for the sake of the Gospel abandoned everything they possessed and followed the Lord.” [Col. 0536C] See Cresollius, first decade of the *Sacred Anthology*, chapter 1, section 9. Thus Cyprian, in Epistle LXXXI, p. 164, says to the confessors that they will judge the nations and reign with Christ. Lactantius, chapter 57 of the *Epitome*: “We ought to await God’s judgment, so that we may afterward judge those who have passed judgment upon us.” Thus the common editions read, certainly better than Pfaff’s edition, in which it is written, “those who pass judgment upon us.” Moreover, one of the seven ancient manuscripts [Col. 0536D] we have mentioned, and the Metz manuscript of Saint Arnulf, read “will be judged.” From this others undoubtedly made “will be vindicated,” as in the Chartres manuscript. For it is a recurrent error. Through the same error, in certain ancient manuscripts and editions of Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, it is written that “Aesculapius is judged by a thunderbolt,” whereas Pamelius’s edition correctly reads “is punished,” as we shall say elsewhere. See Henry Valesius’s annotations on Eusebius, book VI, chapter 42. (I have restored the reading which, except for Morel, was common to all before Baluze. He, on the basis of seven editions, printed “will judge,” which is certainly better because it corresponds to the opinions of that age. Compare Epistle VI [Baluze LXXXI], section 2. Yet better readings are not always genuine. Indeed, it is more probable that some corrector substituted Morel’s reading for the common reading than that he substituted the latter for the former. But the matter cannot easily be settled conclusively unless one knows precisely the character of the editions in which each reading occurs.—GOLDHORN.)]

XXIV. For in the sacrifices first offered by Abel and Cain, God regarded not their gifts but their hearts, so that the man who pleased in his heart would please in his offering (Gen. 4:5 [printed: IX, 5]). Abel, peaceable and righteous, by sacrificing to God innocently taught others also that, when they offer a gift at the altar, they should come in this way: with fear of God, with a sincere heart, with the law of justice, and with the peace of concord. Since he was deservedly such a person in the sacrifice of God, he himself afterward became a sacrifice to God, so that, as the first to display martyrdom, he might inaugurate 212 the Lord’s Passion by the glory of his own blood, since he had also possessed the Lord’s justice [Col. 0536B] and peace. Such people, finally, are crowned by the Lord; such people will judge with the Lord on the day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0535C] “Will be vindicated,” Oxford. Lipsius. All printed editions except Morel and Baluze.]. But one who is discordant and at variance and lacks peace with the brothers, as the blessed Apostle and Holy Scripture testify, even if he should be killed for Christ’s name, will not be able to escape the guilt of fraternal dissension, because, as it is written, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; and a murderer neither reaches the kingdom of heaven nor lives with God (1 John 3:15). One who has chosen to be an imitator of Judas rather than of Christ cannot be with Christ. What kind of offense is it that cannot be washed away even by a baptism of blood? What kind of crime is it that cannot be expiated by martyrdom?

XXV. The Lord also necessarily admonishes us to say in prayer: **AND DO NOT SUFFER US TO BE LED INTO** [Col. 0536C] **TEMPTATION.** In this part it is shown that the adversary can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it, so that all our fear, devotion, and observance may be directed toward God, since in our temptations nothing is permitted to the evil one unless power is granted from there. Divine [Col. 0537A] Scripture confirms this when it says: “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to Jerusalem and besieged it, and the Lord gave it into his hand” (4 Kings 24). Power is given to the evil one against us according to our sins, as it is written: “Who gave Jacob over to plunder, and Israel to those who despoil him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned? And they refused to walk in his ways or hear his law, and he brought upon them the wrath of his indignation” (Isa. 42:24–25 [printed: XLII, 24]). And again, when Solomon sinned and withdrew from the Lord’s commandments and ways, it is written: “And the Lord raised up Satan against Solomon himself” (3 Kings 11:14 [printed: XII]).

[Note: [Col. 0537D]

### XXVI.—“Do not touch him.”

After these words the following is added in the Fuxensis manuscript: “And elsewhere he says: ‘Behold, I deliver him to you. Only preserve his life.’” This is taken from chapter 2 of the book of Job, as cited by Tertullian in his book *On Flight in Persecution*.

**“At the time of the Passion.”** Pamelius added “to Pilate” from the Cambrai manuscript. But I did not find this in our manuscripts, and it is clearly absent from the editions preceding that of Pamelius.

**“But when we ask.”** Saint Augustine cites this passage in book IV, chapter 9, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*. [Col. 0538D]

### XXVI

Power against us is given in two ways: either for punishment when we sin, or for glory when we are tested. We see that this was done in Job’s case, when God declared and said: “Behold, I give into your hands everything that he has; but take care not to touch the man himself” (Job 1:12). [Col. 0537B] And the Lord speaks in his Gospel at the time of his Passion: “You would have no power against me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

But when we ask that we may not come into temptation, we are reminded of our weakness and lack of strength by the very manner of our prayer, lest anyone insolently exalt himself, lest anyone proudly and arrogantly claim anything for himself, lest anyone regard the glory of either confession or suffering as his own, since the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: “Watch and pray, lest you come into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark 14:38). Thus, when humble and submissive confession comes first and everything is attributed to God, whatever is asked suppliantly, with fear and honor of God, may be granted by his loving-kindness.

[Col. 0537C]

[Note: [Col. 0538D]

### XXVII.—“The concluding clause follows.”

Tertullian, in his book *On Prayer*: “And the concluding clause follows, explaining what ‘Lead us not into temptation’ means.”

**“But deliver us from evil.”** See Erasmus’s annotations on chapter 11 of Luke.]

### XXVII

After all these things, at the conclusion of the prayer comes a clause that gathers all our petitions and prayers into a concise summary. For at the end we say, **BUT DELIVER US FROM EVIL**, comprehending all the adversities that the enemy contrives against us in this world. From these there can be trustworthy and secure protection if God delivers us, if he grants his help to those who entreat and implore him.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] “From which there cannot be” was corrected by the Oxford editor, without citing any manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0537D] “Unless … he grants” was corrected by the Oxford editor, who likewise cited no manuscript.]

But when we say, **DELIVER US FROM EVIL**, nothing remains that ought still further to be requested, once we have asked for God’s protection against evil. Having obtained this, we stand safe and secure against everything the devil and the world contrive. For what fear of the world can he have whose protector in the world is God?

[Col. 0538A]

### XXVIII

What wonder is it, dearly beloved brothers, if such is the prayer that God taught, since by his instruction he condensed our every prayer into a brief, saving discourse? This had already been foretold through the prophet Isaiah when, filled with the Holy Spirit, he spoke of God’s majesty and loving-kindness [p. 213]: “Completing and shortening the word in righteousness,” he says, “for God will make a shortened word throughout the whole earth” (Isa. 10:22).

For when the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, came to all and, gathering together the learned and the unlearned alike, issued the precepts of salvation to every sex and age, he made a great compendium of his commandments, so that the memory of those learning the heavenly discipline would not be burdened, but might quickly learn what was necessary for simple faith.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] “The Church might learn,” Pem.]

Thus, when he taught what eternal life is, he embraced the mystery [Col. 0538B] of life in a great and divine brevity, saying: “Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent” (John 17:8).

[Note: [Col. 0537D] “You, the only true God,” Paris.]

Likewise, when he selected the first and greatest commandments from the Law and the Prophets, he said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God. And you shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole strength” (Deut. 6:4–5). “This is the first commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12:29–31).

[Note: [Col. 0538D] “Your neighbor,” Oxford. “Your neighbor,” Ver., MR., Lam., NC. 1. “As yourself,” Paris.]

“On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40). And again: “Whatever good things you would have people do to you, do the same to them. For this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 7:12).

### XXIX

The Lord taught us to pray not only by words but also by deeds, himself praying and making supplication frequently, and demonstrating by the testimony of his own example what we ought to do, as it is written: “But he would withdraw into the wilderness and worship” (Luke 5:16). [Col. 0538C]

[Note: [Col. 0538D] “Praying,” Lam., Ebr., Ar., Bod. 2, 3.]

And again: “He went out upon the mountain to pray, and spent the night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). But if he who was without sin prayed, how much more ought sinners to pray? And if he, keeping watch continually throughout the whole night, prayed with unceasing petitions, how much more ought we to keep watch by night in frequent prayer?

[Note: [Col. 0538D]

### XXX.—“Asked.”

The commonly printed editions, Hilary in book X, chapter 38, *On the Trinity*, and Jerome in book II *Against Pelagius* have “sought,” as it is read in chapter [Col. 0539D] 22 of the Gospel according to Luke. The edition called that of Gravius, however, prefers “asked.” Since I found that reading both in twenty-seven of our manuscripts and in nine English manuscripts, as well as in Tertullian’s *On Flight in Persecution*, in Saint Augustine’s *Exposition of Psalm 100*, and in the Morel edition, I had no doubt that it should be restored in this form, especially because it is so written above in Letter VII, page 14.

**“Might harass.”** In the Gospel of Luke and in one Vatican manuscript, as well as in book II of Saint Augustine *Against Pelagius*, the reading is “might sift.” But three of our manuscripts have “might winnow.” It is also noted in the edition by that excellent and most learned man Pierre Coustant—whom we owe an outstanding edition of the works of that saint—that this was the reading in ancient copies of book X of Saint Hilary’s *On the Trinity*. Tertullian in *On Flight in Persecution* and Hilary in the book just cited have “might separate.”]

### XXX

The Lord prayed and made entreaty not for himself—for what would the innocent one pray on his own behalf?—but for our sins, as he himself declares when he says to Peter: “Behold, Satan has asked [Note: [Col. 0538D] “sought,” Oxford and the early printed editions] to harass you [Col. 0539A] [Note: [Col. 0539C] ‘to sift you,’ Voss. 3] as wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32).

Afterward he entreats the Father for everyone, saying: “I pray not for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John 17:20).

Great indeed is the Lord’s kindness and loving mercy for our salvation: not content with redeeming us by his blood, he also prayed further on our behalf. Observe what the desire of the one praying was: that, just as the Father and the Son are one, so we too might remain in that very unity. From this too it may be understood how greatly one sins who rends unity and peace, since it was for this that the Lord also prayed, wishing, of course, that his people should thus be saved and live in peace,

[Note: [Col. 0539C] Thus commonly in the ancient manuscripts. “His people uniquely,” which Walker approved, *Miscellaneous Observations*, p. 54.]

since he knew that discord cannot enter the kingdom [Col. 0539B] of God.

[Note: [Col. 0540D]

### XXXI.—“Lift up your hearts.”

Commodianus, *Instruction* 76: “When the priest of the Lord commands, ‘Hearts upward.’” For the ancients often wrote *susum* for *sursum* (“upward”), as we said at chapter 19 of Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. I now add Vitruvius, in whom, book X, chapter 8, the words “from the bottom upward” are read in Pierre Pithou’s ancient manuscript. See Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers* and his notes on the *Martyrology of Ado*.]

### XXXI

But when we stand for prayer, dearly beloved brothers, we must keep watch and apply ourselves to our petitions with our whole heart. Let every fleshly and worldly thought depart, and at that time let the mind think of nothing except precisely what it is praying. For this reason the priest also, after first delivering the preface before the prayer, prepares the minds of the brothers by saying, “Lift up your hearts,” so that when the people reply, “We lift them to the Lord,” they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing but the Lord.

Let the breast be closed against the adversary and open to God alone, and let it not permit God’s enemy to approach it during the time of prayer. For he frequently creeps in and penetrates, and, subtly deceiving us, draws our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another in our voice, although it is not the sound of the voice but the mind and understanding that ought to pray to the Lord [Col. 0539C] with sincere attention.

What negligence it is to be distracted and carried away

[Note: [Col. 0539D] “distracted and captivated,” Paris, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, MR., Manut.]

by foolish and profane thoughts when you entreat the Lord [p. 214], as though there were something you ought to think about more than the fact that you are speaking with God! How do you ask to be heard by God when you do not hear yourself? Do you want God to be mindful of you when you ask him, though you are not mindful even of yourself?

This is to take no precautions at all against the enemy; this is, when you pray to God, to offend God’s majesty through negligence in prayer; this is to keep watch with the eyes while sleeping in the heart, although a Christian ought to keep watch in the heart even while sleeping with the eyes, just as [Col. 0540A] it is written in the voice of the Church speaking in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song 5:2).

[Note: [Col. 0540C] “I sleep, it says,” Ar., Lam., NC. 1.]

Therefore the Apostle carefully and cautiously admonishes us, saying: “Persevere in prayer, keeping watch in it” (Col. 4:2), teaching and demonstrating, namely, that those whom God sees keeping watch in prayer are able to obtain from God what they request.

### XXXII

Those who pray should not come to God with fruitless and barren petitions. A request is ineffectual when the prayer that entreats God is sterile. For since every tree that does not bear fruit is cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. 7:19), a discourse without fruit likewise cannot win God’s favor, because it is made fruitful by no deed. Therefore divine Scripture instructs us, saying: “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good” (Tob. 12:9). [Col. 0540B]

For he who on the day of judgment will repay a reward for works and almsgiving is also today a kindly hearer of the one who comes to prayer accompanied by works.

[Note: [Col. 0540C] “With almsgiving,” Ar., Lam., NC. 1.]

Thus, in short, the centurion Cornelius, when he prayed, merited being heard. For he gave many alms among the people and prayed to God continually. As he was praying at about the ninth hour, an angel stood beside him, bearing witness to his deed

[Note: [Col. 0540D] “to his deeds,” Ver., Ebor., Pem., Bod. 4]

and saying: “Cornelius, your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God” (Acts 10:4).

[Note: [Col. 0540D]

### XXXIII.—“Righteous angels.”

Most ancient manuscripts have “holy,” as in the book *On Mortality*, page 232, where the same passage is quoted.]

### XXXIII

Prayers quickly ascend to God when the merits of our works raise them up to God. Thus the angel Raphael bore witness to Tobias, who was always praying and always performing good works, saying:

“It is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God. For when you and Sarah prayed, I offered the memorial of your prayer in the sight of the glory [Col. 0540C] of God. And when you buried the dead in simplicity, and because you did not hesitate to rise and leave your meal but went away and buried the dead man, I was sent to test you; and again God sent me to heal you and Sarah your daughter-in-law. For I am Raphael, one of the seven righteous angels who stand and minister before the glory of God” (Tob. 12:11–15).

Through Isaiah also the Lord admonishes and teaches similar things, solemnly declaring:

“Loosen,” he says, “every bond of injustice; undo the constrictions imposed by oppressive contracts. Release the broken into rest, and tear apart every unjust agreement. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy who lack shelter [Col. 0541A] into your house. If you see one naked, clothe him; and do not despise those of your own household and stock. Then your timely light will break forth, and your garments will quickly arise; righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you; and while you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. 58:6–9).

He promises to be present, and says that he hears and protects those who loosen the bonds of injustice from their hearts and give alms to the members of God’s household according to his commandments: because they listen to what God commands to be done, they themselves also merit being heard by God.

The blessed apostle Paul, having been helped by the brothers in a time of oppressive need, said that the good works

[Note: [Col. 0541D] “the works that are done,” Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1]

that are done are sacrifices to God: “I am satisfied,” he says, “having received from Epaphroditus the things sent by you, an odor of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice [Col. 0541B] pleasing to God” (Phil. 4:18). For when someone has mercy on the poor, he lends to God; and one who gives to the least gives to God, spiritually sacrificing to God an odor of sweetness.

[Note: [Col. 0541D]

### XXXIV.—“Peter at the sixth hour.”

See Tertullian at the beginning of his book *On Fasts*, Jerome in his letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*, and Daniel Heinsius’s annotations on Clement of Alexandria, page 77.]

### XXXIV

In the observance of the hours of prayer, we find that Daniel and the three young men—strong in faith and victorious in captivity—observed the third, sixth, and ninth hours [p. 215], evidently by the mystery

[Note: [Col. 0541D] “mystery,” Ver.; “mysteries,” Vat. 2]

of the Trinity, which was to be manifested in the last times. For the first hour, progressing to the third, displays the completed number of the Trinity; likewise, the fourth, proceeding to the sixth, reveals another trinity; and when the ninth is completed from the seventh, the perfect Trinity is numbered by groups of three hours.

The worshipers of God, having long before determined these intervals of hours spiritually, observed them as fixed and lawful times for prayer. [Col. 0541C]

[Note: [Col. 0541D] “They served the Lord,” Lam., Bod. 2, NC. 1; “they served,” Oxford, Lips.]

Later the matter was made manifest: what the righteous had formerly done in praying in this manner had been mysteries. For at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the disciples, fulfilling the grace of the Lord’s promise. Likewise Peter, ascending to the upper roof at the sixth hour, was instructed by both a sign and the voice of God admonishing him to admit everyone to the grace of salvation, although he had previously doubted that the Gentiles should be cleansed. And the Lord, crucified at the sixth hour, washed away our sins with his blood at the ninth; and so that he might redeem us and give us life, he then completed his victory through suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0541D]

### XXXV.—“Observed.”

Some ancient copies have “to be observed”; one of mine has “appointed.”

**“In the morning I will stand before you.”** The Séguier manuscript has: “In the morning I will stand before you and behold you.” Three others: “In the morning I will stand before you, and you will hear me.”

**“Let us walk.”** Three ancient manuscripts have: “Let us exult and rejoice.” [Col. 0542D] Four others and the Morel edition: “Let us exult and be glad.” The Séguier manuscript: “Let us rejoice and feast in it.”

**“Malachi.”** The old editions and thirteen ancient manuscripts have *Malachim*, the Fuxensis *Malachil*, and the Verona manuscript *Malachiel*.]

### XXXV

But for us, dearly beloved brothers, in addition to the hours observed from antiquity, both the times and [Col. 0541D] the mysteries of prayer have now increased. For prayer must also be offered in the morning, [Col. 0542A] so that the Lord’s resurrection may be celebrated by morning prayer. This the Holy Spirit signified long ago in the Psalms, saying: “My King and my God, for to you I will pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you and contemplate you” (Ps. 5:2).

[Note: [Col. 0541D] “I will worship,” Ver.]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] “I shall stand,” Lam., MA., NC. 1, Bod. 2, 3.]

And again the Lord speaks through the prophet: “At dawn they will keep watch for me, saying: ‘Let us go and return to the Lord our God’” (Hos. 6:1).

Likewise, when the sun withdraws and the day ends, prayer must necessarily be offered again. For because Christ is the true sun and the true day, when the sun and day of this world withdraw and we pray and ask that light may come upon us anew, we are praying for the advent of Christ, who will bestow the grace of eternal light.

The Holy Spirit declares in the Psalms that Christ is called the day: “The stone,” he says, “which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
