This was done by the Lord, [Col. 0542B] and it is wonderful in our eyes. This is the day that the Lord has made; let us walk and be glad in it” (Ps. 117:22–23).

[Note: [Col. 0542D] “This thing was done,” Pem., Paris, Vict.]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] “Wonderful,” Ar., Ben.]

Likewise the prophet Malachi

[Note: [Col. 0542D] “Malachiel,” Ver., Vict.]

attests that he is called the sun, saying: “But for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will arise, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. 4:2).

Thus, if in the Holy Scriptures Christ is the true sun and the true day, no hour is excepted at which God ought not to be worshiped frequently and continually by Christians. Accordingly, we who are in Christ—that is, in the true sun and the true day—should persevere in petitions and pray throughout the whole day. And when, according to the law of the world, the returning night succeeds in alternating cycles, there can be no harm from nocturnal darkness to those who pray, because for the children of light it is day even in the nights. For when is one without light who has light in his heart? Or when does one lack sun and day whose sun and day is Christ?

[Col. 0542C]

[Note: [Col. 0542D]

### XXXVI.—“Having abandoned the light.”

Nearly all the ancient manuscripts read thus. Four, however, have: “abandoned by the light.” Three others: “forsaken by the light.”]

### XXXVI

But since we who are in Christ—that is, in the light—are always in the light, let us not cease from prayer even during the nights. Thus Anna the widow, always petitioning and keeping watch without interruption, persevered in meriting God’s favor, as it is written in the Gospel: “She did not depart,” it says, “from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:37).

Let either the Gentiles, who have not yet been enlightened, or the Jews, who, having abandoned the light, have remained in darkness, look to that. But we, dearly beloved brothers, who are always in the Lord’s light, who remember and hold fast to what we began to be once grace was received, should reckon the night as day. Let us believe that we always walk [Col. 0542D] in the light; let us not be hindered by the darkness from which we have escaped. [Col. 0543A]

Let there be no loss of prayer during the hours of night, no sluggish and idle forfeiture of our devotions. Spiritually renewed [p. 216] and reborn through God’s indulgence, let us imitate what we are to become. Since in the kingdom we are to possess day alone, without the intervention of night, [Col. 0544A] let us keep watch by night as though in the light. Since we are to pray always and give thanks to God, let us not cease here also to pray and give thanks.

[Col. 0543]

# BOOK TO DEMETRIANUS

[Note: [Col. 0543C]

## TO DEMETRIANUS

Nothing is easier, nothing more commonplace, than criticizing the studies of others, since it is clear to everyone that human talents are, as Symmachus says in book IV, Letter 22, ready to find fault. We cited an example of this from Augustine at the beginning of our notes [p. 560] on Cyprian.

Lactantius, book IV, chapter 4, criticizes—or rather, to use Jerome’s word, carps at—Cyprian because in this discourse, which was written against an enemy of the Christian religion, he employs testimonies from Holy Scripture. Demetrianus, of course, regarded Scripture as empty, fabricated, and fictitious, and therefore ought instead to have been refuted by arguments and reason—that is, by human testimony, namely that of philosophers and historians—so that he might most effectively be refuted from his own authorities.

Tertullian, on the contrary, says at the beginning of his book *On the Testimony of the Soul*:

“Great diligence and far greater powers of memory are needed for study if anyone wishes to extract, from the most widely accepted literature, testimonies to Christian truth from the philosophers or poets or any other masters of secular wisdom, so that truth’s rivals and persecutors may be convicted from their own proper instrument both of error against themselves and of injustice against us.” [Col. 0543D]

Some have believed that Saint Jerome too held the same opinion as Lactantius, because in his letter to Magnus he reports this judgment of Lactantius concerning Saint Cyprian’s work against Demetrianus. But in my judgment they were gravely mistaken. For Jerome does not report Lactantius’s judgment as though approving it, but to show that Lactantius believed Cyprian would have done better if, in refuting Demetrianus, he had used the testimony of philosophers and poets rather than that of Holy Scripture against a pagan.

Jerome did this so that, by Lactantius’s testimony as well, he might show that ecclesiastical writers could employ testimonies from secular literature in their writings. In his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, he likewise says that the arguments of heretics—and, through them, of the philosophers—can be refuted with a few brief statements from Scripture. A Luciferian in the same Jerome says: “I ask you to set aside the philosophers’ argumentation and speak with me in Christian simplicity.”

Baronius, however, under the year 256, demonstrates with excellent arguments that Lactantius’s criticism is not legitimate. (Cf. Dom Le Nourry’s dissertation on this work of Saint Cyprian, reprinted in full below in this volume.)]

(C)

## ARGUMENT

Demetrianus, proconsul of Africa, contended that the wars, famine, and pestilence by which the world was then being ravaged ought to be blamed upon the Christians, because they did not worship the gods. Cyprian answers him elegantly—after explaining that everything grows worse as the world ages—that the pagans themselves are instead the cause of such great disasters, because they do not worship God and, moreover, assail Christians with unjust persecutions.

Then, after reproaching him for the unprecedented forms of torture with which he tortured Christians more than other accused persons—not to obtain confession, but denial—Cyprian demonstrates the impotence of the gods. First, they cannot defend themselves, so that Demetrianus, who avenges them, should be worshiped by them rather than himself worshiping them. Second, when expelled by Christians from possessed bodies, they confess what they themselves are.

Nor are the fall of kings, losses of wealth, and similar evils, which by divine action accompanied the persecutions of Christians in retribution, therefore not to be regarded as acts of vengeance merely because Christians also shared in them, since all those things are a joy to Christians rather than a punishment.

Accordingly, he exhorts Demetrianus to return to his right mind while there is still time, or at least through fear of judgment and of the perpetually burning fire of Gehenna. Cyprian himself imitates partly Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* and *To Scapula*, and partly Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*. PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0544B]

[Note: [Col. 0544C]

### I.—“To Demetrianus.”

In the Corbie manuscript this book is entitled: “Here begins the Letter of Saint Cyprian to Demetrianus, pagan bishop.” Nicolas Vignier, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, judged that Demetrianus was proconsul of Africa. [Col. 0544D] Who he actually was is correctly discussed in the notes to the English edition, where it is written that he was more probably a judge in the city of Carthage, or one of the counselors who customarily assisted the governor in judicial proceedings.

**“Nor did I do this without the authority of divine teaching.”** After these words Pamelius added “and of the name,” an addition that I found in three ancient manuscripts. It is, however, absent from the ancient editions, from twenty-one of our manuscripts, and from four English manuscripts. In two others of ours the reading is: “without the teaching of divine authority.” This is also the form written in the margin of the edition called that of Gravius. Pamelius prefers this reading too. Rigaltius and the English editors retained Pamelius’s addition in the text. I deleted it because it is superfluous and the greater part of the ancient copies do not have it.

**“Trample.”** [Col. 0545C] I prefer this reading because I found it in the ancient editions and in seventeen manuscripts. The English editors also preferred it. Tertullian and Cyprian frequently use this word. The First Council of Arles, canon 17: “That no bishop trample another bishop.” See Jacques Godefroy’s notes on book I, chapter 10, of Tertullian’s *To the Nations*.

**“And turn and crush you.”** Although these words occur in all the editions and in five ancient copies, I would readily delete them, both because they are absent from fifteen of our manuscripts and four English manuscripts, and because they have no importance for establishing what Cyprian wished to suggest.]

### I

Demetrianus, I had often treated you with contempt as you barked and clamored against God, who is one and true, with sacrilegious mouth and impious words. I considered it more modest and better to disdain the ignorance of a man in error through silence than, by speaking, to provoke the madness of a lunatic.

Nor did I do this without the authority of divine teaching, since it is written: “Say nothing in the ears of a fool, lest, when he hears it, he mock your sensible words” (Prov. 23:9). And again: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. 26:4).

We are also commanded to preserve what is holy within our conscience and not expose it to be trampled by swine and dogs, for the Lord speaks and says: [Col. 0544C] “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast [Col. 0545A] your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and crush you” (Matt. 7:6).

[Note: [Col. 0545B] “under their own feet,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. “Their own.” For so Ar., Lam., Ebor., Voss. 2.]

For when you often came to me with more eagerness to contradict than desire to learn, and, resounding with clamorous cries, preferred impudently to thrust forward your own views rather than patiently hear ours, it seemed foolish to engage with you, since it would be easier and less difficult to beat back with shouts the agitated waves of a stormy sea than to restrain your rage with reasoned discussions.

Certainly it would be fruitless labor and wholly without effect to offer light to the blind, speech to the deaf, or wisdom to a brute, since a brute cannot understand, the blind cannot receive light, and the deaf cannot hear.

[Note: [Col. 0545C]

### II.—“I overcame through patience.”

Thus Jerome in his letter to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem: “We did not wish to give you an opportunity, for we saw the stratagem of your charity. We overcame injury through patience.”

**“That wars arise more frequently.”** Prudentius, book II *Against Symmachus*:

> And there are those who do not hesitate  
> To reproach us with disastrous wars  
> Since we spurned the altars of the temples.  
> [Col. 0545D]

**“Showers and rains.”** The Novella of Theodosius concerning the Jews and Samaritans:

“Shall we any longer endure the alteration of the seasons’ courses through the angered condition of the sky, which, exasperated by the pagans’ perfidy, no longer knows how to preserve nature’s equilibrium? For why has spring renounced its customary grace? Why has summer, barren of harvest, disappointed the toiling farmer’s hope of ears of grain? Why has winter’s unseasonable ferocity, with piercing cold, condemned the fertility of the lands to the injury of sterility, unless it is because nature’s established order departs from its law to avenge impiety?”

**“Long periods of clear weather.”** Matthew 16: “It will be clear, for the sky is red.” Jerome, book II *Against the Pelagians*: “In clear weather we suffer a storm.” Prudentius, [Col. 0546C] book I *Against Symmachus*: “The stormy air produced a clear sky, transparent from the vault of heaven.” The same author in his morning hymn: “May this light bestow serenity.”

**“Modesty.”** Jerome in his letter to Theophilus of Alexandria: “Honor to your courage, honor to your zeal for the faith. You have shown that your silence until now was a matter of prudential restraint, not consent.” The same author, book I *Against Rufinus*: “And I shall show that my silence until now was due to modesty, not a guilty conscience.” Saint Ambrose, in his letter against Symmachus’s *Memorial*: “interpreting forbearance as consent.”

**“I answer.”** The Saint-Arnoul manuscript and the Morel edition have: “We answer.”]

### II

Considering these things, I often kept silent and overcame your impatience through patience, since I could neither teach one who is unteachable, restrain an impious man through religion, nor check a madman through gentleness. [Col. 0545B]

But now, since you say that many complain that wars arise more frequently, that plague and famine rage, and that long periods of clear weather withhold showers and rains—and that this is blamed upon us—it is no longer right to remain silent. Otherwise, our silence may now begin to be attributed not to modesty but to lack of confidence, and while we disdain to refute false accusations, we may appear to acknowledge the charge.

I therefore answer both you, Demetrianus, and the others whom you may perhaps have incited, sowing hatred against us through your slanderous words and, through the propagation of your own root and stock, producing numerous companions for yourself. Yet I believe that these men will admit the reasonableness of our discourse; [Col. 0546A] for one who has been moved toward evil by a deceiving falsehood will be moved much more toward good by compelling truth.

[Note: [Col. 0546C]

### III.—“Because your gods.”

Lactantius, book V, chapter 8: “Learn, therefore, that human beings are evil for this reason: because gods are worshiped.”

**“With the springtime mildness.”** Previously the reading was: “the crops are joyful from their springtime mildness.” We found the true reading in four ancient copies, and Morel writes that he found it in an ancient manuscript. Even the false reading shows that this one is correct. For since it has *verna de temperie*, it is evident that the error arose from the word *vernante*, which the scribe did not understand and rendered as the single word *vernade* in place of *vernante*. Above, Letter XV, page 25: “Springtime mildness succeeded winter.”

**“In the fields.”** Although I know that the commonly received reading, which has “on the farms,” is excellent, I prefer this one because I found it in fifteen of our manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, and in four Bodleian manuscripts. The Verona manuscript also had this reading, as does the Morel edition.

**“Youth.”** This reading can readily be preferred, since it is found in twenty of our manuscripts and six English manuscripts, as well as in all editions earlier than Pamelius’s. Pamelius printed “in its youth,” declaring that he had found it thus in four ancient manuscripts. It was through a lapse of memory, however, that he stated Morel had also printed it thus.]

### III

You said that all these things by which the world is now shaken and oppressed happen because of us and ought to be blamed upon us, because your gods are not worshiped by us. In this matter, since

[Note: [Col. 0545B] “you who are ignorant,” Bod. 1, 3, 4, Thu., Vict.]

you are ignorant of divine knowledge and estranged from the truth, you must know this first of all: the world has already grown old. It does not stand with the powers with which it formerly stood, nor possess the vigor and strength in which [p. 217] it once flourished.

Even if we remained silent and produced no evidence from Holy Scripture and divine proclamation, the world itself now speaks and testifies to its own decline through the proof furnished by all things that are failing. In winter there is not so great an abundance of rain to nourish the seeds; in summer there is not so great a blaze of sun to ripen the crops;

[Note: [Col. 0546B] “the customary blaze,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Lam., Ebor., Thu., Foss.]

the sown fields are not so joyful under the mildness of spring, nor are the autumns so fruitful in the produce of trees. [Col. 0546B]

Fewer slabs of marble are quarried from mountains now excavated and exhausted; depleted mines supply fewer stores of silver and gold, and their impoverished veins shorten and diminish day by day. In the fields the farmer is failing; at sea, the sailor; in the camp, the soldier; in the forum, innocence; in judgment, justice; in friendships, harmony; in the arts, skill; in morals, discipline.

Do you think that a thing grown old can retain as much vitality as it possessed when its youth was still fresh and vigorous? Whatever is now inclining toward its setting and its final end must necessarily diminish. [Col. 0547A]

Thus the sun at its setting casts its rays with a less brilliant and fiery splendor. Thus the moon, as its course now declines, grows thin as its horns wane. The tree that was formerly green and fruitful, once its branches have dried, is afterward disfigured by sterile old age. And the spring that once flowed abundantly from overflowing veins, failing through age, scarcely trickles with a little moisture.

This decree has been laid upon the world; this is God’s law: that everything which has arisen must perish, everything which has grown must age; that strong things must become weak and great things diminish; and that, once they have been weakened and diminished, they must come to an end.

[Note: [Col. 0547C]

### IV.—That individual things diminish

And yet it is certain, and could easily be proved, that the same evils occurred in the Roman Empire before the Christian religion had been established within it. I shall nevertheless use, as proof of this matter, the testimony of Columella alone, who lived near our own times. In the preface to his books *On Agriculture*, he says that the leading men of the Roman state in his age frequently blamed now the barrenness of the fields, now the intemperateness of the weather, which for many years had been harmful to the crops; and that some had even sought to moderate the complaints just mentioned by what seemed a sound argument, because they believed that the soil, exhausted and worn out by the excessive fertility of an earlier age, [Col. 0547D] could no longer furnish mortals with sustenance with its former bounty. Yet in Book II, chapter 1, he says that this arose not from the exhaustion of the earth, as very many believed, but from human idleness.

And these things indeed occurred before the religion of Christ had been established. Once it had been introduced into the commonwealth, and had become burdensome and hateful to the Gentiles, they attributed those calamities to our people, on the ground that their gods were not worshipped by them. In Rufinus, Book IV, chapter 13, there is reported a rescript of Antoninus Pius to the Asians on behalf of the Christians, in which the emperor says:

> As for the earthquakes that have occurred, or are even now occurring, it will not be inappropriate to console your grief with a just admonition, since I have discovered that in events of this kind you turn disasters common to all into grounds for hostility against them.

Later, when idolatry had ceased, the religion of God had been embraced among all nations everywhere, and the entire commonwealth had become Christian, whenever those evils occurred which the Gentiles had formerly been accustomed to attribute to us, then—human nature being prone to reproach [Col. 0548C] and accusation—they were transferred in subsequent ages to other parties. Thus in the age of the emperor Theodosius they were attributed to Jews, Samaritans, and pagans, as is clear from his Third Novella; and in the age of Charlemagne they were attributed to tempest-makers, against whom there survives a book by Agobard, archbishop of Lyons. In later times they were attributed in Denmark to the sins of priests. Pope Gregory VII bears witness to this matter; writing to the king and people of the Danes in Book I, Letter XXI, he says:

> Meanwhile, it seems that we must not pass over, but must emphatically prohibit by apostolic injunction, what has become known to us concerning your nation: namely, that you attribute the intemperateness of the seasons, corruptions of the air, and every kind of bodily affliction [Col. 0548D] to the sins of priests.

**An age begins with old age.** Seneca, Letter XIII:

> What, moreover, is more disgraceful than an old man beginning to live?

Likewise, Letter XXIII:

> Those who are always beginning to live live badly. Some begin to live when it is time to cease.

Likewise, chapter 4 of *On the Shortness of Life*:

> I hear very many saying: “At fifty I shall retire into leisure; my sixtieth year will release me from official duties.” How late it is [p. 562] to begin living at the time when one ought to cease!

Censorinus, chapter XIV, says that the body begins to grow old for the first time in the sixtieth year. And Cicero, in the *Speech for Roscius of Ameria*, says:

> According to ancestral custom, sixty-year-old men were thrown from the bridge into the Tiber.

Tacitus says that Agricola, who died in the fifty-sixth year of his life, was snatched away midway through the span of an unimpaired lifetime. Elsewhere the same author says that fifteen years constitute a large portion of mortal life.

### IV

You blame the Christians because individual things diminish as the world grows old. What if old men, too, were to blame the Christians because they have less strength in old age, because they do not flourish as before in the hearing of their ears, the speed of their feet, [Col. 0547B] the keenness of their eyes, the vigor of their strength, the vital fluid of their inward parts, and the mass of their limbs; and because, although in former times the long life of human beings extended beyond eight hundred and nine hundred years, it can now scarcely reach the number of one hundred?

We see gray hairs on children; hair fails before it has grown. Nor does an age end in old age, but begins with old age. Thus, even at its very beginning, birth hastens toward its end; thus whatever is now born degenerates through the old age of the world itself. No one, therefore, ought to wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

[Note: [Col. 0548D]

### V.—God is not sought at all

In the Séguier manuscript it is written *colitur* (“is worshipped”).

]

### V

As for the fact that wars continue with greater frequency, that barrenness and famine increase our anxiety, that health is broken by raging diseases, and that the human race is devastated by the destructive spread of pestilence, you should know that this too was foretold: [Col. 0547C] that in the last times evils would multiply and [Col. 0548A] adversities would assume various forms, and that, as the day of judgment now approaches, the chastisement of an indignant God would be kindled more and more into scourges against the human race.

For these things do not happen—as your false complaint, ignorant through its lack of knowledge of the truth, boasts and loudly proclaims—because your gods are not worshipped by us, but because God is not worshipped by you. For since he himself is the Lord and ruler of the world, and all things are governed by his judgment and command, and nothing can occur except what he has either done or himself permitted to be done, certainly, whenever those things occur which manifest the wrath of an indignant God [Note: [Col. 0547C] *Kindle*, Ar. Ben.], they do not occur on our account, by whom God is worshipped, but are inflicted because of your offenses and deserts—you by whom God is neither sought at all nor feared, and by whom, after vain superstitions have been abandoned, the true religion is not acknowledged—so that the one God of all may alone be worshipped and entreated by all.

[Col. 0548B]

### VI

Finally, hear him himself speaking, himself instructing and admonishing us alike with his divine voice:

> You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,

he says (Deut. 6:13). And again:

> You shall have no other gods besides me

(Exod. 20:3). And again:

> [p. 218] Do not walk after foreign gods so as to serve them, and do not worship them; and do not incite [Note: [Col. 0547C] *Provoke*, NC. 2.] me by the works of your hands to destroy you

(Jer. 25:6).

Likewise, the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, solemnly attests and announces the wrath of God, saying:

> Thus says the Lord Almighty: Because my house lies deserted, while each of you hastens to his own house, therefore heaven will withhold its dew, and the earth will withhold [Note: [Col. 0548C] *Withdraw*, Ar.] its produce; and I shall bring the sword upon the earth, and upon the grain, and upon the wine, [Col. 0548C] and upon the oil, and upon human beings, and upon livestock, and upon [Col. 0549A] all the labors of their hands

(Hag. 1:9–11).

Likewise, another prophet repeats and says:

> And I shall rain upon one city, and upon another [Note: [Col. 0549C] *One*, Lam. Ebor. Pem. Lin. NC. 1. Woss. 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] I shall not rain. One portion will be rained upon, and the portion upon which I have not rained will wither. And two or three cities will gather into one city for the sake of drinking water, but they will not be satisfied; and you do not turn back to me, says the Lord

(Amos 4:7–8).

[Note: [Col. 0549C]

### VII.—Nor did they wish to receive

The old editions, including the Aldine, and four old manuscripts add: “nor did they wish to believe or to receive discipline.” But all the other old manuscripts have the reading we have printed.

**Through impunity for crimes.** Cicero, in the *Speech for Milo*:

> As for that which is the chief source of audacity, judges, who does not know [Col. 0549D] that the greatest enticement to wrongdoing is the hope of impunity?

See our notes on Lupus of Ferrières, p. 472.

]

### VII

Behold, the Lord is indignant and angry, and threatens you because you do not turn back to him. Yet, amid this obstinacy and contempt of yours, you are surprised or complain if rain rarely descends from above; if the earth is rough and foul beneath a covering of dust; if a barren clod scarcely produces meager and pallid grasses; if beating hail weakens the vine; if an overturning whirlwind strips the olive tree of its branches; if drought brings the spring to a standstill; if a pestilential breeze corrupts the air; and if diseased health consumes the human being [Col. 0549B]—although all these things come because sins provoke them, and God is exasperated still more [Note: [Col. 0549C] *Is exasperated by offenses*, Pem. Voss. 2.] when such great and numerous things accomplish nothing.

For the same God declares in the Holy Scriptures that these things occur either for the correction of the obstinate or for the punishment of the wicked, saying:

> In vain have I struck your children; they did not receive discipline

(Jer. 2:30).

And the prophet, devoted and consecrated to God, responds to these same things and says:

> You struck them, but they felt no pain; you scourged them, but they did not wish to receive [Note: [Col. 0550C] *And they do not receive*, Bod. 3.] discipline

(Jer. 5:3).

Behold, scourges are divinely inflicted, yet there is no fear of God. Behold, blows and whips from above do not cease, yet there is no trembling, no dread [Note: [Col. 0550C] *There is no hesitation*, Voss. 1, 2. Grav.]. What if even this chastisement did not intervene in human affairs? How much greater would human audacity still be, made secure [Col. 0549C] by impunity for crimes?

[Note: [Col. 0549D]

### VIII.—For you serve God

This is the reading of thirteen old manuscripts. Others and the more ancient editions give: “You do not serve God”; the Grenoble manuscript, “You do not serve the Lord.”

**You minister to him.** This is the reading of nineteen old copies. The Morel edition has the same. The more ancient editions and five old copies read: “You do not minister.”

**The constitution of souls is common.** See the discourse of Vettius Praetextatus on slaves in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 11.

**He himself exercises dominion.** Only this is found in the old editions, twenty-two of our manuscripts, and ten English manuscripts. Goulart likewise read it so in the book of the bishop of Acre. Manutius was the first of all to introduce the reading “he himself exercises dominion over a human being.” Pamelius retained it, while nevertheless observing that Manutius alone had the words [Col. 0550C] “over a human being,” and that he himself preferred the reading “against a human being.”

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book VIII, chapter 12:

> At home, indeed, we assume the dispositions of tyrants, and wish to exercise over our slaves not as much authority as is fitting, but as much as is permitted.

Juvenal, Satire VI:

> “Set up a cross for the slave.” For what crime has the slave  
> Deserved [Col. 0550D] punishment? What witness is present? Who laid the charge? Listen!  
> No delay concerning a person’s death is ever too long.  
> “Madwoman! So a slave is a human being?” “Let him have done nothing—so be it.  
> This I will; thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.”

]

### VIII

You complain that now abundant springs, healthful breezes, frequent rain, and fertile soil render you less service, and that the elements do not so fully minister to your advantages and pleasures. For you serve God, [Col. 0550A] through whom all things serve you; you minister to him by whose command the whole creation ministers to you.

You yourself demand service from your slave, and, though yourself a human being, compel another human being to submit and obey you. And although you share the same lot in being born, the one condition of dying, similar bodily material, and a common constitution of souls; although by equal right and under the same law you both come into this world and afterward depart from the world; nevertheless, unless service is rendered to you according to your judgment, unless obedience is given in compliance with your will, you, as an imperious and excessive exactor of servitude, flog, beat, and afflict and torture with hunger, thirst, nakedness, and frequently even with the sword and prison. Yet you do not acknowledge, wretched man, the Lord your God, although you yourself exercise dominion in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 0550D]

### IX.—There remains afterward

Three old manuscripts read: “It is therefore necessary that there remain afterward.” Morel reports that he likewise read this in two ancient manuscripts.

**With the birds.** The old editions and five old copies read: “with the birds and winged creatures.” The Fux manuscript reads: “with the winged creatures.” But these words are absent from all the other old manuscripts, from those seen by Morel, and from Hosea.

**And is angry.** These words stood in the ancient editions. The Aldine edition removed them. The Morel edition restored them. Pamelius again deleted them. I restore them because, although they are absent from many old manuscripts, they are nevertheless found in seventeen. For Cyprian said a little earlier: “Behold, the Lord is indignant and angry.”

]

### IX

Deservedly, therefore, when scourges assail us, God’s whips and blows do not cease. Since they accomplish nothing here, and do not turn individuals back to God even through such terror of calamities, there remains afterward the eternal prison, the unceasing flame, and perpetual punishment. Nor will the groaning of those who plead be heard there, because the terror of the indignant God was not heard here—God who cries out through the prophet and says:

> Hear the word of the Lord, children of Israel, because the Lord has a judgment against the inhabitants of the land, because there is neither mercy, nor truth, nor knowledge of God [Note: [Col. 0550C] “Nor hearing of God,” NC. 2.] upon the land, but cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have spread over the land; [p. 219] they heap blood upon blood. Therefore the land will mourn together with all its inhabitants, with the beasts of the field, with the creeping things of the earth, and with the birds of heaven; and the fish of the sea will perish. Let no one judge; let no one refute

(Hos. 4:1–4).

God says that he is indignant [Col. 0550C] and angry because there is no knowledge of God upon the earth, and God is neither acknowledged nor feared. God reproves and condemns the offenses of falsehood, lust, fraud, cruelty, impiety, and fury, yet no one turns back to innocence. Behold, the things previously foretold in God’s words are occurring, [Col. 0551A] yet no one is admonished by the reality of the present to take thought for the future. Amid the very adversities by which the soul, scarcely able to breathe, is constrained and hemmed in, people still have leisure to be wicked and, in dangers so great, to pass judgment not upon themselves but rather upon another.

You are indignant that God is indignant, as though by living wickedly you merited anything good, as though all these things that occur were not still smaller and lighter than your sins.

[Note: [Col. 0551C]

### X.—Fear

We added this word from one royal manuscript. The Fux manuscript has “place or shame.” Morel says that in one ancient manuscript he read “dread.” Although the Fux manuscript differs from the royal one, it nevertheless indicates that something is missing here. In one old manuscript the reading is “fear or shame.” In the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul there is only “or shame,” without “fear.” So too in the Morel edition. This indicates that something is missing here.

**As punishments.** The edition called Gravius’s and two [Col. 0551D] old manuscripts give “as scourges.” The Verona manuscript likewise had this. A little above it is written: “the chastisement of an indignant God would be kindled more and more into scourges against the human race.”

**Of barrenness and famine.** Prudentius, Book II, *Against Symmachus*:

> Hence, he says, the barren fields bear crops more rarely,  
> And grim famine rages, and throughout the entire world  
> Destitute mortals grow pale, lacking bread.

For Symmachus had said:

> Public famine followed, and a sickly harvest disappointed the hope of all the provinces.

By contrast, when great fertility occurred in the commonwealth under the emperor Maximinus, [p. 563] the Gentiles ascribed it to the benevolence of the gods, who thereby testified that they approved what was being done against the Christians. Hence Maximinus, seeking glory for himself, issued an edict in which, as Rufinus says, he extolled this abundance with considerable boastfulness and arrogance. And immediately the Christians were treated with savage cruelty. But God at once sent the most violent and severe famine and pestilence [Col. 0552C] upon the commonwealth, so that it might be clear that the good things occurring within it were not granted by the gods as a reward for persecutions, but that, on the contrary, the God of the Christians avenged those who suffered unjustly for his name. See Eusebius, Book IX, chapters 7–8.

]

### X

You who judge others, be at some time also your own judge. Look into the hidden places of your conscience—or rather, because there is now no fear or shame in wrongdoing, and sin is committed as though those very sins made one more pleasing, look upon yourself, who appear transparent and naked to everyone.

For you are either swollen with pride, rapacious through greed, savage in anger, prodigal in gambling, drunken [Col. 0551B] through wine, envious through spite, incestuous through lust, or violent through cruelty. And do you wonder that God’s wrath increases as punishment for the human race, when what deserves punishment increases every day?

You complain that an enemy rises up, as though, even if there were no enemy, peace could exist among the togas themselves [Note: [Col. 0551C] “Togas, the garb of peace,” Bod. 1.]. You complain that an enemy rises up, as though, even if external arms and dangers from the barbarians were suppressed, the weapons of domestic assault arising from the false accusations and injuries of powerful citizens did not rage more fiercely and grievously within.

You complain of barrenness and famine, as though drought produced a greater famine than rapacity, as though a fiercer blaze of want did not arise from profiteering on rises in grain prices and the piling up of prices. You complain that heaven is closed against the rains, while granaries upon earth are closed in just this way. You complain that less is now produced, as though what has been produced [Col. 0551C] were supplied to the needy.

You accuse pestilence and plague, although pestilence [Col. 0552A] and plague themselves have either exposed or increased the crimes of individuals: mercy is not shown to the sick, while greed and plunder gape after the dead. The same people are timid when service of compassion is required, but reckless when impious gains are at stake; they flee the funerals of the dying and seek the spoils of the dead. Thus it becomes apparent that the wretched have perhaps been abandoned in their illness for this very purpose—so that they cannot recover while being cared for; for whoever seizes the property of a dying man has willed the sick man to perish.

[Note: [Col. 0552C]

### XI.—No hesitation

Pamelius afterward added from the Cambron manuscript, “there is no dread.” But I deleted it, because I found this addition nowhere except in the Bec manuscript. In this matter I followed the example [Col. 0552D] of Pamelius, who, when he saw “there is no hesitation” written in the edition called Gravius’s in place of what he himself printed, “there is no trembling,” says that he deleted it because the manuscripts do not have it. To be sure, these two words that I deleted are found in that edition, but printed in smaller type, so that it might be understood that there was some doubt as to whether they belonged to Cyprian. The more ancient editions, however, give: “There is no pretense in plundering, there is no hesitation.” In place of this, the Pithou manuscript and certain others, as well as the Erasmus and Aldine editions, read “concealment.” I found nowhere the word “trembling,” which Pamelius substituted in this reading. Nor does he himself indicate where he found it.

**Those who will judge sell themselves.** Erasmus, Manutius, and Morel printed it thus, and I found this reading in eleven ancient manuscripts. I found the alternative reading, “those who will judge come,” in thirteen. And in three of these thirteen the reading is “the perverse come to judge.” In the Saint-Arnoul manuscript the original reading was “those who will judge sell themselves,” but a more recent hand emended it to read “those who will judge come.”

]

### XI

So great a terror of calamities cannot impart the discipline of innocence [Note: [Col. 0551C] “Can impart discipline,” Ar. Ben.], and amid a people dying in repeated slaughter no one considers that he himself is mortal. Everywhere people rush about, seize, and take possession. There is no concealment in plundering, no hesitation. Each person hastens to seize as though it were permitted, as though it were required, as though the person who does not seize felt that he had suffered personal damage and loss. [Col. 0552B]

Even among robbers there is some measure of shame concerning their crimes: they seek remote mountain passes and deserted solitudes, and wrongdoing is committed there in such a way that darkness and night at least veil the crime of those who commit it. Greed rages openly and, protected by its own audacity, displays in the light of the forum the weapons of unrestrained cupidity. Hence come forgers, hence poisoners, hence assassins in the midst of the city, as headlong in sinning as they are able to sin with impunity.

A crime is committed by the guilty, yet no innocent person who will punish it can be found. There is no fear of accuser or judge [Note: [Col. 0552C] “There is no fear: whatever can be bought off is not feared,” Bod. 3.]. The wicked obtain impunity while the honorable remain silent, accomplices are afraid, and those who will judge sell themselves.

And therefore, through the prophet, by the divine Spirit and inspiration, the truth of the matter is brought forth [Note: [Col. 0552C] “Is discerned,” Bod. 2. MR.] and shown by a sure and [p. 220] manifest argument: God is able to prevent adversities, but the deserts of sinners cause him not to give aid. The prophet says:

> Surely the Lord’s hand has not lost the power to save you, nor has his ear become too heavy to hear. But your sins separate you from God, and because of your offenses he has turned his face away from us, so that he does not show mercy

(Isa. 59:1–2).

Let sins and offenses, therefore, be taken into account; let the wounds of conscience be considered. Then each person will cease complaining about God or about us, if he understands that he deserves what he suffers.

[Note: [Col. 0553C]

### XII.—Hence our chief discourse with you

The old editions before that of Pamelius and thirteen old manuscripts read: “Hence our chief discourse is with us.” Pamelius printed “Hence our chief discourse is with you” from four of his manuscripts and one of Morel’s. Gronovius, chapter 14 of his *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers*, says that this passage should be written: “Hence our discourse is *cummaxime*,” that is, “especially.” I know [Col. 0553D] that *cummaxime* is commonly used by ancient authors who wrote in Latin to mean “very much.” Nevertheless, I think that Pamelius’s edition, which rests upon the authority of more old manuscripts, should be preferred to Gronovius’s conjecture.

**You wear them down with persecutions.** In four ancient copies it is written *flagitatis* (“you demand”), with *vel fatigatis* (“or you wear down”) above the line. But *fatigatis* alone appears in seven others and in some of those seen by Pamelius. He himself printed *agitatis* (“you harass”) without mentioning any old manuscript. Two old manuscripts have only *flagitatis*. Below in this same book, p. 222: “We know that through the very things which torture and wear us down, we are tested and strengthened.”

]

### XII

Behold what that very matter is concerning which our chief discourse is with you: that you persecute us though we are innocent, and that, to the dishonor of God, you assault and oppress the servants of God.

It is not enough that your life is stained by the diversity of raging vices, by the iniquity of deadly crimes, and by the profitable gains of bloody plunder; that the true religion is overthrown by false superstitions; and that God is neither sought at all nor feared. Beyond this, you wear down [Col. 0553B] with unjust persecutions the servants of God, who are consecrated to his majesty and name.

It is not enough that you yourself do not worship God; beyond this, you persecute with sacrilegious hostility those who do worship him. You neither worship God nor permit him to be worshipped at all. And although all others who venerate not only those senseless idols and images made by human hands, but even certain prodigies and monsters, are pleasing to you, the worshipper of God alone displeases you.

Everywhere in your temples the pyres of sacrificial victims and the funeral piles of animals smoke, while God’s altars either do not exist or are concealed. Crocodiles, dog-headed apes, stones [Note: [Col. 0553C] “And *liberides*,” Bod. 3; uncertain reading.], and serpents are worshipped by you; God alone upon earth is either not worshipped, or is not worshipped with impunity. You deprive the innocent, the just, and those dear to God of their homes; you despoil them of their property; you weigh them down with chains; you shut them in prison; you punish them with the sword, wild beasts, and fire. [Col. 0553C]

Nor are you at least content with a swift ending to our sufferings and a simple and rapid brevity of punishment. You apply prolonged tortures to bodies destined to be mangled; you multiply numerous torments for inward parts destined to be torn. Your savagery and brutality cannot be content with customary tortures; [Col. 0554A] ingenious cruelty devises new punishments.

[Note: [Col. 0553D]

### XIII.—Let it be forced out by bodily pain

Minucius Felix:

> Conducting upon them a perverse inquiry, one that would not elicit truth but compel falsehood.

Jerome, in the *Letter concerning the Woman Struck Seven Times*:

> While pain sought the truth.

Cyprian, at the end of the book *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 228:

> Pain, which is the witness of truth, is applied. [Col. 0554C]

Quintilian, Book V, chapter 4:

> So too with torture, a most frequently treated topic: one party calls judicial examination by torture a necessity for confessing the truth; the other calls it frequently even a cause for speaking falsely, since endurance makes falsehood easy for some, and weakness makes it necessary for others.

Likewise, chapter 10:

> A person who can endure pain will lie under torture, and a person who cannot endure it will lie.

Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book III:

> The truth must be elicited by torture, so that under examination he may identify the accomplices in his crime.

Quintus Curtius, Book VII:

> If you believe torture to be more certain than oracles, I do not refuse even this proof for exposing falsehood.

Moreover, that tortures sometimes extort falsehood instead of truth has been shown by us with numerous examples in the notes on the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*, p. 599. Another memorable example of this matter survives in chapter X of Matteo Bossi’s *On the Conduct of Magistracy*; another is found in Petramellarius the continuator of Onofrio Panvinio, p. 225, where he discusses Paolo Aretino. See also Simon Goulart in the *Treasury of Memorable Histories*, vol. I, p. 293.

**Since I confess voluntarily.** Cicero, in the *Speech for Milo*:

> What you wish to discover by torture, I confess.

**Proclamation.** Thus read the editions of Manutius and Morel and sixteen old manuscripts. The ancient editions and eight others give *praeconatione* (“heralding”), and one gives *praeconizatione*. See Du Cange’s Latin glossary.

]

### XIII

What is this insatiable frenzy for butchery? What is this unappeasable lust for cruelty? Choose instead one of two alternatives for yourself: either being a Christian is a crime, or it is not. If it is a crime, why do you not kill one who confesses it? If it is not a crime, why do you persecute an innocent person?

I ought to have been tortured if I had denied it. If, fearing your punishment, I had concealed with deceptive falsehood what I had previously been and the fact that I had not worshipped your gods, then I should have been tortured; then I should have been driven by the force of pain to confess the crime. So in other judicial examinations defendants who deny that they are implicated in the crime of which they are accused are tortured, in order that the truth of the offense, which is not disclosed by an informing voice, may be forced out by bodily pain.

But now, since I confess voluntarily, cry aloud, and repeatedly attest in frequent and reiterated [Col. 0554B] declarations that I am a Christian, why do you apply torture to one who confesses and who denounces your gods—not in hidden and secret [Note: [Col. 0553C] “Secluded,” Bod. 3.] places, but openly, publicly, in the forum itself, while magistrates and governors listen? Thus, even if what you first charged against me had been insufficient, what you ought still more greatly to hate and punish has increased: while I proclaim myself a Christian in a public place and with the people gathered around, I confound both you and your gods [Note: [Col. 0554C] “Both gods and goddesses,” Bod. 1.] by a clear and public proclamation.

[Note: [Col. 0555B]

### XIV.—To be feared as lord

Pamelius was the first to insert these words into Cyprian’s text [p. 564], taking them from Morel’s observations; Morel says that he found the passage thus in a good manuscript. I too found the same addition in five ancient manuscripts. It is not, however, found in the Séguier manuscript. [Col. 0555C]

Jerome, in the *Letter to Nepotian on the Life of Clerics*:

> To love belongs to sons; to fear, to slaves.

The same author, in the *Letter to the Monk Rusticus*:

> Fear the superior of the monastery as a lord; love him as a parent.

Rufinus, on Psalm 27:

> He who serves from fear is a slave; he who obeys from love is a son.

Lactantius, chapter 26 of the *Epitome*, in the ancient editions:

> For what is so just as to acknowledge God as father and to fear him as lord?

In place of this Pfaff printed “to fear him as God,” because that was the reading he found in the Turin manuscript. But apart from the fact that the word “lord” must necessarily be retained for the sense to stand, the same Lactantius writes in chapter 59 of the same *Epitome*:

> The first duty of justice, moreover, is to acknowledge God as father and to fear him as lord.

Entirely correct. For Lactantius is fond of speaking in this way, as is clear from Book IV, chapter 4, and Book V, chapter 19.

Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, in the *Letter to Valerian*:

> Because you call him Lord, fear him; because you call him Father, love him.

Primasius, on Paul’s *Epistle to the Romans*:

> He who fears is a slave, but he who loves is a son.

Vettius Praetextatus, in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 11:

> Let your slaves, therefore, honor you rather than fear you.

John of Salisbury, *Policraticus*, Book VIII, chapter 12:

> Let your slaves honor you rather than fear you.

Ennodius, in the *Panegyric to Theodoric*:

> By God’s inspiration, you possess such gentleness that you believe yourself able to accomplish more through affection than through fear. Noble qualities have been inscribed among the monuments of your glory, so that while kings fear you, servants love you.

Velleius Paterculus notes that Caesar said that he preferred to be loved rather than feared. Cicero, in his book *On Old Age*, writes thus of Appius:

> His slaves feared him; his children revered him.

See above, the notes on the *Letter to Donatus*, p. 384.

]

### XIV

Why do you turn against the weakness of the body? Why do you contend with the frailty of earthly flesh? Engage with the vigor of the spirit; break the strength of the mind; destroy faith. If you can, conquer by debate; conquer by reason. Or, if there is any divine force and power in your gods, let them themselves rise in their own vengeance; [p. 221] let them themselves defend themselves by their own majesty. For what can they provide to those who worship them, when they cannot avenge themselves upon those who do not worship them?

For if the one who avenges is of greater worth than the one who is avenged, you are greater than your gods. But if you are greater than those whom you worship, you ought not to worship them; rather, you ought yourself to be worshipped and feared [Col. 0555A] by them as lord.

Your vengeance defends them when they have been injured, just as your protection guards them when they have been shut away, lest they perish. Be ashamed to worship those whom you yourself defend; be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you yourself protect.

[Note: [Col. 0555D]

### XV.—By the tortures of words

Thus in Petronius I read: “the fabulous torture of maxims.”

**Whom you fear.** I do not know why these words were omitted from the later editions. For although they are absent from several ancient [Col. 0556B] copies, they are found in several other excellent ones and, besides, yield excellent sense. Manutius was the first to delete them. The English editors restored them.

]

### XV

Oh, if only you were willing to hear and see them when they are adjured by us and tortured with spiritual scourges, when they are cast out of possessed bodies by the tortures of words; when, howling and groaning with a human voice, and feeling blows and lashes by divine power, they confess that the judgment is to come!

Come and learn that what we say is true. And since you say that you worship the gods, at least believe those whom you worship. Or, if you are willing to believe even yourself, the one who now possesses your breast [Note: [Col. 0555B] “They possess,” ibid.] and has now blinded your mind with the night of ignorance will speak from within you, in your own hearing [Note: [Col. 0555B] “They themselves will speak,” Bod. 1, 3.].

You will see us being entreated by those whom you entreat, [Col. 0555B] feared by those whom you fear, whom you adore. You will see those whom you receive and venerate as lords stand bound beneath our hand and tremble as captives. Surely, at least in this way, you will be able to be confounded in those errors of yours, when you see and hear your gods disclose at once, under our questioning, what they are and—although you yourselves are present—prove unable to conceal those deceptions and frauds of theirs. [Col. 0556A]

[Note: [Col. 0556B]

### XVI.—Why do you turn toward false gods?

Claudius, bishop of Turin, presented these words as his own, though altering them in places, when writing to Theodemir, abbot of Monte Cassino. For in place of Cyprian’s words “false gods,” Claudius foolishly substituted “false images,” because he maintained that no honor was owed to images of the saints. Since he had written these things as though they were his own, without any mention of Cyprian, Jonas, bishop of Orléans, admonished him that they belonged to the most blessed martyr Cyprian. [Col. 0556C]

**Captive.** Thus read all the old manuscripts except the Moissac manuscript, in which *captiva* (“captive,” feminine) is written, and all the old editions. Pamelius, whose edition was followed by Rigaltius, printed *captiva*, because he saw that *captiva* was read in the book *On the Worship of Images* by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, where this passage is quoted by Claudius of Turin—evidently through an error. For in Dungal, where this passage is also quoted, *captivum* (“captive,” masculine) is correctly written.

**You bow down.** So too in the edition of the fragments of Claudius’s Letter. But an old manuscript reads “you incline.” For I possess a copy of these fragments collated with a manuscript by the hand of the most distinguished Jean [Col. 0556D] Cordes, where “you incline” is read. This is likewise the reading of the Grenoble manuscript.

**Animals bent downward.** The well-known passage of Ovid, from Book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> And although the other animals, bent downward, gaze upon the earth,  
> He gave humanity an uplifted face and commanded it to behold  
> Heaven and to raise its upright countenance toward the stars.

Cicero, Book II of *On the Laws*:

> For although he had cast down the other living creatures toward their food, he raised humanity alone upright and summoned it to the sight of heaven, as though it were beholding its kindred and former home.

Prudentius, Book II, *Against Symmachus*:

> I had created humanity perfect and commanded it to behold  
> The things above, with all its senses turned toward me,  
> Upright in posture and lofty in station, gazing upward.

Very many similar passages could be produced. But these are sufficient. See Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation XXXVIII, and [Col. 0557C] our notes on the book of Lupus of Ferrières *On Three Questions*.

[p. 565]

**The Father sent.** Pamelius inserts “the Son,” on the authority of five manuscripts and one cited by Morel. I too found it written thus in five ancient manuscripts. It is certainly a gloss, for it is absent from twenty-one [Col. 0557D] of our manuscripts and eight English manuscripts.

]

XVI. What sloth of mind, then—indeed, what blind and foolish madness of men bereft of sense—is it to refuse to come from darkness to light, and, though bound in the snares of eternal death, to refuse to embrace the hope of immortality; not to fear God when he threatens and says: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be utterly destroyed, unless it is to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:19). And again: “They worshiped those whom their own fingers had made; and man bowed down, and the man was humbled, and I will not forgive them” [Note: [Col. 0555B] “Them, says the Lord”: NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.] (Isa. 2:8). Why do you humble yourself and bow down before false gods? Why do you bend your captive body before senseless images and earthly fabrications? God made you upright; and whereas the other animals are prone, lowered toward the earth by the downward inclination of their posture, you have an elevated stance, and your face is raised upward [Col. 0556B] toward heaven and toward God [Note: [Col. 0556B] “God”; “his own”: Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3. Thu. Foss.]. Look there; raise your eyes there; seek God in the heights. That you may escape the regions below, lift up your heart, suspended upon lofty and heavenly things. Why do you cast yourself down into the fall of death together with the serpent you worship? Why do you fall into the devil’s ruin through the serpent itself and together with the devil? Preserve the elevation [Col. 0557A] with which you were born; remain such as you were made by God. Set your mind upright together with the posture of your face and body. That you may know God, first know yourself. Abandon the idols that human error devised. Turn to God; if you call upon him, he comes to your aid. Believe in Christ, whom the Father sent to give us life and restore us. Cease injuring the servants of God and of Christ by your persecutions: when they are injured, divine vengeance defends them.

> **Note [Col. 0557D]**
>
> **XVII.—The ruin of affairs.** So read almost all the old copies, including the Verona manuscript. Some, however, have “of kings,” through an obvious error. The care taken by those who refer these “ruins of kings” to the Decian period is therefore superfluous. A similar error was formerly removed by us in Agobard, in the letter of Pope Gregory IV. Thus, in Saint Ambrose’s letter to Chromatius, the oldest manuscript of the Church of Lyon originally had *dat consilium rei dicens* (“he gives counsel, speaking of the matter”), but this was immediately corrected above the line, and *regi* (“to the king”) was inserted. Likewise, where volume IV of Labbe’s *Councils*, p. 920, in the letter of the bishops of Maritime Phoenicia to Emperor Leo, reads *hujus rei gratia* (“for the sake of this matter”), which is the true reading, the oldest manuscripts of the Church of Beauvais and of the monastery of Corbie have *hujus regi gratia*. See also the Notes on the *Capitularies*, pp. 1060, 1105. I shall add other similar passages as well, so that they may be useful to learned men [Col. 0558C] when they encounter books in which the same errors occur and for whose correction the authority of old books is lacking. In Pope Celestine’s letter to the Clergy and People of CP., where the editions correctly have *cum a se commissa sibi rei ratio requiretur* (“when an account of the matter entrusted to him by himself is required of him”), the manuscript of the Church of Beauvais has *regi*. In the same manuscript [Col. 0558D], when the letter of Pope Vigilius to Aurelian, bishop of Arles, is reproduced, it reads: *Dignum est et catholico rei conveniens* (“It is worthy and fitting for a Catholic matter”), whereas *regi* (“for a Catholic king”) must be read, as in the editions. From the same source arose the fact that in canon 40 of the Council of Meaux, where a canon of the Synod of Clermont is quoted, *regiculam* was written in an old Orléans manuscript, whereas *reiculam* must be read. In chapter 8 of Agobard’s book against the Law of Gundobad, *resculas* was formerly read instead of *reiculas*, as I noted there. In volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1426, in a precept of Louis the Pious, *rex* is written instead of *res*.

XVII. Hence it is that none of us, when apprehended, resists, nor avenges himself against your unjust violence, although our people are exceedingly numerous and abundant. Our confidence in the vengeance that is to follow makes us patient. The innocent yield to the guilty; the blameless submit to punishments and tortures, certain [Col. 0557B] and confident that nothing we suffer will remain unavenged; and the greater the injustice of the persecution has been, the more just and severe will the vengeance for that persecution become. Never does the crime of the impious rise against our name without divine vengeance immediately accompanying it. To say nothing of ancient records [Note: [Col. 0557C] “Let us not retain”: an unnamed old manuscript.] and not to rehearse with any proclamation of the voice the acts of vengeance repeatedly inflicted on behalf of God’s worshipers, the recent event is sufficient proof: so swiftly—and, 222 in so swift a response, so mightily—has protection lately followed, in the ruin of affairs, the loss of wealth, the loss of soldiers, and the reduction of military camps. Let no one suppose that this happened by chance or think it accidental, since long ago divine Scripture established and declared: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32:35); and again [Col. 0557C] the Holy Spirit warns beforehand and says: “Do not say, ‘I will avenge myself on my enemy’; but wait for the Lord, that he may come to your aid” (Prov. 20:22). Hence it is clear and manifest that all these things descending from God’s indignation occur not through us, but on our behalf [Note: [Col. 0557C] “On your behalf”: Bod. 1.] [Col. 0558A].

> **Note [Col. 0558D]**
>
> **XVIII.—We murmur.** Certain old books and old editions have *musitamus*. I too thought that this should be the spelling, because I read in Juvencus: “Nor did they fly among themselves with a muttering voice.” But afterward I discovered that this word descends from the verb *mussare*, and consequently believed that *mussitamus* should be written, as it is in the Séguier manuscript. For in Sidonius as well, book VI, [Col. 0559D] Epistle 16, this Sapphic verse is found: “Although the chorus of the envious murmurs.” The grammarians, moreover, cite many authorities that readily prove that it should be written as I have written it.

XVIII. Nor should anyone therefore think that Christians are not vindicated by the things [Note: [Col. 0557C] “In the things which”: Voss. 1.] that happen, because they themselves also appear to be grazed by the onslaught [Note: [Col. 0557C] “Onslaught”: Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] of those events. The person who feels the punishment of the world’s adversities is the one whose entire joy and glory are in the world. The person who grieves and weeps if things go badly for him in this age is the one for whom things cannot go well after this age; whose entire profit from living is acquired here; whose every consolation comes to an end here; whose transient and brief life calculates some sweetness and pleasure here, while, once he has departed from here, punishment alone remains to cause him pain. But those who have confidence in the good things to come feel no pain [Note: [Col. 0558C] “No pain here”: Bod. 3, 4. “For these”: Bod. 1, 2.] from the onslaught of present evils. Thus we are neither dismayed by adversities, nor broken [Col. 0558B], nor grieved; nor do we murmur amid any disaster of affairs or sickness of bodies. Living by the spirit more than by the flesh, we overcome the weakness of the body by the strength of the mind. Through the very things that torment [Note: [Col. 0558C] “Torment you”: Oxon.] and weary us, we know and trust that we are being tested and strengthened.

> **Note [Col. 0559D]**
>
> **XIX.—You see, equally.** So read the old editions. This is also how it is read in nine ancient manuscripts. Manutius deleted *equally*. So too Morell and the English edition. I do not see, however, why it should have been deleted. Certainly the word does not appear necessary. But it is not therefore to be removed. For Cyprian said shortly before: “You think that we suffer adversities equally with you.” And soon afterward: “We encounter the hardships of the flesh equally with you.” Yet the word *equally* is absent there from seventeen old books.

XIX. You think that we suffer adversities equally with you, when you see that the same adversities are not borne equally by us and by you? Among you impatience is always loud and complaining; among us there is courageous and devout patience, always quiet and always grateful to God. It claims nothing joyful or prosperous for itself here, but, gentle and calm and steadfast against all the storms of the wavering world [Note: [Col. 0558C] “A steadfast mind”: Voss. 3. “Steadfast”: Vict. 3.], it awaits the time of the divine promise. For as long as this body remains, it must share the condition common to the rest [Col. 0558C], the common bodily condition; nor is it granted to the human race [Note: [Col. 0558C] “To be separated humanly”: Pem. Voss. 2.] to be separated from one another unless one departs from this world. Meanwhile, within one house, the good and the evil are contained together. Whatever happens within the house we suffer by an equal [Col. 0559A] lot, until, when the end of the temporal age has been completed, we are divided between the abodes either of eternal death or of immortality. We are not, therefore, comparable and equal to you simply because, while still situated in this world and in this flesh, we encounter the hardships of the world and the flesh equally with you. For since everything that punishes consists in the perception of pain, it is manifest that the person whom you see not grieving equally with you does not share your punishment.

> **Note [Col. 0559D]**
>
> **XX.—There will be no produce.** The old editions and six old books have “there will be no generation.” The reading taken from the edition called that of Gravius, which Manutius and others after him followed, and which we too have retained, [Col. 0560D] is supported by nineteen manuscript copies. Morell printed *nascentiae*, perhaps through a printer’s error, for this manner of writing is not Latin. Yet Pamelius was very pleased with that reading. In the Foix manuscript and the Lamonian manuscript one reads “there will be no produce.” See Du Cange’s Latin glossary.
>
> **Food.** The old editions and nine old books support “grain.” Two others and five English manuscripts have “food.” But the greater part of the manuscripts has the reading I retained.

XX. Among us the strength of hope and the firmness of faith flourish. Amid the very ruins of the collapsing world, the mind stands upright, courage is immovable, patience is always joyful, and the soul is always secure in its God, just as the Holy Spirit speaks through the Prophet and exhorts us, strengthening the firmness of our hope and faith with a heavenly voice: “The fig tree,” he says [Col. 0559B], “will not bear fruit, and there will be no produce on the vines. The labor of the olive tree [Note: [Col. 0559C] “Olive tree”: Bod. 1. Voss. 1. Thu. Vict. Grav. Morell.] will prove false, and the fields will not supply food. The sheep will fail from the pasture [Note: [Col. 0559C] “From the fold”: Foss. Spir. unnamed old manuscript, Grav. Morell.], and there will be no cattle in the stalls. But I will exult in the Lord and rejoice in God my Savior” (Hab. 3:17–20). He declares that a man of God and a worshiper of God, sustained by the truth of hope and founded upon the steadfastness of faith, is not moved by the assaults of this world and age. Although the vineyard disappoints and the olive tree deceives, and the sweltering field dries up as its plants die from drought, what is this to Christians? What is it to God’s servants, whom paradise invites and whom all the grace and abundance of the heavenly kingdom await? They always exult in the Lord and rejoice and are glad in their God. They courageously endure the world’s evils and adversities while looking ahead to future gifts and prosperity [Note: [Col. 0559C] “By courageously enduring, they await good and prosperous things to come”: Lam. Ebor. “While good things”: Oxon. from four manuscripts. Voss. 1. Thu. Foss. Vict.]. For we who, having laid aside our earthly birth [Col. 0559C], have been re-created and reborn by the Spirit, and now live not for the world but for God, will receive God’s gifts and promises only when we have come to God. And yet, to ward off enemies and obtain rain, and either to remove or mitigate adversities, we always make supplication and pour out prayers; and, conciliating and appeasing God for your peace and safety [Col. 0560A], we pray continuously and urgently by day and by night.

XXI. Let no one, therefore, flatter himself because, through the equality of flesh and body, we and the profane—that is, the worshipers of God and those opposed to God—temporarily share the condition of worldly hardships, and so suppose that all these things which happen are not inflicted upon you [Note: [Col. 0559D] “Upon us”: Voss. 2. Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4.], since it was foretold beforehand by God’s own proclamation and by prophetic [Note: [Col. 0560C] “And apostolic”: Pem.] attestation that God’s wrath would come upon the unjust, that persecutions which would injure us by human agency would not be lacking, but that acts of vengeance which would defend the injured by divine agency would follow.

> **Note [Col. 0560D]**
>
> **XXII.—Old man or young man.** I retained this reading, which I found in several ancient copies, for the reasons adduced by Pamelius, who correctly notes that the manuscripts vary remarkably. In some it is read as here; elsewhere, “an old man or a young man”; elsewhere, “old men and younger men”; elsewhere, “older and younger men”; and finally elsewhere, “of old men, nor of young men and virgins.” See book II of the *Testimonies*, chapter 22.

XXII. And how great are the things which are meanwhile done here on our behalf! Something is given as an example, so that the wrath of God the avenger may be known. But the day of judgment still lies ahead, which Holy Scripture announces, saying: “Wail, for the day of the Lord is near, and destruction [Note: [Col. 0560C] “And retribution”: Ar.] from God will be at hand. For behold, the day of the Lord comes with incurable indignation and wrath, to make the world desolate and to destroy sinners from it” (Isa. 13:6). And again: “Behold, the day of the Lord comes, burning like an oven [Note: [Col. 0560C] “Fire”: Voss. 1.], and all foreigners and all the wicked will be stubble [Note: [Col. 0560C] “As stubble”: Bod. 3. “Like”: Ar. Lam. Bod. 2. NC. 1.]; and the coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord” (Mal. 4:1). The Lord foretells that foreigners will be set ablaze and burned—that is, those alien to the divine family and profane, not spiritually reborn nor made sons of God. Elsewhere God declares that only those who have been reborn and marked with the sign of Christ can escape, when, sending his angels to devastate the world and destroy the human race, he threatens more severely at the end and says: “Go and strike, and let your eyes show no mercy. Do not pity old man or young man [Col. 0560C]; kill virgins and little children and women, so that they may be utterly destroyed. But do not touch anyone upon whom the sign has been written” (Ezek. 9:5–6). What this sign is, and on what part of the body it is placed, God makes clear elsewhere, saying: “Pass through the midst [Note: [Col. 0560C] “Pass through the midst of”: Lam. Ebor. NC. 2. Voss. 2.] of Jerusalem, and mark a sign upon the foreheads of the men who groan and mourn over the iniquities committed in their midst” [Col. 0561A] (Ezek. 9:4). And that this sign pertains to the passion and blood of Christ, and that whoever is found bearing this sign is preserved safe and unharmed, is likewise confirmed by the testimony of God, who says: “And the blood will be a sign [Note: [Col. 0561C] “This blood will be”: Voss. 1. “As a sign”: Lam. Ebor. Foss. Vict.] for you upon the houses in which you will be [Note: [Col. 0561C] “You will be there”: Bod. 1, 2, 4. “In which you will dwell”: Lin.]; and I will see the blood and protect you, and there will be no plague of destruction among you when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exod. 12:13). What came first as a figure in the slaughtered lamb is fulfilled in Christ when the reality afterward follows. Just as there, when Egypt was struck, the Jewish people could escape only through the lamb’s blood and sign, so too, when the world begins to be devastated and struck, whoever is found in the blood and sign of Christ will alone escape.

XXIII. Therefore, while there is time, look to true [Col. 0561B] and eternal salvation; and because the end of the world is already near, turn your minds to God in the fear of God. Take no delight in that powerless and empty domination which you exercise in this age among the just and gentle [Note: [Col. 0561C] “Among the unjust and merciless”: Bod. 3, 4.], since even in a field darnel and wild oats may dominate among cultivated and fertile crops. Do not say that evils happen because your gods are not worshiped by us; instead, know that this is the judicial sentence of God’s wrath [Note: [Col. 0561C] Thus four English manuscripts. “Know the wrath of God”: Oxon.], so that one who is not brought to understanding by benefits may at least be brought to understanding by blows. Seek God, even if late, because 224 long ago God warned and exhorted through the Prophet, saying: “Seek God, and your soul will live” (Ps. 68:33). Acknowledge God, even if late, because Christ, when he came, gave this admonition and teaching: “Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Believe him [Col. 0561C] who does not deceive at all. Believe him who foretold that all these things would come to pass. Believe him who will give the reward of eternal life to believers. Believe him who will inflict eternal punishments in the fires of Gehenna upon unbelievers.

> **Note [Col. 0561D]**
>
> **XXIV.—Condemned (*addictos*).** That is, adjudged, condemned. In Optatus, book I, *addictus* means “subjected” or “subordinate,” as does *addictus glebae* (“bound to the soil”) in civil law. I shall use this occasion to observe that what seems to me an excellent emendation was attempted by Guillaume Fournier in the final letter of book VII of Cassiodorus, where Mariangelo Accursio printed: *Non dici potest proprium quod liberare dominum non videtur additum* (“That which does not appear to have been added to free the master cannot be called his own” [the text is corrupt]); in place of this Fournier conjectured that 566 *addictum* should be inserted, while noting that he had read *a debito* in an old manuscript. Fournier’s conjecture may be judged sound on the ground that a debtor’s goods are assigned (*addicta*) to the creditor, and consequently so is the debtor himself.
>
> **They will be preserved with their bodies.** See our notes on book III of Salvian’s *Governance of God*.
>
> **Suddenness.** So too in the same chapter of the letter to Fortunatus. Pontius the deacon, in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “At the proconsul’s command, the chief officer suddenly rushed upon his enemies with his soldiers.” Aulus Gellius, book IX, chapter 15, spoke of an “extempore speech” (*subitaria dictio*). Titus [Col. 0562D] Livy also used this word. Boethius, book II of the *Consolation of Philosophy*: “But every sudden change of circumstances occurs not without some agitation of minds.” See the notes on Letter LVII, p. 466.
>
> **Repenting.** We restored this in place of “doing,” which occurs in the common editions, because we found it written so in fifteen of our books and in four English manuscripts. See the letter to Fortunatus, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 12.

XXIV. What glory of faith will there then be, what punishment of faithlessness, when the day of judgment comes? What joy for believers, what sorrow for the faithless, to have refused to believe here beforehand and then to be unable to return in order that they may believe? Gehenna, always burning, will consume the condemned [Col. 0562A], and voracious punishment with living flames [Note: [Col. 0562C] “Punishment will tear apart”: Voss. 1.]; nor will there be any means by which their torments may ever have either respite or end. Souls will be preserved with their bodies for pain in endless tortures. There the person who watched us here for a time will always be watched by us, and the brief pleasure of cruel eyes in the persecutions inflicted will be repaid by perpetual spectacle, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, which says: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished; and they will be a spectacle to all flesh” [Note: [Col. 0562C] “Of the flesh”: Pem. Voss. 2.] (Isa. 66:24). And again: “Then the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labors. When they see them, they will be troubled with dreadful fear and will marvel at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation, saying among themselves, repenting and groaning from anguish [Note: [Col. 0562C] “Through anguish”: Lam. Ver.] of spirit: ‘These are the ones [Col. 0562B] whom we once held in derision [Note: [Col. 0562C] “In derision”: Ar. Lam. Vict. Vat. “In laughter”: Manut.] and as a type of reproach. We fools regarded their way as madness and their end as without honor. How have they been numbered among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints? Therefore we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun did not rise upon us. We wearied ourselves on the way of iniquity and destruction; we walked [Note: [Col. 0562C] “And we walked”: Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] through difficult wastes, but the way of the Lord we did not know. What did pride profit us, or what did the boastfulness of riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow’” (Wis. 5:1–9). Then the pain of punishment will be without the fruit of repentance, lamentation will be empty, and supplication ineffectual. Those who refused to believe unto eternal life will believe too late unto eternal punishment.

> **Note [Col. 0562D]**
>
> **XXV.—From the depths.** I was compelled to write thus because of the authority of the old editions. Pamelius printed “from the deep and dark night of superstition,” because he saw that Morell had noted that an ancient book read thus. Yet Morell did not place this reading in his edition, but the one I restored. I found Pamelius’s reading in only three books.
>
> **To your hatred.** Prosper, at the end of his book *Against the Conferencer*: “With God’s aid, let it be our endeavor, through quiet and modest patience, to return love for hatred.”
>
> [Col. 0563B] **We show the paths of salvation.** Jerome, in the letter to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem: “To those who blaspheme the merciful God we extend a hand.”
>
> **No repentance is late.** Jerome, in the letter to Laeta on the education of her daughter: “Conversion is never late.” John of Salisbury, book VII of the *Policraticus*, chapter 21: “Repentance too is never late, provided it is genuine.” Seneca, *Agamemnon*: “The road to good conduct is never late.” Quintus Curtius, book IX: “Late repentance followed cruelty.” Symmachus, book X, Letter 54 [Col. 0564B]: “The amendment of old age is late and insulting.” Saint Ambrose, in his response to the *Memorial* of Symmachus: “It is certainly true that no age is too late for thorough learning.
