That old age which cannot amend itself should blush.” Cicero, book II of the *Letters to Friends*, Letter VII, says that belated congratulations are not ordinarily criticized.
>
> **Has been made.** So read all the old books except one. The edition called that of Gravius has: “has been made secure concerning immortality.” Pamelius followed this, and Rigault afterward.

XXV. Therefore, while it is permitted, make provision for security and life. We offer you the saving service of our mind and counsel [Col. 0562C]. And because we are not permitted to hate, and because we please God all the more when we return no injury for injury, we exhort you—while the opportunity is present, while something of this age still remains—to make satisfaction to God and to emerge from the depths of dark superstition into the bright light of true religion. We do not begrudge your advantages, nor do we conceal divine benefits. We return goodwill for your hatred, and in return for the torments and punishments inflicted upon us [Col. 0563A], we show you the paths of salvation. Believe and live; and you who persecute us for a time, rejoice with us forever. When departure from here has taken place [Note: [Col. 0563B] “Withdrawal”: Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver.], there is no longer any place for repentance, no effect of satisfaction. Here life is either lost or retained; here provision is made for eternal salvation through the worship of God and the fruit of faith. Let no one be delayed either by sins or by years from coming to attain salvation. For one who still remains in this world, no repentance is late. Access to God’s forgiveness lies open, and entry is easy for those who seek and understand the truth. Although you are at the very point of departure and at the setting of temporal life, if you pray concerning your transgressions and implore God, who alone is true, with confession and faith in the acknowledgment of him, pardon is granted to the one who confesses, saving forgiveness is bestowed upon the believer from divine mercy, and [Col. 0563B] at the very moment of death the passage is made to immortality. 225 Christ bestows this [Col. 0564A] grace; he grants this gift of his mercy by subduing death with the trophy of the cross, redeeming the believer at the price of his blood, reconciling man to God the Father, and giving life to the mortal through heavenly regeneration. Let us all, if possible, follow him; let us be enrolled under his sacrament and sign. He opens the way of life for us; he restores us to paradise; he leads us to the kingdoms of heaven. We shall live with him forever, having been made sons of God through him. We shall exult with him forever, restored by his blood. We Christians will be glorious together with Christ, blessed by God the Father, rejoicing in perpetual delight in the presence of God, and always giving thanks to God. For he who, though subject to death, has been made secure in immortality [Col. 0564B] [Note: [Col. 0564B] “Has been made secure concerning immortality”: Oxon.] cannot but be always joyful and grateful [Note: [Col. 0563B] “Joyful and grateful”: Thu.].

[Col. 0563]

# BOOK ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS: THAT IDOLS ARE NOT GODS, THAT THERE IS ONE GOD, AND THAT THROUGH CHRIST SALVATION HAS BEEN GIVEN TO BELIEVERS

[Note: [Col. 0563D] “That idols are not gods: against the pagans”: Vict. and others. “That it has been granted to believers that there are no gods”: Voss. 4. Lin. [Col. 0564D] Spir. “Confirmed”: Dun. “On the idols of the gentiles”: Goulart.]

> **Note [Col. 0563D]**
>
> **ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS.** It is difficult to determine with certainty what Cyprian placed in the title of this book, if indeed he placed anything there, especially if Erasmus’s opinion is correct that it is only a fragment of a larger work, since it begins abruptly. Many old books, and indeed the best of them, establish the beginning of the work at these words [Col. 0564D]: “That those whom the common people worship are not gods.” In Angelo Poliziano, chapter 34 of the *Miscellanies*, it is called the book *On the Origin and Kinds of Idols*. The diligence of later men gave it the title **ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS**, and Rigault testifies that he found it thus in ancient copies. Although I have nowhere found this title in [Col. 0565A] the manuscripts, I have nevertheless retained it for the convenience of scholars. In editing the beginning of the book itself, however, I followed the wording of the old books and old editions. Yet there are some old books that begin “The gods do not exist” and lack what precedes.
>
> Little mention of this book is found among [Col. 0565B] ancient writers, since I find it cited nowhere except in Jerome and Augustine. Augustine writes as follows in his book *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, chapter 4: “Bishop Cyprian, a follower of this apostolic rule, when disputing concerning the one true God against the worshipers of many false gods, produces many testimonies from the books of those whom they regard as distinguished authors—that is, from that truth which they suppress in unrighteousness.” He also cites it in book VI of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 44. Jerome, however, in his letter to Magnus, places the subject matter of this book at the beginning 567 of his discussion as though it were a title, writing thus: “With what brevity, with what knowledge of every history, with what brilliance of words and thoughts Cyprian touched upon the fact that idols are not gods!” Some think that Pontius the deacon also had the same book in view when, in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, he wrote that through him the gentiles were defeated when the charges they level against us were turned back upon themselves. But since these words of Pontius can also apply to the book *To Demetrianus*, in which the holy Martyr turns against the gentiles [Col. 0565C] their complaints concerning Christians, I do not dare affirm that Pontius’s words must be understood only of the book *On the Vanity of Idols*. For Pontius may have had both works in view. Moreover, concerning the worship of idols nothing is more elegant than Lucian’s *Zeus Tragoedus*. BALUZ.

(C, G, S)*

# ARGUMENT

[Col. 0563C]

The title itself embraces the three chief divisions of this book. The first proves from the following considerations that those in whose honor temples were established, images fashioned, victims sacrificed, and feast days celebrated had been kings and human beings rather than gods; and therefore that their worship could have benefited neither foreign peoples nor the Romans in any respect; that the power of the Roman Empire must be attributed not to them but rather to fortune, since it both arose through a certain alternation of circumstances and blushes at its own origin; and that, from the emptiness of their outcomes, it is evident that nothing should be attributed to auspices or auguries [Col. 0563D]. Indeed [Col. 0564C], these deceptions belong rather to demons, as attested even by the poets, Socrates, Plato, Trismegistus, and Osthanes, who acknowledged both one God and demons. The second division makes it briefly manifest that there is one God, both from the greater dignity of monarchy in comparison with other forms of rule and from the very expressions of the pagan populace—“O God,” and similar phrases. The final division treats Christ more extensively from the Jewish Prophets and the Gospel history. PAMEL.

[Col. 0564D]

> **Note [Col. 0565C]**
>
> **I.—They were formerly kings.** Lactantius, book VI, chapter 8: “How then, someone will say, did they come to be regarded as gods? Doubtless because they were very great or very powerful kings and, on account of the merits of their virtues, their gifts, or the arts they discovered, having been dear to those over whom they ruled, they were consecrated to memory.” The same author, in the book *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 11: “Surely all those who are worshiped as gods were human beings, and they were likewise the first and greatest kings. But who does not know that after death they were either accorded divine honors on account of their valor, because they had ruled over the human race, or attained immortal remembrance on account of the benefits and inventions by which they had refined human life?” So too in the book of the *Recognitions* of Saint Clement. Cicero, book II of *The Nature* [Col. 0565D] *of the Gods*: “Persaeus, a pupil of Zeno, says that those by whom some great benefit for the cultivation of life had been discovered were regarded as gods, and that beneficial and salutary things themselves were designated by the names of gods.” And below: “Human life and common custom adopted the practice of raising men distinguished by their services to heaven through fame and popular consent. Hence Hercules; hence Castor and Pollux.” Horace, book II, Epistle 1:
>
> Romulus and Father Liber, and Pollux with Castor,  
> After mighty deeds were received into the temples of the gods.
>
> Quintus Curtius, book IX, writes that the Persians worship their kings among the gods not only piously but also prudently, for the majesty of imperial power is the safeguard of their security. Julius Firmicus, in the book *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “For the frivolity of the Greeks loves to call by divine names those who have conferred some benefit upon them or aided them by counsel or valor. And gratitude for their benefits is repaid by them in such a way that they call gods, and believe to be gods, those who [Col. 0566A] once ruled over them.” Cicero, in the speech *For Milo*: “The Greeks confer the honors of gods upon those men who have killed tyrants.” Lucian writes in the *Toxaris* that the Scythians sacrificed to Orestes and Pylades, not as gods, but as good men. Julius Firmicus also says that the Egyptians venerate and worship as a god Joseph, who had provided for their destitution for [Col. 0566B] seven years. Epiphanius, in the prologue to his books *Against Heresies*, chapter 7, says that tyrants and deceivers who had misled the whole world by their inventions and falsehoods were consecrated with divine honors. Pietro della Valle, in the *History of His Travels*, testifies that even now the pagan Indians worship as gods their kings and illustrious men who earned divine honors by their splendid deeds. BALUZ.
>
> **The faces of the dead.** Here I shall note only that I use this passage to restore this word to Commodian, in whose *Instruction* 2 one reads: “They prayed to dead gods,” in place of which Rigault printed “dying gods.” So too in *Instruction* 20: “For you fools worship those who died an evil death.” I cite these passages of Commodian as they stand in the old manuscript of Saint-Aubin of Angers. BALUZ.
>
> **And they sacrificed.** The old editions and some old books have: “For they also sacrificed.” Others simply have “and they sacrificed,” a reading I found in fifteen ancient manuscripts. Two old books there have “also” [Col. 0566C] instead of “and.” Neither of these two readings pleased Pamelius. He preferred the one which he says he found in Gravius and Casterius, and wrote: “to whom they also sacrificed.” But I did not see the word “to whom” either in the edition called that of Gravius or in the manuscripts. BALUZ.
>
> **With honor.** I saw it written thus in thirteen old books. Certain others have “honors” or “honor” in the accusative. I retained the reading supported by the authority of the greater number of old books, especially since I found this passage punctuated in this way in the Tournai manuscript of the royal library, in the Bec manuscript, and also in that of Saint-Arnoul at Metz. BALUZ.
>
> **From this they became sacred rites for posterity.** Minucius Felix: “Likewise, indeed, our forefathers also believed rashly, credulously, and with rude simplicity concerning the gods: while they worshiped their kings religiously, while they longed to see those deceased kings in images, while they eagerly sought to retain their memories in statues, 568 the consolations they had adopted became sacred rites.” See Fulgentius Planciades, book I of the *Mythologies*, where he treats the [Col. 0566D] son of the Egyptian Syrophanes. BALUZ.

I. That those whom the common people worship are not gods is evident from this. [Col. 0565A] They were formerly kings who, because of the memory of their kingship, subsequently began to be worshiped by their own people even in death. Hence temples were established for them; hence images were fashioned to preserve through representation the faces of the dead. And they sacrificed [Note: [Col. 0565A] So the oldest manuscripts and the more recent editions. Bal. Lips. “To whom they also sacrificed”: Oxon. “For they also”: Foss. Corb. Gronov. “(To whom) and”: Lindn.] victims and celebrated feast days by rendering honor [Note: [Col. 0565A] “Honors”: Oxon. Lindn. “Honor,” accusative: Lin. Lam. “With such great honor” [Col. 0566A]: Voss. 4. Tew. Routh, *Script. eccl. opusc.*, 1840.]. [Col. 0566A] Hence those things which had initially been adopted as consolations became sacred rites for posterity. And let us see whether this truth holds [Note: [Col. 0566A] “Whether this also holds”: Gronov. Lips. Routh, from two new Oxford manuscripts and the Drury manuscript.] in each individual case.

> **Note [Col. 0566D]**
>
> **II.—Melicertes and Leucothea.** Hyginus, *Fable* II: “Ino threw herself into the sea with her son Melicertes. Liber wished her to be called Leucothea; we call her Mater Matuta. He called Melicertes the god Palaemon, whom we call Portumnus.” Ino, moreover, is represented as the nurse of Liber, or Bacchus. Add Lactantius, book I, chapter 21, section 23. CELL.

Castors. The English editors, who after Morel printed *Castor and Pollux* in their edition, warn that *Castors* ought to have been restored here, if it were worth altering a matter of such slight importance. But this reasoning carries no weight. For they themselves made several alterations in the works of Saint Cyprian which are of no greater importance. I, however, made the change because Cyprian’s own words ought to be restored to him, and because in Minucius Felix, from whom Cyprian seems to have taken this, it is written: “The Castors die by turns that they may live.” So too it is written in all the [Col. 0567B] ancient books, both ours and the English, with the single exception of the Chartres manuscript, which has the reading of Morel’s edition. And since the issue was the correction of Cyprian on the authority of the ancient books, it was necessary to restore the reading found in almost all the manuscripts. Dio Cassius, book XXXVII, notes that the temple of Castor and Pollux at Rome was customarily called the temple of Castor alone. See Erasmus’s annotations on chapter XXVIII of Acts. BALUZE.

Aesculapius is struck by lightning. Lactantius, book I, chapter 10, speaking of Aesculapius, says that “he deserved to be struck by lightning by God.” Pliny, [Col. 0567C] book XXIX, chapter 1, writes that he was struck by lightning because he had restored one of the sons of Tyndareus to life. Cornelius Celsus, in the preface to his books *On Medicine*, says that Aesculapius was enrolled among the gods because he expounded this still rudimentary and commonplace science with somewhat greater refinement. Tertullian writes in the *Apologeticum* that he was “claimed by lightning,” that is, made a god. For this reading, preferred by the editions of Beatus Rhenanus and Pamelius, seems to me better than the one that has “judged.” In the same sense Pliny says in the *Panegyric* that Nerva was “claimed for heaven by the gods.” Thus Optatus, book I, calls a martyr “claimed,” that is, canonized—to use the word of our own times—when it was established that he had suffered tortures and undergone death for the name of Christ. In the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 187, the word “is claimed” has another meaning, as I noted there. The *Passion of Saint Philip the Bishop*, in volume IV of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 140, says: “The fact that Scolapius the physician was struck by lightning on Mount Cynusuris caused him to merit consecration among the nations.” See Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma XII. [Col. 0567D] BALUZE.

Oetean. Nine ancient books prefer *Aetnean*. And it is written in nearly this way in Arnobius in the royal manuscript. Although I do not doubt that this reading is false, I nevertheless think that I may use it to correct a passage of Pacian in the book *On Penitents*, where it reads: “Aetna and Licaniculus and Campanian Vesuvius seethe with unwearied little globes of flame.” But in the ancient manuscript of the Grande Chartreuse it is written: “Sicilian Etna and Campanian Vesevus.” Correctly: for Aetna is in Sicily, and Vesuvius in Campania. On the burning of Hercules, see Fronton du Duc’s notes on Theophilus of Antioch’s books *To Autolycus*. The story of the Hercules of Sufetula in Augustine’s letter to the citizens of the colony of Sufetula is amusing and elegant. BALUZE.

Admetus’s herd. In Commodian, as edited by Rigault, *Instruction* XI reads: “He is also said to have pastured Admetus’s cattle.” But in the manuscript of Saint-Aubin, *a primitia* is written in place of *Admeti*. Ovid, book II of *The Art of Love*:

[Col. 0568B] The Cynthian is said to have pastured Admetus’s cows through the heat  
And to have hidden in a little cottage. BALUZE.

The cave of Jupiter. Minucius Felix: “Even now Jupiter’s cave is visited and his tomb is shown.” Virgil, book IV of the *Georgics*: “They fed the king of heaven beneath the Dictaean cave.” Ovid, book III of the *Amores*, Elegy 9: “Crete, a land proud of having nursed Jupiter.” See Jerome on the first chapter of the Epistle to Titus. BALUZE.

Is visited. In Angelo Poliziano, chapter 34 of the *Miscellanies*, it is written *mutitur* [uncertain reading]. BALUZE.

[Col. 0568C] Latium from a hiding place. Minucius Felix: “And so he preferred his hiding place, because he had lain safely hidden, to be called Latium.” Virgil, book VIII of the *Aeneid*: “And he preferred it to be called Latium because he had lain safely hidden upon these shores.” Ovid, book I of the *Fasti*: “The land was called Latium from the god lying hidden.” See Lactantius, book I, chapter 13. Hence the Latiarian Hill in Varro, book V, *On the Latin Language*. BALUZE.

He [instituted] the imprinting of letters and the stamping of coins. Understand this, indeed, as imprinting letters on stones, parchments, and bark. CELLARIUS. Gronovius: “and to stamp.” LINDNER.

He [instituted] stamping. Tertullian in the *Apologeticum*: “By him first was a coin stamped with a tablet and image, and hence he presides over the treasury.” See the notes of Pamelius. BALUZE.

The Moors worship kings. Tertullian in the *Apologeticum* says that the petty kings of Mauretania were worshipped as gods by their peoples. Lactantius, book I, chapter 15: “It was clearly for this reason that the Romans consecrated their Caesars [p. 569], and the Moors their kings.” Minucius Felix: “Juba is a god to the Moors with their consent.” Valerius Maximus in his preface: “For we received the other gods; the Caesars we made.” Herodian, book IV, says that it is the custom of the Romans to consecrate emperors who die leaving sons or successors alive, and that those who have received this honor are said to have been enrolled among the deified. BALUZE.]

## II

Melicertes and Leucothea are cast into the seas, and afterward become divinities of the sea. The Castors die by turns [Col. 0567A] that they may live. Aesculapius is struck by lightning so that he may rise to godhood [Note: [Col. 0567B] “Rise again,” Gronovius.]. Hercules is consumed in Oetean [Note: [Col. 0567B] “Oeta,” Lin. Thu.] fires so that he may put off the human being. Apollo pastured Admetus’s [Note: [Col. 0567B] “For Admetus,” Gronovius; Routh, from new Oxford MSS. 1, 2.] herd. Neptune constructed walls for Laomedon, and the unfortunate builder did not receive payment for his work. Jupiter’s cave in Crete is visited [Note: [Col. 0567B] “Is seen,” Thu. Foss.; “is said,” Pem. Voss. 2; “is visited,” Voss. 4.], and his tomb is shown, and it is manifest that Saturn was driven away by him [Note: [Col. 0567B] “That Saturn was driven away is manifest,” Pem. Voss. 2. Thu. Mich. Vict.]. Hence Latium received its name from his hiding place [Note: [Col. 0567B] “Hiding places,” Pem. Voss. 2.]. He was the first in Italy to institute the imprinting of letters and the stamping [Note: [Col. 0568B] “And stamping,” Gronovius.] of coins; hence [Note: [Col. 0568B] “Whence,” Oxford.] the treasury is called Saturn’s. He was also a cultivator of rustic life [Note: [Col. 0568B] “For he was also a cultivator of rustic life,” Mich. Vict.]; hence he is depicted as an old man carrying a sickle [Note: [Col. 0568B] “Is depicted carrying,” Lam. Bod. 3. Voss. 2. Spir. Rem. Er. Man. Gronovius; Routh, from three new Oxford MSS. and two of Drury; Tew. Meerm.]. When he had been driven away, Janus had received him as a guest [Col. 0568A] [Note: [Col. 0568B] “Received,” Foss. Mich. Vict. Lindner.]; from Janus’s name the Janiculum was named and the month of January instituted. Janus himself is represented with two faces because, stationed in the middle, he seems to look equally upon the year beginning and the year departing. The Moors, moreover, manifestly worship kings [Note: [Col. 0568B] “Their kings,” Rigault.], and do not conceal this name under any veil.

[Note: [Col. 0568D]

## III.—On the Gods

This passage is written with great variation and confusion in the ancient copies. The edition called that of Gravius reads *concerning all these*; the manuscript of Saint-Éloi at Arras, *from all these*; the Foix, Tours, Corbie, and Lamouignon manuscripts, the editions of Manutius and Morel, and also the variant readings placed in the margin of the book used by Gravius, *concerning gods who were human beings*; the Sorbonne manuscript, *from these human beings*; one royal manuscript, the Thuanean, and also one of mine, *other human beings*, with the preposition *concerning* omitted. The Chartres and Bec manuscripts have *from pious human beings*. Let the reader choose from these variant readings the one he judges best. I would readily believe that the reading preferred by the editions of Manutius and Morel—which Rigault and the English editors also retained—should be preserved, as I have preserved it. BALUZE.

[Col. 0569B] That the memory of ancestors and kings was preserved. Minucius develops this more fully and adds that he traced the lineage from Uranus down to Jupiter. LINDNER.

If at some time the gods were born. Cicero, book I of *The Nature of the Gods*: “If they were born, there were no gods before they were born. And if there was a birth of the gods, there must also be their destruction.” BALUZE.

Unless perhaps Jupiter has grown old. Taken from Felix, chapter XXIII. I add to this argument Pliny’s judgment, book II, chapter VII, concerning the pagan gods: “To believe that there are marriages among the gods, yet that throughout so long an age none is born from them; that some are always aged and gray-haired, others young men and boys; that some are dark-colored, winged, lame, born from an egg, and living and dying on alternate days—this is nearly the delirium of children. But it surpasses all shamelessness to fabricate adulteries among them, then quarrels and hatreds, and even divinities of thefts and crimes.” CELLARIUS.]

## III

Hence among the several nations and provinces the diverse religion of the gods varies, since not one god is worshipped by all, but each people preserves the particular cult of its own ancestors. Alexander the Great, in a notable volume addressed to his mother, writes that a priest, through fear of Alexander’s power, disclosed to him the secret concerning gods who were human beings: [Col. 0569A] that the memory of ancestors and kings had been preserved, and that from this the rites of worship and sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0569A] “Rites of worship,” Ver. Thu. Foss. Corb. Mich. Lin.] had become established. But if the gods were born at some time, why are they not still born today—unless perhaps Jupiter has grown old, or Juno’s capacity for childbirth has failed?

[Note: [Col. 0569B]

## IV.—For Their Own

Certain ancient books and Morel’s edition have “entirely.” That reading seems good. Let learned critics determine whether it should be preferred. BALUZE.

Native gods. So also Minucius Felix. BALUZE.

[Col. 0569C] Picus. Prudentius, in the first book *Against Symmachus*, said that his body was mottled. Plutarch in the *Roman Questions* asks why the Romans venerate Picus. BALUZE.

The god of counsels. Jerome in the *Life of Hilarion*: “This custom has been observed in Roman cities ever since Romulus: because of the successful rape of the Sabine women, chariots also make seven circuits for the god of counsels himself.” Varro, book V, *On the Latin Language*: “The Consualia are named from Consus, because at that time public holidays are held for that god, and at his altar in the circus the priests conduct those games at which the Sabine maidens were abducted.” Ovid, book III of the *Fasti*: “Prepare the festival for Consus; Consus will tell you the rest.” Tertullian in the book *On the Shows*: “Hence the games were called the Consualia; in the beginning they honored Neptune.” For they call the same god Consus. And immediately afterward: “Although they also defend the Consualia as Romulus’s institution, because he dedicated them to the god Consus—supposedly the god of counsel—namely the counsel by which he then devised for his soldiers the abduction of the Sabine maidens as wives.” See Dionysius [Col. 0569D] of Halicarnassus, book I; Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 4; and Plutarch in the book *Roman Questions*. Lilio Gregorio Giraldi relates in Syntagma V of the *History of the Gods* that he remembered, when he was unhappily spending his days at Rome, that a little shrine was excavated at the foot of the Palatine behind the church of Saint Anastasia. Most people then thought it belonged to Consus, that is, Neptune, because of the numerous seashells found there. On the shrine’s vault or arched ceiling there was also the image of a white eagle with a red crest, which most people then interpreted as a symbol of counsel. That the temple of Consus was subterranean in that district is proved from P. Victor. BALUZE.

Cloacina. Lactantius, book I, chapter 20: “Tatius consecrated an image of Cloacina found in the Great Sewer; and because he did not know whose likeness it was, he gave it a name derived from the place.” On Cloacina and the goddesses that follow, see Augustine’s letter to Maximus of Madaura. BALUZE.

[Col. 0570B] Dread and pallor. Lactantius in the same place: “Tullus Hostilius fashioned and worshipped Dread and Pallor.” Saint Augustine, book XX *Against Faustus*, chapter 9: “For the Romans also consecrated images of bodily afflictions, such as pallor and fever.” BALUZE.

Fever. Octavianus Horatianus, book IV, chapter 1: “Hence it is that the Romans established a temple for Fever.” Prudentius in the *Hamartigenia*:

Equal is the madness of those whom report records  
As having consecrated Fever and Scabies as goddesses in dedicated shrines.

Cicero, book II of *The Laws*: “And an ancient altar of Fever stands upon the Palatine.” See Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 5, and Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, Syntagma I of the *History of the Gods*.

Flora. The Floralia were instituted in her honor. Cicero, in the Fifth Action *Against Verres*, said: “Mother Flora must be appeased for the Roman people and commons by the celebration of games.” Lactantius, book I, chapter 20: “After Flora had acquired great wealth from the trade of prostitution, she named the people her heir and left a fixed sum of money, from the annual interest on which her [Col. 0570C] birthday was to be celebrated by the presentation of games called the Floralia.” See there the notes of Joseph Isaeus. Arnobius, book VII: [p. 570] “Flora is thought to be treated with honor if at her games one sees shameful acts performed and transferred from brothels to theaters.” Saint Augustine, in one of the letters that he wrote to Nectarius about the affair at Calama—Letter XCI in the new edition—says: “No fertile soil, no richly endowed virtue, but that goddess Flora was found to be a mother worthy of these flowers. Her theatrical games are celebrated with such lavish and licentious indecency that anyone may understand what kind of demon it is which cannot otherwise be appeased unless there, not birds, not four-footed animals, nor finally human blood, but—far more criminally—human modesty perishes as though sacrificed.” Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 29, records that Numa instituted the Floralia on the fourth day before the Kalends of May. Ovid, book IV of the *Fasti*: “The floral festival extends even into the Kalends of May.” Suetonius in *Galba*: “As praetor, at the opening of the Floralian games, he presented a novel kind of spectacle: elephants walking the tightrope.” See there the commentary [Col. 0570D] of Filippo Beroaldo. Tacitus, book II of the *Annals*, records that the temple of Flora was established by the aediles Lucius and Marcus Publicius beside the Circus Maximus. See Justin, book XLIII; Velleius Paterculus, book I; Martial, book I, Epigram 92; and Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, Syntagma I of the *History of the Gods*. Fulgentius Planciades, book I of the *Mythologies*, called a wanton girl one “sporting with Floralian impudence.” See what we said about the Floralian games in the notes to the *Letter to Donatus*, p. 379. BALUZE.

Prostitutes. We have removed what follows in the edition called that of Gravius and in those of Pamelius, Rigault, and the English editors, because we did not find it in any of the ancient copies we used; because it is absent from several English manuscripts; because it does not appear in the early editions or in Minucius; and because, as Rigault says, it breaks the sense. BALUZE.

The treachery succeeded. It proceeded to a successful outcome. RIGAULT.

[Col. 0571B] The god Viduus. Who could recount all the ridiculous names of the gods? Such too is Scansus, who follows, and such are the other gods and goddesses. Others—Arnobius, book IV; Lactantius, book I, chapter 20; and Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, chapter 8—have recounted many, indeed almost innumerable, names, yet could not include them all. CELLARIUS.

And Forculus from doors, and Limentinus. Augustine, *City of God*, [Col. 0571C] book IV, chapter 8, at the end: “Each man stations one doorkeeper at his house, and because he is human, he is entirely sufficient. These people stationed three gods: Forculus at the doors, Cardea at the hinge, and Limentinus at the threshold. Thus Forculus could not guard the doors and the hinge and threshold at the same time.” Add Tertullian, *On the Crown*, chapter 13, at the end. CELLARIUS.

Orbona from bereavements. Pliny, book II, chapter 7: “A shrine was dedicated to Orbona beside the temple of the Lares, and an altar to Evil Fortune on the Esquiline.” Arnobius, book IV, more clearly: “Parents bereaved of children are under Orbona’s protection; those whose final hour has come are under Naenia’s.” CELLARIUS.

The defeated Penates. Virgil concerning Aeneas, book I, line 72: “Carrying Ilium into Italy, and the defeated Penates.” LINDNER.

Bald Venus. Lactantius, book I, chapter 20: “When the Gauls had occupied the city and the Romans were besieged upon the Capitol, they made torsion engines from the women’s hair and consecrated a temple to Bald Venus.” BALUZE.]

## IV

Why, indeed, do you think those gods can do anything for the Romans [p. 226] when you see [Note: [Col. 0569A] “Whom you more often see,” Gronovius.] that they could do nothing for their own peoples against Roman arms? For we know the Romans’ native gods. [Col. 0570A] Romulus was made a god by Proculus’s perjury; so too Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, and Consus, whom Romulus wished to be worshipped as the god of deceit—or as the god of counsels—after treachery succeeded [Note: [Col. 0569A] “Even today it arrived,” Bod. 3. MR.] in the rape of the Sabine women. Tatius also both discovered and worshipped the goddess Cloacina; Hostilius established Dread and Pallor. Later Fever was dedicated by someone or other, as were the prostitutes Acca and Flora [Note: [Col. 0569A] “Prostitutes. These gods,” Bod. 3. Pem. Voss. 2, 3. Lam. Thu. [Col. 0570A] Foss. Corb. Mich. Vic. Hinc. MR.].

[Sometimes, indeed, names of gods are invented among the Romans: thus they have even the god Viduus, who bereaves the body of its soul. Since he is, as it were, associated with death and funerals, he is not admitted within the walls; and nevertheless, because he has been made an exile, he is condemned by Roman religion rather than worshipped. There is also Scansus, named from acts of ascending [Note: [Col. 0571B] “Named” is absent from Gronovius.], and Forculus from doors, Limentinus from thresholds, Cardea from hinges, and Orbona from bereavements [Note: [Col. 0571B] “Suburbana,” MSS. and printed editions passim.].] [Note: [Col. 0570A] “Sometimes … Orbona.” Besides the editions of Gravius, Pamelius, Rigault, and Fell, these words are also found in the more recent editions of Cellarius, Lindner, Gronovius, and Goldhorn, although the last appears to support Baluze.]

These are the Roman gods. But Thracian Mars, Cretan Jupiter, Juno—whether Argive, Samian, or Punic—Tauric Diana, the Idaean mother of the gods, and the Egyptian gods are monstrosities, not divinities. Surely, if they had possessed any power, they would have preserved their own kingdoms and those of their peoples. The Romans do indeed also have the defeated Penates [Note: [Col. 0571B] “Defeated,” Grav.; “bound,” Camb.], whom the refugee Aeneas brought with him. There is also Bald Venus—far more disgracefully bald here than wounded in Homer.

[Col. 0571B] [Note: [Col. 0571C]

## V.—The Assyrians

So the ancient editions, certain ancient books, and Minucius as well. Other ancient books prefer “Syrians.” Twenty-six others omit mention of the Medes, but four others contain it, as does Minucius. In addition, the Verona manuscript and the manuscript of Saint-Éloi at Arras add the Tyrians. Mention of the Median kingdom is also absent from the editions of Manutius and Morel. Those who were first called Assyrians were afterward called Syrians. See René Massuet’s dissertations on Irenaeus, p. 71, § 142. Arbaces transferred the empire from the Assyrians to the Medes, and it was afterward transferred to the Persians. So Justin teaches in books I and XLI. BALUZE.

Romulus the parricide. Jerome in the *Letter to the Monk Rusticus*: “As soon as Rome was founded, it could not have two brothers as kings at the same time, and it was dedicated by parricide.” Lucan, book I: “The first walls were drenched in a brother’s blood.” BALUZE.

Brutus kills his sons. Lucius Junius Brutus, the first [Col. 0572B] consul. Consult Livy, book II, chapter 5. Virgil also touches upon this in book VI, line 819:

As consul, this man will be the first, and savage, to receive  
Authority and the axes; and as a father he will summon  
His sons, who stir up new wars, to punishment  
For fair liberty—unhappy man. CELLARIUS.

[Col. 0572C] “A time with a fixed end” is the same as “a time by a fixed end.” Thus one is a gloss upon the other. You may also understand the omitted words as follows: “They guard or retain the period of rule received from God until a fixed end, at whose approach it will be taken from them.” LINDNER.

Regulus. This and what follows have been taken almost word for word from Minucius. BALUZE.

And defeated. I added this from the Foix manuscript. Minucius gave me the boldness to do so, for in him it reads: “Mancinus observed the religious rites, and was sent under the standard and surrendered.” In place of what Minucius called “surrendered,” the Foix manuscript has “defeated.” BALUZE.

Greedy chickens. Two ancient books have “vultures.” But that reading does not agree with the story, which is thoroughly amusing. I shall recount it from Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 4. During the First Punic War, when Publius Claudius wished to engage in a naval battle and had sought the auspices according to ancestral custom, the keeper of the sacred chickens announced that the chickens would not come out of their cage. Claudius ordered them to be thrown into the sea, saying: “Since they refuse to eat, let them drink.” Suetonius in *Tiberius*: “Claudius Pulcher, when the chickens would not eat during an augury off Sicily, had them plunged into the sea in contempt of religion, so that they might drink since they refused to eat, and then entered upon a naval battle. After he was defeated and ordered by the senate to name a dictator, he named his courier Ilicius.” Hence Paulus’s joke in Martial, book I, Epigram 29. Cicero, in the first book *On Divination*, tells an almost similar story concerning the consul Gaius Flaminius. These are his words: “Likewise, when he was taking the auspices by means of the sacred chickens, their keeper was postponing the day for joining battle. Flaminius then asked him what he thought should be done if the chickens still would not eat. When the man answered that they must remain inactive, Flaminius said: ‘Splendid auspices indeed, if business can be conducted while the chickens are hungry, but nothing can be done when they are full!’ And so he ordered the standards to be pulled up and the army to follow him. At that time, when the standard-bearer of the first company of *hastati* could not move his standard from its place and made no progress [p. 571] even after several men joined him, [Col. 0573B] Flaminius ignored the report in his customary fashion. And so within three hours the army was cut to pieces, and he himself was killed.” See Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 6. Rosinus, book III, chapter 10 of the *Roman Antiquities*, reproduces from ancient monuments an image of the cage and the chickens. BALUZE.]

## V

Kingdoms, however, do not come by merit, but vary by chance. The Assyrians, Medes, and Persians [Note: [Col. 0571B] “Syrians and Persians,” Lin. Ebor. Lam. Bod. 3. Thu. Foss. Mich.; “and the Tyrians,” Ver. Voss. 4; “Syrian,” Verona and Arras MSS. [Col. 0572B] “And the Medes” omitted by the first edition; Routh, from MSS.] held imperial power before, and we know that the Greeks and Egyptians also ruled. Thus, as the turns of power changed, [Col. 0572A] the time to rule came to the Romans also, just as it had to the others.

But if you return to their origin, you would blush. Their people is gathered from criminals and malefactors, and, once an asylum has been established, impunity for crimes supplies their numbers. Then, so that the king himself [Note: [Col. 0572B] Thus the MSS. In others the first word “Then” is expunged. It is absent from Lindner.] may possess sovereign power, Romulus becomes a parricide—another crime. And so that he may arrange a marriage [Note: [Col. 0572B] “They arrange,” Verona, which agrees with what follows: “They abduct.”], he inaugurates a thing of concord through acts of discord. They abduct, act savagely, and deceive in order to increase the population of their state. Their marriages consist in broken covenants of hospitality and cruel wars with allies.

The consulship is also the highest rank among Roman honors. We see that the consulship began in the same way as the monarchy. Brutus kills his sons so that the dignity of his office may grow in esteem through endorsement of the crime. The Roman kingdoms therefore grew neither through sacred religious observances nor through auspices or auguries; they merely retain for a fixed period the time granted them. Regulus, moreover, observed the auspices and was captured; Mancinus observed the religious rites and was sent under the yoke and defeated [Note: [Col. 0572B] “And defeated” was introduced by Baluze’s edition and omitted by Routh.]. Paulus had greedy chickens, yet was slain at Cannae. Gaius Caesar, [Col. 0573A] though auguries and auspices opposed his sending ships [Note: [Col. 0573B] “A sailor,” Corb.] to Africa before midwinter, disregarded them, and thereby sailed and conquered all the more easily.

[Note: [Col. 0573B]

## VI.—Credulous

I judged that *credulous* should be written, because I found it so written in three manuscripts and in the edition called that of Gravius, instead of the *prodigal* found in the editions and certain ancient books. Even the false reading of the Tours manuscript, which has *cruel*, shows that this is the true one. It is extremely common in ancient manuscripts to find *cruel* in place of *credulous* and conversely, and also *cruelty* in place of *credulity* and conversely, as I have already noted on p. 483. See volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1119. The Corbie manuscript has “foolish [Col. 0573C] and cruel,” which was certainly corrupted from some ancient text that appears to have contained “credulous.” As for “prodigal,” I cannot say how it crept in, unless *lost* was once written; ignorant copyists then changed that *lost* into *betrayed*, and afterward into *prodigal*. “Lost men” means criminal and wicked men. RIGAULT.

Impure spirits. Above, in the *Letter to Donatus*, p. 3: “Unclean and wandering spirits.” Minucius: “They are impure, wandering spirits, weighed down from their heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires.” Lactantius, book II, chapter 14: “Defiled and lost spirits wander throughout the whole earth.” BALUZE.

Wandering. Commodian, *Instruction* IV: “Hence wandering spirits now overthrow many bodies.” Likewise *Instruction* XXII: “Demons wandering in the world.” So the ancient manuscript of Saint-Aubin. In place of this Rigault printed “to wander.” Prudentius in the poem on Saint Vincent: “There too are wandering spirits, [Col. 0573D] powerless and filthy.” BALUZE.

Hostanes. The early editions and almost all the ancient books have *Sosthenes*. Manutius printed *Ostanes*, Pamelius *Hostanes*. But I saw *Ostanes* written in three ancient manuscripts and *Hostanes* in the Tours manuscript. In one ancient manuscript of mine *Ostanes* was originally written, but it was afterward corrected in antiquity so as to show that *Sostanes* should be written. It is also written that way in the Grenoble manuscript. In Apuleius’s *Apology* he is called Hostanes. Saint Augustine cites this passage in book VI of *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chapter 44. See Selden, *On the Law of Nature and Nations*, book V, chapter 11. BALUZE.—Pliny, book XXX, chapter 1: “The first person, so far as I can discover, known to have composed a commentary upon it was Ostanes, who accompanied Xerxes, king of the Persians, in the war that he waged against Greece. He scattered, as it were, seeds of this monstrous art, infecting the world in passing wherever he traveled. This [Col. 0574B] Ostanes especially drove the Greek peoples to madness, and not merely to eagerness for knowledge of it.” RIGAULT.

The form of the true God. Pliny, book II, chapter 7: “I consider it a mark of human weakness to believe in an image and form of God.” Apuleius in the *Apology*: “God can be conceived by few and expressed by none.” When the martyr Attalus, in Rufinus, book V, chapter 3, was asked what name God had, he answered: “Those who are many are distinguished by names. He who is one has no need of a name.” Marius Victorinus at the beginning of the book *On Divine Generation*: “To speak about God is boldness beyond man.” Cicero, book I of *The Nature of the Gods*, says that the appearance of God is perceived by thought, not by the senses. Lucretius, book I: “The god is scarcely seen by the mind of the soul.” Lactantius in the book *On the Anger of God*, chapter 11: “In Xenophon, Socrates says in disputation that one ought not to inquire into the form of God.” Arnobius, book I: “If you wish to hear the true judgment, either God has no form, or, if he has been formed with some form, we certainly do not know what it is.” [Col. 0574C] Dio Cassius, book XXXVII, speaking of the God of the Jews, says that they considered their God ineffable and invisible. Cassian, *Conference* X, chapter 4, argues against the simplicity of those who think that the incomprehensible majesty of the true divinity should be worshipped within the circumscription of some form. See the same author, book VIII *On the Dress of Monks*, chapter 4. Sulpicius Severus, book II of the *Sacred History*: “The reply was that the form of God cannot be perceived by mortal eyes.” In Juvencus, book II of the *Gospel History*, Christ, speaking of the rock, says:

For you were never able to comprehend his voice,  
Nor did he permit you to see his own form.

Rufinus, book I of the *Apologies*: “For the nature of God is not, as some think, visible to some and invisible to others.” See Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* and Novatian’s book *On the Trinity*. See also Jacques de Billy’s scholia on Gregory of Nazianzus’s oration *On the Plague of Hail*. [Col. 0574D] BALUZE.]

## VI

The principle underlying all these things is one that misleads and deceives, leading a foolish and credulous populace astray through illusions that blind them to the truth. They are impure and wandering spirits who, after becoming immersed in earthly vices and withdrawing from heavenly vigor through earthly contagion, do not cease—lost as they are [Note: [Col. 0573B] “Lost” is absent from Gronovius.]—to ruin others and, corrupted themselves, to instill the error of their corruption.

The poets too know these beings as demons; Socrates proclaimed that he was instructed and guided according to a demon’s will, and it is from this that magicians derive their power to perform pernicious or ludicrous deeds. Yet Hostanes, the foremost of them, [Col. 0574A] both denies that the form of the true God can be beheld and says that true angels [Note: [Col. 0573B] “Our angels,” Oxford variant readings. Perhaps *servants* was once read. Routh.] stand beside his throne. Plato agrees with him by a similar line of reasoning: while preserving one God, he calls the others angels or demons. Hermes Trismegistus likewise speaks of one God and acknowledges him to be incomprehensible and beyond estimation.

[Note: [Col. 0574D]

## VII.—They Envelop Falsehoods in Truths

Imitated from the sixth book of the *Aeneid*: “Enveloping truths in obscurities.” Saint Ambrose, book I of *On Duties*, chapter 16: “To envelop truths in obscurities.” The comedy *Querolus*: “This is plainly what I have often heard: to envelop truths in obscurities.” Minucius Felix: “They govern lots and produce oracles enveloped in many falsehoods.” Tertullian, book I *To the Nations*: “So that they may not interweave falsehoods with truths.” Sulpicius Severus, book II of the *Sacred History*, speaking of the eunuch Bagoas, says: “Things undefiled from a corrupt mouth that mingled truths with falsehoods.” BALUZE.

Even spirits slipping in. So the early editions before that of Manutius, in which the word “spirits” was cut out and omitted. Twenty-two ancient copies nevertheless contain it. BALUZE.

Secretly terrify the mind. From the excellent Verona manuscript. The common reading is “minds.” Minucius too, chapter XXVII, section 3, from which these words appear to have been copied, has “minds.” CELLARIUS.

Their assault ceases. Twelve ancient books read: [Col. 0575C] “When the assault or madness of their worshippers ceases.” BALUZE.

Although they are themselves liable to punishment, worthy of punishment. Salvian, *On the Governance of God*, book VI, p. 220: “crimes more liable to punishment.” Nor does the word lack ancient authority. Pliny, book XVIII, chapter 11: “Groats are pounded with a pestle by the penal labor of convicts,” that is, by labor performed as punishment. Thus Prudentius, in *Lawrence*, line 193, called the work of those condemned to the mines “penal labor.” CELLARIUS.

[p. 572] By our voice. The Verona manuscript: “not by our voice, but by our working.” BALUZE.

Might imitate. Although this reading is consistent in all the ancient books and all the editions, and also in Minucius, I nevertheless think that the words “might be able” do not fit this passage and that another expression should be restored, signifying that the pagans feared lest they be compelled or driven to imitate the Christians. Unless perhaps the words should be removed from this passage, so that it reads simply: “lest, once they know us, they either imitate us or be unable to condemn us.” Seneca, *Letter* VII: “You must either imitate or hate.” BALUZE.]

## VII

These spirits, therefore, hide beneath consecrated statues and images [Note: [Col. 0574B] “Gathered,” Lam.; “beneath consecrated,” Routh.]. By their breath they inspire the breasts of prophets, animate the fibers of entrails, govern the flights of birds, direct lots, and produce oracles. They always envelop falsehoods in truths, for they both are deceived and deceive. They disturb life and trouble sleep; even slipping as spirits into bodies [Note: [Col. 0574B] Wopkens, in *Miscellanea Critica*, vol. X, tome 1, on chapter 26 of Minucius, thinks that the phrase “into bodies” should be removed.], they secretly terrify minds, contort limbs, [Col. 0575A] break health, and provoke diseases [Note: [Col. 0575B] “With diseases,” NC. 2. Routh.] in order to compel people to worship them. Then, when they have been fattened by the reek of altars and the pyres of cattle, by releasing what they had [p. 227] bound they appear to have effected a cure. This is the remedy they provide when their assault ceases.

They have no other purpose than to call human beings away from God and turn them aside from understanding true religion toward superstition about themselves; and, although they are themselves liable to punishment, they seek companions for their punishment—people whom they have made sharers in their crime through error [Note: [Col. 0575B] “Through terror,” NC. 3. Routh.]. Yet when adjured by us through the true God, these spirits immediately yield and confess, and are compelled to depart from the bodies they possess. You may see them, by our voice and working [Note: [Col. 0575B] “Voice and prayer,” Bod. 3. Lam. Thu. Foss. Mich. Lin. Corb. Lin. Spir.], beaten by the scourges of hidden majesty, scorched by fire, stretched by the increasing propagation of their punishment, howling, groaning, and pleading; you may hear them confess, even in the hearing of those who worship them, whence they came and when they will depart. They either leap out at once or vanish gradually, according as the faith of the sufferer gives aid or the grace of the healer breathes upon him.

Hence they drive the populace to hatred of our name, so that people may begin to hate us before they know us, lest, once they know us, they should be able either to imitate us or be unable to condemn us.

[Note: [Col. 0575D]

[Col. 0575D] ## VIII.—The Brotherhood of the Thebans

See Rigault’s observations on Minucius, p. 189. BALUZE.

With the pyres at variance. After Eteocles and Polynices had died from wounds inflicted upon each other, the body of the former was placed upon a pyre to be burned; Creon, son of Menoetius, forbade the body of the latter to be given burial because he had come to attack his native land. Nevertheless, his sister Antigone and his wife Argia secretly carried away Polynices’ body by night and placed it upon the same pyre on which they had laid Eteocles. Hyginus relates this in Fable LXXII. I note in passing that in the same author, Fable LXXI, one should read “At Thebes the funeral is divided,” not “the smoke.” For the funeral was certainly divided by the Thebans, but not likewise the smoke rising from the pyre, since the devotion of the sister and wife prevented that from happening. CELLARIUS.

There is one king among the bees. Jerome in the *Letter to the Monk Rusticus*: “Even dumb animals and herds of wild beasts follow their own leaders. Among bees there are rulers.” Varro, book III, chapter 16, *On Agriculture*: “They follow their king wherever he goes, support him when weary, and, if he cannot fly, carry him upon their shoulders.” [Col. 0576B] See Lactantius, book III, chapter 10; Seneca, book I of *On Clemency*, chapter 9; Ovid, [Col. 0576C] book III of the *Fasti*; and Dio Chrysostom, Orations IV and XLVIII. BALUZE.

And since man dwells more spaciously. Minucius, ch. 32: “Since I, a man, dwell more spaciously” (*laxius*). We printed it so there, with Fulvius Ursinus, because Cicero, whom Minucius is accustomed to imitate, used *to dwell spaciously* of his own house in ch. 44. Yet all Cyprian’s manuscripts, if he copied Felix, display *more spaciously* (*latius*), so that I begin to doubt whether the former author too may not have written *latius*, as Sabaeus and François Baudouin read. CELLARIUS.]

## VIII

There is therefore one God, Lord of all [Note: [Col. 0576B] “The Lord is one God,” Gronovius]. [Col. 0576A] For that sublimity cannot have a partner, since it alone possesses all power. Let us borrow from earthly affairs too an illustration of divine sovereignty. When has a partnership in kingship ever begun in good faith, or ended without bloodshed? Thus the brotherhood of the Thebans [Note: [Col. 0576B] “Theban brothers,” Verona; this appears to be a gloss, Cellarius] was broken, and their discord, persisting even in death, continued in their opposing funeral pyres. A single kingdom cannot contain the Roman twins, though the single lodging of the womb made room for them both. Pompey and Caesar were related by marriage, yet the bond of kinship did not hold firm amid rival power. Nor should you marvel at this in the case of human beings, since all nature agrees in this respect. There is one king among the bees, one leader among the flocks, and one ruler among the herds: much more, then, is there one ruler of the world, who commands by his word all things whatsoever that exist, orders them by reason, and brings them to completion by his power.

[Col. 0576B] [Note: [Col. 0576C]

### IX.—I shall confine

Thus all the old editions and all the old copies, except the Pithoean and Metz manuscripts, in which *includam* is written. Manutius preferred this reading, as did others after him. The Bec manuscript has “may be confined” (*includatur*). The Foix manuscript reads: “Do you think that the power of such great majesty can be enclosed within a single little shrine?” To be sure, Minucius reads: “Shall I confine the power of such great majesty within a single little shrine?” But there the construction of the words is different. Novatian, *On the Trinity* [Col. 0576D], ch. 6: “Yet God is not contained, shut within a tabernacle.” Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II: “I know that our fathers’ shrines are within cities; nor do I follow the Persian Magi, on whose advice Xerxes is said to have burned the temples of Greece because they confined within walls the gods, for whom all things ought to be open and free, and whose temple and home this entire world was.” Tacitus writes thus of the Germans: “Moreover, from the greatness of the heavenly beings they judge that the gods should neither be confined within walls nor represented in any likeness of the human face.” Aelius Lampridius, in his *Alexander Severus*: “Hadrian had ordered temples without images to be built in every city.” Saint Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, ch. 2: “Do walls, then, make Christians?” BALUZE.

To be dedicated in our own. Lactantius, *On the Wrath of God*, ch. 23: “Let God be consecrated for us, not in temples, but in our heart.” The same author, *Institutes*, book V, ch. 8, says that God’s temple is not made of stones or clay, but is the human being himself, who bears the image of God. BALUZE.

[Col. 0577B] Do not seek a name for God. Thus the excellent Verona manuscript, and certain manuscripts of Minucius, ch. 18, although there we printed “of God” (*Dei*), following Meursius; he, however, relied chiefly upon Cyprian’s reading, which, as we have seen, is doubtful. CELLARIUS.

[Col. 0577C] God is his name. Below, *Testimonies*, book II, ch. 7, from Isaiah: “I am the Lord God; this is my name.” And in Psalm 67: “God is his name.” BALUZE.

The designation “of God.” Pamelius printed “God” (*Deus*). So too Rigaltius and the English edition. But almost all the old manuscripts and the editions of Manutius and Morel have “of God” (*Dei*). Anyone who considers the matter attentively will readily perceive that this is certainly better. BALUZE.]

## IX

He cannot be seen, for he is brighter than sight; nor comprehended, for he is purer than touch; nor appraised, for he is greater than perception. And therefore we appraise him worthily precisely when we call him inappraisable. What temple, indeed, could God have [Note: [Col. 0576B] “of God,” Oxford], whose temple is the whole world? And since man dwells more spaciously [Note: [Col. 0576B] Perhaps “more freely,” Routh], shall I confine the power of such great majesty within a single little shrine? He must be dedicated in our [Col. 0577A] mind and consecrated in our breast. Do not seek a name for God [Note: [Col. 0577B] “of God,” Thuaneus, Foix, Michaelinus, Victorinus]: God is his name. Names are needed where a multitude must be distinguished by the particular marks of appellations; for God, who alone exists, the designation “of God” is the whole. Therefore he is one, and is wholly diffused everywhere [Note: [Col. 0577B] “He himself is diffused everywhere,” Pamelius, Thuaneus, Foix, Verona, Bodleian 3]. For even the common people naturally acknowledge God in many sayings, when the mind and soul are reminded of their author and ruler. We frequently hear it said: “O God,” “God sees,” “I commend it to God,” “May God repay you,” “What God wills,” and “If God grants it.” And this is the culmination of guilt: to refuse to acknowledge him whom you cannot fail to know.

[Note: [Col. 0577C]

### X.—First with the Jews

Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*: “The Jews enjoyed favor with God because of the remarkable righteousness and faith of their original founders.” BALUZE.

Negligent. The old copies vary greatly at this point. Some of them, together with the old editions, have: “Negligent of discipline, they afterward became proud.” Others omit both “negligent” and “proud,” and have only: “and afterward became undisciplined.” The Foix manuscript reads: “But afterward, neglecting discipline, they became disobedient.” BALUZE.—Undisciplined. The Vulgate translator of the Book of Wisdom also used this word, [Col. 0577D] ch. 17, verse 1. Old Glossary: *indisciplinatus*, ἀμαθής, “ignorant, unlearned.” LINDNER.]

## X

As for the fact that Christ exists, and how salvation came to us through him, this is the order and this the rationale. At first the Jews enjoyed favor with God. Thus in former times they were righteous; thus their ancestors obeyed religious obligations [Col. 0577B] [Note: [Col. 0577B] “They obeyed.” But Cambridge]. Hence both the loftiness of their kingdom flourished and the greatness of their race [Note: [Col. 0577B] “in lineage,” Manutius, Monacensis] arose. But afterward, becoming negligent, undisciplined, and proud, and inflated by confidence in their fathers [Col. 0578A], they despised the divine commandments and lost the favor granted to them. How profane their life became, and what guilt they incurred by violating religion, they themselves also testify: although silent in speech, they confess it by their fate. Scattered and wandering, they roam about; exiles from their own soil and sky, they are tossed among dwellings belonging to others.

[Note: [Col. 0577D]

### XI.—Much more faithful

Tertullian, speaking in the *Apologeticum* of the Jews, who had lost God’s favor through their own fault and were exiles from their own sky and soil, says that holy utterances had foretold to them that, in the final courses of the age, God would choose for himself, from every nation, people, and place, worshippers much more faithful. Lactantius, ch. 43 of the *Epitome*: “He would gather for himself from the foreign nations another, more faithful people.” Several old manuscripts and editions here in Cyprian instead prefer “much better.” The Foix manuscript reads: “much better in obedience and stronger in faith.” The Burgundian, Tournai, and Grenoble manuscripts read: “of much better obedience and stronger faith.” Rigaltius testifies in his *Observations on Tertullian’s Apologeticum* that he read it thus in an ancient copy. Three other old manuscripts have: “of much more faithful and better [Col. 0578B] obedience.” The Tours manuscript: “much stronger in faith.” The Chartres manuscript: “much more compliant.” But *feliciores*, “more fortunate,” is written instead of *faciliores*, “more compliant,” in the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul. BALUZE.

Which, once received. The Foix manuscript reads: “once this too had been received, the Jews, after despising his majesty, lost his indulgence. [Col. 0578C] Therefore the arbiter of the discipline of this favor,” etc. In the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul and in the Bec manuscript these words are absent: “which, once received, the Jews had lost by despising religious obligations.” BALUZE.

573 Illuminator and teacher. See Tertullian in the passage cited just above. BALUZE.—Thus it is also read in the most ancient handwritten book: “teacher of the common people.” But the other reading is preferable because it is more ancient, since the words were drawn from Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, where they occur in this order in ch. 21: “Therefore the Son of God was announced as the arbiter and master of this favor and discipline, the illuminator and guide of the human race.” LINDNER.

The Spirit puts on flesh. Rigaltius printed this in his first edition of this book, issued with Minucius Felix, and says that the older copies have it thus. Some old manuscripts and the standard editions have: “He puts on flesh with the Holy Spirit cooperating.” The word “cooperating” is absent from the Bec manuscript. The Reims, Dijon, recent Victorinus, and one Royal manuscript have: “He is clothed in flesh by the [Col. 0578D] Holy Spirit.” Thus too it was corrected from an old book in the margin of the Lyon edition of 1544. So too it was written in Florus’s manuscript. An ancient Saint-Germain manuscript of the highest quality has: “The Holy Spirit is clothed in flesh.” Pamelius found this wording in four manuscripts. Erasmus retained the common reading, but placed in the margin: “The Holy Spirit puts on flesh.” This reading is to be preferred, both because it is supported by old manuscripts and because the word “cooperating” appears to be a gloss. It is, moreover, customary among the ancient Fathers to call Christ the Holy Spirit. Hermas, book III, *Similitude* 5, speaks thus of Christ’s body: “This body, therefore, into which the Holy Spirit was brought.” Justin, *Apology* II: “It is therefore impious to understand the Spirit and power of God as anything other than the Word,” etc. Irenaeus, book V, ch. 1, after saying, “The Holy Spirit descended upon Mary,” immediately adds: “The Word of the Father [Col. 0579C] and the Spirit of God, united to the ancient substance formed in Adam, made man living and perfect.” Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, no. 18: “Thus, finally, man is with God, when the flesh of man is with the Spirit of God.” See much more in the most learned Benedictine monk Pierre Coustant’s preface to the works of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, §57. I add here, moreover, that the scholastic theologians debate whether the Holy Spirit can be called the father of Jesus Christ. See Thomas of Strasbourg, book III, distinction 4, article 4. BALUZE. (Cf. Nourry’s observations on this passage, the dissertation in the preceding volume, and Lumper, *History of the Fathers*, vol. XI, p. 116 ff.).—Thus from the Benevento manuscript: the others read, “The Holy Spirit puts on flesh”; if this is Cyprian’s genuine wording, the Spirit himself must be understood as the λόγος (*Logos*, “Word”). The standard editions insert “cooperating,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Three notable manuscripts have “descends”; others, “enters.” LINDNER.]

## XI

Moreover, God had foretold that, as the age declined and the end of the world was now drawing near, God would choose for himself from every nation, people, and place worshippers much more faithful and of better obedience [Note: [Col. 0577B] The words “and of better obedience” are absent from some editions, but present in Gronovius. “Better in obedience and stronger in faith,” Leipzig edition, approved by Routh from the new manuscripts Oxford 1 and 2, Tew, Drury. “Of better obedience and stronger faith”], 228 who would draw pardon from the divine gifts [Note: [Col. 0578B] “They would draw”; “of this,” Thuaneus, Michaelinus, Victorinus], which, once received, the Jews had lost by despising religious obligations. Therefore the Word and Son of God is sent as arbiter [Note: [Col. 0578B] “Arbiter of pardon, favor, and discipline,” Oxford, Pamelius, Rigaltius, Lindner. “Therefore arbiter of pardon and favor,” Leipzig] and master of this favor and discipline [Note: [Col. 0578B] “Descends,” Pamelius, Laudianus, Verona, Tew, Drury, Meerman, three new Oxford manuscripts, Cellarius, Lindner, Routh]; through all the Prophets of old he was proclaimed [Col. 0578B] as the illuminator and teacher of the human race [Note: [Col. 0578B] “Is proclaimed,” Thuaneus, Victorinus, Michaelinus. “Guide,” New Collection 1 and 2, Drury 1, Tew, Cellarius, Gronovius, Lindner, Routh]. He is the power of God, he his reason, he his wisdom and glory. He enters into a virgin; the Holy Spirit puts on flesh; God is mingled with man [Col. 0579A]. He is our God, he is Christ, who, as mediator between the two, puts on man so that he may lead man to the Father. Christ willed to be what man is, so that man too might be able to be what Christ is.

[Note: [Col. 0579C]

### XII.—The Jews also knew

These words and nearly everything that follows have been taken from ch. 12 of Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*. BALUZE.

[Col. 0579D] Wisdom. In the Burgundian manuscript it is written: “punished with the blindness of foolishness.” BALUZE.]

## XII

The Jews also knew that Christ was to come. For he was always announced to them as the Prophets admonished them [Note: [Col. 0579B] “This was always,” Pamelius, Vir, Gronovius. “With seven manuscripts and the first edition admonishing,” Routh]. But since his twofold advent was signified—one in which he would fulfill the role and example of a man, and the other in which he would reveal himself as God [Note: [Col. 0579B] “Would reveal.” Not Lindner]—they failed to understand the first advent, which came beforehand, hidden in suffering, and believe only in the one that will be manifest in power. That the Jewish people could not understand this was the consequence of their sins. They were so punished with blindness of wisdom and understanding that, being unworthy of life, they had life before their eyes and did not see it.

[Col. 0579B] [Note: [Col. 0579D]

### XIII.—They had believed him to be merely a man

Rufinus, on Psalm 2, *On Christ against the Jews*: “Because they saw him humble in the flesh, they despised him with a proud and blind heart.” Likewise on Psalm 13: “You have despised the humble advent of the Son of God.” BALUZE.

Governed Syria. “Governed” is correct, because Tacitus called Pontius Pilate a procurator, book XV, ch. 44; but “Syria” is less accurate, since it was under a consular legate. Pilate was governor only of Palestine—and not all of it, but the ethnarchy of Archelaus, reduced to provincial status, that is, Judaea and Samaria. Josephus, *Jewish War*, book II, ch. 14, at the beginning: Πεμφθεὶς δὲ εἰς Ἰουδαίαν ἐπίτροπος ὑπὸ Τιβερίου Πίλατος, “Pilate was sent by Tiberius as procurator into Judaea.” CELLARIUS. Our author errs together with Tertullian, presbyter of the church of Carthage, [Col. 0580C] whom he follows in the *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, where he says: “The leaders of the Jews were so exasperated by his teaching . . . that at last, when Jesus was brought before Pontius Pilate, who at that time governed Syria on Rome’s behalf, they extorted from him, through the violence of their votes, permission to have Jesus delivered to the cross.” LINDNER.

Not merely that he might experience death. The word “merely” does not occur in most manuscripts. Thus “to experience death” will be ἰδεῖν διαφθοράν, “to see corruption,” as the Greek translators rendered Psalm 16:10, and Luke with them in Acts 2:31. LINDNER.

He appeared to his disciples such as he had been before. Gronovius printed it thus because Rigaltius admits that the penultimate word had accidentally dropped out of his edition; the Oxford manuscript supplies the fourth word. LINDNER.]

## XIII

Accordingly, when Christ Jesus, in fulfillment of what had previously been foretold by the Prophets, expelled demons from human beings by his word and the command of his voice, restored paralytics, cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, gave the lame the power to walk, brought the dead back to life, compelled the elements to serve him, the winds to minister, the seas to obey, and the lower regions to yield, the Jews—who, because of the humility of his flesh and body, had believed him to be merely a man [Col. 0580A]—judged him, because of the freedom of his power, to be a magician. Their teachers and leaders, that is, those whom he refuted by both his learning and wisdom, were inflamed with anger [Note: [Col. 0579B] “With anger kindled and indignation aroused,” Thuaneus, Foix, Victorinus, Michaelinus, Lindner] and roused to indignation, and persecuted him [Note: [Col. 0579B] Baluze and Routh add “and added”; why, I do not know, says Goldhorn]. At last, after seizing him, they handed him over to Pontius Pilate, who at that time governed Syria on Rome’s behalf, demanding his crucifixion and death with violent and persistent votes [Note: [Col. 0579B] “With persistent votes.” Pamelius, Thuaneus, [Col. 0580B] Foix, Michaelinus, Victorinus, and Corbie reject the rest; Lindner encloses it in brackets] [Note: [Col. 0580B] “They demanded,” Laudianus, Victorinus].

[Note: [Col. 0580C]

### XIV.—Bound

Nine old manuscripts exhibit this reading, which I consider better. Certain others have “joined”; one old manuscript and some old editions have “conquered.” This may show that “bound” had originally been written, but was later corrected in antiquity so that “conquered” should be read. The reading “bound” therefore appears better, as though Christ had appeared to his disciples [Col. 0580D] with the bands and strips in which his body had been laid in the tomb, together with the linen cloth in which Joseph of Arimathea had wrapped his body. For he also showed the unbelieving his hands and feet, in which the marks of the nails had been impressed; he showed them also to the unbelieving Thomas, as related in ch. 20 of the Gospel according to John. BALUZE.

For forty days. This is entirely certain; I would not mention it had I not seen “on the fiftieth day” written in ch. 47 of Lactantius’s *Epitome* in Pfaff’s edition. For Lactantius himself wrote “forty” in book IV, ch. 21. BALUZE.

Taken up into heaven. There is no mention here of Christ’s descent into the lower regions. But Cyprian recalls this doctrine in the second book of the *Testimonies* and proves it from testimonies of the Old and New Testaments. For ch. 24 reads: “That he would not [Col. 0581A] be conquered by death, nor would he remain among the dead.” And ch. 25: “That on the third day he would rise from the lower regions.” [Col. 0581B] Although writers earlier than Cyprian likewise proclaim the same doctrine, it nevertheless does not appear to have been expressed in explicit words in certain creeds, because the descent into the lower regions seemed sufficiently indicated when Christ was said to have been buried. Hence Rufinus, in his exposition of the Creed, says: “It should certainly be known that the words ‘he descended into the lower regions’ are not added in the Creed of the Roman Church, nor is this phrase found in the Eastern Churches; the force of the expression nevertheless appears to be the same in the statement that he was buried.” From this it may readily be concluded that Rufinus was wrongly criticized by Hendrik Vitus Oosthove in his book *On Christ’s Descent into the Lower Regions*. For Rufinus, who elsewhere writes in more than one passage that Christ descended into the lower regions, does not say that Christ did not descend there, but only that “he descended into the lower regions” is not found in the Creed of the Roman Church or in those of the Eastern Churches. Even in the time of Pope Innocent IV it was absent from the creed that the Catholicos of the Jacobites sent to him to prove that he held the faith of the Roman Church. Oderic Raynaldus published it under the year 1247 [Col. 0581C]. See Bellarmine, *On the Word of God*, book II, ch. 6, and Rigaltius on Tertullian’s book 574, *The Prescription against Heretics*. See also [Col. 0582A] Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s *Apology*, where he discusses Christ’s descent into the lower regions at length, and [Col. 0582B] Pierre du Faur de Saint-Jory, *Agonisticon*, book III, ch. 10, p. 265. BALUZE.

Give sight. That is, “bestow vision.” A word of Tertullian, whom Cyprian frequently used as his master. *On Repentance*, ch. 12: “If the swallow has blinded its chicks, it knows how to give them sight again with its celandine.” And metaphorically in *On Modesty*, ch. 8: “In embellishing garments with purple spots.” LINDNER.]

## XIV

That they would do this he himself had foretold, and the testimony of all the Prophets had likewise preceded it, declaring that he must suffer—not merely that he might experience death [Note: [Col. 0580B] Thus Thuaneus, Foix, Victorinus, Corbie, Michaelinus, Laudianus, Vossius 3, Spirensis, Remensis, Erasmus, Manutius, Routh, Leipzig. “Merely death,” Oxford. Lindner brackets “merely”], but that he might conquer it—and that, after suffering, he would return again to the realms above, so as to demonstrate the power of divine majesty. The course of events therefore fulfilled the promise. For when crucified, forestalling the executioner’s task, he voluntarily yielded up his spirit; and on the [Col. 0580B] third day he voluntarily rose again from the dead. He appeared to his disciples such [Note: [Col. 0580B] Routh omits “such,” following New Collection 2 and 3. “Such as he had been,” New Collection 1, Drury 1, Tew, Meerman] as he had been, presenting himself to the beholders so that he might be recognized, at once bound [Note: [Col. 0580B] “Joined,” Oxford. “With joined [members],” MR, Verona, Lindner, Routh, Goldhorn] and visibly possessing the solidity of bodily substance. He remained for forty days, so that they might be instructed by him in the life-giving commandments and learn what they were to teach. Then, surrounded by a cloud, he was taken up into heaven, so that as victor he might bring to the Father the man whom he loved, whom he put on, and whom he protected from death [Col. 0581A]. He is now to come from heaven for the punishment of the devil and the judgment of the human race [Note: [Col. 0581A] “Against,” conjectured by Routh], with the might of an avenger and the authority of a judge. Meanwhile, his disciples, dispersed throughout the world at the admonition of their Master and God, were to give commandments leading to salvation [Note: [Col. 0581A] “To give . . . to lead . . . to give sight,” Vossius 3], lead people from the error of darkness to the way of light, and give the blind and ignorant the sight by which to recognize the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0582B]

### XV.—Pain, the witness of truth

See what we said above on a similar subject in the *Letter to Demetrianus*, p. 563. Jerome, in his apologetic letter to Asella: “Tortures elicit truth more readily than laughter does.” BALUZE.

Might be proclaimed. The Verona manuscript and seven other old manuscripts have “might be proved.” BALUZE.

Leader of light. The Foix manuscript reads “leader of our hope.” Saint Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book III, ch. 7, calls Christ the leader of humility. BALUZE.

## XV

And lest the proof should be less solid and the confession concerning Christ overly delicate, they are tested through tortures, crosses, [Col. 0582A] and many kinds of punishment. Pain, which is the witness of truth, is applied, so that Christ, the Son of God, who is believed to have been given to humanity for life, might be proclaimed not only by the heralding of the voice but also by the testimony of suffering. Him, therefore, we accompany; him we follow; him we have as the guide of our journey, the leader of light, and the author of salvation, promising both heaven and the Father to those who seek and believe. We Christians shall be what Christ is, if we have imitated Christ [Note: [Col. 0581A] “Followed,” Pamelius, Laudianus, Thuaneus, Victorinus, Foix, Michaelinus, Nov., New Collection, [Col. 0582A] Drury 1, Meerman, Vienna, Remboldt, Froben, Hernagius, Lindner, Routh].
