# 229 BOOK ON MORTALITY

[Note: [Col. 0581D]

### On Mortality

Saint Augustine frequently mentions this book with praise, but especially in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 14, where he says that it is commendably known to many and indeed to almost everyone who loves ecclesiastical literature. The same author, in his letter to Vitalis, says that Cyprian’s whole purpose in this passage is that we should know that faithful people of good character are to be congratulated when they die, since they are removed from the temptations of life and will thereafter remain in most blessed security. Eusebius also mentions this book in his *Chronicle*: “A pestilential disease,” he says, “seized many provinces throughout the whole world, especially Alexandria and Egypt, as Dionysius writes; Cyprian’s book *On Mortality* is also a witness.” See there the notes of Joseph Scaliger. [Col. 0582D] Jordanes gives the same account in his book *On Gothic Affairs*, where he writes that this calamity was tearfully described by Dionysius: “It was also recorded,” he says, “by our venerable martyr of Christ, Bishop Cyprian, in the book entitled *On Mortality*.” Eusebius places that pestilence after the death of Pope Cornelius; Petavius, in *On the Doctrine of Times*, book XIII, places it in the preceding year. Yet Christoph Sand includes this treatise of Cyprian among those falsely attributed to the holy martyr. The celebrated Pearson refutes him splendidly in the *Cyprianic Annals*. It is a wretched thing for a man to be excessively audacious.]

(C)

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0581C]

The blessed Pontius briefly explains the subject in his *Life of Cyprian*: “From this,” he says, “Christians of more tender feeling over the loss of their loved ones—or, what is more serious, of weaker faith—might be consoled by hope of things to come.” For first, after teaching that afflictions of this kind had been foretold by Christ, he teaches that mortality, or pestilence, is not to be feared, because it leads to immortality [Col. 0582C], and hence that faith is lacking in one who does not hasten toward better things. Nor is it surprising that the Christian shares the evils of this life with the Gentiles, since Christians must labor in this age more than others [Col. 0582D]. Accordingly, following the example of the saints Job and Tobit, patience is necessary, and one must not murmur. Unless the struggle has first taken place, victory cannot be attained; and although [Col. 0583A] diseases are shared by virtues and vices alike, death is nevertheless not shared in the same way: the righteous are carried off to refreshment, but the unrighteous to punishment. He next answers the tacit objection that people are deprived of martyrdom by this mortality: martyrdom is not within our power, and even a spirit prepared for martyrdom is crowned by God as judge. Finally, he teaches that the dead should not be mourned in such a way that we become a stumbling block to the Gentiles, as though we lacked hope of the resurrection. Indeed, if the day of our own summons comes, we must depart from here to the Lord with a willing spirit, especially since we are migrating to our homeland. There a great number of our loved ones awaits us; a dense and abundant multitude longs for us, already secure concerning its own immortality yet still concerned for our salvation. Eusebius mentions [Col. 0583B] the circumstances in which Cyprian wrote this book in his *Chronicle*: “A pestilential disease,” he says, “seized many provinces throughout the whole world, especially Alexandria and Egypt, as Dionysius writes; Cyprian’s book *On Mortality* is also a witness.”

[Note: [Col. 0583C]

The present mortality. Pontius describes this miserable calamity elegantly in his *Life of Saint Cyprian*.

Of a delicate mind. Tertullian, in *On the Spectacles*: [Col. 0583D] “You are delicate, Christian, if you desire pleasure in this age as well.”

Is sufficient. I judged that it should be written thus on the authority of the Verona and Séguier manuscripts, and because the same reading is found in twenty other manuscripts of ours and in ten English manuscripts. The old editions and five old manuscripts have “is able.”

Unconquered. Two old manuscripts have “incorrupt.”]

229 Although among very many of you, dearly beloved brothers, there is a sound mind, firm faith, and a devout soul, which is not disturbed by the frequency of the present mortality but, like a strong and steadfast rock, itself breaks the turbulent assaults of the world and the violent waves of the age without being broken by them, and is not conquered by trials but proved through them, I nevertheless observe that some among the people stand less firmly—whether from weakness of spirit, littleness of faith, attachment to secular life, the softness of their sex, or, what is more serious, error concerning the truth—and do not exercise the divine and unconquered strength of their breast. The matter was therefore not to be passed over in silence [Col. 0583C] or left unspoken. Rather, insofar as our modest ability is sufficient, the sluggishness of a delicate mind must be restrained with full vigor and with discourse drawn from the Lord’s teaching, and one who has now begun to be a man of God and of Christ must be regarded as worthy of God and Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0583D]

### II.—Hopes

The English editors printed “breathes,” on the authority of seven old copies. That is certainly a good reading, and two of our old manuscripts confirm it. But because the rest and the other editions have “hopes,” which is also a good reading, we were unwilling to change it.

Disturbance. Formerly “hesitation” was read. But I found this reading in only three ancient manuscripts. The reading I have retained is found in twenty-four of our manuscripts and seven English ones, most notably the Verona manuscript.

Endurance of things to come. Hincmar cites this passage in vol. I, p. 72, from the book *On Mortality*, though [Col. 0584C] Sirmond notes in the margin that it was taken from near the end of *On the Unity of the Church*.

Foretold. This too had to be printed on the authority [Col. 0584D] of the old manuscripts and editions. Erasmus wrote “taught,” as did Manutius. I found that reading in only three ancient manuscripts. The other reading, which is ours, is preferred by nineteen of our manuscripts and eleven English ones. The Verona manuscript also had it thus.

The kingdom of God, brothers. Saint Augustine quotes this passage in *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, ch. 8.

577 To begin. The Sorbonne manuscript has “in perpetuity.” Another old manuscript reads: “to reign perpetually with Christ.” I took this last reading from the margin of the Lyon edition of 1544, where some learned man entered variant readings drawn from ancient manuscripts. Whenever I cite those readings—to mention this too in passing—I state simply that I have taken them from one old manuscript, lest anyone think that I am misleading him because I do not say where the reading was obtained.]

## II

For one who serves as a soldier of God, dearly beloved brothers, [Col. 0584A] who is stationed in the heavenly camp and already hopes for divine [glory?—the noun governed by *divinam* is absent from the supplied Latin], must recognize what he is, so that there may be in us no trembling and no disturbance at the storms and tempests of the world. For the Lord foretold that these things would come, instructing, teaching, preparing, and strengthening the people of his Church by the exhortation of his provident voice for the endurance of all things to come. He announced and foretold that wars, famines, earthquakes, and pestilences would arise in one place after another. And lest an unexpected and novel fear of hostile events strike us down, he warned beforehand that adversities would increase more and more in the final times. See, the things that were spoken are taking place; and since the things foretold beforehand are taking place, all the things promised will follow as well, for the Lord himself promises and says: “But when you see all these things taking place, know that the kingdom of God [Col. 0584B] is near” (Luke 21:31). The kingdom of God, dearly beloved brothers, has begun to draw near. As the world passes away, there now come the reward of life, the joy of eternal salvation, perpetual security [Note: [Col. 0583C] “Gladness”—thus almost all editions and Augustine, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians* IV.8. Baluze, without giving a reason: “Security” [Col. 0584C] (Goldhorn)], and possession of the paradise so recently lost; heavenly things now succeed earthly ones, great things small ones, and eternal things those that pass away. What room is there here for anxiety and concern? Who amid these things is trembling and sorrowful, except one who lacks hope and faith? It belongs to one who is unwilling to go to Christ to fear death. It belongs to one who does not believe that he will begin to reign with Christ to be unwilling to go to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0585C]

### III.—Canceled

Six of our manuscripts, as well as four cited by Pamelius, one Morel manuscript, and one English manuscript, have “conquered”; two others have “extinguished,” and another “expelled.” We have followed the better manuscripts, which have “canceled.”]

## III

For it is written that the righteous person lives by faith (Rom. 1:17). If you are righteous and live by faith, if you truly believe in Christ, why—since you are destined to be with Christ and are secure in the Lord’s promise—do you not embrace the fact that you are being summoned to Christ [Col. 0584C] and rejoice that you are being freed from the devil? Consider, finally, that righteous Simeon, who truly was righteous and observed God’s commandments with complete faith. When it had been divinely disclosed to him that he would not die before he had seen Christ, and the infant Christ had come into the temple with his mother, he recognized in the Spirit that Christ, concerning whom this had previously been foretold to him, had now been born [Col. 0585A]. Upon seeing him, he knew that he himself would soon die. Rejoicing, therefore, in the nearness of death and secure in the imminence of his summons, he received the child into his hands, 230 and, blessing the Lord, cried out and said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30). He was plainly proving and testifying that peace then comes to God’s servants, that free and tranquil rest then comes, when, having been drawn out of these tempests of the world, we seek the harbor of the eternal dwelling-place and security, and when, this death having been canceled, we come to immortality. For that is true [Note: [Col. 0585C] Thus Baluze, without giving a reason; all the others have “our peace”] peace; that is trustworthy tranquility; that is steadfast, firm, and perpetual security.

[Note: [Col. 0585C]

### IV.—With greed

Saint Augustine quotes this passage [Col. 0585D] in *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, ch. 10, and in *Against Julian*, book II, ch. 8.

With carnal vices. Augustine, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book VI, ch. 14: “This is the struggle that the aforementioned martyr carefully and eloquently explains in the book he composed *On Mortality*, saying, among other things, that we have a constant and burdensome struggle with carnal vices and worldly enticements.”

Constant. The old editions and seven old manuscripts have “constant, unremitting, and burdensome.” So too four English manuscripts. But many more do not have “and unremitting.” Those words are also absent from Augustine in the passages about to be cited. Yet at the beginning of the book *On Works and Almsgiving*, p. 237, one reads “constant and unremitting activity.”]

## IV

Moreover, what else is carried on in the world each day but a battle against the devil? What else but combat against his darts and weapons in constant conflicts [Col. 0585B]? We have a struggle with greed, with sexual impurity, with anger, and with ambition; we have a constant and burdensome contest with carnal vices and worldly enticements. The human mind, besieged and hemmed in on every side by the devil’s assault [Note: [Col. 0585C] “Surrounded and hemmed in,” Laudianus, Eboracensis, Bodleian 3 and 4], scarcely manages to meet each attack, scarcely to resist it. If greed is laid low, lust rises up; if lust is restrained, ambition takes its place; if ambition is despised, anger provokes, pride inflates, drunkenness entices, envy breaks concord, and jealousy severs friendship. You are forced to curse, though the divine law forbids it; you are compelled to swear, though it is not permitted.

[Note: [Col. 0585D]

### V.—The devil’s swords

In the Laetiense manuscript one reads “snares,” with “or swords” written above the line. From this arose the discrepancy among the readings in the old manuscripts. Some preferred “snares,” others “swords.” One of my manuscripts has “snares [Col. 0586C] and swords.” Pamelius notes that he saw “snares” written in four old manuscripts, but retained the other reading because it occurs in Augustine.

[When we shall have seen.] Twenty-six ancient manuscripts have *quis vel qui viderit* (“whoever—or he who—shall have seen”). Fourteen others prefer *credendi* (“of believing”) or *credere* (“to believe”).]

V. The soul daily suffers so many persecutions [Note: [Col. 0585C] “The mind is daily buffeted by so many persecutions,” Voss. 1; NC. 2. So also in the book *On Patience*.], the heart is beset by so many dangers; and does it please us to remain here long amid [Col. 0585C] the devil’s swords, when we should rather crave and desire, with death coming more swiftly to our aid [Note: [Col. 0585C] “With swift death,” Pem.; Voss. 2; NC. 2.], to hasten to Christ, since he himself instructs us and says [Note: [Col. 0586C] “And admonishes,” Lam.; Voss. 1; Ebor.; NC. 1; Bod. 2, 3.]: [Col. 0586A] “Amen, amen, I say to you: you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; you shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall turn into joy” (John 16:20). Who would not wish to be free from sorrow? Who would not hasten to enter into joy? And when our sorrow shall turn into joy, the Lord himself again declares, saying: “I shall see you again [Note: [Col. 0586C] “But again,” Lam.; Voss. 1; Ebor.; NC. 1; Voss. 1, 2.], and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (ibid. 22). Since, therefore, to see Christ is to rejoice, and there can be no joy for us unless we have seen Christ, what blindness of mind, what madness it is to love the afflictions, punishments, and tears of the world, and not rather to hasten toward a joy that can never be taken away!

VI. This happens, most beloved brothers, because faith is lacking, because no one believes that the things promised by [Col. 0586B] God are true—God who is truthful, whose word is eternal and steadfast for believers. If a serious and reputable man promised you something, you would surely put faith in the one making the promise [Note: [Col. 0586C] “You would have faith in the one making the promise,” Lam.; Ebor.; NC. 1; Voss. 1, 2.], nor would you believe that you could be misled or deceived by one whom you knew to stand by his words and actions. Now God speaks with you, and you waver faithlessly with an unbelieving mind! God promises you immortality and eternity when you depart from this world, and you doubt! This is to have no knowledge of God at all; this is to offend Christ, the lord and teacher of believers [Note: [Col. 0586C] “Teacher of believing,” Veron.; Ren.; Paris; Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1, d; Voss. 1, 2; Bod. 2, 4; Manut. “Teacher of believers, by the sin,” Routh; Goldhorn.], by the sin of unbelief; this is, while established in the Church, to have no faith in the house of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0586D]

VII.—*Of advantage.* It is doubtful whether the reading should be *utilitatis* (“of advantage”) or *humilitatis* (“of humility”). Four manuscripts prefer *utilitatis*, with *vel humilitatis* (“or, of humility”) above the line. Two others have only *utilitatis*; another two only *humilitatis*. Copyists were therefore free to insert whichever reading they preferred. I would gladly prefer *humilitatis*, because it is certain that Christ was a teacher and master of humility, as Cyprian himself calls him in Letter LVI, p. 91, to the Thibaritans; Jerome in the Letter to Antonius; Augustine in chapter 31 of Book XXXIII *On Virginity* and elsewhere; Saint Ambrose in Book III, chapter 7, *On the Faith*; and Caesarius of Arles at the end of the eleventh of the Homilies published by us. In his third sermon Peter of Blois calls him “the humble master and teacher of humility.” This is also supported by Tertullian’s statement in *On the Veiling of Virgins* that nothing is dearer to God than humility. I have nevertheless retained *utilitatis*, because this reading is good and is found in the more accurate manuscripts.

[Col. 0587D] *The blessed apostle.* Saint Augustine cites this passage in Book IV, chapter 10, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*.]

VII. Christ himself, the master of our salvation and advantage, shows how greatly it benefits us to leave the world. When his disciples were saddened because he said that he was now [Col. 0586C] going to depart, he addressed them, saying: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father” (John 14:23), plainly teaching and showing that when [Col. 0587A] those dear to us whom we love leave the world, we should rejoice rather than grieve. Mindful of this, the blessed apostle Paul states in his Letter: “For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21); he reckons it the greatest gain no longer to be held by the snares of the world [Note: [Col. 0587C] “By worldly snares,” Ar.; Ben.; Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Voss. 1, 2; Lam.; Ebor.], no longer to become liable to any sins or vices of the flesh, but, released from crushing afflictions and freed from the venomous jaws of the devil [Note: [Col. 0587C] “Of the hunting devil,” Morel.], to set out, at Christ’s summons, toward the joy of eternal salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0587D]

VIII.—*May Christ lead us.* I have written this on the authority of four ancient copies, in place of what was previously read, “the Spirit.” In two of those four manuscripts, however, “Christ” is written in the manner in which “Spirit” is sometimes customarily written as an abbreviation, and above the line is written “or, the Spirit.” Furthermore, in ancient manuscripts of the works of Saint Cyprian and other ancient ecclesiastical writers, I have often seen “Spirit” written for “Christ” and conversely—most notably in the author of the book *On Rebaptism*, who, on p. 364, quoting the passage from the First Letter of John that reads, “Christ is the truth,” wrote, “The Spirit is the truth.” I know that Christ is elsewhere called “spirit,” even in Cyprian; but since we possess another and easier reading, there is no need to retain one capable of causing difficulty and introducing obscurity.]

VIII. Yet some 231 are disturbed because the violence of this disease attacks our people equally with the Gentiles—as though the Christian had believed for this purpose: that, immune from contact with evils, he might enjoy the world and this present age in happiness, rather than that, after suffering every adversity here, he might be reserved for future joy. Some are disturbed that this mortality is [Col. 0587B] common to us and to others. For what in this world do we not share with others, so long as this common flesh remains according to the law of our first birth? As long as we are here in the world, we are joined to the human race by our common condition of flesh, though separated from it in spirit. Thus, until this corruptible nature puts on incorruption and this mortal nature receives immortality (1 Cor. 15:53), and Christ [Note: [Col. 0587C] “The Spirit leads us,” common reading; Oxford; Routh; Lips.] leads us to God the Father, all the discomforts of the flesh are common to us and to the human race. Thus, when the earth is barren and yields no produce, famine makes no distinction among people. Thus, when a city has been seized by hostile invasion, captivity lays waste to all alike. And when clear skies withhold rain, there is one drought for everyone. And when jagged rocks crush [Col. 0587C] a ship [Note: [Col. 0588C] “Shatter,” Lam.; Lin.; NC. 1; Ebor.; Bod. 4.], shipwreck is common without exception to all who sail in it. Pain of the eyes, attacks of fever, and sickness of every limb are common to us and to others so long as this common flesh is carried about in the world.

IX. Indeed, if the Christian knows and holds fast under what condition and under what law he has believed, he will know that he must labor in the world more than others, since he must struggle all the more against the devil’s assaults. Divine Scripture teaches and forewarns us, saying: “Son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.” And again: “Endure in suffering, and in your humiliation have patience, because gold and silver [Note: [Col. 0588C] “And silver.” Thus Job; Lam.; Ebor.; Lin.; NC. 1, 2; Paris; Bod. 2, 3, 4.] are tested in fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation” (Sir. 2:1, 4–5).

[Note: [Col. 0587D]

X.—*Naked I shall go.* See Fronton du Duc’s notes on Chrysostom’s Homily VI *To the People of Antioch*. See [Col. 0588D] also Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 6.

*Foolish.* I changed this, since *insipientibus* (“senseless”) was formerly read, because I saw *ineptis* (“foolish”) written in seventeen of our manuscripts, in eight English manuscripts, and in Morel’s edition.

*There is none like him.* Ovid, speaking of Deucalion in Book I of the *Metamorphoses*:

> No better man than he, nor any greater lover  
> Of justice, ever lived.

*The works of God.* So also in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 214. Before these 578 words, however, “It is good to conceal a king’s secret” is written in the Tours and Foix manuscripts. This appears to derive from a gloss. We have therefore not added it to the text, although Tobias 12 reads: “It is good to hide a king’s secret.” Horace, *Epistles* XVIII:

> Nor should you ever pry into anyone’s secret.

*Your daughter-in-law.* These two words are absent from nineteen of our manuscripts and eleven English manuscripts. They are certainly unnecessary, since it is sufficient that they occur a little later, where this passage of Sacred Scripture is quoted.]

X. Thus Job, after the loss of his possessions, after the deaths of his children, and when grievously afflicted also with sores and worms, was not defeated but tested. Showing the patience of a devout mind amid his very struggles and sufferings, he said: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb; naked also shall I go beneath the earth. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so has it been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). And when [Col. 0588B] his wife also urged him, in impatience under the force of his pain, to say something against God in a complaining and spiteful voice, he answered: “You have spoken like one of the foolish women. If we have received good things from the Lord’s hand, why should we not endure evil things? In all these things that befell him, Job sinned nothing with his lips in the sight of the Lord” (Job 2:10). Therefore the Lord God bears witness to him, saying: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth, a man without complaint, a true worshiper of God” (ibid. 1:8).

And Tobias, after his magnificent works and the many glorious proclamations of his mercy, suffered blindness of the eyes; yet by fearing and blessing God in adversity, he grew in praise through the very ruin of his body. His own wife also tried to corrupt him, saying: “Where are your righteous deeds [Col. 0588C] [Note: [Col. 0588C] “And alms,” Voss. 2; Pem.]? Look at what you are suffering” (Tob. 2:14). But he, steadfast and firm in the fear of God and armed by religious faith to endure every suffering, did not yield in his pain to the temptation of his feeble wife, but by greater patience earned still greater favor from God. The angel Raphael afterward praises him, saying: “It is honorable to reveal and acknowledge the works of God. For when you and Sarah your daughter-in-law prayed, I offered the memorial of [Col. 0589A] your prayer in the sight of God’s glory. And when you buried the dead in simplicity, and because you did not hesitate to rise and leave your meal, but went away and buried the dead man, I was sent to test you; and again 232 God sent me to heal you and Sarah your daughter-in-law. For I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels who stand and minister before God’s glory” (Tob. 12:11–15).

[Note: [Col. 0589B]

XI.—*We must not murmur.* Jerome, in the Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus against Rufinus: “It belongs to a prudent man, even if he is in pain, to conceal his state of mind and dispel the cloud upon his heart by serenity of countenance.” Among the instructions that Saint Louis, king of France, gave his son as he was dying, this is especially found: “Furthermore, if the Lord permits you to suffer any tribulation, you should receive it graciously and with thanksgiving.” Fulgentius Placiades, Book II of the *Mythologies*: “For the wise man entrusts his pain either to kindness or to oblivion.” The same author had said above that oblivion is the medicine of miseries. Horace, Book II, Ode 3:

> Remember, amid hardship, to preserve  
> An even mind.

Oenone’s Letter to Paris, in Ovid:

> Whatever you deservedly suffer must be borne calmly;  
> A punishment that comes undeserved comes as a cause for grief.

See Aulus Gellius, Book XIII, chapter 26, and Philiscus’ discourse in Cassius Dio, Book XXXVIII, intended to raise the spirits of Cicero in exile and affliction.]

XI. The righteous always possessed this endurance; the apostles held to this discipline from the Lord’s law: not to mutter in adversity, but bravely and patiently to accept whatever happens in the world. The Jewish people, by contrast, always gave offense in this very matter, because they repeatedly murmured against God, as the Lord God testifies in Numbers, saying: “Let their murmuring against me cease, and they shall not die” (Num. 18:25). We must not murmur [Col. 0589B] in adversity, most beloved brothers, but patiently and bravely endure whatever happens, since it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). In Deuteronomy also, the Holy Spirit admonishes through Moses and says [Note: [Col. 0589B] “Admonishes … says,” Routh, from five manuscripts.]: “The Lord your God will afflict you and inflict hunger upon you, and it shall be known in your heart [Col. 0590A] whether you have faithfully kept his commandments or not” (Deut. 8:2). And again: “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with your whole heart and your whole soul” (Deut. 13:4).

[Note: [Col. 0589C]

XII.—*Though there be loss of property.* Rufinus on Psalm 95: “Let the earth be troubled, let the sea be troubled, let all the elements be troubled; let God’s servant remain undaunted.”

*Tests you.* So also in the book *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 9, and Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 15. See our notes [Col. 0589D] on Agobard, p. 9.

XII.—*The ship’s pilot.* We restored this passage, formerly defective because *nam* (“for”) was read instead of *navis* (“ship”), with the aid of two ancient copies. In three manuscripts the word *nam*, which elsewhere and in the editions is placed before *gubernator* (“pilot”), is absent. It is an error. Yet that very error shows that the reading we present is true. Lactantius, Book III, chapter 13: “A ship without a pilot is lost.” Pope Leo I, in the Letter to Rusticus: “Who will steer the ship amid the waves of the sea if the pilot departs?” Seneca, *On Providence*, chapter 4: “You recognize the pilot in a storm, the soldier in battle.” The same author, Letter 108: “A teacher of that kind can benefit me no more than a seasick pilot in a storm. One must hold the rudder against the snatching wave, struggle with the sea itself, and rescue the sails from the wind.” Cicero, Book II of *On Divination*: “Reason enables the physician to foresee an illness growing worse, the commander an ambush, [Col. 0590B] the pilot a storm.” John Chrysostom, in Letter CLXXXII to Venerius, says that a pilot is recognized in a storm and that the best physician diagnoses the more serious diseases of the body. Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter X: “The physician is recognized in a desperate case, the pilot in a storm.” Quintilian, Book IV, chapter 1: “Surely the worst pilot is one who wrecks the ship as it leaves port”; and chapter 10: “A good pilot has never suffered shipwreck.” Vegetius, Book IV, chapter 15, said: “For what hope of safety remains to one who has lost the rudder?” Cornelius Nepos, in the *Life of Atticus*: “The pilot deserves exceptional praise for courage when he saves the ship from winter and a rocky sea.” Seneca, Letter XXX: “A great pilot sails even with his sail torn; and if he has lost his equipment, he nevertheless fits the wreckage of the ship for continuing its course.” Theodoret, Letter LXXIX, writes that the turmoil of the sea reveals the pilot’s skill. For, as Jerome says in Book I *Against Rufinus*, “an ignorant sailor fears to steer the ship.” In Avitus, Letter XXXI, one reads: “But otherwise, what vengeance is it if the ship in raging winds is yielded to the master, not without their danger, in that crisis?” Perhaps the reading is better in the manuscript of Marnaesius: “If the sailors are without a master, one does not yield to that crisis without danger to them.” Furthermore, R. P. Hardouin published this letter of Avitus in vol. II of the *Councils*, p. 981, as though it were new, from a manuscript in the Royal Library. Yet it had been published by Sirmond in 1643.

[Col. 0590D] *A delicate boast.* Tertullian, in *On the Crown*: “I know their shepherds: lions in peace, deer in battle.” Sidonius, Book V, Letter VII: “Though they are lions in court, they are hares in camp.” Martinus Magistri, in the book *On Fortitude*, fol. 8: “There are many who, in the absence of dangers, make many resolutions—even without any pretense of courage—but who, when dangers present themselves, depart from their upright and holy resolution. Thus we read in the Gospel concerning Peter, who, while danger was absent though already 579 close at hand, said to Christ: ‘Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you’; but when he saw Christ bound, at the voice of a little maidservant he said that he did not know him.” In Livy, Book IV, Vettius Messius, rebuking the Volscians, says that they are turbulent in peace and sluggish in war. Tacitus, Book I of the *Histories*: “All the most cowardly—and, as the event showed, those who would dare nothing in danger—were extravagant in speech and fierce of tongue.” And below: “Fierce before the crisis, timid in danger.” [Col. 0591C] Cassius Dio, Book XLVI, observes that most people are customarily bold before they have come into the sight and experience of danger. Seneca, *The Trojan Women*:

> O boastful man, while prosperous fortune’s state  
> Exalts the spirit; timid when fear has thundered.

To this may also be referred the following from the first chapter of the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*: “Her princes have become like rams that find no pasture, and they have gone without strength before the face of the pursuer” (Lam. 1:6).

[Col. 0591D] *The tree.* Above, in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 197: “The wind does not carry away the wheat, nor does a storm overturn a tree founded upon a solid root.” Seneca, *On Providence*, chapter 4: “No tree is solid or strong unless the wind frequently strikes it. By the very buffeting it is compacted and drives its roots deeper. Fragile are those that have grown in a sunny valley.”]

XII. Thus Abraham pleased God, because, in order to please God, he neither feared to lose his son nor refused to commit the killing of his child (Gen. 22). You who cannot bear to lose a son under the law and lot of mortality—what would you do if you were ordered to kill your son? The fear of God and faith ought to make one ready for everything. Though there be loss of property, though there be continual and bloody torment of the limbs from ravaging diseases, though there be the mournful and sorrowful severing from wife, children, and departing loved ones: let these things not be stumbling blocks to you, but battles. Let them not weaken or break a Christian’s faith [Note: [Col. 0589B] “Christian faith,” Routh, from three manuscripts.], but rather display its [Col. 0590B] strength in the struggle, since every injury inflicted by present evils must be despised through confidence in future blessings. Unless battle has preceded, there can be no victory; when victory has been won in the encounter of battle, then the crown too is given to the victors. A ship’s [Note: [Col. 0590B] “For the pilot.” Ancient and approved reading, Lips. Routh deleted “For” and “ship.”] pilot is recognized in a storm; a soldier is tested in battle. Boasting is delicate when there is no danger. Struggle [Col. 0591A] in adversity is the test of truth [Note: [Col. 0591C] “Of virtue,” Grav.; Routh.]. A tree founded upon a deep root is not moved when the winds press upon it; a ship made solid by strong construction [Note: [Col. 0591C] “Strengthened by its construction,” Lam.; Ebor.; Voss. 1, 2, 3; NC. 1, 2; Lin.; Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Routh; Lips.] is pounded by waves but is not pierced; and when the threshing floor beats out the crops, the strong and sturdy grains defy the winds, while the empty chaff is carried away by the blast.

XIII. So too the apostle Paul, after shipwrecks, after scourgings, after many grievous torments of flesh and body, says that he was not afflicted but corrected by adversity, so that the more grievously he was afflicted, the more genuinely he might be tested: “There was given to me,” he says, “a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me, lest I be exalted. For this I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is perfected in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9). Therefore, when weakness, feebleness, [Col. 0591B] or some devastation rages, then our strength is perfected; then faith, if it persists under trial, is crowned, as it is written: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous men” (Sir. 27:5). This, finally, is the difference between us and those who do not know God: they complain and murmur in adversity, whereas adversities do not call us away from the truth of virtue and faith, but strengthen us [Note: [Col. 0592C] “Prove us,” Ar.; Paris; Lam.; Ebor.; Bod. 2, 3.] in suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0591D]

XIV.—*Devastation.* Thus sixteen ancient manuscripts and the editions of Manutius and Morel. Another reading, however, *vastationis* (“of devastation”), is also found in seven ancient manuscripts. I prefer the one that the greater part of the manuscripts shows to have been more generally received, especially since the holy Martyr customarily uses the word *vastitas*.

*Unshaken.* The ancient copies vary greatly at this point. Some have *inconcussi*, others *inconcussis*. I prefer to relate it to the soul.

*We ought.* I have retained this word, although I found it in only a few ancient manuscripts, because either it or another like it is necessary at this point.

[Col. 0592C] *Those who trust.* Three ancient manuscripts have “the faithful.” See the observations above on Letter V, p. 391.]

XIV. That now a belly loosened into a flux drains the body of its strength; that a fire conceived deep within the marrow blazes up into sores of the throat; that the intestines are shaken by continual vomiting; that the eyes burn with the force of blood; that some people’s feet or other parts of their limbs are amputated through the contagion of diseased putrefaction; that, as weakness bursts forth [Col. 0591C] through the losses and injuries of the body, either the gait is enfeebled, the hearing [Col. 0592A] obstructed, or the sight 233 blinded—all this advances the proof of faith. To contend with unshaken powers of soul against so many assaults of devastation and death—what greatness of heart it is! What sublimity, amid the ruins of the human race, to stand erect and not lie prostrate with those who have no hope in God! We ought rather to rejoice and embrace the gift of the present time, because, while we boldly display our faith and proceed toward Christ along Christ’s narrow way after enduring toil [Note: [Col. 0592C] “In toil,” Lam.; NC. 1; Ebor.; Bod. 2.], we may, by his judgment, receive the reward of his life [Note: [Col. 0592C] “The reward of the way,” Bod. 1, 2, 4; NC. 1; Routh.] and faith.

By all means let him fear to die—but he who, not reborn of water and the Spirit, is consigned to the fires of Gehenna. Let him fear to die who is not enrolled under Christ’s cross and passion. Let him fear to die who will pass from this death into the second death. Let him fear to die whom, when he departs from the world, the eternal flame will torment with everlasting [Col. 0592B] punishments. Let him fear to die for whom a longer delay merely secures this much: that his torments and groans are postponed for the time being.

[Note: [Col. 0592C]

XV.—*Of the coming.* In two ancient manuscripts *venientis* (“of the coming”) is written, with *vel saevientis* (“or, of the raging”) above the line. Morel also testifies that he read it thus in one of his ancient manuscripts.

*Not fearing brothels.* The opponents of the Christian religion who raged against our people sent virgins destined for martyrdom to brothels. They were plainly following the institutions of the ancient Romans, who considered it impious for untouched girls to depart from life. Tertullian, at the [Col. 0592D] end of the *Apology*: “For even quite recently, by condemning a Christian woman to a pimp rather than to a lion, you confessed that among us a stain upon chastity is reckoned more atrocious than every punishment and every death.” Prudentius, in the poem on Saint Agnes:

> It is resolved to hand her to a brothel  
> Unless she bows her head before the altar.

In Rufinus, Book VIII, chapter 12, the story is told of a noble woman of Antioch who, when she saw herself and her daughters being forced to sacrifice to idols, with torture and death threatened if they refused, and when she further feared that violence might be inflicted upon her own and her daughters’ chastity, threw herself with them into a river that lay upon their route. Among the other things she said to persuade her daughters to this end was: “Shall those limbs, then, which even the common air has scarcely known, be prostituted in public brothels?” Hence it came about that, because Christian virgins were cast into brothels, they were believed—although they suffered violence and truly lost their chastity—nevertheless to have remained virgins according to [Col. 0593C] the Gospel, as Algerus, the scholastic of Liège, proves from Jerome and Augustine in chapter 76 of the book *On Mercy and Justice*. From Augustine himself I further add that, in the Letter to Victorianus, he writes that violence inflicted upon a virgin, if she did not consent, must be reckoned not as the shame of corruption but as the wound of suffering; and in the Letter to Honoratus he writes that chastity is not violated by violence if it is preserved in the mind, since neither is it violated in the flesh when the sufferer’s will does not shamefully employ her own flesh but endures without consent what another does. [Col. 0593D] See also Charles Guyet, Book II, chapter 7, p. 173, of the *Heortologia*. Suetonius, in *Tiberius*: “Since, according to ancestral custom, it was impious for immature girls who were virgins to be strangled, they were first violated by the executioner and then strangled.” Cassius Dio, Book LVIII, testifies likewise concerning Sejanus’ daughter. See Baronius under January 21.

*A delicate matron.* Victor of Vita, Book V, chapter 8: “A noble and delicate matron.” Jerome, in the Letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem: “The Son of God carried one diseased sheep upon his shoulders to heaven, bearing with and patiently enduring the delicate sinner.”

580 *Numerous.* Three of our manuscripts and one cited by Morel exhibit *torosus* (“muscular”), that is, one who has a knotty mass of flesh in which strength and vigor reside. Hence “muscular neck” in Catullus’ poem on Berecynthia, “the muscular necks of oxen” in Book [Col. 0594C] II of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, and “muscular youth” in Persius’ Satire III. Minucius Felix, almost at the very beginning, has “delights in those tangled and knotty errors.” In the manuscript of the monastery of Bec, *corrosus* (“gnawed away”) is written instead of *torosus*.]

XV. Many of our people die in this mortality—that is, many of our people are freed from the world. As this mortality is a plague to Jews, Gentiles, and Christ’s enemies, so to God’s servants it is a saving departure. Because the righteous die together with the unrighteous, without any distinction among the human race, you must not suppose that destruction is common to good and evil alike. The righteous are summoned to refreshment; the unrighteous are carried off to punishment. Protection is given more swiftly to those who trust; punishment to the faithless.

We are improvident and ungrateful, most beloved brothers, toward God’s benefits, and we do not recognize what is being bestowed upon us. Look: virgins depart in secure peace with their glory intact, not fearing the threats, corruptions, and brothels [Col. 0592C] of the coming Antichrist. Children escape the danger of their unstable age [Col. 0593A] and happily attain the reward of continence and innocence. The delicate matron no longer fears torments, having gained exemption from the fear of persecution and from the executioner’s hands and tortures through the swiftness of her death. By dread of mortality and of the times, the lukewarm are kindled, the lax are constrained, the slothful are roused, deserters are compelled to return, Gentiles are forced to believe, the old body of the faithful is summoned to rest, and a fresh and numerous army is mustered for the battle line with greater strength. Having enlisted for military service in the time of mortality, it will fight without fear of death when the battle comes.

[Note: [Col. 0594C]

XVI.—*To the needy.* We added this on the authority of two of our ancient manuscripts and likewise two English manuscripts.]

XVI. Then consider this, most beloved brothers—what a thing it is, how pertinent, how necessary—that this plague and pestilence, which appears horrible and deadly, tests the justice of every individual and examines the minds of the human race: [Col. 0593B] whether the healthy serve the sick; whether relatives dutifully love their kindred; whether masters take pity upon their ailing slaves; whether physicians refuse to abandon the sick who implore them; whether the fierce restrain their violence; whether the rapacious extinguish, at least through fear of death, the ever-insatiable fire of raging greed; whether the proud bend their necks; whether the shameless soften their audacity [Note: [Col. 0593C] “Restrain,” Pem.; Voss. 1, 2.]; whether, as their loved ones perish, the rich even then give something to the needy and bestow gifts, since they themselves will die without an heir.

Even if this mortality had conferred nothing else, it has rendered this very great service to Christians and God’s servants: we have begun gladly to seek martyrdom while learning not to fear death. These things are exercises for us, not funerals. They give the soul the glory of courage; through contempt for death they prepare it for the crown.

[Note: [Col. 0594C]

XVII.—*A destructive conception.* The Séguier manuscript has “dangerous.”

*For it is one thing.* Giovanni Pico della Mirandola read differently in his manuscript. For he wrote: “It is one thing for martyrdom to be lacking to the soul, another for the soul to be lacking to martyrdom.” Thus in the *Apology*.

*Desires.* This too we added from certain of our manuscripts and certain English manuscripts. It may, however, be a gloss.]

XVII. But perhaps someone may object and say: “What grieves me, then, in the present mortality is this: although I had been prepared for confession and had devoted myself with my whole heart and full strength to enduring suffering, [Col. 0594A] I am deprived of my martyrdom because death overtakes me first.”

In the first place, martyrdom rests not in your power but in God’s gracious favor, and you cannot say that you have lost what you do not know whether you deserve to receive 234. Then, furthermore, God—the searcher [Note: [Col. 0593C] “Is the searcher,” Voss. 2; Pem.; Saris.; Bod. 1, 4.] of kidney and heart, the beholder and knower of hidden things—sees you, praises you, and approves you; and he who perceives that your courage stood ready will repay a reward for that courage. Had Cain already killed his brother when he offered a gift to God? Yet God in his providence condemned beforehand the fratricide conceived in his mind. Just as in that instance the evil thought and destructive conception were foreseen [Note: [Col. 0594C] “Perceived,” Lips.; Voss. 2, 3.] by God in his providence, so too among God’s servants, in whom confession is contemplated and martyrdom conceived in the mind, the soul devoted to the good is crowned by God as judge.

It is one thing for the soul to be lacking to martyrdom; another for martyrdom to have been lacking to the soul. As the Lord finds you when he calls, so likewise does he judge you, since he himself testifies and says: “And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of kidney and heart” (Rev. 2:23). For God does not desire [Note: [Col. 0594C] “Desires” is absent from the first edition and others; Routh.] our blood, but seeks our faith. Neither Abraham, Isaac, nor Jacob was killed; yet, honored for the merits of faith and justice, they deserved to rank first among the patriarchs. At their banquet is gathered everyone who is found faithful, righteous, and praiseworthy.

[Note: [Col. 0594D]

XVIII.—*How contrary to order.* These words are found in Gratian, Causa XIII, question 2, and in William Durandus’ treatise *On the Manner of Celebrating a General Council*, part III, rubric 6.

*In the manner of obstinate slaves.* Tacitus, Book I of the *Histories*: “Even under torture, the loyalty of slaves is obstinate.” See Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 11. Tacitus likewise relates in Book IV of the *Annals* that Nero’s wife Octavia was accused of intercourse with a slave; her maidservants were therefore interrogated, and although some, overcome by the force of torture, assented to falsehoods, most persisted in defending their mistress’s chastity. Suetonius, in *Caligula*: “He gave eighty [units unspecified in the source] to a freedwoman because, although tortured with the gravest torments, she had kept silent about her patron’s crime.” Tacitus, in Book XV of the *Annals*, mentions another freedwoman named Epicharis, who, although torn apart by torture, never consented to confess the charges brought against her, though they were true. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVIII, mentions a maidservant from whom torments bordering upon death wrung out indirect statements against her master. See Pliny, Book VII, chapter 23; Justin, Book XLIV; Seneca, Book IV of *On Benefits*, chapter 19, and Letter 6, at the passage “Let him hold him on the rack”—that is, as Muretus interprets it, “Let him not reveal his accomplices or betray any of the matters for which he is being tortured.” See also Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 8, and Book VIII, chapter 4; Quintilian, Book II, chapter 20; Cassius Dio, Book XLVII; Victor of Vita, Book V, chapter 2; and Patrick Young’s notes on Clement’s Letter to the Corinthians, p. 9.]

XVIII. We ought to remember that we must do not our own will but God’s, in accordance with what the Lord has commanded us to pray each day. How contrary to order and how perverse it is that, although we ask that his will be done, when God calls us forth and summons us from this [Col. 0594C] world, we do not immediately obey the command of his will. We resist and struggle against it; and, in the manner of obstinate slaves, we are led into the Lord’s presence with sadness [Col. 0595A] and grief, departing from here under the bond of necessity rather than in obedience of will. And we wish to be honored with heavenly rewards by him to whom we come unwillingly!

Why, then, do we pray and ask that the kingdom of heaven may come, if earthly captivity delights us? Why, in frequently repeated prayers, do we ask and entreat that the day of the kingdom be hastened, if our greater desires and stronger wishes are to serve the devil here rather than to reign with Christ?

[Note: [Col. 0595D]

### XIX.—He Heard in Order That He Might Tell

The translator of the preface to the *Disputation of Jason and Papiscus*: “For he had seen for this purpose, that he might report it.” Tertullian, at the end of the book *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “The Lord has also measured out for us the extent of the veil by revelations. For an angel, as though striking the neck of one of our sisters in dreams by way of applause, said: ‘An elegant neck, and deservedly bare! It is good that you should be veiled from the head down to the loins, lest the freedom of your neck prove of no benefit to you either.’ And certainly what you have said to one, you have said to all.” He therefore heard in order that he might tell. The same author in the book *On Idolatry*: “At this point I solemnly declare, on God’s authority, that it is not even safe to suppress anything that has been shown to one person, since it was certainly shown for the sake of all.” Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 5: “But when your servant Simplicianus told me this story about Victorinus, I burned with zeal to imitate him. For this purpose he too had told it.” [Col. 0596D]

**A priest.** The old editions and almost all our old and English manuscripts have only these words. Pamelius, following the edition called that of Gravius and an old manuscript, wrote “a priest of God.” But I found the word “God” in only six ancient manuscripts. The Séguier manuscript does not have it.

### XIX

Finally, so that the indications of divine providence might shine forth more clearly—that the Lord, foreknowing the future, takes thought for his own with a view to true salvation—one of our colleagues and fellow priests, exhausted by illness [Note: [Col. 0595C] Thus ten English MSS.; *nostris* (“our”) in the Oxford edition.] and now anxious because death was approaching, prayed that leave to depart might be granted him. As he prayed and was already almost at the point of death, there stood beside him a young man venerable in dignity and majesty, [Col. 0595B] lofty in stature [Note: [Col. 0595C] Thus six English codices; “exalted,” Oxford.] and radiant in appearance. The human gaze could scarcely have looked upon him with fleshly eyes as he stood there, except that one who was already about to depart from this world was now able to see such a figure.

Then [Note: [Col. 0595C] “To whom he,” Lam., York, NC. 1; Bodl. 2.], not without a certain indignation of spirit and voice, he groaned and said: “You are afraid to suffer; you are unwilling to depart. What am I to do with you?” This is the voice of one both rebuking and admonishing: he does not consent to their present desire when they are anxious about persecution but unconcerned about being summoned away [Note: [Col. 0595C] “Anxious … unconcerned,” in the singular, Routh, from his codices NC. 4 and 5; Pamelius.]; rather, he takes thought for their future. Our brother and colleague, who was about to die, heard what he was to tell the others. For he who heard it when about to die heard it for this purpose: that he might tell it. He did not hear it for himself, but for us. For what could he learn for himself when he was already about to depart? Rather, he learned it for us [Note: [Col. 0595C] “For us” is absent from fourteen English manuscripts. It is rejected by Routh and Lipsius.] who remain, so that, when we learned that the priest who had asked for leave to depart had been rebuked, we might recognize what is expedient for everyone. [Note: [Col. 0595C] “Might know,” Lam., York, NC. 1, 2; Bodl. 1, 2, 3, 4.] [Col. 0595C]

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

### XX.—Black Garments

The ancients used that color in mourning. Vincent of Lérins complains that widows under the Arian persecution had been stripped of their mourning dress, evidently because they wore dark garments, that is, black ones. In Paul, *Opinions*, book I, title 23, and from there in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 743, one reads: “One who mourns ought to abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing.” Yet Herodian, book III, notes that Roman women in mourning wore thin white garments, so as to present the appearance of mourners, whereas men, by contrast, were clothed in black garments. See also Plutarch’s *Roman Questions*.

]

### XX

How often it has also been revealed to us ourselves, the least and last of all [Col. 0596A]; how frequently and manifestly, by God’s gracious favor, I have been commanded to testify continually and preach publicly that our brothers who have been freed from the world by the Lord’s summons are not to be mourned! For we know that they are not lost [Note: [Col. 0596C] “Not lost, but departing,” Ar. and the others just mentioned.] but sent ahead; that in departing they precede us; and that, as is customary with travelers and sailors, they ought to be longed for, not lamented. Nor should black garments be assumed here, 235 when they have already put on white garments there. No occasion should be given to the Gentiles justly and rightly to reproach us because we mourn as extinguished and lost those whom we say are alive with God, and because we fail to prove by the testimony of heart and breast the faith we profess in speech and voice. We betray our hope and faith; the things we say appear pretended, [Note: [Col. 0596C] *Si stimulate*, Voss. 1; Bodl. 4.] feigned, and counterfeit. It profits nothing to parade virtue in words and destroy truth by deeds. [Col. 0596B]

[Note: [Col. 0596D]

### XXI.—We Lament and Grieve

Cyprian tells us [Col. 0597B] that we who possess the hope of resurrection are not permitted to weep for the dead. This must be understood of immoderate weeping. For otherwise Christ, by his own example at Bethany, approved the practice of shedding tears at the deaths of friends. There, when he saw Mary and the Jews weeping over the death of Lazarus, 581 he too wept. From this the Jews concluded that Lazarus had been greatly loved by Christ. For those final tears, as we said in connection with book VI of Salvian, belong more to those who love than to those who mourn, although they also belong to mourners and to those who long for their friends. Seneca therefore spoke elegantly in Letter LXIII: “We, however, may be forgiven if we lapse into tears, provided they have not flowed excessively and we ourselves have checked them. Let the eyes neither be dry when a friend has been lost nor stream without restraint. We should shed tears, not wail.” See Saint John Chrysostom’s homily *On Not Mourning the Dead Immoderately*, and Ruricius, book II, Letter 4. See also above, p. 168, the *Letter to Tyrasius*. Add Dio Chrysostom, who in Oration XXIX teaches that the departed should be honored by remembrance, not by tears.

Among the Romans the period of mourning was formerly prescribed. Seneca says somewhere that women were allotted a year for mourning, not so that they should mourn that long, but so that they should not mourn longer. In Livy, book II, we read that the funeral of the consul Brutus was celebrated with great ceremony. “But,” says Livy, “public grief conferred far greater honor upon his death; it was especially remarkable because the matrons mourned him as a father for a year, since he had been so stern an avenger of violated chastity.” Likewise the matrons mourned Publius Valerius Publicola for one year, as Plutarch testifies. Likewise they also mourned Coriolanus, as the same author testifies. Dio, book LV, recorded that it was decreed that women should mourn for a full year after the death of Augustus. Among the Spartans, as Plutarch relates in his *Lycurgus*, mourning ended on the twelfth day.

**If we believe in Christ.** We judged that the text should be written and punctuated in this way, following the authority of six old copies. For this reading seems to me preferable to the commonly received one, which I append here for the benefit of those who may perhaps think that it ought to have been retained: “If we believe in Christ, let us have faith in his words and promises and, as those who will not die eternally, let us come with joyful confidence to Christ, with whom we shall live and reign forever.” Meanwhile it should be noted that the word “those who will die” does not occur in those six ancient copies, whereas “we die” or “we shall die” [Col. 0598B] is found in several ancient manuscripts and editions.

]

### XXI

Finally, the apostle Paul rebukes [Note: [Col. 0596C] “Disapproves,” all printed editions down to that of Lipsius; the English editors conjecture “upbraids”; “rebukes,” only two English codices.], reproves, and censures any who are saddened at the departure of their own: “We do not wish [Note: [Col. 0596C] “I do not wish,” Bodl. 1, 3.] you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not be saddened like the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so too God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus” (1 Thess. 4:13–14).

He says that those who have no hope are saddened at the departure of their own. But we who live in hope, believe in God, and trust that Christ suffered for us and rose again—we who abide in Christ and rise again through him and in him—why are we ourselves unwilling to depart from this world, or why do we lament and grieve for our own who depart as though they were lost [Col. 0596C], when Christ himself, our Lord and God, admonishes us and says: “I am the resurrection and [Col. 0597A] the life. He who believes in me, though he die, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die eternally” (John 11:25–26)?

If we believe in Christ, if we have faith in his words and promises and do not die eternally, [Note: [Col. 0597B] “If we believe, let us have faith in his words … and, as those who will not die eternally” is the reading common to all editions down to that of Lipsius, with a few exceptions that have “We shall not die.”] let us come with joyful confidence to Christ, with whom we shall both live and reign forever.

[Note: [Col. 0598B]

### XXII.—Dignity

There were anciently two readings of this passage. Some manuscripts present *firmitatem* (“firmness”), with *vel dignitatem* (“or glory”) above the line. Others have only *dignitatem* (“glory”). Florus read it in this way. Hence arose the discrepancy found in the ancient copies. I have read *firmitatem* in three, without any addition.

**Our commonwealth.** See Fronton du Duc’s notes on Saint John Chrysostom’s panegyric on the holy martyr Lucian. [Col. 0598C]

**Conformed.** There were likewise anciently two readings of this passage. Two old books have *configuratum* (“configured”), with *vel conformatum* (“or conformed”) above the line. The ancient copyists inserted whichever reading pleased them more. Pamelius preferred *configuratum*. I write *conformatum*, because I found it written thus in twenty-two of our copies, one of which is the Séguier manuscript, and in five English copies, as well as in the excerpts of Florus; and because it is also so written in book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 11.

By contrast, in Regino, *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, book II, chapter 108, the text should read: “But this opinion is weakened by canonical and apostolic proofs,” rather than *informatur* (“is informed”), as we printed. In Saint Gregory, book I, Letter 71 or 73, to Peter the subdeacon, one reads: “So that, once equity has been preserved, you yourself may be praised in the reports of the aforesaid bishop.” In place of this, three excellent and extremely ancient books have: “That we may be informed by the reports.” I think this is better. And [Col. 0598D] perhaps the text should read: “That we may be informed by the reports, and you yourself may be praised.”

**According to faith in the truth.** This reading, presented by eleven copies, among which I include the Séguier manuscript, is the best. In two others *verbi* (“of the word”) is written. Morel notes that he saw *veri* (“of the truth”) written in ancient copies, but elsewhere *verbi*. This confirms our reading. In the Bec manuscript and Morel’s edition one reads *veritatis* (“of truth”).

]

### XXII

Meanwhile, when we die, through death we pass over to immortality; nor can eternal life follow unless it befalls us to depart from here. This is not an exit, but a passage; when the temporal journey has been completed, it is a crossing over to eternal things.

Who would not hasten to come to what is better [Note: [Col. 0597B] Baluz alone adds “to come,” without giving any reason.]? Who would not desire to be changed and transformed [Note: [Col. 0597B–0598B] All the others have “reformed”; Baluz changed it for an unknown reason.] into the likeness of Christ and to come more quickly to the dignity of heavenly glory, when the apostle Paul proclaims and says: “Our commonwealth,” he says, “is in heaven, [Note: [Col. 0598B] “Is heavenly,” Salisbury.] whence we also await the Lord [Col. 0597B] Jesus Christ, who will transform [Note: [Col. 0598B] “Reform,” Lam., York, Voss. 3.] the body of our lowliness, conformed [Note: [Col. 0598B] “Conformed,” Lam., York, Bodl. 1, 3, 4.] to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21)?

Christ the Lord also promises [Col. 0598A] that we shall be such when, so that we may be with him, live with him in eternal dwellings, and rejoice in the heavenly kingdoms, he prays to the Father for us, saying: “Father, I will that those whom you have given me should also be with me where I shall be, and should see the glory that you gave me before the world was made” (John 17:24).

One who is about to come to Christ’s dwelling, to the glory of the heavenly kingdoms, ought not to mourn or lament, but rather, in accordance with the Lord’s promise and according to faith in the truth, to rejoice in this his journey and translation.

[Note: [Col. 0598D]

### XXIII.—From This Contagion

Although the greater part of the old copies presents this reading, several others and the ancient editions nevertheless read “from this contagion” with a different grammatical form (*de hac contagione*). Manutius was the first to introduce the form we have retained. Both are good.

**But also through Solomon.** See Pamelius’s annotation on this passage.

(**But the Holy Spirit, teaching also through Solomon.**) The Book of Wisdom is attributed to Solomon not only by Cyprian [Col. 0599C]—both here and below, in *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, chapter 1, and in *Testimonies* II, chapter 13, and III, chapters 15, 53, 59, and 66—but also by Hegesippus and Irenaeus, and by “the whole chorus of the ancients,” as Eusebius says in *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 22; also by Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*; Origen, book VIII *On the Epistle to the Romans*; Saint Hilary on Psalm 123; Basil, book V *Against Eunomius*; Evaristus, in the letter to the Africans; Felix, first letter to the Gauls; Felix, second letter to Saint Athanasius; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 76 and the book *On Weights and Measures*; John of Damascus, book IV, chapter 18; Ambrose, on Psalm 1 and *On Paradise*, chapter 12; and even Saint Jerome himself, in the letter to Paulina *On the Education of a Daughter*.

Saint Augustine gives the reason in these words, in *The City of God*, book XVII, chapter 20: “Two other books, one of which is called Wisdom and the other Ecclesiasticus, have acquired the customary attribution to Solomon because of a certain similarity of style.” Yet he still seems to reconsider this very point in book II, chapter 4: “And certainly many statements in chapters VII, VIII, and IX of that book are applicable to Solomon alone.” Its Greek title is also Σολόμοντος (*Solomontos*, “Of Solomon”). Therefore the opinion of the learned John Driedo, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, book I, commends itself to me: namely, that Philo the Jew, more than 160 years before the birth of Christ, in the time of Onias the high priest, gathered into this one volume sayings of Solomon that had been scattered here and there.

This is all the more likely because at the end of 3 Kings it is written that Solomon uttered three thousand parables and five thousand songs, and discoursed on beasts, birds, creeping things, fish, and so forth. It is further confirmed by the fact that his Proverbs were evidently collected into one work, not by him, but much later by the servants of King Hezekiah—or, according to Rabbi Moses, by Isaiah—as is clear from Proverbs chapter 25.

However that may be, Cyprian acknowledges this book as the teaching of the Holy Spirit and as divine Scripture both in this passage and in Letter LXXXI and *To Demetrianus*. The other ancients do no less wherever they cite this book, notably Dionysius the Areopagite, chapter 4 of *The Divine Names*, and the Council of Sardica in its letter to all bishops.

Accordingly, Saint Augustine, citing this passage in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14, says: “Since these things are so, the judgment of the Book of Wisdom ought not to have been rejected—a book which, for so long a succession of years, merited to be read in the Church of Christ from the station of the readers of the Church of Christ, and to be heard with reverence for divine authority by all Christians, from bishops down to the lowest faithful laity, penitents, and catechumens.” And a little later: “They ought to prefer this Book of Wisdom to all commentators, because the distinguished commentators who lived very near the times of the apostles preferred it even to themselves. In employing it as a witness, they believed that they were employing nothing other than divine testimony.”

Indeed, the apostle Paul himself, in Romans 11 and Hebrews 11, alludes to chapters 9, 6, and 15 of the Book of Wisdom. I have discussed these matters at somewhat greater length because of those who even today refuse to receive this book into the canon of Scripture, because Saint Jerome denies that it is included in the Jewish canon; although it is nevertheless numbered in the canon of the Church by Saint Augustine, the Council of Carthage, Innocent, Gelasius, and Isidore, in the passages cited below at *Testimonies* I, chapter 20. —PAMELIUS.)

**He was taken away.** See Saint Augustine, chapter 14 [Col. 0600D] of *On the Predestination of the Saints*.

**A soul devoted to its God.** Jerome, in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*: “Simplicity of heart and a soul devoted to its God.” The author of the *Letter to Oceanus, on Enduring Reproaches*, published under Jerome’s name: “Therefore let the soul devoted to God take care that the laughter of the foolish or the utterly vain speech of stupid people does not disconcert it.” 582

]

### XXIII

Thus, finally, we find that Enoch too was translated, who pleased God, as divine Scripture testifies and declares in Genesis: “And Enoch pleased God [Note: [Col. 0598B] “Pleased God, he says,” Lam., York, NC. 1.], and afterward was not found, because God translated him” (Gen. 5:24). This is what it meant to have pleased in the sight [Col. 0598B] of God: to have merited translation away from this world’s contagion.

But the Holy Spirit also teaches through Solomon that those who please God are taken away from here sooner and are more quickly delivered, [Col. 0599A] lest, by remaining longer in this world, they be polluted through contact with the world. “He was taken away,” he says, “lest wickedness alter his understanding” (Wis. 4:11, 14). “For his soul was pleasing to God. Therefore he hastened to lead him away from the midst of iniquity.” [Note: [Col. 0599B] “From the midst of iniquity,” Oxford.]

So too in the Psalms, with spiritual faith, a soul devoted to its God hastens toward the Lord, saying: “How greatly beloved are your dwellings, O God of hosts! My soul longs and hastens toward the courts of God” [Note: [Col. 0599B] “Toward your courts, O God,” Ver.] (Ps. 83:2–3).

### XXIV

It belongs to one whom the world delights to wish to remain in the world for a long time—to one whom this age, flattering and deceiving him, entices with the allurements of earthly pleasure. Moreover, since the world hates the Christian, 236 why do you love one who hates you, instead of following Christ, who both redeemed you and loves you?

John cries out and speaks in his epistle, exhorting us not to love the world by pursuing fleshly desires: “Do not,” he says, “love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the desire of the world. And the world will pass away, and its desire; but he who does the will of God abides eternally, even as God abides eternally” (1 John 2:15–17).

Rather, dearly beloved brothers, with an uncorrupted mind, firm faith, and steadfast courage, let us be prepared for every will of God. Having cast away the fear of death, let us think upon the immortality that follows. Let us show that we are what we believe ourselves to be, so that we neither mourn the departure of our dear ones nor, when the day of our own summons comes, hesitate to come gladly to the Lord when he himself calls us.

### XXV

Although this has always had to be done by God’s servants, it ought to be done much more now, when the world is already collapsing and is beset by the tempests of assailing evils. Since we see that grievous things have already begun, and know that still more grievous things are imminent, let us reckon it the greatest gain if we depart from here more quickly.

If the walls in your dwelling were tottering from age, the roofs overhead were trembling, and the house, now worn out and exhausted, threatened imminent collapse as its structures gave way through age, would you not move away with all speed? If, while you were sailing, a turbulent and stormy tempest, with waves rising more violently, foretold a coming shipwreck, would you not quickly seek the harbor?

Look: the world is tottering and collapsing, and bears witness to its ruin—not now through the old age of things, but through their end. And do you not thank God and congratulate yourself that, by an earlier departure, you are withdrawn from the impending ruins, shipwrecks, and plagues? [Note: [Col. 0600B] “Are exempted,” Routh.]

[Note: [Col. 0600D]

### XXVI.—Dearly Beloved Brothers

In the Séguier manuscript, both here and elsewhere, these two words are written thus: *FF. DD.* I mention this to demonstrate the scrupulous diligence of the most learned Jean du Tillet. When he was editing the works of Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, and in the *Exhortation to Penitence* read in an old book, “these things are written *FF. DD.* and carved upon everlasting monuments,” he was unwilling to expand the abbreviation, although he could have done so. Instead, he noted in the margin that he thought these signs meant *dilectissimi fratres* (“dearly beloved brothers”), as it is written in the old manuscript of the Grande Chartreuse. Galesini, although he lacked [Col. 0601B] this authority, printed it in his edition just as du Tillet had conjectured it ought to be written.

**Let us embrace the day.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in book IV *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8.

**And to the kingdom.** Previously the text read “and to the heavenly kingdom.” But the word “heavenly” is a gloss by someone who did not know that Cyprian uses the word *kingdom* by itself to signify Christ’s kingdom, that is, the heavenly kingdom. I did indeed find the word “heavenly” in two ancient manuscripts. But [Col. 0601C] it is absent from fourteen others of ours and from eight English manuscripts.

**Secure concerning their own safety.** This is the reading of all the old editions, all our manuscripts, and ten English manuscripts. It is also quoted in this form by Saint Augustine in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 19, and by the author of the *Sermon for the Feast of All Saints*, published in the appendix to volume V of the same saint’s works, p. 350, which also survives in a manuscript of homilies attributed to Alcuin. Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, book II, Letter 4: “Believe me, dearest brothers, she is already secure concerning her own rest and anxious concerning our salvation.” See Maximus of Tyre, Dissertation XXVII. See above, p. 467.

Erasmus was the first to print *immortalitate* (“immortality”). The Manutius edition retained that reading. Morel rejected it and printed *incolumitate* (“safety”). Pamelius, Rigault, and others preferred *immortalitate*. Two or three old copies read: “Already secure concerning themselves, yet anxious concerning our safety.” Wessel Gansfort of Groningen, in his letter to Bernard of Meppen: “The departed pray [Col. 0602C] for us, that we may be brought into their blessed fellowship.” See above, p. 467.

**The victory of suffering.** Two old books read “the glory.”

**Of his glory.** Thirteen old books have *claritatis* (“glory”), a word extremely frequent in Cyprian. Five others have *charitatis* (“love”), evidently through a copyist’s error for *claritatis*. In three others it is written: “Intending to give them most abundant gifts and the rewards of his glory.”

]

### XXVI

We must consider, dearly beloved brothers, and repeatedly reflect that we have renounced the world and are living here meanwhile as guests and strangers [Note: [Col. 0601B] “Here,” Lam., Salisbury, Bodl. 1, 2, 3, 4.]. Let us embrace the day that assigns each of us to his own dwelling, that snatches us from here, frees us from the snares of the age, and restores us to paradise and to the kingdom.

Who, when living abroad, would not hasten to return to his homeland? Who, when eager to sail to his own people, would not all the more ardently desire a favorable wind, so that he might quickly be permitted to embrace his dear ones?

We regard paradise as our homeland [Note: [Col. 0602B] “Let us regard paradise as our homeland,” Bodl. 2.]; we have already begun to regard the patriarchs as our parents. Why do we not hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland and greet our parents? A great number of our dear ones await us there—a dense and abundant multitude of parents, brothers, and children longs for us, already secure concerning their own safety and still anxious concerning our salvation. What common joy there is, both for them and for us, when we come into their sight and embrace!

What delight there is in the heavenly kingdoms, without fear of dying; and what supreme and perpetual happiness, with the eternity of living! There is the glorious choir of the apostles; there the company of exultant prophets; there the innumerable people of the martyrs, crowned because of their victory in struggle and suffering. There are the triumphant virgins, who subdued the desire of flesh and body by the strength of continence. There are the merciful, rewarded because they performed works of righteousness by supplying food and gifts to the poor—those who, observing the Lord’s commands, transferred their earthly patrimonies into heavenly treasuries.

Let us hasten toward them, dearly beloved brothers, with eager longing. Let us desire that it may be granted us soon to be with them, soon to come to Christ. May God see this thought of ours; may Christ the Lord look upon this purpose of our mind and faith. He will give the more abundant rewards of his glory to those whose desires for him have been greater. [Col. 0602B]

[Col. 0601]

### ON WORKS AND ALMSGIVING

Saint Jerome speaks of this book as follows in the *Letter to Pammachius on the Falling Asleep of Paulina*: “How great is the power of mercy and with what rewards it is to be recompensed, the blessed Cyprian pursues in a substantial volume; and he approves Daniel’s counsel, which says that the most impious king, if he had been willing to listen, was to be saved by sustaining the poor.”

]

(C)

[Col. 0601D]

[Note: [Col. 0601D]

### I.—Many and Great

This passage, translated into Greek, was presented at the Council of Ephesus among the testimonies of the Fathers and martyrs against the Nestorian heresy. Consequently, in the ancient translation of that council, Cyprian’s words are not transcribed; instead, other words translated from the Greek text are given. That translation survives among the *Works of Marius Mercator*, p. 180 of our edition. Vincent of Lérins also testifies that this passage was read at the council. [Col. 0602D]

**He sent the Son.** In the later editions and three ancient manuscripts one reads “his Son.” The word “his” does indeed occur in Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, from which this passage was taken. It also occurs in book II of the *Testimonies*, chapter 8. Nevertheless, I have deleted it because it is absent from twenty old books, from Marius Mercator, from the Speyer edition, from the old Venetian edition, and from the Erasmian edition. It was first added in the Manutius edition. Morel expunged it.

**Might treat.** The previous reading was “might heal.” I was compelled to change it because almost all the old books have the reading I present.

**For when the Lord.** Saint Augustine quotes this passage in book IV *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8.

**Ancient.** Thus almost all the old books and old editions. Pamelius printed the masculine form *antiqui*. I found that reading in some ancient books as well.

]

### I

MANY and great, dearest brothers [Note: [Col. 0601D] “Dearly beloved,” Ar.], are the divine benefits through which the generous and abundant mercy of God the Father and of Christ has acted and continues always to act for our salvation: the Father sent the Son to preserve us and give us life, so that he might restore us; and the Son was willing to be sent and to become the Son of Man [Note: [Col. 0603C] Thus Lam., Benedictine, York, Ar., Ver., Bodl. 1, 2, 3. “Was willing to be and to become the Son of Man,” early printed edition. “To call himself also the Son of Man,” Ver.] so that he might make us children of God.

He humbled himself so that he might raise up the people who previously lay prostrate. He was wounded so that he might treat our wounds [Note: [Col. 0603C] Thus West., Lam., York, Ar., Bodl. 1, 3, 4, Geneva, Ver., Thu.; “heal,” Oxford.].
