He became a servant so that he might draw servants forth into freedom. He endured death so that he might bestow immortality upon mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy. [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Works of mercy,” Ar.]

But beyond these, what great providence and how great a mercy it is that provision is made for us by a saving plan, so that fuller care may be taken to preserve the human being who has been redeemed! For when the Lord came and had healed those wounds Adam had borne, and had treated the serpent’s ancient poisons, he gave a law to the man made sound [Note: [Col. 0603C] “To those made sound,” NC. 1; “they sinned,” NC. 1.] and commanded him not to sin any further, lest something worse befall him if he sinned.

We had been constrained and confined within narrow bounds by the injunction of innocence. Nor would [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Nor did … have,” West., Augustine, Salisbury.] the weakness and frailty of human infirmity have had anything it could do, had divine loving-kindness not once again come to our aid and, by revealing works of righteousness and mercy, opened a certain path for safeguarding salvation, so that by almsgiving we might wash away whatever stains we subsequently contract [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Contracted,” NC. 2.].

### II

The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: “By almsgiving and faith sins are cleansed” (Prov. 15:27). This certainly does not mean the sins that had previously been contracted, for those are cleansed by the blood and sanctification of Christ.

Again he says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33). Here too it is shown and proved that, just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the washing of saving water, so by almsgiving and righteous works [Note: [Col. 0603C] “Operations,” Bodl. 1, 2, 3, 4; “works,” Oxford.] the flame of sins [Note: [Col. 0603C] “The tinder of sins,” Bodl. 3.] is put to rest.

And because [Note: [Col. 0603C] “So that because,” Bodl. 1.] the remission of sins is granted once in Baptism [Note: [Col. 0603C] Thus Foss., Lam., York; “remission,” early printed edition; “a continual promised pardon of sins is granted,” Bodl. 3.], continual and unceasing activity, imitating the likeness of Baptism [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Performed after the pattern of Baptism,” Bodl. 4.], once again bestows God’s indulgence [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Indulgence,” Bodl. 4; “may bestow,” Bodl. 1, 4.]. The Lord also teaches this in the Gospel. For [Col. 0604A] when his disciples were reproached because they ate without first washing [Note: [Col. 0604C] Variant form *lavissent*, Ar., Salisbury, Ver., MR.] their hands, he answered and said: “He who made what is within also made what is without. But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:40).

He teaches and shows, namely, that it is not the hands that must be washed, but the breast; that the stains within rather than those without must be removed; and that whoever has purified what is within has also cleansed what is without, and, once the mind is cleansed, has begun to be clean in skin and body as well.

Moreover, in admonishing and showing us how we may be clean and purified, he added that alms must be given. He who is merciful teaches and admonishes us to practice mercy; and because he seeks to preserve those whom he redeemed at a great price [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Whom he greatly redeemed,” Ar., Bodl. 1, 2, 3, 4.], he teaches that those stained after the grace of Baptism can be purified again.

[Col. 0604B]

[Note: [Col. 0603D]

583

### III.—Let Us Therefore Acknowledge

Saint Augustine also quotes this passage in the same work, chapter 10.

**Nor let anyone.** Augustine cites this in the same place and in book II *Against Julian the Pelagian*, chapter 8.

[Col. 0604D]

**Breast.** Previously the reading was “heart,” and there can be no doubt that this reading is excellent. But since “breast” is written in twenty-two of our books and in six English ones, I thought that I ought to yield to their authority, especially since it is also written thus in Saint Augustine, book II *Against Julian the Pelagian*, chapter 8.

**The truth is not in us.** The common editions afterward add: “But if we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.” Yet although these words occur in certain ancient manuscripts, since they are absent from sixteen of ours—especially the Séguier manuscript—from six English manuscripts, and from Saint Augustine in the passages cited above, I thought they were not Cyprian’s, but had been transferred here from Saint John’s epistle by some studious reader. Certainly the sense remains no less complete without them.

]

### III

Let us therefore acknowledge, dearest brothers, the saving gift [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Saving,” as in Augustine.] of divine indulgence, and, for the cleansing and purification of our sins—for we cannot be without some wound 238 to the conscience—let us treat our wounds with spiritual remedies.

Nor let anyone [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Let anyone flatter himself,” Lin., Voss. 1.] so flatter himself concerning a pure and unstained breast [Note: [Col. 0604C] “An unstained breast,” West., Ar., Bodl. 1, 2, 3, 4, Augustine.] that, relying upon his own innocence, he thinks no medicine need be applied to his wounds, since it is written: “Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins?” (Prov. 20:9). And again John states and says in his epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves [Note: [Col. 0604C] “We lead ourselves astray,” Voss. 1.], and the truth is not in us” [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Is not in us. But if no one,” Ar., Salisbury, Bodl. 1, 2, 3, 4, Thu., Augustine. Oxford adds: “But if we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.”] (1 John 1:8).

But if no one can be without sin, and whoever says that he is blameless is either proud or foolish [Note: [Col. 0604C] “Is foolish; because he knows,” Augustine.], how necessary and how kindly is the divine mercy which, because it knows that certain wounds are afterward not absent from those who have been healed, has given saving remedies so that those wounds may once again be treated and healed!

[Col. 0605A]

[Note: [Col. 0605C]

### IV.—Your Garments

I do not know whence arose the wording of the Fuxensis manuscript, in which one reads: “And your prayers will quickly be heard.” In the common edition: “And your health will arise more quickly.” See Jerome on Isaiah chapter 58.

]
] IV. Finally, dearest brothers, divine admonition has never ceased or fallen silent [Note: [Col. 0605C] “Ceased or fallen silent”: thus Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Saris., Lin., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Thu. Oxon. reads: “never ceased.”] from continually and everywhere summoning God’s people, in both the Old and New Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0605C] Thu. reads: “always and everywhere in the Holy Scriptures.”], to works of mercy [Note: [Col. 0605C] West. and Saris. read “peoples were summoned.”]; and, as the Holy Spirit sings and exhorts, whoever is being instructed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms. Through Isaiah God commands and enjoins: “Cry out,” he says, “with strength, and do not hold back. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their crimes” [Note: [Col. 0605C] Saris. reads “the offenses of Jacob.”] (Isa. 58:1). And after he had commanded that their sins be reproached against them, had set forth their crimes with the full force of indignation, and had said that they could not make satisfaction for their offenses even if they employed prayers, entreaties, and fasts, nor appease God’s anger even if they rolled themselves in sackcloth and ashes, [Col. 0605B] nevertheless, in the final part, showing that God can be appeased by alms alone, he added:

“Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not disregard the members of your own family. Then your timely light will break forth, and your garments will quickly arise; righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Here I am’” (ibid., 7–9).

[Note: [Col. 0605C]

**V.—In the heart.** In two ancient books [Col. 0605D] the reading is “bosom,” with “or heart” written above the line. From this arose the divergence of readings in the ancient codices, some of which have “heart,” others “bosom.” The older editions have “bosom.” Manutius printed “heart”; Morellius, “bosom.”

**The Lord’s mercy.** Jonas of Orléans, who cites this passage from the book *On the Lord’s Prayer* in Book III, chapter 10, of *On the Instruction of the Laity*, reads “God’s mercy.” Lamonius’s codex has “God’s pardon”; the Séguier manuscript has simply “God.”

**Forgiving.** In the Fuxensis codex, either “forgiving” or “patient.” From this arose the different reading in certain books, in which “patient” is written. For the rest, I think that “forgiving” ought to be read, chiefly because, in addition to the authority of the ancient books and editions, it is written in the Book of Daniel: “Perhaps he will forgive your offenses.”

**May be filled.** Thus the older editions before the one said to be Gravius’s. The Morellian edition likewise has this reading. Moreover, our twenty books agree, including the Séguier and Verona manuscripts, the oldest of all. There are nevertheless two that have “may be filled” or “may be joined”; six others have only “may be joined.” Seven English manuscripts prefer this last reading, though not in this place, for they put the word “may be joined” in the preceding phrase: “may be joined to almsgiving.” Pamelius, contrary to so many authorities and without the support of any ancient book, merely because the edition said to be Gravius’s reads “may be stuffed full,” and because a certain Cologne book—which is certainly defective in this passage—reads “will be stuffed full,” just as the Fuxensis also erroneously has “may be consecrated”—Pamelius, I say, constructed “may be stuffed full” from the reading of that edition and of the Cologne codex, having no doubt at all that this was the best reading. This certainly cannot be permitted. For if conjectures could be indulged so readily, I would rather print “may be supported” with Goulartius, a reading that I know was approved by Nicolas Le Fèvre. With the same audacity Pamelius printed *sanat* (“heals”) for *satiat* (“fills”) in Epistle 76, page 154, as we noted there. Apuleius, Book II of the *Metamorphoses*: “But this last one, which the final birth poured forth from the satiating spring.” See above, page 515.]

V. Remedies for appeasing God have been given in God’s own words [Note: [Col. 0605C] Bod. 3 reads “remedies concerning.”]; divine instructions have taught what sinners ought to do: that satisfaction is made to God by righteous deeds and sins are cleansed by the merits of mercy. And in Solomon we read: “Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor person” [Note: [Col. 0605C] Lam., NC. 1, Ebor., and Bod. 2 read “in the bosom of the poor person.” Ver. reads: “It will plead for you on the evil day.”], “and it will plead for you against every evil.” And again: [Col. 0605C] “Whoever stops his ears so that he does not hear the weak will himself call upon God, and there will be no one to hear him” (Prov. 21:[Col. 0606A]13). For one who has not himself been merciful will not be able to merit the Lord’s mercy; nor will one who has not been humane toward the poor person’s plea obtain anything from divine loving-kindness through his own prayers.

The Holy Spirit likewise declares and confirms this in the Psalms, saying: “Blessed is he who considers the needy” [Note: [Col. 0605C] Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, and Ver. read “the one in need.”] “and the poor; on an evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:2). Mindful of these precepts, Daniel, when King Nebuchadnezzar was in turmoil, terrified by an ominous dream, gave him a remedy for averting evil and obtaining divine assistance, saying: “Therefore, O king, may my counsel please you: redeem your sins with alms and your injustices with acts of compassion toward the poor, and God will be forgiving” [Note: [Col. 0606C] “God forgiving”: Lam., Lin., Pem., Voss. 1, 2, Bod. 2, 3. Oxon. reads “God patient.”] “toward your sins” (Dan. 4:24). Because the king did not obey him, he suffered the hostile and adverse things he had seen—things he could have escaped and avoided [Col. 0606B] if he had redeemed his sins with alms.

The angel Raphael also testifies to the same things [Note: [Col. 0606C] Ar., Lam., and Bod. 2 read “the same things to Tobias.”], and exhorts that alms be given willingly and generously, saying: “Prayer” [Note: [Col. 0606C] Lam. reads “Prayer, he says, is good.” Ver. reads “from sins.” Bod. 4 reads “Almsgiving with righteousness.”] “with fasting and almsgiving is good, because almsgiving delivers from death and itself cleanses sins” (Tob. 12:8). He shows that our prayers and fasts have less power unless they are assisted by almsgiving [Note: [Col. 0606C] Ar., West., Saris., and Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4 read “are joined to almsgiving.” Others after Pamelius read “are stuffed full.”], and that entreaties alone have little force for obtaining what is sought unless, through the addition of deeds and works, they are filled to satisfaction [239] [Note: [Col. 0606C] Lin. reads “are assisted.”]. The angel reveals, manifests, and confirms that through almsgiving our petitions are made effective, through almsgiving life is redeemed from dangers, and through almsgiving souls are delivered from death.

VI. Nor, dearest brothers, do we set these things forth without confirming what the angel Raphael said by the testimony of truth. In the Acts [Note: [Col. 0606C] West. reads “Thus in Acts.”] of the Apostles, the credibility of this fact is established; and by the proof of an event accomplished [Col. 0606C] and fulfilled, it is shown [Col. 0607A] that souls are delivered by almsgiving not only from the second death but also from the first [Note: [Col. 0607D] Saris. reads “is attested.”].

Tabitha [Note: [Col. 0607D] Bod. 3 reads “Tabitha the almsgiver.” Ar., Saris., and Bod. 2 read “in prayers.”], who was deeply devoted to righteous deeds and the giving of alms, became ill and died. Peter was summoned to her lifeless corpse. When, with apostolic kindness, he had come without delay, the widows stood around him weeping and pleading, showing him the cloaks, tunics, and all the garments that they had previously received. They pleaded for the dead woman not with their own voices but through her works. Peter perceived that what was being sought in this way could be obtained, and that Christ’s help would not fail the pleading widows, since Christ himself had been clothed in the widows.

And so, kneeling down [Note: [Col. 0607D] Ver. reads “on his knees.” Saris. reads “had prayed, and.”], he prayed; and, as a capable advocate for widows and the poor, he carried to the Lord the prayers entrusted to him. Then, turning toward the body, which now lay washed upon the board, he said: “Tabitha, arise in the name of Jesus Christ” [Note: [Col. 0607D] West. reads “in the name of the Lord.”] (Acts 9:40). Nor did the one who had said in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0607D] Voss. 2 and Pem. read “in his Gospel.”] that whatever was requested in his name would be given fail to bring Peter aid immediately. Death, therefore, is suspended and the spirit restored; and, while everyone marvels in astonishment, the body, brought back to life, is animated once more for this light of the world. Such was the power of the merits of mercy; such was the strength of righteous works! She who had bestowed the means of sustaining life upon struggling widows merited being recalled to life at the widows’ petition.

[Note: [Col. 0607D]

**VII.—Moth.** See Fronton du Duc’s notes on Saint Basil’s *Homilies on Fasting*, page 29.

**Sell all that is yours.** Lamonius’s codex reads: “Sell everything you possess and give it to the needy.” Elsewhere also I have seen “the needy” written in place of “the poor.”

**But when he found.** Lamonius’s codex reads: “But when a precious pearl [Col. 0608D] had been found.”]

VII. Accordingly, in the Gospel the Lord—the teacher of our life and master of eternal salvation, who gives life to the people of believers and provides for those he has made alive unto eternity—among his divine mandates and heavenly precepts commands and enjoins nothing more frequently than that we devote ourselves [Col. 0607C] to giving alms and not brood over earthly possessions, but instead lay up heavenly treasures. “Sell your possessions,” he says, “and give alms” (Luke 12:33). And again:

“Do not lay up treasures for yourselves upon earth, where moth and consuming decay destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor consuming decay destroys, and where thieves neither dig through nor steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will also be” (Matt. 6:19–21).

And when he wished to show one who had observed the law how to be perfect and complete, he said: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell everything that is yours” [Note: [Col. 0607D] Voss. 1 reads “everything you have”; NC. 2, “you possess.”], “and give it to the needy, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

Likewise, in another passage he says that the merchant of heavenly grace and purchaser of eternal salvation, after selling [Col. 0607D] all his possessions, ought to purchase the precious pearl—that is, eternal life, made precious by Christ’s blood—with the value of his patrimony: [Col. 0608A] “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a merchant” [Note: [Col. 0608D] Ar., West., Saris., and Bod. 2, 3, 4 read “a man trading.”] “seeking fine pearls. But when he found a precious pearl, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it” (Matt. 13:45).

[Note: [Col. 0608D]

**VIII.—Considers God.** The codex of Saint-Aubin reads “lends to God.” The Burgundian and Lamonian codices have “lends to God.”

**Mammon.** See Celio Calcagnini, Book I, Epistle 39.]

VIII. Finally, he calls those people children of Abraham whom he sees actively helping and feeding the poor. For when Zacchaeus had said, “Behold, I give half of my substance to the needy, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything” [Note: [Col. 0608D] Bod. 3 reads “whomever I have defrauded.”], “I repay fourfold,” Jesus answered and said that “today salvation” [Note: [Col. 0608D] Saris. reads “Salvation, he says.”] “has come to this house, since this man too is a son of Abraham” (Luke 19:8–9).

For if Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, then surely one who gives alms according to God’s precept believes God; and one who possesses the truth of faith preserves the fear of God. But one who [Col. 0608B] preserves the fear of God considers God in acts of compassion toward the poor [Note: [Col. 0608D] Voss. 1, Lam., and NC. 2 read “lends to God.”]. For he acts for this reason [Note: [Col. 0608D] Bod. 1, 2, 3 read “For he works for God.”] [240]: because he believes, because he knows that what was foretold in God’s words is true and that Holy Scripture cannot lie—that unfruitful trees, that is, barren people, are cut down and cast into the fire, while the merciful are called to the kingdom.

Elsewhere, too, the Lord calls working and fruitful people faithful, but denies faith to the unfruitful and barren, saying: “If you have not been faithful with unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you that which is true” [Note: [Col. 0608D] Lam. and Bod. 3, 4 read “that which is yours.”]? “And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:11).

IX. If [Note: [Col. 0608D] Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4 read “But.” Printed editions and Oxon. read “If.”] you are anxious and afraid that, if you begin to perform very many works of charity, the generous exercise of them may exhaust your patrimony and perhaps reduce you to poverty, be fearless [Col. 0608C] and secure in this matter. That from which expenditure is made for Christ’s needs and by which a heavenly work is performed cannot be exhausted. I do not guarantee this to you on my own authority, but promise it on the faith of Holy Scripture and the authority of the divine pledge.

The Holy Spirit speaks through Solomon and says: “Whoever gives to the poor will never be in need; but whoever turns away his eye will be in great poverty” (Prov. 28:27), showing that the merciful and those active in good works cannot be in need, while it is rather the miserly and barren who later fall into want.

Likewise, the blessed apostle Paul, filled with the grace of the Lord’s inspiration, says: “He who supplies seed to the sower will also provide bread for eating, and will multiply your sowing and increase the produce of the fruits of your righteousness, so that you may be enriched in all things.” And again: “The administration [Col. 0608D] of this service will not only supply what the saints lack, [Col. 0609A] but will also abound” [Note: [Col. 0609D] Bod. 4 reads “but also causes abundance.” Above it reads “has supplied and has abounded.”] “through abundant thanksgiving” [Note: [Col. 0609D] Saris. reads “through many thanksgivings.”] “to God” (2 Cor. 9:10–12). For while the thanksgiving of the poor is directed to God in prayer for our alms [Note: [Col. 0609D] Saris. reads “through alms.”] and works, the resources of the one who acts [Note: [Col. 0609D] Bod. 1 reads “of those who act.”] are increased by God’s repayment.

And in the Gospel the Lord, already discerning at that time the hearts of people of this kind and warning the faithless and unbelieving with foreknowing speech, solemnly declares:

“Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the nations seek all these things. But your Father knows” [Note: [Col. 0609D] Bod. 1, 2 and Saris. read “For.”] “that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0609D] Thus Ver., Thu., and Foss.; these words were absent from the printed editions.], “and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:31–33).

He says that all things are added and given to those who seek God’s kingdom and righteousness. For the Lord says that, when the day of judgment comes, those who have performed works in his Church [Col. 0609B] will be admitted to receive the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

**X.—Snare.** Two ancient books add “of the devil.”

] X. You fear that your patrimony may perhaps fail if you begin to give generously from it, and you do not know, wretched man, that while you fear the failure of your property, your very life and salvation are failing; and while you take care that nothing of your possessions be diminished, you do not see that you yourself are being diminished. You are a greater lover of mammon than of your own soul, so that, while you fear losing your patrimony for your own sake, you yourself perish for the sake of your patrimony [Note: [Col. 0609D] West., Ebor., and Foss. read “lest perhaps.” Ver. reads: “lest you lose your patrimony for your own sake, you ensure that you yourself perish for the sake of your patrimony.”].

And therefore the Apostle rightly cries out and says:

“We brought nothing into this world, and indeed we can take nothing away. Therefore, having food and covering, let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many harmful desires, which plunge a person into ruin [Col. 0609C] and destruction. For greed is the root of all evils; some, desiring it, have made shipwreck of the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:7–10).

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

**XI.—Means may be lacking.** The codex of Saint-Aubin reads “substance can be lacking.” So too it was written in the Verona manuscript.

] XI. You fear that your patrimony may perhaps fail if you begin to give generously from it. For when has it ever happened that the means of sustaining life could be lacking to a righteous person [Note: [Col. 0609D] Ver. reads “substance could be lacking.”], when it is written: “The Lord will not kill a righteous soul with hunger” (Prov. 10:3)? Elijah is fed in the wilderness through the service of ravens, and a meal is divinely prepared for Daniel in the den, where he had been shut up by the king’s command as prey for the lions. Yet you fear that food may be lacking to you while you perform good works and merit the Lord’s favor, when he himself, in the Gospel, rebukes those whose [Note: [Col. 0610D] West. reads “of whom.”] mind is doubtful and faith [Col. 0610A] weak, [241] solemnly declaring:

“Look at the birds of heaven, because they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds” [Note: [Col. 0610D] Ar., Lam., and Lin. read “nourishes.”] “them. Are you not worth more than they?” (Matt. 6:26).

God feeds the birds, and daily nourishment is furnished to sparrows; creatures that have no perception of divine things lack neither drink nor food. Do you think, then, that anything will be lacking to you—a Christian, a servant of God, one devoted to good works, one dear to his Lord?

[Note: [Col. 0609D]

**XII.—From earthly gains.** An ancient codex of the monastery [Col. 0610D] of Compiègne reads: “and so that by prudent works we might make for ourselves great gains from earthly resources.”

] XII. Unless you suppose [Note: [Col. 0610D] Ar. and Bod. 2 read “Unless you suppose that.”] that one who feeds Christ is not himself fed by Christ, or that earthly things will be lacking to those upon whom heavenly and divine things are bestowed. From where comes this unbelieving thought? From where this impious and sacrilegious reflection? What is a faithless heart doing in the house of faith? Why is one who does not believe Christ at all called and named a Christian? [Col. 0610B] The name “Pharisee” suits you better.

For when the Lord discussed almsgiving in the Gospel and faithfully and beneficially admonished us to make friends for ourselves by prudent action from our earthly gains—friends who would afterward receive us into the eternal dwellings—Scripture added after these things [Note: [Col. 0610D] Ar., Voss. 1, Lam., and Bod. 2, 3 read “divine Scripture.”]: “But the Pharisees, who were exceedingly greedy, heard all these things and mocked him” (Luke 16:14). Such are certain people [Note: [Col. 0610D] Ar. reads “Such people now.” Oxon. reads “Such people we now see in the Church.”] whom we now see in the Church, whose blocked ears and blinded hearts admit no light from spiritual and saving admonitions. We ought not to be surprised that they despise the servant in his discourses, when we see the Lord himself despised by people of this kind.

[Note: [Col. 0610D]

**XIII.—Burdens by its own weight.** Thus all the old editions, all our books, and [534] eight English manuscripts. Pamelius, as he himself says, added “more heavily” from Gravius’s edition, although that word does not occur in the edition said to be Gravius’s.

[Col. 0611B] **Returns.** *Redditus* ought to be written, not *reditus*. For the word *redditus* derives from the verb *reddo* (“render”), not from *redeo* (“return”). Varro, Book III of *On Agriculture*, chapter 3: “So that in that year that part of the villa yielded sixty, twice as much as your estate yields.” Jerome, Book II, *Against Jovinian*: “For great returns the head of the household exacts payment.” Saint Leo the Pope, Sermon III, *On the Collections*: “For although a greater return may be expected from a greater sowing, [Col. 0611C] the fruit of righteousness can nevertheless arise from a small planting.” And yet Cujacius, Book IX of the *Observations*, chapter 15, writes *reditus*, and Salmasius, in his notes on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, page 3, contends that it ought to be written thus. Here in Cyprian the Compiègne codex has “riches.”

**Of earthly possessions.** I do not disapprove the reading of the old editions: “Make Christ a participant with you from the proceeds of earthly possessions.” Manutius was the first to alter it. The Manutian edition is supported by ancient copies.]

XIII. Why do you flatter yourself with these foolish and senseless thoughts, as though fear and anxiety about the future were holding you back from good works? Why do you put forward shadows and certain illusions of an empty excuse? Rather, confess what is true; and since you cannot deceive those who know, disclose the secret and hidden things of your mind.

The darkness of barrenness has besieged your soul, and, once the light of truth withdrew from it, a deep and profound fog of greed blinded your carnal heart. You are the captive and slave of your money; you are bound by the chains and fetters of covetousness; and though Christ had already set you free, you are bound once more. You preserve money that, though preserved [Note: [Col. 0610D] Saris. reads “preserved by you.”], does not preserve you. You heap up a patrimony that burdens you with its own weight [Note: [Col. 0610D] Thus Ar., West., Lam., Saris., and Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4: “thus burdens.” Oxon. reads “more heavily by its own.”]; and you do not remember what God replied to the rich man who boasted with foolish exultation of his abundance [Note: [Col. 0610D] Ver. reads “abundance, boasting foolishly of himself.”] of overflowing produce: [Col. 0611A] “‘Fool,’ he says, ‘this night your soul is demanded from you. Whose, then, will be the things you have prepared?’” [Note: [Col. 0611B] Ver., Ar., and Saris. read “your soul—which.”] (Luke 12:20).

Why do you brood alone over your riches? Why, to your own punishment, do you increase the weight of your patrimony, so that the richer you become in the world, the poorer you become toward God? Share your returns with the Lord your God; divide your fruits with Christ. Make Christ a participant in your earthly possessions, so that he in turn may make you his coheir in the heavenly kingdoms.

[Note: [Col. 0611C]

**XIV.—And pitiable.** These words are absent from seventeen of our books and from three English manuscripts.

**In the Church of Christ.** I strongly think that these words—which are absent from the old editions, from ten of our codices, and from five English manuscripts, but were added by Manutius—ought not to be in this passage. Nevertheless, I have not ventured to delete them, because I found them in eleven ancient copies.]

XIV. You are mistaken and deceived, whoever you are who believes yourself rich in this world. Hear the voice of your Lord in the Apocalypse rebuking people of this kind with righteous reproaches:

“You say,” he declares, “‘I am rich and have become wealthy and need nothing’” [Note: [Col. 0611B] Saris. reads “and have become wealthy, and need nothing.”]; “and you do not know that you are wretched and pitiable, and poor” [Note: [Col. 0611B] West., Saris., and Bod. 1 read “wretched and poor.”], “and blind, and naked. I counsel you to buy from me gold refined” [Note: [Col. 0611B] Voss. 1 reads “gold tested.”] “by fire, so that you may be rich; and a white garment, so that you may be clothed” [Note: [Col. 0611B] Thus Bod. 1, 3, 4, Thu., and Foss. The printed editions read “may be clothed in white”; Ar., Bod. 2, and MR. read “may be dressed.”], “and the shamefulness of your nakedness may not appear in you; and anoint” [Note: [Col. 0612B] Saris. reads “anoint.”] “your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Rev. 3:17–18).

Therefore, you who are wealthy and rich, buy refined gold for yourself from Christ, so that, once your impurities have been burned away as if by fire, you may be pure gold, if you are cleansed by almsgiving and righteous action. Buy yourself a white garment, so that you who had been naked according to Adam and stood hideously deformed may be clothed in Christ’s radiant garment. And you, a matron who are wealthy [Note: [Col. 0612B] Ar., Saris., and Bod. 1, 2, 4 read “a wealthy matron.”] and rich in the Church of Christ, anoint your eyes not with the devil’s antimony [*stibium*] [Note: [Col. 0612B] Bod. 3 reads “of the deformed devil.”], but with Christ’s eye-salve, so that you may come to see God by meriting God’s favor through both works [Note: [Col. 0612B] Oxon. reads “through good works and conduct.”] and conduct. [242]

[Note: [Col. 0611C]

**XV.—Corban.** I have seen it written thus in nine manuscript codices, including the Séguier manuscript. Others have *Corbona* or *Corbana*. The Fuxensis has *Corban* and *Corbana*. [Col. 0611D] In chapter 7 of the Gospel according to Mark, and in Jerome’s Epistle to Geruntia *On Monogamy*: “*Corban*, which means ‘gift.’” The reading of the Pithoeanus codex may also be good; there it is written: “which, as though wholly orphaned, you do not regard.” For a little earlier Cyprian said that this mother’s eyes were overspread with the darkness of blackness and covered by night. See Cotelier’s notes on Book II of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 36, and Samuel Basnage’s *Exercises on Baronius*, page 597.

**Into the Lord’s house.** That is, into the house in which Christians assemble to celebrate the mysteries. The decree of Galerius Maximinus concerning the Christians, in Rufinus, Book IX, chapter 9: “But we also permit them to restore their houses of prayer—that is, their Lord’s houses—as they wish.” And in Book X, chapter 3, a certain confessor who had defeated a philosopher says: “Arise and follow me to the Lord’s house and receive the seal of this faith.” Jerome in the *Chronicle*: “At Antioch construction began on the Lord’s house that is called the Golden.” Saint Hilary, at the end of the book to Constantius [Col. 0612B] that begins *Benignifico*, says of the Arians: “They therefore fear the judgment of the people; they pass from the Lord’s house to the palace.” See Beveridge’s annotations on canon 15 of the Council of Ancyra, and Jean Étienne Duranti, Book I, chapter 1, *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*.

Since mention has arisen of this most distinguished man, a citizen deeply devoted to his homeland, who was, to use Saint Cyprian’s words, an eminent person, we must seize this [Col. 0612C] opportunity to destroy the fable that has recently emerged in the republic of letters concerning him and Pierre Danès, bishop of Lavaur. A certain recent writer, a witness insufficiently reliable, writes that Duranti was not the author of the work *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*, but rather Pierre Danès, bishop of Lavaur; and that Duranti, who had found it in Danès’s library, which he had purchased for a price, made it his own under the right by which buyers make the things they buy their own.

This author says that he received this account from Pierre de Bertier, bishop of Montauban, who, as he says, had heard it reported by Jean de Bertier, bishop of Rieux, his uncle, who was joined in the closest friendship with Danès and Duranti. It is remarkable how eagerly this new story has been received by some, because, as Cicero says, the multitude judges few things from truth, but many from opinion.

In the first place, it seems fair and entirely consonant with reason that no one should dare call a man of great and good reputation a plagiarist without certain evidence. But the evidence that would take that work away from Duranti is so far from certain [Col. 0612D] that, on the contrary, everything concurs in vindicating it for him. For it is certain that the account concerning the bishop of Montauban, which has now emerged for the first time after so many years, cannot be true. His uncle Jean de Bertier departed this life in July 1620. At that time the bishop of Montauban was a boy only twelve years old. Who could readily bring himself to believe that a boy of that age held conversations with his uncle about such weighty [585] subjects and matters so remote from the experience and understanding of children?

Moreover, it is certain that Danès, advanced in age, withdrew two years before his death to the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where he died and was buried. It is not probable that this learned man wished to tear himself away and separate himself from his library. We should therefore suppose that he transferred it to the house in which he had resolved to live and in which he did in fact live.

This opinion of mine is confirmed by the testimony of Genebrard, who, in the funeral oration [Col. 0613C] delivered for Danès a few days after his departure to heaven, says that Danès’s books were then in the possession of his heirs and had neither been dispersed nor sold. It is confirmed also by the authority of Thevet, who knew Danès most intimately and survived him. In his encomium of Danès, Thevet speaks of his scholarly labors in such a way as to say that he hopes they may be found among his books still held by his relatives. I myself certainly have in my library two manuscript codices that are known once to have been in Danès’s library.

Finally, J. Ang. Papius, who first published the work *On the Rites of the Catholic Church* at Rome in 1591 and dedicated it to Gregory XIV, testifies that Duranti called this work [Col. 0613D] his “nocturnal studies” and sent it to Rome to Cardinal de Pellevé so that it might be printed there. Moreover, a letter by the same Duranti to his friend Jean de la Barrière, abbot of Feuillant, is in circulation. It was written from the prison into which that excellent man had been cast by depraved and factious men, three days before his pitiable death. In it he asks de la Barrière, who was then at Rome, that whenever he himself should depart from human affairs, he should arrange for his book to be approved at Rome and then committed to print.

Is it right to suppose that a grave, good, and wise man, then condemned and near to death, could have been so shameless as, with the greatest audacity and injustice, to attribute to himself a work that he knew had not been composed by him? Far be it that this thought should enter the head of any person of sound mind. Time will destroy the fabrications of this opinion—or rather, this fable—and students of truth and humane letters [Col. 0614C] will willingly dismiss it.

Danès’s glory does not need human falsehoods. In the everlasting course of time, the fame of his achievements will live. For, as the most illustrious president de Thou says, he was a most learned man who, although he published no writings, merited being numbered among the men of this age preeminent in learning and humane letters. Scévole de Sainte-Marthe, concurring with him in his *Eulogies of Frenchmen Illustrious for Learning*, laments that no monuments of so great a talent and such prolonged labor now survive.

**A portion of the sacrifice.** See Petavius’s dissertation *On Penance and Reconciliation as Received in the Customs of the Ancient Church*, chapter 3.

[Col. 0614D] **Merited praise from the judge’s voice.** Jerome, in his Epistle to Demetrias *On the Preservation of Virginity*, speaking of Saint John the Baptist, says: “Praised by the judge’s voice before the day of judgment.”

**Unfaithfulness.** I came very close to printing “unhappiness,” following the reading of the old editions, which is supported by twenty-two of our copies and eleven English manuscripts. Manutius printed “unfaithfulness.” Pamelius thought otherwise.

**And the needy widow.** I have restored this passage on the authority of the Burgundian codex and that of Saint-Arnoul. For the rest, the reading of the Grenoble codex and of one of mine is not bad; in them it is written: “The widow, though needy—not a widow in her work—is found.” Moreover, the word “generous,” which the Manutian edition inserted, is found nowhere in our ancient copies or in the English manuscripts.]

XV. But you who are such a person cannot perform works of charity in the Church. For your eyes, overspread with the darkness of blackness and covered by night [Note: [Col. 0612B] Foss. reads “blinded by night.”], do not see the needy and the poor. [Col. 0612B] You are wealthy and rich, and you believe that you celebrate the Lord’s rite, though you pay no regard at all to the *corban*, though you come [Col. 0613A] into the Lord’s house without a sacrifice, though you take a portion of the sacrifice that a poor person offered.

Look in the Gospel at the widow who was mindful of the heavenly precepts [Note: [Col. 0613B] Lam. and Ebor. read “the divine precepts.”], who acted amid the very pressures and constraints of poverty and put into the treasury the only two small coins [Note: [Col. 0613B] Saris. reads “the only coins.”] she possessed. When the Lord noticed and saw her, assessing her work not by her patrimony but by her disposition, and considering not how much she had given but from how much, he answered and said:

“Amen, I say to you, this widow has put more than everyone else into the gifts of God. For all these others put into the gifts of God from what abounded for them, but she, from her poverty, put in all the livelihood she possessed, whatever it was” (Luke 21:3).

A greatly blessed and glorious woman, who merited praise from the judge’s voice even before the day of judgment! Let the rich be ashamed [Col. 0613B] of their barrenness and unfaithfulness [Note: [Col. 0613B] Ar., Saris., West., Voss. 1, Ebor., Lam. 6, NC. 1, 2, Thu., Foss., and Bod. 1, 2, 3 read “barrenness and unhappiness.”]. She is a widow, and a widow needy in material things, yet she is found rich in works [Note: [Col. 0613B] Thus West., Ar., Lam., Ebor., Lin., and Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Oxon. reads “is found generous in her work.”]. Although everything that is given is conferred upon orphans and widows, she who ought to have received gives instead. Thus we may know what punishment awaits the barren rich person, when, by this very example, even the poor are shown to be obligated to perform good works.

And so that we may understand that these works are given to God and that whoever does them merits the Lord’s favor, Christ calls that offering “the gifts of God” and declares that the widow put two small coins into the gifts of God, so that it may become more and more evident that whoever shows mercy to the poor lends to God [Note: [Col. 0613C] Bod. 1, 2 read “lends to God.”].

[Note: [Col. 0614D]

**XVI.—Nor fellow servants.** The Compiègne codex reads: “Nor should we prefer our servants or children to the Lord.”

] XVI. But neither, dearest brothers, should this consideration restrain or recall a Christian from good and righteous works: that someone might think himself able to be excused on account of his children. For in spiritual expenditures we ought to think of Christ [Note: [Col. 0614B] Saris. reads “give to Christ.”], who has declared that he himself receives them; and we should prefer not fellow servants but the Lord to our children, as he himself instructs and admonishes us:

“He who loves,” he says, “father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

Likewise, in Deuteronomy, comparable words are written to strengthen faith and love of God:

“Those who say,” he declares, “to father or mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and who did not acknowledge their own children—these have kept your precepts and preserved your covenant” (Deut. 33:9).

For if we love God with our whole heart, we ought to prefer neither parents nor children to God. John also sets this forth [Note: [Col. 0614B] Saris. reads “sets forth and says.”] in his Epistle, declaring that the love of God is not present among those whom we see unwilling to act charitably toward the poor:

“Whoever,” he says, “possesses the substance of the world and sees his brother in need” [Note: [Col. 0614B] West. reads “his needy brother”; Ver., “his brother desiring something.”], “and closes his heart, how” [Note: [Col. 0614B] West., Voss. 2, Pem., and Foss. read “closes his heart against him.”] “does the love” [Note: [Col. 0614B] Ver. reads “how can.”] “of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17).

For if God receives a loan through alms given to the poor, and what is given to the least is given to Christ, no one should prefer earthly things to heavenly things or place human things before divine things.

[Note: [Col. 0615C]

### XVII.—The Jar of Meal

The Lamonian codex reads *phial*. The Pithoean manuscript reads: “The jar of flour shall not fail, and the vessel of oil shall not diminish.” Almost the same wording also occurs in chapter 17 of the Third Book of Kings. See St. Ambrose, *On Duties*, book II, chapter 4, and book III, chapter 1.

**The flask of oil.** Prosper—or some other author—*On the Promises and Predictions of God*, book II, chapter 29: “The flask of oil shall not diminish.” Jerome, in the *Letter to Furia on the Preservation of Widowhood*: “The flour is sown, and the flask of oil [Col. 0615D] is found.” Likewise, in the *Letter to Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*: “In a marvelous manner, when the flask had been filled.” Sulpicius Severus, in book I of the *Sacred History*, speaking of the story of Elijah: “Then, warned by the Lord, he made for the town of Zarephath and lodged with a widow. When, being hungry, he asked her for food, she pleaded that she had nothing except a little meal and a little oil; when that was consumed, she would await death together with her children,” etc.

XVII. Thus that widow in the Third Book of Kings, when everything had been consumed by drought and famine, made a hearth-cake from the little meal and oil that remained [Note: [Col. 0614B] “Ash-cake,” Ver. Bod. 1, 2, 4.], after whose consumption she was to die with her children. Elijah arrived and asked that something first be given to him to eat; then she and her children were to eat whatever remained. She did not hesitate to comply, nor did the mother, amid famine and want, put her children before Elijah. Indeed, in the sight [Col. 0615A] of God, what is pleasing to God is done: what was requested is offered promptly and willingly; not a portion from abundance, but the whole from her little store is given; and though her children were hungry, another is fed first. Amid want and famine, she gives thought to mercy before food, so that, while bodily life is disregarded in a saving work [Note: [Col. 0615C] “In a spiritual work,” Saris.], the soul may be spiritually preserved.

Elijah, therefore, bearing the type of Christ, 243 and showing that Christ repays each person in return for mercy, answered and said: “Thus says the Lord: The jar of meal [Note: [Col. 0615C] “The jar of flour,” Saris. “Shall diminish,” Ver.] shall not fail, and the flask of oil shall not diminish until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the earth” (1 Kings 17:14). In accordance with the faithfulness of the divine promise, what the widow had furnished was multiplied and heaped up; and as righteous works [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Furnished in righteous works,” Bod. 1, 4.] and the merits of mercy received increase and growth, the vessels of meal and oil [Col. 0615B] were filled. The mother did not take from her children what she gave to Elijah; rather, through what she did kindly [Note: [Col. 0615C] “She bestowed what she did kindly,” Bod. 1.] and devoutly, she bestowed more upon her children. And she did not yet know Christ, had not yet heard his precepts, and had not been redeemed by his cross and passion; yet she repaid food and drink in return for blood. From this it may become apparent how greatly a person sins within the Church if, placing himself and his children before Christ, he keeps his riches and does not share his abundant patrimony with the poverty of the needy.

[Note: [Col. 0615D]

### XVIII.—Souls to Be Delivered

Some old books and certain editions read “to be redeemed.”

**To be wiped away.** This is the reading of the early editions, including the Manutian, and of almost all the old books. Erasmus advised that this unquestionably was the correct reading. Rightly so. For above, Letter VIII, p. 17: “You may wipe it away with your joy.” Varro, *On Agriculture*, book III, chapter 5: “And rather make it creep through narrow channels, so that they can easily be cleaned out.” Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 2: “Old ditches are to be wiped clean.” Columella, book VI, chapter 9: “Then also it is appropriate for the lips to be wiped with a sponge.” Lucretius, book IV:

[Col. 0616C] “Surely we see many things cast forth and wiped away.”

Likewise book VI:

“Whence that dry sound wipes the ears.”

Horace, *Satires*, book II, satire 2:

“This rather than wipe the palate with a hen.”

The same author, *Odes*, book I, ode 7:

[Col. 0616D] “As the South Wind often wipes away the clouds from the darkened sky and makes it bright.”

Juvenal, Satire V:

“But soon you twist the cups as well,  
Wounded, and he wipes the wounds with a red napkin.”

And Satire XIV:

“Let another wipe the rough vessels.”

Silius Italicus, book II:

“Since opportunity has been given  
To scrape away with iron the long-standing rust.”

Quintus Curtius, book X: “And the oars were wiped clean in turn.” Apuleius, in the *Apology*: “Even the continuation of repeated labor wipes away all grace from the body and makes its condition thin.” Symmachus, book VI, Letter 73: “Let joy wipe away the cloud of present anger”; and often elsewhere in this author.]

XVIII. But there are many children in the household, and the number of your children delays you from applying yourself generously to good works. Yet you ought, for that very reason, to do more, because you are the father of many dear pledges. There are more persons for whom you must entreat the Lord; the offenses of many must be redeemed, the consciences of many cleansed, [Col. 0615C] the souls of many delivered. Just as in this worldly life the greater the number of children to be fed and supported [Col. 0616A] [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Fed and sustained,” Saris.], the greater the expenditure, so also in the spiritual and heavenly life, the more numerous the children, the greater the expenditure on works ought to be.

Thus Job too offered numerous sacrifices for his children: as great as was the number of children in his household, so great also was the number of victims given to God. And because something sinful cannot fail to occur daily in the sight of God, daily sacrifices were not lacking by which sins could be wiped away. Divine Scripture proves this [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Proves this,” West.], saying: “Job, a true and righteous man, had seven sons and three daughters, and he cleansed them, offering victims for them to God according to their number, and one calf for their sins” (Job 1:2, 5). If, therefore, you truly love your children, if you show them the full, fatherly sweetness of charity, [Col. 0616B] you ought all the more to perform good works, so that by righteous action you may commend your children to God.

[Note: [Col. 0616D]

### XIX.—In Need of Bread

Several old books read “seeking bread.” So too does the Vulgate edition.

**Lends at interest.** This is the reading of the later editions and of most of the [Col. 0617D] old books. Other editions and the commonly used Psalter read “lends.” So too does the English edition.]

XIX. Do not regard as the father of your children [Note: [Col. 0615C] “Do not think yourself the father of your children,” Saris. Voss. 1.] one who is both temporary and weak [Note: [Col. 0616C] “You are weak,” Saris. Voss. 1.]; rather, secure for them him [Note: [Col. 0616C] “Father” added by Oxon.] who is the eternal and steadfast Father of spiritual children. Assign to him the resources that you are preserving for your heirs. Let him be your children’s guardian, their trustee, and, by divine majesty, their protector against all worldly injuries. A patrimony entrusted to God [Note: [Col. 0616C] “Of those who believe in God,” Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Lam. “Nor does a thief seize it,” Voss. 2.] is neither taken away by the state nor confiscated by the treasury nor overturned by any legal chicanery. An inheritance is placed in safety when it is preserved with God as its guardian.

This is to provide for dear children’s future; this is to take thought for future heirs with fatherly devotion, in accordance with the faith of Holy Scripture, which says: “I was young [Note: [Col. 0616C] “I was younger,” Bod. 1. Saris.], and I have grown old; and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring [Col. 0616C] in need of bread [Note: [Col. 0616C] “Seeking bread,” Saris. West. Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.]. All day long he has mercy and lends at interest, and his offspring [Col. 0617A] is blessed” [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Will be blessed,” Bod. 1, 3.] (Ps. 36:25). And again: “He who conducts himself blamelessly in righteousness [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Without reproach and injury,” Saris.] will leave blessed children after him” (Prov. 20:7).

You are therefore a transgressor and a traitor as a father unless you faithfully take thought for your children, unless with religious and genuine devotion you provide for their preservation. You who devote yourself more to an earthly than to a heavenly patrimony, preferring to commend your children to the devil [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Would rather commend them to the devil,” Pem. Voss. 2.] than to Christ, sin twice and commit a twofold and double crime: both because you do not prepare for your children the aid of God the Father, and because you teach your children [Note: [Col. 0617C] Thus Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Spir. Vet. innom. Voss. 1. Lam. Ebor. “To the children,” Rigalt.] to love their patrimony more than Christ.

XX. Be rather such a father to your children as Tobias proved to be. Give your dear ones useful and saving precepts such as he gave his son; command your children what he too commanded his son, saying: “And now, son, I command you: serve [Col. 0617B] God in truth, and do before him what is pleasing to him; and command your children 244 to practice righteousness and almsgiving, to remember God, and to bless his name at all times” (Tob. 14:10–11).

And again: “All the days of your life, dearest son, keep God in mind, and do not transgress his commandments. Practice righteousness all the days of your life, and do not walk the path of wickedness, because, when you act in truth, there will be regard for your works. Give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person. Thus it will come about that the face of God will not be turned away from you. Give according to what you have, son. If you have abundant substance, give more alms from it; if you have little, share from that very little. And do not be afraid when you give alms, for you store up a good reward for yourself against the day of necessity, because almsgiving [Col. 0617C] delivers from death and does not permit one to go into Gehenna [Note: [Col. 0617C] Thus. In West. Ar. Ben. Pem. NC. 2. Saris. Voss. 2. Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver. “Gehenna,” Imp.]. Almsgiving is a good gift for all who practice it before the Most High God” (Tob. 4:2–16).

[Note: [Col. 0617D]

### XXI.—To Have Emperors Present

Above, Letter VIII, p. 17, Christ is said to have been present at the martyrs’ contest. Cassian, book VI, chapter 9: “The Lord continually watches the battle of our contest.” The author of the *Letter to Demetrias*, among the works of St. Jerome: “See what spirit and what courage you ought to bring to so great a spectacle, and measure the magnitude of the contest by the dignity of its spectators.”]

XXI. What kind of public exhibition is it, dearest brothers, whose presentation [Note: [Col. 0617C] “Whose provision,” Bod. 1.] is celebrated with God looking on! If, at the pagans’ public exhibition, it is regarded as great and glorious to have proconsuls or emperors present, and if the preparations and expenses of the sponsors are greater so that they may please their superiors, how much more illustrious and greater is the glory of an exhibition that has God and Christ as its spectators! How much more abundant must the preparations and more generous the expense be here, [Col. 0618A] where the Powers of heaven assemble for the spectacle, where all the angels assemble, where the sponsor seeks neither a four-horse chariot nor a consulship, but is granted eternal life; where the empty and temporary favor of the crowd is not courted, but the everlasting reward of the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0617D] “And the heavenly kingdom,” Lin.] is received!

[Note: [Col. 0617D]

### XXII.—Let Each Person Place

This passage is cited by St. Augustine, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, chapter 8.

[Col. 0618D] **Sponsors of public exhibitions.** Jerome, in the *Letter to Pammachius on the Death of Paulina*: “A sponsor for the poor and a candidate for the needy.” See Seneca, *On Benefits*, book II, chapter 21, and Maximus of Turin’s *Homily on the Vigil of the Lord’s Nativity*. Quintilian, book VIII, chapter 3, reports that Augustus was the first to use the word *munerarius* (“sponsor of a public exhibition”).

**Show.** The Manutian edition afterwards continues: “fortified by your precepts and destined to receive heavenly things in return for earthly.” But I, with Morellius, delete these words, because I did not find them in the early editions or in any of the old copies I used, and they are also absent from nine English manuscripts.]

XXII. And so that the sluggish, the barren, and those who, through greed for money, do nothing to produce the fruit of salvation may be put to greater shame—so that the blush of disgrace may strike their filthy conscience more forcefully with its own dishonor and shame [Note: [Col. 0618C] “That a blush may come upon it,” Pem. Voss. 1.]—let each person place before his eyes the devil with his servants [Note: [Col. 0618C] “The devil with his angels,” Voss. 1.], that is, with the people of perdition and death, leaping into the midst and, in Christ’s very presence as judge, challenging Christ’s people [Note: [Col. 0618C] “With Christ present,” Voss. 1. Lam. Bod. 1, 3, 4.] to a test of comparison, saying:

“For these whom you see with me, I [Col. 0618B] neither received blows nor endured scourges, neither bore the cross nor shed my blood; nor did I redeem my household at the price of suffering and gore. Neither do I promise them the heavenly kingdom, nor call them back anew to paradise with immortality restored. Yet what costly public exhibitions they provide for me, how magnificent they are, and through what excessive and prolonged labor they are procured, with the most expensive preparations—their possessions either mortgaged or sold to provide the exhibition! And unless its presentation proves respectable [Note: [Col. 0618C] “Comes to pass,” Saris.], they are driven out with abuse and hissing and sometimes nearly stoned by the fury of the people.

“Show me such sponsors of exhibitions among your own people, Christ: show whether those rich men [Note: [Col. 0618C] “Show the rich,” Ar. West. Lam. Ebor. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], those overflowing with abundant wealth, present such an exhibition in the Church with you presiding and watching—mortgaging or selling their possessions, or rather transferring them to heavenly treasures by changing their ownership for the better. In these fleeting and earthly exhibitions of mine, no one is fed, no one is clothed, no one is sustained by the comfort of any food or drink. Amid the madness of the presenter and the delusion of the spectator, everything perishes in the prodigal and foolish vanity of deceptive pleasures. There, among your poor, it is you who are clothed and fed; it is you who promise eternal life to those who perform good works. And scarcely do your people, who are honored by you with divine recompenses and heavenly rewards, equal mine who are perishing [Note: [Col. 0618C] “Mine who bring about perdition,” Ar. West. Bod. 4. Ver. Corb. Man. [Col. 0618D] Mor.].”

[Col. 0619A] XXIII. What do we answer to this, dearest brothers? By what reasoning do we defend the minds of the rich, shrouded in sacrilegious barrenness [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Sacrilegious barren deeds,” Lam. Bod. 2, 4. Ver.] and, as it were, in a night of darkness? By what excuse do we clear them, when we are inferior to the devil’s servants, inasmuch as we do not repay Christ even in small things for the price of his passion and blood?

He gave us precepts; he instructed us what his servants ought to do; he promised a reward to those who perform good works, 245 and threatened punishment to the barren. He pronounced his sentence and foretold in advance what judgment he would deliver. What excuse can there be [Note: [Col. 0619D] “What defense can there be?” Saris. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] for the idle, what defense for the barren, except that when the servant does not do what [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Whatever the servant,” other witnesses.] is commanded, the Lord will do what he threatens? For he also says:

“When the Son of Man comes in his splendor, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his splendor [Note: [Col. 0619D] “In his splendor,” Ar. West. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, above, *Against the Jews* and *To Quirinus*. “In glory,” Imp.]; and all nations will be gathered [Col. 0619B] before him, and he will separate them from one another, just as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats; and he will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left. Then the king will say to those who will be [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Who are,” Ar. West. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom that was prepared for you from the beginning of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me [Note: [Col. 0619D] “You wove clothing for me,” Ar. West. Saris., above, *Against the Jews* and *To Quirinus*. “You clothed me,” Imp.]; I fell ill, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.’

“Then the righteous will answer him, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, thirsty and give you drink? When did we see you a stranger and take you in, naked and clothe you? And when did we see you fall ill [Note: [Col. 0619D] “Ill,” Bod. 1, above, *Against the Jews* and *To Quirinus*. “I fell ill,” Imp.] or in prison, and come to you?’

“Then the king will answer and say to them: ‘Amen, I say to you: insofar as you did it for one of the least of these [Col. 0619C] my brothers, you did it for me.’

“Then he will also say to those who will be at his left hand [Note: [Col. 0620D] “Who are at his left hand,” Ar. West. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.]: ‘Depart from me, accursed, into the eternal fire that my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; ill and in prison, and you did not visit me [Note: [Col. 0620D] “Come to,” NC. 2. Bod. 3, 4.].’

“Then they too will answer, saying: ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or ill or in prison, and not minister to you?’

“And he will answer them: ‘Amen, I say to you: insofar as you did not do it for one of the least of these, neither did you do it for me.’

“And these will depart into eternal burning [Note: [Col. 0620D] “Conflagration,” Pem. Voss. “Fire,” Lin.], but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:31–46).

What greater declaration could Christ have issued to us? How could he have done more to urge on our works of righteousness and mercy [Col. 0619D] than by saying that whatever is furnished to the needy and poor is furnished [Col. 0620A] to himself, and that he himself is offended if it is not furnished to the needy and poor? Thus, whoever is not moved by consideration for his brother in the Church may at least be moved by contemplation of Christ; and whoever gives no thought to his fellow servant in toil and want may at least think of the Lord as present in that very person whom he despises.

XXIV. And therefore, dearest brothers, whose fear of God is ready, and whose spirit, now that the world has been scorned and trampled underfoot, has been raised toward heavenly and divine things, let us offer service to the Lord in the winning of his favor [Note: [Col. 0620D] “In winning his favor,” Voss. 1.] with full faith, devout mind, and continual action. Let us give earthly garments to Christ, that we may receive heavenly clothing; let us give worldly food and drink, that we may come with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to the heavenly banquet. Lest we reap little [Note: [Col. 0620D] “We shall reap without growing weary,” Bod. 1, 4.], let us sow very much. [Col. 0620B] While there is time, let us provide for eternal security and salvation, as the apostle Paul warns and says: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do what is good toward everyone, but especially toward the household of faith. And let us not fail in doing good, for in due season we shall reap” (Gal. 6:10).

[Note: [Col. 0619D]

### XXV.—Equality

So Erasmus and others after him. I was unwilling to change it, although almost all the [Col. 0620D] old manuscripts and the earlier editions read “equity.”

[Col. 0621B] **Sharing and just.** Commodianus, *Instruction* 30: “Share with the least while you have time.” Likewise, *Instruction* 63.]

XXV. Let us consider, dearest brothers, what the people of believers did under the apostles, when, amid those very beginnings, their minds flourished with greater virtues, when the believers’ Faith still burned with the fresh warmth of faith. They then sold their houses and estates and willingly and generously offered the proceeds to the apostles for distribution to the poor [Note: [Col. 0620D] “The resources to the poor,” West.]. By selling and disposing of their earthly patrimony, they transferred their lands to the place where they might obtain the fruits of an eternal possession [Note: [Col. 0620D] “Of an eternal possession, so that they might procure for them,” Bod. 3, 4.], purchasing [Col. 0620C] houses there where they would begin to dwell forever. Such was then their abundance in works as was their unity in love, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Now the multitude of those who had believed acted with one soul and one mind; nor was there any distinction among them, nor did they regard anything among the goods they possessed as their own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32).

This is truly to become God’s children [Note: [Col. 0620D] “To live spiritually,” West.] by spiritual birth [Note: [Col. 0620D] “A son,” Lam. Ebor. West.]; this is to imitate, by the heavenly law, the equality of God the Father. For whatever belongs to God is common for our use, nor is anyone barred from his benefits and gifts so as to prevent the entire human race from enjoying the divine goodness and generosity equally. Thus daylight gives light equally, the sun shines, rain waters, and wind blows; sleepers have one common sleep, and the radiance [Col. 0620D] of the stars and moon is common to all. Following this example of equality [Note: [Col. 0620D] “This example of equity,” Bod. 1, 2, 3. “Of equality,” NC. 2. Tew. Drur. 2.], the landowner [Col. 0621A] who shares his revenues and produce with the brotherhood, being generous and just through freely bestowed gifts, is an imitator of God the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0621B]

### XXVI.—The White Crown

Above, Letter VIII, p. 18: “It was assuredly white in the brothers’ works; now it has become purple in the blood of the martyrs.” Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Paula to Eustochium*: “For not only the shedding of blood in confession is reckoned as martyrdom; the spotless service of a devout mind is also a daily martyrdom. The former crown is woven from roses and violets, the latter from lilies.”]

XXVI. What glory will belong to those who perform good works, dearest brothers; how great will be the fullness of joy when the Lord begins to review his people and, distributing the promised rewards according to our merits and works, gives heavenly things in return for earthly, everlasting things for temporary, great things for small; presents us to the Father, to whom he restored us by his sanctification [Note: [Col. 0621B] “Who restored us,” Bod. 3. “From sanctification,” Bod. 2.]; bestows eternity and immortality upon us, to which he restored us through the life-giving power of his blood; makes us return anew to paradise; and opens the kingdoms of heaven by the faithfulness and truth of his promise!

Let these things remain firmly fixed in our minds; let them be understood with full faith; let them be loved with the whole heart; let them be purchased by the magnanimity of unceasing works [Col. 0621B] [Note: [Col. 0621B] “Be rendered with magnanimity,” Lin.]. A splendid and divine thing, dearest brothers, is saving action: the great comfort of believers, [Col. 0622A] the saving protection of our security, the fortification of hope, the safeguard of faith, the remedy for sin [Note: [Col. 0621B] “A remedy laid up for sin,” Ar.], a thing placed within the doer’s power, a thing both great and easy, a crown of peace without the danger of persecution, the true and greatest gift of God, necessary for the weak and glorious for the strong. Helped by it, the Christian carries [Note: [Col. 0621B] “Is helped to bear,” Bod. 1. “Prefers,” Rig. “And the righteous man,” West. [Col. 0622B] Lin.] spiritual grace through to completion, wins the favor of Christ the Judge, and reckons God his debtor.

Let us willingly and promptly contend for this palm of saving works; let us all run in the contest of righteousness, with God and Christ looking on. And since we have already begun to be greater than the age and the world, let us not allow any desire for the age and the world to slow our course. If the day either of our rendering an account [Note: [Col. 0622B] “Return,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Veron. Corb. Vet. Inn. Spir. Man. Routh, from four of his manuscripts.] or of persecution [Note: [Col. 0622B] “Striking,” Morel.] finds us unencumbered and swift, running in this contest of works, the Lord will never fail to reward [Col. 0622B] our merits. To those victorious in peace he will give the white crown for their works; in persecution he will double it with the purple crown for suffering.

[Col. 0621]

# 247 BOOK ON THE GOOD OF PATIENCE

[Note: [Col. 0621D] *On Patience*, Bod. 4. Lin. August.]

[Note: [Col. 0621D]

### On the Good of Patience

Cyprian mentions this work of his at the end of the *Letter to Jubaianus*, p. 137. Tertullian wrote a book on the same subject, as did Augustine. A certain bishop Paul also wrote a book *On Patience* long ago, as Gennadius attests.]

(C)

## Argument

[Col. 0621C] Cyprian himself briefly explains the occasion of this writing near the end of the *Letter to Jubaianus*: “We patiently and gently preserve the charity of the mind, the honor of the college, the bond of love, and the concord of the priesthood. For this reason, even now, insofar as our modest ability has availed, with the Lord’s permission and inspiration, we have composed a little book *On the Good of Patience*, which we have sent to you on account of our mutual love.”

Accordingly, after first distinguishing true patience from the philosophers’ false patience, he commends Christian patience by reference to the patience of God, of Christ, and of all the righteous. He then proves, both from the Scriptures and by arguments, that it is not only useful but also necessary, adding the examples of Job and Tobias. And so that the good of patience may shine out more brightly from the vice opposed to it, [Col. 0621D] he expounds how great an evil impatience is. [Col. 0622C] Finally, he censures the desire for vengeance and teaches, in accordance with the Scriptures, that vengeance ought rather to be left to God than claimed for ourselves. If Cyprian imitates Tertullian in any book, he certainly does so in this one—namely, Tertullian’s book *On Patience*. **PAMELIUS.**

[Note: [Col. 0622D]

### I.—The Discipline of Our Faith

Above, Letter XXII, p. 32: “Modest through the humility and fear proper to our discipline.” Likewise, in the [Col. 0623D] *Letter to Quirinus* prefixed to the books of *Testimonies*, p. 274: “Certain chapters pertaining to the religious discipline of our way of life.”]

I. IN intending to speak about patience, dearest brothers, and to proclaim its uses and advantages, where should I begin more appropriately than from the fact that I see patience is necessary for you even now as you listen, so that you cannot even do this very thing—hearing and learning—without patience? For saving discourse [Note: [Col. 0622D] “The discourse of the Lord,” Bod. 4.] and reasoning is effectually learned only when what is said is heard patiently.

Nor do I find, dearest brothers, among the other paths of heavenly discipline by which our profession of hope and faith is directed toward attaining [Col. 0622D] divinely given rewards, [Col. 0623A] anything more [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Anything either more useful for life or more necessary for glory,” Bod. 4.] useful for life or greater for glory than that we, who rely upon the Lord’s precepts with the obedience of fear and devotion, should guard patience above all with complete observance [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Maintain,” Pem. Voss. 1.].

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

### II.—The Wisdom of This World

Celsus, with a malicious disposition against Christians, twisted this statement of the apostle Paul into the opposite meaning, saying that they commonly boasted that wisdom was an evil thing in life, but foolishness a good thing. Origen, writing against him, says that this is pure misrepresentation—as indeed it is, since it is expressly contrary to the Apostle’s words.]

II. Philosophers too profess that they pursue this patience [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Each of the philosophers,” Ver.]. But patience there is as false as their wisdom is false. For how can one be either wise or patient who knows neither the wisdom nor the patience of God [Note: [Col. 0623C] “Knows: and how,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]? For God himself warns concerning those who seem wise to themselves in the world, saying: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (Isa. 29:14).

Likewise the blessed apostle Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit and sent to call and form [Note: [Col. 0623C] “And save the nations,” Lin.] the Gentiles, solemnly warns and instructs them, saying: “See that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deception, according to [Col. 0623B] the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2:8).

And in another place: “Let no one,” he says, “deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks himself wise, let him become foolish to this world, that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘I will rebuke [Note: [Col. 0623D] “I will catch,” Voss. 1. “Rebuking,” Pem. Lin. Voss. 2. NC. 2. “You will rebuke,” above, book III *To Quirinus*, chapter 69.] the wise in their own cunning.’ And again: ‘The Lord [Note: [Col. 0623D] “God,” Saris. Ver.] has known the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish’” (1 Cor. 3:18–20).

Therefore, if true wisdom is not there, true patience cannot be there either. For if the wise person [Note: [Col. 0624C] “For certainly if the patient person,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Pem. Ar. MR. Thu. Foss. “Wise,” Rigalt.] is one who is humble and gentle, yet we see that philosophers are neither humble nor gentle, but are very pleasing to themselves and, by the very fact that they please themselves, displeasing to God, it is apparent that true patience does not exist there [Note: [Col. 0624C] “That patience does not exist there,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], where there is the arrogant audacity of affected [Col. 0623C] freedom and the shameless display of an exposed and half-naked breast.

[Note: [Col. 0623D]

### 587 III.—We Do Not Speak Grandly

Minucius Felix: “We display wisdom not in our clothing, but in our mind. We do not speak great things, but live them.”]

III. But we, dearest brothers, who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, who display wisdom not in clothing but in truth, who know the consciousness of virtues rather than their boastful display, who do not speak great things but live them—as servants [Note: [Col. 0624C] “As servants,” Saris. “Because we are servants,” Bod. 4.] and worshipers of God, let us render in spiritual obedience the patience that we learn from heavenly teachings.

For this virtue is shared by us with [Col. 0624A] God. From him patience begins; from him its splendor and dignity take their origin. The source and greatness of patience proceed from God as their author. Humanity ought to love what is dear [Note: [Col. 0624C] “Is dear, and the good,” Bod. 1.] to God; the divine majesty commends the good that it loves. If God is our Lord and Father, let us pursue alike the patience of both Lord and Father, because servants ought to be obedient, and it is not fitting for children to be degenerate.

[Note: [Col. 0624D]

### IV.—To Ripen

So the early editions and six old books. This reading is plainly excellent. The other reading, “to grow mild,” which Erasmus introduced, is also good and has the agreement of more old books.

**Prefers to maintain patience for a long time.** Above, Letter IX, p. 18: “I maintained my patience for a long time.” Ruricius, book II, Letter 4: “Patience must be maintained in temptation.”

**Return to me.** This clause, which occurs in the early editions, was removed by the Manutian edition; Morellius restored it. Quite rightly, for it appears in eight old books.

[Col. 0625D] **Forbearance and patience.** There can be no doubt that this correction is certain, since this is the reading in chapter 35 of book III of the *Testimonies*, in eighteen of our manuscripts, in seven English manuscripts, and in Florus’s excerpts. Pamelius also attests that it was written thus in the Affligem manuscript, and Rigaltius that it was so written in the Verona and Benevento manuscripts. Below, in this very book, p. 252: “Take away the substance of enduring and tolerating, and perseverance continues with no roots or strength.”]

IV. But what and how great is the patience found in God! Though profane temples, earthly images, and sacrilegious rites have been instituted by human beings in contempt of his majesty and honor, he most patiently endures them; he makes the day dawn and the light of the sun arise equally upon the good and the evil; and when he waters the earth with rains, no one is excluded from his benefits, so as to prevent him from bestowing undifferentiated showers alike upon the righteous [Col. 0624B] and the unrighteous.

We see that, with the inseparable impartiality of patience, at God’s command the seasons obey and the elements serve the guilty and the innocent, the religious and the impious, the grateful and the ungrateful: winds blow, springs flow, the abundance of crops grows great [Note: [Col. 0624D] “The abundance of crops glows white,” Morel. “Fruits ripen,” Foss. “Shines,” Vict. “Ripened fruit,” Lin.], the fruits of the vines ripen, orchards abound with fruit, woodlands grow leafy, and meadows flower.

And though God is provoked by frequent—indeed continual—offenses, he restrains his indignation and patiently awaits the day of retribution once appointed.
