Although vengeance lies within his power, he prefers to maintain patience for a long time, mercifully enduring and delaying, so that, if possible, wickedness, though greatly prolonged, may at last be changed, and the human being, after wallowing in the contagion of errors and crimes, may even belatedly be converted to God, as God himself warns and says: “I do not desire the death of one who is dying, but rather that he return and live” (Ezek. 33:11). And again: “Return to me, says the Lord” (Mal. 3:7). And again: “Return to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious and patient and of great compassion, and turns aside his sentence against inflicted evils [Note: [Col. 0624D] “Inflicted evil,” Ben. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Saris.]” (Joel 2:13).

The blessed apostle Paul likewise recalls this and, calling the sinner back to repentance, sets forth and says: [Col. 0625A] “Or do you perhaps despise the wealth of his goodness, his forbearance, and his patience [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Forbearance and patience,” Ver. Ben. Saris. Bod. 1, 3, 4. Ar. Above, *To Quirinus*, book III, chapter 35. “Of forbearance and patience,” Oxon. and earlier editions.], not knowing that the patience and goodness of God lead you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Against the day of wrath,” Bod. 1, 4. Ver.] and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2:4–6).

He said that God’s judgment is righteous because it comes late, because it is deferred long and greatly, so that God’s long patience may provide for the human being’s attainment of life. Punishment is then exacted from the impious person and sinner, when repentance for sin can no longer be of benefit [Note: [Col. 0625C] Thus Lam. Ver. Thu. Foss. “To the sinner,” Oxon.].

[Note: [Col. 0625D]

### V.—Tax Collectors

That is, those who contracted to collect taxes, says Erasmus on this passage of Matthew; hence they are also called *redemptores* (“contractors”). A class of people once infamous among [Col. 0626D] the Jews, but now regarded among Christians as especially honorable. Nor indeed is that surprising, since merchants and bankers are preferred to almost everyone else by the leading men of both states, although neither Aristotle nor Cicero wishes them to be counted among respectable citizens.

**Tax collectors—Gentiles.** See Cotelerius’s notes on book IV, chapter 6, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*.]

## V

And that we may understand more fully, dearly beloved brothers, that patience is a thing of God, and that whoever is gentle, patient, and meek is an imitator of God the Father, when the Lord in his Gospel gave precepts for salvation [Col. 0625B], and, setting forth divine admonitions, instructed his disciples unto perfection [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Unto advancement,” Ebor. Bod. 3.] [Note: [Col. 0625C] “His disciples,” Pem. Voss. 1.], he declared:

> You have heard that it was said: “You shall love your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0625C] “Your neighbor, and you shall hate your enemy,” Lam. [Col. 0625D] Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Ver.], and you shall hate your enemy.” But I say to you: Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, who causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Do not even the tax collectors do this?” Bod. 1. Thu.]? And if you greet only your brothers, what more do you do [Note: [Col. 0625D] “What more will you do?” Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Foss.]? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? Therefore be perfect [Note: [Col. 0625D] “Therefore you will be,” Bod. 1, 2, 3. Thu. Foss. Ver.], as your heavenly Father [Note: [Col. 0626C] “As the Father,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver.] is perfect.  
> (Matt. 5:43–48)

Thus, he said, the children of God are made perfect; thus he showed and taught that those restored by heavenly birth are brought to completion: if the patience of God the Father remains [Col. 0625C] in us; if the divine likeness, which Adam had lost through sin [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Which Adam had lost by sinning,” Bod. 3.], is manifested and shines in our deeds. What glory it is to become like God! What great happiness it is to possess among one’s virtues something that can be equated with the divine praises!

> **Note: [Col. 0626D]**
>
> **VI.—To receive.** Formerly the reading was *to take*. We have preferred the reading favored by twenty of our manuscripts and five English manuscripts.
>
> **To show.** Tertullian, in his book *On Patience*: “showing God himself as the example of patience.”

## VI

Nor, dearly beloved brothers, did Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, teach this only in words; he also fulfilled it in deeds. And because he had said that he had descended [Col. 0626A] for this purpose, to do the will of the Father [Note: [Col. 0626C] “To fulfill the will of the Father,” Bod. 3.], among the other wonders [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Great works,” Ver.] of his mighty acts by which he displayed the signs of divine majesty, he also preserved his Father’s patience through an uninterrupted course of endurance.

Indeed, all his actions [p. 249], from the very moment of his coming, are marked by patience as their companion [Note: [Col. 0626C] Singular: “is marked,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lam. Thu.]. First of all [Note: [Col. 0626C] “First of all, because,” Lam. Ebor.], descending from that heavenly height to earthly things, the Son of God does not disdain to put on human flesh and, although he himself was not a sinner, to bear the sins of others. Laying aside immortality for a time, he allows himself to become mortal, so that the innocent may be slain for the salvation of the guilty [Note: [Col. 0626C] “Punished for their salvation,” Bod. 3.].

The Lord is baptized by a servant; and, though he is to grant remission of sins, he himself does not disdain to wash his body in the bath of regeneration. For forty days he fasts, though it is through him that others are fed to fullness. He hungers and feels hunger so that those who had suffered hunger for the word and for grace [Col. 0626B] might be filled with heavenly bread. He engages in conflict with the devil when tempted, and, content merely to have defeated the enemy, he attempts nothing beyond words.

He did not preside over his disciples with a master’s authority as though over servants; rather, kind and gentle, he loved them with brotherly charity. He even deigned to wash the Apostles’ feet, so that, by being such a lord toward his servants, he might teach by his own example what a fellow servant ought to be toward his peers and equals.

Nor is it surprising [Note: [Col. 0626D] “Nor is it surprising if,” Bod. 1.] that he proved to be such toward obedient equals [Note: [Col. 0626D] *Obaudientes*, Lin. NC. 2; *obedientes* in others. “Equals”—from where? Baluzius indicates no source for this word.], since he was able to endure Judas to the very end with long patience, to take food with his enemy [Note: [Col. 0626D] “To take with his enemy,” Ar. Bod. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. Ben. Ver.], to know the enemy within his own household and yet not reveal him publicly, and not to refuse the traitor’s kiss.

And in enduring the Jews, what great equanimity and what great patience! To bend unbelievers toward faith by persuasion; to cherish the ungrateful with service; [Col. 0626C] to answer opponents gently; to endure the proud with clemency; humbly to yield to persecutors; and, until the hour of the cross and Passion, to desire to gather together those who killed the Prophets and were always rebellious against God.

> **Note: [Col. 0627C]**
>
> **VII.—Receive the spittle.** Erasmus wrote, “patiently receive the spittle.” It is remarkable how favorably this adverb was received. All the editions published after the Erasmian edition retained it. Yet, among the great number of ancient copies I used, I found it nowhere except in the Lamonian manuscript. It is also absent from seven English manuscripts. I therefore do not think anyone can accuse me of rashness for removing it, especially since it is certain that it is by no means necessary there. Below, p. 255: “He did not turn his face away [Col. 0627D] from the foulness of their spitting.” Tertullian, in his book *On Flight in Persecution*: “He did not turn his face away from their spittle.”
>
> **Innocence itself and justice itself.** Thus most of the ancient manuscripts. Many others have, in the masculine, “he himself and he himself.” Both readings are good.

## VII

During the Passion and cross itself, moreover, before they came to the cruelty of execution and the shedding of blood, what disgraceful abuse he patiently heard, what mockery and insults he endured! He received the spittle of those who insulted him [Note: [Col. 0627C] “Received the spittle,” Ar. Saris. Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver.; Oxon. adds “patiently.”], though shortly before he had formed the eyes of a blind man with his own spittle. He himself suffered scourging, though now, in his name, the devil and his angels are scourged by his servants. He who crowns the martyrs with eternal flowers was crowned with thorns. He who bestows the true palms upon the victorious was struck in the face with palms. He who clothes others in the garment of immortality was stripped of his earthly garment. He who gave heavenly food was fed with gall, and he who offered the saving cup [Note: [Col. 0627C] “With the saving cup,” Bod. 4; “saving cups,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2; “with the saving cup,” Thu.] was given vinegar to drink.

That innocent one, that just one—indeed, innocence itself and justice itself [Note: [Col. 0627C] Masculine: “he himself and he himself,” Bod. 1, 2, 3. Thu. Foss.]—is numbered among criminals; truth is oppressed by false testimonies; the one who will judge is judged; and the Word of God is led silently to sacrifice.

And when, at the Lord’s crucifixion, the stars are confounded, the elements disturbed, [Col. 0627B] the earth trembles, night shuts out day, and the sun withdraws both its rays and its eyes lest it be compelled to behold the crime of the Jews, he does not speak, nor is he moved, nor does he proclaim his majesty even amid the Passion itself. Everything is endured steadfastly and continually to the end, so that full and perfect patience may be consummated in Christ.

## VIII

And after all these things [Note: [Col. 0627C] “After these things, still,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], he still receives his killers if they turn and come to him. Kind and patient, with a saving patience intended to preserve them [Note: [Col. 0627C] “Kind, the Church,” Oxon. ed. Ar. Saris. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Pem. Voss. 1. Lin. Ver. Vet. innom. Spir. Man.; “kind and patient,” Imp.], he closes his Church to no one.

Those adversaries, those blasphemers, those who were always enemies of his name—if they repent of their offense, if they acknowledge the crime they committed [Col. 0628A]—he admits not only to pardon for their crime but also to the reward of the heavenly kingdom. What could be called more patient, what more kind? Even the man who shed Christ’s blood is brought to life by Christ’s blood.

Such and so great is Christ’s patience; and unless it had been such and so great, the Church would not have had the Apostle Paul either.

## IX

But if we too, dearly beloved brothers, are in Christ, if we have put him on, [p. 250] if he is the way of our salvation, then, since we follow Christ in his saving footsteps, let us walk according to Christ’s examples, just as the Apostle John instructs us when he says:

> He who says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked.  
> (1 John 2:6)

Likewise Peter, upon whom the Church was founded by the Lord’s gracious favor, states in his Epistle:

> Christ [Col. 0628B] suffered for us, leaving you [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Us,” Ver.] an example, that you should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return [Note: [Col. 0628C] “He did not revile in return,” Lin. Bod. 4. Saris. NC. 2. Ver. Thu.; “he reviled,” Oxon.]; when he suffered [Note: [Col. 0628C] “He who, when he suffered,” Voss. 1.], he did not threaten, but handed himself over to the one who judged him unjustly [Note: [Col. 0628C] “To the one judging unjustly,” Ar.].  
> (1 Pet. 2:21)

> **Note: [Col. 0627D]**
>
> **X.—Fratricide.** I prefer this reading, both because the word is thoroughly Latin and because it is found in the old editions, including the Morellian, and in several ancient manuscripts; and also because, since it has passed out of common usage, I think those who substituted *parricide* supposed that the other reading was not sound. Cyprian, treating this very subject in his book *On the Good of Patience*, p. 250, calls Cain a fratricide.
>
> Cicero, in his *Speech concerning His House, before the Pontiffs*: “Clodius resolved that nothing should be enacted outside the regular order. What of the measure concerning me which you say you carried, parricide, fratricide, sister-killer? Did you not carry those things outside the regular order?”
>
> Priscian, book I: “From *parenticida*, by syncope, comes *patricida*; from *frater*, ‘brother,’ comes *fratricida*, ‘fratricide’; from *soror*, ‘sister,’ comes *sororicida*, ‘sister-killer.’”
>
> Tertullian [Col. 0628C], in his book *On Patience*: “Cain, that first murderer and first fratricide”; and in his book *On the Shows*: “by a fratricide as founder.”
>
> Lucifer of Cagliari, book II *For Saint Athanasius*: “Let him also be compared to Cain the fratricide; let him be declared to remain in death. Why did you compel me to perform this deed, which would have made me, like Cain, a fratricide and a son of the devil?”
>
> Philastrius, chapter 128: “There is a heresy which does not understand correctly the account of Cain: that after committing fratricide he asks the Lord to let him die rather than be forgiven.”
>
> Salvian, book I of *The Governance of God*, chapter 6, treating [Col. 0628D] this same matter, wrote: “When, as God bears witness, he was about to commit fratricide.”
>
> Cassian, book IX, chapter 9: “To repent after fratricide”; and *Conference* VIII, chapter 21: “By a fratricide and an impious man.”
>
> Primasius, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “The murderer bore the sign of Christ, just as Cain the fratricide bore it.”
>
> Germanus, bishop of Paris, in his letter to Queen Brunhild: “One of them, Cain, committed fratricide.”
>
> Gregory of Tours, book I of the *History*, chapter 2: “Rising up as a new fratricide in the shedding of his brother’s blood.”
>
> Council of Worms, chapter 30: “We decree that parricides and fratricides…”
>
> Council of Trosly, chapter 13, speaking of Cain’s crime: “And he himself, until the seventh generation, was to pay the penalty for his fratricide and envy as a wandering fugitive.”
>
> Alcuin, or whoever else wrote the book *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 13: “A fratricide is one who kills his brother.”
>
> Pope Honorius III, no. 588 in Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1225, §29: “More cruel than Cain the fratricide.”
>
> George of Poděbrady, king of Bohemia, in his apologetic letter to King Matthias of Hungary, his son-in-law, in volume IV of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 411, calls Cain a fratricide.
>
> Quintilian nevertheless teaches, book VIII, chapter 6, that the killer of a mother or brother may be called a *parricide*.

## X

Finally, we find that the Patriarchs, the Prophets, and all the just—who bore the figure of Christ through an image that preceded him—guarded nothing more carefully among their praiseworthy virtues than their maintenance of patience with courageous and steadfast equanimity.

Thus Abel [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Abel, at the beginning of the world, martyrdom,” Voss. 1.], inaugurating and first consecrating the origin of martyrdom and the suffering of a just man [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Inaugurating that of a just man,” Ar. Bod. 2. Ver.], neither resists nor struggles against his fratricidal brother [Note: [Col. 0628C] “Murderous brother,” Lam.; “fratricidal,” Foss.; “parricidal,” Oxon.], but is humbly and meekly put to death with patience.

Thus [Col. 0629A] Abraham, believing God and first establishing the root and foundation of faith, when tested in his son neither doubts nor hesitates, but obeys God’s commands with the complete patience of devotion. Isaac too, prefigured in the likeness of the Lord’s sacrifice, is found patient when he is offered by his father for immolation.

Jacob, driven from his land by his brother, departs patiently; and afterward, with still greater patience, as a suppliant he brings his yet more impious persecutor back to concord through peaceful gifts. Joseph, sold by his brothers and banished [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Bound,” Lam. Pem. Voss. 2.], not only forgives them patiently but also generously [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Freely,” Pem. Voss. 2; “grain and wheat,” Bod. 3.] and mercifully distributes free grain to them when they come [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Distributes,” Bod. 3.].

Moses is frequently despised and nearly stoned by an ungrateful and faithless people, yet, gentle and patient, he entreats the Lord on their behalf.

And in David, from [Col. 0629B] whom Christ’s birth according to the flesh arose, what great, marvelous, and Christian patience there was [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Is recognized to have been,” Bod. 3.]! He often had King Saul—who was persecuting him and desiring to kill him—in his power and could have killed him; yet he preferred to preserve him when Saul had been subjected and handed over to him. He did not repay his enemy in kind; indeed, after Saul had been killed, he even avenged him.

Finally, so many Prophets were killed, so many martyrs honored with glorious deaths—all of them came to heavenly crowns through the praise of patience. For the crown of pains and sufferings cannot be received unless patience in pain and suffering goes before it.

> **Note: [Col. 0629D]**
>
> **XI.—Let God’s sentence be considered.** Saint Augustine cites this passage in book IV of *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, [Col. 0630D] chapter 8.

## XI

But that it may be known more clearly and fully how useful and necessary patience is, dearly beloved brothers, let us consider God’s sentence, which Adam received at the very beginning of the world and of the human race when he forgot the commandment [Col. 0629C] and transgressed the law that had been given [Note: [Col. 0629D] “He did not retain the grace he had received but lost it,” Voss. 1.].

Then we shall know how patient we ought to be in this world, since we are born under such a condition that we labor here amid afflictions and conflicts:

> Because you listened, he says, to your wife’s voice and ate from that tree—the only one concerning which I commanded you not to eat [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Not to eat from it,” Bod. 1.]—the earth shall be cursed in all your works. In sorrow and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you [Note: [Col. 0629D] “It shall sprout for you,” NC. 1.], and you shall eat the produce of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and into the earth you shall go.  
> (Gen. 3:17 ff.)

We are all bound and constrained by the bond of this sentence until, when death has been discharged [Note: [Col. 0629D] “When death has been extinguished,” Bod. 4; “having died,” Bod. 3.], we depart from this world. We must live in sorrow and groaning all the days of our life [Col. 0630A]; we must eat our bread with sweat and labor.

> **Note: [Col. 0630D]**
>
> **XII.—In the world.** Two ancient manuscripts have “in the world,” with “or, in the age” written above the line. Hence it came about that, since some preferred “world” and others “age,” one or the other reading was placed in the ancient copies at the scribes’ discretion.

## XII

Thus each of us, when born [Note: [Col. 0629D] “And each, when born,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Saris.] and received into the lodging-place of this world, begins with tears; and though still wholly without knowledge or awareness, in that very first moment of birth knows nothing except how to weep. By a natural foresight he laments; the inexperienced soul, by its crying and groaning at its very beginning, bears witness to the anxieties, labors, and storms of mortal life [Note: [Col. 0629D] “Temporal life,” Ver.] into which it is entering. [p. 251]

For as long as life is lived here, there is sweating and labor. And for those who sweat and labor, no consolations can assist more than those of patience. Though these are fitting and necessary for everyone in this world, they are all the more so for us, who are battered more severely by the devil’s attacks; who, standing daily in the battle line, are wearied by struggles with an old and well-practiced enemy [Col. 0630B]; and who, besides the varied and unceasing battles of temptations, must also, in the contest of persecutions, abandon our patrimonies, undergo imprisonment [Note: [Col. 0630D] “Undergo imprisonment,” with “must,” Bod. 3.], bear chains, surrender our lives, and endure the sword, wild beasts, fires, crosses, and every kind of torture and punishment through faith and the strength of patience. The Lord himself instructs us and says:

> I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace. In the world, however, you will have affliction; but take courage [Note: [Col. 0630D] “But believe,” NC. 1. Lam. Bod. 1, 2.], because I have overcome the world.  
> (John 16:33)

But if we who have renounced the devil and the world suffer the afflictions and assaults of the devil and the world more frequently and violently, how much more ought we to maintain patience, so that with it as our helper and companion we may endure everything hostile?

> **Note: [Col. 0631D]**
>
> **XIII.—Bringing into present possession.** I do not deny that the common reading, which has “granting,” is excellent. But since our reading rests upon the authority of nineteen of our manuscripts and six English manuscripts, as well as the testimony of Florus, I judged that it should be restored to Cyprian.
>
> **To the crown.** The ancient copies vary greatly at this point. Some present the reading we have retained; others, “to the crown of praise”; and others, together with the old editions, “to the crown and praise already close at hand.” From these, the reader may choose whichever pleases him more.

## XIII

The saving commandment [Col. 0630C] of our Lord and teacher [Note: [Col. 0630D] “Our teacher,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; “the saving commandment of the teacher,” Oxon.] is:

> He who endures [Note: [Col. 0630D] “He who perseveres,” Lin.] to the end shall be saved.  
> (Matt. 10:22)

And again:

> If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples [Note: [Col. 0630D] “You are my disciples,” Ar. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.  
> (John 8:31)

We must endure and persevere, dearly beloved brothers, so that, having been admitted to the hope of truth and liberty, we may be able to attain truth and liberty themselves. For the very fact that we are Christians is a matter of faith and hope; but for hope and faith to attain their fruit, patience is necessary.

For we do not pursue present glory, but future glory, in accordance with the admonition of the Apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0630D] “In accordance with Paul,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], who says:

> By hope we have been saved [Note: [Col. 0630D] “We have been made safe,” Lam. Ebor. Pem. Bod. 2.]. But hope that is seen is not hope; for why does anyone hope for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see [Note: [Col. 0630D] “We hope with expectation,” Saris. Ar. Bod. 2, 4. Ver.], [Col. 0631A] we await it through patience.  
> (Rom. 8:24)

Therefore expectation and patience are necessary, so that we may complete what we have begun and, when God brings it into present possession [Note: [Col. 0631C] “With God brought into present possession,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Saris. Lin. Ver. Benev. Benet.; “with God granting it,” Oxon.], receive what we believe and hope for.

Finally, in another passage the same Apostle instructs and teaches the just—those who work and lay up heavenly treasures for themselves through the increase of divine interest—to be patient as well:

> Therefore, while we have time, let us do what is good toward all, but especially toward the household of faith. Let us not fail in doing good; for in due time we shall reap [Note: [Col. 0631C] “We shall reap, if we are not weary,” NC. 1.].  
> (Gal. 6:9)

He warns that no one should fail in the work through impatience, and that no one, either diverted or defeated by temptations, should stop midway along the path of praise and glory, so that past achievements perish because the things begun cease before they are completed, as it is written:

> The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him on whatever day he goes astray.  
> (Ezek. 33:12)

And again [Col. 0631B]:

> Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown.  
> (Rev. 3:11)

This saying exhorts us to persevere patiently and bravely, so that the person who strives toward the crown, with praise already near at hand [Note: [Col. 0631C] “The crown of praise already close at hand,” Bod. 1, 3, 4. Voss. 1; “praise as nearly as possible,” Morel.; “and praise already close at hand,” Foss. Eras.], may be crowned through continuing patience.

> **Note: [Col. 0630D]**
>
> **XIV.—Carried.** All the old editions and sixteen ancient manuscripts, including the Séguier manuscript, have “tasted”; eight, including the Verona manuscript, have “carried.” Pamelius introduced the latter reading into the text, evidently because the Eucharist is not tasted with the hand but in ancient times was customarily carried in the hand. Rigaltius approved this. It has therefore seemed proper to retain this reading, which is supported, moreover, by the authority of eight ancient manuscripts. For Cyprian, in his book *On the Lapsed*, p. 188 [Col. 0632D], says: “And because he does not immediately receive the Lord’s body with defiled hands.” See Jean Étienne Duranti, book I, chapter 16, *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*; Henri Valois’s annotations on Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43, and book VII, chapter 9; Cardinal Bona, book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 17; and Hospinian, book I *On Churches*, chapter 5.

## XIV

Patience, dearly beloved brothers, not only guards what is good but also repels adversity. Favoring the Holy Spirit and cleaving to heavenly and divine things, it resists, by the bulwark of its virtues, the deeds of flesh and body by which the soul is assaulted and captured [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Shaken,” Pem. Voss. 2. Bod. 2, 4.].

Let us consider a few examples out of many, so that the rest may be understood from the few. Adultery, fraud, and murder are mortal crimes. Let patience be strong and steadfast in the heart [Note: [Col. 0631C] “Thus, while patience remains strong and steadfast in the heart, neither by adultery…,” Saris.]; then neither is the sanctified body and temple of God polluted by adultery, nor is innocence dedicated to justice [Col. 0631C] infected by the contagion of fraud, nor, after the Eucharist has been carried in the hand [Note: [Col. 0631C] “After the Eucharist has been tasted,” Bod. 1, 2. MR. Thu. Foss. [Col. 0632C] Voss. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. and all editions before Pamelius; “the Eucharist having been carried,” Lin.], is that hand stained with sword and bloodshed.

## XV

Charity is the bond of brotherhood, the foundation [p. 252] of peace, the tenacity and strength of unity. It is greater than both hope [Col. 0632A] and faith; it takes precedence over both works and martyrdoms; and it will remain with us forever before God in the heavenly kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Eternally in the kingdoms,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.].

Take patience away from charity, and, left desolate, it does not endure. Take away from it the substance of endurance and forbearance, and it does not persevere with any roots or strength.

Indeed, when the Apostle spoke of charity, he joined endurance and patience to it:

> Charity is magnanimous, charity is kind; charity does not envy, is not puffed up, is not provoked, thinks no evil [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth,” Lin.]; it loves all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.  
> (1 Cor. 13:4–7)

He shows that charity can persevere tenaciously because it knows how to endure all things. And elsewhere he says:

> Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.  
> (Eph. 4:2)

He established that neither unity [Col. 0632B] nor peace can be preserved unless brothers cherish one another through mutual forbearance and, with patience mediating, guard the bond of concord.

> **Note: [Col. 0632D]**
>
> **XVI.—Not only seven times.** Thus the old editions, including the Morellian, and two ancient manuscripts. This is taken from chapter XVIII of Matthew. This passage therefore appears to be defective in the ancient codices, which do not contain this clause. Manutius removed it, Morellius restored it, and Pamelius removed it again. The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul has: “not only seventy-seven times.” The Catholicos of the Armenians used that argument and authority when writing to Pope Innocent IV in 1247, in order to persuade him that Emperor Frederick should be spared, against whom the Pope’s anger had been violently inflamed. See Odoricus Raynaldus, year 1247, §34. See above, p. 463.

## XVI

What then of the commands that you should not swear or curse; that you should not demand back what has been taken from you; that, after receiving one blow, you should offer the other cheek to the person striking you; that you should forgive a brother who sins against you not only seven times, but seventy-seven times [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Seventy and seven,” Bod. 4.], and indeed forgive absolutely every sin; that you should love your enemies; and that you should pray for your adversaries and persecutors? Can you accomplish [Note: [Col. 0632C] “You will not be able to do these things,” Bod. 1, 3.] these things [Note: [Col. 0632C] “Endure,” Ar. Saris. Lam. Ebor. Foss.] unless you maintain the strength of patience and forbearance?

We see this accomplished in Stephen [Note: [Col. 0632C] “By Stephen,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.]. While he was being killed by the Jews with violence and stones, he asked not for vengeance for himself but pardon for his killers, saying:

> Lord, do not charge them with this sin.  
> (Acts 7:59)

Thus it was fitting that he should be Christ’s first martyr. Going before the martyrs who would follow him [Col. 0632C] in a glorious death, he was not only a preacher of the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 0632C] “He deserved to be a preacher,” Saris.] but also an imitator of his supremely patient gentleness.

What shall I say of anger, discord, and hostility, which ought not to exist [Col. 0633A] in a Christian? Let patience be in the breast, and these things cannot find a place there; or, if they attempt to enter, they are quickly excluded and depart, so that the peaceful dwelling may remain in the heart where the God of peace delights to dwell.

Indeed, the Apostle admonishes and teaches us [Note: [Col. 0633D] “Admonishes, saying,” Bod. 1; “the Apostle Paul indeed admonishes,” Ver.]:

> Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption [Note: [Col. 0633D] “On the day of redemption,” Saris. Bod. 1, 2. Vict.]. Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you.  
> (Eph. 4:30)

For if the Christian has escaped from rage and fleshly contention, as though from the storms of the sea, and has now begun to be tranquil and gentle in Christ’s harbor, he must not admit anger or discord into his breast, since he is permitted neither to return evil for evil nor to hate.

## XVII

Patience is also necessary for the various afflictions of the flesh and the frequent, harsh torments of the body by which the human [Col. 0633B] race is daily wearied and shaken. For since, in that first transgression of the commandment, bodily strength departed together with immortality, and weakness came with death, and since strength cannot be recovered unless immortality is recovered with it, we must always struggle and contend in this bodily fragility and weakness [Note: [Col. 0633D] “Always struggle in the body,” Bod. 3, 4.]. This struggle and conflict cannot be sustained except by the strength of patience.

Moreover, for our testing and examination [Note: [Col. 0633D] “Various hardships are inflicted for our proving,” Ver.], diverse sufferings are imposed upon us, and a manifold variety of trials is inflicted: losses of property, the burning of fevers, the torments of wounds, and the loss of loved ones.

Nothing distinguishes the unjust from the just more [Note: [Col. 0633D] “Distinguishes the just more,” Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] than this: in adversity the unjust person complains and blasphemes through impatience, whereas the just person [Col. 0633C] [Note: [Col. 0633D] “The just,” plural, Voss. 1.] is proved by patience, as it is written:

> Endure in suffering, and in your humiliation possess patience, because gold and silver are tested in fire [Note: [Col. 0633D] “But acceptable human beings are tested in the furnace of humiliation,” Bod. 1.].  
> (Sir. 2:4)

> **Note: [Col. 0633D]**
>
> **XVIII.—The blessing of God.** Some ancient manuscripts prefer: “Let the blessing of God accompany victorious patience.” The Séguier manuscript has: “Let the blessing of God be proclaimed by victorious patience.” So also the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul.

## XVIII

Thus Job was examined and proved, and by the virtue of patience [p. 253] was raised to the highest summit of praise. How many darts of the devil were launched against him, how many torments inflicted! The loss of his estate is imposed upon him; bereavement of his numerous offspring is inflicted. A lord rich in possessions and a father richer still in children, he suddenly is neither lord nor father.

The devastation of wounds is added, and the devouring punishment of worms consumes his wasting and suppurating limbs. And lest anything whatsoever should remain which Job had not experienced in his trials, the devil also arms his wife. He employs that ancient device of his wickedness—as though he could deceive and beguile everyone through a woman, as he did at the beginning of the world.

Yet Job is not broken by these grievous and repeated assaults, so as to cease proclaiming the blessing of God amid his hardships and afflictions [Col. 0634A] through victorious patience [Note: [Col. 0633D] “He proclaimed the blessing with victorious patience,” Voss. 1. Pem. Bod. 4. NC. 2.].

Tobit too, after his magnificent works of justice and mercy, was tested by the loss of his sight; and to the degree that he patiently endured blindness, to that same degree, through the praise of his patience, he earned God’s favor in a magnificent way.

> **Note: [Col. 0633D]**
>
> **XIX.—Impatience is the devil’s evil.** See Tertullian’s book *On Repentance*, which is wholly occupied [Col. 0634D] with this argument.
>
> **He was the first to perish.** The Epistle of Pope Siricius to all the bishops: “The ancient enemy—from the beginning a liar, an enemy of truth, and envious of humanity—does not allow us to remain undisturbed and free from his assault. In order to deceive humanity, he first deceived himself.”

## XIX

And that the goodness of patience may shine more brightly, dearly beloved brothers, let us consider what evil [Note: [Col. 0634D] “And what evil,” Saris.] impatience, by contrast, brings upon us. For just as patience is Christ’s good, so, by contrast, impatience is the devil’s evil [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Is an evil,” Bod. 1, 4.]. And just as the person in whom Christ dwells and remains is found to be patient, so the person whose mind is possessed by the devil’s wickedness is always impatient.

Let us therefore examine the beginnings themselves. [Col. 0634B] The devil could not patiently endure that the human being [Note: [Col. 0634D] “God as superior to himself and the human being made in the image…,” ad Vict.] had been made in God’s image. Hence he was the first to perish, and he caused another to perish.

Adam, impatient for the deadly food contrary to the heavenly command, fell into death and did not preserve by the guardianship of patience the grace divinely given to him. Cain killed his brother because he could not patiently bear his brother’s sacrifice and offering. And Esau descended from greater things to lesser because he lost his rights of primacy through impatience over lentils [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Of the mind,” Bod. 1, 3.].

What of the Jewish people, faithless and ungrateful amid God’s benefits? Was not their first withdrawal from God the crime of impatience? While they could not bear Moses’ delay as he spoke with God [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Moses speaking with God,” Ar. Bod. 2. Foss. Vict.], they dared to demand profane gods [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Dared to demand,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; Oxon. omits “dared.”], naming a bull’s head and an earthly fabrication as the guides [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Calling them guides,” Ar.] of their journey.

Nor did they ever desist from that same impatience. Always impatient of instruction and divine [Col. 0634C] admonition, they killed their Prophets and every just person and finally rushed even to the Lord’s cross and blood.

Impatience also creates heretics [Note: [Col. 0634D] “Also in the Church,” Lan. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2.] in the Church and, after the likeness of the Jews, drives those rebelling against Christ’s peace and charity into hostile and frenzied hatreds.

And, lest it take too long to recount each instance, absolutely everything that patience builds through its works unto glory, impatience destroys unto ruin.

## XX

Why then, most beloved brothers, after carefully weighing both the benefits of patience and the evils of impatience, let us hold fast to patience with complete observance—the patience through which we abide in Christ, so that we may come with Christ to God. [Note: [Col. 0634D] “And we can come with Christ to God”: Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] Patience, abundant and manifold, is not confined within a narrow limit or restrained by brief bounds. The power of patience extends widely [Col. 0635A]; and although its richness and bounty issue from the fountain of a single name, they pour through overflowing channels along many paths to glory. Nothing in our actions can advance toward the perfection of praise unless it receives from patience the steadfastness needed for perfection. [Note: [Col. 0635C] “Support” (*firmamentum*): Lin. Pem.]

It is patience that both commends us to God and preserves us. It is patience that moderates anger, bridles the tongue, governs the mind, guards peace, regulates discipline, breaks the assault of lust, represses the violence of arrogance, extinguishes the blaze of hostility, restrains the power of the rich, relieves the poverty of the poor, protects blessed integrity in virgins, laborious chastity in widows, and inseparable love in those joined in marriage. It makes people 254 humble in prosperity, courageous in adversity, [Note: [Col. 0635C] “And courageous in adversity”: Bod. 1.] and gentle in the face of injuries and insults [Col. 0635B]. It teaches us quickly to forgive those who offend, but, if we ourselves offend, to plead long and earnestly. It overcomes temptations, endures persecutions, and brings sufferings and martyrdoms to their consummation. It is patience that firmly fortifies the foundations of our faith; it is patience that raises the growth of hope to sublime heights. [Note: [Col. 0635C] “Advances subtly”: Ar.] It directs our conduct [Note: [Col. 0635C] “Itself directs the recognition of deeds”: Ben. NC. Ebor. Lam. Bod. 2.], so that we may keep to the way of Christ as we walk by means of his endurance. It causes us to persevere as children of God while we imitate the patience of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0635D]

**XXI.—“Nor this at the very end.”** We have restored the reading of the old editions, which is confirmed by twenty-three of our manuscripts and twelve English manuscripts. We were compelled to delete the words that had been altered and added in Morel’s edition, although we had also found them in three ancient codices and knew that Pamelius had likewise found them in four ancient copies. These are the words we deleted, for anyone who thinks it worth knowing what they were: “Nor should we defer the retribution of the wicked [Col. 0636D] until that day of the last judgment; together with us, we exhort you: meanwhile embrace the benefit of patience, so that amid these,” etc.

**“With querulous haste.”** Pamelius adds “and envious” from the Cambrai codex. But I have found this addition nowhere in the ancient books or in editions preceding that of Pamelius.

**“White robes.”** Eleven manuscript books read: “A white robe was given to each.”

[Col. 0637C] **“Of all the righteous.”** The Laetian codex reads: “He will vindicate all the righteous together with himself.”

**“Every knee should bend.”** Seven old books have “should bow”; seven others, “all knees should bow.”

[Col. 0638C] **“God the Father . . . beneath the earth.”** These words are absent from the book of Saint Arnulf, doubtless, as I think, through the copyist’s carelessness. For they occur in the other old books and in the editions.]

## XXI

But since I know, most beloved brothers, that very many people—either under the weight of grievous injuries or from anguish over those who assail and rage against them—desire swift vindication, this too must not be left unmentioned at the end: [Note: [Col. 0635C] Thus Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Ben. Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Foss. Morel, Pamelius, and Oxford read: “Nor should we defer the retribution of the wicked until that day of the last judgment; together with us, we exhort you: meanwhile embrace [Col. 0635D] the benefit of patience, so that amid these,” etc.] situated as we are amid the tempests of this unstable world and the persecutions of Jews, gentiles, and heretics as well [Col. 0635C], we must patiently await the day of vengeance and not hurry, with querulous haste, to avenge our suffering, since it is written:

> Wait for me, says the Lord, on the day of my resurrection [Note: [Col. 0635D] “Of my retribution”: Bod. 3.] as a testimony, for my judgment shall be against the assemblies of the nations, that I may receive kings and pour out my wrath upon them.  
> (Zeph. 3:8)

The Lord commands us to wait [Note: [Col. 0635D] Oxford adds “most beloved brothers”] and to endure the coming day of vengeance with resolute patience. He also speaks in the Apocalypse, saying:

> Do not seal the words [Col. 0636A] of the prophecy of this book, because the time is now near, so that those who persist in doing harm may still do harm, and whoever is filthy may still become filthier; but let the righteous person do still more righteous things, and likewise let the holy person [Note: [Col. 0635D] “The holy person, holier things”: Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver. Man.] do holier things. Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to repay each person according to his deeds.  
> (Rev. 22:10–12)

Thus even the martyrs who cry out and, as their anguish bursts forth, hasten toward their vindication are commanded to wait a little longer and to show patience until the appointed times are completed and the full number of martyrs is attained:

> And when he had opened, it says, the fifth seal, [Note: [Col. 0635D] “The fifth sign”: Lam. Ebor. Saris. Bod. 2, 3, 4. Ver. [Col. 0636C] Thu.] I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and their testimony; and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: “How long, holy and true Lord, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” And individual [Col. 0636B] white robes were given to them, [Note: [Col. 0636C] “A white robe was given to each”: Thu. Shortly afterward, “that they should endure”: Bod. 1.] and they were told to rest for yet a short time, until the number was fulfilled of their fellow servants and brothers who afterward [Note: [Col. 0636C] “Five afterward”: Lam. Pem. Lin. Ebor. Saris. NC. 1. Voss. 1, 2. Thu. Foss. Vict. “Should be slain”: Pem.] would be killed following their example.  
> (Rev. 6:9–11)

## XXII

The Holy Spirit declares through the prophet Malachi when divine vengeance for righteous blood will come:

> Behold, the day of the Lord comes, burning like a furnace; and all foreigners and all the wicked will be stubble, [Note: [Col. 0636C] “Like stubble”: Pem. Voss. 1. “As”: Bod. 1.] and the coming day will set them ablaze, [Note: [Col. 0636C] “Sets ablaze”: Bod. 1.] says the Lord.  
> (Mal. 4:1)

We likewise read this in the Psalms, where the coming of God the Judge is proclaimed as worthy of awe in the majesty of his judicial authority:

> God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and around him will be an exceedingly great tempest. [Note: [Col. 0636D] “His storm”: Bod. 3. “Mighty”: Pem. Bod. 3.] He will summon [Note: [Col. 0636D] “He will call”: Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ar. Lam. Ver.] heaven above and earth below, that he may separate his people. [Col. 0636C] Gather to him his righteous ones, those who establish his covenant through sacrifices; and the heavens will proclaim [Note: [Col. 0636D] “Will announce”: Saris. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] his righteousness, because God is Judge.  
> (Ps. 49:3–6)

And Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0636D] “For Isaiah also”: Bod. 1. Foss.] foretells the same things, saying:

> For behold, the Lord will come like fire, and his chariots like a tempest, to repay vengeance in wrath. For by the Lord’s fire they will be judged, and by his sword they will be wounded.  
> (Isa. 66:15)

And again:

> The Lord God of hosts will go forth and crush war; he will stir up battle [Note: [Col. 0636D] “Will rouse battle”: Voss. 2. Pem.], and with might he will cry out against his enemies [Col. 0637A]. I have been silent; surely I shall not always be silent?  
> (Isa. 42:13)

## XXIII

Who, then, is this who says that he was formerly silent but will not always be silent? Surely it is he who was led like a sheep to slaughter and who, like a lamb before the one shearing it, [Note: [Col. 0637B] “Before the shearer”: Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver.] voicelessly did not open his mouth. [Note: [Col. 0637B] “Thus he did not open”: Lam. Ebor.] Surely it is he who did not cry out, nor was his voice heard in the streets. Surely it is he who was not rebellious and did not contradict when he offered his back to scourges and his cheeks 253 to blows, but did not turn his face away from the vileness of spitting. Surely it is he who, when accused by the priests and elders, answered nothing and, to Pilate’s amazement, maintained a silence of the utmost patience. [Note: [Col. 0637B] “Most patient, maintained silence”: NC. 2.]

This is he who, [Note: [Col. 0637B] “This one who”: Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.] though he was silent during his Passion, [Note: [Col. 0637B] “Previously during his Passion”: Ver.] will afterward not be silent when exacting vengeance. This is our God—that is, the God not [Col. 0637B] of everyone, but of the faithful and believing—who, when he comes manifestly [Note: [Col. 0637B] “More manifestly”: Lin.] at his second advent, will not be silent. For although he was formerly hidden in humility, he will come manifestly in power.

## XXIV

Let us await him, most beloved brothers, as our Judge and Avenger, who will vindicate together with himself the people of his Church and the whole company, from the beginning of the world, of all the righteous. [Note: [Col. 0637B] “All the righteous”: Voss. 1.] Whoever hastens and hurries excessively toward his own vindication [Note: [Col. 0637B] “Vindication of himself”: Bod. 1.] [Col. 0638A] should consider that the one who vindicates has not yet himself been vindicated.

God the Father commanded that his Son be worshiped, and the apostle Paul, mindful of the divine command, states:

> God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, [Note: [Col. 0637C] “That it may be above every name”: Ar. Lam. Ebor. Ver.] so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend [Note: [Col. 0638B] “All knees should bow”: NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1. Ver.]—of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth.  
> (Phil. 2:9–10)

And in the Apocalypse the angel restrains John when he wishes to worship him and says: [Note: [Col. 0638B] “Restrained”: Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3.]

> See that you do not do this, because I am your fellow servant and that of your brothers. Worship the Lord Jesus.  
> [Note: [Col. 0638B] “Worship. Of this one”: Ar. Lin. Pem. Voss. 2.] (Rev. 22:9)

What a Lord Jesus is this, and how great is his patience: he who is worshiped in heaven has not yet been vindicated on earth! Let us ponder his patience, most beloved brothers, amid our persecutions and sufferings. Let us render to his coming an obedience full of expectation. Let us not hurry, with irreligious and shameless haste, [Note: [Col. 0638B] “Ruinous haste”: Saris.] for the servants to be vindicated [Col. 0638B] before the Lord.

Rather, let us persist [Note: [Col. 0638B] “But let us persist”: Saris.] and labor diligently, [Note: [Col. 0638B] “Let us labor”: Lam. Ebor. Ver.] watching with our whole heart [Note: [Col. 0638B] “Watching for God”: Bod. 3.] and remaining steadfast in every kind of endurance; and let us keep the Lord’s commandments, so that when that day of wrath and vengeance comes, we may not be punished with the impious and sinners, but honored [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Crowned”: Vict.] with the righteous and those who fear God.

[Col. 0637]

# BOOK ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY

[Note: [Col. 0637D]

**589 ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY.** After Saint Augustine had quoted the beginning and certain other passages of this book in Book IV, chapter 8, of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, he afterward says: “We recognize how true and how forceful are these words of Cyprian in his letter, which is known to the people. It was indeed fitting that Cyprian should both sternly rebuke and admonish concerning jealousy and envy, since the great abundance of his love proved that his heart was utterly estranged from so [Col. 0638D] deadly an evil.”

The same author says on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Galatians: “Blessed Cyprian also wrote an excellent book *On Jealousy and Envy*; anyone who reads it will not hesitate to number envy among the works of the flesh.”

See Hincmar, *Book of Fifty-Five Capitularies*, chapter 47, page 566.]

(C)

## SUBJECT

[Col. 0637D] In his *Life of Cyprian*, the blessed Pontius gives the subject of this book briefly in these words: “Who,” he asks, “would restrain, by the sweetness of a saving remedy, the envy that proceeds from the poisonous malice of jealousy?”

At the outset, therefore, after teaching that jealousy or envy is a more serious offense because it is a more hidden evil, and that its origin must be ascribed to the devil, he also presents in passing examples of envy from the Old Testament. [Col. 0638D] He then demonstrates, through each individual class of vice, that envy is the root of all evils and thus shows why fraternal hatred was rightly forbidden by Christ and the apostles in more than one passage. Finally, after exhorting them by God’s example to love their enemies, he deters them from this evil by setting before them the crowns of reward.

[Note: [Col. 0639C]

**I.—“Is not easily avoided.”** The *Consultations of Zacchaeus and Apollonius*, chapter 29, in volume X of d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, page 36: “And what is more savage, the evil is not guarded against beneath its appearance of innocence, because people do not believe that it can be avoided.”

**“When it creeps into the breast.”** Ten old books read “shall have crept in.” So too the old editions. Morel’s edition reads “when it may creep into the breast.”

[Col. 0639D] **“Walls.”** Previously “members” was read. We found the true reading in two very ancient copies, namely, the old Victorinus manuscript and the Tournai manuscript. In the Victorinus manuscript “members” is written, with “or walls” above the line; in the Tournai manuscript, “walls,” with “or members” above the line.]

## I

To be jealous of the good you see [Note: [Col. 0637D] “Good people”: Lin.] and to envy those who are better [Col. 0639A] appears to some, most beloved brothers, to be a slight and insignificant offense. Because it is considered slight and insignificant, it is not feared; because it is not feared, it is despised; because it is despised, it is not easily avoided. It thus becomes a blind and hidden source of destruction, which secretly afflicts unwary minds because it is too little discerned to be guarded against by the foresighted. [Note: [Col. 0639C] “By those who foresee”: Voss. 1. “By the prudent”: Pem. Voss. 2.]

But the Lord commanded us to be prudent and instructed us to keep watch with vigilant care, lest the adversary, always watchful [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Always himself”: Ben. Voss. 2.] and always lying in ambush, once he has crept into the breast, [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Creeps in secretly”: Pem. Voss. 2. “Has crept in”: Ar. Bod. 2, 4. Ver. Thu. Foss. “Are creeping in”: Vict.] should fan sparks into fires, magnify small things into the greatest, and—while he caresses the lax and incautious with a gentler breeze and softer breath—raise up storms and whirlwinds and contrive the ruin of faith and shipwrecks of salvation and life.

We must therefore keep watch, most beloved brothers, and labor with all our strength [Col. 0639B], so that with careful and complete vigilance we may resist the raging enemy as he aims his missiles at every part of the body [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Hurling them at the parts”: Bod. 3.] where we can be struck and wounded, 256 just as the apostle Peter forewarns and teaches in his epistle:

> Be sober and vigilant, because your adversary the devil prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.  
> [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Something to devour”: Bod. 1, 2. Ver. Thu.] (1 Pet. 5:8)

[Note: [Col. 0639D]

**II.—“He prowls about.”** The author of the *Letter to Demetrias*, among the works of Jerome: “The author of envy does not cease to envy; and he who was himself once cast away from God is tormented with all the greater jealousy the more distinguished he sees someone to be in God’s sight.” And shortly afterward: “After the manner of a deceitful enemy, he surveys everything and explores every entrance to the soul, to see whether there is anything weak and insufficiently protected through which he might creep.”

**“Melodious music.”** We have decided to retain this reading, which the old editions, including Morel’s, prefer, because it is given by seventeen old books, except that one of them has “resonant” in place of “melodious” [Col. 0640C], and because in Quintilian’s age there was doubt whether the word *musicam* could be used, as he himself says in Book VIII, chapter 3. Nevertheless, certain other old books and the English edition prefer *canoram musicam*; the Moissac codex and Rigault read *canorem musicam*. But this is an error, for *canor* is masculine. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book V: “Yet that melody was not born to charm the ears.” [Col. 0640D] There are other examples as well.

**“Displays false things.”** The author of the *Praedestinatus*, published by Sirmond, quotes this passage in the prologue to Book III: “The book hostile to humanity, fabricated against the Catholic faith, surrounded by fallacies, an adulterator of sound definition, has been completed; and, as Saint Cyprian says, it displays false things in order to steal away the true.”]

## II

He prowls about each one of us and, like an enemy besieging people enclosed within a fortress, examines the walls and tests whether some part of them is less stable and less secure, through whose approach he might penetrate to the interior. He presents seductive forms [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Female forms”: Bod. 3.] and easily obtained pleasures to the eyes, [Note: [Col. 0639C] “Desires”: Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1, 2. NC. 1. Pem. Bod. [Col. 0640C] 2, 4. Vict. Voss.] so that he may destroy chastity through sight. He tempts the ears with melodious music, [Note: [Col. 0640C] “Melodious music”: Ben. Thu. Foss.] so that by hearing a sweeter sound he may loosen and soften Christian vigor.

He provokes the tongue to abuse; through inciting injuries [Col. 0639C] he goads the hand to the violent insolence of killing. To make a person fraudulent, [Col. 0640A] he holds out unjust gains; to capture the soul with money, [Note: [Col. 0640C] “To capture, he displays”: Bod. 1.] he offers ruinous profits; he promises earthly honors so that he may take away heavenly ones; he displays false things so that he may steal away the true. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens expressly and openly, [Note: [Col. 0640C] “And manifestly”: Bod. 1.] holding out the terror of turbulent persecution. Ever restless and always hostile in his assault upon God’s servants, he is treacherous in peace and violent in persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

**III.—“Missiles that secretly.”** Above, at the beginning of the book *On the Unity of the Church*, page 193: “Precaution is easier where the danger is manifest.” Jerome, in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*: “An arrow discharged from a fully drawn bow is difficult to avoid. For it reaches the person at whom it was thrown before it can be frustrated by the barrier of a shield.”]

## III

Therefore, most beloved brothers, the mind must stand equipped and armed against all the devil’s deceitful ambushes and open threats, as constantly prepared [Note: [Col. 0640C] “Let it be as prepared”: Pem. Voss. 2.] to resist as the enemy is constantly prepared to attack.

And since the missiles that creep in secretly are more frequent, and the more hidden and clandestine the assault is, the less it is perceived and the more seriously and frequently it assails us so as to wound us [Col. 0640B], let us be vigilant also in recognizing and repelling such things. Among them is the evil of jealousy and envy. If anyone examines it deeply, he will find that nothing must be guarded against more by a Christian and nothing must be watched more carefully than being captured by envy and jealousy. Otherwise, entangled in the blind snares of the deceitful enemy, [Note: [Col. 0640C] “Of the enemy”: Pem. Voss. 1.] while through jealousy brother turns to hatred of brother, he may unknowingly be destroyed by his own sword.

So that we may understand this more fully and perceive it more clearly, let us return to its source and origin. Let us see whence jealousy arose, and when and how it began. For so pernicious an evil will be more easily avoided by us if both the origin and the magnitude of that evil are known.

[Note: [Col. 0640D]

**IV.—“From this the devil.”** Saint Augustine quotes and explains this passage in Book IV, chapter 9, of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*. See Sirmond’s notes on Rufinus of Palestine’s book *On Faith*, page 91.

[Col. 0641D] **“Of his party.”** The following comes afterward in the Pithou codex: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.” But I have not found this addition elsewhere.]

## IV

Through this evil, at the very beginning of the world, the devil was the first both to perish [Col. 0640C] and to destroy. He who was sustained by angelic majesty, [Note: [Col. 0640C] “He, angelic”: Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1, Voss. 1, 2. “Power”: Bod. 3. “He formerly”: Oxon.] [Col. 0641A] he who was acceptable and dear to God, after he saw the human being made in the image of God, burst into jealousy through malicious envy. He did not cast another down at the prompting of jealousy before he had first himself been cast down by jealousy—captive before taking captive, ruined before ruining. While envy spurred him on, [Note: [Col. 0641C] “And while envy spurred”: NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.] he took from the human being the grace of the immortality that had been given, [Note: [Col. 0641C] Thus Lam. Ebor. Lin. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. “Takes away, he who also”: Imp.] and he too lost what he had formerly been.

What an evil this is, most beloved brothers! Through it an angel fell; through it that lofty and illustrious sublimity could be ensnared and overthrown; through it the very one who deceived was himself deceived. Since then envy has raged upon the earth: the person destined to perish through envy obeys the master of perdition and imitates the jealous devil, as it is written:

> Through the devil’s envy death entered the world.  
> (Wisd. 2:24)

Those who belong to his party therefore imitate him.

[Col. 0641B] [Note: [Col. 0641D]

**V.—“Of the new brotherhood.”** The word “new” is absent from two old books. It certainly seems superfluous. I have nevertheless not deleted it, because it occurs in many manuscript copies.

**“Persecutes through envy.”** In three ancient codices the following comes afterward: “while he imitates the jealous devil.” But this seems to have been repeated by some learned reader from what was said shortly before. Novatian, in his book *On the Trinity*: “It does not descend from the malicious envy of jealousy.”

**“Cain is jealous of righteous Abel.”** For this reason Prosper, in Book II, chapter 6, of *The Promises and Predictions of God*, calls Cain the author of envy. Irenaeus, in Book I, speaking of Cain’s generation, says: “Thus, when he killed his brother Abel, he was the first to manifest jealousy and death.”

**590 “Once.”** In one of my old books “once” is written, with “or together” above the line. From this, therefore, as we have said more than once already, arose the discrepancy found here in the manuscript codices, some of which have “once,” others “together.”]

## V

From this, finally, arose the first hatreds of the new brotherhood; from this began unspeakable acts of fratricide (Gen. 4), when unrighteous Cain was jealous of righteous Abel, when the evil man persecuted the good through envy and jealousy. The fury of rivalry had such power to bring the crime to completion that neither a brother’s love, nor the enormity of the crime, nor the fear of God, nor the punishment of the offense received any consideration. He who had first displayed righteousness was unrighteously crushed; he who had not known how to hate endured hatred; he who did not resist as he died was impiously slain.

And jealousy was the reason why Esau became hostile to his brother Jacob (Gen. 27). For because Jacob had received their father’s blessing, Esau blazed into persecuting hatred, kindled by the torches of envy. And when Joseph’s brothers sold him, the cause of their selling him arose from rivalry (Gen. 37). After he had straightforwardly related to his brothers, as a brother, what had been shown to him as favorable in his visions [Col. 0641C], their malicious disposition burst into envy.

What else but the goad of jealousy provoked King Saul to hate David and, in repeatedly renewed persecutions, to desire to kill an innocent, merciful, gentle man who patiently bore everything with mildness? [Note: [Col. 0641C] “With gentle truthfulness”: Routh, from his codices.] (1 Sam. 18). Because, once Goliath had been killed and so great an enemy destroyed [Note: [Col. 0641C] “Cast down”: Pem. Voss. 2.] by divine help and favor, the admiring people burst into praise of David with the approving acclamation [Note: [Col. 0641C] “With the duty of proclamation”: Bod. 1.] of their testimony (1 Sam. 17), Saul [Note: [Col. 0641C] “King Saul”: Pem. Voss. 2.] conceived from envy the madness of hostility and persecution [Col. 0642A].

And, lest I make this account too long by reviewing individuals, [Note: [Col. 0641C] “By reviewing”: Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, [Col. 0642C] 2, 3, 4. “By kindling”: Oxon.] let us consider the destruction of a people perishing once and for all. [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Of a people perishing together”: Pem. Ebor. Routh, from one codex. “For itself”: Tew.] Do not the Jews suffer precisely because they prefer to envy Christ rather than believe in him? Disparaging the mighty works that he performed, they were deceived because jealousy blinded them, and they could not open the eyes of their hearts to recognize divine realities.

[Note: [Col. 0642D]

**VI.—“From it hatred arises.”** Prudentius in the *Hamartigenia*: “For the spark of hatred burned from the tinder of jealousy.”

**“Higher.”** Thus the old editions and sixteen old books. Manutius printed “more increased.” Morel afterward restored the old reading. Pamelius reinstated that of Manutius, which I found in ten ancient books; but the greater number prevails. And certainly the old edition is much better.

**“Anger grows hot.”** Cassian, Book VIII, chapter 1, calls it “deadly poison.”]

## VI

Considering these things, [Note: [Col. 0642C] Thus Thu. Foss. NC. 2. “Which now”: Oxon.] most beloved brothers, let us vigilantly and courageously fortify against so destructive an evil the hearts we have dedicated to God. Let the death of others contribute to our salvation; let the punishment of the imprudent confer health upon the foresighted.

No one should suppose that this evil is contained within a single form or confined by brief bounds and a narrow limit. The manifold and prolific destructiveness of jealousy extends widely. It is the root [Note: [Col. 0642C] “For it is the root”: Lin. Pem. Voss. 2. Bod. 3, 4.] of all evils, the source of disasters, the seedbed of offenses, and the substance of faults. From it hatred arises; from it animosity proceeds. Jealousy inflames avarice when someone, seeing another person richer, cannot be content with what is his own. Jealousy arouses ambition when someone sees another higher in honors. [Note: [Col. 0642C] Thus Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2, 3. “More increased in honors”: Oxon.]

When jealousy blinds our perception and brings the hidden places of the mind beneath its dominion, the fear of God is despised, Christ’s teaching is neglected, and the day of judgment is not foreseen. Pride swells, cruelty grows bitter, treachery breaks faith, impatience convulses, discord rages, and anger grows hot. A person who has come under another’s power can no longer restrain or govern himself [Col. 0642C].

From this the bond of the Lord’s peace is broken; from this fraternal love is violated; from this truth is adulterated and unity divided; and people rush into heresies and schisms when priests are disparaged, bishops envied, and a person either complains that he himself was not ordained instead [Note: [Col. 0642C] “Honored instead”: Bod. 3.] or disdains to tolerate another as his superior. From this he kicks back; from this he rebels—proud from jealousy [Col. 0643A], perverted by rivalry, and made by animosity and envy the enemy not of the man, but of the honor.

[Note: [Col. 0643C]

**VII.—“Bring executioners to bear.”** Tacitus, *Annals*, Book VI: “Nor was it without reason that the man most eminent in wisdom used to maintain that, if the minds of tyrants were laid open, wounds and blows could then be seen.”

Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*:

> O, if the hearts of the rich lay open,  
> What great commotions lofty  
> Fortune drives within!

Latinus Pacatus, in the *Panegyric to Theodosius*: “My guilty mind has within it certain executioners whose nature I cannot explain.”

Boethius, Book IV of *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> The kings whom you see seated  
> Upon the lofty summit of the throne—  
> If someone strips from the proud  
> The coverings of their empty splendor,  
> He will then see within  
> That the lords bear constricting chains.  
> For from one side lust torments  
> Their hearts with greedy poisons.  
> For from one side lust torments  
> Their hearts with greedy poisons.  
> From another, anger lashes the mind,  
> Raising its turbulent waves;  
> [Col. 0643D] Either grief wears down its captives,  
> Or treacherous hope torments them.

By contrast, Seneca, *Letter* 115: “If we were permitted to look into the soul of a good man, O what a beautiful countenance we would see—how holy, how radiant with magnificence and serenity, shining on one side with courage, on another with temperance and prudence!”

**“Is mangled.”** The codex of Saint Arnulf and the Grenoble codex read “is torn.”]

## VII

What a moth of the soul it is, [Note: [Col. 0643B] Thus Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. “What a thing it is for the soul”: Oxon.] what a corruption of the thoughts, what great rust of the breast, to be jealous of another person’s virtue or happiness—that is, to hate in him either his own merits or God’s benefits; to turn the good things of others into one’s own evil; to be tormented by the prosperity of the illustrious; to make another’s glory one’s own punishment; and, as it were, to bring certain executioners to bear upon one’s breast and employ torturers against one’s own thoughts and perceptions, so that they may mangle one with inward torments and strike the hidden places of the heart with the claws of malice!

For such people no food can be pleasant, no drink enjoyable. They are always sighing, groaning, and grieving; and because envy is never cast off by the envious, their besieged breast is mangled [Col. 0643B] without interruption by day and night.

Other evils have an end, and whatever offense is committed comes to an end when the offense has been consummated. In the adulterer the crime ceases once the violation has been perpetrated; in the robber the wickedness subsides once the murder has been committed; possession of the spoil sets a limit to the plunderer’s rapacity, [Note: [Col. 0643B] “The plunderer’s rapacity”: Ar. Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Vict. “Satisfies”: Vat.] and completion of the deceit sets a boundary for the deceiver. Jealousy has no end: it is a constantly abiding evil and an unending sin. The more the person who is envied 258 advances [Col. 0644A] through greater success, the more the envious person blazes with the fires of envy into a still greater conflagration.

[Note: [Col. 0643D]

**VIII.—“From this comes a threatening countenance.”** One old book reads: “From this comes a defiant countenance.”

**“Trembling of the lips.”** Robert, bishop of Senez and son of Gervase, used these words as though they were his own when describing the vices of Bartholomew, archbishop of Bari, who called himself Urban VI at the beginning of that miserable schism which tore the Church apart after the death of Pope Gregory XI [Col. 0644C], as may be seen on page 1271 of our notes on the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*.

The ancients placed trembling of the lips among the indications of an evil mind. Lactantius, in chapter V of *On the Anger of God*, when enumerating the faults of a disturbed mind, includes among them trembling of the mouth—that is, of the lips. Jerome, on chapter 1 of Paul’s Epistle to Titus: “He, by contrast, with grim countenance, trembling lips, furrowed brow, unbridled abuse, a face shifting between pallor and redness, makes a din with his shouting.”

Likewise, in the letter *On Avoiding Suspicious Cohabitation*: “Why do you suffuse your countenance with the blush of disgrace and confess the impatience of your breast with trembling lips?”

Likewise, in the letter to Pammachius against John of Jerusalem: “With your neck thrown back and your lips trembling, you fell silent.”

Likewise, in the letter to Oceanus *On the Husband of One Wife*: “Yet the brow sweats, the cheeks grow pale, the lips tremble, the saliva dries upon the tongue, and the body contracts more from age than from fear.”

Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* III, chapter 20, speaking of Brice when he was not yet of sound mind: “With trembling lips and an uncertain countenance.”

A fragment of Petronius in Diomedes, Book III: “An old woman well-soaked in wine, with trembling little lips.”

Seneca, at the beginning of his book *On Anger*, includes among the signs of anger the fact that the lips quiver. Elsewhere it is a sign of fear, as in Jerome’s letter to Nepotian *On the Life of Clerics*: “They tremble at the doctor’s entrance and, with quivering lips, ask whether they are improving.”

Silius Italicus, Book VIII:

> Scarcely forming breathless murmurs  
> Amid her sobs, and with trembling lips, Anna—

Seneca, *Letter* 97: “It is characteristic of the guilty to tremble.” See above, page 439.]

## VIII

From this comes a threatening countenance, a grim expression, pallor in the face, trembling of the lips, grinding of the teeth, rabid words, unbridled abuse, and a hand ready for murderous violence—even if for the moment empty of a sword, nevertheless armed with the hatred of an enraged mind. [Note: [Col. 0643B] “Of a frenzied mind”: Pem. Voss. 2.]

For this reason the Holy Spirit says in the Psalms:

> Do not be jealous of the person who walks prosperously in his way.  
> [Note: [Col. 0643B] “Do not make yourself jealous”: Bod. 4.]

And again:

> The sinner will watch the righteous person and will grind [Note: [Col. 0643B] “Grinds”: Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Ver.] his teeth at him. [Note: [Col. 0643B] “Teeth”: Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ben.] But God will laugh at him, because he foresees that his day will come.  
> [Note: [Col. 0644B] “His days will come”: Bod. 4. “Comes”: Bod. 3.] (Ps. 36:7, 12–13)

The blessed apostle Paul marks out and identifies such people when he says:

> The poison of asps is beneath their lips, and their mouth is full of cursing [Note: [Col. 0644B] “A curse”: Bod. 2, 4. Thu. Ver.] and bitterness. Swift [Note: [Col. 0644B] “And swift”: Bod. 3.] are their feet to shed blood. [Col. 0644B] Destruction [Note: [Col. 0644B] “Affliction”: Ar. NC. 1. Voss. 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver. “Misfortune”: Bod. 3.] and calamity are in the ways of those who have not known the way of peace, [Note: [Col. 0644B] “Because the way”: Bod. 1.] and there is no fear of God before their eyes.  
> (Rom. 3:13–18)

[Note: [Col. 0644D]

**IX.—591 “What is seen is brought to recovery.”** Thus the more ancient editions and twenty-six old copies. Erasmus added the word “wound,” producing the reading: “The wound that is seen is brought to recovery”; I too found this reading in five [Col. 0645D] manuscript codices. Nevertheless, I removed the word because of the authority of so many old copies and because the sense stands perfectly well without it.

**“Your adversary is with you.”** Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*: “We can easily be free of other vices. This enemy is enclosed within us. Wherever we go, we carry our enemy with us.”]

IX. The evil is much lighter and the danger less when limbs are wounded by the sword. Treatment is easy where the wound is manifest, and what is visible is quickly restored to health when medicine comes to its aid. [Note: [Col. 0644B] Thus Ar. Lam. Ebor. Thu. Foss. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. “The wound that is visible” Oxon.] The wounds of jealousy are hidden and concealed; those that have shut themselves away with blind pain within the recesses of conscience [Col. 0645A] admit no remedy from a healer’s care. Whoever you are who are envious and malicious, consider how treacherous, destructive, and hostile you are toward those whom you hate. You are the enemy of no one’s salvation more than your own. Whoever it is whom you persecute through jealousy will be able to elude and avoid you; you cannot flee from yourself [Note: [Col. 0645D] “You can avoid, but not flee” Ar. Voss. 2. “Flee, wherever you might flee” Foss.]: wherever you may be, your adversary is with you; the enemy is always in your breast [Note: [Col. 0645D] “Is in your breast” Lam. Ebor. Thu. Bod. 1, 2.]; destruction is enclosed within you. You are bound and fettered by an inescapable chain, a captive under the dominion of jealousy, and no consolations come to your aid. It is an enduring evil to persecute a person who belongs to the grace of God. It is a calamity without remedy to hate one who is blessed.

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

X.—The night has passed. See Erasmus’s *Annotations* on this passage of Paul.

]

X. And therefore, dearly beloved brothers, the Lord, taking thought for this danger lest anyone fall into the snare of death [Col. 0645B] through jealousy of a brother, when the disciples asked him which among them [Note: [Col. 0645D] “Which of them” Lin.] was the greater, said: “Whoever is least among all of you, he will be great” (Luke 9:48). By his answer he cut off all rivalry; he uprooted and severed every cause and source of biting envy. A disciple of Christ [Note: [Col. 0645D] “A disciple of Christ,” accusative, Lam. Lin. Bod. 2.] is not permitted to be jealous [Note: [Col. 0645D] “Ought not” Bod. 2.]; he is not permitted to envy. Among us there can be no contest for exaltation: through humility we rise to the highest things [Note: [Col. 0645D] “We rise, whereby we may please” Pem. Voss. 2.]; we have learned whereby we may please. Finally, the apostle Paul also instructs and admonishes us that, since we have been illuminated by Christ’s light and have escaped the darkness of our nocturnal way of life, we should walk in deeds and works of light. He writes and says: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on [Note: [Col. 0645D] “Let us be clothed with” Ver. Vet. innom.] the weapons of light. Let us walk becomingly [Note: [Col. 0646D] “Honorably” Lin.] as in the day—not in [Col. 0645C] revelries and drunkenness, not in lusts and shameless acts, not in quarrels and jealousy” (Rom. 13:12–13). If darkness has departed from your breast, if the night has been dispelled from it, if the gloom has been wiped away, if the splendor of day has illuminated your understanding, if you have begun to be a person of light, do the things that belong to Christ, because Christ is light and day [Note: [Col. 0646D] “Both light and day” Bod. 1.].

[Note: [Col. 0646D]

XI.—Hates his brother. See Saint Augustine, Tractate V on the Epistle of Saint John, and Cassian, book I, chapter 20. See also Hincmar, vol. I, p. 72.

[Col. 0647D] As to carnal persons, as. In the Apostle’s wording (ῥήσει), I have restored the words “as to carnal persons, as,” which had perhaps fallen out of Baluze’s text. ROUTH.]

XI. Why do you rush into the darkness of jealousy? Why do you envelop yourself in the cloud of spite? Why, through the blindness of envy, do you extinguish all the light of peace and charity? Why do you return to the devil whom you had renounced? Why do you come forward as another Cain? For the apostle John declares in his epistle that anyone who has been jealous of and hated his brother is bound by the crime of murder, saying: “He who hates his brother [Col. 0646A] is a murderer; and you know that no murderer has life abiding in him” (1 John 3:15).
