And again: “He who says that he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness even until now; and he walks in darkness and does not know where he is going [Note: [Col. 0646D] “Does not know where he is going” Bod. 2.], because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (ibid. 2:9–11). “He who hates his brother,” he says, “walks in darkness and does not know where he is going.” For 259 in his ignorance he goes into Gehenna; unaware and blind, he plunges headlong into punishment, having withdrawn from the light of Christ, who admonishes and says: “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). Now the one who follows Christ is he who adheres to his commandments, advances along the way taught by his instruction, follows his footsteps and paths, and imitates what Christ both taught and did, in accordance with [Col. 0646B] what Peter [Note: [Col. 0646D] “The apostle Peter” Bod. 3.] also exhorts and admonishes when he says: “Christ suffered for us [Note: [Col. 0646D] “Suffered for you” Lam. Bod. 1, 2. Thu. Foss.; see book III, *To Quirinus*, chapter 39.], leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

XII. We must remember by what name Christ calls his people and by what title he designates his flock. He names them sheep, so that Christian innocence may be equated with that of sheep (John 10:2; Matt. 10:16); he calls them lambs, so that simplicity of mind may imitate the guileless nature of lambs. Why does a wolf lurk beneath sheep’s clothing? Why does one who falsely claims to be a Christian bring disgrace upon Christ’s flock? To put on the name of Christ and yet not proceed along Christ’s way—what else is this but a violation of the divine name, a desertion of the path of salvation? For he himself teaches and says that the one who keeps the commandments [Note: [Col. 0646D] “His commandments” Ver. Bod. 2.] comes to life, that the one who hears [Col. 0646C] and performs his words is wise, and that the one who acts and teaches accordingly will be called a great teacher in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:19). What has been preached well and profitably will then benefit the preacher if what is uttered by the mouth is fulfilled by the deeds that follow. Yet what did the Lord impress upon his disciples more frequently? Among his saving admonitions and heavenly commands, what did he enjoin them to guard and preserve more carefully than that, with the same love with which he himself loved the disciples, we too should love one another [Note: [Col. 0646D] “We should love one another” Ar. Bod. 2. Thu. Foss.] (John 13:34)? But how does one retain either the Lord’s peace or charity when, because jealousy intervenes, he can be neither peaceable nor beloved?

[Note: [Col. 0647D]

XIII.—Of a confessor and martyr. I judged that this should be written in place of what was formerly read, “of confession and martyrdom,” because I saw it written thus in seventeen of our books and in four English manuscripts. Pamelius also testifies that he found this reading in the Cambrai manuscript. The edition called Gravius’s reads “for a confessor and martyr.” This reading comes very close to the one I have substituted. Eight old copies have the reading I rejected.

Infants. Three old copies have “little children.” In book III of the *Testimonies*, “infants” is written.

I gave you milk to drink. It was formerly read: “I gave you milk as drink, not food.” Although that reading is good, I nevertheless judged that the reading presented by twenty of our books and eight English manuscripts should be preferred, as well as by the Cambrai manuscript praised by Pamelius and the excerpts of Florus. Several old books and editions have the other reading. In book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 3, it reads: “I gave you milk as drink, not solid food.”]

XIII. Therefore the apostle Paul also, when he was setting forth the merits of peace and charity and firmly asserting and teaching that neither faith, nor almsgiving, nor even the suffering itself of a confessor and martyr [Note: [Col. 0647C] Thus Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. “Of confession or martyrdom” Oxon.] would benefit him unless he preserved the bonds of charity whole and inviolate, added and said: “Charity is magnanimous; charity is kind; charity is not jealous” (1 Cor. 13:4). He was plainly teaching and showing that whoever is magnanimous and kind and free of jealousy and spite is capable of retaining charity. Likewise, in another place, when admonishing that a person who is now filled with the Holy Spirit and made a son of God by heavenly birth should pursue nothing but spiritual and divine things, he states and says: “And I, brothers, was indeed unable to speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons, as to infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink [Note: [Col. 0647C] Thus Ar. Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. “I fed you with milk” Bod. 1. “Solid food” book III, *To Quirinus*, chapter 3.], not solid food, for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are unable [Note: [Col. 0647C] “You are able to bear solid food” Voss. 1.]. For you are still carnal. For when jealousy and strife and dissensions are among you [Note: [Col. 0647C] “For when among you” NC. 1. Lam. Bod. 2.], are you not carnal and walking according to man?” (1 Cor. 3:1–3).

[Col. 0647B] XIV. Carnal vices and sins must be crushed, dearly beloved brothers, and the hostile corruption of the earthly body must be trampled down by spiritual strength, lest, while we turn back once more to the way of life of the old man, we become entangled in deadly snares. The Apostle providently [Note: [Col. 0647C] “Providing” Ar. Bod. 2.] and beneficially gives prior warning of this very thing: “Therefore,” he says, “brothers, let us not live according to the flesh; for if you live [Note: [Col. 0647C] “You are living” Bod. 3, 4. Voss. 1. Ver. Ben. “You will die” Bod. 3. Voss. 1.] according to the flesh, you will begin to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death [Note: [Col. 0647C] “You put to death,” present tense, Ver.] the works of the flesh, you will live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Rom. 8:12–14). If we are sons of God, if we have now begun to be his temples, if, having received the Holy Spirit, we live in holiness and spiritually, if we have raised our eyes from the earth to heaven, if we have lifted up to the heavenly and divine things a breast filled with God and Christ, [Col. 0647C] let us do only what is worthy of God and Christ, just as the Apostle also arouses and exhorts us: “If you have risen together [Note: [Col. 0647C] “If,” he says, “you have risen together with Christ” Ver. “If we have risen together” Thu.] with Christ,” he says, “seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God; set your mind on the things that are above, 260 not the things upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0647C] “Not earthly things” Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver. Ben.]. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear [Col. 0648A] with him in glory” (Col. 3:1–4). We, therefore, who in Baptism have both died and been buried with respect to the carnal sins of the old man [Note: [Col. 0647D] “Have died” Ar.], and who through heavenly regeneration have risen with Christ, should alike think and perform the things that belong to Christ, as the same Apostle again teaches and admonishes, saying: “The first man was from the clay of the earth; the second man is from heaven. As was the one from clay, so also are those who are from clay; and as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of him who is from clay, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47–49). But we cannot bear the heavenly image unless, in that which we have now begun to be [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Have begun to be, we persevere” Voss. 1.], we exhibit the likeness of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0648D]

XV.—Born afterward. Rigault preferred *successiva*, “succeeding.” I found that reading in several very ancient copies. In the Bec manuscript it is written *succidua*.

I have begotten. Although the reading “has begotten” is good, I nevertheless decided to restore this one because it appears in every edition preceding Pamelius’s, in twenty-three of our books, and in three English manuscripts. I found the other in only three.

Is born spiritually in such a way. The remainder of this book is absent from the manuscript of Saint-Arnoul.]

XV. For this is what it means to have changed what you were and to have begun to be what you were not: that the divine birth may shine forth in you; [Col. 0648B] that a godlike discipline may answer to God the Father; and that, through the honor and praiseworthiness of one’s manner of life, God may be gloriously manifested in a human being. He himself exhorts and admonishes us and promises a reciprocal return to those who glorify him: “Those,” he says, “who glorify me I shall glorify; and he who despises me will be despised” (1 Sam. 2:30). Forming and preparing us for this glorification [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Conforming us for this glorification” Voss. 1.], and presenting the likeness of God the Father, the Lord and Son of God says in his Gospel: “You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Your neighbor” Ar.] and hate [Note: [Col. 0648C] “And you shall hate” Pem. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 3.] your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Like the Father” Ar. Lin. NC. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. “Your Father” Thu.] who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise over the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Lev. 19; Matt. 5:43–45). If it is joyful and glorious for human beings to have children like themselves, [Col. 0648C] and if one takes greater delight in having begotten them when the offspring born afterward [*soboles subsiciva*] corresponds to its father in matching features, how much greater is the joy of God the Father when someone is born spiritually in such a way that the divine nobility [Note: [Col. 0648C] “Begetting” Ar. Bod. 2.] is proclaimed in his deeds and praises? What a palm of justice, what a crown it is to show oneself such a person [Note: [Col. 0648C] “To be such” Ar. Bod. 2. “Such” [corrupt: *tetalem*] NC. 1. Drur. 1, 2. Meerm.] that God does not say of him: “I have begotten [Note: [Col. 0648C] Thus Bod. 1, 3, 4. “I begot” Oxon.] sons and exalted them, but they have despised me.” [Col. 0649A] (Isa. 1:2). Rather, may Christ praise you and invite you to the reward, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that was prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

[Note: [Col. 0649C]

XVI.—Let divine reading be in your hands. I am surprised that this reading, which is preferred by all the old editions and all the old books, was rejected by Pamelius. Thinking that this passage was defective, he supplemented it from four manuscripts and printed: “Let divine reading be before your eyes, good works in your hands, and reflection upon the Lord in your thoughts.” I have restored the old reading.

Peace too has. Above, Epistle VIII, p. 18: “In the heavenly camps peace and the battle line have their own flowers.” Hilary, bishop of Arles, in his *Sermon on Saint Honoratus*: “Peace too has its martyrs.” Jerome, in the *Epistle to Demetrias on the Preservation of Virginity*: “The preservation of chastity too has its own martyrdom.” See the homily of Saint John Chrysostom in praise of Saint Thecla, the first woman martyr and apostle. Commodianus, *Instructions* LXII: “War is absent; in peace martyrs were advancing.”

Victors, when the adversary has been cast down. The Grenoble manuscript reads: “Victors are crowned when, in the contest, the adversary has been cast down and subdued.”

[Col. 0649D] Lust. Fulgentius Planciades, book II of the *Mythologies*, calls it “the stepmother of honor.”]

XVI. By these meditations the mind must be strengthened, dearly beloved brothers; by exercises of this kind it must be fortified against all the devil’s missiles. Let divine reading be in our hands and reflection upon the Lord in our thoughts. Let unceasing prayer never cease at all; let saving work continue. Let us always be occupied in spiritual acts, so that, whenever the enemy approaches and whenever he attempts to draw near, he may find a breast both closed and armed against him. For there is not merely one crown for a Christian, the crown received in time of persecution. Peace too has its crowns, by which victors in varied and manifold conflict [Col. 0649B] are crowned when the adversary has been cast down and subdued. To have subdued lust is the palm of continence. To have fought against anger and injury is the crown of patience. To despise money is a triumph over avarice. To endure the adversities of the world through confidence in things to come [Note: [Col. 0649B] “Future good things” Bod. 2, 3.] is the praise of faith. And one who is not proud in prosperity obtains glory from humility. One who is inclined toward mercy in supporting the poor acquires the recompense of heavenly treasure. And one who does not know how to be jealous, and who loves his [Col. 0650A] brothers in unanimity and gentleness, is honored with the reward of love and peace. We run daily in this stadium of virtues; without any interruption of time, we attain these palms and crowns of justice.

[Note: [Col. 0649D]

XVII.—Merrah. This is the reading of four excellent old books, including the Verona manuscript. It is also written thus in the translation of the Seventy Interpreters, in Origen’s Homily VII on Exodus; in Saint Cyril of Alexandria, book V of *Worship in Spirit and Truth*; in Saint Ambrose, chapter 5 of *The Institution of a Virgin*; and in Saint Augustine, book II, Question 55 on Exodus. Cotelerius also correctly demonstrates that it must be written precisely thus in his notes on book VI, chapter 19, of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. See also the notes of Fronton du Duc on Poem XVII of Saint Paulinus. Rufinus on Psalm 44: “Myrrh is a very bitter substance with which the body of a dead person is anointed so that it will not decay, and it drives away worms.”

Imitate the good. That well-known saying: “In living, follow the good; in writing, follow the skilled.” Ambrose, book II of *Duties*, [Col. 0650C] chapter 20: “It is therefore of the greatest benefit to everyone to associate with the good. It is also useful for young men to follow illustrious and wise men.” Gregory Nazianzen says in his poem to Nicobulus that it belongs to a prudent and sensible man to measure his life by a great standard and to shape himself in imitation of excellent men. Quintilian, book I, chapter 6: “I shall therefore call linguistic usage the consensus of the learned, just as I call the consensus of the good the rule of life.” 592 Lactantius, book I, chapter 1: “Because speaking well belongs to a few, but living well to everyone.” Ruricius, book II, Epistle IV: “Just as living is common to everyone, truly living well and departing well from this life belong to few.” Seneca, Epistle VII: “Associate with those who will make you better.” Symmachus, book V, Epistle LXIV: “It is the greatest gain to seek the friendship of good people.” Jerome, in the *Epistle to Rusticus*: “Among the clergy, follow the better men.” Cyprian did what he advised. He always imitated the good. For Pontius the deacon writes thus in his *Life* of Cyprian: “And so, running through the examples of all good men, [Col. 0650D] while always imitating those who were better, he also made himself worthy of imitation.” Ennodius, book V, Epistle XX: “Let honorable studies take complete possession of you. Make haste to come to the harvest of your fatherland, cleansing your tongue with the hoe of reading and your character by imitating the good.” Horace, book I, Epistle XVIII:

> Amid your many readings, you will question learned men  
> About the method by which you may pass your life gently.

Tacitus praises Agricola because he strove to learn from the experienced and follow the best men.

Joined. This emendation, which I found in three ancient manuscripts and in the ancient editions, seems certain to me. Nevertheless, almost all the old books prefer “co-heir.” This discrepancy arose because in one old book, as in the Victorinus manuscript, “joined” was written, [Col. 0651B] and above the line perhaps “co-heir.” We have already observed that this frequently occurred in ancient copies of the works of Saint Cyprian.]

XVII. So that you too, who had been possessed by jealousy and spite, may be able to attain these palms and crowns, cast off all that malice by which you were previously held [Note: [Col. 0649B] “Drive away the darkness by which you were held” Bod. 2.]; reform yourself for the way of eternal life with saving footsteps. 261 Tear the thorns and thistles from your breast, so that the Lord’s seed may enrich you with fertile [Note: [Col. 0649B] “Fruitful” Bod. 1.] produce and the divine and spiritual crop may overflow into the abundance of a fruitful harvest. Vomit out the poisons of gall; expel the venom of dissensions. Let the mind infected by serpentine spite be cleansed; let all the bitterness that had settled within be soothed by the sweetness of Christ. If you take both food and drink from the sacrament of the cross, may the wood that, as a figure, proved effective [Col. 0650B] at Merrah [Note: [Col. 0650B] “At Marrah” Ver. “Mara” Oxon.] prove effective for you in the reality by making the taste sweet and soothing your breast to gentleness; nor will you struggle to obtain the remedy of restored health. Seek healing from the very source from which you had been wounded. Love those whom you previously hated; cherish those whom you envied with unjust disparagement. Imitate the good, if you can follow them [Note: [Col. 0650B] “If you cannot follow them” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ver.]. But if you cannot follow them, at least rejoice with your betters and congratulate them [Note: [Col. 0650B] “Congratulate” Voss. 1. “Congratulate” Imp.]. Make yourself a participant with them through united love; make yourself joined to them through the fellowship of charity and the bond of brotherhood. [Col. 0651A] Your debts will be forgiven when you yourself have forgiven; your sacrifices will be accepted when you come to God in peace. Your thoughts and deeds will be directed by God when you have thought upon what is divine and just, as it is written: “Let the heart of a man think just things, so that his steps may be directed by the Lord” (Prov. 16:9).

[Note: [Col. 0651B]

XVIII.—Cain does not enter. I consider this reading, which three old books have, the best; the other, which has “does not return,” is false. For Cain, who [Col. 0652B] was born after his parents had been expelled from paradise, cannot be said not to have returned to paradise, since he had never been in it. I therefore did not doubt that the reading of these three books should be preferred.

His grace. Thus many old books. Others have “of his grace and indulgence.”]

XVIII. You have many things upon which to reflect. Think of paradise, which Cain, who killed his brother through jealousy, does not enter (Gen. 4). Think of the heavenly kingdom, to which the Lord admits only those who are harmonious and of one mind [Note: [Col. 0651A] “Only those of one mind” Lin.]. [Col. 0652A] Think that only those can be called sons of God who are peaceable, who, united through heavenly birth and divine law [Note: [Col. 0651A] “Through birth and law” Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Voss. 1, 2. [Col. 0652A] Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], correspond to the likeness of God the Father and of Christ. Think that we stand beneath the eyes of God and run the courses of our conduct and life while he himself watches and judges; that only then can it befall us to see him, if now we delight him, who sees us, by our deeds; if we show ourselves worthy of his grace and indulgence; if, in order to please him always in the kingdom, we first please him in this world.

[Col. 0651]

# EPISTLE TO FORTUNATUS ON EXHORTATION TO MARTYRDOM

[Note: [Col. 0651C] *On the Good of Martyrdom*. “Read in peace, dearest brother, and, comparing our times with these times, groan silently” NC. 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0651C]

Although there can be no doubt that this book is by Saint Cyprian, to whom it is ascribed in all the ancient manuscripts and editions, nevertheless an old error that crept into the ancient editions of Saint Jerome’s Epistles persuaded Mariano Vittori—as Baronius also observed—that it was by Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, [Col. 0651D] with an argument also being drawn from its style; yet others maintain that the style of this book’s author agrees with Cyprian’s style and does not agree with Hilary’s. The diligence of the most illustrious Dom Pierre Coustant and Dom Jean Martianay, monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, removed the corrupt reading that had crept into Jerome’s Epistles. They testify that the true and genuine reading found in the new edition of Saint Jerome’s works appears in every manuscript without exception. Latino Latini attempted to divine the source of this error, and I think he divined it correctly. For that most learned man conjectured that “to Fortunatus” had been written in the margin of some book, so that this annotation referred to the name of Cyprian, and that it was afterward rashly transferred into the text and placed in the wrong position. That it is by Cyprian is also proved, among other arguments, by the fact that [Col. 0652C] Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, as Sirmond observed in the margin, cites on p. 73 of his book *On Predestination*, as being from Cyprian, a certain passage from book II of Chronicles that appears in chapter eight of this Cyprianic work. As for Pearson’s contention in his *Cyprianic Annals* that the work is not by Cyprian but by [Col. 0652D] an author later than Cyprian, I cannot agree with him, since he offers no good reasons for asserting his opinion. Pamelius is also mistaken when he writes that the first edition of this book was owed to Rembolt. For, as the English editors correctly noted, it is found in the Speyer edition and in the old Venetian edition. (PREFACE. This title and the following one, CHAPTERS OF THE FOLLOWING BOOK, are taken from the Oxford edition, in which, however, nothing is found to indicate whence they were obtained. EDD.]

(C)

[Col. 0651]

# PREFACE

[Col. 0651C]

[Note: [Col. 0652D]

I.—Has already begun. Although I have not resolved to give an account of every change I have made in the works of Saint Cyprian, I nevertheless thought I ought to give one here, even though the matter is of little importance, lest anyone think that I substituted the word “already” for “now” out of a desire to contradict. I did so because all the old books and all the old editions present this reading.

]

I. YOU REQUESTED, dearest Fortunatus, that, since the weight of persecutions and afflictions presses upon us and the hostile time of Antichrist at the end and consummation [Note: [Col. 0652C] “Toward the end and consummation” Bod. 1, 4.] of the world has already begun to approach, I should compose exhortations from the divine Scriptures to prepare [Note: [Col. 0652C] “To prepare the brothers’” Voss. 1.] and strengthen the minds of the brothers, by which I might animate [Col. 0652C] Christ’s soldiers for the heavenly and spiritual contest. A request so necessary had to be obeyed, so that, insofar as our modest ability, instructed by the aid of divine inspiration, suffices, certain weapons and fortifications might be brought forth from the Lord’s commands for our brothers who are about to fight. For it is too little that we rouse God’s people [Col. 0653A] with the trumpet blast of our voice unless we also strengthen, by divine reading, the faith of believers and the courage consecrated and devoted to God.

[Note: [Col. 0653D]

II.—An unprepared soldier. Petronius: “As a soldier, I did not have my weapons ready.”

Adhering to Christ. This reading is consistent in all the ancient editions and in all the old books, both ours and the English manuscripts. I therefore wonder that the English editors retained Pamelius’s reading, [Col. 0654D] which is not good, contrary to the evidence of the old books and editions.]

II. What, moreover, is more fitting or important to our care and concern than that through continual exhortations we should prepare [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Than to prepare the people, etc., committed to us” Ebor. Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Voss. 1, 2.] the people and army divinely entrusted 262 to us and stationed in the heavenly camp against the devil’s weapons and missiles? For one who has not first been trained on the field cannot be a soldier fit for war; nor will anyone [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Or who” Bod. 1.] seeking to obtain the victor’s crown be crowned in the stadium unless he first practices the use and skilled application of his strength. The adversary with whom we wage battle [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Wage war” Lin. “War is waged” Bod. 1.] is old, and the enemy ancient: nearly six thousand years have now been completed since the devil began to assail mankind. Through the experience of antiquity itself he has thoroughly learned every kind of temptation and every art and stratagem of [Col. 0653B] overthrowing. If he finds Christ’s soldier unprepared, untrained, unconcerned [Note: [Col. 0653D] “If with one unconcerned” Ar. Lam. Ebor. Ver. Voss. 3.], and not vigilant with his whole heart, he circumvents the ignorant, ensnares the unwary, and deceives the inexperienced [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Deceives the unprepared” Lam. NC. 1. Ebor. MR.]. But if anyone keeps the Lord’s commands, adheres courageously to Christ [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Adheres to Christ’s footsteps” Oxon.], and stands against him, the devil must be defeated, because Christ, whom that person confesses, is unconquered.

III. And so that I might not extend my discourse at length, dearest brother, and weary the hearer or reader with an abundance of prolix writing, I have made an abridgment. After setting forth headings that everyone [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Everyone who” Bod. 1, 3.] ought both to know and retain, I would attach passages from the Lord and substantiate my proposition by the authority of the divine reading, so that I may seem not so much to have sent you a treatise of my own as to have provided material for those composing treatises. This method [Col. 0653C] benefits individuals in practical use with greater utility. For if I were to give a garment already made and prepared [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Were to send a garment” Ver.], the garment used by another would be mine, and perhaps, since something made for one person might be less suitable for another’s physical build [Note: [Col. 0653D] “Physical bearing” Voss. 1, 3.] and body, it would be regarded as ill-fitting. But now I have sent the wool itself and the purple dye from the Lamb through whom we have been redeemed and made alive. When you receive them, you will make yourself a tunic according to your own wishes; you will take greater delight in it as your own domestic and personal garment [Note: [Col. 0654D] “And in your own garment” Bod. 3, 4.]; and you will also provide what we have sent to others, so that they too may make one according to their own judgment. Thus, when that old nakedness has been covered, all may bear the garments of Christ, clothed by the sanctification of heavenly grace.

[Note: [Col. 0654D]

IV. A greater Baptism, that is, the Baptism of blood, which is explained a little below.

Elements. Five old books and the English edition add “in place of gods.” This is also found shortly afterward at the beginning of the first chapter.]

IV. Furthermore, dearest brother, I have foreseen this [Col. 0654A] useful and salutary principle: in so necessary an exhortation, one that may make martyrs, the delays and hindrances of our own words must be cut away, the circumlocutions of human discourse removed, and only those things spoken by God set forth, by which Christ exhorts his servants to martyrdom. The divine precepts themselves must be supplied as weapons to those who are fighting. Let them be the exhortations of the military trumpet; let them be the trumpet calls for those in battle. From them let ears be raised; by them let minds be instructed; from them let the strength both of mind and body be fortified to endure every suffering. Let us, who with the Lord’s permission have given the first Baptism to believers, merely prepare each individual for the other one as well, impressing upon them and teaching [Note: [Col. 0654D] “Prepare and instruct” Ver.] that this Baptism is greater in grace, more sublime in power, and more precious in honor: a Baptism in which angels baptize; a Baptism [Col. 0654B] [Note: [Col. 0654D] “The Baptism of suffering, in which God and his Christ rejoice” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Ar. Ben. Bod. 1.] in which God and his Christ rejoice; a Baptism after which no one sins any longer; a Baptism that perfects the growth of our faith; a Baptism that, as we depart from the world, immediately unites us with God. In the Baptism of water the forgiveness of sins is received; in the Baptism of blood, the crown of virtues. It is something to be embraced and desired, and to be sought with all the prayers of our petitions, so that we who are servants of God [Note: [Col. 0654D] “Were servants of God” Ver. Ben. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. MR.] may also be his friends.

# CHAPTERS OF THE FOLLOWING BOOK

I. Accordingly, in exhorting and preparing [Note: [Col. 0654D] “Preparing” Ver. “Repairing” Voss. 3.] our brothers and arming them with firmness of courage and faith for the glory of confessing the Lord and for the battle of persecution and suffering [Note: [Col. 0654D] “Arming them for persecution” Ar. NC. 1. Lam. Ebor.], it must first be said [Col. 0654C] that the idols that a person makes for himself are not gods. For things that are made are not greater than their maker and craftsman; 263 nor can things protect and preserve anyone when they themselves perish from their temples unless preserved by a human being. Nor, moreover, are the elements to be worshiped, for they serve mankind in accordance with God’s arrangement and command [Note: [Col. 0654D] “Serve him” Ar.].

II. When the idols have been destroyed and the nature of the elements demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0654D] “When the elements have been cast down” A. Ben.], it must be shown that God alone is to be worshiped.

III. It must then be added what threat God makes against those who sacrifice to idols [Note: [Col. 0654D] “Serve idols” Voss. 3.].

IV. Furthermore, it must be taught that God does not readily pardon idolaters.

[Col. 0655A] V. And that God is so indignant at idolatry that he commanded even those who had urged others to sacrifice to and serve idols to be put to death.

VI. After this it must be added that, having been redeemed and made alive by Christ’s blood, we ought to prefer nothing to Christ, because he too preferred nothing to us, and for our sake he preferred evils to good things: poverty to riches, servitude to dominion, and death to immortality. We, on the contrary, in our sufferings, should prefer the riches and delights of paradise to worldly poverty [Note: [Col. 0655C] “Set before” Ver.], eternal dominion and kingship to temporary servitude, immortality to death, and God and Christ to the devil and Antichrist.

VII. It must also be impressed upon them that, once rescued from the devil’s jaws and freed from the snares of the world, if they begin to experience straits [Col. 0655B] and afflictions [Note: [Col. 0655C] “Freed, if they begin to experience straits and afflictions” Bod. 3, 4.], they should not wish to return to the world again and forfeit their escape.

VIII. Rather, one must remain steadfast and persevere in faith and courage [Note: [Col. 0655C] “Faith and truth” Vat.] and in the perfection of heavenly and spiritual grace, so that the palm and crown may be attained.

[Col. 0656A] IX. For afflictions and persecutions occur for this purpose: that we may be tested.

[Note: [Col. 0655D]

X.—The injuries and punishments. The Grenoble manuscript reads: “the injuries and battles.” The manuscript of Saint-Arnoul likewise reads thus.

]

X. Nor should the injuries and punishments of persecutions be feared, because the Lord is greater in his power to protect than the devil in his power to assail.

XI. And lest anyone be frightened and troubled by the afflictions and persecutions that we suffer in this world, it must be shown that it was foretold beforehand [Note: [Col. 0655C] “Already proved and foretold,” Bod. 4.] that the world would hate us and would stir up persecutions against us, so that, from the very fact that these things occur, the trustworthiness of the divine promise concerning the recompenses and rewards that will follow afterward may be manifest; and so that nothing new may befall Christians, since from the beginning of the world the good have labored and have been oppressed and killed by the unjust. [Note: [Col. 0655C] “And from this,” Voss. 3.]

[Col. 0656B] XII. In the final section it must be set forth what hope and what reward await the righteous and the martyrs after the struggles and sufferings of this present time, and that we shall receive more as recompense for suffering than what we endure here in the suffering itself.

## ON EXHORTATION TO MARTYRDOM

[Note: [Col. 0655D]

**CHAP. I.—That idols.** The English editors erred greatly in this passage and at the beginnings of all the chapters of this book and of those addressed to Quirinus. For they placed in the margin the chapter headings whose proofs Cyprian afterward supplies from Scripture. But who could divine that these were Cyprian’s, since they customarily place in the margin summaries of the matters contained in the text, while those summaries are their own, not Cyprian’s or those of the ancient copyists? Add to this that, as it seems to me, they gave this book an inept beginning by starting with the word “It is shown.” One could readily ask what the word “It is shown” signifies here, since it ought to refer to something preceding. We have restored the chapter summaries [Col. 0656D] to the text, as was proper, judging that this novelty should be rejected and the ancient practice retained. For these summaries are more properly theses, in proof of which Cyprian adduces the following testimonies from Holy Scripture. Therefore, in certain ancient books these summaries are written in larger characters.

**Or the moon.** Pamelius added “the rulers of the terrestrial globe” on the authority of two ancient books, and because it is so read in chapter XIII of the Book of Wisdom and in Cyprian himself, Book III of the *Testimonies*, chap. 29, where the same passage is quoted. But because I found those words in none of the ancient copies that I use, and because they are absent from all editions earlier than that of Pamelius, I removed them from this passage.]

## CHAPTER I.—THAT IDOLS ARE NOT GODS, AND THAT THE ELEMENTS ARE NOT TO BE WORSHIPED IN PLACE OF GODS

It is shown in Psalm 113:

> The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works [Note: [Col. 0655D] “work,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Ver.] of human hands. They have mouths [Col. 0655C] and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear [Note: [Col. 0656C] “They hear; they have nostrils and will not smell; they have hands and will not touch; they will not cry out with their throat,” Lin.]. For there is no breath in their mouths. May those who make them become like them [Note: [Col. 0656C] “May they be like them,” Ben. Ver. Lam. Ebor.; “they are,” Voss. 2.] [Note: [Col. 0656C] “who make them, and all who trust in them,” Bod. 3.].

Likewise in the Wisdom of Solomon:

> They regarded all the idols of the nations as gods, though these have neither the use of eyes for seeing, nor nostrils for drawing breath [Note: [Col. 0656C] “receiving breath,” Bod. 4.], nor ears for hearing, nor fingers on their hands for handling; and even their feet are sluggish for walking. For a human being made them, and one who had borrowed breath fashioned [Col. 0656B] them [Note: [Col. 0656C] “he fashioned them,” Voss.]. But no human being will be able to fashion a god like himself: for, being mortal, he fashions a dead thing with unrighteous hands. Yet he himself is better than those whom he worships, since he indeed has lived, but they never have. (Wis. 15:15–17)

Likewise in Exodus:

> You shall not make for yourself an idol or the likeness [Col. 0656C] of anything. (Exod. 20:4)

Likewise in Solomon concerning the elements:

> Nor, by attending to the works, did they recognize who the craftsman was; instead, they considered either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circuit of the stars, or the mighty water, or the sun, or the moon to be gods. If they judged this because of their beauty, let them know how much more beautiful than these [p. 264] the Lord is. Or if they marveled at their powers and works, let them understand from these that he who established these mighty things is mightier than they. (Wis. 13:1–4) [Note: [Col. 0656D] “He who established these things is mightier than they,” Bod. 4, 2, 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0657D]

**CHAP. II.—That God alone.** There are three beginnings to this chapter in the ancient copies. Some have: “That God alone exists. In Exodus: There shall not be.” Others have: “That God alone is to be worshiped. In Exodus: The Lord your God.” Still others have: “That God is to be worshiped, as it is written: You shall worship your God.” I have adopted this last reading because it rests upon the authority of the ancient copies. To be sure, if account were to be taken of the passages of Holy Scripture quoted here, there would be no doubt that the correction of the later editors should have been retained. For sometimes the ancient [Col. 0658D] writers, through a lapse of memory, cite passages of Holy Scripture as coming from places other than those where they are actually found; nor is it permissible to correct them without the authority of ancient books, as we shall show by examples in the notes on the anonymous book *On Rebaptism*. It therefore seemed safer to retain the reading of the manuscripts.

**Fear rather.** Thus the Speyer edition. Most codices have “fear.” In four it is written: “Hear rather the Lord.” In the Bec manuscript: “See.”]

## CHAPTER II.—THAT GOD ALONE IS TO BE WORSHIPED

[Col. 0657A]

As it is written [Note: [Col. 0657C] “It is written in Deuteronomy,” Oxon. Lam. Ebor. Lin. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.]:

> You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve. (Deut. 6:13)

Likewise in Exodus:

> You shall have no other gods besides me. (Exod. 6:13)

Likewise there [Note: [Col. 0657C] “Likewise in Deuteronomy,” Oxon. Voss. Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Very well.]:

> See, see that I am [Note: [Col. 0657C] “I am the Lord,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.], and there is no God besides me. I shall put to death [Note: [Col. 0657D] “I shall kill,” Bod. 1, 3, 4.] and make alive; I shall strike and I shall heal; and there is no one who can snatch from my hands [Note: [Col. 0657D] “who can rescue from my hand,” Voss. 1, 3.]. (Deut. 32:39)

Likewise in Revelation:

> And I saw another angel flying in midheaven, having the eternal Gospel, that he might proclaim it over the earth and over all nations [Note: [Col. 0657D] “through all nations,” Ben. Ver.], tribes, languages, and peoples, saying with a loud voice: “Fear God rather [Note: [Col. 0657D] “Serve the Lord rather,” Voss. 1. Bod. 3. Voss. 3.], and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all that is in them.” (Rev. 14:6–7)

Thus also the Lord in the Gospel recalls [Col. 0657B] the first and second commandments, saying:

> Hear, Israel. The Lord your God is one God;

and:

> You shall love your Lord with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. This is the first; and the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0657D] “your neighbor as yourself,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] as yourself. On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets. (Matt. 22:39–40)

And again:

> Now this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only and true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. (John 17:3)

## CHAPTER III.—WHAT GOD’S THREAT IS AGAINST THOSE WHO SACRIFICE TO IDOLS

In Exodus [Note: [Col. 0658C] Thus Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ar. Lam. Ebor. Lin.; “It is read,” in Imp. Voss. 3.]:

> He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless it is to the Lord alone. (Exod. 22:19)

Likewise in Deuteronomy:

> They sacrificed to demons and not to God. (Deut. 32:17)

[Col. 0657C] Likewise in Isaiah:

> They worshiped those whom their fingers had made; and the human being bowed down, and the man was humbled, and I shall not pardon them [Note: [Col. 0658C] “I shall pardon them, says the Lord,” Ar. NC. 1. Lam. Ebor. Bod.]. (Isa. 2:8)

And again:

> To them you poured out drink offerings, and upon them you placed sacrifices. Shall I not therefore be indignant over these things? says the Lord. (Isa. 57:6)

Likewise in Jeremiah:

> Do not walk after foreign gods so as to serve them; do not worship them, and do not provoke me by the works of your hands, so that I destroy [Note: [Col. 0658C] “scatter,” Voss. 3.] you. (Jer. 25:6)

Likewise in Revelation:

> If anyone worships [Note: [Col. 0658C] “shall worship,” Bod. 1, 3, 4.] the beast and its image, and receives [Note: [Col. 0658D] “has received,” Bod. 1.] the mark [Col. 0658A] on his forehead or on his hand, he too shall drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed in the cup of his wrath, and shall be punished with fire and sulfur before the eyes of the holy angels and before the eyes of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torments shall ascend forever and ever. Nor shall they have rest by day or night, all those who worship the beast and its image. (Rev. 15:9–11)

[Note: [Col. 0658D]

**CHAP. IV.—Golden gods.** Five ancient books add “and silver.” See the notes on the book *On the Lapsed*.]

## CHAPTER IV.—THAT GOD DOES NOT READILY PARDON IDOLATERS

Moses pleads in Exodus for the people but does not obtain his request:

> I beseech you, Lord, he says, this people has committed a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold [Note: [Col. 0658D] “of gold and silver,” Ar. Bod. 2.]. And now, if you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from the book that you have written.

And the Lord said to Moses:

> Whoever has sinned before me, I shall erase him from my book. (Exod. 32:31–33)

Likewise, when Jeremiah interceded for the people, the Lord spoke to him, saying:

> And you, [Col. 0658B] do not pray for this people, and do not make supplication for them in prayer and petition, because I shall not hear them at the time when they call upon me, at the time of their affliction. (Jer. 11:14)

Ezekiel too announces this same indignation of God against those who sin against God [Note: [Col. 0658D] “abandon the Lord,” Voss. 3.]:

> And the word of the Lord came to me, he says, saying: “Son of man, if any land sins against me by committing a trespass, I shall stretch out my hand over it and crush the support of bread [Note: [Col. 0658D] “of its bread,” Bod. 3.]; I shall send famine upon it and remove from it human beings and cattle. And if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in its midst, they would deliver neither sons nor daughters; they alone would be saved.” (Ezek. 14:12, 14, 16)

Likewise in the First Book of Kingdoms:

> If a man sins by transgressing against a man, they shall pray to the Lord for him. But if a human being sins against God, who shall pray for [Col. 0658C] him? (1 Kings 2:25)

[Note: [Col. 0659D]

**CHAP. V.—If you hear in one.** This passage is quoted by Gratian, XXIII, q. 5, *Si audieris*. There the gloss says that Cyprian was asked whether the wicked, after the Lord’s coming into this world, should be punished with death, and that he answered in the affirmative, because if this was done before Christ’s coming, as is proved by the authority of Deuteronomy and the example of Malachi, it should be done much more after Christ’s coming. John of Torquemada inferred from this that the wicked who corrupt the multitude should not be spared. The author of the gloss did not consult Cyprian, and therefore erred concerning the facts.

**Shall preserve it.** Two ancient books have “shall save it”; another, “shall keep it”; and yet another, “may find.”]

## CHAPTER V.—265 THAT GOD IS SO INDIGNANT AT IDOLATRY THAT HE COMMANDED EVEN THOSE WHO URGED OTHERS TO SACRIFICE TO AND SERVE IDOLS TO BE KILLED

In Deuteronomy:

> But if your brother, or your son, or your daughter, or your wife who is in your bosom, or your friend who is as dear as your own soul, secretly entreats you, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods [Note: [Col. 0658D] “foreign gods,” Ar. Lam. Ebor.], the gods of the nations,” you shall not consent to him and shall not listen to him; [Col. 0659A] your eye shall not spare him, and you shall not conceal him, but you shall assuredly denounce him. Your hand shall be upon him first to kill him, and afterward the hand of all the people; and they shall stone him, and he shall die, because he sought to turn you away from the Lord your God. (Deut. 13:6)

And again the Lord speaks and says that not even a city is to be spared if it has unanimously consented to idolatry:

> Or if you hear in one of the cities that the Lord your God will give you to inhabit, people saying, “Let us go and serve other gods,” whom you have not known [Note: [Col. 0659C] Oxon. adds: “You shall inquire diligently, and if you find that what is said is certain.”], you shall utterly kill all who are in the city with the slaughter of the sword, and you shall burn the city with fire, and it shall remain without habitation forever. It shall not be rebuilt even now, so that the Lord may turn away from the indignation of his wrath. And he shall grant you mercy and have mercy upon you, and multiply you, if you obey the voice of the Lord your God and keep [Col. 0659B] his commandments. (Deut. 13:12)

Mindful of this commandment and its force, Mattathias killed the man who had approached the altar to sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0659C] “had ascended,” Bod. 1.] (1 Macc. 2:24).

But if these commands concerning the worship of God and the rejection of idols [Note: [Col. 0659C] “the casting down of idols,” Bod. 1.] were observed before the coming of Christ, how much more must they be observed after the coming of Christ, since, when he came, he exhorted us not only by words but also by deeds, having suffered and been crucified after every injury and insult, so that by his example he might teach us to suffer and die. Thus no human being has any excuse for not suffering on his own behalf, since Christ suffered for us; and since he suffered for the sins of others, much more ought each person to suffer for his own sins.

Therefore he threatens in the Gospel and says:

> Whoever confesses [Col. 0659C] me before human beings, I too shall confess him [Note: [Col. 0659C] “I shall confess in him,” Ar. Voss. 1.] before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before human beings, I too shall deny him before my Father who is in heaven. (Matt. 10:33)

Likewise the apostle Paul:

> For if we die together, he says, we shall also live together; if we endure, we shall also reign together; if we deny, he too shall deny us. (2 Tim. 2:12)

Likewise John:

> He who denies the Son does not have the Father either; he who confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father. (1 John 2:23)

Accordingly, the Lord exhorts us to contempt of death and strengthens us, saying:

> Do not fear those who kill the body but [Col. 0660A] [Note: [Col. 0659C] “and the soul,” Bod. 2.] cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can kill the soul and the body [Note: [Col. 0659C] “destroy the body,” Ar. Lam. Bod. 2.] in Gehenna. (Matt. 10:28)

And again:

> He who loves his soul shall lose it; and he who hates his soul in this world shall preserve it unto eternal life. (John 12:25)

[Note: [Col. 0660D]

**CHAP. VI.—We are killed.** The Morel edition and certain ancient books have “we are put to death,” and immediately afterward “of killing.”

**Is not worthy of me.** The Séguier codex has: “is not my disciple.”

**We overcome.** The Verona codex has: “we more than conquer.” See [Col. 0661D] the notes on Epistle XXVI, p. 412, where the same word occurs.]

## CHAPTER VI.—THAT, HAVING BEEN REDEEMED AND GIVEN LIFE BY THE BLOOD OF CHRIST, WE OUGHT TO PREFER NOTHING TO CHRIST

In the Gospel the Lord speaks and says:

> He who loves father or mother above me [Note: [Col. 0659D] “mother more than me,” Lin. Ebor. NC. 1.] is not worthy of me. And he who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me [Note: [Col. 0659D] “And he who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Absent from Imp.]. And he who does not take up his cross [Note: [Col. 0659D] “takes up his cross,” Bod. 4.] and follow me is not worthy of me [Note: [Col. 0660C] “is not my disciple,” Ar.]. (Matt. 10:37)

Thus also it is written in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 0660C] “is set down in Deuteronomy,” Bod. 3.]:

> Those who say to father and mother, “I do not know you,” and who did not acknowledge their sons—these have kept your commandments and observed your covenant [Note: [Col. 0660C] “and your commandment,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2.]. (Deut. [Col. 0660B] 33:9)

Likewise the apostle Paul:

> Who, he says, shall separate us from the love of Christ? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: “For your sake we are killed all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter” [Note: [Col. 0660C] “sheep for killing,” Ar. NC. 2. Bod. 2.]. But in all these things we overcome [Note: [Col. 0660C] “In all these things we more than conquer,” Ber.; “For him,” Lam. Ebor. Bod. 1, 2, 4.] because of him who loved us. (Rom. 8:35)

And again:

> You are not your own, for you were bought at a great price [Note: [Col. 0660C] “You were bought at a great price,” Ber. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 3.]. Glorify [Note: [Col. 0660D] “Make manifest,” Ver.] and bear God in your body. (1 Cor. 6:20)

And again:

> Christ died for all, 266 so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them. (2 Cor. 5:15)

[Note: [Col. 0661D]

**CHAP. VII.—In casting out.** The Fux codex has “in leading out,” and shortly afterward “wilderness” in place of “solitude.” Three other ancient books prefer this latter reading.]

## CHAPTER VII.—THAT THOSE RESCUED FROM THE JAWS OF THE DEVIL AND FREED FROM THE SNARES OF THE WORLD OUGHT NOT TO RETURN AGAIN TO THE WORLD, LEST THEY LOSE WHAT THEY HAVE ESCAPED

[Col. 0660C]

In Exodus the Jewish people, prefigured as a shadow and image of us, had—with God as protector and avenger—escaped the harshest servitude of Pharaoh and Egypt, that is, of the devil and the world. Yet, faithless and ungrateful toward God, the people murmured against Moses, looking back upon the hardships of solitude and toil and failing to understand the divine benefits of freedom and salvation. They sought to return to the servitude of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0660D] “Egypt,” Lin. Spir. Bod. 1, 2, 4.], that is, of the world, from which they had been delivered [Note: [Col. 0660D] “from which they had been exempted,” Bod. 3; “withdrawn,” Spir. Morel.], though they ought rather to have trusted in God [Note: [Col. 0660D] “to have faith in God,” Lin.] and believed that he who frees his people from the devil and the world [Col. 0661A] protects them after they have been freed:

> What is this, they say, that you have done to us by casting us out of Egypt? It is better [Note: [Col. 0661C] “It was better,” Bod. 3.] for us to serve the Egyptians than to die [Note: [Col. 0661C] “than to perish,” Ar. Bod. 2.] in this wilderness.

And Moses said to the people:

> Have confidence and stand firm [Note: [Col. 0661C] “Be silent and stand,” Bod. 1; “Stand confidently and see,” Spir.], and behold the salvation that comes from the Lord, which he shall bring about for you today. The Lord himself shall fight for you, and you shall remain silent. (Exod. 14:11)

Admonishing us of this in his Gospel, and teaching us not to return again to the devil and the world, which we renounced and from which we escaped, the Lord says:

> No one who looks backward and lays his hand upon the plow is fit for the kingdom of God. (Luke 9:62)

And again:

> Let him who is in the field not turn back [Note: [Col. 0661C] “to take up his garment,” Ar. Lam. Ebor. Bod. 2. NC. 1, 2. Ben.]. Remember Lot’s wife. (Luke 17:31)

And lest anyone be held back from following [Col. 0641B] Christ either by any desire for possessions or by affection for his family, he adds and says:

> He who does not renounce all that belongs to him [Note: [Col. 0661C] “all that he possesses,” Ar.] cannot be my disciple. (Luke 14:33)

[Note: [Col. 0661D]

**CHAP. VIII.—Happy servants.** Thus all the ancient editions before that of Pamelius. It is written in the same way in our books and in the English books.

[Col. 0662D] **That you may obtain it.** At this point the Manutius and Commelinus editions subsequently contain this passage: “For everyone who competes exercises self-control.” But since it is absent from the Séguier codex, the ancient editions, and all the ancient books except two, having been added by Manutius, omitted by Morel, and then restored by Pamelius, we have deleted it. See the notes on Epistle VIII, p. 395.

**Joshua put to flight.** The Séguier codex has: “Moses put to flight.”]

## CHAPTER VIII.—THAT WE MUST PRESS ON AND PERSEVERE IN FAITH AND VIRTUE, AND IN THE PERFECTION OF HEAVENLY AND SPIRITUAL GRACE, SO THAT WE MAY ATTAIN THE PALM AND THE CROWN

In Chronicles:

> The Lord is with you as long as you [Note: [Col. 0661C] “as long as you,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] are with him. But if you abandon him, he shall abandon you. (2 Chron. 15:2)

Likewise in Ezekiel:

> The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he goes astray [Note: [Col. 0661D] Voss. 1 adds: “And the wickedness of the wicked shall not afflict him on whatever day he turns back from his wickedness.”]. (Ezek. 33:12)

Likewise in the Gospel the Lord speaks and says:

> He who perseveres to the end [Note: [Col. 0661D] “until the end,” Lin.] shall be saved [Note: [Col. 0661D] “will be saved,” Bod. 4.]. (Matt. 10:22)

And again:

> If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, [Col. 0661C] and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall free you. (John 8:31)

Forewarning us also that we must always be prepared and stand firmly equipped for action, he adds and says:

> Let your loins be girded [Note: [Col. 0661D] “your loins belted,” Voss. 4.] and your lamps burning; and be like people awaiting their master when he returns [Note: [Col. 0661D] “when he comes,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 4. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him. Blessed [Note: [Col. 0661D] “Happy,” Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4.] are those servants whom the master, when he comes, finds watching. (Luke 12:35)

Likewise the blessed [Col. 0662A] apostle Paul, so that our faith may advance, grow, and attain the highest things, exhorts us, saying:

> Do you not know that those who run in the race [Note: [Col. 0661D] “that those who run in the stadium,” Bod. 1.] all indeed run, but one [Note: [Col. 0661D] “yet one,” Bod. 1, 3.] receives the palm? Run in such a way that you may obtain it [Note: [Col. 0661D] “that you may grasp it,” Bod.; Oxon. adds: “For everyone who [Col. 0662C] competes exercises self-control in all things.”]. They indeed do so to receive a corruptible crown, but you an incorruptible one. (1 Cor. 9:24)

And again:

> No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly troubles, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. And if anyone competes, he shall not be crowned unless he has fought according to the rules. (2 Tim. 2:4)

And again:

> I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; and do not be conformed [Note: [Col. 0662C] “a living sacrifice,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; “your rational ministry,” Lin. Voss. 1; “your rational service; and do not be conformed,” Bod. 4.] to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of the spirit [Note: [Col. 0662C] “renewal of the mind,” Bod. 3.], that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God. (Rom. 11:1)

And again:

> [Col. 0662B] We are children of God; but if [Note: [Col. 0662C] “We are children; but if,” Bod. 1.] children, then also heirs—heirs indeed of God and coheirs with Christ—provided that we suffer with him, so that we may also be magnified together with him [Note: [Col. 0662C] “be glorified together,” Bod. 3.]. (Rom. 8:17)

And in Revelation the same exhortation of divine proclamation speaks, saying:

> Hold fast [Note: [Col. 0662D] “Hold fast, he says,” Bod. 1, 4.] what you have, lest another receive your crown. (Rev. 3:11)

This example 267 of persevering and remaining steadfast is signified in Exodus, where Moses, in order to overcome Amalek, who bore the figure of the devil, raised his upturned hands in the sign and sacrament of the cross [Note: [Col. 0662D] “in the sign of the cross,” Bod. 1.]. He could not conquer the adversary unless he persevered steadfastly in that sign, with his hands continually raised:

> And it came to pass, he says, that when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered his hands, Amalek grew stronger. And taking [Note: [Col. 0662D] “Amalek grew stronger. But Moses’ hands were heavy, and taking,” Ver.; similarly Book 2 *To Quirinus*, chap. XXI.] a stone, they placed it beneath him, and he sat upon [Col. 0662C] it. And Aaron and Hur supported [Note: [Col. 0662D] “Hur supported,” Voss. NC. 2.] his hands on either side, and Moses’ hands remained steady until sunset. And Joshua put Amalek and all his people to flight [Note: [Col. 0662D] “his people by the edge of the sword,” Ver.]. And the Lord said to Moses: “Write this in a book as a memorial [Note: [Col. 0662D] “as a memorial,” Ar. Bod. 3.], and deliver it to the ears of Joshua: because by an utter blotting out I shall blot out [Note: [Col. 0662D] “I shall blot out,” Bod. 4.] the memory of Amalek from beneath heaven.” (Exod. 17:11)

[Note: [Col. 0662D] “Forever,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]

## CHAPTER IX.—THAT AFFLICTIONS AND PERSECUTIONS OCCUR FOR THIS PURPOSE: THAT WE MAY BE TESTED

[Col. 0663A]

In Deuteronomy:

> The Lord your God tests you, that he may know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. (Deut. 13:3)

And again in Solomon:

> The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous human beings. (Ecclus. 2:5)

Paul too testifies to the same things and speaks, saying:

> We glory in the hope of the glory of God; and not only this, but we also glory in afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance, endurance proof, and proof hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured [Note: [Col. 0663C] Thus Manut. Pam. Rig. Voss. 1, 2. Lin. and Book 3 *To Quirinus*, chap. 6. “Diffused,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 2. Spir. Vet. innom. Eras. Morel. Grav.] into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. (Rom. 5:3)

And Peter sets forth and says in his Epistle:

> Dearest brethren, do not be astonished at the burning trial that comes upon you and occurs for your testing; nor lose heart, as though something new were happening to you. But whenever you share in Christ’s sufferings, rejoice in every way, so that, when the revelation of his glory takes place, you may rejoice and exult [Note: [Col. 0663C] “rejoice and exult,” Bod. 4.]. If you are reproached in the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 0663C] “in the name of Jesus,” Bod. 4.], you are blessed, because the name of the Lord’s majesty and power rests upon you. According to them [Note: [Col. 0663C] “by them,” Spir.] it is indeed blasphemed, but according to us it is honored. (1 Pet. 4:12)

[Note: [Col. 0663D]

**CHAP. X.—That they are not to be feared.** We have restored in this passage two clauses of this sentence that the Manutius edition had omitted but Morel had restored. Since they occur in all the ancient editions, we judged that they should be restored, for the ancient books do not contradict them.

**Because the Lord is greater.** Rufinus, Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 34: “Far greater is he who defends us than he who persecutes us.” The same author on Psalm 62: “The devil is the strong armed man who possessed this world. But Christ, coming as one stronger than he, defeated him.”

**They themselves are bound.** This is the reading of the ancient editions. The author of the book *On the Promises* [Col. 0664D] *and Predictions of God*, among the works of Prosper, also read it in this way. The English editors passed over that reading and printed: “Their feet were bound.” This reading is found in eighteen of our copies, including the Séguier codex, and in the Morel edition, as well as in that called Gravius’s. Nonius Marcellus: “*Copulantur* in place of *copulant*.” And a little later: “*Copulantur* in place of *conjungunt*.”

**By that encounter.** The Séguier codex has: “that encounter of the righteous.”

**Mogilalum.** Nearly all the ancient books that I have used—and above all the Séguier codex—indicate that this is the correct reading. The Manutius edition and the Fux codex prefer *mollegium*. But Latinus Latinius read *mogilalum* in his copies and judged it to be the true reading; the other reading, which has “mute,” he considered to have been substituted through the recklessness of copyists, who altered many things in Cyprian, especially in passages quoted from Holy Scripture, in which every bold and unskilled copyist thought himself at liberty to reduce everything to conformity with the Vulgate edition without penalty. This was also observed somewhere by Francisco Torres. In Mark 9 the Greek reads μογιλάλον (*mogilalon*, “speech-impaired”). See Du Cange’s Greek glossary, p. 941, under the word Μόγγος (*mongos*).]

## CHAPTER X.—THAT THE INJURIES AND PUNISHMENTS OF PERSECUTIONS ARE NOT TO BE FEARED, BECAUSE THE LORD IS GREATER IN PROTECTING THAN THE DEVIL IS IN ATTACKING

John proves this in his Epistle, saying [Note: [Col. 0663C] “sets forth and says,” Spir.]:

> Greater is he who is in you than he who is in this world. (1 John 4:4)

[Col. 0663C] Likewise in Psalm 117:

> I shall not fear what a human being may do to me; the Lord is my helper. (v. 6)

And again:

> Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall be magnified in the name of the Lord our God [Note: [Col. 0663D] “shall call upon,” Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Ben. Ver.; “shall be magnified,” Spir.]. They themselves are bound [Note: [Col. 0663D] “Their feet were bound,” Ar. NC. 1, 2. Lam. Ebor. Voss. 1. Lin. Bod. 1, 2. Ben. Ver. Ox.; “They themselves are bound and,” Imp.] and have fallen; but we have risen and stand upright. (Ps. 19:8)

And the Holy Spirit, teaching still more powerfully and showing that the devil’s camps are not to be feared, and that if the enemy declares war upon us, it is precisely in that war [Col. 0664A] that our hope is rather to be placed, and that through that encounter the righteous attain the reward of the divine throne and eternal salvation, sets forth and says in Psalm 26:

> If camps are arrayed against me, my heart shall not fear; and if war rises against me, in that shall I place my hope [Note: [Col. 0664C] “in it shall I place my hope,” Voss. 1.]. One thing [Note: [Col. 0664C] “One thing I have asked,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. Bod. 1, 4.] I have asked of the Lord; this shall I seek [Note: [Col. 0664C] “This shall I seek,” Bod. 1, 4. Lam. Ebor.]: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.

Likewise in Exodus Divine Scripture declares that through afflictions we are instead multiplied and increased, saying:

> The more they oppressed them, the more numerous they became and the more they grew strong. (Exod. 1:12)

And in Revelation divine protection is promised amid our sufferings:

> Fear none, he says, of the things that you are about to suffer. (Rev. 2:10)

Nor is it anyone other than he who also speaks through the prophet Isaiah who promises us safety and protection, saying:

> Do not fear, because I have redeemed you and called [Col. 0664B] you by your name; you are mine. And if you pass through water, I am with you, and rivers shall not overwhelm you; and if you pass through fire [Note: [Col. 0664C] Thus Ver. Vat. Lam. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Voss. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3; “fire, the flame,” Imp.], you shall not be burned and the flame shall not consume you, because I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who saves you. (Isa. 63:11)

He also promises in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0664C] “Indeed also in the Gospel,” Prior.] that divine aid 268 will not fail God’s servants during persecutions, saying:

> But when they hand you over, do not consider how or what you are to say; for in that hour what you are to say shall be given to you. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in you. (Matt. 10:10)

And again:

> Settle it in your hearts not to prepare your defense beforehand, for I shall give you a mouth and wisdom [Note: [Col. 0664C] “a mouth of wisdom,” Bod. 4.] that your adversaries shall not be able to resist. (Luke 12:11)

Thus in Exodus God speaks [Col. 0664C] to Moses when he hesitates and trembles at going to the people, saying:

> Who gave a mouth to a human being? And who made the *mogilalon*—the speech-impaired person? And who made the deaf [Note: [Col. 0664D] Thus Ver. Benev. Ar. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1, 2. Lam. Bod. 1, 4; “mute,” Imp.; “mute and speaking, hearing and deaf,” Bod. 3.]? And who made the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God? Now therefore go, and I shall open your mouth and instruct you what to say. (Exod. 4:11)

Nor is it difficult for God to open the mouth of a person devoted to him and to inspire his confessor with steadfastness and confidence in speaking, since in Numbers he even caused an ass to speak against the prophet Balaam (Num. 22:30).

Therefore, in [Col. 0665A] persecutions let no one consider what danger the devil brings, but rather what aid God provides. Let human hostility not unsettle the mind, but divine protection strengthen faith, since each person, according to the Lord’s promises [Note: [Col. 0665C] “the Lord’s commandments and promises,” Ar. Bod. 4.] and the merits of his faith, receives as much of God’s help as he believes himself able to receive; nor is there anything that the Almighty cannot provide, unless the failing [Note: [Col. 0665C] “catholic faith,” Ar.] faith of the recipient has given way.

[Note: [Col. 0665D]

**CHAP. XI.—Be mindful.** The Fux codex has: “Remember.”

**Wars and reports.** Two ancient books have: “wars and rumors of wars.” So too in one Bodleian manuscript. See Erasmus’s *Annotations* on this passage of Matthew.

**But in the world, affliction.** Only these words occur in the manuscript codices, including the Séguier codex. Pamelius added “you shall have” from the Afflighem codex, and because it is also so read in the book *On Patience* and in John, both in Greek [Col. 0666D] and Latin. Yet the word “you shall have” is absent from the book *On Patience* in certain ancient books, including the Séguier codex. The ancient editions nevertheless have it. I am surprised that Pamelius did not observe this.

**Of devastation.** Four books and one Bodleian manuscript have “of desolation.” So too in Daniel 9 and in chapter 13 of the Gospel according to John.

**Nursing.** The Pithou codex has *nutricantibus* (“those nursing”).

**All flesh be saved.** Twelve of our books and six English books have: “all flesh might be delivered.”

**This is the Christ.** See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of Matthew.

**Wonders.** I do not know whether this reading should be preferred to that favored by fifteen ancient copies, in which “portents” is written. 2 Esdras 9: “And you gave signs and portents against Pharaoh.” The anonymous book *On Rebaptism*, p. 372: “They shall give great signs and portents.”

**Corpse.** Although the word “body,” which the ancient editions have, fits this passage very well, I am nevertheless compelled to yield [Col. 0667D] to the authority of eighteen of our books and five English books, in which “corpse” is written. And immediately afterward several ancient books have “shall be gathered together” in place of “shall be collected.” See Erasmus on this passage of Matthew.]

Will be darkened. Ten ancient manuscripts have “will darken” or “will be darkened.” See Fronton du Duc’s notes on Chrysostom’s *Homily to the People of Antioch*.

With a great trumpet. Sixteen ancient manuscripts and the early editions have “with great power and glory.” Erasmus, as often happens, combined two readings from ancient manuscripts into one and printed: “with great power and glory, and with a great trumpet.” Morel did likewise. The English editors printed the true reading but cited no manuscript evidence.

Image. Previously the text read “statue.” The English edition printed “image.” We preferred this reading because we found it in twenty of our manuscripts and seven English manuscripts, and also because it occurs [Col. 0668D] in Book III of the *Testimonies*, chapter 10. Philostratus relates a similar story in *The Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, Book I, chapter 19.

Upon Peter. Rigault notes that the Codex Fuxiensis read “upon the rock” (*super petram*), and that he had inspected this himself, but that a later—though still ancient—hand marked the *a* with two obeli and wrote a *u* above it. Since, however, I have not found this in the Codex Fuxiensis, I am compelled to suppose that Rigault, with his attention directed elsewhere, wrote “Foxiensis” for some other manuscript in which he had found it. The Codex Seguierianus originally read “upon the rock,” but in antiquity the letter *u* was afterward placed over the letter *a*, to show that “Peter” (*Petrum*) should be read. Conversely, the Codex Fossatensis originally read “upon Peter,” but in antiquity was afterward corrected to “upon the rock.” The Codex Thuanus and eight others have “upon Peter.” I do not doubt that “Peter” should be read, although ten ancient manuscripts and the early editions have “rock.”

[Col. 0669D] Unrestrained. Erasmus introduced this reading. Several ancient manuscripts and Latin usage confirm it. *Impotentia* signifies excessively violent power, and, as it were, its tyrannical exercise. Some ancient manuscripts and early editions—even Morel’s, surprisingly—prefer “because you are powerful.” See Lambinus on Horace, Book I, Ode 37.

How great. We have restored these two words, which had dropped out of Rigault’s edition and were omitted from the English edition. All the ancient manuscripts and early editions contain them.

[Col. 0670D] Unpunished. So the early editions and nearly all the ancient manuscripts. Erasmus changed it and printed “with impunity.” That reading does indeed occur in some ancient manuscripts.

Ten months. Previously the text read “nine,” because the earlier editors of Saint Cyprian’s works perhaps thought that passages cited in them from Holy Scripture ought to be corrected according to the Vulgate edition. This has always seemed to me a matter of great difficulty, since it is certain—as the most learned men had observed before me—that Cyprian used a different translation. Accordingly, when I noticed this discrepancy and knew [Col. 0671C] that Josephus had treated the same matter in his book *On the Sovereignty of Reason*, I thought I could easily settle the difficulty by his authority. But my expectation deceived me. For after reporting the mother’s statement to her son that she had carried him in her womb for nine months, on the following page he immediately says that the most holy martyrs declared that their mother’s womb had borne them for ten months. Thus the same difficulty always remains. We must therefore have recourse to the authority of the ancient copies. Nearly all that I have seen—and they are many—have “ten.” So too do those used by the English editors. Yet Pamelius, although he thought this reading [Col. 0671D] better, and Rigault too was of the same opinion, preferred to retain the other reading in the text. Pamelius adduces several authorities to prove that the reading “ten” is better. I could adduce many more, but I do not wish to do so, lest reading them weary the readers. I shall therefore note only the passages of ancient authors who say that infants are born in the tenth month. The reader may consult them if desired. See Tertullian, *On the Soul*; Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, Book I; Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*; Lucifer of Cagliari, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*; Jerome, the letter to Rufinus *On the Judgment of Solomon*, and the letter *On Avoiding Suspect Cohabitation*; Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book IV, chapter 5; Prudentius, the poem on Saint Romanus the martyr; Fulgentius Ferrandus, *Letter to Anatolius*; Saint Vincent Ferrer, the sermon for the Vigil of the Nativity of Christ; Plautus, *Amphitryon* and *Cistellaria*; Virgil, the Fourth *Eclogue*; Ovid, Books I and V of the *Fasti*, and the *Letter of Oenone to Macareus*; [Col. 0672C] Seneca, *Thebaid*; Quintilian, *Institutes*, Book VIII, chapter 3; Apuleius, *Apology*; Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 16, and Book VII, chapter 1; Julius Paulus, Book I, title 9; Octavius Horatianus; Ulpian, in the law *Intestato*, Digest, *On Direct and Statutory Heirs*; Petrarch, *Letters on Familiar Matters*, Book XIII, letter 1, to Guido, bishop of Perta, which I published among the supporting documents for the history of the Auvergne family, where the testament of Bernard III de la Tour was also published, in which testimony is given concerning a womb pregnant for ten months. See also Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, Book V, chapter 9. It must nevertheless be admitted that the reading which [Col. 0672D] I reject occurs in four ancient copies and is also found in Jerome’s letter to Eustochium *On Preserving Virginity* and in his letter to Helvidius. But the reading I have retained occurs in nineteen of our manuscripts and four English manuscripts. See the *Pentecontarchus* of Lorenzo Ramírez de Prado, chapter 3.

Persuaded him rather. The letter *On Honoring Parents*, published among Jerome’s works: “Imitate the Maccabean son, who obeyed his mother when she urged him to die and gladly undertook her harsh command, lest he offend his mother. He preferred to be joined to his brothers in death rather than resist his mother’s will.” Comparable in some respect to this mother’s constancy is another mother who would never disclose where she had hidden her son, for whom they were searching, and whose steadfast, noble declaration neither later threats nor death itself could alter: see Tacitus, *Histories*, Book II.

Of the one who denied. The Codex Gratianopolitanus has “to the one who denied.”

Let us proceed through the same testimonies furnished by punishments, through the same martyrdoms of suffering. The Codex Thuanus has: “let us proceed to the glory of martyrdom.” The Codex Gratianopolitanus: “let us proceed to the suffering of martyrdom.”

## CHAPTER XI.—THAT IT WAS FORETOLD THAT THE WORLD WOULD HATE US AND WOULD STIR UP PERSECUTIONS AGAINST US; AND THAT NOTHING NEW HAPPENS TO CHRISTIANS, SINCE FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD THE GOOD HAVE SUFFERED, AND THE JUST HAVE BEEN OPPRESSED AND KILLED BY THE UNJUST

The Lord warns and foretells in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0665C] “in his Gospel,” Lam., Bod. 2], [Col. 0665B] saying: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me first” (John 15:18). “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Remember the saying that I spoke to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you.” And again: “The hour will come when everyone who kills you will think that he is rendering service to God. But they will do this because they have not known the Father or me. I have spoken these things to you so that, when the hour comes, you may remember them, because I told you” (John 16:4). And again: “Amen, amen, I say to you that you will weep and mourn, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy” (ibid., 26). And again: “I have spoken these things to you so that in me you may have peace, but in the world affliction [Note: [Col. 0665C] Oxford adds “you will have”]; but have confidence, because I have overcome the world” (ibid., 38).

And when he was asked by his disciples [Col. 0665C] about the sign of his coming and the consummation of the world [Note: [Col. 0665C] “consummation of the age,” Bod. 4], he answered and said: “Take care that no one deceives you, for many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ,’ and [Col. 0666A] they will deceive many” (Matthew 24:4). “You will begin to hear of wars and reports of wars [Note: [Col. 0665C] “opinions of wars,” Bod. 3]. See that you are not disturbed, for these things must happen, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom [Note: [Col. 0665C] “kingdom against kingdom,” Bod. 1]; and there will be famines, earthquakes, and pestilences in various places. But all these things are the beginnings of birth pangs. Then they will hand you over to affliction and kill you, and you will be hated by all nations because of my name. Then many will be scandalized, will betray one another, and will hate one another. Many false prophets will arise and lead many astray; and because wickedness abounds, the love of many will grow cold. But the one who endures to the [Note: [Col. 0665C] “perseveres to the,” Bod. 1] end will be saved. And this Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0665C] “throughout the whole world,” NC. 2], as a testimony to all nations [Note: [Col. 0665C] “a testimony of all nations,” NC. 2], and then the end will come.

“When, therefore, you see the abomination [Col. 0666B] of devastation [Note: [Col. 0665C] “desolation,” Bod. 4], which was spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from the house; and let the one who is in the 269 field not turn back to take his garment. But woe to those who are pregnant and nursing [Note: [Col. 0666C] “pregnant and breastfeeding,” Voss. 1] in those days! Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.
