For then there will be great affliction, such as has not existed [Note: [Col. 0666C] “such as has not occurred,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 2, Bod. 1, 2, 3] from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will be; and unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved [Note: [Col. 0666C] “all flesh would not be delivered,” Ar., Lam., Ebor., Bod. 1, 2, Ver.]; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened.

“Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘Look, there,’ do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise, and they will produce great signs [Note: [Col. 0666C] “great signs and portents,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Ben., Ver.] and wonders, to lead, if possible, even the elect into error [Note: [Col. 0666C] “terror,” Bod. 1, 2]. But take care: behold, I have foretold everything to you. Therefore, if they say [Col. 0666C] to you, ‘Look, he is in the wilderness’ [Note: [Col. 0666C] “Go out; he is in the wilderness,” Bod. 3], do not go out; ‘Look, he is in the inner rooms’ [Note: [Col. 0666C] “in sleeping places,” Voss. 1], do not believe it. For just as lightning comes [Note: [Col. 0666C] “which comes,” NC. 1, 2, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; “lightning proceeding,” Lin.] from the East and appears as far as the West, so too will be the coming of the Son of Man. Wherever the corpse is [Note: [Col. 0666C] So Ar., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Benev., Ver.; “body,” printed editions], there [Col. 0667A] [Note: [Col. 0667C] “will be gathered,” Bod. 2, 3, Tertull.] the eagles will gather. Immediately after the affliction of those days, the sun will be darkened [Note: [Col. 0667C] So Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Benev., Ver.; “will grow dark,” printed editions], and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn; and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and glory. And he will send his angels with a great trumpet, and they will gather his elect from the four winds [Note: [Col. 0667C] “winds of heaven,” Ver.], from the highest reaches of the heavens to their furthest limits” (Matthew 24; Luke 21).

Nor are the things that now befall Christians new or sudden, since the good and just, devoted to God by the law of innocence and the fear of true religion, have always advanced along the difficult, narrow way through afflictions and injuries [Note: [Col. 0667C] “afflictions and straits,” Bod. 1] and the severe and manifold penalties of hostile attacks [Note: [Col. 0667C] “penalties inflicted by persecutors,” Lam., Ebor., Ben., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4]. Thus, at the very beginning of the world, righteous Abel [Col. 0667B] was the first to be killed by his brother; Jacob was driven into exile; Joseph was sold; King Saul persecuted the merciful David; King Ahab attempted to suppress Elijah when he steadfastly and courageously asserted the majesty of God; and Zechariah the priest was killed between the temple and the altar, so that he himself became a sacrificial victim in the place where he had offered victims to God. In short, so many martyrdoms of the just have repeatedly been celebrated, and so many examples of faith and courage have been produced for posterity.

The three young men—Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael—equal in age, united in love [Note: [Col. 0667C] “love of God,” Bod. 1], steadfast in faith, constant in courage, stronger than the flames and punishments pressing upon them, proclaim [Note: [Col. 0667C] “proclaimed,” Bod. 2, 4] that they serve God alone, know him alone, and worship him alone, saying: “King Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you concerning this matter. For the God whom we serve is able [Col. 0667C] to rescue us from the furnace of burning fire, and he will deliver us from your hands, O king. But if not, let it be known to you that we do not serve your gods, nor do we worship the golden image [Note: [Col. 0667C] So Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Benev., Ver., [Col. 0668C] Oxford; “statue,” printed editions] that you have set up.”

And Daniel, devoted to God and filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out and says: “I worship nothing except the Lord my God, who made heaven and [Col. 0668A] earth” (Daniel 14:4). Tobias too, though under royal and tyrannical servitude, was nevertheless free in mind and spirit; he preserved his confession to God and exaltedly proclaimed the divine power and majesty, saying: “In the land of my captivity I confess him, and I reveal his power among a sinful nation” (Tobit 13:6).

And what of the Maccabees—the seven brothers, alike in the lot both of birth and of courage, fulfilling the number seven in the mystery of perfect consummation? Thus the seven brothers remained united in martyrdom, just as the first seven days in the divine ordering comprise seven thousand years [Note: [Col. 0668D] “by the reckoning of years,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2]; as there are seven Spirits and [Note: [Col. 0668D] “or Spirits,” Benev., Ver.] seven angels who stand and move before the face of God; the seven-branched lamps in the tabernacle of witness; the seven golden lampstands in the Apocalypse; and [Col. 0668B], in Solomon, the seven pillars upon which Wisdom built [Note: [Col. 0668D] “builds,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4] her house (Proverbs 9:1). So too there the number of the seven brothers, embracing the seven churches in the quantity of its own number, accords with what we read in the first Book of Kingdoms [p. 270], that the barren woman bore seven children (2:5); and in Isaiah: “Seven women take hold of one man and ask that his name be invoked over them” (Isaiah 4:1). The apostle Paul also, mindful of this lawful and fixed number, writes to seven churches. And in the Apocalypse (1:19–21), the Lord directs his divine mandates and heavenly precepts to seven churches and their angels. This number is now found there among the brothers, so that the lawful consummation may be completed [Note: [Col. 0668D] “may lawfully be completed,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 2].

[Col. 0668C] The mother too, their origin and root, is plainly joined with her seven children. She later bore the seven churches, having herself first been founded as one upon Peter [Note: [Col. 0668D] So Lam., Voss. 1, Lin., Nup., printed edition; “upon the rock,” Spir., anonymous edition, Remb., Erasmus, Morel, Grav., Fox.] by the Lord’s voice. Nor is it without significance that in their sufferings the mother alone [Note: [Col. 0668D] “consolation in sufferings,” Bod. 4] is with her children. For martyrs, who testify in suffering that they are God’s children, are henceforth acknowledged as having no father except God, as the Lord teaches in the Gospel, saying [Note: [Col. 0668D] “the Lord speaks, saying,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 2]: [Col. 0669A] “Do not call anyone your father [Note: [Col. 0669C] “do not call father,” Ebor.] upon earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matthew 23:9).

What proclamations of confession they uttered! What splendid, what great proofs of faith they furnished! The hostile King Antiochus—or rather Antichrist represented in Antiochus—sought to defile the martyrs’ glorious mouths, unconquered in the spirit of confession, through contact [Note: [Col. 0669C] “by contamination,” Lin.] with swine’s flesh. After beating them severely with whips and accomplishing nothing, he ordered pans to be heated. When these had been made hot and set ablaze, he commanded that the one who had spoken first, and had most provoked the king [Note: [Col. 0669C] “the king’s anger,” Bod. 3] by his steadfast courage and faith, be brought to them and fried, but only after the tongue that had confessed God had first been drawn out and cut off. This befell the martyr to his greater glory, for the tongue that had confessed God’s name ought itself to proceed first to God.

[Col. 0669B] Next, after devising still more savage punishments for the second [Note: [Col. 0669C] “against the second,” Voss. 1], before torturing the rest of his limbs, he stripped the skin from his head together with his hair—plainly from a particular hatred. For since Christ is the head of a man, and God the head of Christ, the one who mangled the martyr’s head was persecuting God and Christ in the head. But he, confident [Note: [Col. 0669C] “strong in his martyrdom,” Bod. 1] in his martyrdom and promising himself the reward of resurrection from God’s recompense, cried out and said: “You, unrestrained as you are [Note: [Col. 0669C] “powerful,” Bod. 2], destroy us from this present life; but the King of the world will raise us, who have died for his laws, to an eternal resurrection of life” (2 Maccabees 7:9).

When the third was asked for his tongue, he quickly put it forward, for he had already learned from his brother to despise the punishment of having it cut out. He also steadfastly extended his hands to be amputated—greatly blessed by this kind of torment, since it fell to him, by stretching out his hands for punishment, to imitate the likeness of the Lord’s passion.

The fourth likewise despised the tortures with equal courage and, answering in a heavenly voice to rebuff the king, cried out and said: “It is better for those given over to death by human beings to await hope from God once again, since they are to be raised by him to eternal life [Note: [Col. 0669C] “to eternal life” omitted by Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Voss. 1, 3, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Ben., Ver.]; but for you there will be no resurrection [Col. 0669C] to life” (ibid., 14).

The fifth, besides trampling underfoot the king’s butchery and his harsh and varied tortures by the vigor of faith [Note: [Col. 0669C] “by faith and vigor,” Bod. 2], was also inspired by the divine Spirit with foreknowledge and knowledge of future events, and prophesied to the king that God’s wrath and vengeance would swiftly follow: [Col. 0670A] “Possessing power among human beings,” he said, “although you are corruptible, you do what you please. But do not think that our race has been abandoned by God. Wait and see his great power [Note: [Col. 0669C] “great is his power,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Voss. 1, Lin., Bod. [Col. 0670C] 1, 2, Benev., Ver.], and how he will torture you and your offspring” (ibid., 16). What relief that was to the martyr [Note: [Col. 0670C] “of the martyr,” Ar.], what great consolation: amid his own torments to think not of his own tortures but to foretell the punishment of his torturer!

In the sixth, however, not courage alone but also humility deserves proclamation. The martyr claimed nothing for himself and did not vaunt the honor of his confession in proud words; rather, he attributed to his own sins the fact that he suffered persecution from the king, but gave to God the fact that he would afterward be avenged. He taught martyrs [p. 271] to be modest, to trust in vengeance, and to boast of nothing in suffering: “Do not,” he said, “wander vainly [Col. 0670B] in error. For we suffer these things because of ourselves, since we have sinned against our God. But do not imagine that you will go unpunished [Note: [Col. 0670C] “will be unpunished,” Lamb., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Lin., Voss. 1, 2, Benev., Ver.], after undertaking to fight against God” (ibid., 18).

Admirable too was their mother. Neither broken by the weakness of her sex nor shaken by repeated bereavement, she willingly watched her children die. She counted those punishments not as the sufferings of her dear ones but as their glories, offering God as great a martyrdom through the steadfastness of her own eyes as her sons had offered through the torments and suffering of their limbs. When six [Note: [Col. 0670C] “the others,” NC. 2] had been punished and killed, one of the brothers remained. The king promised him riches, positions of power, and many other things, so that his cruelty and savagery might be soothed by the consolation of subduing even one; and he asked that the mother too join him in pleading with her son to bring about his downfall. She did plead, but as befitted the mother of martyrs, as befitted one mindful of the law and of God, as befitted one who loved her sons not indulgently but courageously. She pleaded, indeed, but that he should confess God; she pleaded that this brother should not be separated from his brothers in their share of praise and glory. She reckoned herself the mother of seven sons only if it should be her lot to have borne seven sons to God [Col. 0670C] rather [Note: [Col. 0670C] “to have borne them to God, not,” NC. 2; “to have borne them rather than,” Voss. 1] than to the world.

Thus arming and strengthening him, and then giving birth to her son through a happier travail, she said: “Son, have mercy upon me, who carried you in my womb for ten months [Note: [Col. 0670C] “nine months,” Oxford; “ten,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Voss. 1, Ver.], gave you milk for three years, nourished you, and brought you to this age. I ask you, son, to look upon heaven [Col. 0671A] and earth, and, after beholding everything in them, to understand that God made them from nothing, and the human race as well. Therefore, son, [Note: [Col. 0671C] “so it shall be,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, 2, Lin., Ver., Voss. 1, 2, 1, 2, 4, Oxford] do not fear this executioner, but, having become worthy of your brothers, accept death, so that in that mercy I may receive you with your brothers” (2 Maccabees 7:28).

Great was the mother’s praise in her exhortation to courage, but greater in the fear of God and the truth of faith [Note: [Col. 0671C] “faith of the truth,” Bod. 1], because she promised neither herself nor her son anything from the honor of the six martyrs, nor did she believe that the brothers’ prayer would benefit the salvation of one who denied. Rather, she persuaded him to become a sharer in their suffering so that, on the day of judgment, he might be found with his brothers. Afterward the mother too died with her children [Note: [Col. 0671C] “with her children,” Ver.]; for nothing else now befitted her [Note: [Col. 0671C] “was now permitted,” Lam., Ebor., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, NC. 1, Lin.] than that she who had borne and made martyrs should be joined with them in the fellowship of glory, and that she herself [Col. 0671B] should follow those whom she had sent ahead to God.

And lest anyone embrace the evil gift of deceivers when, by means of a certificate or some other thing, an opportunity to deceive is offered to him, Eleazar too must not pass unmentioned. When the king’s servants offered him the opportunity to take meat that he was permitted to eat [Note: [Col. 0671C] “was permitted to eat,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1; “and eat,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4] and, in order to deceive the king, pretend that he was eating the sacrificial and forbidden foods being forced upon him, he refused to consent to this deception. He said that such pretense befitted neither his age nor his nobility, because others would thereby be scandalized and led into error, supposing that Eleazar, at ninety years of age, had abandoned and betrayed God’s law and gone over to the custom of foreigners; and that it was not worth gaining a few brief [Col. 0672A] moments of life only to offend God and incur eternal punishment.

After he had been tortured for a long time and was already at the point of death, dying amid blows and torments, he groaned and said: “Lord, who possess holy knowledge, it is manifest that, although I could be delivered from death, I endure the harshest bodily pains as I am beaten with scourges; but in my soul, because of the fear of you yourself, I willingly suffer these things” (2 Maccabees 6:22). This was altogether sincere faith and whole and sufficiently pure courage: he thought not of King Antiochus but of God the Judge [Note: [Col. 0672C] “feared God the Judge,” Voss. 1], and knew that it could not contribute to his salvation if he mocked and deceived a human being, since God, who is the judge of our conscience and alone is to be feared, can neither be mocked at all nor deceived.

If, therefore, we too live consecrated and devoted to God, if we make our journey upon [Note: [Col. 0672C] “above those very,” Ar., Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4] the ancient [Col. 0672B] and holy footprints of the just, [p. 272] let us proceed through the same lessons of punishments, through the same martyrdoms of suffering. Let us reckon it the greater glory of our own time that, while ancient examples [Note: [Col. 0672C] “since, while ancient examples,” Lam., Bod. 2, NC. 1] can be counted, Christian martyrs cannot be counted, because the abundance of courage and faith has subsequently overflowed. The Apocalypse bears witness and says: “After these things I saw a great multitude [Note: [Col. 0672C] “a large multitude,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Ver.] which no one could number, from every nation and from every tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and the Lamb. They were clothed in white robes [Note: [Col. 0672C] “in white robes,” Voss. 1; “in a white robe,” Ver.], and palms were in their hands, and they cried with a loud voice: ‘Salvation belongs to our God [Note: [Col. 0672C] “Praise to our God,” Bod. 4], who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.’ And one of the elders answered and said to me: [Col. 0673A] ‘Who are these clothed in white robes, and whence have they come?’ And I said to him: ‘My lord, you know.’ And he said to me: ‘These are the ones who have come from the great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple’ [Note: [Col. 0673D] “serve in the temple,” Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4, Ben., Ver.]” (Revelation 7:9).

But if so great a multitude of Christian martyrs is shown and established, let no one think that becoming a martyr is difficult or arduous, when he sees that the multitude of martyrs cannot be numbered.

[Note: [Col. 0673D]

Repenting. So the early editions, fourteen [Col. 0674D] of our manuscripts, and five English manuscripts. See the notes on the concluding part of the letter to Demetrianus.

Their bosoms. Six ancient manuscripts have “their sheaves.”

[Col. 0675C] Eternal things are restored. The Codex Seguierianus has “eternity is represented.”

## CHAPTER XII.—WHAT HOPE AND REWARD AWAIT THE JUST AND THE MARTYRS AFTER THE STRUGGLES AND SUFFERINGS OF THIS TIME

Through Solomon the Holy Spirit shows and foretells [Note: [Col. 0673D] “warns,” Ar., Lam., Ebor., NC.; “foretells,” Bod. 1, 4, Oxford], saying: “Even if they have suffered torments before human beings, [Col. 0673B] their hope is full of immortality. Though troubled in a few things, they will be well provided for in many, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself. Like gold in the furnace he tested them, and like burnt offerings [Note: [Col. 0673D] “a whole-burnt sacrificial victim,” Bod. 1, 4, Benev., Ver.] he accepted them as sacrificial victims; and in due time regard will be shown for them. They will shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds. They will judge nations and rule over peoples, and their Lord will reign forever” (Wisdom 3:4).

Likewise, in the same author our vindication is described, and the repentance of those who persecute and harass us is foretold: “Then,” he says, “the just will stand with great steadfastness against those who oppressed them and took away their labors. Seeing them, they will be disturbed with dreadful fear and will marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation, saying among themselves in repentance [Note: [Col. 0673D] So Lam., Ebor., Voss. 1, Bod. 2, 4] and groaning from anguish [Note: [Col. 0673D] “through anguish,” Bod. 1, 2, Benev., Ver.; cf. *To Quirinus*, Book 3, chapter 16] of spirit: [Col. 0673C] ‘These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as a byword [Note: [Col. 0673D] “in laughter and as an example,” Lam., Bod. 1, 2, 4, Ver.] of reproach. In our folly we considered their life madness and their end without honor. How, then, have they been numbered [Note: [Col. 0673D] “How have they been numbered,” *To Quirinus*, Book 3, chapter 16] among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints? Therefore we strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice did not shine upon us [Note: [Col. 0673D] “shine over us,” NC. 1], nor did the sun rise upon us. We grew weary in the way of iniquity and destruction and walked through trackless wastes, but we did not know the way of the Lord. What profit did pride bring us? Or what did our boasting [Note: [Col. 0674D] “vaunting,” Lam., Ebor.] of riches contribute to us? All those things passed away like a shadow’” (Wisdom 3:1).

Likewise, in Psalm 115 (v. 3), the value and reward of suffering are shown: “Precious,” he says, “in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 0674D] “death of the just,” Bod. 1, 3, Benev., Ver.]. Likewise, in Psalm 125 (v. 8), the sorrow [Col. 0673D] of struggle and the joy of recompense are expressed: “Those who sow,” he says, “in tears will reap in joy. [Col. 0674A] As they went, they walked and wept, casting their seed; but as they return, they will come with exultation, carrying [Note: [Col. 0674D] “bearing,” Bod. 2, 3, 4] their bosoms [Note: [Col. 0674D] “their sheaves,” Bod. 1, Lin.].” And again, in Psalm 118: “Blessed are those who are undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search out his testimonies [Note: [Col. 0674D] “mysteries,” NC. 1; “testimonies,” Lin.]; with their whole heart they seek him.”

Likewise, the Lord in the Gospel, himself the avenger of our persecution and the rewarder [Note: [Col. 0674D] “bestower of gifts,” Bod. 1, 2, 4, Ver.] of suffering, says: “Blessed are those who have suffered persecution for justice’s sake, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:10). And again: “Blessed will you be when people hate you, separate you, drive you out [Note: [Col. 0674D] “attack you,” Ar., Bod. 2], and curse your name as evil because of the Son of Man. Rejoice on that 273 day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke 6:22). And again: “Whoever loses his life [Col. 0674B] because of me will save it” (Luke 9:24).

Nor do the rewards of the divine promise await only those condemned and killed. Even if suffering itself is lacking for the faithful, yet their faith has remained whole and unconquered, and a Christian has shown that, after despising and abandoning everything that is his, he follows Christ, he too is honored by Christ among the martyrs, as Christ himself promises and says: “There is no one who leaves house or field or parents or brothers or wife or children because of the kingdom of God and does not receive seven times as much in this time, and eternal life in the age to come” (Luke 18:29).

Likewise, in the Apocalypse he says the same thing: “And I saw,” he says, “the souls of those killed because of the name of Jesus [Note: [Col. 0674D] “the word of Jesus,” Bod. 2; “the testimony of Jesus,” Ver.] and the word of God.” And after placing first those who had been killed, he added, saying: “And all who did not worship the image of the beast [Col. 0674C] or receive its inscription upon their forehead or hand.” He joins all these together as seen by him in the same place and says: “And they lived and reigned with Christ” (Revelation 20:4). He says that all live and reign with Christ—not only those who have been killed, but also all who, persevering in the steadfastness of their faith and the fear of God, did not worship the image of the beast or consent to its deadly and sacrilegious edicts.

## CHAPTER XIII.—THAT WE RECEIVE MORE AS THE REWARD OF SUFFERING THAN WHAT WE ENDURE HERE IN THE SUFFERING ITSELF
Source/review notes: The supplied source itself ends with an incomplete apparatus-note marker at [Col. 0685D]; the draft faithfully preserves this inherited gap.

The blessed Apostle Paul proves this. By divine favor he was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, and testifies that he heard ineffable words; he boasts, with the assurance of an eyewitness [Note: [Col. 0674D] “With the eye of faith,” Bod. 3; “hidden,” Lam. Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], that he saw the Lord Jesus, and with the greater truthfulness of conscience [Note: [Col. 0674D] “Of a greater conscience,” Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] he professes what he both learned and saw: “The sufferings of this present time,” he says, “are not worthy to be compared [Col. 0675A] with the glory that is to come upon us, which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Who, then, would not strive with all his strength to attain such glory—to become a friend of God, immediately to rejoice with Christ, and after earthly torments and punishments to receive divine rewards? If it is glorious for soldiers of this world to return triumphantly to their homeland after defeating the enemy, how much better and greater is the glory of returning in triumph [Note: [Col. 0675B] “Triumphant,” Bod. 2, 3, 4.] to paradise after defeating the devil, and, once the one who had previously cast Adam down [Note: [Col. 0675B] “Deceived him,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Voss. 1, 2.] has himself been overthrown, of carrying victorious trophies back to the place from which the sinner Adam was expelled; of offering to God a most acceptable gift—faith uncorrupted and the mind’s courage unimpaired, the illustrious praise of devotion; of accompanying him when he begins to come to exact vengeance upon his enemies; of standing at his side when he sits in judgment; [Col. 0675B] of becoming a coheir with Christ; of being made equal to the angels; and of rejoicing with the patriarchs, the apostles, and the prophets in possession of the heavenly kingdom?

What persecution can overcome these thoughts? [Note: [Col. 0675B] “What persecutions can,” Bod. 2. Lam.] What torments can vanquish them? The mind that is brave, steadfast, and founded upon devout meditations [Note: [Col. 0675B] “Devout imitations,” Voss. 1.] endures; and against all the devil’s terrors [Col. 0676A] and the world’s threats the spirit remains immovable, strengthened by a sure [Note: [Col. 0675B] “Welcome faith,” Voss. 1.] and solid faith in things to come. In persecutions the earth is closed [Note: [Col. 0676B] Thus Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. Voss. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Ben. Ver.; printed editions: “the eyes are closed.”], but heaven lies open; Antichrist threatens, but Christ protects; death is inflicted, but immortality follows; when a man is slain, the world is taken from him, but when he is restored, paradise is presented to him; temporal life is extinguished, but eternal life is renewed.

What great dignity and security there is in departing from here with joy, in departing gloriously amid pressures and afflictions! In a moment one closes the eyes with which human beings and the world were seen, and immediately opens those same eyes so that God and Christ may be seen. What speed there is in so blessed a departure [Note: [Col. 0676B] “What happiness,” Lat.]! You are suddenly withdrawn from the earth so that you may be placed in the heavenly kingdoms.

These things must be embraced in mind and thought; these things must be pondered day and night. If persecution [Col. 0676B] finds [Note: [Col. 0676B] “If the persecutor finds,” Bod. 3.] such a soldier of God, courage ready for battle [Note: [Col. 0676B] “Destined for battle,” Bod. 5.] cannot [p. 274] be defeated. Or if the summons comes first, the faith that was prepared for martyrdom will not go unrewarded. With God as judge, the reward is rendered without loss of time: in persecution, military service is crowned; in peace, conscience is crowned.

[Col. 0675]

# THREE BOOKS OF TESTIMONIES [Note: [Col. 0675D] *To Quirinus, On the Mystery of Christ*, NC. 1. Bod. 2. Lam.; *A Book against the Jews*, Rem. Er. Man. Mor.; *A Letter of Cyprian to Quirinus*, Lin.] AGAINST THE JEWS

[Note: [Col. 0675D]

If there are any passages in the works of Saint Cyprian about which it cannot be definitively declared that they are certainly his, this is especially true of the books of *Testimonies to Quirinus*. For several manuscripts contain more than the commonly printed editions, while others contain less. Therefore, since it is impossible to distinguish what is truly Cyprian’s from what was added after him by learned readers, we have retained what is commonly read in the editions and have added what we found in ancient manuscript copies, adding nothing of our own.

Moreover, only the first two books appear in [Col. 0676D] the Speyer edition, the old Venetian edition, and the edition prepared by Remboldus. Erasmus published the third from a manuscript belonging to the monastery of Gembloux. But he says that it seems more probable to him that this work is not Cyprian’s, because in it, apart from the preface, the author never displays his own style. Even if this were true—which it certainly is not—that argument is exceedingly weak, as is also what Priorius thinks concerning the third book. For Saint Augustine cites these books as Cyprian’s in Book IV, chapters 8 and 9, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, as Pamelius noted; Pamelius also adduces other excellent proofs to show that they are truly Cyprian’s. This is further maintained by the note in the English edition on the first book and in its preface to the third book. To these I add that Bishop Fulgentius, in the fragments, and Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, in Letter 128 to King Charles and in his book *On Three Questions*, cite this work as Cyprian’s.

I had twenty-one old copies of these books, although five of them contain only the first two books. A work of nearly the same subject as this work of Cyprian is the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, commonly attributed to Prosper. I further point out that Erasmus, who professed his belief that this work was not Cyprian’s, nevertheless cites chapters 3 and 5 of its second book as Cyprian’s at the beginning of his *Annotations* on the Gospel of John.

**More precise.** The Verona and Corbie manuscripts have “more useful.”

**Could be known.** The edition called that of Gravius, and the Pamelian edition, have: “it can be that he himself is the one who was foretold.” But I found this reading in none of the old copies that I used; nor does it occur in the English manuscripts or in the earlier editions. The English editors nevertheless retained it.

**For readers.** Previously the text read “for you, the reader.” We emended it from the Verona, Foix, and Bec manuscripts; that this emendation is legitimate is also shown by the preface to the third book.]

(C)

[Col. 0675C] CYPRIAN to his son Quirinus [Note: [Col. 0675D] “To his own Quirinus, greetings,” NC. 2.], greetings.

I was obliged, dearest son, to comply [Note: [Col. 0675D] “I was obliged, dearest,” Bod. 1.] with your spiritual desire, which with most earnest [Col. 0675D] entreaty asks for the divine teachings by which [Col. 0676C] the Lord has deigned to educate and instruct us through the Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0676D] Thus Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Veron. Benev. Voss. 3; “educate and establish,” Oxon.], so that, having been led away from the darkness of error [Note: [Col. 0676D] “From the gloom of dark error,” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.] and illuminated by his pure [Col. 0676D] and radiant light, [Note: [Col. 0676D] “And illuminated by his pure and radiant light,” Bod. 1; “to be illuminated,” Voss. 3; “to the light,” etc., Lin.] we may hold to the way of life through the saving [Col. 0677A] mysteries.

And indeed, just as you requested, I have composed the discourse and arranged the little book in an abbreviated compendium [Note: [Col. 0677C] “A short time before,” Voss. 4; “briefly arranged,” Bod. 1, 2; “briefly arranged for you,” Spir.; “with compendious brevity,” Voss. 3.], so that I might not diffuse what was being written [Note: [Col. 0677C] “What is being written,” Lin.] into a broader abundance [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Broader,” Bod. 4.], but, so far as my modest memory suggested [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Had suggested,” NC. 1. Lamb. Bod. 2.], might gather selected headings and append whatever was necessary. Thus we may appear not so much to have treated the subjects ourselves as to have supplied material for those who treat them.

Such brevity is also highly beneficial to readers, since a longer book does not scatter the reader’s understanding and attention [Note: [Col. 0677C] “Would not scatter,” Ver.], but a retentive memory preserves what is read in a more precise compendium [Note: [Col. 0677C] “In a more useful compendium,” Ver.].

I have, in fact, comprised two little books, regulated with equal balance [Note: [Col. 0677C] “With equal quality,” Veron.; “regulated,” Voss. 4.]. In the first we have striven to show [Note: [Col. 0677D] “We may have striven,” most printed editions; “we have striven,” Oxon., from Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lin. NC. 1. Voss. 4.] that, in accordance with what had previously been foretold, the Jews withdrew from God and lost the Lord’s indulgence, which had long before [Col. 0677B] been given to them and promised for the future; and that Christians succeeded into their place, earning the Lord’s favor through faith [Note: [Col. 0677D] “The faith of the Lord,” Bod. 1, 3. Voss. 4.] and coming from every nation and from the whole world.

The other little book contains the mystery of Christ: that the very one has come [Note: [Col. 0677D] “Has now arrived,” NC. 2.] who was announced according to the Scriptures, and that he did and fulfilled all the things by which the one who had been foretold could be understood and recognized [Note: [Col. 0678C] “The one foretold can be recognized,” Lam. NC. 1, 2. Lin.; “could be known, just as he was foretold,” Voss. 2.]. For the present, these things may benefit readers [Note: [Col. 0678C] “You, the reader,” Oxon.] in forming the first outlines of faith.

Greater strength will be given, and the understanding of the heart will work more and more, for one who searches the Old and New Scriptures more fully and reads through all the volumes [Note: [Col. 0678C] “The volumes of the books,” Lam. Lin. NC. 1.] of the spiritual books. For now we have drawn from the divine fountains [Note: [Col. 0678C] “From the fountain of divine fullness,” Voss. 3.] a little to send you for the present. You will be able to drink more abundantly [Note: [Col. 0678C] “More freely,” Bod. 4.] and be filled more copiously if you too approach those same [Col. 0677C] fountains of divine fullness, intending to drink from them together with us.

I wish you always good health, dearest son.

# CHAPTER HEADINGS

I. That the Jews grievously sinned, to the offense [Note: [Col. 0678C] “In offense,” Voss. 4.] of God, because they abandoned the Lord and followed idols.

[Col. 0678A] II. Likewise, that they did not believe the prophets and killed them.

III. That it was foretold beforehand that they would neither know, understand, nor receive the Lord.

IV. That the Jews would not understand the Holy Scriptures, but that they were to be understood in the last times, after Christ had come.

V. That the Jews can understand nothing in the Scriptures unless they first believe in Christ.

VI. That they would lose Jerusalem and abandon the land they had received.

VII. Likewise, that they would lose the light of the Lord.

VIII. That the first, fleshly circumcision has been abolished and a second, spiritual circumcision has been promised.

IX. That the former law, which was given through Moses, [Col. 0678B] would cease.

X. That a new law was to be given.

XI. That another dispensation and a new covenant were to be given. [Note: [Col. 0678C] “Ought to be given,” Voss. 4.]

XII. That the old baptism [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Baptism,” masculine form, Voss. 4.] would cease and the new [Note: [Col. 0678D] “New,” masculine form, Voss. 4.] would begin.

XIII. That the old yoke would be abolished and a new yoke given.

XIV. That the old shepherds would cease and new ones begin.

XV. That Christ would be the house and temple [Note: [Col. 0678D] “Christ would be the temple,” Voss. 4.] of God, and that the old temple would cease and a new one begin.

XVI. That the old sacrifice would be abolished and a new one celebrated.

XVII. That the old priesthood would cease and a new priest [Col. 0678C] would come, who would remain forever.

XVIII. That another prophet like Moses was promised—namely, one who would give a new covenant and who ought to be obeyed all the more.

XIX. That two peoples were foretold, the greater and the lesser: that is, the old people of the Jews and the new people that was to arise from us [Note: [Col. 0678D] “From the new,” Bod. 1.].

[Col. 0679A] XX. That the Church, which had formerly been barren, would have more children from the nations than the synagogue had previously had.

XXI. That it was rather the nations that would believe in Christ.

XXII. That the Jews would lose the bread and cup of Christ and all his grace, whereas we would receive them; and that the new name of Christians would be blessed upon the earth.

[Col. 0680A] XXIII. That the nations rather than the Jews attain the kingdom of heaven.

XXIV. That the Jews can obtain pardon for their sins only in this way: if they wash away the blood of the slain Christ in his baptism and, passing into the Church, obey his commandments.

## CHAPTER I.—THAT THE JEWS GRIEVOUSLY SINNED, TO THE OFFENSE OF GOD, BECAUSE THEY ABANDONED [Note: [Col. 0679C] “Forsook,” Thu. Foss. Corb.] THE LORD AND FOLLOWED IDOLS

[Col. 0679B]

In Exodus, the people say to Aaron: “Rise and make [Note: [Col. 0679C] “Rise, make,” Bod. 2.] gods for us to go before us, because as for this man Moses, who [Note: [Col. 0679C] “The man who,” Corb.] brought us out of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him” (Exod. XXXII, 1).

Likewise there Moses says to the Lord: “‘I beseech you, Lord,’ he says, [Note: [Col. 0679C] “I beseech you, Lord,” Thu. Foss. Corb.] ‘this people has committed a great sin [Note: [Col. 0679C] “This people a great,” Foss.]. They have made for themselves gods of gold and silver. And now, if you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from the book that you have written.’ And the Lord said to Moses: ‘If anyone has sinned before me, I will erase him from my book’” (ibid. 31–33).

Lin. Lamb. Thu. Corb. Benev. Ver.] that were around them, [Col. 0679C] and [Note: [Col. 0679C] “Around them, and,” Thu.] they offended the Lord [Note: [Col. 0679D] “Acted against the Lord,” Ar. Lam. NC. 1. Lin. Thu. Foss. Corb. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. The same below.], and abandoned God, and served Baal.”

Likewise there: “And the children of Israel again proceeded to do what was wicked [Note: [Col. 0679D] “And again they did evil,” Voss. 4.] before the Lord, and served Baal and the gods of foreigners; and they abandoned the Lord and did not serve him” (Judg. II, 11–13).

“Judah has been abandoned, [Note: [Col. 0679D] The entire passage from “Judah has been abandoned” to “In Jeremiah” is absent from Ar. Lam. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. [Col. 0680C] Corb. Voss. 3.] and abomination has been committed in Israel and in Jerusalem, because Judah profaned the holy things of the Lord, in which he delighted, [Col. 0680A] and pursued foreign gods. ## CHAPTER II.—THAT THEY DID NOT BELIEVE THE PROPHETS AND KILLED THEM

In Jeremiah the Lord says: “I sent you my servants the prophets. I sent them before dawn, and you did not hear me [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Obey me,” Foss.] or incline your ears, when I said: ‘Let each person turn from his evil way and from your most wicked pursuits [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Your affections, from age to age,” Spir. Rem. Er. Lin. NC. Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Foss. Corb.]; and you shall dwell in this land, which I gave to you and your fathers from age to age.’ And again: ‘Do not walk after foreign gods so as to serve them, and do not worship them [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Do not worship, and do not,” Spir. Rem. Er. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Foss. Corb.], and do not provoke me by the works of your hands to destroy [Note: [Col. 0680C] “To scatter,” NC. 1.] you.’ But you did not hear me” (Jer. XXV, 4–7).

Likewise, in Book III of *Basileion* [Note: [Col. 0680C] “Likewise in the book of Kings,” Bod. 2. NC. 2.], Elijah says to the Lord: “With jealousy I have been jealous for the Lord God Almighty [Note: [Col. 0680C] “I have been jealous for the Lord God Almighty,” Foss.], [Col. 0680C] because the children of Israel have abandoned you, demolished your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword; I alone remain [Note: [Col. 0680C] “I only,” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2, 4. Lin.], and they seek to take my life [Note: [Col. 0680D] “They seek to take away my life,” Foss. Voss. 3.] from me” [Note: [Col. 0680D] “It from me,” Bod. 2, 4. Voss. 3, 4.] (III Kings XIX, 10).

Likewise in Ezra: “They revolted from you [Note: [Col. 0680D] “They withdrew from you,” Bod. 1, 2, 3. Voss. 5.], cast your law behind their backs [Note: [Col. 0680D] “Behind their body,” Bod. 1, 4. Voss. 3.], and killed your prophets, who solemnly warned them to return to you” (II Esdr. XX, 26).

[Note: [Col. 0681D]

**Give ear.** This is the reading of all the old editions. Pamelius altered it on the authority of a single old book and because Tertullian, in Book III *Against Marcion*, reads, “receive it into your ears.” The Vulgate edition of Isaiah does indeed contain the reading advanced by Pamelius. But since the version used by Cyprian differed from our Vulgate, it is highly probable that the text of the old editions is better. Moreover, it is confirmed by thirteen of our books and six English manuscripts.

**Manger.** I have restored the reading of the Speyer edition, which I also found in ten of our books and [Col. 0682D] four English manuscripts. The edition of Holy Scripture that is our Vulgate does indeed read *praesepe*. But that authority does not prove that Cyprian must likewise be read in this way, for Latin writers of old used both *praesepe* and *praesepium* for “manger.”

**Woe, sinful nation.** We restored the text in this form on the authority of the old books, as we also did in the book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 207, where we gave the reason for this alteration.

**False measuring-line.** Six old books have “your measuring-line.”]

## CHAPTER III.—THAT IT WAS FORETOLD BEFOREHAND THAT THEY WOULD NEITHER KNOW, UNDERSTAND, NOR RECEIVE THE LORD

[Col. 0681A]

In Isaiah: “Hear, heaven, and give ear, [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Give ears,” Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Lam. Thu. Corb. Voss. 4.] earth, for the Lord has spoken: ‘I begot and exalted sons, but they rejected me [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Despised me,” NC. 1. Bod. 2. Lin. Foss. Voss. 3. Thus Tertullian and Irenaeus.]. The ox recognized its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Its master’s manger,” Bod. 2, 4. Thu. Foss. Corb. Voss. 4; *praesepem*, Ver.]; but Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Did not recognize me,” Bod. 3, 4; “the people did not,” Foss.]. Woe, sinful nation, [Note: [Col. 0681C] “Woe to the sinful nation,” Oxon.] a people full [Note: [Col. 0681C] “To a people full,” Oxon.] of sins, a wicked seed, [Note: [Col. 0681C] “A most evil seed,” Bod. 1, 3. Voss. 4.] criminal children! You have abandoned the Lord and driven the Holy One of Israel to indignation’” [Note: [Col. 0681C] “You provoked him to anger,” Ar. Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2; “you drove him to anger and indignation; you provoked the Holy One,” Voss. 2.] (Isa. I, 2–4).

Likewise, in the same prophet the Lord says: “Go and tell this people [Note: [Col. 0681D] “This people,” Bod. 2. Voss. 4.]: ‘With your ear you shall hear and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall see and shall not perceive [Note: [Col. 0681D] “Shall not behold,” Ar. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]. For the heart of this people has grown dull [Note: [Col. 0681D] “For I have made dull,” Foss.]; they have heard heavily with their ears and have closed their eyes, [Col. 0681B] lest perhaps they should see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, return, [Note: [Col. 0682C] “And be converted,” Corb., thus Tertullian; “that I may heal,” Voss. 3.] and I should heal them’” (Isa. VI, 9–10).

Likewise in Jeremiah the Lord says: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves worn-out cisterns that will not be able [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Were not able,” Corb.] to hold water” (Jer. II, 13).

Likewise in the same prophet: “Behold, the word of the Lord has become a curse to them, and they do not [Note: [Col. 0682C] “A curse; they do not,” Thu. Foss.] desire it” (Jer. VI, 10).

Likewise in the same prophet the Lord says: “The kite knows [Note: [Col. 0682C] “The kite knows,” Bod. 3.] its season; the turtledove and swallow, the sparrows of the countryside, [Note: [Col. 0682C] “The swallow, the sparrows,” Corb.] have observed the times of their coming; but my people have not known the judgment of the Lord. How do you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? The false measuring-line [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Adultery,” Afflig.; “your measuring-line,” Bod. 1, 2, 3. Lam. Lin. Thu. Bor. Voss. 3, 4.] has been made in vain; the scribes have been confounded, the wise have trembled and been captured, because they rejected the word of the Lord” (Jer. VIII, 7–9).

Likewise in Solomon: [Col. 0681C] “The evil seek me, [Note: [Col. 0682C] “The evil will seek me,” Thu. 1. Voss. 4.] and they shall not find me. For they hated wisdom and did not receive the word of the Lord” (Prov. I, 28–29).

Likewise in Psalm XXVII: “Render to them their recompense, because they did not understand the works of the Lord” (Ps. XXVII, 45).

Likewise in Psalm LXXXI: “They neither knew nor understood; [Col. 0682A] they shall walk in shadow” (Ps. LXXXI, 5).

Likewise in the Gospel according to John: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But as many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name” (John I, 11–12).

## CHAPTER IV.—THAT THE JEWS WOULD NOT UNDERSTAND THE HOLY SCRIPTURES, BUT THAT THEY WERE TO BE UNDERSTOOD IN THE LAST TIMES, AFTER CHRIST HAD COME

In Isaiah: “And all these words shall be to you like the words of a sealed book. If you give it to a man who knows letters to read, he will say: ‘I cannot read it, for it is sealed.’ But on that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Of this book,” Voss. 4.], and the eyes of the blind, who are in darkness and mist, [Col. 0682B] shall see” (Isa. XXIX, 11, 18).

Likewise in Jeremiah: “At the end of the days [Note: [Col. 0682C] “In the last days,” Voss. 4.] you shall understand these things” (Jer. XXIII, 20).

Likewise in Daniel: “Secure the words [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Secure the book,” Ver.] and seal the book until the time of consummation, until many learn and knowledge is fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0682C] “Until all are filled with knowledge,” Lin.]; for when the dispersion takes place, they shall understand all these things” (Dan. XII, 4, 7).

Likewise in Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud” (I Cor. X, 1).

Likewise in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “Their perceptions have been dulled to this day, while this same veil remains in the reading of the Old Testament, which is not unveiled because it is abolished in Christ; and even to the present day, [Note: [Col. 0682D] “Present day,” NC. 1. Lam. Bod. 2.] whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But as soon as they have turned [Note: [Col. 0682D] “He has turned to the Lord,” Ar. NC. 1. Lin. Lam. Bod. 2. Voss. 3.] to the Lord, the veil shall be removed” [Col. 0682C] (II Cor. III, 14, 16).

In the Gospel, after the resurrection, the Lord says: “These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written [Note: [Col. 0682D] “Everything written,” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.] about me in the law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and said to them: “For thus [Col. 0683A] it is written, and thus it was necessary [Note: [Col. 0683D] “For it is written, and it is necessary,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Lam. NC. 1. Voss. 3.] for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and the remission of sins to be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke XXIV, 44–47).

[Note: [Col. 0683D]

**Are blessed.** The Burgundian manuscript has “are justified.”]

## CHAPTER V.—THAT THE JEWS CAN UNDERSTAND NOTHING IN THE SCRIPTURES UNLESS THEY FIRST BELIEVE IN CHRIST

In Isaiah: “And unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. VII, 9).

Likewise the Lord in the Gospel: “For unless you believe that I am, you shall die in your sins” (John VIII, 24).

That righteousness, moreover, rests upon faith, and that life is found there, was foretold in Habakkuk: “But the righteous person shall live by my faith” [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Shall live by faith,” NC. 1. Bod. 1, 4. Tert.] (Hab. II, 4).

Hence Abraham, the father of the nations, believed. In Genesis: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Gen. [Col. 0683B] XV, 6).

Likewise Paul to the Galatians: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Reckoned,” Bod. 1, 2.] to him as righteousness. You therefore know that those who are of faith are the children [Note: [Col. 0683D] “The Jews,” Lam.] of Abraham. But the divine Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the nations by faith, announced beforehand to Abraham that all nations would be blessed in him. Therefore, those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham” (Gal. III, 6–9).

## CHAPTER VI.—THAT THEY WOULD LOSE JERUSALEM AND ABANDON THE LAND THEY HAD RECEIVED

In Isaiah: “Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire. Foreigners will devour your country in your sight; [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Foreigners shall devour it,” Ben. Ar. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Voss. 3, 4. Mor.] and the daughter of Zion shall be left desolate and overthrown by foreign peoples, like a hut in a vineyard and like a watchman’s shelter in a cucumber field, like a city [Col. 0683C] under siege. And unless the Lord Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” [Note: [Col. 0683D] “We would have been similar,” Ar. NC. 2; “we would have made similar,” Thu. Foss. Corb.] (Isa. I, 7–9).

Likewise in the Gospel the Lord says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Slay,” Thu. Bod. 1, 3, 4. Corb. Voss. 3, 4.] the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children [Note: [Col. 0683D] “Gather the children,” Ar. Lam. NC. 1, 2; “gather you and the children,” Voss. 4; “collect,” Oxon.] as a hen gathers her chicks [Note: [Col. 0683D] “As an eagle its young,” Bod. 3.] beneath her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house shall be left to you [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Behold, your house shall be sent to you,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; “remitted,” Voss. 3.] desolate” [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Desolate” is absent from Ar. Ben. Er. Ver. Man. Voss. 4.] (Matt. XXIII, 37–38).

[Note: [Col. 0683D]

**According to John.** So the old books always read. Sirmond likewise wrote it in this form, although he was skilled in Greek, [Col. 0684D] in the decree of Pope Stephen II concerning the Roman hospice *cata Galla Patricia*, vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 38.]

## CHAPTER VII.—LIKewise, THAT THEY [Note: [Col. 0684D] “That the Jews would,” Lam.] WOULD LOSE THE LIGHT OF THE LORD

In Isaiah: “Come, let us walk in the light of the Lord. For he has forsaken his people, the house of Israel” (Isa. II, 5–6).

Likewise in his Gospel according to John: “He was the true light who illuminates every person coming [Col. 0684A] into this world [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Who comes into this world,” Ver. Benev.]. He was in this world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I, 9–10).

Likewise there: “He who does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: that light came into the world, and human beings loved darkness [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Human beings” is absent from Lam. NC. 1. Voss. 3, 4.] more than light” (John III, 18–19).

## CHAPTER VIII.—THAT THE FIRST, FLESHLY CIRCUMCISION HAS BEEN ABOLISHED AND A SECOND, SPIRITUAL CIRCUMCISION HAS BEEN PROMISED

In Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord to the men of Judah [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Men of Judah,” Corb.] and those who inhabit Jerusalem: ‘Renew new ground among yourselves, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves for your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart, lest my wrath go forth like fire and burn, with no one [Col. 0684B] to extinguish it’” (Jer. IV, 3–4).

Likewise Moses says: “In the last days God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God” (Deut. XXX, 6).

Likewise in Joshua son of Nun: “And the Lord said to Joshua: ‘Make for yourself exceedingly sharp stone knives, and sit down and circumcise the children of Israel a second time’” [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Cut off,” Foss.; “sit down,” Thu. Corb.; “sit beside,” NC. 1. Lam.; “both cut off and circumcise,” Voss. 3; “and sit,” Voss. 4.] (Josh. V, 2).

Likewise Paul to the Colossians: “You have been circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ” (Col. II, 11).

Likewise, Adam, the first man made by God, was uncircumcised; so were righteous Abel; Enoch, who pleased God and was translated; Noah, who, when the earth and its inhabitants were perishing because of their sins, [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Who, among all on earth, because of sins,” NC. 1, 2. Lin. Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Benev. Ver. Man. Voss. 3.] was alone chosen so that the human race might be preserved in him; and Melchizedek the priest, according to whose order Christ was promised. And further, [Col. 0684C] that seal of the seed is of no benefit, whereas all are sealed with the sign of the Lord.

## CHAPTER IX.—THAT THE FORMER LAW, WHICH WAS GIVEN THROUGH MOSES, WOULD CEASE

In Isaiah: “Then those who seal the Law will be revealed, lest they learn” [Note: [Col. 0684D] “Lest they depart,” Bod. 4.]. “And he will say [Note: [Col. 0684D] “And you will say: I await,” Lin. NC. Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Voss. 4.]: ‘I await God, who turns his face away from the house of Jacob, and I will trust in him’” (Isa. VIII, 16–17).

Likewise in the Gospel: “All the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John” (Matt. XI, 13).

[Note: [Col. 0685D]

**The law shall go forth from Zion.** See Avitus, Letter XIX.]

## CHAPTER X.—THAT A NEW LAW WAS TO BE GIVEN

In Micah: “For the Law shall go forth from Zion, and [Col. 0685A] the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many peoples, and shall convict and expose mighty nations” (Mic. IV, 2–3).

Likewise in Isaiah: “For the Law shall proceed from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, [Note: [Col. 0685C] “From Jerusalem,” Lin. NC. 1. Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Voss. 3, 4.] and he shall judge among the nations” (Isa. XI, 3–4).

Likewise in the Gospel according to Matthew: “And behold, a voice from the cloud, saying: ‘This is my most beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased; hear him’” (Matt. XVII, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0685D]

**Because they did not remain.** These words and what follows to the end are absent from fourteen of our manuscripts and nine English manuscripts. They were also absent from one old manuscript of mine, but were added in ancient times in the margin when that manuscript was reviewed and corrected.]

## CHAPTER XI.—THAT ANOTHER DISPENSATION AND A NEW COVENANT WERE TO BE GIVEN

In Jeremiah: “‘Behold, the days are coming,’ says the Lord, ‘and I will consummate a new covenant for the house of Israel and the house of Judah, [Note: [Col. 0685C] “I will consummate the house of Israel and the house of Judah,” NC. 1; “and a covenant,” NC. 1. Lin. Lam. Corb. Bod. 2, 3, 4. Voss. 4.] not according to the covenant that I established for their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0685C] The remainder, from “out of the land of Egypt” to the end of the chapter, is absent from Ar. Thu. Lamb. Foss. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 2, 3, 4. Voss. 3, 4.] because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them,’ says [Col. 0685B] the Lord. ‘For this is the covenant that I shall establish for the house of Israel after those days,’ says the Lord. ‘Putting my laws into their understanding, I shall write them there; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. And each shall no longer teach his brother, saying, “Know the Lord,” because all shall know me, from their least to their greatest; for I shall be gracious toward their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no more’” (Jer. XXXI, 31–34).

## CHAPTER XII.—THAT THE OLD BAPTISM WOULD CEASE AND THE NEW WOULD BEGIN

In Isaiah: “Therefore, do not remember the former things, [Note: [Col. 0685D] “Do not remember the former things,” Ar.] and do not consider the ancient things. Behold, I make new things, which shall now arise, and you shall know them; and I shall make a way in the desert and rivers in a waterless place, to water my chosen race, [Note: [Col. 0685D] “The human race,” Foss.] my people, [Col. 0685C] whom I acquired, [Note: [Col. 0685D] “Whom I chose,” Corb.] so that they might proclaim my mighty works” (Isa. XLIII, 18–21).

Likewise in the same prophet: “If they thirst, he shall lead them through the deserts; [Note: [Col. 0685D] “He shall bring them water from the rock; the rock shall be split,” Bod. 1, 2, 4. Lin. Benev. Voss. 3, 4.] he shall bring forth water for them from the rock; the rock shall be split, and water shall flow, and my people shall drink” [Note: [Col. 0685D] “And my people shall live,” Ar.] (Isa. XLVII, 21).

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, John says: “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance. But he who comes after me is stronger than I, [Note: [Col. 0685D] “The one coming is stronger,” Thu. Foss. Corb.] whose sandals I am not fit [Note: [Col. 0685D] “Worthy,” Lam. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 2, 3, 4.] to carry. He shall baptize you [Note: [Col. 0685D] “Baptizes,” Oxon.; “shall baptize,” Foss. Ar. Lam. Lin. Bod. [Col. 0686C] 1, 2; “with the Holy Spirit,” Bod. 2. Foss.] with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 11).

Likewise according to John: “Unless someone has been born of water and [Col. 0686A] the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. For what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John III, 5–6).

[Note: [Col. 0685D]

### CHAPTER XIII.—“My Yoke Is Good.”

See Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of Matthew. [Col. 0686D]

In Jeremiah. These words also, down to the end of the chapter, are absent from thirteen of our manuscripts and from ten English manuscripts; they were also absent from that old manuscript of mine in which they were added in the margin.]

### CHAPTER XIII.—THAT THE OLD YOKE WOULD BE ABOLISHED AND A NEW YOKE GIVEN

In Psalm 2: Why have the nations been thrown into tumult [Note: [Col. 0686C] Why have they raged, Lin. Lam. NF. 1. Corb. Voss. 3, 4.], and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth [Note: [Col. 0686C] Came together as one, Ar. Corb. NC. 1, 2. Lam. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3. Voss. 3.], and the rulers were gathered [Note: [Col. 0686C] Assembled, Voss. 4.] together as one against the Lord and against his Christ. Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke away from us [Note: [Col. 0686D] Let us throw it away from us, Lam. Thu. Bod. 2, 4. NC. 1, 2. Corb. Lin. Voss. 4.] (Ps. 2:1–3).

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, the Lord says: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest [Note: [Col. 0686D] I will rest you, Thu. Lin. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Voss. 3.]. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me [Note: [Col. 0686D] Know from me, Thu.], because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke [Col. 0686B] is good [Note: [Col. 0686D] My yoke is pleasant, Lin. Thu. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], and my burden light (Matt. 11:28–30).

In Jeremiah: On that [Note: [Col. 0686D] “In Jeremiah: On that” is absent from Ar. Lam. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Corb. Voss. 3.] day I will crush the yoke from their neck and break their bonds; and they will no longer serve others, but will serve the Lord God, and I will raise up David as king for them (Jer. 30:8–9).

[Note: [Col. 0686D]

### CHAPTER XIV.—Likewise in Jeremiah

These words too are absent from the ancient copies mentioned shortly before; in mine they were added in the margin.]

### CHAPTER XIV.—THAT THE OLD SHEPHERDS WOULD CEASE AND NEW ONES BEGIN

In Ezekiel: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep from their hands; I will turn them away so that they do not pasture my sheep, and they will pasture them no longer. I will draw my sheep out of their mouths and pasture them with judgment (Ezek. 34:10, 16).

In Jeremiah the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0686D] “In Jeremiah the Lord says: And I will give” is absent from the same manuscripts.]: And I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will pasture you, feeding you [Col. 0686C] with discipline (Jer. 3:15).

Likewise in Jeremiah: Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and proclaim it to the islands that are far away. Say: He who scattered Israel will gather him and guard him as a shepherd does his flock, because the Lord has rescued Jacob and rescued him from the hand of one stronger than he (Jer. 26:10).

### CHAPTER XV.—THAT CHRIST WOULD BE THE HOUSE AND TEMPLE OF GOD, AND THAT THE OLD TEMPLE WOULD CEASE AND A NEW ONE BEGIN

In the Second Book of Kingdoms: And the word of the Lord came to Nathan [Col. 0687A], saying: Go and say to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: You shall not build me a house to dwell in; but it shall be, when your days have been fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build me a house in my name [Note: [Col. 0687D] A house by name, Bod. 1, 2. Thu. Foss.], and I will establish his throne for ever; I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; and his house and his kingdom shall obtain faithfulness for ever in my sight (3 Kings 7:4, 5, 12, 14, 16).

Likewise in the Gospel the Lord says: In the temple there shall not be left one stone upon another that will not be pulled down [Note: [Col. 0687D] That will not be destroyed, Ar. Bod. e Lam. NC. 1.] (Matt. 24:2); and after three days another will be raised up without hands (Mark 14:58).

### CHAPTER XVI.—THAT THE OLD SACRIFICE WOULD BE ABOLISHED AND A NEW ONE CELEBRATED

[Col. 0687B] In Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0687D] “Isaiah says,” Bod. 1.]: What use to me [Note: [Col. 0687D] What to me, Bod. 3, 4.] is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am sated; I do not desire the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, or the blood of bulls and goats. For who has required these things from your hands? (Isa. 1:11–12.)

Likewise in Psalm 49: I will not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats. Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High. Call upon me in the day of distress [Note: [Col. 0687D] The day of distress, Thu.], and I will rescue you [Note: [Col. 0687D] I will deliver you, Ver. Cam. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Thu. Corb. Ar. Bod. 1, 2, 4.], and you will glorify me (Ps. 49:13–15).

Likewise in the same Psalm: A sacrifice of praise will glorify [Note: [Col. 0687D] Magnify, Lin.; honor, Ar. Corb.] me; there is the way on which I will show him the salvation of God [Note: [Col. 0687D] My salvation, Ar. Cam. NC. 1. Bod. 2.].

Likewise in Psalm 4 [Note: [Col. 0687D] “And there,” Thu. Foss. Corb.]: Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord.

Likewise in Malachi: I take no pleasure in you [Note: [Col. 0687D] Delight concerning you, Voss. Bod. 3, 4; in you, Ver.], says the Lord, and I will not accept [Col. 0687C] a sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0687D] I do not regard it as acceptable, Veron.] from your hands. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place the fragrance of incense is offered [Note: [Col. 0687D] Will be offered, Bod. 1.] to my name, together with a pure sacrifice, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord (Mal. 1:10–11).

### CHAPTER XVII.—THAT THE OLD PRIESTHOOD WOULD CEASE AND A NEW PRIEST COME, WHO WOULD EXIST FOR EVER

In Psalm 109: Before the morning star I begot you [Note: [Col. 0687D] I generated you, Benev. Veron. Thu. Foss.]. The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.

Likewise, in the First Book of Kingdoms, God says to Eli the priest: And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest [Note: [Col. 0687D] A faithful priest, for him, Lam.], who shall do everything that is in my heart; and I will build him a faithful house [Note: [Col. 0688D] A better throne, Lin.; a faithful house for all days, Lin. NC. 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.], and he shall pass before my anointed ones all his days. And it shall be that whoever [Col. 0688A] remains in your house will come to worship for a small coin and a single loaf of bread (1 Kings 2:33, 36).

### CHAPTER XVIII.—THAT ANOTHER PROPHET, LIKE MOSES, WAS PROMISED—NAMELY, ONE WHO WOULD GIVE A NEW COVENANT AND OUGHT TO RECEIVE GREATER HEED

In Deuteronomy, God says to Moses: And the Lord said to me: I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you, and I will put my word in his mouth, and he will speak to them the things that I command him. And whoever does not hear whatever [Note: [Col. 0688D] Whatever he speaks, Bod. 1, 4; he will speak, Bod. 2. Lamb. Thu. Foss. Corb.; what he will speak, Lam.] that prophet speaks in my name, I will exact vengeance (Deut. 18:17–19).

Concerning him Christ also says in the Gospel according to John [Note: [Col. 0688D] “John says,” Bod. 4.]: Search the Scriptures, in which you think that you have eternal life. These are [Note: [Col. 0688D] These things are, Thu. Foss. Corb.; these are the things that serve as testimony, Benev. Ver. Lin. Bod. 2, 3, 4. Thu.] they that bear testimony concerning me; yet you are unwilling to come to me so that you may have life. Do not think [Col. 0688B] that I accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope [Note: [Col. 0688D] In whom you place your hope, Bod. 1, 2.]. For if you had believed Moses, you would also believe me, since he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words? (John 5:39–40, 45, 47.)

### CHAPTER XIX.—THAT TWO PEOPLES WERE FORETOLD, THE GREATER AND THE LESSER: THAT IS, THE OLD PEOPLE OF THE JEWS AND THE NEW PEOPLE, WHICH WOULD ARISE FROM AMONG US

In Genesis: And the Lord said to Rebecca [Note: [Col. 0688D] The Lord said to Rebecca, Bod. 2.]: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly [Note: [Col. 0688D] Shall be divided from your womb, Foss. Corb.]; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger (Gen. 25:23).

Likewise in Hosea: I will call the people that was not my people “my people,” and her who was not beloved “beloved.” For in the place where it shall be said, “You are not my people,” [Col. 0688C] there they shall be called sons of the living God (Hos. 2:24; 1:10).

### CHAPTER XX.—THAT THE CHURCH, WHICH HAD FORMERLY BEEN BARREN, WOULD HAVE MORE CHILDREN FROM THE NATIONS THAN THE SYNAGOGUE [Note: [Col. 0688D] Than the synagogue had had before, Ver.] HAD FORMERLY HAD

In Isaiah: Rejoice, O barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband. For the Lord has said: Enlarge the site of your tent and of your curtains, and fasten them [Note: [Col. 0688D] And fasten your cords, Bod. 1. Mor.; fasten them and do not, Lam.]. Do not hold back; lengthen your measurements and strengthen your stakes [Note: [Col. 0688D] And your pegs, Corb.]. Extend still farther to your right and your left, and your seed will possess the nations [Note: [Col. 0688D] They will possess; uninhabitable places, Thu. Corb. Bod. 1, 4.] and inhabit deserted cities. Do not fear, because you will prevail (Isa. 54:1, 4). Nor be ashamed because you have been accursed, since you will forget your eternal disgrace (Isa. 54:1, 4).

So too, although a son had first been born to Abraham by the slave woman, Sarah remained barren for a long time and only late in her old age bore Isaac, a son given by promise [Col. 0689A] (Gen. 21), who was a type of Christ.

So too Jacob took two wives (Gen. 29–30): the elder, Leah, whose eyes were weaker, was a type [Note: [Col. 0689C] “Whose eyes were weaker, as a type … Rachel as a type,” Oxon.] of the synagogue; the younger and beautiful Rachel was a type of the Church. She too remained barren for a long time and afterward bore Joseph [Note: [Col. 0689C] Bore Joseph, Foss. Corb. Bod. 1, 2, 4; bore a son, Joseph, Oxon.], who was himself also a type of Christ.

And in the First Book of Kingdoms we read that Elkanah had [Note: [Col. 0689C] “In the First, Elkanah,” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4; “Elkanah had,” Ar. Lam. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Corb. Thu.] two wives: Peninnah, who had children, and the barren Hannah, from whom Samuel was born—not according to the ordinary course of generation, but according to God’s mercy and promise, after she had prayed in the temple (1 Kings 1). And when Samuel was born, he was a type of Christ.

Likewise in the First Book of Kingdoms: The barren woman has borne seven, and she who had very many children has grown weak (1 Kings 2:5). The seven children, moreover, are [Note: [Col. 0689C] “The children, moreover, are seven,” Oxon.] the seven churches. Hence Paul too wrote to seven churches, and the Apocalypse sets forth seven churches [Col. 0689B] (Rev. 1), so that the number seven might be maintained: as with the seven days in which God made the world (Gen. 1); the seven angels who stand and conduct themselves before the face of God, as the angel Raphael says in Tobit (Tob. 12); the seven-branched lamp [Note: [Col. 0689D] Seven-branched lamps, Oxon.] in the tabernacle of witness [Note: [Col. 0689C] Tabernacle of Testimony, Foss.] (Exod. 25); the seven eyes of the Lord that survey the world; the stone with seven eyes, as Zechariah says (Zech. 3:9; 4:10); the seven Spirits and the seven lampstands in the Apocalypse; and the seven pillars upon which Wisdom built her house, in Solomon (Prov. 9:1).

### CHAPTER XXI.—“But when he saw”

These words and the remainder, down to “a multitude of nations,” are absent from the Burgundian manuscript [Col. 0689D] and from the Lamonian manuscript.

**Haircloth.** The older editions and all the old copies prefer this reading, except that in the Thuanus manuscript, as in the Fossatensis, *cilium* (“eyelash”) is written—evidently through the carelessness of scribes who did not understand what they were writing. In the same form, if anyone also wishes to know this, it is read in two ancient manuscripts, one royal and the other my own.

Through a similar error, in my manuscript 162 *Cilius* is written in place of *Caecilius* in the book *On the Passion of Saint Cyprian*, as follows: “In the time of Valerian, that most wicked emperor, there was in Carthage, which is in Africa, a most glorious man named Cyprian. At first he taught rhetoric; afterward, having been converted to the faith of Christ by a certain presbyter named Cilius, he also received the name Caelius.” Erasmus, who saw that this passage of Cyprian was lying corrupted by an error, printed *ilicem* (“holm oak”), evidently as a conjecture.

Afterward there appeared the edition called that of Gravius. Its editor advises readers [Col. 0690C] that he had seen *helicem* written here among variant readings entered in Gravius’s copy of an edition of Cyprian [Col. 0690D], implying that Gravius had entered in his own copy, and only in the briefest fashion, corrections noted from a manuscript of Cyprian. It is nevertheless established that not all those readings were taken from an old book and that some of them were merely conjectures of Gravius. And although the author of that edition states that he used several copies for it—including, among others, one particularly distinguished and ancient manuscript from the library of the Cologne Charterhouse—he nevertheless cited none of them in confirmation of the reading found in Gravius’s book. Indeed, he retained Erasmus’s text, which he would not have done if he had possessed the authority of any old book.

For my part, I would certainly embrace and prefer Gravius’s conjecture gladly, were it not opposed by the authority of the old editions and manuscripts and contradicted by certain ancient writers of great renown. For although the reading I have retained is corrupt, it is established as ancient from chapter 4 of Saint Ambrose’s book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*; from book 12, chapter 42, of Saint Augustine’s *Against Faustus the Manichaean*; from book 16, chapter 41, of *The City of God*; and also from Letter 47 of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, to Rufinus, to which Rufinus himself replies in the letter prefixed to the books *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*.

Rufinus thinks that this corrupt reading was placed in the Latin copies by Latin scribes who did not understand what the Greek word ἕλιξ (*helix*, “tendril”) meant and therefore supposed it to be *cilicium* (“haircloth”). For the Greeks call a vine-tendril ἕλιξ—not so much a vine shoot, as our copies have it, as those little curls and coils of the shoot by which a growing vine is accustomed to attach and suspend itself from the branches of a tree, from a stake, or from whatever other supports it rests upon. Farmers call these *capreoli* (“tendrils”). Secured by these bonds and without danger of slipping, the vine shoot either grows heavy with fruit or stretches outward in its roaming length.

Hence Isidore should be corrected in book 17, chapter 1, of the *Etymologies*, where, while treating this very matter, he wrote *sine lapsu periculorum* (“without the fall of dangers”), although it should read *sine lapsus periculo* (“without danger of falling”). Caelius Aurelianus, book 1 of the *Chronica*, chapter 1: “the rings of the vine, which they call *helecos*.”

From what has been said, moreover, it is sufficiently clear that those who assert that *helicem* is read here in corrected copies of Cyprian are mistaken, since it is certain that this word is absent from all ancient copies of the holy Martyr’s works. See Caelius Calcagninus, book 1, Letter 28.

**Fearsome.** So read the old books and the old editions. The author of that ancient translation therefore used a manuscript in which φοβεροὶ οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ (“his eyes were fearsome”) was written. Dom Bernard de Montfaucon, a Benedictine monk highly skilled in these and many other branches of humane learning, and most devoted to me, reported to me that he had seen this wording in an ancient Greek manuscript of the Royal Library. For in the ancient glosses φοβερός (*phoberos*) is translated *formidolosus* (“fearsome”).

This reading is confirmed by the translations of others, which convey the same sense if one is willing to consider them somewhat more carefully. Some translated it “more beautiful,” others “fiery”—*des yeux pleins de feu*, “eyes full of fire,” as we French say—and in chapter 19 of the Apocalypse, “His eyes were like a flame of fire”; or “burning,” as in Livy, Cicero, Virgil, and elsewhere. Others translated “ruddy”; others, finally, “gracious,” as Rufinus does in his book *On the Blessing of Judah*, and as others do. All these meanings are readily compatible with one another. For fiery and burning eyes, which may also be called ruddy, possess splendid and exceptional beauty. These same eyes are “fearsome”: that is, they arouse fear and awe—not, however, the sort of fear that terrifies, but that which proceeds from the reverence we show toward those whom we respect and honor. Thus in chapter 37 of the book of Job there is “fearsome praise toward God”; in Lucretius, “fear of the gods”; and in Jerome, “fear mingled with love.” For by nature we stand in awe of beautiful people. Indeed, as Cicero says, bodily beauty, through the fitting arrangement of the limbs, moves and delights the eyes precisely because all the parts agree with one another in a certain grace.

But, to return to our subject, I am astonished that Manutius and the others printed *formosi* (“beautiful”) here, contrary to the testimony of the old manuscripts and editions, merely because Erasmus had conjectured in the margin of his edition that it should be written so, although he had changed nothing in the text itself. I am astonished, I say, that Manutius and the others preferred this conjecture to so many authorities; for in addition to the old copies that they saw, and those that I saw, Latinus Latinius testifies that the more ancient manuscripts preserve the reading that I have restored.

Certainly, to conceal nothing, the word *formosi* occurs in two ancient manuscripts; but what weight has this against so many that have *formidolosi*? This error therefore arose from the judgment of those who did not understand that the word *formidolosi* could have a favorable meaning in this passage. The English edition approves our reading, although it placed *formosi* in the text.]

[Col. 0693B]

### BOOK TWO.—In Proverbs

I have corrected it thus, because I saw the same wording in certain old books, in the old Venetian edition, in the edition issued by Rembolt, and in Erasmus’s edition; and because in Tertullian’s book *On Modesty* I read: “For, as Solomon says in Proverbs, which we call παροιμίας (*paroimias*, ‘proverbs’)….” Certain manuscripts have *paraemiis*. Pamelius preferred this reading, although he acknowledged that *proverbiis* was written in the commonly available editions. Some manuscripts make no mention of this book of Solomon, nor do the editions of Manutius and Morel. Rigaltius and the English editors wrote *in paraemiis*.]

## CHAPTER I.—THAT CHRIST IS THE FIRSTBORN, AND THAT HE HIMSELF IS THE WISDOM OF GOD, THROUGH WHOM ALL THINGS WERE MADE

In Solomon, in Proverbs: “The Lord established me at the beginning of his ways; before the age he founded me for his works. Thu.], before the mountains were set in place, before all the hills the Lord begot me.
