## CHAPTER LIV.—THAT NO ONE IS WITHOUT DEFILEMENT AND WITHOUT SIN

In Job: “For who is clean from defilements [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Without defilements” Ver. Benev.]? Not even one, though his life on earth should be one [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Not even if it is one” Bod. 1.] day [Note: [Col. 0761D] “On earth: he cannot be without reproach” Cott.]” (Job XIV, 4, 5).

Likewise, in the Psalm: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Behold, I was conceived in wickedness” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Thu. Corb. Voss. 3.], and in offenses my mother conceived [Note: [Col. 0761D] “In sins my mother conceived” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 3, 4. “Nourished me in the womb” Voss. 3.] me” (Ps. L, 7).

Likewise, in John’s Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8).

## CHAPTER LV.—THAT WE MUST PLEASE NOT MEN, BUT GOD

In Psalm LII: “Those who please men 320 have been put to shame, [Col. 0761C] because God has made them nothing.”

Likewise, in Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians: “If I wished to please men [Note: [Col. 0761D] “If I still wished to please men” Lam. NC. 1.] [Note: [Col. 0761D] “If I pleased” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.], I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. I, 10).

## CHAPTER LVI.—THAT NOTHING WHICH IS DONE ESCAPES GOD’S NOTICE

In the Wisdom of Solomon: “In every place the eyes of God observe the good and the evil” (Prov. XV, 3).

Likewise, in Jeremiah: “‘I am a God who is near, and not a God far away [Note: [Col. 0761D] “A God from afar” Lam. NC. “From afar” Cott.]. If a man has hidden himself in secret places [Note: [Col. 0761D] “But if a man has hidden himself in his secret places” Lam. NC. 1. “If he is hidden, then” Corb.], shall I therefore not [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Shall I therefore not” Bod. 3.] see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?’ says the Lord” (Jer. XXIII, 23, 24).

Likewise, [Col. 0762A] in the First Book of Kings: “Man sees the face [Note: [Col. 0761D] “Sees the face, but God the heart” Thu. Lin. “God sees in the heart” Cott.], but God sees the heart” (I Kings XIV, 7).

Likewise, in the Apocalypse: “And all the churches shall know [Note: [Col. 0762C] “And all the nations and churches shall know” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.] that I am the searcher [Note: [Col. 0762C] “I am the Lord, the searcher” Lam. NC. 1.] of the kidneys and the heart, and I will give to each of you according to his works [Note: [Col. 0762C] “Your works” NC. 2. “Works” Thu.]” (Apoc. II, 23).

Likewise, in Psalm XVIII: “Who understands offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults [Note: [Col. 0762C] “From my secrets” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2. Thu. Corb. Voss. 3.], O Lord” (Ps. XVIII, 13).

Likewise, in Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “We must all be made manifest before Christ’s judgment seat, so that each person may receive [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Each person may receive” NC. 2.] the things proper to his body [Note: [Col. 0762D] “What each of us did” Cott.] according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V, 10).

## CHAPTER LVII.—THAT A BELIEVER IS TO BE CORRECTED AND PRESERVED [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Ought to be preserved” Lam. NC. 1.]

In Psalm CXVII: “Correcting, the Lord has corrected me [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Chastening, he has chastened me” Cott. “Chastening, he has corrected me” NC. 1, 2.], and has not delivered me over to death” (Ps. CXVII, 13).

Likewise, in Psalm LXXXVIII: “I will visit their wicked deeds with the rod [Note: [Col. 0762D] “With an iron rod” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.], and their offenses with scourges. But my mercy [Col. 0762B] I will not scatter away [Note: [Col. 0762D] “I will not destroy” Corb. “I will not remove” Bod. 3. Voss. 4.] from them” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 33).

Likewise, in Malachi: “And he shall sit [Note: [Col. 0762D] “And God sat” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Thu.] refining and purifying like gold and silver, and he shall cleanse the sons of Levi” (Mal. III, 3).

Likewise, in the Gospel: “You shall not come out from there until you pay the last farthing” (Matt. V, 26).

## CHAPTER LVIII.—THAT NO ONE OUGHT TO BE GRIEVED BY DEATH, SINCE IN LIVING THERE IS TOIL AND DANGER, BUT IN DYING THERE IS PEACE AND THE ASSURANCE OF RISING AGAIN [Note: [Col. 0762D] “And in rising again there is assurance” Bod. 3.]

In Genesis: Then the Lord said to Adam: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife [Note: [Col. 0762D] “woman” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Voss. 3.], and ate from that tree—the only one from which I had commanded you not to eat [Note: [Col. 0762D] “not to eat, and you ate from it” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]—the earth shall be cursed in all your labors. In sorrow and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life. [Col. 0762C] It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the produce of the field [Note: [Col. 0762D] “you shall eat your bread from the produce of the field” Corb.] in the sweat of your face. You shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III, 17–19). Likewise there: “And Enoch was pleasing to God, and afterward he was not found [Note: [Col. 0762D] “he was not found, because” Cott.], because God translated him” (Gen. V, 24). And in Isaiah: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell; but the word [Note: [Col. 0762D] “utterance” NC. 2. Manut.] of the Lord abides [Note: [Col. 0762D] “shall abide” Bod. 3, 4.] forever” (Isa. XL, 6–8). In Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0762D] “In Ezekiel: They say” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Corb.]: “They say: ‘Our bones have become dry, our hope has perished, we have expired.’ Therefore prophesy and say [Note: [Col. 0762D] “Prophet, say” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Cott. Voss. 3.]: [Col. 0763A] ‘Thus says the Lord [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Thus says the almighty Lord” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2.]: Behold, I shall open your tombs and bring you out of your tombs, and I shall lead you into the land of Israel. And I shall put my Spirit within you, and you shall live. And I shall place you in your own land, and you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken and shall act, says the Lord’” (Ezek. XXXVII, 11–14). Likewise in the Wisdom of Solomon: “He was taken away [Note: [Col. 0763D] “The righteous man was taken away” Cott. “He was remembered in a short time; he fulfilled the times, for he was pleasing to God” Cott.] lest wickedness should alter his understanding. For his soul was pleasing to God” (Wisd. IV, 11–14). Likewise in Psalm LXXXIII: “How dearly beloved [Note: [Col. 0763D] “How lovely” Bod. 3. “Lovely are the tabernacles” Lin.] are your dwellings, God of hosts! My soul longs and hastens [Note: [Col. 0763D] “yearns and faints” Lin. NC. 2.] toward the courts [Note: [Col. 0763D] “into the courts” Bod. 1.] of God” (Ps. LXXXIII, 2, 3). And in Paul’s Epistle to the Thessalonians: “But we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve like the others, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died [Col. 0763B] and rose again, so also will God bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus” (I Thess. IV, 13, 14). Likewise in First Corinthians: “Fool [Note: [Col. 0763D] “You senseless man” Cott.], what you sow is not brought to life unless it first [Note: [Col. 0763D] “unless beforehand” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Voss. 3. “For star” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2. Cott.] dies.” And again: “Star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection [Note: [Col. 0763D] “in the resurrection” Bod. 1. Oxon. adds “of the dead”]. The body is sown in corruption; it rises without corruption [Note: [Col. 0763D] “in incorruption” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.]. It is sown in dishonor [Note: [Col. 0763D] “in ignobility” Cott.]; it rises in glory. It is sown in weakness; it rises in power. An animal body is sown; a spiritual body rises [Note: [Col. 0763D] “the body rises” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.]” (I Cor. XV, 36, 41–44, 53–55). And again: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality. 321 But when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on incorruption, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: ‘Death has been swallowed up [Note: [Col. 0763D] “Death has been taken away” Lam. Bod. 1, 2, 4. NC. 1.] in conflict [Note: [Col. 0764D] “without conflict” Lam. Bod. 2. NC. 1.]. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your conflict [Col. 0763C]?’” Likewise in the Gospel according to John: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may also be with me where I shall be, and may see my glory, which you gave me before the foundation of the world [Note: [Col. 0764D] “before the world came into being” Cott.]” (John XVII, 24). Likewise according to Luke: “Now, Lord, you dismiss your servant according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29, 30). Likewise according to John: “If you had loved me, you would rejoice [Note: [Col. 0764D] “you certainly would rejoice” Lin.] because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

## CHAPTER LIX.—ON THE IDOLS THAT THE GENTILES REGARD AS GODS

In the Wisdom of Solomon: “They regarded all the idols of the nations as gods, though these have neither the use of eyes for seeing, [Col. 0763D] nor nostrils for perceiving breath [Note: [Col. 0764D] “nostrils for smelling” Cott.], nor ears for hearing, nor fingers on their hands for handling [Note: [Col. 0764D] “fingers of the hands for touching” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Voss. 3. “hands for feeling” Cott.]; indeed, their feet are sluggish for walking. [Col. 0764A] For a human being made them, and one who had borrowed breath fashioned them. Yet no human being will be able to fashion a god like himself. For although mortal, he fashions a dead thing [Note: [Col. 0764D] “though mortal, he will fashion a dead thing” Voss. 3, 4.] with unrighteous hands. Yet he himself is better than those whom he worships, since he at least has lived, whereas they never have” (Wisd. XV, 15–17). On this same subject: “Nor, by attending to the works, did they recognize who the craftsman was; instead they regarded as gods either fire, or wind, or the swift-moving air, or the circuit of the stars, or the mighty water, or the sun and moon, the rulers of the terrestrial globe. If it was because of their beauty that they judged them to be so, let them know how much more beautiful than these is the Lord; or if they marveled at their powers and works, let them understand from them that he who established these mighty things is mightier than they” (Wisd. XIII, 1–4). Likewise in Psalm CXXXIV: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. [Col. 0764B] They have a mouth and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear [Note: [Col. 0764D] “they do not hear; they have nostrils and will not smell; they have hands and will not feel; they have feet and will not walk” Bod. 1. Cott. Voss. 3.]. For there is no breath in their mouth. May those who make them become like them [Note: [Col. 0764D] “May all who make them be like them” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Thu. Corb.], and all who trust in them [Note: [Col. 0764D] “make them. Likewise” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.]” (Ps. CXXXIV, 15–18). Likewise in Psalm XCV: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. XCV, 5). Likewise in Exodus: “You shall not make gods of silver or gold for yourselves” (Exod. XX, 23). And again: “You shall not make an idol for yourself, nor the likeness of anything” (ibid. XX, 4). Likewise in Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord: Do not walk according to the ways of the nations, for they fear those things in their outward forms, because the ordinances of the nations are empty. Wood cut from the forest is the work of a craftsman; overlaid with gold and silver, they are beautifully fashioned. They have secured them with hammers and nails, and they shall not move, because they can be fastened down. Silver plating is brought from Tarshish; gold comes from Moab. All are the works of craftsmen. They will clothe it in blue and purple. They will lift them up and carry them, because they cannot walk. Do not fear them, because they do no harm, and there is no good in them. Say this: ‘The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from beneath this heaven.’ Heaven shuddered at this and recoiled with far greater violence, says the Lord. My people have done these wicked things. They have abandoned the fountain of living water and dug for themselves worn-out pits that could not hold water. Your love has scourged you, and your wickedness will accuse you. Know and see that it will be bitter for you that you have abandoned me, says the Lord your God, and have not hoped [Col. 0764D] in me, says the Lord your God; for forever you have afflicted my yoke and broken your bonds, and [Col. 0765A] you said: ‘I shall not serve, but I shall go upon every high mountain, upon every lofty hill, and beneath every shady tree. There I shall be put to shame in fornication.’ They said to wood and stone, ‘You are my father,’ and to stone, ‘You begot me.’ And they turned their back to me, and not their face” (Jer. X, 2–5, 9, 11; II, 12, 13, 19, 20, 27). In Isaiah: “The dragon has fallen or been broken apart. Their carved images have become like beasts and cattle. You shall carry 322 them bound upon the neck like a burden, toiling and hungry and unable” (Isa. XLVI, 1, 2, 5). And again: “Gathered together, they will not be able to be saved from war. They themselves have been led captive with you” (Jer. LI, 15–18). And again: “To whom have you likened me? Look and understand that you err in heart, you who pour gold from a bag and weigh silver in a balance, hiring craftsmen by weight. [Col. 0765B] They made things fashioned by hand; bowing down, they worshiped it, lifted it upon their shoulders, and thus walked. But if they set those things down, they will remain in place and not move; those who cry out to them will not be heard, and they will not save them from evils.” Likewise in Jeremiah: “The Lord, who made heaven and earth, established the terrestrial globe by his power; in his wisdom he stretched out heaven and the multitude of waters in heaven. He brought clouds from the end of the earth, lightning in the clouds, and brought forth the winds from his storehouses. Every human being has been rendered foolish by his own knowledge; every craftsman has been confounded by his carved images, because what he cast is falsehood. There is no breath in them. The enclosed works have been emptied; at the time of their visitation they shall perish.” And in Revelation: “And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet. And I heard one voice from the four corners of the golden ark that is before God saying [Col. 0765C] to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: ‘Release the four angels bound at the great river Euphrates.’ And the four angels were released, who had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year, to kill a third part of humankind; and the number of the mounted armies was two myriads of myriads (*dismyriades myriadōn*). I heard their number. And thus in the vision I saw the horses and those seated upon them, wearing breastplates of fire, blue, and sulfur; and the heads of the horses—and from their mouths came fire and smoke and sulfur. By these three plagues a third part of humankind was killed, by the fire and smoke and sulfur that came from their mouths; it is also in their tails. For their tails are like serpents, having heads, and with them they do harm. And the rest of humankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons [Col. 0765D] and idols—that is, images of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood—which can neither see nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders.” [Col. 0766A] Likewise there: “And a third angel followed them, saying in a loud voice: ‘If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives the inscription upon his forehead or upon his hand, he shall drink of the wine of his wrath and shall be punished with fire and sulfur before the eyes of the holy angels and before the eyes of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torments shall ascend forever and ever’” (Rev. IX, 1, 13–21; XIV, 9–14).

## CHAPTER LX.—AN EXCESSIVE DESIRE FOR FOOD IS NOT TO BE PURSUED

In Isaiah: “Let us eat [Note: [Col. 0765D] “Let us not say: Let us eat and” NC. 1.] and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. This sin shall not be forgiven you until you die” (Isa. XXII, 13, 14). Likewise in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0765D] “Exodus: The people sat down” Bod. 1.]: [Col. 0766B] “And the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose [Note: [Col. 0765D] “rose up” Thu. Voss. 3.] to play” (Exod. XXXII, 6). Paul in First Corinthians: “Food does not commend us to God; neither shall we abound if we eat [Note: [Col. 0765D] “have eaten” Thu.], nor shall we be in want [Note: [Col. 0765D] “shall we fail” Bod. 3.] if we do not eat” (I Cor. VIII, 8). And again: “When you come together [Note: [Col. 0765D] “When you have come together” Lam. NC. 1.] to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry [Note: [Col. 0765D] “should be hungry” Bod. 1, 3.], let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment [Note: [Col. 0765D] “into judgment” Bod. 1, 3, 4.]” (I Cor. XI, 33, 34). Likewise to the Romans: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV, 17). In [Note: [Col. 0765D] “Likewise in the Gospel” Bod. 1, 4.] the Gospel according to John: “I have food [Note: [Col. 0765D] “I have food to eat” Corb. NC. 2.] that you do not know. My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete [Note: [Col. 0765D] “that I may complete” NC. 2.] his work” (John IV, 32, 34).

## CHAPTER LXI.—THE DESIRE TO POSSESS, AND MONEY, ARE NOT TO BE PURSUED

[Col. 0766C]

In Solomon, in Ecclesiasticus: “He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver” (Ecclus. V, 9). Likewise in Proverbs: “He who hoards grain is cursed among the people. But a blessing is upon the head of him who shares it [Note: [Col. 0766D] “who shares with him” Bod. 1.]” (Prov. XI, 26). Likewise in Isaiah: “Woe to those who [Note: [Col. 0766D] “Woe to those who” Cott.] join house [Note: [Col. 0766D] “joins house” Bod. 1.] to house [Note: [Col. 0766D] “to house, estate to estate” Lin. Corb.] and connect field [Note: [Col. 0766D] “field to field” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 3, 4. Thu.] with field, so that they take something away from their neighbor [Note: [Col. 0766D] “their neighbors” Bod. 2, 3. Corb. “of one’s neighbor” Bod. 1, 4.]. Will you 323 dwell alone upon the earth?” (Isa. V, 3). Likewise in Zephaniah: “They shall build houses and not inhabit them [Note: [Col. 0766D] “shall not dwell in them” Lam. NC. 1, 2. Bod. Cott.], and shall plant vineyards and not drink their wine, because the day of the Lord is near” (Zeph. I, 13, 14). Likewise in the Gospel according to Luke: “For what does it profit a person to gain the whole world, but [Col. 0766D] lose himself [Note: [Col. 0766D] “if he should suffer the loss of his soul” NC. 2.]?” (Luke IX, 25). And again: “But the Lord said to him: ‘Fool, this very night your soul is demanded [Note: [Col. 0766D] “your soul is demanded” Lam. NC. 1.] of you [Note: [Col. 0766D] “your soul from you” Lin.]. Therefore, whose shall the things be that you have prepared [Note: [Col. 0766D] “you prepared” Lam.]?’” (Luke XII, 20). And [Col. 0767A] again: “Remember that you received good things [Note: [Col. 0767C] “you received good things” Lam. NC. 1.] in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things [Note: [Col. 0767C] “but Lazarus evil things” NC. 1, 2.]. But now he is entreated here [reading uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0767C] “he rejoices here” Lam. Cott. “he rests here” Bod. 1. “he is comforted here” Bod. 2. Corb.], while you are in pain” (Luke XVI, 25). And in the Acts of the Apostles: “But Peter said to him: ‘Silver and gold I do not have. What I do have, however, I give you: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene [Note: [Col. 0767C] “the Nazarean” Thu.], rise and walk.’ And taking hold of his right hand [Note: [Col. 0767C] “taking his hand” Lin.], he raised [Note: [Col. 0767C] “lifted” Thu.] him up” (Acts III, 6). Likewise [Note: [Col. 0767C] “Likewise Paul” Bod. 2.] in First Timothy: “We brought nothing into this world, and indeed we can take nothing away [Note: [Col. 0767C] “we can take away” Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Thu. Lam. Voss. 3. “we shall be able to take away” Cott.]. Therefore, having sustenance and covering, let us be content with these. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation [Note: [Col. 0767C] “fall into the snares of temptations” Corb. “into the snare of the devil” NC. 2. “the devil’s trap” Cott.] and a trap and many harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and ruin. For covetousness is the root of all evils; by pursuing it, some have made shipwreck [Col. 0767B] of the faith and have pierced themselves with many sorrows” (I Tim. VI, 7–10).

## CHAPTER LXII.—MARRIAGE IS NOT TO BE CONTRACTED WITH GENTILES

In Tobit: “Take a wife from the offspring of your kindred, and do not take a foreign woman [Note: [Col. 0767C] “a foreign wife” Bod. 1, 4. Voss. 3. Thu.] who is not from the tribe of your kindred” (Tob. IV, 12). Likewise in Genesis: Abraham sends his servant to take Rebecca from his own offspring [Note: [Col. 0767C] “that Rebecca might be taken” Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Thu.] for his son Isaac (Gen. XIV). Likewise in Ezra: When the Jews were being laid waste, it was not enough for God unless they abandoned their foreign wives together with the children whom they had fathered by them (I Esd. X). Likewise in Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “A woman is bound [Note: [Col. 0767C] “A woman is tied” NC. 2.] for as long as her husband lives. But if he has fallen asleep, she is free [Col. 0767C] to marry whomever [Note: [Col. 0767C] “she is free; whomever” Voss. 3. Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, [Col. 0767D] 2, 4.] she wishes [Note: [Col. 0768C] “whomever she shall wish” Thu. Corb.], only in the Lord. But she will be happier [Note: [Col. 0768C] “more blessed” Bod. 1. NC. 2.] if she remains thus [Note: [Col. 0768C] “remains. Likewise on this same subject in First Corinthians” Bod. 1, 3, 4.]” (I Cor. VII, 39, 40). And [Col. 0768A] again: “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I take the members of Christ [Note: [Col. 0768C] “Shall I take the members of Christ” Cott. “Taking, therefore” Bod. 2.] and make them members of a prostitute [Note: [Col. 0768C] “members of a fornicating harlot” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 1. Cott. Voss. 3.]? By no means. Or do you not know that those who are joined [Note: [Col. 0768C] “those who are joined” Bod. 2, 4. Thu. Corb. “he who adheres to a harlot” Voss. 3.] to a prostitute are one body? For the two shall be in one flesh. But he who joins himself [Note: [Col. 0768C] “those who join themselves” Cott.] to the Lord is one spirit [Note: [Col. 0768C] “are in one spirit” Cott.]” (ibid. VI, 15–17). Likewise in Second Corinthians: “Do not be joined with unbelievers. For what participation is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship has light [Note: [Col. 0768C] “the light” Voss. 3.] with darkness?” (II Cor. VI, 14). Likewise concerning Solomon in Third Kings: “And the foreign wives turned his heart away after their gods” (III Kings XI, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0767D]

**CHAPTER LXIII.—Of fornication.** Sometimes *fornication* is used improperly, as in Gratian, 31, question 1, chapter *Hac ratione*, where second marriages are said to be true fornication, and it is immediately added that this fornication is honorable. This is true. Yet Michael Siricius, as opponents of clerical celibacy are accustomed to do, eagerly seized upon these words as a weapon against our customs in the preface to the book he wrote *On Having Only One Wife*, in order to show that among us there is some honorable prostitution, and consequently that, according to our judgment, prostitution is not a sin but a virtue. It is evident that these statements were made with great vehemence of intemperance; for that passage does not prove this, but only that the manner of life is honorable which the author, out of devotion to chastity, chose to call fornication, although it is not truly fornication but the lawful union of male and female. For both in the canons of Saint Patrick, bishop of the Irish, and in the Penitential of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, the word *fornication* is used generally for the act of sexual intercourse itself. And Saint Augustine, in chapter six of the book *On the Good of Marriage*, says that even in the more immoderate demanding of the carnal debt, although depraved habits drive them to such intercourse, marriage nevertheless protects them from adultery or fornication.

[Col. 0769D] **For the word of the cross.** See Massuet on the first book of Irenaeus, p. 17.]

## CHAPTER LXIII.—FORNICATION IS A SERIOUS OFFENSE

In Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Every offense whatsoever that a person commits is outside the body. [Col. 0768B] But one who fornicates sins against his own body. You are not your own, for you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear the Lord in your body” (I Cor. VI, 18–20).

## CHAPTER LXIV.—WHICH THINGS ARE CARNAL AND PRODUCE DEATH, AND WHICH ARE SPIRITUAL AND LEAD TO LIFE

Paul to the Galatians: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these oppose one another [Note: [Col. 0768C] “For they are opposed” Voss. 3.], so that you do not do the very things you wish. But the works of the flesh are manifest; they are [Note: [Col. 0768C] “fornication, shamelessness” Cott.]: adulteries, fornications, impurities, obscenities, idolatries, sorceries, murders, enmities, contentions, jealousies [Note: [Col. 0768C] “jealousy, anger, strife, fits of rage” Cott.], fits of rage, provocations, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, revelries, [Col. 0768C] and things like these [Note: [Col. 0768C] “things like these. For those who do such things” Lam. Lin. NC. 1, 2. Bod. Thu. Corb.]. I warn you [Note: [Col. 0768D] “I warn you, as I warned you before, that” Cott.] that those who do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the spirit [Col. 0769A] is charity, joy, [Note: [Col. 0769C] “peace, patience, kindness, goodness” Cott.] peace, magnanimity, goodness, [Note: [Col. 0769C] “faith, modesty, gentleness, self-control, chastity, love; against such things there is no law” Cott.] faith, gentleness, self-control, chastity. For those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0769C] “with its passions and desires” Cott.]” (Gal. V, 17, 19–24).

## CHAPTER LXV.—ALL OFFENSES ARE PUT AWAY IN BAPTISM

In Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who desire males 324 [Note: [Col. 0769C] “men who lie with males” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2. Cott. [Col. 0769D] Voss. 3.], nor thieves, nor defrauders, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers [Note: [Col. 0769D] “nor the rapacious shall inherit the kingdom of God” Cott.] shall attain the kingdom of God. And such indeed you were; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified [Note: [Col. 0769D] “but you have been sanctified, but you have been justified” Lam. Lin. NC. 1, 2.] in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (I Cor. VI, 9–11).

## CHAPTER LXVI.—GOD’S DISCIPLINE IS TO BE OBSERVED IN ECCLESIASTICAL PRECEPTS

[Col. 0769B]

In Jeremiah: “And I shall give you shepherds according to my heart, and they shall feed the sheep, feeding them [Note: [Col. 0769D] “shall feed you with discipline” Cott. Voss. 3.] with discipline” (Jer. III, 15). Likewise in Solomon, in Proverbs: “Son, do not neglect God’s discipline, nor lose heart when corrected by him. For God corrects the one whom he loves” (Prov. III, 11, 12). Likewise in Psalm II: “Hold fast [Note: [Col. 0769D] “Embrace discipline” Bod. 2.] to discipline, lest the Lord perhaps become angry and you perish from the right way [Note: [Col. 0769D] “perish from the just way” Cott.]. When his wrath swiftly blazes against you, blessed are all who trust in him [Note: [Col. 0769D] “Happy are all who trust in him” Cott. Corb.]” (Ps. II, 12). Likewise in Psalm XLIX: “But to the sinner God says: ‘Why do you expound my righteous decrees [Note: [Col. 0769D] “God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts?” Cott. “Why” Voss. 3.], and take up my covenant in your mouth? Yet you hated discipline and cast [Note: [Col. 0769D] “threw . . . behind you” Cott.] my words behind you’?” [Col. 0769C] (Ps. XLIX, 16, 17). Likewise in the Wisdom of Solomon: “Unhappy is the person who rejects discipline” (Wisd. II, 11).

## CHAPTER LXVII.—IT WAS FORETOLD THAT THEY WOULD REJECT SOUND DISCIPLINE

Paul in Second Timothy: “There shall be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires [Note: [Col. 0769D] “walking according to their desires” Lam. NC. 1.] they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their hearing and scratching their ears. They will turn their hearing away from the truth [Note: [Col. 0769D] “turning their hearing away” Lam. Bod. 2. NC. 1. Corb.], but will turn toward fables” (II Tim. IV, 3, 4).

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—ONE MUST WITHDRAW FROM A PERSON WHO LIVES DISORDERLY [Note: [Col. 0769D] “walks disorderly” Corb.] AND CONTRARY TO DISCIPLINE [Note: [Col. 0769D] “lives contrary to God’s discipline” Lam. NC. 1.]

[Col. 0770A]

Paul to the Thessalonians: “But we command you in the name [Note: [Col. 0770C] “you, brothers, in the name” Lam. Lin. NC. 1.] of our Lord [Note: [Col. 0770C] Thus the Greek, Lam. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2. Thu. Corb. Voss. 3. The printed editions omit “of our Lord.”] Jesus Christ to withdraw from all brothers who walk disorderly and not according to the tradition they received from us” (II Thess. III, 6). Likewise in Psalm XLIX: “If you saw a thief, you ran together [Note: [Col. 0770C] “you joined him” Lam. NC. 1. Thu. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4.] with him, and with adulterers [Note: [Col. 0770C] “among adulterers” Bod. 4. “with adulterers” Lam. [Col. 0770D] NC. 1. Bod. 2. Thu. Corb.] you placed your portion” (Ps. XLIX, 13).

## CHAPTER LXIX.—THE KINGDOM OF GOD DOES NOT CONSIST IN THE WISDOM OF THE WORLD OR IN ELOQUENCE, BUT IN FAITH IN THE CROSS AND IN THE POWER OF ONE’S WAY OF LIFE

In Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Christ sent me to proclaim, not in wisdom of speech, lest [Col. 0770B] the cross of Christ be made empty. For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to those who are saved it is the power of God. For it is written: ‘I shall destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent.’ Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator [Note: [Col. 0770D] “investigator of this world” Lam. NC. 1.] of this age? Has God not made foolish [Note: [Col. 0770D] “made the wisdom foolish” Cott. Voss. 3. “God made it foolishness” Bod. 1.] the wisdom of this world? For since [Note: [Col. 0770D] “Since the world did not know the wisdom of God through its own folly, it pleased God through foolishness” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2. “through its own wisdom” Cott.] in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of proclamation to save those who believe. For the Jews desire signs [Note: [Col. 0770D] “ask for signs” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.], and the Greeks seek prudence [Note: [Col. 0770D] “the Greeks seek wisdom” Cott. Voss. 3.]. But we proclaim Christ crucified: indeed a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 17–24). And again: “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among [Col. 0770C] you thinks himself wise, let him become a fool to this world [Note: [Col. 0770D] “a fool to this age” Bod. 1, 3, 4. Voss. 3.], so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. For it is written: ‘You shall rebuke [Note: [Col. 0770D] “Rebuking” Lin. NC. 1. “I shall rebuke” Morel.] the wise in their craftiness’” (I Cor. II, 18–20). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise [Note: [Col. 0770D] “of wise men” Lam.], that they are foolish [Note: [Col. 0770D] “that they are vain” Bod. 1.]” (Ps. XCIII, 11).

## CHAPTER LXX.—PARENTS ARE TO BE OBEYED

In Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians: “Children, be obedient to your parents, for this is right. Honor your father and your mother [Note: [Col. 0770D] “and your mother, which” Bod. 1, 2, 4.], which is the first commandment [Col. 0771A] with a promise [Note: [Col. 0771D] “the first with a renewed promise” Lam. Lin. Bod. 1, 2. Voss. 3.], that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Eph. VI, 1, 7, 9).

## CHAPTER LXXI.—FATHERS [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Parents also” Bod. 2, 4.] ALSO OUGHT NOT TO BE HARSH TOWARD THEIR CHILDREN

Likewise there: “And you [Note: [Col. 0771D] “You fathers” Thu. Voss. 3. Corb. “Parents” Oxon.], fathers, do not provoke [Note: [Col. 0771D] “provoke to anger” NC. 1.] your children to anger, but nourish them in the discipline [Note: [Col. 0771D] “with discipline” Cott. “in the discipline and correction” Lam. Bod. 2. NC. 1. Voss. 3.] and correction of the Lord” (Eph. VI, 4).

## CHAPTER LXXII.—SERVANTS, ONCE THEY HAVE BELIEVED, OUGHT TO SERVE THEIR EARTHLY MASTERS ALL THE MORE

In Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians: “Servants [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Servants of Christ” Lam. NC. 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. Voss. 3.], obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, 325 and in the sincerity of your heart as though obeying Christ, not serving only under observation, [Col. 0771B] as people-pleasers, but as servants of God” (Eph. VI, 5).

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—LIKEWISE, MASTERS OUGHT TO BE GENTLER

Likewise there [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Likewise there” is absent from the printed editions, which transpose the word “there.” I restore it from Lam. NC. 1. Voss. 3. Lin.]: “And you, masters, do the same toward them, relaxing your anger [Note: [Col. 0771D] “setting aside anger” Lam. Cott.], knowing that both your [Note: [Col. 0771D] “your own” Voss. 3.] and their Master is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him [Note: [Col. 0771D] “there is none before him” NC. 2.]” (Eph. VI, 1, 7, 8).

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—ALL WIDOWS WHO HAVE BEEN TESTED ARE TO BE HONORED

In Paul’s First Epistle to Timothy: “Honor widows who are truly widows. But the widow who lives in luxury is dead while living [Note: [Col. 0771D] “is dead while alive” Bod. 1, 4. Corb.]” (I Tim. V, 3). And again: “But pass over younger widows [Note: [Col. 0772D] “Avoid younger widows” Cott. “Omit” Voss. 3.]. For when they have become self-indulgent [Note: [Col. 0772D] “have become self-indulgent” Benev. Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 3, 4. “have lived in luxury” Voss. 3.] [Col. 0771C] against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring judgment because they have rejected their first faith” (I Tim. V, 11).

The Apostle in First Timothy: “If anyone does not take care of his own, and especially of those of his household, he denies the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V, 8). On this same subject in Isaiah: “If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise [Note: [Col. 0772D] “shall have despised” Bod. 1. Voss. 3.] the members of your own stock” (Isa. LVIII, 7). [Col. 0771D] In First Timothy: “Do not receive an accusation against an elder” (I Tim. V, 19).

[Col. 0772A]

In Paul’s First Epistle to Timothy: “Rebuke those who sin before everyone, so that the others also may be afraid” (I Tim. V, 20).

On this same subject in John’s Epistle: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II, 19). [Col. 0772B]

Likewise in the Gospel according to Matthew: “Blessed [Note: [Col. 0772D] “Happy are the pure” Lam. Thu. Corb. Lin. NC. 1. Bod. 1, 2, 4.] are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). Likewise in Psalm XXIII: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? One innocent in hands and pure in heart [Note: [Col. 0772D] “pure of heart” Bod. 4.]” (Ps. XXIII, 3, 4).

Likewise in Third Kings: “And the Lord stirred up Satan against Solomon himself” (III Kings XI, 23). Likewise in Job [Note: [Col. 0772D] “In all things God first” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 2.], God first permitted it, and only then was it allowed to the devil (Job II, 6). And in the Gospel the Lord first [Note: [Col. 0772D] “first gave warning” Bod. 1.] permitted it, saying to Judas: “What you are doing, do more quickly [Note: [Col. 0772D] “do more swiftly” Lam. NC. 1. Bod. 4. Cott. “swiftly” Lin. “sooner” NC. 2. Bod. 3.]” (John XIII, 27). Likewise in Solomon, in Proverbs: “The heart of the king is in God’s hand” (Prov. XXI, 1).

[Col. 0772D] In Deuteronomy: “You shall not interpret omens [Note: [Col. 0772D] “You shall neither interpret omens nor practice augury” Cott.], nor practice augury” (Deut. XVIII, 10).

In Leviticus: “You shall rise before an elder and honor the person [Note: [Col. 0773D] “show honor to the person” Cott.] of the presbyter [Note: [Col. 0773D] “of your presbyter” Bod. 2.]” (Lev. XIX, 32).

[Col. 0773B] In Ecclesiasticus, in Solomon: “He who splits wood will be endangered by it, if the iron should fall out” [p. 326] (Ecclus. X, 9). [Col. 0773C]

In the Gospel according to Matthew: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X, 16). And again: “You are the salt of the earth. In Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Temptation will not overtake you [Note: [Col. 0774D] “Has overtaken.” Oxon. “Will overtake.” Thu. Corb. “Has seized.” Bod. 1.], except what is human. [Col. 0774C]

In Leviticus: “Any person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of well-being, which belongs to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him—that person shall perish from [Col. 0775A] his people” (Lev. ### CHAPTER XCV.—ONE MUST LIVE IN FELLOWSHIP WITH THE GOOD [Note: [Col. 0775D] “With the good.” Lam. NC. 1. Voss. 3.] [Note: [Col. 0775D] “One must associate.” Mor. Man.], BUT AVOID THE EVIL

### CHAPTER XCIX.—THAT JUDGMENT WILL BE ACCORDING TO THE TIMES: EITHER BY EQUITY BEFORE THE LAW, OR BY THE LAW AFTER MOSES

Paul to the Romans: “All who have sinned without the law will perish without the law [Note: [Col. 0775D] “All who have sinned unjustly, unjustly.” Lam. Lin. NC. [Col. 0776D] 1, 2. Bod. 1, 2, 4. Voss. 3.]; and all who have sinned under the law will also be judged through the law” (Rom. II, 12).

### CHAPTER C.—THE GRACE OF GOD IS TO BE GIVEN FREELY

# BOOK CONCERNING PUBLIC SHOWS

[Note: [Col. 0779D]

^604 **CONCERNING PUBLIC SHOWS.**—The first edition of this book was issued from the press of Paulus Manutius. Old copies of it are extremely rare. Morellius, Goulartius, and Rigaltius possessed none, nor did the English scholars; I possessed two, one from the library of the monastery of Saint-Denis at Reims, the other, formerly belonging to the Collège de Foix, from the Colbert Library. On the authority of these manuscripts I corrected this book, adding [Col. 0780D] nothing of my own and changing nothing. Learned men, however, hold various opinions concerning its author. Some, by a decisive judgment, deny that it belongs to Cyprian; on the other hand, several learned and erudite men—namely, the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, Jacques Pamèle, Pierre Faber of Saint-Jory, Jacques Sirmond, Didier Hérault, and perhaps others—cite it as an authentic [Col. 0781D] work of Cyprian. Even the most illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine appears to have considered it Cyprian’s. For my part, amid this diversity of opinions and prejudging no one’s position, I have thought that it ought not rashly to be separated from the authentic works of the holy Martyr, especially since some have observed that it does not differ from his style as greatly as certain people have supposed.]

(C, G, S)\*

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0779D]

The author first argues against those who attempted to defend the public shows of the pagans by the authority of Scripture. Although they are nowhere prohibited in explicit [Col. 0780D] words of Scripture, he nevertheless proves that they are condemned by the prohibition of idolatry, since every kind of show without exception was consecrated to idols. Then, proceeding through the individual kinds of games, he discusses somewhat more fully than in the second Epistle to Donatus the dangers inherent in watching them, especially those through which, as he says, “instruction in obscenity is imparted by images of lust.” Finally, he briefly enumerates the spectacles worthy of a Christian, with which he ought rightly to delight himself. He undoubtedly imitated Tertullian’s book *Concerning Public Shows*, which Tertullian indicates in one place that he wrote both in Greek and in Latin; that work is so replete with everything pertinent to this subject that it may serve as a commentary whenever the diversity of public shows is to be discussed.

[Note: [Col. 0781D]

**I.—To the people standing firm in the Gospel.** Thus, if its title is authentic, the book of Novatian *On Jewish Foods* is inscribed: “To the people persevering in the Gospel.”

[Col. 0782D] **Occasion for writing.** Several Epistles of the holy Martyr were written with the same intention.

**In the conduct of life.** The Foix manuscript reads, “in righteous deeds.”

**Vices.** The same manuscript reads, “disgraceful acts.”

**As innocent.** The old manuscripts read, “innocent and without fault.”]

## I

**CYPRIAN, TO THE PEOPLE STANDING FIRM IN THE GOSPEL, GREETINGS.**

Just as I am deeply saddened and my spirit is grievously afflicted whenever no occasion for writing to you presents itself—for it is a loss to me not to converse with you—so nothing restores such joy and gladness to me as when an occasion once more arises. [Col. 0781B] I consider myself to be with you when I speak to you by letter.

Although, therefore, I know that you are certain that matters are as I say and that you doubt nothing concerning the truth of my words, nevertheless even the evidence confirms the sincerity of the matter. For since no occasion whatsoever is passed over, my affection is thereby proved.

Although, then, I am certain that you are no less serious in the conduct of life than faithful in the sacrament, nevertheless there is no lack of flattering defenders of vices and indulgent advocates who lend authority to vices and—what is worse—turn the judgment of the heavenly Scriptures into an advocacy of crimes, as though the pleasure of shows were sought as an innocent means of relaxing [Col. 0781C] the mind. Indeed, the vigor of ecclesiastical discipline has been so enervated and is being driven so far toward what is worse by every kind of moral languor that now vices are given not merely an excuse but authority. It has therefore seemed good to me now, in a few words, not to instruct you, but to admonish you who are already instructed, lest wounds that have been badly bound break through the scar of an apparent healing. For no evil is more difficult to extinguish than one that possesses easy means of return, while it is both defended by the consent of the multitude and caressed by excuses.

[Note: [Col. 0782D]

**II.—From the heavenly Scriptures.** Tertullian, Cyprian’s teacher, treats this argument in the same way in his book *Concerning Public Shows*.

**Nabla.** See Hospinianus, book II *On Temples*, chapter 23, p. 309.]

## II

Are faithful people—people who claim for themselves the authority of the Christian name—not ashamed, not ashamed, I say, to defend from the heavenly Scriptures the vain superstitions of the pagans mingled with public shows, and to confer divine authority upon idolatry? For how can something performed by pagans [Col. 0781D] in honor of some idol be attended as a spectacle by faithful Christians, pagan idolatry be thereby upheld, and the true and divine religion be trampled underfoot in contempt of God?

I am overcome with shame at recounting their objections [Col. 0782A] and defenses in this matter. “Where,” they say, “are these things written? Where are they forbidden? Otherwise, Elijah too is Israel’s charioteer, and David himself danced before the ark. We read of harps (*nabla*), lyres (*cynarae*), cymbals, drums, pipes, zithers, and dances. The Apostle also presents the contest of boxing and of our wrestling against the spiritual forces of wickedness. Again, when he draws examples from the stadium, he also sets forth crowns as prizes. Why, then, should a faithful Christian not be permitted to watch what the divine Scriptures were permitted to record?”

At this point I might reasonably say that it would have been far better for such people to know no Scriptures at all than to read the Scriptures in this way. For words and examples that were set down to encourage evangelical virtue are transferred into defenses of vice. These things were written not so that they might be watched, but so that greater [Col. 0782B] urgency might be aroused in our minds regarding profitable things, since among the pagans there is such great urgency regarding things that are not profitable.

## III

It is therefore an argument for arousing [p. 340] virtue, not permission or freedom to watch pagan error. Its purpose is that the spirit may thereby be kindled more strongly toward evangelical virtue for the sake of divine rewards, since through the calamity of every labor and sorrow it is granted to attain eternal benefits.

For the fact that Elijah is Israel’s charioteer offers no defense for watching circus races: he never raced in any circus. And the fact that David performed dances in the sight of God is of no help to faithful Christians sitting in a theater: he did not dance out a tale of Greek lust while contorting his limbs with obscene movements. Harps, lyres, pipes, drums, and zithers served the Lord, not idols.

Let no precedent, therefore, be pleaded for watching unlawful things: through the devil’s craftsmanship, things derived from holy uses have been transformed into unlawful ones. Let shame, then, prescribe a rule for these people, even if the holy Scriptures cannot. For Scripture sometimes exercises greater foresight through what it commands. Out of regard for modesty, it prohibited more because it remained silent. If truth had descended so far as to address these things explicitly, it would have formed the worst judgment of its faithful. For even in commandments certain things are generally left unsaid to greater advantage: often, when they are forbidden, they call attention to themselves. Thus, even while they are passed over in silence, they are written in the Scriptures; severity speaks in place of commandments, and reason teaches what Scripture left unspoken.

Let each person deliberate only with himself and converse with the character proper to his profession, and he will never do anything unseemly. For the conscience that owes an account to no one other than itself will carry greater weight.

[Col. 0782D]

[Note: [Col. 0783D]

**IV.—The mother of all games.** See Ovid, book V of the *Fasti*, and Pierre Faber of Saint-Jory, book IV of the *Agonisticon*, chapter 3, where he explains these matters at length. See also Tertullian’s book *Concerning Public Shows*.

**Romulus to Consus.** See above, p. 569.

**Songs.** The Foix manuscript reads “lamentations.” Faber, chapter 4, thinks that what follows afterward derives almost entirely from a gloss.]

## IV

What did Scripture forbid? It forbade people to watch what it prohibits them from doing. It condemned, I say, all these kinds of shows when it abolished idolatry, [Col. 0783A] the mother of all games, from which these monsters of vanity and frivolity arose.

For what spectacle is without an idol? What game is without a sacrifice? What contest is not consecrated to a dead person? What is a faithful Christian doing among these things? If he flees idolatry, why does one who is now holy take pleasure in criminal things? Why does he approve superstitions contrary to God—superstitions which he loves while watching them?

Moreover, let him know that all these things are inventions of demons, not of God. He shamelessly exorcizes demons in the Church while praising their pleasures at public shows. Since, when he once renounced the devil, the entire bond with him was broken in Baptism, by going to a spectacle of the devil after coming to Christ he renounces Christ as though Christ were the devil.

Idolatry, as I have already said, is the mother of all games. To induce faithful Christians to come to her, she entices [Col. 0783B] them through the pleasure of eyes and ears. Romulus first consecrated circus games to Consus, as though to the god of counsel, for the purpose of carrying off the Sabine women. The other theatrical games, however, were later introduced to distract the people when famine had seized the City; they were dedicated to Ceres and Liber, and subsequently to the other idols and to the dead.

Those Greek contests—whether in songs, strings, voices, or feats of strength—have various demons as their presiding powers. Whatever else either moves the eyes of the spectators or charms their ears, if investigated together with its origin and institution, displays as its cause either an idol, a demon, or a dead person. Thus the devil, that craftsman, because he knew that idolatry in its naked form was abhorred, mingled it with public shows so that it might be loved through pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0783D]

**V.—The ancestors of Christ.** Thus the Foix manuscript. Another manuscript and the Manutius edition read “parts,” through an evident error: the comparison is between the genealogy of a horse and the genealogy of Christ. This Christian knows the genealogy of a horse but does not know the genealogy of Christ. A shameful and pitiable thing.

**The holy one with himself.** The Foix manuscript reads, “with himself the body which is holy.” The Reims manuscript and the editions read, “with himself the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 0784D] **Dismissed from the Lord’s service.** The manuscript from which this book was published by Manutius did not contain the words “from the Lord’s service,” and therefore an asterisk was placed in that edition to indicate that something was missing here. Pamèle commends a manuscript in which “dismissed from the Lord’s service” was written, as it is in the Reims manuscript; the Foix manuscript has “having lost the Lord’s service,” through a copyist’s error.

**Carrying the Eucharist.** See above, p. 464, and the notes on the book *On the Good of Patience*.

**Christ’s holy body.** Corrected from the Foix manuscript.]

## V

Why is it necessary to pursue the matter further, or to describe the monstrous kinds of sacrifices [Col. 0783C] performed at the games? Among them, sometimes even a human being becomes the victim through the priest’s act of brigandage: blood, still hot from the throat, is caught in a foaming bowl while it is still seething, and is cruelly offered by being thrown into the face of an idol as though it were thirsty. Amid the spectators’ pleasures, the death of certain persons is dispensed, so that through a bloody spectacle people may learn to behave savagely—as though a person’s own private madness were insufficient unless he also learned it publicly.

[p. 341] A rabid beast is reared as a luxury for the punishment of a human being, so that it may rage more cruelly beneath the spectators’ eyes. The trainer instructs the beast, which perhaps would have been more merciful had a still more cruel master not taught it to be savage.

Therefore, to pass over in silence whatever idolatry commends more broadly, how vain the contests themselves are: quarrels over colors, rivalries in races, partisanship in honors, rejoicing because one horse was faster, grieving [Col. 0783D] because another was slower, counting the years of livestock, knowing the consuls, learning ages, identifying pedigrees, recalling the grandsires and even the great-grandsires! [Col. 0784A]

How completely idle this occupation is—or rather, how shameful and dishonorable! I mean the man who can calculate from memory the entire lineage of a breed of horses and recite it with great speed and without making a mistake in the spectacle. If you question him about the ancestors of Christ, he does not know them, so that the very knowledge he does possess is all the more unfortunate. And if I should ask him again about something pertaining to a particular spectacle, he does not know—or is still more unfortunate if he does know. And if I should ask him in turn by what road he reached a particular spectacle, he will confess that it was past brothels, past the naked bodies of prostitutes, past public lust, past public disgrace, past vulgar wantonness, past the common dishonor of all.

Even if I do not charge him with what he perhaps committed, he nevertheless saw what ought not to have been committed, and through lust he led his eyes to a spectacle of idolatry. He dared to take what was holy with him into a brothel, if that were possible. Hurrying to the spectacle, dismissed from the Lord’s service and still carrying with him, as is customary, the Eucharist, that faithless man carried Christ’s holy body among the obscene bodies of prostitutes, meriting greater condemnation from his journey than from the pleasure of the spectacle.

[Note: [Col. 0784D]

**VI.—The twists of plots.** Thus the old manuscripts. Earlier editions read “the twists of the actors,” which makes no sense. See Martini’s *Lexicon* and Gerardus Joannes Vossius’s *Etymologicon of the Latin Language*.

**Amid the laws themselves.** See above, p. 381.

[Col. 0785D] ^605 **Adultery with the eyes.** See above, p. 379.

**Broken in every limb.** See above, p. 380.

**Womanly softness.** See above, p. 381.]

## VI

But, to pass now from this shameless pollution of the stage, I am ashamed to report what is said; I am ashamed even to accuse what is done: the twists of plots, the deceits of adulterers, the immodesty of women, buffoonish jokes, filthy parasites, and even the toga-clad heads of households themselves—now witless, now obscene, foolish in everything, shameless in everything. [Col. 0784C] And although no class or profession of human beings is spared by the speech of these reprobates, people of every class nevertheless assemble for the spectacle. The common disgrace gives pleasure: they come to see, recognize, or learn idle vices. There they flock to the public shame of a brothel, to a school of obscenity, lest anything less be done in private than is learned in public; and amid the very laws themselves, everything forbidden by the laws is taught.

What is a faithful Christian doing among these things, when he is not permitted even to think of vices? Why does he take pleasure in representations of lust, so that, once modesty has been cast aside in their presence, he may become bolder in committing crimes? By growing accustomed to seeing, he also learns to do. Yet those women whom their misfortune has brought down and cast into servitude conceal their public lusts and console their disgrace in hiding places. Even those who have sold their modesty blush [Col. 0784D] to be seen. But this public [Col. 0785A] monstrosity is enacted before everyone’s eyes, and even the obscenity of prostitutes is surpassed. The question was how adultery might be admitted through the eyes. Upon this disgrace another disgrace worthy of it is superimposed: a man broken in all his limbs and enervated beyond womanly softness, whose art consists in expressing words with his hands. And on account of one creature who is somehow neither man nor woman, the whole city is stirred up, so that the fabulous lusts of antiquity may be performed in dance. Thus everything forbidden is so loved that even the things an earlier age had concealed are recalled to the memory of the eyes.

## VII

Lust is not content to employ its own present evils unless it makes into a spectacle for itself that in which an earlier age also went astray. Faithful Christians are not permitted, I say, to attend—absolutely not—even those performers whom [Col. 0785B] Greece, trained everywhere in all its empty arts, sends to entice the ears. One imitates the hoarse, warlike blasts of a trumpet; another regulates mournful sounds by blowing his breath into a pipe; another, competing both with choruses and with the melodious human voice, modulates through the holes of pipes the breath that, straining, he had drawn from his entrails into the upper parts of his body—now pouring it forth, now confining it within and releasing it into the air through particular passages in the holes, now breaking the sound at a finger-joint. He labors to speak with his fingers, ungrateful to the Craftsman who gave him a tongue.

Why should I speak of comic and useless preoccupations? Why of those grand insanities of the tragic voice? Why of strings joined to shouting? Even if these things had not been dedicated to idols, faithful Christians still ought not to approach or behold them; for although [Col. 0785C] they might contain no crime, they contain within themselves the greatest vanity, one scarcely compatible with the faithful.

## VIII

For that other madness of the remaining spectacles is an obvious occupation for idle people. The first victory is for the stomach to have been able to hunger beyond the human measure, under the title of crowned gluttony—a shameful commercial exhibition. The wretched face is hired out to the blows of wounds so that an even more wretched stomach may be fattened. Besides, how foul are those wrestling matches, in which one man, lying beneath another, is entangled in dishonorable embraces and holds! In such a contest, whether one watches or wins, modesty nevertheless has been defeated.

See: another man leaps naked before you; another hurls a brazen discus with all his strength into the air. This is not glory but madness. In short, remove the spectator and you will have abolished the vanity. Faithful Christians must flee these things—as we have already [Col. 0785D] said repeatedly—spectacles so vain, so destructive, so sacrilegious, from which both our eyes and our ears should be guarded. We quickly grow accustomed to what we hear and what we see. For since the human mind is drawn toward the vices themselves, what will it do if it has slippery examples of bodily nature, which falls of its own accord? What will it do [Col. 0786A] if it is actually impelled? The mind must therefore be called away from these things.

## IX

The Christian has better spectacles, if he wishes; he has true and profitable pleasures, if he recognizes himself. And, to omit those things that cannot yet be contemplated, he has this beauty of the world to see and admire. Let him behold the rising of the sun and, again, its setting, which in mutual succession recalls days and nights; the globe of the moon, marking the courses of the seasons by its waxing and waning; the choirs of glittering stars, shining continually from their supreme mobility; the principal divisions of the whole year, apportioned in succession from one extremity to the other; and the days themselves, together with the nights, arranged into intervals of hours; the mass of the earth held in balance with its mountains; flowing rivers with their springs; the outstretched seas with their waves [Col. 0786B] and shores; and meanwhile the air spread between them, equally stable through the supreme harmony and bonds of concord, by its subtlety giving life to all things—now pouring out rain from gathered clouds, now restoring clear weather when its thinness has been renewed. Let him behold, too, the proper inhabitants of all these realms: birds in the air, fish in the waters, and humanity on the earth.

These, I say, and the other works of God should be the spectacles of faithful Christians. What theater constructed by human hands could be compared with these works? Though it be built from great masses of stone, the crests of the mountains are higher; and though its paneled ceilings gleam with gold, they will be surpassed by the brilliance of the stars. Whoever recognizes himself as a son of God will never marvel at human works. A person casts himself down from the summit of his nobility if he can admire anything apart from the Lord.

[Col. 0786C]

> **Note [Col. 0785D]**
>
> **X.—*Detriumphaverat*.** Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*: “We never triumph more completely over them than when we are condemned for our steadfastness in the faith.” Minucius Felix: “They began to worship those whom they had devastated and paraded in triumph.” Thus they also used *depompare* to mean “to subject to insult,” as we have shown by numerous examples in our new collection of Councils, pp. 716, 724. In the old translation of the Sixth Council, session 12, in the letter of Sergius of Constantinople to Pope Honorius, we read: “When he had refuted and publicly disgraced his depraved impiety.”

## X

Let the faithful Christian, I say, devote himself to the sacred Scriptures; there [p. 343] he will find spectacles worthy of the faith. He will see God establishing his world and, together with the other living creatures, making that marvelous structure of the human being, and making it superior. He will behold the world amid its transgressions, righteous shipwrecks, the rewards of the devout, and the punishments of the impious; seas dried up for a people, and again seas of water supplied to a people from a rock. He will behold harvests descending from heaven, not furrowed by the plow; rivers presenting dry crossings when the ranks of their waters have been restrained. He will see faith in certain persons struggling with fire, wild beasts overcome by religion and turned to gentleness. He will contemplate souls recalled even from death itself. He will also consider the marvelous restoration from their tombs to life of the bodies of those already consumed; and amid all these things he will now see a still greater spectacle: that devil who had triumphantly humiliated the whole world lying beneath the feet of Christ. [Col. 0786D]

What a beautiful spectacle this is, brothers; how delightful, how necessary—to contemplate one’s hope continually and to open one’s eyes to one’s salvation! This is a spectacle [Col. 0787A] that can be seen even when the physical eyes have been lost. This is a spectacle presented not by a praetor or consul, but by him who alone exists before all things and above all things—indeed, from whom are all things—the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and honor for ever and ever. I pray that you may always fare well, brothers. Amen.

[Col. 0787]

# BOOK ON THE PRAISE OF MARTYRDOM

> **Note [Col. 0787C]**
>
> **ON THE PRAISE OF MARTYRDOM.—**This book was published by Erasmus from a very corrupt Gembloux manuscript. Erasmus, however, says in his annotations that no one will have so dull a nose as not immediately to perceive that the style of this work differs far and wide from Cyprian’s diction. Baronius, on the contrary, judges it to be Cyprian’s and refutes Erasmus’s opinion concerning the difference of style by an argument drawn from Book IV of Saint Augustine’s *On Christian Doctrine*. From that work he concluded that Cyprian did not always maintain the same manner of speaking: at times, namely, he pursued the sublime and was copious in his abundance of words, while at other times he used a lowly and subdued manner of expression. This is true. Bellarmine also thinks it to be Cyprian’s.
>
> Some infer that this work is not Cyprian’s because it was addressed to Moses and Maximus, and because it is established [Col. 0787D] that Moses died before the election of Pope Cornelius, and therefore before the plague and pestilence that ravaged the entire world in the year 252, on the occasion of which Cyprian wrote his book *On Mortality*. But this argument is of no weight. For we possess many excellent and very ancient manuscripts in which there is no mention of Moses and Maximus, and in which the title of the book is written simply: *Here Begins On the Praise of Martyrdom*, or something similar. The names of Moses and Maximus were therefore added by some scholar who, understanding from the words of this book that the work was addressed to confessors, persuaded himself that they could be none other than Moses, Maximus, and the other confessors to whom Letters XV and XXIV are addressed.
>
> Add in favor of this work that it is consistently found everywhere, in all the ancient manuscripts, among those works of Saint Cyprian about which there is no difficulty concerning whether they are Cyprian’s. Moreover, Florus, deacon of the church of Lyons, transcribed [Col. 0788C] various passages from it in his excerpts from the works of Saint Cyprian, in which he includes no passages that are not genuinely Cyprian’s.
>
> As for the style, I can use the same kind of argument employed by the most learned Jacques de Billy to attribute to Gregory Thaumaturgus the *Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes*, despite the protest of its style: it was found among his authentic works in the Queen’s manuscript, written in capital letters and almost equaling Gregory in antiquity—a fact which, he says, carried great weight with him. So too can I speak of the book *On the Praise of Martyrdom*, which survives in the Séguier manuscript, written in majuscule letters a thousand years ago. I had sixteen old copies of it, against which I corrected the text. I shall not, however, present all their variant readings; I shall note only certain ones that seem to me of some importance.
>
> Above all I shall warn the reader that I do not know by what mischance a large part of this work came to be omitted in the Thuana manuscript and in the Metz manuscript of Saint Arnulf. In these, after the words on page 343, “the capacity is burdened,” much is missing, omitted by the copyists, down to these words on page 343, “the chief point, namely.” Again, through the same error, on page 350, after “the elect are crowned,” the rest is similarly missing through omission by the copyists; and there, to mention this also, those manuscripts read “are tended” instead of “are crowned.” [Col. 0788D]

*(C, G, S)\**

# ARGUMENT

[Col. 0787A]

In an elevated style, the author pursues the praise of martyrdom, treating three matters in particular at length throughout the book: namely, what it is, how great it is, and to what purpose it is profitable. Meanwhile, by beautiful comparisons and by an argument drawn from the funerals that occur every day, he exhorts his readers willingly to undergo death for Christ. Among the virtues of martyrdom he then enumerates this: that the Lord’s propitiation crowns martyrs as exempt from every kind of suffering, so that Christ’s saying about paying to the last farthing does not apply to them.

As their reward, he sets forth both security from the fear of Gehenna and the attainment of eternal life, describing each briefly in a certain poetic manner; then he explains that martyrdom serves as a crown for some, and as redemption from sins for others who are washed in their own blood. Finally, after encouraging them through several scriptural passages to confess the name of Christ, he asks them to remember him when the Lord has begun to honor martyrdom in them, since it is believed that the Lord will not refuse those who make this request.

[Col. 0788A]

> **Note [Col. 0788D]**
>
> **I.—*Animum*.** The Saint-Arnulf and Thuana manuscripts have “by the deliberation of my mind.” The Saint-Denis manuscript of Reims likewise reads this way, except that through a copyist’s error the word “my” is missing. Nicolas Le Fèvre made the same correction in his printed book, in which he noted variant readings from the manuscripts.
>
> [Col. 0789D] **“Capacity in speaking.”** Thus the Manutius edition. Previously “faith” was read, a reading also found in certain old books.
>
> **“Fortified by the discourse.”** Thus the old editions and several old books. The Reims manuscript has, “may fortify the discourse and pour forth freely.”

## I

Although, dearly beloved brothers, it is incongruous to bring any trepidation into this favorably received discourse, and although it is by no means fitting to diminish the glory of such great devotion by confessing that I have begun to doubt, nevertheless I say repeatedly [Col. 0788B] that the mind itself is broken by deliberation, since it is kindled by the desire to carry out this praise and restrained from speaking by the greatness of the virtue. It is either unfitting to remain silent or dangerous to say too little. Yet this one consideration comes to the aid of a person in such agitation: it seems that pardon may readily be granted to one who was not afraid to dare.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, although the capacity of my talent is burdened [Col. 0788C] by the power of the subject, so that the further it advances in expressing the dignity of martyrdom, the more it is oppressed by the very weight of its praise and, weakened and broken by its estimation of all the matters about which it is now speaking, fails within itself, entangled in its own discourse, and cannot, with free and loosened reins, express in open eloquence the power of such great praise—nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, there will be some capacity [Col. 0789A] for speaking which, fortified by the discourse of the work itself, may pour forth freely what consciousness of unequal talent had driven away from speech.

Since, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, though entangled in so many and such great matters, we strive with every zeal and labor to establish the exceptional and most beautiful outcomes of salvation, I do not fear that, terrified by some fear born of indolence, I shall either turn back or be extinguished. For if anyone wishes to consider the matter of which we are treating, after weighing the hope inspired by devotion and pondering the greatness of the subject itself, he will marvel all the more that I was able to dare, placed as I am where both the magnitude of the subject presses upon me and the fervor of the mind’s desire drives a mind confused by joy into narrow straits. For who is there whom this subject would not terrify? Whom would it not overthrow with the awe of his own wonder?

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0787C] “The mind itself is broken by my deliberation”: thus Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “I shall break”: Thu.
- [Col. 0788C] “Therefore, although the power”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “May express such great praise”: Lam., Lin.
- [Col. 0789C] “Faith in speaking”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Lin.
- “Fortified by reason”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “May pour forth abundantly”: Oxon. “May pour forth freely”: Lam., Lin., Ebor., NC. 1.
- [Col. 0789D] “To strengthen”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.

> **Note [Col. 0789D]**
>
> **II.—606 *Formido* (“awe”).** Not the kind that terrifies, but that which proceeds from the reverence with which we regard those whom we revere and honor, as I said on Book I of the *Testimonies*, chapter 21, p. 281, under the word *formidolosi*.
>
> **“Of life and faith.”** Certain old books do not have “of life,” etc.

## II

For there is indeed, unless I am mistaken, even within the very strength [Col. 0789B] of conscience, a marvelous awe that both agitates and inflames us. The more deeply you examine its power, the more, from the very sight of its venerable splendor, it sends before itself the shudder proper to its sacred character.

For you surely ought to consider how great a glory it is to expiate by the remedy of a single stroke every stain of one’s life, the filth of a polluted body, the contagions accumulated through the long corruption of vices, and the guilt received from the world over so protracted a span of time—a stroke by which the reward may both be increased and the guilt excluded. Hence the whole consummation and condition of life is placed in martyrdom. This is the foundation of life and faith, this the defense of salvation, this the bond of liberty and honor. And although there are other means by which the light may be attained, nevertheless one reaches the immediate vicinity of the promised gift better when sufferings act as advocates.

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0789D] “Courage”: Lam.
- “Honor”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Lin.

> **Note [Col. 0789D]**
>
> **III.—“Banished.”** Certain old books have “conquered”; [Col. 0790D] others, “revealed.”

## III

Consider how great a glory it is, after banishing the desires of this life [Col. 0789C] and separating the mind from all intercourse with nature and the world, to set it against the peril posed by the adversary; not to dread the cruelty of the torturer; for a person to be given courage by the pain through which it is believed that he is being destroyed; and to assume as an increase of virtue for himself precisely what the one punishing him thinks contributes to his torture.

For although the rebounding claw may strike again against ribs hardened in endurance, and although, as the scourges move, a vein may be drawn out behind them along with a piece of flesh torn away, he nevertheless stands immovable, stronger than his own sufferings, turning over only this within himself: that amid this cruelty of the executioners Christ himself, for whom he suffers, suffers still more. For since, if he denies the Lord, he incurs guilt on account of the one for whom he ought to have conquered, the man to whom victory and suffering are owed must necessarily be seen to endure all things. [Col. 0790A]

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0789D] “Relieved”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- [Col. 0790C] Thus Oxon., Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, and Imp.

> **Note [Col. 0790D]**
>
> **IV.—*Redampliatur*.** That is, “is increased.”
>
> **“The surrounding populace.”** See above, p. 455.
>
> **“Immovable strength.”** The word “strength,” which is not necessary, is absent from certain old books. It is readily possible to suppose that the word “immovable” refers to the breakwater.
>
> **“The conquered sea.”** Certain books have “the struck sea”; one of my manuscripts has “the sea itself.”

## IV

Therefore, since martyrdom is a matter of supreme importance, there are three things that we have proposed to discuss concerning it: what it is, how great it is, and to what purpose it is profitable.

What, then, is martyrdom? The end of transgressions, the termination of danger, the guide of salvation, the teacher of endurance, the house of life, whereby even those things perish which, in the future crisis, could have been reckoned as torments. Through it, both testimony is rendered to the Name and the majesty of the Name is further magnified—not because its greatness could be diminished in itself or broken by the crime of one who withdraws his confession, but because it overflows [Col. 0790B] toward the culmination of glory. For the terror of the surrounding populace renders souls fearless in the face of pain, and adds to the title of honor amid the threats of snarling envy: the mind grows as greatly in the struggle as the adversary believes that he is conquering through the one whom Christ has resolved to crown.

Then, therefore, all the strength of faith is brought forth; then belief is proved, when you come into the talk and reproach of the common people and, with a devout mind, fortify yourself against their popular madness, refuting and resisting whatever profane speech may cast against Christ by attacking your person. It is as when a breakwater placed against a hostile sea struggles in opposition: although the waves strike it and the returning sea repeatedly beats against it, its immovable strength nevertheless holds fast and does not succumb when covered by the foaming waters, until the force, dispersed among the crags, subsides, and the conquered sea, flowing over the rocks, escapes into the open spaces of the shore. [Col. 0790C]

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0790C] “What this is”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “Thus”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Oxon. Imp. has: “The path of endurance, teacher [Col. 0790D] of the house of life.”
- [Col. 0790D] “Of one treating it”: Imp.

> **Note [Col. 0790D]**
>
> **V.—“Empty.”** Five old books read “alienates the mind.”

## V

For what is there in those people but empty speech, idle conversation, and a depraved delight in empty words? As it is written: “They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear” (Ps. CXIII, 13). “Their foolish heart has been weighed down, lest at any time they be converted and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 10).

There is no doubt that he said this concerning all [p. 345] whose hard mind and stubborn savagery of heart, driven away from life-giving devotion, remains in dissent—madness leading them, fury carrying them off, [Col. 0791A] and, finally, every form of brutality tormenting them, by which they are alike goaded and swept along. Thus, although their own deeds would have sufficed for their punishment, the guilt of the persecution they have stirred up adds weight to the punishment itself.

### Variant Reading

- [Col. 0790D] “And save them”: Oxon.; the other reading is attested by Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.

> **Note [Col. 0791D]**
>
> **VI.—“Most hideous corruption.”** The Saint-Arnulf and Thuana manuscripts have “the corruption most thoroughly warded off.” Nicolas Le Fèvre placed “things most thoroughly warded off” in his book; this is also how it is written in the Saint-Denis manuscript of Reims.

## VI

All this pertains to the praise of martyrdom; all of it illuminates the glory of suffering. In martyrdom the hope of the age to come is discerned; in it Christ himself is at work—he whose examples, which we seek to follow, are enacted, and whose is also the power by which we resist.

And because something presents itself for mention at this point, this is surely a supreme and marvelous condescension, one which we can neither conceive in the mind nor fulfill in words. For what more could he have bestowed upon us in his abundant kindness than first to show in himself what he would crown in others? He became mortal so that we might be immortal, and he through whom human affairs are governed endured [Col. 0791B] the end of the human lot. And, to make what he suffered appear to have been granted to us, he bestowed confession, placed martyrdoms before us, and, finally, by the merits of his birth assigned to a saving remedy everything by which the light could be oppressed: in supreme humility, yet with divine power. Whoever have deserved to be worthy of this have escaped death; by subduing the condition of death, they have conquered all this most hideous corruption of the world.

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0791D] “Destruction”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “Oppressed”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “Suppressed”: Oxon.

> **Note [Col. 0791D]**
>
> **VII.—“Harvests are gathered.”** Four old books have “are ripened.”

## VII

There is no doubt how much they obtain from the Lord who have preferred the name of God to their own safety: so that, on that day of judgment, their bloodshed might make them better and their poured-out blood reveal them to be stainless. Death indeed renders life more complete; death conducts one more surely to glory.

Thus, whenever rain-swollen grain swells while the stubble rejoices and fruitful harvests are gathered in summer; thus, whenever the vine is cut back with iron, its grapes are clothed more richly as the shoots burst forth. [Col. 0791C] For whatever advances through its own injury contributes to an increase in the yield of the coming season.
