Indeed, it has often benefited the fields to set fire to them, so that the heat of the spreading conflagration may open the earth’s hidden breathing passages. It has been beneficial to parch the light stubble with crackling fire, so that the pregnant crop might rise higher and a denser ear blossom upon the fruit-bearing stalks. Thus martyrdom likewise has first a fall, afterward a fruit: it so despises death that it preserves life by death.

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0791D] “Hidden stubble”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “Harvests are ripened in summer”: Oxon., from manuscripts; Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- [Col. 0792D] “The ear may blossom”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “And their own blood would make them”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “Whom their own blood would show to be martyrs”: Oxon.

> **Note [Col. 0791D]**
>
> **VIII.—“Instruments.”** The Saint-Arnulf manuscript has “straw.”

## VIII

For what is so exceptional and sublime as to preserve all the strength of faith through robust devotion amid so many instruments of the executioners? What is so great and beautiful [Col. 0792A] as, amid so many swords of those standing around, repeatedly and openly to profess the Lord of one’s liberty and the author of one’s salvation? Especially if you set before your eyes that nothing is more detestable than disgrace, nothing fouler than servitude, and that you should now seek and desire nothing other than to be rescued from the calamities of the age, stripped of the world’s evils, and, amid the ruins of a world already on the verge of perishing, to live as one estranged from earthly contagion.

For what have you to do with this light, when eternal light has been promised to you? What have you to do with this intercourse of life and nature, when the vastness of heaven calls for you? By all means let this desire for life possess those whom a raging fire will torment with eternal vengeance for their crimes—an evil that cannot be expiated. Let this desire for life possess those for whom both dying is punishment and continuing to live is torment. The world itself now yields to you, and the earth gives way before you, [Col. 0792B] who, while all others are dying, have been preserved for this purpose: that you might be a martyr.

Do we not daily see funerals? Do we not see new forms of bodily death after prolonged suffering, the destructions of some unprecedented calamity as diseases rage, and the devastation of plundered cities? From these [Col. 0792D] we can recognize how great the dignity of martyrdom must be, since even the plague has begun to compel us toward its glory.

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0792D] “To disclose”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “Deaths of the body after prolonged suffering”: Lam., Ebor.
- “From which we might be able”: Lam., Ebor., Lin. “So that we might be able”: Oxon.

> **Note [Col. 0791D]**
>
> **IX.—“New deaths.”** Two old books and Morel’s edition have, [Col. 0792D] “different deaths resulting from deeds and raging forces.”
>
> **“The plague has begun.”** In certain old books it is written “may have begun.” The author is referring to the plague and pestilence that was then ravaging the world, on the occasion of which Cyprian wrote the book *On Mortality*.
>
> **“Of all who stand.”** The Saint-Arnulf and Thuana manuscripts have “in the standing.”
>
> **“Among all marks of glory.”** The Saint-Arnulf manuscript has “among all glories.” So too the Thuana manuscript, except that it has “of all.”

## IX

Indeed, dearly beloved brothers, consider this, I beg you, [p. 346] more fully, for in it salvation turns and sublimity is reckoned. Yet I am not unaware that you too know most fully that we are held within the judgments of all who stand, nor are you ignorant that this discipline has been handed down to us: that without any fear of warfare we should defend the power of so great a Name. For the desire of eternal remembrance has long since drawn you away from longing for this light; hopes for the future have torn you away; and the desirable fellowship of Christ has separated you from every vice.

But if we hesitate to succumb to destruction and offer our soul to death, the divine benefits—whose reward beyond the fervor of earthly things is so great that human mediocrity can scarcely give it full expression—must no longer be held and embraced by us. Heaven lies open to our blood; before our blood the habitation of Gehenna yields; and among all marks of glory a more beautiful title of blood and a more spotless crown are inscribed. [Col. 0792C]

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0792D] “Have long deceived”: Lin.
- “Among all of the glories”: Saint-Arnulf; Thuana has “of all.”

## X

Thus, whenever a soldier enters laden with triumphal spoils taken from the enemy, he rejoices in his wounds. Thus, whenever a sailor long wearied by storms reaches safe shores, he derives his happiness from the danger he has endured. There is indeed, unless I am mistaken, a joyful labor [Col. 0793A] through which security is found.

Therefore, all things must be endured, everything must be suffered; nor must one seek a way to rejoice for a brief time and be punished perpetually by fire. For you must remember that you are bound, as it were, by a certain covenantal agreement, under which either there is a just condition for obtaining salvation or the dreadful prospect of deserved punishment—amid adversity and prosperity alike, amid weapons and missiles. On one side worldly ambition solicits you; on the other, heavenly greatness admonishes you.

> **Note [Col. 0793D]**
>
> **XI.—“Of the Lord’s Passion.”** The same manuscripts have “of the promise.”

## XI

If you fear losing salvation, know that you are capable of dying. Moreover, death must be despised by you, for whom Christ was slain. Let the examples of the Lord’s Passion, I beg you, converge before your eyes; let both the rewards offered and the perils prepared converge there, and observe how great a difference there is between the two. For you will not be able [Col. 0793B] to confess unless you know how greatly you harm yourself if you deny.

The martyrs rejoice in heaven; fire will consume the enemies of truth. God’s paradise blossoms with his witnesses; Gehenna embraces the deniers, and eternal fire will blaze. And, to say nothing of the rest, this above all surely ought to exhort us: that the confession of the one name of Christ is preserved by an everlasting confession, as it is written: “Whoever confesses me on earth before men, him will I also confess before my Father and before his angels” (Luke XXII, 8).

The ornaments of the virtues are added further to the culmination of glory. For Scripture says: “The righteous will shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds; they will judge nations and rule over peoples” (Wis. III, 7).

### Variant Reading

- [Col. 0793D] “How greatly it may harm”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.

> **Note [Col. 0793D]**
>
> **XII.—“To kill.”** The same manuscripts and certain others have “to have killed.”

## XII

For it is a great splendor, dearly beloved brothers, to adorn one’s life with the honor of suffering for eternal salvation; [Col. 0793C] it is great sublimity, before the face of the Lord and under Christ’s gaze, to despise and not dread the torments inflicted by human power.

Thus Daniel overcame the threats of the king and the fury of roaring lions through the constancy of his faith, because he believed that none other than God was to be worshiped. Thus, when the young men were placed in the furnace, the conflagration burned against itself, because the righteous endured the fires while, through belief in the Lord, they feared those of Gehenna.

Hence they also received a worthy return, without being deferred to the future or reserved for the reward of eternal salvation. God saw their faith, so that they deserved to see in the body what they had promised themselves after their departure. Nor can it be estimated how great a reward there is in present tribulation, if savagery flees, if flame yields. For all had one mind, which neither violence could break [Col. 0793D], nor anger overthrow, nor fear of death restrain from the obedience of devotion. Hence, by the Lord’s grace, it came about that the king himself seemed rather to have been punished in them, when those whom he believed he had killed escaped. [Col. 0794A]

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0793D] “Through the substance of his faith”: Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.
- “Whom”: Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.
- “In present tribulation”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “How great a reward has been allotted in the present”: Oxon.
- “Subsided”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “If there was savagery, it yielded; if there was flame, it stood still”: Oxon.

> **Note [Col. 0793D]**
>
> **XIII.—“Now more.”** The Saint-Arnulf and [Col. 0794D] Thuana manuscripts have “is it not more?”
>
> **“The Lord’s commandments.”** Three old books have “promises.”
>
> **“To set forth.”** The Saint-Arnulf manuscript has “to weigh.”

## XIII

Now, dearly beloved brothers, I shall come [p. 347] to that matter from which I can sufficiently show how great the power contained in martyrdom is. Although it is known to everyone and should be desired for the distinctions of its innate splendor, nevertheless the necessity of the time has added more to the longing of the will. For among great gifts is this: that one should be crowned at the very time when, if perhaps he should die, he thinks himself crowned.

Therefore, since martyrdom is sublime and exalted, it is now all the more necessary, when the world itself is being overturned and, with the globe partly shaken, failing nature bears witness to the moments of its final end. For when rain presses upon the sky, [Col. 0794B] the air holds forth the prospect of mournful rainfall; and whenever a black tempest hangs over the bristling sea, lightning flashes through the open spaces between clouds that gleam in the night. And when the sea rolls in great waves, little by little the water rises and little by little its surface grows white, until afterward you see it rush so violently that upon the rocks against which it is broken it casts its foam higher than the swelling sea had spewed forth its wave.

You read that it is written that we must repay even to the last farthing. But this part has been taken away from martyrs alone. For those who, relying upon their desire for eternal salvation, have conquered the desires of this life have been made exempt from all suffering by the Lord’s commandments. From this point first, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we shall be able to set forth how much the power of martyrdom can accomplish. [Col. 0794C]

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0793D] “Desire of the will”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “Of pleasure”: Oxon.
- [Col. 0794D] “It is a great gift”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “The sorrowful air displays the rains”: Oxon. “Holds forth the prospect”: Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.
- “Against the rocks struck by them”: Oxon., from manuscripts; Lam., Ebor., NC. 1, Imp. The printed text has “upon those.”
- “Even to the very last farthing”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “But this portion belongs only”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1.
- “The promises of the Lord have made them”: Lam., Ebor., NC. 1. “The Lord’s propitiation crowns them”: Oxon.

> **Note [Col. 0794D]**
>
> **XIV.—“Ravaging.”** The Saint-Arnulf manuscript incorrectly has “being flogged.”

## XIV

And, to pass over everything else, we must remember how great a glory it is to come stainless to Christ, to become a sharer in his suffering, and to reign with the Lord in perpetual eternity; to escape the impending destructions of the age and not, amid the bloody devastation of ravaging diseases, be mingled with the rest in their common lot.

And, to say nothing of the crown, if, while you were placed amid these slippery evils of nature, departure from life were promised to you, would you not rejoice with your whole mind? If, I say, while you were tossed about amid the whirlwinds of this world, a repose close at hand summoned you, would you not reckon death as a remedy?

Placed amid the weapons of the executioners and the missiles of interrogations that put you to the test, stand lofty and strong, considering how great the punishment is for denying at a time when you cannot enjoy the world for whose sake you would deny. For the Lord knew that grievous torments and pernicious arts of punishment were being armed for our destruction, so that he might make us strong for every endurance. “Son,” he says, “when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II, 1). And the most blessed apostle Paul also exclaimed and said: “For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21). [Col. 0795A]

### Variant Readings

- [Col. 0794D] “If perhaps”: Lam., Ebor., Lin., NC. 1.
- [Col. 0795D] “Exclaims and says”: Lam.

> **Note [Col. 0795D]**
>
> **XV.—“A companion within the household.”** Erasmus’s edition and certain old books prefer “fellowship.”

Source/review notes: The source phrase “Christi sui gloriam interque comitetur” is materially defective or incomplete; the draft’s unsupported “walking in his midst” has therefore been replaced with an explicit textual uncertainty.

] **XV.** Therefore, dearest brothers, with steadfast faith and resolute devotion we must oppose with contrary courage the savage threats of the world and the harsh roaring of our persecutors [Note: [Col. 0795D] “Against all,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]; nor must those whose hope is eternity and heavenly life be afraid—those whose ardor is kindled with desire for the light, and whose salvation rejoices in the immortality promised them. The fact that hands are tightly bound by constricting chains, that heavy fetters wound about the neck press down with their solid [Col. 0795B] weight, or that the body, stretched upon the rack, groans as it descends toward the metal plates—this is occasioned not by a desire for blood, but by trial. For how could we recognize the very dignity of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0795D] “Favor,” Lin.] unless we were compelled to desire it even at the cost of our own body?

I indeed perceived—and the truth does not deceive me—when the savage [Note: [Col. 0795D] “Often,” Lam. Ebor. Lin.] hands of those assailing me tore my limbs apart and the raging torturer furrowed my mangled joints, yet still did not prevail, that those standing around said [Note: [Col. 0795D] “It was said in words,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]: “That is something great indeed, something beyond my knowing [Note: [Col. 0795D] “Something,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1. “It is indeed said: not to be subdued by pains,” Oxon.]—not to be subdued by pain, not to be broken by agonizing punishments.” But there were other voices saying: “And I think he has children. For he has a wife as his companion at home; yet he neither yields to the bond of his dear ones nor, drawn away by the obligations of affection, abandons his purpose.” The matter must be understood and this courage searched to its very depths. For it is no slight [p. 348] confession, whatever its nature may be, for the sake of which a man suffers and is able to die.

**XVI.** Indeed, dearest brothers, so great is the power of martyrdom that through it even the man who wished to kill you is compelled [Note: [Col. 0795D] “Through that,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] to believe. It is written, and we read: “Endure in suffering, and in your humiliation have patience, for gold and silver are tested by fire” (Ecclus. II, 4). Since, therefore, the Lord tests us by earthly trials and Christ the Examiner weighs us by these evils of the world, we must congratulate ourselves and rejoice that he does not reserve us for those everlasting destructions, but delights in us once we have been cleansed of every contamination. For what else does he seek but the full compass of integrity from those whom he summons [Note: [Col. 0796D] “Whom he summoned,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] to share in the inheritance and gladly receives into the kingdoms of heaven?

He himself declared that all things were his: both those spread out over the level plains and those rising into sloping hills, as well as whatever the vastness of heaven [Col. 0796A] encompasses and whatever the encircling sea encloses within its shifting surface. But if all things belong to him and he asks nothing of us except sincere deeds, we ought, as he himself said, to be like gold. For when you see gold shining on the gleaming earth beneath a flickering light [Note: [Col. 0796D] “The light is beneficial,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and being dissolved into liquid by consuming flames—for such, generally, is also the craftsman’s method: whenever the blazing fire is vomited from the panting furnaces, a rich [Note: [Col. 0796D] “Every rich,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] flame is drawn through the earth’s narrow channel, and, as the clods flow back, the sand is retained—it follows that we must endure all things so that we may be free of every crime, just as he said through his prophet: “And though in the sight of men they suffered torments, yet their hope is full of immortality; and, having been afflicted in a few things, they shall be well rewarded in many, because God tested them and found them [Col. 0796B] worthy of himself [Note: [Col. 0796D] Thus Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; “of him,” Oxon.], and accepted them as a sacrificial victim of a whole burnt offering” (Wisdom III, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0795D]

**XVII.—Purple running into figures.** Tertullian appears to explain this [Col. 0796D] in his book *On Modesty*, where he discusses garments ornamented with spots of purple.

]

**XVII.** But if ostentatious rank deters you, and the great quantity of money amassed in treasuries admonishes you—a thing that always [Note: [Col. 0796D] “Often,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] turns a well-disposed mind away from its purpose and drives a soul devoted to its Lord with frenzied terror—I beg you to recall the heavenly words. For this too is the voice of Christ, who says: “Whoever loses his life for my name shall receive a hundredfold in this world, and in the world to come shall possess eternal life” (Matt. X, 39); and surely we ought to reckon nothing greater or more advantageous than this.

For although, as in costly garments, purple may run into figures, and gold may wander along the softening threads to form a design, and although your treasures, upon which you brood, may not lack heavy metals dug from the earth, nevertheless, unless [Col. 0796C] I am mistaken, those things will be reckoned empty and vain if, while everything lies ready to hand for you [Note: [Col. 0796D] “If they lie ready to hand for you,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1.], salvation alone appears to be lacking. So too the Holy Spirit says that we can give nothing in exchange for our soul. For he says: “If you gain the whole world and lose your soul, what will it profit you? Or what exchange will a man give [Note: [Col. 0796D] “Can give,” Lam. Ebor.] for his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26).

All the things we behold are empty, for, established upon feeble roots, they cannot sustain the strength of their own solidity. Whatever is obtained from the world is undone by the passage of time. Therefore, lest there be anything sweet or dear that could be preferred to the desires of eternal salvation, such things have been cut away by the Lord’s commandments and deprived of any right or law of their own: lest, that is, a son should break a father placed under torture [Note: [Col. 0796D] “The father placed under torture,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.], or affection should turn a heart bound fast in hardened strength toward another resolve. By his own authority Christ ordained that truth alone and salvation alone must be embraced amid great tortures; in him a wife and children and grandchildren—in him every offspring of one’s own flesh—must be claimed through a happy victory.

**XVIII.** For Abraham too pleased God in this way: when tested by God, he did not spare even his own son; yet perhaps he might have been pardoned if he had hesitated to kill him. Religious devotion armed his hands, and paternal affection disregarded every tender impulse at the command [Note: [Col. 0797C] “Commands,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] of the Lord who gave the order. He did not recoil from shedding the blood of his child, nor did he tremble at the command—and at that time [p. 349] Christ had not yet been slain for him.

For what is dearer than he who, lest you should today suffer anything against your will, first suffered what he taught? What is sweeter than he who, although he is himself our God and Lord, nevertheless makes the man who suffers for him a coheir of the heavenly kingdom? O how great a thing this is beyond my knowing—whether because the judgment of conscience can scarcely bear to comprehend it, [Col. 0797B] although it always marvels at great gifts, or because the majesty of God is so generous that, when no one expects them, it offers even those things which, in contemplation of what has been done, it would have been impious for us to desire.

Indeed, if eternal salvation alone were given, we would owe gratitude for the very perpetuity of life [Note: [Col. 0797C] “We would be ungrateful,” Oxon., from the codices Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]. But now, since he grants us heaven and the power to judge others in the everlasting age, in what respect could human frailty not find itself equal to all these things? If you are harried by injuries, he was harried first. If you are oppressed by insults, you imitate the gift of God. Hence, whatever you endure for him is little, since you can do nothing more than that upon which salvation in its entirety rests, because in martyrdom he promised everything.

Finally, when the Apostle, to whom all things were always dear, marveled profoundly at the magnitude of the promised gifts, he said: “I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory to come that shall be revealed [Note: [Col. 0797C] “Is revealed,” Oxon.; “shall be revealed,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] in us” (Rom. VIII, 18). For he was considering within himself how great the recompense was: that to one for whom escape from death would have been enough, there should be given not only the reward of salvation but also ascent into heaven—a heaven which neither banished light compels into night nor day, in alternating succession, opens into light, but where the serene mildness of the clear air, across [Col. 0798A] the cloudless sky glowing with fiery brilliance, unfolds a pure radiance.

**XIX.** It now remains, dearest brothers, for us to show what purpose martyrdom serves and, in particular, to teach that fear of things to come should rouse us toward this title of glory. For those to whom great things have been promised have correspondingly great things that they should fear. A soldier does not rouse himself to arms before the enemy has set hostile weapons in motion; no one draws a ship out from its anchorage unless dread of the sea has gripped his mind; and the farmer, keeping a careful eye upon his resources, does not stir the earth with his fruitful plow until the crumbling clod, having absorbed the rain, is dissolved into dust. Such is every natural practice here: one does not know what is beneficial unless one has recognized what is deadly. [Col. 0798B] Hence a reward is given to all the saints while the unjust are subjected to the torments merited by their deeds.

No one who knows what the Lord has promised to his own can doubt it; nor is there any doubt about how great the fires of punishment are with which he threatens. And since the discourse has brought itself to the point where an account must be given of both, I shall briefly set forth a few things concerning each, as I said.

[Note: [Col. 0797D]

**XX.—The place called Gehenna.** A description of Gehenna occurs in the book *To Demetrian*, p. 224.

**Belching flames.** Above, Epistle XV, p. 25: “Stationed on the Lord’s threshing floor, you behold the chaff being burned in unquenchable fire.” Epistle LV, p. 81: “When, writhing under torture, he is burned by the heat of a consuming flame.” Epistle LVI, p. 94: “Our persecutors shall burn in the perpetual heat of the penal flame.” *To Demetrian*, p. 224: “Gehenna, always burning, shall consume the condemned, and a devouring punishment with living flames.” See Arnobius, book II, and Lactantius, book VII, chapter 26.

**Some, indeed, are.** Here he begins an enumeration of the torments by which the damned are tortured in Tartarus; and he does this in almost the same manner in which the Gentiles described the punishments of their Tartarus. For in Epistle XXXI, p. 44, he too used “Tartarus” for hell. There will perhaps be those who, from the description of Tartarus which the author of this [Col. 0798D] book presents here, will infer that these words are not Cyprian’s, because the description appears to approach too closely the Gentile opinions concerning Tartarus. Nothing can be replied to this objection except that Cyprian, wishing to impress upon Christians the dreadful punishments of the damned, so that by this enumeration of torments he might persuade them that every effort must be made to live piously and according to the rules of the Gospel, lest they fall into those punishments, digressed after the manner of rhetoricians through those kinds of punishment which the Gentiles believed to exist in the underworld; for, as Cicero says in book II of *On the Laws*, fear of divine punishment recalls many people from crime. See Prosper, book III, chapter 12, *On the Contemplative Life*, and Saint Gregory, book IX of the *Morals on Job*, chapter 39, or the penultimate chapter. See also our notes on the relevant passage in book III of Salvian, “the torments of eternal fire.”

]

**XX.** The raging place called Gehenna, amid the loud murmuring and groaning of those who lament [Note: [Col. 0797C] “Murmurs with groaning” (reading uncertain), Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.], and amid belching flames, always exhales the savage conflagrations of its smoking furnace through the dreadful gloom of dense night. A compressed mass of fire is confined and then released into the various forms of punishment. Then there are manifold kinds of torment, as the devouring flame rolls back upon itself [Note: [Col. 0797C] “When it rolls entirely back upon itself,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; [Col. 0798C] “Then upon itself,” Oxon. Pamel.] whatever its emitted heat has tortured.

It restrains with diverse forms of destruction those who rejected the Lord’s voice [Col. 0798C] and despised his commands; and, according to the degree of forfeited salvation, it calls forth its powers, as each man’s share in crime [Note: [Col. 0798C] “Of the crime,” Pamel. Oxon.; “to crime,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] determines his peril. Some, indeed, are bent down by an intolerable mass; others are hurled by a savage force down the precipice of a steep and sloping path; and the heavy weight of clanking chains pulls them downward by their bond [Note: [Col. 0798C] “By a bond,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]. There are also some whom a wheel driving swiftly [Note: [Col. 0798C] “An untiring wheel turns,” Lam.] and an unceasing whirl spins about; others, compressed together in a tightly packed mass, are enclosed as body clings to body, [Col. 0799A] so that fire consumes them, iron weighs them down, and the multitude of bodies tortures itself.

**XXI.** But for those by whom God was always sought or known, the dwelling place of Christ has never failed: there grace abides; there the luxuriant earth in verdant fields clothes itself in nurturing [p. 350] grass and is sustained by fragrant flowers; there groves rise high toward their summits, and there thicker foliage clothes the trees and casts a canopy of shade over whatever their bending branches cover.

There all things are subject neither to cold nor heat, nor do the fields rest as in autumn, only for the fertile earth to give birth again in a new spring. All things belong to a single season; the fruits of a single summer are borne. For then the moon does not serve out its appointed months, nor does the sun pass through the intervals of the hours, [Col. 0799B] nor does vanquished light withdraw into night. Joyful repose possesses its peoples, and a peaceful dwelling holds them. There a spring gushes forth in the midst, rising from the bosom of its overflowing channel, and, with a murmuring course at intervals, glides through winding turns, so that at its outlets it divides into rivers newly born from itself.

From this, therefore, comes the great praise of the martyrs; from this comes the noble crown of the victors, to whom greater things than these have been promised and whose rewards are more abundant. The fact that the body is cast to wild beasts or the threatening sword is not feared reveals the principle of God’s favor and makes his choice manifest. For it would have been incongruous for him to retain amid earthly vices and filth one whom he had judged worthy of so great a gift.

[Note: [Col. 0799D]

**XXII.—Nothing has been denied you.** Above, Epistle XV, p. 26: “For what do you ask of the Lord’s indulgence which [Col. 0800D] you do not deserve to obtain?”

]

**XXII.** Deservedly, then, nothing has been denied you, O good martyrs: you whom the hope of eternity and of light sustains, and whose entire devotion and mind are seen to be dedicated [Col. 0799C] to heavenly service. Deservedly, I say—deservedly nothing is forbidden for you to desire, since in your minds this world is despised, and the estranged face of the age has become dreadful, like the confused blindness of darkness. For you this world is always a prison, its houses are cells, and everything possessed in life is merely traveling provision. For the person whom vain ambition has not brought beneath its pompous tread, and whom popular greatness has not exalted, but whom Christ has added to his kingdom as one burning with heavenly desire, is carried away from these evils by triumphant victory.

**XXIII.** Nothing, therefore, is so great and venerable as that which frees from death, causes one to live, and grants perpetual reign. This is fitting for God’s saints, necessary for the wretched, welcome to all: by it the good rejoice, the downtrodden are raised up, and the elect are crowned.

For God, the cultivator of all, gave martyrdom as a kind of remedy [Note: [Col. 0799D] Thus Imp.; “a certain remedy in martyrdom,” Oxon. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] for life, when he bestowed it upon some according to their merit and delivered it to others according to his mercy. We have indeed seen many, noble in faith, attain this title of the name [Note: [Col. 0799D] “Men,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.], so that death might honor the obedience of their devotion. But we have also frequently beheld others standing fearless, so that, redeeming the sins they had committed and washed by their own blood, they might be regarded as cleansed in blood and, having been slain, might come to life again—those who, while alive, were reckoned dead. [Col. 0800A]

Death, indeed, makes life more complete; death recovers lost glory. Through it hope already lost is regained; through it salvation in its entirety is restored. So, when seed has failed in parched fields [Note: [Col. 0800D] “Clods,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and the earth has sweltered as its plants die, it has been beneficial to draw down a river from the upturned hills and to refresh the thirsty fields with flowing streams, so that the vanquished barrenness of the soil might pour itself forth into fruitful stalks and a denser crop, counterfeiting the effect of rain, might bristle over the field.

**XXIV.** What, then, dearest brothers, should I report above all; what should I say? When so many titles of dignity converge upon one point, the mind is confounded, thought is drawn away, and in the very effort of striving eloquence, speech proves unequal and fades away. What can be said that could be sufficient, [Col. 0800B] when, if you express the power of eternal salvation, its grandeur confronts you, and if you speak of its grandeur, its magnitude outstrips you? The realities harmonize and converge at once, and nothing appears capable of being uttered that is worthy of them. Thus the examples of martyrdom, coming from the opposite direction, have caught and held the onrush of my daring discourse as though entangled and ensnared.

What voice, what lungs, what strength can undertake to sustain a gift so great? By the confession of a single utterance, adversities collapse and blessings arise; kingdoms lie open, sovereignties are prepared, punishment is conquered, death is subjected, and life is brought forth; [p. 351] the hostile weapons of the attacking enemy are broken [Note: [Col. 0800D] “Are broken apart,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.]. If there is sin, it kills it; if there is guilt, it puts an end to it. Therefore, I beg you, weigh this in your own minds, and take from my discourse only so much as you know yourselves able to apprehend.

[Col. 0800C] **XXV.** Let that day come before your eyes: when, as the people watch and all look on, unshaken devotion struggles against earthly crosses and the threats of the world; when the suspended hearts and anxious minds of those wavering in uncertain trepidation are shaken by the fearful horror of their apprehensive rejoicing; what anxiety there is, what longing in their prayers, what vows are recalled, while victory still hangs in the balance and the victor’s crown, by the uncertainty of chance, hangs above a head facing an uncertain outcome; while that pestilent and furious avowal is kindled to wrath, inflamed to madness, and finally scorched by all the frenzy of the heart and by grinding threats.

For who does not know how great a thing this is: that despite the pain of wounds and the blows of interrogation, our frailty is, as it were, despised and the unexpected boldness of human courage does not yield; that a man stands and is not moved, is tortured [Col. 0800D] and yet not conquered, but is instead armed by the very punishment with which he is tortured?

**XXVI.** Consider what this means, dearest brothers; set the entire steadfastness of martyrdom before your senses and your souls. For behold: at the suffering of anyone who has been called, the martyrs long since summoned from the world already rejoice; the heralds of every good thing rejoice; the elect likewise rejoice. There the Lord rejoices in his soldier; there Christ rejoices in the witness [Col. 0801A] to his name.

What I say is too little, dearest brothers, too little. So great a task and so marvelous a weight have I undertaken in this kind of discourse. Yet, I beg you, let the gravity of your judgment not fall short of its own intention, knowing that only so much can be said about martyrdom as it has been possible to comprehend. This alone, therefore, was the reason for undertaking its praise: not because I judged myself equal or adequate to its glory, but because I perceived so great a power in it that, even if I said little about it, I would profess myself to have said a very great deal.

For although justice, the guardian of faith, may be preferred to goodness, and immaculate virginity may recognize itself as superior among all forms of praise, it must nevertheless yield to blood [Note: [Col. 0801D] “Nevertheless yield to blood,” Oxon.; “it must,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.] and submit to gore. The former chose the good; the latter imitated Christ.

[Col. 0801B] **XXVII.** Now, however, dearest brothers, lest anyone suppose that I have placed all salvation in no condition other than martyrdom, let him first consider this: it is not I alone who seem to speak, nor is the order of things such that the promised hope of immortality strives to remain confined within a single part. But since the Lord testified with his own mouth that there are many dwellings with the Father, I have believed nothing greater than that glory by which these men are approved as unworthy of worldly life [Note: [Col. 0801D] Thus Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; Imp.: “They are unworthy. Therefore.”].

Therefore, dearest brothers, contending in emulous devotion and driven as though by the spur of reward [Note: [Col. 0801D] “By the impulse,” Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.], let us undertake every exertion of our strength and endurance. For perishable things ought not to move us: they are always hastening toward their own overthrow, not only by the law laid down for them but also by the very end of time. John cries out and says: [Col. 0801C] “Already the axe is laid to the root of the tree” (John XII, 35), plainly indicating and showing that all things have reached their final old age. But the Lord himself also says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (Matt. III, 10). If he foretold that we must walk at that time, he has surely shown that we should walk all the more [Note: [Col. 0801D] Thus Imp.; “that we should walk now,” Oxon. Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.].

**XXVIII.** And, to return to the praise of martyrdom, there is the utterance of the most blessed Paul, who says: “Do you not know that those who run in the contest—many compete, but one receives the palm? You, however, run in such a way that you may all obtain it” (I Cor. IX, 24). Elsewhere too, in words capable of exhorting us to martyrdom, he called us coheirs of Christ. Indeed, so as to omit nothing, he says: “If you have died together with Christ, why do you make decrees as though still living in this world?” [Col. 0801D] (Col. II, 20).

For, [p. 352] dearest brothers, we who await the rewards of resurrection, who seek the day of judgment, and who finally trust that we shall reign with Christ, ought to be dead to the world. You cannot desire martyrdom unless you have first hated the world, nor can you attain God’s reward unless you have loved Christ. But whoever loves Christ does not love the world. For Christ has been cast aside by the world, [Col. 0802A] just as the world has been cast aside by Christ, as it is written: “The world is crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

The world was lovable to no one unless the Lord had first condemned him; nor could one who gloried in the life of the world enjoy eternal salvation. This is the utterance of Christ, who says: “Whoever loves his life in this world shall lose it in the world to come; but whoever hates it in this world shall find it in the world to come” (Matt. X, 39). The apostle Paul also says: “Be imitators of me, as I too am of Christ” (I Cor. VI, 1). And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0801D] Thus Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1.] he himself says: “I wish you all, if it is possible, to be imitators of me” (I Cor. VII, 7).

**XXIX.** He who suffered said this, and he suffered for this purpose: that he might imitate the Lord. Surely, then, he wished us also to suffer for this purpose, that through him we might imitate Christ. If you are righteous and believe in God, why do you fear to shed your blood [Col. 0802B] for him whom you know to have suffered so many times for you? He was sawn asunder in Isaiah, slain in Abel, offered in Isaac, sold in Joseph, and crucified in man.

I say nothing of the other things, which speech cannot express and the mind cannot bear. Conscience is overcome by the example of his humility; and as it considers how many things occurred while he suffered, it marvels that he suffered for whose sake all things trembled. Day fled into night; all light withdrew into darkness; and, its weight tilting in alternating motion, the entire earth was shaken and split apart. The shades were thrown into confusion, the tombs laid bare, and, as the earth’s sepulchers gaped open, bodies restored to the light stood forth [Note: [Col. 0802D] “Stood,” Oxon., from the codices Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; Imp.: “Restored.”]. The world trembled at the flow of blood; the curtains hanging at the doors were torn, and the whole temple groaned.

It is therefore a great thing to imitate him who by dying [Note: [Col. 0802D] Thus Lam. Ebor. NC. 1.; Imp.: “The curtains hanging at the doors were torn, and the whole temple groaned: he who by dying.”] [Col. 0802C] condemned the world. Accordingly, when, after the example of the Lord’s Passion and for every testimony to Christ, you lay down your life and do not fear to shed your blood, everything must yield to martyrdom. Inestimable is martyrdom’s glory, infinite its measure, immaculate its victory, inestimable its title, immeasurable its triumph; for it is exalted by the confessor’s own glory [Note: [Col. 0802D] “Of the one standing firm,” Lam. Ebor. Lin. NC. 1.], and is adorned, as it were, by sharing in Christ’s blood.

**XXX.** Therefore, dearest brothers, although all this belongs to the Lord’s promise and gift, although it is bestowed from on high and cannot be received except by his command, and although it can neither be conceived by the mind, expressed in words, traversed in discourse, nor fully encompassed by any powers of eloquence, nevertheless it will be a work of your benevolence, charity, and love if you are willing to remember me [Col. 0802D] when the Lord begins to honor martyrdom in you.

That holy altar encloses you within itself; that great seat of the venerable name contains you within itself, as though in the bosom of an embracing lap. The dominions of everlasting time await you, as does that realm in which you shall always reign and always live. O blessed are you, whose sins have truly been forgiven—if indeed you, who are Christ’s companions, have ever sinned! O blessed are those whom the Lord’s blood has stained from the beginning [Col. 0803A] of the world, and whom this splendor of a snow-white garment has deservedly clothed and the brightness of an enveloping robe adorned!

Indeed, I already seem to myself to behold it, and according to the judgment of the human mind that divine and glorious vision comes before my eyes and sight. I seem, I say, already to behold that truly noble company accompanying the glory of its Christ and—[the text following *interque* is defective or incomplete]. Before his face shall go the blessed throng of victors [Note: [Col. 0803A] Thus Lam. Imp.; “of men.”], and, with the ranks pressing thickly together, [Col. 0804A] like the rising of the sun it shall bring forth its entire illuminated host into dominion. And would that, though I am utterly abject, it might be granted me to see this! But the Lord will be able to accomplish what he is believed not to deny when you ask it.

Following these doubtful works of the divine Cyprian in Baluze’s edition was a treatise *On Rebaptism* by an anonymous author, which we inserted in a more suitable place in the preceding volume.

# APPENDICES TO THE GENUINE WORKS OF THE DIVINE CYPRIAN

[Col. 0803]

# PROLEGOMENA ON THE DOUBTFUL AND LOST WRITINGS OF SAINT CYPRIAN, AND ON WORKS FALSELY ATTRIBUTED TO HIM

## ARTICLE I. The Doubtful Works of the Divine Cyprian

[Col. 0803B]

Besides the works universally acknowledged to be the genuine productions of Saint Cyprian, several others circulate under his name in manuscripts and printed books. Some of these are doubtful; others were certainly falsely attributed to him. I shall discuss them briefly here, following the order in which they are listed in the Venetian edition of Baluze.

**I.** First comes the distinguished book *On the Public Shows* [Note: [Col. 0803C] This book and the following one were printed above according to the standard of Baluze’s Paris edition. EDD.]. It is not unworthy of Cyprian, and many have indeed ascribed it to him—namely Baronius, Jacques Pamèle, Pierre du Faur, Sanjorianus, Jacques Sirmond, Desiderius Heraldus, and Bellarmine.

Supporting their view is, first, the book’s own inscription: “Cyprian to the people who stand firm in the Gospel, [Col. 0803C] greetings”; then the identity assumed by its writer, who presents himself as a prelate absent from his Church and is distressed because he cannot address his people either face to face or, as often as he wishes, through his letters. This appropriately fits our holy bishop, whether hiding in seclusion or living in exile at Curubis.

The indications of date also support it: the work was written while paganism still flourished, and it mentions the custom then prevailing by which the faithful carried the most holy Eucharist home from the Church, as well as the exorcisms then frequently performed; these same practices are known to have flourished at Carthage in Cyprian’s age. Finally, the case is supported by the fact that the author of this little work imitated here and there Tertullian’s books [Col. 0804B] *On the Public Shows*, with which, as no one is unaware, our saint was familiar.

The book’s style also approaches Cyprian’s to no small degree, so that to some learned men it appears to differ from his style only very slightly. Nevertheless, anyone accustomed to reading Cyprian must acknowledge that this difference of style is by no means doubtful. Nor is there to be found here that force and effectiveness of expression so characteristic of him, or that use of sacred texts in which his works excel to a remarkable degree.

Add that, apart from Cyprian’s name, nothing is read in this little work to suggest that it was written to the Carthaginians rather than to the faithful of another Church. Indeed, since the author mentions the origin of the games in the city of Rome and nowhere else, and since, after much else, near the end of the work he summons his flock [Col. 0804C] to a spectacle worthy of Christians—namely, the fabric of the world and the sacred writings—saying:

> “This is the spectacle presented not by a praetor or consul, but by him who alone exists before all things and above all things—indeed, from whom are all things—the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

Since, I say, he speaks these words there, one might suspect that this book was written to the Romans rather than to the Carthaginians. The latter had not a consul but a proconsul, and therefore it appears that the latter, not the former, should have been named here.

As for Cyprian’s name, it could have been added by a copyist who believed the book to be his. We therefore judge that this little work must be left among Saint Cyprian’s doubtful writings until something more certain has been produced in favor of one side or the other.

II. The book *On the Praise of Martyrdom* is likewise an excellent work, [Col. 0805A] written in an oratorical and more highly wrought style than the unquestionably authentic minor works of St. Cyprian, if one excepts the *Letter to Donatus*. Erasmus—and after him John Fell and Elias Dupin [Note: [Col. 0805D] Dupin, *Biblioth.*, vol. I, pp. 267 and 278; Tillemont, vol. IV, note 14, on Cyprian; Ceillier, vol. III, p. 154.]—therefore denied it to St. Cyprian and judged it to be the production of some idle rhetorician. Baronius, on the contrary, [Note: [Col. 0805D] Baronius, at the year 255, no. 37 ff.] severely reproves Erasmus for judging thus merely on account of the difference in style, and proves from St. Augustine [Note: [Col. 0805D] Augustine, book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 21.] that St. Cyprian did not always employ the same manner of writing. Rather, as St. Augustine observes in the same place, he used at one time the plain style, as in the book—or Letter LXIII—*On the Lord’s Cup*, to Caecilianus; at another the temperate style, as in the book *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*; and at another even the grand style, as in this same book, whenever the subject so required.

Fell further attacks this minor work on the ground [Col. 0805B] that it mentions the plague then raging, although it is addressed to Moses, Maximus, and the other confessors. For since it is established that St. Moses was crowned with martyrdom under Decius, in the year 251, whereas Fell maintains that the plague first arose during the reign of Gallus, he therefore infers that the book was written by an author poorly informed about events remote from his own age. To this one may reply, with Tillemont, that it has not been proved that this plague first broke out under Gallus, although it did rage more fiercely at that time; and consequently the book in question cannot be denied to St. Cyprian on this ground.

Baluzius, in his annotations, employs another reply: namely, that the dedication of the book to Moses and Maximus is not found in the many excellent and very ancient codices that he possessed. He asserts that in these only [Col. 0805C] something like the following is prefixed: *Here begins On the Praise of Martyrdom*. Accordingly, in his edition he omitted the former dedication as an addition made by someone else. John Fell likewise testifies that the same dedication is absent from three ancient codices. But there is no need to have recourse to this, since the letter of St. Moses, Maximus, Nicostratus, and the other Roman confessors—which is Letter XXVI among the Cyprianic letters—provides by no means an empty argument for vindicating the same book to St. Cyprian. His Eminence Cardinal Bellarmine undoubtedly intimated this in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under St. Cyprian, when he said that the aforesaid confessors mention it in that letter.

I shall set out the matter itself. Among other things, those confessors write:

> “We have therefore received—we say it again, brother Cyprian—great joys, great consolations, great encouragements, especially because you followed the glorious, I will not say deaths, but immortalities of the martyrs with glorious and fitting praises. For such departures had to be celebrated in such language, so that the things recounted might be spoken of just as they occurred. From your letter, therefore, we saw those glorious triumphs of the martyrs, and with our own eyes, as it were, we followed them as they sought heaven, and we beheld them established among the Angels, Powers, and heavenly Dominions. And with our own ears, as it were, we also perceived the Lord bearing before the Father the testimony he had promised them.” [Col. 0806A]

It is therefore certain that, among other things, St. Cyprian set before them the glory of the martyrs in heaven and Christ’s testimony before God the Father, in order to rouse them all the more vehemently to martyrdom. Now we do indeed possess two letters of the holy martyr Cyprian to these same men, the one numbered XV and the other XXV in the Venetian edition of Baluzius that we use. But although both contain some exhortation to the same contest, neither mentions the heavenly glory of the martyrs or Christ’s testimony. It is therefore necessary that they designated by the words quoted above some other minor work of the same saint. Yet both of these subjects occur in the book *On the Praise of Martyrdom*.

First, concerning Christ bearing witness before his Father, it says:

> “And, to pass over the rest in silence, this surely ought to exhort us all the more: that the confession of a single utterance is preserved by Christ’s everlasting confession, as it is written: ‘Whoever confesses me on earth before men, I too shall confess him before my Father and before his Angels.’” [Col. 0806B]

In the same place he also discusses the glory of the martyrs at length and, finally, toward the end, says:

> “O blessed are those whom the Lord’s blood has stained from the beginning of the world, and whom, by their merit, this brilliance of snow-white raiment has clothed and the whiteness of the encircling robe adorned! Indeed, I now seem to myself to behold them, and, according to the capacity of the human mind, that divine and illustrious sight rises before my eyes and gaze. I seem, I say, already to behold how that truly noble company accompanies the glory and the journey of its Christ. There, before his face, the happy band [Col. 0806C] of victors, its ranks pressing densely together, will display its power like an entire host illuminated by the rising of the sun. And may it be granted to me, though most abject, to see this!”

These and other things, which the diligent reader will discover by comparing the confessors’ letter with the book in question, arouse a strong suspicion that they had read it. Hence the aforesaid Cardinal Bellarmine listed it among the doubtful works of St. Cyprian, not because he himself judged it such, but because Erasmus had doubted it. Nor did he think its style differed from that of Cyprian’s other minor works, except in being more highly wrought than the others—but not more than all of them, since the *Letter to Donatus* is in no way inferior to it.

In asserting it for the same holy martyr, Baluzius also observes in his annotations that in every [Col. 0806D] ancient codex everywhere—among which he counts one belonging to Séguier, written in majuscule letters a thousand years ago—it is “consistently found among those works of St. Cyprian concerning which there is no difficulty that they are St. Cyprian’s.” He further commends Florus of Lyon’s excerpts from the works of St. Cyprian, in which, he says, various passages from this same book occur, although all the other excerpts are certainly Cyprian’s.

Nevertheless, we cannot deny that, in addition to the difference in style, certain rather obscure phrases are also found here and there in it, such as are not easily found in the saint’s undisputed works. Moreover, in recalling the punishments of the underworld it follows the manner of the pagans to some extent, and I do not know whether this sufficiently savors of St. Cyprian. Accordingly, although I am strongly inclined [Col. 0807A] to attribute the book in question to him, I would not venture to do so with certainty. The Louvain editors, and afterward the Paris editors, of the works of St. Augustine did indeed judge that the same book was cited by the holy Doctor in book I, chapter 30, *Against Gaudentius*; but what Augustine there recalls from St. Cyprian is found properly and much more closely in the *Letter to Donatus*.

III. Baluzius listed first among the minor works commonly attributed to St. Cyprian the book *On Discipline and the Good of Chastity*. Bellarmine and Pamelius judged it to be his genuine production, against Erasmus and others [Note: [Col. 0807D] Dupin, *Biblioth.*, vol. I, p. 267; Ceillier, *Histoire*, vol. II, p. 153.], who denied it to him because of the difference in style. Its author was certainly a bishop absent from his flock, who was accustomed to stir it continually to the pursuit of the virtues, as is beyond doubt from [Col. 0807B] the very opening of the book. It may also be gathered that it was written in times of persecution, since it says:

> “Virginity cannot fear persecution, since it can challenge him from a position of security.”

Pamelius therefore thought that it was published during Cyprian’s retirement under Decius. But this is scarcely probable, since Pontius did not mention it, although he so diligently commended the usefulness of the saint’s retirement from the works produced by him; he would therefore undoubtedly have mentioned above all a book written during that very retirement.

Besides the discrepancy in style, Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0807D] Tillemont, vol. IV, art. 28, pp. 46 and 81.] thought he had also detected in it a certain passage on divine grace from which its author might be judged later than St. Augustine, were it not that persecution is mentioned there. He nevertheless suspected that this persecution might refer to the Vandals [Col. 0807C] or other heretics. But Maran rightly replied to this [Note: [Col. 0807D] Maran, in the *Life*, § 35, p. 118.] that the conjecture was less probable, since many more testimonies of this kind—and perhaps more explicit ones—concerning divine grace occur in St. Cyprian’s undisputed works.

Furthermore, Pamelius notes that this book is ascribed to St. Cyprian both in the notable and ancient codex of the Cologne Charterhouse, according to Gravius, and in the codices of Louis Carrion and St. Pantaleon at Cologne. He also notes that the author greatly imitated Tertullian in his book *On Chastity* and borrowed many things from it; and, as regards style, that short aphorisms and enthymemes of this kind are also found in the book *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, and wherever the holy prelate imitated Tertullian. This much is certain: apart from the dissimilarity of style—and St. Cyprian did not always employ the same style—nothing prevents its being attributed to him.

IV. Erasmus, Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0807D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, art. 41, p. 56.], and others judged that the book entitled *To the Heretic Novatian, on Not Denying the Hope of Pardon* should be assigned to another author because of a similar difference in diction, although they acknowledged that in all other respects it was neither unworthy of St. Cyprian nor remote from his age. Certainly the author, who reveals at the very beginning of the book that he is a bishop, mentions only one persecution after that [Col. 0808A] which Decius had provoked, and affirms that in this later persecution many who had fallen in the first stood unconquered. Maran therefore [Note: [Col. 0808D] Maran, loc. cit.] reasonably supposed that he wrote it after the persecution of Gallus, during the peaceful beginnings of Valerian’s reign.

Scholars commonly gather that he was an African, because he seems to allude to the schism of Felicissimus, which was known almost exclusively in Africa, when he says:

> “What can the few most perverse Novatians—or now, the most unhappy (*infelicissimi*)—answer to these things?”

That it was not the work of St. Cornelius, as Erasmus suspected, is suggested by these words of the same author:

> “The sacrament of Baptism, which was provided for the salvation of the human race, and which Christ showed beforehand through his own mouth that the Church alone may celebrate according to a heavenly ordinance.”

These words savor of St. Cyprian’s error concerning the baptism of heretics, from which St. Cornelius was always very far removed. [Col. 0808B]

Maran, however, thinks he has noticed in the same book, besides the divergence in style, something else because of which it cannot be attributed to the holy martyr. The author began the book as follows:

> “While I was considering, and my mind was boiling intolerably, what I ought to do concerning our pitiable brethren, who, wounded not by their own will but by the onslaught of the raging devil, were still, that is, throughout a long succession of time, doing penance and paying the penalty—behold, another enemy arose in opposition, an adversary of paternal compassion itself, the heretic Novatian, etc.”

And again, after saying that many of those who had been wounded “in the first battle line,” that is, in the Decian persecution, “afterward, that is, in the second battle . . . persevered courageously,” he added:

> “Behold, these schismatics do not hesitate to call those who are so glorious and so dear to the Lord ‘wood, hay, and stubble’; yet they presume that their equals—that is, those still placed in the same guilt of their fall—must not be admitted even to penance.” [Col. 0808C]

From these passages Maran infers two things. First, the author of the book was a bishop who took it ill that Novatian impiously opposed him in treating the penitent lapsed with humanity. Second, when this author was writing, he had not yet granted peace to those who had lapsed under Decius. Consequently, he was not St. Cyprian, who, it is established, when the persecution of Gallus was imminent, decreed in the Council of Carthage that peace should be granted to the lapsed even before their whole penance had been completed, lest they succumb to the persecution.

Maran’s argument is not without force, yet it is not as certain as it appeared to him. First, what was said in the former passage about penance prolonged “throughout a long succession of time” cannot be taken literally unless someone wishes to say that Novatian first began to spread his heresy under Valerian, or at least that knowledge of this matter reached the author of the book only then. Neither can be maintained. The first cannot, because it is established from the preceding commentary that under Decius he stirred up his heresy together with the schism. Nor can the second, because no plausible reason can be given why an African bishop—such as Maran admits the author of the book to have been—could for so long have remained ignorant of Novatian’s heresy, which was very well known in Africa [Col. 0809A] and condemned in the Council of Carthage. The writer therefore seems to have spoken less precisely about the time; and the words “still, that is, throughout a long succession of time” must be referred not to Valerian’s reign, but to the beginning of Gallus’s.

Nor can the conclusion Maran drew from the second text be inferred with certainty: namely, that when the author was writing, he had not yet granted peace to those who had lapsed under Decius. For he does not deny that this had been granted to them by himself; rather, he affirms that down to that very time it had been so harshly denied to penitents of this kind by Novatian and his followers that, if their judgment were to prevail, the penitent lapsed should not even then be admitted to penance.

It is likewise not sufficiently plausible that the same author, when Valerian was already emperor, was still considering [Col. 0809B] what ought to be done with the penitent lapsed, since already under Decius it had been decreed in the Council of Carthage as well as in the Roman council that the lapsed should be admitted to full penance and, once this had been completed, to peace. Moreover, afterward, in another synod of Carthage under the emperor Gallus, it was decreed that, because of the impending persecution, all the lapsed who had begun to do penance from the first day of their fall and had not withdrawn from the Church should immediately be granted that same peace. Therefore, if that African bishop even then was truly considering what he ought to do concerning the lapsed, it must be said that he was speaking of those who were not included in the later decree. On this reasoning the whole difficulty vanishes, since such a deliberation could have applied just as well to St. Cyprian as to anyone else. [Col. 0809C] Maran’s observation therefore does indeed make it more doubtful whether the book in question should be attributed to someone other than St. Cyprian, but it does not prove that it must certainly be denied to him.

V. The *Exhortation to Penance of the Divine Cyprian* was brought to light in the middle of this century and first appeared at Bologna in the year 1751, from the press of St. Thomas Aquinas, at the establishment of Girolamo Corciolani. It was published from a manuscript codex in the Library of the Canons Regular of the Congregation of St. Savior at Bologna by the most learned and most reverend lord John Chrysostom Trombelli, formerly Abbot General of that same congregation. With the support of others from his congregation—which abounds in highly learned canons—he had already published one volume of similar unedited minor works of the Latin Fathers. In the first part of volume II, entitled *Minor Works of Cyprian, Hilary, and Other Ancient Latin Fathers, Now Published for the First Time by the Canons Regular of St. Savior*, he shared this little work of Cyprian with the learned. [Col. 0809D]

Although the highly perceptive editor does not assert with complete certainty that this little work is the work of the divine Cyprian himself, he is nevertheless wholly inclined to vindicate it for that holy Doctor. His reasons are: first, that the codex places Cyprian’s name before it; second, that the same method of argument and of citing testimonies from Scripture that Cyprian employs in the books of *Testimonies* is used here; and third, that a discipline is established here which, since it was being attacked in Cyprian’s time, had need of such a champion. For it is indicated there with sufficient clarity that the lapsed must be received into the Church, and that those guilty of any crimes whatsoever must by no means be barred from the hope of pardon, provided that they have submitted themselves to canonical penance. [Col. 0810A]

Nor does he remain silent about the arguments on the other side, though he weakens them. The first is that an interpretation of Scripture is cited here that differs greatly from the one Cyprian uses. Trombelli replies that the ancients followed now one, now another interpretation of Scripture, and that there are so many and such manifest proofs of this fact that no one now doubts it. He adduces one clear example from Augustine, who quotes verse 22 of Ezekiel chapter XVIII four times, always in a different form. He also lays blame on copyists because they assumed no slight liberty in frequently substituting the interpretation they themselves preferred for the one used by the author they were copying. [Col. 0810B]

The second argument is that none of the ancients cites this little work or attributes it to Cyprian. Trombelli thinks it should be answered that it must not be asserted so rashly that no other ancient cited the work, since we still lack the works of so many Doctors; and that a negative argument drawn from the silence of the ancients should not be given much weight. A sufficiently plausible reason can also be given why none of the ancient authors whom we do possess cites this little work: the error refuted by it ceased not long after Cyprian’s time, and therefore so did the occasion for which it might have been cited.

He further adds this reason for doubting the authorship of the work: that long ago there were some, even among Latin writers, who imitated Cyprian in this manner of writing, among whom Pelagius was preeminent. Yet, after weighing all these considerations, it is highly probable that this little work belongs to Cyprian, or at least to an ancient, highly credible writer contemporary with Cyprian and so closely matched to the books of *Testimonies* that, if joined to them, it should appear to form virtually one body with them. And since, in Trombelli’s judgment, its usefulness is by no means slight, “I judged,” says the distinguished Oberthür, [Note: [Col. 0810D] Oberthür, *Opera omnia SS. PP.*, vol. III, *Works of St. Cyprian*, vol. I, Würzburg, 1782, in the letter to the distinguished Michael Ignatius Schmidt, p. 20.] “that it could neither be passed over nor ought to be separated from the books of *Testimonies*.” [Col. 0810C]

Concerning the usefulness of this little work itself, however, the most learned editor argues as follows:

> “Is not a little work highly useful in which the Church’s most customary practice stands out”—namely, that an error, once it has arisen, is immediately checked by adducing numerous testimonies from Scripture—“and which contains so large a portion of the most ancient version? But if you believe that the sacred books are cited here in the order in which codices of that period were arranged, you at once have another advantage in it—one that it is quite unnecessary to commend at length here, but that is certainly not slight. It also has this benefit: in citing the sacred Scriptures, it adduces the book of Ecclesiasticus and shows by its example how highly that book—which Protestants now hold in the least esteem—was valued in the earliest centuries of the Church.” [Col. 0810D]

## ARTICLE II. Works Falsely Attributed to the Divine Cyprian

[Col. 0811A]

I. Baluzius further contains various minor works that were likewise formerly attributed to St. Cyprian, but which learned critics sufficiently agree are not his. Among these, the book *On Gamblers* seems, in Bellarmine’s judgment, rather to be the work of some Roman Pontiff, since its author writes at the beginning:

> “Since divine and paternal compassion has conferred upon us the leadership of the apostolate, has by heavenly favor established the vicarial see of the Lord, and since in our higher office we bear the origin of the authoritative apostolate upon which Christ founded the Church, having received at the same time the power of loosing and binding and the ministry of forgiving sins.”

In Dupin’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0811D] Dupin, *Bibliothec. Auctor.*, vol. I, p. 278, note o, Cologne Latin ed., and p. 267.], it was indeed written [Col. 0811B] by a bishop, but one must not conclude from the quoted words that he was the Roman Pope merely because he calls himself Christ’s Vicar, for among the ancients that title was given to all bishops. The style of this tract is still less similar to Cyprian’s style, since it is convoluted, obscure, and full of words that are scarcely Latin. Sacred Scripture is cited in it differently from the manner found in Cyprian’s books, and its author mentions a book entitled *Teaching*, or *The Teaching of the Apostles*, which was in all probability composed after St. Cyprian.

II. The book *On the Singularity of Clerics* is a highly useful work, in which it is proved that clerics ought not to live with women. Some have falsely assigned it to Origen, others to St. Augustine. Baronius [Note: [Col. 0811D] Baronius, at the year 253, no. 44.] maintained that it could be attributed to no one more fittingly [Col. 0811C] than to our St. Cyprian. Bellarmine, Pamelius, and the other modern writers dissent from this opinion. Although they commonly acknowledge that the book is notable, useful, and the work of an ancient writer, they rightly declare its style and the barbarous words that occur here and there in it to be unworthy of St. Cyprian. [Note: [Col. 0811D] Such barbarous words are: *repulsarium*, *constitutionarios*, *vulgaritatis*, *flumirorum* [uncertain reading], *probrositatis*, *participia*, *adunari*, *vanificat*, *egestosam*, *procurativa*, *absentarii*, etc., and *conjugaliter*.]

Others have also attributed this tract to Jerome, and some to Gaudentius of Brescia. But it is written in neither Jerome’s nor Origen’s style [Note: [Col. 0811D] See *Hist. Theolog. Critic.*, vol. IX, on the writings of Origen, p. 260 ff.], and it would approach more closely the style of Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, were it not contradicted by the manuscripts and printed editions, none of which attributes it to him. The author of the English edition contends that this tract was composed in the time of the Venerable Bede, when the question of celibacy was being debated in the West; but this conjecture rests on no solid reason. [Note: [Col. 0811D] See Maran, in the *Life of Cyprian*, § 36, p. 120 f., Venice ed., 1728.]

III. The book *On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*, which is also attributed to Augustine, has, in Maran’s judgment, neither this Father nor Cyprian as its author. For, as Dupin says, besides the fact that its style and manner of writing are entirely different, Sacred Scripture is always cited in it according to Jerome’s version. [Col. 0812A] Pamelius attributes it to a certain Erradus, whose name he found written in the margin of this book in a manuscript of Augustine; others assign it to Patrick, bishop of Ireland, and still others to Clymacus. This tract was published among the works of the divine Augustine. Fell further testifies that it was once translated into the English language and is found in a manuscript volume of Saxon homilies under this title: *On the Twelve Abuses, According to the Disputation of St. Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr*.

IV. To these tracts must be added the *Oration in Praise of Martyrdom* and another, *On the Twofold Martyrdom, to Fortunatus*, [Col. 0812B] which were composed for amusement by some later author. The former is written in an ornate and excessively affected style, and it is evident that its author’s intention was to compose a speech according to rhetorical form. At its opening it begins just as though the author were addressing the people in a public sermon; its periods are elaborately fashioned, its thoughts attenuated by excessive scrupulousness, and its arrangement highly constrained.

The *Oration on the Twofold Martyrdom* was written less carefully by some later author who wished to imitate Cyprian’s style. Henry Gravius and Pamelius believed Erasmus to be the author of this fraud; but without solid foundation they branded Erasmus’s name with this considerable disgrace. Certainly that learned man would have concealed the fraud better. For although the author pretends that he is writing in the year 240, or thereabouts, after Christ, he nevertheless says that religion is spreading more widely [Col. 0812C] than the empire. He mentions the persecutions of Diocletian and Maximus—or Maximian—the war against the Turks, and monks and their arts.

V. The tract *On the Cardinal, or Principal, Works of Christ*, attributed to Cyprian although its style is entirely different, has on the authority of many manuscripts been restored to Arnold of Bonneval, an abbot in the diocese of Chartres and a friend of Bernard, who flourished around the middle of the twelfth century. He had dedicated it to Pope Adrian IV, and in the same style he wrote other tracts included in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*: *On the Words of Christ*, *On the Cross*, *On the Works of the Six Days*, and *On the Praises of the Virgin Mary*. Finally, he wrote the book of *Meditations*, which, though not previously published, was added to Cyprian’s works in the most recent Oxford printing issued in England. [Col. 0812D] [Note: [Col. 0812D] As was certainly fitting, God willing, in the course of this Library we shall take care that these minor works are returned to their own medieval period and attributed to their lawful author. **EDS.**]

VI. I shall say nothing about the *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, an excellent work also attributed to Jerome but now, by the judgment of all, restored to its lawful parent, Rufinus of Torano, presbyter of the Church of Aquileia. Gennadius mentions this exposition in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, when he says:

> “By his own labor—indeed, by the gift of God’s grace—the same Rufinus expounded the Creed in such a way that, by comparison with him, others might be thought not to have expounded it.”

It still appears even now among the spurious works of Jerome. [Col. 0813A] [Note: [Col. 0813D] We shall likewise give this book with the works of Rufinus. **EDS.**]

VII. The tract *On the Baptism of Heretics*, which opposes the opinion of St. Cyprian and was first brought to light by the highly learned Rigault, is the work of an ancient author who lived before Augustine’s time and perhaps in Cyprian’s own age. Baluzius—first prompted by Philippe Labbe—believes that this little book *On Rebaptism* was written [Note: [Col. 0813D] Baluzius’s note a on the anonymous book *On Rebaptism*, p. 735, Venice ed., 1748.] by Ursinus, an African monk whom Gennadius names in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* among the writers of the closing years of the fourth century. Gennadius reports that Ursinus wrote against those who decree that heretics must be rebaptized, and taught that those who are baptized either simply in the name of Christ or in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—even if with an erroneous understanding—must not be rebaptized; but that after a simple confession of the Trinity, the laying on of hands is sufficient for their salvation. [Col. 0813B] [Note: [Col. 0813D] See the preceding volume.]

What especially persuaded Baluzius to attribute this minor work to Ursinus—although William Cave assigns it to the age of Cyprian, since it seems to have been written when persecution was increasing—were the words, “after so long a succession of so many centuries,” which had elapsed between the author and the Apostles. Baluzius thinks Cave’s judgment is demolished by the fact that, as he himself had shown elsewhere concerning the date of the Council of Elvira, persecution was also mentioned in antiquity by people who lived long after persecution had ceased. Rigault, by contrast, together with the Oxford editor, Tillemont, Cave, Maran, and Gallandi, considers it the work of an author not far removed from Cyprian’s age. [Note: [Col. 0813D] Maran, in the *Life of St. Cyprian*, § 35, p. 117; Gallandi, *Biblioth. SS. Patrum*, vol. III, Prolegomena, p. 23; and Walch, *Histor. der Ketzer*, vol. II, p. 368 ff.]

[Col. 0813C] VIII. No more can the following be counted among the genuine works of St. Cyprian: the tract *On Mounts Sinai and Zion, Against the Jews*; the book *To Bishop Vigilius, on Jewish Unbelief*; and the tract *Against the Jews Who Persecuted Our Lord Jesus Christ*. The first was composed by a man who placed faith in the ravings of the rabbis and Kabbalists, and it contains trifles wholly unworthy of Cyprian’s genius.

It is evident to anyone who reads it that the second minor work, *On Jewish Unbelief*, is merely a preface by a certain elderly Christian who calls himself Celsus to the dialogue between Jason the Christian and Papiscus the Jew, which he himself had rendered from Greek into Latin. This preface was perhaps once adopted among Cyprian’s works—although by an excessively hasty judgment—because in the Colbertine codex numbered 1453 its beginning reads: “Cyprian to his brother Vigilius, greetings!” This dialogue, moreover, is an ancient Greek work, since Origen mentions it in book IV *Against Celsus*. [Col. 0813D] [Note: [Col. 0813D] See *Hist. Theolog. critic.*, vol. I, on Aristo of Pella, art. II, pp. 386, 392.]

Who and what manner of man this Celsus was, who translated these things into Latin and augmented them with a rather lengthy preface dedicated [Col. 0814A] to Bishop Vigilius, [Note: [Col. 0814D] Pamelius conjectures that this Vigilius was bishop of Trent. But Celsus congratulates his Vigilius on his future martyrdom and says that, in God’s judgment, he had been destined to be a martyr when he was appointed bishop in a miraculous manner. This cannot be applied to Vigilius of Trent, for no one could have spoken of that man—living toward the end of the fourth century amid the Church’s profound peace—as a martyr in hope and expectation.] is not known. This alone is evident from many passages of the preface: that he wrote while persecutions were still flourishing and before the emperors had embraced the Christian faith.

IX. Finally, critics likewise agree that the third tract *Against the Jews* cannot be attributed to Cyprian because of its excessive divergence in style. The distinguished Dupin further observes that in these two works—namely, the preface dedicated to Vigilius and the tract *Against the Jews*—nothing coherent or substantial is found. [Note: [Col. 0814D] Dupin, *Bibl. Auctor.*, vol. I, p. 269, Cologne Latin ed.]

X. Pamelius thought Cyprian to be the author of the poems entitled *Genesis* and *Sodom*, because they are attributed to him by Georg Fabricius, Morel, and a manuscript codex of the Library of St. Victor at Paris, [Col. 0814B] and because he thought he had detected certain Cyprianic phrases in them. But these arguments are of little weight, and the poems mentioned are not sufficiently worthy of the holy martyr; they are more rightly believed to be the work of some unknown author.

Likewise, nothing recommends vindicating to our saint another poem addressed to a senator who had turned from the Christian religion to idols. Nor does anything recommend the *Hymn on the Lord’s Cross*, or *On the Lord’s Passover*, as Pamelius read the title, or *The Tree of Life*, as Fabricius read it. According to the same Pamelius, the codex of Dunes attributes it to Victorinus; and after its conclusion another codex belonging to Cornelius Gualter has:

> “The Hymn of Caelius Cyprian, Bishop and Martyr, on the Passover of Our Lord Jesus Christ; or, according to some, of Victorinus *Pictabronensis* (that is, *Petabonensis* or *Petavionensis*), Bishop.”
