It is also said to survive under Victorinus’s name [Col. 0814C] in other manuscript codices. In Baluzius’s Venetian edition it bears the name Victorinus of Poitiers.

XI. Other tracts inscribed with Cyprian’s name are not merely spurious, but also contain trifles and falsehoods. Thus the work *On the Supper* is ridiculous and filled with absurdities, and is therefore unworthy not merely of our holy martyr, but even of a Christian man. It is plainly the production of some trifler who abused the narratives of Sacred Scripture for his own foolish tales, so that it is astonishing that it could ever have been attributed to our St. Cyprian.

Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0814D] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, p. 81, art. 65, “On St. Cyprian.”], on account of its utterly absurd jokes, drawn by fair means or foul not merely from profane subjects but even from Sacred Scripture, rightly and deservedly judges it worthier of a Turk than of a Christian. Salmasius testifies in his *Notes* [Col. 0814D] on Flavius Vopiscus, p. 396, that through the kindness of the highly learned jurist Juretus he had obtained this little work in manuscript, rendered into verse by Azelin, a monk of Reims, with this title: *The Supper of Azelin, Monk of Reims, Which He Composed for Emperor Henry in Imitation of Cyprian of Carthage*. [Col. 0815A]

Concerning the same book Casimir Oudin relates the following: [Note: [Col. 0815D] Casimir Oudin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, pp. 275–276.]

> “The man most illustrious for learning, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, also advised me of one thing concerning the minor work entitled *Cyprian’s Supper* among his works, in a letter written at Hanover on December 29, 1707: that he possessed an edition of this little production made in Germany in the year 1681, in a small format, with a translation of it into German verse; and that in this edition—which was undoubtedly made on the authority of an ancient and authentic manuscript codex—the work consists of twenty chapters, and a certain Maurus, a Gaul as I suppose, dedicated it to Lothair, King of the Franks, son of Louis IV, called ‘d’Outremer,’ who obtained the kingdom in the year 954 and held it for thirty-two years, down to the year 985. From this it is evident that this little work, devoid of any merit and utterly unworthy of dedication to a king of the Franks, is the production of an ignorant man from the profoundly dark tenth century, very far removed from Cyprian’s time. I did not wish to conceal from posterity what the most distinguished Leibniz communicated to me.” [Col. 0815B]

XII. Of the same kind are two tracts filled with superstition and impiety [Note: [Col. 0815D] Dupin, *Biblioth. Auctor.*, vol. I, p. 269.] that the Oxford editor found under Cyprian’s name, one written in Latin and the other in Greek. The title of the first is *Cyprian’s Secrets, or Mysteries*; that of the second, *εὐχαὶ Κυπριανοῦ* (*Prayers of Cyprian*). He judged both utterly unworthy of the light of publication, since they were full of the foulest superstition. In Maran’s judgment, [Note: [Col. 0815D] Maran, in the *Life of Cyprian*, § 36, p. 124.] they appear to have been falsely attributed [Col. 0815C] to Cyprian of Antioch.

XIII. Likewise, the *Revelation of the Head of St. John the Baptist*, a fabulous little work found under the name of St. Cyprian in the very old Speyer edition printed by Vindelinus, is a legendary narrative written after Athanasius, Cyril, Theodosius, the Vandals, and the Chronicles of Marcellinus and Pippin, all of whom are mentioned in it.

XIV. Nor does the *Confession of St. Cyprian*, extant in Greek and Latin in Baluze and listed among the apocrypha in the Decree of Gelasius, pertain to our saint. It is instead believed to belong to a saint of the same name, the Antiochene or Nicomedian martyr who, together with St. Justina, virgin and martyr, is entered in the Roman Martyrology under September 27. This *Confession*, or his *Penitence*, in which [Col. 0815D] he most abundantly laments the crimes of his former life, was first published by the Oxford editor of Cyprian’s works, and after him by Baluze. Baluze, however, also produced the Greek text itself from the Colbertine Library and placed it alongside the Latin translation, since the latter teems with numerous blemishes that might perhaps be more readily corrected from the Greek. Some say that this man was bishop of Antioch and suffered martyrdom at Nicomedia under Diocletian together with the virgin Justina, with whom he was madly in love. Nazianzen, Prudentius, Metaphrastes, and others confuse him with Cyprian of Carthage [Col. 0816A]. The Oxford editor of Cyprian’s works, supported by conjectures not to be despised, expressly affirms that no such Cyprian of Antioch ever existed; indeed, that the entire narrative circulated about him—certainly marvelous, yet a very ancient fable already in existence before the time of Nazianzen, which the empress Eudocia once also depicted in a heroic poem of three books—is nothing other than the history of Cyprian of Carthage, wondrously interpolated, or rather newly fabricated, by one of those who eagerly sought to embellish the deeds of the martyrs with novel material.

XV. The *Prayer for the Martyrs* and the *Prayer Which He Spoke on the Day of His Passion* are likewise falsely attributed to St. Cyprian. Maran assigns both [Note: [Col. 0816D] See Maran, *Life of Cyprian*, § 37, p. 124 ff.] to Cyprian [Col. 0816B] of Antioch. Dupin judges that the two treatises addressed to the martyrs, and the *Confession* or *Penitence of Cyprian the Martyr*, are works attributed by later Greeks to Cyprian the martyr, who perhaps was Cyprian himself, bishop of Carthage, whose life was amplified [Note: [Col. 0816D] The same, ibid.].

XVI. Several other works bear the name of Cyprian, such as the shorthand signs of Tiro and Seneca, which Gruter, following Trithemius, believes Cyprian augmented with words suited to Christian usage; these signs were published by Gruter [Note: [Col. 0816D] The reader should be advised that a certain little book survives which, although it does not have Cyprian as its author, nevertheless acknowledges him as its restorer: I mean the shorthand signs of Tiro and Seneca, which our prelate and martyr enriched with a quite substantial supplement, adding words necessary for Christian use, which appear in abundance in the codex published by Gruter. The Oxford editors, at the end of the index to Cyprian’s work.]. The English published under Cyprian’s name a Paschal computation, which they believe Paul the Deacon designated when he said: “Cyprian composed a very useful Chronicle.” The computation indicates the author’s date, for it is carried down to the fifth year of Gordian and the consulship of Arianus and Papus [Col. 0816C]. It is not altogether impossible to suppose that Cyprian had already been converted by that time, although Pontius the Deacon suggests that this occurred later. But the barbarity of this writer’s style does not accord with that elegance of expression which, as is evident from the *Letter to Donatus*, Cyprian cultivated in the earliest period of his conversion [Note: [Col. 0816D] To make the barbarity evident, the first sentence should be transcribed: “For a certainly not inconsiderable time we have been anxious, and, burning with eagerness, seeking to discover—not now in secular writings, but also in the holy and divine Scriptures—what is the first day, not of the month, in which month the Jews in Egypt were commanded to eat the Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon.” Cyprian would never have expressed his thought in that manner.]. This author says that Christ celebrated the Passover for the fifth time and died on the sixth, in the sixteenth year of Tiberius, after he had proclaimed the Gospel for only one year. That system is ancient, from which Dupin concludes that the work is by an ancient author.

XVII. Finally, the book *On the Trinity* was falsely attributed to St. Cyprian of Carthage; its author is Novatian [Col. 0817A], the Roman pseudo-bishop whom we discussed at length in Section II.

XVIII. In addition to the little works already reviewed, Baluze appended immediately after St. Cyprian’s letters three others as doubtful. He affirms that the first was drawn from two old manuscripts, one belonging to the library of the most illustrious Jean Bohier and the other to that of the monastery of St. Remigius at Reims; the second from a Foix manuscript in the Colbertine Library; and the third, finally, from this same manuscript and another belonging to St. Remigius at Reims. The first is extant under the name of Pope Cornelius and addressed to Cyprian; it is a brief but sharp rebuke of the error concerning the rebaptism of heretics. But, as we have already said elsewhere, we do not believe that this controversy ever arose between St. Cornelius and Cyprian, nor [Col. 0817B] do we accept Rufinus’s authority on this point. This letter of Cornelius is therefore apocryphal.

The heading of the second is: “Cyprian to the people residing at Carthage, eternal salvation in the Lord.” It not only differs too greatly from St. Cyprian’s style but also does not reflect his age, since it was written against the *traditores*—betrayers of Holy Scripture—who first became known under Diocletian.

The third begins as follows: “Cyprian to his blessed and most beloved father Turabius, eternal salvation in the Lord”; it is a letter of consolation addressed to him in his grief over the death of his daughter. This same letter formerly circulated under the name of St. Jerome, addressed to Tyrasius; but scholars have entirely denied it to him, and it is now included among his spurious works. The meanness of its inelegant style [Col. 0817C] and the obscurity of its diction prove no more that it pertains to our St. Cyprian.

XIX. The most distinguished pair of scholars, Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand, in volume IX of their very extensive *Collection of Ancient Writers and Historical Monuments, etc.*, place first St. Cyprian’s *Poem to Felix on the Resurrection of the Dead*, recovered from a Corbie manuscript copied more than nine hundred years ago. Although the distinguished editors were unwilling to affirm with certainty in their preliminary observation which Cyprian was the author of this poem, they nevertheless deny that it should be attributed to that most celebrated bishop and martyr of Carthage, both because of its excessively rough expression and because of its more frequent violations of the laws of meter. This poem had indeed already been published at the end of Tertullian’s works, but the editor proved himself excessively bold: unable to tolerate the metrical laws violated by Cyprian, whoever he may have been, and his humble style [Col. 0817D], he attempted to recast this little work in more elegant verse. Martène and Durand therefore took pains to restore from the aforementioned manuscript this poem, as it came from its author, to its original integrity.

## ARTICLE III. Concerning Certain Lost Works of St. Cyprian

I. Of those thirteen letters which, as we know from his fourteenth letter [Col. 0818A], St. Cyprian sent to the Roman clergy as witnesses to his pastoral vigilance [Note: [Col. 0818D] Cyprian, Ep. XIV, otherwise XV and XX, to the Roman Clergy.], the distinguished Maran demonstrated by arguments not to be despised that seven survive and the remainder are missing [Note: [Col. 0818D] Maran, *Life of Cyprian*, I, § IX, p. 27, Venice edition, 1758.].

The two letters which St. Cyprian had previously written to his clergy and people concerning the ordination of Felicissimus and the case of Felicissimus and the presbyters who adhered to him have likewise perished. He had earlier sent copies of these through Caldonius and Fortunatus to Cornelius, as Cyprian himself relates in Letter XLII, otherwise XLV, to that same Cornelius.

The circular letter which St. Cyprian sent to all the provinces subject to the metropolitan see of Carthage has also perished. Its purpose was to establish among everyone the legitimacy of Cornelius’s episcopate, and for the individual bishops to be admonished to repudiate Novatian and adhere to Cornelius. We learn this [Col. 0818B] from Letter XLV, otherwise XLVIII, to Cornelius.

In Letter LV, otherwise LIX, to Cornelius, he mentions two letters. In the first he had recently sent Cornelius the names of all the Catholic bishops subject to the metropolitan see of Carthage, with the intention that, if anyone other than they wrote to him, he should know that such a man was one of those who had sacrificed, one of the *libellatici* who had obtained certificates of sacrifice, or one of the heretics. The other letter informed him, among other things, of Fortunatus’s pseudo-episcopate. Both letters have perished.

It is evident from Letter LVIII, otherwise LXI, to Lucius that St. Cyprian, together with the other bishops of Africa, sent a joint letter to that same Lucius, the Roman pontiff, in which he congratulated him both upon attaining the summit of the pontificate and upon the glory of his confession. This letter [Col. 0818C] is likewise missing. Finally, the letter of St. Cyprian sent through the deacon Rogatianus to Firmilian, in which he informed him of his disagreement with Stephen—as is inferred from Firmilian’s Letter LXXV to Cyprian—has also perished.

II. Pontius the Deacon concludes his enumeration of St. Cyprian’s writings with these words [Note: [Col. 0818D] Pontius, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 5.]:

> Who, finally, would have inspired with the clarion call of the heavenly trumpet so many confessors, branded with a second inscription upon their marked foreheads and preserved alive as exemplars of martyrdom?

Since the holy Pontius did not count Cyprian’s letters among his works, the very learned Ceillier judges [Note: [Col. 0818D] Ceillier, vol. III, *Histoire générale des auteurs*, p. 152.] that the quoted words cannot refer to Letter LXXVII, in which he consoles the confessors condemned to the mines [Col. 0818D] under Valerian. Rather, they must designate some distinct little work, also different from the *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, which Pontius had discussed previously [Note: [Col. 0818D] “Who would have driven the martyrs onward with so powerful an exhortation from the divine word?” Pontius, *Life*, loc. cit.].

Ceillier consequently concludes that this little work has perished, as have the letters which St. Cyprian sent to St. Augustine and St. Felicitas, the martyrs of Capua in [Col. 0819A] Campania, during the persecution of Valerian [Note: [Col. 0819A] In a very old manuscript cited by the Oxford editor at the end of the index of Scripture, these letters are mentioned as follows: “The Christians suffered the fourth persecution under the emperor Decius, the author of those evils. During this persecution Cyprian exhorted by letters Augustine and Felicitas, who [Col. 0819B] suffered at the city of Capua, the metropolis of Campania, during the reign of Valerian.”]. For St. Cyprian extended his solicitude and charity even beyond Africa [Note: [Col. 0819B] Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, p. 73.].

III. To these we further append a brief observation concerning Letter Sixty-Eight: whether it should truly be attributed to St. Cyprian. We already noted above, while discussing the holy martyr’s letters, that Launoy regarded the aforementioned letter to Stephen concerning the excommunication of Marcian, bishop of Arles—which not only Cyprian’s editors Pamelius, Baluze, and Fell, but also writers of sound reputation [Col. 0820A], claim for Cyprian—as apocryphal and therefore unworthy of him.

Many considerations, however, prevent us from subscribing to that learned man’s opinion. For, as Basnage observed [Note: [Col. 0820B] Basnage, *Annales politico-ecclesiastici*, under the year 254.], not only is it written in Cyprian’s style, but it also contains material that most strongly reflects Cyprian’s times, customs, and discipline, so that one egg is not more like another than this letter is like Cyprian’s other letters. Fell also vindicates it for its author by another argument. St. Augustine, namely, mentions a certain letter of Cyprian to Stephen that has nothing whatsoever to do with the question of baptism. Since only two letters from Cyprian to Stephen survive, and one of them—Letter Seventy—concerns baptism, it is altogether probable that Augustine had the present letter, Letter Sixty-Eight, in view.

# FIRST APPENDIX. DOUBTFUL WORKS

[Col. 0819]

## BOOK ON DISCIPLINE AND THE BENEFIT OF CHASTITY. A LETTER BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR. (C, G, S)\*

[Col. 0819C]

[Note: [Col. 0819D]

**I.—On discipline.** I have not had the opportunity to see this letter in any manuscript.

**I shall not think myself absent.** Pamelius says: “Thus Gravius in the margin and the manuscript, instead of *I do not believe*.” PAMELIUS.

**Nevertheless, all things that are profitably brought forward.** Pamelius says: “Gravius has this from the same manuscript, instead of what the others have, *bring forward*; but I do not approve of what Manutius alone has, *manfully*.” PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0820D] **To fulfill the things that we know.** Pamelius says: “Gravius, Manutius, and Morel follow this conjecture of Erasmus. The word *quaque* could be understood as *quacumque*, especially since the manuscripts also read it thus.” PAMELIUS.]

I. I do not consider that I have neglected any portion of my duties, since I always strive—especially through daily expositions of the Gospels—to provide you, through the Lord, with growth in faith and knowledge. For what more useful thing can be done in the Lord’s Church, what can be found more fitting to the office of a bishop, than that believers should be able to attain the promised kingdom of heaven through instruction in the divine words, imparted and bestowed by the Lord himself?

This is certainly the daily task of prayer belonging both to my work and to my office, which, although absent, I strive to maintain; and through letters I endeavor to restore my presence to you. While I address you in the customary manner with communications sent to strengthen you in faith, I therefore call upon you always to stand armed against all the devil’s assaults, firmly established upon the root of the Gospel. I shall not think myself [Col. 0819D] absent if I can be free from anxiety.

Nevertheless, all things that are profitably brought forward, and that either define or promise the condition of eternal life to those who discuss them, are fruitful only if, through the power of divine indulgence, they are assisted toward the advantage of action [Col. 0820C]. We not only bring forward words that come from the sacred springs of Scripture, but join to those very words prayers and petitions to the Lord, so that he may both open to us and to you the treasures of his mysteries and grant the strength to fulfill the things that we know. For the greater danger is to have known the will of the Lord and then to have ceased from performing God’s will.

[Note: [Col. 0820D]

**II.—Apart from the will which we ought to will as our own.** Pamelius says: “From Coster I have *ut* (‘as’) instead of *et* (‘and’); nevertheless, the entire passage is still obscure. The manuscript codex has *and it comes to be in our own*, but this does not please me.” PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0821D] **Which has been consecrated by Christ.** Pamelius says: “Here again Coster has *because by Christ*; but the meaning is sound even on Erasmus’s testimony, and the manuscript codices also read thus.” PAMELIUS.]

II. Although, therefore, as you know, I always exhort you to many duties and to the commandments of divine admonition—for what else could be more the object of my prayer, or greater, than that you should stand perfect in the Lord in all respects?—I nevertheless admonish you above all to preserve the defenses of chastity, as indeed you do. You know that you are the temple of the Lord, the members of Christ, the dwelling of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0820D], chosen for hope, consecrated to faith, destined for salvation; sons of God, brothers of Christ, sharers in the Holy Spirit, owing nothing any longer to the flesh, as though reborn from water and chastity, apart from the will (John 1:13) [Col. 0821A] which we ought to will as our own. Let this be maintained also on account of redemption, so that what has been consecrated by Christ cannot be corrupted.

For if the Apostle declares the Church to be the bride of Christ (2 Cor. 11), I ask you, how great a chastity is required where, amid marriages, the Church is maintained as a virgin bride? As for myself, were it not that I have resolved to admonish you briefly, I believe I could produce sufficiently extensive and abundant praises of chastity; but I have deemed it superfluous to praise it at greater length among those who practice it. For you adorn it by putting it into practice, and by exercising it you bring forth more praises of it. You become its ornament even as it is yours, each lending beauty to the other in mutual exchange. It supplies you with the discipline of good morals; you provide it with the service of holy works. For both how much and what it can accomplish [Col. 0821B] have become manifest through you, and it itself has demonstrated and taught what you desire. Thus the two goods of commandments and deeds are joined into one, lest anything appear incomplete if either service were lacking to the commandments or commandments to the service.

III. Chastity is the honor of bodies, the adornment of morals, the holiness of the sexes, the bond of modesty, the fountain of purity, the peace of the household, and the chief principle of concord. Chastity is not concerned with pleasing anyone but itself. Chastity is always modest, since it is the mother of innocence. Chastity is always adorned by modesty alone, rightly conscious that it is beautiful if it displeases the wicked. Chastity seeks no ornaments; it is its own adornment.

It commends us to the Lord and unites us with Christ. It drives every unlawful conflict of desires from our members [Col. 0821C] and brings peace to our bodies. It is blessed in itself and renders blessed all those with whom it deigns to dwell. Even those who do not possess it can never accuse it. It is venerable even to its enemies, since those who cannot overcome it admire it all the more.

But just as chastity is always mature and proven in men, and to be sought by women, so its enemy, immodesty, must always be detested. It renders its servants an obscene mockery, sparing neither their bodies nor their minds. For once it has overcome their proper morals, it subjects the whole person to the triumph of lust. At first it is flattering, so that it may do greater harm while pleasing; it exhausts one’s property together with one’s modesty. It is the enemy of continence, a hostile frenzy that frequently proceeds through the bloodshed caused by desires, a conflagration of a good conscience, the mother of impenitence [Col. 0821D], the ruin of the better years of life, an insult to one’s lineage. It overthrows fidelity to blood and family, inserting its own children into the affections of strangers and introducing into other men’s wills offspring of an unknown and corrupted stock. Often burning beyond the bounds of its own sex, since it does not contain itself within what is permitted, it considers itself insufficiently satisfied unless in male bodies also it seeks—not some new pleasure, but extraordinary and monstrous perversions against nature itself, from men through men.

[Col. 0822A] IV. Chastity, however, holds the first place in virgins, the second in the continent, and the third in marriages. Yet in all these, with its respective degrees, it is glorious. For it is praiseworthy to preserve marital fidelity amid so many conflicts of the body; and to have set within marriage a limit derived from continence is a matter of greater virtue, since even lawful things are then rejected. Certainly, to have preserved holiness from the womb, and to have maintained oneself as an infant throughout the whole span of one’s life into old age, is a work of truly admirable power. Yet not to know the body’s enticing laws belongs more to good fortune; to overcome them once they have become known belongs to virtue—provided, nevertheless, that this virtue too comes from the gift of God, although it displays itself in human limbs.

V. The precepts of chastity, brothers, are ancient. Why do I call them ancient? Because they were established together with humanity itself [Col. 0822B]. For a woman has her husband precisely so that she may know no other besides him; and a woman was given to a man so that, once what was his own had been placed under his authority, he might seek nothing belonging to another. Thus, Scripture says, “the two shall be in one flesh” (Matt. 19:6), so that what had been one might return to unity, lest separation without reunion afford an occasion for union with another.

Hence the Apostle too declared that the man is the head of the woman (1 Cor. 11:3), so that he might affirm chastity through the union of the two. For just as another’s head cannot be fitted to someone else’s limbs, so neither can limbs that are not its own be fitted to another head. The head corresponds to its own limbs, and the limbs to their own head. Both adhere in mutual concord by a natural clasp, lest, through any discord arising from the division of the limbs, the covenant of the divine bond should be broken. Yet he also adds and says: “For he who [Col. 0822C] loves his wife loves himself” (Eph. 5:28–29). “For no one hates his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church.” From this follows a powerful rule concerning charity together with chastity: husbands must love their wives just as Christ loved the Church, and wives likewise ought to love their husbands as the Church loves Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0821D]

**VI.—For the adulterer has no excuse.** Pamelius [Col. 0822D] says: “This again comes from Tertullian, *On Chastity*, not far from the beginning, where he refers it to the excusing of a sin which, in accordance with his error, he wrongly admits to pardon.” PAMELIUS.]

VI. Christ gave so great an honor to chastity when, in response to a question, he said that a wife was not to be dismissed except on account of adultery (Matt. 5:32). Hence arose that sentence: “You shall not permit adulteresses to live” (Lev. 20:10). Hence the Apostle says: “This is the will of God: that you abstain from fornication” (1 Thess. 4:3). Hence he also says that the members of Christ must not be joined to the members of a prostitute (1 Cor. 6:9, 15) [Col. 0822D]. Hence the man who, trampling upon the law of chastity, practices the vices of the flesh is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. Hence adulterers deservedly do not possess the kingdom of heaven. Hence every sin is said to be outside the body, while the adulterer alone sins against his own body. Hence arise the Teacher’s other authoritative precepts, all of which it is unnecessary to recall now, especially among you, who frequently know and practice them. Although they have not been transcribed here, you still cannot complain of their omission. For the adulterer [Col. 0823A] has no excuse, nor could he have had one, since he was permitted to marry a wife.

[Note: [Col. 0823D]

**VII.—Which are so bound together that they cannot be torn apart.** Pamelius says: “A passage supporting the indissolubility of marriage. This passage is, however, defective, as Manutius also indicated with an asterisk. Some manuscripts continue what follows with different punctuation, in this manner: ‘By its loftiness it surpasses all things. If any perverse human beings dare to overstep the laws, virginity makes itself equal to the angels of God.’ But even thus they do not provide a satisfactory reading.” PAMELIUS.

**Virginity is confined to neither sex.** Pamelius says: “Gravius in the margin and the codex of St. Pantaleon have *neuter*; but the former reading pleases me.” PAMELIUS.]

VII. But just as laws have been prescribed for married women and are so firmly bound together that they cannot be torn apart, virginity and continence stand outside every law. Nothing from the laws of marriage pertains to virginity; by its loftiness it surpasses all things. If any perverse attempts of human beings seek to overstep the laws, virginity makes itself equal to the angels. Indeed, if we examine the matter, it even exceeds them, since, struggling in the flesh, it wins a victory even against nature—a victory the angels do not possess.

What else is virginity but a glorious contemplation of the life to come? Virginity is confined to neither sex. Virginity is infancy persevering. Virginity is a triumph over pleasures. Virginity has no children; but, what is more, it possesses contempt for having children. It does not have fecundity, but neither does it suffer bereavement. It is happy because it is free from the pain of childbirth, but happier because it is free from the calamity of its children’s funerals.

What else is virginity but liberty released from bonds? It does not have a husband as master. Virginity is free from every attachment; it is dedicated neither to marriage, nor to the world, nor to children. It cannot fear persecution, since its freedom from anxiety enables it to challenge persecution.

[Note: [Col. 0823D]

**Sold off by his brothers.** *Distrahere* means not to assign something offered for sale to one person, but to sell it to a number of persons carrying it to various places. Joseph was “sold off” in this sense, because his brothers sold him not to any single master, but to a company of Midianite merchants [Col. 0824D].

**To the charge of immodesty.** Pamelius says: “The manuscript codices have the excellent reading *immodesty*, instead of *chastity*.” PAMELIUS.

**He who was lesser in the household.** The manuscript codices also correctly have this instead of *in a lesser [danger]*, for Joseph was not in lesser but in greater danger there.]

VIII. But since the precepts of chastity have been briefly set forth for us, let us now present an example of chastity. For greater progress is made when one comes to the actual matter; nor will there be any doubt about the virtue when what is commanded is also attested by examples.

The example of chastity began with Joseph (Gen. 39:7). A Hebrew youth, noble through his father and nobler through his innocence, he was sold off by his brothers to the Ishmaelites because of envy arising from his revelations [Col. 0823C], and came into the household of an Egyptian. By his obedience, innocence, and complete fidelity in servitude, he easily won his master’s favorable and benevolent disposition toward him; both his cultivated speech and his age commended his appearance to everyone.

But this nobility was received by his master’s wife in a manner other than was proper. In a secluded part of the house, without witnesses, deep within and suited to crimes, the incontinent woman thought that through her own immodesty she could overcome the young man’s chastity, now by promises, now by threats. When she caught hold of his clothing as he attempted to flee, he abandoned even his garments because of the audacity of so great a crime, intending the purity of his naked body to serve as a witness to his innocence. The foolish woman did not hesitate to add slander [Col. 0823D] to the crime of her own immodesty. Disheveled and inflamed because her desire had been spurned, she complained both to the others and to her husband, with pretended grief [Col. 0824A], that the Hebrew youth had attempted to inflict upon her the violence which she herself had attempted to inflict.

Her husband’s passion, ignorant of the facts and fiercely kindled by his wife’s accusation, burst into flame. But the chaste young man, because he had not joined his conscience to the offense, was thrust into the depths of prison. Yet chastity was not alone in prison: for God was with Joseph, and the guilty were delivered into his hand because he had been innocent. Moreover, he unraveled the obscurities of dreams, because his spirit had remained watchful amid temptation, and through the Lord he was released from his chains. He who had been a subordinate in a household amid danger was made master of the royal house without danger. Restored to his nobility, he received, with God as judge, the fruit of chastity and innocence which he had merited from him.

IX. But no less, from the opposite sex, there arises for us another similar example of chastity drawn from the continence of women. As we read, Susanna (Dan. 13), the daughter of Hilkiah and wife of Joachim, was very beautiful, but more beautiful in character. No artificial appearance commended her beauty, for she was unaffected. Chastity and nature alone had adorned her.

Two of the elders had begun to lust madly after her, remembering neither the fear of God nor even their own age, already withering with years. Thus the flame of reviving lust recalled them to the fires of their long-past youth, setting them ablaze. These robbers of chastity professed love, but in fact hated it. When she resisted, they threatened her with false accusations; desiring to commit adultery themselves, they said that they would accuse her of adultery.

Amid these rocks of lust she sought help from the Lord, because she was unable to resist by the strength of her body. And from heaven the Lord heard chastity crying out to him [Col. 0824C]. When she was being led to punishment, oppressed by injustice, she was freed and saw vengeance inflicted upon her enemies. Twice victorious, although so fatally beset both times in her danger, she escaped both lust and death.

It would be endless if I were to pursue more examples. I am content with these two, especially since through them chastity was defended with every power.

[Note: [Col. 0824D]

**X.—So that, like a flower hastening swiftly through the passing span of life.** Pamelius says: “Gravius beautifully restored this passage in this form, instead of what others read: ‘like a flower indeed hastening swiftly to pass through life.’ The manuscript codices also agree, and they likewise read *extended* instead of what the others have, *extending*.” PAMELIUS.]

X. The memory of noble blood could not soften them in life—a memory that in some serves license and wantonness. Nor could bodily beauty and the well-proportioned form of the limbs soften them; such beauty often suggests that, like a flower hastening swiftly through the passing span of life, it should be nourished by the opportunity for pleasure extended to it. Nor could their early years in the bloom not merely of youth but of more advanced maturity soften them, when still-new and seething blood kindles the flames of nature [Col. 0824D], and blind fires working in the marrow are ready to proceed toward their remedy even through danger to modesty.

Nor could any opportunity furnished by a hiding place without a single witness soften them—an opportunity considered safe by some and the strongest inducement to admitting crime, when impunity presents itself to one’s deliberations [Col. 0825A]. Nor could compulsion imposed by the authority of those commanding, or by the rashness of accomplices and associates, soften them; upright resolutions are often broken in this manner. Nor could rewards themselves and kindnesses, accusations, threats, punishments, or deaths soften them. Nothing was so savage, so harsh, or so grievous as falling from the lofty rank of chastity.

They were worthy of so great a reward from the divine Judge: the one was raised to distinction almost upon a royal throne, while the other, endowed with restored concord with her husband, was redeemed through the deaths of her enemies. These and examples like them must always be placed before our eyes; matters equal to them must be contemplated by us day and night.

[Col. 0825B]

[Note: [Col. 0825D]

**XI.—For that consummated will.** Pamelius says: “Gravius has *pleasure* in the margin, but not even this makes the passage clear.” PAMELIUS.]

XI. Nothing so delights a faithful soul as the unbroken consciousness of undefiled modesty. To have conquered pleasure is the greatest pleasure; nor is there any greater victory than one won over desires. He who has conquered an enemy was stronger, but stronger than another; he who has restrained lust was stronger than himself. He who struck down an enemy smote an external foe; he who subdued desire overcame a domestic enemy.

Every evil is more easily conquered than pleasure, because every other evil, whatever it may be, is repellent, while pleasure is enticing. Nothing is so difficult to overcome as that through which the enemy is armed. He who removes desires also removes fears, for fears arise from desires. He who conquers desires triumphs over sin. He who conquers desires shows that the evil of the human race lies beneath his feet [Col. 0825C]. He who has conquered desires has given himself perpetual peace. He who has conquered desires restores to himself liberty, a thing most difficult even for the freeborn.

Therefore, brothers, as the facts teach, chastity must always be cultivated by us. To make it easier, it requires no contrivances. For that consummated will which, unless it were hindered, remains far off, is nevertheless ours. Thus what is ours need not be acquired, but fostered.

[Note: [Col. 0825D]

**XII.—Next, to see that nothing in oneself is fashioned beyond due measure.** Pamelius says: “He borrowed this from the beginning of Tertullian’s book *On the Dress of Women*, where Tertullian teaches that chastity also consists in adornment. Cyprian himself treated this subject above in the book *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*, where similar passages of Tertullian are discussed more fully. Erasmus rightly conjectured, however, that *is made alluring* should be read instead of *of those making alluring*.” PAMELIUS.

**Why are the edges of the eyes darkened?** Pamelius says: “Erasmus judges that this should be read instead of what the old printed codex had, *are suffocated*, because, he says, dark coloring was customarily applied beneath the eyes. But if one reads *are painted* or *are colored*, it will come closer to Cyprian’s expression in the cited book: ‘to color the eyes with encircling blackness.’” PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0826D] **They exceed anyone’s account book.** Tertullian similarly says in *On Women’s Dress*: “Ten thousand sesterces are spent upon a single thread; a delicate neck bears estates and islands; the slender flesh of the ears consumes an account book; and on the left hand each individual finger plays with the wealth of separate moneybags.” Explaining himself, he says: “These are the powers of ambition: to carry upon one little female body wealth bearing so much interest.” For a *kalendarium*, or *book of accounts*—as Seneca calls it in Letter 88—means both household accounts in which sums received in individual months are recorded, and those accounts in which interest payable on the Kalends was entered, as Rhenanus rightly observed. The jurists Ulpian and Africanus use it in this latter sense. It is therefore unnecessary to have recourse to Erasmus’s conjecture that the reading should be “they exceed the weight of the cylinders.”]

XII. For what else is chastity but an honorable mind appointed to guard the body, so that modesty restored to the sexes and sealed by strictness might preserve the honor of fidelity through uncorrupted offspring? To chastity, brothers, belong—and are recognized as belonging above all—reverence for God, holy meditation upon his precepts, a soul inclined toward faith, and a mind awestruck before sacred religion [Col. 0826A].

Next, it requires seeing that nothing in oneself is fashioned beyond due measure, extended beyond propriety, exposed, artificially painted, or made alluring so as to provoke or revive seduction. A woman who aims to stir another’s desire is not chaste, even if her bodily purity remains intact. Far removed from us should be those by whom beauty is not adorned but prostituted. For preoccupation with beauty is both an indication of an evil mind and a judgment that one is deformed.

Let the body’s natural condition remain free, and let no violence be done to God’s works. A woman who does not please herself as she is must always be wretched. Why is the color of the hair changed? Why are the edges of the eyes darkened? Why is the face transformed by artifices into a different shape? Finally, why is the mirror consulted, unless because the woman fears being herself?

The dress of a chaste woman should itself be chaste; a faithful woman should not know adultery even in colors [Col. 0826B]. To weave gold into clothing is, as it were, to ruin the clothing by means of its cost. What are hard metals doing among the delicate threads of the warp, unless they are to weigh down flowing shoulders and display the extravagance of a mind unhappily vaunting itself? Why are necks burdened and concealed by foreign stones whose prices, even apart from the workmanship, exceed anyone’s account book? The woman is not adorned; rather, the woman’s vices are displayed. Why, when fingers are so burdened with gold that they can neither enter nor withdraw—is this required by practical use, or is an empty display of estates being exhibited? A remarkable circumstance: women who are delicate in all other respects are stronger than men when bearing the burdens of vice.

### XIII

But, to return to what I had begun: chastity must always be cultivated by men and women, and must be preserved with every safeguard [Col. 0826C] within its proper bounds. The bodily nature is quickly endangered in the body, since the flesh—which is always tending toward a fall—carries it away with itself. Under the pretext of nature, which continually urges human beings toward those affections by which the ruins of the fallen race are repaired, the flesh deceives them with the enticement of pleasure: it does not lead offspring toward the continence of lawful union, but casts them into guilt. Therefore, against these snares of the flesh, in which the devil intrudes as both companion and leader, one must struggle with every kind of virtue. Let this struggle be undertaken, according to the Apostle, with Christ’s aid, and let the soul withdraw as far as it can from association with the flesh. Let consent be separated from the body; let vices always be chastised, so that they may be hated. Let that shame of sin, hideous and degraded, be kept before the eyes. Repentance itself, with its lamentations, is a dishonorable [Col. 0827A] attestation of crimes committed. Let nothing in the faces of others be examined with curiosity. Let speech be brief and laughter restrained, for laughter is a sign of a compliant and relaxed mind; and let even honorable physical contact be avoided. Let nothing be permitted to the body where bodily vice must be avoided. Let one consider how honorable it is to have conquered disgrace, and how dishonorable to have been conquered by disgrace.

### XIV

It must also be said that adultery is not pleasure but mutual dishonor, nor can that give delight which kills both soul and modesty. Let the soul restrain the goads of the flesh and curb the body’s impulse. For it has received this power, so that the members might serve at its command and so that, like a lawful and accomplished [Col. 0828A] charioteer, it might rein back with the reins of the heavenly precepts the impulses of the flesh when they rise beyond the body’s permitted limits, lest this chariot of the body, carried beyond its bounds, drag the charioteer himself with it into danger.

But amid these things—indeed, before them—aid must be sought from the divine camp against every disturbance and vice. For God alone is powerful: he who deigned to make human beings and to furnish them with complete assistance. I have dictated only a few things, since my purpose is not to write a volume but to send an address. Consult the Scriptures; seek in those very precepts greater examples for yourselves concerning this matter. Farewell, dearly beloved brothers.

[Col. 0827]

## NOTICE

At this point the recent editors had both the opportunity and the intention of publishing anew a little work recently assigned to St. Cyprian, entitled *Exhortation to Repentance*, from the unpublished materials of the Most Illustrious Gentlemen Trombelli and Mingarelli, Canons Regular, who were the first to bring this book forth from very ancient manuscripts and make it public property at Bologna in the year 1751. But since this book is exceedingly difficult to find, lies hidden in Italian booksellers’ catalogues, and, although sought by every means, has not yet been found in time, we promise that it will be included later in the course of this Library.

# SECOND APPENDIX: SPURIOUS WORKS

[Col. 0827]

## THE BOOK ON GAMBLERS  
### A TREATISE WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED TO CYPRIAN  
(C, G, S)

[Col. 0827B]

> **Note [Col. 0827C]**
>
> **I.—“Great concern for us from the whole brotherhood.”** Perhaps it should read: “concern for the whole brotherhood.” Yet the opening of this book is still plainly mutilated. —PAM.
>
> **“And since to us.”** I have omitted the superfluous word *in*. —RIGALT.
>
> **“And since the divine and paternal loving-kindness,” etc.** Nor does Faber note that this Treatise is not Cyprian’s. For [Col. 0828C] from this passage it appears to have been written by some Roman Pontiff. —PAMEL.

### I

Great concern for us has arisen from the whole brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0827C] Thus the York, Imperial edition. *The concern of the faithful*], especially from the guilty [Note: [Col. 0827C] Thus the York, Imperial edition. *And guilty*] audacity of all the ruined—that is, of gamblers—which entices their minds into wickedness within itself, so as to plunge them into the pit of death [Note: [Col. 0827C] Thus Bodl. 1, York, Imperial edition: *into wickedness, into the pit*. *Let them be stained by the snare of death*, York].

And since the divine and paternal loving-kindness has bestowed upon us the leadership of the apostolate, has adorned the Lord’s vicarial see with heavenly favor, and since in our predecessor [Note: [Col. 0827C] Thus Bodl. 1, Corb., Imperial edition. *In yours*] we bear the origin of the authentic apostolate upon which Christ founded the Church—having received at the same time the power of loosing and binding and the ministry of forgiving sins—we are admonished by saving [Note: [Col. 0827C] Thus Bodl. 1, Imperial edition. *Of loosing; saving*, Bodl. 1] doctrine, lest, while continually pardoning offenders, we ourselves should be tormented together with them.

[Col. 0828B]

> **Note [Col. 0828C]**
>
> **II.—“Lest, secure in the Church.”** Here too the superfluous particle *cum* had been inserted. —PAMEL.
>
> **“While the Lord is indignant, we should lose it as he reproaches us.”** I think it should read: “and while he reproaches us.” —PAMEL.
>
> [Col. 0829D] **“They sought you as a ruler.”** Here too I would prefer “they appointed.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Regard the priest.”** I do not know to what Scripture this alludes, unless perhaps it refers to those passages concerning the cultivation of the word. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Lest any defect of mange be found among them.”** So I read in place of the former *with mange*; yet the passage is still obscure and mutilated. —PAMEL.

### II

We are therefore called the salt of the earth so that the whole brotherhood may be salted with heavenly wisdom through us. For since he says, “But if the salt should become tasteless [Note: [Col. 0828C] *Foolish*, Bodl. 1], it will be worth nothing [Note: [Col. 0828C] *In no respect*, Bodl.] except to be cast outside and trampled by men,” we dread and fear that, being secure in [Note: [Col. 0828C] *When in*, Bodl. 1] the Church because priestly dignity has been entrusted to us [Note: [Col. 0828C] *The dignity is*, Bodl. 1], and becoming negligent, we may be found idle alongside certain brothers; or that, while granting false communion, we may lose—while the Lord is indignant and reproaches us—that which we received with honor through God’s favor. For divine Scripture says: “Woe shall be to the shepherds.”

But if the shepherds themselves are found negligent, what answer will they give [Note: [Col. 0828C] *Entrusted by the Lord*, Bodl. 1] to the Lord concerning [Col. 0829A] the sheep? What will they say to the Lord about the sheep—that they were harassed by the sheep? They will not be believed. It is incredible that shepherds could suffer anything at the hands of a sheep; rather, they will be punished for their lie.

And another Scripture says: “They sought you as a ruler; do not be exalted. Be among them as one of themselves; take care of them and give heed.” And again: “Regard the priest as a cultivator, and let every kind of delight be found in his keeping, the granaries full, so that he may satisfy the sheep with whatever fodder they desire” [Note: [Col. 0829C] Thus Bodl. 1, Imperial edition. *They considered*, Bodl. 1, 2].

For, to establish that we—that is, the bishops—are shepherds of spiritual sheep, namely faithful human beings placed under our care, lest any [Note: [Col. 0829C] *No*, Bodl. 1] defect of mange be found among them, they should all the more be examined by us every day, so that, when heavenly medicine has been applied, flourishing fleeces may grow upon them and contribute to the nature of the garment [Col. 0829B] of salvation.

> **Note [Col. 0829D]**
>
> **III.—“He confirmed.”** Thus Pamel., Baluz., Oxford. Or should it be “he has confirmed,” the manuscripts having been misread? —EDITORS.

### III

In the Gospel the Lord said to Peter: “Peter,” he said, “do you love me?” And Peter answered: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” He said: “Feed my sheep”; and, earnestly enjoining it for the third time, he confirmed it by saying: “Feed [Note: [Col. 0829C] Thus Lam., York, Bodl. 1, Corb., Imperial edition: *He said to Peter, Feed*] my sheep.”

> **Note [Col. 0829D]**
>
> **IV.—“To our fellow inhabitant.”** The superfluous particle *and* was rendering the passage obscure. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Without bodily tribulation.”** Here I would like *also* to be added. —PAMEL.
>
> [Col. 0830D] **“And with a worthy status.”** I certainly read “with a corresponding status.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Provident and solicitous, he says.”** I certainly read this too in place of “saying.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“And in the Teachings of the Apostles.”** I do not know whence he cites these words, for they are found neither in the Canons nor in the Apostolic Constitutions. —PAMEL.

### IV

And since we have received the episcopate [*Episcopium*; Note: [Col. 0829C] *The bishop*, Bodl. 1]—that is, the Holy Spirit through the laying on of a hand—as a guest within the heart, let us place no [Note: [Col. 0829C] *And no … for our fellow inhabitant*, Bodl. 1] cause of distress before our fellow inhabitant. The Apostle [Note: [Col. 0829C] *The Lord*, Bodl. 1] admonishes us and says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit who is within you; and do not extinguish the light that has shone within you.”

As many corresponding martyrdoms as await [Note: [Col. 0829D] *May there be*, Bodl. 1] a bishop who acts well and admonishes for salvation without bodily tribulation, so many torments are heaped [Col. 0829C] upon a negligent bishop [Note: [Col. 0830C] *So much also upon a negligent bishop*, Bodl. 1] who produces no testimonies from the Holy Scriptures. The Apostle Paul rouses us, places bishops and stewards of evangelical teaching in a corresponding status, and says: “As long as he is a child, he has stewards and managers; but when he has grown, he claims his inheritance.”

We too are dispensers and stewards of the Gospel; and this too is required among dispensers and stewards: that each be found faithful and just. If, therefore, it is required among dispensers and stewards that each be found faithful and just, what if the sheep [Note: [Col. 0830C] *All*, Bodl. 1, Corb.] sin [Col. 0830A], and the dispensers sin together with them? Do they not burden themselves with the weight of those who sin?

The Apostle [Note: [Col. 0830C] *The same Apostle Paul*, Bodl. 1] Paul recalls how, when instructing Timothy and strengthening him in firmness of faith—lest he fail God in anything and lest the evil one interpose himself amid the prayers of the just—he says with foresight and solicitude:

> O Timothy, my son, preserve what has been entrusted to you. Do not neglect the gift that is within you through the laying on of the elders’ hands. Gird yourself bravely, and perform your ministry manfully and fulfill it with integrity. Be a good [Note: [Col. 0830C] *For good*, Bodl. 1] example to the rest. Let no one contradict you; let no one despise your youth. Rebuke a sinner in the presence of many, so that the rest too may be afraid; and do not share in the sins of others.

And again:

> If anyone called a brother is a fornicator, an idolater, a miser, a robber, or an unjust man, [Col. 0830B] do not even take food with such a person.

And elsewhere:

> Any brother who lives after the manner of foreigners and admits things resembling their deeds—cease to associate with him; for unless you do so [Note: [Col. 0830C] *Unless you do it*, Bodl. 1], you too will share in his guilt.

And in the *Teachings of the Apostles*:

> If any brother sins in the Church and does not obey the law, let him not be joined to the community until he repents, and let him not be received, lest your prayer be defiled and obstructed.

And the Apostle says yet again:

> Remove the wicked from your midst [Note: [Col. 0830C] *I do not know*, Bodl. 1].

> **Note [Col. 0830D]**
>
> **V.—“With offending persons.”** Again we have omitted the superfluous particle *lest*. —PAMEL.
>
> **“How great and abundant is the loving-kindness of the Lord’s son.”** I read “of God.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Tempting in no single kind.”** I think it should read “with no single kind of temptation.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Adulteries.”** Certainly either this or the singular “adultery” should be read in place of the former corrupt reading. —PAMEL.

### V

But if, through the varied and concordant warning of many witnesses, we are taught [Note: [Col. 0830C–D] *We are taught a unified and concordant warning, lest we take food with offending brothers*, Bodl. 1] not even to eat food with brothers who sin, how much more ought such a person to be barred from Christ’s sacrifice?

How great and abundant is the loving-kindness of God the Son, since in his foreknowledge he takes counsel for us concerning the future, lest any unwary person among the brothers be caught anew in the devil’s snares! [Col. 0830C] He commanded us to be watchful, provident, and instructed, because that ancient enemy prowls about, assailing God’s servants and tempting them with no single kind of temptation. For his temptations are many, chief among them being idolatry, adulteries, thefts, robberies, avarice, fraud, drunkenness, impatience, adultery, murder, jealousy, treachery, false testimony, false speech, envy, pride, cursing, error, and any similar things that accord with these. Among them is the gaming board.

[Col. 0831A]

> **Note [Col. 0831C]**
>
> **VI.—“A great destruction is concealed in its embrace.”** The passage is corrupt in many respects. —PAMEL.
>
> **“The hand which has already.”** I certainly read *which has already* in place of *so*; moreover, I add *is*, from Antoninus. [Col. 0831D] —PAMEL.
>
> **“Admitted to the Lord’s sacrifice.”** Either he alludes to the ancient custom discussed in the book *On the Lapsed*, or—as appears more likely from what follows—he is speaking about presbyters. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Which rises in praise of the Lord.”** Thus Antoninus rightly reads, as does a certain manuscript of Morel, in place of *itself*. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Which imprints the sign of the cross,” etc.** This again is from Antoninus, in place of the former: “itself, through which we are protected, the sign of the cross upon foreheads.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Itself which completes the divine sacraments.”** In accordance with Antoninus’s preceding reading, I have not hesitated to insert *which*. —PAMEL.
>
> **“What is it, I ask.”** I have added the particle *I ask* from the same Antoninus; for in his text it should undoubtedly be read thus in place of the word *he says*. —PAMEL.
>
> **“The devil’s hunting spear and the wound of sin.”** I prefer this reading of his too over the common text, “the evil of Zabulus and the devil’s wound.” Following him, we have again omitted *and* a little later. [Col. 0832C] —PAMEL.
>
> **“Where madness and frenzy.”** Antoninus: “where frenzy of mind.” —PAMEL.
>
> [Col. 0832D] **“There, rabid friendship.”** Thus he too, and another manuscript of Morel, in place of *rabidosa*. —PAMEL.
>
> **“A brotherhood of crime.”** Thus another manuscript of Morel, in place of “monstrosity.” —PAMEL.

### VI

The devil’s manifest snare is at hand [Note: [Col. 0831C] Thus Bodl. 1, Imperial edition. *It is ready*], bearing the serpent’s deadly poison and a corrupting enticement. Although it appears to be nothing, a great destruction is concealed in its embrace [Note: [Col. 0831C] *Embraces*, Bodl. 1].

What is the meaning of this, I ask, faithful people? The hand which has already been cleansed from injuries to human beings and admitted to the Lord’s sacrifice receives through divine favor that which pertains to the salvation of the whole person [Note: [Col. 0831C] *Itself through favor*, Bodl. 1]; it rises in the sanctuary in praise of the Lord; it [Note: [Col. 0831C] *Itself the sign*, Bodl. 1] imprints upon foreheads the sign of the cross by which we are protected; it is the very hand which [Note: [Col. 0831C] *Itself, to*, Bodl. 1] completes the divine sacraments. What is the meaning of this, I ask, that it should again be entangled in the devil’s snares, from which it was stripped free, and be condemned through those very sacraments?

Gambling hands have become accustomed, with lustful zeal, to the gaming board; this is the devil’s hunting spear [Note: [Col. 0831C] *The evil of Zabulus*, Bodl. 1] and the incurable wound of sin. I speak of the gaming board, where the devil is at hand, crouching low to capture a friend [*amicapiendum*, an uncertain reading], and, once he has captured him, triumphs over his captive through treachery and false testimony. I speak of the gaming board, where there is madness, frenzy, perjury for sale, and the serpent’s command and conversation. There is rabid friendship; there is the discordant brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0831C] *Monstrosity; there*, Bodl. 1] of most atrocious crime; there are insults, savage audacity, an insane mind, and ferocious impatience. I speak of the gaming board, where possessions are lost and enormous sums of money [Note: [Col. 0832C] *Lost, and madness …*, Bodl. 1] destroyed—a monstrosity displaying a quarrelsome, thieving madness.

> **Note [Col. 0832D]**
>
> **VII.—“The wealth of their ancestors, acquired by sweat.”** Another manuscript of Morel has “by their labors”; so too Antoninus. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Although there were so many means for increasing their estate,” etc.** Something is missing, namely “opportunities,” or something similar. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Gambling is a channel of evil,” etc.** This again is from Antoninus, in place of “it is that snare of evil and the overthrow of the enemy, which.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Without any legal chicanery.”** From the same source, *of the law court* in place of *strong*. But conversely, in his text *chicanery* should be restored in place of *money*. —PAMEL.

### VII

O harmful, sedentary, and idle wickedness of gamblers! O cruel hands, armed to endanger themselves, which squander through shameful zeal their paternal goods and their ancestors’ wealth acquired by sweat! A savage, harmful, and sleepless hand, night and day the continual bearer of its implements [Col. 0831C], which has condemned itself by sinning and does not cease its course even after its sins! O wicked hand, armed for the destruction of its master, which loses his entire substance for the sake of the basest bronze coins; although there were so many means for increasing [Col. 0832A] his household property and the abundance of his great wealth, he is now destitute and poor!

Gambling is what the law hates. Gambling is what an ignoble crime follows [Note: [Col. 0832C] *Pursues*, Bodl. 1]; in it temptation is manifest but punishment concealed. Gambling is a channel [Note: [Col. 0832C] *It is that snare of evil*, Bodl. 1] of evil and the overthrow of a friend; it brings no profit but consumes everything. From this men become poor; from this they lose their wealth; from this, after all their property has been consumed, they bury themselves beneath borrowed money; from this they lose their patrimony without any legal chicanery. What kind of lawsuit is this, that those whom no one is prosecuting should prosecute themselves out of malice, and dissipate their paternal inheritances beneath the manifold numbers upon the dice [Note: [Col. 0832C] Thus Corb., Imperial edition. *Beneath the manifold number of their enemies. They destroy*, Bodl. 1]?

> **Note [Col. 0832D]**
>
> **VIII.—“At the instigation of Zabulus alone.”** This too is from the same author, in place of “at the prompting”; he also reads “filled” in place of “had filled,” but wrongly. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Into his folds.”** Perhaps “in his fold”; yet the passage is still obscure and mutilated. —PAMEL.
>
> [Col. 0833D] **“In statuettes and images.”** We have added the previously missing *and*. —PAMEL.
>
> **“By which he established that he was to be worshiped by his imitators,”** etc. Thus again from that author, in place of the former “he declared that he was to be worshiped and determined the rule that sacrifice be offered to him.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“Under the fictitious name of a god.”** Certainly read thus in place of “fabricated.” —PAMEL.

### VIII

There are also times when gamblers themselves, together with prostitutes, keep nocturnal vigils beside their author behind closed doors. The wretches are armed against one another [Col. 0832B], filled with the spirit of the devil, and there commit a double or twofold crime. Here the sound of the dice rattles; there incest works in silence. Here, without any regard for his dignity and without any excuse, a man is compelled by this pestilential pursuit to yield up his goods; there deadly poison is secretly drunk.

Whence came the devising of these sacrileges? Whence came this crime? We establish it through the testimony of its authors. For a certain man, well educated in the study of letters, after long meditation invented this evil [Note: [Col. 0832C] *Evil*, Lam.] and so destructive a pursuit, at the instigation of Zabulus alone, who had filled him with his arts. He therefore displayed this thing, which he fashioned in carvings together with his own image, intending it also to be worshiped. And so, at the suggestion of the friend who prompted him inwardly to devise this art, he set up his own image with an inscription of his name [Note: [Col. 0832C] Thus Corb., Imperial edition. *He came to the sinner’s aid*].

Displaying himself in a handsome image, he accordingly placed it in a certain elevated location. Carrying this gaming board in his own folds, as though he might appear to be both the player and inventor of this wickedness—a man whose name ought not to be spoken by God’s servants [Col. 0833A], for he is as shameful in name as he is unjust in deed—he arranged that every servant of God who embraced the gaming board should be called by its author’s name.

For when he formed representations of himself in statuettes and images, he invented another crime, by which he established that he was to be worshiped by his imitators [Note: [Col. 0833C] “He declared that he was to be worshiped and determined the rule that sacrifice be offered to him”; thus Bodl. 1], and instituted that sacrifice should be offered to him. Thus anyone wishing to adhere to his pursuit would not stretch his hand toward the board before first sacrificing to its author. Hence it came about that one who had once been a human being and the adulterous perpetrator of a crime, after his death deserved to be worshiped by profane [Note: [Col. 0833C] Thus Bodl. 1, Imperial edition. *Prostrate*] and erring people under the fictitious name of a god.

> **Note [Col. 0833D]**
>
> **IX.—“A sorcerer and poisoner.”** A new word, apparently derived from the idols being worshiped. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Every man who eats the flesh of the sacrifice.”** I have fully restored this passage from the book *On the Lapsed*, where this Scripture is cited in this form, in place of the former *begging*; from the same source I read “uncleanness” in place of “of uncleanness.” —PAMEL.

### IX

Whoever plays at the gaming board must also know its sorceries [Note: [Col. 0833C] *Sorcery*, Bodl. 1], knowing that this is far removed from God’s servants, since [Note: [Col. 0833C] *Since they know*, Bodl. 1] the sorcerer and poisoner remains outside and, again, on the day of judgment will be tormented in revolving fire.

Whoever plays at the gaming board must first sacrifice to its author, something Christians may not do, since the Lord says: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, unless he sacrifices to God alone”; and again: “Do not sacrifice to foreign gods, lest you provoke me by the works of your hands to destroy you.”

You who are a Christian and play at the gaming board—even if you do not sacrifice, you share in the guilt under the law of this crime. And surely the Lord confronts you and says: “Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins.” And again: “Depart, depart from there; come out from her midst, you who carry the vessels of the Lord, and do not touch anything unclean.”

Whoever you are, Christian, if you gamble, you must believe first [Note: [Col. 0833C] Thus Bodl. 1. *Firstly*, Imperial edition] of all that your name is not Christian but pagan, and you receive in vain that which pertains to the Lord’s sacrifice. For thus [Note: [Col. 0833C] *For the Lord*, Bodl. 1] he says: “No unclean person shall [Col. 0833C] touch [Note: [Col. 0834C] *Let … touch*, Bodl. 1] the sacrifice of the Holy One.” For Scripture says: “Every man who eats the flesh of the sacrifice while his uncleanness is upon him—that soul shall perish from my people.”

> **Note [Col. 0833D]**
>
> **X.—“Surely, what madness.”** Antoninus: “O what madness”; he also reads “they swear falsely” in place of “they perjure themselves.” —PAMEL.
>
> [Col. 0834D] **“And blinded by the darkness of Zabulus.”** Antoninus: “of the devil.” Moreover, *deorbati* (“blinded”) is a new word. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Before the crowds present.”** I have restored this from the same author in place of the former “before the shameful,” a very bad reading. —PAMEL.
>
> **“While sacrificing beside the author.”** Again, an obscure passage. The same expression occurs above. —PAMEL.
>
> **“And do not do anything evil.”** I certainly read thus, since “refrain” precedes it. —PAMEL.
>
> **“See, brothers, that you are not misshapen.”** Everywhere else Cyprian has “conformed.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“And pardon is granted to no one.”** I read this too in place of “pardon”; this, however, seems to pertain to the error of the Novatians. —PAMEL.
>
> **“If a man sins by transgressing.”** This too is from other passages of Cyprian, in place of “sin is committed.” —PAMEL.

### X

Gambler, whoever you are, you call yourself a Christian; but you are not, because you share in the world. Nor can you be Christ’s friend when you maintain friendship with Christ’s enemy.

Surely, what madness possesses faithful gamblers when they rage and perjure themselves with the most rapacious cries! [Col. 0834A] Blinded by the darkness of Zabulus, they lay hands upon one another, curse, invoke damnation upon themselves, and dishonor the lineage of their parents before the crowds present. The clatter of the dice sounds publicly; hands hasten to slaughter their inheritance. Nor does the wretch understand what harm he does himself when he binds himself as a pledged servant to gambling. And one who has already been defeated repeatedly is once more incited, at Zabulus’s urging, to the still more harmful pursuit.

O art hostile to its devotees, and lustful debauchery! It provides not riches but nakedness and want. An executioner of a hand, a harmful hand, which does not desist even after winnings but continues to play after losses! The Christian who gambles pollutes his hand at the sacrifice of Zabulus while sacrifices are offered beside its author [Note: [Col. 0834C] Thus Corb., Imperial edition. *By the author’s punishments*].

For this reason the Lord declares his indignation at this:

> Do not stretch out your hands unjustly, lest you provoke me, and I shall not permit [Col. 0834B] you to remain long upon the earth.

And again:

> Refrain your hands from injustice, and do not do anything evil.

And the most blessed Apostle Paul likewise says:

> See, brothers, that you are not misshapen [Note: [Col. 0834C] *Conformed*, Bodl. 1] after this world and its pomp, luxury, and pleasures; but restrain yourselves from every injustice [Note: [Col. 0834C] *The injustice of the world*, Bodl. 1].

For whoever sins against God receives no excuse [Note: [Col. 0834C] *Because there is no excuse for an offense against God*, Bodl. 1] and no indulgence, and pardon is granted to no one. In the Gospel the Lord says:

> If anyone speaks blasphemies against the Son of Man, he shall be forgiven; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either here or in the age to come.

And again the Prophet says:

> If a man sins by transgressing [Note: [Col. 0834C] *If sin is committed against*, Bodl. 1] against a man, prayer shall be made to the Lord for him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?

And the blessed Apostle Paul, the steward and vicar of Christ, exercising ecclesiastical care [Col. 0834C], sets forth and says:

> You are the temple of God, and Christ dwells within you. If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.

Again the Lord in his Gospel repudiates sinners and reproaches them, saying:

> Depart from me, all you who work injustice; I never knew you.

And the Apostle John says:

> Everyone who sins is not of God but is of the devil; and you know that the Son of God is to come for this reason: to destroy the children of the devil.

[Col. 0835A]

> **Note [Col. 0835B]**
>
> **XI.—“Transfer them to paradise.”** Perhaps “send them back.” —PAMEL.
>
> **“And a mortal crime.”** I certainly read thus with another manuscript of Morel, in place of “immortal.” —PAMEL.
>
> [Col. 0836B] **“A fold of lies.”** Another manuscript reads “the wickedness of falsehood.” —PAMEL.

### XI

If you are a Christian gambler, you are the enemy both of yourself and of your inheritance. Whoever you are, wretch, cease from that madness. Why do you continue to hurl yourself with the devil into the snare of death? Why do you stake your wealth and riches for the basest bronze coins [Note: [Col. 0835B] Thus Corb., Imperial edition. *The basest man of bronze*]? Why do you entangle yourself in worldly snares, so that you may be judged together with the world [Note: [Col. 0835B] *With the world*, Bodl. 1, Corb.]? Why do you sin by praising your enemy with acclamations, when you must necessarily be punished together with him?

Be, rather, not a gambler but a Christian. With Christ seated beside you, the angels watching, and the martyrs present, scatter your money upon the Lord’s table. Distribute to the poor your patrimony, which perhaps you would otherwise have lost through that savage pursuit. Entrust your riches to Christ, who wins. Be called a servant together with your Lord; devote yourself to the pursuit of divine service; imitate the Lord’s art, which does not lose but rather gains.

[Col. 0835B] Cease from those most rapacious habits of yours; restrain your headlong wickedness. Let your daily play be with the poor; let your work with widows be frequent. [Col. 0836A] Convert all your property and provisions to the service of the Church. Store your gold, silver, and money in heavenly treasuries. By righteous work transfer your lands and villas to paradise. Apply yourself to almsgiving and continual prayer, so that your sins may be forgiven.

Do not gamble, for there the game is harmful and the crime mortal [Note: [Col. 0836B] *An immortal crime*, Corb.]; there is madness without reflection; there is no truth, but a fold of lies. Cut your hand away from it and turn your heart away from it. Draw the enemy’s darkness from your eyes and purify your hand from the sacrifices of Zabulus. Drive rapacious habits away from yourself. Be patient and Christian; be just and provident toward yourself and your life in your works. Flee the pursuing devil, and flee gambling, the enemy of your property. Let your pursuit be that of wisdom: be instructed by the admonitions of the Gospel [Col. 0836B]; stretch pure hands toward Christ, so that you may be able to merit the Lord. Do not look upon gambling. Amen.

[Col. 0835]

## ON THE SOLITARY LIVING OF CLERICS  
### A TREATISE WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED TO CYPRIAN, AND ALSO, ACCORDING TO SOME, TO AUGUSTINE AND ORIGEN  
(C, G, S)

[Col. 0835C]

> **Note [Col. 0835D]**
>
> **On the Solitary Living of Clerics.** This book appears to have been written around the time of our countryman Bede, when controversy concerning the celibacy of clerics was especially intense, particularly in the West. An argument drawn from a revelation corresponds to that age. For it was reported that the angel Gabriel had delivered twelve sealed articles declaring that the marriage of priests was not to be tolerated. It is established that the work was written after the commonly accepted version had come into use. Nor does it matter that the author seems to defend the opinion of Origen, since this belonged to the hypothesis he had undertaken. Rigaltius says that the Fossatensis manuscript attributes it to Cyprian. In the Corbie manuscript it is entitled *Augustine, On the Solitary Living of Clerics*.
>
> **“But because some among you have now fallen into disgrace through dwelling with women.”** Pamelius [Col. 0836D] says that Manutius and Morel, together with Landulf of Colonna, read “through mention of women.” But Antoninus, together with the old printed edition, has the former reading, which accords better with the argument of the book. If Landulf too did not read the word *concerning*, I would regard it as superfluous and omit it with Antoninus. —PAMEL.
>
> **“They have fallen into disgrace.”** Pamelius says: Through an error in Rembold’s manuscript, “of disgrace” was read. Since this alone was unsatisfactory, Erasmus substituted “disgracefully”; Antoninus and the old printed edition also read that. —PAMEL.
>
> **“By the Lord’s rebuke.”** Pamelius says: Manutius and Morel read “rebuke”; but the former reading, “obedience,” is preferable, especially if with Antoninus we read “rebuking” in place of “befitting.” —PAMEL.

I had indeed promised you some time ago, dearly beloved sons, a letter which, commending from the law the principles governing every kind of conduct, would also contain in summary everything that pertains generally to all clerics for the direction of their rule of discipline. But because some among you have now commonly fallen into disgrace through dwelling with women, I have been compelled to write to you specifically about this matter as well, by the Lord’s rebuke. For, severely rebuking me in my wretchedness because of your negligence, he commanded me to direct that clerics must not dwell with women.

And although this admonition by the authority of my letter alone would suffice, nevertheless, lest anyone mock me as a dreamer, as Joseph’s brothers mocked him, we add the confirmation [Col. 0836C] of the Scriptures. Thus all may know that even now, through revelation, the Lord commands what he is known to have commanded previously in writing; and that we are not adulterating the Lord’s word or wishing boastfully to glory in revelations, but that, in reporting the matter thus before the Lord’s sight, we do not lie in what we say—just as we trust that we have not heard a falsehood from the Lord. We rely upon the declaration of the Apostle Paul:

> For we are not, he says, like the many who adulterate the word of God; but from sincerity, as from God, we speak before him in Christ.

We are therefore afflicted with the greatest sorrow concerning certain putrefied members of our body, and lament with groaning the Church’s loss, as it is reduced day by day through our sloth to an exceedingly small number. [Col. 0837A]

> **Note [Col. 0837D]**
>
> **“Let him record himself as guilty.”** Pamelius says: Here too Rembold substituted “of things,” a thoroughly corrupt reading; the old printed editions, Gravius, and Morel have the former reading. —PAMEL.
>
> **“When destruction comes upon you.”** Pamelius says: Neither the old printed editions nor Rembold have these words, but they occur in the Septuagint. We have therefore rightly added them on Cauchius’s conjecture, together with what follows. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Confidence is adversarial.”** Pamelius says: He too reads thus, more correctly than the common “adverse.” [Col. 0838D] —PAMEL.
>
> **“Indeed, rather than our own.”** Pamelius says: He uses *quin immo* in the sense of “rather”; for neither the old printed editions nor Rembold have the word “more,” which Erasmus first added. —PAMEL.
>
> **“Which has bestowed upon each human being his own glory.”** Pamelius says: Through a compositor’s error Rembold had “his,” which did not fit; Erasmus therefore substituted “from every side” for “upon each.” But the former is genuine. —PAMEL.

We believe that we are relieved in some measure by the fact that our diligence cannot be thwarted by the negligence of certain persons. Our letters have never failed them; during our absence, their frequency has compensated everyone for the frequency of their own dissimulation. Thus every contemptuous person may record himself as guilty, while we, with untroubled brow, may cry aloud against the contemptuous what Solomon confidently declares in reproach:

> Because I called, he says, and you did not obey; and I extended my words, and you did not give heed, but rendered my counsels ineffectual, and paid no heed to my rebukes: therefore I too shall laugh at your destruction. I shall rejoice against you when destruction comes upon you, and when tumult suddenly comes upon you—overthrow together with tempests—and [Col. 0837B] when affliction and conquest come upon you. For the time shall come when you invoke me, but I shall not hear you. The wicked will seek me and will not find me, for they hated wisdom. They did not receive the word of the Lord, nor did they wish to heed my counsels. For they despised my rebukes; therefore they shall eat the fruits of their own way and be filled with their own impiety.

My exhortation now turns to you, whom we do not wish to experience such sheer precipices of ruin. Fear, as much as you can, the deadly consequences of such falls; and in this overthrow let the examples of those who are falling terrify you. A man is excessively reckless if he strives to pass where he has seen another fall, and utterly unbridled if fear is not struck into him when another person perishes. But he is a lover of his own salvation who avoids the assault of another’s death.
