And he is provident who becomes watchful through the disasters of others, as Solomon confirms when he says: “The astute man, on seeing the wicked punished, will be thoroughly instructed.” And again: “When the impious fall, the just will be greatly terrified.”

Overconfidence is an enemy: it entrusts its life to dangers as though the outcome were certain. Slippery is the hope that expects to be saved amid the kindling of sin. Victory is uncertain when one fights amid hostile weapons. And deliverance is impossible when one is surrounded by flames yet does not burn. Solomon does not deny this when he says:

> Who will bind fire in his bosom without burning his garments? Or who will walk upon fiery coals without burning his feet? So too, whoever goes in to his neighbor’s wife will not be innocent—nor will anyone who touches her.

Believe, I beg you; believe divine assurance, indeed, rather than our own [Col. 0837D], because it cannot deceive in anything whatsoever that it promises, as the Lord says: “It is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one point of the law to fall.” And again: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.”

We therefore deceive ourselves whenever we believe in a disorderly fashion, supposing that the precepts of the [Col. 0838A] law are changed by our faith, so that we may hope that immutable chastity will everywhere be preserved between men and women.

A person will scarcely drink poison and live. One sleeping on a riverbank must fear lest he fall, since the Apostle says: “Let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.” In this matter it is better to fear well than to trust badly. And it is more useful for a person to recognize himself as weak, so that he may prove strong, than to wish to appear strong and emerge weak. Concerning this, the Apostle rebukes the presumptuous, saying: “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” Certainly, one who entrusts himself to harmful things by failing to guard against opposing dangers has become his own deceiver and has deceived his own soul. But the person who, always distrustful amid evils, fears every kind of harmful appearance takes safer counsel for himself. Solomon expounded the difference between them, saying: [Col. 0838B] “The wise man will turn away from every evil through fear, but the fool, trusting in himself, mingles with the wicked.”

A great counsel of divine wisdom has been devised whereby we are delivered with the aid of fear. It is a great expedient of providence that virtue and victory may sometimes come through fear. The Lord has bestowed great remedies for salvation, so that even the fearful person may receive praise, as Solomon repeats, saying: “Blessed is the man who fears all things through apprehension.” Inestimable is the Lord’s mercy, which has bestowed upon each person his own glory; and incomprehensible is the loving-kindness that has assigned palms of victory according to the struggles, so that by making confession we may overcome the savagery of men, and by fearing we may conquer the enticements of women—provided that the Lord accomplishes glories over us both through strength and through weakness, so that in all things and through all things he may testify himself to be omnipotent, [Col. 0838C] apportioning different kinds of triumph, so that wars may be won by us through counsel as well as through strength. Otherwise, if we were to conquer solely by the fortitude of faith, the works of wisdom would, contrary to Solomon, be empty.

Now, therefore, the weapons of wisdom must be borne where a contest between the female and male sexes is declared. Hence Solomon instructs us as follows: “Make prudence known to yourself, so that it may preserve you from a strange and most wicked woman.” Observe now that in this war prudence, not faith, has been given to us as the victor, since prudence would deliver us by the remedy of timidity; and consider what weapons must now be taken up if you wish to have the law’s assistance. Be fearful, so that you may be undaunted. Although fear may appear to be weakness in a contest, nevertheless, according to the Apostle’s word, “strength is perfected in weakness.” Separate yourselves, I beseech you; fence yourselves off [Col. 0838D] from the pestilential contagion.

The farther each person is from adverse things, the less he feels their adversity. One is less goaded by pleasures when one is not where pleasures abound. And one suffers fewer torments of avarice when one does not see riches—if we accept the Apostle’s promise: [Col. 0839A]

> **[Note: Col. 0839D]**
>
> **And into snares.** Pamelius says: “We have omitted the word *of the devil*, because neither the old printed edition nor Rembold has it, nor does Cyprian have it elsewhere; nevertheless, he everywhere reads *snare*.” PAMEL.
>
> **He makes prey of great men.** Pamelius says: “Antoninus adds *his* in place of *his own*; but another old manuscript of Morel reads quite differently: *he makes his mingled prey only of the great and strong*.” PAMEL.
>
> **While he considers them deserving or feeble.** Pamelius says: “Erasmus’s *emeritos*—‘distinguished’—is also not bad, were it not followed by *but himself to be highly deserving*; for that reason we have restored this reading from the old printed edition and Rembold.” PAMEL.
>
> **O how disorderly.** Pamelius says: “Antoninus also reads thus. The old printed edition and Rembold, however, have *in ordinalis*; the passage is obscure. Gravius conjectures that *pandering* should be read in place of *robbery*, but this is not satisfactory.” PAMEL.
>
> **Everything belonging to a woman is causative.** Pamelius says: “Erasmus reads *Casuale*—‘accidental’—but the former reading is in the old printed edition and Rembold. It seems to allude to this:
>
> ‘A shared bed always brings disputes and alternating quarrels.’” PAMEL.

“Those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and snares, and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and ruin.” In no different way is the man who is joined to a woman subjected to temptations, since there is nothing in her that does not strike the person who draws near. Female beauty has become the sting of sin, and the condition of death arose from no other source than womanly substance. Solomon recalls this to make us vigilant, saying: “From a woman came the beginning of sin; because of her we all die.” Through her we are held mortal, yet we are not afraid. What if we were already mortal? Christ indeed delivered us through a woman, but we must fear that from which we still die. That deliverance itself will then be established in woman if death, which had come through a woman, [Col. 0839B] is conquered in turn by us. But if scandals still rule over us through woman, we have certainly squandered Christ’s deliverance.

Indeed, this hope of liberty, which we believe Christ has bestowed upon our faith, remains for the future: namely, that woman will then do us no harm at all, when death itself has also been abolished. For if we now think ourselves proof against the darts of women, what then remains for the heavenly kingdoms? Not undeservedly does the Apostle rebuke such thinking, saying: “Already you are filled; already you have become rich; without us you reign—and would that you did reign!” The time of struggle, therefore, is still under way, and death through woman continues to rage even now. I am lying if we do not see the destruction of very many arising from this source. How many bishops and clerics, together with laymen, and what men they were, are known to have suffered shipwreck with all these achievements, when they wished to sail in a fragile ship—after they had trodden through contests of confession and victory, [Col. 0839C] after mighty deeds, signs, and wonders had been displayed everywhere! How many lions has a single sinful womanly weakness subdued—a thing which, although cheap and wretched, makes prey of great men! Solomon speaks of this, saying: “The price of a prostitute is only one loaf of bread, but a woman captures precious souls.”

These things happen before us, yet we are restrained by no terrors. What would we do if we heard only stories that were carried along by report? But such is always the unbelief of human hardness: it does not believe that others have perished merely by hearing or even by seeing, unless it has also seen itself perish. Nor is it shaken by its companions’ deaths, while it supposes that they deserved them or were feeble. [Col. 0839D] Yet it confidently imagines itself to be highly deserving or very strong, not knowing that examples are furnished for everyone when punishments have been inflicted upon some, just as the Lord sets forth in the Gospel and says: “Do you think that these Galileans were sinners beyond all Galileans because they suffered such things? No, I tell you. Unless you repent, you will perish in the same way, just as those upon whom the tower in Siloam fell [Col. 0840A] and killed them. Do you think that they too were guilty beyond all the people living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. If you do not repent, you will perish in the same way.”

We marvel that Adam was seduced through Eve, although no examples of dying persons had preceded him and only a single command had constrained him, whereas now neither innumerable deaths nor countless commands restrain us. To us it is fittingly said, in accordance with the Lord’s rebuke: “If Adam had seen the deaths that have occurred among you, he would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable for Adam on the day [Col. 0840B] of judgment than for you.”

Far away be that pestilence, that plague, and that secret destruction. O how wildly proximity to a woman hurls its darts; her nearness is a brigandage of sins [the reading is obscure]. There is in this association no commendable sincerity, for it experiences collisions as turbulent as waves. Friendly concord does not dwell in this intimacy, since it creates nothing but discordant hostilities. The Lord indeed made woman as a helper for man, but through the serpent’s envy she assumed a hostile role. If she, born from her own husband, even to this day tempts the very man to whom she is joined, how much more does a woman who is coupled with a man without being joined to him by any law? And if those two who have been formed together into one flesh prick one another with mutual temptations, what will those do who have neither been born nor joined together in one flesh? Especially because one who is called away by affection for another is no longer permitted [Col. 0840C] even to call upon God; nor is the man who has sought someone to whom he might devote domestic care allowed to think upon divine things. For this reason the Apostle gives the following counsel: “I wish you to be without anxiety. The man who is without a wife is concerned about how he may please God; but the man who has a wife thinks about the things of this world, how he may please his wife.” What is there now to delight anyone in this union, in which there are only conflicts? Or what advantage favors it, where there are no marital duties, when not even these can be secure?

Everything belonging to a woman is causative, and union with her is always hostile. By its bond it brings great troubles; and upon anyone to whom she unlawfully adheres, she inflicts an incurable wound. Sparks leap from coals; rust is nourished by iron; asps hiss forth diseases; and woman pours out the pestilence of lust. Solomon compares it thus: “From garments proceeds the moth, and from woman the wickedness of a man.” I wish [Col. 0841A]

> **[Note: Col. 0841D]**
>
> **Everyone who has not eaten flesh.** Clerics seem at that time to have abstained from meat and wine. PAMEL.
>
> **Enjoys the pleasure of seeing.** Thus I read with the old printed edition, in place of *of wine*; Rembold has neither reading. PAMEL.
>
> **A suspect resolution.** *Placitum* means “decree.” Manutius alone reads *placidum*—“peaceful.” PAMEL.
>
> **Who causes it to be discredited outwardly.** Thus from Antoninus and a certain manuscript of Morel, in place of *which outwardly*; that manuscript also reads *permits* in place of *causes*. PAMEL.
>
> **He brings blasphemy upon the religion he practices.** Thus, excellently, a certain manuscript of Morel, in place of *has bestowed*. PAMEL.
>
> **Worthy indeed of his old age.** We add *indeed* from an old manuscript, for so it is read in Maccabees. PAMEL.

to know what sort of common affection this is, what sort of always-ambiguous discord of sickness, which attacks and disturbs its own purpose with wavering counsels. Why did a man take a woman into his company when he disdained to marry a wife? Why does everyone who has not eaten flesh fill his dwelling with preparations of flesh? And why does one who has not drunk wine enjoy the pleasure of seeing it? As though the mind were not sometimes fed by an abundance of food merely through seeing, without tasting, and as though the mind were not often excited by the fragrance alone of aromatic wine. Why, through hypocrisy, does he wish to be called abstinent by men, yet in secret be distended with flesh and drunkenness? Many possess riches which they deny to their own use but preserve out of covetousness; if no covetousness adhered to them, they would not possess the marks of covetousness. But because they are possessed by covetousness, [Col. 0841B] they enjoy in their minds what they do not touch in practice. So too does the man who has despised the bond of marriage bind himself instead with womanly bonds. Although he is mingled with her in no act of intercourse, he nevertheless always delights in desire, sight, conversation, and association. For if he had no desire for a woman, he would never take a woman to himself for his pleasures.

Indeed, furthermore, he has given me a suspect resolution: he has not taken a lawful wife and has refused a lawful wife. Unless I am mistaken, he has argued in public that he promises sanctity to men, while in private he is not without a wife. Two evidences—of sanctity and lust—must here and there be wondered at: each conceals the other and each betrays the other. The ingenious eunuch and adulterer works against himself while taking counsel for himself; and while he seeks [Col. 0841C] both things, he accomplishes neither. Thus he is by no means reckoned holy, because he does not enjoy a true union, since the Apostle Paul says: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife.”

But I grant that the chastity of this continence has not been violated. Nevertheless, it presents a bad reputation to suspicious persons; and he guards the good of chastity inwardly through a laborious struggle in vain, since he causes it to be discredited outwardly, destroying the teaching of Paul, who both provides for the future and warns: “Why,” he says, “is my liberty judged by an unbelieving conscience? If, therefore, I partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks?” It is worse than adultery to render continence criminal and to make sanctity infamous. He brings blasphemy upon the religion he practices [Col. 0841D] when he does not fulfill before everyone what he professes, lest Christianity be believed a fraud and adultery appear clothed in the veil of sanctity. For this reason the Lord gives advance warning in the Gospel, saying: “Let your light so shine before men that, seeing [Col. 0842A] your good works, they may magnify your Father who is in heaven.” The Apostle Paul follows this as well, saying: “Therefore let not your good be blasphemed.” And again: “Providing good things not only before God but also before men.” And elsewhere: “Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do all things for the glory of God. And be without scandal to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God, just as I too please everyone in all things.”

But perhaps it is objected: What, then, does he mean when he himself says elsewhere: “If I wished to please men, I would not be Christ’s servant”? The various sayings of the law never exclude one another; rather, all its answers are fixed in their proper contexts. It is not permissible to please men where the will of men does not contain the Lord’s will. But where people accept [Col. 0842B] what advances the glory of God, the Apostle Paul himself commanded that it be made known to everyone: “Let each of us,” he says, “please his neighbor for good edification.”

What reward of sanctity, then, does a man expect when he not only provokes unbelievers to blaspheme sanctity but also furnishes the faithful with a destructive example, so that the weak may subtly fornicate under the pretext of affection, and a chaste man may furnish instruction in the most shameless kind of chastity? He destroys what the Apostle Paul threatens: “Has the weak brother perished in your conscience—the one for whom Christ suffered? But by thus sinning against the brethren and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.”

Indeed, it is fitting not only for young men but also for the old to take thought for their brothers’ weakness, lest old age [Col. 0842C] provoke youth to perish, although from old age every salutary lesson ought to proceed. Thus Eleazar professes in the book of Maccabees and says: “I would rather be sent ahead into the underworld than abandon the ancestral laws. For it is not worthy of our age to pretend, lest many of the young, supposing that Eleazar at ninety years of age had gone over to the way of life of foreigners, should themselves be led astray through my pretense and for the sake of my brief and corruptible span of life, and I should acquire hatred and a stain upon my old age.” He preferred to expose his life to torments rather than become a teacher of perdition to anyone. Yet where there are no torments, we are unwilling to place the brothers who must be saved ahead of mere indulgences; nor are we content, without any tortures, to benefit both ourselves and others, although he refused to live when he was going to die, [Col. 0842D] as he continued below, saying: “Therefore, by departing life courageously, I shall appear worthy indeed of my old age, and shall leave the young a strong example, so that with a ready spirit and courageously they may submit to an honorable death for the grave and holy laws.” Although [Col. 0843A]

> **[Note: Col. 0843D]**
>
> **Indeed, he is consummate.** I read exactly thus with Morel, in place of *who in the least*. For we had this word above in the same meaning, and the old printed edition and Rembold agree. PAMEL.
>
> **Certainly, even for anyone alone.** I add *alone* from the same sources. PAMEL.
>
> **To suffer from an incurable semitertian fever.** According to Rembold, a semitertian fever (*hemitritaeus*) is one and a half tertian fevers. PAMEL.
>
> **But someone.** We have omitted the interjected word *if*, following the old manuscript and Rembold. PAMEL.
>
> **Unexpectedly or in passing.** Antoninus reads *in passing*, but the former is repeated twice or three times below. PAMEL.
>
> **Or sometimes relaxes in ordinary activity.** Rembold read *in laughter*; Erasmus more correctly emended this to *into laughter*, but the former reading is in the old printed edition. PAMEL.

this also befits laypeople, so that they may not present outsiders with an occasion for blasphemy or the brotherhood with an opportunity for fornication, this necessity binds clerics with especial force; for either blasphemed religion or a lost brotherhood will inflict double penalties upon them. Nor will those who have furnished foreigners and brethren with fuel for sinning find any consolation at all in the Lord’s judgment. For this reason the Apostle Paul instructs Titus as follows: “Present yourself as an example of good works, in teaching, in integrity, in gravity, in sound and irreproachable speech, so that the adversary may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say of us.” And again: “Show good faith in all things, so that in all things they may commend the good teaching of our Lord and Savior.” So too he writes [Col. 0843B] to Timothy, saying: “Be an example to the faithful in speech, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity.” The Apostle Peter also exhorts this, saying: “Let your conduct among the Gentiles be good, so that in the very matter in which they malign you as evildoers, they may glorify God because of your good works.” And again: “For this is the will of God: that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men.”

Let no one propose to himself and say: “I wish to have something to conquer.” For this is to say: “I desire to live beneath a ruin.” Who is so foolish as to wish to be forced into hardship when an effortless triumph is offered him? For it is no greater a triumph to be proved victorious in a woman’s presence than it is to preserve inviolate the pledge of sanctity in solitude. And since there is one [Col. 0843C] title of glory, in this situation one courageous man labors greatly, yet he is rewarded equally with the man who conquered with little labor. What of the fact that the man who shows himself at all times cut off from womanly affections is indeed reckoned consummate? For in the Gospel the Lord calls the man perfect who has cut away his entire inheritance from his own use.

Certainly, even for anyone alone, daily triumphs for chastity are not lacking, because the human body never ceases to assail the spirit with carnal desires. The Apostle affirms this, saying: “The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever things you wish.” You now have your own flesh to overcome continually; why do you wish to hire another against yourself as well? [Col. 0843D] No one desires to add a worse fever on top of one fever, lest he begin to suffer from an incurable semitertian fever, for which no physician is able to provide relief. Nor does anyone take up another person’s burden in addition to his own, lest, crushed by two burdens, he be plunged as far as the underworld. Hence the prophet Jeremiah teaches that the weight of sanctity must be borne alone: “It is good,” he says, “for a man when he has borne the heavy yoke in his youth; he will sit alone and be silent, because he has taken the heavy yoke upon himself.” [Col. 0844A]

But some malicious supporter will take refuge in the saying of the Apostle Paul: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” These are not the burdens which the Apostle Paul commands us to help carry; rather, he commands that no discord separate us as we bear with one another, and that we provide assistance to brothers who are undergoing temptations. He does not command us to procure temptations for ourselves through women, but instead to lighten the weight of temptations, since he knows what sort of yoke sanctity is—one that can scarcely be carried even alone. Concerning this, not only he but even the Lord refused to define a fixed command, saying: “Not all receive [Col. 0844B] this word, but only those to whom it has been given.” And again: “He who can receive it, let him receive it.”

If, therefore, the greatness of this weight is borne with difficulty when it is alone, how will it be borne if one is weighed down by doubled burdens? And if almost all who are alone scarcely endure the snares of the flesh, what do those do who do not hesitate to lie down beneath swords hanging over them from both sides? I say more: if husbands and wives, experiencing marital desires every day, are not sufficient for one another, what are those doing who associate with women in order to increase their assaults?

A woman’s appearance, encountered unexpectedly or in passing for an hour, casts arrows, as it were, into others’ eyes. When even simple respectful regard is not safe, what takes place where, in shared lodging, a woman acquires the settled confidence of freedom? In domestic tasks, she now bares her upper arms [Col. 0844C] and thighs for wool-working; now, growing hot, she uncovers her limbs; now, fatigued, she tosses herself about or sometimes relaxes in ordinary activity; now she displays enticements; and, what is more poisonous than all these things, she delights in singing psalms or songs. It is more tolerable to hear a basilisk hissing than to hear her singing. Solomon makes us cautious against her as follows: “Do not remain continually with a singing woman, nor listen to her, lest perhaps you perish through her influence.”

I pass over the rest, which is more shameful than can be spoken of. I say only this: even to watch a woman broken by grief or anger is no longer without allure. What are we to say if you see her rejoicing, or, what is worse, enticing you? Let me say it once: every unfitting companionship with women is the glue of sins and poisoned birdlime with which the devil hunts his prey. Companionship with women is incongruous; Solomon again teaches us to take every precaution against their companionship: “Do not sit at all with another man’s wife,” he says, “and do not dispute with her over wine, lest perhaps your heart incline toward her and you slide through your own blood into destruction.” [Col. 0844D]

Finally, even if we trust that our mind will always remain steadfast in this [Col. 0845A]

> **[Note: Col. 0845D]**
>
> **Nor to display.** This is not found in the Apostle today. PAMEL.
>
> **[Col. 0846D] By the Apostle Paul.** Erasmus reads *with the Apostle as witness*, but the former reading is pleasing because it is in the old manuscript. PAMEL.
>
> **In the assembly for the sacred rites, however, etc.** This is a fine passage concerning the Church’s sacred rites, since he says that heavenly things are discussed there, holy mysteries are celebrated, the spiritual work of angels is performed, and God’s precepts assemble and gather us there. PAMEL.

community, we ought to regard even this as suspect, lest the very women who associate with us perhaps become stirred toward us, or be driven by their headlong age and maddening incitements toward other loves. We shall then be the cause—or, what is worse, without being the cause—of being stained by another person’s fornication, since with us the occasion of a brothel is suggested to others; and we shall be swallowed up by the guilt of another’s crime, because we ourselves procure the pandering of uncleanness. For this reason the Apostle Paul instructs us concerning similar matters: “If your brother is scandalized because of food, you are no longer walking in charity. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died.” And again: “It is good neither to eat flesh nor to drink wine nor to display anything by which your brother [Col. 0845B] is offended, scandalized, or weakened.” And elsewhere: “Judge this instead: that you should not place a stumbling block or scandal before a brother.” Concerning himself he also says: “Therefore, if food scandalizes my brother, I shall never eat flesh again, lest I scandalize my brother.”

Since, therefore, the detestable trouble of this association assails us, even if it cannot make people adulterers, it nevertheless makes them worse than adulterers and the incestuous. For who, as an examiner of another’s heart, could weigh the quality of each person, and who could presume to be a combatant against Satan on behalf of another person, and an adequate guarantor before God? A man is mad if he promises anything concerning himself—to say nothing of appearing to pledge a guarantee even for a woman—since the Apostle Paul pronounces concerning himself as follows: “Not that I have already received, or have already been justified, or have already been made perfect; but I pursue, if by any means I may apprehend that for which I also have been apprehended by Christ. [Col. 0845C] Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. Yet one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching toward what is before my feet, I pursue along the rule toward the prize of the heavenly calling of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, as many of us as are perfect, let us think this way.” “It is,” he says, “of the least importance to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; but I do not even judge myself. The one who judges me is the Lord.” And elsewhere: “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who does not judge himself in what he approves in another.”

Although, therefore, we possess nothing certain even concerning our own stability, since we are shaken without ceasing as we endure the stormy assaults of the world’s waves, nevertheless, if anyone has such confidence in the immovability of his own steadfastness, let him at least anxiously fear lest he himself become a scandal to the eyes of others. Let him be terrified by the Lord’s threatening voice: “Woe,” he says, “to this world because of scandals; nevertheless, woe to that man through whom scandal comes.” [Col. 0845D] If we fear and dread these threats of the Lord with a religious heart, let us fear our own danger more on account of others than on account of ourselves, since we are bound to mutual benefit, as the Apostle Paul says: “Let each consider not the things that are his own, [Col. 0846A] but those of others.” And again: “Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another.”

But someone may seize upon a saying of Paul himself to object: “Each of you will render an account for himself to God,” and “Each will bear his own burden.” Therefore, the man who does not wish to render an account for another must not take an illicit part in that person’s affairs or business; and the man who endeavors to remain free or immune from others’ burdens must, by the contrary condition, keep nothing belonging to another under his control. For one who has conducted another’s business must necessarily be subjected to the other’s accounting. The man in whose possession his brother’s burdens have perished through unsafe custody must be held liable for their loss or destruction. For whatever is lost in our house through insufficiently competent protection, or whatever thieves break in and steal, is our responsibility; and whatever is badly guarded after being entrusted to us through our negligence will be exacted from us. [Col. 0846B] We are free from one another only when nothing belonging to another is kept in our possession.

Perhaps someone may say: “Then we ought not to assemble together even at the house of prayer, lest one person scandalize another.” This slanderous objection belongs to a heretical profession: it argues from good things in order to assert evil ones, prejudges sanctity in order subtly to introduce uncleanness, and brings accusations against what is lawful so that it may secure what is unlawful. For this reason the Apostle Paul anticipates this heresy, saying: “Nevertheless, neither is woman without man nor man without woman in the Lord.”

Far be it—far be it—that women should be forbidden everywhere, or permission be granted everywhere. They have their proper places with a husband, with children, with brothers, with parents, and with servants; and in the house of prayer alone, beside all the clerics. But in one dwelling, apart from kinship, they properly have no companions. She is free who stands firm. But whatever has bent aside cannot stand free, as Scripture says: “You shall turn aside neither to the right nor to the left.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever is more than this is from evil.” Learn now the measure of temperance, you who seek excess through license. Love women amid sacred solemnities, and hate them in private association, if you wish to hold Solomon’s teaching: “There is a time to love and a time to hate.” [Col. 0846C]

Association with a woman must therefore be avoided when there is an uninterrupted, mutually shared routine of carnal concerns, because amid its own concerns the flesh always provokes incitements of desire. It engenders fuel for sinning where, while considering the advantages of temporal life, it has perceived itself to be somewhat relaxed in its thoughts, as Solomon asserts: “Earthly thought weighs down the mind that considers many things.” In the assembly for the sacred rites, however, where the spirit rules, the handmaid recognizes herself and loses the exercise of her own pleasure; she also loses her luxury while heavenly matters are discussed and holy [Col. 0846D] mysteries are celebrated. The whole of human nature is occupied where all things are not human but divine, where reverence—or trembling and terror—is inspired; in every soul the entire substance of the flesh lies buried.

Even amid the very commerce of the flesh, many people neglect bodily pleasure—for example, when the legions rehearse exercises in arms, when the forum resounds with lawsuits, when lecture halls echo with learning, when merchants urgently attend to trade, or when craftsmen are intent upon their crafts. How much more must this be so where the work being performed is not the carnal work of human beings but the spiritual work of angels? Assaults have no power there, where even the demons themselves withdraw; and no distinction of any sex is permitted to be considered where neither age nor rank but equality alone reigns. To speak more fully, everyone there [Col. 0847B] receives such dispositions that marriage itself is ignored, where Christ speaks, is heard, and is attended to, and through all things and in all people he alone is everything. The Apostle testifies to this, saying: “Where there is neither Jew nor Greek, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, male nor female, slave nor free, but Christ is all things and in all.” [Col. 0847A]

It is plainly a glory to celebrate this assembly with women, for in it there is no distinction of condition, and there alone it is permissible to make everyone equal without any difference. Thus not even in Baptism does anyone blush at another’s nakedness, where the infancy of Adam and Eve is renewed; nor does Baptism expose anyone; rather, one receives a tunic.

But even if someone worse than the devil should be struck there by the sight of women, your congregation is nevertheless blamed for nothing, since it is gathered for heavenly things, not earthly ones. Yet if anyone there indulges lustful gazes, he in no way harms another who has come forward not toward a human being but toward Christ for salvation. Indeed, I shall confute the objectors from their own objections, so that they may yield not to my propositions but to their own. If a common assembly can be scandalized amid holy festivals, where the tempter, the devil himself, trembles, who promises himself that he will be steadfast there where the tempter boldly confronts him? [Col. 0847C] And if we are endangered there where God’s commandments gather us, what are we doing where God’s commands separate us? If we are disturbed there where we are fortified by God’s will, how much more where we have not only the devil but also the Lord against us? For divine protection is supplied to us together with sacrosanct commands, as Isaiah says: “He gave the law as an aid”; but without divine commands there can be no protection. [Col. 0847D]

> **[Note: Col. 0847D]**
>
> **Since it cannot exist without justice.** This is the author’s idiom. The old printed edition and Rembold read *without victory*, but that does not please us. PAMEL.
>
> **[Col. 0848D] For the thoughts of mortals.** Gravius and Morel rightly read thus, in place of what others have, *the thoughts of immortals*. For this is the reading of the Book of Wisdom, which he cites under Solomon’s name, just as shortly afterward he cites the book of Ecclesiasticus. PAMEL.

It is one thing to do what God commands, and another to resist his will. His commands must be observed in such a way that, if he orders something which seems unjust according to human judgment, it is believed to be just and is done; and if he orders what is just, it is reckoned just and is done. For nothing that he commands can be without [Col. 0848A] justice, since he has the power, by justifying injustice, to call it justice, and, by rejecting justice, to declare justice turned awry to be injustice; his will alone is true justice. For if everything we do, we do solely in order to please the Lord, then surely whatever the God whom we strive to please wills, commands, and approves will alone be just.

For servants cannot know by themselves what pleases their masters unless they follow their masters’ commands; and certainly human beings cannot discern the wills of other human beings like themselves unless they have received something to observe. Much more, therefore, are mortals unable to comprehend the justice of the immortal God unless he himself deigns to reveal the tokens of his acts of justice, as Solomon confirms when he says:

> For what [Col. 0848B] human being will be able to know the counsel of God? Or who will be able to conceive what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans uncertain. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and its earthly habitation burdens the mind that thinks upon many things. We can scarcely judge the things that are upon the earth, and we discover with toil the things that lie before our eyes; but who will investigate the things that are in heaven? And who knows your mind unless you have given him wisdom and sent the Holy Spirit from on high? Thus the paths of those who are upon the earth have been corrected, human beings have learned the things that please you, and they have been healed through wisdom.

Those who walk in darkness cannot show themselves light unless the light freely offers itself to those who cannot see. Thus human blindness does not find the way to [Col. 0848C] God unless he himself displays the lamp of the law. Hence David speaks as follows:

> Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.

And again:

> The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes.

Whatever, therefore, has been disclosed by God is light-bearing; and what is worthy of God is that which God himself acknowledges as acceptable to his will, so that he may exercise dominion in all things. Otherwise neither would we be enrolled as servants nor would he be regarded as Lord, if we were permitted to render service according to our own will and to choose the exercises of justice by our judgment rather than God’s. The apostle Paul renders such people’s claims void when he says:

> Being ignorant of God’s justice and wishing to establish their own, they have not subjected themselves to the justice of God.

Let these utterly vain evasions, [Col. 0848D] and these groundlessly slanderous complaints, now be removed from our midst. With God’s help, we do not fear to assemble with women for spiritual acts, because we believe that, by God’s command, we are performing an act of justice, from which we know that protections are supplied to us. In private, however, lodgings must be kept separate for clerics who practice continence and for virgins, especially because what God judges iniquitous cannot be just. Cohabitation, even if no shameful conduct is known within that cohabitation itself, [Col. 0849A] inflames desire, because it is impossible for integrity to attain victory when it strives to fight against God’s commands. For as much aid as the law furnishes to the obedient, so much does it provoke sin in the disobedient, as the Apostle says:

> The power of sin is the law.

Therefore, he who commanded us to triumph alongside women in his sacred rites also commands us to beware, in private, of conflicts involving women.

There are, to be sure, other necessities which compel us to see women even in private; but these too require the effective discharge of a divine work or command: that we visit them, provide consolation, and beneficially impart life-giving exhortations. Yet even in these duties no less care must be taken for our conduct, so that signs of purity may shine in our actions. There must be no lack of severity [Col. 0849B] capable of constraining a woman in the presence of a cleric, so that she receives our very consolation with trembling and experiences the affection of the visitation in such a way that she reverences the cleric.

And lest it take too long to range through every particular: whatever we do in your company can be honorable, provided that signs of honor always shine forth in us. The apostle Paul encompassed everything when he said:

> Let all your affairs be conducted honorably.

And again:

> As we commanded you, walk honorably.

Whatever is done indiscriminately does not turn out well; and a sacred thing that is done is not sacred unless what is sacred is carried out sacredly, as Solomon asserts when he says:

> Those who have justly preserved just things will be justified.

Sincerity itself must therefore be preserved sincerely, and everything pertaining to one’s vow must also be marked in one’s conduct, lest vows commend one thing [Col. 0849C] while actions intimate another. The commitment of the will must be proved on every side, and the course of each person’s contest must be completed in every respect, lest something necessary for triumph be lacking because the struggle was not fully fought. Hence the apostle Paul introduces lessons drawn from contests:

> Even one who competes in the contest will not be crowned unless he has competed according to the rules.

And again:

> Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. Everyone who competes in the contest abstains from everything; and they do so to receive a corruptible crown, but you an incorruptible one.

The fullness of holiness and the perfect palm of victory, therefore, consists in having nothing about oneself, on any side, that one must reject, lest by retaining what one professes to hate, one appear to love it.

[Col. 0849D] But if someone says, “I hold my adversary captive so that I may always insult him,” let him take care that the captive does not perhaps begin to prevail [Col. 0850A] against him. A robber is never safely confined together with a treasure, nor is a lamb safe when dwelling in one cage with a wolf. A man has chosen to be defeated when he introduces his own enemy within his gates; and he himself has placed a sword within his own body when he opens his dwelling place to his adversary’s entrance. The man who trusts himself to associate with a cause of scandal says without justification, “I wish to be at peace with the devil,” contrary to the Apostle’s words:

> Do not give place to the devil.

Therefore the place where the treasure is hidden must be fortified in every way, lest through one opening the robber undermine the entire wall. For if he is scarcely repelled by walls when he assaults from outside, how powerful will he be if he receives a dwelling within the walls? And if those who shut him out are sometimes captured by him, [Col. 0850B] how much more is the man deceived who willingly opens an entrance to him? Solomon says:

> If the just man is scarcely saved, where will the unjust man appear?

Every crack, therefore—to say nothing of every gate—must be closed, lest the entire camp be penetrated through a single opening. All the defenses must be put in order, lest the whole city collapse through one small place left unfortified, as Solomon reiterates:

> He who despises small things will gradually fall.

It happens, I think, through deliberate pursuit of this perversity that a woman rather than a man is chosen by clerics for communal living. Is a woman so much more useful to a cleric’s material interests than a continent man, or a boy, is useful to a continent man? Or will that benefit be seemly which an unseemly companionship makes possible? And what becomes of Solomon’s statement:

> Every animal loves its [Col. 0850C] like?

And again:

> Birds flock together with those like themselves.

But even if a woman is considered more useful, carnal advantages ought not to be preferred to the benefits of spiritual advantages. It would have been more expedient to endure any useless man for the sake of safeguarding one’s reputation than to enjoy the good services of a woman together with an utterly shameful reputation. Solomon makes this comparison when he says:

> Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman who does good.

The devil’s poisons are therefore always artfully prepared. Exercising the ingenuity of his cunning through them, he assists those devoted to chastity with deceptive advantages in order to destroy them. Supplying apparently necessary benefits among continent persons through their mutual assistance, he first induces a man and a woman to live together; then, after making them inseparable through reciprocal consolations, [Col. 0850D] he can kill those who have offered their simple souls for the observance of vows of chastity.

Meanwhile, withdrawing the weapons of his assault, like a peaceful patron he presents [Col. 0851A] arguments for holiness, until over a long period he nourishes a hostile concord between the two. He makes them affable to one another and ready to serve each other; and, as a hostile flatterer removing every obstacle, he rejoices to lend efficacy to their advantages. By commending each to the other through every necessity, he renders them dependent upon their customary mutual consolation. He does not wish to hinder them in anything, lest he separate them spiritually as well as carnally. He causes them to live undisturbed, lest at an immature stage the first beginnings of their partnership unsettle the covenant they have commenced. Before the eyes of everyone, he goes so far as to invite, cherish, and support them toward the perfection of holiness, so that they reckon as God’s benefits the very things working against them, through which they are induced to perish, not knowing that God never assists what he forbids.

By flattering them in this way, the devil prepares such a sense of security [Col. 0851B] for their chastity that, when joined together, they consider themselves more able to remain immovable against lust than when separated. Leading them onward in complete tranquility, he disturbs them with no storms or waves; and, as though in the middle of the sea, he induces the incautious to slacken their sails and not to seek the helm, so that, when a sudden tempest is stirred up, he may plunge them, shipwrecked, beneath an unforeseen disturbance.

At first he displays this gentleness so that he may entice two ships to come together. Once he has joined them, he can drive them against each other in sudden whirlwinds and shatter them. He uses these flatteries so that, after removing every missile, restraining adversity, and suggesting prosperity, he may keep a sleeping fire concealed without any flames until, by joining two torches, he ignites both together. He refrains from applying the weapons of his savagery [Col. 0851C] until, like an expert hunter, he binds those whom he intends to kill in the cords of his snare. But when he has fastened them together in an indissoluble chain, like a trainer of gladiators he immediately forces the two to arm themselves against each other. Then, goading their bodies, he at once fits swords to their hands, at once kindles madness, and, driving them into wounding embraces, kills both together with a single stroke.

Thus he unfolds what at first he appeared to bestow; thus from simple charity he forges illicit love; thus through holiness he brings ruin upon them. By being content to give way, he is able to seize possession more powerfully; and by submitting and allowing himself to appear defeated, he boasts of conquering more completely. The apostle Paul shows that he understands his stratagems when he says:

> For we are not ignorant of his devices.

[Col. 0851D] Thus those who are at peace in this partnership are at peace to their harm, because through the devil’s peacemaking they are led to war. Nor do those make good progress in holiness whose very progress is contrived by the enemy’s craft to their detriment. Neither do those strive to ascend the steps of continence by a straight course whom the adversary labors to extend upward to the summit so that he may hurl them down from on high. Those who have taken a slippery road must necessarily be dashed down in ruinous falls. Of this road Solomon proclaims:

> There is a way that appears right to human beings, but its final ends descend into the depth of hell.

[Col. 0852A] But they say: “If clerics are censured for this association, then many saints must also be censured along with us: Elijah, who stayed with a widow; the Apostles, who took women with them as companions; John, who received the Lord’s mother when the Lord himself entrusted her to him; and the Lord himself, to whom certain religious women supplied sustenance from their possessions, whom Martha also served at table, who sat at the well and spoke alone with the foreign Samaritan [Col. 0852B] woman, and whose feet a woman washed with tears and wiped with her hair while he reclined at table.”

Cunning advocates and deceitful legal experts! In their desire to violate the rules governing disputes and legal proceedings, they overturn the laws themselves. Because they refuse to be restrained by the appropriate commands of the laws, they set before the judges unsuitable examples as though they were analogous legal precedents, in order to mock them. They are exposed by Solomon through the very sagacity of the law:

> A sinful man avoids correction and finds a comparison to suit his own will.

Such people must therefore be refuted not by argument but rather by correction, so that they are not instructed by arguments already interpreted for them before they have admitted what they discovered as an aid to their defense. Solomon [Col. 0852C] teaches us how to deal with such people when he says:

> Do not answer a fool according to his own folly, lest you become like him; but answer a fool contrary to his own folly, lest he appear wise to himself.

Truly, they must be great men who compare themselves to the saints, and ours must be an extraordinary way of life if it seems equal to that of the Prophets or Apostles. For the sake of indulging our lust, we wish perversely to imitate the saints, while in all other actions we refuse to follow the footsteps of the just. In some matters we excuse ourselves as too weak to imitate the deeds of our superiors; in others we proclaim ourselves equal to those superiors—even though Elijah himself, when placed in distress, confessed before God that he was unequal to his fathers:

> Am I better than my fathers?

Elijah was compelled to cry this out concerning his predecessors in his weakness; [Col. 0852D] and do we not hesitate to equate our strength with Elijah, with the Prophets, with the Apostles, and with the Lord?

I plainly see avarice trampled down among you just as the Apostles abandoned all their possessions. I see gluttony [Col. 0853A] and drunkenness absent from your banquets just as the Apostles, possessing nothing, were often compelled to go hungry. I recognize fasting, thirst, hunger, and nakedness flourishing among us everywhere for the sake of the urgent work of teaching alone, just as we read that they triumphed among the Apostles. The same exercises of virtue through which the Apostles made every vice tremble are proved to burn fervently among us. Plainly we practice the Lord’s forty-day fast and the prayers and vigils with which he broke even the nightly silence throughout the wilderness.

Do we truly undertake comparable contests against the struggles of vice? Do we act with such rigor, austerity, vigils, sufferings, labor, hardship, affliction, and abstinence—the things by which sins are trampled down—that no one suspects any evil of us? Through these things the apostle Paul boasts that [Col. 0853B] his conscience had become known to all:

> In all things commending ourselves as ministers of God: in great endurance, in afflictions, in trials, in tribulations, in distresses, in beatings, in custody, in prisons, in tumults, in invocations, in labors, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in charity unfeigned, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of justice on the right hand and on the left.

For these imitations we are too weak; but for taking women about with us, we claim for ourselves the capacity to imitate them. Even if someone were to boast that he fulfilled all the Apostles’ practices, no one’s persuasion could incline me to believe that there are new Apostles today, contrary to the apostle Paul’s declaration:

> [Col. 0853C] Are all Apostles? Are all Prophets?

If Christ dared to compare himself with God, although he said, “The Father is greater than I,” or if the Apostles dared to equate themselves with Christ, then similar courage makes us equal to the Apostles today. Miserable humanity, do you not fear being struck by lightning for this claim of equality, when you do not hesitate to borrow apparently similar precedents for your sins from the Son of God or the sons of thunder? Although it is the exalted boastfulness of pride even to desire anyone to be recorded as comparable to the least members of the Church, Paul admonishes us:

> Each esteeming the other superior to himself.

And shortly afterward he added:

> Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although established in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, [Col. 0853D] taking the form of a servant.

We must therefore think less of our own powers, and our weakness must not be compared with the strength of the saints. The apostle Paul offers us instruction from his own example when he says:

> For we do not dare to compare or associate ourselves with certain people who commend themselves; but we, commending ourselves within ourselves to ourselves, do not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of grace which God has apportioned to us.

[Col. 0854A] For we also consider what he said elsewhere:

> I labored more than all of them.

Nothing better, nothing more appropriate, is set before me as the means by which I may prevail than that I myself should prescribe from the very authority that is cited prescriptively against me. Certainly Paul himself labored more than all; and yet he trembled to imitate his colleagues in taking women about with him, lest he subject himself to destruction through carnal temptation. Hence he himself gave this explanation:

> I therefore run, not as though toward uncertainty; I fight, not as one beating the air. Rather, I discipline my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate.

Compare yourself, then, with this man, you who boast of the Apostle; and learn from him what you should fear, for he cries out:

> I beseech you, be imitators of me.

[Col. 0854B] He therefore refused to place confidence in taking women about with him, because he was not unaware how greatly some virtues differ from others. He had shown this by comparing the Church’s spiritual gifts to the differing brightness of the sun, the moon, and the stars. But we, on the contrary, flatter ourselves with equality to the Apostles, paying no attention whatever to what the Apostles and all the saints accomplished through unconquered strength. We seek to force open a difficult path when an easier and more level one has been placed before us, contrary to Solomon’s words:

> Do not entrust yourself to a laborious road, lest you place a stumbling block before your soul.

Nor does anyone consider that one man walks safely upon a slippery place while another, who is unequal to it, slips; one man ascends mountains at a run over crags, while another falls if he constrains himself to attempt it. One man succeeds in guiding ships safely through storms, [Col. 0854C] while another cannot attain such good fortune. The apostle Paul decides the matter when he says:

> Each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.

But those who attempt to prejudice my case by appealing to the saints’ example—why do they refuse to contemplate another example, one they should fear? And why does the man who strives to be equated with the Apostles not rather set before himself, as a warning, the adulterous presbyters in Daniel? I do not put these examples forward in order to oppose those who truly imitate the Apostles, but to confound those who equate themselves with the saints. Nor do I deny that those whom we have all received as teachers must be followed. Rather, I contend against those who, desiring to distort the histories of the good for the benefit of their own evils, suppose that the law of God supports them. [Col. 0854D] So do all who hasten to perish and wish their disgraces to be concealed under the saints’ protection, so that, under the guise of imitating their superiors, they may commit every contrary deed. The apostle Paul exposes and makes them public when he says:

> What I do, and will continue to do, is to cut off the opportunity of those who desire an opportunity, so that in the matter of which they boast they may be found such as we are.

For pseudo-apostles of this sort [Col. 0855A] are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into Apostles of Christ. They add this to the accumulated fullness of their destruction: they defame the good, whose example they use for evil. It would be sufficiently useful and salutary for them if they believed that they themselves had failed to understand the rationale of some history rather than suppose that anything dishonorable existed in the law. The apostle Paul rebukes and confounds them:

> Understanding neither the things they say nor the matters about which they make assertions.

And again:

> If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet understood how he ought to know it.

The prejudicial claims of the insolent are therefore void. The wandering inventions of their perversity lead them astray, and they seek out histories suited to their opinions so that they may expound them—people who act wickedly yet borrow the protection of the law. [Col. 0855B] For those who act well, all things that have been written are good, since they receive blessed things properly, as the apostle Paul promises:

> We know that the law is good if one uses it lawfully.

We have prevailed by confounding our opponents. Let us now turn to instructing the very people we have defeated, lest we either allow them to remain in their offense as though they were holy or be judged incapable of giving an account, so that, having been publicly defeated, they may repent. Or, if they refuse, we have discharged what pertains to our diligence. Thus, just as we have satisfied the statement of Solomon cited above, let us also satisfy the apostle Paul when he proclaims:

> The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with complete modesty those who resist the truth, in [Col. 0855C] case God should grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth and they should recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will.

Everything done by our authorities was done with reason, so that an authority fortified on every side against transgressors might be handed down to us, their successors. This was to cut off the heresy censured above concerning the receiving of women—a practice which the Lord relaxed to a small degree, whether through himself or through his servants, lest the Lord’s entire creation be condemned through excessive rigor. The Lord foresaw the heretics who abolish marriage and strive to separate those whom the Lord joined, contrary to the principle of nature [Col. 0855D] and contrary to the Gospel. An authority forbidding them was therefore already being prepared at that time, lest married women who served in his presence be prohibited from approaching Christ.

Yet even that permission was granted with restraint, since what it accomplished was not for itself but for others. For the Lord spoke to the Samaritan woman, taught her for a time, and departed; he did not thereby create a defense for continuing excesses. He likewise allowed Martha to serve him for a time. But what else could serving the Lord mean except serving the banquet of the heavenly kingdom? [Col. 0856A] Were there no meals in the Lord’s presence? Or, in the presence of his majesty, was there any other food or drink than the teaching alone that nourished them? The Lord himself testifies:

> My food is to do the will of him who sent me.

Thus the company of women was fitting for the Apostles, not so that the women might destroy them but so that they might learn reverence; and they followed in order to provide the service proper to humanity, as the Gospel records concerning the Lord and the Apostles together:

> And it came to pass afterward that he journeyed through the cities and villages, evangelizing the kingdom of God, and the Twelve with him, and women who had been healed of unclean spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward; [Col. 0856B] Susanna; and many others, who also ministered to him from their possessions.

Did individual women attach themselves individually to individual men? Or did they remain there without discipline, persisting in enticing companionship? Almost the whole Church appears to have been present there, so that they followed not for disreputable feasting together but to learn the practices of a good manner of life. For that reason nothing is written there that could equate the occasion with our feasts together: neither laughter nor joking is said to have been present. Nor, as is still customary among certain people today, is a choir of psalm-singing virgins said to have caressed their ears with poisonous songs.

To demonstrate briefly from the Apostles how greatly they could disapprove of lax familiarity: they were compelled to be suspicious even of the Lord himself when he spoke with a woman, and only their established knowledge of his majesty restrained them, as the Evangelist relates:

> Meanwhile his disciples came and marveled that he was speaking with a woman. Yet no one said to him, “What are you seeking?” or “Why are you speaking with her?”

[Col. 0856C] And what am I to say about the woman who approached and prostrated herself at the Lord’s feet, whose mourning and lamentation shameless people are not ashamed to demand as a defense of their own wantonness? Their own blindness carries them so far that they do not even dare to contest matters on comparable grounds. Solomon says of them:

> Their malice blinded them, so that they did not know the mysteries of God.

John, moreover, appears to have received the Lord’s mother—but she was a mother whose conduct the very name of “mother” reveals. Yet I cannot admit other mothers of Christ as well, nor may the woman who gave birth to Majesty be equated with all women.

Elijah too [Col. 0856D] was commanded by the Lord to leave the wilderness and enter the widow’s lodging. He labored under the Lord’s command to remain in a house, although solitude had provided him comfort and rest. The Lord offered him an occasion to perform mighty deeds, so that in time of famine he might supply sufficient nourishment both to the widow herself and to her orphans, although he had endured want, afflicted everywhere by fasting. [Col. 0857A] He had been sent to receive food, but instead, by giving food to the wretched, he banished the wretchedness of their poverty.

This cannot lend support to anyone’s lust. There was no opportunity for scandal where, in passing, he had as his lodging what was worse—a poverty-stricken household—from which any ordinary guest would have fled. But here, among those with whom he lodged, he fulfilled his task and returned; and even if he had remained, he could not have been suspected. What sort of benefit could companionship have had there, where there was no sustenance? What sort of access did Elijah have to the widow, when famine gave him his lodging?

Whoever you are who wish to be called Elijah’s disciple because he stayed with a widow, first endure the wilderness’s afflictions and the completion of a forty-day fast. Then either you will not seek a woman, or there will be no man left capable of staying with one. Yet if you can do so, [Col. 0857B] keep that accomplishment for yourself. As for us, both the angel and the Lord Christ indicate no one other than John alone as coming in the spirit and power of Elijah.

Alas! We are compelled to grieve over what we teach, for we have come so far that, in comparison with lax men, we must argue about the awe-inspiring virtues of the saints. Spare us, insolence—spare us now! The saints will never consent to your case. Their dealings with women were religious, restrained, venerable, chaste, and modest.

Or, if you still strive to seek out tortuous quibbles through the saints, we nevertheless know that the friends of God are to be commemorated only with reverence, as David taught:

> But your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored by me.

Let the plunderers of modesty and kidnappers of chastity now go and set forth their burdensome [Col. 0857C] complaints to their little women. They have no refuge whatever among our saints; Paul’s apostolic authority forbids association with them:

> Avoid these also; for from among them are those who creep into houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, who are led by various desires.

After this edict, would that they might venture to believe that the examples of angels support them. They can no longer bend us, for we know that even angels fell with women. They do indeed borrow their defenses aptly from such beings; but we listen to no angel against the apostle Paul:

> Even if I or an angel of God should evangelize to you otherwise than what we evangelized to you, let him be anathema.

All who do not yield to this prohibition are utterly mad and burn with desire for women. [Col. 0857D] Gaping after obscenities, they prefer to die rather than consent to be torn away from women’s sides by any separation. Thus, to fill the maw of their own greed, they will not be without the pleasure of a woman even for an instant. This is the fruit they obtain from women: with their attention always fixed upon them, they satiate the desires of their eyes, [Col. 0858A] lest even a moment pass in which they lack what they crave.

Thus integrity dies among them, where every period of association—whether spent dining together or dwelling together—is defiled by corrupt affections. The holy apostle Peter identified them when he said:

> Reveling in their feasts, having eyes full of adulteries and unceasing sins, ensnaring weak souls.

Solomon likewise censures them:

> Fixing one’s eye is an abomination before the Lord.

By contrast, Job testifies that he possesses a pure eye when he says:

> And if my heart has consented to my eyes.

For a man can avoid being held guilty on account of his eyes when an unexpected encounter with a woman, contrary to his will, stirs a temptation which his mind immediately expels because he did not desire it. [Col. 0858B] But the man who retains in his own company the material of scandal does not deserve to escape the disturbance of his sight: the man who wishes to enjoy the affections of his fixed attention and desires to possess what presents an offense to his eyes. Their insatiable greed can in no way be entirely restrained amid continual stumbling blocks, as Solomon confirms:

> Hell and destruction are not satisfied; likewise, the eyes of human beings are insatiable.

And elsewhere:

> The eye is not satisfied with seeing.

And again:

> What has been created more wicked than the eye?

---

[Note: Col. 0849D]

**“So that she receives our very consolation.”** The old printed edition and Rembold read both this and the following words in the plural, but the word “woman” precedes. —PAMELIUS.

**“And everything pertaining to one’s vow.”** From this passage is confirmed the unspoken vow of chastity attached to clerical celibacy, about which he speaks more openly a little later.

**“And the perfect palm.”** From this it is apparent that one must also read: “one received the palm.” Cyprian reads it this way everywhere. —PAMELIUS.

**“He himself chose to be defeated.”** The old printed edition and Rembold have *penetrari*, “to be penetrated.” —PAMELIUS.

**“He says without justification.”** The old printed edition has “does not say”; but the former reading [Col. 0850D] is preferable. —PAMELIUS.

**“He who despises small things will gradually fall.”** Erasmus incorrectly has “falls,” for Ecclesiasticus has the former reading. —PAMELIUS.

**“It happens, however, through deliberate pursuit,” etc.** Erasmus prefers this in place of what stood there, *arbitrio* (“by judgment”). It appears that one should read *fit studio* (“it happens through deliberate pursuit”). —PAMELIUS.

**“Than the good effects of a woman.”** Erasmus reads “affections,” less correctly. —PAMELIUS.

**“He first induces a man and a woman,” etc.** Rembold had omitted *conversari* (“to live together”), and Erasmus adds it on conjecture; but the old printed edition does contain it. —PAMELIUS.

[Note: Col. 0851D]

**“Drive them against themselves.”** I judge that one should read *illidere* (“drive against”) rather than *elidere* (“dash out”). —PAMELIUS.

**“May keep a fire concealed without any flames.”** Morellius and Gravius rightly read this with the old printed edition and Rembold, in place of what others have, *occultat* (“he conceals”). —PAMELIUS.

**“And while submitting.”** I add *dum* (“while”) with the old printed edition. —PAMELIUS.

**“Disputes and legal proceedings.”** This too is the genuine reading, and that of Rembold, in place of Erasmus’ substitution: “disputed proceedings, which belong to legal cases.” —PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0852D]

**“But rather by correction.”** This reading too is preferable to *correptionem* (“rebuke”). —PAMELIUS.

**“And in all other actions.”** This too is preferable to *inter* (“among”). —PAMELIUS.

**“I plainly see.”** Both here and a little later Erasmus added the negation “not,” but it is unnecessary, since the passage is ironic, as is also the following “I recognize,” etc. The same judgment applies to the places where he added a negation to the statement “If Christ himself,” etc., especially if we read with those editions *facit* (“makes”) rather than *faciet* (“will make”). —PAMELIUS.

[Note: Col. 0853D]

**“In invocations.”** Certain redundant words here appear to have slipped from the margin into the text.

**“One man over crags.”** The old printed edition and Rembold have *ripas* (“banks”). —PAMELIUS.

**“The apostle Paul decides, saying.”** I add “saying” [Col. 0854D] from the old printed edition. —PAMELIUS.

**“What other example do they refuse?”** From the same edition, with Morellius, I read it thus in place of “do they wish?” —PAMELIUS.

**“And he who [compares himself] with the Apostles.”** Manutius alone has “apostolic.” —PAMELIUS.

[Note: Col. 0855D]

**“Those whom the Lord joined.”** Either one must read it thus with Erasmus, or, with the old printed edition and Rembold, “what the Lord commanded”; the former, however, is more attractive. —PAMELIUS.

**“Thus the company of women was fitting for the Apostles.”** The old printed edition has: “Thus the Apostle taught that the company of women,” etc. —PAMELIUS.

**“Where almost the whole Church appears to have been present.”** The passage is thoroughly obscure. The old printed edition and Rembold read “shameful conspiracies” in place of “disreputable feasting together,” incorrectly. —PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0856D]

**“For that reason nothing is written there.”** This is from the old printed codex; Rembold has *adeo* (“so greatly”), while Erasmus has “it is well described for those purposes.” Morellius reads “so greatly, not well.” —PAMELIUS.

**“Yet I cannot.”** This again is from both of those editions, in place of Erasmus’ “they cannot.” —PAMELIUS.

[Note: Col. 0857D]

**“Poverty-stricken.”** Morellius, Rembold, and the old printed edition correctly have *egestosam*, while others have *egestuosam*. —PAMELIUS.

**“We know that the friends of God are to be commemorated only with reverence.”** A notable passage in support of the veneration of the saints. —PAMELIUS.

**“For we know that even angels fell with women.”** Here too the author interprets the “sons of God” in Genesis 6 as angels. —PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0858D]

**“The maw of their own greed.”** The old printed edition and Rembold have *illuviem* (“filth” or “flood”); neither reading is displeasing. —PAMELIUS.

**“In which they lack.”** We have certainly restored this from that edition in place of *cum* (“when”). —PAMELIUS.

**“If such Christian charity is recorded.”** The old printed edition and Rembold more correctly have *adnotatur* (“is recorded”) than the *advocatur* (“is invoked”) found in others. —PAMELIUS.

Unmoved by this rebuke, they stubbornly disregard the divine prohibitions against this abominable intimacy; and, what is more, they plead charity as their excuse. In the words of Isaiah, they devour bitterness as sweetness and cover naked foulness with the veil of a good name, while among them true love is violated under the guise of false affection. [Col. 0858C] But Charity cries out and protests: “I did not join such people together; it is another, false charity that has fashioned a counterfeit of me. I never oppose God’s commandments; I never favor the dissolute; I do not desire holiness to be blamed through me. A perverted brotherhood slanders me; I too have encountered dangers among false brethren. Come to my aid, my herald; come to my aid, Paul the apostle. Bear witness for me, lest what you proclaim about me be distorted: ‘The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.’”

Shall that be reckoned love through which an injury to holiness is exposed to accusations? Or shall the brotherhood of those through whom daughters of Mother Church are led into guilt be judged sincere? If this is to be recorded as Christian charity, then hatreds are unquestionably better, for although they separate people, they stain no one. [Col. 0858D] This parricidal love, however, is accustomed to unite brothers who are persecutors, who willingly suffer daughters of the Church to be defamed as fornicators because of their companionship—contrary to the charity taught by the apostle Paul when he said: “Love of one’s neighbor works no evil.” An outstanding proof of charity indeed: it not only harms one’s neighbor by a destructive brotherhood, [Col. 0859A] but also refuses to be subject to the prescriptions of the apostolic command.

> **Note [Col. 0859D]**
>
> **I still have something at which to marvel.** Erasmus’ restoration, *at which I cannot marvel*, is unsatisfactory unless *enough* is added. Certainly the old printed edition and Remboldus have the former reading. The passage concerns a vow of continence made by married persons. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Our eunuchs do not endure.** Here too Erasmus’ reading, *And the eunuchs hesitate*, is not pleasing. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **The right of one person.** Erasmus had added *of companionship*, but unnecessarily. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **They did not hesitate to send away.** This again is taken from the old printed edition, together with Gravius and Morellius, in place of the corrupt reading *contati* in Remboldus and the others. Manutius, however, reads *contenti*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **But I shall confess the truth, if I am permitted.** This too is the authentic reading of Morellius and those editions, instead of Erasmus’ *I confess, if I should be permitted*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Nor do they confound them any less; indeed, they do so even more severely.** The error of Remboldus’ codex has also remained until now in the printed editions: *nor by threats against them, but by punishments*. —PAMELIUS.

Let the champions of such love be confounded by those who, for the sake of common advantages, forsake even the love owed to their own blood relatives.

Throughout almost the entire world the whole human race is bound together, and everywhere natural kinship is divided by mutual separation abroad. Parents can, children can, brothers can, and even spouses themselves—which is more—can break the bonds of nature granted them by God; yet clerics, though God does not permit it and indeed prohibits it, cannot refuse a love enslaved to ties with women? The desirable companionship of relatives is continually deprived of the presence of those closest to them, yet clerics resist living apart from unrelated women? [Col. 0859B] They ought to have done so even if the Lord had commanded something peculiar or unusual, since they possess the Holy Spirit for accomplishing impossibilities, whom worldly people do not possess. Hence the apostle John admonishes them as follows: “Little children, overcome them, because he who is in you is greater than he who is in this world.”

Yet what is now seen to be possible and easy even for pagans—not merely for Christians—is rendered ineffectual among clerics, without any results at all. It is not enough for them to despise God’s commands unless they also have this further disgrace: that they neither follow—let alone surpass—the custom of all nations. Through Ezekiel the Lord reproaches them, saying: “You have not walked according to my laws, nor have you carried out my ordinances. But neither have you acted according to the ordinances of the nations that surround you.” This so-called love signifies some shameful thing, which they think cannot be wrested from them without violating nature. [Col. 0859C]

I still have something at which to marvel. I see that very many Christian husbands and wives, when they jointly resolve upon continence, choose separate dwellings, so that through mutual consent to their common vows they may attain their purpose without the provocation caused by one another’s presence and through a harmonious withdrawal. Yet our eunuchs cannot endure sleeping without a woman’s companionship? Among the former, conjugal love is weighed against love of continence; but among eunuchs, cohabitation with a woman can never become distasteful. Let the charity of the eunuchs speak; let it say whether perhaps conjugal charity sins more grievously in such separation—so that the apostle Paul’s counsel might appear to have recommended divorce to married persons: “The time that remains,” he says, “is short. It remains that those who have wives should strive to be as though they had none, while those who do not have them should glory as though they did.” Of these the Apostle himself says: “Their glory is in their shame.” [Col. 0859D]

[Col. 0860A] “It is love,” they say. O love that begrudges itself! O charity that desires to be praised amid reproach! A great miracle indeed: that the charity of virgins should cause virgins to be believed to be like married persons, while the charity of married persons should cause married persons to be regarded as virgins. Behold true love, which separates within marriage so that it may unite in chastity. Behold holy love, which leads married persons to absence from one another for the sake of their common praise.
