Certainly those people love one another inseparably who, in order to win triumphs for themselves, withdraw from one another. Neither crime, nor nature, nor law, nor the Lord, nor the Apostle has forbidden or taken from them the right belonging to one partner; yet, to safeguard their equal vows, with their united life set aside, they have vowed a love expressed in absence—people who yield neither to crime, nor nature, nor law, nor the Lord, nor the Apostle, nor marriage itself. [Col. 0860B] Shameful virginity condemns these men just as greatly as disciplined marriage glorifies those married persons. Let it suffice for their disgraceful punishment that eunuchs are judged by married people.

To rebuke them, we must not pass over the children of Israel, who in the time of Ezra did not hesitate to send away wives and children whom they had taken contrary to divine law, nor did they attempt to excuse themselves by appealing to the Lord’s charity. But I shall confess the truth, if I am permitted. Those who now cling to unrelated women rather than dismiss them—what would they do if they were ordered to cast out their children and wives? Or when will they be capable of renouncing their relatives for Christ, when they prefer women who are not even their own to Christ’s commandments? I say that they could more easily deny their own parents for the sake of these same little women than abandon the little women themselves for Christ’s sake. They despise what the Lord himself said in the Gospel: [Col. 0860C] “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, or mother, or wife, or children, or brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.”

If those who hesitate to cast aside their parents are unworthy of Christ, what do those men promise themselves whom not parental affection, but something else, causes to appear as despisers of Christ? Accordingly, they are made worthless by comparison with the merits of those whom they see making no exception for any relative out of regard for Christ. Nor do they confound them any less; indeed, those men confound them even more severely who, fearing not merely to struggle with another’s flesh but even with their own, depart after cutting off their genitals. Concerning these I suspend judgment for the present by way of inquiry, leaving the matter to be brought forward in another discussion. To the confusion of these eunuchs, I do not hesitate to declare better [Col. 0860D] those who do not even spare themselves than, I would say, those who dare offer temptations to women.

Let the spiritual eunuchs answer: what madness is there in the love of women, or what mystery is there in sharing quarters with a woman, that they indulge alien members to their own destruction, [Col. 0861A] while the others cut off even their own without hesitation?

> **Note [Col. 0861D]**
>
> **Concerning their Galli.** The *Galli*, as Remboldus correctly noted, were priests of Cybele, so called from the river Gallus. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **They merited pardon through martyrdom.** Erasmus restored *palm*, but because the author is speaking of sinners who obtained pardon through martyrdom itself, the reading of those editions is preferable. —PAMELIUS.

The latter cast away members firmly attached to themselves; the former glue themselves to hostile members. The latter do not hesitate to fight for spiritual integrity with the torment of a body no longer intact; the former, without torment and with their bodies intact, refuse to be whole without their female halves.

But no comparison should be made between our own people and those men, lest persons condemned by any Christian judgment take comfort from it. There are still worse examples that must be recalled, so that it may be an even greater punishment to be condemned by one who is mutilated. Let them consider that, even to the present day, Jews cut off a portion of their own flesh in circumcision at the law’s command. Let them recognize what they deserve who, when the Gospel commands, neglect to carry out the Lord’s will after being circumcised of the presence of women. They fail to understand what the Lord himself said: “Unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” [Col. 0861B]

I think that even idolaters may reproachfully taunt us concerning their Galli. These men willingly torture themselves by mutilation, provided that, at the cost of their bodily condition, they may obey the pretenses demanded by idols. Our clerics, by contrast, prefer to preserve their own bodies while imposing loss upon the women who dwell with them. They ought to tear such women even from their own flesh, if they happened to be related to them by birth, lest they be ashamed when compared with idolaters and sacrilegious men. The Lord also rebukes such despisers, saying: “The children of this age are more prudent than the children of light.” Thus the profane devotion of such men must be preferred to that of our clerics, for whom shameful priesthoods remain desirable despite such dreadful consequences.

Our clerics, for the sake of the dignity of the heavenly priesthood, shed no blood, endure no blade, suffer no wound or torture; only the sight of a woman holds them against the Lord. [Col. 0861C] They rush upon women and love women as though they expected the impure mysteries of their affection never to be revealed, although such mysteries have been shamefully disclosed and exposed through others like them. The apostle Paul foresaw them even then, saying: “The sins of some people are manifest, preceding them to judgment; but those of others follow after them. Likewise good works are manifest, and whatever is otherwise cannot be hidden.”

They reply, however: “Some among those whom we despise likewise kept women in their houses and yet attained martyrdom, so that their innocent conscience was thereby proved.” [Col. 0861D] I do not want anyone to mount a case against me on the basis of martyrdom, because adulterers, murderers, drunkards, and persons guilty of every crime have often been converted when an opportunity for combat presented itself and have merited pardon through martyrdom. Martyrdom is therefore called both a crown and a baptism, because it baptizes and crowns alike.

Go further now: even if certain people were permitted to merit martyrdom while preserving their association with women inviolate, martyrdom itself was nevertheless not without pardon for those whom [Col. 0862A] the guilt of prohibited cohabitation did not absolve. Nor could martyrdom prove them innocent in that very innocence, for it is seen to have forgiven them contempt for the law, the foulness of unlawful companionship, and—what is graver than everything else—the crime committed against the Church. For an innocence that harms the reputation of Christ’s bride is itself guilty.

Christ, the innocent Lamb—or rather, more truly, heavenly Innocence itself—so completely despised his own welfare for the Church that he might render her inviolate, without any spot or wrinkle. What sort of cleric, then, is he to whom Christ’s bride is entrusted for the very purpose that, out of love for one woman, he should allow the entire Church to be blamed? We dare to say: the Son was sent by God the Father from the Father’s bosom and endured absence from his kingdom in order to make the Church innocent, yet a cleric cannot leave a woman’s side to keep Christ’s Church [Col. 0862B] from being rendered infamous?

But they say: “In martyrdom we are forgiven, just as indulgence was granted to our fathers.” Then let us all place the same confidence in regard to our sins. Let those of us who labor to act rightly roam amid debauchery, run along the paths of sinners, release the reins, and loosen every bridle. Let us go wherever the world carries us and wherever the devil invites us; let us fornicate freely, envy, plunder, and defraud; let us securely commit every evil—martyrdom will come to our aid, and we shall escape! For so the apostle Paul promises: “Let us do evil that good may come—whose condemnation is just.”

Let those whom astrologers have taught to possess foreknowledge of tomorrow entrust their hope to this martyrdom. Let those who have learned from astrologers to know, beyond the angels and Christ, the times that the Father has placed within his own authority await these crowns, so that at least then they may remember that they ought to have lived well before the time of their martyrdom, when they perceived the day of the Lord coming like a thief. [Col. 0862C] But let us suppose that martyrdom is already hanging immediately over them. In the meantime, before they become martyrs, they remain subject to the laws and must undergo judgment unless they are disarmed by armed conflict.

It is an outrageous audacity for them to set the example of their fathers against the Lord’s authority, since the Lord himself deprived them of any voice for this objection: “Do not walk,” he says, “according to the laws of your fathers, and do not observe their ordinances; do not associate yourselves with their pursuits, and do not be defiled. I am the Lord your God: walk in my commandments and observe my ordinances.”

[Col. 0862D] Let those who run this way and that seeking hiding places for their objections, lest they ever lack women, now understand that the protection offered by their fathers has been taken from them. Since they are abandoned on every side by every supporting defense, after exhausting every last argument they imagine that a statement of the apostle Paul comes to their aid, and they say: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” Paul the apostle certainly recognizes the words taken from his own ordinance, but he does not recognize those who appeal to and put forward that ordinance. [Col. 0863A]

> **Note [Col. 0863D]**
>
> **He discusses the right to live, and not to eat.** An obscure passage. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Transgressors of an established transgression.** Erasmus correctly reads thus in place of their reading *ordinari*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Reasonable.** Here, as also somewhere above, the old printed edition and Remboldus read *rationali*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Those who live for others ought to please those others.** This too is the authentic reading, in place of Erasmus’ not inappropriate emendation: *Those who live from the altars ought to please the altars.* —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Our ministry.** This must plainly be read with Morellius instead of *your ministry*, because the Apostle agrees with it. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **It raises up falls.** Erasmus wrongly reads *houses*. Nor is the reading he himself restored, *it demands plunder*, satisfactory in place of their metaphorical expression, *it tears away banks*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **It brings manifold deaths.** The old printed edition reads *simple minds*. Remboldus and most others read *simple deaths*, in place of which Gravius and Manutius have *morals*; Morellius, however, reads *manifold deaths*, which is by far the most satisfactory. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **And of the worst manner of life.** Remboldus had again inserted *devastations*, but this is unnecessary. —PAMELIUS.

For Paul granted a defense to those who oppose no part of the law; and he offered protection to those who act according to their own choice and do not hinder any ecclesiastical right. He discusses the right to live, and not to eat, thereby confirming each person’s individual choice. He commanded no one to be judged concerning matters of this kind, which divine authority, conceding them to individual wills, mercifully permitted on either side, both to do and not to do.

But he subjected to ecclesiastical tribunals those transgressors guilty of an established transgression whom no immunity from punishment excused. Thus, when they indiscriminately produce against us—like a written objection—the words, “Who are you to judge another’s servant?”, let them also acknowledge as reasonable and certain the answer we receive from the same apostle Paul: “We command you, brothers,” he says, [Col. 0863B] “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to separate yourselves from brothers who walk disorderly and not according to the tradition that you received from us.”

We have escaped, I think, the many entanglements of arguments with which women’s embraces have bound the enamored eunuchs. They are compelled to alter the decrees of the law by perverse interpretations and prefer to be heard when they put forward empty and fabulous inventions rather than themselves to hear what is true. The apostle Paul foretells them, saying: “They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables.” Let them seek out whatever else they please so as to oppose the truth on behalf of women. Those among whom a woman has prevailed against Ezra rather than truth possess no victory.

But you, dearest sons, I address not only by persuasion but by authority. [Col. 0863C] Despise such delirium. You know that Paul the apostle everywhere condemned their disputes, as he wrote to the Romans: “I ask you, brothers, carefully to observe those who either speak or act so as to cause dissensions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and turn away from them.” So too he directs Timothy: “Do not,” he says, “contend over words, for that is useful for nothing except the overthrow of those who hear. Take diligent care to present yourself approved to God, an irreproachable workman, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid foolish and empty utterances, for they advance greatly toward impiety, and their speech creeps like a cancer.”

And to show clerics who are to be appointed what teaching is suitable for bringing such disputes to nothing, he also instructs Titus as follows: “But you, speak [Col. 0863D] what accords with sound doctrine: that the elders should be sober, prudent, sound in faith, in charity, and in sincere patience.”

Your obedience, therefore, must receive plain instruction [Col. 0864A] and avoid the shape-shifting deceitfulness of objections. Clear a pure path for your steps; do not sow or tread upon thorns and thistles, lest the good seed be unable, because of thorn-bushes, to produce for you the fruit of holiness. Hence the prophet Jeremiah exhorts and teaches as follows: “Do not,” he says, “sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves for your God; circumcise the foreskin of your heart.”

Everything accustomed to prick and tear must therefore be cut away from our field, lest the mind of the cultivator become entangled in malignant briars within his own possession. We must also amputate everything by which the furnace of boiling flesh—seething with the sulfurous flames of fire-bearing tinder—blazes up, lest even a slender spark that has been preserved kindle greater conflagrations. Solomon makes this plain, saying: [Col. 0864B] “From one spark a fire increases.” Turn away impure occasions by which the inner chambers of the breast are penetrated, so that transparent clarity may be honored in you. Be content to endure the laboriousness of solitude for the sake of preserving modesty rather than to arrive effortlessly at disgrace.

Contemplate what it means to preside over a holy people, and consider what it means to attend to the divine sacraments. Those who live for others ought to please those others, and those who are consecrated should exercise a care for purity corresponding to the sacred things themselves to which they render the service of their ministry. Thus they will not offend the Lord through the very things they handle, nor begin to obstruct among the people what they preach. For this reason the apostle Paul testifies: “We endure all things,” he says, “lest we place any obstacle in the way of Christ’s Gospel.” [Col. 0864C] And again: “Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be reviled.”

You must therefore labor as much as possible under this rule, especially in matters in which solitude rather than company is the truer witness for manifesting seriousness. Consider how many evils this manner of life acquires. It sows nothing but corruption; it causes vices to sprout, conceives desire, gives birth to disgrace, provokes rage, extends fury, feeds wantonness, nourishes insolence, raises up falls, builds ruins, tears away banks, constructs precipices, sails amid dangers, spreads its sails toward shipwrecks, rejoices in perdition, fosters destruction, purchases confusion, stores up reproach, multiplies incriminations, inflames accusations, and, gathering together in one mass whole troops of the many snares of entrapments, brings through endless disgraces manifold deaths upon the destruction of the lost. [Col. 0864D]

No one casts down, tramples upon, or puts to death so many and such great devastations of calamity and of the worst manner of life [Col. 0865A] except solitary chastity alone.

> **Note [Col. 0865D]**
>
> **And barrenness of crimes.** This reading of the old printed edition is authentic, since *abundance* precedes it. Where Remboldus read *desire*, Erasmus restored *captivity*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **For its memory is immortality.** Here, by contrast, Erasmus correctly did not write, *For immortality is its memory*, because the former wording is found verbatim in Greek. He also correctly reads *because* instead of *which*, for the Greek is ὅτι (*hoti*, “because”). —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Of suspect company.** Here again, through an error in Remboldus’ codex, *equality* was read. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **It does not possess brightness.** I consider the negative superfluous. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **So that all do not hesitate to shine on its behalf.** Paraphrase led Erasmus to restore *to vouch* instead of *to shine*. —PAMELIUS.

Solitary chastity is the unconquered defense of holiness and the mighty overthrow of infamy; the firmness of fortitude and the weakness of insolent wantonness; the protection of uprightness and the destruction of wickedness; the soul’s victory and the body’s spoil; an abundance of glories and a barrenness of crimes; the bridesmaid of holiness and the repudiation of shame; the sign of purity and the abolition of scandals; the practice of continence and the complete emptying-out of lust; the secure peace of virtues and the tranquil defeat of wars; the summit of purity and the prison of libido; the harbor of honor and the shipwrecking place of disgrace; the mother of virginity and the enemy of uncleanness; the breastplate of modesty and the stripping away of shamefulness; the destruction of corruption, the wall of strictness, and the destruction of common baseness; [Col. 0865B] the sword of severity, the conqueror and slayer of dissolution; the armor of the strong and the disarming of the dissolute; the dignity of integrity and the condemnation of fornication; the pinnacle of brightness and the precipice of dishonor; the will to good works and the affliction of vices; the refreshment of chastity and the punishment of insolence; the acquisition of triumphs and the loss of crimes; the repose of salvation and the exile of perdition; the life of the spirit and the death of the flesh; the state of angelic being and the death of human nature.

By its reins all obscenity is bridled, and by its shackles the heels of raging libido are restrained. Against it, as against rocks, every surge of inundating blood is shattered; and within it the foaming madness of bodily fluid is calmed. By withdrawing from itself the supports of concupiscence, it is recognized as carrying its own dead members, [Col. 0865C] concerning which the apostle Paul warns: “Therefore mortify the members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and avarice, which is the service of idols; because of these the wrath of God comes.”

Human nature is castrated from all these things only by the shining knife of solitude, so that, through the administration of circumcision, it may introduce inviolate eunuchs to the banquet of holiness. Holiness has promised to solitary chastity the nuptial seal of its ring in such a manner that virginity without it is unsealed. Content with itself alone, it tames desire, rectifies the mind, subjects concupiscence, extinguishes burning desires, weakens the limbs, and enslaves the body. It so crucifies carnal things that both male and female seem to belie their sex in their manner of life, for it laboriously cuts them off from the activity of either sex; [Col. 0865D] or, making neither one of the two, it glories in conferring upon both a third form, so that before the resurrection it is known to practice an image of the resurrection after the likeness of the angels.

The Lord promised that this would come to pass: “Those,” he says, “who are accounted worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead will neither marry nor be given in marriage, nor indeed will they die. For they are like the angels of God, because they are children of the resurrection.” [Col. 0866A] This is what the holy solitude of clerics demands: that before it is transfigured, it should already appear transfigured into the aspect of angelic brightness, cutting away all things from itself and stripping concupiscence of every means of combat.

Solomon recounts its praises, saying: “It is better to be without children and with brightness. For its memory is immortality, because it is known both before God and among human beings. When it is present, they imitate it; they desire it when it has departed; and, crowned, it triumphs forever, victorious in the contest of undefiled struggles.”

Nothing is without children and with brightness except solitude alone, which not only keeps its own conscience unstained by any filth, but is also defamed by no suspicions arising from suspect company. [Col. 0866B] For if chastity—which is difficult—should preserve a man and a woman together in virginity, it does not possess brightness; their companionship itself cannot fail to obscure it with certain shadows of disgrace. Solitude, by contrast, is so bright and manifest to everyone that, through the brilliance of its whiteness, it is revealed to all as pure and luminous.

Hence the Apostle teaches us: “Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light is in all goodness, righteousness, and truth, proving what is pleasing to God.” And again: “Do all things,” he says, “without murmuring and hesitation, and be irreproachable and simple, like spotless children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world.” [Col. 0866C]

Thus solitude shines everywhere, so that all do not hesitate to shine on its behalf; and it so illuminates holiness within itself that it wrests praise for itself even from its enemies. Paul the apostle commands this especially concerning every prelate: “He must also possess a good testimony from those who are outside, so that he does not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare.”

Love this solitude, therefore, and hold fast to it, for it alone can vanquish women. While no concupiscence yet strikes the breast, and while uncorrupted simplicity still remains calm, hasten quickly to the protection of secluded solitude, lest afterward you be unable to escape.

The entrance must be occupied in advance against every ambush, lest hostile force slip in first and fall upon the unwary. [Col. 0866D] It is a saving remedy to forestall rather than be forestalled; and to anticipate rather than be anticipated befits strong powers. Wherever foresight is present, every opposing force is frustrated; but where foresight is neglected, every opposing force gains mastery. Before hunger comes, we struggle; before want comes, we weary ourselves by labor. Thus in every matter we remove the opportunity for calamities [Col. 0867A] by exercising foresight concerning future times.

> **Note [Col. 0867D]**
>
> **That it may protect the provident, not the headlong.** With Morellius, from the old printed edition and Remboldus, we have added *that*, while nevertheless omitting the word *us*, in agreement with those same witnesses. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Eager boldly to carry out the dispositions, etc.** With the same witnesses we have added *boldly*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Much more does he expend courage perversely.** Until now this was read, in an extremely corrupt form derived from a defect in Remboldus’ codex, as *through what was about to perish*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Remember what befits spiritual persons.** Remboldus again corruptly reads *let him remember*, for which Erasmus has *let us remember*. The former reading, however, is authentic. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Among the weapons of the shameful.** Erasmus had restored *herds*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Of insolence.** These words are poorly connected, nor is it easy to conjecture what this writer means here; he also twists at will the Holy Scriptures that he adduces throughout. He appears to mean by *beginnings* the initial stages.

How much more, then, must the calamity of women be forestalled by every provision, since, if desire for a woman is allowed to begin, it never comes to an end at all? Solomon explains the comparison: “The underworld, the love of a woman, the earth that is not satisfied with water, and the fire do not say: ‘It is enough.’”

Let everyone, therefore, who feels secure because he is not yet tempted be afraid; because nothing is yet being said about him, let him take care lest it be said: “We are human beings; we carry our frailty in the flesh.” We must therefore surround and gird ourselves on every side with vigilant circumspection, so that no part may waver. We do indeed receive spiritual strength by which the frailty of our substance is fortified. But spiritual strength has been bestowed upon us [Col. 0867B] so as to protect the provident, not the headlong; to fortify those who renounce the assaults of sins, not those who immerse themselves ever more deeply in assailing sins.

The Spirit has been given to us as a guardian, but so that, by standing beside those who avoid hostile things, he may come to their aid—not so that he may favor those who choose them. Nor does he strengthen those who willingly and eagerly rush into adversity, but he confirms those who strive to separate themselves from it. For whoever dares to exercise his courage through destructive attempts does not possess the assistance of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit does not will any self-willed strong man to be driven into treacherous victories. He does not protect such a man; rather, he abandons one whom he recognizes as rushing into dangers and seeking triumphs through unlawful outcomes. As he himself spoke even then through Solomon: “He who loves danger will perish in it.”

[Col. 0867C] The power of the Holy Spirit is therefore administered according to his order, not according to our choice, and battles prosper according to his ordinance. No army that rushed headlong has ever failed to fall when, eager to act boldly, it violated the dispositions of its leader or commander. Much more does he expend courage perversely who presumes to triumph without the weapons supplied by the teaching of the Spirit, his master, since the Spirit says: “Woe to those who do anything through their own presumption, not through God.”

If, then, there is any confidence in spiritual strength among you, remember what befits spiritual persons. If you believe that you are serving as spiritual soldiers, recognize that what we teach is not carnal, as the apostle Paul says: “If anyone thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize the things that I write to you.”

You have no reason to flatter yourselves with this deceitful persuasion: that because you are spiritual, you may choose to move among the weapons of the shameful, or that you are not unequal to the dignity of clerical office. For greater conflicts are accustomed to confront greater persons. [Col. 0867D] The rich are envied more fiercely than the poor, and the savage assault of robbers troubles not the needy but the wealthy. Leaders and princes are attacked by enemies in battle more than soldiers are; and whatever heights are loftier are battered by violent winds and tempests. Therefore, the more each person is capable of beyond others, the more and more he should know that he must be afraid lest he be diminished in some respect. Hence Solomon admonishes: “He who glories,” he says, “in riches should fear poverty.” [Col. 0868A]

I beg you with all my strength, and beyond my strength: let all clerics devote themselves to this, that they practice an irreproachable withdrawal into solitude, lest either they through women, or women through them, be provoked to disgraceful mockeries.

If anyone has a mother, daughter, sister, wife, or female relative, let him keep her in such a way that no maidservant is present and no unrelated woman enters. Otherwise, he may seem to retain his close female relatives precisely so that, because of them, he may freely bring unrelated women into his company. But if the women who are his close relatives cannot live without the service of maids or the companionship of female friends, it is expedient that they move to another dwelling rather than that unsuitable persons be retained because of them. [Col. 0868B] For it is humane that the cleric should neither deprive them of the women they require nor permit them to defile the cleric through unwelcome women.

They can be entrusted to holy women with whom they may live, provided that no woman dwells with the cleric. No woman—whether unattractive, elderly, or unrelated—is to be individually received for domestic service. For sin is committed more readily where wrongdoing can be secure from suspicion, especially since lust finds no deformity, unattractiveness, or lowliness distasteful or contemptible; rather, the devil paints whatever is foul or horrible and renders it beautiful. [Col. 0868C]

If, however, anyone is compelled by travel to lodge among brothers or strangers where women are present, let him restrain himself completely, lest he be corrupted by any susceptibility to passion. Let him remain apart and in private, attending to God and himself, lest he be captured inwardly by the devil, and lest one who could not be captured among outsiders should fall among his own people. After escaping enemies, let him appear in their presence for a time when wholesome reasons require it, and then hasten quickly to withdraw again from their sight.

In every place one’s presence with women is to be tasted briefly, not prolonged. Access to women should be granted only as one passes by, in a manner almost fugitive. For the beginnings of insolence consist in constantly appearing in their midst, and it is preparation for destruction to make one’s appearance among women repeatedly and ceremonially. Concerning this matter Solomon imposed a limit upon us, [Col. 0868D] saying: “Do not remain continually in the midst of women.”

Walk and act, therefore, in such a way that the Church’s white-robed senate may always remain steadfast among its clerics. Let severity toward women flourish in you; let authority prevail, vigor be maintained, and gravity be revered.

To gather everything together once and for all in conclusion, we read over to you a summary that the apostle Paul presents by reducing the matter to concise completeness: [Col. 0869A] “For the rest, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever modest, whatever holy, whatever lovely, whatever of good reputation—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline—think upon these things, which you have received and learned and heard and seen in me. Practice these things, and the God of peace and love will be with you. Amen.” [Col. 0870A]

[Col. 0869]

# A TREATISE ON THE TWELVE ABUSES OF THE AGE, WRONGLY ATTRIBUTED TO CYPRIAN AND AUGUSTINE  
(C, G, S)

> **Note [Col. 0869D]**
>
> **Of the one who establishes.** In Augustine, vol. 6, the reading is *of the one who preaches*. Shortly before this, the same author reads *to complete*.
>
> **Of the ruler.** *Of the giver*, in the Corbie manuscript.
>
> **And by graver punishments.** Thus two manuscripts, the Royal and the Colbertine. The editions read differently: *he will be beaten with sharper scourges and graver punishments*. Shortly before this, Augustine reads: *by his own merit alone*.

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0869B]

The first degree of abuse is a wise man and preacher without good works—one who neglects to carry out in deeds what he teaches in speech. For those who hear his teaching disdain to practice what is said when they see the preacher’s deeds diverging from the words of his preaching. The authority of one who lays down a rule never becomes effective unless he has fixed it in the hearer’s heart by putting it into practice—especially since the teacher himself, if he has fallen into love of vice, makes light of applying another teacher’s remedy to his own wounds. Hence the Lord himself, wishing in the Gospel to instruct his disciples concerning both teaching and good works, warned them what caution they should exercise in these matters, saying: “But if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5:13). That is, if the teacher has gone astray, [Col. 0869C] by what other teacher will he be corrected? And: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be!” (Matt. 6:23). For if the eye ceases to perform the office of seeing, who will demand that service from the hand, the foot, or the rest of the body? Therefore teachers should consider whether they may be liable to a greater punishment if they furnish more abundant occasion for the ruin of very many. For even Solomon, when he fell into transgression despite his great wisdom, by his own fault alone occasioned the division of the kingdom of the whole Israelite people. Those, therefore, to whom many things are entrusted suffer greater losses if they do not rightly administer the gifts they have received from their ruler. For more is required from the one to whom more is entrusted. And the servant who understands his master’s will but does not do it will be beaten with the harsher and heavier scourges of punishment [Col. 0869D] (Luke 12:47).

[Note: [Col. 0869D]

CHAPTER II.—“Is fitting” (*competit*). In Augustine: “is appropriate” (*convenit*).

“Has left behind” (*deseruit*). “Leaves behind” (*deserit*) in two manuscripts and Morel. In the following [Col. 0870D] sentence we likewise read, as in Augustine, *deseruit*, although *deserit* is read in the manuscripts and printed editions of Cyprian’s works.

“Which” (*quam*). I added this word from the edition of Augustine, where the passage reads: “how access to the future may swiftly be secured.” In the Corbie manuscript: “access to future prosperity”; we follow the same edition in several other places about which it is unnecessary to give notice.

“With himself” (*secum*). This word is absent from two manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER II

The second degree of abuse is an old man found to be without religion. Although the members of his outward man are growing old, [Col. 0870B] the powers of his soul—that is, the members of the inward man—gain no increase in strength. It is fitting above all for the elderly to devote themselves to religion, since the flowering season of this present age has passed and left them behind. For just as among trees that tree is rejected which, after flowering, does not offer its cultivator excellent fruit, so also among human beings that man is rejected whom the flower of youth has left behind and who nevertheless, in the old age of his body, makes light of producing the mature fruits of good works. What could be more foolish than for the mind not to strive to hasten toward perfection when the whole bodily frame, worn out by old age, is hastening toward destruction? The eyes grow dim, the ears hear poorly, the hair falls out, the face [Col. 0870C] turns pale, the teeth fall out and diminish in number, the skin dries up, the breath smells unpleasant, the chest is constricted, the cough cackles, the knees tremble, and swelling distends the ankles and feet; even the inward man, who does not grow old, is weighed down by all these things. And all these swiftly foretell that the house of the body is now about to fall. What remains, then, except that, as the decline of this life approaches, every old man should desire to think of nothing other than how his future dwelling may successfully be secured? For the uncertain end of this life hangs over the young, whereas a more mature departure from this light shortly awaits all the old. A person must therefore beware of two little members that do not grow old in his flesh and that drag the whole man with them into sin: namely, the heart and the tongue. For the heart never ceases to devise new [Col. 0870D] thoughts, and the tongue readily speaks whatever it perceives the heart devising. Old age, therefore, must take care that these still-youthful members do not deceive the harmony of its whole being and, through foolish conduct, make a mockery of the gravity of the rest of the body. Each person [Col. 0871A] [Note: [Col. 0871D]

“Or to an elder.” Thus the Regius manuscript; the edition has “to an elder who admonishes.” Shortly afterward, before “the disgrace of the cross,” we deleted the words “but death,” which are absent from two manuscripts and from Augustine.

“Therefore a young man without discipline.” Augustine, by contrast: [Col. 0872D] “Therefore a young man without obedience is a young man without discipline.”

must consider what befits advanced age, so that he may act in a manner that renders neither his life, nor his age, nor his ministry contemptible.

## CHAPTER III

The third degree of abuse is a young man without obedience, through whom the world is distorted from the right order of reason. For how will he command service from others in old age if in youth he disdains to show himself obedient to his elders? Hence there is also an ancient proverb that one who refuses first to render service to someone cannot rule. For this reason the Lord Jesus too, in the days of his flesh, while he had not yet reached the lawful age of a teacher, obediently rendered service to his parents. [Col. 0871B] Thus, just as sobriety and perfection of character are required in the elderly, so service, submission, and obedience are rightly required in the young. Consequently, among the commandments of the Law, the first of those concerning human beings enjoins honor for father and mother. For although one’s natural father may not have survived, or may be unworthy, it is shown that sons must nevertheless render paternal honor to some worthy and living father until they reach a fitting age. In divine Scripture, indeed, men are called fathers in four ways: by nature, by nation, by admonition, and by age. Concerning a natural father, Jacob says to Laban: “If the fear of my father Isaac had not been present, you would have taken everything that is mine” (Gen. 31:42). One is called a father by nation when the Lord spoke to Moses from the bush: “I am,” he said, “the God of your fathers, [Col. 0871C] the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:6). One is called a father by age and admonition together when Moses says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; ask your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7). If, therefore, one’s natural father is no longer alive or is unworthy, a young man must nevertheless offer obedience to one who admonishes him or to an elder. How, then, will one appear worthy of honor in old age if he has not endured the labor of discipline in youth? Whatever a person has labored at, that too he will reap. For all discipline in the present seems to be a matter not of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, the training it provides will yield the most peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb. 12:11). Just as fruit is not found on a tree on which shoot or flower did not first appear, so in old age one will not be able to attain due [Col. 0871D] honor if in youth he has not labored in the exercise of some discipline. How, then, can discipline exist without obedience? A young man without discipline is therefore a young man without obedience, [Col. 0872A] since obedience itself, which is the mother of all disciplines, requires great exercise. It took the pattern of its practice from Christ the Lord, who, obedient to the Father even unto death, willingly endured the disgrace of the cross.

## CHAPTER IV

The fourth degree of abuse is a rich man without almsgiving, who does not distribute to the needy and those who have nothing the surplus beyond his own use that he stores away to preserve for the future. The result is that, while he carefully guards on earth what he has acquired, he loses the perpetual treasure of the heavenly homeland. The Lord Jesus invited the rich young man who had questioned him about perfection to this treasure when he answered: “If [Col. 0872B] you wish to be perfect, go and sell everything you have and give to the poor; then come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matt. 19:21). No human being can ever possess this treasure except one who provides relief to the poor or is himself poor. Therefore, let nothing lie idle in your treasuries that prevents the poor from sleeping. For although a rich man has amassed many things, he cannot possibly enjoy them all by himself, because the nature of one person has no use for so many things. What, then, is more foolish than, for the sake of one person’s food and clothing, to lose all the perpetual delight of the kingdom of heaven and to undergo the eternal torments of hell without expectation of consolation? What must at some time be lost through necessity should therefore be freely distributed for an eternal reward. For all things that are seen [Col. 0872C] are temporal, while those that are unseen are eternal (2 Cor. 5:18). So long as we are temporal, temporal things provide temporal services; and when we have passed from here, eternal consolations will be provided by eternal things. Therefore, we ought not to love things that we shall not always possess—especially since his own treasure and field, and everything he possesses, show the covetous rich man to be devoid of reason, because with the whole gaze of his heart he loves things that never love him. For if someone loves gold and silver, fields, clothing, food, metals, and brute animals, the very nature of these things shows that none of them can repay his love in kind. What, then, is further removed from reason than to love what is incapable of loving you, and to neglect the one who, in return for your love, provides you with everything in love? For this reason, therefore, [Col. 0872D] God commands that the world not be loved but one’s neighbor be loved, since one’s neighbor can repay one’s love in kind, something the world assuredly cannot do. Indeed, the Lord commanded even an enemy to be loved, [Col. 0873A] [Note: [Col. 0873D]

“Enlivens the soul” (*animam vegetat*). Morel and two manuscripts: “fixes the mind” (*animum figit*).

“Inferior to no one.” Two manuscripts: “inferior to no one in what has been begun.”

“Of the weak.” Augustine: “of the lowly.”

[Col. 0874D] “Friendship.” Two manuscripts: “friendly” (*amica*).

“Than of the mind.” The printed editions add “has need” before these words and “in good character” before “be exercised.” I have followed two manuscripts.

“Strength.” Augustine: “the virtue of ruling.”

“Of a judge.” Thus two manuscripts, in place of “of judgment,” which stood in the editions.

“Harshly.” Absent from Augustine.]

so that this love might turn him from an enemy into a friend. Therefore, any covetous rich man who wishes to have eternal riches should provide for the needy by distributing what meanwhile will not endure. For if he does not sell what he loves, no one can purchase what he desires. The covetous are called accursed at the judgment by the perfectly righteous Judge because those who passed by their dwellings did not say: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 128:8). Unhappy, therefore, are the covetous rich, who because of transitory possessions sink into eternal damnation. Conversely: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Happy, therefore, is the merciful person, since in this virtue God requires not material wealth but disposition.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0873B] The fifth degree of abuse is a woman without modest chastity. For just as prudence provides for and preserves every good character in men, so modest chastity nurtures, fosters, and preserves in women every honorable action. Modest chastity guards purity, restrains avarice, avoids quarrels, mitigates anger, forestalls lust, moderates covetousness, chastises wantonness, guards against drunkenness, does not multiply words, cleanses the cravings of gluttony, and wholly condemns theft. What more need be said? It restrains every vice and nurtures every virtue and whatever is praiseworthy before God and good people. An immodest life expects neither praise from human beings in the present age nor reward from God in the age to come. A modestly chaste life, however, possesses a good [Col. 0873C] reputation among human beings and rejoices in the hope of future blessedness. It makes itself worthy of imitation by those now living and leaves a cherished memory to posterity. It always delights in and assents to good conduct, and enlivens the soul by constant meditation on and utterance of the Scriptures. It preserves the examples of the virtuous who have gone before and forms inseparable companionships with the perfect. The exercise of true modest chastity, therefore, consists in two forms: the condition and outward appearance of the body, and the inward disposition of the soul. By the outward form, we provide good works before God. Bodily modest chastity consists in not coveting the possessions of others; avoiding every impurity; not wishing to taste food before the proper hour; not provoking laughter; not speaking vain and false words; maintaining in every respect an orderly bearing, and a fitting arrangement both of the hair [Col. 0873D] and of clothing, as is proper; not entering into companionship with the unworthy; looking at no one with a haughty gaze; not allowing the eyes to wander; not walking with a pompous and seductive gait; appearing inferior to no one in a good work once begun; inflicting neither insult [Col. 0874A] nor shame upon anyone; blaspheming no one; not mocking the elderly; not envying the good; not disputing with one’s superior; not discussing matters of which one is ignorant; and not disclosing everything one knows. These things make a person lovable to one’s neighbors and acceptable to God.

The modest chastity of the soul consists in doing every good deed more for the eyes of God than for those of human beings; suppressing desires for shameful thoughts; esteeming everyone better than oneself; envying no one; placing no confidence in oneself; always committing everything to God’s help; setting oneself before God’s eyes; not defiling one’s understanding with heretical depravity; agreeing in all things with Catholics; clinging to God alone; offering the chastity of an eternal mind to Christ God; bringing every good work begun to an end only at death; disregarding and making light of [Col. 0874B] present tribulations through strength of soul; loving nothing on earth except one’s neighbors; storing up the treasure of all one’s love in heaven; and hoping for a reward from God in heaven for every good deed. Modest chastity is the adornment of the noble, the exaltation of the humble, the nobility of the ignoble, the beauty of the weak, the prosperity of those who labor, the consolation of those who mourn, the increase of every beauty, the glory of religion, a defense against accusations, a multiplication of merits, and friendship with God, the Creator of all.

## CHAPTER VI

The sixth degree of abuse is a lord without virtue, because possessing the power to rule is of no benefit if the lord himself does not possess the rigor of virtue. [Col. 0874C] But this rigor of virtue must be exercised not so much through external strength—which is itself necessary for secular lords—as through inward strength of mind. For the strength needed to rule is often lost through negligence of mind, as is proved to have happened in the case of Eli the priest. Because he did not restrain his sinning sons with the severity of a judge, the Lord, in punishing them, harshly did not spare him, as though he had consented. Those who rule must therefore possess three necessary things: fear, order, and love. For unless a lord is both loved and feared, his ordering cannot possibly remain firm. By benefits and affability, therefore, he should ensure that he is loved; and by just punishments—not for an injury done to himself, but for violation of God’s law—he should strive to be feared. Moreover, because many depend [Col. 0874D] upon him, he himself must cling to God, who appointed him to leadership and strengthened him as one stronger than others to bear the burdens of many. For unless a peg is fixed securely and firmly and attached to something stronger, everything hanging from it soon falls; and the peg itself, loosened [Col. 0875A] [Note: [Col. 0875D]

“Rise higher” (*transcendunt*). Thus the Colbert manuscript. The edition has “descend” (*condescendunt*).

“Needs glory.” Thus Morel and two manuscripts; others have “needs all glory.”

[Col. 0876D] “One another.” I added this phrase from two manuscripts, Morel, and Augustine.]

from the firmness of its support, falls to the ground together with its burdens. So too, unless a prince clings steadfastly to his Creator, both he and everything he sustains quickly perish. Some, indeed, draw closer to God through the office of ruling, while others become worse after the honor of high rank has been imposed upon them. Moses, upon receiving leadership of the people, enjoyed more intimate converse with God. Saul son of Kish, however, after receiving the royal scepter, offended God through the pride of disobedience. After King Solomon obtained the throne of his father David, God enriched him beyond all mortals with the gift of wisdom, as befitted the governance of an innumerable people. By contrast, Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, after he seized part of the kingdom of the house of David, turned the ten tribes of Israel located [Col. 0875B] in the region of Samaria toward the worship of idols. These examples clearly show that some grow toward greater perfection in a more exalted station, whereas others sink into worse things through the arrogance of dominion. From both cases it is understood that those who rise toward better things are able to do so through strength of mind and God’s help, while those who turn aside toward worse things go astray through both weakness of mind and negligence. It is therefore improper for a lord to be without virtue, though he cannot possess virtue without God’s help. For if one who oversees many does not possess strength of mind, he cannot perform that task, because great things are ordinarily beset by great attacks or adversities. Everyone who presides, therefore, should first endeavor with the whole intention of his mind never to doubt God’s assistance in any matter. For if he begins to have the Lord of lords as his helper in his deeds, no human being will be able to treat his rule with contempt: “For there is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1). He raises the needy from the dung heap and makes him sit with the princes of his people; he casts the powerful down from their seat and exalts the humble, so that the whole world may become subject to God and stand in need of the glory of God.

## CHAPTER VII

The seventh degree of abuse is a contentious Christian, who, although he has received a share in Christ’s name through faith and Baptism, loves the fleeting delights of the world, contrary to Christ’s words and purpose. For every object of contention is sought either because of love for the thing itself that is at issue, [Col. 0875D] or because of love for some other thing concealed beneath an odious appearance. Thus, for example, although war is an odious thing, waged in the spirited conflict of combatants, it is pursued because of love for victory and freedom; and many other beloved ends are sought with great contention beneath odious toil or fear. From this it is plainly understood that nothing can be contended for except through love—that is, for an expected and subsequently attractive reward. Therefore, whoever contends for any reason concerning the present world [Col. 0876A] plainly shows that he loves it. Yet the words of the Holy Spirit through John forbid the world to be loved, for he says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15). For love of the world and love of God cannot dwell together in one heart, just as the same eyes cannot look at heaven and earth simultaneously. But one must inquire whether there is truly anything in the world that ought to be loved, and what that world is which divine utterances forbid us to love. We are therefore commanded not to love the earth, together with what springs from it, its metals and living creatures, the beauty of clothing, the pleasures of food, and the things pertaining to these; but we are commanded to love our neighbor, for whose sake all these things were made. All the aforementioned things, [Col. 0876B] since they will not endure, cannot accompany those journeying toward the heavenly homeland. Neighbors, however, as those who will endure as the King’s fellow heirs, may rightly love one another. Therefore, what does not always remain in the world, but will perish together with the world—and the world itself—is commanded not to be loved. One’s neighbor, however, who is part of the kingdom of heaven, is fittingly loved on earth and among the lowest elements by those who desire the kingdom of heaven, since in that highest homeland he will be possessed forever as a fellow heir. The present world is therefore commanded not to be loved, lest anyone, through love of the age, become alienated from the love of God. One ought not, then, to contend for what it is not lawful to love. Accordingly, a Christian who bears the likeness of Christ’s name must also possess the likeness of his character. For no one is rightly [Col. 0876C] called a Christian unless he is conformed to Christ in character. Concerning Christ it is written through the Prophet: “Behold my son, whom I have chosen; my elect, in whom my soul has been well pleased. I shall place my Spirit upon him. He will not contend or cry out, nor will anyone hear his voice in the street” (Isa. 42:1; Matt. 12:18). Behold, Christ neither contended nor cried out; and if you wish to possess the likeness of Christ’s character, do not contend, lest you prove to be a Christian only improperly so called within the Church. For Christ commanded his followers: “Do not be called Rabbi; for one is your Father, who is in heaven. For you are all brothers” (Matt. 23:8). He commanded them to pray, saying: “You shall pray in this way: Our Father who is in heaven, may your name be sanctified” (Matt. 6:9). Therefore, one who professes that he has his Father and homeland in heaven contends in vain that he has a father on earth. [Col. 0876D] No one becomes a possessor of that homeland unless he is free from contention over an earthly homeland.

## CHAPTER VIII

The eighth degree of abuse is a proud poor man, who, though possessing nothing, is lifted up in pride—even though, conversely, the rich of this age are commanded through the apostle Paul not to be proud-minded. What, then, could be more foolish than for one who, cast down as it were to the earth through feeble [Col. 0877A] [Note: [Col. 0877D]

“Pass by” (*praetereunt*). Augustine: “lose” (*perdunt*).

“Lest they be unjust” (*ne iniqui*). Augustine: “if unjust” (*si iniqui*).

“Not to lift up the mind.” Augustine: “not to be lifted up in mind.”

“The fruitfulness of the lands, etc.” Thus we emended the text on the authority of the Colbert manuscript and Augustine. Other witnesses wrongly read, “when the fertility of things, the sea, etc., has been disturbed.” The same manuscript has “when fair weather has been disturbed” before “of the lands.” Shortly afterward, I read from two manuscripts “scorch the vine shoots,” in place of the edition’s “scorch all the vine shoots.”]

poverty, ought to have walked as the lowest and humblest of men and to have been sorrowful, instead raising a mind swollen with the haughty inflation of pride against God? Through this vice those who had been created at the highest summit of heaven slipped and fell. Why, then, does one who ought to appear humble above all human beings wish to behave proudly on earth as though powerful? But lest the poor be saddened by their poverty, let them consider what they are to receive from God; for he himself says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). By right ordering, the merciful Judge entrusts the kingdom of heaven to those from whom he has taken participation in earthly kingdoms among mortals, so that one who possesses absolutely nothing on earth may appear rich upon heaven’s throne. The poor must therefore beware lest, while [Col. 0877B] through want and necessity they pass by the earthly kingdom, they also lose the kingdoms of heaven through shamelessness of mind. For although by God’s dispensation they have received unavoidable poverty, whether they are poor in spirit lies within their own choice. The kingdoms of heaven are not promised to every sort of poor person, but only to those in whom lack of riches is accompanied by humility of mind. The humble poor person is called poor in spirit: although seen to be needy outwardly, he is never lifted up in pride, since lowliness of mind has greater power to attain the kingdoms of heaven than temporal poverty in present riches. Indeed, humble people who rightly possess wealth can be called poor in spirit; but there is no doubt that proud people who possess nothing are deprived of the blessedness [Col. 0877C] of poverty. Concerning both, Holy Scripture says: “There is one who is as though rich while possessing nothing, and there is one who is as though poor while possessing great riches” (Prov. 13:7). The humble rich man is thus as though poor amid great riches because he is poor in spirit; and the proud poor man, although possessing nothing, is as though rich in his mental disposition. Humility of mind, therefore, is noble poverty, while arrogance of spirit is foolish wealth. The poor must therefore take care to understand what they are and, because they cannot obtain by possessions what they desire, to cease acting proudly through swelling of mind.

## CHAPTER IX

The ninth degree of abuse is an unjust king. For a king ought not to be unjust, but a corrector of the unjust. Hence he must preserve in himself the dignity of his [Col. 0877D] title, for the meaning of the name “king” entails that he fulfill the office of ruler toward all his subjects. But how will he be able to correct others if he does not correct his own character lest it be unjust? For a king’s throne is exalted in justice, and the governance of peoples is made firm through a king’s truthfulness. [Col. 0878A]

A king’s justice consists in oppressing no one unjustly by power; judging justly between a man and his neighbor, without partiality; being a defender of strangers, orphans, and widows; restraining thefts; punishing adulteries; not exalting the wicked; not maintaining the immodest and stage performers; destroying the impious from the land; not permitting parricides and perjurers to live; defending churches; feeding the poor with alms; appointing the just over the affairs of the kingdom; having elderly, wise, and sober counselors; paying no heed to the superstitions of magicians, soothsayers, and female mediums; deferring anger; defending the homeland bravely and justly against adversaries; trusting in God in all things; not lifting up his mind amid prosperity; patiently enduring every adversity; possessing the catholic faith in God; not allowing his sons to act impiously; devoting himself to prayers at fixed hours; [Col. 0878B] and not tasting food before the proper hours. “Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. 10:10). These things bring prosperity to the kingdom in the present and lead the king to the better kingdoms of heaven.

But one who does not administer his kingdom according to this law will assuredly endure many adversities in his rule. For this reason the peace of peoples is often broken, stumbling blocks arise even from within the kingdom, the fruits of the lands diminish, the services of the peoples are impeded, and many varied afflictions taint the prosperity of the kingdom. The deaths of loved ones and children bring sorrow; hostile incursions devastate the provinces on every side; wild beasts tear apart herds of cattle and flocks of sheep; storms of air and winter prevent the fruitfulness of the lands and the services [Col. 0878C] of the sea; and sometimes lightning strikes scorch the crops, the blossoms of trees, and the vine shoots. Above all, however, a king’s injustice not only darkens the present face of his rule but also casts a shadow over his sons and grandsons, preventing them from possessing the kingdom as their inheritance after him. For because of Solomon’s transgression, the Lord divided the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hands of his sons. And because of the justice of King David, he always left a lamp from his seed in Jerusalem (3 Kings 11:31–35).

Behold, it is plainly evident to those who consider it how powerful a king’s justice is in this age. It is the peace of peoples, the protection of the homeland, the security of the common people, the defense of the nation, care for the sick, the joy of human beings, the mildness of the air, the serenity of the sea, the fertility of the earth, the relief of the poor, the inheritance of children, and for the king himself the hope [Col. 0878D] of future blessedness. Nevertheless, the king must know that just as he has been established first upon the throne of human beings, so, if he has not practiced justice, he will hold first place in punishment. For in that future punishment he will have above him, in an implacable manner, all the sinners whom he had beneath him in the present.

[Note: [Col. 0879D]

“In which” (*in quo*). Thus the Regius manuscript; the edition has “which” (*quod*).

“Mute” (*muti*). Thus the Corbie manuscript cited in Augustine. Morel and Pamel have “many” (*multi*); my editions of Augustine have “my” (*mei*).

“But that very.” Thus two manuscripts; the edition has “for that very.”]

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0879A]

The tenth degree of abuse is a negligent bishop, who seeks the honor of his rank among human beings but does not preserve before God—on whose behalf he serves as an ambassador—the dignity of his ministry. First, therefore, inquiry should be made of the bishop as to what the dignity of his name entails; for since “bishop” is a Greek word, it is interpreted as “watchman.” Why he is appointed a watchman, and what is required of a watchman, the Lord himself reveals when, under the persona of the prophet Ezekiel, he declares to the bishop the account demanded by his office, saying: “I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel. When, therefore, you hear a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. But if you see the sword coming and do not announce it, so that the impious man may turn back from his way, that impious man indeed [Col. 0879B] will die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it and he does not turn back, he indeed will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul” (Ezek. 3:17).

It therefore befits the bishop, who has been appointed watchman over all, diligently to observe sins and, after observing them, to correct them by word and, if he can, by deed. If he cannot, he must avoid the perpetrators of crimes according to the rule of the Gospel. “For if,” the Lord says in the Gospel, “your brother sins against you, correct him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you one or two more witnesses, so that every word may be established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. If he does not hear them, tell the Church. If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. [Col. 0879C] 18:15). In this order anyone who refuses to adhere to his teacher or bishop must be expelled. And one expelled in this order must not be received by any other teacher or bishop. For concerning a priest it is written in the Law: “He shall not take a widow or a divorced woman as wife” (Lev. 21:7). Therefore, one who joins to himself a person excommunicated by a catholic bishop, without that bishop’s permission, transgresses the laws of the holy priesthood into which the race of Christians has been chosen.

The bishop ought to conduct himself according to this principle toward those whom he has been appointed to watch. Paul the apostle, however, explains what he ought to be in himself: one coming to the rank of bishop should be sober, prudent, chaste, wise, modest, hospitable, having submissive children with all chastity, having a good testimony from those [Col. 0879D] who are outside, and setting forth the trustworthy word of doctrine; before becoming a bishop, he should not have had more than one wife; he should not be violent, double-tongued, drunken, or a recent convert, so that through these qualities he himself may demonstrate in deed what he teaches others in the discourse of doctrine (1 Tim. 3:2).

Negligent bishops, therefore, should beware of that concerning which the Lord complains through the Prophet at the time of punishment, saying: “Mute shepherds have destroyed my people, and the shepherds did not feed my flock, but fed themselves” (Ezek. 34:8). Rather, those whom the Lord has appointed over his household should take care to give [Col. 0880A] them food in due season—the measure of wheat, namely pure and proven doctrine—so that when the Lord comes they may deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I shall appoint you over many. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:23).

## CHAPTER XI
The eleventh degree of abuse is a people without discipline. When it does not submit to the exercises of discipline, it binds itself in the common snare of perdition; for without the rigor of discipline it does not escape the wrath of the Lord. Therefore, in the Psalmist’s words, the undisciplined people is admonished: “Embrace discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry” (Ps. II, 12). Discipline of conduct, however, is orderly correction and the observance of the rules established by those who have gone before. Concerning this discipline [Col. 0880B] the apostle Paul speaks as follows: “Persevere under discipline; God presents himself to you as to sons. But if you are outside discipline, in which all have become participants, then you are illegitimate children, and not sons” (Heb. XII, 8). Those, therefore, who are illegitimate are without discipline and do not obtain the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven; but if they are sons, they endure the corrections of paternal discipline and should not despair of someday being able to receive the inheritance. Concerning this discipline Isaiah also preaches to an undisciplined people, saying: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do well” (Isa. I, 16). And the Psalmist sings in harmony with him concerning the same thing, saying: “Turn away from evil, and do good” (Ps. XXIII, 15).

Unhappy, therefore, is the man who casts off discipline. For whoever [Col. 0880C] rends the discipline of Christ’s Church dares to do something beyond even the soldiers who crucified the Lord but did not tear his tunic. For just as the tunic covers the whole body except the head, so the whole Church is protected and adorned by discipline, except for Christ, who is the head of the Church and is not under discipline. That tunic, moreover, had been woven throughout from above, because this same discipline of the Church is bestowed from heaven by the Lord and is made complete by him. Concerning it the Lord, after he had risen from the dead and was about to ascend to the Father, spoke to his apostles, saying: “But remain here in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49). The tunic of Christ’s body, therefore, is the discipline of the Church; but whoever is outside discipline is alien to the body of Christ. Let us therefore not tear it, but cast lots to determine whose it shall be (John XIX, 24); that is, let us not dissolve anything belonging to the Lord’s commandments, but [Col. 0880D] let each person remain with the Lord in the state in which he was called.

## CHAPTER XII

The twelfth degree of abuse is a people without law. By despising the words of God and the determinations of the laws, such a people falls by various paths of error into that same snare of perdition. Under the figure of a transgressing people, the Prophet thus laments the human race concerning these paths: “But we have gone astray like sheep; each of us has turned aside into his own way” (Isa. LIII, 6). Concerning these paths Wisdom also speaks through Solomon: “Many [Col. 0881A] paths seem right to men, but their ends lead down to death” (Prov. XIV, 12).

> **Note [Col. 0881D].**  
> “Without law.” The Colbert manuscript reads: “without Christ.”

Those many paths of perdition are indeed traveled whenever the one royal road—the law of God, which turns aside neither to the right nor to the left—is abandoned through negligence. Concerning this road the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes, declares: “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV, 6). He invites all people together to this way, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI, 28); for “there is no partiality with God” (Rom. II, 11), where there is neither Jew nor Greek, male nor female, slave nor free, barbarian nor Scythian, but Christ is all and in all; for all are one [Col. 0881B] in Christ Jesus.

Since, therefore, Christ is the end of the law, those who are without law become without Christ. Consequently, a people [Col. 0882A] without law is a people without Christ. It is therefore an abuse for a people to become lawless in the age of the Gospel, when the apostles were given leave to preach among all nations; when the thunder of the Gospel resounded throughout every part of the world; when the Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness attained righteousness; when those who had been far off were brought near in the blood of Christ; when those who once were not a people are now the people of God in Christ; when it is the acceptable time, the day of salvation, and the times of refreshment in the sight of the Most High; when every nation has a witness to the resurrection; when the Lord himself bears witness, saying: “Behold, I am with you every day, even to the consummation of the world” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Let us therefore not be without Christ in this [Col. 0882B] transitory age, lest in the age to come Christ begin to be without us.

[Col. 0881]

# BOOK ON THE TWO KINDS OF MARTYRDOM, ADDRESSED TO FORTUNATUS, BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR  
(C, G, S)

[Col. 0881C]

> **Note [Col. 0881D].**  
> “That the pious desire of my Fortunatus,” etc. Although, in order to persuade readers that this book was Cyprian’s, the author mentions another book addressed to Fortunatus, the style itself nevertheless speaks against that attribution. For the ancient Fathers never used the verb *fortunare* (“to make fortunate”), lest they should appear to attribute anything to Fortune.
>
> **[Col. 0882D.]** “Those who persevered under tortures even to death.” We have already said more than enough above about the various senses in which Cyprian understands “martyrs,” especially in volume I, Epistle IX. —PAMELIUS

## I

IN MANY AND VARIOUS WAYS I give thanks, my Fortunatus, most dear to me in the Lord, to the divine kindness: both because it stirred up your piety to spur me to my duty, so that in a single little book I might furnish our fellow soldiers with material from which, with the grace of the Spirit assisting them, they might fashion defenses and weapons against the assaults of persecution; and because, when I attempted what you requested, that kindness did not disdain to be present with me, nor did it permit the labor of either of us to be fruitless—that is, it brought the pious desire of my Fortunatus to a fortunate outcome and willed that the service of its minister should become a benefit to its flock.

For you write that from that book the vigorous gained much strength and eagerness, while so much courage was added to the more timid and weak that through God’s grace we ought to promise ourselves a certain victory [Col. 0881D] even from them. I have therefore complied all the more willingly with your later letter, in which your charity asks that, since this undertaking has succeeded well under the auspices of our Lord Jesus Christ, I should add another volume on the twofold kind of martyrdom. One kind is displayed when the savagery of torturers rages; the other is indeed more hidden, but nevertheless demands a courageous spirit fortified with much armor from God. May the Spirit of Christ deign through me to bestow this gift also upon our brothers and fellow soldiers, and may he [Col. 0882C] bring what he has given to a prosperous outcome! For just as nothing is holy unless he sanctifies it, and nothing powerful unless he strengthens it, so nothing is happy or auspicious unless he makes it prosper. Assured, then, both by your prayers and by the Lord’s goodness, I shall begin.

## II

“Martyr,” as is known even to those who do not know Greek, means “witness.” Although, after the light of evangelical truth had arisen, ecclesiastical usage properly bestowed the honor of this title upon those who persevered under tortures even to death in professing the name of Jesus Christ and, as it were, sealed the Gospel instrument with their blood before unbelievers, nevertheless the whole life of the devout bears witness to God. This is not because he needs anyone’s testimony: he is in himself the fountain of eternal glory, so that no [Col. 0882D] honors paid by men can make him more honorable, nor any dishonors inflicted by mortals render him more obscure. Yet it so pleased his eternal and divine counsel that he should will his goodness, wisdom, and power to be made illustrious among men through men—just as he willed the world to be governed through angels, although he has no need of angelic ministry, and bestows upon human beings through human beings many things that he could have given directly, since whatever he wills he can accomplish by a nod, and for him to have willed is to have done.

And although, as I have said, no dishonor reaches that ineffable majesty, [Col. 0883A] Scripture nevertheless speaks as though he were honored or dishonored through us.

> **Note [Col. 0883D].**  
> “Because of a shortage of water.” Manutius and Morellius incorrectly read *taricis*. Nor does Cyprian elsewhere use this form; indeed, even the word *herus* (“master”) is unknown to him. —PAMELIUS
>
> **179.** “Or they are said to be one for this reason,” etc. This interpretation plainly agrees with Erasmus’s annotations on this passage of [Col. 0884D] John’s Epistle. Cyprian himself, however, interprets it very differently, of the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in his book *On the Unity of the Church*. So too do the other ancient writers. —PAMELIUS

For in Deuteronomy he reproaches Moses because, when the people murmured over the shortage of water at Kadesh in the wilderness of Sin, at the waters of contradiction, Moses did not sanctify him among the children of Israel. Because of this offense, neither Moses nor Aaron was permitted to enter the promised land, which they had awaited for so many years; Moses was allowed only to look upon it from afar, from the summit of the mountain.

## III

Moreover, those skilled in Hebrew letters affirm that the use of “sanctify” in the sense of “glorify” is a peculiarity of that language. Yet this can also be made clear from other passages of Scripture, if we are less inclined to trust their testimony. For in the Lord’s Prayer, “Hallowed be thy name” (Matt. [Col. 0883B] VI, 9) is said in the sense of “May thy name be glorified,” or “made illustrious.” So too Paul exhorts the Corinthians to glorify and bear God in their body.

For just as God’s name is glorified by the life of devout people, in whom he himself through his Spirit works whatever good they do, so, conversely, it is polluted and brought into disrepute by the evil deeds of those who profess themselves worshipers of God. Just as the courage of a soldier or the uprightness of a servant contributes to the glory of his commander or master, so the cowardice of the soldier or the wickedness of the servant brings disgrace upon the commander or master, because the conduct of such persons depends in large measure upon the character of those under whose authority they stand. Even if their superiors are entirely free from blame, popular opinion nevertheless commonly judges the character of masters from the behavior of their servants.

Thus here too we see divine [Col. 0883C] Scripture frequently speaking in accordance with mortal feelings. In Leviticus, for example, concerning the man who gave some of his offspring to the idol Moloch, it says: “Because he has polluted my holy name” (Lev. XX, 3). Yet what has been sanctified by men can be polluted, whereas God’s name is always glorious in itself and is contaminated only among men, just as a lying accusation does not pollute an upright man. So too in Ezekiel God cries out that his name had been polluted among the Gentiles by the impious conduct of the Israelites. Indeed, the most blessed Paul, writing to the Romans, speaks on the Prophet’s authority and says, addressing Jews who profess the law while doing what the law forbids: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles” (Rom. II, 24).

And in the Lord’s Prayer, as I mentioned just now, we pray on the Redeemer’s authority that [Col. 0883D] the name of God the Father may be sanctified—that is, that it may become famous and illustrious among men, certainly through men, or rather in men. It is made illustrious if his Spirit reigns in us and if his will is obeyed on earth, just as there is no rebellion in heaven. But since human beings possess no virtue from themselves, whatever is rightly done through us redounds to God’s glory. For this reason the treasure of divine power sometimes shines forth from earthen [Col. 0884A] vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us.

## IV

Therefore, although the whole life of the devout glorifies God and Christ his Son through its martyrdom—that is, its witness—there is nevertheless no testimony more illustrious among men than the testimony of blood, that is, of a life held in contempt for God’s sake and a death courageously endured.
