Miracles too bore witness to divine power, especially before unbelievers, for signs were properly given for these, as the blessed Apostle writes; yet the testimony of blood poured out has always been more effective.

How many incurable diseases had the Lord healed by a word! How many blind people had he given sight! How many maimed, paralyzed, and infirm people had he restored! How many lifeless bodies had he recalled to life! Yet few believed in him, and he heard it said: “He casts out demons [Col. 0884B] by Beelzebub” (Luke XI, 15). But when it came to blood, there Satan’s kingdom was cast down, there the world was subdued.

John the Evangelist also records a threefold testimony on earth—the Spirit, the water, and the blood—mentioning the most effective of these last. John the Baptist was privileged to see the Spirit descending upon Jesus in the form of a dove; whether others saw it is uncertain. Certainly this testimony was given to John so that he might cease to doubt whether the Lord Jesus was the one who would baptize with the Spirit and with fire. John the Evangelist saw the testimony of the water, though it is not sufficiently clear whether he alone saw it or saw it together with many others. This was indeed a mighty mystery of the sacred washing by which sins are blotted out; yet he saw the water flow forth together with the blood, without which the water would have been ineffective. For what advantage is there in having sins abolished unless they are succeeded by the life of righteousness conferred by the blood?

[Col. 0884C] Nevertheless, these three are one: for there is one God who through the Spirit, the water, and the blood reveals his power and goodness to the human race. Or they are said to be one because the testimony agrees with itself from every side and is discordant in no respect—just as those joined by the closest friendship are said, because of the supreme agreement of their minds, to be one soul.

## V

According to a more literal understanding, these three are also the principal signs and even instruments of life in a human being. For so long as breath is alternately drawn in and given out again through the operation of the lungs, it is a sure indication of life. Hence, in customary speech, those who live are said to “breathe” (*spirare*), while those who have ended their life are said to have “breathed out” (*expirasse*). Indeed, [Col. 0884D] the soul in Latin is called *anima*, “breath,” in imitation of the Greek word, for the Greeks call wind ἄνεμος (*anemos*).

Furthermore, within the human being himself are very subtle spirits, dispersed throughout the entire body from the heart, where they have their source, but traveling chiefly through the arteries, although they are mingled with all the other parts as well. If these suddenly fly out, they bring immediate death; if they are shut in, they consume the person through a lingering illness. There is also [Col. 0885A] a certain natural fluid, which I think physicians call phlegm, likewise dispersed throughout the whole body. We never perceive its use more clearly than in the sense of taste, for unless it is interposed between the tongue and the palate, the palate will have no power of judgment.

Yet these things are so intermingled in a human being that there is no blood without spirit and phlegm, and all contribute equally to sustaining life. We see every animal die as soon as its blood has flowed out; and when the fluid that physicians call “radical moisture” has been consumed, a human being dies just as a lamp goes out when its oil has been exhausted.

But we are lingering too long in contemplation of nature. Nevertheless, I think this has not been done uselessly by us, since it makes clearer to your charity the mystery upon whose contemplation we dwell all the more willingly because it is more salutary. [Col. 0885B] For according to the consideration of nature, these things possess great power when they perform their functions in a living body; but according to mystical philosophy, they possess their greatest power only when they leave the body.

## VI

No one marveled at the Lord when he breathed in and out in the human manner. But when, upon the cross, he sent forth his spirit with a loud cry, it was understood at once that he had been both true man and true God: man, because in accordance with the order of nature, after sending forth the breath of life, he ceased to live; God, because he died together with a mighty cry, thereby declaring that he laid down his life willingly and of his own accord—something that everyone knows lies beyond human strength.

The centurion nearby perceived the effective testimony of the spirit; for the blessed Mark relates it in these words: “When the centurion [Col. 0885C] who stood opposite saw that he had breathed his last in this manner, he said, ‘Truly this man was the Son of God’” (Mark XV, 39). What is more abject than death according to the flesh? Yet nothing is more powerful than death according to the spirit.

It was also contrary to the course of nature that blood and water flowed from the side of a lifeless body, so that the threefold testimony might be completed. He poured out his whole spirit so that we might breathe again. He pressed out whatever watery moisture remained so that we might be washed. He sent forth whatever blood had settled in the heart so that we might be strengthened.

And I hardly know whether I am acting wrongly by comparing these three with one another, since they are one—not by nature, but in mystery. Yet if there is any distinction among them, blood is especially celebrated as testimony, because Scripture testifies that the life of an animate creature is in the blood, and for that reason blood was excluded from food by decree of the law. [Col. 0885D] Moreover, blood is more exposed to human sight than either spirit or water.

> **Note [Col. 0885D].**  
> “The life of the Lord, who was the supreme martyr.” I do not think that Christ is called a martyr among the ancient writers. —PAMELIUS
>
> “Satan claimed a right over us.” Through a printer’s negligence, Manutius’s edition read “judged” instead of “claimed.” —PAMELIUS
>
> “Behold him who takes away the sin of the world.” The Lyons edition and Manutius read “sins,” but both [Col. 0886D] Froben editions and that of Gravius have “sin.” That this is the genuine reading is clear from the author’s interpretation, which is the same as that given by Erasmus in his *Annotations on John*; this provides further confirmation for H. Gravius’s conjecture. —PAMELIUS

## VII

The life of the Lord—who was the supreme martyr, and who even today fights and conquers in very many martyrs—was a cause of offense. I am no longer speaking of the Pharisees and scribes: even to his own relatives and brothers he was detestable, since they said that he had gone mad. But his death was marvelous not only to the devout but even to the impious, and [Col. 0886A] nowhere was it more true that God’s power is perfected in weakness (II Cor. XII, 9). There Satan’s tyranny was broken; there the infernal powers were defeated; there the devil was triumphed over; there hell was cast down and heaven opened.

This, surely, was what the Lord prayed for as the hour of death approached: “Father, glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee” (John XVII, 1). What is more contemptible than a dead man? For who would fear even Caesar once he was dead? Yet what is more effective than Christ’s death? The veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom; the earth was shaken; rocks were split; tombs were opened; the bodies of the buried came back to life; the sun covered its face at midday (Matt. XXVII). Never throughout his whole life did he reveal his power more fully. Soon, after breaking through all the barriers of death, he [Col. 0886B] presented himself alive to his disciples.

This, surely, is that effective testimony of the most sacred blood, which alone could demolish the wall separating God from the human race; which alone could, with a single erasure, cancel that entire bond that stood against us and by which Satan claimed a right over us. For the blood of goats or calves could not abolish sin; those were shadows and types of things to come. Nor could any human being’s blood take away the sin of the world except the blood of that unique Lamb to whom the Baptist bore witness, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29).

## VIII

It is a greater thing to take away “sin” than “sins,” and the sin not merely of this person or that one, but of the world. For the body of sin had occupied the whole world. Christ’s blood, poured out for us, bears evident witness that this body has been taken away through [Col. 0886C] Christ, speaking better things for us, as the Apostle says, than the blood of Abel. Abel’s blood, crying out from the earth, spoke of vengeance; but Christ’s blood, crying from the cross, speaks peace and reconciliation.

Indeed, because that same blood is drunk by us—provided it is drunk worthily—it cries out within our hearts words full of peace and consolation. There too is a threefold testimony, though in a certain spiritual manner. The Spirit, who has been given to us as a pledge, cries out, “Abba, Father,” bearing witness that we are children of God (Rom. VIII, 16). The water through which we have been reborn cries out that all our sins have been forgiven us. And if anyone still doubts, there is added the testimony of the blood, crying out: “Why do you still hesitate? Why do you still fear the tyrant [Col. 0886D] Satan? Behold the price by which the Son of God redeemed you. If God had not willed you to be saved, he would not have delivered his Only-Begotten Son to death.”

## IX

“No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). If there is no greater testimony of extraordinary goodwill than for someone to bestow his life upon a friend, more weighty still is the testimony of the Lord’s blood, which was poured out for enemies. [Col. 0887A] Poured out for enemies, it made them friends and children of God. And so that we might understand that this friendship would be perpetual, he left us his flesh to eat and his blood to drink, so that we might be nourished by the very things through which we were redeemed.

> **Note [Col. 0887D].**  
> “More or less two hundred and forty years have passed.” The author added this so that the work might be thought ancient, but he contradicts himself in this very sentence when he says that already at that time the faith had spread more widely than the Roman Empire. For it is not sufficiently established that this was true before the time of the emperor Constantine. —PAMELIUS
>
> **[Col. 0888D.]** “We act in his place.” The author again added this so that he might be thought a bishop. —PAMELIUS
>
> “When that blood of Christ was still fresh,” etc. This too belongs to the imposture. Nor does Cyprian anywhere call bad shepherds “wolves,” but applies the term, in accordance with Scripture, only to heretics. —PAMELIUS

The Old Testament was confirmed by the sprinkling of blood, as the most blessed Paul splendidly teaches in writing to the Hebrews. The New Testament was signed and strengthened by Christ’s blood—that is, the testament and covenant of grace and the forgiveness of sins—through the blood of the spotless Lamb, who deigned to take upon himself the sin of the whole world: the sin that all who come into this life contract from Adam, and by whose infection all who sin commit their sins.

Yet Christ’s sublimity is so great that perhaps no other [Col. 0887B] human being ought to be compared with him, had he himself not granted us such great confidence by not disdaining to call his disciples friends, and his servants brothers and fellow heirs. Therefore, just as he by his marvelous testimony glorified the Father in this world and also in heaven, so his testimony is in a certain sense completed by the testimony of the saints, as though the Lord and his servants shared one passion.

Lest anyone think that this has been said with insufficient reverence, the blessed Paul speaks in our defense when he writes thus to the Colossians: “I now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my flesh I complete what is lacking in Christ’s sufferings for the sake of his body, which is the Church” (Col. I, 24). For who does not know, brothers, what an abundant harvest the field of the Church has yielded, watered by the blood of the apostles and the other martyrs? [Col. 0887C] The more blood was poured out, the more luxuriantly the multitude of believers blossomed; the more widely that blessed vine, springing from Christ as its root, spread its branches and occupied the whole world, wherever it extends from East to West and from North to South.

## X

Behold, most beloved brothers, more or less two hundred and forty years have passed since the days of the Lord our Redeemer; and already the branches of this vine have spread almost more widely than the Roman Empire, intoxicating even savage nations with the new wine of the Spirit. Those whom no force of iron could subdue are softened by the blood of that white Lamb.

Those who investigate the causes of nature report that a diamond, which yields to no hardness of steel, will, when [Col. 0887D] soaked in goat’s blood, shatter under blows of the hammer. But no diamond is harder than the stony heart of sinners. This iron heart, therefore—this stony heart, this heart harder than diamond—is softened by the blood of Christ and by that of his martyrs, who supplied what was lacking in his sufferings.

By this proof that supreme Shepherd—and, as Peter says, Prince of Shepherds—testified that he was the good shepherd, because he laid down his life for the sheep, providing us [Col. 0888A] an example so that we too, who in our own poor measure act in his place, may be prepared to shed our blood for the Lord’s flock, unless we prefer to appear hirelings rather than shepherds.

The words of the disciple accord with the Lord’s words. For after Paul said that he rejoiced in the sufferings by which he completed Christ’s sufferings, himself enduring for Christ’s body, the Church, sufferings like those the Lord had endured, he added the reason why he willingly suffered them: “Of which,” he says, “I was made a minister according to the stewardship of God that was given to me for you, that I might fulfill the word of God” (Col. I, 25). And elsewhere he writes that he has fulfilled the Gospel. Therefore, just as Christ’s sufferings are completed by the deaths of the martyrs, so Christ’s promises are confirmed by the blood of shepherds. [Col. 0888B] For no instrument is more indubitable than one signed with the blood of so many martyrs. This, surely, is what it means to fulfill the word of God; this is what it means to fulfill the Gospel.

## XI

But meanwhile a most grievous sorrow arises in my soul, beloved, when I reflect that, although that blood of Christ is still fresh and ought to be fervent in the hearts of the faithful, there are so many in whom charity has grown cold. I am tortured all the more severely because the Church has not a few such shepherds, who not only fail to interpose their own bodies against the assaults of the wolves, but themselves behave as wolves, slaughtering and destroying the souls of the simple while serving their own belly, profit, and ambition.

So far are they from fulfilling the word of God that they instead [Col. 0888C] hawk it for profit and adulterate it with impious teachings. Nor do they consider that the Prince of Shepherds, in his most severe judgment, will demand from their hands every single sheep for whose redemption he poured out his blood. But their punishment awaits them. For now, it is better that we set aside our complaints and exhort one another to the duty that we owe to Christ.

## XII

We have received a threefold testimony from Christ; we must render him a threefold testimony in return. Let us faithfully hand on the elementary teachings to those preparing for baptism, and the more perfect teachings to those who have been baptized. Let us strengthen them with the fruits of the Spirit, summoning them to heavenly life; and if circumstances demand it, let us willingly expend even our life for the flock entrusted to us, and in turn glorify God by our death.

And lest it appear strange to anyone that God should be glorified by the death of human beings, hear the blessed John speaking in the Gospel concerning Peter. The Lord had [Col. 0888D] foretold to him that, when he had grown old, another would gird him and lead him where he did not wish to go; John says: “signifying by what death he was to glorify God.” Therefore, all who since the foundation of the world have died for God, for righteousness, and for piety have glorified God by their death.

For even hypocrites feign almsgiving, fasting, prayers, and other exercises of piety; but no one has willingly and eagerly accepted death unless he was [Col. 0889A] firmly persuaded that nothing adverse could happen to those who persevere in the love of God.

> **Note [Col. 0889D].**  
> “It is not the punishment that makes the martyr, but the cause.” The author indeed took this from St. Cyprian, but what Cyprian said against heretics, this author applies against those who inflict death upon themselves and against sorcerers brought forward for punishment. —PAMELIUS
>
> “They do not threaten the tyrant.” That this is not universally true is evident even from Prudentius alone, where the [Col. 0890D] martyrs Lawrence and Romanus do the opposite. Indeed, not even the Maccabees will be martyrs if this author is to be believed. This passage must therefore be read cautiously, lest it appear to favor the pseudo-martyrs of our own age. —PAMELIUS
>
> “Not all martyrs now have equal eagerness under torture.” Morellius and Manutius read “martyrdom,” but this does not please me. —PAMELIUS

## XIII

Yet someone is not immediately a martyr merely because he is killed: assassins and pirates are killed too. It is not the punishment that makes the martyr, but the cause. If some are read of as having courageously inflicted death upon themselves, that was either weakness seeking through death an end to pain, or ambition, or madness. Nor is it bearing witness to God to do what is both displeasing to God and forbidden even by the laws of the nations.

There is the greatest possible difference between barbarous savagery and the most modest constancy of the martyrs—weak in itself, strong in Christ. Some people employ particular arts to numb the body so that they may not feel tortures; in this way sorcerers fortify themselves against the executioners’ hands. There are also violent passions that [Col. 0889B] deprive the mind of sensation, so that people endure even death without fear. But that peaceful and gentle quality, that which is humbly exalted and exaltedly humble, we see only in Christ’s martyrs.

They do not stare at the executioner with savage eyes; they do not threaten the tyrant. They grieve more over their tormentors’ blindness than over their own afflictions. Christ himself, surely, cries out in them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). They look to nothing but heaven, where all their hope has been stored up.

Thus the Lord himself was led like a voiceless lamb to slaughter. If he uttered any words, they revealed a gentle and peaceful spirit more fully than any silence could have done. With what gentle speech he addresses Judas the traitor! How calmly he answers after being struck with a slap! How entirely without savagery he speaks to Annas [Col. 0889C] and Caiaphas! How tranquilly he answers Pilate! Finally, when the Pharisees, as though victorious, shook their heads and raged against him with the bitterest insults, he cried out in the utmost gentleness: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

## XIV

To die, therefore, is not in itself testimony; but to die in this manner is to bear witness to God. Stephen, a young man among murderers, a lamb among wolves, stood with a peaceful, angelic face and, after the Lord’s example, prayed for those who stoned him, keeping his eyes nowhere but on heaven. There he was privileged to see the one by whose protection he was stronger than his persecutors.

The man who fears God does not fear human savagery. The man who sincerely loves heavenly life readily holds his earthly life cheap; and for him, with the blessed Paul, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21). Is it not an immense gain to exchange this life, both brief and defiled by innumerable evils, for eternal happiness?

Here the Lord, as in all other things, presented himself to us as a model. When the final act of his martyrdom approached—the act that, as they say in stories, ought to be the best—he withdrew, cast himself upon the ground, and prayed at length and repeatedly. [Col. 0890A] Soaked in bloody sweat, he expressed in himself the weakness of our nature, having first testified to weariness and sorrow of spirit even unto death, lest we fall into despair if, when everything threatens immediate death, we experience nature’s horror.

For if there were no sensation of pain, martyrdom would possess nothing marvelous; but to overcome pain is worthy of a crown. To dread death belongs to nature; to conquer nature by courage of spirit belongs to grace. Paul can do all things, but only in the one who strengthens him.

By what defenses, then, is the weakness of nature conquered? If we cast ourselves wholly upon the ground—that is, if we attribute absolutely nothing to our own strength; if we remain watchful and pray earnestly; if we submit our will to the divine will and speak these words sincerely, from our whole heart: [Col. 0890B] “Let this cup pass from me, if it is possible; nevertheless, let it be done not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. XXVI, 39).

## XV

I have known and wept over certain men endowed with great courage who, when already near the crown, failed and denied the one whom they had long professed. What caused this? They had turned their eyes away from him who alone gives strength to the weak; they had ceased praying and begun to look toward human defenses.

They contemplated the fetters of their own nature; they considered the goads, claws, red-hot plates, iron, fire, and the rest of the apparatus of the torture chamber, dreadful even to behold. They compared the atrocity of the torments with their own strength, and therefore lost victory from their hands. Whenever someone thinks in this way—“I can endure this, but I cannot endure that”—he will never bring his martyrdom to a successful completion.

But [Col. 0890C] the person who surrenders himself entirely to the divine will, looking nowhere but to God’s aid, is at last steadfast and unconquered. This cannot happen unless true and living faith is present, neither hesitating nor prying into questions. Do not consider how great the tyrant’s savagery is or how great human weakness is, but how great the Lord’s power is—the Lord who fights and conquers in his members.

## XVI

Therefore, to turn back from our digression to the point proposed: just as the Lord’s death was more powerful than his life, so he willed the death of his martyrs to be powerful. For what is weaker than to be bound, condemned, beaten, tortured, killed, and to surrender one’s body to the executioner’s will? This spectacle sometimes moves even the most savage tyrants to pity.

But when [Col. 0890D] diseases are driven away at the martyrs’ tombs, demons roar, monarchs are terrified, miracles flash forth, and idols fall, then it becomes apparent how effective and powerful the martyrs’ blood is. “His bodily presence is weak, but his letters are weighty” (II Cor. X, 10), the most blessed Teacher of the Gentiles once heard. This may rightly be applied to the martyrs as well: their life is weak and despised, but their death is weighty and powerful.

Not all martyrs now have equal eagerness under [Col. 0891A] torture—

> **Note [Col. 0891D].**  
> “As human history indeed records.” This phrase too was unknown to the ancient writers, who spoke not of “human” but of “ecclesiastical” histories. —PAMELIUS
>
> “Of Diocletian.” Morellius conjectures that “of Valerian” should be read. Yet even if this correction is made, there are many other things proving [Col. 0892D] that the work is not Cyprian’s. Nor does Cyprian anywhere speak of this second kind of martyrdom. —PAMELIUS
>
> “The apostle Paul wrote to the Galatians.” Manutius correctly reads “Galatians” here instead of “Corinthians.” —PAMELIUS
cheerfulness under torture, just as not all meet their end by the same kind of death. Those three blessed youths found refreshment amid the flames, and the seven sang a hymn to the Lord in the harmless element as though in a chamber. Daniel likewise suffered no harm while enjoying the company of lions. Blessed Andrew, according to secular history—though history of sufficiently well-established credibility—went to the cross rejoicing and congratulating himself. Others die only gradually, amid prolonged and varied tortures, yet are not permitted to end their pain by death. It therefore belongs to the true martyr to commit this entire matter also to God’s decision. He knows what is expedient for us and what is most conducive to his own glory. Only this must continually be kept in mind: “Whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. 14:8). And no one should be displeased with himself if he feels severe and prolonged distress alike in body and in [Col. 0891B] mind, provided that he trusts in the one for whom he contends. He will not allow anyone to be tempted beyond what he is able to bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out (1 Cor. 10:13). Sometimes he permits certain of his elect to falter under torture, so that they may recognize their own weakness; afterward he makes those same persons exceedingly brave in the contest. By this dispensation Peter denied the Lord three times, so that, having learned how powerless he was in his own strength, he might strengthen his brethren. But how was he to strengthen them? By teaching them to distrust themselves and place all their confidence in the Lord.

### XVII

But now it is time for us to discuss with your Charity the second kind of martyrdom. This requires even more careful treatment, because it is hidden and common to every age. For [Col. 0891C] Neroes, Diocletians, Deciuses, and Maximins do not always rage, yet the devil never ceases to put those who have professed service in Christ’s army through their exercises. And perhaps, by Christ’s gift, times will come hereafter in which no persecutions by tyrants will afflict the Church; yet there will never cease to be contests, never cease to be martyrdoms by which devout people glorify God. The Church, indeed, while still militant in this exile, applauds with particular rejoicing those who faithfully laid down their lives in confessing the name of Jesus, and people hasten to their memorials with great eagerness. But the heavenly theater—the myriads of angels and the innumerable multitude of the just who reign with Christ—applauds all those who bear witness, by the integrity and innocence of their lives, to the sincere faith and unconquered charity that they have toward the Lord Jesus.

[Col. 0891D]

### XVIII

God is glorified not only by the profession of faith, which, according to Paul, is made with the mouth unto salvation, but also by the confession of sins committed. Lest we appear to be saying this rashly on our own authority, testimonies from Scripture must be adduced. Therefore, if the life of the devout did not redound to God’s glory, Christ would not say in the Gospel: “That they may see your good works and glorify your Father [Col. 0892A] who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16); nor would Paul the Apostle write to the Galatians: “And they glorified God in me” (Gal. 1:24). This is also confirmed by the contrary, on the basis of what we have said. For if the name of God is polluted and dishonored by the impious life of his people, then surely it is honored by their good life. The Apostle also condemns the impious wisdom of the philosophers who, although they had known God, nevertheless did not glorify him as God (Rom. 1:21). They professed wisdom and displayed consummate folly. Thus, although they professed that God existed, nevertheless, by living shamefully and sacrificing to idols, they obscured God’s glory as though by false testimony—as though he were neither just nor truthful, or as though he were not one but many, or as though he resembled stones. The most blessed Paul bears even clearer witness to this when writing to the Corinthians: “You were bought,” he says, “at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). God therefore redeemed us at the price of his own blood so that, once cleansed from sins, we might thereafter lead a life worthy of him.

### XIX

And we bear the emperor’s emblem stamped upon our foreheads. What if someone who bears the sign of Christ performs the works of Belial? Is not the one whose insignia we bear dishonored? Conversely, just as an emperor takes satisfaction in a highly energetic soldier, judging that soldier’s courage to be an honor and adornment to himself, so God glories in those whom he has redeemed, washed, and sanctified, and whom he has deemed worthy of the Spirit’s donative, if by holiness of life they demonstrate that the Lord’s grace in them has not been empty. If Paul glories in the devotion of his disciples, [Col. 0892C] calling them his joy and crown, although he was nothing but a steward of another’s gift, does not the Lord glory still more in those for whom he died? Again, when the Lord speaks to Satan in this manner in the book of Job—“Have you considered my servant Job, how there is none like him upon the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and withdrawing from evil?” (Job 1:8)—does he not speak like one glorying in his worshiper? Blessed Paul, however, used an even more splendid expression [Col. 0892B] when writing the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of the knowledge of himself; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:4). “A good name is better than precious ointments” (Ecclus. 7:2). Scripture is accustomed to call a glorious reputation [Col. 0892D] a fragrance. God, however, does not glory in the human manner, taking complacent and excited pleasure in himself; rather, he regards our salvation as his glory. The Apostle therefore added: “Among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing.” How is God glorified among those who are being saved? Because his mercy is made illustrious. How among those who are perishing? Because his justice is manifested in them.

[Col. 0893A]

> **Note [Col. 0893D]**
>
> **Achan.** Morelius has *Achar*. So also the Septuagint; but this version is a mixture of Jerome’s Vulgate edition and the Septuagint. What is remarkable, however, is that the author seems to make the repentance of the fallen into a kind of martyrdom. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **Kata Lucam.** Manutius, both here and below, substituted *secundum* (“according to”). But because the former expression is Cyprianic, I think the author deliberately wrote it in that form. The interpretation of this passage, however, is also contrary to the opinion of the ancients. **PAMELIUS.** [Col. 0894D]

### XX

The course of the discourse itself has now led us to teach that God is also glorified by the confession of sins. Here Achan immediately presents himself from the book of Joshua. Because, contrary to the divine edict, he had taken from what was under the ban a distinguished scarlet cloak, two hundred shekels of silver, and a golden bar weighing fifty shekels, the people of Israel turned their backs upon their enemies. Joshua therefore said to Achan: “My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel, and confess and tell me what you have done; do not conceal it” (Josh. 7:19). He confessed, suffered punishment, and the Lord’s wrath was turned away. That confession made God’s justice and wisdom illustrious: his wisdom, because nothing was hidden from his eyes; his justice, because he had not without cause allowed the enemy to prevail against Israel, and because no human being violates his laws [Col. 0893B] with impunity. What Achan had stolen was not of great value; nevertheless, it was a great lesson to the entire people concerning how dangerous it is to neglect God’s commands and to attempt to deceive him, as though anything could escape his notice or as though he favored transgressors. And although that man was a Jew, for a single sin that seemed trivial to him he paid the severest penalty: he was stoned by the entire people, redeeming the salvation of his soul by the destruction of his body. For God does not judge twice for the same offense.

### XXI

But what punishment awaits those who, after so great a light and grace of the Gospel—after once being enlightened, tasting the heavenly gift, becoming participants in the Holy Spirit, and likewise tasting the good word of God and the powers of the age to come—relapse into many monstrous crimes, crucifying [Col. 0893C] the Son of God again for themselves and exposing him to public shame? They are all the more pitiable because, although they are such people, they nevertheless spurn the remedy of saving repentance and despise the Church as she offers her maternal bosom and invites them to restoration of health. How great a disgrace do you think such a defection brands upon the Church? Nor can that disgrace fail to touch Christ, who is the head of the Church and regards as entirely his own whatever belongs to his body and its members. Conversely, how great is the exultation of the whole Church when one who has fallen is reconciled to the Church through repentance! And lest we suppose that this joy exists only among us, let us hear the Lord speaking in the Gospel κατὰ Lucam (“according to Luke”): “Thus I say to you that there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-[Col. 0893D]nine just persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:9). For this concluding clause ends the parable of the shepherd who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep, sought with great labor the one that had wandered from the flock, and at last, when he had found it, placed it upon his shoulders and restored it to the fold. With a similar statement he closes the parable of the woman who found the lost drachma: “Thus, I say to you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner [Col. 0894A] who repents” (*ibid.*). Yet this must not be understood as though it were more pleasing to God and his angels to return to devotion after a fall than to persevere in innocence without falling. Rather, Scripture speaks in its customary manner, in accordance with human affections, intending to attest that the conversion of sinners is most pleasing to God: “For he does not seek the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live” (Ezek. 18:32).

### XXII

And sometimes the falls of devout people, although enormous, are turned by divine dispensation to the greatest advancement of the Church. Thus fell the prince of the apostles; thus Paul, teacher of the Gentiles; thus Mary Magdalene—those in whom the Church now especially glories, and whose falls redounded to the strengthening and consolation of the house of God. Moreover, he is not speaking here of those who are truly just, [Col. 0894B] but of Pharisaic righteousness, just as he says elsewhere: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12). Yet those to whom the Lord said this were not well; rather, puffed up by some manner of observance of the Law, they thought themselves well and therefore did not desire a physician.

### XXIII

Since matters stand thus, beloved brother, let us strive by continual exhortations to stir the souls of the faithful, so that their entire life may render martyrdom—that is, testimony—to God. This testimony is so far from being negligible that, unless it has gone before, the martyrdom borne by blood is not martyrdom. For you will have offered your neck to the executioner in vain unless you have first put to death the members that are upon the earth—that is, the affections that wage war against the spirit: hatred, envy, greed, and lust. Whoever serves these has in a certain manner denied [Col. 0894C] God and, while professing Christ with his mouth, confesses Satan as god by his life. Nor should this discourse appear excessively harsh to anyone, since it is truthful and conducive to salvation. Whatever any human being places before God, he makes into a god for himself; nor can we serve two masters, for there is one God, who must be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one’s strength.

### XXIV

Therefore, whoever says with his mouth, “I believe in one God,” yet serves greed, lust, or luxury, lies to himself and contradicts himself, sounding one thing with his tongue while concealing another in his mind. He bears witness to God with his voice alone, while worshiping Satan by his life. The testimony of life, however, is more effective than that of the tongue: “Not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom, but he who does the will [Col. 0894D] of the heavenly Father” (Matt. 7:21). Works too have their own eloquent language, even when the tongue is silent. Therefore the Lord speaks thus in the Gospel κατὰ Joannem (“according to John”): “The works that the Father gave me to accomplish, those very works that I do bear witness concerning me” (John 5:36). Therefore, just as good works profess God, so evil works in a certain manner say: “There is no God, nor any knowledge in the Most High.” Who would not tremble, [Col. 0895A] who would not shudder, who would not tear his garments, who would not stop his ears if he heard such words from a Christian?

> **Note [Col. 0895D]**
>
> **Moreover, drunkenness is so common in Africa, etc.** What he said first about bishops he takes from Cyprian’s book *On the Lapsed*; this, however, he takes from St. Augustine’s *Letter to Auxilius*, so that he may be thought an African. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **Prisons, chains, hooks.** This is unquestionably the correct reading. **PAMELIUS.** [Col. 0896D]

How great a horror and how great a grief seize our minds when someone, overcome by torture and ordered to deny Christ, does deny him and burns incense before the statue of Jupiter! How we tremble, fearing that God in his anger may hurl against us the thunderbolt of his wrath, or that the earth may open and swallow us—since sometimes the impiety of one person involves many others in a common punishment. And there are crimes so monstrous that even to have seen or heard them is detestable. But why, at other times, do we shut our eyes to an equivalent crime? Why do we flatter both ourselves and others so greatly? See what the Apostle says about such people when writing to Titus: “They profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16). The same Apostle, in his First Epistle to Timothy, says of the widow who neglects her family: “But if anyone [Col. 0895B] does not take care of her own, especially those of her household, she has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8). If a woman who is somewhat negligent in caring for her family has denied the faith, what do you think he would say of those who have surrendered themselves entirely to Mammon and the belly? Paul is certainly speaking about Christians when he says in writing to the Philippians: “Their end is destruction; their god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19). He censures the same people when writing to the Romans: “People of this kind do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly” (Rom. 16:18). In accordance with Scriptural usage, he said “serve” in the sense of “worship.” They worship their belly, which they take for their god. Concerning greed, he makes an even more explicit pronouncement when writing to the Colossians: “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, [Col. 0895C] and greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5).

### XXV

We execrate those who prostrate themselves before the image of Diana. How much more justly do we execrate those who serve Mammon with their whole heart and sacrifice to him every day? And if the greedy person is an idolater who is held fast by zeal for money—who stores away what has come to him by inheritance or been acquired by his own labor and does not distribute it to the needy—what must be judged concerning those who amass wealth by pimping, usury, plunder, fraud, false accusations, and the oppression of the poor? And this service of idols is found not only among Christians but even—lamentably—among bishops. Moreover, drunkenness is so common in our Africa that people almost do not regard it as a crime. Do we not see [Col. 0895D] one Christian compelling another Christian to drunkenness at the memorials of the martyrs? Do we consider this a lighter crime than sacrificing a goat to Bacchus? It seems to me much graver, if we wish to weigh the matter by right reason.

When a tyrant says, “Deny Christ, sacrifice to Jupiter, and become our friend—or die,” often the tongue denies while the heart protests, and the hand burns incense while the mind inwardly worships Christ. Although this too is a most grievous crime, the weakness of human nature nevertheless mitigates some part of the guilt of impiety. There Satan speaks to you [Col. 0896A] through the tyrant’s voice. But what does he say to you through your own desire? “Deny Christ and be rich; sacrifice to Mammon and give Christ your notice of departure.” What does he promise? Gold and silver, useless matter unless you put it to use. Nor does he say, “Die,” but, “Delight your eyes.” Indeed, he says rather: “Gain money, which you will possess for a short time; lose your soul forever.” And yet here you voluntarily bend your knees to Satan and, having denied Christ, surrender yourself entirely into his bondage.

But what does Christ say? “Be mine and live forever. Despise those temporary riches, and I shall repay you a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the age to come. Leave earth and receive heaven.” Yet God, who promises these things, is deserted, while the devil, falsely promising things of so little worth, is worshiped. O foul [Col. 0896B] defection! O shameful idolatry! O unjust exchange! With what reward did he entice the first parents of the human race? He displayed an apple and gave death. He deceived them with a lie: “You shall not die, but shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:4–5). And when they had been deceived, what sort of master did they desert, and to whom did they defect? From what happiness did they fall, and into what miseries did they cast themselves?

But that same prince of darkness who spoke to Eve through the serpent speaks to us through his attendants and ministers: through procuresses and pimps, through those who entice us to the love of money, ambition, and pleasure, drawing us away from the sincerity that is in Christ Jesus. The same one speaks to us through our desires, which live in our members. Nor does he say what a human tyrant says: [Col. 0896C] “Either obey me or die.” He does not display prisons, chains, hooks, frying pans, or blazing furnaces, nor crosses, nooses, or swords. He merely says: “Despise God, renounce the inheritance of heavenly life, commit adultery, and you will obtain pleasure.” But what kind of pleasure? Momentary, belonging only to the body—and seasoned with how many bitter things? Disgrace, danger, and, above all, the hidden torment of conscience. This is the devil’s bait; this is his enlistment bounty. And what is the pay? Let the blessed Apostle declare it with greater trustworthiness: “The wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23). What death? The death of the body, which alone the human tyrant threatens and is able to inflict? No, but the death of Gehenna, which knows no end.

A human tyrant has more power than the devil. The former in some manner compels human nature; the latter can do nothing [Col. 0896D] but entice. He cannot cast you down unless you consent: to despise him is to conquer him.

### XXVI

Greater pardon is therefore owed to one who denies Christ under torture than to one who voluntarily consents to the devil, for to believe the devil is to deny Christ. He is a liar and the father of every lie. His promises, however flattering their outward appearance, are nothing but illusions enticing people to destruction. Therefore let no one flatter himself thus: “I am a sinner; I love money, serve lust, pursue honors, indulge vengeance, [Col. 0897A] and am devoted to pleasures—but I have not denied Christ.”

> **Note [Col. 0897D]**
>
> **The name of one who offered incense or obtained a certificate.** This is again taken from St. Cyprian, who nevertheless calls the latter *libellatici*. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **So that you might have no doubt.** He insists all too frequently upon this sure confidence in God. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **The Turk.** Thus the shrew is detected by the evidence it gives against itself. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **However much you may profess Christ with your tongue and dress.** This too must be read cautiously. [Col. 0898D]
>
> **From which evil the Lord’s mercy delivered us.** He added this too so that the book might appear to be Cyprian’s, since some report—though wrongly—that Cyprian practiced the magical arts. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **Maccabees.** Manutius correctly reads *Machabaei* in place of the previous *Maccabaei*. **PAMELIUS.**

But the Lord himself answers you: “You cannot serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24). Meanwhile, you shudder at the abominable designation “incense-offerer” (*thurificatus*) or “certificate-holder” (*libellatus*), though perhaps you yourself are worse than those who offered incense or obtained certificates. They were driven by human fear—too violent for human nature to overcome—to utter impious words with the tongue while conscience protested. You, enticed by so paltry a reward, voluntarily defect to the one from whose tyranny Christ redeemed you by his blood. You have now become entirely Christ’s, as the Apostle says: “You were bought at a great price,” and, “You are no longer your own” (1 Cor. 6:20, 19). You professed service in his army at the saving bath; you enrolled your name under him; you were initiated into his mysteries; you received the donative and pledge of the Spirit, so that you might have no doubt [Col. 0897B] about the promised pay. At the same time you declared perpetual hostilities against the devil and renounced all his pomps and pleasures. You blew and hissed at him and swore allegiance to the Redeemer; yet although you serve so many vices, you are pleased with yourself because you have not yet offered incense or obtained a certificate.

### XXVII

If a soldier who had sworn allegiance to Caesar were to flee to the Turk and, at the latter’s command, do things that he knew were utterly displeasing to Caesar, would he not, when captured, be dragged away to punishment as a deserter, a perjurer, and a renegade? Who would listen to him if he defended himself thus: “I am not a deserter; I have not denied Caesar”? Would he not immediately hear: “What difference does it make that your tongue was silent? You denied him in deed—and did more than deny him, since you not only deserted his army but also fled to the tyrant and irreconcilable enemy of your emperor”? [Col. 0897C]

The ears of the faithful rightly abominate the word “apostate.” Yet apostasy is not to be execrated only where the profession of Christ’s name is renounced by burning a little incense or by means of a written certificate, but wherever Christ’s laws are despised and Satan is obeyed. It makes no difference what the tongue sounds forth. If it sounds forth Christ while the mind is devoted to crimes, this is not profession but hypocrisy—hypocrisy that would deny Christ if pressed by the fear that oppresses incense-offerers and certificate-holders.

And in matters so opposed to one another that neither admits association with the other, whenever we embrace one, we have renounced the other; whenever we reject one, we acknowledge the other. Such are light and darkness, war and peace, death and life, God and Belial, as blessed Paul also testifies in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: [Col. 0897D] “For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? And what agreement has Christ with Belial?” To adhere to Belial is to deny Christ, however much you may profess Christ with your tongue or dress.

### XXVIII

If any simpler person doubts this, I shall give a plain and evident proof. Let us imagine a tyrant [Col. 0898A] speaking thus to a Christian: “Burn incense to Jupiter,” adding nothing and not demanding that he deny Christ. If the Christian burns incense, will it not be evident to everyone that by this very act of making an offering of incense to Jupiter he has denied Christ, even though he utters nothing impious against Christ? In the same way, those who practice the magical arts—from which evil the Lord’s mercy delivered us, as from all the others by which we were once held while walking according to the old man—silently deny Christ when they enter into a compact with demons.

Again, if the Maccabean brothers together with their mother preferred to be killed by so many tortures rather than eat pork, because they judged that doing so would deny God, the author of the Law, how do those who knowingly and willingly violate the Law’s commands flatter themselves when they grow old in luxury, drunkenness, greed, robbery, [Col. 0898B] adultery, and other crimes that even the laws of the Gentiles refused to leave unpunished? Although they deny Christ in so many ways and sacrifice to demons so many times, do they demand to be regarded as Christians? Among these are some who commit such things openly and almost even glory in the vilest deeds, so little are they ashamed or grieved by what they have done! Yet they dare to enter the Church of the saints; they dare to mingle with the Lord’s flock.

The Church sometimes tolerates such people lest, if provoked, they disturb God’s people still further. But what benefit is there in not being expelled from the assembly of the devout if you have deserved expulsion? For expulsion is a remedy and a step toward recovering health; to have deserved expulsion is the greatest of evils. And one mingles in vain with the assembly of the saints in a temple made by hands if he has been removed from fellowship with God and with the whole [Col. 0898C] mystical body of Christ.

### XXIX

We must also consider how greatly Christians recoil from things sacrificed to idols, from entering pagan temples, and even from the images themselves. Although blessed Paul cries aloud that neither an idol nor food sacrificed to idols is anything, much less is a temple built from stones anything. Nevertheless, the minds of very many are held by such religious scruple that they would sooner meet death than taste what has been sacrificed to idols, and they regard it as an inexpiable offense to enter a temple of Jupiter, Apollo, or Diana, thinking themselves gravely contaminated by contact with an image. I indeed approve the religious scruple of such people, provided that it is consistent in all matters. But now, alas, one may see certain people almost superstitiously fearful in these matters, while in others, where there was graver cause for fear, they are excessively [Col. 0898D] unconcerned.

Contact with an idol does not of itself pollute the soul, nor does entering a pagan temple or eating something sacrificed to idols. But the love of money, incest, robbery, hypocrisy, and similar monstrosities do of themselves pollute the conscience. How fitting, then, to shudder at entering a pagan temple but not to shudder at sacrificing victims to demons in a temple consecrated to the Spirit!

[Col. 0899A]

> **Note [Col. 0899D]**
>
> **There he loves a victim to be offered to him, etc.** The author astonishingly distorts this passage of Malachi. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **Therefore let no one flatter himself in vain.** This again is borrowed word for word from Cyprian’s book *On the Lapsed*. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **The usage of the Church, indeed, etc.** We have sufficiently shown in volume I, Epistle IX, that this distinction between martyr and confessor is not Cyprianic in every respect. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **But monks above all.** Here too the disguised actor tears away his own mask, for he did not know that in Cyprian’s age monasticism had not yet been born. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **For neither a desert place.** These are plainly Erasmian words, and consequently must also be read with caution. **PAMELIUS.**

Holy Paul cries aloud in writing to the Corinthians: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:16). Again, in the same Epistle: “Do you not know that your members are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” (1 Cor. 6:19).

If God has consecrated the hearts of Christians to himself so that he may dwell in them through his Spirit, there he delights and walks; there he loves a pure victim to be offered to him in every place. Yet one who, after driving out the Holy Spirit, brings into this temple sacred to God the abominations that Ezekiel saw in his mystical vision—one who there establishes a seat for Mammon, Venus, Comus, Bacchus, and other monstrosities; one who there sacrifices the filthiest victims to demons—fears to enter [Col. 0899B] a pagan temple lest he be contaminated.

Therefore let no one flatter himself in vain: “God is not mocked” (Gal. 6). Let our religion be consistent with itself. Let us not detest others while being ourselves liable to graver crimes, nor be religiously fearful in one matter and shamelessly impious in another. Rather, having once professed Christ, let us bear witness to him by our whole life and glorify him in every respect, obeying his commands, so that by this people may know that we truly trust in him, love him sincerely, and did not hypocritically present ourselves at the sacred bath for service in his army.

### XXX

The blessed Apostle foretold that persecution would never be lacking for anyone who wished to live devoutly in Christ Jesus. If there is no tyrant, torturer, or plunderer, desire will not be lacking, daily providing us [Col. 0899C] with material for martyrdom. Finally, these very evils that mortal life brings with it, and which are common to the devout and the impious, will prepare for us the crown of martyrdom if we endure them calmly and with thanksgiving. Nor are those who were not brought to their end by violent death deprived of the glory of martyrdom. Who would dare to exclude from the number of the martyrs either the patriarch Abraham, his son Isaac, or blessed Job? What executioners’ workshops ever tortured a body more severely than natural affection tortured the Patriarch’s mind when, without hesitation and at God’s command, he prepared to sacrifice his only and uniquely beloved son, in whom rested his entire hope of posterity? What was lacking from Isaac’s martyrdom, when without murmuring he allowed himself to be bound and placed upon the funeral pyre, and did not recoil from the sword raised above his neck? With whose martyrdom, moreover, [Col. 0899D] shall we dare compare the things Job suffered?

### XXXI

And if anyone still distrusts our discourse, he certainly cannot distrust the words of blessed Paul. Writing to the Hebrews and beginning with Abel, he recounts a vast catalogue of saints down to Gideon. It includes many who did not die a violent death—indeed, [Col. 0900A] there are few who did die in that manner—yet concerning them all he pronounces: “And these were found approved through the testimony of faith” (Heb. 11:39), clearly declaring that the martyrdom of faith is also accomplished by a good life.

The usage of the Church, indeed, distinguishes them by particular names. It calls “martyrs” those who died a violent death, and “confessors” those who steadfastly professed the name of the Lord Jesus amid tortures and threats of death, prepared to meet death—or rather, eagerly seeking the supreme crown of martyrdom. Before God, however, all who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, all who have truly died with Christ and been buried with him in Baptism so that they no longer live for themselves or for the world to which they once died, but for him who died for them, are martyrs and will not be deprived of the martyrs’ crown—above all [Col. 0900B] monks who are truly monks, and virgins who are truly virgins.

For neither a desert place, sackcloth for clothing, vegetables for food, fasts, nor *chamenniae* [probably “sleeping on the ground”; reading uncertain] constitute a monk. Beneath these coverings there sometimes lies a thoroughly worldly mind. This is discovered if such persons are called to some ecclesiastical office. There you may see some of them very easily overcome by luxuries, more impatient of injuries and more eager for revenge than any ordinary member of the common people. What is the reason? Because they exercised the body more than the mind, although blessed Paul teaches that bodily exercise is profitable for a little, while devotion avails for everything (1 Tim. 4:18).

### XXXII

I would not say these things because those who chastise their bodies and reduce them to servitude [Col. 0900C] in such ways are to be condemned, but because Satan, equipped with a thousand arts, sometimes mocks the unwary, transforming himself into an angel of light. From such bodily exercises he induces in them a false conviction of holiness; and although they are inwardly saturated with spiritual vices, both they themselves and others regard them as devout. Such was the righteousness of the Pharisees, to which, by Christ’s judgment, the unrighteousness of the publican was preferred.

Thus there are also foolish virgins who suppose that solid devotion consists in keeping the body untouched by a man, although the mind is thoroughly corrupted by greed, pride, envy, and slander. There are also false widows who, while they live in pleasures, are dead to Christ. In sum, however, everyone who is truly a Christian, whatever his state or order, has his own contests and his own cross. If he takes it up patiently and bears it steadfastly, he glorifies the Lord by his testimony [Col. 0900D]—provided only that he does not claim for himself the praise of his good works, for this is not to glorify God but to glorify oneself.

### XXXIII

Each of the faithful has his own contests. He has the devil as his adversary, God as the director of the contest, and as his theater not only the Church and the angels but also unbelievers, as Paul [Col. 0901A] says to the Corinthians: “We have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9).

> **Note [Col. 0901D]**
>
> **Lower their faces.** Some read *dimittere* (“let go”), incorrectly. **PAMELIUS.**
>
> **One who, on account of a slight fever, has recourse to the remedies of enchantresses.** I do not know what remedies of enchantresses he means. Everyone knows that old women everywhere promise remedies to fever patients through magical charms and incantations. **PAMELIUS.** [Col. 0902D]
>
> **His confidence in all his happiness.** Here too the text is corruptly printed *infelicitatis* (“unhappiness”); and because a little later it had also omitted the word *es* (“you are”), this passage too must be read cautiously. **PAMELIUS.**

If we conquer, the angels glory, the churches of the faithful glory, and Christ himself glories in his members. But if we are defeated through our own sloth, Satan triumphs with his angels, unbelievers insult us, and they assail God with reproaches, saying:

“Look at those who boast that they have been redeemed from Satan’s tyranny and proclaim that they have died to the world. Nevertheless, they are overcome by their desires no less than we are, whom they say are still held under Satan’s reign. What benefit is their Baptism, by which they say that they put off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God? What benefit is the Holy Spirit, by whose direction they say they are governed? Why do they always have ‘The Gospel, the Gospel’ [Col. 0901B] upon their lips, when their entire life is at variance with the Gospel’s commands?”

With how great a shame do you think the Church is suffused when enemies hurl these accusations against her and she has no means of refuting their reproaches! Do we not see the entire assembly of the Church lower its face and blush whenever some virgin who had married Christ, slipping away from angelic fellowship, defects to fornication or marriage? How great a grief seizes all our minds, but especially those of the pastors, if ever a soldier of Christ, overcome by torture, has renounced his emperor! And how great, on the other hand, is Satan’s triumph!

### XXXIV

Therefore, dearly beloved brethren, if we truly love God, if we daily pray sincerely, “Hallowed be your name,” let us watch with the greatest zeal, not only lest we pollute his name, but also that by both death and life we may glorify [Col. 0901C] him, in accordance with blessed Paul’s admonition:

“Living without complaint as innocent children of God, blameless in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom let us shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, to the glory of Christ Jesus, our king and director of the contest, who regards as his own whatever is done in his members.”

Let us suffer with him so that we may be glorified with him on the day of the Lord. Let us glorify him here among human beings, so that he may glorify us with his glory before his angels, when, as blessed Paul says, he comes to be glorified in his saints. No one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules. Those who seek a corruptible crown abstain from everything (1 Thess. 1:9; 2 Tim. 2:5; 1 Cor. 9), leaving nothing undone that conduces to victory. What, then, is it fitting for us to do so that [Col. 0901D] we may obtain in heaven that incorruptible and unfading crown of immortal life?

### XXXV

Here, if anyone asks how a person can be a martyr without the shedding of blood: whoever pursues righteousness with such a disposition that he would sooner accept death than consent to turn aside from righteousness—his ready will shall be reckoned as martyrdom. For God judges no one by the outcome of events, but by his disposition. [Col. 0902A] For why should someone be deprived of the glory of martyrdom when it was no fault of his that he did not complete his martyrdom? Conversely, whoever lives with the disposition that he would deny Christ if he had to accept the loss of his property, bodily torture, or death will receive the reward of an apostate.

Will someone who perjures himself for a little money be afraid to deny Christ if his entire fortune is endangered, if disgrace, imprisonment, and death are threatened? Will someone who, because of a slight fever, takes refuge in the remedies of enchantresses prefer to endure tortures more bitter than death rather than renounce Christ? Indeed, will someone who so often deserts Christ for a brief little pleasure of the flesh or for momentary glory hold his life cheap for Christ? It is not the tyrant who made such a man an apostate; rather, an apostate came before the tyrant.

Now, since the manner of the contest is similar, the hearts of the brethren must be armed for these struggles [Col. 0902B] with the same weapons by which we have shown that they must be strengthened for martyrdom. It is faith that fights and conquers in the martyrs; and no one has failed under torture except through a failure of faith.

### XXXVI

God must therefore be prayed to continually, that he may increase faith in us; for it is God’s gift, and to him is owed all the glory of every victory. Let us press upon their minds and impress upon them how dreadful a crime every form of idolatry is, and how severely it was punished by God under the Old Law—how many thousands Moses slaughtered because of the golden calf.

Next, let an explicit comparison be presented between open idolatry, when sacrifice is offered to images, and hidden idolatry, when, in contempt of God, obedience is rendered through desire to Satan. Then let God, the source of every good, be compared with the devil, the prince of all wickedness. Let the inequality [Col. 0902C] of the two fellowships also be shown: on the one side are the children of God, fellow citizens of the angels, and heirs of blessed immortality; on the other are the children of Belial, the company of all the demons, and the heirs of Gehenna. Let the unequal character of their wickedness also be compared, and let their differing wages be set beside one another. If these things have first been accepted and planted deep within the heart, victory will be easy.

As things now stand, faith floats upon the lips of many, while in the heart it is either altogether absent or exceedingly feeble. For who does not profess what we read in Deuteronomy: “Hear: the Lord your God is one Lord”? And: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6). Who does not recite daily with his mouth, “I believe in God the Father Almighty”? Yet a person does not believe in God if he does not place the confidence of his entire happiness in him alone; nor does someone have one God and Lord [Col. 0902D] if through fornication, luxury, and avarice he carries out Satan’s commands; nor does someone serve him alone if he serves his belly, if he is devoted to this world, or if he is situated in wickedness.

### XXXVII

The pagans believe that there are many gods, and do you therefore consider yourself a perfect Christian merely because you are persuaded that there is one God? What great thing are you doing? The Jews, who daily blaspheme in their synagogues, [Col. 0903A] believe the same.

> **Note [Col. 0903D]**
>
> **For they themselves shall receive consolation.** This is also Erasmus’s translation. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Like pleurisy.** I prefer this reading of Morel to that of the earlier printed editions, *pleuretis*, or that of Manutius, *pleuresis*. —PAMELIUS. [Col. 0904D]

The demons also believe the same—and tremble. If you truly believe in God, believe that he is just and truthful: just in rewarding the devout and punishing the impious, truthful in his promises. Believe that there is no hope of salvation except through his Son, whom he delivered up to death for us all. Believe that no evil can befall those who have surrendered themselves wholly to his will and persevere in him.

This is to believe in God the Father; this is to believe in his Son; this is to believe in the Holy Spirit, one God, and in the holy Church, the mystical body of Christ, outside which there is no salvation and within which there is no destruction.

### XXXVIII

Whoever plants the feet of his soul upon such a rock will stand immovable against every assault of temptation. For example: you have been provoked by an insult, and the flesh suggests [Col. 0903B] to you a desire for revenge. Before you answer, think to yourself as follows: “The devil has incited this abusive man to cast me down and, when I have fallen, to destroy me. But listen to what the emperor under whom you serve advises: ‘Blessed,’ he says, ‘are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.’ And: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.’ What does that most valiant commander of Christ, Paul, advise? ‘Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath.’”

The devil says: “Enjoy revenge and lose eternal life.” God says: “Overcome evil with good, and do not resist evil; and receive, together with my Son, possession of the kingdom of heaven.” Then consider at once which of the two it is better to obey.

The devil says to you through your desire: “Commit adultery, enjoy a temporary bodily pleasure, and become my slave and fellow heir of Gehenna.” [Col. 0903C] Listen instead to what God says to you: “Despise temporary pleasure and receive a hundredfold: the joy of a good conscience in this age, and eternal life in the age to come.” Then weigh which of the two should rather be heard.

Through the inclination of the flesh, as though through Eve, Satan suggests to you: “Live pleasurably.” In opposition Christ says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they themselves shall receive consolation.”

In the same way, in all other temptations hold up against the tempter the shield of the Scriptures, in which God speaks to you with no less claim upon your faith than if he were speaking to you face to face and mouth to mouth. From these torrents take up stones with which to strike down proud Goliath. You have the example of your Lord: this is how he laid the devil low.

Do not lose heart if the devil attacks repeatedly and from time to time assails you with greater engines of war. He can do nothing against [Col. 0903D] him who is with you. Say those words of John: “Greater is he who is in us than he who is in this world.” Let this saying of the Lord come to your aid: “Take courage, for I have conquered the world.” If Christ’s soldier has been trained for conflict by these prayers, he will find his antagonist weaker day by day.

### XXXIX

Yet the watches must not be relaxed if the enemy should at some time feign tranquillity. Rather, while observing his snares, let a person say with blessed Habakkuk: “I shall stand upon my watch and plant my foot firmly upon the rock,” [Col. 0904A] guarding my heart with every vigilance, lest any entrance lie open to the one who prowls about seeking someone to devour.

The safest fortification of the heart is sobriety together with persistent prayer and continual meditation upon the Scriptures: “For every Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. 3:16).

From Scripture, therefore, sayings must be gathered that you may have close at hand and, as it were, ready for battle, so that with them you may immediately strike down the serpent when it raises its head. For there is no disease of the soul for which divine Scripture does not furnish a present remedy. From it each person should obtain examples of the devout—and above all of Christ—by which he may either take courage or be consoled.

### XL

[Col. 0904B] I now come to those evils which either accompany human nature itself or seem to befall us by chance. A devout soul trained for combat will turn these also into material for a crown.

I shall make what I mean clearer by an example. Someone is stripped of his possessions, whether by war, shipwreck, or robbery. He should not immediately contemplate a noose, or a means of replacing by evil practices what has been lost, but should speak to himself as follows:

“The Lord is testing whether I love him with all my heart. He gave; he has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

Let him give thanks for having received from the Lord’s kindness, and give thanks for having lost it as a trial of his faith. If he has said these things with the disposition with which holy Job said them, he will receive the reward together with Job. The Lord judges not how much anyone loses, but how patiently he loses it, [Col. 0904C] just as he does not regard how much anyone gives to the needy, but with what disposition he gives it.

Someone has a uniquely beloved son; premature death takes him from you. A plague strips you of those dearest to you—a spouse, children, and friends. Bear it patiently, and say: “Thus it seemed good to the Lord; and perhaps it was expedient both for us and for our loved ones. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

There are also diseases that involve tortures no less atrocious than any cruelty of torturers can inflict, such as pleurisy, sciatica, gout, paralysis, a stone, and ulceration of the kidneys and bladder. If anything of this sort should happen, let the mind not be provoked into impatience, nor the tongue burst forth into blasphemous words, but let it say with blessed David and Eli the priest: “He is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes.”

In this way we shall turn even those evils which are not inflicted because of the profession of Christ [Col. 0904D] into a crown for ourselves and glory for Christ. And perhaps it will happen that the Lord, propitiated by our endurance, will either remove our afflictions or mitigate them. But if this does not happen, we shall nevertheless ensure by this means that what would have been unbearable to an impatient spirit becomes gentler through patience.

With these and similar arguments we shall not cease to exhort one another to manifest the Lord’s glory, whose title and insignia we bear. Let each of us offer him martyrdom in his own station and rank, not only in adversity but also in prosperity.

[Col. 0905A] In adversity, let us recognize the love of a father who scourges us for correction, and let us give thanks for the charity with which he loves us as children whom he does not wish to disown, but to receive back after correcting them. In prosperity, let us likewise give thanks for his goodness, by which he consoles us so that we may bear the weight of temptations. [Col. 0906A] Thus it will come about that our whole life is nothing other than a testimony declaring, before believers and unbelievers alike, the wisdom, goodness, mercy, and truth of God the Father, of his Son Jesus, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0905]

# A Prayer of Cyprian of Antioch for the Martyrs

> **Note [Col. 0905C]**
>
> **Of Cyprian of Antioch.** Who this Cyprian was—the Antiochene magician and lover of Justina—will be stated below. —OXFORD EDITOR.
>
> **You are visible to the Son alone.** All the manuscripts and old editions read *conspectabilis*. But the other reading is preferable, because Prudentius similarly said: “He shone before his face, visible.” —PAMELIUS.
>
> [Col. 0906C] **Pure innocence.** Once again we owe the word *pure* to Morel, and, a little afterward, the word *enemy* in the phrase “the bloodthirsty enemy,” both of which are missing elsewhere. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **That we may carry the sign of eternal salvation inviolate.** The Church still uses almost the same words in the ceremonies of Baptism. —PAMELIUS.

(G, S)\*

Holy, holy, holy (*hagios, hagios, hagios*), Holy of Holies, Father of our fathers, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God of the Apostles, God of the Prophets, God [Col. 0905B] of virgins, God of those who live well, God of believers, God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ your Son: we invoke you as suppliants and likewise entreat you, only-begotten Son, who were begotten from the mouth of the Most High before the ordering of the world and, through the mystery, born from the womb of the holy Virgin Mary.

As we pray, deign to grant us spiritual growth in holy desire and integrity of heart, so that the breast renewed by the saving laver may remain inviolate by carnal offenses. With uncorrupted faith, an undefiled mind, steadfast devotion, and continual action or love, we ask that you permit us to flourish in your holy Church. For we bend our knees and bow our necks to you, in whose glory angels and archangels, thousands upon thousands of martyrs, and the choir of apostles and prophets exult; to you all [Col. 0905C] birds sing praises, and the tongues of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth confess; to you all the waters in heaven and beneath heaven confess; things without sensation perceive you. You alone exist, and apart from you and outside you there is no one.

We beseech you, Lord, almighty Father, who are visible to the Son alone, whose angels and archangels obey you—Lord and Father, we pray that you grant us an uncorrupted mind, pure innocence, sincere devotion, and a conscience that is holy, pure, sober, [Col. 0906A] and chaste, passing through this age in glorious faith against all its snares. Grant us a breast fortified against the devil’s threats and the enticements of the flesh, lest we become entangled in the deadly snares of the violent [Col. 0906B] and bloodthirsty enemy, so that we may carry the sign of eternal salvation inviolate.

Drive from us all the filth of this age and every persuasion of the devil. Let him be ensnared, fall, and be overcome by us; let him be driven away, just as Asmodeus, that most wicked demon, was driven from Sarah your servant and destroyed through your holy angel Raphael. Just as you were present with Tobias, deign to be present with me. And just as you showed mercy to the three youths in the furnace and to Daniel, deign to act likewise toward us, your servants.

You who raised the dead, gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, movement to the lame, and health to lepers: grant likewise to your servants, who with all the strength of our mind believe that you were born, suffered, and will come to judge the living and the dead. Stand by us as you stood by the Apostles in their chains, Thecla in [Col. 0906C] the flames, Paul in his persecutions, and Peter amid the waves.

You who sit upon the seven thrones at the Father’s right hand, look upon us and deliver us from the destruction of eternal death: one in one—the Father and the Son [the Latin is uncertain here], the Son in the Father, the Holy Spirit—through whom and with whom there belong to you in the holy Church honor, power, splendor, majesty, dominion, blessing, and immortality, both now and forever, always and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0905]

# A Prayer of Cyprian of Antioch, Which He Spoke on the Day of His Passion

(G)\*

[Col. 0905D]

> **Note [Col. 0905D]**
>
> **God of Abraham.** Gravius places before it the same words, “God of our fathers,” which in the common text appear afterward, [Col. 0906D] because Scripture generally reads this way. The manuscripts, however, agree with our reading. —PAMELIUS.

Holy Lord, holy Father (*hagios*), holy God (*hagie*), and holy, my God—for who is greater than you? I return thanks and praise to you, God of Abraham and God of Isaac and God [Col. 0906D] of Jacob, God of our fathers, God of the Apostles, God of the Prophets, and God of the Martyrs, who existed before the ordering of the world, God of the living, who are coming [Col. 0907A] to judge the living and the dead.

> **Note [Col. 0907D]**
>
> **Who have power to kill.** I add *to kill* from Morel’s manuscript. Gravius further adds: “who have power to put to death and again to give life,” but this does not seem preferable, since the same thing would then be repeated twice. From Gravius, however, I have added the words “and to make the dry green.” —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Before the Lord.** This too comes from Gravius. A little afterward, however, we have omitted with the manuscript the superfluous word *and*.

You are the true God, who sit upon the cherubim and seraphim, the throne of your honor, and look into the abysses; who see all things before they come into being; who have power to kill and to restore again; who have power to make the dry green. You are the Lord and ruler of all.
