Deliver me from this age and hear me as I pray, just as you heard the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, though they did not believe you or your servant Moses.

Woe for my sins! When you rise to shatter the earth, beneath what cleft in the rocks shall I hide myself from before your power? To what mountain shall I say, “Fall upon me,” and to what hill, “Cover me from before the fear of the Lord,” when you rise to shatter the earth?

I beseech you, Lord, help me. Do not judge me [Col. 0907B] according to my conduct, for I have obeyed none of your commandments. Hear me as I pray, just as you heard Jonah from the belly of the sea monster; so may you hear me and cast me out from death into life.

The Ninevites put on ashes and sackcloth and did penance before the Lord. As I make confession (*exomologesis*) before you for all my sins, you who love repentance, have mercy on me. David also says: “Lord, for the sake of your name, blot out my sin.” And I too entreat your majesty: blot out all my sins, and hear me as I pray, just as you heard the three youths—Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael—from the furnace of fire, and sent your angel with a cloud of dew, so that Nebuchadnezzar, ruler of the kingdom, was confounded. For you are the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule; you alone [Col. 0907C] possess immortality and dwell in inaccessible light, which no human being has seen or can see.

Hear me as I pray, just as you heard Daniel from the lions’ den and sent the prophet Habakkuk, who brought him a meal and said: “Eat the meal that God has sent you.” And Daniel said: “The Lord will not abandon those who seek him.”

Hear me as I pray, just as you heard Tobias and Sarah while they were praying in the courtyard of their house. Then the angel Raphael offered their prayers on their behalf. So too may you hear my petitions, admit my prayers to your holy court, and continually send your angel to blot out all my offenses, just as you removed the unclean spirit from Sarah, the daughter of Raguel; and enlighten my heart, just as you enlightened the eyes of Tobias.

Hear me as I pray, just as [Col. 0907D] you heard Susanna in the hands of the elders; so may you deliver me from this age, because you love a pure conscience. Hear me as I pray, just as you heard Hezekiah, king of Judah, and removed his illness from him. So too remove from me the infirmity of the flesh, and grant me an increase for faith [the object of “increase” is unstated in the Latin], just as you added fifteen years to his life. Deliver me from the midst of this age, just as you delivered Thecla from the midst of the amphitheater. Deliver me from every infirmity of my flesh.

[Col. 0908A] I entreat you, Father of majesty, who at the end of the times had mercy upon us by sending us your Son Jesus Christ, our Lord, God, and Savior, born of the Virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit at the announcement of the angel Gabriel, through whom you delivered us from the danger of imminent death.

And I entreat you, Son of the living God, who performed such great wonders; who at Cana of Galilee made wine from water for Israel; who opened the eyes of the blind; who made the deaf hear; who restored paralytics to the use of their limbs; who loosed the tongues of those with impeded speech; who healed those tormented by demons; who made the lame run like deer; who delivered the woman from her flow of blood; who raised the dead; who walked with your feet upon the water; who extended your hand to Peter as he sank; who established the sea, [Col. 0908B] set its boundary, and said: “Thus far shall you come, and here shall you break yourself in your strength.”

I entreat you, Son of the living God, concerning all my offenses—you who are in heaven, the Son in the Father and the Father in you forever, who sit upon the cherubim and seraphim, the throne of your honor.

Angels and archangels stand before you, a number beyond numbering, fearing and trembling before your honor and power, crying out with a loud voice and saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth.”

You yourself established a covenant with us: “Ask and you shall receive; knock and it shall be opened to you. Whatever you ask of my Father in my name, I ask the Father that you may receive it.” I ask, that I may receive; I seek, that I may find; I knock, that it may be opened to me. In your name [Col. 0908C] I ask, that you may ask the Father and it may be given to me.

I am ready to pour out my blood as a sacrifice for your name and to endure every kind of torment. You, Lord, are my hearer and defender; defend me from my adversary. May your angel of light protect me, for you said: “Whatever you ask in faith through prayer shall be given to you.”

Every human being is a liar; you are truthful. Just as you promised, you have power, Lord, to grant me every heavenly mystery of yours, so that I may be worthy to behold the face of your saints. May the Spirit work within me; may your will be done in me, for I have pledged myself to you for all the days of my life.

Under Pontius Pilate you endured the good confession; you were crucified, descended, and trampled down the sting of death. Death was conquered; [Col. 0908D] the enemy, the devil, was conquered. You rose from the dead and appeared to your Apostles. You sit at the Father’s right hand and will come to judge the living and the dead.

You shall reign: deliver me from the hand of the one who seeks my soul. Through your name deliver me from the hostile power, so that you may grant me the aid to conquer my enemy; for you are the mighty champion and advocate of the prayers and petitions of our souls. Intercede day and night for my sins, [Col. 0909A] and carry my prayer to your Father.

And you, holy Lord and Father, deign to look upon my petitions, just as you looked upon Abel’s offerings. Deign to deliver me from fire and everlasting punishment and from every [Col. 0910A] torment that you have prepared for the wicked, through the good and blessed Jesus Christ our Savior, through whom praise, honor, power, and glory belong to you throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0909]

# A Treatise by an Unknown Author on Mounts Sinai and Zion, Against the Jews

(C, G, S)

[Col. 0909B]

> **Note [Col. 0909D]**
>
> **I.—Proof of the chapters.** The opening of this book is mutilated and therefore obscure. Nevertheless, all the printed editions and manuscript codices read it in this way, with the exception of the Cambrai manuscript, which has: “That the proof of the chapters,” etc. Nor is that reading satisfactory. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **By Jesus himself.** The Cambrai manuscript reads *by Christ*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **According to John.** This comes from the Cambrai, Marchiennes, Dunes, and Affligem manuscripts—the last in the margin—and agrees with Morel, in place of what the Affligem manuscript has in the text itself and the old printed editions have, namely *beside*; the others, however, read *according to*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **For from Zion the law shall go forth.** This too agrees with Morel and comes from three manuscript codices, in place of *shall come forth*. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **How are we to understand this?** We have added the question mark in agreement with the old printed editions, Gravius, and Cauchius; and, since none of them read it there, we removed the phrase *whether one* from the place where it stood. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **But the Latin interpretation.** Manutius reads, “but the interpretation is Latin.” The former, however, is genuine. —PAMELIUS.

### I

The proof of the chapters contained in the divinely inspired Scriptures is as follows: the things that were written figuratively in the Old Testament must be understood spiritually through the New Testament, since they were fulfilled in truth through Christ.

For spiritual understanding has been given to us through Jesus Christ, as Jesus himself says: “To you it has indeed been given to understand the mysteries of God, but to others they are given in similitudes.”

We find it written in the Gospel according to (*kata*, κατὰ) John: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” This Law was given to Moses on Mount Sinai. Yet again we find it written: “For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

How are we to understand this? Are Mount Sinai, where the Law was given by God to Moses, and Mount Zion, from which the Law went forth, one and the same mountain? Or is Mount Sinai [Col. 0909C] one mountain and Mount Zion another? For we find that these names of the two mountains are Hebrew; but the Latin interpretation of the names, which differ from one another, shows that Mount Sinai is one thing and Mount Zion another.

> **Note [Col. 0909D]**
>
> **II.—Mount Sinai is interpreted.** Our author everywhere uses the verb *interpretor* as though it were entirely passive; he is no less a stranger to grammar than to theology. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **In Psalm II.** I read it precisely thus, not “in the first Psalm,” since Cyprian too, above in *Testimonies*, Book III, chapter 29, calls this Psalm the second when quoting these words, not the first. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **And Mount Sinai.** I add *mount* from the Cambrai manuscript. From the same manuscript I have restored the words, “Since the whole world has evil deeds and has been stained by the devil,” in place of the reading, “Since the whole world, because of evil deeds, by the devil.” —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Because I too [hate] it.** The Cambrai manuscript omits *because* and reads, “And I hate it.” Neither reading is satisfactory, because the Evangelist reads quite differently: “Because I bear testimony concerning it.” —PAMELIUS.

### II

This is the translation from the Hebrew language into Latin. Mount Sinai is interpreted as “eternal temptation” and “hatred”; likewise, Zion is interpreted as “the temptation of provocation” and “watchtower.”

You see, therefore, that in their Hebrew interpretation they are not alike, nor are they one mountain, but rather two mountains differing from one another [Col. 0910B] in grace and honor.

Moreover, the prophet David says in Psalm II: “But I have been appointed king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his dominion.” See, then, how he designates Mount Zion as holy. From this it is evident that Mount Zion is heavenly and spiritual, whereas Mount Sinai is earthly. For nothing that is on earth can be holy, since the whole world has evil deeds and has been stained by the devil, as Jesus says: “The world hates me, and I hate it, because its deeds are evil.”

> **Variant [Col. 0909C]:** “Its deeds are evil.” —Fossius, Michaelis, Victorius.

For this reason, whatever exists in this earthly age cannot be holy.

> **Note [Col. 0910D]**
>
> **III.—The Holy Spirit, the Son of God.** On this ancient form of expression, see above the book *That Idols Are Not Gods*. Consequently, these words should not trouble the reader, nor should the two similar expressions below. For before heresies concerning the Holy Spirit arose, the ancients did not write with such caution. —PAMELIUS.
>
> [Col. 0911C] **Although by sacred fingers, yet by fingers in a figure of the flesh.** Manutius omits the word *although*, recites the words “by sacred fingers” only once, and places them a little earlier. Our manuscripts, however, agree with the common reading; and if the words are enclosed in parentheses, the sense will be clear. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Thus, indeed, this truth, etc.** I restored this exceedingly corrupt passage from the manuscript codices—partly from Affligem, Dunes, Marchiennes, and the old printed editions, and partly from the Cambrai manuscript—as follows:
>
> “Thus, from the beginning of the world and thereafter, all human beings at their birth received names from their parents based on time and deed. They did not do so of themselves, but were impelled in mind by God, who, before things come to pass, has foreknowledge of what will be, so that Hebrew words and names might later indicate what those persons would become after reaching maturity, and the interpretation of the names might reveal the truth about what would befall each one.” —PAMELIUS.

### III

It is established from the prophetic saying that Mount Zion is holy and spiritual.

> **Variant [Col. 0909C]:** Thus Fossius, Michaelis, Victorius, and the Imperial edition; *non tam ex* (“not so much from”) [the apparatus wording is uncertain].

Upon this mountain the Holy Spirit—

> **Variant [Col. 0909C]:** “By the Holy Spirit.” —Fossius, Michaelis, Victorius.

—the Son of God, was appointed king, proclaiming [Col. 0910C] the will and dominion of God his Father.

> **Variant [Col. 0910C]:** “Of God and the Father.” —Fossius, Michaelis, Victorius, the Imperial edition.

Mount Sinai, however, is an earthly mountain situated in an arid land, in Syria-Palestine, where the land of Judaea is, and where that city is—

> **Variant [Col. 0910C]:** “Where the city is.” —Fossius, Michaelis, Victorius, the Imperial edition.

—the murderess of the Prophets, before whose gate Christ was crucified by the Jews in a garden. Through the prophet Isaiah that city is called Jerusalem, but spiritually it is accursed and forsaken.

Nor is this without reason, because upon that same earthly Mount Sinai, through Moses—who was still clothed in the earthly flesh of the first man—the earthly and carnal people of the Jews received from God the law that was to be delivered to them [the Latin syntax is corrupt]. It was written by sacred fingers upon two [Col. 0911A] tablets of stone—although by sacred fingers, yet by fingers in a figure of the flesh—as befitted a carnal and exceedingly hard people, just as the stone tablets upon which they received the Law were exceedingly hard.

There were two tablets because they signified that the unity of the people would be divided into two parts: the part that is saved, and the unbelieving part that perishes. Thus the angel said to Rebecca, the wife of Isaac:

“Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall overcome the other people, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

Rebecca bore the figure of the Church, just as her husband Isaac bore within himself the type of Christ. Therefore, when the angel says, “Two nations are in your womb,” he was indicating that two parts would also arise from the nations: a lost, idolatrous part and a believing part that lives through faith. He indicates that this one part of the nations will remain [Col. 0911B] in the womb of the Church unto eternal generation, in the figure of Rebecca; and that the portion belonging to the people of the unbelieving Jews would then be divided from Rebecca’s belly and separated from the birth of the Church.

This was the prefiguration spiritually announced through the angel in Genesis.

Now, the names of the mountains have such an interpretation in the Latin language as to reveal the truth about what these two mountains, Sinai and Zion, are. We shall speak of this a little later. Thus, indeed, we have established this interpretation of the truth as coming from the beginning of the human race.

Thus, from the beginning of the world and thereafter, all human beings at their birth received names from their parents based on time and deed. They did not do so of themselves, but were impelled in mind by God, who, before things come to pass, has foreknowledge of what will be. In this way, Hebrew words and names might later indicate what those persons would become after reaching maturity, [Col. 0911C] and the interpretation of the names might reveal the truth about what would befall each one.

This was fulfilled at that time in the Patriarchs. In accordance with the fact that the flesh of the first man was made from the soil of the earth, we establish the truth from that first-formed man himself.

> **Note [Col. 0911D]**
>
> **He gathered it in his fist from the four cardinal regions of the world.** These things were drawn from rabbinical refuse. In the *Pirke Rabbi Eliezer* it is said:
>
> “God began to gather the dust of the first man from the four corners of the earth—namely red, black, white, and green. The red dust became blood; the black was for the entrails; the white for the bones and sinews; the green became the body. Why did he gather his dust from the four corners of the world? Because the Holy and Blessed One had said: Whether a person goes from east [Col. 0912C] to west, or from west to east, or travels to any place whatever, and his appointed time comes to depart from this world, the earth should not then say: ‘In this place there is no dust of your body taken from me,’” etc. —OXFORD EDITOR.
>
> **In the four cardinal letters you have the name Adam.** Our cabbalist did not know that only three letters are found in the name. But if a more suitable author for such trifles is wanted, the reader may consult volume nine of the works of St. Augustine, Tractate 10 on the Gospel of John, where all these things occur. —OXFORD EDITOR.
>
> **That is, one, etc.** Both this and the phrases that follow—“that is, four,” “that is, one,” and again “that is, forty”—were written in the Dunes manuscript alongside the interpretation of the Greek words; they are entirely missing from the other manuscripts and the old printed editions. We nevertheless thought they should be retained for greater clarity. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **That flesh which he bore within himself figuratively.** Manutius correctly noted that this must certainly be understood cautiously. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **This number, 46.** This wooden reckoner constructs the number 46 from the number 6,000, the number 6, and 40. —PAMELIUS.
>
> **Destroy this temple.** Gravius writes *phanum* both here and twice afterward. All the manuscripts, however, consistently have *fanum*; and not only Festus, but also Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book V, and Livy, first decade, Book X, derive *fanum* from *fando*.

### IV

He received from God the name Adam. The Hebrew *Adam* is interpreted in [Col. 0912A] Latin as “earth made flesh,” because God gathered it in his fist from the four cardinal regions of the world, as it is written:

“I measured heaven with my palm, gathered the earth in my fist, and fashioned the human being from all the soil of the earth; I made him in the image of God.”

He therefore had to bear within himself the name Adam derived from these four cardinal regions of the earth.

We find in the Scriptures that the Creator of the world appointed four stars, one in each cardinal region of the earth. The first, the eastern star, is called *anatolē* (ἀνατολή, “rising”); the second, the western, *dysis* (δύσις, “setting”); the third, the northern star, *arktos* (ἄρκτος, “the Bear”); and the fourth, the southern, is called *mesēmbria* (μεσημβρία, “midday” or “south”).

From the names of these four stars, take the first letter of each star’s name: from the star *Anatolē*, A; from the star *Dysis*, D; from the star *Arktos*, A; and from the star *Mesēmbria*, [Col. 0912B] M. In these four cardinal letters you have the name ADAM.

Indeed, the name is indicated numerically by the four Greek letters ἀδάμ: α, μία, that is, one; δ, τέσσαρα, that is, four; α, μία, that is, one; μ, τεσσαράκοντα, that is, forty. Add them together and you will find the number forty-six.

This number, 46, signifies the passion of Adam’s flesh, which Christ bore within himself figuratively and suspended upon the wood. This flesh was called Jesus by God the Father; the Holy Spirit descended from heaven; Christ—that is, “Anointed”—was named by God, the living God; spirit was mingled with flesh: Jesus Christ.

This number 46 therefore declares the Passion, because he suffered in the six-thousandth year, at the sixth hour; rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven on the fortieth day. Or it signifies the Passion because Solomon built the temple for God in forty-six [Col. 0912C] years.

Jesus said that his flesh was the likeness of this temple when he said to the Pharisees: “Destroy this temple, and I shall raise it up in three days.” And the Pharisees said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will this man raise it up in three days?” But Jesus was speaking of the temple of his body.

[Col. 0913A]

### V

Then Abel, the son of Adam, received a Hebrew name signifying his murder by his brother and the mourning of his parents.

Likewise Enoch, who before the Flood pleased God as a righteous man and was therefore taken alive in his flesh from this world to a place known to God. From that place, at the consummation of the world, he is to be restored to this world, from which he was transferred, in order to confound and refute Antichrist. After they have been slain by him, they will complete their martyrdoms and live eternally throughout the ages of ages. Enoch is therefore interpreted as “renewed.”

Then there was righteous Job, who even before the day of judgment merited praise from the Judge’s own voice. Therefore, because he defeated and overcame the devil, Job is interpreted as “dearest to God.”

Likewise, Abraham was called Abram by his parents at his birth. But after he was tested by God and found faithful, [Col. 0913B] God blessed him and appointed him father of many nations. Therefore, after God changed his name, he was called Abraham, which is interpreted as “father of many peoples.”

> **Note [Col. 0913D]:** [The supplied source breaks off here.]

### VI.—“And Mount Zion: a trial of provocation.”

Others added “eternal”; but Manutius rightly omitted it, together with the Cambrai manuscript, because it is not read above. —PAMELIUS.

“They were found.” On the authority of the same manuscript I have omitted the superfluous particle “and.” —PAMELIUS.

“Clearly, moreover, Moses,” etc. If its sound is considered, *Massa*, which denotes “trial,” appears to approximate the name Moses. —OXFORD EDITOR.

The passage is so corrupt that it has not been possible to repair it from the manuscripts. Four of them agree with the common printed editions, as do the early printed editions, except that they read “Moses,” as does Morel, who also reads “He makes manifest.” The Cambrai manuscript, however, reads quite differently: “Clearly, moreover, to Moses and Aaron, through whom God tried them by the Law, it is interpreted in Latin [Col. 0914D]. Similarly, when they were tried by God on the mountain, they were found to be alien,” etc. Perhaps it should be read thus: “And the interpretation of Sinai was fulfilled, being made manifest to Moses and Aaron, through whom God tried them by the Law,” with everything else omitted, since the same words were placed earlier and therefore seem superfluous here. —PAMELIUS.

VI. Behold, meanwhile, we have said a little concerning many proofs, so that, having reached the names of the two mountains, we may demonstrate the interpretations of those mountains’ names and how they were designated for our instruction; so that from this interpretation of the names we may understand Mount Sinai to be earthly and Mount Zion to be heavenly. Spiritually interpreted, Sinai means “eternal trial and hatred,” and Mount Zion means “trial of provocation and watch.” Thus it is understood when Mount Sinai is called “eternal trial and hatred,” because from that mountain Moses received the Law for a most hard-hearted [Col. 0913C] and obstinate people. When they were tried by the eternal God through that Law, they were found unable to endure that same Law forever; thereafter they were turned into objects of hatred to God. Therefore, in the name of Mount Sinai, from which they had received the Law, the interpretation of the name designated a people tried by God and turned into objects of eternal hatred. Sinai is therefore called “eternal trial and hatred.”

For we find in the Scriptures that they were tried by God. Thus it is written, when the Lord says to Moses: “Let this people go out and gather for themselves each day’s provision on that day, and I shall try them, whether they can endure my Law or not.” And when they were tried by God through the Law, they were found alien to that Law. Thereafter they were turned into objects of eternal hatred to God, and the interpretation of Sinai was fulfilled.

Moses too, through whom God tried them by the Law, clearly bears a similar interpretation in Latin [Col. 0913D]: Moses means “God’s trial and finding” [Col. 0914A]. Through him, when they were tried by God, they were found alien to the observance of the Law; therefore they were turned into objects of eternal hatred to God.

We find this hatred written into the very lineage of the Jews, when Isaac says of his two sons, the elder Esau and the younger Jacob: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Now the elder Esau was wholly hairy, Scripture says, “like a hairy hide,” as a figure of the elder people, established in the impiety of their transgressions. Jacob, however, was smooth and younger, as a figure of the newer people, who, by hearing the word and through the faith of belief, were turned from the roughness of the world to the gentleness of Christ, God and Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0914D]

### VII.—“Trial of provocation.”

The author appears to have been deceived by the sound of the word when deriving his interpretation from it. —OXFORD EDITOR.

“And let us try what will happen to him.” This again is taken from the Cambrai manuscript in place of “what is to happen”; for in the Greek of the Septuagint it reads, *τὰ ἐν ἐκβάσει* (“the things in the outcome”). The manuscripts, however, omit the little word “and” shortly afterward.]

VII. Behold, we have demonstrated through the testimony of the Scriptures that the elder and more ancient people were turned into objects of hatred to God, in accordance with the interpretation of Mount Sinai, which says: “eternal trial and hatred.” Likewise, Mount Zion is interpreted as “trial of provocation and watch.” This Latin interpretation signifies the Passion upon the sacred wood, as Solomon says concerning the Lord’s Passion itself:

“Let us question him with insult and torture, that we may know his reverence and test his patience; and let us try what will happen to him. For if he is truly the Son of God, God will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his adversaries. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death. These things they devised, and they went astray; their own malice blinded them, and they did not understand the mysteries of God.”

Behold the Jewish tempters. Likewise, it is written: “And they tempted God in a waterless place.”

The “watch,” moreover, signifies the height of the wood, as Solomon says: “They stationed me like a watchman [Col. 0914C] over an orchard,” because in a garden he hung fastened to the wood between two robbers. From the height of the wood he watches both of them, as a figure of two evildoing peoples: the Gentiles, lying amid the evil deeds of the world, and the Jews, the slayers of the Prophets. These are the two evildoing peoples, whose figure was borne by the two robbers between whom the Innocent One hung. One blasphemed, while the other confessed that the Innocent One was suffering unjustly. Jesus, moreover, watched both of them from the watchtower of the wood, the blasphemer and the confessor. He saved the confessor and destroyed the blasphemer, just as he did with the two peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0915D]

### VIII.—“And they cast out their bodies and sent them forth from themselves.”

We have thus supplied the mutilated passage from the Cambrai and Cauchius manuscripts. The common editions had only: “and the bodies from himself,” for which Manutius, together with other manuscripts, reads, not badly: “and he sent the bodies forth.” —PAMELIUS.

“Prostrate on their faces.” I have this from all the manuscripts, in place of “prostrate on the face.” —PAMELIUS.]

VIII. The persecutors who have been abandoned, and who have not placed their faith in him, lie under sentence of eternal death; if they depart from the world in this condition, they will perish. The Gentiles, however, who have been converted to him and who have faith in him that he is [the] Son of God, will be saved and will behold their emperor and king forever and ever [Col. 0914D–0915A].

But while hanging upon the wood during the Passion itself, he looked out from the height of the wood and watched the two portions of the people. One portion of the people, who had seen his marvelous and divine works, grieved and wept as he suffered injuries. Other Jews, however, mocked him, striking his head with a reed, blaspheming and saying: “Hail, King of the Jews! Where is your father? Let him come and deliver you from the cross.”

At this the Father was provoked and caused heaven to be opened; there were thunderclaps and unbearable darkness; the earth was shaken, tombs were opened, and they cast out their bodies and sent them forth from themselves; the veil of the temple was torn. At so great a crashing of heaven and shaking of the earth, all who stood before the wood—some grieving, others blaspheming and mocking—fell prostrate on their faces, trembling [Col. 0915B] like dead men. Then the Jews understood that they had offended God, and they turned to mourning; and there was the provocation.

For at the time when he hung fastened to the wood, it was the period of Unleavened Bread, which comprises the Jewish feast days. On that day, frightened by the earthquake and the crashing of heaven, they lay prostrate on their faces, lamenting upon the ground, and turned to mourning. Thus in his Passion itself he fulfilled the prophetic saying: “And I shall turn their feast days into mourning, and their songs into lamentation.”

For earlier, when they were held captive in Babylon, the Babylonians said to them: “Sing us songs from the songs of Zion.” And the Jews, lamenting their captivity, said to the Babylonians, as we have stated, in lamentation: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?”

[Col. 0915C]

[Note: [Col. 0915D]

### IX.—“Pontius Pilate, his mind impelled.”

Because Rembold’s edition, through the printers’ negligence, had “unstained,” Erasmus conjecturally restored “infused.” But “impelled” is the genuine reading. —PAMELIUS.

“Thus, moreover, another prophet.” Manutius reads “but another”; our manuscripts, however, have the former. It is remarkable that he calls him another prophet, since it was the same David who pronounced it. —PAMELIUS.

“And did not swear deceitfully.” Since Cyprian reads it thus elsewhere, I prefer this reading, with three manuscripts and the common printed editions, to “in deceit” in the Cambrai manuscript, or “under deceit” in Manutius. —PAMELIUS.]

IX. Behold how the interpretation of Mount Zion—“trial of provocation and watch”—was fulfilled. Hence it is manifest that Mount Zion is the kingdom of the sacred wood, justified in holiness, as David says: “Proclaim the kingdom of God among the Gentiles, for the Lord reigned from the wood and passed over to the Gentiles.”

Concerning this kingdom of the royal wood, the same prophet says: “But I was appointed by him as king over Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his dominion.” While hanging upon the wood during his Passion, he fulfilled this prophetic saying through Pontius Pilate. Pontius Pilate, his mind impelled by God, took a tablet and wrote the title in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: “Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews.” He fastened the tablet bearing the name of the King of the Jews to the head of the wood with a nail. Then he made manifest the prophetic [Col. 0915D] saying, because spiritually Mount Zion is the cross, which is the power of God, as the Apostle says: “The cross of Christ is foolishness to unbelievers, but to believers the cross [Col. 0916A] is the power of God.” And again he says: “But we proclaim to you Christ, and him crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

Thus, moreover, another prophet declares that the wood of the Lord’s Passion is holy Mount Zion, saying in the Spirit: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? One innocent in his hands”—demonstrating his innocence with right and left hands extended and fixed by nails. Therefore he says: “One innocent in his hands and pure of heart, who has not received his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor: he shall receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior.”

Every human passion ends with one falling to the ground; this Passion of the cross alone displays one standing upright. Hence we truly say [Col. 0916B] that the holy mountain is the wood of the Passion. Moses was not innocent in his hands and pure of heart. For he was not pure of heart, because in Egypt he struck an Egyptian with his heel, killed him, and buried him in the sand with his own hands. Christ, however, ascended the holy mountain, the wood of his kingdom, to die at the hands of the Jews, although he himself killed no human being, but only the devil, the enemy of the human race. Therefore the one innocent and pure of heart ascended the mountain; and thus the prophet says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place? One innocent in his hands and pure of heart.”

He also declared holy Mount Zion to be the holy cross, as the prophet likewise says: “From Zion shall go forth the Law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The law of Christians is the holy cross of Christ, [Col. 0916C] the Son of the living God, as the prophet likewise says: “Your law is in the midst of my belly.” When he was struck by the lance in the belly of his side, blood mingled with water poured forth and flowed. From it he fashioned for himself the holy Church, in which he consecrated the law of his Passion, as he himself says: “Let anyone who thirsts come and drink. Whoever believes in me, as it is written, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.”

Likewise in the Psalms: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season.” Behold the prophetic word, whose “fruit” is spiritually to be understood as the Resurrection on the third day, saying: “From Zion shall go forth the Law”—that is, from the royal wood—“and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem,” which is the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0916D]

### X.—“He calls Jerusalem.”

Erasmus had added, to make the sense coherent, “concerning which it is said in the Apocalypse: I saw.” No manuscripts have this; but the early printed codices read the preceding words with them. —PAMELIUS.]

X. The flesh fastened to the wood uttered the Lord’s word, saying: “Eli, Eli.” And the spiritual prophecy spoken beforehand was fulfilled [Col. 0916D]: “From Zion shall go forth the Law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

He calls Jerusalem the new city descending from heaven, made four-square by the four [Col. 0917A] Gospels, having twelve foundations belonging to the twelve Prophets and twelve gates belonging to the twelve Apostles. Through their proclamation Christians entered this holy and new city, which is the spiritual Church.

XI. Behold, we have demonstrated through the testimony of all the divine Scriptures that the two mountains—Sinai on earth and Zion in heaven—bear the figure of the two Testaments: Sinai of the old and Zion of the new. From these two mountains, that is, the two Testaments, we have two peoples shown and revealed in the later period: the old and earlier people of the Jews, and the new and later people of the Christians. The Jews are earthly and carnal, having received from God the promised land; Christians are heavenly, and will receive from God the promised kingdoms of heaven [Col. 0917B] in the age to come. For the flesh of Christians will be spiritual and immortal.

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

### XII.—“From Hebrew into Greek or Latin.”

This comes from three other manuscripts, in place of what stood there: “in Greek and Latin.” The passage nevertheless remains obscure. What follows should be understood as above. —PAMELIUS.]

XII. Since another proof of the truth is set forth in the Scriptures, from that heavenly truth we make a spiritual comparison of the figures, drawn from the practices of this world. For we have said that the holy Mount Zion, which is the royal and sacred wood, had as its interpretation from Hebrew into Greek or Latin: “trial of provocation” or “watch,” because from the wood he watched those who stood before him, both good and evil.

[Note: [Col. 0917D]

### XIII.—“Through Solomon.”

Here as earlier he also attributes the Book of Wisdom to Solomon. —PAMELIUS.

“In the epistle of John his disciple.” The catholic epistles of John nowhere contain anything of the kind. It therefore seems that “James” should be restored, so that it may allude to the saying: “He shall be compared to a man considering his face in a mirror.” I am therefore all the more surprised that the Cambrai manuscript reads “to Paul.” —PAMELIUS.]

XIII. Thus we find that the Savior himself was called by Solomon the spotless mirror of the Father, because the Holy Spirit, the Son of God, sees himself doubled: the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father; each sees himself in the other [Col. 0917C], and therefore he is the spotless mirror.

For we too, who believe in him, see Christ in ourselves as in a mirror, as he himself instructs and admonishes us in the epistle of John his disciple to the people: “See me in yourselves as each one of you sees himself in water or in a mirror.” And he confirms Solomon’s saying concerning himself when he says: “Who is the spotless mirror of the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

### XIV.—“A four-square watchtower.”

This fine author believed that *speculum*, “mirror,” and *specula*, “watchtower,” differed in no respect: equally skilled in derivations and in the interpretation of mysteries. —PAMELIUS.]

XIV. Moreover, he also said that he himself was the eternal and true vine, and that his Father was the husbandman. Therefore, if Christ is the true vine, it is surely established that we too, who believe in him and have put him on, are the true vine, which is the Lord’s vineyard; and Christ is the keeper of his vineyard, as Solomon says: “They appointed me keeper in the vineyard.”

In the practices of this world, moreover, we find that, in a spiritual likeness, there is figuratively a vineyard having its own lord and owner. At the season of ripeness, near the days of the vintage, a boy is stationed as keeper in the vineyard upon a high wooden structure fixed in the middle of the vineyard. Upon this wooden structure they make a four-square watchtower from battered reeds, and on each side of the square watchtower they make three openings, making twelve openings in all. Through this square arrangement of openings, the boy who is keeper looks out over and guards the whole vineyard, singing so that no traveler entering the Lord’s vineyard entrusted to him may damage it, and so that thieves may not trample the vineyard’s grapes.

But if some importunate and needy thief wishes to enter the vineyard and take a cluster of grapes, the vigilant boy there [Col. 0918B], from within his watchtower over the vineyard, raises a threatening voice, cursing and warning the traveler-thief not to dare approach the vineyard, saying: “Walk straight on.” The thief, fearing the voice of the boy who threatens him, flees from the vineyard. He sees the watchtower and hears the voice, but does not see the boy within the watchtower who is threatening him; and, afraid, he continues on his way.

[Note: [Col. 0918D]

### XV.—“And in his name the Gentiles will believe and hope.”

This too is found in the same manuscripts, which surprises me, since both Isaiah and Matthew have nothing but “they will hope,” in Greek and Latin; nor does Cyprian earlier, in Book II of the *Testimonies*, chapter 13, read anything but “they will believe.” —PAMELIUS.]

XV. This worldly practice is likened to spiritual grace. For so it is among the divine people just as it is in an earthly vineyard. The Lord’s spiritual vineyard is the Christian people, who are guarded at the command of God the Father by the boy Christ, raised up in the watchtower of the wood.

But if the traveler, the devil, walking along the road of this world, dares to separate and afflict a person from the Lord’s spiritual vineyard, he is immediately rebuked by the heavenly boy’s voice [Col. 0918C] and chastened by spiritual scourges; banished “to the hundredth” [an uncertain reading], he flees into dry and deserted places.

This boy who keeps watch is the Lord’s Son, who received his vineyard from the Father with the charge that it be saved and preserved. Concerning him the prophet Isaiah sings, saying: “Behold my most beloved servant; I shall place my Spirit upon him, and he shall proclaim judgment to the Gentiles. He shall not cry out or contend. He shall not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoking flax, until he casts forth judgment in victory; and in his name the Gentiles shall believe and hope.”

[Col. 0919]

# A TREATISE AGAINST THE JEWS WHO PERSECUTED OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR  
(C, G, S)

[Col. 0919A]

[Note: [Col. 0919C]

### I.—“In the Spirit.”

Pamelius wrongly reads “and in the Spirit.” —MARAN.

“Attend to your sense and understanding.” This appears to allude to Philippians 4: “May the peace of God guard your senses and understandings.” —PAMELIUS.

“Like things.” Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “like.” A little afterward, “the trumpet’s sounds” comes from the Colbert manuscript; the printed editions have “the trumpet,” while two other manuscripts have “of the trumpet.” —MARAN.

“The soldier [recognizes] the trumpet.” He would have spoken more correctly if he had said “the horse [recognizes] the trumpet,” since the soldier is not a dumb animal. —PAMELIUS.

“Their own.” We add this word from three manuscripts and Morel. —MARAN.]

I. ATTEND to your sense and understanding in the Holy Spirit, so that you may not only hear with your ears but also behold with your eyes the divine mystery of Christ. You behold it through your faith. Hearing, indeed, belongs to necessity; believing, to careful judgment. It is the function of the ears indiscriminately to apprehend both vain and useful things alike; it is the function of faith to believe only what it has approved. For it is of no benefit to hear gladly unless belief confirms what is heard.

The eyes of faith are the spirit, through which spiritual things are seen. Therefore, if you are spiritual, understand heavenly things. Like things recognize their own likenesses. Even dumb animals understand one another from the sound of the voice: lions recognize roaring, bulls lowing, and the soldier the trumpet’s sounds! How much more truly, then, do spiritual persons understand spiritual things, and heavenly persons and heirs understand [Col. 0919B] the precepts of their Father and the provisions secured in their Father’s testament?

Since you, therefore, are Christ’s heirs, understand his testament. But if anyone, by reason of age, is less teachable and cannot understand it, he has the Holy Spirit as interpreter; let him follow the Spirit. With him as guide and teacher, he will very easily be able to know the rights and power of the New Testament, namely, that the inheritance was bestowed upon the Gentiles in the following manner.

[Note: [Col. 0919D]

### II.—“Fixed.”

Two manuscripts read: “by a fixed joining of measurements.” —MARAN.

[Col. 0920C] “With his brothers.” Pamelius thinks that “sons” should be read, and so the Oxford edition reads; but all the ancient manuscripts, together with Morel, have “brothers.” —MARAN.

“With his sons.” This must certainly be read in place of “brothers.” For Noah did not enter the ark with his brothers, but with his sons. Similarly, a little afterward, “rainbow” should stand in place of “ark.” For God placed the testimony of the covenant in the bow of heaven, that is, the rainbow. —PAMELIUS.

“In the rainbow.” Thus Pamelius, although Morel and the manuscripts have “in the ark.” —MARAN.

“On Mount Horeb.” Following all the other versions, he likewise cites this passage according to the Septuagint, which reads “Horeb” in place of “Oreb.” —PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0921D] “Agag.” Thus Pamelius by conjecture, since the Jews are nowhere said to have spared Achan, whereas 1 Kings 15 relates that Saul and the people spared Agag, king of Amalek. Morel and three manuscripts read “Achan.” —MARAN.]

II. In the beginning God the Father made the human being with his own hand and placed him in Paradise, giving him a fixed condition consisting of the precepts of life, law, and testament. But he, having despised his Father’s precepts, was expelled from Paradise into his earthborn nativity, in which he also died.

God, however, raised up a righteous race from the seed of Adam, which seed he preserved as a people [Col. 0919C] through Noah’s son and his heirs. From that race he found a righteous man and commanded him to make a structure in the form of a vessel, with a fixed capacity produced by the joining of its measurements, so that Noah, sheltered within it with his brothers, might be preserved for the sake of that race. For because of humanity’s injustice God had decreed that the world should perish beneath inundating waters.

Thereafter, therefore, Noah was saved with his own people. God established with him an attestation of his commandment, saying: “Every living thing shall be food for you, like the produce of vegetables, except flesh with its lifeblood” (Gen. 9:3); and he placed the sign of this attestation in the rainbow.

After this the Lord God again gave testimony to Abraham concerning Isaac, saying in this manner: “To you and your seed I shall give this land, and I shall make you the father of many nations” (Gen. 17:8). Thereafter the seed increased into a numerous people and was divided among twelve Patriarchs. The Lord likewise established an attestation for them on Mount Horeb through Moses. Having driven the nations from that place, he established there the people whom he had taken and possessed as an inheritance assigned to himself. God also showed them very many signs [Col. 0920B] and miracles, as to a most beloved son.

But that same people, after receiving so many and such great benefits, opposed their Father and abandoned the living God. For Israel abandoned the Lord, showing him its back and not its face; it turned its face toward idols. By killing the Prophets sent to it, who preached concerning Christ, Israel thereby grew accustomed to persecuting Christ, not only when he came in the body, but even when he was proclaimed by the Prophets.

For they persecuted all the seers. Some they attacked with stones, and others they destroyed by shamefully torturing them—not only the Prophets themselves, but, through them, the Lord Christ as well. What proof is there of this? Namely, that they accepted the accused, the unbelieving and faithless, liars and adversaries of Christ, while they attacked those who were true [Col. 0920C] and full of faith.

They reviled Moses because he proclaimed Christ; they loved Dathan because he did not proclaim Christ. They repudiated Aaron from the priesthood because he displayed the likeness of Christ; they appointed Abiron because he contradicted Christ. They hated David because he sang of Christ; they exalted Saul because he did not speak of Christ. They rejected Samuel because he spoke of Christ; they preserved Agag, for he said nothing about Christ. They stoned Jeremiah when he prophesied Christ; they loved Ananias when he opposed Christ. They sawed Isaiah apart when he cried out concerning Christ; they magnified Manasseh when he persecuted Christ. They killed John when he pointed out Christ; they slaughtered Zechariah when he loved Christ. They loved Judas when he betrayed Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0921D]

### III.—“Unworthy.”

We have thus corrected the reading on the authority of three manuscripts; the printed editions have “worthy.” —MARAN.

“They were dying.” Three manuscripts have “he was dying.” —MARAN.

“Because of indignation.” Thus Morel and two manuscripts; Pamelius has “in indignation.” —MARAN.]

III. You see how those who love Christ are hated, while those who hate him are cherished with love among an unworthy people. O unworthy obstinacy in persecution, extending even to annihilation by death! For they not only attacked the Lord’s witnesses; those faithless tenants also insulted the Father in the Son, even the Lord himself [Col. 0921B].

What, therefore, did they deserve to suffer for this crime? Surely to be driven from the kingdom and disinherited from the inheritance. And so it was done, and so it happened: things worthy of such persons befell them. For the Father suffered insult in the Son, and the Son suffered it in the Prophets at the time when they were dying. In his own time he was compelled by indignation to write a new testament, calling heaven and earth as witnesses, as well as the angel from the temple, while Moses and Elijah stood by. For he summoned these witnesses when he suffered in Israel.

He foretold through the Prophets that these things would happen thus, in these words: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, because the Lord has spoken: I begot sons and exalted them, but they despised me” (Isa. 1:2).

[Note: [Col. 0921D]

### IV.—“Poured forth.”

The Colbert manuscript has “pours forth.” —MARAN.

“All creation was shaken.” *Nativitas*, “creation,” stands for *creatura*. It is remarkable, however, that he says: “The angel fled away in repentance when the veil was cut.” —PAMELIUS.

“The Lord was tortured.” I added the absolutely necessary word “Lord.” —PAMELIUS.]

IV. The Lord poured forth these words against Israel, crying aloud and saying: “You did not want me; others who have not yet even heard mention of me will receive me. You despised my wedding feast; others who were not invited will attend. You refused to cultivate my field and my vineyard, from which the fruits of righteousness arise; others will cultivate them and gather their fruits in God.”

What is this dreadful disposition and accursed design? Were you therefore able to kill the king and bridegroom? For this reason heaven and earth and the elements within them are witnesses; indeed, every creature is a witness to the death of Christ.

O new cruelty! All creation was shaken during the Lord’s Passion, but the people remained unmoved and without trembling. The angel fled away in repentance when the veil was cut, while the people remained without fear and with their garment intact. The elements were transformed and thrown into confusion; Israel continued unconcerned. O new hardness! O singular audacity! O bloodstained faithlessness! [Col. 0921D]

Pilate, a secular judge of a foreign nation and holding temporal authority, cleansed his hands and washed away the guilt forced upon him, saying: “I am innocent and free of his blood” (Matt. 27:24). But the people did not imitate even a stranger and foreigner; instead, they cried out: “Fasten him to the cross! Away with him! His blood be upon us and upon our children” (ibid.).

Violent cruelty, an inhuman people, unfeeling hearts, and wide-open eyes! They killed their benefactor and shed no tears. The Apostles mourned, and the people gloried. The earth trembled, and the people rejoiced. The Lord was judged, and Israel exulted. Christ suffered, and the impious cried out. The Lord was tortured, and the people rejoiced. The Lord was suspended, and the people feasted. By this shameful solemnity of theirs, they sealed their wicked designs with their own crime and cruelty.

[Note: [Col. 0922D]

### V.—“Most beloved.”

One manuscript has the singular, “most beloved thing.” —MARAN.

“Sealed with seven seals.” Since this appears to allude to the book mentioned in Revelation 1, “sealed with seven seals,” I consider that “with seven seals” must certainly be read, unless someone should prefer “by the seven spirits,” since they too are mentioned in Revelation 1. —PAMELIUS.

“To feast at the wedding.” Thus the Colbert manuscript; another manuscript has “to feast toward [or at] the wedding”; the printed edition, “to feast upon the wedding.” —MARAN.]

V. Tell me and speak, impious Israel: did you offer such a sacrifice by immolating the Father’s own Son to him? Did you pour forth such libations—the blood of the pledge most beloved [Col. 0922B] by God? Were you leading dances, Jerusalem, while Christ was being killed? Were you offering songs with auspicious cries when you said: “Fasten him up! Suspend him!”

Because of this, amid famine and sickness, the Lord complains of you: “People of Israel, I cannot endure,” he says, “new moons, sabbath, and the great day; my soul abhors your festivals and fasting” (Isa. 1:13). Not without cause did God hate your ceremonies, in which you destroyed his sole and foremost Son.

O harsh day, mournful hour, sorrowful solemnity, ill-fated land, profane city, and people bloodied by the killing of the Lord! For they killed the Lord and released the robber.

For this reason, therefore, the Lord was compelled to make a new testament, sealed with seven seals, with Moses and Elijah as witnesses on the mountain. There he commanded that the mystery of Scripture should not be disclosed until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. But as soon as the Lord rose on the third day, he opened the New Testament, the life-giving testament, and spoke thus:

“Come, foreign nations, my heirs; for Israel did not obey. Therefore go, disciples, even to the farthest limits of the earth, and preach throughout the world in these words: ‘Come from every direction, countries of the Gentiles; enter the eternal inheritance, for Israel refused it. Do not hesitate. Here there is no distinction based on free birth, dignity, condition, station, appearance, or age. Whether eminent in dignity or noble, whether old or young, whether poor or rich, good or evil, masters or slaves—enter the inheritance on equal terms. Even if someone is crippled in his feet or deformed in body; even if he is disfigured by blemishes [Col. 0922D] or appears deficient in his head; even if he is deprived of his eyes—everyone is freely permitted to recline at the banquet and feast at the Bridegroom’s wedding.’”

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

### VI.—“Who has stolen what belongs to others.”

Thus two manuscripts; the printed edition has “who steals what belongs to others.” —MARAN.

“Fort **munitions**.” Thus the Colbert manuscript; the printed edition has the singular, “of a fortification.” —MARAN.]

VI. Let no person be ashamed of his age, lowliness, ill health, or condition [Col. 0923A], for the Lord is accustomed to sustain such a person. He restored sight to the blind, made the lame walk, restored speech to the mute, cleansed those afflicted with blemishes, and raised the dead.

Do not be afraid, you who have sinned; come first to life. Let no one who has committed murder be afraid because he committed it; let no one who has stolen another’s property despair because he took it; and let no tax collector be afraid because he extorted money. For forgiveness of sins has been established for everyone, and the Lord desires such persons: those cast down by lowliness, unsightly in appearance, broken in health, and oppressed by servitude.

For the blessed, glorious, eminent, powerful, rich, and strong refused to submit to the Lord or to enter the Bridegroom’s wedding feast; indeed, they killed him in a most unworthy manner. Consequently, each one among them who was highest became lowest; the strongest became weak; the prudent, foolish; the noble and rich, utterly poor; and the heir, disinherited. For they disowned the most gentle and benevolent King, saying (John 19:15): “We do not know who this man is, for he is not our king; we have another king, Caesar.” Therefore they have the king for whom they asked.

Then the voice of the prophecy was fulfilled which had foretold to them: “You rejected the water of Siloam, which flows silently, and preferred the water of Rassin. Therefore I am bringing upon you the king of the Assyrians, who will level your mountains and enter your lands” (Isa. 8:6). And so it happened. For when Christ had been rejected by the people, he sent the tyrant whom they had desired. He destroyed their cities, condemned the people to captivity, took their spoils, [Col. 0923C] and reduced their homeland to the desolation of Sodom.

For in his indignation the Lord took away from Jerusalem the strength of bread and water, the mighty man, the giant, the warrior, the judge, the prophet, the diviner, the venerable elder, the counselor, the skilled architect, and the prudent assistant (Isa. 3:1). He transferred all these aids, defenses, and fortifications to the Gentiles, together with his entire kingdom, its standard planted firmly. He dwelt among them, pitched camp at the threshold, established there the army of his power, and there he reigned.

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

### VII.—“To the possession of his good things.”

I have likewise restored this passage conjecturally, in place of “passion.” —PAMELIUS.

“Having obtained.” This passage was altered in the Oxford edition without notification to the reader and without any authority. There it reads: “For they were cast out from heaven, deprived of every implement they possessed—the lamp of seven lights, and the structure,” etc. [Col. 0924D] —MARAN.

“Prayer.” Thus two manuscripts; the printed edition has “a prayer.” —MARAN.

“You wept a prayer with the voice of suppliants.” The expression is extraordinary, unless indeed the passage is mutilated. Likewise, I do not know what is meant by: “Be an heir with the virgin.” —PAMELIUS.]

VII. The kingdom is no longer in Jerusalem, but in us: here is the camp, here the army, here the commander, here the power, here the bridegroom, here the wedding, here the King, here Christ, here life, here resurrection, here eternity. He is the one who was prefigured from the beginning, honored by the Prophets, embodied in the womb, [Col. 0923D] immersed in the Jordan, despised by the people, suspended upon the wood, and buried in the earth. He is the one who broke his old covenant and wrote the new, by which he called the Gentiles to the possession of his good things. And therefore we Gentiles bear upon our [Col. 0924A] shoulders the cross of our Lord, the cross which Israel acknowledged as Lord. He addressed them gently in these words: “Come to me, all you who labor under a burden, and I will refresh you. For my yoke is gentle, and my burden is very light” (Matt. 11:28–30). But they answered, “We will not listen.” Our Gentiles, however, heard and believed the saving word, by which their ears were opened, the eyes of the blind were enlightened, the tongues of those impeded in speech became eloquent, and the lame leapt like a frolicking wild animal.

For Christ established his throne with his kingdom among them; but the people were left abandoned, naked, deserted, and bereft of both the heavenly and the earthly kingdom. For they were cast out from the heavenly kingdom, having obtained all the implements that they possessed: the lampstand of seven lights, the apparatus of the Covenant, the bronze vessels, the trumpets, the [Col. 0924B] bread from heaven, and the holy land flowing with milk and honey. Israel was deprived of this inheritance and is now abandoned throughout its entire land, without nourishment and without the aid of light. For you destroyed your help and protection, persecuted the light, rejected the protector, fastened the bridegroom to the cross, and suspended the king. Therefore you are an exile from your homeland, wandering about the rivers of the Gentiles; with the voice and prayer of suppliants you wept, saying: “In my misery I have been driven from my own dwelling places; I have become a guest and stranger in another’s possession, without house or roof. Have mercy on one deserted, impious, and shamefully defeated.”

[Note: [Col. 0924D]

VIII.—**When you stretch out your hands.** This is how it must be read, for this is the reading of the Seventy at Isaiah 1, from which the following words were taken. PAMELIUS.]

VIII. This is the punishment upon Israel; this is the condition of Jerusalem. Unless they turn their minds and say, “The Lord lives forever,” they will not be able to enter into [Col. 0924C] the Lord’s rest. For he lives, and his inheritances live, and he whom you impiously killed in Jerusalem lives. And yet the Lord has not denied you all hope: he has granted the pardon that comes through repentance, if by any means you can repent. Who is so good, who so loving, so merciful?

“Receive salvation,” he says, “even though you killed me. Be an heir with the free woman, although you do not deserve it. I forgive you, if you repent.”

Therefore, if it is possible, take up a good disposition in this way; whether late or slowly, understand the new covenant. Come now, you Gentiles: explain their own Scriptures to them, and say: “Worship the Lord as his merits deserve. When you stretch out your hands, though you multiply your prayer, he does not hear you; for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, be clean, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord God. Wash the blood from yourselves, and he will cleanse [Col. 0924D] your hearts whiter than snow, your souls whiter than milk” (Isa. 1:15).

[Note: [Col. 0924D]

IX.—**From Zion shall go forth.** We emended this passage on the authority of the Colbert manuscript, which, however, has *has gone forth*. Another manuscript reads: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The printed editions read: “From Zion of God shall go forth the word from Jerusalem.” MARAN.

**Have mercy on those who stray.** Once again, this passage appears to be mutilated. PAMELIUS.

**The poor.** I restored this word, which was absent from the printed editions, from three manuscripts that were also used in emending the other passages. For the printed editions had: “The rich reduced to poverty, slaves ruling over the inheritance, those subjected to dominion called to the kingdom.” Pamelius reads *to dominion*. MARAN.]

IX. Draw near; believe the Scriptures; here is salvation: “From Zion shall go forth the word, and the law from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). He shall judge in the midst of the Gentiles and rebuke many peoples. [Col. 0925A] Let them beat their swords into plowshares and change their spears into sickles. Nation shall not take up sword against nation, for they shall cease to wage war.

“And you, house of Jacob, come; let us walk in the light of the Lord. For he has sent away his people. Your land has been filled with foreign omens, and the children have become estranged.” For it is your own land, yet the Lord’s race has become foreign. Come, therefore; enter and become, as it were, one nation. Have mercy on those who stray. It is right that the judgment of God be honored: how the great have been cast down and the lowly raised up; the strong weakened and the weak strengthened; the rich reduced to poverty and the poor brought into the inheritance; slaves made masters over their masters, rulers made subject; those who saw deprived of sight and those deprived of sight enlightened; the wise turned to foolishness, and fools to wisdom.

[Col. 0925B]

[Note: [Col. 0926B]

X.—**What was done.** The Royal manuscript reads *what was done* in the singular; another, *what was done on Horeb*. MARAN.

**In the law.** Thus the Colbert manuscript; the printed editions have *understand*. MARAN.

**They learn.** Thus the Colbert manuscript; the printed edition has *discum*. From this Pamelius, to complete the sense, had added *are taught* before the words “those who once taught.” MARAN.]

X. Indeed, those who were formerly senseless and uneducated in spirit now teach the Scriptures, and know and understand them. But those who from the beginning were learned and skilled and knew the discipline of the law do not know the law, do not know how to read, nor do they understand spiritual things. And when one of those learned men, desiring [Col. 0926A] to see, comes and understands, he asks a boy or a little child, an old woman, a widow, or a peasant, saying:

“I desire to live; be my guide in Zion. Explain the New Covenant to me; reconcile me to the Lord. See, I hand myself over to you as a disciple. Interpret the law for me; expound what was done on Horeb, the commandments given in Zion, and in the law.”

Without letters he expounds the Scriptures to them; a boy teaches an old man, and an old woman persuades an eloquent speaker. Israel, therefore, having been corrected, follows when taken by the hand to the washing-place; there he bears witness to what he has believed and, having received the sign and been purified through the Spirit, asks to receive life through the food of grace—the bread that is in the blessing. And a wondrous spectacle occurs: those who served as Levites, the priests who offered sacrifice, and the chief pontiffs who poured libations stand before a boy making the offering. Those who once taught now learn; those who gave commands [Col. 0926B] are themselves commanded; those who baptize are immersed, and those who circumcised are circumcised. Thus the Lord willed the Gentiles to flourish. You see how Christ has loved you.

[Col. 0925]

# THE SUPPER, FALSELY ATTRIBUTED TO CYPRIAN  
*(C, G, S)*

[Col. 0925C]

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

A certain king named Joel was holding a wedding in the region of the East, at Cana of Galilee. Many were invited to this wedding. Those, therefore, who had washed rather early in the Jordan attended the banquet. Then Naaman commended [it; the object is unstated], Amos sprinkled water, James and Andrew brought hay, Matthew and Peter spread it out, Solomon set the table, and all the multitude reclined.

But when the places for those reclining were already full, those who arrived later found places for themselves as best they could. First of all, therefore, Adam sat in the middle; Eve upon leaves; Cain upon a plow; Abel upon a milking vessel; Noah upon the ark; Japheth upon bricks; Abraham beneath a tree; Isaac upon an altar; Lot beside the [Col. 0926C] door; Jacob upon a rock; Moses upon a stone; Elijah upon a hide; Daniel upon a tribunal; Tobit upon a bed; Joseph upon a bushel measure; Benjamin upon a sack; David upon a little hill; John upon the ground; Pharaoh upon sand; Lazarus upon a board; Jesus upon a well; Zacchaeus upon a tree; Matthew upon a bench; Rebecca upon a water jar; Rahab upon tow; Ruth upon straw; Thecla upon a window; Susanna in a garden; Absalom among foliage; Judas upon a money-box; Peter upon a chair; James upon a net; Samson upon a column; Eli upon a seat; Rachel upon a bundle. Patiently Paul remained standing; Esau murmured; and Job grieved because he alone sat [Col. 0927A] upon dung.

When everything had been removed, Pilate asked for water for his hands; Judas handed it to him; Martha served; Hermocrates poured it out; Peter held out a linen towel; Isaiah brought in a lamp; Simeon gave thanks; Anna blessed; Rachel brought in garlands; David held out hyssop; Mary gave ointment; Martha anointed them; Adam brought in fruit; Samson held out a honeycomb; David struck the lyre; Mary the timbrel; Jubal played the psaltery; Judith led the dances; Asael sang; Herodias danced; Azariah rendered praises; Mambres played more vigorously; Isaac caused laughter; [Col. 0930B] Judas offered a kiss; Lot said farewell.

And so Jesus went out first of all as master; John as guard; Peter as net-fighter; Pharaoh as pursuing gladiator; Nimrod as hunter; Judas as informer; Adam as gardener; Eve as opening performer; Cain as robber; Abel as shepherd; Jacob as runner; Zechariah as priest; David as king; Jubal as lyre-player; James as fisherman; Antiochus as cook; Rebecca as water-carrier; Ananias as oven-tender; Thecla as beast-fighter; Molessadon as fool; Solomon as religious man; Martha as serving-woman; [Col. 0930C] Uriah as soldier; Herod as madman; Ham as servant; Tobit as physician; Noah as drunkard; Isaac as laugher; Job as mourner; Daniel as judge; Joseph as craftsman; Tamar as prostitute; Rachel as beautiful woman; Leah as hateful woman; Mary as lady; Lot as impious man; Amalek as adversary; Shem as builder; Esau as little peasant; Goliath as strongman; Jeroboam as baker.

But because Dinah was quarreling, Aaron was pouring out water, and Jonah was naked, Hoshea then asked for the sun so that Bathsheba might be dried. When this had been done, the king commanded them to come to him. They came on the next day and offered him gifts. First [Col. 0931A] of all Abraham offered a ram; Thecla, a bull; Noah, a little sheep; Rebecca, a camel; Samson, a lion; Esau, a deer; Jesus, a calf; Jacob, a beast of burden; Elijah, a chariot; Judith, a garment; Bathsheba, hair; Isaac, wood; Joseph, grain; Reuben, resin; Abimelech, money; Levi, fir cones; Moses, a box; Peter, a honeycomb; Abigail, supplies.

[Note: [Col. 0931C]

**Is discovered.** I emended thus, for the printed editions’ *is compelled*, on the authority of the Colbert manuscript. [Col. 0932C]

**Was seeking.** The printed editions have “was being sought.” We emended the text on the authority of four manuscripts.]

But because, before the day of the banquet, certain things had been stolen from the banquet, they were investigated by order of the king. Hagar had wrapped up a multicolored necklace; Rachel, a golden seal; Thecla, a silver mirror; Benjamin, a drinking cup; Tamar, a signet ring; Judith, a silk-lined covering; David, a royal spear; Abimelech had carried off another man’s wife.

Then the king commanded that all who had attended the banquet be led [Col. 0931B] to torture. When this had been done, John, though innocent, was the first to be beheaded; Abel was killed; Adam was cast outside; Zechariah fell silent from fear; Jacob fled; Enoch complained; Abimelech was disturbed; Nebuchadnezzar was transformed; Abraham made supplication; Elijah was taken away; Dinah was suppressed; Noah was shut in; Lot was struck; Jesus was crucified; Daniel was condemned; Susanna was accused; Joseph was bound; Martha was killed; Habakkuk was carried away; Thecla was given to the beasts; Ananias was cast into the furnace; Samson was restrained with bonds; Uriah was punished; Paul was scourged; Isaiah was stretched out; Jonah was stripped; Jeremiah was stoned; Tobit was blinded; Moses was not believed; Abiram was carried away; Absalom was hanged; Rebecca was put to confusion; Hagar was led away; Pharaoh was accused; [Col. 0931C] Dathan was abandoned; Korah was crushed; Isaac was bound; [Col. 0932A] Nathan was sent away; Amalek was convicted; Judas was cursed; Mambres was dishonored; Lot was discovered; Phinehas was killed; Hophni was dismissed; Eli died in fear; Dinah was restrained; Esau was deceived; Saul was bound beneath; Job grieved over what had been done; Eve was questioned; Cain cried, “I do not know”; Peter was seized and denied it.

But because many were privy to the theft, Rahab was receiving what was involved in it; Laban was seeking; Susanna was defamed; John was accusing; Rachel was denying; Moses was instructing; Tryphaena was weeping; Mary was observing; Onesiphorus was watching; Paul was sad; Jacob was swearing; Pharaoh did not believe; Jeroboam lied; Susanna was afraid; Rebecca blushed; Jeremiah lamented.

Afterward, when everyone had been searched, the stolen property was found with Benjamin, though Joseph was privy to it. But after it was proved to the king that Achan son of Carmi was the sole culprit in the theft, he ordered him to die and handed him over to everyone. Then, seizing the opportunity, Moses was the first to strike him with his heel; Jacob moved in to grapple with him; Thecla stripped off his garment; Daniel dashed him to the ground; David struck him with a stone; Aaron with a rod; Jesus with a scourge; Judas split him through the middle; Eleazar pierced him with a spear.

Then the king commanded that the dead man be buried. Laban sold a field; Abraham bought it; Joseph made the tomb; Nahor built it; Mary placed spices there; Noah closed it; Pilate wrote an inscription over it; Judas received the price. When this had been done, Zechariah cried out for joy; Elizabeth was confused; Mary was astonished; Sarah laughed at what had happened. When [Col. 0932C] all was completed, they returned to their homes.

[Col. 0931]

# TREATISE ON THE REVELATION OF THE HEAD OF BLESSED JOHN THE BAPTIST  
*By an uncertain author (G, S)*

[Col. 0931D]

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

I.—**Josephus relates.** We append this utterly astonishing narrative lest anything formerly attached to Cyprian should be missed. Pamelius appears to be washing a brick—that is, laboring in vain—when he attempts in his notes to cleanse this cesspool of falsehoods. OXFORD EDITORS.

**Josephus relates.** Namely, book XVIII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 10, or chapter 7 according to the new version. Eusebius repeats the same account from him in book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 11—or 11 according to the Greek copy—and afterward Bede in his commentary on Mark 14. Since Bede uses the same words, and these words therefore appear to have been copied verbatim from there, I did not hesitate to restore: “taken away to the fortress of Machaerus.” PAMELIUS.

**The ecclesiastical history relates, etc.** This is how I read it, because Josephus makes no mention of this matter; it occurs instead in book XI, chapter 28, of the [Col. 0932D] *Ecclesiastical History*, in Rufinus’s appendix to Eusebius. PAMELIUS.

**But after a long time.** Namely, in the time of Julian the Apostate, says Bede together with Rufinus. They also relate more correctly that monks were present when the bones of John the Baptist were scattered, not that they arrived afterward. On their authority I also judge that *Philip* must certainly be read for *Joseph*, especially since Peter of Troyes agrees in the *Scholastic History*, not to mention a certain manuscript treatise on this matter and Ado in the *Martyrology* at August 29; following Rufinus, they say that these bones were sent to Athanasius through Julian the deacon. PAMELIUS.]

I. Josephus relates that John the Baptist was taken away in chains to the fortress of Machaerus, and that his head was cut off there. The ecclesiastical history relates that he was buried at Sebaste, a city in the region of Palestine [Col. 0932D] formerly called Samaria.

But after a long time, pagans invaded his tomb and scattered his bones across the open plain. They gathered them again, burned them in a fire, and afterward cast the burned remains over the fields. [Col. 0933A] Later certain monks, religious men, came from Jerusalem to the site of that tomb. When they heard what had happened to John, they gathered whatever they could from his bones and carried them to their father Philip at Jerusalem. He sent them with other religious men to Athanasius, the most faithful pontiff of Alexandria.

There they were preserved in a wondrous manner until the time of Theophilus, bishop of that same city. At the command of the emperor Theodosius, and with Christ’s favor, this Theophilus destroyed all the temples of idols in that region, built a church of wondrous size, and consecrated it in honor of Saint John the Baptist. The bones that the aforesaid Athanasius had sent to him he honorably deposited in that church, after the neighboring bishops had assembled there in throngs from every direction, [Col. 0933B] together with all orders of clergy and people.

Now, as the Paschal festival approached, John the Baptist was beheaded under the rule of the most wicked Herod, who commanded that his head be given to the dancing girl. Long after his beheading, when the year arrived in which the church had been built in his name and his bones deposited there by the pontiff Theophilus at the command of the emperor Theodosius, the church was consecrated in his honor on August 29. His solemnity was magnificently celebrated at the dedication.

At that time, however, his head remained deposited in the place where Herod’s wife had secretly laid it, with no one knowing, after she received it from her daughter upon a platter.

[Note: [Col. 0933C]

II.—**The chronicle of the prince Marcellinus.** The text previously read incorrectly *Marcellus*. For Bede, in the passage cited, likewise quotes the chronicle of Marcellinus Comes. Marcellinus wrote an appendix to the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and Jerome and continued it as far as the age of Justinian. It was printed with the consular fasti [Col. 0933D] of Onofrio Panvinio. PAMELIUS.—The manuscripts formerly had *Chronica*. BALUZE.

**Placing it in a certain cave.** The author says that the most sacred head of the Baptist was stolen by robbers; Marcellinus Comes and Symeon Metaphrastes say by a certain potter. I think this is why Bede preferred, both in the passage cited and in his homily *On the Deposition, or Feast, of the Lord’s John the Baptist*, to write merely that it was lost through negligence. This was also copied verbatim into the martyrologies of Bede and Ado at February 24. Metaphrastes calls the potter Peritius. In those passages, as also in Usuard, it is evident from Marcellinus, Metaphrastes, Peter of Troyes, the aforesaid narrative, the manuscript martyrology of St. Donatian, and Ado’s own *Chronicles*, that *Emesa*—or rather *Emesium*, the city of Phoenicia—must be read, not *Edessa*. PAMELIUS.

[Col. 0934C]

**Bishop Jurannus.** Bede reads *Julioramus*; Peter of Troyes, *Juliaramus*. The former comes closer to the reading of Metaphrastes, who together with the manuscript reads *Uranius*, especially since Marcellinus Comes reads *Juliuranius*. All of them, however, report that he was bishop not of Alexandria but of Emesa. The author therefore appears to have suffered a lapse of memory in making him bishop of Alexandria and successor to Theophilus, [Col. 0934D] for neither Uranius nor Julioranus is numbered among the bishops of Alexandria. PAMELIUS.

**To the city of Alexandria.** Here too the author appears to have forgotten himself, perhaps because, as he said above, the bones of the Lord’s John the Baptist were deposited near Alexandria and a church had been built there in his honor. The reading of Sigebert’s *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 761 also supports the others: “The head of John the Baptist is transferred from the city of Edessa”—for I judge that *from Edessa* must be read in place of *in Edessa*. That this must be understood of its translation into Gaul is evident from Vincent of Beauvais, Peter of Troyes, Antonius, and also from a certain manuscript chronicle of the Guillelmite order by an unknown author. PAMELIUS.]

II. If anyone wishes to know everything more fully, let him read the chronicle [Col. 0933C] of the prince Marcellinus. There he will find that, in the time of the emperor Marcian, two monks came from the East to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer. In an angelic vision these monks were told:

“Go to Herod’s palace—the Herod who was once the faithless ruler here. Enter it and look carefully. Wherever you see smoke rising from the earth, dig there, and without delay you will find the head of John the Baptist.”

They did so and secretly carried it with them to Jerusalem with great honor. Not long afterward, it was stolen by robbers, [Col. 0934A] who placed it in a certain cave and left it there, until John himself, with Christ’s help, revealed it to a religious man named Marcellus, a priest who lived in that cave as a hermit, saying:
