“Take my head, which was deposited in this cave by robbers, and carry it to Bishop Jurannus, who now presides over the city of Alexandria after Theophilus, beloved of God, where the relics of my body rest.”

And Marcellus did so, with Christ’s assent.

Thus, at that same solemnity of the collection of his relics, their translation, and the consecration of the church, the head of John the Baptist was brought to the city of Alexandria by Marcellus the priest and given to Bishop Jurannus on August 29. Jurannus received it and wondrously deposited it in that same place, to be guarded perpetually. Therefore today’s festival, with Christ’s assent, should be called the collection of the relics of blessed John the Baptist, not his beheading, and also the finding and revelation of his head.

By then that same man of the Lord, Bishop Jurannus, and the priest Marcellus had peacefully and happily departed from this world to the Lord.

III. After not very many years had passed, an angelic vision spoke to a certain devout man, a priest and monk named Felix, who in those days had journeyed from the West to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer: “Felix, rise quickly and go to the city of Alexandria. There you will find a church consecrated in honor of Saint John the Baptist, where his head is hidden together with three of the little Innocents. Take it and convey it to the regions of Gaul, to the territory of Aquitaine, [Col. 0934C] to a place that I shall show you.”

Assured of this vision and now awake, the venerable old man was filled with immense joy. He immediately went where he had been commanded and, finding everything just as he had been told, rendered countless thanks to the guide of his journey. Hastening to the place, he enclosed within a single small basket the treasure appointed for him by God. He immediately set out on the return journey, joined by his companions, his seven brothers who had gone with him. Secretly traversing that whole region, he reached the seashore and found a ship, with oars and [Col. 0935A] rudders, prepared by God. He boarded it with the treasure and the pearls of great price. His brothers and companions therefore embarked with him; giving thanks and blessing God with hymns and praises, they made for the open sea.

IV. When he had begun his voyage across the sea, Felix raised his eyes, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and said: “Lord Jesus Christ, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, and who beholds the depth of the abyss; who walked with dry feet upon the waves of the sea, raised the sinking Peter with your hand, and delivered Paul three times from shipwreck: deliver us from the great waves of this sea, so that, while we live, we may bless your name for ever and ever. Deign also, Lord, to send your holy angel from heaven to be the guide of our [Col. 0935B] journey, as he once was for our fathers when you led them out of the land of Egypt with great might and with your strong hand; and lead us by a straight course to the desired place, where the holy and precious pearls are to be deposited.”

[Note: [Col. 0935D]

V.—That is, the king of the Vandals. This must be understood either of the slaughter of Chilxingus, count of Auvergne, and Amingus, count of Poitiers—Sigebert indicates something of the kind—who had come to the aid of the duke of Aquitaine against Pepin; or of the killing of Duke Waylar as though he were a king, slain near Périgueux according to Ado and Aimoin, with the men in question being called Vandals because they were descended from the Vascones, and hence also from the Vandals. Or they may have been some remnant of the Vandals then again harassing Gaul, as Robert Gaguin writes that they did shortly before Charles Martel, Pepin’s father, began to reign. PAMELIUS.

]

V. While the blessed Felix was praying these and similar words, behold, a luminous cloud descended above the ship, and from the midst of the cloud emerged a dove as white as snow. It remained motionless above the ship’s stern, by day and by night alike, until they reached the shore of the Ocean in the regions of Aquitaine. When they realized that they were not far from land, they turned aside to the harbor called Angoulême, situated in the district of Aulnay. There they left the ship for the land and rested for a little while.

Setting out from that place and traveling two miles, they found in the distance the bodies of the dead [Col. 0935C] lying upon the face of the earth: namely, the king of the Vandals with his entire army, numbering, as I estimate, about twenty thousand men. For that stiff-necked people had set out upon its wandering over the sea with a great fleet, and a violent wind had fallen upon them and carried them into the western regions, to the aforementioned harbor of Angoulême.

Word was brought to Pepin, king of the Aquitanians, that the Vandal nation was invading his kingdom. He therefore sent throughout all the territories of Aquitaine and Saintonge, as well as Angoulême—in fact, throughout all their territories—ordering the inhabitants to march against them and engage them in battle. For King Pepin was then staying in the territory of Aulnay, above the river Boutonne, at the palace called Angériacum, between the territories of Poitou and Saintonge. At length, when King Pepin with the whole multitude [Col. 0935D] of armed men encountered his enemies, the Lord wrought a great deliverance for his entire army, so that no one escaped from that multitude without being destroyed in the slaughter.

The aforesaid king saw that aid from heaven and vengeance upon his enemies had been granted him by the Lord, so that no men from his army had been lost except twenty whom he loved exceedingly above the rest. Taking them up, [Col. 0936A] he placed each upon a bier. Joyful over the victory but sorrowful over the deaths of those lost, he recalled his army, wishing to return home.

VI. When they had withdrawn about four miles from the site of the slaughter, he ordered the tents to be pitched. Overcome by sleep, he commanded that his bed be prepared in the pavilions. Then, as sleep came upon him because of his exhaustion, a divine voice addressed him, saying: “Why has sluggish sleep so overwhelmed you? Know that the head of the great man John the Baptist, together with three little Innocents, is being brought to this district from the lands beyond the sea in the East, and that because of his merit victory in this battle has been divinely granted to you by God.”

King Pepin answered the voice in the vision: “If such great benefits are in force for me because of his merit, tell me what I should do, or how [Col. 0936B] I shall be able to seek him out and find him.”

The divine voice replied: “Behold, behind you seven brothers in the garb of pilgrims are following you, and the one who appears to preside over the others is called Felix. Go to meet them with a few men and receive them kindly in humility of heart. Endeavor to bring the richly adorned and exceedingly precious pearls peacefully with you, and you will see the mighty works of God.”

Felix, the man of God, was terrified at the sight of so great a multitude of slaughtered bodies. Nevertheless, trusting in God’s assistance, he encouraged his companions and urged them to continue their journey for a little while. Turning aside opposite that place, they established a small shelter for themselves, so that they might remain there that night until morning.

VII. The aforesaid King Pepin awoke from sleep [Col. 0936C] and silently began to ponder within himself what he should do in consequence of the vision he had seen, reflecting that wisdom is found among the ancients and prudence among those of long experience. He quickly sent for a prudent man, eminent in good works, named Felix, so that concerning so manifest a vision he might petition the Lord to deign to suggest sound counsel to him.

It was therefore resolved in council that they should remove their clothing and footwear, put on ashes and sackcloth, and walk barefoot to meet the servants of God, just as he had been admonished by the divine oracle. When they caught sight of one another, both the king himself and all who were present fell prostrate upon the ground and continued in adoration until the servants of God reached the place where they lay.

When they had blessed the Lord and greeted one another, [Col. 0936D] they gave each other the kiss of peace. Rising from the ground, they tearfully questioned one another as to why the things they had seen and heard had occurred. Felix, the man of God, understanding that everything had been disclosed by God, recounted the story of how he had gone to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer and how, through divine mercy, the hidden treasure had been revealed to him.

After prayer had been offered and all had answered, “Amen,” [Col. 0937A] Felix raised aloft the exceedingly precious pearls—that is, the head of John the Baptist and the relics of his companions, the blessed martyr Innocents—and led the choir of people singing psalms with hymns and praises.

VII. On hearing this, the entire army in the camp, numbering thirty thousand men, came out to meet him as though it were one man. Carrying with them the bodies of the dead who had fallen in battle, they sought aid from heaven from the Lord through John his forerunner, asking that divine grace might deign to reveal whose relics were being carried. They declared that they had such great faith that Saint John, with the Lord’s approval, could grant whatever was asked.

Taking the small basket in which the head of the blessed John the Baptist was contained, they placed it upon each bier, touching the dead [Col. 0937B] with it. In a marvelous and inestimable manner, as soon as it touched the bones of those lying there, life was restored to the dead through one who was dead. At that very hour twenty men rose from the funeral rites as quickly as if they had been awakened from sleep; those who were being carried for burial by their weeping friends returned to life amid those same friends’ rejoicing.

When King Pepin and the entire army saw the mighty works that the Lord had wrought among them through John the Baptist, his forerunner, they clapped their hands and blessed the Lord, who performed wonders in heaven and upon earth. Felix, the man of God, and his companions were filled with joy. Together with King Pepin and his army, they raised aloft the head of the blessed and preeminent forerunner of Christ, John the Baptist, and the relics of the blessed Innocents, and began their journey with joy and gladness.

Proceeding without delay, [Col. 0937C] they came to a certain village called Vultronia. After resting there for a little while, they were met by a blind man, who was immediately restored to health through the merits of the most blessed Forerunner. When they decided to depart from that place, they took the road leading to the marsh called Mathevallis. When they had decided to rest there for a little while, behold, a man disabled in his feet, who was wholly unable to stand erect, dragged himself forward by crawling to meet them. Invoking the merit of the blessed John, he was so completely restored to health that, firm and steady and without pain, he walked with the crowds.

VIII. Now approaching the place toward which they were traveling, they reached the palace called [Col. 0938A] Angériacum, above the river Boutonne. When all the people heard of it, from the greatest to the least, men and women alike, they gathered into one body and came out to meet them. When they arrived there before King Pepin’s palace, they immediately deposited the relics for safekeeping, with great fervor and devotion, in the basilica of the most blessed and glorious ever-Virgin Mary.

All the people rejoiced with great joy, celebrated the solemn observance of that day on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, and each returned to his own dwelling. The blessed Felix and his companions, together with the venerable king, entreated the Lord, among other things, to suggest sound counsel to them concerning the place in which they should lay the holy remains.

They built a basilica, and within it a hollow ciborium supported by six marble columns, well fashioned in workmanship of marvelous beauty, not far from the bank of the Boutonne—about one hundred stadia away, as I estimate. [Col. 0938B] Having embalmed with spices and many fragrant substances the head of the blessed John the Baptist, the gracious forerunner of Christ, and the bodies of the three blessed Innocents, they enclosed them together within this ciborium and secured it with a seal of bitumen. With the Lord’s assistance, the building was happily completed.

The same king also constructed a conduit fountain. Its water was led from a distance of almost two miles through channels deep beneath the earth to his palace; it was conducted into the basilica through iron and bronze pipes and bubbled up beneath the ciborium through a hollow marble column. There the washing of holy baptism was performed, after which the water was redirected to its original point of entry.

King Pepin and the blessed Felix then summoned bishops [Col. 0938C] and priests and all the nobles of the country. They blessed the church and, dedicating it in honor of John the Baptist, consecrated it with marvelous solemnity. They endowed it nobly with estates and possessions bequeathed to them by their ancestors. After arranging everything necessary, they established monks there who would serve God in perpetuity. Thereafter the Lord worked many wonders through his servant John the Baptist.

At last, setting a limit to our narrative, let us implore the immeasurable goodness of Christ, that, sustained by his mighty right hand, he may lead us to the haven of eternal rest—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages.

[Col. 0937]

## THE COMPUTATION OF EASTER (C, G, S)

### ADMONITION TO THE READER  
JOHN WALLIS, DOCTOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY AND PROFESSOR OF GEOMETRY AT OXFORD, SENDS GREETINGS

[Col. 0937C] When the most reverend John Fell, bishop of Oxford, recently asked me to read through the treatise that follows here—which is said to be Cyprian’s and is now to be published with Cyprian’s other works—and at least to examine the numbers, which he suspected [Col. 0938C] had been corrupted, I must briefly explain what I have done in the matter.

This treatise was once found in manuscript in the Cottonian Library, but in a defective state. The most reverend James Ussher, lately archbishop of Armagh, had caused it to be copied, [Col. 0939A] and inserted with his own pen into his transcript his conjectures concerning its correction; from this we obtained the copy now under discussion. Finally, the reverend Thomas Gale, professor of sacred theology, collated the copy we possess with that Cottonian codex, restoring it wherever it had departed from the manuscript. He also added several observations of his own, in which he either suggested corrections or noted certain expressions occurring here that agree with statements by Cyprian elsewhere, thus furnishing grounds for a conjecture about the author.

When these materials had been brought to me, I arranged the matter in approximately the order you see. At one point I had thought of inserting into the text the conjectural emendations—whether Ussher’s, Gale’s, or my own—but enclosing them in brackets, and printing in a different typeface those words of the text itself that appeared to require alteration, so that [Col. 0939B] I might both reproduce the manuscript faithfully and place the correction immediately before the reader’s eye. But I changed my plan at the direction of the reverend bishop who is overseeing the publication of the whole work, so that this part might conform to the rest. I have therefore printed the emended text continuously, whether the correction derived from their conjectures or ours, and consigned to the foot of the page both the readings that were, or were considered to be, erroneous in the manuscript, and alternative conjectural emendations differing from those appearing in the text.

This codex uses Roman numerals alone, not the Indian numerals commonly called barbaric. Among them it has the letter I marked above to represent one thousand, and IIII, VIIII, XXXX, and LXXXX for four, nine, forty, and ninety, where M, IV, IX, XL, and XC are now generally written. Wherever the practice differs, I judge that it derives from the copyist, not the original manuscript. Indian numerals—2, 3, 4, and so forth—do indeed occur several times in our copy; but, after more scrupulous investigation, I understand this to be the work of the copyist and not to be found in the original. For at the date at which the Cottonian codex is thought to have been written, [Col. 0939C] toward the end of the ninth century after Christ, such numerals had not yet come into use among Europeans, but only in at least the eleventh century or later.

Nor do parentheses appear there; I do not know whether punctuation marks do. I have therefore supplied them according to my judgment. The numbers, which were defective and corrupted throughout, I restored by calculation and by consulting those passages of Holy Scripture to which they referred. A great many other scribal errors I corrected conjecturally, whether as the principles of syntax required or on other grounds. Nevertheless, I have indicated the manuscript codex’s reading so that, if anyone can form a better conjecture from it, he may freely do so. These are the matters that, several months ago, I thought ought to be brought to the reader’s attention.

After we had completed these things in this fashion and the printers had set their type, which was soon to be put to press, hope arose that a copy would be brought from a codex at Reims. The reverend bishop therefore directed that the press be halted and that we wait until that copy was delivered. This occurred several weeks later through the kindness of the reverend and most learned Father Mabillon of the Benedictine Order. It bore this title: *The Computation of Easter by Caecilius Cyprian Begins*; and the following heading was prefixed: *From Manuscript C of the Library of Saint Remigius at Reims, formerly numbered LXXI, but now 133.*

Having obtained this copy, [Col. 0940B] I collated it with ours and found it differing from ours in the ways noted in the annotations, but no less defective. At least it happened fortunately that the two codices were not always defective in the same place: sometimes ours had to be corrected from that one, and sometimes that one from ours. Moreover, in a great many places this codex confirms corrections I had made from Ussher’s, Gale’s, or my own conjectures. In such cases I omit those conjectures and cite the authority of this codex among the variant readings; I introduce conjectures only when both codices appear faulty.

This codex likewise contains Roman numerals alone, of the same forms as in the other—except for the symbol for one thousand—not Indian numerals, and no parentheses; I do not know whether any attention at all was paid to punctuation in the original. For *Calendis* it has *Kl.*, since in ancient writing K was customarily written for *Ca*, as *krus* for *carus*, and so forth. The other copy does indeed have *Kal.*, but I believe this was substituted by the copyist, who was not concerned with every individual stroke of the letters but was content to reproduce the words themselves. I suspect that the same occurred in both copies.

By the letters U, G, and W, moreover, I designate the notes and conjectures of Ussher, Gale, and myself; by the letters C and R, the Cottonian and Reims codices—or at least the copies transcribed from them for us. The errors that still remain—for some do remain—I leave, reader, to your judgment, together with the assessment of either our conjectures or the work itself and its author. Farewell. The twenty-second day of July, in the year 1682 of the Dionysian era.

## AN EXPOSITION OF THE LEAP YEAR BEGINS

### ALTERNATIVELY: THE COMPUTATION OF EASTER BY CAECILIUS CYPRIAN BEGINS

[Col. 0939]

[Col. 0939C] [Note: [Col. 0939C]

*An Exposition of the Leap Year.* Words prefixed by Ussher to his copy. From an ancient Cottonian codex written in Lombardic characters [Col. 0940C] toward the end of the ninth century after Christ. In the Cottonian manuscript the following title was wrongly assigned to this treatise, which was copied in an exceedingly corrupt form: *An Exposition of the Leap Year Begins, written in the year of Christ 243.* Gale, who collated the copy with the Cottonian codex, notes beside the words “wrongly assigned”: “Yet by a contemporary hand and in capital letters.”

Michael Seneschal, in his *Evangelical Triad, or Threefold Question concerning the Year, Month, and Day of Christ’s Birth, Baptism, and Death*, published at Liège in 1669, question 3, chapter 2, records on the authority of Godfrey Wendelin that Sirmond found at Reims and sent to Bucherius in 1648 an old manuscript bearing this title: *The Computation of Easter by Caecilius Cyprian*. We conjectured that it was the same as this treatise because of the following words that he quotes from it: “Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior, 1,579 years after the first Passover of the Hebrews in Egypt, ate the Passover with his learners on the sixth day before the Ides of April, on the fifth day of the week, and suffered on the next day, the sixth day of the week.” These words occur below, [Col. 0941C] with slight differences—a fact that, after finally obtaining a copy of the Reims codex, we have established with certainty.

Yet after inspecting this single passage, Seneschal denies that this work is Saint Cyprian’s: first, because no one before now has attributed such a work to that saint; second, because the expression *cum discentibus suis* (“with his learners”) is far removed from Cyprian’s customary elegance; and third, because Cyprian was not the sort of man to commit such gross errors concerning the art he had undertaken to explain.

I do not pledge myself as guarantor. But as to the first objection: if the work is pseudepigraphical, it is certainly neither spurious nor falsely fabricated; its antiquity is evident, and its subject matter itself shows that it was written in Cyprian’s age. And if no one has attributed it to Cyprian, neither, so far as I know, has anyone attributed it to anybody else. It remained hidden in libraries, not yet published and perhaps observed by few. Nor is it true that no one has attributed such a work to Cyprian, for Paul the Deacon does so in his *Life of Cyprian*: “He also composed a very useful chronicle.”

As to the second objection, the word *discentibus* does not occur in our codex, either here or in another passage where it appears in [Col. 0941D] the Reims codex; instead, ours has *discipulis* (“disciples”). Besides, in that age the word *discentes* (“learners”) was not considered so barbarous in this sense, since Tertullian used it several times—as the reverend bishop of Oxford points out. Cyprian especially imitated and revered Tertullian, whom, according to Pamelius in his *Life of Cyprian*, he customarily called “the Master.”

In *On Patience*, chapter III: “He for whom, had he wished it, legions of angels would have come from heaven at a single word did not approve even the sword of one learner as an instrument of vengeance.”

And in *On Prescription*, chapter XXX: “There still remain in the world those who remember them, even their own learners and successors, lest those who came later be able to deny it.”

In *On Baptism*, chapter II: “There is no other baptism except the later baptism of Christ, which at that time could certainly not have been administered by his learners.”

As for elegance, it is unsurprising if writings otherwise genuine lost much of their polish through being defectively copied by scribes unskilled in these matters.

As to the third objection—that the author erred [Col. 0942B] in assigning to Christ’s Passion a year and day inconsistent with astronomical calculations of the moon’s age—it is unsurprising if this happened to Cyprian at a time when exceedingly few people, even among the holy Fathers, were so skilled in astronomy that they could not err.

At least the following considerations favor Cyprian: first, a sufficiently ancient manuscript codex names him as the author, and no one else is named; second, the distinguished Mr. Gale observes here several distinctive turns of phrase that occur elsewhere in Cyprian; and finally, as the reverend William Lloyd, bishop of St Asaph, a man sufficiently inquisitive in these matters, points out, although there were several Latin versions of Holy Scripture, this author follows precisely the version used by Cyprian.

Lloyd nevertheless does not conclude that Cyprian is the author, because toward the end of the work the author terminates his computation in the fifth year of Gordian, during the consulship of Arrianus and Papus. That year is one year earlier [Col. 0942C] than the year in which Cyprian professed himself a Christian. Yet this is possible, since writers of history and chronology do not always carry their accounts down to the very year in which they write, but often stop at a somewhat earlier year. This would be in no way surprising here if the Easter of Gordian’s fifth year was the last celebrated under that emperor, Philip the Arab—who succeeded him in the following year—having begun his reign before Easter. It would be more surprising if Cyprian, living in another region, had mentioned the Roman consuls for the very year in which he was writing elsewhere.

Moreover, the distinct mention near the beginning of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit; likewise of Christ’s Passion and his resurrection on the third day, and of the salvation to be obtained through him; the explicit acknowledgment of the gifts of the Holy Spirit conferred as a pledge; and other things of this kind strongly suggest a man recently converted to Christianity and wishing to set forth distinctly these principal articles of Christianity.

For my part, [Col. 0942D] I determine nothing in the meantime; nor is the matter important enough for us to be greatly concerned about the author.

“Distressed.” Gale: compare Cyprian, *On the Praise of Martyrdom*, except that it has, “while distressed,” and so forth.

“In secular matters.” Gale: Proterius, bishop, to Pope Leo, *On the Method of Calculating Easter*: “The Fathers [of Nicaea] established the computation, not according to the now-introduced . . . proceedings of the Jews, nor according to external, supposed, and fabricated wisdom, but instructed by the grace of the Holy Spirit.”

]

For no inconsiderable length of time indeed [Note: [Col. 0939C] W.: Thus I restore the text and supply *fuimus* (“we were”). R.: “Year XII.” C.: “Many indeed were distressed for a period of years.” G.: “Many indeed [Col. 0940C] were distressed in the time of the ancients.”] we were anxious [Col. 0940C] and distressed—not over secular matters [Note: [Col. 0940C] C. R.: *saecul.*; and so almost always.], but while searching in the holy and [Col. 0941A] divine Scriptures to discover what [Note: [Col. 0941A] R.: “was.”] is the first day of the new month, the month in which the Jews in Egypt were commanded [Note: [Col. 0941A] R. omits “the Jews.”] to sacrifice the Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon. [Note: [Col. 0941A] R.: “to sacrifice from the fourteenth day of the moon.”]

[Note: [Col. 0942D]

“Most Holy.” C.: “I am holy, who will divide.” Gale: The word *sum* (“I am”) that follows in the manuscript is written above the line by another hand, and incorrectly for *sp.* W.: This is not a bad proposal, but I should prefer *sanctissimus* (“the Most Holy”), because he presently speaks distinctly of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and for *dividet* (“will divide”) I read *id vidit et* (“saw it, and”), and with codex R I supply *invenimus* (“we found”), which the scribe had perhaps omitted as superfluous because it was repeated.

]

The Most Holy One, who saw this, granted his favor, and we found it. [Note: [Col. 0941A] W.: Thus I restore the text. C.: “The Holy One who will divide—I am—therefore granted his favor.” R.: “The Holy One who saw it granted his favor, and we found.”] We found it, moreover, through the immense goodness and justice of almighty God the Father and through the incomparable mercy of Christ his Son, our Lord and God, [Note: [Col. 0941B] R.: “through incomparable mercy.”] who, obedient to his Father on account of our sins, [Note: [Col. 0941B] R.: “hearkening.”] laid down his life. Rising with it from the dead on the third day, [Col. 0942A] he promised his disciples eternal life [Note: [Col. 0942A] R.: “his learners.”] and gave believers in his Passion and resurrection the grace of the Holy Spirit as a pledge. [Note: [Col. 0942A] C. omits “as a pledge.”]

In him, the Spirit, himself the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0942A] R.: “the Spirit himself, the Lord.”] reveals deep mysteries [Note: [Col. 0942A] C. omits “deep.”] and makes obscure sacred truths manifest [Note: [Col. 0942A] R.: “manifest things.”] to his willing servants—that is, to those who seek with all the powers of faith. [Note: [Col. 0942A] C.: “these”; and so several times in place of “and.”] Therefore, believing and knowing with certainty that God denies nothing, but grants to everyone who wills and desires according as he himself wills, we committed ourselves [Note: [Col. 0942A] C.: “when we are.” G.: “we agreed.”] [Col. 0943A] to so laborious an undertaking.

[Note: [Col. 0943D]

“Unblemished,” and so forth. G.: Cyprian similarly writes elsewhere, “unblemished, one year old, perfect,” book II, *Against the Jews*.

“With bitter herbs.” G.: Greek *ἐπὶ πικρίδων* (“with bitter herbs”); Cyprian, as above.

“You shall devour from its entrails after the slaughter.” G.: Whence comes this?

“According to the image.” G.: Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*: “What first occurs in the image, when the lamb is slain, is fulfilled in Christ when the reality follows.”

]

In this undertaking we were not abandoned [Note: [Col. 0943C] R.: “being abandoned.”], but rather inspired by God himself [Note: [Col. 0943C] C.: “unexpected.” U.: “inspired.” R.: “inspired and illuminated.”]. We wish to show those who love and desire divine studies [Note: [Col. 0943C] G.: “those who appear.” U.: “those who desire.” G.: “those who approve.” R.: “those who desire.”] that Christians can never stray from the way of truth and, as though ignorant [Note: [Col. 0943C] R.: “what.”] of the date of Easter, follow after blind and dull-witted Jews. Since we plainly begin from God, [Note: [Col. 0943C] C. and R.: “when, when we.” U.: “a burden.” G.: “And since God [begins] us.”] we shall demonstrate not only the first day on which the lamb was slain in Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0943C] C.: “to be noted.” R.: “on which from Egypt.”] but also the dates of the Jewish and Christian Easter in past and future time. [Note: [Col. 0943C] R.: “and, moreover, of future time.”]

Let us therefore begin, dearly beloved brothers, with the reading from Exodus. [Note: [Col. 0943C] C.: “Let us begin; therefore, accordingly,” and omits “dearly beloved.” R.: “I shall therefore begin, dearly beloved brothers, from the delight of Exodus.”] In that reading we recognize God and the Lord himself [Note: [Col. 0943C] C.: “we recognize him.” R.: “we recognize our Lord himself.”] as having said to Moses and his brother Aaron in the land of Egypt [Note: [Col. 0943C] R.: “these lands.”]:

> “This month shall be for you the beginning of months, the first among the months of the year. Speak [Note: [Col. 0943C] C.: “To do.” G.: “Speak.” R.: “Say.”] to [Col. 0943B] the whole congregation of the children of Israel, saying: ‘On the tenth day of this month [Note: [Col. 0943C] C.: “the tenth.”], let each man take for himself, according to the households of the tribes, a sheep for each household; [Note: [Col. 0943D] C.: “households.”] and if they are too few in a household [Note: [Col. 0943D] C.: “house.”] to be sufficient for a sheep, he shall take with him his nearest neighbor, [Note: [Col. 0943D] C.: “a neighbor and the nearest.”] according to the number of their persons. [Note: [Col. 0943D] R. omits “their.”] Each shall calculate for a sheep whatever amount will suffice for him: [Note: [Col. 0943D] C.: “let him calculate.”] one that is unblemished, one year old, perfect, and male. [Note: [Col. 0943D] R.: “perfect, male, one year old.”] You shall take it from the lambs or from the kids. [Note: [Col. 0943D] R.: “and from.”] It shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole multitude of the congregation of the children of Israel shall kill it [Note: [Col. 0943D] C. and R.: “shall kill.” R.: “the whole.”] at evening.
>
> “‘They shall take some of the blood and put it upon the two doorposts and upon the lintel [Note: [Col. 0944C] R.: “lintels.”] in the houses in which they eat it. [Note: [Col. 0944C] C.: “you eat.”] They shall eat that flesh by night, roasted with fire; they shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs. [Note: [Col. 0944C] R.: “with bitterness.”] You shall eat none of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted: the head with the feet and the entrails. You shall leave none of it until morning, and you shall break no bone from it. Whatever remains of it until morning shall be burned with fire. You shall devour from its entrails after its slaughter. [Note: [Col. 0944C] R. correctly omits “you shall devour from its entrails after its slaughter.”]
>
> “‘You shall eat it in this fashion: your loins girded, your shoes upon your feet, [Note: [Col. 0944C] C. omits “and your staffs in your hands.”] and your staffs in your hands. You shall eat it in haste, for it is the Passover of the Lord.’”

Thus, through Moses, God commanded the entire congregation of the children of Israel, in the new month that is the beginning of months and the first among the months of the year, in what attire they were to eat the Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon. This was surely for the purpose [Note: [Col. 0944C] C.: “still.”] both of revealing his divinity to us who believe in Christ and of demonstrating, even then from the beginning of the world, their act of brigandage.

For in Egypt at evening—[Col. 0944B] that is, in the final times of the world—they went out girded and shod, [Note: [Col. 0944C] C. omits “and those who in Egypt at evening.”] with swords and clubs against the unblemished Lamb of God, [Note: [Col. 0944D] R.: “the Lamb of God.”] on the evening of the first day of Unleavened Bread; and they perpetrated against him everything that had been foretold by all God’s prophets. [Note: [Col. 0944D] C. omits “all.” R. omits “God’s.” R.: “foretold.”]

Therefore, since we now celebrate Easter not according to the image as they did, but according to the reality, in commemoration of the Passion of the Son of God, [Note: [Col. 0944D] C.: “because.” C. omits “of the Passion.” R.: “for them also.” C.: “formerly.”] the first thing we must do is diligently inquire, with all the strength of our faith, into nothing other than what the new month is, where it begins, and where it ends. Then, and not before, we shall discover that the Passover cannot be observed by the Jews themselves either before or after the fourteenth day of the moon. [Note: [Col. 0944D] R.: “when the fourteenth day of the moon has been found.” C.: “to observe.”]

Holy and divine Scripture in Genesis plainly begins to show us this very thing, saying: [Col. 0944C] “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. The earth [Col. 0945A]

[Note: [Col. 0945C]

Which is now understood to be. W. Codex C has this entire passage very differently, and plainly has a different calculation (from that of the others): “On this” (I read, “It is now”) “is understood to be the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. From which day, reckoning” (I read “computing”), “some of us who were former” (I read “earlier”) “wished to identify this new month.” For they said that this same month began on the eighth day before the Ides of March and ended on the day of the Nones of April; and” (I read “And”) “therefore those twenty-nine days. Let us return to Genesis,” etc. Thus the author here rejects two opinions held by those who sought—before his time—the beginning of the first month: one in codex R, which, because it is set out at greater length, we admit into the text; the other in codex C, which we present in the notes. Those whom codex R mentions seem to have believed that the moon, created with the sun on the fourth day of the world, was as though fourteen days old; so that at the close of that day and the beginning of the second there was the full moon, which they call the fifteenth moon, and this precisely at the equinox. Consequently, on the first day it had been the eleventh moon. Therefore, reckoning the year of the world to begin from the first day, they divided the thirty [Col. 0945D] days of which they wished the full month to consist into two parts, one of eleven days and one of nineteen. Thus, when the twelfth month of the lunar year had ended—that is, after 354 days—then, for the new moon of the first month, either one had to go back eleven days in the common solar year, which is eleven days longer than the common lunar year, or, when an embolismic thirteenth month of thirty days had been inserted, go forward nineteen days. The author does not here reject this division of the thirty days, but he does reject their choice of the day in the solar year on which they supposed that the world had been created on the first day, and therefore the moon on the fourth. For they reckoned that first day on which the world was created as the eighth day before the Kalends of April, that is, March 25. In order that the moon might be eleven days old on that date, they reckoned that the month had begun, as it were, on the Ides of March, that is, March 15; and consequently, since it consisted of thirty days, that it ended on the Ides of April, which is April 13; and therefore that the moon was fourteen days old on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, that is, March 28, when the moon was created. Those whom codex C mentions, however, reckoned that first day of the world as the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, that is, March 22; and that this first month of twenty-nine days had begun on the eighth day before the Ides of March, that is, March 8, and ended on the Nones of April themselves, that is, April 5. Thus the moon would have been fourteen days old on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, that is, March 21, and that first day of the world would have been the full moon, or the fifteenth moon. Codex C indeed appears to agree with them in the paragraph “After this I shall speak briefly” (which follows here in the notes), where it is said that the Hebrews never celebrated Passover before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, because on that day the moon born on the eighth day before the Ides of March was fourteen days old. Yet even here that codex is not consistent with itself, since immediately afterward it says [Col. 0946D] that the moon, on the fourth day of the week, became the fifteenth moon at the equinox on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. This comes closer to the former opinion, which said that the moon was made fourteen days old on that day. But codex R—and indeed codex C in what follows—also rejects this opinion, assigning the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that is, March 17, as the first day on which Passover can be celebrated, at the fourteenth moon. Its new moon, or first moon, would therefore have been the fourth day before the Nones of March, which is March 4. In what follows he strives to establish this opinion, so that there can be no doubt that codex C is corrupt in that passage.

[…] however, was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the [Note: [Col. 0945B] C. water.] waters. And God said: “Let there be light”; and light was made, and God saw the light, that it was good. And God divided between the light and [Note: [Col. 0945B] C. omits between.] the darkness. And God called the light day, and the darkness [Note: [Col. 0945B] C. omits called.] he called night. And [Note: [Col. 0945B] C. evening was made,] evening came and morning came, one day.”

[Note: [Col. 0945B] C. It should be referred, and omits therefore.] By relating and thus intimating to us that the Lord himself divided between the light and [Note: [Col. 0945B] R. omits between.] the darkness—that is, between day and night—Holy Scripture clearly [Note: [Col. 0945B] R. we show.] shows that this is the first day and [Note: [Col. 0945B] C. its following night.] its succeeding night. Between these the artificer of all things divided equally, that is, faultlessly. [Note: [Col. 0945B] C. wrongly inserts night between “between these” and “the day of all.”]

[Note: [Col. 0945B] C. on this. G. it is now. R. “who now,” etc.; but codex C has this whole passage very differently, as in the notes appended below.] This day is now understood to be the eighth day before the Kalends of April. From that day, some of us who came earlier, wishing to identify this new month and, once the fourteenth moon had been found within it, to demonstrate the day of Passover according to the Jews, calculated and said that this same month began on [Note: [Col. 0945B] R. the Ides.] the Ides of March and ended on the Ides of April; and so they stumbled. Consequently, although they correctly divided those [Note: [Col. 0945B] R. thirty of Genesis although.] thirty days [Col. 0946A] into [Note: [Col. 0945B] R. eleven and ten and nine.] eleven and nineteen—namely, [Note: [Col. 0946B] W. I rewrite thus. R. “they know and into.”] counting eleven backward in a common year and arriving at the Ides of March, and carrying [Note: [Col. 0946B] R. ten and nine.] nineteen forward into that former year in which an embolism occurs and arriving at the Ides of April—they erred in this, as I have said, because they could not ascertain the true first day of the new month. That matter will now be demonstrated as truly established, since in the *Pinax* composed by us no year will be found to cause an error.

Therefore, wishing to show truly where this month begins and where it ends, let us return to Genesis, which has related to us that [Note: [Col. 0946B] R. the Lord.] God himself divided between the first day and the first night. From this we recognize that no one other than [Note: [Col. 0946B] R. the Lord.] God himself divided also between the second and [Note: [Col. 0946B] C. omits between.] the third day and night [Note: [Col. 0946B] C. omits also.], [Col. 0946B] and thus, from the fourth day onward, [Note: [Col. 0946B] R. “caused this office of the sun and moon to shine.”] assigned this office to the sun and moon. For these are the two greater luminaries of which [Note: [Col. 0946B] R. “the Lord said.”] God said: “Let luminaries be made in the firmament of heaven [Note: [Col. 0946B] C. “so that they may bring forth”; U. “may obey”; G. “so that they may appear”; R. “so that they may shine.”] so that they may appear over the earth and divide between day and night; and let them be [Note: [Col. 0946B] C. “for signs, and for days and months and seasons and years.”] for signs, for seasons, [Col. 0947A] [Note: [Col. 0947C]

For this reason. W. Codex C likewise has this entire passage very differently and adapts to the eighth day before the Kalends of April what codex R adapts to the fifth day before the Kalends of April. It reads as follows: “After this I shall speak briefly: those Hebrews who were then worthy, taught by the Spirit of God, also [calculated] each year according to the course of the moon; they never celebrated Passover before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. The moon born on the eighth day before the Ides of March is fourteen days old on the eleventh” (read “twelfth”) “day before the Kalends of April, together with which it had acquired so great an office. This, therefore, is why, when the fifteenth moon is renewed in each month, it is cut off” (read “the sun advances ahead of it”); “and therefore the sun is found to travel eleven days and a quarter of a day more during a year. And thus the moon that on the fourth day of the week at the equinox, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, had become the fifteenth moon, was found, when the first year was completed, to be the twenty-sixth moon on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Likewise” (read “Again”) “in the second year, after nineteen was subtracted, it was found to be the seventh. In the third year, the eighteenth; in the fourth, the thirtieth; in the fifth, the eleventh; in the sixth, the twenty-second; in the seventh, the third; but in the eighth year it was found to be the fifteenth, just as it had been placed in the firmament of heaven in the beginning, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the fourth day of the week.” On this Galaeus makes the following note: “After this I shall state everything briefly: Passover was never celebrated among the Jews before the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. The moon born on the eighth day before the Ides of March is fourteen days old on the eleventh” (read “twelfth”) “day before the Kalends of April.” Obs. This is from the discussion *On the Paschal Reckoning* by Murinus, bishop of Alexandria. I do not know who Murinus is. It is found together with this writer (Cyprian) in the Cottonian codex and is written in precisely the same hand. He commends Josephus, who first composed a cycle of nineteen years, Anastasius, Theophilus, Cyril, Dionysius Exiguus, and Victorinus, who wrote to Pope Hilary, bishop of the city of Rome. [Col. 0948C]

It makes a month of twenty-nine. W. I supply the sign S, meaning one-half, which appears to have dropped out, and similarly after thirty immediately below. For 354 divided by 12 gives 29½; likewise 365¼ divided by 12 gives approximately 30½. Thus the Hebrew month was 29½ days and the Roman month approximately 30½ days. Accordingly, one should read XXIX S, and likewise XXX S, and immediately afterward, “Therefore between XXIX S and XXX S,” etc.

Eleven hours and a quarter of an hour. W. This is not to be understood of the increase of the whole month, for eleven and a quarter hours, multiplied twelve times according to the number of months, will not amount to the corresponding number of days. It refers rather to the increase of a half-month: how much the sun has gained from the beginning of the month to the full moon. That is, by the time of the full moon, when half the month has passed, the sun will have advanced by the same amount, or will have traveled ahead—meaning that it will have spent more time traversing its half-month than the moon spent traversing its own. Taken twenty-four times—for there are that many half-months in the year—this will amount to the corresponding number of days, [Col. 0949C] namely eleven and a quarter days, the amount by which the solar year exceeds the lunar year.]

and for days, and for years; and let them shine in the [Note: [Col. 0947B] R. solid structure.] firmament of heaven, [Note: [Col. 0947B] C. so that.] so that they may shine over [Note: [Col. 0947B] C. “the earth,” etc., omitting what follows.] the earth.” And so it was done. And God made two greater luminaries, the greater luminary as the beginning of the day and the lesser luminary as the beginning of the night,” etc. These, then, are the two luminaries that received not only this office, of dividing between day and night, but also that of serving for signs, seasons, days, and years.

[Note: [Col. 0947C] W. Codex C has this entire passage very differently, as in the notes appended below.] For this reason, therefore, those Hebrews who were then worthy, having been taught [Note: [Col. 0947C] R. the Spirit.] by the Spirit of God, also calculated each year according to the course of the moon. And, in order to bring it into correspondence with the course of the sun, within sixteen years they divided the thirty days of the first month into two parts—not equally, but according to calculation. As we said above, our predecessors, following the Hebrews, correctly divided them [Note: [Col. 0947C] “eleven and nine”; read “into eleven and nineteen.”] into eleven and nineteen, but failed to ascertain the first day of the first month and therefore erred. The first day of the new month, according to the course of the moon as it decreases twelve times, is recognized as the [Note: [Col. 0947C] R. seventeenth.] sixteenth day before the Kalends of April. On that day, at the same hour, the moon was found in the same condition in which it had been made on the fifth day before the Kalends of April in the preceding year. The Hebrews count [Note: [Col. 0947C] C. 257.] 354 days in that year, down to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April. Those who calculate according to the course of the sun, however, after eleven days and a quarter of a day, find that the year has been completed on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, when 365 days and [Note: [Col. 0947C] W. I supply “a quarter of a day,” because of the “and” that still remains.] a quarter of a day have been completed; and thus they designate the fifth day before the Kalends of April [Col. 0948A] as the first day of the coming new month. Consequently, combining the four quarter-days of a four-year period into one day, in every fifth year they insert it not on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, but [Note: [Col. 0948B] R. “they insert the fifth day before the Kalends of March.”] on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, lest they add a whole day to the first day of the coming new month and overturn this entire order, which the earlier Hebrews had established by a sure calculation even before Rome itself was founded.

The Hebrew year, therefore, divided into twelve months, makes each month 29½ days. Similarly the Roman year, divided [Note: [Col. 0948B] R. “into twelve tenths,” which should be read “into twelve also.”] also into twelve parts, makes [Note: [Col. 0948B] R. months.] each month 30½ days. Therefore, the difference between 29½ and [Note: [Col. 0948C] R. 31.] 30½ is understood to be eleven hours and [Note: [Col. 0948C] R. a fourth.] a quarter of an hour. The sun, when it was made the beginning of the day, traveled ahead during those eleven and a quarter hours. Likewise, since the moon was promised that it would become the beginning of the night, it was not fitting for it to come into being after sunset and thus be seen in heaven, since it ought to have been visible and to have followed from the [Note: [Col. 0948C] W. I would prefer “first,” because of the following “together with which.”] first day, together with which it had acquired so great an office. This, therefore, is why, whenever the fifteenth moon is renewed each month, the sun advances ahead of it. And therefore the sun is found to travel eleven days and a quarter of a day more during a year.

And thus the moon that had been made the fifteenth moon on the fourth day of the week, the fifth day before the Kalends of April, was found, when the first year was completed, to be the twenty-sixth and one-quarter moon on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 0948C] W. I supply what had dropped out: *qu.* for one-quarter and *dod.* for three-quarters, because 7½ and 22½ still appear.] Again, in the second year, after eleven and one-quarter days were added, it was found to be 7½ on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. In the third year, 18¾ on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. In the fourth year, 30 on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. In the fifth year, 11¼. In the sixth year, 22½. In the seventh year, 3¾. But in the eighth year [Col. 0949A] [Note: [Col. 0949C]

Concerning the lunar course. G. Observe, therefore, the lunar course according to the Greeks’ first rule, in the Egyptian manner and not according to the epacts.

After eighteen days had been carried forward, on the second day before the Kalends of May. W. Codex R has nineteen, perhaps because an embolismic month is customarily thirty days long, and therefore nineteen days must be taken in the forward direction. But this is not so with the first month of the new year. This may have caused the copyist to put nineteen here in place of eighteen, as is commonly done elsewhere when there is an embolism. But XVIII must certainly be read, with codex C. For nineteen days carried forward after the day before the Ides of April would extend not to the day before the Kalends, but to the Kalends of May themselves; that, therefore, would have to be substituted here if XIX were retained there. Similarly, where codex C has “after eighteen days had been carried forward, on the third day before the Kalends of May,” one must read “the second day,” or “the day before the Kalends.”

But lest in the second month. W. Codex C has: “But lest they begin to celebrate Passover in the second month, [I supply: counting not forward] but backward—that is, subtracting the days of that moon—they found the fourteenth moon and the sixth day of the week on the Kalends of April.” These words are clear enough and sufficient for the point being stated. Codex R, however, perhaps through interpolation, has the matter at greater length as follows: “But lest they begin to celebrate Passover in the second month, and not in the first month, which runs from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, counting backward from the twenty-five days of the moon”—for it had that many on the day before the Ides [Col. 0950C] of April—“that is, subtracting eleven days of that moon, they found fourteen ten” (the “ten” is superfluous) “and the sixth day of the week, on the Kalends of April themselves.” These words cannot be correct, for from the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May there are only seventeen days, even if both endpoints are included. One must certainly read “from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.”

For at the first time. This passage, which is entirely absent from codex C, is defective in R; I have supplied it as best I could. The meaning is this: since the solar year of 365¼ days exceeds the common lunar year [Col. 0950D] of 354 days by 11¼ days, in the first common solar year of 365 days a quarter-day is lacking; in the second year, because of a similar deficiency, one-half will be lacking; in the third, three-quarters. When this is joined to the similar quarter in the fourth year, it completes an *as*, that is, one whole day. Inserted into that fourth year, it therefore makes the year one of 366 days, called bissextile because the sixth day before the Kalends of March is placed twice. The result is that the fifth day before the Kalends of March, and every day following it, occurs one day later than it would have if that intercalation had not been made. Consequently, the retrogression of eleven days which had to be made for a common lunar year in a common solar year must now, in a bissextile year, be made by twelve days, because the solar year now extends twelve days beyond it. Conversely, the advancement for an embolismic year, otherwise nineteen days, must now be eighteen days.]

it was found to be the fifteenth moon on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, just as it had been made in the beginning.

Thus instructed by this calculation—not by their own wisdom, but by God’s—the Hebrews could not [Note: [Col. 0949B] C. err.] err concerning the [Note: [Col. 0949B] R. moon’s.] lunar course, [Note: [Col. 0949B] R. omits “according to the Greeks’ first rule, in the Egyptian manner and not according to the lunar epacts.”] according to the Greeks’ first rule, in the Egyptian manner and not according to the lunar epacts. And therefore, when they first sacrificed the Passover in Egypt, on the day before [Note: [Col. 0949B] R. the Ides of April.] the Ides of April, the second day of the week, at the fourteenth moon, then, when the first year had been completed, they could not again [Note: [Col. 0949B] R. on the day before the Ides of April.] celebrate Passover on the second day before the Ides of April, because the moon was found by them to be not the [Note: [Col. 0949B] R. fourteen-tenth.] fourteenth but the twenty-fifth. Therefore, seeking the [Note: [Col. 0949B] R. fourteenth.] fourteenth, they necessarily had to find the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 0949C] R. omits moon.] moon on the second day before the Kalends of May by carrying [Note: [Col. 0949C] C., correctly, eighteen; R. nineteen.] eighteen days forward.

But lest they begin to celebrate Passover in the second month and not in the first month—which [Col. 0949B] runs from the [Note: [Col. 0949C] R. thirteenth.] sixteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May—they counted backward from the twenty-five days of the moon [Note: [Col. 0949C] C. omits “and not in the first month, which runs from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, from the twenty-five days of the moon.”], [Note: [Col. 0949C] C. “but backward” (read “not forward, but backward”).] that is, subtracting eleven days of that moon, and found the moon to be fourteen days old on the sixth day of the week, the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 0949C] R. “fourteen ten.”] [Note: [Col. 0950B] R. “on the Kalends themselves.”] This was the first common year.

Likewise, in the second common year, the fourteenth moon occurred on the [Note: [Col. 0950B] R. eleventh day.] twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the third day of the week. But in the third year, they did not count backward, lest they pass beyond the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, which is the first day of the first month, [Note: [Col. 0950B] C. “But in the third year, in the *Pinax*, in which the bissextile day and embolism are found,” etc., omitting several intervening lines.] and fall within the twelfth month of the preceding year. [Note: [Col. 0950B] R. “and it had fallen in the month twelve of the preceding year.”] Instead they calculated differently. For this was the year in which they had to carry forward not [Note: [Col. 0950B] R. “ninth ten.”] nineteen days, but, after subtracting one, [Note: [Col. 0950B] R. “nineteen eight.”] eighteen. By God’s grace we shall explain what this one day is that is subtracted [Note: [Col. 0950B] R. “which new day is subtracted from nineteen.”] from the nineteen.

For at the first time, when Passover was observed in Egypt, a quarter-day was owing in that very year. In the first following year it became one-half; with the addition of the second year it became three-quarters; but in the third year it became an *as*, a whole day. Thus this is the third year in the *Pinax* in which [Note: [Col. 0950B] W. I thus supply what is defective in R: “For at the first time when Passover was observed in Egypt, there was an amount owing in that very year. In the second year, when it was added, it became …; but in the fourth year it became an *as*” (among other things, the signs for one-quarter, one-half, and three-quarters have dropped out).] the bissextile day and embolism are now found. [Note: [Col. 0950C] C. “the bissextile day,” and omits now.] In that year Passover is shown to have occurred at the fourteenth moon, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, the second day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0950C] C. omits “to have occurred.”] [Col. 0950B]

In the fourth, a common year, it occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day of the week. Likewise, in the fifth common year, the [Note: [Col. 0950C] R. omits fourteenth moon.] fourteenth moon occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends [Note: [Col. 0950C] C. omits of April.] of April, the third day of the week. In the sixth year, an embolismic year, it occurred on the Nones of April, the second day of the week. In the seventh year, a bissextile year, it occurred on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0950C] C. omits: “In the sixth year, an embolismic year, on the Nones of April, the second day of the week. In the seventh year, a bissextile year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day of the week.”] [Note: [Col. 0950C] R. “a bissextile but common year.”] [Note: [Col. 0950C] R. “with an embolism, on the second day before the Ides.”] In the eighth year, an embolismic year, it occurred on the day before [Col. 0951A] [Note: [Col. 0951C]

We calculated above. Ussher indicates that *compotavimus* should be substituted for *computavimus* (and similarly several times), since in that age *compotus*, *compotista*, etc., were commonly used for *computus*, *computista*, etc.

And therefore. According to this hypothesis he could have arranged the *Pinax* in periods of eight years, since after eight years the fourteenth moon returns to the same calendar [Col. 0952C] date, though not to the same day of the week; indeed, not even after sixteen years does it return to the same day of the week. He preferred, however, to calculate by periods of sixteen years—which he calls a *sedecennitas*; I would prefer *sedecennium*—perhaps because after sixteen years it returns to the immediately preceding day of the week, which does not happen after eight years. We have here reconstructed, according to the author’s intention, the *Pinax* itself, which had been lost.

The immediately following Lord’s Day is the Christian Passover.] the Ides of April, the fifth day of the week.

Behold, therefore, how we calculated above that after eight years the fifteenth moon was again found on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 0951B] C. adds: “after the eighth year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April,” which accords with its own calculation reviewed above.] Thus after eight years the fourteenth moon was found on the day before the Ides of April, [Note: [Col. 0951B] C. “after the eighth year, on the second day before the Ides.”] but it was found to be the fifth day of the week, not the second as before. [Note: [Col. 0951B] C. omits is.] [Note: [Col. 0951B] R. “but the day of the week was found to be not the second but the fifth,” omitting “as before.”] And therefore we show that, in the same *Pinax*, the fourteenth moon returns to its original day not after eight years, but after sixteen years; [Note: [Col. 0951B] W. I supply thus. C. “not this same *Pinax*.” R. “this same *Pinax*.”] [Note: [Col. 0951B] C. “not for eight, but sixteen to the day,” in place of “not after eight years, but after sixteen years, to its day.”] and in it we marked the bissextile years according to the course of the sun, without the error of the ignorant. [Note: [Col. 0951B] R. “therefore.”] Although, when this same cycle has completed sixteen years and an embolism has been inserted, the fourteenth moon then occurs on its fixed date, it nevertheless does not occur on the second day of the week, but on the first. [Note: [Col. 0951B] R. “the sixteenth year completed.” C. “sixteen years completed.”] [Note: [Col. 0951B] R. “heaven.”] [Note: [Col. 0951B] R. and C. “in the embolism.”] [Note: [Col. 0951B] R. and C. omit “nevertheless it does not occur on the second day of the week.” R. “nevertheless it does not occur on the second day of the week, but on the first.”]

Likewise, when the second sixteen-year period is completed, it occurs on the seventh day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0951B] C. “when completed it occurs.”] The third occurs on the sixth day of the week; the fourth on the fifth. [Note: [Col. 0951C] C. omits “The third, however, on the sixth day of the week; but the fourth on the fifth.”] The fifth [Col. 0951B] sixteen-year period occurs on the fourth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0951C] R. “the sixteen-year period shows the day.”] The sixth sixteen-year period occurs on the fourth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0951C] omits “the fourth day of the week; the sixth sixteen-year period.”] [Note: [Col. 0951C] R. ten-year period.] But the seventh, when it has completed 112 years, returns to the second day before the Ides of April and the moon is found to be fourteen days old on the second day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. “when the sevenfold period has completed the year.”] [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. “the day before the Ides.”] [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. comes.] [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. “the fourteenth moon and the second day of the week.”]

These, therefore, are the 112 years through which we cycle; and, calculating the years from the first day on which Passover was observed in Egypt, we arrive at Christ and demonstrate the day of his Passion and Resurrection. [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. omits “112 through.” R. “cycling, and calculating the years to the first day of Passover observed in Egypt.”] [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. “we shall arrive.”] [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. omits “and Resurrection.”]

First, however, we must set out the remaining eight years of the *Pinax*, for we have calculated only through the eighth. [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. “First, so that the remaining year, the eight *Pinakes*.”] Thus in the ninth, a common year, the fourteenth moon and the second day of the week coincide on the Kalends of April. Likewise, in the tenth common year, they coincide on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day of the week. In the eleventh year, a bissextile and embolismic year, they coincide on the sixth day before the Ides of April, the fifth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. “a bissextile year and with embolism.” R. “a bissextile year and embolism.”] [Note: [Col. 0952B] C. fourth.] In the twelfth common year, they coincide on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the second day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. “the fifth Kalends.”] Likewise, in the thirteenth common year, they coincide on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, the sixth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. fourteen.] [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. thirteenth.] [Note: [Col. 0952B] R. “the sixth day of the week.”] In the fourteenth year, an embolismic year, they coincide on the Nones of April, the fifth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0952C] C. “with embolism.”] In the fifteenth, a bissextile common year, they coincide on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, the second day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0952C] R. “In year twelve, a bissextile year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, the second day of the week.”] [Col. 0953A] [Note: [Col. 0953C]

Passover on the Kalends. Namely, in the ninth year of the third sixteen-year period.

Passover on the sixth. Namely, after an entire *Pinax* of 112 years had been completed seven times—or 784 years—in year 83 of the eighth *Pinax*, that is, in the third year of the sixth sixteen-year period.

Passover on the twelfth. Namely, after eight *Pinakes*, in year 74 of the following one, or the tenth year of its fifth sixteen-year period.

Passover on the twelfth. Namely, after nine *Pinakes*, in year 106 of the following one, that is, in the tenth year of its final sixteen-year period. As is clear below, however, he counts 995 years from the Exodus to the captivity of Jeconiah; from there to the edict of Cyrus, 70 years; and from there to the end of the seven weeks, 49 years, making 1,114.

But Jesus himself also. G. The passage is cited by Bucherius.

Passover on the sixth. Namely, after fourteen *Pinakes*, in year 11 of the following one. This is also the passage—though corrupt—which Seneschallus cites from Bucherius and which confirms the correction of the calculation that I had proposed above. Ussher had already restored 1,579 in place of I DLXXIV, where V had dropped out, as is evidently required by the computation of all the years that follows below. From the *Pinax* I had accordingly restored the date, as you see. Codex R confirms this correction.

His own 318. This passage is defective in both codices and therefore obscure; but what follows makes clear that it must be restored with this meaning: when Abraham defeated his adversaries and freed his friends (Gen. 14), he numbered his home-born men, that is, his own servants, as 318. This author believes the following prophetic mysteries to be contained in that number. Namely, the numeral sign C for one hundred signifies that a son [Col. 0954D] Isaac would be born to Abraham when he was a hundred years old. He repeated this letter three times (CCC) to signify three hundreds, corresponding to the three days’ journey made by Isaac when he was to be sacrificed—a type of Christ—who also carried the wood, that is, the sign of the cross. The sign of the cross is the Greek letter τ, signifying the number 300. But in addition to those three hundred he further adds eighteen, that is, in Greek letters, ιη. He thinks that these signify the name Jesus, Ἰησοῦς (*Iēsous*), as its initial letters. Thus, just as Lot was freed through Abraham’s 318 servants, so through τιη—which signify the same number—that is, through the sign of the cross and the name of Jesus, Isaac was freed and rendered death void, or escaped it, on that third day. All of this pertains not so much ultimately to Isaac, in whom no one obtains mercy, but to Jesus Christ, whose type he was and who is called the seed of Abraham.]

In the sixteenth year, when an embolism had been made, the fourteenth moon was found once again at the head, that is, in the first line, on the first day of the week, the day before the Ides of April. [Note: [Col. 0953B] C. therefore.] [Note: [Col. 0953B] C. seventeen, and below, the second day before the Ides of April.] On that day, we have said, the Jews first observed Passover in Egypt. [Note: [Col. 0953B] R. at first.]

From that point until Joshua son of Nun, after forty-one years had been completed, the children of Israel sacrificed the Passover on the Kalends of April, the Sabbath. [Note: [Col. 0953B] C. “ten years completed.”] [Note: [Col. 0953B] R. on Sabbaths.] Hezekiah, moreover, from the departure out of Egypt to the first year of his reign, after [Note: [Col. 0953B] W. I supply thus. C. and R. “from Egypt.”] [Note: [Col. 0953B] R. to.] 867 years, celebrated Passover on the sixth day before the Ides of April, the fourth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0953B] R. 868.] [Note: [Col. 0953B] C. third.] Likewise Josiah, in the eighteenth year of his reign, after 970 years, sacrificed the Passover on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the second day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0953B] R. 870.] [Note: [Col. 0953B] C. seventeenth.]

Ezra, however, at the time when the seven weeks had been completed, [Note: [Col. 0953B] R. Ezra.] [Note: [Col. 0953C] C. at the same.] [Note: [Col. 0953C] C. “because the week has been completed from the time.”] [Note: [Col. 0953C] W. I emend thus. [Note: [Col. 0953C] R. omits from.] [Note: [Col. 0953C] R. “the city restored.”] [Note: [Col. 0953C] R. “two hundred 578,” but “two hundred” stands for ….] [Col. 0953B]

But Jesus himself, our Lord [Note: [Col. 0953C] C. omits and.] and Savior, after 1,573 years, ate the Passover with his disciples on the sixth day before the Ides of April, the fifth day of the week; and he suffered on the following day, the fifth day before the Ides of April, the sixth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0953C] C. I DLXXIV, with V having dropped out.] [Note: [Col. 0953C] U. I DLXXIX. [Col. 0954A] This is Christ Jesus, who according to the flesh was the son of Abraham. In his mystery, Isaac, born to his father when the latter was a hundred years old, carried the wood upon his shoulders, so that from this it might be demonstrated both that adversaries are defeated and that believers obtain salvation through the wood, that is, through the sign of the cross. [Note: [Col. 0954B] C. omits “when the latter was a hundred years old.”] [Note: [Col. 0954B] C. “the same was shown.”] [Note: [Col. 0954B] C. “that the opposing sex is resisted.”] [Note: [Col. 0954B] R. “of the cross + as a sign.”]

This is Abraham, to whom God said: “In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.” [Note: [Col. 0954B] R. inserts “in you.”] Does anyone, therefore, obtain mercy in Isaac? No; rather, every person who believes God in Christ will be blessed. [Note: [Col. 0954B] R. anyone.] [Note: [Col. 0954B] C. all.] [Note: [Col. 0954B] C. shall be blessed.] And therefore Abraham, because he was called a prophet by the Lord God, knew clearly that, in the sacrament of Christ, a son had been born to him when he was a hundred years old—a son who, after the third day, rendered death void and bound that strong one, our enemy. [Note: [Col. 0954B] R. “concerning the Lord.”] [Note: [Col. 0954B] C. evident things.] [Note: [Col. 0954C] R. “the son born.”] [Note: [Col. 0954C] C. omits and.]

Then he numbered all his home-born servants: 318. That is, to signify the generation in his hundredth year, he repeated C three times, and made τ, the sign of the cross; to these he joined ιη, the name of Jesus. He then defeated his adversaries and freed his brother’s son Lot from their captivity. [Note: [Col. 0954C] W. I supply thus what is defective in the manuscripts. And rightly did the Lord himself, our teacher, say to the Jews: “If you were children of Abraham, the deeds [Note: [Col. 0954C] R. “If you are children of Abraham, do the works of your father.”] [Col. 0955A] [Note: [Col. 0955D]

Eight years. I retain Athaliah’s eight years—both codices call her Godoliah—although 2 Chronicles 22:12; 23:1; 24:1 and elsewhere variously mention six or seven, because this author’s calculation appears to require it; moreover, other chronologists count at least seven, and both codices agree.

But from the Exodus, 995. We have restored the numbers, which are corrupt throughout, from the passages of Holy Scripture to which they refer. Thus corrected, they produce the number he intends, namely 995. This is done by counting David’s six months, Jehoahaz’s three, and Jeconiah’s three months and ten days—for which one hundred days are here entered—as one complete year.]
you would do the works of Abraham.” [Note: [Col. 0955B] C. And.] But those who heard these things from Christ chose to do the wicked works not of Abraham but of the devil. [Note: [Col. 0955B] C.
