After these [Note: [Col. 0959C] C. omits and the street and wall will be restored and built, and the times will be emptied out; and after these sixty-two weeks.] sixty-two weeks, [Note: [Col. 0959C] R. 72.] the anointing will perish, and there is no judgment in him; and he will destroy the city and that holy place together with the leader who is to come, and they will be cut off in a flood, and until the end of the shortened war of extermination. [Note: [Col. 0959C] C. and devastations.] And [Note: [Col. 0959C] R. but.] he will confirm [Note: [Col. 0959C] C. confirmed.] the covenant with many for one week; and in the middle of the week [Note: [Col. 0959C] C. and half a week.] my sacrifice and libation will be taken away; [Note: [Col. 0959C] C. omits and.] and over [Note: [Col. 0959C] R. that.] the holy place will be [Note: [Col. 0959C] C. from the beginning.] the abomination of desolations; and until the completion of the time, consummation will be imposed upon this desolation.”

“‘And he will confirm,’ he says, ‘the covenant with many for one week.’” [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. confirmed.] This, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. week, and omits therefore.] is the one week that the angel separated [Col. 0959B] from [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. 670.] the seventy and placed in the last times of the age. We understand this week to contain seven years, in which Enoch and Elijah must first come and, through [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. their.] their prophecy, confirm the Gospel—that is, the new covenant—for a great multitude. For thus we heard the angel saying [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. as we heard.] to Daniel: [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. to Daniel. C. by Daniel.] “He will confirm [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. and he confirmed.] the covenant with many for one week. And in the middle of the week,” he says, “my sacrifice and libation will be taken away.”

Half a week, however, signifies “a time, times, and half a time,” which is three years and six months; these make, according to [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. what days.] the Apocalypse, [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. in the Apocalypse.] 1,260 days. During those days that Antichrist will cause great devastation. Consequently, no Christian will then be able to offer sacrifice to God, because [Col. 0959C] that most wicked one [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. Antichrist.] will begin to sit [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. sit together.] in God’s temple and declare himself to be God to the ignorant. [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. affirm himself the Lord.] The Lord Jesus our Savior must kill him [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. Christ and.] with the spirit of his mouth, abolish him by the presence of his coming, and in that very event bring the world to its consummation, as it is written: [Col. 0960A] “And over that holy place will be the abomination [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. of desolation.] of desolations, and until the completion of the time consummation will be imposed [Note: [Col. 0959D] C. and upon.] upon this desolation.”

[Note: [Col. 0959D] R. After this.] After this, let us return to the seven and then to the [Note: [Col. 0959D] R. 72. C. seventy-two.] sixty-two weeks. Those seven weeks contain forty-nine years. When they were completed, Jerusalem was known at that time to have been restored; a street was seen to have been built through its center; and a wall, raised around the city itself, strongly protected [Note: [Col. 0960C] R. were protecting.] everything within it. In that city, the temple that had been destroyed in the [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. likeness.] likeness of Adam was rebuilt in his [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. omen.] name over the course of forty-six years, [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. omits was built over the course of forty-five years.] and in the mystery [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. sacrament.] of the Holy Spirit it was anointed with oil, just as the angel had said: “So that vision and [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. may be brought to completion.] prophecy [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. prophecies. R. prophet.] may be brought to completion, and the [Col. 0960B] Holy of Holies may be anointed.” [Note: [Col. 0960C] R. may be anointed.] [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. holy.] That very Holy of Holies was anointed as the image of the human being; [Note: [Col. 0960C] I transcribe it thus, but C. and R. it itself.] and because of the Jews’ unbelief it was destroyed once again, together with the city itself, by our Lord himself in the time of Vespasian. [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. conquered.] [Note: [Col. 0960C] W. I write thus. C. with. R. through.]

For so it had been written in the same chapter that we are expounding: [Note: [Col. 0960C] C. just as it had also been in the same chapter that we have expounded. [Col. 0960D] R. which we are expounding. W. I rewrite that.] “And after [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. 72. C. seventy-one.] sixty-two weeks the anointing [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. will perish.] will perish, and there is no judgment in him; and he will destroy the city and that holy place together with the leader who is to come; [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. omits and.] and they will be cut off [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. omits in.] in a flood; [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. omits and.] and until the end of the shortened war of extermination.” [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. from the boundaries.] “They will be cut off,” he says, “in a flood.” [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. in what—in the flood of the deluge.] About whom did he say this? [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. is this said.] Surely about the Jews themselves, who, after Christ’s coming, were cut down and expelled from their own city during that [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. omits in.] siege [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. because of sedition.] and conquest [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. battle.] by Vespasian; and they do not return to it now, nor [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. omits in.] during the very end of the shortened war. [Col. 0960C]

What, then, [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. But what also in this.] is [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. omits this.] this shortened war, if not the kingdom of Antichrist, which is destined to rise against the Christian people? These [Note: [Col. 0960D] C. These very.] are the days of which the Lord [Note: [Col. 0960D] R. God.] says in the Gospel: “And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved.”

[Col. 0961A] The temple was therefore restored [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. therefore.] in the name of the first-formed man, who was called Adam, as we said [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. above.] above, in forty-six years. [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. after thirty-six years.] That it was restored in Adam’s name is demonstrated thus: among the Greeks, the first letter of his name is called alpha, μία (“one”); the second, delta, [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. is called a, alpha, one; the second delta, four; the third alpha again; and the fourth mu, forty.] τέσσαρες (“four”); again alpha, μία (“one”); and the fourth, mu, τεσσαράκοντα (“forty”). [Note: [Col. 0961C] C. τέσσαρα (“four”).] Thus the number is forty-six. [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. thus.]

This number of years is comprised [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. will be comprised.] as follows. From [Note: [Col. 0961C] R. with that one added.] the day on which the Jewish people returned to their own land, Cyrus reigned over the Persians for thirty-one years; after him [Note: [Col. 0961C] Meabesses.] Cambyses reigned for nine years, completing forty. After the forty years, however, [Note: [Col. 0961D] I rewrite it thus. R. Zmeridius. C. Hysmerius.] Smerdis the Magus reigned for seven months; [Note: [Col. 0961D] C. six.] but we do not count those months. Why? [Note: [Col. 0961D] C. omits Why?] Because they had laid [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. he had laid.] the foundations of the temple in Cyrus’s seventh month, [Note: [Col. 0961D] C. him.] and from that time until the second year [Col. 0961B] of Darius they did not complete [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. had not completed.] the work upon it. [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. omits upon.] Then Aggaeus and Zacharias prophesied; through them the Lord exhorted the people, and they came together with one accord and completed the remainder of the temple’s construction in four years. Indeed, it is clearly demonstrated in the first book [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. of Esdras.] of Esdras that the temple of God was completed in every respect [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. was in every respect.] in the sixth year of Darius.

Let us add Darius’s [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. omits of Darius.] six years to the forty, making forty-six. To those years three were added in the mystery of Christ’s passion and resurrection, and the seventh [Note: [Col. 0961D] C. weeks.] week was completed. Then, when the forty-ninth year was completed, the [Note: [Col. 0961D] C. streets.] street, temple, wall, and city itself were shown to be wholly perfected and [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. protected.] fortified. But this entire work was being accomplished in the mystery of the Church.

Finally, let us see what those forty-nine years signify. [Col. 0961C] For it was not without reason that God willed so great—that is, [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. perfect.] so prophetic—a work to be completed [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. weeks.] in seven weeks. [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. completed, and so frequently.] It is understood [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. therefore.] to have been [Note: [Col. 0961D] R. perfect.] prophetic [Note: [Col. 0961D] C. omits in this way.] in this way: from the forty-nine years, eighteen are set apart [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. gathered together.] in the name of Jesus Christ, and thirty-one remain. When these were completed, Christ Jesus suffered and rose again for the salvation of believers, and through himself showed all things to be perfected. The temple, [Col. 0962A] which he fashioned [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. formed.] not with human hands but with his own sacred hands, according to his Father’s command, [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. because of the command.] he anointed not with oil but with the Spirit of God. He built the city—that is, the Church—with sanctified stones, and within it he established [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. omits established the street.] the street. The street, moreover, is the straight [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. omits and level.] and level way by which those who walk upon it attain eternal life. For this city he established a strong and impregnable wall—that is, his holy name—through which name he subjects every adversary beneath his feet.

Behold, [Note: [Col. 0962C] R. and behold.] by God’s grace, what splendid and wondrous things [Note: [Col. 0962C] C. inserts noble.] have been shown to us through the forty-nine years. Conversely, those years demonstrate that a great calamity will overtake unbelievers and those who persecute God’s servants. [Note: [Col. 0962C] C. continuing souls.] Let us see by what reasoning. [Note: [Col. 0962C] C. because, however, the reasoning.] This [Note: [Col. 0962D] R. For this.] world, in which the righteous and unrighteous have lived [Note: [Col. 0962D] R. habitation.] from the beginning of the age, [Col. 0962B] was completed in six days. When they had been completed, the seventh day was blessed: [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. that one, namely. R. that.] namely, the coming day of the eternal Sabbath. In these days, therefore, from the beginning, God has prepared fire not only for the devil and his [Note: [Col. 0962D] R. will be.] angels but also for all sinners. The Son of God himself showed that the rich man Phineas [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. from the beginning, and omits Phineas.] was burned in its flame. This is the fire [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. Gehenna.] of Gehenna. In its likeness, the furnace, heated sevenfold at the king’s command, rose to forty-nine cubits [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. likeness.] and consumed [Note: [Col. 0962D] R. exercised.] the adversaries of Ananias, Azarias, and Misahel; but it did not afflict the three youths themselves, who were protected by the Son of God—in the mystery of us, who are the third race [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. omits of human beings.] of human beings. [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. the youths themselves … protected, and omits by.]

Thus, [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. completed.] when forty-nine years had been completed after the seventy [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. captivity.] years of captivity, they made 119 years. [Note: [Col. 0962D] R. 114.] These 119 years are joined [Col. 0962C] to the 995 years counted from the Exodus to Jechonias, making altogether 1,114 years down to the restoration of Jerusalem, when the seventh week had been completed. [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. omits years.]

With the seventh [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. omits however.] week completed, we must turn [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. return.] to the [Note: [Col. 0962D] C. 72.] sixty-two weeks, [Note: [Col. 0962D] weeks.] which contain 434 years. When these had been completed, Christ had to be born according to the flesh. Concerning him, [Col. 0963A] immediately thereafter Simeon, [Note: [Col. 0963D]

Concerning whom immediately afterward Simeon. C. *contenentissimus*. U. *continentissimus*. νουνεχέστατος (“most intelligent”), for which the translator—if indeed there was a translator—had read συνεχέστατος (“most closely connected”). G. Rather, *contentissimus* (“most content”), as one content with his lot; for Simeon himself said, “Lord, now dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes,” etc.

Which day. W. He assigns Christ’s nativity, contrary to the received opinion, to March 28—unless perhaps what he says about the nativity should be understood of the conception, which is believed to have occurred around this time, [Col. 0964D] namely March 25.

A fourth part of a day contains three hours. W. Rather, six hours, for the discussion here concerns a day of twenty-four hours—unless either he wishes the entire νυχθήμερον (“day and night”) to be divided into twelve hours, each twice as long as ours, or he wishes to distinguish three daylight hours from the same number of nighttime hours, of which he takes no account here.

Through four seasons. W. That is, on four occasions, or four times.

] a righteous man, [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. *contenentissimus*.] holding him in [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. his hands.] his hands, said to Mary his mother: “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many [Note: [Col. 0963C] W. I rewrite it thus. C. and R. of the dead.] in Israel, and as a sign that will be contradicted.” [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. is contradicted.]

Yet not only Simeon, but also the 434 years, [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. 424.] demonstrated the sign of the cross, the time of the passion, and the third day of his resurrection. Let us see how. [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. But in what, in what way.] Above we said that a son was born to Abraham when he was one hundred years old, in the mystery of Christ; and we demonstrated that no one in Israel obtained the blessing, or can now obtain the blessing, except in the seed of Abraham himself, who is [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. of Christ.] Christ. Therefore, in the mystery of Christ, one hundred are first set apart from the 434 years, [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. 437 years.] leaving 334. [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. 337.] Three hundred [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. Three hundred.] years, namely, [Col. 0963B] signified the τ (*tau*), the sign of the cross, [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. the sign of the cross, omitting τ. C. τ, the sign of tau, omitting of the cross.] and thirty-four remained. From these, three [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. from.] were subtracted [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. three.] on account of the day [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. omits day.] of his resurrection, leaving thirty-one years. [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. 33.] When these had been completed, Christ had to suffer for the sins of believers.

Let us therefore add these [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. For these, therefore.] 434 years [Note: [Col. 0963C] C. 334.] to the preceding total, and we find that there were 1,548 years [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. 538.] from the Exodus to the birth [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. of the Lord.] of Christ. Desiring to learn the date of his birth, let us carefully count those 1,548 years from the Exodus—[Note: [Col. 0963C] R. omits that is, from the first row of the table.] that is, from the first row of the table—and we shall arrive at the day of his birth. [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. Let us count.] This day is found in the thirteenth row of the sixth sixteen-year cycle: [Note: [Col. 0963C] R. sixteen-year cycle.] the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the fourth day of the week [Wednesday]. [Note: [Col. 0963D] C. omits fifth day before the Kalends of April, fourth day of the week.]

O how splendid and divine is the Lord’s providence! [Col. 0964A] Christ was born on the very day on which the sun was made—the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the fourth day of the week. [Note: [Col. 0963D] C. omits that Christ was born on the very day on which the sun was made, the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the fourth day of the week; and therefore concerning him.] And therefore the prophet Malachias rightly [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. omits rightly.] said concerning him to the people: “The sun of righteousness will rise for you, and healing is in its wings.” This is the sun of righteousness, in whose wings healing was foreshown. [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. wings.] [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. in whose wings it was shown.] Moses too is recognized [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. is known.] as speaking of him in the canticle: “And he yearned over [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. yearned over his people.] his young and spread out [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. spreading out his wings.] his wings.”

He is the Lord in whose [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. likeness.] likeness this yearly sun completes its course in 365 [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. omits days.] days and a fourth part [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. days.] of a day. This fourth part of a day contains three hours. The three hours, moreover, bear the image of those three days at the beginning of the age that existed without the sun and moon. [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. were made.] And therefore, [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. omits just as.] just as three hours, counted four times in [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. a four-year period.] a four-year period, produced one day of twelve [Col. 0964B] hours, [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. produced, so that those three hours also [produced] a day.] so those three days, maintaining three months apiece through the four seasons, demonstrated a year completed after twelve months. [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. and R. defending. G. depending.] [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. counted.]

And thus, through this manifold triad, both the [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. omits twelve.] twelve hours signified the one Gospel divided into four parts, [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. eternal; perhaps “and three.”] and the three months through four seasons—that is, through the four [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. Evangelists—the twelve apostles chosen by Christ.] Gospels—demonstrated to us the twelve apostles chosen by Christ. [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. apostle chosen.] [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. manifested.] These are the apostles by whose words we have been built up, and through whom we learned that our Lord suffered in the [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. fifteenth.] sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when he himself was [Note: [Col. 0964C] R. in the year.] thirty-one years old. [Note: [Col. 0964C] C. thirty-one.]

To the sixteenth [Note: [Col. 0964D] C. fifteenth.] year and the thirty-one, [Note: [Col. 0964D] R. omits year and.] therefore, let us add eighteen in the name of Jesus himself, producing the number sixty-five. Three hundred are lacking from this number for the year to be completed [Col. 0965A] according to the course [Note: [Col. 0965B] R. omits course.] of the sun.

Among the Greeks, moreover, 300 is denoted by one letter called *tau* (τ), and *tau* plainly demonstrates to everyone the sign of the cross. [Note: [Col. 0965B] R. by one letter.] [Note: [Col. 0965B] C. τ, *tau*, the sign of the cross, and man.] [Note: [Col. 0965B] R. the cross, a sign.] Behold, then: let us now truly believe that Christ was born according to the flesh on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which we have proved that the sun was made. [Note: [Col. 0965B] C. omits: Behold, then: let us now truly believe that Christ was born according to the flesh on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which we have proved that the sun was made.]

We must show that this fact itself was not [Note: [Col. 0965B] C omits “and this fact.”] without significance [Note: [Col. 0965B] C: “unique.”], but [Note: [Col. 0965B] R omits “for.”] was prefigured for our salvation. For on the fourth day, when the sun was made, on that same day the moon also became fifteen days old; [Note: [Col. 0965B] C: “which on the next day.”] on the next day, however, it was sixteen, and on the third, seventeen. And thus Adam was fashioned from the earth; through his disobedience he had brought death not only upon himself but also upon us. Our Lord Jesus, trampling down that death [Note: [Col. 0965B] R: “the unjust one whom.”], suffered when the moon was fifteen days old; he rested in the heart of the earth when it was sixteen; and on the third day, when the moon was found to be [Col. 0965B] seventeen days old, [Note: [Col. 0965C] C: “ascended from.”] he returned from the lower regions, from the foundations of the earth; and thus he restored eternal life to Adam himself and to all who believe in him. Therefore, just as by the course of the sun [Note: [Col. 0965C] R: “the course of the time of the Passion.”] the sign tau and the time of the Passion were shown, so also by the course of the moon the third day of his resurrection was clearly revealed. For from the [Note: [Col. 0965C] C: “many.”] first day on which the moon was made fifteen days old, [Col. 0966A] it was thereafter seen in heaven for [Note: [Col. 0965C] R: “twelve.”] fifteen days; but on the sixteenth day, just as in the sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, it was not [Note: [Col. 0965C] C omits “was.”] seen by human beings, as though dead. Likewise, on the [Note: [Col. 0966B] C omits “also.”] seventeenth [Note: [Col. 0966B] R omits “day.”] day it was not seen; but on the [Note: [Col. 0966B] R: “eighteenth.”] eighteenth day, in the [Note: [Col. 0966B] C: “likeness and name.”] likeness and name of Jesus himself, it too, restored at evening after [Note: [Col. 0966B] R: “the third.”] the third day, rose again and demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0966B] R: “showed.”] the future resurrection of us all at evening, that is, [Note: [Col. 0966B] R omits “in.”] in the last hour of the age.

See, then, [Note: [Col. 0966B] C: “what great things the day of the Lord’s nativity shows us!”] what great things the day of the Lord’s nativity has shown us! That [Note: [Col. 0966B] C omits “of the nativity.”] day of the nativity was found from the Exodus, as we have said, after 1,548 years. We have shown that these years [Note: [Col. 0966B] R omits “from the Exodus.”] were thus truly reckoned by us [Note: [Col. 0966B] C: “we shall show.”] from the Exodus, since we also demonstrate that the numerical reckoning of those years is not without significance. [Note: [Col. 0966C] C: “He showed, who has foreknowledge of future things.”] For the holy [Col. 0966B] and divine Lord, in order to show us that he has foreknowledge of future things, revealed even in those years the time when the water that washes away sins had to be sanctified [Note: [Col. 0966C] C: “his Son by water.”] by his Son, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. And therefore, just as Abraham, when he wished to vanquish [Note: [Col. 0966C] R omits “those.”] those who had taken Lot, his brother’s son, captive [Note: [Col. 0966C] R: “had taken.”], counted his household servants—first eighteen in the name [Col. 0967A] [Note: [Col. 0967B]

In the consulship of Arrianus and Papus. W. The calculation is carried down to this year, which is 243 of the Common Era. In that year Cyprian is said not yet to have professed himself a Christian, but to have done so one or two years later. Whether this treatise was written in the year at which the calculation terminates is unclear. It should hardly be supposed that Cyprian wrote it then, before he was a Christian. If, therefore, he is its author, we shall have to say that it was written somewhat later, after he became a Christian. Indeed, it rarely happens that writers of chronicles [Col. 0967C] carry events down to the very year in which they write; rather, they stop at some more notable year shortly past. That appears to have been done here as well—namely, at the last year of the emperor Gordian. For his fifth year ends and his sixth begins in the year of the consulship of Arrianus and Papus. After his sixth year had begun but before it was completed, and before another Easter, he was killed by his successor Philip the Arab; and indeed, according to Julius Capitolinus, Arrianus and Papus were still consuls.

Two hundred and fifteen years were completed. W. The manuscripts vary in this number. Manuscript C has 215, and more correctly. For since both assign Christ’s death to the sixteenth year of Tiberius, which is the year 29 of the common Dionysian era, from then to the consulship of Arrianus and Papus, which is the year 243 of the same era, there are 214 years, or 215 if both terminal years are counted. But manuscript R has 220; consequently it counts 1,791 years from the Exodus instead of 1,794, and seeks the Jewish Passover for that year not, as manuscript C does, in the third line, but in the eighth line [Col. 0967D] of the first sixteen-year cycle. It sets it not, as C does, on 12 Kalends of April, the third weekday, but on 9 Kalends of April, the sixth weekday. Yet the manuscripts agree in this—that which is common to both years—that our Easter, on the immediately following Sunday, falls on 7 Kalends of April. For whether 11 Kalends of April, that is, March 21, [Col. 0968B] was the third weekday, or 9 Kalends of April, that is, March 24, was the sixth weekday, 7 Kalends of April, that is, March 26, will be Sunday. But I conjecture that the cause of the error was this. Both manuscripts assign to Christ’s nativity the year 1548 from the Exodus, and both agree that thirty-one years must be added for the Passion. These indeed make 1579 years, but manuscript R says—because the V has dropped out—that they make 1574 years. And when the copyist, unconcerned about this, saw that according to the reckoning of others there were [Col. 0968C] 1,794 years from the Exodus to that year of Gordian, and perceived an interval of not 215 but 220 years, he assigned this number to that interval, interpolating here the five years that had dropped out there. Once these figures had been set down, that man—or perhaps someone else—observed that, if 1,548 years were assigned from the Exodus to Christ’s birth, then the agreed thirty-one years from there to the Passion, and from there to Gordian’s fifth year the 220 years that R had already set down, the total from the Exodus to Gordian’s fifth year came to 1,799 years. He therefore substituted 1,799 years for 1,794. To this corresponds the eighth line of the first sixteen-year cycle, and consequently 9 Kalends of April, the sixth weekday, for the Jewish Passover. And since, given these figures, the Christians’ Easter would fall on the following Sunday, 7 Kalends of April—which, as it appears, actually occurred, and indeed according to the canons subsequently established by the Council of Nicaea had to occur—he was sufficiently confident that the calculation had been properly set down. But the same result would have occurred, as has just been said, even if this error of five years had not entered: namely, that the Christians’ Easter in that year was on 7 Kalends of April, as [Col. 0968D] actually occurred. Thus that error in calculation belonged to the copyist, not the author. The present author congratulates himself greatly upon this agreement and concludes from it that his *Pinax* was correctly constructed.]—

of Jesus; and, because of the generation of one hundred, counting [Note: [Col. 0967B] C: “another.”] the others threefold in the mystery of the three days [Note: [Col. 0967B] C: “repeating.”], he counted 300 and made [Note: [Col. 0967B] R adds “the sign.”] τ, tau, the sign of the cross. So too, from [Note: [Col. 0967B] C: “in.”] the 1,548 years, let us deduct fifteen hundreds, and forty-eight remain. From these, when eighteen are subtracted [Note: [Col. 0967B] R: “removed.”] in the name of Jesus, thirty years are found. When these were completed, the Lord Jesus, thirty years from his nativity, was baptized by John in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar; in his sixteenth year he suffered and rose again. Let us therefore add thirty-one years to the sum, and all the years from the Exodus to the Passion together amount to [Note: [Col. 0967B] W. Thus I restore the figure from the calculation; C: 1,588. R: 1,574.] 1,579. From that time—that is, from the Passion—to the fifth year [Note: [Col. 0967B] R: “Gordian.”] of Gordian, in the consulship [Note: [Col. 0967B] C: “of the consuls Arianus and Papa”; I read “in the consulship.”] of Arrianus and Papus, [Note: [Col. 0967B] R: 220.] 215 years were completed. All the years from the Exodus, however, were [Note: [Col. 0968B] W. Thus I restore the figure. C: 1,798. R: 1,799.] 1,794.

[Col. 0968A] By numbering all these years from the Exodus—that is, from the first line of the *Pinax*—through seven sixteen-year cycles [Note: [Col. 0968B] R: “proceeding through seven sixteen-year cycles, we shall find.”], let us complete all the aforementioned years; and then, [Note: [Col. 0968B] W. I supply “to.”] upon reaching the third line of the first sixteen-year cycle [Note: [Col. 0968B] W. I supply from the other manuscript “upon reaching.”], we shall find that according to the Jews Passover fell on [Note: [Col. 0968B] R: “9 Kalends of April, the sixth weekday.”] 12 Kalends of April, the third weekday. According to our reckoning, however, [Note: [Col. 0968B] R: “the eighth.”] on the third line of the first sixteen-year cycle, Sunday falls on 7 Kalends of April. Thus, following the same sequence onward until the end of the age, we have not erred in seeking to determine [Note: [Col. 0968B] C omits “seeking to determine.”] the Jewish and Christian days of Passover. [Note: [Col. 0968B] C: “for this.”] And therefore let us always and without ceasing give thanks to God the almighty Father, who has called us to such great grace and revealed the divine mysteries through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord [Note: [Col. 0968B] C omits “and.”] and Savior.

[Col. 0971B] W. After the printers had reached this point and blank space remained at the bottom of the page, it seemed appropriate to insert here, from Bucherius, Hippolytus’s Paschal Canon, which is entirely similar to this one of Cyprian. For Hippolytus too [Col. 0971C] divided his cycle into *heccaedecaeterides*, or sixteen-year cycles—that is, paired eight-year cycles—just as [Col. 0972B] our Cyprian did. And, as here, he teaches that after seven sixteen-year cycles, or 112 years, Passover returns to the same day of the month and the same weekday. I here recast that canon, which Bucherius arranged somewhat differently, into the form in which we set out Cyprian’s canon above. [Col. 0972C]

The Sunday immediately following not the fourteenth but the fifteenth lunar day is, according to Hippolytus, the Christians’ Easter.

[Col. 0971D] The head of this canon, or the first year of its first sixteen-year cycle, is assigned to the first year of the emperor Alexander, which is the common year of the Lord 222. Consequently, the common year 243—which is the close of Gordian’s fifth year and the beginning of his sixth—is year 22 of this canon, that is, the sixth year of its second sixteen-year cycle. In Cyprian’s canon, the same year was the third line, and consequently the second year, of the first sixteen-year cycle. Therefore, although both canons have exactly the same form, they do not begin from the same starting point: the first year of Cyprian’s canon is the twenty-first in Hippolytus’s canon.

Likewise, the first day of the first month is reckoned in Cyprian’s canon as March 4, or 4 Nones of March, so that the fourteenth lunar day can fall on March 17, or 16 Kalends of April. But in Hippolytus’s canon that first day is reckoned as March 5, or 3 Nones of March; consequently, the fourteenth lunar day does not occur before March 18, or 15 Kalends of April. [Col. 0972D]

Moreover, Hippolytus assigns as the Christians’ Easter the Sunday that immediately follows not the fourteenth but the fifteenth lunar day. Thus, if the fifteenth lunar day is a Sunday, Easter is not to be celebrated on that day—which, I believe, is what Cyprian intends, although he does not say it in so many words—but on the Sunday following the full moon, or the fifteenth lunar day, and not on the full moon itself. It is indeed possible that Cyprian too, like Hippolytus, intended Easter to be celebrated not on the full moon itself when it was a Sunday, but on the following Sunday. The remains of the table in manuscript R also appear to support this.

[Col. 0973A] Finally, they disagree concerning the age of the moon. For the common year 243, which is the second year in Cyprian’s canon and the twenty-second in Hippolytus’s, Cyprian places the fourteenth lunar day on 12 Kalends of April, the third weekday; Hippolytus, however, places it on 15 Kalends of April, the seventh weekday. The full moon therefore fell on 14 Kalends of April, the first weekday—that is, Sunday, March 19—and Hippolytus’s Easter, not on that Sunday but on the following one, fell on March 26, or 7 Kalends of April. According to Cyprian, Easter likewise had to be celebrated on that very day, since it was the first Sunday after 12 Kalends of April, the third weekday. The Paschal canons of Dionysius—which we now use in Julian computation according to the intention of the Council of Nicaea—also designate [Col. 0974A] that same day as Easter for that year.

Besides these canons of Hippolytus and Cyprian, there were also other canons of similar form—namely, arranged in sixteen-year cycles or doubled eight-year cycles, and thus recurring after 112, or even fifty-six, years. This is evident from our Cyprian, who rejects one or another canon of this kind, and from Bucherius’s notes on the canon of Hippolytus.]

## THIRD APPENDIX

[Col. 0973]

## DISSERTATION ON CYPRIAN’S BOOKS *TO DEMETRIANUS* AND *ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS*

BY DOM NICOLAS LE NOURRY, O.S.B.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the Book *To Demetrianus*

[Col. 0973B]

### ARTICLE I  
#### Analysis of This Book

Demetrianus, deeply devoted to the impious worship of false gods, had frequently met with Cyprian to debate with him, not for the purpose of ever investigating the truth, but solely to defend his own religion (p. 185). Cyprian therefore disdained this unteachable, contentious, and exceedingly obstinate man, and judged that he should be refuted by silence and patience rather than by words, as our sacred Scriptures teach. But when the world was then being afflicted by the most dreadful calamities of war, famine, and pestilence, that madman [Col. 0973C] began to make an even louder clamor and openly to shout that very many people were rightly complaining along with him that the Christians were the cause of those disasters because they did not venerate the gods of the other nations. Therefore Cyprian, lest he appear to admit this by his silence, finally undertook to refute these accusations, however foolish and contemptible, in a public writing (p. 186).

He utterly demolishes them by several weighty arguments. First, he says, those very great calamities showed that the world was growing old and failing in strength. There was not, indeed, so great an abundance of rain in winter, so mild a spring, so intense a heat of the sun [Col. 0973D] in summer, or so great an abundance of crops and fruits in autumn. Moreover, metals were diminishing in the bowels of the earth, and the number of farmers, sailors, and soldiers was decreasing. Innocence was lacking in the forum, harmony among friends, skill in the arts, and discipline in morals. The calamities of an aging world, therefore, were no more to be attributed to the Christians than the fact that a man worn out by age is assailed and overcome by the diseases of old age (p. 187).

Our author then makes it plain that the Christians were by no means the authors of these calamities; rather, [Col. 0974B] the gentiles themselves were, since they had offended God—whom they had entirely and utterly abandoned—by their criminal worship of false gods, their various superstitions, and their innumerable crimes. Indeed, for that reason, and so that they might return to a sounder mind, that perfectly just God permitted the world to be shaken and almost overwhelmed by those most disastrous afflictions which his sacred prophets, cited there by Cyprian, had foretold. But such was the blindness of the impious and criminal gentiles that, in no way moved by so many and such great blows, they did not fear the wrath of God, which they were continually provoking with new crimes. Who, therefore, would not condemn those who, although they demanded the servitude owed to them by their own servants and punished those who did not obey their commands with scourges, hunger, thirst, nakedness, the sword, and imprisonment, nevertheless refused [Col. 0974C] to obey and serve the almighty Lord (p. 188)? Since they were not corrected by so many and such great blows—though these were less severe than they deserved—nothing remained for them but eternal imprisonment and the perpetual punishment of fire.

He there appeals to the conscience of Demetrianus as judge and asks by what right he himself, guilty of avarice, envy, lust, and every kind of crime, could complain of divine vengeance (p. 189). For what just complaint could he and the other gentiles then make about wars, when there was no peace among those wearing the toga? What complaint could they make about barrenness and famine, which their rapacity made still worse? What grievance could they voice about the pestilence, when their cruelty toward the dying and the dead, and their eagerness to seize those people’s goods, [Col. 0974D] was fiercer than the plague itself? Were not forgers, poisoners, assassins, and utterly unjust judges also ranging abroad with impunity at that time? God therefore, in rightful and wholly deserved vengeance for so many crimes, allowed the world to be afflicted by the greatest calamities, although he could have prevented them (p. 190).

Moreover, his perfectly just wrath was aroused by the insatiable fury of the gentiles, with which, contrary to every law of equity, they tortured and [Col. 0975A] killed Christians by every most atrocious punishment merely because of their name. For if the Christians had injured their gods, why did those gods calmly allow injuries to themselves to go unpunished, or leave it to those same gentiles, as though more powerful, to ward them off? But these gods were so feeble that they needed human protection; and when adjured by Christians, they were compelled by their words—as though beaten with scourges and blows—to depart from the bodies they possessed (p. 191). Indeed, they were forced openly, before the mouths and eyes even of all the gentiles, to disclose their deceptions and confess the coming judgment. Yet what could be more foolish and absurd than for these false gods to be worshiped with impious rites and by a human being prostrating his body, when the human being’s upright stature and heavenward gaze admonished him to acknowledge and honor the true and almighty God (p. 192)?

[Col. 0975B] He therefore exhorts Demetrianus and the other gentiles to turn to the true God, believe in Christ, and cease injuring his servants, whom confidence in future vengeance made patient. For God had shortly before given a most evident proof of his vengeance and their defense “in the downfall of kings, the loss of wealth, the depletion of soldiers, and the reduction of military camps.” From this our author therefore concludes that public calamities occurred not as punishment and vengeance upon the Christians, but upon the gentiles.

Nor does he permit the objection that God would be unjust for allowing Christians, like gentiles, to be engulfed and overwhelmed by such great disasters. For it was only the gentiles who mourned them, and by no means the Christians, who, having been made more certain of future blessings and living by the spirit rather than the flesh, overcame bodily weakness with great steadfastness of soul [Col. 0975C] (p. 193). They knew, moreover, that they were tested and strengthened by adversities, and that although all who remain in this world, as in the same house, share a common condition, nevertheless after this life they would be separated from the gentiles and obtain eternal happiness. They were therefore not disturbed by public calamities. For, having put aside earthly birth and been reborn in the spirit, they did not live for the world but for God, to whom “continually and insistently, by day and by night,” they prayed for calamities to be removed or moderated, for enemies to be driven away, for rains to be obtained, and indeed even for the peace and safety of the gentiles themselves.

The gentiles therefore could not flatter themselves because, amid public calamities, their condition and that of the Christians was common, at least [Col. 0975D] as regards the body. For the world was being oppressed not because of the Christians but because of the crimes of those same gentiles and as vengeance upon them, just as had been foretold by the sacred prophets (p. 194).

Furthermore, after the imminently approaching day of the Last Judgment, the wicked gentiles will be tormented by punishments more cruel still, likewise foretold by those same prophets. For just as the Israelites who had sprinkled the thresholds of their houses with the blood of the lamb once escaped safely from Egypt, so only those who bear before them the sign of Christ’s blood will escape eternal torments.

Our author therefore again exhorts the gentiles to [Col. 0976A] come to their senses and, though late, at last acknowledge God, in whom, as the prophets and Christ teach, is life. For they must believe Christ, who never deceives, who foretold that all these things would come to pass, who will give the reward of eternal life, and who after the final judgment will command the faithless and unbelieving to be burned in the living flames of eternal fire (p. 195). Those impious people, tormented by such great sufferings, will be beheld—the very people who had fed their cruel eyes on the horrific but brief spectacle of tortures inflicted on Christians. Then, as the prophet says, those same people will marvel at the Christians’ unexpected salvation, and will repent too late of their errors and crimes.

Moreover, Christians, who had learned to hate no one and to return good for evil, repaid the gentiles’ hatred with benevolence and, in return for torments and punishments, [Col. 0976B] showed them the path of eternal salvation. All people, so long as some part of this life remains, can obtain that salvation, provided that, after embracing the true religion, they make satisfaction to God. For while one remains in this world, no repentance is too late: pardon is given to the one who confesses, and forgiveness to the one who believes, which Christ bestows at the price of his own blood. Cyprian therefore once again exhorts everyone to follow Christ as leader, if it is possible, in such a way that after death they may enjoy eternal happiness with him (p. 196).

### ARTICLE II  
#### Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and Martyr, Is Shown to Be the True Author of This Book; Who He Was, and Whether He Was the First Martyr in Africa

[Col. 0976C]

There has never been, nor can there now be, any question concerning the author of this treatise. For all have always confessed with one voice, and still confess, that it was written by Thascius Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. There is therefore no need to prove once again, by the testimony of various manuscripts and authors of every age whose credibility is beyond all challenge, a fact that is certain, acknowledged, and accepted by everyone without dissent. Nevertheless, we cannot entirely pass over two men distinguished for their learning and authority, Lactantius and Jerome. The first explicitly cites this treatise, which he had undoubtedly read, “To Demetrianus” (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, ch. 4, p. 471); the second testifies that it was published “Against Demetrianus” [Col. 0976D] (Jerome, Epistle LXXXIII, *To Magnus*, p. 655; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 3, art. 2). We reproduced the words of both in our third dissertation on the works of Lactantius. Is this not also one of those treatises Cyprian composed against the gentiles, of which Pontius, his deacon, made only this general mention: “Through whom”—Cyprian—“the blasphemous gentiles would be defeated by refuting the charges they bring against us” (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, p. 4)? Although he does not call this treatise by its particular name and title, he could scarcely have indicated it in clearer words, as will be evident from what has already been said and what remains to be said.

[Col. 0977A] We believe that no one, however little educated, can be unaware who that most holy man was who illuminated the Church in a truly marvelous manner, not only by the sanctity of his life and the shedding of his blood, but also by his writings. He was African by origin and, as seems more likely, was born at Carthage. He had imbibed the impious superstitions of the gentiles with his mother’s milk. He was still following them when, as Jerome says, “he taught rhetoric with distinction” (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, §67, p. 119). Later, however, he embraced the Christian religion at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius, whose additional name he consequently adopted. As soon as he accepted that religion, he was so inflamed with the desire to attain its perfection that, while still a catechumen, he resolved to preserve continence and [Col. 0977B] distributed all his possessions to the poor, so that, stripped of them, he might more fully imitate the poor Christ. Not long afterward, because of his exceptional virtues, he was made a presbyter and then bishop of Carthage, although he sought to decline each of those burdens as far as he could. With how great piety, prudence, charity, holiness, and other episcopal virtues he flourished, no one can fail to know unless wholly unfamiliar with ecclesiastical history. Indeed, his works, “brighter than light,” as Jerome says (*ibid.*), breathe forth these marvelous virtues. He completed the course of so holy a life by an utterly unconquered confession of Christ, for which he was beheaded and deserved to be crowned with martyrdom.

Yet his triumph was certainly the greater because, as Pontius says, “he was the first in the province” [Col. 0977C] of Africa “to consecrate the first fruits of martyrdom”; and shortly afterward: “He was the first in Africa to imbue the priestly crowns” with blood (Pontius, *Life of St. Cyprian*, p. 10). But Cyprian himself appears to oppose this opinion. When Papinianus raised against him a certain scruple—though one resting only on ridiculous slanders—as a reason not to communicate with him, Cyprian replied: “Why did so many bishops, my fellow colleagues, not fall into this scruple—those who, when they departed from our midst, were proscribed; or who, after being arrested, were held in prison and chains; or who, banished into exile, went to the Lord by an illustrious journey; or who, executed in certain places, received heavenly crowns from the glorification of the Lord?” (Cyprian, Epistle LXVI, *To Papinianus*, p. 166 ff.). He there mentions several [Col. 0977D] bishops, his colleagues, who undoubtedly had ended their lives in martyrdom in Africa. For why does he call them his colleagues unless they had in fact held episcopal rank in his province? Therefore, in order to reconcile Pontius the disciple with Cyprian his teacher, certain more expert critics think that Pontius’s cited words should be understood not of the whole of Africa but of Africa in the narrower sense. But what if we say that he is not speaking with complete precision and that by the general name of Africa he denotes nothing other than Carthage, the capital of all Africa? For a very few words later he continues thus: “From the time that the order of the episcopate at Carthage is reckoned, no one among its good men and priests is recorded as having come to suffering . . . so that in the very city [Col. 0978A] where he had lived in such a manner, and where he had been the first to accomplish many glorious deeds, he might also be the first to adorn the insignia of the heavenly priesthood with glorious blood” (Pontius, p. 10). Pontius’s meaning therefore appears to be that Cyprian was the first bishop of Carthage in Africa to attain the palm of martyrdom through the shedding of his blood. Some, moreover, think these words designate only the persecution stirred up by Valerian and Gallienus, and that Cyprian was the first of all in Africa who, under those rulers, “suffered,” as Jerome says (Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, §67, p. 119). We shall not strongly oppose this opinion if it is established by sufficiently compelling arguments.

### ARTICLE III  
#### On the Title of This Book, and Whether It Was Written Against Demetrianus Alone

[Col. 0978B]

This book was written “To Demetrianus,” as Lactantius says, or “Against Demetrianus,” as Jerome says (locations cited above). For both titles are found prefixed in our unpublished manuscripts: in the very ancient Colbert manuscript, first, “Here begins the work of the same author, Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*”; in the Tarn manuscript, “Here begins the book of Caecilius Cyprian *Against Demetrianus*.” In the old editions, however, it reads: “Treatise of Saint Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, *Against Demetrianus*”; and in by far the greater number of the others, simply “*To Demetrianus*.” But however this title was written, it is certain that this work is not a letter but a treatise which Cyprian was compelled to publish [Col. 0978C] against Demetrianus, who was endeavoring with all the powers of his intellect to defend the abominable errors of the gentiles.

Although the title of this book displays only the name of Demetrianus, it is nevertheless clear that not only he, but also all the pagans, are refuted in it. For just as Cyprian names him specifically, so too he addresses them. Indeed, throughout the entire conclusion of this book—which is certainly no small part of it—he addresses pagans of every kind and exhorts them to come to their senses and, rejecting the impious worship of the gods, to embrace the religion of the Christians. Moreover, does he not seem, under the name of Demetrianus himself, to rebuke all pagans no less than him in these words: “Either you are swollen with pride, or besotted with drunkenness, or envious through spite, or [Col. 0978D] incestuous through lust, or violent through cruelty” (Cyprian, p. 189)? Was Demetrianus, then, guilty of all these crimes? But certainly, when Cyprian immediately added, “And you wonder that the wrath of God increases in punishment of the human race, when that which deserves punishment increases daily” (*ibid.*), he indicates plainly enough that the wrath of God had been aroused not merely by the crimes of Demetrianus, but by those of all the pagans, and that the world had been shaken by public calamities. To this may be added that shortly afterward he addresses all pagans as follows:

> See what sort of thing this very matter is about which our discourse with you is chiefly concerned: that you have harassed us, though innocent; that, in contempt of God, you attack and oppress God’s servants. It is not enough that your life is stained by the variety of raging vices, by the wickedness [Col. 0979A] of deadly crimes, and by the gain from bloody robberies; that true religion is overthrown by false superstitions; that God is neither sought at all nor feared. Beyond all this, you still harass by unjust persecutions the servants of God, who are consecrated to His majesty and name (*ibid.*, p. 190).

In the first Royal manuscript and the Targny manuscript, the reading is *flagitatis* (“you importune” or “harass”). So too in the older Colbert manuscript, except that a second hand, though writing in the same script, has written *flagellatis* (“you scourge”). That reading appears in the third Royal manuscript, while the second has *fatigatis* (“you weary” or “harass”).

This book, therefore, was published by Cyprian not against Demetrianus alone, but against all pagans as well, and with the intention that it should come into everyone’s hands. No lengthy argument is needed to prove what he declares in these perfectly explicit words: “I reply both to you, Demetrianus, and likewise to the others whom you may perhaps have stirred up.” It is nevertheless equally certain that it was addressed primarily to him, since Cyprian, repeatedly provoked by his shameless accusations—which will be discussed shortly—was at last compelled to set his hand to this work.

## ARTICLE IV. Who Demetrianus Was, to Whom This Book Was Addressed: Whether He Was a Proconsul or a Judge of Inferior Rank

Who Demetrianus was can be learned from no better source than this very book with which we are dealing. From it, however, it is most clearly gathered that he was a pagan [Col. 0979C] who had met very frequently with Cyprian, then bishop of Carthage. Yet Demetrianus would not have had such easy access to Cyprian’s house unless he had been connected with Cyprian—perhaps while Cyprian himself was still a pagan—by some longstanding familiarity. But with as much piety as the latter gave his name to the Christian religion, with equal impiety and obstinacy was the former enslaved to the abominable worship of false gods. For he had indeed come to Cyprian frequently, but never for the purpose of investigating the truth or learning anything; rather, as Cyprian says, with the “single purpose” (Cyprian, p. 185) of contradicting him—that is, merely to defend, with truly astonishing shamelessness, the impious worship of false gods and the absurd superstitions of his fellow pagans. But because he strove to defend his errors only with “clamorous words,” with utterly ungovernable [Col. 0979D] obstinacy, and without any argument of even the slightest weight, Cyprian scorned him—as he barked with sacrilegious mouth against the true God and raised a din with impious words—as ignorant, blind, deaf, brutish, unteachable, shameless, insane, impious, frenzied, and rabid. These, indeed, are the many distinctions with which he adorns him.

At that time, therefore, this furious man was living at Carthage, as was Cyprian; and everyone thinks—not without reason—that from this very treatise it can be established that he had there been raised to some judicial office. Yet there is no small disagreement among them as to what that office was. Very many have believed that he [Col. 0980A] was the proconsul of Africa, who possessed supreme authority in that province. Others, however, think that he was a judge of inferior rank, and perhaps an assessor of the proconsul himself. For it does not seem probable to them that Demetrianus, had he been proconsul of all Africa, would have visited Cyprian so readily and so frequently merely to force his false religion upon an unwilling man, after the fashion of a pettifogger, with nothing but “clamorous words.” Moreover, why would Cyprian, who judged that persecutors of Christians ought to be avoided, have so readily entrusted himself to the good faith of a raging proconsul and received him so frequently into his home? Why would he have treated with such contempt the man whom he had more reason to fear than anyone else—so much so that, in the course of so many discussions held in his own house, he did not deem him worthy of even a single word in reply when he disputed with such ardor, not about some trivial matter, but [Col. 0980B] about religion? Would not a proconsul, inflamed by anger and his innate fury at such contempt, immediately have exacted punishment from him, as he had the power to do? Why did this furious man, driven to madness, not at once cast Cyprian—by whom he was so despised—into chains, send him into exile, or condemn him to death? Finally, for what reason would this man, inflamed by so ardent and blind a zeal for his religion, have spared Cyprian alone, when Cyprian describes his extreme cruelty toward Christians in these words:

> You deprive the innocent, the just, and those dear to God of their homes; you strip them of their property; you burden them with chains; you shut them in prison; you punish them with wild beasts, the sword, and fire. Nor are you content even with a summary of our sufferings and with the simple and rapid brevity of punishments: you apply [Col. 0980C] prolonged tortures to bodies that are to be mangled; you multiply manifold torments for the tearing of their entrails; nor can your savagery and brutality be content with customary tortures: inventive cruelty devises new punishments (Cyprian, p. 190).

Who, then, will persuade himself that a proconsul of such great power and such great inhumanity spared Cyprian, the bishop and leader of the Christians, upon whom he could daily and easily lay hands? Would he not, by Cyprian’s death, have satisfied both himself and all the other pagans, their implacable enemies?

Why, moreover, would he not have attempted, by killing Cyprian, to win the favor of those whom—in consequence of the hatred with which he burned against the Christians—he left no stone unturned to rouse to anger against them and draw to his own side? For Cyprian openly reproached him for this in the following [Col. 0980D] words:

> I reply to you, Demetrianus, and likewise to the others whom you may perhaps have stirred up: by sowing hatred against us with your slanderous words, you have made many into shoots springing from your root and origin (*ibid.*, p. 186).

Was it, I ask you, also the duty of the proconsul of Africa to lead others, if possible, to the worship of false gods by arousing hatred against Christians through shameless accusations? Could he not have achieved this more easily and promptly by torturing and killing Christians with the most atrocious punishments? Finally, would Cyprian have assailed a proconsul in a public writing with such harsh and bitter words?

Others nevertheless insist that the words addressed by Cyprian to this Demetrianus, cited shortly above, indicate plainly enough that he really [Col. 0981A] was the proconsul of Africa. For who could torture and kill Christians with so many and such great, both ordinary and extraordinary, torments unless he had been invested with proconsular rank? Furthermore, Cyprian acknowledges that he was a judge when he addresses him in this manner: “You who judge others, be at some point your own judge” (*ibid.*, p. 189). But if he was a judge, then he must undoubtedly have been a proconsul. For afterward he again addresses him thus: “Cease to injure the servants of God and Christ with your persecutions; when they are injured, divine vengeance defends them” (*ibid.*, p. 192). Thus he persecuted Christians with the utmost inhumanity, and it lay within his power to quell this persecution. But who possessed such power except the proconsul?

Others, however, concede that these words may establish that Demetrianus [Col. 0981B] was some judge at Carthage, and perhaps the proconsul’s assessor, but not for that reason the proconsul himself, as they believe has been sufficiently proved by the preceding arguments. For judges of inferior tribunals, though of lower rank, ordered Christians to be tortured and killed with no less cruelty than did proconsuls. Yet even if this were so, others will object, Cyprian ought to have feared these men no less than the proconsul. It lay within their power to lay hands upon him, torture and kill him, or at least drag him before the proconsul’s tribunal. But because the latter’s rank and power were far greater, it seems scarcely probable that Cyprian could have treated him with such indignity and such harsh words. Yet whatever rank of judge he may have held, it is certainly clear that he was so inflamed [Col. 0981C] by an utterly ungovernable zeal for his false gods that he repeatedly disputed against the Christians with nothing but a clamorous voice, without ever adducing any argument of even the slightest weight, in order either to lead them to the impious worship of those gods or to increase the pagans’ fury against those who refused.

## ARTICLE V. The Reasons That Compelled Cyprian to Write and Publish This Book

Although Cyprian had at first judged that no reply should be made to Demetrianus, who barked against the Christian religion and raised a din against it with nothing but impious words, he was nevertheless afterward compelled to break his silence. At that time, destructive wars were shaking the Roman [Col. 0981D] Empire, while a most dreadful famine and a horrifying plague were miserably devastating and depopulating cities, villages, and individual homes. Seizing this opportunity, Demetrianus summoned his associates in impiety and stubbornness and began openly to proclaim that very many people complained that there was no cause for such great calamities other than the obstinacy and impiety of the Christians, who refused to worship the false gods. Therefore, lest the pagans should as usual attribute his prolonged silence to lack of confidence and inability to answer, Cyprian undertook in this book to repel their empty and futile accusations:

> We ought no longer to remain silent, he says, lest our silence now begin to appear the result not of modesty but of lack of confidence, and lest, while we disdain to refute [Col. 0982A] false accusations, we seem to acknowledge the charge (Cyprian, p. 186).

No one, therefore, should be surprised that he again refutes such senseless accusations, which had frequently been repelled by other defenders of our religion, as we have said. For the pagans exploited these bitter disasters more frequently and boldly, and thereby deceived ignorant worshipers of the gods all the more easily, in proportion as the disasters were greater and inflicted greater harm upon the whole world (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 4, art. 1 ff.; *on Tertullian*, ch. 1 ff.). How savage and destructive were the wars in which the Roman Empire then burned may be inferred from this: after his revolt from the emperor Philip and the ensuing civil war, Decius had scarcely begun the third year of his reign when, defeated by the Goths in a great [Col. 0982B] battle, he was miserably killed together with his three sons, Decius, Etruscus, and Trajan. Gallus, his successor, in the eighteenth month of his reign, while preparing to fight Aemilianus, who had usurped imperial power, was killed by his soldiers together with his colleague (*Dissertation on Caecilius’ Book On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 7, art. 1). Nor did Aemilianus long enjoy the fruit of his crime, but after three months ended his life by a similar death. Zosimus and other writers of Roman history committed further details concerning these wars to writing (Zosimus, *History*, bk. I, p. 643 ff.; Orosius, *History*, bk. VII, ch. 20 ff.; Eutropius, *Breviary*, bk. IX, p. 123).

Eutropius relates that nothing memorable was accomplished by these emperors and that their reign became known to men through nothing other than “pestilence and various [Col. 0982C] diseases.” We find this confirmed by Orosius as well (Orosius, passage cited, ch. 21). Concerning both these public calamities, Zosimus, whom we cited shortly above, recorded the following:

> Οὐκ ἧττον δὲ, τοῦ πανταχόθεν ἐπιβρύσαντος πολέμου, καὶ ὁ λοιμὸς πόλεσί τε καὶ κώμαις ἐπιγενόμενος, εἴ τι λελειμένον ἦν ἀθρώπειον γένος, διέφθειρεν, οὓπω πρότερον ἐν τοῖς φθάσασι χρόνοις τοσαύτην ἀνθρώπων ἀπώλειαν ἐργασάμενος (Zosimus, passage cited, p. 644): “No less, while war was flooding in from every side, did a plague come upon cities and villages and destroy whatever remained of the human race, never before in preceding ages having caused so great a loss of human life.”

How true these things are, and how widely that deadly plague spread, is attested by witnesses beyond all challenge as to [Col. 0982D] credibility: Dionysius of Alexandria, Pontius the deacon of our Cyprian, and Cyprian himself. The first, in fragments of his letters collected by Eusebius, is said to have related the following concerning the plague that occurred when Gallienus reigned shortly after Gallus (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VII, ch. 22, p. 268 ff.). The plague, he says, most terrifying and calamitous of all, raged among the pagans with a severity hitherto unheard of. Everything was filled with lamentation; everyone mourned; and because of the multitude of those who had died and were dying daily, the whole city resounded with grief. There was no house at all in which there had not been at least one funeral.

[Col. 0983A] Pontius, moreover, an eyewitness, describes this plague and its terrible effects in the *Life* of the same Cyprian as follows:

> Afterward there broke out a dreadful plague and an excessively destructive devastation, which, with sudden violence, carried off countless people each day, each from his own dwelling, and invaded in succession the continuous rows of houses belonging to the trembling populace. Everyone shuddered, fled, avoided contagion, and impiously exposed his own relatives, as though by casting out the person who was going to die of the plague one could also shut out death itself. Meanwhile, throughout the entire city there lay no longer bodies, but the corpses of very many people (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, p. 5).

Cyprian himself, in the book that he wrote to console Christians amid this calamity, portrayed its horrifying violence and the intolerable sufferings of the sick in these words:

> The fact that now the bowels, loosened into a flux, drain the body’s [Col. 0983B] strength; that a fire conceived deep in the marrow burns up into wounds in the throat; that the intestines are shaken by continual vomiting; that the eyes burn with the force of the blood; that in some persons either the feet or other parts of the limbs are amputated through the contagion of diseased putrefaction; that, as weakness breaks forth through losses and injuries of the body, either the gait is enfeebled, or the hearing obstructed, or the sight blinded—all this serves as a proof of faith (Cyprian, *On Mortality*, p. 162).

It is therefore with good reason that the author of the Eusebian Chronicle (*Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the year of Christ 253) and Jordanes direct us to this book of Cyprian (Jordanes, *On the Deeds of the Goths*, ch. 19) and to the cited letter of Dionysius of Alexandria, so that we may learn how dreadful and horrifying that plague was. In the present book of Cyprian, [Col. 0983C] with which we are dealing, he says concerning it and the other calamities then arising: “Wars continue with increasing frequency; barrenness and famine compound anxiety; health is broken by raging diseases; the human race is devastated by the ravages of pestilence” (*ibid.*, *To Demetrianus*, p. 187). A little earlier, moreover, he had said: “In the fields the farmer fails” (the older Colbert manuscript: “in the plowed lands”), “on the sea the sailor, in the camps the soldier” (*ibid.*, p. 186).

Thus, while the world was being devastated by such great disasters and by so great a slaughter of nearly all mankind, Demetrianus and the others whom he had joined to himself cried out more loudly and at the top of their voices that the world was afflicted, and almost entirely overwhelmed, by that hitherto unheard-of plague and by the other calamities of famine and war for this reason: because Christians refused to worship their [Col. 0983D] false gods. Cyprian, therefore, in order at last to stop the impure mouth of Demetrianus and the other pagans and, if possible, to recall them to a sounder mind, judged it necessary to suppress their complaints, however absurd, in this public book with which we are dealing.

# CHAPTER II. The Subject, Date, Manuscripts, Editions, and Notes by Certain Scholars on This Book

## ARTICLE I. The Subject of This Work, and Whether Cyprian Failed, as Lactantius Contends, Fully to Discharge the Office He Undertook as Defender of the Christian Religion

[Col. 0984A]

What we have just said concerning the occasion and necessity for writing this book makes its subject plain to everyone. For in it Cyprian undertook to demonstrate, against the false and public accusations of Demetrianus and the other pagans, that the true cause of the public disasters was not the Christians, who worshiped the one true God and lived pious, chaste lives free from crime, but the pagans themselves, worshipers of false gods and guilty of every kind of most grievous crime. He proves this by various weighty arguments and by many oracles of our sacred Prophets, who, inspired by the divine Spirit, had not only [Col. 0984B] foretold those calamities, but also foretold that Almighty God, the perfectly just avenger of crimes, would one day exact due punishment from those wicked and impious people.

But Lactantius, as we observed in the appropriate place (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 3, art. 2; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 1, p. 459, and ch. 5, p. 471), censures Cyprian for this, not only freely but rather severely: namely, that he refutes and attacks Demetrianus solely with testimonies from sacred Scripture, which that pagan man regarded as “empty, fabricated, and fictitious.” Accordingly, he asserts without hesitation that in that “discourse,” as he calls it, Cyprian discharged the office he had undertaken as defender of the Christian religion neither fully nor properly. He therefore believes that Cyprian can be excused [Col. 0984C] only because he was “carried away by his extraordinary learning in the divine Scriptures, so that he was content with those things alone upon which faith rests.”

Yet although Demetrianus was profoundly devoted to the abominable superstitions of the pagans and rejected the authority of our sacred Scripture, our Cyprian did not rashly employ its true testimonies to repel his unjust accusations. For at the beginning of this book he cites certain precepts from Proverbs and Matthew by which one is forbidden to answer an insane man who barks foolishly. But what, I ask, prevents statements that agree entirely with right reason and are observed by all men of sound mind from being advanced even against the most obstinate pagan? He also [Col. 0984D] adduced many other testimonies in which those public disasters about which the pagans complained had, as we have said, been foretold by our sacred Prophets. But since he clearly demonstrates that these predictions had attained their fulfillment, did he not derive from them a decidedly strong argument against the pagans?

Moreover, Demetrianus had frequently met Cyprian, as Cyprian himself acknowledges and as we have already observed, in order to dispute with him about his own religion and the Christian religion. Although Cyprian prudently disdained him in silence as a thoroughly inept trifler who proclaimed with as much obstinacy as falsehood that Christians were the authors of all public calamities, he did not [Col. 0985A] always remain silent. For he says, “Considering these things, I have often kept silent” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 185). You hear him say “often,” but not “I always kept silent.” If, therefore, he sometimes answered him, could he not then have demonstrated how great is the authority of our Old Testament, which we received after it had always been preserved with the greatest care by the Jews, although they are our most bitter enemies?

But why, you will ask, did he not prove this in the public work by which he wished to lead not only Demetrianus but also the other pagans “toward the good,” as he himself says, “under the compulsion of truth”? Yet why, I ask you, was there then any need for this proof if he had demonstrated it in private discussions with Demetrianus and in another book previously published? Very many, as we shall say below, [Col. 0985B] believe that he did so in the book *On the Vanity of Idols*.

Furthermore, what of the fact that, in this book *To Demetrianus*, he proves and affirms the principal doctrines of the Christian religion concerning the one true God and Christ the Lord by certain arguments drawn from reason alone, by which pagans who were not utterly blinded could very easily be convinced? For he demonstrates both doctrines fully through the public confession of the demons, whom Christians cast out of the possessed bodies of the pagans themselves by adjuring them solely in the name of their master Christ (*ibid.*, p. 192). Nothing more certain or clearer than this proof could be advanced, as we have seen more than once elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 2, art. 3; *on Lactantius*, ch. 9, art. 2; and *on Tertullian*, ch. 10, art. 7).

[Col. 0985C] Finally, he also refutes Demetrianus, who babbled that Christians were the cause of public calamities, on the ground that these are inflicted as punishment upon criminal men. Yet in this book he made it perfectly clear to everyone that the morals of the pagans were as corrupt as those of the Christians were chaste and holy. He therefore rightly concludes from this that these calamities are brought upon the world not by the Christians, but by the pagans themselves, calamities by which God chastises wicked men according to their deserts but tests the virtue of the good. These three points, and no more, were what he had proposed to treat in this book. He therefore properly discharged the office he had undertaken of defending the Christian religion against the accusations made by Demetrianus and the other pagans. We have discussed more fully in our preceding dissertations [Col. 0985D] this criticism by Lactantius, with which he assailed not only Cyprian but also Tertullian and Minucius Felix (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 2, art. 4; and *on Minucius*, ch. 2, art. 2).

For the rest, Lactantius did not deprive Cyprian of his deserved praise, but extols his talent and eloquence in these words:

> Cyprian alone stood forth as preeminent and illustrious, since he had both acquired great glory for himself through the profession of oratory and written a very great deal in his own manner. For his talent was fluent, copious, pleasing, and—what is the greatest virtue of discourse—clear, so that one cannot determine whether he was more ornate in speaking, more lucid in exposition, or more powerful [Col. 0986A] in persuasion (Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 1, p. 459).

It would be very easy to accumulate here many other encomia bestowed upon this most sacred martyr by trustworthy writers of every age. But because they have been prefixed to nearly all editions of his works, we did not think that what had already been done needed to be done again.

## ARTICLE II. The Date of This Book

We believe that there is no one who, after hearing what we related shortly above concerning the terrible devastation caused by the plague in Africa, would not readily acknowledge that this book was composed by Cyprian while it was [Col. 0986B] raging with particular cruelty among mankind. It arose in the year of Christ 250, when Decius was already emperor. It is said to have lasted for at least ten years, though in such a manner that it sometimes appeared to diminish and abate. It cannot therefore be gathered with certainty from this alone at precisely what time the book was published, unless we compare the greater violence of the plague with other things done and declared by Cyprian himself. It is clear, however, that he published it after he had heard Demetrianus complain very frequently in his home about the plague and other public disasters. Cyprian was therefore staying at Carthage, where he admitted Demetrianus into his home, and he had less fear of the fury and persecution of tyrants against the Christians. But when Decius, having become emperor toward the end of the year 249, stirred up a new persecution against them, [Col. 0986C] Cyprian withdrew from Carthage and returned there in the following year, around the month of April, when that persecution is said to have subsided. Indeed, the councils that he held there sufficiently demonstrate this first return. He remained there until the year 258, when he again avoided another persecution stirred up by the emperor Valerian, and shortly afterward ended his life in illustrious martyrdom. He therefore wrote this book between the years 252 and 258. We have already seen that, during the reign of Gallus, the violence of the plague and diseases was so great that writers testify that his reign was known solely from them, as we have said. Gallus ruled the Romans after the death of the emperor Decius, from the end of the year 251 until 253. It therefore seems, not without reason, that this book *To Demetrianus* was written by Cyprian [Col. 0986D] about that time.

That it was not composed—or at least not published—while Gallus was reigning may be inferred from the fact that our author himself affirms that God, the perfectly just avenger of crimes, never allowed the cruelty of tyrants against Christians to go unpunished:

> For, to pass over ancient memories, he says, and not to recount with any proclamation of the voice the vengeance repeatedly exacted on behalf of God’s worshipers, the proof supplied by a recent event is sufficient: the defense that lately followed so swiftly, and in its very swiftness with such magnitude, through the downfall of kings, losses of wealth, destruction of soldiers, and reduction of military camps (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 192).

Some believe that these words indicate the disastrous death of Decius [Col. 0987A] and his sons, who were destroyed utterly and perished miserably, their camps having been plundered and their wealth carried off. We do not deny this, but we believe that something more is signified. For when Cyprian wrote these things, the plague had never raged more fiercely nor inflicted greater devastation upon mankind. But we have shown that this occurred during the reign of Gallus, the successor of that same Decius. After the eighteenth month of his reign, Gallus and his son Volusianus, whom he had made Caesar, were killed by their own soldiers. Aemilianus, who was then proclaimed emperor, met a similar fate after three months. Valerian, moreover, who was appointed in his place around the month of August in the year 253, embraced the Christians at the beginning of his reign with remarkable friendship and affection, until, toward the end of the year 256 or at the beginning of the following year, he stirred up a new persecution against them. Having therefore obtained so favorable an opportunity, Cyprian [Col. 0987B] most probably published this book against Demetrianus and the other pagans either in September of that same year, 253, or shortly afterward. At that time, indeed, he had better grounds than before the deaths of Gallus and Volusianus for saying that the injuries inflicted upon Christians contrary to every right had been avenged by the supreme and perfectly just God through the downfall of kings. If anyone should nevertheless continue to contend that these words must be understood solely of the death of Decius, and should prove this with stronger arguments, we shall immediately yield and subscribe to his opinion.
