## ARTICLE III. The Manuscripts of This Book

[Col. 0987C]

We had several manuscripts of this book from the Royal and Colbert libraries, copied at different times and by different scribes; while examining this same book, we collated them with the printed editions. At the command of the most illustrious Abbé Le Tellier de Louvois, the first set was supplied to us by Jean Boivin, another keeper of the same Royal Library, a man highly celebrated not only for Greek but also for Latin learning. Other manuscripts were communicated to us by the distinguished Charles Duchesne through the customary favor of the most illustrious Abbé Colbert—a favor that can never be sufficiently praised. One further manuscript was furnished to us by Monsieur de Targny, a doctor of the Sorbonne, and another by the library of our monastery of Saint-Germain.

[Col. 0987D] Very many others still exist in other libraries. Étienne Baluze, a man universally renowned for both his writings and his learning, examined twenty-one of them, gathered from every quarter, for the preparation of the edition of all Cyprian’s works that he had long ago undertaken; and he deigned to communicate their catalogue to us. In identifying these and the others, we shall follow the chronological order in which each of them appears to expert judges and to Baluze himself to have been written.

The first of all to be named is the Séguier manuscript, which once belonged to the library of the most illustrious Séguier, Chancellor of France, but now belongs to the most illustrious du Cambout de Coislin, bishop of the church of Metz, Duke and Peer of France, and Prince of the Empire. This [Col. 0988A] manuscript is said to have been written a thousand years ago.

Five others are said to have been copied eight hundred years ago. The first is the Pithou manuscript, the second the Colbert manuscript, the third is held in our monastery of Saint-Aubin at Angers, the fourth—formerly in the Abbey of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés—is now in the library of the distinguished Étienne Baluze, and the fifth is in the library of Saint-Martin at Tours.

Three others display an age of seven hundred or six hundred years: the first is a Royal manuscript, the second belongs to Baluze, and the third is the Targny manuscript. Two are five hundred years old: one from Saint-Pierre-le-Moûtier, and the other from Notre-Dame de la Liesse. Five are four hundred years old: the first from Saint-Remi at Reims, the second from the Sorbonne, the third and fourth from Saint-Victor [Col. 0988B] in Paris, the fifth belonging to the distinguished Monsieur Bohier, president of the Parlement of Dijon, and the sixth belonging to Baluze. Finally, five are either three hundred or two hundred and fifty years old: two belong to our Most Christian King, the third to Saint-Denis at Reims, the fourth is from Grenoble, and the fifth belongs to the distinguished Monsieur de Lamoignon, first president of the Parlement of Paris.

## ARTICLE IV. The Editions of This Book

In proportion to Cyprian’s great renown for holiness of life and learning, the editions of his works multiplied. An edition that bears no indication of date, place, or printer’s [Col. 0988C] name appears to many to be the earliest; some believe it was printed immediately after the invention of the art of printing. A second was published at Speyer in 1471, but was everywhere disfigured by errors. Another afterward appeared at Venice in 1483 from the press of Lucas Venetus. Subsequently, another edition, enlarged by the addition of certain works of Cyprian, whether genuine or spurious, was prepared at Paris in 1512 through the labor of the printer Rembold and others. This was revised by Erasmus, who prefixed to it a preface and certain annotations; editions of it were issued to the public from Froben’s press in the years 1520, 1525, and 1528.

Afterward, the same works of Cyprian were printed in 1541 by Hervagius, in that same year at Antwerp by Johann Crinitus, and at Paris by Langelier. They were subsequently published at Basel in [Col. 0988D] 1544 from the Quentel press through the efforts of Heinrich Gavius, by the already commended Froben in 1549, and again by Hervagius in 1550.

Just as the aforementioned Antwerp edition was published in octavo, as they are fond of saying, so too were the Lyon editions of 1537, 1549, and 1556, the Venetian edition of 1547, and Froben’s edition of 1603. Most scholars, however, judge neither these nor the earlier editions to be complete or accurate.

Later, the works of St. Cyprian, corrected against manuscripts through the care and labor of Guillaume Morel and printed in an elegant type, were issued to the public at Rome in 1563. They were reprinted at Paris in the following year, but with additions and corrections. In that same year, 1564, the treatises of Cyprian alone [Col. 0989A] were published at Paris by Claude Frémy after the works of Leo the Great.

Pamelius prepared a new edition of all Cyprian’s works, corrected from ancient manuscript and printed copies. It was first committed to type at Antwerp in 1568 and was afterward printed there again in 1589, as well as at Paris in 1574. Then, in 1593, Simon Goulart, an adherent of the Calvinist sect, prepared a new edition of Cyprian’s works, printed by Jean Le Preux; it was also published at Paris in the years 1532, 1603, and 1644. Earlier, however—namely in 1616—an edition had appeared at Paris from the press of Michel Chapelet; it is attested to have been corrected with the aid of the editions of Paulus Manutius and Guillaume Morel and of several manuscripts.

[Col. 0989B] Rigault subsequently devoted fresh care to another edition and made it public (Rigault, *Observations*, p. 170). He declares that he revised it by means of variant readings collected by Pope Marcellus II and Bishop Antonio Agustín from what he calls the excellent Verona and Benevento copies. He wished us to be advised, however, that he took these variant readings from a volume of Cyprian in which Charles de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse, had transcribed them in his own hand; yet for this book he presents only nine, taken from the Verona manuscript. This edition was first made available for public use at Paris in 1646, and again in 1666, together with certain observations by Pamelius, from the press of the widow of Mathurin Dupuis.

We owe the latest edition of Cyprian’s works, published at Oxford [Col. 0989C] in 1682, to the illustrious John Fell, bishop of Oxford. With great labor, deserving the praise of all, he revised and annotated it according to eighteen English manuscripts written by different hands and according to various readings sent to him from England and France. We judge no less worthy of praise the integrity of this most learned writer, who openly professed that he was far removed from those who—not without serious injury to religion—devote their labor to exposing the blemishes of the ancient Fathers. Whether he kept his promises everywhere and at all times will be made more certain to us by the distinguished Étienne Baluze, who, having gathered from every quarter manuscripts of Cyprian’s works, has long been planning a new edition of them. The more confidently we expect [Col. 0989D] that his edition will be more accurate than the others, the more surely we await his judgment concerning all the editions published thus far.

### ARTICLE V. On the Various Annotations upon This Work

There are various notes and observations by learned men upon the work under discussion. Erasmus, however, left only two upon it. In the first, he expresses surprise that someone preferred to call this work a treatise rather than a letter. He then added that Cyprian appears to have thought that this world was growing worse through old age. But what we have noted concerning the title of this work sufficiently shows by what right it is designated a “treatise” [Col. 0990A]. Moreover, our author was not alone—as we shall see below—in thinking that the world was growing old and becoming worse with age, or rather, that it was afflicted by the infirmities of old age just as a human being is.

William Morel published more numerous, though very brief, observations upon this work. In them he did nothing more than indicate how Cyprian’s text should be corrected from ancient manuscripts or from the books of sacred Scripture. He made only one substantive observation: namely, that Cyprian was speaking there of exorcists when, in disputing against the pagans, he treated of demons whom Christians cast out of the bodies of the possessed. But it seems to us, as must be said below, that he was speaking not only of exorcists but of absolutely all [Col. 0990B] Christians.

Pamelius likewise composed fifty-nine notes upon this work. Almost all of them concern corruptions in its text; in a smaller number, however, he endeavors either to elucidate or to confirm Cyprian’s statements by the authority of other ancient writers. But because he attempted through them to illustrate the teachings of the Catholic Church, not all of them pleased Goulart. He therefore attempted to bring them into conformity with the tenets of his Calvinist sect. Moreover, he arranged for all of Pamelius’s observations on this work to be reprinted, adding a few of his own, distinguished by the mark §. In almost all of these he indicates certain variant readings from a single manuscript codex communicated to him by Bovaeus. For he added only five notes of his own. The first [Col. 0990C] reminds us that the old age of the world consists especially in the corruption of morals. The second observes that the long life spans of primeval human beings are confirmed by the history of the universal flood. The third then remarks that the ancient Christians directed their prayers to God through Christ, without invoking the saints. But he ought to have shown whether Cyprian had denied such invocation anywhere at all. Fourth, he admits that the ancient Christians used the external sign of Christ’s cross, but without superstition and without any diminution of the doctrine concerning Christ’s merit. It is certainly good that he approves the use of this venerable sign. But who has ever approved its superstitious abuse, or allowed the doctrine concerning Christ’s merit to be weakened with impunity? Finally, he proves from various testimonies of the ancient Fathers of the Church that after this [Col. 0990D] life there is no place for repentance. But there he cites as genuine a spurious work attributed to Justin Martyr.

Rigault afterward compiled a few notes upon this work; in his edition of 1664 they are not distinguished from his notes on *The Lord’s Prayer*. There are, indeed, no more than nineteen. Nine of them present readings from the Verona manuscript, as we have said; in the others—which, with one exception, are extremely brief—he attempts to explain or confirm certain words of Cyprian.

In the Oxford edition there are two classes of notes, arranged in a reasonably convenient order. The first, printed in smaller type, present variant readings from manuscript codices, but none at all from old [Col. 0991A] editions. Why the latter were omitted, we have not ascertained. Notes of the second class serve to explain and establish Cyprian’s text. In these, moreover, that learned man undoubtedly took care to maintain commendable brevity. The first two are longer than the rest. One refutes the opinion of those who suppose that Demetrian was proconsul of Africa. The other answers Lactantius, who, as we said above, reproaches Cyprian because he argued from the authority of sacred Scripture against a pagan who wholly and utterly rejected and scorned it. We cannot conceal, moreover, that certain observations by this admittedly learned editor are less worthy of approval, particularly the penultimate one, in which he contends that Cyprian rejected purgatorial fires, although [Col. 0991B] Cyprian had no thought of them whatsoever. But these matters must be treated below in their proper place.

## CHAPTER III. NEW OBSERVATIONS UPON THIS WORK

### ARTICLE I. On the Authority of Sacred Scripture and Certain Passages in It

We shall certainly gladly admit as true what Lactantius asserted: that Cyprian was carried away by his exceptional learning in the divine writings (*Lactant.*, *Institutions*, book V, ch. 4, p. 471). For how could he not have been captivated by their teaching, when he ascribed to them the authority of the divine instruction and name (*Cyprian*, [Col. 0991C] *To Demetrian*, p. 185)? In the old editions and in many manuscript copies, the two words *and name* are absent (*ibid.*, pp. 187 and 188); but they are read in five others and do not appear to have been added there rashly. He so emphatically proclaims the supreme authority of our sacred Scriptures (*ibid.*, pp. 187, 188, 190, 192, 193, 194, and 195) because he was fully persuaded that God himself and the Holy Spirit had spoken in them, and that they had been composed by prophets and writers who were filled with the same Holy Spirit. This conviction of Cyprian was always constant. In this work and in almost all his writings—especially in his three books *Against the Jews*—he posits and follows it as certain and by no means doubtful. There is therefore no need for us to prove it [Col. 0991D] at greater length.

Yet it may perhaps be worth observing that certain words of Ezekiel are cited in one manner in this work *To Demetrian* and in another in his second book *Against the Jews*. For he addresses them to Demetrian (*ibid.*, p. 194) and the other pagans as follows:

> “Go and slay, and do not spare with your eyes. Have no mercy upon old man, young man, or virgin; kill little children and women, that they may be utterly destroyed. But touch no one upon whom the sign has been written. What this sign is, and upon what part of the body it is placed, God makes clear in another passage, saying: Pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a sign upon the foreheads of the men who groan and mourn over the iniquities [Col. 0992A] that are committed in their midst” (Ezek. 9:4).

But in the second book *Against the Jews*:

> “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a sign upon the foreheads of the men who groan and mourn over the iniquities that are committed in their midst. Likewise there: Go and slay, and do not spare with your eyes. . . . But touch no one upon whom the sign has been written” (*idem*, book II, *Against the Jews*, §22, p. 47).

In this second passage he follows the order of the sacred Bible, which, as you see, is reversed in the former. But no one will ever deny that Cyprian was entitled to do this, since by this means he wished to connect the sequence of his discourse with a more suitable transition. Some may therefore find it more surprising that in this latter passage he said, “Likewise there,” but in the former, “He makes clear in another passage” [Col. 0992B]. For these words are written in the same passage. Did careless copyists therefore err in transcribing our author’s text, where they ought to have written “in that passage” rather than “in another passage”? Or did he have some other passage in view, which we can scarcely believe?

Moreover, there, as elsewhere (*idem*, *To Demetrian*, p. 94), he follows the translation of the Seventy-two, as he does when he also quotes these words:

> “Seek God, and your soul shall live” (Ps. 68:33).

These words were taken not from the prophet Amos, who is cited in the Oxford edition, but from Psalm 69 according to the same translation of the Elders.

Some may perhaps be more surprised that he cited certain words of the New Testament against a pagan; but these are very few and are [Col. 0992C] Christ’s own words. He gives us two reasons why he quoted them. First, because Christ never deceived anyone. Second, because he foretold many things exactly as they in fact occurred. Accordingly, with this proviso, he addresses the pagans as follows:

> “Believe him who never deceives at all; believe him who foretold that all these things would come to pass” (*Cypr.*, *ibid.*, p. 195).

With still greater right he presses the testimonies of the Old Testament against those who could not have been unaware that Christians had received them from their bitterest enemies, the Jews, by whom it had been preserved entire and uncorrupted (*Dissertation above*, ch. 5, art. 3 ff.).

### ARTICLE II. How Cyprian Demonstrates God’s Existence from the Upright Posture of the Human Body, from the Creation of the Sun and Other Things, and from the Public Confession of Demons Cast Out by Christians from the Bodies of the Possessed

[Col. 0992D]

Although in this book *To Demetrian* Cyprian assumes as certain, and as already proved by himself elsewhere, that there is only one God, he nevertheless demonstrates it both clearly and briefly by certain arguments of no little weight. The first is that with which he argues against the pagan as follows:

> “God made you upright. . . . Yours is a lofty stature, and your countenance is raised upward toward the heavens and toward God [the better manuscripts read *suum*, ‘its own’]. Look there; raise your eyes there, and seek God above. . . . With the posture of your face and body, set your mind upright. That you may be able to know God, first know yourself” (*Cyprian*, *To Demetrian*, p. 192).

[Col. 0993A] From the fact that a human being, if he knows himself and his own mind, attends to his lofty posture, and seriously considers his face raised toward heaven, will then be compelled to confess that he was fashioned by God and that the heavens and all created things were made by him, Cyprian therefore plainly concludes that God truly exists and is one. We examined and explained this argument in our dissertation on the books of Lactantius. Indeed, the sun alone most evidently reveals to everyone that its most brilliant light—as Lactantius himself says and as we have noted elsewhere—is a proof of the divine and unique majesty (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 7, art. 3, and ch. 11, art. 2; *ibid.*, ch. 12, art. 1); that is, it proves that the true and one God exists, by whom it was created. Both authors selected the examples of the sun and heaven above all other creatures because the creation of the sun and heaven demonstrates to all people the supreme majesty and power of almighty God.

[Col. 0993B] Cyprian therefore rightly concludes from this that idols—that is, the false gods of the pagans invented by human error—must be abandoned, and that the true and one God must be acknowledged and worshiped, since he can aid those who implore his help as easily as the false gods are invoked in vain by human prayers.

He then proves God’s existence by another, truly invincible argument, drawn from the public confession of demons whom the pagans regarded as gods. For when adjured by Christians, they were not only cast out of the bodies of the possessed by their words, as though by spiritual scourges and tortures, but were also compelled publicly [Col. 0993C] to confess that they were not gods, that they deluded human beings by their tricks and deceptions, and that there was only one God, whom those same Christians worshiped. It is useful to observe with what confidence he presses this argument against the pagans. For he addresses Demetrian and all the other pagans in these words:

> “O, if only you were willing to hear [our manuscript codices read *velis*, ‘you be willing’] and to see when they are adjured by us and tortured with spiritual scourges, and are cast from possessed bodies by the tortures of words; when, howling and groaning, speaking with a human voice, and feeling lashes and blows by divine power, they confess the coming judgment” (*Cyprian*, *To Demetrian*, p. 191).

He presses still more sharply and challenges them to test so great a power and that public confession of the demons:

[Col. 0993D]

> “Come and learn that the things we have said are true” (*idem*, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14).

Nor did he say this only once, but repeated it in two other books (*To Donatus*, p. 4). We have already observed (*Dissertation above*, ch. 10, arts. 6 and 7 [printed “79”]) that Tertullian challenged the same pagans no less boldly, and that this can never be called into doubt by any person of sound mind.

It is therefore more certain than certainty itself that demons were then expelled by Christians from the bodies of the possessed. But if that is marvelous, far more marvelous indeed is the manner in which they were driven away. They were compelled to depart from bodies they had possessed for however long, howling, our author says, and groaning, not by a human voice, certainly, but by divine power; [Col. 0994A] and they were struck and mangled by the words of the Christians who adjured them, just as though by spiritual scourges, blows, and tortures. For this reason he wrote to Donatus that Christians had been given a power by which they could compel those unclean and wandering spirits

> “to confession by threatening rebukes; press them with harsh blows to depart; stretch them upon the rack as they struggle, howl, and groan under an ever-increasing punishment; strike them with scourges; and scorch them with fire. The thing is done there, yet is not seen: the wound is hidden, but the punishment manifest” (*Cypr.*, *To Donatus*, p. 4).

Again, in another book:

> “You may see them struck with scourges by our voice and by the operation of a hidden majesty, scorched with fire, stretched upon the rack under an ever-increasing punishment, howling, groaning, and pleading” (*idem*, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14).

For this reason he confidently [Col. 0994B] said to any pagan:

> “You will see us entreated by those whom you entreat, feared by those whom you fear and whom you adore. You will see standing bound beneath our hand, and trembling as captives, those whom you look up to and venerate as masters” (*idem*, *To Demetrian*, p. 191).

Thus demons were not only tortured and cast out by Christians, but, when departing however unwillingly from the possessed bodies of human beings, were also forced publicly to declare by what tricks they deceived people, that they were not gods, and that only the God of the Christians was God. Certainly nothing was truer, more certain, or more manifest than this public confession of theirs. Cyprian therefore draws with perfect justice the following conclusion against the pagans:

> “Surely even in this way you will be able to be confounded in these errors of yours, when [Col. 0994C] you see your gods disclose immediately, under our questioning, what they are, and, even though you are present, prove unable to conceal their tricks and deceptions” (*ibid.*).

Or, as he had said in another book:

> “To confess, even in the hearing of those who worship them, whence they come and when they depart” (*idem*, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 14).

In other dissertations of ours we have expounded this entire argument and made it plain to everyone that its force is such that it most invincibly demonstrates both that the gods of the pagans are false and that God is one; and consequently that the religion of those same pagans is false, while the religion of the Christians is true (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 20, art. 3; *on Lactantius*, ch. 10, art. 2; and *on Tertullian*, ch. 10, arts. 6 and 7).

Morel, moreover, observed in his notes upon this book [Col. 0994D] that Cyprian was there speaking of Christian exorcists, who cast demons from the bodies of the possessed. But if he thinks that Cyprian spoke only of those who had been initiated into the order of exorcists, he is certainly mistaken. For in the already-cited book *To Donatus*, Cyprian expressly asserts that the power of casting out demons had been granted to every Christian. We too showed in our preceding dissertation that demons were then cast out and driven away by Christians of every kind, just as by exorcists (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, loc. cit.).

### ARTICLE III. That Christ Must Be Believed, Who at the Price of His Blood Regenerates a Human Being through Holy Baptism; on the Twofold Sign of His Death; on Repentance; and in What Sense It Is Said to Be Too Late for No One Who Is Still Living This Life

[Col. 0995A]

It is not enough for a human being to know God; he must also believe God and Christ, who was sent by his eternal Father and

> “redeemed the believer at the price of his blood, reconciling the human being to God the Father and giving life to the mortal by heavenly regeneration” (*Cyprian*, *To Demetrian*).

But what is that heavenly regeneration if not the sacrament of holy Baptism, by which, as the Apostle says, we were buried with Christ

> “into death, so that, just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (St. Paul, *Epistle to the Romans* 6:4)?

For this reason Cyprian had written a little [Col. 0995B] earlier:

> “We who, having cast off our earthly birth, have been recreated and reborn by the Spirit, now live no longer for the world but for God” (*Cypr.*, *ibid.*, p. 193).

He said *exposita*, that is, “laid aside and cast off,” with reference to earthly birth; Tertullian and Lactantius use this verb in the same sense, as we observed in our preceding dissertations. Nor does our author employ it only once, but elsewhere as well, especially in his treatise *To Donatus*, where with all the force of his eloquence he describes and proclaims the marvelous effects of Baptism (*idem*, *To Donatus*, p. 3).

But just as he rightly teaches that the grace of Baptism is the price of Christ’s blood, so too he asserts that the sign by which anyone found marked will be preserved safe [Col. 0995C] and unharmed pertains to that same blood of Christ and to the torment of the cross (*ibid.*, p. 194). He proves this from the testimony of Ezekiel cited above, and further from these words of Moses in Exodus:

> “And the blood shall be a sign for you upon the houses in which you shall be; and I shall see the blood and protect you, and there shall not be among you a plague of destruction when I strike the land of Egypt” (Exod. 12:13).

What that sign is he himself indicates to us in chapter twenty-two of the second book *Against the Jews*, where he relates both the testimony of Ezekiel and that of Moses (*Cypr.*, book II, *Against the Jews*, ch. 22, p. 46). The title of this chapter is:

> “That in this sign of the cross there is salvation for all who are marked upon their foreheads.”

Elsewhere, following Augustine, we have noted that this and the other chapter headings came from Cyprian himself. [Col. 0995D] The cited words of Exodus are written in the same way in this book and in our manuscripts of the treatise *To Demetrian*. But in its editions, instead of “in which you shall be,” we read: “in which you yourselves shall be.”

He adds that the Passover lamb was the shadow and image of this sign, whose reality was fulfilled in the dying Christ. He immediately gives this reason:

> “And just as there, when Egypt was struck, the Jewish people could escape only by the sign and blood of the lamb, so too, when the world begins to be devastated and struck, whoever is found in the blood and sign of Christ will alone escape” (*idem*, *To Demetrian*, p. 194).

By this comparison and argument he again proves that no one will be saved at the end of the world unless he bears the sign of Christ’s cross, [Col. 0996A] just as no one escaped safe and unharmed from Egypt unless marked with the sign and blood of the lamb.

No one, however, should suppose that Cyprian thought that anyone would be saved by that sign of the cross alone, merely placed upon his forehead. For good works are also required to obtain eternal happiness. Nor was it in any other sense that he said:

> “Believe him who will give believers the reward of eternal life” (*ibid.*, p. 195).

For throughout his writings, including entire works such as *On Works and Almsgiving* and the third book *Against the Jews*, he plainly shows that, in addition to faith and the sign of Christ’s cross, good works are necessary, by whose merit we may attain everlasting blessedness.

He enumerates and proclaims many good works of Christians [Col. 0996B], which must be treated later. Yet no one will deny that one of them is repentance for the impious worship of false gods and for former offenses. For if repentance is true and sincere:

> “Pardon,” he says, “is granted to the one who confesses, and saving forgiveness is bestowed upon the believer from divine compassion” (*ibid.*, p. 196).

Nor can anyone plead in any way the difficulty of obtaining it. For, he says,

> “the approach to God’s forgiveness lies open, and access is easy for those who seek and understand the truth” (*ibid.*).

Indeed, he does not wish anyone to be hindered either by infirmity or by advanced age from obtaining salvation through repentance, because, as he says,

> “while one is still in this world, no repentance is too late” (*ibid.*).

For so great is the price of Christ’s blood that

> “[Col. 0996C] even at the very departure and setting of temporal life,”

he further says,

> “pardon is granted to the one who confesses, and forgiveness to the believer”;

and thus

> “at the very point of death one passes to immortality.”

But there the learned Oxford editor, although a bishop of the Anglican Church, shrewdly observes that these words were addressed to a pagan who had not yet been reborn in the sacred waters of Baptism, since such easy pardon cannot be promised to wicked Christians who repent only late. And Cyprian certainly proves this more than once, particularly throughout his treatise *On the Lapsed*, from which it is enough to transcribe the following:

> “As greatly as we have sinned, so greatly let us weep. Let diligent and prolonged treatment not be lacking for a deep wound; let repentance not be less than the crime” (*On the Lapsed*, p. 137).

### ARTICLE IV. Whether Cyprian Denied Purgatorial Fires; How Explicitly He Asserts That the Punishments of the Damned Will Be Eternal, Whose Brief Pleasure of the Eyes Will Be Weighed Against Perpetual Viewing; and with What Varied and Horrible Torments Christians Were Mangled by Them

[Col. 0996D]

After this life, says Cyprian, there is no place for repentance and satisfaction, but

> “here life is either lost or retained” (*Cyprian*, *To Demetrian*, p. 197).

But the clearer and more certain these latter words are, the less probable this observation by the bishop of Oxford seems to us:

> “As for purgatorial fires,” he says, “no one should flatter himself and [Col. 0997A] hope for a restoration to life from the underworld.”

Did Cyprian there deny purgatorial fires, of which he made no mention there? Was he necessarily obliged to indicate them there? Not in the least. For, as the same bishop of Oxford admits, Cyprian is there arguing against pagans. If they persist until death in the impious worship of false gods, they will be tortured by the eternal punishments and fires of hell; but if, when death is imminent, they believe, are converted, and depart from this life regenerated by “heavenly regeneration,” or Baptism, they will immediately attain blessed immortality. Who, then, does not see that nothing against purgatorial fires can be concluded from this?

After our author had plainly declared that the souls [Col. 0997B] of unbelieving and wicked people would be tortured together with their bodies by eternal pains and punishments, he immediately added:

> “There he who watched us here for a time will always be watched by us, and the brief pleasure of cruel eyes in the persecutions that took place will be weighed against perpetual viewing” (*ibid.*, p. 195).

But once again the bishop of Oxford observes that these words assail the fleeting and savage delights of the theaters, which feasted the eyes of pagans and persecutors of the Christian religion. Yet, with the learned man’s pardon, we may say that Cyprian is not speaking there—indeed, was not even thinking—of the public pleasures of the theaters, but of the most cruel spectacle enjoyed by pagans who watched most eagerly as Christians were mangled and killed by the most dreadful torments. His meaning, therefore, is that the brief pleasure enjoyed by those cruel eyes with which pagans, not without great delight, watched Christians cruelly [Col. 0997C] tortured and slain with monstrous savagery during the persecutions,

> “will be weighed against perpetual viewing,”

that is, will be considered and assessed,

> “according to the testimony of sacred Scripture,”

as he says there,

> “which declares: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh” (Isa. 66:24).

Although he said that the pleasure of the pagans who delighted their cruel eyes with the horrible spectacle of slaughtered Christians was brief, those same Christians were very often killed by torments as prolonged as they were horrible. Cyprian depicted their various kinds as follows:

> “You deprive the innocent of their homes, despoil them of their property, weigh them down with chains, shut them in prison, and punish them with wild beasts, the sword, and fires. Nor are you content [Col. 0997D] even with a swift conclusion to our sufferings and the simple and rapid brevity of punishments: you apply prolonged tortures to bodies to be mangled, multiply numerous punishments for entrails to be torn apart, and your savagery and brutality cannot be satisfied with customary tortures; ingenious cruelty devises new punishments” (*Cyprian*, *ibid.*, p. 190).

He therefore makes it clear that the punishments by which our most holy martyrs were tortured were of two kinds. Some were ordinary: namely, exile, confiscation of property, chains by which they were weighed down, prison in which they were confined, wild beasts by which they were devoured, the sword by which they were beheaded, and fires by which they were commonly burned. Others were extraordinary: namely, more prolonged and multiplied punishments, and all those which ingenious cruelty and [Col. 0998A], as he further says,

> “the insatiable frenzy of butchery and the inexpressible lust for savagery” (*ibid.*)

could ever devise. But we have treated these matters abundantly in our preceding dissertations, and they will also be treated in the following one (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 10, art. 2; *on Tertullian*, ch. 16, art. 1; and *on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. 8 and ch. 12).

### ARTICLE V. With What Injustice the Pagans Condemned Christians without Allowing Them a Defense or a Hearing; How Marvelous Was Their Patience, Though Their Number Was Always Increasing; and How God Avenged Them by the Ruin of Kings, Losses of Wealth, Destruction of Soldiers, and Diminution of Military Camps

The greater the cruelty of the pagans in mangling and killing [Col. 0998B] Christians, the greater was their injustice in condemning them. For, contrary to the prescribed laws of natural, divine, and human law, they tortured, condemned, and killed them—without allowing them a defense or a hearing—by every kind of punishment hitherto unheard of. Cyprian therefore overthrows and refutes those most unjust people with this argument:

> “Being a Christian either is a crime or it is not” (*Cyprian*, *To Demetrian*, p. 191).

If it is not a crime, the innocent person ought certainly to have been acquitted. But if it is a crime, one who denied that he was a Christian ought, like other defendants, to have been tortured under examination until he confessed his crime. For judicial examination of defendants was established by law so that bodily pain might elicit whether the crime of which the accused stood charged was real. But the pagans, scorning these most equitable laws, [Col. 0998C] attempted by the cruelest examination to compel a person who voluntarily and repeatedly confessed himself a Christian—who proclaimed it in the very forum, in the hearing of magistrates and governors, and who overthrew the false gods of the pagans—to deny that he was a Christian, that is, to deny what they considered his crime. Cyprian therefore assails the pagans in these words:

> “When I voluntarily confess and cry aloud, and repeatedly and again and again attest that I am a Christian, why do you apply tortures to one who confesses? . . . While I pronounce myself a Christian in a public place and with the people standing about, and confound both you and your gods by clear and public proclamation, why do you turn against the weakness of the body? Why do you contend with the frailty of the flesh?” (*ibid.*).

Who could deny that nothing more unjust, or more contrary to every human, civil, and divine law [Col. 0998D], could ever be done than to compel a person by the most dreadful tortures to deny the crime of which he is accused—even by a deceitful lie—and then to acquit him upon his denial? We have expounded and examined this entire argument in our preceding dissertations on the books of Minucius Felix and Tertullian, from whom Cyprian seems, not without good reason, to have drawn it (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 8, art. 2; and *on Tertullian*, ch. 17, art. 2).

But he presses the point still further and rightly teaches that a Christian must not be compelled by force or tortures to reject or deny his religion, but must be defeated by reason, and his faith refuted by valid arguments. He therefore addresses the pagan as follows:

> “[Col. 0999A] Engage with the vigor of the mind; break the strength of the intellect; destroy faith; defeat it by disputation, if you can; defeat it by reason” (*Cyprian*, *ibid.*).

As we have shown, this is the same argument used by Tertullian and Lactantius; the latter expresses it in this manner:

> “Religion cannot be compelled. The matter must be conducted by words rather than blows, so that there may be willingness.”

We have discussed these matters more fully and, unless we are mistaken, sufficiently abundantly in our preceding dissertations (*Lactant.*, *Institutions*, book V, ch. 19, p. 518; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 10, art. 3; and *on Tertullian*, ch. 19, art. 1).

Although Christians saw themselves condemned and slaughtered by the pagans with the utmost injustice of every kind and solely because of their name, they nevertheless endured horrible tortures without any ill will toward their persecutors, [Col. 0999B] but with patience as great as their fortitude. For they knew that God had commanded them never to hate any human being and to love even their enemies (*Cyprian*, *To Demetrian*, p. 197). They therefore returned no injury for injury, but goodwill for hatred; and in return for the punishments inflicted upon them, they showed the way of salvation (*ibid.*, p. 172). Accordingly, no one resisted when apprehended by tyrants; indeed, when mangled by torture, he gloried and gave thanks. These matters were explained in our preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 21, art. 1).

Nor should this be attributed to weakness or impotence, for, as Cyprian says, their number was exceedingly great and abundant (*Cyprian*, loc. cit.). [Col. 0999C] And we have certainly seen how great their multitude was in the time of Tertullian. Since they multiplied daily, they must undoubtedly have been far more numerous when our author was writing (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, loc. cit.). He therefore judged that there was no need to prove something known to everyone and deeply resented by the pagans. By their numbers, then, the Christians could easily have avenged the cruelty of the pagans, as we have also demonstrated in our preceding dissertation (*ibid.*, ch. 22, art. 1).

Moreover, they knew with certainty that the horrible brutality of the pagans would not be left unpunished by God, the most just judge:

> “The assurance of vengeance to come,”

Cyprian therefore says,

> “made them patient” (*Cypr.*, *ibid.*, p. 192).

But whence, someone will ask, came such assurance? [Col. 0999D] First, because almighty God himself had promised in clear and solemn words that this would come to pass. Second, our author concludes that God had in fact kept his promises from the fact that

> “an impious crime never rises against our name without divine vengeance immediately following” (*ibid.*).

Nor did he assert that this was difficult for him to prove, since it was evident from all the histories of past events. He therefore thought it sufficient to present an example from recent memory in which God exacted the gravest punishments from the persecutors of Christians through

> “the ruin of kings, losses of wealth, destruction of soldiers, and diminution of military camps.”

We have already seen that these words designate the most disastrous defeat and death of the emperor Decius and of his sons Decius, Trajan [Col. 1000A], and Etruscus. How evident and remarkable a proof this was of divine vengeance, as our author calls it, we shall show in the subsequent dissertation on Lucius Caecilius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. By this and many other examples he made plain to everyone what punishments Decius and the other most brutal tyrants of the Christians paid to God. In our other dissertations as well, we have clearly considered how strong and invincible an argument can be drawn from these events in vindication of the truth of the Christian religion (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. 7, art. 1).

## CHAPTER IV. Cyprian’s Arguments Are Examined by Which He Refutes Demetrian and the Other Pagans Who Accused Christians of Being the Cause of the Public Calamities of War, Famine, and Pestilence

[Col. 1000B]

### ARTICLE I. Cyprian’s First Argument, Drawn from the Old Age of the World, Is Examined
In our preceding dissertations we have seen how often and how shamelessly the pagans charged that Christians were the cause of all the public calamities by which the world was afflicted, because they did not venerate the pagans’ gods (Dissert. on Arnobius, chap. 6, art. 1 ff.; on Tertullian, chap. 23, art. 1 ff.). Although this absurd accusation had been utterly overthrown by the defenders of our religion as often as it was repeated by those same pagans, [Col. 1000C] Demetrianus and others were nevertheless not ashamed to revive it when, in the time of our Cyprian, the world was oppressed by the threefold scourge of war, famine, and a dreadful plague. Cyprian was therefore compelled to write this book in order to refute them once again, as we have noted. Since, however, he checked their effrontery—which had already been more than sufficiently repulsed by others—with certain new and weighty arguments, these must now be examined in our customary manner.

First, therefore, he demonstrates that these and other public disasters, considered either collectively or individually, were by no means caused by the Christians, but arose sometimes from natural causes, far more often from the very great crimes of the pagans themselves, and always as punishment for wicked men. He thinks that one may infer that, in general, they should be attributed [Col. 1000D] to natural causes from the old age of the world, which he believed was tending toward decline and destruction (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 186). For, he said, the four seasons of the year had been disordered. There was, indeed, a smaller supply of rain in winter, less blazing heat from the sun in summer, less mildness of the sky in spring, and less abundance of fruit in autumn. Moreover, gold, silver, and other metals were diminishing in the bowels of the earth, while farmers, sailors, and soldiers were everywhere failing. Indeed, he says: “We see gray hairs in children; hair fails before it grows; nor does life end in old age, but begins with old age” (*ibid.*, p. 187). Finally, there was the greatest corruption of morals. From all these things he concludes that the world was growing old, and that it was no wonder if, in its old age, as [Col. 1001A] in that of other living things, everything degenerated and failed.

But just as there is no room for doubt that all these things which Cyprian so positively asserts were true, so, with due respect to the most holy Martyr, we may be permitted to say that they did not occur because the world—which remained intact for so many centuries after his death—had already grown old and was near its end. Furthermore, gold and silver were diminishing because their veins had been exhausted only in certain places, not everywhere on earth. More frequent deaths among human beings could have resulted from the intemperateness and corruption of the air, from which also arose that dreadful plague that was laying everything waste. The pestilential air could likewise have caused children to turn gray entirely before their time, and their strength, which [Col. 1001B] ought to have increased, to diminish as it does in the aged. Yet even if all these things were most clearly proved to have arisen from natural causes, it is nonetheless certain that such great disasters befell men in vengeance for their wickedness, as we shall soon see.

Cyprian’s opinion concerning the imminent end of the world was not peculiar to him, but was shared with him by Fathers of various ages. Lactantius and very many others, as we have observed in the proper place, were persuaded that the whole world would be destroyed when the number of six thousand years from its beginning had been completed. Others, however, such as Tertullian, thought that its fall and that of the Roman Empire would be the same. Finally, others, such as Ambrose and Gregory the Great, like our Cyprian, proclaimed that the end of the world was imminent whenever [Col. 1001C] it was afflicted by public calamities of famine, plague, and other extraordinary disasters (Dissert. on Lactantius, chap. 29, art. 1; and on Tertullian, chap. 15, art. 1, and chap. 21, art. 1; Ambrose, book X, *Exposition on Luke*, § 10, p. 1506; Gregory, *Homily 35 on the Gospels*, p. 1612). But do not, I beg you, readily suppose that all of them pronounced as certain and entirely beyond doubt that which they had learned from Christ’s most certain words was known to God alone. Rather, because they saw that certain signs foretold by Christ himself of the world’s decline had occurred, they thought Christians should be warned about them, so that, although wholly uncertain about what would follow, they might lead holier lives and not promise themselves a longer span. No one has ever been able to infer [Col. 1001D] with certainty from public calamities, any more than from the corruption of morals, that the end of the world was near. Yet no one either, as we think, can deny that our Cyprian concluded entirely correctly that public calamities had been stirred up by the pagans’ most grievous offenses, crimes, impious superstitions, and general corruption of morals. Let us now examine, if you please, how he derives his second argument from this.

## ARTICLE II. How clearly Cyprian demonstrates that public calamities occurred not because Christians worshiped the true God, but because the pagans worshiped false gods and were guilty of other most grievous crimes; with a discussion of the punishments of slaves

It is certainly established that the world was not created by itself, as we have demonstrated elsewhere, [Col. 1002A] but by the true and omnipotent God, by whose will and judgment all things are governed, and whom human beings and all creatures ought to obey and serve (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 187). But he commanded that false gods should never be worshiped, and that he alone should be worshiped and adored by all human beings. For, Cyprian says, he had commanded in a “divine utterance”: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13). In another book he reported precisely these same words and testifies that they were written in Deuteronomy (Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 171, and book III *Against the Jews*, § 11, p. 65). In the Greek translation of the Seventy, however, it reads: Κύριον τὸν θεόν σου φοβηθήσῃ, καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις, “You shall fear the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” But in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, προσκυνήσεις, “you shall worship,” occurs in place of φοβηθήσῃ, “you shall fear.”

Elsewhere God forbade [Col. 1002B] the gods fabricated by human beings ever to be worshiped by anyone. These are the very words of his quoted by Cyprian: “You shall have no foreign gods apart from me” (Exod. 20:3). He repeats the same words in another book (Cyprian, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, *ibid.*), which the Seventy rendered in Greek as follows: Οὐκ ἔσονταί σοι θεοὶ ἔτεροι πλὴν ἐμοῦ, “You shall have no other gods besides me.” In the Latin Vulgate, however: “You shall not have foreign gods before me.”

Jeremiah too, cited by our same author, had announced to the Jews and to all others that prophets had been sent by God to warn them that his wrath was being provoked by this impious worship of foreign gods. “Do not,” he said, “serve foreign gods and worship them. Do not provoke me by the works of your hands to destroy you” (Jer. 26:6). He reported these same words in another book (Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, [Col. 1002C] book I, § 2, p. 21; idem, *To Demetrianus*, p. 189); in the Greek of the Septuagint: Ὅπως μὴ παροργίζητέ με ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τῶν χειρῶν ὑμῶν, τοῦ κακῶσαι ὑμᾶς, “So that you may not provoke me to anger by the works of your hands, to bring harm upon yourselves.” In the Vulgate, however, we read: “And do not provoke me to anger by the works of your hands, so that I may not afflict you.”

But the pagans’ crime was all the more grievous because they not only worshiped false gods and spurned the one true God, but also condemned Christians who worshiped him, contrary to all human and divine laws, as we have seen, without ever giving them a hearing or allowing them a defense, and killed them by every kind of torture. Rightly and deservedly, therefore, God, offended by such great injustice and impiety on their part, avenged these and their many other crimes by public calamities.

Indeed, in addition to those two atrocities of idolatry [Col. 1002D] and supreme injustice, “Innocence,” says our author, “had failed in the forum, justice in the court, concord in friendships, and discipline in conduct” (*ibid.*, p. 186). He pursues these matters much more fully in his book *To Donatus*, where he gives the reasons why he himself, after renouncing the pagans’ accursed superstitions, embraced the Christian religion:

> “Although the laws have been engraved on twelve tablets and legal rights publicly prescribed on displayed bronze, transgression occurs amid the laws themselves and sin amid legal rights. Innocence is not preserved even there where it is defended. The fury of men at variance rages against one another, and amid the togas, with peace broken, the forum bellows in the madness of litigation. . . . Crimes blaze everywhere, and everywhere, through manifold kinds of sinning, a harmful poison [Col. 1003A] works through wicked minds. . . . To be innocent now among the guilty is a crime. Whoever does not imitate the wicked gives offense. The laws have come to an agreement with sins, and what is public has begun to be lawful” (Cyprian, *To Donatus*, p. 7 ff.).

The rest, which it would take too long to transcribe here, you may read there. If anyone could doubt how true these things were, he will become still more certain from what has often been observed in our preceding dissertations concerning the utterly corrupt morals of the pagans, and from what must be said a little later.

Since, therefore, the pagans overthrew so many and such important divine and human laws with truly astonishing audacity and rashness through so many and such great crimes, they certainly could not complain that God chastised them with public disasters. But Cyprian additionally convicts them completely through the comparison, obvious to everyone, [Col. 1003B] between master and slave. If you have a slave who is defiant, insolent, unfaithful, and does not obey your commands, do you not, Cyprian says, “scourge him, beat him, and frequently afflict and torture him with hunger, thirst, nakedness, iron, and prison” (*ibid.*, *To Demetrianus*, p. 188)?

But someone will ask whether masters were lawfully permitted to punish their slaves with so many kinds of penalty. Yes, we reply, and with many others which Plautus expressed in these verses:

> Great praise and thanks we deservedly give to perfidy,  
> Together with our swindling, tricks, and cunning,  
> Trusting in the endurance of our shoulder blades, relying on the strength of the elms  
> (variant: “of our shoulders”),  
> Against goads, metal plates, crosses, and fetters,  
> Ropes, chains, prisons, wooden collars, shackles, and neck-irons,  
> And the fiercest instructors, well acquainted with our backs,  
> Who have often before laid scars upon our shoulders.

But someone else will ask us why Cyprian [Col. 1003C] added “iron” there. Could masters, he will ask, kill their slaves with impunity? We answer that, under the most ancient Roman law, masters had indeed been granted the power of life and death over their slaves. Later, however, the emperor Hadrian, according to Spartianus, not only forbade slaves to be killed by their masters, but also commanded judges to condemn masters who were proved to have punished their slaves too harshly (Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, past the midpoint; *Theodosian Code*, book IX, title 11, *On the Correction of Slaves*, laws 1 and 2, p. 79).

In the books of the *Institutes*, moreover, mention is made of a law issued by Antoninus, by which “one who has killed his own slave without cause is commanded to be punished no less than if he had killed another man’s slave. But the excessive harshness of masters is also restrained by a constitution of the same emperor” (*Institutes*, book [Col. 1003D] I, title 8, *On Those Who Are Independent*). Finally, Constantine the Great entirely and utterly abolished this right of masters over slaves by two laws, and further prohibited them ever to rage against slaves too savagely. In the cited *Theodosian Code* you have both of those laws.

In any case, although masters could still have killed their slaves in Cyprian’s time, we may nonetheless readily be persuaded that the word “iron” does not denote this power, but rather certain instruments of iron, like the metal plates mentioned by Plautus—that is, glowing plates of bronze and iron—with which slaves were tortured.

Furthermore, even if a master does not possess the right of life and death over his slave, he nevertheless rightly [Col. 1004A] demands the service owed to him by one who shares the same nature as himself. Thus, when the master corrects the slave who resists and refuses obedience, that slave himself is the cause of his punishments. How much more, therefore, are wicked human beings the cause of public calamities when, after abandoning the true God, the lord and governor of all things, and after despising and undermining all his laws, they worship false gods and wallow in every kind of crime! Yet these were not Christians but pagans, whose complaint about public disasters was therefore utterly unjust. Accordingly, Cyprian rightly presses them as follows: “Do not say that evils occur because your gods are not worshiped by us; but know”—so reads the oldest Colbert manuscript—“that this wrath is God’s sentence, so that one who does not understand through blessings may at least understand through blows” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 194). But these matters will become still clearer and more evident [Col. 1004B] from what he said about each particular disaster, which must now be explained.

## ARTICLE III. How Cyprian proved that the Christians were by no means the cause of wars, but the pagans were

The pagans’ complaint concerning wars was indeed great, or, to use Cyprian’s words: “You complain that an enemy is rising up” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 189), who was ravaging and laying waste the Roman Empire. But this was certainly by no means to be attributed to the Christians, but to these very pagans: “Among whom,” our author continues, “even if an external enemy were absent, could there be peace among the togas themselves?” (*ibid.*). By the term “togas” he includes all Roman magistrates, governors, and judges who wore the toga. [Col. 1004C] For we have already seen how great were the quarrels and dissensions among them, and how great their crimes of avarice and injustice, by which human beings were very often afflicted more cruelly than by war.

To this must be added that, “Even if the frontier arms and dangers arising from the barbarians”—“frontier” (*extrema*) in our oldest manuscript; “external” (*externa*) in the other manuscripts and printed editions—“are checked,” nevertheless internal and domestic wars were waged more savagely by means of “false accusations and injuries,” through which they invaded the property of others. For was less harm done to the commonwealth by wars than when, as he says, “a crime is committed by the guilty, and no innocent person is found to exact punishment; when neither accuser nor judge is feared? The wicked obtain impunity: while the modest are silent, the complicit are afraid, and those who will judge are bought” (*ibid.*, p. 190)?

But in *To Donatus* he wrote more fully about these matters in the following words:

> “Crimes blaze everywhere. . . . Here one substitutes a will; there another composes a false one through a fraud punishable by death. Here children are excluded from inheritances; there strangers are endowed with estates. An enemy accuses, a slanderer attacks, a witness defames; on every side the venal audacity of a prostituted voice runs riot in lying accusations, while in the meantime the guilty do not perish even together with the innocent” (idem, *To Donatus*, p. 7).

Because, therefore, there was such contempt for the laws and such impunity even for the gravest crimes, “There is no fear”—this word is absent from several manuscript copies—“or shame in wrongdoing,” he says; “and people sin as if they gained greater approval through the very sins themselves” (idem, *To Demetrianus*, p. 189). What wonder, then, [Col. 1005A] if so many impious and disgraceful men were found everywhere? What wonder if “forgers and poisoners” shamelessly raised their deadly heads? What wonder if “assassins were seen in the midst of the city, as headlong in sinning as they were free from punishment for their sins?” (*ibid.*, p. 190). But these most criminal men were discussed in the preceding dissertation (Dissert. on Tertullian, chap. 24, art. 4). Who can doubt that these internal wars were far worse than the external ones being waged on the remotest borders of the Roman Empire? But consider, I ask, whether by these words, “external arms arising from the barbarians,” he was aiming especially at those by which Decius and other emperors—who, as we saw above, were slain to a man while raging more fiercely against the Christians—paid with their deaths the penalty for their cruelty.

[Col. 1005B] But these wars, says Cyprian, were waged neither by some fortuitous chance nor in vengeance upon the Christians, but upon the pagans who had provoked God. For, he says, “It is clear and manifest that all these things which descend from God’s indignation occur not through us, but on our behalf”—so the older and better manuscripts read (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 192). These disasters of war, therefore, did not happen “through us,” that is, because of us and because we do not worship false gods, but “on our behalf,” since by these wars God was avenging the injuries done to us and, by punishing our persecutors, restoring to our churches the peace they desired.

## ARTICLE IV. By what reasoning Cyprian shows that the Christians were not the cause of barrenness and famine, but the pagans were

[Col. 1005C]

The pagans were still crying out that they were being killed by famine, barrenness of the fields, and scarcity of crops because Christians did not venerate their gods (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 189). But this second complaint of theirs was plainly absurd. For the true God willed that the world be afflicted by this public calamity, not indeed because of the Christians, who worshiped him piously and obeyed his precepts, but because of the pagans themselves, who denied that he was the true God and were always offending him with the gravest crimes.

For although the world was struck by so great a scourge through God’s just judgment, the pagans nevertheless did not thereby become better. Avaricious men, in order to sell grain more dearly, [Col. 1005D] shut their granaries and preferred the poor to perish from hunger rather than fail to increase their own wealth through the poor’s need. Their rapacity and avarice therefore created a greater and far crueler famine than the barrenness of the earth. For what, as Gregory Nazianzen rightly argues, is “more grievous and bitter than the cruelty and insatiable greed of those who possess grain? For they watch for difficult times, trade in famine, and reap a harvest from the calamities of others” (Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 20, p. 558). Therefore those savage and brutal men, who had cast off all humanity, were detestable both to God and to other human beings. For Solomon declares [Col. 1006A] in the Proverbs cited by the same Gregory and by our Cyprian: “He who lies in wait for the grain supply is accursed among the peoples” (Gregory, *ibid.*; Cyprian, book III *Against the Jews*, § 61, p. 82); or, as we read in the Vulgate: “He who hides grain is cursed among the peoples.”

Nor is this cruelty condemned only by divine laws, but also by human ones. For we have as a witness the jurist Paulus, who left it written: “The *Dardanarii* [grain speculators] are especially accustomed to manipulate and distress the grain supply; their avarice has been opposed both by official instructions and by imperial constitutions” (*Digest*, book LX, title 11, *On Extraordinary Crimes*, law 6).

But those hard and iron-hearted pagans ruined these most equitable laws and, moreover, held in utter contempt the salutary warnings of God, by which his sacred prophets had foretold a coming famine because of their offenses. [Col. 1006B] For what could be clearer than this warning of Haggai cited by Cyprian (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 187)?

> “Because my house lies desolate, while each of you pursues”—διώκετε, “pursues” (Vulgate: “hastens”)—“his own house, therefore heaven will withhold the dew, and the earth will hold back its produce, and I shall bring a sword upon the earth”—καὶ ἐπάξω ῥομφαίαν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, “and I shall bring a sword upon the earth.”

The Vulgate reads:

> “And I called drought upon the earth, and upon the grain, and upon the wine, and upon the oil, and upon human beings, and upon beasts of burden, and upon all the works of their hands” (Hag. 1:9–10).

He had therefore foretold the future barrenness of the earth because human beings would abandon God’s house—that is, his worship, or the house in which he was customarily worshiped—so that each might go away into his own house, where he would venerate idols and false gods. [Col. 1006C] Although Cyprian, following the Seventy, said “sword,” nevertheless that term undoubtedly signifies drought and barrenness, by which death was inflicted upon human beings.

Accordingly, he added this prophecy of the prophet Amos:

> “And I shall rain”—the Septuagint: καὶ βρέξω, “and I shall rain”; the Vulgate, as a little later—“and I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain. . . . And two and three cities will gather in one city for the sake of drinking water, and they will not be satisfied. And you do not return to me, says the Lord” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 187; Amos 4:7 ff.).

But so far were they from then returning to this one true God that they instead offended him still more grievously, not only during the famine and barrenness, but also during the more bitterly raging plague, as must now be demonstrated.

[Col. 1006D]

## ARTICLE V. So far were the pagans from attempting to appease God, who had been offended by their crimes, during the plague that they instead provoked him with still more grievous offenses

We have already observed how the most disastrous plague was laying everything waste in a manner dreadful and hitherto unheard of, as Cyprian, Eusebius, and others record (above, chap. 1, art. 5). But what do you suppose was then done by the pagans who accused the Christians of this third disaster? Did they thereby become better? By no means. Indeed, they provoked with new crimes—crimes that can never be sufficiently detested—the God whom they had compelled, [Col. 1007A] because of their offenses, to chastise them with this horrible plague. For, Cyprian says, “Through the plague and pestilence itself, the crimes of individuals were either revealed or increased, since no mercy was shown to the sick, while avarice and plunder gaped after the dead” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 189).

He charges them with two kinds of crimes into which men both cruel and avaricious openly rushed. First, their inhumanity toward the sick, the dying, and the dead was extreme and horrible to describe. They offered no assistance to those suffering from the plague, utterly abandoned the dying, fled from the funerals of the dead, and left the bodies of the deceased unburied, just like those of dogs. But Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon and an eyewitness, portrays these things in colors [Col. 1007B] as vivid as they are tragic:

> “All shuddered, fled, and avoided contagion, impiously casting out their own. . . . Meanwhile, throughout the whole city there lay, no longer bodies, but the corpses of very many; and by the sight of the fate common to all they demanded mercy from those passing by. No one regarded anything but cruel gains. No one trembled at the recollection that the same outcome might befall him. No one did to another what he wished to be done to himself” (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, p. 5).

Dionysius of Alexandria likewise wrote the same things about these same pagans:

> Νοσεῖν ἀρχομένους ἀπωθοῦντο, καὶ ἀπέφευγον τοὺς φιλτάτους, κἀν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἐῤῥίπτουν ἡμιθνῆτας, καὶ νεκροὺς ἀτάφους ἀπεσκυβαλίζοντο· τὴν τοῦ θανάτου διάδοσιν, καὶ κοινωνίαν ἐκτρεπόμενοι, ἣν οὐκ ἦν πολλὰ μηχανωμένοις ἐκκλῖναι ῥᾴδιον.
>
> “They drove away those who were beginning to fall ill and fled from their dearest loved ones; [Col. 1007C] they abandoned the half-dead in the streets and cast out the dead unburied, shunning the transmission and shared experience of death—something which, despite employing many precautions and every diligence, they nevertheless could not readily avoid” (Eusebius, book VII, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 22, p. 269).

The second kind of crime committed by these people, wholly devoid of every sense of humanity and no less wicked than the former, was that they seemed to have abandoned the dying precisely “lest they should be able to escape death while receiving care” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 189). For they desired not their recovery but their swiftest possible death, so that they might more quickly rush upon their property and possessions. For no one, as Pontius, whom we cited just now, said, regarded anything but cruel gains. [Col. 1007D] Nor did they attempt to conceal this. For, Cyprian continues, “There was no concealment in plundering, no hesitation, no fear” (*ibid.*, p. 190). They could be seen running about everywhere, seizing and appropriating the property of the deceased. And lest someone else, gaping with equal avarice, forestall their robberies, forgers stood ready to substitute fraudulent wills for those of the dying, which were immediately approved as genuine by the authority of judges corrupted by bribes.

So far, therefore, were these most wicked men, afflicted by so many and such great disasters, from coming to their senses that, without fearing the wrath of God, they continually aroused it more fiercely against themselves by still more grievous crimes (*ibid.*, p. 188). Justly, therefore, did the prophets cited by our author [Col. 1008A] complain that those who neither felt pain nor wished to accept discipline were being struck and beaten with these blows in vain (Jer. 2:30). What, then, says Cyprian, would they not have done if they had not been struck? Would not their boldness in sinning have increased through the impunity of their crimes? These, then, are the arguments by which our author clearly demonstrates that the pagans, and by no means the Christians, were the cause of the public calamities, as must still be proved.

## ARTICLE VI. How great were the works of mercy that Christians showed to all who were infected by the plague, dying, or dead

If the Christians could not avert the public calamities by which the world was convulsed [Col. 1008B] because of the pagans’ many and great crimes, as we have said, they attempted either to alleviate them by pious works or to obtain from almighty God that a limit be set to them. For by day and night, “unceasingly and insistently,” says Cyprian, they entreated him “that enemies might be warded off, rains obtained, adversities either removed or moderated, and for your peace and safety,” that is, the pagans’ (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 193).

The editor of the Oxford edition notes at that passage that in these words Cyprian referred to the memorable deed of the Christians who, under the emperor Aurelius, obtained from God the rain utterly necessary for the army—a subject we treated in the preceding dissertation. But since Cyprian said that Christians implored God’s mercy “unceasingly and insistently,” [Col. 1008C] did he not rather denote by these words their daily prayers, by which, both privately and publicly in their assemblies, as we have also noted, they prayed to God for the emperors and for the condition of the age? (Dissert. on Tertullian, chap. 19, art. 2; chap. 23, art. 4; *ibid.*, chap. 15, art. 1.)

As great as was the pagans’ inhumanity toward their companions suffering from the plague, dying, or dead, and the insatiable cruelty of avaricious men, as we have just said, so great was the Christians’ piety, charity, and compassion toward them. At the risk of their own lives, they brought every assistance to the sick and the dead. For, as Pontius relates, Cyprian immediately assembled the people entrusted to him and exhorted them with such force of eloquence to show every work of mercy to the sick that what was performed by the Christians [Col. 1008D] can scarcely be described (Pontius, *Life of Cyprian*, pp. 5–6). Duties were assigned to individuals according to their station, by which they might bring their aid to those infected by the plague. Without any delay, the rich bestowed with marvelous generosity everything necessary upon those in need. The poorer, meanwhile, furnished through their labor a recompense more precious than every form of wealth. But in this they surpassed the incomparable piety of Tobias—with whose pardon Pontius wished this to be said—because by these offices of mercy they attempted to relieve not only the household of the faith, but also the pagans most hostile to them, whom, even when dead, they committed to burial no differently from Christians.

[Col. 1009A] Dionysius of Alexandria explains these matters more fully. Very many, he says, while continually attending upon the sick and restoring them to health, themselves perished by a death as holy as it was glorious. Others, after closing the eyes and mouths of the dead, carrying their bodies on their shoulders, washing them, laying them out, and clothing them according to customary practice, themselves died shortly afterward and received the same offices from others. And this kind of death, as Dionysius rightly says, is judged, because of their piety and steadfastness in the faith, to be no less than martyrdom (Eusebius, book VII, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 22, p. 269). Who, then, does not see how different were the deeds of Christians and pagans during that calamitous plague, and which of them offended God or were capable of appeasing him when angry?

## ARTICLE VII. Why entirely innocent Christians were afflicted by the same public calamities as the wicked pagans

[Col. 1009B]

In no way moved by the Christians’ truly marvelous works of supreme piety toward all, the pagans pressed their case more fiercely and cried out openly that God would be altogether unjust if, in punishing the wicked through public calamities, he afflicted and overwhelmed the deserving and undeserving alike (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 192). But our Cyprian refutes this argument, which they had often repeated, as we have seen, by various considerations (Dissert. on Tertullian, chap. 23, arts. 1 and 5; Cyprian, *ibid.*, p. 192).

First, he acknowledges that God [Col. 1009C] could prohibit these evils whenever he wished, but that he had been unwilling to do so because of the pagans’ wickedness and crimes, as we have shown—crimes which, as the Prophet says, separate human beings from him (Isa. 59:2). Therefore, if the pagans had not sinned, or if they had sincerely repented of their crimes, then, not being separated from God, they would certainly have had no cause to complain about him and about the Christians.

Next, although Christians led an entirely pious and chaste life, nevertheless, because for as long as they are in this world their bodily condition must be the same as that of the pagans, just as with people living in the same house, both groups must therefore be affected by the same adverse and troublesome circumstances. But they were very different in spirit. For which of them could be said to be afflicted and disquieted by public [Col. 1009D] disasters? Were they not only the pagans, who grieved, sorrowed, and lamented their wretched lot with voices as clamorous as they were querulous? Christians, on the contrary, says Cyprian, “living more by the spirit than by the flesh,” overcame “the weakness of the body by firmness of mind” (Cyprian, *ibid.*, p. 193). Therefore, never dismayed or broken in spirit by any adversity, they neither grieved over these things nor murmured about them.

Furthermore, the pagans bewailed their miseries and hardships because they could enjoy well-being only in this age, and nothing afterward remained for them but punishment and sorrow (*ibid.*, p. 192). The minds of Christians, on the contrary, who despised the transitory goods of this life, remained uplifted amid these very ruins of a passing age; [Col. 1010A] their virtue was immovable, their endurance joyful, their faith firm, and their hope and expectation certain of the eternal happiness promised to them by God.

Next, the world was not oppressed by so many disasters because Christians did not worship false gods; rather, the true God permitted it to be afflicted by these things so that, as Cyprian says, “one who does not understand through blessings may at least understand through blows” (*ibid.*, p. 195). The pagans, therefore, were punished by these calamities so that they might repent of their crimes and, having at last rejected the insane worship of false gods, acknowledge and worship the one omnipotent God and embrace the true religion.

In addition, Christians knew and trusted that they were being tested and strengthened by these same adversities. Therefore, in another book Cyprian said: [Col. 1010B]

> “How necessary it is that this plague and pestilence, which seems dreadful and deadly, tests the righteousness of each individual: whether the healthy serve the sick; whether relatives dutifully cherish their kindred; whether masters show mercy to their ailing slaves; whether physicians do not abandon the sick who implore them; whether the rapacious extinguish, at least through fear of death, the ever-insatiable blaze of raging avarice; whether the proud bend their necks; whether the wicked soften their audacity; whether, as their dear ones perish, the rich even thus bestow and give something, since they themselves are to die without an heir” (*ibid.*, p. 193; idem, *On Mortality*, p. 162).

For just as the skill of a shipmaster is discerned in a storm, just as the spirit of a soldier is tested in battle, and just as Abraham’s faith was tried by the command to sacrifice his son, so by these public disasters the virtue and patience of Christians were tested and, [Col. 1010C] once tested, crowned (*ibid.*). Why so? “Because,” he says, “unless the struggle has preceded, there can be no victory; when victory has been achieved in the encounter of battle, then the crown also is given to the victors” (*ibid.*, p. 160).

After confirming this by the examples of certain persons, especially the apostle Paul, and also by the words of Paul and Ecclesiastes, he concludes from it that the condition of Christians in the public calamity of the plague and in other adversities is far different from that of pagans and Jews. For to these enemies of Christ the dreadful plague, concerning which we have spoken sufficiently, was an incurable and deadly stroke by which the dying were carried away to everlasting punishment; but to Christians it was a saving departure, by which they were summoned to eternal refreshment (*ibid.*, p. 161).

[Col. 1010D] Therefore, however greatly the pagans and Jews complained and grieved over plague, famine, and war, to the same degree Christians showed, with calm and joyful spirits, the truth of what the prophet Habakkuk, cited by Cyprian, had foretold long before in these words (idem, *Against Demetrianus*, p. 193):

> “The fig tree will bear no fruit, and there will be no produce on the vines”—Οὐ καρποφορήσει καὶ οὐκ ἔσται γεννήματα ἐν ταῖς ἀμπέλοις, “It will not bear fruit, and there will be no produce on the vines.”  
> “The labor of the olive will fail, and the fields will provide no food. The sheep will fail from the pasture”—Ἐξέλιπεν ἀπὸ βρώσεως πρόβατα, “The sheep have failed for lack of food.”  
> “And there will be no cattle in the stalls. But I shall rejoice in the Lord, and in God my Savior”—Χαρήσομαι ἐπὶ τῷ Θεῷ σωτῆρί μου, “I shall rejoice in God my Savior” (Hab. IV, 17–18).

Nor indeed was their joy feigned or empty, because [Col. 1011A] they firmly expected that eternal happiness would be given to them by God.

Cyprian afterward confirms this at much greater length with words taken from the Book of Wisdom, which he cited in full elsewhere and elsewhere reported only their final portion (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 195). Solomon—to whom Cyprian expressly attributes this very book—there clearly recounts how bitterly impious and unjust men, tormented in the eternal fires of hell, will bewail their most wretched lot and eternal condemnation when they behold the blessedness of Christians (Wis. 5:1 ff.; Cyprian, book III, *Testimonies*, p. 68; *On the Dress of Virgins*, p. 97; and *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 182).

Moreover, in our preceding dissertations we saw that this argument of the pagans, drawn from the Christians’ adversities and [Col. 1011B] persecutions, militates not so much against them as against the providence of God; and we saw how it is answered and overthrown by the most learned defenders of the Christian religion.

## CHAPTER V. ON CYPRIAN’S BOOK *ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS*

### ARTICLE I. Analysis of This Book

This book is divided into three parts. In the first, Cyprian shows that the gods of the pagans are altogether false (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 11).
