For dead kings began to be worshiped by them; thereafter their likenesses were represented in images, temples were built, victims were sacrificed, and feast days were celebrated in their honor. In this way not only Melicertes and Leucothea, Castor and Pollux, Aesculapius, Apollo, and Neptune were made gods, but also Jupiter, whose tomb is displayed in Crete, and Saturn, who gave Latium its name and was the first in Italy to teach the impressing of letters and the stamping of coins. When Jupiter drove him out, he was received by two-faced Janus, from whom the Janiculum and the month of January derived their names. The Moors, however, worshiped their kings more plainly and openly. The religion of the pagans was then propagated through this unrestrained and impious license. For in the provinces individual peoples worshiped not the one true God, but numerous fictitious gods handed down by their ancestors. Our author proves this from a letter of Alexander the Great and makes it plain that nothing could be more absurd to say [Col. 1011D] than that power to beget other gods was either given to or taken away from gods of this kind (*ibid.*, p. 12).

Nor does he allow it to be objected that the Romans merited dominion over the whole world through their piety toward their gods. For they never received it from their own native and indigenous gods or goddesses, nor from other foreign deities adopted from elsewhere. They did not receive it from the former, such as Romulus, Picus, Tiberinus, Pilumnus, Consus, Viduus, Scansus, Forculus, and Limentinus; nor from the goddesses Cloacina, Fear, Pallor, Fever, or Acca and Flora, both prostitutes, or Cardea and Orbona. Indeed, to name such gods and goddesses is to refute them (p. 13).

Assuredly for the same reason—and indeed for a still stronger one—[Col. 1012A] the Romans’ foreign gods, such as Thracian and Cretan Mars, or their adopted goddesses, such as Argive, Samian, or Punic Juno, Tauric Diana, the Idaean Mother of the Gods, or Bald Venus, neither gave nor enlarged the Romans’ empire. For if they were unable to protect the kingdoms of those by whom they were worshiped, how could they establish and enlarge the empire of others to whom they had never been known? In addition, the Penates whom Aeneas carried with him into Italy had been conquered. Furthermore, before the Romans there flourished the kingdoms of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Egyptians, and Greeks. The gods of the Romans therefore govern neither these kingdoms nor any others.

But come now, and tell us, please, how dominion was bestowed upon the Romans because of their piety toward their gods, when it began with parricide, the abduction of virgins, and other unspeakable crimes [Col. 1012B]. Nor may you say that it was enlarged through auspices, auguries, and other superstitions of this kind, by which certain future events were either foretold or something was believed to occur outside the customary order of nature. For the examples of Regulus, Mancinus, and Gaius Caesar demonstrate their falsity. And what of the fact that these and all the other things at which the pagans marveled were not performed by the power of their false gods, but by the frauds and deceptions of demons, who were known to poets, to Socrates, to the Magi, to Hostanes, and to Plato, although both Hostanes and Plato taught that there is only one God (p. 14)? For these demons are impure and depraved spirits who, hiding beneath the statues and images of the gods, attempted to persuade credulous and unwary people that these things were done by those very gods [Col. 1012C], lest they be led away from their worship to the true religion. For all their deceptions and frauds were exposed when Christians, adjuring them by the true God, compelled them not only to depart from the bodies they possessed, but also openly to confess who they themselves were and that he in whose name they were adjured is the one true God.

Passing from there to the second part of this treatise, Cyprian proves with the utmost clarity that he alone is God, the creator of all things. For, he says, the supreme majesty of divinity can neither be divided nor admit a partner. Indeed, even earthly kings—such as the “brotherhood of the Thebans,” the Roman twins, and the kinsmen Pompey and Caesar—were unable to endure association with another reigning sovereign. And what of the fact that, if we consider natural things [Col. 1012D], we see that bees, flocks, and herds have a single leader, just as there is one ruler of the world, who can neither be seen nor comprehended nor ever adequately estimated? Since he is one, he is not called by many names; rather, his entire name is God. And because he is diffused everywhere, he cannot be confined within a single little shrine, but the whole world is his temple. Finally, the common people, however ignorant, very frequently invoke him naturally by their exclamations and confess that he exists.

Finally, in the third part of this work Cyprian makes plain to everyone what the Christians’ genuine doctrine concerning Christ is. The kingdom of the Jews, he says, flourished so long as they obeyed the divine commandments. [Col. 1013A] But after they had spurned them, they lost the grace given to them by God and, exiles from earth and heaven, wander scattered throughout the whole world. Accordingly, as he had promised, God chose for himself another and more faithful people, who would receive the grace and pardon lost by the Jews. At the appointed time, therefore, he sent his Son, who is Word, power, reason, wisdom, and glory. Descending into a virgin through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, he became man mingled with God. He is therefore the Christians’ judge, master, illuminator, teacher, and mediator, who leads us to the Father.

The Jews indeed knew that this was he whom their sacred prophets had foretold would come both then and at the end of the world; but, blinded by their crimes, they deny this first advent of his and await the second. [Col. 1013B] And because he performed almost countless miracles, they said that he was great. Yet certainly, while he lived among human beings as himself a man, all those things occurred which had been foretold about him by those same prophets. Toward the end of his life, the teachers and leading men of the Jews, angered by his divine teaching, extorted from Pontius Pilate, who governed Syria on behalf of Rome, the sentence that he should be affixed to a cross. But as he died upon it, he voluntarily gave up his spirit; and, returning to life on the third day thereafter, he presented himself to his disciples to be seen. For forty days he taught those with whom he associated the things which they were afterward to teach others. Finally, he was taken up into heaven, from which, after the world has been destroyed, he will come to judge all humanity. His disciples everywhere disseminated the teaching they had received from him [Col. 1013C], and demonstrated its truth not only by their words, but also by the astonishing constancy with which they endured tortures, crosses, and other kinds of punishment, even unto death.

### ARTICLE II. On the Author, Title, Beginning, Integrity, and Subject of This Book, and Why It Is Sometimes Entitled an Epistle

With one voice and great unanimity, everyone acknowledges—and has always acknowledged—that Cyprian is the author of this book. Who, indeed, could doubt this, when Augustine indicates it in no obscure terms with these words?

> “Bishop Cyprian, a follower of the apostolic rule, arguing concerning the one true God against the worshipers of many false gods, adduces many testimonies from the books of those whom they regard as eminent authors—that is, from that truth which they suppress in unrighteousness” (Augustine, *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, chap. 4, § 6, p. 530, vol. IX).

Jerome, however, wrote still more explicitly to Magnus:

> “With what brevity, with what knowledge of all history, and with what brilliance of words and thoughts did Cyprian dispatch the subject that idols are not gods?” (Jerome, *Epistle* 83, p. 937).

It would be as easy for us to cite numerous other writers of different ages who attest the same thing as it would be useless to others. There is therefore no need to prove more fully what no one calls into controversy.

[Col. 1014A] It seems far more difficult, however, to say what the true and genuine title of this book is, and what its beginning was. For in the older Colbert manuscript, written, as is believed, eight hundred years ago, the following occurs:

> “Here begins *That Idols Are Not Gods*.”

Then the book immediately begins as follows:

> “That idols are not gods, and that there is one God, and that it has been granted to believers that the beings worshiped by the common people are not gods, is known from this. Kings in ancient times, etc.”

Precisely the same is presented in Royal Codex 3974 and several others, except that the words *Against the Pagans* have been added to the title—two words which certainly were never Cyprian’s.

In the ancient manuscript of our monastery, formerly belonging to Corbie, which is said to be of approximately the same age as the Colbert manuscript, we read:

> “Here begins the Epistle of Caecilius [Col. 1014B] Cyprian, *That Idols Are Not Gods*.”

The first three words, however, were not written initially, but were added later by the same hand. The book—or, as it is called there, the Epistle—begins thus:

> “That the beings worshiped by the common people are not gods is known from this. Kings in ancient times, etc.”

Not very different are the words set down in the Tarn manuscript:

> “The Epistle of Caecilius Cyprian concerning the fact that idols are not gods.”

Then:

> “That the beings worshiped by the common people are not gods is known from this. Kings in ancient times, etc.”

The beginning of the more recent Colbert codex, without a title, is:

> “That the beings worshiped by the world are not gods is known from this,” etc.

And at the end:

> “Here ends *That Idols Are Not Gods*.”

The most distinguished Baluze, moreover, informed us that in almost all the manuscripts of this book which he possesses or has collected from elsewhere [Col. 1014C], it begins without any other heading with the words which, as we have just noted, are written in the Colbert manuscript.

We have additionally seen certain codices mutilated by half or more, at the beginning of which is prefixed a table of all the books of Cyprian copied in them. In this table, however, the following simple title of this book is presented:

> “That Idols Are Not Gods.”

No one could readily say whether the copyists transcribed it from the words of Jerome just cited or from elsewhere. But it is certain and evident that this title is incomplete, since it represents only the first part of this treatise.

The editions vary no less. For in those printed in 1540 and the following year, it is entitled:

> “Fourth Treatise, *On the Vanity of Idols*”;

while the beginning of the book is:

> “That idols are not gods, and that there is one God, and that it has been granted to believers that the beings worshiped by the common people are not gods, is known from this. Kings in ancient times, etc.”

In the edition prepared by Morel in 1564, however, the title is:

> “That Idols Are Not Gods”;

while the opening of the book is:

> “That idols are not gods, and that there is one God, etc.,”

as in the preceding edition. But in the editions of 1593 and 1606, the title is:

> “That Idols Are Not Gods, and That There Is One God, and That Christ Has Been Given as Salvation to Believers; or, *On the Vanity of Idols*”;

while the beginning of the book is:

> “That the beings worshiped by the common people are not gods is known from this. Kings in ancient times, etc.”

[Col. 1015A] Rigaltius retained both the same title and the same beginning of the book in the careful edition he prepared. Finally, the editor of the Oxford edition rejected all these things, prefixed the title *On the Vanity of Idols*, and began the book with these words:

> “That the beings worshiped by the common people are not gods is known from this. Kings in ancient times, etc.”

He testifies, however, that he retained only those words which seemed to him better suited to identifying the book. But who would deny that this title of the book is no better than “That Idols Are Not Gods,” which can be confirmed by Jerome’s authority? Yet, as we have said, that title presents only the first part of this book, not its whole subject.

We therefore cannot affirm with certainty what the true title of this book is or what its opening was. [Col. 1015B] Erasmus suspected that those words had been added by some learned man and that nothing survives for us except a fragment of this work, whose beginning has been cut off (Erasmus, *Notes on This Book*). For Lactantius, he says, is our witness that numerous volumes were written by Cyprian. Lactantius did indeed say that many works were published by him, but he was wholly silent about the subjects on which they were written, and afterward mentioned by name only a single address to Demetrianus (Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. V, chap. 1, p. 459, and chap. 4, p. 471). Erasmus could also have cited Augustine and Jerome, whom we quoted shortly before. The former testified that in his book against the pagans Cyprian adduces many testimonies from them; the latter, that knowledge of all history is displayed in it (Augustine, *On the One Baptism, Against Petilian*, chap. 4, § 6, p. 530, vol. IX). But Jerome said that this was done with the utmost brevity. And certainly in this book the only work cited by its own name is the notable letter of Alexander the Great to his mother. Yet because Cyprian gathered many things against the pagans concerning their gods, which many persons had handed down in memory and writing, Augustine doubtless said that these matters too were confirmed by the testimonies of pagan writers.

Erasmus further bases his conjecture that this book is mutilated upon the fact that it begins abruptly. Nor shall we oppose him and others who may think and demonstrate that in the earliest codices, or in others copied not long after Cyprian’s age, there was no title and the book began with these words:

> “Kings in ancient times, etc.”

[Col. 1015D] But they will have to prove what is most difficult: to whom the omission of this title should be attributed—whether to Cyprian himself, writing in great haste, or to the negligence of scribes who, according to a not uncommon practice, had left an empty space in which they intended to write the title in larger letters and even in red ink. It is sufficient merely to note that the title, which is read in such different forms in various manuscripts and printed editions, does not appear to have proceeded from Cyprian. Several scholars furthermore consider a fragment in the first part of this book, which we shall discuss later, to be spurious and supposititious. There is therefore no slight reason to doubt whether this book has come down to us wholly uncorrupted.

Yet the more obscure that question is, the more evident it is to everyone [Col. 1016A] what the subject of the book is. For who, after reading this very brief work rapidly, does not immediately notice that it demonstrates that the gods of the pagans are false, that there is one God, and that Christ his Son is our teacher and redeemer?

Finally, we have already seen that this little work is entitled an Epistle in many manuscript copies. But this should seem surprising to no one, since most of Cyprian’s works are called indifferently *Epistles*, *Treatises*, and *Books* by ancient writers. Nor is there any need for us to demonstrate what has been sufficiently and abundantly proved by others, especially by the Bishop of Oxford. But because this treatise displays no epistolary character, it seems preferable [Col. 1016B] to abide by the judgment of those who have thought that it should be placed among the treatises (*Oxford Preface to the Annals of Cyprian*, p. 4).

### ARTICLE III. At What Time and with What Haste This Book Was Written by Cyprian

Although no indication of the time when this book was written can be discovered in it, some nevertheless think that it was published by Cyprian immediately after he had been regenerated in the sacred waters of baptism and before he was initiated into the order of the presbyterate. They attempt to confirm their opinion by certain conjectures. They derive the first from the fact that more learned men who rejected the false religion of the pagans and embraced Christianity [Col. 1016C] were accustomed to prove the sincerity of their conversion in some public writing. But did all men—not merely all Christians, I mean, but even all defenders of the Christian religion—write books immediately upon their conversion, by which they might provide a surer pledge and memorial of their faith? Surely no one would say so. Moreover, before Cyprian published this book, he had sufficiently proved the integrity of his faith both in writing and in deed. For he had already, as they acknowledge, written the book *To Donatus*, in which he openly gave an account of the Christian religion he had embraced. Furthermore, while still a catechumen he had given the surest pledge of it, when he was inflamed with such zeal for Christian perfection that, after selling all his estates, he distributed the money thereby collected to the poor. What further need was there, then, that by publishing another book [Col. 1016D] he should prove anew a faith already proved more than sufficiently?

The second conjecture of those who believe that this book was composed by Cyprian when he had only very recently become a Christian is taken from the fact that he used words in this book that are scarcely Christian, as in these phrases:

> “Kingdoms . . . are changed by fortune”;

and afterward, concerning Christ restored to life:

> “To return again to the world above” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, pp. 13 and 16).

They also say that Cyprian assembled numerous profane histories and did not cite testimonies of sacred Scripture, which in his other books he adduced abundantly and sometimes, as they continue to allege, more frequently than was proper. Finally, this entire book is composed of materials which he sometimes copied word for word from the books of Minucius [Col. 1017A] Felix and Tertullian. Yet in his other books we see nothing at all similar. From all these considerations they therefore think it rightly follows that Cyprian published this book as soon as he enrolled himself in the Christian religion.

But those who argue in this way cannot be unaware that the word *sors* (“lot” or “fortune”) is frequently used in the sacred Scriptures of both the Old and New Testaments in the same sense as by Cyprian (Num. 26:33, 36; Josh. 16–17, etc.). Moreover, what is less Christian in the words concerning Christ, “to return to the world above,” than in these words of Christ himself:

> “You are from below; I am from above,”

that is, from the upper regions, or seats above (Luke 1; Acts 1, etc.; John 8:23)? [Col. 1017B] Cyprian said that Christ, raised from the dead, “returned to the world above”—not, indeed, to the gods, but to the earth, which lies above the lower regions into which he had descended when dead. As for profane histories, do not Tertullian and Minucius Felix, Arnobius and Lactantius, and other defenders of the Christians argue against the pagans by employing the same or similar histories? Furthermore, no one should find it surprising that in this book, which he wrote hastily, he excerpted many things from Tertullian and Minucius Felix; that he expressly adduces no testimonies of sacred Scripture; that he speaks in it less elegantly than in his other works; and, finally, that, because he had no leisure, he borrowed not his own arguments but those of others, and sometimes even their words.

How hurriedly he composed this book may be inferred [Col. 1017C] from the fact that what is written in its second part, though shorter than the other two, could easily have been arranged in a better order. Furthermore, where he discusses earthly kingdoms, he repeats the adverb *caeterum* (“moreover” or “but”) three times within a few lines. First, he says:

> “Moreover, the Assyrians held kingdoms” (Cyprian, p. 14).

And two lines later:

> “But if you return to the order.”

Finally, shortly thereafter:

> “Moreover, Regulus also observed the auspices” (*ibid.*, p. 13).

Since, therefore, he was compelled to compose this book with great speed, might this not indicate that it was published by him when he withdrew from Carthage in order to escape persecution? At that time, indeed, he considered it part of his pastoral duty to strengthen Christians in the faith, to refute the pagans, and to restrain the rash assaults of Demetrianus [Col. 1017D], who, as we said in the preceding chapter, had rather frequently come to him for no other reason, surely, than to defend his false religion with loud cries. But those more expert will judge these conjectures of ours and of others. For nothing wholly certain occurs by which the true date of this treatise may be assigned. A more certain judgment about it could certainly be made if we possessed its genuine title and an undoubted beginning.

### ARTICLE IV. On the Manuscript and Printed Copies of This Book, and the Notes of Various Scholars upon It

Numerous codices of this little work, copied by scribes of different ages [Col. 1018A], are found in various libraries. We had four at hand: the older Colbert manuscript, copied eight hundred years ago; the Corbie manuscript of equal antiquity, now the Saint-Germain manuscript; a third, the Tarn manuscript, one century later than those; and finally another Colbert manuscript, written three hundred years ago. Baluze collected several others for the preparation of a new edition of Cyprian’s works, and gave us the following catalogue of them. The first four are eight hundred years old: namely, the Pithou manuscript, those of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne, Saint-Martin at Tours, and Saint-Remi at Reims. One, seven hundred years old, belongs to the monastery of Saint-Michel-en-Péril-de-la-Mer. Two are six hundred years old: the Saint-Maur-des-Fossés and Baluze manuscripts. Three are five hundred years old: the first from the monastery of Saint-Pierre in the district of Nevers, the second [Col. 1018B] from Saint-Victor in Paris, and the third from Notre-Dame de la Joie. Five other codices are four hundred years old: one of Baluze, another of Bohier, one from the Sorbonne, one from Saint-Éloi at Arras, and one from Saint-Victor in Paris. Finally, four are three hundred or two hundred and fifty years old: those of Saint-Denis at Reims, Saint-Corneille at Compiègne, Grenoble, and Monsieur de Lamoignon, président à mortier of the Parlement of Paris.

As for editions of this book, they are the same as those of the other works printed together with it, which we listed above. There is therefore no need to prolong our discussion of them.

The same scholars who composed notes and observations on the preceding book also composed them on this one. Erasmus, however, published a single note upon it which, as we have already said, concerns the title [Col. 1018C] and beginning of this little work. Pamelius wrote seventy-nine notes; in the first forty-nine he explains the points adduced by Cyprian in the first part of this book for overthrowing the false religion of the pagans. The remaining notes on the other two parts of the same book are shorter; in those parts Cyprian explains and establishes the Christians’ doctrine concerning God and Christ the Lord.

Goulart arranged for all these observations to be reprinted verbatim in the edition of Cyprian’s works which he prepared. He added nothing of his own except that the crime of idolatry is extremely ancient; he believes that it arose among Noah’s descendants when, after the Flood, they departed from the worship of God. For when, he says, Rachel is said in the book of Genesis to have stolen her father’s idols [Col. 1018D] (Gen. 31:19, 34), they are spoken of as things already widely diffused and common at that time. Others, however, believe that the origin of idolatry was far more ancient, as we have shown elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 720 ff.).

The observations afterward produced by Rigaltius are useful for correcting the text by means of variant readings from ancient codices. In several other notes, he endeavored to explain Cyprian’s words, or to elucidate and confirm them by testimonies from other ancient writers.

The editor of the Oxford edition furthermore prepared two kinds of notes, just as he did for the preceding and other works of Cyprian. In the first kind he presents variant readings from certain ancient codices which he himself collected [Col. 1019A] or which were transmitted to him by others. In the second, which are certainly quite extensive, he elucidates or confirms by the authority of others the statements made against the fictitious gods of the pagans in the first part of this book; in his notes on the other parts, however, he is far briefer.

## CHAPTER VI. NEW OBSERVATIONS ON THIS BOOK

### ARTICLE I. On the Materials Cyprian Excerpted from Tertullian and Minucius Felix, and How in Two Other Books He Proved by Testimonies of Sacred Scripture What He Briefly Relates in This One Concerning the Jews, Christians, and Christ the Lord

[Col. 1019B] This book has three parts. As we have said, Cyprian excerpted the first and second from the *Octavius* of Minucius, and the third from Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, sometimes using the same words as both, and especially those of Tertullian (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. XXI, p. 21). Nearly all the passages he excerpted from Minucius were quoted together in our dissertation on the latter’s *Octavius*. Those which he borrowed from his teacher Tertullian were elucidated in our preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. II, art. 6; and *On Tertullian*, chap. IX, art. 2 ff.). Yet it does not seem to us that he excerpted every individual passage from one rather than the other. For no one can affirm, either certainly or readily, whether what he relates concerning demons in the first part of this book was drawn from Minucius Felix [Col. 1019C] rather than from Tertullian. Furthermore, if anyone wishes to investigate more carefully where in our dissertations we attempt to explain the passages excerpted by Cyprian from each of them, he will find them identified without much difficulty in the summaries of the chapters or in the general index to our entire book. There is therefore no need to enumerate them individually, since doing so might prove tedious to most and of little use to many.

Since we also attempted in those same dissertations to elucidate, illustrate, and smooth out nearly everything difficult or somewhat obscure that occurs in this treatise of Cyprian, it would likewise be useless labor now to repeat and reprint our observations. We shall therefore touch only upon those points which are peculiar to our author and which we ought not to pass over without some comment [Col. 1019D].

First, then, it must be noted that the things which Cyprian related in the third part of this book—concerning the Jews rejected by God because of their crimes, concerning the Christians substituted in their place, concerning Christ as God and man, and concerning his mortal life—are clearly demonstrated by numerous testimonies of sacred Scripture in two of his books *To Quirinus, Against the Jews* (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 15 ff.). Indeed, in their proem he prefaces them as follows:

> “I have compiled two little books, regulated with equal balance: one in which we have endeavored to show that the Jews, in accordance with what had previously been foretold, departed from God and lost the Lord’s favor, which had long before been given to them and promised for the future; [Col. 1020A] but that Christians succeeded in their place, winning the Lord’s favor through faith and coming from all nations and from the whole world. Likewise, the other little book contains the mystery of Christ: that the very one who came is he who was announced according to the Scriptures, and that he did and accomplished all the things by which it can be understood and known that he is the one who was foretold” (Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, proem, p. 18).

In these two books, therefore, the most holy Martyr satisfied those who might have desired the things he related in this shorter exposition concerning all these matters to be proved by testimonies of sacred Scripture.

### ARTICLE II. How Clearly Cyprian Affirms the Orthodox Doctrine concerning the Supreme Divinity of Christ and the Mystery of the Most Holy Trinity

[Col. 1020B]

We cannot pass over without some observation how manifestly Cyprian affirms and proclaims the supreme divinity of the Son of God, Christ the Lord. For after proving with the utmost clarity against the pagans, by various lines of reasoning examined in our preceding dissertations, that there is one almighty God, he pronounces the following concerning Christ:

> “This is our God; this is Christ” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 15).

Since, therefore, he first demonstrated against all the pagans that there is only one God, and now most explicitly affirms that Christ too is God, it necessarily follows that he and all other Christians of his time believed that the divinity of Christ is the same as that of his eternal Father. [Col. 1020C] For if by these words he had intended to signify that they were two Gods, or that one was more powerful than the other, he would have exposed himself to his pagan adversaries, who proclaimed that there were many gods and that Jupiter was more powerful than the others. Thus he firmly affirms that Christ is true God and one God with his Father. Consequently, without any hesitation he added in the same place:

> “This is the power of God; this is his reason, this his wisdom and glory”;

and shortly before:

> “The Word and Son of God” (*ibid.*).

Yet the power, reason, Word, and Son of God possess the same nature, substance, and eternity as his eternal Father himself, as we demonstrated in the preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, chap. VIII, art. 1 ff.).

Furthermore, he unhesitatingly declares that Christ was restored from death to life

> “in order that he might reveal the power of divine majesty” (Cyprian, *ibid.*, p. 16).

[Col. 1020D] But what divinity could he reveal except the very divinity which he had possessed before and always? Thus, when he returned to life not by another’s power but by his own, he showed that he had always possessed the power of divine majesty—that is, the same divinity as his Father.

And this is said by him not only in this book, but also twice in his epistle to Caecilius:

> “Jesus Christ, our Lord and God” (Cyprian, *Epistle* 63, to Caecilius, pp. 148 and 135).

Elsewhere, when discussing Christ’s second advent at the end of the world, he teaches that it is foretold in these words of the Psalmist:

> “God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not be silent”;

and also in these words [Col. 1021A] of Isaiah:

> “The Lord God of hosts will go forth.”

After proving this, he draws the following conclusion:

> “This is our God—that is, the God not of all but of the faithful and believing—who, when he comes manifestly at his second advent, will not be silent” (Cyprian, *On the Good of Patience*, p. 220; Ps. 49:3; Isa. 42:13).

But how, I ask you, could he have said and repeated so frequently and so often that Christ is God unless he had regarded it as altogether certain that this was the doctrine both of those to whom he wrote and of all other Christians, apart from heretics?

Nevertheless, he did not stop there, but proceeded further and plainly and openly declared that Christ ascended into heaven

> “so that the disciples, dispersed throughout the world at the admonition of their master and God, might deliver God’s precepts for salvation” [Col. 1021B] (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 16).

Do you see how explicitly Christ is called by him not only the master of his disciples but also God—true God, certainly, and the same as the Father, since, as he had demonstrated in the same work, there cannot be many gods? Moreover, in the second book *Against the Jews*, he clearly proves by various testimonies of sacred Scripture that Christ is true God and coeternal with his Father (Cyprian, *Against the Jews*, bk. II, §§ 5–6, p. 34 ff.).

No less clearly does he affirm and proclaim the divinity of the Holy Spirit and the orthodox doctrine concerning the Most Holy Trinity in the epistle which he wrote, in his own name and that of his fellow bishops assembled in synod, to Jubaianus concerning the baptism of heretics. For first he determined in it that their baptism was valid:

> “If they confess with us the same Father, the same Son, the same Holy Spirit, and the same Church” (Cyprian, *Epistle* 73, to Jubaianus, p. 200).

[Col. 1021C] Then, if someone baptized among the heretics has become a temple of God:

> “I ask,” he says, “of which God? If of the Creator, he could not”

become his temple,

> “since he did not believe in him,”

as is the case with a Marcionite.

> “If of Christ, neither can he become his temple if he denies that Christ is God. If of the Holy Spirit, since the three are one, how can the Holy Spirit be propitious toward someone who is an enemy either of the Father,”

as are the Patripassians,

> “or of the Son,”

as are the Anthropians,

> “and the other plagues of heretics,”

as he himself calls them? (*Ibid.*)

But when he said there that those three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity are one, does he not follow his teacher Tertullian, who, in his book *Against Praxeas*, as we noted in the preceding dissertation, had said:

> “The three are one, not one person” (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, chap. 8, art. 3)?

Who, then, does not see that the opinion of both men concerning the three divine Persons and their one and the same nature is identical? And how can three be one, unless it is because the three divine Persons possess one nature, by which those three are one and the same God?

Finally, shortly afterward he teaches that Christ’s command concerning the baptism of the nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit enjoins that they

> “be baptized in the full and united Trinity” (Cyprian, *ibid.*, p. 206).

But how can the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 1022A] be one united Trinity unless their nature is the same and they are one and the same God?

Nor should anyone object to us Cyprian’s subsequent words, in which he plainly said that the Father is called by Christ

> “his Lord and his God.”

For there he speaks of Christ insofar as he is man, who asks to be glorified by the Father and was obedient to him even unto death. Away, then, with the utterly foolish cavils of a certain impious Socinian, who wished to infer from this and several other similar forms of expression that Cyprian denied the divinity of Christ, which he proclaimed as frequently as he did openly and plainly.

### ARTICLE III. On Christ as Man, and in What Sense It Could Have Been Said: “The Holy Spirit Is Clothed with Flesh”

[Col. 1022B] Let us proceed, if you please, and see how clearly and plainly Cyprian asserts that Christ is not only true God but also true man. He was sent, he says—doubtless by his eternal Father—as “the Enlightener and Teacher of the human race,” just as had previously been foretold “through all the prophets” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 15). He did indeed say “all the prophets”; but because he aimed at brevity in this work, he did not think it necessary to prove the point there at greater length. Yet he certainly proved it expressly, especially in the second book *Against the Jews* (Idem, bk. II, *Against the Jews*, § 10, p. 37). To the same point, moreover, tend all those testimonies of the Old Testament by which, as he shows, it had been foretold that the old law would be abolished and a new one substituted, [Col. 1022C] that Christ would come, and that the true religion would be founded by him (And bk. I, p. 17 ff.). Since no one can deny that all these things concern that same Christ and his mortal life, Cyprian undoubtedly concluded from this that he had been announced through all the prophets. For some foretold his coming, others more things about him, and others fewer. In our preceding dissertations, moreover, we have expounded and elucidated numerous predictions by the sacred seers concerning the future Christ, cited by Lactantius and Tertullian.

Cyprian then continues: “This Word and Son of God,” he says, “descends into the Virgin and, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, is clothed in flesh.” So indeed the text stands in the printed editions and in certain more recent manuscripts. In the margin of the older editions, however, the following is noted: [Col. 1022D] “Alternatively: *the Spirit is clothed in flesh* [*carne spiritus induitur*].” But what else, I ask you, does this annotation signify except that this was the reading of other copies? And certainly the words are written thus not only in the Corbie, or Saint-Germain, manuscript, but also in no fewer than seven other older and better-quality copies. In some, however, the reading is “flesh by the Holy Spirit” [*carnem Spiritu sancto*]; in the Tarn manuscript, “he is clothed in flesh through the operation of the Holy Spirit” [*carne Spiritus sancti operatione induitur*]. You plainly see how diverse the manuscript readings are at this point.

But because the words “the Spirit is clothed in flesh” [*carne Spiritus induitur*]—with “Holy” [*sanctus*] added in some copies—might appear rather harsh to certain readers, the following was added by way of explanation in the margin of the manuscript of Saint-Martin of Tournai and of two others cited by Pamelius: “When he says, ‘the Holy Spirit is clothed in flesh,’ [Col. 1023A] he does not mean the person of the Holy Spirit, but that of the Son, who is himself also called spirit, in accordance with the saying, ‘God is spirit.’” Pamelius indeed testifies that the copyists of the Affligem and Blandinium manuscripts intruded these words into Cyprian’s text itself.

Rigault, however, although he admitted the former reading, “with the Holy Spirit cooperating,” into Cyprian’s text, nevertheless rejects it altogether in his notes as an invention of the subtler school of later ages. But if it is spurious and fabricated by overly ingenious scholastics, why did he leave it in Cyprian’s text? And on what grounds did he also reject the other reading, which, by his own admission, is found in the older copies and which he acknowledges can be explained in this catholic sense: “The Holy Spirit”—that is, the person of the Son of God, who is spirit—[Col. 1023B] “is clothed in flesh”? Yet this explanation is far older than Rigault, since, as we noted shortly before, it is found in the margins of three old manuscripts and in the text of two others.

But because Cyprian drew this part of his book chiefly from Tertullian, as we have said, it may perhaps be worthwhile to consider somewhat more carefully whether the words of the master can shed any light upon this passage of his disciple. Tertullian had said: The Word, or Discourse, of God, “having descended into a certain virgin and been fashioned as flesh in her womb, is born as man mingled with God: flesh endowed with spirit is nourished, grows to maturity, speaks, teaches, acts, and is Christ” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 21, p. 21). Do you see that what Tertullian conveyed in more [Col. 1023C] words Cyprian rendered in fewer? Since the intention and meaning of both are therefore the same, we must inquire what Tertullian—and consequently Cyprian—understood by the terms “flesh and spirit.” By “flesh” Tertullian seems frequently to signify the whole human nature of Christ, in virtue of which, having been fashioned in the Virgin’s womb, “he is born as man”; doubtless because the evangelist had written: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). But if that is so, it must be said that by “Spirit,” or “Holy Spirit,” Tertullian designated not the third person of the Most Holy Trinity but the second person, that of the divine Word, who is truly spirit and holy.

Nevertheless, if we were allowed room for conjecture, [Col. 1023D] we would propose the following. Could it not be said that Tertullian there used “flesh” to indicate Christ’s body alone, and “spirit” to indicate his soul? For, he says, “flesh endowed with spirit”—that is, his flesh or body was endowed and informed by spirit, or soul. For although by this very term “flesh” he frequently designates the whole human being, that is, body and soul, this does not prevent him from also often understanding by “flesh” the body alone. For what else does he do throughout the whole book *On the Flesh of Christ* but show against the heretics that the flesh assumed by Christ was not fictitious and simulated, but real? There he seems to denote only Christ’s body by the term “flesh.” In the same way, in the following book, while discussing the resurrection of the flesh, [Col. 1024A] he sets it in opposition to the soul (*On the Resurrection*, ch. 8, p. 330 ff.). Yet in his book *On the Soul* he expressly defines the soul and the spirit of a human being as one and the same thing (Idem, *On the Soul*, ch. 11, p. 271). For, to omit much else: “When the soul and spirit are in question,” he says, “the soul itself will be the spirit, just as the day itself is the light.”

What, then, prevents Tertullian from having said in the *Apologeticum* that Christ’s flesh was fashioned in the Virgin’s womb and, endowed with spirit or soul, performed all the works of his human and mortal life? But if this is Tertullian’s true meaning, can we not say that Cyprian’s meaning is the same: the Word of God, having descended into the Virgin, is clothed with the flesh of the spirit—that is, with his soul? It certainly matters little whether “Holy” [*sanctus*] [Col. 1024B] was added after “spirit.” For who does not know that Christ’s soul is holy? We offer this explanation, however, only to those who can sometimes pardon conjectures, in which we rarely indulge.

Finally, our author said, “God is mingled with man,” which he likewise drew from these words of his master Tertullian: “He is born as man mingled with God.” Once again you see the same thing expressed by both authors, though in different words. How these statements are to be understood we explained in the preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 9, art. 1).

## ARTICLE IV  
### On the origin of idolatry; on certain ridiculous gods of the Romans mentioned in a doubtful or spurious fragment of this book; and on the cruel beginning of the Roman consulship

[Col. 1024C]

Whatever Cyprian argues against the pagans concerning the origin of idolatry and their many false gods, insofar as it deserves any notice, we have endeavored to elucidate and illustrate in our preceding dissertations. Very little therefore remains for us to observe. At the very beginning of the book, when our author traces the origin of the impious worship of false gods back to Saturn, he follows his teacher Tertullian, as we have already noted. A little later, like that same Tertullian and Minucius Felix, he refutes the pagan Romans, who prattled that by their piety toward the gods they had merited dominion over the whole terrestrial globe (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 13; *Dissertation* [Col. 1024D] *on Tertullian*, ch. 25, art. 1; *Dissertation on Minucius*, chs. 18 and 19; and *on Tertullian*, ch. 27, art. 3 ff.). But at that point the editions of Rigault and Oxford, and certain others, read as follows:

> “Acca and Flora, prostitutes. Indeed, among the Romans the names of gods are invented to such an extent that they even have the god Viduus, who bereaves the body of its soul. Being as it were death-bearing and funereal, he is not kept within the walls but is placed outside them; and nevertheless, because he has been made an exile, he is condemned by Roman religion rather than worshiped. There is also Scansus, named from acts of ascending; Forculus, from doors; Limentinus, from thresholds; Cardea, from hinges; and Orbona, from bereavements. These are the Roman gods” (Cyprian, ibid., pp. 12–13).

In our manuscripts, however, only the following is found: “Acca and Flora, [Col. 1025A] prostitutes. These are the Roman gods”; all the rest is absent, just as in the editions published in 1540, 1541, 1564, and 1593. The editor who prefaced the Oxford edition likewise admits that these words are lacking in the most highly approved copies and that they disrupt Cyprian’s meaning. Nevertheless, he retained them in his text because, he says, they occur in the Benevento manuscript, the Verona manuscript, at least one of the four Vossian manuscripts, and the Corbie manuscript. As for what should be said of the first three—which he cited on another’s authority and which we have not seen—we have been able to learn nothing. But this we certainly know: none of these words is found in the Corbie, or Saint-Germain, manuscript that we have before us. It is therefore remarkable how these by no means few words could have been omitted from so many manuscripts written in different ages and in different regions. [Col. 1025B] Do they not therefore savor strongly of being a pure and simple addition? Yet the most distinguished Étienne Baluze, who consulted so many manuscripts that we were not permitted to see, as we have said, will doubtless untie the knot of this difficulty with his customary sagacity.

But although these words are plainly spurious and adulterated, some may perhaps ask us who those gods were. We shall therefore answer such curious persons, if there are any, that we have already treated Forculus, Limentinus, Cardea, and Orbona in our dissertation on the books of Arnobius (*Dissertation on Arnobius*, ch. 13, arts. 5 and 6). There we plainly showed that these divinities were placed by the pagans among those whom they imagined to preside over each individual thing. [Col. 1025C] Such also were Viduus and Scansus, described clearly enough in the editions of the book under discussion that contain the disputed passage. Augustine, however, reported much more about all these ridiculous gods from Varro, whom anyone can consult very easily (Augustine, bk. IV, *City of God*, [Col. 1026A] ch. 8, p. 93 f.; and bk. VI, ch. 9, p. 150).

Finally, Cyprian shows that dominion was neither granted to the Romans nor enlarged because of their piety toward their fictitious gods. “For we see,” he says, “that the consulship began just as the monarchy did. Brutus kills his sons so that the prestige of his office may be enhanced by the commendation earned through crime” (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 13). Everyone knows the history of Tarquinius Superbus, who was expelled from the monarchy by the Romans. Brutus, who subsequently became the first consul, ordered his sons and his wife’s brothers to be scourged and beheaded because they had conspired with others to restore Tarquin. If you desire a witness to this event, Augustine cites Virgil, whose verses are these:

> Would you also see the Tarquin kings, the haughty soul  
> [Col. 1026B] of Brutus the avenger, and the recovered fasces?  
> He will be the first to receive the consul’s authority  
> and cruel axes; and, though a father, he will summon  
> his sons, who stir up new wars, to punishment  
> for the sake of glorious liberty.  
>   
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. VI, v. 812 ff.)

If you desire more, consult Servius on these verses of Virgil, Titus Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Valerius Maximus, and other writers of Roman history. By many other weighty arguments, moreover, Cyprian manifestly proves how false and absurd was the Romans’ boast that through piety toward their gods they had founded their empire and extended it to the furthest regions of the earth (Augustine, bk. III, *City of God*, ch. 16, p. 72; Livy, beginning of bk. II; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. V, *Roman Antiquities*; Valerius Maximus, bk. V, ch. 8, § 1). But unless we are wholly mistaken, these arguments have been sufficiently explained in our preceding [Col. 1026C] dissertations (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chs. 18 and 19; *on Lactantius*, ch. 32, art. 1 ff.; and *on Tertullian*, ch. 27, art. 3 ff.).

[Col. 1025]

# A POEM ADDRESSED TO FELIX, ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE DEAD

*(From the* Most Extensive Collection of Ancient Writers and Monuments, *vol. IX.)* (C, S)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION BY DOM EDMOND MARTÈNE

[Col. 1025D] The *Poem on the Resurrection of the Dead*, which we place at the beginning of this volume, bears the name of St. Cyprian in a very ancient Corbie manuscript written in uncial letters nine hundred years ago. It is not easy, however, to divine who this Cyprian was. For its excessively rough diction and its frequent violations of the rules of meter appear to prevent us from attributing it to that most celebrated bishop and martyr of Carthage whose excellent writings are read with such delight, [Col. 1026D] although its grave and vigorous thoughts are by no means foreign to him or to be judged unworthy of so great a teacher. Nor does the author’s age appear remote from that of Cyprian of Carthage. For if he was not earlier than Cyprian, several indications prove that he was at least approximately contemporary. He certainly intimates in the following verses—where he depicts the impious at the Last Judgment, tormented by the stings of conscience and detesting that same worship of idols—that he lived particularly in a time [Col. 1027A] when idolatry still flourished:

> There each will confess the savagery of his own life.  
> First, whoever formerly thought wrongly of God,  
> worshiped wandering stones under a fictitious divinity,  
> consecrated bloodstained altars with fire,  
> and feared painted figures without a voice, etc.

He also sufficiently shows that he flourished during the most turbulent times of the nascent Church, when heralds of the sacred Word were consigned to a cruel death and, as unconquered witnesses, sealed with the shedding of their blood the faith of Christ that they preached, for he rebukes the savagery of tyrants against Christians in these words:

> Yet you denied this Lord of heaven and earth  
> and instead slew the just with cruel slaughter;  
> most of you often drove away the heralds of God;  
> truth among you was always treated as a crime.

Add to these considerations the fact that he rather clearly intimates the millenarians’ opinion about Christ’s earthly kingdom after the resurrection, an opinion that scarcely reached the end of the third century. It has no less of the flavor of antiquity that, gathering arguments from every quarter, he appears very probably to have used this poem to attack the mad philosophers of his age who denied the future resurrection of bodies.

Someone may perhaps identify the author of this poem as Cyprian, who was converted from a magician into a Christian and then became bishop and martyr at Antioch in [Col. 1028A] Phoenicia; his acts, divided into three books by a contemporary writer, we first published in volume III of our *Anecdota*. But that Cyprian would have written not in Latin but in Greek.

Moreover, the value of this little work is demonstrated by the principal doctrines of the Christian religion asserted in it: original sin, the necessity of Baptism, the mystery of the Trinity, and the resurrection of the dead. These doctrines certainly appeared so important in a very ancient author that we could by no means be deterred from publishing him by his semi-barbarous diction. Although the text was copied by an unskilled, albeit very ancient, scribe and is so corrupted that one must often remain in doubt, learned men will not, we believe, complain on that account that we have expended our labor in vain.

After I had written this, I noticed that the following poem [Col. 1028B] had been published at the end of Tertullian’s works. When I read it there and compared it with our manuscript, I discovered a bold editor who, impatient of the metrical laws violated by Cyprian—whoever he was—and of his humble style, attempted to render this little work in more elegant verses and thus published not Cyprian’s composition but his own. Therefore, since learned men customarily revere even the errors in ancient writers, we thought it worthwhile to restore the same poem to its authentic form, just as it issued from its author.

## I

I who chose the country-loving Muses for my song,  
and adorned the spring breezes with rosy flowers,  
ripened for summer the heavy ears of harvest,  
cut down autumn’s swelling grapes upon the vines,  
[Col. 1027C] and always praised winter’s peaceful olives,  
released measured streams from their springs,  
and sang of leafy woods amid the wandering grass—  
I shall now attune my song to the ethereal breezes of light.

May I now be allowed to touch the light-bearing Muses,  
to disclose secret nymphs at the river’s source,  
and joyful woods set beneath another star;  
and I shall likewise commemorate the eternal Muses in song.

Whence the boundless sea swells with towering waves;  
what power commands the solid earth to tremble;  
and whence golden light first shone upon the newborn world;  
who could fashion man from fruitful clay;  
whence the race could increase in an empty age;  
what diverse desire for life exists among the people;  
what offspring, first created through evil, was doomed to die;  
whence come the pleasing fragrance and modest grace of rosy garlands;  
what makes the vine glow with joyful grapes;  
how new barley grows milky upon the old stalks;  
how the tree grows dark beneath its frosty olives;  
who, by varied shoots amid the waning of verdure,  
protects the mother of its offspring with gentle shade.

It is good to know the origins of all the branches,  
[Col. 1027D] so that through all things we may recognize the true God,  
who fashioned light, seas, heaven, and earth  
and adorned the newborn world with varied stars;  
who first commanded cattle and birds to come forth,  
gave fish the waters of the sea to fill,  
and caused the sands to teem with animals.

Such songs I shall draw forth with well-ordered Muses;  
for you I shall reveal wholesome water from the springs  
and the welcome rain that comes in tranquil clouds,  
flowing freely and deep into the souls of men;  
I shall receive it in full streams upon our fallow fields.

## II

Come now: approach the safe and living water,  
and readily drink the swift-flowing draught of life.

If anyone should wish to escape the punishments of eternal flame,  
though ignorant of the Day and unaware of the coming age,  
and instead attain the rewards of a righteous life,  
let him remember this one God and pray to him alone,  
who set the whole world upon a balance beneath its boundary;  
who remains eternal and will always exist forever,  
[Col. 1028B] holding all the ages, and alone before every age;  
God unbegotten and without end, who alone possesses  
the divine throne and forever towers above the lofty heaven.

He alone is almighty; all created things obey him:  
Father, Son, and Spirit, who are always one.

He fashioned man for his eternal pleasure,  
gave him as shepherd of the flocks and master of wild beasts,  
and granted him dominion over the race of birds, the sea, and the land.

By speech alone he could stretch out heaven;  
by a word he commanded the solid earth to hang suspended;  
faster than speech he separated the waters of the sea;  
yet he loved to fashion this dear form with his hands  
and willed his own beautiful likeness to be present in it.  
By his Spirit he breathed the life-giving air upon its face.

## III

Forgetful of God, that man rashly committed so great a wrong.  
Nothing beyond the single admonition was to be touched,  
through which he would know evil and discern what was right.  
God immediately forbade him to touch the unlawful fruit.

How many gifts of the world God granted to man!  
He marked out an exceedingly sweet pledge of his love  
and gave them dear commandments conducive to salvation.  
He placed beneath their dominion the lands and every living creature,  
the winged race, the herds, every kind of wild beast,  
the creatures of the sea, and all swimming animals.

But because the first man transgressed the law in the first offense  
and straightway violated the Lord’s commandments,  
[Col. 1028D] he perished through death when his wife persuaded him to every evil.

For the woman first committed the evil of sin;  
she betrayed and deceived her husband concerning the law.  
Eve, wrongly persuaded, opened the gates to death  
and brought death upon herself and her whole race.

From this unwary transgression death flowed forth forever.  
Thereafter deep wickedness spread all the more readily,  
and the farmer’s toil troubled the year more cruelly.  
The crafty serpent inflicted this through malicious envy.

From that time the peoples’ many evil deeds increased,  
and impious seeds produced further wicked acts.

## IV

Therefore God alone, to whom belongs supreme power,  
who possesses the highest summit of lofty heaven,  
dwelling on high in inaccessible light forever,  
mindful of the past and foreknowing the future,  
preserves forever the decree governing the offspring according to its deserts,  
and all the souls that govern sluggish bodies  
and move rationally throughout a wandering human being’s limbs.

When, at the body’s first laying down, they relinquish the weight of its members  
[Col. 1029A] and, freed from earthly bonds, depart in lightness,  
they travel to their appointed places in different regions of the world.

He immediately decrees that some be enclosed in hidden darkness,  
but others he at once recalls to joyful breezes,  
to be preserved for the rewards ordained by the law,  
until their bodies rise once more from death with their members.

Now men must weigh the interest owed on their former life,  
and, remembering the judgment of God, stand before the deeds gone by;  
each must await the penalty due for his own offense.

Or do they suppose that, like nameless beasts, without weight or breath,  
they may utterly and vainly pour out the breath of God when life ends?  
[The text and syntax of these last two lines are uncertain.]

## V

Can almighty God, beneath whose command all things are ruled,  
not restore life after death?  
Or does the Lord appear unable to accomplish anything?

If he could bring bright light forth from darkness,  
and by his word could arrange all the masses of creation,  
preparing all things from nothing by his mighty voice,  
why can he not join together again, from existing matter,  
the familiar shape that once existed and once lived,  
and command it to rise again in a form like its own?

Since all things belong to God, they will surely return everything:  
the earth, when commanded, will call back whatever it once covered—  
if perhaps the flame of a funeral pyre destroyed someone laid in sleep,  
[Col. 1029B] or the sea cast another into its blind waters;  
if fish filled their bellies with someone’s flesh,  
or wild beasts fashioned a cruel death from his limbs,  
or his blood lay in a body torn apart by birds.

Nor will death’s realms deny anyone to the Lord any longer.  
They must produce the living for God from among the dead,  
and human beings must stand before him in their restored forms.

Thus dry seeds are entrusted to the upturned earth  
and, fastened deep in furrows, putrefy as though dead;  
from them the stalk is brought back to life with restored ears,  
and strong grains grow golden once more with living seed;  
new harvests rise with manifold increase.

All the stars will fall, then shine after being born anew.  
Day dies with its light in the dense night;  
night falls away into day and rests as light returns to things;  
and day will rise again on high among its stars.

The sun too falls, though it bears splendor in its brilliant light;  
its light dies when evening’s shadow comes upon the world,  
then returns renewed as joy for the whole age.

Thus the phoenix, burned, lives again from its own death  
and immediately rises, a bird, from its own tomb.

A tree stripped of leaves bears fruit in its season  
[Col. 1029C] and is again bent down with apples upon its newly sprouted branches.

## VI

Therefore, at the divine voice, while the world trembles  
and the powers of the lofty air are shaken to their depths,  
an unfamiliar crash and tremendous rumblings of heaven arise.  
As God advances and the Judge of the world arrives,  
innumerable ministers immediately hasten together  
and surround the Lord in his heavenly majesty;  
angelic hosts descend across the breadth of the earth.

They are all messengers of God, endowed with divine power,  
every spirit possessing the form and efficacy of might.  
Fiery vigor is theirs, their bodies gleaming with heaven’s radiance;  
divine force flashes forth. At this the whole earth groans;  
at this the trembling earth groans throughout its whole extent,  
laboring to give birth to the human beings whom justice commands it to return.

His companions marvel; at last the clouds are thrown into confusion;  
the astonished stars fear the sudden power from on high.

Here, at God’s command and the voice of the Mighty One,  
all the tombs throughout every realm are immediately shattered;  
the entire earth pours out bones through gaping clefts,  
and the sand, their mother, disgorges living peoples.

Limbs adhere to hair; bones are bound together by marrow;  
joined sinews govern the breathing bodies,  
and veins infused with blood begin to move together.

[Col. 1029D] Souls released from their hidden chambers are restored  
and each returns to its own rising bodily organs.

O wondrous faith! Every age now springs forth.  
The ancient multitude of the dead springs from the dust.  
Mothers and men rise again when light is restored;  
great-hearted young men, boys, and maidens once brides,  
and departed old men stand there with living souls;  
the world resounds with the wailing cries of infants.

Various nations come from their lowest habitations:  
the hosts of the East, and those whom the furthest land beholds;  
those who inhabit the central zones beneath the sloping sky,  
and those who occupy the Riphaean heights beneath the frosty constellation.

Every inhabitant of every region is present in fear:  
farmer and soldier; kings with their diadems laid aside;  
the rich man mingled with the poor in an equal company.

A profound trembling is everywhere; the world now groans in prayer,  
and the peoples stretch out their hands, marveling as they cry aloud.

## VII

The Lord himself, radiant with transcendent light  
and supremely powerful in every fiery might,  
flashes from his exalted throne in the heavenly abode,  
[Col. 1030A] surrounded by a shining company of martyrs  
and attended by his blessed prophets,  
whose brows gleam brightly beneath snow-white bands.

Now priests also stand present in shining garments,  
wearing as the reward of life their radiant crowns;  
bowing low, all worship with knees bent.

“Alone *hagios* [ἅγιος, holy], alone holy is God!”  
This is the single voice of all.

Then the Lord will command the twofold people to stand before him  
and order the righteous to be separated from the number of the wicked.  
He commands those clothed in vigor, death having been conquered,  
to possess forever the never-extinguished breezes of light;  
to enter the ancient kingdoms that forever bloom,  
through rich groves and ever-pleasant lawns;  
and to live an everlasting life in a glorious body.

## VIII

There is a place on the Aeolian shores beloved by the Lord,  
where the light is bright and a more wholesome breeze blows,  
where day is eternal and time unchanging;  
a region set apart for God, exceedingly rich in fields,  
a dwelling greatly blessed beneath a tranquil pole.

The air is always joyful and will always remain in light,  
gentle, breathing life-giving currents upon its winds.  
There the earth, with its exceedingly fertile soil, produces everything in due proportion.

Floral purple blazes across the level meadows.  
[Col. 1030B] All things intermingle their brilliant light without envy;  
each joyful flower clothes another in its own radiant garment.

Here rosy fields are variegated with snow-white seed,  
and the snow-white air ripples with rosy flowers,  
though one cannot know by which of them the fields grow more sweetly fragrant,  
which is superior in beauty or excels more greatly in honor.

Their like is never born in flower-bearing gardens;  
no such lilies ever bloomed in our fields.  
Nor, when the rose opens, does it redden our familiar fields so deeply;  
nor is Tyrian purple so deeply dyed with red.

The precious jewel gleams among many-colored stones:  
here the green gem shines, there the carbuncle burns,  
and the emerald casts forth flashing rays of light.

Here cinnamon also grows upon fragrant shoots,  
and amomum blazes with joyful green leaves.

Here lies uncreated gold of radiant light,  
and lofty, blossoming groves touch heaven with their crowns;  
abundant shoots weigh down the verdant branches.

No India has ever stretched out groves to equal these;  
no green pine raises such densely clustered treetops;  
no branch blooms better in the season of spring;  
no lofty cypress waves and curls its foliage so.

[Col. 1030C] Here enclosed fir trees blossom black at their summits,  
and only these forests remain green forever, untouched by hail.  
No leaves fall; no flower is ever absent in its season.  
Their compact crowns remain green with redness; the tree is purple.

But I think that flower is a rose, for its redness is uniform;  
thus its appearance breathes such fragrance through its leaves.

The most beautiful tree stands with flowers and new fruits;  
fertile oaks thicken their branches with life-giving produce.  
Rich apples [*metella*, an uncertain reading] blaze upon the verdant branches,  
and drinkable milk flows in full rivers.

Whatever grows green in that holy land breathes life;  
whatever blossoms from its shoots makes its inhabitants blessed;  
even the soil of that beautiful earth is fragrant and healing.

A tranquil spring there waters the grassy fields;  
from it four rivers irrigate the divided land.

I think spring reigns forever, the heavens clothed with flowers.  
No winter constellation alters the breezes with cold,  
nor does a radiant season flash with oppressive heat.  
Heaven tempers the serene breezes with its own light  
and renews the fertile land, making it better with its breath.

There is no night; the stars pour away their darkness.

## IX

Anger and treachery are absent, as is dreadful desire;  
fear is shut out, and cares have been driven from the threshold.

[Col. 1030D] The evil one is banished from here, an exile to the furthest shores;  
toil too, fearing even to touch those blessed boundaries, is driven away.

There ancient faith rests in its chosen dwelling;  
justice lives rejoicing in an eternal covenant;  
and secure salvation delights in the tranquil fields,  
destined always to live, always to remain in light.

Here dwells every righteous cultivator of equity and goodness,  
everyone who feared the Lord, the Thunderer, with an innocent mind,  
honored his parents with sacred devotion,  
and always cultivated a holy life without offense;

or whenever he comforted a needy person with friendly resources,  
and brought relief to the excessively burdened poor;  
was the poor man’s helper and accustomed to release orphans;  
rescued the endangered and aided those oppressed by accusation;  
offered guests the dear pledges of his own table;  
performed all his duties according to divine commands;  
harmed no one and coveted nothing belonging to another.

All these, exulting in divine praises  
and praying together, lift their voices to the stars.  
Singing psalms to the Lord, they celebrate their gratitude amid rejoicing,  
[Col. 1031A] and will travel the blessed way with angelic messengers as companions.

## X

After the Lord has bestowed these happy gifts  
and sent the righteous together into the eternal kingdoms,  
the pitiable multitude comes forward, mourning its own offenses.

Here all groan and grieve as their tears increase;  
with repeated wailing they bear witness to their deeds  
and tremble at the fiery weapons threatening them according to their deserts.

The angels seize them and now prevent them from praying;  
they prevent them from uttering belated words of repentance.  
Now pardon in answer to prayer is denied as the flame approaches.

O wretched ones, how often was divine power made known to you?  
How often was the majesty of truth recognized?

You heard the thunder and saw the lightning of heaven;  
how often you experienced continual rain,  
the wrath of winds and hail, and clear nights and days.

God’s gifts enriched the seasons with their bounty:  
spring supplied roses in abundance; summer lacked no crops;  
autumn offered varied mellow fruits;  
icy winter always governed the thriving olives.

God provided everything; no act of goodness was lacking,  
yet through all these things the whole human race failed to know God.

The earth trembled before God; the sea hung upon God’s command;  
the frightened river flowed backward over dry sands,  
[Col. 1031B] and all joyful nature acknowledged God.

## XI

Yet you denied this Lord of heaven and earth  
and instead slew the righteous with cruel slaughter.  
Most of you often drove away the heralds of God;  
truth among you was always treated as a crime.

And therefore you will reap the fruit of unrighteous seed.  
Behold, you do not recognize the Day that you habitually ridicule.

You will enter the deep darkness of fire and sulfur,  
burning as you endure savage wrath amid torments.

The Lord commands these people to depart to eternal punishment,  
to pass beneath the flames of Gehenna forever without end,  
to be crushed beneath a mass amid the surging pools of flame.

He commands the threatening elements to turn into flames  
and all the fire of heaven to descend from the clouds.

## XII

Then the devouring, swift fire of Tartarus encloses them,  
and the seas will belch forth tempestuous flames;  
the whole earth will overwhelm the living with ashes,  
and the fiery air will brandish furrows of wrath.

The world will be armed with every kind of blazing torch;  
hellish fires rage violently against the world.

Driven headlong, they are swept up into the heat;  
[Col. 1031C] they flee this way, then are carried back that way in swift flight.  
The wrath of the savage flame meets them as they flee,  
and only then do they recognize the punishment due for their offense.

Now the earth is possessed by no wandering inhabitant  
and is submerged at its furthest bounds beneath the depths of the sea,  
where the sun ends its rays after traversing Olympus  
and the constellations rise beyond the world that it has crossed.

The air swells with dense darkness, its light concealed;  
the furthest pools burn with hidden streams.

The place has a fiery nature appointed for punishments,  
and the marsh of hell, rising with flames from the depths,  
thunders and moves in punishment through dreadful furnaces.

The flame boils and is convulsed in its swift-whirling vortex;  
a river rushes into torments with a surging flood;  
all the scorching sand mingles with mire.

Here the captive multitude of the wicked will be sent, groaning—  
the host of sinful flesh destined to burn.

Great lamentation is there, weeping accompanied by shouting,  
and a violent gnashing; then the cries of the suffering  
will rise far from the flame; the fire and the deep groans  
of those who burn ascend into the resounding air.

## XIII

Then the image of evil hangs there—the promised offspring.  
[The Latin of this line is materially uncertain.]  
[Col. 1031D] and belated prayers will begin to rise toward heaven.  
Now they will wish to know the God whom they refused to know.

There each will confess the savagery of his own life:  
his guilty hands and a mind made cruel by crime.  
[Col. 1032A] He will testify to the unspeakable savagery of his life.

First, whoever formerly thought wrongly of God,  
worshiped wandering stones under a fictitious divinity,  
consecrated bloodstained altars with fire,  
feared painted figures without a voice,  
and adored the insubstantial waves of a false divine power;

and everyone whom evil error immediately led astray:  
if anyone was an adulterer, or had killed his children;  
if anyone lived with a mind conscious of any evil;  
if he went about violently with plunder, or defrauded a client;  
if anyone stained his palms with human blood  
or secretly mixed poisons to cause death;

then, if anyone defiled his heart through hidden theft,  
or rejoiced in unrighteous profit from another’s misfortune—  
whoever committed any wicked deed among all these evils,  
a deep blaze will torment him with bitter fire.

The deaths of all will inflict punishment upon the living,  
thus preserving the whole sorrowing multitude of humanity.  
[The final line is textually or syntactically uncertain.]

## XIV

How often did the holy prophets sing of these things!  
How often, admonished by the Spirit of God, did they speak of what was to come!

No one—how wretched!—no one, alas, lent an ear.

Thus almighty God willed his rewards to be known,  
and also the many threats of the law set forth through such warnings,  
[Col. 1032B] sending many men who proclaimed the words of heaven.

Finally, at God’s command, the prophet joined the bones together  
and marveled when the tombs suddenly moved, though not by their own power;  
he saw bodies formed from scattered ashes lying there,  
then marveled as they rose alive when the soul returned  
and stretched their hands toward heaven at his voice.

They give thanks to God and to Christ the victor for such wonders.  
Those bodies then sought the tomb in silence  
and withdrew to await the future day appointed by God.

He commanded them to be kept for a little while in their deepest chambers,  
until that great Day should arrive when the appointed time was complete.

All of you, recognize the true Lord,  
who alone causes the soul to ascend into the light,
And can thrust that same soul down into penal Tartarus,

And to him lies open all power over life and death.

For God, to be able is enough; there is no need to will: by speaking, the deed is done.

He alone is to be feared by me in my inmost thoughts.

And since every course is concluded by death,

Whoever exists today will carry his life away with him.

### XV

Therefore, while life remains, while it is granted to enjoy the light,

While repentance is permitted, before the end of the age

Overtakes the unwary and closes their unknowing eyes—

[Col. 1032C] That final day of death which is bound by law—

Above all, vigilantly cherish the salvation that remains,

And it will be easy to turn your course toward the good.

After your bronze-bound expiations, burdened with their rites [Latin text uncertain],

And after the storms that have vexed the wandering far too much [Latin text uncertain],

Enter upon straight paths and keep to favorable winds.

From this point, first drive guilt away with joyful spirits,

And let corrected guilt long be washed from the heart.

Then, grown gentle, blot out the wicked evils you have committed,

And appease the God who is to be feared with everlasting prayers.

Let all the worst mortal things yield to the good among the living.

Preserve henceforth a new life free from guilt,

And keep devout minds in the true name.

As suppliants, ask forgiveness for your former offenses.

Henceforth let pure hearts ripen for devout cultivators,

And raise innocent hands in righteous prayers;

Readily render your voices to divine praises.

Let your minds begin to grow accustomed to things good and true;

Let the gifts of the divine law be celebrated more fully.

Call good things to mind, and at once undertake good deeds.

Let the filthy evils once committed be made clean,

And everything better will burn brightly for you who are devout.

[Col. 1032D] Life will at the same time be freed from dreadful dangers,

And, in accordance with its prayers, will attain eternal rewards.

**THE END**

# FOURTH APPENDIX

[Col. 1033]

## SELECT NOTES ON CYPRIAN FROM THE OXFORD EDITION

# LETTER I

[Col. 1033A]

**Those standing firm.** This formula occurs rather frequently and appears to mean more than merely identifying the brethren who had been at Furni, or those who stood while the presbyters sat in attendance. We should rather believe it was added with the same meaning with which, below, the brethren are called “standing” and “standing firm”: namely, to distinguish them from the apostates (*ἀποστάται*), the lapsed, schismatics, and heretics.

**My colleagues who were present.** The most eminent Baronius, Pamelius, and those who have recently edited the councils maintain that this letter was written at some synod after Cyprian’s return from retirement. On the contrary, however, it is almost Cyprian’s regular practice to append the bishops’ names to synodical letters. It therefore seems quite probable that the bishops mentioned here were present for some less formal reason when news arrived of the appointment made by Victor. Certainly, in Letter XXXIV—number XXVIII in Pamelius—[Col. 1033B] mention is made of “colleagues who were present,” although there can be no suspicion there that a council had been held.

The passage in the Council of Carthage of eighty-seven bishops concerning the baptism of heretics, where the name Geminius of Furni occurs, appears to have supplied the grounds for the learned men’s conjecture about the date when this letter was written. They believed this man to be the same as Geminius Victor and therefore supposed that he died sometime after that synod. But it is rather less credible that this Geminius was a bishop, both because of the disgrace attached to his act and because Cyprian calls him a “brother,” not a “colleague.”

But grant that Geminius Victor was a bishop: is it not equally probable that Geminius Faustinus also became a bishop? When he was appointed guardian under the testament of the other Geminius, he was a presbyter of the church of Furni; afterward, and particularly by the date of the aforesaid council, he had been promoted to the episcopate. It may also be added that, according to the authority of certain manuscripts and also of St. Augustine, the bishop of Furni in that synod is said to have been not *Geminius* but *Geminus*. [Col. 1033C]

But, leaving aside this controversy over the name, let us explain the altered order and why we judge this letter to have been written not after Cyprian’s return from retirement, as the most learned men have thought, but at the very beginning of his episcopate, while the Philips still held imperial power.
