First, Victor’s act appears to reflect those times of peace which Cyprian describes in his book *On the Lapsed*: when—to use his own words—there was no devout religion among the priests, no unbroken faith among the ministers, no mercy in works, no discipline in conduct; when very many bishops, who ought to have served the rest both as exhortation and as example, neglected the divine administration and became agents of secular business.

Geminius would indeed have seemed hardly sound of mind if, in his final testament, he had named a Christian presbyter as guardian amid the heat of the Decian persecution—or even while it had not yet burned itself out—and had appointed as the protector of another’s welfare a man whose own life would daily be in danger.

Moreover, [Col. 1033D] Cyprian expressly says in this letter that the canon forbidding clerics to be named guardians by any of the faithful [Col. 1034A] had been enacted by the bishops who preceded him, yet that this provision had been issued only recently. The closing years of his episcopate therefore do not at all suit the date of this event.

It must not be concealed that Cyprian also says this had “long ago” been established in council. Yet those words, according to Cyprian’s manner of speaking, denote a very brief interval. We shall see this below in Letter LVII—number LIV in Pamelius—where our author says that a measure enacted scarcely a year earlier had been established “long ago.” On these matters, however, see the *Annals*, year 249, § 9.

**The presbyters who sat beside us.** That is, on either side of the bishop. Ignatius, in the letter to the Magnesians, greets them “together with the most dignified bishop and the spiritual crown of the presbyterate” (*μετὰ τοῦ ἀξιοπρεπεστάτου ἐπισκόπου, καὶ πνευματικοῦ στεφάνου τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου*). Theodoret, Book V, chapter 3, teaches that “the middle seat” (*ὁ μέσος θῶκος*) belongs to the bishop. Indeed, learned men refer even the passage in Revelation 5:2 to this custom whereby the bishop sat in the midst of the clergy.

**The presbyter Geminius Faustinus as guardian.** [Col. 1034B] It should be observed here that under Roman law the guardianship of minors, being regarded as a public office, was a burden from which exemption was granted only for certain very serious reasons defined by law. Anyone wishing to know them should consult Book I of the *Institutes*, title 25.

Although it could hardly be expected that Christian priests would enjoy so peculiar a privilege through the indulgence of pagan emperors, it could nevertheless be provided by mutual agreement and through the force of canons that no Christian should seek to impose this burden upon any member of the clergy, under the penalties contained in those same canons.

Indeed, as soon as the emperor Constantine obtained control of affairs, nothing was more urgent to him than to confirm by enacted laws, and with manifold additions, the immunities privately granted to the Christian clergy. Relevant here is the rescript to Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, which Eusebius records in Book X, chapter 7, and which Anulinus himself mentions in his letter to Constantine. St. Augustine cites it in Letter LXVIII to Januarius, and it is included in the acts [Col. 1034C] of the Conference of Carthage, day 3, numbers 216 and 220.

Also relevant is the law published on the day before the Kalends of November, in the third consulship of Constantine Augustus and the third of Licinius—that is, in the year of Christ 313:

> We have learned that, through the faction of the heretics, the clerics of the Catholic Church are being so harassed that, contrary to the privileges granted them, they are burdened by nominations or undertakings of the kind imposed by public custom. It is therefore our will that, if Your Excellency finds anyone thus harassed, another be substituted for him, and that henceforth injuries of this sort against men of the aforesaid religion be prohibited.

Indeed, the troublesome fury of the Donatists subsequently extorted still other laws.

Yet in virtually that same age, once peace had been restored to the Church and the evils of a long peace were sprouting up, clerics began to involve themselves in secular concerns for the sake of shameful gain. Their imperial successors, as well as synods, therefore considered it necessary that clerics should not merely be excused by privilege, but should be driven away from such affairs by enacted laws.

Thus, among the three provisions proposed by Marcian to the Council of Chalcedon and enacted in canon 3, [Col. 1034D] we find the decree:

> Henceforth no bishop, cleric, or monk is to lease estates or undertake business, or involve himself [Col. 1035A] in secular administrations  
> (*μηδένα τοῦ λοιποῦ, μή ἐπίσκοπον, μὴ κληρικόν, μὴ μονάζοντα, ἢ μισθοῦσθαι κτήματα, ἢ πράγματα, ἢ ἐπεισάγειν ἑαυτὸν κοσμικαῖς διοικήσεσιν*).

Similarly, Justinian, *Novel* 123, chapter 6, prohibits those established in the clergy from becoming, under any law, guardians or curators of any person whatsoever, and so forth.

**In honor of the brethren receiving allowances.** The gifts classed under the name *sportulae* were sufficiently honorable—namely, of a kind that the highest magistrates did not disdain to receive. A limit was therefore fixed for them by legislation. Thus a rescript of Theodosius the Great provided:

> With the exception of ordinary consuls, absolutely no one else is to be permitted to give a golden *sportula*. When public offices are celebrated, however, the coin used for *sportulae* is to be silver; nor may a silver coin of greater value be expended than the kind customarily minted when we divide one pound of silver into sixty silver coins.

Relevant here appear to be Pliny’s remarks about the honoraria of decurions in Book X, Letter 114, and also the material found in Book V, final section, of the *Digest*, *On Gifts between Living Persons*.

In ecclesiastical usage, however, regard appears to have been paid not only to Roman *sportulae* but also to the custom of the Jewish Church, in which offerings were to be placed in baskets, as may be seen in Deuteronomy 26:2. Certainly, [Col. 1035B] in his annotation on Apostolic Canons 3 and 4—where the Christian people are forbidden to offer honey, milk, strong drink, and so forth at the altar, but are ordered to send them to the homes of the bishops and presbyters—Balsamon says that these are called *κανίσκια*, “little baskets,” or *sportulae*.

**Receiving, as it were, tithes from the produce.** The payment of tithes preceded the Mosaic law by long intervals of time and by no means derives its right from that law. Just as we still dedicate the seventh portion of the time granted us as owed to God, so we rightly continue to pay a tenth of our means.

Christian priests did indeed begin to receive tithes from produce at a later date, because rural inhabitants and those who practiced agriculture were converted to the faith only late; hence the name “pagans,” that is, country people, adhered to the heathen. Even now among us, where tithes are paid everywhere, city parish priests are supported chiefly from offerings or *sportulae*. [Col. 1035C] The most learned Rigaltius therefore appears rather inopportunely to cast odium upon the payment of tithes in this passage. This subject is treated more fully near the end of the book *On the Unity of the Church*.

# LETTER II

**To the disgrace of his profession.** Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 22, says that those who practiced these arts were condemned to infamy and loss of civil status; they were excluded from the council chamber, the rostra, the senate, equestrian rank, and all other honors, as well as from certain insignia.

Similarly, Augustine, *City of God*, Book II, chapter 14, says that performers of poetic plays were removed from the fellowship of the state and repelled from all honors. Hence Laberius, when compelled by Caesar to perform a mime, grieved as one who had suffered the gravest injury, although the payment of five hundred thousand sesterces was of no avail, and said:

> A Roman knight, I left my home;  
> I shall return to it a mime.  
> This day I have lived one day too many—  
> more than I ought to have lived.

And surely the Church is more chaste than the state. It was therefore an empty excuse that this actor had withdrawn from the theater and taught privately. Those who are not permitted even to think [Col. 1035D] what is evil can certainly not be permitted to perpetrate it in private.

**Men are forbidden in the law.** Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 23, says:

> Since the law declares accursed the man who dresses in women’s clothing, what judgment will it pass upon the pantomime, who is even adorned in women’s apparel?

**That he should be redeemed by a salary.** By provisions (*σιτηρέσια*) and generous terms of support, such as were paid from the public treasury to military tribunes and commanders. Thus Pliny, Book III, chapter 7: “[It] is placed among civil honors and military service, whence the term ‘salaries.’” Moreover, this expression penetrated even to the peoples of the East. For in Ezra 4:14 the speaker is a dependent of the Persian court.

**He will be able to transfer himself to us.** In the African council of eighty-seven bishops, Eucratius is said to have been bishop of Thenae, a city in Byzacena situated on the military road to Carthage, as is clear from the *Antonine Itinerary*. It therefore afforded a convenient passage for a traveler.

# LETTER III

[Col. 1036A]

**Rogatianus.** Pamelius conjectures that this is the same man who, in the council of eighty-seven bishops, is called the bishop “of Nova.” But this is rather improbable, both because of the old age of the Rogatianus mentioned here and because the other Rogatianus, the bishop of Nova, did not cast his vote among the first—as the number of episcopal years that had elapsed would have required according to the custom of the African Church—but among the last.

The Lincoln manuscript supplies us with the deacon’s name and calls him Cassius. We do not agree with Cardinal Baronius, who in the year 257, chapter 12, declares this letter to have been written in a synod, for the reasons given above under Letter I.

Rigaltius observes that in this letter Cyprian gives Rogatianus advice which he himself declined to adopt in other letters, where he says to the bishops and presbyters:

> As for the other matter about which our fellow-presbyters wrote to us, I could make no reply by myself, since from the beginning of my episcopate I resolved to do nothing on my own private judgment without your counsel and without the consent of the people.

But anyone who considers with how much hostility [Col. 1036B] Cyprian, a neophyte and altogether a newcomer, reached the summit of the see of Carthage will not be surprised that he found it necessary to employ popular methods and to relinquish his own right in many matters, particularly at the beginning of his administration. There was no need at all for the aged Rogatianus, bishop of an unimportant little town, to do the same.

**Three of the ministers: Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.** It is certain that Korah alone was a Levite, whereas Dathan and Abiram sprang from the tribe of Reuben. But the crime that defiles them also makes them equal; and those who sided with the rebellious Levites are not undeservedly numbered among them. Hence Moses himself spoke to Korah and the whole multitude, without excepting Dathan and Abiram: “You exalt yourselves too greatly, sons of Levi.”

**Reproach concerning the evil.** The Greek reads, “Bear witness concerning the evil” (*μαρτύρησον περὶ τοῦ κακοῦ*). It would be quite appropriate for the Jewish priest to speak abusively of the accused; our Lord, however provoked, did not repay such treatment in kind. Perhaps the text was *exproba*, “produce as proof”: that is, “Employ as evidence against me [Col. 1036C] those things that I have said.”

**Deacons ought, however, to remember.** This warning applies equally to presbyters, who were admitted by bishops to a share in their responsibilities, yet in such a manner that they remained in obedience to them.

**The apostles, that is, the bishops.** Thus Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 3, quoted by Eusebius in *History*, Book V, chapter 6, says that bishops were appointed by the apostles and that their successors continued down to us. He then lists the bishops who succeeded the apostles in the more celebrated churches.

Similarly Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chapter 32:

> Let them display the origins of their churches; let them unfold the succession of their bishops, running down through succession from the beginning in such a manner that the first bishop had as his founder and predecessor one of the apostles or one of the apostolic men who nevertheless persevered with the apostles. For in this manner the apostolic churches present their registers: as the church of Smyrna reports that Polycarp was installed by John; as the church of Rome reports, and so forth.

Moreover, [Col. 1036D] Clement of Rome, almost a contemporary of the apostles, describes this appointment and succession of bishops in his *Letter to the Corinthians*, chapter 44.

# LETTER IV

**To remain in her proper state.** Three states of women are enumerated: virgins, widows, and married women. Virgins were held in the first place of honor above the others. A special place in the church was assigned to them not merely for protection but also for honor. Those who entered this state wore not the attire of matrons but that of virgins—that is, the veil—and openly professed that they followed that distinguished manner of life.

The word *status* signifies either civil condition—namely, the dignities and rights of a free person—or belongs to the language of contests, where one is trained to defend one’s position or to dislodge an opponent from his footing.

[Col. 1037A] **That one was a deacon.** The sin was therefore committed with graver scandal. The sexual offense of a deacon in the Church of Constantinople under Nectarius very nearly overthrew the ancient discipline of penance among the Easterners. See Socrates, Book V, chapter 14.

**At his whim and belching.** With Rigaltius, we consider this reading entirely correct, particularly since Pontius spoke in almost the same formula: “Far be it from us that the belching of a man should pass judgment upon so blessed a martyr.” No one customarily indulges in belching except among lackeys and parasites, with whom anything is permitted. Hence the satirist’s line: “If he has belched well,” and so forth.

**By excluding the deacon.** According to the custom long received in the Church, offenses of laypeople were customarily punished by excommunication and the other censures of the Church, but those of clerics by deposition. Yet it is manifest that during the first three centuries bishops, presbyters, and deacons were, like laypeople, subject to public penance and the imposition of hands. The reader should consult Morinus, *On the Administration of the Sacrament of Penance*, Book IV, chapter 12.

[Col. 1037B] **An adulteress not of a husband, but of Christ.** Although she has no husband, she is called an adulteress. Every faithful woman is a bride of Christ, but much more one who has professed virginity.

# LETTER V

**I greet you, being safe.** When Cyprian had safely reached his appointed hiding place, it was altogether fitting that, because of the deep affection existing between himself and the brethren, he should as soon as possible relieve by letter their longing occasioned by his absence, assure them of his safety and circumstances, and finally admonish them carefully about matters concerning the condition of the Church. All these things are accomplished most fully in this letter.

It therefore appears very probable not merely that this letter was written before all the others, but that it was written immediately after his withdrawal. It is followed by another of almost the same subject and composed in the same words, namely Letter VI, number 81 in Pamelius. Cyprian himself testifies in Letter XX—number 15 in Pamelius—that the letters written in this hiding place were thirteen in number. [Col. 1037C] They are all presented here, although other editors regarded some of them as lost.

It may further be noted that this letter appears only very rarely in the old manuscripts and was committed to print quite late—namely, after all the editions of Erasmus.

**The circumstances of the place do not permit it.** A disturbance had arisen at Carthage, in which Cyprian was demanded for the lion amid popular uproar in the circus and amphitheater, and was finally proscribed, as is said in Letter LIX, number LV in Pamelius. Speaking below of the same matter, he says: “Would that the circumstances of my position and rank permitted it.”

**The total sum that has been collected.** The whole fund that, after accounts had been settled, consisted of money intended for the poor. For just as, at the Church’s birth, the proceeds from property sold out of piety were laid at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4:35), so afterward what had been dedicated to God was entrusted to the bishops’ fidelity. [Col. 1037D] Justin Martyr reports this in the clearest terms in the *Apology*. A division was made: one part went to the bishop, another to the clergy, and a third to the needs of the poor.

Accordingly, as Cyprian hastened into retirement, he deposited this money after dividing it among the clerics, so that they might distribute it again more easily.

**The confessors are to be visited.** Visiting the sick or those placed in any other calamity is rightly regarded as a duty of piety. See Matthew 25:36. Another reason will also appear below why very many people gathered in crowds around the martyrs: namely, first to extort peace from them, and then from the Church.

It should incidentally be noted here that Cyprian, here as elsewhere, uses the names “confessor” and “martyr” interchangeably. Strictly speaking, however, only those who suffered for the name of Christ should be called martyrs, while confessors are those who professed themselves Christians before the tribunal without subsequent punishments.

**Those who offer among the confessors.** [Col. 1038A] Before the first ardors of piety cooled, Christians participated in the sacred mysteries every day, or at least every Lord’s Day. The martyrs, who continually stood beneath the blow of suffering, were especially anxious never to be without that divine viaticum.

Because it was necessary at these solemn rites for a deacon to assist the presbyter, so that the presbyter could not go alone, Cyprian advises them to alternate by turns and, by varying those who came, to lessen the resentment.

What it means “to offer among the confessors” we learn from Cyprian in Letter XXXIV, number 28 in Pamelius:

> You acted uprightly and with discipline, dearly beloved brethren, when, upon the advice of my colleagues who were present, you judged that communion should not be granted to Gaius, the presbyter of Didda, and his deacon; for by communicating with the lapsed and offering their oblations, they had frequently been found involved in perverse errors, and so forth.

Here it should incidentally be noted that particular deacons were sometimes assigned to presbyters to assist them.

To communicate with certain persons and to offer their oblations were indeed distinct things. Yet because no one [Col. 1038B] participated in the sacred mysteries without first offering a gift to God, the whole sacred office is very often understood when either expression is used.

Similarly, although, as St. Paul says in Hebrews 13:10, “we have an altar,” nevertheless the sacrifices of Christian devotion differ utterly from the immolations of the Gentiles and Jews. Some therefore act wrongly when, upon hearing the name of altar, oblation, or sacrifice, they inopportunely introduce a bloody victim and a slaughtered sacrificial animal. The ancient Fathers vigorously removed the odium of all such accusations in their apologies.

**To accommodate oneself to the times.** This reading is supported not only by the testimony of very many manuscripts but also recommended by its antiquity. For this appears to have been the reading not only of Origen in his commentary and of our author here, but also of Ignatius in his letter to Polycarp. The abbreviation *κω* can equally represent *κυρίῳ* (“the Lord”) and *καιρῷ* (“the occasion”); this may perhaps have given rise to the variant reading.

# LETTER VI

[Col. 1038C]

**Cyprian’s letter to the martyrs.** It matters little that some manuscripts, as well as printed copies, read: “To the younger Rogatianus and the other confessors.” Such titles are due to the care and ingenuity of copyists, and the reader can usually dispense with them without loss.

They supposed that the presbyter Rogatianus—the glorious old man who, receiving the assault of the raging populace, first prepared lodging in prison and in a sense went ahead as a quartermaster—had been crowned with martyrdom. They therefore thought it impossible that this letter could be addressed to him and accordingly invented another Rogatianus, as unlike the first as possible—that is, a younger man.

But it is manifest that nothing is said here of the elder Rogatianus except that, as a result of the popular disturbance, he had been committed to prison. Indeed, it is implied rather that he still survived as an example and continued to lead these men as well when this letter was written. Nor is it unusual, when a letter is written jointly to several persons, for one of them to receive particular mention as occasion arises.

Moreover, [Col. 1038D] if conjectures from names have any force, the Rogatianus described here was certainly the very man mentioned in the following Letter VII, number 36 in Pamelius; in Letter XIV, number 6 in Pamelius; and in Letter XLI, number 38 in Pamelius. Concerning the date when this letter was sent, the reader should consult the very careful discussion by the Most Reverend Bishop of Chester in the *Annals of Cyprian* prefixed to this work.

**The kiss of the Lord.** The Hebrews devise many things in their theology concerning the kiss of the Lord and profess that Moses departed from life in this manner. Indeed, in Deuteronomy 34:5 it occurs that “Moses died”—so the rabbis say [the remainder of the citation is apparently missing]. In this matter, however, Jews differ widely from Christians: among the former, a quiet and peaceful death was regarded as the kiss of the Lord; [Col. 1039A] among the latter, a bloody and violent death is judged most blessed and most desirable.

**Quartermaster.** Vegetius says in Book II, chapter 7: “Those who go ahead and choose a place suitable for a camp are called quartermasters (*metatores*) in the army.” Thus Caesar’s man in Lucan says: “Boldly I shall come as quartermaster into the western fields.” It was therefore most aptly said of Rogatianus and Felicissimus that they entered prison first, as if quartermasters.

# LETTER VII

**The Lord may have deigned to reveal.** Cyprian rather frequently appeals to revelations made to him. He does this, however, not to impose doctrines of faith upon others, but to defend his innocence when assailed by the envious.

His withdrawal was spoken of disparagingly as a shameful flight. He therefore shows that he feared only for the sake of his flock and that he complied not with his own inclination but with a divine command. Moreover, it was honorable for him among the clergy and people that God should deem him worthy of divine communications and [Col. 1039B] knowledge of future events. This was especially influential in the African Church, where heretics—particularly Montanus—put forward prophecies and revelations with great display.

**He willed him to believe and to grow.** At Carthage, namely, where he had been converted to the faith and promoted to the episcopate: he was fixed to that see as though rooted there.

**From my own portion.** See what was said above concerning the division of offerings into three parts, one of which went to the bishop. As to the property that he had possessed while still a pagan, Pontius teaches us that, as soon as Cyprian embraced the Christian faith, he sold his possessions to relieve the need of the poor and disposed of whole estates, leaving himself nothing that he could give away anew.

**Acolyte.** Hesychius says: “Acolyte (*ἀκόλουθος*): the younger boy; an attendant, one in personal service” (*ὁ νεώτερος παῖς· θεράπων, ὁ περὶ τὸ σῶμα*). This office, if any was, was most widely received throughout the whole Church in this century.

As regards the Easterners, the name taken from Greek shows that it was in use among them. Concerning the Roman [Col. 1039C] Church, the letter of Cornelius to Fabius of Antioch, which we shall quote below, abundantly attests it. Concerning the African Church, our author will be a substantial witness throughout his letters. More on this subject may be seen in the annotations on the following letter.

# LETTER VIII

**Of the Roman clergy.** Although these words belong to the title of this letter—a title added by a copyist according to his own understanding and therefore incapable of possessing any weight or authority—the most learned Rigaltius takes occasion from it to show that the term *clergy* (*clerus*) is wrongly applied to ecclesiastical persons and to designate men initiated into holy orders.

He first says that *κλῆρος* signifies three things: the little lot we use in casting lots; the allotment or act of receiving by lot, that is, the very action of casting lots; and what falls to each person by lot.

He adds that Greek writers on Hebrew affairs, and Latin writers following them, [Col. 1039D] called a *clerus* that portion which fell by lot to each tribe from the vast tract of land divided, at Joshua’s command, among the eleven tribes of the Hebrews. He explains this by an example. When the lots for the tribe of Benjamin had been cast into the urn, the urn was shaken; whichever lot came out when the tribe of Benjamin drew was called Benjamin’s *clerus*, or allotment. The same applied to the portions of the other eleven tribes.

From this he proceeds as follows:

> After Christian truth succeeded the Mosaic figures and, because the Hebrews had behaved ill, divine grace was turned toward the Gentiles, what the Hellenists had called the Church they also called the *Clerus*.

After inserting much material by which he nevertheless by no means establishes that the Hellenists employed *clerus* as a synonym for the Church, the learned man adduces the passage of St. Peter and says that the depraved blindness of mortals, neglecting Christian simplicity, restored Pharisaic pride and overwhelmed heavenly things with earthly:

> Peter appears to have been the first to transfer the word *cleri* to Christian matters, in his First Canonical Epistle. [Col. 1040A] Himself a fellow-presbyter, he exhorts presbyters to feed the flock God committed to them, watching over the sheep not from desire for shameful gain, but freely; nor as lording it over the *cleri*—that is, the Christian people.

Finally, Rigaltius complains that the pastors made the name *clergy*, which had been common to the whole body of the sheep, so exclusively their own that the very name of the sheepfold was degraded into the designation “people,” “commonalty,” or “laity.” Thus, already by the age of Tertullian and Cyprian, so great a distinction arose between clerics and laity that laypeople were not understood under the designation “clergy.”

What the learned man intends by this lengthy discussion is not easy to conjecture. Is he offended that there are bishops and pastors in the Church? It does not appear so, since he acknowledges that the Lord appointed numerous pastors over his sheepfold. Certainly, diversity of things not only permits but even requires diversity of terms.

Or, since St. Peter addresses presbyters as a fellow-presbyter, will it be a sign of neglected Christian simplicity and Pharisaic pride if an apostle or bishop [Col. 1040B] claims right and authority over the ecclesiastical clergy? St. Paul admonishes in 1 Timothy 5:1, “Do not rebuke an elder” (*πρεσβύτερον ἐπιπλήξῃς*); yet in verse 20 of the same chapter, when presbyters have been found guilty of crimes, it will be necessary, at the Apostle’s own command, to “rebuke them before everyone” (*ἐνώπιον πάντων ἐλέγξας*).

Or is the offense that, although the word *clergy* sometimes includes all Christians, it is sometimes restricted to ministers of the word? Yet this occurs everywhere in common usage. Not only the supreme Deity but magistrates too are called “gods”; and in Revelation 5:10 all the faithful are called kings and priests. Nevertheless, no one would say that secular princes and those who perform sacred rites in any order whatsoever wickedly appropriate those names to themselves.

We acknowledge that the lots of the Israelite tribes are called *cleri*, allotments. Yet the sacred text itself teaches us that the case of the Levites was far different from that of the remaining tribes. Numbers 18:20 says:

> You shall possess no inheritance in their land, nor shall you have a portion among them, because I am your portion and your inheritance among the children of Israel  
> (*Ἐν τῇ γῇ αὐτῶν οὐ κληρονομήσεις, καὶ μερὶς οὐκ ἔσται σοι ἐν αὐτοῖς, ὅτι ἐγὼ μερίς σου, καὶ κληρονομία σου ἐν μέσῳ τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ*).

It is surely one thing for the portions of land assigned to the tribes to be called their *cleri*, and another for the Levites themselves, whom the Lord acknowledges as his own allotted portion, [Col. 1040C] to be called his *clerus*.

We do not deny that St. Peter in his First Epistle called all Christians the Lord’s *clerus*. Yet that same Peter, in Acts 1:17, does not hesitate to call the apostolic office “the allotted share of ministry” (*κλῆρον διακονίας*).

Finally, if it is not enough for Rigaltius that by the age of Cyprian and even Tertullian the distinction between clerics and laity was so great that laypeople were not understood by the word *clergy*, Clement of Rome will testify that this was already so in the apostolic age. In his *Letter to the Corinthians* he says:

> Particular services have been assigned to the high priest; to the priests their particular place has been appointed; and upon the Levites particular ministries are imposed. The layperson is bound by the ordinances pertaining to the laity  
> (*Ἀρχιερεῖ ἴδιαι λειτουργίαι δεδομέναι εἰσί, καὶ τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἴδιος ὁ τόπος προστέτακται, καὶ λευΐταις ἴδιαι διακονίαι ἐπίκεινται· ὁ λαϊκὸς ἄνθρωπος τοῖς λαϊκοῖς προστάγμασιν δέδεται*).

But more than enough has been said on these matters.

**We have learned that the blessed Pope Cyprian has withdrawn.** Rigaltius says that Cyprian’s withdrawal was not entirely free from the reproach of flight among certain members of the Christian brotherhood who had read Tertullian’s discussion *On Flight in Persecution*.

I do not doubt that the very severity of so great a master so overwhelmed the disciple’s mind—or [Col. 1040D] at least pricked it with some scruple—that Cyprian strove with great care to remove from himself the suspicion of flight. The rather intricate diligence of his intimate friend Pontius also persuades us of this; Cyprian’s own following letters declare it; and, if we love the truth, nothing is more strongly censured by this Roman clergy’s admonition, as elaborately argued as it is disorderly.

Cyprian’s strongest defense is that he withdrew at God’s prompting—indeed, at his command. For what is clearer than the divine command delivered by Christ to the apostles: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another”? If you deny that this command applied to anyone other than the apostles, who would demand from Cyprian a witness to the Lord’s command, the Holy Spirit, and God’s favor specifically toward himself?

His friends also alleged several reasons of human prudence. He was a prominent person. Cyprian alone visibly embodied the Church; if he were removed, the whole brotherhood would collapse. Cyprian’s presence alone inflamed the powers hostile to the Christian name. [Col. 1041A] The enraged populace had particularly demanded that Cyprian alone be thrown to the lion. If he were removed for a time, their frenzy appeared capable of subsiding. Finally, although absent, he nevertheless supplied and suggested everything necessary for his Church through agents or deputies and through very frequent letters.

That these reasons for withdrawal, highly plausible at the time, served as a precedent for later centuries is shown by Augustine’s splendid letter to Honoratus. It also offers the most salutary counsels against all the subtleties of such human prudence.

Writers on strategy discuss a question not unlike ours: whether a commander in war should be praised if he does not hesitate to expose his own life everywhere to dangers boldly and vigorously. The matter admits this determination: the safety of the commander must be considered first when his removal would necessarily overthrow the safety of the people, for then “the first work of virtue is to preserve the man who preserves all the rest” (*πρῶτον ἔργον ἀρετῆς εἶναι, σώζειν τὸν ἅπαντα τἆλλα σώζοντα*). But when the entire army’s steadfastness depends upon the commander’s example, then neither hands nor head are to be spared. Plutarch wisely observed this in the case of Pelopidas.

**By Clementius.** See the letter immediately following below.

[Col. 1041B] **“To the subdeacon.”** Rigaltius complains that in this way, little by little and beginning with the lowest ranks, kingship and the lust for domination entered the Church. The apostles had spoken only of deacons. Cyprian’s age admitted subdeacons; the following age, archdeacons, and thereafter archbishops and patriarchs. The apostles had spoken only of bishops and presbyters. Tertullian said that the bishop was the high priest. With Rigaltius’s leave, I would believe that the subdiaconate and the other grades of the clergy, both lower and higher, were introduced into the Church not for ostentation, kingship, and the lust for domination, but to serve the necessary purposes of Christian piety. What could have contributed more to the unity of the African Church and to other public advantages than that all the bishops of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania should be subject to the governance of Cyprian alone? Conversely, as regards the lower grades, if anyone considers the condition of the primitive Church—the need to summon every individual to solemn assemblies, and afterward to admit them only with discrimination and watchfulness; repeatedly to dispatch messengers [Col. 1041C] not merely to neighboring regions but to places far distant; perpetually to care for the sick, the poor, catechumens, the lapsed, martyrs, prisoners, those condemned to the mines, and finally the dead—he will not be surprised that, amid so many affairs, so pressing, so varied, so laborious, and so full of danger, very many persons were employed to manage them; and that, after bishops, presbyters, and deacons, subdeacons, readers, acolytes, and doorkeepers were appointed to share in ecclesiastical responsibility.

Cornelius, who at this very time was bishop of the Roman Church, distinctly reports how many persons had been appointed to the clergy in the city, in his Letter to Fabius of Antioch, preserved in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43: namely, there were “forty-six presbyters; seven deacons; seven subdeacons; forty-two acolytes; and fifty-two exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers together” (*πρεσβυτέρους τεσσαράκοντα ἕξ· διακόνους ἑπτά· ὑποδιακόνους ἑπτά· ἀκολούθους δύο καὶ τεσσαράκοντα· ἐξορκιστὰς δὲ καὶ ἀναγνώστας ἅμα πυλωροῖς δύο καὶ πεντήκοντα*). To these he adds that there were “more than fifteen hundred widows and persons in distress, all of whom the Master’s grace and loving-kindness supports” (*χήρας σὺν θλιβομένοις, ὑπὲρ τὰς χιλίας πεντακοσίας, οὓς πάντας ἡ τοῦ Δεσπότου χάρις καὶ φιλανθρωπία διατρέφει*). Finally, he concludes concerning them all: “so great and so necessary a multitude in the Church, a number rich and increasing through God’s providence, together with an exceedingly great and innumerable people” (*τοσοῦτο πλῆθος καὶ οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ διὰ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας πλούσιός τε καὶ πληθύων ἀριθμός, μετὰ μεγίστου καὶ ἀναριθμήτου λαοῦ*). [Col. 1041D] And indeed it would be reasonable to believe that Carthage, Rome’s rival, yielded little to it even in matters pertaining to Christian piety.

**“For a definite reason—which, assuredly, he did rightly.”** Rigaltius says that the words should be connected thus: “For a definite reason; which, assuredly, he did rightly, since he is a distinguished person and the contest is imminent.” These appear to be the words of the Carthaginian clergy, written in Cyprian’s favor and support in order to excuse his withdrawal.

**“Upon us who appear to have been placed in authority.”** Rigaltius says: When Fabian had departed this life and Cyprian had withdrawn, both sees, the Roman and the Carthaginian, were vacant. In each place, therefore, the clergy had undertaken the care of its own Church, and the Carthaginian clergy had sent a letter to the Roman clergy concerning this withdrawal of their Cyprian. The Roman clergy, replying to the Carthaginian, said: “Since it is incumbent upon us, who [Col. 1042A] appear to have been placed in authority and to guard the flock in the shepherd’s stead, if we are found negligent, it will be said to us,” etc. Since these words are general and concern a responsibility shared on both sides, they signify a courteous and modest solicitude most appropriate to Christian charity, rather than the arrogance of any command or power. Of lesser—indeed, of greater, according to the editions—importance is what he adds: something no sane person would deny, namely that the honor of the Roman See had long since been preeminent and primary. For both the letter sent by the Carthaginian clergy to the Roman clergy concerning Cyprian’s withdrawal renders, as it were, an account; and the words of the Romans that follow here, “We therefore do not wish to find you hirelings,” although exhortatory rather than commanding, and counsels rather than orders, sufficiently indicate that even then Rome held the foremost position in the pontifical See.

**“To our predecessors.”** To the priests of the Jews. On the words that follow, **“We did not correct the one who was straying,”** Rigaltius says: Tertullian renders it thus: “What was driven away you did not bring back.” In the book *On Modesty*.

**“The lame.”** Rigaltius says that Tertullian has “the broken”; the Septuagint, [Col. 1042B] *συντετριμμένον*, in Psalm 145: “Who heals their infirmities and binds up their broken places.”

**“From the very act by which he withdrew.”** Rigaltius says: From Peter’s action, who, when Christ had been apprehended by the Jews, did not strictly speaking flee, but withdrew—that is, departed or retired. For, as it is stated in the Gospel, he followed Christ, but at a great distance, which gave the appearance of flight; indeed, the Gospel says that all the disciples abandoned Christ and fled. This letter of the Roman clergy, however, appears to lay an even heavier charge upon Peter when it says: “And the other disciples did likewise”—as though following Peter’s example. The Romans twist this against Cyprian’s withdrawal, not without the reproach of flight.

At this same time, under the same odium attached to the word “flight,” Dionysius of Alexandria—a man of equal standing in dignity and learning, and the great glory of Egypt—was also suffering criticism. He likewise defended himself on the ground that he had sought concealment after being warned by a divine voice: “I speak before God, and he himself knows that I am not lying: I did not undertake my flight on my own impulse, nor without God” (*Ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ λαλῶ, καὶ αὐτὸς οἶδεν ὅτι οὐ ψεύδομαι, οὐδεμίαν ἐπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ βαλλόμενος οὐδὲ ἀθεεὶ πεποίημαι τὴν φυγήν*); and much more to this effect in Eusebius, book VI, [Col. 1042C] chapter 40.

**“Ascending to that which they were being compelled to do.”** They shrink from declaring the deed itself in explicit words. Rigaltius says that they ascended the Capitol in order to place incense in the censer. Thus in the book *On the Lapsed*: “They had not waited even to be apprehended before ascending, so that they might deny when questioned.” And shortly afterward: “When they came voluntarily to the Capitol, did not their step falter?” And in the same book: “One of those who voluntarily ascended the Capitol in order to deny.” Canon 59 of the Council of Elvira: “No Christian is to ascend to the idol of the Capitol for the purpose of sacrificing.”

Latinius’s manuscript presents the matter differently: namely, that the presbyters of the Roman Church, observing that weak Christians, driven by fear, were ascending to the Capitol, had given them courage and recalled them to the Church by timely admonitions. What is said below in the printed texts—that “those who had been apprehended returned through fear of men”—does not appear to correspond to the context.

**“That Church, strong in faith.”** While retaining Pamelius’s reading, Rigaltius notes that [Col. 1042D] by this boast of their own fortitude the Romans cast odium upon the Carthaginians. Indeed, Tertullian himself, a Carthaginian, proclaims the prerogative of the Roman faith in his book *On Prescriptions*: “But if you are near Italy,” he says, “you have Rome, from which authority is also ready at hand for us. How blessed is that Church, upon which the apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood!” And in the fourth book *Against Marcion*: “Let us see what the Romans nearby also proclaim.” But Latinius’s reading assigns the praise of fortitude not to the Roman Church but to the clergy.

**“If in any way they could receive indulgence.”** Rigaltius says: the indulgence of penance. Moreover, the words “from him who is able to grant it” are added because the Church had not yet admitted idolaters to penance by any decree, although it did so immediately afterward.

**“Whether widows or the afflicted.”** Rigaltius says: William Morel was the first to publish this Letter, and he did not indicate where he had obtained his copy. It is not found in Pamelius’s manuscripts, [Col. 1043A] nor in the Italian manuscripts, nor in those of our country. Yet it is highly authentic and does not teem with as many errors as Pamelius supposed. Morel therefore printed *clydomeni* in this passage, which we do not deny to be corrupt; indeed, we believe Pamelius’s conjecture to be correct, that the archetype read *clinomeni*. This opinion appears all the more firmly established because it is known that among Christians of that age the designation “clinics” was commonly reproachful. These were persons who, while lying ill in bed, received baptism by having water poured over them because of the imminent danger of death—as though they had not been properly baptized, since they were sprinkled rather than immersed. They are discussed in Cyprian’s Letter to Magnus.

The Roman clergy, therefore, in undertaking the care even of these bed-bound persons, soften the sadness of the term and, by altering the ending, call them *κλινομένοις* (“those lying down”), not *κλινικοῖς* (“clinics”). With similar kindness, Tertullian in the *Apologeticum* declined to call Christians nearly exhausted by advanced age “clinics,” but instead called them “old men already belonging to the household.” As regards the authenticity of the Letter, besides the manuscripts of Latinius, which acknowledge it, it is also found in one of the Bodleian manuscripts. [Col. 1043B] As for the present word, the approved reading is the one we employ; support for it is provided by Cornelius’s Letter to Fabius, cited above, where on a similar occasion mention is made of “widows and persons in distress” (*χηρῶν καὶ θλιβομένων*). We showed in book III, *To Quirinus*, chapter 61, that “to support” means to supply someone with what is necessary for life.

**“The catechumens ought not to be deceived.”** Rigaltius says: For this was among the first things they heard from a bishop or presbyter—that among Christians the care of charity or love was of the highest importance; and they could complain that they had been deceived if they happened to be abandoned in the very heat of persecution.

## LETTER IX

**“To the presbyters and deacons at Rome.”** Rigaltius says: When the persecution raised against the Christians under the emperor Decius had killed Fabian, the head of the Roman Church, the Roman clergy sent a letter to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, through Clement the subdeacon, and informed him of Fabian’s [Col. 1043C] glorious end. Soon afterward, when the same destructive persecution was raging throughout Africa, Cyprian—by then demanded for the lion—departed into seclusion, with God so directing, and gave no notice of his withdrawal to the Roman Church. But subsequently the Carthaginian clergy, in a letter sent to the Roman clergy, disclosed what course Cyprian had decided upon. The Roman clergy then replied to the Carthaginian clergy that they were touched with no slight grief because the shepherd had sought concealment after abandoning the sheep.

This is the subject of the preceding Letter, which Pamelius testifies that we owe to Morel, and which is the very letter that Cyprian complained had come into his hands not without some suspicion of fraud. He sent it back to Rome to the presbyters and deacons so that they might determine whether it was that letter of their clergy which they had entrusted to Clementius for delivery. We do not possess the Romans’ reply. It is permissible to infer only this much by conjecture: the Romans acknowledged the Letter as their own. It so stung Cyprian’s mind that he considered it necessary to write them a letter rendering an account both of his conduct and of his discipline and diligence. This he indeed accomplished in the Letter numbered XX [Col. 1043D] in this Oxford edition.

**“To the deacons.”** Rigaltius says: Those forms of declension, *diacones* and *diaconibus*, are ancient. Yet they had the Apostle in their hands, in whom one reads *διάκονοι*, *διακόνοις*, and *διακόνους*; and in the Old Latin version, *diaconi*, *diacones*, and *diaconos*. I do not know how they came to prefer saying *diacones* and *diaconibus*. They certainly treated the word “bishops” with greater reverence. Those who said *episcopus* did not say *diaconas* for women, but *diaconissas*. Justinian, *Novel* III, uses what is virtually a common-gender form: “one hundred male deacons and forty female” (*διακόνους ἄρρενας ἑκατόν, τεσσαράκοντα δὲ θηλείας*).

**“When, concerning the departure of my good colleague.”** Rigaltius says that “departure” means death, which is presently called “consummation.” Christians avoided the word “death” as far as they could because of their hope of resurrection and everlasting life. Accordingly, they said “sent on ahead” instead of “dead,” and “passing” or “departure” instead of “death.” Borrowing a term from the art of calculation, they spoke of a person as “consummated” and of the “consummation” of years, days, [Col. 1044A] and hours, as though these had been gathered and reckoned like coins into a final sum. Expressions of this kind occur frequently in Tertullian.

**“His honorable consummation took place.”** Rigaltius says: “Fabian having been perfected by martyrdom at Rome” (*Φαβιανοῦ ἐπὶ Ῥώμης μαρτυρίῳ τελειωθέντος*), Eusebius VI.39. Rufinus: “Fabian having been crowned with martyrdom in the city of Rome.”

**“The memory of the one placed in authority.”** Rigaltius says: Fabian, bishop of Rome, whom the Roman clergy also calls “the one placed in authority” in the preceding Letter, and by the same name designates the other rulers of the Churches as well. Justin had called such a person *προεστῶτα*, “the one presiding”; Tertullian, in the *Apologeticum*, “the president.” He is the bishop, whom the same Tertullian also calls the high priest.

**“I also read other letters.”** Rigaltius says: I agree with Pamelius that these were nothing other than the foregoing pages of Letter II.

**“In which neither those who wrote nor those to whom it was written were identified.”** Rigaltius says: We must therefore conclude that the title was omitted in the archetype. This was perhaps an act of caution or prudence on the Romans’ part amid the dangers of the Decian persecution.

**“I sent the same authentic Letter back to you.”** Rigaltius [Col. 1044B] says: He calls it “authentic,” although he doubted its genuineness; nevertheless it was authentic in the sense that it was exactly the same letter as had been brought by Clementius. This Letter should be called “clerical” for two reasons: first, because it was directed by the Roman clergy to the Carthaginian clergy; and second—and chiefly—because it had been sent through a messenger initiated into holy orders. Concerning the order of these Letters, consult the *Annals* for the year 250, § VIII.

## LETTER X

**“To the Martyrs and Confessors.”** Nicolas Le Fèvre notes that those were called “confessors” who, when questioned before the judges, had professed Christ; “martyrs” were those who, after professing Christ, were also tortured in order to make them deny him and nevertheless persevered. All martyrs, therefore, were confessors, but confessors were not yet martyrs, except as “designated”—as Tertullian elegantly calls them at the beginning of the book *To the Martyrs*—or, as he calls them elsewhere, “candidates for martyrdom.”

**“The present confession, however.”** [Col. 1044C] The persecution initiated by the ordinary magistrates proceeded only as far as exile. When the proconsul arrived, he added torture and death.

**“I have already learned that some have been crowned.”** We learn who they were from Lucian’s Letter: namely Bassus, Mappalicus, Fortunio, Paul, Fortuna, Victorinus, Victor, Herenius, Credulus, Herena, Donatus, Firmus, Ventus, Fructus, Julia, Martialis, and Aristo.

**“With an unrestrained voice.”** With the voice by which they professed themselves Christians before the tribunal.

**“Giving believers as much as the recipient believes himself to receive.”** Thus above, in the book *To Donatus*: “As much capacity for faith as we bring, so much cleansing grace do we drink in.”

**“God provides the contest.”** See what is stated above on this subject in book II, *Against the Jews*, chapter 9.

**“He is self-controlled in all things.”** Rigaltius says: Paul, in 1 Corinthians, has, “he exercises self-control in all things” (*πάντα ἐγκρατεύεται*). And the Vulgate version: “he abstains from all things.” [Col. 1044D] Priorius adds that Cyprian here compares the Christian contest with the competitions of the gentiles, who carefully regulated the athletes’ diet and exercises. They were not allowed every kind of food, but were subjected to “necessary eating” (*ἀναγκοφαγία*), as Aristotle calls it. Their bread was called *coliphium*. They abstained from all pleasures for the sake of bodily training, as Clement of Alexandria indicates in *Stromata* III. Plato has the same in book III of the *Republic*: “The other athletes also know this: that the man who intends to keep his body in good condition must abstain from all such things” (*Τοῦτο μὲν καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι ἀσκηταὶ ἴσασιν, ὅτι τῷ μέλλοντι σώματι εὖ ἕξειν ἀφετέον τῶν τοιούτων ἁπάντων*). He means pleasures and harmful enticements. To these may be added what Tertullian says in the *Exhortation to Martyrdom*: “Athletes are set apart for a stricter discipline so that they may devote themselves to building strength; they are restrained from luxury, richer foods, more delightful drink,” etc.

**“Of my assumption.”** He reads *ἀναλήψεως*, “taking up”; in our manuscripts *ἀναλύσεως*, “departure,” occurs. See book III, *To Quirinus*, chapter 16. Tertullian in the *Scorpiace* has: “the time of separation.”

[Col. 1045A] **“He mourns the falls and deaths of very many.”** Rigaltius says: Thus in the preceding Letter, “amid the falls of those who mourn.” By “falls” he means those of the lapsed brethren whom the tortures overthrew and who, through the cruelty of the torments, offered incense to idols or denied Christ. The falls belong to the lapsed; the deaths to the deniers.

**“Peace should supervene.”** Rigaltius says: This is the peace concerning which the head of the household had sent word in the following Letter, through that anxious young man, in these words: “Tell him to be secure, because peace is coming.”

**“Having received a reprieve after glory.”** Rigaltius says: “After glory” means after the glory of an unimpaired will and a glorious conscience, which makes us martyrs before God—even if, through God’s own indulgence, an unexpected and unhoped-for peace should supervene, granting us a reprieve to remain still longer in the world and in the Church, flourishing in praise after the world itself has already been trampled down. Thus elsewhere: “if, after peace has been received, a reprieve is given by God”—that is, if brethren in danger of death, after receiving peace from the Church, escape that danger by God’s will, a reprieve for living [Col. 1045B] having been granted to them by God—they should nevertheless continue to enjoy the peace which the Church had granted in consideration of their approaching death. And in the book *On Mortality*: “When one of our colleagues and fellow priests, exhausted by illness and anxious about approaching death, prayed that a reprieve might be granted him”—that is, he asked God to indulge him by allowing him to remain among the living for a little longer.

**“That he may be crowned for glory.”** That is, for the glorious contest of temperance, chastity, and piety in time of peace, and of constancy, patience, and faith in the encounter.

## LETTER XI

**“Although I know.”** Rigaltius says: Augustine, in book IV of *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, mentions this Letter under the title *To the Clergy, on Praying to God*. He acknowledges this title as genuinely Cyprian’s; and says that, as though addressing words to the clergy, Cyprian also addressed himself, “representing in his own person, like holy Daniel, the sins of his people.”

[Col. 1045C] **“Renouncing the world in words alone and not in deeds.”** Augustine adds from Paul’s Letter to Titus: “For they confess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds.” Moreover, he cites this passage in the final chapter of *On Faith and Works*, in Letter 89.9.4, and also in book II *Against Cresconius*, chapter 15.

**“Torments without end from the torturer, without the release of condemnation, without the consolation of death.”** Rigaltius says: Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*: “all the ingenuity of the executioner in tortures.” Rufinus, in his translation of book VI of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, where he treats Origen’s persecution under Decius: “So that he was tormented by a thousand deaths, yet not even the single death he expected befell him, since the persecutor took the greatest pains to ensure that neither release through death was granted nor the punishment ceased.” Eusebius had written only: “The judge contentiously exerted all his strength to ensure that he should by no means be killed” (*Μηδαμῶς αὐτὸν ἀνελεῖν παντὶ σθένει τοῦ δικαστοῦ φιλονείκως ἐνστάντος*). Pamelius rightly notes that this supplies evidence for determining when this Letter was written.

**“Until they cast down.”** Until. Until.

**“He failed amid the very tortures.”** [Col. 1045D] I consider this reading the most genuine; for one who has expired under torture is rightly said to have attained glory not through the termination of the punishment but through the speed of his death.

**“It was said in a vision.”** Rigaltius says: The books of both sacred libraries, Mosaic and Christian, supply examples of visions; for the patriarchs relate many things divinely revealed to them, and so do the prophets. Peter saw a great vessel lowered to him from heaven, and Paul saw things which neither ear had ever heard nor eye seen. Then the Christian Fathers of the Church committed to writing many things signified to them in dreams. Tertullian, too, cites the testimony of visions more than once.

Accordingly, during this Decian persecution of the Christian people, Cyprian acts in a manner most fitting for a bishop: while the storm rages, he contemplates heaven like a helmsman skilled in the stars, and impresses upon his passengers the commands given him from heaven, employing a most effective kind of persuasion—a vision divinely presented to him and particularly suited to the matter he was handling. Letter XVI, where it speaks of ecstasy, will make clear that this [Col. 1046A] vision occurred in sleep.

**“That they should petition for certain persons specifically designated to them.”** Rigaltius says: This recalls the memory of some event involving the repentance of certain lapsed persons, concerning whom the votes of the brethren had been discordant.

**“In accordance with the peace that the Lord gave us.”** Rigaltius says: He said to the apostles in John 14:27: “My peace I give you. Not as the world gives do I give to you.” For he was giving the apostles mutual peace among themselves. Chrysostom understood it thus: “I give such peace that you may be at peace with one another, which makes you stronger” (*Ἐγὼ δίδωμι τοιαύτην, ὥστε μετ’ ἀλλήλων εἰρηνεύειν, ὅπερ ὑμᾶς ἰσχυροτέρους ποιεῖ*).

**“The brotherhood animated as one.”** “With one accord” (*ὁμοθυμαδόν*).

**“He was carrying a net.”** Rigaltius says: This vision portrays the devil equipped as a retiarius, who fought with a cast-net and a trident or fishing-spear.

**“In order to catch the surrounding people.”** Rigaltius says: The devil, Christ’s rival, catches human beings by tricks and fraud. Christ, however, said to the fishermen Simon and Andrew, [Col. 1046B] while they were intent on catching fish: “Come, I shall make you fishers of men.” In place of nets and a dragnet, he gave them the commands of God the almighty Father, most effective for eternal salvation, so that by those precepts or commands they might recover for life the human beings whom the devil had deceived into death.

**“Cover them with a cast of the net.”** Rigaltius says: With a net cast over them—a casting-net, *ἀμφίβληστρον*, a *funda*. Servius, on that passage of Virgil’s *Georgics*—“now the casting-net lashes the river”—says: “The *funda* is a kind of net, so called from its being cast—that is, it is a casting-net, called *βόλος*.” Thus, when a retiarius was matched against a Thracian, murmillo, or secutor, the technique of the contest was that the retiarius should draw together his cast net with such agility that he seized his opponent. Tertullian called that contraction or seizure a “sponge” in the book *On the Spectacles*: “fixed upon the bites of bears and the sponges of the retiarii.”

**“That he might afflict you.”** *Τοῦ σινιάσαι*. He understood it in the ordinary sense of the word, namely, as signifying “to maltreat” (*κακουργεῖν*) or [Col. 1046C] “to harm” (*βλάπτειν*), not “to shake” (*σεῖσαι*) or “to sift” (*κοσκινεῦσαι*), concerning which see Hesychius.

**“The Father also corrects us.”** The words that follow—“and firmly adhering to his Christ”—support this as the genuine reading, since those words certainly determine that the preceding reference is to the Father. The other reading, “he both corrects and protects us,” refers back to what was said above concerning Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, with which it by no means fits.

**“Although established in very many offenses.”** In the same spirit Tertullian, in the book *On Repentance*, calls himself “a sinner bearing every mark.”

**“Tell him,” he said, “to be secure, because peace is coming.”** Rigaltius says: Accordingly, near the end of the Letter he says: “Let us pray that peace may be restored sooner and that assistance may quickly be brought to us in our hiding places and dangers.” This vision is mentioned in Letters 4 and 16. The head of the household addresses the young man who appeared above to Cyprian in a state of anxiety and some sadness. “Tell him,” that is, Cyprian.

**“No one looking back.”** Some Greek manuscripts [Col. 1046D] also read the words in this order.

**“She lost what she had completed.”** The whole journey she had traversed came to nothing. We have discussed above Cyprian’s use of this word.

**“Of those who are weak.”** Of the lapsed.

**“That the repentance of the lapsed may be reformed.”** Rigaltius says: So that it may not be accepted while crude, premature, incomplete, or insufficiently sincere.

## LETTER XII

**“That care may not be lacking for them.”** Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*: “I say nothing yet of the reward to which God invites martyrs. Meanwhile let us compare the very manner of life in the world and in prison, and see whether the spirit does not gain more in prison than the flesh loses; indeed, through the Church’s care the flesh does not lose even the things that are its due.”

**“Record the days on which they depart.”** Tertullian, in the book *On the Crown*, [Col. 1047A] addresses the Christian thus: “You have your own registers, your own calendars; you have nothing to do with the world’s festivities—indeed, you owe the contrary.” The account books that contained the expenditures made in relieving the poor were the faithful’s registration tablets; martyrologies were their calendars.

At approximately this time, at the beginning of Decius’s reign, Fabian is said to have appointed seven subdeacons at Rome to oversee seven notaries and collect the acts of the martyrs in their entirety. Moreover, Cyprian says in Letter XXXIX that the martyrs’ sufferings and their anniversaries were celebrated with commemoration throughout Africa. Indeed, an illustrious monument survives concerning the singular diligence of the ancient Eastern Church in this matter. Eusebius preserved part of it in book IX, chapter 15, while the Most Reverend Ussher has recently presented it in full. I mean the Letter of the Church of Smyrna written to the Churches of Pontus concerning the Martyrdom of Polycarp.

There, after recounting the acts of his martyrdom, the brethren promise, with divine favor, “to celebrate the anniversary of his martyrdom, both in remembrance of those who had already contended and for the training and preparation of those who would do so in the future” (*ἐπιτελεῖν τὴν τοῦ μαρτυρίου αὐτοῦ ἡμέραν γενέθλιον, εἴς τε τῶν προηθληκότων μνήμην, καὶ τῶν μελλόντων ἄσκησίν τε καὶ ἑτοιμασίαν*). [Col. 1047B] They report that the passion occurred “on the second day of the opening of the month Xanthicus, seven days before the Kalends of March, on the Great Sabbath, at the eighth hour; he was arrested by Herod the chief of police, under Philip of Tralles the high priest, while Statius Quadratus was proconsul” (*μηνὸς Ξαντικοῦ δευτέρᾳ ἱσταμένου, πρὸ ἑπτὰ καλανδῶν μαρτίων, σαββάτῳ μεγάλῳ, ὥρᾳ ὀγδόῃ, συνελήφθη ὑπὸ Ἡρώδου εἰρηνάρχου, ὑπὸ ἀρχιερέως Φιλίππου τραλλιανοῦ, ἀνθυπατεύοντος Στατίου Κοδράτου*). Nothing more precisely recorded can be said or imagined.

## LETTER XIII

**“We contend daily for our life.”** Rigaltius says: By this the author means eternal life, as above, page 187: “It accords with the discipline and with the very life of us all.” But the more obvious meaning is that we are daily exposed to death; hence Tertullian, in *On the Spectacles*, chapter 1, calls Christians “a race ready for death.” And if any ominous or fateful event occurred, it was immediately “Christians to the lion!” The same author, *Apologeticum*, chapter 40.

**“The faith and birth received.”** Rigaltius says: He speaks of “received faith” and “received birth” for the adoption of the Christian faith [Col. 1047C] and the reception of baptism. Thus Tertullian also spoke of “lost baptism” in the book *On Baptism*; and in ancient inscriptions concerning the rites of the Great Mother one reads: “He received and obtained the taurobolium”; “He performed the taurobolium”; and somewhere even, “He was tauroboliated.” Just as they spoke of “receiving” rites, so also of “delivering” them. Ancient stones read: “They delivered the Leontic rites”; “They delivered the Coracic rites”; “They delivered the Patric rites.”

**“Attainment.”** Baptism. See book III, *To Quirinus*, chapters 42 and 97.

**“Shine like lights.”** Pamelius notes that the Greek word *φαίνεθε* is ambiguous. Moreover, Ambrose too, in his commentary, construed it in the imperative sense employed here by Cyprian.

**“So that, while they deliberate about you.”** Rigaltius says: While the gentiles hold an inquiry concerning you, investigate you, examine you, and speak against you. 1 Peter 2: “wherein they speak against you” (*ἐν ᾧ καταλαλοῦσιν ὑμῶν*). The Vulgate version has *detrectant*, “they disparage.” The old glosses: “To disparage” (*detrectare*), *λοιδορεῖν*, “to revile”; “he disparages” (*detrectat*), *ἀπωθεῖ*, “he rejects.”

**“As though evildoers.”** *Ὡς κακοποιῶν.*

[Col. 1047D] **“Of the preeminent name.”** Namely, Christians. James 2:7, “the noble name” (*καλὸν ὄνομα*).

**“When one person is drunken toward another.”** Rigaltius says: All previous editions read “when some other person,” or “when some one person is drunken.” Thus, up to now, the extremely corrupt text of the printed Cyprian has distorted his meaning. “How greatly,” he says, “is your name disgraced by wrongdoing, when someone, drunken from the waters and behaving wantonly, lingers?” “From the waters,” that is, from baptism. The man who has given his name to Christ, who has been dipped or baptized into Christ’s name, binds himself by this sacrament to become a worthy and temperate person. Accordingly, if he thereafter appears drunken or worthless, he brings great dishonor and reproach upon his religion. For although *temulentus*, “drunken,” derives from *temetum*, “wine,” and wine is diluted with water, this man, contrary to nature, becomes drunken from the waters, wanton and shameful from the laver. He renounced Satan and returns to Satan’s camp. He returns to the place from which he was made an exile.

With Rigaltius’s leave, I would say [Col. 1048A] that it is not all the old editions, but his own emendation, that is extremely corrupt, being supported by no manuscript evidence and no rational argument. For in this passage the subject is not the newly baptized, but the confessors—namely, those returning from the proconsul’s tribunal, not from the Church’s baptistery. It is indeed a common practice for critics, when they pursue a reading that appears ingenious to them, to abandon the genuine and obvious one.

**“Having been made an exile from the place,” etc.** Pamelius says: You see from the explicit words that the rebuke is directed at exiles. It alludes to 1 Peter 2: “For what glory is it if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it?” It signifies that those who had returned from exile without being ordered to do so were thereafter killed not as Christians but as criminals. Rigaltius wrongly diverts these words to another meaning, as though Cyprian’s thought were this: that the confessors had indeed been driven into exile for Christ’s sake, but behaved so wickedly there that, after their return, they were condemned by the judge no longer as Christians but as criminals. Could the proconsul of Africa punish at Carthage offenses that exiles had committed in another province?

[Col. 1048B] **“Illuminated members.”** *Φωτισθέντα*, “illuminated.” For martyrdom is a baptism of blood.

**“We had renounced the world.”** There is no need to repeat so often the same observations concerning the solemn formula of renunciation employed in the Church throughout every age.

**“Discipline in conduct.”** Rigaltius says: After these words, the following passage is read in the Reims manuscript:

> And although I have written most fully to our clergy—both recently, while you were still confined in prison, and now again—so that whatever you might need for clothing or food should be supplied, nevertheless I myself have also sent you 250 from the small funds of my own that I carried with me; and I had recently sent another 250. Victor too, formerly a reader and now a deacon, who is with me, has sent you 425. I rejoice, moreover, when I learn that very many of our brethren, in accordance with their love, eagerly vie with one another in coming forward and assisting your necessities by their contributions. I wish you, etc.

[Col. 1048C] This addition ought to be considered all the more valuable because it supplies us with a clearer example of Caecilian’s charity toward the brethren. For in the other Letters we indeed find him generous from his own resources; here, however, he gives even from the modest funds that he carried with him to meet his own necessities. We may now understand that he relieved his brethren’s needs even from what was necessary for himself. For he defrayed his own necessities from his own resources. Yet nothing is more burdensome than a slender provision for a journey. In the manuscripts that I have had occasion to see, however, these words occur nowhere.

## LETTER XIV

**“We might refine.”** Rigaltius says: The old glosses: “He refines” (*limat*), *ῥινίζει*, “he files,” and *ζητεῖ*, “he investigates.” Phaedrus: “If he had subtly refined the lie from its roots, he would not have overthrown the household by a deadly crime.”

**“To Tertullus.”** The man praised before and to be praised repeatedly. For if he was a man of thoroughly recognized courage and exceptional diligence in managing the martyrs’ affairs, no suspicion could arise that he had suggested timid counsels to his bishop. Cyprian thus seizes every opportunity to defend his withdrawal.

[Col. 1048D] **“Let them learn what ecclesiastical discipline requires in accordance with the teaching of the Scriptures.”** Rigaltius says: He impresses upon them what he already admonished in the preceding Letter: those who now glory in the title of confession must nevertheless be humble, modest, and peaceful. They must not by their arrogance provoke the gentiles’ cruelty against themselves, as though they were rebels and insolent persons, and so bring odium upon the Christian name.

It will be worth the effort to observe here once for all that in these Letters our Caecilius chiefly strives to make the people peaceable and genuinely Christian. For he knew that very many troublesome persons, through their insolent boasting of the Christian name, had so often provoked even the secular authorities—frequently while they were occupied with other matters—that those authorities felt compelled to restrain the disturbers of public peace with the utmost cruelty and excessively aggravated punishments. This had brought great disgrace upon the Christian faith.

He likewise knew that in his own Church there were many who, excessively secure in their confidence in the saving laver, were forgetful of discipline and of the whole brotherhood: [Col. 1049A] greedy for gain, devoted to ambition, factious, given to luxury, taking pleasure in their arrogant conduct, displeasing to everyone, and, in short, Christians in name alone. Cyprian therefore says that these ways of life are the causes of the great sorrows by which the Church, crushed down, is being destroyed. But why should we marvel at these things in a Church already two centuries old, when we so often hear or read Paul reproaching his Corinthians with things even worse?

**“To follies and dissensions.”** Rigaltius says: Cyprian warns these confessors in the same way that Septimius warned those blessed persons designated for martyrdom, whom he says were tempted by the devil in prison itself through “petty quarrels, partialities, or dissensions among themselves.” These certainly brought many evils upon the Christian commonwealth. Here Cyprian calls “follies” what Tertullian calls “petty quarrels” or “petty disputes.”

**“As for what our fellow presbyters wrote to me.”** Rigaltius says: Namely, concerning the lapsed who were to be received into penance.

**“Nothing without your counsel and the consent of the people.”** Rigaltius says: That is, together with the whole Church, as the apostles had done [Col. 1049B] in that first synod described in Acts 15:22: “Then it pleased the apostles and elders, together with the whole Church” (*Ἔδοξε τοῖς Ἀποστόλοις καὶ τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις σὺν ὅλῃ τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ*). On that passage Chrysostom speaks admirably: “So as to show that it was not done tyrannically, because these things pleased everyone” (*Ὥστε δεῖξαι ὅτι οὐ τυραννικῶς, ὅτι πᾶσι ταῦτα δοκεῖ*); and shortly afterward: “Thus there was no arrogance in the Church” (*οὕτως οὐδεὶς τύφος ἦν ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ*).

Thus the Romans themselves say below, in Letter 3: “By comparing counsels with the bishops, presbyters, deacons, confessors, and likewise with the laity who stand firm.” We noted above that Cyprian took pains to remove odium from himself; here, however, he says that he determines nothing pertaining to the principles of ecclesiastical discipline without consulting the people. For since the external effect of the power of the keys consisted chiefly in the people’s treating those subjected to censure as gentiles and tax collectors, it certainly could not be expected that they would all abandon friends, close associates, and brethren struck by the thunderbolt of excommunication, or readmit others whom they had expelled, until they themselves had been satisfied concerning those persons’ crimes or repentance.

Moreover, it should be observed here [Col. 1049C] that the case of the lapsed was handled not according to the customs received in the Church, but with a leniency hitherto unheard of; it was therefore all the more appropriate that an account should be given of the reason for this innovation.

## LETTER XV
An honorable petition. He immediately calls the martyrs’ wishes this. Whatever the martyrs did on behalf of the lapsed was done wholly by way of intercession—an intercession indeed highly honorable and not easily to be disregarded; yet it remained a petition and possessed only the prerogatives of favor. Cyprian discusses the matter at length in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 92 of this edition, and thereafter. “Do the martyrs,” he says, “direct that something be done? If it is just, if lawful, if not contrary to the Lord himself, it must be done by God’s priest: there should be a ready and willing assent on the part of him who complies, provided that there has been religious moderation on the part of him who petitions,” etc. The intercessions of the martyrs were believed to have very great weight with God, because they were called [Col. 1049D] and believed to be friends of God in a special sense. In the Church they possessed a prerogative because, if the lapsed had been a scandal to her, the martyrs, by contrast, lent her praise and honor and increased them. But it seems probable that, in this passage, the modest and sober certificate (*libellus*) which the martyrs had first sent is called, in a special sense, a petition worthy and honorable in them. It should further be observed, as we have also noted elsewhere, that the commands of martyrs who had been crowned and had departed from the living carried far more weight than those of persons who still survived and were themselves in danger of losing their crown and peace.

The ancient simplicity of the martyrs is depicted in vivid colors by the Church of Lyons and Vienne, in the letter concerning the suffering of the martyrs under Marcus Aurelius which they wrote to the churches of Asia and Phrygia:

> “Although they had borne witness not once or twice, but many times, and had again been rescued from the beasts, and bore upon them the brands, bruises, and wounds, they neither proclaimed themselves martyrs nor permitted us [Col. 1050A] to address them by that name,” etc.

Moreover, those excellent martyrs did not enrich the lapsed as though scattering largesses and gifts among a crowd, nor did they command them to regard themselves as secure and blessed. Rather, they took care to restore them to sound conduct through admonitions and the offices of solicitous devotion:

> “For they took no occasion for boasting against those who had fallen, but from that in which they themselves abounded they supplied the needier, having a mother’s compassion and shedding many tears for them before the Father,” etc.

Eusebius, book V, chapter 2.

Finally, in this letter Cyprian, after mentioning the honorable petition of the martyrs, passes to the penance performed; he then recounts the *exomologesis*—the confession—of the gravest and most extreme offense, namely idolatry. Afterward he mentions the laying-on of hands in penance by the bishop and clergy; and finally he relates that peace was offered to the lapsed and the Eucharist given to them. In these words, which occur in almost the same form in the next letter, a pattern of the whole ancient ecclesiastical discipline is presented.

The first step toward pardon and peace was the admission of the guilty person to penance; this was effected not without the laying-on of hands and *exomologesis*, or confession [Col. 1050B]. The second step was completed by passing through the imposed penance in its various periods of weeping, hearing, and standing. The third was a second *exomologesis*, that is, the solemn and public confession of the sin after the penance had been performed. This was followed, in the fourth place, by the laying-on of hands once again by the bishop and clergy as a token of reconciliation. Once these things had been duly performed, access to the mysteries of the Eucharist was at last opened.

But by a marvelous shortening of the path, the martyrs were now contriving that the lapsed, while still almost belching the deadly food of idols, their throats still breathing forth their crime and reeking of its fatal contagion, should immediately rush upon the body of the Lord. These are Cyprian’s words in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 92.

We showed from Tertullian, on p. 93 of this work, that the recommendations of martyrs had formerly carried weight in the Church in the case of the lapsed. Hence it is rightly said below: “Such concessions as your predecessors, the martyrs, made in the past.” Cyprian shows in Letter 27 (Pamelius’s no. 23), [Col. 1050C] that Paulus, Aurelius, and above all Lucianus were those who had exceeded due measure in recklessly granting certificates.

**Of the gravest and most extreme offense.** Rigaltius says: Elsewhere he said, “Of an eternal sin”; he means idolatry. “A vast sin, surpassing all others.” “The chief crime of the human race.” “The supreme guilt of the age.” “The entire ground of judgment.” Tertullian.

**To make an offering for them.** This is certainly the truer reading and is supported by Letter 2, where mention is made of a synodical decree that no brother, when dying, should appoint a cleric as guardian or curator; and if anyone did so, “an offering shall not be made for him.” Thus in the following letter: “Their name is presented in the offering,” and, “Let them be forbidden to make offerings.” By contrast, “to offer peace” is not said so appropriately.

**The lapsed may indeed be granted pardon in this matter.** Rigaltius says: That is, in this—that they press urgently, that they hasten, and that they wish to anticipate the appointed periods of penance.
