**Let the mother first receive it.** Rigaltius says: In the following letter, “Our mother the Church”; Tertullian, in his book *To the Martyrs*, “Lady Mother Church.” With the greatest prudence Cyprian reserves the martyrs’ wishes [Col. 1050D] concerning the granting of peace to the lapsed for the time when Mother Church herself shall enjoy peace. This was so that, while the heat of persecution was intensifying, those newly fallen into ruin and immediately admitted to peace might not, by their example, harm the others who were still standing, causing them to contend less steadfastly in the struggle because they were enticed by the pleasant hope that, after a lapse and fall, the same indulgence might be expected for themselves.

**Abruptly and unworthily promised either by you.** Rigaltius says: As one would speak before martyrs, he first sets down censorious words in such a way that they may be tempered by those which follow: “or done by us.”

**Our Church begins to blush even before the Gentiles themselves.** Rigaltius says: Thus above, “of whom the Church does not afterward blush”—that is, before the Gentiles. Such shame arose either from the dissolute conduct of certain persons or because discipline had not been maintained when faith was shamefully overthrown at the very beginning of the contest.

**Showing partiality toward persons.** Rigaltius says: Matthew and Mark said, βλέπειν εἰς πρόσωπον, “to look upon a person” (Matthew 22:16; Mark 12:14). [Col. 1051A] Luke 20:21 has λαμβάνειν πρόσωπον, “to accept a person.” Opposed to this is ἐπ’ ἀληθείας τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ θεοῦ διδάσκειν, “to teach the way of God in truth.” God is not a προσωπολήπτης, “one who shows partiality.”

**They hunt for gain.** Rigaltius says: What a foul corruption laid low even the martyrs of that Church! For Cyprian means that even among the martyrs there were some who offered certificates of peace for sale. It would be far more shameful, however, if the pontiffs themselves were the retailers and hawkers of such merchandise.

**To the clergy and to the people.** That this letter was written at the same time as the two following is shown by the fact that, although Cyprian mentions them here, they in turn mention this one. See Letters XVI and XVII toward the end.

## LETTER XVI

**For a long time I restrained my patience.** Our author had previously written several letters from his place of retirement to the presbyters and deacons. In the case of the lapsed, however, after receiving the insolent demand of Donatus, Fortunatus, Novatus, and Gordius [Col. 1051B]—which he had hoped to satisfy when he said that the matter should be deferred until his return—he now writes to them for the first time.

**Some of the presbyters.** Namely, those named in the preceding letter. Some among them are known to have been the very men who afterward became hostile to our Cyprian and were designated by the title “the five presbyters.” Yet, in order to soothe them, he calls them his fellow presbyters.

**Nor mindful of their place.** Rigaltius says: The presbyteral rank, which is subordinate to the episcopal. For such was the ecclesiastical order under Cyprian, and it had already been exactly the same in the age of Tertullian. For when he discusses the authority to confer baptism, he says: “The chief priest, who is the bishop, indeed possesses the right of conferring it; then the presbyters and deacons—but not without the bishop’s authority, on account of the honor of the Church; when this is preserved, peace is preserved.” Indeed, that had been the order from the beginnings of Christian devotion, at least from the time when bishops admitted presbyters to a share in their pastoral responsibilities. Hence he says that this presbyteral attempt [Col. 1051C] had never at all been made under his predecessors. Ignatius says that it is lawful μηδὲν ἄνευ γνώμης ἐπισκόπου ποιεῖν, οὔτε βαπτίζειν, οὔτε προσφέρειν, οὔτε θυσίαν προσκομίζειν, “to do nothing without the bishop’s approval—neither to baptize, nor to make an offering, nor to present a sacrifice.”

**In contempt of the superior, they claim everything for themselves.** They do not remain within the limits of a petition, to such a degree that they leave nothing to the bishop except the glory of complying or the necessity of obeying.

**Without any orderly means of restoring salvation.** Rigaltius says: That is, communion, outside which there is no salvation.

**All sins shall be forgiven the sons of men.** Rigaltius says: These are the words of Mark, chapter 3: πάντα ἀφεθήσεται τὰ ἁμαρτήματα τοῖς υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, “all sins shall be forgiven the sons of men.” The author of the Vulgate version rendered the meaning of these words ambiguous by transposing the verb “shall be forgiven,” a transposition which Cyprian has preserved here. But in book III *To Quirinus* he said with complete clarity that a person who sins against God cannot be forgiven in the Church. He then quotes from the Gospel according to Matthew: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.” And immediately [Col. 1051D] he adds from Mark: “All sins shall be forgiven the sons of men, and blasphemies,” etc.

From these passages it is perfectly clear that in this letter and in the book *To Quirinus* Cyprian’s meaning is that all sins committed against the sons of men—that is, against human beings—are forgiven, but not those committed against the Holy Spirit. Cyprian derives this from his teacher. For in the book *On Modesty*, Tertullian says: “You forgive, so that you may be forgiven by God. Offenses are cleansed which a person has committed against his brother, not against God. Finally, in prayer we profess that we will forgive our debtors.” Septimius undoubtedly understood this as “our debtors,” not God’s.

With Rigaltius’s kind permission, a meaning must be assigned to these words of Cyprian which can accord with his purpose. He cites this passage to show that pardon must not rashly be granted to the lapsed, yet in such a way that it is not denied to the penitent. I therefore think that our author held that to blaspheme the Holy [Col. 1052A] Spirit is precisely the same thing as to deny Christ. Indeed, in Luke 12 these words are immediately joined to the following: “Everyone who confesses me before men, the Son of Man will also confess before the angels of God; but whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.” Moreover, where the same saying of the Lord occurs in Matthew 12 and Mark 3, it is directed against those who blaspheme him. See what is noted in book III *To Quirinus*, chapter 28: “He shall not obtain forgiveness.” This is because he must be expelled from the Church and cannot be restored except through penance, which is the one plank left after shipwreck.

**Of an eternal sin.** Some Greek copies read ἁμαρτίας, “sin.” By “eternal sin” he means that supreme crime of idolatry which banishes a person from the Church.

**They will fall still further.** Rigaltius says: Those who have already fallen away from the faith pledged to Christ now fall away also from the discipline of Christ’s Church.

**In lesser sins.** Lesser, at least, in comparison with apostasy; for among other things he means adultery and [Col. 1052B] homicide. Cyprian makes the same comparison in the following letter.

**Their name is presented in the offering.** Rigaltius says: They are named during the sacrifices of prayer. Prayers or petitions for them are presented by name to God through the presbyters. Their name is offered together with the prayers offered for them. Pamelius observes that in manuscript copies the Canon is worded thus: “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants; names.” This should be understood to mean that after the words “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” the word “names” was written as an instruction, thereby reminding the presbyter who acts on behalf of the people that certain persons must be mentioned by name at this point.

**After *exomologesis* had been made.** We noted above, in the book *On the Lapsed*, that public confession is meant here. Thus in the letter to Antonianus: “It was resolved that those who had sacrificed should be assisted at the point of death, because there is no *exomologesis* in the underworld.” It is entirely clear that the words of the Psalmist are cited there: “In the underworld, [Col. 1052C] who will confess to you?” It is then expressly added: “And because there is no confession in the underworld, nor can *exomologesis* be made there.”

Thus in the book *On the Lapsed*: “How much greater in faith and better in fear are those who, though bound by no crime of sacrifice or of obtaining a certificate, nevertheless, because they even thought of doing so, sorrowfully and simply confess this very thing before God’s priests, make *exomologesis* of their conscience, and disclose the burden of their soul.” Immediately afterward he says of the three youths: “They made *exomologesis* to God in the midst of the fire.” Similarly, he says of Daniel: “Making *exomologesis* in sorrow, he said: ‘Lord, great God,’ etc. ‘We have sinned, we have committed wickedness,’” etc.

**They set the servants of God at odds with God’s priest.** Rigaltius says: That is, with the bishop. Thus Letter 52: “God’s priest appointed at Rome.” It should be noticed here that God’s servants are set against God’s priest. But God’s priest ought to remember that he too is God’s servant.

**Mindful of our place.** Rigaltius says: His episcopal place, and specifically that of the Church of Carthage, which was the first see of the province and therefore bore responsibility for many churches. [Col. 1052D] Thus, in the African Ecclesiastical Code, Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, says: “By God’s favor, as you know, brothers, I bear responsibility for all the churches.” In the same work Numidius, a bishop, says to Aurelius: “This see has always possessed the authority to ordain a bishop in accordance with the desire of each church.” Epigonius, likewise a bishop, says: “You are bound to support all the churches.” Accordingly Cyprian himself begins Letter 15 thus: “Responsibility arising from our office and fear of the Lord compel us.”

**Day after day among us the innocent age of children is also filled with the Holy Spirit and sees in ecstasy.** Rigaltius says: Men most highly praised for Christian devotion received divine forewarnings of various events not only from dreams, but also from inspired frenzy. We noted above examples of dreams which our Caecilius relates to the presbyters of his Church. In this letter he inculcates certain warnings or commands through the ecstatic utterances of innocent children. “Day after day,” he says, “among [Col. 1053A] us the innocent age of children is filled with the Holy Spirit; in ecstasy it sees with its eyes, hears, and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to warn and instruct us.”

He rightly says “in ecstasy.” For the power of the divine Spirit coming upon the children displaced whatever in them belonged to their own indwelling or native mind, so that each, no longer in possession of himself but filled with that mighty inhabitant, perceived, saw, and spoke of nothing except his guest.

How nearly Aristotle had investigated this grace of divine frenzy in his book *On Divination through Dreams*, where he admits that ecstatic persons sometimes foresee the future! He says:

> τοῦ δὲ ἐνίους τῶν ἐκστατικῶν προορᾶν αἴτιον ὅτι αἱ οἰκεῖαι κινήσεις οὐκ ἐνοχλοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ ἀπορραπίζονται· τῶν ξενικῶν οὖν μάλιστα αἰσθάνονται.

> “The reason why some ecstatic persons foresee the future is that their own movements do not trouble them but are beaten away; consequently they are especially conscious of movements foreign to them.”

But whence came those ξενικά, “foreign movements,” unless brought and introduced by that divine guest?

Philo speaks admirably in his treatise *Who Is the Heir of Divine Things*:

> ἐξοικίζεται μὲν γὰρ ἐν ἡμῖν ὁ νοῦς κατὰ τὴν τοῦ θείου πνεύματος ἄφιξιν· θέμις γὰρ οὐκ ἔστι θνητὸν ἀθανάτῳ συνοικῆσαι. Διὰ τοῦτο ἡ δύσις τοῦ λογισμοῦ καὶ τὸ περὶ αὐτὸν σκότος ἔκστασιν καὶ θεοφόρητον μανίαν ἐγέννησε.

> “For the mind dwelling within us leaves its home at the arrival of the divine Spirit, since it is not lawful for the mortal to dwell together with the immortal. Therefore the setting of reason, and the darkness surrounding it, produced ecstasy and a God-borne frenzy.”

The same author calls this frenzy [Col. 1053B] ἔνθεον κατοχωτικήν τε μανίαν, “a divinely inspired and possessing frenzy.” For this reason Tertullian, against Marcion, also maintains that ecstasy—that is, loss of reason—is compatible with grace. “For when a man is placed in the Spirit,” he says, “he must necessarily fall away from ordinary sense.” Thus, in ecstatic persons, wisdom dies for a little while. Human wisdom is so obscured and overshadowed by the advent of the divine that it seems meanwhile to have departed.

Chrysostom, speaking of the vision in which Peter beheld a great vessel let down from heaven, says:

> ἔκστασις, πνευματικὴ θεωρία γέγονεν αὐτῷ· τοῦ σώματος, ὡς ἂν εἴποι τις, ἐξέστη ἡ ψυχή.

> “An ecstasy, a spiritual vision, came upon him; the soul, so to speak, stood outside the body.”

## LETTER XVII

**Among the people who are standing.** See what was said on Letter 1.

**For whom divine mercy has power to provide a remedy.** The followers of Montanus and Novatian also held the opinion that persons convicted of the gravest crimes, although they might not obtain pardon from the Church, could nevertheless obtain it from God. The matter therefore did not turn on this point for them. Our author rightly applies this restraint to the lapsed who [Col. 1053C] were hastening toward peace: one must not conclude that the salvation of those who happened to die before completing the course of penance was lost.

## LETTER XVIII

**That summer had begun.** Letter 20 to Pamelius, no. 15, supplies another reason for relaxing the discipline: namely, not only the lapsed and many of the Carthaginian presbyters, but also the Roman Church had judged that indulgence should be employed. It would have been altogether harsh to incur, all at once, the ill will and anger not only of his own people but also of the neighboring Church, where his withdrawal was already being criticized.

**To make *exomologesis* also before a deacon.** Rigaltius says: For there is priesthood even in the diaconate. Thus Letter XX: “Nor did the vigor of the priesthood fail the presbyters and deacons.”

Rigaltius must be read cautiously here when [Col. 1053D] he says that there is priesthood in the diaconate. Whatever necessity compels, it also justifies—but only for as long as the necessity presses. The story in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 44, of the Eucharist being conveyed to Serapion by a boy is well known; yet no one would say that it is lawful for boys to distribute those sacred mysteries.

Moreover, Rigaltius departs far from the truth when he adduces in support of his statement the words found below: “Nor did the vigor of the priesthood fail the presbyters and deacons.” For Cyprian means there that his power over the offenders themselves, whether they were presbyters or deacons, had not failed, since he had admonished both groups.

Furthermore, the *exomologesis* is said to have been made before a deacon, not because he alone was privy to it—for the penance even of the sick was public in those centuries, insofar as this could be arranged—but because, in the absence of a presbyter, to whom that duty primarily belonged, the presence of a deacon was regarded as absolutely necessary, however many members of the laity might happen to be present. For since the Church [Col. 1054A] consisted of clergy and people, it was proper that, when satisfaction was made to the Church through *exomologesis*, persons should be present who represented both parts.

The form was prescribed by Bishop Cyprian: that is, he prescribed the condition under which the lapsed were to be received into the Church, as is abundantly clear from this and the following letter and from many others. Once the form or condition had been fulfilled, the deacon and the lay brothers summoned for this purpose were witnesses and arbiters in the Church’s name.

This was the principle of ancient ecclesiastical discipline: the superiors, assembling with the clergy and in the presence of the standing laity—to whom honor must also be paid on account of their faith and fear—were to arrange all matters with the conscientiousness of common deliberation. Thus, in the conferral of holy orders, κατάστασις, “appointment,” belonged to the bishops, while συνευδόκησις, “joint approval,” belonged to the people. See Letter LXVII and Clement’s *Letter to the Romans*, paragraph 44.

**The part of the people which has lapsed.** The lapsed who were commended by no recommendations from the martyrs, or who had not yet even been admitted to penance, were in the second class. Warned of their danger by the threat of approaching death, they begged to be admitted to peace. Although these persons were not to be [Col. 1054B] received on an equal footing, they were nevertheless to be commended to divine mercy, by whose protection their souls were to be sustained until fuller remedies could be provided. That this is the meaning of the words is plainly apparent from the following letter.

**Those who are hearers also.** The third order is that of the catechumens. Since they had not yet bound their faith to Christ, they appeared to have lapsed less seriously than the others and could therefore expect a readier pardon.

## LETTER XX

**An account of our conduct.** Rigaltius says: By “conduct” he means ministry, administration, and discipline. And toward the end of this letter: “Our conduct, which ought to be united and to agree in all matters.” Thus also Letter XXVI: “They desire their conduct to be approved even by their own brothers.”

[Col. 1054C] **As the Lord’s commands instruct us.** Namely Matthew 10:23, to which his example may also be added, since it is equivalent to a command: Luke 4:30 and elsewhere. Hence Origen, *On John* XVIII.12, says:

> διδάσκει ἡμᾶς ἐν διωγμοῖς καὶ ταῖς καθ’ ἡμῶν ἐπιβουλαῖς ἀναχωρεῖν.

> “He teaches us to withdraw amid persecutions and plots against us.”

Clement of Alexandria speaks to the same effect in *Stromata* IV. In explaining why the Lord commanded flight, he says:

> Βούλεται ἡμᾶς μηδενὶ αἰτίους μηδὲ συναιτίους κακοῦ τινος γίνεσθαι, σφίσιν τε αὐτοῖς, πρὸς δὲ καὶ τῷ διώκοντι καὶ τῷ ἀναιροῦντι. Τρόπον γάρ τινα προσαγγέλλει ἑαυτὸν περιστέλλεσθαι. Ὁ δὲ παρακούων, τολμηρὸς καὶ ῥιψοκίνδυνος. Εἰ δὲ ὁ ἀναιρῶν ἄνθρωπον θεοῦ εἰς θεὸν ἁμαρτάνει, καὶ τοῦ ἀποκτιννύντος αὐτὸν ἔνοχος καθίσταται ὁ ἑαυτὸν προσάγων τῷ δικαστηρίῳ. Οὗτος δ’ ἂν εἴη ὁ μὴ περιστελλόμενος τὸν διωγμόν, ἁλώσιμον διὰ θράσος παρέχων ἑαυτόν· οὗτός ἐστι, τὸ ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ, ὁ συνεργὸς γινόμενος τῇ τοῦ διώκοντος πονηρίᾳ.

> “He wishes us to become neither the causes nor the joint causes of any evil to anyone—to ourselves, and moreover to the persecutor and the executioner. For in a certain manner he gives advance notice that one should protect oneself. But the person who disobeys is rash and reckless. If the person who kills a man of God sins against God, then the one who presents himself before the tribunal also becomes implicated in the act of the person who kills him. Such is the person who does not protect himself from persecution, but through audacity makes himself easy to capture. So far as it lies with him, he becomes an accomplice in the persecutor’s wickedness.”

Similarly, the Church of Smyrna, describing the passion of Polycarp—which indeed occurred after his withdrawal—calls it τὸ κατ’ εὐαγγέλιον μαρτύριον, “martyrdom according to the Gospel.” It adds:

> περιέμενεν γὰρ ἵνα παραδοθῇ ὡς ὁ κύριος, ἵνα μιμηταὶ καὶ ἡμεῖς αὐτοῦ γενώμεθα, μὴ μόνον [Col. 1054D] σκοποῦντες τὸ καθ’ ἑαυτούς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ κατὰ τοὺς πέλας, etc.

> “For he waited to be delivered up, as the Lord did, so that we too might become his imitators, looking not only to what concerns ourselves but also to what concerns our neighbors,” etc.

The passages advanced on the other side with great pomp savor more of Montanus than of Christ.

**They had stained their hands and mouths with sacrilegious contacts.** Rigaltius says: Those were called *sacrificati*, “persons who had sacrificed,” who had stained their hands by placing incense upon the incense-box, or had stained their mouths by eating food offered to idols.

**Thousands of certificates were issued every day.** From this alone it may be seen how great was the number of the lapsed in the Decian persecution, especially since the martyrs commonly included whole families in a single certificate. “Let him communicate with his own.” See Letter 15 and elsewhere Letter 25: “We have granted peace to all.” And further: “Let not only these have peace, but also those whom you know to be dear to us.” Letter 22. Certainly thousands of certificates of this kind would seem sufficient for the whole fallen human race.

## LETTER XXI

[Col. 1055A]

**Celerinus to Lucianus.** This letter, sent by Celerinus while he was at Rome to Lucianus, a Carthaginian confessor, together with the letters that follow it, contributes greatly to explaining the controversy over the restoration of the lapsed. It also demonstrates the singular shamelessness of Lucianus, which caused Cyprian and his Church a very great deal of trouble. It was therefore useful for Cyprian to collect these letters and arrange for them to be appended to his own. See Letters XXXVII and XXXIX.

**Of this world.** This correction of the received reading, like those that follow, is so manifest that there is no need either to defend or elucidate it with commentary.

**In so blooming a confession.** Rigaltius says: That is, a purple confession, in which blood was shed for the name of Christ. Thus Tertullian, in the book *On the Crown*, called the soldier of Christ “clad in red with the hope of his own blood.” Shortly afterward our Caecilius will call the martyrs or confessors “blooming,” that is, clothed in purple by the shedding of blood.

Salmasius long ago proved that Greek writers used ἀνθηρά, “blooming,” of purple [Col. 1055B] possessing true brilliance—that is, a color of outstanding quality and in the most perfect bloom. Latin authors around Cyprian’s age likewise called verses “blooming” when they were distinguished by exquisite thoughts, and certain extracts from Apuleius are called *Florida*. A “blooming” color is opposed to an austere one. Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 6.

**Yet I ask, dearest brother, of the Lord.** As though he had said: If you undergo martyrdom before my letter reaches you, I ask the Lord to have mercy on my wretched sisters. But if my letter reaches you while you are alive, I beg you to give an answer, to ask God that I too may be worthy to be crowned, and to grant my desire on behalf of my sisters.

**And therefore I ask you to grant my desire.** That is, to grant a certificate to Numeria and Candida, who had lapsed. The most illustrious Baronius offers a quite plausible conjecture about the origin of these certificates under the year of Christ 253, paragraph 60.

The custom seems to have arisen from the practice by which bishops sent the lapsed to the confessors to obtain peace before they were reconciled to the Church. They were first to seek pardon from those against whom they had behaved with particular shamelessness [Col. 1055C] when, while those persons were courageously confessing, they themselves had cowardly denied the faith. Certainly, at the outset it seemed a severe punishment for persons disfigured by a shameful denial even to look upon the faces of those who shone and were adorned with the glory of confession.

By this method provision was made both for the dignity of the confessors and for the benefit of the lapsed. The latter were thus compelled to submit themselves as defeated persons to the victors and, through that humiliation of spirit, to merit pardon from the Church by means of the confessors’ prayers.

But what had formerly been introduced as a remedy began, through human wickedness, to be turned into an offense. The lapsed, scorning the bishop and the other priests, flocked to the martyrs of their own accord. After wresting from them certificates petitioning the bishop for communion, they demanded communion from the Church rather than requesting it, as though it had been pledged to them and were owed to them by virtue of the martyrs’ prayers.

Indeed, that the confessors enlarged their privileges from small beginnings to an immense extent is shown by their undertaking at Rome at almost this very time, when by their letters they were thrusting a pseudo-bishop upon the Church. Thus Pacianus says in Letter II [Col. 1055D] that Novatian was made bishop by a letter from persons who falsely presented themselves as confessors. And in Letter III: “By the authority of letters, when contrary to divine law the sole lawful priest was already seated at Rome, that man assumed for himself the title of another bishop.”

But in the present case something especially unexpected occurs. Celerinus, residing at Rome, asks Lucianus, a Carthaginian confessor, to grant peace to Numeria and Candida, who had lapsed at Rome and remained excluded from the Church there. This prerogative far surpasses the rights of bishops, whose authority is confined within the boundaries of their dioceses.

In truth, however, from the earliest centuries of the Christian faith, martyrs were assigned not to one particular Church but to them all. We see the acts of martyrs transmitted from one Church to others, and the martyrologies of individual Churches containing the names not only of their own members but also of persons who lived far away.

Moreover, Moses and Maximus and other confessors were nearby at Rome [Col. 1056A], and some of them—Moses at least—were crowned with martyrdom. Why, then, did Celerinus not request pardon for his lapsed sisters from them? Was it because Numeria and Candida were Africans and, although they had offended at Rome, were considered members of the Carthaginian Church and therefore were to be assisted by the recommendations of the martyrs of the Church of Carthage? Or was a milder persecution being conducted at Rome, so that capital punishments were not expected there? Moses certainly appears to have died from illness after the long filth and misery of imprisonment, while the others eventually escaped. Or, finally, because there was no bishop at Rome, and no hope that the lapsed women would be fully restored until a bishop was appointed, did they therefore look elsewhere and appeal to the good faith of the Carthaginian prelate? I do not wish to decide any of these questions; let the learned reader consider them.

**Until the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ.** Supply “is present,” or “is furnished.”

**The ministry of the blooming confessors.** Rigaltius says: We judge that this is how the passage should be read. He calls those confessors “blooming” who were already distinguished by a blooming confession. They had already been tortured on the rack or torn [Col. 1056B] by claws, had preserved their faith in Christ with the greatest steadfastness, and were accordingly awaiting the proconsul’s decision in prison. Meanwhile they nourished their constancy from the sacred Scriptures, lifted up their hope, strengthened their confidence, and in short discussed everything which the circumstances of the present time advised them either to anticipate or to reconsider.

Lucianus, accordingly, having been made the superintendent of those imprisoned with him and himself illustrious through a blooming confession, ministered to the brothers shut up with him in these offices of Christian devotion. He wrote out the wishes of the confessors to the brothers who perhaps preserved the structure of the Church nearby, or distributed the relief sent from the breasts of Lady Mother Church.

**Made a priest of God.** Perhaps this is meant in the same sense in which, in Revelation 5:10, the martyrs are called kings and priests to God. Or perhaps “the ministry of the blooming confessors” is meant specifically: he was made superintendent over the martyrs, that is, he administered matters on their behalf. But the passage is in fact corrupt, and no sound sense can readily be extracted from what follows. Perhaps it should be restored as “friend of God,” for martyrs are repeatedly honored with this designation.

[Col. 1056C] **Because she paid bribes on her own behalf so that she would not sacrifice.** Rigaltius says: She had redeemed herself with money from the necessity of sacrificing. Many who distrusted their own strength to endure tortures were accustomed to do this. They therefore made an agreement with an informer, a soldier, or some petty rogue of a governor.

Toward such persons our Caecilius was much more humane and kindly than Tertullian, who judged that persecution should neither be fled nor bought off. “It is the price that makes the difference,” he says; “otherwise, just as flight is a gratuitous redemption, so monetary redemption is a form of flight.”

Peter of Alexandria, canon XII, not only excuses but defends the monetary redemption of a person from persecution, citing the example of Jason in Acts 17, who was released after money had been paid, and that passage of Holy Scripture: “A man’s own riches are the price of his soul’s redemption.” Concerning those who gave money in this manner, he expressly says: Οὐκ ἔστιν ἔγκλημα προσάγειν, “No charge is to be brought against them.”

**Sixty-five.** All who were proscribed after making confession were regarded as exiles, even if they went to Rome. Nowhere were hiding places safer than in the city. [Col. 1056D] Those who secured their safety by flight before they were dragged before the tribunal were called fugitives. By this extraordinary expenditure and lavish generosity toward so great a number of confessors, those sisters sought to redeem the offense they had committed.

## LETTER XXII

**If I shall have been worthy to be called your colleague.** Rigaltius says: Celerinus had written to Lucianus: “So that your brother may also speak to you from the lowest place, if I, Celerinus, shall have been worthy to hear myself so called.” Lucianus therefore returns Celerinus’s own words to him in a beautiful contest of Christian humility. The letter itself will presently explain this; although no more elegant than the preceding letter, it is no less Christian.

**I received your letter, in which you burdened me so greatly.** Rigaltius says: The diction of this entire letter is very harsh and unpolished, but its beginning is especially intricate; its thought, however, is worthy of a good confessor of Christ.

Lucianus replies [Col. 1057A] to Celerinus’s letter and says that he was burdened with such shame as soon as he read Celerinus’s words, “If I shall have been worthy to be called your brother,” that, overwhelmed by shame thereafter, he almost lost the joy he had felt most intensely on reading after so long a time the letter for which he had longed.

“I exulted,” he says, “when I read the most honorable mention of myself; but because of so great a kindness arising from your humility, by which you think so humbly of yourself and so magnificently of me as to say, ‘If I shall have been worthy to be called your brother,’ I was so overcome with embarrassment that all my joy, thrown into confusion, almost collapsed. For what is my confession before a petty magistrate compared with yours, which confessed Christ’s name not merely before a soldier or some governor, but before Caesar himself? And this you did with noble utterances and plainly divine words, by which, I know, you conquered that greater serpent, the surveyor of Antichrist—as lovers of the faith and zealous guardians of Christ’s discipline know. I rejoice again and again that you continue in the living vigor of that steadfastness.”

**The surveyor of Antichrist.** Rigaltius says: According to Paul’s words to the Thessalonians, Antichrist will come at the end [Col. 1057B] of the Roman Empire. He cleverly says “serpent,” as though it were the line or cord of a surveyor, and alludes to the devil, whom Holy Scripture calls the serpent.

Rather, the “surveyor of Antichrist” is Antichrist’s forerunner, just as military surveyors went ahead of the army to designate suitable sites for camps. See what was said on Letter VI.

**By confessing you terrified him.** This is an incurable ulcer for which neither the Vatican nor the Bodleian Library—where alone we found copies of this and the preceding letter—provides a remedy. If conjecture is permitted, I would believe that the words “I know, as it were, lovers of the faith” [or possibly “I know them as lovers of the faith”] and “zealous guardians of Christ’s discipline” were words spoken by Celerinus before the emperor when he was questioned about the affairs of the Christians.

The sentence should accordingly be constructed thus: “For, by God’s will, you not only terrified the greater serpent himself, the surveyor of Antichrist, by your confession, but also conquered him by those utterances and deifying words: ‘I know them as lovers of the faith’ and ‘zealous guardians of Christ’s discipline’ [Col. 1057C]—in the living vigor of whose steadfastness I rejoice that you continue.” By his confession he terrified Decius, while by his defense he conquered him.

Or perhaps the text should be written: “By which I know what sort of encourager of the faith and zealous guardian of Christ’s discipline you are,” so that these are Lucianus’s own words. But perhaps others will offer readings sounder than these.

**After my summons.** Rigaltius says: After the Lord has called me. Christians are unwilling to speak of death, and martyrs least of all, since the crown lies ready for them.

**If anyone asks peace from you, grant it in my name.** Rigaltius says: Rather, it ought to have been granted in Christ’s name, if it was expedient to grant it—not in the name of that Paulus, although he was a blessed martyr. For that reason Cyprian deservedly censures Lucianus’s shamelessness in the letter immediately following, which is full of Christian gravity and prudence.

**Bassus in the stone quarry.** Rigaltius says: The manuscript should be examined to see whether there remain any traces of the reading *in petrario*, “in the stone quarry,” which would have been in the mines. The manuscripts having been consulted—since one reads *perario*, another *pegrario*, and the printed text *pejerario*, which makes no sense at all—there can be no doubt that the true reading is the one we have given.

[Col. 1057D] It is sufficiently well known that among Greek and Latin authors the term “quarries” denotes a prison or the mines. Plautus, in the *Captives*: “You will go straight to the stone quarries.”

**Paulus after the interrogation under torture.** Rigaltius says: Thus, in the synodical acts collected by Hilary of Poitiers, “Liberius after his exile.” But since Mappalicus is said to have died “during the interrogation under torture,” while Paulus died “after the interrogation,” it seems probable that the former died amid the torments and the latter after them.

**After the case had been set forth before the bishop.** Pamelius says: You see here that Lucianus, however indiscreet, nevertheless observed the practice which Cyprian so often censures the presbyters for neglecting: the cases had to be laid before the bishop and *exomologesis* had to precede the granting of peace, even when it was granted at the prayers of the martyrs.

Although the persecution was still being directed at least against those who had been committed to custody, circumstances nevertheless appeared to be tending toward peace, so that Christians would no longer be sought out. Thus Lucianus asks that peace now [Col. 1058A] be granted to the lapsed “when the Lord has begun to grant peace to the Church herself,” without awaiting, that is, its complete arrival and the return of the bishop and confessors. Otherwise there would have been no dispute between Cyprian and Lucianus, if the latter had merely maintained that the lapsed should be restored once peace had been returned to the Church.

## LETTER XXIII

**What they have done since committing the offense.** Those who, after being admitted to penance, have so conducted themselves in it as to give no offense to the bishop and the faithful are to be received immediately, even though they have by no means completed the period assigned to them. This is to be done not only at Carthage but everywhere throughout Africa.

We desire you to have peace with the holy martyrs. These words contain a threat: namely, that if Cyprian did not adequately comply, the martyrs would not remain in communion with him—as though it rested with them not merely to grant communion to anyone they wished, but even to take it away from the bishops themselves.

[Col. 1058B] In the presence of one of the clergy. In ancient times, communications among Christians were carried on only at the greatest risk. Their letters were therefore continually entrusted to the fidelity of clerics and were consequently also called *clerical letters*—so much so that Cyprian found it necessary to ordain a reader for the express purpose of carrying letters to Rome. See Epistle XXIX. Lucian, however, in order to lend some authority to his letters, employed witnesses who belonged to the clergy, but by no means distinguished ones: an unnamed exorcist and likewise an unnamed reader.

## EPISTLE XXIV

To Cyprian and his fellow presbyters. I punctuate the passage so that “residing at Carthage” refers to the presbyters, not to Cyprian. For it is evident from the opening words that this letter was written while the persecution was raging. From Epistles XLI and XLVIII we know that Caldonius was a bishop, although it is not sufficiently established of what city. When he wished to consult [Col. 1058C] the Church of Carthage concerning a doubtful matter and what ought to be done about it, he deemed it proper to address his letter not only to Cyprian, who was in hiding, but also to his presbyters who were at Carthage—especially since the letter could scarcely have been delivered except with their help. Near the end of this persecution, this same Caldonius received delegated authority from Cyprian to administer in his name and stead the business of restoring the lapsed. Consequently, at least by then, he had been adequately instructed concerning what ought to be done in that entire matter. Saint Peter, in 1 Peter 5, calls himself a *fellow presbyter* (συμπρεσβύτερον).

Felix, who was supplying the service of a presbyter. Pamelius says that “to supply the service of a presbyter” appears to mean nothing other than what we now call acting as a presbyter’s vicar. Such persons among us seem to be the curates of parish priests. Rigaltius says: “One who assisted presbyters by frequent service.” Thus, in the letter of Celerinus which immediately follows, Numeria and Candida are said to have ministered to sixty-five confessors [Col. 1058D] and sustained them in every respect. Perhaps “to supply the presbyterate” means the same as to minister or discharge that office, so that this Felix was the presbyter of Decimus, Caldonius’s predecessor in the episcopate. Meanwhile, it must be acknowledged that in Cyprian’s century *presbyterium* denoted an ecclesiastical council. Thus, in Cornelius’s letter concerning the confessors who returned to unity, it is said: “It was resolved that the presbyteral council should be convened.” It may therefore be that the scribe or notary of this confessor is said to “supply the presbyteral council.” If conjectural emendation of the writings of the ancients were permissible, however, I would conclude that the genuine reading was: “Felix, who supplied a presbyter to Decimus”—that is, the man who, when the martyr Decimus was at the point of death, arranged for a presbyter to attend him.

## EPISTLE XXV

They ought not, as though prostrate. The very dress and bearing of penitents professed their fall; for this reason they were called ὑποπίπτοντες, “those who lie beneath,” namely, those lying subject and prostrate. Cyprian, however, says that they not only knelt before the brethren but lay prostrate beneath the devil.

I sent you the book. Rigaltius says: “The book *On the Lapsed*.” But that book does not yet appear to have been written. It is probable that by the word “book” Cyprian meant the bundle of letters that he sent.

That there may be one course of action among all. Rigaltius says: “In a matter of faith, that is.” For in the administration of the Church, Cyprian says that every superior has freedom to exercise his own judgment, in the letter to Stephen, Bishop of Rome. The Roman presbyters themselves write to Cyprian in Epistle XXXI: “Let them know that in conscience they owe an account to God alone as judge.” See the concluding clauses of the letters to Stephen and Jubaianus. Indeed, every effort must be made, so far as possible, that there be one disciplinary practice in the administration of the Church. For the ancient Church understood what great disturbances had been caused by differing customs in the celebration of Easter, which set East against West. And here, certainly, the dispute concerned no article of faith but discipline—namely, the administration of penance.

## EPISTLE XXVI

[Col. 1059B]

What they have done after their offense. Rigaltius says: “What penance they have performed for their deed.” Above: “Lest they have committed anything of which the Church might be ashamed.” “You are to examine the conduct, works, and merits of each.” We have an example of such an inquiry in Celerinus’s letter to Lucian concerning Numeria and Candida. Intending to entreat from the eminent and most courageous confessor Lucian letters or certificates for obtaining peace on their behalf, Celerinus recounts what they had done after their offense: “They themselves,” he says, “went down to the harbor to meet the confessors who came here after their ill-treatment, brought them up into the city, ministered to sixty-five, and have sustained them in all respects down to the present day. For they are all in their care.” Another example is furnished by Caldonius’s letter entreating Cyprian on behalf of certain lapsed persons who, after sacrificing, were tested a second time and became exiles. “They appear to me,” says Caldonius, [Col. 1059C] “to have washed away their former offense by abandoning their possessions and homes and, doing penance, following Christ. They left behind the possessions which the imperial treasury now holds.” Cyprian therefore answers Caldonius that he had judged rightly concerning the granting of peace to the brethren, who had restored it to themselves through true repentance and the glory of confessing the Lord, being justified by the words with which they had formerly condemned themselves.

## EPISTLE XXVII

When the martyr Mappalicus. And yet Lucian did not hesitate to say that Mappalicus had ordered the indiscriminate peace that Lucian was granting everywhere to be given. But he betrayed his shamelessness still more when, after being admonished by Cyprian, he proceeded from bad to worse and threatened the bishop himself with excommunication.

While he was still confined in prison. When as yet he enjoyed no privilege under the Church’s ordinances, since he had not yet been crowned. Moreover, for a martyr after death to bequeath to an heir, as though by a last will and testament, the right to grant peace [Col. 1059D] was unprecedented.

Our sect. Pamelius says: Tertullian frequently uses the word *sect* in a favorable sense for the Christian confession, as may be seen in his books *On Flight in Persecution*, *On the Pallium*, and the *Apology against the Gentiles*. Cyprian imitates him in his customary manner, both here and in Epistle XXXIII concerning Celerinus and in the preface to Book I of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*. Bede, in his retraction concerning Acts, is likewise witness that in Acts 26 the Apostle uses αἵρεσιν, “sect,” in a favorable sense. Our translator therefore did not render it badly as “sect.”

Into the grace. He appears intentionally to have omitted the word χριστοῦ, “of Christ,” concerning which the Greek manuscripts vary: some have θεοῦ, “of God,” and others Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, “of Jesus Christ.” For Cyprian reads this passage in the same way in his letter to Caecilius concerning the sacrament of the cup. Tertullian also reads it thus in *Against Heresies*, chapter 27.

To turn the Gospel of Christ. μεταστρέψαι: “to pervert.”

## EPISTLE XXVIII

[Col. 1060A]

You have imbued the spiritual contest with your virtues. Rigaltius says: “You have begun.” It is a phrase of Tertullian’s in *On Fasting*: “where now even a people belonging to God began to be chosen, and the restoration of humanity could be begun.” And in *On Modesty*, where he speaks of Peter: “He himself initiated the key,” that is, began to use the key—namely, by the Gospel of the Lord’s word.

Crowns woven by your hand. Rigaltius says: “The Corbie manuscript reads: ‘Your crown your hands.’ This is certainly corrupt, but from it the reading ‘crowns sewn by your hand’ may be elicited. Nevertheless, ‘woven’ does not displease me. For one who inserts and binds flowers into a ribbon for use as a crown—a στεφανοπλόκος, ‘wreath-weaver’—may be said to ‘weave a crown.’”

Title. A constant expression in Tertullian: “title of ambition,” “of idolatry,” “of lusts,” “of office,” “of injuries,” and very many similar instances. Indeed, he quite frequently has “to entitle” and “entitled.”

## EPISTLE XXIX

[Col. 1060B] Since it was necessary for me to write by means of clerics. Rigaltius says: “Christian affairs were conducted with such reverence that a bishop did not write to the clergy except through clerics.” It should be observed, however, that from the very period when the Christian people judged matters of the Church together with the clerics, the laity were so clearly distinguished from the clergy that bishops’ letters were carried only by clerics. This was perhaps prudent, so that, if it seemed safer, they might also deliver instructions orally. We observed above that Rigaltius rather unfairly ridicules the distinction between the lay people and the clergy. See what was said there.

Those nearest to the clergy. Rigaltius says: “There was therefore a certain dignity of being ‘next to the clergy,’ and perhaps a grade preparatory to such proximity. Cyprian admitted men even to this lowest dignity by common counsel. Those ‘nearest to the clergy’ were instituted after the example of those who served near the emperor in the imperial record offices. There is also in Book XII of the Code a title, *On Those Nearest to the Imperial Record Offices*. Publicly reading in church at the bishop’s command was a formal designation to the office of reader. He therefore immediately adds: ‘Nothing was done by me in your absence.’” [Col. 1060C]

Or recently with the presbyters. Certain members of the clergy appear to have visited Cyprian in his retreat and, by common counsel, to have settled matters of the greatest importance to the condition of the Church. He says that Saturus had long ago been designated for the office of reader. Optatus, however—a reader now devoted to instructing catechumens and distinguished by the glory of his confession—had already been declared a subdeacon. Saint Paul appears to have distinguished in ancient times between presbyters who governed and those who taught, in 1 Timothy 5:17.

Among the readers, a teacher of the hearers. Rigaltius says: “Thus, at that time, learning and teaching existed even among the readers.” And rightly so, since they were appointed to instruct catechumens.

## EPISTLE XXX

By the profession contained in their impious certificates. Rigaltius says: This epistle identifies two classes of *libellatici*, those who obtained certificates. One consisted of those who had entered their names upon certificates professing the worship of Jupiter, Mars, and other gods of that kind. The other consisted of those who had not personally offered certificates bearing their own profession to the pagan authorities, but had received and signed certificates submitted by others, perhaps even by the authorities themselves. There was, however, a third class of *libellatici*: namely, those who, by giving or receiving a certificate, professed that they were Christians and that for this reason it was not lawful for them to ascend the Capitol or sacrifice, but that they were giving a payment precisely so that they would not do what was unlawful. This class of *libellatici* will be discussed at Cyprian’s epistle to Antonianus. See what we said in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 95.

Which they themselves had attested. Rigaltius says: “Namely, that they had approached the impious altars.” From this it is evident that this class of *libellatici* differed from those discussed in the epistle to Antonianus.

But also against those who had ratified what they received. Rigaltius [Col. 1061A] says: “That is, those who had accepted certificates submitted on their behalf; for in this way they had accepted and ratified whatever those certificates contained. What they contained was that the person in question had on that day ascended the Capitol and offered incense to Jupiter. Although he had not done it, he nevertheless caused it to be publicly read that he had done it—namely, through the reading of a certificate by which he wished to appear to have satisfied the edicts issued against the Gospel. This was to abandon the faith pledged to Christ.”

The whole sacrament of faith. Rigaltius says: “The whole Christian faith.” Thus Facundus of Hermiane, in Book IX addressed to the emperor Justinian, says that “the sacrament of Christian adoption” can mean Christian adoption. Cyprian himself likewise says in Epistle LI: “those who had previously been united by the sacrament of unanimity,” that is, joined in unanimity. No word occurs more frequently among the ancients, nor is there any in whose use they allow themselves greater liberty. It will be discussed again shortly, toward the end of this epistle.

He seeks deceptive tricks in his excuse. Rigaltius says: “Psalm 140 condemns these tricks.”

Penance cut short. Rigaltius says: “He calls that penance ‘cut short’ whose appointed duration a presbyter curtailed through ill-timed compassion and did not permit to continue as long as it should have. Even for diseases of the body to be cured, penance is necessary. An undisciplined patient makes his physician cruel.” [Col. 1061B]

Of the confessors whom the dignity of their confession still confines here in prison. Rigaltius says: It will be useful here to make a single observation about the term *confessors*. Just as legal authorities, in questions concerning servitudes, call an action “confessory” when someone claims a servitude for himself, and “negatory” when someone denies the servitude claimed by another, so in questions of faith the Christian Fathers call those “confessors” who, when questioned about their faith or religion, courageously assert the name of Christ and affirm that they are Christians; but they call those “deniers” who faithlessly abandon Christ and conceal or deny that they are Christians. Meanwhile, one appears to be playing with words if he derives the term “confessor” from any source other than the words of our Lord in Matthew 10.

The dignity of confession. Rigaltius says: “Of a flourishing confession,” that is, a steadfast, vigorous, and nobly exemplary one—or, as follows shortly afterward, a glorious one: “which divine favor has raised to so great a summit of glory.” A little later this epistle calls this “favor” the “divine indulgence.” [Col. 1061C]

He preserves it in him from whom he possesses it. Cyprian had said above to the confessors that they were martyrs by virtue of the Gospel.

Let them perform the office of advocates. Rigaltius says: “Let groans and bitter weeping take the place of advocates in meriting or obtaining pardon and mercy.”

Except that it again entails greater danger and shame. Rigaltius says: “Tertullian, toward the end of the book *On Penance*.”

Not to have sought the assistance of peace. Rigaltius says: “That is, of pardon or indulgence.”

But all this lies in the sacrament. Rigaltius says: For these are the signs, mysteries, and sacraments of a grieving and truly penitent soul: a modest request, a reverent petition, necessary humility, active patience, and keeping watch at the gates of the heavenly camp—that is, at the threshold of the Church. Tertullian splendidly describes all the sacraments of ἐξομολόγησις, “public confession,” [Col. 1061D] in his book *On Penance*: “Thus *exomologesis* is a discipline for prostrating and humbling a person, prescribing a manner of life calculated to attract mercy. Regarding dress and food, it commands him to lie in sackcloth and ashes, to defile the body with filth, to cast down the mind with grief, and by sorrowful treatment to alter those things wherein he sinned. Furthermore, it commands him to know only plain food and drink; to nourish prayers by fasts; to groan, weep, and cry aloud to the Lord day and night; to throw himself at the feet of the presbyters, kneel before God’s beloved, and enjoin upon all the brethren embassies of supplication on his behalf.” He will interpret it more correctly who understands by *sacrament* simply the Christian law, which above is called the “sacrament of faith.” Tertullian also uses this phrase in *On the Soul* and frequently elsewhere. The same Tertullian calls the Mosaic law “the Jewish sacrament” in *Apology*, chapter 19, contrasting it with ours, that is, the Christian sacrament.

Penance performed. Although the Church took care that no one should die without peace, it nevertheless required that at least some penance [Col. 1062A] had been performed and that the person had repeatedly professed his abhorrence of his own deeds. Tears, moreover, and groans and weeping had to manifest the signs of a grieving and truly penitent soul. Only then was the sick person to be left to divine mercy, since God himself knows what to do with such people and how to weigh the balances of his judgment. In those centuries the priest had not yet been constituted a judge.

Most blessed and most glorious Pope. Rigaltius says: “Thus the Roman clergy address Cyprian, bishop of Carthage.”

## EPISTLE XXXI

And the other confessors. Rigaltius says: Eusebius appears to mention these men in Book VI, chapter 43 of his *History*, drawing on a letter of Cornelius to Fabius. He says that Novatus, at the very beginning, drew to himself certain excellent men from among the confessors, including Maximus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, and Urbanus, who had both become confessors for the second time; and also Sidonius and Celerinus, who were held in great renown [Col. 1062B] among the confessors because they had overcome every kind of torture. This title of Christian honor, “confessor,” should be noted.

Those among them not sufficiently fed for the contest with the enemy. Neither gladiators entering the arena nor soldiers going into battle customarily did so without having eaten.

To possess the heavenly kingdom without any hesitation. The ancients continually insist upon this privilege of the martyrs.

Their fathers. Pamelius says: “This sentence is compiled from the Gospels of Matthew and Luke. For the words, ‘for so their fathers treated the prophets,’ belong to Luke; while Matthew has: ‘for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.’”

For him who loved us. See what was said on Book III *To Quirinus*, chapter 18.

To the presbyters, deacons, confessors, and the steadfast laity themselves. Rigaltius says: In Cyprian’s age there were subdeacons and readers. Are they omitted here because they are understood under the name of deacons? And why does he append the confessors to the deacons as though they constituted an order, when confessors could also be found among the presbyters and deacons? Or was it enough that such confessors should be conspicuous among the presbyters and deacons, while the others were distinguished from the laity merely to signify their virtue? Thus, finally, “the steadfast laity” would denote that part of the Church consisting numerically of the faithful from whom confessors, subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters were made. [Col. 1062C]

And again. Perhaps the alternative reading, “not only once, but again,” is more approved. Yet because a large part of idolatrous worship consisted in funeral rites and mourning, I judged that nothing should be changed. The sense would then be: whereas they formerly accompanied idols with lamentations, now at last they should mourn their sins.

A necessity sought of their own accord. Rigaltius says: “A sought-out necessity is not necessity, but a sought-out appearance and pretext of necessity—a fabricated and feigned necessity.”

## EPISTLE XXXII

[Col. 1062D] Concerning bishops from abroad. Rigaltius says: Cyprian shows honor even to bishops from abroad and calls them his colleagues; and in canon 19 of Arles they are granted a place to sacrifice: “It is resolved that they be given a place so that they may offer.” Noteworthy is the admonition of Avitus of Vienne concerning a certain Bishop Maximianus, addressed to Caesarius of Arles in Epistle IX: “However great the length of time or the vastness of the journey by which he leaves the dwelling of his native land, a priest cannot be called a foreigner wherever the Catholic Church may be found.” In this sense it can also be said that “a foreign bishop” is by no means a reproachful designation for one whom a church receives from somewhere other than its own presbyterate or native land. The “communion of strangers” of which the canons speak was so far from honorable that it served as a punishment. But here the words “concerning bishops from abroad” appear to denote only those who were staying outside their own dioceses—namely, those who had come to Carthage for some business, perhaps ecclesiastical.

## EPISTLE XXXIII

[Col. 1063A]

That they should draw up letters in the Church’s name. The matter itself shows that these formerly missing words must certainly be inserted into the text.

They acted grandly. Rigaltius says: “Magnificently, in a manner worthy of the majesty and discipline of the Christian faith.” Thus Martial, in secular matters, had spoken of “a grand work” and “grand words.” The ancient glosses give μεγαλοεργῶς, “magnificently,” and μεγαλοεργία, “magnificence.” Tertullian has “grand service”; Juvenal, “grand song,” meaning tragic song; and Tertullian, “grander fables.” Cicero speaks of “grandeur of words” in *On Famous Orators*, where he discusses the grandiloquence of Demosthenes. Cyprian himself says below in Epistle XXXIII: “He spoke sublime words, words which bore witness to the Christian faith.”

They credited them to the Lord. Whatever they themselves had done well, they attributed to divine grace. Or, if the reading of the Bodleian manuscript is to be admitted, they did not set their former good deeds against their fall, as though God owed them pardon because of their merits.

[Col. 1063B] Who deigned to reveal. Rigaltius says: “In dreams; through a vision; in a vision.” See above, Epistle VII.

Since I received those letters only recently. Pamelius says: “Both these letters of the lapsed and those to which he replies are missing. If they survived, the form of the martyrs’ certificates would now be known to us.” Indeed, it is known from Epistle XXIII.

## EPISTLE XXXIV

To Gaius of Didda. Pamelius says: If conjecture is permissible in an uncertain matter, it seems probable to me that Didda was some village in the diocese of Carthage and that this Gaius was the presbyter of that place—that is, the man whom we now call its pastor or curate—because Cyprian mentions his deacon. Moreover, one may infer that the place was extremely obscure, since it is mentioned nowhere else.

By offering their offerings. Rigaltius says: By communing with the lapsed at an untimely and premature stage, the presbyters and deacons would have presented their offerings—that is, their prayers [Col. 1063C] and alms, their penance not yet duly authenticated, and their still-unripe works, which were therefore by no means pleasing to the divine majesty. For penitents enjoined upon the presbyters, deacons, and all the brethren embassies of supplication on their behalf, as Tertullian says in *On Penance*. See what was said in the notes to Epistle V, and concerning offerings for the dead in the notes to Epistle II. It may further be observed that in Epistle XVI, where the manuscripts commonly read, “Their name is offered,” Latinus Latinius, appealing to the authority of a certain Vatican manuscript, recommends the reading, “It is offered in their name,” which indeed appears more appropriate.

They interpose with tears. They place an obstacle before them; they hinder them. In the same way the tribunes “interposed,” that is, by virtue of their magisterial authority, they prevented the action.

While many still. This question concerns not only Philumenus, Fortunatus, and Favorinus, but many others who perhaps deserved a more severe punishment, [Col. 1063D] since they did not think that they should reclaim their position even belatedly.

Meanwhile, let them merely abstain from the monthly distribution. Rigaltius says: Pamelius printed the passage thus, although printed books had formerly read “from the distribution of those measuring,” some manuscripts “from the dominion,” and others “from the approach.” In some manuscripts, however, a third reading has been formed from both, and this I believe to be the true one: “Meanwhile, let them abstain from calling themselves monthly recipients.” That is, let them not call themselves recipients of the monthly allowance; let them not be counted among such recipients; let them receive nothing from the monthly distributions mentioned in Epistle XXXIX. Certainly the conjecture of Pamelius is all the less tolerable because it most openly contradicts the author’s intention. For Cyprian takes particular care that nothing be decided in his absence in the case of Philumenus, Fortunatus, and Favorinus, but that everything be kept unchanged and deferred until his return. Pamelius’s reading, by contrast, means that meanwhile they should merely abstain from the monthly distribution. Cyprian excludes them from the Church in such a way [Col. 1064A] that he does not even wish them to be called recipients of the monthly allowance. Traces of this designation, like those of *sportulantes*, “stipend-recipients,” are rare in books today. Rigaltius’s conjecture is contradicted not only by Epistle XXXIX but also by the first and best Bodleian manuscript, which expressly reads, “from the monthly distribution.” Nor does Latinius’s conjecture have any place; he recommends reading “from association with the monthly recipients,” that is, from intercourse with the other presbyters. In Tertullian’s age everyone contributed a modest payment on a monthly day. Tertullian calls the money thus collected “a fund of piety” in *Apology*, chapter 39. These fugitives appear to have been subjected to the ecclesiastical censure called suspension from benefice. But it seemed necessary to handle this case more cautiously because Cyprian himself, on account of his withdrawal, was burdened by similar ill will.

## EPISTLE XXXV

With deliberate rashness. “Deliberate.” Tertullian says in *Apology*, chapter 6: “Even regarding your very gods, you, their most obedient descendants, have rescinded the measures which your fathers had deliberately decreed.” [Col. 1064B]

The Lord commanded that action be taken. Namely, what is said in Matthew 18:17: “If he does not hear the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.”

To the privilege of indulgence. Pamelius says: “Here, Christian reader, you see the word *indulgence* used twice in precisely the same sense in which we now use it. You find it repeated twice above in Epistle XX and also in the following epistle.”

## EPISTLE XXXVI

They refer them to the bishop. Rigaltius says: “The blessed martyr judged that the sinew of discipline was broken in this respect: certificates were solicited from the martyrs, although they could not grant peace but were accustomed to send each person to his own bishops.”

You, nevertheless, brother. Rigaltius says: “They call the bishop of Carthage ‘brother,’ though at the beginning of the epistle they called him ‘Pope.’” [Col. 1064C]

We know the faith of the Church of Carthage. Rigaltius says: “The Romans themselves praise the faith of the Church of Carthage.”

Cast against you by means of a letter. Spoken insultingly against you.

As for Privatus of Lambaesis. Rigaltius says: “In Epistle LV he will say that this heretic was condemned in the colony of Lambaesis by the judgment of ninety bishops for many grave offenses.” See the seventy-fifth vote of the Council of Carthage.

A matter causing us concern. That about which we are especially anxious—namely, the unity of the Church. Hence, when heretics were deprived of communion by decrees of councils, the neighboring churches were immediately informed.

On behalf of the body of the whole Church, whose members are distributed throughout all the various provinces. Rigaltius says: “This pertains to Cyprian’s concern for all the churches and to that single episcopate, a share of which, he says in the book *On the Unity of the Church*, is held wholly and jointly by each bishop.” [Col. 1064D]

## EPISTLE XXXVII

Exhortations of divine favor. In place of this Rigaltius substituted “ornaments”; but since Cyprian says that in the words of Celerinus he heard the martyrs, it is more relevant for him to add that he perceived exhortations together with those words than ornaments.

We make our prayer together with many others. Rigaltius says: “Sacrifices of prayer were offered by the presbyter who acted on behalf of the people, that is, who presented the people’s prayers to God. It is as though he had said: ‘Through the Church’s public prayer and our private prayer.’”

Already breathing only heavenly things. Rigaltius says: “In the book *On Mortality*: ‘Stationed in the heavenly camp, he already breathes divine things.’”

[Col. 1065A] As often as you are urged to withdraw from prison. Rigaltius says: The formula of exhortation was, “Save your life. Take thought for yourself.” With these words non-Christian friends and relatives customarily advised and urged their friends or relatives not to perish without cause. So spoke those ignorant of Christian truth and heavenly things. For discipline indeed forbade anyone to offer himself voluntarily; such conduct belongs to the headlong and the *parabolanus*, the reckless risk-taker. But the same discipline provided that no one should so love his life that he was unwilling to lay it down for Christ’s name. The proconsul himself urged Cyprian, whom the emperors’ edicts had now ordered to be brought before him: “The emperors have commanded you to perform the rites.” Cyprian answered, “I will not.” The proconsul added: “Take thought for yourself.” Augustine, *On the Passion of Saint Cyprian the Martyr*.

The winter season has crossed over. I would consider the reading commended by most manuscripts, “winter has crossed over,” to be more genuine. Thus Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book I: “The whole year is winter.” We have discussed that word above.

The dreadful lodging of the prison. Priorius says: “In chapter 2 of *To the Martyrs*, Tertullian thunders in the same style as he exhorts the martyrs to overcome even the perils of prison—filth and destitution. There he calls the prison a *custodiarium*, a place of confinement.” [Col. 1065B]

To the embrace and kiss of the Lord. Rigaltius says: For the propagation of the Christian name amid so many and such savage storms of persecution—which not infrequently overthrew both the people and even those appointed to govern them—the bishop had to labor in every way to maintain a people and clergy most firmly devoted to faith in Christ. Since this could be accomplished by no better means than by setting before Christ’s confessors a happiness immediately present to them, martyrdom was granted the prerogative of abolishing every delay in obtaining it, lest the postponement of the hope of attaining it until the time of judgment or resurrection should make the soldiers less vigorous. Thus the martyrs were sent immediately from the contest to the crown—that is, to the embrace and kiss of the Lord. Meanwhile, even before the consummation of martyrdom, the best confessors were granted the privilege of obtaining peace for the lapsed, who under the Church’s discipline could otherwise have hoped for it only through the most grievous austerities of a long period. In this epistle, therefore, Cyprian sets before the confessors the joys of eternal happiness as immediately ready, in order that by their example he might raise and kindle the others to steadfastness in martyrdom. The kiss of the Lord was discussed above. Rigaltius explains this matter as though the immediate happiness of Christ’s confessors had been proposed through the counsel and contrivance of the bishops. They derived this belief from Holy Scripture: Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; Revelation 14:14; and frequently elsewhere. [Col. 1065C]

That voice illustrious through the purification of confession. Rigaltius says: “‘I am a Christian.’ Tertullian in the *Apology*, addressing the tyrannical governor: ‘The man cries aloud, “I am a Christian.” He says what he is, while you wish to hear what he is not.’ Cyprian calls it the ‘purification of confession’ because through the baptism of martyrdom, or the washing of blood shed for Christ, all offenses are cleansed. He calls the voice ‘illustrious’ just as Celerinus, in his epistle to Lucian, calls the confession ‘flourishing’—that is, purple, bloody.”

Founded with a strong mass upon the rock. Rigaltius says: “Thus in Epistle IV: ‘grave men founded once for all upon the rock with solid stability.’” [Col. 1065D]

## EPISTLE XXXVIII

In clerical ordinations. Rigaltius says: “To ordain” means to appoint as superiors, in Lampridius: “Whenever Alexander Severus wished to appoint governors to provinces, or procurators or financial administrators, he published their names and said that it was a serious matter that, although Christians did this in publicly announcing priests who were to be ordained, it was not done in the appointment of provincial governors.”

To weigh by common counsel. Rigaltius says: “Above: ‘What had long ago been begun by the common counsel of us all has, under pressure of necessity, been advanced.’”

Sublime words. Rigaltius says: “Just as Persius spoke of the ‘grand words of Cato about to die.’ Sublime words, which confessed Christ sublimely—such as those of the Roman martyr in Prudentius.”

To come to the pulpit after the torture-platform. Rigaltius says: [Col. 1066A] The Roman martyr declares: “Hear, all of you; I cry far and wide, I proclaim, I send forth my voice higher from the *catasta*.” Casaubon says that *catasta*, usually a wooden platform, is a Roman word, but of Greek—or rather Sicilian—origin, in connection with that passage of Persius: “lest another be more outstanding, fat Cappadocians applauded on the rigid *catasta*.” Martial called them “stages.” Martyrs placed upon iron *catastae* were there exposed to the gaze of the pagan multitude. It was therefore most glorious for Aurelius to come from that *catasta*, where he had most courageously confessed Christ, to a similar structure in the Church, so that he might proclaim the divine readings in the sight of the brethren. Readers in church recited the sacred readings from a pulpit or ambo. Hence also those expressions in ecclesiastical writers: καθίσταται ἐν ἄμβωνι, “he is stationed in the ambo,” and ἐν δεικτηρίῳ, “in the place of display.” The following epistle will say that the glorious faces—that is, those of the confessors who still belonged to the order of readers—were to be placed in a higher location.

And because joy always hastens. Rigaltius says: “What follows from this point is extremely corrupt in Pamelius’s edition. We emended it from the Verona and Corbie manuscripts: ‘And because joy always hastens, nor can gladness endure delay, meanwhile he reads to us on the Lord’s Day’; that is, ‘he inaugurated peace by dedicating his reading.’” This, then, is Cyprian’s meaning: Our Aurelius, ordained by us as reader, should have inaugurated that office in the presence of the Church. But since he arrived here after returning so gloriously from martyrdom, he certainly had to be received by us with the greatest gladness. “And because joy always hastens, nor can gladness endure delay,” meanwhile, until by God’s favor he presents himself to you in peace, he will read here among us on the Lord’s Days. That is, he will perform among us what he would have performed before the Church if it enjoyed peace—namely, once the fury of the persecutions had subsided. He inaugurated the Church’s most longed-for peace among us when he dedicated among us his new office of reading for the Church. [Col. 1066B]

May he quickly restore to his people their priest unharmed. Rigaltius says: “Me, namely, Cyprian, your bishop and priest.” He modestly calls himself only “priest.” In Cyprian’s usage, however, “priest” means a bishop.

## EPISTLE XXXIX

[Col. 1066C] By granting a furlough to the good confessors. Rigaltius says: “A furlough for remaining yet a little while in this world, as above: ‘having received, after glory, a furlough to flourish in the praise of the Church.’” “Withdrawn by the Lord from the midst of death for this purpose,” as below in this epistle.

We refer it to you. In the sense in which a matter is said to be referred to the senate—namely, so that what has been done may be ratified by your vote, at least with respect to the more effective exercise of his office.

Since he hesitated to consent. Rigaltius says: Cyprian, in exile, writes to the presbyters, deacons, and people of his Church that he, together with his colleagues who perhaps were then present, had ordained as reader Celerinus, a man distinguished by many virtues. When Celerinus, because of his modesty and humility, declined the offered office and hesitated, the Church appeared in a dream and compelled him not to delay any longer in obeying Cyprian’s counsel. Cyprian therefore says that he himself, by his own persuasion, adopted Celerinus into the clergy, but that the Church, whose authority was greater, compelled and constrained him. Here again Cyprian’s dexterity in making such gentle use of the efficacy of visions should be noted. [Col. 1066D]

Their feet bound in the stocks. Priorius says: I remember that I once noted that the *nervus* was an instrument of torturers by which Christians’ feet and legs were bound. It was made of wood and divided by many holes, so that the limbs might more easily be tortured—with such force, indeed, that they were often dislocated. Plutarch, *On the Daimonion of Socrates*: τοὺς πόδας ἐν τῷ ξύλῳ δεδεμένοι, “their feet bound in the wooden stocks.”

Sacrifices for them always. Rigaltius says: The Greeks celebrated public festivals (*panegyrica*) in honor of brave men who had overthrown a tyrant or had otherwise fought successfully for their country, so that by their example they might inspire their people to illustrious deeds. At sacred anniversaries Christians offer praises to God, commemorating by name those who bravely suffered martyrdom for faith in Christ. See the notes on Epistle II. Perhaps the passages in Tertullian’s *On the Soldier’s Crown* pertain to this.

[Col. 1067A] The sufferings of the martyrs. Priorius says: Tertullian calls them “birthdays” (*natalia*), meaning, of course, the day on which they were born into heaven.

Of the very man who had persecuted him. Understand Decius. Above he says: “When he had entered into conflict with the very chief and author of the persecution.”

Whose following and conduct. Rigaltius says: From a predecessor or preceptor come a follower and a following; from a teacher, a disciple and discipline; from a master, a servant and service.

As though a kind of resurrection had taken place in their case. Rigaltius says: Those who rise again appear to return to life—whether they awaken from sleep or recover from illness, especially a severe one.

Monthly distributions. Rigaltius says: That is, from the common fund contributed by the whole Church of Carthage for disbursement. Apart from this common fund, there was another from Cyprian’s personal resources; see Epistle XXX.

In no respect inferior. Here “inferior” refers to age: he had not yet reached his twenty-fifth year and was therefore, according to the customs of the Church, too young for holy orders. Thus above, Epistle XXXVIII: “Younger in the promise of his age”; and in this Epistle: “Nor could he be younger.”

## EPISTLE XL

[Col. 1067B]

For you should know that we have been admonished and instructed by divine favor. Rigaltius says: Cyprian customarily attributes to a divine admonition what, in the clergy’s absence, he appeared to do by himself in making an ordination. Accordingly, below he will say: “Meanwhile, let what is revealed be done.” Similarly, in the preceding Epistle he says that Celerinus undertook the office of reader at the admonition of divine favor; and in Epistle XXXII likewise, that divine testimonies preceded Aurelius’s ordination. From this infer that the ordinations of clerics—not only subdeacons, deacons, and presbyters, but even readers—were already regarded in antiquity not as profane but as sacred, to such a degree that certain signs sent by God commonly occurred before their ordination.

That Numidicus the presbyter be enrolled. Baronius says: Numidicus was by no means ordained a presbyter by St. Cyprian. Rather, since he was already a presbyter of some other church and had endured so glorious a martyrdom, he was deemed worthy of the honor of exercising the presbyterate in the principal church of all Africa, [Col. 1067C] the Church of Carthage. For this is suggested by the words: “That Numidicus the presbyter be enrolled in the number of the presbyters of Carthage.” There is not even a word about a new ordination of him, as we have seen in the case of several readers recently ordained. It was indeed considered a great honor to sit among the presbyters with the bishop in the cathedral church. Those admitted in this fashion were said to be “incardinated,” and those thus admitted were also called “cardinals.” But the most illustrious annalist is always engaged in adapting the customs of the ancient Church to the practice of the present age. It is not, however, so easy to believe that presbyters of the Roman Church were admitted from elsewhere in such a fashion that they were all thereafter called cardinals.

Revived by his companions. Drawn out from the heap of the dead and relieved of that fatal burden.

He remained unwillingly. Rigaltius says: Because the Lord had imposed upon him a further period of residence in the flesh.

He will be advanced to a higher position. Rigaltius says: To the position of the high priest, that is, of bishop. Meanwhile he will sit [Col. 1067D] in the second order, which is the presbyterate.
