For the diaconate too is the third grade of priesthood—namely, the *diaconium*, just as there is a *presbyterium*.

## EPISTLE XLI

To divide a portion of the people with the bishop. Rigaltius says: The saying “Do not divide with your brother” is well known; it has been extended to shameful and obscene matters.

I sent you as my deputies. Rigaltius says: And among them, indeed, Rogatianus himself, whom he named above in Epistle VII.

So that the needs of our brethren might be discharged by means of the funds. Rigaltius says: The register of needs contained the names of needy persons. Thus, when someone’s need was relieved by the brethren’s beneficence, his name too was struck out; in this way beneficence struck out the need and, together with the need, the needy person’s name.

To practice their trades. Rigaltius says: Tertullian treated this question concerning trades in his book *On Idolatry*. Understand here trades by no means unworthy of a Christian—not theatrical occupations or ones favorable to idolatry. [Col. 1068A] And this, indeed, is the true method of relieving the poor: those utterly worn out by old age and illnesses should be supported entirely at public expense; but those who, although able by their labor to obtain some means of sustaining life, nevertheless could not earn enough to support their family, should be assisted by a supplement sufficient for the purpose.

I might advance them to offices of ecclesiastical administration. For doorkeepers and clerics of the lower ranks were chosen from those who were on the register of the poor. This arrangement served to economize the Church’s resources.

Those who had first come forward to be struck off. Rigaltius says: Tertullian had similarly said, “They are present to be witnesses.” One manuscript reads: “those who were first summoned to be struck off.”

That they would not communicate with him on the mountain. Rigaltius says: Thus above: “because they would not communicate with him on the mountain.” This is the reading of all editions and manuscripts except two Vatican codices, both of which read [Col. 1068B] “in death.” On that reading, this Felicissimus would have threatened not to grant peace, even at the point of death, to those who obeyed Cyprian, nor to celebrate offerings and sacrifices in commemoration of them. Nevertheless, we consider the commonly received reading to be correct: Felicissimus had hurried away with a great many people and, through factionalism, had withdrawn to the mountain in opposition to the Church; therefore Cyprian, in turn, rebuts him as the author of a perverse conspiracy with a contrary threat. “Let him know,” he says, “that he will not communicate with us in the Church.” He opposes the Church of the faithful to the mountain of the factious. “He threatened you and said that you would not communicate with him on the mountain; we threaten him in turn and say that he will not communicate with you in the Church.” Yet a difficulty remains: in the following Epistles Cyprian makes no mention of the mountain, although he says much about Felicissimus and about his faction and secession. Mountains were always held in veneration as places close to heaven. Perhaps Felicissimus, through perverse imitation, therefore taught on the mountain and withdrew there to pray, [Col. 1068C] because the Lord had done so; Matthew V and Luke VI. Certainly the Donatists, followers of the Novatians here in Africa, were called *Montenses*. But there was also a city near Carthage that bore the name *Mons*. In truth, by analogy they would more properly be called *Montenses* from a city than from mountains; those who dwell near mountains are called *montani* and *monticolae*. Here, however, it appears most probable that a place within the city itself is designated. Thus at Rome someone is said to live “on the Palatine hill” or “on the Viminal,” or at Corinth, “on the Acrocorinth.” The citadel of Carthage, called Byrsa, is described by Strabo, book XVII, as ὀφρὺς ἱκανῶς ὀρθία, “a sufficiently steep brow”; and perhaps Felicissimus held his assemblies in that part of the city.

All of which we shall investigate. “I shall conduct a judicial examination. I shall inquire.” Hence the saying: “If you are a judge, investigate; if you are a king, command.”

Send it also to the clergy at Carthage. The letter appears first to have been transmitted to Caldonius, who was acting in his own diocese. It was likewise to be delivered to Herculanus, also a bishop, before it was handed to the brethren at Carthage.

## EPISTLE XLII

[Col. 1068D]

We have excluded them from communion. By carrying into execution the sentence pronounced by Cyprian.

Repostus, one of the exiles. Rigaltius says: He, of course, who, while belonging to the Church, had been made an exile for the name of Christ. Irene of the Rutili appears to have confessed Christ in a radiant confession; for martyrs were called “radiant,” “ruddy,” and “clad in red.”

With my notation. That is, Caldonius’s, who alone wrote the letter, although the others confirmed it with their signatures.

You ought to have known. That is, Cyprian, who may perhaps be addressed in the plural as a mark of honor. I would think it should be written in the singular: “You ought to have known.”

Likewise, we excluded Sophronius. Rigaltius says: This clause appears to require the following reading: “Likewise, we excluded Sophronius, himself also one of the exiles; Soliassus; and Budinarius,” [Col. 1069A] so that we understand three persons to have been excluded here: Sophronius, one of the exiles; Soliassus; and Budinarius. I consider that it must certainly be read “Soliassus the *burdonarius*,” or muleteer. In IV Kings V, “the load of a pair of pack-mules” is mentioned; the word is perhaps derived from Hebrew. It was granted citizenship as a Greek word—that is, βόρδον, βορδῶνα, and βορδόνιον are found in glossaries. Moreover, the word occurs in the *Digest*, book XXXII, law XLIX: “The bequest includes slaves—for example, litter-bearers who carried only the mistress of the household—or a litter, sedan chair, or pack-mules.” Nor is it surprising if, after Paula the mender of sacks, we encounter Soliassus the muleteer as well.

## EPISTLE XLIII

The most faithful Britius. Britius, Rogatianus, and Numidicus—three presbyters in all—remained in the faith when five defected to Felicissimus’s party: namely Fortunatus, Jovinus, Maximus, Donatus, and Gordius. On them, see the *Annals*, year 251, paragraph 2. [Col. 1069B] And perhaps the pretext for innovation here was that, since the presbyters acted with equal rights in the bishop’s absence and administered the Church’s affairs by common vote, as though they were its senate, the larger number was among the schismatics; those who supported the opposing side had therefore been regarded as schismatics.

That it was not permitted me to come to you before Easter Day. Rigaltius says: At that time the schismatics had thrown everything into disorder in the Church of Carthage, arrogating to themselves authority to grant peace to the lapsed before the case had been sufficiently examined according to the standard of ecclesiastical discipline. Cyprian therefore decided that he must postpone his return, lest, during the solemnities of the Easter festival, the gathering of the people and the unwelcome presence of the returning bishop offer the factious an occasion for fresh disturbances. Cyprian’s own words on the following page sufficiently intimate this: “While we guard against the threats and plots of the treacherous, lest a greater tumult arise there upon our arrival.” Indeed, Cyprian gained this advantage from the delay: he was not exposed alone to the hostility of the schismatics, but was supported by the votes and authority of the bishops, who customarily assembled after Easter.

[Col. 1069C] These presbyters are nothing other than those five leading men. Rigaltius says: How carefully he collects everything favorable to his cause so as to bring odium upon his opponent! He says that the five presbyters who had allied themselves with Felicissimus in order to create slander and danger for Cyprian were shown and signified to him by God through those five leading men who had subscribed to the magistrates’ edict against the Christians. Consequently, those five presbyters were no less deserving of hatred than those five leading supporters of the persecution.

## A.D. 252. EPISTLE LIV

Cyprian to Maximus. This Epistle belongs among those written in the year of Christ 252 and appears to have been sent at the very beginning of the year.

That the Church is one. For we profess this in the creed when we say: “I BELIEVE IN THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.” For this reason the Nicene Fathers explicitly say: [Col. 1069D] “I BELIEVE IN ONE CATHOLIC AND APOSTOLIC CHURCH.”

After schismatic and heretical error received you as you came out of prison. Rigaltius says: These words sufficiently prove the vanity of Pamelius’s observation that Cyprian here, and in other passages of this kind, is to be understood not of schismatics or heretics but of other wicked persons. What Pamelius adduces from Augustine’s books proves only this: according to the varying forms of the cases, that most holy teacher thought differently from Cyprian concerning the punishment of heretics. St. Augustine mentions this passage in book II of *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, chapters 34 and 37, and in Epistle 255 to Macrobius the Donatist. This passage is also adduced in the *Conference of Carthage*.

It is granted to the Son alone to shatter vessels of clay. Rigaltius says: He shortly afterward says: “Nor can anyone claim for himself what the Father assigned to the Son alone.”

That he himself can carry a shovel. A shovel (*pala*) is a broad and somewhat concave agricultural implement, of which Pliny says in book XVIII, [Col. 1070A] chapter 6: “Rushy ground should be turned with a shovel, but stony ground with mattocks.” This implement was employed to clean grain, and those who think it was a winnowing fan appear to be mistaken. The prophet Isaiah, chapter XXX, verse 24, distinguishes the shovel from the winnowing fan in the Hebrew text and teaches that grain is cleaned with both: “winnowed with shovel and fan.” St. Augustine, in his Epistle to Macrobius, reads the passage thus: “As though he thinks himself able to carry both shovel and fan for winnowing and cleansing the threshing floor.”

## EPISTLE LVI

In the city of Capsa. This is a city of Byzacena, mentioned in the sixty-ninth vote of the Council of Carthage. The treasures of Jugurtha were stored there.

The violence of the magistracy. It has been noted elsewhere that the Decian persecution was first stirred up by the magistracy of the cities and by popular tumult; afterward the proconsul conducted a more severe investigation.

Undertaken not voluntarily but under compulsion. Rigaltius [Col. 1070B] says: He attributes to compulsion the violence of the tortures and their prolonged repetition.

During these three years. This appears to approach closely to the proper duration of penance.

That they had confessed the Name. Rigaltius says: That is, they had pronounced openly and clearly: “We are Christians.” Thus in the preceding Epistle: “Killed for the Name,” namely, the name of Christ, while constantly crying aloud that they were Christians.

And had not previously failed in the struggle. Rigaltius says: “Previously,” that is, before the tortures had exhausted their flesh.

When they have begun to come to me. Fixed synods were held twice each year, after Easter and in the autumn; when occasion arose, they were prolonged or held more frequently.

## EPISTLE LVIII

To the people residing at Thibaris. This appears to be a city of Zeugitana. Pamelius says: Since, when writing to larger cities, he customarily addresses his Epistle both to clergy and people, it is surprising [Col. 1070C] that he writes this Epistle to the people alone, particularly since Vincentius of Thibaris is mentioned among the bishops of Africa. It was observed above, concerning the Epistle to Cornelius about Polycarp of Hadrumetum, that omission of a bishop’s name indicates that the church lacked a bishop at the time of writing. In this passage, however, both bishop and clergy appear to have been passed over because a reply is here being made to requests from the people of Thibaris that had previously and repeatedly been conveyed to Cyprian, either by letter or messenger. But it is nothing novel for Cyprian to write to the people separately from the clergy, for he did so above in Epistle XVII.

If the state of affairs and the circumstances of the time. Rigaltius says: Thus Cyprian, even while serving the Lord, does not consider himself forbidden to serve the occasion prudently as well—that is, as befits a servant of God, δουλεύειν καιρῷ καὶ κυρίῳ, “to serve the occasion and the Lord”; Romans XII.11.

The day of affliction, the setting of the age, the time of Antichrist. Rigaltius says: Paul had already said that “the time was shortened” and that the last times were approaching. Cyprian himself will shortly say in this Epistle, “in the last times.” Below [Col. 1070D] he will say, “the most evil day.” This is precisely what Tertullian calls, in *Apology*, chapter 32, “the greatest violence impending over the whole world, and the very close of the age, threatening dreadful severities”; and in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 27: “the ends of the age, under the final wrath.” He then says explicitly: “After the eradication of Antichrist, the resurrection will be set in motion.”

From the age now dying. Rigaltius says: Above he said, “the setting of the age.”

While afflictions hem us in. Rigaltius says: Paul in II Corinthians: θλιβόμενοι, ἀλλ’ οὐ στενοχωρούμενοι, “afflicted, but not hemmed in.” The ancient glosses: “He hems in: θλίβει, στενοχωρεῖ, ἄγχει, πνίγει—he afflicts, confines, strangles, chokes.” Here, therefore, “to be hemmed in” or “confined” means more than to suffer affliction, as in IV Esdras: “But the righteous will endure narrow things, hoping for spacious things.” Psalm IV: ἐν θλίψει ἐπλάτυνάς μοι, “In affliction you enlarged me.” Cyprian himself will say in Epistle LVIII: “He was oppressed by sins that hemmed him in.”

Do not marvel at the burning that befalls you. Rigaltius says: I Peter 4: Μὴ ξενίζεσθαι τῇ ἐν ὑμῖν πυρώσει, “Do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you.” Tertullian, in *Scorpiace*: “Beloved, do not be terrified at the burning that is taking place among you [Col. 1071A] as a trial, as though something new were happening to you.” Punishment by fire is the supreme punishment in Tertullian’s book *To the Martyrs*; and the Apostle, to show the supreme test of Christian faith, says: καὶ ἐὰν παραδῶ τὸ σῶμά μου ἵνα καυθήσομαι, “and if I surrender my body to be burned.” Thus also the torments of eternal damnation are signified by the fire of Gehenna.

Lest you be thrown into consternation. He appears to have read: μηδὲ ἐξίστασθε ὡς ξένου ὑμῖν συμβαίνοντος, “nor be dismayed as though something strange were happening to you.”

Then the heavens stand open to the martyrs. Rigaltius says: He alludes to Stephen’s words: “I see the heavens opened.” Tertullian: “Your blood is the whole key to paradise.” Cyprian himself in Epistle LIV: “He who receives martyrdom is baptized in his own blood.” This was the chief concern of bishops and presbyters: to render the people brave and steadfast in undergoing martyrdom for Christ’s name.

When he sees our people being scattered by fear of persecution. Rigaltius says: He does not condemn flight during persecution, being gentler and more accommodating than Tertullian. Indeed, he is obliged to defend it; otherwise he would condemn himself.

Nor hear the bishop discoursing. Rigaltius says: That is, teaching and expounding. Cyprian himself, in the Epistle to Antonianus: [Col. 1071B] “I had read it previously and had learned, while the bishop was discoursing, that sacrifice must not be offered to idols.” Pontius, in the *Life of Cyprian*: “O blessed people of the Church, who had always listened while their bishop discoursed!”

Who are not permitted to kill. Rigaltius says: Christians’ weapons are prayers and tears, sometimes flight, but most often the steadfastness of courageous endurance for Christ’s name. Tertullian in the *Apology*: “Under this discipline it is more permissible to be killed than to kill.” By disarming Peter, Christ unbelted every Christian. Accordingly, in the following Epistle Cyprian says to Cornelius that Christ’s soldiers are now keeping sober watch and standing armed for battle; that they cannot be conquered, though they can die; and that precisely in this they are invincible, because they do not fear to die or fight back against their assailants, since the innocent are not permitted to kill even the guilty.

Of this darkness. By transposing the words, he appears to have read: πρὸς τοὺς κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ αἰῶνος τοῦ σκότους τούτου, “against the world-rulers of this age of darkness.”

On the most evil day. Rigaltius says: That is, the day of Antichrist: τοῦ πονηροῦ, “of the evil one.”

[Col. 1071C] As the sign of God. Impressed upon the forehead among the rites of baptism.

Mindful of the Eucharist, which received the Lord’s body. Rigaltius says: Ambrose, book IV of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 2: “The priest says to you, ‘The body of Christ,’ and you say, ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘True.’ Let the disposition hold fast what the tongue confesses.” Priorius says: He is speaking here according to the rite by which the Eucharist was placed in the hands of the laity, not in their mouths. Hence the Council in Trullo, canon 28, says concerning a presbyter: μήτε τοίνυν δημοσίᾳ μήτε ἰδίᾳ εὐλογείτω, μήτε τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ κατανεμέτω ἑτέροις, “Let him therefore neither bless publicly nor privately, nor distribute the body of Christ to others.” The First Council of Toledo, chapter 14: “But if anyone does not consume the Eucharist received from the priest, let him be expelled as sacrilegious.” See also canon 3 of the Council of Saragossa. Here it should be observed that laypeople receive with the hand but consume with the mouth. The Roman Church, which altered this custom, appears to have believed the hands of laypeople more profane than their mouths.

## A.D. 253. EPISTLE LXII

[Col. 1071D]

With the greatest grief of our spirit. This Epistle, whose genuineness we by no means doubt, occurs extremely rarely in manuscript copies. Indeed, among all those made available to me, I have not seen a single one containing it. There is no need to refute the wholly implausible conjecture of Pamelius, who imagines that these Africans were captured by Goths. Nor, certainly, was Africa—most prolific in prodigies—so thoroughly cultivated and pacified as to harbor no barbarians, so that they would have to be sought on the opposite quarter of the globe. On this matter consult the *Cyprianic Annals*.

He wrests them from the jaws of the devil. Rigaltius says: Thus in Epistle IV he says: “The burden must be rescued from the fire.”

Members dedicated to Christ. By a settled intention of the mind directed toward chastity. For at that time those women were not enclosed within cloisters. Pamelius says: You have a similar expression concerning holy virgins both in the Epistle to Pomponius and in the book *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*.

[Col. 1072A] I was a captive, and you redeemed me. The redemption of captives was always reckoned among the principal duties of charity in the Church. Lactantius calls it a great and illustrious work of justice. Ambrose even broke consecrated vessels of the Church for such purposes, book II of *On Duties*, chapter 28. Augustine, according to Possidius, did the same; as did Deogratias, according to Victor of Vita, book I.

We have sent one hundred thousand sesterces in coin. Rigaltius says: Johann Friedrich Gronovius, in *On Sesterces*, no. 18, very correctly observed that Pamelius had no reason to doubt the corruption of the common reading. For that reading is not Latin and does not signify any sum in proper Latin. Accordingly, it must undoubtedly be written: “one hundred thousand sesterces in coin.” This reading yields a sum of 25,000 of our present-day pounds. Lombert reduces Rigaltius’s valuation to 7,500 French livres. Capellus calculates differently, arriving at 9,639 livres, 17 sous, and 10 deniers. If we calculate according to English currency, perhaps the person who says that the sum designated here amounts to 781 pounds sterling and 5 shillings comes closest [Col. 1072B] to the truth. We have restored the manifest copyist’s error according to the analogy of the Latin language, for it is sufficiently certain that Cyprian spoke correctly. Nor do we approve the solemn method of critics who leave errors in the text so that they may laboriously correct them in their notes.

I have appended the names of each contributor. Rigaltius says: Not without reason or unnecessarily. For in the sacrifices of prayers, the names of those who had acted promptly and willingly in so necessary a work were offered up. We showed above, in the note on Epistle I, that exclusion from this privilege was regarded as a most severe punishment.

## EPISTLE LXIII

Although I know. In this Epistle Cyprian is not refuting the Aquarians, or Hydroparastatae, an offshoot of the Ebionites according to Epiphanius, *Heresy* XXX, nor the Encratites, followers of Tatian, [Col. 1072C] whose error chiefly consisted in rejecting wine as something profane and abominable. As Epiphanius says, they called it διαβολικόν, “diabolical,” asserting with fabulous vanity that vines had sprung from Satan and the earth. Our author says that these people had erred through ignorance or simplicity. Because they received the Eucharist before dawn, at a time when no one drank wine, as the Apostle reports in Acts II.15, it is credible that they substituted water as a more respectable kind of drink and one less exposed to suspicion. This was especially so because pagans might have detected by the smell of wine that those who reeked of it were Christians—a matter discussed at the end of this Epistle. This Epistle was solemnly mentioned by St. Augustine in book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21, where passages found right at its beginning are adduced as an example of the plain style of discourse.

By a human and novel institution. Rigaltius says: Thus a little later he will say, “to set down things of our own and merely human.” See what we observed above concerning the “human Church,” [Col. 1072D] “human credulity,” and “human tradition” in the notes on Epistles LVII and LX.

What the author and teacher of this sacrifice did and taught. Rigaltius says: The Gospels recount what he did and what he taught. Paul handed down nothing different to his Corinthians. What Christ instituted at the supper Christians afterward called a sacrifice, and they called the ministers of the sacred supper priests.

And that nothing else should be done by us than what the Lord first did for us. Rigaltius says: In this same Epistle he will say: “But if it is not permitted to relax even the least of the Lord’s commands, how much less is it lawful to infringe things so great, so weighty, and so closely pertaining to the mystery of the Lord’s passion itself and of our redemption, or to alter them by human tradition into anything other than what was divinely instituted?”

Nor can it be seen to be his blood in the cup. Rigaltius says: Thus Tertullian, in his book *On Prayer*: “His body is represented in the bread.” Cyprian himself shortly afterward says, “the cup in which Christ’s blood is shown”; and, concerning the water, “which cannot express Christ’s [Col. 1073A] blood.” When he insists so repeatedly that the cup must be mixed, his principal concern is that wine not be absent from it. For although, in order to conciliate the Aquarians’ minds and defend the custom received in the Church, Cyprian acknowledges that water is rightly used in the Eucharist, by which the Christian people are symbolized, and although he thought that Christ had used ordinary diluted wine, he nevertheless maintains that everything must be measured wholly by the standard of the Lord’s institution. That is, what must be done is what Jesus Christ our Lord and God, the author and teacher of the sacrifice, not only did but taught. He repeatedly states similar things throughout, adding that the images of Christ’s sacrifice are constituted by bread and wine.

Noah, drinking wine, expressed an image of the Lord’s passion. Rigaltius says: The Fathers greatly indulged their ingenuity wherever bread and wine occur in the Scriptures. From I Peter III.21, it is entirely clear that Noah bore a type of the redemption gained through Christ; and, surviving the waters of the flood, he more truly foreshadowed the saving waters of Baptism. What wonder is it, then, if a step is laid in advance toward the Church’s other [Col. 1073B] sacrament as well; and if, since he fell asleep after drinking wine, he is said to have prefigured the eucharistic cup and the Lord’s death? Meanwhile, for the logic of the type to stand, it is necessary that the Lord drank wine no less than Noah did.

Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth bread and wine. Rigaltius says: The Septuagint translators, Genesis XIV: καὶ Μελχισεδὲκ βασιλεὺς Σαλὴμ ἐξήεγεν ἄρτους καὶ οἶνον, “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth loaves and wine.” The Complutensian edition reads ἐξήνεγκεν αὐτῶν ἄρτους, “he brought forth loaves for them,” just as Ambrose also cited it in book I of *On Abraham*: “And Melchizedek, king of Salem, brought forth loaves and wine for him.” Tertullian, however, had said most explicitly in *Against the Jews*: “Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham himself as he returned from battle.” Josephus has τῷ Ἀβραάμου στρατῷ, “to Abraham’s army,” and in place of “bread and wine,” πολλὴν ἀφθονίαν τῶν ἐπιτηδείων, “a great abundance of provisions.” The author of the *Commentaries on Genesis* attributed to Eucherius, book XI, no. 17, says that it is not surprising if Melchizedek went out to meet the victorious Abraham and brought forth bread and wine to refresh both him and his soldiers. [Col. 1073C] What follows in those same commentaries concerning this history, however, reveals the hand of an interpolator. Jean Mercier and Hugo Grotius acknowledge that the opinion of those who think this was done after a preceding sacrifice is not improbable.

In the person of the Father. Our Lord not only claims this Psalm for himself in Matthew XXII.44 and elsewhere, but the Jews also commonly acknowledge it. Moses ha-Darshan on Genesis XXXVII.12; *Midrash Tehillim* on Psalm II; Rabbi Saadia Gaon on Daniel VII.13; Talmud, tractate *Berakhot*, chapter 5.

Making mention of the Apostles. By the servants who are said to have been sent, he understands the Apostles.

To the mixing bowl. See what was said on book II *To Quirinus*, chapter 2. When he says that she mixed the wine, according to Jansenius’s interpretation, only this should be understood: that she served and prepared it.

Full and trodden. The Septuagint has πλήρους καταπεπατημένης, “full, trodden down.” Evidently they took the word that signifies a winepress for another word of almost the same form, one that signifies abundance of possessions and fruitfulness in produce. St. Jerome, in accordance with the sense of the Hebrew text, reads: “I alone have trodden the winepress.”

[Col. 1073D] Do not, he says, remember the former things. He similarly interprets this of Baptism in book I *To Quirinus*, chapter 12.

Christ, who is the rock. Rigaltius says: The rock upon which Christ built his Church. Yet in very many passages Cyprian transferred what is said of the rock to Simon, to whom Christ gave the name Peter because of his correct declaration concerning the Son of God.

He taught by the example of his instruction that the cup should be mixed by combining wine and water. Cyprian says below that we do not observe what was commanded unless we too do the same things that the Lord did and, mixing the Lord’s cup in the same manner, do not depart from divine instruction. He appears to insist on this still more strongly afterward. Furthermore, most writers of the ancient Church agree that the Lord offered wine diluted with water at his supper. Thus Justin, *Apology* II; Clement of Alexandria, book II of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 2. The Fathers of the Council in Trullo derive the custom from tradition in canon XXXII; but the most certain evidence for the matter must be drawn [Col. 1074A] from Jewish rites. For it is reasonable to believe that our Lord accommodated himself in this respect to the customs received in the community. Thus the paschal reading is called a “proclamation,” and so the Apostles are commanded to “proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.” They called the paschal lamb “the body of the Passover”; similarly, the Lord says of the eucharistic bread: “This is my body.” Just as the head of the household, when the blessing has been completed in the celebration of Passover, breaks the bread, so too the Lord took bread and, after giving thanks, broke it. Concerning wine, however, the Hebrew teachers say that it was all the same whether the wine employed was unmixed or diluted, as is transmitted in the *Tosefta*. Hence Aquinas correctly says in Part III, question 74, article 7, and question 83, article 6, reply 4, and Bonaventure in book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 11, part 2, question 3, that the admixture of water does not belong to the necessity or integrity of the sacrament. The Armenians, indeed, held the heresy that water must be altogether absent from the wine in the Eucharist; they were condemned by the Quinisext Synod. Although the Roman Church appears to decree [Col. 1074B] that the cup of the blood of Christ the Lord must be consecrated neither in pure water nor in pure wine—that is, wine without water—but in wine mixed with water, nevertheless, if the matter is attentively considered, they intend it to be consecrated in wine alone. For they instruct that the water be added in a very small quantity—“the smallest possible,” in Eugenius’s words—and that some interval elapse between the mixing and the consecration, so that the water may at length be converted into wine. See the *Roman Catechism*, chapter IV, paragraph 17, and the *Roman Sacerdotal*, part I, treatise XIX, chapter 2. In this matter the testimony of Aristotle, book I of *On Generation and Corruption*, final chapter, is customarily adduced. There he says that wine introduced in a very small quantity into water is transformed into water: μεταβάλλει θάτερον εἰς τὸ κρατοῦν· οἷον σταλαγμὸς οἴνου μυρίοις χοεῦσιν ὕδατος οὐ μίγνυται· λύεται γὰρ τὸ εἶδος καὶ μεταβάλλει εἰς τὸ πᾶν ὕδωρ, “The one substance changes into the predominant one; for example, a drop of wine does not mix with ten thousand measures of water, for its form is dissolved and it changes entirely into water.” Thus the Roman Church recognizes not merely one transubstantiation in the Eucharist, but two. Furthermore, the practice [Col. 1074C] of the Greek Church should be observed. Concerning it Balsamon says: πρὸ τοῦ ἁγιασθῆναι τὸ ἅγιον ποτήριον, οὐ βάλλεται τὸ ζέον εἰς τὴν ἕνωσιν, ἀλλὰ μετὰ τὸν ἁγιασμόν, “Before the holy cup is consecrated, the hot water is not poured into the mixture, but after the consecration.” Consequently, in their judgment, the water follows this sacred mystery; it does not enter into it.

Will be poured out. Cyprian supports the reading of those manuscripts that have ἐκχυθησόμενον, “which will be poured out.”

Produce of the vine. γεννήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου, “produce of the vine.” The Vulgate translation retained the very term: “I shall not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine.”

To pervert the Gospel of Christ. μεταστρέψαι, “to pervert.” Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine similarly use that expression.

Your intoxicating cup. The Septuagint: ποτήριόν σου μεθύσκον, ὡσεὶ κράτιστον, “your cup, making drunk, as though most excellent”—intoxicating like wine of the finest quality. In Hebrew it is “my cup,” and Jerome, *To Sunnias and Fretela*, says that the Septuagint wrote ποτήριόν μου, “my cup.”

From that worldly taste. Rigaltius says: He calls the taste of ordinary and profane wine a worldly taste, to which he opposes divine understanding, so that it is now understood not as wine but as the [Col. 1074D] Lord’s blood.

By that ordinary wine the mind is loosened. Rigaltius says: He calls it “ordinary wine” because it has not yet been sanctified or consecrated into Christ’s blood. Accordingly, he will shortly oppose the Lord’s blood to that ordinary wine. He no longer calls it wine, but blood.

All sorrow is removed. We have repeatedly noted that in Cyprian “to remove” (*exponere*) means the same as “to take away from the midst.”

He was oppressed by sins that hemmed him in. Rigaltius says: Thus above, in Epistle LVI, he said: “He is frequently beset by afflictions that hem him in.”

We see that the people are understood in the water. Bertram, in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, written about the middle of the ninth century, argues as follows from these words:

> It should also be considered that in that bread not only Christ’s body but also the body of the people who believe in him is represented figuratively. It is therefore made from many grains of wheat, because the body of the believing people is joined together from many [Col. 1075A] believers through Christ’s word. For this reason, just as in the mystery that bread is received as Christ’s body, so also in the mystery the members of the believing people are indicated; and just as that bread is called the believers’ body not corporeally but spiritually, so too Christ’s body must necessarily be understood not corporeally but spiritually.
>
> So too water is commanded to be mixed into the wine that is called Christ’s blood, and neither is permitted to be offered without the other, because neither the people without Christ nor Christ without the people can exist, just as neither the head without the body nor the body without the head can exist. Finally, in the sacrament the water bears the representation of the people. Therefore, if that wine, sanctified through the ministry of the ministers, is corporeally converted into Christ’s blood, the water likewise mixed with it must necessarily be corporeally converted into the blood of the believing people. For where there is one sanctification, there is consequently one operation; and where the principle is equal, an equal mystery also follows. Yet we see that nothing in the water has been changed corporeally; consequently, therefore, nothing has been manifested corporeally in the wine either. Whatever is signified [Col. 1075B] in the water concerning the body of the people is received spiritually; therefore, whatever is indicated in the wine concerning Christ’s blood must necessarily be received spiritually as well.

In the wine, however, he shows the blood of Christ. Rigaltius says: Above in this Epistle: “The wine by which Christ’s blood is shown.” And here, a little later, where he speaks of the water: “By this sacrament also the people are shown to be united.” “Is shown,” in the sense in which he said in this very passage: “We see that the people are understood in the water.” See Epistle LXIX.

How neither can wine alone. That is, while the usage received in the Church remains in force. But it should be noted that what is said to contain a mystery within itself does not always remain perpetually ratified and sacred in the Church. Formerly the faithful used a rather large loaf in the Eucharist, so that all who partook of the same loaf might be shown to be one bread and to have been endowed with communion in the broken body of the Lord. Subsequently it became customary to use small cakes, but the mystery has not thereby perished; for these represent little coins, [Col. 1075C] the price of the Lord’s body. Thus in this very Epistle our author relates that the Eucharist was first celebrated by the Lord at night—and this too was not without mystery—so that the very hour of the sacrifice might show the evening of the world, as it is written in Exodus: “And the whole multitude of the congregation of the children of Israel shall kill it at evening.” He then adds: “We, however, celebrate the Lord’s resurrection in the morning”; from this it will also be evident that we wish to walk in Christ’s light. Moreover, by a decree of Eugene, Roman Pontiff, water is ordered to be mixed in a small quantity into the chalice that is to be consecrated; thus, through the wine’s exceeding the quantity of water, there is signified the superiority of the merits of Christ the Lord and of his dignity above human nature and above the sins of the human race. Yet no less appropriately, when unmixed wine is used, it is shown that we are saved solely by Christ’s merits and blood. Similarly, the Greeks pour hot water into the consecrated chalice to signify, according to Balsamon’s interpretation of canon XXXII of the Council in Trullo, “that the fluids which flowed from the holy side of our Lord Jesus Christ are life-giving” (τοῦ εἶναι ζωοποιὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁγίας πλευρᾶς τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ῥεύσαντα). The Latins use cold water, to testify [Col. 1075D] that Christ truly died and that we are saved only by his death. The same has occurred in Baptism: formerly triple immersion was required, so that the doctrine of the Holy Trinity might be made manifest; afterward a single immersion took its place, so that we might profess our acknowledgment of one God. Immersion also appeared necessary so that we might be seen to have been buried with Christ through Baptism; afterward we were sprinkled with water, so that we might be known to have been cleansed by the sprinkling of his blood. In like manner, a harmonious mixture of milk and honey was added to the baptismal water, and for this reason these were offered at the altar together with wine and ears of grain; yet these practices later fell into disuse by decrees of the canons, while the mystery of the sacrament remained unimpaired.

In the sacrifice which Christ offered. Rigaltius says: In the sacrifice Christ offered himself to the Father; in the sacrament of his sacrifice he made the bread and wine his body and gave them to his disciples while they were dining. For what the Lord said stands ratified: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” That is, provided that those communicating worthily [Col. 1076A] become, through faith, participants in his body and blood and are transformed unto eternal life.

Only Christ must be followed. Christ alone must be heard. Rigaltius says: This is the safest rule for preserving traditions, which Cyprian repeatedly impresses upon his readers in many places in this Epistle. At its beginning he says: “Nor should anything else be done by us than what the Lord first did for us.” And in this very passage: “It is not lawful to violate the sacrament of our redemption or, by human tradition, to alter it into something other than what was divinely instituted.” And: “For one ought not to follow human custom, but the truth of God.” Yet this same Cyprian will say in this very Epistle: “But the Lord offered the mixed chalice not in the morning, but after supper. Are we therefore to celebrate the Lord’s Supper after supper?” Tertullian’s book *On the Crown* was written against the Psychics and Gnostics. It was also a tenet of theirs that, even under the pretext of tradition, written authority must be demanded. Accordingly, against these people he begins by discussing the many traditions that had been received without written authority, both concerning Baptism and concerning the Eucharist, [Col. 1076B] and he acknowledges that obedience is owed to them. Thus each man trims his sails to his own opinion and cause.

In the morning sacrifices. Rigaltius says: Tertullian: “even at meetings before dawn.” They celebrated the Eucharist in the hours before dawn because, if they had postponed it until suppertime, the congregation could not have been summoned to the banquet. What follows a little later in Cyprian indicates this. Tertullian, however, when he says that the Eucharist was celebrated even at meetings before dawn, acknowledges that it was also celebrated at mealtime.

Through the taste of wine. Tertullian treats the entire matter in Book II *To His Wife*, chapter 5: “The more pains you take to conceal such things, the more suspicious you will make them and the more readily they will be detected by pagan curiosity. Will you escape notice when you sign your bed and your little body; when you blow away something unclean; when you rise even during the night to pray? Will you not appear to be practicing some magic? Will your husband not know what you taste in secret before all other food? And if he learns that it is bread, will he not believe it to be the bread it is said to be?” In fact, morning breakfasts consisted of a draught of unmixed wine; hence ἀκρατίζεσθαι [Col. 1076C] among the Greeks means “to breakfast,” and ἀκράτισμα the taking of breakfast. But these things did not apply to women, for whom merely to have tasted wine was regarded as a capital crime. The reading on which the best manuscripts agree—the Lambeth, York, second Bodleian, Lincoln, Benedictine, and London manuscripts—appears by no means to be rejected, especially since it corresponds most closely to Tertullian’s thought. What is there called “the unbelieving conscience” Septimius used to mean the conscience of the other person, the husband. But I alter nothing.

When we come to supper, we offer the mixed chalice. It is evident from this that these “water-drinkers” had not imbibed the error of the Manichaeans, Tatianists, or Elchasaites, so as to think that wine, as though it were the devil’s blood, must be utterly abominated. For these words are spoken in the person of those who offered water alone only in the morning. It is also evident that the Eucharist, although received in the hours before dawn, was customarily distributed in the evening as well. Tertullian is a substantial witness to this fact in *On the Crown*, chapter 3: “At mealtime we receive the sacrament of the Eucharist from the hands of those presiding [Col. 1076D].” Elsewhere he advises that it be received when the stations have ended. The custom of communicating after supper long endured in the Church; for Socrates, Book V, chapter 22, says: “The Egyptians who are neighbors of the Alexandrians, and those who inhabit the Thebaid, hold assemblies on the Sabbath; but they partake of the mysteries in a manner contrary to the custom of Christians. For after they have feasted and filled themselves with every kind of food, toward evening they make the offering and partake of the mysteries” (Αἰγύπτιοι γείτονες ὄντες Ἀλεξανδρέων, καὶ οἱ τὴν Θηβαΐδα οἰκοῦντες, ἐν σαββάτῳ μὲν ποιοῦνται συνάξεις· οὐχ ὡς ἔθος δὲ χριστιανοῖς τῶν μυστηρίων μεταλαμβάνουσι· μετὰ γὰρ τὸ εὐωχηθῆναι, καὶ παντοίων ἐδεσμάτων ἐμφορηθῆναι, περὶ ἑσπέραν προσφέροντες, τῶν μυστηρίων μεταλαμβάνουσι).

The truth of the sacrament. Rigaltius says: “The mixed chalice, and with the entire brotherhood present.” Thus we truly observe everything Christ handed down by offering the mixed chalice, at mealtime, and with the whole brotherhood present.

But the Lord offered the mixed chalice not in the morning, but after supper. Are we therefore to celebrate the Lord’s Supper after supper? Rigaltius says: Above he said that it is unlawful to violate matters belonging to the sacrament of the Lord’s institution itself, or by human tradition to alter them into something other than what was divinely instituted. Here, however, [Col. 1077A] he ingeniously devises causes and reasons why we ought not to celebrate the Lord’s Supper after supper, even though the Lord instituted it after supper. Someone will say that the causes or reasons Cyprian offers are spiritual and divine: namely, that Christ instituted the memorial of his Passion—which took place toward the evening of the day—after evening; whereas we celebrate in the morning the Lord’s resurrection, which the Lord himself accomplished in the morning, and that consequently what was divinely instituted does not appear to have been altered by human tradition or presumption. It may be gathered that already in Tertullian’s age something had been altered regarding this sacrament; and these words from *On the Crown* show that the sacrament of Christ’s body was celebrated not only in the evening, at mealtime, but also in the hours before dawn: “The sacrament of the Eucharist, commanded by the Lord at mealtime, we receive even in the hours before dawn.” Human presumption had not yet gained such force, however, that it was not also received at mealtime. But it is evident from what Cyprian relates in this Epistle that it gained complete ascendancy shortly afterward. Augustine indeed says [Col. 1077B] that this pleased the Holy Spirit—not on account of the reasons Cyprian offered, but so that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body might enter the Christian’s mouth before any other food. “For this reason,” he says, “that custom is observed throughout the entire world.” And yet he likewise notes that some are pleased by a certain plausible argument that, on one fixed day of the year—the day on which the Lord gave the Supper itself—the body and blood of the Lord may, as a more distinguished commemoration, lawfully be offered and received after food. Then that most holy man concludes his discussion as though doubtful and uncertain: “Accordingly, we compel no one to eat before that Lord’s Supper, but neither do we dare contradict anyone.” This discussion is found in Epistle CXVIII, where one may also observe that on the day on which the Lord gave the Supper itself, almost everyone in most places bathed. Augustine therefore adds: “And because some also maintain the fast, the offering is made in the morning for those who eat, since they cannot endure both fasting and bathing; but in the evening for those who fast.”

[Col. 1077C] For it is the Lord’s Passion. Its “memorial” (ἀνάμνησις). Luke XXII.19; 1 Corinthians XI.24, 25.

If someone in simplicity has not observed this. Rigaltius says: Thus below, near the end of the Epistle, he will say: “What we have erred in simplicity.”

His second advent draws near. Rigaltius says: Above he said: “the decline of the age.” Epistle LVIII.

Illuminates more fully. Not through the delusions of Montanus and his prophetesses, as Tertullian would have said, but through diligent observance of the admonitions of Christ and the Apostles.

The truth of the Lord’s tradition. Rigaltius says: Above he said “the truth of the sacrament”: that is, precisely what the Lord taught and did.

## EPISTLE LXIV

To brother Fidus. Pamelius says: It is not known in what place Fidus was bishop; it is nevertheless likely that his see was near that of Therapius, who in the synod is surnamed “of Bulla.” See Suffrage 61 of the Council of Carthage.

## EPISTLE LXV

[Col. 1077D]

To Epictetus. Pamelius says: It is likely that this man was bishop of Assuras; but since another bishop of Assuras, named Victor, delivered his opinion at the synod, Epictetus seems to have died before the synod. See Suffrage 68 of the Council of Carthage.

Fortunatian, formerly bishop among you. Pamelius says: Fortunatian had indeed been their bishop, but because he had lapsed, he was now deprived of the episcopate; and from what follows it is evident that he also belonged to Novatian’s faction. He is said to wish “to act as though restored to his former standing”: as if, after lapsing and completing his penance, he had been restored to the Church’s communion and thereby reinstated in full, or were permitted to assume its government again, as though by the right of postliminy. But it appears that Fortunatian had not been granted penance—indeed, had not even sought it; so far was it from having been completed.

[Col. 1078A] I shall therefore not be indignant over these things. The Septuagint reads: “I shall be angry over these things” (ἐπὶ τούτοις ὀργισθήσομαι), omitting “all” (πᾶσι).

I shall not release them. Rigaltius says: They will remain bound; it will not be remitted to them; they will not be absolved: “I shall certainly not release them” (οὐ μὴ ἀνήσω αὐτούς). This text is cited more than once in the same form.

Lest perhaps he abandon. The Septuagint reads ἀπαλλάξῃ, “remove.” Aquila, more in accordance with the meaning of the sacred text, has διακόψῃ, “cut off,” and Symmachus διαφθείρῃ, “destroy.” At 1 Samuel XXV.10 the Septuagint renders this word by ἀναχωρέω, “withdraw”; elsewhere it commonly explains it by διακόπτω, “cut off,” καθαιρέω, “take down,” and synonymous verbs.

The altar of the Holy One. The Septuagint reads: “to the altar of the Holy One; and they shall not bring sin upon themselves, lest they die” (πρὸς τὸ θυσιαστήριον τοῦ ἁγίου· καὶ οὐκ ἐπάξονται ἐφ’ ἑαυτοὺς ἁμαρτίαν, ἵνα μὴ ἀποθάνωσι). Editors previously thought that Exodus XXX.20 was being cited as far as this point, and that error produced others.

Although. That is, “in whatever way,” “even though,” as in: “A deep gloom of encroaching darkness blinded the hearts of some.” For no correlative clause follows here.

They desire contributions, offerings, and profits. Rigaltius says: Thus already in Cyprian’s century bad priests appropriated gain or profit from the offerings of the faithful. [Col. 1078B] Augustine, Book IV *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*. Sulpicius Severus complained in the clearest terms that this most loathsome plague had invaded later generations, *History*, Book I: “Sitting,” he says, “they await gifts, and they hold every distinction of life corrupted by payment, while they parade holiness as though it were for sale.”

Lapsed laymen. Read: “the lapse of laymen,” for this sense better serves Cyprian’s point.

The offering to be sanctified. Rigaltius says: The offering is sanctified when it becomes the body of Christ, which is called absolutely “the Holy.” We have noted in Tertullian, *On Prayer*: “From the mouth with which you have uttered ‘Amen’ over the Holy.” And in *The Prescription Against Heretics*: “Lest he cast the holy to dogs.” Later, however, it became customary to say “consecration” in place of “sanctification,” since the common people believed that the term “consecrating” signified something more excellent than sanctification. We have often discussed the extent to which the elements in the Eucharist are and are called Christ’s body.

When not even the offering can be sanctified there. Rigaltius [Col. 1078C] says: Pamelius opposes to Cyprian’s opinion the opinion of Augustine, who determined that sacraments administered by impious and criminal bishops or presbyters—and even baptisms conferred by heretics—are valid: Tractate V on John, and Books VI and VII *Against the Donatists*. This matter requires a distinction concerning the factual case brought into controversy. For here Cyprian is dealing with a certain Fortunatian, bishop of Assuras, who through idolatry had fallen away from the faith and therefore from the episcopate, priesthood, and Church, and was no longer regarded as a Christian, much less a presbyter or priest, much less a bishop. According to the discipline prevailing in Cyprian’s time, if he had obtained a period of penance, then after completing it and rendering lawful satisfaction he could indeed be readmitted to Christian communion, but by no means to the episcopate or to any rank of priesthood in the Church. The Church was restored to the lapsed man, but not his place or rank; for he had lost his place or rank. He was therefore reduced to the congregation or laity in such a way that no character or power of the priesthood remained with him. In a case of idolatry of this kind, Cyprian therefore denied that Fortunatian [Col. 1078D]—an idolater turned schismatic, who without having obtained penance claimed episcopal rank for himself and arrogantly and contumaciously gathered a petty congregation—could sanctify any offerings, prayers, or petitions. The reason was that he was outside the Church in such a way that he no longer belonged to Christ, whom he had denied by sacrificing to idols: he had effaced Christ’s character by superimposing the character of Jupiter, the Antichrist. From the same discipline came Cyprian’s denial that those baptized by heretics or schismatics had received Christ’s Baptism. For he says that such ministers of the sacraments, when ministering outside the Church, minister nothing, with this argument: since the Church is one, those who are not in that one Church are in none; nor do they possess any capacity by which they can receive from that one Church something received that they might communicate or confer. Cyprian and the other [Col. 1079A] fellow bishops, presbyters, and deacons throughout Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania thought it fitting to establish and sanction doctrines of this kind in an age most grievously afflicted by the persecutions of secular powers and the factions of the Church’s ministers, so as to make their people more tenacious of the Christian faith and their ministers more devoted to ecclesiastical peace and unity. This, then, was the target toward which the most holy Fathers at that time bent all the resources of Scripture. In the age immediately following theirs, either because it had better pagans—that is, pagans less hostile to the Christian name—or because it obtained better ministers of the Church, discipline began to be relaxed, and subtlety in argument was gradually sharpened in its zeal for the Catholic name. Accordingly, under Augustine a more humane opinion found favor, one that established a cause for heretics or schismatics very different from that of idolaters. For those who departed from Catholic doctrine were indeed said to be cut off from the Church, but nevertheless in such a condition that if, after peace had been made, they returned to the Catholic Church, they were deemed, as though by right of postliminy, never to have departed and thus recovered their former place in the Church. For they had not denied the head of that Church—namely Christ—as idolaters had; and therefore the baptisms they had administered in schism [Col. 1079B] were not rendered void. Hence those statements of Augustine: “I grant that heretics are wicked; but the heretics gave Christ’s Baptism.” And: “Thus, therefore, those whom a drunkard baptized, whom a murderer baptized, whom an adulterer baptized—if it was Christ’s Baptism, Christ baptized them.” And: “That sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer.” The same Augustine, in Epistle CLXVI, cites in support of this opinion of his the words of Constantine: “Observe,” he says, “what the prince’s words contain: For if, in those who were first initiated, the sacred efficacy of Baptism is judged weak merely because those from whom it is received are thought to be sinners, the sacrament once delivered will have to be renewed as many times as the administrator of the conferred Baptism is found unworthy; and our faith will depend not upon the choice of our own will, nor upon the grace of the divine gift, but upon the merits and character of priests and clerics.”

## IN THE YEAR 254. EPISTLE LXVI

[Col. 1079C] Cyprian, who is also Thascius. Pamelius says: It seems to me that Cyprian wished “to Cretanize with a Cretan”; and because Florentius had prefixed his own name together with his praenomen, Cyprian did the same. This very praenomen may be found in the Acts of his Passion and in Pontius the deacon. I would indeed believe that Pupianus begrudged Cyprian the name Caecilius, which he had received from the presbyter of blessed memory by whom he was converted to the faith, and that in contempt he greeted him by the title Thascius, by which he had been known among the pagans.

I [write to] you, brother. Rigaltius says: Although Florentius was now a schismatic, Cyprian nevertheless calls him brother, just as Optatus calls the Donatists brothers, rebuking them because they themselves refused to call Catholics brothers: “They refuse,” he says, “to be called our brothers; nevertheless, we cannot depart from the fear of God, for the Holy Spirit exhorts us through Isaiah the Prophet, saying: ‘You who fear the name of the Lord, hear the name of the Lord. Those who hate and execrate you, and refuse to be called our brothers—you nevertheless say to them: You are our brothers.’ They are therefore brothers beyond doubt, although not good ones. The name of brotherhood is not laid aside even when sin intervenes.”

The dignity of your martyrdom. Rigaltius says: Before the schism Florentius was in communion with Cyprian and, during the persecution, had advanced to the supreme sublimity of martyrdom, as Cyprian says below.

Unworthy and unchaste men. Rigaltius says: These words indicate sufficiently what sort of reproaches Florentius had poured upon Cyprian—unspeakable and shameful things, execrable even to pagans.

In our declarations. Rigaltius says: When we ourselves declare and say something about ourselves, let the declarant be one person and the witness another. Let the declarant and the witness not be the same person. “No one who bears witness to himself is trustworthy” (Οὐδεὶς ἑαυτῷ μαρτυρῶν ἀξιόπιστος).

My testimony is not true. Rigaltius says: It is not lawful or just. Horace: “It is right that each man measure himself by his own measure and foot.”

[Col. 1080A] Thus you assail the priest. We have frequently discussed this passage of Holy Scripture and the meaning of the word *incitas* (“you assail”). Moreover, we have observed that Cyprian regularly draws forth testimonies of Scripture in masses, as though from an armory. See what was said at Epistles III and LIX.

Bishop of the Christians. Rigaltius says: Above, in Epistle LIX, he said: “with the designation of his episcopate appended and added.” Thus he was proscribed because he was a bishop: solely for this reason, not because he was bishop of Carthage, but because he was a bishop of Christians.

Nor do I boast of these things, but relate them in sorrow. Rigaltius says: Epistle LIX: “For I speak when provoked; I speak in sorrow; I speak under compulsion,” etc.

The new people of believers. Pagans converted to the faith, to whom Baptism was not granted “without the bishop’s judgment” (ἄνευ γνώμης ἐπισκόπου), as Ignatius relates.

Bees have a king. Rigaltius says: The same author, in *On Idolatry*: “Bees have one king, flocks one leader, and herds one ruler.” Such ingenious arguments are customarily treated in the schools, concerning the quail-king that leads each flight of quails, and concerning cranes. For they too choose a leader whom they follow and who, with neck erect, keeps watch, and other things of this kind. From these examples this is inferred: individual hives, flocks, herds, and companies each have their own king, leader, and ruler; none has an ecumenical one.

Robbers in the employ of a contractor. Rigaltius says: The man by whom they were hired for some crime. He calls the ringleader of the faction a contractor (*manceps*).

Into the presence of God. By the prerogative of martyrdom, which has been discussed elsewhere.

When they withdrew from the midst. Rigaltius says: When, after the synod had been dissolved and the hand had been laid upon me, they withdrew. But since peace prevailed in the Church at the time Cyprian was advanced to the episcopate, these words should instead be understood of the Decian persecution.

Confessors subjected to examination. Rigaltius says: From judicial examination (*quaestio*). Thus the martyr Lucian, in Epistle XXI, said: “Paul [returned] from examination.” It should be noted here that the confessors are said first to have been examined and then tortured. For once cognizance of the case has been granted, the judicial examination comes first, and then tortures are applied.

The bishop is in the Church, and the Church in the bishop. It is altogether conducive to the unity of the Church that the bishop has not lapsed through heresy or idolatry, or been excluded from the right of communion for some other offense; and that the congregation likewise adheres to its own bishop, since he who is not with the bishop is certainly not in the Church, nor with Christ. These ideas appear to have been taken from Ignatius the God-bearer (θεοφόρος).

With a pure and unstained mouth I offer sacrifices without ceasing. Rigaltius says: Prayers from a sincere heart, from a pure and chaste conscience.

For I remember what has already been shown to me. Rigaltius says: Here too he employs revelations and visions, a weapon especially powerful for crushing adversaries in the hand of Cyprian, a most excellent and divine man, but otherwise vain and futile. For both a cunning rhetorician and an artful sophist could fabricate visions of this sort most aptly suited to his cause and deceive the unwary and simple. But since Pupianus had thought that credence should be given to rumors, it was fair that he should not be angry with Cyprian for believing dreams.

And afterward, “the dreamer.” This refers to the words of the brothers who mocked him: “Then it will become apparent what benefit his dreams bring him.”

On the day of judgment both sets [of letters] will be read before Christ’s tribunal. According to Plato’s opinion, the Great Year will one day restore the events performed in the earthly world; but in reality the great and manifest day of the Lord, Acts II.20, will bring about the “restoration” (ἀποκατάστασις) of all past deeds, Acts III.21. For an examination so exacting, many learned men believed that a thousand years would be required. But however the matter of reading those letters may turn out, it is entirely certain that an account must be rendered of both sets, since the Lord said this concerning every idle word, Matthew XII.36.

## IN THE YEAR 256. EPISTLE LXXXVI

[Col. 1081A]

To Nemesianus. The names of all these bishops of Numidia appear at the Synod of Carthage. Nemesianus is called “of Thubunae” in Suffrage 5. Felix is listed as “of Bagai” in Suffrage 12, and “of Amaccura” in Suffrage 33. There are indeed other men named Felix there, but they belonged to Byzacena and are not relevant to this passage. Lucius is mentioned in Suffrages 7 and 31, both men being Numidians; others of that name belong to Zeugitana. Litteus occurs in Suffrage 82. We have Polianus in Suffrage 15; a man of that name is called “of Milevis” in Suffrage 78. Suffrage 8 presents Victor of Octavum, a Numidian; another Victor, of Gor, does not appear relevant here. Jader of Midila occurs in Suffrage 45. Finally, Dativus of Badis is mentioned in Suffrage 15. Only concerning Nemesianus could there be doubt whether he was a Numidian or a Moor, except that Tubiana occurs in Numidia no less than in Mauretania, as appears from the Carthaginian Conference and the *Notitia* [Col. 1081B] *Imperii*. Indeed Ptolemy’s Θιβινίς should apparently be referred here, although I determined otherwise in my notes on the Council of Carthage. From their three separate replies, it appears that the aforesaid bishops were condemned separately to three mines, although there is no agreement as to which was the mine of Siguensis mentioned in Epistle LXXVIII. The name of Litteus is absent from the replies; hence one may conjecture that he had died.

The boundaries of the assigned place confined him. Rigaltius says: Thus in Epistles IV and LXXXI he excuses himself on account of the conditions of the place—namely, the place within whose assigned boundaries he was confined.

This thing is not execrable to us. Rigaltius says: So far is it from being execrable to us that it ought to be accepted as a sacrament of eternal salvation.

Whose entire hope is in the wood. Rigaltius says: That is, in Christ, who hung upon the wood for sinners. Thus Paul glories in the cross, that is, in the crucified Lord.

The sacrament of our salvation. Rigaltius says: In this sense all the things Christ performed in the flesh are sacraments of [Col. 1081C] our salvation.

And the places that [produce] gold. It is by no means necessary that the confessors were condemned to gold or silver mines; it is enough that those incitements to evil are customarily dug from the earth’s innards. Certainly Pliny says in Book IV that Numidia is distinguished for the production of nothing except Numidian marble and wild beasts.

Crossbars. Rigaltius says: He calls those things “crossbars” which restrain and impede “from the side” (ἐκ πλαγίου). Vitruvius, Book VIII, chapter 6, and Book X, chapter 11. Chains adapt themselves to every movement by means of the links of which they consist; but crosswise iron bars inserted between fetters twist like wooden neck-yokes.

The hair of the half-shorn head bristles. Rigaltius says: By its deformity it strikes horror into those who see it. In the following Epistle: “You have made yourself like the hair of a half-shorn head.” Horace: “His hair cropped by an uneven barber.” Thus those condemned to the oars are shaved so that, if they attempt to escape by flight, they can be recognized and brought back.

[Col. 1081D] No opportunity to offer is granted. This privilege was not denied to martyrs, however harshly treated in the Decian persecution. See Epistle IV.

To premeditate an answer. “To rehearse beforehand how to make one’s defense” (προμελετᾶν ἀπολογηθῆναι). This translation has been discussed elsewhere.

Sixtyfold fruit. The hundredfold yield of martyrs and sixtyfold yield of virgins were discussed in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*.

To stand awaiting God’s promised reward. To this standing is opposed, in the book *On the Lapsed*, “to stand awaiting pardon.” Moreover, we have repeatedly observed that, according to the opinion of the ancient Church, martyrs by a special privilege attain consummation without awaiting the day of judgment. Hence below he calls them “all prepared for divine and heavenly glory”—that is, for martyrdom.

These darknesses of the world. These perhaps exist beneath the open sky and shining sun; they are more oppressive than those felt by men condemned to the mines and buried within the earth’s innards.

[Col. 1082A] Against the wrongs of heretics. It was observed above that these Numidians stood with Cyprian in the council on the question of the baptism of heretics.

## IN THE YEAR 257. EPISTLE LXXVII

To uncover hidden sacraments. Rigaltius says: The secrets, mysteries, difficulties, and hidden meanings of Sacred Scripture: the uncertain and hidden things of divine wisdom.

To come to belief. Rigaltius says: To the Christian faith.

Helpers one of another. Rigaltius says: Mutually helping one another. Above, Epistle LXIV: “coming one to another.”

## EPISTLE LXXVIII

According to its breadth. Rigaltius says: By “breadth of breast” he means the breast of a holy man, which is customarily [Col. 1082B] fruitful and magnificent in praises of God and good works.

We have received the sacrifice that you sent from Quirinus and from yourself. This is mentioned in the preceding Epistle, and perhaps in the books dedicated to Quirinus.

With a clean work. That is, with a clean creature or animal. He appears to have read “from every creature” (ἀπὸ πάσης κτίσεως) instead of “from all the cattle” (πάντων τῶν κτηνῶν).

So also may he look upon yours. Rigaltius says: In the following Epistle: “And it will be in the time of their visitation.”

## EPISTLE LXXIX

We have received an amount under the name of an offering. Rigaltius says: The sum of money that each man contributed from his own resources; or which Cyprian sent from his own private means. We have commented on this at the preceding Epistles.

I, Felix, have written. This reading appears altogether worthy of acceptance; for it would be wholly contrary to [Col. 1082C] common usage if Felix, who appears first in the heading of the Epistle, were passed over entirely at its close. Indeed, it appears quite inappropriate that the others who had either subscribed or read it should be mentioned, while the man who wrote it was omitted. It is not easy to conjecture who Eutychianus is, whom Bishop Polianus calls “lord.” It is a sufficiently common form of salutation for someone to be called “lord brother.” See Epistle LXXVII and elsewhere.

## EPISTLE LXXX

Under the stroke of the contest. Rigaltius says: In the following Epistle he will say: “at that moment of confession.”

That Valerian had sent a rescript to the Senate. This remarkable change of fortune should not, it seems, be passed over in silence. This is that Emperor Valerian concerning whom Trebellius Pollio relates: “Noble by birth, the son of Valerius, formerly censor, and advancing in his day through every rank of dignity to the highest summit on earth, his praiseworthy life of seventy years had risen to such glory that, after discharging all honors and magistracies with distinction, he became emperor—not, as usually happens, through a disorderly concourse of the people or the clamor of soldiers, but by right of merit and, as it were, by the unanimous judgment of the whole world. Indeed, had everyone been given the power to declare whom they wished as emperor, no other man would have been chosen. And so that the greatness of Valerian’s public merits may be known, I shall set forth the decrees of the Senate by which all may perceive what the most august order always judged concerning him.

“On October 27, in the consulship of the two Decii, when a meeting of the Senate was being held in the Temple of Castor on account of imperial letters and individual opinions were being taken as to whom the censorship should be entrusted—for the Decii had placed this within the power of the most august Senate—when the praetor first proclaimed, ‘What is your judgment, Conscript Fathers, concerning the choice of a censor?’ and had asked the man who was then chief of the Senate for his opinion, Valerian being absent—for he was serving in the field with Decius—all cried out with one voice, interrupting the customary procedure for delivering opinions: ‘Valerian’s life is itself a censorship. Let him judge concerning everyone, for he is better than everyone. [Col. 1083A] Let him judge concerning the Senate, for he has no crime. Let him deliver judgment concerning our life, for nothing can be alleged against him. Valerian was a censor from his earliest childhood. Valerian was a censor throughout his entire life. A prudent senator, a modest senator, a dignified senator; a friend of the good, an enemy of tyrants, a foe of crimes, a foe of vices. We all accept this man as censor; we all wish to imitate him. Foremost in lineage, noble in blood, blameless in life, renowned for learning, singular in conduct, an exemplar of antiquity.’ When these words had been repeated many times, they all added [their assent], and thus the meeting was adjourned.”

It adds to this man’s praise that he was exceedingly favorable to Christians, so that, according to Dionysius of Alexandria, “he was gentle and friendly toward the people of God. For no other among the emperors before him was so favorably and kindly disposed toward them—not even those who were said openly to have become Christians—as he manifestly was at the beginning of his reign, receiving them with the greatest familiarity and affection. His entire household was filled with worshipers of God and was a church of God” (ἤπιος καὶ φιλόφρων πρὸς τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τοῦ θεοῦ· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄλλος τις οὕτω τῶν πρὸ αὐτοῦ βασιλέων εὐμενῶς καὶ δεξιῶς πρὸς αὐτοὺς διετέθη· οὐδ’ οἱ λεχθέντες ἀναφανδὸν χριστιανοὶ γεγονέναι, ὡς ἐκεῖνος οἰκειότατα ἐν ἀρχῇ καὶ προσφιλέστατα φανερὸς ἦν αὐτοὺς ἀποδεχόμενος· καὶ πᾶς ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ θεοσεβῶν πεπλήρωται, καὶ ἦν ἐκκλησία θεοῦ).

But after all this, led astray by the counsels of Macrianus, an impious man and magician, he turned to attacking [Col. 1083B] the Church. Becoming entangled in the Persian war and betrayed by that very Macrianus who had instigated the counsels against the Church, he fell into the power of the barbarian enemy. There, for as long as he lived, he endured the most wretched servitude and served as a mounting-block: the unrestrained victor trod upon him and, when about to mount his horse, raised himself by placing his foot upon Valerian’s neck as he bent his back. Neither the intercession of the kings who attended the Persian, nor fear of the Roman people and of Valerian’s sons who succeeded him in the empire, availed anything. Indeed, he would have perished utterly unavenged had not Odaenathus of Palmyra assembled an army and broken the assault of the raging barbarian, and had he not moreover utterly destroyed the wretched remnants of Macrianus’ family after Macrianus was slain by Aureolus.

Let them be punished immediately. Rigaltius says: Sometimes a day for denial—that is, for renouncing Christ—was appointed, as in the book *On the Lapsed*: “when the day appointed for those who were to deny had passed.”

Registered on the imperial estates. The reading of the Verona manuscript, which has *et scripti* (“and enrolled”), leads toward the more [Col. 1083C] approved reading *ascripti* (“registered”). It is sufficiently well known from the writers on imperial law what sort of servitude was borne by the *ascripticii glebae*, those registered to the soil.

The Emperor Valerian, in his address. Rigaltius says: He here calls an “address” what he said above Caesar had sent in a rescript. An emperor, moreover, by delivering an address in the Senate, advised the Senate to decree what then appeared to serve the public interest. Of that kind is Antoninus’ address concerning gifts between husband and wife, which Ulpian records. Whatever was formerly proposed in the Senate by emperors with the prerogative of an oracle, as something likely to conduce to the commonwealth’s advantage, was called an “address”; hence all constitutions inscribed to the Senate were called addresses of the emperors. Thus in a law of Theodosius and Valens addressed to the Senate it is said: “By this address we decree that a father shall succeed even to infant children, whether, when the child’s mother died, he fulfilled the duty of entering upon the inheritance or seeking possession of the goods, or neglected these things; when his infant child dies, he shall succeed [Col. 1083D] without ambiguity, at whatever age.”

In the Cemetery. That is, the open ground where he had assembled with the Christian people for the solemn worship of God, despite the emperor Valerian’s prohibition; hence, to inspire greater terror, punishment was inflicted upon him in that very place. The *Roman Martyrology* reports that he suffered in the cemetery of Callistus, where the martyrdom of Cornelius was also commemorated, as was that of blessed Cyprian. This is said to have been done so that the holy prelates who, during the Decian persecution, had been united by holiness of life, strength of spirit, and frequent correspondence with one another, and had been crowned on the same day, should not be separated even in their place of veneration. I reproduce the words of Francesco Maria Florentini in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*.

And with him, Quartus. This man appears to have been a presbyter, or else someone bearing that name, since he is designated without any qualification. The additions commonly made concerning Felix, Agapetus, Donatianus, Faustinus, Praetextatus, Laurentius, Hippolytus, Afra, and the Soldiers [Col. 1084A] 165 require an authority more trustworthy than the commonly circulated martyrologies.

The Prefects in the City. It was the duty of the prefect of the city to suppress unlawful associations; but Cyprian appears to understand by this designation all the other magistrates as well.

## LETTER LXXXI

That *frumentarii* had been sent to take me to Utica. While traveling to Utica, the proconsul dispatched his *frumentarii* to arrest Cyprian; likewise, after returning to Carthage, he employed the services of mounted orderlies. Both were suitable agents for deadly commands. Thus, pace Rigaltius, what is read here and in the Acts is perfectly consistent. Rigaltius says:

> The *Life of Cyprian*, said to have been written by his deacon Pontius, displays the charm of rhetorical diction more than the care of historical narration. Thus it says nothing of the deeds of that most holy man which are contained in his own Letters, nor even of this circumstance pertaining to his martyrdom: that when he learned that the *frumentarii* were looking for him in order to take him to Utica, [Col. 1084B] he concealed himself for a time, lest he be taken away from his own Carthaginians, before whose eyes he wished to undergo martyrdom, so that by his own example in death he might confirm what in speech and writing he had taught must be endured for Christ’s name. He therefore remained hidden in a secluded retreat. For so he himself says in this Letter. But he does not say where he had his retreat—prudently, certainly, for it would not then have been safe for him to do so. Yet after the contest had ended in his death, when Pontius the deacon, who had also been his companion and intimate in exile, transmitted his bishop’s life to posterity, who could suppose that he performed this task so meagerly and inadequately as not to indicate the place to which Cyprian had withdrawn on the advice of his dearest friends—indeed, to omit the entire history of this withdrawal? For what we read in the circulating treatise of Pontius, that he was exiled to Curubis, has nothing to do with the retreat under discussion here. Nor should one be said to have hidden from the *frumentarii* when he moved to the place to which he had been ordered to go into exile.

> Moreover, if anyone misses either fidelity or diligence in that little work on Cyprian’s life, he must necessarily feel the same dissatisfaction concerning the Acts of the Passion published by Lazius and Morellius. [Col. 1084C] For they do not present this withdrawal of Cyprian from his gardens; they say only that, after returning from exile to his gardens, he was summoned from there and taken to the proconsul. Nor does Augustine mention the *frumentarii*, since he followed certain martyrologies resembling those Acts. For he related that Cyprian was carried by carriage to his passion between two attendants; the Acts say that two senior officials came to the martyr, an orderly of the staff and a mounted orderly. These things plainly betray the ignorance or negligence of the writers of that period.

> Far from the mark has strayed the man who suspects that by metaphor the *frumentarii* here mean the very lictors who dragged Christians to execution, as though, after the manner of grain-dealers, they were storing the Lord’s grain in the Lord’s granary. Anyone may laugh all the more at this conjecture when the correct interpretation is sufficiently plain and easy. It required no great scholarly labor to perceive that by *frumentarii* Cyprian here meant none other than that class of men who, enrolled among the military services under the pretext of procuring grain throughout the various provinces, listened and investigated whether anything was being stirred up against the majesty of Caesar or of the Roman people, [Col. 1084D] arrested the authors of plots and disturbances, and took them wherever they had been ordered, or even killed them on the spot.
