In Eusebius, *History*, book VI, there is a letter of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, writing to a certain Germanus in these words: “Sabinus”—he was prefect under Decius—“sent a *frumentarius* to search for me” (φρουμετάριον ἔπεμψεν εἰς ἀναζήτησίν μου). And in many passages in Spartianus, Lampridius, and Capitolinus, *frumentarii* are found to signify scouts or spies—messengers (ἀγγελιαφόρους), overseers (ἐπόπτηρας), observers (διόπτας), investigators (ἐρευνητάς), and secret agents (κατασκόπους). Thus the emperor Hadrian was so inquisitive, not only about his own household but also about those of his friends, that through the *frumentarii* he investigated every secret; nor did his friends realize that the emperor knew of their private lives until the emperor himself revealed it. Famous is the passage of Capitolinus concerning Maximinus: “Instructions were sent in writing to all the provinces, with *frumentarii* dispatched, that anyone who had assisted Maximinus was to be counted among the public enemies.” [Col. 1085A] Jerome, on Obadiah, chapter I: “For those whom they now call *agentes in rebus* or mounted couriers, the ancients called *frumentarii*.” See what is said concerning the inquisitive *beneficiarii* in the notes on Tertullian.

His honor will be impaired. Martyrs were an honor to their churches and were likewise to be honored by them. But owing to the disposition of men, to whom nothing moderate is pleasing, respect readily passed into worship, to such an extent that souls lying beneath the altar were everywhere brought close to altars, and “angels of the churches” crowned with martyrdom were thereafter regarded as the guardian angels of their cities. Concerning our Cyprian as the avenger of his Carthaginian people, there is a memorable account in Procopius, *History of the Vandal War*, book II, chapter 1:

> During the reign of Huneric, the Vandals seized Cyprian’s church after using violence against the Christians; they immediately drove the priests from it with great dishonor and thereafter themselves tended the sacred things as though these belonged to the Arians. While the Libyans were distressed and deeply troubled by this, Cyprian, they say, often appeared in a dream and instructed them that the Christians should have no anxiety at all concerning him, for in the course of time he himself would become their avenger. When this report had circulated [Col. 1085B] and reached all the Libyans, they waited expectantly for some event that would befall the Vandals because of these sacred places, although they could not determine how the vision in the dream would be fulfilled for them.

> Now, when the emperor’s fleet arrived in Libya—for the recurring anniversary was already at hand, and on the following day they were to celebrate Cyprian’s festival—the Arian priests, although [someone] had then led the Vandals toward Decimum [text corrupt], thoroughly cleansed the entire sanctuary, hung up the finest of the votive offerings there, prepared the lamps, brought the sacred vessels out of the storerooms, and arranged everything with exact care so that each article was suitably ready for its proper use. But events at Decimum happened as I have already explained: the Arian priests fled and departed, while the Christians whose practice regarding the faith was orthodox came to Cyprian’s church, lit all the lamps, and tended the sacred things according to the customary rite by which these ceremonies were performed. Thus what the dream-vision had foretold became known to everyone.

Victor of Vita deals with this expulsion of the orthodox from the churches dedicated to Cyprian.

[Col. 1085C] I, a bishop placed over another church. He presided by metropolitan right over all the churches of Africa; for in Letter XLVI he says: “Our province extends more widely, for it has Numidia and the two Mauretanias joined to it.” Yet episcopal jurisdiction was bound by a certain narrower bond. In the bishop’s words the prayers of the whole Church were formally addressed to God; likewise in his words its solemn confession was established. Therefore, above all, that confession which was sealed with blood ought to be made by the bishop himself. Thus in Letter LX he says that in Cornelius “the entire Roman Church confessed.”

Sentence received on account of the confession. Rigaltius says: “That is, on account of the confession of the name—namely, the Christian name.” Augustine, *Against the Letter of Gaudentius*: “Instructed by these sacred writings, blessed Cyprian said in his Confession: ‘Discipline forbids anyone to offer himself.’”

And to suffer there. Rigaltius says: “Among you, in the sight of the Church over which God has placed me.”

Nor should any of you voluntarily offer himself to the pagans. Those who provoke the persecutors’ fury and bring death upon themselves should be called Circumcellions rather than martyrs. [Col. 1085D] And indeed such rashness most often ended unhappily. Those who were excessively eager to enter the contest were equally precipitate in shrinking from it, and this headlong course merely prepared the step toward a fall. Rightly, therefore, did the Church apply a brake to this growing evil, lest overheated and arrogant men combine public disaster with their private ruin. The theologians also rightly maintain that men ought not unconditionally to ask God, even in their prayers, that they become martyrs, since such an act, without the reservation of the divine good pleasure, would appear to flow from presumption or rashness rather than from true hope, faith, or Christian charity.

The Fathers of Elvira themselves, though by no means favorably disposed toward images, decreed in canon 60:

> If anyone breaks idols and is killed on the spot, since this is not written in the Gospel nor is it found ever to have been done under the Apostles, it has been decided that he is not to be received into the number of the martyrs.

[Col. 1086A] Rigaltius says: “Augustine relates that Cyprian said this in his Confession, in the passage already cited.” And in the ancient Acts:

> When the proconsul Paternus made inquiry, Cyprian said: “Since discipline forbids anyone voluntarily to offer himself, and since this is likewise displeasing to your own judicial authority, they cannot present themselves of their own accord; but if sought by you, they will be found”—that is, in their own cities.

The antiquity of these Acts is therefore confirmed by the clear testimony of this great man. One might indeed wish that the things we know to have been ancient were likewise preserved in an authentic form.

We shall make arrangements by common counsel. Rigaltius says:

> He does not insist so carefully upon the phrase “by common counsel” without reason. He foresaw the vices of monarchy and recoiled from the seedbed of the greatest evil. Yet perhaps a man may be said to consult for the common good when he alone provides for the public interest.

## ABOUT THE YEAR 246  
## TO DONATUS: BOOK ON THE GRACE OF GOD

Caecilius Cyprianus. The same man as Thascius. [Col. 1086B] See Letter LXVII, numbered 69 by Pamelius, and also the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Cyprian*. Hence it was with too little judgment that, in the Roman synod of seventy bishops attributed to Gelasius, the works of the martyr Cyprian were admitted, while the writings of Thascius Cyprian were condemned as apocryphal.

To Donatus. The Speyer edition, almost contemporary with the invention of printing, has this title: *The Book of Cyprian to Donatus*. And indeed very many manuscript codices agree; in them the customary opening words of an epistolary composition and the introductory salutation are often absent at the very beginning. Moreover, in no copies, whether printed or manuscript, is a valedictory conclusion added anywhere. I acknowledge that St. Augustine calls it a letter; but it should equally be remembered that he commonly designates by that same title the treatises *On the Lord’s Prayer*, *On Mortality*, *On Works and Almsgiving*, *On the Dress of Virgins*, and *On Patience*. This was presumably because, after writing those books, the author sent them to a particular friend or to the community of the whole Church, [Col. 1086C] as is known to have happened in many cases; or because short treatises and pamphlets that do not exceed the dimensions of a letter are commonly called letters.

The character of this work is entirely foreign to the epistolary form, and it actually appears to have been written with the same purpose as Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, and similar works, as a defense of the Christian religion. For, as the very learned Rigaltius rightly observes, more educated men, when first professing their allegiance to the Church, were accustomed to compose defenses of the sect they had embraced and of their own way of life. But what the same learned man adds—that in Augustine’s time this work was customarily placed first in the copies, and that this is evident from the book *On Christian Doctrine*—is not equally clear. For in the passage cited, that most holy Father quotes it in the following form: “in a certain Letter”; but if he had derived the designation from its order, he would undoubtedly have called it “the first.” Indeed, the order of this author’s works varies so greatly that neither in printed books nor in manuscripts—and I speak of a fact most thoroughly ascertained—does either this treatise or any other occupy a fixed place.

[Col. 1086D] On the Grace of God. We retain this title as the simplest and as having been supplied by Cyprian himself, with this preliminary observation: this title and almost all the others were added according to the fancy of copyists. For Pontius appears certainly to have referred to this work when he said: “Who would show the benefit of grace advancing through faith?” Although in that passage his purpose is to undertake a defense of the blessed martyr’s withdrawal, adducing those writings of which the Church of God would have been deprived if Cyprian had been taken away in the first tempest of the Decian persecution, nevertheless, since the earlier writings also borrowed authority and illumination from the events subsequently accomplished during the ten years after that withdrawal, Pontius not rashly credited them as well to that withdrawal and to the preservation obtained through it.

### I

You advise me well. Rufinus mentions this passage in the prologue to Origen’s homilies on Numbers, saying: “I shall use for you, brother, the words of the blessed martyr: ‘You advise me well, dearest Donatus.’”

[Col. 1087A] I remember that I promised. These words and many that follow appear to have been inserted for ornament, after the example of the writings of Plato and Cicero, and especially of Minucius Felix in his *Octavius*, whom Cyprian manifestly imitates throughout this entire framework. Cicero reminds Varro of this genre of writing in the preface to the *Academic Questions*: “I think that when you read it, you will marvel that we said to one another what we never actually said; but you know the convention of dialogues.”

Thus some pedant, lest anything perhaps be lacking, foolishly fabricated in Donatus’s name a letter that would provide an entrance to Cyprian’s reply. Although found in a single copy, it nevertheless earned credence from Pamelius, with his characteristic readiness, and praise from Cardinal Baronius. Lest the reader suspect that a fraud has been played upon him, I shall not begrudge the inclusion of this excellent little letter. It reads as follows:

> I believe you remember, most holy Cyprian, how talkative we were among the orators: one understanding, one thought, an undivided course of reading. [Col. 1087B] Why, then, are we not strengthened in spirit in the same way through divine reading? Or was it not always our intention that we should believe together?

With the vintage season granting leisure. Although Christians regarded the festivals of the pagans as impious and profane, they judged the vintage holidays more leniently, since these provided relief after the labors of the harvest rather than professing the worship of deities. For that reason the Christian emperors retained them while abolishing other festivals. Law *All Days*, Code, *On Holidays*:

> It shall be lawful for those days alone to remain holidays which the more indulgent year accepts in two months as a rest from labor, for mitigating the summer heat and gathering the produce of autumn, etc.

For carefully composed narratives—that is, discourse composed with study and care, such as the “stories” (μῦθοι) of the rhetoricians commonly are. Below it is said, “we offer studied compositions to your ears”; and Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*: “Where pleasure is, there is interest, through which, of course, pleasure acquires its savor; where interest is, there is also rivalry, through which interest acquires its savor.” By the word *fabula*, however, the narration of an event is designated. Thus Minucius Felix: “We pursued our journey with stories that beguiled the way,” etc.

[Col. 1087C] Let us seek this seat. St. Augustine adduces this passage as an example of pictorial diction overflowing in a frothy circuit of words. Cyprian is perhaps depicting those very gardens which Pontius records that he sold upon his conversion to the faith and to which he withdrew shortly before his martyrdom.

### II

Let it enter into your breast. So that I may earn your goodwill.

Divine indulgence. By this expression our author everywhere understands divine grace, as does Tertullian. Because of its marvelous and sudden effects, it is immediately called “the benefit of grace.” But this entire passage was taken from Tertullian, *On Baptism*: “Is it not marvelous that death should be washed away by bathing?” And shortly afterward: “We too marvel, but because we believe; unbelief, on the other hand, marvels and does not believe, for it marvels at simple things as though they were empty, and at magnificent things as though they were impossible,” etc.

Would put off. That is, would lay aside—a sense very commonly used by our author [Col. 1087D] and by Tertullian.

Native by the corruption of matter. Natural evils that are, as it were, overlaid by the decay and filth of the old man from whom they have arisen. To these are opposed voluntary evils, transferred through long habit into a second nature, which our author calls “acquired.” The third Bodleian codex not unsuitably reads “begotten” (*genitum*); but I do not readily alter the text.

### III

This death of crimes. Baptism, namely, in which we die with Christ: Romans 6:4; Colossians 2:12—yet in such a way that thereafter we live to God and to his righteousness, as the Apostle subsequently concludes in the passages just cited and commonly elsewhere.

Has begun to belong to faith. If we now do anything worthy of praise, it must be ascribed to divine grace; if we committed anything in the past, the most merciful God will impute it to human error. See Acts 17:30; 1 Timothy 1:13–14.

Shone upon. This reading is approved and is derived from the African dialect. Thus Tertullian, *On the Soul*: “The emanation of Valentinus shone the seed of wisdom upon the soul.” [Col. 1088A] Nevertheless, the reading “flowed in,” which others restored, is not to be wholly rejected. Minucius Felix: “Though weights founded the earth, and though liquid flowed into the sea,” etc. But “shone within” could also have been said.

### IV

—With unfallen firmness. Stable, upright, without falling. In the same form Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, says: “if a brother has died without children.” By this word he appears to censure those who have fallen into some shameful act.

It is granted into freedom. You can do as much as you believe. Thus below: “The Spirit received enters into possession of its freedom,” and elsewhere: “Giving to believers as much as each believes himself able to receive.” See chapter 42, book III, *To Quirinus*.

For the healing of those in pain. The formerly received reading was “in the marrow of the young,” etc.—a somewhat harsh phrase, but by no means foreign to the African dialect. The sense would certainly proceed very suitably in this way: the author would say that baptism has bestowed a power by which the venom of poisons implanted by nature in our innermost marrow is extinguished, and the stain of the mind, conceived by the will from evil habits, is cleansed. This follows the same thought as the words above: [Col. 1088B] “Or what is native through the corruption of matter,” etc. But I alter nothing.

Unclean and wandering spirits. Demons are everywhere called “unclean spirits” in the Gospel; they are likewise also called wandering spirits: Job 1; Matthew 12:43; 1 Peter 5:8. But after the Lord’s promise in Mark, final chapter, verse 17, that these signs would follow those who believed—that in his name they would cast out demons, etc.—and after that right and power was held to belong to all ordinary Christians, so that Tertullian in the *Apologeticus* presumed to pledge that if anyone possessed by a demon were ordered by any Christian whatever to speak, that spirit would as truly confess itself a demon in the one case as elsewhere falsely a god; and that, “if they do not confess themselves demons, not daring to lie to a Christian, then shed the blood of that most insolent Christian on the spot”—it consequently happened that, as among the Jews in Acts 19:13, scoundrels and impostors passed themselves off as exorcists.

They are even censured in imperial law, Digest, law I, title *On Extraordinary Proceedings*: “If he has enchanted, if he has uttered an imprecation, if—to use the common word of impostors—he has exorcized.” [Col. 1088C] To confront this evil, the Church arranged for approved men to be assigned to this office. Moreover, because very many pagans had wholly enslaved themselves to the power of demons through abominable mysteries, they could not be claimed for the service of Christ—which is true freedom—until the possessor of bad faith had been expelled and a place left for a better guest. Consequently, the same men who presided over the instruction of catechumens likewise discharged the office of exorcists.

See canon X of Antioch and canon XXVI of Laodicea, where, at the mention of the exorcist, Balsamon says: “Exorcists, that is, catechists” (ἐφορκισταὶ ἤτοι κατηχηταί); and: “Some attempted to exorcize—that is, to catechize unbelievers—without having received this through episcopal laying on of hands” (τινὲς ἐπεχείρουν ἐφορκίζειν, τουτέστι κατηχεῖν ἀπίστους, μὴ λαβόντες τοῦτο δι’ ἐπισκοπῆς χειροθεσίας), etc. Harmenopulus likewise, in the *Epitome of the Canons*, section I, title 9, interprets “exorcists” as “catechists” (ἐξορκισταί, κατηχηταί). In the Theodosian Code, law 121, *On Decurions*, exorcists, as clergy of higher rank, are exempted from civil burdens. The formula for ordaining an exorcist is found in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 7. Moreover, not only presbyters but even bishops themselves performed this office when occasion offered. Paulinus relates this of Ambrose, Possidius of Augustine, [Col. 1088D] to omit others.

A hidden blow. Below, in *To Demetrianus*, he says that they are “beaten with spiritual scourges,” and in *On Idolatry*, “with the scourges of a hidden majesty’s operation.” Minucius Felix likewise:

> When adjured by the true and only God, they unwillingly and wretchedly shudder within the bodies, and either leap out at once or vanish by degrees, according as the sufferer’s faith assists or the healer’s grace breathes upon him.

Not yet the body and its members. Meanwhile, before we have been changed. Although we are still burdened with the load of the body, we are nevertheless not wholly blinded by the cloud of the world. The Holy Spirit promises many things for the future, but also makes many things present. We do indeed hope, but we also possess.

### V

Wars divided everywhere. Below he says: “after manifold battles scattered throughout the whole world.”

### VI

It is filled out into substance. The Speyer and Rembolt editions read: “The body is filled out dry with stronger foods, and with the dew of fat.” [Col. 1089A] If only other editors had been willing to err so simply and candidly—namely, by setting down what they found in their copy—for from that point the passage to the true reading would have been very easy. But after Erasmus, according to his critical method, had substituted “the continual odor,” forgetting *muscular masses*, for “the dew of fat,” and after other copyists with equal success emended it to “the ruin of the body,” the wound was almost beyond hope and, had the earliest copies not been consulted, wholly incurable.

In costly clothing. Juvenal, *Satire* 3, refers to this: “the *pinnirapi* and well-dressed young men” [syntax fragment]. It contributed to luxury that the eyes should feast not merely upon human but upon noble blood, and that a handsome face and splendid clothing should commend the spectacle. Moreover, it is established from the Acts of Felicitas and Perpetua, upon whom the robe of Saturn was placed, that the condemned were customarily dressed in a garment sacred to the god for whom the games were held.

To the beasts without any crime. Pamelius and Rigaltius read: “Beasts fight against beasts.” But the author is speaking of human beings, whom he should hardly be thought to have called beasts by means of a feeble, popular insult.

[Col. 1089B] The mother also buys. She purchases a convenient seat. Perhaps she would not have attended the spectacle unless invited by the danger to her son.

### VII

The ancient crimes of poems. Pamelius and Rigaltius read: “Ancient crimes in song.” Supported by the manuscripts, with the learned Gronovius agreeing, I have judged that their reading should be abandoned.

In incestuous acts, error. Pace Rigaltius and others who substituted “horror,” I follow the manuscripts and Gronovius. The matter is well known: the plots of almost all plays owe their existence to mistakes. Hence the banquet of Thyestes, the parricides of Hercules and Theseus, and the incest of Oedipus, which fills both pages of the tragic writers and which Cyprian has in view in this passage. Tertullian confirms this reading when, speaking of this very matter in the *Apologeticus*, he says: “As soon as an error has struck, thereafter the propagated branch of incest will advance, the lineage creeping onward together with the crime.” And again, speaking of incest in *To the Nations*, he has: “Nor is it opposed to ignorance, error, or accident,” etc.

Yet the substitution of “horror” [Col. 1089C] for “error” is not an isolated mistake. The Speyer edition, Rembolt, and Erasmus read above: “the horrors of the former life,” instead of “the errors.”

The endurance of incestuous vileness. Every abominable sexual practice, even if not committed with relatives, is so called. Thus violated Vestal virgins were to be prosecuted for incest. Yet meanwhile none are so closely related as those of the same sex, among whom, as our author rightly says, sin is committed against the right and covenant of birth.

### VIII

He believes him privy to it. That is, one who is privy only to himself and whom an informer cannot bring before the court.

Acting in concert with vices. Taking the side of vice and worthy of the worst morals.

### IX

The Twelve Tables. After a colony of Roman citizens was established at Carthage, that city thereafter became Rome’s rival in another form. Hence among them likewise were theaters, baths, forums, the laws of the Twelve Tables, and even a Capitol. See below, *On the Lapsed*.

[Col. 1089D] Innocence is not preserved even there where it is defended. “Protected,” “preserved.”

By a capital fraud. Such, namely, as is excepted under the Digest, *On the Aediles’ Edict*. A capital penalty is one that entails death or loss of citizenship: law CIII, *On the Meaning of Words*. Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 9, calls idolatry, blasphemy, homicide, adultery, fornication, false testimony, and fraud the seven stains of capital sins. Thus in *On Repentance*: “The graver and deadly offenses that do not obtain pardon—homicide, idolatry, fraud, denial, blasphemy, and certainly adultery and fornication, and any other violation of God’s temple.” These are scarcely anything other than the three notorious crimes divided into various branches. For the Catholic Church itself allowed a single penance for these.

A lie of crimes. False accusations. Thus Tertullian, *On the Crown*: “If the devil fabricates a lie of divinity, [Col. 1090A] being from the beginning a liar in this form also, he had doubtless himself foreseen those in whom the lie of divinity would be practiced.”

The guilty do not perish together with the innocent. By a double injustice: the innocent perish and the wicked are preserved.

A deserter, he defiled his follower. He left him exposed.

### X

Of a deceptive spectacle. Distributions of money, gift-baskets, things thrown to the crowd, and remissions of taxes truly benefit the people to whom they are given; spectacles, however, merely corrupt them. It is therefore fitting that in gifts of this kind both parties should alike gain nothing, and that the candidate for office should lose what the people received without benefit.

### XIV

The gift of the Lord. Baptism, namely. Elsewhere here it is everywhere called the Grace of God; below, “the freely given gift from God.”

Let him see to what is against us. This form of expression is virtually constant in our author and in Tertullian. In the *Apologeticus*: “Let the outward form be what it may, provided that the quality of the material is the same; [Col. 1090B] let the shape be what it may, provided that it is the very body of God.”

### XV

Constant prayer or reading. What follows proves that the reading of the Holy Scriptures is meant. For in those centuries those sacred volumes were not forbidden to laypeople, still less to the newly baptized.

Let us illuminate with the light of righteousness. I agree with the learned Gronovius, who judges that this is how the passage should be read, with the manuscript copies supporting him. In the book *On Works and Almsgiving* it is said: “The sun radiates; the day gives light,” just as in this very passage, one or two lines earlier, very many codices read. Hence among writers of the Middle Ages, “to illuminate” means to paint, and in our vernacular language an illuminator is called a painter. Meanwhile, it must not be concealed that both “to enlighten” and “to illuminate” are read very frequently.

### XVI

From goodness, patience. Patience consonant with goodness and flowing from it—a manner of speaking virtually constant in Tertullian. In *Against Marcion*, book II, he says: “God alone is blessed by virtue of the property of incorruptibility.” In the book *On Patience*: “He reserves every display of wisdom as derived from patience.” [Col. 1090C] A little above our author says: “the freely given gift from God.”

The learned Gronovius suspects that the period should be framed thus: “A mind made compliant by the goodness of patience, secure in God through steadfast faith, is delighted by saving hearing.” The second codex belonging to the most learned Vossius supports this conjecture.

Undertake this duty according to custom. Tertullian describes this custom more fully in the *Apologeticus*:

> They do not recline at table before prayer to God is first tasted. They eat as much as hungry people desire; they drink as much as is useful to the chaste. They satisfy themselves as people who remember that they must worship God during the night also. They converse as people who know that God hears. After water for the hands and lights have been brought, each person is invited into the midst to sing to God, as he is able, either from the Holy Scriptures or from his own composition. From this it is proved how he has drunk. Prayer likewise concludes the banquet.

Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII, similarly says, in speaking of Christian conduct:

> His whole life is a holy festival. His sacrifices are prayers and praises; [Col. 1090D] before the meal there are readings of the Scriptures, and during the meal psalms and hymns (ἅπας ὁ βίος αὐτοῦ, πανήγυρις ἁγία· αὐτίκα θυσίαι μὲν αὐτῷ εὐχαί τε καὶ αἶνοι, καὶ πρὸ τῆς ἑστιάσεως ἐντεύξεις τῶν γραφῶν, ψαλμοὶ δὲ καὶ ὕμνοι παρὰ τὴν ἑστίασιν), etc.

That is, just as Christian piety derived other rites from the Jewish church, so it also borrowed this custom of sacred readings and the solemn giving of thanks over food. Indeed, this very practice was established by the public religions of humankind. “Before eating, men instituted the practice of offering a libation to the gods,” says Censorinus. Hence arose the custom among the pagans of branding as utterly impious and wicked those “who consumed sacrifices without offering them” (ἄθυτα ἱερὰ κατεσθίοντες) and those “without libations” (ἄσπονδοι). Consequently, in the writings of the ancients, *sacrificial victims* (ἱερεῖα) commonly denoted the flesh of animals.

All the less tolerable, therefore, are those who, without any preliminary prayer to God, hold dogs’ feasts and, like Harpies, swoop down upon the food set before them. Scaliger’s criticism in this passage consequently appears superfluous, when he says the period should be framed thus: “Undertake this duty rather with your own mouth.” Morellius followed him.

## YEAR 247  
## BOOK ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS

[Col. 1091A]

On the Vanity of Idols. What in the old printed editions was prefixed as a title should in fact have been called an Argument or summary of the contents of the ensuing work. We retain only those words that appear best suited to designate the writing. It should further be noted that the very same reasons which suggest that the little book *To Donatus* was composed by Cyprian immediately after he received the faith likewise assign the birth of this thoroughly apologetic treatise to the same period. Accordingly, since the former is assigned to the vintage holidays at the end of the year 246, the latter may reasonably be assigned to the beginning of the following year, that is, 247.

St. Jerome, Letter LXXXIV, *To Magnus*, adorns this treatise with a distinguished encomium: “In *That Idols Are Not Gods*, with what brevity, with what knowledge of every history, with what brilliance of words and thoughts did Cyprian strike home?” Meanwhile, it must not be concealed that quite a few passages were transferred here word for word from Tertullian, and very many from Minucius. [Col. 1091B] But the first Christians had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them, as is said in Acts 4:32; therefore no action for plagiarism could exist.

For this reason Athenagoras, Justin, Clement, Tatian, Arnobius, Augustine, and all the Fathers who wrote against pagan worship likewise fought with the same weapons. Indeed—and one might less readily have expected this—Varro, Cicero, and Pliny had used them before, not to mention the Greeks, as had other pagan writers everywhere. Hence St. Augustine, speaking of this very matter in the book *On Baptism, Against Petilian*, states with good reason:

> Cyprian, disputing about the one true God against the worshipers of many gods, adduces many testimonies from the books of those whom they regard as distinguished authors.

For what could be more suitable for removing the hostility of pagans who accused Christians of atheism because they despised the pagans’ deities, than [Col. 1091C] openly to demonstrate, by bringing forward the testimony of the most learned men among the pagans, that they had held the same view of the gods as the Christians?

Moreover, Pontius, designating this little book by sufficiently evident indications, says: “Through what work would the blasphemous pagans be defeated by having turned back upon themselves those charges which they cast against us?” We have explained above by what right that author mentioned this work, together with several others that preceded Cyprian’s withdrawal, in a wholly inappropriate place.

### I

They were once kings. Or at least royal offspring. Thus Ino, or Leucothoe, was the daughter of Cadmus, king of Thebes; the Tyndarids were sons of the king of Oebalia; Hercules was the son of Jupiter, etc. “For a mortal to help a mortal,” says Pliny, book II, chapter 7, “is godhood, and this is the road to eternal glory. By this road the Roman nobles advanced. By it now, with heavenly stride and together with his children, Vespasian Augustus, the greatest ruler of every age, proceeds, bringing aid to an exhausted world. This is the most ancient custom of returning thanks to benefactors: that they should be enrolled among the divinities.”

Cicero likewise, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II:

> Human life and common custom undertake to raise beneficent and outstanding [Col. 1091D] men to heaven through reputation and goodwill. Hence Hercules, hence Castor and Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber also, hence Romulus, etc.

He has similar statements in book III as well. Cyprian therefore rightly calls them gods—not those whom the wise worship, but those whom the common people worship.

### II

Castor and Pollux. If it were worth altering a matter of slight importance, one ought to substitute “the Castors” here; for so writes Minucius, from whom these words appear to have been taken, and very many manuscripts support that reading.

Hercules, so that he may put off the human being. “I do not see,” says the same Cicero, “how the man upon whom burning torches were cast on Mount Oeta, as Accius says, passed from that fire into his father’s eternal home.”

The cave of Jupiter in Crete. “Three Jupiters,” says Cicero in the passage cited above, “are enumerated, of whom the first and second were born in Arcadia; the third, the Cretan, was the son of Saturn, whose tomb is shown on that island.”

To stamp coins. Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 10: “By him tablets were first produced, [Col. 1092A] and coin was stamped with an image; hence he presides over the treasury.” Nevertheless, Servius Tullius was the first to strike coins at Rome, if Pliny is to be trusted.

Of rusticity. That is, of the countryside, although Papias distinguishes the terms: “Rusticity pertains to manners; rural labor pertains to work—the cultivation of the soil.”

The Moors, however. Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*: “Each province and city has its own god: Syria has Astarte, Arabia Dusares, Noricum Belenus, Africa Caelestis, and Mauretania its own petty kings.”

Worship. Thus Tertullian, *On Idolatry*: “Idolatry consists in the worship of human beings.”

Alexander M. Rigaltius contends that this is so, and that these passages in fact pertain to another Alexander, namely Polyhistor. This conjecture pleased him so greatly that he introduced it three times: here, of course, in his notes on Tertullian, and also on Minucius. Cyprian, Athenagoras, Minucius, and Augustine were therefore mistaken—as were even the most highly regarded pagan writers—all of whom refer to letters written by Alexander the Great to his mother Olympias [Col. 1092B], in which this secret concerning the origins of the divinities is said to have been wrung from the priests by fear of his power. Tertullian alone, however, if Rigaltius is to be believed, is said to have grasped the matter itself. Rigaltius shows that it should be attributed to the tutor of Cornelius Lentulus, since Tertullian says: “What the Egyptians relate, Alexander arranges, and his mother reads.” Here he wishes the words *Alexander arranges* to refer to a compiler (*syntaktēs*, συντάκτην), while the following words, *his mother reads*, he says clearly denote some writings or other dedicated to Alexander’s mother. For my part, I have not yet established that the Egyptian priests so greatly feared the power of a petty Greek slave, nor have I yet learned that Polyhistor dedicated a book to his impoverished mother. This one thing I know: among our writers the verb *digerere*, “to arrange,” implies nothing more than some manner of narrating a subject. Thus Tertullian says in his book *On Patience*: “If the discussion concerns some good, the subject requires that the contrary of that good also be reviewed; for you will more clearly illuminate what should be pursued if you similarly set forth what should be avoided,” etc. So too Pontius: “That the example may be set down in writing.” [Col. 1092C]

Moreover, who will believe that Cyprian could have erred in praising a volume which he regarded as distinguished? Or Athenagoras, who expressly says that these conversations with the priests took place “in Heliopolis, Memphis, and Thebes” (*en tē Hēliopolei, kai Memfei kai Thēbais*, ἐν τῇ Ἡλιοπόλει, καὶ Μέμφει καὶ Θήβαις)? Or that Augustine was mistaken, when he cites this letter three times in the books *On the City of God*, says that these things were disclosed to Alexander by the priest Leo, and admonishes his readers to consult the letter itself and recall what they have read? But let Plutarch settle the dispute, for he was, if anyone was, thoroughly versed in the affairs of Alexander and was an abundant witness in matters of history. In his *Life of Alexander* he says:

> “Alexander says in a letter to his mother that certain secret oracles were given to him, which he himself, upon his return, would disclose to her alone. It is also said that, after hearing Psammon the philosopher in Egypt, he especially approved this among the things stated: that all human beings are ruled by God, for that which governs and exercises dominion in each person is divine,” etc.  
> (*Alexandros en epistolē pros tēn mētera phēsin, gegonenai tinas autō manteias aporrhētous, has autos epanelthōn phrasei pros monēn ekeinēn; legetai de kai Psammōnos en Aigyptō tou philosophou diakousas, apodexasthai malista tōn lechthentōn, hoti pantes anthrōpoi basileuontai hypo theou, to gar archon en hekastō kai kratoun theion estin*, Ἀλέξανδρος ἐν ἐπιστολῇ πρὸς τὴν μητέρα φησὶν, γεγονέναι τινὰς αὐτῷ μαντείας ἀπορρήτους, ἃς αὐτὸς ἐπανελθὼν φράσει πρὸς μόνην ἐκείνην· λέγεται δὲ καὶ Ψάμμωνος ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ τοῦ φιλοσόφου διακούσας, ἀποδέξασθαι μάλιστα τῶν λεχθέντων, ὅτι πάντες ἄνθρωποι βασιλεύονται ὑπὸ θεοῦ, τὸ γὰρ ἄρχον ἐν ἑκάστῳ καὶ κρατοῦν θεῖόν ἐστιν*), etc.

**Why, then, are none born even today?** Pliny, book II, chapter 7:

> To believe that there are marriages among the gods, yet that in so long an age no one is born from them; and that some are always aged and gray-haired, [Col. 1092D] others young men and boys, some dark-skinned, winged, lame, hatched from eggs, and living and dying on alternate days—this is nearly the delirium of children.

### IV. Treachery prospered

That is, it succeeded happily. Thus below: “the greatness of the race prospered.” See Tertullian, *On the Shows*, and *Against Marcion*, book I.

**The goddess Cloacina also.** Tatius consecrated an image of Cloacina found in the Great Sewer; and because he did not know whose likeness it was, he gave it a name derived from the place. Arnobius, book I.

**Fear and Pallor.** Similarly, Cicero discusses the matter in book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*:

> Love, deceit, fear, toil, envy, fate, old age, death, darkness, misery, complaint, the Graces, fraud, obstinacy, the Fates, the Hesperides, dreams—all of whom they say were born of Erebus and Night. Either, therefore, these monsters must be approved, or the original ones must be abolished.

**From bereavements, Orbona.** All these words are absent from the most highly regarded manuscripts [Col. 1093A] and disturb the sense. Nevertheless, because they appear in the Beneventan, Veronese, and Corbie manuscripts and in at least one of the four Vossian manuscripts, we retain them. Orbona is mentioned by Pliny, book II, and Cicero, book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*. “Parents bereaved of their children are under the guardianship of Orbona,” says Arnobius. This perhaps gave rise to *Suburbanae*, which was the received reading. Or else, through reversal of the final letters, “from bereavements, Orbona” became “from a suburban bereavement.”

**But Mars is Thracian.** Lycophron calls him *Mamertus* (μαμερτόν).

**There is also Bald Venus.** Lactantius, book I, chapter 20:

> After the city had been captured by the Gauls, the Romans, while besieged on the Capitol, made artillery cords from the women’s hair and consecrated a temple to Bald Venus.

**Regulus observed the auspices.** Valerius Maximus, book I, in the chapter *On Religion Preserved*, says:

> In matters pertaining to the preservation of religion, I am inclined to think that Marcus Atilius Regulus surpassed everyone.

Then, after a few intervening words, he adds:

> The immortal gods could certainly have mitigated their savage cruelty; [Col. 1093B] but, so that the glory of Atilius might be more illustrious, they allowed the Carthaginians to act according to their own character.

**Mancinus maintained religious observance.** To this extent, namely: after prodigies had occurred to him at Lanuvium when he was about to depart for Spain, he became frightened, reversed his route, and made for Genoa. There, after boarding a small boat, he was frightened by another prodigy, which he nevertheless disregarded. See Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter *On Prodigies*.

**The ravenous chickens.** Cicero, book II of *On Divination*:

> Flaminius did not obey the auspices, and so perished with his army. But in the following year Paulus did obey them: did he therefore fall any less, together with his army, at the battle of Cannae?

**Gaius Caesar before.** Cicero, *On Divination*, book II:

> What of Caesar himself? When the chief haruspex warned him not to cross over into Africa before the winter solstice, did he not cross over? Had he not done so, all the enemy forces would have assembled in one place.

So too Suetonius, *Julius*, chapter 95.

### VI. The poets also knew these as demons

It should be noted that this word was formerly neutral in meaning, and indeed commendatory: they received the designation from knowledge no less than “intelligences” did. Hence in Holy Scripture evil spirits are called *demons* only five times [Col. 1093C], though everywhere they are called *demonia*. But after the Valentinians and other Gnostics proclaimed their *daimones* (δαίμονας), or Aeons, as the creators of the world and arbiters of affairs, the Fathers of the Church called evil spirits *demons*; good spirits, however, they always called angels.

**The foremost, Hostanes.** Pliny, book XXX, chapter 1:

> The first person who, so far as I find, produced a commentary on this subject was Ostanes, who accompanied Xerxes, king of the Persians, in the war which he brought upon Greece. He scattered, as it were, the seeds of this monstrous art, infecting in passing the world through every place he traveled. This Ostanes especially drove the peoples of Greece not merely to eagerness for this knowledge, but to madness.

**Plato and Hermes.** The former in the *Timaeus*, the latter in the *Poemander*.

### VII. They disturb sleep

To this perhaps pertain those words of the Apostle Jude: “Dreaming, they defile the flesh” (*enypniazomenoi sarka men miainousi*, ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι σάρκα μὲν μιαίνουσι).

### IX. But as for a temple

Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 10, has: “We spit upon temples no less than tombs.” Minucius [Col. 1093D] Felix: “They despise temples as tombs.” Arnobius likewise, in book I, Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*, and others among the Fathers inveigh against those sepulchers of the dead and enclosures of the divinities. Meanwhile, they always accepted churches—“upper rooms of the Lord” (*hyperōa Kyriaka*, ὑπερῷα Κυριακά), “houses of prayer” (*euktērious oikous*, Εὐκτηρίους οἴκους), precincts, and places sacred to the worship of almighty God. A similar observation may be made concerning the word *ara*, “sacrificial altar,” or *bōmos* (βωμός), from which Christians continually recoiled; but they freely embraced the name *altare*, “altar,” or *thysiastērion* (θυσιαστήριον).

**Do not seek a name for God.** “No one is able to utter a name for the ineffable God” (*onoma tō arrhētō theō oudeis echei eipein*, ὄνομα τῷ ἀρρήτῳ θεῷ οὐδεὶς ἔχει εἰπεῖν), etc. Justin, *Apology* II. Thus every name of God is *anekphōnēton* (ἀνεκφώνητον), “unutterable.” Minucius: “Do not seek a name for God; ‘God’ is his name.”

**The common people naturally confess God in many things.** This matter supplied the argument for a special treatise by Tertullian, namely *On the Testimony of the Soul*.

### XIV. That they might give eyes to the acknowledgment of the truth

The expression is borrowed from Tertullian:

> If a swallow has blinded its young, [Col. 1094A] it knows how to give them sight again with its own celandine.

He similarly uses this word in his book *On Modesty*.

**Which is Christ.** Now the members of his mystical body, and thereafter sharers in his glory.

## About the Year 248: *Testimonies to Quirinus against the Jews*

## Preface to the First Two Books

**It was necessary to comply.** That Cyprian wrote these treatises, and that they were formerly called the books of *Testimonies*, is attested not only by Bede, Gennadius, and other authors of later times, but also by Pelagius, Jerome, and Augustine. Pelagius, namely, when writing books of *Testimonies*, confesses that he is “an imitator, indeed a completer, of the work of the blessed martyr Cyprian, who wrote to Quirinus,” as Jerome says in book I, chapter 9, *Against the Pelagians*. Augustine repeats this in nearly the same words in book IV, chapters 8 and 10, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*. Indeed, one may observe that, in the judgment of the aforesaid Fathers, not [Col. 1094B] merely the first two books but also the third must be attributed to Cyprian. For the passages from Job 25, 1 John 1, and Psalm 51—cited by them from Cyprian’s book to Quirinus—are found not in either of the earlier books but in the last. Jerome, moreover, in the clearest possible words identifies not merely the book but even the chapter, saying that they are placed under the fifty-fourth heading of the third book, where they are still found. Accordingly, to Rigaltius’s question whence came the third book, which the old edition certainly does not contain, one may answer that it proceeded from the same Cyprian, though somewhat later, from whom the first two proceeded.

That this treatise was not transmitted until after Cyprian’s episcopate might be shown by his address to Quirinus under the title “son,” were that title not lacking from certain manuscripts, and were it not also established that not only bishops but presbyters likewise addressed their disciples by this title. That Quirinus was a neophyte when this work was directed to him is suggested by Cyprian’s words: “Meanwhile, may these things profit you as you read, in forming the first outlines of faith”; and later: “You will be able to drink more fully and be more abundantly satisfied if you too approach those same fountains of divine fullness, to drink together with us.” [Col. 1094C] Hence, if these words pertain to the Quirinus named almost side by side with Cyprian in Letters 77 and 78—as seems quite probable—it will be evident that they were written long before the closing period of Cyprian’s life. Or if perhaps these little books were sent somewhat later, I would nevertheless have no doubt that the mass of material had long before been collected and arranged. Consequently, that reading in the manuscript codex of the distinguished Vossius was not altogether absurd: “The little book was arranged beforehand in a brief compendium.”

Indeed, anyone who carefully considers the method of writing employed by Cyprian will readily perceive that, after receiving the faith, his first pursuit was not merely to become thoroughly versed in Holy Scripture, but to keep its contents ready to hand, accurately arranged, as it were, under common headings. For this is his customary and almost [Col. 1094D] constant practice: whatever subject he treats, he presents testimonies from Holy Scripture in clusters and leads them into battle as though from a most fully equipped armory. It will by no means be burdensome for the reader to have observed this almost at the threshold of the work.

Finally, since both the formula under which the testimonies of Holy Scripture are everywhere cited in these writings and the titles of the books of Scripture themselves are altogether different from those occurring in the rest of his work, scarcely any explanation can be given for this variation—once it is established that the author of both was the same—except that they were written at different times. It must therefore be said that this treatise preceded all the other works that follow.

I had indeed hoped that the abundant gleaning of Scripture contained in this treatise might have prepared some way toward restoring the Latin version that preceded Jerome’s. And certainly, if [Col. 1095A] Cyprian’s text were everywhere self-consistent, we might deservedly regard those places found to differ from the Vulgate reading as remnants of the ancient version. But since the variation of readings in the manuscript codices is such that several readings differing from the Vulgate occur at once, and since, because the codices do not agree with one another, it is by no means established which of these Cyprian wrote; and further, since the Fathers of the earliest centuries differ in their manner of citing Holy Scripture, we regard this undertaking as all but hopeless. Flaminius Nobilius and other learned men profusely adduce scriptural readings from Tertullian, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine on the basis of printed books, insufficiently mindful that the matter is constantly presented differently in the manuscript codices. Meanwhile, immortal thanks must be given to God, best and greatest, whose providence has so arranged matters that amid an almost infinite diversity of minor words, the substance of the matters and the order of doctrine remain continually inviolate. There is almost no dispute concerning the Scriptures, although their precise wording is everywhere disputed.

[Col. 1095B] **The Jews according to the things which had been.** Cyprian occupied himself so willingly and almost continually with the writings of his Master that very few subjects were omitted which he did not treat anew in a work of precisely the same argument. Thus, just as Tertullian published a commentary *On Baptism*, our Martyr wrote *On the Grace of God*, or *On Baptism, to Donatus*—to pass over his letters to Jubaianus, Pompeius, and others on that subject. As Tertullian treated *On Idolatry*, so Cyprian discussed *The Vanity of Idols*. Furthermore, one will later see Tertullian’s treatises *On the Apparel of Women* and *On the Veiling of Virgins*; *On Patience*; *To Scapula*; *To the Martyrs*; *On Prayer*; *On Repentance*; and *On Prescription* reflected, as if correspondingly (*antistoichōs*, ἀντιστοίχως), in our author’s writings *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*; *On the Good of Patience*; *To Demetrianus*; *Exhortation to Martyrdom*; *On the Lord’s Prayer*; *On the Lapsed*; and *On the Unity of the Church*. It is enough to have indicated all these things here once.

## Book One

[Col. 1095C]

### I. The Jews into offense

The pride of the Jews placed a most powerful obstacle in their way, preventing them from coming into the obedience of faith. The beginning is therefore most properly taken from this point, just as was formerly done by Saint Stephen and, as we see, accomplished by the Apostles in Acts and the Epistles.

**He cast out of Egypt.** This reading is almost constant in Cyprian as well as Tertullian. It appears to have arisen from the homonymy of the word, which denotes not only the ascent of a thing but almost every change of condition or place. This usage is common in Greek *airō* (ἀίρω), Latin *tollo*, and also in our vernacular languages.

**Judah was forsaken.** Although in most manuscripts the words that follow, down to the end of this chapter, are lacking, nevertheless, since they appear in the Speyer manuscript and the other printed editions, and also do not follow the Vulgate version, we by no means regard them as a recent addition.

### II. In *Basileion*

That is, the books of Kings—of Judah and of the ten tribes, or Israel. [Col. 1095D] Christians drew from the Hebrew sources only at a very late date; hence even now the Greek nomenclature of most books of the sacred codex has passed into our vernacular languages. Accordingly, we call them Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, etc. Some manuscript codices express these names in Latin words, but they are few compared with the others, which acknowledge the Greek nomenclature; we therefore judge that nothing should be changed. The same must be said of the formula for citing the Gospels: *kata* Matthew, *kata* John, etc.

### III. Sparrows of the countryside

*Strouthion* (στρουθίον) means a bird or sparrow. In the Hebrew text there is [a word absent from the supplied text], which Aquila and Symmachus retained; and they wrote *agrou* (ἄγρου), “of the field.” Thus, with both words retained, the reading *agrou strouthia* (ἀγροῦ στρουθία), “sparrows of the field,” prevailed in the Greek copies.

**False measuring-line.** In Hebrew, *schoinos pseudēs* (σχοῖνος ψευδής), “a false measuring cord”; but because the ancients not only wrote with a reed but also measured with one, “measuring” was substituted for “the scribe’s pen.” In Zechariah 2:1 a measuring cord made from twisted reeds is called a *schoinion geōmetrikon* (σχοινίον γεωμετρικόν), “surveyor’s cord.” [Col. 1096A]

### V. By my faith

The Greek text has: “My righteous one shall live by faith” (*dikaios mou ek pisteōs zēsetai*, δίκαιός μου ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται). Other copies, perhaps older ones, read, with the words transposed, “by my faith” (*ek pisteōs mou*, ἐκ πίστεώς μου), a reading followed by some copies of the New Testament at Hebrews 10:38. See book III of this work, chapter 42.

### VIII. Renew newness among yourselves

“Break up for yourselves fallow ground,” says the Vulgate Translator; but the former reading is Tertullian’s, who sometimes renders the word as *novitas*, “newness,” and sometimes as *novamen*, “a new thing.”

### IX. Lest they should say

The Septuagint translators have “so as not to learn” (*tou mē mathein*, τοῦ μὴ μαθεῖν). The Chaldean Paraphrast recognizes this reading and renders [the source’s non-Latin text is absent]. Procopius explains the passage according to our author’s meaning as follows:

> Bind up the law, for there is no longer need of the law of Moses or of the testimonies from him, now that the new teaching has been handed down to his disciples, those called from among the gentiles. These will be made manifest as sealing up the law so as not to learn it, since it is no longer useful beside the presentation of the better teaching.  
> (*Dēson ton nomon, ouketi gar chreia tou Mōyseōs nomou, oude tōn par’ autou martyriōn, tēs kainēs paradedomenēs didaskalias tois didaktois autou, tois ex ethnōn keklēmenois, hoitines* [Col. 1096B] *phaneroi esontai sphragizontes ton nomon tou mē mathein auton, ouk eti onta chrēsimon tē parathesei tou kreittonos*, Δῆσον τὸν νόμον, οὐκέτι γὰρ χρεία τοῦ Μωϋσέως νόμου, οὐδὲ τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῦ μαρτυρίων, τῆς καινῆς παραδεδομένης διδασκαλίας τοῖς διδακτοῖς αὐτοῦ, τοῖς ἐξ ἐθνῶν κεκλημένοις, οἵτινες φανεροὶ ἔσονται σφραγίζοντες τὸν νόμον τοῦ μὴ μαθεῖν αὐτόν, οὐκ ἔτι ὄντα χρήσιμον τῇ παραθέσει τοῦ κρείττονος).

### XI. Because they did not remain

Although these words lack manuscript support, nevertheless they authenticate themselves because their version differs from the Vulgate and agrees with Cyprian. The same must be said of the following words, likewise absent from the copies.

**Into a people.** To distinguish the Israelite nation from the gentiles, Hellenists prefer to call it *laos* (λαός), “people.” Our author carefully renders this word as *plebs*, “people” or “congregation”; it is his custom to call the faithful “the people” and “the steadfast people.” Tertullian less accurately says *populus*, “people,” as do the Vulgate translator and other ancient writers everywhere.

### XV. A house in the name

There God truly dwelt among human beings and displayed the propitiatory for the sins of the whole world. Our Lord everywhere in the Gospel declares that the Jerusalem Temple prefigured his body.

[Col. 1096C]

### XVI. Whole burnt offerings of rams

Irenaeus and Tertullian use this word, as do old copies of the Vulgate version.

**I have no pleasure.** Almost none of the ancient Fathers passed over this passage when discussion arose concerning the sacrifice of the new covenant. Irenaeus explains it at length in *Against Heresies*, book IV, chapter 30:

> Our Lord, giving counsel to his disciples to offer the firstfruits of his own creatures to God—not as though God were in need, but so that they themselves might be neither unfruitful nor ungrateful—took that bread which comes from creation and gave thanks, saying: “This is my body.” Similarly, he acknowledged as his blood the cup, which comes from the creation that belongs to us. He taught the new offering of the New Testament, which the Church, having received it from the apostles, offers throughout the whole world to God, who provides us with nourishment: the firstfruits of his gifts in the New Testament. Concerning this, Malachi among the Twelve Prophets thus gave advance indication: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifice from your hands; for from the rising of the sun to [Col. 1096D] its setting, my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place incense is offered to my name and a pure sacrifice, for great is my name among the nations, says the Lord Almighty.” By these words he most plainly signifies that the former people has indeed ceased to offer to God, while in every place sacrifice is offered to God, and this sacrifice is pure; and his name is glorified among the nations.

And in chapter 33 he adds:

> Since the Son’s own name belongs to the Father, and the Church offers to God Almighty through Jesus Christ, he rightly says with respect to both: “And in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice.” John, however, says in the Apocalypse that incense is the prayers of the saints.

And in chapter 34:

> We offer to him the things that are his, fittingly proclaiming the communion and unity of flesh and spirit. For just as bread, which comes from the earth, upon receiving the invocation of God, is no longer common bread but Eucharist, consisting of two realities, an earthly and a heavenly; so too our bodies, on receiving the Eucharist, [Col. 1097A] are no longer corruptible, since they possess the hope of resurrection.

Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 344 D, Paris edition, 1636:

> We are the true high-priestly race of God, as God himself also testifies when he says that in every place among the nations we offer sacrifices pleasing and pure to him. But God accepts sacrifices from no one except through his priests. God therefore bears advance witness that all those sacrifices which Jesus Christ handed down to be performed through this name—that is, in the Eucharist of the bread and the cup—and which are performed by Christians in every place on earth, are pleasing to him. But he rejects those performed by you and by those priests of yours, saying: “And I will not accept your sacrifices from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations,” he says, “but you profane it.” And even to this day you contentiously say that God does not accept the sacrifices offered in Jerusalem by those then dwelling there who were called Israelites, but that he said he accepts the prayers of those members of that nation who were then in the diaspora.  
> (*Archieratikon to alēthinon genos esmen tou Theou, hōs kai autos ho Theos martyrei, eipōn hoti en panti topō en tois ethnesi thysias enaretous autō kai katharas prospherontes. Ou dechetai de par’ oudenos thysias ho Theos, ei mē dia tōn hiereōn autou. Pantas oun hoi dia tou onomatos toutou thysias has paredōken Iēsous ho Christos ginesthai, toutestin epi tē eucharistia tou artou kai tou potēriou, tas en panti topō tēs gēs ginomenas hypo tōn Christianōn, prolaborōn ho Theos, martyrei eucharistous hyparchein autō; tas dē hyph’ hymōn kai di’ ekeinōn hymōn tōn hiereōn ginomenas apanainetai, legōn, kai tas thysias hymōn ou prosdexomai ek tōn cheirōn hymōn; dioti apo anatolēs hēliou heōs dysmōn, to onoma mou dedoxastai, legei, en tois ethnesin; hymeis de bebēloute auto kai mechri nyn philoneikountes legete, hoti tas men en Hierousalēm epi tōn ekei tote oikountōn Israēlitōn kaloumenōn thysias ou prosdechetai ho Theos; tas de dia tōn en tē diaspora tote dē ontōn apo tou genous ekeinou anthrōpōn euchas prosesthai auton eirēkenai*, Ἀρχιερατικὸν τὸ ἀληθινὸν γένος ἐσμὲν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς μαρτυρεῖ, εἰπὼν ὅτι ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσι θυσίας ἐναρέτους αὐτῷ καὶ καθαρὰς προσφέροντες. Οὐ δέχεται δὲ παρ’ οὐδενὸς θυσίας ὁ Θεός, εἰ μὴ διὰ τῶν ἱερέων αὐτοῦ. Πάντας οὖν οἳ διὰ τοῦ ὀνόματος τούτου θυσίας ἃς παρέδωκεν Ἰησοῦς ὁ Χριστὸς γίνεσθαι, τουτέστιν ἐπὶ τῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ τοῦ ἄρτου καὶ τοῦ ποτηρίου, τὰς ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ τῆς γῆς γινομένας ὑπὸ τῶν Χριστιανῶν, προλαβὼν ὁ Θεός, μαρτυρεῖ εὐχαρίστους ὑπάρχειν αὐτῷ· τὰς δὴ ὑφ’ ὑμῶν καὶ δι’ ἐκείνων ὑμῶν τῶν ἱερέων γινομένας ἀπαναίνεται, λέγων, καὶ τὰς θυσίας ὑμῶν οὐ προσδέξομαι ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν ὑμῶν· διότι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῆς ἡλίου ἕως δυσμῶν, τὸ ὄνομά μου δεδόξασται, λέγει, ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν· ὑμεῖς δὲ βεβηλοῦτε αὐτό· καὶ μέχρι νῦν φιλονεικοῦντες λέγετε, ὅτι τὰς μὲν ἐν Ἱερουσαλὴμ ἐπὶ τῶν ἐκεῖ τότε οἰκούντων Ἰσραηλιτῶν καλουμένων θυσίας οὐ προσδέχεται ὁ Θεός· τὰς δὲ διὰ τῶν ἐν τῇ διασπορᾷ τότε δὴ ὄντων ἀπὸ τοῦ γένους ἐκείνου ἀνθρώπων εὐχὰς προσίεσθαι αὐτὸν εἰρηκέναι.)

[Col. 1097B]

[The Greek text appears textually disordered at this point in the supplied source:]

> And thanksgivings performed by the worthy are the only perfect and well-pleasing sacrifices to God; this I too affirm. For Christians alone received the tradition of performing these things, also in remembrance of their dry and liquid nourishment, in which there is remembrance also of the suffering which the Son of God endured through him.  
> (*Kai eucharistiai hypo tōn axiōn ginomenai, teleiai monai kai euarestoi eisi tō Theō thysiai, kai autos phēmi. Tauta gar mona kai Christianoi parelabon poiein, kai ep’ anamnēsei de tēs trophēs autōn xēras te kai hygras, en hē kai tou pathous ho peponthen di’ autou ho huios tou Theou memnētai*, καὶ εὐχαριστίαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀξίων γινόμεναι, τέλειαι μόναι καὶ εὐάρεστοί εἰσι τῷ Θεῷ θυσίαι, καὶ αὐτός φημι. Ταῦτα γὰρ μόνα καὶ Χριστιανοὶ παρέλαβον ποιεῖν, καὶ ἐπ’ ἀναμνήσει δὲ τῆς τροφῆς αὐτῶν ξηρᾶς τε καὶ ὑγρᾶς, ἐν ᾗ καὶ τοῦ πάθους ὃ πέπονθεν δι’ αὐτοῦ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ μέμνηται.)

Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 21:

> So that Malachi’s prophecy might likewise concur: “I have no pleasure, says the Lord, and I will not accept your sacrifices; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice”—namely, the ascription of glory, and blessing, and praise, and hymns.

In book IV, chapter 1, he interprets the “pure sacrifice” as simple prayer from a pure conscience. Therefore, in place of victims and the dismemberment of slaughtered animals, there remains among Christians only a rational and bloodless sacrifice. In the words of Malachi, it consists of *mincha teora*, that is, a grain offering with its libation—namely, bread and wine—in that Eucharistic sacrifice which is always to endure, [Col. 1097C] and in the incense of devout prayers.

### XVII. Before Lucifer

Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 9, refutes the Jews, who attempted to argue that these words signified Hezekiah’s birth by night, and he claims the prophecy for the birth of our Lord.

### XX. The seven angels

In accordance with that custom, at the Persian court the seven principal satraps enjoyed the privilege of standing and conversing before the king’s face. From this writer, cited here and elsewhere, Pamelius rather inappropriately says that the canonical status of the book of Tobit has been established. There can be no doubt that the books of the Old Testament called Apocrypha, which do not appear in the Hebrew sources, were commonly found in the Greek books used by the Hellenists. Consequently Christians, who borrowed the sacred Bible from Hellenistic Jews, rightly and deservedly drew testimonies from them without distinction, especially against the Hellenists.

After enumerating the twenty-two volumes of the sacred codex in book I of *Against Apion*, Josephus calls them “the writings justly believed” (*ta dikaiōs pepisteumena*, τὰ δικαίως πεπιστευμένα), [Col. 1097D] and adds:

> From Artaxerxes down to our own time, every event has indeed been written down, but these writings have not been deemed worthy of the same trust as those preceding them, because there was no exact succession of the prophets. It is evident in practice how firmly we have trusted our own writings; for although so long an age has now passed, no one has dared either to add anything to them, remove anything from them, or alter them.  
> (*Apo de Artaxerxou mechri tou kath’ hēmas chronou, gegraptai men hekasta, pisteōs de ouch homoiōs ēxiōtai tois pro autōn, dia to mē genesthai tēn tōn prophētōn akribē diadochēn; dēlon d’ estin ergō pōs hēmeis tois idiois grammasi pepisteukamen; tosoutou gar aiōnos ēdē parōchēkotos, oute prostheinai tis ouden, oute aphelein autōn oute metatheinai tetolmēken*, Ἀπὸ δὲ Ἀρταξέρξου μέχρι τοῦ καθ’ ἡμᾶς χρόνου, γέγραπται μὲν ἕκαστα, πίστεως δὲ οὐχ ὁμοίως ἠξίωται τοῖς πρὸ αὐτῶν, διὰ τὸ μὴ γενέσθαι τὴν τῶν προφητῶν ἀκριβῆ διαδοχήν· δῆλον δ’ ἔστιν ἔργῳ πῶς ἡμεῖς τοῖς ἰδίοις γράμμασι πεπιστεύκαμεν· τοσούτου γὰρ αἰῶνος ἤδη παρῳχηκότος, οὔτε προσθεῖναί τις οὐδέν, οὔτε ἀφελεῖν αὐτῶν οὔτε μεταθεῖναι τετόλμηκεν), etc.

But if anyone should judge the ancient character of the Jews from the opinions of more recent rabbis—sworn enemies of the Christian name, who especially abhor the Greek version and the books composed by Hellenists in the vernacular tongue—and measure Jewish institutions accordingly, he will certainly stray from the truth by the whole breadth of heaven, as they say. For the ancient Jews regarded nothing as more important than committing their nation’s sacred philosophy and historical deeds to writing, and they most zealously encouraged the studies of others in that arena. This is discernible not only from the writings of Sirach, Tobit, Ezra, Baruch, Philo, Aristobulus, Demetrius, Eupolemus, and Josephus, [Col. 1098A] but is also manifest from the Sibylline verses, Phocylides, and other literary works written by Jews under assumed identities.

### XXI. Beautiful eyes

*Charopoi* (χαροποί) means “terrifying.” The true reading appears to be *Formidolosi*, “fearsome,” in a passive sense. Thus Sallust says: “To kings the good are more suspect than the wicked, and the virtue of another is always fearsome to them.” Cicero likewise: “The steadfast preservation of judgment in matters which appear fearsome.”

**To my Christ, Cyrus.** “To my anointed, Cyrus” (*Christō mou Kyrō*, Χριστῷ μου Κύρῳ). Scribes, whose custom it is to change what they do not understand, substituted *Kyriō* (κυρίῳ), “Lord.” That reading prevailed among almost all the ancients. And indeed, since Cyrus, the liberator of God’s people, is called his Messiah or anointed one and bore a type of our Lord, these words are most properly attributed to our Lord.

### XXIX. Like purple-red

We do not readily alter this reading, especially since it is abundantly supported by the manuscripts. Meanwhile, it must be said that it appears entirely probable that the author wrote “as though russet-red,” the reading of the Veronese codex, traces of which remain in those books in which “as though rose-colored” is written. [Col. 1098B] The same must be said of the passages in Tertullian’s *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 10, and also in the *Scorpiace*. Everyone knows that a red color is called *russeus*, “russet.”

## Book Two of the *Testimonies*

### I. The Lord created

Eusebius and Jerome contend that *ektēsato* (ἐκτήσατο), “acquired” or “possessed,” should be read instead of *ektisato* (ἐκτίσατο), “created”; the Hebrew text agrees with them. But Philo the Jew, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, and Origen preceded our author in this reading and attributed those words to our Lord. The Arians did the same and employed them as the surest defense of their wicked doctrine. But grant that the Father created the Son—by eternal generation, namely. The Son of the eternal Father can surely be nothing other than coeternal with him.

### II. Wisdom built

Almost the whole of the eighth chapter, which provides the approach to this one, is fully and carefully assigned to our Lord by Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 37; [Col. 1098C] Justin Martyr, *Against Trypho*; Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*; Cyprian, book I *To Quirinus*, chapter 1; and Origen, *On First Principles* (*Peri Archōn*, περὶ Ἀρχῶν), book I, chapter 2. Thus Cyprian deservedly employs in this context the things said concerning that same Wisdom of God to explain the mysteries of his Church.

The statement here concerning “a lofty proclamation over the mixing bowl” must be ascribed to the Septuagint translators, who had written *hypsēlon kērygma epi kratēra* (ὑψηλὸν κήρυγμα ἐπὶ κρατῆρα). They appear to have read [a Hebrew form absent from the supplied text] in place of [another Hebrew form absent from the supplied text], with the letters not greatly altered and the sound only minimally varied. It was said in chapter 20 of the preceding book that the Church is denoted by the number seven. In chapter 15 of that same book, Christ is taught to be the house and temple of God. The chapter’s title explains the rest.

### III. My heart uttered forth

The Arians pleasantly mock the Nicene Fathers and the orthodox writers of our own age for adducing this and similar passages of Holy Scripture to establish the divinity of our Lord. But it should have been considered that the Nicene Fathers were especially [Col. 1098D] intent upon proving that the faith commended by them had formerly been received in the Church, and that they interpreted Holy Scripture in precisely the same manner as ecclesiastical writers had interpreted it before the controversy arose. This Psalm is attributed to the Messiah not only by the author of Hebrews 1:8, Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 66, Justin Martyr, *Against Trypho*, Origen on Psalm 1, and nearly all the Fathers, but also by the Jews themselves—the Chaldean Paraphrast, Kimchi, Solomon Jarchi, and Aben Ezra. It is established that not only Cyprian in this passage, but Tertullian in numerous passages, understood this text concerning the “good word” as referring to the essential Word of God. It should further be noted that the ancients called the divine *Logos* (λόγος) “Speech” rather than “Word.”

### IV. The arm is high

Although the distinguished Jerome greatly altered this version, which corresponds to the Septuagint, he acknowledges in his Commentary that the passage can be understood of [Col. 1099A] the Jews, who did not recognize Christ, the arm of the Lord. Nor does the Chaldean Paraphrast disagree, for he says [the source’s non-Latin text is absent]. Certainly Justin Martyr, *Apology* II and *Against Trypho*, as well as Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, paragraphs 71 and 72, and *On the Resurrection*, chapter 59, taught that Christ is the arm of God, in addition to Procopius on this passage and others on similar passages. For testimony that the Lord’s hand is the divine *Logos* (λόγος), we summon the Chaldean Paraphrast, who frequently renders what occurs in the Hebrew text by [words absent from the supplied source]; it is very well known that among that writer these words designate God, best and greatest.

**Into fashioned saws.** This reading is most certain and agrees with the Greek version, which has: “I made you like new threshing-cart wheels fashioned in the form of a saw” (*epoiēsa se hōs trochous hamaxēs aloōnta kainous peristēroeideis*, ἐποίησά σε ὡς τροχοὺς ἁμάξης ἀλοῶντα καινοὺς περιστηροειδεῖς). Traces of it survive in those manuscripts that had “into fashioned *seres*.” The reading received until now, which has “turned back upon itself,” appears to be the invention of some Italian scribe [Col. 1099B] who—as is customary with that sort of person—inserted the words that he thought he himself understood better. Although this entire passage was lacking in the Speyer manuscript and the editions of Rembold, Erasmus, and Manutius, nevertheless, since it appears in other printed editions, is present in very many manuscripts, and moreover does not at all reproduce the Vulgate version, it appears that it must unquestionably be retained.

### V. The angel of the Lord called him

To vindicate our author’s judgment concerning Christ as the angel of the covenant, it might have been sufficient—according to the method I have employed—to adduce the parallel passage of the New Testament, namely 1 Corinthians 10:9. For what interpreter of the Old Testament should be heard in opposition to the Lord himself or his Apostles?

But since innovators have believed that nothing whatever is impermissible to them in this argument, and boldly teach that the Angel who once appeared to the Patriarchs and to Moses, and who is almost continually called Jehovah, must be numbered among the attendants of created and ministering spirits—thus opening the widest possible entrance to the opinions of the Socinians; for what advantage will it be to have shown that our Lord [Col. 1099C] is called God and Jehovah in Holy Scripture if this is likewise attributed to any angels whatsoever who discharge some embassy in God’s stead?—it will not be burdensome to state that this doctrine is wholly abhorrent to the judgment and faith of the universal primitive Church.

Justin, over many pages in his *Dialogue against Trypho*, and also in *Apology* II, proves most carefully that Christ, as the angel of the covenant, “was the one who appeared and spoke to Moses and Abraham and, in short, the other Patriarchs” (*ēn ho Mōsei kai tō Abraam kai tois allois haplōs Patriarchais phaneis kai homilēsas*, ἦν ὁ Μωσεῖ καὶ τῷ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἁπλῶς Πατριάρχαις φανεὶς καὶ ὁμιλήσας). Irenaeus similarly argues at length in book III, chapter 6, and book IV, chapters 17 and 26; Clement of Alexandria, *Pedagogue*, book I, chapter 7; Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 9, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 27, and *Against Praxeas*, chapter 16; and Origen, Homily I on Isaiah. Moreover, the Fathers who followed held the same judgment: Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 2; Basil, *Against Eunomius*, books II and IV; Athanasius, book IV *Against the Arians*; Hilary, *On the Trinity*, books IV and XII; Gregory Nazianzen, Orations 35 and 49; Ambrose on Colossians 1:15 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16; Augustine, Letter 112; and the Synods of Antioch and Sirmium cited by Athanasius.

[Col. 1099D] **He will not fail.** The Septuagint has *hyposteilētai* (ὑποστείληται): “through fear he will abandon his protection.” Tertullian has “he will conceal”: “through fear he will withdraw himself.”

### VI. To that God

The Septuagint placed the emphatic phrase “to the God who appeared” (*tō theō tō ophthenti*, τῷ θεῷ τῷ ὀφθέντι), which our author judged should by no means be omitted. Justin likewise cites the passage in *Against Trypho*.

**Every stream.** [The Hebrew term absent from the supplied text] means not merely a valley but also a stream; Isaiah, however, uses another word here, namely [absent from the supplied text]. Nearly all the codices agree in the present reading.

**They shall glory in his name.** [A Hebrew term absent from the supplied text], or “the Name,” signifies God among the Hebrews. It will therefore be permissible to judge that it is understood here under this designation. Certainly the Septuagint, which placed *katakauchēsontai* (κατακαυχήσονται), “they shall glory,” did not read [the term is absent from the supplied text].

**God blessed.** Irenaeus cites this passage in book III, chapter 18, and Tertullian presses it most carefully in *Against Praxeas*, paragraphs 13 and 15. And rightly so, since—as Proclus [Col. 1100A] most correctly says concerning the faith—it “walls off the infiltration of calumny” (*pareisdysin sykophantias apoteichizei*, παρείσδυσιν συκοφαντίας ἀποτειχίζει), and contains the especially solemn formula by which honor was rendered to God, best and greatest, in the Jewish Church.

Meanwhile, it must be acknowledged that the word *God* is absent from the Speyer manuscript, the old unnamed edition, and the editions of Rembold and Erasmus. But it occurs in those that follow and also in all the manuscripts I have consulted. Erasmus therefore rightly and deservedly attributes this omission to the scribes, especially since that word occurs everywhere in Paul’s text. Moreover, in accordance with the idiom of the sacred language, [a Hebrew expression absent from the supplied text], without any word added, everywhere signifies God.

**He shall possess these things.** Very many copies read “he shall inherit all things” (*klēronomēsei panta*, κληρονομήσει πάντα), but others, and by no means contemptible ones, have “he shall inherit these things” (*klēronomēsei tauta*, κληρονομήσει ταῦτα). We see not only our author but also the Vulgate translator supporting this reading.

### VII. Neither elder nor angel

The explanation for the difference appearing among the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and the present version must be sought in the varying meaning of the word [the original term is absent from the supplied text]. The Septuagint considered it defectively written for [another absent term], and placed *presbys* (πρέσβυς), [Col. 1100B] “envoy” or “ambassador.” Tertullian follows them in *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 22, and claims the prophecy for our Lord. The Latin version, however, understood *presbys* in the sense in which it denotes an old man. Jerome, following the sense of the root, renders it “afflicted.”

### IX. He furnishes the contest

The Septuagint copies everywhere, and Justin Martyr, read: “Furnish a contest to the Lord” (*Kyriō parechete agōna*, κυρίῳ παρέχετε ἀγῶνα). But it appears that in ancient times the text was also read: “The Lord furnishes a contest” (*Kyrios parechei agōna*, κύριος παρέχει ἀγῶνα), for thus not only our author in this passage but also elsewhere in his Letters, and likewise Irenaeus and Tertullian, express the passage.

**Let him know so as to prefer evil; he will change the good.** I think this reading genuine, since it is secured by the support of almost all the manuscripts, confirmed by the testimony of Irenaeus—who very rarely differs from our author in the recension of Scripture—and, finally, approaches more closely to the meaning of the Septuagint.
