I acknowledge that in Irenaeus, book III, chapter 26, Feuardentius changed *commutabit*, “he will change,” into *communicavit*, “he communicated”; but he himself admits that it is otherwise in other editions, [Col. 1100C] and certainly in the Arundel manuscript I find it written in the former manner. Perhaps the words transcribed by the Vulgate translator would express the Hebrew truth more successfully; but the question is not what is best, but what Cyprian wrote.

**He himself will watch over you.** The Vulgate reading, which retains “her,” would have no supporters in this learned age if devotion to party, rather than to truth however manifest, did not carry greater weight. Certainly Irenaeus cites the passage three times in precisely the same manner as our author. It must be observed that the Greek copies formerly read “he himself will watch over you” (*autos sou tērēsei*, αὐτός σου τηρήσει), although there can be no doubt that they themselves wrote [uncertain OCR: *teirēsei*, τειρήσει].

### X. And he is a man

The Vulgate says “inscrutable”; others, “desperately diseased.” In the Hebrew there is [a word absent from the supplied text], which is very often written defectively, so that final *shin* serves as a support for the *ḥolem*, and signifies “man.” Certainly Tertullian rendered this text in such a way as to show—to use Jerome’s words—“that the Lord [Col. 1100D] and Savior is man according to the dispensation of the flesh assumed, and that no one can know the mystery of his birth.” The passages occur in *Against the Jews*, *On the Flesh of Christ*, and *Against Marcion*, book III.

A man shall proceed from his seed. The Septuagint has, “A man shall come forth from his seed” (*exeleusetai anthrōpos ek tou spermatos autou*). The phrase “from the bucket,” a proverbial expression among the Hebrews, denotes the derivation of human beings from their parents. Hence not only do the Septuagint here render the word as “man” (*anthrōpon*), but the Targum also translates it by [text missing]. It may also be noted that the word which follows appears to have been understood in the sense in which it denotes an arm. “To rule over many nations” (*kyrieuein ethnōn pollōn*) is precisely the same as what is said in Ps. 88:25: “to have his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers” (*echein en thalassē cheira autou, kai en potamois dexian autou*). Finally, it may be observed that in the words immediately following the Septuagint read, as it were, “Gog shall be exalted” (*hypsōthēsetai hē Gōg*). Indeed, Symmachus likewise has, “He shall be exalted above Gog” (*hypsōthēsetai hyper Gōg*). From Ezek. 38 and 39 and Rev. 20:8, we learn that Gog and Magog—especially the barbarian nations—designate the enemies of the Church; but here it is said that they will become Christ’s kingdom, something most happily accomplished through the preaching of the Gospel. [Col. 1101A]

XI.—And he shall attain faith. “I shall establish him in the house” (*pistōsō auton en tō oikō*) is still read in copies of the Septuagint. It is credible, however, that they wrote *epistēsō*, “I shall establish,” for in the Hebrew there is: [text missing].

XII.—You are not insignificant. The Hebrew text appears to profess the contradictory of this. Likewise the Septuagint has, “You are very small” (*oligostos ei*). But our author follows the reading of St. Matthew, who says, “You are by no means the least” (*oudamōs elachistē ei*). Indeed, if Rabbi Tanchum, a learned Jew, is to be trusted, St. Matthew’s reading represents the Hebrew truth. For he notes that the word which is said to mean “small” actually denotes something great in value.

XIII.—Jesus the priest. Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, attributes this passage to our Lord, as does Tertullian in *Against the Jews* and *Against Marcion*, book III, [Col. 1101B] chapter 7, who says: “Zechariah, in the person of Christ himself, and indeed in the mystery of his very name, is the true high priest.”

XIV.—The righteous man perishes. That these words pertain to our Lord is taught by Justin Martyr in *Apology* II and the *Dialogue with Trypho*; Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 67; and Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 22. Jerome likewise says: “The righteous man perishes—he of whom Pilate’s wife says, ‘Have nothing to do with that righteous man.’ Having washed his hands, he says, ‘I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.’”

XV.—Come, let us cast wood. Others render this passage differently, namely: “Let us destroy the tree with its fruit”; or, “Let us cast wood upon his flesh,” that is, “Let us restrain him with clubs.” But the most literal sense appears to be the one retained by the Septuagint and the Vulgate translator and acknowledged by the Targum of Jonathan. Justin cites the passage in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, as does Tertullian in *Against the Jews*, chapter 10. Some of the Rabbis identify the particular kind of wood and maintain that it was yew, [Col. 1101C] from whose poisonous sap they suppose that poisons were prepared.

And he took a great stone. It must by no means be supposed that our author believed that stone to have been Christ; rather, that the stone prefigured him who truly heard everything that was said. Similarly, Tertullian says that the Israelites were circumcised by Joshua with a rocky edge, that is, by Christ’s precepts, “for the rock was Christ”: *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 16, and book IV, chapter 13. In precisely the same way, the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 10:4 that “all drank the same spiritual drink,” and “they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.”

XVI.—Behold, we. He appears to have read *idou* (“behold”) instead of *ei* (“if”).

XVIII.—Let us ascend the mountain. Tertullian carefully treats this passage in *Against the Jews*, chapter 3, and *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 21.

XIX.—Appoint a service. The Septuagint has *therapeian*, that is, “solemn worship.” But since that word likewise denotes the services rendered to the sick, [Col. 1101D] the Latin translator rendered it in this sense.

Let the Bridegroom proceed. It is abundantly established that our Lord was distinguished by the title “Bridegroom.” But lest anyone suppose that this passage has been rashly cited in a matter of this kind, it should be recalled that in Acts 2:19 this prophecy is claimed for the Messiah by the Apostle. St. Jerome, in his commentaries, interprets the following passage from Jeremiah 16 in the same manner. Tertullian likewise interprets the next passage, from Psalm 18, in *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 11.

Of the might of the Lord. The Septuagint reads “of the might of the Lord” (*dynameōs kyriou*), in the manner in which they commonly render the word.

XX.—I stretched out my hands. Justin, in *Apology* II and the *Dialogue with Trypho*, as well as Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 13, interpret this text in the same sense.

Your life shall hang before you. Tertullian interprets this passage thus in *Against the Jews*, chapter 11.

They dug hands. This psalm pertains so certainly to the Messiah that even the Jews confess it. Yet, in order to extricate themselves, they invent a twofold Messiah: the one, son of Joseph, humble indeed and described in this passage; the other, son of David, a prince and warrior. As for these words, they are among those that have received two readings among the Hebrews. And learned men, although elsewhere deeply devoted to the reading received among the Hebrews, judge that the form of expression followed by the Septuagint—which has *ōryxan*, “they dug”—should be preferred to the present reading, which gives *hōs leōn*, “like a lion.” [Col. 1102A]

Fasten with nails. The Septuagint has, “Nail my flesh because of fear of you” (*kathēlōson ek tou phobou sou tas sarkas mou*). Aquila has *ēlōthē*, “I fastened.” From this one may conjecture that the original text was *kathēlōsen*, “he fastened with nails.” Solomon uses this form of speech in Eccles. 12:12: “The words of the wise are like ox-goads and like glowing nails” (*logoi sophōn, hōs ta boukentra, kai hōs hēloi pyroumenoi*); or, as Theodotion has it, “nails firmly fixed” (*hēloi pepēgotes*). The Hebrew signifies not only “he shuddered,” but also “he fastened with nails.”

His day. It is well known that “the day of the Lord” designates the times of the Messiah. See Acts 2:20. Our author appears to have read *eklektous*, “elect,” instead of [Col. 1102B] *klētous*, “called.”

God is suspended. The Septuagint has, “God is not like a man, so as to be suspended” (*ouk hōs anthrōpos ho theos diartēthēnai*). A Greek scholiast interprets this not inappropriately: “To be suspended—that is, to be shaken; for things that hang are shaken” (*Diartēthēnai, tout’ esti saleuthēnai; ta gar kremamena saleuontai*).

XXII.—His might covered the heavens. This passage describes the entire apparatus of the Law delivered of old, whose mediator was the Angel of the Covenant, that is, our Lord. Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 22, maintains that those words present the Lord’s transfiguration, which was indeed a foreshadowing of his coming Passion, according to the testimony of St. Luke 9:33. It should be noted that the words, “and there the might of his glory was established,” and, “he established a strong love,” are two versions of the same Hebrew text [Hebrew omitted], arising from the homonymy of that language. A similar instance occurs in the following word, which means both “word” and “pestilence,” and in the next, which denotes both parched earth and a burning coal.

Government upon his shoulders. Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 10: [Col. 1102C] “What king at all bears the emblem of his authority upon his shoulder, rather than a diadem on his head, a scepter in his hand, or some mark upon his distinctive garment? But Christ Jesus alone, the new King of the ages, bore upon his shoulder both the authority and sublimity of his new glory—namely, the cross.”

When he raised his hands. Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 10, and *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 18: “Why, indeed, did Moses at that particular time—when Jesus was fighting against Amalek—pray while seated with outstretched hands, when amid such alarming circumstances he ought rather to have commended his prayer on bended knees, with his hands beating his breast and his face cast down upon the ground? Unless it was because there, where the name of Jesus was fighting, the posture of the cross was also necessary, since Jesus would one day fight against the devil and through the cross obtain victory.” Justin Martyr writes similarly in the *Dialogue with Trypho*.

Upon the wood of life. This was so that the second Adam might correspond more exactly to the first: just as the one brought death into the world through wood, the other gave life. Likewise, when the world was restored after the flood, “Noah was saved in wood, borne upon the waters” (*ho Nōs en xylō diesōthē, epochoumenos tois hydasi*), says Justin Martyr in the *Dialogue*. [Col. 1102D]

XXIII.—The sun shall set at midday. This prophecy is referred to the Lord’s Passion not only by our author, but also by Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 66, and Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 42. Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 66, similarly interprets the following passage from Jeremiah. The word “seven” is omitted by both.

XXV.—He will give us life after two days. Thus Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 14, and *Against Marcion*, book IV, chapter 43.

Let them wash their garment. St. John appears to have had this passage from Exodus in view in Rev. 7:14.

XXVI.—Those who stood by him presented him. In place of “he was brought before him” (*enōpion autou prosēchthē*), a reading corresponding to the Chaldean, the text once read, “those standing by brought him forward” (*hoi parestēkotes prosēgagon auton*), as is clear from Justin in the *Dialogue*. Moreover, Tertullian reads, “those who stood by led him forward,” in *Against Marcion*, book III, chapter 9. Hence, in place of “were bringing,” copyists appear to have written “were presenting.” In the remainder too, our author and Tertullian [Col. 1103A] follow Justin Martyr’s reading, leaving aside the Septuagint.

That they may be raised up. The manuscript codices agree in this reading; more correctly it would be said, “that they may be judged.”

XXVIII.—Behold, the day of the Lord comes. The Lord claims this prophecy of Malachi for himself in Matt. 11:14. The Chaldean paraphrast notes that the following passage concerns the Day of Judgment, teaching that Psalm 49 concerns the day of the great judgment. Augustine agrees with him in *The City of God*, book XX, chapter 24. Similarly, Psalm 67, which is devoted to celebrating the Ark of the Covenant and the divine presence there, treats far more splendidly of his “dwelling” (*skēnōsin*) in the flesh, as St. Paul notes in Eph. 4:9.

That he may separate. The Septuagint reads, “for the purpose of separating” (*tou diakrinai*). In truth, the last judgment will be accomplished through separation; see Matt. 25:32.

They shall be troubled before his face. Although these words appear in the Greek copies, they are absent from the Hebrew sources.

You shall exterminate among all nations. The Septuagint has *kataklēronomēseis*, “you shall take possession.” Whoever claims something for himself excludes others from its possession. [Col. 1103B]

XXIX.—Who will announce it to you? The Septuagint has, “Who will announce it to you?” (*tis anangelei hymin*), for they appear to have read [Hebrew text omitted]. What follows concerning the “eternal place” (*topos aiōnios*) appears to savor of a Hebrew euphemism; St. Luke calls it a “place of torment” (*topos basanēs*). It was at a later date that hell was designated through Tophet and Gehenna.

Remove the gates. I consider this reading genuine, although Pamelius thought otherwise, for it appears to have arisen from the homonymy of the Greek text *arate pylas*, which can mean “lift up the gates” or “remove the gates,” and could not have resulted from a copyist’s error. It would be superfluous labor to vindicate for our Lord the passages from the Psalms gathered here, since most of them are attributed to the Messiah by the Jews themselves. Our Lord, in John 10:1, declares himself to be the gate; and in this sense Clement, in his *Epistle to the Corinthians*, interprets the twofold passage from Psalm 118, “Open to me the gates of righteousness” (*anoixate moi pylas dikaiosynēs*).

My ministers would be troubled. “They would struggle” (*ēgōnizonto*), says the Apostle; that is, they would be engaged in an agony. When the Lord is about to describe his own agony, he says, “Now my soul is troubled.” [Col. 1103C]

My Father has prepared. Our author is consistent in this reading, as is Irenaeus. The very ancient Cambridge manuscript acknowledges it, as do other Greek codices, which read, “which my Father has prepared” (*ho hētoimase ho patēr mou*).

**ABOUT THE YEAR 249. THE THIRD BOOK OF TESTIMONIES**

The third book. Although this book is absent from the Speyer edition, the old unnamed edition, and Rembold’s, it is found in Erasmus’s edition and in all those which subsequently followed it. Moreover, the manuscript codices commonly contain it. We showed above, from the supporting testimony of Jerome, Augustine, and other ancient writers, that it is a genuine work of our author. By way of a further supplement, [Col. 1103D] it may now be added that not only was heading 54 of this book expressly cited by Jerome, but the fourth heading was also cited repeatedly by Augustine, namely in *Retractions*, book II, chapter 1; *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 9; and *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3. I would not deny that certain testimonies occur which were interpolated by copyists, and others copied in the words of the Vulgate translator; but these points do not concern the standing of the book itself, and they affect almost all the writings of the ancients equally. It might more properly be doubted whether this book should be called the third to Quirinus, or rather a separate and independent work. The testimonies against the Jews given above appear to constitute a single work, although divided into two parts; both the nature of its argument and the prefixed epistle would suggest this. Indeed, the testimonies which follow have a wholly different subject, and the addition of another epistle shows that this treatise was written under new auspices. Hence the Lambeth codex does not improperly count the preceding booklets as one and calls the following work not the third but the second book to [Col. 1104A] Quirinus. But since the other manner of numbering has prevailed, we have judged that we should not depart from it.

I.—The year 249. We have judged that this book, composed under wholly new auspices and yet before the persecution, should be assigned to the year 249, toward the close of which persecution was threatening. But so that it would not be separated from the other books of testimonies, we have placed it before the treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*, which we believe was written before Cyprian’s episcopate, thereby somewhat reversing chronological order.

II.—For either you prick those subject to you. Tertullian likewise reads with a disjunctive particle: “or you fast for lawsuits.” Hence both appear to have read, “For either you prick those under your authority, or for lawsuits,” etc. (*ē gar tous hypocheirious hymōn hyponyssete, ē eis kriseis*, etc.).

And your garments. The Septuagint has “your remedies” (*ta iamata sou*). The Vulgate translator has, “Your health shall arise more quickly.” Our author appears to have read “your garments” (*ta himatia sou*). Indeed, Tertullian likewise read it so.

I wait for you. That is, “I await; I expect.”

With alms and faith. Copies of the Septuagint—which present the book of Proverbs in a sufficiently disordered form—insert these words in an improper place, namely chapter 15, verse 29. But the fact that they once appeared in chapter 6 is suggested by their presence in the Syriac and Arabic versions. [Col. 1104B]

In the heart of the poor. The Septuagint reads, “in your storehouses” (*en tameiois sou*), in place of which it appears that “in the heart of the poor” (*en kardia ptōchou*) was once read.

More than sacrifice. In place of *ou thysian*, “not sacrifice,” our author appears to have read *ē thysian*, “than sacrifice.” Many copies of the Septuagint acknowledge this reading. The former reading, however, which agrees with the Hebrew text, is consistently retained in Matt. 9:13 and 12:7.

All these things I have observed. Our author omitted the words that follow in the sacred text, “from my youth.” Let the reader note, however, that these very passages are likewise gathered together in the book *On Works and Almsgiving*; this entirely accords with what we said above, on page 13, concerning Cyprian’s method of citing Holy Scripture. Indeed, it also vindicates this book as his.

That you may be enriched in all things. Some Greek codices read thus: “that in all things” (*hina en pasi*).

Nor the rich. The Greek manuscripts support this reading, having “nor the rich” (*mēde tous plousious*). Indeed, what follows on the opposite side—namely, the distinct mention of the poor, the infirm, the blind, and the lame—appears to favor this reading. [Col. 1104C]

III.—For while you were still little ones. This was perhaps an addition made by a copyist, for it is absent from the book *On Jealousy and Envy*, where this text is cited. A similar passage occurs in Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 75: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to receive solid food.”

Charity is magnanimous. The Greek is *makrothymei*, “is long-suffering.” Tertullian calls it “magnanimous” in his book *On Patience*. But “long-suffering,” an equally barbarous word, became more prevalent.

It is not puffed up; it is not provoked. The Greek codices commonly read, “it is not puffed up; it does not behave unseemly” (*ou physioutai, ouk aschēmonei*); but very many manuscripts have, “it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious” (*ou physioutai, ou philotimei*), which our author appears to have followed. In the book *On the Unity of the Church*, this text is expressed in the same manner.

Any division. This reading is supported by the most highly regarded Greek manuscript codices. The Bodleian manuscript, venerable for its antiquity if any is, and written in uncial letters, reads, “there was no division whatsoever among them” (*ouk ēn chōrismos en autois tis*). But Beza’s manuscript, preserved at Cambridge, has, “there was no distinction at all among them” (*ou diakrisis en autois oudemia*). I pass over copies of a later period. Moreover, it should be noted that our countryman Bede observed this discrepancy long ago in his *Retractation on the Acts of the Apostles*. [Col. 1104D]

Offer your gift at the altar. The words “at the altar” are redundant.

He walks in darkness. Although the word “walks” is not found here, it occurs below, in verse 11.

IV.—That one must glory in nothing. We noted above that Augustine repeatedly cited this passage while opposing the madness of Pelagius.

V.—But do not call anyone rabbi. If that title is not permitted to be accepted, it is likewise forbidden to confer it. Our Greek copies have, “Do not be called” (*mē klēthēte*). The Vulgate translator has, “Do not wish to be called.”

VI.—Naked shall I also go beneath the earth. These words are supplied by way of interpretation for what the Septuagint expresses more briefly: “I shall depart there” (*apeleusomai ekei*). For the words added below in the same manner, the translators of the Septuagint are the authorities: “In the things that befell him, Job did not sin, nor with his lips” (*en tois symbebēkosin autō ouch hēmarten Iōb, oude en tois cheilesin autou*). [Col. 1105A]

A thorn of my flesh. The word “my” is redundant. What follows, “strength is perfected in weakness,” with the word “my” omitted, forms a more universal lemma.

How narrow! The Complutensian Bible, as well as almost all the older manuscript codices, likewise reads *ti stenē*, “how narrow!”, with exclamatory force.

In the places of the impious. The Septuagint translators appear to have read [text missing] in place of [text missing]. Pamelius notes that printed codices had “Ecclesiastes III” in the margin. But it is found neither there in Greek nor in the book of Wisdom. Goulartius maintains that it is written in Ecclesiastes III. In truth, however, it is found in Proverbs of Solomon 28; our author frequently calls that book “the Wisdom of Solomon.” [Col. 1105B]

VII.—On the day of redemption. This agrees with the Greek codices that read “on the day” (*en hēmera*).

IX.—Thus you shall fulfill the law of Christ. This text is cited in the same manner in the epistle to Antonianus, as though the reading had been, “Thus you shall fulfill the law of Christ” (*houtōs plērōsete ton nomon tou Christou*).

X.—Subject to none but God alone. The Septuagint reads, “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” (*Ouchi tō theō hypotagēsetai hē psychē mou?*). Our author appears to have read, “To none but God” (*ouk ē tō theō*). The Vulgate translator expresses it as an imperative: “Nevertheless, be subject to God, O my soul.”

But Shadrach answered. This passage was almost always present to Cyprian’s mind. It is brought forward not only in these books, but also in the *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, the Epistle to the Thibaritans, and the Epistle to Rogatianus.

XI.—Your loins girded. Our author rightly adduces this passage in proof of his lemma. For the servitude in Egypt and the passage into the land of Canaan foreshadowed our state under the tyranny of sin and under evangelical liberty.

For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear. Our author appears to have read, “For you were bought at a great price; glorify and bear” (*ēgorasthēte gar timēs megalēs, doxasate, kai bastasate*). Indeed, manuscript copies favor the latter addition; certainly our author is consistent in this reading. [Col. 1105C]

As though they did not use. The Greek text has, “as though not using fully” (*hōs mē katachrōmenoi*). These words admit this translation well enough. Thus Plato, *Epistle* VIII: “He has not made proper use of the gift” (*ouk orthōs katakechretai dōrea*).

Let us also bear the image. This accords with those copies which read *pherōsōmen*, “let us bear.”

To please him to whom he has proved himself. Many imperial laws survive concerning military approval. First, a man’s origin was investigated, lest some escape their municipal duties under the pretext of military service. Second, his age was considered, namely, that his eighteenth year had been completed. Third, his stature, so that he was five feet and seven inches tall. Fourth, his status, so that slaves and those practicing an ignoble way of life were excluded. Fifth, his strength and bodily condition, for which the standard differed according to the difference between cavalry and infantry service. Sixth, his religious sect: thus Jews and, at times, Christians were prohibited from armed military service. [Col. 1105D]

You pursue vain things. That is, you adhere to absurd sects; the Greek text has *dogmatizesthe*, “you submit to ordinances.”

In the spirit of your understanding: *noos hymōn*, “of your mind.” Tertullian expresses this passage in the same words in *On the Soul*, chapter 45.

In righteousness, in holiness, and in truth. Printed books commonly read, “in righteousness and holiness of truth” (*en dikaiosynē kai hosiotēti tēs alētheias*). But many manuscripts approach the reading of our author, namely, “in righteousness, and holiness, and truth” (*en dikaiosynē, kai hosiotēti, kai alētheia*).

Just as God abides forever. This addition appears to have been taken from elsewhere.

Christ our Passover was sacrificed. Printed copies read, “Christ our Passover was sacrificed for us” (*Pascha hēmōn hyper hēmōn ethythē Christos*). But manuscript copies commonly have, “Christ our Passover was sacrificed” (*Pascha hēmōn ethythē Christos*). The Vulgate translator agrees with this reading.

XII.—And if he swears vainly. After verse 10, the eleventh is omitted and the twelfth appended, because there is no need [Col. 1106A] to aggravate the crime of perjury when it is established that one may not swear truly on frequent or trivial grounds.

XIII.—For the edification of faith. Printed copies have, “for the edification of need” (*pros oikodomēn tēs chreias*); but many manuscripts support our author’s reading and have, “for the edification of faith” (*pros oikodomēn tēs pisteōs*).

Blessing and not cursing. In place of “Bless, and do not curse” (*eulogeite, kai mē katarasthe*), our author appears to have read, “blessing and not cursing” (*eulogountes, kai mē katarōmenoi*).

XV.—As a sacrifice. This text occurs in the Epistle to Rogatianus, and in both places it reads, “as a whole burnt-offering, a sacrifice.” I nevertheless think that Cyprian wrote *in holocaustoma*, “as a burnt-offering”; but copyists, prompted by the following passage from Wisdom 3:4 and by their own minds, which were excessively prone to alter everything, thought it should be corrected and substituted, “as a whole burnt-offering, a sacrifice.”

XVI.—He delivers from evils. If a truthful witness has such force in civil cases and the affairs of ordinary life, how much more does one who is a martyr for God’s cause.

Lifting bundles of brushwood. *Gremia* is the same as *cremia*, bundles of dry twigs, which are collected in much the same manner as sheaves of grain. Ulpian, book LV, *On Legacies and Trusts*, book XXXII: “But if the intention does not oppose it, rods, bundles of brushwood, vine-shoots, and remnants of timber will also be included.” Columella, book XII, chapter 32: “We shall carry the must into boiling vessels, at first over a gentle fire made from very slender pieces of wood, which country people call *gremia*.” [Col. 1106B]

XVIII.—He is not my disciple. Cyprian appears to have read *mou mathētēs*, “my disciple,” in place of *mou axios*, “worthy of me.” So it is found in Luke 14:26.

Through him who loved us: *dia tou agapēsantos hēmas*. Other codices read *dia ton agapēsanta*, “on account of him who loved us.” The Vulgate has “because of him.”

XXI.—For you do the same things that you judge. In our copies we read, “For you who judge practice the same things” (*ta gar auta prasseis ho krinōn*), but our author appears to have read, “You practice the things that you judge” (*anta prasseis ha krineis* [uncertain reading]). And afterward, in place of *toiauta*, “such things,” he appears to have read *ta kaka*, “evil things.”

XXVII.—Shine like lights. He understood the word *phainesthe* not indicatively, “you shine,” but imperatively, “shine.” [Col. 1106C]

XXVIII.—That it cannot be remitted in the Church. At first sight these words appear to favor the Novatian hypothesis; but the testimonies of Scripture that are adduced are restricted to sin against the Holy Spirit, or at least to graver crimes—and indeed, in the earliest Christian period no pardon was granted for them. Moreover, since according to ancient customs public sinners had to be expelled from the Church before they were admitted to repentance, it will rightly be said that such criminals could not be remitted into the Church. In the same sense our author says in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*: “Let there be no further permission to sin after you have begun to know God.” See Heb. 6:4.

XXIX.—You would belong to the world. To corrupt and to be corrupted is called “the world.”

XXX.—What anyone has vowed to God. Pamelius, in his customary manner, commends monastic vows to us from this passage, scarcely remembering that neither the period nor the nature of this work can have reference to vows of that kind. [Col. 1106D]

Cursed is he who performs the works of God negligently. The Canaanite nations were under anathema, that is, devoted to destruction; hence anyone who spared the defeated in those wars waged under God’s auspices was prosecuted as guilty of violating an oath. Moreover, it is evident from the examples of Abraham, Jephthah, and the Israelites throughout Scripture that wars were formerly undertaken with vows.

XXXI.—The impious shall not rise in judgment. The Jews held the opinion that they alone would be brought before the coming judgment.

XXXII.—They beget and are begotten. Certain Greek copies, with the kind permission of Pamelius, read, “they are begotten and they beget” (*gennōntai kai gennōsi*). What follows, though less than idiomatic Latin—“they do not marry, nor are they married”—is retained by almost all the Latin Fathers; for the words in the Greek text, “neither do they marry, nor are they given in marriage” (*oute gamousin, oute ekgamiskontai*), could scarcely be rendered otherwise in the same number of words. The Vulgate translator has at Luke 20:34: “The children of this world marry and are given in marriage.” What immediately follows, “for neither shall they begin to die,” [Col. 1107A] must be traced to the Greek text which reads, “For neither can they die any longer, since they are equal to the angels of God and are children of the resurrection” (*oute gar apothanein eti, isangeloi tō Theō, tēs anastaseōs huioi ontes*).

So too the woman and the virgin. This agrees with the Greek manuscripts which read, “Both the woman and the unmarried virgin care for the things of the Lord” (*kai hē gynē, kai hē parthenos hē agamos, merimna ta tou Kyriou*).

Unless there is one holy loaf. Some codices of the Septuagint have, “unless there is the holy loaf” (*ei mē artos ho hagios*), words that our author believed denoted a single loaf. But printed copies commonly read, “or they are holy loaves” (*ē hagioi artoi eisin*).

XXXIII.—O God, give your judgment to the King. Our author claimed this passage for the Messiah in chapter 2 of the preceding book. The following passage, Gen. 19:24, is commonly adduced by the Fathers to prove the distinction of Persons in the Godhead. The reader may consult Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*; Irenaeus, book III, chapter 6; Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*; Cyril, book I on John; Athanasius, *Epistle on the Synods*; Hilary, *On the Synods*; Jerome on Isaiah 45; and Ambrose, book I of *On the Faith*.

XXXVI.—To the people of Pontus. Thus Tertullian in the *Scorpiace*.

XXXIX.—But he delivered himself to one judging unjustly. Our codices [Col. 1107B] read, “to the one judging justly” (*krinonti dikaiōs*). But our author appears to have read, “He delivered him to the one judging unjustly” (*paredōken auton tō krinonti adikōs*), with reference to Pilate and Caiaphas.

Established in the figure of God. Tertullian reads, “established in the image of God,” in *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 20. The Vulgate has “in the form.”

XL.—He will repay you in secret. What follows, “openly” (*en phanerō*), is absent from many manuscripts, as St. Augustine observed long ago in *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book II, chapter 5.

XLII.—Faith altogether. Thus, in the following chapter, “It is altogether an offense among you.”

But the righteous man from my faith. We treated this passage above, in book I to Quirinus, heading 5.

XLIV.—To attain immediately. Elsewhere *consecutio*, “attainment,” is used for baptism, in chapter 97: “One must hasten to faith and attainment.” Tertullian likewise says in *On Baptism*, chapter 19: “If any understand the weight of baptism, they will fear attainment all the more.” The status of catechumens seeking baptism is opposed to this. Ecclesiastical laws, which after the gift of discerning spirits had ceased took care that Jews, Gentiles, and other unworthy persons should not be hastily admitted through baptism and thereby brand the Christian name with disgrace, neither ought nor are able to prejudice divine grace. [Col. 1107C]

XLV.—Through patience we wait. Thus it reads in the book *On the Good of Patience*, and the approved manuscripts read so here. The former reading, “through expectation we hope,” must be attributed to the barbarism of copyists.

XLVII.—Let him utterly fail. It will be worthwhile to observe that *ta panta*, “all things,” is absent not only here but also from many Greek copies. The immediately following clause likewise has, “and the impious shall grow weak” (*kai asthenēsousi hoi asebeis*), which was an addition by Theodotion so that the Greek would correspond to the Hebrew. Symmachus translates more correctly, “and stumbling blocks together with the impious” (*kai skandala met’ asebōn*).

XLVIII.—That one must not lend at interest. Usury is consistently ill regarded among ecclesiastical writers, and rightly so whenever payment is demanded for the delay of money left unpaid because of poverty. The case may perhaps be different with money which the recipient puts to profitable use—except insofar as positive laws determine otherwise, or the avoidance of scandal counsels otherwise. [Col. 1107D]

But the man who shall be righteous. These words have been supplied from what follows in order to complete the sense.

The mystery of faith. That is, mysteries which must not be publicly disclosed, a practice that has always prevailed in every religion.

What we had to do. This expression is frequent in Tertullian. *On the Soul*, chapter 55: “You have also to believe that the region of the lower world is subterranean.” *On Modesty*, chapter 13: “They would have to be instructed that one must not blaspheme.”

LII.—The kingdom of God is within you. One could scarcely show by a clearer example that human beings can place an obstacle in the way of divine grace than the fact that the Jews continued to seek the Messiah even when he was present; indeed, they pursued him with implacable hatred.

Not one. The Vulgate translators, more in accordance with the sense of the Hebrew truth, have: “Are you not the only one? [Col. 1108A] Behold, man’s days are short.” But our author follows the Septuagint.

LVII.—You shall not come out from there. This text is adduced to prove that the faithful person is corrected by evils sent by God in this world. For hell alone is the place of punishments properly so called.

LVIII.—Concerning this alone. The Septuagint has, “I commanded you concerning this alone” (*eneteilamēn soi toutou monou*); they anticipated him in adding the word “alone.”

This corruptible thing. Tertullian commonly reads it in the same manner in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*.

Death into contention. The Apostle has *eis nikos*, “into victory”; but our author and Tertullian also appear to have read *eis neikos*, “into contention.” In Hos. 13:14 the Septuagint put: “Where is your judgment, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?” (*pou hē dikē sou, thanate? pou to kentron sou, Hadē?*). And in truth, forensic judgments are not conducted without contention, and one who prevails in a case is commonly said to have conquered. It should be noted that the Greek translators understood [the Hebrew word] not as “plague,” but as a sentence pronounced by a judge. Moreover, it is clear from verse 10 that they read [text missing], not as we do but as the Chaldean translator did. It may further be observed that some [Col. 1108B] Greek copies, in place of “Hades” (*Hadē*), read “O death” (*thanate*) a second time, agreeing with our author.

LIX.—Let them become like them. Nothing more grievous can befall an idolater than to be made like his god.

LXI.—That they may take [something] from their neighbor. Thus the Septuagint; but Symmachus and Theodotion more correctly have, “until no place remains” (*heōs tou mē hyparchein topon*). The Vulgate reads, “As far as the boundary of the place.”

Here he begs. The Greek is *parakaleitai*. Now, after the reversal of their fortunes, the Rich Man plays the beggar’s part and beseeches Lazarus. The Vulgate translator and others render the word in its other sense: “Here he is comforted.”

Having maintenance. This phrase is constant in Tertullian when he treats of daily sustenance. See *On Idolatry*, chapters 6, 8, and 12; *On the Crown*, chapter 7; and *On Monogamy*, chapter 16. Indeed, the expression was taken from forensic usage, which both writers employed; for there “to maintain” means to supply the necessities of life. Paulus, in the law *Nesennius*, *Digest*, *On the Management of Another’s Affairs*: “Suppose that his father had gone abroad and that, while the mother was returning to her homeland, she had maintained both his son and his daughter.” [Col. 1108C] Thus Ulpian, book I, *Digest*, *On the Office of the Prefect of the City*: “He shall also hear patrons in need who complain of their freedmen, especially if they say that they are ill and desire to be maintained by their freedmen.”

And a mousetrap. “Mousetrap,” *pagis* (“snare”). An old glossary. A device sufficiently suitable for catching a greedy little animal, but wholly unworthy of a human being.

LXIV.—Continence, chastity. This agrees with the manuscripts which add *hagneia*, “chastity.”

LXVI.—Embrace discipline. He renders the passage thus in the book *On the Dress of Virgins*. The Septuagint reads, “Take hold of discipline” (*draxasthe paideias*). Perhaps it was once written, “Embrace the child” (*draxasthe paidiou*).

LXVII.—Itching to hear, scratching their ears. One of these expressions appears to have been taken from the margin.

LXIX.—If anyone among you thinks himself wise, let him become a fool to this world. Our copies read: “If anyone thinks himself wise in this age, let him become a fool” (*ei tis dokei sophos einai en tō aiōni toutō, mōros genesthō*). Our author appears to have punctuated it differently, namely: “If anyone thinks himself [Col. 1108D] wise among you, let him become a fool to this age” (*ei tis dokei sophos einai en hymin, tō aiōni toutō mōros genesthō*).

LXXIX.—For they shall see God. Those who pray are said to seek the face of the Lord; and God is said to turn his face away from those whom he rejects.

LXXX.—You would have no power. These words, though spoken to Pilate, are rightly referred to the Devil; for the Lord likewise says that this was their hour—namely, the Jews’—and then immediately adds, “and the power of darkness,” Luke 22:53.

LXXXIII.—You shall not make a sidelock. The Septuagint translates the word as *sitoēn* [uncertain Greek reading], which Hesychius explains—if one may conjecture after Casaubon and Heinsius—as “a form of cutting among the Phaselites” (*koura para Phasēlitais*). Thus the Israelites were forbidden the hairstyle used among the Phaselites, a people neighboring Palestine, etc. Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, notes the sidelocks of the Germans. According to Tacitus’s explanation in *Germania*, this means “to turn the hair sideways and bind it beneath in a knot.” “The appearance of the beard” is *opsis tou pōgōnos* in the Septuagint.

LXXXIV.—He will be endangered by them if the iron falls out. This reading is taken from the Septuagint, though with altered punctuation. In them the words are divided into two sentences: “He who splits wood will be endangered by it. If the iron falls out,” etc. (*Schizōn xyla kindyneusei en autois. Ean ekpesē to sidērion*, etc.). The Vulgate translator more correctly represents the Hebrew truth: “He who splits wood will be wounded by it. If the iron has grown blunt and is not as before, but has become dull, it will be sharpened with much labor.” [Col. 1109A]

XCIV.—Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup. In commenting upon this passage in the book *On the Lapsed*, Pamelius says that this reading deserves notice against those who insist upon the necessity of communion under both kinds. Evidently, in his judgment, it follows from this that for the reception of the Eucharist it is enough that one merely eat the bread; consequently, he should likewise say that it is no less sufficient for one merely to drink the cup. Moreover, he says that the interpretation of this passage should be noted concerning the necessity of placing *exomologesis* before the Eucharist. That is, auricular confession must necessarily precede those sacred mysteries; namely, the command that one examine oneself absolutely requires each person to undergo another’s examination. Certainly, one who supports his hypothesis in this way would have commended it more earnestly by remaining silent.

XCV.—Do not bring the impious man into the habitation of the righteous. The sacred text has [Hebrew text omitted], which the Vulgate translator renders, “Do not lie in wait,” etc. But the Septuagint, whom our author follows, renders it by a not inappropriate paraphrase: “Do not bring an impious man into the pasture of the righteous” (*mē prosagagēs asebē nomē dikaiōn*). They appear to have read [Hebrew text omitted] in place of [Hebrew text omitted]. [Col. 1109B]

XCVI.—Blessed is he who finds a true friend. The Septuagint has, “as one who found prudence” (*hōs heuren phronēsin*). But Cyprian appears to have read, “as one who found a friend” (*hōs heuren philon*), or “a faithful friend” (*philon piston*).

XCVII.—One must hasten to attainment. It was said above that “attainment” denotes baptism. Because of this delay of baptism, those baptized on a sickbed were formerly held in disrepute in the Church, although practice varied in this matter according to the circumstances of the times. Tertullian held the contrary opinion in *On Baptism*, chapter 19: “If any understand the weight of baptism, they will fear attainment more than delay.”

XCVIII.—While good things are coming. Cyprian seems to have read [Col. 1109C] ἕως (“until”) or ἐφ’ ᾧ (“on condition that”). That is: let us enjoy this interval and indulge in pleasures until baptism has granted pardon for all that has gone before.

C.—He who sees them will possess them. See what we said in chapter 6 of Book II, *To Quirinus*.

CVII.—Do not love to disparage, lest you be taken away. The Hebrew text and the Vulgate have: “Do not love sleep, lest poverty overwhelm you.” But the Septuagint, together with our author, reads: μὴ ἀγάπα καταλαλεῖν, ἵνα μὴ ἐξαρθῇς, “Do not love to speak evil, lest you be taken away.” The reason for this variation seems to be sought in the homonymy of a word that signifies not only sleep but also repetition, and, in the Hebrew dialect, cursing and disparagement. Proverbs VII.9 is rendered by the Vulgate translator, “He who repeats a saying to another”; and XXVI.11 can likewise be rendered, “A fool repeating himself in his folly.” The expression “be taken away” appears to mean the same as “be removed from the midst.”

CXIII.—A son of the Most High, if you obey. The words “if you obey” [Col. 1109D] are redundant, unless perhaps the words that follow, καὶ ἀγαπήσει (“and he will love”), were mistakenly read as εἰ ἀγαπήσῃς (“if you love”) or something similar.

CXIV.—*Exomologesis*. Penitence, of course. For *exomologesis*, by Tertullian’s definition, is a discipline of prostrating and humbling a person. To carve numerous meanings out of this word in the passage is to look for a knot in a bulrush; we gladly leave that labor to Pamelius.

CXVII.—Of this darkness. The word αἰῶνος (“of the age”) is also absent from certain Greek manuscripts.

When you have completed, stand. This agrees with those manuscripts that omit σητε οὖν [an uncertain OCR reading; apparently “therefore stand”].

CXIX.—Let him come in human form. He will be a man. What the Assyrian and Chaldean kings were to the Israelites, Antichrist will be to Christians. Therefore, just as the downfall of the king of Babylon was represented under the figure of Lucifer falling from heaven, Isaiah XIV.12, so too Antichrist was described by the earliest Christians with a similar apparatus of terror, as, namely, [Col. 1110A] a kind of evil genius and prince of evil spirits. Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 25: “The beast Antichrist, together with his false prophet, brings conflict upon the Church of God, and so, when the Devil has been consigned to the abyss,” etc. These words appear to refer to Revelation XX, where the Dragon, the ancient Serpent, who is the Devil and Satan, is described. Certainly the martyr Hippolytus openly held the opinion that Antichrist was the Devil himself, clothed in an illusory and aerial body.

By the shedding of blood. The Greek has καὶ αἵματος, καὶ πνικτοῦ, “and from blood, and from what is strangled.” If these words prohibited the consumption of blood, Christians would be so far from being commanded to abstain from shedding blood that, as Augustine rightly observes against Faustus the Manichaean, Book XXXII, chapter 19, it would have been necessary to provide that “they should eat no flesh whose blood had not been shed.” Hence in Leviticus XVII.13 this very thing is commanded: that “the blood should be poured out like water.” For this reason most of the ancients who held that the mention of blood prohibited its consumption passed over the mention of “what is strangled” [Col. 1110B] as superfluous. But of what kind and how great an importance is the addition καὶ ὅσα ἂν μὴ θέλητε ὑμῖν γίνεσθαι, ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖν, “and whatever you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to others,” and whether these words refer to the precepts given to the sons of Noah, let the learned determine.

## ON THE DRESS OF VIRGINS

Pontius, Jerome, Augustine, and others among the ancients attribute this book to Cyprian, so that there is no controversy over its author. The date of its composition, however, is not equally agreed upon. The very learned Rigault judges that it was composed after Cyprian’s episcopate began, and reproaches Pamelius, I might say, for thinking that it was written by the author when he had first emerged from the laity in Christ’s Church. Rigault believes the matter conclusively settled beyond the reach of controversy by the words of Pontius, who says: “Imagine him now translated by the honor of martyrdom. Who would restrain virgins within a discipline appropriate to chastity and a manner of dress worthy of holiness?” [Col. 1110C] These words, he says, signify as clearly that this little book concerning virgins was published by Cyprian after the persecution as does its title, *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*.

We, however, observed at the beginning of this work that Pontius’s words, “Who would have shown the benefit of grace advancing to its completion?” refer to the book *To Donatus, on the Grace of God*, notwithstanding the defense of Cyprian’s withdrawal undertaken there from the writings mentioned in that passage. And since everyone, including Rigault himself, admits that the book *To Donatus* was written by Cyprian when he first professed the Christian name before the Church, we do not hesitate to affirm that nothing certain can be inferred from the foregoing words of Pontius concerning the order of our martyr’s writings.

The most learned Lombert strives to defend Rigault’s opinion with another argument, taken from the words of Jeremiah quoted below, where the prophet says: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, feeding with discipline”—as though the kind of ecclesiastical discipline represented by the book *On the Dress of Virgins* [Col. 1110D] belonged to a bishop alone. But no one who remembers that several books on that subject were composed by Tertullian the presbyter will say this.

Certainly the words cited by Pamelius in support of his position seem to carry greater weight: our author says that he addresses virgins and exhorts virgins “more from affection than from authority”; not because, being the last and least and acutely conscious of his humility, he claimed any right to censure license, etc. Cyprian is wholly unfamiliar to those who suppose that after becoming bishop he spoke in this way merely as a rhetorical figure.

Finally, if anyone observes the lax morals of women, the indiscriminate use of the baths, and the splendid display of clothing censured in this work, he will hardly persuade himself that the period of the Decian persecution is being described. Let it therefore stand that this treatise should be assigned to the year 243 and to those works which, according to Pontius, Cyprian produced as a presbyter.

We have judged that the old title of this little book should be retained. It is supported by [Col. 1111A] the Speyer edition, the old unnamed edition, those of Rembold, Erasmus, Manutius, Gravius, and most manuscript codices; it appears the simplest, represents the contents of the work most conveniently, and comes closest to Tertullian’s terminology. Tertullian, in *On the Apparel of Women*, teaches that “dress” comprises two forms, grooming and adornment. Septimius had treated these separately in the books *On the Apparel of Women* and *On the Veiling of Virgins*. But since Cyprian had determined to complete the whole subject in a single volume, nothing could have been more appropriate to his design than to place at the head of the work the word “dress,” a term of the broadest signification.

It is evident that Pontius describes rather than cites the books of the holy martyr. Thus, although he mentions a “discipline appropriate to chastity and a manner of dress worthy of holiness,” we do not therefore think the book’s title should be expanded. Nor do we judge that it should be entitled *A Volume on Virginity* merely because Saint Jerome calls this book by that name in his letter to Eustochium.

[Col. 1111B] I.—Discipline, the guardian of hope. The word “discipline” fills nearly every page of Tertullian, and in his writings every duty of piety is honored with this designation. He everywhere commends the discipline of patience, faith, prayer, holiness, monogamy, and chastity. He also begins the closely related treatise *On the Veiling of Virgins* by repeatedly mentioning discipline, and in that same work assigns this prerogative of instruction to his Paraclete.

Cyprian, however, follows his master right up to the altars, under the happiest auspices, always imitating him in such a way as to correct him, and so as himself to become one whom others might safely imitate. The testimonies from Holy Scripture assembled here can be found in Epistle IV—62 in Pamelius’s numbering—*Concerning Virgins*. Indeed, it is customary for our author, when dealing with the same cause, to fight with the same weapons drawn from Scripture.

A retaining-cable of faith. To it, as to a ship’s rope, the anchor of faith is fastened. But Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, II, uses the phrase “the retaining-cables of our hope” of feminine finery in precisely the opposite sense: namely, things that do not sustain hope but [Col. 1111C] hold it back.

II.—The fear governing life. He said above: “The entire foundation of religion and faith proceeds from observance and fear.” And immediately afterward: “Lest what is received as holy and pure through the Lord’s favor should be held with insufficiently vigilant fear.”

III.—Now our discourse is addressed to virgins. Saint Augustine cites this passage in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book IV, chapter 21, as an example of the temperate style. He further observes that in this little book the martyr Cyprian wrote about the dress of virgins, not about undertaking the profession of virginity.

We exhort them more from affection than from authority. Similarly Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, Book II: “Handmaids of the living God, my fellow-servants and sisters, by what right am I counted with you, the very least?” And later: “Would that I, most wretched man, might on that day of Christian exultation raise my head even beneath your heels.”

Eunuchs who have castrated themselves. Tertullian said: “Those who seal themselves for the state of eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 1111D] V.—For it is not right that a virgin should arrange herself for the display of her beauty. He interprets himself below when he says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient.”

VI.—When she is tortured for confessing the Name. Tertullian had previously said: “When, having been torn for Christ, she has endured.”

VII.—And destined here to remain with the world. Things that those about to die are compelled to leave behind.

Whose pomp and pleasures we renounced even then. Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter IV: “When we entered the water and professed the Christian faith in the words of its rule, we testified with our own mouths that we had renounced the Devil, his pomp, and his angel.”

Just as God also remains. This addition does not appear in the Greek.

IX.—You live in such a way that you can be loved. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, explains the matter thus: “The pagan women of Arabia cover not only the head but the entire face in such a way that, leaving one eye uncovered, they are content to enjoy half the light [Col. 1112A] rather than prostitute the whole face.” A certain Roman queen accordingly called them most unfortunate, because they could love rather than be loved.

X.—Let them not use them. See Book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*, chapter 2.

Peter also. If an apostle enjoying so great a favor endured the most extreme poverty, a Christian woman takes pleasure in her abundance of riches in vain.

XI.—The harlot city is described. Tertullian likewise cites this passage in Book II of *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 12: “That mighty city which presides over seven mountains and many waters,” etc. See Book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*, chapter 36.

XIII.—Dragging their robes as they walk. Homer calls such women by the single word ἑλκεσίπεπλοι, “trailing-robed.”

The foremost daughters of Zion. The Vulgate renders the Hebrew text more suitably: “The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion.” What is then said afterward, “the Lord will uncover their attire,” ἀνακαλύψαι τὸ σχῆμα, is more successfully read by certain copies as αἰσχύνωμα, “their shame.”

Crescents. The μηνίσκοι (“little moons” or “crescents”) are, according to Symmachus, [Col. 1112B] μανιάκια (“necklaces”), and according to Hesychius περιτραχήλια, μανιάκια, περιδέραια (“neckbands, necklaces, collars”). The Septuagint in fact joins μηνίσκους καὶ τὸ κάθεμα, “the crescents and the pendant.” According to the same Hesychius, κάθεμα means ὁ κατὰ στήθους ὅρμος, “the necklace lying upon the breast,” that is, a necklace placed around the neck and customarily adorned with a hanging jewel. With reference to this Jerome translates it “crescents,” pendants resembling the moon.

Hair-dividers. The hair-dividing pin is well known among Latin writers. With one of these Fulvia pierced the tongue of the dead Cicero.

Clustered ornament. Whatever Rhenanus and Pamelius may have thought to the contrary, the *botronatus* appears to have been an ornament for the ears. Hesychius says: βοτροειδία, ἐνωταρίων εἶδος, “grape-cluster ornaments, a kind of earring.” Tertullian mentions these clustered ornaments in Book II of *On Apparel*.

Right-arm ornaments. What these ἐπιδέξια were can scarcely be understood more successfully than from the bargain of the maiden Tarpeia, who, according to Plutarch, is said to have betrayed Rome’s citadel to the Sabines ἐπιθυμήσασα τῶν χρυσῶν βραχιονιστήρων, “because she desired their golden armlets.” See Exodus XXXV.21; Numbers XXXI.50; II Kings I.10. Aquila translates it χλιδῶνα βραχίονος, βραχιόλιον, “an arm ornament, a bracelet.” But no one will be surprised that in [Col. 1112C] all these passages the Greek differs greatly from the Hebrew, the Latin from both, and our author from them all, if he considers the infinite variety of articles worn—especially by women—among every nation and in every age.

XIV.—For neither did God make scarlet-colored things. Tertullian, *On the Apparel of Women*, Book II, chapter 10: “God, of course, showed us how to steep wool in the juices of plants and the secretions of shellfish. When he commanded all things to come into being, it escaped him to order purple and scarlet sheep.” Jerome employs the same rhetoric in the *Life of Marcella*.

Sinful and apostate angels. Tertullian, Book I of *On the Apparel of Women*, chapter 2: “Those angels, namely, who fell from heaven to the daughters of men,” etc. Lactantius, Book II, chapter 15; Eusebius, *Preparation*, Book V; and Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XV, chapter 23, also held this opinion.

XV.—If some painter. Saint Augustine discusses this passage at length as an example of the grand style in the previously cited passage of *On Christian Doctrine*.

[Col. 1112D] With a rival color. One whose beauty all might emulate.

You, in order to overcome the word of your Lord. Thus Tertullian, *On Apparel*, Book II, chapter 6: “But the Lord says: ‘Which of you can make black hair white, or white hair black?’ Thus they refute God.” And shortly afterward: “It is surprising that no contest is also raised against the Lord’s precepts: it has been declared that no one can add to his stature, yet you add to your weight certain rolls of hair,” etc.

XVI.—You already take fiery-red hair as an omen for yourself. Tertullian, in the same place: “May your fiery-red head prove the worst of omens for you.”

You sin against your head. This appears to refer, not, as Rigault would have it, to *diminutio capitis* under Roman law, but to the Apostle’s words in I Corinthians XI.10, καταισχύνει τὴν κεφαλήν, “she dishonors her head.” I would further suppose that Cyprian remembered the words of his master: “Let them know that the whole of a woman is ‘head’; its bounds and limits extend as far as the point where her clothing begins.”

XVII.—When the day of resurrection comes. The same author says above in that work: [Col. 1113A] “I shall see whether you rise again with white lead, rouge, saffron, and all that elaborate arrangement of the head.”

XVIII.—And because. The sense of these words appears unable to stand unless they are connected with what follows.

Shameful words. Fescennine verses, altogether obscene, which, as Festus says, were sung at weddings.

XXIII.—The reward of greater grace. Beyond the measure of baptismal grace, God grants richer gifts to those mature alike in years and piety; but scarcely any are more desirable than those which supply strength for subduing the desires of the flesh.

## THE BOOK ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH

*On the Unity of the Church.* This book, written to resolve the schism of Novatian, is attributed to Cyprian not only because Pontius, Saint Augustine in Book II *Against Cresconius*, chapter 33, and other ancients mention it, but also by the testimony of Cyprian himself in Epistle LIV—51 in Pamelius’s numbering—[Col. 1113B] for there he acknowledges a little book composed by himself “which set forth the unity of the Catholic Church.” No one will readily doubt that these words refer to this volume.

We have omitted the addition of the word “Catholic” in the title of the little book, though it has commonly prevailed and is supported by very many manuscripts, especially since Pontius further abbreviated the title, designating this treatise by the single word “Unity.” Moreover, it is certain that Saint Augustine, in the passage cited above, expressly called this book the *Epistle on Unity*. Facundus, Book I, page 16, appears to follow this terminology in a passage badly mutilated by copyists, as the most learned Lombert rightly observes. For he intended to cite not a nonexistent book of Cyprian *On the Trinity*, but the book *On Unity*, as will be evident to anyone who examines the passage itself.

Rembold’s edition supplied another title, namely *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, taken from the beginning of the little book, where we are said to be admonished to be innocent in simplicity and yet prudent along with that simplicity. We observed that something similar occurred in the preceding [Col. 1113C] treatise among those who devised the title *On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins*.

As for the time when the work was composed, we judge from its argument and from the epistle cited above that it was written after Cornelius’s accession to the pontificate, the schism of Novatian, and the defection of the confessors, but before the martyrdom of Cornelius himself, indeed before the confessors returned to the Church; that is, that it was sent to Rome in the year 251.

VI.—These three are one. Faustus Socinus says in his commentary upon this passage that it is sufficiently established that the clause is spurious and was inserted here by men who wished, by whatever means, to defend and propagate their dogma concerning the triune and one God. He further adds that Jerome—one who, as Erasmus rightly writes of him somewhere, often drew many things toward victory and toward the defense and favor of his own cause with insufficient prudence—perhaps obtained some copy, or even several copies, in which this clause, namely the threefold testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit [Col. 1113D] bearing witness in heaven, had been added in such a way that the fraud could not be detected. Contrary to the testimony of all other copies, Latin as well as Greek, Jerome then began to defend and promote the reading of that clause as genuine, publicly complaining that it had been erased from the commonly used codices through the fault and fraud of heretics.

To repel this exceedingly grave accusation that Saint Jerome was a forger and an interpolator of Holy Scripture, it may suffice that Cyprian cited this passage not only before Jerome’s time but before Arius himself and before the controversy over that dogma—so displeasing to Socinus—concerning the triune and one God. Yet Cyprian acknowledges this passage both here and in his epistle to Jubaianus. Indeed, Tertullian did the same in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 25.

Meanwhile it is astonishing that this epistle of Saint Jerome—which first tortured Erasmus, and then Socinus and his followers, and which is acknowledged not only by them but generally by the manuscripts, by almost all the older printed codices, and by the [Col. 1114A] commentaries of interpreters—has in our own century utterly disappeared, as if some enchantment had dazzled men’s eyes. To speak somewhat more distinctly: it is found in the Latin Bibles published at Nuremberg in 1475, Venice in 1498, Basel in 1506, Lyon in 1520, Paris in 1563, Lyon in 1589, and Antwerp in 1617. Whether this happened by chance or through wrongdoing, let the learned investigate. Since the epistle itself is brief and is not readily available nowadays, it will not be burdensome to append it.

The Prologue to the Canonical Epistles begins:

> Among the Greeks who are wholly sound in doctrine and follow the right faith, the order of the seven epistles called canonical is not the same as that found in the Latin codices. For because Peter is first in the order of the apostles, his epistles also stand first in the order of the others. But just as we formerly corrected the Evangelists according to the standard of truth, so, with God’s help, we have restored these epistles to their proper order. The first of them is one epistle of James, then two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude.
>
> If these were faithfully translated into Latin by interpreters in the order in which their authors arranged them, [Col. 1114B] they would neither create ambiguity for readers nor conflict with one another through variations of expression. This is especially true of the passage in the First Epistle of John where we read about the unity of the Trinity. There we have discovered that unfaithful translators departed greatly from the truth of the faith, placing in their edition only the names of three—the Water, the Blood, and the Spirit—and omitting the testimony of the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, by which both the Catholic faith is most firmly strengthened and the single substance of the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is confirmed.
>
> As for the other epistles, I leave it to the reader’s judgment to determine how far the edition of others differs from ours. But you, Eustochium, virgin of Christ, by earnestly demanding from me the truth of Scripture, in a sense expose my old age to be gnawed by the teeth of the envious, who proclaim me a forger and corrupter of the holy Scriptures. Yet in such a work I neither fear the envy of my rivals [Col. 1114C] nor will I deny the truth of Holy Scripture to those who ask for it.

VII.—From the upper part. Our Lord speaks everywhere of himself, his doctrine, and the second birth of the regenerate as coming ἄνωθεν, “from above.” Saint Cyprian therefore draws that word here toward the same meaning and holds that Unity, as though fallen from heaven, was prefigured by Christ’s tunic, which was ἄνωθεν ὑφαντὸς δι’ ὅλου, “woven throughout from above.” Chrysostom mentions this interpretation in Homily 85, but concludes: τοῦτο δὲ ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ λέγειν αἰνιττόμενος τὸ εὐτελὲς τῶν ἱματίων, “But he seems to me to say this as an allusion to the plainness of the garments.”

IX.—When they breed, they bring forth their young together. “Their love for both offspring is equal,” says Pliny, who in Book X, chapter 34, describes the domestic life of doves at length: “Chastity holds first place among them, and adultery is unknown to either sex; they do not violate marital fidelity and maintain a common home. Except when unmarried or widowed, a dove does not leave the nest,” etc.

X.—They assume for themselves the name of bishop. Such, of course, was Novatian. By “reckless outsiders” [Col. 1114D] are meant the three bishops summoned from Italy who lent their hands to Novatian’s ordination.

Treatises; discourses. Thus in Epistle LXXVII—78 in Pamelius’s numbering—it is said: “You do not cease in your treatises to unveil hidden mysteries”; and immediately afterward: “Greater than all in exposition, more eloquent in discourse.” Indeed, in this very work: “in a lengthy treatise.” Hence in later centuries those who delivered sermons before the people were called *tractatores*, “expositors.” Glossary of Cyril: ὁμιλητικός, “a preacher,” *tractator*.

XI.—In my substance. This is given for what the Septuagint has, ἐν ὑποστήματι, “in my subsistence.” They appear to have read [a word is absent in the source]. Hesychius explains ὑπόστημα by πλῆθος, “multitude.”

When there is another baptism. An occasion to discuss this doctrine will be given elsewhere.

XII.—Corrupters of the Gospel. On this sacrilege of the heretics, see Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 5; Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chapters 17 and 33, and *Against Marcion*, Book V, chapter 18; Eusebius, *History*, Book V, chapter 28; Augustine, *Heresies* 46, on the Manichaeans, and 70; Theodoret, Book II of *Heretical Fables*, chapter 5.

[Col. 1115A] With the spirit of dew. They had been bedewed with the refreshment of the Spirit. But if this is the meaning of the words, it would be more appropriate to say that they had been animated by “the dew of the Spirit.” Hence the suspicion arises that the author wrote: “God animated the simple and mutually harmonious with the spirit of his mouth.” This manner of speaking is sufficiently common in Holy Scripture.

XIV.—Such persons, even if slain. This maxim, which Cyprian continually inculcates, passed into the Eastern Church. For Saint Chrysostom, referring to it in Sermon 11 on the Epistle to the Ephesians, says: Ἀνήρ τις ἅγιος εἶπέ τι δοκοῦν εἶναι τολμηρόν, πλὴν ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἐφθέγξατο· τί δὴ τοῦτό ἐστιν; οὐδὲ μαρτυρίου αἷμα ταύτην δύνασθαι ἐξαλείφειν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ἔφησεν, “A certain holy man said something that seemed daring, yet he nevertheless uttered it. What was it? He said that not even the blood of martyrdom can wipe away this sin.”

How great a wickedness schism is, and how utterly incapable of expiation, the remaining Fathers teach us everywhere: Clement, *Epistle to the Corinthians*; Ignatius, epistles to the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians; Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 62; Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 45; Firmilian’s epistle to Cyprian; Optatus, Book I; Fulgentius, *To Monimus*, Book II; Augustine, *Against Parmenian*, Book II, chapter 2; Vincent of Lérins, chapter 34; Prosper, *On the Fulfillment of Promises and Predictions*, chapter 5.

[Col. 1115B] XV.—Our merits a reward. That reward proceeds from God’s good pleasure, for he crowns his own gifts in us. Whenever our author mentions merits, recourse must be had to his most celebrated maxim, frequently cited by Saint Augustine as an oracle, in Book III *To Quirinus*, chapter 4: “We must glory in nothing, since nothing is ours.”

By a shortening abridgment. Our author uses the same phrase in the preface to the first book *To Quirinus*.

XVI.—Having a representation of religion. The Apostle says μόρφωσιν εὐσεβείας, “a form of godliness.” Tertullian frequently uses *deformatio* in the sense of a description: “depicting the end of each, the torments of Herod and the refreshments of John,” *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 34; “He does not first fashion the idol out of clay,” *Apology*, chapter 12.

XVII.—Condemned by himself. Certainly these words of the Apostle fit no mortals better than Novatus and Novatian, for they separated from themselves before they separated from the Church. The former, after contending in Africa [Col. 1115C] that all the lapsed should be admitted without delay, sailed to Rome and advanced the contrary doctrine: namely, that it should be regarded as an inexpiable crime if they were ever admitted. The latter not only took part in but presided over the judgment of the Roman clergy concerning the reception of the lapsed. With his own hand he wrote, and with his own mouth publicly read, the letter transmitted to the African Church on that matter. Yet in that same Rome he taught that defenders of that opinion—that is, of his own opinion—were to be numbered among apostates and the lapsed; and there, after swearing that he would not accept the episcopate, he usurped it.

XVIII.—Where those who earn the Lord’s favor are signed. Christians impressed the sign of the cross upon their foreheads not only during the solemn rites of baptism, but “at every advance and movement forward, at every entrance and departure, when dressing and putting on shoes, at the baths, at tables, when lighting lamps, when going to bed, when sitting down—whatever occupation engaged them—they wore away their foreheads with the sign of the cross.” So reports Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3. Religious worship of crosses, meanwhile, was absent. “We neither worship crosses,” says Octavius in Minucius [Col. 1115D], “nor desire them.”

XIX.—With full satisfactions. What full satisfaction means will be discussed below in the book *On the Lapsed*.

XX.—Some of the confessors. He censures Maximus, Nicostratus, Evaristus, and others who in their letters recommended Novatian for the episcopate and supported his party.

XXII.—They fell away from the faith. The Vulgate translator renders ἠπίστησαν as “they did not believe”; but our author appears to have understood it more correctly as “they acted faithlessly.” For that word refers to what had been said above: ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ, “they were entrusted with the oracles of God.”

XXIII.—With the glue of concord. Namely, through one bishop. In the epistle to Pupianus he says: “The Church is the people united to the priest and the flock adhering to its shepherd.” Optatus calls the bishop “the bridegroom, the bond of peace.”

XXVI.—Nor do we give tithes. Tithes were paid by a prescription of nature long before the Mosaic Law. Even if the words found in the Septuagint at Genesis IV.7 do not sufficiently establish this—οὐκ ἐὰν ὀρθῶς προσενέγκῃς [Col. 1116A] ὀρθῶς δὲ μὴ διέλῃς, ἥμαρτες, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?”—certainly what is read in chapter XIV.18 concerning the tithes paid by Abraham proves it, especially since this custom formerly prevailed throughout the whole world, as though by a public decree of the human race.

The most substantial witnesses to this fact are Herodotus, Books I, II, III, and IX, and throughout; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Books I, IV, and VI; Pausanias, *Elis* and *Phocis*; Diodorus Siculus, Book I; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, *Camillus*, *Sulla*, *Lucullus*, etc.; Aristotle, *Economics*, Book II; Thucydides, Book III; Justin, Book XVIII, chapter 20; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III; Livy, Book V, chapter 21.

When the world was first flooded with the light of the Gospel, nothing was more frequently proclaimed than offerings, first fruits, charitable distributions, and the sale of one’s entire property for the support of the Church. Indeed, the most ancient Fathers expressly command the payment of tithes. Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 20, says:

> All the apostles of the Lord are priests; they inherit neither fields nor houses here, but always serve the altar and God. Concerning them Moses also says: “The Levitical priests shall have neither part nor substance with Israel in the whole tribe of Levi; they shall eat the fruit-offerings of the Lord, their substance.” [Col. 1116B] For this reason Paul also says: “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit.”

And in the same book, chapter 27:

> For this reason the Lord, in place of “You shall not commit adultery,” commanded them not even to lust; in place of “You shall not kill,” not even to be angry; and in place of tithing, to distribute everything they possess to the poor. All these things were the acts not of one abolishing the Law, but of one extending and enlarging it.

Furthermore, in chapter 34:

> They had indeed consecrated the tithes of their possessions; but those who have received liberty assign everything they possess to the Lord’s uses, giving cheerfully and freely things that are not less, since they possess a greater hope.

Thus Origen, on Numbers XVIII:

> No one lawfully or legitimately uses the fruits produced by the earth or the living creatures brought forth as offspring by the flock unless first fruits from each and every thing are offered to God—that is, to the priests. I therefore consider it necessary that this law, like certain others, be observed even according to the letter.

He then adds:

> The Lord says in the Gospels: “Woe to you, scribes [Col. 1116C] and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint”—that is, give a tenth part of mint—“and cumin and dill, and pass over the weightier matters of the Law. Hypocrites, these things ought to be done, and those not omitted.” Consider more carefully, therefore, how the Lord’s word wills that the weightier matters of the Law should be performed in every way, but nevertheless that those things which are designated according to the letter should not be omitted.
>
> But if you say that he spoke these words to the Pharisees, not to the disciples, hear him again saying to the disciples: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Pharisees and scribes, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” What he wishes the Pharisees to do, therefore, he wishes the disciples to fulfill much more and with greater abundance, etc.

It would take too long to survey every relevant passage. Anyone with leisure should consult Hilary on Matthew XXIV and the exposition of Psalm CXVIII, the octonary *He*; Nazianzen, Oration V; Jerome on Malachi III; Chrysostom, Homily 35 on Genesis; XVIII on Acts of the Apostles; XIV and Homily 4 on chapter II of Ephesians [citation numbering uncertain in the source]; Ambrose, commentary on Luke XI, Book VII, [Col. 1116D] Sermon 34 for Tuesday, and the sermon for Ascension Day; Augustine on Psalm CXLVI, Sermons 166 and 219 *On Time*, and Homily 48.

Indeed, see what our own author says in Epistle I—66 in Pamelius’s numbering—where he states:

> The tribe of Levi received tithes from the fruits that were produced. All this was done by divine authority and arrangement, so that those who devoted themselves to divine prayers might be distracted by no concern, nor be compelled to think about or conduct secular business. This same principle and form is now maintained among the clergy, so that those who are advanced by clerical ordination in the Lord’s Church may in no respect be distracted from the divine ministry, etc.

## ON THE LAPSED

When conduct is under discussion, *lapsus*, “a fall,” commonly signifies any graver offense by which a person, in the course of life, not only stumbles and is displaced from his footing, but is prostrated and falls down. Thus Adam’s sin is everywhere called his fall. In ecclesiastical usage, however, [Col. 1117A] “the lapsed” generally means those who yielded to threats or tortures in time of persecution; they are called below “scattered,” “prostrated,” and “lying fallen.” Those who remained steadfast in the faith, by contrast, were called “the standing.” The prophet Zechariah appears to have prefigured them in chapter III.7, where a place “among those standing” is promised to the person who walks in the Lord’s ways and keeps his charge.

There were various classes of the lapsed:

1. Those who obtained security by means of certificates and were called *libellatici*, “certificate-holders.”
2. Those who burned incense or feasted upon the sacrificial victims and were called *thurificati* and *sacrificati*, “incense-offerers” and “sacrificers.”
3. Those who compounded their crime with blasphemies, abjured the Christian name, and were called apostates.
