But when the Decian calamity had struck down very many people by these various kinds of ruin, and they—supported by the faction of Novatus and Felicissimus and certain presbyters who agreed with them, or even by the excessively indulgent recommendations of the martyrs—shamelessly demanded readmission to the Church, Cyprian did what he had formerly promised he would do. Once peace had been restored to the Church, and after weighing the matter in consultation with the brethren, [Col. 1117B] he determined what should be decided concerning each class.

This little book, like the preceding one *On Unity*, was first read at Carthage—and, as it is reasonable to believe, in the council itself—and was then sent to Rome, as we learn from Epistle 54, number 51 in Pamelius. The words at the beginning of the work—“Behold, dearly beloved brethren, peace has been restored to the Church; and what recently seemed difficult to the unbelieving and impossible to the faithless, our security has been restored by divine aid and vengeance”—sufficiently indicate that this little book was sent to Rome after the death of Decius, and immediately after news of it had been received.

I have no doubt, however, that it had been written somewhat earlier and publicly read at Carthage. For several months elapsed between Cyprian’s return and the death of Decius and the reporting of that death in Africa, during which a council concerning the cause of the lapsed was frequently held. But authors continually claim for themselves the right to add from time to time things newly arisen, to remove material, and to make various alterations in their writings; [Col. 1117C] and I believe that Cyprian did so here as well. Pontius, Eusebius, Rufinus, Augustine, Fulgentius, Pacianus, and many other ancient writers mention this work.

II.—A white-clad cohort. Likewise the martyrs are called by our author the *Massa Candida*, the “White-Clad Company.” Thus Tertullian, *On the Crown*: “To be crowned more nobly with the white laurel of martyrdom.” With regard to their shed blood, however, they are elsewhere called “florid” and “clad in red.”

From the impious and criminal veil. Nearly the whole religion of the pagans was occupied with the cult of the dead and the appeasement of the divine shades; hence their sacred rites were generally performed in mourning dress and with veiled head. Christians, by contrast, following the Apostle in I Corinthians XI.10, offered prayers with uncovered heads, while women alone were veiled in church for the sake of modesty and submission.

Moreover, a covered head was a sign of servile status. Hence a person about to undergo a slave’s punishment was covered with a veil. “Go, lictor,” says the father of Horatius when his son was in danger, in Livy, Book I; “bind the hands which, armed only a little while ago, [Col. 1117D] won sovereignty for the Roman people. Go, cover the head of the city’s liberator,” etc.

A forehead pure with the sign of God. That is, marked in the laver of Baptism and mindful of the thorny garland of the Lord Jesus, it cannot admit any other head-covering, or any attire introduced by the devil’s candidates. So says Tertullian in his book *On the Crown*, where he also reports that Claudius Saturninus, in his book *On Crowns*, explains their origins, causes, kinds, and ceremonies in such a way that one will find no charm of flower, no delight of foliage, no turf or vine-shoot, that has not been consecrated to someone’s head.

II.—*Weakens them by malicious disparagement.* In order to make themselves appear more excusable, the lapsed maintained that very many of those who remained standing would have fallen together with them if they had likewise been tried—if they had not then escaped by flight, as Cyprian did. In a not dissimilar case it was said: “She is chaste whom no one has propositioned.”

*The day appointed for those who denied has passed.* Edicts had been issued [Col. 1118A] against the Christians, requiring every Christian, within a prescribed day, to declare before the governor, proconsul, or another magistrate that he renounced Christ. If he did not, he was to be punished with death, or perhaps with confiscation of property or exile. Once that period had elapsed, all who had not made such a declaration became liable to the announced penalties and therefore had to be numbered among the confessors. For this reason our author says that neither the prescribed exiles, nor the appointed tortures, nor losses of private property terrified the bishops.

V.—*A long peace had corrupted discipline.* Sulpicius Severus reckons thirty-eight years of peace for the Church, namely from the emperor Severus to Decius, since Maximinus’s attacks had struck only the clergy of certain churches and had left Africa untouched. Almost the same statements occur in Epistle XIII, Pamelian number 7.

VI.—*With beard disfigured.* He has in view Leviticus 19:27, where it is forbidden to disfigure the corners of the beard. On this matter see Book III, chapter 84, *To Quirinus*. He treated the conduct [Col. 1118B] of women in the book *On Dress*.

*To join with unbelievers.* The author has in view the admonition of St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 6:14 and 1 Corinthians 7. See Book III of the *Testimonies to Quirinus*, chapter 62.

*Very many bishops.* St. Augustine touches on this passage frequently against the Donatists; see Book III, chapter 2, *Against the Epistle of Parmenian*, and Book IV, chapter 26, *Against Cresconius*.

*While the brethren in the Church were starving.* Although it seemed good to the Apostles, Acts 6, that they should not forsake the word of God to serve tables, and deacons were consequently appointed in their place, care of the poor nevertheless remained permanently with the bishops. How diligently St. Paul attended to this, his Epistles teach us throughout. Justin, *Apology* II, gives an account of the conduct of Christians in the following century: “What is collected is deposited with the presiding minister, and he himself assists orphans and widows, those in want through illness or some other cause, those who are in prison, and strangers staying among us; in short, he becomes the guardian of all who are in need.” Cyprian’s Epistles prevent us from being ignorant that this was his perpetual [Col. 1118C] concern, especially Epistle LXII, Pamelian number 60, where, if Rigaltius has calculated correctly, 25,000 pounds were expended to ransom captives.

*At the very first words.* Cyprian, Epistle LX, Pamelian number 57, calls those struck down by this unexpected terror “taken by surprise.” Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 41, describes at length a similar devastation among the lapsed in Egypt at this very time.

VIII.—*Those arrested should go up.* This reading, supported by most manuscripts, is commended by a similar expression in Epistle VIII of the Roman clergy, Pamelian number 3: “We recalled those who were going up from that which they were being compelled to do.”

*People went voluntarily to the Capitol.* This means the citadel of Carthage, an imitation of the Roman Capitol. The Novatians and Donatists contemptuously called the Catholics “Capitolines” because they had received back those who had lapsed by going up there. Thus Pacian, Epistle II: “Does it harm the holy man Cyprian that his people bear the name Apostolic, or [Col. 1118D] Capitoline, or Synedrium?”

*He who had already renounced the devil.* Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 4, and elsewhere throughout, repeatedly invokes these solemn words of Baptism, as do our Cyprian and other Fathers. This most ancient formula had no other origin than the beginnings of Christianity and appears to be that “pledge” (*eperōtēma*, ἐπερώτημα) of which St. Peter speaks in 1 Peter 3:21. In Jewish baptism the proselyte renounced his native land, parents, and humanity; the Christian, however, renounces and dismisses harmful desires, the pomps of the world, and the wickedness of the devil.

IX.—*It was offered in a lethal cup.* He has in view the libations of the Gentiles, concerning which St. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10:21: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.”

*Infants also.* On their Baptism, see the letter *To Fidus*. Rigaltius attacks this custom at length in his notes on that Epistle and says here: “Moved by this consideration, they decreed that infants should be baptized; they gave the sign of faith to a human being before he was capable of faith. [Col. 1119A] They made a sign without the reality a substitute for the reality itself.” A fanatic from the dregs of the Anabaptists could have written nothing different. Are infants, then, utterly incapable of faith? If this is accepted, how were John the Baptist and others filled with the Holy Spirit from their mother’s womb? Moreover, circumcision both before the Law and under it was a covenantal rite whose foundation was faith in the Messiah who was afterward to come, just as its antitype, Baptism under the Gospel, rests upon faith in the same Messiah who had come. But if Israelite infants, though incapable of actual faith, were fit to receive circumcision, then likewise the children of Christian parents may be able to partake of Baptism notwithstanding the same obstacle, namely the lack of faith. Those infants had long since been baptized who gave examples of that keen and lively awareness mentioned above; hence it is plainly wrong to say that the Church was thereby moved to decree that infants should be baptized. Moreover, Irenaeus teaches us that infant Baptism was received in the Church before Cyprian’s age, Book II, chapter 39, where he says that infants, little children, [Col. 1119B] boys, young people, and the elderly are reborn unto God. Similarly Origen, on Romans 6, says: “The Church received from the Apostles the tradition of giving Baptism even to little children.” That this custom prevailed in Tertullian’s age is evident even from the fact that he advises the contrary: “Why should an innocent age hasten to the remission of sins?” This opinion pleased so many that they considered Baptism should be postponed until extreme old age. They were plainly striving to secure for themselves leave to sin, confident of pardon through expiation in the saving laver.

*The little ones lost.* St. Augustine, Epistle XXIII to Boniface, resolves the matter thus: “He said, ‘They lost,’ so far as concerned the crime of those by whom they were forced to lose it. They lost it in the mind and will of those who committed so great an outrage against them. For if they had lost it in themselves, they would certainly have remained liable to condemnation by the divine sentence. If holy Cyprian had thought this, he would not immediately have added their defense, saying,” etc.

X.—*Depart, depart.* Cyprian pleads his own cause [Col. 1119C] against the detractors who reproached him for his flight as something shameful. He appears not only to defend it as lawful but to commend it as something commanded, departing widely on this point from his master Tertullian.

XIII.—*Now the scourges would tear them.* Tertullian likewise describes these tortures in *Apology*, chapter 30: “Let claws gouge them as they are stretched out; let crosses suspend them; let flames lick them; let swords sever their throats; let beasts leap upon them.”

*At one time the Lord forgave Aemilius.* According to the teaching of the ancient Church, the baptism of blood washed away every stain of one’s past life no less certainly than the laver of water. Consequently, since Castus and Aemilius were admitted to the honor of martyrdom, there was no room for doubt that pardon had been granted them. Hence in Epistle XVIII, Pamelian number 13, Cyprian addresses thus those among the lapsed who were hastening to peace: “The battle line is still engaged, and the contest is celebrated daily. If one truly and steadfastly repents of what he has committed, and the ardor of faith prevails, he who cannot be postponed can be crowned.” The statement that the Lord [Col. 1119D] had “at one time” forgiven him appears to indicate that this had occurred previously at Carthage.

XV.—*The holy thing of the Lord.* Below he calls the food and drink sanctified in the blood of the Lord, as Rigaltius rightly observes.

*They assail the Lord’s body.* Our author explains himself by two testimonies of Holy Scripture, namely Leviticus 17:3, where it is said: “The flesh of the sacrifice which belongs to the Lord,” and 1 Corinthians 11:27: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord,” etc. Facundus, Cyprian’s most faithful follower, explains it very clearly in Book IX, chapter 5: “We call the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, which is in the consecrated bread and cup, his body and blood—not because the bread is properly his body and the cup his blood, but because they contain within themselves the mystery of his body and blood. Hence the Lord himself called the blessed bread and cup which he handed to his disciples his body and blood.”

XVII.—*But when the day of judgment comes.* He has in view [Col. 1120A] the passage of St. John, Revelation 6:10, which he immediately cites, where it is said that beneath God’s altar the souls of the slain martyrs cry with a loud voice, saying, “How long?” etc. The ancients held the view that sentence had been pronounced before the day of judgment only upon the martyrs, while the cases of all others were adjourned.

XVIII.—*Before he is vindicated.* Peace granted by martyrs was not entirely valid before they had been crowned. See the Epistle of Lucian, where, after Paul and other martyrs had been summoned to execution, peace is declared to be granted in their name. This was done with good reason, since not a few confessors afterward lapsed themselves.

XIX.—*For Moses also.* Pacian cites this passage in Epistle III and teaches that the prayers of the saints suffer rejection if they petition for those who do not themselves ask, if they intercede for those who persist in crime, or if they defend not individuals or a few persons but many thousands.

XX.—*Let no one defame the dignity of the martyrs.* Let no one, he says, overthrow the privilege formerly granted them of interceding for the lapsed, provided that it remains within its prescribed limits. [Col. 1120B] That is, provided they grant what is described in Epistle 17, Pamelian number 10: “Such things as their predecessors, the martyrs, granted in the past.” Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*: “Certain persons who did not possess peace in the Church were accustomed to entreat it from the martyrs in prison.” The pardon granted to the lapsed was called “peace,” because through it they were admitted to participation in the sacred rites and, specifically, in prayer and the kiss of peace—“the seal of prayer,” in Tertullian’s words.

XXI.—*The wrath of indignation.* The Septuagint has “wrath of fury” (ὀργὴν θυμοῦ).

XXIV.—*To implore mercy.* From God the Father and from his Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, both of whom he had renounced.

XXV.—*While we are sacrificing.* See what we said on Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 16. Infants were formerly admitted to participation in the mysteries of the Eucharist immediately after Baptism, on the strength of the Lord’s words in John 6:53: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you.” This was later postponed in consequence of the Apostle’s admonition in 1 Corinthians 11:28: “Let a man examine [Col. 1120C] himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup.”

XXVI.—*To carry ashes.* It was customary for participants in the Eucharist, after receiving a portion of the bread, not only to eat it during the sacred ceremonies but also to reserve some of it and carry it home, where they consumed it either before food, in times of danger, or at the outset of undertakings, just as was afterward done with *eulogiae*, or blessed loaves. This custom appears to have lasted until the Council of Saragossa. To this pertains Tertullian’s statement in Book II *To His Wife*: “Let your husband not know what you taste in secret before all other food”; and in *On Prayer*: “After receiving and reserving the Lord’s body.” That the Eucharistic bread should be transubstantiated into the Lord’s body appears to surpass belief; yet something still greater, if that is possible, and something no one could readily assert, would be that the Lord’s body was turned into ashes.

XXVII.—*He said that he had done it.* The most learned Rigaltius thinks that this passage will be illuminated by the Epistle of the clergy of the Roman Church, where a fearful Christian declares [Col. 1120D] that he gave a payment to an extortioner—whether soldier or governor—so that he would not do what was unlawful, namely, so that he would not be compelled to sacrifice to idols. Certainly this could be more fully elucidated from the Epistle to Antonianus, namely Epistle 55, Pamelian number 52. Yet these words seem to suggest something else: namely, that in place of the *libellaticus*, someone else had done or said that which, being justly imputed to its author, constituted him a denier or a lapsed person. The kind of deed Cyprian has in view here will therefore more probably have been this. A Christian, fearing harm to himself, either sent in a pagan who, assuming his identity, would sacrifice, renounce the faith, and obtain a *libellus* or certificate in the other man’s name, by which the latter could defend himself and turn away informers if he happened to be called into question, as though he himself had fully satisfied the emperors’ laws; or at least he obtained by payment or entreaty a token certifying that these acts had been performed. In this case the *libellaticus* will most properly be said to have “done” whatever another committed by doing it, and to have disclosed himself as unfaithful through the unlawful [Col. 1121A] declaration contained in those accursed certificates. Certainly, in recent times among us under Cromwell’s tyranny, when the rebels’ arms had overthrown an excellent sovereign and the victors raged without restraint against all who remained faithful, many crossed over to the opposing camp and openly defected, and are therefore to be numbered among the apostates. There were also many who did evil in what seemed to them a more restrained manner: they secured safety by tokens—of the sort given to those who had pledged their allegiance to the rebels—either bought for a price or obtained from persons who had assumed their identities. Meanwhile they boasted that they had remained faithful and had not consented to the conspirators through accursed covenants, although they had protected themselves by the expedient lie of a token affirming that very thing. This class of persons appears to be numbered among the *libellatici*. The aforesaid Epistle to Antonianus teaches us that this whole scene was sometimes arranged in the presence of the governor himself. Indeed, it could scarcely have been conducted conveniently without his knowledge. More than this: Epistle 66, Pamelian number 68, establishes that the *libellatici* sometimes [Col. 1121B] renounced Christ before the governor himself in explicit words, though privately. There Martialis and Basilides are said to have been stained by certificates of idolatry, bound by consciousness of their abominable deeds, and, again, defiled by an accursed certificate of idolatry. Thus the public records also contained the statement that Martialis had attested that he had complied with idolatry, and Christ… [source text breaks off]. So very little separated this class of *libellatici* from shameless and open apostasy.

*All will be written.* Thus the Septuagint, as though reference were being made to the Book of Life and the records of God the Judge.

XXVIII.—*They even thought of this.* The most learned Lombert rightly infers from this that secret sins must be expiated by confession and repentance before God, and that auricular confession, contrary to Pamelius’s wish, is not thereby established. The aforementioned learned man further says that Cyprian is speaking here only of public penance, and in support cites Morinus, who assigns private penance to the seventh century in Book VII of *The Administration of Penance*. Certainly Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 16, plainly teaches that in the age of Valentinian and Theodosius, in the Roman Church, [Col. 1121C] penance was imposed not privately by a presbyter but publicly by the bishop, “in a conspicuous place” (ἐν τόπῳ ἐκδήλῳ). On this matter the annotations of the most learned Valesius should be consulted.

XXX.—*He visits the baths daily.* Tertullian paints this delicate and self-indulgent penance in vivid colors near the end of his book *On Penance*.

XXXI.—*They should make exomologesis to God.* He has in view the additional narrative of the Septuagint translators, in which the three Youths in the midst of the furnace confess at length their own sins and the offenses of the whole people. From it one must also derive the explanation of the statements in the preceding book, namely that the aforesaid youths were sustained by a dewy spirit; for it says there that the Angel of the Lord made the furnace “like a wind of dew blowing through it” (ὡς πνεῦμα δρόσου διασυρίζον). What was said above on this subject, p. 81, must be assessed by these considerations.

*To make satisfaction to the Lord.* These satisfactions appear to consist in such a course and rule of life as demonstrates that repentance has been undertaken seriously and advances [Col. 1121D] and promotes it through every discipline for prostrating and humbling the person, imposing “a manner of life which entices mercy,” as Tertullian says in *On Penance*. It was indeed unfortunate that, when ancient writers adorned *exomologesis* and the solemn hardships of penance with the name “satisfaction,” the Socinians and other heretics seized the opportunity to teach that our Lord himself made satisfaction in no other way. Conversely, when others undertook to defend the merits of Christ, they maintained that he made satisfaction in such a way that it amounts to sacrilege for us to employ any penal acts of penance. Certainly St. Paul appears to have required of his Corinthians, in 2 Corinthians 7:11, not merely earnestness, but defense, indignation, fear, zeal, and punishment; and the same Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 5:2 and 2 Corinthians 12:21, shows that the Church’s censures against offenders were imposed with public mourning. It would be altogether absurd for those free of the guilt to remain in grief while the wicked wallowed in luxury and [Col. 1122A] indulged their appetites. Tertullian describes the outward form of this mournful condition in *On Penance*: “It consists in lying in sackcloth and ashes, obscuring the body with filth, casting down the spirit with sorrows, and exchanging the things by which one sinned for mournful treatment; furthermore, in knowing only plain food and drink—not, of course, for the belly’s sake but the soul’s; ordinarily, moreover, in nourishing prayers with fasts, groaning, weeping, and crying aloud to the Lord God day and night, falling at the feet of the presbyters, kneeling before God’s beloved ones, and enjoining upon all the brethren embassies of intercession. All this is *exomologesis*.” Therefore, if anything among these were lacking, the satisfaction would not be complete. Yet no empty or perfunctory taste of these works would suffice. Elsewhere our author requires a long and complete penance: that penance be protracted for a long time, that the lapsed perform penance for a proper period, and that peace not be granted before the lawful and complete period of satisfaction; to this he opposes pardon granted while the time is still unripe. But what span of time should be regarded as mature and lawful is not so easy to determine. It is sufficiently established that shortly before and after the Council [Col. 1122B] of Nicaea and the halcyon age of Constantine, when the world poured into the Church and peace was followed by license, sterner examples were required, so much so that for certain crimes periods of eight, twelve, or fifteen years—or even the whole of life, however long it might extend—were prescribed. But it seems probable that in the age of the Apostles and afterward until Montanus, except in cases of idolatry, adultery, and murder, which may perhaps require exception, the treatment was milder. Certainly the penance imposed upon the incestuous Corinthian, who used the rights of marriage as a pretext for his crime, did not continue beyond the interval between the writing of the First and Second Epistles. This interval appears to be comprised of the time spent on Timothy’s journey from Macedonia to Corinth and his return from there. It may further be observed that Cyprian himself, who so rigorously requires long and complete satisfaction, a proper period, and protracted penance—and who was perhaps the first of all to grant any pardon to idolaters—nevertheless, by decree of the council held there, urged and maintained that peace should immediately be granted to the lapsed upon whom he had imposed [Col. 1122C] that penance, that is, after an interval of about six months. Indeed, even if the whole period after the commission of the crime, namely from the beginning of Decius’s reign, is added, it will certainly be contained within three years. See Epistle LVII, Pamelian number 54. Penance is indeed a second baptism. Just as the delay of the catechumenate and the stage of the *competentes* had arisen from the faithlessness of those who, immediately admitted into the Church, abandoned it with equal readiness, so the intervals of weeping, hearing, and standing had intervened as restraints of a kind upon restoration through penance and upon that second plank after shipwreck, in order to counter the wickedness of those who, confident in the remedy, again rushed headlong into destruction.

XXXIII.—*A spirit of piercing (transpunctio).* Here the Vulgate translator renders κατάνυξις as “slumber,” but at Romans 11:8 he has “compunction.” Theophylact, following Chrysostom’s meaning, defines κατάνυξις as “the soul’s persistent and unchangeable [Col. 1122D] disposition toward evil; for to be pierced through (*katanyssesthai*, κατανύσσεσθαι) is to be fixed fast somewhere and nailed to it.” Hesychius, however, renders it “stillness” (ἡσυχία).

*Love of the truth.* That is, “love” (*dilectionem*); “love of the truth” (ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας). The Vulgate has “charity of the truth.”

XXXVI.—*When you have turned back and groaned.* The Septuagint translators preceded him in this reading, which one could not readily derive from the Hebrew text. Jerome nevertheless acknowledges it, not only in the Epistle to Sabinianus but also in his Commentary, and says that according to the spiritual sense the divine word exhorts all sinners, and heretics especially, to repentance: when they have turned back from their vices, groaned, and performed penance, they are saved, and then understand where they formerly were and that they had vainly placed their hope in empty things.

*The evils inflicted.* Understand this as penal evils. The Septuagint has: “repenting of the evils” (μετανοῶν ἐπὶ ταῖς κακίαις). Tertullian, Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 24, says: “And the Lord repented of the evil which he had said that he would do to them, and did not do it.”

## ON THE LORD’S PRAYER

[Col. 1123A]

*On Prayer.* In his catalogue of St. Cyprian’s works, Pontius mentions this work after the treatises *On the Lapsed* and *On Unity*, saying that it teaches the rule of the Gospel prayer. Nearly all editors have placed it in this order—certainly the editions of Spira, Vetus, the unnamed edition, Rembolt, and Erasmus, to omit the others—so that it immediately followed the book *On the Lapsed*. And indeed, if anyone considers the continuous admonitions for preserving unity that fill both sides of the page here, he will judge that it was written with no purpose or at no time different from the preceding works. But since the earlier writings are known to have been sent to Rome near the end of the year 251, this one appears to be assignable to the following year, namely 252. Among our martyr’s compositions, scarcely any other was more highly commended by St. Augustine. In his book *On Grace and Free Will*, he says: “I admonish and exhort you diligently to read the book which blessed Cyprian wrote *On the Lord’s Prayer*, to understand it as far as the Lord assists you, and to commit it to memory.” He likewise praises it in Epistles XLVII [Col. 1123B] and CVII, as well as in Book IV, chapter 9, *To Boniface, Against Two Epistles of the Pelagians*, in Book II *On the Gift of Perseverance*, and in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 5. Moreover, St. Hilary judged this Treatise so perfect in every respect that, in Canon 5 of his Commentary on Matthew, he said that “Cyprian, a man of holy memory, freed us from the necessity of commenting upon the mystery of Prayer,” although Tertullian too had written a most suitable volume on the subject, etc.

II.—*For what prayer can be more spiritual?* Fanatical innovators regard only that prayer as spiritual which is poured forth in extemporaneous fervor; in this they differ widely from our Cyprian. Tertullian said in *On Prayer* that the prayer instituted by Christ is composed of three things: the utterance by which it is pronounced, the spirit by which it has such power, and the understanding by which it is received.

III.—*With disorderly cries.* “When we worship with modesty and humility,” says Septimius, “we shall more effectively commend our prayers to God—not even raising our hands too high, but lifting them moderately and only slightly; [Col. 1123C] nor raising our faces with audacity. For that publican, who prayed not only with his prayer but with his countenance humbled and cast down, departed more justified than the exceedingly insolent Pharisee. The sounds of the voice should also be subdued. Otherwise, how powerful must our lungs be if we are heard according to loudness? God, however, is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart, just as he is its beholder.” Cyprian perhaps has in view the pagan vain repetition censured by the Lord in Matthew 6:7 and described in 1 Kings 18:26, an example of which Aeschylus gives in the *Seven Against Thebes* (Ἑπτὰ ἐπὶ Θήβαις). The Gentiles placed such confidence in using the correct nomenclature of the gods that they protected themselves with lists of divine appellations, lest through a lapse of memory they confuse the rites and offend the divine powers they were trying to appease.

*Through Jeremiah also.* In Greek manuscripts the sixth chapter of Baruch is called the “Epistle of Jeremiah” (Ἐπιστολὴ Ἱερεμίου). We explained above, in the annotations on Book I *Against the Jews*, why our author repeatedly employed the apocryphal books when citing Holy Scripture.

*But God must be worshipped by you in the understanding.* Worship must be rendered to you in the mind or intellect, O God. [Col. 1123D] The Septuagint has: “In the understanding you must be worshipped, O Master” (Τῇ διανοίᾳ σοὶ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν, δέσποτα).

VII.—*Our Father.* Lucian, in the *Philopatris*, calls the Lord’s Prayer “the prayer beginning with ‘Father’” (τὴν εὐχὴν ἀπὸ πατρός). Thus our customary designation, derived from its first words, appears by no means new.

VIII.—*Individually.* A word employed by Tertullian: “Demons have no name individually,” in *On Idolatry*.

IX.—*The mysteries of the Lord’s Prayer.* No word has a broader meaning among ecclesiastical writers than *sacramentum*, “mystery” or “sacrament.” St. Hilary spoke of the Lord’s Prayer in this form in the passage cited above.

*Gathered briefly into speech.* For this reason shorter prayers are repeatedly called *Collects*. Tertullian calls this Prayer “a compendium of the whole Gospel,” *On Prayer*, chapter 1. Chrysostom says that the Lord taught this “measure of prayer” (μέτρον εὐχῆς), Homily *On Hannah*. Tertullian calls it “the lawful prayer” and also “the regular prayer,” *On Flight*, chapter 2.

[Col. 1124A] X.—*A voice which also reproves the Jews.* Similarly Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 2: “This is what is charged against Israel.”

*You sent him, the holy one.* The word “him” is superfluous, unless perhaps, when the Septuagint had “the holy one” (τὸν ἅγιον), the Latin translator thought the emphasis of the Greek article should be expressed in this way.

*Remission of sins is granted.* Our author drew this word from his Master. In *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 18, Tertullian says: “We have spoken about the remission of sins.”

*Not because we wish anything for God.* Similarly Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 3: “Not that it is fitting for human beings to wish God well, as though there were someone else from whom one could wish something for him, or as though he would suffer unless we wished it.”

XII.—*Besides, by whom can God be sanctified, who himself sanctifies?* Tertullian uses almost the same words in the same place: “Besides, when is the name of God not holy and sanctified through itself, since he sanctifies all others from himself?”

*Such indeed you were.* The reading is the same in Book III *To Quirinus*, chapter 65; in both places it is a manifest but inveterate error shared by Irenaeus, Book IV, chapter 46 and Book V, chapter 10; Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 10; and Augustine, *On Penance*, chapter 10. [Col. 1124B] The Greek text has “such were some of you” (ταῦτά τινες ἦτε), that is, “some of you were once such.” But I alter nothing, for we are considering not what ought to have been written, but what was in fact written.

XIII.—*We ask that it be made present to us.* Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 5, says: “The manifestation of the Lord’s kingdom belongs to the object of our expectation.”

XIV.—*For who resists God?* Thus Tertullian in the same place: “Not because anyone can obstruct the accomplishment of God’s will.”

*No one is strong by his own powers.* No Father supplies more generous weapons for repelling the madness of Pelagius; hence St. Augustine continually summons Cyprian to his side. See *To Boniface*, Book IV, chapter 9, where almost entire pages are transcribed.

*The Son obeyed.* Scarcely any word is more customary for Cyprian. Tertullian says in *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 2: “God’s will had come into obedience. Accordingly, if you too do not obey God,” etc. The ancients, as Festus observes, used *obaudivit* in place of *obedivit*.

XVIII.—*Just as we say “Our Father,” because he is the Father of those who understand [Col. 1124C] and believe, so also we call the bread “ours.”* St. Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, Book III, near the end, says: “The Lord taught his Apostles that daily, in the sacrifice of his body, believers should dare to say: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.’ They desire that God’s name, which is holy in itself, be hallowed in themselves. They add: ‘Thy kingdom come,’ awaiting the hope of the kingdom in the future, so that when Christ reigns, sin may by no means reign in their mortal body. And they join to it: ‘Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven,’ so that human frailty may imitate the angels and God’s will be fulfilled on earth. The Apostles pray for daily bread, or that which is to come above every substance, so that they may be worthy to receive Christ’s body,” etc. If, in prayers to God that were less solemn, praying otherwise than the Lord taught was, in Cyprian’s judgment, the result not only of ignorance but also of fault, it must certainly not be thought that the Church ever omitted the Lord’s Prayer during the mysteries of the Holy Eucharist, especially since the Eucharistic bread was regarded by them as altogether daily. [Col. 1124D] Tertullian, *On Prayer*: “‘Give us today our daily bread’: let us understand this spiritually. For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life and the bread of life. ‘I am,’ he says, ‘the bread of life.’” And shortly afterward: “The bread is the word of the living God who descended from heaven. Then also because his body is reckoned in the bread.” That is, as the most learned Rigaltius interprets it: “Through the sacrament of bread he commends his body,” just as Augustine says in Book I, *Questions on the Gospels* 43: “Through the sacrament of wine he commends his blood.”

*We touch his body.* One who is connected by some relationship with any family or person is said by Latin authors to “touch” or “be related to” them. So Cicero in *Against Verres*, Suetonius in *Galba*, and Valerius Maximus, Book X, chapter 8. The Christian is the Lord’s brother and, indeed, a member of his body; thus joined to him by an indivisible bond, he not only touches him but participates in him. Below he says that by right of communion we touch Christ. These words refer to St. Paul’s statement [Col. 1125A] in 1 Corinthians 10:16, where the Eucharistic wine is called “communion in the blood of Christ” (κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ).

*The Eucharist daily.* The Eucharistic bread was daily for Christians down to the times of Jerome, Ambrose, and St. Augustine, as may be seen from Jerome’s Epistle to Luca of Baetica [name as transmitted in the source] and his *Apology to Pammachius*; from the final chapter of Books IV and V of Ambrose’s *On the Sacraments*; and from Augustine, Epistle CXVIII. Moreover, Apostolic Canon 9 and Canon 2 of the Council of Antioch decree: “All the faithful who enter and listen to the Scriptures but do not remain for the prayer and holy communion must be excommunicated as persons who cause disorder in the Church” (Πάντας τοὺς εἰσιόντας πιστούς, καὶ τῶν γραφῶν ἀκούοντας, μὴ παραμένοντας δὲ τῇ προσευχῇ καὶ τῇ ἁγίᾳ μεταλήψει, ὡς ἀταξίας ἐμποιοῦντας τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀφορίζεσθαι χρή). In Tertullian’s time, when a scruple arose as to how the faithful might partake of the sacred mysteries on station days without risking the breaking of the fast, he answers: “Will not your station be more solemn if you stand at God’s altar? When the Lord’s body has been received and reserved, both things are preserved: participation in the sacrifice and fulfillment of the duty,” *On Prayer*, near the end. It should be noted in passing that Septimius proposes not the Church’s custom but an invention of his own.

[Col. 1125B] XX.—*To be able to follow him.* In the book *On the Lapsed* it is said: “Nor could he be conquered by the world who had nothing in the world from which he might be conquered; released and free, he would follow the Lord like the Apostles,” etc. There, contrary to the evidence of the copies, the very learned Gronovius maintains that it should read “by which he might be bound,” etc.

XXII.—*And forgive us.* Grave controversies once arose over these words, and Erasmus was criticized for printing “dismiss for us” (*dimitte nobis*). This was undeserved, since the matter itself is of the slightest importance and it is established that the ancients spoke in both ways. Certainly the very ancient Verona manuscript of Cyprian, written in capital letters, everywhere retains *Dimitte*, *Dimisi*, and *Dimittimus*; and every manuscript that exists uses them at least somewhere.

*Preserving faith in his promise.* *Reservare* has the same meaning as *servare*, “to preserve.” Thus Tertullian, *Against the Jews*: “Isaac was preserved with the wood.”

XXIII.—*He will forgive you your sins.* After these words, the Paris edition of 1541 inserts an addition [Col. 1125C] of nearly twenty lines, which afterward deceived many. Another of the same kind occurs near the end of the same paragraph. Neither is supported by the authority of any manuscript codex; the crime of forgery ought to be punished with the severest penalties. Yet that accursed desire long possessed human minds—to insert a base and spurious offspring into the noblest families.

*The sacrifice to God is greater.* Not the sacrifice of a turtledove or ewe lamb, but of an ox—indeed, of a hecatomb. “Greater” means “greatest.” Thus Tertullian, *On Prescription*, chapter 2: “Heresies bringing eternal death and the burning of a greater fire,” etc.

XXV.—*Do not permit us to be led.* Our author substitutes Tertullian’s interpretation for the text itself. For Tertullian says in *On Prayer*: “‘Lead us not into temptation’; that is, do not permit us to be led into it—by him, certainly, who tempts. Besides, far be it from the Lord to appear to tempt, as though he either did not know each person’s faith or desired to cast him down.” Cyril, *Mystagogical Catechesis* V, says: “‘Not to enter [Col. 1125D] into temptation’ means not to be submerged by temptation” (Τὸ μὴ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς πειρασμόν ἐστι τὸ μὴ καταβαπτισθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ πειρασμοῦ).

*The wrath of indignation.* See what was said in the book *On the Lapsed*.

*The Lord stirred up Satan.* This passage is cited in the same way in Book III *To Quirinus*, chapter 80.

XXVIII.—*Bringing the word to completion.* Origen, Procopius, Tertullian, and Jerome likewise interpret this passage. St. Paul, Romans 9:28, attributes it to our Lord. For “completed,” Tertullian translates “a word cut short,” *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 1.

*May people do good things to you.* The word “good” was understood in the text itself, since the adjective “equal things” (ἴσα) requires a substantive. Thus what is said in Luke 18, “What shall I do?” (τί ποιήσω), is, in Matthew 19:16, “What good thing shall I do?” (τί καλὸν ποιήσω).

### XXXI.—Lift Up Your Hearts

Nothing in Christian devotion is more ancient than fixed formulas of prayer. The priest led with prescribed words, and the people responded in turn, without a prompter—something customary among the Gentiles—because, as Tertullian says (*Apology*, ch. 30), they prayed “from the heart,” that is, [Col. 1126A] they knew the prayers by memory. We learn from Cyril that the same formula prevailed in the Eastern Church; there, after the words just mentioned, followed the solemn words still in use: “Let us give thanks to the Lord,” with the people’s response, “It is fitting and right.” *Mystagogical Catechesis* V.

Justin Martyr, describing the ancient liturgy in *Apology* II, says that after the reading of the Scriptures and the discourse of the presiding minister:

> “Then we all rise together and send up prayers. And, as we said before, when we have finished the prayer, bread, wine, and water are brought forward; and the presiding minister likewise sends up prayers and thanksgivings to the best of his ability, and the people voice their assent: ‘Amen.’”

The solemn words used in Baptism have been discussed elsewhere.

### XXXIII.—The Dead Simply (*simpliciter*)

The reading should be *similiter* (“in like manner”), for the Septuagint has: “When you buried the dead, in like manner I accompanied you.” And there can certainly be no doubt that this is the genuine reading; but because all the manuscripts agree in the error—not only here but also below in the book *On Mortality*—there was a conscientious reluctance to alter anything.

[Col. 1126B] **I was sent to test you.** As though the angel had inflicted Tobit’s blindness. Although the Greek copies we use, as well as the Latin version, do not recognize this reading, we learn from the Syriac version that it formerly prevailed.

### XXXIV.—The Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours

Tertullian, *On Fasting*, ch. 10:

> Since in the same commentary on Luke the third hour is shown to be an hour of prayer—the hour at which those initiated by the Holy Spirit were regarded as drunk—as also the sixth, when Peter went up to the upper room, and the ninth, when they entered the Temple, why should we not understand that, while the complete freedom to pray always, everywhere, and at every time remains unimpaired, these three hours nevertheless—being more conspicuous in human affairs, since they divide the day, distinguish its occupations, and are publicly sounded—were likewise more solemn for divine prayers? This is also suggested by the example of Daniel, who prayed three times a day, certainly through the selection of particular hours; and these were none other than those [Col. 1126C] subsequently distinguished by apostolic observance: the third, sixth, and ninth.

### XXXV.—This Is the Day Which the Lord Has Made

Our author adduces this passage in Book II *To Quirinus*, ch. 16, to prove that the Lord Jesus was called a stone. There—although some copies follow the Vulgate—he likewise appears to have read: “This was made by the Lord,” which is the reading of the Septuagint translators and is recognized by St. Mark. Here, however, the text is employed to establish that Christ was called “the day.” This interpretation appears peculiar to Cyprian, although it may be derived quite suitably from other grounds.

### XXXVI.—Let There Be No Loss of Prayer During the Hours of the Night

It is well known that Christians held assemblies at night. Tertullian, *To His Wife*, Book II, calls them “nocturnal gatherings”; Pliny, in his *Letter to Trajan*, calls them “before-dawn” gatherings. Moreover, out of private devotion the faithful tore themselves from bed and rose during the night to pray, as Tertullian says in the passage cited above. Thus also in the *Apology*:

> “They satisfy themselves in such a way as people who remember that they must worship [Col. 1126D] God even during the night.”

## ON MORTALITY

### On Mortality—or the Deadly Epidemic

Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 51, gives a precise explanation:

> “One thing is mortal, and another is mortality; for one is that which suffers, and another that which causes suffering.”

In truth, this epidemic disease had symptoms so varied and erratic that it did not correspond at all to the proper type of plague. The bowels, loosened into a flux, drained the body’s strength. A fire conceived deep within the marrow surged up into wounds of the throat. The intestines were shaken by continual vomiting; the eyes burned with the force of the blood; in some, the feet or other parts of the limbs were amputated because of infection by diseased putrefaction; the ability to walk was impaired, hearing was obstructed, and sight was blinded.

This most dreadful epidemic first arose in Arabia, was then carried into Egypt, and afterward [Col. 1127A] advanced into Africa; from there it raged through the western regions of the Roman Empire, rivaling in fury the Athenian plague described by Thucydides, and following its customary route, as though along a royal highway. For Pliny says, Book VII, ch. 50: “It has been observed that pestilence always travels from the southern regions toward the setting of the sun.”

This calamity occurred during the reigns of Gallus and Volusianus, as Eusebius testifies in the *Chronicle*, together with Orosius, Book VII, and Zonaras, *Annals*, Book II. Moreover, Eusebius, Book VII, ch. 22, teaches from the letters of Dionysius of Alexandria that it occurred during a time of peace:

> “We rejoiced once again in the peace of Christ, which he gave to us alone; but after both we and they had enjoyed only the briefest respite, this disease descended upon us.”

These points being established, we declare that this book was written in the year 252 [the printed “152” is evidently erroneous], before the renewal of the persecution, as the whole tenor of the treatise confirms. Pontius mentions this work and also relates at some length the outstanding service rendered by Cyprian to those suffering from the epidemic and consequently dying from it.

Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, says that Cyprian’s book [Col. 1127B] *On Mortality* was laudably known to many, indeed to almost all who loved ecclesiastical literature. He also cites it in Epistle 107, *To Vitalis*, as well as in Book II *Against Julian* and in *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book IV, ch. 8. Eusebius—or at least Jerome—likewise praises it in the *Chronicle*.

### IV.—You Are Compelled to Curse

That is, to curse Christ. Paul began his career of persecution in this manner, as he himself confesses in Acts 26:11, and thereafter pagan governors conducted persecution in the same way. Thus Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, ch. 15, speaking of Polycarp’s martyrdom, describes the proconsul as saying:

> “Revile Christ.”

The holy martyr replied:

> “For eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?”

**You are compelled to swear.** By the *genius* of Caesar, or by his fortune. Thus the proconsul in Eusebius, Book IV, ch. 15, in the passage cited above, presses Polycarp:

> “Swear by Caesar’s fortune.”

He replied:

> “I am a Christian,”

and did so with boldness. Accordingly, Tertullian says in *Apology*, ch. 32, that Christians swear, though not by the *genii* of the Caesars, [Col. 1127C] but by their welfare—that is, by God—who is more august than all *genii*. Meanwhile, it must not be concealed that these words may rightly be referred to cursing and to the use of oaths in ordinary life.

**But the world will rejoice.** He means the Greek *kosmos* (κόσμος), or “world,” and our author everywhere translates that word in this way.

### VIII.—The State of This Disease

That is, its bad state of health; hence the feeble and infirm are called *valetudinarii*, “invalids.” Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, says: “Aesculapius can prescribe in a dream a cure for an illness.”

**This corruptible thing.** Tertullian reads thus in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 41, and frequently elsewhere.

**Clouds delay clear skies.** Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40: “When wintry weather caused by rains delays summer weather, and the year becomes an object of anxiety.”

**Jagged rocks constrict the ship.** Thus Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book II, ch. 16: “You blame the physician’s instruments because they cut, cauterize, amputate, and constrict.”

[Col. 1127D] ### IX.—Stand in Righteousness and Fear

These words do not occur in the Greek copies, but the Vulgate translator has them.

### X.—With Wounds Also and Worms

So too below in the book *On Patience*, as though Job had suffered from *phthiriasis*, or infestation with lice. The passage of Job intended is 7:4, where dust is mentioned no less than worms. But these words do not in the least—at least according to the common view—describe a dead man, for worms never appear in their tombs. The additional words, “Naked also shall I go beneath the earth,” are an interpretation of the Septuagint’s words ἀπελεύσομαι ἐκεῖ, “I shall go there.”

**I offered a memorial.** Thus in Revelation 8:3 an angel is said to have stood before the altar holding a golden censer, and much incense was given to him so that he might offer it with the prayers of the saints, etc.

**And again.** The Septuagint reads καὶ νῦν, “and now.” Our author appears to have read καὶ πάλιν, “and again.” In place of “we stand by,” the same translators read: “who offer up the prayers of the saints.”

[Col. 1128A] **How God remains forever.** See what was said in Book III *To Quirinus*, ch. 11.

**Behold, the world totters and slips away.** Scarcely for any other reason did Christians stir up more serious hostility against themselves than because they prophesied evil concerning human affairs. Nor did they reach this opinion rashly, since the apostles repeatedly testify not only that the end of all things is at hand and that the last days have come, but add further that the last hour has arrived, 1 John 2:18.

In *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 22, Tertullian says: “Our prayers sigh for the passing away of this age,” etc. Yet when writing to the Gentiles, in order to soothe them, he says the contrary in *Apology*, ch. 32:

> “There is also another and greater necessity for us to pray for the emperors, and indeed for the whole condition of the empire and for Roman affairs, because we know that the immense force threatening the whole world, and the very close of the age, which threatens dreadful calamities, is delayed by the continuance of the Roman Empire.”

**Let us embrace the day which assigns each person to his own dwelling.** The day of death is rightly called the day of particular judgment, [Col. 1128B] just as the end of the world is declared to be the universal judgment. Devout antiquity knew absolutely nothing of a third day or place.

**A multitude of our dear ones awaits us.** Although souls received into heaven are not free from concern for this age, nothing prevents them from wishing the same felicity for their own people and finally congratulating them upon it, for charity never fails. What follows concerning the glorious choir of the apostles, the exultant company of the prophets, and the innumerable people of the martyrs appears to have provided the occasion for the expressions found in the Ambrosian hymn called the *Te Deum*.

## ON EXHORTATION TO MARTYRDOM

### On Exhortation to Martyrdom

Tertullian gave a little book a similar title, *On Exhortation to Chastity*. Of Cyprian’s writings, scarcely any is praised more splendidly by Pontius:

> “Who,” he says, “would raise up so many martyrs by the exhortation [Col. 1128C] of the divine word? Who, finally, would animate by the trumpet-call of heaven so many confessors, marked upon their foreheads with a second inscription and preserved alive as an example of martyrdom?”

Indeed, the letters to the distinguished confessors Moses and Maximus, as well as to the Thibaritans, and several others besides, are entirely devoted to kindling zeal for martyrdom. But that the exhortation is conducted by means of the divine word and the trumpet-call of heaven appears to be the special character of this work, and one that corresponds exactly to the design of the books *To Quirinus*. Moreover, the passages of Holy Scripture cited in the same manner in both works openly proclaim the same author.

It is not easy to say who the Fortunatus was to whom this book is dedicated, since several persons of that name occur in Cyprian’s writings; and it may ultimately be that these words concern someone different from all those mentioned elsewhere. I would nevertheless think that they refer to the bishop to whom Epistle 56—number 53 in Pamelius—is addressed, perhaps the man called Fortunatus [Col. 1128D] of Thuccabori at the Council of Carthage.

Finally, I judge that it was composed on the occasion of the persecution renewed under Gallus and Volusianus. Cyprian, warned of it through heavenly visions, did not cease warning others. The Decian disaster overwhelmed everyone in its way by its unexpected violence, so that the sole remaining concern was the restoration of the lapsed. The persecutions that followed under Valerian and Gallienus appear far too savage for the remedies to have been delayed until then, given our martyr’s diligence. It remains, therefore, that the origin of this little book should be assigned to the intervening period, namely the year 252 [the printed “232” is evidently erroneous].

What is adduced by some from Jerome, *Epistle to Pammachius*, ch. 50, in order to suggest that St. Hilary was the author of this treatise—because mention is made of his books *To Fortunatus*—appears to carry no weight. If one considers Hilary’s age, a book about martyrdom against the fury of the Gentiles would have been singularly inopportune under Christian emperors. Moreover, an argument drawn from the name of the person is wholly precarious. Nor, furthermore, do the dates of the Fortunatus [Col. 1129A] who wrote the life of Hilary’s daughter correspond; and finally, in very many manuscript copies of Jerome, not the name of Hilary but that of Cyprian appears.

Meanwhile, it is difficult to guess what came into Pamelius’s mind when he said that Rembold was the first of all to publish this treatise, since it appears in the Speyer edition, which was contemporary with the art of printing, and also in an old anonymous edition that certainly long preceded Rembold.

**Our humble ability, equipped with the aid of divine inspiration.** Whatever is done with the support of divine grace, our author attributes to inspiration. Thus Tertullian, *On Patience*, ch. 1, says:

> “The greatness of certain good things, as also of evil things, is unbearable, so that divine inspirational grace alone operates to enable us to receive and perform them.”

**Six thousand years are now almost complete.** Our author follows the ancient calculation received in Africa in his own time, namely that which assigns the Christian era to the year 5500 from the creation of the world. If 252 years are added to that number, the result is 5752, which is not far from [Col. 1129B] 6000. It is well known that in stating numbers it was customary to use the nearest round number.

St. Peter had said in his Second Epistle, 3:8, that a thousand years with God are as one day; hence the ancients believed that, once the six days were completed, the eternal Sabbath and the end of the world would follow. Moreover, because the Lord had promised, Matthew 24:22, that those days would be shortened for the sake of the elect, the opinion had taken possession of almost everyone’s mind that the consummation of the world and the hostile age of Antichrist were at hand. See what was said on this subject in the book *On Mortality*.

**Snares for casting us down.** “Our wrestling,” says the Apostle in Ephesians 6:12, “is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers,” etc.

**With the headings set forth.** Those copies therefore appear to approach the author’s intention most closely which present all these headings together at the beginning of the book.

**Wool and purple.** Among the offerings admitted for the use of the tabernacle in Exodus 25 were blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. But for the adornment of the Christian Church, the colors of innocence and [Col. 1129C] martyrdom suffice.

**With the Lord’s permission, we first gave Baptism to believers.** In ancient times Baptism was celebrated only by command of the bishop. “It is not lawful apart from the bishop either to baptize or to hold an *agape*,” etc., says Ignatius, *Epistle to the Smyrnaeans*. Hence the baptistery existed only in the church in which the bishop himself had his seat. Martyrdom received the name of Baptism from the Lord’s words in Matthew 20:22.

**Angels baptize.** They perform the office of sponsors and carry the souls of the martyrs, purified in the washing of blood, into heaven. See Luke 16:22.

**It completes the growth of our faith.** On this τελείωσις, “perfecting” or “completion,” see Luke 13:32 and Hebrews 2:10.

**Let us also be friends.** Martyrs are perfected in love, 1 John 4:18. Thus Tertullian, commenting on that passage of John in *Scorpiace*, ch. 12, says:

> “Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment, and he who fears is not perfected in love. What fear should we understand except that which produces denial? What love does he affirm to be [Col. 1129D] perfect except that which drives fear away and gives courage for confession? With what punishment does it punish fear”—not “what punishment,” as appears in the printed editions—“except that which the denier will suffer when he is destroyed in both body and soul in Gehenna?”

Hence the martyrs, by right of friendship, stand perpetually at the Lord’s side and follow the Lamb wherever he goes, Revelation 14:4.

**Let them lose what they have attained.** That is, let them lose the progress they have made. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, says that the soul “turns out” (*evadere*) in various ways through accidental conditions, that is, it advances; and in *On Patience*, that a man “turns out” unto salvation, that is, proceeds. He frequently uses the word in almost the same sense, as does Virgil likewise: “I make my way to the summit’s highest roof.” Or perhaps the word is used in the sense in which it signifies “to be” or “to become,” so that the meaning is: Those who return to the world after they have become Christians fall away from Christianity.

## NOTES ON THE BOOK *ON EXHORTATION TO MARTYRDOM*

**Those whom he worships.** The Greek has τῶν σεβασμάτων αὐτοῦ, “his objects of worship.” St. Paul uses the same word in Acts 17:23 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4.

[Col. 1130A] **An idol for yourself.** Thus the Septuagint renders it εἴδωλον, “idol,” not γλυπτόν, “carved image”; for it makes no difference whether the object worshiped is produced by the art of sculpture or of painting.

**And all things that are in them.** The Greek has καὶ πηγὰς ὑδάτων, “and springs of waters,” a reading recognized by the manuscript codices.

**He asks and does not obtain.** See what was said in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 93.

**At the time when they call upon me, in the time of their affliction.** All these words are superfluous and appear to have been inserted in the wrong place.

**But if he should ask.** This passage is not transcribed in full, and many words are omitted immediately afterward.

**Equal to your soul.** Ὁ ἴσος τῇ ψυχῇ σου, “one equal to your soul.” From this should be sought the explanation of St. Paul’s expression in Philippians 2:20, οὐδένα ἔχω ἰσόψυχον, “I have no one of equal soul.”

**Because of him who loved us.** Our author agrees with those copies which read διὰ τὸν ἀγαπήσαντα, “because of him who loved us.”

[Col. 1130B] **Take courage, stand, and behold.** The Septuagint reads θαρσεῖτε, στῆτε καὶ ὁρᾶτε, “take courage, stand, and behold,” but the first word does not appear in the sacred text.

**In the renewal of the spirit.** Our author appears to have understood the Holy Spirit, but the Greek copies have not πνεύματος ἁγίου, “of the Holy Spirit,” but νοὸς ὑμῶν, “of your mind.”

**Who bore the figure of the devil.** Thus Book II *To Quirinus*, ch. 16: “Amalek was overcome by Jesus—that is, the devil was conquered by Christ.”

**Nor fall away.** Although no trace of this reading appears in the Greek text, our author reads it similarly in the *Epistle to the Thibaritans*, as though he had read μήτε ἐκπέσητε, “nor fall away.”

**Whenever you share.** Quite a few manuscript codices likewise read κοινωνοῦντες, “sharing,” and immediately afterward τῆς δόξης τῆς δυνάμεως, “of the glory of the power.”

**The name of the Lord.** Our author appears to have read not πνεῦμα, “spirit,” but ὄνομα, “name,” and ἡμᾶς, “us,” in place of ὑμᾶς, “you.”

**Their feet were entangled.** The Septuagint has Αὐτοὶ συνεποδίσθησαν, “they themselves were entangled by the feet.”

[Col. 1130C] **One thing I asked.** The Septuagint reads μίαν ᾐτησάμην, “one thing I asked,” with αἴτησιν, “request,” understood. See 3 Kingdoms 2:20.

**You shall not be burned.** The manuscript codices agree in this reading, and the Septuagint version requires it:

> “If you pass through fire, you shall certainly not be burned, nor shall the flame burn you.”

Moreover, the Hebrew truth also demands it. These words were therefore wrongly omitted in the printed editions until now.

**To premeditate an excuse.** The Greek text has ἀπολογηθῆναι, “to make a defense”; and indeed every defense is a kind of excuse. The Vulgate has “what you are to answer.”

**Mogilalum (“one who speaks with difficulty”).** There can be no doubt that Cyprian wrote *mogilalum*. No adequate reason can be given why so many copies should have conspired to introduce an unusual word; but there is a sufficiently obvious reason why recent copyists altered it, as they have frequently done elsewhere: so that everything might correspond more closely to the Vulgate edition. The Greek copies in fact have δύσκωφον, “deaf and scarcely speaking”; but [Col. 1130D] Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion agree upon μογιλάλῳ, a word used in Mark 7:32.

**Let him receive only so much from God’s assistance.** See Book VII *To Quirinus*, ch. 42.

**If you were of the world.** Since St. John uses the same word in chapters 15 and 16, it is not easy to say why our author translated it differently. But all the books agree in this reading, notwithstanding the reading of the Vulgate translator, to which copyists everywhere tend to accommodate everything.

**David, the merciful man.** Tertullian treats this passage in *Scorpiace*, ch. 8:

> “David is harassed, Elijah is put to flight, Jeremiah is stoned, Isaiah is sawn apart, Zechariah is slaughtered between the altar and the Temple,” etc.

**Seven days, seven thousand years.** That is, the duration of the world. Elsewhere our author limits the world’s age to the span of six days, or six thousand years. Nor need he appear here to have gone over to the camp of Papias, for there are some who hold that the Day of Judgment itself will last a thousand years.

[Col. 1131A] **He writes to seven churches.** Namely, to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Thessalonians. If it is asked in what passage Paul mentions this legitimate and definite number, it might perhaps be said that he did so in Hebrews 11:30.

**One upon the rock.** The first person to change this reading and substitute “Peter” was Manutius. See what was said on the book *On the Unity of the Church*, p. 76. It should moreover be noted that our judgment concerning the additions there made to Cyprian’s text is excellently confirmed by the most learned Latino Latini in his *Sacred and Profane Library*, published at Rome in 1677, pp. 178–79. In the clearest words the Lord says: ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω, “Upon this rock I will build.”

**Nor is it without significance.** That is, it is not devoid of mystery; it is not said rashly or without purpose.

**To be raised by him.** The printed editions add “unto eternal life,” but contrary to the authority of the manuscript copies and [Col. 1131B] the Greek text.

**Nor will the prayer of the brethren be of benefit.** He censures the martyrs who thought themselves able to grant pardon to anyone whatsoever. Tertullian, in the decidedly bad book *On Modesty*, nevertheless says well:

> “Let it suffice for a martyr to have purged his own sins. It is the act of an ungrateful or proud man to scatter upon others also what he obtained as a great favor. Who has discharged another’s death by his own, except the Son of God alone? For even during his Passion he delivered the thief. He had come for this purpose: that, himself pure from sin and entirely holy, he might die for sinners. Accordingly, you who emulate him, if you yourself have committed no sin, by all means suffer for me; but if you are a sinner, how will the oil of your lamp be able to suffice both for you and for me?”

**And lest anyone even by means of certificates.** These words fully confirm our opinion concerning the *libellatici*—those who procured certificates of sacrifice—on which see the book *On the Lapsed*.

**Whole burnt offerings of a sacrifice.** See what was said in Book III *To Quirinus*, ch. 15. The Septuagint read ὁλοκάρπωμα θυσίας, “a whole burnt offering of sacrifice,” and perhaps the truest reading was *Holocaustum hostiae*, “the whole burnt offering of the victim.”

[Col. 1131C] **Carrying their laps.** See what was said in Book III *To Quirinus*, ch. 16.

**They are shut away during persecutions of the earth.** That is, they are proscribed and deported. The reading found in earlier editions, “their eyes are closed during persecutions of the earth,” arose from the most unfortunate criticism of copyists, who create an error by emendation when they cannot find one. Below they read that “in a moment the eyes are closed, through which men and the world were seen,” and therefore supposed that nothing except eyes could be closed.

**Without loss of time.** In every respect confessors are equated with martyrs if they too are exempt from the delay of judgment, which was regarded as the peculiar prerogative of the Baptism of blood. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, said: “Lesser sins are paid for by a delay of resurrection,” judging that they were punished there by this penalty of loss. The doctors of later times added the penalty of sense and purgatorial fires. Origen even held the fires of Gehenna to be purgatorial.

The passages adduced by some on this question from the *Epistle to Antonianus* refer entirely to the censures imposed upon the lapsed here in the Church; they have nothing in common with the punishments that afflict those who have departed this life.

[Col. 1131D] **The conscience is crowned.** By “conscience” he means courage ready for battle and faith prepared for martyrdom.

## NOTES ON *TO DEMETRIANUS*

### To Demetrianus

Baronius, Pamelius, Lombertus, and others who have written about Cyprian unanimously say that this man was proconsul of Africa. But it is scarcely credible that the highest magistrate, laying aside the fasces and insignia of command, would come to the home of a Christian bishop—not once but repeatedly. Nor are the following words more applicable to a proconsul: that he stirred up others and, by sowing hatred through his slanderous words, made many companions for himself through the sprouting of his own root and origin. Provincial governors showed their anger differently and fought with more decisive weapons.

Moreover, [Col. 1132A] it appears wholly alien to Cyprian’s character that he would address a leading man in less than respectful language, professing that he despised him as one barking and clamoring against the truth with sacrilegious mouth and impious words, and addressing him as unteachable, impious, raging, blind, deaf, and brutish. It must therefore be said that Demetrianus was at least a judge in the city of Carthage, or one of the legal advisers who customarily assisted the governor in trials; concerning these, see Acts 25:12. It is not improbable that a man of this kind, personally known to Cyprian through studies they had once shared, should have wished sometimes to visit his former companion.

Pontius certainly adorns him with no title other than “a blaspheming Gentile,” and Lactantius, without any honorific preface, calls him “a man ignorant of the truth.” Nor does it matter that Demetrianus is said to deprive those dear to God of their homes, despoil them of their property, load them with chains, confine them in prison, and punish them by wild beasts, the sword, and fire. These acts are entirely consistent with a persecutor occupying an inferior tribunal and are reported in Acts 8 and 9 of Saul, who certainly was not a provincial governor.

Our author declares plainly enough that this defense was occasioned by the epidemic discussed above [Col. 1132B] in the book *On Mortality*, and by the famine that commonly follows a pestilence. And since famine is known to follow upon the cessation of agriculture—that is, once the epidemic has become established and prolonged—we judge that this book was written no earlier than the second year after the disease began, namely 253.

**For since you have often come to me.** Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book V, ch. 4—with Jerome, *Epistle to Magnus*, joining him as a supporter—says that Cyprian, in the discourse in which he attempts, as he himself says, to refute Demetrianus, who was barking and clamoring against the truth, did not handle the subject as he should have. For Demetrianus should have been refuted not by testimonies of Scripture, which he naturally regarded as worthless, fictitious, and fabricated, but by arguments and reason. Since Cyprian was dealing with a man ignorant of the truth, he should have postponed the divine readings for a little while, formed him from the beginning as though uneducated, and gradually shown him the first principles of light, lest he be blinded when the whole radiance was set before him.

But this charge and [Col. 1132C] calumny will vanish entirely as soon as it is established that Cyprian was not dealing with a man so uneducated and ignorant of the truth, but with one who had often come to Cyprian and had repeatedly disputed sharply about articles of the faith.

It should moreover be observed that the passages of Holy Scripture which St. Cyprian adduces throughout this work are taken almost entirely from the prophets; and no method is better suited to refuting an unbeliever. Hence St. Augustine, in his discourse *On the Five Heresies*, after adducing testimonies of the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament, says:

> “Be present here, pagan, and listen to what the Prophet says. I did not write whatever I pleased for myself. The codex in which these things are written is kept in the Jew’s bookcase. My enemy is my witness. Ask him: open, read, and believe.”

Indeed, the same most holy Father treats this argument at length in *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, Book XIII.

**It is no longer right to remain silent.** It was long before the pagans abandoned this accusation; so much so that St. Augustine himself had to write *The City of God*, and Orosius his history, in order to refute it.

[Col. 1132D] **The world has now grown old.** That the structure of the universe is disintegrating through old age and tending toward destruction is very different from the close of the age and the end of the world brought by the Day of Judgment. They differ as natural death differs from violent death. Nevertheless, the first Christians expected both destructions alike and threatened the Gentiles with them.

**Springtime in its own mildness.** This reading is approved and accords with Tertullian’s phrasing. In *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 12, he says: “Winters and summers, springs and autumns return.” The editors, with misplaced generosity, added *sata*, “crops.”

**They increase anxiety.** Tertullian, on a similar occasion in the *Apology*, said that “the year becomes an object of anxiety.”

**A barren clod produces pale grasses.** Thus Tertullian, *To Scapula*:

> “We must grieve because no city will escape punishment if it sheds our blood. Thus, under the governor Hilarianus, when they shouted concerning our burial grounds, ‘Let there be no threshing floors!’ their own threshing floors came to nothing, for they did not gather their harvests.”

[Col. 1133A] **Who is transparent and naked.** Juvenal likewise assails an effeminate judge in *Satire* 2, dressed not in ordinary clothing but in translucent garments.

**Granaries are shut upon the earth.** The person guilty of this offense is called in Proverbs 11:26 συνέχων σῖτον, “one who holds back grain.” Nazianzen elegantly describes the matter as καταπραγματεύεσθαι τῆς ἐνδείας, καὶ γεωργεῖν τὰς συμφοράς, “to speculate upon want and cultivate calamities.” Although the name *dardanarii*, “grain profiteers,” was infamous and their conduct punished by law, those who held governing power in the provinces were not at all ashamed to make profits from it.

**By the guilty man (*a nocente*) [reading uncertain].** Many things are said with this meaning in the book *To Donatus*. Nor is it novel for authors repeatedly to use what they had written previously as their own material.

**The guilty are afraid.** That is, to accuse and inform against others.

**Crocodiles and dog-headed apes.** Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 6, says that when Piso and Gabinius were consuls they barred these Egyptian monstrosities from the Capitol and, after overthrowing their altars as well, formally repudiated them. Later, however, when they were restored to their former state, supreme majesty was conferred upon them.

**For I ought to have been tortured if I denied it.** Tertullian treats this argument extensively in *Apology*, ch. 2, and *To the Nations*, Book I, ch. 2. So does Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*, where he says that a perverse examination was conducted, not one that elicited the truth but one that compelled a lie.

[Col. 1133B] **By the ruin of kings.** That is, the Decii, whose downfall our author attributes to divine vengeance at the beginning of the book *On the Lapsed*. This subject provided Lactantius with the theme of a separate book. Orosius also treats it in his *History*, Book VII, ch. 31.

**We mutter at ill health.** So far are we from uttering blasphemous words, or even murmuring with a growl, that we do not so much as whisper a complaint.

**Sheep from their food.** The Septuagint has ἐξέλιπον ἀπὸ βρώσεως πρόβατα, “the sheep failed for lack of food.” But the alternative reading, “Sheep shall disappear from the fold,” would correspond more closely to the Hebrew truth, for this renders it very well. The Septuagint translators appear to have read [the underlying Hebrew reading is absent from the supplied text].

**For repelling enemies and obtaining rain.** He refers to the memorable deed of the Christian soldiers under Emperor Aurelius, concerning which see Justin Martyr and Tertullian in the *Apology*.

[Col. 1133C] **Do not touch.** They read μὴ ἐγγίσητε, “do not approach.” Cyprian appears to have read μὴ θίγητε, “do not touch.”

**The brief pleasure of cruel eyes.** Those fleeting and savage delights of the theaters, which fed the eyes of the persecutors, the wretches will pay for when they are tortured eternally in the flames of Gehenna, and when from afar they behold the poor received into Abraham’s bosom.

**At the very moment of death one passes to immortality.** All these words are addressed to a Gentile who has not yet been reborn through Baptism. So ready a pardon cannot be promised to wicked Christians who repent only at the last moment.

## NOTES ON THE BOOK *ON WORKS AND ALMSGIVING*

### On Works and Almsgiving

In nothing did primitive piety shine more brightly than in the abundant generosity by which the needs of the poor were relieved. [Col. 1133D] Nor was greater diligence expended by either the apostles or the holy Fathers in commending any duties to the Christian people.

Indeed, the excellent collection of material on this subject in the present little book appears to have been written under something like divine guidance, so that the minds of the brethren at Carthage would be more ready to bring aid to the suffering Numidians who at that time were taken captive by barbarians. This event is mentioned in Epistle 62, number 60 in Pamelius.

That this little book was written before that disaster is sufficiently established by the fact that, among its exhortations, no mention occurs of so compelling a cause. We therefore assign the treatise itself to the year 254, since it appears to have preceded the aforesaid incursion of the barbarians. St. Jerome praises this book in his *Epistle to Pammachius*, as does St. Augustine *Against the Pelagians*, in *Against Julian*, and frequently elsewhere. Pontius appears to mention the same work under the title *On Mercy*.

**Adam had brought it.** *Apportaverat*: he had brought it upon us, had inflicted it. St. Augustine [Col. 1134A] frequently cites this passage and says that two Pelagian falsehoods are refuted here: first, their claim that the human race derives no defect from Adam that must be healed and cured through Christ; and second, their claim that after Baptism the saints have no sin. See *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians to Boniface*, Book IV, ch. 8.

**Not, of course, those sins which had previously been contracted.** The very great care of the ancient writers must be observed here, lest anything they said weaken the absolutely certain faith that all the sins of one’s previous life are cleansed in the washing of Baptism. It appears that all who gave their names to the Christian faith were drawn to Baptism above all by this hope and expectation.
