**Continual working.** By this expression our author frequently denotes everything understood among us under the designation “good works.” Hence it is used in the title of this book as equivalent to almsgiving; and the first chapter of the third book *To Quirinus* is entitled “On the Good of Works and Mercy.” See what was said there.

**Already washed upon a board.** The text should be Ἐν τῷ ὑπερώῳ, “in the upper room.” Acts 9 means the dining chamber, [Col. 1134B] that is, on the upper story. The copyists, following their own understanding and thinking chiefly of a table, substituted *in tabula jam*, “already upon a board.” The custom of washing the dead prevailed among the Gentiles; hence Ennius had said:

> A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin.

**Support.** See what was said in Book III *To Quirinus*, ch. 61.

**High and deep.** Papias says: “Height is a general term for both that which is lofty and that which is deep.” The darkness that fills the entire intervening space, heaven and earth, is meant.

**Not with the devil’s stibium.** That this pigment was used among the Jews is clear from 2 Kings 9:30; Jeremiah 4:30; and Ezekiel 23:40. The Greeks called it πλατυόφθαλμον, “eye-widener,” and ὀμματογράφον, “eye-paint.” Nor was it unknown to the Romans. Pliny, Book XXXIII, ch. 6, says that among women’s eye cosmetics it enlarges the eyes. Tertullian, in *On the Dress of Women* and elsewhere, formerly attributed the arts of cosmetics to the devil, the falsifier of nature.

You believe that you celebrate the Lord’s Day. Our author seems to have in view the passage of St. Paul, 1 Cor. 16:2, where [Col. 1134C] the individual faithful are commanded, on the first day of the week, or on any Lord’s Day, to set aside whatever they please. Justin Martyr explains the Christian Church’s custom in this regard, *Apology* II: “On the day called the Day of the Sun, all who dwell in towns or in the countryside assemble together in one place.” After describing the solemn observances of prayer and the Eucharist, he adds: “Those who are prosperous and willing give whatever each chooses according to his own purpose; and what is collected is deposited with the presiding minister, who himself assists orphans and widows,” etc.

It should be observed that among the ancients the word *Dominicum* signifies three things. First, the day itself: so it occurs at Rev. 1:9 and in Ignatius, *Epistle to the Trallians*. Second, the church: thus the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 5, commands a catechumen entering “the Lord’s house” (*es to kyriakon*) to remain in the place of the catechumens. Jerome likewise uses *Dominicum* in this sense in the *Chronicle*; and the words in our vernacular languages, the English *Church* and the German *Dohm*, are plainly derived from this source. Third, it is used for the mysteries customarily celebrated at the place and time just mentioned; [Col. 1134D] thus “to perform the Lord’s rite” (*kyriakon telein*) means to officiate at Christian sacred rites. And perhaps the words used here—“Do you believe that you celebrate the Lord’s Day?”—belong to this sense. Certainly the bond between receiving the Eucharist and the right to share in the offerings was so close that the two always proceeded in step, and those denied this privilege of “communion with an offering” (*koinōnias meta prosphoras*) were regarded as excluded. On this matter, see the Council of Ancyra, canon 5, as well as what is said in Epistle 2. St. Augustine seems to have spoken in this sense in *Sermon* 213, *On Time*: “Offer the oblations that are consecrated upon the altar; a man capable of offering should be ashamed if he communicates from another’s oblation.”

Ash-baked bread. The Septuagint has “a little cake baked in the ashes” (*enkryphian mikron*). According to Hesychius: “*Enkyphias*: a kind of bread made in ashes because there is no oven.”

A jar of meal. An earthenware vessel. The Septuagint: “The jar of flour did not fail, nor the flask of oil.”

True and just. Our author follows the reading that has: “That man was true, just” (*anthrōpos ekeinos alēthinos, dikaios*) [Col. 1135A]; in place of this some copies give “blameless” (*amemptos*), and others “without blemish” (*amōmos*). The words here concerning the offering of a calf for sins, which are superfluous, occur widely in Greek copies; and indeed “the things concerning sin” (*ta peri hamartias*) are commonly added to “sacrifices” (*thysiais*). See Ps. 39:10.

For it is a good prize. The Vulgate translator likewise reads this way. The Greek has “a good prize” (*thema agathon*), whence the expression “prize contests” (*thematikoi agōnes*), in which the competitors contend for a prize that has been deposited. These are also called *argyritai*, as opposed to *stephanitai* and *phyllitai*—contests for crowns and leaves.

What a gift. Among the pagans, the expenditure of those who furnished public entertainments was devoted to the slaughter and destruction of human beings; Christians spent their resources upon relieving those same human beings. The latter was a spectacle worthy of God most good and great, the former of the devil. Moreover, not only through their largesse, but much more through their sufferings, Christians became a spectacle to God, angels, and men, as the Apostle relates at 1 Cor. 9:9. “A gift before the supreme God” seems to be contrasted with those gifts made before men.

A four-horse chariot or the consulship. The honors and insignia of the higher magistracies. “Curule horses,” says Festus, “are horses harnessed to a four-horse chariot.”

[Col. 1135B] And unless an honorable production succeeds. Similarly in the book *To Donatus*: “An utterly foolish and empty loss—to have wished to procure, by the pleasure of a disappointing spectacle, that which the people would not accept and the magistrate would lose.”

Burning. The Greek has “eternal punishment” (*kolasin aiōnion*). Our author, consistent in this reading, seems to have read “burning” (*pyrōsin*).

What the people of believers did under the Apostles. Our author likewise appeals to those times near the end of the book *On Prayer*.

The day of our repayment. Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 32, uses *redhibitio*, “restitution.” The alternative reading *reditio*, “return,” does not displease Rigault: thus a return, which appears voluntary, would be opposed to persecution, which is violent. Or, rather, *return* may mean admission into Paradise, from which the sinner Adam and Adam’s progeny, tainted with sin, were expelled. Christ abolished this sin, and consequently good Christians return to Paradise, to which Cain did not return after his fratricide, as Cyprian says near the end of *On Jealousy and Envy*. [Col. 1135C]

## ON THE BOOK *ON THE GOOD OF PATIENCE*

On the Good of Patience. Cyprian himself supports this title in his celebrated letter to Jubaianus, where he says: “For this reason we have also composed a little book *On the Good of Patience*, insofar as our limited ability was capable of it, with the Lord permitting and inspiring us.” From this it is also easy to learn at what time and on what occasion he published the treatise. He evidently wrote it after the controversy over the baptism of heretics had arisen, namely around the year 255, in order to provide a remedy for the partisan feelings embittered on both sides. To address this matter more properly, throughout the entire course of the work he does not insert even a single word—and this may be evidence of the exceptional prudence he employed in conducting affairs—that might reopen the memory of that unhappy controversy. Moreover, not only Pontius mentions this little book, but also Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*; Augustine, book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 1; also book VII [Col. 1135D] *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, chapter 54; book IV *To Boniface*, chapter 8; and frequently elsewhere.

Philosophers too profess that they pursue this virtue. Tertullian likewise says in the book *On Patience*: “The philosophers, indeed, who are regarded as creatures possessing some degree of wisdom, esteem patience so highly that, although they disagree among themselves through the various caprices of their schools and rivalries of opinion, they nevertheless remember patience alone in common and have entrusted to this one virtue the peace of their studies. Upon it they unite, upon it they form a compact; they pursue it unanimously in their aspiration to virtue and base every display of wisdom upon patience.”

This virtue is shared with God. Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 3: “Among us, reason and its structure demonstrate clearly enough—not only through words in giving commands but also through sufferings in enduring—to those to whom it has been granted to believe, that patience is God’s nature, the operation and excellence of a certain innate property.”

His immortality laid aside for the time being. Princes are similarly said to lay aside their majesty [Col. 1136A] when, taking off the insignia of their rank, they appear in public in the dress of a commoner.

He had formed eyes a little before. As though he had not opened the man’s eyes but made them. Thus Nonnus, chapter 9 of his paraphrase of John, writes of “a face without light”:

> Possessing a conjoined, undivided, unshaped power of sight,  
> which nature had not fashioned; but within the circle of the lidless eye  
> he bore a swollen, alien orb beneath the mist that attended his birth.

That it might be consummated in Christ. Our author seems to have in view the Savior’s words, “It is finished” (*tetelestai*), John 19:30, as though he had fulfilled not the prophecies but patience.

Upon whom the Church. Similar expressions occur in the letters to Florentius Pupianus, Jubaianus, and Quintus, and elsewhere. For when our author cites a testimony of Scripture, he customarily embellishes it with praise of the sacred writer himself. In *On Work and Almsgiving*, when citing St. Paul, he says: “The Apostle Paul, filled with the grace of the Lord’s inspiration.” And in this [Col. 1136B] very book: “The blessed Apostle Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit and sent to summon and form the Gentiles.” And a little later: “Paul, mindful of the divine command,” as frequently elsewhere.

His fratricidal brother. The Pompeian Law on parricide provides that a person is liable for parricide not only if he kills his father or mother, but also if he kills a brother, sister, paternal cousin, and so forth.

He begins with tears. Pliny treats this at length in the preface to book VII: “On the day of birth, nature casts man naked upon the naked ground, at once to wailing and weeping; and of all the many living creatures, none other is born to tears—and those immediately at the beginning of life. But, by Hercules, that early and very swift smile is granted to none before the fortieth day.”

Innocence dedicated to righteousness. Baptismal innocence, of course.

Nor after carrying the Eucharist. We retain Pamelius’s reading, although it is supported by the authority of only a few manuscripts; for *gestata Eucharistia*, “the Eucharist having been carried,” actually corresponds better to the hand mentioned here than *gustata Eucharistia*, “the Eucharist having been tasted.” [Col. 1136C] Indeed, Cyprian elsewhere used a not dissimilar manner of speaking, namely in the *Epistle to the Thibaritans*: “Let us arm,” he says, “the right hand with the spiritual sword, that it may resolutely reject deadly sacrifices, mindful of the Eucharist by which it received the Lord’s body.” Likewise in *On the Lapsed*: “That it may not immediately receive the Lord’s body with hands of wickedness.” Furthermore, it is evident from that book that the Eucharistic bread was not merely distributed to the faithful by the priest, but was also carried home by them.

The punishment of worms consumes. Our author spoke to this effect above in *On Mortality*. Tertullian calls them “creatures breaking forth” in the book *On Patience*.

That they might call a bovine head and an earthly image the guides of their journey. Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 1, says that “a bovine head came forth for them,” and that “all Israel, abandoning God, gave honor to this image, saying: ‘These are the gods who brought us out of the land of Egypt.’” Our author has, however, composed these words in such a way as to relate that the Israelites [Col. 1136D] worshiped not a single idol but several. Indeed, it was not rashly, or merely because of a Hebrew idiom, that the Septuagint translators used the plural number, saying: “These are your gods, O Israel,” and, “Make us gods who will go before us.” For the prophecy of Amos 5:26, quoted by St. Stephen, establishes that the Israelites fashioned not only a golden calf, but also “the tabernacle of Moloch, and the image of the idols, the star of the god Remphan—the figures which they made.”

The Psalmist, Ps. 77:64, says that by this crime the Israelites provoked God to jealousy—and rightly so. The worship due to God most good and great, who had appeared visibly in the Tabernacle in the pillar of fire and cloud, they bestowed upon Moloch, or the Sun, as upon a deity more immediately present; and they carried about his own tabernacle or seven-chambered processional car, corresponding to the number of the planets, as Rabbi Simeon reports in the *Jalkut*. Furthermore, the worship proper to Jehovah, or the supreme God, who is, was, and will be, they transferred to Rephan, or Saturn—for so he is called among the Egyptians—the god of time and supreme among the planets. His emblem was the star-marked ox, because of the agriculture over which he presided; and his star was “upon the highest part of his brow” (*epi metōpou akrou*), as Cyril says. [Col. 1137A]

The goods of patience and the evils of impatience. Tertullian uses precisely the same method in his book *On Patience*.

Laborious chastity in widows. In a similar phrase Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, mentions a “more laborious continence.” Comparing virgins and widows, he says: “Virginity consists in grace, but continence in virtue. Not to desire what you have become accustomed to desiring is a great contest. But if you have never known the fruit of desiring a thing, you will easily refrain from desiring it.”

A separate white robe for each. Not a few manuscripts read: “A white robe was given to each of them” (*edothē autois hekastō stolē leukē*). Thereafter the Greek text contains only “they shall be fulfilled” (*plērōsontai*); what is said here about the number is added by way of interpretation.

For by the Lord’s fire. The Septuagint reads: “A casting away in a flame of fire; for by the Lord’s fire the whole earth shall be judged, and by his sword all flesh.”

[Col. 1137B] Worship the Lord. Cyprian seems to have read not “Worship God” (*tō Theō proskynēson*) but “Worship the Lord” (*tō Kyriō*).

## ON THE BOOK *ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY*

On Jealousy and Envy. This book, having almost the same subject as the preceding one, also seems to have been written on the same occasion. But since in the Epistle to Jubaianus Cyprian mentions the treatise *On Patience*, but not this one *On Jealousy and Envy*, it is reasonable to believe that at the time that epistle was written only one of the two treatises had been composed. Consequently, our author did not publish this work before the immediately following year, namely 256. That it was not delayed any further is suggested by the fact that persecution immediately threatened—a persecution which would extinguish private animosities by a public catastrophe, just as falling ruins commonly extinguish fires, and which also struck Cyprian himself and banished him to Curubis.

Pontius clearly [Col. 1137C] identifies this little book when he says: “Who would restrain envy, arising from the venomous malignity of jealousy, with the sweetness of a saving remedy?” Jerome likewise mentions it in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 5, where he calls *On Jealousy and Envy* “a most excellent book,” adding this commendation: “Whoever reads it will not hesitate to number envy among the works of the flesh.” Augustine likewise praises it in *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, book IV, chapters 8, 9, and 11, and also book V, chapter 14. Our Bede also cites it in his commentary on the First Epistle of St. Peter, final chapter.

He goes about seeking someone to devour. The sacred text has “he walks about” (*peripatei*); most manuscripts have “he goes around” (*perierchetai*). Thus the Israelites destroyed the city of Jericho by walking around it. [Col. 1138A] In the book of Job, the devil is said to roam throughout the world; here he is declared to circle around each one of us—so intent is he upon the destruction of each individual as though upon that of all.

Himself first cast down by jealousy. Some attribute the fall of the angels to pride rather than envy; but these vices are joined by such an indivisible bond that neither can exist separately. Indeed, each is at once the parent and offspring of the other.

Envy is removed. It is taken out of the way, according to an idiom of the author that we noted above in the book *To Donatus*.

He halts rapacity. That is, he makes it stand still; he restrains it. Thus above drought is said to halt rivers.

You may see what you are. That is, “Consider; reflect upon it.” We have discussed this phrase of Cyprian in the book *To Donatus*.

Christ suffered. This passage is cited rather frequently.

Him also a very great teacher. The sacred text has only: “He shall be called great” (*megas klēthēsetai*). Those, however, who seem better acquainted with the constitution of the heavenly kingdom than with their own household assign a special aureole to teachers, [Col. 1138B] so that even in heaven an academic degree as teacher must be attained. See Dan. 12:3.

Nor loving. That is, a cultivator of charity, benevolent and friendly.

You will begin to die. “You are about to die” (*mellete apothnēskein*).

Let us also bear the image. We have frequently commented on this reading.

Cut-off offspring. Rigault proposes that *subsiciva*, “cut-off,” should be read as *successiva*, “successive,” but he lacks manuscript support. I think the received reading should be retained. According to an ordinary manner of speaking, children may be regarded as shoots cut, as it were, from the stock of their parents, answering to the nature of the tree. Thus in Romans 11 the Apostle calls the Jews shoots of a good olive tree and the Gentiles shoots of a wild olive. Likewise Isaiah, chapter 5, compares the Israelites to a shoot of a noble vine that produced wild grapes instead of grapes. In the *Epistle to Euchratius Concerning an Actor*, our author speaks in almost the same way: “He cannot be regarded as having ceased who appoints substitutes and supplies several replacements in place of himself alone.”

Let a man’s heart devise righteous things. You will seek these words in vain in [Col. 1138C] Bibles that follow the Hebrew text, but they correspond exactly to the Septuagint reading. Indeed, nothing is more disordered than this book of Proverbs in the Greek manuscripts. The words themselves are: “Let a man’s heart devise righteous things, so that his steps may be directed by God.” But if we consider the matter more attentively, it will appear that the Septuagint translators did not wander far from the sense here. They read, namely, in place of [text apparently lost or corrupt]; as the Chaldean paraphrast seems to have read when he says [text apparently lost], or at least they held “the secrets of men’s ways” to be the same thing as “his spirit.”

[Col. 1138]

## SELECT ANNOTATIONS OF MARTIN JOSEPH ROUTH, DOCTOR OF SACRED THEOLOGY AND PRESIDENT OF ST. MARY MAGDALEN COLLEGE, OXFORD, ON FOUR BOOKS OF ST. CYPRIAN

*(From* Certain Principal Minor Works of Ecclesiastical Writers, *vol. I, second edition, Oxford, 1840, pp. 330–359.)*

## ON THE BOOK *ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS*

[Col. 1137D]

### CHAPTER I.—That Idols Are Not Gods; That There Is One God; and That Salvation Has Been Given to Believers Through Christ

Since in some manuscripts and in several old editions preceding that of Baluze, or the Benedictine edition, all these words are rightly set apart as the title—or rather the summary—of the work, I have arranged for them to be printed in that form. As for the third clause of this title, which in its present form first appeared in the Manutian edition, the author writes similarly below: [Col. 1138D] “But as to who Christ is and how salvation came to us through him, this is the order, this the rationale.”

And they celebrated feast days with such great honor. I ventured to restore the passage in this form, substituting *tanto*, “such great,” for *dando*, “giving,” on the authority of two manuscripts: one Vossian, cited among the variant readings in the Oxford, or Fell, edition; and the other my own, which I recently acquired from the Tewater collection. For *honore*, “honor,” the editions before Baluze offered *honores* or *honorem*, except for those very old editions preceding Erasmus’s.

Whether this truth is thus also among individuals. So Jacob Gronovius, who before Baluze furnished his own edition of this little book, had printed it, putting *an sit et hoc* in place of the common reading *an stet haec*. This emendation, neglected by Baluze—if indeed it ever came to his attention—is confirmed [Col. 1139A] by two manuscripts of Cyprian preserved at New College, Oxford, which I have designated by the numbers 2 and 3. Another manuscript of Cyprian is also extant in that college; but no variant readings from any of these manuscripts, at least as regards this little book, appear in the Oxford edition. A manuscript of Cyprian formerly belonging to the distinguished Drury, and now acquired by me, also agrees with the improved reading.

### CHAPTER II.—Apollo Tended Admetus’s Flock

Gronovius had substituted this for the common *Admeti* in the aforementioned edition of this little book, which was appended to Minucius Felix and appeared in 1705, about twenty years before Baluze’s edition of Cyprian. Since the two aforementioned manuscripts of New College support it, I have preferred this reading. Wherever I depart from that edition of Baluze in these shorter works of Cyprian, I shall always note the fact, as I have already done in Firmilian’s epistle, while seldom citing variant readings elsewhere.

Hence he is depicted carrying a sickle. The common text adds *senex*, “as an old man,” after “carrying,” which Gronovius rightly omitted from his edition. Pamelius was the first to admit the word, from the Cambon manuscript; but it is unknown to the four manuscripts cited in the Oxford edition, as well as to the three New College manuscripts, my manuscript mentioned above, formerly Tewater’s, and the oldest editions of Cyprian. I have therefore omitted the word. Two Drury manuscripts and another formerly belonging to the distinguished Meerman, now mine and written in the twelfth century, may now be added to the evidence.

### CHAPTER III.—Alexander Says That This Is So

*(See the note on this passage in the Oxford edition, to which Routh added the following.)* The most learned Bishop of Oxford wrote this and more about letters seen by Plutarch and other ancient writers, not about those that circulate today under Alexander’s name. In Baluze’s text, however, the verb *esse*, “to be,” is wrongly omitted after *ita*, and a full stop is wrongly placed after *scribit*, “writes”; hence, as I noted long ago, these errors passed into my own text. [Col. 1139C]

### CHAPTER IV.—Prostitutes

In many editions preceding Baluze’s, the words that follow are enclosed in brackets, and they are not recognized by the three New College manuscripts, the two formerly belonging to Drury, or the Meerman manuscript. They do, however, occur in the Tewater manuscript mentioned above.

There is also Bald Venus. Lactantius, book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 20: “When the city had been occupied by the Gauls, the Romans, besieged on the Capitol, made cords for artillery from the women’s hair and consecrated a temple to Bald Venus.” Baluze cited this passage after Fell. Yet, although authors offer several reasons for this title, Cyprian here intimates that Venus was so called for some less honorable reason.

### CHAPTER V.—Both the Assyrians and the Persians

Since nearly all the manuscripts omit the words “and the Medes,” [Col. 1139D] I have followed the first edition here. Many manuscripts, however, offer “Syrians” for “Assyrians.”

They do … they take the auspices. Jacob Gronovius, following Cellarius, substituted these plurals for the common singulars “he does” and “he takes the auspices.” Cellarius calls the manuscript used in his edition of this little book appended to Minucius Felix the Verona manuscript. That edition of Cellarius was printed at Halle in 1699. Rigault, however, had already cited the Verona manuscript’s reading with approval in his notes on Cyprian. New College manuscript 2, the Tewater manuscript, and the older Drury manuscript should be added to its support. Meanwhile, in his *Italian Journey*, p. 23, Mabillon reported that this Verona manuscript had been written in rather large letters a thousand years before.

But they keep the allotted time within a fixed limit. That is, the Roman kingdoms possess the time assigned to them within a fixed and determined limit.

And defeated. I have disregarded these words, which Baluze added without adequate reason; meanwhile, contrary to his intention, they were placed in that posthumous edition of Baluze after the words “and was captured.” [Col. 1140A]

And the more easily he both sailed and conquered. I restored the particle *et*, “and,” which in the Oxford and other editions precedes the words “the more easily”; the same particle, however, is omitted in those books before the verb “sailed.” The New College manuscript that I call the second preserves it in both places, as does the more recent Drury manuscript; but the older Drury manuscript, like the Meerman manuscript, omits it before “sailed.”

### CHAPTER VI.—Foolish and Prodigal

Baluze reads “credulous,” preferring this admittedly easier reading to the alternative “prodigal,” which is supplied by all editions except that of Gravius and by nearly all the manuscripts. The words occur in combination below: “All things prodigal and foolish,” Cyprian says, “perish amid delusive pleasures,” *On Work and Almsgiving*, chapter 16. My manuscript formerly belonging to Tewater, however, has “incredulous.” Rigault once conjectured that *perditum*, “lost,” had been written instead of *prodigum*, “prodigal”; and in the same chapter you have “with the people of perdition and death.” I, however, would prefer to substitute *proditum*, “betrayed,” for *prodigum*. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* III.15: “I was betrayed, misled, and cast into deception.” See Forcellini’s *Lexicon* under the word.

Hostanes. Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, chapter 2: “The first extant writer, so far as I can discover, who composed a treatise on it—magic—was Osthanes, who accompanied Xerxes, king of the Persians, in the war that he waged against Greece; and he scattered, as it were, the seeds of that monstrous art, infecting in passing the whole world through whatever regions he traveled. More careful authorities place shortly before him another Zoroaster of Proconnesus. This at least is certain: this Osthanes drove the peoples of Greece to a frenzy for this science, and not merely to an eagerness for it.” Fell cited this passage from Pliny; it is now reproduced from Hardouin’s edition.

And he says that true angels stand beside his throne. A manuscript among the variant readings of the Oxford edition has “our angels” for “true angels.” Perhaps the word “servants” was once corrupted into “true.”

Consecrated. Baluze’s text has the singular “consecrated,” [Col. 1140C] and one manuscript cited in the Oxford edition, as well as the New College manuscript I have designated number 1, has “assembled.” Moreover, *conservati*, “preserved,” is retained as a variant reading in the margin of the Erasmian edition. Since, however, I judge the reading *consecratis*, “consecrated,” found in the earlier editions to be best—a reading confirmed by the other two New College manuscripts, my former Tewater manuscript, and both Drury manuscripts—I have restored it here in place of Baluze’s singular *consecrati*, following Cellarius, while John Lindner also retained it in his edition.

### CHAPTER VII.—They Assail with Diseases

The common reading is “they assail diseases.” I corrected the passage from New College manuscript 2.

To superstition concerning themselves. That is, concerning the demons; above the author wrote, “to the worship of themselves.”

They have made them sharers through terror. The common reading is “through error”; relying upon New College manuscript 3, I changed it to “through terror.” This reading is also written in the margin of the manuscript that I call New College manuscript 2. Lactantius, discussing demons in his *Epitome*, chapter 28, wrote: “They send dreams, or even outright terrors.” [Col. 1140D]

### CHAPTER VIII.—Therefore There Is One Lord God of All

The common text has the verb *est*, “is,” after “Lord”; at the prompting of the three New College manuscripts and the Erasmian edition, I deleted it. Both Drury manuscripts may now be added. The Tewater manuscript has: “One, therefore, is the Lord of all, one God.” The editions of Cellarius, Gronovius, and Lindner add “one is” before “God.”

Nor here should you marvel concerning a human being. In place of Fell’s reading, “Nor should you marvel at this only concerning a human being,” which was preferred by Gronovius, Cellarius, and Lindner, my opinion is that the reading of the first edition, *nec hic tu*, should be restored. In the Tewater manuscript also, *hic* is written by the same hand as a variant above the word *hoc*.

### CHAPTER IX.—He Is Greater Than Perception

Someone cited in Marshall’s English translation of the works of St. Cyprian conjectured that *censu*, “in estimation,” should be written for *sensu*, “than sense.” I once said that these words are often confused with one another, and acknowledged that *census* is a Cyprianic word. Nevertheless, the words of Lactantius in the *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*, chapter 2, show that nothing should be changed: “Therefore there is one God … whom the human mind cannot evaluate by sense, nor mortal tongue express. For he is too sublime and too great to be comprehended either by human thought or speech.” [Col. 1141A]

And although man dwells more broadly—perhaps, more spaciously. Minucius, chapter 32, §1, has: “although I, a man, dwell *taxius*.” With Fulvius Ursinus we printed *laxius*, “more spaciously,” there, because Cicero, whom Minucius commonly imitates, used “to dwell spaciously” of his house in chapter 44. But all manuscripts of Cyprian, if he transcribed Felix, openly offer *latius*, “more broadly,” so that I am beginning to wonder whether the earlier author too did not write *latius*, as Sabaeus and François Baudouin read. —CELLARIUS, as cited by Lindner. I think *laxius* should be attributed to both authors; it could easily have passed into *latius* or *lacius*, the latter being what the manuscripts have. Galerius complained before the emperor Diocletian that fifteen years had already “flowed away”; that he had been banished to Illyricum or the bank of the Danube and had struggled with barbarian peoples, while others ruled delicately within more spacious and tranquil lands. Lactantius, *On the Deaths* [Col. 1141B] *of the Persecutors*, chapter 18.

The designation “God” is all that is needed. The expression is obscure. Perhaps *solum*, “alone,” should be restored for *totum*, “whole.” Lactantius also says in the *Epitome* that God does not need a proper designation, using these words: “and that he is without a name, because he does not need a proper designation, since he is alone,” chapter 4. New College manuscripts 2 and 3 omit the word. The editions after Pamelius and before Baluze have “God,” not “of God”; Baluze restored “of God.” The more recent Drury manuscript has “God,” but the older one “of God.” Moreover, since in the following line, before the word “diffused,” the oldest editions and the five manuscripts mentioned in the Oxford edition, as well as all the other manuscripts I used in editing this little book, read *ipse*, “he himself,” for *totus*, “whole,” I have arranged for *ipse* to be printed, following Gronovius’s precedent.

### CHAPTER X.—But as to Who Christ Is, Etc.

In the words “this is the order, this the rationale,” I have deleted the verb “is” before “rationale,” which Baluze added against the testimony of the other witnesses.

Subsequently becoming undisciplined and proud. “Negligent [Col. 1141C] and undisciplined, etc.” in Baluze’s edition. The Vossian manuscript cited in the Oxford edition and my Tewater manuscript give “neglectful of disciplines.” Two New College manuscripts have “neglectful of discipline.” Another manuscript of the same college, however, gives: “But they subsequently became undisciplined and were puffed up by confidence in their fathers”; the older Drury manuscript agrees with it. The reading *indisciplinati*, “undisciplined,” was admitted into the text in Morel’s edition of Cyprian, printed in 1564. Concerning the same word, Cellarius noted in his edition of this treatise that the Vulgate translator used it in Wisdom 17:1 and that the Old Glosses have “*indisciplinatus*: unlearned” (*amathēs*). Meanwhile, rejecting the words “negligent and,” which the Meerman manuscript nevertheless also recognizes, I believe that Cyprian wrote: “But they subsequently became undisciplined and proud,” and that “neglectful of disciplines,” or “of discipline,” is to be regarded as a gloss on the Cyprianic word *indisciplinati*.

Exiles from both sun and sky. Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 21: [Col. 1141D] “Scattered, wandering, and exiles from both sky and sun, they roam throughout the world.”

### CHAPTER XI.—Of Much Better Obedience and Stronger Faith

“Of much more faithful and better obedience,” in Baluze’s edition. From New College manuscripts 2 and 3 and my manuscript formerly belonging to Tewater, I admitted the words “of better obedience and stronger faith” into the text. In New College manuscript 1 and the older Drury manuscript, however, only the words “much more faithful” occur, while “of better obedience and stronger faith” are omitted; Gronovius’s edition does the same. The more recent Drury manuscript has “of better obedience and stronger faith,” omitting “much.” My manuscript formerly belonging to Meerman agrees with Baluze’s reading.

Illuminator and guide of the human race. The common reading is “teacher,” but Cellarius and Gronovius formerly adopted “guide,” and Lindner did so more recently, whereas long before them Rigault had noted: “‘Guide of the human race’: so it is read in the oldest copies of Cyprian and Tertullian.” Moreover, *deductor*, “guide,” occurs in two New College manuscripts and in my older Drury and Tewater manuscripts. It is a word of Tertullian, occurring elsewhere and also in the very passage of the *Apologeticus* that Cyprian transferred here. The more recent Drury manuscript has “ruler” in its place, and the Meerman manuscript “teacher.” [Col. 1142A]

This is the power of God, etc. Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 23: “The power of God, and the spirit of God, and the Word, and wisdom, and reason, and the Son of God.” Compare also the beginning of his book *On Prayer*, above, p. 97. Similarly, much in what follows has been transferred here from chapter 20 of the same *Apologeticus*, just as above the author already owed a great deal to Minucius Felix.

He descends into the virgin. Since three manuscripts cited in the Oxford edition, the three at New College, and likewise my own manuscripts offer this reading, *delabitur*, in place of the common *illabitur*, “enters into,” I have preferred it, as did Lindner following Cellarius; Tertullian supplies the verb.

The Holy Spirit is clothed with flesh. Compare Rom. 1:3–4, where the two natures of Christ are thus designated.

[Col. 1142B] ### CHAPTER XII.—It Will Be Announced to Those Who Warn

I have restored this reading of the first edition, which is confirmed by at least seven manuscripts, in place of *admonentibus*, “to those who admonish.”

As one who would discharge the function of man by both practice and example. What the author wrote here rather obscurely occurs in all the books.

### CHAPTER XIII.—They Thought Him a Magician from the Unrestricted Scope of His Power

“Unrestricted scope of power” is used to mean its amplitude. Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 20: “Since they had presumed him to be merely a man because of his lowliness, it followed that they should think him a magician because of his power.” Cyprian imitated Tertullian, and Arnobius in turn imitated Cyprian, book I, chapter 46.

The teachers of the Jews … handed him over. This passage is presented somewhat differently in the Manutian edition, with support both from the manuscripts I used and from Tertullian’s words in *Apologeticus*, chapter 21, which Cyprian imitates. It does not, however, seem worth the effort [Col. 1142C] to alter the words adopted here, since they signify the same thing. Among other things here, Tertullian, like Minucius in the earlier part of the little book, served as the author’s model.

### CHAPTER XIV.—For Even When Crucified, Anticipating the Executioner’s Office, Etc.

Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 21: “And yet, when fastened to the cross, he voluntarily dismissed his spirit with a word, anticipating the executioner’s office.”

Such as he had also been. So New College manuscripts 2 and 3. Baluze printed, “the same such as he had also been,” whereas previously the text had either “such as he had been” or “such as he had been before.” New College manuscript 1 and the Meerman, Tewater, and older Drury manuscripts have “such as he had been.” The more recent Drury manuscript has “as he had been,” without “such.”

Joined together. Rigault noted that this reading occurs in the Royal and Verona manuscripts. “*Junctis*,” he says, “represents Luke’s phrase, ‘when the eleven were assembled together’ (*synēthroismenois tois hendeka*), Luke 24:33.” Lindner, following Cellarius, admitted the same reading before me. The editions of Manutius, Fell, [Col. 1142D] and Gronovius, the Pamelius manuscripts and several of Baluze’s manuscripts, New College manuscript 1, my former Tewater manuscript, and the more recent Drury manuscript give the singular “joined.”

But *vinctus*, “bound,” is the reading of the first edition, supported by New College manuscript 2, my Meerman and older Drury manuscripts, and nine further manuscripts cited by Baluze. Baluze indeed so preferred it that he restored it to his edition: “as though Christ had appeared to his disciples with the bands and clothing in which his body had been placed in the tomb, together with the linen cloth in which Joseph of Arimathea had wrapped his body.” So Baluze; yet this would conflict too greatly with the sacred history.

In the Venetian edition, however, published in the same year as that first Roman edition of Cyprian and, so far as I know, scarcely differing from it elsewhere, *victus*, “defeated,” was printed. This word likewise appears in an old edition without place or year, in the Erasmian edition, and in New College manuscript 3, though it makes no sense. How easily *junctus* or *junctis* could have passed into [Col. 1143A] *vinctus* is meanwhile apparent from the fact that in New College manuscript 1 these words are confused with each other in Firmilian’s epistle. See §32.

With the vigor of an avenger and the authority of a judge. Perhaps one should read “in the capacity of an avenger.” A little above Cyprian writes: “Failing to understand the first advent, which preceded in the Passion hidden from view, they believe only in the one that will be manifested in power.” Compare the final chapter of Tertullian’s book *Against the Jews*. “As an avenger” occurs in New College manuscript 1.

As teacher and God. Perhaps “and” should be deleted. The Verona manuscript, with Rigault’s approval, has “not as teacher, but as God,” and New College manuscript 1 has “the Lord God.” But I would prefer to read “God as teacher,” on the authority of Tertullian, whom Cyprian has drawn upon here: “The disciples also,” he says, “dispersed throughout the world in obedience to the command of God their teacher.”

### CHAPTER XV.—If We Shall Have Followed Christ

“Imitated” in Baluze’s and Fell’s editions and others. I judged that the earlier reading “followed” should be restored; it was supplied [Col. 1143B] by the six manuscripts named in the Oxford edition, New College manuscript 1, and two of my own—the Meerman and the older Drury manuscripts. Add the ninth-century Vienna manuscript, as is evident from Denis’s *Catalogue*, vol. I, col. 582. Why should not the alternative reading “imitated” be regarded as a gloss upon this one?

## ON THE BOOK *ON MORTALITY*
That the highly learned Fell was right to add what he placed concerning Jerome at the end of his note is shown by the Armenian version of Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, which has at last been published in our own times; there no trace appears of the words added by Jerome. See the edition of Eusebius’ *Chronicle* by Joannes Baptista Aucher, Venice, 1818, vol. II, p. 299.

CHAPTER I.—*Through an error concerning the truth.* Tacitus, *Histories* II.72, has *errore veri*, that is, ignorance of the matter or fact. Compare Forcellini, *Lexicon Latinum*, under *Error*.

CHAP. II.—*Perpetual joy.* In Baluze’s text [Col. 1143C] there appears *perpetual security*; but the other reading, which I have restored, is found both in all the printed books and in the manuscripts that I was able to consult—namely, the two New College codices and the four parchment manuscripts in my possession, of which the Meerman manuscript was written in the twelfth century, besides the more recent Drury manuscript, which I do not possess. The word *joy* likewise appears in a certain thirteenth-century Vienna codex. See Denis, *Catalogus*, vol. II, col. 2129. Add that no variant is noted at this point in the readings appended to the Oxford edition.

*To begin to reign.* The Sorbonne codex has *in perpetuity*. Another old codex: *that he will reign perpetually with Christ*. BAL. Joannes Fredericus Gronovius once wrote in his *Observationes de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*, after citing this passage of Cyprian:

> “To begin to reign.” The manuscripts have: “who does not believe that he will reign perpetually with Christ.” I believe this was changed by those to whom the simple word *reign* seemed inappropriately placed, as though they were reigning even now. Yet among the best authors the present infinitive is commonly used for the future. [Col. 1143D] Cicero, book IV *To Atticus*: “Cato nevertheless declares that, while he is alive, the man will not triumph.” Livy, book XXXIV: “On the following day Nabis said that he would withdraw from Argos and remove the garrison, since this was the Romans’ pleasure, and that he would return the prisoners and deserters.” Plautus, *The Rope*: “Or that the pimp will do what he has done,” chap. XIV, p. 150, Deventer edition.

Nevertheless, Cyprian writes as follows below: “providing homes there, where they would begin to dwell forever,” *On Works and Almsgiving*, penultimate chapter. Moreover, some manuscripts have in St. Paul, Romans 8:13: “For if you live according to the flesh, you will begin to die”—*μέλλετε ἀποθνῄσκειν*, “you are going to die.” Nor do the manuscripts I have used change anything in this passage of Cyprian.

CHAP. IV.—*Drunkenness incites.* Perhaps one should read *irritates*.

*You are compelled to curse.* Sometimes even against Christ.

*You are forced to swear, which is not permitted.* Cyprian, *On the Good of Patience*, p. 252, Baluze’s edition:

> …then, that you should not swear or curse; that you should not demand back what has been taken from you; that, [Col. 1144A] after receiving a blow, you should offer the other cheek to the one striking you; that, toward a brother sinning against you, etc.

But although it must by no means be denied that very many ancient writers interpreted *κατὰ τὴν λέξιν*—literally—the command of Christ and of the apostle James against swearing, we nevertheless learn from reading other ecclesiastical authors that among Christians the custom of swearing duly and religiously always prevailed. Compare, besides Tertullian cited above, *Apostolic Constitutions* VII.3; François Baudouin, *On the Laws of Constantine the Great*, book II, p. 209, Leipzig edition; Optatus, *On the Donatist Schism*, book II, chap. 22, p. 45, Du Pin’s edition; St. Gregory Nazianzen, Letter 219. Compare also the passages of Holy Scripture concerning the same matter that I shall mention here: Revelation 10:6; Hebrews 6:16–17; 1 Thessalonians 5:27.

CHAP. VI.—*And does it delight us here*, etc. This should be read *ἐρωτηματικῶς*, interrogatively.

CHAP. VII.—*Christ, the teacher of believers.* The common reading is: *Christ, the Lord and teacher of believers*. But since this addition is unknown both to the older editions [Col. 1144B] of Cyprian and to the manuscripts I collated myself, besides nine others whose variants are cited in the Oxford edition, I expunged it. For a similar reason I judged that the word *namely* after *teaching* should be deleted. I now see, moreover, that the same has recently been done in both places in the edition of St. Cyprian’s *Letters to the Martyrs and Confessors*, for the use of the confessors of the Gallican Church, London, 1792. There the editor declares that he followed the Oxford edition but nevertheless sometimes selected readings from the variants appended to it.

CHAP. VIII.—*And may the Spirit lead us to God the Father.* Baluze has: *And may Christ lead us to God the Father.* Yet because of the preceding words I have restored the old reading, which is supported, so far as I know, by all the manuscripts except a few of Baluze’s more than thirty codices. Indeed, in altering this passage the highly learned man forgot the canon of textual criticism that bids us embrace the more difficult reading, provided it is otherwise sound.

CHAP. IX.—*Divine Scripture, saying*, etc. See below [Col. 1144C] what we have noted concerning this book of Ecclesiasticus on § 1 of the treatise *On Works and Almsgiving*.

CHAP. XI.—*He warns … he says.* I adopted these words in place of the printed subjunctives *may warn … may say*, on the authority of New College codex 2 and four of my manuscripts.

CHAP. XII.—*The Christian faith.* The common reading is *the faith of a Christian*. In New College codex 2 and in two of my manuscripts I found not *of a Christian* but *Christian*, which is perhaps better here.

*Helmsman.* *The helmsman of a ship.* This previously mutilated passage, where *nam* (“for”) was read instead of *navis* (“of a ship”), we supplied with the aid of two old copies. In three the word *nam*, which elsewhere and in the editions is placed before *helmsman*, is absent. It is an error; yet that error shows that the reading we present is the true one. Thus BALUZE. But apart from the fact that the particle *nam*, found in the old editions, could have arisen from the preceding word *corona*, neither word—*nam* or *navis*—is recognized by almost any manuscript, since neither appears [Col. 1144D] in those three manuscripts of Baluze, nor in the books collated for the Oxford edition, nor in the seven codices I inspected; the word *navis* is placed only in the margin of the Tewater manuscript. I therefore judged that it should be removed from the text as a marginal gloss first introduced by Baluze. Add that the word was unknown to Florus of Lyon, who wrote before the middle of the ninth century. For it is absent from an old codex of his unpublished *Commentary on the Pauline Epistles*, compiled from Cyprian and eleven other Fathers, where Cyprian’s words are quoted. Let me note in passing that the distinguished Mabillon, in his investigation *On the Commentary on Paul by Bede and Florus, Deacon of Lyon*, records that another copy of this work of Florus besides my own exists at the Grande Chartreuse. That investigation concerns, of course, another commentary by the same Florus—not by Bede, as is commonly believed—drawn from Augustine. See p. 488 of the new edition of Mabillon’s *Veterum Analectorum*.

*Struggle amid adversity is a proof of virtue.* The common reading is [Col. 1145A] *truth*. That reading does indeed appear in New College codex 1; but from one Bodleian codex mentioned in the variant readings of the Oxford edition, another New College codex, and my Tewater manuscript, I adopted *virtue*, which I had formerly conjectured should be read. In the margin of the New College codex, however, appears the alternative reading *truth*, and something else that I cannot identify has been entered in one of my manuscripts.

*Has been made firm.* Baluze’s edition, like the Oxford edition, has *is firm*. But since the word *has been made firm* appears in the twelve manuscripts mentioned by the Oxford editor, with both New College codices and four of my own supporting them, I judged that this reading of the first and the other older editions should be restored. I have now seen the same thing done in the edition that I mentioned just above, prepared for the use of the confessors of the Gallican Church.

CHAP. XIV.—*The reward of his way.* For *the reward of life*, I gladly adopted *the reward of the way* from three manuscripts mentioned in the Oxford edition and New College MS 1.

CHAP. XV.—*Through fear of mortality and of time.* [Col. 1145B] I formerly thought that the conjunction *and* should be deleted, because shortly afterward one reads *in a time of mortality*. I would now prefer to write *terrors* in place of *of time*.

CHAP. XVII.—*For God does not seek our blood, but our faith.*—Baluze reads: *For God does not desire our blood, but seeks our faith.* “We added the word *desires* from certain manuscripts of ours and certain English manuscripts. It may, however, be a gloss.” BALUZE. I have restored the text of the first and other editions and of one parchment manuscript in my possession. New College codex 1 has only a different word order: *For God does not seek our blood, but our faith.* The manuscript formerly belonging to Meerman has: *For God does not seek our blood, but seeks our faith.* Likewise the Oxford edition: *For God does not seek our blood, but seeks our faith.* But in my book formerly belonging to Tewater the passage reads: *For God does not desire our blood, but only our faith.* New College MS 2 and the more recent Drury manuscript agree with Baluze’s reading, but the older Drury manuscript [Col. 1145C] has: *For our God does not seek blood, but faith.*

CHAP. XIX.—*He prayed for leave for himself.* Fell explains: permission from the Lord for a longer absence—that is, a prolongation of life here on earth. The ancients called relief from pain or death *leave*. Lexicographers cite this statement of Seneca: “My illness had granted me a long leave; suddenly it attacked me.”

CHAP. XX.—*Anxious about persecution, secure about his summons.* Before finding this reading in my codices and those of New College—to which five manuscripts of Pamelius may be added—I had conjectured that it should be written thus, instead of the ablatives *anxious* and *secure*. The sense of the passage appears to be: “Anxious on their behalf about persecution, lest, compelled by its violence, they deny the faith; secure concerning their summons, since he is certain that by a divine summons they will be delivered from the world.” See a little below. And above, near the beginning of § 2, one already finds: “Joyful, therefore, concerning his now imminent death, and secure concerning his approaching summons.” Indeed, a parallel expression appears at the end [Col. 1145D] of the treatise: “Already secure concerning her own immortality, still anxious concerning our safety.” Fell, however, noted on the words *anxious about persecution, secure about their summons*: “They shrink from the martyr’s crown; they do not desire the joys of heaven.” Take whichever interpretation you prefer.

*Indeed, he has learned concerning those who remain.* Relying on the Tewater manuscript and fourteen others mentioned in the Oxford edition—including the two New College codices, which contain all Cyprian’s treatises—I expunged the pronoun *for us*, added in the printed editions before *those who remain* but making the discourse more obscure. Neither Drury manuscript knows it.

CHAP. XXI.—*Finally, the apostle Paul disapproves.* Baluze, for reasons unknown to me, exchanged this reading of all the editions for the alternative *rebukes*. In the Oxford edition, which, like the others, presents *disapproves*, only two codices are mentioned in which the verb *rebukes* appears; yet there it is noted without reason: “Perhaps one should read *reproaches*.” Moreover, all the manuscripts I use support the reading *disapproves*. [Col. 1146A]

CHAP. XXII.—*Who would not hasten toward better things?* Baluze’s text has: *Who would not hasten to come to better things?* But since the verb *to come* is sought in vain either in the printed books or in the manuscripts I used, it appears that it should be deleted. Add that neither Pamelius nor the variant readings printed in the Oxford edition mention it. Likewise, immediately afterward and for the same reason, I have thought it proper to restore *be reformed* in place of *be transformed*, which appears in Baluze’s text.

CHAP. XXIII.—*According to faith in the truth.* This reading, presented by eleven copies, among which I include the Séguier manuscript, is the best. Two others have *of the word*. Morel notes that he had seen *of the truth* written in old copies, with *of the word* as an alternative. This confirms our reading. The Bec codex and Morel’s edition read *truth*. Thus BALUZE, who was the first to place *of the truth* in place of the common reading *truth*, supported also by New College codex 2 and my Tewater manuscript. But since, besides two of Baluze’s manuscripts, the older Drury codex also presents the word *of the word*, I wonder whether one should restore: *according to faith in the word of truth*. Below, however—if this is relevant—there appears in *On Works and Almsgiving*, chap. 4: “He who possesses the truth of faith preserves the fear of God.” [Col. 1146B]

CHAP. XXIV.—*Just as God also abides forever.* This addition from Holy Scripture is omitted in Cyprian’s Tewater codex, as also in at least the older Drury manuscript; but it is cited in Cyprian’s *Testimonies*, book III, chap. 2, and in the works of other Fathers.

CHAP. XXV.—*You may be delivered.* I restored this reading in place of the common *you may be stripped*, relying on one codex among the variant readings of the Oxford edition; but perhaps some will think that the other reading should be retained, unless the author’s words on p. 291, line 20, persuade them otherwise. I now see, moreover, that the verb *you may be delivered* has been preferred in the edition for the use of the Gallican exiles that I mentioned just above.

[Col. 1146C] CHAP. XXVI.—*To dwell here in the meantime.* Relying on the authority of many manuscripts, I have restored the reading of the first and other editions in place of *there*, which was substituted without reason.

*Still anxious concerning our safety.* I deleted the conjunction *and* commonly placed before *still*, which is unknown to the first edition and the seven manuscripts I collated. The Tewater manuscript, however, omitted the words *and still*, while one codex cited in the Oxford edition has *but still*.

*The exulting prophets.* Cyprian was thinking of the evangelist John’s words: “Your father Abraham exulted that he might see my day: he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

*The triumphant virgins.* The common reading is *the virgins triumphing there*; but the manuscript formerly belonging to Tewater, while preserving a better order of words, has *there the triumphant virgins*. Perhaps more correctly, however, the first edition and the six manuscripts I collated do not recognize the adverb *there*. Yet the Tewater manuscript also prefixed *there* to the word *rewarded*.

[Col. 1146D] *That we may soon be with them.* The first and other old editions do indeed add *be able*. But since that verb is recognized by only one of the manuscripts collated for the Oxford edition and only one of my own, I now think it perhaps right to omit it, although the recent editor of certain works of Cyprian whom I mentioned above thought otherwise.

ON THE BOOK *ON WORKS AND ALMSGIVING*

CHAP. VI.—*And of widows and the poor.* I have restored the conjunction *and*, which is prefixed to this sentence in the first and other editions and in the seven codices I myself collated, but was wrongly omitted in Baluze’s and the Oxford editions; perhaps in the manuscripts it had been absorbed by the preceding word *orasset*.

*Rise up in the name of Jesus Christ.* Certain versions add the words *in the name of Jesus Christ*, together with these Fathers: Cyprian, Ambrose, and Cassiodorus.

[Col. 1147A] CHAP. VII.—*There will your heart be also.* I restored *there* in place of *in that place* from the manuscripts, because in Cyprian’s own *Testimonies of Holy Scripture*, book III, p. 59 of the Oxford edition, the evangelist’s passage is cited in this form.

CHAP. IX.—*But you are apprehensive and afraid.* Baluze restored the earlier reading, *If you are apprehensive and afraid*, which Fell had changed on the authority of four manuscripts. I now add to these seven others that present the reading I prefer; the sentence is constructed in precisely the same way shortly below, where the verb *you are afraid* occurs.

CHAP. XI.—*Assistance.* The editions following the Aldine add *of life*, but I deleted the word because Pamelius warned that no codex except the Aldine reads it. Nevertheless, I found it in the Lyon edition, which preceded the Aldine. Moreover, the codices I inspected do not know the word *for you* after *working*; I note this because the word is not greatly missed.

CHAP. XIII.—*Divide your income.* I restored the more correct spelling; but in Cyprian’s editions and [Col. 1147B] manuscripts *redditus* is frequently written instead of *reditus*, and Baluze defends it.

CHAP. XIV.—*What wealthy matron.* Baluze’s text reads: *What wealthy matron in the Church of Christ.*

> I strongly believe that the words *in the Church of Christ*, which are absent from the old editions and from ten of our codices and five English codices, but were added by Manutius, ought not to occur in this passage. I did not, however, dare to expunge them, because I found them in eleven old copies.

Thus BALUZE. They also appear in my Tewater and Meerman manuscripts, together with one of the two Drury manuscripts. But since perhaps eleven of Baluze’s codices and five English codices omit them, and since they occur neither in the older Drury manuscript, nor in my other manuscript, nor in New College codex 1, I judged that these intrusive words, unknown to the oldest editions, should be omitted.

CHAP. XV.—*You believe that you celebrate the Lord’s Supper.* It must be held with Fell that the Eucharist, which is the Lord’s Supper, is meant here. Meanwhile, after I had long ago decided to remove the conjunction [Col. 1147C] *and* placed before *the Lord’s feast*, which is unknown to the first and Erasmian editions as well as to our manuscripts, I later observed that it was absent from three other manuscripts.

CHAP. XVI.—*Unfruitfulness.* The common reading is *unbelief*.

> “I came very close,” says Baluze, “to printing *unfruitfulness*, in accordance with the reading of the old editions, which twenty-two of our copies and eleven English copies confirm. Manutius printed *unbelief*. Pamelius thought otherwise.”

Thus Baluze. I scarcely doubt that the word *unfruitfulness* ought to be restored in this passage, since it is commonly joined with *barrenness*; for soil is often called *barren and unfruitful*. I have therefore restored this word, which was also approved by Rigault and which I saw in six manuscripts; but another of my codices reads *unbelief*.

*A widow and destitute, she is found active in good works.* Before Baluze, most printed editions presented: *a widow and destitute, a widow is found generous in good works*. I preferred the text of almost all my codices; only in New College codex 1 and both Drury manuscripts is the word *widow* repeated, while New College codex 2 presents *rich in good works*. There is, as rhetoricians say, a play on words between *inops* (“destitute”) and *opere* (“in work”). Erasmus’ edition does not know the word *generous*. [Col. 1147D]

*Christ calls that the gifts of God.* The word *that* appears to refer to the treasury mentioned above.

CHAP. XX.—*And now, my son, I command*, etc. In the margin of the more recent Drury manuscript the scribe wrote: “Tobit’s most wholesome commands to his sons.” Shortly afterward Fell, on the authority of manuscripts, substituted *into darkness* for the words *into Gehenna*; but the manuscripts themselves also vary here.

CHAP. XXI.—*Four-horse chariot.* The honors and insignia of the higher magistrates. “Curule,” says Festus, “means horses harnessed four abreast.” FELL.

CHAP. XXII.—*And unless an honorable expenditure follows.* Thus in the book *To Donatus*: “An altogether foolish and empty loss—to have wished to purchase, through enjoyment of a disappointing spectacle, that which the people would not accept and the magistrate would lose.” FELL.

[Col. 1148A] *And yours scarcely equal mine as they perish.* In number, as becomes clear immediately afterward.

CHAP. XXV.—*Equality.* So Erasmus and others after him. “I was unwilling to alter it, although almost all the old codices and the earlier editions read *equity*.” BALUZE. New College codex 2, my former Tewater manuscript, and the more recent Drury manuscript correctly present *equality*. To these books I also add the unpublished *Commentary on the Pauline Epistles* by Florus of Lyon in my possession, which I mentioned earlier. Immediately before, the author had written *equally*.

CHAP. XXVI.—*An excellent and divine thing.* The sentence would proceed better if one read: *is a thing*.

*The day of our return.* Earlier in this treatise Cyprian has “to make us return to paradise,” and near the end of *On Mortality*, “restores us to paradise and the kingdom,” p. 281. See also the end of the letter *To Demetrianus*. Pamelius was the first to adopt *repayment* from manuscripts and the corrections of Joannes Coster. That word does indeed appear in New College codex 2 and means the same as *recompense*, [Col. 1148B] which is certainly a Cyprianic word. Nevertheless, approving the old reading *return* with Rigault, I decided to restore it. It is found in six manuscripts cited by the Oxford editor and in four of my manuscripts; indeed, it had originally been written in the Tewater manuscript. Plautus recognizes the word *return*. And the words *return* and *persecution* placed here correspond to *summons* and *persecution*, which occurred above in the book *On Mortality*, § 13.

ON THE BOOK *ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY*

CHAP. II.—*He prowls around*, etc. From this passage the excellent conjecture of the distinguished Oberthür at the end of Tertullian’s book *On Prayer* is confirmed.

*He provokes the tongue to abuse.* The sentence would perhaps be more complete if *to insolence* were added from what follows, and if *violence* were written there in place of the word *insolence*. [Col. 1148C] Below one finds: “hands ready for the violence of murder.”

CHAP. III.—*Either deceptive snares or open threats.* I restored *either* before *deceptive*, which Baluze omitted, with New College codex 2 and both of my manuscripts supporting me, as do the editions before Baluze’s. I now add the Meerman manuscript and both Drury manuscripts.

CHAP. IV.—*While he imitates the devil whom he envies.* One of my codices—a parchment manuscript—presents *Zabulus*, not *diabolus*, and the word is written in that form in several editions of Cyprian. “*Zabolus* means *diabolus*, for the Aetolians said *za* (ζα) instead of *dia* (διά).” Gesner, *Thesaurus Linguae Latinae*, under the word.

CHAP. V.—*He blazed up into the hatred of persecution with the torches of envy.* *Hatred of persecution*, which is the reading of both manuscripts and printed books, means the hatred from which persecution arose.

*Patient with gentle mildness.* Although the word *gentle* was restored in place of *with gentleness* in the Benedictine edition, I have now preferred the other reading, supported by my manuscripts. [Col. 1148D]

*At the same time.* In one of my books *once* is written, and above the line “or *at the same time*.” Hence, therefore—as we have said more than once—arose the discrepancy found there in the manuscripts, some of which have *once*, others *at the same time*. BALUZE. I restored *at the same time*, which is the reading of the first edition and is supported by one of my manuscripts, although the ancients sometimes use *once* to mean “altogether” and “forever.” My former Tewater codex, written in 1396, has *to himself* in place of *at the same time*, and *each thing* in place of *each person*. Shortly afterward, at line 30, the author used *see* in the sense of “consider” or “reflect”; and in § 6 I restored from the older editions the words “who falsely claims to be a Christian,” whose order Manutius was the first to alter without reason to “who claims himself falsely to be a Christian.”

CHAP. XIII.—*And free from jealousy and envy.* The construction of *free from* with these genitives, first adopted by Manutius, is supported by both New College codices and my Tewater manuscript. I now add both Drury manuscripts and the Meerman manuscript, together with the unpublished commentary of Florus of Lyon on the Pauline Epistles. One of my books, however, has the alternative construction printed in editions preceding the Aldine: *free from jealousy and envy*. Immediately afterward I restored the words *as though to carnal men* in the apostle’s saying (*ῥήσει*), since they had perhaps fallen out of Baluze’s text. [Col. 1149A]

CHAP. XIV.—*The second man is from heaven.* Concerning this variant, consult editions of the New Testament. Consult them also below concerning the reading *let us bear* in place of *we shall bear*, since very many Greek manuscripts and Fathers have *φορήσωμεν* (“let us bear”) in place of *φορήσομεν* (“we shall bear”).

CHAP. XV.—*To be such.* Baluze’s edition has *oneself to be such*, not, as previously printed, *you to be such*. But I expunged *oneself*, which may have arisen from the preceding word, relying on the authority of two codices cited in the Oxford edition, New College MS 2, and two of my own. New College MS 1, however, has *you to be such*. [Col. 1149B] Now add both Drury manuscripts and the Meerman manuscript. Shortly after the word *to be strengthened*, my former Tewater manuscript has *and to be adorned*.

CHAP. XVI.—*Saving operation.* That is, almsgiving effectual for eternal salvation. The same manner of speaking already occurs near the end of the book *On Works and Almsgiving*.

CHAP. XVII.—*You will labor.* The first edition and one of my codices prefer *you labor*, a reading that I formerly approved, but less correctly. Health is to be promoted when it needs to become stronger.

*If you cannot follow.* The common reading is: *But if you cannot follow them*. [Col. 1150A] I have restored the reading of the older editions, approved by Rigault and supported by five codices cited in the Oxford edition, both New College codices, and the Tewater manuscript. I now add the very old Meerman codex and the older of the two Drury manuscripts. This clause, however, is absent from the other Drury manuscript and from one further manuscript.

CHAP. XVIII.—*To which Cain does not return.* Baluze adopted into his edition *which Cain does not enter*, and says that he considers this reading, found in three old books, to be the best, while the alternative *returns* is false. For Cain, who was born after his parents had been expelled from paradise, could not be said to have returned to paradise, since he had never been there. He therefore adds that he had no hesitation in preferring the reading of these three books. Yet I do not think this argument has such force that the verb *enters* should be substituted for the formerly received reading, which is confirmed by almost all the manuscripts. Of the codices I used, only New College MS 2 [Col. 1150B] and the more recent Drury manuscript present *enters*. Cyprian says here that Cain does not return to paradise, the ancient possession of his parents; indeed, the mind is also commonly said to “return to God.” Compare the end of the treatise *On Works and Almsgiving*, where one finds “us returning to paradise,” and the note on that passage.

*By heavenly birth and divine law.* The word *heavenly* is recognized neither by the ten manuscripts mentioned in the Oxford edition nor by six of the seven that I used in editing these treatises; the entire clause is lacking in the Meerman manuscript. Above, however, one finds the same words, “by heavenly birth.”

[Col. 1149]

ST. CYPRIAN’S EXHORTATION TO REPENTANCE. (C, G, S)

NOTICE

[Col. 1149B] The reader should remember how, a little above, while we were preparing the [Col. 1149C] first appendix, we regretted that, although searching diligently here and there, we had been unable to find J. C. Trombelli’s unpublished materials in sufficiently good time for them to be published, most appropriately inserted in their proper place; yet we did not despair that by favorable providence we might eventually come upon them. Now that hope has not disappointed us. Behold, before this volume was completed, this last work of St. Cyprian, so long undiscovered, came into our hands [Col. 1150B] in the excellent library of the Seminary of Saint-Sulpice, [Col. 1150C] through the gracious courtesy and benevolence of its devout administrators. Therefore, good reader, with due thanks rendered, use and enjoy both this work and Trombelli’s outstanding discussions upon it.

PREFACE OF JOANNES CHRYSOSTOMUS TROMBELLI

[Col. 1149D] I. Although I examined our codices carefully and with the greatest diligence, especially those containing the letters and shorter works of ancient authors—for precious remains of ancient writers often lie hidden in them, remains whose collection and publication are of the greatest importance to the republic of letters—nevertheless, when I came to those containing Cyprian’s writings, I increased my diligence, hoping that what had happened to Erasmus, Manutius, [Col. 1150D] and Morel would also happen to me. When they carefully and meticulously went through the codices of Cyprian, they discovered certain things that had escaped earlier printers but that, by reason of their excellence, seemed to demand that they be brought to light.

My expectation did not wholly disappoint me. Of the two Cyprian codices we possess, one is more extensive than the other, so much so that it contains almost all Cyprian’s letters [Col. 1151A] and shorter works. While I was most carefully examining these and comparing them with the printed texts, there presented itself to me a little book that I sought in vain among the published works. In the codex in question it bears the title: “Cyprian’s Exhortation concerning Repentance”—a title, as I shall show below, assigned to it by the copyist.

I shall explain presently how great the excellence and usefulness of this little work are. I certainly dare to affirm boldly that it has undeservedly remained hidden until now. For although it contains no historical monument, displays no eloquence, and also lacks arguments drawn from reason or from the authority of the ancients, but relies on Scripture alone, set forth plainly and without any ornament, it is not therefore to be despised. Otherwise one would necessarily have to despise those excellent [Col. 1151B] books of Cyprian that contain the *Testimonies to Quirinus*. For in them, without any display of eloquence or verbal ornament, without any support from arguments or the ancients, errors are combated and the doctrines of our faith are established by Scripture alone.

II. The author whose little work I publish here adopted the same design. He was certainly an ancient and highly credible writer: either Cyprian himself, that is, or, if you prefer, another unknown author nevertheless contemporary with Cyprian, following Cyprian’s footsteps and method. The manner of disputation he employs and of citing testimonies from Scripture appears to point to Cyprian, since it is very similar to that which Cyprian observed in the book of *Testimonies*. This conjecture is also favored by Cyprian’s name prefixed to the little work in the codex; for although copyists sometimes erred in this matter, they nevertheless often identified the true authors of books. [Col. 1151C]

Yet because the author of our little work cites a version of Scripture very different from that used by Cyprian, and because none of the ancient writers attributed this treatise to Cyprian, I remain uncertain to whom I should ascribe it. I know indeed that these latter arguments are by no means unanswerable. The ancients sometimes followed one translation of Scripture, sometimes another. We possess so many and such evident proofs of this that no one now doubts it.

> **Note [Col. 1151D].** I offer a single example, but a clear one. Augustine, Sermon 20, no. 3, cites verse 22 of Ezekiel 18 as follows: “On whatever day the wicked man turns back and practices justice, I shall forget the years of his wickedness.” But in Sermon 39, no. 1, he cites it in this form: “On the day you turn back, God forgets your former evils.” In Sermon 82, *On the Words of the Gospel*, Matthew 18, no. 14, he again adduces it, though with a slight difference, as follows: “On whatever day the wicked man turns back from his iniquities and practices justice, I shall forget all his iniquities.” Elsewhere too, when citing the same verse, he presents it with some variation: “He knocks and cries out,” Augustine says in no. 10 of Sermon 87, *On the Words of Matthew 20*, “through the prophet Ezekiel: ‘On whatever day a man turns back from his most evil way, I shall forget all his iniquities.’”

Copyists too arrogated to themselves no slight license and often substituted the translation they preferred for the translation used by [Col. 1151D] the author they were copying.

[Col. 1152A] III. That none of the ancient writers whose works we now possess cites this little book is not surprising. For the error that this treatise refutes disappeared not long after Cyprian’s time; consequently, the occasion for citing the treatise also ceased to exist. Moreover, how do we know that other ancient writers whose books we lack did not cite it? The difficulty drawn from the silence of the ancients is therefore slight. Yet although, as I have said, I acknowledge that these arguments can be answered, they are nevertheless probable.

IV. Whoever composed this little book, it is highly probable that he was a contemporary of Cyprian, or at least was not far removed from his period, and that he was thoroughly versed in the reading of Scripture. Does not the translation of Scripture that he follows, together with the discipline he attempts to establish, show him to have been Cyprian’s contemporary, or at least not far removed [Col. 1152B] from Cyprian’s period? This writer indicates clearly enough that those who had lapsed were indeed to be received into the Church, and that persons guilty of any crimes whatsoever were by no means to be barred from the hope of pardon, provided that they submitted themselves to canonical penance. Since this question was especially prominent in Cyprian’s time, it indicates clearly enough the period in which this book was written.

V. Moreover, who could deny that he was thoroughly versed in the reading of Scripture after seeing him range through so many books of Scripture and select from them passages that wonderfully confirm the catholic doctrine and support the practice that Cyprian judged should be maintained in the Church?

[Col. 1152C] VI. I consider what I have said about Cyprian as the author of this little book to be only highly probable, and I have not ventured to establish anything certain on the matter, because I know that there have long existed certain writers—

> **Note [Col. 1152C–D].** Here is what Baluze notes concerning Cyprian’s books of *Testimonies*: “If there are any passages in the works of St. Cyprian about which it cannot be declared with certainty that they are his, this can be asserted especially of the books of *Testimonies to Quirinus*. For several codices contain more than the common editions, others less.” But why are quite a few codices so extensive? Is it not because they were enlarged through the labors of later teachers? I said “even among Latin writers”; for among the Greeks John of Damascus excelled in this kind of writing, publishing several books on a similar subject, which he called *Parallels*, or, if you prefer, *Selections*.

—even among the Latins who imitated Cyprian in this kind of writing. Among their number that Pelagius was outstanding,

> **Note [Col. 1152D].** “A work of almost the same subject as this work of Cyprian is the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, which is commonly attributed to Prosper.” Baluze, note 1 on the books of St. Cyprian’s *Testimonies*.

> **Note [Col. 1152D].** See what Vossius relates “concerning the writings of Pelagius” in *Historia Pelagiana*, book I, chap. 4, and Cave in his *Historia Litteraria*, under Pelagius, at the year 405, p. 383, vol. I, Basel edition of 1741.

but he afterward deprived himself of the praise he had acquired elsewhere by contending against divine grace. Since, moreover, things that are highly probable may fittingly be accepted, who will hold it against me if henceforth, whenever discussion arises concerning the author of this little work—and it will arise often—I call him Cyprian?

[Col. 1153A] VII. In my judgment, the usefulness of this little work is by no means slight. Is not a work exceedingly useful in which a very common practice of the Church stands out—namely, that whenever an error arose, it was immediately checked by adducing numerous testimonies from Scripture—and which contains so large a portion of the most ancient version? But if you believe that the sacred books are cited here in the order in which the manuscripts of those times were arranged, you immediately have another advantage [Col. 1154A] in it. There is certainly no need to commend this advantage here in many words; yet it is assuredly not insignificant. It also has this benefit: in citing the sacred Scriptures, it adduces the book of Ecclesiasticus, thereby showing through its own example how highly that book—which Protestants now esteem very little—was valued in the earliest centuries of the Church. But enough thus far concerning the author and excellence of the little work. Here now is the work itself:

## THE EXHORTATION OF ST. CYPRIAN ON REPENTANCE BEGINS
