[Note: [Col. 1153D] Perhaps: *An Exhortation to Repentance*.]

[Col. 1153]

[Col. 1153B] **That through repentance all sins can be forgiven to one who has turned to God with his whole heart.**

In Psalm eighty-eight (v. 31): If his sons forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but I will not scatter my mercy away from them.

Likewise in Isaiah (30:15): Thus says the Holy Lord of Israel: When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been.

Likewise there (30:1): Woe, children of desertion, says the Lord. You have formed a plan not through me, and made my covenant not through my spirit, adding sin upon sin.

Likewise in Jeremiah (2:25): Turn [Note: [Col. 1153D] *Turn*, as I think.] your foot away from the rough road, and your face from thirst. But she [Col. 1153C] said: I shall be strengthened; I will it, because she loved strangers and went after them.

Likewise in Isaiah (31:6): Turn back, because you [Note: [Col. 1153D] *Who*, as I think.] devise a lofty and wicked thought.

Likewise there (43:25): I am, I am he who blots out your injustices, and I will not remember them. But do you remember, and let us be judged together; state your injustices first.

Likewise there (55:6): Seek God, and when you have found him, call upon him. But when he has drawn near to you, let the impious man forsake his ways and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him turn to the Lord; and mercy will be prepared for him, because he does not forgive your sins only a little.

Likewise there (44:1): Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, because you are my servant. I have called you my servant; and you, Israel, do not forget me. For behold, I have wiped away like . . . . . . . your injustices, and like rain your sins. Turn [Col. 1153D] to me, and I will redeem you.

Likewise there (46:8): Keep these things in mind and groan. Repent, you who have been led astray; turn to me in your heart, and keep former ages in mind, because I am God.

Likewise there (54:8): For a brief time I forsook you, and with great mercy I will have mercy upon you. In a brief fury [Col. 1154B] I turned my face away from you; in everlasting mercy I will have mercy upon you.

Likewise there (57:15): Thus said the Most High, dwelling in the heights, eternally holy among the holy; his name is the Lord, the Most High resting among the holy and giving equanimity to the fainthearted, and giving life to those afflicted in heart. I am not angry with you forever, nor will I exact vengeance upon you in every respect; for the spirit will go forth from me, and I have made every breath. And because of a slight sin I grieved him, and I turned my face away from him; and he became contemptible and departed sorrowfully upon his ways. I saw his ways and healed him; I consoled him and gave him true consolation, and peace upon peace to those far away and those nearby. And the Lord said: I have healed them; but the unjust, like a troubled sea, will be tossed about and [Col. 1154C] cannot rest. There is no rejoicing for the impious, says the Lord.

Likewise in Jeremiah (2:32): Will a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin the band across her breast? But my people have forgotten me for days [Note: [Col. 1154D] I think *in days* should be read.] beyond number.

Likewise there (18:7): In sum, I shall speak against a nation or against a kingdom, either to remove them and destroy them. And if that nation turns from its evils, I shall repent of the evils which [Note: [Col. 1154D] *Which*.] I planned to do to them. And in sum, I shall speak concerning a nation or kingdom, to rebuild and plant it; and they will do evil before me, so that they do not hear my voice, and I shall repent of the good things which I said I would do for them.

Likewise there (3:12): Return to me, dwelling-place of Israel, says the Lord, and I shall not set my face firmly against you, because I am merciful, says the Lord, and [Col. 1154D] I shall not be angry with you forever.

Likewise there (3:14): Turn back, children who have departed, says the Lord, because I will rule over you; and I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you into Zion. And I shall give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you, shepherding with discipline.

Likewise there (3:22): Turn back, children who are turning back, and I will heal your brokenness.

[Col. 1155A] Likewise there (4:14): Wash your heart clean of wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be healed. How long will the thoughts of your sorrows remain within you?

Likewise there (8:4): Thus says the Lord: Does one who falls not rise again, or will one who turns away not turn back? For this people has turned away from a wicked vision; they have persisted in their presumption and refused to turn back.

Likewise there (8:6): There is no man repenting of his wickedness and saying, “What have I done?” He who runs has failed in his course, like a horse urging itself on with its neighing.

Likewise there (18:11): Let each person, therefore, turn away from his evil way, and improve your pursuits. And they said: We shall be strengthened, because we shall go after your [Note: [Col. 1155D] *Our*, as I think.] inventions, and each of us will do the evils that please his own heart.

Likewise there (Lam. 2:18): Pour out tears like a torrent [Col. 1155B] day and night. Give yourself no rest; let the pupil of your eye not be silent.

Likewise there (Lam. 3:40): Let us examine our ways and turn to the Lord. Let us cleanse our hearts together with our hands, and look to the Lord who dwells in heaven. We have sinned and provoked you, and you have not been appeased.

Likewise there (3:6): And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what the dwelling-place of the house [Note: [Col. 1155D] Delete the words *voice of the house*.] of Israel has done to me? She went upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and fornicated there. And I said: After she had committed all these fornications, “Turn to me”; yet she did not return.

Likewise there (Lam. 3:31): The Lord will not reject forever; and when he has humbled, he will have mercy according to [Col. 1155C] the multitude of his mercy, because he will not humble from his whole heart, nor reject the children of men.

Likewise in Ezekiel (33:12): And the righteous man will not be able to be saved on the day of sin. When I say to the righteous man, “You shall surely live,” but he trusts [Note: [Col. 1155D] *If he trusts*, as I think.] in his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered; in the iniquity he committed, in that he will die. And when I say to the impious man, “You shall surely die,” and he turns away from his sin and performs justice and judgment, and restores the pledge to his debtor, and returns what he has seized, and walks in the precepts of life so as not to act unjustly, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the sins he committed will be held against him, because he performed judgment and justice; in these he will live.

Likewise there (17:24): I am the Lord, for I humble [Col. 1155D] the tall tree and exalt the lowly tree; I dry up the green tree and make the dry tree live again.

Likewise there (33:10): And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Just as you have spoken, saying, “Our errors and our iniquities are upon us, and in them we waste away; how then shall we live?” say to them: As I live, says the Lord, do I desire the death of the impious man? Only let him turn away from his way, and he will live.

Likewise there (36:36): I, the Lord, have rebuilt what was demolished and replanted what was laid waste.

Likewise there (18:21): And if the unjust man turns away from [Col. 1156A] all the injustices he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and performs judgment and justice and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the offenses he committed will be remembered; in the righteousness he has performed, he will live. Do I willfully desire the death of the unjust man, says Adonai the Lord, rather than that he should turn away from his evil way and live?

Likewise there (18:30): Turn back and turn yourselves away from all your acts of impiety, and they will not become a punishment for you. Cast away from yourselves all your injustices, by which you have acted impiously against me, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why should you die, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of one who is dying, says Adonai the Lord.

Likewise in Daniel (4:31): And after the completion of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes to heaven; and [Col. 1156B] my understanding returned to me, and I praised the Most High, blessed the King of heaven, and praised him who lives forever, because his power is eternal, his kingdom endures from generation to generation, and all who dwell upon the earth are nothing.

Likewise in Micah (7:1ff.): Woe is me, my soul, because truth has perished from the earth, and among all there is no one who corrects; they all judge with bloodshed. Each one afflicts his neighbor with affliction; they prepare their hands for evil.

Likewise there (7:8): Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; rather, I shall rise again. For even if I sit in darkness, the Lord will shine upon me. I shall endure the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him, until he himself vindicates my cause.

Likewise in Zephaniah (2:1): Assemble and pray, undisciplined nation, before you become like [Col. 1156C] a passing flower, before the Lord’s anger comes upon you, before the day of the Lord’s fury comes upon you. Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth; practice judgment, seek justice, and seek meekness, and answer him, that you may be protected on the day of the Lord’s anger.

Likewise in Zechariah (1:3): Turn to me, and I shall turn to you.

Likewise in Hosea (14:2): Turn, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have been weakened by your injustices. Take many with you, and turn to the Lord your God; say to him in adoration: You are able to forgive our sins, so that you do not receive iniquity, but receive good things.

Likewise in Ecclesiasticus (17:23): Turn to the Lord [Col. 1156D] and abandon your sins; hate abomination exceedingly, acknowledge the just ordinances and judgments of God, stand in the allotted place of propitiation before the Most High, and go to the portion of the age with the living and with those who offer confession. Do not linger in the error of the impious. From the dead, as from one who is nothing, confession perishes. While alive and healthy, you will confess to God and glory in his acts of compassion, because great is God’s mercy and his propitiation toward those who turn to him.

Likewise there (20:4): How good it is for an upright heart to manifest repentance! For thus you will escape deliberate sin.

Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles (8:19): But Peter said to him: Let your money perish with you, because you think that you can obtain the grace of God through money. You have neither part nor lot in this faith, because your heart [Col. 1157A] is not right before the Lord. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord, in case the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the bond of iniquity and the bitterness of gall.

Likewise in the Second Epistle of blessed Paul [Note: [Col. 1157B] *Blessed*, unless we are mistaken.] to the Corinthians (7:10): For sorrow that is according to God produces a steadfast repentance leading to salvation; but the sorrow of the world produces death.

Likewise there, on this very matter (2:10): But if you have forgiven anyone anything, so have I. For whatever I have forgiven, I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.

Likewise there (12:20): But I fear that perhaps, when I come to you, God may humble me among you once again, and I may mourn many of those who sinned before and have not [Col. 1157B] repented of the fornication and shamelessness they committed.

Likewise there (13:2): I foretold and now foretell, as though seated there when present, and now while absent, to those who sinned before and to all the rest, that if I come again, I will not spare them.

Likewise in the Second Epistle to Timothy (2:21): Avoid profane novelties of words, for they make great progress toward impiety; their discourse spreads like a cancer. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth, [Col. 1158A] saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they have overturned the faith of some. But the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: God has known those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from all iniquity. Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware, some indeed for honor and others for dishonor. If anyone, therefore, has corrected [Note: [Col. 1158B] The Vulgate, which the copyist otherwise follows in this passage, has *cleansed*.] himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. But flee youthful desires. Pursue justice, faith, charity, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, able to teach, patient, and correcting [Col. 1158B] with modesty those who resist, in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance unto knowledge of the truth, and they recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will.

Likewise in the Apocalypse (2:5): Remember whence you have fallen, and repent; otherwise, I shall come to you quickly and remove the lampstand from its place.

## ON THE TITLE AND AIM, OR SUBJECT, OF THE PRECEDING LITTLE WORK

[Col. 1157]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1157C]

I. Since the custom has prevailed that books of the ancients now being published should be elucidated by the person who brings them to light, I comply with that custom. First I shall discuss the title of the preceding little work and the subject pursued in it by its author; then I shall append certain notes to that work, explaining passages which have appeared somewhat obscure to some and removing doubts that might creep into the reader’s mind.

II. Yet there is something in the title itself that may cause difficulty for students little accustomed to reading manuscripts. They might readily suppose that the words *Exhortation on Repentance* were either prefixed to the published work by Cyprian himself or at least possess great antiquity and authority. Then, indeed, they will be troubled by the syntax of those words, which departs markedly from Latin usage.

[Col. 1158C] III. But this difficulty is very slight, for the error must be assigned to the copyist. Those who copied books were accustomed, if they happened to find the books themselves without titles, to supply titles of their own devising. They also often altered old titles of which they did not approve at all, substituting new ones at pleasure. For this reason, the titles prefixed to books vary greatly among manuscripts and are sometimes utterly worthless and exceedingly remote from the author’s intention.

IV. Accordingly, the title of this little work appears to be the one that immediately follows, namely: “That through repentance all sins can be forgiven to one who has turned to God with his whole heart.” For this is the subject that this writer, whoever he was, undertook to discuss and prove by the authority of Scripture. Nor is this surprising. For, to confine myself to Cyprian, a not dissimilar title is prefixed to the little work that we customarily entitle *On the Vanity of Idols*, [Col. 1159A] namely: “That idols are not gods, and that through Christ salvation has been given to believers.” Nor is the title prefixed to the books of *Testimonies* very different.

V. But, you will say, a title of this kind does not accord very well with some of the testimonies cited in the same little work, especially numbers 12 and 43. By what reasoning, I ask, will you be able to derive the proposition, “Through repentance sins can be forgiven to one who turns to God with his whole heart,” from the statement that “a bride cannot forget her adornment, nor a virgin the band across her breast, yet the people forgot God for very many years”? Again, by what reasoning will you be able to derive the same thesis from the following teaching of the apostle Paul? “I foretold and now foretell, as though seated there [Col. 1159B] when present, and now while absent, to those who sinned before and to all the rest, that if I come again, I will not spare them.”

VI. This difficulty appears by no means slight. Yet you will readily resolve it if you observe that the ancient Fathers who taught that all crimes could be forgiven through repentance were not speaking of just any sort of repentance, but of the repentance required by the Church in reliance upon ancient discipline and custom. Thus they warned that three errors must be avoided: the error constructed by the cruelty and obstinacy of the Novatians against the Church’s authority—namely, their denial that graver sins could be forgiven; likewise, the error which the excessive severity of certain Catholics sought to establish—namely, that although they acknowledged that all crimes were indeed remissible, they nevertheless denied that remission and pardon should be granted to those who had fallen into graver sins, [Col. 1159C] and repelled them from the Church and from hope of pardon; finally, the error which the excessive indulgence and leniency of others sought to introduce. These admitted the lapsed into the Church and received them into communion while requiring no repentance from them, or at least only the slightest, certainly not that demanded by ecclesiastical custom and by the steadfastness of the wiser and more eminent bishops.

VII. It is beyond doubt that the Novatians, after fomenting a schism and forming a sect separated from Catholic communion, taught that certain sins were unforgivable; and Cyprian indeed points out this error in Epistle LII [Note: [Col. 1159D] P. 157; consult his words at passage VIII.]. But it is plainly refuted by the author of the book *To Novatian the Heretic*, a contemporary of Cyprian, [Col. 1159D] from which we shall often quote passages; it is also refuted by Pacianus, whom we shall sometimes cite below.

VIII. Nor was I rash in saying that in Cyprian’s age some were excessively severe—to such a degree, namely, that they altogether denied pardon and ecclesiastical communion to criminals—while others, by contrast, were so indulgent that they immediately received into the Church those stained by the gravest crimes and did not require from them those salutary afflictions which the Church had prescribed. For, as we learn from Cyprian’s books, some, as I have already said, were wholly unwilling to receive those guilty of grave crimes into repentance [Note: [Col. 1159D] “Indeed, among our predecessors certain [Col. 1160C] of these bishops in our province did not think peace should be granted to adulterers, and altogether closed the place of repentance against acts of adultery” (*Epistle* LII, p. 155). See Baluzius’s notes 59 and 62 on this epistle. That severity was revived by a certain Januarius, who refused to admit to repentance a monk guilty of intercourse with a consecrated virgin. He was therefore reproved by Bacharius, a very learned man, who judged that the same monk should be received into repentance. See the works of Bacharius, edited by Franciscus Florius, p. 36.], nor to admit into the Church [Col. 1160A] those who had at some time defected from it without schism, whether by means of certificates or in some other way [Note: [Col. 1160D] “And therefore it was resolved, dearest brother, after the cases of each had been examined, that for the present those who had obtained certificates should be admitted, and that those who had sacrificed should be aided when near death. . . . Nor should you think, dearest brother, that the courage of the brethren is thereby diminished or martyrdoms cease, because repentance has been relaxed for the lapsed and a hope of peace offered to the penitent” (*Epistle* LII, to Antonianus, concerning Cornelius and Novatian, pp. 153–154).]. Others, by contrast, during the very heat of persecution, before repentance had been completed and without the bishop’s consent, very readily admitted the lapsed to communion in the sacraments [Note: [Col. 1160D] See *Epistle* IX, p. 47, and *Epistle* XII, p. 57; and again *Epistle* LII, p. 140: “Finally, when the presbyters and deacons had written to me about certain persons, saying that they were immoderate and were urgently pressing to be received into communion, etc.”]. Consequently, some, although stained by very grave crimes, wished pardon to be granted them so promptly and readily that they demanded the immediate remission, without any canonical repentance—in a manner far different from that prescribed by the ancient canons and ecclesiastical custom—of whatever sins they had previously committed, not even excepting the crime of schism and apostasy. To obtain pardon more promptly and surely, they fled for recourse to confessors and martyrs, so that by their letters of recommendation—as by a kind of aid and, if we wish so to speak, [Col. 1160B] “a supplement to the repentance owed by them”—they might be admitted to the congregation of the faithful and to ecclesiastical communion [Note: [Col. 1160D] This is stated most plainly in Cyprian’s *Epistle* LV to Cornelius, especially in these words: “But when I read the other letter of yours, brother, which you appended to the first, I was sufficiently astonished when I observed that you had been somewhat disturbed by the threats and terrors of those who had come to you, since, as you wrote, they had assailed you with utter desperation, threatening that if you did not accept the letters they had brought, they would read them publicly and utter many foul and disgraceful things worthy of their own mouths.”]. But if the bishops did not receive them immediately and required them to submit to the ancient laws of repentance, those petitioners sometimes reached such audacity that they threatened to read those same letters before the people, from whom they would readily obtain the communion and pardon which the bishops had been unwilling to impart of their own accord [Note: [Col. 1160D] See the preceding note.]. In Cyprian’s fifty-fifth epistle we have such clear examples of this matter that we certainly cannot doubt it. I nevertheless indicate at the foot of the page some passages from that epistle, perhaps the more important ones; the reader himself will be able to consult the others [Note: [Col. 1160D] “But when I read, etc.” Recall the preceding notes. “And those sacrilegious men against God, rash in impious fury against God’s priests, withdrawing from the Church and taking up parricidal arms against the Church, [Col. 1161B] labor to complete their work by the devil’s malice, lest divine clemency heal the wounded in his Church. By the deceit of their lies they corrupt the repentance of the wretched, lest satisfaction be made to an indignant God, lest one who formerly blushed or feared to be a Christian should afterward seek Christ his Lord, and lest one who had withdrawn from the Church should return to it. They strive to prevent offenses from being redeemed through just acts of satisfaction and lamentations, and wounds from being washed with tears. . . . What honor, then, is given to God when God’s majesty and judgment are so despised that, although he says he is indignant and angry with those who sacrifice, and threatens eternal punishments and perpetual torments, sacrilegious men put forward [Col. 1161C] and declare that God’s anger should not be considered, that the Lord’s judgment should not be feared, that one should not knock at the Church of Christ; but that, once repentance has been removed and no confession (*exomologesis*) of the crime made, bishops despised and trampled underfoot, peace should be proclaimed by presbyters with deceitful words, and that, lest the lapsed rise or those placed outside return to the Church, communion should be offered to those not in communion. Nor was it enough for them to have withdrawn from the Gospel, to have taken away from the lapsed the hope of satisfaction and repentance, and to have removed from every sense and fruit of repentance those entangled in frauds, stained by adulteries, or polluted by the deadly contagion of sacrifices, so that they would not pray to God or make confession (*exomologesis*) of their crimes in the Church” (pp. 181–182). . . . “But if there are any who think they can return to the Church not by prayers but by threats, or suppose they can make an entrance for themselves not by lamentations and acts of satisfaction but by terrors, let them know for certain that the Lord’s Church stands closed against such persons, and that the unconquered and strong camp of Christ, [Col. 1161D] protected and fortified by the Lord, does not yield to threats. A priest of God who holds fast to the Gospel and keeps Christ’s precepts can be killed; he cannot be conquered. Zechariah, God’s high priest, furnishes and supplies us with examples of courage and faith: when he could not be terrified by threats and stoning, he was killed in God’s temple, crying out and repeatedly saying what we too cry out and say against heretics: ‘Thus says the Lord’ (2 Chron. 24): ‘You have forsaken the ways of the Lord, and the Lord will forsake you.’ For because a few rash and wicked men forsake the heavenly and saving ways of the Lord and, by not doing holy things, are forsaken by the Holy Spirit, we must not therefore be forgetful of divine tradition, so as to judge the crimes of raging men greater than the judgments of priests, or to suppose that human efforts have more power to attack than divine protection has strength to defend” (p. 184).].

[Col. 1161A] Both extremes displeased Cyprian. Most people embraced his position while he was still alive [Note: [Col. 1162D] See *Epistle* LIV, written in the name of many bishops.], and others subsequently followed it, especially Pacianus, who frequently cites Cyprian. Cyprian vigorously refuted excessive leniency, both elsewhere and certainly in *Epistle* LV, in which, among many other things, there are these extensive passages worthy of reading:

“For certain putrid members must not be gathered in such a way that those which are whole and sound are wounded; nor is that shepherd useful or prudent who so mingles diseased and infected sheep with the flock that he contaminates the entire flock by the affliction of the clinging evil. Do not look to their number, for one who fears God is better than a thousand impious sons, as the Lord spoke through the prophet, [Col. 1161B] saying: ‘Son, do not rejoice in impious sons if they are multiplied for you, when the fear of God is not in them’ (Ecclus. 16). O if only you could, dearest brother, [Col. 1162A] be present here with us when these insignificant and perverse men return from schism! You would see how much labor it costs me to persuade our brothers to patience, so that, once their anguish of mind is soothed, they may consent to receive and treat the wicked. For just as they rejoice and are glad when those who can be tolerated and are less blameworthy return, so by contrast they murmur and resist whenever the incorrigible and insolent—men stained either by adulteries or by sacrifices, and after these things still arrogant besides—return to the Church in such a state that they corrupt the good dispositions within” (p. 183).

Add what he discusses at length in the book *On the Lapsed* against this excessive and harmful leniency: “The physician is unskilled, etc.” (p. 377); “This leniency does not grant peace but takes it away, etc.” (p. 378). [Col. 1162B] And in this passage he reproves those martyrs who, through letters of recommendation, pressed too vehemently for the Church to receive persons guilty of crimes without repentance: “He alone can grant pardon for sins committed against himself who bore our sins, etc.”

Elsewhere, however, he earnestly entreats the same martyrs and confessors to be more cautious in granting letters of recommendation [Note: [Col. 1162D] *Epistle* X, to the Martyrs, etc., p. 51.], for not a few persons guilty of monstrous crimes abused these letters in order to be received into the Church without repentance.

IX. He was likewise displeased by the utmost severity, through which those who had fallen into crimes might easily be driven to despair and persist in impiety. He therefore judged that severity should be tempered by leniency, so that the opportunity for repentance would be closed to no one, [Col. 1162C] and consequently that everyone, although previously stained by atrocious crimes, could indeed be received, provided that they underwent the repentance imposed by the bishop. Consult the passages I cited just above. Indeed, the words I indicated from the book *On the Lapsed* deserve to be transcribed here in full:

“The physician is unskilled who handles the swollen hollows of wounds with a sparing hand, and, by preserving the poison enclosed in the deep recesses of the inward parts, aggravates it. The wound must be opened and cut, and, once the decayed parts have been amputated, treated with a stronger remedy. Though the impatient sick man cry aloud and shout and complain through his pain, afterward he will give thanks when he experiences health. For there has arisen, dearest brothers, a new kind of disaster; and as though the tempest [Col. 1162D] of persecution had raged too little, there has been added to the sum, under the title of mercy, a deceptive evil and flattering destruction. Contrary to the vigor of the Gospel, contrary to the law of the Lord and God, through the rashness of certain persons an ineffectual communion and false peace are granted to the incautious, dangerous to those who give them and of no benefit to those who receive. . . .” (p. 377).

“This leniency does not grant peace but takes it away; it does not bestow communion but obstructs the way to salvation. This is another persecution and another temptation, through which the subtle enemy, by concealed devastation, assails those who are still fallen: so that lamentation may cease, [Col. 1163A] grief fall silent, the memory of the offense disappear, the groaning over sins be suppressed, the weeping of the eyes be stayed, and the gravely offended Lord not be entreated by long and full repentance, although it is written: ‘Remember whence you have fallen, and repent.’ Let no one delude himself; let no one deceive himself” (p. 378).

But if they did not refuse to repent and underwent the penalties he himself prescribed, he showed himself entirely ready to exercise the greatest possible leniency toward them. We have a clear proof of this leniency in *Epistle* XII, which I beg the reader to read (p. 55).

X. Hence, concerning the utterly wicked followers of Felicissimus—whose monstrous crimes, execrable life, schism, and defection from the Church he had described [Col. 1163B] immediately before—he does not hesitate to pronounce as follows (*Epistle* LV, p. 84):

“If they wish to undergo our judgment, let them come. Finally, if any excuse and defense can be made for them, let us see what sense of satisfaction they possess and what fruit of repentance they bring. The Church here is closed to no one, nor is the bishop denied to anyone. Our repentance, leniency, and humanity are available to those who come. I desire all to return to the Church; I desire all our fellow soldiers to be enclosed within Christ’s camp and the dwelling-places of God the Father. I forgive everything; I overlook much, from the desire and purpose of gathering the brotherhood together. Even those offenses committed against God I do not examine with the full rigor of religious judgment. By forgiving offenses more than I ought, I almost offend myself. With ready and complete love I embrace those who return in repentance, confessing their sin through humble and sincere satisfaction.” [Col. 1163C]

XI. I judge that what I have reported is sufficiently suited to what I proposed to demonstrate. But if you still desire other testimonies from the same Cyprian on this matter, consult what he himself teaches in the book *On the Lapsed* and in *Epistle* LV. Moreover, he encompasses both extremes and explains his own position most plainly in *Epistle* LII (p. 155), in these words: “But I marvel that certain men are so obstinate, etc.” We shall cite these words in the notes on the final testimony, that is, Apocalypse 2:5.

XII. Therefore, in order both to censure the error and schism of the Novatians and to vindicate from reproach his own purpose and the discipline he had introduced into the Church, either Cyprian [Col. 1163D] himself composed this little work, or certainly another person contending for Cyprian’s position did so, gathering passages that could subsequently be distributed, if you wish, into three arguments or heads of discussion: the first would condemn the schism and errors of the Novatians; the second would refute the opinion of those who, although acknowledging that all crimes fell under the Church’s authority, nevertheless barred criminals from the Church and from undertaking repentance; the third would approve the discipline proposed by Cyprian. In the notes on them we shall show that the two testimonies we mentioned are fittingly included under one of these heads. I suspect, moreover, that this little work was composed with the intention that it be appended to the other parts of the third book of the *Testimonies*.

[Col. 1164A] But now at last let us provide the notes we promised.

## We Append Certain Notes to the Passages of Scripture Cited in the Preceding Little Work

### CHAPTER II

I would not wish the reader to suppose that only those passages of Scripture contained in this little work concern repentance. You will find others, and not a few, in Bacharius’s book sent to Januarius, and also in the *Parallels* of John Damascene (letter μ, title III, περὶ μετανοίας, “On Repentance,” etc.), in the chapter which I cite at the foot of the page. If you compare that chapter with this little work, the exercise will be most pleasant and highly useful. Accordingly, the passages enumerated here are either some portion of a larger [Col. 1164B] book which contained many more, or, if you prefer, they are selected passages as being more suitable than the rest—not, indeed, for establishing the usefulness and necessity of repentance considered generally, but for establishing the usefulness and necessity of that kind of repentance which I discussed in sections 6, 7, and the subsequent sections of the preceding chapter. Recall, therefore, what we taught in those sections.

I now come to the passage which first presents itself in this little work, and which reads as follows:

## I

**If his children forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes; but I will not withdraw my mercy from them** (Ps. 88:31).

[Col. 1164C] I once thought that this passage had been altered through a certain license on the part of a copyist, and that the Vulgate rendering had been substituted for the ancient one—something I have often observed to have happened in manuscripts. But afterward I remained uncertain when I saw the same passage cited in almost the same form in the book of Bacharius [Note: [Col. 1164D] No. 22, p. 115, in the edition of François Florio.] as it is presented in this little work. Either, therefore, both copyists arrogated the same license to themselves, or, more probably, even in ancient times there existed another translation of this passage which rendered it in the manner in which the Vulgate now renders it.

Moreover, this passage from Psalm 88 appears as follows in that very ancient little book [Note: [Col. 1164D] It is established that the author of the *Book to Novatian* was a contemporary of Cyprian, etc. See the *Life of St. Cyprian* prefixed to Baluze’s edition, § 35, p. 94.], which was written against Novatian in the time of Novatian and Cyprian themselves:

> If his children forsake my [Col. 1164D] law, and do not walk in my commandments; and if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my precepts, I will visit their crimes with a rod and their offenses with scourges; but I will not withdraw my mercy from them.

Cyprian does not differ greatly, citing the same passage thus [Note: [Col. 1164D] In Epistle VII, p. 41; Epistle LII, p. 155; and again in the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 314.]:

> If they forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not observe my precepts, [Col. 1165A] I will visit their crimes with a rod and their offenses with scourges; but I will not withdraw my mercy from them, etc.

It is, moreover, no wonder that this passage is presented first. For it refutes the severity of those who, being excessively austere, refused to receive penitents into the Church. Hence the author of the book addressed to the heretic Novatian says (p. 11):

> What madness is this of yours, Novatian, that you read only those things which pertain to the destruction of salvation, while passing over those which pertain to mercy? Scripture cries out and says: “Repent. . . .” We have heard that the Lord is therefore of great compassion; let us hear what the Holy Spirit declares through David: “If his children forsake,” etc.

Bacharius also, a very ancient writer—for he is believed to have been a contemporary of Augustine—[Col. 1165B] and a very trustworthy one, similarly refutes in these same words the severity of those who denied an opportunity for penance to certain graver sins:

> Come then, my friend, he says [Note: [Col. 1165D] Vol. III of the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, p. 133; in François Florio’s edition, as I have said, p. 115, no. 22.] in his letter to Januarius, rise up; and, though your reward and substance have been lost amid the waves of the world, like a shipwrecked man take hold of the last plank—that is, knowledge of the divine Canon—which may bring you to the shore, where it says: “If his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes; but I will not withdraw my mercy from them, nor will I impair my truth.” Of whose children is this said? Are they not the children of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the womb of the ecclesiastical font and the hidden matrix of an intricate [Col. 1165C] mystery brought forth; whose birth the cradle of the cross received and the breast of the Gospel suckled? Do you wish to know that the baptized, and not catechumens, are called children? Observe what he himself says to his apostles: “I shall no longer call you servants, but sons.”

This passage also refutes the leniency and laxity of those who received into the Church, without any penance, persons who had fallen into crimes. When God promises mercy to David’s descendants, does he not also promise that he will impose penance upon them? “I will visit with a rod . . . but I will not withdraw my mercy.” Cyprian puts it beautifully (Epistle LII, p. 155):

> In the Psalms also we read alike of the severity and the clemency of God, who at once threatens and spares, who punishes in order to correct and, when [Col. 1165D] he has corrected, preserves: “I will visit,” he says, “their crimes with a rod and their offenses with scourges. But I will not withdraw my mercy from them.”

## II

**Likewise in Isaiah** (30:15): **As the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, says: When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been.**

By these words the Novatians are invited back to the Church, insofar as they are assured that, if they groan—that is, if they repent of their schism and their other crimes—they will be saved. Once restored to the Church, and once their former errors have been effaced by salutary penance, they will then at last recognize the gravity of the schism and heresy in which they had previously been entangled: “And you will know where you have been.”

[Col. 1166A] Moreover, the very point that we deduced from the immediately preceding testimony may readily be deduced also from the one cited here. For the person who turns to God must groan—that is, must perform true, not counterfeit, penance. If he does this, he will be saved by the Lord and, when he has repented, will recognize the detestable state in which he formerly was: “And you will know where you have been.”

But you will readily ask where the cited words are to be found, since they are cited also by Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1166D] In the book *On the Lapsed*, p. 386.] and Pacian [Note: [Col. 1166D] *Against Novatian’s Treatise*, and vol. III of the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, p. 61: “What if I had added that saying of Isaiah: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been’?” And in the *Exhortation to Penance*, p. 75: “And again: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been’?”], and indeed, if you believe the distinguished Calmet, by Origen, Jerome, and Fulgentius. Look for them in the ancient version adhering to the Septuagint translators, and you will find them in verse 15 of Isaiah 30. I have noted this all the more gladly because I saw that in the edition of Cyprian prepared by Baluze the marginal citation is: Ezekiel [Col. 1166B] 18 and 33. Jerome, whom I shall cite under no. 4, certainly quotes it from Isaiah.

## III

**Likewise there** (30:1): **Woe, children of desertion, says the Lord; you have formed a plan not through me, and made my covenant not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sin.**

This passage is undoubtedly the very one that appears in the Vulgate at Isaiah 30:1, translated into Latin as follows:

> Woe, rebellious children, says the Lord, that you should form a plan, but not from me, and weave a web, but not through my Spirit, so that you might add sin upon sin.

Our writer, moreover, follows the Septuagint translators in the manner of the ancients. The passage seems to have been introduced so that we might be warned that God does not approve the plan [Col. 1166C] of those who—to use Cyprian’s words (Epistle LV, p. 181)—

> sacrilegiously oppose God and with impious fury rashly oppose the priests of God; withdrawing from the Church and taking up parricidal weapons against the Church, they labor to complete their work with the devil’s malice, lest divine clemency heal the wounded within his Church. By the fraud of their lies they corrupt the repentance of the wretched, so that satisfaction may not be made to the indignant God.

By these words, I think, he means the Novatians, who, in order to increase the number of their followers, readily received the lapsed and the criminal into their own heaven, and did not demand from them those prayers and afflictions that the Catholic Church demanded. Yet I also think that the same Novatians are reproved because [Col. 1166D] they had revolted from the Church, setting up schismatic leaders against the Catholics. Cyprian certainly indicates this when he says (Epistle LV, p. 178):

> It is clear that those do not become bishops by the will of God who are made bishops outside the Church, who are made contrary to the ordering and tradition of the Gospel, as the Lord himself declares among the Twelve Prophets, saying: “They appointed a king for themselves, and not through me.” And again: “[Col. 1167A] Their sacrifices are like the bread of mourning; all who eat them will be defiled.” And through Isaiah also (Isa. 30) the Holy Spirit cries out and says: “Woe to you, rebellious children. Thus says the Lord: You formed a plan, but not through me, and made a covenant, but not through my Spirit, adding sins upon sins.”

The author of the book addressed to the heretic Novatian, whom I have often cited, also appears to have the same point in view when he commits the following to writing (p. 8):

> For he who did not enter the sheepfold through the door, but descended by another way, is a thief and a robber. Likewise, in the same Gospel he also says: “All who came were thieves and robbers.” Who are these, if not deserters from the faith and transgressors against the Church of God, who struggle against God’s ordinance? The Holy Spirit rightly rebukes them through the Prophet, [Col. 1167B] saying: “You formed a plan not through me, and a covenant not through my Spirit, adding sins upon sins.” What answer can these utterly perverse Novatians make to these things—or now those few most wretched men who have burst forth into such insane fury that they have reverence neither for God nor for man?

## IV

**Likewise in Jeremiah** (2:25): **To turn [Note: [Col. 1167D] I think it should read: “Turn.”] your foot away from the rough road, and your face from thirst. But she said: “I shall be strengthened; I will it,” because she loved strangers and went after them.**

This passage of Jeremiah, which is now presented, is very effective in breaking down the obstinacy of the Novatians. In the Vulgate you will read it as follows:

> Keep your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst; and you said: “I have despaired; I will by no means do it, for I have loved strangers and will walk after [Col. 1167C] them.”

Jerome uses this passage to invite the lapsed Rusticus to penance, writing the following to him [Note: [Col. 1167D] Formerly Epistle 46; in the Verona edition, Epistle 122, no. 1, p. 885.]:

> Nothing so offends God as clinging to worse things through despair of better ones, although despair itself is a sign of unbelief. For one who despairs of salvation does not believe that there will be a judgment. But if he feared it, he would certainly prepare himself for the Judge by good works. Let us hear God speaking through Jeremiah: “Turn your foot away from the rough road, and your throat from thirst.” And again: “Will not one who falls rise again, or one who has turned away return?” And through Isaiah: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved, and you will know where you have been.”

## V

**Likewise in Isaiah: Turn back, because [Note: [Col. 1167D] “You who,” unless a plausible conjecture deceives me.] you conceive a lofty and wicked thought** (Isa. 31:6).

[Col. 1167D] This passage serves both to call sinners to true, not counterfeit, penance and to recall the Novatians from schism to the Church. Very similar to it is another passage that Cyprian quotes from Joel in his book *On the Lapsed* [Note: [Col. 1167D] P. 386.]: “Return to the Lord your God,” etc.

The distinguished Calmet notes that Symmachus explained this passage in the following manner:

> Repent, just as you have withdrawn from God by a profound transgression.

But the Septuagint has:

> Turn back, you who were devising a profound [Col. 1168A] and wicked plan.

Accordingly, the word “lofty” in “a lofty thought” here signifies the same as “profound.” According to Augustine, it is also used with this meaning elsewhere. For the holy Doctor explains the seventh verse of Psalm 63, “Man will approach a deep heart,” etc., as follows:

> Man approached a deep heart, that is, a secret heart—

where “secret” seems here to signify the same as “profound”—“presenting man to outward sight while preserving God within.”

## VI

**Likewise there** (Isa. 43:25): **I am, I am he who wipes away your injustices, and I will not remember them; but you, remember, and let us be judged together. Speak first of your injustices.**

The Vulgate has:

> I am, I am he who wipes away your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Bring me to remembrance, and let us be judged together; [Col. 1168B] tell me, if you have anything, so that you may be justified.

But the author of the little book addressed to the heretic Novatian, whom I have cited rather often, agrees almost entirely with our writer. This is how he reads the passage [Note: [Col. 1168D] P. 16.]:

> I am, I am he who wipes away your crimes, and I shall not be reminded of you; but keep them in mind, and let us judge. Speak first of your crimes, so that you may be justified.

The purpose of this passage seems to me plainly the same as that which I said belonged to the passage from Jeremiah cited a little earlier. Indeed, after reciting it, the author of the little book addressed to Novatian immediately adds:

> While access to pardon lies open, brothers, let us entreat God with full acts of satisfaction. Let us entreat him, so that we may be exalted.

This passage also seems to have been presented so that we might be taught how abundantly and with what supreme generosity God has mercy upon us, since he utterly forgets the sins over which we grieve. Nevertheless, he admonishes us [Col. 1168C] to remember them ourselves—that is, by lamenting them. He likewise admonishes us to lament our sins before we request their pardon from the Church: “Speak first of your injustices,” etc. These words therefore condemn the overhasty penance of some and the excessive readiness of certain presbyters in granting pardon to the lapsed. Damascene also adduces this passage to impress upon us the necessity of penance [Note: [Col. 1168D] *Parallels*, letter μ, title III, p. 578, vol. II of Le Quien’s edition.].

## VII

**Likewise there** (Isa. 55:6): **Seek God, and when you have found him, call upon him. But when he has drawn near to you, let the impious man forsake his ways, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him turn to the Lord, and mercy will be prepared for him, because he does not remit your sins greatly.**

These words of Isaiah, with which we are now dealing, condemn that same overhasty penance and [Col. 1168D] excessive readiness. The sinner must seek God, and, when God illuminates and moves that sinner’s heart by his grace, the sinner must forsake his way. Then mercy will be prepared for him—a mercy which God does not grant without prayers and punishments to which the sinner must submit. For God—to use our writer’s words—“does not remit greatly,” that is, not without some punishment and affliction on our part.

The words “not greatly” may perhaps also bear other senses, but certainly these two. The first is this: as soon as the sinner sincerely laments his sin, God will forgive whatever [Col. 1169A] wrongs he has committed, to such a degree that he does not allow himself to be entreated for long before granting pardon. The second is: while God and the Church are calling you back to themselves, O Novatians, obey the one who calls, for he will not long—“not greatly”—endure your obstinacy and insolence.

Calmet favors this latter explanation when he warns the reader to compare this passage with the other one, John 12:35:

> The light is among you for a little while longer; walk while you have the light.

However that may be, hear how the Vulgate translator rendered into Latin the words with which we are dealing:

> Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the impious man forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.

[Col. 1169B] Saint Pacian does not pass over this passage when disputing against the Novatians (Epistle III), nor does Damascene (*Parallels*, letter μ, title III).

## VIII

**Likewise there** (Isa. 44:1): **Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, because you are my servant; I have called you my servant, and you, Israel, do not forget me; for behold, I have wiped away your injustices like . . . and your sins like rain. Turn to me, and I will redeem you.**

For a long time I searched both in the Vulgate version and in Bibles translated into Latin from the Septuagint for the passage cited here, but I searched in vain. For although something akin to it appears in 41:8–9, 42:1, again in 43:1 and 5, and elsewhere as well, nevertheless in those passages you will find other things that [Col. 1169C] differ greatly from the words cited.

I therefore suspect that what is adduced here, from some ancient translation, is the first, second, and third verses of Isaiah 43, which are translated into Latin from the Septuagint reading as follows:

> And now thus says the Lord God, who made you, Jacob, and who formed you, Israel: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name. You are mine. And if you pass through water, I am with you, and the rivers will not cover you. And if you pass through fire, you will not be burned; the flame will not consume you, because I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior.

But in the Vulgate it reads as follows:

> And now thus says the Lord, who creates you, Jacob, and forms you, Israel: Do not fear, because I have redeemed you and called you by your name. You are mine. [Col. 1169D] When you pass through the waters, I shall be with you, and the rivers will not cover you.

Or rather, I suspect that what is adduced here is the first five verses of Isaiah 44, which are nevertheless read very differently in the Vulgate, in the following manner:

> And now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen. Thus says the Lord, who makes and forms you, your helper from the womb: Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and most upright one, whom I have chosen; for I will pour waters upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit upon your seed and my blessing upon your offspring. And they will spring up among the grasses like flints beside flowing waters. This one will say: “I belong to the Lord”; another will call himself by the name of Jacob; and this one will write with his hand: “For the Lord” . . . the King of Israel and his Redeemer.

But the Latin translation adhering to the translation of the [Col. 1170A] Seventy [the Septuagint] renders it as follows:

> But now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen. Thus says the Lord God, who made you and loved you from the womb: You will still have help. Do not fear, my servant Jacob, and beloved Israel, whom I have chosen. For I will give water in thirst to those who walk in watery places; I will place my Spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children. And they will spring up like grass in the midst of water and like a willow beside flowing water. This one will say: “I belong to God”; another will cry out in the name of Jacob; and another will write upon his hand: “I belong to God,” and will cry out in the name of Israel.

The difference—and it is no slight one—between these translations I attribute to the copies possessed by the translator whom our writer consulted. Perhaps he himself also translated the foregoing words, somewhat ambiguous in the Hebrew [Col. 1170B] or, if you prefer, in the Greek, in the manner he judged suitable for recalling the erring to the Church. Moreover, if you prefer to say that the words “Turn to me and I will redeem you” were taken from another passage of Scripture which a careless copyist failed to identify and separate from the foregoing, I shall not oppose you.

## IX

**Likewise there** (Isa. 46:8): **Keep these things in mind and groan; repent, you who have been led astray, and turn to me in your heart, and keep former ages in mind, because I am God.**

In the Vulgate these words are rendered thus:

> Remember this and be confounded; return to your heart, transgressors. Remember the former age, because I am God.

[Col. 1170C] But our writer, adhering to the Septuagint version, translates somewhat differently. These words invite those who have fallen into grave crimes to true penance—“Turn to me in your heart”—and remind them of the discipline of earlier Christians and of the judgments of God, who does not allow crimes to go unpunished: “Keep former ages in mind, because I am God.” They also invite, if you prefer, the Novatians back to the Church which they had forsaken, and admonish them not to continue provoking God with new crimes and with obstinacy in the schism they had undertaken.

## X

**Likewise there** (Isa. 54:8): **For a little time I forsook you, and with great mercy I shall have mercy upon you. In a little fury I turned my face away from you; with eternal mercy I shall have mercy upon you.**

[Col. 1170D] Unless we are mistaken, this passage indicates that through a brief penance—during which the Church seems to forsake the guilty when it excludes them from communion and from the assembly of the faithful—they will obtain most abundant and enduring mercy. It also indicates, if you prefer, that sinners are not wholly forsaken by God and that, if they obey his call, they will obtain most abundant mercy. The Vulgate has it thus:

> In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while, and with everlasting mercy I had mercy upon you.

## XI

**Likewise there** (Isa. 57:15):

> **Thus said the Most High, dwelling on high forever, holy among the holy; his name is the Lord: the Most High, resting among the holy, giving composure of spirit to the fainthearted, and giving life to those afflicted in heart. I am not angry with you forever, nor [Col. 1171A] will I take vengeance upon you in all things; for the spirit will go forth from me, and I have made every breath. Because of sin I grieved him for a little while and turned my face away from him; he was brought low and departed sorrowful along his ways. I saw his ways and healed him; I myself comforted him and gave him true consolation and peace upon peace, to those who are far away and to those who are near. And the Lord said: I have healed them. But the unrighteous will be tossed about like a troubled sea and cannot rest. There is no rejoicing for the impious, says the Lord.**

This passage admits an explanation akin to the preceding one. The author of the book addressed to Novatian uses it to commend the divine kindness toward all the unrighteous and to invite them to penance:

> And since, he says (p. 11), the prophet Jeremiah entreats the Lord in the person [Col. 1171B] of the sinful people, saying: “Correct us, Lord, but in judgment and not in anger, lest you make us few,” Isaiah added and said: “Because of sin I grieved him a little and struck him, and I turned my face away from him; and he was grieved and departed sorrowful along his ways.” And because he acts, he added and said: “I saw his ways and healed him, and I gave him true exhortation, peace upon peace”; thereby showing that, for those who repent, entreat, and act, what they wickedly lost or turned away from Christ can be restored.

The Vulgate, moreover, renders this passage as follows:

> Thus said the High and Exalted One, who inhabits eternity—and holy is his name—dwelling in the high and holy place, and with a contrite and humble spirit, that he may give life to the spirit of the humble [Col. 1171C] and give life to the heart of the contrite. For I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry to the end, because the spirit will go forth from before my face, and I will make the breath. Because of the iniquity of his avarice I was angry and struck him; I hid my face from you and was indignant, and he went wandering in the way of his heart. I saw his ways and healed him, and brought him back, and restored consolations to him and to those who mourn for him. I created the fruit of the lips: peace, peace to him who is far away and to him who is near, said the Lord, and I healed him. But the impious are like a raging sea which cannot rest, and its waves overflow with trampling and mud. There is no peace for the impious, says the Lord God.

See the commentators on this passage.

## XII

**Likewise in Jeremiah** (Jer. 2:32): **Will a bride forget her ornament, or a virgin her breast-band? [Col. 1171D] Yet my people have forgotten me for days [Note: [Col. 1171D] “For days,” as I think.] without number.**

If you think that this book was written against the Novatians, who had already defected from the Church and had bound themselves by numerous crimes, you readily see the object of these admonitions: namely, to point out their crimes and obstinacy, and to teach that they foolishly defected from the Church, which had already been waiting for them for a long time and inviting them to penance, and that they likewise foolishly persisted so long—“for innumerable days”—in error.

But if you think that it was written to confirm the leniency introduced by Cyprian, say that the passage was presented in order to show [Col. 1172A] that God desires anyone who has defected from him to return to him at last, and has therefore waited for innumerable days; and also that the Lord complains because he sees the impious persisting in their unrighteous purpose and ancient obstinacy. Why, then, should these people be rejected if at long last they take refuge in the Church in order to lament their former crimes?

The Vulgate version does not differ greatly from the one our writer uses, for it is as follows:

> Will a virgin forget her ornament, or a bride her breast-band? Yet my people have forgotten me for innumerable days.

## XIII

**Likewise there** (Jer. 18:7):

> **In an instant I shall speak concerning a nation or concerning a kingdom, or I shall remove and destroy them. And if the nation turns from its evils, I will repent of the evils which [Note: [Col. 1172D] “Which,” feminine.] I thought to do to them. And in an instant I shall speak [Col. 1172B] concerning a nation or kingdom, that I may rebuild and plant it; and they will do evil before me, so that they do not hear my voice, and I will repent of the good things which I said I would do for them.**

In my judgment, the purpose of the cited passage is this: the Lord testifies that he has indeed threatened the destruction of peoples and nations, yet if they repent of their crimes, he will immediately turn away the punishments which he had previously threatened. Conversely, if upright men defect from righteousness, he will by no means grant the rewards which he had previously promised. In short, he testifies that he hates no one who repents and regards no one who departs from uprightness.

Why, therefore, should peoples be turned away from penance because of former crimes which they now lament and are prepared to efface by chastisements and afflictions? Why should both Novatian [Col. 1172C] and those who adhered to Novatian persist in obstinacy and schism, and place their confidence in their former merits? The material that we shall present concerning passage XV illustrates this very passage.

If you desire the Vulgate, here it is:

> Suddenly I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, that I may uproot, destroy, and bring it to ruin. If that nation repents of its evil, against which I spoke, I too will repent of the evil which I intended to do to it. And suddenly I shall speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, that I may build and plant it. If it does evil in my sight by not hearing my voice, I will repent of the good which I said I would do to it.

Damascene also cites this passage [Note: [Col. 1172D] *Parallels*, letter μ, title III, p. 578, vol. II.].

## XIV

**Likewise there** (Jer. 3:12): **Return to me, dwelling of Israel, says the Lord, and I will not set my face firmly [Col. 1172D] against you, because I am merciful, says the Lord, and I will not be angry with you forever.**

The present passage from Jeremiah has the same object as the first part of the preceding passage and requires no particular annotation. Our Vulgate translator renders the words as follows:

> Return, apostate Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn my face away from you, because I am holy, says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever.

Consult, I pray, what the most distinguished Calmet teaches concerning this passage, which Damascene does not pass over.

It is remarkable, moreover, that Joel is not subsequently cited to the same effect, although Cyprian, [Col. 1173A] [Note: [Col. 1173C] “And the prophet Joel, with the Lord himself admonishing, declares the Lord’s kindness: ‘Return,’ he says, ‘to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious, patient and of great compassion, and one who turns aside his sentence against inflicted evils.’ After reciting these words, Cyprian adds: ‘He can grant pardon; he can turn aside his sentence. He can mercifully forgive one who repents, acts, and entreats’” (*On the Lapsed*, p. 386). Elsewhere also, namely in Epistle LII, p. 155: “For since it is written, ‘God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living,’ certainly he who desires no one [Col. 1173D] to perish desires sinners to repent and through penance to return anew to life. Therefore he also cries out through the prophet Joel and says: ‘And now thus says the Lord your God: Return to me with your whole heart, together with fasting, weeping, and lamentation; and rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious, patient and of great compassion, and one who turns aside his sentence against inflicted evil.’” The words in which Pacian cites Joel may be found in Epistle I, p. 52, and Epistle III, p. 65. As for Damascene, consult the *Parallels*, letter μ, title 3, p. 578, vol. II of Le Quien’s edition.], Pacian, and Damascene frequently cited him. But this should perhaps be attributed to the copyist’s fault and negligence.

## XV

**Likewise there** (Jer. 3:14):

> **Turn back, children who have withdrawn, says the Lord. For I will rule over you, and I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you into Zion; and I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will shepherd you, feeding you with discipline.**

The meaning of the words I have just cited, which are separated from the preceding words by only a single verse, is not dissimilar. In the Vulgate, moreover, they are translated into Latin as follows:

> Turn back, returning children, says the Lord, because I am your husband; and I will take you, one from a city and two from a kindred, and I will bring you into Zion; and I will give you shepherds according to my [Col. 1173B] heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and doctrine.

If anyone affirms that these words are expressly directed to the Novatians, and that, if they recover their senses from heresy and schism and return to the Church, they are promised legitimate and true shepherds—whereas they previously had only illegitimate and spurious ones—he will certainly be affirming what I regard as highly probable.

Read, I pray, what Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1173C] “And the prophet Joel, with the Lord himself admonishing, declares the Lord’s kindness: ‘Return,’ he says, ‘to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious, patient and of great compassion, and one who turns aside his sentence against inflicted evils.’ After reciting these words, Cyprian adds: ‘He can grant pardon; he can turn aside his sentence. He can mercifully forgive one who repents, acts, and entreats’” (*On the Lapsed*, p. 386). Elsewhere also, namely in Epistle LII, p. 155: “For since it is written, ‘God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living,’ certainly he who desires no one [Col. 1173D] to perish desires sinners to repent and through penance to return anew to life. Therefore he also cries out through the prophet Joel and says: ‘And now thus says the Lord your God: Return to me with your whole heart, together with fasting, weeping, and lamentation; and rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, because he is merciful and gracious, patient and of great compassion, and one who turns aside his sentence against inflicted evil.’” The words in which Pacian cites Joel may be found in Epistle I, p. 52, and Epistle III, p. 65. As for Damascene, consult the *Parallels*, letter μ, title 3, p. 578, vol. II of Le Quien’s edition.] and Pacian [Note: [Col. 1173D] *On the Unity of the Church*; Epistle XLI, p. 123; Epistle XLVIII, p. 130; and Epistle XLIX, p. 141, etc.] relate concerning the criminal ordination of Novatian and the other schismatics. To these, I ask you to add what the author of the book addressed to Novatian discusses at length on this subject [Note: [Col. 1173D] Epistle III, p. 60, vol. II of the Paris *Library*.].

## XVI

**Likewise there** (Jer. 3:22): **Turn back, returning children, and I will heal your brokenness.**

What I said concerning the two immediately preceding passages of Scripture I do not hesitate [Col. 1173C] to affirm also of the one I have just cited, which reads as follows in the Vulgate:

> Turn back, returning children, and I will heal your apostasies.

See the commentators on this passage.

## XVII

**Likewise there** (Jer. 4:14): **Wash your heart from wickedness, [Col. 1174A] Jerusalem, that you may be healed. How long will the thoughts of your sorrows remain within you?**

To grasp the force of the testimony cited here, consult what was set forth concerning Scriptural passages IV, V, and IX. The Vulgate presents it as follows:

> Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, that you may be saved. How long will harmful thoughts linger within you?

## XVIII

**Likewise there** (Jer. 8:4):

> **Thus says the Lord: Will not one who falls rise again, or one who turns himself away turn back? For this people turned itself away from a wicked vision, persisted in its presumption, and refused to turn back.**

Bacharius applies precisely the same explanation to the words of Jeremiah which I have just cited [Note: [Col. 1174D] P. 3 of François Florio’s edition.], writing as follows:

> And elsewhere: “Will not one who falls rise again, or one who turns away turn back?”

[Col. 1174B] The Vulgate, however, reports it in the following form:

> Thus says the Lord: Will not one who falls rise again? And will not one who has turned away return? Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away in contentious apostasy?

## XIX

**Likewise there** (Jer. 8:6): **There is no man repenting of his wickedness and saying, “What have I done?” He who runs has failed in his course, like a horse persuading [Note: [Col. 1174D] I think it should read: “sweating.”] in its neighing.**
What is set down in this passage is explained in almost the same manner as the passage set down in the twelfth place. Recall, therefore, what was said there. The Vulgate renders these words somewhat differently, namely: “There is no one who repents of his sin, saying, ‘What have I done?’ They have all turned to their own course, like a horse [Col. 1174C] rushing headlong into battle.” The interpretation followed by our author, therefore, derives from the Septuagint translators. Theodoret explains it thus [Note: [Col. 1174D] Book II of the *Commentary on Jeremiah*, chapter VIII]: “A horse running with violent impetus and neighing comes to a halt after its exertion; but these men—namely, the impious and most wicked—did not halt at all in the course of their crimes.” John Damascene also cites this passage [Note: [Col. 1174D] *Parallels*, letter μ, title III].

XX. Likewise in the same place (Jeremiah 18:11–12): “Let each person, therefore, turn away from his evil way, and make your endeavors better.” And they said: “We shall be strengthened, because we shall follow your inventions [Note: [Col. 1174D] ‘Our,’ as I think], and each one of us shall do the evil things that please his own heart.”

If you remember what we noted on passage XII, as well as on XIV, XV, and those following, [Col. 1174D] you will readily perceive the direction in which the preceding words are aimed. Moreover, I think they were introduced here so that, just as in ancient times the Hebrew people, bound fast by their crimes, refused to obey the Lord when he called them to repentance and preferred to serve foreign gods and their own depraved inclinations rather than God, so those wicked men whom our author rebukes—namely, the Novatians, unless we are altogether mistaken—hindered by their schism and errors, refused to obey God and the Church when he called them, stubbornly wishing to persist in their schism and adopted error. Very closely akin [Note: [Col. 1173D] “The Lord indeed had foretold that many ravenous wolves would come in sheep’s clothing, etc.,” pp. 13–14] [Col. 1175A] to the interpretation proposed by our author is that of the Vulgate, namely: “Let each one return from his evil way, and make straight your ways and your endeavors.” But they said: “We have despaired; for we shall follow our own thoughts, and each one of us shall practice the wickedness of his evil heart.”

XXI. Likewise in the same place (Lamentations 2:18): “Pour out tears like a torrent day and night; give yourself no rest; let the pupil of your eye not be silent.”

These words beautifully invite one to repentance. The Vulgate has them thus: “Let tears flow down like a torrent by day and night; give yourself no rest, nor let the pupil of your eye be silent.” Here I note in passing that in the first centuries of the Church Jeremiah’s Lamentations did not constitute a separate book distinct from the Prophecy. It is therefore not surprising [Col. 1175B] if our author cites these words as though they were contained in a single book: “Likewise in the same place.”

XXII. Likewise in the same place (Lamentations 3:40): “Let us examine our ways and turn to the Lord. Let us cleanse our hearts together with our hands, and let us look to the Lord who dwells in heaven. We have sinned and provoked you, and you have not been propitiated.”

These words express the utterances of a penitent crying out to God and seeking pardon and compassion from him. First, therefore, all sinners whatsoever—and consequently the Novatians themselves and the schismatics—are invited by them to repentance. They also show that the path to repentance is wrongfully closed, since the Holy Spirit through Jeremiah presents and praises the examples of those who, [Col. 1175C] detesting their own depravity, say: “Let us examine”—for I prefer to follow the Vulgate—“our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord. Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in heaven. We have acted wickedly and provoked you to anger; therefore you are inexorable.” I once suspected that the latter words, “We have sinned . . . and you have not been propitiated,” indicate why the Novatians were then harassed both by Christians and by the Gentiles themselves—namely, because they had provoked God by their crimes and schism. Whether my suspicion was correct or otherwise, let the reader judge.

XXIII. Likewise in the same place (Jeremiah 3:6): “And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you seen what the dwelling of Israel has done to me? She went upon every high mountain and [Col. 1175D] went beneath every wooded tree, and there committed fornication. And after she had committed all these acts of fornication, I said: ‘Turn to me,’ but she did not return.”

This passage is cited in the manuscript in such a way as to retain both terms, “dwelling” and “house,” one of which is certainly redundant. I have advised that the word “house” be deleted—not because the word displeased me, but because I thought that it had subsequently passed into the text itself from the margin, where it had first been placed for purposes of explanation. Elsewhere, indeed, our author expressly translates it as “dwelling”: “Return to me, dwelling of Israel,” no. 14. I now come to the explanation. First, God’s extraordinary goodness and love toward those guilty of monstrous crimes are commended here, for the Lord still calls them to repentance. The Lord next complains that they persisted in their [Col. 1176A] obstinacy, although he had offered them pardon so frequently and in such unmistakable words. See what we said on passage XII, and likewise on XIV and those following. If you desire the Vulgate interpretation, I provide it at once: “And the Lord said to me in the days of King Josiah: Have you not seen what apostate Israel has done? She went by herself upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and there committed fornication. And after she had done all these things, I said: ‘Return to me,’ but she did not return.”

XXIV. Likewise in the same place (Lamentations 3:31): “The Lord will not reject forever; and when he has humbled, he will have mercy according to the abundance of his mercy, because he will not humble from his whole heart, nor reject the children of men.”

The points presented under testimony XIII and other related passages [Col. 1176B] are again impressed upon us by the words we are now considering. In the Vulgate they read thus: “For the Lord will not reject forever. For if he has cast aside, he will also have mercy according to the abundance of his mercies; for he has not humbled from his heart and cast aside the children of men.”

XXV. Likewise in Ezekiel (33:12): “And the righteous man will not be able to be saved on the day of sin. When I say to the righteous man, ‘You shall surely live,’ but he trusts in his own righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds will be remembered; in the iniquity that he has committed, in that he shall die. And when I say to the impious man, ‘You shall surely die,’ but he turns away from his sin and practices righteousness and justice, returns a pledge to his debtor, restores what he has taken by robbery, and walks in the commandments of life so as not to do [Col. 1176C] what is unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the sins that he has committed shall be brought against him, because he has practiced justice and righteousness; in these he shall live.”

The passage from Ezekiel cited here is very similar to the one he introduced from Jeremiah in no. XIII, and therefore admits the same explanation. The author of the book *Against Novatian* uses these words of Ezekiel to refute Novatian himself in this manner (p. 13):

> “How, therefore, this Novatian came to be so criminal, so utterly lost, and so mad with the fury of dissension, I cannot discover. He who, while he was still in the one house—that is, Christ’s Church—wept over his neighbors’ transgressions as though they were his own, bore the burdens of his brethren, as the Apostle exhorts, and strengthened with heavenly consolation those who were wavering in the faith. But now, since [Col. 1176D] he began to practice that Cain-like heresy, which strives after nothing but killing, he does not spare even himself in the end. But if he had read that the righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him on the day when he goes astray, and that the impiety of the impious man will not harm him from the day on which he is converted, he who always opposes penitents would long ago have repented in ashes. He finds it easier to bring about the collapse of structures that stand than to rebuild fallen ruins.
