By his false opposition he has terrified many of our most wretched brethren and made them pagans again, saying that the repentance of the lapsed is vain and cannot benefit them unto salvation.”

The Vulgate translator, moreover, rendered the same thought into Latin in these words: “And the righteous man will not be able to live in his righteousness on any day on which he sins. Even if [Col. 1177A] I say to the righteous man that he shall surely live, but, trusting in his own righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteous deeds shall be consigned to oblivion, and in the iniquity that he has committed, in that he shall die. But if I say to the impious man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin, practices justice and righteousness, returns the pledge—that impious man—and gives back what he has taken by robbery, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die.” You have the same admonitions in verses 21 and 24 of chapter 18 of the same Ezekiel.

XXVI. Likewise in the same place (Ezekiel 17:24): “I am the Lord, because I humble the tall tree and exalt the lowly tree; I cause the green tree to wither and make the dry tree live again.”

What was just conveyed in express terms is now placed before our eyes in an elegant allegory. It indicates that God is able, as he pleases, both to bring down the proud and to raise up the humble who grieve over their crimes. [Col. 1177B] This pronouncement therefore strikes at the Novatians, swollen and exalted in their schism. It also strikes all those who bar sinners from pardon and repentance, since the Lord exalts the lowly shrub and imparts life and vigor to the dry tree. But if you think precisely the same explanation should be applied to this testimony as I applied to the preceding one, you certainly have my permission. Although the Vulgate interpretation scarcely differs from the one I have just presented, nevertheless, since thus far I have added the Vulgate to the Old Latin interpretation, I add it here as well: “For I, the Lord, have humbled the lofty tree and exalted the lowly tree; I have dried up the green tree and made the dry tree put forth leaves.”

[Col. 1177C] XXVII. Likewise in the same place (Ezekiel 33:10): “And you, son of man, say to the house of Israel: As you have spoken, saying, ‘Our errors and our iniquities are within us, and in them we waste away. How, then, shall we live?’ Say to them: ‘As I live, says the Lord, I do not will the death of the impious man; only let him turn away from his way and live.’”

This statement is clear. In it God’s goodness shines forth in calling people who have long clung to iniquity and almost despaired. It also appears as a certain divine testimony to the will to grant pardon to even the most thoroughly lost. By these words, indeed, those are especially refuted who attempt to impose limits upon divine love and forbid repentance to criminals. If God does not will the sinner’s death, but rather that he be converted and live, who will call any crimes inexpiable [Col. 1177D] or bar those desiring repentance from it, and therefore from the Church? The author of the book *Against Novatian*, whom I have frequently cited, employs this passage of Ezekiel in the same sense (p. 11), saying:

> “Likewise the Lord says to the same prophet Ezekiel: ‘Son of man, say to the people of Israel: Why have you spoken, saying, “We waste away in our errors, and how shall we be able to be saved?” Say to them: “As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but I desire that the sinner turn away from his most evil way and live.”’”

Cyprian also employs it—to avoid listing everyone—near the end of the book *On the Lapsed* and near the beginning of the book *On the Benefit of Patience*, as does Jerome. See what I shall say in no. 30.

The Vulgate translator rendered the same thought into Latin [Col. 1178A] in these words: “You, therefore, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying, ‘Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and in them we waste away; how, therefore, shall we be able to live?’ Say to them: ‘As I live, says the Lord God, I do not will the death of the impious man, but rather that the impious man be converted from his way and live.’”

XXVIII. Likewise in the same place (Ezekiel 36:36): “I, the Lord, have rebuilt what was demolished and planted what was uprooted.”

A second allegory, akin to the one introduced in no. 26, is proposed here. Since I have reported it in our author’s words, I should also like to present it in the words of the Vulgate, which are as follows: “I, the Lord, have rebuilt what was scattered and planted what was uncultivated.”

XXIX. Likewise in the same place (Ezekiel 18:21): “And if the unrighteous man turns away from all the iniquities that he has committed, keeps [Col. 1178B] all my commandments, and practices justice, righteousness, and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the transgressions that he has committed shall be remembered; in the righteousness that he has practiced, he shall live. Do I will by my will the death of the unjust man, says Adonai the Lord, rather than that he turn away from his evil way and live?”

The very point conveyed a little earlier by the admonitions of the prophet Ezekiel is here again impressed upon us in other words very closely resembling the preceding ones.

Recall no. XXV. Here I note only that this passage of Ezekiel was perhaps cited in the same sense by Cyprian when he taught as follows (*On the Benefit of Patience*, p. 496):

> “He admonishes us lest anyone, growing impatient, fail in his labor; lest anyone, either distracted or overcome by temptations, stop midway along the path of praise and glory, [Col. 1178C] and the things of the past perish when what had been begun ceases to be brought to completion, as it is written: ‘The righteousness of the righteous man will not deliver him on any day on which he strays.’ And again: ‘Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown.’ This declaration exhorts us to persevere patiently and courageously, so that he who is already striving toward the crown, with praise now close at hand, may be crowned through enduring patience.”

In the Vulgate, however, those words are rendered thus: “But if the impious man repents of all the sins he has committed, keeps all my precepts, and practices justice and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die. I shall not remember any of the iniquities that he has committed; in the righteousness he has practiced, he shall live. Is the death of the impious man my will, says the Lord God, and not rather that he be converted from his ways and live?”

[Col. 1178D] With this interpretation established—and indeed from the very etymology of the name *Adonai*—one of these terms, “Adonai” or “Lord,” appears to be redundant. Yet I was unwilling, meanwhile, to lay hands upon the preceding interpretation. The frequently cited John Damascene does not omit this passage (*Parallels*, etc.).

XXX. Likewise in the same place (Ezekiel 18:30): “Be converted, and turn away from all your impieties, and they shall not become a punishment to you. Cast away from yourselves all your iniquities, by which you acted impiously against me, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, house of Israel? For I do not will the death of one who is dying, says Adonai the Lord.”

In the same eighteenth chapter that I cited just now, [Col. 1179A] though with several verses intervening—namely, at verse 30—you will find the words introduced here. Through them the Lord invites criminals to repentance and promises them not only life but also pardon for even the gravest crimes whatsoever. See what we said on passages XIV, XV, and other related ones.

The author of the book *Against Novatian* employs this same explanation, writing as follows (p. 16):

> “Let us therefore, with all the strength of our faith, give praise to God; let us make a full confession, since the powers of heaven rejoice over our repentance, all the angels rejoice, and Christ too rejoices. Although we are again burdened with sins and overwhelmed by transgressions, he exhorts us with full and merciful moderation to cease from crime, saying: ‘Turn yourselves and return from your impieties, and [Col. 1179B] your iniquities shall not become a punishment to you. Cast away from yourselves all your impieties that you have committed against me, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why do you deliver yourselves over to death, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the sinner.’”

Jerome likewise employs the passage, writing as follows to the lapsed Rusticus [Note: [Col. 1179D] In the epistle formerly numbered XLVI; in the Verona edition, 122, p. 1]:

> “Ezekiel too, because inspired by the same Spirit, speaks in the same words: ‘Be converted,’ he says, ‘and return from your iniquities, house of Israel, and your impieties shall not become a torment to you. Cast away all your impieties by which you have acted impiously against me, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why should you die, house of Israel? For I do not will the death of the sinner, says the Lord.’ Hence he also says in what follows: ‘As I live, says the Lord, I do not will the death of the sinner, except that he return from his way [Col. 1179C] and live,’ lest an unbelieving mind despair of the promise of good things, and a soul that has once resigned itself to perdition fail to apply a cure to its wound because it believes that it can by no means be healed.”

The Vulgate translator wished this passage to be read in Latin as follows: “Be converted and repent of all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not become your ruin. Cast away from yourselves all your transgressions in which you have transgressed, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. And why should you die, house of Israel? For I do not will the death of one who is dying, says the Lord God.”

XXXI. Likewise in Daniel (4:31): “And after the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned within me; and I praised the Most High, blessed the King of heaven, and praised him who lives forever, because his power is eternal, his kingdom is in [every] generation, and all who inhabit the earth are nothing.”

The words introduced from Daniel invite peoples long habituated to impiety to repentance and detestation of their crimes by the example of Nebuchadnezzar. They readily show that the opportunity for repentance is closed to no one, since even Nebuchadnezzar, who for many years had despised the supreme deity, was at last granted pardon by the Lord for his past crimes because of his humility and acknowledgment of the truth.

In the Vulgate these words read thus: “Therefore, after the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes to heaven, and my understanding was restored to me; and I blessed the Most High, [Col. 1180A] and praised and glorified him who lives forever, because his power is everlasting power and his kingdom endures from generation to generation. And all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing before him.”

XXXII. Likewise in Micah (7:2): “Woe is me, my soul, because truth has perished from the earth, and among them all there is no one who corrects. They all judge in bloodshed; each man afflicts his neighbor with affliction; they prepare their hands for evil.”

If this passage of Micah is taken by itself, it appears to assail the Novatians, over whose crimes and schism God complains. Yet in order to attain a fuller and, if you permit the expression, complete and integral sense of these words, you must add what follows. You will then say that the Prophet complains [Col. 1180B] because there was the most complete agreement of all in crimes and iniquity. Nevertheless, the Prophet says that he rejects their example, since he had resolved to call upon and worship the Lord and to repent of his sins. Once he had done so, he would escape the torments and punishments that his former crimes deserved.

Anyone who reads the seventh and following verses of the same chapter will acknowledge that what I say is true. I transcribe them here from the Vulgate, since you possess the greater part of the Old Latin version from our author: “My soul desired early figs. The holy man has perished from the earth, and there is no upright man among human beings. They all lie in wait for blood; a man hunts his brother to death . . . But I shall look to the Lord; I shall wait for God my Savior. My God [Col. 1180C] will hear me. Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall rise again. When I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light. I shall bear the Lord’s wrath because I have sinned against him, until he judges my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out into the light; I shall see his righteousness. And my enemy shall look upon me and be covered with confusion—she who says to me, ‘Where is the Lord your God?’ My eyes shall look upon her; now she shall be trodden down like the mud of the streets.”

XXXIII. Likewise in the same place (Micah 7:8): “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; rather, I shall rise again. For if I sit in darkness, the Lord will shine upon me. I shall endure the Lord’s wrath because I have sinned against him, until he himself vindicates my cause.”

Concerning this testimony, recall what we have just said. [Col. 1180D] These passages of Micah have this advantage: in addition to the admonitions we have just considered, they exhibit an ancient version somewhat removed from the Vulgate, one that you would nevertheless have difficulty finding elsewhere. Furthermore, if you desire the first verse of this chapter from the Septuagint version in order to complete the thought, here it is: “Woe is me, because I have become like one gathering stubble at harvest and clusters in the vintage. There are no firstfruits from the good things to eat—woe, my soul!”

It is surprising, moreover, that another passage of Micah, not far removed from the preceding one, is not introduced—namely, verse 19 of the same chapter, which Saint Jerome [Note: [Col. 1180D] In the epistle to Oceanus, formerly numbered LXXXIII; in the Verona edition, 69, no. 6] reads in this manner: “He himself will turn again and have mercy [Col. 1181A] upon us; he will sink our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depth of the sea.” But perhaps our author here refrained from citing it because he thought those words much better suited to Baptism than to repentance. Indeed, the same Jerome whom I cited teaches that the grace of Baptism is denoted by those words: “Micah prophesies concerning the grace of Baptism: ‘He himself will turn again,’ etc.”

XXXIV. Likewise in Zephaniah (2:1): “Assemble and pray, undisciplined nation, before you become like a passing flower, before the Lord’s wrath comes upon you, before the day of the Lord’s fury comes upon you. Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth; practice justice, seek righteousness, and seek meekness, and answer him, so that you may be protected on the day of the Lord’s wrath.”

[Col. 1181B] What could be more fitting for terrifying the Novatians and turning them away from schism and heresy, and for bringing them back to the Church they had abandoned, than the words introduced here from Zephaniah? What, likewise, could be more effective in urgently driving to repentance those who had provoked God’s wrath against themselves by their crimes? Our author undoubtedly adheres to the Septuagint interpretation. The Vulgate translator, however, rendered the same words into Latin thus: “Assemble, gather together, unlovable nation, before the command brings forth the passing day like dust, before the wrath of the Lord’s fury comes upon you, before the day of the Lord’s indignation comes upon you. Seek the Lord, all you meek of the earth who have practiced his judgment. Seek what is just; seek what is meek, if perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the Lord’s fury.”

[Col. 1181C] XXXV. Likewise in Zechariah (1:3): “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you.”

This passage is so clear that it requires no explanation whatsoever. See what we said on passages 15, 16, and those following. It also agrees completely with the Vulgate.

XXXVI. Likewise in Hosea (14:2): “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have been weakened by your iniquities. Take many with you, and return to the Lord your God. Say to him in adoration: ‘You have power to forgive our sins,’ so that you may not receive iniquity, but may receive good things.”

Recall what we said concerning the passages just cited and others explained earlier, and you will plainly see the object of the words of Hosea that we are now considering. Here I note only [Col. 1181D] that if you wish the words “Take many with you” to be directed to the Novatians, they invite them to return to the Church, as it were, in groups and with many gathered together. If they are directed to those who fled to the Church for the sake of repentance but were repelled by certain more severe and austere persons, then they indicate that they should gather the supporting petitions of many, especially of martyrs and confessors. With their aid, either the resolve of the more austere might be bent toward leniency, or it might at least be overcome by the number and authority of those interceding. The words can also signify the prayers of the Church, through which penitents might both receive canonical reconciliation and move God to mercy. Saint Pacian favors this last interpretation when he says (*Epistle* I, p. 53):

> “I know, brother, that this very pardon granted through repentance [Col. 1182A] is not indiscriminately given to everyone, nor is it relaxed before there has been either an interpretation of the divine will or perhaps a visitation: with great weight and careful balancing, after many groans and an outpouring of tears, after the prayers of the whole Church.”

Take the term “iniquity” in the phrase “so that you may not receive iniquity” to mean the punishment to be inflicted for iniquity. Interpreters have long since warned that these terms—“sin,” “iniquity,” and other related words—are ambiguous, and signify both sin and iniquity themselves and the punishment to be imposed for sin and iniquity. The Vulgate differs somewhat from the preceding interpretation; it is as follows: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, because you have fallen in your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord, and say to him: ‘Take away all iniquity, [Col. 1182B] accept what is good, and we shall render the calves of our lips.’”

XXXVII. Likewise in Ecclesiasticus (17:23): “Return to the Lord, and forsake your sins; hate abomination exceedingly, acknowledge the righteous ordinances and judgments of God, stand in the allotted place of the Most High’s propitiation, and go to the portion of the age with the living and with those who offer confession. Do not linger in the error of the impious. From a dead person confession perishes as though it were nothing. Living and sound, you shall confess to God and glory in his mercies, because great is God’s mercy and his propitiation toward those who turn to him.”

If the observations I made on testimony XXXIV are recalled here, they will, I think, sufficiently illuminate the passage we introduce here. The Novatians certainly appear to be indicated and admonished at last to return from heresy to the Church by these words: “Return to the Lord, [Col. 1182C] and forsake your sins . . . stand in the allotted place of the Most High’s propitiation, and go to the portion of the age with the living and with those who offer confession.” Sinners in general are aroused to true, sincere, and solid repentance—in short, to the repentance prescribed by the Church: “Hate abomination exceedingly, acknowledge the righteous ordinances and judgments of God, and stand in the allotted place of the Most High’s propitiation.” For what could more expressly denote the Church and the repentance prescribed by her? They are also admonished not to delay returning to God, for death is imminent. Therefore, while life and health still remain, let them humbly ask pardon from him, which he, being supremely merciful, will grant abundantly: “Living and sound, you shall confess to God and glory in his mercies, because [Col. 1182D] great is God’s mercy and his propitiation toward those who turn to him.” The Vulgate translator rendered those words into Latin thus: “Return to the Lord and turn away from your injustice; hate abomination exceedingly, acknowledge the righteous ordinances and judgments of God, and stand in the allotted place of the ordinance and prayer of God Most High. Go into the portions of the holy age, with the living and those who offer confession to God. Do not linger in the error of the impious; confess before death. From a dead person confession perishes as though it were nothing. You shall confess while living; living and sound, you shall confess and praise God and glory in his mercies. For great is the Lord’s mercy and his propitiation toward those who turn to him.”

XXXVIII. Likewise in the same place (Ecclesiasticus 20:4): “How good it is for one who has been corrected to make his repentance manifest! For thus you shall escape voluntary sin.”

[Col. 1183A] This passage appears to be directed toward those who testified that they repented of their crimes and therefore did not refuse to call themselves corrected, but were unwilling to submit to the repentance prescribed by the Church. Our author exhorts them to perform the public repentance established by the Church, for this is most fitting; if they act otherwise, they will by no means escape voluntary sin.

But what, you will ask, is that voluntary sin said to be inescapable for one who refuses to perform public penance? Is it disobedience toward the Church, which prescribed that penance? Or the scandal given to the rest of the faithful? I would readily admit either explanation. Yet I would not censure those who observe that voluntary sin cannot be escaped by persons who do not perform the repentance for their former crimes [Col. 1183B] prescribed by the Church. For one who performs either no repentance or only slight repentance for former crimes readily returns to sin and shows contempt for the customs and sanctions of the Church. The Vulgate interpretation agrees almost entirely with the preceding one, differing only in that it reads “rebuked” where our author has “corrected.”

XXXIX. Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles (8:19): “But Peter said to him: May your money be with you unto perdition, because you think that you can obtain God’s grace through money. You have neither part nor lot in this faith, because your heart is not upright before the Lord. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the bond of iniquity and the bitterness of gall.”

[Col. 1183C] That room for repentance can be open to sins of every kind, and consequently even to the gravest, is readily demonstrated from the words of Peter cited here, since Peter exhorts Simon Magus—who sought to purchase the gifts of the Holy Spirit and was therefore guilty of a monstrous crime—to repentance. The same words are also suited to recalling from schism and heresy the Novatians, some of whom perhaps had been led to that sect and retained in it by money, or at least by the advantages offered to them. Although the difference between this interpretation and the Vulgate is slight, I nevertheless choose to introduce the Vulgate as well: “But Peter said to him: May your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. You have [Col. 1183D] neither part nor lot in this word, for your heart is not upright before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.”

XL. Likewise in the Epistle of blessed Paul [Note: [Col. 1183D] *Benedicti* (“blessed”), unless we are mistaken; for the ancients often referred to Christ and the Apostles with this appellation placed before their names] to the Corinthians, the second (7:10): “For sorrow that is according to God works steadfast repentance unto salvation, but the sorrow of the world works death.”

The passage of the Apostle that we are now examining celebrates the usefulness of ecclesiastical repentance, which is carried out even through bodily afflictions, and testifies that it will be both steadfast and salutary—“unto salvation.” [Col. 1184A] But it condemns as harmful and even deadly that kind of repentance approved by the world. By the name “world” it means the flesh that flatters us and opposes the law of God, and therefore ecclesiastical discipline—or, if you prefer, the blandishments of schismatics and of certain lax persons. Cyprian, indeed, approves only that repentance which also displays external afflictions and manifest sorrow. Hence, in the book *On the Lapsed* (p. 384), he says:

> “Perform full repentance; prove the sorrow of a grieving and lamenting spirit. And do not be disturbed by the improvident error or vain insensibility of certain persons who, although held fast in so grave a crime, have been stricken with such blindness of mind that they neither understand their transgressions nor mourn them. [Col. 1184B] This is a greater stroke from an indignant God.”

The same passage also shows that there are no unpardonable sins. For how could repentance be called “steadfast unto salvation” if some sins were unpardonable? Hence Saint Pacian, disputing against the Novatians, rightly employs this same passage (*Epistle* I, p. 53). It also commends the leniency urged by Cyprian, and in it the leaders of the churches are admonished not to bar repentance from those seeking pardon for their crimes, for repentance is “steadfast unto salvation.” Why, then, should the faithful who desire to bewail their crimes be barred from it? I do not introduce the Vulgate here, for it has the same interpretation as the preceding one. John Damascene declares that he sets great value on this passage by citing it in the *Parallels*.

[Col. 1184C] XLI. Likewise in the same place, concerning this very matter (2 Corinthians 2:10): “But if you have forgiven anyone anything, so have I; for what I have forgiven, I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we may not be circumvented by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his stratagems.”

Here too bishops are admonished to grant pardon to penitents; for the Apostle Paul approved the indulgence and leniency—if we may so speak—which the faithful had shown toward penitents. Accordingly, this passage condemns that rigor and severity which some were striving to introduce into the Church by denying pardon to penitents, even if they submitted themselves to the Church’s judgment. Saint Pacianus indeed uses it in this sense when he writes [Note: [Col. 1184D] Epistle I, p. 53, vol. III, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris.]:

> “What will be denied to the bishop, in whom the name of God is operative? [Col. 1184D] He will indeed render an account to God if he has done anything wrongly, or judged corruptly and impiously. Nor is God thereby prejudiced or prevented from undoing the works of an evil builder; meanwhile, if that administration is pious, the bishop continues as a helper in the works of God. Behold, the Apostle writes to the laity: ‘If you have forgiven anyone anything, I also have; for what I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have done for your sake in the person of Christ, so that he may not be possessed by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices.’ But if the Apostle says that he himself has forgiven what the laity forgive, how shall what a bishop has done be rejected? . . . . I know, brother, that this very pardon through penance is not granted indiscriminately to everyone, nor is it conferred before either an interpretation of the divine will or perhaps a visitation has occurred. It is granted with great seriousness [Col. 1185A] and careful deliberation: after many groans and an outpouring of tears, after the prayers of the whole Church. Thus pardon is not denied to true repentance, yet no one prejudges Christ, who will judge.”

The passage also condemns the error of those who considered some sins incapable of expiation. For who will consider any sins incapable of expiation when Paul, without any restriction or exception of offenses, affirms that he forgives those who had sinned whatever had previously been forgiven them by the faithful? That same Pacianus whom I have just cited, after quoting these very words of the Apostle, “If you have forgiven anyone,” and so forth, aptly adds [Note: [Col. 1185D] Epistle III, p. 65, vol. III, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Paris.]:

> “Do you see the Apostle’s indulgence, tempering even his own judgments? Do you see a most gentle leniency, far removed from your arrogance, wholly unlike the scowling brow of Novatian, [Col. 1185B] and concerned instead for our common life and the salvation of all? Or do you still assail us as a severe censor?”

The further words, “So that we may not be circumvented by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his devices,” have, in my judgment, the following meaning: I forgive whatever you have forgiven precisely so that we may not be circumvented by Satan. For Satan circumvents believers who have fallen into offenses if we employ against them excessive austerity and rigor untempered by any leniency; by this means they are easily driven to despair. We take precautions against precisely this, since we know the demon’s deceits and devices well.

The Vulgate differs scarcely at all from the interpretation given above; here it is at once: “But if you have forgiven anyone anything, I also have; for what I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have done for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be circumvented by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his thoughts.”

[Col. 1185C] XLII. Likewise in the same place (2 Cor. 12:20–21): “But I fear lest perhaps, when I come to you, God may humble me among you once again, and I may mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the fornication and shameless conduct which they committed.”

Following the example of the Apostle Paul, who feared an evil outcome for those who had not repented of the fornication and shameless conduct which they had committed, and who foretold that many of them would be such that he would have to mourn their destruction, Cyprian—or whoever is the author of this little work—fears an evil outcome for those who, although guilty of very many offenses, nevertheless wished to be admitted into the Church without penance. He therefore requires penance from the shameless and the criminal so that they might obtain ecclesiastical communion [Col. 1185D] and pardon.

This passage is also rightly pressed against the Novatians, since Paul would not have required penance from criminals if their crimes were unpardonable. Were the things that the Apostle Paul designates here by the terms “fornication” and “shameless conduct” merely slight offenses? Saint Pacianus, disputing against the Novatians, does not omit this testimony of Paul; for he refutes them as follows (Epistle I, p. 52):

> “Review what the Spirit says to the churches. He accuses the Ephesians of having abandoned their love; he charges the Thyatirans with sexual immorality; he rebukes the Sardians for failing in their work, the Pergamenes for teaching divergent doctrines; he brands the riches of the Laodiceans; and yet [Col. 1186A] he invites them all through satisfaction to repentance. What does the Apostle say to the Corinthians when he speaks thus: ‘Lest, when I come, I may mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of what they formerly committed in fornication and their uncleannesses’?”

Cyprian had preceded Pacianus (Epistle LII, p. 157), committing the following words to writing:

> “‘Every sin whatsoever that a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits adultery sins against his own body’ (1 Cor. 6). Yet even to these penance is granted, and the hope of mourning and making satisfaction is left open, according to the Apostle himself when he says: ‘I fear lest perhaps, when I come to you, I may mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleannesses, fornications, and lustful acts that they committed.’”

See also, I beg you, [Col. 1186B] how Jerome uses this passage to correct the fallen Sabinianus (in the Verona edition, Epistle CXLVII, no. 1, p. 1078).

But who could omit Bachiarius, who not only cites this passage but even uses the very version employed by our author? I am especially pleased to summon Bachiarius as a witness because the reader will clearly recognize from his admonitions that the passage of Paul which we are discussing can also be cited for another purpose. Here are Bachiarius’s own words (*Book to Januarius*, p. 54, edition of Franciscus Florius):

> “Do not, I beg you, despise your dead brother. He is the son of the barren Shunammite woman, that is, of the Church; this one who has died was born by promise. For the Lord once promised and pledged his birth to a second Abraham in the seed of Isaac. His head was struck by heat during the harvest, [Col. 1186C] that is, the ruling part of his mind grew hot amid the very flame of lustful hope. Let his mother run to Elisha; that is, let the Church mourn earnestly, for he will rise again if we have faithfully hoped for this from Christ. And you, most blessed one, imitate Elisha’s work upon your dead brother: place hand upon hands, feet upon feet, mouth upon mouth. First, have compassion upon him who lies dead. Do not, elated by the triumph of your integrity, tower over him or stretch yourself beyond one whom sudden death has seized; instead imitate the Apostle, who says: ‘I fear lest the Lord my God humble me among you and I may mourn many of those who sinned before.’ Moreover, set your eyes upon his eyes so that they may no longer wander to his destruction; your mouth upon his mouth so that it may not speak wicked things; your hands upon his hands so that they may not perform [Col. 1186D] hostile deeds; your feet upon his feet so that they may not stray into shameful things. And thus, when your limbs have been joined to his limbs for his protection, not only will he have no further opportunity to sin, but he will also receive hope of rising again, so that one who has died from the cold of sin may, at the time of consolation, be recalled to life.”

In the Vulgate you will find these words translated in the following manner: “For I fear lest perhaps, when I come . . . lest once again, when I come, God may humble me among you, and I may mourn many of those who sinned before and have not repented of the uncleanness, fornication, and shameless conduct which they committed.”

XLIII. Likewise in the same place (2 Cor. 13:2): “I foretold and foretell, as when present, so now while absent, to those who sinned before, [Col. 1187A] and to all the rest, that if I come again I will not spare.”

In this passage the Apostle teaches that criminals must be subjected to penance, for he says that he cannot possibly leave unpunished the grave crimes into which some had fallen. Therefore, he neither wishes the opportunity of pardon to be closed to penitents (see Testimony XLI), nor does he allow grave crimes to remain unpunished and without penance. This too was earnestly desired not only by Cyprian (see what we taught in nos. 8, 9, and the following sections of chapter 1), but also by Pacianus (consult Pacianus’s words concerning Testimony XLI).

These words also indicate the authority of ecclesiastical rulers over every kind of offense and every criminal, especially if they are not separated from the words discussed under no. XLI, insofar as they indicate the full and supreme judgment [Col. 1187B] which the Apostle declares himself able to exercise against believers who had fallen into offenses. But if certain sins were incapable of expiation, could he have sat in judgment over the criminals and passed sentence? Such sins, since they would be unpardonable, would plainly not have been subject to his judgment and sentence. Moreover, who does not know that bishops succeed the Apostles in what is called ordinary authority? Bishops will therefore possess authority over every kind of offense, and consequently none will be unpardonable, whatever nonsense the Novatians might utter to the contrary.

In the Vulgate Paul’s words are set down thus: “I foretold and foretell, as when present and now absent, to those who sinned before and to all the rest, that if I come again I will not spare.”

XLIV. Likewise in the Second Epistle to Timothy (2 Tim. 2:16): “But avoid profane novelties of words, [Col. 1187C] for they make great progress toward impiety; for their speech creeps like a cancer. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and have overturned the faith of certain persons. But God’s firm foundation stands, having this seal: ‘God knows those who are his,’ and, ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from all iniquity.’ Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen vessels, some indeed for honor and others for dishonor. Therefore, if anyone corrects himself by withdrawing from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. But flee youthful desires. Pursue justice, faith, charity, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, [Col. 1187D] knowing that they produce quarrels. But the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle, teachable toward all, patient, and to correct with modesty those who resist, in case God should grant them repentance unto the knowledge of the truth and they should come to their senses, escaping the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive to do his will.”

Our writer directs these admonitions of the Apostle Paul against the Novatians, and impresses them upon the ears of the faithful so that they may abstain from the stratagems and companionship of heretics and schismatics, and not allow themselves to be deceived by their cunning and evil devices: “But their speech creeps like a cancer”; this is both the blemish upon unity and its wrinkle (see Saint Pacianus, Epistle III). For although there must be evil persons in this world, and even [Col. 1188A] in the Church—“some vessels for honor, others for dishonor” (see Saint Pacianus again, Epistle III)—the greatest care must nevertheless be taken lest we be led into error by their examples and their flattering and cunning speeches.

Cyprian expresses this beautifully (Epistle LV, p. 186):

> “Now I both admonish and ask you to do at my request what at other times you do spontaneously and honorably: when this letter of mine has been read, if any contagion of poisonous discourse and pestilential sowing has crept in there, let all of it be removed from the ears and hearts of the brethren, and let the pure and sincere love of the good be cleansed anew of every defilement of heretical disparagement. Henceforth let our most beloved brethren steadfastly shun and avoid the words and conversations of those whose speech creeps like a cancer, [Col. 1188B] as the Apostle says: ‘The worst conversations corrupt good characters.’”

He further commands the faithful so to deal with those same schismatics that they first lead them back to the Church, softened by examples and then by leniency and moderation, while entirely avoiding disputes, harsh words, and threats: “But the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle.”

The Vulgate translation is almost presented here. Whether this resulted from a copyist’s license or some accident, others may determine. Yet because the Vulgate differs to some degree from the version exhibited by the author of this little work in the first two verses, I reproduce those two verses of the Vulgate here: “But avoid profane and vain talk, for it makes great progress toward impiety, and their speech creeps like a cancer.”

[Col. 1188C] XLV. Likewise in the Apocalypse (2:5): “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent; but if not, I shall come to you quickly and move the lampstand from its place.”

This passage has almost the same aim as that cited from Zephaniah under no. 34. These passages therefore invite people to the penance prescribed by ecclesiastical laws; they show that an opportunity for pardon remains for sinners; and finally, they threaten schismatics and sinners with grave punishments unless they come to their senses and repent.

That these admonitions invite fallen believers to the penance prescribed by ecclesiastical laws is shown by the following words of Cyprian [Note: [Col. 1188D] Epistle XIII, p. 57, *To the Clergy concerning Those Who Hurry toward Peace*.]:

> “I have read your letters, most beloved brethren, in which you wrote that your salutary counsel was not lacking to our brethren: that, laying aside reckless haste, [Col. 1188D] they should offer religious patience to God, so that when, through his mercy, we have assembled in one place, we may be able to deal with every individual case according to ecclesiastical discipline, especially since it is written: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and repent.’ But he repents who, mindful of the divine command, gentle and patient, and obedient to the priests of God, earns the Lord’s favor through his acts of submission and righteous works.”

And again elsewhere (*On the Lapsed*, p. 378):

> “This leniency does not grant peace but takes it away; it does not bestow communion but obstructs the way to salvation. This is another persecution and another temptation, through which the subtle enemy advances by hidden devastation to attack [Col. 1189A] those who have fallen even now: so that lamentation may cease, grief fall silent, the memory of the offense vanish, the groaning of hearts be suppressed, the weeping of eyes be stopped, and the Lord, who has been gravely offended, not be entreated through long and complete penance, although it is written: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and repent’ (Apoc. 2).”

That these words of the Apocalypse show that an opportunity for pardon remains for sinners is both declared by the words themselves—inasmuch as they invite to penance the very bishop whom they rebuke—and proved by Cyprian’s own example when he uses them to establish the doctrine under discussion:

> “I wonder,” he says (Epistle LII, p. 155), “that some are so obstinate that they do not think penance should be granted to the lapsed, [Col. 1189B] or believe that pardon should be denied to the penitent, although it is written: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and perform the former works.’ This is certainly said to one who is known to have fallen and whom the Lord exhorts to rise again through works.”

It would moreover be wrong to omit what the author of the book *To Novatian* committed to writing (p. 13):

> “By his false arguments he terrified many of our most wretched brethren and made them pagans again, saying that the penance of the lapsed is vain and cannot benefit them unto salvation, though Scripture cries out and says: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and repent; otherwise I shall come to you unless you repent.’ And indeed, writing to the seven Churches and confronting each one [Col. 1189C] with its particular crimes and offenses, he said: ‘Repent.’ To whom? Surely to those whom he had redeemed at the great price of his own blood.”

Let us add to these statements what Bachiarius wrote to Januarius on this subject [Note: [Col. 1189C] In the edition of Franciscus Florius, p. 117, no. 22.]:

> “And what [Col. 1190A] of what he says to his Churches in the Apocalypse, which are compared, under angelic guardianship, to sevenfold lampstands among the number of the faithful: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and repent, and perform the former works; otherwise I shall come to you quickly and remove your lampstand.’ And in the earlier part of the book he says that he saw an innumerable people who washed their robes in tribulation and made them white in the blood of the Lamb, because, he says, the Lamb of God leads them to the fountains of life. Yet we understand this to be the number of penitents, because they were saved only through tribulation and mourning. You too, therefore, wash your robe in the fountain of tears.”

To all these let Saint Pacianus be added, who declared the following [Note: [Col. 1190C] In the *Exhortation to Penance*, p. 74.]:

> “Behold, I promise and pledge that if you return to your Father [Col. 1190B] with true satisfaction, wandering no further and adding nothing to your former sins, and also saying something humble and tearful—‘We have sinned in your sight, Father; now we are not worthy of the name of sons’—then immediately that unclean animal and the shameful food of husks will withdraw from you. . . . . Surely he would not threaten the unrepentant unless he forgave the penitent. God himself also says: ‘Remember—behold—from where you have fallen, and repent.’ . . . . The Lord wishes none of you to perish. Even the insignificant and the least are sought.”

Finally, it is readily proved that in these words the Lord threatens schismatics and sinners with punishments unless they come to their senses and repent. For what is [Col. 1190C] that coming of the Lord spoken of here, if not the visitation which he describes elsewhere in these words: “I shall visit the men settled upon their dregs”? And what else is the removal of the lampstand from its place but removal from that place in the Church which a person holds?

[Col. 1193] B

Cyprian and other Africans held that baptism could be separated neither from the Church nor from the Spirit, III, 1129, 1132, 1165, 1170, 1188. Among heretics everything is empty and false, III, 1043. Such things must be regarded as profane, ibid. Heretics have no power, 1161. Where the Church is not, sins cannot be forgiven, 1040. Those returning from heresy must be baptized so that original sin and heresy may be cleansed away, 1043, 1187. Acts performed outside have no saving effect, 1046. Heretics will return more willingly if they are baptized, 1125. No heresy is to be excepted, 1158, 1176. Those returning from heresy must be born through both sacraments, III, 1046, 1081, 1117.
