Oil sanctified on the altar, III, 1041. Good works commanded by Christ, 619. The reward promised to those who work, ibid.; punishment for the barren, ibid. Merits of good works, 417, 422, 443, 446. To merit God’s favor by works, 613. Eternal life is bestowed for good works, 618. Works of righteousness are rewarded, 602. Sins are purged by the merits of mercy, 492. Sins are purged by righteous works, ibid. On the day of judgment God will render a reward for works and almsgiving, 540. Prayers alone, without works, are of little avail, 606. Good works are sacrifices, 541. A sacrifice from every pure work, 423. The merciful cannot be in want, 608. Those who work, 608. The service of active charity, 329. Good works: good and necessary activity, 361. Saving activity, 649. One must work in secret, 757. Liberality in active charity, 518. Let charitable action be done generously, 493. One must act by deeds, not words, 775. Even the poor ought to practice charitable works, 613. The more children there are, the more one must give, 616. Those who do not give for fear of poverty are censured, 610, 611. Barren people will be cast into the fire, 608. We must not allow the temples of God to remain captive, 360. Everyone willingly and generously contributed monetary assistance toward ransoming the captives, 361. One hundred thousand sesterces were collected from contributions by the clergy and people, ibid. Cyprian adds the names of the individuals so that prayers may be offered for them, 362. In addition, certain bishops contributed in their own name and that of their people; their names are added, ibid. Ophites, III, 1112. Optatus, 346. Optatus, subdeacon, 287, 302.

Prayer that is peaceful, simple, and spiritual, 524. Conditions of prayer, 241, 242, 243, 509, 525. Why God does not hear, 242. Those who keep watch in prayer obtain what they ask, 539. Those whose hearts sleep are censured, ibid. Those who do not hear themselves, ibid. Christ gave the form of prayer, 520. The prayer taught by Christ, who is God, 538. We obtain our requests more readily if we ask in Christ’s prayer, 520. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to petition God with words that are his own, 521. “Our Father,” that is, the Father of those who believe, 525. When we call God Father, we ought to act as children of God, 526. To pray otherwise than Christ taught is not only ignorance but also fault, 521. In the Lord’s Prayer heavenly teaching is comprehended in summary form, 525. Supplication in church in someone’s name, 399. Prayers borne up to God by the merits of works ascend swiftly, 540. Prayer is ineffectual without works, ibid. Private prayers, 265. Prayers with a congregation during the sacrifices, ibid. Our prayer is public and communal, 524. We must pray for everyone, 244. We pray for the salvation of all, 530. Prayer must be made for the lapsed and for those who stand firm, 313. Prayers for heretics, III, 825. Christians always pray for the fruits of the earth, 559. For the peace and well-being of the citizens, ibid. Prayer must be made lest anyone who has been excluded remain far from salvation, 532. Let there be no loss of prayer during the hours of the night, 543. Let us count the night as day, ibid. For Christians, the occasions and mysteries of prayer have increased, 541. Prayer must be made in the morning, ibid. At the departure of the day, 542. Likewise at night, ibid. Prayer must be made throughout the whole day, ibid. Prayer must be made in the morning so that the Lord’s resurrection may be celebrated, 242. As the day departs, we ask that light may come upon us again, ibid. Worshipers of God formerly observed the third, sixth, and ninth hours in the celebration of prayers, 541. Continual prayer is necessary lest we fall away from the kingdom of heaven, 528. To pray by day and by night, 560. Let us consider that we stand in the sight of God, 521. The adversary diverts our prayers from God, 539. The divine eyes must be pleased by the posture of the body and the manner of the voice, 521. Christ did not wish [Col. 1223] anyone to pray only for himself, 523, 524. Prayers are not to be tossed about noisily during the sacrifices, 522. A petition must be commended to God modestly, ibid. Prayer offered with discipline, maintaining quietness and modesty, 521. It should not be the sound of the voice, but the mind and understanding, that prays, 539.

A bronze disk thrown into the air is not glory but madness, 785. Clerical ordination, 317, 398; III, 1161. Vicarious ordination, III, 1168. The procedure for clerical ordinations, 318. Ordination of a successor, III, 1144. In ordinations the clergy are consulted, as are the people, 317, 318 ff. Cyprian ordains clerics together with his colleagues, 321. Cyprian examined everything that ought to be present in those being prepared for the clergy, 287. The ages, circumstances, and merits of individuals are distinguished so that worthy men may be promoted to ecclesiastical ranks, 330. Human testimonies are not to be awaited when divine endorsements have preceded them, 318. Sabinus was appointed in place of Basilides by the vote of the whole brotherhood and by the judgment of the bishops who were present or had written, III, 766, 1027. What ordination is just and legitimate, III, 1022. It is decreed that those ordained by heretics are to be received as laymen, III, 1049. There is no ecclesiastical ordination where the unity of the Church does not exist, 764. The ordination of heretics is rejected, III, 1049.

Immodest adornment, 448. Chastity is also situated in dress and adornment, 444. A face conquered by falsehood, 456. Those who transform what God fashioned lay hands upon God, 455. One should glory in the flesh only when it is tortured, 446. Costly is the attire of women whose modesty is cheap, 450. Wounds must not be inflicted upon the ears, 457, 459. A woman clothed in costly apparel does not mourn the garment of Christ that she has lost, 489, 490. Fiery-colored hair is an evil omen of things to come, 456. Manifestations, 407. Frequent and continual displays, III, 855. Christ calls his flock sheep, 646. God did not make sheep scarlet or purple, 452. Uzziah stained with the mottling of leprosy, 514.

## P

Paconius, 364. The unhappiness of pagans, 558. Wandering sheep, III, 707. To separate the chaff from the wheat, III, 791. Pallor is cultivated among the pagans, 570. The wayward trailing of vine shoots, 195. Pernicious caresses, 300. To stroke with flattering blandishments, 477. Christ is the bread of life, 531. Many grains make one loaf, 384. Bread mixed with unmixed wine, 485. To eat bread with sweat and labor, 630. Heavenly bread, 626. Pope Cyprian, 224, 268, 303, 307.

God’s paradise blooms with witnesses, 793. Wholesome and saving draughts of paradise, III, 1116. Paradise is the homeland of Christians, 601. Death restores Christians to paradise and the kingdom, ibid. Through death we pass over to immortality, 597. We come to Christ’s seat, to the splendor of the heavenly kingdoms, 598. See MARTYRS and DEATH.

The paralytic of the Gospel, III, 1149. Parents must be obeyed, 770. Parricidal weapons, III, 813. Parricidal words, III, 799. A little girl carried to the idols, 484, 485. The solemnities of Easter, 348. Easter Day, III, 1159. Daily nourishment is provided for sparrows, 610. Examples of the Lord’s passion, 793. A likeness of the Lord’s passion, 669. Christ’s passion, 715. The crown of suffering, III, 833. The crown of suffering is not to be assigned to heretics, III, 1123. Shepherds through whom the Lord’s sheep are neglected and perish, 448. Shepherds old and new, 686.

The FATHER must be known before the Son, III, 1120. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, 504. The Father judges nothing, 754. He cannot have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother, 503. Honor due to fathers, III, 1121. The affection of fathers toward their children, 436.

Patience necessary for the lapsed, 314. Patience must be maintained amid injuries, 777. On patience in adversity, 589. Christians share patience with God, 623, 624. Patience is a quality of God, 624. God’s patience is described, ibid. The crown of patience, 649. Patience enables us to persevere, 633. Religious patience, 558. The good of patience, III, 1127. The virtue of patience extends widely, 633. Patience with incestuous depravity, 211. The patriarchs bore the figure of Christ, 628. To be of patrician rank is a matter of praise, 323.

A great patrimony is a temptation, 450. Individuals were intent on enlarging their patrimony, 469. To prefer one’s patrimony to God, 492. The bond of patrimony, 475. Lend your patrimony to God at interest, 448. Love of patrimony is condemned, 608. To love patrimony more than Christ, 617. PATRIPASSIANS, III, 1112. Punishments that serve as advocates, 789. Paula, seamstress, 332.

Paul caught up to the third heaven, 674. A passage of the Apostle Paul [Col. 1224] explained, III, 1117, 1118. The humility of the Apostle Paul, 233. Paul of Obba, III, 1067. Paul, martyr, 280, 281, 286, 303. Paul had voracious chickens, 572.

The poor must be fed, 541. Care of the poor is commended, 230, 232, 240, 327, 329. Greater care and affection should be shown to the poor who stand firm, 329. Those supported by the Church should be content with more frugal food, 363. Corban in the Church, 612. Fear, 570.

Peace granted by the martyrs, 270, 272, 273, 281. Peace worse than persecution, 492. That is not peace but war, 479. Deceptive peace, 334. True peace is deceived by the lie of false peace, III, 814. Invalid and false peace, 478. If they seek peace, let them lay down their weapons, III, 826. To seek peace deceitfully, III, 857. Peace is necessary for the brave, III, 856. Peace must not be granted rashly, 257, 260, 294, 296. False peace is dangerous to those granting it, 478. It will profit its recipients nothing, ibid. Martyrs shed their blood so that they may not lose the peace of the Church, 305. Peace is won not by indulgence but by arms, III, 857. The bond of peace and concord, III, 1050, 1108. The bond of the Lord’s peace, 642. The Lord’s peace, III, 1127. Peace and battle each have their flowers, 250. Diversity of opinions while preserving the bond of peace, III, 1050. Stephen’s predecessors preserved peace with the Africans, III, 1159. Peace has its own crowns, 649. Peace restored to the Church, 465. It seemed impossible to unbelievers and the faithless, ibid. The children of God ought to be peacemakers, 518.

The sin of unbelief, 586. Laws have assented to sins, 215. Each person is held accountable for his own sin, III, 793. Remission of sins, III, 1172. To purge all sins through suffering, III, 786. All sins are remitted in baptism, 285, 769; III, 1146. Remission of sins is not given except in the Church, III, 1040, 1043. Sins unto death, III, 1169. Mortal sins, 768. Enumeration of grave sins, 585. No sin can be greater than schism, III, 1049. The filth of the ancient contagion, 463. The ancient serpent’s poisons, 603. The wounds borne by Adam, ibid. We all have sin, 761. We transgress daily, 527. We need daily sanctification, ibid. We sin daily, 555. Every day there cannot fail to be something in which one sins, 616. No one can be without sin, 604. He is proud or foolish who says that he is blameless, ibid. We cannot be without some wound of conscience, ibid. Let no one take pleasure in himself as though innocent, 534. Even after people have been healed, some wounds subsequently remain, 604. One who ignorantly and in simplicity offers water in the sacrifice may be granted pardon through the Lord’s indulgence; otherwise after admonition, 387. Christ instructs for the future and forgives what in the past was done wrongly in simplicity, 388. The power of remitting sins was granted to the apostles and to the churches that they established, III, 1168. They do not obtain remission as though from us, III, 1147. Even one who has sinned against God cannot be forgiven in the Church, 751. Christ alone can forgive sins committed against himself, 480. There is no pardon for continuing to sin after knowing God, 443. See PENANCE. Christians and philosophers hold different opinions concerning sins, III, 782. Obstinate sinners, 494. One who sins publicly must be rebuked, 772.

The shameless display of exposed and half-naked chests among philosophers, 623. To bring torturers against one’s own breast, 643. The hiding places of a closed breast, 488. The obstinate savagery of the breast, 790. Enslaved to money, 475. Money must not be sought, 766. A captive and slave of money, 610. Feet happily bound, 416. Feet shod and armed with evangelical teaching, 356. Why Christ washed the apostles’ feet, 626. To swear falsely, 470. A perjurer, 281. The conquered household gods whom the fugitive Aeneas brought, 571.

Pentecost, III, 1189. The day of Pentecost, III, 1202. Care of strangers is commended, 327. Faithlessness and faith can have no fellowship, III, 829. Discordant faithlessness does not maintain unity, 507. The punishment of faithlessness, 511. Those baptized by affusion, III, 1148. The grief of those in danger, 360. No one near danger is safe for long, 366. Great danger hangs over those who neglect their duty, 227. The kingdom of the Persians, 571.

Persecution of the Christian name because of public calamities, III, 1163. Persecutions foretold, 350, 356, 665. The corruption of discipline during peace as the cause of persecution, 469. Persecution comes because of sins, 241. Torments came when certain persons grew proud because of their confession, ibid. Persecution by domestic enemies crowns no less than persecution by outsiders, III, 799. One of the Maccabees ascribes his suffering of persecution to his own sins, 669. He gave to God what would afterward be vindicated, ibid. Persecutions take place so that we may be tested, 581, 656, 665. Persecution arose so that God might raise up prostrate faith, 468. It was an examination rather than a persecution, 469. Persecution arose so that it might become apparent what the Church is, III, 974. Persecution is an examination of our heart, 243, 244. Let no one be terrified by fear of persecutions, 355. The reward of persecutions, [Col. 1225] 673. The fruits of persecutions, 351, 352. What good can you think of someone whom persecution itself has not reformed? 483. Unless the struggle has preceded, there can be no victory, 590. Greater hope in war, 663. No one has an excuse for not suffering for Christ, 660. Let no one voluntarily offer himself for persecution, 432. The persecutor is compelled to believe, 795. Some hasten too eagerly toward their own vindication, 638. Let them consider that the one who vindicates has not yet himself been vindicated, ibid. Persecution not throughout the whole world, but local, III, 1164. The fall of the brethren throughout almost the whole world, 290, 295. Ruins are still falling throughout the whole world, 310. A very great number were struck down at the enemy’s first words, 471. Of their own accord they ran to the forum; they begged not to be delayed, 472. Driven to destruction by mutual exhortations, ibid. Love of patrimony compelled many to sacrifice, 473, 474. Days were appointed in advance for the testing of faith, 467. A day was fixed for those who denied, ibid. In the persecution of Decius, tortures came after exiles, 319. Persecution prevented Novatus’s case from being heard, III, 730. Persecution under Valerian, 430.

Perseus, bishop, III, 809. Perseverance of faith, 219. One must persevere in faith, 655, 661. See GRACE. God shows no partiality, III, 1016. Harmful and poisonous persuasion, 492. The plagues of heretics, III, 1112. Plagues and pestilences of the faith, 507. The plague described, 590 ff., 791, 792. The rock of Christian truth, III, 1169.

Peter readily agreed with the legitimate reasoning that Paul upheld, 410. He did not say that he held the primacy and that those who were newer and later than himself ought rather to obey him, ibid. To Peter first the Lord gave the power of binding and loosing, III, 1114. The Church was founded upon Peter as the source of unity, 410; III, 1043, 1114. The Church was to be built upon Peter, 406. Peter speaks in the name of the Church, ibid. The Lord first chose Peter and built the Church upon him, 410. From Peter Christ established the source of unity, III, 1114. The source of unity beginning from one, 499, 500. To Peter alone Christ said: “Whatever you bind,” etc., III, 1168. Peter, one man, speaks for all and answers with the voice of the Church, III, 806, 807. Christ entrusts his sheep to Peter, 449. Peter’s confession concerning Christ, III, 1191. Peter denied Christ, III, 1190, 1193. Peter raises Tabitha, 607. The apostles Peter and Paul, III, 1159. Peter and Paul knew one another in the City, III, 1202. A passage of the Apostle Peter is explained, III, 1120. Peter’s preaching, III, 1196. Peter’s chair, III, 818, 1169. Peter’s succession, III, 1169. Peter of Hippo Diarrhytus, III, 1070.

The example of Pharaoh, III, 1150. Pharaoh’s extremely harsh servitude, 660. The distinction between the Pharisee and the tax collector, 523. Philip, deacon, III, 1115. To preach philosophy, III, 790. The presumption of a harsher philosophy, III, 782. The false patience of philosophers, 623. Phinehas pleased God, III, 1115. Picus, 570. The pledge of life, III, 780. God, not men, must be pleased, 761. Heads of decrees, III, 767. A conspicuous wound is easily cured, 644. One who mourns stirs up mercy, III, 788. The groaning of mourners must be admitted, III, 789. The tears of mourners, III, 793. The divine handiwork, 363. God’s workmanship must not be adulterated, 454. Plato acknowledged one God, 574. He calls the others angels or demons, ibid.

The people joined to the priests in danger, III, 836. The incorrupt majesty of the faithful people, III, 826. The most holy and very great Roman people, III, 828. The presence of the people at synods, 253, 260, 261, 264, 271, 274, 295, 302, 312, 339. A council held in the presence of the greater part of the people, III, 1052. Cyprian does not number the people among those who rendered judgment at the council, III, 823. Cyprian does nothing without the people’s consent, 234. Cyprian consults the people in the ordination of clerics, 318. Honor must be shown to the people who stand firm, because of their faith and reverence, 261. Every act was made known to the people, III, 721. The people oppose the reception of the insolent, III, 824. Priests are elected in the presence of the people, III, 1025. In their presence either the crimes of the wicked are exposed or the merits of the good proclaimed, III, 1026. A people who consent to an unjust and unlawful episcopate are not immune from the contagion of the offense, III, 1023. They must separate themselves from a sinful prelate whom the bishops have deposed, III, 1025.

Rain falls without distinction upon the just and unjust, 625. The cup of martyrdom, III, 856. Punishment began from the same source as the crime, 484.

Penance has been driven from men’s hearts, 478. The way of penance, III, 765. A pretense of penance, III, 783. Penance [Col. 1226] necessary for the lapsed, III, 812. Let the penance be no less than the crime, 492. The penance of the lapsed is to be fostered, III, 712. It must be prolonged, III, 767. How it is to be proved, 296. Marks of a true penitent, 260, 261, 296, 299, 489, 492. The fruit of penance, 562; III, 794. Penance strengthens one to renew the contest, 494. A true penitent is made stronger for battle through sorrow, ibid. True penance merits not only pardon but a crown, ibid. No penance is too late for one who still remains in this world, 563. The Lord promises indulgence to penitents, III, 786, 788, 789, 792. Penance is taken away if the fruit of penance is intercepted, III, 794. In the Church the contumacious are slain with the spiritual sword when they are cast out of the Church, 371. When some graver offense intervenes, the faithful are excluded and separated from the body of Christ, 531. The penance of certificate-holders (*libellatici*) must not be rejected, III, 781. The penance of those returning to the Church, III, 1197. Hands laid upon penitents, 410. At a council penance was decreed not only by agreement but also under threat, III, 816. Against those who grant peace without penance, III, 817, 818. A period of penance is granted to adulterers and peace is given, III, 785. For lesser offenses of idolatry, penance is performed for an appropriate period, 251, 257. Full penance, 370, 489, 492. Certificate-holders subject to penance, 487. Likewise those who contemplated the crime either of sacrifice or of obtaining a certificate, 484. Concerning the woman who, when her hands were seized for sacrificing, did not consent, 272. Full penance for corrupted virgins, 370. Lighter penance for those who were found with males but discovered to be intact, 370. Let them be expelled under a graver censure if they have lived with those same men under one roof, ibid. At the Council of Carthage it was resolved that the lapsed should be assisted at the point of death, III, 784. Meanwhile, certificate-holders were to be admitted, ibid. Penance is rightly prolonged while there is tranquility, III, 855, 856. It is otherwise when persecution is imminent, ibid. Pardon may quickly be granted to the lapsed amid torture, 476. For these, penance begun after three years may suffice, 347. Peace is granted to the lapsed who subsequently confess, 274. Bishop Therapius is rebuked for granting peace prematurely, III, 1014. Nevertheless, the peace granted is not withdrawn, ibid. God knows what to do with those who die before completing their penance, 315. Schismatic confessors are received without penance, III, 711. Bishops submit themselves to penance, III, 1029. The Council of Carthage decreed that lapsed bishops could be admitted to perform penance but were to be barred from priestly honor, III, 1031. Cornelius, together with absolutely all the bishops, decreed the same, ibid. For a bishop deposed for idolatry, lay communion is like an act of grace, III, 1030. A deacon must be deposed or excluded if he persists in insulting his bishop, 397. When Bishop Trophimus returns with his people, he communicates as a layman, III, 777. Penance was denied to adulterers under Cyprian’s predecessors, III, 787. Those who did not perform penance were barred from the hope of communion and peace if they began to plead for it when in danger, III, 789. Cyprian threatens that whoever joins Felicissimus will not communicate in the Church, 330. He will be unable afterward to return to the Church and communicate, 339. Cyprian carefully weighs who ought to be received and admitted into the Church, III, 812 ff. The people resist whenever the incorrigible return to the Church, III, 813.

The necessity of the sacrament of penance, 403. A priest is guilty if a good soldier, while in flight, dies without peace and communion, III, 857. The sacrament of penance must be administered to the dying, 227. In danger of illness, confession (*exomologesis*) must be made before any presbyter who is present, or before a deacon if no presbyter can be found or if death begins to press, 259. Many in the Church of Arles died without peace, III, 991. There is no place for penance after death, 562, 563. Here life is either lost or retained, 563. What is loosed on earth is loosed in heaven, III, 855. Satisfaction and remission effected through the priests are pleasing to the Lord, 489. Whatever priests do for a true penitent, God reckons as acceptable, 494. Penitents receive the Spirit of the Father when they receive peace, III, 858.

Polianus, 414, 424. Polianus of Milevis, III, 1061. Polycarp, bishop, III, 852, 1021, 1036. Polycarp, bishop of Hadrumetum, III, 710. Polycarp of Hadrumetum, III, 1056. Pompeius, bishop, III, 701, 852. Pompeius of Sabrata, III, 1073. Cyprian’s letter to Pompeius, III, 1128. Pomponius, bishop, III, 852, 1021, 1036. Pomponius of Dionysiana, III, 1067. The people of Christ cannot be divided, 505. The united Christian people are compared to the Lord’s bread, 384; III, 1150. The people are united to Christ when water is mixed with wine in the cup, 384. We, the entire people, are one, 524. The onslaught of the raging populace against the martyrs, 346. A people of perdition and death, 618. A sinful people cannot [Col. 1227] be the child of God, 526. The two peoples foretold, the elder and the younger, 688. Monstrous prodigies are worshiped, 553. A vine-covered portico, 196. Those who are possessed believe that they possess, 475.

The power of heavenly grace, III, 1169. The divine precepts are not impossible, III, 1015 ff. Predictions of a woman seized by a demon, III, 1164. The battle of the glorious contest, III, 765. God watches those who fight; the angels watch, and Christ also watches, 356. To despise prelates with proud arrogance, 470. Prelates appointed without the law of ordination, 507. The privilege of communion, 304. Deceptive tricks in excuse-making, 310. Tricks of demons, 556. The presumption of a harsher philosophy, III, 782. Condemned presumption, III, 1117, 1119. Betrayers of the truth, III, 1116.

Prayer offered with discipline, 521. The trumpet of prayers, 313. To offer prayer during the sacrifices, 265. Presbyters sit with the bishop among the clergy, 324, 325. Presbyters are called priests by Cyprian, 325, 334. They are called prelates, 252, 261, 278. Presbyters and deacons must nurture the sheep entrusted to them, 252, 254, 257. They must govern and teach confessors, ibid. One must rise in the presence of presbyters, 773. The honor of the presbyterate is designated for certain readers, 323. The same monthly allotment as for presbyters, 324. Numidicus the presbyter is enrolled among the presbyters of Carthage, 325. While the see is vacant, presbyters reserve certain matters until the election of a bishop, 278, 312. Five presbyters delay Cyprian’s return, 334. Five presbyters claim everything for themselves, 250, 254. Rash presbyters are to plead their case before the bishop and clergy, and before the confessors and people, 253. Meanwhile the rash presbyters are forbidden to offer, ibid. Presbyters and deacons who depart from the Church communicate as laymen when they return, III, 1050. Those ordained outside communicate as laymen when they return, ibid. Presbyters and deacons ought to preside over purity and continence, 369. To convene the presbyterate, III, 720.

Tribulations occur so that we may be tested, 656, 663. Tribulations inflicted by the pagans, 419, 426. To assume the primacy, III, 1144. To hold the primacy, 410. Esau lost his prerogatives of primogeniture, 634; III, 1126. Primitivus, presbyter, III, 701, 710. Primus, bishop, III, 1021, 1036. Primus of Misgirpa, III, 1055. Primus, schismatic, III, 713. Prisca, companion of Montanus, III, 1161. Priscus, bishop, III, 852. Privatia­nus, 346; III, 852. Privatianus of Sufetula, III, 1062. Privatus of Lambaesis, 306. Privatus of Sufes, III, 1062.

A storm does not overturn a sturdy tree, 507. Proculus, bishop, 359; III, 1036. Proculus swears falsely; Romulus becomes a god, 570. Betrayers of unity, III, 1116. Another prophet like Moses was promised, 688. The prophets bore the figure of Christ, 628. Christ foretold his advent through the prophets, ibid. A resolve of continence, III, 786. Formula of proscription, 403. The burden of proscription, ibid. To prostitute the members of Christ to the pagans, 470. The audacity of a prostituted voice, 214. The protection of Christ’s body and blood, III, 856. A protected flank, 220. A province extending more widely, III, 710. Psalms at Christian banquets, 222, 223. Our prayer is public and communal, 524. The distinction between the tax collector and the Pharisee, 522, 523. Pudentianus of Cuicul, III, 1070. Chastity preserves the course of its glory, III, 786. The modesty of the marital bond, 360. Children’s virtue greater than their age, 419. Children crowned with martyrdom, 427. A teacher who leads children to perdition, 362. Voracious chickens, 572. The pulpit, that is, the tribunal of the Church, 319, 323. Orphans must be protected, 778.

Purgatory. Others are contrasted with those who are crowned immediately: those who await pardon and pay the last farthing, III, 786. They are cleansed and purged, after being tormented for their sins by long suffering and for a long time by fire, ibid. They remain in suspense until the day of judgment, ibid. On the day of judgment the merits of the martyrs and works of the righteous will benefit many, 480. Apostates and deserters, even if slain for the Name, will not then be capable of being admitted to the peace of the Church, III, 790. A sacrifice for someone’s repose, 399.

Christian women should not wear purple, 452. The purple blood of the Lamb through whom we were redeemed, 653. Purple dye flows onto images, 796. Pusillus of Lamasba, III, 1071. Shells, III, 823. A well of living water, III, 1139. With the rotten branches cut away, 477.

The missiles of probing questions, 794. A most difficult interrogation, 246, 249. The torments of interrogations, 554. Quantity. Cyprian supplies expenses from his own resources, 327. ## TABLE OF THE CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

[Col. 1233] General Survey of the Entire Edition. Explanation of the Sigla.

PREFACE, in which, after an enumeration of the editions of St. Cyprian’s works, the teaching of the holy Martyr is discussed at greater length, by Dom Prudentius Maran, O.S.B. 10

I.—Cyprian’s position on the unity and infallibility of the Church. 15

II.—Those who deny that, in Cyprian, bishops are distinguished from presbyters by divine law are refuted. 21

III.—The primacy of the Roman Church was always acknowledged by St. Cyprian. 23

IV.—On St. Cyprian’s disagreement with St. Stephen. Stephen approved no Baptism except that conferred according to the form prescribed by Christ. 27

V.—St. Cyprian understood his opponents’ position less fully. On Baptism in the name of Christ. Stephen’s position originated with the Apostles. 31

VI.—The principal arguments by which St. Cyprian defended himself. He rejected neither sacraments administered by wicked persons within the Church nor tradition. 35

VII.—St. Cyprian does not confuse Confirmation with the imposition of hands upon returning heretics. He numbers Confirmation among the sacraments. 39

VIII.—The sacrament of Penance is defended from St. Cyprian’s testimony; it is shown how necessary he judged it and how reverently he wished it to be administered. Certain statements of his are explained. 42

IX.—Whether in Africa before St. Cyprian communion after penance had been denied for the gravest crimes. 47

X.—Whether a new discipline was introduced under St. Cyprian, and the former severity retained only for apostates and deserters. 51

XI.—Whether St. Cyprian denied peace to the lapsed who died in the course of their penance, excepting only those who had received certificates from the martyrs. 55

XII.—Whether the Council of Carthage imposed penance upon those who had sacrificed for the whole duration of their lives. 59

XIII.—On Christ’s presence in the Eucharist. 61

XIV.—On communion under both kinds. 65

XV.—St. Cyprian’s position on the Sacrifice, Purgatory, and the invocation of the Saints. 67

XVI.—On Christ’s divinity and his grace. 71

LIFE OF ST. CYPRIAN, prepared under the supervision of Dom Prudentius Maran. 73

I.—On St. Cyprian before he became a Christian. He must be distinguished from Cyprian of Antioch. 75

II.—On St. Cyprian’s conversion. While a catechumen, he distributed his possessions and bound himself by a vow of continence. The year and time of his baptism are uncertain. 77

III.—On St. Cyprian’s studies and writings from his Baptism until his Ordination. 81

IV.—Cyprian immediately receives the presbyterate and the episcopate. In what year he was ordained bishop. His deeds and writings at the beginning of his episcopate. 82

V.—On the persecution of Decius and its beginnings, and on the great number of the lapsed and the confessors. 86

VI.—In what consisted the offense of those called *libellatici*—holders of certificates. 89

VII.—Cyprian withdrew during the persecution for entirely just reasons. 93

VIII.—On the letter sent by the Roman clergy to Carthage after it had been reported that Cyprian had withdrawn. 95

IX.—On Cyprian’s first response to the Romans’ letter. On the thirteen letters written before the second response and conveyed to Rome together with it, many of which are shown to be missing. 96

X.—The order of Cyprian’s letters written before the fifteenth letter to the Romans; first, on the fifth and ninth. The thirty-seventh must be assigned to another time. 99

XI.—Five letters of St. Cyprian concerning the lapsed. He did not overlook the crime of the presbyters who had given communion to the lapsed.—He threatens them not with suspension but with excommunication. 101

XII.—On St. Cyprian’s fifteenth letter and several others written shortly afterward, when a new disturbance arose. 106

XIII.—On Celerinus’s letter to Lucianus and Lucianus’s response. 108

XIV.—St. Cyprian writes to the clergy concerning the ordination of Saturus and Optatus. Various letters from the lapsed to St. Cyprian. The clergy exclude Gaius of Didda from their communion. When Letters XXV and XXIX were written. On the letters of the Roman clergy and confessors. 110

XV.—The persecution intensifies again; the coming peace is revealed to St. Cyprian. His deeds and writings at the close of the year 250 are reviewed. 113

XVI.—Cyprian sends deputies to act in his place. The threats of Felicissimus. 115

[Col. 1235]

PART ONE OF THE WORKS OF THE DIVINE THASCIUS CAECILIUS CYPRIAN, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE AND MARTYR.—LETTERS. 191

LETTER I. To Donatus.—Cyprian converses with Donatus about divine matters. Commending the grace of God conferred through Baptism, he explains how greatly he has been changed by it; and, after demonstrating before his eyes the errors of the world, exhorts him to contempt of the world and, finally, to constant reading and prayer. 191

LETTER II. From the Roman clergy to the clergy of Carthage concerning the withdrawal of St. Cyprian.—After Cyprian’s withdrawal, the Roman clergy, in accordance with their zeal for the faith, remind the Carthaginian clergy of their duty and instruct them what should be done concerning the lapsed while their bishop is absent. 225

LETTER III. To the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome.—A personal letter. 230

LETTER IV. To the presbyters and deacons.—St. Cyprian, now in retreat, exhorts his clergy to discharge his duties properly, and to ensure that neither those confined in prison nor the other poor lack anything. He then urges them to keep the people peaceful, lest, if they flock in crowds to visit the martyrs in prison, this should eventually be forbidden them. 232

LETTER V. To the presbyters and deacons.—He wishes the confessors to be reminded of their duty by the clergy, so that they may devote themselves to humility and obey the presbyters and deacons; incidentally, he also gives the reason for his withdrawal. This too is one of the thirteen Letters mentioned below at Letter XV. 233

LETTER VI. To the presbyter Rogatianus and the other confessors.—He exhorts Rogatianus and the other confessors to observe discipline, lest those who had confessed Christ with their voice should appear to deny him by their deeds. Incidentally, he rebukes certain among them who, though banished on account of the faith, did not fear to return to their homeland without authorization. This is what Cyprian says below, in Letter XV: that those in exile had not lacked reproof when it was necessary. It is clear, therefore, that this Letter was written during his withdrawal. 235

LETTER VII. To the clergy, on praying to God.—Its subject is nearly the same as that of the two preceding letters, except that here he exhorts them to constant prayer. 240

LETTER VIII. To the martyrs and confessors.—Cyprian commends the martyrs of Africa in extraordinary terms for their steadfastness and invites them to persevere, following the example of their colleague Mappalicus. 245

LETTER IX. To the clergy, concerning certain presbyters who rashly granted peace to the lapsed while the persecution was not yet over and without the bishops’ knowledge. 250

LETTER X. To the martyrs and confessors who asked that peace be granted to the lapsed.—By his counsel St. Cyprian recalls the martyrs and confessors, as far as he can, to the Lord’s precepts. 253

LETTER XI. To the people.—St. Cyprian composes the spirit of the people themselves as far as he can and instructs them to remain within ecclesiastical discipline. 256

LETTER XII. To the clergy, concerning the lapsed and catechumens, that they should not depart empty-handed.—When some of the lapsed rushed forward with brazen demands and attempted to extort the peace promised to them by the martyrs and confessors, St. Cyprian wrote twice to the clergy on this matter, so that they might restrain their violence and, after they had made *exomologesis*—public confession—they might be sent to the Lord in peace. 259

LETTER XIII. To the clergy, concerning those who hasten toward peace. Peace must be attained through penance, and penance is performed by keeping the commandments. Those afflicted by illness may be admitted to peace if supported by the intercession of the martyrs; the rest must be held back until peace has been restored to the Church. 260

LETTER XIV. To the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome.—He gives an account of his withdrawal and of what he did during it, sending to Rome, in his own defense, copies of the Letters he had written to his people; indeed, he uses the same words here as there. Compare Letter XXII, to the Roman Clergy. 261

LETTER XV. To Moses, Maximus, and the other confessors.—In this gracious letter Cyprian refreshes with his words the spirits of the martyrs, made strong by their faith and confession; and, extolling their blessed state with fitting praise, kindles in them a much more ardent desire for heavenly glory. 265

LETTER XVI. From the confessors to Cyprian.—A certificate written by Lucianus in the name of the martyrs. 268

LETTER XVII. To the presbyters and deacons, concerning the preceding and the two following letters.—No account is to be taken of the martyrs’ certificates before peace has been restored to the Church. 269

LETTER XVIII. From Caldonius to Cyprian.—Since some of the lapsed, under pressure from a renewed persecution, had confessed Christ and therefore sought peace before setting out into exile, Caldonius consults Cyprian on whether peace should be granted to them. 272

LETTER XIX. He replies to Caldonius.—Cyprian treats nothing distinctive in this letter except that he agrees with Caldonius’s position: namely, that peace must not be denied to those lapsed persons who have merited it by true penance and confession of Christ’s name, and thereby have restored it to themselves. 237

[Col. 1236]

LETTER XX. From Celerinus to Lucianus.—Celerinus asks the Carthaginian confessors for peace on behalf of his sisters, who had lapsed at Rome. 274

LETTER XXI. Lucianus replies to Celerinus.—Lucianus grants Celerinus’s request. 279

LETTER XXII. To the clergy residing at Rome, concerning many confessors, Lucianus’s shamelessness, and the modesty of the confessor Celerinus.—Through this letter Cyprian informs the Roman clergy of the seditious demand of the lapsed that they be restored to peace, and of Lucianus’s shamelessness. To make these matters better understood, Cyprian arranges for both his own letters and those of Celerinus and Lucianus to be transmitted. 282

LETTER XXIII.—This letter is absent in number, but not in fact. 286

LETTER XXIV. To the clergy, concerning the letters sent to Rome and the appointment of Saturus as reader and Optatus as subdeacon.—Through this letter the clergy are informed of the ordination of Saturus and Optatus and of what Cyprian wrote to Rome. 287

LETTER XXV. To Moses, Maximus, and the other confessors.—This is a letter of congratulation to the Roman confessors. 288

LETTER XXVI. Moses, Maximus, Nicostratus, and the other confessors reply to the preceding letter.—The Roman confessors gratefully acknowledge the comfort they received from Cyprian’s letter.—Martyrdom is not a punishment but blessedness.—The words of the Gospel are torches for kindling faith.—Cyprian’s position in the case of the lapsed is accepted. 290

LETTER XXVII. Cyprian to the lapsed.—The subject of this letter is given below at Letter XXIX. “They wrote letters to me,” he says, “not asking that peace be given to them, but claiming it as though it had already been given, because they say that Paul granted peace to everyone, as you will read in their letter, a copy of which I have sent to you, together with the brief reply that I made to them.” The letter of the lapsed to whom he replies is missing. 300

LETTER XXVIII. To the presbyters and deacons.—The subject of this letter agrees sufficiently with that of the preceding one, and I think it is the letter of which he speaks in the following letter. For he commends his clergy because they had excluded from communion Gaius, a presbyter of Didda, and his deacon, who were rashly communicating with the lapsed; and he exhorts them to do the same with certain others. 302

LETTER XXIX. To the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome.—The Roman clergy are informed of the rashness of the lapsed who were demanding peace. 304

LETTER XXX. From the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome to Cyprian.—The Roman Church sets forth its position on the lapsed, in agreement with the decrees of the Church of Carthage.—Indulgence shown to the lapsed must be measured by the standard of the Gospel.—That the peace granted by the confessors rested only upon grace and personal favor is evident from the fact that the lapsed are referred to the bishops.—The seditious demand for peace is to be attributed to the faction of Felicissimus. 305

LETTER XXXI. From the Roman clergy to Cyprian.—What the Roman clergy treated briefly in the preceding letter they now discuss more broadly and soundly, also replying to another letter of Cyprian, from which they quote several words, though that letter is believed no longer to survive. Incidentally, they also thank Cyprian for the letters sent to the Roman martyrs and confessors. Like the preceding letters of the Roman clergy, it was written while the See was vacant after Fabian’s death. 309

LETTER XXXII. To the clergy of Carthage, concerning the letters sent to Rome and those received from there.—The Carthaginian clergy are instructed to arrange for the letters of the Roman clergy and Cyprian’s replies to be circulated. 318

LETTER XXXIII. To the clergy and people, concerning the ordination of Aurelius as reader.—Cyprian announces to the clergy and people that he has ordained the confessor Aurelius as reader, incidentally commending his virtue and constancy of spirit, by which he also merited a higher rank in the Church. 319

LETTER XXXIV. To the clergy and people, concerning the ordination of Celerinus as reader.—Its subject is almost the same as that of the preceding letter, except that he commends at length Celerinus’s steadfastness in confessing the faith. The circumstances of the text itself sufficiently indicate that both letters were written during the withdrawal. 322

LETTER XXXV. To the same, concerning the ordination of Numidicus as presbyter.—He announces to the clergy and people that he has ordained Numidicus as presbyter, briefly commending his worthiness. 326

LETTER XXXVI. To the clergy, concerning the care of the poor and strangers.—He admonishes them not to visit the martyrs in crowds and not to neglect widows, the sick, the poor, or strangers. 328

LETTER XXXVII. To the clergy, that every kindness be shown to the confessors confined in prison.—He exhorts his clergy to show every kindness and care toward the confessors, both those living and those who have died in prison; to record carefully the dates of their deaths so that their memory may be celebrated each year; and, finally, not to forget the poor. 329

[Col. 1237]

LETTER XXXVIII. To Caldonius, Herculanus, and the others, concerning the exclusion of Felicissimus.—Felicissimus, together with the associates in his sedition, is to be barred from everyone’s communion. 331

LETTER XXXIX. Letter of Caldonius, Herculanus, and the others to Cyprian, concerning the exclusion of Felicissimus and his associates.—Caldonius, Herculanus, and the others carry out what he had commanded them in the preceding letter. 333

LETTER XL. To the people, concerning the five schismatic presbyters of Felicissimus’s faction.—Just as Cyprian, in the second letter before this one, informed the clergy, so now he informs the people that Felicissimus must be avoided, together with the five presbyters of his faction, who both granted peace indiscriminately to the lapsed and stirred up sedition and schism against Cyprian. 334

LETTER XLI. To Cornelius, because he had not accepted Novatian’s ordination.—The messengers sent by Novatian, who had notified the Church of Carthage of his ordination, are rejected by Cyprian. (See vol. III, col. 699.) 341

LETTER XLII. To Cornelius, concerning Cyprian’s approval of his ordination and concerning Felicissimus.—Cyprian excuses himself for not placing unquestioning confidence in Cornelius’s ordination before he received the letters of his colleagues Caldonius and Fortunatus, which confirmed that it was legitimate. Incidentally returning to this matter because of the opposing faction of Novatian’s party, he explains that he did not immediately adhere to that party at the very outset, but rather to Cornelius—so much so that he refused to entertain accusations against him. (See vol. III, col. 702.) Ibid.

LETTER XLIII. To the same, because he had written to the confessors seduced by Novatian.—The title sufficiently indicates the subject of the letter; a report establishes that this letter and the following one were sent together with the present letter. (See vol. III, col. 708.) Ibid.

LETTER XLIV. To the Roman confessors, that they should return to unity.—He exhorts the Roman confessors seduced by the faction of Novatian and Novatus to return to unity. 342

LETTER XLV. To Cornelius, concerning Polycarp of Hadrumetum.—In this letter Cyprian explains how it happened that, while he was at Hadrumetum, the clergy under Polycarp wrote from there not to Cornelius but to the Roman clergy, although Polycarp himself had previously written to Cornelius instead. The text itself establishes that this letter was composed shortly after the preceding ones. (See vol. III, col. 709.) 343

LETTER XLVI. From Cornelius to Cyprian, concerning the confessors who returned to unity.—Cornelius informs Cyprian of the confessors’ solemn return to the Church, which he describes. (See vol. III, col. 716.) Ibid.

LETTER XLVII. Cyprian’s congratulatory reply to Cornelius concerning their return from schism. (See vol. III, col. 730.) Ibid.

LETTER XLVIII. From Cornelius to Cyprian concerning Novatian’s faction and its adherents.—Cornelius gives Cyprian an account of the Novatian faction. (See vol. III, col. 712.) 344

LETTER XLIX. Cyprian’s reply to Cornelius concerning the crimes of Novatus.—He commends Cornelius for having warned him at an opportune moment, since he received Cornelius’s letter on the day after the guilty faction came to him. He then describes at length the crimes of Novatus and the schism previously stirred up by him in Africa. (See vol. III, col. 725.) Ibid.

LETTER L. From Maximus and the other confessors to Cyprian, concerning their return from schism.—They inform Cyprian that they have returned to the Church. Ibid.

LETTER LI. Cyprian’s letter of congratulation to the confessors concerning their return from schism.—Cyprian congratulates the Roman confessors upon their return to the Church and replies to their letter. Ibid.

LETTER LII. To Antonianus, concerning Cornelius and Novatian.—When Antonianus, after receiving a letter from Novatian, began to incline in spirit toward his party, Cyprian confirms him in his former position: namely, that he should continue in communion with Cornelius, that is, with the Catholic Church. To persuade him, he sets forth the history of the whole tragedy between Cornelius and Novatian and teaches that Cornelius was an excellent man and legitimately elected, whereas Novatian, guilty of many crimes, had usurped an illegitimate election. Incidentally, at the beginning of the letter he excuses himself for having changed his position concerning the treatment of the lapsed, and at the end he explains wherein the Novatian heresy consists. 347

LETTER LIII. To Fortunatus and other colleagues, concerning those overcome by torture.—When his colleagues consulted Cyprian on whether lapsed persons who had been overcome under torture should be admitted to communion, he replied that, because they had already performed penance for three years, they seemed to him worthy of admission; but since a council of bishops was to be held at his residence after the Easter solemnities, he would discuss the matter with them. 348

LETTER LIV. To Cornelius, concerning the granting of peace to the lapsed.—The African bishops had previously decreed in a council that the lapsed should not be admitted to peace unless they had performed penance for a long time, except perhaps when the danger of illness was pressing. Now, with a new persecution imminent, they decreed that peace should be given to all who had performed penance,

[Col. 1238]

so that they might be stronger for the battle of suffering. Cyprian announces this decree of the bishops to Pope Cornelius in the name of the whole synod; this letter therefore belongs not so much to Cyprian himself as to the African synod. (See vol. III, col. 851.) 350

LETTER LV. To Cornelius, concerning Fortunatus and Felicissimus, or Against the Heretics.—At the outset of this letter Cyprian warns Cornelius not to listen to the slanders of Felicissimus and Fortunatus against him, nor to be frightened by their threats, but to be courageous, as befits a priest of God confronting heretics. For, according to the custom common among heretics, they began their heresy and schisms from contempt for the one bishop in the Church. Incidentally, he also indicates the usual sources of heresies and schisms, so that Morel rightly entitled the letter *Against the Heretics*. (See vol. III, col. 795.) 305

LETTER LVI. To the people of Thibaris, an Exhortation to Martyrdom.—Cyprian first excuses himself to the Thibaritans for not having visited them and warns them of the approaching persecution; he then adds incentives to undergo martyrdom cheerfully.—Examples are then presented of the righteous from the beginning of the world who suffered martyrdom. Foremost is the Passion of our Lord, which surpasses all those examples.—What of the contests of the stadium and theater, bravely and cheerfully endured, which provide an incentive to undergo the sufferings of martyrdom?—Finally, the future reward should be considered; it already gives more than sufficient encouragement and ardor to endure everything. 351

LETTER LVII. To Cornelius in exile, concerning his confession.—Cyprian praises Cornelius and his people for confessing Christ’s name even unto exile, and exhorts them to steadfastness and to mutual prayers for one another, both in view of the imminent day of contest in this life and after death. Damasus mentions this letter in the *Life of Cornelius*, since, on account of it, a calumny was raised and the tyrant seized upon an occasion to put him to death. (See vol. III, col. 829.) 358

LETTER LVIII. To Lucius, Roman pope, returned from exile.—Cyprian and his colleagues congratulate Lucius on his return from exile, teaching that delayed martyrdom does not diminish its glory. Then, indicating that Cornelius’s martyrdom and Lucius’s exile occurred by divine providence in order to confound the Novatians, he predicts Lucius’s imminent martyrdom; God so arranging matters that his martyrdom would be consummated not abroad but among his own people. (See vol. III, col. 971.) 358

LETTER LIX. To Fidus, concerning the baptism of infants.—Cyprian says that those who thought an infant should not be baptized before the eighth day after birth must be corrected; together with certain of his fellow bishops, he judges that a newborn may properly be baptized immediately. (See vol. III, col. 1011.) 359

LETTER LX. To the Numidian bishops, concerning the redemption of the brethren from barbarian captivity.—After lamenting at the beginning the captivity of the brethren reported to him by the Numidian bishops, Cyprian says that he is sending one hundred thousand sesterces, attaching the names both of the individual brothers and sisters and of the colleagues who had contributed something. It is probable that this captivity was inflicted by those barbarians against whom Decius marched to war and was killed. Manutius and Morel were the first to publish this letter in recent times. Ibid.

LETTER LXI. To Euchratius, concerning an actor.—He forbids an actor who persists in his shameful profession to communicate in the Church. Nor, indeed, should he be excused on the ground that he does not himself practice acting, so long as he teaches it to others; nor on account of poverty, since maintenance may be provided for him at the Church’s expense. Accordingly, if the resources of Euchratius’s church are insufficient, he tells him to come to Carthage. 360

LETTER LXII. To Pomponius, concerning Virgins.—Cyprian and several colleagues reply to their colleague Pomponius: virgins who had resolved to maintain their state continently and firmly but were afterward found in the same bed with men, if they are still found to be virgins, are to receive communion and be admitted to the Church; but if otherwise, since they are adulteresses not against a husband but against Christ, they are to be compelled to undergo full penance. Those who obstinately persist are to be expelled from the Church. Incidentally, he introduces a form of discipline by which virgins may be kept to their duty, and says certain things concerning the Church’s power to excommunicate. 364

LETTER LXIII. To Caecilius, concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s cup.—This letter and the following two contain nothing other than replies to the preceding Letter, since they offer thanksgiving both for the consolation supplied by the letter and for the assistance sent together with it. From the fact that three different letters were written in reply to Cyprian’s single letter, it may be gathered that the bishops who wrote them were confined in different mines. This is confirmed by Letter LXXX, where a particular mine is mentioned. 372

LETTER LXIV. To Epictetus and the people of Assura concerning Fortunatianus, formerly their bishop.—He warns Epictetus and the people of Assura not to permit Fortunatianus, once their bishop but now lapsed, to return to the episcopate, both for other reasons and because it had been decreed that

[Col. 1239]

lapsed bishops should not be restored to their former rank. 389

LETTER LXV. To Rogatianus, concerning a deacon who opposed his Bishop.—Cyprian admonishes Bishop Rogatianus to restrain the pride of the deacon who had provoked him with insults and to compel him to do penance for his audacity. On this occasion he again repeats what was said above, in Letter LV, concerning sacerdotal or episcopal authority. It is not sufficiently certain when it was written, except that the similar beginnings of this and the following letter suggest that they were written during the same synod. 395

LETTER LXVI. To the clergy and people residing at Furni, concerning Victor, who appointed the presbyter Faustinus as guardian.—Because Geminius Victor, contrary to the decree of the council of bishops, had appointed the presbyter Geminius Faustinus in his will as his guardian or trustee, Cyprian forbids offerings to be made for Victor or a sacrifice to be celebrated for his repose. Incidentally, from the example of the Levitical tribe, he concludes that clerics ought not to involve themselves in secular burdens. 399

LETTER LXVII. To Stephen, concerning Marcian of Arles, who adhered to Novatian.—Because Marcian, bishop of Arles, had followed Novatian’s sect, seduced many, and separated himself by schism from the communion of the other bishops, Cyprian admonishes Stephen, the supreme pontiff, to use his authority, in Marcian’s absence, to substitute another in his place; and that, after penance has been performed, peace should be granted both to the lapsed and to those seduced by Marcian, and their return to the Church permitted. (See vol. III, col. 989.) 401

LETTER LXVIII. To the clergy and congregations residing in Spain, concerning Basilides and Martialis.—Because the bishops Basilides and Martialis had lapsed and been defiled by certificates of idolatry, Cyprian and his fellow bishops commend the clergy and people of the Spanish churches for having substituted Sabinus and Felix in their place by a legitimate election. This was especially proper since, according to Cornelius’s decree, lapsed bishops could indeed be admitted to perform penance but were to be barred from sacerdotal honor. Incidentally, he also touches upon certain matters concerning the ancient rite of episcopal election. The context indicates that it was written under Stephen. (See vol. III, col. 1019.) 402

LETTER LXIX. To Florentius Pupianus, concerning detractors.—Cyprian clears himself before Florentius Pupianus of various crimes charged against him, and rebukes his fickleness of mind because he so rashly believed detractors. Since he says that he had by then discharged the episcopal office for six years, it is sufficiently clear that the letter was written under Stephen. Ibid.

LETTER LXX. To Januarius and the other Numidian bishops, concerning the baptism of heretics.—Cyprian contends that what heretics use is not Baptism and that no one among those who oppose Christ can advance through Christ’s grace. (See vol. III, col. 1035.) 410

LETTER LXXI. To Quintus, concerning the baptism of heretics.—A reply is given to Quintus, a bishop in Mauretania, who had consulted him concerning the baptism of heretics. Ibid.

LETTER LXXII. To Pope Stephen, concerning the Council.—Cyprian and his colleagues at a certain council announce to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, that they have decreed both that persons returning from heresy to the Church should be baptized and that bishops or presbyters coming from the same groups should be received on no other condition than that they communicate as laymen. (See vol. III, col. 1044.) 413

LETTER LXXIII. To Jubaianus, concerning the baptism of heretics.—Questioned by Jubaianus concerning the baptism of heretics, Cyprian replies that he judges heretics coming to the Church ought to be sanctified by the Church’s Baptism. (See vol. III, col. 1109.) 414

LETTER LXXIV. To Pompeius, against Stephen’s letter concerning the baptism of heretics.—On this question Cyprian openly indicates that Stephen, whom we know to have been bishop of the Roman Church at that time, not only did not agree with him but also wrote and issued instructions against him. (See vol. III, col. 1127.) Ibid.

LETTER LXXV. From Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to Cyprian, against Stephen’s letter.—He holds the same position as Cyprian concerning Stephen, though more harshly, and congratulates himself upon this agreement, giving thanks to God. Then, examining Stephen’s words concerning the baptism of heretics, he shows that Stephen opposes the Apostle Paul, while he himself agrees with Paul. (See vol. III, col. 1153.) 415

LETTER LXXVI. To Magnus, concerning the baptism of Novatians and those who receive grace upon a sickbed.—The first part of the Letter has the same subject as the preceding ones, except that here he presses against the Novatians what he had previously said generally concerning all heretics. Incidentally, he also intimates that legitimate succession in the Chair of Peter is a mark by which the Church may be recognized. In the second part—which, as the title sufficiently indicates, has hitherto wrongly been published as a separate Letter—he teaches that Baptism performed by sprinkling upon a sickbed is just as valid as that performed by immersion in church. (See vol. III, col. 1137.) 416

[Col. 1240]

LETTER LXXVII. To Nemesianus and the other martyrs confined in the mines.—He extols with extraordinary praise the martyrs condemned to the mines, setting a corresponding consolation against each individual torment in a beautiful antithesis. It may be gathered from these words that it was written in exile: “Unless the boundaries prescribed for me, banished for confessing the Name, kept me back.” 416

LETTER LXXVIII.—Reply of Nemesianus, Dativus, Felix, and Victor to Cyprian.—This letter and the following two contain nothing other than replies to the preceding letter, since they offer thanksgiving both for the consolation supplied by the letter and for the assistance sent together with it. From the fact that three different letters were written in reply to Cyprian’s single letter, it may be gathered that the bishops who wrote them were confined in different mines. This is confirmed by Letter LXXX, where a particular mine is mentioned. 422

LETTER LXXIX. Reply of Lucius and the other martyrs to the same.—The words of the letter itself demonstrate that its subject is the same as that of the preceding one. It is therefore a letter not of Lucius, the Roman pontiff, but of Lucius, an African martyr and bishop; still less is it a letter from Cyprian to Pope Lucius. 424

LETTER LXXX. Reply of Felix, Jader, Polianus, and the other martyrs to Cyprian.—The aforesaid martyrs gratefully acknowledge the assistance transmitted by Cyprian. 425

LETTER LXXXI. Cyprian to Sergius, Rogatianus, and the other confessors confined in prison.—He consoles Rogatianus and his fellow confessors confined in prison, and fortifies their spirits by the example of the martyrs Rogatianus the elder and Felicissimus. The letter itself indicates that it was written in exile. 426

LETTER LXXXII. To Successus, concerning the messengers who returned from Rome reporting the persecution.—Cyprian informs Bishop Successus that, after the emperor Valerian—doubtless together with Gallienus—had decreed a more severe persecution, Pope Xystus suffered martyrdom at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of August. He asks Successus to make this known to his other colleagues, so that each may encourage his flock toward martyrdom. Since Cyprian himself suffered shortly afterward, in September, there can be no doubt that this letter was written near the end of his life. 431

To the people of Carthage. 435

To the presbyter Turasius. 436

LETTER LXXXIII. To the Clergy and People, concerning his withdrawal shortly before his passion.—When, near the end of his life, Cyprian had returned to his gardens and was informed that men had been sent who would—[source breaks off]
they might drag him to Utica for execution, he withdrew. But lest it be believed that he had done this from fear of death, he explains his reason in this letter: namely, that he might undergo martyrdom nowhere other than at Carthage, in the sight of his own people. 437

**LETTER OF POPE CORNELIUS TO CYPRIAN.** 438

**PART II.—SHORT WORKS.** 441

**BOOK ON THE DRESS OF VIRGINS.**—Pontius, in his *Life of St. Cyprian*, sums up the subject of this book in a few words: “Who,” he says, “would restrain virgins, as though with the reins of the Lord’s teaching, within a discipline befitting chastity and a manner of dress worthy of holiness?”

First—to explain the subject somewhat more fully—Cyprian celebrates the praises of discipline and demonstrates its usefulness from Scripture. He then treats of the glory, honor, and merits of virginity and of those women who had vowed and dedicated their virginity to Christ. He teaches that continence consists not only in the integrity of the flesh, but also in dignity of dress and adornment. Nor, indeed, can wealth excuse excessive concern for adornment among women who have already renounced the world. On the contrary, since the Apostle prescribes that even married women must keep their adornment within proper bounds, a virgin ought to observe this much more strictly. Thus, although they may be wealthy, they ought to consider that riches should indeed be used, but devoted to good purposes—to those things that God has commanded, namely, expenditure upon the poor.

After this he teaches from the Apocalypse that the display of ornaments and clothing is more fitting for prostitutes than for virgins; and from Isaiah chapter 3 he likewise deduces how greatly such varied and costly feminine ornaments offend God. Accordingly, passing from excessive adornment to the various kinds of cosmetics, he absolutely forbids them not only to virgins but also to married women, since they will not go unpunished for attempting to reshape, transform, and adulterate God’s handiwork.

Furthermore, he also forbids virgins practices that had come into use through negligence: both attending weddings and frequenting mixed public baths. Finally, in a brief epilogue, having described in very few words, as they say, what good the virtue of continence contains and from what evil it is free, he concludes the book with this exclamation: “Persevere courageously; advance spiritually; attain your goal happily. Only remember us then, when virginity begins to be honored in you.” Ibid.

**BOOK ON THE LAPSED.**—Cyprian had frequently promised that, as soon as peace was restored to the Church, he would write something more definite concerning the treatment of the lapsed; in this book, therefore, he fulfills his promises.

First, he sets before their eyes with joy [Col. 1241] the Church’s wholly unexpected peace and the steadfastness in the faith of the confessors and of the others who had stood firm; then, with the deepest grief, the ruin of the lapsed. After explaining the causes of the preceding persecution—namely, the neglect of discipline and the sins of the faithful—he severely rebukes the lapsed because, at the very first words of the threatening enemy, they sacrificed to idols instead of withdrawing in accordance with Christ’s counsel. He likewise rebukes them because, already defiled by sacrifices and contrary to the law of the Gospel, before their offenses had been expiated and before confession (*exomologesis*) of their crime had been made, they did violence to the body and blood of the Lord and extorted communion and peace from certain presbyters without the bishop’s judgment.

He therefore seeks to deter them by the divine punishment of several of the lapsed who had communicated unworthily—incidentally mentioning those who had obtained certificates of sacrifice (*libellatici*), since they were not thereby excused from guilt—and to encourage them by the example of those who, although implicated in no crime of sacrifice or certificate, nevertheless, because they had so much as contemplated it, painfully and straightforwardly confessed this very thing before the priests of God and made *exomologesis*. With many exhortations he urges them to confession of their offense, public repentance, and full satisfaction.

Lastly, he warns that the Novatianists must be avoided, refuting their heresy from several passages of Scripture. 467

**BOOK ON THE UNITY OF THE CHURCH.**—Cyprian wrote this book on the occasion of the Novatian schism, in order to deter his own Carthaginians, who otherwise were not greatly averse to it because Novatus and certain other presbyters of his Church were the authors of the entire tragedy.

First, after fortifying them against the schismatics’ snares and exhorting them to steadfastness, he teaches that the cause of heresies is that the head of the Church is not sought, Peter’s primacy is despised, and the one Chair, the one Church, and the one episcopate are abandoned. He then demonstrates the unity of the Church both from Scripture and from figures of the Old and New Testaments.

Further, while ostensibly treating another subject, he briefly discusses the ambition of Novatian in usurping the Roman episcopate. He argues at length that their fewness accomplishes nothing against the Church by appeal to Matthew 18: “Wherever two or three have been gathered in my name, etc.”; and that martyrdom outside the Church cannot profit them.

After this he teaches that they ought not to marvel that heresies flourished, since these had long ago been foretold by Christ—here incidentally introducing the punishments of schismatics—nor that certain Roman confessors assented to the schism, since no one is blessed before death and Judas proved a traitor even within the company of the Apostles. He likewise teaches that fellowship with schismatics and heretics must be avoided. Finally, through Scripture, he exhorts them to peace and unanimity. 493

**BOOK ON THE LORD’S PRAYER.**—St. Cyprian’s treatise on the Lord’s Prayer, in which he imitates Tertullian’s book *On Prayer*, comprises three parts. In the first, he shows that the Lord’s Prayer is the most excellent of all prayers, supremely spiritual, and supremely efficacious for obtaining what is sought. In the second part, he gives an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer and, following in Tertullian’s footsteps, proceeds through its seven principal parts.

Finally, in the third part, he examines the conditions of prayer and teaches that prayer ought to be:

1. persevering and constant, after the example of Christ the Lord;

2. vigilant and poured forth with the whole heart, after the example of the priest who, “before the prayer, after first reciting the preface, prepares the minds of the brethren by saying, ‘Lift up your hearts,’ and the people respond, ‘We have them with the Lord’”;

3. joined with good works and almsgiving, as in the cases of Tobit and Cornelius;

4. offered at every hour of the day, and especially at the three hours appointed by the Church for prayer—namely, the third, sixth, and ninth hours—as well as in the morning and evening. 521

**BOOK TO DEMETRIANUS.**—To Demetrianus, proconsul of Africa, who contended that the wars, famine, and plague by which the world was then being ravaged ought to be blamed upon the Christians because they did not worship the gods, Cyprian gives an admirable reply. After arguing that all things deteriorate as the world grows old, he maintains that the pagans themselves are rather the cause of such great disasters, because they do not worship God and, moreover, harass Christians with unjust persecutions.

Then, after reproaching him for the unprecedented kinds of torture with which he tormented Christians beyond other accused persons—not to elicit confession, but denial—he demonstrates the gods’ impotence: first, because they cannot defend themselves, so that Demetrianus, who avenged them, ought rather to be worshiped by them than to worship them himself; and second, because, when expelled by Christians from possessed bodies, they confess what they themselves are.

Nor should the downfall of kings, losses of wealth, and similar evils that, as divine vengeance, accompanied persecutions of Christians be judged not to be punishments merely because Christians shared in them as well, since all these things are a source of joy to Christians rather than a punishment. Accordingly, while there is time, he exhorts Demetrianus to come to his senses, if only from fear of judgment and of the fire of Gehenna that burns forever. Cyprian himself partly imitates Tertullian’s *Apology* and his book *To Scapula*, and partly Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*. 545

**BOOK ON THE VANITY OF IDOLS.**—The title itself embraces the three principal subjects of this book.

First, Cyprian proves [Col. 1242] that those in whose honor temples were founded, images fashioned, victims sacrificed, and feast days celebrated were kings and human beings rather than gods. Accordingly, their worship could have profited neither foreign peoples nor Romans. The power of the Roman Empire must be attributed not to them but rather to fortune, since it came about through a kind of alternation and is ashamed of its own origin. From the empty outcome of auspices and auguries, it is evident that nothing should be attributed to them. Rather, these are the deceptions of demons, as even the poets, Socrates, Plato, Trismegistus, and Hostanes bear witness, for they acknowledged both one God and demons.

The second subject—that there is one God—he briefly establishes both from the superior dignity of monarchy over other forms of rule and from the very expressions of the pagan populace, such as “O God,” and similar utterances.

The final subject, concerning Christ, he treats at greater length from the prophets of the Jews and the Gospel history. 565

**BOOK ON MORTALITY.**—St. Pontius briefly explains its subject in his *Life of Cyprian*: “By whom,” he says, “would Christians of too tender an affection concerning the loss of their own—or, what is more serious, of too little faith—be consoled by the hope of things to come?”

First, after teaching that afflictions of this kind had been foretold by Christ, Cyprian teaches that mortality, or plague, must not be feared, because it leads to immortality; and accordingly that faith is lacking in one who does not hasten toward better things. Nor is it surprising that the Christian shares the evils of this life with the Gentiles, since the Christian must labor in the world more than others. Accordingly, following the examples of the saints Job and Tobit, there is need of patience, and there must be no murmuring. For unless the struggle has preceded, victory cannot be attained, etc. 583

**BOOK ON WORK AND ALMSGIVING.** 601

**BOOK ON THE GOOD OF PATIENCE.**—Cyprian himself explains the occasion of this work in a few words near the end of his letter to Jubaianus: “We patiently and gently preserve charity of mind, the honor of the college, the bond of affection, and the harmony of the priesthood. For this reason, even now, with the Lord permitting and inspiring, we have composed, to the extent that our modest ability availed, a little book *On the Good of Patience*, which I have sent to you in view of our mutual affection.”

Accordingly, after first distinguishing true patience from the false patience of the philosophers, he commends Christian patience by appeal to the patience of God, of Christ, and of all the righteous. He then proves, both from Scripture and from reason, as well as by the examples of Job and Tobit, that patience is not only useful but also necessary. And so that the good of patience might shine forth more clearly from its opposing vice, he explains how great an evil impatience is.

Lastly, he censures the desire for vengeance and teaches that, according to Scripture, vengeance should be left to God rather than arrogated to ourselves. If in any book Cyprian imitates Tertullian, it is certainly in this one—namely, Tertullian’s book *On Patience*. 621

**BOOK ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY.**—St. Pontius gives the subject of this book in a few words in his *Life of Cyprian*: “Who,” he says, “would restrain envy, arising from the poisonous malignity of jealousy, by the sweetness of a saving remedy?”

At the outset, therefore, after teaching that jealousy or envy is the graver a crime the more hidden the evil is, and that its origin must be attributed to the devil, he also incidentally sets forth examples of envy from the Old Testament. He then demonstrates, by proceeding through the individual kinds of vice, that envy is the root of all evils; and accordingly that fraternal hatred was rightly forbidden by both Christ and the Apostles in more than one passage.

Lastly, after exhorting them, by God’s example, to love their enemies, he deters them from this evil by setting before them the crowns of reward. 637

**LETTER TO FORTUNATUS: AN EXHORTATION TO MARTYRDOM.** 651

**Preface.** Ibid.

**Chapter I.—That idols are not gods, and that the elements must not be worshiped in place of gods.** 655

**Chapter II.—That God alone must be worshiped.** 657

## BOOK ON THE SPECTACLES

The author first argues against those who attempted to vindicate the public spectacles of the Gentiles by the authority of Scripture. Although they are nowhere prohibited in express words of Scripture, he nevertheless proves that they are condemned by the prohibition of idolatry, on the ground that every kind of spectacle without exception has been consecrated to idols. He then treats, one by one, the dangers involved in watching each kind of entertainment, at somewhat greater length than in the second epistle to Donatus, especially the dangers of those performances in which, he says, “instruction in obscenity is delivered through images of lust.” Finally, he briefly enumerates the spectacles worthy of a Christian, in which a Christian ought rightly to take delight. He undoubtedly imitated Tertullian’s book *On the Spectacles*, which Tertullian indicates somewhere that he wrote both in Greek and in Latin. That book is so replete with everything pertinent to this subject that it may serve as a commentary whenever the diversity of spectacles is under discussion. 779  

## BOOK IN PRAISE OF MARTYRDOM

He develops the praise of martyrdom in an elevated style, treating at length throughout the book three matters above all: namely, what martyrdom is, how great it is, and what purpose it serves. Meanwhile, through beautiful comparisons and an argument drawn from everyday funerals, he exhorts his readers willingly to undergo death for Christ. Among the virtues of martyrdom he then includes this: that the Lord’s propitiation crowns the martyrs, freed from every suffering, so that Christ’s saying about paying the last farthing does not apply to them. As their reward, he sets forth both security from the fear of Gehenna and the attainment of eternal life, briefly describing each in a somewhat poetic manner; and then he explains that for some martyrdom serves as a crown, while for others, who are washed in their own blood, it is redemption from sins. Finally, after encouraging them toward confession of the name of Christ with several passages of Scripture, he asks them to remember him when the Lord begins to honor martyrdom in them, since it is believed that the Lord will not [Col. 1247] refuse them when they ask.
